**Second Series, in Which Are Published the Fathers, Doctors, and Writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III.** Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or Complete Courses in the Individual Branches of Ecclesiastical Learning.

The Patrology has been printed in two editions: one Latin, the other Greek-Latin. The Latin edition is sold in 1,200 volumes; the Greek-Latin edition in 1,300. The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the Eastern authors are presented in it only in Latin translation.

# In the Year of Our Lord 840. Hilduinus, Abbot of Saint-Denis

[Col. 0009]

[Col. 0009A]

## Historical Notice on Hilduinus

*[Gallia Christiana, among the abbots of Saint-Denis.]*

[Col. 0009]

[Col. 0009A] Hildumus, also at times called Aldoinus, a disciple of Alcuin and born of an illustrious family—for he was the brother of Wigrinus, count of Périgord and Angoulême and a relative of Charles the Bald, as well as the brother of Count Bernard and Gairold, who are remembered in the necrology of Saint-Germain—whether or not he was a monk when he came to the monastery of Saint-Denis, may reasonably be inferred from the ancient necrology of Argentolium and also from the Dionysian necrology, where on the tenth day before the Kalends of December he is called “the blessed Dionysius’s monk and abbot,” to have assumed the monastic habit there.

He was elected abbot in 814, according to Book I of *The Miracles of Saint-Denis*, chapter 1—or in 815 according to the present method of reckoning the beginning of the year. Certainly, in that year, the first of Louis Augustus, on the Kalends of December, in the eighth indiction, he obtained from that prince two privileges concerning royal protection. Around the year 822 the same prince also issued a charter concerning the exchange of certain estates between Abbot Hilduinus and Hidulfus, involving certain properties situated in Alsace.

Louis and Lothair Augustus granted Hilduinus remission of an annual payment of two hundred measures of wine [Col. 0009B]. At first the Dionysian abbot had furnished these freely, on the occasion of a shortage of wine, to the palace at Vern—Vernvilla—and later his successors had paid them by custom; but now the royal collectors were demanding them as a legal and due census. This charter was issued around the year 823, by which time Hilduinus was archchaplain, or chief almoner, and abbot of Saint-Médard at Soissons and Saint-Germain-des-Prés.

In the following year, when the Emperor Louis the Pious sent Lothair to Rome to settle the disturbances that had arisen concerning the election of Pope Eugene II, he employed Abbot Hilduinus as a counselor. For the year 828 there is a charter of Louis and Lothair concerning an exchange of certain properties in the county of Anjou between Fulcricus and Abbot Hilduinus. In that same period he is also mentioned in a charter of those emperors decreeing, at the request of Theodrada, abbess of Saint Mary of Argentolium, that after her death this church should return to Saint-Denis [Col. 0009C].

Around 830, Rabanus, abbot of Fulda, sent his commentaries on the Book of Kings to Hilduinus, abbot and archchaplain of the imperial palace. Hilduinus had requested from him some writing of Rabanus that would be useful to him, through a Fulda monk whom Rabanus had sent to the palace.

Hilduinus is praised by all the writers of that age in many ways. Lupus, abbot of Ferrières, with whom he had lived in his youth, calls him “a most excellent abbot.” In Letter 110 he likewise declares him “conspicuous at the summit of nobility, dignity, and moderation,” namely because of the dignity of archchaplain that he possessed; hence the same author also calls him “master of ecclesiastical affairs.”

Bishop Frotharius, in Letter 11, addresses him as “a man of the highest nobility, raised to the summit of glorious dignity, a father and teacher chosen by God”; and in Letter 16 as “illustrious and distinguished by every kind of nobility.” In the letter of the church of Sens concerning the election of Jeremiah, he is described as “advanced by God for sacred affairs” [Col. 0009D], because he alone—or at least together with the king—directed ecclesiastical matters.

Theganus also lists him among the emperor’s magnates [Col. 0010A], together with Jesse, bishop of Amiens. Walafrid Strabo, in poems written to him and contained in the sixth volume of Canisius’s *Ancient Readings*, calls him “a great Aaron,” whose moral radiance is commended together with the soundness of his understanding.

Finally, Agobard, archbishop of Lyon, calls him “most holy and most blessed” in a letter to the palace nobles, and, almost alone together with Abbot Wala, “the helper of the most Christian Emperor Louis in the way of God.”

Nevertheless, when in 830 he had joined Wala, abbot of Corbie, in supporting the emperor’s sons, who had rebelled against their father, he lost that emperor’s favor and was sent into exile at the monastery of Corbie in Saxony. Shortly afterward, recalled through the influence of his disciple Hincmar, he recovered his former offices, namely the prefectures of Saint-Denis and Saint-Germain.

It then happened that Hilduinus, having become freer—for he was no longer distracted by the affairs of others and had devoted himself entirely to governing his own sheep—persuaded Louis the Pious, by his petitions, to renew through the bishops the monastic order in the abbey of Saint-Denis, so that he might lead his flock to better pastures.

Louis must be heard on this subject in his diploma:

> “Among other matters, it seemed good to them”—the bishops who, at Louis’s command, were holding an assembly at Paris—“that the monastery of the most illustrious and distinguished martyr of Christ, the blessed Dionysius, and of his companions, which is known to have been dedicated in the name of so many martyrs and enriched with the most ample possessions by the kings of the Franks and the ancestors of our glory, so that the monastic order might religiously serve God there, required extensive correction and reform . . . . This matter they brought to the ears of our serenity both directly and through the venerable and prudent man Hilduinus, the religious abbot of the aforesaid monastery, so that it might be corrected through their authority by our most pious imperial power. Given on the seventh day before the Kalends of September, in the nineteenth year, by Christ’s favor, of the reign of Louis, most serene emperor, in the tenth indiction (832). Enacted at the monastery of Saint-Denis, successfully, in the name of God. Amen.”

To this charter of Louis [Col. 0010C] another was added, issued there at the same time, by which he confirmed the division of the possessions that Hilduinus had made for the monks.

Hilduinus’s letters on this subject, taken from an authentic document that is mutilated in several places, were published by Mabillon in Book VI of *On Diplomatics*, p. 519, and after him by Félibien in *Historical Proofs of Saint-Denis*, no. 72. There Hilduinus says that he made this division “not from ambition for an empty name or desire for present glory, but solely for the reward of future recompense, with the counsel and consent of Louis my lord, so that the monastic order might never fail in this place, as happened in former times, to such an extent that, through prolonged pastoral negligence and lack of temporal support, the monks had for the most part abandoned the habit itself . . . . Therefore, lest at some time, through lack of temporal support, the monks should fall into a similar collapse,” and “lest by any sophistry they should in future stray or deviate from the path of righteousness and the institution of the rule of Saint Benedict,” Hilduinus decreed that every year they should be given:

> “of pure wheat, for their use and that of the guests who come to the refectory, 2,100 measures”; for “the provision of the servants who serve them, 900 measures of rye; of pure wine, for the use of the same monks and guests, 2,500 measures, besides beer for the use of the servants; of legumes, 300 measures; of fat, thirty-five measures; of butter, thirty sesters; poultry at Easter and Christmas, etc.”

All these provisions, “assigned for a number of 150 monks,” he forbids his successor abbots ever to reduce; rather, he wishes them increased, so that “as their resources multiply, the worshipers of divine service may also be increased,” and so forth.

The subscribers are Aldric, archbishop of Sens; Ebo, archbishop of Reims; Otgar, archbishop of Mainz; Drogo, bishop of Metz; Witgar, bishop of Turin; Erchanrad, bishop of Paris; Jonas, bishop of Orléans; Heribald, bishop of Auxerre; and Tractarius, bishop of an unknown see.

> “Enacted in the monastery of the holy chief of the apostles and of the most distinguished martyrs Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius, in the nineteenth year of Louis, most serene emperor, in the tenth indiction. Given on the eleventh day before the Kalends of February, successfully, in the name of God.”

[Col. 0011B] As stated above, the Emperor Louis later ratified this constitution of Abbot Hilduinus on the seventh day before the Kalends of September, in the same year and indiction, and indeed in the monastery of Saint-Denis.

From this, says Mabillon, it follows that the nineteenth year of Louis’s reign expressed in the aforesaid letter of Hilduinus must be reckoned from the time when Louis was declared co-emperor by his father, not from the death of his father Charles, which occurred only on the fifth day before the Kalends of February.

Around the same year Hilduinus built a church, or rather an oratory, of the Blessed Mary. It is still visible in the underground crypt at the foot of the ancient tomb of Saint Dionysius and his companions. This is clear from his somewhat mutilated letter, in which he assigns to this oratory—whose dedication is said to have taken place on the Kalends of November—as an endowment “the little village called Ermedon and an estate at Aqua Picta,” to provide lighting, in addition to what was customarily donated from the treasury at the feet of the saints.

[Col. 0011C] Moreover, he decreed that “eight monks of this holy congregation, in rotation, should continually perform in that chapel both the daytime and nighttime office according to Roman custom.”

This is further confirmed by a diploma of the Emperor Louis, by which he granted to the church a village in the county of Paris called Mintriacum, or Mitry. The church had recently been built by “the venerable man Hilduinus, religious abbot of the monastery of the holy chief of the apostles and of the most distinguished martyrs Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius”—whom the emperor calls his special protectors—“before the feet of those same most blessed martyrs,” for the praise of God and the Lord Jesus Christ, “in honor of the holy and ever-undefiled Virgin of Heaven, Queen of the whole world, and of the holy precursor of Christ,” for the safety of the emperor, his wife, and his offspring. There he placed “very many and most precious relics of the saints.”

This donation was made to that place for the provision of lights and ornaments, on the condition that on the Purification of Saint Mary, on the day of the martyrdom of the most blessed Peter and Paul, on the solemnity of the most glorious martyr Sebastian, and on the anniversary of the emperor and his beloved wife Judith, when they had departed from this world, the monks of that holy monastery should receive a meal from the resources of the village, excluding the charitable provisions “which, by imperial authority, they already received from the resources of the church assigned for the solemnities,” and that on those same days, as far as possible, the poor should also be fed.

> “Given on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of February, in the nineteenth year, by Christ’s favor, of the reign of our lord Louis, most pious Augustus, in the eleventh indiction. Enacted at the royal palace of Vern.”

In the year 836 Hilduinus undertook to write the *Areopagitica*—this is what they call the works that he composed concerning the deeds of the blessed Dionysius—at the command expressed in a letter of Louis the Pious, which is found prefixed to the same *Areopagitica*.

In that same year, having recently been exiled to New Corbie, he had promised certain relics of the holy martyrs to Warinus, abbot of that place and likewise of the monastery of Rebais. He therefore gave him, with the assent of the emperor, the bishop of Paris, and the neighboring nobles, the body of the boy and martyr Saint Vitus of Lucania. During the reign of Pepin it had been transferred to Francia and kept in a Dionysian cell in the territory of Paris.

Nithard, in Book I of his *History*, states that in 838 Hilduinus, together with Gerard, count of Paris, confirmed his loyalty by oath to Charles—not 828, as is read, perhaps through a printer’s error, in the first volume of the *History of the University of Paris*, p. 604.

In the same year Hilduinus and the brothers of Saint-Denis decided to enter into a confraternity of prayers with the monks of Saint-Remi, who willingly consented to the sacred alliance, unless indeed they themselves were its first authors. Letters concerning this matter were published from the parchment of Saint-Remi in volume IV of the *Spicilegium*, p. 229, and in the *Historical Proofs of Saint-Denis*, no. 77; there the act is attributed to Fulco, abbot of Saint-Remi.

The names of the monks from the monastery of Saint-Denis are appended in the old parchment [Col. 0012B], together with the names of those to whom they had granted communion in their prayers, who were called enrolled brothers by the others.

Among these, the first listed are the Emperor Louis, then King Louis, then Abbot Hilduinus, and then Abbot Louis. The first of the two latter was abbot of Saint-Denis; the other two were confederates and perhaps had been taken from the Dionysian community. Although Abbot Louis seems to have been the brother of Louis Augustus, who succeeded Hilduinus as Dionysian abbot, while already being abbot of other monasteries.

These are followed by the names of 123 monks of the same place. Mabillon, in volume II of the *Annals*, p. 608, gives 127, among whom Bishop Godfrey is mentioned.

In the year 839 the Emperor Louis ratified, on the tenth day before the Kalends of February, in the second indiction and the twenty-sixth year of his reign, an exchange of possessions made between Hilduinus, abbot of Saint-Denis, and Ermentrude, abbess of Saint Mary of Jouarre.

[Col. 0012C] In the following year, the twenty-seventh of the reign of Louis, most serene Augustus, on the ninth day of February, two noble spouses, Lantfrid and Teutgild, donated various estates situated at Bidolidum to Hilduinus, abbot of Saint-Denis.

After Louis died on Sunday, 20 June of that same year, 840, while Lothair was journeying from Italy toward Paris to seize the entire empire if he could, Hilduinus, together with Gerard, count of Paris, went out to meet Lothair, having broken faith with Charles. At that time, while brother rose against brother and the Northmen, taking the opportunity as favorable for ravaging the coastal regions, had just plundered Rouen, Hilduinus wished the treasure of Saint-Denis to be carried to the abbey of Ferrières. But when Lupus, abbot of Ferrières, warned in Letter 110 that the place was not sufficiently secure, it is uncertain where Hilduinus turned.

Certainly, around this year 840 there survive in the *Proofs of the History of Saint-Denis*, nos. 81 and 84, two privileges of the Emperor Lothair, granted to Saint-Denis at Hilduinus’s request, concerning the valley of Tillina, or Valtellina, in Italy. In the first diploma Hilduinus is simply called “the venerable abbot”; in the second, “the venerable man called archbishop and chief notary of our sacred palace.”

The authors disagree about the year of Hilduinus’s death. To Mabillon he seems not to have lived beyond 840; the author of the *Genealogical History of the Nobility of France*, volume VI, p. 242, agrees, assigning his death to the year 840. Jacobus Brolius is mistaken, however, when he places his death one year earlier, as Astronomus contradicts him by stating that after Louis’s death Hilduinus, abbot of Saint-Denis, went out with Gerard, count of Paris, to meet Lothair as he approached Paris.

The writer of the *History of the University of Paris* appears no less distant from the truth both as to the year and the day when, in volume I, p. 604, he reports that Hilduinus died in 842, on 30 October.

In the necrology of Saint-Germain, written in his time, there is an entry on the tenth day before the Kalends of December: “The burial of Lord Hilduinus, abbot”; and likewise in the Dionysian necrology:

> “Hilduinus, monk and abbot of the blessed Dionysius, died; destined to be glorious in every respect, had he not betrayed his loyalty to the Emperor Louis and afterward to his son Charles, in order to curry favor with Lothair.”

The aforementioned Brolius, followed by the author of the *History of the University of Paris*, volume I, p. 604, asserts that Hilduinus was buried in the choir of Saint-Médard at Soissons, opposite the principal altar, where a gravestone could still be seen before the church was destroyed by the Calvinists. If this is so, says Mabillon, it must be conceded that he remained abbot of that place until his death.

# The *Areopagitica*, or Life of Saint Dionysius

Written by Hilduinus at the command of Louis the Pious.

*(From Surius.)*

[Col. 0013B]

## Prolegomena

### I

[Col. 0013]

Letter of the most pious Augustus, Lord Louis, to Hilduinus, venerable abbot of the monastery of the most holy martyrs Dionysius and his companions, concerning the gathering into a single work of the things that he had found scattered through the Greek histories concerning the account of the most precious martyr Dionysius.

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divine clemency’s merciful favor, Emperor Augustus, to Hilduinus, etc.

*(This letter is to be sought among the works of Louis the Pious in volume 104 of this Patrology, col. 1326.)*

### II

[Col. 0013]

Reply of Hilduinus, abbot, to the most serene Emperor, Lord Louis. It explains from where and in what manner the materials were taken which, at his command, Hilduinus had compiled into a single work from Greek and Latin histories concerning the account of the most distinguished martyr Dionysius.

To Louis the Pious, ever Augustus, honored with wondrously gracious kindness and reverence for his authority, Hilduinus, humble servant of Christ and keeper of the register of my lord Dionysius, the precious martyr, and of his companions, and in all things most devoted to your imperial dominion, wishes present prosperity in Christ, the blessing of eternal happiness, and glory.

#### I

“My heart exults in the Lord, and my horn is exalted in my God. My mouth is opened wide, and my lips shall rejoice, so that I may proclaim the praises of my lord, the most glorious martyr Dionysius.” I was commanded to do this by my distinguished emperor and lord; I could not have kept silent about it even if someone had perhaps forbidden me. Indeed, I have great reason to rejoice, because divine condescension has wished to grant me my desire in fuller measure: I have learned that the conception of my mind was pleasing to him, since your sublimity, pleasing to God, lent the hand of authority to the work that my humility had spontaneously resolved to undertake.

For this reason, it is beyond doubt that he is the author of good works and of every spiritual endeavor who both stirs minds to action and, by whatever means pleases him, assists their actions.

My spirit also greatly rejoices in God my Savior because your most Christian soul so clearly recognizes in itself the benefits of divine goodness and the consolations of the saints, and so readily shows itself inflamed with reverence and devotion toward its author and restorer, and toward its special intercessors.

For your pious soul would not so deeply confess the true and just judgments of God unless it recognized itself illumined by the Holy Spirit. Nor would your wisdom of supreme discernment so devotedly seek out the good deeds and words of God’s friends unless it loved the supreme Good, from whom and through whom all good things exist [Col. 0014C].

It is recognized that your religious devotion is inflamed by love of him, so that you sought the glorious triumphs of Christ’s soldiers. Once you know them, you will fight more vigorously against vices and the authors of vices through their help, so that by following the examples of the martyrs, who fought courageously and won faithfully, you too may reach the palm with which they were rewarded.

This also contributes to the encouragement of your vow and concern: Ezra, the restorer of Sacred Scripture, thereby earned from God the great gift of reward and acquired for himself a praiseworthy name among human beings.

#### II

Therefore, since the diligence of your efforts is directed toward a matter that, because of the great antiquity of this most holy father of ours—so far as his earthly origin, conversion, and death are concerned—has become known to almost the entire world through wondrous holiness and miraculous signs, while knowledge of him remains known to only a few of our people and still unknown to many, when it is made manifest through your efforts you will both win for yourself, as you know better, great merit and acquire an everlasting memorial.

May the Lord grant that we too may be found suitable fellow workers for the completion of your good will. We obey your commands without hesitation, just as diligently as you request what we willingly undertake to execute.

Because you ask us to send you as quickly as possible all that has been found in both Greek and Latin books concerning our lord and patron Dionysius, matters that until now we have known only imperfectly, we consider it unfitting to delay what the pious desire of your authority rightly expects from our service.

As the shortness of time permits, whatever our swiftly recollecting memory shall suggest to our lips, with the Lord’s favor we shall rapidly commit to the pens of scribes. We humbly ask your wisdom not to seek in what we undertake to write out of reverence and love for the most holy martyr, and in obedience to your command, any pomp of words or elegance of composition, but the sincerity of the purest truth, as we have received it from the statements of the ancients.

Do not rebuke us concerning the force of cases, prepositions, and conjunctions, or concerning the alteration of letters in what follows, or the placement of punctuation according to grammatical art. We have undertaken to hasten not these things, but the service of our devotion and the duty of commending your authority.

This is especially so because we shall weave together what we have expressed from a foreign language in the sequence of the text just as it has been strained from the press. Although in translation it may not retain the corresponding fragrance of the language, it nevertheless conveys the savory flavor of truth and of its meaning.

Accordingly, we shall disclose to all readers and hearers the order of the history, gathered into one work as your dominion commanded, and afterward its fullness divided out item by item. For what we desire to reveal with faithful heart will demonstrate itself to be true and probable through divine inspiration and execution.

We do not therefore judge that we have much to labor over, since trustworthy statements of recognized and highly approved persons make clear what should be held and believed concerning this most holy martyr of Christ.

#### III

From ancient times and down to the present, both the testimony of other histories and that of the *Acts of the Apostles* have known that he was of exceedingly noble birth and distinguished at Athens by instruction in philosophy.

This is especially clear from the history of Aristarchus, the Greek chronicler, who, writing in a letter to Onesiphorus, the *primicerius* (chief official), about the city of Athens and the deeds of the apostles in that place, orderly recounts his family origin, his learning, the course of his life, the period of his age, his ordination, his preaching, the appointment of a successor to his episcopal office, and his arrival at Rome.

We are sending this letter to your dominion, and any diligent person among us can obtain it. A curious reader may borrow it from the Greek sources, from which we too took it.

That before his conversion he traveled to Heliopolis for the sake of astrology, where, together with his companion Apollophanius, he saw the darkness at the crucifixion of our Savior, he himself demonstrates in letters sent to Polycarp, bishop of the Smyrnaeans, and to that same Apollophanius; for he was then twenty-five years old.

That he believed together with his entire household and his wife Damaris, the reading of the *Acts of the Apostles* teaches, and the dialogue of Basil and John demonstrates even more clearly, in chapter 5 of Book IV.

Blessed Ambrose also plainly reveals the same fact in his letter to the people of Vercelli, identifying his wife by name.

Finally, blessed Father Augustine, in the beautiful sermon [Note: Possidius, in his index, calls this sermon a tractate; and it is indeed Augustine’s.] that he wrote on the sower of the word, says:

> “When the apostle had finished speaking, after the resurrection of the dead—which is especially the faith of Christians—had been proclaimed there, the Athenians are reported to have said, ‘We shall hear you about this again.’ For some among them were mocking, some doubting, and some believing; and among them a certain Dionysius the Areopagite is named, that is, the chief man of the Athenians, and a certain noble woman named Damaris, and many others.”

In the same sermon, where he writes about the scandal of the Jews and the foolishness of the Gentiles, he says:

> “To the Jews a stumbling block, but to the Gentiles foolishness; yet to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks—that is, to Paul himself from Saul, and to Dionysius the Areopagite, to such persons as these and those—Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God.”

### IV

As for knowledge of his books, which he wrote in his native language and composed for those who requested them, our reading—through the grace of God and your direction, by whose provision translated books are returned from our archives to those who request them—satisfies us.

We received the authentic books, written in the Greek language, as a great gift when the treasurer of the church of Constantinople and the other envoys sent on Michael’s public embassy, after completing their mission at Compiegne, presented them to your glory on the very eve of the solemnity of Saint Dionysius.

Divine grace followed this gift, which seemed to have been brought to our devotion from heaven, so greatly that on that same night the Lord Christ deigned to work, for the praise and glory of his name and through the prayers and merits of his most distinguished martyr, nineteen very famous miracles involving the healing of various illnesses in persons well known to us and to our neighbors.

### V

Since blessed Clement had sent him here, namely to the people of Gaul, the most ancient little book of his passion explains how he reached Christ through the palm of martyrdom after suffering diverse and most cruel tortures; how his own head, honored with the reverent service of the heavenly army under angelic guidance during the celebration of his funeral rites, was carried to the place where he now rests; and in what manner he was buried by a certain Catulla, a married woman.

Especially worthy of mention, however, is the writing of Visbius, which by divine providence was discovered in Paris in a volume that had been hidden away for a very long time. Among other things worth remembering, it is known to contain—as you read there—the words of our Lord Jesus Christ spoken to him when he was celebrating the sacred mysteries and the Lord appeared to all who were present.

The very ancient Mass books, almost worn away by excessive age, seem to support this account. They contain the order of the Mass according to the Gallican custom that was observed in this western region from the beginning of the received faith until it adopted the form it now uses, the Roman form.

In these volumes there are two Masses that, during the celebration, briefly recall the tortures of the martyr and his companions in order to invoke the mercy of divine compassion and stir the hearts of the people to devotion, just as the other Masses written there chant the sufferings of other Apostles or martyrs whose passions are well known.

The chant, meaning, and words of these Masses seem to correspond so closely to the account of their passion that we sent you that no one can doubt that their struggles were described by a witness of their martyrdom, and that, from the same truthful history, remembrance of their torments was prescribed in the prayers mentioned above.

### VI

Moreover, these supplications of the Mass seem to possess no negligible authority concerning the passion of the saints in question. For among us there exist letters of Innocent, and after him of Gelasius, as well as more recent letters of blessed Pope Gregory and other pontiffs to the bishops of the cities of Gaul, and letters of our own bishops to them, concerning the imitation of Roman custom in all matters belonging to ecclesiastical authority.

From these it can be understood that for many years this form of the Mass had departed from Gallican custom, and that remembrance of the passion of these martyrs had long been established in these western regions through petitions of supplication [perhaps: “supplications”]. We place our faith in these testimonies all the more certainly because we firmly believe, without doubt, that they were composed shortly after the completion of the martyrs’ course.

## VII

Nevertheless, no one should think that blessed Dionysius and his successors departed from apostolic institution because of this order of the Mass, originally handed down according to Gallican customs, if it is established that its proper character belongs to the apostles themselves, to apostolic men, and even to the city of Rome. Nor can anyone wonder why we possess the hymn of Saint Eugenius of Toledo concerning blessed Dionysius, while we seem to lack the writings of neighboring learned men, with only a few exceptions. For even those works that we do possess—we say this after asking pardon of our predecessors—we found hidden away and negligently left behind; and we rejoice that we possess others not yet published, because they have not yet been fully clarified.

## VIII

Moreover, we have been amazed at the babbling frivolity of those who, arguing that this Dionysius cannot have been the Areopagite, foolishly gather the following material to support their position. They claim that the venerable and holy presbyter Bede said in his exposition of the Acts of the Apostles that Dionysius the Areopagite was bishop not of Athens but of Corinth, adding that he died there.

Since the booklet of this martyr’s Passion testifies that he was ordained bishop by Clement, Roman pontiff, and sent into these regions of Gaul, and since the Passions of various holy martyrs killed under different emperors state that they came to these regions together with this most holy man, this is plainly refuted by the hearing of sensible men. Gregory of Tours, as he said he had read in the Passion of Saint Saturninus, mentions by way of conjecture that this same man was sent into these regions during the persecution of Decius, under blessed Sixtus, together with six other bishops—although their lives or Passions in no way accord with his statements regarding chronology.

## IX

Behold the authority of those who know little, contradicting itself. We answer it, as though in excess, for the satisfaction of the foolish, since we have before us a true account of this holy pontiff and martyr drawn from truthful histories.

First, we ask that those who are contentious in this matter wipe from their eyes the cataract contracted through arrogance and assumed learning, since they wish to appear clever, so that they may read with clear perception and faithfully reread what is true. And if they have opened only one eye when reading what the venerable presbyter Bede had said improperly, through an inadvertence, in the work mentioned above—where he corrected himself and, anticipating the voice of his critics, wrote a retraction—let them open the hollow in which the other eye ought to have been, and learn from ecclesiastical history that Dionysius, bishop of Corinth, mentions Dionysius, bishop of Athens, in his letter addressed to those same Athenians. For it is written there, in Book IV, chapter 23:

> There is also another letter of his—Dionysius, bishop of Corinth—to the Athenians, in which he invites them to belief in the Gospel and stirs up the more sluggish; at the same time he reproves certain people, as though they had almost fallen away from the faith, since their bishop Publius had completed his martyrdom. He also mentions Quadratus, who had succeeded the martyr Publius in the priesthood, and records that through his labor and diligence a certain revived warmth of faith had been restored among them.

> In the same letter he also points out that Dionysius the Areopagite, who, instructed by the apostle Paul, believed in Christ according to what is recorded in the Acts of the Apostles, was the first person ordained bishop at Athens by that same Apostle.

Blessed Jerome very clearly mentions this letter, as well as other letters of that Dionysius, bishop of Corinth, including the one he had sent to Bishop Soter, in his book *On Illustrious Men*. Therefore, anyone who observes under which emperors each of these men lived can plainly gather how absurd this argument is, since the periods separating these two Dionysiuses are so widely distinct.

## X

The same ecclesiastical history also reads as follows, in Book III, chapter 4:

> Among Paul’s companions, Crescens is said to have gone to the Galatians, while Linus and Clement presided over the Church in the city of Rome. They are said by Paul himself to have been his companions and assistants. It is also established that Dionysius the Areopagite at Athens, whom Luke described, believed when Paul first preached and became one of his companions, and that he assumed the priesthood of the Athenian Church.

Concerning the death of this Dionysius the Areopagite, Greek writers said nothing, because, owing to the great distance between the lands, his passing was entirely unknown to them. We nevertheless possess a Martyrology of Greek authority, obtained from Constantinopolitan parchment codices, so ancient that it demands the greatest caution from those who handle it. In it we find his dies natalis designated, together with the note that he had been bishop of Athens.

As its antiquity indicates, we reasonably suppose that this Martyrology may have been composed in the period when, at Constantine’s command, an opportunity having arisen, the martyrdoms of the Lord’s saints were collected from the whole world and brought to Caesarea.

To this day, moreover, the elders of the Greeks and the inhabitants of Athens, instructed by written histories and traditions of succession, maintain that Dionysius was at that time the first bishop of that city, when Timothy, likewise a disciple of Paul, governed the Church of the Ephesians. They also say that Dionysius, having appointed a bishop in his place, went to Rome and, as they learned, completed his life by a glorious martyrdom among the people of Gaul.

Patriarch Tarasius of Constantinople also carefully investigated this matter through his legates. Once convinced that it was so, he restored to the city of Athens the archiepiscopal pallium that had already long been withheld from it because of a certain dispute, and by synodal agreement honored it with the authority of a metropolis, which it had formerly possessed. For during the preceding years and up to that time, the bishop of that city had been subject to no one except the patriarch, nor were the bishops of the cities that owed him jurisdiction subject to any other authority.

## XI

As for what they say is written in the Passion of this blessed Dionysius—that Saint Clement ordained him bishop and sent him to Gaul—they should know without doubt that either they did not obtain the aforesaid Passion from truthful and more carefully corrected copies, or they read it corrupted through the fault of scribes. For it is not written there that he was consecrated bishop by blessed Clement, but that he was appointed apostle of all Gaul.

If our purpose were directed to other matters, we could sufficiently adduce examples of the authority of this apostolic ordination both from the Acts of the Apostles and from the deeds of the Lord himself. It is possible, as we have said, that they do not possess the text of this holy man of God’s Passion copied from authentic sources, and that therefore they are mistaken in this matter. We ourselves have seen several little codices derived from it. In some, the meaning seemed to agree, but the wording differed; in others, neither the meaning nor the continuity of the phrasing could be reconciled.

This plainly happened because of the great antiquity of this venerable and most ancient father and because of ignorance of the unknown and foreign language in which the account of him was principally written—or perhaps through the devotion of the faithful. They did not take pains to return to the ancient histories for knowledge of him; instead, like Gregory of Tours, who did not err through deliberate deception, they committed to writing what they had gathered by hearsay, according as each person’s understanding allowed, seeing the magnificent and innumerable wonders performed through him.

We read that the same thing happened with the deeds and Passions of the holy apostles, and we plainly discover it in other histories necessary to the Church. There were those who told the truth about the virtues of the blessed apostles but composed false accounts concerning their teaching. Likewise, concerning ecclesiastical histories and the origin, deeds, or deaths of the Fathers, some wrote truthfully as far as the factual substance of events was concerned, but less cautiously fabricated details regarding times or places.

Thus, as is well known, there has been variety among different translators in the canonical Scriptures. In these works, some said less, while others added certain things, until through blessed Jerome our language received their unalloyed truth from the very source.

## XII

Therefore no history can or should be regarded as equally probable unless it can be gathered from the comparison of truthful witnesses, especially orthodox ones. For this reason, what we now write after collecting the material concerning this distinguished martyr is to be held more securely than what we casually reread about any other saint without the author’s name—especially since what we are writing comes from the ancient writing of the Antiquarians, as from a meadow not Parisian but Paradisiacal.

Nevertheless, we must spare the simplicity of the religious man Gregory, bishop of Tours. He assessed many things otherwise than the truth actually was, and committed them to writing not through cunning deceit but from a good-hearted and simple intention.

We can plainly recognize that he did not investigate certain matters very carefully, since Fortunatus, a prudent and highly learned man who lived at the same time as he and frequently wrote many things to him, composed a most beautiful hymn in rhythmic form about this glorious martyr. In it he records that Dionysius was sent by blessed Clement, as he had learned from the pages of the Latins. But he makes no mention of Dionysius’s nation or episcopal ordination, because he was entirely ignorant of the Greek language.

## XIII

In view, therefore, of such numerous and manifest assertions of testimony concerning this most holy and ancient Father—of the truth fully brought to light and revealed to all who wish to know it, and of so certain an argument pressed upon those who wish not to know it that, even if they desire it, they cannot fail to recognize what is true—let the ruinous and excessively profane contention cease that this Areopagite was not Dionysius.

For whoever in any way seeks to diminish the martyr’s reputation is plainly attempting, with blind arrogance and feeble strength, to detract from the truth for which he bore witness, crossing so many seas, suffering exile in so distant a region, and enduring such bitter torments for its sake.

Just as one must judge truly impious and obstinate anyone who, after so many established judgments, leaves something in his perverse mind to be contrived against this conclusion, so whoever, after the truth has been discovered, continues to doubt anything about it will rightly be declared, by the decree of the upright, a companion and disciple of him who was a liar from the beginning and the father of lies.

## XIV

I cannot estimate the extent of the dullness of these whisperers, the worst kind of men. If they sought the glory of their homeland and their own glory, they ought to have contended that they possessed so excellent a teacher and distinguished a martyr. Instead, although they possess him, they murmur that they do not.

## XV

Nor can I grieve as the matter demands over the perversity of the mad. Although they ought, through prayers and proclamations of praise, to make the glorious martyr favorable toward them despite their iniquities, they labor through detraction and diminution of his reputation to make him, as far as lies within them, hostile to themselves.

Yet he does not grow in heaven through the praise of such people, nor diminish through their disparagement. Joined to the Savior and made a fellow citizen of the angels, he observes the wills of all from the highest citadel of heaven; following the Lamb wherever he goes, he searches and penetrates the hearts of all, filled with divine light.

Even in this world he does not need the testimony to his glory provided by such men—if indeed they should be called men, since they disparage one who reigns immortally in heaven, whom, while he was still in mortal flesh, beasts revered as he struggled in the contest.

For him and his companions, that praise in this world is sufficient which their most splendid monuments attest, and which nearly the entire Christian world proclaims in celebrated veneration.

Nor is it surprising if the martyr of the Lord Jesus endures their quibbling, since the same God of majesty, who, having risen from the dead, dies no more and sits at the right hand of the Father in heaven, with principalities and the powers of all the angels subject to him (Rom. VI), continues through so many centuries to endure undeserved prejudices from unbelievers.

## XVI

Meanwhile, until you receive more concerning the knowledge of your advocate, most serene Augustus, accept this and make it truthfully known to all: we send these things faithfully to your lordship, since we have diligently endeavored to gather them truthfully from truthful historians and the pages of histories.

For the truth, on behalf of which this servant and friend of the Lord shed his precious blood, has no need of our false testimony. It is sufficient for itself by its own testimony, and it makes those whom it fills into the most truthful witnesses who testify to the truth.

Finally, something that we sought for a long time with great anxiety may perhaps cause someone else to wonder: why, after all their torments, these holy men were finally stripped naked and publicly beaten with rods, as though from the beginning, and then deliberately beheaded with axes. This may seem all the more astonishing because this manner of execution is more rarely, or nowhere, recorded as having been inflicted upon other saints of God.

Anyone who knows the matter will understand—as we infer from the words of their Passion and learn by reviewing many deeds of the ancients—that in ancient times it was the Roman custom for anyone of the nobility accused of treason, who had withdrawn from military service and the defense of the Republic to go elsewhere and acted against the will of the Senate, or who had presumed to teach otherwise than the sentence prescribed, to be ignominiously killed with an axe after being publicly beaten with scourges, amid every form of disgrace.

Thus, in the 111th Olympiad, the Roman consul Manlius Torquatus struck his son with an axe after having him beaten with rods, although he was victorious, because he had fought the enemy against orders.

Therefore, from these things you and all readers should observe how noble this holy Dionysius was according to earthly birth in the world; how exalted according to spiritual rebirth in the Lord; how great in fervor and faith, as he traversed such vast expanses of land in the pious zeal of truth within the Christian religion; how highly regarded even by the ruler of the world, who sent his officers here from Rome to have him slaughtered; how noble in the dignity of his lineage and in the overthrow of pagan worship; how courageous in enduring torments; how utterly degraded in his execution; how supremely holy before God in death; how excellent and inconceivably glorious with Christ in heaven; how powerful in virtue for the assistance of our weakness, while we still labor in the contest; and how blessed he will rejoice eternally with his own body, received again in blessedness, together with his companions, all the angelic choirs, and all the saints and elect of the Lord, in eternal happiness.

This will be through the same Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, true God and Son of God and man, who in the perfect Trinity of one substance and power lives and reigns as God forever and ever. Amen.

# III

[Col. 0022C]

### Letter of the unworthy abbot Hilduin to all the sons and faithful of the holy Catholic mother Church, explaining how anyone who wishes to know may discover, in the letter addressed on this matter to the most Christian emperor, Lord Louis, from what sources and in what manner the material that he had assembled into a single continuous text at the emperor’s command was taken from Greek and Latin histories concerning the knowledge of the most excellent martyr of Christ, Dionysius.

Hilduin, humble servant of Christ and keeper of the register of my lord Dionysius the precious and of his companions, wishes continual peace and eternal glory to all Catholic love, spread everywhere by the Holy Spirit.

## I

Since Scripture admonishes us by a general definition, saying, “Whatever your hand is able to do, do it earnestly” (Eccl. IX), and since I recognized the desire of the pious Augustus and of very many others eagerly striving toward this purpose, it seemed to me that I should expend some sweat in this matter as well, so that, with Christ’s help, I might bring to light the account of the conversion [or: conduct], preaching, arrival at Rome, and triumphant martyrdom of the most blessed Dionysius.

This material is contained chiefly in Greek histories and, as though buried, was preserved among the Latins in no small portion, concealed in ancient archives. I did this so that devotion among the devout toward the worship of God and of his distinguished martyr might increase through the accumulation of further devotion, and so that, in the house of the Lord, the glorious intercession of that friend of God, for whose love we have undertaken this work, might obtain divine mercy for our due service, offering the faithful a taste in a cup, insofar as our smallness and our little intellect permit.

For, as was said before us, the deeds of those who live well are the alphabet of those who desire life, and the examples of martyrs are exhortations to martyrdom. Therefore, as you reread what follows, intoxicated with this splendid cup, let faith in piety burst forth, and do not assign our service to rash presumption in the name of this man.

Since, however, as a certain wise man says, truth is often despised in a lowly person, although nothing ought to have been preferred to it, I humbly beg all into whose hands these writings may come not to attend to the humility of our person or the undisciplined rusticity of our speech. Let them know that, in this particular matter, the Lord is not a respecter of persons. 

In this respect, I confess myself unskilled in expression, though not in knowledge. Rather, let them place before their eyes this renowned and true soldier of Christ, the subject of this work. Whatever any mortal may now say in his praise will be unequal to his dignity, since he can be praised worthily only by the one by whom and through whom he merited becoming such a man.

Let them therefore faithfully reread what truthful men have written truthfully about him and have simply gathered into one account. If they are displeased by our ignorance, let them return to the monuments of antiquity. We forge neither our own material nor anything new; instead, we draw out the ancient words of the ancients from deeply hidden volumes and, preserving the sincerity of the truth, place them in clearer pages.

## II

We do not think that anyone of sound mind will judge these things less acceptable because they had not previously been repeated, since anyone can plainly recognize that the one who created all things together (Eccli. XVIII) did not wish everything to be revealed either all at once or to everyone at once. Many things that had once been manifest have again been hidden by time.

One should recall what is read in the divinely inspired writings (IV Kings XXII) concerning the book of the Law, which had long lain hidden and was afterward discovered amid astonishment.

And when Daniel says, “Many shall pass through, and knowledge shall be multiplied” (Daniel XII), how much more should no one deny that, while many companions are looking elsewhere, some sluggish or slow person following behind may nevertheless discover on the road the destruction that those going ahead had worn smooth.

Therefore, every ambiguity having been cast aside, concerning the claim that this very Dionysius, whose deeds are written here, was not the Areopagite and bishop of Athens, whatever anyone may have said—whether in Gregory, bishop of Tours, by way of conjecture, or through the inadvertence of the holy presbyter Bede, or through the unsupported assertions of others—anyone who wishes to know the matter more carefully should seek out and reread, to identify at least some of the sources by name, the history of Eusebius of Caesarea, the letter of Aristarchus, the Greek chronographer, to Onesiphorus the primicerius, and the writing of Visbius.

There he will be able to learn who this Dionysius was and how he reached Christ through the palm of martyrdom, if he is unwilling to lend them the hand of faith in their connection with one another.

As for these and any other sources from which everything now collected before us was taken, if it is useful and pleasing to the kindness of the reader, and if he cannot find them elsewhere, this letter of our smallness to the most serene Augustus will abundantly illuminate the matter.

Even if he does not deign to believe us, the sources themselves will nevertheless reveal to him, without any haughtiness, where, how, and in what order he may plainly find all these things stated. If he needs it, he will also be able to borrow the complete books from the archive of our Church.

May every faithful and dear brother in the Lord prosper, with piety and grace, remembering us.

[Col. 0023D]

# The Passion of the Most Holy Dionysius Begins

Dionysius, who from the place called the Areopagus and by his ancestral name was called **Ionicus**, but by his Christian surname was called **Macarius**, was ordained archbishop of the Athenians by the holy apostle Paul and, by the apostolic authority of blessed Pope Clement, appointed apostle of all Gaul.

His unconquered devotion to the faith of Christ, under the emperor Domitian [Note: [Col. 0023D] Rather, under Trajan or Hadrian.] and the prefect Sisinnius, after many contests in the city of Paris, during which our Lord Jesus Christ appeared to him before a great number of witnesses, he completed in martyrdom on the seventh day before the Ides of October, together with Rusticus and Eleutherius. Saint Dionysius carried his own head to the place where he now rests.

## CHAPTER ONE

After the blessed and saving Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ, his worshipful resurrection from the dead, and his glorious ascension into heaven—by which he manifested that he had never been absent in his divinity, to which he returned—the preaching of the apostles among all nations succeeded, so that, as faith grew, many deserved to become confessors of the name of Christ.

The Catholic mother Church afterward rejoiced that these men had merited becoming martyrs and warriors of the faith, just as she rejoiced in having such leaders and governors among the apostles. When they saw their own Passions approaching, they taught, filled with the grace of the Holy Spirit, what they had learned from the teaching of the Lord Jesus, so that they might pass over to the glory and reward of holy confession.

Therefore we give thanks to you, Lord Jesus Christ, who granted that the darts of the hostile enemy should be a trial and not wounds for your faithful. Among the other gifts of grace, you bestowed such a reward for the labor upon your witnesses that no enemy might rejoice that any of yours had been unwarlike. Rather, you granted them perpetual triumph, so that they might always be an example to your Church.

Among their company was the blessed apostle Paul. The humanity and kindness of our Savior and God, presiding in heaven, addressed Saul, struck him down, established him as Paul, and joined him to their merit and number. Filled with the Gospel of Christ, he traversed not only from Jerusalem to Illyricum but also to the furthest boundaries, as God-appointed teacher of all nations.

Traveling through the upper and neighboring cities, at the time when the emperor Claudius held the scepter, he came to Athens.

## CHAPTER TWO

Athens is one of the great cities, a metropolis situated on the border of Thrace and overlooking the boundaries of Lacedaemonia, lying midway between Achaea and Macedonia. Greece possessed nothing more splendid in the situation of its lands. It was mountainous, with lofty and numerous hills, and ancient literary eloquence called it the paternal womb and maternal breasts.

Confined like a double sea within the straits of the Ionian Sea, it touches the Aegean Sea on the left. It is a renowned and ancient city, glorious by itself apart from foreign additions. Its gathered population did not give it its origin; the place that is its seat is also its origin.

Rich in the fertility of its lands, nurse of speech and eloquence, mother of philosophers and sages, and abundant in the liberal arts and every kind of wealth, it stood out above all cities.

It is situated in the province of Attica in Hellas, where Cecrops and Menander, noble kings, shone. There Apollo, Hippocrates, Aristotle, and the other inventors and transmitters of every kind of knowledge arose, and their presence in the whole world and their memory in our own times continue to shine.

In this exceedingly distinguished city, during the time of Cecrops, Menander, and the kings who succeeded them, the worship of images and statues and the superstitious religion of idols was first devised and proclaimed by ordinances.

It was also consecrated in its development to Minerva, and its name was adapted from her name. It was the first of all cities to establish laws, either handing rights down to others or borrowing them [reading uncertain: *mutavit*, “altered them”].

## CHAPTER THREE

The city is marked out and divided into five regions.

The first region is the one facing the Aegean Sea. In it stands a mountain rising above the city, where golden statues of Saturn and Priapus were worshiped in the madness of various delusions. This region is called **Kronos Pagos**, from the name of Saturn, who is called *Kronos* in Greek.

The second region is Athens itself, facing Thrace. There stood a terebinth tree of astonishing size, beneath which, on appointed days, shepherds worshiped images of Silvani and Fauns, rustic beings. This region is called **Pagos** from the name of Silvanus and Faunus. For the Greeks call Silvanus *Pan*, and they call the Fauns *Ficarii* or *Panitae*.

The third region is called **Possedonos Pagos**, facing the harbor of Neptune. For *Possedon* is what the Greeks call Neptune. There they worshiped an image of him and an effigy of Diana at Aegium, and, when the moon was renewed, the entire population gathered there for many public functions.

The fourth region is in the same city, where an idol of Mars and an image of Hercules had stood on the hill of Mount Triton, situated in the middle of the city. Many sacrifices and offerings were made there to Mars and Hercules, whom they worshiped as the greatest and strongest gods.

There too judgments were conducted, courts were taught, and every skill of intellect was practiced. This place is called the **Areopagus**, after Mars; for Mars is called *Ares* in Greek.

The fifth region of the same city faces the Scaean Gate. It is called **Hermis Pagus**, from the name of Mercury, who is called *Hermes* in Greek. In it, a small shrine of Mercury had captivated the city through reverence for itself.

## CHAPTER FOUR

This city, fortified with very strong walls and enriched beyond other cities by a flourishing sea; honey-sweet, as the expression goes, streams and rivers; sufficiently rich groves planted with fragrant spices; nectar-like vineyards flowing with abundant produce; exceptionally plentiful olive groves; flourishing green spaces; pastures fully sufficient for livestock; supplies of gold, silver, and every other metal; the traffic of ships and customs revenues; and an abundance of every pleasure—once flourished with the greatest nobility.

But although in its earlier age it surpassed all the felicities of the world, it is now overwhelmed and broken by the frequent and dense assault of peoples.

At the time of Paul’s arrival there was a certain nobleman, Apollo the **Kronospagite**, called **Symmistes**, that is, a fellow-priest, because he surpassed the others in that region of the city. He was descended from the lineage of a most noble Apollo, a leader of the Athenians.

His father Nicolaus was a man of great intellect, distinguished as a citizen by his devotion to literary study and a master of Argolic art. Apollo, therefore, while he was renowned among the schools of philosophers, was turning over authoritative libraries and devoting himself to philosophy and to vain superstitions according to pagan ritual.

He heard the apostle Paul preaching doctrines that were new and previously unheard. Unable to resist him, he discovered that the teaching Paul delivered at Athens was true.

Therefore, abandoning demonic deceptions and pagan inventions, he fell at the apostle’s feet and begged him to show him the true doctrine and the way of salvation. He professed himself to be a disciple of Christ, not of Saturn.

## CHAPTER FIVE

When these things had taken place, the Athenians, stirred by the novelty of his preaching, one day led Paul to the Areopagus so that his teaching might be examined there.

Paul addressed Dionysius, who, because of his full knowledge of the divine science of the heavenly powers, was called **Theosophus**, that is, “wise concerning God.” From the region of the city where he habitually lived and where he had been born and held authority, he used the designation “Areopagite” as though it were his natural name.

He was descended through a long and illustrious line from the high blood of the first and great Dionysius—not the Dionysius of Semele or Deucalion, but the one who is renowned at Athens as the inventor of the vine.

When he was twenty-five years old and richly instructed in almost every art, stirred by a desire for advancement, he migrated to Heliopolis in Egypt together with his fellow philosopher Apollophanius, out of a desire to study astrology.

While he was living there with Apollophanius, at the time when God made man, our Lord Jesus Christ, was hanging crucified on the cross for the salvation of the world through the envy of the Jews, and the sun, fearful at the death of its Lord, changed the rays of its light into the horror of a dark night, while the regions of the world were covered by the darkness of the gloom, Dionysius was astonished at this sign of darkness, previously unseen and unheard of.

Since he had been trained in every branch of learning, he said:

> “This night, which we marvel to see descend newly upon our eyes, signifies that the true light of the whole world is about to come, and declares that God will shine upon the human race in serene graciousness.”

## CHAPTER SIX

Having happily completed the matters for which he had gone there, he returned and presided over the citadel of the entire city of Athens. As president of the court of the Areopagus, he arranged the administration of all public and private affairs, as a nobleman among the noblest.

Among the foremost of the foremost, clad in the philosophical toga, he poured forth to the citizens and to those flocking from every direction for that study the subtleties and turns of sophistic and syllogistic reasoning, the acumen of universal disciplines.

This prophet, while still a pagan, had been able to disclose in advance the inward meaning of the great mystery that had come, as though it were yet to come. When Paul had entered the Areopagus, with everyone’s ears alert to his word, he began to question Dionysius in particular: what did he worship, and which divinities did he serve in so spacious and venerable a place?

Dionysius replied:

> “We worship and adore the gods whom our fathers worshiped, through whose power and skill the mother earth is sustained. The altars you see are consecrated in the name and honor of Mars, Hercules, Mercury, and Priapus.”

When Paul had examined the individual altars and images of the false gods, he found among the other altars one altar with an inscription above it: **To the Unknown God**.

Paul turned to Dionysius and asked him:

> “Who is that unknown God?”

Dionysius answered:

> “That God has not yet been demonstrated among the gods. He is unknown to us and is to come in the age that lies ahead. For he is the God who will reign in heaven and on earth, and his kingdom will have no end.”

Paul added:

> “What do you think? Will he be a man, or a spirit of the gods?”

Dionysius replied:

> “True God and true man. He will renew the world. But he is still unknown to human beings, because his dwelling is with God in heaven.”

Paul said:

> “I proclaim to you that God whom you call unknown. For he was born of the Virgin Mary, suffered under Pontius Pilate, died for the salvation of humanity, rose again, and, ascending into heaven, sits at the right hand of God the Father—true God and true man, through whom all things were made. He will come at the end of the age as judge of all that is done.

> “He was born in Judea, God and great in Israel, and holy is his name” (Ps. LXXV).

> “Therefore, recognize now the one whom until this time you have held as unknown, for he alone is God and there is no other besides him” (I Kings II). He brought us back from death to life at the price of his blood. He joined heaven and earth—that is, human beings and angels—in the unity of his kingdom. He kills, being just, and gives life, being merciful. He shuts, and no one opens; he opens, and no one shuts” (Apoc. III).

## CHAPTER SEVEN

While Paul preached these and many other things and visited the individual temples, commending Christ Jesus as the Son of God and true God, the Athenians received his words with the greatest attentiveness, moved by friendly curiosity because of their very novelty.

Dionysius heard the true doctrine and the teaching of salvation. He recognized that the idols whom he served were nothing, or rather that they were demons rather than gods. He clearly perceived the Holy Spirit and the words of life in Paul’s teaching. Touched in heart by divine light, he yielded to Paul and asked him to pray on his behalf for the mercy of the very God whom Paul proclaimed, so that he might merit becoming that God's true worshiper and Paul's disciple.

## CHAPTER EIGHT
The next day, as Paul was continuing on his journey, a certain blind man began to address him with urgent pleas. The holy apostle made the sign of the cross over his eyes, which had been closed from birth, saying:

“Christ the Lord and our teacher, who placed mud upon the eyes of the man born blind and restored his sight (John 9), may he himself enlighten you by his power.”

Then, as soon as the man could see, Paul addressed him in these words:

“Go,” he said to Dionysius, “and tell him that Paul, the servant of Jesus Christ, has sent me to you, so that, mindful of your promise, you may not delay coming to him. There, receiving the baptism of salvation, you may be absolved from all the bonds of sins.”

The man who had received his sight obediently fulfilled the command, and, hastening to Dionysius, reported Paul’s words to him in order.

But Dionysius, already anticipated by the grace of election, looked at the blind man, who now gazed upon him with eyes that had not previously possessed light, and said to him:

“Are you that man whom all his relatives knew to have been born blind?”

He replied:

“I am indeed the one whose eyes, though born blind, have until now never been illumined by the sun. But Paul himself, whose saving commands I bring to you, invoking the power of Jesus Christ, his teacher, granted me the light of health.”

Dionysius immediately arose and, together with his entire household and his wife Damaris—whom his parents had compelled him to marry according to the custom of earthly nobility, because they desired to receive dear offspring—hastened to the command of Saint Paul. Believing faithfully and renouncing the errors of the pagans, he was sprinkled with the water of holy baptism. At last he surrendered himself to be more fully instructed in Paul’s teaching, in the faith of the Holy Trinity, and in the mystery of the incarnation, passion, and resurrection of Jesus Christ our Lord, as well as in all the secrets of ecclesiastical holiness. Thus, as his inseparable companion, he was instructed by blessed Paul for three years, wherever Paul moved his steps.

Returning to Thessalonica in obedience to his teacher, he was ordained bishop of the Athenians by that same blessed apostle Paul. Thereafter, at Paul’s command, he preached the Gospel of Christ, and converted that city and a very large part of his homeland to the faith of the truth.

## CHAPTER IX

During the same period he also wrote to Timothy, bishop of the Ephesians and his fellow disciple. Using a divine pen and thunderous language, he showed himself filled with the word of that same bread by which the angels live. He wrote with distinguished eloquence and reverent, profound understanding concerning the heavenly principate—that is, concerning the orders of angels—as was fitting for one who had placed his mouth in heaven, since, when he spoke of heavenly things, he dwelt there in heart and conduct.

He discussed these matters most fully in the following chapters:

First, that every divine splendor, proceeding variously according to goodness in those who exercise providence, remains simple; and not only this, but also unites those who receive that splendor.

Second, that divine and heavenly things are suitably displayed through symbols of dissimilarity.

Third, what the hierarchy—that is, the sacred principate—is, and what progress is made with respect to the hierarchy.

Fourth, what the designation “angels” signifies.

Fifth, why all heavenly substances are commonly called angels.

Sixth, what is the first adornment of the heavenly substances, what is the middle, and what is the last.

Seventh, concerning the seraphim, cherubim, and thrones, and concerning their first hierarchy—that is, their first sacred principate.

Eighth, concerning the dominions, virtues, and powers, and concerning their middle hierarchy—that is, their sacred principate.

Ninth, concerning the principalities, archangels, and angels, and their final hierarchy—that is, their sacred principate.

Tenth, a repetition and gathering together of the good and angelic choir [order].

Eleventh, why all heavenly powers are commonly called heavenly virtues.

Twelfth, why those who are hierarchs among human beings—that is, sacred princes, namely priests—are called angels.

Thirteenth, why Isaiah is said to be cleansed by a seraph.

Fourteenth, what the number assigned to the angels signifies.

Fifteenth, what the formal images of the angelic virtues are, and what their orders are; what is meant by that which is fiery; and what it means that angels appear in human form. What are those eyes? What are those nostrils? What are those ears? What is that mouth? What are those senses of touch? What are those eyelids? What are those eyebrows? What is that hearing? What are those teeth? What are those shoulders? What are those arms and hands? What is that bone? What are those breasts? What are those backs? What are those feet? What are those wings? What is that nakedness? What is that clothing? What is that most splendid garment? What is that priestly garment? What are the belts? What are those rods? What are those spears? What are those axes? What is that geometrical cord? What are those winds? What are those clouds? What is that bronze? What is that electrum? What are the colors of the different stones? What is the leonine appearance? What is the aquiline appearance? What is the calf-like appearance? What are those horses? What are the differences among the colored horses? What are those rivers? What are the chariots? What are the wheels? What is that which is called the joy of the angels?

## CHAPTER X

He also wrote a second book to the same Timothy concerning the ecclesiastical sacred principate. It was divided into chapters, which follow below. First he placed the most elegant mystical sacrament, and then appended to each chapter the contemplation of the mystical sacraments appropriate to it.

In these writings he shows that everything performed in the ecclesiastical and most sacred consecrations of the mysteries is carried out through angelic ministry, according to the fittingness of each order, together with the ministers of the holy altar and especially the hierarch—that is, the priest—who, in accordance with sacred law, is made one of the angels to perform his work from heaven.

Above all, in the ministry of the sacred sacrifice of the Lord’s passion, the most holy principate of the heavenly host, with its companions, is always present in its own order and office of praise. He also shows this in the consecration of the most holy chrism, which is uniform and of one order in the symbols of the most holy Eucharist. In this initiation of the chrism, he clearly manifests that the order of the seraphim surrounds the gracious Jesus, who, being holy in all things, sanctifies himself for us and fills us with every sanctification, perfect in him and born of God; and that, together with the other angelic choirs, they intelligibly praise our same Lord Jesus Christ with that many-praised hymnody which the prophet describes the seraphim as having heard them proclaim, while they sing “Alleluia” sensibly.

The first division of this book is as follows: the transmission of the ecclesiastical principate, and what its contemplation is. Concerning the things accomplished in the illumination of baptism. Concerning the things accomplished in the bestowal of the Eucharist. Concerning the things accomplished in the chrism and consecrated in it. Concerning priestly perfections. Concerning the perfect orders—that is, monks and those who renounce the world—even after baptism. Concerning the things accomplished in those who sleep.

## CHAPTER XI

He also composed a third volume for the same Timothy, concerning the divine names, which he calls *On Symbolic Theology*. In it he argues with exactness and orthodoxy, as far as is sufficient.

In the first chapter: what the contemplation of the Word is, and what the transmission concerning the divine names is. Concerning united and differentiated theology; what divine union and divine distinction are; what the power of prayer is; and concerning blessed Hierotheus, reverence, and theological composition. In this work he shows that, in the holy city beside the tomb of Jesus, the prince of life, he heard a discussion from James, the brother of the Lord, and Peter, the chief of the apostles, as well as from John the Theologian, together with the aforementioned Hierotheus, holy Timothy, and many other holy brothers. He heard from them the mystery of the faith, as all theologians held it, concerning the divinity and humanity of the Lord and Savior. In what follows, he also demonstrates—suppressing his name—that blessed Paul was present among them.

Concerning goodness, light, the good, desire, ecstasy, and zeal; and that evil neither exists nor belongs to what exists, nor is it in existing things. In this chapter, asserting that the desire of blessed Ignatius must also be understood with reference to the good, he recalls him with praise and reverence as writing in a certain place:

“‘My desire,’ he says, ‘has been crucified,” intending the Lord Jesus.

[Note: Others translate it, “My love has been crucified.”]

He also inserts no few chapters from the aforementioned Hierotheus against the philosophers. In these, arguing about evil through twisted syllogisms, he constrains them so thoroughly that they can turn aside in neither direction, nor go back behind them, nor direct themselves elsewhere, except where he himself compels them to stumble.

Concerning being and paradigms. In this section he sharply rebukes the opinion of the philosopher Clymis [reading uncertain]. Concerning life; and in this section he refutes the madness of Simon Magus and drives his contentious arguments away from the divine choir.

Concerning wisdom, mind, word, truth, and faith. Concerning virtue, justice, salvation, redemption, and inequality. There he strikes Elymas the Magus (Acts 13) with a two-edged sword, saying:

“If God is almighty, how is it said that he is unable to do something?”

He also pierces Paul, who was making accusations, with a syllogistic needle, and pierces and crushes his heart and brain—that is, his understanding and perception.

Concerning the greater and the lesser; concerning the same and the other; concerning the similar and the dissimilar; concerning stability, motion, and equality; concerning the almighty; concerning the Ancient of Days; concerning the age and time; concerning peace; what it means that something is called “the same”; what life itself and virtue itself are; and what the other such expressions mean.

Concerning the Holy of holies, the King of kings, and the Lord of lords. Concerning the God of gods. Concerning the perfect and the one.

## CHAPTER XII

He also composed for the same Timothy an epitome, arranged by chapters, concerning mystical theology: through *kataphasis*, that is, affirmation; through *apophasis*, that is, negation; and through hypothetical—that is, conditional—syllogisms. Transcending by understanding all sensible and intelligible things, both those on earth and those in heaven, and proceeding as far as is possible and permitted to a mortal, he penetrated into the sanctuary of divinity itself.

For this reason Dionysius has since then, and still today, been called by the wise men of the Greeks **πτερύγιον τοῦ οὐρανοῦ**, which Latin speech explains as “the wing of heaven.” For, flying there through spiritual understanding and the grace of a most reverent revelation, he learned not only the manifold, magnificent mysteries and ministries of the holy spirits, but also tasted with the palate of his heart the savor of the eternal Godhead. From this he poured forth these things in writings for human knowledge.

In the first chapter of this book he says that blessed Bartholomew the apostle made known to him how he ought to understand theology and the holy Gospel. He began this skillfully and defined it by inserting into his writings the apostle’s words, brief but exceedingly profound.

In the second chapter he taught how it is necessary to be united and to offer hymns to the cause of all things and to that which is above all.

In the third, what belongs to kataphatic—that is, affirmative—theology, and what belongs to apophatic—that is, negative—theology.

In the fourth, that the transcendent cause of every sensible thing is none of the sensible things.

In the fifth, that the transcendent cause of every intelligible thing is none of the intelligible things.

## CHAPTER XIII

He also wrote a letter to Gaius, expounding through propositions how God is known by a certain ignorance, and how he was seen by those who are recorded to have seen him; and how he is understood in some manner through a gift that makes one good and divine. He explained that not only the ministry of Christ’s divinity but also that of his humanity remains secret in speech and unknown to understanding.

He explained how Jesus, who is above all things, was substantially established among human beings, and how, according to human nature and from the substance of human beings, he was substantially constituted, as the virgin showed by giving birth in a transcendent manner, and as unstable water showed by sustaining material and earthly weight. He explained that gracious Jesus did not perform divine things only according to God, nor human things only according to humanity; but that, God having become man, he made known to us a certain new divine-human operation.

He also sent letters to Dorotheus, a minister, making known that the divine darkness is the inaccessible light in which God is said to dwell, and in which everyone worthy of knowing and seeing him in this body is found.

In a brief letter he admonished the priest Sosipater not to judge his good deeds, when they had not been made manifest, to have been neglected, and urged him to avoid contention over words.

## CHAPTER XIV

He also sent a letter, almost apologetic in character, to Polycarp, bishop of the Smyrnaeans and specifically a disciple of the blessed apostle John. He indicated that stubborn contradictors of the truth, though often rebuked, should be avoided to some extent.

At the same time he accused the Greeks of attempting, through the wisdom received from God, to draw out divine worship while using divine things in an unholy manner, and of striving, through the great vanity of poets, to impose servitude upon the creature rather than upon the Creator.

He therefore mentions Apollophanius the sophist, a worshiper of the sun, and advises Saint Polycarp concerning him.
