He recalls the miracle performed in the sun under Hezekiah, to which that same Apollophanius refused to give credence. So that Polycarp might be unable to resist his admonition, he instructs him to remember with Apollophanius the sign of darkness that occurred at the Savior’s crucifixion, and the wondrous advance and retreat of that darkness from west to east, as they had both seen while living in the city of Heliopolis. He also adds the words that Apollophanius had often spoken to him at that time, as will be explained more fully below in the letter addressed to him.

For a fuller knowledge of the events, we have decided to append that letter here. It reads as follows:

“An address to Apollophanius, my intimate and fellow philosopher.

“Now my speech is directed to you, my innermost love, recalling to you many anguished cares concerning you, and, with a gentle mind, reproaching you for the long-standing persistence of the foolish frivolity known to you. I mock the fanatical phantoms of your illusions, while worshiping with the greatest reverence and diligence the supernatural transformation brought about by the magnificent goodness of God. To you, now rightly repentant, the part of my soul, I offer my rejoicing, and I shall address you concerning your own contempt, so that I may again commend to you those things whose knowledge you formerly despised.

“Very frequently and carefully I explained to you, as Moses relates, that the Lord made the human being from clay, and that his transgressions were cleansed by the flood. I then explained that he was received into friendship, and that the Lord performed many great deeds for him and in him in Egypt and during his journey of departure; and that he produced many kinds of theologians, through whose foreknowledge God was pleased to become incarnate from a virgin.

“In reply, you often sent me word not only that you were utterly ignorant of the truth of these things, but also that you did not know who this Moses was. You rejected the Gospel of Jesus Christ, the fullness of God’s majesty, which you called mine. You refused to accept Paul, a wanderer throughout the world and a sower of words, from material things to immaterial things. Rather, by refuting me, you urged me to unlearn the things upon which I relied, saying that I had degenerated by abandoning the laws of my ancestral religion and had transferred myself into sacrilegious wickedness. You urged me either to abandon those things upon which I depended or, after leaving them behind [or: erasing them], to be content with what was mine and not to disparage the divine powers or the laws of our fathers.

“But when the light from above determined to make the splendor of the Father’s glory shine into the darkness of your mind, it poured into the innermost chamber of my heart the memory of how, when we were nearly the same age at Heliopolis, I spent almost twenty-five years living there with you. It happened that, on a certain Friday, at about the sixth hour—almost the sixth hour—the sun was horribly darkened, as the moon moved in front of it. For the sun, which is not God but God’s creature, could not shine when its own light had set.

“I complained to you and asked what, most learned one, you thought of this. Your answer was so firmly fixed in the heart of my mind that it cannot be scraped away by any oblivion or erased by any image of death.

“When the whole world had been uniformly obscured and was wasting away in the gloom of darkness, and the sun’s disk returned as though cleansed, we took up the rule of Philip of Aridaeus [reading uncertain]. When we discovered what was already most familiar—that the sun ought not to suffer such distress through the force of an eclipse, and that the moon, covering the solar radiance with Ethiopian veils from the east, normally sought to seize it at the western horizon—then, although the moon was absent and the time of conjunction was not approaching, the treasuries of light, concealing the darkness they had produced, seemed to carry it as far as the boundaries of Ilium [or: Italy; reading uncertain] and to hide it in the West.

“Then I said to you, the sanctuary of immense learning, still ignorant of the mystery of so great a matter: ‘What, Apollophanius, mirror of learning, do you ascribe to these secrets?’

“To this you replied, not in the language of human understanding but, as though under a divine omen:

“‘These, good Dionysius, are the recompenses of divine things.’

“Finally, when I discovered that the day and year of that Friday corresponded with the proclamation that Paul sounded into our attentive ears, with signs crying out in agreement, I surrendered myself to the truth and was released from the bonds of falsehood. How ineffably I extol it and bring it to you! It is both the way and the life, and it is the true light that enlightens every person coming into the world (John 1). To it at last, as one truly wise, you yielded; you yielded to life when you renounced death. You will do well to cling to it, when you are joined more closely with us hereafter.

“That one is he who is” [Note: He alludes to the words of Exodus, “He who is sent me,” and likewise, “I am who I am.”]. With his radiance I used to blind you, when you were accustomed to darken the inner chambers here and there with multicolored and manifold cosmetics, and to obscure them with sharpened darts.

“For, as you confessed, the knowledge of him whom you longed to know deliciously echoed upon the palate of your mind; yet, disdaining him, you refused to let him take up residence in the belly of your knowledge.

“Therefore, if you now bear a knowing and provident heart, receive him, so that you may not fear on behalf of those who do not exist what truly is. Be more obstinate in testing falsehood than you were in resisting the truth that our prayers urged upon you.

“Thus, by Jesus, my being and my life, I shall now die joyful, when you yourself live in him.’”

## CHAPTER XV

He likewise wrote a very useful letter to Demophilus, severely rebuking him for having prevented the reception of one who had apostatized from the faith. It is fragrant with examples and testimonies of Scripture, like a garland gathered from a field full of sacred Scripture, which the Lord has blessed.

Whenever the occasion required him to use the name of the Lord and Savior, he calls him “the gracious one.” Anyone who reads this letter attentively will perceive, to no small degree, what sort of graciousness and mercy Jesus the Lord possesses, insofar as it is possible for a human being to know; and he will understand with what confidence a person ought, after a fall if one should occur, to return to the gracious one.

In it he also demonstrates fully enough the order, excellence, and authority of the ecclesiastical ministers and of the priests. To this he appends the following—not, I would say, a fable, but a spiritual event spiritually accomplished. For the benefit of those who read these things, into whose hands the complete text of the letters may perhaps not come, we have decided to relate it here.

After many other things he says:

“‘We do not have a high priest who cannot sympathize with our weaknesses, but he himself, innocent and merciful, will not break forth or cry out. For he is gentle and the propitiation for our sins.

“‘Therefore, O Demophilus, we will not accept your zealous impulses, even if you take up Phinehas and Elijah ten thousand times over, when we hear what was pleasing and displeasing to gracious Jesus from his disciples, who, during their dwelling in the flesh, shared in his gentle and gracious spirit.

“‘The ignorant must be taught, not tortured. Just as we do not torture the blind, but lead them by the hand, so the gracious one seeks the person who has gone astray, calls the one who has fled, and, having scarcely found him, carries him upon his shoulders.

“‘He eagerly joins himself to those who flee and does not disdain to be disdained by those who reject him. He endures those who provoke him without cause and excuses them himself. Indeed, he promises to heal them. He goes before those who approach him and meets them; embracing them all completely, he kisses them, and he does not accuse them or reproach them for their former deeds. Rather, he loves what is present, celebrates a feast, and calls together his friends—namely, the gracious angels—so that it may be the dwelling place of all who rejoice.

“‘Therefore, all who begin to act wickedly or to do good join themselves, through their goodness or wickedness, to those spirits whose will they begin to do. The latter, disciples and companions of the gracious angels, consign their blessed ends to the ever-existing mirror, where they will always be with God—which is the greatest of all good things. The former, however, will fall away even here from divine and perpetual peace, and after death will be with their familiar demons.

“‘Therefore ought we not, through abundant goodness and mercy, to become and remain with the gracious God, and to be separated from the evils that make us unjust?’

“And shortly afterward:

“‘If you wish,’ he said, ‘I shall recount to you a divine vision of a certain holy man, which you will not mock. For I shall speak the truth.

“‘When I was once near Crete, Saint Carpus received me as a guest. If any other man could be compared with him, he was most worthy of divine visions because of the great purity of his mind. He did not begin the sacred consecrations of the mysteries unless a favorable vision from above had first been shown to him while he was praying before the offering of the most holy sacrifice.

“‘As we were discussing certain matters with one another, he himself told me that he had been greatly saddened by one of the unbelievers. The cause of his sadness was that, while the unbelievers were celebrating their festivals, this unbeliever had led a certain faithful man astray from gracious Jesus our Lord.

“‘I consoled him and advised him that it would be appropriate for him to ask for divine clemency on behalf of those people. Receiving assistance from God the Savior, he should convert the unbeliever, overcome the apostate through graciousness, and not cease urging them to convert even to this day, thus leading them into divine knowledge.

“‘But he could not bear this patiently. Wasting away with great agitation and bitterness—I do not know in what manner—he went to sleep, troubled by this matter, for it was evening.

“‘Around midnight—for he was accustomed at that time to awaken for the divine hymns—he arose from sleep. Tormented by excessive agitation, he stood for prayer without blessing himself. He was grieving and burdened beyond measure, saying that it was unjust for men who were without God and perverted the straight ways of the Lord to live.

“‘As he said these things, he asked the Lord to send heavenly fire and mercilessly destroy them both. When he had said this, he was immediately carried away in spirit. He said that it seemed to him that he suddenly saw the house in which he was standing shaken and divided from the roof down the middle into two parts, so that he remained beneath the open sky.

“‘He also saw a funeral pyre blazing with much fire and descending all the way to him; and the entire heaven itself set ablaze. In the southern region he saw gracious Jesus seated upon a throne, with an immeasurable number of angels standing before him in human form.

“‘Seeing these things from above and wondering at them, Carpus bent downward and saw the earth opened by a dreadful chasm, with a dark abyss gaping open. The same men concerning whom he had been troubled stood before him on the slippery edge of the darkest abyss, trembling and exceedingly miserable. They had not yet been thrown down from the unstable slope on which they were staggering and collapsing.

“‘From below in the abyss he saw horrible serpents crawling and placing themselves around their feet, sometimes dragging them, wrapping themselves around them, and tormenting them at the same time. At other times the same serpents dragged them with their teeth and tore at those same men, who were being consumed by heavenly fire; they tried to pull them into the abyss from which they themselves had emerged.

“‘He also saw certain men in the midst of the serpents, making a tumult with their voices, striking and pushing those who were being tormented into the abyss. Likewise, it seemed to him that other men had approached them, wishing these wretched people to be tormented briefly and make satisfaction; but those who were striking and pushing them did not wish this.

“‘While Carpus was concentrating on what he had seen below and neglecting the heavenly things he had previously seen, he began to grow weary and cease paying attention, because the men were no longer falling into the depth of the chasm. Moreover, he had cursed them without mercy. Then he looked upward and said that he could scarcely see the sky again.

“‘But he saw gracious Jesus taking pity on the sinners who were being tormented. Jesus rose from the heavenly throne and descended all the way to them, stretching out his gracious hand to those placed in torment. Immediately the multitudes of angels who had descended with him seized them on both sides where they stood while being tormented, at the moment when gracious Jesus extended his hand to them, and they rescued them.

“‘Then Jesus turned to Carpus and said to him:

“‘“Carpus, strike these people with the hand you have raised against them, and do not withdraw it out of mercy. Strike against me, for I am ready to suffer again in order to save human beings once more, and I take greater pleasure in them than in other human beings who have not sinned.

“‘“Nevertheless, consider whether it would be better for you to exchange dwellings with the serpents in the abyss, or to be with me and with the gracious and humane angels.”

“‘These are the things that I heard, and I believe them to be true.’”

These things were spoken to Demophilus.

## CHAPTER XVI

To Titus, who asked by letter what the house of wisdom is, what its cup is, what its foods are, and what its drink is, he responds with great clarity and eloquence.

Although brief, his letter to the apostle and evangelist John, exiled on the island of Patmos, is nevertheless consolatory and prophetic, distinguished by the charm of its language and the dignity of its meaning. In it he foretold, as he had learned from God, that John would still return from that exile and preach the Gospel in Asia.

We have also judged it worthy to insert the letter here into the account of these events. It begins as follows:

“To John the Theologian, apostle and evangelist, appointed and entrusted to the island of Patmos.

“Most beloved, I regard the sacred soul as something especially precious to me among the apostles. Hail, truly most beloved, from one beloved, desired, dear, and greatly loved.

“What wonder is it if Christ spoke the truth, and if his wicked persecutors drive his disciples from the cities? They do things worthy of themselves, since the wicked separate themselves from the holy. Yet, by driving them away and separating them, they present from visible things an image of invisible realities.

“Nor will God be blamed in the ages to come for just separations, when the impious have made themselves separate from the righteous, and we see the pious already made one with God there.

“Since they are lovers of the truth, they withdraw from the desire for material things and, freed from the desire for every evil, love the divine peace and sanctification of all good things. They begin the future life from the present, living fittingly and angelically among human beings, with every affection of the soul, divine invocation, and graciousness, together with the other good things.

“Therefore let this not disturb you, as though you suspected that you did not suffer, and as though you judged only the sufferings of the body. I do not believe that you feel them. Concerning those who act wickedly toward you and unjustly determine your fate, I fittingly invoke the sun of the Gospel.

“Leaving these matters aside, I desire to join you to us, since you bring yourselves toward the good, and to make you participants in the light. No adversity will deprive us of John’s most splendid ray.

“For now I appeal to the memory and renewal of your true theology. Shortly afterward, even if I speak boldly, I say that you yourselves will be united with me.

“I am altogether capable of announcing this to you, learning it from God and saying: you will be released from the prison of Patmos and will return to the land of Asia. There you will practice imitations of the gracious God and hand them on to those who will come after you.”

## CHAPTER XVII

[Note: See Baronius, year 109.]

Moreover, he produced many works, both volumes and letters addressed to various people. Like a river of mystical eloquence and as an oracle of the Holy Spirit, he foretold with exceptional labor and true philosophical instruction the overthrow of pagan errors, the destruction of the knots of their syllogisms, the emptying of the worship of idols, and the commendation of the blessedness of the heavenly homeland and the immortality of eternal life. Their magnificent excellence seems to exceed the smallness of our understanding.

He also wrote many things which undoubtedly remain hidden from our joy.

While Paul was in Rome, and afterward, following his first defense in the western regions, just as he himself had foretold, the precious and eloquent Dionysius—who by homeland was Ionian, but who, because of his great holiness, was called by the Christian surname Macarius, which means “blessed”—strove with abundant care to water the Lord’s sheep planted by his teacher, lest, after the teacher’s departure, ravenous wolves that spare not the flock should attack them.

Therefore, passing through neighboring and distant cities, preaching, converting peoples to the faith, strengthening the faithful in the word, and healing those oppressed by various illnesses, he withdrew as far as Troas for the sake of the Gospel. He remained for some time in those regions.

Several years later, when he was staying with Pelio of the Lacedaemonians and learned through widespread report that Peter and Paul, the chief apostles, were being held at Rome—Peter in prison and Paul in chains for a second time—he returned to Athens. Having appointed a bishop in his place, he entrusted the people to him. Then, scattering the seeds of the word through the neighboring parishes, he served diligently until he reached Rome, accompanied by certain officials whom he had taken as his companions.

Thus, as a son of Achaea by fortune and a learned architect, he devoted himself to the greatness of the Roman Church, while by no means abandoning Greece, where the memory of his teaching and miracles remains.

For, driven forward by his great love for the apostles and his desire for martyrdom, he hastened along the road to Rome, so that, if Christ so willed, he might die together with them. But divine providence and the exceedingly mad insanity of a diabolical man forestalled his wishes.

For when the most impious Nero had loosened the reins of his empire on land and sea, and when, amid the accumulation of his other wickednesses, the success of excessive pleasure had caused the frenzy of his cruelty to boil over in dreadful rage against Christ’s servants, in the fourteenth year of his reign—before blessed Dionysius reached Rome—he sent the holy apostles of God to heaven, one by the trophy of the cross and the other by execution with the sword, drenched in blessed blood and deemed worthy of the glory of martyrdom.

[Note: Baronius teaches that Peter and Paul suffered martyrdom in the thirteenth year of Nero, in the year 69 of Christ.]

Then, bringing his life to an end by a dreadful death, as his life itself had been, he was soon destined for the underworld.

## CHAPTER XVIII

[Col. 0038D]

Finally, when precious Dionysius, with Christ as his guide, entered within the walls of the Roman citadel, he found that the necessity of the faith and the evident opening of a door among the peoples through whom he had passed had detained him for some time. He found blessed Clement already governing the summit of the holy and supreme apostolic see.

As soon as they were able to greet one another, the same glorious Dionysius, archbishop of the Athenians and servant of the Lord, was received by him with due honor. Because of the reverence owed to his holiness and learning, as well as because of their earlier fraternal bond, Dionysius was held in a place of the greatest veneration.

Living with Clement for some time in the closest familiarity, both through mutual conversation concerning apostolic decrees and through the sweetness of spiritual affection, they bound themselves to one another with the ties of immeasurable love.

But when almighty God wished, through the most splendid and eastern ray of the true Sun—namely, the Lord Jesus Christ, in the person of the most holy Dionysius—to illumine the western darkness by his grace, and foresaw that the strongest wall of unbelief, which had occupied nearly the whole of Gaul and Germany beyond hope of repair, should be destroyed by such a battering ram; and when he wished paganism to be pierced by the dart of such consummate eloquence, and all this Gaul to be raised up through the apostolate of Dionysius, since it was known to be miserably enslaved to the demonic service of Mercury, he touched the heart of blessed Clement and kindled him to address precious Dionysius in words of this kind.

## CHAPTER XIX
You see, said Saint Clement, my dearest brother Macarius Dionysius, how great is the harvest of the Lord’s sowing, and how few are the laborers. Since, therefore, you have been sufficiently instructed in every aspect of catholic piety and thoroughly strengthened in every Christian virtue and religious discipline, go in the name of the Lord, entering the regions of the West, and, like a good soldier of Christ, wage the battles of the Lord your God. And just as the Lord Jesus Christ entrusted to my teacher Peter—and I received by right of sacred inheritance—the divine power by which you may always be supported in the authority of binding and loosing, so, accompanied by our prayers and strengthened by the intercessions of the holy apostles, receive all Gaul within the portion of your apostleship, by our apostolic authority. Do the work of an evangelist; fulfill your ministry, so that, through you, knowledge of Christ may be spread everywhere and you may deserve to hear from the Lord on the day of recompense: “Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your Lord.” And do not fear the multitude and ferocity of the barbarian people, knowing for certain that whoever labors more will receive the greater reward.

He also assigned to him several tested men as companions and fellow ministers of the word, and said to him: “As the Lord was with our lords, fathers, and teachers, his apostles Peter and Paul, so may he be with you in everything, wherever you turn. Be strong, for you will bring an immense and innumerable multitude of people into the true promised land of the children of Israel.” And, giving peace to all, he released them to depart in this fellowship of true brotherhood.

## CHAPTER XX

They hastened on together, preaching the Lord in every direction, and arrived at the harbor of the city of Arles. From there, after sending certain men to the regions where they were needed, as he judged appropriate, Macarius Dionysius—the man who, by the privilege of the apostolic see, when blessed Clement, successor of the apostle Peter, entrusted it to him, had received the seeds of the divine word to distribute among the Gallic peoples—following the example of the most blessed prince of the apostles and his master, who had plunged himself into Roman cruelty for the name of Jesus Christ, went fearlessly and armed with the fervor of faith to wherever he knew the error of paganism to be raging most fiercely among the Gauls. Under the Lord’s guidance he reached Lutetia of the Parisians, and, renowned for his teaching, shining with miracles and signs of virtue—which he had learned from the teacher of the Athenians, Paul—he ministered to Gaul.

He did not fear to confront the savagery of the unbelieving people, because the memory of former punishments strengthened his courage: having experienced many torments, he knew that he would finally attain life through death. Nevertheless, with all his desire he longed that he who was already a perfected confessor of Christ’s name amid many lashes of torment might, through the penalty of death, deserve also to become a martyr.

At that time the aforesaid city of the Parisians flourished as a royal seat, a meeting-place of Gauls and Germans, and a center of nobility. Its air was healthful, its river pleasant, its soil fertile, its woods rich in trees, and its vineyards abundant. It was crowded with people and filled with commerce and varied traffic, while the river’s waters flowed around it. Among its many advantages, the riverbed also supplied the inhabitants with a great abundance of fish.

## CHAPTER XXI

Therefore the servant of God chose this place as one to be sought out. When he first approached it fearlessly, armed with faith and strengthened by steadfast confession, he addressed a certain Lisbius, a most distinguished man of the city of Paris, who had believed in the Lord Jesus Christ through his preaching and faithfully adhered to him, saying:

“Most illustrious man, since now, through the working of the grace of Jesus Christ our Lord, a very great multitude of people is being consecrated in belief and confession of his holy name by the blessing of baptism, and the number of the faithful increases daily, it seems to me that I should receive from your fraternity, at a price, the field belonging to your secretary, build there a baptismal house, and receive the divine charisms.”

Lisbius replied: “Most blessed father, I offer it freely to the Lord Jesus Christ through your holiness.”

Blessed Dionysius answered: “No, we must not act in this way in such a matter. For our God and Lord Jesus Christ, working through the Holy Spirit, was born from blessed Mary, ever-virgin, for our salvation, when he himself had made the world, in a rented lodging. Therefore it does not seem right that, having received the field for nothing, I should prepare a house in which, through our ministry, his adopted sons may be reborn. Moreover, the burial of captives has been purchased from its price. It is therefore reasonable that I should take the place at a price where those who, through the commerce of his blood and by passing through death, have been baptized and redeemed from the captivity of the devil and everlasting death may be buried. You, however, will distribute the payment for it to Christ’s poor—you who have devotedly offered yourself to him.”

## CHAPTER XXII

When these things had been accomplished, and with the help of almighty God always accompanying him in everything and everywhere, he built there, according to the measure of his strength and as a newcomer was able, a church in honor of our Lord Jesus Christ, whose name was not yet known in those places and among those peoples. According to custom, he established the offices of clerics devotedly serving the Lord, and advanced approved persons to the honor of the second order, ceaselessly restoring to the Creator the peoples whom he had recalled from the deviant worship of the creature.

Thus girded with the faith and devotion of the people, which he saw in the construction and reverent attendance of the basilica, and greatly strengthened by it, he did not cease to make known to the nations God and our Lord Jesus Christ, whom he knew with a pure heart and loved with the ardor of his soul. Presenting to everyone his mercy in the present time and the judgment to come, he gradually joined to God those whom he was rescuing from the devil. With every effort of exhortation and by prodigies of signs, he strove to make those whom he was snatching from the world worthy of heaven.

For the Lord deigned to perform such great works of power through him that he won the hearts of rebellious pagans no less by miracles than by preaching. And whenever the priests of idols stirred up sedition among the people against him—so that countless multitudes, even from neighboring regions, came in groups with weapons and military equipment to destroy the faithful who had already believed in Christ through him, wherever they heard that he was—no sooner could they see him than such an ineffable light of heavenly grace shone in him that either, laying aside all their ferocity together with their weapons, they prostrated themselves before him, or, if they had not yet been pierced by the gift of the Holy Spirit so as to believe, they melted away in extreme fear and fled terrified from his presence.

In a wondrous manner, an armed multitude could not resist an unarmed man; rather, the Gallic cothurnus and German stubbornness alike submitted themselves eagerly to him and asked that Christ’s easy yoke be placed upon them. The idols that had been fashioned at their expense and by their efforts were themselves destroyed by them; and, having found the harbor of salvation, they rejoiced at the shipwreck of their idols. The portion conquered from the devil also mourned, while the victorious legion of the Church triumphed over it.

## CHAPTER XXIII

Then the ancient enemy, seeing that what was known to prosper through the Lord by the continual conversion of peoples was perishing for him, turned the entire machinery of his craft toward attacking what had been built. Therefore he instructed the leaders of his faction—who were mourning the exile of their gods, and whom he had armed for the impious persecution of those who preached that the one true God, the Lord Jesus Christ with the Father and the Holy Spirit, must be worshiped and feared—and likewise against those who had received this faith of salvation with devoted hearts.

Since, because of the multitude of the faithful, they could not accomplish what they had wickedly desired, he furnished them with this cunning device of his art, by which they might attain their wish: they were to report to Domitian, who after Nero, the son of perdition, had carried out the second persecution against Christians, that the power and proclamation of the holy man’s preaching had already spread far and wide, so that he might quickly take measures for the reverence of their gods, which, as they claimed, was already being abolished even from human memory by a certain Dionysius, an invincible sorcerer and magician, and by his followers.

When Domitian, that monstrous beast of the most savage cruelty, heard this, he burned with such rage of indignation that wherever he found any Christian, whether in person or through his agents, he either forced him to sacrifice to the obscene gods or, after imposing various punishments, handed him over to the sword for execution.

Moreover, throughout the whole world subject to him, a public edict was posted in every city, town, municipality, and village, ordering those serving in official positions to hasten to expose all lovers of Christ’s name to every variety of punishment, so that no one might remain who could acquire what was being destroyed.

## CHAPTER XXIV

When the decree of persecution had been published, the rejoicing crowd of wicked men advanced in frenzy into every part of the world and conspired to fight against the Lord’s people. They did not hesitate to attack with the sword those whom the Lord had shown to be his own by the sign of faith. Consequently, no tranquility of the present life was now granted to those fighting for Christ, and no liberty of the holy martyrs was spared. All, alas, either obeyed the impious commands or endured what had been decreed by the most savage emperor.

Accordingly, the prefect Fescennius Sisinnius was dispatched, accompanied by a select official retinue, with immense clamor to the regions of the West. He was to search wherever he could find the holy old man, the renowned man of learning and foremost in the signs of his virtues, Macarius Dionysius, and either compel him by the emperor’s decree to burn incense to idols or, after tearing him apart with immense tortures and inflicting the most elaborate punishments, to strike him with an axe—according to Roman law—since he had flourished in outstanding earthly nobility and had acted against the decrees of the Senate and the Republic and against imperial authority. He was to be stripped naked, publicly beaten with rods, and struck with the axe.

## CHAPTER XXV

When the aforesaid Fescennius Sisinnius and his fellow soldiers had received the emperor’s command, they entered the borders of Gaul in search of Macarius Dionysius. While they were still far away, the holy man’s famous name became known to them. They were therefore still more enraged and, with faster movement, swelling hearts, and savage faces, approached Paris. There they found blessed Dionysius fighting against unbelievers and continually exhorting a multitude of people to the faith by his preaching.

With him the persecutors’ savage fury also encountered the blessed man Rusticus, archpresbyter, and Eleutherius, archdeacon, whom the servant of the Lord himself had consecrated in their orders as fellow ministers of preaching and divine service.

These holy men never endured being absent from the presence of the most blessed Dionysius. Divine favor already knew them to be destined to share in the eternal kingdom, and the persecution of the fiery tempest, through the contests of martyrdom, could not separate them from one another by any artifice of its cunning or severity.

At last the arrival of the prefect Fescennius Sisinnius, with a retinue of Roman soldiers, suddenly resounded throughout the city of Paris and the entire region. The leading men of the cities of Gaul came out to meet him, and the imperial order concerning the capture of the holy bishop Macarius Dionysius was urgently and publicly proclaimed with full authority.

## CHAPTER XXVI

Because the Lord Jesus Christ had determined to wash away, in the fountain of his own blood, the labors of his most holy old servant, who had long struggled, so that, freed from the burden of the flesh and made white beyond snow, he might stand more freely in the Lord’s presence—and so that he who was offering himself as a fragrant holocaust might continually offer a sacrifice of praise—he was seen by an almost innumerable crowd of demonic men. The Lord’s saint was captured, mocked, cruelly bound with exceedingly hard thongs, dragged away, and brought, together with holy Rusticus the archpresbyter and his archdeacon Eleutherius, before the prefect.

The prefect addressed him with excessive severity, saying:

“Are you that utterly infamous old man who is said to be Dionysius the Ionian and is surnamed Macarius, who even abolishes the worship of our gods and despises the decrees of the invincible emperor?”

Blessed Dionysius replied:

“I am indeed old in body, but through the fervor of devotion and faith and through the saving confession of my Lord and Savior Jesus Christ I remain forever new. I do not cease, without deceit, to nourish with rational milk those newly begotten for him through the ministry of my preaching, whom the font of holy baptism brings forth for him. I also preserve, by innocent conduct and a pure heart, the commands of that prince who truly is invincible.”

The prefect said: “Tell me, then, whose divinity you profess to worship and of what condition you declare yourself to be.”

Then the three most blessed men—Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius—thus inspired by the gift of the Holy Spirit and inflamed by zeal for the faith, although only one had been questioned, gave their answer in one voice and with the same words, as though speech proceeded from the mouth of a single man:

“By this it is manifest that we are most genuine Christians: we believe with the heart, confess with the mouth, and worship through pious action the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, one God and Lord, so that in the perfect Trinity there is both the fullness of divinity and the unity of power.

“We faithfully preach our Lord Jesus Christ, one person of that same holy Trinity, God before the ages of the world, and true man, made for the salvation of human beings from blessed Mary, ever-virgin, at the end of the ages; who suffered, died, and was buried, was raised from the dead, and sits at the right hand of the Father’s majesty in the heights, above every heavenly principality and power; who will come to judge the living and the dead, and the age, which will be changed for the better through fire.”

Then the prefect said:

“I have not been ordered to discuss any of these matters with you, especially since it has become known throughout almost the whole Roman world that, despite your decrepit and wretched old age, you possess excessive eloquence, evasive profundity of speech, and an ability beyond human nature to seduce the people, together with magical tricks. We have heard enough of this in Rome. Tell me only whether you intend to obey the commands of the great emperor Domitian and revere the laws of the immortal gods. If not, I shall fight you manfully—not with a contest of words, but of blows.”

## CHAPTER XXVII

While these things were taking place and the prefect and the Lord’s saints were being questioned, a noble matron of an illustrious family, named Larcia, arrived with a large retinue. She addressed the prefect, saying that her husband Lisbius had been mentally captivated by the magical arts of Dionysius the Ionian, surnamed Macarius, and had joined himself to his transgressions.

Lisbius was immediately sought, found, and brought in. When the prefect pronounced the sentence of death, he received it in confession of Christ’s name and was transferred to eternal life.

The Lord’s saints, however, were handed over to the torturers and led to the places of punishment. In the presence of the holy Rusticus and Eleutherius, so that fear of the torments might make them abandon their purpose, their precious commander and the Lord’s strongest athlete, Dionysius, was stripped. Naked over his entire body, he was flogged in turn by three groups of three soldiers, but was not conquered.

Amid the crackling of the blows he did not cease to praise God and urge his fellow soldiers to prepare themselves undefeated for such things, nor to preach to all the faithful that they should be strengthened in the Lord’s faith, saying:

“My mouth shall speak the praise of the Lord, and let every flesh bless his holy name, because I have been judged worthy to bear the marks of Christ’s passion in my body for the confession of him. This is your glory, O faithful men and most beloved brothers. Therefore see to it that you do not fail amid my tribulations; rather, let your hearts be armed, and be most ready to offer your bodies to similar things for the love of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

## CHAPTER XXVIII

Rusticus and Eleutherius were also flogged with great severity, and the holy men were loaded together with an immense weight of chains and thrust into a dungeon of the darkest prison.

From there they were brought again before the prefect’s tribunal, stretched upon the racks, and flogged, yet they gave thanks to the Lord.

Then Dionysius, the most blessed and acceptable sacrifice to the Lord, was stretched naked before the eyes of his companions upon an iron bed with flames placed beneath it. He sang, saying:

“Your word is greatly refined, O Lord, and your servant has loved it. Therefore, Lord Jesus Christ, power and wisdom of God the Father Almighty, who said, ‘When you pass through fire, the flames shall not harm you,’ and who gave me the more perilous fire to conquer in my desires, grant that, to the glory of your name, I may also overcome this burning.” And when his whole body had been scorched, he was lifted up and thrown to most ferocious beasts, driven into frenzy by prolonged fasting. When he saw them rushing toward him with the greatest force, he made the sign of the cross against them and, looking up to heaven, said: “You, Lord, who are always the same, be present with me now, exercising the same power that you mercifully granted to your servant Daniel in the den.” But when the beasts reached him, they fell down before him most gently.

Huge fires were also prepared in furnaces, and the man of God, Saint Dionysius, armed with the banner of the holy cross, was thrown into them. He said:

“Here too, Lord Jesus Christ, you will not fail me, so that I may emerge unharmed from this symbolic burning of everlasting torment. By the dew of your Holy Spirit extinguish these fires, the seats of my faith, just as you extinguished the flaming sword guarding paradise, giving your faithful passage to life through the liquid of your blood.”

## CHAPTER XXIX

Meanwhile the holy men Rusticus and Eleutherius, weeping and hastening with eager desire toward similar punishments, were led away in chains rather than released.

When, at his prayer, the fire of the furnace had been extinguished and the blessed bishop of the Lord, Dionysius, had emerged more radiant than gold, he was hung upon a cross-shaped gallows, fastened there by the piercing of instruments of torture. From there he continued to preach to all who watched that Jesus Christ was the true Lord. After being tortured for a long time without dying, he was taken down, and the three chosen servants of the Lord were confined together with a multitude of the faithful in the prison of Glaucinus.

The righteous were led by those bound by crime; those condemned were led by the condemned; and the innocent were delivered up by the guilty.

There, after many and most necessary exhortations to the people who, following him, had broken into the prison, and after instructions addressed to those absent, he celebrated the solemnity of the Lord’s Mass, so that the faithful might be strengthened by participation in the Lord’s body and blood, as though he were already placed in heaven.

At the hour when the holy bread was broken, by which he and the people were to communicate, a light of such kind shone from heaven upon him and all who were present that none of them had ever seen anything like it before. Within it the Lord Jesus Christ appeared to him, also visible to all who were granted the sight, together with a multitude of angels. Taking the holy bread, he gave it to him, saying:

“Receive this, my dear one, which I shall soon complete for you together with my Father, because your reward is exceedingly great with me, and salvation in my kingdom awaits those who will hear you. Now act courageously, and your memory shall be in praise. The love and kindness that you always possess will obtain whatever you ask for anyone.”

Larcia, the woman mentioned above, was present at the mystery of this terrible and wondrous spectacle, although she was still motivated by pagan curiosity and yet attentive to the miracles.

## CHAPTER XXX

When these things had also been completed, executioners arrived. They brought the servants of Christ out of the filth of the prison and presented them again before the prefect.

The prefect said to them:

“If at last you are pursuing life by wise counsel, sacrifice to the gods and live. But if you choose to die, go and look upon the corpses of those whom you seduced, unhappily unburied and still bearing the marks of their torments. If you do not recoil, surpass their misery with your own misery and die unhappily, as you desire.”

At these words the martyrs of Christ—Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius—strengthened in a common confession of faith and steadfastness of virtue, chose, after excessive torments, to complete a glorious martyrdom.

Removed from the judge’s presence and shown the bodies of the holy dead, they praised the just and hidden judgments of God, who had determined thus to humble in the present those whom, before all time, he had decreed to exalt so gloriously in the heavenly kingdom.

Then, after terror had been added, and after they had been worn down by many insults and punishments they had not previously endured, they openly declared themselves servants of Christ in a loud confession.

The holy priest of God was especially mangled by human savagery, and the beast also served that savagery. He hastened toward torments so that he would not be slow in reaching glory. He provoked punishment against himself so that the victory might be greater. On one side the executioners struggled; on the other, the martyr’s voice, bearing the palm of victory. He embraced the punishments so that, as the torment increased, the crown might also increase.

Therefore, once again, as at the beginning, all the holy martyrs were beaten naked with rods in the presence of everyone, then clothed again in their garments, and led out opposite the idol of Mercury to the appointed place, where they were ordered to kneel for beheading.

## CHAPTER XXXI

Then blessed Dionysius, the Lord’s bishop, stretched out his hands and raised his eyes to heaven, saying:

“God, my God, who created me and by your grace brought me into this life; who by your eternal wisdom taught me and did not hide from me the counsels of your mysteries; who have always consoled me with mercy and abundant compassion, and have been with me in everything wherever I went: I give you thanks for all that you have done and shown me, and for what you have deigned to accomplish through me.

“Above all, because now you have visited my humility through yourself and called my old age, wearied by your desire, to yourself, knowing that for a long time I have greatly longed to see you. Now, Lord, receive me through the crown of martyrdom together with my brothers, your servants. I commend to your protection those whom through our ministry you acquired for yourself by your blood. Mercifully hear, as you promised, all who through us ask you in your name, for yours is the kingdom and the power with the Father and the Holy Spirit, before all things and throughout all ages of ages.”

When blessed Rusticus and Eleutherius, all the faithful, and many pagans who followed him in mourning had answered “Amen,” they knelt and stretched out their necks. At one and the same moment, according to the emperor’s command, their heads were severed with axes whose edges had been blunted. Remaining steadfast in this faith, they gave their bodies to the earth and brought their blessed souls to heaven.

By such a confession they deserved to depart to the Lord that, even after their heads had been cut off, the quivering tongue was thought still to confess Jesus Christ the Lord. For the love that had been present in their minds, although their heads had been severed, continued to pour forth in speech the ardor that their mouths had already embraced.

Truly this was an exceedingly blessed fellowship, pleasing to our God. Among them neither one could be first nor another third; but, confessing the Trinity, they deserved to be adorned with a threefold martyrdom, so that, equal in faith, they might be crowned with equal glory.

## CHAPTER XXXII

On that same day, the great multitude of the faithful who had believed through him, together with him and around the city, was killed for Christ’s name and subjected to punishments of every kind, even punishments previously unheard of, so that at Paris it seemed fulfilled what had been proclaimed in prophetic prediction concerning Jerusalem:

“They have laid the dead bodies of your servants around it, and there was no one to bury them.”

To manifest the glorious merits of the holy martyr and first priest of Gaul, and so that, where the life-giving fruit had first begun to arise, the triumph of his glory might be displayed more fully, the greatest honor seized all who were present, and an ineffable light shone upon everyone.

The corpse of the most blessed Dionysius rose, and his holy hand began to carry his head, severed from his body by the executioner’s axe, with his arms hanging down. An angelic guide directed his steps, and heavenly light surrounded him.

A multitude of the heavenly army became companion to his lifeless body as it carried its own head from the very mountain where he had been beheaded for nearly two thousand paces, to the place where, by God’s disposition and his own choice, it now rests buried. Without ceasing, the multitude praised God with sweet-sounding hymns.

Countless ranks of divine spirits were also heard ascending to heaven and singing with inestimable sweetness: “Glory to you, O Lord,” frequently adding, “Alleluia.” As far as that immense sound could be distinguished, angelic choirs seemed to sing these and other things whose meaning could not be perceived, answering one another antiphonally.

When countless peoples saw and heard this, and many of the persecutors as well, they believed in the Lord. Those who did not believe, struck with overwhelming terror, fled each to his own side.

## CHAPTER XXXIII

It was entirely fitting that divine favor should thus display on earth its glorified saint, who, as a renowned messenger to the fiercest peoples and God’s precious confessor, inflamed by the fire of divine love, steadfastly endured the punishments of passion and through monstrous torments reached the fellowship of the angels.

It was a new, unprecedented, and unheard-of miracle: a lifeless body running as though alive, and a man already dead walking with upright steps.

Yet although it is wondrous, it is not difficult for the body of the most holy man, with his head severed, to walk by angelic ministry in the manner of a living person. The same God, by his omnipotence, after the spirit had departed, could easily direct his corpse to walk, in testimony to the faith that his faithful servant had preached. He had formed that very body from the dust of the earth and deigned to breathe into it the spirit by which it was enlivened; and he will likewise deign to restore it when reduced to ashes and to make it eternally living with the soul by which it had lived.

When the aforesaid Larcia witnessed this astonishing miracle, she sprang into the crowds of unbelievers and cried out that by the grace of Christ she was a Christian. She was immediately seized and, while confessing Christ our Lord, was baptized in the fountain of her blood for the remission of sins and died cleansed of the impurity of idols.

Her son Visbius, whom she had received from her husband Lisbius, was taken to Rome and, after Domitian had been carried away by the corpse-bearers [Note: *Evespillato*, that is, “carried away by the corpse-bearers.” This was written in the margin of an ancient manuscript codex.], served under three Caesars. On returning under the holy bishop Masso, who governed the Church of Paris as the third after blessed Dionysius, he abandoned everything that belongs to the world, was baptized, and joined the company of religious men and Christ’s poor.

Meanwhile, the persecutors and the phalanxes of pagans feared that the most faithful and proven devotion of the converted people might gather and bury the bodies of the saints Rusticus and Eleutherius, which lay on the mountain where they had been martyred together with blessed Dionysius, for the people’s protection. They therefore make an initial plan and choose to consign the martyrs’ bodies to the deep waters and profound currents of the Seine, so that they might be destroyed by the earth’s waters.

They placed the bodies in boats and ordered their servants to carry them to the chosen whirlpool and sink them there. But almighty God, who knows the future, who changes times but does not change the plan he has predestined, and who altered the evil plan of Holofernes through the wisdom of a kindly woman, compelled the schemes of the wicked to serve the craft of his own providence by whatever means he wished.

## CHAPTER XXXIV

For a certain noble matron, named Catulla, although she was still held captive by the errors of the pagans more by necessity than by choice, nevertheless showed by both mind and action that she desired to be converted to the faith of Christ through the examples of the martyrs and to attain the grace of baptism. Inspired by God’s mercy, she sought a plan of admirable courage and asked to come to a banquet with those who were to destroy the holy bodies.

While she lavished upon them the resources of her offered hospitality, she distracted them from remembering what they had undertaken to do. By a secret arrangement she entrusted her faithful servants and those aware of her intimate plan with the task of carefully concealing the precious bodies by theft.

When they learned their mistress’s will and command, they hastened to carry out what had been ordered. They concealed the laudable theft—which injured no one and brought the greatest gain to all who believed piously—six miles from the city mentioned above, in the furrows of autumn fields that the matron had then prepared abundantly for sowing seed. They pretended to be farmers, as though engaged in rural labor, and took care to mark the place with a definite sign.

Later, when the same woman, more fully aware of God’s future purposes, and her Christian companions, amid the silent secrecy of night, took up the bodies of the martyrs mentioned above, they joined them to the body of blessed Dionysius and, with whatever reverence they could offer amid the fury of the persecutors, visited them with the utmost devotion.

Afterward the field was sown, and the crop did not refuse its service. It was fertilized with such richness, and the gift of abundance poured itself over it so fully, that the most devoted cultivator obtained a hundredfold harvest and deserved the salvation of her homeland.

## CHAPTER XXXV

When the matron mentioned above first saw that the violence of the persecution had grown weak, she approached with suitable honor and the greatest reverence the place that preserved the bones of so many martyrs, together with the holy priests of the Lord and crowds of the faithful. She openly made known to everyone the incomparable treasure that she had preserved for a long time for the benefit of herself and her descendants, on that same most sacred day on which blessed Dionysius, triumphing with his companions, completed the contest and deserved to receive the crown of victory from the hand of the Lord, and on which the precious witness of the Lord Jesus gained a place in the heavenly senate.

She marked the place by building a distinguished mausoleum. After the bodies of the saints had been buried with fitting reverence, their garments were preserved, with the reverence of due worship, down to the present day: namely, the tunic, hair shirt, and boots of the precious Dionysius; the *casula* of Saint Rusticus, the archpresbyter; and the *dalmatica* of blessed Eleutherius, the archdeacon—except for portions taken by the devotion of the faithful as relics of the Lord’s chosen ones.

Through the merits and prayers of these saints, the same venerable woman, reborn from water and the Holy Spirit in the name of the Holy Trinity, gave to the Lord Jesus Christ our Savior and to the martyrs themselves everything she was able to possess. Celebrating sacred vigils at their bodies for as long as she lived, she deserved, in good confession and conduct, to depart to the glory of Christ and the holy martyrs, through their intercession.

## CHAPTER XXXVI

As time passed and the number of the faithful increased, Christians devoted to the protection of blessed Dionysius built a basilica over the bodies of the precious martyrs at great expense and with exceptional adornment. There, every day, through the working of our Lord Jesus Christ, the frequency of their miracles is proved and displayed.

The magnificence of these miracles cannot be adequately narrated even by speech, nor can they be comprehended by human minds. Therefore the dignity of their honor and splendor cannot be reached even by human thought.

Nevertheless, the sick and those afflicted by every kind of distress experience, in that place and wherever they invoke the Lord’s mercy through the merits of these same martyrs, how greatly God’s servants ought to be honored. Through their intervention, blindness receives sight, weakness receives the power to walk, and ears whose gates were closed deserve to receive hearing.

Nor must this be left unmentioned: those tormented by the infestation of unclean spirits, when they are brought to the tombs of the aforesaid witnesses of Christ to be examined by divine power, are compelled by the command of the saints themselves to indicate by name where each of the martyrs has been placed.

Their memorable and most glorious passion was celebrated opposite the city of Paris, on the hill that was formerly called Mount Mercury because the idol of Mercury was chiefly worshiped there by the Gauls, but which is now called the Mount of Martyrs, through the grace of the Lord’s saints who accomplished their triumphant martyrdom there: on the seventh day before the Ides of October, in the ninety-sixth year from the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the sixty-fourth from his passion; while the age of the most blessed Dionysius was approximately ninety years and the sixteenth year of the reign of Domitian, that most savage Caesar, was beginning.

Divine vengeance followed him, as it had Nero, whose portion he had been, after the killing of the apostles, without any delay. Struck down, he miserably and deservedly lost his life together with his tyrannical rule.

Our Lord Jesus Christ reigns, to whom are honor and glory, power and dominion, with the Father, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, from eternity and now and throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

# In the Year of Our Lord 840: Maxentius, Patriarch of Aquileia

[Col. 0049]

[Col. 0049C]

## Historical Notice on Maxentius

(Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, vol. IV, p. 38.)

[Col. 0049]

[Col. 0049D] Maxentius, the successor of Urbanus, subscribed to the donation of Rotaldus, bishop of Verona, in the year 813 [Note: [Col. 0049D] Or rather, 814.] on June 24. He consecrated Erulfus, bishop of Mantua and his suffragan, in the year 823. Concerning him Dandulus writes in his chronicle:

“Maxentius, patriarch of Aquileia, supported by the favor of King Lothair, endeavored to disturb the Church of Grado and the suffragans of Istria; nor, when admonished by Pope Gregory, did he wish to desist. Indeed, having again obtained secular assistance, he compelled the aforesaid bishops entirely to render him the reverence and subjection owed to a metropolitan.”

Candidus, however, relates the following about him:

“Urbanus was succeeded by Maxentius. At his urging, and through the efforts of Lothair, Pope Eugenius II convened a council at Mantua, at which the island of Grado was adjudged to the Church of Aquileia, while Venereus, who falsely used the title of patriarch, was deposed. From the ruins of the temple of the ancient native god Belus, he built at Aquileia the monastery of Saint Benedict for monks, called Belinense. Eventually, because it had been completely abandoned on account of the harshness of the climate, Pope Gregory XI attached it to the monastery at Udine of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, of the same order, granting its estates and revenues under equal right. Urbanus and Boniface later confirmed this privilege at great length. Yet, through the treachery of those who had seized the administration of the state, everything, as with most other possessions, was overturned, since they impiously claimed for themselves a large part of them in their customary fashion. The remainder, being likewise neglected, the collegiate chapter of the canons of Aquileia appropriated to itself by grant of Pope Nicholas V. Thus, almost like public plunderers, while they are excessively attentive to their own interests, they overturn the commonwealth by making common possessions insignificant.”

After he had lived fifteen years in the patriarchate, he died in the city of Austria.” This is what Candidus says about Maxentius. The year in which Maxentius died is not known. Nevertheless, he must have died after the Council of Mantua, held by the authority of Pope Eugenius II in the year 826.

[Col. 0051B]

# LETTER OF MAXENTIUS TO THE EMPEROR CHARLEMAGNE ON THE MEANING OF THE RITES OF BAPTISM

(Pez, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*.)

[Col. 0051]

[Col. 0051B] To the most devout, most Christian, and glorious prince, crowned and preserved by God, peaceful, victorious, triumphant, most serene, and perpetual Augustus, Lord Charles the Great, emperor and ruler of the Roman Empire: Maxentius, the least of the servants of the Lord, humble bishop of the holy Catholic Church of Aquileia, sends eternal salvation in the Lord.

## I

We therefore give great thanks to our Lord, because you have deigned to recall this holy Church, or rather me, your very insignificant servant, to the memory of your Highness. For although I am the least of all my predecessors, your kindly clemency did not disdain to admonish me through familiar conversation and sacred letters, diligently inquiring and encouraging me to address each of the needs of the holy Church of God. Concerning what you wish to know—how we and our suffragans teach and instruct the priests of the Lord and the people entrusted to us by God regarding the sacraments of baptism—we hasten to bring to the knowledge of your Excellence whatever, with the Lord’s help, we are able to understand according to the limited capacity of our intelligence.

## II

We do not contemplate idly what the holy Church uniformly does concerning those who are to be baptized. Whether children or young people come to the sacrament of regeneration, they do not approach the fountain of life before they become catechumens. Catechumens are so called because they are instructed, or because they are subject to correction and possess free choice directed toward Christ. For the beginning of holiness is to confess the Lord Christ, the Son of God, according to what is written: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but confession is made by action unto salvation.”

The place of those who confess is the place of those who, hastening toward the grace of God, desire to become something more than they have been. For this reason they are called *competentes*, that is, those asking for the grace of God, so that before they receive baptism they may serve the Lord through faith, and after receiving faith they may not lose God’s gifts or make void his grace, whom they have wished to serve.

Salt is therefore given to catechumens in the ministry so that we may be what the Lord said in the Gospel: “You are the salt of the earth,” that is, the seasoning of God’s wisdom. And, as the same rite says: “Receive the salt of wisdom; may God be gracious to you unto eternal life.” For what is accomplished through the ministry of priests is sanctified by the Lord and becomes for those who receive it a perfect medicine, remaining within their inward parts.

Then they are exorcised and breathed upon, so that the unclean spirit may be cast out from them. It is not God’s creature in infants that is exorcised or breathed upon, but the one under whose power are all who are born with sin, so that it may then truly appear, according to what is written, that “the prince of this world” is cast out, and how the strong man is first bound and afterward his vessels are plundered and transferred into the possession of the victor.

For *scrutiny* means inquiry or investigation: through the mouths of priests and the laying on of hands, that vessel, formed from the clay of the earth and given life, which the works and pomp of the devil had separated from God’s command in paradise through wicked suggestion and infected with the poison of his malice, is scrutinized and cleansed. Once the unclean spirit has been expelled from it, it is marked in every part with sanctified oil, recalled to the grace of blessing, and made the Lord’s vessel and a temple of the Holy Spirit, as the Apostle says: “It will be a vessel sanctified unto honor, useful to the Lord, prepared for every good work.”

## III

To renounce means to reject and refuse; that is, after abandoning the error of paganism and the worship of images, to worship God the almighty Father, Jesus Christ his Son, and the Holy Spirit. It means stripping off the old human being with his deeds, as the Apostle says, and putting on the new, who has been created according to God in righteousness and the holiness of truth.

After this they enter the baptismal font and are baptized under a threefold immersion in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Then, through the washing of regeneration, they are transferred into the embrace of Mother Church, made children by adoption, and enrolled in the book of the life of Christ our Lord. From his holy name the chrism received its name. They are also anointed with the chrism of this sacred anointing, the chrism of salvation—that is, with the most abundant outpouring of the Holy Spirit in Christ Jesus our Lord unto eternal life.

Regenerated also, following Jesus as their leader, and washed in the blood of the Lamb, they arrive clothed in white garments—that is, in wedding garments—for the table of the heavenly kingdom and for that true promised land, covered with the sacred veil of faith and destined to receive crowns.

## IV

The Creed has been called by many names for many reasons. *Symbolum* is Greek; in Latin it may be called a token, a contribution, a compact, or an agreement of faith—something that many people contribute into one whole.

The structure of this Creed is therefore bound together with the utmost brevity. Its words are few, but its mysteries are great. Here the power of God the Father and the Son, who is his equal, is proclaimed. Here the Only-Begotten Son of God is shown to have been born according to the flesh from the Virgin Mary and the Holy Spirit. Here his crucifixion, burial, and resurrection on the third day are proclaimed. Here his ascension above the heavens and his being seated at the right hand of the Father’s majesty are acknowledged, and he is declared to be coming to judge the living and the dead. Here the Holy Spirit is received as undivided in the same divinity as the Father and the Son. Finally, here the calling of the Church, the remission of sins, the resurrection of the flesh, and eternal life are proclaimed.

## V

Concerning the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord himself deigned to say nothing other than this in the Gospel:

“I am the living bread which came down from heaven”; and: “Whoever eats of this bread will live forever, and the bread which I will give is my flesh for the life of the world.” For he says: “My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink. Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him.”

To eat that flesh and drink that blood, therefore, is to remain in Christ through faith and to have him who remains in us through grace. For what is offered by many is brought into one body of Christ through the infusion of the Holy Spirit; and when each receives the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, the remission of all sins is effected for them.

## VI

It is doubtless known that all these things are written in the books of your library. Yet we believe that they are more fully and more sacredly retained in the treasury of your most holy heart, or in the spiritual tablets of your heart, which is guided by the hand of God.

We also know that the most learned men stand before the serenity of your countenance and, instructed by your most salutary teaching, are known to retain these matters here in their fullness. We, for our part, hold, proclaim, and teach according to what, with God inspiring us and his grace going before us, our powers of understanding permit: what the apostles proclaimed, what the evangelists announced, what we read in the sacred writings and in the well-ordered rule of the canons of the holy Fathers, and also what we follow with the pure sincerity of faith—the most sacred teachings of the venerable Catholic bishops of the Roman Church and of the holy Apostolic See.

Having set forth these preliminary matters, we wish your Imperial Excellence always to remain safe and sound. We wish you to live out the present life for a long time in joy and tranquility. We wish you to possess without end the joys of eternal life with all the saints.

May the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus our Lord, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God, forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0053C]

# COLLECTANEA OF MAXENTIUS ON THE ANCIENT RITES OF BAPTISM

(Pez., same work.)

[Col. 0053]

## On the Catechumens

[Col. 0053C] I. Catechumens are those who first come from paganism, possessing the will to believe in Christ. The command of exhortation is found in the Law: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God.” Hence the person to whom the Lord first speaks through the priest, as through Moses, is called a catechumen—that is, a hearer—so that, acknowledging the one Lord, he may abandon the various errors of idols. I also think that all those baptized by John unto repentance prefigured the catechumens.

II. They are first exorcised, then receive salt and are anointed with sanctified oil. Exorcism is a speech of rebuke made against the unclean spirit in the possessed or in catechumens, through which the devil’s most wicked power, his long-standing malice, violence, and assault are driven out and flee from them.

This was signified by the lunatic whom the Lord Jesus rebuked, and from whom the demon departed. The devil’s power is exorcised and breathed upon in them, so that they may renounce him and, delivered from the power of darkness, be transferred into the kingdom of their Lord through the sacrament of baptism.

Since infants cannot renounce him by themselves, this is fulfilled through the hearts and mouths of those who carry them. But the Fathers established that salt should be given to catechumens in the rite so that, by tasting it, they might receive the seasoning of wisdom from the taste of Christ, lest they be foolish and look back like Lot’s wife; lest, by giving a bad example, they themselves remain behind and crush others, as she did who, when she was being rescued from Sodom, afterward looked back on the way and remained there, becoming a pillar of salt.

By this sign those who, through faith, renounce the world, its deeds, and its desires are to be seasoned, so that they do not remember their former attachment or return to the allurements of the age. For, according to the Savior’s saying, whoever puts his hand to the plow and looks back cannot be fit for the kingdom of heaven.

## On the Competentes

[Col. 0055A]

III. After the catechumens comes the second order, that of the *competentes*. The *competentes* are those who, after instruction in the faith and after a disciplined life, hasten to receive the grace of Christ. For this reason they are called *competentes*, that is, those seeking the grace of Christ.

Catechumens merely hear and do not yet ask. They are like guests and neighbors of the faithful: from outside they hear the mysteries and hear of grace, but they are not yet called faithful. The *competentes*, however, already ask, already receive, and are already catechized—that is, imbued with instruction in the sacraments.

To these the saving Creed is handed over as a reminder of the faith and a token of holy confession, so that, instructed by it, they may recognize what sort of persons they must now present themselves to be in order to receive the grace of Christ.

## On the Creed

[Col. 0055B]

IV. Our ancestors, it is said, established the Creed, which these same *competentes* receive, for the following reason. They relate that after our Lord and Savior had ascended to the Father, when his disciples, through the coming of the Holy Spirit, spoke in the tongues of flame of all nations, this sign resulted: no foreign nation, no language inaccessible or impassable to barbarians, seemed beyond their reach. They received from the Lord the command to go to each nation to preach the word of God.

Therefore, as they were about to depart from one another, they first established together a rule for their future preaching, so that, departing from one another geographically, they would not proclaim anything different or discordant to those who were being invited to the faith of Christ. Thus, all gathered together as one and filled with the Holy Spirit, they composed from what they each believed a brief common token of their preaching, and determined that this rule should be given to believers.

They wished to call it the Creed for many and very just reasons. *Symbolum* is Greek; it may be rendered in Latin as a token or contribution—that is, something that many contribute into one whole. The apostles did this in these words, each contributing into one whole what he believed.

It is called a judgment or sign because at that time, as the Apostle says and the Acts of the Apostles reports, many pretended to be apostles of Christ. They named Christ, but did not announce the tradition according to its full and unbroken lines. Therefore, as they were about to depart, the apostles established this token by which those who truly preached Christ according to the apostolic rules could be recognized.

Finally, they report that this practice was also observed in civil wars. For among combatants there are martial bearing, the sound of a voice, and the same customs and institutions. Each commander gives his soldiers distinctive tokens, called in Latin signs or tokens. If someone should appear whose identity was in doubt, he was questioned about the *symbolum*, and thereby revealed whether he was an enemy or an ally.

The Fathers therefore handed this down not to be written on parchment but to be retained in the heart, so that it would be certain that no one had learned it from reading—which sometimes even reaches unbelievers—but from the tradition of the apostles. Thus, as has been said, when they were about to depart to preach, the apostles imposed this token of their unanimity and faith.

V. The Creed is a sign by which God is recognized, and which believers accordingly receive so that they may know how to prepare themselves for the struggles of faith against the devil. Its words are few, but all the sacraments are contained in it.

The apostles gathered into it, in brief, everything from the whole of Scripture, so that believers who do not know letters—or those who do know them but cannot read Scripture because of the preoccupations of the world—might retain this in their hearts and possess sufficient saving knowledge. It is a brief word of faith, formerly foretold by the prophet: “The Lord will make a brief word upon the earth.”

VI. Anyone coming from the pagans or from paganism becomes a catechumen, possessing the will to believe in God. The priest instructs him how he ought to believe, and he receives the command of exhortation concerning what sort of person he must show himself to be according to the rule of faith and in the worship of the living God.

The Lord speaks to him through the priest, just as the command was given through Moses in the Law: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God.” The catechumen is exorcised—that is, the evil spirit is adjured to depart and withdraw, giving place to the true God.

The catechumen receives salt so that, as an initial nourishment, the divine gift of the salt of vigorous wisdom may cleanse away the flowing and putrid sins at the beginnings of faith. Catechumens are called hearers or listeners; nevertheless, they cannot be present with the faithful when the divine mysteries are celebrated. This was determined by the ancient institution of the Fathers.

The second order after the catechumens is that of the *competentes*. Catechumens merely hear and do not yet ask; the *competentes*, after instruction, ask and hasten to seek the grace of Christ. They give their names before the priest at the doors of the Church through an acolyte. Moreover, they are now catechized concerning those by whom they are to be received—that is, they are imbued with instruction in the sacraments and taught purity of faith.

VII. Scrutinies are performed among these people. The servants are examined as to whether they remain in the same doctrine of faith in which they had previously been instructed by the priests, and whether they renounce the evil spirit, his malice, and his destructive pomps.

They are also breathed upon so that, once the devil has been driven away and they have been admonished to renounce him, an entrance may be prepared for Christ our Lord. The faith of the apostolic Creed is handed over to them, so that, like an empty house abandoned by its former inhabitant, their dwelling may be adorned and prepared for God by the perfected order of faith.

Their breasts are anointed with oil while the holy cross is traced, so that the entrance of the devil may thereby be closed. Their noses are also touched so that they may enjoy the fragrance of the knowledge of God and that the apostolic saying may be fulfilled in them: “Thanks be to God, who always causes us to triumph in Christ Jesus and manifests through us the fragrance of his knowledge in every place.”

This may also be understood under the following pledge: as long as they draw breath through their nostrils, they are to persevere in that same profession of faith. Their shoulders are signed so that they may be fortified on every side. Thus, in the anointing of the breast and shoulders, the firmness of faith and perseverance in good works are signified.

When they come to the font, the priest examines them as to whether they truly wish to renounce everything, as they had previously been admonished. After they have renounced in the customary manner, they are again questioned concerning the faith of the Creed. When they have correctly answered everything in due order, and have professed that they believe according to the integrity of that Creed, they are baptized in the name of the holy Trinity by threefold immersion.

And rightly so: the human being, created in the image of the holy Trinity, is renewed into that same image through the invocation of the holy Trinity. The one who fell into death through the third stage of sin—that is, consent—is raised from the font a third time by grace and rises to life.

VIII. Then they are clothed in white garments because of the joy of regeneration and as a prefiguration of angelic life, so that they may be adorned by its splendor. The whiteness of their garments mystically prefigures the joy of those dwelling in the heavenly Jerusalem, as Isaiah’s prophecy testifies: “There,” he says, “thousands of rejoicing ones dwell.”

Through the washing of regeneration, they begin, as far as they are able, to imitate their fellow citizens who have attained eternal blessedness, so that they may enjoy their blessed fellowship forever.
