Then their heads are anointed with sacred chrism and they are covered with a mystical veil, so that they may understand that they will bear the dignity of the diademed kingdom and of the priesthood. For such people the blessed Apostle Peter says: “You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood.”

Finally, they are strengthened with the body and blood of the Lord, so that they may be members of that head who suffered and rose again for us. For they eat and drink the price of our redemption: “You were bought,” says the distinguished preacher, “with a great price; glorify and bear God in your body.”

Finally, through the laying on of hands of the high priest, they receive the sevenfold grace of the Spirit, so that they may be strengthened by the Holy Spirit to preach to others who, through grace in baptism, have been given eternal life.

# IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 840. CANDIDUS, MONK OF FULDA

[Col. 0057]

[Col. 0057B]

# HISTORICAL NOTICE CONCERNING CANDIDUS

(Fabricius, *Bibliotheca medii et infimi Latini*.)

[Col. 0057]

[Col. 0057C] Candidus of Fulda, the author of the *Life of Saint Eigil*, which is also found in Brower’s *Fuldensian Antiquities*, was a monk around the year 822. He is distinct from Candidus the priest in Britain, to whom Alcuin dedicated several works around the year 790. Candidus of Fulda also wrote a short work on the Passion of the Lord, which Pez published in volume I, page 239, of the *Newest Treasury of Anecdotes*.

[Col. 0057C]

# THE PROSE AND METRICAL LIFE OF SAINT EIGIL, BY CANDIDUS, MONK OF FULDA

(See *Patrologia*, volume CV, column 377.)

[Col. 0057]

[Col. 0057D]

# THE SHORT WORK OF CANDIDUS ON THE PASSION OF THE LORD

(Pez, *Newest Treasury of Anecdotes*.)

[Col. 0057]

## PREFACE

[Col. 0057D]

It is known to you, dearest brothers, and you have learned it through frequent reading of the holy Gospel, that almighty God deigned to send his only-begotten Son into this world for the salvation of the human race. Although he was always co-eternal and co-omnipotent with God, he is said to have come to us when he assumed human nature, so that he could be seen by human beings.

For, brothers, the divine nature is invisible, incomprehensible, and wholly present everywhere. This, then, is what we say to you: he is everywhere in his divine nature; but he is said to come to us into this world when he assumes human nature so that he may be seen.

He was born, as you know, from the holy Virgin Mary in these last times; he who was born before the ages from God the Father and is co-eternal with the Father and the Holy Spirit. He was born, I say, according to his humanity, while in his divinity he was always born from God.

He was born for this purpose: to teach human beings by his example and word, and to be the way for all believers to the kingdom of heaven. I say “the way,” because just as people come by a road, so we must come to the kingdom of heaven through his teaching and examples.

The Son of God therefore came to teach; he came to fulfill what he taught. He taught that every human being should love God and love his neighbor as himself. He always loved God, and he loves his neighbors—that is, faithful souls whom he made his neighbors, because he assumed a human soul into the unity of his person.

He loved his neighbors, I say, to such an extent that he handed himself over to death for his brothers and neighbors. For the human race could not otherwise be redeemed from eternal death except by an innocent person dying for all.

But after the transgression of the first human beings, no one born of man and woman appeared innocent. Therefore the Son of God, born from the Virgin alone, appeared in the world innocent and without sin, so that one might die for many sinners—not a sinner, but the redeemer of sinners.

We now celebrate the sacrament of the Lord’s Passion in accordance with the time in which it is read to have taken place. For the holy Church of God customarily solemnly celebrates every year the memory of that same Passion, through which the world was redeemed from eternal death, and prepares itself by good works to deserve a share in his resurrection. This should indeed be done at all times, but most devoutly at this time.

Let us therefore hear, brothers, with attentive heart and devoted mind, how our Lord himself deigned to come to undergo this Passion for our salvation, how patiently he endured what was inflicted upon him, and what example of patience he deigned to offer his faithful so that they might follow him. Having heard and committed these things to memory, may we, with God’s help, be able to arrive prepared for the joy of his resurrection and filled with good works.

For, as the Apostle says, “If we suffer with him, we shall also be glorified with him.” And if we follow the traces of his death, we shall likewise share in his resurrection. For if such necessity should arise, we must be prepared to die for Christ, just as he died for us.

Nevertheless, if no one persecutes us unto death, we must still be prepared in mind to die with him, so that we may also deserve to live with him. Let us always give thanks to divine mercy, which has deigned to love us so greatly. Let us prove, not only by words but also by the commandments he himself gave, that we love him who first loved us and handed himself over to death for us.

The four evangelists—Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John—relate to us the history of the Lord’s Passion and the order in which it was accomplished. But since it would be lengthy to explain to you all the words of each of them in order, we wish to relate and briefly interpret the Lord’s Passion for you from all four together, as though they were the words of one.

# CHAPTER I. AN ORDERED TEXT OF THE PASSION OF THE LORD ACCORDING TO THE FOUR EVANGELISTS

As we have learned from the accounts of the evangelists, when Jesus had completed his words of instruction to the whole people, saying, “Having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end,” he said to his disciples: “You know that after two days the Passover will take place, and the Son of Man will be handed over to be crucified” (John XIII; Matthew XXVI).

When, as we have said, he had completed the teaching of the Gospel by which he had determined to instruct the whole people, he then foretold to the disciples that the Passover was near—that is, after two days. He left us to understand this as meaning after the two days of the natural law and the written law.

He came to show us by his example what the Passover was, for, as the evangelist says, he knew that his hour had come, that he should pass from this world to the Father (John XIII). By these words he wished to show the disciples that the Son of Man was to be handed over into the hands of those who would kill him, so that after death he might pass to the Father.

For *Passover* is interpreted as “Passage.” By those words, therefore, he showed what the Passover was: that the Son of Man should be handed over, crucified, and pass from death to the Father, with whom he had always been.

Then the chief priests and the elders of the people gathered in the courtyard of the high priest, who was called Caiaphas, and took counsel to seize and kill Jesus by deceit. But they said: “Not on the feast day, lest perhaps a tumult arise among the people.”

Those chief priests and elders of the Jewish people had been appointed to meditate on the law of God and preach it to the people. They changed their office and gathered for the purpose of removing salvation from themselves and, so far as it lay with them, killing it.

They said that this should not be done on the feast day, that is, on the Passover, lest a tumult arise among the people. They feared the people more than God. A multitude of people customarily gathered for the solemnity of the Passover, and they feared that the people would take him from their hands.

But whether they wished it or not, that time had been both appointed by God and prefigured long beforehand: at the time when the paschal lamb was customarily sacrificed, the true Lamb would come and be sacrificed for the salvation of the whole world. For he is the Lamb of God who took away the sins of the world; he was handed over because of our offenses.

His betrayer was one of the twelve disciples whom he had chosen. For, as John the evangelist says:

# CHAPTER II

Six days before the Passover Jesus came to Bethany, where Lazarus, whom Jesus had raised, was. They made him a supper there in the house of a certain Simon the leper. Martha, the sister of Lazarus, served, while Lazarus himself was one of those reclining at table with him.

Then Mary, his other sister, came, took a pound of costly genuine nard ointment, anointed the head and feet of Jesus as he reclined, wiped his feet with her hair, and the house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment (John XII).

My brothers, this supper took place, as I said, six days before the Passover. But it is mentioned to you now so that you may know how that wicked traitor Judas came to hand the Lord over to the Jews, as you will hear in what follows.

The Lord therefore came to Bethany. Bethany is a village in Judea, and its name is interpreted as “house of obedience.” It signifies the Church of Christ, which is not truly his Church unless it is a house of obedience.

Christ Jesus the Lord, who first founded it, was obedient to God the Father unto death. Whoever, therefore, wishes to share in his Church should know that he can merit this through obedience.

But in this Church of Christ there are customarily two classes of people: one consists of those who preach the faith of Christ; the other of those who, receiving the teaching of faith from the preachers, support the preachers from their earthly possessions so that they may carry out the work of preaching.

This supper is said to have taken place in Bethany, as though in the Church, and in the house of Simon the leper, as though among the Gentile people, who had previously been leprous with sins but were cleansed by God and made worthy for the Lord’s supper to be held in their house.

As we have said, there are two classes of people who serve Christ: preachers and those to whom they preach. There were likewise two sisters at this Lord’s supper, Martha and Mary. Martha served, and Mary anointed the Lord with ointment.

The one who served signifies those who support and assist their preachers from their own possessions in the work of preaching. Mary, however, represents the preachers themselves, who anointed the Lord. For whoever preaches Christ as true God anoints the Lord’s head; and whoever preaches him as human anoints his feet and wipes the Lord’s feet with his hair.

Preachers ought to be prepared for this: just as he deigned to die for us, so they too should always be prepared to die for his faith. For Christ suffered for us, leaving us an example so that we might follow in his footsteps.

If a time should come when it is necessary to suffer death for him, let us be prepared. But if not, let us at least wipe his feet with our hair—that is, let us abandon worldly riches and honors for his name. For this is signified by the hair with which that woman wiped the Lord’s feet.

“The house,” he says, “was filled with the fragrance of the ointment.” We said earlier that the house of Simon the leper signifies the Gentile people, formerly leprous with many and various sins but cleansed by the Lord through the blood of his Passion. For he is the Lamb who took away the sins of the world.

The Lord was therefore anointed with ointment in Simon’s house; that is, the Gospel of Christ was preached among the Gentile people, and the house was filled with its fragrance, because, as the Lord commanded, they went and taught all nations. And as the Psalmist says: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth” (Psalm XVIII).

When the disciples saw this, they were indignant. One of them, Judas Iscariot, who was about to betray him, said: “Why this waste? Why was this ointment not sold for three hundred denarii and given to the poor?” He said this not because he cared about the poor, but because he was a thief; and since he kept the money box, he carried away what was put into it (John XII).

You see, brothers, that this wretched Judas did not first sin when, through greed, he sold the Lord for money. He had already been a thief and had stolen by carrying away what was given to them.

The ministers of the Church resemble this Judas when they serve the Church in order to collect money from it for themselves. Pursuing shameful gain, they use the Church just as Judas then used the Lord, collecting money and treasures for themselves in his name.

And alas, what sorrow! There are already many such traitorous Judases in the world. To this day the Jewish people do what Judas did then: they are indignant that the Church of the Gentiles anoints God through its faith and belief.

Jesus therefore said: “Leave her, so that she may keep it for the day of my burial. Why do you trouble the woman? She has performed a good work upon me. For you always have the poor with you, and whenever you wish you can do good to them; but you will not always have me with you.

“For in pouring this ointment upon my body, she has done what she could and has anticipated anointing it for burial. Amen, I say to you: wherever this Gospel is preached in the whole world, what she has done will also be told in memory of her” (John XII; Matthew XXVI; Mark XIV).

The other disciples of the Lord were indignant over the ointment that seemed to them to have been wasted, since it was worth three hundred denarii. The others truly wanted the money to be given to the poor; but Judas alone, who was a thief, wanted to steal it.

Jesus therefore answered them—that is, the other disciples, not Judas—and showed them that the woman had acted well. She anointed the Lord’s body with that ointment because, after his death, when she wished to do the same thing again, she did not find his body in the tomb, for the Lord had already risen.

This is what the Lord means when he says: “She has anticipated anointing my body.” Therefore, he says, “Leave her, so that she may keep it for the day of my burial”—that is, let her do in this manner what she would have done then had she found him.

“Amen,” he says, “I say to you: wherever this Gospel is preached…” Recall now, brothers, what I said above: that this ointment signifies the Gospel. What he said there—“the house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment”—he says here: “This Gospel will be preached throughout the whole world.”

For this reason, after what seemed to him the waste of the ointment, which he had wanted to turn into shameful profit, that same man departed four days later, two days before the Passover.

Judas, one of the twelve, who was called Judas Iscariot, went to the chief priests and said to them: “What are you willing to give me, and I will hand him over to you?” But they rejoiced and agreed to give him money—thirty silver pieces—and he promised, and he sought an opportunity to hand him over without the crowds (Matt. 26; Luke 22). [Col. 0063A] He said: “What are you willing to give me, so that I may hand him over to you?” In their estimation he assigned a price to his Lord.

Now on the first day of Unleavened Bread, when it was necessary for the Passover to be sacrificed, the disciples approached Jesus, saying: “Where do you wish us to prepare for you to eat the Passover?” But Jesus sent Peter and John, saying: “Go and prepare the Passover for us,” and “Go into the city, and a man carrying a water jar will meet you. Follow him into the house he enters, and say to the master of the house: ‘The Teacher says: My time is near; I will celebrate the Passover with my disciples at your house. Where is the guest room where I may eat the Passover?’ And he himself will show you a large upper room furnished; prepare there.” They went and found it just as he had told them, and they prepared the Passover [Col. 0063B] (Luke 22; Matt. 26).

The Lord sent two disciples to prepare for himself the passage by which he would pass from this world to the Father. These two were Peter and John. Peter signifies faith, John charity; for through these he passes to the glory of incorruption and to blessed life: through faith, by which we believe in God the Father, in his Son himself, and in the Holy Spirit; and through charity, by which we love him in whom we believe.

Thus the Lord deigns to recline at such a passage. For among the Jews that solemnity was called *Azyma*, which means “without leaven.” The apostle Paul showed what this signified when he said: “Let us celebrate the feast, not with the old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.”

See, brothers, what two disciples are sent [Col. 0063C] to prepare the Passover: sincerity and truth. Sincerity of heart belongs to charity; truth to faith. For in the old law it is written: “You shall love your friend, and hate your enemy.” The leaven of hatred and malice remained there in the heart of the one who hated his enemy. But Christ desires a Passover without leaven, for he says: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself,” and he did not leave anyone whom you were to hate; for he says: “You are all brothers.”

The old law commanded that the blood of one’s neighbor be avenged; there the leaven of anger remained. But Christ says: “Pray for those who persecute you”; and again: “Forgive the sins of your brothers from your hearts.” For, as I have said, he wants the place where he deigns to dwell to have a dwelling without the leaven of malice.

Therefore the heart in which Christ wishes to eat the Passover must be prepared with faith and charity, and then it is worthy that Christ remain in it. “Go,” he says, “to a certain man.” He did not name anyone, to indicate that it is free for each person whether or not he receives Christ.

“My time,” he says, “is near”—namely, the time when the old leaven had to be brought to an end, so that the spotless Lamb might be sacrificed for the sins of humanity. For this is the Passover, as we said above, by which he passed from death to eternal life.

When evening came and the supper had taken place, the devil having already put it into the heart of Judas Iscariot to betray him, Jesus knew that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he had come forth from God and was going to God (John 13). This Lord’s Supper was good for the good and chosen disciples [Col. 0064A], and a revelation of many mysteries and the beginning of the New Testament; but for that wretched betrayer it was the beginning of complete destruction.

For then the devil put it into his heart that Judas should betray him. This is especially accustomed to be the cause of destruction for the wicked: when someone dares to approach the sacraments of God with a wicked heart and an evil thought, and strives bodily to join himself to the holy things from which malice is far removed.

You must beware of this, brothers, and beware greatly, lest you presume to approach the sacred mysteries with the leaven of malice. For whoever is conscious of anger and malice, or of lust that has been committed, or of other evil crimes, and does not drive these things from his heart and has not done penance for what he has committed—if he approaches the divine sacraments, he gives the devil access, so that the devil may tempt him and hurl him into the abyss of destruction from which he will not escape. Therefore, brothers, as the Apostle says: “Let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit.” And “Let each person examine himself, and so eat of that bread and drink from the cup.”

## CHAPTER III

The Lord rises from the supper, lays aside his garments, and, taking a linen cloth, girds himself. Then he pours water into a basin and begins to wash the feet of his disciples (John 12). This humble service, which the Lord deigned to offer his disciples, gives us outwardly a great lesson in humility, while inwardly it is entirely filled with the mysteries of our salvation and redemption.

It is a great and truly immeasurable humility that our Lord—according to his divinity, God and creator of all things, and according to his humanity, our head and the head of the whole Church—deigned to wash the feet of his disciples and to give us an example, so that we might take care to serve one another both in washing feet and in every need that may arise. For feet are the lowest members of the body and are nearest to the earth.

So, brothers, so must we assist the weaker members of Christ in their needs, and, as much as we are able, care for them through our humility and charity.

That is what is indicated to us outwardly in this mystical service of the Lord, but a great mystery is also contained inwardly in this deed. The Lord rises from the supper when, exalted for us on the cross, he was raised up through the preaching of the holy Gospel. He lays aside his garments when the soul that he assumed for us, abandoning the body for a time, tasted death for everyone. At that very moment of death he took the linen cloth and girded himself, enduring the harsh passion of the flesh through which he gave up his spirit.

He poured water into the basin because from his side flowed the blood of our redemption and the water of baptism by which the sins of the faithful are washed: with blood daily, but with water once—and this in the basin. For only in the Church is the remission of sins effected through baptism.

As I said, water and blood came out from Christ’s side. We are washed with water once for the remission of sins, but with blood it is necessary that we be washed daily. This is what he says: “He began to wash and to wipe them with the linen cloth with which he was girded.” For the linen cloth, as you heard above, [Col. 0065A] signifies the painful harshness of the passion that he undertook for us; through that passion Christ himself intercedes for us at the right hand of God the Father.

Therefore he comes to Simon Peter, and Peter says to him: “Lord, are you washing my feet?” Jesus answered and said to him: “What I am doing you do not know now, but afterward you will know.” Peter said to him: “You shall never wash my feet.” Jesus answered him: “If I do not wash you, you will have no share with me.” Peter says to him: “Not only my feet, but also my hands and my head” (John 13).

Jesus came to Simon Peter, for he began with him first. But Peter, being a human being, was frightened at the service whose mystery he did not know. Although he was good, and although the Church was to be founded upon his faith, he was nevertheless afraid—afraid, I say, that God should serve him. [Col. 0065B] But he did not know what this signified: namely, that the Lord would wash the world from sins through his passion, and that, whatever sins we have committed after baptism, we need his mercy daily in order that they may be cleansed.

Still not knowing what the Lord wished to signify, Peter said: “You shall never wash my feet.” All would certainly have said this if they had not been frightened by his example and by what the Lord said: “If I do not wash you, you will have no share with me.” Fearing this, and perceiving however slightly the meaning of the deed, they consented—something no one would have consented to if they had not heard these words spoken to Peter.

Jesus answered: “If I do not wash you, you will have no share with me.” For unless someone is reborn of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God. [Col. 0065C] And unless we cry out to him daily, “Forgive us our debts,” we will not be able to reach his share—that is, the kingdom of heaven.

He therefore washes once in baptism all previously committed sins; he washes daily, through our repentance, the sins that we commit.

Jesus therefore says to him: “The one who has been washed does not need anything except to wash his feet, but is entirely clean. And you are clean, but not all”; for he knew who would betray him, and therefore said: “You are not all clean” (John 13).

“The one who has been washed,” he says, “does not need anything except to wash his feet.” Whoever has been washed in baptism does not need—in fact, must not—be baptized again. For whoever is baptized is baptized into Christ’s death, namely, so that he may die to all previously committed sins. Therefore whoever is baptized into Christ’s death, which happened once, is baptized once; and whoever wishes to be rebaptized is as though he wished Christ to die again.

Therefore, brothers, the Lord said: “The one who has been washed does not need anything except to wash his feet.” For when we commit many sins after baptism, they must be washed daily. The feet signify this earthly conduct: just as dust clings to feet touching the earth, so, while we live in this world, sin from worldly occupation often clings to us even against our will; and it needs daily repentance in order to be washed.

“And you,” he says, “are clean, but not all.” That is: through what I wish to signify by this service, you are to be cleansed, and are as though already clean, because what was to happen to human beings had already been accomplished by the Lord. For they—and the whole human race—[Col. 0066A] were to be cleansed by Christ’s death.

“But,” he says, “if I have cleansed you who were predestined to eternal life, nevertheless”—even though unbelievers and betrayers of the faith, namely heretics and schismatics, are cleansed outwardly with you—“they will not remain clean.” For after their sins have been forgiven, they return to their former evils and are therefore polluted by themselves, although they have been cleansed by me.

He said this then about Judas the betrayer. Although he was being washed with the apostles, Satan nevertheless immediately entered him after the washing and destroyed him.

That Judas therefore signifies those who in the Church indeed receive baptism together with the chosen, but nevertheless will not reach eternal life with the chosen, because they repeat their forgiven sins and, acting wickedly, either openly resist the Church of God [Col. 0066B] or, what is worse, secretly deceive it.

## CHAPTER IV

After he had washed their feet, he took his garments and, when he had reclined again, said to them: “Do you know what I have done to you? You call me Teacher and Lord, and you speak rightly, for so I am. If I, then, the Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet. For I have given you an example, so that just as I have done to you, you also may do” (John 13).

After he had washed the disciples’ feet, he took his garments—that is, after he had washed our sins by his blood and tasted an undeserved death for us, he rose on the third day and appeared alive to his disciples in the body in which he had suffered.

When he had reclined again, he said to them: “Do you know what I have done to you?” You call me Teacher and Lord. Do you know what commands I have given you? If you call me Teacher, do what I teach; and if you call me Lord, serve as the Lord’s servants. “For I am,” he says, “the Teacher who gave the commands, and the Lord who created you and redeemed you when you were lost.”

“If I, then, the Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet”—if, he says, I who redeemed you, who taught and instructed you, if I have forgiven your sins, though you have nothing to forgive me—“you also ought to forgive one another’s sins,” since each of you certainly has something to forgive another.

“For I have given you an example, so that just as I have done to you, you also may do.” The Lord gave us an example by forgiving our sins and redeeming us through his passion, so that we too may follow his footsteps, forgiving sins among ourselves daily and, if necessity should arise, being ready to die for Christ’s name, just as he deigned to die for us.

“Amen, amen, I say to you: a servant is not greater than his master, nor an apostle greater than the one who sent him” (John 13).

“You call me,” he says, “Lord and Teacher. Therefore, if you are servants, as you truly are, you are not greater than I, your Lord; and if you are my apostles, you are not greater than I, who sent you. For *apostle* is said in Greek, and in Latin means ‘one who is sent.’

“If you are not greater, follow me, who am greater than you. And if I have done such things for you, who are lesser, how much more ought you to assist your brothers in their needs? Just as I was beneficial to you, though I had no need of your beneficence, so you also should be beneficial to your brothers.

“If you know these things,” he says, “you will be blessed if you do them”—not, that is, being justified merely by knowing them, but by doing what you know.

“I do not speak about all of you. I know whom I have chosen. But this is so that Scripture may be fulfilled: ‘The one who eats my bread has raised his heel against me.’ I tell you this now, before it happens, so that when it has happened you may believe that I am he” (John 13).

“I do not say,” he says, “that all of you are blessed or will do what I have commanded you. But I know whom I have chosen. For he chose all twelve of them, but Judas alone so that this Scripture might be fulfilled: ‘The one who eats my bread has raised his heel against me.’ The others he chose to sow the seed of the holy Gospel throughout the world.

“Thus, brothers, you see daily in the Church false Christians who eat bread with us—that is, who share in Christ’s body and blood. You see them, I say, raising their heel against the Church, because at the end it will become clear what they were before, when they seemed to be with us but were not of us.

“They too are chosen, but for the Church’s testing, so that scandals may arise through them and the Church may advance through patience. For it is always necessary that scandals arise in the world, but woe to that person through whom scandals come.

“‘So that you may believe that I am he’—that is, that I am the one to whom this Scripture and all the holy Scriptures bear witness. For whatever was foretold in the old law was entirely fulfilled in Christ, while what remains is to be fulfilled at his second coming, when he comes, brings an end to all scandals, and leads the Church, cleansed from every stain and wrinkle, into his kingdom, but burns the chaff with unquenchable fire.” [Col. 0067C]

“Amen, I say to you: whoever receives the one whom I send receives me; and whoever receives me receives the one who sent me” (John 13).

This is known to you, brothers: Christ is received in his preachers. For at the end of the world he will say: “As often as you did it for one of the least of these who are mine, you did it for me.” And whoever receives Christ will rejoice at the coming of the entire holy Trinity.

When Jesus had said these things, he was troubled in spirit, and testified and said: “Amen, amen, I say to you: one of you will betray me.” The disciples were greatly saddened and looked at one another, uncertain of whom he was speaking. And they began one by one to say: “Surely it is I, Lord?”

One of his disciples was reclining at Jesus’ breast, the one whom Jesus loved. Simon Peter therefore beckoned to him and said to him: “Who is he, about whom he speaks?” So, when he had reclined upon Jesus’ breast, he said to him: “Lord, who is it?” Jesus answered: “It is the one to whom I shall give the morsel after dipping it.”

“The Son of Man indeed goes as it is written of him; but woe to that man through whom the Son of Man will be betrayed. It would have been better for that man if he had not been born” (John 13; Matt. 26).

The Lord foretold, with the betrayer himself listening, that one of them would betray him, giving him an opportunity for repentance, so that, if he wished, he might still refrain from so great a crime. When he did not recover his senses even through these words, he added something that identified him more clearly.

[Col. 0068A] “The one,” he says, “to whom I shall give the dipped morsel—he is the one.”

Judas, who betrayed him, answered and said: “Surely it is I, Rabbi?” He said to him: “You have said it.”

And while they were eating, Jesus said: “I have earnestly desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer.” And taking bread, he blessed it, broke it, and gave it to the disciples, saying: “Take and eat; this is my body, which will be handed over for you. Do this in remembrance of me.” And taking the cup, he gave thanks and gave it to them, saying: “Drink from it, all of you; for this is my blood of the New Testament, which will be poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins. I say to you that from now on I will not drink of this fruit of the vine until that day when I shall drink it new with you in the kingdom of my Father.”

“Nevertheless, behold, the hand of the one who betrays me is with me at the table.” And when he had dipped the bread, he gave it to Judas Iscariot; and after the morsel, Satan entered him (Matt. 26; Luke 22).

Judas, he says, answered: “Surely it is I, Rabbi?” He no longer deigned to call him Lord, as the other disciples did. For this is characteristic of the lost: when they are caught and reproved for a crime, they immediately begin to grow angry and swell with pride, as though by this they were excusing themselves from their sin.

And Jesus said: “You have said it.” He neither revealed it openly nor denied it, but said: “You have said it.” He answered Pilate the governor in the same way, for the question he asked was not worthy of being answered.

## CHAPTER V

While they were eating, Jesus took bread, and so forth.

These are the sacraments of our salvation, brothers; this is our spiritual nourishment; this is the salvation of our souls. We celebrate this sacrament daily on the holy altar. It began in this manner, after the old Passover had been completed by the Lord, as you have heard.

He therefore took bread. For this reason he wished this sacrament to be celebrated in bread: bread appropriately corresponds to the likeness of the Church. Bread passes through fire after being made from many grains that have been crushed and joined together, and becomes suitable for sustaining human life. The Church, joined from many holy people and crushed, as it were, by many tribulations, both internal and external, passes through death to heavenly life.

The Lord took this bread when he assumed a human body, and by taking it he blessed it. For it was said to our first parent Adam after the transgression: “Cursed is the earth in your work.”

[Col. 0068D] When Christ therefore assumed a body from this earth—from which Adam too was made—he blessed that earth by his assumption, releasing it from the curse. He broke it when he permitted himself to die on the cross, and he gave it to his disciples when he entrusted them with the ministry of preaching among the nations, saying: “Go, teach all nations.”

This is what he says here: “Take and eat.” That is: “Nations, make my body, which you already are. This is the body that is given for us.” For what he assumed from that mass of the human race, he broke through his passion and, once broken, raised it again. For bread must pass through fire.

Therefore what began from us he handed over for us. And “you also eat”—that is, perfect the body of the Church, [Col. 0069A] so that the whole perfected body may become one bread, as one body whose head is Christ.

And if you are still eating the bread of sorrow, although God will give his beloved sleep after their labors, then this is the Lord’s inheritance, in which it will remain forever.

And taking the cup, he gave thanks (Matt. 26). He gave thanks to God, who gives all things with the Father, so that he might give us an example, that we may know that we have received everything we possess from God.

“He gave it,” he says, “to them, saying: ‘Drink from this, all of you; for this is my blood of the New Testament’” (Matt. 26).

Every human being consists of two substances, namely body and soul. Therefore, so that both might be saved, both were assumed by the Lord. For this reason we are commanded in our sacrament to commemorate both his body and his blood [Col. 0069B]—that is, the soul which he handed over for us.

“This is,” he says, “the blood of the New Testament.” As a prefiguration of this, in the Old Testament the two doorposts of the houses of the children of Israel were marked with the blood of a lamb, so that the destroying angel might not enter. And as the Apostle says: “Moses sprinkled all the people with blood, saying: ‘This is the blood of the covenant that God commanded for you.’” And according to the law, almost everything is cleansed with blood.

The bread, then, is Christ’s body, which he assumed from the body of his Church; the blood, however, signifies his soul, which he received into the unity of his person. And just as you heard the Apostle say: “Almost everything was cleansed with blood,” so all our sins were cleansed by Christ’s blood poured out—that is, by his spirit being released.

For the same Apostle adds: “Let us draw near,” he says, “with a true heart in full faith, our hearts sprinkled with a good conscience.” Here you see, brothers, that that blood represents Christ’s soul, when he says “our hearts sprinkled.” For spirit can sprinkle spirit through a good example, but blood cannot sprinkle the heart.

The bread is compared with his body. When his soul left his body—for this was his death—our souls, sprinkled and sanctified by that soul, I say, become clean and immaculate. And for this reason the Lord said: “This is,” he says, “the blood of the New Testament.”

For Moses, speaking of the blood of the calf with which he sprinkled the people of Israel, said: “This is the blood of the covenant that the Lord commanded you.” But this blood of Christ was poured out for the forgiveness of sins; for the blood of the Old Testament forgave no one’s sins, since it held the figure of this blood but was not capable of bringing about the forgiveness of sins.

“I say,” he says, “to you: I will not drink from this fruit of the vine until I drink it new with you in the kingdom of my Father” (Matt. 26; Mark 14).

The Lord appears to have said this about the cup that he then gave the disciples to drink, because the time was near when, redeeming the world and giving it life through his death, he would establish the kingdom of God the Father.

“Nevertheless,” he says, “the hand of the one who betrays me is with me at the table” (Luke 22).

“If I,” he says, “will not drink of this fruit of the vine, nevertheless at this table—that is, with the Church present—even now the hand of the one who betrays me is with me. And so there will be many belonging to the portion of that same betrayer who put their hand upon my altar, yet do not belong to the kingdom of my Father. To that kingdom I will lead those souls whom I will drink in the kingdom of my Father”—that is, those whom I will make one in myself.

For many now put their hand to Christ’s sacraments in this Church, yet will not come to the heavenly kingdom. For although they appear outwardly to be sheep, inwardly they are ravenous wolves.

The Lord therefore dipped the bread and gave it to Judas Simon Iscariot, and after the morsel Satan then entered him (John 13).

This is it, my brothers; this is what customarily takes place in this Church. For when people presume to approach Christ’s sacraments with an unclean and wicked conscience, then indeed they eat and drink judgment upon themselves—namely, the judgment by which they are handed over to Satan. For after he had received the morsel, Satan entered Judas.

But you, brothers, examine yourselves, cleanse your consciences from hatred and every kind of malice, and so eat of that bread and drink from the cup.

Jesus said to him: “What you are doing, do quickly.” But none of those reclining knew why he had said this to him. Some thought, because Judas had the money box, that Jesus was saying to him: “Buy what we need for the feast,” or that he should give something to the poor.

When he had received the morsel, he went out immediately; and it was night (John 13).

“What you are doing,” he says, “do quickly”—not because the Lord commanded him to perish, but because he had already been judged, and the Lord wished what was to happen to be fulfilled through him.

“Do it quickly,” he says, “so that the Scriptures may be fulfilled” [Col. 0070C], which foretold my betrayal and death.

None of those reclining knew this. The other disciples understood simply everything that was said, just as earlier, concerning the ointment that had been poured out, the other disciples genuinely spoke on behalf of the poor: “Why this waste? For this could have been sold for much and given to the poor.”

So here too some thought—because Judas had the money box—that Jesus was saying to him: “Buy what we need for the feast,” or that he should give something to the poor. Perhaps Judas had previously been accustomed, when something was to be given to the poor, to steal it away; and earlier he had already secretly sold the Lord, which he now completed openly.

When Judas had received the morsel, he went out immediately. For darkness could not remain any longer with the light.

“It was night,” he says. Truly he was night [Col. 0070D] and darkness, because he was already wholly possessed by the devil.

## CHAPTER VI

When he had gone out, Jesus said: “Now the Son of Man has been glorified, and God has been glorified in him. If God has been glorified in him, God will also glorify him in himself, and will glorify him immediately.

“Little children, I am with you only a little longer. You will seek me; and as I said to the Jews, ‘Where I am going, you cannot come,’ so now I say to you.

“I give you a new commandment: that you love one another as I have loved you, and that you love one another. By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13).

When Judas had gone out—having become night and darkness—Jesus said: “Now the Son of Man has been glorified.” For that Judas represented all lost human beings; and therefore, when he had gone out, the Lord said: “Now the Son of Man has been glorified.” When night went out, day alone remained.

So, brothers, so it will be when all the lost go into eternal fire. Then the righteous will go into eternal life. Then the Son of God will become glorious, when in his body—that is, in the Church—nothing dark remains, but everything is bright.

“And God,” he says, “has been glorified in him.” For the Son of God himself, insofar as he is God, is always glorious and remains so. But in his body, which is the Church, much darkness still remains; when all of it has gone out, Christ’s Church will remain without stain.

“If God,” he says, “has been glorified in him, God also glorified him in himself.” For the Son is in the Father, and the Father in the Son. According to that nature by which he is in the Father and the Father in him, he is always glorious, as I have said, and there is no darkness in him.

“But God,” he says, “will immediately glorify him.” For it will happen, he says, that God will also glorify my body—that is, the Church—entirely, so that it too may be glorious. And this was soon to happen: namely, that the body which he assumed from us for us would be glorified through the glory of resurrection and immortality and placed at the right hand of God the Father.

“I am with you only a little while,” he says, “and where I am going, you cannot come” (John 13).

It was only a short time that he was then mortal with the disciples. And where he was going—that is, to the glory of immortality—they could not yet come. But so that they might know how they were to go there, he says: “Now I say to you: I give you a new commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you.”

“This,” he says, “is the way by which you must come to the glory of immortality: that you love one another as I have loved you.” For the same Lord said above: “I am the way and the truth.” He therefore became the way for the disciples to immortality and eternal life, saying: “Love one another as I have loved you.”

It is as though he said: “Go there in the way you have seen me going.” “By this,” he says, “everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another,” and the other things that he had told them at length about the same love of God and neighbor.

When that betrayer Judas went out, and the chosen disciples remained with him, he revealed many mysteries that he had not revealed to them before, while the one who was destined to perish had been present.

“By this,” he says, “everyone will know that you are my disciples”—that is, this is the sign of the Lord’s discipleship.

By this, brothers, the disciples of God and the disciples of the devil are always recognized. If you see someone loving his brother, know that he is Christ’s disciple. But if you see him hating his brother, whom he sees, know that he does not love God either, whom he does not see. Therefore he must belong to the devil, since he does not belong to God.

Always keep these words of the Lord in mind, my brothers; always demonstrate them by your deeds. For by this you will be recognized as belonging to God, if you love your brothers.

When, as I have said, the Lord was discussing at length with his disciples the love of God and neighbor, he raised his eyes to heaven and said:

“Father, the hour has come. Glorify your Son, so that your Son may glorify you, just as you gave him authority over all flesh, so that he may give eternal life to all whom you have given him. This is eternal life: that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent.

“I glorified you on earth; I completed the work that you gave me to do. And now glorify me, Father, with yourself, with the glory that I had with you before the world existed.

“I manifested your name to the people whom you gave me from the world. They were yours, and you gave them to me, and they have kept your word. Now they have come to know that everything you gave me is from you, because I gave them the words that you gave me, and they received them [Col. 0072B] and truly came to know that I came forth from you, and they believed that you sent me.

“I pray for them; I do not pray for the world, but for those whom you have given me, because they are yours. All mine are yours, and yours are mine, and I have been glorified in them.

“And now I am no longer in the world, but they are in the world, and I am coming to you. Holy Father, keep them in your name, whom you have given me, so that they may be one as we are.

“When I was with them, I kept them in your name. Those whom you gave me I guarded, and none of them perished except the son of perdition, so that Scripture might be fulfilled.

“But now I am coming to you, and I speak these things in the world so that they may have my joy fulfilled in themselves.

“I gave them your word, and the world hated them, because they are not of the world, just as I am not of the world. I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you preserve them from evil.

“They are not of the world, just as I am not of the world. Sanctify them in the truth. Your word is truth.

“As you sent me into the world, so I sent them into the world. And for their sake I sanctify myself, so that they too may be sanctified in truth.

“I do not pray for these only, but also for those who will believe in me through their word, so that all may be one, just as you, Father, are in me and I am in you; so that they too may be one in us, so that the world may believe that you sent me.

“And I have given them the glory that you gave me, so that they may be one as we are one. I in them and you in me, so that they may be perfected in one, and the world may know that you sent me and that you loved them as you loved me.

“Father, I desire that those whom you gave me be with me where I am, so that they may see my glory, which you gave me, because you loved me before the foundation of the world.

“Righteous Father, the world has not known you, but I have known you, and these have known that you sent me. I made your name known to them, and I will make it known, so that the love with which you loved me may be in them, and I in them” (John 17).

## CHAPTER VII

And after the hymn had been sung, they went out to the Mount of Olives (Matt. 26).

After he had offered to God a hymn of praise and a prayer for all believers—as you have just heard, brothers—they rose and went to the Mount of Olives. By this he signified that through the prayer which he prayed for them they would ascend the mountain of God’s mercy. For the oil that abounded on that mountain usually signifies mercy in holy Scripture.

Thus the disciples came to the Mount of Olives, as though to the height of God’s mercy, by the way that he was then showing them.

Then Jesus said to them:

“All of you will be scandalized because of me on this night. For it is written: ‘I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered.’ But after I have risen, I will go before you into Galilee” (Matt. 26).

The Lord foretold to his disciples that they would abandon him, and that they would do so on that very night. Therefore, my brothers, he took care to foretell it to them, so that when they had abandoned him and been scandalized because of him, they would not despair of salvation.

For just as he terrified them when he foretold that they would deny him, so he promised them mercy when he promised that he would rise and go before them into Galilee—as though he were saying: “You will indeed deny me, but my mercy will not abandon you.”

“I will go before you into Galilee”—that is, I will become immortal, and by passing over to that glory I will go before you; do not be afraid, for you too will follow me there. For *Galilee* is interpreted as “passing over.”

“When I have passed,” he says, “from this mortality to the glory of immortality, then you too will follow me as I go before you.”

Peter, however, answered him: “Even if all are scandalized because of you, I will never be scandalized.” Jesus said to him: “Amen I say to you, this very night, before the cock crows, you will deny me three times.” Peter said to him: “Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you.” And all the disciples said likewise (Matt. XXVI).

It was not, brothers, out of falsehood or rashness that Peter and the other apostles promised that they would die with the Lord even then and would never deny him; rather, their affection toward the Lord was ardent, but carnal. For the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified. They did indeed have the Spirit given by the Lord, but they were to receive him more fully after the Lord’s resurrection, so that they would not fear dying for the Lord. At that time, moved in spirit, they did not hesitate to make the promise, but, weakened in the flesh, they could not fulfill it.

The Lord therefore permitted Peter to deny him then, so that he might learn that the carnal affection he then held toward Christ had to be removed, and that Christ must be loved with the love of God, as he did afterward. Once he had done this, no power of the world could compel him to deny Christ. He permitted him to deny him then so that afterward, as the future leader of the Church, he himself might forgive sinners when he saw that the sin of denial had been forgiven him by the Lord.

And truly the blessed apostle Peter said that, even if he had to die, he would not deny the Lord—but that time had not yet come. For he was not to die with the Lord, but after the Lord and for the Lord. First Christ died for Peter and for all the faithful; afterward Peter died, not with him, but for him. No one could die with the Lord, because he alone died without guilt; for all other human beings, death is the punishment of sin. He died for our sin, not for his own, and we die for our sin, not for his. [Col. 0074A]

Then Jesus came with his disciples to a village called Gethsemane, where there was a garden. He entered it himself with his disciples. Judas, who was betraying him, also knew the place, because Jesus had often gone there with his disciples. The Lord said to his disciples: “Sit here while I go over there and pray.” And taking Peter and the two sons of Zebedee, he began to be sorrowful and troubled (Matt. XXVI; John XVIII).

The Lord came to the place called Gethsemane. He went there because he knew that his betrayer was accustomed to come there, so that, when he sought him, he would find him. For he was not fleeing from the passion for which he had come into the world, and which he had repeatedly foretold that he would undergo for us. [Col. 0074B]

He therefore took Peter and the two sons of Zebedee and began to be sorrowful and troubled. He took these disciples to witness the truth of his humanity, just as earlier he had taken them to witness his glory on the mountain, where Moses and Elijah were seen with him in majesty. Thus those who had been witnesses of his glory might also become witnesses of his humanity; and those who, taught by many signs, did not doubt that he was God might also know from this sign of sorrow that he was human.

He was sorrowful not for his own death, which, as we have said, he had come into the world to undergo, but for the destruction of that disciple of his who was the betrayer, and for the blindness of that people who had handed him over to death. For why would he be sorrowful on his own account as he was about to die, when he had earlier foretold to the disciples: “The Son of Man,” he said, “will be handed over to be crucified”? [Col. 0074C] By repeatedly proclaiming this beforehand to his disciples, he showed that he did not fear what he had graciously come into the world to accomplish. Rather, as he said above: “The Son of Man goes, as it is written.” He was not sorrowful about this, but about what follows: “But woe to that man through whom he will be betrayed.” For he was betrayed to the Jews by Judas, and by the Jews to the Gentiles.

He was therefore sorrowful for their destruction, not for his own passion, without which the world could not have been saved. He therefore said to the disciples:

“My soul is sorrowful even unto death; remain here and keep watch with me” (Matt. XXVI; Mark XIV).

You have heard, brothers, what the Lord said: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death”—not because of death. That passion prevailed over him only to the extent that he permitted it; for this reason also he said: “He began to be sorrowful.” He was sorrowful only as much as he wished to be. In this he differed from other human beings: he made use of every human emotion, but only to the extent that he chose.

CHAPTER VIII

“And going forward,” he says, “about a stone’s throw, he fell on his face, praying and saying: ‘My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will’” (Luke XXII; Matt. XXVI).

It was the human nature that he had assumed from the Jews that prayed this—not that he might refuse to undergo death, but that he might not receive it from those who were his relatives according to the flesh. “Nevertheless,” he says, “not as I will, but as you will.” He does not say, “Let it happen according to the will of the humanity assumed from the Jews,” but, “According to our one and eternal will, this and all things will happen.” For everything that the Lord willed, he did through his Son, and the will of the Father and the Son is always one. The Lord prayed these things so that human beings might know that this was indeed his will, and might not commit so great a crime against him as to crucify the Lord of glory. For he wills that all should be saved and that no one should perish.

“An angel of the Lord appeared to him from heaven, strengthening him; and, being in agony, he prayed more earnestly. And his sweat became like drops of blood falling to the ground” (Luke XXII).

The Lord’s angel appeared to him from heaven and strengthened him, just as earlier, when he was hungry, angels came and ministered to him. Whenever he himself wished it, those heavenly angelic spirits were present to him.

“And being in agony, he prayed more earnestly.” One prayed for all: the Lord for his servants, in order to make his servants friends. Great indeed were human beings’ sins, and therefore Christ worked their salvation through every kind of goodness. He gave them an example, being baptized in the Jordan while always without sin; he gave them commandments for living; he faithfully granted bodily health to everyone who asked; he devoted himself frequently to prayer, sometimes spending the night in it; he fasted; and finally, as you have just heard, he prayed for us with such intense struggle that his sweat became like drops of blood falling to the ground.

He did all these things by giving us examples, not because he needed any of them, but to provide an example for us, whom he had come to save. He sweated in order to free Adam, who had sweated. For it had been said to him: “By the sweat of your face you shall eat bread.” As if it were said: “You will not eat heavenly bread until one born from your flesh sweats for you.”

“And,” he says, “his sweat was like drops of blood falling to the ground.” By this sweat and this blood the earth—that is, the human race—was washed from the curse under which it had fallen when it was first said to the sweating man: “Cursed is the earth in your work”; and to the first who shed blood: “Cursed,” he says, “shall you be upon the earth, which has opened its mouth and received your brother’s blood from your hand.”

And he came to his disciples and found them sleeping. He said to Peter: “So, you could not keep watch with me for one hour? Keep watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation; the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matt. XXIV; Mark XIV). The apostles, not yet strengthened by the Holy Spirit, were overcome by sleep. He said to them: “Keep watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation.” The Church does this every day when it says: “Do not lead us into temptation.” For it is one thing not to be tempted, which cannot happen in this world; it is another not to be led into temptation. We pray daily that this may happen—not that he should lead us into temptation so that we fall when tempted, but that, standing firm, we may fight temptation courageously. Thus the apostle Paul also says: “Keep watch and stand firm in the faith, and act courageously.” “Your spirit,” he says, “is willing, but the flesh is weak”—willing to make promises, but burdened by fragile flesh and unable to fulfill what it has promised. [Col. 0076A]

Again, a second time he went away and prayed, saying: “My Father, if this cup cannot pass unless I drink it, let your will be done.” And he came again and found them sleeping, for their eyes were heavy, and they did not know what to answer him. Leaving them, he went away and prayed a third time, saying the same words (Matt. XXVI; Mark XIV).

In the second and third prayer he said: “Let your will be done, my Father,” as if he were saying: “If I am to drink this cup, let your will be done, as in heaven so also on earth, so that, through the taste of this cup, peace may come to people of good will throughout the whole earth. And if I am to be killed by the Jews, let your will be done among all the other nations, so that through their offense salvation may come to the Gentiles.” And he prayed this a third time, so that, when the fullness of the Gentiles had entered, all Israel might be saved. First he asks that he not receive the cup of death from the Jews. Second, that, if this could not be changed because it had been ordained by his and the Father’s counsel, the salvation of the Gentiles might come through their offense. Again, third, that after the salvation of the Gentiles the salvation of the Jews might also come.

Then he came to his disciples and said to them: “Sleep now and rest. It is enough. Behold, the hour has drawn near, and the Son of Man will be handed over into the hands of sinners. Rise, let us go. Behold, he who betrays me has drawn near” (Matt. XXVI).

CHAPTER IX

When Judas had received a cohort and attendants from the chief priests and Pharisees, he came there, and with him a large crowd with swords, clubs, lanterns, and torches, sent by the chief priests and the elders of the people (John XVIII).

Judas came with a large crowd and weapons so that, if the Lord happened to be found with a crowd of people, either he himself would be seized as the betrayer of his Lord, or Jesus would be defended by the crowd. They also brought lanterns and torches because it was night. And appropriately so: they were carrying out works of darkness in the darkness. Therefore, as the evangelist John says, “the darkness did not comprehend the light” so that it might shine for them; rather, as far as lay within them, they killed it so that it would not shine for others.

Jesus, knowing all that was about to happen to him, went forward and said to them: “Whom do you seek?” They answered him: “Jesus the Nazarene.” Jesus said to them: “I am he.” Judas, who was betraying him, was also standing with them. When he said to them, “I am he,” they went backward and fell to the ground.

See, brothers, what sort of power that darkness had against the light! At the one word with which he said to them, “I am he,” they all went backward and fell to the ground. Such is the power of human beings against God, and this regularly happens: wherever the light comes, the darkness flees as though going backward.

But the Lord also indicated something else by doing this. When he had first told the Jews that he himself was Jesus, the Jews did not then believe; rather, they went backward, remaining unbelieving, and fell into earthly works. But:

“Again,” he says, “he asked them: ‘Whom do you seek?’ They said: ‘Jesus the Nazarene’” (John XVIII). [Col. 0077A] Then they did not fall, because those who did not believe at first will believe at the end of the world.

Jesus answered: “I told you that I am he. If therefore you seek me, let these go, so that the word might be fulfilled which he spoke: ‘Of those whom you gave me, I have lost none’” (John XVIII).

When he asked them again whom they were seeking and they said, “Jesus the Nazarene,” he said: “If you seek me, let these go.” He could have allowed the apostles to leave while the Jews lay fallen on the ground; he could also have caused them not to rise again. But he said these words so that, if he did not allow them to seize him, the redemption of the human race might not be accomplished—the redemption for which he had come. And if he had not said to them, “Let these go,” they would have seized the disciples as well and handed them over to death, because they had been predestined for this: through them the Gentiles were to believe. [Col. 0077B]

These words may also be understood in another way, as though the Lord were saying openly to them: “Let these go first and preach to the Gentiles, so that, after the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, you too may be converted and saved. Thus, from all those whom God the Father gave him to become his body, he would not lose anyone, but would save both groups—that is, Jews and Gentiles.”

Now the one who betrayed him had given them a sign, saying: “Whomever I kiss, that is he; seize him.” And immediately approaching Jesus to kiss him, he said: “Hail, Rabbi,” and kissed him. Jesus said to him: “Friend, why have you come? Do you betray the Son of Man with a kiss?” (Matt. XXVI; Luke XXII).

Because it was night, the one who knew him gave them the sign of a kiss so that they would know whom to seize. He made the sign of peace into a sign of war. How many people today, brothers, touch with their lips while being far away in mind! With their mouths they offer peace, while their hearts plot wickedness. Here was fulfilled what the Lord said through the prophet: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me.”

Jesus said to him: “Friend, why have you come?” He calls him what he could have been, if he had wished; for he also said to the other disciples: “I will no longer call you servants, but friends.”

Then they approached, laid hands on Jesus, and seized him. Those who were around him, seeing what was about to happen, said to him: “Lord, shall we strike with the sword?” And behold, Simon Peter, having a sword, drew it, struck the servant of the chief priest, and cut off his right ear. [Col. 0077D] The servant’s name was Malchus.

Jesus answered: “Let it go as far as this. Put your sword back in its place, for all who take the sword will perish by the sword. Do you think that I cannot ask my Father, and he would immediately provide me with more than twelve legions of angels? Shall I not drink the cup which the Father has given me? How then will the Scriptures be fulfilled? For this must happen.” And when he had touched the man’s ear, he healed it (Matt. XXVI; Luke XXII; John XVIII).

Peter and the apostles were doing these things out of the carnal love with which they still loved the Lord. But this can also signify something for our understanding: when Peter and his fellow apostles preached to the Gentiles while the Jews refused to believe, they removed, as it were, the right ear—that is, the spiritual understanding of the law—so that they would not hear what the apostle Paul says: “The letter kills.” All these things happened to them in figure, and they did not know that “the spirit gives life”; and they were written for our justification.

The servant whose ear was cut off was named Malchus. This name is interpreted in Latin as “king,” because the kingdom that the Jews formerly possessed passed away from them, as the Lord himself said: “The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits.”

“All,” he says, “who take the sword will perish by the sword.” Everyone who takes that sword of which the Lord said, “I have not come to bring peace upon the earth, but a sword”—namely, the word of the love of God—will perish by this visible sword. For the preacher does not use a sword to take revenge on an adversary by shedding blood; rather, he must use the sword, that is, the word of God, so that by it he may defend the faithful and separate unbelievers from them.

When Elymas, a certain magician, opposed Paul the preacher of the word of God, Paul said to him: “Enemy, son of the devil, will you not cease subverting the straight paths of the Lord? And now, behold, the hand of the Lord is upon you, and you shall be blind.” Peter himself also used another sword against Simon Magus. For he said: “You have neither part nor share in this word,” separating him from those whose part he had been in the preaching of the Gospel.

The preacher of the faith must therefore use such a sword. By that visible sword he perished when he accepted the work of preaching, just as he dies to all the affairs of the world when he gives himself to the service of Christ alone. [Col. 0078C]

“Do you think that I cannot ask my Father, and he would immediately provide me with more than twelve legions of angels?” I do not need the assistance of twelve apostles; the whole earth and its fullness are mine. A legion, according to ancient custom, consisted of six thousand men; therefore twelve legions are seventy-two thousand, and there are that many languages among the nations.

“Why,” he says, “would I need such assistance from you, so that you might fight for me, when, if I wished to gather together all the languages of the nations with the angels who preside over each nation, I could do so?” The Lord himself will do this on the day of judgment, when all nations, tribes, and languages will be gathered to him.

As if he were saying: “Even now I could gather all the nations to myself; nevertheless, I do not do so now. I will first be judged unjustly by human beings, so that I may come again to judge the living and the dead justly.”

“How then will the Scriptures be fulfilled, for this must happen?” The Scriptures could not be fulfilled in any other way unless he allowed himself to be seized, scourged, and killed. Indeed, the salvation of the entire human race had to be accomplished through his passion.

And Jesus, taking hold of the ear, healed it. When the apostles went out to preach to the Gentiles, the Jews’ right ear was removed—that is, those people who possessed the right understanding of the Holy Scriptures. But when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then the right ear itself will also be restored to them by the Lord.

CHAPTER X

At that hour Jesus said to the crowds: “Have you come out as against a robber, with swords and clubs, to seize me? Every day I sat among you, teaching in the temple, and you did not seize me. But this is your hour, and the power of darkness.” All this happened so that the Scriptures of the prophets might be fulfilled. Then all the disciples, abandoning him, fled (Matt. XXVI; Luke XXII).

The armed Jews had gone out with a crowd against Jesus as against a robber, although he had so often been among them and they had not seized him. Nor would they have done so now if he himself had not wished it. For, as you heard above, with a single word he struck all of them down; and previously they had often wanted to seize him but could not, because his hour had not yet come.

“But now,” says the Lord, “this is your hour, and the power of darkness.” For darkness had come in darkness to seize the light. [Col. 0079B]

“All the disciples, abandoning him, fled.” He had said this to them above: “You will all be scandalized because of me this night.” For they had not yet been strengthened by the Spirit, and darkness still prevailed against them. Darkness held them so that they fled. Later, however, after receiving the Holy Spirit, they despised the threats of the rulers and priests and yielded neither to their scourges nor to their swords.

The cohort, the tribune, and the attendants of the Jews then seized Jesus, bound him, and brought him first to Annas. He was the father-in-law of Caiaphas, who was high priest that year. It was Caiaphas who had given the Jews the counsel that it was expedient for one man to die for the people (John XVIII).

The cohort and the tribune were Roman soldiers, whom the Jews sent with their men to seize Jesus. For they did not have the authority to presume to seize him without Roman soldiers. They therefore bound the Lord. For he came for this purpose: by his bonds to release us from the bonds of our sins.

Long before, the Jews had done spiritually what they then did bodily, binding Jesus—that is, holding the key of knowledge, the law, and the prophets—and neither entering themselves nor allowing others to enter.

Peter was following him from a distance, and so was another disciple. That disciple was known to the high priest, and he entered with Jesus into the courtyard of the high priest. Peter, however, stood outside at the door. The other disciple, who was known to the high priest, went out, spoke to the doorkeeper, and brought Peter in. After entering, he sat with the attendants to see the outcome (John XVIII; Matt. XXVI).

Peter followed the Lord from a distance with another disciple, namely the one who was going to deny the Lord. For that other disciple too had later fled after abandoning him.

But this may also be understood in another way: certain disciples followed the Lord more than the others—Peter and, as is thought, John—because these two customarily signify the whole Church in the holy Gospel. Peter signifies the faith of the Church, while John signifies love. These therefore followed the Lord because the Church imitated the faith and love of Christ. [Col. 0080A]

But they followed from a distance because Christ died for the Church without his own sin, whereas the Church dies for itself; and there is a great difference between dying for oneself and dying for another. Peter still feared human beings and at the same time loved the Lord. But when perfect love came to him, it cast out the fear of human beings, so that he loved the Lord alone and no longer feared their threats and terrors.

The high priest therefore questioned Jesus about his disciples and his teaching. Jesus answered him: “I have spoken openly, and I have always taught in the synagogue and in the temple, where all the Jews gathered. Why do you question me? Question those who heard what I spoke to them. Behold, they know what I said” (John XVIII). [Col. 0080B]

He did not question him in order to learn the truth—for, had he wished to hear it, he could have learned it many times before—but to lay a trap for him, in case he might hear him say something against God or against Caesar, so that he could judge him guilty of death.

When he had said this, one of the attendants standing nearby struck Jesus on the face, saying: “Is that how you answer the high priest?” Jesus answered him: “If I have spoken wrongly, bear witness to the wrong; but if I have spoken rightly, why do you strike me?” (John XVIII).

The Lord said to the high priest: “Why do you question me? Question those who heard me,” because it was not fitting for him to hear instruction in the truth from one whom he was holding bound. For this answer one of the attendants struck Jesus on the face.

O wicked hand and mind of the unrighteous, striking one who answers rightly! Behold, brothers, it is clear why Christ is called the Lamb who takes away the sins of the world. The Creator is struck by the creature, and he endures it, answering with nothing but words of justice and gentleness.

“If I have spoken wrongly,” he says, “bear witness to the wrong; but if I have spoken rightly, why do you strike me?” For their law says: “You shall not afflict the innocent and the just.” He ought therefore first to have given testimony concerning the crime and then to have struck him. But he not only failed to prove a crime, which he could not find in the Lord; he also struck him because of his words of truth.

O wondrous and ineffable patience! He whose hands made and formed us, who holds the earth in his fist and weighs the heavens in his palm, endured being struck by a servant of the Jewish high priest! He fulfilled what he had earlier commanded the disciples: “If anyone strikes you on the right cheek,” he says, “offer him the other also.” He offered it when he said: “If I have spoken wrongly, bear witness; and strike me if you find a crime.”

CHAPTER XI

Annas sent him bound to Caiaphas the high priest, where the scribes were and where the elders had gathered. The chief priests and the whole council were seeking false testimony against Jesus in order to hand him over to death. For many were giving false testimony against him, but their testimonies did not agree (John XVIII; Mark XIV).

They were seeking false testimony by which he might be found guilty of death, for they could not find true testimony. For how could they find a true accusation of crime in one who came without sin to take away the sins of the world? They sought false testimonies in order to punish him. But, as Solomon says: “A false witness will not go unpunished.” And their testimonies did not agree, because falsehood is usually divided against itself.

When many false witnesses had come forward, at last two false witnesses came and said: “We heard him say: ‘I will destroy this temple made with hands, and after three days I will build another not made with hands.’” Their testimony did not agree.

The high priest rose and stood in the midst, questioning him: “Do you answer nothing to what these men testify against you?” Jesus remained silent.

The high priest again questioned him, saying: “I adjure you by the living God: tell us whether you are the Christ, the Son of God.” Jesus said to him: “You have said so. Nevertheless, I say to you: From now on you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power and coming on the clouds of heaven.”

Then the high priest tore his garments, saying: “He has blasphemed! What further need have we of witnesses? Behold, now you have heard the blasphemy. What is your judgment?” And they all condemned him as deserving death (Matt. XXVI; Mark XIV).

“Last,” he says, “two false witnesses came.” They were false witnesses because they said what they had not heard the Lord say. The Lord had said: “Destroy this temple.” They reported that he had said: “I will destroy this temple.” But the Lord foretold what was going to happen. They, however, gave false testimony against him.

The Lord said to the Jews: “Destroy this temple,” because the Jews were going to kill the Lord; and “after three days,” he says, “I will raise it up”—not, as the false witnesses said, “I will rebuild it.” He was speaking about his body, which, as I have said, the Jews were going to kill, and which he raised up on the third day.

The high priest said to him: “Do you answer nothing to what these men testify against you?” But Jesus remained silent. For the Lord knew that the high priest was questioning him deceitfully so that he might be able to accuse him. Therefore he did not answer him. Why should he answer one whom he knew would not believe?

The high priest said: “I adjure you by the living God.” As I said above, he did this to compel him to say something by which he could accuse him and condemn him to death. But the Lord then answered him and said: “From now on you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power.” [Col. 0081D]

The Lord foretold the judgment that would come, at which he would judge the human race. As if he were saying: “Since you have now adjured me by that great name of my Father, I tell you what will happen, whether you wish it or not. You will see the one whom you now unjustly judge while he is bound, sitting at the right hand of the Father and coming to judge justly the one whom you now judge unjustly.”

Then the high priest tore his garments. It is the custom of the Jews that, when they hear some word against God, they tear their garments because they cannot endure blasphemy. At that time he thought that the Lord had spoken against God when he said that they would see him sitting at the right hand of the power of God. [Col. 0082A]

But this was not against God. In truth, he ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of God, and from there he will come to judge the living and the dead.

They condemned him as deserving death. Behold, brothers, for what crime Christ was judged deserving of death: because he foretold that he would sit at the right hand of God and come on the clouds of heaven.

Then the men who were holding him spat in his face and struck him with blows. Others slapped his face; others covered his face and, striking him, said: “Prophesy to us, Christ! Who is it that struck you?” And they said many other blasphemous things against him (Matt. XXVI).

The Lord endured all these kinds of insults for us, in order to free us from eternal disgrace. They covered his face and, striking him, said: “Prophesy! Who struck you?” It would have been easier for him to say this than to reveal what they were thinking in their hearts. Yet he, who can do all things, could do both; but it was not then the time to display signs to unbelievers. For above in the Gospel we read that the Lord himself revealed the thoughts of their hearts when he said: “Why do you think evil in your hearts?”

He who fills heaven and earth could easily have said which of those standing nearby had struck him. But then was the time when he was to be judged.
