The time will come when he himself will judge, bringing to light the hidden things of darkness, revealing the purposes of hearts, and repaying each person according to the deeds of his hands, whether good or evil.

CHAPTER XII

Peter was sitting outside in the courtyard warming himself, because it was cold. One maidservant approached him, and when she saw him sitting by the light and had looked at him closely, she said: “This man also was with Jesus the Galilean.” But he denied it before everyone, saying: “I do not know what you are saying.”

As he was going out through the doorway, another maidservant saw him and said to those who were there: “This man also was with Jesus the Nazarene.” Again he denied it with an oath, saying: “I do not know the man.”

After a little while those who were standing there approached and said: “Truly, you are one of them, for your speech makes it clear that you are a Galilean.” Then he began to curse and swear that he did not know the man.

Immediately, while he was still speaking, the cock crowed. The Lord turned and looked at Peter, and Peter remembered the word of the Lord, as he had said: “Before the cock crows, you will deny me three times.” And he went outside and wept bitterly (John XVIII; Luke XXII; Matt. XXVI). [Col. 0082D]

The fact that Peter, the chief of the apostles and, after the Lord, appointed the first shepherd of the Church, was permitted to deny him was not without purpose. It happened so that all preachers and leaders of the holy Church might learn from his example that sins can be forgiven those who sin and repent, since so great a crime of denial had been forgiven that leader of the Church. It also happened so that everyone might learn not to trust in his own strength, but to know that all the good accomplished by us depends upon God’s gift.

For the most blessed apostle Peter had not yet received the fullness of the gift of the Holy Spirit. Therefore he immediately experienced what human frailty can do if it is not raised up by God’s gift. He who then, timid and weak, was terrified by the words of a lowly maidservant later despised the threats and words of the emperor Nero, who at that time held power over the whole world. He possessed the fullness of the grace of the Holy Spirit, which, burning within him, did not allow him to be tested by the cold of unbelief, just as you have now heard in the Gospel that he was warming himself because it was cold. [Col. 0083A]

For then what the Lord had earlier foretold would happen was truly fulfilled in him: “Because lawlessness will abound, the love of many will grow cold.” But he who had been permitted to fall was immediately raised up by God’s mercy. For when Peter had denied him three times, the Lord looked at him, and Peter remembered the word by which he had foretold his fall.

“And he went outside,” it says, “and wept bitterly.” By weeping he wiped away what he had committed through presumption. “Immediately,” it says, “the cock crowed.” For after someone has sinned, it is necessary that he be summoned immediately to repentance by the preacher’s word, as by the voice of a crowing cock. The crowing cock foretells the approaching light, and the preacher ought to proclaim that through repentance the way back to the light of God’s mercy has been prepared.

You should also know, brothers, that because the one who accused Peter said, “Your speech makes it clear,” Peter should not be thought to have spoken a language different from that of the other Jews. Rather, as you yourselves know, every province and region has something distinctive in its speech, which it preserves as native to itself; and from this it is customary to infer from what province or region the speaker comes.

They also called Jesus a Galilean or Nazarene because he had been raised there by his parents out of fear of King Herod and his son Archelaus. For Nazareth is a city in Galilee. He was born in Bethlehem according to the prophecies of the prophets, because his parents too were from the house and family of David, whose lineage and birth belonged to Bethlehem.

Therefore, brothers, having heard Peter, the chief of the apostles, deny the Lord, let us also hear and do what he did after his denial. For he wept bitterly. If we weep but do not weep bitterly, our repentance is not yet complete. Rather, let the sins we have committed become bitter to us, and let us flee from them, because they are bitter. If we act in this way, the Lord will also be present to us, as he was present to Peter, and he will restore us to what we were when things were well with us.

CHAPTER XIII
[Col. 0083D] When morning came, all the chief priests and the elders of the people took counsel against Jesus and brought him before their council, saying: “If you are the Christ, tell us,” so that they might hand him over to death. And Jesus said to them: “If I tell you, you will not believe me; and if I question you, you will not answer me, nor release me.” Then the whole assembly of them rose, bound him, led him away, and handed him over to Pontius Pilate the governor. But they themselves did not enter the praetorium, so that they would not be defiled, but might eat the Passover (Matthew XXVII; Luke XXII; John XVIII).

What the Lord had foretold was fulfilled: “It is necessary,” he said, “[for the Son of Man] to go to Jerusalem and suffer many things from the elders, scribes, and chief priests, and afterward be handed over [Col. 0084A] to the Gentiles to be mocked, scourged, and crucified.” Yet although the Jews themselves and the Gentiles would have done these things with evil intent, it was nevertheless carried out by God’s dispensation, namely, so that this might signify that the first preachers, from among the Jews, would hand over the faith of Christ to the Gentiles, and that his glory would there be exalted over the whole earth.

“They themselves,” he says, “did not enter the praetorium, so that they would not be defiled.” They regarded it as defilement if they were in the same house with Gentiles, but did not see the greater defilement within themselves: that, filled with wicked thoughts, they had taken counsel about how to hand Jesus over to death—and this through the testimony of false witnesses. For the Lord had also foretold this about them: “Straining out the gnat, but swallowing the camel,” he said. And this is what they did: while avoiding that small, or rather nonexistent, [Col. 0084B] defilement, they incurred the great crime of homicide.

Then Judas, who had betrayed him, seeing that he had been condemned, was moved with repentance and returned the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and elders, saying: “I have sinned by betraying innocent blood.” But they said: “What is that to us? You see to it.” And throwing the pieces of silver into the temple, he departed, and going away he hanged himself with a noose (Matthew XXVII).

This repentance of Judas was indeed fruitless, but it happened for this reason: so that the Jews might become inexcusable, since Judas himself, the betrayer, declared to them that the Lord was innocent and that his blood had been unjustly shed. “And going away,” he says, “he hanged himself with a noose.” For he was not worthy, in dying, either to touch heaven or earth; but he perished between the two, having handed over to death the Lord of both.

Yet the wretched traitor himself hoped that they would release the Lord after he had been scourged. But when he saw that he had already been handed over to the Gentiles, he understood that he was to be condemned to death; for it was the custom of the Jews that anyone whom they found guilty of death they should hand over to the governor for punishment.

But the chief priests, having received the pieces of silver, said: “It is not lawful to put them into the *corbanan* [Vulgate, *corbonam*], because it is the price of blood.” After taking counsel, they bought with them the potter’s field as a burial place for foreigners. For this reason that field was called *Acheldemach* [Vulgate, *Haceldama*], that is, “Field of Blood,” to this day. Then what was spoken through the prophet Jeremiah was fulfilled, saying: “And they took the thirty pieces of silver, the price of the one whose price had been set, whom they priced among the children of Israel, and they gave them for the potter’s field, as the Lord appointed for me” (Matthew XXVII).

*Corbanan*, in Hebrew, may be called in Latin something like “a gift” or “offering”; it was the place into which the gifts offered to God were deposited by the people. The Jews did this with evil intent, but although they did not wish it, their deed became for us a prophecy. For at the price of Christ’s blood the field was purchased for us—that is, the Church—in which, dying to sins, we are buried in baptism, so that, living in righteousness, we may rest in it. The Church is the potter’s field, that is, the Lord’s, who first fashioned humanity from the clay of the earth.

Pilate therefore went outside the praetorium to the Jews and said: “What accusation do you bring against this man?” They answered and said to him: “If he were not a criminal, we would not have handed him over to you.” They accused him, saying that they had found him subverting their nation, forbidding the payment of taxes to Caesar, and saying that he himself was Christ the king.

When he was accused by the chief priests, he answered nothing. Then Pilate said to him: “Do you not hear how many testimonies they bring against you?” And he did not answer him a single word, so that the governor was greatly astonished.

Pilate said to the Jews: “Take him yourselves and judge him according to your law.” The Jews said: “It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death”—so that the word of Jesus might be fulfilled, by which he signified what kind of death he was to die (John XVIII; Luke XXIII; Matthew XXVII).

The Jews said: “It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death,” while Pilate wanted them to judge him according to their law. Why would it not have been lawful for them to put him to death if he had been a criminal, since it is written in their law: “You shall not permit sorcerers to live”? But the Lord, who was not a criminal but the author of every good thing, had foretold that he would be handed over to the Gentiles to be scourged and crucified. This is what the evangelist means when he says, “signifying what kind of death he was to die.”

It was necessary that what Truth itself had foretold concerning himself should be fulfilled—namely, that he would be handed over to the Gentiles, as we said above. Nor is there no mystery in the fact that the Jews, although they themselves did this with evil intent, handed the Lord over to the Gentiles. For the apostles, from among the Jews, preached Christ to the Gentiles, among whom his body—that is, the Church—has suffered many adversities from that time to this day. “Through many tribulations,” the Apostle says, “we must enter the kingdom of God.” For the Church herself, which is the body of Christ, does not cease to labor under persecutions until the end of the world; yet all these will end on the final day of the resurrection of all, and thereafter they will never again occur throughout eternity.

## CHAPTER XIV

Pilate entered the praetorium again, summoned Jesus, who stood before him, and the governor questioned him, saying: “Are you the king of the Jews?” Jesus said to him: “Do you say this of your own accord, or have others told you about me?” Pilate answered: “Am I a Jew? Your nation and the chief priests have handed you over to me. What have you done?” (John XII.)

Jesus stood before the governor: the just Judge of heaven stood before an unjust judge of earth. The first man, Adam, stood before God in pride, excusing himself for the sin he had committed. The Lord, the Redeemer of the human race, did not excuse himself, although he was conscious of no sin whatsoever, having committed none. Yet in order to free us from our pride through his humility, he deigned to endure the judgment of the wicked—he who is to come to judge all the righteous and the wicked.

Jesus answered Pilate: “My kingdom is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would certainly fight so that I would not be handed over to the Jews; but now my kingdom is not from here” (John XVIII).

“My kingdom,” he says, “is not of this world,” because he received from God the Father, as King and Son of God, that he should be almighty—not from the mortality of the world. His kingdom therefore did not begin with that mortality which he assumed from the world. Rather, he himself, eternally King and God without beginning, became a mortal human being for us, so that he might reign temporally in this world, but might make those for whose redemption he had come his eternal kingdom.

“If my kingdom were of this world,” he says, “my servants would fight so that I would not be handed over to the Jews.” If he had wished to rule human beings as a mortal in a temporal kingdom, he could have employed angelic ministries for this purpose. After he had fasted forty days and nights, angels came and ministered to him, never abandoning him, because they were always present to serve him—indeed, they came with him from heaven when he was born of the Virgin, and with them he will come to judgment in the glory of his Father.

Thus angelic ministries were never lacking even to him after he had become human; through them he, being almighty, could accomplish whatever he wished. He would not therefore have been handed over to the Jews if he had not wished it, for thousands upon thousands of angels stood beside him. When he wished to be handed over to the Jews, the extent of his power was nevertheless revealed: at the sound of a single word from him, they went backward and fell to the ground—earth which, had he wished it, would immediately have swallowed them alive.

This saying of the Lord—“My kingdom is not of this world”—may also be understood of the Jews. For when Pilate had said, “Your nation and your chief priests have handed you over to me,” he replied: “My kingdom is not of this world”—that is, because their sins demanded it, my kingdom is no longer of this world of the Jews and their chief priests. The kingdom of God had then been taken away from them and given to a nation producing its fruits.

Pilate said to him: “Then you are a king?” Jesus answered: “You say that I am a king. For this I was born, and for this I came into the world: to bear witness to the truth. Everyone who is of the truth hears my voice.” Pilate said to him: “What is truth?” And after saying this, he went outside again to the Jews (John XVIII).

“I was born for this,” the Lord says, “and for this I came into the world: to bear witness to the truth.” The Lord was born for this and came into the world for this: to reveal to the world the truth, which is the Lord himself. For he himself is the truth, and he bore witness to the truth when he preached it in the world.

The old law was, as it were, certain members of Christ’s future coming; Christ himself, however, is the truth. “Everyone,” he says, “who is of the truth hears my voice.” For whoever is from Christ and in Christ hears Christ’s voice. We are his members, and therefore we hear his voice—that is, we believe the truth as it teaches us.

Pilate therefore went outside again to the Jews and said to them: “I find no case against him.” But they grew more insistent, saying: “He stirs up the people, teaching throughout all Judea, beginning from Galilee and reaching even to here.”

When Pilate heard this, he asked whether the man was a Galilean. And when he learned that he belonged to Herod’s jurisdiction, he sent him to Herod, who himself was also in Jerusalem in those days. When Herod saw Jesus, he rejoiced greatly [Col. 0087A], for he had long desired to see him, because he had heard many things about him, and he hoped to see some sign performed by him. He questioned him at length, but he answered nothing.

The chief priests and scribes stood by, persistently accusing him. Herod, with his soldiers, despised him and mocked him; he dressed him in a white garment and sent him back to Pilate. And Herod and Pilate became friends on that very day, for previously they had been enemies of one another (John XVIII; Luke XXIII).

The fact that the Lord was sent by the governor to the king of the Gentiles, although they themselves did not understand it, signified what was taking place: Christ was to be preached by the Jews and, as it were, sent to the Gentiles. Then he was sent back again from the king of the Gentiles to the governor of the Jews, because at the end of the world, when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, all Israel will be saved.

“And Herod and Pilate became friends,” he says. The unjust condemnation of Christ produced an impious and treacherous concord between wicked kings. But, as the Psalmist says, “They are to be destroyed, not built up,” being enemies of the truth. For Christ is the peace of angels and human beings; whoever is opposed to peace cannot be a friend either to himself or to anyone else.

Pilate, having summoned the chief priests, the magistrates, and the people, said to them: “You brought me this man as one who was subverting the people. And behold, I have examined him in your presence and found no case in this man concerning the matters of which you now accuse him. Nor did Herod; for I sent you to him, and behold, nothing deserving death has been done by him. Therefore, after correcting him, I will release him.”

Now on the solemn day the governor was accustomed [Col. 0087C] to release to the people one prisoner whom they wished. At that time they had a notorious prisoner called Barabbas, who was imprisoned with the rebels and had committed murder during the insurrection. When the crowd had gathered, Pilate began to ask them, as he always did for them.

Pilate said to them: “It is customary for me to release one prisoner to you at the Passover. Whom do you want me to release to you: Barabbas, or Jesus who is called Christ?” For he knew that they had handed him over out of envy. But the chief priests stirred up the crowd to ask for Barabbas and destroy Jesus.

The entire crowd cried out together, saying: “Take this man away, and release Barabbas to us.” Pilate said to them: “What then shall I do with Jesus who is called Christ?” They all said: “Let him be crucified.” The governor said to them: “What evil has he done?” But they cried out even more loudly, saying: “Let him be crucified” (Luke XXIII; Matthew XXVII; Mark XV).

The reason the people and the leaders of the Jews burned with such hatred against Jesus that they handed him over to death was nothing other than this: they themselves were enemies of the truth and could not endure the truth present among them. Their previous sins had also brought it about that all love of God and neighbor departed from their hearts.

If they had loved God, they would never have persecuted him who preached daily in the temple, teaching them God’s commandments. Or if they had loved their neighbor, remembering his benefits—by which he restored sight to the blind, movement to the lame, and lost life even to the dead—they could have ceased persecuting him.

But because, as we said, they had been deprived of love of God and neighbor [Col. 0088A], they had no place within themselves for goodwill or justice, by which they might have known that a benefactor ought not to be condemned. Even the Gentile governor Pilate seemed more devoted to justice, since he repeatedly tried to declare him innocent.

Therefore, brothers, whenever you see anyone devoted to love of God and of the brethren, do not doubt that he is God’s temple and that God’s Spirit dwells in him. But whoever is without charity can never possess any true virtue.

The hearts of the Jews, being empty of charity, could not love Christ. Therefore they preferred to have a rebellious robber released to them rather than hold fast to peace, which is Christ. They rejected him who healed the people and chose the one who had committed murder in an insurrection.

*Barabbas* is interpreted as “son of their master.” The Jews chose the son of their master—that is, of the devil. For he himself, as the Lord says, “was a murderer from the beginning and did not stand in the truth.”

## CHAPTER XV

Then Pilate took Jesus and scourged him. The soldiers plaited a crown of thorns, placed it on his head, wrapped him in a purple garment, and came to him, saying: “Hail, King of the Jews” (John XIX).

Pilate did this according to Roman custom. Considering Jesus guilty, he wished to determine by the scourging the measure of the offense for which he had been handed over to him. But by his divine and gracious dispensation, Christ deigned to endure this form of punishment for us, so that he might heal the wounds of the sins we had contracted with his innocent wounds.

Mystically, too, this action of Pilate and the Roman soldiers signified that the future body of Christ—that is, the Church—would be torn by the repeated scourges of Gentile persecutions, and yet that those same persecutors would afterward believe in him and worship him as the King of glory.

The crown of thorns placed upon Christ’s head may also signify the crime of idolatry, by which the Gentiles, ignorant of his true divinity, bestowed the divine name upon various inventions of idols. By wrapping Christ’s body in a purple garment, they foreshadowed the frequent, indeed continual, outpourings of blood—from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of the Lord himself and of his body—with which those who shed the innocent blood of the saints surrounded the body of Christ, that is, the Church.

Pilate therefore went outside again and said to the Jews: “Behold, I am bringing him outside to you, so that you may know that I find no case against him.” Jesus therefore came out, wearing the crown of thorns and the purple garment. And he said to them: “Behold the man.”

When the chief priests and the attendants saw him, they cried out, saying: “Crucify him, crucify him!” Pilate said to them: “Take him yourselves and crucify him, for I find no case against him.” The Jews answered him: “We have a law, and according to the law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God” (John XIX).

As was their custom, the Jewish people held the law in words, not in deeds. Here they falsely interpreted the law they had received, saying that Christ ought to die because he had made himself the Son of God.

For the Lord himself says in the law: “I have begotten and exalted sons.” And: “I said, ‘You are gods and sons of the Most High.’” And: “Israel is my firstborn son.” And: “From Egypt I called my son.” And to our Lord Jesus Christ himself he said: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you.”

How, then, could he who had made himself the Son of God die according to the law, when God the Father himself had so often called him Son—not only him, but also that whole people, whom he frequently called by the name of sons? He ought not therefore to have died for this reason, that he made himself the Son of God, since he truly was so.

When Pilate heard this statement, he became even more afraid. He entered the praetorium again and said to Jesus: “Where are you from?” But Jesus gave him no answer (John XIX).

The Lord had answered some of Pilate’s other questions; but when Pilate asked him where he was from, he did not answer him, because he knew that Pilate was not worthy to have so great a mystery revealed to him. For he is from the Father, as he himself says: “I came forth from the Father and came into the world”; and: “I proceeded from God.” This, then, was not to be said to unbelieving Pilate—where the Lord was from.

Pilate said to him: “You will not speak to me? Do you not know that I have authority to crucify you, and authority to release you?” Jesus answered: “You would have no authority against me unless it had been given to you from above. Therefore the one who handed me over to you has the greater sin” (John XIX).

Pilate would have had no authority against the Lord unless the Lord himself had handed him over to Pilate. And the one who handed him over to Pilate himself had no authority to hand him over except insofar as the Lord permitted it. He was therefore handed over because he willed it, just as he became human because he willed it.

The Jews handed him over to Pilate, and they themselves had the greater sin, since they handed him over to death, rather than those who crucified him. Hence the evangelist Mark reports that he was crucified at that time—that is, at the third hour of the day—when the people were demanding that he be crucified. By this he clearly showed that he was crucified by those who, with evil intent, handed him over to death.

From then on Pilate sought to release him, but the Jews cried out, saying: “If you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend. Everyone who makes himself a king opposes Caesar” (John XIX).

O cruel treachery and savage wickedness! Earlier they had said that he ought to die because he had made himself the Son of God. But when they saw that they were accomplishing nothing by this, they turned to another argument, saying that he was guilty of death because he had rebelled against Caesar.

But they said this falsely. They had never seen Christ seek the power of an earthly kingdom, since heaven and earth and all their fullness belong to him. Indeed, he did not refuse to pay the census tax for himself and his disciples; and at the first registration he deigned to be born and wished his parents to come for the census enrollment.

When Pilate heard these statements, he brought Jesus outside and sat on the tribunal, in the place called the Lithostrotos, and in Hebrew *Gabbatha*. It was the day of Preparation for the Passover, about the sixth hour. As he sat on the tribunal, his wife sent to him, saying: “Have nothing to do with that righteous man; for today I have suffered many things in a dream because of him.”

Pilate therefore said to the Jews: “Behold your king.” But they cried out: “Take him away, take him away; crucify him!” (John XIX; Matthew XXVI.)

As Pilate sat on the tribunal, his wife sent to him, saying that he should have nothing to do with that righteous man, since he had done no evil. Many think that the devil had already begun to understand the benefit of the Lord’s passion and the good that would come from it for the human race, and had persuaded the woman to impede the benefit of Christ’s death.

Pilate said to them: “Shall I crucify your king?” The chief priests answered: “We have no king but Caesar.”

This is what the Lord had said above: “My kingdom is not of this world.” For that world—that is, the unbelieving people—denied Christ as king and subjected themselves to Caesar’s kingdom, lest they become God’s kingdom.

But we, my brothers, pray daily in prayer that his kingdom may come and that he himself may reign in us, since he has made us a chosen race, a royal priesthood. Hence the Lord himself says: “I have been established as king by him”—not over those who said, “We have no king but Caesar,” but over his holy Mount Zion, to proclaim the Lord’s commandment: namely, the Church of the Gentiles, or rather one Church from both peoples, Jews and Gentiles.

When Pilate saw that he was accomplishing nothing, but that rather a riot was arising, he took water and washed his hands before the people, saying: “I am innocent of the blood of this righteous man; you see to it.” And the whole people answered: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matthew XXVII).

Pilate washing his hands signifies the people cleansing themselves through baptism from the impurity of innocent blood. It is said that this was customary among the ancients: whenever someone wished to show himself innocent, he washed his hands with water before witnesses. Hence the Psalmist also says: “I will wash my hands among the innocent.”

## CHAPTER XVI

Then he handed him over to them to be crucified. The soldiers of the governor took Jesus into the praetorium and gathered the whole cohort around him. They stripped him and wrapped him in a scarlet cloak. They plaited a crown of thorns, placed it on his head, and put a reed in his right hand. Kneeling before him, they mocked him, saying: “Hail, King of the Jews.” They spat upon him, took the reed, and struck his head (John XIX; Matthew XXVII).

The Lord endured all these kinds of insults for us, so that he might free us from the reproach of the devil. Yet each individual detail may also be understood, although those who performed these acts did not know it, as a mystery concerning Christ and the Church.

After they had mocked him, they stripped him of the cloak and dressed him in his garments, and led him away to crucify him (Matthew XXVII).

The soldiers’ mockery, as we said above, was, although unknown to them, a saving prophetic sign understood by us. For the fact that they stripped him of his garments signifies that human cruelty has often chosen to extinguish the saints of God, who are his garments.

They wrapped his body in a scarlet cloak. By repeated outpourings of blood and slaughters of the saints, they stained the Church of Christ with blood. They plaited a crown and placed it on his head. The head of Christ is God the Father. Thus, by that worship with which God ought to be served, human beings or animals of every kind were worshiped.

They placed a reed in his right hand. This signifies that they preferred the temporal kingdom of the world to the right hand, which is the heavenly kingdom. In Scripture the Lord’s left hand generally signifies the present age, while the right hand signifies the eternal kingdom of the saints in heaven.

A reed is therefore given into Christ’s right hand whenever the fragile things of this left hand are preferred by fools to the eternal kingdom of God. Again, they themselves took it and struck his head. This is what the fragile power of this world tends to do: not only does it refuse to submit itself to God in worthy service, but it also provokes persecutions against his name insofar as it is able.

They stripped him of the cloak and dressed him in his garments. Those who had first persecuted him afterward clothed the Lord in his garments; indeed, the persecutors themselves became the Lord’s garments when they believed in him whom they had hated without cause.

They took Jesus and led him away. Carrying his own cross, he went out. As they went out, they found a man of Cyrene coming from the countryside, the father of Alexander and Rufus. They compelled him to carry his cross. They came to the place called the Place of the Skull, which in Hebrew is *Golgotha*, and they gave him wine mixed with gall to drink. When he had tasted it, he refused to drink. And they crucified him, with two others, one on each side, and Jesus in the middle (John XIX; Mark XV; Matthew XXVII).

As the Lord went out from the praetorium, he carried his own cross. He carried the cross for himself—the one who had previously commanded his own: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him take up his cross and follow me.” He therefore went ahead so that the others might follow.

Simon was found and compelled to carry the Lord’s cross. *Simon* is interpreted as “obedient.” Whoever therefore wishes to obey the command of the Lord who goes before him takes up the cross and follows the Lord.

See, brothers, that this Simon was compelled to carry the Lord’s cross, whereas the Lord himself carried it willingly. The Lord’s passion was indeed voluntary; but although the holy martyrs accepted theirs with as good a will as they could, each nevertheless died for his own sins. He, however, deigned to undergo a necessary death not for himself but for us.

And we, brothers, although we do not suffer persecution from anyone unto death, can nevertheless carry the Lord’s cross by putting to death our members—that is, the unlawful desires that are upon the earth—by disciplining our bodies and bringing them into subjection, so that the body may be subject to the soul as a maidservant to her mistress.

And whenever our brothers commit something against us, we carry the Lord’s cross if we forgive what they have done and return good to them with a kindly heart instead of evil.

They gave him wine mixed with gall to drink. The Jews, who possessed knowledge of the one God but did not keep his law, gave the Lord something like wine mixed with gall when they opposed him, whom they knew, through their wicked deeds, making knowledge bitter with sins. Even to this day those who know God well but despise his commandments give him wine mixed with gall.

They crucified Jesus between two robbers. He wished to suffer this kind of death so that the human race, which had perished through the fruit of the forbidden tree, might be saved through the wood of the cross. Eve ate the forbidden fruit hanging upon the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, and she died; and through the fruit of eternal life hanging upon the wood of the cross, the human race was raised from death.

“He who eats,” he says, “my flesh has eternal life.”

The Lord was also stretched out upon the cross in order to signify that the kingdom of the whole world would be his. For by his outstretched arms he showed that the breadth of the whole world was to be drawn toward him. “If I am lifted up,” he says, “I will draw all things to myself.”

He was crucified in the midst of robbers, one of whom remained unbelieving, while the other became faithful and merited entry into the kingdom of heaven. For Christ is the just Judge who will come between two peoples: assigning one to eternal fire for its evil merits, while saving the other by his mercy and rewarding it with the eternal kingdom of his Father.

Pilate also wrote the title of his charge and placed it above his head. It was written: “Jesus the Nazarene, King of the Jews.” Many of the Jews read this title, because the place where Jesus was crucified was near the city. It was written in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin.

The chief priests of the Jews therefore said to Pilate: “Do not write, ‘King of the Jews,’ but that he himself said, ‘I am King of the Jews.’” Pilate answered: “What I have written, I have written” (John XIX).

When Pilate wrote the title and said, “This is the King of the Jews,” he signified the future faith of the Gentiles. But when the Jews opposed what he had written, they were doing what that nation continues to do to this day: opposing the Gentiles who believe that Jesus is Christ, the Son of God.

But whether they wish it or not, Jesus is the King of the Jews—that is, of those who confess him. For whoever confesses him before human beings, he too will confess him before the angels of God. The Lord is therefore the King of such confessors: “I have been established by him over his holy Mount Zion,” he says.

A psalm’s inscription speaks of this title: “Do not destroy the inscription of the title.”

Jesus said: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke XXIII).

The Lord fulfilled what he had previously commanded his disciples: “Pray,” he says, “for those who persecute and slander you.” His prayer could certainly not have been without effect. Many of the Jews for whom he prayed at that time, not knowing that the one whom they were condemning to death was the Son of God, afterward converted and believed, and were added to the number of the faithful. It is reported that three thousand of them believed on one day and five thousand on another.

## CHAPTER XVII

When the soldiers had crucified Jesus, they took his garments and divided them into four parts, one part for each soldier, as well as the tunic. The tunic was seamless, woven from the top throughout. They therefore said to one another: “Let us not tear it, but cast lots for it, to decide whose it shall be,” so that the Scripture might be fulfilled: “They divided my garments among themselves, and for my clothing they cast lots” [Col. 0093A] (John XIX).

The soldiers who crucified the Lord took his garments and divided them into four parts. These four soldiers signify the four regions of the whole world. From these regions, all the nations, receiving Christ’s garments—that is, the apostles and preachers—form one Catholic Church through faith.

Although these garments are divided among the four regions of the world, they are nevertheless one tunic through the one charity of Christ. The Church of Christ is divided in place but joined by the unity of charity. Of this it is said: “The tunic was seamless, woven from the top throughout.”

Charity was not constructed by human art or ingenuity. Rather, the unity and charity of the Church is God’s gift, woven from the indissoluble fellowship of many souls. The tunic therefore was not to be torn, because neither can the charity of the saints be torn nor their unity divided.

Let a Christian therefore fear doing what a pagan was not bold enough to do. For the soldiers said: “Let us not tear it, but cast lots for it, to decide whose it shall be.” The Lord is our lot and our portion; by this lot we shall possess charity.

Or the four soldiers may signify the four evangelists, who divided among themselves the deeds of the Lord to be narrated, while all four preached one tunic, that is, the charity of Christ. For, as the Apostle says, the whole law is fulfilled in one word of love. Everything, therefore, that the four evangelists relate concerning the Lord’s deeds tends toward the one end of charity, which, woven from above, cannot be torn or divided.

Those passing by blasphemed him, shaking their heads and saying: “Ah, you who destroy the temple of God and rebuild it in three days, save yourself! If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross” (Matthew XXVII).

They were speaking without understanding. What the Lord was doing at that time concerned the destruction and restoration of the temple of God—namely, his body—which, after raising it from the dead on the third day, he rebuilt.

Those who mocked him, and the soldiers who came near and offered him vinegar, said: “If you are the King of the Jews, save yourself.”

Similarly, the chief priests, mocking him with the scribes and elders, said: “He saved others; he cannot save himself. If he is the King of Israel, let him now come down from the cross, and we will believe him. He trusted in God; let him deliver him now, if he wants him. For he said, ‘I am the Son of God’” (Luke XXIII; Matthew XXVII).

The chief priests were saying this in a certain way prophetically: “He saved others; he cannot save himself.” For he saved the Gentiles, while the Jews, related and close to him according to the flesh, remained unbelieving.

“If he is the King of Israel, let him now come down from the cross, and we will believe him.” The Lord did what seemed more impossible: he rose from the tomb after dying. Yet those who had promised that they would believe if he came down alive from the cross did not believe him when he rose.

One of the criminals who were hanging there was blaspheming him, saying: “If you are the Christ, save yourself and us.” But the other answered and rebuked him, saying: “Do you not even fear God, since you are under the same condemnation? And we indeed justly, for we are receiving what our deeds deserve; but this man has done nothing wrong.” And he said to Jesus: “Lord, remember me when you come into your kingdom.” And Jesus said to him: “Amen, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke XXIII).

Here too this righteous man displayed the judgment of his equity between a believing and an unbelieving criminal. One of the criminals blasphemed him together with the Jews, saying: “If you are the Christ, save yourself and us.” For this man signifies that body of the devil which, remaining unbelieving, is alienated from the truth of God; the head of that body expressed the same word of doubt: “If you are,” he said, “the Son of God, command that these stones become bread.” But the other confessed that he and his companion had justly received the sentence of condemnation, while he recognized that the Lord, who had done nothing wrong, was suffering for his own sins and for those of the whole faithful people. “We are condemned justly,” he said, “for we are receiving what our deeds deserve; but this man has done nothing wrong” [Col. 0094B].

O great faith of the criminal—or rather, a great work in the criminal belonging to the same Lord and filled with his compassion! He saw a man hanging on a tree. He did not see him illuminating the blind, cleansing lepers, casting out demons, restoring hearing to the deaf, raising the dead, feeding five thousand people with five loaves, or walking upon the sea; but, although he saw him afflicted with torments alongside himself, he nevertheless believed him to be the Lord of majesty and recognized him as king. “Lord,” he said, “remember me when you come into your kingdom!” He saw him crucified and called him Lord; he did not doubt that he would die, yet he believed that after his death there would be a kingdom.

This, brothers, was not the work of that man but the marvelous work of God in the human heart. He heard nothing outwardly of his teaching, but the one who taught was within. And Jesus said to him: “Amen, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise.”

At the very time of the Lord’s passion, of the criminals crucified with the Lord one was found reprobate and the other chosen; so that we might be warned that there are two classes of human beings. To the one, whom he will place on the left, the Lord himself will say: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire”; to the other, whom he promises to glorify on the right, he will say: “Come, you blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.” For this chosen man also prayed for that very thing, saying: “Lord, remember me when you come into your kingdom.” He requested entry into the kingdom which the Lord promised would be given at the end to his chosen ones.

See, brothers, what a great manifestation of God’s mercy was accomplished in one word: he, now on the point of death, erased all the sins of the former life. He confessed the Lord, and by that confession earned entry into paradise; for he became a martyr from being a criminal. When he climbed onto the cross, he was a criminal; when he hung on the cross, he became a confessor and martyr.

Let us not despair, brothers, over past sins. There is no delay with the Lord who forgives, if our spirit is ready to confess and abandon the sins we have committed; for the bosom of his mercy is always ready. And observe that both had previously been criminals, since the whole human race was subject to sins; but the portion of the chosen, turning away from sins and converting to faith, was made worthy of entry into paradise [Col. 0094D]. The rejected portion, however, remaining like the unbelieving criminal, is to be punished with eternal fire.

“Today,” he says, “you will be with me in paradise.” Christ, the Son of God, is always in paradise according to his divinity; indeed, he himself is the paradise of his faithful, that is, their delight and eternal happiness. Therefore the man who was to be brought to knowledge of his divinity was going to be with the Lord in paradise; he recognized his humanity as empowered by divinity even while he hung upon the cross. For on that day the soul of Christ, despoiling hell, led the souls of his chosen ones forth to the joys of paradise; but his body, placed in the tomb, was raised from death on the third day, having been assumed for us.

Therefore the soul of the criminal was led with the soul of the Lord to the joys of paradise on the very day on which the Lord promised this. “You will be with me,” he says, “in paradise” [Col. 0095A]; that is: Just as my soul is always blessed by the contemplation of God and is free from every corruption and mutability of sin, so, by God’s mercy, your soul too will be blessed with the same happiness. And rightly does he say “today”; for that blessed soul was to be led to the delights of eternal life, where there is not night and day, but one single eternal day.

## CHAPTER XVIII

Now there stood beside the cross of Jesus his mother and his mother’s sister, Mary of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene. When Jesus therefore saw his mother and the disciple standing whom he loved, he said to his mother: “Woman, behold your son.” Then he said to the disciple: “Behold your mother.” And from that hour the disciple took her into his own household (John XIX).

The merciful Lord displayed an outstanding proof of his compassion: he did not disregard the mother of his flesh as he was about to pass to the Father of his divinity, but entrusted her to the beloved disciple, clearly instructing us to show devoted affection toward our parents. And see, brothers, that he deigned to entrust a virgin mother to a virgin disciple, so that the guardian of his mother’s virginity might be one who, for love of her, had deserved to preserve his own body inviolate from carnal defilement.

Moreover, these three women signify the three classes of Christ’s Church, which in the Lord’s field produce a threefold harvest: a hundredfold, sixtyfold, and thirtyfold. His mother was a virgin; his mother’s sister, Mary, was married; and Mary Magdalene was already practicing continence. Thus the whole Church of the saints consists of these three degrees: virgins, continent persons, and married people [Col. 0095D]; yet the name of all three is none other than Mary. For from all these are chosen those of whom he himself says: “Whoever does the will of my Father is my brother, sister, and mother.” A brother, like the virgin John; a sister, like married people who beget virgins; a mother, like the woman who, having abstained from carnal marriage, spiritually begets Christ in her heart through continence. In this way the sons of the Church are made every day, just as John is read to have become the son of Mary.

But the Lord also seems to indicate another mystery in this passage: namely, that just as he did this near his death, entrusting his mother to the disciple, so near the end of the world the Jewish people, from whom he was born according to the flesh, is to be entrusted to the people of believers. For when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered [Col. 0096A], then all Israel will be saved, which may be understood as represented by Mary. “From that hour,” he says, “the disciple took her into his own household.” For after that Jewish people has believed, then the two will become one flock and one shepherd.

From the sixth hour darkness came over the whole earth until the ninth hour; and around the ninth hour Jesus cried out with a loud voice, saying: “Heloi, Eloi, lama sabacthani!” That is: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” But some standing there and hearing this said: “This man is calling Elijah” (Matthew XXVII).

From the sixth hour darkness came until the ninth hour. The luminaries that God placed to shine in the firmament of heaven could not see their Creator hanging on the tree or offer him the light of their splendor; their hearts were darkened, and they called good evil, evil good, darkness light, and light darkness, choosing Barabbas and asking that Jesus be destroyed.

But another, more secret mystery may also be understood as signified in the hour of darkness: namely, that after Adam’s sin, committed in the afternoon breeze, darkness lay over the whole earth, with human beings ignorant of their Creator God, until in the last times the Lord, taking pity on the human race, assumed flesh and underwent the punishment of the cross. At the ninth hour, after giving up his spirit and immediately rising again, he deigned to illuminate the world with his truth.

And around the ninth hour Jesus cried out with a loud voice: “My God, why have you forsaken me?” [Col. 0096C] Christ prayed on behalf of the human race from which he had assumed his body. He spoke as though he himself had been forsaken, since darkness of ignorance of God held the human race, which according to his humanity was close to him. These, then, are the darknesses that arose from the sixth hour of Adam’s sin until the ninth hour of Christ’s death: people who did not know the true light, which is God, were confined in the darkness of sins.

For them, therefore, the Lord prayed, and obtained that they should not be forsaken. For when the Lord’s day dawned, he rose from the dead and said: “All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me,” and so that the darknesses might be removed from the world: “Go,” he said, “into the whole world and preach the Gospel to every creature.”

“My God, why have you forsaken me?” That is: Why has the human race been forsaken by you for so long that it does not receive knowledge of you [Col. 0096D], knowledge whose absence is a darkness than which none greater can exist?

But some said: “This man is calling Elijah.” Because of a slight similarity between the divine name *Heloi* and the name Elijah, those ignorant of the Hebrew language thought that the Lord was calling Elijah to his aid.

Afterward, knowing that all things had now been completed, so that Scripture might be fulfilled, Jesus said: “I thirst.” Now a vessel stood there full of vinegar, and immediately one of them ran, filled a sponge with vinegar, and, putting it on hyssop, offered it to his mouth. But the others said: “Let us see whether Elijah will come to save him” (Matthew XXVII).

The Lord, having become human, admitted human feelings to himself when he wished, and used them as he wished [Col. 0097A]. He said that he was thirsty, and he certainly spoke truly; therefore he thirsted when he wished and as much as he wished. Thus, so that Scripture might be fulfilled, he said: “I thirst.” He thirsted for this purpose: that the Scripture might be fulfilled which says: “In my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink.”

But this thirst of the Lord reveals to us a great sacrament of his goodness. For earlier in the Gospel he said that he would give water which whoever drank would never thirst forever—living water springing up into eternal life. Therefore the one who was able to give this to others certainly gave what he himself possessed.

He therefore thirsted and hungered for something: namely, for that which he said, “My food is to do the will of him who sent me, so that I may complete his work.” The Lord’s thirst and hunger were that God’s work might be completed, that the human race might be saved. He wished this to be understood while hanging on the cross when he said that he thirsted: namely, that God’s work might be completed and that, after the work of his fleshly death had been accomplished, the human race might be freed from eternal death after the death of his flesh had been accomplished.

But while he himself willed this, the Jews offered him vinegar, acting in opposition to God’s merciful will and remaining its adversaries to this day. They also offer vinegar to the Lord—that is, their faithlessness and malice against the preaching of evangelical teaching, setting their most bitter vinegar against the Lord’s mouth. For when the wholesome wine that the Lord gave, saying, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and you shall love your neighbor as yourself,” should have been life-giving, the Jews turned this most salutary drink into vinegar of dreadful bitterness. They preferred to hear the Lord giving salutary commands rather than obey the one who taught them; and they did not love him, who had become God and a human being near to them, as they loved themselves, but condemned him to the most shameful kind of death as though he were the enemy of their salvation [Col. 0097C].

When Jesus had received the vinegar, he said: “It is completed.” And crying out with a loud voice, he said: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit”; and saying this, he bowed his head and gave up his spirit (John XIX; Luke XXIII).

He said that the Old Testament was completed, whatever had to be completed before his death; or he said that the work of human salvation was completed, concerning which, as we said above, the Lord himself said: “My food is to do the will of my Father, so that I may complete his work.” And elsewhere: “I have glorified you on earth; I have completed the work that you gave me.”

When, therefore, he had completed this work, he bowed his head and gave up his spirit [Col. 0097D]. For it was as though Christ’s bowing of the head consisted in this: that God, who is the life of all, deigned to die in the body for us, becoming, as the Apostle says, obedient to the Father unto death. The bowing of the head, therefore, was his humble obedience, by which he died so that the work the Father had given him might be completed, in order that he might offer us, made alive, to God the Father.

“He gave up his spirit,” he says, as one having the power to lay down his life and the power to take it up again. He gave up his spirit, saying: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit.” No spirit had been handed over into the hands of God from the beginning of the world before the Lord handed his own into God’s hands.

When, therefore, he handed his own into the hands of the Father, he offered to God the Father the spirits of all his chosen ones, whether those who came before his incarnation or those who came after it. For this is what the Apostle says will happen at the end of the world: “When he has handed over the kingdom to God the Father”—that is, when he has made all his chosen ones alone the kingdom of God—“and when sin no longer reigns, they will reign in God, and God in them,” as he himself says: “Come, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.”

Thus he gave his immaculate and sinless spirit into the hands of the Father, and this he works in us: that he may hand over his Church, without spot or wrinkle, into the hands of the one to whom he commended his spirit.

## CHAPTER XIX

And behold, the veil of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom; and the earth was shaken, and the rocks were split, and the tombs were opened; and many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep rose, and, coming out of the tombs after his resurrection, they came into the holy city and appeared to many (Matthew XIX [sic]).

When Christ died, the veil stretched before the Holy of Holies was torn in two from top to bottom. My brothers, Christ’s death opened to us the hidden things of the heavenly mysteries. For us who believe, the divine mysteries that are veiled from unbelievers have been opened.

For as long as the Jewish people and all unbelievers do not believe in Christ, a veil is placed before their eyes, so that they do not see that those ancient events signified the new life of evangelical grace. But when one believes Christ to have been incarnate, to have suffered, to have been raised from the dead, and to be seated at the right hand of God, the veil will be torn for him, and the hidden mysteries of the divine dispensation, which had previously been veiled, will be opened.

For this purpose the veil hung in the temple of the Old Testament: so that the people and all who entered would not indiscriminately see the Holy of Holies, in which were the Lord’s ark, and above it the two cherubim, and the other things that were intended to be seen not by the whole people but only by the priests.

When, therefore, Christ deigned to die for us, the mysteries of the Old Testament that had previously been veiled were opened. For all those kinds of victims and sacrifices that were commanded to be offered in the old law foretold that one holy and singular sacrifice of the Lord’s passion. When, therefore, he himself was sacrificed for the salvation of the world to God upon the altar of the cross as an offering of most sweet fragrance [Col. 0098D], then it was opened what had long before been concealed—namely, what those things enacted there signified.

“And the earth,” he says, “was shaken.” This refers to earthly promises, such as that land promised to them, flowing with milk and honey, the multitude of children and grandchildren, and the other promises in which that people then took delight. Through Christ’s death these things began to grow cheap, as those who hoped for better and more lasting promises of eternal happiness.

“And the rocks were split.” The hard and burdensome obligations of the old law are transferred to the mercy of the new grace, so that sins, which were then always punished by death alone, are now erased by the gentle medicine of repentance.

“And the tombs were opened.” The prophecies of the prophets are disclosed when the truth appears [Col. 0099A]. Nor was it without cause, my brothers, that when Christ rose, the bodies of many also came out of the tombs and appeared to many: namely, so that, just as Christ, the firstfruits of those who die, rose from the dead, so we too might not doubt that we will rise in the flesh on the last day.

For he alone died for all, but he did not rise alone. His death is the vivification of the dead, because no one else could die in such a way as to raise the dead by his death. He alone, therefore, as we said, died in such a way that death itself became the resurrection of the dead.

Now when the centurion and those who were with him, guarding Jesus, saw the earthquake and the things that were happening, they were greatly afraid and glorified God, saying: “Truly this was the Son of God.” And the whole crowd of those who were present together for that spectacle, seeing what was happening, returned beating their breasts (Matthew XXVII; Luke XXIII).

While the Jews remained in unbelief, the Gentile centurion and the Roman soldiers, seeing the miracles that were happening and being afraid, confessed the Son of God: “Truly,” they said, “this was the Son of God.” They already saw him dead, yet they confessed him to be the Son of God; and this foreshadowed the future faith of the Gentiles.

“Look,” says the Lord, “at the regions, for they are already white for harvest.” For the hearts of the Gentiles were already prepared to believe. Before they heard the voice of any preacher, these men were moved to faith by the signs of the Lord’s passion alone.

“Beating,” he says, “their breasts.” That is, grieving that they were witnessing the things being done against the Lord by the Jews.

Now there were many women there at a distance, who had followed Jesus from Galilee, ministering to him. Among them were Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Joseph, and Mary the mother of the sons of Zebedee, and many other women who had gone up with him to Jerusalem (Matthew XXVII; Mark XV).

These women, who were wealthy, ministered to Christ from their own possessions, to him who had wished to possess nothing of his own in this world, although the whole earth and its fullness are his. But he became poor for us, so that in him we might be rich.

With the same devotion, therefore, they desired to minister to him when he was dead with which they had previously served him while he was alive. Moreover, where no man dared to approach, no one prevented the women from standing near him. They desired to care for his body and perform the funeral rites, but the joy of the resurrection forestalled them; they were the first to deserve to see it, so that the sex that had brought the cause of curse and disobedience into the world might itself first announce to the world the reward of obedience and the glory of the resurrection.

The Jews, therefore, because it was Preparation Day, and so that the bodies might not remain on the cross on the Sabbath—for that Sabbath was a great day—asked Pilate that their legs be broken and that they be taken away. So the soldiers came and first broke the legs of the one and of the other who had been crucified with him. But when they came to Jesus, seeing that he was already dead, they did not break his legs. Instead, one of the soldiers opened his side with a lance, and immediately blood and water came out. The one who saw this has testified, and his testimony is true; and he knows that he speaks the truth, so that you too may believe.

For these things happened so that Scripture might be fulfilled: “You shall not break a bone of him.” And again another Scripture says: “They will look upon the one whom they pierced” (John XIX).

Preparation Day, brothers, was the name given among the ancients to the day that we call Friday. It was called Preparation, because on it they prepared what they would live on during the Sabbath; for on the Sabbath they were not permitted to carry out any work. Therefore that day was called Sabbath, that is, rest.

But because they understood these things according to the letter alone, they were entirely ignorant of the divine mystery contained in them. For us, however, brothers, as we said above, the veil of the temple having been torn, the mysteries that remain veiled from those who still do not believe have been opened.

Friday holds the figure of the present age, which was made in six days [Col. 0100B]. This age is plainly a preparation for the life to come; for here the merit by which we may have eternal rest must be prepared for us. Our Preparation Day, therefore—that is, the day of preparation—is the present age, subject to many narrow straits of affliction. It is followed by the Sabbath, that is, the rest of souls. After the Sabbath will come the Lord’s Day, when, having also received their bodies, the whole human being will be received into everlasting glory.

Just as Christ suffered on Friday, rested in the tomb on the Sabbath, sanctified the Lord’s Day by the glory of his resurrection, and, rising from the dead, no longer dies, so that death no longer rules over him, so also his Church, when the passions and hardships of the present age have ended, having received blessed rest, awaits the coming of the resurrection of bodies. Then, rising, it too will no longer die, and death will no longer rule over it; possessing one eternal and infinite Lord’s Day, which has no evening, it will enjoy eternal light.

This is the figure of Friday, on which the Lord suffered; of the Sabbath, on which he rested in the tomb; and of the Lord’s Day, on which he rose from the dead: namely, the present age, the future rest of souls, and the final resurrection of all, in which merits blessed without end will be received.

The Jews, therefore, wishing to prevent the holy day of the Sabbath from being defiled by the punishment of the crucified, asked Pilate that their legs be broken and that they be taken away. But the Lord himself, who was crucified, did not need their foresight; he himself was the dispenser and governor of all times. For when he willed, he suffered and died, just as, when he willed, he conquered death and rose from the dead.

He who formed the human being on the sixth day redeemed him by his death on Friday. He who, after completing his works, rested from them on the seventh day also rested in the tomb on the seventh day, that is, the Sabbath, when the works of human salvation for which he had come to accomplish them had been completed.

For on the cross, when he had received the vinegar, the Lord himself also said: “It is completed”; and, bowing his head, he gave up his spirit. When this work had therefore been completed, the Lord rested bodily in the tomb, while his soul triumphed in paradise.

He who on the first day, the Lord’s Day, commanded light to be made also deigned to illuminate the world with the light of his resurrection on the Lord’s Day. He will also glorify the final Lord’s Day by the resurrection of all human beings, when we will all rise and we will be changed into glory [Col. 0101A].

Of that day the Psalmist says: “One day in your courts is better than thousands.”

The Jews asked that the legs of those who had been crucified be broken and that they be taken away, but the Lord’s legs were not broken, since he was already dead. My brothers, whatever was done in the Lord’s passion was done for our salvation and as a salutary example.

That he was crucified with the wicked was an example for us, so that we should not be burdened even though, during the passing time of this age, we are not permitted to exist without wicked people. That his head was turned toward heaven and his feet toward the earth signifies that our head, Christ, has gone before us to the heavens, and that we, who are the feet—that is, the extremity of the body—will follow him.

That his hands were stretched out to the right and left signifies, as we may understand it, the twofold love of God and neighbor to be preached throughout the breadth of the world. That his side was pierced with a lance, from which water and blood came forth, signifies that there is one entrance into the catholic Church: water, namely baptism, or the baptism of blood.

“Unless,” he says, “one has been born again of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God.” Whether one is baptized with water or with blood, baptism is nevertheless the entrance into the Church.

Thus all the other things done in the Lord’s passion are either instructions or signs of our life and salvation. So too the fact that the Lord’s legs were not broken, which happened after the Lord’s death had already taken place, signifies that the pillars of Christ’s body—that is, the pastors of the Church—are not to be broken either by threats or softened by flattery [Col. 0101C].

This was done because Christ suffered for us, leaving us an example so that we might follow his footsteps. For Christ’s death, held before the eyes of the heart, strengthens the hearts of the faithful, so that they will not fear suffering for him.

These things happened so that Scripture might be fulfilled: “A bone of him shall not be broken.” And another Scripture says: “They will look upon the one whom they pierced.”

Two events in the Lord’s passion are accompanied by these two testimonies of holy Scripture. The fact that his legs were not broken corresponds to “A bone of him shall not be broken.” The fact that the soldier opened his side with a lance corresponds to what the prophet says: “They will look upon the one whom they pierced.”

For through Moses the Lord commanded that, when the paschal lamb was sacrificed, its bone should not be broken [Col. 0101D]. So too whoever is a bone in the body of the Lord—that is, a strong member in Christ’s Church—cannot be broken by any terrors or threats.

And what that other Scripture said, “They will look upon the one whom they pierced,” will take place at the final judgment, so that the persecutors of Christ may see the one whose body they now afflict with various kinds of suffering.

## CHAPTER XX

When evening had come, a certain rich man from Arimathea arrived, a noble decurion, who himself was awaiting the kingdom of God and was also a disciple of Jesus, though secretly because of fear of the Jews. He had not consented to their counsel and actions. He was a good and righteous man named Joseph. He boldly entered before Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus [Col. 0102A].

Pilate was astonished that he had already died; and summoning the centurion, he asked him whether he had already died. When he had learned from the centurion that he had, he granted Joseph the body of Jesus.

Joseph therefore came and took the body. Nicodemus also came, he who had first come to Jesus by night, bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about a hundred pounds. They took the body of Jesus, and Joseph bought a linen cloth; they bound him in linen cloths with spices, as is the Jews’ custom in burial.

Now in the place where he was crucified there was a garden, and in the garden a new tomb, which Joseph had cut out of rock, in which no one had yet been placed. There, because of the Jews’ Preparation Day and because the tomb was nearby, they placed Jesus. They rolled a large stone to the entrance of the tomb and went away.

Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joseph were there, sitting opposite the tomb; and they saw how the body had been placed. Returning, they prepared spices and ointments so that they might come and anoint him; but on the Sabbath they remained silent according to the commandment (Matthew XXVII; Luke XXIII; John XIX; Mark XV).

A certain rich man came to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus. For no poor man could approach the governor and obtain this from him, although it necessarily had to be done: the Lord himself had foretold that his body would remain in the earth for three days.

And observe the Lord between two Josephs: one, the husband of Mary, a witness to her integrity; the other, this man, who placed the body of Jesus in his own tomb, in which no one had yet been placed, so that if someone else had previously been placed there, it could be said that Jesus had not risen from it [Col. 0102C].

And observe two undefiled wombs: Mary’s, from whom the undefiled Lord was born; and the new tomb, in which no human being had been placed either before or after the Lord.

For the body of the Lord, assumed from a human being, had to be placed in the earth because the Lord had said to the first parent of the human race, Adam, from whom every human body has been sown, after the fault: “You are earth, and into earth you will go.” To fulfill, therefore, the debt of the human condition, the Lord’s body was placed in the earth.

Brothers, you must know that the Son of God died in order to redeem the human race—not as himself a debtor to death, but willingly paying the debt of death, which he did not owe, out of the love with which he loved us.

When the first man Adam was punished with the penalty of death for the fault of disobedience, the condition of death remained throughout the whole mass of the human race. For all came from one, and all sinned in one, and, born with sins, all were compelled to pay the penalty of sin.

The human race could not be freed from the bond of this curse before someone came who, born without sin, would not become liable to the penalty of sin. For the penalty was owed to all the others because all were born with sins. Therefore the penalty was not owed to the one alone who had not committed the sin for which the penalty was imposed, since he alone was born without it.

The Son of God therefore came, assuming the human race without guilt. His mother was impregnated not by the desire of a man but by the love of the Holy Spirit, and she bore a Son without sin, whom she conceived without desire [Col. 0103A].

By his voluntary death he was able to redeem those who were held under the debt of death. All the others died unwillingly, compelled by sin. Therefore they could not be redeemers of others, since they themselves were debtors to punishment.

The Son of God came, as I said, and became the redeemer of all. He did not assume death because of a debt of sin, since he committed no sin, but out of the love with which he loved us. He received as the reward of this love the salvation of all of us who believe in him and love him as he loved us and handed himself over for us as an offering to God for a fragrant odor.

This, my brothers, was the reason for Christ’s incarnation. For this he was born in the flesh: that he might die in the flesh. For this he died willingly: that he might free us from the necessity of eternal death. For this also he was placed in the tomb: because just as it was said to the first man, “You will surely die,” so it was said to him, “You are earth, and into earth you will go.” Thus he paid the entire debt of the sinner, so that he might redeem the whole human nature that he had assumed.

[Col. 0103B]

## HERE BEGINS THE LETTER OF CANDIDUS, MONK OF FULDA

**Whether Christ could see God with bodily eyes**

(Pez., *Thesaurus novissimus Anecdotorum*)

[Col. 0103]

[Col. 0103B] **I.** To the venerable lord in Christ, a brother to be loved with the greatest affection, the presbyter Candidus [Note: [Col. 0103D] Thus I read it. Perhaps it should be read *Pater*. The manuscript has PR.] sends greetings.

You do not act altogether inappropriately when, speaking in the customary relational manner, you call yourself a son and me a father; for you certainly have Christ as your Father in heaven, and you do not hesitate to honor and embrace him because of his dignity and love. But we all believe, hope in, and love this Father who is common to us all.

As for your wish to call me “father” in connection with what you have decided to undertake, this does not seem inappropriate. For since the Holy Scriptures command that fathers be questioned so that they may declare, and elders so that they may tell, if the person questioned is a father and a presbyter, why do you not rightly call “father” the man whom you do not hesitate to question?

Would that I might be as useful to you in answering your questions as you desire—since you think me a man who wishes, in true charity, and is able, through knowledge, to resolve what you ask! The question, you say, was put to you by someone: Could Christ our Lord, insofar as he was human, while he lived here as a mortal among mortals, have seen God?

If this question was raised and solved long ago by the holy Fathers, I do not know whether it is held to have been explained either by you or by any of the ancients in the manner in which the man about whom you wrote is said to have asked it—namely, whether the Father could be seen by Christ’s bodily eyes. But whether you have already received an explanation of that question from others or not, I will not conceal from you what I think about it.

**II.** Just as God is the highest spirit, so he is supremely incorporeal. I say this because angels, souls, and whatever created spirits there are, although they are both called and are incorporeal, are nevertheless, in comparison with that incorporeality—or, so to speak, spirituality—of God, corporeal in a certain way.

Although souls or angels may perhaps be called nonlocal in another respect, they are nevertheless local in comparison with that supreme divinity, because, even if they are not contained by anything else, they are contained by the very world, which is certainly a place. God, however, is contained neither by the world nor by any creature, because all created things are contained by him, so that they may exist and remain.

Therefore let the one who asked you this—namely, whether God is seen, or could be seen, or is to be seen with bodily eyes—hear this answer from me and from all Catholic Christians: God, who is spirit, is seen by spirit, not by flesh. He is seen by human beings who are pure in heart, not by the body, however pure; he is seen and is to be seen by spiritual substance, but not by carnal substance through the flesh.

### III.

But if he should perhaps reply and say: “What we now see through the body, the spirit sees through the body; and it has been promised to all of us that after the judgment, when our bodies have become incorruptible, we shall rejoice in the eternal vision of God”—whoever says this is speaking truly, as the matter stands. Yet the spirit now sees bodies through the body for this reason: bodies cannot be seen in any other way than through the body; nor can anything else be seen through the body except a body.

For if you ask whether Christ saw God with bodily eyes, I in turn ask whether you now can—or, if you can, whether you wish to—see the truth with bodily eyes. And if you tell me that you neither wish nor are able to do so, know that Christ likewise wished to see God in no other way than as he can be seen. He neither wills nor willed anything that he could not; nor can he do anything that he does not will, because the will and power of God are God himself [or: “God itself”], not something else.

Therefore Christ, by himself, insofar as he is spirit, and by that very Spirit with which he was filled, assumed a human being and saw God—by himself, I say, and by that Spirit with which he was filled. But to behold him with bodily eyes, since he is the supreme Spirit, he did not wish, if I am not mistaken, because he could not; and he could not because he did not wish to. For, as I said, he wills everything that he can, and can everything that he wills.

### IV.

And so that this may become clearer to you through some small example—if indeed one can be found; rather, because no example similar to such a matter can be found, what I shall say is similar only in part—it is as though, in the middle of the day, with the sun shining, you wished to use some material lamp, although the sun’s radiance, diffused all around you, was sufficient for you.

This is similar to the matter under discussion only in this respect: God, whom he always saw in spirit, was not to be sought by bodily sight.

I speak of myself: if bodies were not made necessary for seeing, I would take no care to see anything with bodily eyes; and perhaps this is true of everyone. For tell me: if you knew and retained in your memory, without letters, everything that you wished to know, would you have cared either to possess or to see letters?

Certainly, I use letters unwillingly, either to remind myself or to teach others. If I could forget nothing of what I have learned, or if I were able to know without letters whatever ought to be known, and to know it continually, I would no longer need letters. The same will happen to me and to everyone: namely, that without letters we shall both know and not forget what we are destined to know.

### V.

It was therefore not by a weaker kind of sight that God was to be sought as visible to Christ, who was always seen by him—and is to be seen by him—by a firmer and better kind of sight.

I do not say this as though I thought that God could not have granted his body something more excellent than other bodies. He could have done so, and he did, granting his body the great and ineffable grace that ought to be granted above other bodies: first—if this is indeed the first point—that it should become the flesh of God; that flesh should be made without sin from human flesh, and specifically from the flesh of a virgin; that in being born it should not stain its mother; indeed, that she should be called, and should be, the mother of God because of him; that he should live without sin; that those who touched him in faith should be healed; and—what seems to me either the greatest or at least not the least—that he should become such a sacrifice as would be more acceptable to God the Father than all bodily creatures, on behalf of all those who share human nature and are predestined to salvation.

He also granted that, after death, he should not see corruption; and that, exalted in the glory of resurrection above the heavens, he should become eternally blessed in a heavenly dwelling.

These are the things that are acknowledged without doubt as having been granted, and as needing to be granted, to the same flesh of Christ. But how it would contribute to that supreme and inviolable order for him to see his Father, the supreme Spirit, through his bodily senses does not sufficiently appear to me.

Since human nature was seeking this—that, because it was not yet able to see through the spirit, God should be seen bodily—God himself, taking account of the weakness of that nature, became bodily in order to be seen by bodily eyes and touched bodily. For this reason the whole uniquely marvelous and marvelously unique dispensation of Christ’s incarnation took place: namely, so that through the one whom human beings had seen as mortal and bodily, they might be led to the vision of the one who is to be seen not bodily but spiritually.

### VI.
