To the one, therefore, who put this kind of question to you, answer in this way: “If you desire to see God, purify your heart, and you will see him.”

For Christ wished to see God the Father as he was able, and was able as he wished. Since he foretold that we would see God with pure hearts, there can be no doubt that he himself saw him in the way in which he taught us that we could attain to seeing him.

Three points now occur to me. First, God can be seen by created spirits that are pure—not to the extent that he sees himself, but to the extent that he permits himself to be seen. God himself, in his divine nature, cannot be seen by bodies, however pure. By the impure—whether spirits or bodies—he is not only not seen, but withdraws far from their sight; and the farther he, who is life and salvation, withdraws from them, the more wretched and unhappy they become.

God, therefore, is seen in his entirety by himself; by a good created spirit, to the extent that he permits; by a good human being, through the spirit; and by the impure, in no way. For the spirit sees bodies through the body; and the body sees the uncreated Spirit through a created spirit, but not by itself.

O soul, purify yourself through faith, rule over the body, and use it for good; strive to enjoy God.

### VII.

As for the soul of Christ, whether it sees God the Father in this way, there can be no doubt that it sees him more than all creatures do. For, as stated above, the vision of God is promised at the end to our purified souls; that vision the soul of Christ, which is already and always pure, continually enjoys.

When the Evangelist said, “No one has ever seen God,” consider what he means by “no one”: no human being—no one, that is, among humankind—has ever seen God in the nature of his divinity. But that one, who is God and man, is undoubtedly seen to see him through his spirit, except by unbelievers.

And when he said, “No one has seen God,” observe that he used the past tense, “has seen,” not “no one will see.” For, as the same Evangelist says, “We shall see him as he is”—a vision that the soul of Christ has always possessed from the time it was assumed and filled by him.

Unless someone should perhaps say that there had once been a time when that holy, indeed most holy, soul of Christ, holier than all creatures, existed without God, and that divinity later came to it. But this is contrary to the Catholic faith.

Hold firmly, therefore, that the soul was always full of God and always saw God as he is. Hold this firmly, and do not doubt that, from the moment he began to be human, Christ always saw God through his own spirit—the God whom he had always seen even before assuming human nature.

For our angels also see the face of the Father who is in heaven; how much more, then, that soul which, being full of God, is more excellent than all creatures?

No human being, therefore, has seen God in his own nature, except that one alone who alone is without sin. But all the righteous and those purified from sins will see him.

For if the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, himself declares him, consider to whom he will declare him—namely, to a creature. And to what creature would he declare him, if he did not declare him to his own soul, which he assumed?

He does declare him to it; and, as I said, he made it see God more excellently and magnificently than all creatures.

### VIII.

If these matters seem to you to stand as I have said, be satisfied with them. But if you see anything beyond this, forgive me, because I am human and can be mistaken; nevertheless, I love the truth, and therefore I am also willing to be corrected.

I beg your fraternity to commend me frequently to your fellow soldiers. If I have any ability to contribute something useful to them, I desire this greatly, since I understand that I am a debtor both to them and to all the sons of the Catholic Church.

Also admonish them, in my words and your own, to conduct themselves soberly, piously, and justly. And since they are held in high esteem among human beings, let them take care to be before God what they are said to be.

For they are called servants of God, and they do not doubt what is required of servants of God: namely, that a servant should serve his lord. For you are servants of God, not of this world, nor of mammon. He, therefore, must be served whom we are servants of, even if we do not wish it.

Let the right faith be read and held; let unwavering hope be possessed; and let all our actions begin, continue, and end with charity. May charity never fail.

Among all the virtues of the soul, nothing should be more distinctive, more familiar, or more beloved to you than charity; and it is such a virtue that, when it alone is complete, it is sufficient.

Humility is the foundation of your conversion; patience, its walls; faith, its roof; hope in God, its summit. Yet all these are effective only if they are accompanied by charity; without it, none of them is anything.

For if you are humble but do not love the one before whom you humble yourself—God—your humility is false. If you are patient but do not love the one for whose sake you suffer, your patience is empty. If you believe but do not love the God in whom you believe, the demons do the same. If you hope but do not love the one from whom you hope, you nourish an empty hope.

Therefore let everything be done with charity: first toward God, then toward your neighbor, and again toward God, so that everything that is done may be done out of love of God. Let him be the author of the work, its guide, its perfecter, its reward, and the perfection of the work.

### IX.

Humble yourselves before one another; love one another; be patient with one another; love one another. Believe in God, and love one another. Hope in God, and love one another.

Let the one who knows [*sciat*, thus the codex] instruct the one who does not know; let the one who does not know love the one who instructs; and let both love God, who made the one who knows able to know and gave him to the one who did not know, so that the latter might also learn to know.

Let the one who knows not become puffed up against the one who does not know, because knowledge puffs up, whereas charity does not puff up but builds up.

Let the one who knows understand that he is obliged to build up. For this reason God made him knowledgeable: so that the one who does not know might be built up through him, because God is the God of both.

Indeed, just as the Almighty could have made everyone rich if he had wished, but wished some, not all, to be rich, so that the mercy of the rich might become useful and the humility of the poor might arise, so also the Almighty could indeed have made everyone knowledgeable, since he wishes all to be saved. But he wished some to teach by themselves, so that others might be taught through them and charity might be firmly maintained among all: the knowledgeable person loving the humble learner, and the learner loving the well-disposed teacher.

### X.

I do not say these things, my brother, most beloved in Christ, as though I had heard anything unfavorable about you. Rather, your sublime and holy way of life is praised by all who know it.

But because you are good and wise, you gladly tolerate me in my foolishness when I press upon you the one thing that I know nothing better than: charity. I have said little about it, although no one can say as much about it as it deserves.

For it is the greatest virtue, and God himself is charity; whoever truly loves God and neighbor should have no doubt that God is in him.

I commend myself to your charity—as a son to all the fathers, as a brother to the brothers, and as a father to the sons.

May Almighty God, in his mercy, protect and govern you, and bring you, as you advance in him, to the perfection of holiness. Fare always well in Christ.

If perhaps an answer was given to you otherwise than your question required, and this offended your charity somewhat, know that the reason for this was the following. When I first wrote, I did not then have your letter with me, and for that reason I did not remember well what you had asked. But after I found it, I also answered what you had asked.

If any scruple still remains in your mind, make this known in writing as well, so that, by God’s gift, it too may be illumined by the open truth.

There will be a time when brother will speak with brother. There will be a time when the one who rejoices will enjoy the one who rejoices. All things have their time; charity has no end. Farewell.

At the command of devout Christ, feed fathers and young novices,

so that they may be able to taste sweet words.

*The end.*

## In the Year of Our Lord 840. Dodana or Duodena

## Historical Notice

Dodana, or Duodena, a pious woman, says Fabricius (*Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis*), married Bernard, duke of Septimania and count of Barcelona, the son of Saint William, in the year of Christ 814. Mabillon published her *Manual Book* addressed to her son William in the fourth volume of the *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*. From that edition we reprint it, including the gaps present in the manuscript. —Editor.

## In the Name of the Holy and Undivided Trinity

Here begins Dodana’s Manual Book, which she sent to her son William.

Seeing many people rejoice in the world with their offspring, and seeing myself, Dodana, far removed from you, my son William, I have therefore, as though anxious and full of the desire to be useful, sent this little work, written in my name, to be read outwardly in your form—that is, as though addressed personally to you. I rejoice that, although I am absent in body, this present little book may, when you read it, bring back to your mind what you, my son, ought to do toward me.

## Preface

In the eleventh year, happily and with Christ’s favor, when our lord Louis was then shining in the imperial power, on the day of the eighth day before the Kalends of July, at the palace of Aachen, I legally entered marriage as wife to my lord and your father, Bernard.

Then again, in the thirteenth year of his reign, on the third day before the Kalends of December, with God’s help, as I believe, your birth from me, most desired firstborn son, came forth into the world.

As the wretched misery of this world turned and increased, amid the many upheavals and conflicts of the kingdom, there is no doubt that the emperor mentioned above went the way of all. For before reaching the summit of the twenty-eighth year of his reign, he completed the life owed to this world.

After his death, in the following year, the birth of your brother, who came second from my womb after you, arose by God’s mercy on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April in the city of Uzès.

Indeed, before that little one had received the grace of baptism, the lord and father of you both, B. [Bernard], together with Elefantus, bishop of the aforesaid city, and his other faithful men, had him brought into his presence in the regions of Aquitaine.

But while, because of your absence, I remained for a long time in that city under the command of my lord, already rejoicing in his struggle, I undertook, out of desire for you both, to have this little book transcribed and sent to you according to the measure of my small understanding.

## The Same Author Again

Although I am occupied by many anxieties and would at some time behold your face, nevertheless this one matter is, according to God, established in the Lord’s prior decision.

I had indeed wished, if strength were granted me by God; but since salvation is far from me, a sinner, I desire it, and in this desire my spirit withers.

For I have heard that your father Bernard has entrusted you to the hands of the lord King Charles. I admonish you to devote yourself to the dignity of this task until its completion. Yet, as Scripture says, “Seek first in all things the kingdom of God,” and then those things necessary for your soul and body will be added for you to enjoy happily.

## The Chapters of the Following Book Begin

I. On loving God.  
II. On seeking God.  
III. On the greatness of God.  
IV. On the height of God.  
V. Again, by the same author, on God.  
VI. A moral chapter by the same author.  
VII. An admonition by the same author.  
VIII. On the Holy Trinity.  
IX. On faith, hope, and charity.  
X. On reverence in prayer.  
XI. Again, by the same author.  
XII. On reverence toward your father.  
XIII. Again, by the same author, on the father.  
XIV. On receiving examples from pious Fathers.  
XV. On your lord: another matter, another matter.  
XVI. On receiving counsel: another matter, another matter.  
XVII. Again, by the same author, on counselors: another matter, another matter.  
XVIII. A special admonition addressed to you.  
XIX. To the relatives of your lords: another matter, another matter.  
XX. To the leading men of the dukes.  
XXI. That you should show honor to priests.  
XXII. That you should bend your spirit toward great and small.  
XXIII. An admonition by the same author to correct your conduct.  
XXIV. Again, by the same author, another matter concerning the foregoing.  
XXV. That you should flee pride.  
XXVI. That you should serve in the sevenfold gift of the Holy Spirit. Again, by the same author.  
XXVII. A useful admonition for restraining vices.  
XXVIII. That you should oppose virtues to vices.  
XXIX. That you should maintain patience of mind and body.  
XXX. That you may easily conquer vices: read the eight beatitudes aloud and always retain them in your heart.  
XXXI. That, when you are able, you should help the poor.  
XXXII. On various tribulations, should they befall you.  
XXXIII. On reconciliation, should you commit some offense.  
XXXIV. On various temptations, should they befall you.  
XXXV. If there is tribulation.  
XXXVI. If there is persecution.  
XXXVII. If there is necessity.  
XXXVIII. If distress comes upon you.  
XXXIX. If there is sickness. Again, by the same author.  
XL. That you should give glory to God in all things.  
XLI. Again, a comparison of the six and eight beatitudes that confer virtues upon you.  
XLII. I admonish you so that you may be able to be a perfect man.  
XLIII. I show you how, with God’s help, you can be without blemish.  
XLIV. On the sevenfold reckoning of what should be proposed to those who have sinned against you, so that you may forgive them.  
XLV. On understanding the twofold birth.  
XLVI. I desire that you flourish in the first birth.  
XLVII. I admonish you to persevere in the second.  
XLVIII. On the first and second death.  
XLIX. I declare that you should contemplate the first death.  
L. That you should strive to flee the second death.  
LI. I admonish you to flourish in understanding and prayer.  
LII. On past, present, and future things.  
LIII. I explain how you should pray for all the orders of the Church.  
LIV. For bishops and priests.  
LV. For kings and their exalted dignity.  
LVI. For your lord.  
LVII. I admonish you to pray constantly for your father.  
LVIII. Again, for all who follow; conclude here with the words: “and for all the holy people of God.”  
LIX. That you should pray for all faithful departed, for the very good and for those who are not very good.  
LX. For the undeserving, you will find worthy things to do.  
LXI. Pray for the deceased parents of your father.  
LXII. For Lord Theuderic in particular, and again for all the deceased, that they may rest in peace.  
LXIII. Again, specifically for the father.  
LXIV. On articles and composed meters.  
LXV. On the letters of Adam and their meanings.  
LXVI. On the five groups of three blessings that are offered upon you and remain always.  
LXVII. Again, on the same matter, addressed to the same person.  
LXVIII. On your ages. Again, by the same author.  
LXIX. On your composed verses and letters.  
LXX. After the words prescribed, on public affairs.  
LXXI. I ask you to pray for me, both while I am still living in the body and after the funeral of the tomb, for the salvation of my soul.  
LXXII. The names of the deceased transcribed below.  
LXXIII. I ask you to write an epitaph for my tomb.

## Chapter One: On Loving God

God is to be loved and praised not only by the heavenly powers but also by every human creature that walks upon the earth and strives toward heaven.

Among these I exhort you, son W., insofar as you are able, always to seek those things by which, together with the worthy and suitable—those who love God—you may be able to climb to a sure summit and, together with them, reach a kingdom that will endure without end. Amen.

Again, I ask and humbly urge your noble youth, as though I were present, and also those to whom you may show this little book for reading, not to condemn or criticize me because I am rash enough to enter into so sharp and difficult a contest of labor that I dare to send you some discourse concerning God, and so forth.

## Chapter VII: Again, an Admonition by the Same Author

I also admonish you, my beautiful and beloved son W., not to disdain acquiring for yourself many volumes of books amid the worldly cares of this age. In them you ought to understand and learn something about God, the creator of all that belongs to you, from the most sacred teachers—indeed, more and greater things than have been written above.

Entreat him, cherish him, and love him. If you do this, he will be your guardian, guide, companion, homeland, way, truth, and life; he will grant you prosperity in the world most generously and turn all your enemies toward peace.

But you, as it is written in Job, “Gird up your loins like a man.” Be humble in heart and chaste in body, and rise upward. Be very glorious, and clothe yourself in splendid garments.

And what more? Your exhorter, D. [Dodana], is always present, my son. And if I should be absent—being destined to become absent—you have here a memorial, a little book, O. M. R., so that, as though in the image of a mirror, you may behold me in mind and body by reading and praying to God; and you can fully see what service you ought to render toward me.

My son, you will have teachers who will teach you more and greater lessons of usefulness, but not with the same disposition: none with a heart so ardent in the breast as I, your mother.

Son W., my firstborn, read, understand, and fulfill in action these words sent to you by me. And do not neglect to commend, nourish, love, and urge your little brother from good to better, once he has received the grace of baptism in Christ—although at present I do not know his name.

When he has reached the proper age for speaking or reading, show him this little *Manual* composed by me and written in your name, and admonish him through reading it; for he is your flesh and your brother.

I admonish you both, as though I, D., your mother, were already addressing you together: though oppressed by the worldly cares of the age, at least for a time keep your hearts raised above. Look upon him who reigns in heaven, the one called God.

May he, the Almighty, of whom I make mention despite my unworthiness, together with your father, our lord and my master B., frequently make you happy and joyful in the present world, prospering in all things; and after the course of this life has been completed, may he make you known as entering joyfully with the saints. Amen.

## Chapter X: On Reverence in Prayer

Prayer is so called as though it were “the reason of the mouth.”

Pray with your mouth, cry out with your heart, and ask through your deeds, so that God may always come to your aid by days and nights, at hours and moments.

When you have rested in bed, say then:

> God, attend to my aid. Lord, hasten to help me. And “Glory” to the end.

Then say the Lord’s Prayer. When it is completed, say:

> You have guarded me, God, throughout the day; guard me also during this night, if you command it. May I deserve to be protected beneath the shadow of your wings, filled with the Holy Spirit, surrounded by royal defense, and encircled by the guardianship of angels, so that during this night, although resting only briefly, I may sleep the sleep of peace. And whenever I awaken, may I sense within sleep that you are my guardian—the one who appeared to blessed Jacob as he leaned upon the ladder, O Savior.

When you have completed this, make the sign of the cross upon your forehead and over your bed, in the likeness of the cross by which you were redeemed, in this manner: +, saying:

> I adore your cross, Lord, and I believe in your holy resurrection. May your holy cross be with me. The cross is what I have come to know; I have always loved it and always adore it. The cross is salvation for me; the cross is defense for me; the cross is protection and always a refuge for me; the cross is life for me. Death to you, devil, enemy of truth, worshiper of vanity; the cross is life for me, death to you forever.

And again:

> I adore your + cross, Lord, and recall your glorious passion, you who deigned to be born, suffer, die, and rise from the dead, you who are with the Father and the Holy Spirit +. May the blessing of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit descend and remain upon me, your servant W., the least. Amen.

May this cross and blessing always be with those whom I, fragile D., frequently mention above. And just as the dew of Hermon that descends upon Mount Zion, or as ointment poured upon the head and flowing down upon the beard, the beard of Aaron, so may the outpouring of Jesus the Nazarene, Son of God, descend and remain upon you wherever you go, and upon your brother, who came second from my womb after you.

If there are more of them, with God’s help, may they obtain together with you what I have invoked above, through him who lives and reigns throughout endless ages of ages. Amen.

### Again

When, with God’s help, you have risen in the morning, or at whatever hour time allows you, say again three times, “God,” as above, and then the Lord’s Prayer. When it is completed, say:

> My God and my God, arise and help me; understand my cry. In the morning I pray to you; hear my voice. Arise and attend to my judgment, so that today you may be present in my cause, my God.

And what more, son? Rise, put on your shoes as is customary, and prepare yourself in the preparation of the Gospel of peace. Chant the canonical hours; complete your office, as it is written: “Seven times a day I have praised you.”

Recite the chapters of all your preparations as you know them best, or as you find them. When these have been completed as above, say the prayers appropriate to the individual hours. Then, in the name of the supreme God, go out to the temporal service that is increasing for you, or to whatever your lord and father B. has ordered, or your master K. has commanded to be done—provided that God permits it.

## XI: Again

When you go outside, keep God in mind with the sign of the cross, and say:

> Have mercy on me, merciful Father, and complete my steps today in your paths. Lead me in your way and direct me in your truth. Help me today and always, my God, so that slanders do not assail me and no injustice rule over me. Rather, gladden my heart as I walk toward goodness, so that, by doing what pleases you, I may deserve, with your help, to reach evening.

Also say:

> Blessed are you, Lord God, who have helped me and comforted me. You are blessed, from whom all good things proceed, who live, and so forth.

## XV: An Admonition to Be Shown Toward Your Lord

Keep the lord you have, K. [Charles], whom God, as I believe, and your father B. chose in the flower-bearing strength of your beginning youth for you to serve.

Continue to hold fast to him, who is sprung from a great lineage of noble stock on both sides [the Latin is corrupt]; serve not merely to please the eyes, but with understanding as well. In both body and soul, keep for him in all things a pure, reliable, and useful loyalty.

## XIX: To the Relatives of Your Lords

If you reach the point at which, together with your fellow soldiers, you may deserve to be a useful servant within the royal and imperial court, or anywhere else, fear, love, honor, and cherish the illustrious and distinguished parents and relatives of your lord, eminent in royal power, arising both from the dignity of paternal descent and from the dignity of marriage.

In every affair, prepare for all of them a pure and suitable service, with reliable fidelity in carrying out their interests, both in mind and body, and so forth.

You, therefore, son V., likewise obey the yoke * and the rule of servitude. Be faithful to your lord K., whoever he may be, and to the worthy parents of both sexes who are sprung from royal lineage.

It is fitting for you to act in this way, and I desire that all who serve under their royal rule should strive with all their strength to serve usefully and faithfully among them.

For God, as we believe, chose and especially chose them for the kingdom, giving them a glory tending toward that great likeness of resemblance which he promised to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. May the gracious Almighty, the strong and most distinguished King, make them like and harmonious with their worthy offspring and their descendants.

May they, following the peace of their forefathers, shine prosperously in this present world; bravely rule, protect, govern, and defend the world and its people in the service of God and the saints; resist and defend against the bands of enemies and foes rising up everywhere; and unite the holy Church of God more firmly in true religion in Christ.

May they see the offspring of their children pleasing God worthily, growing and flourishing, and tending upward through the course of many years, and so forth.

## XX: To the Leading Men of the Dukes

Love, cherish, and frequently serve the leading men of the dukes and their counselors, those who faithfully serve them and their equals—everything in the parts, and the parts through the whole, whoever he or they may be who shine in the court.

Humbly seek out examples of their dignities and hold them most firmly. For in a great house such as that one was, is, and will be, many exchanges of instruction take place.

There one person can, if he wishes, learn from another humility, charity, chastity, patience, gentleness, moderation, sobriety, prudence, and the other virtues that accompany the earnest practice of good works.

You, therefore, as a growing boy, learn from your elders and from those capable of understanding whatever good you can receive from them, with the help of the supreme and gracious God, so that you may first of all please God, and so forth.

## LX

Pray for the parents of your father, who left their possessions to him in lawful inheritance—those who were, or whose names you will find written in the chapters of this little book at the end.

Although Scripture says, “Another rejoices in another’s goods,” nevertheless, as I said above, their inheritances are not possessed by strangers but by your lord and father B. [Bernard], insofar as they remained to him. Pray for him who possesses them; pray that you may enjoy them happily for a very long time while you live.

For I believe that if you strive toward him worthily and humbly, he will thereby increase for you the pious growth of the frugality of his dignities, just as, with the prior clemency of Almighty God, your father may have ordered something from them to be bestowed upon you in proportion to your ability to make them greater, so that the reward may increase for him from the souls to whom all those things belonged.

Because of his many responsibilities, he does not have the opportunity for a time. But you, while you are able and have permission, pray continually for their souls.

Nor should this be passed over, my son: pray for the one who, receiving you from my arms, adopted you as a son in Christ through the bath of regeneration. His name, while he lived, was Lord Theodoric [Note: Was Theodoric the brother of Count Heccard, whose testament is found in Perard, p. 25?]. He had been your former nourisher and also your lover in all things, if it had been permitted him.

We believe that Abraham’s bosom received him. Leaving you, as though a firstborn little child, in this world, all his possessions remained with our lord and master so that they might benefit you.

Offer more numerous and special prayers for him, together with the very good, at night, at matins, at vespers, and at the other hours, throughout the times of the hours and the spaces of places. If he did anything unjustly and did not repent, command that a sacrifice be offered to the Lord for him frequently, insofar as you are able, through the prayers of holy priests and by distributing alms to the poor.

When you have poured out your prayers to the Lord for him, say the following capitular prayers:

> Eternal rest, and so forth. May his soul dwell among good things. The righteous shall be in eternal remembrance.

Or as you know better.

When you have completed this, say the prayer:

> May you deign, Lord, to place the body and soul of your servant Theodoric in the bosoms of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, so that, when the day of your judgment has come, you may command him to be raised among your saints and elect, through the Lord.

## LXI

Frequently have the solemnities of Masses and sacrifices offered not only for him but also for all faithful departed.

For no prayer is better in this matter than offerings of sacrifices. It is said of the very brave man Judas: “It is a holy and salutary thought to pray for the dead and to offer sacrifice for them, so that they may be released from sins.”

May he rest in peace. Amen.

## LXVIII

You have now reached four years completed. If a second child had had as much time, I would have transcribed another little book for him personally; and if he had had as much again, and as much again, and half of half as much, turning through the years, I would have joined stronger words to you in extended speech, so that I might behold your appearance.

But because the time of my dissolution does not delay me, and the illness of anxieties crushes my body on every side, I exhort you, in haste and knowing that I cannot reach the appointed time, to taste this little book, which I have gathered for you and your brother so that it may be useful, like a honey-sweet drink and a honeycomb mixed into food for the mouth.

For from the time when I came to your father, or when your state from us came forth into the world, everything is reckoned among us on the Kalends of the months [read: December].

From the first verse of this little book to its final syllable, know that everything has been written for you as a measure of salvation. Read what is contained there in the headings of the verses, so that you may more easily enter into what follows below.

## LXXI

Returning to me, I mourn.

From the excessive sweetness of my love and longing for your beauty, postponing myself, as though forgetful of myself, I sometimes desire to enter within when the doors are closed. But since I am not worthy to be counted among the prescribed number, nevertheless I ask that you not cease to pray for the remedy of my soul with an affection that makes the countless countable.

W., it is not hidden from you how, because of my continual infirmities and for certain reasons, I have endured in my fragile body all these things—or others like them—because of my merits, which hinder me, in accordance with the saying of someone who says: “Dangers from kindred, dangers from the nations,” and so forth. With God’s help and through the merit of your father, I confidently escaped all these things. Yet my mind turns back to these deliverances, and during the recurring seasons I remained sluggish in many divine praises; what I ought to have done during seven hours, I negligently failed to do for seven times seven.

Therefore, with a suppliant affection and all my strength, I beg you to take pleasure in continually imploring the Lord’s mercy for my offenses and sins, and to deign to raise me, crushed and weighed down, to the heights. While you see me alive in this world, strive with watchful devotion to contend on my behalf, not only through vigils and prayers, but also through alms for the poor, so that, once physically released from the bond of my sins, I may deservedly be received with mercy in all things by the merciful Judge.

At present I need your frequent prayer, and that of others; afterward there will be even more need, and, as I believe, it will come more quickly. Because of the excessive pain of love, my mind is greatly troubled on every side by what may happen to me in the future; and I am uncertain, considering my merits, how I shall be able to be delivered at the end. Why? Because I have sinned in thought and speech. Indeed, my useless speech proceeded as far as evil action.

Although this is so, I shall never despair of God’s mercy, nor do I now despair, nor ever shall. And so that I may at some time attain restoration, I leave no survivor like you, who will strive on my behalf as you do—and, noble boy, many through you—for the interests of my lord and master, so that my service toward him in the marches, [Col. 0117B] or in many places, would not become worthless; nor would he have separated himself from you or from me, as is customary. In some respects I feel myself greatly burdened by obligations.

From many needy people—not only Christians but also Jews—I have often received many things from their possessions through my hands. As much as I was able, I repaid; and as much as I can, I shall always repay hereafter. But if, after my departure, anything remains to be paid, I ask and beg you yourself to inquire carefully who my creditors are. Once they have been found, see that everything is paid in full, not only from my resources, if any remain, but also from what you possess and what, with God’s help, you may justly acquire hereafter.

What more? Concerning your youngest brother, I have advised above what you ought to do toward him, and I advise it again hereafter. This I ask: if he reaches that time, may he himself also deign to pray for me. For now I admonish both of you together, as though joined as one, and ask that you deign frequently to offer on my behalf the offerings of sacrifices together with sacrificial oblations, and so forth.

The Book of the Manual ends here. Amen. Thanks be to God.

## Names of the Dead

Recognize these as abbreviated names of certain persons mentioned above but previously omitted: Willelmus, Cuhngundis, Cariberga, Withburgis, Theodericus, Gothzelmus, Guarnarius, Rodlindis. They belong to the genealogy mentioned above and, with God’s help, are joined together in this world; their calling remains with the One who created them all as He willed.

What is to be done concerning them, my son, except to say with the Psalmist: “We who live bless the Lord, from this time forth and forever.”

## Likewise

[Col. 0118B] Whoever from your lineage departs—which is subject to no one’s power except God’s, whenever He gives the command—and likewise your uncle Lord Aribertus [Note: [Col. 0117D] Heribertus, who was blinded in the year 830, according to the *Life of Louis the Pious*], I ask that, if you survive, you order his name to be transcribed together with the persons listed above, praying for him.

## LXXII

When I myself have completed my days, order my name also to be transcribed as deceased among their names. What I desire, and what I demand with all my strength as though it were already present, is that, in the place where I am buried, you order these verses to be firmly inscribed upon the very roof of the tomb covering my body, so that those who see the epitaph of the tomb may be commanded to pour forth worthy prayers to God for me, unworthy as I am: S S S.

Also, whoever may ever read this Manual which you are reading, let that person meditate upon the words that follow below, and commend me—already, as it were, shut within—to God, that I may be released.

## In the Year of the Lord 842. Jonas, Bishop of Orléans

[Col. 0117]

[Col. 0117D]

## Historical Notice

*(From* Gallia Christiana*.)*

[Col. 0117]

[Col. 0117D] Jonas, successor of Theodulf, wishing the monastic order restored by him in the monastery of Micy to remain undisturbed, arranged for it to be secured by imperial authority through a privilege granted on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of March, in the twelfth year of Louis, in the third indiction. This is the year 825, when he attended the assembly held at Paris on the first of November concerning the veneration of images. In order to review its acts carefully and present the reviewed material to Pope Eugene II for reading, he was sent as an envoy by Louis Augustus together with Jeremiah, archbishop of Sens.

He is listed among the bishops who attended another synod at Paris in the year 829. He subscribed the partition of the goods of Saint-Denis, made in the year 832 by Abbot Hilduin. At the Synod of Sens in 833, he subscribed the privilege issued for the monks of Saint Remigius of Sens. He attended the Synod of Thionville in 835 and the deposition of Ebo, archbishop of Reims.

In the same year, on the ninth day before the Kalends of September, he was delegated by Louis the Pious together with Count Hugh to place the monks of Fleury in possession of the estate of Suncant, which nobles had violently usurped, although his grandfather Pippin had granted it to them. At the request of Jonas, Louis Augustus granted another privilege to the monastery of Micy on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May in the year 836.

He subscribed the testament of Aldric, bishop of Le Mans, in the year 837, on the Kalends of April, on Holy Easter Day, in the fifteenth indiction. In the same year, on the day before the Kalends of May, he attended at Aachen the judgment rendered in the case of the monks of Anisolum, and on the eighth day before the Ides of September he attended a hearing at Quierzy concerning the same matter.

In Baluze there are two letters from the emperor to Jonas, both without a date. In the first, the emperor assigns Jonas and Abbot Henry the task of ensuring that the ecclesiastical property taken from the monks of Saint-Calais is restored. The second, which perhaps preceded the hearing at Quierzy, declares them to be his envoys so that they might compel the monks who had left the monastery to return, while ordering the disobedient to appear at the next hearing at Quierzy.

Lupus, abbot of Ferrières, speaks of Jonas with praise and writes to him in Letters 21, 27, and 28. In the first, however, he seems to criticize him for failing to restrain the rapacity of his relative Agius, whom it is likely was Jonas’s successor.

Adrevald of Fleury, in *Miracles of Saint Benedict*, Book I, chapter 25, recounts a lawsuit instituted between the advocates of Fleury and those of Saint-Denis. To settle it, Jonas the bishop and Donatus, count of Melun, were sent; he calls them judges according to the Salic Law.

Jonas was also distinguished for his writings. At the command of Louis the Pious, he composed three books against Claudius, bishop of Turin, in defense of the sacred images. He dedicated them to Charles, Louis’s son, in the year 840, from whom he obtained confirmation of the lands of the Church of Orléans. At the request of the same Louis, he wrote a book on the veneration of the Lord’s Cross, which he sent to Claudius, bishop of Turin; this may perhaps be the same work as the earlier one.

He also wrote three books *On Clerical Instruction*, first published by D. Luke d’Achery, as well as another short work *On Royal Instruction*. Baluze also attributes to him the *Life of Saint Hubert, Bishop of Liège*, in his notes on the Capitularies.

Jonas died in the year 843, after spending twenty-two years in the episcopate. Let these verses of Bertold, a monk of Micy, serve in place of an epitaph. Bertold dedicated them to Jonas when writing the *Life of Saint Maximin*, whose relics Jonas had removed from their burial place and transferred to the place where they are now venerated, during the reign of Emperor Louis:

> If indeed you excel in talent and overflow with wisdom,  
> You shine, prudent, in eloquence like Ambrose.  
> You are now called a second Homer in our age;  
> Publius Maro himself is the model for your speech.  
> You are pleasing in character, surpassed by none in piety,  
> Gentle in countenance and dignified in speech.

Ludovico Cavalli, in the *Catalogue of Authors Used in Composing the Gate of the Muses*, says that Varanius wrote in heroic verse a *Life of Jonas of Orléans*.

[Col. 0119]

## Literary Notice

*(From Fabricius, the* Bibliotheca medii et infimi Latini*.)*

[Col. 0119]

[Col. 0119C] Jonas, bishop of Orléans from the year 821 [Note: [Col. 0119D] Alberic under that year, p. 167; Andrea Saussay, *Annals of the Church of Orléans*, p. 313; Charles le Cointe, vol. VIII of the *Frankish Annals*, pp. 613 ff.; the Sammarthani, vol. II, p. 239], after Theodulf until the year 843, attended various councils and the Council of Paris in 824. In 840 he presented to King Charles, son of Louis, three books against the deceased Claudius, bishop of Turin, in opposition to his work against the veneration of images [Note: [Col. 0120D] See the *Orthodoxographi*, p. 1199 of the first edition]. Jonas testified that he had seen only excerpts of Claudius’s work.

Jonas submitted his work to the judgment of Lupus of Ferrières, who decided that nothing in it needed to be changed. See Pagi under the year 825, no. 16; and Baluze’s notes on Lupus, p. 355, where he reports that he handled with his own hands a very old and elegant copy of Jonas’s books—indeed, the very copy that Jonas presented to Charles the Bald.

This is Jonas’s position [Note: [Col. 0120D] Compare Dallæus, *On Images*, IV, 5; the works of Friedrich Spanheim, vol. II, p. 863]: people who venerate images are not all to be regarded as idolaters, since he himself also venerates them in the ecclesiastical manner—that is, he greets them. Some honor and veneration are indeed to be shown to the saints, their memory, and their relics; yet he certainly does not adore them as the Lord. Rather, the superstitious and harmful adoration of images requires correction.

Nor does he adore Mary, but he venerates her with fitting honor and implores her intercession with God; this intercession, like that of the other saints, is neither to be denied nor treated as insignificant. Their images are not to be expelled from churches, but preserved for the adornment of the churches, for remembrance, and for the instruction of the faithful.

These books were first published at Cologne in 1554, then in both editions of the *Orthodoxographi* at Basel in 1555, p. 1199, and in 1569, p. 1526; then at Antwerp in 1565, in octavo, in more corrected form, by Christopher Plantin. They were later included in all editions of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*: those of Paris and Cologne, volume IX, and also the latest edition of Lyon, volume XIV, p. 167. The other two opponents of Claudius of Turin, Dungal and Abbot Theodemir, as well as Claudius himself, have been discussed in their proper place.

Three books *On the Instruction of Laymen*, addressed to Matfred, count of Orléans, were published from the Corbie manuscript by d’Achery in volume I of the *Spicilegium*, p. 1203 (new edition, volume I, p. 258).

*On Royal Instruction*, a book addressed to King Pippin, a large part of which is repeated in the Sixth Council of Paris in 829, was first published complete by the same highly praised d’Achery in volume V of the *Spicilegium*, p. 57 (new edition, volume I, pp. 324–335).

That Jonas was also competent in verse is evident from the twelve-line poem prefixed to this work of instruction, in which he says, among other things:

> I once played readily in metrical odes;  
> Now, with my body broken, I wish to do nothing but weep.

But the Sapphic ode published by Canisius under Jonas’s name, and subsequently by Andrew Rivinus at Leipzig in 1653 in octavo together with poems of Drepanius Florus and others, beginning “Behold, the pious and gracious Caesar has arrived,” and discussed by Barthius in *Adversaria* XIX, 17, has Theodulf of Orléans as its author. It was dedicated by him to the arrival of Louis Augustus at Orléans. See Canisius’s *Ancient Readings*, latest Basnage edition, vol. II, part II, p. 75.

The Jonas who committed to writing the translation of Hubert, bishop of Liège, is not a different person from our Jonas.

[Col. 0121]

## Second Literary Notice

*(From Bellarmine,* On Ecclesiastical Writers*.)*

[Col. 0121]

[Col. 0121B] Jonas, bishop of Orléans under Louis the Pious, wrote three extant books against Claudius, bishop of Turin, in defense of the sacred images, and so forth. Yet this author must be read cautiously, since he suffers from the same error as Agobard and the other Gauls of his age, who denied that any religious veneration was owed to sacred images. On this matter, see Anastasius the Librarian’s preface to the Seventh Council.

## [On Lay Instruction]

[Col. 0121]

## Basnage’s Prefatory Notice to the Following Work

[Col. 0121]

This golden work ought to be continually handled not only by laymen, but especially by those who tend Christ’s sheep, says d’Achery. For Jonas’s sole aim, and the whole direction of his labor, was to draw out, like a resourceful bee, the honeyed juices of Christian doctrine from excerpts of sacred Scripture and from the particularly pleasing writings of the holy Fathers; to distribute them through the ordered parts of this work as so many honeycombs and cells of his own hive; and to offer them for the healing and nourishment of human hearts.

The old library of Corbie supplied me with a single copy, transcribed approximately five hundred years ago. That prelate conducted his episcopate so religiously, prudently, and learnedly, and shone among the more celebrated bishops of Gaul under Charles the Bald; he dedicated this work, divided into three books, to Matfred, count of Orléans. In what state of mind he did so, you will discover in the preface to this very work.

He produced many other works of profound learning, but it is not my purpose here to list their titles. If you wish, read, among other works, the *Annals of the Church of Orléans* by Charles Saussay of Orléans, p. 313.

Later, D. Peter Sauret supplied d’Achery with various readings from a manuscript of the Discalced Carmelites at Clermont in Auvergne, formerly belonging to the cathedral church of Laon. We used these readings to correct the text, just as we used those noted by Baluze from an old edition of this work, published at Douai in 1645 from a manuscript of the monastery of Elnon, as well as those that we ourselves discovered when comparing several chapters of Book I with Jonas’s short work *On Royal Instruction*, which we publish below.

[Col. 0121]

# Three Books of Jonas on Lay Instruction

[Col. 0121]

## Jonas’s Preface

[Col. 0121D] To his beloved in Christ, Matfred: Jonas, everlasting salvation in the Lord.

Recently I received the letter of your earnestness, in which you admonished my lowliness [Note: “Lowliness” (*extremitatem*). Acherius conjectured that this ought to be read thus, and it was so printed at Douai; but the text here read *extrenuitatem*. Below, wherever this has been restored from the Clermont manuscript; and, lest we repeat the same thing too often, we wish the reader to know that we have had everything added from that manuscript enclosed in brackets.] to write to you as quickly and as briefly as possible concerning how you and the others who are bound by the marriage bond ought to lead a life pleasing to God. This is indeed a great task, my dearest friend, which you demand from me, the most ignorant of all people; it utterly exceeds the powers of my understanding, and ought to be undertaken only by learned and eloquent men.

Since, then, [in all matters]* pertaining to the salvation of your soul, [I have always wished to comply with your most humble petition, only in this special request of yours] I had initially decided, conscious of my weakness and ignorance, to resist rather than obey, because I feel myself unequal and unfit to complete it. For your request and my incapacity generated a great struggle in my heart: the former urging me to undertake the work, the latter refusing to undergo the burden of so great a task.

[Col. 0123B] Since my mind had long been divided in this struggle, and since, weighing itself with the most subtle judgment on the scale of its own discernment, it recognized itself to be wholly incapable of undertaking the work, deliberation reached the point at which the work would be abandoned.

But charity, which “bears all things, hopes all things, believes all things, endures all things” (I Corinthians XIII, 4), unable to tolerate such an omission, sprang into the midst of the conflict, driving away the weakness of fear, granting courage to undertake the work, and promising through Him who opens the mouths of the mute and makes the tongues of infants eloquent (Wisdom X, 21) an abundance of ability. At last it compelled me to undertake the work.

Trusting in this, I have to a considerable extent succeeded in undertaking it, because I shall not weave into this work words expressing my own thoughts, written in an eloquent style—a style entirely lacking to me—but rather the doctrines proclaimed in the divine oracles and most elegantly polished by the holy Fathers.

Accordingly, it was my purpose, as far as my intelligence allowed, to search out the divine utterances and the sayings of the holy Fathers; and, like someone picking various little flowers from different meadows and gathering them into a kind of basket, to compose this little commentary for your pious devotion, and also for those who may perhaps find it pleasing. Thus, as in a mirror, you may continually contemplate yourself in it and, through frequent reading, be instructed concerning how you ought to lead your married life honorably.

But if someone should wish to object that I have labored in vain and superfluously on this little work, especially since the Christian way of life is established in the legal, prophetic, evangelical, and apostolic writings, and since, as blessed Augustine says, that same way has been perfectly set out in the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount, let that person know that the ancient Fathers, penetrating the forest of sacred Scripture, cut from it various and innumerable branches of sound faith. For the benefit of many and in honor of divine service, they produced saving rules from those branches; from these, too, there consists the canonical and monastic discipline that devoutly serves Christ.

Although lay instruction is scattered through the divine writings, nevertheless, for those who either lack the inclination or the ability to traverse the broad fields of sacred Scripture, it was judged useful and worthwhile to assent to your kindly request in this matter, to excerpt—as has been said—sentences from the Old and New Testaments and sayings of the holy Fathers, and to assemble this work from them in response to your request and dedicate it to your devotion; indeed, for you and for others who are willing to undertake it with zeal, to receive it with charity and embrace it with pious devotion.

And so that its length would not weary its readers, I divided it into three little books [Note: [Col. 0124C] “I divided it into three little books.” Thus the Clermont manuscript and the Douai edition read; the Paris edition had “I divided it into three little books for you.”]: the first and last are intended generally for all the faithful, while the middle one is, for the greater part, especially suitable for those leading a married life.

Meanwhile, I admonish your most experienced discernment and your humble devotion to the service of Christ to read this frequently, or have it read to you. Do not readily disclose it to those who are more inclined to criticize what belongs to others than to love with fraternal affection.

If I have assembled anything in this work otherwise than I ought, I humbly ask the Lord that I may be forgiven. But if readers or hearers discover anything in it that may benefit them, let them remember to give thanks, together with me, not to me but to God.

# Book One

[Col. 0123]

## Chapter One

### What all the faithful ought generally to know: into what condemnation through the Fall they have come because of the guilt of the first man

The first-created man, the parent of the entire human race, was wondrously created by God from the clay of the earth and placed in the happiness of paradise. But because, wrongly persuaded by his wife’s counsel, he consented and ate the fruit of the forbidden tree, he not only became himself a transgressor of the divine command, but also passed on to us, who are born from the stock of that sin, the guilt of his transgression and the punishment of just condemnation.

For it is clear that, when he transgressed, we too transgressed the Lord’s covenant together with him. Hence the Psalmist says: “I have counted all the sinners of the earth as transgressors” (Psalm CXVIII, 119). And the Apostle says: “Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin, death; and thus death passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Romans V, 12).

Behold what inheritance that same father of ours left us—the one to whom, when he sinned, it was said: “You are earth, and into earth you shall go” (Genesis III, 19): exile instead of a homeland, misery instead of happiness, dishonor instead of glory, and the death of body and soul instead of immortality.

He made a deeply miserable bargain with the devil. The devil, who through pride fell from angelic dignity into apostasy, through whose envy death entered the world (Romans V, 12), envying Adam’s happiness, promised him divinity but took away immortality, and made the inhabitant of paradise an exile of the world. Nor did he subjugate only Adam; he also subjected his offspring to his destructive rule. Humanity remained held under it, miserably and fatally, until that Samaritan—the Lord Jesus Christ—while traveling, moved by mercy, approached him, bound up his wounds, poured in wine and oil, placed him upon his own beast, and brought him to an inn. On the following day he brought the innkeeper two denarii for the healing of the wounded man, and promised that, on his return, he would repay whatever more the innkeeper had spent (Luke X, 33).

Augustine writes in his *Book of Sermons to the People*: “The fallen one envied the one standing and cast him down; but Christ, descending, raised up the one lying fallen.”

He also writes in the *Enchiridion* (chapter XXXIII):

> “The human race was held under just condemnation, and all were children of wrath. Concerning this wrath it is written: ‘For all our days have failed, and in your wrath we have wasted away. Our years shall be meditated upon like a spider’” (Psalm LXXXIX, 9). “Concerning this wrath Job also says: ‘A human being born of woman is short-lived and full of wrath’” (Job XIV, 1). “Concerning this wrath the Lord Jesus Christ says: ‘Whoever believes in the Son of God has eternal life; but whoever does not believe in the Son does not have life, but the wrath of God remains upon him’” (John III, 36). He does not say “will come,” but “remains,” since every human being is born with it. Therefore the Apostle says: “We too were by nature children of wrath, like the rest” (Ephesians II, 3). Since human beings were in this condition through original sin—and all the more gravely and harmfully insofar as they added greater or more numerous sins besides—it was necessary to have a mediator, that is, a reconciler, who would appease this wrath by an offering. All the sacrifices of the Law and the Prophets were its shadows (Hebrews VIII, 6; IX, 11). Hence the Apostle says: ‘For if, while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, having now been reconciled in his blood, shall we be saved from wrath through him’” (Romans V, 10).

[Col. 0125D] Prosper writes [Note: [Col. 0125D] Rather, Julianus Pomerius, *On the Contemplative Life*, Book II, chapter 20]:

> “In Adam we lost all the good things that we could have possessed; in Christ we shall receive again even greater things, to be possessed without end, if we persevere in following his footsteps. Adam made us liable to every evil through his own fault; Christ’s coming freed us from them through grace. Adam transmitted his guilt and punishment to us; Christ, who could not assume our guilt, since he was conceived and born without sin, by assuming our punishment abolished both our guilt and our punishment.” [Note: “By assuming punishment.” The first edition read “by assuming guilt,” which could not be accepted.] “In short, Adam deprived us of paradise; Christ gave us heaven as well.”

It is therefore clear that the original sin by which the human race was damnably bound could not be loosed and washed away except through that same mediator between God and humanity, the man Jesus Christ. Nor could humanity be freed through him in any other way than if he were true man and also true God.

It is therefore manifest that we have been saved through the grace of our Redeemer Jesus Christ. Through his undeserved death, although we are not exempt from ordinary death, we have nevertheless been rescued from the death that was owed to us and that would have been everlasting; from children of darkness we have become children of light, and from vessels of wrath we have become vessels of mercy.

Therefore every faithful person ought to recognize where he fell through his own merit and from where he was rescued through Christ’s gratuitous compassion. He should strive to love so great a rescuer and deliverer with all his heart, all his soul, and all his strength, and not grow cold in love for him in any respect, but spend every moment of his life in his service.

## Chapter Two

### That in baptism the old person is stripped off and the new person put on, and that one dies and is buried with Christ

The Apostle admonishes us to strip off the old person with his deeds and put on the new, saying: “Strip off the old person with his deeds, and put on the new person, who is renewed in the knowledge of God” (Colossians III, 9). And elsewhere: “All who have been baptized in Christ have put on Christ” (Galatians III, 27). Again: “Put on the Lord Jesus Christ” (Romans XIII, 14). Again: “Put on the new person, who was created according to God” (Ephesians IV, 23).

This is the new person with whom all believers ought to be clothed and dressed. Hence it is written in the Apocalypse: “Blessed is the one who watches and guards his garments, lest he walk naked and his shame be seen” (Revelation XVI, 15). And in Ecclesiastes: “At all times let your garments be white, and let oil not fail from your head” (Ecclesiastes IX, 8).

They were clothed in the garments of this new person of whom it is read in the same Apocalypse: “I have a few names in Sardis that have not defiled their garments, and they shall walk with me in white garments. Whoever conquers shall be clothed in white garments, and I shall not erase his name from the book of life” (Revelation III, 4).

Hypocrites and wicked people of this kind cannot be clothed in the garments of this new person. For whoever is truly clothed in his garments—that is, in his virtues—will rightly be able to say with the Apostle: “I live, yet it is no longer I; Christ lives in me” (Galatians II, 20).

What is the old person except the former life that we led in sins? What is the new person except Christ, who is justice, truth, and sanctification? According to the Apostle, we die and are buried with him in baptism, as he says: “Do you not know that all who have been baptized in Christ Jesus have been baptized into his death?” (Romans VI, 3.)

Blessed Augustine explains these words as follows [Note: *Enchiridion*, chapter 52]:

> “So that we understand nothing else in Christ’s baptism except the likeness of Christ’s death, and nothing else in the death of crucified Christ except the likeness of the remission of sin: so that, just as true death took place in him, so true remission of sins may take place in us; and just as true resurrection took place in him, so true justification may take place in us.”

And a little later:

> “The Apostle so presented the death of Christ that he even said that Christ himself died to sin. To what sin, except that of the flesh in which he was present—not as sin, but as the likeness of sinful flesh—and therefore he calls it by the name of sin? You are therefore baptized into the death of Christ, in which not only adults but also infants are baptized. He says: ‘So also you’—that is, just as Christ—‘so also consider yourselves dead to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus’” (ibid., 11).

The same Apostle writes to the Colossians: “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Colossians III, 3). You have died, that is, because you have been baptized into his death. And since “our old person was crucified together with him” (Romans VI, 6), just as Christ was crucified, died, and was buried for us, and rose again, so we too ought, in imitation of his passion, to crucify our wills and desires and to imitate in baptism the mystery of his death, burial, and resurrection.

Again he says: “If we have died with Christ, we believe that we shall also live with him” (ibid., 8).

We must therefore labor so that nothing of the filth of the old person remains in us. Christ was crucified not in part but whole, so that we might die entirely to sin and live to God.

That person lives to God who follows Christ’s footsteps in humility, sanctification, and piety. I say, that person lives to God and becomes his temple who has been clothed in the heavenly commandments that constitute the garment of the new person—commandments lacking to the one who entered the wedding feast in a filthy garment.

Blessed Jerome says in his commentaries [Note: *Commentary on Matthew*, chapter XXII, verse 11]:

> “If, then, at the time of judgment someone is found under the Christian name not to possess the wedding garment—that is, the garment of the heavenly person—but a defiled garment, namely, the castoff clothing of the old person, he is immediately reproved and told: ‘Friend, how did you come in here?’” (Matthew XXII, 12.) “He calls him friend because he was invited to the wedding; he accuses him of shamelessness because, wearing a filthy garment, he defiled the purity of the wedding feast. But he was speechless. At that time there will be no opportunity for shamelessness [Note: “Opportunity for shamelessness.” Thus the excellent Clermont manuscript reads; the earlier reading, “opportunity for repentance,” was entirely inappropriate], nor any possibility of denial, since all the angels and the world itself are witnesses to the sins.”

Therefore every faithful person ought to know that unless he is clothed with this new person—namely, the Lord Christ Jesus—even if he now walks adorned with purple and fine linen, gold and jewels, he nevertheless exists miserably and lamentably naked in the eyes of the divine majesty. And if he ends his days in this nakedness, he will not only be reproved in the future by Christ the King, but will also be excluded from the wedding feast, which is eternal.

But if someone wishes to know what the garments of this new person are, let him know that his garments are innocence, patience, kindness, gentleness, faith, humility, charity, modesty, chastity—without which no one will see God—and the other virtues, whose enumeration would be lengthy.

It is also necessary to take care not to return to the sin to which one died in baptism, since baptism cannot be repeated, nor will Christ, having died once for that person, return again to suffer. Concerning this the Apostle says: “Christ, rising from the dead, no longer dies; death shall no longer rule over him” (Romans VI, 9).

## Chapter Three

### That the faithful ought always to remember the covenant they made with God in baptism

Every faithful person bound himself to God in baptism by the bonds of two covenants. In the first, he renounced the devil, all his works, and all his pomps. In the second, he professed that he believed in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Thus, under the invocation of that same Holy Trinity, he deserved to receive the grace of baptism.

Therefore, if anyone, after such a renunciation, enticed by any allurements of vice, returns to the things he renounced; and if, after receiving so great a faith, he falls into apostasy, unbelief, heretical depravity, or fraternal schism, he is undoubtedly a transgressor of both covenants.

The first covenant, since it cannot be cleansed by a repetition of baptism, can be cleansed through the tears of repentance, generous almsgiving, and the performance of other good works. But the second covenant, once stained by the leprosy of the contamination described above, cannot be cleansed or recover the color of its former faith and the vigor of health unless it first becomes free from that contamination through Christ’s grace and returns to the unity of the Church.

Because it is established that, on account of the sin of the first man, that flaming sword by whose barrier the gate of paradise was closed to human beings was extinguished in the most holy font of baptism, and that the same gate was opened to believers, all the faithful ought always to remember the covenant and pledge which they made with God [in baptism]. They must take care lest, by defiling themselves with any filth of vices, they not only rekindle that same fire for themselves, but also cause the unclean spirit expelled from them at the time of baptism to return to them, together with the addition of a sevenfold number of demons; and thus, as the Lord says, “the last state of those men becomes worse than the first” (Matt. XII, 45). And what the blessed Apostle Peter said may be fulfilled in them: “For it would have been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness than, after knowing it, to turn back from the holy commandment delivered to them.” And what he says shortly afterward may apply to them: “The dog has returned to its vomit, and the washed sow to wallowing in the mud” (II Pet. II, 21–22).

Therefore all Christians must earnestly strive, remembering so great a pledge and so salutary a covenant, and keeping it without dispute and inviolate, while despising the ancient enemy, together with his vices, whom they renounced, to ascend without weariness to the courts of the heavenly city, which through the mystery of holy baptism and the gift of the Holy Spirit have been opened to believers. [Col. 0129A]

## CHAPTER IV. That there were various baptisms in the Old Testament, but that in the New Testament there is one baptism which grants remission of sins in three ways

We read in Exodus that Moses, who bore the type of Christ, baptized the people of God in the Red Sea, which bears the figure of baptism because it was reddened with the blood of Christ, as the Apostle testifies and says: “For I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that all our fathers were under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea” (I Cor. X, 1). The sea, as has been said, bore the figure of baptism; the cloud, of the Holy Spirit; and the manna, of the bread of life. Other baptisms also took place in the Old Testament, which were practiced according to the dispensation of the times; but nowhere before John the Baptist is baptism said to have been given for repentance. [Note: “[But up to.]” Thus I emended the text, whereas it formerly read “if up to.” Below, where the text reads “nor merely in the Spirit,” Acherius rightly saw that it should read “nor yet.”]

For Isidore writes in the second book of *The Offices* (Book II, chap. 24):

> “John also baptized, but not wholly in the Jewish manner. For he baptized not only in water, nor merely * in the Spirit; but he added this alone: that he baptized in repentance, as Paul says in the Acts of the Apostles: ‘John baptized the people with the baptism of repentance, saying that they should believe in the one who was to come after him, that is, in Jesus’ (Acts XIX, 4). Thus perfect baptism began with Jesus. He therefore first baptized in the Holy Spirit, as John says: ‘I indeed baptize you in water; but in your midst there stands one whom you do not know; he will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire’ (John I, 26). This is the perfection of baptism: for it is God who baptizes, so that those who are baptized may also become children of God.”

This is indeed the one saving baptism, concerning which the Apostle says: “One Lord, one faith, one baptism” (Eph. IV, 5). Although it grants remission of sins in three ways, it is nevertheless one baptism through which sins are cleansed.

For the aforementioned Isidore writes in the same little book that there are three baptisms:

> “The first,” he says, “is that of which the Apostle speaks, by which the filth of sins is washed away through the laver of regeneration.”  
> 
> “In this baptism,” as the blessed Augustine says, “little children die only to original sin; adults die also to all those sins which, by living wickedly, they have added to what they drew from birth” [Note: *Enchiridion*, chap. 44.].

> “The second baptism,” says the aforementioned Isidore, “is that by which a person is baptized in his own blood through martyrdom. Christ too was baptized with this baptism, so that in this, as in other matters, he might give believers an example, just as he said to the disciples, the sons of Zebedee: ‘Can you drink the cup which I am going to drink, and be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized?’” (Matt. XX, 22; Mark X, 38).

Thus water and blood are a twofold figure of baptism: one by which we are regenerated through baptism, [Note: “Through baptism.” Here Acherius also correctly emends the text to “through the washing of water.” Above, from the Claromontane manuscript, I restored “are a figure of baptism,” for the printed edition had “is a figure.” Whether “the conversion of Manasseh” should subsequently be restored, as Acherius thought, others may decide; it seems to me that the word “confession” is not improperly used.] the other by which we are consecrated in blood.

There is also a third baptism, that of tears, which is undergone with greater labor; as was done by the one who watered his bed with tears each night (Ps. VI, 7), or by those who imitate the confession of * Manasseh and the humility of the Ninevites, through which they obtained mercy, and the prayer of that tax collector standing far off in the temple and beating his breast, who did not even dare to raise his eyes toward heaven. Their eyes, moreover, according to the prophet, “pour forth streams of water,” etc. (Lam. III, 48). Such people, without doubt, are known to cleanse their sins through the baptism of tears. [Col. 0130B]

Of these three baptisms, although the order has been stated differently above, the Psalmist says: “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered” (Ps. XXXI, 1). That is, in baptism through the confession of sins and streams of tears: “Blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not imputed sin, and in whose spirit there is no deceit” (ibid., 2), through the crown of martyrdom.

Since the first baptism is knowingly sought on account of faith in Christ, it is received for salvation. The second, because Christ grants peace to his Church, is not achieved today through the blood of martyrdom. The third, however, which is exceedingly necessary, must be sought and embraced by all Christians—not lazily, nor with any discouragement, as many customarily do, which is dangerous, but with great haste and the most devoted intention of mind, while the acceptable time remains, while it is the day of salvation, and while the Lord may be found. [Col. 0130C]

## CHAPTER V. On the seven remissions of sins

In the preceding chapter it was said that there are three baptisms through which the washing and purification of sins takes place. In this chapter it must be demonstrated by what means remission of sins occurs.

For Origen writes as follows in the first homily of his book on Leviticus:

> “Hear now how many there are of the remissions of sins. There is the remission by which we are baptized for the remission of sins. The second is in the passion of martyrdom. The third is that which is granted through almsgiving; for the Savior says: ‘Nevertheless, give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you’ (Luke XI, 41). The fourth remission of sins comes to us through our forgiving the sins of our brothers; for the Lord and Savior himself says: ‘If you forgive your brothers their sins from your heart, your heavenly Father will also forgive you your sins. But if you do not forgive your brothers from your heart, neither will your Father forgive you your sins’ (Matt. XVIII, 35). And as he taught us to say in prayer: ‘Forgive us our debts’ (Matt. VI, 12). [Col. 0131A]
>
> “The fifth remission of sins occurs when someone turns a sinner back from the error of his way; for divine Scripture says: ‘Whoever turns a sinner back from the error of his way will save his soul from death and cover a multitude of sins’ (James V, 20). The sixth remission of sins likewise takes place through an abundance of charity, as the Lord himself says: ‘Amen I say to you, her sins are forgiven, because she loved much’ (Luke VII, 47). And the Apostle says: ‘Because charity covers a multitude of sins’ (I Pet. IV, 8).
>
> “There is still a seventh remission of sins, although laborious and difficult, through repentance: when the sinner washes his bed with tears, and his tears become his bread by day and by night (Ps. XLI, 4); when he is not ashamed to disclose his sin to the priest of the Lord in order to obtain medicine, according to the one who says: ‘I said: I will declare my injustice against myself; and you forgave the impiety of my sin’ (ibid., 5). And this saying: ‘I turned in my anguish, while the thorn was being fixed’ (Ps. XLI, 4).”

The sacrifices that were performed under the Law were therefore types of these remissions, which now take place in the Church. Nor is it without mystical significance that there are said to be seven remissions, since the Holy Spirit, through whom remission of sins is granted, is said to possess a sevenfold grace.

When Isaiah prophesied concerning Christ, who is the Lord’s rod of power, he said of the Spirit’s gifts: “A rod shall go forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root, and the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isa. XI, 1). [Note: “The rod of power.” Acherius printed “a rod and power,” not entirely without justification, but the reading of the Claromontane manuscript seemed preferable; for Jonas appears thereby to have referred to that passage of Psalm CIX: “The Lord will send forth the rod of your power,” etc.]

This does not mean that the same Holy Spirit is different according to the distinctions of his names, but that one and the same Spirit is the source and origin of all virtues. For just as, according to the Apostle’s testimony, Christ is called the power and wisdom of God; and in Proverbs we read, “God founded the earth by his wisdom and prepared the heavens by his prudence” (Prov. III, 19); and just as the same Word is called light, life, and resurrection, so the Holy Spirit is called the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, of knowledge and piety, and of the fear of the Lord.

The number seven therefore contains within it the numbers three and four: in three, the mystery of the Holy Trinity; in four, the Gospel. For whether three is multiplied by four or four by three, the number twelve is reached, because the mystery of the Holy Trinity and the doctrine of the Gospel are extended through the twelve apostles to the four quarters of the world. If anyone desires to know more fully and extensively about the mystery of this number seven, let him read the first book of Pope Gregory’s *Moralia*, where he will find it discussed at very great length.

## CHAPTER VI. [Col. 0132A] That spiritual fathers ought to urge those whom they receive from the holy font toward better things by words and examples

We are prompted by the teaching of the prophet Daniel not only to stir ourselves to undertake saving instruction, but also to teach others righteousness; for he says: “Those who are learned shall shine like the splendor of the firmament, and those who instruct others in righteousness like the stars for everlasting eternities” (Dan. XII, 3).

The blessed Augustine also says to the people in a sermon [Note: Sermon 163, *On Time*]:

> “Therefore, whatever men or women have spiritually received children from the holy font must recognize that they have become their guarantors before God. Consequently, it is necessary that they always devote to them the care of true charity, admonish, discipline, and correct them, so that they may preserve chastity and keep virginity until marriage; restrain their tongues from cursing and perjury; utter no shameful or lustful songs from their mouths; not become proud, not be envious, and not retain anger or hatred in their hearts; not observe omens, and never hang amulets or demonic signs on themselves or their own people; flee enchanters and ministers of the devil; hold the Catholic faith truly; assemble more frequently at church; and, setting aside verbosity, listen attentively with their ears to the divine readings.
>
> “Let them feed the hungry, give drink to the thirsty, clothe the naked, receive the poor and strangers, visit the sick and those confined in prison, and take care to minister to them in their necessities; let them keep peace, strive to recall those at variance to harmony, and show honor to priests. If, therefore, you strive to admonish your sons and daughters concerning all these things and things like them, you will happily arrive with them at eternal blessedness.
>
> “Let no one deceive himself, dearest brothers; no person dies for himself alone. Rather, as I have often advised, however many people someone has edified by the example of a holy life, with so many and for so many will he receive the reward of blessed recompense. And whoever gives as many an example of evil conduct, even if they do not follow him, must know that he will render an account for so many evils.
>
> “Therefore, as I have already advised, with the Lord’s help we must show our neophytes an example of good conduct as far as we can, so that we may deserve to attain forgiveness of sins not by receiving punishment for their destruction, but rather through their edification.”

And since it has frequently been shown to you what you ought to avoid and flee, and by constant preaching it has been demonstrated what you ought to do and seek, act, with God’s help, so that our admonition may benefit you more as a reward than as a judgment before the tribunal of the eternal Judge. [Note: No one can fail to understand that these words are presented as from Saint Augustine, although they do not occur in the passage cited. What follows in brackets was wholly absent from the earlier edition.]
