[Col. 0133A] [By these and similar instructions of so great a teacher we are clearly taught that, although we ought to form all whom we can, by words and examples, toward the integrity of a holy life and urge them to devote themselves to good works, nevertheless we ought to act with particular care and vigilance toward those whom we have received from the holy font. Many people, in fact, practice this saving reception not for the sake of the salvation of the one received, but rather out of love for the world. Let them decide for themselves whether such people ought rightly to be called spiritual fathers. Whoever, therefore, becomes a spiritual father to anyone in baptism must labor as much as he can so that the one whom he has received may remain his spiritual son, lest by living wickedly he become once again the son of the one from whose service he was rescued through the grace of baptism and made a son of God through adoption.] [Col. 0133B]

## CHAPTER VII. That people should come eagerly and devoutly to receive the gift of the Holy Spirit through the laying on of the bishop’s hands

The reception of the Holy Spirit, which is bestowed by bishops through the laying on of hands, is sought appropriately by some and negligently by others. There are certain noble people—which is praiseworthy—who eagerly hasten to have themselves and their own distinguished by such a gift. There are also others—which deserves correction—who delay doing this for a long time. The lower classes, moreover, are negligent in this matter partly through carelessness and partly through ignorance, to such an extent that some of them do not receive the consecration of this gift until they are already of decrepit age. [Col. 0133C]

That it belongs to the bishop alone to transmit the Holy Spirit to the faithful through the laying on of hands is shown by the Acts of the Apostles, where we read:

> “It happened that while Apollos was at Corinth, Paul, after passing through the upper regions, came to Ephesus. There he found certain disciples and said to them: ‘Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?’ But they said to him: ‘We have not even heard whether there is a Holy Spirit.’ And he said to them: ‘Into what, then, were you baptized?’ They said: ‘Into John’s baptism.’ Then Paul said: ‘John baptized the people with a baptism of repentance, saying that they should believe in the one who was to come after him, that is, in Jesus.’ When they heard this, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. And when Paul had laid his hands upon them, the Holy Spirit came upon them; and they spoke in tongues and prophesied” (Acts XIX, 1).

Observe that, after receiving baptism, they immediately received the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands by the blessed Paul.

Likewise, in another passage:

> “When the apostles who were in Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent Peter and John to them. When they had arrived, they prayed for them that they might receive the Holy Spirit; for he had not yet come upon any of them, but they had only been baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. Then they laid their hands upon them, and they received the Holy Spirit” (Acts VIII, 16).

It must be noted that the Holy Spirit came upon none of the baptized except through the laying on of the apostles’ hands. We must believe, moreover, that just as the sacraments of baptism and of the Lord’s body and blood are made visible through the mysteries administered by priests and consecrated invisibly by the Lord, so indeed the grace of the Holy Spirit is invisibly bestowed upon the faithful through the laying on of hands, by the ministry administered by bishops.

Why, however, the foreheads of believers are signed with sacred chrism for the reception of the gift of the Holy Spirit not by presbyters but by bishops, the successors of the apostles, Pope Innocent writes about most fully in his decretal letters. To that passage I refer anyone who wishes to know carefully and diligently [Note: Innocent I, Letter 1, chap. 3.].

By the foregoing teachings, therefore, it is fully demonstrated that the faithful must by no means negligently delay receiving so great a gift. Rather, casting off the torpor of negligence, they must seek and receive it with great eagerness of mind and devotion, lest—God forbid—anyone be taken from human affairs without the gift itself. [Col. 0134B]

## CHAPTER VIII. That children, when they have reached the age of understanding, must be instructed in the sacrament of faith, the mystery of baptism, and the gift of the Spirit’s sevenfold grace

The Church, as the blessed Augustine says, is the house of saving discipline, in which one is said to live well in order to arrive at everlasting life. Therefore, whoever is in the school of this discipline, in which Christ, the supreme teacher and master, instructs, must humbly submit his neck to the instruction of so great a teacher. For in this school the manifold precepts of sound faith are learned. Since they are many, yet flow from one fountain of wisdom, and exercise little ones in what is clear and adults in what is obscure, those who are not yet able to learn Christ’s deeper commandments ought meanwhile to strive to learn the humbler ones, until, with divine mercy assisting them, they can grasp higher things. Hence the Lord teaches his disciples on the mountain, but feeds the crowds in the plains. [Col. 0134C]

If, however, there should be someone who displays slowness and dullness of understanding and says, “I cannot learn, because I do not possess enough capacity to learn all the many and great commandments of Christ, which are certainly wondrous and innumerable,” let him hear what the aforementioned blessed Augustine writes in his book *On Christian Discipline* [Note: Sermon *On Christian Discipline*, chap. 2]:

> “There are many precepts in the Law,” he says, “by which the good life itself is contained, commanded, and learned. There are altogether many precepts, and they are innumerable. Hardly anyone can count even the pages of the precepts themselves—how much less the precepts? Yet the Lord wished, on account of those who might excuse themselves either because they have no leisure to read, or because they do not know how to read, or because they cannot easily understand, that no one should have an excuse on the day of judgment. He wished, as it is written, to complete and abbreviate the word upon the earth, as the prophet had foretold concerning him: ‘For the Lord, completing and abbreviating the word, will accomplish it upon the earth’ (Isa. X, 23; Rom. IX, 28).
>
> “God did not wish this completed and abbreviated word to be obscure. It is brief so that there may be time to read it; it is clear so that you may not say, ‘I was not permitted to understand it.’ The treasure of the divine Scriptures is therefore great, containing within itself wondrous things and many commandments, like many gems, precious necklaces, and immense vessels of great metal. But who can search out this treasure, make use of it, and reach everything that is in it?
>
> “When the Lord gave this comparison in his Gospel and said, ‘The kingdom of heaven is like a treasure discovered in a field’ (Matt. XIII, 44), lest anyone should say that he was unequal to searching the treasure, he immediately gave another comparison: ‘The kingdom of heaven is like a merchant seeking fine pearls, who, having found one precious pearl, sold all that he had and bought it’ (ibid., 45). Thus, if you were too lazy to search the treasure, do not be too lazy to carry one pearl beneath your tongue and walk securely wherever you wish.
>
> “What, then, is the word that is completed and abbreviated? [Note: St. Augustine, in the passage cited above, chap. 7.] ‘You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind’ (Matt. XXII, 37), and ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’ On these two commandments hang the whole Law and the Prophets (ibid., 39). Behold what is learned in the house of discipline: to love God and to love one’s neighbor—God as God, and one’s neighbor as oneself.”

In the beginning of the holy Church of God, no one was baptized unless he had first been instructed both in the faith of the Holy Trinity and in the mystery of holy baptism. Now, however, because the name of Christ prevails everywhere, and children born of Christian parents are brought without hesitation to receive the grace of baptism before they can speak—and not without reason, since those who are subject to the sins of others may, through the carrying and response of others, be absolved from the transgression of original sin, so that, rescued from the power of darkness, they may be transferred into the kingdom of their Lord—it must be diligently ensured, whether by their parents or by those who have received them from the washing of the holy font, that when they reach the age of understanding they are instructed in the faith and the mystery of baptism. Thus, even if they should be unwilling or unable to progress more broadly and abundantly in their understanding of the divine Scriptures, at least they will be found instructed, without excuse, in the faith of the Holy Trinity and the mystery of holy baptism. [Col. 0135D]

## CHAPTER IX. That, because baptism cannot be repeated, a second baptism must necessarily be repentance

Divine mercy has absolved us through the grace of baptism from the guilt of the first man, made us sons of salvation from sons of perdition, and made us sons of adoption from alien sons, as was also said above. But because after baptism we have lost much and have fallen in many ways, and because baptism cannot in any way be repeated, that same merciful divinity has granted us the certain and most salutary remedy of repentance. Through prophetic and evangelical admonition it urges us all alike to hasten to it.

For the prophet Isaiah cries: “Seek the Lord while he may be found; call upon him while he is near. Let the wicked abandon his way, and the unjust man his thoughts, and let him return to the Lord, and he will have mercy on him; and to our God, for he is generous in forgiving” (Isa. LV, 6).

And the Lord says through Ezekiel: “I do not desire the death of the wicked, but that the wicked should turn from his way and live” (Ezek. XXXIII, 11). Again: “Turn and do penance for all your iniquities, and iniquity will not be your ruin” (ibid., XVIII, 30). Again: “On whatever day the sinner turns, all his iniquities will be forgotten” (ibid., XXXIII, 12).

And Solomon says: “Do not be without fear because of a committed sin, and do not add sin upon sin” (Ecclus. V, 5). Again: “Do not delay turning to the Lord, and do not put it off from day to day” (ibid., 8). Again: “The Most High hates sinners, and he has mercy on the penitent” (ibid. XII, 3). Again: “Abandon your sins and turn to the Lord” (ibid., XVII, 21). Again: “My son, you have sinned; do not sin again, but also plead concerning your former sins, that they may be forgiven you” (ibid., XXI, 1).

And the Lord says in the Gospel: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. III, 2). John the Baptist says: “Produce fruits worthy of repentance” (Luke III, 8). And the Apostle Paul says: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (II Cor. VI, 2). And Peter says: “Repent therefore and turn back, so that your sins may be blotted out” (Acts III, 19).

Jerome, in his exposition of Ecclesiastes, writes:

> “Do not act impiously to excess, and do not be foolish, when you die before your time, since the Lord says: ‘I do not desire the death of the one who dies, but only that he return and live.’ Let it be enough to have sinned once. Therefore we must raise ourselves up after a fall. For if, according to those who discuss natural science, the swallow knows how to restore the sight of its young with the juice of celandine, and wounded goats seek dittany, why do we not know that a remedy has been provided for sinners?”

Augustine writes in his *Book of Sermons* [Note: *On the Words of the Lord*, Sermon 16, chap. 11]:

> “I know,” he says, “and so does every person who considers the matter a little more attentively, that no one who fears the Lord fails to correct himself under his words, except one who thinks that he has more time to live. This very thing destroys many when they say, ‘Tomorrow, tomorrow,’ and suddenly the door is closed. He remained outside with the raven’s voice, because he did not have the dove’s lament; it is the raven’s voice. Mourn like a dove and beat your breast; but by striking yourself, let yourself be corrected under the blows.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Tell me, I beg you. Behold, I agree, I concede, and I acknowledge that God has promised you forgiveness. But who promised you tomorrow? Tell me where you read that you will receive forgiveness if you do not correct yourself. Read to me how long you are going to live. ‘I do not read it,’ he says. Then you do not know how long you will live. Be corrected and always be ready. Do not fear the final day as a thief who might break through the wall while you sleep; but keep watch and correct today what you are postponing until tomorrow.”

Gregory, in his homily on the nine orders of angels [Note: Homily 34, toward the middle], writes:

> “The Lord opens the bosom of his mercy and seeks to receive us into himself through repentance; but we cannot perform repentance worthily unless we also know the proper manner of that repentance. For truly to do penance is to mourn the evil one has committed and not to commit again what must be mourned. Whoever laments some sins while nevertheless committing others either pretends to do penance or does not understand it.
>
> “What benefit is there if someone mourns the sins of lust while still panting with the fever of greed? Or what benefit is there if he now grieves the faults of anger while still wasting away in the flames of envy? Yet what I have said is still too little: the one who mourns sins must in no way commit what is to be mourned, and the one who laments vices must fear committing vices.
>
> “For it must be considered with the greatest care that one who remembers having committed unlawful acts should strive to abstain even from certain lawful things”—as in the example of David, who refused to drink water brought at the risk of his men.

The same author writes elsewhere [Note: Homily 20, toward the beginning]:

> “Produce fruits worthy of repentance” (Luke III, 8). In these words it must be noted that the friend of the Bridegroom urges us to produce not merely fruits of repentance, but fruits worthy of repentance [to be produced. For it is one thing to produce fruits, another to produce fruits worthy of repentance].
>
> “To speak, therefore, of fruits worthy of repentance, it must be understood that whoever has committed no unlawful acts is rightly permitted to make use of lawful things; and he may perform works of mercy while, if he does not wish to do so, he is not required to abandon the things of the world. But if someone has fallen into the guilt of fornication, or perhaps—which is more serious—into adultery, he must cut away from himself lawful things to the same degree that he remembers having committed unlawful things.
>
> “For the good work of one who has sinned less ought not to be equal to that of one who has sinned more; nor should the fruit of one who has fallen into no crimes equal that of one who has fallen into some crimes, or that of one who has fallen into many. Therefore, when it is said, ‘Produce fruits worthy of repentance,’ each person’s conscience is confronted, so that the profits of good works may increase through repentance in proportion as he has inflicted more grievous losses upon himself through guilt.”

The same author writes in the *Moralia*:

> “Every sinner ought to have a twofold lament in repentance: namely, because he did not do the good he could have done, and because he did the evil he ought not to have done. When we do not rise to good works, we must mourn ourselves doubly, because we have not done what was right and have practiced what was wrong.”

There are indeed many other testimonies of divine Scripture which urge us to turn to God without delay concerning our committed sins and promise that through repentance we can obtain the forgiveness of divine mercy. The medicine of repentance must therefore not be disregarded; for when it is disregarded, the disease grows stronger and is shown to produce death for the sick person. [Note: “The disease grows stronger.” We emended this conjecturally; previously the text read, “it is disregarded by habits, growing stronger.”] [Col. 0137D]

## CHAPTER X. [Col. 0138A] That the manner of repentance has been placed in the judgment of priests

That the wound of sin can be healed by the remedy of repentance is testified by the matters collected in the preceding chapter. But the manner of that repentance, and the time for repenting, have been placed in the judgment of priests, to whom Christ has granted the power of binding and loosing.

Hence the blessed Augustine writes in the *Enchiridion* (chap. 65):

> “Definite periods of repentance are established by those who preside in the churches, so that satisfaction may also be made to the Church, in which the sins themselves are forgiven; for outside it they are not forgiven. For it has received the Holy Spirit as a pledge, without whom no sins are forgiven, so that those whose sins are forgiven may obtain eternal life.”

For very few people today in the Church perform such repentance as the examples of the penitent ancient Fathers and canonical authority prescribe. What guilty person, who certainly ought to have been punished with public penance, lays aside his military belt, is kept away from the thresholds of the Church and the assembly of the faithful, and is separated from the body of Christ? Who nowadays receives the lamentations of repentance in ashes and sackcloth, according to the custom of the ancient penitents?

Isidore also writes in the *Book of Sentences* [Note: Book II of *The Offices*, chap. 16]:

> “The penitent rightly mourns his sin in sackcloth and ashes, because in sackcloth there is the harshness and contrition of sins, while in ashes the dust of the dead is shown. Therefore in both we do penance: in the punishment of sackcloth, so that we may recognize the vices we committed through guilt, and in the ashes of dust, so that we may understand the sentence of death to which, by sinning, we have come.”

[Note: “In the punishment of sackcloth.” No one can doubt that the reading Acherius noted in the margin—“in the contrition of sackcloth”—is better.]

From this it follows that in the ancient times of our religion, whenever someone was seen, according to the priest’s prescribed decision, clothed in sackcloth until satisfaction had been made, sprinkled with ashes, unkempt in appearance, prostrate on the ground, and pouring forth tears, he was immediately recognized as a penitent, and everyone prayed that the Lord might forgive him.

Now, however, a penitent is scarcely recognized in the Christian assembly, because almost none of these things is done toward penitents. It is therefore believable that, just as many other things in the Christian religion have become despised, so too the aforementioned manner of repentance has, fearfully, withdrawn from use. [Col. 0138D] Consequently, many commit various crimes boldly.

Indeed, if a Christian of our time today were to commit homicide or some other offense, because he is not punished with such repentance he does not hesitate, on the following day, to join the assembly of the faithful without reverence. And thus he is found to scandalize the Church, to which he ought to have made satisfaction by repenting.

For people commonly say, either publicly or silently within themselves, concerning such a person: “O murderer! O criminal! Yesterday you committed this and that, and today you shamelessly insert yourself into our fellowship with your hands stained by the blood of your neighbor [Note: “By the blood of your neighbor.” Thus the excellent Claromontane manuscript. The earlier edition had “with hands full of blood.” What follows, transcribed from Sozomen and Pope Innocent, is taken from the Claromontane manuscript.]; and, what is even more shameless, you do not fear to share with us in the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ!” I say this from experience, more from what is customary than from what I wish.

Since, therefore, periods of repentance are established so that the penitent may make satisfaction to the Church, which he injured by sinning, I do not know whether that person is performing repentance worthily who first injured the Church by sinning and afterward, through such shameless association, compels the Church to fall into murmuring and detraction concerning him.

These statements have been made not about hidden but about manifest crimes. Since such crimes are committed publicly, they must necessarily be washed away by public satisfaction in repentance.

[How, in ancient times, penitential discipline was observed toward penitents in these Western regions, Sozomen transcribes in the Ecclesiastical History in Three Parts [Col. 0139B]: “Since, he says, it is recognized that to sin not at all is divine and above human nature, the Lord has commanded that forgiveness be granted to those who sin and do penance; but those who refuse to confess acquire a greater sin. Therefore the ancient bishops deemed it appropriate that, as in a theater before the testimony of the Church, the people’s offenses should be disclosed; and for this purpose they appointed a trustworthy and well-conducted man who could keep a secret and was wise. Those who had committed offenses came to him and confessed their own sins. He, according to each person’s fault, prescribed the penalty. This is still carefully observed in the churches of the West, especially [Col. 0139C] at Rome, where a place for penitents has also been established. For the accused stand there as though placed among mourners; when the sacred celebration has been completed, they do not receive Communion but prostrate themselves on the ground with groaning and lamentation. The bishop then approaches them and, himself with tears and spiritual groaning, prostrates himself, so that the whole congregation of the Church may devote itself to weeping. After this the bishop rises first and lifts those lying on the ground. Then, after offering an appropriate prayer for the penitents, he dismisses everyone. They, meanwhile, willingly devote themselves to disciplines—fasts, abstinence from bathing, restriction of food, or other things that are prescribed—and await the common time determined by the bishop. When the appointed time arrives, they fulfill their discipline as though paying a debt; healed of their sin, they share Communion with the people.” Thus the Roman bishops preserved this practice from ancient times down to our own day. But how and in what manner penitents should approach to receive the grace of the Lord’s body and blood, Pope Innocent teaches most fully in his Decretals, transcribing the following: “Concerning penitents, whether they are doing penance for graver offenses or for lesser ones, the custom of the Roman Church shows that, if no illness intervenes, they are to be released on the Thursday before Easter [Col. 0140A]. As for assessing the seriousness of sins, it belongs to the priest to judge, so that he may attend to the penitent’s confession and to the tears and weeping of the one who is being corrected, and then order him to be released when he sees that suitable satisfaction has been made. Certainly, if anyone falls ill and reaches the point of despair, he is to be released before Easter, lest he depart from this world without Communion.”]

One matter must by no means be passed over: some people who are conscious of their sins seek out inexperienced physicians of their souls, so that they may impose upon them penitential periods according to their wishes; and for this reason they avoid the experienced, lest the latter subject them to a more severe penance. If an experienced physician is sought to drive away diseases of the body, how much more should the most skilled physician of the soul be sought [Col. 0140B]? Thus, just as an unskilled physician, when he does not know how to treat a bodily wound, does not lessen it but very often adds to its growth, so an inexperienced physician of souls, when he wishes to appear to heal their weaknesses, is thought to increase those same weaknesses because he does not know how to apply suitable remedies. Concerning such men the Lord says through the prophet: “They revived souls that were not alive, and they put to death souls that were not dying” (Ezek. XIII, 18).

There are also many spiritual physicians who possess the knowledge required to heal the wounds of souls, but who, either out of self-love or for the sake of flattery, refuse to strike with the rigor of the most salutary penance the faults of those who make their confession to them [Col. 0140C]. Concerning these the Lord again says through the prophet: “Woe to those who sew pillows under every elbow and make cushions under the head of every age, to capture souls” (ibid.). Pope Gregory explains this passage in his Pastoral Book as follows: “To put a pillow under every elbow is to soothe with flattering praise souls falling from their uprightness and reclining with pleasure in such things. For an elbow is received by a pillow, or the head of one lying down by cushions, when the harshness of correction is withdrawn from the sinner and the softness of favor is applied to him, so that he may lie comfortably in error, struck by no harshness of opposition.”

Those who seek inexperienced flatterers as physicians of their souls deceive themselves with a vain sense of security [Col. 0140D]. They commonly seek such men so that, in doing penance, their bodies may feel almost no affliction—especially since the aforementioned Pope Gregory says: “Flesh that rejoices has drawn us to death; when afflicted, let it lead us back to pardon.”

As for abstinence, to which some penitents subject themselves discreetly and commendably, but others indiscreetly and negligently, Prosper gives the following judgment [Note: [Col. 0140D] Book II, On Contempt of the World, chapter 22.]: “They mortify their members that are upon the earth when they chastise their undisciplined body by continual fasts; when they keep their appetite within its necessary limit; when they abstain with measured strictness not only from more delicate foods, but also, among ordinary foods, allow their flesh nothing according to desire, but only what is necessary to sustain life. They are certain that no delicacy is harmful if it is consumed without desire, while cheap foods often hinder the progress of abstinence if they are eaten greedily.

“This is why holy David restrained his desire for water when he saw it, and poured out the water brought to him by his men lest he appear to satisfy his desire by drinking it. And the eating of meat did not harm holy Elijah, because he did not crave it. Hence it is understood that those who truly abstain condemn not the natures of foods but their cravings, and mortify their pleasures by abusing the food or drink they desire [Col. 0141B].

“Those who wish to abstain not only from the quality but also from the quantity of foods strive for nothing other than to allow themselves as much as seems sufficient for restoring the stomach and removing hunger; they do not satisfy their appetites through greedy consumption, but restrain them. Their eating is brought to an end not by satiety but by their will. For those who refuse either to be dissolved by richer foods, with the flesh luxuriating, or to be burdened by cheap foods through the distension of the belly, restrain their minds both from the desire for more precious foods and from excessive consumption of cheap ones. Abstinent men are generally neither luxurious nor greedy.”

[Note: “The water that he saw.” Acherius prefers “the water within itself.” Below, instead of “from excessive consumption,” the best Claromontanus manuscript reads “from excessive consumption of cheap [foods].” The earlier edition was badly corrupt at this point, reading: “which they will restrain from the perception of the mind of cheap [foods].”]

“What shall I say about abstaining from wine or consuming it? The holy Apostle established a definite rule when he said: ‘Do not become drunk with wine, in which there is debauchery’ (Eph. V, 18). It is as though he were saying: Excessive consumption of wine, not its nature, produces and nourishes debauchery; therefore I forbid you not to use wine, but to become drunk. For moderate use of wine strengthens a weak stomach, while drunkenness weakens both mind and body.

“Finally, he commanded his disciple Timothy, who had already weakened himself through the prolonged rigor of abstinence and had damaged his stomach by drinking water, to use a little wine, saying: ‘Do not continue to drink water, but use a little wine for the sake of your stomach and your frequent illnesses’ (I Tim. V, 23). Accordingly, those who take wine not for drunkenness but only for the health of the body do nothing contrary to abstinence. Their will does not offer it to them; illness permits it. If illness is absent, they should abstain from wine, lest the consumption of wine—which supports the sick—set the healthy body aflame. For no one would say that using wine or having oil for use is a sin. Yet we ought not to provide these things to the desiring flesh, lest, once we begin to grant it what is lawful, it should demand what is unlawful and, by making us obedient to it in small matters, compel us to punishable crimes. When the natural order has been disturbed, the body would then rule the spirit, and the spirit would serve the body’s domination.”

And shortly afterward: “But if, while abstaining from quadrupeds, they enjoy pheasants, goats, peacocks, or other costly birds, or fish, they do not seem to me to cut off the pleasures of their bodies but to change them. They reject ordinary and cheap meats not for the sake of abstinence, but as though because of some uncleanness—or, more truly, because of the delicacy of a nauseated stomach—so that they may satisfy their pleasures with other meats, and even with more delicate and expensive ones.

“As has already been made clear, we are not to condemn the natures of any meats that have been granted for human use and that God established; rather, we must flee carnal desires, which the devil introduced into the perception of the flesh. Those who wish to appear more frugal and acquire glory for themselves as though from the strictness of abstinence judge that one must abstain from all animals, yet fill the appetite of their bodies to excess with foreign fruits, delicate drinks of rowan berries [Note: [Col. 0141D] “Drinks of rowan berries.” Elsewhere Acherius prefers “little spoonfuls of rowan-berry drink.”], and other things. Spiritual abstinence does not counsel the abandonment of the use of particular foods, but the restraint of desire.

“Those, therefore, are to be judged more devoted to moderation who forbid themselves not the consumption of particular things but bodily pleasures. Nor do those who deny themselves wine but inundate themselves with drinks from various cups seem to me to fulfill abstinence. Perhaps they also abstain from wine for this reason: that they may purchase praise from human beings, and compensate for the wine forbidden to them with the pleasure of sweeter drinks.”

It is therefore clear [Note: [Col. 0141D] “It is therefore clear.” The remainder of the chapter is absent from the Claromontanus manuscript after these words. In its place it contains the following, which I prefer to the printed text: “It is therefore evident that the consumption of food and drink should be moderately avoided by those who abstain, not for pleasure but for the body’s necessity [I read: ‘should be used’], and that the fault lies not in their consumption but rather in immoderate enjoyment. Therefore, when someone wishes to do penance, he ought to observe in taking food and drink the measure described above. It is fitting that one who has committed unlawful acts should also forbid himself lawful ones. Let him also chastise his members that are upon the earth with fasts, vigils, prayers, and other salutary afflictions, so that, according to the Apostle, he may become a living, holy, and pleasing sacrifice to the Lord, and may be able to say with the Psalmist: ‘My soul thirsted for you, and my flesh in how many ways!’”] that, for the healing of the wounds of sinners, learned and spiritual physicians—not ignorant men who favor sins—should be sought; that penitential periods should humbly be undertaken according to their judgment; and that public penance for capital and manifest sins should be performed without retraction. As for the measure and consumption of food and drink, penitents who decide to discipline their bodies discreetly through the rigor of abstinence should deliberately follow the judgment of Prosper set out above. It is fitting that, when someone is given over to penance, he should strive to discipline his body by continued fasts, constant vigils and prayers, and the practice of the other holy virtues, so that he may rightly say with the Psalmist: “My soul thirsted for you; how greatly my flesh also thirsted” (Ps. LXII, 2).

## CHAPTER XI. That the faithful ought frequently to assemble in church for the sake of prayer

Because in the present age the devotion of the Christian people falls far short of the devotion of the faithful communities that existed under the apostles, this will be briefly recalled in the final chapter of this little book. The devotion of certain Christians is far removed from the religious devotion of that community—not only in various other respects, but also in the fact that they assemble at church sluggishly. Yet just as many people frequently attend church with pious and religious zeal for the sake of prayer, so, on the contrary, there are some who, although they have a basilica nearby, do this very rarely, even though the matter deserves correction.

That temples dedicated to divine worship ought to be visited frequently, and that God ought there to be invoked steadfastly and devoutly, is attested by the testimonies of divine Scripture collected below. Thus it is read in the Book of Chronicles: “The Lord appeared to Solomon by night and said: ‘I have heard your prayer, and I have chosen this place for myself as a house of sacrifice,’” and so forth (II Chron. XII). A little later: “My eyes also shall be open and my ears attentive to the prayer of the one who prays in this place. For I have chosen and sanctified this place, so that my name may be there forever; and my eyes and my heart shall remain there all days.”

And in the Gospel of Luke: “And it came to pass, while he blessed them, that he departed from them and was carried up into heaven. And they, worshiping, returned to Jerusalem with great joy. And they were continually in the temple, praising and blessing God” (Luke XXIV, 52).

And in the Acts of the Apostles: “They continued steadfastly in the apostles’ teaching, in fellowship, in the breaking of bread, and in prayers” (Acts II, 42). A little later: “Every day they continued with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread from house to house, they took their food with gladness and simplicity of heart, praising God and having favor with all the people” (ibid., 46). Again there: “Peter and John went up into the temple at the ninth hour of prayer” (ibid., III, 1).

Origen, too, in his homily on Rebecca [Note: [Col. 0143D] Homily 10 on Genesis.], says: “I fear that you are still causing your mother, the Church, sorrow and groaning, since you do not assemble to hear the word of God and scarcely go to church except on feast days—and then not so much from desire for the word as from an interest in the solemnity and the opportunity for public relaxation. What, then, shall I do, to whom the stewardship of the word has been entrusted? Where or when shall I find your time? You spend most of it—or almost all of it—in worldly occupations. You devote one part to the marketplace and another to business; another is occupied with lawsuits, and no one, or hardly anyone, makes time to hear the word of God.

“But why do I blame you for your occupations? Why do I complain about those who are absent? Even those who are present in the church are not attentive. Instead, they spend their time in ordinary, habitual conversations and turn their backs on the word of God and the divine readings. I fear that the Lord may say to you also: ‘They turned their backs to me and not their faces’ (Jer. I, 12).”

And a little later in the same work: “Tell me, you who assemble at church only on feast days: Are the other days not feast days? Are they not the Lord’s days? It belongs to the Jews to observe certain rare days as solemn; therefore the Lord says to them: ‘I cannot endure your new moons and Sabbaths and great day. Your fasts, holidays, and feast days my soul hates’ (Isa. I, 13). Does God, then, hate those who think that the Lord’s feast occurs on only one day?”

Since Christians, in imitation of the temple of Jerusalem where the blood of brute animals was poured out, build basilicas in honor and love of God, where the blood of bulls is no longer poured out but the body and blood of Christ are consecrated and received by the faithful; since God, through such clear oracles, deigns to promise that he will dwell in places dedicated to his name and hear the prayers of those who entreat him there; and since bishops dedicate them to God with such solemn invocation that all who assemble there to pray, and cry out to him from whatever tribulation, may obtain the benefits of his consolation—it is necessary that the faithful, putting aside the lukewarmness of negligence, frequently and devoutly visit such places to entreat God and make him favorable to them, and show themselves worthy of the sight of the angels, whose assembly is undoubtedly present there.

But if the aforementioned temple, in which animals were slaughtered, was held in such veneration that not only Jews acquainted with the knowledge of the divine law but also nations far removed from God’s covenant came to it for the sake of prayer—as is related in the Acts of the Apostles concerning the Ethiopian eunuch, who had come to worship in Jerusalem and was returning when Philip catechized and baptized him (Acts VIII, 26)—how much more should the temples of Christ, where his flesh and blood are sacrificed, be venerated by the faithful with religious service and frequented unexcusedly with continual prayers?

Therefore, contrary to the reprehensible and correctable custom of some people, churches dedicated to the divine name through the ministry of priests are not to be wholly neglected and abandoned because they build little chapels for themselves according to their own wishes and insist that sacrifice can and ought to be offered there—especially since the Lord says in the Law: “To the place which the Lord your God shall choose from all your tribes, to establish his name there and dwell in it, you shall come and offer in that place your burnt offerings and sacrifices” (Deut. XII, 6). And a little later: “Beware lest you offer your burnt offerings in every place that you see; but in the place which the Lord shall choose in one of your tribes, there you shall offer sacrifices” (ibid., 13).

And in the sacred canons, specifically in the Council of Laodicea, it was established (Canon 58): “Offerings are not to be made in houses by bishops and presbyters.”

## CHAPTER XII. On perseverance in prayer

Many people do not devote themselves to the religious practice of prayer as they ought, and as the examples of the holy fathers of old teach. The concentration of some in prayer is also pitifully hindered by concerns about earthly matters and by unlawful thoughts. Since this is so, the more fiercely we are shaken by the world’s adversities in prayer, and the heavier the tumult of carnal thoughts we endure, the more ardently and vigorously we must persist in prayer. Perseverance in prayer grants us assistance amid adversity, because where human help is insufficient, divine aid must be implored through prayers.

The following passages teach how persistently we should devote ourselves to prayer. The Psalmist says: “[I remembered your name in the night, Lord (Ps. CXVIII, 55). Again: In the middle of the night I rose to confess to you (ibid., XII). Again: In the nights lift up your hands in the holy place, and bless the Lord (Ps. CXXXIII, 2). Again:] Every night I wash my bed; I water my couch with my tears” (Ps. VI, 7).

There are also many other teachings of the same psalmist concerning the continual practice of prayer, but they are not set down here for reasons of length. You have also in the Book of Ecclesiasticus: “Do not be hindered from praying always, and do not fear to be justified even unto death, because the reward of the Lord remains forever” (Ecclus. XVIII, 22). “Before prayer, prepare your soul, and do not be like one who tempts God” (ibid., 23). “Whoever keeps the law multiplies prayer. The Lord will hear the prayer of the injured” (ibid., XXXV, 1). “Prayer with humility will penetrate the clouds” (ibid., XXI).

The Lord also says in the Gospel: “It is necessary always to pray and not to grow weary” (Luke XVIII, 1). And elsewhere: “Ask, and it shall be given to you; seek, and you shall find; knock, and it shall be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives; and whoever seeks finds; and to the one who knocks it shall be opened” (Matt. VII, 7). Again: “Watch, therefore, at all times, that you may be counted worthy to escape all these things that are to come and to stand before the Son of Man” (Luke XXI, 26).

And the Apostle: “Rejoice always; pray without ceasing; give thanks in all things” (I Thess. V, 17). Again, the same: “Persist in prayer, being watchful in it” (Col. IV, 2). Again, the same: “The Lord is near. Be anxious about nothing, but in every prayer and supplication, with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known before God” (Phil. IV, 6). And Peter says: “Be prudent and watchful in prayers” (I Pet. IV, 7).

Isidore, in the Book of Sentences: “By prayers we are cleansed; by readings we are instructed. Both are good if possible; if it is not possible, it is better to pray than to read, because in readings we learn what we ought to do, while in prayers we receive the very things for which we ask.”

Jerome, to Eustochium [Note: [Col. 0145D] Letter 22.]: “Although the Apostle commands us to pray always, and although even sleep itself is prayer to the saints, nevertheless we ought to have fixed hours for prayer, so that, if we should happen to be detained by some task, the appointed time itself may remind us of our duty. Everyone knows the third, sixth, and ninth hours, as well as dawn and evening. No food should be taken before prayer has been offered; nor should one leave the table without giving thanks to the Creator. [At night] one should rise twice or three times and turn over in one’s mind the passages of Scripture that one has committed to memory.”

Again, Isidore [Note: [Col. 0145D] Isidore, Sentences, Book III, chapter 7.]: “Just as it is not fitting for a soldier to go out to war without weapons, so it is not beneficial for any Christian to proceed anywhere without prayer. [Note: Acherius says that these words, down to “This is the remedy,” are no longer found in Isidore. In the same passage, he advises reading “he should turn himself to prayer” in place of “he should submit himself in prayer.”] This is the remedy for one who is seething with the heat of vices: whenever he is attacked by any vice, he should submit himself in prayer, [Col. 0146B] * because frequent prayer extinguishes the assault of vices. We must apply our mind to praying and knocking with such perseverance that, by the strongest concentration, we overcome the importunate suggestions of carnal desires that creep into our senses, and we must persist until, by rising up, we conquer them.”

And a little later: “Prayer belongs to the heart, not to the lips. For God does not attend to the words of the one who pleads, but looks upon the heart of the one who prays. If the heart prays silently and the voice is quiet, although this is hidden from human beings, it cannot be hidden from God, who is present to the conscience. It is better to pray in the heart with silence and without the sound of the voice than with words alone, without the mind’s attention. One should never pray without groaning, for remembrance of sins produces sorrow. While we pray, we recall our guilt and then recognize more clearly that we are guilty. Therefore, when we stand before God, we ought to groan and weep, remembering how grievous are the crimes we have committed and how terrible are the punishments of hell that we fear.”

There are, moreover, some who persist frequently in prayer while neglecting the other good works. They must join the practice of the other virtues to their prayer as well. Conversely, there are those who devote themselves to other good works and neglect continual prayer. They too ought to attach constant prayer to their good works. The prophet Jeremiah says: “Let us lift up our hearts with our hands to the Lord” (Lam. IX, 41). Isidore explains this as follows [Note: [Col. 0146D] In the same work, as above.]: “He lifts his heart with his hands who supports prayer with work. For whoever prays and does not work lifts his heart but does not lift his hands. Whoever works and does not pray lifts his hands but does not lift his heart. But because it is necessary both to work and to pray, the saying is rightly expressed with reference to both: ‘Let us lift up our hearts with our hands to the Lord.’”

Since our Savior therefore taught not only the form of prayer but also the persistence and frequency with which we should pray, we ought to imitate the persistence of the widow who repeatedly appealed to the unjust judge, and also of the friend who continually knocked at his friend’s door and asked that three loaves be lent to him—examples he set before us to teach perseverance in prayer and to show us how continually and humbly we should entreat him (Luke XI, 5). Thus, casting aside the torpor of laziness, let us continually implore the same Lord and Savior to absolve us from all our errors and make us sharers in the eternal homeland.

## CHAPTER XIII. That in the Church of God one must not devote oneself to idle and shameful conversations; and that those who do so not only fail to lessen their sin but also pile up greater sins

Many people enter the church without directing pure and simple prayer to God, because they do not meditate in their minds on what they pray with their mouths. Concerning such people Bede says in Homily 17 on the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0147D] The second Sunday in Lent.]: “There are some who enter the church and prolong the psalmody or prayer with many words, but, directing their attention elsewhere in their hearts, do not even remember what they are saying. They pray with their mouths while their minds wander outside, and thus deprive themselves of all the fruit of prayer, thinking that a prayer is heard by God which they themselves, who utter it, do not hear. No one can fail to perceive that this occurs at the instigation of the ancient enemy. Knowing the benefit of prayer and envying human beings the grace of obtaining what they ask, he sends those who pray various images of frivolous thoughts, and sometimes even shameful and harmful fantasies, by which he may hinder prayer. Thus it is that at times, prostrate in prayer, we endure such great waves of wandering thoughts.”

There are therefore many people who care more to devote themselves to vain and obscene conversations than to lend an ear to the divine readings. Nowhere do they seem to find it more pleasurable to pour the whispers of others into people’s ears, to split their faces with laughter, than in the Church of God, where they ought humbly and devoutly to have invoked him and mourned their sins. There is no doubt that this too occurs at the instigation of the same ancient enemy.

That the house of God is not a place for such unlawful activities but rather for prayers, the Lord teaches in the Gospel, saying: “My house is a house of prayer, but you have made it a den of thieves” (Luke XIX, 46).

Origen, writing about the veil of Moses [Col. 0147D] [Note: [Col. 0147D] On Exodus, chapter 34, Homily 12.], says: “We must first explain what it means to be turned away from the Lord, so that we may know what it means to be turned toward him. Everyone who, while the words of the law are being read, is occupied with ordinary conversations is turned away. Everyone who, while Moses is being read, is anxious about worldly business, money, and profits is turned away. Everyone who is constrained by concern for possessions and stretched taut by desire for riches, who boasts in the world and pursues the honors of the world, is turned away.

“But there is another who seems to be free from these things: he stands present and hears the words of the law, and his face and eyes are attentive, but in his heart and thoughts he wanders. He too is turned away. What, then, does it mean to be converted? If you turn your backs on all these things and devote yourselves to the word of God with zeal and concern of mind, meditating on his law day and night, this is to be turned toward the Lord [Note: [Col. 0147D] The same work, shortly afterward.].

“Some of you, as soon as you have heard what is read, immediately depart. There is no mutual inquiry about what has been read, no discussion, nowhere any remembrance of the command by which the divine law admonishes you: ‘Ask your fathers, and they will tell you; your elders, and they will declare it to you’ (Deut. XXXII, 7). Others do not even patiently wait for the readings to be recited in the church. Still others do not know whether they are being recited, but occupy themselves with worldly conversations in the more remote parts of the Lord’s house. Of such people I have dared to say that, when Moses is read, not merely a veil lies over their hearts, but a certain wall and barrier has been placed there.”

Augustine, in his homilies to the people [Note: [Col. 0148D] Sermon 214, On the Season.]: “When you assemble in church, pray for your sins. Do not engage in quarrels, do not stir up disputes and scandals, and do not utter idle conversations. [Whoever does these things when coming to church wounds himself by quarreling in the very place where he could have been healed by prayer.] Standing in church, do not be talkative, but listen patiently to the sacred Scriptures. Whoever speaks vain words in church will have to give an account both for himself and for others on the day of judgment, because he neither hears the word of God himself nor permits others to hear it.”

Again, the same: “There are many whose destruction causes me exceedingly great sorrow. I mean those who, coming to church, are more eager to quarrel than to pray, and, when they ought to receive the divine readings in church with attentive ears and complete devotion, strive instead to conduct lawsuits outside and assail themselves with various slanders. Sometimes, what is worse, some are inflamed by excessive anger, quarrel most bitterly, and disgracefully strike one another with insults and accusations, with kicks and fists. It would have been better for such people not to come to church than to provoke divine anger against themselves by so many evils. For although they come to church with lesser sins, they return from church with many crimes.”

Again, the same: “There are some who, on the birthdays of the saints or on any festival, wish either to plead or to hear lawsuits—and, what is worse, not for the sake of truth but for avarice and greed. They ought to plead cases and deliberate with justice, but on other days and at another time, not during the solemnity of the saints, when everyone ought to devote himself to God rather than attack others through various disputes.”

Again, the same: “When you assemble at church, do not occupy yourselves with such conversations that you may acquire sins through them. Do not occupy yourselves with quarrelling, but rather with praying, so that by supplication you may obtain God’s grace instead of offending him through disputes.”

Bede, in Homily 20 on the Gospel [Col. 0149A]: “When the Lord had made a kind of whip from cords, he drove them all out of the temple” (John II, 15). “What, then, my brothers, what do you think the Lord would do if he found people divided by quarrels, occupied with conversations, dissolved in laughter, or entangled in any other crime—he who saw people buying the victims to be sacrificed to him in the temple [and] hastened to drive them out? We have said this on account of those who enter the church and not only neglect the intention of praying but also increase the very things for which they ought to have prayed.

“Moreover, when they are reproved for such folly, they pursue their reprovers with insults, hatred, or slander—adding sins to sins and, as it were, carelessly weaving for themselves an exceedingly long rope by increasing them, without fearing that they will be condemned by the examination of the strict Judge because of it.”

And a little later [Col. 0149B]: “Therefore, beloved, these things must be greatly feared and dreaded with worthy fear, and we must take careful precautions lest, when he comes unexpectedly, he find in us something perverse for which we rightly deserve to be scourged and driven from the church. Above all, we must be watchful in that place which is especially called a house of prayer, lest we do anything foolish, lest we hear from the Apostle, as did the Corinthians: ‘Do you not have houses for conducting or discussing worldly matters, or do you despise the Church of God?’ (I Cor. XI, 22).”

Again, the same in the same work: “‘Zeal for your house has consumed me’ (John II, 18). Let us also be zealous for the house of God, dearest brothers, and, as far as we can, persist in ensuring that nothing wrong is done there. If we see a brother who belongs to the house of God swollen with pride, accustomed to slander, enslaved to drunkenness, weakened by luxury, turbulent with anger, or subject to any other vice, let us strive, insofar as our ability permits, to correct him and to set right what has been polluted and perverted. If we cannot correct anything of this sort, let us nevertheless endure it with the sharpest anguish of mind. Above all, in the very house of prayer, where the Lord’s body is consecrated and where the presence of angels is certainly always present, let us act with all our strength so that nothing foolish may hinder either our own prayer or that of our brother.”

The Apostle therefore decrees that all Christians must entirely avoid foolish talk and vulgar jesting. It is more fitting for them to mourn than to laugh, in accordance with the Gospel saying: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. V, 5). Consequently, all the faithful must take the greatest care not to do anything dishonorable in church, whether in thought, word, or deed, lest, by piling up sins upon the sins for which they had gathered to obtain absolution, they acquire not absolution from sins but rather accumulate for themselves ropes by which they are, so to speak, bound.

## CHAPTER XIV. That prayer to God and confession of sins may and ought to be made in other suitable places also, if the basilica is far away
Some people neglect to frequent the threshold of the church for the sake of prayer; conversely, there are many who, because they cannot visit basilicas and do not have the relics of the saints at hand, therefore do not pour out the vows of their prayers to the Lord with the humble devotion they ought to show. They fail to observe that God is no less present in a part than in the whole, but is everywhere wholly present, everywhere present, everywhere wondrous. Hence the Psalmist says: “Where shall I go from your spirit, and where shall I flee from your face? If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present” (Ps. 138:7). Likewise: “Bless the Lord, my soul, in every place of his dominion” (ibid. 102:22).

Thus we read in the Book of Kings: “If your people go out to war against their enemies by the road along which you send them, and they pray to you toward the direction of the city which you have chosen and toward the house which I have built for your name, then you will hear in heaven their prayer and supplication, and you will execute judgment for them. But if they sin—for there is no one who does not sin—and, being angry, you deliver them to their enemies, and they are led captive into the land of their enemies, whether far or near, and in their heart they repent in the place of their captivity, and, converted, entreat you in their captivity, saying, ‘We have sinned, we have acted wickedly, we have behaved impiously’; and if they return to you with all their heart and all their soul in the land of their enemies to which they were led captive, and pray to you toward the direction of their land which you gave to their fathers, and of the city which you chose, and of the temple which I built for your name, then you will hear in heaven, in the firmament of your throne, their prayer and supplication, and you will execute judgment for them” (1 Kings 8:44).

And in the Book of Daniel: “When Daniel learned of this—that is, of the law that had been established—he entered his house, and, with the windows of his upper room open toward Jerusalem, he knelt three times a day and worshiped, confessing to his God, just as he had been accustomed to do before” (Dan. 6:10).

The Apostle likewise says: “I desire, therefore, that men pray in every place, lifting up pure hands without anger or disputation” (1 Tim. 2:8).

Jerome, in his letter to Eustochium [Note: Letter 22, toward the end.]: “As you leave your lodging, let prayer arm you; as you return from the street, let prayer meet you before you sit down. Let the little body not rest before the soul has been nourished by the word of God. At every action, at every step, let the hand trace the cross.”

John Chrysostom [literally, “Golden Mouth”]: “When,” he says, “you have lain down upon your bed and are troubled by no one, before sleep comes to you, bring forth the book of your conscience into the midst; recall your sins, whether you have sinned in word, deed, or thought. For the Prophet says: ‘Be angry, and do not sin; what you say in your hearts, and be pricked in your beds’ (Ps. 4:5).

“During the day you had no time, but judgments occupied you; business was imposed upon you, conversation with friends, household necessity, care of children, concern for your wife, fear of military service, and a thousand circumstances surrounded you. When you come to your little bed to surrender your limbs to sleep, no one troubles you, no one knocks: say in your heart and to your soul, ‘We have spent the day, O soul; what good have we done, or what evil have we committed?’ If you have done some good, give thanks to your God; but if some evil, do not do it again. Recalling your sins, pour out tears, and, lying upon your bed, you will be able to erase them. Pray to your Lord, and then allow your soul to fall asleep.”

By these and countless other testimonies of Holy Scripture it is plainly demonstrated that, if a basilica is nearby and circumstances permit, God should be entreated for sins in the basilica; but if it is far away, he should be entreated everywhere, confession of sins should be made to him, and the intercession of the citizens above, whose power with the Most High is great, should be sought.

## CHAPTER XV. That confession of sins, except the confession made to priests in order to receive counsel and appease God, is to be made to God in prayer

The faithful therefore confess their sins to priests because the Lord has granted them the power to bind and loose. They also undergo periods of penance according to their judgment. But the fact that penance is not to be measured by the length of time, but by contrition of heart, is evident from the penance of David and of the other holy penitents.

Although someone may confess his sins to a priest and perform periods of penance according to the priest’s counsel, he must nevertheless confess his sins in prayer to God, whom he has made angry with himself by sinning, and must ask forgiveness from him with a contrite heart and tearful sighs. Then the sinner may rightly say to God: “Turn your face away from my sins, and blot out all my iniquities” (Ps. 50:11), when he sets his sins before himself through repentance and weeping, in accordance with the Psalmist’s words: “And my sin is always before me” (ibid., v. 5). And again: “I turned in my anguish while the thorn was fixed. I made my sin known to you, and I did not conceal my injustices. I said: ‘I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord,’ and you forgave the wickedness of my sin” (ibid. 31:4). And again: “Reveal your way to the Lord, and hope in him, and he will act” (ibid. 36:5).

Solomon likewise says: “Whoever conceals his crimes will not prosper; but whoever turns back and abandons them will obtain mercy” (Prov. 28:13). The Apostle John says: “But if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and cleanse us from every sin” (1 John 1:9).

John Chrysostom: “For I acknowledge my iniquity, and my sin is always before me” (Ps. 50:5). O integrity of mind! He did not forget his sin and iniquity. Although it had been granted to him, he nevertheless had adultery and murder depicted in his conscience as in an image, and each day he saw their corruption; therefore he said: “And my sin is always before me.” I see it; you, Lord, consider it. I write it; you, as Lord, erase it.

“See what this means: if you remember, God will not remember; if you forget it, God will remember it. For God does not fail to know these things if you do not speak of them. Does he wish to learn them from you, when he was present while you were committing them and knew them when you perpetrated them? You were not ashamed to sin, and are you ashamed to confess? Speak in this life, so that you may have rest in that one. Speak with groaning and weeping. Your sins are written in a book; your tears are the sponge of your sins. Great indeed is their power. I shall tell you what tears can accomplish. What is greater than the martyrs, who lay down their lives for their friend? Great is the glory of the martyrs. Martyrs pour out blood; sinners pour out tears. That prostitute did not pour out blood, but poured forth springs of tears and erased her sins.

“And what shall I say about the prostitute and impure woman? Peter, the pillar of the Church and foundation of the faith, the foremost Apostle, denied God three times at the questioning of a most contemptible little maidservant. Did he shed blood? Did he not pour forth bitter tears, take away his sin, and recover his former dignity? Keep the book of your conscience, and write down your daily sins.”

The highly salutary testimonies cited above therefore show that, apart from the confession which must unquestionably be made to priests, each person ought continually to confess his sins to God in prayer and wash them away with groans and tears.

But if anyone wishes to know carefully where the New Testament says that sinners ought to make confession of their sins to priests, let him hear that, according to the testimony of the Evangelist Mark, those who were baptized by John were confessing their sins (Mark 1:5). Let him also hear that, while Paul was preaching at Ephesus, “many of those who believed came, confessing and declaring their deeds” (Acts 19:18). And in the Epistle of the Apostle John: “But if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins” (1 John 1:9). Likewise in the Epistle of the Apostle James: “Confess your sins to one another, and pray for one another, so that you may be saved” (James 5:16).

## CHAPTER XVI. That greater sins are to be disclosed to a priest, while daily and lesser sins are to be disclosed to one another

It is the custom of the Church to confess more serious sins to priests, through whom people are reconciled to God. Regarding daily and lesser sins, however, very few make confession to one another, except monks, who do this every day.

That mutual confession should be made concerning lesser and daily sins is shown by what follows. Jesus son of Sirach said: “Do not be ashamed to confess your sins” (Sirach 4:31). And elsewhere: “The righteous man is his own accuser at the beginning” (Prov. 18:17). And the Lord in the Gospel: “Narrow and constricted is the way that leads to life” (Matt. 7:14)—that is, the confession of sins.

The Apostle James says: “Confess your sins to one another, and pray for one another, so that you may be saved” (James 5:16). Bede the Venerable, a presbyter, explains this passage as follows [Note: On chapter 5 of the Epistle of James.]: “In this statement there should be the following distinction: we should confess daily and lesser sins to one another, as equals, and believe that we are saved by their daily prayer. But let us disclose the uncleanness of more serious leprosy to a priest, according to the Law, and according to his judgment let us take care to be purified in the manner and for the length of time he prescribes.”

Jerome, in his exposition of Ecclesiastes [Note: Jerome’s Commentary on chapter 10, verse 11.]: “If the devil-serpent secretly bites someone and infects him with the poison of sin, while no one knows; if the one who has been struck keeps silent and does not repent, and does not wish to confess his wound to a brother and teacher, then the teacher and brother, who possess tongues for healing, will not easily be able to help him. For if the sick person is ashamed to confess his wound to the physician, medicine cannot cure what it does not know.”

Likewise, in his exposition of Proverbs [Note: In the exposition, chapter 10.]: “The mouth of the wicked conceals iniquity” (Prov. 10:11). “The wicked are those who, by defending them, conceal their own wounds or the errors of their neighbors, so that they may not reach health. The Prophet, abhorring this, prays to the Lord that he not incline his heart to an evil word, to make excuses for sins” (Ps. 140:4).

Gregory, in his Homilies [Note: Something similar is found in the third Penitential Psalm, verse 4.]:  “Proofs of humility are for each person to recognize his own iniquity and to disclose what he has recognized by the voice of confession. It is a customary vice of the human race both to commit sin by falling and, after committing it, not to reveal it by confessing, but to defend it by denial and, when convicted, to multiply it by defending it. From the fall of the first man we derive these increases of wickedness, since from that fall we drew the very root of guilt.

“For this reason the first man had been questioned: so that he might erase by confessing the sin he had committed by transgression; and he was asked where he was, so that by confessing he might recognize the guilt he had perpetrated and how far he was from the face of his Creator.”

“Signs of true confession are present if, when someone calls himself a sinner, he does not contradict another who says the same thing about him. It is written: ‘The righteous man is his own accuser at the beginning’ (Prov. 18:17). Someone desires to appear not a sinner but righteous when, although no one accuses him, he confesses himself a sinner” [Note: Moral Reflections, book XXII, chapter 10.].

And shortly afterward: “The greatest care must be taken that we both confess willingly the evils we have committed and do not deny them when others accuse us. It is a vice of pride that someone should disdain to have others say to him what he considers himself worthy to confess of his own accord.”

Confession is the pledge of the debtor. A pledge is taken from a debtor when confession of sin has already been obtained from a sinner.

Origen, in his exposition of the Book of Leviticus [Note: Origen, on Leviticus 3, Homily 3.]: “‘If he sins,’ he says, ‘in any one of these matters, let him declare the sin that he has committed.’ There is something wonderfully secret in this: he commands that the sin be declared. Indeed, everything we do must be declared and brought into the open—whatever we do in secret, whatever we commit in speech alone or even in the hidden recesses of our thoughts; everything must be made public. But it must be brought forth by the one who is both the accuser and instigator of sin. For he incites us to sin, and, when we have sinned, he also accuses us.

“If, therefore, we anticipate him in this life and become our own accusers, we escape the wickedness of the devil, our enemy and accuser. Thus the Prophet says elsewhere: ‘You speak first of your iniquities, so that you may be justified’ (Isa. 43:26). Does he not clearly reveal the mystery we are treating when he says, ‘You speak first’? He shows you that you must anticipate the one who is ready to accuse. ‘You,’ he says, ‘speak first,’ lest he anticipate you. For if you speak first, offer the sacrifice of repentance, and hand over your flesh to destruction so that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord (1 Cor. 5:5), it will also be said to you: ‘You received your evil things during your lifetime; now rest here’ (Luke 16:25).”

For the person who is not pricked voluntarily but is convicted by another’s accusation obtains a remedy with greater difficulty.

From these testimonies it can be gathered that, just as we offend in many ways every day, so every day we ought mutually to confess what we have done and cleanse these sins through prayers, almsgiving, humility, and contrition of heart and body.

## CHAPTER XVII. On avoiding unclean thoughts, and the ways in which sin is committed in the heart and brought to completion in deed

Just as there are many who devote themselves to foul speech, buffoonery, insults, and idle talk, so there are very many who, while taking pleasure in vain and unclean thoughts, believe that they have not sinned at all. Such thoughts bring the stain of sin not only upon those who speak them but also upon those who willingly lend them an ear.

Moreover, unclean thoughts usually draw people toward evil deeds, in accordance with the Gospel saying: “For out of the heart come evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, and the rest” (Matt. 15:19). It is clear that, just as holy thoughts preserve a person, so unclean thoughts, when they delight, defile. Whatever, as the presbyter Bede the Venerable wrote, we are accustomed to do, say, or hear more frequently, must necessarily return more frequently to the mind as to its customary and proper dwelling.

And just as swine usually frequent muddy wallows while doves frequent clear streams, so unclean thoughts disturb an impure mind, whereas spiritual thoughts sanctify a chaste one.

Isidore also writes in the Book of Sentences: “Even if someone refrains from an evil deed, nevertheless, because of the wickedness of the thought alone, he will not be innocent.” Hence the Lord says through Isaiah: “Take away the evil of your thoughts from my eyes” (Isa. 1:16).

For we sin not only by deeds but also by thoughts, if we take pleasure in them when they unlawfully present themselves. Just as a viper is killed when it is torn apart by its offspring in the womb, so our thoughts, nourished within us, kill us; conceived within, they consume us with viperous poison and destroy our soul with a cruel wound.

[Note: “Our [thoughts] within us.” Thus the Clar. manuscript reads correctly; the earlier edition has nostrae, not corruptly. Below, where “in ambush he may be able” is read, Acherius rightly noted that “set in ambush” (in insidiis positus) should be read.]

It is a matter of our own will to turn illicit thoughts over in the mind and take pleasure in them; it belongs to demons to provide them with incitements. The devil, therefore, is not the author but the instigator of unclean thoughts, as blessed Jerome says in his commentaries on the Gospel of Matthew [Note: From the Commentary on Matthew, chapter 15.]: “Those who think that thoughts are injected by the devil and do not arise from their own will must be rebuked. The devil can be the helper and instigator of evil thoughts, but he cannot be their author. But if, always lying in ambush, he has kindled the slight spark of our thoughts with his fuel, we should not suppose that he can also search out the hidden things of the heart; rather, he infers what we are turning over within from the condition and gestures of the body.

“For example, if he frequently sees us looking at a beautiful woman, he understands that the heart has been wounded by the dart of love. There are certainly some who conceive sin in their hearts and deliberate about committing it, but either omit it through fear or are unable to carry it out because of difficulty. Such people plainly die in the house—that is, in the heart—and therefore must recognize that they have sinned in thoughts of this kind, flee through confession to the lamentation of penance, and seek the intercessions and assistance of the saints, so that by the Lord Jesus Christ, to whom all things live, they may deserve to be raised to life in the house—that is, in the heart—like the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue.”

It is therefore necessary for everyone, with divine aid, to drive harmful thoughts from the heart like unclean flies. Just as someone immediately throws off anything dirty that falls upon his garment, so he must likewise cast unclean thoughts from his heart. For just as a burning coal, when it falls upon any part of the body, burns it unless it is immediately thrown off, so filthy thoughts, which intrude upon human minds at an inconvenient time, produce, so to speak, a wound of sin unless they are quickly driven away from the mind.

It is necessary to know in how many ways sin is committed in the heart and in how many ways it is brought to completion in deed. Hence blessed Gregory says in the Moral Reflections [Note: Book IV, chapter 25, on Job 3.]: “Sin is committed in the heart in four ways; it is brought to completion in deed in four ways. In the heart it is committed by suggestion, pleasure, consent, and the boldness of self-defense. Suggestion comes through the adversary, pleasure through the flesh, consent through the spirit, and the boldness of self-defense through pride.

“Often a fault that ought to terrify the mind raises it up, and by casting it down elevates it; but by elevating it more gravely overthrows it. Thus the ancient enemy broke the uprightness of the first man with these four blows. The serpent suggested; Eve took pleasure; Adam consented; and, when questioned, he refused through boldness to confess his guilt.”

Sin is likewise brought to completion in deed in four ways. First, guilt is enacted inwardly; afterward the offense is openly revealed before the eyes of human beings without shame; then it is turned into a habit; and finally it is nourished either by the seductions of false hope or by the miserable obstinacy of despair.

These four stages of sin may rightly be understood as the chariot of Pharaoh—that is, of the devil—and therefore everyone must beware of them. When resistance is first made to suggestion, pleasure does not follow; if pleasure is resisted, the deed of evil consent is not completed. But if consent is not driven away, the person miserably slips into the boldness of self-defense and the obstinacy of despair. His bones—that is, the virtues of his soul, once enslaved to these vices—grow old, in accordance with the Psalmist’s words. For he says: “Because I was silent,” that is, because I did not confess my sins, “all my bones grew old,” that is, the virtues of my soul.

What he adds, “while I cried out all day” (Ps. 31:3), means the same as if he had said: “while I defended my sins.” In Holy Scripture, the defense and obstinacy of sins are called a cry. Therefore those who take pleasure in harmful thoughts must carefully consider into what sort of guilt they customarily fall through them.

## CHAPTER XVIII. That those who are aware of the sins of others become guilty unless they correct them or disclose them for the sake of correction and salvation

Those who confess their sins privately to priests and erase them by the satisfaction of worthy penance are by no means to be exposed. But concerning sins which one brother has committed against another, the Gospel’s instruction must be followed entirely.

That those who are aware of the sins of others are brought into danger unless they either correct them or disclose them for the sake of correction is shown by what follows. [Note: “That, however, those who are aware.” We have deleted the little word est after the adverb autem. Acherius’s reading, qui autem sunt conscii (“but those who are aware”), is plainly correct.] Origen writes in a homily on the Book of Leviticus [Note: Homily 3 on Leviticus, chapter 3, verse 1.]: “Let us now see what this soul says, which hears the voice of an oath and is a witness, or which has seen something and is aware of it but does not report it. From this it undoubtedly receives the sin of the one who acted wickedly or swore falsely. This also instructs us according to the historical sense, teaching us never to pollute our consciences with another’s sins or to give our consent to those who act wickedly.

“By consent I mean not only acting together, but also remaining silent about what has been done unlawfully. Do you wish to know that these matters also agree with the Gospel commandments? The Lord himself says: ‘If you see your brother sinning, rebuke him between you and him alone. If he listens to you, you have gained your brother. But if he does not listen, take with you one or two others. And if he does not listen to them either, tell the Church. But if he does not listen to the Church, let him be to you as a heathen and a tax collector’ (Matt. 18:15).

“And shortly afterward: ‘Since the commandment of the Gospel is such, and the Law prescribes that, if he remains silent, he will bear the other’s sin, it must be understood that if someone either does not report what he sees his neighbor doing wrong, according to the rule stated above, or, when called as a witness, does not speak the truth, he will take upon himself the sin committed by the person whom he conceals, and the punishment for the offense will fall back upon the one who was aware of it.’”

The same author, in a homily on Achan stealing the golden tongue: “‘If a soul sins and hears the voice of one who swears an oath, and is a witness to what he has seen or of which he is aware, unless he reports it, he shall bear his iniquity’ (Lev. 5:1).”

The same author, in the same work [Note: Homily 7 on Joshua]: “Nor should this be passed over without attention: when one person sinned, anger came upon the whole people. How did this happen? It happened when priests who preside over the people wished to appear lenient toward offenders.
