Fearing the tongues of sinners, lest they speak evil of them, and forgetting priestly severity, they refused to fulfill what is written: ‘Rebuke sinners in the presence of all, so that the others may have fear’ (1 Tim. 5:20). And again: ‘Remove the evil person from among yourselves’ (1 Cor. 5:13).

“Nor, being inflamed with zeal for God, did they imitate the Apostle, who says: ‘I have handed such a person over to the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved’ (ibid. 5:5). Nor did they take care to follow the Gospel command: if they saw someone sinning, they should first approach him privately; afterward they should speak with two or three witnesses; and if he despised them and was not corrected after the Church’s rebuke, they should regard him as a heathen and a tax collector.

“While sparing one person, they plot the destruction of the whole Church. What kind of goodness is this? What kind of mercy is it—to spare one and bring everyone into danger? For the people are polluted by one sinner. Just as one diseased sheep infects the entire flock, so when one person commits fornication or any other crime, the whole people are polluted.

“Therefore let us watch over one another, so that everyone’s conduct may be known, especially to priests and ministers. Let them not think of saying secretly, ‘What does it concern me if someone else acts wickedly?’ This is like the head saying to the feet, ‘What does it matter to me if my feet are in pain or in bad condition? It does not concern me, so long as the head remains healthy.’ Or if the eye should say to the hand, ‘I do not need your work; what does it matter to me if you are in pain because you are wounded? Surely I, the eye, am not troubled by your illness?’

“Such, then, is the conduct of those who preside over Churches, because they do not consider that all who believe are one body, having one God who binds and holds us together in unity.”

And the Apostle says: “Not only those who do these things, but also those who approve of those who do them, are worthy of death” (Rom. 1:32). Likewise, in the same Apostle’s Epistle to the Corinthians: “Do you not know that a little leaven corrupts the whole lump? Purge out the old leaven, so that you may be a new dough, as you are unleavened” (1 Cor. 5:6–7).

Gregory, in the Book of Pastoral Care: “Those who observe the evils of their neighbors and nevertheless restrain their tongue in silence are like people who, after seeing wounds, withhold the use of medicine. They become the authors of death precisely because they refuse to cure the poison which they could have healed.”

Let those who, out of love, fear, or acceptance of a gift, shrink from exposing the deadly sins of wicked people hear this: unless they disclose those sins for the sake of correction and salvation, they become like the sinner; and when one person sins while the others remain silent and do not rebuke him, danger threatens them all.

Whoever sees evil and remains silent falls not only into the words of the Psalmist: “If you saw a thief, you ran with him, and you made your portion with adulterers” (Ps. 50:18), but must also cry out with Isaiah and say: “Woe is me, because I have been silent; for I am a man of unclean lips” (Isa. 6:5). Whoever, therefore, sees evil and remains silent is undoubtedly a man of unclean lips, and turns the sinner’s crime back upon himself.

## CHAPTER XIX. That those who have received the faith of Christ and ended their lives in wickedness are punished more severely than those who died without faith but nevertheless performed good works

Some Christians are accustomed to say that those who have been reborn in Christ, although they live wickedly and close their lives in evil deeds, are not to be punished with everlasting fire, but with a long-lasting and purifying fire. Since many assert this and none of them can establish its truth from the divine oracles [Note: “And none of them.” In chapter 12 of the Institutions, below: “and no one is able to affirm from the divine oracles that this is true.” This reading seems better to me.], they must take care not only not to believe it but even not to utter it. By saying such things, they might deceive themselves and others with a kind of empty security.

That no one is brought to the eternal kingdom by faith in Christ alone without works will be demonstrated in the following chapter. But that those who live in crimes, do not redeem them either by the lamentation of penance or by generous almsgiving, and instead persevere in them until death will suffer harsher torments than those who, although they were not baptized in the Church by Christ’s washing, nevertheless performed good works, is demonstrated by the testimonies collected below.

Peter says: “For it would have been better for them not to know the way of righteousness than, after knowing it, to turn back from the holy commandment delivered to them. What has happened to them is expressed by the true proverb: ‘The dog has returned to its own vomit,’ and ‘the washed sow to wallowing in the mud’” (2 Pet. 2:21–22).

And the Lord in the Gospel: “That servant who knew his master’s will and did not prepare himself or act according to his will shall be beaten with many blows; but the one who did not know and did things deserving blows shall be beaten with few. Everyone to whom much has been given, much will be required; and from the one to whom much has been entrusted, more will be demanded” (Luke 12:47–48).

Likewise: “When the unclean spirit has gone out from a person, it passes through dry places, seeking rest, and does not find it. Then it says, ‘I will return to my house from which I came.’ And when it comes and finds it empty, swept, and decorated, it goes and takes with it seven other spirits more wicked than itself; they enter and dwell there. And the last state of that person becomes worse than the first” (Matt. 12:43–45).

Origen likewise, in a homily on the beginning of the Decalogue [Note: Homily 8 on Exodus.]: “The unclean spirit dwelt in us before we believed, before we came to Christ, while our soul was still committing fornication against God and was with its lovers, the demons. But afterward, when it said, ‘I will return to my former husband,’ and came to Christ, who created it from the beginning in his own image, the adulterous spirit necessarily gave way, since the soul had gone to its legitimate husband.

“We were therefore received by Christ; our house was cleansed from its former sins and decorated with the ornaments of the sacraments of the faithful, which those who have been initiated know.”

And shortly afterward: “For it must be not merely a house but a temple in which God dwells. If, therefore, it neglects the grace it has received and entangles itself in worldly affairs, immediately that unclean spirit returns and claims for itself the empty house. And, so that it may not be expelled again, it brings with it seven other spirits more wicked than itself, and the last state of the person becomes worse than the first.”

Bede, in his exposition of the Gospel of Luke [Note: On the exposition of chapter 11, verse 26.]: “Whoever, after baptism, is seized either by heretical depravity or by worldly desire will immediately be cast down into the depths of every vice. Hence the spirits are rightly called more wicked when they enter, because the person will not only possess those seven vices that oppose the seven spiritual virtues, but will also pretend through hypocrisy to possess the virtues themselves; and the last state of that person will be worse than the first. For it would have been better for him not to know the way of truth than, after knowing it, to turn back” (2 Pet. 2:21). We read that this was especially fulfilled in Judas the traitor, Simon Magus, and others of the same kind.

Augustine likewise, in the Enchiridion [Note: Enchiridion, chapter 67.]: “Some people believe that even those who do not abandon the name of Christ, who are initiated into his holy washing, and who are not cut off from him by any schism or heresy, will be saved through fire, no matter how great the crimes in which they live—crimes which they neither wash away by repentance nor redeem by almsgiving, but in which they persist most stubbornly until the final day of this life—although, because of the magnitude of their crimes and wickedness, they will be punished in a long-lasting but not eternal fire.

“But those who believe this and are nevertheless Catholics seem to me to be deceived by a certain human benevolence; for, when consulted, divine Scripture gives a different answer.”

And shortly afterward: “Moreover, if a wicked person is saved through fire on account of faith alone, and if this is how we must understand what blessed Paul says, ‘He himself will be saved, yet so as through fire’ (1 Cor. 3:15), then faith will be able to save without works, and what his fellow Apostle James said will be false. The statement that Paul himself made will also be false: ‘Do not be deceived: neither fornicators, nor idolaters, nor the effeminate, nor men who lie with males, nor thieves, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor extortioners will possess the kingdom of God’ (1 Cor. 6:9–10). If those who persist in these crimes will nevertheless be saved because of faith in Christ, how will they not be in the kingdom of God?”

If, therefore, according to the Gospel’s judgment, after knowing Christ a person lives wickedly and causes the unclean spirit that was expelled from him at baptism to return, adding to himself the sevenfold number of demons, and allows it in a certain sense to reclaim its former house in him, then “the last state of that person becomes worse than the first.” It is plainly evident that, if he ends his life in the same wickedness, he must be punished more severely than those who, although they did not receive the faith of Christ, nevertheless devoted themselves to good works.

Therefore each person must adorn the faith of Christ he has received with works. And just as no one should despair of God’s mercy, so no one, after this life, should soften or temper God’s judgment—which can be nothing but just—in his own favor or that of others, and therefore neglect to devote himself to good works in this life.

Accordingly, care must be taken that, while we live in this life, we devote ourselves to good works, as the Lord warns through the Prophet: “Give glory to the Lord your God before it grows dark, and before your feet stumble against the dark mountains” (Jer. 13:16). And elsewhere: “Seek the Lord while he may be found; call upon him while he is near. Let the wicked abandon his way, and the unjust man his thoughts,” and so forth (Isa. 55:6–7).

And the Lord in the Gospel: “Watch and pray, for you do not know the day or the hour” (Matt. 26:41). Likewise: “The day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night” (2 Pet. 3:10). Likewise: “Walk while you have the light, lest darkness overtake you” (John 12:35). And the Apostle: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Cor. 6:2).

By these teachings we are thoroughly instructed not to waste in vain the time granted for repentance, but rather to devote ourselves continually to good works.

[Col. 0160D] Up to this point, it should suffice to have briefly shown from the divine oracles and the judgments of the holy Fathers what generally befits all the faithful. [Note: “To have briefly shown.” It could be restored as “to have briefly indicated,” or something similar; it is also acceptable to read “to have demonstrated briefly by connected exposition.” I immediately read “for the purpose of instruction.” “They are bound, by rules most fitting for service to the divine power, to the purpose of a saving institution.” I understand this to refer to the omission of matters pertaining to the orders of clerics, monks, and others, who by their very condition are bound to serve God in a particular way. I think the word *debeat* (“ought”) should also be added after *conjugatorum* (“of married people”).] From this point onward, omitting the orders which, by forms most appropriate to the proposed *institution of salvation*, are constrained to serve divine power, it will be shown from the authorities cited above what married people should be like and how they ought to live. First, however, something must be said about the Christian profession, which by many is not adorned with works as it ought to be; afterward, what has been promised will be pursued chapter by chapter.

## CHAPTER XX  
### That many hold the Christian profession in words but neglect it in works

If men eagerly strive to learn and most keenly understand the laws of the world, promulgated by mortals to settle the business of lawsuits, so that, once these laws are well known, they may clearly distinguish on this earth of the dying what is true and what is false, what is just and what is unjust, how much more ought all the faithful to make it their concern to learn and understand the heavenly laws promulgated for human beings by God, the supreme Maker and Creator of all, and mercifully bestowed upon them—laws by which they are thoroughly taught what evil must be avoided and what good must be done, and which also raise their followers to the land of the living.

The law of Christ, therefore, was given by the Lord not specifically for clerics but generally for all the faithful to observe. Although the Gospel contains certain special commandments applicable only to those who have renounced the world and follow the apostles, the rest are judged to be observed without concealment by all the faithful, each in the order in which he has vowed to serve God. For there are many laypeople who believe that the evangelical and apostolic law was given to them, endeavor to understand it, and diligently strive to live according to it as far as they can. There are others who believe that it was given to them, but refuse to understand it and to live according to it. Concerning such people, blessed Augustine says in his book of Sermons to the People [Note: *On the Words of the Apostle*, Sermon 13]: “A person, sometimes with a mind perversely disposed, is excessively afraid to understand, lest he be compelled to do what he has understood. Hence the Psalmist says: ‘He did not wish to understand, so as to do good’ (Ps. 35:4). But if such people take care to consider what will happen to them in the future unless they correct themselves immediately, they have the answer readily available both in the Gospel and in the Apostle.”

There are others, moreover, of such great foolishness that they maintain that the law pertains not to them but only to clerics. They glory in being marked by the name of Christ and think that they can be saved by faith alone, although the Lord says in the Gospel: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven will enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 7:21). And the apostle James says: “Faith without works is useless” (Jas. 2:26). Again: “What good is it, my brothers, if someone says he has faith but does not have works? Can faith save him?” (ibid. 14). And shortly afterward: “If faith does not have works, it is dead in itself.” The apostle John says: “Whoever says that he knows God but does not keep his commandments is a liar, and the truth is not in him” (1 John 2:4). Paul says: “They profess that they know God, but by their deeds they deny him” (Titus 1:16). Again, elsewhere: “Those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires” (Gal. 5:24).

Blessed Augustine says in the aforementioned book of sermons [Note: *On the Words of the Apostle*, Sermon 31, chapter 9]: “I say to your charity, brothers: all bad Catholics confess that Christ came in the flesh, but by their deeds they deny him. Do not, therefore, be as though secure in faith; join a right life to right faith, so that you may confess that Christ came in the flesh both by speaking the truth in words and by living well in your deeds. For if you confess him in words but deny him by your deeds, the faith of such people is almost the faith of demons. Thus the apostle James, when speaking about faith and works against those who thought that faith was sufficient for them and did not want to have good works, says: ‘You believe that God is one; you do well. Even the demons believe—and tremble’ (Jas. 2:19). Will the demons therefore be freed from eternal fire because they believe and tremble?” A wretched and deeply lamentable faith indeed is that which is compared with the faith of demons. The Apostle, distinguishing the faith of believers from the faith of demons, says: “Faith which works through love” (Gal. 5:6). It is clear, therefore, that unless faith loves what it believes and adorns itself with good works, it loses the merit of faith.

How many there are today in the Church—a matter that cannot be considered without great sorrow of heart—who have received the faith of Christ but scorn to have works, serve vices, and think that the name of Christianity is sufficient for them. Will faith alone carry to the kingdom of God the proud, the envious, the greedy, adulterers, perjurers, robbers, fornicators, murderers, and those enslaved to countless other vices, when the Lord in the Gospel and the Apostle say that people of this kind will not possess the kingdom of God? How many there are also who, because of love of the world and love of themselves, make little of the Creator, although the world and its desire are passing away, while the one who clings to Christ remains forever, just as Christ remains forever; and whoever, as he himself testifies, keeps his word “will never see death” (John 8:51).

The Lord says through the Prophet: “Give attention, my people, to my law; incline your ear to the words of my mouth” (Ps. 77:1). Whoever is the Lord’s people should take care to attend to his law and lend an ear to his words; but whoever neglects to do so demonstrates that he is not his people.

There are, however, some who not only do not deign to fulfill the divine law in deed but do not even deign to hear it. What, I ask, do they make of what is written: “Whoever stops his ear so as not to hear the law, his prayer will be accursed” (Prov. 28:9)? If the prayer of one unwilling to hear the divine law is accursed, then his heart is likewise despised; if his heart is despised, Christ disdains to dwell in him. Therefore he who hates Christ’s laws does not have Christ come to his heart, because a heart of this kind, subjected to sin, does not deserve to have such a guest, as Scripture testifies when it says: “The holy spirit of discipline will flee deceit, and will not dwell in a body subject to sins” (Wis. 1:5).

Let those who spend their days in sins hear this: those subjected to vices cannot have the Holy Spirit as their inhabitant, and no one can serve sin and Christ at the same time, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “No one can serve two masters” (Matt. 6:24; Luke 16:13). And through the Prophet: “The bed is too narrow; the covering is too short; it cannot cover both” (Isa. 28:20). It is as though he plainly said: No one can receive me and the author of sin together in the bed of his mind. For, as the Apostle says, “What agreement does Christ have with Belial? And what partnership does light have with darkness?” (2 Cor. 6:15).

The Christian profession is also neglected by many, and in many respects, because of carnal pleasures and the widely differing vanities of this age. The more excessively—indeed, pointlessly—they serve these, the less they are found to devote themselves to the works of the Christian profession. If we reread the Acts of the Apostles and carefully observe the devotion of the Christian people who flourished under those same apostles, we shall find that the devotion of the Christian people of our age differs greatly from theirs. And in proportion as those people followed it more ardently and devoutly, so some have departed farther from its works.

Therefore, just as at the beginning of the newborn Church that same faith flourished through works, so now, when works are neglected, it withers among certain people. To use the words of blessed Augustine [Note: Sermon of Saint Maximus, bishop, *On Various Matters*, among the Ambrosian sermons, 9]: “Christ is the same in us as he was in them; the same faith is in us, but not the same devotion. In them the brotherhood of Christ was greater than that of blood. In them, as there was one faith, so there was also one substance; and those who shared Christ also shared their resources. They considered it wrong not to admit as a participant in their substance one who was a participant in grace. They were not afraid that they themselves would be hungry; rather, they feared that others would be hungry. But now, as the same blessed Augustine says, one gives so little thought to another’s poverty that what the Apostle says has become true: ‘One is hungry, another is drunk’ (1 Cor. 11:21).”

And shortly afterward: “Now is the time of which the Lord says in the Gospel: ‘Iniquity will abound; the love of many will grow cold’ (Matt. 24:12). For now greed and iniquity abound, whereas formerly they were restrained by the goodness of generosity, and the love of brotherhood grows cold, although previously it burned with love for Christ. In those days, under the apostles, such great love of brotherhood existed that no want was found in their assembly. But now such dissimulation of Christianity exists that in our gathering you can scarcely find a rich person. When I say that a rich person can scarcely be found, I mean rich not in possessions but in works. The Apostle says: ‘Let them be rich in good works’ (1 Tim. 6:18). In the Church, he intended the person to be understood as rich who is rich in Christ.”

And the same writer adds shortly afterward: “Rarely, therefore, in this age do we find a rich person among the Christian people; and although many are rich in gold at home, in the Church they are beggars. For since they do not use their means for the poor in proportion to their ability, neither is what they bring acceptable nor what they keep sufficient. The Lord said to Cain when he offered gifts: ‘If you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, you have sinned. Be still.’ So you, Christian, do not divide rightly, if from your great store of gold you reserve a larger portion for mammon than you give to God.”

At the beginning, therefore, of the holy Church of God, the fervor of faith among believers was so vigorous that they persevered in the apostles’ teaching, in fellowship, in the breaking of bread, and in prayers; they held everything in common and took their food with gladness and simplicity of heart, praising God.

Now, however, the devotion of Christianity among most people is very different. [Note: “For among some.” We have corrected this passage, formerly teeming with foul errors, by comparison with chapter 11 of the little work on royal instruction which we publish below.] For among some, love of earthly affairs is placed above the apostles’ teaching; greed above fellowship in the breaking of bread; coldness of love and the desire to seize another’s property above giving away one’s own; and the pleasures of the flesh, curiosity about worldly matters, anxiety about the world, and the mind’s manifold wandering in different directions above prayers. What was common to those people is now so private to certain individuals that scarcely ever is anything from it redirected to another’s use.

Those people took their food with gladness and simplicity of heart, praising God. Now, however, some scarcely take food without gossip, hypocrisy, mockery, the dancing of actors, obscene joking, filthy speech, buffoonery, and countless other vanities that weaken the Christian soul from the vigor of its proper condition. They were simple in heart; these, by contrast, are deceitful and double-minded, although Scripture says: “Think of the Lord in goodness, and seek him in simplicity of heart” (Wis. 1:1).

When those people took food, they praised God; these, demanding various kinds of food according to their own pleasure, praise the skill of cooks in preparing the most luxurious dishes for them. Consequently they are excessive in eating and drinking, so that Nabuzardan, the chief of the cooks, seems to be demolishing the walls of Jerusalem—that is, the virtues of their souls.

They are also so forgetful of that evangelical command—“See to it that your hearts are not weighed down with drunkenness, excess, and the cares of this life” (Luke 21:34)—that, with their bellies stuffed with exquisite foods and irrigated with various drinks, they open their mouths not for the praises of God but for laughter. They pay no attention to what the Lord says in the Gospel: “Woe to you who laugh now, for you will mourn and weep” (ibid. 6:25). And elsewhere Scripture says: “Laughter will be mixed with sorrow, and mourning takes hold of the end of joy” (Prov. 14:13). Conversely, concerning the righteous: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted” (Matt. 5:5).

It is not without profound mystery that our Lord Jesus Christ is read in the Gospel to have wept, not laughed: namely, so that in this, as in his other members, he might give an example that in this valley of tears we should not laugh for the sake of smoky and fleeting joys, but rather should weep over the loss of our inheritance of the eternal homeland, from which we have long been exiles.

Those who devote themselves to banquets and excessive talk must therefore be terrified by the condemnation of the purple-clad rich man, who refused to give crumbs to the needy Lazarus (Luke 16:24); and for that reason, as blessed Gregory says, he came to the point of asking even for the smallest things. He asked that his tongue be cooled because he had insolently devoted himself to the talkativeness that usually occurs especially during banquets.

They must indeed be softened and urged toward works of mercy by the example of blessed Job, who says: “If I have denied the poor what they desired, and have made the eyes of the widow wait; if I ate my morsel alone, and the little one did not eat from it” (Job 31:16).

Therefore, lest anyone think that he can devote himself to excessive talk with impunity, let him hear what the Psalmist sings: “Who is the person who desires life and loves to see good days? Let him restrain his tongue from evil and his lips from speaking deceit. Let him turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. 33:13). Many, indeed, because of the evil days which, deceived by the love of the world, they think good, lose the eternal good days in which there is perfect happiness and the unspeakable blessedness of perpetual joy.

There is also something else in the Christian religion worthy of great amazement: human laws, which generally instill fear in those wishing to sin more than Christ’s commandments do, seem to have greater force than the divine laws, although the former free those who obey them from temporal punishment, while the latter free them from eternal punishment.

When someone occupying the summit of royal or imperial dignity, ruling mortals temporarily, issues an edict that he wishes his subjects both carefully to hear and faithfully and prudently to fulfill, what subject, I ask, does not listen to it eagerly and hasten faithfully to obey his commands? Who would dare to break out into such great audacity? Who would presume to disregard it except at his own peril?

When I say these things, amazement and indescribable wonder arise in my mind. Human beings make laws, and subjects observe them; but God, the Creator of all, ruling eternally—who is not increased by our advancement nor diminished by our loss, in whose hand we are like clay in the hand of a potter—has given a law for the salvation of souls to be embraced, and it is despised. Even if it is heard by the bodily ear, it is not received by the ear of the heart and is not fulfilled in deed.

What excuse will Christians be able to offer the Lord when they accept the strictness of worldly law out of fear of the world, yet refuse to bow their necks to the yoke of Christ, which is light and easy and leads to eternal life? The Lord says: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you.” And again elsewhere: “Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls; for my yoke is easy and my burden is light” (Matt. 11:28–30).

Yet people refuse to come to such a great caller, to learn humility and gentleness from him, and to take up his yoke. What else do those who do this do except fall away from their own salvation? How pitiable and destructive this is cannot be expressed.

All the faithful must therefore take care not to place human laws above divine laws, or love of the world above love of God. For those who love the world there is a broad and spacious way that leads to death; for those who love Christ there is a narrow and constricted way that leads to life.

Today there are more people in the Church—and this is deeply mournful—who strive to walk along the broad and spacious way leading to death than those who endeavor to enter by the narrow and constricted way leading to life. This happens because what the Apostle writes to Timothy seems to have been fulfilled: “Know this,” he says, “that in the last days perilous times will come. People will be lovers of themselves,” and so forth, as he continues in that Epistle (2 Tim. 3:2). And again elsewhere: “For they all seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ” (Phil. 2:21).

I clearly perceive that in modern times the Christian profession is not honored by most people with the same devotion and reverence with which it was honored by the Christians of old.

The apostles—or rather, through the apostles, Christ—judged that this rule of faith, about which I have spoken briefly above and at full length in the Acts of the Apostles mentioned earlier, was to be held by the faithful. If Christ taught this, indeed because he taught it, why is it despised in accordance with so many and such great customs devised to suit the wishes of certain people? Although this rule is truly received with God’s approval, some neglect it in works in many different ways.

I think this has happened because among certain laypeople a deeply lamentable custom has crept in. They have not paid proper attention to the divine laws to which they have submitted themselves through faith. They make a law for themselves not only of what they desire—which is not lawful—but also of what is lawful yet not expedient; and they believe that they can live blamelessly according to whatever happens to please them. Since demonstrating this point individually from the divine oracles and the judgments of the holy Fathers would require great length, it will be shown in the following chapters, insofar as God grants the ability.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0167]

## CHAPTER I  
### That marriage was instituted by God, and should not be desired for the sake of lust but for the procreation of children

[Note: “For the procreation of children.” As in the table of chapters, so here Codex Claromontanus adds: “and that the life of good married people is signified through Job”; its absence from the earlier edition is unsurprising, since that edition was prepared from a manuscript lacking the material concerning Job which we shall copy from the Claromontanus.] 

[Col. 0167A] Since God is supremely good, all the things he made are very good, as Scripture says: “God saw all that he had made, and it was very good” (Gen. 1:31). Yet many people are known to turn into evil for themselves certain good things created by the good God, because they use them badly.

His goods are innumerable and ineffable. Among them is marriage, which is good and was instituted by God at the beginning of human creation, as the book of Genesis makes clear, where we read: “For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two will be one flesh” (ibid. 2:25). It also says there: “God made humankind; in the image of God he made him; male and female he created them, and he blessed them, saying: ‘Increase and multiply, and fill the earth’” (ibid. 1:27).

And Solomon says: “A wife is prepared for a man by God” (Prov. 19:14). And in the Gospel: “Have you not read that the one who created them from the beginning made them male and female? Therefore what God has joined together, let no human being separate” (Matt. 19:6). And Paul says to the Corinthians: “If you take a wife, you have not sinned; and if a virgin marries, she has not sinned” (1 Cor. 7:28). The same writer says to the Hebrews: “Marriage is honorable, and the marriage bed undefiled” (Heb. 13:4).

That this great good is turned into guilt if it is sought for the sake of lust and not rather for the fruit of procreation is shown in blessed Augustine’s book *On the Good of Marriage* (chapter 19): “Marriage is therefore good,” he says, “and married people are better in proportion as they are more chaste and faithful, if they fear God, and especially if they spiritually nourish the children whom they desire carnally.”

The same writer says in the same work (chapter 9): “It must certainly be observed that God gives us some goods which are to be desired for their own sake, such as wisdom, health, and friendship; and others which are necessary for the sake of something else, such as instruction, food, drink, sleep, marriage, and sexual intercourse. Some of these are necessary for wisdom, such as instruction; some for health, such as food, drink, and sleep; and some for friendship, such as marriage or sexual intercourse. Through these the propagation of the human race is sustained, and in it the fellowship of friendship is a great good.

“Whoever does not use these goods, which are necessary for the sake of other things, for the purpose for which they were instituted, sins—sometimes venially, sometimes damnably. Whoever uses them for the purpose for which they were given acts well. Therefore, whoever does not need them acts better if he does not use them.”

Again, the same writer says in the same work (chapter 3): “We are now speaking according to this condition of being born and dying which we know and in which we were created: that the marriage of male and female is something good. Divine Scripture so commends its *se detractionem* [an uncertain reading; Acherius proposes *confoederationem*, “covenant,” which is not displeasing if *quorum* is written] that neither may a woman who has been sent away by her husband marry another while her husband lives, nor may a man dismissed by his wife take another unless the woman who departed has died.

“Marriage is therefore good, and the Lord also confirmed it in the Gospel—not only because he prohibited sending away one’s wife except for the cause of fornication, but also because, when invited, he came to a wedding.”

The same writer says in the same work: “Why marriage is good is rightly asked. It does not seem to me to be good solely for the procreation of children, but also for the natural fellowship itself between the two sexes. Otherwise marriage would no longer be called marriage among the elderly, especially if they had either lost their children or never had any. But now, even in an old marriage that is good, although the ardor of chastity between male and female has faded, the order of love between husband and wife remains strong. For the better they are, the sooner they began, by mutual consent, to abstain from mingling their bodies—not because necessity later prevented them from doing what they wished, but so that it might be praiseworthy that they had earlier refused to do what they could.”

The same blessed Augustine also writes to Count Valerius [Note: *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, chapter 4]: “The union of male and female for the purpose of begetting is a natural good of marriage; but one makes bad use of this good if one uses it like a beast, so that one’s intention is directed toward the pleasure of lust and not toward the will to propagate.”

And shortly afterward: “What I said belongs to the nature of marriage: that male and female are joined in a partnership for begetting, and therefore do not defraud one another, just as every partnership naturally refuses to tolerate a fraudulent partner. When unbelievers possess this evident good, because they use it unbelievingly, they turn it into evil and sin.”

The same writer adds shortly afterward (chapter 7): “Marriage therefore boasts because it makes some good even from that evil; but because it cannot take place without it, it is ashamed—just as if someone with an injured foot reached some good destination while limping. The arrival itself is not bad because of the evil of limping, nor is the limping good because of the benefit of arriving. In the same way, we should neither condemn marriage because of the evil of lust nor praise lust because of the good of marriage.”

[Col. 0168D] Isidore says in book two of his *Offices* [Note: Book II, chapter 19]: “Those marriages are undefiled which seek offspring, not lust, within marriage. They were not instituted to serve the pleasures of the flesh, but only to seek the fruit of procreation. For, as the marriage documents themselves indicate, a wife is taken for the purpose of begetting children. Therefore, when someone lives more luxuriously than the necessity of begetting children requires, it is already sin.”

Marriage is therefore good, but it is not to be placed on an equal footing with virginal goodness and widowly continence. Isidore says in the same little book: “Marriage is good in itself, but because of the things surrounding it, it becomes bad. It is bad because of what the Apostle says: ‘The married man thinks about the things of the world.’ And again: ‘Because of fornication, let each man have his own wife’ (1 Cor. 7:34).

“That not one man and several women, but one man and one woman are joined, is first demonstrated by the union divinely made as an example. For when the Lord had formed the man and saw that a companion equal to him was necessary, he took one of his ribs and fashioned one woman for him. Thus Adam and the woman Eve, joined to one another in marriage, established for humankind, by the authority of their origin and by God’s first will, the form of marriage.”

The aforementioned Augustine also writes in his book of sermons about the praise of married people [Note: *On the Words of the Lord*, Sermon 53, chapter 4]: “Married life is praiseworthy,” he says, “and it has its place in the body of Christ.” And shortly afterward: “We know that those who lead married lives are members of Christ, if they are members of Christ—that is, if they are faithful.” Again the same writer says: “I dare to say that those who lead married lives, if they possess humility, are better than chaste people who are proud.”

These and countless other testimonies make clear that marriage, from which holy and humble virginity is born, is good and honorable, provided it is used chastely. Whoever desires it for the purpose for which it was instituted uses a good thing well; whoever uses it badly is undoubtedly shown to turn a good thing into sin for himself.

Accordingly, married people must understand that they have committed such a fault and must take care not to turn what is lawful into sin for themselves by using it for the sake of lust. Those who have stained the chastity of the marriage bed with the blemishes of such incontinence must strive to wash it away by daily gifts of alms, continual prayers, tears of repentance, and other good works.

[This ought not improperly to have been added to this chapter: the prophet Ezekiel asserts that he heard of three men who were delivered, namely Noah, Daniel, and Job. And since through Noah [lacuna] the order of those set over others is signified, while through Job the life of good married people is also signified, it remains for married people to imitate, insofar as they can and with the support of divine grace, the life and deeds of this man, praised by the Lord with such great integrity and by so many and such great praises of sacred virtues, so that they may deserve to be rightly admitted to his fellowship.

For in the house of the wedding feast, which is the Church of Christ, a dining room is described; these are evidently the three orders of the faithful in the Church: teachers, abstainers, and married people. Elsewhere in the Gospel these same three orders of the faithful are distinguished in such a way that the life of the continent is shown by two lying in bed, that of those set over others by two in the field, and that of married people by two women grinding together.

Concerning the third order, therefore, the presbyter Venerable Bede writes: “There will be two women grinding together.” He calls those people “grinding” who, established among the congregations, are governed by teachers while carrying on the affairs of the world. He signified them also under the name of women, because, as I have said, it is fitting that they be governed by the counsels of the experienced. He called them “grinding” because of the cycle and round of temporal affairs; yet he said that they were grinding together insofar as the Church’s needs are supplied from those very matters and affairs.

“Every activity of this world is a mill, which, while it heaps up many cares, turns human minds around as though in a circle and casts out from itself something like flour, because it always produces the smallest thoughts for a restless heart.

“One will be taken, and the other will be left. The part will be taken that practiced marriage only for the love of producing offspring and distributed earthly substance in order to acquire heavenly things; but the part will be left that [lacuna] served the allurements of the flesh for the sake of marriage; and, if it gave any earthly thing to the Church or to the poor, did so as though it were adding still more to a Lord redeemed by these gifts [the wording is corrupt].”]

It is therefore clear, in accordance with the prophecy of the prophet Ezekiel and the evangelical teaching, that there are three orders and distinctions of the faithful in the Church. Since this discussion concerns the order of married people, they must take the greatest care to conduct the affairs of the world in such a way that they do not in the least displease their Creator.

Let them therefore beware of being left behind, a fate that the Lord threatens with terror, and embrace being taken up, which the same Lord happily promises in his proclamation, so that they may not be counted among the company of those who are to be left behind.

To use the words of blessed Gregory in the eighth homily on the prophet Ezekiel: “The life of good married people must be regulated in the camp of the Lord in such a way that, while living together in harmony in the love of the almighty Lord, they pay one another the debt of the flesh in such a manner that they never forget what they owe the Lord in good works; and if, as human beings, they commit any offenses, they constantly redeem them through acts of piety.”

## CHAPTER II  
### That those who wish to take wives should strive to approach them chaste and undefiled, just as they desire to find them chaste and undefiled

[Col. 0170D] Some laypeople, overcome by the love of lust, and others, led by desire to seek earthly honor—or rather, while awaiting the time when they may obtain the honors of the world—roll about in the mud of lust. Before approaching the marriage union, they corrupt themselves in various ways and lose the virginal honor which they ought to have preserved until the time of taking a lawful wife.

They also deprive themselves of the blessing with which God blessed the union of the first human beings, and of that blessing which is now bestowed in the Church through the ministry of priests [Note: “The ministry of priests.” We have corrected the text in this way, admittedly by conjecture, but by a conjecture that cannot be wrong. Previously it read “mysteries”], according to canonical authority and the custom of the holy Roman Church, upon those about to marry.

From what source, indeed, has the condemnable custom arisen that the bridegroom and bride are very rarely blessed during the celebration of Mass according to the order stated above? The children born from such intercourse, moreover, although both parents are free in status, are nevertheless unable—what a sorrow—to succeed to the inheritance together with brothers born from a lawful marriage, according to the judgment of worldly law.

Concerning this matter blessed Ambrose writes in book one of his work entitled *On Abraham*: “Let people therefore learn not to despise marriage and not to join themselves to unequal partners, lest they receive children whom they cannot have as heirs. If they are moved by no consideration of modesty, let them at least strive toward a worthy marriage for the sake of transmitting an inheritance.”

Let those who desire to take wives therefore hear how the angel Raphael instructed Tobias concerning the wife he was to join to himself: “Those who receive marriage in such a way that they exclude God from their mind and devote themselves to their lust, like a horse and mule that have no understanding, over them the demon has power. But when you have taken her, after entering the bedroom, remain continent from her for three days; devote yourself with her to nothing except prayer. On the first night, when the fish’s liver has been burned, the demon will be driven away. On the second night, you will be admitted to the union of the holy patriarchs. On the third night, you will obtain a blessing, so that children may be safely procreated from you. After the third night has passed, you will take the virgin with fear of the Lord, led more by love of children than by lust, so that you may obtain the blessing in your children in the seed of Abraham” (Tob. 6:16).

If there happen to be people who, in taking wives chastely, wish to think lightly of priestly admonition, they must by all means hold angelic instruction in the highest regard.

But those who are impure and unchaste, yet wish to marry chaste and pure wives, should hear what blessed Augustine says in the Book of Sermons [Note: [Col. 0171D] On the Words of the Lord, Sermon 46, chapter 2]:

> “You who are going to take wives, keep yourselves for your wives. What sort of women you wish to find them, such ought they also to find you. What young man is there who does not wish to marry a chaste wife? And if he is going to take a virgin, who does not desire her untouched? You seek one untouched: remain untouched yourself. You seek one pure: do not be impure. For she can, and you can. If it could not be done, neither could she do it. But since she can, let her teach you that it can be done. And that she may be able, God governs her. Yet you will be more glorious if you do it. Why more glorious? The guardianship of her parents restrains her, and the very modesty of the weaker sex holds her back. Finally, she fears laws that you do not fear. Therefore you will be more glorious if you do it, because, if you do it, you fear God. She has many things to fear besides God; you fear God alone. But the one whom you fear is greater than all” (chapter 3).

“He himself must be feared in public, he himself in secret. You go out: you are seen; you enter: you are seen; the lamp burns: he sees you; the lamp is extinguished: he sees you; you enter the bedroom: he sees you; you move within your heart: he sees you. Fear him—the one who is concerned to see you—and, by fearing, be chaste. Or, if you wish to sin, seek a place where he does not see you, and do what you wish.”

Likewise, the same author, in his sermon to the people entitled *On the Ten Strings* (chapter 20):

> “Do not say to yourself, whenever you perhaps wish to do something wanton: ‘I do not yet have a wife; I do what I wish. For I do not sin after I have a wife.’ You already know your price; you already know where you are approaching, what you eat, and what you drink. Abstain from fornications, lest you say to me: ‘I go to the brothel, I go to a prostitute, I go to a harlot; nor do I violate that commandment which says, “You shall not commit adultery” (Exod. 20:14), because I do not yet have a wife, and I do nothing after having one; nor do I violate that commandment which says, “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife” (ibid., 17), because I go to a public prostitute.’ Against which commandment do I offend? We do not find the string that we should strike. With what cord shall we bind this fugitive? Let him not flee: he has something by which he may be bound. For the ten commandments are referred to those two, as we have heard, namely, that we should love God and our neighbor. And those two are referred to that one commandment: ‘What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another’ (Matt. 7:14).

> “Let your holiness understand. Indeed, ‘What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another’ pertains to those two commandments. If you do not do to a human being what you do not wish to suffer from a human being, it pertains to the commandment concerning your neighbor. But if you wish to do to God what you do not wish to suffer from a human being, are you not doing to another what you do not wish to suffer? A human being has become dearer to you than God. ‘Then how do I do it to God?’ you ask. You corrupt yourself. ‘And how do I wrong God, since I corrupt myself?’ Hear the Apostle: ‘Do you not know that you are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?’ (1 Cor. 3:16). He says this to Christians; he says this to the faithful: ‘If anyone corrupts the temple of God, God will destroy him’ (ibid., 17). Do you see how he threatens? You do not wish your own house to be corrupted; why do you corrupt God’s house? Certainly you are doing to someone what you do not wish to suffer. There is therefore no escape. The one who did not think he could be held is held.”

When, therefore, the matters mentioned above have been carefully considered, those who approach the marriage bond should take the greatest care not to be corrupted either secretly with prostitutes or openly with servant girls before they bind themselves by the marital bond. Thus, since they cannot obtain the hundredfold fruit of virginity, at least, being joined in chastity, they may be able to receive from the Lord the thirtieth fruit.

## CHAPTER III. [Col. 0172D] That married persons ought not indiscriminately to serve carnal intercourse

There are many who lead married lives and strive most modestly to distinguish the times for intercourse and abstinence with their wives. There are also those who not only refuse to observe any limit to this discernment, but habitually make shameless objections against those who chastise and rebuke them. “Our wives,” they say, “are joined to us by law. If we use them whenever and however we wish, according to our desire, we do not sin. Rather, we become guilty of a greater crime if we abstain from the embraces of our wives and do not beget the children whom we ought to beget.”

What I say has very often been put to me. Ecclesiastes resists their most shameless assertion—or rather, the lustful will by which they strive to make such conduct a law for themselves—saying: “A time for embracing, and a time to be far from embraces” (Eccles. 3:5). And the Apostle says: “The time is short. It remains that those who have wives should be as though they had none; those who use this world, as though they did not use it; those who rejoice, as though they did not rejoice; and those who buy, as though they did not possess. For the form of this world is passing away” (1 Cor. 7:29–31).

[Jerome writes in his *Commentary on the Prophet Ezekiel*:

> “Men are therefore commanded,” he says, “to know definite times for intercourse, not only with other men’s wives, but also with their own, with whom they seem to be joined by law, as Scripture says: ‘Increase and multiply, and fill the earth’ (Gen. 1:28)—to know when they should have intercourse and when they should abstain from their wives. Ecclesiastes also proclaims this: ‘A time for embracing, and a time to be far from embraces’ (Eccles. 3:5). Let the wife therefore beware lest, overcome by desire for intercourse, she conceal the husband [text corrupt; see note], and let the husband beware lest he use force against his wife, thinking that the pleasure of marriage ought to be subject to him at all times.”

[Note: [Col. 0173D] “She conceal herself from her husband.” Although we understand that our labor in correcting such passages will be of little use, since very few readers will be concerned with matters of this kind, nevertheless, because we are unwilling to leave corrupted anything that we can remedy, we point out that an appropriate meaning can be obtained from this absurd sentence by changing one word. For if one reads *cogat virum* (“force her husband”), it becomes clear from the author’s meaning that the condition of husband and wife is equal with respect to what, following Paul, is called the marital obligation, and that neither may demand it from the other at certain times, either through importunity or by force inflicted upon the body. Below, in chapter 10, where the same passage is copied, Acherius notes that another reading is found, *illiciat virum* (“entice her husband”), which is not objectionable.]

For Pope Gregory, in the *Pastoral Book* (Part III, chapter 28), says:

> “Those bound by marriage must be admonished that, when they consider what belongs to the other, each should strive to please the spouse in such a way as not to displease the Creator; that they should engage in the affairs of this world in such a way that they do not neglect to desire the things of God. Let them rejoice in present goods in such a way that they nevertheless fear eternal evils with watchful concern. Let them grieve over temporal evils in such a way that they nevertheless fix their hope, with undiminished consolation, on future goods [Col. 0173C] [Note: [Col. 0174D] ‘On future goods.’ Acherius says that another reading is found: ‘on everlasting goods,’ which he prefers. We immediately removed the little word *se* after the verb *cognoscunt*. Not long afterward, where the text has *se contingere*, a much better reading stood in the margin: *aeternis se conjungere* (‘to join themselves to eternal things’). Likewise below, where the text has *servet quae Dei sunt* (‘let him preserve the things that are God’s’), Acherius notes that the reading *speret* (‘let him hope’) found elsewhere is as suitable as this reading is inept.], so that, while in their passage they recognize that what they do exists* [text corrupt], and in their abiding-place [recognize] what they desire, neither do the evils of the world break their hearts, since the hope of heavenly goods strengthens them, nor do the goods of the present life deceive them, since the evils of the coming judgment make them apprehensive.

> “Thus the spirit of Christian spouses, both weak and faithful—unable wholly to despise temporal things, yet able, through desire, to come into contact with itself* [text corrupt]—even while it lies for a time in the pleasure of the flesh, is restored by the refreshment of heavenly hope. And if it possesses the things of the world for the use of the journey, let it preserve* the things of God for the fruit of arrival. Let it not devote its whole self to what it is doing, nor fall completely away from what it ought firmly to hope for. Paul expresses this well and briefly when he says: ‘Those who have wives should be as though they had none; those who weep, as though they did not weep; and those who rejoice, as though they did not rejoice’ (1 Cor. 7:30).

> “He has a wife as though he did not have one who uses her for carnal consolation in such a way that he is never bent by love of her into evil works away from the uprightness of a better purpose. He has a wife as though he did not have one who, seeing that all things are transitory, endures care for the flesh out of necessity but awaits the eternal joys of the spirit out of desire. To weep without weeping is to lament outward adversities while nevertheless knowing how to rejoice in the consolation of eternal hope. Likewise, to rejoice without rejoicing is to lift the mind above lowly things while never ceasing to fear what is highest.

> “A little later he appropriately adds: ‘For the form of this world is passing away’ (ibid., 31), as though he were plainly saying: ‘Do not love the world steadfastly, since even the world itself, which you love, cannot stand.’ In vain, therefore, do you fix your heart as though it were on something permanent, while the very thing you love is fleeing.

> “Spouses must be admonished to endure patiently whatever in one another sometimes displeases them, and to save one another by mutual exhortation. For it is written: ‘Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ’ (Gal. 6:2). The law of Christ is love, because through it he both generously bestowed his goods upon us and patiently bore our evils. We fulfill the law of Christ and his commandments when we kindly bestow our own goods and piously endure the evils of our own.”

After hearing and carefully considering what has been said above, married persons who are unchaste should cease making their lustful desire a law for themselves. From the authorities cited above, they should learn that they ought not to use their wives immoderately.

## CHAPTER IV. [Col. 0174C] On preserving fidelity between husband and wife, and that it is not permissible [to have either a mistress or] a concubine

It is incompatible with the Christian religion for one man to join several women, or one woman several men, in a single body. Among the Jews and certain other unbelievers, this shameful custom continues. For it is neither lawful nor fitting for a Christian, having abandoned fidelity to the marriage bed, to wander among various prostitutes. The passages that follow also demonstrate that this must not be done.

The Lord says through Malachi:

> “You have done this again: you covered the altar of the Lord with tears, with weeping and groaning, so that I will no longer look upon the sacrifice or accept anything pleasing from your hand. And you said: ‘For what reason?’ Because the Lord has been witness between you and the wife of your youth, whom you have despised. Yet she is your companion and the wife of your covenant. Did not one make her, and is there not a remnant of his spirit? And what does each person seek except the offspring of God? Guard your spirit, and do not despise the wife of your youth” (Mal. 2:13–15).

And the Apostle says: “Let the husband render the debt to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband” (1 Cor. 7:3). And shortly afterward: “Do not defraud one another, unless perhaps by mutual agreement for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer. Then return again to the same relationship, lest Satan tempt you because of your lack of self-control” (ibid., 5). Likewise, the same author says: “The woman does not have authority over her own body, but the husband; and likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife” (ibid., 4).

Augustine, in the *Book on the Good of Marriage* (chapter 11), says:

> “The honor of marriage is therefore chastity in begetting children and keeping faith in rendering the carnal debt. This is the work of marriage. The Apostle defends it from every crime when he says: ‘If you take a wife, you have not sinned; and if a virgin marries, she does not sin; and let her do what she wishes—she does not sin if she marries’ (1 Cor. 7:28). But a more immoderate advance by either sex in demanding the debt is permitted as a concession, on account of the matters we mentioned above.”

Likewise, the same author in the same work (chapter 23):

> “For chastity includes not committing fornication, not committing adultery, and not defiling oneself by any illicit intercourse. Those who do not observe these things act against the Lord’s command, and for this reason they are excluded from the virtue of obedience.”

Likewise (chapter 6):

> “Married persons therefore owe one another not only the fidelity of joining with one another for the purpose of begetting children—which is the first association of the human race in this mortality—but also, for the avoidance of illicit intercourse, a mutual kind of service in bearing one another’s weakness, so that even if perpetual continence pleases one of them, it cannot be practiced without the consent of the other. For this reason also, the wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband.”

Likewise, the same author in the same work (chapter 3):

> “If therefore the fidelity of honor and of the mutual services owed by either sex is preserved, chastity will remain in the properly married souls all the more sincere as it is more powerful, and all the more secure as it is more peaceful—even if the limbs of both are languishing and almost corpse-like.”

Likewise, the same author in the *Book on the Ten Strings* (chapter 9):

> “Consider the word of God: ‘You shall not commit adultery’ (Exod. 20:14). Do not commit adultery after your wives, because you do not want your wives to commit adultery after you. Do not go where you do not want them to follow. You try in vain to excuse yourselves when you say: ‘Am I going to another man’s wife? I am going to my servant girl.’ Would you like your wife to say to you: ‘Am I going to another man, to my male servant’?

> “You say: ‘The woman to whom I go is not another man’s wife.’ God forbid that she should say this; it is better that she grieve over you than imitate you. That chaste and holy woman, truly Christian, grieves when her husband fornicates—not for the sake of the flesh, but for the sake of love. She does not refuse you because she herself does not do it, but because it is not good for you. For if she abstains for the reason that you should not do it, then, if you do it, she will do it too. But if she owes it to God, if she owes it to Christ, what you demand from her, and she renders because he commands it, then, even if her husband fornicates, she offers her chastity to God.

> “Christ speaks in the hearts of good women, speaking inwardly with words such as these: ‘You are tormented by your husband’s injuries. Grieve over what he does to you, but do not imitate him by doing evil; let him imitate you in doing good. In what he does badly, do not consider him your head, but me. For if he is your head in what he does badly, the body will follow its head, and both will plunge headlong. But so that she may not follow her evil head, let her hold fast to Christ, the Head of the Church. To him she owes her love; to him she gives her honor. Whether her husband is absent or present, she does not sin, because the one to whom she owes her refusal to sin is never absent.’”

Likewise, the same author in the *Book on Adulterous Marriages* (Book II, chapter 8):

> “Those who are displeased that an equal standard of chastity should be maintained between husband and wife, and who prefer—and especially in this matter—to be subject to the laws of the world rather than to those of Christ, should read what the emperor Antoninus, who was certainly not a Christian, decreed concerning this matter. Among other things he says:

> “‘For it seems to me exceedingly unjust that a husband should demand chastity from his wife when he does not himself offer it; this can both condemn the husband and, through the confession of mutual guilt, settle the matter between the two or remove the cause of the action.’”

> “If these things must be observed for the honor of an earthly state, how much greater chastity does the heavenly homeland and the fellowship of angels require!”

Bede, in his *Commentary on Proverbs*:

> “‘A most beloved hind and a most delightful fawn’ (Prov. 5:19). Let that wife always be most beloved to you who, like a hind pursuing serpents, pursues prostitutes and drives them from her house.”

Jerome, in his *Letter on the Death of Fabiola* (Letter 30):

> “Whatever is commanded to men consequently extends to women. For an adulterous wife is not to be dismissed while an adulterous husband is retained. If someone joins himself to a prostitute, he makes one body with her. Therefore a woman who joins herself to a fornicator and an impure man becomes one body with him.

> “The laws of the Caesars are one thing; the laws of Christ another. Papinianus commands one thing; our Paul another. Among the former, the reins of chastity are loosened for men; once only fornication and adultery have been condemned, lust is freely permitted in brothels and with servant girls—as though dignity, rather than pleasure, made the fault. Among us, what is not permitted to women is equally not permitted to men; the same servitude is judged by the same standard.”

Lactantius also writes [Note: [Col. 0175D] “Lactantius also.” This passage is indeed from Lactantius, *On True Worship*, Book VI, chapter 23, but not in these same words]:

> “When someone has a wife, he may not have either a female slave or a free woman, if he is to preserve fidelity to his marriage. For it is not the case—as is publicly asserted concerning men—that only the woman is adulterous who, having a husband, is polluted by another man. Since divine law has joined two people in the body of one marriage, anyone who tears the bond of that body apart in different directions is an adulterer. For it is unjust that a husband should demand from his wife what he cannot himself provide.”

Ambrose, in the *Book on Abraham* (Book I, chapter 3):

> “Let us therefore imitate Abraham, so that we may be heirs of the earth through the righteousness of faith, through which he became heir of the world. But perhaps someone may say: ‘How do you propose Abraham to us for imitation, when he received a son from a servant girl? Or what does it mean that so great a man was subject to this error, whose deeds we admire so greatly?’

> “Let us consider first that Abraham lived before the law of Moses and before the Gospel; adultery did not yet seem to be forbidden. Punishment for a crime comes from the time of the law that prohibited the crime; before the law there is no condemnation of the matter, but only from the law. Although God praised marriage in paradise, he had not condemned adultery. You have one defense of Abraham.

> “The second is that he did not, inflamed by the ardor of wandering lust or captivated by the beauty of a wanton appearance, prefer the companionship of a servant girl to the marriage bed; rather, he did so out of concern for posterity and the propagation of offspring. After the Flood, the human race was still sparse. It was also a matter of religious duty, lest someone seem not to have discharged the debt owed to nature.”

I therefore admonish you, men above all, who are striving toward the grace of the Lord: do not join yourselves to an adulterous body. For whoever joins himself to a prostitute is one body with her. Do not give women this occasion for divorce. Let no one flatter himself on the basis of human laws: every act of fornication is adultery, and what is not permitted to a woman is not permitted to a man. The same chastity is owed by the husband as by the wife. Whatever is committed with a woman who is not a legitimate wife is condemned under the charge of adultery.

You have therefore understood what you must avoid, lest anyone make himself unworthy of the sacraments. Understand also this: such intemperance dissolves marital love, makes servant girls proud, matrons angry, discordant, and rebellious, concubines shameless, and husbands immodest. As soon as a servant girl conceives by her master, she despises her mistress as though she were made richer by childbirth; the mistress grieves that she is despised and accuses her husband as the author of her injuries.

It is clear, therefore, that an equal standard of chastity between husband and wife and fidelity to the marriage bed must be preserved. It is not lawful for a man, whether for the sake of offspring or for the sake of lust, to dissolve the marital bond with another woman, nor for a woman to do so with another man.

## CHAPTER V. That husbands ought to love their wives in chastity and should honor them as the weaker vessel

In the preceding chapter we briefly gathered what concerns the preservation of fidelity between husband and wife. In this following chapter, what concerns wives being loved by their husbands with chaste love remains to be gathered.

It is written in Proverbs:

> “Let your fountain be blessed, and rejoice with the wife of your youth, a most beloved hind and a most delightful fawn; let her breasts intoxicate you at all times, and delight continually in her love” (Prov. 5:18–19).

And in Ecclesiastes:

> “Enjoy life with the wife whom you love, all the days of your unstable life, which have been given to you beneath the sun, throughout all the days of your vanity” (Eccles. 9:9).

The Apostle Peter says:

> “Husbands, likewise, live together with your wives according to knowledge, granting honor to the female vessel as the weaker vessel, as co-heirs of your grace, so that your prayers may not be hindered” (1 Pet. 3:7).

Paul also says:

> “Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ loved the Church” (Col. 3:19).

Likewise, the same author:

> “No one has ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it. Thus husbands ought also to love their wives as their own bodies” (Eph. 5:29).

Augustine likewise, in his book to Valerius against Pelagius [Note: [Col. 0177D] *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, chapter 9]:

> “There can be no doubt that, according to the natural order, men rule women rather than women men. In preserving this order, the Apostle says: ‘The head of the woman is the man’; and, ‘Wives, be subject to your husbands’ (Col. 3:18). The Apostle Peter likewise says: ‘Thus Sarah obeyed Abraham, calling him lord’ (1 Pet. 3:6).

> “Although this is so, in such a way that nature loves singularity among those who rule, we nevertheless more readily see plurality among those who are subject. Yet several women would never lawfully be joined to one man unless several children were born from this arrangement. Therefore, if one woman has intercourse with several men, since this produces no multiplication of offspring for her but only a repetition of lust, she cannot be a wife but is a prostitute” (chapter 10).

> “For among faithful married persons, not only fertility, whose fruit is offspring, and not only chastity, whose bond is fidelity, but also a certain sacrament of marriage is commended. Hence the Apostle says: ‘Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ loved the Church’ (Col. 3:19). The reality of this sacrament is undoubtedly that a male and female joined in marriage remain inseparably together as long as they live, and that it is not permissible, except on account of fornication, for one spouse to be separated from the other.”

Jerome, in the *Book Against Jovinianus* (Book I):

> “If Christ loves the Church holily, chastely, and without any stain, husbands too should love their wives in chastity, and each should know how to possess his own vessel in sanctification and honor” (1 Thess. 4:4).

Ambrose, in the first book entitled *On Abraham*, where he describes the hospitality Abraham showed to the angels (Gen. 18:6), says the following (Book I, chapter 5):

> “And he said to Sarah: ‘Hurry, knead three measures of fine flour and make cakes baked under the ashes.’ A good husband does not allow his wife to be excluded from a religious service, nor does he greedily claim the whole service for himself. Thus it is rightly preserved for the sake both of devotion and of modesty. What belongs to devotion he wishes to be shared; what belongs to modesty remains intact for Sarah. Outside the tent, the husband investigates the arrival of the guests; inside the tent, Sarah guards the woman’s modesty and performs the work proper to a woman with complete modesty. Outside, the husband invites; inside, Sarah prepares the meal. Abraham himself does not merely hurry, but also tells his wife to hurry, showing her to be a partner in devotion and not unequal in faith.”

Those, therefore, who love in their wives the beauty of the body and the desire for pleasure more than the beauty of the mind should hear what the aforementioned Ambrose says in the same first book (Book I, chapter 2):

> “Everyone is taught not to seek above all the beauty of a spouse, which is often accustomed to bring death to the husband. For it is not so much a woman’s beauty as her virtue and dignity that delights a husband. Whoever seeks the sweetness of marriage should not pursue a woman of higher rank than the marital necessities can sustain—not one adorned with necklaces, but one adorned with character.”

Augustine, in his *Book on the Sermon on the Mount* (chapter 15):

> “A good Christian is found to love in one woman the creature of God, which he desires to be renewed and reformed, but to hate the corruptible and mortal union and intercourse—that is, to love in her what she is as a human being and to hate what she is as a wife.”

And shortly afterward:

> “A Christian can therefore live harmoniously with his wife, whether by supplying with her the indulgence of the flesh—which the Apostle says is granted as a concession, not as a command—or by the propagation of children, which can already be praiseworthy to some degree—or by fraternal fellowship without any mingling of bodies, having a wife as though he did not have one, which is the most excellent and sublime condition among Christian marriages. Yet he must hate in her the name of temporal necessity and love eternal blessedness.”

The same author also writes to Count Valerius [Note: [Col. 0179D] *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, chapter 18]:

> “Far be it, therefore, that a faithful man, when he hears the Apostle say, ‘Love your wives’ (Col. 3:19), should love the lust of the flesh in his wife—a lust he ought not to love even in himself—when he hears another Apostle say: ‘Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world’ (1 John 2:15).”

Let married persons therefore consider that, as the documents cited above make clear, outward beauty and carnal pleasure in wives must in no way be preferred to their inward chaste love. What must be sought in wives, therefore, is not merely wealth and beauty, but rather chastity and moral integrity.

## CHAPTER VI. That intercourse with wives ought to take place for the sake of offspring, not pleasure

[Col. 0179C]

Let faithful married persons hear this—those among whom almost anything they desire is considered permissible in satisfying carnal pleasure with their wives: they must not, following the custom of the nations that do not know God, possess their vessels, that is, their wives, in the sickness of desire, but in sanctification and honor, as the teachings of the holy Fathers appended below make entirely clear.

Jerome, in his commentary on Ecclesiastes (chapter 3:5):

> “‘Do not defraud one another, unless perhaps by mutual agreement for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer’ (1 Cor. 7:5)—that is, devote yourselves to children, and then again to continence.”

Likewise, the same author, treating impurity and luxury in his commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians, says:

> “Luxury follows impurity as its companion. For just as, in the old law, Scripture embraced in a general statement the unspeakable crimes committed in secret, whose very naming is most shameful lest both the mouth of the speaker and the ears of the hearers be polluted, saying, ‘Make the children of Israel modest or reverent toward every impurity,’ so here it has called the other extraordinary pleasures—and even the acts of marriage themselves, if they are not performed modestly and honorably, as though under the eyes of God, so that attention is given only to children—impurity and luxury.”

It should be noted that the Apostle calls intercourse with one’s wife impurity and luxury unless it takes place for the sake of offspring.

Blessed Augustine also, in the book [Note: [Col. 0179D] *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, chapter 8] that he wrote to Count Valerius, explaining Paul’s statement, “For this is the will of God, your sanctification: that you abstain from fornication; that each of you should know how to possess his own vessel in sanctification and honor, not in the sickness of desire, like the nations that do not know God” (1 Thess. 4:3–5), says:

> “A faithful married person therefore not only does not use another’s vessel, as those do who desire other men’s wives; he must also know that he ought not to possess his own vessel in the sickness of carnal desire. This must not be understood as though the Apostle had forbidden marital intercourse—that is, lawful and honorable intercourse—but rather that this intercourse—which would have had no diseased lust attached to it if freedom of choice had not perished in it through preceding sin—now has that lust attached to it so that it may be a matter not of pleasure but of necessity; yet without it the will itself cannot attain its fruit in begetting children. This pleasure [Note: [Col. 0180D] “This pleasure.” Read, as Acherius had advised should be read in the margin of the earlier edition, “this will”] in the marriages of the faithful is not directed toward the end that children who will pass away may be born in this world, but that those who will remain may be reborn in Christ.

> “If this result follows, there will be a full reward for marriage faithfully lived; if it does not follow, there will still be peace for spouses of good will. With this intention of heart, one who possesses his own vessel—that is, his wife—undoubtedly does not possess it in the sickness of desire like the nations that do not know God, but in sanctification and honor like the faithful who hope in God.

> “A person uses that evil of desire rather than being overcome by it when he restrains and checks it as it seethes with disordered and shameful movements, and releases and employs it only while caring for the propagation of offspring: so that he may beget children carnally in order to bring forth spiritual children, not so that he may subject the spirit to the flesh in sordid servitude.”

Likewise, the same author in the *Book on the Good of Marriage* (chapter 10):

> “Intercourse necessary for begetting, blameless and alone, is marital intercourse. But intercourse that goes beyond this necessity already serves not reason but lust.”

Likewise, the same author in the same work:

> “The use of marriage is such that if anything occurs in it through the mingling of bodies that exceeds the necessity of begetting, even if it has been done venially, it is contamination.”

And shortly afterward (chapter 6):

> “Marital intercourse for the sake of begetting has no guilt; intercourse for the satisfaction of desire, though with one’s spouse and on account of fidelity to the marriage bed, has venial guilt. Adultery, however, or fornication, has deadly guilt. Accordingly, continence from all intercourse is better even than marital intercourse undertaken for the sake of begetting” (chapter 7).
