> “But because that continence has greater merit, while rendering the marital debt is no crime, demanding it beyond the necessity of begetting is venial guilt, and committing fornication or adultery is a punishable crime, beloved chastity must take care lest, while seeking a means by which it may be honored more greatly, it give a spouse a means by which he or she may be condemned.”

Likewise, the same author in the same work (chapter 16):

> “What food is for the preservation of human beings, intercourse is for the preservation of the human race; and neither is without carnal pleasure. Yet when this pleasure is moderated and, under the restraint of temperance, reduced to natural use, it cannot be lust.

> “What illicit food is in the maintenance of bodily nourishment, fornication or adulterous intercourse is in the seeking of offspring. What illicit food is in the luxury of the belly and throat, illicit intercourse is in desire that seeks no offspring. What excessive appetite is in lawful food, that is the venial intercourse found among married persons.

> “Therefore, just as it is better to die of hunger than to eat food sacrificed to idols, so it is better to die without children than to seek offspring through illicit intercourse. Wherever human beings are born, if they do not follow the vices of their parents and worship God rightly, they will be honorable and saved. The seed of a human being, from whatever human being, is a creature of God; for those who use it badly, it will be bad, but it will never itself become evil.

> “Just as the goodness of children born to adulterers is no defense of adulteries, so the wickedness of children born to married persons is no crime of marriage.”

Likewise, the same author in the *Book on Christian Doctrine* (Book III, chapter 18):

> “For if someone could for a time use many wives chastely, another person can use one lustfully. I approve more of the man who uses the fruitfulness of many for some other purpose than of the man who enjoys the flesh of one for its own sake. In the former case, a usefulness appropriate to the opportunities of the times is sought; in the latter, desire entangled in temporal pleasures is satisfied.

> “Those who, in accordance with the Apostle’s concession, engage in carnal relations with individual spouses on account of their lack of self-control are at a lower level before God than those who, while each having several wives—as the wise person looks to nothing but bodily health in food and drink—look to nothing but the begetting of children in intercourse.”

Gregory, in the *Pastoral Rule* (Part III, chapter 28):

“Married couples must be admonished to remember that they were joined for the purpose of receiving offspring. When, by indulging in immoderate intercourse, they turn the occasion of procreation into an occasion of pleasure, they should consider that, although by this they do not go beyond what is permitted outwardly, nevertheless within marriage itself they transgress both marriage and its rights. Therefore they must lament with frequent prayers that they stain the beautiful appearance of intercourse with mingled pleasures. For this reason the Apostle, skilled in heavenly medicine, did not so much instruct the healthy as show remedies to the sick, saying: ‘Concerning the matters about which you wrote to me, it is good for a man not to touch a woman. But because of fornication, let each man have his own wife, and let each woman have her own husband’ (1 Cor. 7:1).

[Note: “Permitted the fear.” Acherius notes in the margin that elsewhere *praemisit* (“sent before”) is read—a reading as good as this one is bad.]

“He who permitted this because of the fear of fornication certainly did not give a command to those who were standing firm; rather, lest they should perhaps fall to the ground, he showed a bed to those who were falling. Therefore, still addressing the weak, he adds: ‘Let the husband render the debt to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband’ (ibid., 3). While granting them something of pleasure within the great dignity of marriage, shortly afterward he adds: ‘But I say this by way of indulgence, not by way of command’ (ibid., 6). For he indicates that what is granted by indulgence is a fault. Yet the fault is forgiven all the more readily because through it nothing illicit is done; rather, what is permitted is not held within moderation.”

The example of Lot is also relevant: so that he would not perish with the Sodomites as though in a fire of lust, he did not climb the mountain of chastity but remained in Segor, that is, in marriage (Gen. 19).

It is also read in the *History of the English* [Note: Bede, *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*, Book I, chapter 27, and Gregory, Letter 31, Book XII] that the blessed Gregory wrote the following in reply to Augustine’s questions:

“Therefore legitimate intercourse of the flesh ought to be for the sake of offspring, not pleasure; and the mingling of the flesh ought to be for the purpose of begetting children, not the satisfaction of vices. But when it is not love of begetting offspring, but pleasure, that dominates in the act of intercourse, married couples have something to lament even in their intercourse.”

Since so many and such great testimonies declare that this must be lamented, it must unquestionably be avoided. Therefore married people should take heed that intercourse with one’s wife, when it occurs not from love of receiving offspring but for the sake of lust, requires tears.

## CHAPTER VII. Against those who maintain that they ought not at all to abstain from intercourse with pregnant wives

If a wife is taken for the sake of offspring, and the intercourse of male and female is to be practiced out of love for children, not from the heat of lust, then, once the swollen belly of the wife has shown the fruit of the offspring conceived, what does intercourse with one’s wife signify except an indication of lust? Does the Lord not, in a certain sense, say to the man unwilling to abstain from such intercourse:

“If you took a wife for the sake of children, now, through my work, you have obtained what you wanted. Why have you presumed to add anything of diseased lust to my work?”

Those who maintain that they may freely have intercourse with pregnant wives should read what the blessed Ambrose wrote in his *Exposition of the Gospel according to Luke*:

“What wonder is there concerning human beings, if even animals, by a certain mute action, declare that their concern is to beget, not a desire to have intercourse?” For once they have felt their womb become heavy and have received the seed in their generative womb, they no longer indulge in intercourse or love wantonness, but undertake the care of parenthood. Human beings, however, spare neither what has been conceived nor the Lord: they pollute the former and provoke the latter.

“‘Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you, and in the womb I sanctified you’ (Jer. 15). Do you observe the hands of your Creator, once forming a human being in the womb, as a restraint upon your wantonness?” He is at work, while you defile the secrecy of the womb with lust. Either imitate the animals or reverence the Lord.

“What shall I say about animals? The earth itself often rests from the work of generation; and if, through the impatient desire of human beings, it is repeatedly occupied by scattered seeds, it punishes the farmer’s lack of judgment and changes fertility into sterility. Thus, in the very elements and in animals, it is a shame for nature not to cease from the practice of generation.”

Let them also read what the blessed Augustine wrote in his book *On the Good of Marriage* [Note: In the commentary on Ezekiel, chapter 18, verse 6]:

“There are likewise men so incontinent that they do not spare even pregnant wives. Whatever married people do among themselves that is immoderate, shameless, or filthy is a vice of the people, not a fault of marriage.

“There is also a saying of a certain wise man, approved by the blessed Jerome [Note: From the sayings of Xystus the Pythagorean, in *Bibliotheca Patrum*, p. 222.], which runs as follows: ‘He is an adulterer,’ he says, ‘who is an excessively ardent lover of his own wife.’ With another man’s wife every love is disgraceful; with one’s own, excessive love is so. A wise man ought to love his wife by judgment, not by passion. He controls the impulses of pleasure and is not carried headlong into intercourse. Nothing is uglier than to love one’s wife as though she were an adulteress.

“Certainly, those who say that they join themselves to wives and raise children for the sake of the commonwealth and the human race should at least imitate the animals. After the bellies of their wives have grown large, let them not destroy their children, nor present themselves to their wives as lovers, but as husbands.”

[Note: “It is therefore plainly evident.” In the Claromontanus manuscript the following, which is preferable, is read in place of these words: “Married people should therefore consider that, in accordance with the dignity of human nature and the most salutary instruction of so many most illustrious Fathers, they ought in every respect to abstain from intercourse with pregnant wives. And when they are admonished concerning such intercourse, they ought not to open their mouths in laughter, but should instead turn themselves toward correction, and toward contrition and repentance of heart.”]

It is therefore plainly evident that, as the statements of the most illustrious teachers establish and the ancient married Fathers provide an example, intercourse with pregnant wives must altogether be avoided. But if anyone wishes to maintain that he either does not want, or is unable, or certainly ought not, to abstain from such intercourse, let him know that intercourse with a wife is not free from fault when it is practiced not for the sake of offspring but for the sake of lust.

## CHAPTER VIII. On incest

Since every illicit intercourse is incestuous, intercourse with relatives and with women consecrated to God is much more properly considered incestuous. Those who have intercourse either with virgins consecrated to God or with blood-relatives are judged incestuous—that is, unchaste.

As the Christian religion and the authority of the holy Church have established, marriages between relatives are to be avoided for as long as the names of the relationships remain. For it is never fitting among Christians that two or three relationships, as the blessed Augustine says [Note: *City of God*, Book XV, chapter 16], should exist in one person.

By the authority of the holy Church of God, which is believed to observe what was handed down to it by the apostles and to which it is not lawful to oppose oneself; and also by the judgment of secular law, as well as by the most honorable order of nature itself, it is clearly taught that marriages between relatives are to be deferred until the seventh degree [Col. 0183D]. Then, as the same blessed Augustine says in his book *On the City of God*, lest the relationship itself should extend farther and cease to be relationship, it is to be bound again by the bond of marriage and, so to speak, the fugitive is to be recalled.

Isidore speaks as follows about consanguinity [Col. 0184A]:

“Its succession is divided by seven degrees in the following manner: son and daughter; grandson and granddaughter; great-grandson and great-granddaughter; great-great-grandson and great-great-granddaughter; great-great-great-grandson and great-great-great-granddaughter; triple-great-grandson and triple-great-granddaughter; and the son of the triple-great-grandson and the daughter of the triple-great-granddaughter.

“When this consanguinity, gradually separating itself through the ordered lines of descent, has withdrawn as far as the final degree and has ceased to be kinship, the law of marriage takes it up again and, so to speak, recalls the fugitive. Consanguinity of lineage was therefore established up to the sixth degree, so that the kinship of lineage might be terminated by so many degrees.”

Pope Gregory the Younger likewise [Note: Thus the Claromontanus manuscript. The earlier edition read, “The blessed Pope Gregory also,” as though these were words of Gregory the Great.], in his decretals, strikes with apostolic anathema, among others, those who take wives from their own kindred, saying [Note: Gregory II, Roman Council I, chapter 1 and following]:

“If anyone takes his brother’s wife in marriage, let him be anathema.” And all answered three times, “Let him be anathema.”

“If anyone takes a married woman in marriage, let him be anathema.” And all answered, “Let him be anathema.”

“If anyone takes his stepmother or his daughter-in-law in marriage, let him be anathema.” And all answered three times, “Let him be anathema.”

“If anyone takes his cousin in marriage, let him be anathema.” And all answered three times, “Let him be anathema.”

“If anyone takes a wife from his own kindred, or one whom a relative has had, let him be anathema.” And all answered three times, “Let him be anathema.”

But if anyone should object that the blessed Pope Gregory wrote differently to Augustine, bishop of the English, concerning the degrees of kinship [Note: Book XII, Letter 31, response 7], let him know that he did this not in order to oppose the authority of the Church, but rather to provide for that untrained people.

Since, therefore, it is clearly demonstrated that incestuous marriages must altogether be avoided by Christians, why is such a marriage desired, in which both guilt is implied and the nobility of worldly rank is marked with disgrace? I say that it is marked with disgrace because whoever is entangled in such a marriage is stripped of noble status, and the children born from such a marriage are not admitted to inheritance according to the judgment of human law.

It is therefore necessary that every believer beware of such incestuous marriages, lest, by doing illicitly and culpably with relatives what he could do lawfully and without blame with others, he both incur the fall of sin and be struck with apostolic anathema.

## CHAPTER IX. Against the shameless, who say that, since the sexual organs were created by the all-wise Creator, mutual ardor must be endured, rather than lust exercised according to each person’s will

There are people who wish to devote themselves to their lust and who say: “The sexual organs were created by God, the supreme Maker, in both sexes for the purpose of mutual union. What offense do we therefore commit if we practice intercourse according to our desire?”

Those who say this must carefully consider that God created not only the sexual organs but also the other members of the body for the purpose of doing lawful things with them, not unlawful things. [With his members, therefore, as long as a person uses them in an orderly manner and according to their proper law, he undoubtedly uses good things well; but if he turns them to illicit and extraordinary uses, he turns the good things that he ought to have used well toward his own destruction.]

The blessed Jerome therefore writes against the objections of Jovinian (Book I), who says:

“Why,” he says, “were the sexual organs created, and why were we created by so wise a Creator in such a way that we suffer mutual heat and burn with desire for natural intercourse? Thus we are endangered by the shamefulness of the answer, and, as though between two cliffs and certain necessities—the *Symplegades* (Greek: συμπληγάδες, “Clashing Rocks”) of chastity—we suffer shipwreck either of shame or of the argument.

“I could indeed say how the posterior part of the body, and the passage through which the excrement of the bowels is discharged, has been banished from the eyes and placed, so to speak, behind the back; [so too this part, which is beneath the belly and was placed there to digest the humors] by which the veins of the body are irrigated, was created by God. I am compelled to say something and to become foolish, but you have forced me to dare to speak.

“Our Lord and Savior, although he was in the form of God, deigned to take the form of a servant, becoming obedient unto death, even the death of the cross (Phil. 2). Why was it necessary that he be born with those members which he was not going to use? Certainly, in order to display his sex, he was also circumcised. Why did his love castrate John the Apostle and John the Baptist, whom he had caused to be born men? We who believe in Christ should follow Christ’s examples. And although we once knew him according to the flesh, now we know him no longer in that way.”

The same writer says in his exposition of the book of Ecclesiastes (chapter 3, verse 11):

“For the Lord made all things good in their time. It is good to keep watch and to sleep; yet it is not always good either to keep watch or to sleep, because in turn, according to God’s arrangement, each thing is good when it is needed.”

From these things we are not, as some suppose, urged toward luxury and delicacies in the manner of animals. The Psalmist says:

“Do not become like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding.”

And again:

“Man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared with foolish beasts and became like them” (Ps. 31:11 and 48:13).

Likewise, in the book of Tobit:

“For those who receive marriage in such a way that they exclude God from their mind and devote themselves to their lust like the horse and the mule, the demon has power over them” (Tob. 6:16).

Convicted by these testimonies, the defenders of such great shamelessness should understand that, although the sexual organs were created by the good God, it is not permitted to use them according to each person’s desire, but according to the purposes for which they were orderly established by God, in accordance with his will, at their proper time and in their proper order.

## CHAPTER X. That one must altogether abstain from wives during menstruation

[Since the dignity of the human condition, after the fall of the first parent, has through the grace of Christ obtained the ability to reach the fellowship of the citizens above by the purity of good works, married people must take the greatest care not to make themselves in some way unworthy of their fellowship by enslaving themselves to any impurities. For just as one reaches that fellowship through purity, so one withdraws from it through impurity.

“There are many,” says the blessed Jerome, “who think that the pleasure of marriage ought to be subject to them at all times, and they do not distinguish the proper times for intercourse—when intercourse should take place and when they should abstain from their wives. Therefore, just as they do not spare pregnant women, so they also do not abstain at all from women who are menstruating. Some do this unknowingly, and some knowingly. How greatly this must be avoided, as something subject to danger by the Lord’s command, is shown below by the divine oracles collected here.”]

When the prophet Ezekiel was enumerating the justified deeds of a good man, he included this in sixth place:

“He has not approached a menstruating woman” (Ezek. 18:6).

The blessed Jerome explains this passage as follows [Note: In the commentary on Ezekiel, on the same verse]:

“Every month, women’s heavy and sluggish bodies are relieved by the discharge of unclean blood. If a man has intercourse with a woman at that time, the fetuses conceived are said to draw a defect from the seed, so that lepers and elephantiasis sufferers are born from such conception, and corrupted bodily fluid degenerates into deformed bodies of either sex, with members either too small or excessively large.

“Men are therefore commanded to know definite times for intercourse, not only with other men’s wives but also with their own, to whom they appear to be joined by law, since Scripture says: ‘Increase and multiply, and fill the earth’ (Gen. 1:18)—times when intercourse should take place and times when they should abstain from their wives.

“This is also expressed by the Apostle and Ecclesiastes: ‘A time to embrace,’ he says, ‘and a time to refrain from embracing’ (1 Cor. 7; Eccles. 3:5).

“Let the wife also beware lest, overcome by the desire for intercourse, she conceal it from her husband [Note: ‘Conceal it from her husband.’ We noted above that one should read *compel* or *entice*]; and let the husband not use force against his wife, thinking that the pleasure of marriage ought to be subject to him at all times.”

Hence Paul also says:

“Let each one know how to possess his own vessel in sanctification and righteousness” (1 Thess. 4:4).

Augustine, in his book of sermons [Note: *On Time*, Sermon 3, toward the middle], says to the people:

“Whenever the Lord’s Day or a feast day arrives, let no one know his wife. Whenever women suffer the flow of blood, the same observance must be maintained, because those conceived at that time will be either possessed by demons, or hunchbacked, or epileptic. And if animals without understanding do not join themselves except at a definite and proper time, how much more ought human beings, who were created in the image and likeness of God, to exercise restraint?”

It is also written in Leviticus:

“A woman who suffers a discharge of blood at the return of her month shall be separated for seven days. Everyone who touches her shall be unclean until evening. Anything on which she has slept or sat during the days of her separation shall be polluted. Whoever touches her bed shall wash his clothes; and after washing himself with water, he shall be unclean until evening. Whoever touches any vessel on which she has sat shall wash his clothes; and after washing himself with water, he shall be unclean until evening.

“If a man has intercourse with her during her menstrual period, he shall be unclean for seven days, and every bed on which he sleeps shall be polluted.

“A woman who suffers a discharge of blood for many days outside the time of her menstruation, or whose discharge continues beyond her menstrual period, shall be unclean for as long as she is subject to this condition, as during her menstrual period. Every bed on which she sleeps and every vessel on which she sits shall be polluted. Whoever touches her shall wash his clothes; and after washing himself with water, he shall be unclean until evening.

“You shall therefore teach the children of Israel to beware of their uncleannesses, lest they die in their filth when they have polluted my tabernacle, which is among them.

“Again, it is written there: ‘You shall not approach a woman who is menstruating, nor uncover her nakedness.’

“And again: ‘If a man has intercourse with a woman during her menstrual discharge and uncovers her nakedness, she who has opened the source of her blood shall perish; both shall be cut off from the midst of their people’” (Lev. 15:19–24; 18:19; 20:18).

Since the Apostle says, “Whatever was written was written for our instruction” (Rom. 15:4), and since the law is spiritual and ought to be understood spiritually, in this passage—as the testimonies of the holy Fathers cited above make clear and the surface of the text itself demonstrates—without prejudice to the spiritual meaning, men must altogether abstain from wives who are suffering menstruation.

## CHAPTER XI. After how many days a woman who has given birth may enter the church, and after how much time she may unite with her husband in intercourse; and that a husband who has had intercourse with his wife ought to enter the church only after first washing with water

[Note: This heading has been restored from the Claromontanus manuscript in place of the heading printed by Acherius, as noted above in the table of chapters.]

Although the faithful people are free through the grace of Christ from the burdens of the law under which the Jewish people are still weighed down because of their unbelief, since the Christian people are spiritual and understand and judge the law spiritually, there are nevertheless certain practices that Christian custom still observes, without prejudice to their mystical meaning, for the sake of bodily propriety and purity.

This is the case with women who have given birth, who refrain from entering the church; and likewise with those who suffer menstrual bleeding, who in many provinces, on account of bodily impurity, are similarly kept away from the buildings of the basilica.

And although, as the blessed Pope Gregory teaches, these matters are to be understood spiritually, it is nevertheless neither improper nor dishonorable nor contrary to spiritual understanding if they are observed literally, according to the practice of the early Christians, because of what was stated above [Note: “Because of what was stated above.” I printed this reading, whereas the earlier edition had “because of what was permitted.”]

The same Pope Gregory therefore writes to Augustine, bishop of the English, who had consulted him [Note: Book XII, Letter 12; and Bede, *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*, Book I, chapter 27]:

“When a woman has given birth, after how many days ought she to enter the church? You have learned from the precept of the Old Testament that she ought to abstain for thirty-three days in the case of a male child and sixty-six days in the case of a female child [Note: “She ought to abstain.” In the Claromontanus manuscript, what follows in Gregory’s letter is written continuously here, beginning with the words “But a wicked…”].”

And shortly afterward:

“But,” he says, “a wicked custom has crept into the conduct of married people: they disdain to nurse the children they have begotten and hand them over to other women to be raised. This seems to have been invented solely because of incontinence, since, because they do not wish to practice continence, they disdain to nurse the children they have begotten” (ibid., shortly afterward).

“A man who sleeps with his own wife ought not to enter the church unless he has washed with water; but even after washing he ought not to enter immediately. The law commanded the ancient people that a man who had intercourse with a woman should wash with water and should not enter the church before sunset.

“This can nevertheless be understood spiritually, because a man is joined to a woman when the mind, through pleasure, is joined in thought to an illicit desire. Unless the fire of desire has first cooled in his mind, he ought not to consider himself worthy of the assembly of the brethren, since he sees himself weighed down by the wickedness of depraved pleasure.

“Although different nations have different opinions about this matter and appear to observe different practices, it has nevertheless always been the custom of the Romans, from ancient times, after intercourse with one’s own wife, to seek purification through washing and to refrain for a short time, reverently, from entering the church.”

Here the discussion concerns those [Note: “Here, against those.” This passage is set out at greater length and more clearly in the Claromontanus manuscript]:

“If there should perhaps be incontinent persons who maintain that, before the child born has been weaned, they may and ought to approach their wives for intercourse, and that after intercourse with their own wives they may irreverently enter the church before purification by washing, let them carefully consider how strongly the divine oracles and the teaching of so eminent a doctor forbid such incontinence.

“There are therefore some—something deserving correction—who, rising from intercourse with their wives, enter the church irreverently without waiting for purification by washing. They not only approach the most holy altar indiscriminately but also receive the body and blood of the Lord without distinction. Therefore they must understand that one ought to enter the church of Christ reverently, and that his body and blood ought to be received salutarily only with a clean body and a pure heart.”

Those who, rising from intercourse with their wives, enter the church irreverently are therefore addressed here: they not only approach the most holy altar indiscriminately but also receive the body and blood of the Lord without distinction. Let them understand, then, that once they have entered the church of Christ, they ought to receive his body and blood only with a clean body and a pure heart.

## CHAPTER XII. That, unless for the cause of fornication, a wife ought not to be dismissed, as the Lord says, but rather endured

Some people habitually dismiss their wives for various reasons. There are four qualities by which women become desirable to men: lineage, intelligence, wealth, and beauty.

Some men, thinking that they have married wives of free status, immediately separate them from the right of marriage if, after some circumstance, those women have been reduced to slavery. They do this according to the law of the world, not according to the law of Christ.

Others, when they have married intelligent, beautiful, and wealthy women, shamelessly dismiss them if the women later become mentally incapacitated, are afflicted by some other bodily disability, or are reduced to poverty after their inheritance has been squandered through reckless spending. These men take pleasure in women who are more intelligent, more beautiful, and richer.

The Lord’s judgment forbids this, saying in the Gospel that whoever dismisses his wife, except for the cause of fornication, commits adultery, and whoever marries a dismissed woman commits adultery in the same way (Matt. 19).

There are many laymen who resist this judgment, indeed the law of Christ, and are not ashamed to make their own desire a law for their flesh. How great a crime this is and how far removed from the Christian religion is shown by what follows.

For it is written in Genesis:

“Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and shall cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh” (Gen. 2:24).

And in the Gospel:

“What God has joined, let no man separate” (Matt. 19:6).

And the Apostle says:

“To those who are joined in marriage I give this command—not I, but the Lord—that a wife should not depart from her husband; but if she has departed, she should remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband; and a husband should not dismiss his wife” (1 Cor. 7:10).

And shortly afterward:

“Let each one walk as God has called him, as I teach in all the churches. Was anyone called while circumcised? Let him not draw over the foreskin. Was anyone called while uncircumcised? Let him not be circumcised. Circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing, but keeping the commandments of God is what matters. Let each one remain in the calling in which he was called” (ibid., 17).

Augustine, in *The Sermon on the Mount* (Book III, chapter 14), says:

“It was also said: ‘Whoever dismisses his wife, let him give her a certificate of divorce’ (Matt. 5:31). This is the lesser righteousness of the Pharisees. It is not contrary to what the Lord says: ‘But I say to you, whoever dismisses his wife, except for the cause of fornication, commits adultery; and whoever marries a woman released from her husband commits adultery’ (ibid., 19:7).

“For he who commanded that a certificate of divorce be given did not command that the wife be dismissed. Rather, he says, ‘Whoever has dismissed her, let him give her a certificate of divorce,’ so that the consideration of the certificate might restrain the rash anger of the man casting out his wife.

“The one who sought delay in dismissing her signified, as far as he could to hard-hearted men, that he did not wish for separation. Therefore, when the Lord himself was asked about this on another occasion, he replied: ‘Moses did this because of the hardness of your hearts’ (ibid.).

“However hard-hearted the man who wanted to dismiss his wife might be, if he reflected that, once the certificate of divorce had been given, she could marry another without danger, he could easily be appeased. Therefore, to establish that a wife should not easily be dismissed, the Lord excepted only the cause of fornication. He commands that all other hardships, if any should arise, be endured bravely for the sake of marital fidelity and chastity. He also calls the man an adulterer who marries a woman who has been released from her husband.”

And shortly afterward (chapter 16):

“For nothing is more unjust than to dismiss a wife because of fornication if the husband himself is also convicted of fornication. The saying presents itself: ‘In whatever you judge another, you condemn yourself, for you do the same things when you judge’ (Rom. 2:1). Therefore whoever wishes to cast away his wife because of fornication must first be cleansed from fornication himself. I would say the same concerning a woman.”

Jerome, in his commentaries on the Gospel of Matthew (on chapter 19, verse 4), says:

“When the Lord was questioned, he said: ‘Have you not read that he who made them in the beginning made them male and female?’ This is written at the beginning of Genesis. By saying ‘male and female,’ he showed that second marriages are to be avoided. For he did not say, ‘He made males and females,’ which would have been sought from the dismissal of the former wives, but ‘male and female,’ so that they might be bound together in the companionship of one spouse.

“For this reason ‘a man shall leave his father and mother and cling to his wife’ (Matt. 19:5). Likewise he says, ‘and he shall cling to his wife,’ not ‘to his wives.’ ‘And the two shall be one flesh.’ The reward of marriage is for two to become one flesh. Joined to the spirit through chastity, one spirit is produced.

“Therefore, what God has joined, let no man separate. God joined them by making one flesh of man and woman; a man cannot separate this, unless perhaps God alone does so. A man separates them when, because of his desire for a second wife, he dismisses the first. God separates them—he who had joined them—when, by mutual consent, for the sake of serving God, because the time is short, we have wives as though we had none.

“They say to him: ‘What then did Moses command—to give a certificate of divorce and to dismiss her?’ (ibid., 7). They disclose the accusation they had prepared. Certainly, the Lord had not offered his own judgment, but had recalled the ancient history and the commandments of God. He says to them: ‘Moses permitted you to dismiss your wives because of the hardness of your hearts; but from the beginning it was not so’ (ibid., 8).

“What he says means this: Can the Lord be inconsistent with himself, so that he earlier commanded one thing and then overturns his judgment by a new command? This must not be thought. Rather, when Moses saw that, because of desire for second wives—who might be richer, younger, or more beautiful—men were inclined either to dismiss their first wives, to kill them, or to lead a miserable life with them, he preferred to intervene in the quarrel rather than allow hatred and murder to continue.”

And shortly afterward:

“The disciples say to him: ‘If such is the situation of a man with his wife, it is not advantageous to marry.’ Wives are a heavy burden if it is not permitted to dismiss them except for the cause of fornication. What if she is drunk, irritable, of bad character, extravagant, gluttonous, wandering, quarrelsome, and abusive? Must such a woman be kept? Whether we wish it or not, she must be endured.”

It has been established by the clearest evidence that wives can neither be wholly dismissed nor ought to be dismissed, unless the cause of fornication intervenes.

Just as husbands, broken by no adversity and impaired by no bodily affliction, do not allow themselves to be dismissed or neglected by their wives, so likewise husbands cannot, without danger to their souls, dismiss or neglect their wives because of certain adversities and misfortunes, unless, as stated above, the cause of fornication intervenes.

And just as it is customary for chaste and honorable women to sit constantly at the bedsides of their sick husbands, wasting away under prolonged illness, to serve them, assist them according to their strength, and fail in nothing regarding the fidelity of the marriage bed, so it is entirely fitting and consistent with the Christian profession that husbands should repay the same service to their wives.

## CHAPTER XIII. That those who, after dismissing their wives because of fornication, marry others are declared adulterers by the Lord’s judgment

It has already been declared above from the Lord’s judgment that whoever dismisses his wife, except for the cause of fornication, and marries another is an adulterer; and that whoever marries a dismissed woman is likewise an adulterer. It is not superfluous to repeat this in the present chapter.

The Apostle also says:

“If she has departed, let her remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband” (1 Cor. 7).

Jerome likewise, in his commentaries on the Gospel of Matthew (chapter 19), says:

“Because it could happen that someone might falsely accuse an innocent woman and, because of a second marriage, bring a charge against the first, he is commanded to dismiss his former wife in such a way that he may not have a second wife while the first is alive.

“For what he says means this: If you dismiss your wife not because of lust but because of an injury, why, after experiencing the unhappiness of a first marriage, do you expose yourself to the danger of a new one?

“And because it could also happen that, under the same law, a wife might give her husband a certificate of divorce, the same precaution is prescribed, so that she should not take a second husband.

“And because a prostitute and a woman who had once committed adultery did not fear disgrace, the second husband is warned that, if he marries such a woman, he is liable to the charge of adultery.”

Augustine, in his book to Valerius against Pelagius [Note: *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, chapter 10], says:

“For this is preserved in Christ and in the Church: that the living, united with the living, should not be separated forever by any divorce. Such observance of this sacrament exists in the city of our God, on his holy mountain—that is, in the Church of Christ—among all the faithful who are married and who are undoubtedly members of Christ.

“Thus, although women marry or are taken as wives for the purpose of begetting children, it is not lawful to leave a barren wife in order to take a fertile one.

“If anyone does this, he is not guilty according to the law of this world, where, when a divorce intervenes, it is permitted without crime for one person to contract another marriage with another person. The Lord testifies that, according to Moses, this was permitted to the Israelites because of the hardness of their hearts. But according to the law of the Gospel, he is guilty of adultery, just as the woman herself is if she marries another.

“So firmly do the rights of a marriage once entered into remain between the living that those who have been separated from one another are rather still spouses of each other than spouses of those to whom they have attached themselves afterward. For they would not be adulterers with others unless they remained spouses of one another.

“Finally, when the husband with whom there had been a true marriage has died, a true marriage can be formed with the man with whom there had previously been adultery. Thus, while both are alive, a certain marital bond remains, which neither separation nor union with an adulterer can remove.”

The same writer, in *The Sermon on the Mount* (Book I, chapter 14), says:

“He calls the man an adulterer who marries the woman who has been released from her husband. The Apostle shows the limit of this matter, saying that it must be observed for as long as her husband lives; but when he has died, he grants permission to marry.”

There is no doubt that this great abomination against the commandment of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ concerning dismissing wives and taking others has become entrenched because the perpetrators of so grave a crime are not struck, as they ought to be, by the severest canonical censure. Concerning this matter Pope Innocent writes in his decretals [Note: [Col. 0192D] Innocent I, Letter 3, chapter 6]:

“Your Charity also inquired about those who, after a divorce had intervened, have joined themselves in marriage to others; it is clear that they are adulterers on both sides. Those, however, who, while their wife is still alive—even though the marriage may appear to have been dissolved—have hastened to unite themselves with another cannot fail to be regarded as adulterers, to such an extent that even the women joined to such men appear themselves to have committed adultery, according to what is read in the Gospel: ‘Whoever dismisses his wife and marries another commits adultery; likewise, whoever marries a dismissed woman commits adultery’ (Matt. V, 32). Therefore all such persons must be kept from communion with the faithful.”

## CHAPTER XIV

That parents should diligently educate their children in the fear of God, teaching them how they ought to live chastely, worship God, and show honor to their parents; and what danger threatens those who neglect to do so.

There are many who love their children more in spirit than in the flesh, and there are others who love them more in the flesh than in spirit. Likewise, some persuade them to learn the law of heaven more than that of the world, while others, conversely, persuade them to learn the laws of the world more than those of heaven. There are also those who teach them to strive after heavenly things more than earthly things, while others, conversely, teach them to desire earthly things more than heavenly ones.

Let those, therefore, who love their children carnally and strive to instruct them in the laws of the world rather than in those of heaven hear what the Lord says in Deuteronomy: “These words of mine, which I command you today, shall be in your heart; and you shall teach them to your children, and meditate upon them while sitting in your house” (Deut. VI, 6). Likewise, shortly afterward: “Place these words of mine in your hearts and in your souls, and fasten them as a sign upon your hands, and place them between your eyes. Teach your children to meditate upon them.”

Let them, therefore, imitate blessed Job, whose devotion to educating his children was such that he not only made them outwardly perfect in deed and word, but also cleansed their hearts by offering sacrifice. For blessed Gregory writes in the *Moralia* (Book I, chapter 4):

“When the days of the feast had gone round, Job would send for them and sanctify them, rising early and offering holocausts for each one. When it is said, ‘He would send for them and sanctify them,’ it is plainly shown what he carefully did for them when present, and how, though absent, he was not lacking to them in solicitude.”

The same author shortly afterward:

“But because the sons of blessed Job had been so firmly girded with the discipline of good instruction that they did not sin either by their conduct at the feasts or by their words, this is plainly shown when it is added: ‘Perhaps my sons have sinned and blessed God in their hearts’ (Job I, 5). He had taught them to be perfect in deed and in word; yet he feared for them solely on account of their thoughts.”

And shortly afterward (same work, chapter 5):

“But in this matter one must carefully consider with what severity a father could correct the conduct of his children and with what solicitude he strove to cleanse their hearts.”

[Col. 0193B] Let them also attend to David instructing his son Solomon. Of him it is read in the First Book of Kings: “I am entering the way of all the earth. Be strong and be a man, and observe the observances of the Lord your God, so that you may walk in his ways and keep his ceremonies, judgments, commandments, and testimonies” (III Kings II, 2), as it is written in the Law of Moses and in the Book of Chronicles:

“But you, Solomon my son, know the God of your father and serve him with a perfect heart and a willing mind. For he searches all hearts and understands every thought of the mind. If you seek him, you will find him; but if you abandon him, he will cast you away forever” (I Chronicles XXVIII, 9).

Let them also attend to Tobit. Of him it is read that, when he had become a man, he took Anna, a wife from his own tribe; [Col. 0193C] and he begot a son by her, giving him his own name. From his infancy he taught him to fear God and to abstain from every sin (Tobit I, 9).

Likewise, shortly afterward, addressing his son Tobias, he said:

“Listen, my son, to the words of my mouth, and establish them in your heart as a foundation. When God takes my soul, bury my body; and you shall honor your mother all the days of her life. For you must remember what dangers, and how many, she suffered for your sake in her womb. When she too has completed the time of her life, bury her beside me.

“Keep God in mind all the days of your life, and take care never to consent to sin or neglect the commandments of our God. From your possessions give alms, and do not turn your face away from any poor person. For then it will happen that the face of the Lord will not be turned away from you either. Be merciful as you are able: if you have much, give abundantly; if you have little, strive to distribute even a little willingly. For you are storing up a good reward for yourself on the day of necessity, because almsgiving delivers from every sin and from death, and does not allow the soul to go into darkness. Almsgiving will bring great confidence before the supreme God to all who practice it.

“Guard yourself, my son, against every form of fornication, and never permit yourself to know a crime apart from your wife. Never allow pride to dominate your thoughts or your speech, for in pride every ruin had its beginning. Whoever has worked for you, immediately give him his wage, and do not let a hired worker’s pay remain with you at all. [Col. 0194A] What you hate to have done to you by another, see that you never do to another. Eat your bread with the hungry and the needy, and clothe the naked with your garments. Set out your bread and your wine upon the tomb of the righteous, and do not eat or drink from it with sinners. Always seek counsel from the wise. Bless God at all times, and ask him to direct your ways, and let all your plans remain in him.”

Likewise, the same author says:

“Listen, therefore, my sons, to your father: serve the Lord in truth, and seek to do what is pleasing to him. Command your sons to practice justice and almsgiving, so that they may remember God and bless him at all times in truth and with all their strength” (same work XIV, 10).

It is also read in Proverbs:

“Discipline your son, and do not despair; but do not set your soul upon killing him” (Prov. XIX, 18).

“Do not withdraw discipline from a boy; for if you strike him with a rod, he will not die. You shall strike him with the rod, and you will deliver his soul from hell” (Prov. XXIII, 13–14).

“Discipline your son, and he will refresh you and give delight to your soul” (same work XXIX, 17).

“He who spares the rod hates his son, but he who loves him diligently disciplines him” (same work XIII, 24).

Jesus son of Sirach says:

“If you have sons, educate them and bend them from their childhood. If you have daughters, guard their bodies, and do not show them a cheerful face” (Sirach VII, 25–26).

The Apostle also says:

“Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord” (Eph. VI, 4).

Likewise, the same author:

“Fathers, do not provoke your children to indignation, so that they may not become dispirited” (Col. III, 21).

Jerome, to Laeta (Letter 7):

“If mature age and the exercise of one’s own will are attributed to parents, how much more are infancy and weakness—and she who, according to the Lord’s saying, does not know the right hand from the left (John VII), that is, does not know the difference between good and evil? If you carefully provide that your daughter not be struck by a viper, why do you not take the same care that she not be struck by the hammer of the whole earth; that she not drink from Babylon’s golden cup (Jer. L, 51); that she not go out with Dinah and wish to see the daughters of a foreign land (Gen. XXXIV); that she not play with her feet; that she not drag her tunics? Poisons are given only when coated with honey. Vices deceive only under the appearance and shadow of virtues.”

And below:

“But whoever is a child and thinks as a child, until he reaches the years of wisdom and Pythagoras’ letter brings him to the crossroads, both his good and his evil are attributed to his parents—unless perhaps you suppose that the children of Christians, if they do not receive baptism, are themselves alone guilty of sin, and that the crime is not also referred to those who were unwilling to give it to them, especially at a time when they could not resist what they were going to receive; just as, conversely, the salvation of infants is the gain of their elders.”

Ambrose, in his book *On Joseph* (chapter 2):

“We are therefore instructed what the affection of parents and the benefit of children ought to be; but often paternal love itself, unless it observes moderation, harms children—whether excessive indulgence dissolves wrongdoing, or preference for one turns the others away from brotherly affection. More is gained for a son when he gains the love of his brothers. This is the more splendid generosity of fathers; this is the richer inheritance of sons. Let equal affection join those whom equal nature has joined. Piety knows no monetary profit in that which entails a loss of piety. Why are you surprised that quarrels arise among brothers over a field or a house, when envy burned among the holy sons of Jacob over a tunic?

“What, then? Is Jacob to be reproved because he preferred one to the others? Yet neither can we take away parents’ freedom, preventing them from loving more those whom they believe deserve more, nor should we cut off from children their eagerness to please more. Indeed, Jacob loved that one more because he foresaw in him greater marks of virtue.”

[Col. 0195B] There are some who exhort their children only with gentle words and are not deterred by the example of Eli the priest, who restrained his sons with words alone and refused to strike them with the strictest severity (I Kings II). Moreover, there are many parents who, while their children are still in the slippery age of youth, neglect to correct them with blows so that they may act rightly. When such children reach the age of understanding and begin to devote themselves to evil deeds, they cannot easily be restrained from evil by parental chastisement. There is no doubt that their sins are imputed to the parents who were unwilling to chastise them in their tender years.

## CHAPTER XV

That children ought to render their parents the honor due to them.

[Col. 0195C] Just as there are those who render their parents honor worthily and reverently, so, conversely, there are those who neglect to do so. They fail to observe—or at least are unwilling to observe—that those who dishonor their parents commit an injury against God, who is the true Creator and Father of all, and that the Lord does not permit injuries against parents to remain unpunished unless worthy repentance follows. The testimonies briefly collected below demonstrate how great a condemnation it is, and how far removed from human dignity, not to recognize one’s parents reverently, and how great a reward belongs to those who obediently render them their due honor.

God says in the Law:

“Honor your father and your mother, so that you may live long upon the land which the Lord your God will give you” (Exod. XX, 12).

Likewise there:

“Whoever curses his father and mother shall be put to death” (same work XXI, 17).

Solomon says:

“The eye that mocks its father and despises the birth of its mother, let the ravens of the valleys pluck it out and the young of the eagle devour it” (Prov. XXX, 17).

Likewise:

“A fool mocks his father’s discipline, but whoever guards reproofs will become more prudent” (same work XV, 5).

Likewise:

“A wise son makes his father glad, and a foolish one despises his mother” (same work II, 20).

Likewise:

“Whoever afflicts his father and drives away his mother is dishonorable and unfortunate.”

Likewise:

“Whoever curses his father and mother—his lamp will be extinguished in the midst of darkness.”

And the Apostle:

“Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right: ‘Honor your father and your mother’ (which is the first commandment with a promise), ‘so that it may be well with you and you may live long upon the earth’” (Eph. VI, 1).

And Tobias, instructing his son, said:

“When God takes my soul, bury my body; and you shall honor your mother all the days of her life. For you must remember what dangers, and how many, she suffered for your sake in her womb. When she too has completed the time of her life, bury her beside me” (Tobit IV, 3).

Augustine writes as follows in his exposition of the Ten Commandments:

“The fourth commandment is: ‘Honor your father and your mother.’ The creature corresponding to this in the fifth plague of the Egyptians is the dog-fly. What is the dog-fly? It is a canine fly; the word is Greek. It is characteristic of a dog not to recognize its parents. Nothing is more doglike than for those who gave birth to someone not to be recognized. It is therefore fitting that puppies of dogs are born blind.”

Jerome [Note: [Col. 0195D] Jerome indeed wrote this at the cited place, but not in precisely these words.] in his Letter to Furia (Letter 10):

“It is indeed good for parents to be loved by their children after God; but if the necessity arises that the love of parents and children must be compared with the love of God, and both cannot be preserved, then hatred toward relatives is devotion toward God. ‘Honor your father’ (Exod. XX), but only if he does not separate you from the true Father. Know that the bond of blood lasts only so long as he acknowledges his Creator.”

Ambrose, in the book entitled *On Joseph* [Note: [Col. 0196D] *On the Blessing of the Patriarchs*, chapter 1.]:

“First of all, how great a reverence do we learn to show to parents when we read that the one blessed by his father was blessed, and the one cursed by him was cursed? For this reason God granted such power to parents, so that the devotion of children might be stirred up. The prerogative of parents is the discipline of children. Honor your father, therefore, so that he may bless you; let the devout honor his father out of gratitude, the ungrateful out of fear.

“Even if a father is poor and does not possess an abundance of wealth to leave to his children, he nevertheless possesses the inheritance of a final blessing, by which he may bestow upon his heirs the riches of sanctification. And rightly, it is better to become blessed than rich.”

There are, indeed, sons of perverse will who misunderstand the honor due to their parents and pretend that it consists solely in recognizing their parents and humbling themselves before them bodily but not in spirit; they also refuse to provide them with the things they need. Let them observe, therefore, that, as blessed Jerome says in Scripture [Note: [Col. 0196D] From the commentary on Matthew, chapter IV, verse 4.], honor is understood not so much in the duties of offering greetings as in almsgiving and the presentation of gifts.

And the same author shortly afterward:

“The Lord commanded, considering the weaknesses, ages, and poverty of parents, that children should honor them even by supplying what is necessary for life.”

Children therefore render their parents the honor due to them worthily when they humbly and reverently recognize them as their parents and provide them with what they need.

## CHAPTER XVI

That married people should know that they ought to exercise pastoral ministry in their households.

There are people of both sexes who seek among those subject to them the gain of souls rather than earthly advantage. Conversely, there are certain powerful men and some noble matrons who greedily demand from them only earthly profit, while either disregarding the salvation of their souls or utterly undervaluing it. They imagine that they will incur no danger through their falls and that they will have to render no account to God on their behalf. One must fear lest the prophetic saying be applied to them in any way:

“You ate the milk and clothed yourselves with the wool; you killed what was fat, but you did not feed my flock,”

and the rest that the prophetic discourse declares concerning shepherds (Ezek. XXXIV, 3).

If the head is sick, as blessed Gregory says [Note: [Col. 0197D] *Pastoral Care*, Part II, chapter 7], the limbs are strong in vain; when the limbs are sick, the head too must necessarily be either sick or close to sickness.

What kind of solicitude and care such people ought to show toward the household subject to them is taught by what follows. Solomon says in Proverbs:

“Pay careful attention to the face of your flock, and consider your herds.”

Likewise:

“Where there is no governor, the people fall. A man is known by his instruction; the heart of the wise seeks instruction” (Prov. XXVII, 23; XI, 14; XII, 8; XV, 14).

Bede, in his homilies on shepherds [Note: [Col. 0197D] From the homily on the dawn of the Nativity of the Lord, Luke II, among the winter homilies on the saints.]:

“Not only shepherds—that is, bishops, priests, and deacons, and also rulers of monasteries—are rightly called shepherds, but all the faithful who take charge of guarding their small household, insofar as they preside over that household with vigilant care. And whoever among you governs even one or two brothers by daily administration ought to fulfill the office of shepherd toward them, because he is commanded, insofar as he is able, to feed them with the nourishment of the word.

“Indeed, each one of you, brothers, who is thought to live as a private person holds the office of shepherd and feeds a spiritual flock and keeps watch over it through the night, if he strives, having gathered around himself a multitude of good works and pure thoughts, to govern it with just moderation, nourish it with the heavenly pastures of the Scriptures, and guard it with watchful diligence against the snares of unclean spirits.”

Gregory, in a homily on the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0198D] Homily 6.]:

“Would that, dearest brothers, we should not say to our condemnation that all who are designated by the name of priest are called angels, as the prophet testifies, saying: ‘The lips of the priest shall guard knowledge, and they shall seek the law from his mouth, for he is the angel of the Lord of hosts’ (Mal. II, 7).

“But you too, if you wish, can deserve the dignity of this name. For each one of you is capable of it to the extent that he has received the grace of heavenly inspiration: if he recalls his neighbor from his wickedness; if he takes care to exhort him to do good; if he announces to one who is in error the eternal kingdom or punishment. When he offers the words of holy proclamation, he truly becomes an angel.

“And let no one say, ‘I am not capable of admonishing; I am not fit to exhort.’ Offer as much as you can, lest, because you badly preserved what you had received, you be required to suffer torments. For the one who hid the talent rather than distribute it had not received more than one talent.

“And we know that in the tabernacle of God not only bowls but, at the Lord’s command, cups were also made. By the bowls is signified overflowing doctrine; by the cups, a small and limited measure of knowledge. One person, full of the doctrine of truth, makes the minds of his hearers drunk; by this act he offers a bowl. Another cannot express fully what he understands; but because he announces it somehow, he offers a taste through a cup.

“Therefore, placed in God’s tabernacle—that is, in the holy Church—if you cannot minister bowls through the wisdom of doctrine, give your neighbors cups of good words to the extent that divine generosity enables you. To the extent that you think you have been perfected, draw others also after you; desire to have companions with you on the way of God.

“If one of you, brothers, goes to the marketplace or perhaps to the baths and sees someone idle, he invites him to come along. Let earthly activity itself admonish you: if you are journeying toward God, take care not to come to him alone. Hence it is written: ‘Let the one who hears say, “Come”’ (Rev. XXII, 17).”

Likewise, the same author in a homily on the nine orders of angels [Note: [Col. 0198D] Homily 34.]:

“For there are many who grasp little, yet do not cease piously to announce these same small things to their brothers. These therefore move among the number of angels.”

Augustine, in a sermon to the people:

“Warn your children and all your households to live chastely, justly, and soberly, and encourage them toward good example and good works.”

Likewise, the same author in his book of sermons [Note: [Col. 0198D] *On the Words of the Lord*, sermon 18, chapter 18.]:

“Always separate yourselves in heart from evil people; for a time, cautiously associate with them bodily. Yet do not be negligent in correcting those who belong in some way to your care. Act by admonishing, exhorting, teaching, frightening—by whatever means you can.

“And when you find in the Scriptures and in the examples of the saints, whether those who lived before or after the Lord’s coming, that evil people do not defile the good within unity, do not become sluggish in correcting the evil.”

For the prophet Isaiah cries out:

“Withdraw, go out from there; do not touch what is polluted” (Isa. XV, 11).

Blessed Augustine explains this in the following way (chapter 20):

“For what is it to touch what is unclean except to consent to sins? And what is it to go out from there except to do what pertains to the correction of evil people, insofar as this can be done according to each person’s rank and standing, while preserving peace? You were displeased that someone sinned; you did not touch what was unclean. You rebuked, corrected, admonished, and, if the matter required it, applied suitable discipline that did not violate unity: you went out from there.”

There are many, indeed, who think little of making this withdrawal and departure and of not touching what is unclean. For when they permit robberies, oppression of the poor, thefts, adulteries, and countless other evils to occur in their households, and are softened by the services of such people and delighted by their companionship, they are undoubtedly shown not to withdraw from them. When they consent to such people in their sins, they do not leave their company. Since, therefore, they do not apply suitable discipline to such offenders, they take no care to avoid touching what is polluted and unclean.

Let such rulers therefore observe the strictness of discipline that blessed Job exercised toward those who acted wickedly, and the works of mercy he performed toward the oppressed. For he says:

“The ear that heard me blessed me, and the eye that saw me bore witness to me, because I delivered the poor man crying out, and the orphan who had no helper. The blessing of the one who was perishing came upon me, and I comforted the widow’s heart. I clothed myself with justice, and I dressed myself in judgment like a garment and a diadem. I was an eye to the blind and a foot to the lame; I was a father to the poor, and the case I did not know I investigated most diligently. I crushed the jaws of the wicked and snatched the prey from his teeth” (Job XXIX, 11 and following).

Likewise, shortly afterward:

“Though I sat like a king with the army surrounding me, I was nevertheless a comforter of the sorrowful” (same work, 25).

Let them also observe the care that blessed Tobit, blind in body but seeing in heart, exercised over his household. When he heard the voice of a bleating kid, he said:

“See whether it may perhaps be stolen. Return it to its owners, because it is not lawful for us either to eat anything stolen or to touch it” (Tobit II, 21).

By these words it is implied that, just as he kept his household free from theft, so also by watchful care he kept it free from all other vices. Those who preside must therefore take the greatest care to maintain vigilant concern for their household without ceasing, lest—God forbid—any of their subjects be deceived by the instigation of the ancient enemy and, while they dissemble, consent, or fail to rebuke, be turned toward sin.

## CHAPTER XVII

That sins must first be forgiven to one’s brothers, and then the gift must be offered to God.

There are very many who with a cold heart, kindled by no fire of charity, offer gifts to God at the altar and do not cease to frequent prayers and almsgiving, supposing that these things please God without charity—especially since no good thing pleases without charity, whereas with charity all things please him. External things can then be freely given and offered to God when the inner person has been kindled by the fire of charity and has become a temple of the Holy Spirit.

The Lord teaches in the Gospel how a gift ought to be offered to God, saying:

“If you offer your gift at the altar and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go first to be reconciled with your brother; and then, when you have come, offer your gift” (Matt. V, 23).

And elsewhere in the Gospel:

“Peter approached Jesus and said: ‘Lord, how often shall my brother sin against me and I forgive him—up to seven times?’ The Lord answered him: ‘Not up to seven times, but up to seventy times seven’” (same work XVIII, 21).

And afterward:

“So also my heavenly Father will do to you, unless each of you forgives his brother from your hearts” (same work, 35).

Blessed Jerome explains this as follows [Note: [Col. 0199D] Book III on Matthew, chapter 18.]:

“A fearful sentence, if God’s judgment is bent and altered according to our judgment. If we do not forgive our brothers small offenses, greater ones are not forgiven us by God.

“And because someone may say, ‘I have nothing against him; he knows it himself. He has God as judge; I do not care what he wishes to do. I have forgiven him,’ he confirms his sentence and overturns every pretense of feigned peace by saying: ‘Unless each of you forgives his brother from your hearts’ (same work, 35).”

Augustine, in his book *On the Sermon on the Mount* (Book I, chapter 10):

“We are therefore commanded, when bringing a gift to the altar, if we remember that our brother has something against us, to leave the gift before the altar, go, and be reconciled with our brother; then to come and offer the gift.

“If this is understood literally, perhaps someone may think that it must be done only if the brother is present; for the matter cannot be delayed when you are commanded to leave your gift before the altar. If, however, something of this kind comes to mind concerning someone who is absent, or even, as may happen, across the sea, it is absurd to believe that your gift should be left before the altar and that you should offer it to God only after traveling over lands and seas.

“We are therefore compelled to take refuge entirely in spiritual meanings, so that what was said may be understood without absurdity. Spiritually, we may understand the altar as faith itself in the inner temple of God, of which the visible altar is a sign. Whatever gift we offer to God—whether prophecy, teaching, prayer, hymn, psalm, or any other such spiritual gift that comes to mind—cannot be acceptable to God unless it is supported by the sincerity of faith.”

Gregory, in the *Moralia* (Book XXII, chapter 8):

“God Almighty does not receive a gift from the hand that is offered with a heart bound by wickedness. The mind that wishes to offer a gift to God must first be cleansed, because everything given to God is weighed according to the mind of the giver. Every stain of wickedness must be wiped away from our inner person by a change of thought, because an offering does not know how to appease the Judge’s anger unless the purity of the offerer makes it pleasing.

“Thus it is written in the Book of Genesis: ‘The Lord looked upon Abel and his gifts; but he did not look upon Cain and his gifts’ (Gen. IV, 4). Sacred Scripture does not say: ‘He looked upon Abel’s gifts, but did not look upon Cain’s gifts.’ Rather, it first says: ‘The Lord looked upon Abel,’ and then adds: ‘and upon his gifts.’ Again it says that he did not look upon Cain, and afterward adds: ‘nor upon his gifts.’ What is done is accepted from the heart of the giver. Therefore the offerings pleased not Abel because of his gifts, but the gifts pleased because of Abel. For we read that the Lord first looked upon the one who gave, and afterward upon what he gave.”

When we have heard the order of this account, we learn that external gifts are made acceptable by the inward purity of the heart, so that the force of this distinction may teach each of us what we ought to be in ourselves when we provide external goods not only to God through the vow of offering but also to our neighbors.

God does not wish to receive sacrifice from those who are at enmity; he refuses to accept a holocaust. From this one should therefore estimate how great is the evil of discord, on account of which that is rejected by which guilt is loosened.

It is written in the Book of Ecclesiasticus:

“Whoever offers sacrifice from the property of the poor is like one who sacrifices a son before his father” (Sirach XXXIV, 24).

What could be more intolerable than the death of a son before his father’s eyes? The extent to which this sacrifice is regarded with anger is therefore shown when it is compared with the grief of a father deprived of his child.

It is one thing to practice mercy on account of sins, and another to sin in order to practice mercy. The latter can no longer be called mercy, because what becomes bitter through the poison of a diseased root does not contribute to a sweet fruit.

Through the prophet the Lord rejects the sacrifices of wicked people, saying:

“I am the Lord, loving judgment and hating robbery in a holocaust” (Isa. LXI, 8).

For many take away from the needy what they give to God. The Lord shows with what severity he rejects them, saying:

“The sacrifices of the wicked are abominable, offered from crime” (Prov. XXI, 27).

Very often the worst people consider how much they give to God through an offering, but refuse to consider how much they steal. They count, as it were, the reward of their works while refusing to weigh the guilt of their crimes.

Likewise, in his *Pastoral Book*:

“If you offer your gift at the altar,” and so forth (Matt. XV, 23). [Note: [Col. 0201D] From Gregory, cited above, chapter 23.]

“From this perception one must weigh whose sacrifice is rejected and how intolerable the guilt is shown to be. For since all evils are washed away by good deeds that follow, let us consider how great are the evils of discord, which, unless they are utterly extinguished, do not permit good to follow.”

Having briefly set forth these judgments, we are fully instructed that we can offer an outwardly pure victim to God only when we have wiped every cloud of discord from our heart and, in accordance with the Apostle, presented ourselves before the eyes of the divine majesty as “a living, holy, and pleasing sacrifice to God” (Rom. XII, 1).

## CHAPTER XVIII

That one should approach frequently and with discernment to receive the Lord’s body and blood.

The most holy body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, in which both the redemption of complete salvation and the mystery of our faith reside, are received by some reverently and beneficially, but by others indiscreetly and unworthily. [Col. 0202A] There are also some who, because they are bound by the guilt of their offenses, are rightly deprived of participation in so great a sacrament by the judgment of the priest.

There are likewise many—something exceedingly dangerous and deserving of suitable correction—who withdraw from this sacrament partly through carelessness and partly through sluggishness to such an extent that they scarcely receive it once a year, except on only three especially celebrated feasts [out of custom [Note: [Col. 0202D] Out of custom. We have added these words, which were entirely necessary.]], doing so from custom rather than devotion. They do not know, or are unwilling to know, that just as the body dies without food and drink, so the soul dies without spiritual food.

How great the danger is if it is not received, and how great the danger is if it is received indiscreetly, is briefly demonstrated by the following collected evangelical and apostolic testimonies and sayings of the holy Fathers.

The Lord says in the Gospel:

“Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him” (John VI, 57).

And elsewhere:

“Amen, I say to you: unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves. Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day” (same work, 54–55).

Paul to the Corinthians:

“The cup of blessing which we bless—is it not a participation in the blood of Christ? And the bread which we break—is it not a participation in the body of the Lord?” (I Cor. X, 16).

Likewise:

“Therefore whoever eats the bread and drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself, not discerning the body of the Lord” (same work XI, 27).

Jerome, in his book *Against Jovinianus* (Book I):

“All the people who were going to approach Mount Sinai and hear God’s word were commanded to sanctify themselves for three days and abstain from their wives. We know that the same thing was said to David when he was fleeing from the priest Abimelech: ‘Are the young men clean from their wives?’ And he replied: ‘They have been so since yesterday and the day before’ (I Kings XXI, 4).

“For they could not eat the showbread, which is like the body of Christ, if they had risen from the beds of their wives. And in passing one should contemplate what he had said: ‘Are the young men clean from their wives?’—namely, that with regard to the purity of Christ’s body every intercourse is unclean.”

Gregory, in the *Book of the Moralia*:

“We learn what the blood of Christ is not now merely by hearing but by drinking. This blood is placed upon both doorposts according to the example of the ancient people when it is imbibed not only by the mouth of the body but also by the mouth of the heart.

“For the blood of the lamb is placed upon both doorposts when the sacrament of Christ’s Passion is received by the mouth for redemption and is also contemplated with an attentive mind for imitation. We eat the lamb’s flesh at night when, in the sacrament, we receive the Lord’s body, while we do not yet see one another’s consciences.

“For it does no good to receive the body and blood of Jesus Christ with the mouth while contradicting him by wicked conduct. Let those who live wickedly in the Church and do not cease to receive Communion, supposing that they are cleansed by such communion, learn that it contributes nothing to their purification, as the prophet says:

‘Why has my beloved committed many crimes in my house? Will holy flesh take away your wickedness?’ (Jer. XI, 15).

“And the Apostle says:

‘Whoever receives this unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself’ (I Cor. XI, 29).”

Isidore, in the first book of the *Offices* (Book I, chapter 18):

“Some say,” he remarks, “that unless some intervening sin prevents it, we daily ask for the Eucharist, at the Lord’s command, saying: ‘Give us this day our daily bread’ (Luke 11:3). They speak rightly, provided that they receive it with religion, devotion, and humility, and do not do so with proud presumption, trusting in their own righteousness. But if their sins are such as to remove them from the altar like a dead person, they must first perform penance, and only then receive the life-giving medicine; for the Apostle says: ‘Whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself’ (1 Corinthians 11:29). To receive unworthily means to receive at a time when one ought to be doing penance.

“On the other hand, if the sins are not so serious that a person should be judged excommunicated, he ought not to separate himself from the medicine of the Lord’s body, lest, while he is forbidden to abstain for a long time, he become separated from Christ’s body. For it is evident that those who touch his body live. Hence one must fear that, while someone is separated for a long time from Christ’s body, he may remain alienated from salvation, since the Lord himself teaches: ‘Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves’ (John 6:54). Whoever has now ceased to sin should not cease to communicate. Married people, however, should abstain from sexual intercourse, devote themselves to prayer for many days, and then approach Christ’s body.”

A little later he adds:

“Therefore certain days should be chosen during which a person first lives more continently, so that he may be worthy to approach so great a sacrament.”

The same author, in the little book entitled *Synonyma* [Note: This is Saint Augustine, chapter 53, *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*.]:

“To receive communion in the Eucharist every day I neither praise nor condemn; nevertheless, I advise and exhort everyone to communicate on every Sunday, provided that the mind is not inclined to sin. For I say that one who still has the will to sin is burdened more by receiving the Eucharist than purified by it. Therefore, although someone is troubled by sin, if he no longer intends to sin thereafter, and if, when he is about to communicate, he makes satisfaction with tears and prayers, and, trusting in the Lord’s mercy—which is accustomed to forgive sins confessed devoutly—approaches the Eucharist fearlessly and securely, I say this concerning one who is not weighed down by grave and mortal sins. But whoever is burdened by mortal crimes committed after baptism, I urge first to make satisfaction through public penance and, having thus been reconciled by the priest’s judgment, to be joined to communion, if he wishes to receive the Eucharist not for his judgment and condemnation.

Since, therefore, the assembly of Christians is especially established for the purpose that, amid the solemn celebration of hymns and praises, participation in the Lord’s body and blood may be celebrated, it is impossible not to wonder sufficiently at how a highly reprehensible practice has crept in: namely, that some do not fear being deprived of so great a sacrament; and, if it happens that they are separated from it because of some intervening sin, they are not crushed either by grief or by contrition of heart. Moreover, this reprehensible practice has become so deeply rooted that it seems almost to be regarded as law and to promise a kind of impunity to those who do not participate in so great a sacrament.
