“Therefore each believer must recognize that dangers threaten him on every side: unless he eats and drinks, he will not have life in himself; but if he eats and drinks unworthily, he eats and drinks judgment upon himself. Let him therefore prepare himself so that, with a pure heart and body, he may be able to receive frequently and prudently the gift of his redemption, so that he may deserve to have Christ with him in the present and to be raised by him to life in the future.”

## CHAPTER XIX  
### On the Tithes of the Faithful

Although the offerings and tithes of the faithful ought to be given for God alone, many customarily give them with a manifold distribution that greatly needs correction. For just as there are some who give them devoutly to God, so there are very many who distribute them to priests not for the sake of divine honor but for their own profit, and compel those under their authority to distribute them likewise—namely, so that whatever has been given may be turned, wholly or almost wholly, to the uses of themselves and their own people. For although they wish to appear to men as honoring God, they are in fact dishonorers of God, indeed, robbers of what has been given to God, and they exist to their own destruction.

There are also many who, confined within the boundaries of their possessions and lacking revenues, possess basilicas either as their own legal property or certainly through the gift of some powerful person. To these the religious devotion of the faithful commonly contributes a large abundance of offerings and tithes. Led by greed of this sort, they are accustomed to say: “That priest acquires much from my church; therefore I want him to serve me according to my desire from what he acquires from me. Otherwise he will no longer have my church.” In such basilicas, too, they do not allow priests to be appointed unless they receive from them the gift they desire.

There are also many powerful men who, forgetting their rank and ministry, possess basilicas, while they themselves are poor in resources but abound in the very generous tithes of the faithful. Contrary to what is lawful, they confer these basilicas on their own clerics or laymen as benefices, so that those men may serve them from such offerings and tithes. Anyone who notices understands how extraordinary this is, how incompatible with Christian religion, and how dangerous to those who do it.

For it belongs not to laymen but to the ministry of bishops—through whom basilicas are dedicated to God—to regulate how the offerings and tithes offered to God by the faithful are distributed. It is properly the bishops’ ministry to determine how much of these offerings of the faithful is applied to the construction and repair of the church, how much to preparing lights, how much to receiving guests and relieving the poor, and how much is spent on the needs of priests and of those who together with them serve in Christ’s army. It is not the ministry of laymen to demand that anything from these offerings be turned to the uses of themselves and their own people.

This kind of greed had so bound certain laymen that they thought they could pursue it justly and reasonably, indeed without blame, until the glorious orthodox lord Emperor Louis [Note: Louis the Pious, *Capitularies*, Book V, chapter 22], among the other benefits of his piety that he conferred upon the holy Church in honor and love of our Lord Jesus Christ, also freed the Church from this abuse. Laymen must therefore beware of desiring the tithes and offerings of the faithful. They should know that they cannot claim anything from them by force except at their own peril, and should be content with their own ministry, lest, while they usurp another’s ministry, they in some manner make themselves unworthy of the ministry with which they ought to be content, turn the pious vows of others into sin for themselves, and incur the mark of sacrilege.

Thus King Uzziah, because he rashly seized the priestly ministry, was immediately punished with the uncleanness of leprosy. King Belshazzar also, because he unlawfully turned vessels consecrated for divine use to his own uses, lost both his life and his kingdom.

Therefore, whoever promises himself impunity in this kind of greed should hear what the sacred canons decree on this matter at the Council of Gangra [Note: Chapter 7, from the translation of Dionysius Exiguus]:

“If anyone wishes to receive or give the offerings of the Church outside the church, without the consent of the bishop or of the person to whom such duties have been entrusted, and does not wish to act with his counsel, let him be anathema.”

Jerome also writes in his letter to Nepotian (Letter 2):

“To defraud the Church is sacrilege.”

And below:

“To take anything away from it—which is the most manifest of crimes—surpasses the cruelty of all robbers.”

He also writes in his *Commentaries on the Gospel of Matthew*:

“All who misuse the temple’s offerings and the things contributed for the uses of the Church, applying them to other matters with which to satisfy their own will, are like the scribes and priests who purchase falsehood and the Savior’s blood.”

That tithes ought to be given to priests—or rather, in the priests, to God—is demonstrated by the testimonies collected below.

It is written in Genesis:

“And he gave him”—that is, Abraham gave Melchizedek—“tithes of everything” (Genesis 14).

Again:

“Jacob made a vow, saying: ‘If God will be with me and will guard me on the way by which I walk, and will give me bread to eat and clothing to wear, and if I return safely to my father’s house, then the Lord shall be my God; and this stone which I have set up as a pillar shall be called the house of God; and of everything that you give me I will offer you tithes’” (ibid. 28:20).

And in Exodus:

“You shall not delay to offer your tithes and firstfruits” (Exodus 22:29).

In Leviticus:

“All the tithes of the land, whether of grain or of the fruits of the trees, belong to the Lord; and they are consecrated to him” (Leviticus 27:30).

Again:

“All the tithes of cattle and sheep, and everything that passes under the rod, every tenth animal that comes forth, shall be consecrated to the Lord. You shall not exchange it, the good for the bad or the bad for the good” [citation as printed: Numbers 15:17].

In the Book of Numbers:

“You shall separate firstfruits for the Lord from your foods; from your threshing floors you shall separate firstfruits, and likewise you shall give firstfruits from your preparations to the Lord.”

Again:

“I have given you all the best of the wine, oil, and grain, whatever they offer as firstfruits to the Lord” (ibid. 18:12).

Again:

“And the Lord said to Aaron: ‘You shall possess nothing in their land, nor shall you have a portion among them. I am your portion and inheritance in the midst of the children of Israel. To the sons of Levi I have given all the tithes of Israel as a possession, in return for the ministry by which they serve me in the tent of meeting.’”

In Deuteronomy:

“In the place that the Lord your God will choose so that his name may dwell there, you shall bring there everything that I command you: burnt offerings and sacrifices, victims, tithes and firstfruits of your hands, and whatever is most excellent among the gifts that you have vowed to the Lord” (Deuteronomy 12:11).

Again:

“You shall set apart a tenth part of all your crops that are born in the land year by year, and you shall eat it in the sight of the Lord your God, in the place that he will choose, so that his name may be invoked there: the tenth of your grain, wine, and oil, and the firstborn of your herds and sheep, so that you may learn to fear the Lord your God at all times” (ibid. 14:22).

In the Book of Tobit:

“He alone withdrew from the company of everyone and went to Jerusalem, to the temple of the Lord, and there worshiped the Lord, the God of Israel, faithfully offering all his firstfruits and tithes” (Tobit 1:6).

In Malachi:

“Bring the whole tithe into my storehouse, so that there may be food in my house, and test me in this, says the Lord. If I will not open for you the floodgates of heaven and pour out a blessing upon you in abundance; and I will rebuke the devourer for your sake, and he shall not destroy the fruit of your land; nor shall your vineyard be barren in the field, says the Lord of hosts. And all nations shall call you blessed” (Malachi 3:10).

Jesus son of Sirach:

“In every gift make your face cheerful; and sanctify your tithes with rejoicing” (Sirach 35:11).

Paul:

“Indeed, those among the sons of Levi who receive the priesthood have a commandment to take tithes from the people according to the law, that is, from their brothers” (Hebrews 7:5).

Augustine, in a sermon to the people [Note: *On the Time*, sermon 219]:

“Give thanks to Christ, most beloved brothers. The days are already near when we ought to gather the fruit of the earth and the harvests; and therefore, while giving thanks to God who gave them, let us think about offering—or rather, returning—tithes. For our God, who deigned to give everything, deigns to demand a tenth from us, which will undoubtedly benefit not him but us. Thus he himself promises through the prophet, saying: ‘Bring,’ he says, ‘the whole tithe into my storehouses, and let there be food in my house; and test me in this, says the Lord, whether I will not open for you the floodgates of heaven and give you fruits in abundance’ (Malachi 3:10).

“Behold, we have proved how tithes benefit us more than God. O foolish people, what evil does God command, that he should not deserve to be obeyed? For he says: ‘You shall not delay to offer me the firstfruits of your threshing floor and your winepress’ (Numbers 18:30). If giving late is a sin, how much worse is it not to have given? And again he says: ‘Honor the Lord your God from your just labors; offer him something from the fruits of your righteousness, so that your storehouses may be filled with grain and your winepresses overflow with wine’ (Proverbs 3:10). You do not offer this for nothing; you will soon receive it back with great interest.

“Perhaps you ask whom it benefits that God receives what he will return. Again you ask whom it benefits that what is given is given to the poor. If you believe, it benefits you; if you doubt, you have lost it. For tithes, most beloved brothers, are the taxes of needy souls. Therefore pay the taxes to the poor; offer libations to the priests.

“But if, as a farmer, you do not have tithes of earthly crops, whatever your skill provides for your sustenance belongs to God. From the source of your livelihood he demands tithes: from military service, from trade, from your craft, return tithes. We pay one thing for the land; we reckon another for the use of life. Therefore, human being, pay because you possess; pay because you have deserved to be born. For thus the Lord says: ‘Each shall give the redemption of his soul, and there shall be among them neither sickness nor calamity.’

“Behold, you have in the Holy Scriptures the guarantee of your Lord, by which he promised you that if you give tithes, you will receive not only an abundance of crops but also bodily health. ‘Your threshing floors,’ he says, ‘will be filled with grain, and your winepresses will overflow with wine; and there will be among them neither sickness nor calamity’ (ibid. 3). Since by giving tithes you can earn both earthly and heavenly gifts, why through greed do you defraud yourself of a double blessing?

“Hear, therefore, O faithless humanity. You know that everything you receive belongs to God, yet you do not lend anything of his to the Creator of all things. The Lord has no need; he does not ask for a reward, but for honor. He demands something of your possessions in order to return it. He asks for the firstfruits of your goods and tithes, and you greedily refuse.

“What would you do if, having taken nine parts for himself, he had left you the tenth? That has already happened when your harvest, deprived of the blessing of rain, has withered in barrenness, and hail has struck your vintage or frost has scorched it. What is it that is counted so greedily? Nine parts have been taken back from you because you were unwilling to give the tenth. It is indeed certain that you did not give it, but nevertheless God exacted it. For this is the Lord’s most just custom: if you do not give him the tenth, you will be reduced to the tenth.

“For it is written that the tithes of your field and the firstfruits of the earth are with you. I see you, and you thought you could deceive me. Within your treasuries and your houses there will be plunder. You will give to the wicked soldier what you are unwilling to give to the priest.

“What would the Lord say? Surely this: ‘The human being is mine, whom I made; the earth is mine, which you cultivate; the seeds are mine, which you sow; the animals are mine, which you wear out; the rains and showers are mine; the blasts of the winds are mine; the warmth of the sun is mine. Since all the elements are mine, you who merely lend your hands deserved only the tenth.’

“Whoever therefore wishes either to acquire a reward or to merit forgiveness of sins should pay tithes, even from the nine parts, and should strive to give alms. Let it be done in such a way, however, that whatever remains beyond moderate food and reasonable clothing is not reserved for luxury but stored in the heavenly treasury through almsgiving to the poor. For whatever God has given us beyond what we need, he has not given to us for ourselves alone, but has conveyed it through us to be distributed to others. If we do not give it, we have invaded another’s property.”

Thus, by evident indications, it has been made clear how tithes ought to be given to God. If, therefore, as Scripture teaches, God is honored through tithes, firstfruits, and the other fruits of the earth, then certainly—because he is honored [Note: “Certainly, because he is honored.” No suitable sense can be drawn from this passage unless one reads “certainly, he is dishonored by him,” or something similar. Nevertheless, I prefer to preserve these words and add “he dishonors God.” Below, the text has been ineptly printed: “offered to God for his soldiers.” “Given by God to his ministers” would not be objectionable.], whoever neglects to give these things to God—and if the one who does not give them dishonors God—much more does the one dishonor God who unlawfully appropriates for his own soldiers what has been offered to God.*

For it is precisely because of this greed, which has emptied the Lord’s priests and reduced them to poverty, that some basilicas now exist so decayed and lacking roofs, and—what is worse—so nearly collapsed to the ground because poverty prevents repairs, that Christ cannot be served in them, nor can his body and blood be worthily consecrated. When pagans and unbelievers see these churches, they blaspheme the name of Christians, saying: “Look at the kind of temples Christians build for Christ their God.” Thus the Apostle’s saying is fulfilled: “The name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you” (Romans 2:24).

For just as the devotion of the ancient Christians burned to build basilicas for Christ, to heap them with various gifts, and to honor their priests, so now, as perverse and disordered customs arise, the greed of many burns to strip and dishonor them—something that deserves correction. Whoever wishes to be counted by Christ the Lord among the number of those same Christians should not neglect to follow their examples and should make himself a son, not a robber, of the Church.

## CHAPTER XX  
### That due honor should be shown to priests, through whom human beings are reconciled to God

Since priests are mediators, so to speak, between the Lord and the people, they ought to be venerated with appropriate honor, without regard to persons, wealth, or status, because of love and honor for the one whose ministry they exercise. Yet many venerate in them not Christ’s ministry but what is unlawful: the riches and honors of the world. The more powerful and wealthy they are, the greater the honor and veneration they receive from such people.

There are also some priests who lack worldly wealth and honors, and who are held in such contempt by certain laymen that those laymen not only make them administrators and stewards of their possessions but also compel them to serve them in the manner of laymen, while disdaining to have them as guests at their table. Such people apparently wish to have priests in name only; in reality, they do not want them for the very purpose for which priests ought to be had, and they wish to have as intercessors with God men whom they utterly despise as such. It is not lawful to express in words how dangerous, reprehensible, incompatible with Christian religion, and dishonorable this is. There is no doubt that it happens not only because of the negligence of certain priests but also because of the pride and ignorance of certain laymen.

How greatly priests ought to be venerated is briefly established below by legal, evangelical, and apostolic ordinances and by the sayings of the holy Fathers.

For it is written in Deuteronomy:

“You shall not speak evil of the gods, nor curse the ruler of your people” (Exodus 22:28).

Again:

“If you perceive that a judgment is difficult and ambiguous for you, between blood and blood, case and case, leprosy and non-leprosy, and you see that the words of judgment differ within your gates, arise and go up to the place that the Lord your God will choose. You shall come to the priests of the Levitical race and to the judge who is at that time, and you shall ask them; they will show you the truth of the judgment. And you shall do whatever those who preside in the place that the Lord has chosen tell you and teach you. You shall follow their sentence according to his law, and you shall not turn aside to the right or to the left. But the person who acts proudly and refuses to obey the command of the priest who at that time ministers to the Lord your God shall die by the judge’s decree. Thus you shall remove the evil from Israel, and all the people, hearing of it, shall fear, so that no one thereafter may swell with pride” (Deuteronomy 17:8 and following).

And in Ecclesiastes:

“With all your soul fear the Lord, and sanctify his priests. Love with all your strength him who made you, and do not forsake his ministers. Honor God with all your soul, and honor his priests.”

Again:

“Do not despise the account of wise elders, and converse with their proverbs. For from them you will learn instruction and understanding, and how to serve the commandments without complaint” (Ecclesiastes 7:30 and following).

And in the Gospel:

“Whoever receives you receives me.”

Again:

“Whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward. And whoever receives a righteous person in the name of a righteous person will receive a righteous person’s reward.”

Again:

“Whatever city or town you enter, inquire who in it is worthy, and remain there until you depart. … Whoever does not receive you or hear your words, when you go out of the house or city, shake the dust from your feet. Amen I say to you, it will be more tolerable for the land of Sodom and Gomorrah on the day of judgment than for that city” (Matthew 10:40 and following).

Paul says:

“Obey your leaders and be subject to them. For they keep watch as those who will render an account for your souls, so that they may do this with joy and not with groaning” (Hebrews 13:17).

Paul says again:

“Let the presbyters who preside well be held worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in word and doctrine” (1 Timothy 5:17).

Jerome, to Heliodorus (Letter 1):

“Far be it from me,” he says, “to speak anything unfavorable about those who, succeeding to the apostolic rank, consecrate Christ’s body with their sacred mouth; through whom we too are Christians; who, possessing the keys of the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 16:18), in a certain manner judge before the day of judgment; who preserve the Lord’s bride in sober chastity. Clerics feed the sheep; I am fed.”

John of Constantinople [Note: *Homily on receiving Severianus*]:

“Just as it is necessary for the body to be joined to the head, so it is necessary for the Church to be joined to the priest and ruler of the people; and as branches are joined to roots and rivers to springs, so are children joined to their father and disciples to their teacher. Let the obedience of disciples shine forth in you, and let it be evident how much affection you show your father. Adorn me, children, and place upon me the crown of your obedience. Make me be judged blessed by all, and magnify my teaching through your obedience, according to the Apostle’s words: ‘Obey your leaders and be subject to them, because they keep watch for you as those who will render an account for your souls’ (Hebrews 13:17).

“This, therefore, I warn beforehand: let no one regard our admonition as insignificant. For I am a father, and it is necessary that I offer counsel to my children. What nature in the fleshly fathers accomplishes through the nature of the flesh, grace through the Spirit accomplishes in us.”

[Col. 0210C] From Eusebius’s *Ecclesiastical History* [Note: Rufinus, Book I, chapter 5], an address of Constantine to the bishops:

“God has appointed you priests and has given you the power to judge even us; therefore we are rightly judged by you. But you cannot be judged by human beings; for this reason, await among yourselves the judgment of God alone, so that whatever disputes you have may be reserved for that divine examination. For you have been given to us by God as gods, and it is not fitting that a human being should judge gods, but only he of whom it is written: ‘God stands in the assembly of gods; in the midst he judges the gods’ (Psalm 81:1).”

As in certain other matters, so also in this the form of Christian life is darkened because some laymen do not venerate the Lord’s priests with the honor due to them.

Gregory says in the *Pastoral Rule*:

“The deeds of rulers must not be struck with the sword of the mouth, even when they are judged rightly deserving of correction. If the tongue ever slips against them, even in the smallest matters, the heart must necessarily be pressed through the suffering of penance, so that it may return to itself and, having offended against the authority placed over it, may fear the judgment of the one from whom that authority was received. For when we offend those set over us, we oppose the ordering of the one who placed them above us.”

Isidore also writes in the third book of the *Sentences* (Book III, chapter 39):

“Rulers are to be judged by God, but they are in no way to be judged by their own subjects.”

And a little later:

“But if a ruler deviates from the faith, then he is to be corrected by his subjects. For lesser faults, however, he is to be tolerated by the people rather than disciplined.”

Therefore, priests who act rightly are not to be held in contempt because some priests live negligently. Those who act well are not only to be venerated but also imitated; those who act badly are indeed to be venerated because of Christ’s ministry, but not imitated. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel:

“Therefore, whatever they tell you, observe and do; but do not act according to their works” (Matthew 23:3).

For this reason certain laymen must beware lest they hold the Lord’s priests in such contempt that they oppress and strip them, bind them by legal process, and inflict upon them the various injuries they are accustomed to inflict. For when they dishonor them in any way, they dishonor Christ, whose ministers they are, who says in the Gospel:

“Whoever despises you despises me, and whoever receives you receives me” (Luke 10:16).

Blessed Augustine explains this in his book of sermons [Note: *On the Words of the Lord*, sermon 24, chapter 1]:

“If he said only to the Apostles, ‘Whoever despises you despises me,’ then despise us too. But if his word has reached us, and he has called us and placed us in their position, see to it that you do not despise us, lest the injury you inflict upon us reach him. For if you do not fear us, fear him who said: ‘Whoever despises you despises me.’”

Therefore, in venerating and obeying priests, let them imitate the orthodox Emperor Theodosius, exalted by power and the most abundant honors, and observe how humbly and reverently he obeyed the admonitions, rebukes, and excommunications of the blessed Ambrose, that memorable man. He knew that the imperial power with which he was distinguished depended upon the power of the one whose servant and minister Ambrose was. Whoever wishes to know this more fully should read the ninth book of the *Tripartite History*, under title thirty (Book IX, chapter 30).

## CHAPTER XXI  
### That laymen ought to know that the Lord has granted priests the power of binding and loosing, and that they ought willingly to obey their admonitions and humbly submit to their excommunications

Some laymen are so reckless that they regard the admonitions, rebukes, and excommunications of priests as nothing. Anyone who notices understands how far this is from Christian profession. This highly reprehensible and detestable practice has grown so greatly among some—and, so to speak, become law—that they regard a priest’s command and excommunication as no more important than those of some layman. I urge such people to consider carefully what follows.

The Lord says in the Gospel specifically to the blessed Apostle Peter, the head of the Church:

“I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew 16:19).

He also says generally to all the disciples:

“Amen I say to you: whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven.”

Blessed Jerome explains this passage in his *Commentaries* (chapter 18):

“Because he had said, ‘If he does not hear the Church, let him be to you as a pagan and a tax collector,’ a contemptuous brother could have made this secret response or silent thought: ‘If you despise me, I despise you too; if you condemn me, you are condemned by my judgment.’ He grants the Apostles authority so that those who are condemned by such persons may know that they are strengthened by divine judgment, and that whatever has been bound on earth is likewise bound in heaven.”

Again, the Lord says in the Gospel:

“Receive the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven; and whose sins you retain, they are retained” (John 20:23).

Blessed Gregory explains these words as follows [Note: Homily 26]:

“It is pleasing to contemplate to what summit of glory those disciples who were called to the burdens of humility have been led. Behold, they are made secure not only concerning themselves, but they also receive the power to release the bonds of others; they are given authority over the heavenly judgment, so that in God’s place they may retain the sins of some and release those of others. It was fitting that God should raise up in this way those who had consented to humble themselves so greatly for God.

“Behold, those who fear God’s strict judgment become judges of souls; and those who feared being condemned themselves condemn or release others. The bishops of the Church now occupy their place: those who receive the rank of governance take up the authority of binding and loosing.

“And after much else in the same place:

“Therefore the pastors of the Church should strive to loose or to bind with great restraint. But whether the pastor binds justly or unjustly, the pastor’s sentence is nevertheless to be feared by the flock, lest the subordinate, even when perhaps unjustly bound, deserve the sentence of his own binding through some other fault. The pastor, therefore, must fear absolving indiscriminately or binding indiscriminately; but the one who is under the pastor’s hand must fear being bound, whether justly or unjustly, and must not rashly criticize his pastor’s judgment. Otherwise, even if he has been bound unjustly, through the pride of his swollen criticism the fault that did not exist may come into being.”

Jerome, to Heliodorus (Letter 1):

“Clerics live from the altar; for me, as for a barren tree, the axe is laid at the root. If I do not bring a gift to the altar, I cannot plead poverty, since in the Gospel the Lord praises the widow who cast in the two coins that were all she had left. I am not permitted to sit before the presbyter. If I sin, he is permitted to hand me over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord Jesus. Under the old law, whoever did not obey the priests was either placed outside the camp and stoned by the people, or, with his neck subjected to the sword, atoned for his contempt with blood. Now the disobedient is cut down by a spiritual blade, or, expelled from the Church, is torn apart by the ravenous mouth of demons.”

From many sources, a few testimonies have been collected concerning the power granted by the Lord to priests. Let laymen therefore know that they ought to be subject to this power; and since whoever grows proud against it or remains obstinate in any matter is shown to resist most proudly, indeed most dangerously, the ordering of the one by whom it was granted.

## CHAPTER XXII  
### On those who are so exalted by earthly and transient honors that they do not recognize the poor, who are naturally their equals

Those who preside must beware lest they think that their subjects are inferior to them in nature just as they are in rank. For by God’s provident ordering it has been arranged that one mortal should be protected by another mortal—not because of natural superiority, but because of a certain worldly dignity: the weak by the strong through benevolent authority and governance. This is so arranged, however, that natural equality is always recognized.

Yet many, swollen with perishable and quickly passing possessions, do not recognize as naturally equal either those over whom they preside or those whom they surpass in power, honors, and wealth. Even if they acknowledge this in words, they do not acknowledge it in their affections. It is clear that this vice flows from the source of pride. For why should master and servant, rich and poor, not be equal by nature, since they have one God in heaven who shows no partiality?

Therefore Paul teaches that masters ought to render to their servants what is fair and just, saying: “Masters, provide your servants with what is just and equitable, knowing that you too have a Master in heaven” (Col. 4:1). Concerning this matter blessed Gregory also says:

[Note: *Moralia on Job*, Book XXI, chapter 10.]

“For powerful men, the virtue of humility is great when they consider the equality of their condition. For by nature we are all equal; but, by a providential ordering, it has come about that we appear to be set over some. [Col. 0213C] If, therefore, we remove from our minds what has been added temporarily, we quickly discover what we are by nature. For power once received often confronts the mind and deceives it with proud thoughts. Thus, by the hand of the most humble reflection, the swelling of elevation must be pressed down. If the mind descends within itself from the summit of its eminence, it quickly finds the level ground of natural equality.

“For, as we have already said, nature brought forth all human beings equal; but, through the varying order of merits, a hidden dispensation places some below others. This very diversity, which arose from sin, has rightly been ordered by divine judgments, so that, because every human being does not walk the path of life in the same way, one may be governed by another. But holy men, when they preside, attend not to the power of their rank but to the equality of their condition; nor do they rejoice to rule human beings, but to benefit them. For they know that our ancient fathers are remembered as having been not so much kings of men as shepherds of animals.

“And when the Lord said to Noah and his sons, ‘Increase and multiply, and fill the earth,’ he added: ‘And let your terror and dread be upon all the animals of the earth’ (Gen. 9:2). He did not say, ‘Let it be upon the human beings who are to come,’ but, ‘Let it be upon all the animals of the earth.’ For by nature the human being has been placed above irrational animals, but not above other human beings; and therefore it is said that he is to be feared by animals, not by human beings, because it is contrary to nature to be proud and wish to be feared by one’s equal.”

[Col. 0214A] Augustine, in a sermon to the people:

“Some, however, forgetful of the divine commandments, exercise such power of domination over their servants and subjects that, even on days of fasting, they do not hesitate to beat them with whips, inflict punishments upon them, and restrain them with fetters. And if perhaps, when the time comes to eat, a servant arrives somewhat late, they immediately tear him with blows and satisfy themselves first with the servant’s blood rather than with the pleasure of the banquet. Such is the fasting of these people: they fast not to call forth the mercy of God, but to pour out the cry of a groaning household.

“Whoever desires to merit God’s mercy must himself be merciful first; for it is written: ‘With whatever measure you measure, it will be measured back to you’ (Matt. 7:2). And what is even more grievous, a Christian master does not spare a Christian servant on these days, paying no attention to the fact that, although the servant is a slave by condition, he is nevertheless a brother by grace. For he too has put on Christ, shares in the same sacraments, and worships the same God the Father as you do. Why should he not use you as a brother?”

The same, in his book of sermons:

[Note: *On the Words of the Lord*, Sermon 5, chapter 7.]

“We are God’s beggars. In order that he may recognize his beggars, let us recognize our own. But let us also consider, when people ask something of us, who those are who ask, from whom they ask, and what they ask.

“Who are they who ask? Human beings. From whom do they ask? From human beings. Who are they who ask? Mortals. From whom do they ask? From mortals. Who are they who ask? Frail creatures. From whom do they ask? From the frail. Who are they who ask? Miserable people. From whom? From the miserable. Apart from the substance of their possessions, those who ask are such as those from whom they ask.

“What kind of face do you present when asking from your Lord, if you do not recognize your brother? ‘I am not like that,’ he says; ‘far be it from me to be such.’ The inflated and hardened man says this about the ragged poor man. But I question the naked; I do not ask what sort of people you are in your clothing, but what sort you were when you were born. Both were naked, both were weak, both were beginning a miserable life, and therefore both were crying.

“Come now, rich man, recall your beginnings; see whether you brought anything here. You have already come, and you found so much here (chapter 8). Tell me, I ask you, what did you bring? Tell me what you brought. Or, if you are ashamed to say it, listen to the Apostle: ‘We brought nothing into this world’ (1 Tim. 6:7).

“But perhaps, because you brought nothing and found many things here, you will take something away with you? Perhaps even to admit this you tremble out of love for riches. Listen, and let the Apostle say this too—he does not flatter you: ‘We brought nothing into this world’ (ibid.), certainly when we were born, ‘nor can we take anything away,’ certainly when we leave the body. You brought nothing; you will take nothing away from here. Why do you puff yourself up against the poor?

“When infants are born, let parents, servants, clients, and the crowds of attendants withdraw; let the rich children be recognized as crying. Let a rich woman and a poor woman give birth at the same time; let them not consider what they are giving birth to. Let them withdraw for a little while, then return and recognize them. See, rich man: you brought nothing into this world, nor can you take anything away from here.”

The same, in a sermon to the people:

“Why does the poor man not receive food with you, when he is going to receive the kingdom with you? Why does the poor man not receive your old tunic, when he is going to receive with you the robe of immortality? Why does the poor man not deserve to receive your bread, when he deserved to receive with you the sacrament of baptism? Why is he unworthy to receive even the remains of your food, when he will come with you to the banquets of the angels?”

Instructed by these and by the sayings of the other divine writings, let the powerful and the rich recognize both their servants and the poor, who are naturally equal to them. If, therefore, servants are naturally equal to their masters—and indeed they are—let masters not suppose that they will escape punishment while, inflamed by turbulent indignation and the agitated fury of their spirit against the faults of their servants, they behave excessively toward them, either by beating them with the most savage blows or by weakening them through the amputation of limbs, since they have one God in heaven. And those whom in this world they see to be weak and lowly in clothing, appearance, and resources, let them fully recognize as naturally equal and their equals.

## CHAPTER XXIII. Concerning those who neglect the cause of the poor because of hunting and their love of dogs

Although some, swollen with the pride of power, some, delighted by prolonged leisure, and others, embracing bodily pleasures in which they become dissipated by exceeding the bounds of moderation, are not accustomed to regard Christ’s cause among the poor as important, nevertheless there are very many who, because of their love of dogs and of various kinds of hunting, to which they devote themselves miserably, neglect in some measure both themselves and concern for the poor. It is plainly a miserable and deeply lamentable matter when, for the sake of wild animals, which human care has not nourished but which God has granted for the common use of mortals, the poor are stripped, beaten, thrust into prisons, and made to suffer many other things by the powerful.

Those who do this contend that they may justly do so under the law of the world. I call upon them to decide with a just balance whether the law of the world ought to nullify the law of Christ. They will certainly answer, as the faithful ought to answer, that the law of the world must in no way be preferred to the law of Christ. For Christ teaches in the Gospel that, if anyone takes away what is ours, we should not demand it back. And the Apostle says: “It is already altogether a fault that you have lawsuits among yourselves. Why do you not rather suffer injustice? Why do you not rather allow yourselves to be defrauded?” (1 Cor. 6:7).

For if the person who demands back what has been taken from him acts against the Gospel, much more does the person sin against the author of the Gospel who violently exacts things that were not his. Who, then, could deny that it is contrary to the rule of Christianity when, for the pleasure of one person, so many of Christ’s poor are subjected to injuries of every kind? This happens in so many ways that it can scarcely be described.

Let those who wish and dare to do so flatter such people and promise them impunity. I, however, dare not flatter anyone or make anyone secure in this matter by claiming that he can do such things with impunity in any way. Whoever promises himself impunity for this deed should consider—I warn him—what reward those who follow Christ’s law will receive on the day of the dread judgment, and what condemnation those will receive who deviate from Christ’s law because of the law of the world.

For it is also the height of madness when, because of hunting, someone is absent on the Lord’s days and other feast days from the solemn celebration of Mass and the divine praises; and because of such hunting neglects the salvation of his own soul and of those over whom he presides and whom he ought to benefit. Such people take more delight in the barking of dogs than in attending the melodies of the heavenly hymns.

Accordingly blessed Augustine, in homilies to the people, addresses those who devote themselves excessively to hunting as follows:

“Do you think, brothers, that the person is fasting who at first light does not keep vigil for the church, does not seek out the places of the blessed martyrs, but rises, gathers his servants, arranges his nets, brings out his dogs, and traverses the forests? He drags his servants along with him—perhaps they were hastening more eagerly to the church—and heaps upon his own pleasures the sins of others, not knowing that he will be held guilty both for his own offense and for the destruction of his servants.

“Thus he spends the whole day hunting, at one moment raising an excessive shout, at another secretly imposing silence; happy if he has caught something, angry if he has let go of what he did not possess, and pursuing the hunt with such eagerness. In these luxuries, brothers, tell me what worship of God there can be, what devotion of mind there can be. He fasts for this reason—not to devote himself to God or to prayers, but to spend the entire day idle and free to exercise his own will.

“Although, then, you who are such a person, brother, return home in the evening; although you eat when the sun is already declining, can you be thought to have carried out the Lord’s will while pursuing your pleasure? For this is the Lord’s will: that we fast from food and from sins alike. We prescribe abstinence to the body so that we may be able to abstain more from vices in the soul. An exhausted body is a kind of bridle for a soul given to excess. But whoever fasts and sins appears to have gained the profit of food, not of salvation; to have filled the storeroom by sparing provisions, not to have fattened the mind with virtues.

“For there are many who, returning from the hunt, care more for their dogs than for their servants. They make the dogs sleep or recline beside them and have their daily food served in their presence, while they do not know whether one of their servants is dying of hunger. And what is more grievous, if food has not been carefully prepared for these dogs, the servant is killed on the dog’s behalf. You see sleek and fat dogs running about in the houses of some people, while human beings walk about pale and staggering. Such people, then, will never have pity on the poor, since they have no pity for their own servants.”

The same, in his exposition of Psalm 102:

“Let your charity attend for a little while, until this matter is unfolded by examples that are very useful for understanding. He said this when someone—I do not know who—was hungry: if you have something from which you can give, give; if you see that something should be given to provide assistance, give. Let the inward parts of mercy not grow sluggish within you because a sinner has encountered you.

“For a sinful human being has encountered you. When I say, ‘A sinful human being has encountered you,’ I have spoken two names; these names are not superfluous. One name is ‘human being,’ the other is ‘sinner.’ The fact that he is human is the work of God; the fact that he is a sinner is the work of the human being. Give to the work of God; do not give to the work of the human being.

“‘And how,’ you ask, ‘do you forbid me to give to the work of the human being?’ What does it mean to give to the work of the human being? It means giving to a sinner on account of his sin, giving to someone because his sin pleases you.

“‘And who,’ you ask, ‘would do this?’ Who would do this? Would that no one would; would that only a few would; would that it were not done publicly. Why do those who give to hunters give to them? Let them tell me why they give to hunters. They love in him that which makes him utterly wicked; they spare him in that respect and clothe him in that respect, displaying that very wickedness publicly before everyone.

“Those who give to actors, who give to diviners, who give to prostitutes—why do they give? Yet they do not attend there to the nature of God’s work, but to the wickedness of the human work. Do you want to see what you honor in the hunter when you clothe him? Let someone say to you, ‘Be such a person’; you love him, rejoice in him, and in a sense wish to strip yourself in order to clothe him.

“Do not take offense if someone says to you concerning prostitutes, ‘Such are your daughters.’ ‘It is an insult,’ he says. Why is it an insult, unless because that is iniquity? Why is it an insult, unless because that is disgrace? Therefore, when you give, you do not give to strength but to disgrace.

“Thus the person who gives to a hunter gives not to a human being but to a most wicked profession. For if he were merely a human being and were not a hunter, you would not give to him. You honor the vice in him, not his nature.

“By contrast, if you give something to a righteous person, to a prophet, or to a disciple of Christ who needs it, and do not consider there that he is a disciple of Christ or a minister of God…”

Let those, therefore, who devote themselves to hunting consider that they ought to care more for themselves than to serve such pursuits, and that they ought to care more for the poor and their own servants than for dogs. In no way, then, should the care of dogs be preferred by Christ’s faithful to the care of a human being created in the image of God.

Having said these things, it remains necessary to speak about gamblers. Let gamblers know that, as blessed Cyprian, the distinguished martyr, writes, while they serve others, they commit sin. He so condemns and detests that activity that he declares it to be the devil’s snare, and he announces that it must be avoided by all the faithful in every way. For when he had written at length about gamblers, he concluded:

“Do not play at dice. There the game is harmful and a mortal sin; there is madness without reflection; there is no truth, but a company of lies. Cut off your hand from there, and turn your heart away from there. Remove the enemy’s darkness from your eyes.”

And below:

“Be just and prudent toward yourself and your life in your actions. Flee the devil who pursues you, and flee dice, the enemy of your possessions. Let wisdom be your pursuit; be instructed by evangelical admonitions; stretch out pure hands to Christ, so that you may be able to win the Lord’s favor. Do not look at dice.”

Whoever wishes to know more fully about this matter should read the complete address that the same holy man composed on it. There he will certainly discover how much that activity must be rejected by every Christian.

For I know what lovers of dice say: “What evil do we do, or what sin do we commit, if we play at dice?” They must be answered that sin is committed in the same game in many ways. First, because it is scarcely conducted without lying, perjury, anger, or discord. But even if someone happens to commit none of these sins, he undoubtedly sins in this one respect: he serves idleness, which is the enemy of the soul.

Know, therefore, whoever you are, O gambler, that you will have to render an account to God for each day and hour that you spend serving dice.

I also know that many will answer this with turbulent indignation: “What good is this world to a secular person,” they will say, “if he does not enjoy these and the many other kinds of games that have been discovered to satisfy his desires?”

To them I answer with the words of the Lord: “What does it profit a person if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul?” (Matt. 16:26). It is clear, however, that while one serves dice, no gain for the soul is acquired from it.

Let such people also hear the Apostle John warning and saying: “Do not love the world or the things that are in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him, because everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life, which is not from the Father but from the world. And the world is passing away, together with its desire; but whoever does the will of God remains forever” (1 John 2:15–18).

Let them also hear James: “Whoever wishes to be a friend of this world will be constituted an enemy of God” (Jas. 4:4).

Since, then, love of the world is so prohibited by the Apostles, why are fleeting and smoky things loved with such empty affection? Why is the world loved so greatly, when it will not be possessed for long? Why is love of what passes away preferred to love of the eternal kingdom? Thus a Christian should love the world in such a way that, when it falls, the Christian does not fall with it.

## CHAPTER XXIV. The necessity of judging justly and avoiding the acceptance of gifts

There are people who use good things well, and, conversely, there are people who use good things badly. Whoever uses God’s gifts not according to God’s will but according to his own desire, proving himself ungrateful to God, is shown to use good things badly.

There is no doubt that the knowledge of judging rightly is bestowed by God upon mortals, as the Apostle James testifies and says: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (Jas. 1:17). Therefore whoever is turned aside from the path of justice—which gives each person his due—by fear, desire, hatred, or love is certainly convicted of dishonoring Christ, who is justice.

For just as it is fair that one who thinks rightly should act rightly, so it is unjust to think rightly and not act rightly. A kingdom is established through justice and overthrown through injustice; hence many kingdoms already overturned by injustice stand as examples.

Since both the legal and evangelical writings teach that God dwells among those who obey his admonitions and do not deviate from the path of justice, why do human beings—whom he created in his own image, enriched with nobility, and elevated with the knowledge of judging rightly—drive him away from their midst by judging wrongly?

Those who drive him away from themselves by judging perversely undoubtedly establish the enemy of their salvation in their midst. For just as those who pursue justice and truth cling to Christ, so those who judge unjustly in place of justly and falsely in place of truly, without doubt, in some way enslave themselves to the one who is a liar and the father of it.

What could be more unjust and more hateful to God than when, in the courts, love of money is pursued more than Christ? For those who accept money for judging rightly sell Christ, who is justice, like Judas, after receiving payment. Likewise, the person who judges falsely for the sake of something, and the person who conceals the truth, is hateful to God and held guilty before him of an almost equal offense.

Therefore those who are endowed with judicial power need great caution and vigilance, lest right judgment be overturned in any way by them or before them. For if, through their negligence and prolonged leisure, and through the various pleasures to which they devote themselves more than is right, the cause of the poor is disregarded and the equity of judgment is often violated, whatever crooked and unjust act has been committed will undoubtedly be charged against them.

That judgment must be rendered rightly, with partiality toward neither persons nor gifts, is indicated by what follows. It is written in Exodus:

“You shall not turn aside in judgment against the poor. You shall flee falsehood. You shall not kill the innocent and the just, for I abhor the wicked; nor shall you accept gifts, which blind even the prudent and subvert the words of the just” (Exod. 23:3, 7–8).

The same book also says: “You shall not despise the poor in judgment.”

In Leviticus:

“You shall do nothing unjust; you shall not judge unjustly; you shall not consider the person of the poor, nor honor the face of the powerful. Judge your neighbor justly” (Lev. 19:15).

And there:

“You shall not commit anything unjust in judgment, in rule, in weight, or in measure. Let the balance and the weights be just and equal; let the measure be just and the sextarius equal. I am the Lord your God.”

In Deuteronomy Moses said—without doubt addressing judges:

“Command them, saying: Hear them and judge what is just, whether he is a citizen or a foreigner; there shall be no distinction of persons. You shall hear the small as well as the great, and you shall not accept anyone’s person, because judgment belongs to God” (Deut. 1:17).

Also:

“You shall appoint judges and magistrates in all your gates that the Lord your God gives you, throughout each of your tribes, so that they may judge the people with righteous judgment and not incline to either side. They shall not accept persons or gifts, for gifts blind the eyes of the wise and alter the words of the just. You shall pursue justice, and justice alone.”

The same book also says: “Cursed is the one who perverts the judgment of the foreigner” (ibid. 27:19).

In the Second Book of Chronicles:

“Jehoshaphat appointed judges in the land, in all the fortified cities, city by city, and he commanded the judges: ‘Consider what you are doing. For you do not exercise the judgment of a human being, but of the Lord, and whatever judgment you render will return upon you. Let the fear of the Lord be with you, and perform everything carefully. For with the Lord our God there is no iniquity, no partiality, and no desire for gifts’” (2 Chron. 19:5–7).

In the Psalms:

“If indeed you speak justice, judge rightly, sons of men” (Ps. 58:1).

Also:

“Judge the needy and the orphan; justify the humble and the poor” (ibid. 82:3).

In Proverbs:

“Let mercy and truth not abandon you” (Prov. 3:3 and following).

Also:

“The wicked accepts gifts from his bosom in order to pervert the paths of judgment.”

And there:

“Whoever considers the face of a person in judgment does not act well.”

And there:

“To practice mercy and judgment pleases the Lord more than sacrifices.”

And there:

“To accept the person of the wicked is not good in judgment.”

Also:

“Whoever justifies the wicked and condemns the just is hateful to God.”

Also:

“The just person knows the cause of the poor; the wicked does not understand knowledge.”

In Isaiah:

“Woe to those who justify the wicked for gifts, and take away the justice of the just from him; woe to those who devise unjust laws and, writing, write injustices, in order to oppress the poor in judgment and do violence to the cause of the humble among my people, so that widows may become their prey and they may plunder orphans. What will you do on the day of visitation and calamity?” (Isa. 5:23 and following).

Also:

“Thus says the Lord: Keep judgment and practice justice, for my salvation is near, that it may come, and my justice, that it may be revealed. Blessed is the person who does this, and the son of man who holds fast to it; who keeps the sabbath, so as not to profane it, and keeps his hands from doing any evil.”

In Zechariah:

“These are the words that you shall do: Speak truth, each one with his neighbor; judge truth and the judgment of peace in your gates. And let none of you devise evil against his friend in your hearts, and do not love a false oath. For all these are things that I hate, says the Lord” (Zech. 8:16, 17).

It is written in Job:

“The assembly of the hypocrite is barren, and fire will devour the tents of those who willingly accept gifts” (Job 15:34).

In the Gospel:

“Do not judge, and you will not be judged; do not condemn, and you will not be condemned. For with the judgment with which you judge, you will be judged” (Matt. 7:1–2).

John, in his Epistle, says:

“Do not judge according to appearance, but judge a just judgment” (John 7:24).

Gregory, in the *Moralia*:

“The judges of this world endure many injuries for earthly profits, yet for heavenly reward they refuse to bear insults even for the slightest word. They are strong enough to devote the entire day to earthly judgment, but in prayer before the Lord they grow weary after a single hour.

“Often some judges desire earthly rewards and defend justice; they consider themselves innocent and rejoice that they are defenders of uprightness. But if the hope of money is taken away from them, they immediately cease defending justice. Yet they imagine themselves defenders of justice and assert themselves to be its guardians, although they seek not uprightness but money.”

Isidore, in the book of the *Sentences*:

[Book III, chapter 54.]

“It belongs to the offense of rulers when they place wicked judges over faithful peoples contrary to the will of God. For just as it is the people’s sin when their rulers are wicked, so it is the ruler’s sin when judges are unjust.”

The same:

[Chapter 55.]

“The poor are torn apart more grievously by wicked judges than by the most bloodthirsty enemies. For no plunderer is so greedy for what belongs to others as an unjust judge is for what belongs to his own.”

And shortly afterward:

“Often judges destroy, by accepting gifts, the very justice that they undertake in order to obtain eternal salvation. And when they seek temporal profits from just judgment, they are deprived of the eternal reward.”

The same:

[Chapter 38.]

“Whoever judges rightly and expects a reward for it commits fraud against God, because he sells for money the justice that he ought to have bestowed freely.”

And shortly afterward:

“There are three forms of accepting gifts by which human vanity wars against justice: the favor of friendship, the flattery of praise, and the acceptance of a bodily gift.”

The same, a little later:

“Human judgment is perverted in four ways: by fear, desire, hatred, and love. By fear, when we are afraid to speak the truth because we dread someone’s power; by desire, when we are corrupted by the reward of a gift; by hatred, when we contrive adversity against someone; by love, when we strive to favor a friend or relative. In these four ways equity is often violated and innocence often harmed.”

Many other commands of divine authority concerning the pursuit of justice and avoidance of the acceptance of gifts also exist. Everyone who has undertaken the office of judging rightly must carefully weigh and consider them, and strive both to live rightly and to judge rightly according to them.

Let him therefore beware lest, after accepting money, he sell Christ; lest, for the sake of earthly profit, he deprive himself of eternal reward. Let him always place God’s judgments before his eyes, fearing and trembling lest, by deviating from the path of justice, he fall and be condemned precisely where he ought to have been justified.

## CHAPTER XXV. Concerning the avoidance of oaths

Although, as the Apostle James testifies, we all offend in many ways, both orders—clerical and lay—and indeed both sexes, sin greatly and miserably through careless oath-taking. Some think that only the person who swears falsely by the bones of some holy man, or by relics, or by an altar, or by the Gospels, is liable to the crime of perjury; but that the person who calls God as witness for any matter, great or small, and does not hesitate to swear by the Holy Trinity and the citizens above, should be considered free from perjury.

Yet everyone who calls upon God as witness is proved to swear, as blessed Augustine says in his book of sermons:

[Note: Sermon on the Beheading of Saint John, chapter 3.]

The Lord also says in the Law:

“You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain, for the Lord will not hold him innocent who takes the name of his God in vain” (Exod. 20:7).

And the prophet Zechariah:

“Do not love a false oath” (Zech. 8:17).

And Solomon:

“Do not accustom your mouth to swearing” (Ecclus. 23:9).

Also:

“Whoever swears much will not escape sin.”

Also:

“A man who swears much will be filled with iniquity, and punishment will not depart from his house” (ibid. 23:12).

And in the Gospel:

“You have heard that it was said to the ancients, ‘You shall fulfill your oaths to the Lord.’ But I say to you, do not swear at all, neither by heaven, because it is the throne of God; nor by the earth, because it is the footstool of his feet; nor by your head, because you cannot make one hair white or black. Let your speech be ‘Yes, yes; no, no.’ Whatever is more than these comes from evil” (Matt. 5:33–34).

Augustine, *On the Sermon on the Mount*:

[Book I, chapter 17.]

“Thus the Lord is understood to have commanded that one should not swear, so that no one might seek an oath as though it were a good thing and, through the habit of swearing frequently, slip into perjury. Therefore the person who understands that an oath belongs not among good things but among necessities should restrain himself as much as he can, so that he may not use it except under necessity, when he sees that people are slow to believe what it is useful for them to believe unless it is confirmed by an oath.

“To this belongs what is said: ‘Let your speech be “Yes, yes; no, no.”’ This is good and desirable. ‘Whatever is more than these comes from evil’ (Matt. 5:37). That is, if you are compelled to swear, know that this arises from the weakness of those whom you persuade of something. That weakness is certainly an evil; hence we pray daily to be delivered from it when we say: ‘Deliver us from evil’ (ibid. 6:13).

“Thus he said: ‘Whatever is more than these comes from evil’ (Luke 11:4). But you do not do evil when you make good use of an oath. Although an oath is not good, it is nevertheless necessary in order that you may persuade another of something which you rightly persuade him of. But it comes from the evil of the person whose weakness compels you to swear.

“Yet no one knows, except the person who has experienced it, how difficult it is both to extinguish the habit of swearing and never to do rashly what necessity sometimes compels one to do.

“Someone may ask: When he said, ‘But I say to you, do not swear at all,’ why did he add, ‘Neither by heaven, because it is God’s throne,’ and the rest, up to what is said, ‘Nor by your head’ (Matt. 5:34)?

“I believe it was because the Jews did not think themselves bound by an oath if they had sworn by these things. And because they had heard, ‘You shall fulfill your oath to the Lord’ (ibid. 5:33), they did not think that they owed an oath to the Lord if they swore by heaven, or earth, or Jerusalem, or by their own head. This happened not through any fault in the one giving the command, but through the misunderstanding of the one who understood it badly.

“Thus the Lord teaches that nothing among God’s creatures is so insignificant that anyone may consider it permissible to swear falsely by it, since divine providence governs all created things, from the highest to the lowest, beginning with God’s throne and extending even to a white or black hair. ‘Neither by heaven,’ he says, ‘because it is God’s throne; nor by the earth, which is the footstool of his feet’” (ibid. 5:35).

Again, the same author in the Book of Sermons [Note: [Col. 0222D] On the Words of the Apostle, Sermon 28, chapter 2]:

“There are generally more oaths than words. If a person were to consider how often he swears throughout the entire day, how often he wounds himself, how often he strikes and pierces his tongue with a sword, what healthy place would be found in him? Since, therefore, perjury is a grave sin, Scripture has given you a shortcut: ‘Do not swear’ (James 5:12).”

Again:

“Do you therefore wish to be far from perjury? Do not swear. For one who swears can sometimes swear to the truth; but one who does not swear can never swear falsely. Let God swear, who swears safely, whom nothing deceives, from whom nothing is hidden, who altogether knows not how to deceive, since he cannot be deceived. For when he swears, he makes himself a witness. Just as you make God a witness when you swear, so he makes himself a witness when he swears. When you call him as witness, perhaps over your lie you take in vain the name of the Lord your God. Therefore, lest you swear to a lie, do not swear. This is the narrow way: perjury is a precipice. The one who swears is near it; the one who does not swear is far away. He who swears falsely sins, and sins grievously; he who swears truthfully does not sin; nor does he sin who does not swear at all. But the one who does not swear both does not sin and is far from sin; the one who swears truthfully does not sin, but is near sin—near the transition from sin to sin.”

Again (chapter 6):

“Pay attention, I beg you, and take heed. Do not let those deceive you who, I do not know how, wishing to distinguish oaths—or rather, not understanding them—say that it is not an oath when a person says: ‘God knows’; ‘God is my witness’; ‘I call God to witness over my soul that I am telling the truth.’ ‘He invoked God,’ they say; ‘he made God his witness. Did he swear?’ Those who say this want nothing else than to lie after invoking God as their witness. What! Are you a person of a depraved and perverse heart, if you say, ‘By God,’ and you swear, but if you say, ‘God is my witness,’ you do not swear? For what is ‘By God’ except ‘God is my witness’? Or what is ‘God is my witness’ except ‘By God’?”

Again:

“But if you were doing something in the presence of your son as witness, and said to a friend, neighbor, or any other person, ‘I did not do it,’ and touched the head of your son, in whose presence you had done it, saying, ‘By the life of this child, I did not do it,’ your son might cry out, trembling beneath his father’s hand—not fearing his father’s hand, but the divine hand: ‘Do not, father! Do not regard my life as worthless. You have invoked God over me. I saw you; you did it. Do not commit perjury. I regard you as my father, but I fear even more my Creator and yours’” (chapter 7).

“But because God, when you swear by him, does not say to you, ‘I saw you; you did it; do not swear,’ you fear that he may kill you, and you kill yourself beforehand. Since, therefore, he does not say, ‘I saw you,’ you think that he did not see. And what of the words: ‘I kept silent, I kept silent; shall I always be silent?’”

Again (chapter 8):

“Hear briefly, my brothers. I shall conclude the sermon, fixing a salutary concern in your hearts: above all, do not swear.”

Again (chapter 10):

“Therefore, restrain your tongue and your habit as much as you can—not like certain people who, when they are told, ‘You are telling the truth? I do not believe you. You did not do it? I do not believe you. May God judge; swear to me,’ demand an oath. It makes a great difference whether the one who demands the oath does not know that the other is going to swear falsely, or knows it. If he does not know, and therefore says, ‘Swear to me,’ so that he may believe him, I do not dare to say that it is not a sin; nevertheless, it is a human temptation. But if he knows that the other did it—knows that he did it, saw that he did it—and compels him to swear, he is a murderer. The other kills himself by his perjury; but this man both puts forward and presses the hand of the killer.”

Again (chapter 11):

“For an oath contains so much evil that those who worship stones fear to swear falsely by stones. Do you not fear the God who is present, the living God, the God who knows, the God who remains, the God who takes vengeance on the one who despises him? The idolater shuts the temple over the stone and goes away to his house; he shuts it over his own house, and yet, when someone says to him, ‘Swear by Jupiter,’ he fears the eyes of the one who is present.”

And again (chapter 12):

“Behold, I say to your charity: he who swears falsely by a stone is perjured. Why do I say this? Because many are deceived even in this matter and think that, since there is nothing by which they swear, they are not held guilty of perjury. You are altogether perjured if you swear falsely by that which you regard as sacred. But I do not regard that as sacred. You regard as sacred the one by whom you swear. For when you swear, you do not swear to yourself, nor do you swear to the stone—no, but you swear to your neighbor. You swear to a human being before the stone; but are you not also before God? The stone does not hear you speaking, but God punishes you for deceiving.”

Bede, in his Exposition of the Canonical Epistles [Note: [Col. 0223D] On the exposition of the Epistle of James, chapter 5, verse 12]:

“He who forbade slander against another, who forbade judging one’s neighbor, who prohibited mutual lamentation in adversity—these being manifest sins—also added this, which seems trivial to some: that he should abolish the habit of swearing as well. For this too plainly appears not to be regarded as insignificant by those who carefully consider the Lord’s statement in which he says: ‘For every idle word that people speak, they will give an account of it on the day of judgment’ (Matthew 12:36), ‘so that you may not fall under judgment.’ ‘Therefore,’ he says, ‘I restrain you from the fault of swearing, lest by frequently swearing even to the truth you fall into perjury, but rather stand farther from the vice of perjury by being unwilling to swear even to the truth except in the most immediate necessity.’”

Isidore, in the Book of Sentences (Book II, chapter 31):

“We therefore say that an oath must be avoided and must not be used except in necessity alone. It is not contrary to God’s command to swear; but by making a practice of swearing we incur the crime of perjury. Therefore, let the one who fears perjury never swear. Many people delight in swearing whenever they speak, although these words alone ought to be in their mouths: ‘Yes, yes; No, no.’ For anything beyond ‘Yes’ and ‘No’ is from evil (Matthew 5:37).

“Many commit perjury in order to deceive, so that by the trustworthiness of an oath they may lend credibility to their words; and thus, while deceiving through perjury and lying, they mislead the unwary person. Sometimes we are also deceived by false tears, and people are believed while they weep who ought not to have been believed. Often we intend to speak without an oath, but because of the unbelief of those who do not believe what we say, we are compelled to swear; and through such necessity of swearing we form a habit. There are many slow to believe, who are not moved to faith in a person’s word. But those who compel people speaking to them to swear commit a grave offense.

“However someone may swear by any verbal device, God, who is the witness of the conscience, receives it in the manner understood by the one to whom the oath is given. The person who both takes God’s name in vain and deceives his neighbor by fraud is guilty in two ways. An oath that carelessly promises something evil must not be kept—for example, if someone were to promise an adulteress perpetual fidelity to remain with her. It is more tolerable not to fulfill such an oath than to persist in the disgrace of fornication.”

Thus, clear testimonies establish that one ought not to accept oaths indiscriminately, as many are accustomed to do; nor ought one to use even an oath that is free from sin except in necessity alone, lest, while it is employed too frequently, one slip into the crime of perjury.

## CHAPTER XXVI  
### On False Testimony

Among the Ten Commandments that the Lord gave to the Israelite people on Mount Sinai through his servant Moses, he expressly prohibited false testimony: “You shall not bear false witness” (Luke 18:20). The just Lord therefore taught that justice should be loved and forbade falsehood to be uttered. Consider what sort of decree the King of kings, the Lord of lords, and Creator of all things proposed for mortals to observe. Amid flames of fire, flashing lightning, the crash of thunder, and the blare of the trumpet, he solemnly proclaimed this law, by which evil is forbidden and good commanded, by which truth is to be pursued and falsehood avoided. What is greatly to be feared and dreaded is nevertheless despised, because transgression of this commandment of the Lord has become so habitual among some that they almost frequent it as though it were a law; and when they utter it, they think they are committing little or no offense unless they confirm by oath that what they have falsely stated is true.

Such people certainly deceive themselves with a vain hope. Let them therefore see that in his holy law the Lord expressly prohibited false testimony, expressly prohibited perjury, and expressly prohibited lying. Whoever, then, transgresses any one of these is without doubt a violator of the Lord’s commandment. Those who set falsehood against justice are like the false witnesses who, at Christ’s passion, gave false testimony against him.

It is an exceedingly mournful matter that some people regard nothing as cheaper—or rather, nothing as more saleable—in this mortal life than their own souls. When they receive various sums of money and gorge themselves with gluttony and drunkenness even to the point of vomiting in order to utter falsehood, what else are they doing but making their souls available for sale? They sell a great thing for a paltry price. What they receive is smoky and momentary; what they lose is eternal and destined to remain without end. It is truly a wretched bargain when someone, in exchange for another person’s coins, food, and drink, hands his soul over to the devil.

Nor should the person who, unwilling to be justly defeated, to lose what he unjustly retains, or to incur public shame and suffer a small legal loss, corrupts such witnesses with various gifts—and, as commonly happens, also drives them into perjury—consider himself in any way secure from their destruction. Let him know for certain that before the Lord he will be held guilty for all the souls whom he has led either into falsehood or into perjury. Therefore, careful and extremely exact investigation is necessary for judges, so that, following the example of the prophet Daniel, they may examine false witnesses separately and be able to recognize what is lawful, what is true, and what is false.

False witnesses are also commanded to be diligently investigated in the Book of Deuteronomy:

“If a lying witness rises against someone, accusing him of wrongdoing, both parties whose case it is shall stand before the Lord, in the presence of the priests and the judges who are in office in those days. When, after very careful investigation, they discover that the witness has testified falsely against his brother, declaring a lie, they shall do to him as he intended to do to his brother, and you shall remove the evil from your midst. When the others hear, they will fear and will never again dare to do such a thing, and you shall not pity him” (Deuteronomy 19:18).

Solomon also says concerning false witnesses: “A false witness will not go unpunished” (Proverbs 19:5, 9). Elsewhere God says that he hates a deceitful witness and one who utters lies for gifts (ibid., 6:19).” [Note: [Col. 0225D] “A lie for gifts.” I have preferred to emend the text in this way, since what was previously read, *admunerat*, was altogether nonsensical.]

Bede also, in his exposition of Luke (chapter 22, verse 5):

“Many people today recoil from Judas’s crime—his selling the Lord, his Master and his God—as monstrous and abominable, yet they do not take care to avoid it. For when they give false testimony against anyone in exchange for gifts, they plainly sell God for money, because they deny the truth in place of justice. He himself said: ‘I am the truth’ (John 14:6).

“Even when no one gives them money, they sell the Lord for silver, because they take upon themselves the image of the prince of this world—that is, the examples of the ancient enemy—while neglecting the image of the Creator, in whose image they were made. For just as John the Baptist, who died not for confessing Christ but for defending the truth, nevertheless accepted martyrdom for Christ because he accepted it for the truth, so, conversely, whoever despises the rights of charity and truth certainly betrays Christ, who is truth and charity. This is especially so when he does not sin through weakness or the intrusion of ignorance, but, like Judas, seeks an opportunity, with the arbiters absent, to exchange truth for falsehood and virtue for crime.”

Isidore, in the Book of Sentences (Book III, chapter 59):

“A deceitful witness is liable to three persons: first to God, whom he despises by committing perjury; next to the judge, whom he deceives by lying; and finally to the innocent person whom he injures by false testimony. When false witnesses have been convicted, the falsity of their lie is discovered only with difficulty; but if they are examined separately, it is quickly revealed by the judge’s investigation.”

Behold: a brief collection has shown how abominable and hateful to God false testimony is. Judges must therefore strive carefully and vigilantly to hear the causes of judgment patiently, examine them diligently, and decide with a just balance, lest anyone be unjustly deprived by them or before them either of liberty or of any possessions.

Those who, through acceptance of gifts or for the sake of anything else, by judging unjustly and giving false testimony consign people to slavery or cause them to be unjustly deprived of their possessions acquire for themselves a great accumulation of condemnation. For they harm not only those who are alive in the present, but also transmit the same injustice to their descendants in the future.

## CHAPTER XXVII  
### On Lying

The entire sequence of the Old and New Testaments demonstrates that every lie must be avoided. Many people become involved in it lamentably under compulsion, and many voluntarily, without suspecting that they are committing an offense, although Scripture says: “The mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wisdom 1:11). Elsewhere: “You will destroy all who speak lies” (Psalm 5:7). And in the Law the Lord forbids it: “You shall not lie, and no one shall deceive his neighbor” (Leviticus 19:11).

Solomon says: “Whoever lies is a deceitful witness, but a hasty witness fashions a tongue of falsehood” (Proverbs 12:17). “The tongue of lying is an abomination” (ibid., 19). “A faithful witness delivers souls, but the deceitful person utters lies” (Proverbs 14:25). “A faithful witness will not lie, but a deceitful witness brings forth lies” (ibid., 5). Jesus son of Sirach says: “Do not lie with every lie; for its continual practice is not good” (Ecclesiasticus 7:14). In the Gospel: “Every lie is from the devil.” And the Apostle says: “Putting away lying, speak the truth, each one with his neighbor” (Ephesians 4:25). Again: “Do not lie to one another” (Colossians 3:9).

Augustine, in his Book Against Lying (chapter 14):

“The first and capital lie, which must be avoided by a great distance, is the lie committed in teaching religion; no one should be led to this lie under any condition. The second is one that unjustly harms someone, being such that it benefits no one and harms someone. The third is one that benefits one person while harming another, although not harming him with bodily impurity.
