The fourth is committed solely from the desire to lie and to do so; this is lying in the strict sense. The fifth is committed from the desire to please, through agreeable speech.

“After all these have been entirely avoided and rejected, there follows the sixth kind, which harms no one and benefits someone—for example, if someone, knowing where another person’s money is that is unjustly sought, pretends not to know where it is. The seventh is one that harms no one and benefits someone—for example, when a person unwilling to betray someone sought for execution lies, whether that person is just and innocent or guilty, because it belongs to Christian discipline neither to despair of anyone’s correction nor to close the way of repentance to anyone.

“We have treated sufficiently these two kinds, which commonly give rise to great controversy, and have shown what seems right to us: that these kinds too should be avoided by strong, faithful, and truthful men and women, by accepting hardships that can be honorably and courageously endured.”

Therefore, one must not lie to someone asking where a person is who has entrusted himself to one’s faith. Rather, one should answer:

(Chapter 13.) “I will neither betray him nor lie. This was done by the sometime bishop of the Church of Tagaste, Firmus by name, firmer in will. When a man who had fled to him and whom he was concealing with all the care he could was sought by the emperor’s order through officials sent by the emperor, he replied to those asking that he could neither lie nor betray the man. He endured many bodily tortures—for the emperors were not yet Christians—and remained steadfast in his position. Then, when he was brought before the emperor, he appeared so admirable that he himself obtained without difficulty a pardon for the man whom Firmus had protected. What could be stronger or more steadfast than this?

(Chapter 14.) The eighth kind of lie is one that harms no one and is useful for protecting someone from bodily impurity. One must not, therefore, lie in teaching piety. For this is a great crime and the first kind of detestable lie.”

(Chapter 21):

“One must not lie in the second manner, because no one may be wronged. One must not lie in the third manner, because no one should be helped through another person’s injury. One must not lie in the fourth manner, because the desire to lie is itself vicious. One must not lie in the fifth manner, because even truth should not be spoken merely to please people; how much more should one avoid a lie, which is shameful in itself precisely because it is a lie!

“One must not lie in the sixth manner. For even the truth of testimony must not rightly be corrupted for anyone’s temporal advantage or safety. No one may be led to eternal salvation with the assistance of a lie. No one should be converted to good morals by the evil morals of those converting him, since what ought to be done toward him he himself, once converted, ought to do toward others. Thus he will be converted not to good but to evil morals, when he is given as an example for his conduct after conversion what was done to him in order to convert him.

“Nor should one lie in the seventh manner. No person’s temporal advantage or safety should be preferred to the completion of faith. Nor, if someone is so badly disturbed by our rightly performed deeds that he becomes worse in spirit and much farther removed from piety, should we on that account abandon right actions. We must especially keep before us the goal toward which we ought to call and invite those whom we love as ourselves. With the greatest courage we must drink in the Apostle’s statement: ‘To some we are the fragrance of life leading to life, and to others the fragrance of death leading to death’ (2 Corinthians 2:2). And who is sufficient for these things?

“Nor should one lie in the eighth manner, because among good things there is purity of spirit and chastity of body, while among evil things what we ourselves do is worse than what we permit to be done. In these eight kinds, a person sins less by lying the more he rises toward the eighth, and sins more the more he rises toward the first. Whoever thinks that there is any kind of lie that is not sin deceives himself shamefully, considering himself an honorable deceiver of others.”

Isidore, in the Book of Sentences (Book II, chapter 3):

“Liars cause even those who speak the truth not to be believed. For much falsehood often makes a person suspect even when he speaks the truth. Someone who is about to speak falsely often begins with truths, so that, having first acquired credibility, he may make his hearers trusting toward the remaining lies. Many things that are false seem true to people; and therefore they speak not from God but from their own lie. Sometimes falsehood is joined to truth-speaking, and often the person who fabricates falsehood begins with truth.”

A little later:

“Every lie must be avoided with the greatest care. Yet if anyone lies for the sake of human salvation, this kind of lie is never without some lesser degree of fault. But because it is written, ‘The mouth that lies kills the soul’ (Wisdom 1:11), and, ‘You will destroy all who speak lies’ (Psalm 5:7), even this kind of lie is assiduously avoided by perfect men, so that neither anyone’s life may be defended through their deceit nor may they harm their own souls while striving to benefit another’s flesh. Nevertheless, we readily believe that this particular kind of sin is easily forgiven. For if any fault is cleansed by a subsequent reward, how much more easily is this one wiped away, when the reward itself accompanies it!”

That every lie must therefore be avoided is abundantly clear. Accordingly, each person must strive to avoid this vice. Whoever is enslaved to it must abandon it completely, return to the lamentations of repentance, and not neglect to confess it to God and to a priest among the other sins he has committed.

## CHAPTER XXVIII  
### On Curiosity

Many people knowingly, and many unknowingly, fall into the vice of curiosity. While serving it, a person lamentably neglects himself. We ought to mourn the evils we ourselves have committed, not inquisitively investigate and criticize with the bite of detraction the errors of others—errors that we neither wish nor are able to correct.

There are, to be sure, pious deeds of certain people that we ought carefully to examine and take as examples of good action. There are also deeds of certain people that, while unknown to us, bring us no danger and, once known, no benefit. But when we spend our days inquisitively examining such matters, we certainly commit an offense. Many canons and monks suffer from this vice, neglecting their own vocation.

There are also many laypeople who occupy themselves pleasurably with this kind of curiosity almost from morning until evening, either failing to understand that they are sinning or refusing to understand it. They must consider what happened to Dinah, daughter of Jacob. Led by curiosity, she went out to see the women of a foreign region; Shechem, son of Hamor, became enamored of her, seized her, violated her by force, and was joined to her in a detestable [union; text defective] (Genesis 34:1). [Note: [Col. 0229D] “Joined to her in a detestable …” Acherius says that either a linking word (*copula*) or *commercio* (“intercourse”) is missing; I prefer the former.]

“For Dinah,” as blessed Gregory writes in the Pastoral Book (Part III, chapter 30), “goes out to see the women of a foreign region when each mind, neglecting its own pursuits, attends to the actions of others and wanders outside its own bounds and proper order. Shechem, the prince of the land, violates her, because the devil corrupts a mind when he finds it occupied with external concerns.”

Many other teachings of the divine Scriptures exist that demonstrate that the vice of curiosity must be avoided. A few of them are briefly appended here. Jesus son of Sirach says: “Do not investigate unnecessary matters, lest they be multiplied” (Ecclesiasticus 3:24). “It is not necessary for you to see with your eyes the things that are hidden” (Ecclesiasticus 3:23). “Do not quarrel over a matter that does not trouble you” (ibid., 11:9).

In the Book of Ecclesiastes he also says: “Do not apply your heart to all the words that are spoken, lest perhaps you hear your servant cursing you; for your conscience knows that you yourself have often cursed others” (Ecclesiastes 7:22).

Prosper says: [Note: [Col. 0229D] Or Julianus Pomerius, On the Contemplative Life, chapter 6.]

“For as long as a person remains inquisitively occupied with the sins of others, he remains unaware of his own sins, which he ought to know and mourn. But if, returning to himself, he observes his own conduct, he should not seek what he may specially criticize in others, but rather what he may mourn in himself. Therefore, we ought not readily to accuse the vices of our brothers, but to lament them, so that, bearing one another’s burdens, we may fulfill the law of Christ.”

Gregory, in his exposition of the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0230D] Homily 36]:

“Another said: ‘I have bought five yoke of oxen, and I am going to test them; I ask you to hold me excused’ (Luke 14:19). What do we understand by the five yoke of oxen except the five bodily senses? They are rightly called yokes because they are doubled in the two sexes. These bodily senses, since they cannot grasp inward things but know only external things, and since, abandoning what is within, they touch what is outside, rightly signify curiosity. For, while curiosity seeks to scrutinize another’s life, it is always ignorant of its own inward state and strives to think about external matters.

“Curiosity is a grave vice. While it leads a person’s mind outward to investigate the life of his neighbor, it always conceals his own inward state from him, so that, knowing what belongs to another, he does not know himself. The more the mind of the curious person has become knowledgeable about another’s merit, the more ignorant it becomes of its own.

“For this reason it is said concerning those five yoke of oxen: ‘I am going to test them; I ask you to hold me excused.’ The very words of the person making excuses agree with the meaning of his vice when he says, ‘I am going to test them,’ because testing sometimes belongs to curiosity.”

You also have, in the little book called the *Synonyma* [Note: [Col. 0230D] Book II of the *Synonyma*, chapter 15, on curiosity, though in different words]:

“Do not seek what does not concern you. Never desire to know what people say among themselves. Do not ask what each person says or does. Avoid curiosity. Abandon concern for what does not belong to your own case. Curiosity is a dangerous presumption. Many discern the vices of others but do not look at their own.”

It is therefore clear that all Christians must avoid the vice of curiosity with the greatest care. Since the Lord will demand from us the fruit of good action concerning each period of time in which we ought to have spoken and acted, every believer must make himself entirely free from such curiosities and from investigating unnecessary matters.

## CHAPTER XXIX  
### On the Pursuit of Hospitality

Although hospitality is briefly mentioned in the Gospel among the six works of mercy, longer testimonies nevertheless remain to be collected in this chapter for the sake of certain people who neglect it.

Among the many practices contrary to the Christian religion that the arbitrary choices of some have introduced into custom, so that they seem to persist in them as though they were laws, hospitality—an eminent and supremely excellent work of mercy among Christians—is neglected by so many that, in this matter as in several others, the glory of Christianity is greatly darkened. For some regard it so lightly that, although they possess large and spacious houses, they scarcely deign to receive a stranger under their roof—or rather, Christ in the stranger—who says in the Gospel: “I was a stranger, and you welcomed me” (Matthew 25:35).

Nor do they receive travelers lacking lodging into their houses in any other way unless an agreement is first established concerning what they must pay for the ground alone, for each vessel, for the fire that has been lit, and for countless other things that they may use. Indeed, if it happens that they first appear to receive them graciously and with a pretended act of charity without such an agreement, afterward they afflict them with such harassment that they do not cease until they compel them to give what they greedily demand.

Such conduct is so contrary to the Christian religion that whoever persists in this vice, although a disciple of Christ in name, is not one in deed. He will not deserve to be called blessed by that same Christ on the day of the fearful judgment—unless he corrects himself before the final day closes—since Christ says in the Gospel: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom, because I was a stranger and you welcomed me,” and so forth (ibid., 34).

With what confidence does the person who refused to receive Christ in strangers await the day of judgment? The inhuman will therefore hear: “Depart into eternal fire” (ibid., 41). The humane and benevolent, however, will hear: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (ibid., 34). Behold what blessing those who pursue hospitality will receive. For this is why we Christians have been called: “that, as blessed Peter the Apostle testifies, we may inherit the same blessing” (1 Peter 3:9).

Whoever fears being deprived of that blessing must devote himself to hospitality during this pilgrimage. The following passages briefly indicate how it must be pursued.

The prophet Isaiah says: “Bring the wandering strangers into your house” (Isaiah 58:7).

Job says: “The stranger did not remain outside; my door was open to the traveler” (Job 31:32).

And in the Gospel: “I was a stranger, and you welcomed me” (Matthew 25:35).

Peter says: “Pursuing hospitality.”

Paul says: “Let brotherly charity remain among you” (Romans 12:13). And: “Do not neglect hospitality” (Hebrews 13:1).

Ambrose, in the first book On Abraham (Book V):

“Learn how eager you ought to be, so that you may anticipate hospitality and no one else may anticipate you and deprive you of the opportunity for a good work. For it is not enough to do what is right unless you also do it promptly; devotion hastened has richer fruits.

“Hospitality is good. It has its reward: first, human goodwill; then—and this is more important—the reward of divine recompense. We are all guests in this dwelling place, for we have a lodging for a temporary stay. We are quickly departing. Let us beware lest, if we are harsh or negligent in receiving guests, the lodging of the saints also be denied to us after the course of this life.

“But you plead poverty. Your guest does not demand wealth from you, but goodwill; not an adorned banquet, but readily available food. These things are pleasing to human beings and acceptable to God. Hence the Lord Jesus in the Gospel declares that whoever gives a guest a cup of cold water will not be deprived of heavenly rewards (Matthew 10:42).”

Augustine, in the Book of Sermons [Note: [Col. 0231D] On the Words of the Lord, Sermon 32]:

“We are compelled to tell you what we ought not to have had to tell you. For we ought to have found in you something to praise, not to seek something for which we must admonish you. Nevertheless, I shall speak briefly and will not linger.

“Recognize hospitality. Through it one reaches God. You receive a guest whose companion you also are on the road, because we are all strangers. A Christian is one who recognizes that he is a stranger both in his own house and in his own country. Our homeland is above; there we shall not be guests. Here each person is a guest even in his own house, but he will leave that house to his children—a guest to guests.

“Why? If you were in an inn, would you not depart when another arrived? You do the same in your own house. Your father yielded a place to you; you will yield it to your children. You neither remain nor leave it as one who will remain. If we all pass away, let us do something that cannot pass away, so that when we have passed away and arrived where we shall not pass away, we may find our good works there. Christ is the guardian. Why are you afraid that you will lose what you give?”

Gregory, in the *Moralia*:

“It is most necessary for us to love the hospitality of our brothers through the love of fraternity and the works of charity. Therefore the distinguished Preacher, commending both to us, says: ‘Let brotherly charity remain among you,’ and, ‘Do not neglect hospitality’ (Hebrews 13:1).

“The blessed prince of the Apostles commends to us the grace of this hospitality, to be shown kindly to our brothers, saying: ‘Be hospitable to one another without grumbling’ (1 Peter 4:9).

“Hence Truth itself says: ‘I was a stranger, and you welcomed me’ (Matthew 25:35). With wondrous compassion our Redeemer speaks from the sympathy of his members, saying: ‘Whatever you did for one of the least of mine, you did for me’ (ibid., 40).

“Therefore he himself helps us through this—[he] who is our head—since he is helped in his members through our good works. We must consider how much hospitality born of brotherly compassion is worth, and how greatly the inward organs of mercy join us to the almighty Lord. For we draw near to him who is above all precisely from the point at which, through compassion for our neighbor, we humble ourselves even beneath ourselves.

“In bodily matters no one touches high things except one who stretches upward. In spiritual matters, however, it is certain that the more deeply we are drawn through compassion, the more truly and more highly we draw near.”

Many other teachings of the holy Fathers exist, but they are not included here because of the need for brevity. Every believer must therefore keep the rule of Christianity in pursuing hospitality and must pursue it for the love of Christ, not in expectation of temporal reward.

Let no one plead poverty by saying: “I cannot receive guests, because I have nothing with which to provide what they need.” The Lord Jesus Christ, in order to remove this excuse, promised that he would repay even a cup of cold water offered to the thirsty.

## BOOK THREE

[Col. 0233]

## CHAPTER ONE  
### On Charity
He possesses charity who loves God more than himself and his neighbor as himself: “On these two commandments [Col. 0233B] depend the whole Law and the Prophets” (Matt. 22:40). Moreover, it is characteristic of Christians both to love a friend in God and an enemy for God’s sake. Hence it is said in the Psalm: “Your commandment is exceedingly broad” (Ps. 118:96). It is called broad because it embraces friend and enemy alike in equal love.

It is indeed customary among the Jews to love a friend and pursue an enemy with detestable hatred. But among Christians, by the Lord’s command in the Gospel, both are to be loved equally: “You have heard,” he says, “that it was said to the ancients: ‘You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy.’ But I say to you: Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven, who makes his sun rise over good and bad, and sends rain upon just and unjust,” and so forth (Matt. 5:43 ff.). And elsewhere: “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another. By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13:34).

In this commandment the love not only of friends but also of enemies is contained; nor can anyone truthfully boast that he loves God if he has strayed from love of his enemy. [Note: [Col. 0233D] “From his enemy.” Thus Jonas certainly wrote it; and nothing was further from his intention than what Acherius had published, “from his friend.”]

For the Lord says in the Gospel: “If you forgive people their sins, your heavenly Father will also forgive you your sins. But if you do not forgive people, neither will your Father forgive you your sins” (Matt. 6:14). At such a great thunderclap, as blessed Augustine says, who would not awaken? Whoever does not awaken is not asleep but dead. Yet the Lord is also powerful enough to raise the dead. [Col. 0233D]

Concerning charity, Solomon says: “Hatred stirs up quarrels, but charity covers all offenses” (Prov. 10:12). Peter says: “Above all, maintain constant charity among yourselves, because charity covers a multitude of sins” (1 Pet. 4:8). Paul says: “Charity is patient, charity is kind,” and the rest (1 Cor. 13:4). John says: “God is charity, and whoever remains in charity remains in God, and God in him” (1 John 4:8).

Gregory, in the *Pastoral Book* [Note: [Col. 0234D] Homily 35.]: “Therefore, it is a virtue before human beings to endure adversaries; but it is a virtue before God to love them. For God accepts only that sacrifice which the flame of charity kindles before his eyes upon the altar of good works.”

The same author also says: “Since all the sacred writings are full of the Lord’s commandments, why does the Lord speak of love as though it were a singular commandment, saying: ‘This is my commandment, that you love one another’ (John 15:12), unless it is because every commandment concerns love alone, and all the commandments are one commandment? For whatever is commanded is established in charity alone. Just as many branches of a tree grow from one root, so many virtues arise from one charity; and a branch of good work has no greenness if it does not remain in the root of charity. The Lord’s commandments are therefore both many and one: many in the diversity of their works, one in the root of love.

“He himself indicates how this love is to be maintained, for in many passages of his Scripture he commands that a friend be loved in him and enemies for his sake. He truly possesses charity who loves a friend in God and an enemy for God’s sake.”

The same author also says: “‘To everyone who has, more will be given and he will abound; but from the one who does not have, even what he seems to have will be taken away’ (Matt. 13:12). To the one who has, therefore, it will be given and he will abound, because whoever has charity also receives the other gifts; while whoever does not have charity loses even the gifts that he seemed to have received.”

[“Since, as the Apostle bears witness, love is the fullness of the Law, it must be understood that no one can love his neighbor without the love of God, nor God without the love of his neighbor. Therefore, since a few things have been gathered here concerning charity, which is God, whoever desires to reach him who is charity must truly be aflame with love of God and neighbor.”]

## CHAPTER II. On Humility

As pride made demons from angels, so humility makes human beings fellow citizens of the angels. The devil, having fallen from heaven through pride, struck down the first human being and expelled him from paradise. But Christ, the Son of God, came humbly into the world to redeem the human race. Hence the Apostle says: “Although he was in the form of God, he did not consider equality with God something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. 2:6). And below: “He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death—even death on a cross” (ibid., v. 8).

Concerning humility the Lord says through the Prophet: “Upon whom shall my Spirit rest, if not upon the humble, the peaceful, and the one who trembles at my words?” (Isa. 66:2). Solomon says: “Where there is pride, there too is insult; but where there is humility, there too is wisdom. Humility follows the proud, and glory receives the humble in spirit. Before he is crushed, the human heart is exalted; and before he is glorified, it is humbled” (Prov. 11:2; 18:12; 20:23; 29:23). And in the Gospel: “Whoever therefore humbles himself like this child is the greater in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 18:14).

Peter says in his first Epistle: “All of you practice humility toward one another, because God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble” (1 Pet. 5:5). And: “Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he will exalt you” (Jas. 4:10). Jesus son of Sirach says: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things, and you will find grace before God” (Sir. 3:20).

Gregory, in the *Moralia* [Note: [Col. 0235D] Book 34, on Job 42, chapter 18.]: “For this reason the only-begotten Son of God assumed the form of humility; for this reason the invisible one appeared not merely visible but even despised; for this reason he endured the mockery of insults, the disgrace of derision, and the torments of suffering: so that humble God might teach proud humanity not to be proud. How great, therefore, is the virtue of humility, and how sublime is its height, for the sake of teaching which alone he who is great beyond estimation came to suffering and became small!

“Pride of the devil offered itself as the origin of our destruction; the humility of God was found to be the instrument of our redemption. Our great enemy, created among all things, wished in his elevation to appear above all things. But our great Redeemer, remaining above all things, deigned to become small among all things.”

And humility is the teacher of all and the mother of virtues, as Truth says: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matt. 11:29). For when humble people abase themselves, they rise to the likeness of God. What, then, is more exalted than humility? While it lowers itself into the depths, it joins itself to its Creator, who remains above the highest things.

Caesarius, bishop, in his homilies [Note: [Col. 0235D] Homily 18.]: “Let us therefore, dearly beloved brothers, hold humility above all else—not the humility that is sometimes displayed outwardly only, but that which is retained in the conscience. There are some who, whenever there is a certain calm, customarily display humility both in speech and in bodily demeanor. But if, as often happens, some tribulation or storm of scandal arises, pride—which had been concealed in the heart—is brought forth from the mouth through many insults, with unrestrained speech and an erect neck.

“Why has this happened, brothers? Because he did not possess the foundation of true humility; because he did not have in his heart the humility that he had previously professed in his bodily behavior. Let us therefore be humble, dearest brothers, not only toward our elders but also toward our equals and our juniors, lest God resist the proud, lest he humble those who exalt themselves, and lest, puffed up, we be unable to pass along the narrow way.”

Behold, it has been briefly shown how earnestly humility must be pursued. Therefore pride, together with its author the devil, must be vigilantly avoided, and the humility of Christ obediently embraced; for just as pride casts down those who imitate it into the depths, so humility raises those who embrace it to the heights.

## CHAPTER III. On Patience

Patience endured for the love of Christ is to be praised and proclaimed. But when it arises from love of earthly things, it should not be called the virtue of patience—which it is not—but, as blessed Augustine writes [Note: [Col. 0236D] *On Patience*, chapter 2], “astonishing hardness, and patience to be denied.”

Patience is therefore to be praised and proclaimed as a virtue when, for the love of Christ, it is maintained not only amid external adversities and misfortunes but especially retained in the heart. For it is of no benefit to display patience outwardly while inwardly retaining the wars of dissension and the fuel of other vices. Thus, when wisdom is outwardly exhibited but the wars of the vices reign within, this is not the virtue of patience but a pretense of virtue.

Blessed Job is therefore an example of both external and internal patience. He endured patiently not only the loss of external possessions, the deaths of his children, and the injuries inflicted by his friends, but also the scourging of his own body; and amid so many adversities he broke forth not into murmuring but into praise of God, saying: “If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, why should we not endure evil?” (Job 2:10). Likewise: “The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has happened. Blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1:21).

Concerning patience Solomon says: “The patient man governs with great prudence, but the impatient man exalts his folly” (Prov. 14:29). Likewise: “The patient man is better than the strong, and he who rules his spirit than one who captures cities” (Prov. 16:32). Likewise: “A person’s understanding is known through patience” (Prov. 19:11).

The Lord says in the Gospel: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matt. 5:9). Likewise: “By your patience you will possess your souls” (Luke 21:19). Paul says: “If it is possible, insofar as it depends on you, live at peace with all people” (Rom. 12:18). Likewise: “You need patience, so that, having done the will of God, you may receive the promise” (Heb. 10:36). Likewise: “Pursue peace with all and holiness, without which no one will see God” (Heb. 12:14).

When blessed Augustine was speaking in the book *On the Good of Patience* about those who, in order to obtain earthly honors, satisfy various desires, pursue amusements, manifold pleasures, and vanities, patiently, painfully, and perilously endure many hardships, he concluded as follows [Note: [Col. 0236D] Chapters 5–10.]:

“Such people,” he says, “deserve patience to be wondered at rather than praised—or rather, neither wondered at nor praised, since it is no patience at all, but astonishing hardness and patience to be denied. Nothing there is rightly to be praised, nothing usefully to be admired. You will judge a spirit worthy of all the greater punishment, and rightly so, the more it subjects the instruments of virtue to vices. Patience is the companion of wisdom, not the servant of lust. Patience is the friend of a good conscience, not the enemy of innocence.

“When, therefore, you see someone enduring something patiently, do not immediately praise the patience, which is revealed only by the reason for enduring. When the cause is good, then the patience is true; when the cause is not polluted by desire, then patience is distinguished from falsehood. But when that cause is held in crime, the name of patience is greatly misapplied. For not all who suffer share in patience, any more than all who know share in knowledge; rather, those who use suffering rightly are praised for the truth of patience, and are crowned with the reward of patience.

“Nevertheless, when people endure many horrifying things with remarkable fortitude for the sake of lusts, or even crimes, and finally for the sake of this temporal life and health, they sufficiently warn us how much must be endured for the sake of the good life, so that it may also be eternal, without any limit of time, without loss of any benefit, and secure in true happiness. Hence the Lord says: ‘By your patience you will possess your souls’ (Luke 21:19). He did not say, ‘your estates, your praises, or your pleasures,’ but ‘your souls.’ If the soul endures so much in order to possess what may perish, how much ought it to endure so that it may not perish?”

A little later he says:

“Although patience is a virtue of the spirit, the spirit uses it partly in itself and partly in its own body. It uses patience in itself when, while the body remains unharmed and untouched, it is provoked by any adversities, repulsivenesses of things, or goads of words to do or say something that is not expedient or proper, yet patiently endures all evils and itself commits nothing evil either in deed or in speech. By this patience, even while we are physically healthy, we endure the postponement of our blessedness amid the scandals of this age.”

After some intervening material he says:

“All these things, and any others too numerous to mention, belong to that form of patience by which the spirit patiently endures in itself not its own sins but whatever evils come from outside, while its own body remains completely unharmed. There is another form of patience, by which this same spirit endures whatever is painful and grievous in the sufferings of its body—not like foolish or wicked people, for the sake of gaining vanities or committing crimes, but, as the Lord has defined, for the sake of righteousness (Matt. 5:10).

“In both forms the holy martyrs contended. They were filled with [lacuna] of the impious, where the spirit, with the body unharmed, endured certain wounds as it were; and they were bound in their bodies, shut in, afflicted by hunger and thirst, tortured, cut apart, torn to pieces, burned, and slaughtered. With steadfast devotion they subjected their minds to God while suffering in the flesh whatever cruelty, in its search for torment, devised.”

Gregory, in his *Homilies on the Gospel* [Note: [Col. 0237D] Homily 35.]: “It should also be known that patience is ordinarily exercised in three ways. Some things we endure from God, some from the adversary, and some from our neighbor. From our neighbor we endure persecutions, losses, and insults; from the adversary, temptations; and from God, scourges.

“But in all three cases the mind must watch itself with vigilant attention: lest, in response to the evils of our neighbor, it be drawn into repaying evil with evil; lest, in response to the adversary’s temptations, it be seduced into the pleasure of sin or consent to it; and lest, in response to the Creator’s scourges, it fall into excessive murmuring.

“The adversary is perfectly conquered when our mind is wholly restrained from pleasure and consent even amid his temptations, guarded from hatred amid our neighbor’s insults, and restrained from murmuring amid God’s scourges. Nor, when we do these things, should we seek present goods as recompense. Rather, we should hope for the goods of the life to come as the reward of patience, so that the reward for our labor may begin when all labor has completely ceased.”

The same author also says:

“‘By your patience you will possess your souls’ (Luke 21:19). The possession of the soul is therefore placed in the virtue of patience because patience is the root and guardian of all the virtues. Through patience we possess our souls because, as we learn to rule ourselves, we begin to possess that which we are.

“True patience is to endure the evils of others with equanimity and not to be inwardly wounded by pain even against the person who inflicts the evil. For whoever bears the evil of another in such a way that he nevertheless grieves silently and waits for a suitable time for retaliation does not exhibit patience but merely pretends to it.

“For it is written: ‘Charity is kind; it is patient’ (1 Cor. 13:4). It is patient so that it may endure the evils of others; it is kind so that it may love even those whom it bears. Hence Truth itself says: ‘Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you’ (Matt. 5:44).

“It is therefore a virtue before human beings to endure adversaries, but a virtue before God to love them; for God accepts only that sacrifice which the flame of charity kindles before his eyes upon the altar of good works.

“It must also be known that we often seem patient because we cannot repay evil. But whoever does not repay evil only because he is utterly unable to do so is certainly not patient, as we have said; for patience is not acquired in outward display but in the heart.”

These and similar excellent and salutary testimonies instruct us in the virtue of patience. And because true patience cannot exist in us without charity, let us imitate the example of him who for our sake patiently endured scourges, mockery, and the cross, so that by displaying the virtue of patience outwardly and inwardly through love of him, we may after death reach the place to which he went before us.

## CHAPTER IV. On Pride

A person falls into pride sometimes because of the gift of some virtue, sometimes because of the honors of the world, and sometimes because of the weakness of the flesh. Pride is the beginning of every sin. Hence it is written: “Pride is the beginning of every sin” (Sir. 10:15). Pride made demons from angels, while humility restores human beings to equality with angels.

Concerning pride the Psalmist says: “You will save the humble people, but you will humble the eyes of the proud” (Ps. 17:28). Likewise: “The proud acted wickedly everywhere, but I did not turn aside from your law” (Ps. 118:51). Likewise: “You rebuked the proud; cursed are those who depart from your commandments” (ibid., v. 21). Likewise: “The one who practices pride shall not dwell in the midst of my house” (Ps. 100:7).

In Proverbs: “The Lord demolishes the houses of the proud” (Prov. 15:25). In Ecclesiasticus: “Why are you proud, earth and ashes?” (Sir. 10:9). In Amos: “The Lord has sworn by his own life, says the Lord of hosts: I detest the pride of Jacob, and I hate his houses” (Amos 6:8).

Tobias, addressing his son, says: “Never permit pride to rule in your thoughts or in your speech; for every destruction began with it” (Tob. 4:14). And Solomon says: “Where there is pride, there will also be insult” (Prov. 11:2). Likewise: “It is better to be humbled with the meek than to divide spoils with the proud” (Prov. 16:19).

Jesus son of Sirach says: “Pride is hateful before God and human beings. The beginning of human pride is to apostatize from God. Pride is the beginning of every sin. Whoever touches pitch will be defiled by it, and whoever associates with the proud will be clothed in pride” (Sir. 10:7 ff.).

And the Lord says in the Gospel: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 14:11). Peter says: “God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble” (1 Pet. 5:5). Paul says: “Do not be high-minded, but fear” (Rom. 11:20).

Augustine, in the book of sermons [Note: [Col. 0239D] *On the Words of the Lord*, sermon 53, chapters 4 and 5.]: “Only the devil’s pride and envy send a person into eternal fire. The proud cannot be without envy; envy is the daughter of pride. But this mother, pride, does not know how to be barren: wherever she is, she immediately gives birth.”

A little later he says: “Pride comes first among the vices, and envy afterward. Envy did not give birth to pride; pride gave birth to envy. For no one envies except because of a love of superiority. The love of superiority is called pride.”

Gregory, in the *Moralia* [Note: [Col. 0239D] Book 34, chapter 18.]: “The occasion of our destruction was the devil’s pride; the instrument of our redemption was found to be God’s humility. What is more abject than elevation, which, when it stretches above itself, is removed from the height of true exaltation?

“Pride is the beginning of every sin. What, then, is pride except a desire for a perverse height? Height is perverse when, abandoning the beginning to which the spirit ought to cling, it wishes in some manner to become and to be its own beginning.

“Pride has often been the seedbed of lust, because while the spirit raised people as though on high, the flesh plunged them into the depths. Those who are first raised up by pride in the secret of the heart afterward fall publicly; for while they swell inwardly through hidden movements of the heart, they fall through manifest lapses of the body.

“Hence, through the prophet Hosea, it is said against the Israelites: ‘The spirit of fornication is among them, and they have not known the Lord’ (Hos. 5:4). To show that the cause of lust had burst forth from the fault of elation, he immediately added: ‘The arrogance of Israel will answer to his face’ (ibid., v. 5).

“When a human being, through pride, scorns his Creator, he rightly receives warfare from the subjected flesh. Thus the first disobedient one, as soon as he sinned through pride, covered his shameful parts; because, having brought accusation against God in spirit, he immediately found accusation in the flesh.”

A little later he says:

“The proud, by the very fact that they desire to appear lofty, become through their elation far from the true being of God. Those who are separated from the solidity of eternal being cannot endure; as the Psalmist says: ‘You cast them down when they were lifted up’ (Ps. 72:18). They fall inwardly precisely where they rise inwardly in a wrongful manner.

“Thus straw is carried upward by the breath of the wind, but by a swift fall is brought back to the depths. Thus smoke rises toward the clouds, but suddenly, swelling, is dispersed into nothing. Thus mist rises from the lowest places as it thickens, but the ray of the rising sun wipes it away as though it had never existed. Thus moisture is sprinkled upon the surface of grasses during the night, but is dried by the sudden heat of lasting light. Thus foaming bubbles of water, stirred up by the beginning rains, emerge eagerly from the depths, but burst and perish all the more quickly the higher they are stretched by inflation; and as they grow so as to appear, by growing they bring about their own inability to remain.

“It is written: ‘The wicked is proud all his days.’ The elect too sometimes grow proud in certain thoughts and actions of theirs, but because they are elect they cannot be proud all their days; for before they finish their life, they change their hearts from elation to the fear of humility.”

Caesarius, bishop of Massilia [Note: [Col. 0239D] “Bishop of Massilia.” He meant the bishop of Arles, as Acherius correctly observed.], in his homilies (Homily 18): “Two buildings and two cities have been constructed from the beginning of the world. Christ builds one, the devil the other: one is humble, the other proud.

“Let each person therefore attend to his conscience, and if he sees pride ruling within him, let him not doubt that he is unhappily building himself in the devil’s city—or rather, plunging himself into ruin. The sons of God and the sons of the devil are distinguished by nothing except humility and pride.

“Whenever you see someone who is proud, do not doubt that he is a son of the devil. Whenever you see someone who is humble, you ought truly to believe that he is a son of God. And so that you may know this to be true, hear Scripture saying: ‘Every pride is the beginning of apostasy from God’ (Sir. 10:14). From pride arises contempt for God’s commandments, and from the good works that are done arises the desire for empty praise.” Thus Caesarius spoke.

Pride also arises when someone considers himself better than others because of virtues or because of the riches of the world, even though he is certainly worse precisely in that respect in which he considers himself better than others. [Note: [Col. 0240D] “He is worse in that respect.” Previously it was read “he is superior in that respect,” falsely and contrary to the author’s meaning.]

From pride also arise obstinacy, disobedience, quarrels, heresies, and countless other vices, all of which a servant of God can very easily overcome through humility. Some are thought to swell with pride because of the style and splendor of their clothing. Although such adornment often does flow from the fountain of pride, there are nevertheless many who are adorned with these things outwardly and abound in humility inwardly.

Such was that man clothed in purple and adorned with a royal diadem, who said: “See my humility and rescue me, because I have not forgotten your law” (Ps. 118:153). Likewise: “See my humility and my labor, and forgive all my sins” (Ps. 24:18).

Therefore, since we fell through the pride of our parent Adam and rose again through the humility of Christ, we must take care to avoid pride, the devil’s poison, and always cling to the humility of Christ, who says in the Gospel: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matt. 11:29). Whoever has served the vice of pride must therefore confess it to a priest, as he must the other vices, and beseech God to deign to forgive him.

## CHAPTER V. On Hatred and Envy

Just as small things grow through concord, so, conversely, great things diminish through hatred and ill will. Hatred and envy affect many people miserably and fatally. These two destructive sins are also all the more harmful and dangerous the more hidden they are.

Although their disease corrodes the minds of many, some nevertheless reveal by certain outward signs that they are suffering inwardly from the same disease. When such a person is admonished to beware of hatred, he ordinarily replies: “I cannot tear this evil from my heart, because the person about whom you admonish me has inflicted many injuries and various evils upon me. Let God do what he wills; I will not rest until I have taken revenge on him.”

When admonition is given concerning the avoidance of envy and the embrace of charity, people of this kind usually respond: “This person or that person did not deserve to possess what he acquired, because he was not born noble enough to merit attaining it.” They also tend to add: “I, who have spent many years laboring in service, have not attained honor; yet he, who served for a short time or almost no time at all, has preceded me in receiving honor.”

This vice of envy occurs both in great matters and in small ones. Indeed, if discussion concerns the holiness and uprightness of the life of some envious person, and what is said is asserted to be true, those wasting away with such envy insist that everything being said is false. Many other signs also appear by which haters and envious people commonly reveal themselves, and perhaps they do not know how greatly they sin in this matter.

Although these are capital crimes, very few—which is exceedingly dangerous—make confession of them to God and a priest or attempt to wipe them away through the satisfaction of penance. But while they return evil for evil according to the law of the world rather than the law of Christ, despising those whom they envy and harassing them with insults and every kind of abuse, although the deadly crime is plainly evident, they prefer to bear the name of a strong man rather than that of one who blushes with shame and repents.

The divine oracles gathered below teach how vigilantly these vices must be avoided. In the old Law you have: “You shall not hate your brother in your heart, but openly reprove him, lest you bear sin because of him” (Lev. 19:17). In Solomon: “The health of the heart is the life of the flesh, but envy is the rottenness of the bones” (Prov. 14:30). Likewise: “Anger kills the foolish man, and envy slays the simple” (Job 5:2). Jesus son of Sirach says: “Through the envy of the devil death entered the world” (Wis. 2:24). The apostle John says: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3:15). The same author also says: “Whoever says that he is in the light and hates his brother is in darkness, and walks in darkness, and does not know where he is going, because darkness has blinded his eyes” (1 John 2:9–11).

Concerning envy Augustine writes in the book *On the Discipline of Christians* (Book 2, chapter 7):

“May God turn the plague of envy away from the souls of all human beings, let alone Christians. It is the devil’s vice, for which the devil alone is guilty and irredeemably guilty. For the devil is not told, in order to condemn him, ‘You committed adultery,’ or ‘You stole,’ or ‘You seized another’s estate’; rather, he is condemned because he envied the human being, who stood upright.

“Envy is a diabolical vice, but it has its mother. She is called pride. Pride makes people envious. Suffocate the mother, and the daughter will not exist. For this reason Christ taught humility. I am not speaking to the envious, but to those who wish good. I am speaking to those who wish their friends well, so that they may possess as much as they themselves possess.”

Prosper also writes [Note: [Col. 0241D] *On Contempt for the World*, chapter 5.]:

“Certainly an envious person makes another’s good his own punishment through envy. He seems to be provoked to envy by no desire, but merely tormented in the manner of pride. Yet if you examine subtly and deeply the plague of his soul by which, inflamed, he is driven to ruin, you will find him eager for the destruction of the person whose ruin he desires, and held by the evil of pride, since he continually laments that the person whom he envies is better than he is.

“Who could easily express in words the nature of this evil, by which the envious person pursues the divine gift in another with hatred, when the person himself ought rather to be loved, even for the holiness of his merit? The envious person has as many just punishments tormenting him as the envied person has praisers. Excellence of merit makes one envied; the punishment of sin makes the other envious. No human being can apply a remedy to him whose wound is hidden.”

Gregory, in the *Moralia* (Book 5, chapter 31):

“We can envy only those whom we think better than ourselves in some respect. The one killed by envy is therefore a small person, because he himself bears witness that he is less than the person by whose envy he is tormented.

“Hence the crafty enemy secretly attacked the first human being by envy, because, having lost blessedness, he recognized himself to be inferior to the immortality of that person. Cain fell into the perpetration of fratricide because, despising his own sacrifice, he raged against the one whose sacrifice God accepted and whom he dreaded as better than himself; lest he should be in any way superior, he cut him off.

“For this reason Esau burned with persecution against his brother: having lost the blessing of the firstborn—which Esau himself had sold for lentils—he lamented that he was inferior to the one whom he surpassed by birth. Joseph’s brothers sold the holy man to passing Ishmaelites because, having learned the mystery of his revelation, they tried to obstruct his advancement lest he become better than they were.”

It must be understood with the greatest care that although the ancient enemy pours his poison into the human heart through every vice that is committed, in this wickedness the serpent shakes all its vitals and spews forth the plague of malice. Through envy the complexion is affected by pallor, the eyes are cast down, the mind is inflamed, the limbs grow cold, madness arises in thought, and there is gnashing of teeth.

Isidore, in the book of *Sentences* (Book 3, chapter 25):

“An envious person is a member of the devil, through whose envy death entered the world. There is no virtue that does not have the opposing evil of envy; only misery is free from envy, because no one envies the miserable.”

And shortly afterward:

“Every envious person does to another’s virtues what Satan did to blessed Job. For, while he envies prosperity, he stirs up adversity.”

It is not human beings but vices that must be hated. Those who waste away in hatred of a brother and preserve a destructive deceit of the soul against others are to be lamented with tears; for those who separate themselves from charity separate themselves from the kingdom of God.

Bede, in his exposition of John’s Epistle (chapter 2, verse 9; chapter 3, verse 15):

“The Lord commands in the Gospel that enemies be loved. Whoever therefore says that he is a Christian and hates his brother remains in sins until now. He rightly added ‘until now,’ because all human beings are born in the darkness of vices. Human beings remain in darkness until they are enlightened through the grace of baptism in Christ.

“But the person who approaches the fountain of life, in order to be reborn, with hatred for his brother, and approaches the drink of precious blood, by which he is to be redeemed—even if he considers himself enlightened by the Lord—is still in darkness until now. He could not in any way cast off the shadows of sins who did not take care to put on the inner organs of charity.”

The same author also says:

“‘Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer.’ If someone despised hatred of his brother, would he not also despise murder in his heart? He did not move his hands to kill a human being, yet he is already held by God as a murderer. The other is alive, but this one is already judged a killer.

“And you know that every murderer does not have eternal life abiding in him. Even if he appears to live among the saints through faith, he does not have eternal life abiding in him. For when the time of recompense comes, he will be condemned with Cain, who was of the evil one: likewise, the one held by this kind of murder, who disagrees, quarrels, and does not have peace with his brothers.

“It should be noted that he does not say simply, ‘A murderer does not have life abiding in him,’ but: ‘Every murderer’—that is, not only the one who pursues his brother with a sword, but also the one who pursues his brother with hatred.” [Col. 0244A]

By these and similar authorities of divine Scripture, hatred—which spiritually kills those who follow it—is judged something to be avoided, and envy—which consumes the minds of the envious with its rust—is judged something to be shunned. No one whose mind has been infected by these evils will deserve to be the temple of the Holy Spirit unless he has been rid of them.

## CHAPTER VI. On the Eight Principal Vices
Because it is lengthy to enumerate the eight principal vices individually, it has been judged useful to gather them under a single chapter heading. The first of these is pride, which was discussed above. The second is gluttony, a vice into which many fall while promising themselves impunity and saying: “What wrong do we do if we partake at our own discretion of drink and food, which God has granted for human use?” But when they consume these either before the proper time or at the proper time beyond the measure of moderation, without discernment, they unquestionably do wrong.

They should weigh what God says in the Gospel: “See that your hearts are not weighed down by drunkenness, and debauchery, and the cares of this life” (Luke 21:34). And the Apostle: “Food and drink do not commend us to God” (1 Corinthians 8:8). And Isaiah: “Woe to you who are mighty for drinking wine, and strong men for mixing drunkenness” (Isaiah 5:22). Again: “Behold, joy and gladness: slaughtering calves, killing rams, eating meat, and drinking wine. As I live, says the Lord, this iniquity shall not be forgiven you until you die” (Isaiah 22:13). And Solomon: “Wine is a luxurious thing, and drunkenness is tumultuous; whoever delights in these will not be wise” (Proverbs 20:1). Again: “Do not look upon wine when it glows, when its color shines in the glass; it enters pleasantly, but at the end it will bite like a serpent, and like an asp it will spread its poisons. No secret remains where drunkenness reigns” (Proverbs 23:31). Again: “If the powerful are prone to anger, let them not drink wine, lest, when they have drunk, they forget wisdom” (Proverbs 31:4).

The prophet Joel says: “Awake, drunkards, and weep; howl, all you who drink wine in sweetness” (Joel 1:5). Job says: “When he is filled, he will be constricted, and every pain will rush upon him” (Job 20:22). Jesus son of Sirach says: “A drunken laborer will not become rich. Wine and women make the wise apostatize, and they rebuke the sensible. Drinking much wine produces irritation, anger, and many ruinous consequences” (Sirach 19:1; 31:28).

From gluttony arise foolish merriment, buffoonery, frivolity, empty talk, bodily uncleanness, instability of mind, drunkenness, and lust. For, as blessed Jerome says, sexual pleasure immediately follows a belly distended with food and irrigated with various drinks.

The third vice is called fornication, which is accustomed to occur not only through the body but also through the mind. Through the body it occurs by the mingling of the flesh with any woman, or through any other uncleanness intended to satisfy the ardor of lust. Through the mind it occurs when the soul, having abandoned the marriage of its lawful husband—that is, Christ—joins itself to the ancient enemy in an adulterous, indeed destructive, marriage, whether through idolatry or through any other sin.

Concerning this fornication the Psalmist says: “You will destroy all who fornicate away from you” (Psalm 72:27). From fornication arise blindness of mind, inconstancy of the eyes and of the whole body, immoderate love, often danger to life, licentiousness, jokes, wantonness, and every form of incontinence; hatred of God’s commandments, weakening of the mind, unjust desires, neglect of the life to come, and delight in the present life.

The fourth vice is avarice, concerning which Solomon writes: “The miser is not filled with money” (Sirach 5:9). In the Gospel it is compared by God to the disease of dropsy: the more a person drinks, the more he thirsts. So also the avaricious person, the more he has, the more he desires to have; and because he does not maintain moderation in possessing, he loses it through excessive coveting.

A dreadful sentence concerning the avaricious is drawn from the Lord in the Gospel and from the Apostle: the avaricious will not possess the kingdom of God. From the tree of avarice grow poisonous branches, namely envy, thefts, robberies, murders, lies, perjuries, plunder, violence, unrest, unjust judgments, contempt for the truth, forgetfulness of future blessedness, and hardening of the heart, which is opposed to works of mercy.

The fifth vice is anger, concerning which Solomon says: “An angry man provokes quarrels; the patient man calms those that have been stirred up” (Proverbs 5:18). Again: “Do not be quick to anger, because anger rests in the bosom of a fool” (Sirach 7:10). “The wicked always seeks quarrels, but a cruel angel will be sent against him. Who can endure a spirit easily provoked to anger?” (Proverbs 27:11; 18:14.) Again: “Anger has no mercy, nor does bursting fury; who can withstand the force of one aroused?” (Proverbs 27:4.)

Jesus son of Sirach says: “Do not quarrel with an angry man” (Sirach 8:19). Again: “An angry man kindles a fire. Jealousy and anger shorten one’s days and bring one to old age before the time” (Sirach 28:11; 20:26). And in the Gospel: “Everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment” (Matthew 5:22). Paul says: “Let not the sun go down upon your anger” (Ephesians 4:26). James says: “For the anger of man does not accomplish the righteousness of God” (James 1:20).

Whoever does not govern the movement of his own mind by reason easily falls into fury, and is shown to do everything he does precipitately. For one seized by this vice readily loses both the maturity of counsel, the measure of sound discernment, and the dignity of devout action. From anger also grow swelling of the mind, quarrels, insults, shouting, indignation, presumption, blasphemies, bloodshed, murders, desire for revenge, and remembrance of injuries, along with very many other things.

The sixth vice is acedia, that is, idleness, concerning which Solomon says: “Idleness is hostile to the soul” (Proverbs 20:4). Again: “Because of the cold the sluggard would not plow; he will beg in summer, and nothing will be given him.” The Lord rebukes the idle in the Gospel, saying: “Why do you stand here idle all day? Go into my vineyard” (Matthew 20:7).

Many clerics and laypeople suffer from this plague and have no understanding that they are sinning. For just as the exercise of good work gladdens the spirit and kindles it to do ever better things, [lacuna] from this vice arise sleepiness, laziness concerning good work, instability of place, wandering from place to place, tepidity in labor, weariness of heart, murmuring, and empty talk.

The seventh vice is sadness. Sadness occurs in two ways: sometimes beneficially, sometimes destructively. When it occurs beneficially, it is not to be counted as a vice but as a virtue. It is beneficial when someone, worn down by prolonged fasting and every other bodily discipline, and exercised through many struggles for holy virtues, grieves that he has long been exiled from the sweetness of his eternal homeland. Concerning such people the Lord says in the Gospel: “Your sadness will be turned into joy” (John 16:20).

Sadness is destructive when someone grieves over the loss of earthly goods and the injuries inflicted upon him by others to such an extent that he takes no pleasure in doing any good work. For when these things happen to him, they customarily disturb his mind so greatly that they not only draw him away from good things but also compel him to go headlong into the precipice of despair.

Whoever is thus swallowed up by sadness plainly shows that he has placed earthly love above the love of Christ in the foundation of his mind. That those who are sad ought to turn not to murmuring but rather to prayer and the praise of God, the Apostle James teaches, saying: “Is anyone among you sad? Let him pray. Is he cheerful? Let him sing psalms” (James 5:23).

The venerable presbyter Bede explains these words as follows:

> “If,” he says, “anyone among you is weighed down by some sadness—whether perhaps an injury inflicted by other people has fallen upon him, or guilt has intervened, or domestic loss has overtaken him, or it has happened that you have been saddened for any other reason—do not at that hour gather together to murmur against one another and complain about God’s judgments. Rather, hastening to the church, pray to the Lord on bended knees, that he may send the grace of his consolation, lest the sadness of the world, which produces death, swallow you up. You too should drive the harmful plague of grief from your heart by the repeated sweetness of psalmody.”

The eighth is cenodoxy, that is, vainglory, which properly belongs to the arrogant and to lovers of empty praise. Concerning this the Lord says in the Gospel: “They do all their works so that they may be seen by people” (Matthew 23:5). Again: “Amen, I say to you, they have received their reward.”

There are four kinds of arrogant people: when they think that they possess good from themselves; or when they suppose that what has been given to them from above was received on account of their own merits; or when they boast that they possess what they do not possess; or when, despising others, they desire singularly to appear to possess what they do not possess.

The Apostle teaches that “whoever boasts should boast in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 1:31). And the Lord says to his disciples in the Gospel: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). Therefore, when someone does good works, he should by no means seek praise from human beings, but ought to await eternal reward from God.

> “These,” as the venerable master Alcuin writes [Note: [Col. 0247D] *Book on Virtues and Vices*, chapter 34], “are the eight leaders of all impiety with their armies, and the strongest warriors of diabolical fraud against the human race. With God’s help, they are most easily conquered by Christ’s warriors through holy virtues: pride, namely, by humility; gluttony, by abstinence; fornication, by chastity; avarice, by generosity; anger, by patience; acedia, by zeal for good work; evil sadness, by spiritual joy; and vainglory, by the love of God.”

Many people are subjected to these eight principal vices, some understanding them and others not understanding them. They have become so customary that some consider them either no sins or scarcely any sins. Many sayings of the holy Fathers could have been gathered here concerning them, but they have been omitted to avoid excessive length. Nevertheless, each person ought, with the help of God, to avoid these vices; and if anyone has finally become enslaved to them, he should not neglect to make a pure and humble confession of them to God and to a priest.

## CHAPTER VII. On Detraction

Divine Scripture plainly indicates that one ought not to engage in detraction. Thus it is read in the Book of Numbers: “The Lord descended in a column of cloud and stood at the entrance of the tabernacle, calling Aaron and Miriam” (Numbers 12:5). And below: “Why, then, were you not afraid to speak against my servant Moses?” And, becoming angry with them, he departed; the cloud that had been over the tabernacle also withdrew, and behold, Miriam appeared white with leprosy like snow.

You also have in the Psalm: “The one who secretly slanders his neighbor, him I persecuted” (Psalm 100:5). And Solomon: “Put away from you the perverse mouth, and let lips that speak detraction be far from you. Whoever detracts from anyone binds himself for the future; but whoever fears the commandment lives in peace. Do not associate with detractors, because their destruction will suddenly arise, and who knows the ruin of both?” (Proverbs 4:24; 13:13; 24:21.)

The Apostle James says: “If anyone thinks that he is religious but does not bridle his tongue, deceiving his own heart, his religion is worthless” (James 1:26). The venerable presbyter Bede explains this passage as follows:

> “Above,” he says, “he had admonished us not only to hear the word of God but also to do it. Now he adds that, even if someone appears to exercise in deeds the Lord’s commandments that he has learned, if he does not also restrain his tongue from detractions, lies, blasphemies, foolish talk, even excessive speech itself, and the other things by which people commonly sin, he boasts of the righteousness of his works in vain.”

Again: “Do not slander one another, my brothers. Whoever slanders his brother, or judges his brother, slanders the law and judges the law” (James 4:11).

Jerome, to Nepotianus (*Letter* 2):

> “Beware of having either an itching tongue or itching ears—that is, beware either of slandering others yourself or of listening to others who slander. ‘You sat speaking against your brother, and you placed a stumbling-block against the son of your mother. You did these things, and I was silent. You thought wickedly that I would be like you; I will rebuke you and set you before your face’ (Psalm 49:26)—that is, your words and everything you have said about others—so that you may be judged by your own sentence, having been caught in the very things you accused others of doing.
>
> “Nor is this a just excuse: ‘I cannot injure others by reporting what I have heard.’ No one willingly reports anything to an unwilling listener. An arrow is sometimes fixed in a stone; at other times, rebounding from it, it strikes the one who directed it. Let the detractor learn, when he sees that you do not willingly listen, not to slander easily. ‘Do not associate with detractors,’ says Solomon, ‘because their destruction will suddenly come, and who knows the ruin of both?’ (Proverbs 24:21)—that is, both of the one who slanders and of the one who lends an ear to the slanderer.”

Gregory, in the *Moralia*:

> “Those who feed upon the lives of others through detraction are unquestionably satisfied with the flesh of others, as it is written: ‘Do not eat with those who provide meats for eating’ (Proverbs 23:20). To provide meats for eating is, in speech of disparagement, to recount one another’s faults.
>
> “Concerning detractors Solomon rightly says: ‘Those who devote themselves to drinking and give contributions will be consumed, and drowsiness will clothe itself in rags’ (ibid., verse 21). They devote themselves to drinking who intoxicate themselves with the disgrace of another’s life. To give contributions means to contribute words in a conversation of detraction, just as each person commonly brings a portion of food for eating.
>
> “‘Those who devote themselves to drinking and give contributions will be consumed,’ because, as it is written, ‘Every detractor will be uprooted.’ Indeed, many among the Christian people, while suffering from this vice, do not know how far they fall short of their own salvation.
>
> “Often detractors declare the devout actions of their neighbors to be evil through perverse intent. Often, too, they desire to know the errors of others, not out of a desire to correct or out of compassion, but solely from curiosity, so that they may feed upon their detraction. Beyond doubt, they make the sins of others their own through detraction, since those who do this show that they do not possess the inner organs of charity.
>
> “One ought to rejoice with neighbors who live and act rightly, not slander them. One ought also to grieve and sympathize with those who stray from the paths of righteousness, not insult them.”

## CHAPTER VIII. On Avoiding Insults, Idle Speech, and Curses

There are certain sins which, as blessed Gregory says, when they have become customary, are thought to be either trivial or no sins at all. Among these are insults, idle speech, and curses. The ingrained habit of insulting others, uttering idle words, and attacking the lives of others with execrable curses falsely promises that these things are now almost free of guilt. Perfect men, however, take the greatest care to avoid these vices.

Some weak and infirm people, in understanding and in action, persist in these things most dangerously and, what is worse, do not recognize that they are sinning in them. Solomon says: “Because of the sins of the lips, ruin comes near the wicked” (Proverbs 12:13). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “I tell you that for every idle word people speak, they will give an account on the day of judgment” (Matthew 12:36). For each person will be justified by his words or condemned by his words.

The Apostle Paul says: “Avoid foolish and empty tales” (1 Timothy 4:7). Again, in the Gospel: “Whoever says to his brother, ‘Raca,’ will be liable to the fire of Gehenna” (Matthew 5:22).

Jerome, in his *Commentary on Matthew* (on chapter 5):

> “Raca,” he says, “means empty and vain; we can call such a person, in the common insult, ‘brainless.’ If we are to give an account for an idle word, how much more for an insult? The text pointedly adds: ‘Whoever says to his brother, Raca.’ No one is our brother except one who has the same father as we do. Therefore, since he likewise believes in God and knows Christ, the Wisdom of God, how can he be branded with the epithet of folly?”

Augustine, in *The Sermon on the Mount* (Book 1, chapter 9):

> “There are stages in these sins. First, someone becomes angry and retains that movement, conceived in the mind, within his heart. If this agitation forces out an angry voice—not signifying anything specific, but revealing by its eruption the movement of the soul against the one with whom he is angry—that is certainly more than if the anger, once it arose, were suppressed in silence.
>
> “But if not only the voice of the angry person is heard, but also a word that now clearly designates and marks the insult against the person to whom it is directed, who would doubt that this is more serious than if only the sound of indignation had been uttered?
>
> “Thus in the first case there is one thing: anger alone. In the second there are two: anger and a voice signifying anger. In the third there are three: anger, a voice signifying anger, and within the voice itself a clear expression of insult. Hence there are also three forms of liability: judgment, the council, and the fire of Gehenna.”

Gregory, in his *Homilies on the Gospel*:

> “Together with you I offer this warning. Let us spare ourselves idle speech; let us avoid speaking uselessly, insofar as we are able to bridle our tongues. Let our words not flow away into the wind, since the Judge says: ‘For every idle word that people speak, they will give an account on the day of judgment’ (Matthew 12:36). An idle word is one that lacks either the usefulness of righteousness or the reason of just necessity.”

Concerning the avoidance of curses, the Lord says in the Law: “You shall not curse the deaf, nor place a stumbling-block before the blind” (Leviticus 19:14). And Solomon: “A father’s blessing strengthens the houses of his sons; a mother’s curse uproots their foundations” (Sirach 27:16).

Therefore, let both sexes—whoever are accustomed to engage in curses—consider what blessed Augustine says in *The City of God* about a certain woman who, at the prompting of the ancient enemy, cursed her children; what punishment they suffered under that same curse, and what she ultimately endured. For while they were shaken throughout the joints of their limbs, she, moved by grief over their torments, hanged herself with a noose. Whoever wishes to know this more fully should read blessed Augustine’s sermon on this matter, delivered to the people.

Therefore all must restrain themselves from such curses, bearing in mind what the blessed Apostle Paul says: “Nor will those who curse possess the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians 6:10). The Apostle James also says:

> “No human being can tame the tongue; it is a restless evil, full of deadly poison. With it we bless the Lord and Father, and with it we curse human beings who are made in the image and likeness of God. From the same mouth proceed blessing and cursing. This ought not to be so, my brothers. Does a spring pour forth sweet and bitter water from the same opening?” (James 3:8–11.)

Bede explains this as follows [Note: [Col. 0249D] Chapter 3, on the Epistle of Blessed James]:

> “Just as sweet and bitter water cannot simultaneously well up from one vein of a spring, and even if they are mixed in a vessel or cistern, the sweet water immediately becomes bitter through the bitter, while the bitter water, even when sweetness is mixed into it, does not know how to be changed into sweetness, so blessing and cursing can in no way coexist in one mouth.
>
> “Whoever is accustomed to bless God in prayer or to preach his word, yet does not cease to curse human beings, plainly shows that the bitterness of cursing consumes the sweetness of his blessing. For, according to the Apostle, ‘a little leaven corrupts the whole lump,’ and ‘praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner.’”

## CHAPTER IX. On Obscene Speech and Buffoonery

Not only those who devote themselves to obscene speech and buffoonery are shown to sin; so too are those who spend their time excessively even on matters that we recognize to be necessary. Obscene speech and buffoonery are forbidden by the Apostle.

Concerning excessive speech Solomon says: “In much speaking sin will not be absent” (Proverbs 10:19). James says: “If anyone does not stumble in word, that person is perfect” (James 3:2). As Bede explains, this means a word whose offense human weakness can avoid: a word of deceit, detraction, cursing, pride, boasting, excuses for sins, rivalry, dissension, heresy, lying, perjury, idle speech, and also excessive speech about matters that appear necessary.

Whoever guards himself from offense in this kind of speech is a perfect person. For “whoever guards his mouth and his tongue guards his soul from distress” (Proverbs 21:23).

Paul says: “Fornication and every impurity or avarice must not even be named among you, as is fitting for saints, nor obscenity, nor foolish talk, nor buffoonery, which does not pertain to the matter, but rather thanksgiving” (Ephesians 5:3).

Jerome, in his exposition of the Epistle to the Ephesians:

> “I consider foolish talk to belong not only to those who recount obscene things in order to provoke laughter, and, by feigning stupidity, mock even more those whom they desire to please, but also to those who are thought wise according to the world and, disputing about physical matters, say that they have clearly comprehended the sands of the shores, the drops of the ocean, the expanse of the heavens, and the point of the earth.
>
> “The difference between foolish talk and buffoonery is that foolish talk contains nothing wise in itself, whereas buffoonery proceeds from a prudent mind and deliberately seeks certain urbane, rustic, or witty expressions—what we might call joking—to provoke laughter in its hearers. But even this must be driven entirely away from holy men, for whom mourning is more fitting: ‘Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted’ (Matthew 5:5).”

Augustine, in his *Sermons to the People* (sermon 215):

> “Above all, wherever you are—whether in the house, on a journey, at a banquet, or in an assembly—do not utter obscene and licentious words from your mouth. Rather, always strive to speak what is good and honorable.”

It can clearly and evidently be observed that God did not wish sin to have any place either in the house of the inner person or in any member of the outer person. Rather, he wished all of that person’s inner and outer parts to serve him, not sin.

## CHAPTER X. On Works of Mercy, and That Each Person Ought to Begin Almsgiving with Himself

Whoever dreads hearing an evil sentence on the day of the dreadful judgment, and desires to be called blessed of the Father by Christ, should devote himself to the works of mercy proclaimed in the Gospel by that same Lord Jesus Christ. Only the person who first begins to practice almsgiving toward himself can worthily persist in these works.

Concerning mercy the Lord says through the prophet: “I desire mercy, and not sacrifice” (Matthew 9:13). And Job: “From infancy, compassion grew with me, and it came forth with me from my mother’s womb” (Job 31:18). Solomon says: “Let mercy and truth not forsake you” (Proverbs 3:3). Again, the same author: “A merciful man does good to his own soul, but the cruel man rejects even his relatives. To practice mercy and judgment is more pleasing to God than sacrifices” (Proverbs 11:17; 21:3).

Jesus son of Sirach says: “My son, have mercy on your soul, pleasing God” (Sirach 30:14). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “Therefore be merciful, just as your Father is merciful” (Luke 6:36). Again: “Blessed are the merciful, for God will have mercy on them” (Matthew 5:7). Paul says: “Be kind and merciful to one another” (Ephesians 4:32). “Put on, as God’s chosen ones, compassionate hearts” (Colossians 3:12).

Augustine, in *The Sermon on the Mount* (chapter 2):

> “He says that those who assist the wretched are blessed, because they are repaid in such a way that they are freed from misery.”

And shortly afterward (chapter 4):

> “To the merciful—those who use mercy as a true and excellent counsel—mercy is shown by the more powerful in the same manner as they show it to the weaker.”

Cyprian, in his exposition of the Lord’s Prayer [Note: [Col. 0251D] In the book *On Works and Almsgiving*]:

> “Nor,” he says, “can the person who has not himself been merciful deserve God’s mercy; nor will the one who has not been humane toward the poor person’s plea obtain anything from divine compassion in his prayers.”

Isidore, in *The Book of Sentences* (Book 3, chapter 64):

> “It is true that all sins are cleansed by works of mercy, but only if the person who bestows mercy already takes care not to sin. Otherwise there is no forgiveness of sin when mercy precedes in such a way that sins follow it.
>
> “For when a poor person is fed for the sake of boasting, the very work of mercy is turned into sin. Works of mercy extinguish sins to such an extent that the heavenly Judge, coming in the future judgment, says to those standing on his right: ‘Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.
