For I was hungry and you gave me food; I was thirsty and you gave me drink; I was a stranger and you welcomed me; I was naked and you clothed me; I was sick and you visited me; I was in prison and you came to me’ (Matthew 25:34–36).”

That no one can worthily show these same works of mercy to others if he is cruel to himself, the Lord teaches in the Gospel. He rebuked the Pharisees because they washed themselves outwardly but inwardly were full of plunder and iniquity, and, instructing them concerning an almsgiving that a person ought first to give himself, he said that the inner parts should be cleansed: “Nevertheless, give alms, and behold, everything will be clean for you” (Luke 11:41). Shortly afterward he explains this more clearly, saying: “Cleanse what is within, and what is outside will be clean.”

Blessed Augustine says in the *Enchiridion* (chapter 75):

> “Those who live most wickedly and do not care to correct such a life and such conduct, yet do not cease to give alms frequently amid their very crimes and sins, flatter themselves in vain because the Lord says: ‘Give alms, and behold, everything will be clean for you.’”

And shortly afterward (chapter 76):

> “Whoever wishes to give alms in an orderly manner ought to begin with himself and first give alms to himself. For almsgiving is a work of mercy, and it has been said most truly: ‘Have mercy on your soul, pleasing God’ (Sirach 30:24).”

In the same work, shortly afterward (chapter 77):

> “Let those who imagine that through whatever most lavish almsgiving of their produce or of any money they can purchase impunity to persist in the enormity of their crimes and the wickedness of their sins not deceive themselves. They not only do these things but love them, always wishing, if they can do so with impunity, to remain involved in them.
>
> “‘Whoever loves iniquity hates his own soul’ (Psalm 10:6); and whoever hates his own soul is not merciful but cruel. By loving it according to the world, he hates it according to God. If, therefore, he wished to give it alms by which everything might be made clean for it, he would hate it according to the world and love it according to God.”

Again, the same author in the same work (chapter 70):

> “Certainly one must beware lest anyone suppose that those abominable crimes—of which those who commit them will not possess the kingdom of God—may be perpetrated daily and redeemed daily by almsgiving. Life must be changed for the better, and God must be appeased through almsgiving concerning past sins, not somehow purchased so that it may always be permitted to commit them with impunity.
>
> “He has given no one license to sin, although in his mercy he erases sins already committed, if suitable satisfaction is not neglected.”

And shortly afterward (chapters 71–72):

> “Almsgiving,” he says, “is forgiving the person who asks pardon. Accordingly, the Lord’s saying applies to everything done through useful mercy: ‘Give alms, and behold, everything will be clean for you’ (Luke 11:41).
>
> “Therefore not only does the person who gives food to the hungry, drink to the thirsty, clothing to the naked, lodging to the stranger, shelter to the fugitive, visitation to the sick or imprisoned, ransom to the captive, assistance to the weak, guidance to the blind, consolation to the sad, healing to the sick, a way to the one who has gone astray, counsel to the one deliberating, and whatever is necessary to anyone in need give alms; the person who forgives the sinner also gives alms.
>
> “The one who corrects by punishment a person over whom authority has been given, or restrains him by some discipline, yet forgives from the heart the sin by which he was injured or offended, or prays that it may be forgiven him, gives alms—not only in forgiving and praying, but also in rebuking and imposing another corrective punishment—for he shows mercy.”

Gregory, in the *Book of the Moralia* (Book 29, chapter 14):

> “Whoever supplies external substance to a needy neighbor but does not guard his own life from wickedness gives his property to God and himself to sin. What is lesser he offers to the Creator, and what is greater he preserves for iniquity.”

And shortly afterward (Book 12, chapter 23):

> “For whoever both wishes always to sin and, as though always to give alms, offers a price in vain, because he does not redeem the soul that he does not restrain from vices.”

Again, the same author [Note: [Col. 0253D] *Pastoral Book*, Part 3, chapter 21]:

> “Whoever gives food and clothing generously to the poor, yet is polluted by iniquity of soul or body, offers what is lesser to justice and gives what is greater to sins: he has given his possessions to God and prepared himself for the devil.”

Behold, as the divine oracles and the outstanding teachings of the most illustrious doctors show, no one can both devote himself to crimes and properly apply himself to works of mercy. There are many, as was said above, who live wickedly and think that what they commit can be redeemed by lavish distributions of alms.

Hence many, deceived by a vain, indeed perverse, confidence, boldly commit adulteries, murders, false testimonies, perjuries, and many other such things. When someone of this kind is rebuked, he commonly objects: “If I avenge myself for the injuries inflicted upon me, and commit this or that which I have in mind, I praise God: I have many resources by which I can easily redeem such an act”—as though he could hire God with a reward so that, at his own pleasure, he might be permitted to do what God’s holy law forbids.

God is therefore not to be hired so that we may sin for a reward; rather, he is to be entreated that we may not sin and that we may be absolved from past sins. Whoever, lifted up by the pride of power and trusting in an abundance of riches, commits such a deed should not easily believe that it can be expiated by such wealth. Instead, it is necessary for him to turn with his whole heart to the lamentations of repentance and to strive, through bodily contrition, to cleanse what he has wickedly committed.

## CHAPTER XI. On Stinginess

There are many things that are thought trivial but are not, such as stinginess, wasteful extravagance, and many things similar to these. Just as robbery is abominable to God, so stinginess is reprehensible.

Concerning the need to avoid it, the Lord says in the Law:

> “If one of your brothers who dwell within the gates of your city, in the land that the Lord your God is going to give you, has fallen into poverty, you shall not harden your heart or withdraw your hand. Instead, you shall open it to the poor person and lend whatever you see him need.
>
> “Beware lest an impious thought secretly seize you and you say in your heart: ‘The seventh year of remission is approaching,’ and turn your eyes away from your poor brother, unwilling to lend him what he asks, lest he cry out against you to the Lord and it become sin for you.
>
> “Rather, you shall give to him, and you shall do nothing deceitful in relieving his needs, so that the Lord your God may bless you at all times and in everything to which you set your hand. There will be no shortage of poor people in the land of your dwelling. Therefore I command you to open your hand to your needy and poor brother who lives with you in the land” (Deuteronomy 15:7ff.).

And the Lord says in the Gospel: “See and beware of all avarice, because a person’s life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions” (Luke 12:15). Having first presented the parable of a certain rich man whose field had yielded abundant crops, he finally added that God said to this rich man: “Fool, this night your soul will be required of you; whose will the things be that you have prepared?” And he concluded: “So is the one who stores up treasure for himself and is not rich toward God” (ibid., verse 20).

Concerning the stinginess of that same rich man, blessed Augustine says in the Book of Sermons (Sermon 19, chapter 2):

> “When does a Christian dare to tell me that it is good to seize what belongs to others, since he does not dare to say that it is good to cling tenaciously to what belongs to himself? Was that rich man, whose estate had yielded abundant crops and who could not find where to store his produce, and who rejoiced that he had found the plan of demolishing his old storehouses and building larger ones so that he could fill them and say to his soul, ‘Soul, you have many good things stored up for many years; rejoice, enjoy yourself, feast,’—was that rich man seeking what belonged to others? He was not troubling over the boundary of a neighbor’s field; he was not stripping a poor man; he was not deceiving a simple person. He was thinking only about gathering his own things. Hear what he heard, since he guarded his own things so tenaciously; and from this understand what those who seize what belongs to others should expect. When, then, he thought that he had found the wisest plan—demolishing his old, cramped storehouses, building new and larger ones, and gathering and storing all his produce in them, without coveting or seizing what belonged to others—the Lord said to him: ‘Fool, where you think yourself wise, there you are a fool. Fool,’ he said, ‘this night they will demand your soul from you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?’ (Luke 12:21.) If you preserve them, they will not be yours; if you distribute them, they will be yours.”

The same author, in a homily for the Day of Judgment:

> “Pay attention, brothers, and see that the Lord does not say, ‘Depart from me, accursed ones, because you committed theft, because you gave false testimony, because you committed murder and adultery’—which is more serious. He did not say this, but said: ‘For I was hungry, and you did not give me food’ (Matthew 25:35). He did not say, ‘Depart from me because you took what belonged to others,’ which is more unjust; but he said, ‘because you did not give to the poor from your own substance.’ Not because you did evil deeds, but because you were unwilling to do good deeds. Just as mercy alone will deliver those who are on the right, so stinginess alone will condemn those who are on the left. For in that sentence of the Lord, in which he said that the one who did not feed the hungry and clothe the naked would be sent into eternal fire, we can clearly recognize, brothers, with what torment or punishment those who do evil will be condemned, when those who do not do good are sent into the fire. If the one who did not give his bread to the poor is condemned with the devil, where will the one who took what belonged to another be condemned? If the one who did not clothe the naked is sent into the fire, where, do you think, will the one who stripped him be condemned?”

Gregory, in his homily on the rich man and Lazarus:

> “For it is not said that the rich man violently oppressed anyone, but that he exalted himself in the possessions he had received. From this, therefore, one must carefully infer with what punishment he should be chastised who seizes what belongs to others, if the one who does not distribute what belongs to himself is struck by condemnation to hell. Let no one, then, consider himself secure by saying, ‘Look, I do not seize what belongs to others, but I enjoy possessions lawfully granted to me’; for that rich man was not punished because he took what belonged to others, but because, amid the possessions he had received, he abandoned himself to evil. This is what handed him over to hell: he was not fearful in his prosperity; he bent the gifts he had received toward the use of arrogance; he ignored the bowels of compassion; and, even while he had abundant means, he was unwilling to redeem his sins.”

How pestilential and detestable the vice of stinginess is is therefore plainly indicated. All the faithful must take great care to avoid it, lest—God forbid—by following it they should either, like the rich man who thought of hoarding his possessions tenaciously, be branded with the title of folly, or, like the other rich man who did not seize what belonged to others but neglected to distribute what belonged to himself, be condemned. Let them therefore give to the poor, if they do not wish to be consumed by flames; let them give to Christ on earth what he may repay to them in heaven.

## CHAPTER XII. That death must always be set before our eyes

Whoever places before his eyes the final hour of his life, in which he must be taken from this clay dwelling, and remembers that he carries a fragile vessel, soon to be shattered and reduced to dust, and diligently meditates upon the punishments of the wicked and the glory of the saints, sins either scarcely at all or only rarely. Since we do not remember these things as we ought, we consequently fall into many precipitous places of offense.

That we must be ready to meet the Lord is taught most abundantly by the pages of both Testaments. We ought therefore to obey so many and such salutary admonitions and exhortations, to set death daily before our eyes, and to prepare ourselves in such a way that, when the Lord comes and knocks, we may immediately open to him. Then the Gospel saying will be fulfilled in us:

> “Blessed are those servants whom, when the Lord comes, he finds watching” (Luke 12:37);

and we may deserve to receive what follows:

> “Truly I say to you, he will set him over all his possessions” (ibid., verse 44).

That in all our actions we ought to remember our last things is affirmed by Solomon:

> “In all your works remember your last things, and you will never sin” (Ecclesiasticus 7:40).

And the Lord says in the Gospel:

> “Watch therefore, because you do not know the day or the hour” (Matthew 25:13).

Blessed Gregory explains this in his homilies (Homily 12):

> “Because,” he says, “the Lord receives repentance after sins, if each person knew at what time he would depart from the present age, he could assign one period to pleasures and another to repentance. But he who promised pardon to the penitent did not promise tomorrow to the sinner. We must therefore always fear the final day, which we can never foresee. Look: we receive this very day on which we are speaking as a postponement for conversion, and yet we refuse to mourn the evils we have committed. We not only fail to lament what we have omitted, but we also increase the things that must be lamented. Yet if some illness should seize us, if signs of illness should announce approaching death, we seek a postponement of life so that we may mourn our sins, and we ask with great fervor of desire for those postponements which, when granted to us now, we regard as worthless.”

A little later:

> “Let us therefore, brothers, carefully consider these things, lest our time pass away in vain and we then seek to live for doing good when we are already compelled to leave the body. Remember what the Truth says: ‘Pray that your flight may not be in winter or on the Sabbath’ (Matthew 24:20). For by the commandment of the Law it is not permitted to travel a long distance on the Sabbath. Winter is an impediment to walking, because the stiffness of the cold restrains the steps of those who walk. He therefore says: ‘Pray that your flight may not be in winter or on the Sabbath.’ It is as though he said plainly: ‘See to it that you do not then seek to flee from your sins, when it is no longer permitted to walk.’ That time in which flight is not permitted ought therefore to be considered now, while it is permitted. The hour of our departure must always be kept in view; this admonition of the Redeemer must always be placed before the eyes of the mind: ‘Watch therefore, because you do not know the day or the hour’ (ibid. 25:13).”

The same author (Homily 13):

> “Our Lord wished the final hour to be unknown to us so that it might always be regarded with suspicion, so that, since we cannot foresee it, we might prepare for it without interruption. Therefore, my brothers, fix the eyes of your mind upon the condition of your mortality; prepare yourselves daily through tears and lamentations for the Judge who is coming. Since certain death awaits everyone, do not occupy yourselves with uncertain plans for temporal life. Let concern for earthly things not weigh you down. For however great the masses of silver and gold with which the flesh is surrounded, and whatever precious garments it wears, what else is it than flesh? Do not therefore consider what you have, but what you are. Do you wish to hear what you are? The Prophet indicates it, saying: ‘Truly, the people are grass’ (Isaiah 40:7). For if the people are not grass, where are those who, together with you, celebrated last year the birthday feast of blessed Felicity, while today we celebrate it? Oh, how many and how great plans they were making concerning the care of the present life! But when the moment of death stole upon them, they were suddenly found amid the things they had been unwilling to foresee; and all the temporal things which, as though securely, they seemed to possess after careful consideration, they lost at once. If, then, the multitude of the human race flourished in the flesh through birth and withered into dust through death, it was plainly grass. Since the hours flee in their moments, act therefore, dearest brothers, so that they may be held fast in the reward of a good work. Hear what wise Solomon says: ‘Whatever your hand can do, do it promptly, because there is neither work, nor reason, nor knowledge, nor wisdom in the underworld, where you are hastening’ (Ecclesiasticus 9:10). Since we do not know the time of approaching death and cannot work after death, it remains for us to seize the time granted before death. Death itself is conquered when it is feared before it comes.”

Prosper [Note: *On Contempt for the World*, book III, chapter 11, in the middle]:

> “If, at the time when someone is deliberating about sinning, he should consider with a sound mind what punishment awaits those caught in their crimes and wickedness, what torment tortures the convicted, what trembling shakes them, what pallor covers their faces, and, finally, how greatly even the disgrace of a sordid reputation humiliates them and makes them detestable to everyone, I do not know whether he could give his consent to any vices.”

There are also countless other testimonies concerning the hour of the final day, which must constantly be considered and placed before our eyes. Having carefully attended to these things, then, while we can and have the time, let us work unfailingly at what is good, according to the Apostle’s saying:

> “Let us not grow weary in doing good, for in due season we shall reap without growing weary” (Galatians 6:9).

For the present life is the time for sowing, that is, for good works … [lacuna] for receiving the fruit. No one can reap such a harvest while growing weary:

> “The one who perseveres,” says the Lord, “to the end will be saved.”

## CHAPTER XIII. That the Lord will demand from us the fruit of whatever good we ought to have said or done in each period of life; and that an angel is appointed to each person for his protection

We must cultivate the vineyard—which tropologically signifies our soul, which the Lord freed from the dark Egypt of this world, carried through the Red Sea, that is, baptism, betrothed with the ring of his faith, and established in the watchtower of his knowledge and vision—through continual cultivation with holy works, so that when its Lord comes, we may be able to render him worthy fruits of good works for each period of life. Thus blessed Jerome writes in his Commentaries on the Evangelist Matthew:

> “When, therefore, the lord of the vineyard comes, what will he do to those tenants, and so forth” (Matthew 21:49; Luke 22:16). “The Lord,” he says, “asks them not because he does not know what they will answer, but so that they may be condemned by their own answer. The vineyard has been entrusted to us, and entrusted on the condition that we return fruit to the Lord in its seasons, and know what we ought to say or do at each time.”

Observe that fruits of good speech or good action must be rendered to the Lord for each period of life. The periods allotted to slander, perjury, lying, giving false testimony, foul speech, buffoonery, insults, idle talk, and the pursuit of countless other vanities are therefore excluded. Instead, the periods of our life are commanded to be spent in speaking and doing what is good, without interruption by evil words and actions.

That an angel is appointed to each person for his protection is written by the aforementioned Jerome in the same Commentary:

> “Truly I say to you, the angels always see the face of the Father.” Great is the dignity of souls, since each one has an angel assigned to guard it from the beginning of birth. Hence we read in the Apocalypse of John: ‘Write to the angel of Ephesus, of Thyatira, and to the angel of Philadelphia, and to the angels of the four remaining churches.’”

Bede therefore writes in his Exposition of the Acts of the Apostles:

> “‘Now I truly know that the Lord sent his angel and rescued me from the hand of Herod,’ and so forth (Acts 12:11). That each one of us has angels is found both in the *Book of the Shepherd* and in many passages of Holy Scripture. For the Lord also says concerning little ones: ‘Their angels always see the face of my Father’ (Matthew 18:10). Jacob too speaks of himself: ‘The angel who rescued me from all evils’ (Genesis 48:16). And these disciples believed that the angel of the apostle Peter had come.”

Since it is therefore established that we are protected by the guardianship of angels, it is right and necessary that, in their sight, we should not in any way make ourselves unworthy—whether in thought, speech, or deed. The more we persist in unlawful thoughts, words, and wicked works, the farther they withdraw from us, and the enemies of our souls draw nearer. But when, by speaking and acting well, we make ourselves cheerful and pure, we are not only [lacuna] under their protection, but are also pleasing in their sight, so that we may rightly say with the Psalmist:

> “In the sight of the angels I will sing praise to you, my God” (Psalm 137:1).

If we prove to be such that we can worthily sing praise to our God in the sight of the angels, and can be protected by their guardianship in this life, then, when we depart from it, having scorned the mockery of our enemies—of whom the Psalmist says, “My God, in you I trust; I shall not be put to shame; let not my enemies mock me” (Psalm 24:2)—we shall deserve happily to pass into their fellowship.

## CHAPTER XIV. On visiting the sick and anointing them with holy oil

As the Gospel trumpet solemnly proclaims:

> “When the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty” (Matthew 19:28),

he will therefore place the wicked on the left because they were barren in the six works of mercy, and the good on the right because they devoted themselves to those works. One of these works is visiting the sick, as he himself will say on the day of that fearful examination:

> “I was sick, and you visited me” (Matthew 25:35).

Since he who wished to be visited in the sick shows no partiality, some people nevertheless appear to fulfill this command in a personal and preferential manner, in a way unworthy of Christians. When powerful and rich people fall ill, they are visited not by the poor, whose persons are not admitted for such visits, but by their social equals, so that they may repay one another in such matters. The poor, however, are scarcely ever visited by the powerful. Since all are equal by the condition of nature, all must likewise be visited equally when they fall ill, with partiality toward persons set aside.

The sick person, when visited, must not only be admonished not to murmur under God’s chastisements, but rather to recognize that he is being chastised because of his sins and to give thanks to his Creator; he must also be supplied with whatever he needs.

To confound the pride of those who, swollen with the arrogance of power and wealth, visit only the powerful and rich and disdain to go to the poor, the Lord did not wish to go to the son of the ruler, but promised that he would go to the centurion’s servant. Blessed Pope Gregory says in a homily on this Gospel (Homily 28):

> “What does it mean that the ruler asks him to come to his son, yet he refuses to go bodily, while he is not invited to the centurion’s servant and nevertheless promises that he will go bodily? He does not deem himself worthy to be present bodily for the ruler’s son, but does not disdain to meet the centurion’s servant. What does this mean except that our pride is rebuked? We honor in human beings not the nature by which we were made in the image of God, but honors and riches. When we weigh what surrounds them, we plainly fail to perceive their interior qualities, because we consider what is despised in their bodies. Our Redeemer, however, to show that what is exalted among human beings must be despised by the holy, and what is despised among human beings must not be despised, did not wish to go to the ruler’s son, while the Son of God was ready to go to the centurion’s servant. Our pride is therefore rebuked: it does not know how to value people for the sake of their humanity, but, as we have said, values only what surrounds them; it does not look at their nature or recognize God’s honor in human beings. Look: the Son of God does not wish to go to the ruler’s son, yet he is ready to come for the salvation of a servant. Certainly, if the servant of some person were to ask us to go to him, our pride would immediately answer us in silent thought: ‘Do not go, because you are degrading yourself; your honor is being despised; the place is becoming base.’ Look: he has come from heaven and does not disdain to meet a servant on earth; yet we, who are from the earth, disdain to humble ourselves on earth. What can be baser or more contemptible before God than to preserve one’s honor before human beings and not fear the eyes of the inward witness?”

There are also many people, both of higher and lower rank, who, hindered by weakness of mind, refuse to visit the sick, fearing that they might contract some contagion from the visit itself—as though death could find them only while they were visiting the sick, and as though they themselves could evade the death which no mortal can in any way avoid. Hence someone says:

> Who among the timid does not avoid the contagion of the sick,  
> fearing that he may thereby contract a neighboring evil?

There are likewise many who, when either they themselves or their parents and relatives fall ill, do not ask that priests of the Church be brought to them, nor that they be anointed with consecrated oil according to apostolic tradition and the custom of the holy Church. Instead, they prefer to consult male and female diviners—indeed, to consult the devil in them—and have it divined by what circumstance they contracted the illness and whether or not they can escape it.

Those who do this imitate the example of Ahaziah, the impious king, who, because he had abandoned the God of Israel and consulted Beelzebub, the god of Ekron, through messengers, deserved to hear from the Lord through the prophet Elijah:

> “From the bed on which you have climbed, you shall not come down; rather, you shall surely die” (2 Kings 1:4).

King Saul also, abandoned by the Lord because of his disobedience, since he asked to have his future divined by the pythoness, deserved to hear:

> “God will also deliver Israel with you into the hands of the Philistines. Tomorrow you and your sons shall be with me” (1 Samuel 28:19).

That such divinations must be entirely avoided by everyone, and that anointing with consecrated oil must be sought, is indicated by the evangelist Mark:

> “And going out, they preached that people should repent, and they cast out many demons, and anointed many sick people with oil, and healed them” (Mark 6:13).

From this it is clear, as Bede writes [Note: *On the Epistle of Blessed James*, chapter 5], that this custom was handed down to the holy Church: that the possessed, or any other sick persons, should be anointed with oil consecrated by episcopal blessing.

The apostle James also teaches:

> “Is anyone among you sick? Let him bring in the priests of the Church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord; and the prayer of faith will save the sick person, and the Lord will raise him up; and if he is in sins, they will be forgiven him” (James 5:14).

The aforementioned Bede explains this as follows:

> “Just as he had given counsel to the sorrowful, so he also gives counsel to the sick concerning how to protect himself from the folly of murmuring. In proportion to the wound he establishes the remedy: commanding the sorrowful to pray and sing psalms for himself, while directing the one sick either in body or in faith—since he has suffered the greater wound—to remember that he must be healed through the assistance of many, and of elders in particular. He should not entrust the care of his weakness to younger and less learned men, lest perhaps he receive from them some harmful consolation or advice. ‘And let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord’ (ibid., verse 14). The apostles are also read to have done this in the Gospel, and now the custom of the Church holds that the sick are anointed with consecrated oil by priests and healed with prayer accompanying the anointing.”

Not only priests, but, as Pope Innocent wrote [Note: *Epistle I*, chapter 8; and Bede at the place cited above], all Christians are permitted in the same passage to use it in their own necessity or that of their relatives. This oil, however, may be prepared only by bishops. For when he says, “with oil consecrated in the name of the Lord,” he may mean either that the oil is consecrated in the Lord’s name, or certainly that, when they anoint the sick person, they must likewise invoke the Lord’s name over him:

> “And if he is in sins, they will be forgiven him.”

Many are afflicted with bodily illness or even death because of sins committed in the soul. Thus the Apostle says to the Corinthians, because they were accustomed to receive the Lord’s body unworthily:

> “For this reason many among you are sick and weak, and many sleep” (1 Corinthians 11:30).

If, then, the sick are in sins, and confess them to the priests of the Church, and earnestly strive to abandon and amend them with a perfect heart, they will be forgiven. For sins cannot be forgiven without confession and amendment.

For many, through ignorance, and for many others through negligence, this anointing with oil has fallen out of use. For those among whom it is not customary, it is necessary that it come into use. Therefore, when someone falls ill, he ought to seek a remedy from the Church, its priests, and the anointing with consecrated oil—not from male and female diviners, who are certainly dwelling places of demons—and he should ask the Lord Jesus Christ for a remedy not only for the body but also for the soul.

## CHAPTER XV. On burying the dead and caring for their souls

In burying corpses, humanity must be shown toward all the dead in general, not merely affection toward those who are dear to us. In both the Old and the New Testament, those who have shown the greatest devotion and humanity toward burying the dead are praised with great commendation.

In the Old Testament, as you have in the case of Tobit:

> “He fed the hungry and provided clothing for the naked” (Tobit 1:20).

And shortly afterward:

> “When he had gone out, he returned and reported that one of the children of Israel lay slaughtered in the street. Immediately he leaped up from his couch, left his meal while still fasting, went to the body, took it, and carried it secretly into his house, so that after the sun had set he might bury it carefully” (Tobit 2:3).

And later, the angel says to Tobit:

> “When you prayed with tears, buried the dead, left your meal, concealed the dead during the day in your house, and buried them at night, I offered your prayer to the Lord” (Tobit 12:12).

You also have many other examples in the same Testament of those who showed the greatest generosity and devotion in burying kings, prophets, and other holy men.

In the New Testament there are not only Joseph, who wrapped Christ’s body in a shroud and buried him in his own new tomb, but also countless other holy men set before you as examples. They showed devoted humanity not only in burying the bodies of the holy martyrs but also in burying the corpses of all sorts of other people.

Although this is so, many Christians today deprive the funerals of the poor of the consolation of this service, and lavish it only upon the rich, the powerful, and their own dear ones, with conspicuousness and ambition—although, as blessed Jerome says, all ambition ought to cease in death. Just as rich and poor must be visited equally by all Christians, so likewise they must all be buried by everyone, since all who are born from Adam’s mass of sin must die.

This debt is so unavoidable and inescapable that none of Adam’s children can be free from it. The blood of Christ frees us from perpetual death, not from common death. In Adam, according to the Apostle, we all die; but in Christ we are made alive. In Adam, therefore, we fell, but in Christ we rose again. Thus we grew better after our fall.

Since we are earth and must be reduced to earth, and at the time of resurrection must be restored to a better state, Christian devotion, raised up by hope of the resurrection, ought to show the most devoted care of mercy in burying the dead and caring for their souls. Hence blessed Augustine says in the Book of Sermons [Note: *On the Words of the Apostle*, Sermon 32, chapter 3]:

> “Let there be care, according to one’s ability, for burying and constructing tombs, because these too are counted among good works in the Holy Scriptures. And not only in the bodies of patriarchs and other saints, and in the human corpses of all who lie dead, but also in the very body of the Lord, those who did these things are praised and commended. Let people perform these duties of a final service toward their own, and the lamentations of their human grief.”

We are therefore saddened by the loss of those dear to us, but raised up by hope of future immortality; through the gift of resurrection we rejoice and are consoled. The Apostle admonishes us not to grieve concerning those who sleep—that is, the dead—like the others who have no hope (1 Thessalonians 4:12): namely, the hope of resurrection and eternal incorruption. He calls them sleeping and thereby shows that they will eventually awaken.

Augustine likewise says in the same book (chapters 1–2):

> “We are saddened at the deaths of our own because we are necessarily deprived of them, but with the hope of receiving them again. From one side we are distressed; from the other we are consoled. From one side human weakness afflicts us; from the other faith restores us. From one side human condition causes grief; from the other divine promise heals. Therefore the funeral procession, the ranks of mourners, the costly care of burial, and the lavish construction of monuments are whatever consolations of the living, not aids for the dead. Yet there is no doubt that the dead are helped by the prayers of the holy Church, by the saving sacrifice, and by almsgiving distributed for their spirits—but only those who lived before death in such a way that these things could be useful to them after death. New merits are not acquired for the dead when something good is done on their behalf; rather, these consequent benefits are returned according to their preceding merits.”

It is clear, then, that the work of mercy must be performed in burying human bodies. If this humanity does not benefit them in obtaining a remedy for the soul, it certainly benefits us; and if it benefits those who perform it, it harms no one. Therefore, if it is pious to bury the dead, it is impious and inhuman not to bury them.

What, moreover, should we think of those who neither bury the dead in their fields nor permit them to be buried there without payment of some fee? Those who freely bury the dead in their fields imitate Joseph, who buried the Lord’s body in his own tomb. But those who, inflamed by avarice, do not permit the dead to be buried in their fields without payment seem to imitate Ephron, who demanded and received money from Abraham, the servant of God, and sold him the field where he was to bury his dead.

Those who judge that corpses should be buried in basilicas and that burial there is beneficial should read the Book of Dialogues [Note: Blessed Gregory, *Dialogues*, book IV, chapter 50 and following], and they will discover for whom burial in a church is beneficial and for whom it is harmful.

There are some who, in order to build beautiful houses for themselves, do not hesitate to dig up the graves of the dead and expose their bones and ashes to the sun. This custom has crept in among certain people to such an extent that they do not understand that they are sinning by this act. They say that it does no harm to those whose bones they profane. Yet even if it does not harm them, it harms the perpetrators greatly. Nothing harmed the martyrs when their bodies were thrown to be torn apart by beasts and birds; there is no doubt that it harmed greatly those who threw them out.

It is inhuman to dig up the bodies of the dead and expose them to the sun; it is humane and pious to commit them to the earth. Whoever therefore violates and digs up the graves of the dead without unavoidable necessity and without the honor due to piety is rightly compared to the Assyrians, who, according to the Lord’s previously mentioned threat, cast the bones of kings, prophets, and those who had dwelt in Jerusalem from their tombs and exposed them to the sun. How greatly this impiety harmed the Assyrians among the other things they inflicted upon the people of God because of their sins was demonstrated by the outcome.

Let people therefore cease to profane the bones of the dead and allow them to await the day of resurrection in their urns. Rather, let them perform the work of piety by burying the dead.

Concerning this matter Lactantius writes in his book *On the Workmanship of God* [Note: *On True Worship*, book VI, chapter 12]:

> “Let us not, therefore, allow the image and workmanship of God to lie exposed as prey for wild beasts and birds, but let us return it to the earth from which it arose. And although, in the case of an unknown person, we have fulfilled the duty owed to those close to him, let humanity take the place of those who are absent; and wherever a human being is in need, let us consider our duty to be required there. In what does the principle of justice consist more than in this: that what we provide to our own through affection, we should provide to strangers through humanity, which is much more reliable and just? For we are no longer providing it to a human being, who feels nothing, but to God alone, for whom a just work is a most beloved sacrifice.”

It is necessary, then, that when the heavenly origin has left the material of the flesh which it inhabited and ruled until that time, human piety should not allow it to be torn apart by wild beasts and birds, but should carefully strive to commit it to the earth.

It is the duty of Christians not only to bury the bodies of the dead carefully and devoutly, but rather also to aid their spirits through prayers and almsgiving. Even if parents, relatives, and friends are absent who might perform these duties in particular for the dead, Mother Church, which spiritually gave them birth, does not cease to perform these things for them in general.

Hence, as blessed Augustine says in the Book of Sermons, the Church observes the universal tradition handed down by the holy Fathers:

> “That when those who have died in communion with the body and blood of Christ are commemorated in their appointed place at the sacrifice itself, prayer should be made for them, and that it should also be commemorated that an offering is made for them.”

Those who say that no other almsgiving can help the dead except what is given to priests, and the sacrifices offered to God through them, must not be listened to at all. Those who believe and say this are deceived either through ignorance or through the persuasion of others. It is quite believable that this persuasion, by which simple people appear to be induced to believe and say such things, arose from the source of avarice.

For holy Mother Church is accustomed to offer for her dead not only the sacrifices of the altar but also every other kind of almsgiving. Thus every day sacrifices are offered to God for the spirits of those who offered their possessions to God, together with prayers and supplications of many kinds, hospitality toward guests, refreshment for the poor, redemption of captives, and countless other forms of assistance. Yet these benefit those who lived in such a way that these things could also benefit them after death, as blessed Augustine says in the *Enchiridion* (chapters 109–110):

> “The time that lies between a person’s death and the final resurrection holds souls in hidden places, according as each is worthy either of rest or of distress, in accordance with what each received as his lot in the flesh while he lived. Nor should it be denied that the souls of the dead are relieved by the piety of their living relatives when the sacrifice of the Mediator is offered for them or when almsgiving is performed in the Church. But these things benefit those who, while they lived, merited that they could afterward benefit from them. There is one manner of life—not so good that it does not require these things after death; there is another so good that it does not require them; and again there is another so evil that, when this life has passed, it cannot be helped even by these things. Therefore, all merit by which someone may be relieved or burdened after this life is acquired here. Let no one hope to obtain merit before God after death for what he neglected here.
>
> “Therefore, the things which the Church regularly performs for commending the dead are not contrary to that apostolic sentence which says: ‘We shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ, so that each one may receive according to what he has done through the body, whether good or evil’ (Romans 14:10). For each person also acquired this merit for himself while he lived in the body, so that these things might benefit him; they cannot benefit everyone. And why can they not benefit everyone, except because of the difference in the life each person led in the body?
>
> “When, therefore, sacrifices are offered for all baptized dead, whether of the altar or of any kind of almsgiving, they are thanksgivings for the very good, propitiations for those who are not very evil, and, for the very evil—even if they provide no assistance to the dead—they are some kind of consolation for the living. For those whom they benefit, they do not benefit them so that there may be complete remission, or certainly so that the condemnation itself may become more tolerable.”

If anyone therefore wishes to know more fully and extensively about this matter, let him read the book of the same blessed Augustine, *On the Care to Be Taken for the Dead*.

## CHAPTER XVI. That the faithful must not doubt at all concerning the resurrection of the dead

Although we are afflicted by the condition of the death that has been brought upon us, we are nevertheless raised up by hope of the future resurrection. Since some, hindered by weakness of mind, doubt concerning the resurrection of the dead, it is necessary to demonstrate from the pages of both Testaments and from the judgments of the holy Fathers that there must be no doubt at all concerning it.

The Lord declares in the Law: “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob”; he is not the God of the dead, but of the living (Mark XII, 27; Luke XX, 38). And Job says: “I know that my Redeemer lives, and on the last day I shall rise from the earth, and again I shall be clothed with my skin, and in my flesh I shall see God. Whom I myself shall see, and not another: my eyes shall behold him, and this hope of mine is stored in my bosom” (Job XIX, 27). Again: “All the days in which I now serve, I await until my transformation comes” (Job XIV, 14).

Ezekiel says: “O dry bones, hear the word of the Lord. Thus says the Lord God to these bones: Behold, I will bring spirit into you, and you shall live; and I will put sinews upon you, and I will cause flesh to grow over you, and I will stretch skin over you, and I will give you spirit, and you shall know that I am the Lord,” etc. (Ezekiel XXXVII, 4 ff.).

In the Gospel: “For just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he wills” (John V, 11). Again: “For this is the will of him who sent me, the Father: that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me, but raise it up on the last day” (John VI, 39). Again: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day” (ibid., v. 55).

Paul says to the Thessalonians: “For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, so also God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep through Jesus” (I Thessalonians IV, 13).

[Col. 0265C] The same apostle says to the Corinthians: “But if Christ is preached as risen from the dead, how do some among you say that there is no resurrection of the dead? For if there is no resurrection of the dead, neither has Christ risen. For our preaching is empty, and therefore our faith is empty. We are even found to be false witnesses of God, because we have testified against God that he raised Christ, whom he did not raise, if the dead are not raised. For if the dead are not raised, neither has Christ risen. But if Christ has not risen, your faith is vain; for you are still in your sins. Therefore those also who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished. If in this life only we have hope in Christ, we are more pitiable than all human beings.

[Col. 0266A] “But now Christ has risen from the dead, the firstfruits of those who sleep; for since death came through a human being, the resurrection of the dead also came through a human being. And just as all die in Adam, so also all shall be made alive in Christ. But each in his own order: Christ the firstfruits; then those who belong to Christ at his coming; then the end, when he has handed over the kingdom to God and the Father.”

[Col. 0266B] Again, in the same epistle: “But someone will say: How are the dead raised? And with what sort of body do they come? Fool, what you sow is not brought to life unless it first dies; and what you sow, you do not sow as the body that is to be, but a bare grain.” And below: “There is one glory of heavenly bodies, and another of earthly bodies; one brightness of the sun, another of the moon, and another brightness of the stars. For star differs from star in brightness; so also is the resurrection of the dead. It is sown in corruption, it shall rise in incorruption. It is sown in dishonor, it shall rise in glory. It is sown in weakness, it shall rise in power. It is sown an animal body, it shall rise a spiritual body” (I Corinthians XV, 12 ff.).

[Col. 0266C] Augustine, in the *Enchiridion* (chapter 84):

“Now concerning the resurrection of the flesh—not as some have risen and then died again, but into eternal life, as the flesh of Christ himself rose—I do not find how I can discuss it briefly and satisfy all the questions that are usually raised concerning this matter. Nevertheless, a Christian ought in no way to doubt that the flesh of human beings who have been born or will be born, who have died or will die, shall rise again.”

And shortly afterward (chapter 86):

“From the moment a human being begins to live, from that moment he can already die. But once dead, wherever death may have overtaken him, I cannot discover how he should not belong to the resurrection of the dead.”

And shortly afterward (chapter 88):

[Col. 0266D] “The earthly material from which the flesh of mortals is created does not perish for God. Let it be dissolved into whatever dust or ashes, let it disperse into whatever winds and airs, let it be changed into the substance of whatever other bodies, or even into the elements themselves, let it become the food of whatever animals, including human beings, and be transformed into flesh: God restores it to the human soul in an instant of time, he who first animated it so that the human being might come into existence, grow, and live.

[Col. 0267A] “(Chapter 89.) That earthly material itself, which becomes a corpse when the soul departs, shall not be restored in the resurrection in such a way that whatever things have dispersed and been transformed into the various species and forms of other things—although they return to the body from which they dispersed—must necessarily return to the very same bodily parts where they had been. Otherwise, if what frequent cutting removed from the hair returns as hair, and what repeated clipping removed from the nails returns as nails, an excessive and indecorous deformity would confront those who imagine this and therefore do not believe in the resurrection of the flesh.

“But just as, if a statue of some meltable metal were liquefied by fire, or crushed into powder, or mixed into a mass, and an artisan wished to restore it from the quantity of that material, it would make no difference to its integrity which portion of the material were returned to which member of the statue, provided that the whole from which it had been constituted were recovered, so God, the wondrous and ineffable artisan, will restore our flesh from the whole of that material of which it had consisted, with wondrous and ineffable speed. Nor will it matter to its restoration whether hairs return to hairs and nails to nails, or whether whatever of them had perished is changed into flesh and recalled to other parts of the body, since the artisan’s wisdom will ensure that nothing indecorous occurs.

[Col. 0267B] “(Chapter 90.) Nor does it follow that each of those who rise again must have a different stature because the living had different statures, or that the thin must rise again with the same thinness, or the fat with the same fatness. But if it is the Creator’s plan that each person’s individual character and recognizable likeness be preserved in his appearance, while in the remaining good aspects all bodies are made equal, then the material in each person will be so purified that nothing of it will perish, and whatever was lacking in anyone will be supplied by him who was able to create whatever he willed even from nothing.

[Col. 0267C] “But if there is to be a rational inequality in the bodies of those who rise again, as there is among the voices with which a song is filled, then each person’s bodily material will produce what makes the human being suited to the angelic assemblies and introduces nothing incongruous to their senses. For nothing indecorous will exist there; whatever is to be will be fitting, since it would not be destined to exist if it were not fitting.

“(Chapter 91.) The bodies of the saints will therefore rise without any defect, without any deformity, just as they will be without any corruption, burden, or difficulty. In them there will be as much ease as there is blessedness. For this reason they are also called spiritual, although they will unquestionably be bodies, not spirits. But just as what is now called an animal body is nevertheless a body and not a soul, so then the spiritual body will nevertheless not be a spirit.

[Col. 0267D] “Accordingly, insofar as corruption is concerned—which now weighs down the soul—and insofar as the vices by which the flesh lusts against the spirit are concerned, then there will no longer be flesh but a body, since heavenly bodies too are so called.”

[Note: [Col. 0267D] What follows has been taken from various works: *Moralia on Job*, book XIV, chapter 28; likewise book II on Ezekiel, homily 20; and homily 27 on the Gospels.]

Gregory, in the *Moralia*:

[Col. 0268A] “There are some who are uncertain about the resurrection of the flesh. When they see flesh reduced to corruption and bones to dust in the tombs, they doubt that flesh and bones can be restored from dust; and so they reason within themselves, saying: ‘When a human being is restored from dust, how can it happen that ashes are given life?’ It is much less for God to restore what has existed than to create what did not exist. Or what is surprising if he raises a human being from dust, who created all things together from nothing? It is more wondrous for God to establish heaven and earth from things that did not exist than to restore the human being from earth.

“What is surprising if God restores bones, sinews, flesh, and hair from dust, when every day he restores wood, fruits, and leaves in the great mass of a tree from a small seed? When the doubting mind seeks a rational account of the power of the resurrection, questions concerning those very things should be brought before it—things that occur continually and yet cannot in any way be explained by reason—so that, while it cannot penetrate through the sight of what it sees, it may believe from the promise of divine power what it hears.

[Col. 0268B] “Often unbelieving people, when they look upon the dust of decaying flesh, say: ‘From where will bones and marrow, from where flesh and hair, be restored in the resurrection?’ Let them therefore, while asking such questions, look at the small seeds of enormous trees and, if they can, say where in them lies hidden such a mass of timber, such a diversity of branches, such a multitude and luxuriance of leaves, such beauty of flowers, and such abundance of the flavors and fragrances of fruit. Do the seeds of trees have the fragrance or flavor that the trees themselves later produce in their fruits?

“If you cannot comprehend the effect of the resurrection by reasoning, consider how many things there are whose manner of existence you do not understand, yet whose existence you do not doubt. The resurrection of the dead can plainly be established truly and faithfully by these and very many other examples, and above all by the resurrection of our own head, our Lord Jesus Christ, in whom we have all risen and are given life together.

[Col. 0268C] “For what is more consonant with sound faith, or more credible, than that the members should follow the head? Therefore, where the head has gone before, the members must follow.”

That the resurrection is for some unto life and for others unto punishment is attested by the prophet Daniel: “Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to eternal life and others to reproach” (Daniel XII, 2).

In the Second Book of Maccabees: “You, most wicked man, destroy us in the present life; but the King of the world will raise us, who have died for his laws, to the resurrection of eternal life” (II Maccabees VII, 9). Again: “It is better, having been put to death by human beings, to await the hope from God that we shall be raised again by him; but for you there will be no resurrection to life” (ibid., v. 14).

And the Lord in the Gospel: “Do not marvel at this, because the hour is coming in which all who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of God, and they will come forth: those who have done good deeds, to the resurrection of life; but those who have done evil, to the resurrection of judgment” (John V, 28).

Again: “These will go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life.” And the apostle Paul: “We shall all indeed rise, but we shall not all be changed” (I Corinthians XV, 51). All will rise, both the righteous and the unrighteous; but the righteous will rise to be changed, that is, from corruption to incorruption, while the unrighteous will rise from corruption to perpetual and ineffable corruption. Of them it is said through the prophet: “Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched” (Isaiah LXVI, 24).

[Col. 0269A] Therefore all must strive so that the resurrection may come to us for glory, not for reproach; for incorruption, not for corruption.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the Day of Judgment

On the day of the dread judgment scarcely anyone’s conscience can be secure, especially since there we shall have to give an account to God not only for our deeds but also for every idle word. But we, against whom the world and its concupiscence contend—those who run in its stadium and contend in its arena, still uncertain of receiving the crown of immortality, and who also offend in many things and need daily remissions of sins—rightly fear and dread that same terrifying day.

[Note: [Col. 0269D] “The world is delighted.” *Delectatur?* Rather, “struggles” (*luctatur*), and I judge that Jonah wrote it thus. Below I restored *pertimescitur* (“is greatly feared”), where *pertimescitur* had previously been printed.]

[Col. 0269B] For, according to the Apostle, “We shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ” (Romans XIV, 10), to render an account of what we have done through the body, whether good or evil. It is therefore perfectly clear that no mortal should fix the love of his attention upon transitory and swiftly passing things, but rather upon heavenly things with all his strength; and that he should prepare himself for such a great assembly and be able to render his account before Christ God the judge in such a way that he may deserve not to be condemned for evil deeds, but rather to be rewarded for good.

[Col. 0269C] But by those who regard this world as a prison, not as their homeland but as a place of pilgrimage, and to whom life itself is burdensome—whose citizenship, that is, is in heaven—of whom was that man who said, “I desire to depart and be with Christ” (Philippians I, 23), and who said elsewhere, “I have fought the good fight; I have finished the course; I have kept the faith. From now on the crown of righteousness is laid up for me, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will give me on that day—not only to me, but also to those who love his appearing” (II Timothy IV, 7)—that day is not feared as much as it is by us, who are of far lesser merit.

It is therefore credible that by the spirits of the saints, for whom there is the Sabbath of perpetual rest, who await the resurrection of their bodies, that true circumcision and true jubilee are sought, when they will return to their ancient possession, receiving, according to the Apocalypse, two robes; and the prophetic saying will be fulfilled in them: “The saints shall possess double things in their land” (Isaiah LXI, 7). The dread day of which we have spoken is loved beyond explanation by them, and they desire that it come.

[Col. 0269D] That this same day must be set before the eyes of all mortals, considered day and night, feared and dreaded, is indicated by the testimonies collected below. Concerning this day the Lord says through the prophet: “The great day of the Lord is near, and exceedingly bitter. The voice of the day of the Lord is very bitter; there the strong man will be troubled: a day of wrath, that day, a day of tribulation and distress, a day of calamity and misery, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of cloud and storm, a day of trumpet and blast” (Zephaniah I, 14).

[Col. 0270A] For concerning this day it is again said through the prophet: “Yet once more, and I will shake not only the earth but also heaven” (Jeremiah XII, 26). Again: “Wail, for the day of the Lord is near” (Isaiah XIII, 6).

And the Lord in the Gospel: “For the Son of Man will come in the glory of his Father with his angels, and then he will repay each one according to his work” (Matthew XXIV, 44). And elsewhere: “For just as lightning comes forth from the east and appears even to the west, so will be the coming of the Son of Man. Wherever the body is, there the eagles will also be gathered. Immediately after the tribulation of those days the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light; and the stars will fall from heaven, and the powers of heaven will be shaken.

[Col. 0270B] “And then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven, and then all the tribes of the earth will mourn, and they will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds of heaven with great power and majesty. And he will send his angels with a trumpet and a loud voice, and they will gather his elect from the four winds, from the highest parts of heaven to their boundaries” (ibid., v. 27 ff.).

And the Apostle:

[Col. 0270C] “We ought always to give thanks to God for you, brothers, as is fitting, because your faith is greatly increasing and the love of each of you for one another is abounding, so that we ourselves glory in you among the churches of God for your patience and faith in all your persecutions and tribulations that you endure as an example of the just judgment of God, so that you may be deemed worthy of the kingdom of God, for which you also suffer—if indeed it is just before God to repay tribulation to those who trouble you, and to you who are troubled, rest with us, at the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ from heaven with the angels of his power, in flaming fire, taking vengeance on those who do not know God and who do not obey the Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ. They will suffer eternal punishment in destruction, away from the face of the Lord and from the glory of his power, when he comes to be glorified in his saints and to be wonderful among all who have believed” (I Thessalonians I, 5 ff.).

Peter: “The day of the Lord will come like a thief; on it the heavens will pass away with great violence, and the elements will be dissolved by heat” (II Peter III, 10).

In the Apocalypse: “But for the proud, unbelieving, accursed, murderers, fornicators, sorcerers, idolaters, and all liars, their portion will be in the pool burning with fire and sulphur, which is the second death” (Apocalypse XXII, 8).

[Col. 0270D] Prosper [Note: [Col. 0270D] *On Contemplative Life*, book III, chapter 12]:

“Come now, when we have reached that final judgment, we shall be judged by a judge who cannot be deceived by the concealment of crimes or bribed by anyone’s offering to obtain impunity, when the secrets of all begin to be revealed, and not only deeds and words but even thoughts themselves are displayed. What shall we do under the majesty of so great a judge? What excuse shall we be able to put forward? By what art of defense shall we clear ourselves? What repentance will come to our aid, which we despised in this flesh? What good works will defend us, which we did not perform in this life? To what apostles, or to what other saints, shall we flee, whose examples and words alike we scorned?

[Col. 0271A] “Or perhaps the frailty of the body will excuse some there? But the examples of all the saints will protest against their excuse: those who, while living in the flesh with the frailty of the flesh, overcame the frailty of the flesh in the flesh, and by what they did taught that it could indeed be done. Especially since they too resisted sin not by their own power but by the help of the Lord who showed himself to those who did not seek him, so that they might seek him, and showed himself in order that he might be believed; and who, when they believed in him, defended them by invincible protection so that they would not be conquered by sin.

[Col. 0271B] “What, then, will they answer if the Lord says to them: ‘If you were able, why did you not resist sinful desires? If you were unable, why did you not seek my help against sins? Or, having been wounded, why did you not apply the remedy of repentance to your wound?’ Will they not then fall silent, having no excuse to offer, and will he not say: ‘Bind them hand and foot, and cast them into the outer darkness; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth’ (Matthew XXII, 13), where ‘their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched’?” (Isaiah LXVI, 24).

[Col. 0271C] Since, therefore, the day of judgment is announced with terror by so many utterly clear testimonies, and no avenue of escape will be open to us, since we shall come to it to render an account, and since there will be no place there for fruitful repentance, nor any postponement for repenting, nor any escape by seeking the intercession of the saints, it remains that, while we live, we should not waste the time granted for repentance. While we can, and while we have the Lord near us, let us flee to him by repentance, by changing our life for the better, and by correcting our conduct—we who, through sinning, have fallen away in flight from him—so that on that same day we may deserve to experience him as a most merciful judge.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the Four Orders That Will Exist on the Day of Judgment

That there will be four orders on the day of the fearful judgment is clearly demonstrated in the Gospel: namely, two of the elect and two of the reprobate. Concerning them, in a homily on the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0271D] In the homily on the Gospel “Behold, we have left all things,” etc., on the feast of Saint Benedict, namely Biscop]:

[Col. 0271D] “It should be noted,” he says, “that there are two orders of the elect in the future judgment: one of those who judge with the Lord, concerning whom it is mentioned here, who left everything and followed him; the other of those who are judged by the Lord, who did not likewise leave all their possessions, but nevertheless took care to give daily alms to the poor of Christ from what they possessed. Therefore we shall hear at the judgment: ‘Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world’ (Matthew XXV, 34).

[Col. 0272A] “But we also learn from the Lord’s account that there will be two orders of the reprobate there. One consists of those who, having been initiated into the mysteries of the Christian faith, refuse to practice the works of faith; to them, he testifies, it will be said at the judgment: ‘Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels. For I was hungry, and you did not give me food,’ etc. (John III, 18). The other consists of those who either never accepted the faith and mysteries of Christ or rejected them after accepting them through apostasy. Concerning them he says: ‘Whoever does not believe has already been judged, because he does not believe in the name of the only-begotten Son.’ Since they did not wish to honor Christ even in word, they do not deserve to hear even his words by which they might be convicted at the judgment; but they will come to judgment only so that they may be sent into eternal condemnation with those sinful people who are judged.”

Isidore, in the *Book of Sentences* (book III, chapter 30):

[Col. 0272B] “There are,” he says, “two distinctions, or orders, of people at the judgment, namely the elect and the reprobate; yet they are divided into four. There is one order of the perfect, who judge with the Lord, and another of those who are judged; nevertheless both will reign with Christ.

“Similarly, the order of the reprobate is divided into two: those who are evil within the Church are to be judged and condemned; those who are found outside the Church are not to be judged, but only condemned. The first order, of those who are judged and perish, is opposed to that order of the good among whom are those who are judged and reign. The second order, of those who are not judged and perish, is opposed to that order of the perfect among whom are those who are not judged and reign. The third order, of those who are judged and reign, is contrary to that order consisting of those who are judged and perish. The fourth, of those who are not judged and reign, is opposed to the contrary order in which are those who are not judged and perish.”

[Col. 0272C] These four orders—two to be feared and two to be imitated with all one’s strength—are as follows. Whoever fears being counted among those of whom it is said, “Whoever does not believe has already been judged” (John III, 18), ought truly to receive the faith of Christ and beware lest he depart wholly from it through apostasy. Whoever desires to be separated from the number of those to whom it is said, “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire,” etc. (Matthew XXIV, 34), must join right works to right faith, so that he may be not barren but generous and cheerful in all works of mercy.

Behold how every Catholic, with divine mercy going before and following after, can be made free from the two orders of the reprobate, which are greatly to be feared and dreaded. Two remain: one of the perfect—or rather, of the few—and the other, generally, of the rest of the righteous.

[Col. 0272D] Whoever, aided by divine assistance, is able to ascend to the summit of perfection, so that out of love for the apostolic life he leaves all his possessions and, poor, follows the poor Christ, will unquestionably not be judged with God in the judgment, but will sit in order to judge. Whoever cannot climb to the stronghold of the contemplative life, if he is devoted to works of mercy in the active life, will deserve on that same day of judgment to be separated from the number of the reprobate and admitted among those to whom it will be said: “Receive the kingdom of God, which was prepared for you from the beginning of the world.”

## CHAPTER XIX. On the Eternal Punishments of the Reprobate

[Col. 0273A] That the rewards of the righteous are ineffable the Evangelist testifies, saying: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, those things God has prepared for those who love him” (I Corinthians II, 9). Hence it is also credible that, just as the rewards of the righteous are incomprehensible to mortals, so the torments of the impious are ineffable. Since both are incomprehensible, it is necessary that we strive fervently to attain the rewards of the righteous and, while we can and have time, avoid the punishments of the reprobate by doing good.

[Col. 0273B] Concerning the punishments of the reprobate the prophet Isaiah says: “Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched” (Isaiah LXVI, 24). And the Lord in the Gospel: “Cast him into the outer darkness; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matthew XXII, 13). Again: “Therefore, just as the weeds are gathered and burned with fire, so shall it be at the consummation of the age. The Son of Man will send his angels, and they will gather from his kingdom all scandals and those who commit iniquity, and they will cast them into the furnace of fire; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.”

Gregory [Note: [Col. 0273D] *Moralia on Job*, book XXV, chapter 17]:

[Col. 0273C] “The justice of almighty God, foreknowing the future, created the fire of Gehenna from the very beginning of the world, so that it would begin to exist once for the punishment of the reprobate, but would never bring its burning to an end even without wood. It must be understood that all the reprobate, because they sinned with both soul and flesh, will be tortured in eternal punishment in both soul and flesh.

“Therefore the prophet Daniel rightly says: ‘You will place them like a furnace of fire at the time of your presence’ (Psalm XX, 10). A furnace burns inwardly, while that which is devoured by fire begins to be consumed from the outside, so that the sacred writings demonstrate that the reprobate burn both outwardly and inwardly: they are devoured by fire and, like a furnace, are placed there, so that they are tortured in body by fire and burn in mind through pain.”

[Col. 0273D] At the time of the Lord’s presence all the unrighteous are placed like a furnace and devoured by fire, because when the judge appears, their multitude is repelled by the sight of him; inwardly their conscience burns through desire, and outwardly Gehenna torments the flesh.

The prophet Isaiah says: “Therefore Sheol has enlarged its soul and opened its mouth without limit” (Isaiah V, 14). For just as Sheol is said to have been enlarged without limit because it draws many to itself, so it is not improperly called deep and bottomless, because it absorbs those whom it receives into itself as though into an abyss of its immensity. Sheol is rightly believed to have no bottom, because whoever is snatched away by it is swallowed up as though in an immensity.

Although this Gehenna is one for all, it is not kindled with one and the same degree of intensity for everyone. Just as one sun usually touches us all, yet we are not all heated under it to the same degree, because the burden of heat is felt according to the quality of the body, so there is one Gehenna that afflicts the condemned, yet it does not burn all with one and the same intensity. What differing conditions of bodies accomplish here, differing causes of deserts accomplish there.

In the *Book of Dialogues* [Note: [Col. 0273D] Saint Gregory, *Dialogues*, book IV, chapter 44]:

Peter: “I ask you, do we say that those who have once been plunged there will burn forever?”

Gregory: “It is certainly established and unquestionably true that just as there is no end to the joys of the good, so there will be no end to the torments of the wicked.”

Peter: “I would like to know how it is just that a sin committed within a finite time should be punished without end.”

Gregory: “That would rightly be said if the strict judge weighed not the hearts of human beings but their deeds. The wicked sinned within a finite time because they lived within a finite time. For they would certainly have wished, if they could, to live without end, so that they might sin without end. They show that they desire to live always in sin by never ceasing to sin while they live. It therefore belongs to the great justice of the avenger that those should never be without punishment who in this life never wished to be without sin.”

Prosper [Note: [Col. 0274D] *On Contemplative Life*, book III, chapter 12]:

[Col. 0274C] “Weeping and gnashing of teeth,” he says, “show the most acute pains of those who, condemned to the punishment of eternal death, will not possess the sensation of seeing but only of suffering. Their continual groaning, eternal torture, supreme pain, and penal sensation torment their souls but do not destroy them; they punish their condemned bodies but do not bring them to an end. Therefore the unquenchable fire assigned to them is not extinguished, so that, while the life of sensation endures, punishment may endure, and so that it may hold eternal bodies bound more for suffering than for seeing, killing them in living flames with the second death of immortality.

[Col. 0274D] “Now what he says—‘Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched’ (Isaiah LXVI, 24)—refers to the whole punishment of the condemned person, whom the fire of ineffectual repentance burns and the worm of a consuming conscience gnaws immortally. Accordingly, all those who are said to be killed in Gehenna are not dealt with in such a way that, consumed by the greatest pains, they eventually perish, but so that they live in them punitively.”

[Col. 0275A] To hear or read these things and others like them willingly, to bring them continually before the eyes of the mind, to believe that they are future, and truly to consider what an evil it is to be excluded from the joy of divine contemplation, to be deprived of the most blessed fellowship of all the saints, to become exiles from the heavenly homeland, to die to blessed life, to live for everlasting death, to be cast into eternal fire with the devil and his angels—where the second death is for the condemned exile, life, and punishment; where they do not experience in that fire what gives light, but experience what torments; to endure the terrible noises of the overflowing conflagration, to have the eyes blinded by the bitter darkness of the smoking abyss, to be plunged into the depths of fluctuating Gehenna, to be torn forever by the most ravenous worms and never brought to an end—to think upon these things and many similar ones is nothing other than to reject every vice and restrain all carnal allurements.

Who is so foolish in mind, so hard of heart, that these things would not terrify him? Truly miserable and exceedingly mournful is the human condition, which in this mortality never lives without labor. What, I ask, could be more miserable and unhappy than to pass from present labor into eternal labor that will have no end? Would it not have been better never to have been born than, after being born, instructed in the sacraments of the faith, and released from the dangers of this life, to be handed over to eternal punishments because of the enormity of one’s crimes?

Therefore everyone must strive to live in this brief span of time in such a way that, when departure from it comes, eternal punishments may be escaped and the rewards of perpetual life attained.

## CHAPTER XX. On the Everlasting Reward of the Elect

[Col. 0275B] What greater reward can the saints obtain after the resurrection than to be forever with their Lord? Hence Christ says to the Father: “I desire that where I am, they also may be with me” (John XVII, 14). For he himself is our head, and where he has ascended, we shall unquestionably ascend and attain it.

Therefore the Psalmist eagerly said: “How great is the abundance of your sweetness, Lord, which you have stored up for those who fear you” (Psalm XXX, 20), etc. Again: “The Lord shepherds me, and I shall lack nothing; in a place of pasture he has settled me” (Psalm XXII, 1). Again: “But I, like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God, have hoped in the mercy of God forever and unto ages of ages” (Psalm LI, 10). Again: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Psalm XXVI, 13).

[Col. 0275C] In the Book of Wisdom: “Though the righteous be overtaken by whatever death, his soul will be in refreshment” (Wisdom IV, 7). Again: “Blessed is the man who endures temptation, for when he has been tested, he will receive the crown of life, which the Lord promised to those who love him” (James I, 12). Again: “But the righteous will live forever, and their reward is with the Lord, and their thought is with the Most High; therefore they will receive a kingdom of honor and a crown of beauty from the hand of the Lord” (Wisdom V, 10).

The prophet Daniel: “Those who are wise will shine like the splendor of the firmament, and those who lead many to righteousness like stars unto everlasting eternities” (Daniel XII, 3).

In the Gospel: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the beginning of the world” (Matthew XXIV, 34). Again: “Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matthew XIII, 41).

[Col. 0275D] Paul: “When Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory” (Colossians III, 4). Again: “From now on the crown of righteousness is laid up for me, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will give me on that day—not only to me, but also to those who love his coming” (II Timothy IV, 7).

In the Apocalypse:

“These are those who came out of the great tribulation and washed their robes in the blood of the Lamb. Therefore they are before the throne of God and serve him day and night in his temple; and he who sits upon the throne will dwell over them.
