They shall hunger no more, nor thirst anymore; neither shall the sun fall upon them, nor any heat, because the Lamb who is in the midst of the throne will shepherd them and lead them to the springs of the waters of life; and the Lord will wipe away every tear from their eyes” (Apocalypse VII, 14).

[Col. 0276A]

In the book *Enchiridion* (ch. 94): “Therefore, when the reprobate angels and human beings remain in eternal punishment, the saints will then know more fully what good grace has bestowed upon them. Then, when the realities themselves are evident, what is written in the psalm will appear: ‘I will sing to you of mercy and judgment, O Lord’ (Ps. 100:1).”

Gregory, in the *Moralia* (Book 35, ch. 9; the beginning is phrased differently elsewhere), says:

Holy Church receives a double reward after the end of this age. Hence the prophet rightly says: “They shall possess double things in their own land” (Isa. 61:7). For the saints possess double things in the land of the living, since they enjoy at once the blessedness of mind and of body. John in the Apocalypse, when he saw the souls of the saints crying out for the resurrection of their bodies, beheld that individual robes had been given to them, saying: “And individual white robes were given to them, and they were told to rest yet a little while, until the number of their fellow servants and brothers should be completed” (Apoc. 6:11). Before the resurrection, the saints are said to have received individual robes because they still enjoy only the blessedness of the mind. They will therefore receive double robes when, together with the perfect joy of their souls, they are also clothed with the incorruption of their bodies. For then true freedom will exist in us, when our adoption has attained the glory of the children of God.

[Col. 0276B] The multitude of the elect is now drawn to faith through holy teachers, but will one day be gathered into the heavenly homeland, so that there all the elect may praise without end when they see without end him whom they praise. In eternal life the entire multitude of saints is perfectly made the body of the Redeemer, and then clings to him in such a way that nothing of the corruption overcome through resurrection any longer resists them in their holy love, but it is made one with the glory of its Redeemer. The outstanding preacher says: “Creation itself will be set free from the bondage of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God” (Rom. 8:21).

[Note: Col. 0275D. Gregory, *Moralia*, Book 8, ch. 4.]

For the punishment of corruption now weighs upon the elect, but then the glory of incorruption makes them rejoice. And as regards the burdens of present necessity, nothing of freedom is now displayed in the children of God; but as regards the glory of the freedom to come, then nothing of servitude will appear in the servants of God. Thus creation, stripped of the bondage of corruption and having received the dignity of freedom, is clothed in the glory of the children of God; for, united to God through the Spirit, it is shown as though it had passed beyond and subdued this very condition of being a creature.

[Col. 0276C] Hence the Psalmist says: “In a place of pasture he has set me” (Ps. 22:1). Sacred Scripture calls pasture the nourishment of that eternal greenness, where our refreshment no longer withers through the dryness of any lack. Again he says of that shepherd: “But we are his people and the sheep of his pasture.” Hence Truth himself says: “If anyone enters through me, he will be saved; he will go in and go out and find pasture” (John 10).

When the righteous see all the wicked struck by final vengeance, they themselves rejoice in the glory of their deserved recompense. Nor will they then compassionately suffer with the condemned from fellow-feeling, because, cleaving to divine justice in its manifestation, they are strengthened by the unshaken force of inward strictness.

[Col. 0277A] No misery afflicts the minds of the elect, raised upright in the highest clarity of righteousness, because the height of blessedness renders them strangers to miseries. The Psalmist rightly says: “The righteous will see and fear, and will laugh over him and say: ‘Behold the man who did not make God his helper’” (Ps. 51:8). The righteous now see the wicked and fear; then they will see and laugh. For since they can now slip into imitation of them, they have fear; but because they can then be of no benefit to the condemned, they read in the very justice of the Judge in which they are blessed that no pity is to be shown to those given over to eternal punishments, lest they have suffering there.

Prosper [Note: Col. 0277B. *On the Contemplative Life*, Book 1, ch. 4] says:

“This is the blessed life, to which those who have attained through the completion of good works will come: they will be like the blessed angels and will reign without end together with their God. What they believed here, they will see there; contemplating with pure hearts the substance of their Creator, they will rejoice in eternal exultation. Possessed by divine and mutual love, they will adhere happily forever to their God and to one another. Having received their bodies with incorruption and immortality, they will receive citizenship in the heavenly homeland; and, made its citizens forever, they will obtain the promised rewards.

[Col. 0278A] There such great gladness and such grace of heavenly joys will abound for them that they will give thanks to their rewarder for such gifts and will endure no weariness from the very enjoyment of the good things flowing upon them. There the minds of each will be open to each, just as bodily faces lie open to bodily eyes; for there will be such great and perfect cleansing from human sins that they will have reason to give thanks to God their cleanser, not to blush because of any stains that have offended them. For there will be neither sins nor sinners there, and those who are there will no longer be able to sin. Nothing secret will remain hidden from the perfectly blessed, who, what is far more excellent, will see God himself with pure hearts.”

See what glory is promised to us. The Lord exhorts us to strive for it untiringly, and that we may finally deserve to attain it, we are aided by the same exhorter. Why are we sluggish? Why do we neglect to do good works? Why do we disdain to listen to the giver of so great a glory and reward? We ought not to hesitate to follow such a caller and obey his admonitions, so that we may be able to obtain such great glory from him. For this purpose we are born: that we may be born again to Christ. For this also we are reborn, that we may live forever with the same Christ the Lord.

**The Book of Lord Jonas, on How Laypeople Ought to Live, Ends**

[Note: *Ought to live.* In the manuscript used by Acherius, this is added: “I beseech you, reader, remember Herbert of Durs, who, for the love of God and the benefit of readers, had this book renewed.”]

# ON ROYAL INSTRUCTION

[Col. 0277C]

## EDITORIAL NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING LITTLE WORK

[Col. 0277]

Jonas, bishop of Orléans, composed this little work in the same style and by the same method as the *Instruction of Laypeople*; indeed, he repeats five chapters of that same *Instruction*. Therefore, if Jonas is asserted to be the author of this work, he must necessarily be asserted to be the author of that one as well. Since this little work bore no title, we have assigned it the title *On Royal Instruction*, so that it might serve as a kind of second part to the moral, or lay, *Instruction*.

Moreover, this work of Jonas should be valued all the more because, apart from the Preface and the two final chapters, it is preserved in its entirety in the Sixth Council of Paris, celebrated in the year of Christ 829. Either the fathers of the council, wishing to provide the emperors Louis the Pious and Lothair with the admonitions they had requested, judged it expedient to weave the work of Orléans into their decrees; or, rather, I would say that Jonas, who attended the council, had been commissioned by those same fathers to arrange the acts of the council. Since the writings that he had produced shortly before suited the council’s purpose, he may have considered it worthwhile to insert them into royal exhortations. Whichever alternative you choose, reader, you must nevertheless judge that, before the council was held, Jonas had dedicated his little work to Pippin.

[Col. 0277D] Here, then, is what I think the true conclusion is: that little work was composed before that Council of Paris took place, and while Pippin, together with his brothers and others, had not yet undertaken anything against the emperor Louis; indeed, while he still persevered in dutiful obedience to his father—that is, after secret factions, disturbances, barbarian incursions, and various disasters, when the kingdom had been pacified by victories; specifically, in the year 828. Nor need I seek far for proof of this conclusion, since Jonas’s own words are at hand in the Preface, where he addresses Pippin as follows: “Since, therefore, insofar as an orthodox man…” And there are also the passages in which he describes the calamities exhausted before the year 828: “For what loss…”

[Col. 0278C] The letter of the emperors Louis and Lothair, in which they order councils to be held at Mainz, Paris, Lyon, and Toulouse, supports these words of Jonas. Among other things, it says:

“For we had wished, at a suitable time, to hold our general assembly and to deal there with a common correction. And this would have been accomplished by God’s mercy, had the disturbance of our enemies, as you know, not prevented it.”

Further on:

“Nor do we doubt that this too has occurred as a just punishment for that reason: that scandals often arise in this kingdom through tyrants who, by their wickedness, strive to tear apart the peace of the people and the unity of the empire. For it must likewise be counted among our sins that, in the previous year, the enemies of the Christian name entered this kingdom and openly and with impunity—indeed, cruelly—carried out plunderings, burnings of churches, captivities of Christians, and killings of the servants of God.”

[Col. 0278D] Do you wish, learned reader, that I summon writers who show that not before, nor long after, the year 828 did Pippin, with shamefully alienated mind, withdraw from filial reverence, and that he was aware of all the injuries and miseries inflicted upon Augustus, especially his captivity and deposition? They are present: Einhard, Thegan, the author of the *Life of Louis the Pious*, the *Annals of Fulda*, and the annals of Saint-Bertin and Metz. I do not append the years here or quote their words; I am writing for the learned. Let those who have either not read them or do not give them credence consult them.

Moreover, learned reader, observe that the reasons and arguments I set forth above most clearly prove that the words “and you bore his dishonor grievously,” when Jonas addresses Pippin, are by no means to be understood of the emperor’s deposition, but of the insults and disgrace inflicted upon the emperor before the year 828, while Pippin himself was rendering faithful service and loving him deeply. “You were faithfully and humbly subject to him in all things,” Jonas says.

For it is wholly contrary to truth, in view of everything mentioned above and written by authors both contemporary and nearly contemporary, to represent the king of Aquitaine as having shown fidelity and obedience after the emperor’s deposition. On the contrary, he consented to the deposition once and again for his own private advantage. [Col. 0279B] Nor was he later guided by any other spirit when he took Louis the Pious’s side, as Nithard clearly teaches in describing what was done in the years 829, 830, 831, and so forth.

In addition, other arguments help establish more firmly the date of the little work *On Royal Instruction*:

1. If Jonas had already published it through the Synod of Paris and had presented it to Pippin several years later, with what confidence could he have addressed the king at the beginning of the final chapter in these words: “This little work, excellent king, we have arranged out of love for your salvation, humbly beseeching you to deign to read and hear it willingly”? Could Pippin not have accused Jonas of repeating what had already been done, by offering him again what had been prescribed three years earlier at the Council of Paris and dedicated to his father and brother?

2. Jonas himself usually indicates the places from which he borrowed his teaching, so that he seems to take pleasure in citing his authors accurately, as will become clear to anyone who reads through the work. Let us hear him openly acknowledging this in the Preface to the *Instruction of Laypeople*:

“For, relying upon this purpose in undertaking the work, I was guided for the most part by the fact that I was not going to weave into this work words of my own understanding, written in the style of eloquence—which is entirely absent from me—but rather statements proclaimed from the divine oracles and most elegantly refined by the holy Fathers,” and so forth.

How, I ask, could this happen if the bishop of Orléans took this little work from the Council of Paris, yet did not indicate it even with a word, when he noted all the other matters so conscientiously? No one will easily persuade me of this. Let this conclusion, then, stand: Jonas’s royal little work was composed in the year 828. Enough on this matter; let those with keener eyes debate it. I leave the judgment to them.

[Col. 0280B] Thus far Acherius, with the greatest learning. He further notes that this little work was recovered by one of his associates, D. Arnaud Boisserie, from the archive of the canons of the church of Saint Peter at Rome. Baluzius later discovered another manuscript at Orléans. After he had transcribed from it various readings—neither few nor negligible—they provided us with considerable assistance in purifying the text.

[Col. 0279C]

# JONAS’S LITTLE WORK ON ROYAL INSTRUCTION

## HIS LETTER TO PIPPIN, THE KING

[Col. 0279C] To the most noble Pippin, outstanding in lineage, beauty, and wisdom, most glorious king, Jonas, the least servant of the servants of Christ, wishing you blessedness in the present and future life.

That so much time has passed since I was ignorant of your great prudence regarding royal dignity, your great devotion toward divine worship, your great willingness toward the fear and love of God, and also your great humility toward the priestly ministry—qualities which, as I recently learned, are present in you—I attribute to nothing but my own dullness. And rightly so: since I was born and raised in your kingdom, thoroughly trained in letters, and, having laid aside the hair of my head, enlisted in the service of Christ, I ought by right and faithfully to have obeyed your authority in every way.

[Col. 0279D] Yet, out of reverence and concealment, or rather through evasion, because of the blasphemies, insults, and lies of certain wicked men who, through a diabolical cunning filled with hatred and envy, have very often slandered my lowliness before your serenity, I withdrew from you in body, not in mind. I did not heed what the Lord says through the prophet Isaiah for the consolation of those whose lives are torn apart by the mouths of malicious people:

“Do not fear the reproaches of men, and do not regard their blasphemies; for just as fire, so the worm will devour them; and just as a garment, so the moth will consume them. But my salvation will be forever, and my righteousness throughout generations of generations” (Isa. 51:7).

[Col. 0280C] I would not, therefore, presume to write anything by way of admonition to your Highness, had I not been confident in your humble sublimity and learned by experience that you fervently wish to learn and willingly hear those matters that concern the love and fear of God and the salvation of souls. Since you remember the saying, “The prayer of one who closes his ear so as not to hear the law will be accursed” (Prov. 21:13), you lay aside royal pride, offer service to our Creator, and incline the ear of both heart and body to his saving commands.

[Col. 0280D] Although, through the gift of him from whom every good gift and every perfect gift comes, you know very well what you must do and what you must avoid, and although you have at hand many servants of Christ as counselors, nevertheless, because I count myself among the most faithful part of that company and henceforth desire with all my strength to count myself among them, it ought not to seem absurd or be regarded as an idle trifle that I dare to offer you, my lord, a small gift of admonition from the modest treasure of my heart.

[Col. 0281A] Therefore, my most serene lord king, mindful of my duty and being a faithful and undissembling debtor of your salvation, which I greatly desire, I humbly admonish your Highness to consider carefully how the times of the world pass away in perpetual course, and how its joys end for all mortals in mourning; how its honor and love, its splendor and sweetness, produce bitterness for everyone; and also that every son of Adam is worm and decay, and that, according to what the Lord’s voice says to our first parent, he is dust and is quickly reduced to dust.

[Col. 0281B] Hence someone writes:

> Strong men do not draw back their arms, nor purple robes kings;  
> But whoever comes from dust will be dust.

Since it is evident, therefore, that this life assigned to mortals is so unstable and fragile, filled with various kinds of illness and the miseries of manifold calamities, everyone ought, while he is permitted to live, to take care lest, weighed down by some torpor, or enticed by any carelessness or false security, he waste the time granted for repentance. Rather, stirred beneficially by prophetic, evangelical, and apostolic utterances, he should strive through repentance to seek his Creator, from whom he withdrew by sinning, and endeavor to make him favorable to himself through worthy penitential satisfaction and the distribution of alms, according to the prophetic saying:

[Col. 0281C] “Seek the Lord while he may be found; call upon him while he is near. Let the wicked abandon his way, and the unjust man his thoughts, and let him return to the Lord, and he will have mercy on him, and to our God, for he is abundant in forgiving” (Isa. 55:6–7).

And this: “Give glory to your Lord before it grows dark, and before your feet stumble upon the dark mountains” (Jer. 13:16).

And this evangelical saying: “Walk while you have the light, lest darkness overtake you” (John 12:35).

And this: “Watch, because you do not know the day or the hour” (Matt. 25:12).

And this: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Cor. 6:2).

And many similar passages, which the prophetic, evangelical, and apostolic writings set forth at greater length.

[Col. 0281D] Thus instructed by these saving exhortations, every believer is raised from the depths to the heights and hangs with complete trust and hope upon his Creator. Beyond doubt, he takes care not to fall in mind, but rather clings with all his strength to Christ his Redeemer, who cannot fall, saying joyfully with the Psalmist: “But for me it is good to cling to God, to place my hope in the Lord God” (Ps. 73:28).

But this too must nevertheless be avoided by everyone: that he love earth more than heaven, or love this pilgrimage, filled with afflictions, as his homeland. He must know that here he is a pilgrim and a stranger, but that elsewhere he is destined to be a citizen and member of the household. Hence the prophet David says:

[Col. 0282A] “For I am a stranger with you and a pilgrim, as all my fathers were” (Ps. 39:12).

And the Apostle says: “For we know that if our earthly house of this dwelling is dissolved, we have an edifice from God, a house not made by hands, eternal in the heavens” (2 Cor. 5:1).

Therefore, since each person’s fragile and earthen dwelling, in which he makes his pilgrimage, is soon to be dissolved, he must take the greatest care lest, because of love for it, the incitements of desire, and the vain and harmful pleasures of the world, the soul—which has a heavenly origin—perish forever. Rather, the outward man must be subjected as a servant to corruption, so that the inward man, renewed day by day, may be happily prepared to attain eternal glory.

[Col. 0282B] Indeed, it would have been better for every mortal not to exist than to be expelled from the happiness of paradise and from the fellowship of the holy angels and human beings because of carnal pleasures and the smoky, fleeting joys of the world. But because the human condition and the course of this world are as they are, the world itself and its riches must be held not in desire but in use, according to the Apostle’s saying: “Those who use this world should be as though they did not use it” (1 Cor. 7:31). It must also be understood that friendship with it, as the Apostle James testifies, is hostile to God, who says: “Whoever wishes to be a friend of this world is constituted an enemy of God” (James 4:4).

From these words it is plainly gathered that no friend of God ought to embrace friendship with this world, and that it has always been an enemy to the friends of God. It is a wretched and deeply lamentable thing when someone joins himself to friendship with his enemy and, because of that harmful and deadly friendship, loses his eternal and immortal friend, namely his Creator.

[Col. 0282C] Therefore, all who are considered Christians must vigilantly and diligently ensure that they do not postpone conversion to God from day to day, nor deceive themselves with a vain hope by promising themselves a long life on account either of youth or of bodily health. They must know that death spares no age and that the end of each person’s day is uncertain.

Thus, rejecting the ancient enemy, rejecting the world that lies in wickedness, and rejecting and trampling upon its riches, let them make a saving transition each day from vices to virtues, from visible things to invisible things, and from transitory things to eternal things. In this way, when the course of this fleeting life has ended, they may reach him by whom they were created when they did not yet exist, by whom they were recreated when they had perished, and by whose faith they were savingly marked; and from him may receive those things “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, which God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Cor. 2:9).

[Col. 0282D] Having set forth these matters in advance, my modest discourse is once again directed particularly to you, good king, most excellent king. I beseech you, therefore, and entreat you by the Lord, that your Excellence deign to take personally those matters which were stated somewhat above in general terms. I also humbly suggest to your gentleness that you always love the Lord your God, just as he commanded his worshipers to love him: “with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your strength” (Deut. 6:5), and that you place nothing before his love.

[Col. 0283A] As for the command that you ought to love your neighbor as yourself, you do not need my admonition. Since you have shown to everyone—nobly, indeed memorably—how deeply you have loved the orthodox and pious man, our lord and emperor, your father, how faithfully and humbly you have been subject to him in all things, and how grievously you have suffered his dishonor, I pray the Lord in my inmost prayers, and humbly admonish you, that, with the Lord’s help, you may remain most sincerely in that same love forever, and that under no circumstance or anyone’s urging you allow yourself to be separated from his love, nor grieve him in any way.

[Col. 0283B] For, as divine Scripture testifies, among the other instructions by which it teaches that a father is to be loved and cherished, it commands that a son not grieve his father during his lifetime. Finally, the Lord specifically demonstrates how greatly a father ought to be loved and honored by his son. Having given commandments concerning his own worship and love on the first tablet, he gave the first commandment on the second tablet concerning the honoring of one’s father, saying:

“Honor your father and your mother, so that you may live long upon the land which the Lord your God will give you” (the same passage).

There are indeed many legal, evangelical, and apostolic commandments proclaimed by the Lord, by which a father is commanded to be loved and honored by his son. Since these are known to your wisdom, they are omitted here. But it must certainly be understood that whoever honors his father honors God, who is the Father of all; and whoever dishonors him undoubtedly inflicts an injury upon God, because God is the Father of all and ordains that a father be honored by his sons.

[Col. 0283C] What loss, what evils, what sorrow, what oppression, and what miseries did the hostilities and dissensions that arose in the previous year, as your Excellence knows, inflict upon the people of God! This kingdom experienced them miserably, and great delight was thereby produced for the devil and his members.

But because, as I believe, the Lord, moved by the prayers of his servants, and evidently made favorable toward your father on account of his pious and religious deeds, and toward you and your brothers, our lords, in order to strengthen mutual love, averted the war that was being prepared through diabolical cunning, lest the blood of the Christian people entrusted to you—which the devil greatly thirsted for—be shed in civil conflict or in anything worse than civil conflict, it is fitting, indeed necessary, that you and your brothers, our lords, remain indissolubly united in mutual love; that, in accordance with filial reverence and divine ordering and command, you unanimously render suitable submission to your father; that you preserve the honor owed to him and display undissembling honor toward him.

[Col. 0283D] Then, while he rules temporally and you obey him, the people entrusted to you may live quietly and peacefully, and you, because you have vigorously and faithfully administered the office entrusted to you by God, may deserve to reign happily with Christ forever.

There are therefore four things, my lord king, brief to state but, with Christ’s grace assisting, easy to accomplish and highly beneficial to those who observe them. I greatly desire that your diligence both willingly hear them and eagerly fulfill them.

[Col. 0284A] First, that each day everyone take care of the soul rather than the body and acquire for his soul something great and special, which he may possess forever. For, as we are instructed by the evangelical oracle, from all the periods of our life—years, months, days, and hours—from the time when God granted us the discernment of good and evil, he will demand the fruit of good works from our vineyard, that is, from the soul.

Second, that each day, apart from the confession he makes to priests in order to receive counsel for his salvation and to make God favorable toward him, he confess all his sins to his Creator and set his sins before himself, saying with the Prophet:

[Col. 0284B] “For I acknowledge my iniquity, and my sin is always before me” (Ps. 51:5).

When a person now sets his sins before himself by confessing them to God, he then healthfully and truly sings to God that verse which says: “Turn your face away from my sins, and blot out all my iniquities” (the same Psalm, verse 9). Many other things concerning this confession are contained in the divine utterances.

Third, that he place the day of his death before his eyes every day, so that his soul may not blush at the mockery of its enemies when it is summoned to leave the body; rather, enriched by good works, what is said may be fulfilled in it: “He will not be put to shame when he speaks with his enemies in the gate” (Ps. 127:5).

[Col. 0284C] How dreadful that day and that hour are must be carefully considered day and night. For this reason Scripture gives warning: “My son, remember your last things in all your works, and you will never sin” (Ecclus. 7:4). But if we were to contemplate that hour diligently, and if we took care to consider how dreadful it is because it is unavoidable and inescapable, we would presume to sin either rarely or never.

Fourth, that we always keep before our eyes and ponder in our minds the day of the dreadful examination, which is called by the prophet “a day of wrath, a day of tribulation and distress, a day of calamity and misery, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of cloud and tempest, a day of trumpet and blast” (Zeph. 1:16), together with the other things written at greater length about it in the divine utterances.

[Col. 0284D] Then we shall stand before Christ’s tribunal and give an account of what we have done through the body, whether good or evil. We must remove every deadly false security and every bodily pleasure, keep that day constantly before our eyes, and consider it in our minds. With the Lord’s help, we must prepare ourselves so that, when we come before him, we may not be condemned forever with the rejected, but rather, blessed with the elect, may deserve to receive a kingdom with them forever.

Many further matters ought to be written to your Highness, dictated by charity, if I had not feared both exceeding the proper measure of a letter and becoming in some way a burden to your graciousness. Since they are omitted here, they are set out in the following sections, arranged in brief chapters and gathered from the divine oracles and the sayings of the holy Fathers. If you read them, or have someone assist you in reading them, their usefulness cannot be adequately stated.

[Col. 0285A] May the holy and undivided Trinity guard you, good king, inwardly and outwardly; fortify and defend you against the snares of visible and invisible enemies; and, after this pilgrimage, make you a companion of the holy kings.

# HERE BEGIN VERSES BRIEFLY ARRANGED AND FAITHFULLY ADDRESSED TO THE LORD PIPPIN, THE KING

> Pious king, supreme, I beg that you accept the small gift I bring,  
> So that I may often willingly bring you pleasing gifts.  
>
> But if it proves suitable in your sight,  
> My Thalia will more quickly offer something more suitable.  
>
> For the learned, skilled in the art of Maro, produce better things,  
> Since they devote themselves to this and possess a renowned art.  
>
> I, who once played readily in measured odes,  
> Now, with my body weakened, desire to do nothing but weep.  
>
> May God himself be your protector and your supporter throughout the ages;  
> Through him, all your people love you to reign.  
>
> May you hold the heights of ruling with such caution in the fields,  
> That after death you may dwell in the citadel of heaven.

[Col. 0286A]

# THE LITTLE WORK FOLLOWS, VERY BRIEF IN WRITING, BUT HEAVILY LADEN WITH DIVINE ORACLES AND PROFITABLE TO ITS FOLLOWERS

[Col. 0285]

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0285B] **That the Church Is the Body of Christ, That There Are in It Two Principal Eminent Persons, and That Priests Will Render an Account to God for Kings**

All the faithful must know that the universal Church is the body of Christ and that Christ himself is its head. In it there are principally two eminent persons, namely, the priestly and the royal.

[Note: “Namely, the priestly.” Everything from this point until the word *priestly* is repeated was absent from the earlier edition and has been restored from the Orléans manuscript. From that manuscript we have also printed below “and very necessary,” where the reading was “indeed necessary,” and immediately afterward “or from the ministry,” where the reading was “in the ministry.”]

The priestly person is so much more excellent as it will render an account to God for the kings themselves. Hence Gelasius, venerable pontiff of the Roman Church, writing to the emperor Anastasius (*Letter* 8), says:

[Col. 0285C] “For there are two powers, august emperor, by which this world is principally governed: the sacred authority of pontiffs and royal power. Among them, the burden of the priests is so much heavier, as they will also render an account for the kings themselves before the divine tribunal.”

Fulgentius likewise writes in Book 2 of *On the Truth of Predestination and Grace*:

“​​As far as the life of this present age is concerned, no one in the Church is superior to the pontiff, and in the Christian world no one is found higher than the emperor.”

Therefore, since the ministry of priests is a matter of such great authority, indeed of such great danger, that they will render an account to God even for kings themselves, it is fitting and exceedingly necessary that we always be concerned for your salvation, and that we vigilantly admonish you lest, God forbid, you stray from the will of God or from the ministry he has entrusted to you. And if, God forbid, you should in any way depart from it, we must, with pontifical diligence, humbly admonish you and beneficially care for you, so that we may offer timely counsel for your salvation and not be condemned for the silence of our reticence, but rather deserve to be rewarded by Christ for our most diligent care and saving admonition.

## CHAPTER TWO

[Col. 0286B] **On Priestly Power and Authority**

That the power and authority of loosing and binding were bestowed by Christ upon priests, that is, upon the successors of the apostles, the Gospel plainly declares—a matter which the fullness of your wisdom does not fail to know. Therefore we humbly appeal to your Excellence so that, through you, your nobles and all your other faithful subjects may recognize the name, power, strength, authority, and dignity of the priesthood, lest, through ignorance of it, they in any way incur danger to their souls.

What the power and authority of the priesthood are can easily be discerned from the words of the Lord, which he addressed to blessed Peter, whose place we unworthily hold:

[Col. 0286C] “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. 16:19).

And elsewhere he says generally to the disciples:

“Whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven” (Matt. 18:18).

And elsewhere:

“Receive the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them; and whose you retain, they are retained” (John 20:23).

The Gospel text clearly brings forth many similar statements in greater abundance. That other saying should also be recalled to them, indeed presented as an example: in ecclesiastical history the emperor Constantine said to the bishops:

[Col. 0286D] “God established you as priests and gave you the power to judge even us; therefore we are rightly judged by you. But you cannot be judged by human beings. For this reason, await among yourselves the judgment of God alone, so that whatever disputes you have may be reserved for that divine examination. For you have been given to us by God as gods, and it is not fitting that a human being judge gods, but only he of whom it is written: ‘God has stood in the assembly of the gods; in the midst he judges the gods’ (Ps. 82:1).”

[Col. 0287A] Although priests in the present age are negligent in many respects, they are nevertheless not to be blamed or despised; rather, for the sake of him whose ministry they perform, they are to be heard and honored with fitting respect. [Note: [Col. 0287D] “Whose ministry.” Thus the Aurelian codex, correctly; the earlier edition has “whose mystery,” corruptly. There are other passages that we have corrected from the same Aurelian codex, but they are less significant.] For after the apostles this saying of the Lord is directed to them: “Whoever hears you hears me; and whoever despises you despises me” (Luke 10:16). It must be understood that contempt for Christ’s priests constitutes an injury to Christ: for there are many legal and evangelical precepts by which obedience to priests is commanded. What sort of life and conduct priests ought to have, what sort of men they ought to be, how they ought to come to the summit of governance, how they ought to live, and how they ought to teach their subjects by words and examples—this has been sufficiently set forth elsewhere by holy and venerable teachers. Here, however, we must proceed to speak of kings, whose salvation the ministry of priests ought diligently to promote, and by whose arms and protection the Church of Christ ought to be defended.

## CHAPTER III. What a king is, what he ought to be, and what he ought to avoid

A king is so called from ruling rightly; for if he rules piously, justly, and mercifully, he is rightly called a king. If he lacks these qualities, he loses the name of king. In ancient times, however, all kings were called tyrants; but afterward those who ruled piously, justly, and mercifully acquired the name of king. To those who ruled impiously, unjustly, and cruelly, the name not of king but of tyrant was appropriately applied.

Since, therefore, a king is so called from acting rightly, he must first strive, with the help of Christ’s grace, to cleanse himself and his household from wicked deeds and make them abound in good works, so that all the other subjects may always take a good example from them. He himself must also faithfully and obediently submit to Christ’s saving commands; and by acting rightly he must cause those over whom he exercises temporal authority to remain, insofar as this is divinely granted to him, in peace and concord and charity, and in the practice of all other good works. By words and examples he must diligently urge them to works of piety, justice, and mercy, mindful that he will have to render an account to God for them, so that by acting in this way he may, after this pilgrimage, become a companion of the holy kings who pleased God by serving him sincerely.

Concerning what sort of person a king ought to be, and what he ought to avoid, we read in Deuteronomy:

“When you have entered the land that the Lord your God will give you, and possess it and dwell in it, and say, ‘I will set a king over me, as all the nations around me have,’ you shall appoint as king the one whom the Lord your God chooses, from among your brothers. You may not make a man of another nation king who is not your brother. When he has been appointed, he shall not multiply horses for himself, nor lead the people back into Egypt, relying on the number of his cavalry, especially since the Lord has commanded you never again to return by the same way. He shall not have many wives, who might entice his heart, nor immense quantities of silver and gold.

“After he has taken his seat upon the throne of his kingdom, he shall write for himself in a book a copy of this law, taking the exemplar from the priests of the Levitical tribe. He shall keep it with him and read it all the days of his life, so that he may learn to fear the Lord his God and observe his words and ordinances, which are commanded in the law. His heart shall not be lifted up in pride above his brothers, nor shall he turn aside to the right or to the left, so that he and his sons may reign for a long time over Israel” (Deut. 17:14 ff.).

Observe that the fear of God, the keeping of his commandments, humility—which does not allow him to exalt himself above his brothers—and uprightness in justice cause not only the king but also his sons to reign for a long time. Therefore, to warn that a ruler ought to avoid arrogance, Ecclesiasticus says: “They have appointed you ruler; do not exalt yourself, but be among them as one of themselves” (Ecclus. 32:1). In Proverbs: “The king who judges the poor in truth—his throne shall be established forever” (Prov. 29:14). Likewise: “Mercy and truth preserve the king, and his throne is strengthened by clemency” (Prov. 20:28).

But because we do not doubt that the teachings of the saints who reign with the Lord, produced by the gift of the Holy Spirit, have greater force in the hearts of their hearers than the words of our insignificance, we have therefore inserted into this little work of our smallness a few passages from the words of blessed Cyprian, martyr of Christ. We offer them to your serenity to keep at hand, to read and consider often, so that in his words, as in a kind of mirror, you may continually contemplate what you ought to be, what you ought to do, and what you ought to avoid. His words are these:

[Note: [Col. 0288D] Cyprian, or another author, chapter on the Twelve Abuses of the World.]

“The ninth degree of abuse,” he says, “is an unjust king. For a king ought not to be unjust but to be the corrector of the unjust; therefore, he must preserve within himself the dignity of his name. For the name ‘king’ retains this meaning in an intellectual sense: that he should provide the office of a ruler for all his subjects. But how will he be able to correct others who does not correct his own conduct so that it is not unjust? For the justice of a king exalts his throne, and truth makes the governance of peoples firm.

“Now the justice of a king is to oppress no one unjustly by force; to judge without partiality between one man and his neighbor; to be a defender of strangers, orphans, and widows; to restrain thefts and punish adulteries; not to exalt the wicked; not to support the shameless and stage performers; to destroy the impious from the land; not to allow parricides and perjurers to live; to defend the churches; to nourish the poor with alms; to appoint just men over the affairs of the kingdom; to have as counselors old men, wise men, and sober men; not to heed the superstitions of magicians, diviners, and female soothsayers; to defer anger; to defend his country bravely and justly against its adversaries; to live entirely in God; not to let prosperity raise his spirit; to bear every adversity patiently; to hold the Catholic faith in God; not to allow his sons to act impiously; to devote himself to prayers at appointed hours; and not to taste food before the proper hours. For ‘Woe to the land whose king is a child and whose princes eat in the morning’ (Ecclus. 10:16).

“These things produce the prosperity of the kingdom in the present life and lead the king to better heavenly kingdoms. But whoever does not administer according to this rule undoubtedly endures many adversities in his government. For this reason the peace of peoples is often broken, offenses also arise against the kingdom, the fruits of the earth are diminished, and the services of peoples are hindered. Many sorrows also infect the prosperity of the kingdom; the deaths of loved ones and children bring grief; the incursions of enemies ravage the provinces on every side; wild beasts tear apart the herds of cattle and flocks of sheep; storms of spring and winter hinder the fertility of the lands and the services of the sea; and sometimes flashes of lightning burn the crops, the blossoms of trees, and the vine shoots.

“Above all, the injustice of a king not only darkens the appearance of the present government but also obscures his sons and grandsons, so that they may not hold the inheritance of the kingdom after him. Because of the offense of Solomon, the Lord scattered the kingdom of the house of Israel from the hands of his sons; and because of the merit of King David, he left a lamp from his seed perpetually in Jerusalem.

“Behold how greatly the justice of a king benefits the world: it is the peace of peoples, the protection of the fatherland, the security of the common people, the defense of the nation, care for the sick, joy for humanity, moderation of the air, calmness of the sea, fertility of the earth, consolation of the poor, inheritance for children, and hope of future blessedness for himself. Nevertheless, he should know that just as he has been placed first on the throne of men, so also he will hold first place in punishments if he has not practiced justice. For all the sinners whom he has had beneath him in the present life he will have above him in that future punishment.”

Fulgentius, in his book *On the Truth of Predestination and Grace*, says:

“Most merciful emperor, he is not a vessel prepared for mercy unto glory because he has received the summit of earthly rule; rather, he is such if he lives with right faith at the imperial height, and, endowed with true humility of heart, subjects the height of royal dignity to holy religion; if he takes greater delight in serving God in fear than in ruling the people in fear; if gentleness in him moderates anger and kindness adorns authority; if he shows himself to all as more worthy of love than of fear; if he wisely provides for his subjects; if he holds justice in such a way that he does not abandon mercy; if, above all, he remembers himself to be a son of the holy mother, the Catholic Church, in such a way that he makes his rule beneficial to her peace and tranquility throughout the whole world. For the Christian empire is governed and enlarged more when provision is made for the ecclesiastical order throughout the whole earth than when war is waged in some part of the world for temporal security.”

[Note: [Col. 0289D] “For temporal security.” The best reading is found in the Aurelian codex. Acherius had published “for the security of the temple,” an error that arose from an abbreviation in writing.]

Isidore [Note: [Col. 0289D] Book II of the *Sentences*, chapters 49 and 48.] says:

“He who rightly uses the power of kingship ought to conduct himself toward all in such a way that, the more he shines by the height of his honor, the more he humbles himself in mind, setting before himself the example of David’s humility. David did not grow proud of his merits, but humbly abasing himself said: ‘I shall go about in a lowly manner and shall appear lowly before the Lord who chose me’ (2 Sam. 6:22).”

Isidore likewise says:

“He who rules well in temporal affairs within this world reigns forever without end, and passes from the glory of this world to eternal glory. But those who exercise kingship wickedly, after their shining garments and the gleam of their jewels, will descend naked and wretched to be tormented in hell. [Col. 0290B] Kings are called from acting rightly, because by doing what is right the name of king is retained, and by sinning it is lost.”

Gregory, in the *Moralia* [Note: [Col. 0290D] Or Isidore, Book III of the *Sentences*, chapter 48.], says:

“We know that holy men are also called kings in the sacred writings for this reason: that they act rightly, govern their own thoughts well, and compose their movements that resist them by rational discernment. Therefore those are rightly called kings who know how to bring peace, by good governance, both to themselves and to their subjects.”

[Note: [Col. 0290D] “Bring peace.” The earlier edition has “modify”; the same edition immediately below had “immunity.”]

And shortly afterward:

“When the kings of the world feel themselves superior to others, let them nevertheless recognize that they are mortal, and let them not look upon the glory of the kingdom by which they are exalted in this world, but attend to the work that they carry away with them.”

Again, not long afterward:

“When kings are good, it is the gift of God; when they are evil, it is the fault of the people. For the life of rulers is arranged according to the merit of the peoples, as Job testifies: ‘He makes a hypocrite reign because of the sins of the people’ (Job 34:30). When God is angry, the people receive such a ruler as they deserve for their sin. Sometimes kings are changed because of the wickedness of the people; and those who previously seemed good, after receiving the kingdom, become unjust.”

With these matters thus set forth, the king must strive to fulfill the name of king not only in himself but also in those subject to him. He must ensure that the people subject to him abound in piety, peace, charity, justice, mercy, concord, unanimity, and other good works, so that, possessing these qualities, they may deserve to have God with them. He must know with absolute certainty that the Lord will demand from him the good fruit of good works not only concerning himself but also concerning them.

## CHAPTER IV. What properly constitutes the ministry of a king

The royal ministry consists especially in governing and ruling the people of God with equity and justice, and in striving that they may have peace and concord. He himself ought first to be the defender of the churches and of the servants of God. It is also his duty diligently to provide for the welfare and ministry of priests, and the Church of Christ ought to be protected by their arms and defense. The poverty of widows, orphans, and the other poor, as well as of all those in need, must be defended.

[Note: [Col. 0291D] “It is also their duty.” From this point through the word “protected,” these words have been added from the Aurelian codex; from the same source we have also added below “to be defended in their need.” That codex immediately reads, “so that he may commit no injustice,” which is unobjectionable.]

His fear and zeal ought to have this character, insofar as possible: first, that no injustice be committed; then, if one occurs, that he in no way permit it to continue, nor leave anyone hope of concealment or boldness in wrongdoing. But let everyone know that, if any evil they have committed comes to his attention, it will by no means remain uncorrected [Note: [Col. 0291D] “By no means uncorrected.” Here too we used the Aurelian codex to correct the earlier edition, which previously read “and not incorrected”; the same error below, “of just correction,” has been removed by the same means.] or unpunished [Col. 0291B]; rather, the manner of just correction will correspond to the nature of the deed.

Therefore, he has been placed upon the throne of government in order to administer right judgments, so that he may personally take care and investigate lest anyone in judgment turn aside from truth and equity. He must also know that the case which he administers according to the ministry entrusted to him is God’s case, not that of human beings; and for the ministry he has undertaken he will have to render an account on the day of the dread judgment. Therefore, he who is judge of judges ought to cause the case of the poor to come before him and inquire into it carefully, lest those whom he has appointed and who ought to act in his place among the people allow the poor to suffer oppression unjustly or negligently.

[Note: [Col. 0291D] “Allow the poor to suffer oppression.” The earlier edition had “of the poor”; [Col. 0292D] below, the passage from the Book of Job that you see here ended with the words “the comforter of the sorrowful.”]

Concerning the ministry of a king, Job speaks as follows:

“When I sat as a king, with the army standing around me, I was nevertheless a comforter of the sorrowful. The ear that heard me blessed me, and the eye that saw me bore witness to me, because I had delivered the poor man who cried out, and the orphan who had no helper. The blessing of the perishing came upon me, and I comforted the heart of the widow. I put on justice, and it clothed me as with a garment; and my judgment was as a robe and a diadem. I was an eye to the blind and a foot to the lame. I was a father to the poor, and I investigated most diligently the case that I did not know. I crushed the jaws of the unjust and snatched the prey from his teeth” (Job 29:25).

Solomon: “The king who sits upon the throne of judgment scatters all evil from his sight” (Prov. 20:8). Likewise: “A wise king scatters the wicked and bends an arch over them” (ibid., v. 26). Likewise: “A wise judge will judge his people, and the rule of a discerning man will be stable” (Ecclus. 10:1).

[Note: [Col. 0292D] “A wise judge will judge.” The Aurelian codex has “will avenge,” a reading that is all the less to be disregarded because it is clear that, in accordance with the author’s intention, he ought to have written it thus.]

Likewise: “A just king raises up the land, and a greedy man destroys it” (Prov. 29:4). In the Book of Wisdom: “Love justice, you who judge the earth. Think of the Lord in goodness, and seek him in simplicity of heart” (Wis. 1:1). Likewise there: “Hear, therefore, O kings, and understand; learn, you judges of the ends of the earth. Give ear, you who hold the multitudes and take pride in the throngs of nations. For power has been given to you by the Lord, and strength by the Most High, who will examine your works and scrutinize your thoughts. For although you were ministers of his kingdom, you did not judge rightly, nor keep the law of justice, nor walk according to the will of God. He will appear to you terribly and swiftly, because a very strict judgment will be made upon those who rule. To the lowly, mercy is granted; but the powerful will suffer powerful torments. For God will not withdraw from anyone’s person, nor will he fear anyone’s greatness, because he himself made the small and the great, and he cares equally for all; but a stronger punishment awaits the stronger” (Wis. 6:2 ff.).

[Col. 0292B] Isidore [Note: [Col. 0292D] Isidore, Book III of the *Sentences*, chapter 51.] says:

“Secular princes sometimes hold the heights of the power they have obtained within the Church, so that through that same power they may strengthen ecclesiastical discipline. Otherwise, powers would not be necessary within the Church, except that what the priest is able to accomplish through the word of teaching, authority may command through the terror of discipline. Often the heavenly kingdom benefits from the earthly kingdom, so that those placed within the Church who act against the faith and discipline of the Church may be crushed by the severity of princes; and so that the principal power may impose upon the necks of the proud the discipline which the utility of the Church is unable to enforce; and so that authority may bestow strength, by which it may deserve veneration.

“Let secular princes recognize that they must render an account to God concerning the Church which they undertake to protect on Christ’s behalf. For whether the peace and discipline of the Church are increased through faithful princes, or dissolved, he will demand an account from them who entrusted his Church to their power.”

There are also many other oracles of both Testaments by which it is sufficiently established that a king ought to exercise and fulfill the ministry entrusted to him according to the will of God. These we omit here in order to avoid excessive length.

[Note: [Col. 0292D] “It is sufficiently established.” In the Aurelian codex: “we are sufficiently instructed”; whichever reading one adopts, the sense is the same. The following chapter is not found in that praised codex.]

## CHAPTER V. On the danger of a king, and that he ought to reward those who act well, restrain those who act badly by his authority, and cause the case of the poor to come before him

It is counted as a king’s sin when he entrusts the fulfillment of his ministry to unjust judges and ministers; for he ought not merely to administer his ministry through others and withdraw himself from it. We do not mean, therefore, that he alone should hear, investigate, and decide all the disputes and complaints of the people, since he is by no means capable of handling all these matters. Rather, he should appoint under himself men who fear God and hate avarice, through whom he may not offend the King of kings.

What sort of men ought to be appointed is clearly shown by the Book of Deuteronomy, in which we read:

“You shall appoint judges and magistrates in all your gates which the Lord your God gives you, throughout each of your tribes, so that they may judge the people with just judgment and not turn aside to either side” (Deut. 16:18).

Likewise:

“I said to you at that time: ‘I am not able to bear you alone, because the Lord your God has multiplied you, and today you are as numerous as the stars of heaven’—may the Lord, the God of your fathers, add many thousands to this number and bless you as he has spoken. ‘I am not able by myself to bear your affairs, your burden, and your disputes. Choose from among yourselves wise and experienced men, whose conduct is approved in your tribes’” (Deut. 1:9).

Job says:

“When I went out to the gate of the city, and in the square they prepared a seat for me, the young men saw me and hid themselves; the old men rose and stood. The princes ceased speaking and placed their finger upon their mouth” (Job 27:9).

The Book of Exodus shows that the king ought to share the burden of his rule with such men. There we read:

“Provide from all the people capable men who fear God, in whom there is truth, and who hate avarice; and appoint them as tribunes, commanders of hundreds, commanders of fifties, and commanders of tens. Let them judge the people at all times. Whatever matter is greater, let them refer to you, and let them judge only the smaller matters; thus the burden, divided among others, will be lighter for you. If you do this, you will fulfill God’s command, and you will be able to bear his precepts; and all this people will return peacefully to their places” (Exod. 18:21).

When Moses heard this, he did everything that the other man had suggested. Choosing capable men from all Israel, he appointed them as leaders of the people, tribunes, commanders of hundreds, commanders of fifties, and commanders of tens. They judged the people at all times; whatever matter was more serious, they referred to him.

That a king ought to cause the case of the poor to come before him and investigate it carefully is indicated by what we read: in ancient times judges sat at the gate for judgment so that no one would have difficulty approaching, and so that no citizen would be forced to endure violence or accusation. For this reason Jerusalem was also called the city of the just so long as judgments were administered there, since its rulers were not permitted to remain in it.

That a king ought to exalt the good and restrain the wicked is taught by the apostle Peter, who says: “Therefore be subject to every human creature for the Lord’s sake, whether to the king as supreme, or to governors as sent by him for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of those who do good” (1 Pet. 2:13).

Bede explains these words as follows [Note: [Col. 0293D] Bede, in his exposition of the same Epistle.]:

“Not that all governors sent by kings know how either to punish evildoers or to praise those who do good; rather, the action that a good governor ought to perform is simply described, namely, that he restrain evildoers and reward those who act well. Hence, in secular history it is reported that it was the custom of the Romans:

‘To spare the conquered and subdue the proud’” [Note: [Col. 0293D] Virgil, *Aeneid* VI.]

That it is counted as the fault of the one who appoints them when wicked judges are placed over the people of God is made clear by the words of Isidore, who says [Note: [Col. 0294D] Isidore, Book III of the *Sentences*, chapter 52.]:

“It is counted as the sin of princes when they place wicked judges over faithful peoples against the will of God. For just as it is the sin of the people when their princes are wicked, so it is the sin of the prince when the judges are unjust. A good judge knows neither how to harm citizens nor how not to benefit everyone. He offers some the severity of justice, and receives others with the goodness of judgment, without partiality. The flame of avarice does not weaken justice, nor does he strive to take from another what he desires for himself. Good judges embrace justice solely for the attainment of eternal salvation, and do not distribute it in exchange for gifts received; so that, by not seeking temporal profit from just judgment, they may be enriched with an eternal reward.

“From what has been set forth it is made clear that those who are to govern the people of God after the king—that is, dukes and counts—must necessarily be chosen in such a way that those who appoint them can do so without danger to themselves. They must know that they have been placed in office so that they may recognize Christ’s people, naturally their equals, and save and govern them mercifully and justly—not so that they may dominate and oppress them, nor regard the people as their own, nor subject them to themselves for their own glory. This does not belong to justice but rather to tyranny and unjust power.

“For it is an urgent necessity that, since the king himself will undoubtedly render an account before the most just judge for the ministry entrusted to him, he should also diligently investigate each of the ministers placed under him, lest he incur divine judgment on their account. Those ministers themselves must also be warned that whatever they judge will rebound upon them, according to what is written in the Book of Chronicles:

“‘Therefore Jehoshaphat dwelt in Jerusalem; and again he went out among the people from Beersheba to Mount Ephraim and brought them back to the Lord, the God of their fathers. He appointed judges in the land throughout all the fortified cities of Judah, in each place, and he commanded the judges: “Consider what you are doing, for you do not exercise judgment on behalf of man but on behalf of the Lord, and whatever you judge will rebound upon you. Let the fear of the Lord be with you, and act with diligence in all things; for with the Lord our God there is no iniquity, nor partiality, nor desire for gifts”’ (2 Chron. 19:4).

“These things, and others like them that have been mentioned above, the king and his ministers ought to weigh not lazily but diligently, and they ought to apply themselves to the ministry entrusted to them in such a way that they may deserve not to be eternally condemned for it, but rather to be happily rewarded by the Lord.”

## CHAPTER VI. That equity in judgment is the foundation of the kingdom, and injustice its overthrow

That a kingdom stands through justice Solomon establishes in Proverbs, saying: “Justice exalts a nation, but sin makes peoples miserable” (Prov. 14:34). Likewise: “Mercy and truth preserve the king, and his throne is strengthened by justice” (Prov. 20:28). Likewise: “Take away wickedness from the face of the king, and his throne shall be established by justice” (Prov. 25:5). Likewise: “To practice mercy and judgment is more pleasing to the Lord than sacrifices” (Prov. 21:3). And below: “The robberies of the wicked will drag them down, because they refused to practice judgment” (ibid., v. 7). Likewise there: “He who pursues justice and mercy will find life, justice, and glory” (ibid., v. 21).

That a kingdom falls through injustice Isaiah demonstrates:

“For you have laid waste your land,” he says; “you have slain your people. The seed of the wicked shall not be called forever. Prepare his sons for slaughter because of the iniquity of their fathers; they shall not rise up, nor inherit the land, nor fill the face of the world with cities” (Isa. 14:20).

In Amos: “Behold, the eyes of the Lord are upon the sinful kingdom, and I will destroy it from the face of the earth, says the Lord” (Amos 9:8).

Daniel speaks to Belshazzar:

“O king, the Most High God gave your father Nebuchadnezzar a kingdom, magnificence, glory, and honor. Because of the magnificence that he had given him, all peoples, tribes, and languages trembled and feared him. Whomever he wished, he killed; whomever he wished, he struck; whomever he wished, he exalted; and whomever he wished, he humbled. But when his heart was lifted up and his spirit was hardened in pride, he was deposed from the throne of his kingdom, and his glory was taken away. He was cast out from the sons of men, and his heart was placed with the beasts” (Dan. 5:18).

In the Book of Wisdom: “God cast down the seats of proud rulers and caused the meek to sit in their place” (Ecclus. 10:17). Likewise: “God dried up the roots of proud nations and planted the humble from among those nations” (ibid., v. 18). Likewise: “A kingdom is transferred from nation to nation because of injustices, insults, and various deceits” (ibid., v. 8).

From these words it is plainly clear that piety, justice, and mercy establish a kingdom, while injuries to widows and orphans, accusations against the wretched, violent judgments, and the perversion of justice clearly overthrow it. Hence the collapse of many kingdoms, because they had no foundation of piety, justice, and mercy, plainly lends support to what has been set forth above.

[Note: [Col. 0295D] “He attributes credibility to it.” The following material is not found in the Aurelian codex; instead, as Baluzius writes, it contains *Chapters of Various Sentences for the Administration of Public Affairs*.]

## CHAPTER VII. That a kingdom is given not by human beings but by God, in whose hand all kingdoms exist

No king ought to believe, with truth and humility, that his kingdom is administered to him by his ancestors, but rather that it is given by God, who says: “Counsel and equity are mine; prudence is mine, and strength is mine. Through me kings reign, and lawgivers decree what is just” (Prov. 18:14).

That an earthly kingdom is bestowed not by human beings but by God is testified by the prophet Daniel, who says:

“By the decision of the watchers it has been decreed, and by the word of the holy ones, and by the petition, until the living know that the Most High rules in the kingdom of men, and that he gives it to whomever he wishes, and sets the lowliest of men over it” (Dan. 4:14).

Likewise, speaking of Nebuchadnezzar to Belshazzar:

“Until he knew that the Most High had power in the kingdom of men, and that he would raise up over it whomever he wished” (Dan. 5:21).

And through Jeremiah:

“Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Thus shall you say to your masters: ‘I made the earth and human beings and the beasts that are upon the face of the earth, by my great power and my outstretched arm; and I gave it to the one who was pleasing in my eyes’” (Jer. 27:5).

But those who think that an earthly kingdom passes to them by succession from their ancestors, and not rather that it is given by the Lord, are subject to what the Lord condemns through the prophet, saying: “They have reigned, but not from me; they have become princes, and I did not know them” (Hos. 8:4). To be ignorant of God is undoubtedly to be rejected by God.

Therefore, whoever exercises temporal rule over other mortals should believe that the kingdom has been entrusted to him not by human beings but by God. For many reign by the gift of God, and many also reign by God’s permission. Those who reign piously, justly, and mercifully undoubtedly reign through God; those who act otherwise reign not by his gift but only by his permission. Concerning such men the Lord says through the prophet: “I will give you a king in my anger” (Hos. 13:10). And Job: “He makes a hypocrite reign because of the sins of the people” (Job 34:30).

As Isidore explains [Note: [Col. 0296D] Book III of the *Sentences*, chapter 48.]:

“When God is angry, the people receive such a ruler as they deserve for their sin.”

It is therefore established that an earthly kingdom is bestowed not by cunning, not by desire, nor by the strength of human might, but by power—or rather, by the hidden judgment of divine dispensation. Therefore, whoever receives it from God should strive to arrange and govern it according to his will, so that he may be able to reign happily forever with him from whom he received it. For it benefits no one to rule an earthly kingdom if—as may God forbid—it should happen that he becomes an exile from the eternal kingdom.

## CHAPTER VIII. That all ought humbly and faithfully to obey royal authority, which has been ordained only by God

It is established that royal authority ought to provide for all its subjects according to the order of equity. Therefore all subjects ought to obey that authority faithfully, usefully, and obediently, because whoever resists authority ordained by God resists, according to the apostle’s teaching, God’s ordinance.

Just as subjects wish the king to assist them piously and justly, so they ought especially to offer him suitable assistance, first for securing the salvation of his soul, and then generally for arranging and administering the honor and welfare of the kingdom according to God’s will, without concealment or hesitation. When they do this, they are clearly shown both to fulfill the divine commandment and to preserve the faith owed to the king.

That such obedience ought to be rendered by subjects to royal authority is openly testified by the legal precepts, and the Lord admonishes it in the Gospel, saying: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Matt. 22:21). Peter likewise says: “Therefore be subject to every creature for God’s sake, whether to the king as supreme, or to governors as sent by him” (1 Pet. 2:13). And shortly afterward: “Fear God; honor the king” (ibid., v. 17).

The apostle Paul also agrees in the same matter, saying: “Let every soul be subject to higher authorities. For there is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been ordained by God. Therefore whoever resists authority resists God’s ordinance” (Rom. 13:1), and so forth, as the apostolic discourse continues concerning this authority.

He likewise writes to Titus: “Remind them to be subject to princes and authorities” (Tit. 3:1).

To Timothy he shows how highly he regards the case and salvation of the king, writing as follows:

“I urge, therefore, first of all, that supplications, prayers, petitions, and thanksgivings be made for all people, for kings and for all who are in high positions, so that we may lead a quiet and peaceful life in all piety and chastity. For this is good and acceptable before God our Savior, who desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (1 Tim. 2:1).

If the prophet Jeremiah admonishes the people of God to pray for the life of the idolatrous king Nebuchadnezzar, how much more ought all orders of people humbly to entreat God for the salvation of Christian kings!

Thus, how royal authority must be obeyed and how provision must be made for its salvation has been stated briefly from divine authorities. Therefore each believer must offer appropriate assistance to so great an authority, both for his own salvation and for the honor of the kingdom according to God’s will, as a member offers assistance to the head. He should seek in the king the general advancement, welfare, and honor of the kingdom more than the profits of the world, so that, mutually supporting one another through these most salutary services, they may together deserve happily to enjoy the eternal kingdom.

## CHAPTER IX. That where charity is absent, no good can exist
We recognize that there is great danger in both orders—namely, the clerical and the lay—because charity, which is God and the glory of Christianity, and in which the whole substance of our faith consists, is demonstrably not reigning in many of either order—something we say not without great sorrow of heart. What kind of virtue charity is, both the Gospel and apostolic reading, and the expositions of the holy Fathers, teach most fully. For the apostle John says with the greatest clarity that God is charity:

> In this the charity of God appeared in us: because God sent his only-begotten Son into the world, so that we might live through him. In this is charity: not that we loved God, but that he first loved us and sent his Son as an atonement for our sins. Beloved, if God so loved us, we also ought to love one another. No one has ever seen God. If we love one another, God remains in us, and his charity is perfected in us. In this we know that we remain in him and he in us, because he has given us of his Spirit; and we have seen and testify that the Father sent his Son as the Savior of the world. Whoever confesses that Jesus is the Son of God, God remains in him and he in God. And we have known and believed the charity that God has in us. God is charity, and whoever remains in charity remains in God, and God in him (1 John 4:6 ff.).

Let each person consider: if he remains in charity, God remains in him; if he does not have charity, not God but the enemy of his soul dwells in him. With charity, indeed, all good things can be possessed; without charity, none can be possessed. Nor can one who lacks charity worthily sing the angelic hymn to the Lord. But why, you ask? Consider why: because he is not of good will. For charity is defined—as our teachers hand down—as good will. Therefore whoever does not have good will is shown not to have charity; and for this reason he does not deserve to possess peace, who is Christ, because he is not of good will. “Glory,” says the multitude of the heavenly host, “to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14).

Most pitiably, many are deceived: without charity they think either that they can please God or that they can reach him. But if charity is not in us, and hatred, envy, greed, discord, hypocrisy, lust, and the other evils reign—in short, all that is contrary to the purpose of Christianity—it is no wonder if divine punishments strike us inwardly and outwardly with the most varied evils and stir up the assault of enemies against us. Therefore, if we wish to pass through times of peace quietly and calmly, let us love and fear the lover of peace and charity, and humbly submit our necks to his commands.

Those who are supported by palatine honors, whether clerics or laymen, ought to be bound together by the bond of charity. They should not plot against one another’s injury or dishonor contrary to what is right; they should not be sluggish or deceitful toward one another, lest those who are deceitful fall under the words of the Psalmist:

> They speak peace with their neighbor, but evil is in their hearts. Give them, Lord, according to their works and according to the wickedness of their devices, etc. (Psalm 27:3).

[Note: [Col. 0297D] “But those who are sluggish.” This plainly does not cohere with what precedes. Should one read, “but those who are authors of discord”? Certainly something of this sort is required.]

Those who are sluggish are plainly cut off from the unanimity that Paul teaches should dwell in Christ, and they should beware the hypocrisy of Judas, the Lord’s betrayer. There are other matters relevant to this subject, but it would take too long to enumerate them. Certainly, when such men, supported by the honors of palatine rank, tear one another apart with the bites of envy, burn with desire for the ruin and dishonor of their neighbor, and inflict injury on God—whose gifts they enjoy—through their neighbor’s misfortunes; when they do not preserve the proper loyalty owed to the king, to whom they are familiarly attached and to whom they ought to be helpers according to God; when they stain palatine honor by giving others a bad example; and, what is more disgraceful for them, send great rejoicing to the enemies of Christ’s name—

## CHAPTER X  
### On Transgressors of God’s Commandments

If anyone wishes clearly to know the evils by which God is offended or the kingdom endangered, let him examine divine authority—that is, the legal, prophetic, Gospel, and apostolic authority. There he will find fully all the commandments and precepts by which God’s will is fulfilled; there also he will find what God has forbidden to be done. On account of these things there are many divine threats against every order, and in certain cases, against those who scorned to listen, divine vengeance has been completed.

The first human being, because of his transgression of God’s command, was expelled from paradise, condemned to exile, and punished with death; and the human race still experiences this evil today as though implanted in its very nature. Then came the other universal condemnation in the Flood, which plainly is shown to have occurred when vices and various evils multiplied and the natural law was corrupted. How grave and dangerous is the presumption born from contempt of God’s commandments is revealed by the building of the tower and the confusion of languages. As for Sodom and Gomorrah and the neighboring cities, it is clear by what crimes they were destroyed and how they were ruined as an example of eternal condemnation for the human race. Yet, in comparison with them, Jerusalem is recorded to have committed a double evil, because it possessed knowledge of and commandment from God, but scorned to keep it, following its own will.

For, according to the prophet, the iniquity of Sodom was pride, fullness and abundance, and leisure, together with the fact that they did not extend a hand to the needy and poor. Hence forgetfulness of God arose, and they continued to commit abominations. The obstinacy of the Egyptians, who could be corrected neither by signs and wonders nor by scourges, and the end to which it came, are well known. Likewise, it is clear how Dathan, Abiron, and Korah, together with their companions who perished with them, were consumed for their contempt and disobedience toward God by the horrifying opening of the earth. It is also evident how the multitude of God’s people perished in the wilderness because of desire, contempt, and perverse practices forbidden to them by God, until they were consumed by various disasters—so that none of them reached the promised land except only two who obeyed the Lord’s voice.

It would take too long to enumerate how often the people have fallen, or a kingdom perished, because of the sin or disobedience of one person, whether superior or subordinate. Such was the case with Saul: because of his disobedience, we read that the kingdom was taken from him and given to another. His son Jonathan too, through whose faithful courage victory had been granted over the enemies, later transgressed the vow of consecration. Although unaware, he desired the forbidden thing and disturbed the victory of the whole people.

Eli also, of the priestly order, fell because he did not correct his sons sufficiently; indeed, when his sons fell deservedly because of their iniquity, he fell with them, and the priesthood was taken away from his descendants. Through their negligence and iniquity the people were routed and slain in battle, and glory, together with the ark of God, was transferred from Israel; at the same time their place was destroyed. Achan, however, having become disobedient through desire, disturbed the whole people.

We have pursued only a few examples from among many, so that it may be carefully observed: if those who despised God’s commandments—whose number is infinite—were subjected to so many divine acts of vengeance, so many dangers, and so many condemnations, and not only those who received the commandments but also those who corrupted the natural law, how great a guilt do you think will rest upon those redeemed by Christ’s grace and taught and instructed by the same Lord in the way of righteousness, if they scorn to obey his commandments?

Therefore each person must strive in his own order to the best of his ability.
