In proportion to his love for God, let him fulfill what God has commanded and beware what he has forbidden, so that he may not be condemned with those who despise the commandments but may rather be rewarded with those who carry them out; for there is no doubt that through disobedience to and contempt of God’s commandments come both the endangerment of kingdoms and the condemnation of souls.

## CHAPTER XI  
### That Many Hold the Christian Profession Only in Words but Neglect It in Their Works

If human beings eagerly strive to learn and understand with the greatest precision the rights of worldly laws, established by mortals to settle disputes in court, and so on, as in chapter 20 of Book I of *The Instruction of the Layman*, up to “are judged to be observed without concealment”—

That faith alone brings no one to the kingdom of heaven has already been demonstrated in the preceding chapters. But the Christian profession is miserably neglected by many and in many ways, because of carnal pleasures, the most varied vanities of this world, and exceedingly perverse customs. The more pointlessly they devote themselves to these things, the less they devote themselves to the works of the Christian profession. And if the *Acts*, and so on, as in the same chapter 20 of Book I, up to “they praise the skill of cooks in preparing the most sumptuous foods for themselves”—

[Note: [Col. 0299D] “There is also another matter.” This too is found in the chapter cited above, though generally in different wording.]

There is another matter in the Christian religion worthy of great admiration: human laws, which for the most part strike terror into those who wish to sin more effectively than Christ’s commandments do, appear to possess greater force than divine laws, although the former free their subjects from temporal punishment and the latter from eternal punishment.

When someone who holds the summit of royal or imperial dignity, ruling temporally over the rest of mortals, issues an edict that he wishes his subjects both carefully to hear and diligently and faithfully to fulfill, who among his subjects, I ask, does not eagerly obey and strive to comply with his commands? Who would dare burst into such audacity as to presume to disregard it except at his own peril? Therefore one cannot sufficiently wonder why people exist so stricken by blindness that they set aside the law of their Creator with such reckless presumption.

Human beings make laws, and their subjects observe them. God, the Creator of all, ruling eternally—who does not grow through our advancement, in whose hand we are like clay in the hand of the potter—gave a law for the attainment of the salvation of souls, yet people disdain to hear it. Even if it is heard by the bodily ear, it is not perceived by the ear of the heart; and if it is perceived by the ear of the heart, it is not fulfilled in deed.

What excuse will Christians be able to offer the Lord, when they accept the judgment of worldly law through fear of the world, but refuse to submit their necks to Christ’s yoke, which is gentle and light and leads to eternal life? The Lord says:

> Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart; and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is gentle and my burden is light (Matthew 11:28).

Yet they refuse to come to such a great caller, to learn humility and gentleness from him, and to take up his yoke. What else do those who do this do except fall away from their own salvation? How pitiable and destructive this is cannot be expressed.

It can plainly be observed that in the present age the Christian profession is not honored by most people with the devotion and religious commitment with which it was honored by the Christians of old.

The apostles—or rather, Christ through the apostles—judged that this rule of faith, about which we spoke briefly above and which is treated most fully in the aforementioned *Acts of the Apostles*, must be held by the faithful. If Christ taught this, why is it despised through so many and such great perverse customs, devised to satisfy the wishes of certain people? Although, with God’s assent, it is truly perceived, nevertheless some neglect it in their works in various ways. We recognize that this has happened because a deeply lamentable custom has crept in among certain people. Failing to attend as they ought to the divine laws to which they have subjected themselves through faith, they make a law for themselves out of whatever they desire and whatever is not unlawful, and even out of what is lawful but nevertheless inexpedient; they believe that they can live blamelessly according to whatever pleases them.

With these matters established beforehand, each believer must search the innermost recesses of his heart. If he does not adorn the faith of Christ that he has received with works, he must recognize that he has violated the covenant he made with God in baptism. While he still has time, with Christ’s grace assisting him, let him seek again the way of salvation not only in words but also in works.

It is therefore no wonder if the divine sword rages where the faith of Christ is held not truthfully but hypocritically. We always say that we wish to seek God and ask him for forgiveness for our past sins, yet we lie, because we delay fulfilling what we say. Every day we also say that we wish to seek the way of God, from which we have strayed through sinning, by which we may return to God; God has laid it before our eyes, yet we scorn to walk along it.

Who, possessing reason, does not know that we must always choose better things and despise those of lesser worth? We are rightly worn down by various disasters of divine vengeance because of our iniquity, yet we scorn to return to him by whom we are struck, fulfilling the prophetic word:

> The people have not returned to him who struck them, and they have not sought the Lord of hosts (Isaiah 9:13).

It is greatly to be feared that, although we have so often been warned and scourged by the Lord through legal, prophetic, Gospel, and apostolic denunciations or threats, and scorn to return truly to God, what happened to the Israelite people may finally happen to us. They insulted the Lord’s prophets and scorned to return to God. The Lord patiently endured their iniquities for a long time, but at last, unwilling to show them mercy, he permitted them to migrate into Assyrian captivity.

[Note: [Col. 0301D] “For they signify.” The printed edition had: “For the Lord signifies.”]

For the Assyrians signify and are interpreted as “captors.” Therefore we must watch carefully lest, as they were physically, so we—God forbid—become spiritually subject to their captivity.

## CHAPTER XII  
### That Those Who Have Received the Faith of Christ and Ended Their Lives in Evil Are Punished More Severely Than Those Who Died without Faith but Nevertheless Performed Good Works

Some Christians are accustomed to say that those who have been reborn in Christ, although they live wickedly and close their final day in evil works, with prolonged …, and so on, as in Book I, chapter 19, *The Instruction of the Layman*, up to “than to turn back after receiving knowledge.”

Therefore we must ensure that, while we live in this life, we devote ourselves to good works. For the Lord warns in the Gospel:

> Keep watch and pray, because you do not know the day or the hour (Matthew 25:13).

Likewise:

> The day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night (2 Peter 3:10).

Likewise:

> Walk while you have the light, so that darkness may not overtake you (John 12:35).

And the Apostle says:

> Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation (2 Corinthians 6).

By these teachings we are thoroughly instructed that the times granted for repentance must not be wasted, and that the faith of Christ must always be adorned with good works.

## CHAPTER XIII  
### That People Should Frequently Assemble in Church for the Sake of Prayer

It has already been mentioned in the preceding discussion that in the present age the devotion of Christian peoples falls far short of the devotion of the faithful communities that existed under the apostles, and so on, as in Book I, chapter 11, *The Instruction of the Layman*.

## CHAPTER XIV  
### That in the Church of Christ One Must Not Devote Oneself to Idle and Shameful Talk; and That Those Who Do So Not Only Fail to Diminish Their Sins but Accumulate Greater Ones

Many who enter a church do not direct pure and simple prayer to God, because they do not meditate in their minds upon what they pray with their mouths, and so on, as in Book I, chapter 13, *The Instruction of the Layman*.

## CHAPTER XV

### That Prayer and Confession of Sins Can and Ought to Be Made in Other Suitable Places as Well, If the Basilica Is Far Away

[Note: [Col. 0303D] “As there are some.” This entire chapter is indeed found above, in chapter 14 of the book *The Instruction of the Layman*. We nevertheless judged that it ought to be printed again because, in the material that Jonas here transcribes from the Third Book of Kings, there occur quite a few variant readings.]

Just as there are some who neglect to frequent the thresholds of the church for the sake of prayer, so, on the other hand, there are many who, because they cannot visit basilicas and do not have the relics of the saints available, therefore fail to pour out the vows of their prayers to the Lord with the humble devotion that is fitting. They do not consider that God is no less in a part than in the whole, but is wholly everywhere, present everywhere, and wondrous everywhere.

Therefore the Psalmist says:

> Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your presence? If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present (Psalm 138:7).

> In every place of his dominion, bless the Lord, my soul (Psalm 102:22).

Thus we read in the Book of Kings:

> If your people go out to battle against their enemies by the way in which you send them, they will worship you in the direction of this city that you have chosen and of the house that I have built for your name; you will hear their prayers and supplication from heaven and execute judgment. But if they sin against you—for there is no human being who does not sin—and you become angry with them and deliver them to their enemies, and they are led captive into a distant land or one that is nearby, and, having been converted in their heart in the land to which they have been led captive, they do penance and entreat you in the land of their captivity, saying, “We have sinned, we have acted wickedly, we have acted unjustly,” and they return to you with all their heart and with all their soul in the land of their captivity to which they have been led, they will worship you toward the direction of their land that you gave to their fathers, and of the city that you chose, and of the house that I built for your name. You will hear their prayers from heaven, that is, from your firm dwelling place, and you will execute their judgment (1 Kings 8:44 ff.; 2 Chronicles 6:34 ff.).

And in the Book of Daniel:

> When Daniel learned of the established law, he entered his house, and with the windows open in the upper room toward Jerusalem, three times a day he bent his knees, worshiped, and confessed before his God, just as he had been accustomed to do before (Daniel 6:10).

The Apostle also says:

> Therefore I wish men to pray in every place, lifting up pure hands without anger or dispute (1 Timothy 2:8).

Jerome, in his letter to Eustochium, says:

> “As they leave their lodging, let prayer arm them; as they return from the street, let prayer meet them before they sit down. Let the little body not rest before the soul is nourished. At every action, at every step, let the hand trace the cross.”

## CHAPTER XVI  
### On Observing the Lord’s Day and Receiving the Body and Blood of Our Lord Jesus Christ

For in this matter too we earnestly beseech you that, in observing the Lord’s Day—on which God created the light of the world, on which the author of life rose from the dead, and on which he also sent the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, from heaven to the apostles—you show proper care, as we previously entreated your father in our admonitions, and render to so great a day the honor due to it.

That is, on that day, as far as you are able, strip yourselves of worldly cares and anxieties; do what is appropriate to the veneration of so great a day, and teach and instruct your own people by your example to do the same.

With regard to receiving the sacred body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, we likewise admonish you to prepare yourselves healthfully at suitable times, as is fitting for the Christian religion, attending to the Gospel saying:

> Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day. For my flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink. Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him (John 6:55).

By carrying this out, instruct those who serve you, through your example, to do the same.

## CHAPTER XVII  
### Which Emperors or Kings Can and Ought Truly to Be Called Happy

We have arranged this little work, excellent king, out of love for your salvation. We humbly ask you to deign to read and hear it willingly, as was already said above, so that hereafter I may write with a more willing and frequent spirit to your serenity whatever I learn to pertain to the salvation of your soul and the honor of the kingdom.

Nevertheless, I have judged it right and worthy to bring this little work to an end not with my own words but with those of the blessed Augustine, that outstanding teacher, so that you may clearly learn from them which emperors and kings can and ought to be called happy. In Book V of *The City of God* (chapter 24), among other things, he writes as follows:

> “Nor do we now call certain Christian emperors happy because they ruled for a longer time, or because they left behind sons who were emperors and died a peaceful death, or because they subdued the enemies of the state, or because they were able both to guard against and suppress hostile citizens rising up against them. For certain worshipers of demons, who do not belong to the kingdom of God to which these men belong, have also been deemed worthy to receive these and other gifts or consolations of this wretched life. This happened through his mercy, so that those who believed in him would not desire such things from him as the highest goods.

> “Rather, we call them happy if they rule justly; if, amid the tongues of those who honor them loftily and the excessively humble services of those who greet them, they are not elated but remember that they are human beings; if they make their power serve God’s majesty, especially for the widest possible extension of his worship; if they fear, love, and worship God; if they love more the kingdom where they do not fear having fellow-heirs; if they are slow to punish and quick to forgive; if they exercise punishment for the necessity of governing and protecting the state, not for satisfying the hatred of enmities; if they grant pardon not for the impunity of iniquity but in hope of correction; if they compensate what they are often compelled to decree harshly with the gentleness of mercy and the generosity of benefactions; if their luxury is more restrained in proportion as their freedom permits greater indulgence; if they prefer to rule over wicked desires rather than over any nations; and if they do all these things not for the passion of empty glory but for the love of eternal happiness; if they do not neglect to offer to their true God the sacrifice of humility, compassion, and prayer for their sins. Such Christian emperors we call happy—happy for the present in hope, and afterward in reality, when what we await has arrived.”

Thanks be to God.

[Col. 0305B]

# JONAS, THREE BOOKS ON THE CULT OF IMAGES

Published under the rule of Louis Caesar against the blasphemies of Claudius, bishop of the Church of Turin.

*(From the Library of the Ancient Fathers, ninth century.)*

[Col. 0305]

## [BOOK ONE]

### PREFACE OF JONAS TO THE FOLLOWING LITTLE WORK, PRESENTED TO KING CHARLES

[Col. 0305B]

To Charles, beloved and illustrious king, Jonas, the least of the servants of Christ, wishes a twofold salvation.

How great our most glorious lord, your father, the most beloved of God, Louis Caesar, most devout, proved to be in the sincerity of faith, in every virtue of goodness, in the splendor of upright morals, in the gift of wisdom and holiness, and in the fervor of divine love and fear; how outstanding he was, with the Lord’s assistance, in increasing and governing ecclesiastical affairs pertaining to divine honor and worship; how, having lawfully obtained the paternal empire—because God so willed—he held and governed it with the most upright balance of justice; how he fortified it militarily against the attacks of enemies; and how, imitating—or rather surpassing—the conduct of your father, namely the pious and like-named man Charles, the most noble Augustus, he educated the Church of Christ, redeemed by precious blood and divinely entrusted to his rule, in the disciplines of the liberal arts and instructed and caused it to be instructed in the sacred pages of both Testaments and in the sayings of outstanding Fathers, so as to repel the poisonous doctrines of heretics—all this is plainly known to all the sons of the catholic and apostolic faith, since what is said is visibly evident in fact.

For that prince, most beloved of God, among his other zealous efforts to magnify divine worship, carried out with fervor in many ways, caused a certain priest of Spanish nationality, named Claudius, who had for some time served in the honor of the priesthood at his palace and in whom there seemed to be some slight knowledge of explaining the readings of the holy Gospels, to be appointed bishop of the Church of Turin, so that he might provide sacred instruction to the Italian people, who for the most part were far removed from the meaning of the holy evangelists.

But how pestilential a doctrine, abhorrent to the authority of the Church, he poured into the people entrusted to him, is plainly demonstrated by the little book that he wrote to the venerable abbot Theodemir, who, impelled by charity, was correcting him and wishing to turn him away from his superstitious doctrine; this is clear to anyone who wishes to read and know it.

In the end, the aforementioned little book was brought to our lord, your father, who most sincerely and devoutly cultivated the orthodox faith, for the defense of holy Mother Church, which, as the wording of Claudius’s own letter reveals, was being attacked by him in a hostile manner. After being examined by him and by the wisest men of his palace, it was rejected by a just judgment.

Although I neither read nor saw the work itself, I received an excerpt from it, sent by that same father of yours. The aforesaid Caesar, beloved of God, instructed and admonished me [Perhaps: “was instructing and admonishing me”] not to omit writing, insofar as God might grant and according to the weakness of my understanding, a response for refuting and condemning the statements of Claudius contained in that excerpt—statements that were most perverse and had been irreverently hurled into blasphemy and reproach against the holy Church of God.

Obeying his command with the greatest willingness, insofar as God granted me ability and the time allowed, I began to compose a little work and had arranged a large part of it. But when I heard that Claudius, in accordance with the human condition, had ended his final day, I decided to strike my pen from completing the work. For I thought that when he died, his error too would disappear completely, in accordance with the Lord’s saying:

> I will wipe out the memory of Amalek from under heaven (Exodus 17).

I also thought that the memory of that perverse doctrine would be erased from the hearts of all prudent men. But because, as I learned from a truthful report, not only is the error in question reviving in the minds of his disciples, but, according to his teaching, the Arian heresy is discovered to be sprouting—of which he is said to have collected certain written records and, in a clandestine act of cunning, left them in the archives of his bishopric to attack the simplicity and purity of the catholic and apostolic faith—I did not dare fail to resume, at the urging and encouragement of the sons of the holy Church of God, the work I had set aside, so that I might examine it minutely and answer clearly each of the remaining perverse objections with rational and devout counterarguments.

Having carried this out to the best of my ability, and arranging the work according to the command of your father, insofar as my understanding could contain it, I rightly judged that it should be offered to you, so that what I was unable to return to your father while he ruled, I might return equally to you and to him.

It might have been enough for Claudius, as an addition to his miseries, that he followed the error of two heretics, Eustathius and Vigilantius. But not content with these twin plagues, he plunged himself into a deeper abyss of perdition when he showed himself, both in life and in death, to have been a follower and disciple of Arius, the most hostile enemy of the holy Church of God: in life, by teaching and preaching; in death, by leaving the same error written by him in his wicked books.

The sect of that same Arius, long ago condemned by the holy Fathers and pierced by the catholic sword under perpetual anathema, is said by Claudius to have been revived. It is therefore necessary that it be discovered through the most discerning inquiry and the most diligent investigation and brought into the light [Perhaps: “brought forward”], and that, together with its reviver, it be struck down and rendered ineffective once again by ecclesiastical men with the weapons of the holy Scriptures. Otherwise, God forbid, if it remains hidden, it may over time pour deadly poison into the minds of the simple and lead them into perpetual damnation.

I therefore humbly beg your serene clemency, most prudent king: if you find anything useful in this little work, receive it gratefully, keep it and cause it to be kept, read it yourself, and order it to be read to you.

[Note: [Col. 0307C] The excerpt mentioned here is missing. It is not greatly needed, however, since the author attacks each of its individual statements in what follows; moreover, it is found below, before the book of Dungal’s response against the same Claudius (*Patrologia*, vol. 105, col. 459).]

I have inserted the excerpt sent to me between this preface and the following work for this reason: whoever wishes to read and examine it, I ask first to read this preface and then to read and investigate the excerpt. Only afterward should he put his hand to the aforementioned work, either to approve or to disapprove it. Whatever he finds insufficiently answered or insufficiently opposed to the preceding perverse objections, let him supplement with the writings and statements of his own sounder and fuller understanding, for the honor and defense of the holy Church of God.

[Col. 0307]

# BOOK ONE

[Col. 0307C]

It is manifest that Spain has produced men most eloquent and learned, and most invincible in defense of the catholic and apostolic faith. Since their examples are available for imitation and their teachings for following, and since the Church embraces them, the holy Church is beneficially instructed and nourished by them, with Christ’s favor, and not without good reason [the text is uncertain; perhaps: “to depart”].

But since it has very often produced—and to this day does not cease to produce—both heresiarchs attempting to stain the simplicity of the catholic faith with perverse doctrines and men who oppose the authority of the holy Church of God through manifold superstitions, all the faithful must greatly grieve.

To omit the others, from that same Spain there emerged, in the time of Charles, Augustus of holy memory, most pious and invincible, a certain man named Felix, unhappy in his conduct, bishop of the city of Urgel. Joining his most wicked error to that of Elipandus, bishop of the city of Toledo, he dared to preach that, according to his humanity, Christ was not the proper Son of God but an adoptive son; and by this poisonous doctrine both of them infected a large part of Spain.

Then, wishing to appear to imitate the acts of Christ’s apostles, although they themselves were not apostles of Christ but heralds of the ancient enemy, each separately sought out different provinces to imbue with the same insane doctrine. Elipandus sought Asturias and Galicia. I remember having once seen some of his disciples among the Asturians; from the report of the catholic men of that region, who rationally resisted their insane doctrine according to sound teaching, and from the evidence of my own observation, I clearly discovered, from their conduct and appearance, that they were unmistakable antichrists. In them I plainly saw the saying of blessed Ambrose fulfilled:

[Note: [Col. 0309D] Ambrose, on the First Epistle to Timothy.]

> The disposition of the mind is seen in the bearing of the body.

And also the saying of someone else:

> The brow of a human being reveals the garment of his own mind.

What sort of countenance he has, such hearts does he bear. When I had learned these things with complete truth and clarity—and since they had already been admonished, in accordance with the apostolic injunction, to desist from that same erroneous preaching of theirs, yet persisted in the same error—I avoided them as heretics.

Moreover, the same Felix, after having offered that poisonous draught to many in Septimania, nevertheless wished, as far as lay in him, to administer it to Gaul and Germany as well. But, with divine grace lending its aid, his error could find no place in Gaul or Germany, since not only in Germany was there a devotion to letters and a love of the sacred Scriptures, but also in that same Gaul—which alone, according to Jerome’s testimony, had no monsters, but had always abounded in men of great courage and eloquence—the exceptionally diligent zeal and fervent desire of that illustrious man had brought it about that, with the Lord’s help, the sons of the Church entrusted to him should excel both in the disciplines of the liberal arts and in perfect understanding of the divine Scriptures. As soldiers of Christ, equipped with invincible weapons, they drove back his mad doctrine.

By order of that same prince, they assembled in council and, with the authority of the holy Roman Church also brought to bear, condemned that same Felix; indeed, together with the author of his error, Nestorius, whom he had imitated, they consigned him to perpetual anathema.

After the orthodox prince Charles had been removed from human affairs, his glorious son Louis—so like his father in piety, wisdom, and courage—received, by God’s will, the paternal empire in triumph. While he was governing happily, that same Felix was reborn in one of his disciples, named Claudius, just as—in the words of blessed Jerome—“Euphorbus was reborn in Pythagoras.” How he attempted through this same disciple to hurl, with poisonous weapons, not indeed—as formerly—the rule of the Catholic faith, but ecclesiastical traditions, must briefly be recalled.

For the ancient enemy, the foe of the human race, impatient of ecclesiastical peace, who never ceases, insofar as divine permission allows, continually to sow the tares of his malice over the field of God’s holy Church, stirred up the aforementioned Claudius with certain frenzies of his snares and persuaded him to burst into such audacity that he wrote various frivolous and foolish things against the authority of the Church, as will be demonstrated below. I therefore suppose that he imagined that, after the pious and revered prince Charles had died, knowledge of the divine Scriptures in the Church—which that illustrious son, by divine will, had undertaken to govern and defend through the holy merits that had gone before—had been so weakened that he could shake it with the battering rams of his mad doctrine and everywhere force it to yield to him. But how greatly he mocked himself in this expectation is perfectly clear.

For through the exceptionally diligent zeal of that most pious prince, the Church, with the Lord’s assistance, daily grows toward better things, so that it is evident to all of sound faith that she is both healthfully strengthened in the sincerity of faith, wisely enlarged in the knowledge of the divine Scriptures, and made spiritually fruitful. She also stands founded upon the firmest rock, so that neither the gates of hell can prevail against her (Matt. XVI), nor the force of rivers nor the blasts of winds can in any way move her from her foundation. Hence that Gospel saying is appropriately sung concerning her:

“Rivers came, winds blew, and they could not move her, for she was founded upon a rock” (Matt. VII; Luke VI).

Since, therefore, that most beloved prince of God, more completely inflamed with divine love and aided by heavenly grace, diligently instructs the Church entrusted to him and fortifies her with spiritual weapons, continually raising her to higher things by both words and example, it is fitting that, just as his father condemned the error of that same Claudius after bringing forward the authority of the sacred Scriptures, so this glorious son of his—second to none in piety, wisdom, and courage—should likewise condemn the mad blasphemies of that disciple of Felix, pierce them with the weapons of the divine Scriptures, and, with Christ fighting alongside him, make the Church entrusted to him free and immune from these and similar errors.

[Note: Charles the Great condemned the error of Claudius the iconoclast on the authority of the Scriptures; it is therefore far from the case that he wrote that impious book which emerged from the workshop of the heretics under his name against images, in the year 1549.]

How this was accomplished through his pious and exceedingly astute zeal will become clear, God willing, in the course of this work.

The man under discussion, then, born in that same Spain and attached from an early age to the discipleship of the same Felix, served for some time in the priestly office at the palace of the aforementioned most glorious and serene Augustus, beloved of God. But so that he might contribute to the benefit of others through the teaching of evangelical preaching—which seemed to be strongly present in him—the clemency of that most pious prince appointed him to the bishopric of the Church of Turin.

While he watched over the flock entrusted to him as vigorously as he could and strove, insofar as appeared possible, to kindle it through the urgency of his preaching to love of the heavenly homeland, he observed that, among the other things in his conduct deserving correction, he was devoted, through long-established custom, to the superstitious—or rather pernicious—worship of images, with which many in those regions are greatly afflicted.

Therefore, inflamed by excessive and indiscriminate zeal, he is said to have removed, overturned, and entirely renounced from all the churches of his parish not only paintings of sacred events—paintings which, as blessed Gregory testifies, had anciently been permitted in churches not for worship but solely to instruct the minds of the unlearned—but also material crosses, which the holy Church is accustomed to use in honor and remembrance of its redemption.

But because he failed to correct the error of his flock by reason, he generated scandal in their minds and in a certain way drove them to break out in hatred of him. For if he had wished obediently to follow the words of blessed Gregory in his letter to Serenus, bishop of Marseille, and likewise to imitate the salutary deeds of the apostle Paul, he would never have thrown himself headlong into so irrational an action.

For, as we have learned from the book of the Acts of the Apostles (ch. XVII), and as we know with the supporting testimony of the author of the Tripartite History, when blessed Paul came to Athens and saw that the city was full of idols, he did not destroy the altars honored by the people; rather, by reason, he reproved their ignorance and demonstrated the rights of truth.

It is also said that this same Claudius dogmatized, and continues to dogmatize to the present day, certain abominable things against the relics of the saints—which ought not to be despised, since their death is precious in the sight of the Lord and their tombs, as the holy Fathers have handed down, are to be honored. Although the sequence of his writings does not clearly indicate this, it is nevertheless plainly evident from what he suggests and from the truthful report of certain faithful people that the matter stands thus.

Accordingly, it seems plausible that the soul of this novice enemy of the holy Church was composed from the souls of two men of old and allotted to one body—namely Vigilantius and Eustathius, who, to use Sedulius’s words, were alike in error, although they pursued different paths. For although in many respects they departed from one another, they were perversely of one mind in despising the relics of the holy martyrs and dishonoring their tombs, and in criticizing certain ecclesiastical traditions.

The error of one of them was vigorously overcome by blessed Jerome, that outstanding teacher of the holy Church of God, most faithful defender of the truth, and most experienced opponent of mad error; the error of the other was destroyed by the holy Fathers at the Council of Gangra and condemned to perpetual anathema.

It is therefore necessary that whoever imitates errors of this kind, already condemned, should be struck down by canonical authority and joined to their perpetual anathema.

The man of whom we are speaking, since he does not walk simply but, straying from the straight path, arrogantly transgresses the boundaries established by the holy Fathers, did not receive the name Claudius without reason, but, as is believed, by a kind of prophecy. For although he does not seem openly to follow the error of his master—may he who governs us keep that far from us!—nevertheless, in attempting to oppose ecclesiastical authority by limping against it, he rightly receives the name Claudius and is justly counted among those of whom the Psalmist says:

“Foreign sons have lied to me; foreign sons have grown old, and they have limped from their paths” (Ps. XVII).

A certain man, venerable for his dedication to holy religion, worthy of imitation for the uprightness of his life, and deserving of honor in name—Theodemir, father of the monks, now removed from human affairs—had learned, as rumor spread far and wide, that such things were being done and preached by the same Claudius against ecclesiastical authority. Moved by the duty of charity and prompted by love for a single people, he arranged for a letter full of charity to be sent to Claudius, urging him to restrain himself from the things he was reprehensibly doing and teaching.

Claudius, on the contrary, impatient of fraternal admonition and stirred by turbulent indignation, hurled darts of various accusations and reproaches not only at the man who was justly correcting him, but also at all the most sincere worshipers of the holy Catholic and apostolic Church who dwelt in Gaul and Germany, served Christ the Lord with the greatest devotion, and were free from superstitious worship of images. As the text of his letter demonstrates, he did not blush to call them entangled in the abomination of idolatry, in the superstition of false religion, and in countless other crimes.

I therefore cannot sufficiently wonder at a man who does not know the discipline of speaking correctly, yet presumes not only to teach and to criticize others, but—more foolish still—to vomit forth a book in condemnation of learned men. Indeed, were it not necessary to refute his utterly vain error and to guard against the deception of certain simple people—lest his pestilential doctrine somehow become their miserable ruin—his ignorant writings should never be taken into anyone’s hands.

For if they are even lightly examined by those trained in literary art, scarcely anything will be found in them that does not offend the art of speaking and writing correctly, except what he secretly stole from the little works of others and, after subtracting and altering certain things, inserted into his own work as his own, acting in the manner of a compiler.

Meanwhile, it is reported that, to the disparagement of that same abbot and of the whole Gallican Church, he vomited forth a book of such great length that by its size it surpassed David’s Psalter of one hundred and fifty psalms. Only an extract from it has come into the hands of my smallness, and this is its beginning:

**TITLE OF THE BOOK**

**The Defence and Reply of Bishop Claudius against Theodemir the Abbot**

How absurd and ridiculous, and how repellent this title’s construction is to the ears of learned men, can easily and plainly be demonstrated by the judgment even of boys who are still being introduced to the liberal disciplines. We do not openly attribute the rusticity of this title to any particular person, however, because it is uncertain whether it should be attributed to the dictating author, the writer, or indeed the copyist.

We therefore turn by apostrophe to what we do not doubt is your own, Claudius, and wish to engage with you directly—not concerning the things you perversely wrote in that work of yours together with others, but rather concerning you yourself.

For you say against the aforementioned venerable abbot Theodemir:

> “I received your letter, together with the accompanying chapters, full of loquacity and stupidity, through a certain rustic courier. In these chapters you declare yourself troubled, saying that rumor has spread from Italy concerning me throughout all Gaul, even to the end of Spain, as though I had preached some new sect against the rule of the Catholic faith; this is entirely false.”

If you wrote these things apologetically to Abbot Theodemir, why, in your excessive intemperance, do you stain innocent men with the blemish of falsehood by injuring others? For if your writings are carefully examined, you will doubtless be found to have belched forth, not only against that same Abbot Theodemir but also against the Italians, the Gauls, and the Germans, the poison which you had drunk—poison which you belched forth with deadly effect.

Indeed, if we began to examine and refute one by one the constructions of your monstrous words, the execution of the task would be immense and the expenditure of time excessive and pointless. Leaving them to be censured at the proper time by the reader’s most prudent judgment, let us attempt, according to the capacity of our understanding, to investigate the meaning contained in the text of your letters.

You therefore appear first to deserve censure in the opening of those same letters for impatience, levity, and anger, because, forgetful of fraternal love and setting aside measured expression and priestly gravity, you branded a man who was writing to you amicably and familiarly with the epithet “loquacity and stupidity.”

You also say shortly afterward:

> “Nor is it surprising if these members of the devil have said such things about me, since they proclaimed our very head to be both a seducer and demoniac.”

Whom do you call “members of the devil” here, with the reins of restraint cast aside—those who proclaimed our very head to be a seducer and demoniac—unless you mean the Gauls, to whom you wrote above that your rumor had reached and whom, as you wrote later, you said had opened their mouths to blaspheme against you?

I therefore ask you patiently: who ought rather to be called members of the devil? Those who are not separated from ecclesiastical authority by heresy, schism, or any other error whatsoever, or those who, puffed up by the arrogance of pride, dare in some way to resist it?

When you answer that “insulters,” or rather “attackers,” deservedly ought to be called members of the devil, such a dreadful name could be applied to another Church subdued by errors of this kind, but not to the Gallican Church. She does not, in the manner of unbelieving Jews, believe and faithfully proclaim that her head, Christ, is demoniac—a designation proper to them and to those who are driven by an unclean spirit—but believes and truthfully proclaims him, in the Holy Spirit, to be the expeller of demons.

As for “seducer,” which you indiscriminately placed in the negative sense with your ineffective pen, you show by this expression, as by many others, that you are ignorant of ecclesiastical tradition, which, according to the teaching of the holy Fathers, understands “seducer” in both a good and a bad sense.

For it is evident that you were completely ignorant of what blessed Augustine says in his Exposition of the Gospel of John the Evangelist (Tractate VII), although you boasted that nothing in his statements was unknown to you. His words are these:

> “Some were saying, ‘He is good,’ while others said, ‘No, but he deceives the crowds’” (John VII). This was said for the consolation of those who would later preach the word of God and would be called both deceivers and truthful men. For if to seduce is to deceive, neither Christ nor his apostles, nor any Christian, ought to be a seducer. But if to seduce is to lead someone from one place to another by persuading him, we must ask: from where and to where? If from evil to good, he is a good seducer; if from good to evil, he is a bad seducer.

If the sayings of so great a man had been known to you, Claudius, you would not have so rashly, with open mouth and foaming lips, placed “seducer” only in the negative sense.

Since it is therefore established that we truthfully believe, proclaim, and preach Christ our head—not as members of the devil, as you wrote, but rather as his faithful members—to be a good seducer, it is undoubtedly most just that this detestable vice should be attributed not to one who condemns it, but rather to one who infidelously hurls it as a weapon.

The same work continues:

> “For I do not teach a sect, you say, since I hold unity and proclaim truth; rather, I have suppressed, crushed, and conquered sects, schisms, superstitions, and heresies insofar as I have been able, and, insofar as I can, I do not cease to conquer them, with God’s help.”

I cannot sufficiently wonder that a man ignorant of grammatical art, yet possessing at least some understanding of the divine Scriptures, should be seized by such forgetfulness that he denies teaching a sect and professes to hold unity and proclaim truth. For a preacher of Christ can both teach a sect, hold the unity of the Catholic faith, and preach the truth.

We call a sect that which pursues the end of the good. Hence blessed Augustine says in the book On the City of God (Book IX, chapter 1):

> “There is therefore no reason for philosophizing except the end of the good. Consequently, whatever pursues no end of the good ought not to be called a philosophical sect.”

The same author says shortly afterward:

> “Therefore, since Marcus Varro, employing these four distinctions—that is, from social life, from the New Academics, from the Cynics, and from this threefold kind of life—arrived at two hundred and eighty-eight sects, and since other distinctions can likewise be added to all these, because they raise no question concerning the pursuit of the highest good, they are not sects and ought not to be called sects, and so forth.”

Blessed Augustine said these things about the sect that pursues only the highest good, in opposition to the philosophers.

Moreover, that “sect” is understood in both a good and a bad sense, we learn from apostolic teaching: in the good sense, as you find in the Epistle to Timothy:

> “But pursue righteousness, true faith, charity, and peace with those who call upon the Lord from a pure heart” (II Tim. II);

and in the bad sense, as you find in the same apostle’s Epistle to the Galatians (chapter V), where, among the works of the flesh, he places sects in twelfth position.

Thus, what are called *sectae* in Latin are called *haíreseis* (‘heresies’) in Greek, for sects are named from *sectari*, “to pursue.”

But when you say that you have suppressed schisms and superstitions with all your strength, you plainly appear to contradict yourself. For the man who irrationally scandalizes the minds of the peoples subject to him, shamelessly criticizes ecclesiastical traditions, and does not fear to apply the names of abominations to so many and such sincere worshipers of sound faith, ought in no way to be judged a suppressor, but rather a fomenter and author of schisms and superstitions.

As for your claim that you have crushed and conquered sects and heresies, you make great promises to yourself deceitfully. If they have been crushed, why do they rise again at the devil’s prompting? If they have been conquered, why do they return and hurl themselves against the peace of ecclesiastical authority?

But if the catalogue of illustrious men who fought manfully in the battle line of the faith and overthrew the armies of heretics in their ranks were carefully reviewed, your name would certainly not be found in it.

As for the heresies which, as you say, you still do not cease to conquer, since nowhere throughout the whole breadth of the world are they known or heard to be conquered by you, you can more readily suppose no one than your hearers to be those whom you conquer—whom, perhaps because you cannot make them companions of your schism, you therefore write that you conquer as heretics.

The work continues:

> “This has happened, you say, because, after I was compelled to undertake the burden of pastoral office, sent by the pious prince Louis, son of the holy Church of God, I came to Italy and found all the basilicas in Turin full of the filth of anathemas and of images, contrary to the order of truth.”

We disdainfully pass over the extremely malformed construction of these words, filled with barbarisms and solecisms, and investigate their meaning as best we can.

It is true, I say, that what you stated is the case: you were appointed by the pious prince, Lord Louis, son of the holy Church of God, to the Church of Turin. Whether you were compelled, as you assert, or acted voluntarily, is left to God alone.

But in the ineffective construction with which you continue, saying:

> “I found all the basilicas full of the filth of anathemas and of images,”

you accuse your predecessors of having filled those same basilicas not with divine worship but with anathemas, and accuse them of having made not only themselves but also the people of that parish serve the anathemas of those basilicas rather than divine worship.

If it is true that the whole clerical order of your parish, having abandoned divine worship, worships and adores the filth of anathemas in place of God, this must be mourned and lamented with the most abundant tears of the faithful, and God’s immeasurable mercy must be earnestly entreated, so that those who have strayed from their own salvation in this way may quickly recover and return to the path of truth, and may worship and adore him who rightly ought to be worshiped and adored.

But it is credible that, although through the deception of ignorance they may have spent some time in the worship and adoration of images, they should nevertheless by no means be believed to have defected from the unity of the Catholic faith or turned to idols. Hence it is clear that you ought not to have compared such an error so grandly and indiscriminately to the filth of anathemas, but rather, using more measured language, to have attributed it to ignorance.

Moreover, if your predecessors held anything simply and without compromising the faith of Christ, it was in no way fitting for them, now resting in the house of the heavenly Father, to be so arrogantly defamed far and wide by their successor and branded with the epithet of anathema—especially since the unwary simplicity of those earlier men could do no harm to the sound doctrine of those now living.

How great the crime, and how great the arrogance, of a man who, in order to establish his own actions as praiseworthy, indiscriminately and irrationally criticizes the errors of others, is not for me to say. The teachings of the holy Fathers are abundantly available: let them be read and examined, and let their words be salutarily obeyed, lest one fall into such offenses.

I suppose, therefore, that if you were present, Claudius, you might answer:

“I called images anathemas because those who worship them with the worship due to God alone thereby make themselves accursed.”

You would answer well, because in this statement you would agree soberly with us—or rather, with the whole Catholic Church.

For everything divinely prohibited, although not accursed by its own nature, must nevertheless, by the very prohibition through which it has been prohibited, necessarily plunge into the destruction of anathema the person who unlawfully seeks, honors, or worships it. Hence the statement in the book of Joshua:

> “Anathema is in your midst, Israel” (Josh. VII).

On account of this guilt Achan, the transgressor of the Lord’s command, perished beneath a hail of stones. Many other examples of this matter can be found in the divine utterances.

Nevertheless, although these things are so, no one who is not unsound in mind can fail to see how boldly and culpably you have acted in reviling and criticizing your predecessors, and in refusing to correct that same error discreetly, reasonably, and patiently.

You add the following in the continuation of your writing:

> “And because people were worshiping something, I alone began to destroy it [*destruere*, ‘to destroy,’ rather than *destrui*, ‘to be destroyed’].”

Perhaps you were afraid that you might seem to be calling them asses, and therefore unnecessarily chose to add “people worshiping I know not what.” Although one may infer that you wished either images, or crosses, or the relics of the holy martyr-saints, or certainly their precious bodies, to be understood, we do not know which of these you intended to be supplied.

This much we know that you know along with us: worship concerns diverse things and properly belongs to rational creatures. Brute and irrational animals do not worship; they are worshiped. Therefore, you yourself must see how superfluously you inserted “people.”

If, then, you had rationally turned people away—as was fitting—from the worship of superstitious things, you would certainly have acted commendably and would have escaped the censure of indiscriminate action. But because you refused to do this, you deserve criticism.

As for your statement, “I alone began to destroy,” when you perhaps wished to adorn your diction with the figure called *homoioteleuton* (similarity of endings), you fell into the fault of a solecism.

Let us now examine what meaning your letter contains.

In your statement, “I alone began *destrui* (‘to be destroyed’; where *destruere*, ‘to destroy,’ was intended),” let us see whether, perhaps inspired by the spirit of prophecy, you fashioned this phrase concerning the ruin of your own utterly disordered distinction. But in saying that you alone were destroying, you unquestionably contradicted the truth, since not you alone but anyone else may be destroyed in his frivolous and foolish expressions—and not only in such expressions, but also in the things they think wrongly and perversely.

Let us also examine the meaning which we suppose you intended, since your purpose and subject move in one direction while your dictation runs in another. For, ignorant of grammatical art, you used the passive infinitive *destrui*—“to be destroyed”—in place of the active infinitive *destruere*—“to destroy.”

The verb *struere*, “to build,” has its contrary in *destruere*, “to destroy.” Therefore, since you did not permit the structure of the worship which you boast of having destroyed, you used the verb *destruere* with great ignorance and impropriety.

Moreover, in saying that you alone were the destroyer, anyone could have been left wavering in uncertainty as to whether you were proclaiming yourself the overthrower of good things or of sinister ones, unless perhaps you attempt to resolve the ambiguity by appearing to abuse the words of the holy prophet Elijah, who says:

> “Lord, they have destroyed your altars, they have killed your prophets, and I alone have remained, and they seek my life” (III Kings XIX).

But you know very well, as we do, what Elijah heard from the Lord.

You must also consider, for your own good, how great an injury you inflict upon the outstanding teachers of the holy Church of God when you attribute so much to yourself alone. If you alone are the destroyer of perverse doctrines and superstitious things, then all the teachers who fought bravely for the Catholic Church alone, and who now happily obtain the reward of their struggle, are excluded.

And if you have excluded the others, you ought in no way to have excluded blessed Augustine, whom everyone acknowledges to have been the most eloquent teacher among the Latin doctors and the strongest defender and champion of the holy Church of God.

Although not alone, yet with divine grace aiding him, he more eloquently and abundantly than others bravely and reasonably overturned, destroyed, and utterly overthrew the perverse decrees of various heresies and schismatics.

Since you were accustomed to extol him among others with deserved proclamations of great praise, having been continually trained by meditation upon his salutary teachings, you ought in no way to have excluded him.

But if you had been willing to be content with his teachings, you would never have boasted of being alone the destroyer of badly constructed things. And if you had at least deigned to take him as your companion, your destruction, because it would have been guided by his doctrine, might indeed have been regarded as reasonable.

Since, therefore, you have presumptuously placed yourself above not only blessed Augustine but also the other outstanding teachers, your solitary boast of destruction—extending itself to immeasurable proportions—is rightly brought to nothing.

For, in accordance with the saying of Ecclesiastes, woe threatens that same boast of yours, because, having no warmth from the companionship of others, it grows numb in solitary cold; and when it falls, it will have no one to raise it up.

You add the following:

> “For this reason they all opened their mouths to blaspheme against me, and, if the Lord had not helped me, perhaps they would have swallowed me alive.”

This must be attributed to no one but you. You ought to have taken care not to criticize the followers of Christ so disastrously, to brand them with the charge of sacrilege, and to approve—if not by your assent, at least by your silence, with gravity as your teacher—the traditions which the holy Church simply holds as handed down to her by the holy Fathers.

For every faithful person ought, for the love of God, to bear with equanimity an injury inflicted upon him. But who can patiently endure the disparagement and criticism of ecclesiastical authority or the contempt of God’s saints?

It remains, therefore, that you are the author of this offense: you vomited forth such blasphemous words to the disparagement of ecclesiastical authority and its devoted servants, not those whom, as you claim, you compelled by these actions to open their mouths to blaspheme against you and rationally resist your foolish songs.

A little later in the same writings you continue:

> “For when it is expressly said, ‘You shall not make a likeness of anything that is in heaven or on earth’ (Exod. XX), this is understood to have been said not only concerning the likenesses of foreign gods but also concerning heavenly creatures.”

This, then, is also our opinion. It is true, I say, and entirely consistent with sound faith, that no likeness whatsoever of anything in heaven, on earth, or under the earth should be made in such a way that worship or adoration, which is due to God alone, is in some manner offered to it.

Since God is everywhere and contains all things, while he himself is contained nowhere, and is invisible, as the Apostle testifies (I Tim. I and VI), we are forbidden to make a likeness of any of his creatures, lest he be believed to be corporeal.

But since the meaning of this statement is clear—and since it is certainly established that the holy Fathers have explained it to us at length—and since it does not sufficiently pertain to the matter under discussion, we must consider whether perhaps you intend to include under the name “likeness” the images of the saints and the histories of sacred events painted in churches for the sake of beauty and remembrance.

If so, I ask you why, at the Lord’s command, Moses made two golden cherubim and the other things read in Exodus (chapter XXXVII) in the tabernacle of the Lord, and why Solomon fashioned likenesses of oxen and lions in the house of the Lord (III Kings VII).

When you answer—as we believe you will—that these things were made beforehand as figures of mysteries, you will nevertheless be entirely unable to deny that they were likenesses of heavenly and earthly creatures.

And if those things were made in the tabernacle and in the house of the Lord not by God for the purpose of worship but to foreshadow future realities, then allow images of the saints and the histories of the saints to be painted in churches—not so that they may be worshiped, but rather so that they may provide a certain beauty and bring the memory of past events before the senses of the unlearned.

We judge it impious for a creature to be worshiped or for anything of divine service to be offered to it, and with a free voice we proclaim that the perpetrator of this crime is to be detested and anathematized. The Lord thunders terribly how great its punishment is, saying:

> “He who sacrifices to anyone except the Lord alone shall be destroyed” (Exod. XXII).

But as for what you add, saying:

“Or what the human mind devises to place in honor of the Creator”—what sense this may bear is not sufficiently clear. The human mind is not permitted to imagine anything corporeal concerning God, as you seem to have wished it to understand.

Nor can I sufficiently wonder that, when you had undertaken from the commandment of the Decalogue the matter of making no image at all, you were carried away by a certain wanton agility and attempted to explain the conclusion of that same commandment, which you omitted. It reads as follows: “You shall not adore them, nor worship them; I am the Lord your God, mighty, jealous” [Col. 0319A] (Exod. XX), and the rest that follows. It is therefore clear—as I may say with your permission—that in this matter you acted with insufficient skill. For by wishing to explain adoration and worship with many inappropriate words, you both violated the rule of correct expression and failed fully to reach the meaning you intended to convey.

You ought rather to have followed the exposition of the holy Fathers in explaining these same words, not your own. Since you refused to do so, you did not sufficiently make clear the force and proper meaning of those words. For one kind of adoration is owed exclusively to God; another is offered by mortals to mortals equally, as an expression of humility and submission. Again, one kind of worship is that by which only divine power must be served; another is offered, according to its proper measure, not only to rational creatures but also to irrational ones.

On the distinction between forms of worship, you have with us the blessed Augustine teaching most fully in the tenth book of *The City of God* (ch. 1):

> “This is the worship owed to divinity—or, to speak more precisely, to deity. Since I have no sufficiently suitable Latin word by which to signify it in a single term, I indicate in Greek, where necessary, what I mean to say. For wherever it occurs in the holy Scriptures, our translators have rendered *λατρεία* (*latreia*) as *servitus*, ‘service.’ But the service owed to human beings—the service according to which the Apostle commanded servants to be subject to their masters (Eph. VI)—is ordinarily called by another name in Greek.”

[Note: [Col. 0319D] Namely, *δουλεία* (*douleia*).]

> “But *λατρεία*, according to the usage of those who composed the divine utterances for us, always, or so frequently that it is practically always so, denotes that service which pertains to the worship of God. Therefore, if the worship itself is simply called *cultus*, it does not appear to be owed exclusively to God. For we are said to worship human beings as well, whom we regularly visit either in honor or in remembrance. Nor are only those things said to be worshiped to which we subject ourselves with religious respect; certain things also that are subject to us are said to be worshiped. For from this word come *agricolae*, ‘farmers,’ *coloni*, ‘cultivators’ or ‘colonists,’ and *incolae*, ‘inhabitants.’ The gods themselves are called *coelicolas*, ‘inhabitants of heaven,’ for no other reason than that they inhabit heaven—not, of course, by venerating it, but by dwelling in it, as though they were certain colonists of heaven. They are not called *coloni* in the manner of those who, because of agriculture, owe their status to the native soil under a possessing master, but as a great author of Latin eloquence says (Virgil, *Aeneid* I.12):

> *There was an ancient city, which Tyrian colonists held.*

> “He called them *coloni* from inhabiting, not from agriculture. Hence cities founded by larger cities, like swarms of peoples, are called colonies. In this respect, then, it is entirely true that worship is owed only to God, according to a certain proper meaning of this word; but since the worship of other things is also spoken of, the worship owed to God cannot be signified by a single Latin word.

> “Even *religio*, although it seems more distinctly to signify not just any worship but the worship of God—for this reason our translators rendered by this name what is called *θρησκεία* (*threskeia*) in Greek—does not avoid ambiguity when the question concerns the worship of the Divinity. For in the Latin usage not only of the uneducated but also of the most learned, *religio* is said to be owed to human relationships, affinities, and every kind of connection. Thus we cannot confidently say that *religio* means nothing other than the worship of God, since the word seems improperly to have been taken away from its meaning of observance toward human kinship.

> “*Pietas* likewise is ordinarily understood properly as the worship of God, which the Greeks call *εὐσέβεια* (*eusebeia*). Yet this term is also said to be applied dutifully toward parents. In popular usage, moreover, the word is frequently employed for works of mercy. I think this happened because God chiefly commands such works and testifies that they please him either in place of sacrifices or above sacrifices.

> “From this usage it has come about that God himself is also called *pius*, ‘pious’ or ‘merciful.’ The Greeks, to be sure, do not, in any usage of their language, call God *εὐσεβεῖν* (*eusebein*), although even the common people among them use *εὐσέβεια* for mercy. Hence in certain passages of Scripture, so that the distinction might appear more clearly, they preferred to say *θεοσέβεια* (*theosebeia*), a term formed from the worship of God, rather than *εὐσέβεια*, which derives from good worship.

> “Neither of these expressions can we render in Latin with a single word. What is called *λατρεία* in Greek and rendered in Latin as *servitus*, ‘service,’ is the service by which we worship God; what is called *θρησκεία* in Greek and *religio* in Latin is that which we practice toward God; and what they call *εὐσέβεια*, which we cannot express in one word but may call the worship of God—this, we say, is owed exclusively to that God who is the true God and who makes his worshipers gods.

> “Therefore, whatever immortal and blessed beings exist in heavenly dwellings, if they do not love us and do not wish us to be blessed, they are certainly not to be worshiped. But if they love us and wish us to be blessed, they surely wish this for us from the source from which they themselves possess it.”

These statements, which we have brought forward from the blessed Augustine, are more than sufficient for the prudent reader concerning the diversity of worship.

As for the adoration offered by mortals to mortals as an expression of humility and submission, many examples are found in the divine utterances. Among them is this passage in the book of Genesis: “Abraham rose and adored the people of the land, namely the sons of Heth” (Gen. XXIII). Elsewhere in the same book: “When Joseph’s brothers had adored him and he had recognized them, he spoke harshly to them as though they were strangers.” A little later: “Then Joseph entered his house, and they brought him gifts in their hands, and they adored him, prostrate upon the ground” (Gen. XXIV). And in the book of *Melachim* [Kings]: “Bathsheba bowed and adored the king” (III Kings I). A little later: “They announced to the king, saying: ‘The prophet Nathan is here.’ When he had entered the king’s presence and had adored him, prostrate upon the ground, Nathan told the king what follows there.”

Let this suffice for the present. Whoever is inclined to read the pages of the divine Scriptures carefully can very easily find more abundant testimonies of this kind of adoration.

Concerning the adoration owed exclusively to God, there are many and innumerable salutary teachings throughout both Testaments. Since they are so numerous that even the most learned and eloquent men could not easily explain them all, it remains for us to append to this work, in pursuit of brevity, a few of the many expositions arranged and transmitted to our knowledge by holy Fathers inspired by the Holy Spirit.

Origen writes in his *Exposition of the Epistle to the Romans* (Book I):

> “Although human beings could acknowledge God, they turned away from his worship and turned instead to the adoration of images of human beings and animals. To state the matter briefly and gather everything into a single definition: to adore anyone other than the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is the crime of impiety.”

The same author writes again in the same work:

> “I think the following should be understood in this way. If, for example, someone makes out of any metal—gold, silver, wood, or stone—the form of some quadruped, serpent, or bird, and fashions that statue, not as an idol but as a likeness; or even if he sets up paintings for this same purpose, he must nevertheless be said to have made a likeness. The word of God, embracing everything, at once forbids and rejects both. It prohibits not only the making of an idol but also the making of a likeness of everything that is on earth, in the waters, and in heaven. It adds and says: ‘You shall not adore them, nor worship them’ (Exod. XX).

> “To worship is one thing; to adore is another. Someone may sometimes adore even unwillingly, just as certain people who flatter kings, when they see them devoted to such pursuits, pretend to adore idols, although it is certain in their hearts that an idol is nothing. To worship is to devote oneself to it with one’s whole affection and zeal. The divine word therefore cuts off both practices, so that you may neither worship with affection nor adore by outward form.”

Jerome, in his exposition of the prophet Daniel:

> “Let it be known to you, O king, that we do not worship your gods, and that we do not adore the golden statue which you have erected” (Dan. III). Whether we wish to read *statue*, as Symmachus has it, or *golden image*, as the others translated it, the worshipers of God ought not to adore it. Therefore, let the judges and rulers of the world who adore the statues and images of emperors understand that they are doing what the three young men refused to do, and by refusing pleased God. The precise wording should be noted: they say that gods are to be worshiped and an image adored; neither practice is fitting for the servants of God.”

The same author, in his exposition of the prophet Ezekiel:

> “And seventy men of the elders of the house of Israel, with Jezonias son of Saphan standing in their midst before the paintings; and each had a censer in his hand, and a cloud of smoke rose from the incense” (Ezek. VIII). When he says that seventy men from the elders of the house of Israel held censers in their hands, he shows that many other presbyters existed who did not do this but were perhaps held by other sins. He also shows that one man, named Jezonias son of Saphan, stood in their midst as though he were the leader of their crime and sacrilege—those who, having abandoned the worship of God, worshiped idols and, in the temple, did not adore God, whose temple it was, but paintings on the walls.”

The holy Augustine, in the seventh book of *The City of God*:

> “Let everyone strive to worship the one true God, that is, the creator of every soul and body. A person does not sin because what he worships is not to be worshiped, but because he worships what should be worshiped not as it ought to be worshiped. But whoever worships such things—that is, shameful and criminal things—and not the true God, the maker of soul and body, but a creature, even if that creature is not vicious—whether it is soul, body, or soul and body together—sins twice against God: first, because he worships in place of God something that is not God; second, because he worships him with things by which even God himself ought not to be worshiped.”

The same author, in Book X of *The City of God*:

> “Finally, many practices taken from divine worship were transferred to human honors, whether through excessive humility or through destructive flattery. Nevertheless, those to whom such honors were offered were regarded as human beings, who are said to be worthy of worship and veneration; and if much more is added to them, of adoration. But who has judged that sacrifice should be offered except to one whom he knew, believed, or imagined to be a god?”

Again, in the same work, Book X:

> “Some thought that angels should be given the honor—whether by adoring or sacrificing—that is owed to God, but they were forbidden to do so by the angels’ own admonition and were commanded to offer these things to the one to whom alone they knew it was lawful to offer them. Holy men of God imitated the holy angels. For Paul and Barnabas, after a miracle of healing in Lycaonia, were thought to be gods, and the Lycaonians wished to sacrifice victims to them. They humbly prevented this and announced to them the God in whom they believed (Acts XIV.4).”

A little later (chapter 4):

> “Therefore, whatever immortal power, endowed with however great a virtue, loves us, it wishes us to be subject, as it is subject, to the one by whom we may be blessed and under whom it too is blessed. If it does not worship God, it is wretched, because it is deprived of God; but if it worships God, it does not wish to be worshiped in place of God. For it rather supports the divine judgment and favors the powers of love, because it is written: ‘He who sacrifices to gods shall be eradicated, unless to the Lord alone’ (Exod. XXII). To say nothing now of the other matters belonging to the religious service by which God is worshiped, there is certainly no human being who would dare say that sacrifice is owed to anyone except God alone.”

Again, in the same work, Book X (chapter 26):

> “We therefore ought not to fear that immortal and blessed beings, who are subject to the one God, will be offended because we do not sacrifice to them. For what the holy know is due only to the one true God—the one to whom they too cling and by whom they are blessed—they certainly do not wish to have offered to themselves, either through any signifying figure or through the thing itself signified by the sacraments. Such arrogance belongs to proud and wretched demons; the piety of those subject to God is wholly different.”

Again, in the same work, the final book, chapter 10:

> “We build for our martyrs not temples as for gods, but memorials as for dead human beings, whose spirits live with God. Nor do we erect altars there on which to sacrifice to the martyrs, but to the one God, both theirs and ours, we offer sacrifice. At that sacrifice they are named in their proper place and order as human beings of God who conquered the world in their confession, but they are not invoked by the priest who offers the sacrifice. For he sacrifices to God, not to them, although he sacrifices in their memory, because he is God’s priest, not theirs. The true sacrifice itself is the body of Christ. It is not offered to them, because they themselves are this body.”

The same author, in the book *Questions on the Old and New Testaments*:

> “Christians, who are poor and whom they call foolish, worship one God in mystery, from whom all things come, and venerate nothing that has been created by him. For they know that he alone is sufficient and abundant for their salvation.”

A little later:

> “It therefore does not seem right to us that what a human being makes should be adored. For the maker is judged to be adored by the work, not the work by the maker.”

Again, in his exposition of Psalm CXIII:

> “Do not, therefore, add the hands of human beings, so that from the same metal which the true God made you may wish to make a false god—or rather, a false human being—whom you may venerate in place of the true God. Whoever were to receive such a figure into true friendship in place of the true God would be insane. For the likeness of form, and the structure that imitates the arrangement of limbs, leads on and, by a certain weak affection, carries away the weak hearts of mortals.”

Again, in the same work, on Psalm XCVI:

> “But as for human beings, attend to the saints, who are like angels. When you find some holy human being, a servant of God, if you wish to worship and adore him in place of God, he forbids you. He does not wish to claim for himself the honor of God; he does not wish to be God for you, but with you to be under God.”

A little later:

> “So too the holy angels seek the glory of the one whom they love. They strive to draw and inflame all whom they love toward his worship, his adoration, and his contemplation. They announce him to them, not themselves; for, since they are angels and soldiers, they know no glory except that of their emperor.”

Again, a little later:

> “Let no one say: ‘I fear that the angel will be angry with me if I do not worship him in place of my God.’ He is angry with you precisely when you wish to worship him; for he is good and loves God. Just as demons are angry when they are not worshiped, so angels are indignant when they are worshiped in place of God.”

The same author, in his letter to Maximus the grammarian:

> “Know that among the Catholic Christians—whose Church has also been established in your town—no dead person is worshiped, and nothing made or created by God is adored. They worship only God himself, who made and created all things.”

Again, in the book *On True Religion*, among other things, he says (chapter 3):

> “For the apprehension of truth, nothing is more obstructive than a life given over to lust and the false images of sensible things which, impressed upon us through the body by this sensible world, generate various opinions and errors. Nor could there have been error in religion if the soul had not worshiped, in place of its God, either another soul or body, or its own phantasms, which are nothing other than images drawn from the appearance of a body through bodily sensation.”

Again, in the same work:

> “Let the worship of human works not be our religion.”

[Note: [Col. 0323D] That is, worship arising from service, not from love; for a little below he expresses in this way what he calls *latria* and *dulia*.]

> “For the artisans who make such things are better than the things themselves, yet we ought not to worship the artisans. Let our religion not consist in our phantasms. For whatever truth may be, it is better than everything that can be invented according to one’s will. Yet we ought not to worship the soul itself, although it is a true soul, when it imagines false things. True straw is better than a light formed in empty thought according to the fancy of one who suspects; yet it is the belief of a madman that the straw which we perceive and touch should be worshiped.”

Again, in his evangelical sermon concerning the power given to demons to enter the swine:

> “Do not bow down to angels, thinking that sacrifice should be offered to them; they do not wish it. When you do so, they do not understand it; they love it when you adore with them the one whom they adore.”

Again, in the book *On the Quantity of the Soul*:

> “Any other human being, however wise and perfect, or absolutely any rational and blessed soul, is to be loved and imitated only; and to each, according to merit and rank, what is appropriate to it should be offered. For ‘you shall adore the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve’ (Deut. VI).”

Again, in *On True Religion* (chapter 55):

> “Our religion is not the worship of ethereal and heavenly bodies, but of the one by whose contemplation they are blessed. For we too are not blessed by seeing an angel, but by seeing the Truth, through which we also love the angels and rejoice with them. Nor do we see that they enjoy it more readily and without the hindrance of any trouble; rather, we love them because we too have been commanded to hope for something of this kind from the common Lord. Therefore, we honor them with love, not with service. Nor do we build temples for them, for they do not wish to be honored by us in this way, since they know that we ourselves, when we are good, are temples of the Most High God.”

Fulgentius, in the book *On Faith to Donatus*:

> “Because God himself, commanding that he alone be served and ordering that he be adored by the faithful, strictly forbade anyone to adore a creature or serve a creature, for this reason at the end of that commandment he speaks concerning everything he created as follows: ‘You shall not adore them, nor serve them.’”

A little later:

> “True religion consists in the service of the one God.”

Again, a little later:

> “If true faith adores one God with the Father and the Son, it knows that God is to be served by all creatures in such a way that it also knows that the service due to God is not owed to a creature.”

Firmianus Lactantius, Book II of *On False Religion*:

> “The foolish sin in two ways. First, they place the elements—that is, the works of God—above God; then they worship representations of the elements fashioned in human form.”

Again:

> “Let us adore nothing else and worship nothing else except the one name of our only maker and father.”

Again:
