> “God is therefore above, not below; he is not to be sought in the depths but rather in the highest religion.”

And below:

> “Nothing that mortal eyes perceive is to be worshiped.”

More abundant statements of the holy Fathers concerning the worship and adoration owed exclusively to God could certainly have been brought forward, if they had not been omitted in order to avoid excessive length.

The work of Claudius follows.

[Col. 0325A] “These are the people,” you say, “against whom we have undertaken to defend the Church.” An excellent and splendid boast of yours. Earlier you claimed great things for yourself, saying that you were a suppressor and crusher of sects, schisms, superstitions, and heresies; now you add that you have undertaken to defend the Church of God against the adorers of images.

You assume their person in the plural when you say, “These are the people against whom we have undertaken to defend the Church of God,” and then, addressing them individually, you add a little later, “To whom we reply.” We therefore pass over this faulty expression of yours, which grammarians call a solecism of number, and leave it to be associated with your other faulty and disorderly expressions, while investigating only the meaning that has been awkwardly expressed by one who is himself awkward.

The blessed Augustine, therefore, writing against the pagans, rightly says that he undertook to defend the Church of God. He powerfully and rationally refuted their infidelity and furnished the holy Church with salutary admonitions—or rather, fully armed it with spiritual weapons—to refute and overcome their unbelief. You, however, will nowhere be found to have done anything of the kind. I therefore cannot sufficiently wonder why you boasted that you alone had undertaken to defend the Church of God.

But because, abusing the words of that same teacher, you judged that the adorers of images in your parish should be struck with such an attack, you do not appear to have excluded from the same persecution the most sincere worshipers of the holy Church of God who inhabit Gaul and are free from this superstition—people whom, in both your preceding and your subsequent writings, you call worshipers of false religion and superstition.

What you wrote that the adorers of images replied to you in order to defend their error is as follows:

> “We do not think that anything divine is present in the image which we adore; rather, out of respect for the one whose likeness it is, we adore it with such veneration.”

We reproach and detest only this one thing: although they know that there is nothing divine in images, they nevertheless deserve a greater rebuke because they have offered to a feeble and impoverished image the honor due to the Divinity. It is unnecessary for me to explain point by point how far the followers and defenders of this error have departed from true religion.

Some of the Easterners who are enslaved to the same most criminal error likewise customarily respond in this way to those who rebuke them. May the Lord, in his freely given goodness, grant that both these people and those others may at last be rescued from the same superstition and, salutarily instructed in apostolic discipline, be recalled to ecclesiastical tradition.

But what you add is this:

> “If the images of the saints are venerated in the worship of demons, they have not abandoned idols but have changed their names.”

Immediately afterward you add:

> “If you write on a wall or paint images of Peter and Paul, or of Jupiter and Saturn, neither these are gods nor those apostles; neither these nor those are human beings, and thus the name is changed, but the error both then and now always remains the same.”

Who would not perceive in this continuation of your argument, full of frivolity and indiscretion, that you have included Gaul as well, just as you did in the other matters? Gaul both possesses images of the saints and permits them to be possessed for the reasons stated above; but it regards their being adored and venerated in the worship of demons with profound detestation and abhorrence.

Therefore, as you assert, it does not worship idols and change their name, because it abandoned the devil and followed Christ, and from unbelieving became believing. As has been said, it possesses images of the saints, but it does not venerate them in the worship of demons.

As for those who, through excessive and indiscriminate love, supplicate the images of the saints in honor of the saints, I do not know whether they should rashly be called idolaters. They seem rather to require recall from this superstition through the application of rational moderation than to be designated idolaters, since they sincerely believe and proclaim the faith of the holy Trinity.

In the rest of this assertion you agree with us, except for the final statement you added:

> “And thus the name is changed, but the error both then and now always remains the same.”

This can appropriately be applied to what you said above: “They have not abandoned idols but have changed their names.”

Again, you say:

> “Certainly, if they were to be adored, the living rather than the dead ought to have been adored, as you have stated.”

You should have written: “They would have had to be adored,” or, certainly, “They ought to have been adored.”

> “That is, wherever they possess the likeness of God.”

In these words you agree soberly with us. Concerning this matter there are sufficient testimonies in divine Scripture, which are not included here for the sake of brevity.

But what you immediately add is:

> “Not where they possess the likeness of cattle—or, what is more accurate, of stones or woods—lacking life, sense, and reason, as you have stated.”

You should have written: “Where they possess the likeness of things lacking life, sense, and reason.”

How perversely you disagree with those who think soundly is plainly revealed by the matter itself. Your words, which you uttered with shameless insolence in contempt of the saints, are full of blasphemy. Thus, by erring excessively and disastrously, you departed from the understanding of all the faithful when you equated the precious bodies of the saints—bodies which they dedicated to God and in which they served him most dutifully, bodies which were indeed instruments of the Holy Spirit—with cattle and, as you more accurately claimed to have written, with stones and woods.

By this continuation of your argument, in which you clearly show contempt for the bodies of the saints, you are proved altogether to follow the error of Eustathius and Vigilantius. As has already been stated, both of them, in their madness, dogmatized that the relics of the saints should be despised, along with many other things contrary to ecclesiastical decrees; and for this reason they were deservedly assigned to the company of heretics under perpetual anathema.

If, therefore, as you assert, the bodies of the saints possess the likeness of cattle, then they should not be committed to the earth in the human manner but, according to the erroneous doctrine of a certain person—namely, Diogenes the Cynic—should be thrown to wild beasts and birds; or certainly scattered in every direction like a useless stone or an unfruitful piece of wood.

Which Catholic person, I ask you, could patiently read or hear such impious and blasphemous words? Who, I ask, except someone bereft of reason, would not reject such profane statements with abhorrence?

Or do you not know that it was the custom of the pagans, when they killed martyrs by the most varied kinds of death, to hide their bones in many different ways so that Christians could not bury them honorably, or to burn them in fire, or certainly to expose them to wild beasts and birds? Through these actions, impure spirits took care, as far as they could, to prevent the benefits bestowed upon mortals from being increased through the ashes of the saints, to confound the obstinacy of unbelievers, and to expose their deceitfulness.

For, as the blessed Jerome writes against Vigilantius, demons howl at the ashes of the saints and flee from possessed bodies; and many other innumerable things occur through their intervention, with the grace of Christ cooperating. It is beyond doubt that nothing of this kind occurs at the corpses of cattle, or at stones, or at pieces of wood.

The blessed Augustine writes in the eighth book of *The City of God*:

> “Indeed, the deceitful spirit, at whose prompting Hermes was saying these things, was compelled by that very fact to confess that the land was even then utterly full of the tombs of the dead whom they worshiped as gods. But the grief of the demons was speaking through him, for they mourned that their future punishments were impending at the memorials of the holy martyrs. For in many such places they are tortured and confess, and they are driven out of the bodies of human beings whom they possessed.”

John Chrysostom, in his homily on the Nativity of the Maccabees:

> “What a beautiful and welcome festival has shone forth for us, and how much more splendid than all the days of the year does this day gleam! It is not illuminated more brilliantly by the concentrated rays of the sun, but it is exalted and illumined by the light of the martyrs, which shines more brightly than lightning. For the martyrs are brighter than many suns and more radiant than great lights. Therefore today, if it may be said, the earth rejoices, adorned more splendidly than heaven itself.

> “But in this comparison do not consider the ash of the saints’ bodies, nor the embers of the relics of the flesh, nor all the bones consumed by time. Rather, open the eyes of faith and see them clothed with divine power and the grace of the Holy Spirit, radiant with the brilliance of divine light.

> “These very rays are sent forth from the circuit of the heavenly Sun upon the earth by Christ. Leaping forth from their bodies with flashing brilliance, they illuminate the face of the rejoicing Church, just as they blind the face of the envious devil.

> “For if bold leaders of robbers, or impious plunderers of tombs, while carrying off spoils or seeking booty, should happen to come upon the weapons or ornaments of an emperor, then, however greedy for plunder they may be, once they recognize the insignia of the king they are terrified into flight. They do not dare approach or touch them closely, since they foresee that, if they attempt to seize anything from them, not advantage but danger awaits them.

> “So too the demons, who are truly both leaders and teachers of robbers, as soon as they see the bodies of crowned martyrs laid out, immediately flee and leap away from their sight in fear. For they do not attend to their nature, but to the mysterious dignity and glory of Christ, who, in the contest of battle, bore the bodies of his martyrs as weapons.

> “No angel, no archangel, and no other created power has been clothed with such weapons; rather, the Lord of powers and of angels himself has been clothed with them, as Paul cries out, saying in II Corinthians XIII: ‘If you seek proof of Christ speaking in me.’

> “The bodies of the martyrs are precious because they received wounds for the Lord and because they bear upon their limbs the marks impressed for Christ. Just as a royal crown, adorned on every side, sends forth varied splendors, so the bodies of the holy martyrs, distinguished by wounds received for Christ as though by precious stones, are made more precious and more splendid than every diadem of kings.”

Such are his words.

Since these and innumerable other teachings of the holy Fathers make clear that the bodies of the saints are precious and to be venerated and honored by all the faithful, it is plainly evident that it belongs to unbelievers to despise them, whereas it belongs to the faithful to commit them humanely to the earth and to honor them out of love for the one whose name they suffered.

The former is indeed a sign of impiety; the latter clearly a sign of piety. Therefore, whoever judges that they should be despised, or insists that they are like the bodies of cattle, stones, or even pieces of wood, must be regarded not as a Christian but as an Eustathian and Vigilantian—or, more accurately and more gravely, as an unbeliever.

But if, as you perversely believe, the precious bodies of the saints possess the likeness of cattle, stones, and wood, what will you say about the miracles that are wondrously performed at their memorials through the power of Christ?

It is manifest to all the faithful that the bodies of these saints are divinely honored by many great miracles—and not without reason. For it is fitting that those who usefully presented their bodies as instruments of righteousness and triumphed over the devil in them should shine forth through such evident miracles, so that the illustrious signs of divine reward may reveal how precious death is in the sight of the Lord and how great their power is with the Most High (Ps. XXV).

But if bodies of the saints, now almost reduced to dust and ashes, are endowed by divine mercy with such great miracles, with how many perpetual rewards do you think they will be gifted at the time of the resurrection?

The blessed Augustine teaches that the bodies of the dead, especially of the just, should not be cast away but rather committed to the earth, in the first book of *The City of God*:

> “Nor should the bodies of the dead, especially of the just and faithful, be despised and cast away. The Holy Spirit used them as instruments and vessels for every good work. For if a father’s garment, ring, or anything of this kind is dearer to descendants in proportion to the greater affection they bear toward their parents, then the bodies themselves should in no way be spurned—bodies which we bear much more familiarly and intimately than any clothing.”

That the bodies of the saints should be honored by the faithful, the blessed Jerome writes to Riparius against Vigilantius:

> “We honor the relics of the martyrs so that we may adore the one whose martyrs they are. We honor the servants so that the honor of the servants may redound to the Lord, who says: ‘Whoever receives you …’” (Matt. X).

The salutary teachings of so many doctors therefore make clear that the bodies of the saints are not, according to your babblings and absurdities, to be equated with cattle, stones, or pieces of wood, but rather are to be embraced and honored by all the faithful with pious love.

Since it is therefore clear that you cannot deny that the bodies of the saints should not be compared with the things you have written, but should rather be honored by the children of the Catholic Church, and that, because of the preeminence of their merits, they shine with so many and such great miracles, it is necessary for you, removing all obstinacy, humbly to confess that you were in error when you said that they possessed the likeness of cattle, stones, and wood. Even if, devoted to obstinacy, you have refused to do so, you are nevertheless clearly proved by truth and reason to have been in error.

Whether the saints themselves are present with their lifeless bodies when benefits are granted to mortals or not, we are fully instructed by the salutary teachings of the blessed Augustine in his books *The City of God* and *On Care to Be Taken for the Dead*, as well as by the blessed Gregory in the book of the *Dialogues*. We refer the curious reader to a careful reading of these works.

The following occurs in your same work:

“From this, then,” he says, “it must be carefully considered that, if the works of God’s hands are not to be worshiped and honored, how much less are the works of human hands to be worshiped and honored? Certainly not even in the honor of those whose likenesses they are said to be.”

In the sense of this statement you think soberly with us. It is true, I say, that the works of human hands are not to be worshiped and honored with that worship and adoration which belong to Divinity alone. For the works of God’s hands, namely the bodies of the saints, are what you yourself disclose that you mentioned in the preceding part of your little work: they are not to be adored with the adoration owed to Divinity, but are to be embraced and honored with pious love, as consecrated temples of the Holy Spirit. But also what you add:

“Since, if the image which you adore is not God, it is by no means to be venerated with the honor due to the saints, who in no way claim divine honors for themselves”—we entirely approve this and judge it to accord with the Catholic faith. Again, a little later:

“And therefore,” he says, “it must be known with the greatest care that not only he who worships visible figures and images, but also whoever worships any creature, whether heavenly, earthly, spiritual, or bodily, in place of the name of God, and hopes from them the salvation of his soul, which comes from God alone, belongs to those of whom the Apostle says: ‘And they worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator’ (Romans I).”

We reply briefly to these words of yours: We do not worship figures or images. Nevertheless, we possess images, and we do not condemn those who possess them. Whoever, however, worships visible figures and images, or any heavenly, earthly, spiritual, or bodily creature, in place of God, is plainly convicted of serving the creature rather than the Creator. We certainly believe faithfully that the salvation of our soul is given by God alone; but because, being hindered by our merits, we do not deserve to obtain it from him, if we sincerely trust that through the intercessions of heavenly or spiritual creatures we shall become participants in it, we are proved to serve not the creature, as you have written, but rather the Creator. But if the salvation of souls is not acquired through the intercessions of the saints, why is their intercession sought before the divine majesty in the celebration of Masses and in other most humble supplications? Therefore, we know that the soul’s salvation is given only by God; but we faithfully believe that through their intervention it is bestowed upon us, though undeserving, by him. And because we believe and hope this, we serve not the creature but our Creator.

Again you say:

“Why do you humble and bow yourself before false images? Why do you bend your bodily form, captive, before foolish idols and earthly figures? God made you upright; and while the other animals, compelled by their posture, are prone and pressed down toward the earth, your stature is exalted, and your face is upright toward heaven and toward the Lord. Look there; raise your eyes there; seek God on high. So that you may be able to escape the lower regions, lift your breast, suspended toward the heights and heavenly things. Why do you cast yourself into the fall of death together with the senseless image that you worship? Why do you fall into the devil’s ruin through it and with it? Preserve the exalted state in which you were born; remain such as God made you.”

These are not your words, Claudius, but those of the blessed martyr Cyprian. From them you removed some things, altered others, and presented them as your own. That distinguished teacher therefore writes to Demetrianus, devoted to the worship of idolatry, as follows:

“Why do you humble and bow yourself before false gods? Why do you bend your captive body before foolish idols and earthly figures? God made you upright; and while the other animals are prone and pressed down toward the earth, their posture inclining downward, your stature is exalted, and your face is raised toward heaven and toward your God. Look there; raise your eyes there; seek God on high, so that you may be able to escape the lower regions. Lift your breast, suspended toward the heights and heavenly things. Why do you cast yourself into the fall of death together with the serpent whom you worship? Why do you fall into the devil’s ruin through it and with it? Preserve the exalted state in which you were born; remain such as God made you. Establish your soul upright together with the posture of your face and body, so that you may be able to know God; first know yourself.”

I cannot sufficiently wonder that you wished to steal another man’s words so secretly, and that you thought this theft could remain hidden from others. Do you not know what the Lord says through the prophet about those who steal his words? (Jeremiah XXIII.) I believe that you have also read Cassiodorus, who explains fully in his exposition of the Psalms what the office of compilers is.

It is therefore clear that in this action you acted unskillfully and reprehensibly, and for that reason you must openly confess that you erred in the same act. But whoever refuses to confess his own errors is plainly unable either to rebuke or correct those of others with an untroubled face, hearing the Lord say: “Why do you recite my ordinances and take my covenant upon your lips? You hate discipline and cast my words behind you” (Psalm XLIX). And in the Gospel: “Why, then, do you see the splinter in your brother’s eye but do not consider the beam that is in your own eye?” and what follows (Matthew VII; Luke VI).

Since it is therefore certain that you violently made another man’s words your own, I ask you why, where blessed Cyprian wrote, “Why do you humble and bow yourself before false gods?”, you wrote “false images.” He said “false gods” because they are not true. But images, if they are images either of human beings or of any other things, I do not sufficiently see how it could be false that they are images. And if you reply that they are false because they contain no truth in themselves—since, although they have the likenesses of human bodies, they are nevertheless not real bodies—you may for that reason rightly call them false; yet you will in no way be able to deny that they are truly images. Since you cannot deny this, you are deservedly marked out for having needlessly inserted the word “false.”

For also in what you wrote a little later—“Why do you bend your captive body before foolish idols and earthly figures?”—you must explain why you wished to call earthly figures “captive.” We do not fail to understand what earthly figures are; but how they can be called captive is rightly questioned. If they are captive, by whom did they come into such captivity? Since this requires no explanation from you, because the expression itself is absurd, it is clear that you were seized by such mad frenzy that you simply do not know what you are saying.

There are also other passages that you furtively appropriated from the words of the same most holy man, twisting them violently according to your own whim—not in the order of words in which he set them down, nor in the sense in which they were spoken—but toward some alien interpretation [Note: This is how heretics customarily act.]. If a prudent reader begins to examine and scrutinize them as you altered and presented them, it will plainly become evident how absurd and reprehensible they are, and how forcefully you have disturbed, with the foot of a perverse understanding, streams that you drank in clear form.

Again you say:

“But these worshipers of false religion and superstition say: ‘We worship, venerate, and adore the painted cross and the cross represented in his honor, on account of the remembrance of our Savior.’”

Those whom above you called members of the devil, here, with an ill-omened and shameless mouth, you call worshipers of false religion and superstition. You immediately appear to wish to give the reason why they are called worshipers of false religion and superstition: namely, because they worship, venerate, and adore, in memory of Christ’s Passion, the painted cross and the cross represented in his honor.

That the holy Church, following the tradition of the holy Fathers, venerates, adores, and worships the cross of Christ in remembrance of his redemption—not with the worship and adoration that belong to Divinity alone, but rather in the manner sufficiently and abundantly explained above—no one who disagrees with ecclesiastical tradition fails to know. Thus, in remembrance of the Lord’s saving Passion, every year on the most holy day of Good Friday, according to ecclesiastical tradition, she adores the cross of Christ—that is, she greets it with supplication. Spread throughout the whole world, she bursts forth in praise of Christ and sings joyfully:

“We adore your cross, O Lord, and we praise and glorify your holy resurrection.”

And again:

“Behold the wood of the cross, on which hung the salvation of the world; come, let us adore.”

Blessed Gregory also, concerning whose words no one who is mindful of his salvation is doubtful, records in the Book of Sacraments:

“O God, who in your mercy deigned to redeem the human race by the precious blood of your only-begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, graciously grant that those who come to adore the life-giving cross may be freed from the bonds of their sins.”

I ask you, Claudius, if you ever sang this prayer to the Lord, when you came to the place where the cross was to be adored, what did you say there? But I think that you imitated the Jews, whom the Apostle, weeping, calls enemies of the cross of Christ (Philippians III). You have become so hostile to that same cross that you either entirely omitted the words “to adore the cross,” or, certainly, by changing them according to your familiar practice, said one thing in place of another, as you are convicted of having done in the words of the blessed martyr Cyprian.

Therefore, just as in overturning the images of the saints and expelling them entirely from the churches you stubbornly opposed the salutary words of the blessed and most distinguished teacher Gregory, who was writing to Serenus, bishop of Marseilles, so likewise, in rejecting crosses from the Church of Christ and treating them with contempt, you are proved irreverently and foolishly to have opposed the deeds and words of that same teacher.

The same teacher writes to Bishop Januarius as follows:

“The Jews who came here from your city complained to us that Peter, who, by God’s will, had been led from their superstition to the worship of the Christian faith, after enlisting certain undisciplined men, had on the following day after his baptism—that is, on the very feast of Easter Sunday—seized their synagogue, situated at Caralis, with grave scandal and without your consent, and had placed there an image of the Mother of God and of our Lord, as well as the venerable cross and the white fillet that had risen from his forehead and with which he had been clothed.”

And a little later:

“Considering your intention in this matter, and especially your judgment, we exhort you in these words: after removing from that place the image and the cross, with the veneration that is proper to them, you must restore what was taken away by violence.”

The same man also writes, among other things, to Reccared, king of the Visigoths:

“We have also given the bearer of this letter a cross to present to you, in which there is a piece of the wood of the Lord’s cross and some hairs of blessed John the Baptist. Through it, by the intercession of the Lord’s Forerunner, may you always have the consolation of our Savior.”

The venerable priest Bede, the most learned and distinguished teacher of his own age, also writes in his History of the English how, under the salutary direction and teaching of that same blessed Gregory, Bishop Augustine came to Britain with his companions and approached the king of the English. He says:

“After some days the king came to the island and, sitting under the open sky, ordered Augustine with his companions to come there to an interview with him. For he had taken precautions that they should not enter any house to meet him, following an old augury lest, if they possessed any magical art, they might overcome and deceive him by their arrival. But they came endowed not with demonic, but with divine power, carrying a silver cross as their standard and an image of the Lord and Savior painted on a panel, and singing litanies. For their own salvation and that of those for whom they had come, they were entreating the Lord with prayers for eternal salvation.”

And shortly afterward:

“It is reported that, as they approached the city, according to their custom, with the holy cross and the image of the great King, our Lord Jesus Christ, they sang this litany with harmonious voices:

‘We beseech you, O Lord, in all your mercy, that your fury and your anger may be taken away from this city and from your holy house, for we have sinned, alleluia.’”

Attend, I urge you, Claudius, patiently to what a great and distinguished teacher Gregory was, who both establishes above, according to the manner already stated, that the cross is to be adored, and in his writings teaches that the cross is to be venerated, and who sent a cross to King Reccared as a token of veneration and blessing. Consider also with what instruction he imbued his disciple Augustine and his companions, so that they might carry with them the cross and the image of our God Jesus Christ to subdue and preach to the savage hearts of the gentiles and convert them to the faith of Christ.

And consider that your insane and foolish teaching is a contradiction of his sound and sober doctrine. For what he taught should be held concerning the cross and the images of the saints, with the most eloquent assertion and the most careful instruction, you, a man, bark that it should be overthrown by monstrous arguments.

Know, then, that unless you hasten humbly to confess and correct your errors, you have undoubtedly proclaimed doctrines contrary to the excellent words and discerning instructions of so great a teacher, to the danger of your salvation and the ruin of your office.

Why, I ask you, are you seized by such mad frenzy that, imitating Julian the Apostate, you removed from the church the cross bearing the image of Christ and forbade it to be kept by the faithful in the basilicas of Christ according to ecclesiastical tradition? Why do you also shudder at the standard of the cross? Do you not know that it belongs to demons to shudder at that standard of the cross?

What, I ask, made the cross of Christ so offensive to you? I believe that if you had faithfully believed that you were redeemed by the cross of Christ, you would never have made yourself its hostile enemy, its execrator, and its repudiator. For through the cross the author of death was overcome, and life was restored to mortals. No believer can cross the sea of this world and reach the harbor of eternal salvation unless he is spiritually borne by the cross of Christ.

Do you not know that the cross of Christ is the weapon of the faithful? By this standard the foreheads of the faithful are fortified. By this standard invisible enemies are driven away. Through this sign all things are sanctified for us.

Therefore blessed Augustine writes in his Exposition of the Gospel of John, homily sixty-four:

“What is the sign of Christ that everyone knows? What sign is it that, unless it is applied either to the foreheads of the faithful, or to the water itself in which they are regenerated, or to the oil with which they are anointed in confirmation, or to the sacrifice by which they are nourished, none of these things is properly accomplished?”

But for now we are fully instructed concerning the mystery of the cross, which apostolic speech expounds, by the abundant—indeed salutary—exposition of blessed Augustine, who writes in his book On Christian Doctrine and also in the homily on the Gospel of John mentioned shortly before. It is not our purpose to discuss anything here.

Because I recognize myself unequal to understanding so great a subject and unable to express it, I have judged it better for the moment to restrain my own words concerning how great the power and glory of the standard of the cross are. Nevertheless, when we come to the passage where, to the dishonor of the cross, you taught that an ass should be worshiped, and appended many ravings, like a man bereft of reason, it will be necessary, as God permits, briefly to add what the holy and distinguished teachers have said in explanation, in order to refute your ill-formed statements.

It is therefore established and made clear by evident reasoning that it is not those who venerate and adore the cross of Christ according to the manner stated above, but rather you who are its accuser, a worshiper of false religion and superstition.

Since we have said a few things by way of digression, we are necessarily compelled to return to the place in your writings from which we departed. There you say:

“They are pleased with nothing else in our Savior except what pleased the impious: the disgrace of the Passion and the mockery of death. They believe about him what impious men believe, whether Jews or pagans, who doubt that he rose again and know nothing else to think about him except that they believe and retain in their heart that he is wholly dead and always remains in his Passion. They do not heed or understand what the Apostle says: ‘And if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him’ (II Corinthians V).”

If you had cared to do so, Claudius, your unskilled and uncultivated pen could by now have rested and set some kind of limit to its immoderate and unrestrained speech. But you are content neither with a subdued nor with a measured manner of speaking. Instead, you always speak grandly and rage without rule, sparing no Italian, no Gaul, and no German Catholic, but rushing headlong against everyone after casting away the reins of reason and discernment, and uselessly hurling at them such accusations of various superstitions and abominations.

The many and great preceding words of reproach that you unjustly hurled at us could also have been more than sufficient to satisfy the rage of your fury. But everyone who believes rightly and understands rightly easily observes how impious and false is the fiction that you spew forth in unlearned—indeed poisonous—speech, and how utterly contrary to the Christian religion is what you say.

If we are pleased with nothing else in our Savior, as you falsely argue, except what pleased the impious—namely, the disgrace of the Passion, the mockery of death, and the other things you enumerate that belong to the detestable sense of your blasphemy—then we confess that Christ endured the mystery of our redemption without cause for our salvation.

But we truly and faithfully believe and confess that Christ endured these things for our deliverance. Therefore, the mockeries inflicted upon him by the impious in his Passion, shamefully yet innocently, neither displease us nor please us without reason. Nor do we believe about him only what the impious believe, whether Jews or pagans, who doubt that he rose again.

Thus, with evident and shameless disregard for every obstacle of reverence, you accuse us of impiety and unbelief and write that, together with Jews and pagans, we doubt that Christ rose from the dead.

I know and most certainly believe that if you had been inwardly and outwardly fortified by the standard of the cross—which, as the sequence of your writings shows, you curse—the spirit that is a liar in the mouth of the false prophets of the idolatrous king Ahab (III Kings XXII) could never have exercised such power in your mouth as to persuade you to say things so sacrilegious and profane.

But when you say that the various mockeries, insults, and taunts that our Redeemer endured in his Passion please us together with pagans and Jews, I truly confess that you are speaking falsely. They do not please us together with them, for we have neither shared in their unbelief nor have they shared in our redemption.

These mockeries, and the other things you feverishly spew forth with a mind gone astray, were spectacles to the impious, but to the pious they became inborn mysteries and mighty supports of faith.

It is clear that we steadfastly preserve true and sincere devotion toward the faith of our Redeemer Jesus Christ and execrate the impiety of Jews and pagans. Therefore, we rightly repel with the shield of faith the weapons of your wicked assertion and consign them to be pierced by the sword of the Holy Spirit; indeed, we devote them to perpetual anathema.

But if, together with Jews and pagans, we doubt that Christ rose again, and know nothing else to think about him except that we believe and retain in our heart that he was tortured and died and always remains in his Passion, and if we do not heed or understand what the Apostle says—“And if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him” (II Corinthians V)—then, to use the words of blessed Paul, we are of all people the most pitiable.

Therefore, it is not by our own words but by those of the same Apostle that we convict and refute your utterly false and impious objection. Truly, if we doubt that Christ rose again, we do not believe in the resurrection at all. For “if Christ has not risen, neither will the dead rise, and our faith is vain” (I Corinthians VI); the preaching of that same distinguished teacher is vain.

We therefore faithfully believe in the resurrection of the dead, because we in no way doubt that Christ rose again. And because we are his members, we have no doubt that we shall arrive where our head has gone before us.

But what you placed at the conclusion of that same chapter of yours, saying, “They neither heed nor understand what the Apostle says: ‘And if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him’ (II Corinthians V),” we reject along with your other ravings and prove false by the most truthful affirmation of the Catholic faith that we hold.

For we do heed and understand what the Apostle says: “And if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him.” We do know Christ according to the flesh, because he who in his own substance had eternally existed with the Father invisible, impassible, and immortal deigned temporally to become visible, passible, and mortal in our nature. But according to the flesh we no longer know him now, because, as the same Apostle says: “Christ, rising from the dead, no longer dies; death shall no longer rule over him” (Romans VI).

Let us examine the remainder of your work:

“Against these people,” you say, “it must be answered that if they wish to adore every piece of wood made in the shape of a cross because Christ hung upon the cross, then many other things that Christ did in the flesh ought also to be adored by them. For he hung upon the cross scarcely six hours, yet he was in the Virgin’s womb for nine lunar months and more than eleven days, which together amount to 276 solar days—that is, nine months and six additional days. Therefore, let virgin girls be adored, because a virgin gave birth to Christ. Let the mangers also be adored, because immediately after he was born he was laid in a manger. Let the old cloths also be adored, because as soon as he was born he was wrapped in old cloths. Let ships also be adored, because he often sailed in ships, taught the crowds from a small boat, slept in a boat, and commanded that the net be cast on the right side of the vessel, when that great catch of fish was made. Let asses be adored, because, sitting upon a young ass, he reached Jerusalem. Let lambs be adored, because it is written of him: ‘Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world’ (John I); but these worshipers of perverse doctrines wish to devour living lambs and adore lambs painted on a wall. Let lions also be adored, because it is written of him: ‘The lion of the tribe of Judah, the root of David, has conquered’ (Revelation V). Let rocks also be adored, because when he was taken down from the cross, he was placed in a stone tomb. And the Apostle says of him: ‘The rock was Christ’ (I Corinthians X). But Christ was called rock, lamb, and lion tropologically, not properly—by signification, not by substance. Let the thorns of bramble bushes also be adored, because from them a crown of thorns was placed upon his head at the time of his Passion. Let reeds also be adored, because his head was struck with blows by them by the soldiers. Finally, let spears also be adored, because one of the soldiers opened his side with a spear, from which flowed blood and water, the Sacraments from which the Church is formed.”

Although you ought, Claudius, to remember your salvation and finally put an end to your most empty chatter, you are instead so pitiably plunged into the abyss of blasphemy that you attempt, through certain discordant comparisons and frivolous explanations and arguments, in some way to nullify the power and veneration of the cross.

Since, therefore, your persecuting argument has been supported by a fragile structure both according to the rules of literary discipline and according to Catholic understanding, lacking a foundation upon the rock, it is rightly shaken in both respects.

As for the criticisms contained in this passage according to the most expert writers on the art of grammar, we omit them, being concerned with the brevity of our argument, and we shall attempt, according to the measure of our capacity, to examine what you wished to imply in this most foolish exposition of yours. For you say:

“If the cross is adored, let virgin girls also be adored, because a virgin gave birth to Christ.”

Attend, I beg you, most sincere worshipers and lovers of piety and ecclesiastical authority. This teacher speaks metaphorically and syllogistically. For, making a transition from the inanimate to the animate, he argues and says: “If the cross is adored, let virgin girls also be adored, because a virgin gave birth to Christ.”

Concerning how the adoration and veneration of the cross should be understood and practiced with discernment in remembrance of the Lord’s Passion, the blessed Gregory, that distinguished teacher, as has already been said above, gives complete instruction. But that virgin girls, mangers, old cloths, ships, lambs, lions, rocks, thorn bushes, reeds, and spears should be adored, no teacher teaches except a madman and one out of his mind—and Claudius alone teaches it.

Therefore, wherever this Claudius speaks about the cross contrary to blessed Gregory, blessed Gregory, not Claudius, must be followed by all the sons of the Catholic and apostolic Church. But the new and foolish things that he alone pursues as objects of worship must in every way not only be rejected along with him but also detested.

In this little book, therefore, studying brevity, we have determined to refute your, Claudius, utterly absurd teaching concerning the worship of the cross and the ass, which you likewise taught should be done by a syllogistic declamation. But the other things that you wrote to the injury of the cross that is to be adored we decide to disprove more suitably in the following book.

Moreover, this sort of proof of such worship is astonishing and worthy of wonder—indeed, new and unheard-of and, to speak more accurately, most suitable for the laughter of children. Perhaps you appended other ravings to that same worship, namely of the cross and the ass, as objects of worship, so that if you were held in contempt and abhorrence in the worship just mentioned—as indeed you are—you might more easily provoke your hearers to worship them.

Thus you say: “If the cross is adored, let asses also be adored,” immediately giving the reason that the Lord reached Jerusalem while sitting upon a young ass.

Since, then, you propose that asses be worshiped, you must seek for us such as are worthy to be worshiped. For you know that Italian and German asses are poorly endowed with hearing and, because of the deformity and smallness of their bodies, do not deserve to be worshiped.

It is clear, however, that the asses of your region have large bodies and large ears, and by their beauty visibly turn toward themselves the eyes of those who look upon them. Since you therefore preach that asses are to be worshiped, take two of them as an imitation of the idolatrous king Jeroboam, so that, just as he, wishing to turn the people of God away from divine worship, fashioned two golden calves, setting one in Dan and the other in Bethel (III Kings XII), so you too, following his example, turn Christ’s people away from ecclesiastical traditions and choose for them two asses to be worshiped, as has been said: establish one in the city of Turin, to be worshiped by Italy, and the other in some city of Gaul, to be worshiped humbly not only by that same Gaul but also by Germany.

O detestable and abominable preaching! O ill-formed and discordant comparison of the cross and the ass! What madness seized you, Claudius, that you burst forth in writing and preaching such insane things, so abhorrent to all Catholics?

The Apostle, not in an ass but in the cross, glories, saying: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me and I to the world” (Galatians VI), along with the other things concerning the cross that are found in the words of that same Apostle.

And you, answering that Apostle obliquely, what do you appear to say in your statement, “If the cross is adored, let the ass also be adored,” except that if anyone glories in the cross, he should likewise glory in the ass?

I seem to see you, then, clad in an ass’s hide in a theater and being driven about childishly in every direction, while many people surround you—or rather gaze at you in amazement—and point their fingers at you, saying to one another: “Behold the man who, although he was placed in episcopal honor, did not understand, and therefore, compared with an ass, became like it” (Psalm XLVIII).

For you are not thought, Claudius, to have proposed that the ass be worshiped and to have proclaimed that one should glory in it as in the cross without some definite reason for the mystery. Certainly, in the worship of the ass that you taught, you acquired a great mark of stupidity.

For the ass signifies a foolish man, according to the passage in Deuteronomy: “You shall not plow with an ox and an ass together” (Deuteronomy XXII)—that is, you should not join a fool to a wise man in preaching.

But although in this present little book we have, as best we could, opposed your foolishness concerning worshiping the ass in the same way as the cross, and although in the following book, with the Lord in whose hand we and our words are, we shall treat more fully and at greater length the worship that you propose here concerning the cross and the ass, and concerning other senseless things that, with a senseless mind, you proposed to be worshiped as the cross, we have nevertheless determined to examine the conclusion that you appended to the worship of those same things according to your doctrine. There you say:

“All these things are ridiculous and ought rather to be mourned than written; and we are compelled to propose foolish things against fools, and against hearts of stone to hurl not arrows or sayings of the word but blows of stone.”

It is true that all those things are ridiculous and ought rather to be mourned than written—those things that, with a mind gone astray, you have repeatedly written concerning the worship of the ass, the execration of the cross, and the other matters composed against ecclesiastical tradition. We are compelled to write such things against your foolishness and, using Solomon’s words (Proverbs XXVI), to answer you according to your foolishness, lest you appear wise to yourself.

To pierce and wound your heart of stone, and to overthrow the utterly perverse doctrine of your error, we must choose the sharp arrows of the divine word and heap up the sentences of the holy Fathers; with these, as with blows of flint, we must crush and seal up your blasphemous mouth.

Thus, openly taking the very weapons that you attempted to hurl at us, we turn them manfully against you and, reversing their direction, cast them back. With these weapons, like David, we strike down you, the most proud Goliath, with your deadly doctrine.

Again, misusing prophetic speech in part, you say:

“Return to your heart, transgressors” (Isaiah XLVI), “who have departed from the truth, love vanity, and have become vain.”

And immediately you append the teaching of the Apostle Paul writing to the Hebrews, adding:

“Who crucify the Son of God again and hold him up to contempt” (Hebrews VI).

Then, because you are using not another’s words but your own, you introduce inert and uncomposed diction, adding as follows:

“And through this you have made the souls of the wretched companions of demons in great numbers, alienating them from their Creator through the unspeakable sacrileges of images; you have cast them down and thrown them into everlasting damnation.”

Wherever in your little work, which we are examining, you use the words of others, the construction of the sentence retains the literary force that it received from its author; yet it loses its proper sense—corrupted, alas, by the perversity of a tavernkeeper—for you neither set down nor understand the words in the manner in which they were placed, or with the meaning in which they were spoken or understood. Wherever, however, you attempt to construct a sentence in your own words, because the blemish of grammatical art, which you are said to hold in contempt, is not smoothed away, one immediately recognizes how fragile it is and how close to collapse. For rightly the ruin is plastered without straw, and long ago was foretold by the prophet (Ezek. XIII).

Yet, although ignorant of proper expression, because you have nevertheless been thoroughly worn down by constant reading, search out carefully and minutely the pages of the divine utterances, and not only the precise statements of the holy Fathers but also those of pagan philosophers; and you will by no means be able to find in them examples of your constructions. Hence you are held in great astonishment; and although you do not know how to speak correctly, you do not understand that you yourself do not know this, nor can you keep silent, driven on by folly, in accordance with the counsel of the wisest man: “If a fool keeps silent, he will be considered wise; and if he restrains his lips, intelligent” (Prov. XVII).

Therefore you must look to your own welfare and restrain yourself from such constructions as you use in an extraordinary manner—namely, so that you do not teach what you have not learned, and do not presume to compose books, since when they come into the hands of learned men they will certainly not escape the bite of criticism and reproach.

Let us therefore return to what you introduced, where you say with the Prophet: “Return, transgressors, to your heart” (Isa. XLVI). For the Lord very often inculcates and repeats this saying through the Prophet, and rightly calls His people transgressors, because, having turned away from the worship of the divine law, they turned to idols; and He admonishes them to return to their heart—that is, having abandoned the superstition of idolatry, to return to God with their whole heart.

But how this prophetic saying can apply to us, who hold the Catholic and apostolic faith unwaveringly and preserve incorruptly the ecclesiastical traditions that we received from the holy Fathers—since you are able to approve it by no indications and by no proofs—it remains for you to understand that it is not we but rather you who are the transgressor, since you rashly attempt to tear down ecclesiastical statutes, and that you should hasten as quickly as possible to return to your heart, that is, to a sense consonant with ecclesiastical tradition. Know that it will not go unpunished for anyone who wanders away from Him in another direction and fornicates with a stranger.

By doing this, you will prove—not us, as you wrote, but yourself—to be turning away from the truth, loving vanity, and having become vain, as your foolish writings demonstrate.

Let us also repeat the apostolic saying which you presented as your own words, in which you say: “You who crucify the Son of God again and hold Him up to contempt” (Heb. VI). For you suppose that you can strike us with the apostolic saying, and you accuse us of crucifying the Son of God again and holding Him up to contempt, because, in memory of the Lord’s Passion, we represent the image of Christ crucified in gold or silver, or certainly paint it on panels with pigments of various colors.

But if this is so, anyone who reads with the utmost care what precedes and follows in that same Apostle’s Epistle will clearly perceive how far this interpretation departs from the apostolic meaning. For the Apostle speaks of those who had once been enlightened by the grace of baptism and had received the other gifts of the Holy Spirit that he enumerates. Those who thought that the sins they had committed after baptism could be cleansed only by a repetition of baptism are rightly rebuked by the same Apostle, because they would thereby crucify the Son of God again for themselves and hold Him up to contempt—something he declares to be utterly impossible.

For the one who thinks that he can be baptized a second time crucifies Christ again for himself, as we have received from the tradition of the Fathers, and holds Him up to contempt. Therefore, just as it is impossible for Christ to be crucified again—that is, to be held up to contempt—because, as the Apostle says, “Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more; death shall no longer rule over Him” (Rom. VI), so it is plainly impossible for sins committed after baptism to be cleansed by a repetition of baptism.

For just as Christ died once in the flesh upon the cross, so we die once in baptism—not in the flesh, but to sin. Accordingly, just as He cannot be crucified again, so we cannot be baptized again. The sins committed after baptism, however, are washed away by the tears of repentance and the generosity of almsgiving.

Because we hold and believe this, we by no means, as you falsely assert, crucify the Son of God again for ourselves and hold Him up to contempt. Thus, in this argument of yours, as in the others, it is shown by evident indications that you have raved.

As for the weapon of your ridiculous construction, which you fashioned from your own understanding, by which you say: “And through this you have made the souls of the wretched companions of demons in great numbers, alienating them from their Creator through the unspeakable sacrileges of images; you have cast them down and thrown them into everlasting damnation”—because it is hurled against us in vain, it will rightly be blunted and, sharpened against its author, deservedly turned back upon his head.

For it is fitting that, since it found nothing in us to strike, it should return to the one by whom it was directed in vain and pierce him. For it was not we who made the souls of the wretched companions of demons, turned them away from their Creator through the unspeakable sacrileges of images, and cast them into everlasting damnation; rather, it was the one who joined them to demons and cast them into everlasting damnation—the one who taught them to hold the bodies of the saints in contempt, to abominate the standard of the cross, to despise the other ecclesiastical traditions contrary to all right, and to worship an ass.

We are compelled to refute your vain and foolish objections with appropriate and fitting replies. Since, to avoid excessive length, we omit doing this point by point in this little book, we now bring it to an end. And lest we seem to have passed over any part of so many absurd tales without examination, we have deferred the matters that remain for discussion in the following book.

## [BOOK TWO]

[Col. 0341]

## PREFACE TO THE SECOND BOOK

[Col. 0341]

[Col. 0341B] In the preceding little book, O Claudius, it is clear that, insofar as divine aid was granted, we have partly opposed your monstrous objections, which are unworthy of our religion. For it has been briefly proved, and will be proved at greater length, that an ass must not be equated with the veneration and worship of the saving cross.

It remains, therefore, that the matters which, although mentioned, have nevertheless been left unexamined and postponed until this work—namely, those things which you taught were to be honored as the cross, equally with the cross, to the dishonor of the cross—should be examined in detail. Accordingly, our discussion will proceed through each of the things with which you attempted to equate the cause of abolishing the cross; it will investigate fully what each of your absurdities contains, and we shall contemplate with simple eyes why the cross is held in veneration by the sons of the Church, while those things are set aside.

Let us first see, however, how the teacher of the nations instructs us beneficially to glory in the cross and to comprehend its mystery (Gal. IX), through which the great condescension of divine mercy supplied us with the armor of its strength. Through it He made him a preacher from a persecutor and gave him to us as a vessel of election from a vessel of iniquity; and, having been caught up to the third heaven, he heard secret words which it is not permitted a human being to speak.

Having been taught by heavenly revelation and intoxicated with the grace of the Holy Spirit, among the other instructions of his preaching he taught us to glory, after his own example, not in an ass but in the cross, saying: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (II Cor. XII).

And when writing to the Ephesians, he does not urge us to grasp either the tail or the sides of your little ass; rather, bending his knee, he prays and entreats that, rooted and founded in charity, they may comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth, length, height, sublimity, and depth of His cross—not of an ass (Eph. III). In these words the holy Church holds the mystery of the cross—not of an ass—as handed down to the Apostle Paul himself. They plainly demonstrate how absurd is the comparison of your little ass with our life-giving cross, and this is manifest to all who truly worship Christ.

For the same Apostle (Eph. VI) does not say that Christ conquered the principalities and powers of these darknesses—spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places—by means of your little ass, but that He defeated them by triumphing over them through the cross.

Your little ass, Claudius, brays, driven by hunger or goaded by fear of wolves; the cross of Christ glows red with His precious purple blood. Upon it the true vine hung; from its cluster the radiant stem of the shining cross gleams forth, and it embraces the square world with its four sacred horns. Fixed upon the foreheads of the faithful, it drives far from them the deceits of demons.

For if Isaac carried not an ass to be slaughtered—he himself being destined to be the victim—but wood (Gen. XXII), then assuredly our true Isaac carried not your little ass but the cross, destined to be that saving Victim of the Father.

In the Gospel according to Matthew also He says: “And then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven” (Matt. XXIV). He did not say “the ass of Claudius,” but “the sign of the Son of Man.”

Moreover, more than a thousand examples are found, both in the Old Testament preceding as types of the saving cross and in the New Testament, where its honor has already been spread far and wide throughout the four regions of the world, which may also appropriately be understood as corresponding to the four horns of that same cross.

Finally, there are many things which the custom of the holy Church, as they were handed down and left by our forebears, regularly celebrates with a certain innate and natural observance. For it was not in our own time that the practice arose of setting up the figure of the cross in the basilicas of the saints; rather, the legitimate custom of ancient observance established it, so that for all, wise and rustic alike, not only does the memory spiritually recall a certain image of the cross, but the repeated sight of the bodily image also fixes in the mind the victory of the Lord’s Passion.

If the quantity of that venerable wood on which our Lord and Savior hung had been so great that, after being divided into small pieces, all temples dedicated to God could have an image of the cross made from it, we would certainly not place its form in the basilicas from other kinds of wood.

Yet we do not worship the cross as the Lord; rather, we worship Him who through the cross destroyed the dominion of death and fastened to it the record of our sin, making peace through His blood between the things on earth and those in heaven.

Even if we imprint kisses upon it, we do this not because of the wood, but rather out of love for Him who on it restored the losses caused by the former wood (Col. I).

I wonder whether you have ever laid your head upon and kissed the law of God, which is of course arranged on skins and in ink. Perhaps you will answer—if you are willing to speak the truth—that you have done so many times. I want you, then, to answer me: for whose sake did you bow your head—to the skins or the ink, or to God, the author of that law?

For the practice of sacred religion is still preserved in the holy Church, if indeed among you, after the reading of the sacred Gospel has been completed, the book in which the Gospel reading was recited is honored with many kisses by the bishop or presbyters and the other religious ministers of the sacred order. But for whose sake do we do this, if not for the sake of Him whose words they are believed to be?

Accordingly, whatever we offer to the cross, we do wholly for the honor, love, and veneration of Him who hung upon it; and would that we venerated Him with as much honor as would be fitting for you.

Therefore cease to intoxicate yourself with the preparations of the seplasiarii [Note: Lampridius uses this word in *Heliogabalus* for an ointment], lest by yapping such things you instill terror into gentle birds which have not yet been able, with a stronger wing, stoutly to pass beyond the clear air. Apply to your own side the saying that “whoever causes one of these little ones to stumble, it is better for him that an ass-millstone be hung around his neck and that he be cast into the depth” (Matt. XI).

For it is perfectly clear that you cannot scandalize your elders, since you have not yet been steeped in the learning of letters, nor have the pages of the holy teachers instructed you so thoroughly that you could rightly do this.

Therefore you ought to think cautiously of yourself, lest, while you attempt to cross the boundaries of the earlier Fathers, you prove unable to reach the final boundary, where, exhausted on the road, you may be overwhelmed by the rains of storms, failing to reach the house immovably built upon the firm rock (Luke VI).

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 0343B] Behold, now the time requires and the place is suitable for us, as we promised a little above, to append a few of the many statements of the holy Fathers concerning the praise and power of the cross.

Origen writes in Book VI of his *Exposition of Paul’s Epistle to the Romans*: “For such is the power of Christ’s cross that, if it is placed before the eyes and faithfully retained in the mind, so that the death of Christ is viewed with the attentive eyes of the mind, no lust, no desire, and no envy can prevail; rather, immediately at its presence, that entire army of sin and the flesh which we listed above is driven away.”

John Chrysostom writes in his homily *On the Cross and the Thief*: “Today,” he says, “our Lord hung upon the cross, and let us celebrate His outstanding feast with exceedingly great joy, so that we may learn that the cross is the substance of all spiritual rejoicing.

“For previously the very name of the cross was a punishment, but now it is called glory. Previously it bore the horror of condemnation; now it is the sign of salvation. For the cross is the cause of every blessedness for us. It freed us from the blindness of error; it restored us from darkness to light; it joined the conquered to peace; it united those estranged to God; it brought those who were far away near; it showed wanderers to be citizens; it is the cutting off of discord; it is the foundation of peace; it is the abundant bestowal of all good things.”

And shortly afterward: “I also want you to understand by another argument. He did not leave the cross alone on earth, but carried it with Him to heaven. But you say: ‘How is this demonstrated?’ Therefore listen: when He comes with it, when with it He makes His second glorious appearance, for this reason I called it the glorious cross.”

Again, shortly afterward: “And then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven” (Eph. VI). Have you seen the glory of the sign, that is, of the cross? The light of the sun will be made dark; the moon will not be granted its brilliance; but that light will radiate and shine.

And just as a royal procession precedes an emperor, and a military order customarily carries standards upon its shoulders as it advances, thereby announcing his arrival, so, when the Lord comes from heaven, a company of angels and a multitude of archangels will carry that sign upon lofty shoulders and announce to us the royal arrival.

For the cross of Christ alone dissolves the darkness, scatters the kingdom of demons, and removes all terror of the wicked. The cross has provided holiness; the cross has become the sun of righteousness for us, so that, enlightened by His mercy, we may glorify the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.”

The same author, in his homily *On the Lord’s Cross*: “If you desire to know, beloved, the power of the cross, and how much I can say in its praise, listen:

“The cross is the hope of Christians; the cross is the resurrection of the dead; the cross is the guide of the blind; the cross is the way of the despairing; the cross is the staff of the lame; the cross is the consolation of the poor; the cross is the restraint of the rich; the cross is the destruction of the proud; the cross is the punishment of those who live wickedly; the cross is triumph over demons; the cross is the defeat of the devil; the cross is the pedagogue of the young; the cross is the support of the needy; the cross is the hope of the despairing; the cross is the steering of sailors; the cross is the harbor of those in danger; the cross is the wall of the possessed; the cross is the father of orphans; the cross is the defender of widows; the cross is the judge of the unjust; the cross is the counselor of the just; the cross is rest for the afflicted; the cross is the guardian of little ones; the cross is the head of men; the cross is the end of the old; the cross is light for those sitting in darkness; the cross is the magnificence of kings; the cross is an everlasting shield; the cross is the wisdom of the senseless; the cross is the freedom of slaves; the cross is the philosophy of emperors; the cross is the law of the impious; the cross is the proclamation of the prophets; the cross is the announcement of the apostles; the cross is the glorying of martyrs; the cross is the abstinence of monks; the cross is the chastity of virgins; the cross is the joy of priests; the cross is the foundation of the Church; the cross is the protection [variant: guardianship] of the whole world; the cross is the destruction of temples; the cross is the rejection of idols; the cross is the scandal of the Jews; the cross is the ruin of the impious; the cross is the strength of the weak; the cross is the physician of the sick; the cross is the cleansing of lepers; the cross is the rest of preachers [variant: paralytics]; the cross is the bread of the hungry; the cross is the fountain of the thirsty; the cross is the protection of the naked.

“When I say ‘nakedness,’ do not understand bodily nakedness, but the punishment of unbelief; when he believes in Christ, he will be found clothed.”

Consider, I beg you, Claudius, and I ask you: how marvelous and how outstanding a teacher this is, whose most salutary doctrine the holy Church reverently receives, when he proclaims and asserts that at the second coming of the eternal Judge, angels and archangels will carry the cross—not an ass—upon their lofty shoulders, and that through the cross—not through an ass—the various gifts of grace which the same teacher enumerates will be bestowed upon us.

And be ashamed that, seized by insane fury, you have equated the cross with an ass.

Hear also what Eusebius writes about the cross in his *Ecclesiastical History*, among the other things that he commendably reports concerning the deeds of the Emperor Constantine:

“Although he was already a supporter of the Christian religion and a worshiper of the true God, he had not yet, as was customary, been initiated among us, nor had he received the solemn sign of the Lord’s Passion.

“While he was therefore traveling anxiously and turning over many thoughts within himself about the necessity of the approaching war, often lifting his eyes to heaven and praying there for divine assistance, he saw in sleep, in the eastern part of the sky, the sign of the cross gleaming with fiery brilliance.

“When he had been terrified by so great a vision and disturbed by the strangeness of the sight, he saw angels standing beside him and saying: ‘Constantine, conquer by this.’

“Then restored to joy and already confident of victory, he marked upon his forehead the sign of the cross that he had seen in heaven. Thus invited from heaven to the faith, he seems to me not inferior to the one to whom it was similarly said from heaven: ‘Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me? I am Jesus the Nazarene’ (Acts IX), except that the former was invited while still persecuting, whereas this man was invited when he was already following Him.

“From then on he transformed the sign that had been shown to him from heaven into military standards, and fashioned the labarum—which they call the dragon—in the form of the Lord’s cross. Thus equipped with the weapons and standards of religion, he set out against the arms of the impious.

“It is also reported that he had in his right hand a sign of the cross skillfully made of gold.

“It is written also in the *Tripartite History*, Book I:

“‘While he was occupied with these anxieties, he saw in sleep the sign of the cross splendidly set in the sky. As he marveled at the vision, angels stood beside him and said: “O Constantine, conquer by this.” It is also reported that Christ Himself appeared to him, showed him the sign of the cross, and commanded him to make a similar figure and to have this aid in battles, by which he might win the rights of victory.

“‘Eusebius Pamphili, therefore, reports that he heard the emperor himself swear that, when, around noon, the sun was already declining, he had seen a sign of the cross made of light, with an inscription joined to it saying: “By this conquer”; and that the soldiers who were with him at the time had seen it as well.

“‘As he was traveling somewhere with his army, he says, this miracle was shown to him on the road. While he was considering what it might be, night came; and as he slept, Christ appeared with the sign that he had seen in heaven, and commanded that an image of it be made which would serve as an aid in the encounters of battle.

“‘The same author, in the same work, says:

“‘“This military standard was more precious than the others because it was customary for it to precede the emperor and for the soldiers to worship it. For this reason I think Constantine, the noblest ornament of the Roman Empire, changed the standard into the sign of the cross, so that by frequent sight of it and care for it they might grow unaccustomed to their former practice of subjection and might consider as God alone the one whom the emperor worshiped, or under whose leadership and aid he fought against his enemies.

“‘“This sign was always placed before all the ranks, and he especially ordered it to be present for those laboring in battle. He therefore appointed particular standard-bearers to attend to it; their duty was to carry it upon their shoulders by turns and to pass through all the battle lines.

“‘“It is reported that a certain man, because at one time he was carrying this sign and suddenly became terrified when the enemy attacked, gave it to another to carry; and when he had withdrawn from the battle and avoided the javelins, he was suddenly struck and died.

“‘“But the man who received the sacred trophy remained unharmed, although many were hurling javelins at him. For, by the wondrous direction of divine power, the arrows of the enemy fixed themselves in the sign and immediately flew away from the standard-bearer amid the dangers.

“‘“It is said that no other attendant of this sign ever died of a wound in war, as usually happens, or suffered the disaster of captivity.”’”

The same author, in Book II of the same work:

“I also heard of Probianus, a man holding military service at the palace, who was afflicted with a cruel attack of gout and was there freed from his pains, and to whom a holy and wondrous vision appeared.

“Although he had long been a pagan and later became a Christian, he followed the doctrine only to some extent. Yet he was unwilling to worship the cause of all salvation, namely, the most sacred cross.

“To him, holding this opinion, divine power appeared and showed the sign of the cross that had been placed upon the altar of that same church; and it openly made clear that, since Christ was crucified, nothing done for the benefit of the human race could have been accomplished in any manner apart from the power of the cross, which is to be adored—not by holy angels and not by human beings.”

Again, in the same work, Book IX:

“At that time many among the bishops shone forth, such as Donatus Hiperi, concerning whom, although the provincials testify to many miracles, the greatest is what he did concerning a dragon.

“It lay near a bridge on a public road and had food by seizing and devouring sheep, goats, horses, cattle, and human beings. Donatus approached the beast without a sword or any weapon. When it raised its head as though about to devour the man, he marked the sign of the cross in the air with his finger before its face and spat into its mouth. The beast received the spittle in its mouth and died.”

Blessed Augustine also writes in Book XXII, chapter 8, of *The City of God*:

“In Carthage, Innocentia, a most devout woman from one of the leading families of that city, had a cancer in her breast—a condition which, as physicians say, could be cured by no medicines. Either the affected member is ordinarily cut away and separated from the body, or, so that a person may live somewhat more comfortably, the disease must be eased by frequent applications.

“For, if we are to trust the opinion of Hippocrates, as it is reported, and believe that death will come only somewhat later, all treatment must be abandoned.

“She had received this advice from an expert physician, a close friend of her household, and had turned herself in prayer to God alone. As Easter approached, she was instructed in a dream that, as she watched in the women’s section at the baptistery, the first baptized woman whom she encountered should make the sign of Christ’s cross upon the affected place. She did so, and immediately healing followed.”

Jerome writes as follows about the cross in Book I of his exposition of the Epistle to the Ephesians:

“Moreover, whoever reads what the Apostle says when he recalls Christ—‘making peace through the blood of His cross between those things which were on earth and those which are in heaven,’ and the rest that is said in the same passage (Gal. I)—will not think that we, who according to the spirit are called Israel, were far away, and that the Jews, who are called Israel only according to the flesh, were near. Nor will he apply the whole of this understanding to angels and heavenly powers and to human souls, namely, that Christ joined together in His blood both earthly and heavenly things, which had previously been at odds with one another; that the good shepherd, carrying the sick sheep back to the mountains, made it one with the others; that He joined the lost drachma to the drachmas that had been preserved (Luke XV); and that He brought the legal commandments back to those doctrines after whose pattern and image Moses saw the things that were to be fashioned in the tabernacle.

“Thus it comes about that the Lord’s cross benefited not only the earth but also heaven, not only human beings but also angels, and that every creature of the Lord was cleansed by His blood.”

Cassiodorus writes in his exposition of the first Psalm, “And he will be like a tree planted beside running waters”:

“Rightly, I think, the Lord Christ was compared to a fruitful tree because of the cross which He took up for the salvation of human beings. It is rightly called the tree of life, since there the Lord Christ, who is our life, was suspended, and to the thief who confessed on it He said: ‘Amen I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise’ (Luke XXIII).

“Indeed, even today everyone who believes in it receives the gifts of eternal life. For just as flowing earthly water is the life of green trees, so spiritual water floods the sign of the cross, which is known to be the salvation of faithful souls.”

Again, in his exposition of the fourth Psalm:

“The light of Your countenance, O Lord, has been marked upon us” (ibid.). “Just as the coin of the emperor bears his image, so the signs of the heavenly ruler are impressed upon the faithful. By this protection the many-formed devil is driven out, and through fraudulent plotting he cannot overcome the one whom he had held captive by the persuasion of the first man.

“For the cross is the unconquerable protection of the humble, the overthrow of the proud, the victory of Christ, the destruction of the devil, the ruin of the underworld, the strengthening of heavenly things, the death of unbelievers, and the life of the just.

“Behold the true gifts; behold the present gifts by which the tongues of the slanderers are stopped, their throats condemned.”

The same author continues:

“‘The light of Your countenance, O Lord’ (Ps. IV), in the imprint of the cross, is the light of God’s countenance, because it is always known to shine in those who do not choose to defile themselves by any wickedness, as the Apostle says: ‘Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption.’”

Again, in his exposition of the twenty-first Psalm:

“But before we come,” he says, “to the beginning of the Passion, we must examine why He who said, ‘I have power to lay down my life and to take it up again’ (John X), chose such a death for Himself.

“First, the position of the cross itself was such that its upper part looked toward heaven, while its lower part did not leave the earth; fixed at the bottom, it touched the ground; and, as though with arms extended, its breadth reached toward all the regions of the world. Lying down, it marks the four hinges of the globe. Thus placed in a small space, it appears to have embraced everything.
