“I speak of the Lord’s cross, which from a penal instrument for sinners became an honorable redemption, thereafter bestowing salvation: a gallows made salutary, death indicating life, and the humility of divinity proclaiming the height of majesty. Thus you may know Christ in heaven, Christ on earth, Christ throughout the whole world, and Christ even in the underworld through the figure of the cross.

“But if He had been overtaken by any other kind of death, by what sign, I ask, would the devil have been driven away? By what standard would the foreheads of Christians have remained safe? By what figure would the weakness of body and soul have been strengthened? No death could better suit such majesty except the one that left us the signs of perfect salvation.

“Therefore the cross was rightly chosen by Christ, in which He would both die uniquely and die according to the common lot.”

Sedulius, in Book III of the *Paschal Poem*:

> He Himself was the peace of the cross, and, illuminating  
>   
> Its violent timbers with His own limbs, clothed punishment with honor,  
>   
> And made the penalty a sign more truly of salvation;  
>   
> Himself sanctifying the torments, He blessed them.  
>   
>   
> And lest anyone fail to know that the form of the cross is to be honored,  
>   
> Which in its mighty power carried the Lord in triumph,  
>   
> From it He gathers the four regions of the square world.  
>   
>   
> The splendor of the Author shines from the eastern crown of His head;  
>   
> The soles of His sacred feet descend beneath the setting star;  
>   
> His right hand holds the North, His left raises the central axis.  
>   
>   
> All nature lives from the limbs of its Creator,  
>   
> And Christ governs the whole world, embraced on every side by the cross.

Paulinus, in Book VIII of the *Deeds of Saint Felix the Martyr*:

> The sign and confession of the unconquered cross fortify us;  
>   
> Armed by God in mind, we do not seek weapons  
>   
> For the body; and although we seem unarmed in our limbs,  
>   
> We nevertheless carry weapons with which, even amid serene peace,  
>   
> We contend in spirit against incorporeal enemies.

Again, in Book X of the same work:

> Returning home, I bring forth a small but great means of salvation,  
>   
> A fragment taken from the wood of the eternal cross;  
>   
> Holding it in my hand, I thrust it far before the hostile flames,  
>   
> As one holding a shield before his breast with which to cover myself,  
>   
> And to repel the enemy, striking it with the boss of my shield.  
>   
>   
> Believe it, and do not attribute it to me, but render thanks to Christ;  
>   
> Give just praises to the Almighty.  
>   
>   
> For our salvation rests in the cross and name of Christ.  
>   
> From it comes our faith, and, resting upon this cross, it helped us in danger;  
>   
> The flame recognized our salvation.  
>   
>   
> It was neither my voice nor my right hand that terrified the fire,  
>   
> But the power of the cross; and in the place from which it had risen,  
>   
> It compelled the flame, enclosed within the prescribed boundary,  
>   
> To stand still, and to be extinguished with its roar dying away.  
>   
>   
> It compelled the storm, arisen from ashes, to return to ashes.  
>   
> Such is the power of the cross, that nature abandons itself:  
>   
> The fire that devours all wood is itself burned by the wood of the cross.  
>   
>   
> Many hands then, sprinkling those fires repeatedly with vessels,  
>   
> Sought to conquer them with abundant water;  
>   
> But although they balanced the flames with emptied springs,  
>   
> The fire, with greater force, overcame all the water  
>   
> While the weary sprinklers labored; yet by the wood we extinguished the fire,  
>   
> And what the water could not accomplish, a brief draught overcame in the flame.

Again I ask you, Claudius, to observe attentively how great the praise and how great the power of the cross worthy of adoration—not of the ass—are described by so many distinguished teachers, [Col. 0349B] and to be salutarily ashamed that you compared the cross with an ass, old rags, mangers, thorns, and the other things you pursued with an unsound mind. Do you not know that it is not through the things you listed, but through the cross, that heavenly things are reconciled with earthly things, and earthly things with heavenly things? For, as the Apostle says: “In him it pleased the whole fullness of divinity to dwell bodily, and through him to reconcile all things to himself, making peace through the blood of his cross, whether things on earth or things in heaven” (Col. I).

Therefore, leaving aside the typological figures by which this same cross was represented in many ways in the Old Testament, figures which have now been fulfilled in reality, we do not hesitate to testify with the clarity of daylight that all things are sanctified for us through the sign of the cross, not through the ass. Armed with its weapons, we drive evil spirits away from us and, in a certain manner, secure for ourselves the presence of the holy angels. We also read that by the banner of the cross, not by the ass, countless holy men have raised the dead, driven demons from possessed bodies, given sight to the blind, and performed many similar deeds.

It is therefore clear that no member of the faithful has ever been so insane and so sluggish in mind as to attempt to apply such comparisons to the cross—except you alone. And you are believed to have done this because, as can plainly be inferred, you hold the banner of the cross in no account. For the same banner of the cross is known to have enjoyed greater honor and reverence among pagans than among you—a matter we pursue not without great anguish of heart.

It is therefore read in the *Tripartite History*, [Col. 0349D] book two, that the Sibyl said of this wood among the pagans: “O thrice-blessed wood, on which God was stretched out.” And elsewhere in the same work, book six, chapter two, that Julian, desiring the imperial scepters and gradually defecting from Christianity to paganism, found a man who admitted that he could tell him what he desired. This man led him to a certain place of idols, brought him into the sanctuary, and summoned deceptive demons. When they appeared solemnly, Julian was compelled by terror to form the sign of the cross upon his forehead. Then, looking upon the figure of the Lord’s trophy and remembering their defeat, the demons suddenly disappeared.

It is also read in book three of the *Dialogues*, chapter seven, that a certain Jew, although he had no faith in the cross, nevertheless took care to fortify himself with the sign of the cross. When necessity compelled him to go and stay near the temple of Apollo, and suddenly a crowd of evil spirits appeared, the wicked spirit who presided over the others ordered them to inquire who the man was who had dared to lie down in that very temple. The evil spirits approached him and examined him more closely; they saw that he was marked with the mystery of the cross, and, astonished, said: “Ha, ha! An empty vessel, but marked.” When this was reported, the entire crowd of evil spirits disappeared.

O the cross’s power and praise, more worthy of wonder than of description! What mortal, endowed with such understanding and such eloquence, could comprehend its power and praise in his mind or explain them in words? If this banner so greatly protected an unbeliever—indeed, an enemy of the cross—from invisible enemies, and compelled a crowd of evil spirits to depart from a place polluted by idolatrous filth, how much more, do you suppose, will it be a source of power, salvation, and protection to those who embrace it devoutly, while to foolishly loathing and rejecting it there will result the most wretched destruction?

Hence comes the Apostle’s saying: “For the word of the cross is folly to those who are perishing, but to those who are being saved it is the power of God” (I Cor. I). More abundant statements by the holy Fathers concerning the praise and power of the cross could indeed be collected, but these, briefly gathered together, are sufficient to expose and reasonably refute your error, although you are extremely obstinate.

Having thus briefly explained these matters concerning the praise and power of the cross, let us examine the remainder of your work. For you say:

> “God commanded one thing, but these people do otherwise.”

The learned cannot fail to notice how incorrectly you have composed this clause. You ought to have written: “God commanded one thing; these people do another.” Or certainly: “God commanded in one way; these people act in another way.” Since you did not write it thus, recognize that you have spoken incompetently.

Let us then examine the meaning of this ill-formed statement of yours. It is true, I confess, that you show by these words that this is what you mean: God commanded one thing, and we do another. We can offer no defense against what you have asserted, since we offend in many things, as the Apostle James bears witness: “In many things we all offend” (Jas. III). We sin when we fail to fulfill the divine commands; we also sin when we do what has been forbidden. Because of these evils we were expelled with our father Adam from the dwelling places of paradise and plunged into this valley of tears.

Although we have been raised from this fall through Christ’s grace and made sons of God by adoption, alas, once again, as human beings surrounded by the frailty of the flesh, we omit by wrongdoing many things that ought to be done, and by sin we admit many things that have been forbidden. Since the human condition is thus, I ask you—if you recognize that you are a human being—to remember that you are altogether a participant in human frailty. And if you cannot deny that you share in it, you ought not to attack our weakness so arrogantly, but rather, remembering our common frailty—or, better, fraternal charity—you ought in some way to have compassion on us.

But if you think that you have been so strengthened by the solidity of virtues in the dwelling of this mortality that you have no fear whatsoever of human collapse, you flatter yourself in vain, disregarding the prophetic saying: “Cursed is the man who trusts in man, makes flesh his arm, and whose heart departs from the Lord” (Jer. XVI); and the Apostle’s saying: “Let the one who thinks he stands take heed lest he fall” (I Cor. X); and this statement of blessed Jerome in his exposition of the prophet Ezekiel (Vol. V): “It is always necessary to fear and take care lest the storm of a single hour overturn the ancient glory and solid firmness.” Many further and innumerable testimonies could be assembled on this matter, but we omit them to avoid excessive length.

A little later you also add:

> “God commanded the cross to be carried (Luke XIV), not to be adored; these people wish to adore it because they do not wish to carry it with them either spiritually or bodily.”

That God the Son commanded his followers to carry the cross, and taught that no one can cling to his discipleship or prove worthy of him without carrying and bearing it, we learn fully from the pages of the holy evangelists, and we make use of the abundant and eloquent explanations of the distinguished Fathers. Therefore, avoiding prolixity—or rather, pursuing brevity—we omit inserting here the testimonies of the Gospel and the statements of the holy Fathers.

Let it suffice to have said enough about the bearing of the cross: how it is held by us both bodily and spiritually. Concerning its adoration—not that adoration which belongs to divinity alone, but rather the kind about which enough and more than enough has been said above and remains to be said below—we consider it unnecessary at this point to respond to your frivolous objection.

Of the two statements that you join together shortly afterward, saying, “These people wish to adore it because they do not wish to carry it with them either spiritually or bodily,” in one you are shown to speak the truth, but in the other you are convicted of lying and falsehood. We do indeed wish, according to ecclesiastical custom and in remembrance of the Lord’s Passion, to adore the cross in the manner stated above—that is, to salute it. Taught by apostolic instruction, however, “bearing the marks of Jesus in our body” (Gal. VI), we both desire and desirably long to carry his cross with us spiritually and bodily, insofar as he who commands permits.

That Christ’s cross is to be carried in two ways requires neither our explanation nor, in any respect, your portentous demonstration. For blessed Gregory, that eminent teacher, explains fully in his evangelical expositions how it is to be carried both bodily and spiritually.

What must be examined more subtly is what bubbled up from the muddy spring of your mouth: namely, that we do not wish to carry Christ’s cross either spiritually or bodily. In writing that we generally wish to carry it in neither way, you have certainly boasted that you alone—indeed, boastfully above all mortals—carry it in both ways. Look to yourself, I warn you, and consider how haughtily and arrogantly you have preferred yourself to other mortals in these words.

I seem to see you, like a proud Pharisee, swollen with the tumor of arrogance, standing in the Church of Christ and scorning the merits of others’ holy works while attributing them uniquely to yourself and saying: “God, I thank you that I am not like other men” (Luke XVIII)—that is, the inhabitants of Gaul and Germany, who do not wish to carry the cross of Christ either spiritually or bodily as I do; and for that reason I am rightly preferred to those who do not deserve to be compared with me in the virtue and holiness of carrying the cross.

O tumor of your singular righteousness, something to be feared and detested! For it is clear, and no doubt remains, that anyone afflicted with this disease of arrogance falls away from his own salvation. While he does not know how to lie and desires to be preferred to others, carried upward by the punishment of pride he climbs ever higher, until he falls into the pit of wretched humiliation, as the Lord testifies and says: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled.”

Again, a little later you say:

> “To worship God in this manner is to depart from him.”

Here, too, it is not sufficiently clear what kind of worship your invention says is worship of God and departure from him. But from the foolish assertions throughout the preceding and following parts of your work, it can be inferred that you intended this same worship to be understood as reverence and adoration of the cross, and that because we revere Christ’s cross and, in the manner described above, adore it—that is, salute it—we depart from God.

O tongue that does not speak truth but composes lies; O throat that is an open tomb; O tongue that acts deceitfully; O lips that drip the poison of asps (Ps. III); O tongue, I say, which, according to the teaching of blessed Jerome, ought to be cut off and exposed piece by piece for wild beasts and birds to devour! What Catholic would not shudder at an author speaking such things? Who would not judge the speaker of such words worthy of perpetual anathema?

Therefore, as you falsely assert, we do not depart from God by venerating and adoring Christ’s cross. Rather, you, like one possessed and deprived of reason, are convicted of departing from him, since you have written so many foolish things to dishonor that same cross.

Regarding the evangelical testimony you cited, you then add:

> “For he said: ‘Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me’” (Matt. XVI).

You seem to have wished to claim that we do not come after the Lord, do not deny ourselves, do not carry his cross, and do not wish to follow him because we do not wish to carry his cross with us either spiritually or bodily. What else, I ask, is meant by our not carrying Christ’s cross with us spiritually or bodily except openly to say that we disdain coming after him, denying ourselves, carrying his cross, and following him?

It is therefore clearer than daylight that no one deserves to be his follower—indeed, his disciple—unless he is a carrier and bearer of Christ’s cross. Since we know that we possess no good will of ourselves and can have no strength of our own, “for it depends not on human willing or running but on God who shows mercy” (Rom. IX), we do not distrust that strength is supplied to us by him on whom it is good to rely and to whom it is good to cling (Ps. LXXII), from whom both our willing and our ability arise. Thus, I say, we do not doubt that he supplies us with strength sufficient for us, encouraged and strengthened by which we may come after the Lord, deny ourselves, take up his cross, and follow him, so that we may deserve to be worthy of him.

But you, most foolish of mortals, should not suppose that you follow Christ while you are afflicted by so great a disease of empty boasting. Like the one to whom it was said, “Are you wiser than Daniel?” (Ezek. XXVIII), you are swept along by the arrogance of pride, so that you boast that you alone follow Christ and shamelessly strive to oppose the authority of the Church, contrary to Christian discipline.

Hear therefore blessed Augustine, writing in the ninth chapter of *The Sermon on the Mount*: “For the one who is not called a Christian according to the true faith and Catholic discipline does not follow Christ.” Although you do not appear openly to attack the true Catholic faith, nevertheless, in trying to overthrow ecclesiastical statutes contrary to Christian discipline, you are shown to disdain following Christ.

These statements, then, which you attached shortly afterward and did not fit very appropriately to what preceded, you have, in your customary manner and in the role of a compiler, presented as your own. They are as follows:

[Col. 0353C]

> “For unless someone departs from himself toward the one who is above him, he does not draw near, nor can he grasp what is beyond him, if he has not learned to slaughter what he is.”

Since these words agree with neither your style nor your meaning in any way, and are known to belong to blessed Gregory, we entirely approve them and raise them aloft with proclamations of praise.

After the adoration of the ass—which with an unsound mind you equated with the cross worthy of adoration and reverence—the first of your supposedly syllogistic conclusions is, as you see it, this:

> “If the cross is adored, let virgin girls be adored also”—

and immediately you supplied the reason:

> “because a virgin gave birth to Christ.”

What, I ask you, could be more absurd or foolish than this conclusion? “If the cross is adored,” you say, “let virgin girls be adored also, because a virgin gave birth to Christ.”

The cross, then, is saluted through adoration in the manner stated above. The virgin who gave birth to Christ, however, we do not adore; rather, we venerate the holy Mother of God with fitting honor and humbly implore her intercession before the divine majesty. Nor is this without reason, since through her we deserved to receive the author of life. Because that same holy and undefiled virgin Mary gave birth to God and man for us—namely, the Lord Jesus—she is rightly honored by all the faithful with devout love and venerated with due honor.

But that we should offer adoration to virgin girls, as you proclaim while snoring, we consider extremely foolish—indeed, we judge it utterly perverse.

Let us therefore speak still more subtly about this utterly absurd adoration that you proclaim. The sons of the one virgin, namely the holy Church, know that the ever-Virgin received the author of life, and that the birth of that same virgin would not have benefited them without the ascent of the cross. They also remember that, persuaded by the ancient virgin, they came into exile, from which they were redeemed through the cross. For this reason they offer adoration to no virgin, since from one of them they tasted death, and from the other salvation.

They know and believe that they recovered through the cross what they suffered through the persuasion of the first virgin, and that the enemy who had cast them into the bonds of harsh captivity was struck down by its power, while the way into the heavenly homeland was opened for them. Armed with faith, they also know that by this banner of the cross they repel all the darts of the most wicked enemy. Therefore, rightly setting aside the adoration of any virgin girls, they decree that so great and such a trophy of their King is to be venerated—a trophy which they see to have released mortals from captivity, restored the losses of paradise, condemned the infernal powers, crushed the enemy’s strength, and erased the sin of the first virgin, not so much through the childbirth of the second virgin as through the death of the cross.

In the midst of these matters, it seems necessary to consider with what clarity the holy Apostle long ago foresaw the novice enemies of the venerable cross and, with the Holy Spirit guiding the pen of his word, depicted their deadly teaching. For he says: “Watch those who walk in this way, of whom I often told you, and now tell you with tears: enemies of the cross of Christ. Their end is destruction, their god is their belly, and their glory is in their shame; they set their minds on earthly things” (Phil. III).

How well and elegantly he said that the enemies of Christ’s cross have their belly as their god and their glory in their shame! For a belly distended with excessive banquets belches forth the foam of lust, to which the girl is closely related, since, to use the words of blessed Jerome, “genital pleasure immediately follows a belly distended with food and irrigated by various passions.”

These, then—the enemies of Christ’s cross, I say—were marked out before they were born. They now multiply under the devil’s authorship and equate the power of the cross with girls who are devoted to shame, that is, to lust.

By contrast, the same Apostle says of Christ’s lovers: “Those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires.” Consider, I ask you, Claudius, how far this foolish comparison is removed from the power of the cross. The Apostle says that each person who belongs to Christ has crucified his members; understand, therefore, that the one who abhors the crucifixion of his members is shown not to belong to Christ, and that no one can glory both in his shame and in the cross.

If, then, you command girls to be adored as the cross is, you ought to show us those whom you would honor with so great an honor—girls who perhaps are still hiding somewhere and whom, after the manner of Montanus, you regard as prophetesses in place of Maximilla and Prisca.

Let a girl be an object of adoration for the enemy of the cross, whose god is his belly, so that his glory may be in his shame, if that pleases him. But we who wish to belong to Christ crucify our members, honor the Crucified One with the religion due to him, and rejoice both to be and to be called friends of the cross. Accordingly, we venerate not girls but the cross.

Your second proposition contains the following:

> “Let the mangers be adored also, because, as soon as he was born, he was laid in a manger.”

This comparison makes me so astonished by its indecency that I think either that the person writing such things dreamed them while snoring in deepest sleep, or certainly indulged so excessively in wine that he lost his memory. For Solomon is reported, among the other things by which he offended God, to have had many mangers for horses contrary to God’s law. Scripture, as is its custom, silently indicates that he thereby supplied food both for himself and for others who followed his example in evil to the wicked spirits, who are represented under the name of horses.

Therefore the one who builds mangers for horses—namely, impure spirits—is anyone who, setting aside the fear and love of God, constructs some perverse doctrine or schism in which the devil delights and is nourished. Thus it is not every most sincere worshiper of the Catholic faith who is worthy to be called an adorer, but rather the builder of such mangers.

The Lord formerly promised the salutary ruin of these horses through the Lord’s cross, when he testifies through Zechariah, saying: “So shall be the ruin of the horse and the mule, the camel and the ass, and all the animals that are in those camps, like this ruin” (Zech. XIV).

Having understood these matters, we venerate the cross with appropriate moderation, but we judge mangers unworthy of our adoration. Rather, we decree that they should be built for the benefit of animals.

After this you say:

> “Let the old rags be adored also, because, as soon as he was born, he was wrapped in old rags.”

It is characteristic of you, Claudius, to steal certain things from the little works of others, remove some, alter others, add still others from your own contrary to law, and secretly adapt them to your own expressions as though they were your own. You are shown to have done this very often in the preceding parts of this work, and for that reason you are rightly assailed by the darts of reproach.

No one can add anything to, alter, or remove anything from the words of the holy Gospel at will without bringing about his own ruin. Where, I ask you, did you read that the Lord, when born, was immediately wrapped in old rags? Perhaps, just as you shamelessly insult ecclesiastical traditions, you also refuse irreverently to conform to the Gospel translation that we use. Thus, just as you possess schismatic traditions with which you slander ours, you may also possess interpreters of the Gospels whom the Catholic Church does not receive. Having become accustomed to their reading, you insist that the Lord was wrapped in old rags.

Be content with these things if you please. But we, as we have learned from the account of the evangelist Luke, faithfully hold and preach to all the faithful that this is to be held. For he says:

> “And it happened that, while they were there, the days were fulfilled for her to give birth, and she gave birth to her firstborn son, and wrapped him in swaddling cloths, and laid him in a manger, because there was no place for them in the inn.”

And a little later:

> “And the angel said: ‘Do not be afraid, for behold, I announce to you great joy, which will be for all the people, because today a Savior has been born for you, who is Christ the Lord, in the city of David. And this will be a sign for you: you will find an infant wrapped in swaddling cloths and lying in a manger’” (Luke II).

We are instructed by this Gospel oracle that, not as you dream, but simply, the Lord was wrapped at his birth in swaddling cloths. I also believe that, unless forgetfulness had dulled your mind—or some other loss of reason— you could not have forgotten that the Apostle Paul so frequently commanded us to strip off the old man with his deeds and put on the new (Col. III). For if you remembered these things, it is astonishing that, while he always commands us to be clothed in new garments, you have taught the opposite: that, with the same worship by which we venerate the cross, we should also serve old rags.

We continually mark the cross upon our foreheads. We either attach old rags to our bodies to resist the cold, or, compelled by charity, distribute them so that they may benefit the poor. If, however, we turn to the mystery, we drive away the enemy’s assault with the cross. And if, through sinning, we have turned the silk garment that we received new from the Lord in baptism into old rags, we desire to renew it through the power of the cross.

Let the one who is not afraid to stain Christ’s tunic by sinning adore old rags, and let him tear it apart in the peace of the Church, though even the soldier could not tear it during the Passion. We rejoice that we are clothed in the tunic of the new man. We strive, insofar as he grants us the ability, to preserve it new and sound—that is, free from heretical perversity—or to wash away its stains through the cross. And, since Christ was fastened upon it, we stretch out the wrinkles of its old age, so that we may be members of the Church, of which the Apostle said: “that he might present to himself”—without doubt, Christ—“a glorious Church, not having spot or wrinkle or anything of that kind” (Eph. V).

Let anyone who wishes worship the old man with his old rags. But we, putting on the new man, venerate his new insignia, triumphing most victoriously over the world and the prince of the world.

After this you assert:

> “Let ships be adored also, because he often sailed in a ship, taught the crowds from a little boat, slept in a ship, commanded the winds from a ship, and ordered the net to be cast on the right side of the vessel, when that great catch of fish was made.”

It is astonishing that, on account of what we believe the Lord did in a ship—namely, that he sat in it, taught, and performed the other things—you wished to make the ship comparable to the cross.

It is established that in the Flood human beings were saved from the world’s impending catastrophe in the ark, which bore the figure of the cross. Yet none of their successors, although they were superstitious and devoted to needless worship, included the ark or ship among the number of the gods on account of so great a benefit.

How much less, then, is it fitting for us, who venerate the Holy Trinity and abhor any worship apart from that owed to the Divinity, to offer honor to ships! We therefore owe ships no adoration such as is owed to the cross. Rather, since they are necessary in the liquid element, they are believed to be useful for human needs.

If, however, one attends to the mysteries, the holy Church offers no veneration to ships in which the Chaldeans—whose name is interpreted as “captivators,” or as demons—glory. Thus the prophet says: “For your sake I sent into Babylon and brought down all the bars, and the Chaldeans glorying in their ships” (Isa. XLIII).

We do not adore these ships. We know that their deceptive arts—by which the devil gloried and lay in wait for human life—have been shattered and, with Christ’s favor, destroyed by the invincible banner of the cross.

The ship of Tyre is comparable to these. Adorned with the world’s diverse furnishings and made exceedingly secure with different kinds of timber, it was overturned when the sign of the cross arrived: what had stood wrongly was thrown down, and what had been adorned perniciously was stripped away for salvation.

We embrace the victorious cross over these ships, and we exclude both their physical forms and their meanings from adoration. Certainly, we escape the waves of the present world as they rise against it from every side, and we desire to be carried to the lands of the living with Christ as our pilot. We also watch for its enemy with all our strength, according to the Apostle’s command (Phil. III)—that is, we avoid him.

Nor do we adore the ship made into the Church, of which that ship was a type. Rather, we strive to become its members. From this ship he continues to teach crowds of believers (Matt. VIII), and to the contrary winds—namely, the impure spirits that stir up storms of heresies—he continues to command silence, saying: “Be silent and be still” (Mark IV).

Then you say:

> “Let lambs be adored also, because it is written of him: ‘Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world’” (John I).

Unless I understand from you the reason that compelled you to compare a lamb with the cross, I cannot know it by myself. For nowhere do I find that any benefit has been conferred on any mortal through a lamb, except when some dish is prepared from it to relieve hunger.

Even if this name is written of the Lord, it must be understood that he was not given this name because he is an animal, but because, more than other animals, he remains free from external injury and silent at the time of mistreatment.

But if you object that some benefit was conferred upon the Israelite people through a lamb, know that salvation was given not through its body or image, but through blood—and not through it simply, but through blood with which the doorposts of the houses were sprinkled (Exod. I).

The Holy Spirit, whose prompting brought those things about, was already signifying by this that we cannot otherwise keep the adversary away from our homes unless the wood of the Passion has been smeared with the blood of the spotless Lamb, and this sacred banner has marked the entrance to our houses.

For when that blood is sprinkled upon both doorposts and upon the lintels of the houses as protection against the enemy, the cross itself is not merely prefigured but represented, both by the arrangement of its parts and by the weight of its mysteries.

[Note: The passage is obscure and perhaps corrupt.]

Therefore, we embrace, love, and venerate with fitting honor the invincible triumph of the Lord’s cross, through which we know that our fathers also obtained salvation, and on which King Ait (Josh. VII, VIII), whose name is interpreted as “Chaos,” that is, “confusion”—“A indeed, confusion; I, man” [the transmitted gloss is corrupt]—was fastened and overcome, as the Apostle also bears witness.

As for any of the animal lambs, we consider none worthy of adoration.

Among the other ravings of your little songs, you also add:

> “But these worshipers of perverse doctrines wish to devour living lambs and adore those painted on the wall.”

Who, I ask you, are these people who wish to adore painted lambs? Surely not the Gauls and Germans, who not only refuse to offer adoration to any painting whatsoever, but openly oppose those who adore them, rebuke them with all the invective they can, and exert themselves with every effort to bring them back to a sound mind?

If such people are found, then, while preserving brotherly love, we detest them along with you insofar as they are such.

As for lambs, we have them not alive, as you slanderously claim, but prepared by the cooks; we have them as food, and we do not condemn those who eat their flesh. On this matter a remarkable consideration presents itself to the mind. Either you yourself eat lambs, and are shown to have written such things pointlessly, or, if superstition dictates that you abstain from their flesh, you are shown not to have escaped the abyss of the Manichaean and Novatian heresies, and consequently are shown in such conduct rather to serve the worship of a perverse doctrine.

But if you refrain from such food out of temperance, you ought not to become so angry with those who eat it innocently, lest you oppose apostolic teaching, which commands: “Let the one who does not eat not judge the one who eats” (Rom. XIV).

[Col. 0358C]

> “After this,” he says, “let lions be adored also, because it is written of him: ‘The lion from the tribe of Judah, the root of David, has conquered’” (Rev. V).

Anyone who attempts to attribute something to some object must show that it resembles, either wholly or in part, the one to which he compares it. This is what the person did who likened the lion to the Lord. He observed in him the commanding power of beasts, but not their savage and merciless cruelty.

But I do not see how the comparison of the lion with the cross can be made. When I review the lives of the saints, I frequently find that their ferocity yielded to the power of the cross; yet nowhere do I find the memory of lions—creatures ignorant of reason—without ferocity, except insofar as divine omnipotence subdues them.

How, then, the cross, which has benefited all visible and invisible creatures subject to God, and the lion, which has benefited none of the invisible beings and rages with all possible savagery against the bodies of living creatures, can be made to agree, you yourself must see.

Certainly, the signification placed before us—which now rejoices in the meaning of Christ, as in “the lion’s cub of Judah,” and now terrifies the minds of the faithful through its reference to the devil, of whom it is said, “Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour”—is received by us piously insofar as it approaches Christ; and it is not the lion, but Christ, who is adored on that account.

But whenever it signifies the devil himself or some servant lying in wait for the Lord’s flock, who subjects the sons of the holy Church to his doctrine—of him and of such servants it is said through Nahum, “The lion seized enough for his cubs” (Nahum II)—we abhor it in every way. So that we may be able to avoid them, we hold the cross in our minds like a very strong fortress and impress it upon our bodies.

After this you add:

> “Let rocks be adored also, because, when he was taken down from the cross, he was placed in a stone tomb,”

and so forth.

If your words contained anything wise or close to wisdom, you might rightly be heard to some extent, since from your rubbish someone might perceive something sound and wise. But because you put forward things that are utterly foolish and, as the Book of Wisdom says, wish to adorn a clay vessel with tarnished silver (Prov. XVI), you must fear being numbered among those who praised stone gods among the other gods at the banquet of King Belshazzar (Dan. V).

But I think you paid this honor to rocks by equating them with the cross because you felt their stupidity to be present in your own heart. Rather, we must pray to the one who accomplishes all things by the nod of his will, of whom the prophet says: “His indignation is poured out like fire, and the rocks are dissolved by him” (Nahum I), so that he may dissolve this hardness and stupidity of yours with the fire of his mercy.

Then you may understand why the Lord, who had determined to die for our salvation, delayed the death by stones offered by the Jews by hiding himself (John VIII, XII), but, when he was sought for crucifixion, offered himself willingly, saying to his disciples: “Rise, let us go from here” (John XIV).

We use rocks to build the masonry of our walls and houses, and also of our churches. But crosses we either set up in churches with fitting honor in memory of the Lord’s Passion, or, according to what we have learned in the prophet Ezekiel (Ezek. IX), set them before our doors—that is, upon our foreheads—and upon the five bodily senses for our protection.

Then you say:

“Let the thorns of bushes also be adored, because from them a crown of thorns was placed upon his head at the time of the Passion.”

Let whoever possesses sound judgment see how well, how elegantly, and how tastefully you have woven this comparison, as you have the others. For from the turbid little spring of your arrogance, wholly alien to the clearest streams of grammatical art, this comparison has flowed forth—like the other comparisons among your nonsense—in so indecorous and irrational a manner that it is undoubtedly proved both absurd and false. Absurd, indeed, because thorns cannot in any way be compared with the cross, as will be demonstrated below, with the Lord’s help. False, moreover, because in the writings of the three Evangelists—Matthew, Mark, and John (Matt. 27; Mark 15; John 19)—whose testimony we salutarily use and in which we firmly establish the anchor of our faith, although they certainly mention the crown of thorns placed upon the Lord’s head, it can nowhere be found that this crown was fashioned from the thorns of bushes, as you have conjectured. Rather, those holy Evangelists simply record that the soldiers placed a crown of thorns upon his head as an act of mockery.

It is therefore evident, and no one can doubt, that the ancient enemy has made a dwelling for himself in your heart and has opened your mouth to utter so execrable a lie. I mean the one who from the beginning did not stand in the truth, who is a liar and its father, under whose prompting you have rashly and recklessly presumed to assert this same lie against the truth of the Gospel, which is wholly free from such blemish.

Yet although there are different kinds of lies, and in this mortal life we can scarcely be free from falsehood (John 1)—from whose fall, which is almost daily for us, we daily require the remission of divine mercy, and trust that we are mercifully forgiven—nevertheless, that lie which conflicts with the truth of the Gospel we detest in every way and, with divine grace assisting us, earnestly strive to avoid. We grieve and lament that you have fallen into it, as charity commands, imitating the Apostle’s words: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not burning?” (1 Cor. 12).

For no one may add, subtract, or alter anything in the Gospel pages composed by the pen of the Holy Spirit, where, as has been said, our faith rests, thereby dishonoring the one about whom they were written, insulting our faith, and bringing destruction upon his own soul. Therefore you must take care for yourself and consider how greatly you have gone astray by this erroneous addition—namely, by asserting that a crown woven from the thorns of bushes was placed upon the Lord’s head.

I do not know whether knowingly or unknowingly, but you have plunged yourself terribly into the bond of canonical excommunication, since you presumed to add something of your own to the evangelical faith. The definition of the holy Fathers at the Council of Chalcedon concerning those who presume to add anything to the evangelical and apostolic faith is as follows (Act 15):

“The holy and universal synod decrees that no one may bring forward, write down, compose, hold, or teach another faith. But those who have dared to compose another faith, or to bring forward or teach or hand on another creed to those wishing to turn to the knowledge of the truth, whether from the Gentiles, from the Jews, or from any heresy—if they are bishops or clerics, we decree that bishops shall be excluded from the episcopate and clerics from the clergy; but if they are monks or laymen, we decree that they shall be anathematized.”

Since, then, you are plainly struck by the anathema of the holy Fathers, to whom the power of binding and loosing has been granted by the Lord (Matt. 16), if you wish to be saved, return in repentance to that in whose words you erred, so that, by the gift of him who wills all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth, you may deservedly be healed from this blow.

We know, and with tears we confess, that God most justly imposed upon sinful humanity as a punishment that the earth should produce thorns and thistles. The one who had refused to be subject to God and to remain happily and without toil in his homeland was cast into exile and compelled to endure the pricks of thorns. Since the Savior mercifully wished to free him from this exile, he deigned to mount the cross and on it to triumph over the enemy.

Is it therefore fitting that the punishment of exile should likewise accompany one who is returning to his homeland? To make my point clearer: can anyone embrace a piercing thorn with the same love with which he embraces the one who frees him from the devil and opens the entrance to the heavenly kingdom? The cross was fixed so that the thorns of our exile might be consumed.

Would you like to know this more certainly? When the angel, in the person of the Lord, spoke to Moses about leading out the people (Exod. 3)—the people to whom he was about to give the law and grant many other benefits—Moses saw a bush burning, yet not being consumed. This already proclaimed through visible events that the law would indeed inflame the people’s sins by exposing and reproving them, but would not consume them.

The cross, therefore, is more rightly venerated than the thorn: the thorn torments the captive and exile, whereas the cross both removes captivity and burns up the piercing thorn.

After this you add:

“Let the reeds also be adored, because by them the soldiers beat his head with blows.”

The rest is either suitable for provoking laughter or, because it bears some resemblance to a signification of the Lord, can somehow be tolerated. But the comparison of reeds with the cross is so utterly remote that it seems to have proceeded neither from a wakeful person nor from a sound mind, but rather from one who should be handed over to be bound with the cords of Hippocrates as a madman.

We read that, as a figure of the Lord’s cross, the bitter waters once put aside their insipid tastes through the insertion of wood (Exod. 15). Could the power of the Almighty not have sweetened their taste in any other way than by touching them with wood? But, as the time required, through various shadows of figures and figurative allegories he was foreshadowing the usefulness of the most victorious wood. By its touch, the letter of the law—which had previously been impossible because of the bitterness obstructing it—has now, through that same contact, become fit to drink.

We also read that this was foretold concerning the cross: “And he shall be like a tree planted beside the courses of waters” (Ps. 1)—there can be no doubt that this refers either to the blessed man from whom all who are blessed receive blessedness, or to any of his members. Does it say, “And he shall be like a reed beside the banks of marshy rivers”?

I know, certainly I know, what you intend by these things. Perhaps you recalled that dryness was threatened by the Lord to the Egyptian reed—that is, to empty speech containing nothing solid within itself—when it is said: “The channels of the embankments shall be weakened and dried up; the reed and the rush shall wither” (Isa. 19). Thus you wished to console your reed, utterly empty of reason, in this fashion: you tried to show it to be like the cross, and in the same way that the cross is adored by the faithful, you would compel them to adore your reed as well.

Finally, as though adding the crowning achievement of your nonsense, you append:

“Let the spears also be adored, because one of the soldiers opened his side on the cross, from which flowed blood and water, the sacraments from which the Church is formed.”

I have long been stunned with admiration at you, my throat constricted; overcome by such astonishment, my words fail me, and I can only wonder at so extraordinary a thing: when mentioning the spear of the Lord’s Passion, what was it that you failed to recall about what the Lord said to blessed Peter concerning his sword at the time of the Passion: “All who take the sword will perish by the sword” (Matt. 16)?

For if the cross and the spear were to be weighed in an equal balance, just as the Lord said, “All who take the sword will perish by the sword,” so he would have added: “All who take the cross will perish by the cross.” Likewise, when he said to his disciples, “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me,” and, “Whoever does not carry his cross and follow me is not worthy of me” (Luke 14), he would have said in the same way: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him take his spear in his hand and follow me. And whoever does not carry his spear in his hand is not worthy of me.”

For Peter was rebuked when he took the sword, and he was instructed to carry the cross when he was told, “Follow me.” The Lord clearly showed him in what respect he was to follow him when he said: “When you were younger, you girded yourself and walked where you wished,” and so forth (John 21). And lest our minds be led into doubt about the meaning of this, the Evangelist followed with these words: “Now he said this to signify by what death he would glorify God” (ibid.).

Let any heretic, then, adore the spear—namely, the wickedness of his own doctrine—and, joining the forces of Gog and Magog, whose names are interpreted as “roof” or “from the roof,” let him go forth against the holy Church with great arrogance and a display of arms, despising her poor weapons [perhaps: her poorest weapons]. His part will be to trust in the strength of his king, to fortify himself with the banner of the cross, and, after defeating them, to burn their weapons in fire for seven years—that is, to burn all their armor in the sacred and perfect number seven, consecrated to the gifts of the Holy Spirit: their spears, lances, staffs, and hands [reading uncertain]. As it is written: “He will break the bow and shatter the weapons, and burn the shields with fire” (Ps. 45). By the same fire—not momentary but eternal—the weapons of your perverse doctrine must also be burned.

Thus far, with the authority of divine teaching and the doctrine of the holy Fathers, and from what the Lord has deigned soberly to supply, it should suffice that by the course of our writing we have reasonably countered your foolish and most senseless objections, O Claudius.

But since it is clear that, because you preached the worship of asses and of other senseless things—which in your madness you dogmatized as worthy of worship just like the venerable cross—your doctrine cannot in any way be compared with any sound and true doctrine of faith, it seems that we must ask with what false doctrine it can be compared. Since it cannot be equated or in any respect likened to the teachers of the Catholic faith, it is rightly to be matched with the words and deeds of those who are outside the Church.

Since, then, we are compelled to liken the teachings of your preaching to the deeds and words of the pagans, nothing can be more aptly or suitably equated with it in word and deed than Silenus, the drunken prophet, very much like you, of whom Naso writes:

> Behold the drunken old man Silenus on a bent-backed ass;  
> He can scarcely sit, and with skill restrains its pressed-down mane.

Of him Maro writes as follows (Eclogue 6.13):

> Go on, Pierian Muses. Chromis and Mnasyllus in a cave  
> Saw Silenus lying asleep;  
> His veins swollen, as always, with yesterday’s wine,  
> While far away his garlands had slipped from his head  
> And the heavy wine-cup hung by its worn handle.

And shortly afterward:

> Release me, boys; it is enough to have been seen.  
> Learn the songs you wish; songs for you—

We are compelled to oppose vanity with vanity, folly with folly, and falsehood with falsehood.

Since both poets have described the same Silenus drunk with poetic vanity, one of them depicts him sitting on a bent-backed ass, scarcely able to remain seated because of his excessive drunkenness. Having lost the reins by which that ass was to be controlled, he keeps himself from falling only through his weak skill, holding on to the ass’s pressed-down mane. The other, as may be inferred, depicts him as having already fallen from that same ass, lying like a corpse, his veins swollen with yesterday’s wine, as was his habit, the handle of the heavy wine-cup broken by his excessive drinking, his garlands fallen from his head and lying at a distance, and himself ensnared through the trickery of two boys, bound by them with the cords of his own garlands. As is customary with wanton boys toward those who are emptied by excessive unmixed wine and lie snoring, he is mocked, awakened by the same mockery, and promises the boys that he will compose whatever songs they wish—something which, as the following passages of that book testify, he indeed did.

Nevertheless, the resemblance of his deed can appropriately be applied to you, Claudius. For, as some maintain, Virgil wished allegorically, in the person of Silenus, to suggest the person of another.

You therefore appear to sit upon a bent-backed ass, like that same Silenus who so closely resembles you. You have indulged in unmixed wine to such an extent, and so dulled your mind through enormous drinking, that you have lost the reins of moderation and discernment and carried out the other actions which Naso recounts of him, when you taught that an ass should be adored just like the cross.

Moreover, you ought to have proposed for worship that same ass upon which you were sitting, and no others. But I suppose that, because it was bent-backed, you judged it worthy of supporting your sitting. For our worship, however, you rightly judged worthy not bent-backed asses, but noble asses of great stature, well-eared, walking with tower-like necks and holding their heads high.

Yet, according to Virgil, you are proved to have possessed the likeness of that same Silenus. For unless you had been thoroughly drenched in wine, surely not in the wine of which the Psalmist says, “Wine gladdens the heart of man” (Ps. 103), nor in that of which the Book of Judges says that it “gladdens God and human beings” (Judg. 6), but rather in the wine of which the song of Moses says, “Their wine is the gall of dragons and the incurable poison of asps” (Deut. 32), you would never have turned away from ecclesiastical traditions and proposed that asses and the other foolish things you wrote should be worshiped.

The boys who found you swollen with that same gall-filled wine and lying like a corpse, and who bound you with your own cords, can be understood as nothing more fittingly than your spirit—which, according to the Apostle (Eph. 4), ought to be renewed and to put on the new man, namely Christ our Lord—and your understanding, which ought to have produced sound doctrine.

You were therefore made such a mockery and object of derision to these boys that, just as the boys mentioned above forced Silenus to compose foolish songs for them, so your boys—namely, your spirit and your small understanding—plunged you into so deep an abyss of presumption and rashness that, through their persuasion and agreement, or rather through the ancient enemy’s stealthy seizure and triumph, you preached doctrines by which you displayed yourself as mentally captive and incapable of reason.

You thus unhappily made yourself an exile from the catalog of the children of the Church, because they utterly despise your doctrines, full of error and blasphemies, along with you, and decree that they should be consigned to the refuse.

As for your wine-cup with its broken handle, from which, as from a Babylonian chalice, you drank deadly poison and drained it to the dregs: since they know that it is fit for no human use, they rightly cast it away. And lest anyone of sound mind should drink from it, they judge that it must remain forever crushed, useless, and unfit for service.

Certainly, if you had preached things sober and suitable to ecclesiastical dignity, a garland—that is, a priestly crown—would rightly have remained upon your head. But because you presumed to write against the authority and religion of the holy Church of God, you have caused the crown of your episcopal office to fall far from your head, to your disgrace and dishonor, and to be most unbecomingly absent from you.

Recognize, then, O Claudius, this comparison taken from the fables of the poets and not inappropriately applied to you. Take care that you do not henceforth presume to assail the holy Church of God with your poisonous objections.

But lest the length and excessive prolixity of this little book produce weariness in its readers, let its course come to an end here. The remaining portions of your work, O Claudius, will be examined in the third book that follows this one, with the Lord’s help.

## [BOOK THREE]

### PREFACE TO THE THIRD BOOK

[Col. 0363]

[Col. 0363D] In the two little books completed before this one, your most absurd and dishonorable propositions, O Claudius, were not refuted in every respect. Nevertheless, in refuting and rejecting the things which you were not ashamed to proclaim worthy of worship just like the venerable cross, enough—and, as I believe, abundantly enough, insofar as God permitted—has been set forth in the course of our opposition.

There remain, therefore, matters to be observed and examined with the clearest and simplest eyes, to be thoroughly sifted with sound and sober understanding, and to be destroyed by the weapons of the sacred Scriptures and the writings of distinguished teachers. These are the matters which, forgetful of priestly reverence and fraternal love, you spewed forth with shameless lips against the venerable man already so often mentioned, the abbot Theodemir, who, moved by charity, admonished you and wished to recall you from your superstitions—superstitions which you uselessly served and in which you were miserably entangled—without any restraint of discernment or moderation, or, to speak more truly, with the most impudent mouth.

If, then, so many and such great foolish trifles of yours, contained in the extract mentioned above, have produced only three books because of the enormity of your awkward and defective expressions, how long and how extensive do you think the books will necessarily have to be, and how many of them will have to be assembled and written, when the complete codex of this foolish and execrable work of yours—which you composed against the authority and simplicity of ecclesiastical discipline and have now sent to the venerable abbot Theodemir—falls into the hands of learned men?

For, as the things written by you in that extract testify and give credibility to those who see and read them, much more wicked and detestable things will be found in that same perverse codex of yours: things which you repeatedly wrote against our holy mother and nurse, the Catholic and Apostolic Church, for the sake of reproach and insult.

Therefore, if it is still hidden in darkness, it must be brought into the light, so that it may be seen, read, and examined, and so that whatever error and blasphemy it contains, hurled by you against us, may become known and may rightly and reasonably be opposed by ecclesiastical arguments.

For unless, in the present time and after a thorough search, it is found and brought into the open, examined with diligent care, rejected, and committed to the fire, there is reason to fear that, if in future times it should come to the knowledge of simple brethren, its deadly text, read and learned by them, may infect them with the disease of its fatal error, make them wounded, and grievously pour its pestilential destruction into their souls.

[Col. 0365]

## BOOK THREE

[Col. 0365B] Behold, the time has now come, and the order of the matter under discussion demands that we finally come to those things which you specifically objected to the venerable abbot Theodemir, O Claudius, and which through him you prepared craftily to turn back against us. For while you pretended to strike another with your missile, you wished openly and fraudulently to pierce us with that same weapon.

Indeed, when you attempted to infect us with the many other foolish trifles of your insane doctrine, you also constituted yourself so much an enemy and adversary of the holy Church of God that, with shameless face, you presumed to nullify the honor of divine worship which we religiously hold and venerate, and to dogmatize that the intercession of God’s saints should be wholly disregarded and despised.

Accordingly, after gradually reading through and observing your writings, we have resolved in this book to set against each of your false objections, both on our own behalf and on behalf of the same venerable abbot—or rather, in defense of our holy mother, the Catholic Church—answers filled with appropriate truth, and apostolic weapons sharpened by the whetstone of the Holy Spirit.

The course of your argument, in which you attack the aforementioned venerable abbot Theodemir so violently and rashly, proceeds as follows:

[Col. 0365D] “But as for your claim that I forbid people to go to Rome for the sake of penance, you speak falsely.”

I am greatly astonished—though I do not know whether you deserve the astonishment—that you have been so deprived of your senses, or at least that forgetfulness has so dulled your mind, that after making this statement you do not remember what you said earlier.

For in your subsequent words you are found not merely to have prohibited that journey, insofar as you were able, but also, with the reins of moderation broken and wholly drenched in gall, to have raged in insult against those going to Rome and seeking apostolic intercession by that route, branding them with the mark of ignorance and stupidity.

But this is what the flighty and empty instability that knows no firmness brings about: because it is not rooted like a tree of wisdom watered by divine waters, it rushes about heedlessly and ignorantly in every direction, like fine dust carried wherever the breath of levity happens to blow.

Thus you are proved to have incurred, through your own words, the charge of falsehood which you try to bring against your brother, and you yourself testify that the same venerable man escaped it, as far as the present matter is concerned. For he too was free from falsehood, since he said that you had forbidden what you condemn in your writing; and you prove yourself a liar, since what you now deny having forbidden you plainly reveal in what follows that you think, by condemning and insulting it.

But then, as though you were about to give a reason, you add:

[Col. 0366C] “For I do not approve of that journey.”

And as though explaining why you said this, you continue:

“Because I know that it harms neither everyone nor benefits everyone, neither profits everyone nor injures everyone.”

What could be found more foolish than these words I would not easily discover.

What then? Are those things which are called morally indifferent in the actions of our life—that is, things which can be turned by their users toward either a good or an evil purpose—not to be approved at all? Are fasts and bodily abstinence, to mention briefly a few matters while passing over many others, to be rejected because they prepare glory and eternal satisfaction for some, when the Judge says, “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world; for I was hungry and you gave me food,” and so forth, while for others, undertaken through empty display and the desire for popular praise, they drive those who pursue them empty of reward into the punishment of Gehenna, as the examiner of hearts says: “Truly I tell you, they have received their reward”?

Is chastity to be rejected—a virtue that will not only make its followers equal to the angels in future blessedness, but also seeks to display an angelic imitation while they are still in mortal bodies—because many, although they do not approach women’s bodies, nevertheless suffer shipwreck in modesty either through impure desire or through the vice of boasting? Is the distribution of alms perhaps to be nullified on this account, although Scripture says that it resists sins as water extinguishes fire (Sir. 3), because some abuse the money given to sustain their fragile life and perhaps, through its generosity, fall into shameful acts? And among those who give, some await a future reward, while others seek favor, asking for human profit in place of seeking divine reward.

It would therefore have been better for you to weigh this matter by the judgment of your mind and, just like the other morally indifferent goods, to have judged this one useful through devotion of heart, or else decreed that through lack of devotion it would be less beneficial.

For if it benefits one person but harms another, this does not proceed from the nature of the act, but from the character of the person performing it. The act which would have benefited him in the branches of the work he injured at the root of his intention; and because he did not possess a pure eye of intention, the whole body of his action suffered darkness.

We certainly know some who made it their purpose to visit the shrines of the holy apostles and humbly seek their intercession. They were not only praised by holy men, but were also divinely admonished not to cease from this intention. Thus blessed Gregory writes in the book of the Dialogues about a certain man who, among his other exercises of good works, made it his practice every year to visit the relics of the apostles. He was admonished to continue doing what he was doing, so that neither his hand nor his foot should cease, and that on the feast day of the apostles, whom he regularly visited, he would receive the reward of his merits.

Nor is it a new practice for certain places to be frequented by human gatherings for the sake of prayer. Rather, the authority of the ancient Fathers and the authority of the divine utterances urge us to do this.

Although God is present everywhere and his hands established every place, nevertheless, wishing to test the faith of blessed Abraham, he commanded that his son be offered not in any place whatsoever but on the mountain that pleased him, and he required the aforesaid man to travel for three days to that place.

That place is said thereafter to have become renowned and distinguished for this reason and to have been frequented by many. Hence it was marked by the name, “On the mountain the Lord will see.”

The same blessed Moses, who had taught the people of Israel that the earth and its fullness belong to the Lord, as do the heavens and the heavens of heavens, nevertheless commanded them not to offer victims and sacrifices in every place they saw—that is, wherever they wished—but ordered them to ascend to the place which the Lord their God had chosen and there sacrifice victims (Deut. 32).

Although, by a subtler understanding, he wished to signify the unity of the holy Church through the designation of a single place, nevertheless God, considering the mind of the human race, did not wish his worship to become cheapened and lukewarm through the multitude of many places. Rather, he wished to make it commendable through the famous gathering at one place.

If the place containing the ark, constructed from insensible wood and gilded inside and out, containing an urn full of manna, one staff, and the stone tablets, deserved to be ennobled and honored by so great a gathering of people (Exod. 25; Heb. 9), of how great religious reverence must that place be deemed which embraces the body of an Apostle, like an ark of heavenly treasure, conspicuous in body and soul through virtue, containing within it a splendid vessel—the soul—filled with the sweetness of wisdom, and the spiritual law written not on stone tablets but on the fleshy tablets of the heart (2 Cor. 5), together with the staff of pastoral authority by which he may spare the devout and conquer the proud?

It would also take a long time to enumerate how testimonies to this matter are scattered throughout the sacred Scriptures, like little flowers blooming with purple and rose-colored brilliance.

For example, how David received a command from the Lord to offer an appeasing sacrifice on the threshing floor of Araunah (2 Sam. 24); and how Solomon first said to the Lord, “If heaven and the heaven of heavens cannot contain you, how much less this house which I have built” (2 Chron. 7), and then, praying that the Lord’s eyes might be open and his ears attentive in that place, offered his most devout prayer. It is recorded by the Lord’s own testimony that he was heard, both for the native inhabitants praying there and for those who came together from every direction, even for those who came from the ends of the earth to pray in that same place.

We may also consider how blessed Elijah did not establish a new altar, but approached and cared for the ancient one, and how he frequently visited Mount Carmel for the sake of prayer (1 Kings 18).

By all these examples we are taught that those who visit the shrines of the apostles in order to increase their devotion and seek intercession through their suffrages are not to be disapproved or, as you do, called foolish and senseless. For we believe that through these visits not only does love of the service of divine worship grow in their minds, but they are also rewarded for the labor and journey which they willingly undertake out of divine love.

It is also characteristic of the human mind not to be moved as deeply by what it hears as by what it sees. For just as, according to blessed Jerome, the person who travels through and visits the places and cities named understands the divine Scriptures better, so we must believe that those who visit the apostles’ shrines can acquire greater devotion. They hear that one apostle was tortured in one place, another beheaded or crucified in another, and elsewhere inspect with their bodily eyes the place where one was committed to the earth.

For this reason blessed Jerome, expressing astonishment at the fall of a certain man who had contemplated committing fornication inside the enclosure of the cave in which the Son of God was born, is amazed that the man was not deterred from the crime he had conceived by seeing the holy places. He says [Note: [Col. 0367D] Letter to Sabinianus]:

“Most wretched of mortals, you enter that cave in which the Son of God was born, in which Truth arose from the earth and the earth yielded its fruit, intending to arrange a sexual crime. Are you not afraid that the infant may cry from the manger, that the virgin mother may see you, that the mother of the Lord may behold you? The angels cry out, the shepherds run, the star shines above, the Magi adore, Herod is terrified, Jerusalem is troubled, and you creep into the Virgin’s chamber intending to deceive a virgin?”

And shortly afterward:

“Then you run to the place of the shepherds, and while the angels resound above in harmonious song, you testify to the same things in the same words.”

Again, not long afterward:

“The journey has now been arranged, the ships agreed upon, the day fixed, the escape contemplated in your mind. And behold, that angel who was the doorkeeper of Mary’s chamber, the guardian of the Lord’s cradle, and the bearer of the infant Christ—the very one before whom you were committing all these acts—himself exposed you.”

Certainly, to come to the apostles, we know that as long as the Temple of Jerusalem stood, they frequently gathered there for the sake of prayer. Hence in the Acts of the Apostles they are read to have taught every day in the Temple and around the houses, celebrated the mysteries of the Lord’s body in the breaking of bread, and distributed them to the people for consumption.

For this reason, at the ninth hour, as ecclesiastical custom has it, Peter and John approach the Temple in order to worship there, and by their authoritative command release the lame man lying at the threshold of the house of the Lord from the bonds with which he was divinely bound (Acts 9).

For this reason Paul greatly desired and hastened with all his strength to spend the day of Pentecost in Jerusalem.

Since these things are so, let your irrational argument, so to speak, finally be gone. You strive to persuade the minds of little women, and, like a scorpion, while stroking them with your mouth, you secretly attempt to pour in poison with your tail, so that you may turn the minds of the faithful away from love of the holy places and of the apostles.

After this, as though wrapping up a horned syllogism, you try to entangle the same venerable man, who, as far as such an act permits one to understand, was correcting you in the exercise of charity, in the following manner:

[Col. 0369C] “I want first to question you yourself: If you know that doing penance means going to Rome, why have you for so long destroyed so many souls whom you retained in the monastery, received into the monastery for the sake of penance, and did not send to Rome, but instead made them serve you?”

Everyone who is contained within the bosom of Holy Church with a sound mind knows that she consists of various orders of profession—not in a different faith, though differing in manner of life: some devote themselves to marriage, others to celibacy; some offer obedience to prelates, while others restrain the flocks entrusted to them under a divinely given rule; some roam wherever they wish through the various [Col. 0369D] regions of the world with general freedom, while others, constrained by a regular and canonical bridle, have left themselves no avenue by which they may go or return, because of the command of their elders and prelates.

Since these matters stand thus, we reply in the words of that same venerable abbot: “Therefore, O Claudius, I did not destroy for so long so many souls whom I retained in the monastery because, following the commands of our father—namely, blessed Benedict—I have learned that the workshop in which the instruments of good works are exercised is the enclosure of the monastery and stability in the congregation. I also retain the judgment of the canons, which you are shown to ignore at the peril of your soul, and which agrees with this judgment. In the Council of Chalcedon, in the [act . . .], it reads as follows:

‘We decree that monks in every city or region be subject to the bishop, love quiet, and devote themselves solely to fasting and prayers, remaining in the places where they have renounced the world. They are not to participate in ecclesiastical or secular affairs, nor trouble anyone, abandoning their own monasteries, unless perhaps the bishop of the city commands them to do so for some necessary work.’

And shortly afterward:

‘We decree that anyone who transgresses this definition of ours be excommunicated, lest the name of God be blasphemed.’

Those who are not restrained by this profession, if for love of their heavenly homeland they undertake the arduous dangers of such great journeys, and, since they cannot yet be joined to the spirits of the apostles, nevertheless wear out the thresholds of their basilicas and humbly seek their intercession, I consider worthy of praise. For although the Apostle says, ‘I want men to pray in every place, lifting up pure hands without anger or disputation’ (I Tim. II), I understand this to have been said for those who do not know how to pray except where they see an erected altar or at least the relics of saints.

The Apostle himself testifies what opinion he held concerning this matter: he went to worship in the temple, where he was also arrested, and he was hastening there in order to celebrate Pentecost (Acts XX). But those who, so that they may be secure from external disturbances, seek the seclusion of a monastery—if, on the pretext of external wandering, they attempt to undertake secular business—I condemn and rebuke, and I do not doubt that this pertains to the destruction of their souls, because I recall the judgment of my teacher, who says that monks should have no necessity to wander outside, since this is wholly unprofitable for their souls.

As for your claim that I made them serve me, although I do not judge myself immune from this charge—for I have many deformities of character which the pious devotion of the brothers must endure in supporting me—I nevertheless try to follow divine authority, which says: ‘Whoever wishes to be greater among you, let him be your least’; and: ‘Let the one who presides be as one who serves.’

There is also a reciprocal servitude among us, concerning which the precepts of our institution say: ‘Let the brothers serve one another’; and elsewhere: ‘Let them bear with the greatest patience their infirmities, whether of body or of character.’ Likewise, let them eagerly render obedience to one another. The Apostle also says: ‘Through love, he says, serve one another in spirit’ (Gal. V).

Except for this, I know that I ought neither to impose private servitude upon my subjects nor recall having imposed it. Rather, I use Gideon’s words concerning his subjects: ‘I will not rule over you, nor will my son rule over you; the Lord will rule over you.’ For I fear that I may be assigned a portion with proud and faithless shepherds, and that at the fearful judgment the Shepherd of shepherds may say to me, as to them: ‘You ruled over them with authority and with power.’

Indeed, if the fulfillment of my desire is not denied me, I wish truly to say with the Apostle: ‘Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not inflamed?’ (II Cor. XI). And likewise: ‘I became a little one in the midst of you, as a nurse cherishes her children’ (II Thess. II). Hear also the salutary counsel of the wisest man, who says: ‘They have appointed you ruler? Do not exalt yourself, but be among them as one of themselves’ (Eccli. XXXII).

As for what you add, as though in my own words:

“‘I have a band of one hundred and forty monks, all of whom came to me for the sake of penance’”—

I recognize the number, but I not only deny that what follows was said by me; I shudder that it should be said by anyone else. For all those who, as the truth stands, entrusted themselves to the monastery for the sake of penance did not come to me, as you assert, but fled to the mercy of the Lord, to whom the Psalmist says: ‘To you all flesh shall come’ (Ps. LXIV); and to whom the penitent said in the psalm: ‘Lord, I have fled to you; teach me to do your will, for you are my God’ (Ps. CXLII); and to whom Jeremiah says: ‘Lord, my strength and my stronghold, to you the nations shall come from the ends of the earth’ (Jer. XVI).

Holy Scripture rightly indicates that the most just and devout prince—I mean Hezekiah—offended the Lord in these words (IV Kings XX). After, in a certain sense, he had taken away the right of nature and had confronted the swift course of the sun according to his own will, when envoys of a foreign nation came to question him about the portent, and the prophet asked him where those men had come from, he did not answer, as the truth required, that they had come to inquire of the Lord; rather, swollen with excessive pride, he said: ‘They have come to me from a distant land, from Babylon.’ And lest you think that this was said merely according to my interpretation and not on divine authority, hear the Book of Chronicles:

‘In those days Hezekiah became sick unto death, and he prayed to the Lord, who heard him and gave him a sign; but he did not repay according to the benefits he had received, because his heart was exalted, and wrath came against him, against Judah and Jerusalem. Afterwards he humbled himself because his heart had been lifted up, both he and the inhabitants of Jerusalem; therefore the wrath of the Lord did not come upon them in the days of Hezekiah.’

And shortly afterward:

‘Nevertheless, in the matter of the envoys of the princes of Babylon who had been sent to him to inquire about the portent that had occurred in the land, God abandoned him in order to test him, so that everything in his heart might become known’ (II Chron. XXXII).

Therefore I would not say that they came to me, since they renounced the world not for my sake but for their own salvation. I will never admit that they fled to me, for that is characteristic of the proud and of those who seek the favor of their own name. The Apostle long ago marks such men and calls them false Christs, who labor to lead disciples after themselves (II Cor. XI).

I do not therefore demand my own servitude from them because I retain them in the monastery; rather, I strive that our common order may be fulfilled by me and by them. But hear with what favor Jerome, the interpreter of the sacred law and, so to speak, the library of Mother Church, embraces the bodies of the martyrs, and with what authority he defends their honor against your kinsman, who barks against ecclesiastical custom and is your equal in wickedness:

[Note: [Col. 0371D] Jerome against Vigilantius.]

When Vigilantius says:
