“Why is it necessary not only to honor with such great honor, but even to adore, that something-or-other which is transported in a small vessel from place to place? And again: Why do you kiss and adore dust wrapped in linen?”

Jerome drives the hammer of the word against his mad brain:

“Who, O insane head, has ever adored martyrs? Who has considered a man to be God?”

And shortly afterward:

“What is that ‘something-or-other’? I want to know; explain it more clearly, so that you may blaspheme with complete freedom.”

“Some little bit of dust,” he says, “wrapped in linen in a small precious vessel.”

“He is distressed that the relics of the martyrs are covered with a precious cloth, rather than gathered up in rags or sackcloth, or thrown onto a dung heap, so that the drunken and sleeping Vigilantius alone may be adored.

“Are we therefore sacrilegious when we enter the basilicas of the apostles? Was the emperor Constantius sacrilegious, who transferred to Constantinople the relics of Saint Andrew, Luke, and Timothy, at which demons roar and whose presence the inhabitants of Vigilantius confess that they feel? Is Augustus Arcadius now also to be called sacrilegious, who long afterward transferred the bones of blessed Samuel from Judea to Thrace? Are all bishops to be judged not only sacrilegious but fools, who carried a most worthless object and dissolving ashes in silk and a golden vessel? Are the peoples of all the churches fools, who went out to meet the sacred relics and received them with such joy as though they were seeing someone present and alive, so that throngs of people joined together from Palestine as far as Chalcedon and resounded with one voice in the praises of Christ?

“Clearly, they were worshiping Samuel and not Christ, of whom Samuel was both Levite and prophet. You suppose him dead, and therefore you blaspheme. Read the Gospel: ‘The God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob: he is not the God of the dead but of the living’ (Exod. III; Matt. XXII).

“Listen, I ask you, to the custom and ancient practice of Holy Church, and do not transgress the boundaries established by your fathers (Prov. XXII), lest perhaps, despising their lowliness and thinking that you are flying to the heights, the more highly you raise yourself in your own estimation, the more deeply you may be plunged by the condemner of the proud into the depths of Tartarus.”

From these teachings you can be instructed—if the hardness of your leftward-leaning mind does not resist—that in the veneration of the holy relics Christ is worshiped by Holy Church as their sanctifier and vivifier.

John Chrysostom, in his homily on the Ascension of the Lord, says:

“When prayer proceeded from our cross, we celebrated the festival outside the city; and now, when we are discussing the ascension of the Crucified One, we go beyond the boundaries of the city and celebrate with the greatest rejoicing this illustrious day, radiant with every joy. This is observed not as an insult to the city but for the honor of the saints, lest they accuse us of neglect, saying: ‘How many torments did we endure for the Lord? We see all our bones stripped of flesh by the hands of our tormentors; the enraged torturer yielded to our endurance; our blood was poured out willingly for Christ; heads were cut off for his glory. We deserved to endure all these things, yet the mysteries are not celebrated in our tabernacles.’

“Therefore, beloved brothers, today we gather at the places of the blessed martyrs; we hasten to the dwellings of the saints, so that our assembly might be made more glorious by their presence as well. For the martyrs do not preside only in this theater; the attendance of angels also adorns the place, for angels are present too.

“If you desire to see the martyrs, if you wish to behold the angels, open the eyes of faith, and that theater will easily be shown to you. For if a multitude of angels is present throughout the air, much more are they present in the church, and much more abundantly today, when their Lord ascended into heaven.

“And so that you may know that angels are everywhere, hear what blessed Paul says while instructing women concerning modesty: ‘Women ought to have a veil upon their head, because of the angels’ (I Cor. XI). Jacob likewise says: ‘The angel who delivered me from my youth’ (Gen. XLVIII). And those who were with the apostles say to Rhoda: ‘It is his angel’ (Acts XI). Jacob also says: ‘I saw the camps of angels’ (Gen. XXXII).

“And rightly were camps of angels seen on earth. For just as all the cities, every town, and each fortress of an excellent emperor are fortified by military force against the approach of an enemy, and all places are carefully armed lest they be destroyed by a barbarian incursion, so God, because demons who seize with a barbarous and savage mind are everywhere active in overturning peace, established armies of angels for our protection, so that by their presence the audacity of demons might be broken and through them the grace of peace might be ministered to us.

“You see that angels preside, martyrs assist, and help is prepared for us everywhere. What, then, is more miserable than those who abandon this splendid assembly? And what is more blessed for you, who have wished to hasten to so great a solemnity?”

Gregory, too—the singular and foremost ornament of Holy Church in eloquence, and, after blessed Peter, the glory of the Roman see—will instruct you in the Book of Dialogues concerning his view of the bodies and patronage of the saints, in these words:

Peter: “What are we to say about what we often perceive even in the very patronage of the martyrs: that they display not so many benefits through their bodies as through their relics, and perform greater signs there where they themselves are not physically present?”

Gregory: “Where the holy martyrs lie in their own bodies, there is no doubt, Peter, that they are able to display many signs, as they indeed do, and to show countless miracles to those who seek them with a pure mind. But because weak minds may doubt whether they are present there to hear petitions where it is certain that they are not present in their bodies, they must display greater signs there where a weak mind can doubt their presence. But those whose minds are fixed upon God have the greater merit of faith, since they know that the saints are there, though not lying bodily there, and yet are not absent from hearing petitions.”

Let these barriers therefore close your mouth, so that henceforth the dignity of the martyrs may not be torn apart.

Your conclusion, which seems syllogistic to you, is brought to its end in this way:

[Col. 0373D] “If these things are as you say, and doing penance means going to Rome, what will you do with that saying in which the Lord says: ‘Whoever scandalizes one of these little ones who believe in me, it would be better for him that a millstone be hung around his neck and he be plunged into the depth of the sea, than that he should scandalize one of these little ones who believe in me’ (Matt. XVIII; Mark IX)?”

With the deity propitious, we leap over the nets you have cast uselessly before our eyes, for, supported by manifold authority as though by the aid of wings, we are lifted up.

Following the manner of our earlier response, we say that those who are free to go wherever they wish—if they desire to go to Rome and visit the tombs of the apostles in order to mourn their own offenses and thereby commend themselves more greatly to the sight of the Lord—we judge such an act not only not useless but highly beneficial. For, as we have said, not only the institution of the Fathers but also the oracles of the divine Scriptures favor our opinion.

Thus John Chrysostom, in an address on the Acts of the Apostles, exhorts us:

“Moreover, if any one of us is lame, if any is blind in one eye, if any is weak, he cannot enter the temple. But although we are weak, let us appeal to Peter and John; they will give us their hand, they will raise us up, and when we have become well, then we shall be able to enter the temple.”

As for those whom love of Christ, not I, retains in our little monastery, I do not scandalize them because, according to the canon and regular authority mentioned above, they are not granted the freedom to wander here and there; rather, secluded withdrawal is enjoined upon them. They rejoice that they abandoned the millstone long ago, because, by Christ’s favor, they escaped with me the laborious circuit of life which the wicked still traverse, concerning whom it is said: “The wicked walk in a circle” (Ps. XI).

We rejoice that we have escaped the depth of the sea, because, carried by the apostolic net out of the turbulent and filthy waves of worldly pleasures, we seem at last to have been brought to the monastic shore. There the Lord first fished for that one whose tomb you forbid us to visit—I mean Peter—when he said:

“Whoever has left house, or brothers, or sisters, and so forth, for my name’s sake, shall receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life” (Matt. VIII).

And to another he says:

“If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have, and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me” (Matt. XIX; Luke XVIII).

But, as is your custom, you are found to have brought forward the evangelical testimony according to none of the evangelists, mixing everything together at your own pleasure, omitting some things from one and taking others from another.

For when you say: “Whoever scandalizes one of these little ones who believe in me, it would be better for him that a millstone be hung around his neck and he be plunged into the depth of the sea, and so forth” (Matt. XVIII), you omit “of the sea,” although you are known to agree with none of the evangelists in that omission. When you add, “than that he should scandalize one of these little ones,” you seem to have borrowed this from Luke, who added it after the preceding words because he had not previously stated the comparison—namely, of scandal and drowning with a millstone in the depth.

But when you append “who believe in me,” you are found to be entirely alien to the wording of all the evangelists and to the sense [Note: [Col. 0375D] Jonas is mistaken, since Matthew expressly has the words “who believe in me,” chapter XVIII.]

Let your compilation cease at last, then; it is convicted of ignorance even according to the secular letters and, according to ecclesiastical discipline, either of folly or certainly of insanity. For it is not the act of a sound mind to mutilate the sentences of the divine Scriptures with such audacity.

As for what you say last:

“‘No scandal is greater than preventing a man from going along that road by which he can proceed to everlasting joys,’”

the stream of your expression would seem to flow clearly, unless the channel of your intention were perceived to be corrupted. For, on the contrary, you rebuke me because I reproved you for forbidding those traveling to Rome to go there, as though I were doing something else while reproving you for doing that very thing.

But I know that the highest perfection does not consist in the journey by which one goes to Rome. I also know that those who hasten there devoutly receive very great benefit, provided that their profession does not resist it. Therefore the missile of your rebuke, with the lightness of its insult, returns upon the head of its own hurler, because you try to silence the mouths of the weak so that they may not seek the intercession of those who, having conquered the world, enjoy secure access to the presence of the Lord, while those who remain weighed down by an earthly dwelling are compelled to think about many things belonging to the perishing world.

Having explained these matters from the apology of Theodemir, let us examine what follows.

[Col. 0375C] “We know that the words of the Lord and Savior in the Gospel are not understood, where he said to the blessed apostle Peter: ‘You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven’ (Matt. XVI). Because of these words of the Lord already quoted, an unlearned class of people, in order to acquire eternal life, setting aside all spiritual understanding, wish to go to Rome.”

No one who recalls either the times or the actions of heretics doubts that those who strive to overturn ecclesiastical institutions have always brought forward the weaker matters, so that by these, as by the battering rams of their engines, they may be able to shake the purpose of their superiors.

Therefore we are not surprised that you, bringing forward the ignorance of the ignorant and unlearned, also attempt to provoke the devotion of those who seem to excel others. For we know—and do not doubt that this will continue from the beginning of the Church’s birth until its end—that there will be few who shine with doctrine, but many who, content with simplicity, believe that what they recognize must be done is sufficient for their salvation.

The simplicity of these people is always exposed to the mockery of the enemies of Holy Church. Since they are thought to have less strength for resistance, their fragile outer defenses are first trampled down, so that the way may lie more open for battering the walls of the holy city, the Church.

Therefore you, O Claudius, as an enemy of the apostolic relics, first seek to turn the minds of the simple away from love of them, so that, as the attendance of the unlearned gradually ceases, the chill of your poison may extinguish the fire of love even in the hearts of those who are seen to excel others.

This is what you are trying to do when, with the arrogance of disdain, you say that an unlearned class of people, in order to acquire eternal life, sets aside all spiritual understanding of the Lord’s words and wishes to go to Rome.

Many, indeed almost all, understand the rock upon which the Church is built as the faith of blessed Peter, which is common to the whole of Holy Church—namely, the faith that preceded this promise a little earlier: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. XVI)—and that the Lord promised to build his Church upon this rock.

Who is there, even of limited understanding, who does not hold this faith and say: “I believe in God the Father almighty, and in Jesus Christ, his Son”?

As for the keys of the kingdom of heaven, the power of binding and loosing, although not everyone understands them as the matter truly stands, the ignorance of the unlearned does not prejudice the knowledge of those who discern. Therefore you vainly claim for yourself the palm of singular knowledge, while, as far as your words are concerned, you try to envelop everyone in the darkness of ignorance.

For what is an “unlearned class of people” except all unlearned people? If you had said “of unlearned people,” you might in some way have excluded certain persons. But since you accuse everyone generally of ignorance, you do not appear to have excluded yourself—unless perhaps you are trying to separate yourself from the human race.

It is therefore the task of wise men who abide in the bosom of Holy Church to understand the Savior’s words and, for the absolution of their souls, to beseech blessed Peter and the other saints not as gods but as God’s familiars, and, impelled by love, to visit the places of their confession and burial.

It is the task of the simple to imitate the footsteps of their elders and, insofar as they are able, to be united within the body of the Church.

But it is the task of you, your followers, and your predecessors to boast against your mother as though possessing singular knowledge, to despise her lowly members, and, at times, openly led by pride, to be cut off from her body, so that you may deserve to be separated from her future blessedness, in which those who are harmonious and united will rejoice—when her King and Bridegroom himself withdraws from the proud, saying: “Depart from me,” while he grants the humble perpetual blessedness, adding: “Come, you blessed of my Father” (Matt. XXVI), and so forth.

Having said these things, let us pass on to what remains.

[Col. 0376D] “Whoever understands the keys of the kingdom of heaven in this way, as was said above, does not require the intercession of blessed Peter locally.”

Your words are recognized as so full of folly and stupidity that it is merely astonishing if you yourself have understood what you are saying.

For what if, as was said above, I understand the keys of the kingdom of heaven to have been entrusted to the most eminent member of Holy Church—namely, blessed Peter—so that through him this dignity might pass to the others? Will my mind for that reason grow cold in love for him, whom I see honored more greatly by the Lord?

Rather, the fire of loving devotion burns more intensely toward him, who is established as so distinguished among the others that what belongs to all in common seems in some manner to have been received by him individually.

We do not require his intercession locally in such a way as though we were not open to his sight except in the place where we know his relics to be venerated. We firmly hold that every creature is confined for him who sees the one who sees all things and clings to the one who contains all things.

But we satisfy the devotion of the soul, which strives, insofar as it is able, to possess in every way those things which it has persuaded itself to love above all. We believe that the one who loved those who loved him unto death rewards such a fervor of devotion. He exalted women beyond their sex when they approached and frequently visited his tomb, and he made them, so to speak, preachers of the apostles; he first made known to mortals that he had risen.

Finally, hear blessed Augustine in the first book of *The City of God* (chapter 13), how highly he regards the bodies of the saints:

“Bodies of the dead are not to be despised and cast away, especially those of the just and faithful, whom the Holy Spirit used as instruments and vessels for every good work. For if a father’s garment, or a ring, or anything of that kind, is dearer to descendants in proportion to the greater affection they have for their parents, then by no means should the bodies themselves be despised—bodies which we bear much more familiarly and closely than any garments.”

Receive these words of the venerable man, instructed by them, and cease to turn the minds of the faithful away from love of the bodies of the saints.

The same most holy man and defender of the Catholic faith reports in the same books many miracles performed at the relics of the saints. Among them he adds that the bodies of the blessed holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, which had lain concealed and were entirely unknown, were revealed to Bishop Ambrose in a dream and found, where a blind man, the old darkness having been driven away, saw daylight.

Why, I ask you, Claudius, did the Lord wish the bodies of his saints to be revealed so earnestly through the venerable Bishop Ambrose, unless he knew that they would benefit mortals?

Meanwhile, that same mighty wall of Holy Church reports another miracle of this kind, among the others, in the twenty-second book of *The City of God*, saying:

“Hesperius has an estate in the territory of Fussala called Cubedi. When he discovered that his house was suffering from the harmful violence of evil spirits, through the affliction of his animals and servants, he asked our presbyters, while I was absent, that one of them should go there, whose prayers might make the spirits withdraw.

“One went, offered there the sacrifice of the body of Christ, and prayed as much as he could that the affliction might cease. Immediately, by God’s mercy, it ceased.

“Hesperius had received from a friend of his some holy earth brought from Jerusalem, where Christ was buried and rose again on the third day; he had hung it in his bedroom so that he himself might suffer no harm.

“But when his house had been cleansed of that infestation, he wondered what should be done with the earth, since he did not wish to keep it longer in his bedroom out of reverence. It happened by chance that I and my colleague, the bishop Maximus of the Church of Sinnita, were nearby. He asked us to come, and we came.

“When he had related everything to us, he also asked that it be buried somewhere and that a place of prayer be established there, where Christians might gather to celebrate the things of God. We did not resist; it was done.”

Consider, I ask you, Claudius, how highly blessed Augustine valued the dust brought from Jerusalem, since he ordered it to be hidden somewhere so that places of prayer might be established there, where a multitude of the faithful could also gather to celebrate the things of God.

It deserved to be honored by the prerogative of so great a miracle because there its author suffered, rose again, and displayed the other mysteries of our redemption, although the dust itself, being insensible, had no awareness of any of these things.

Consider also how much greater is the merit of the apostle’s body, and how much more powerful its authority for driving away harmful things and obtaining beneficial ones, since it was God’s dwelling and personally completed the traces of the Lord’s Passion by experiencing them.

Now what do you say?

[Col. 0378B] “For if we carefully consider the precise wording of the Lord’s words, it was not said to him: ‘And whatever you bind shall be bound on earth, and whatever you loose in heaven shall be loosed also on earth.’”

Who does not see the utterly foolish twists of your evasion? You suddenly pass from the intercession of the saints to the judicial dignity of the apostles. And, in order to deceive foolish minds and remove hope of intercession, you attempt to assert that the saints do not intercede for us because they do not remain in corruptible bodies.

Just as Peter is not seen sitting in the chair of the city of Rome, so, you claim, he no longer has care for the defense of the Church—as though, freed from the vanity of mortality, he could not intervene for us much more fully and familiarly than when he was once weighed down by an earthly dwelling.

But hear what blessed Augustine says against this in the twenty-second book of *The City of God*. After enumerating the miracles performed at the memorials of the saints, he continues:

“To what do these miracles bear witness, if not to this faith, in which Christ is proclaimed to have risen in the flesh and to have ascended into heaven with the flesh? For the martyrs themselves were martyrs—that is, witnesses—of this faith. Bearing witness to this faith, they endured a world most hostile and cruel, and conquered it not by resisting but by dying.

“For this faith died those who can obtain these things from the Lord, for whose name they were slain. For this faith their wonderful endurance went before, so that in these miracles such great power might follow.”

Jerome, *Against Vigilantius*:

“You say in your little book that while we live we can pray for one another; but after we have died, no one’s prayer can be heard on behalf of another, especially since the martyrs, while imploring vengeance for their blood, were unable to obtain it.

“If the apostles and martyrs, while still established in the body, can pray for others when they ought still to be anxious for themselves, how much more after their crowns, victories, and triumphs? One man, Moses, obtains pardon from God for six hundred thousand armed men; and Stephen, the imitator of his Lord and the first martyr in Christ, pleads for pardon for his persecutors. Once they have begun to be with Christ, will they be less powerful? The Apostle Paul says that 276 souls in the ship were granted to him; and once he has begun to be released to be with Christ, will he then close his lips and be unable to utter a word for those throughout the whole world who have believed his Gospel?

“Will the living dog Vigilantius be better than that dead lion? I would rightly propose this from Ecclesiastes if I confessed that Paul was dead in spirit.

“Finally, the saints are not called dead but sleeping. Thus Lazarus, who was going to rise again, is said to have slept. The Apostle forbids the Thessalonians to grieve concerning those who sleep.”

John Chrysostom, in his homily on Psalm 50:

“You see, beloved, how great is the power of penance and conversion to God from evil works. Here the holy David not only pleased God while he was in the body, but after his death he is found to have provided great consolation to the living.

“It happened in the time of King Hezekiah that the Philistines—hostile nations of the Jews—surrounded the city of Jerusalem. Although Hezekiah was a just man, he petitioned the Lord, prostrated himself, and prayed with tears, seeking vengeance upon his adversaries.

“Isaiah came to him and said that he should not think he had been heard because of his own righteousness—and certainly David had already died and had been resting for many years. What, then, does he say to him? ‘I will protect this city for my own sake and for the sake of David my servant’ (III Kings XIX).

“David is dead, but his merits live. O astonishing thing! O ineffable clemency of God! A dead man intercedes for the living! O the unconquerable struggle of the just, even after their completion!”

As though explaining the subtlety of your reasoning, you add the following:

[Col. 0379C] “And thus it must be understood that this ministry was granted to the bishops of the Church only so long as they themselves journey in this mortal body; but when they have paid the debt of death, others succeed in their place, who receive the same judicial power.”

You also add the example of blessed David:

“‘In place of your fathers, sons have been born to you; you will appoint them princes over all the earth’” (Ps. XLIV).

It is indeed true that, when the holy apostles and the successors of the apostles die, others are appointed in their place, so that, because they depart from the present light through a frail passing and the unavoidable debt of mortals, others may be substituted in their stead, by whom Holy Church may be governed with pastoral authority.

Nevertheless, it is not to be believed either that these successors receive the dignity of their predecessors except insofar as they have maintained the balance of equity, [Col. 0380A] or that the predecessors lose their judicial rights when, putting off the human being, they pass into the better life.

[Note: [Col. 0379D] Here Jonas asserts two things contrary to the sense of sound doctrine. First, that unjust priests lack the dignity and authority attributed to holy prelates; second, that just prelates retain after death the same jurisdictional authority that they possessed while alive. The first is the heresy of the Hussites, condemned at the Council of Constance, session 15, in articles 22 and 30, and [in the case of] John Hus, and at the Council of Trent, session 4, under Julius III, canon 10. See Thomas Waldensis, volume I, book III, chapter 81 and following, and Alfonso de Castro, book XII, *Against Heresies*, chapter “Power.” The second, however, conflicts with the opinions of theologians, who teach that the power of order—that is, the character—remains in the blessed, but not the power of jurisdiction that they possessed here in life. For the judicial authority that will be granted to the apostles at the universal judgment will be new and of a different kind from that which they had while alive.]

Since unjust priests lack the authority attributed to holy pastors if they have lost their rights, blessed Gregory bears witness to this when he says: “Thus it comes about that the one who exercises this power of binding and loosing for his own pleasures, and not for the conduct of his subjects, deprives himself of it.” But that the prerogative of judging remains intact for the saints who leave their souls’ bodily remains to the earth, Paul testifies concerning himself and those like him. “Do you not know,” he says, “that we shall judge angels, how much more the affairs of this world?” (I Cor. VI). Hence Isaiah says: “The Lord will come to judgment with the elders of his people” (Isa. III). Hence Solomon declares concerning the Lord, saying: “Her husband is renowned in the gates” (there is no doubt that he means the holy Church), “when he sits with the senators of the land” (Prov. XXXI). And the Lord Himself in the Gospel says: “Amen I say to you, that you who have left everything, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of His majesty, you also shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. XIX).

Cease, then, to rend so enviously the repose of the saints and, as far as lies within you, to annul their authority, lest you find against yourself as severe judges those whom you despise as though they were to be considered of no account. Meanwhile, from his unbridled, frivolous, and insulting boasting, with which he had long assailed the heavenly powers, he returns to tearing apart mortals and attacks the entire camp of the faithful of the holy Church with bitter words, saying:

> “Return, blind men, to the true light, which enlightens every person coming into this world; that light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it” (John I). “Because you do not look upon this light, you are in darkness and walk in darkness, and you do not know where you are going, because darkness has blinded your eyes” (II John II).

Whom, I ask you, do you call blind, unless perhaps the venerators of the relics of the blessed apostles? We do not deny it. For we, who embrace their ashes with devout love and venerate them with submissive devotion, are known to have been led by their preaching from the blindness of our hearts to the light of truth, as Isaiah bears witness, who long ago said concerning us: “Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened” (Isa. XXXV).

But, I ask you, are we therefore blind because we are moved by kindly affection toward the ashes of the bodies of the saints, whom the Son of God proves Himself to have loved so greatly that He does not allow even the least thing belonging to them to perish in vain, saying: “And not a hair of your head shall perish” (Luke XXI)? Or perhaps—and this is truer—we find that you wish to be called the true light, and assert, after Manichaeus, that the Paraclete has descended into you? For you would not utter such detestable boasts unless you were struggling with vanities, or certainly with things very like them.

But I think you will take greater pleasure in Eunomius, whose follower you are shown almost step by step to be: he wanted the books in which he spewed forth the poisons of his wickedness to possess greater authority than the Gospels. Perhaps, then, you assert that you are the light that has come into this world; and this is not surprising, since the Apostle says: “For Satan himself transforms himself into an angel of light” (II Cor. XI). You are the light; you are the brightness shining in darkness! Lying in the darkness of your perversity, you seem to yourself to shine, when it is plain that, by the very merit of your perversity, you are becoming darker.

But the darkness does not comprehend you, because those who humbly say, “I dwelt with the inhabitants of Cedar” (Ps. CXIX)—which is interpreted as “darkness”—and likewise with Job, “For we are wrapped in darkness” (Job XXXVII), disdain to comprehend your light. By not looking upon this light, they still remain in the darkness of humility and in the distress of the present life, and they do not know where they are going, because darkness has blinded their eyes: they do not submit themselves in the present to the Lord’s power and disposition, and in trembling expectation they await the Bridegroom of their uncertain destiny, wondering when He will return from the wedding.

These things, which you have raved against us in a frenzied manner, have been understood by us in this way. For it is the custom of the sons of the Church to turn even the words of their enemies toward an understanding useful to themselves. After this you continue:

> “You say that each faithful person ought to believe God when He promises; how much more when He swears?”

All who think soundly and believe God as He ought to be believed give Him faith when He promises, and likewise when He swears. God does not swear in order that the bond of an oath may deter Him from changing His decision, as happens with mortals, who bind themselves by oaths so that they may not fail in their promises; rather, for God to swear means to promise firmly and immutably.

For what is the meaning of the words “As I live” except “I say”? His decision does not change by bending in another direction, since He does not know change. Since these things are so, I do not know what distinction you wish to make between God’s promise and His oath, unless perhaps, falling into the error of the Anthropomorphites, you attribute human passions to God just as they attribute bodily features to Him, and measure God according to your own standard: you, who do not know how to fulfill your promises unless you happen to confirm them by an oath.

For us, God is believed when He promises and likewise when He swears. And because He swears by Himself, He is understood not to confirm by an oath what He has decreed, but to commend His unbounded and incomprehensible nature, since, as the Apostle says, “He has no one greater by whom He might swear” (Heb. VI).

Then you add:

> “What does it mean to say: ‘If Noah, Daniel, and Job were in the midst of it’ (Ezek. XIV)—that is, if they were of such holiness, such justice, and such merit as those men possessed, they would not deliver son or daughter?”

In saying this, you agree with us. For we believe the same things, instructed not by your writings but by the authority of divine speech, which says through the lawgiver: “The fathers shall not die for the sons, nor the sons for the fathers” (IV Kings XIV). Likewise through the prophet: “The soul that sins, it shall die. The father shall not bear the iniquity of the son, nor shall the son bear the iniquity of the father. The justice of the just shall be upon him, and the impiety of the wicked shall be upon him” (Ezek. XVIII).

But one can see you advancing with the tortoise’s gait, as nature is said to characterize the scorpion: flattering with your mouth and, as though seeking what is harmless, approaching with your teeth, while in your hindquarters, through a curved wound and a tube filled with the devil’s poison, you intend to pour venom into the hearts of those who hear you. For immediately you add, as though explaining the prophetic statement:

> “I say this so that no one may rely upon the merit or intercession of the saints.”

In the preceding passages, as the testimonies came to hand that were taken from ecclesiastical writers, we demonstrated that you had repeatedly pursued the false claim that holy men do not pray for the living. But why are you inflamed with such rage that you attempt to annihilate the honor and power bestowed by the Divinity upon the relics of the apostles and martyrs? Since perhaps you deserve to hear this from us, you must be struck by the words of the holy doctors.

For blessed Augustine, in the eighth book of *The City of God* (chapter 26), says that a certain Hermes sorrowfully foretold that the celebrated temples of his own time would later become tombs of martyrs, in these words:

> “Then this most holy land, the seat of shrines and temples, will be full of tombs and the dead.”

Against this, he responds to him—and to you, who grieve in the same way—as follows:

> “Certainly the lying spirit, at whose prompting Hermes said these things, was compelled by that very man to confess that even then that land was full of tombs and of the dead whom they worshiped as gods. But the grief of demons was speaking through him: they were mourning that their future punishments would draw near in the memorials of the holy martyrs. For in many such places they are tortured, confess, and are expelled from the bodies of possessed human beings.”

And Jerome, against Vigilantius:

> “But answer: how can such a presence of signs and powers exist in the most worthless dust and ash? I know, I know, most wretched of mortals, what you grieve over and what you fear. That unclean spirit which compels you to write these things has often been tormented by this most worthless dust—indeed, it is tormented by it even today—and the spirit that conceals its wounds in you confesses them in others. Or perhaps, following the custom of the impious Gentiles Porphyry and Eunomius, you pretend that these are the tricks of demons, and that the demons do not truly cry out but conceal their torments.”

If, entangled in such matters, you refuse to heed the advice of men of our own time, at least you ought to obey the counsels of the doctor mentioned above. “I give you advice: enter the basilicas of the martyrs, and at last you will be cleansed.” There you will find many companions of yours burned—not by the martyrs’ candles, which displease you, but by invisible flames. Then you will confess what you now deny, and you will openly proclaim your own name, you who speak in Vigilantius: that you are either Mercury, because of your greed for money; or Nocturnius, after Plautus’ *Amphitryon*, with whom Jupiter joined two nights together during Alcmena’s adultery while Amphitryon slept, so that Hercules of great strength might be born; or certainly Liber Pater, because of drunkenness, with a wine-cup hanging from your shoulders, your face always flushed, your lips foaming, and your insults unbridled.

Certainly, what you add is true:

> “For unless he holds the same faith, justice, and truth that they held, by which they pleased God, he cannot be saved.”

We certainly know that “without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. XI), and that each person is farther from salvation in proportion as he is distant from faith. But if he holds the justice—which is the general name for the whole body of good virtues—and the truth that the saints held, and by these pleases God as they pleased Him, I do not see clearly how he would need the intercession of those whose merit is equal to his own.

Yet I know and truly recognize that, unless faith remains unimpaired in anyone, unbelief separates him from entry into the heavenly kingdom. But if he falls into injustice or into some falsehood, and, according to the Apostle (I Cor. III), builds wood, hay, and straw upon the foundation of faith—that is, if he commits sins that are pardonable and slight—these things must be refined by the fire of tribulation, and, so that he may be freed from them more quickly, he must be helped by the intercessions of the saints.

For if we believe that we are cleansed from sins by the mutual sighs of intercession, since the Apostle says, “Confess your sins to one another, and pray for one another, that you may be saved” (James V), how much more credible is it that we can obtain forgiveness very quickly through the prayers of those who are joined more familiarly to God—provided that our heart is crushed by the pains of repentance? Consider, then, that you have spoken here also with insufficient care, and remember henceforth to avoid so deadly a doctrine.

After this you continue:

> “Hear this, foolish people, and at last become wise, you who seek the intercession of the apostle by going to Rome: hear what the often-mentioned blessed Augustine says against you.”

At last your impure mouth ought to have been stopped from insulting the members of Christ, if not by obedience to honor, at least by yielding to shame, and you ought to have remembered what punishment awaits those who utter insults. For when the Lord says in terrifying terms, “Whoever says to his brother, ‘You fool,’ shall be liable to the fire of Gehenna” (Matt. V), what refuge do you suppose you have, so that you may not be punished by such a sentence, when without cause you cast the charge of folly and stupidity upon your brothers?

Blessed David rightly used these words against those who thought that God had given eyes to others but did not Himself see what mortals did, and had given hearing to others but was Himself deprived of hearing. He says:

> “Hear, you foolish people, and at last become wise. He who planted the ear, shall He not hear? And He who formed the eye, does He not consider? He who corrects the nations, shall He not rebuke—He who teaches human beings knowledge?”

And what he himself thought about these matters, condemning their error, he makes clear by adding: “The Lord knows the thoughts of human beings, that they are vain.”

It is therefore evident that you have misused this testimony not only foolishly but also cunningly. Foolishly, indeed, since you wished to mock so many and such great men who now flourish in the studies of the holy Church. But as far as it seemed to you cunningly, you placed one person’s interpretation in the place of another’s, attempting to strengthen it, as though from the divine Scriptures, so that you might have some accomplices in your own understanding.

But when you claimed that blessed Augustine spoke these words against those who go to Rome to pray, this is in no way consistent with the truth. For the venerable Father, in the book you yourself cited—that is, the eighth book *On the Trinity*—was attempting to draw human minds away from the images of things that they read or hear in the holy Scriptures, so that no reader would dare to fashion for himself some imaginary conception of God.

As an example he brings forward not only blessed Paul but also the blessed Virgin Mary and the very face of our Lord Jesus Christ. He shows by reasoning that, just as no one truly imagines their faces or likenesses exactly as they were, or at least ought to believe that they were precisely as the mind depicts them, so no one ought in any way to doubt that they truly were human beings.

Among other things, therefore, he says:

> “Return with me, then, to the reasoning from which he had briefly departed”—for he had begun to show that each person ought to erase from his heart the image of the Apostle formed from his face, but ought in no way to doubt that he was a human being, and had admonished that everyone should not only believe this about him but also love him. “Let us consider,” he says, “why we love the Apostle. Is it perhaps because of the human appearance that we know so well, because we believe that he was a human being? Certainly not. Otherwise there is no one for us to love now, since that man is no longer a human being: his soul has been separated from his body. But what we love in him we believe still lives even now.”

I do not see what this passage of the venerable Augustine has to do against those who seek the apostles’ intercession. He says that he does not love the Apostle because of his human appearance, and no faithful person does so. For it neither diminishes our love nor adds to it whether his body was longer or shorter; nor does it matter to us whether—as rumor has it—baldness laid his forehead bare or a thick mass of hair covered it.

Nor is he loved because he was a human being, but because he was just. When Augustine adds, “Now there is no one for us to love, since that man is no longer a human being,” he explains this by continuing: “For his soul has been separated from his body.” He plainly shows that he was speaking of the likeness of his face, which his limbs, reduced to dust, certainly cannot preserve.

No faithful person, then, would say that he loves him because of those bodily features, nor would anyone visit his tomb on account of them, since, as Augustine himself said, they no longer exist. Rather, he is loved because he was just, and because, by the demands of his merits, he lives with God and his intercession has great power.

Therefore, Claudius, these words of blessed Augustine do not, as you falsely claim, work against us but for us. We consider the relics of the holy Apostle worthy of veneration because we know that he lives through the works of justice and his merits, and, as charity requires, we visit those ashes that once obeyed a righteous mind in the performance of works of justice.

Let us examine your final response, at least those of your writings that have come into our hands. It is of this kind. Replying to the abbot mentioned above, you say:

> “Your fifth objection against me is that you say you are displeased because the apostolic lord has become angry with me.”

As far as we understand from your words, this venerable abbot was greatly charitable toward you: he kindly corrected you when you taught empty things, admonished you with salutary advice to restrain yourself from them, and grieved because the prelate of the Roman Church had become angry with you. But let us hear with what disposition you received this correction from him.

> “You said this,” you say, “about Paschal, the bishop of the Roman Church, who has now fallen from this present life.”

What of it? If Paschal has died, will there be no one who can resist either your frivolous actions or your wicked words? But human wickedness has this characteristic: it promises itself impunity for crimes if it happens to escape the severity of human judgment. And so, although you ought to have returned to yourself when admonished and carefully guarded against anything sinister that might provoke anger against you, you are seen indirectly to attack the life of that same Paschal with the bite of slander when you add:

> “But he is called *Apostolicus*, as though he were the guardian of the apostle.”

This is contrary to reason. For what reason is he called *Apostolicus*, “guardian of the apostle,” when he is not appointed as the apostle’s tutor or, certainly, as his caretaker, but is substituted for the apostle as his vicar?

Thus your following interpretation, although incorrectly expressed according to the structure of the words, is nevertheless found to be close to the truth in meaning. When you ought to have said, “Fulfilling the office of an apostle,” you incorrectly used the accusative case instead of the ablative. For *Apostolicus* means “like an apostle”; hence we say *aspectum angelicum*, “an angelic appearance,” as though “like that of angels,” and *urbicum ius*, “urban law,” meaning law like that of those who belong to cities.

But that this interpretation of yours is directed toward criticizing the life of the man mentioned above, your subsequent attack makes clear, when you say:

> “Certainly he should not be called *Apostolicus* who sits in the apostle’s chair, but he who fulfills the apostolic office.”

[Note: [Col. 0385D] Read carefully.]

We admit that it is true that no one is raised to the dignity of the apostles merely by being placed upon the apostolic seat, unless it is established that he fulfills apostolic work. But you ought to have been careful lest, through your incautious criticism, you injure one whom you knew to be set over you, in accordance with the counsel of the Wise Man: “My son, do not despise your father’s old age, and if he fail in understanding, grant pardon” (Ecclus. III).

For how could you have borne his burden under the guidance of charity if you had seen him straying from the path of truth, when you could not bear him once you perceived him correcting your trifles? Hear, finally, what blessed Gregory says about incautious critics in the twenty-sixth homily on the holy Gospel:

> “Let the one who is under the hand of a pastor fear being bound, even unjustly; nor should he rashly criticize the judgment of his pastor, lest, even if he has been unjustly bound, through the pride of his swollen criticism the fault that was not there should come into being.”

The example of blessed David ought also to have come to your mind. Although he knew that he had been chosen for the kingship after Saul had been rejected, saw Saul often driven by the frenzies of an evil spirit, and perceived himself to be gravely oppressed by Saul’s persecutions, David not only refrained from harming him but also prevented any of his companions from rising against him, saying: “Who shall put forth his hand against the Lord’s anointed and be innocent?” (I Kings XXVI).

Finally, as though confirming your opinion with a Gospel example, you append the following:

> “Concerning those who occupy his place and do not fulfill his office, the Lord says: ‘The scribes and Pharisees have sat upon the chair of Moses. Therefore, whatever they shall say to you, observe and do; but do not act according to their works’ (Matt. XXIV).”

These words indeed rejoice in the fullness of truth, since they were spoken by Him whose judgment does not fall into any snare of falsehood. But it must be understood that good things are spoken well when they are uttered with a good intention; yet even words well spoken lose, so far as the speaker is concerned, the force of their goodness when they do not proceed from the source of love.

Read the words of the friends of holy Job. They inserted many good and salutary things into their speeches, but by the judgment of the Judge, who weighs the mind more than the words, they deserved to be reproved. He says: “You have not spoken rightly before me, as my servant Job has” (Job XLII).

The Pharisees could therefore rightly be reproved by the Lord and marked with such a rebuke by Him who examines the heart and remained free from every stain. Nevertheless, because they were prelates and claimed for themselves the honor of the priesthood, after doing what was His own task—that is, showing that their crooked actions deserved correction—He instructs us in the following discourse what reverence ought to be shown to such men.

For He urges us to submit to them, considering not their works but their teaching. Recall the striking of Uzzah (II Kings VI; I Chronicles XIII). Because he presumptuously wished to support the ark of God, he immediately deserved to experience the sentence of death. This example touches upon those who, by carelessly criticizing and despising prelates unworthy of their criticism, attempt, as though with the hand of criticism, to support their lives lest they fall—and thus offend God, whose representatives those who preside in authority are.

Learn also, believing the Apostle Paul (Rom. XI), not to judge another’s servant who stands or falls before his own master; and henceforth restrain your mind and mouth from such superfluous and frivolous criticism.

Meanwhile, the ship of this work, passing through the dangers of the world’s sea, with Christ as helmsman and the Holy Spirit blowing, protecting itself from contrary winds—that is, from unclean spirits—and spreading its sails straight ahead successfully, finally reaches here a safe and desired shore.

But if any reader or hearer should judge this worthy of criticism because the long and substantial responses to brief and slight objections are longer and greater than they ought to be, and therefore should rightly be rejected, I humbly ask and beseech you by the Lord that he, according to the fuller and more perfect understanding of his knowledge, should compose a shorter and more concise work to refute the objections mentioned above, which have certainly been hurled against the Christian religion, and, having been appeased, allow it to be brought forth for the hands and reading and hearing of those who wish to possess it.

# History of the Translation of Saint Hucbert, Bishop of Tongeren, into the Monastery of Andage

Written by Jonas while he was still alive. [Col. 0387]

(From Mabillon, *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, volume V, p. 293.)

## Preliminary Observations

### 1

Hucbert—or Hugbert, and in later writers Hubert—became bishop of Tongeren after Saint Ladebert from the year 709 and departed to heaven in the year 728. He was buried at Liège in the oratory of Saint Peter, which he himself had built. His body was placed in the tomb with the ornaments that he had been accustomed to wear when assisting at the divine altar, namely a linen undergarment and a planeta, or chasuble.

“But in the sixteenth year of his most blessed departure,” which was the third year of King Karloman—that is, of the duke or mayor of the palace—corresponding to the year 744 of Christ, his body was lifted from the tomb and found intact. Karloman took part in the sacred ceremony. He “together with the nobles and magnates of his palace lifted the limbs of the most holy man from the tomb-vessel, placed them in a casket, and carried them before the holy altar. There he vowed and bestowed upon him the greatest gifts: namely, silver vessels and cloaks elaborated in foreign workmanship, as well as estates and the revenues of estates, and likewise the servants of the properties.” [Col. 0387C]

### 2

Because the church of Saint Peter was humble and small, Walcandus, bishop of Liège, who had recently restored the monastery of Andage, transferred the body of Saint Hucbert there; it is this translation that we are discussing here. At Walcandus’s request, Bishop Jonas—undoubtedly Jonas of Orléans—committed the history of the event to writing and prefixed a dedicatory letter to the book on the life of Saint Hucbert, which book had been composed by one of Hucbert’s disciples. Both works are preserved in John Roberti of the Society of Jesus’ *History of Saint Hucbert*, together with a book on the miracles of the same saint, which we shall place after the following history of the translation.

### 3

The monastery of Andage, or Andain, so called from the stream flowing past it, later became the monastery of Saint Hucbert. It is situated in the Ardennes forest and in the diocese of Liège. The founder and first abbot of the monastery was Saint Beregisus, who had been educated in the monastery of Saint Trudo and is said to have governed canons at Andage. This occurred at the time when Pippin of Herstal was administering the royal household.

Later, when affairs declined, this community was reduced to a few clerics, while Walcandus, bishop of Liège, restored the collapsing buildings and assigned them to monks of our order. Afterwards he ordered the body of Saint Hucbert to be transferred there to increase the religious standing of the place; from that time onward monastic discipline has continued there down to the present. In the eleventh century the place was governed by Saint Theodoric, its abbot, whom we shall discuss in his proper place. Meanwhile, something must be prefaced here concerning Saint Beregisus and the cult of Saint Hucbert.

### 4

An anonymous monk of Andage wrote a little book on the life of Saint Beregisus, abbot, “in the second year of Otto, son of Henry, king of the Saxons or Austrasians, ruling over the Austrasians, which is the nine-hundred and thirty-seventh year from the Incarnation of the Lord,” as he himself marked the date. In his prologue he complains that “through the sloth of writers” the deeds of Saint Beregisus had until then lain in darkness. He testifies, however, that he undertook the work “at the request of the brothers,” and that he learned what he reports chiefly from the elderly monks Otbert, Wlbert, and Beregrinnus.

He first establishes the period in which Beregisus lived, namely under Pippin, mayor of the palace of Francia, whose chaplain Beregisus was. Since the author was concerned to establish the date of Beregisus, he says:

> “It happened that a charter was found, preserved and deposited under the church’s protection. For it had been given in the name of that venerable abbot during his own time by a certain count of that period, named Grimbert, and by it a donation of vineyards at Trier, which are still retained under the monastery’s ownership, had been made. When I examined it,” he says, “and could not easily penetrate the difficulty of its barbarous script, I finally noticed at the end that it stated that it had been issued in the fifth year of King Theodoric. From there I returned to the volumes in which the deeds of the kings mentioned above are described, and I found that under Theodoric, king of the Franks, Pippin, surnamed the Younger, son of Ansegisel, held the duchy over the Austrasians together with a certain Martin.”

Having established these matters concerning the date, the author begins the Life, of which this is the summary:

> “Beregisus was born in the district of Condroz in Austrasia, in a village called Spongius, to parents who were not free according to worldly status, but who nevertheless, by birth, were wealthy and religious. His father’s name has been torn from memory, but his mother is said to have been called Berilla. He was handed over by his parents and educated at Hasbania, within the monastery of Saint Trudo, under the religious habit, and was so profitably advanced in literary learning and divine law that by pontifical authority he was initiated into the sacred orders and raised to the venerable rank of the priesthood.”

Then Pippin, son of Ansegisel, took him into his household “as a chief priest, submitting himself, together with his wife and offspring, to be instructed by Beregisus’s teaching. But the prudent man, not forgetting to what waves of the shipwrecked world he was being driven, courageously turned back the ship of his mind by the rudder of faith and steadily strove to return to the harbor of repose.”

He incurred Pippin’s anger because, when Pippin alone in the church wore an ornament of the hair and was unwilling to remove it, Beregisus refused to admit him to the kiss.

After this, while Beregisus was once walking through the Ardennes forest with Plectrude, Pippin’s wife, he understood that the place of Andage had been divinely granted to him for habitation, and he obtained it from Pippin. There he “established a monastery, consecrated the basilica, which had been built in the name of the blessed prince of the apostles, with relics, and assigned the clerics their duties. While those clerics were serving in canonical order, the Father himself joined them in the same dwelling.”

After his death, his body “was buried in that very church and glorified by the manifestation of miracles.” His “deposition is celebrated on the sixth day before the Nones of October.”

This has been excerpted from the little book of the aforementioned anonymous author.

### 5

From these facts we first understand that the monastery of Andage had already been founded “in the fifth year of King Theodoric.” I interpret this as referring to Theodoric of Châlons, not to Theodoric, son of the younger Chlodoyei. In the fifth year of the latter Theodoric, Pippin, called the prince of Herstal, was not yet mayor of the palace; indeed, the monastery of Trudo, where Beregisus was educated, had scarcely yet been built.

Second, the monastery of Andage was founded for canons from the beginning, and Beregisus presided over them “in the canonical habit.” Jonas also attests this in the book that follows, writing that “the cell of Andage once flourished with inhabitants in the canonical habit.”

From this someone might argue that the monastery of Saint Trudo, in which Beregisus is said to have been “educated under the religious habit,” was likewise devoted to the same rule. But it can be answered that he was indeed educated there “under the religious habit,” but had not professed monastic vows, which were observed there by others.

Walcandus, the restorer of the monastery of Andage, assumed the see of Liège in the year 810. Later, “having changed the clerical order, in the year of the Lord 817, on the Ides of August, the day of Saint Lawrence the martyr, with the counsel of Pope Leo and the Emperor Louis, he established the religious life of monks there, assigning them possessions sufficient for those serving God there,” as Giles, monk of Aulne—or Aurea Vallis—writes. Altueus, or Alveus, was the first abbot placed over the monks.

### 6

The monastery of Saint Hucbert at Andage has since then been famous, distinguished by the crowds of peoples who gather there, especially those who have been afflicted by the bite of mad dogs. That this devotion is ancient is clear from the book on the miracles of the same saint, particularly from chapters 21 and 29, where mention is also made of an incision and of a piece cut from Saint Hucbert’s stole, which is customarily inserted into the forehead of those who have been bitten. [Col. 0390B]

# Here Begins the History of the Translation of Saint Hucbert

[Col. 0389]

### 1

In the year 813 of the most blessed Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, after the most renowned emperor, the most victorious and most pious Augustus Charles, had been removed from human affairs—he who had extended the bounds of the Frankish kingdom far and wide and enlarged the glory of Christ within his territories; who moreover struck the blindness of many peoples with all the strength he could command and, having snatched them from deep darkness, made them visible in the brightness of light—his glorious son Louis thereafter happily governed the imperial scepters owed to him and entrusted to him by God.

It was fitting that Christ should place over His empire such a great and worthy prince, in whom not only the splendor of ancestral rule should shine, but who, distinguished by nobility of mind, singular in prudence, and blameless in conduct, should become, through the excellence of so many virtues, an example to all subject to him.

He therefore resolved to dedicate the beginning of his reign to such great and worthy auspices that wrongs might be corrected, fallen good things raised up, and standing things strengthened. Each order in the kingdom entrusted to him was not to be tossed about indiscriminately by frivolity and depart from its proper rule. Rather, the secular order was to serve justice and defend the peace of the holy Church with arms; the monastic order was to love quiet, devote itself to prayer, and, having withdrawn from the activities of the world, not submit itself again to them either by choice or necessity.

The episcopal order, however, was to supervise all these matters, so that if any should deviate from them either by choice or necessity, they might, through the diligent judgment and prudent counsel of the bishops, be corrected and brought back to the line of rectitude.

## 2

In these matters, as was truly fitting, while many by their obedience to such exhortations offered an example worthy of imitation, Walcand, the venerable bishop, was no small one among them. For, partly through the prompting of the Godhead and in view of his reward, and partly stirred by the exhortations of this most sacred prince, he labored earnestly to ennoble the people entrusted to him by the Lord through exercises of good works, and always to raise them from good things to better ones; and if anything in his bishopric had remained in need of correction, he strove with all his strength to restore it to a better condition.

Accordingly, among the other things that required correction, a certain cell presented itself to his munificence, called by its ancient name Andage. It had once flourished with inhabitants living according to the canonical rule; but through the passage of time, having collapsed from excessive age and with its inhabitants failing away, it had almost been destroyed. It therefore offered itself as a kind of opportunity for his munificence, in which, with the reins of his generosity loosened, he showed by the execution of his work, rather than by empty words, how free he was from the vice of possessiveness.

For after restoring it almost from its foundations and renewing it again into a better condition, nobly setting aside avarice, he put its affairs in order, ennobled it with worthy buildings, and, in addition to the estates that it had formerly possessed through the generosity of religious men, added others from his own bishopric. He wished its inhabitants to be monks. He carefully anticipated and nobly arranged matters so that they would not be driven by want to extend the hand of need for anything, and so that they would not abandon their holy purpose.

He therefore acted so that, just as he supplied whatever was necessary, they too might perform whatever was pleasing to the divine will, and that they might in no way turn away from whatever the Godhead enabled them to accomplish. Having brought in the finest teachers of the regular life, he instructed them in the monastic way of life, and urged them, both by his own voice and by divine authority, to devote themselves to exercises of good works. Thus it came about that his labor was not frustrated by fruitless toil, but that, once the seed of the word had been cast upon very good soil, the fruit was quickly multiplied a hundredfold through the increase of the word’s harvest.

## 3

Thus, from every direction, devotees of religion began to gather at that same place, especially noble men from the monastery of Saint Lambert [Note: This is the name given to the cathedral church of the city of Liège, whose canons, in considerable numbers, withdrew to the monastery of Andage. For at that time the name “monastery” was also applied to cathedral churches. See Aegidius, the monk of Aigremont, in chapter 34, concerning Walcand.]. They had been inflamed by a desire for the apostolic life and were manfully maintaining the life of that same order through the uprightness of their conduct and deeds.

After, under Christ’s guidance, they had begun to find easy the road of holy conduct, which had formerly been rough for them, they sought increases in their perfection and devotion. They approached the aforementioned venerable and devout bishop Walcand, asking that he permit them to transfer the bones of the most blessed bishop Hubert from the place of his burial and transport them to the cell where they lived, both for their consolation and for the greater honor of the Lord’s confessor.

When the pious Father mercifully heard their request, he judged unworthy the place in which the holy limbs of so great a confessor lay. Nor did he deny that their pious request could and ought to be fulfilled. Nevertheless, lest he seem to have acted rashly and indiscriminately at the prompting of frivolity, he delayed their request for nearly three years.

But when the venerable men themselves insistently demanded that he grant it to them, he proceeded in all things with prudent counsel and consulted his own metropolitan, the venerable man Adebald [Note: Adabald, or Hadabald, succeeded Hildebold the archchaplain in the see of Cologne around the year 817. He also attended the council at Thionville in 821 and the council of Mainz in 828.], about the matter. The metropolitan, himself judging his own counsel, as befitted a man of the utmost humility, to be of least account in so great a matter, thought it best that they should approach the most Christian and orthodox prince, the emperor Louis [Col. 0391C], and jointly declare to him what the petition of the brothers, which had impelled them, was.

That glorious and unconquered Augustus, considering that the matter was extremely important and exceeded the capacity of a few because of its magnitude, decided that it should be referred to the venerable council of bishops then assembled at Aachen, and strongly demanded that the judgment of the holy assembly determine what should be done concerning the matter.

That same venerable and wholly God-beloved assembly, having considered every aspect—namely, who was asking and what they were asking, as well as the reverence due to the Lord’s confessor—decreed that the bones of the holy man should be entrusted to the request of so many religious men and placed in the monastery mentioned above, where they would be honored with greater religious devotion.

The often-mentioned bishop obeyed their decision, assented to their counsel, and granted the body of the most holy man Hubert to the aforesaid venerable men who had made the request.

[Note: Observe here that the transfer of relics required the consent of the metropolitan, the king, and the synod. This had in fact been established in chapter 50 of the Council of Mainz in 813. This council at Aachen seems to have been different from the one held in 817. Otherwise, why would the translation have been delayed until 825?]

## 4

For in the sixteenth year of his ordination [Col. 0392A], which was the year 825 from the Lord’s incarnation, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of October, they came to the urn of the most blessed confessor. The priests dug it up from the place of his burial with the greatest reverence, and from there the holy bones were carried in a procession attended by a great crowd of religious people and members of the clergy to the church of Saint Lambert.

After they had been accompanied there for three days with prayers and vigils, on the day before the Kalends of October they were carried with their reliquary to the aforesaid monastery. There, with Christ’s favor, they were magnificently deposited, as was fitting for so great a confessor.

## 5

But since the outstanding miracles of Christ, by which he glorifies his saints in many ways, must in no way be concealed, but rather, insofar as mortals are permitted to speak, must be proclaimed more and more faithfully for his praise and glory [Col. 0392B], we judged it highly improper and unworthy to cover with silence the magnificence that wonderfully shone forth in our own age around the corpse of the aforesaid holy man.

Indeed, as we learned from the truthful account of the often-mentioned venerable bishop Walcand and of certain other religious men, the entire structure of the body of that most blessed man was found wholly free and immune from that corruption which, because of the transgression of our first parent, was most justly inflicted as a punishment upon human nature—just as it is recorded to have been found and committed to the earth in the time of King Carloman [Note: That is, the mayor of the palace, in whose third year the body of Saint Hubert was raised, as was observed above: namely, in the year 744, the third year after the death of his father Charles Martel.].

If anyone desires to know fully how clearly divine power was manifested in the fact that, throughout so many elapsed ages, the body of the aforesaid holy man was preserved incorrupt during that prince’s time [Note: Jonas appears here to understand “ages” as years. At the time of Hubert’s death, not yet two centuries had elapsed.], let him carefully read through the account of this little book a little above. There he will very easily be able rationally to gather and faithfully observe with what honor, and with how great a state of preservation and incorruption, divine protection endowed it.

Since he has learned that no damage or corruption whatsoever was found in the body of that same holy man during its first translation, which took place under the aforementioned prince, he will in no way doubt that during this second translation, carried out by Bishop Walcand under the most pious and God-beloved emperor Louis, the body of the aforesaid holy man could be found solid and unharmed, protected by the same grace of Christ.

Thus, freed from every cloud of doubt and illumined by the clear light of truth, finding nothing except what he may marvel at and for which he may worthily render manifold thanks to divine power [Col. 0392D], he will undoubtedly proclaim with bowed head and loud voice that God is wondrous and glorious—not only in his other saints, but also in the body of this most faithful little servant of his, honored and glorified by the prerogatives of so many and such great gifts that violate the law of nature [Col. 0393A].

## 6

A period of approximately seventy-five years elapsed between the first and the second translation [Note: Rather, eighty-one years; that is the number of years counted from 744 to 825], while our Lord Jesus Christ reigned and promised that he would remain with his faithful until the consummation of the age [Col. 0394A], mercifully assisting them in their struggles and faithfully, happily, and ineffably rewarding their triumphs. He lives with God the Father and reigns as God in the unity of the Holy Spirit, throughout infinite ages of ages. Amen.

# In the Year of the Lord 843. Hildemar and Lambertus

## Historical Notice

(In Fabricius, *Bibliotheca medii et infimi Latini*.)

Hildemar, a monk from the regions of France who had been summoned to Milan with Leutgar, wrote around the middle of the ninth century an *Exposition of the Rule of Saint Benedict*. Leo of Marsica and Peter the Deacon incorrectly attributed it to Paul the Deacon; a codex of the monastery of Reichenau, which Mabillon examined, attributes it to a certain abbot Basil.

But in the codex of the monastery of Saint Benignus at Dijon, now preserved in the library of Saint-Germain in Paris, no. 667 [Note: Oudinus, vol. II, p. 47], it is found under this title:

> Here begins the teaching concerning the Rule of Saint Benedict, which Master Hildemar the monk taught and explained to his disciples. Therefore, I beg that whenever anything disordered or improper is found there, it be attributed not to the master but to the disciples.

This exposition of Hildemar is cited by Guido in the *Farfa Monastic Discipline*, recently published in the *Collection of Writers on the Ancient Monastic Discipline*, Paris, 1726, quarto, p. 48. At that place the learned editor notes [Note: In the *Catalogue of the Library of the Illustrious Lord Zacharias Conrad von Uffenbach*, 1735, part II, p. 250 [Col. 0396A], no. 59, the editor of this distinguished *Collection* is identified as Marquard Herrgott.] on p. 48 that he intends to publish Hildemar’s *Exposition* in a *Catena of Commentaries on the Rule of Saint Benedict*. Mabillon too had undertaken to publish this commentary with others in vol. II of the *Analecta*, p. 86 (new edition, p. 418), where he notes that chapter 14 of it contains Hildemar’s letter to Ursus, bishop of Benevento.

I read in the catalogue of the Melk monastery library, published at Vienna not many years ago, that a work of commentaries by Hildemar the monk on the thirty-eight chapters of the Rule of Saint Benedict exists in a manuscript codex of that library [Col. 0396A]. There is also there, without the author’s name, a letter to Ursus, the designated and elected bishop of Benevento, concerning the manner of reading. This letter is not inserted within the commentary; rather, it is prefixed to a treatise on the manner of reading and pronouncing the words collected both from the teaching of modern masters and from the authority of Blessed Augustine and the other doctors. Among these, Hildemar’s treatise on Luke is praised.

If this latter letter was written by Hildemar, as may reasonably be inferred from the codex examined by Mabillon, we obtain a definite indication of the year in which Hildemar was writing: for Ughelli notes that Ursus assumed the leadership of the Beneventan Church around the year 833.

## Letter of Hildemar to Ursus, Bishop of Benevento, Concerning the Proper Manner of Reading

To make it increasingly clear, we first wish to append the letter that Hildemar the master wrote to Ursus, the designated and elected bishop of the holy Beneventan Church, concerning the manner of reading well. Then we shall add below the other matters pertaining to reading, drawn both from the teaching of certain modern masters and from the authority of Augustine and the other doctors. This is the aforesaid letter:

> To his most holy lord Ursus, Hildemar, an unworthy servant, sends greetings.
>
> Finally, let your holy blessedness know, most sweet Father, that I love no mortal more than I love you. Therefore, since I cannot now benefit you in any other way, I continually beseech divine clemency for the salvation of your soul, so that, through the regard of that same loving mercy, you may be delivered from all the schemes of the ancient enemy, enjoy here the abundance of many virtues, and after the course of this mortal life deserve to attain the company of the citizens above [Col. 0395D].
>
> I, indeed, being sufficiently more wretched than all the most wretched, remain here devoted to a life of quiet, and could scarcely write what you commanded without anxiety of heart—especially since these matters are unnecessary for you, who know much more, unless I were mindful of the benefits of your divine charity, which your broad charity earnestly strives to bestow upon us.
>
> Therefore, for the sake of your affection, exceeding the measure of my knowledge and office, I shall endeavor to obey your command. Although the art of reading distinctly consists chiefly in punctuation marks, certain accents are nevertheless useful in some way to uneducated readers, and Donatus enumerates them.
>
> No one, after all, is unaware that the section entitled “On Accents” was published especially for the pronunciation of syllables, since through the force of accents the manner of sounding words is demonstrated. For we do not know how we ought to sound a long or short syllable, whether with the circumflex or the grave, except through accent, as Isidore says.
>
> The word “accent” is so called as though from *ad cantus*, “according to song,” because it is placed in relation to song. And although Pompeius says that only two accents are necessary in Latin, namely the acute and the circumflex, Sergius nevertheless says: “There are eight Latin accents: the acute, grave, circumflex, long, *yfen*, *diastole*, apostrophe; to these are added *dasian* and *psilen*, that is, aspiration and lack of aspiration.”
>
> Since the force of these accents is clear to you, I shall say a little about punctuation marks, especially since your letter instructed me to explain the art of reading distinctly—that is, the signs by which a reader can recognize cola, commas, and periods. Their explanation is contained more fully in the section entitled “On Punctuation Marks.”
>
> There are three punctuation marks, as Donatus says: *distinctio*, where a complete sentence ends; its point is placed at the top of the letter. *Subdistinctio*, where not much remains of the sentence; its point is placed at the bottom of the letter. The middle distinction is where approximately as much of the sentence remains as has already been spoken; its point is placed at the middle of the letter.
>
> “Distinction,” as Isidore says, is the figure of a punctuation mark for distinguishing meanings by cola, commas, and periods; when it is placed in its proper order, it reveals to us the sense of what is being read.
>
> Sergius says that a colon is where there are two independent feet, as in “he terrified the cities”; a comma, however, is when, after two or three feet, a proclitic follows that concludes a part of the utterance, as in the first verse of the first book of the *Aeneid*:
>
> > I sing of arms and the man, who first from the shores of Troy.
>
> But that concerns meter. In prose, the following is distinguished by these three points:
>
> > Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the wicked, and has not stood in the way of sinners, and has not sat in the seat of pestilence.
>
> Therefore do not be surprised that they placed the sign of the acute accent in the middle of the sense. As I have learned from learned men, these three accents correspond to these three points: up to the middle of the entire sense, the grave; in the middle of the sense alone, the acute; and thereafter up to the complete sense, the circumflex.
