Thus there is neither a circumflex before the acute nor a grave in any way after the acute.
>
> The reader must observe this above all: only in the middle of the sense of the entire utterance should his voice be raised somewhat more prominently; before the raising, it should be lowered at each point of subdistinction; and after the aforesaid raising, it should be circumflexed at each point, subject to the sense that Donatus discusses in his treatment of accents.
>
> For among other things he says that monosyllables having a shortened vowel are to be pronounced with the acute accent, such as *fax*, *pax*, *nix*, *nux*; but those having a lengthened vowel are to be pronounced with the circumflex, such as *res*, *dos*, *spes*.
>
> In the middle of the sense of an utterance, we should not sharpen the final syllable, which the art permits only in a few cases for the sake of distinction. Rather, we say that the whole final part of the utterance should be pronounced higher, lowered, or circumflexed, while each part and proclitic retain its natural sound.
>
> In questions and inquiries, the reader’s voice must be raised, but somewhat more forcefully than with the acute accent. These are the signs of questioning: `?`; this is the sign of inquiry: `῏`; this is the sign of negation: `ῃ`.
>
> The ancients, with Augustine as their authority, said that inquiry and questioning differ in this respect: many answers can be given to an inquiry, whereas a question receives either “no” or “yes.”
>
> For example, we read as an inquiry:
>
> > Who will bring an accusation against God’s elect? ῏
>
> What follows is pronounced in the tone of a question:
>
> > God, who justifies?
>
> so that the unspoken answer may be “no.”
>
> Likewise, as an inquiry:
>
> > Who is he who condemns? ῏
>
> What follows is pronounced as a question:
>
> > Christ Jesus, and so forth, up to “for us”?
>
> so that the answer may be “no.”
>
> These punctuation marks are so called either because they are marked by placed points, or because, where the voice is lowered or raised or circumflexed on account of the interval of distinction, they are used accordingly.
>
> The sign whose name is *yfen* must join words that have been wrongly separated, as in *antetulit*. An apostrophe, however, separates words that have been wrongly joined, as in *conspicitur’sus*.
>
> Nor should this be omitted: for the sake of inactive readers, syllables and sometimes feet are occasionally marked in prose, as in: *édomo, édocet, sáturo, imitor, álacer, qúandiu, Híeremiás, Isaiás, trucído, addícit, revéra, pudícus, íllicit, íbidem*. Such notation is found very rarely in ancient books.
>
> O my lord, here is what you requested. I could not write it either more briefly or more clearly. Nevertheless, it seems to me, rustic and ignorant as I am, that these matters suffice as far as skill in reading is concerned. Only the sound of the voice is lacking, which must vary according to the various points and signs, and therefore cannot be written.
>
> Indeed, it is apparent only to the eyes of the holy and indivisible Trinity how much I cannot fully disclose to your nobility through a written inquiry—how much I trust in your prayers, or how mindful I myself remain of you. I commend myself to Father Leo and to the other brothers who are with you, begging through our common Redeemer that they at least remember me once when praying to God.
>
> I nevertheless earnestly beg you to remember all the brothers living here, so that they may be protected from every evil by your prayers, strengthened in good devotion, and adorned with the jewels of hope, faith, and charity.
>
> May the loving mercy of the Almighty grant you to escape all the snares of the sins that steal upon us, to run with devoted mind along the way of salvation, and, when your course is completed, to pass by the straight path into the heavenly kingdoms.

## Letter of Lambert of Pultaria, Monk, to Alberic the Abbot, Concerning the Proper Manner of Reading

To Lord Abbot Alberic and the brothers who are with him, Brother Lambert of Saint Peter of Pultaria sends greetings.

What you sent to me, so that you might be instructed by an unlearned man contrary to your expectation, seemed almost like irony rather than a genuine need for knowledge, since your life and conduct appeared to be devoted to the cultivation of righteousness. For you sent, as the proverb says, a sheep to a goat to borrow wool, so that I—already senile, already delirious, already covered with lethargy [Col. 0398D], and stammering with a toothless mouth—might teach Minerva herself.

Nevertheless, lest you perhaps think that I rejected your request not because of a true awareness of my ignorance or a poverty of understanding, but rather from laziness or contempt, I have attempted, with a timid hand, to jot down in the manner of a Psalter certain matters that I either learned from masters and could scarcely recall, or retained through long practice.

I have regarded you, our friends, as supporters of my ignorance, not mockers. If anything here pleases you, attribute it to the merit of God’s mercy shown toward you; but if anything displeases you, attribute it to my error. And yet, if I have become a fool, you compelled me to do so.

Thus far we say *usque modo*, although it would seem more correct to accent the antepenultimate syllable. We say *aliquó módo*, *quoquo módo*, *quonam módo*, *quodam módo*, *nullo módo*. For, as Priscian says, there are cases in which two parts are taken as one, with different meanings among adverbs, such as *ullómodo*, *nullátenus*, *omnino*, *usquémodo*, and others of this kind.

We say *alicujus* and *alicujúsmodi*, *nulliúsmodi*, *istiúsmodi*, *aliunde*, *próinde*, *éxinde*, *súbinde*, *déinde*, *abintus*, *déintus*, *dé intro*, *déforis*, *áforis*.

Priscian says that when, among the Greeks, a preposition compounded with certain words causes the penultimate syllable to bear an acute accent, it makes the antepenultimate likewise acute. Among us, this occurs in only one place, namely in adverbs: the antepenultimate is made acute in *inde*, *déinde*; *intus*, *déintus*, *ábintus*; *intro*, *déintro*; *lónge*, *délonge*, *álonge*, *ámodo*, and so forth. Otherwise, if the preposition were lowered rather than accented, it might be thought to stand before the adverb as a separate word, which is not permitted.

From these and the matters mentioned above it can be inferred how *usquemodo* ought to be accented. And note that in some cases usage prevails, in others reason, and in still others usage, reason, and authority agree.

Some say *enimvero*, others *enimvéro*. But because here my usage is uncertain, authority does not support me, and my reasoning is not firm, I leave the matter to your judgment or superior intelligence.

We say *équidem*, *quandóquidem*, *quoniámquidem*, *átubi*, *ástubi*, *úbiubi*, *úbinam*, *quisnam*, *quinam*, where the syllabic epenthesis does not appear to have been displaced, as it is found in certain nouns, pronouns, and adverbs.

We say *quamóbrem*; *áttamen*, *sédtamen*, *úttamen*; *siquando*, *néquando*, *aliquando*. For these are compounded from the primitive temporal adverb *quando*: *siquando*, *néquando*, and *aliquando*. As Priscian says, they have an acute antepenultimate so that they will not be thought to consist of two separate parts. To distinguish it from *aliquanto*, which seems to have a similar sound, the penultimate syllable of *alíquando* is accented.

We say *quámdiu*, *támdiu*, *aliquámdiu*, *tantómagis*, *quantómagis*, *multómagis*, *siquóminus*, *paulóminus*, *nihilóminus*, *multominus*, *tantominus*, *quantominus*, *quominus*, *multominus*, *tantominus*, *quantominus*, *quominus*, *paulópost*, *alióquin*, and so forth.

We say *propémodum*, *alphabétum*, *intérsit*, *interest*, *monarchia*.

Nevertheless, we say *neoménia* and *scenophigia* with a shortened penultimate syllable, following the analogy of Latin nouns, in which a long *i* before *a* or another vowel is rarely found, although in such words the Greek form should, in our language, be changed to a long *i*.

For the Greeks say *tragedeia*, *comedeia*, *Alexandreia*. In our language, with *ei* changed into a long *i*, we ought to say *tragedia*, *Alexandria*, and so forth, with the *i* lengthened. But in this matter we sometimes follow the Latin poets, who pronounced the *i* shortened according to their custom, as Horace:

> To utter light verses, an unworthy tragedy.

And Juvenal:

> … For what mime is better in comedy, with a weeping throat?

We corrected in the Psalter: *dirumpamus* and *dirupisti*, removing the *s*. For, as Priscian testifies, although the prepositions *dis-* and *di-*, which are found only in compounds, have the same meaning, *dis-* is used only when it is followed by *e*, *f*, *s*, *p*, or *t*, or by *i* in the place of a consonant, as in *discumbo*, *differo*, *dispergo*, *distraho*, *disjungo*.

But when any other consonant follows, *di-* is prefixed, as in *dimitto*, *diduco*, *digero*, *diluo*, *dirimo*, *diruo*, *dirumpo*, *dirigo*.

Isidore says in the book of his *Etymologies*:

> Emor built Sichem, a city of Samaria, which in Latin and Greek is called *Sychima*, and named it after his son Sichem. It is now the city of Neapolis among the Samaritans.

We find this name written everywhere in the history with an *h*.

In the words *cássia* and *pellícanus*, we find *s* and *l* doubled in most ancient books. But whether this doubling ought to arise from the formation of the names themselves, we do not read.

This is all that Isidore says about these matters in his book of *Etymologies*:

> The pelican is an Egyptian bird, living in the solitude of the River Nile; hence it also received its name, for Canopus is called Egyptian.

So much for the word.

Again, when he was treating of aromatic trees, he says:

> Cassia grows in Arabia, a branch with a strong and purple bark, with leaves like those of pepper.

Nothing more.

Whatever value these observations may have, both here and in the Psalter, accept them for the time being as arising from the feeble knowledge of your friend, which you have, as it were, extorted from me when I was afraid not to obey. If they do not displease you, accept them; and if something more accurate should elsewhere shine upon you, do not delay entirely erasing these observations of ours—or rather not ours, except insofar as they have been reviewed by us—lest, God forbid, they cause someone’s sincerity to grow sour.

Farewell, and lend a hand of prayer and counsel to us, who are sailing between Scylla and Charybdis but, because of the excessive storm, can scarcely manage to row, lest we be swallowed up.

# In the Year of the Lord 843. Theganus, Chorepiscopus of the Church of Trier

## Historical Notice

(In Fabricius, *Bibliotheca medii et infimae Latinitatis*.)

Theganus, chorepiscopus of the Church of Trier, wrote in the ninth century a book on the deeds of Louis the Pious, extending to the year 837, more honestly than learnedly, as Miraeus judges. It was published with other writers of Frankish history by Pierre Pithou, and also in the *Writers of German History*, which bear the name of Culpis or, alternatively, Schilter, p. 69.

The Vindobonensis Library preserves a much more extensive copy than Pithou’s, according to Lambecius, vol. II, p. 391.

He also wrote a letter to Hatto, bishop of Mainz, when he sent him Alcuin’s book *On the Trinity*. It was published in the *Ample Collection* of Edmond Martène and Ursin Durand, vol. I, p. 84.

# Theganus’s Life of the Emperor Louis

(Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*.)

## Pertz’s Preliminary Notice

We learn from the entire work, and especially from chapters 3, 20, and 50, that the author of the following work was a cleric and the younger son of a certain noble family. The preface of Walafrid Strabo prefixed to the work names Theganus, a Frank by nation and chorepiscopus of the Church of Trier.

There survives a letter of his to Hatto, written when he sent him Alcuin’s book *On the Trinity*, as well as verses by Walafrid Strabo addressed to him in the person of Tatto, his teacher at Reichenau. We reproduce here the verses from Canisius’s *Ancient Readings*, vol. VI, p. 643, and the letter from the *Ample Collection* of Martène and Durand, vol. I, p. 84:

> In these little verses, most holy teacher Thegan,  
> Tatto, humble, sends you words of greeting with joy.
>
> I am constrained amid doubtful matters, with varying restraint,  
> Whether I should say little or rather remain silent.
>
> Mutual affection compels me to write,  
> But I fear, Father, that I may not offer you worthy words.
>
> Even if Tullius should return from the deepest underworld,  
> Or great Plato open his eloquent mouth;
>
> Or Titus Livius himself bring Cato with him,  
> Or the talkative Sappho sharpen her polished tongue,
>
> They could never worthily proclaim  
> The wondrous praises of you, for they are very many.
>
> We rightly marvel at the gifts of your wise mind,  
> Your learning, character, poems, words, and spirit.
>
> No less do we marvel outwardly at the holy growth  
> Of your stature, your limbs, hands, and face.
>
> We are small and humble; our form has reduced us to a mouse,  
> While the glory of your great bulk makes you a giant.
>
> But setting these things aside, with all our strength we ask  
> That you not tear apart the verses given, beloved bishop.
>
> Rather, provide writings answering our writings,  
> By which, we ask, you may admonish us when corrected.
>
> Indeed, we shall also give you a few things for the boys to read,  
> Some of our jokes, so that you may cut away what is faulty.
>
> But as for the rest, if you wish to command anything,  
> We are wholly ready to follow your orders.
>
> We earnestly ask that you not deprive us, whom you love,  
> Of the honey-sweet measures of your teaching.
>
> Thus indeed we ourselves shall dare humbly, in words,  
> Likewise to send you gifts of salvation.
>
> May divine majesty provide you with every good  
> And make you joyful in attaining the kingdoms of heaven.
>
> Farewell now; may you flourish for ages, rich in merits,  
> And remember us, as we remember you in our prayers.

The same to the same:

> Receive, most holy bishop Thegan, the small gifts  
> Of your Strabo, which he sends you with joy.
>
> Remember Strabo in your prayers while you offer vows to the Thunderer;  
> He too is always mindful of you.
>
> I shall send the verses of the pygmy as soon as the giant  
> Has leisure. Farewell always and everywhere.

Amen.

### Theganus to Hatto

> “To the venerable lord and most noble father in Christ, Hatto, duke and consul, Theganus, a sinner, although a bishop, sends greetings in the Lord Jesus Christ.
>
> “After I had long considered what I might present from my poverty to your serene presence, in view of your immense kindness—which you have continually deigned to show, although my merits did not demand it—and wishing to commend the memory of my name to your piety, nothing else occurred to me except that I should send you some little work of the holy Fathers, in which your holy intellect might exercise itself.
>
> “Therefore I sent you this volume, which the holy Alcuin, the supreme teacher, gathered into one from various books of Saint Augustine and presented to the most learned and noble emperor Charles, as the prologue to this book indicates. In it may be found, as is of the greatest necessity for mortals, material concerning the divine nature and essence, the eternal generation by God the Father, the eternal birth of the Son of God, the eternal procession of the Holy Spirit, the incarnation of Jesus Christ the Son of God, and how God is one and triune, and triune and one, as the true faith commands us to believe. Whoever does not believe in this way is alien from Christ.
>
> “And in another hand: May the renowned glory of Christ deign to preserve and protect you for a long time in this age, and after these mortal times lead you to that blessedness whose end cannot draw near. Farewell.
>
> > Hail, great father; may you always be happy forever.  
> > May God everywhere add heavenly gifts to you.  
> > Thus Thegan prays; thus he always makes his petition;  
> > May the Lord who sits on the lofty throne also be his hearer.”

He should be thought to have written the *Life of Louis* in 835, for in chapter 55 the death of Lothair’s friends, which occurred in the autumn of 836, and in chapter 57 the rebellion of King Louis, which began only in 838, are mentioned. These passages seem to have been added after the work had already been completed.

The appendix for the years 836 and 837 was added either by Theganus or, certainly, by a cleric of Trier and a member of Archbishop Hetti’s household. He begins the year on the day of the Lord’s Nativity (chapter 56).

Since Walafrid has already passed sound judgment on the work itself, there is no need for us to add much. Nevertheless, we cannot refrain from observing that what precedes the year 830 is found for the most part in much fuller form in the *Annals of Einhard*, whose *Life* he must also be considered to have had before his eyes when describing the emperor’s character and appearance. His style of writing reveals no exceptional cultivation of mind.

The first editor of the work, Pierre Pithou, in *Contemporary Writers*, XII, pp. 291–321, used, as he himself reports, a paper codex of comparatively recent date, in which Theganus’s work was followed by the document of the division of the empire by Charlemagne. Following traces of this manuscript, without using any other aids, Culpis p. 67, Chesnius vol. II, p. 273, and Bouquet vol. VI, p. 72, added nothing beyond the testimony concerning Theganus by Christoph Brower, a recent writer, together with Walafrid’s verses, a few notes, and the appendix for the years 836 and 837, published by Lambecius in his *Commentaries on the Imperial Library of Vienna*, vol. II, p. 341 (Kollarius, *Analecta*, vol. I, p. 595). Bouquet rendered valuable service through several notes.

The sources used for our edition were:

1. A codex of the Imperial Library of Vienna, listed in the catalogue of profane history under no. 332, formerly belonging to the celebrated monastery of Admont. It is written on parchment in two columns per page, dating from the eleventh century or the beginning of the twelfth, and also contains the *Chronicle of Regino*. Of all the manuscripts known up to now, it alone contains the appendix. At its end, verses added in the same hand state that the codex was written by Gauzbald at the command of Prince John, or Jordan:

> This genealogy the prince ordered to be made.  
> The aforesaid John was once Jordan.

[Col. 0403D] At the command of Lord Gauspaldus, [I caused] these letters to be inscribed.

May he who sits upon the lofty throne preserve both of them.

May illustrious John be safe and learned throughout the world.

May he fill his house and indeed nourish orphans.

May the Lord repay him here and in the future.

May the Lord preserve him and also his sons,

and may he guard this man together with his father forever.

I have composed these little hexameter verses

in honor of him who ordered them to be written.

The identity of both persons may be questioned. The barbarous manner of writing is by no means inconsistent with that of the Lombards of the period; the title *princeps*, virtually a proper name among the princes and counts of Salerno, Benevento, and Capua, also fits; and the name Jordan, familiar among them but scarcely encountered in Germany, is appropriate. The date of the manuscript, moreover, and the fact that “that John or Jordan” was probably Jordan I, prince of Capua from 1058 and again from 1078 to 1090, father of Richard and Jordan II, readily persuade me of this. I nevertheless regard Gauszbaldus as a foreigner, since he does not use the Beneventan script. [Col. 0404A] Nor is it altogether extraordinary that Thegan’s work should have reached Capua, since the Cassinese possess even today excellent Beneventan manuscripts of Gregory of Tours and Widukind of Corvey, written in the eleventh century or at the beginning of the twelfth. I used the manuscript at Vienna in 1820.

2) A manuscript of the ecclesiastical library of Schaffhausen, transmitted to us by the illustrious Ittner Dumgius, of blessed memory, and collated by him with the printed editions, is assigned to the tenth or eleventh century; in the words of chapter 43 it ends with “for all indeed.”

3) A manuscript formerly belonging to Prüm, now at Trier, written on parchment in 1084 by the scribe Arnold at the direction of Wolfram, abbot of the monastery of Prüm, was collated for our purposes by the distinguished Wyttenbach with the printed editions.

4) The Bouquet edition, or rather the Pithou edition reproduced by Bouquet.

5) A paper manuscript of the Royal Library at Hanover, written in quarto toward the end of the fourteenth century, [Col. 0404B] containing excerpts from the entire work, using the author’s own words wherever possible.

6) A paper manuscript of the Steinwehr Library, now located at Wrocław, apparently from the sixteenth century (cf. Bredow, *On Charlemagne*, 1814, p. 180); we owe its more noteworthy readings to the distinguished Stenzel, an excellent promoter of the history of his native land and a public professor at Wrocław.

When all these witnesses were collated with one another and with the fragment of Thegan inserted under the year 838 in the *Annals of Metz*, written at the end of the tenth or in the eleventh century, the following conclusions emerge:

a. The Bouquet edition conflicts with all the manuscripts and with the Metz annalist; the latter witnesses, however, agree with one another.

b. The Vienna manuscript, which agrees almost word for word with the Metz witness, is superior to the others.

c. The Schaffhausen and Trier manuscripts, both in grammar and in individual words and syntax, have modernized Thegan’s distinctive language; the Schaffhausen manuscript has in this respect often departed farther from our author, and its testimony is confirmed only once, as regards word order, by the Metz witness.

d. The Hanover manuscript follows the Vienna manuscript chiefly in the writing and placement of words.

e. The Wrocław manuscript comes next in proximity to these.

f. Pithou, in editing Thegan, and Chesne, in editing the *Annals of Metz*, attributed too much authority to their own grammatical rules. Thus, in chapter 19, they changed *tenuis* to *tenuibus*, *graciles* to *gracilibus*, and *femoralia* to *feminalia*, although all the manuscripts alike reject these forms. Pithou inserted words at will—for example, “a golden crown shining with gold”—and, apparently believing himself to be correcting the numbers and cases of nouns, the tenses and moods of verbs, and the order of words, omitted or altered them.

The principle of our edition was therefore to adopt in the text the reading of the Vienna manuscript wherever it was supported by the authority of either the Schaffhausen or the Trier manuscript, or of both, while eliminating, with the help of the other witnesses, the errors attributable to its unskilled scribe. This applied especially where one, two, or three letters had been omitted and could easily be restored from the Schaffhausen manuscript. We likewise decided not to follow the spelling of the Vienna manuscript in forms such as *precium*, *tercius*, *pocius*, and the like, since these occur only there and were not accepted in the ninth century. In reporting the readings of the other manuscripts, I thought it unnecessary to include everything occurring in only one manuscript and of no importance, but attributable merely to scribal negligence, such as transpositions of words. I retained, for the convenience of readers, the division of the work into chapters instituted by Walafrid, although it is found only in the manuscripts of Pithou and Hanover. Very few notes were needed, since Einhard’s *Annals*, down to the year 829, serve as an extensive commentary; with their help I also added the years in the margin and retained those added by Bouquet.

[Col. 0405A]

# WALAFRID STRABO’S PREFACE

[Note: [Col. 0405C] I have taken the preface and the chapter summaries from Pithou’s edition; the manuscripts acknowledge neither the preface nor these summaries.]

[Col. 0405]

[Col. 0405A] This little work, in the manner of annals, was composed by Thegan, a Frank by nation and chorepiscopus of the Church of Trier—briefly, indeed, and more truthfully than elegantly. In some of his statements he may appear too expansive and impassioned in speech; yet, as a noble-minded and spirited man, he could not remain silent about what grief, arising from the unworthiness of base persons, had suggested to him. Moreover, his excessive love of justice and of its most Christian executor, the emperor, intensified his natural zeal and grief. Hence, however useful his work may be because of its good intention, it should not be rejected on account of however much rusticity it may contain. We too know the man to have been instructed by extensive reading, but occupied with the purposes of preaching and correction. I, Strabo, inserted certain divisions and chapters into this little work because I often desire either to hear or to recount the deeds and praises of the emperor Louis, of blessed memory, so that individual matters might more easily be made clear to those wishing to know them through a brief table of contents.

1. The succession of the royal line of the Franks from Saint Arnulf to Charlemagne, and Charlemagne’s consecration. [Col. 0405B]  
2. Hiltigard and her three sons.  
3. The younger Louis and his goodness, with examples from antiquity.  
4. Queen Irmingard and the sons born of her.  
5. The death of Pippin and Charles, the sons of Emperor Charles.  
6. How Emperor Charles, with the agreement of the Franks, entrusted the supreme authority of the kingdom to Louis.  
7. What the same emperor did during his final days, and his death and burial.  
8. How Louis, succeeding his father, distributed his father’s possessions.  
9. He received and dismissed various embassies, especially those of the Greeks.  
10. How he confirmed the decrees of his fathers.  
11. The embassy of the Beneventans, declaring the payment of tribute.  
12. Bernard, son of Pippin, submitted himself to his uncle.  
13. How, after sending envoys throughout the entire kingdom, he learned what needed correction and corrected it. [Col. 0405C]  
14. After holding an assembly in Saxony, he received and dismissed envoys of the Danes and Bernard.  
15. He sent an army against the Slavs and conquered.  
16. How Pope Stephen, succeeding Leo, came to Francia and met the king at Reims.  
17. How the same pope consecrated him emperor and they honored one another with mutual gifts.  
18. After Stephen’s death, Paschal succeeded him.  
19. The character of the pious emperor, his daily habits, and his manifold praise.  
20. The unsuitable promotion of base persons to ecclesiastical dignities and their vices.  
21. His father designated Lothar as emperor.  
22. Bernard’s conspiracy against the emperor discovered and defeated. [Col. 0406A]  
23. The emperor’s repentance for Bernard’s death.  
24. The emperor compelled his brothers to change their garb.  
25. Murmann the Breton is killed, and Irmingard dies.  
26. Judith is taken into the kingdom.  
27. An army is sent against Liduit.  
28. When Lothar took Irmingard as his wife.  
29. Lothar sent to Italy.  
30. Pope Paschal’s purification from the charges brought against him before the emperor’s envoys; after his death, Pope Eugenius succeeded him.  
31. The emperor again ravaged Brittany.  
32. The Bulgarian envoys received and dismissed.  
33. Heriold the Northman and his followers become Christians.  
34. An army is sent to meet the Saracens.  
35. The emperor gave Alamannia and Rhaetia to his son Charles.  
36. The force that Pippin, together with the treacherous nobles, brought against his father, and the dishonoring of Judith and her brothers. [Col. 0406B]  
37. By what authority the emperor defeated his enemies and took the queen.  
38. Where Bernard cleared himself of the charges brought against him.  
39. Louis’s first revolt against his father, healed by reconciliation.  
40. Lothar wished to prove himself free from participation in the plan for this revolt.  
41. When Pippin, ordered by his father to go to Francia, turned back in flight.  
42. What took place at the Field of Lies.  
43. How much the most pious emperor suffered, especially at Compiègne.  
44. An attack on Ebbo and his associates.  
45. Louis’s envoys are sent to Lothar on behalf of their father.  
46. Their conference near Mainz.  
47. Louis’s envoys come to his father.  
48. How Emperor Louis was freed from Lothar and Ebbo was arrested. [Col. 0406C]  
49. The indulgence and patience of the pious emperor.  
50. Base counselors to be avoided or suppressed.  
51. The empress Judith recalled from Italy.  
52. What Lothar did at the city of Chalon.  
53. A warning from the father to Lothar delivered through envoys.  
54. How Lothar agreed to return to his father.  
55. On what terms they separated from one another, and the punishment of the treacherous.  
56. Ebbo deposed from the episcopal rank.  
57. The emperor’s envoys are sent from Lyons to Lothar.  
58. The death of Berengar, and the conclusion of the little book.

[Col. 0405D]

# THE LIFE BEGINS

[Col. 0405]

[Col. 0405D] [Note: [Col. 0405D] The inscription of manuscript 2 is: “The Life of Emperor Louis, who is also called the Pious”; that of manuscript 5: “Thegan, chorepiscopus of Trier, on the deeds of Louis the Pious”; the remaining manuscripts have no title.] With our Lord Jesus Christ reigning forever. [Note: [Col. 0405D] “forever” is absent in manuscripts 3 and 4.] In the year 813 of his incarnation, which was the forty-fifth year of the reign of the glorious and orthodox [Col. 0406D] emperor Charles—that Charles who was born from the line of Saint Arnulf, bishop of Christ, as we have learned from paternal report and as many histories attest. [Note: [Col. 0407D] The following material is taken from the *Genealogy of the Kings of the Franks*.] When Saint Arnulf [Note: [Col. 0407C] *Arnolfus* in manuscript 5.] was a duke in his youth, he fathered Duke Ansgisus; Duke Ansgisus fathered Pippin the Elder and Duke Pippin; Pippin the Elder and Duke Pippin fathered Charles the Elder and Duke Charles; Charles the Elder and Duke Charles fathered Pippin, whom Stephen, the Roman pontiff [Note: [Col. 0407C] *Romanus* is absent in manuscript 4.], consecrated and anointed king; Pippin the Elder and King [Note: [Col. 0407C] “the Elder and” is absent in manuscripts 2–4.] Pippin fathered Charles, whom Leo, the Roman pontiff [Note: [Col. 0407C] “the Roman pope” in manuscript 4.], consecrated and anointed emperor in the church where the most blessed body of the chief of the apostles, Peter [Note: [Col. 0407C] manuscripts 3 and 4 have *p. a.*, an abbreviation for “chief of the apostles.”], rests, on the day [Note: [Col. 0407C] “on the day” in manuscript 2.] of the nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ [Note: [Col. 0407C] “Christ” is absent in manuscript 3.].

2. When the aforesaid emperor was in his youth, he betrothed himself to a girl of the noblest lineage of the Suevi [Note: [Col. 0407C] “Suevi” in manuscript 4.], named Hildigard [Note: [Col. 0407C] Manuscript 1 has *Hildegardam*; manuscript 2, *Hiltigardam*; manuscript 4, *Hiltegardam*; manuscript 5, *Hiltigarda*.], who was related to Gotefrid [Note: [Col. 0407C] Manuscripts 2 and 3 have *Godefridus*; manuscript 4, *Gothefridus*; manuscript 5, *Godafredus*.], duke of the Alamanni [Note: [Col. 0407C] manuscript 1: *Almannorum*; manuscript 2: *Alemannorum*.]. Duke Gotefrid [Note: [Col. 0407C] manuscripts 2 and 3: *Godefridus*; manuscript 4: *Gothefridus*.] fathered Huoching; Huoching [Note: [Col. 0407C] manuscripts 4: *Houchingum–Houchingus*.] fathered Nebi; Nebe [Note: [Col. 0407C] manuscripts 2–4: “Nebi, moreover, fathered.”] fathered Imma; and Imma fathered Hiltigard [Note: [Col. 0407C] *Hildegardam* in manuscript 2.], the most blessed queen. After the aforesaid emperor had taken her in marriage [Note: [Col. 0407C] “in marriage” in manuscript 4.], he fathered three sons by her while their father was still alive [Note: [Col. 0407C] manuscripts 2 and 4: “while their father lived.”] One was named after his father, Charles; another was Pippin, who was king over Italy; the third [Note: [Col. 0407C] *tercius* in manuscript 1.] was named Louis [Note: [Col. 0407C] *Ludewicus* in manuscript 4; likewise frequently thereafter.], who was king over Aquitaine [Note: [Col. 0407C] absent in manuscript 3.]. Their father lived happily with them for a long time [Note: [Col. 0407C] manuscripts 2–4: “while.”] and usefully instructed them in the liberal arts and worldly laws.

3. But the one who was younger by birth [Note: [Col. 0407C] “who was the younger by birth” in manuscript 3.] had learned from childhood always to fear God and love him, and whatever he possessed [Note: [Col. 0407C] manuscripts 2–4 and 6: “whatever he had above himself”; manuscript 1: “whatever he possessed.”] he distributed to the poor for the sake of the Lord’s name. For he was the best of his sons, just as, from the beginning of the world, the younger brother has often surpassed the elder brother in merit [Note: [Col. 0407C] manuscript 1: “the younger brother in merits.”] The first example was declared among the sons of the first parents of the human race: the one whom the Lord in his Gospel calls righteous, Abel [Note: [Col. 0407C] “called” in manuscripts 2–4.]. Abraham [Note: [Col. 0407C] *Habraham* in manuscript 3.] had two sons, but the younger became better than the elder [Note: [Col. 0407C] “than the elder” in manuscript 4.]. Isaac had two sons, but the younger was chosen [Note: [Col. 0407C] “Isaac … was chosen” is absent in manuscript 4.]. Jesse had many sons, but the youngest, who was a shepherd of sheep, was chosen and anointed king, at God’s command, to govern the kingdom over all Israel. From whose seed Christ, long ago promised, deigned to become incarnate [Col. 0408A] [Note: [Col. 0407C] “was incarnate.”] It would be lengthy to enumerate such examples and others like them.

4. When the aforesaid Louis [Note: [Col. 0407C] “the aforementioned” in manuscripts 2–4.] reached adulthood, he betrothed himself to the daughter of the most noble duke Ingoram [Note: [Col. 0407C] manuscript 1: *Ingrammi*; manuscript 2: *Ingerrani*; manuscript 3: *Ingorammi*; manuscript 4: *Ingorrammi*; manuscript 5: *Ingoramni*.], who was the son of the brother of Saint Bishop Hruotgang [Note: [Col. 0407C] manuscript 1: “of Bishop Ruotgang”; manuscript 4: “of the holy bishop Ruthgang.”] The aforesaid maiden was named Irmingard [Note: [Col. 0407C] manuscript 3: *Irmigarda*; manuscript 4: *Irmincarta*; manuscript 5: *Irmingarta*.]. With the counsel and consent [Note: [Col. 0407C] *consensu* in manuscript 1.] of her father [Note: [Col. 0407C] “with his consent” in manuscript 1.] he made her queen, and had three sons by her while his father was still alive [Note: [Col. 0407C] manuscripts 2 and 4: “while his father lived.”] One was named Lothar [Note: [Col. 0407C] manuscript 2: *Hlotharius*; manuscript 3: *Lutharius*; manuscript 4: *Lotharius*; manuscript 5: *Hlodharius*.], another Pippin, and the third, his namesake, Louis.

5. The great emperor Charles governed and loved his kingdom well and wisely. In the forty-second year of his reign (810), his son Pippin died at the age of thirty-three. In the following year [Col. 0408B] (811), Charles, his first-born son [Note: [Col. 0407C] “son” is absent in manuscripts 2 and 4.] by the aforesaid queen Hiltigard [Note: [Col. 0407C] manuscript 2: *Hildigarda*; manuscript 3: *Hildegarda*; manuscript 4: *Hiltegarda*.], died [Note: [Col. 0407C] *eius obiit* is absent in manuscript 3.]. Louis alone remained to govern the kingdom.

6. When the aforesaid emperor realized [Note: [Col. 0407C] manuscripts 2–4: “had realized.”] that the day of his death was approaching (813)—for he had grown very old—he summoned his son Louis to him, together with the entire army, the bishops, abbots, dukes, counts, and local officials [Note: [Col. 0407D] “vicars.”] He held a general [Note: [Col. 0407C] “great” in manuscript 4.] assembly with them peacefully [Note: [Col. 0407C] manuscript 4: “peacefully and honorably.”] and honorably at the palace of Aachen, urging them to show loyalty toward his son. He asked everyone, from the greatest to the least, whether it pleased them that he should hand over to his son Louis his title—that is, the imperial dignity. They all replied joyfully [Note: [Col. 0407C] absent in manuscripts 2 and 4.] that it was God’s admonition [Note: [Col. 0407C] manuscript 4: “that it was the admonition of God.”] that he should do this [Note: [Col. 0407C] manuscript 2: “of this.”] for the king [Note: [Col. 0407C] manuscripts 2–4 have *rei*, “matter,” rather than *regi*, “king.”] [Note: [Col. 0408D] That is, *rei*; the form *regi* frequently occurs in monuments of the ninth century.]

Having done this, on the following Sunday [Note: [Col. 0407C] manuscript 4: “the first Sunday.”] he adorned himself in royal dress [Note: [Col. 0407C] manuscript 4: “the dress of a king.”] and placed a crown upon his head. He went forth brightly adorned and decked out, as was fitting for him [Note: [Col. 0407C] manuscripts 2 and 4: “as became him.”] He proceeded to the church that he himself had built from its foundation [Note: [Col. 0407C] manuscript 4: “from its foundations.”], and came before the altar that had been built in a higher place than the other altars [Note: [Col. 0407C] “the altar that he himself had built” in manuscript 3; the phrase “that had been built in a higher place than the other altars” is absent in manuscript 4.] and consecrated in honor of our Lord Jesus Christ [Note: [Col. 0407C] “in honor” in manuscripts 3 and 4.]. Upon it he ordered a golden crown to be placed, other than the one he wore on his head [Note: [Col. 0407C] manuscript 1: “another, I mean”; manuscript 4: “the very one”; manuscript 2 omits “which he wore on his head.”] [Note: [Col. 0407C] “to be placed” in manuscripts 2–4.]

After he and his son had prayed for a long time, he spoke to his son before the entire company of his bishops and nobles [Col. 0409A], urging him above all to love and fear almighty God, to keep his commandments in all things, and to govern and defend God’s churches from wicked men [Note: [Col. 0409C] manuscript 1: “to keep the commandments.”] He ordered him always to show unfailing mercy to his sisters and to his younger brothers, to his nephews, and to all his relatives [Note: [Col. 0409C] manuscripts 2–4: “unfailing.”] Then he was to honor priests as fathers, love the people as sons, force proud and utterly wicked men onto the way of salvation, and be a comforter of monasteries [Note: [Col. 0409C] manuscript 3: “should be”; absent in manuscripts 2 and 4.] and a father to the poor [Note: [Col. 0409C] manuscript 4: “and be a father to the poor. Faithful …”]. He was to appoint faithful ministers who feared God and hated unjust gifts [Note: [Col. 0409C] manuscript 1: “as”; that is, “appoint ministers as faithful and God-fearing men.”] He was not to remove anyone from his honor without a just cause of discernment [Note: [Col. 0409C] manuscripts 2–4: “should not remove.”], and was to show himself at all times irreproachable before God and all the people [Note: [Col. 0409C] manuscripts 2–4: “should preserve himself”; manuscript 3: “should show himself”; manuscript 4: “should show himself.”]

[Col. 0409B] After he had set forth these and many other words before the assembly to his son [Note: [Col. 0409C] manuscript 2: “had set forth”; manuscripts 3 and 4: “had shown.”], he asked him [Note: [Col. 0409C] absent in manuscript 4.] whether he wished to be obedient [Note: [Col. 0409C] manuscript 3: “obedient to him.”] to his commands. He replied that he would gladly obey and, with God’s help, keep all the commands his father had given him.

Then the father ordered him to lift with his own hands the crown that was upon the altar and place it upon his own head, in remembrance of all the commands his father had given him. He carried out his father’s command. When this had been done [Note: [Col. 0409C] manuscript 4: “and when this had been done.”], they went to the palace, hearing the solemn celebration of Mass [Note: [Col. 0409C] manuscripts 2 and 3: *solempnia*; manuscript 4: *solemnia*.]. For as long as the son was with him, the son supported his father both on the way there and on the way back [Note: [Col. 0409C] manuscript 5: “had been”; manuscript 4: the phrase “for as long as the son was with him” is absent in manuscript 2.].

Not many days later, his father honored him with splendid and countless gifts [Note: [Col. 0409C] “and countless” is absent in manuscript 4.] and dismissed him to go to Aquitaine [Note: [Col. 0409C] manuscripts 2–4: “into Aquitaine.”] Before they had separated [Col. 0409C] [Note: [Col. 0409C] manuscript 4: “before they had done so.”], embracing and kissing one another—for joy born of love—they began to weep [Note: [Col. 0409C] absent in manuscripts 2 and 4.] He proceeded to Aquitaine, while the lord emperor retained his kingdom and his title honorably, as was fitting.

7. After they had separated, the lord emperor began to do nothing else [Note: [Col. 0409C] manuscript 2: “he began to think of nothing except prayers”; manuscript 4: “he began to do nothing except devote himself to prayers.”] except devote himself to prayers and almsgiving [Note: [Col. 0409C] manuscripts 2–4: “almsgiving.”] and correct books. For he had very carefully corrected the four Gospels of Christ, entitled by the names of Matthew [Note: [Col. 0409C] manuscripts 2–4: “Matthew.”], Mark, Luke, and John, during the final days before his death, with the help of Greeks and Syrians [Note: [Col. 0409C] manuscripts 2–4: “Syrians.”] [Note: [Col. 0409C] “before” is absent in manuscript 1.]

In the following year, which was the forty-sixth year of his reign (814), in the month of January, the lord emperor was seized with a fever after bathing [Note: [Col. 0409C] manuscript 4: “a fever after bathing.”] As the illness grew worse day by day [Note: [Col. 0409C] manuscript 4: “as his suffering increased.”], he ate and drank nothing except a little water to refresh his body. On the seventh day after he had begun to suffer severely [Note: [Col. 0409C] manuscripts 2–4 omit “with himself.”], he ordered his most intimate bishop, Hildibald [Note: [Col. 0409C] manuscripts 2 and 3: *Hildebaldus*; manuscript 4: *Hiltibaldus*.] [Note: [Col. 0409D] of Cologne], to come to him so that he might administer to him the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood, that he might fortify him for his departure [Note: [Col. 0409C] manuscript 2: “and”]. Having done this [Note: [Col. 0409C] manuscripts 3 and 4: “and when this had been done.”], he remained in his illness through that day and the following night.

On the next day, when daylight came, knowing what he was about to do [Note: [Col. 0409C] manuscript 3: “what would happen.”], he extended his right hand, and with what strength he possessed impressed the sign of the holy cross upon his forehead, then marked his breast and his whole body with it. Finally, drawing up his feet, extending his arms [Note: [Col. 0409C] manuscript 2: “his arms.”] and hands over his body, he closed his eyes [Note: [Col. 0409C] absent in manuscripts 1, 2, and 4.], softly chanting this verse: “Into your hands, Lord, [Note: [Col. 0409C] absent in manuscript 4.] I commend my spirit” [Note: [Col. 0410D] Luke 23:46; and Psalm 31:6.]

Immediately afterward, full of days in a good old age, he departed in peace. On that same day his body was buried in the church that he himself had built [Note: [Col. 0409C] absent in manuscript 1.] at the palace of Aachen, in the seventy-second year of his life, in the seventh indiction.

8. After the death of the most glorious aforesaid emperor Charles [Note: [Col. 0409C] absent in manuscripts 3 and 4.], his son Louis proceeded [Note: [Col. 0409C] manuscript 2: “came.”] from the regions of Aquitaine, came [Note: [Col. 0409C] manuscript 2 omits “and came”; manuscript 4: “and came”; manuscript 3: “and coming.”] to the palace of Aachen, and without any opposition took possession of all the kingdoms that God had handed over to his father [Note: [Col. 0409C] manuscript 1: “contradiction.”] This was the year 814 of the Lord’s incarnation and the first year of his reign.

After his father’s death, he took his seat in the aforesaid palace and first, with the greatest haste [Note: [Col. 0409C] manuscript 3: “great”; manuscript 2: “great,” corrected to “greatest.”], ordered all his father’s treasures to be shown to him: gold, silver, extremely precious gems, and every kind of household property. He gave his sisters their lawful share [Col. 0410C] [Note: [Col. 0409C] manuscript 1 omits “their”; manuscript 3: “royal.”], and whatever remained he gave for his father’s soul. He sent the greater part of the treasure to Rome in the time of the blessed Pope Leo. Whatever remained after this he distributed among priests and the poor, strangers, widows, and orphans [Note: [Col. 0409C] manuscript 3: “and orphans”; manuscript 4: “and orphans.”], reserving nothing for himself except a single silver table, which is three-sided, shaped somewhat like three shields joined into one [Note: [Col. 0409C] manuscripts 2 and 4: “in the middle.”] He kept it for himself out of love for his father, yet redeemed it at another price, which he delivered for his father.

9. When this had been done [Note: [Col. 0409C] manuscript 2: “when this was done.”], envoys came to him from all kingdoms and provinces, from foreign and other nations [Note: [Col. 0409C] manuscript 3: “and the other”; manuscripts 2 and 4: “and from the other.”], and all who had been under his father’s authority, announcing peace and declaring that they would observe loyalty toward him. They offered spontaneous service, not under compulsion [Note: [Col. 0409C] manuscript 2: “Those who had been under his father’s authority announced peace, observed loyalty toward him, and offered spontaneous service without compulsion.”]

Among them came Greek envoys with Amalarius [Note: [Col. 0411] manuscripts 2 and 3: *Almaharius*.], bishop of Trier [Note: [Col. 0411] manuscript 4: “of Trier.”], who had been the ambassador of Charles, of pious memory, to the ruler of Constantinople, whose name does not now come to mind [Note: [Col. 0411D] They had been sent to Michael. Cf. Einhard’s *Annals*.] [Note: [Col. 0411] “whose name does not now come to mind” is absent in manuscript 4; “to … come to mind” is absent in manuscript 1.]

When they arrived, they found Lord Louis seated upon his father’s throne, because God had so ordained. He received them kindly and accepted their gifts with thanksgiving [Note: [Col. 0411] manuscripts 2 and 4: “accepting them.”] While they remained with him, he held familiar conversation with them. Not many days later [Note: [Col. 0411] manuscripts 2–4: “after not many days.”], he honored them with great distinctions and dismissed them to return home. He sent his own messengers ahead of them to prepare whatever they desired for their journey [Note: [Col. 0411] manuscript 2: “whatever was necessary for them until they came into their own region”; manuscript 3: “whatever things were necessary for them until they were in his kingdom.”] until they had reached his kingdom [Note: [Col. 0411] absent in manuscript 4.]

10. In the same year, the aforesaid prince ordered all the charters that had been issued to the churches of God under the rule of his fathers [Col. 0411B] to be renewed, and he personally confirmed them with his subscription [Note: [Col. 0411] manuscript 3: “with his transcription.”] [Note: [Col. 0411D] In Louis’s authentic charters, a transverse line forming the letter H in the monogram was drawn by the emperor’s own hand.] [Note: [Col. 0411] In manuscript 3 this chapter is followed by chapter 11.]

11. Meanwhile envoys of the Beneventans [Note: [Col. 0411] manuscript 4: “of the Beneventans.”] came, surrendering the entire land of Benevento to his authority and promising to pay an annual tribute of many thousands of gold pieces [Note: [Col. 0411] manuscript 5 corrects “many” to “seven”; cf. Einhard’s *Annals*.]. They fulfilled this promise in this manner up to the present day [Note: [Col. 0411] manuscripts 2 and 3: “carried it out.”].

12. At the same time Bernard, the son of his brother Pippin, came and submitted himself to him as prince [Note: [Col. 0411] manuscript 2 reads *ad obsequium*, “for service”; manuscript 3 has *sibi*, “to himself.”], and promised loyalty with an oath [Note: [Col. 0411] manuscripts 2–4: “loyalty to him with an oath.”] Lord Louis received him gladly and honored him with great and honorable gifts [Note: [Col. 0411] manuscripts 3 and 4: “honored him and permitted him.”] He allowed him to return safely [Note: [Col. 0411] absent in manuscripts 2 and 4.] to Italy.

13. At the same time the aforesaid prince sent his envoys throughout [Note: [Col. 0411] manuscripts 2 and 4: “above.”] all his kingdoms [Note: [Col. 0411] absent in manuscript 2.] to inquire [Col. 0411C] and investigate whether any injustice had been committed against anyone [Note: [Col. 0411] manuscript 4: “had been.”], and whether they found anyone who wished to speak of such matters [Note: [Col. 0411] manuscripts 1 and 4: “this.”] and could prove it with wholly reliable witnesses [Note: [Col. 0411] manuscript 1 appears to read “with very just garments,” an obvious textual corruption.], he immediately ordered them to come with the envoys into his presence [Note: [Col. 0411] manuscript 4: “into the province.”]

When they went out, they found an innumerable multitude of people oppressed either by the seizure of their property or by the stripping away of their freedom. Wicked ministers, counts, and local officials [Note: [Col. 0411] manuscript 1: *compositi*; manuscript 5: *locispositi*.] perpetrated these abuses through evil cunning. The aforesaid prince ordered all the records to be annulled that had been made impiously in his father’s days by the hands [Note: [Col. 0411] manuscripts 3 and 4: “through the schemes.”] of wicked ministers [Note: [Col. 0411] manuscript 3: “impious ministers.”] He restored their patrimonies to the oppressed, freed those who had been unjustly forced into servitude, ordered charters to be issued for everyone, and confirmed them personally with his subscription [Note: [Col. 0411] manuscripts 2 and 4: “with his signature.”] He did this for a long time [Note: [Col. 0411] manuscripts 3 and 4: “for a long period”; manuscript 2: “he did this for a long time.”].

14. In another year of his reign he held his general assembly in the regions of Saxony (815), and there established many good measures. An embassy of the Danes [Note: [Col. 0411] manuscripts 2–4: “of the Danes.”] came to him requesting peace, and all the surrounding peoples of the pagan nations [Note: [Col. 0411] manuscripts 3 and 4: “of pagan nations.”] came to him [Note: [Col. 0411] manuscript 2: “nations.”] The aforesaid Bernard [Note: [Col. 0411] manuscript 2: “Bernard.”] also came to him there, and he dismissed him to return to Italy.

After Lord Louis had secured the boundaries of his kingdom in those regions [Note: [Col. 0411] manuscript 4: “in those regions”; manuscript 2: “in those regions.”], he returned [Note: [Col. 0411] manuscripts 2 and 3: “returns.”] to his seat at the palace of Aachen, and spent the winter there [Note: [Col. 0411] manuscripts 2–4: “at Aachen and there.”].

15. In the following year (816) he sent [Note: [Col. 0411] manuscript 4: “directed.”] his army [Col. 0412B] against the Slavs [Note: [Col. 0411] manuscript 2: “Suevi.”] located in the east. They severely oppressed them and, by God’s gift, emerged victorious. When this was done, each man returned to his own place.

16. In the same year Pope Leo the Roman died, and Stephen succeeded him [Note: [Col. 0411] the words “and Stephen succeeded him” are absent in manuscript 1.] Immediately after he assumed the pontificate, he ordered the entire Roman people to promise loyalty on oath to Louis [Note: [Col. 0411] manuscript 1: “to Louis”; manuscript 2: “to King Louis”; the form *Ludowicus* occurs frequently thereafter.] He then sent his envoys to the aforesaid prince, informing him [Note: [Col. 0411] manuscript 2: “he ordered”; manuscript 3: “he announced”; manuscript 4: “he announced.”] that he would gladly see him wherever it pleased him [Note: [Col. 0411] manuscripts 2 and 4: “wherever it pleased him,” referring to the pope.]

When he heard this [Note: [Col. 0411] manuscript 2: “when Lord Louis heard this.”], he was filled with great joy and began to rejoice. He immediately [Note: [Col. 0411] manuscript 4: “at once.”] ordered his messengers to go to meet the holy pontiff with great greetings [Note: [Col. 0411] manuscripts 2–4: “the greatest greetings.”] and to prepare the necessary services. Lord Louis followed his messengers to meet the aforesaid pontiff. When they met one another [Note: [Col. 0411] manuscript 4: “when he met him”; manuscript 2: “when he had met him.”] in the great field of the people of Reims [Col. 0412C], each dismounted from his horse. The prince prostrated his whole body upon the ground three times before the feet of so great a pontiff; then, rising on the third occasion, he greeted the pontiff with these words: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord. The Lord God has shone upon us” [Note: [Col. 0412D] Psalm 118:26.]

The pontiff replied: “Blessed be the Lord our God, who has granted our eyes to see, in accordance with King David.” Then, embracing and kissing one another peacefully [Note: [Col. 0411] manuscript 4: “embracing and kissing peacefully.”], they proceeded to the church. After they had prayed for a long time [Note: [Col. 0411] manuscript 2: “had prayed”; manuscript 4: “prayed.”], the pontiff arose and, in a loud voice, with his clergy, offered him royal praises.

[Col. 0413A] 17. Afterward the pontiff honored him with great and numerous honors, as well as Queen Irmingard [Note: [Col. 0413] manuscript 2: “Ermengard.”] and all his nobles and ministers. On the following Sunday, in the church, before the solemn celebration of Mass and in the presence of the clergy and the whole people, he consecrated and anointed him [Note: [Col. 0413] absent in manuscripts 2–4.] emperor. He placed upon his head a golden crown of marvelous beauty, adorned with the most precious gems [Note: [Col. 0413] absent in manuscripts 2 and 4.], which he had brought with him [Note: [Col. 0413] manuscript 2: “had caused to be carried”; manuscript 3: “had carried”; manuscript 4: “had brought.”] He called Queen Irmingard [Note: [Col. 0413] manuscript 2: “Ermengard.”] Augusta and placed a golden crown upon her head.

As long as the most blessed pope remained there [Note: [Col. 0413] “he remained” in the manuscripts.], they held daily conversations about the welfare of the holy Church of God [Note: [Col. 0413] manuscript 4: “daily.”] After the lord emperor had honored him with great and countless gifts—three times, and more, than he had received from him, as he always used to do, giving more than receiving—he dismissed him to return to Rome with his envoys, whom he instructed to provide him with honorable service everywhere along the journey.

18. After he came to Rome, the aforesaid pope died not many days later (817). Subsequently [Note: [Col. 0413] manuscript 4: “after an excessive number of days”; some words are missing in the manuscripts.] it became clear through God’s manifestation in certain miracles that, while alive, he had been a true worshiper of God. After him Pope Paschal succeeded him [Note: [Col. 0413D] Cf. Einhard’s *Life of Charlemagne*, chapter 22 and following.].

## Exact-form apparatus supplement for chapters 1–18

The inline notes above translate the apparatus in context. This supplement preserves source forms and distinctions that the earlier compressed version normalized or omitted.

- **Preface and title.** The preface and chapter summaries come from Pithou's edition; the manuscripts recognize neither. Manuscript 2's title is `VITA HLUDOUUICI IMPERATORIS QUI DICITUR ET PIUS`, “The Life of Emperor Louis, who is also called the Pious”; manuscript 5 has `THEGANUS COREPISCOPUS TREBERENSIS IN GESTA LODOICI PII`, “Thegan, chorepiscopus of Trier, on the deeds of Louis the Pious”; the others have no title. Manuscripts 3 and 4 omit `in perpetuum`, “forever.”
- **Chapter 1, Arnulf and Pippin.** Manuscript 3's corrupt `ar uolfi` is retained for *Arnulfi*; manuscript 5 reads `arnolfus`. Manuscript 4 omits `Romanus`, “Roman,” after Stephen. Printed `uncxit`, “anointed,” is spelled `unxit` in manuscripts 2–4, “and so subsequently” (`ita deinceps`). Manuscripts 2–4 omit `senior et`, “the Elder and.” Manuscript 4 reads `papa Romanus`, “the Roman pope,” for `Romanus pontifex`. Manuscripts 3 and 4 abbreviate `principis apostolorum`, “chief of the apostles,” as `p. a.`; manuscript 2 adds `in` to `die`, “on the day”; manuscript 3 omits `Christi`, “Christ.”
- **Chapter 2, Hildigard's genealogy.** Manuscript 4 has `imperator sibi iunxit`, “the emperor joined to himself,” for `desponsavit sibi`, “betrothed to himself,” and `Suevorum` for *Suavorum*. Hildigard appears as `hildegardam` (1 and 2), `hiltegardam` (4), and `hiltigarda` (5); Gotefrid as `godefridi` (2, 3), `gothefridi` (4), and `godafredi` (5); Alamanni as `almannorum` (1) and `alemannorum` (2). Manuscript 4 has the linked forms `houchingum---houchingus`; manuscripts 2–4 read `Nebi autem genuit`, “Nebi, however, fathered,” and `peperit`, “bore,” for Imma's `genuit`, “fathered.” Manuscripts 2–4 omit `autem`, “however,” after `Postquam`; manuscript 4 has ablative `matrimonio`, “in marriage.” `tertius` is spelled `tercius` in manuscript 1; manuscript 4 repeatedly uses `Ludewicus`; manuscript 3 omits `rex`, “king,” and manuscripts 2–4 read `dum`, “while,” for `diu`, “for a long time.”
- **Chapter 3, the younger son.** Manuscript 3 reads `qui natu minor`, “who was younger by birth.” Manuscripts 2–4 and 6 have `quicquid super se`, literally “whatever he had above himself,” while manuscript 1 agrees with printed `quicquid sui`, “whatever of his own.” Manuscript 1's abbreviated/corrupt `iunior frater fr meritis` still preserves “the younger brother ... in merits.” Manuscripts 3 and 4 read `quod`, “which,” for `quem`, “whom”; manuscripts 2–4 read past `nominavit`, “called,” for present `nominat`, “calls.” Manuscript 4 has ablative `seniore`, “than the elder,” and omits the full clause `Isaac ... electus est`, “Isaac had two sons, but the younger was chosen.” It also reads `Domino`, “the Lord,” for `Deo`, “God.” Manuscript 2 has `in regem rex`, literally “as king, king,” and manuscripts 2 and 4 reverse `cuius de` to `de cuius`, “from whose.” The alternate `incarnatus est` means “was incarnate,” rather than `incarnari dignatus est`, “deigned to become incarnate.”
- **Chapter 4, Irmingard.** Manuscripts 2–4 read `suprafatus`, “aforementioned,” for `supradictus`. Ingoram's name appears as `ingrammi` (1), `ingerrani` (2), `ingorammi` (3), `ingorrammi` (4), and `ingoramni` (5). Manuscript 1's corrupt `ruotgangiscim pontificis` and manuscript 4's `ruthgangi sancti pontificis`, “of the holy bishop Ruthgang,” are retained. Irmingard appears as `irmigarda`, `irmincarta`, and `irmingarta`. Manuscripts 3 and 4 omit `cum`, “with,” before “counsel”; manuscript 1 reduces `consilio et consensu`, “with counsel and consent,” to `consensu`, “with consent.” Manuscripts 2 and 4 abbreviate `patre vivente`, “while his father lived,” as `p. V.` Lothar's name appears as `hlotharius`, `lutharius`, `lotharius`, and `hlodharius` in manuscripts 2–5.
- **Chapter 5.** Manuscripts 2 and 4 omit `filius`, “son.” Manuscript 3's note `eius obiit` supplies “his [son] died”; manuscript 4 reads `et`, “and,” for `ex`, “from/by.” Hiltigard's name forms are `hildigarda`, `hildegarda`, and `hiltegarda` in manuscripts 2–4.
- **Chapter 6, the imperial succession.** Manuscripts 2–4 read pluperfect `intellexisset`, “had realized,” for `intellexit`, “realized.” `locopositis` is glossed “vicars/local officials.” Manuscript 4 has `grande`, “great,” for `generale`, “general,” and `pacifice et honorabiliter`, “peacefully and honorably.” Manuscripts 2 and 4 omit `exultando`, “joyfully.” Manuscript 4 reverses `ammonitionem esse` to `esse ammonitionem`, “to be an admonition”; manuscript 2 reads `huius`, “of this,” for `illius`, “of that.” Manuscripts 2–4 read `rei`, “of/for the matter,” for `regi`, “for the king”; the editor notes that the form *regi* often occurs in ninth-century monuments where *rei* is meant.
- **Chapter 6, crown and exhortation.** Manuscript 4 reads `prima`, “first,” for `proxima`, “following,” and `cultu regis`, “in the dress of a king,” for `cultu regio`, “in royal dress.” Its `incedebatque clare vestitus` means “and he proceeded brightly dressed.” Manuscripts 2 and 4 read `eum`, “him,” for dative `ei`, “for him,” and manuscript 2 uses imperfect `decebat`, “was fitting,” for pluperfect `decuerat`, “had been fitting.” Manuscript 4 has plural `fundamentis`, “foundations,” and `pervenitque`, “and he came”; manuscript 3 reads `ad altare`, “to the altar,” for `ante altare`, “before the altar.” Manuscript 4 omits `quod erat ... caeteris altaribus`, “which had been built in a higher place than the other altars”; manuscript 3 instead reads `quod ipse construxerat in`, “which he himself had built in.” Manuscripts 3 and 4 use accusative `honorem`, “in honor,” after `in`. Manuscript 1 reads `alia inquam`, “another, I say,” for `aliam quam`, “another than”; manuscript 4 reads `ipsa`, “the very [crown],” while manuscript 2 omits `ille`, “that one.” Manuscripts 2–4 read `poni`, “to be placed,” for `inponi`, “to be placed upon.”
- **Chapter 6, conduct commanded.** Printed `hac` is the orthographic form of `ac`, “and”; manuscripts 2 and 3 read `ac`, manuscript 4 `et`, and the editor explicitly glosses `hac` as `ac`. Manuscript 1's `praeceptis servare` changes “keep his commands” to an awkward case construction. Printed `deffendere`, “defend,” is spelled `defendere` in manuscripts 2–4. Printed `indeficientem`, “unfailing,” appears correctly as `indeficientem` in manuscripts 2–4. At “comforter of monasteries,” manuscript 3 reads `esset`, “should be,” while manuscripts 2 and 4 omit the verb; manuscript 4 continues `et pauperum esse. Fideles`, “and to be a father of the poor. Faithful ...” Manuscript 1 reads `ut`, “as,” for `et`, “and,” before God-fearing ministers. Manuscripts 2–4 read `eiiceret`, “should remove,” for `eiecisset`, “had removed”; manuscripts 2 and 4 omit the following `et`. At the final command, manuscripts 2, 3, and 4 read respectively `custodire`, “preserve,” and `demonstraret`, “should show,” for infinitive `demonstrare`, “to show.”
- **Chapter 6, response and departure.** Manuscripts 2–4 read `ostenderat`, “had set forth/shown,” for `ostenderet`; manuscript 4 omits `eum`, “him,” and manuscript 3 adds `ei`, “to him,” to “obedient.” Manuscripts 2 and 4 read `elevaret`, “should lift,” for pluperfect `elevasset`, “had lifted.” Manuscript 4 reads `quo facto`, “when this had been done,” for `quod factum`; `sollemnia` appears as `solempnia` (2, 3) and `solemnia` (4). Manuscripts 4 and 5 read `fuerat`, “had been,” for `erat`, “was”; manuscript 2 omits `quamdiu cum eo erat filius`, “for as long as the son was with him.” Manuscript 4 omits `et innumeris`, “and countless”; manuscripts 2–4 add `in` before Aquitaine. Manuscript 4 reads `essent`, “were,” for `fuissent`, “had been”; manuscripts 2 and 4 omit `amplexantes enim`, “for embracing.” Manuscript 4 repeatedly spells `domnus` as `dominus`.
- **Chapter 7, prayer and final illness.** Manuscript 2 reads `cogitare cepit nisi orationibus`, “he began to think of nothing except prayers,” in place of “began to do nothing else”; `elemosinis` appears as `eleemosynis` in manuscripts 2–4. At the Gospels, manuscript 2 reads `nam et`, “for also,” and manuscript 4 `nam`, “for,” for printed `Et`; manuscripts 2 and 4 read `intitulantur`, “are entitled,” for `praetitulantur`; Matthew and Syrians appear as `matthaei` and `syris`. Manuscript 1 omits `ante`, “before.” Manuscript 4 reverses `febris post balneum` to `post balneum febris`, “a fever after bathing,” and reads `laboribus`, “sufferings,” for `languor`, “illness.” Manuscript 1 reads `atque`, “and,” for `aquae`, “water”; manuscripts 2–4 omit `nimis secum`, “severely within himself.” Hildibald appears as `hildebaldum` (2, 3) and `hiltibaldum` (4), and is identified as bishop of Cologne. Manuscript 2 reads `et`, “and,” for the second `ut`, “so that”; manuscripts 3 and 4 read `quo facto`, “when this had been done.” Manuscript 3 has `futurus`, “what was going to happen,” for `facturus`, “what he was going to do.” Manuscript 2 adds `sua`, “his,” to “arms”; manuscripts 1, 2, and 4 omit `clausit oculos suos`, “he closed his eyes,” and manuscript 4 omits `Domine`, “Lord.” Luke 23:46 and Psalm 31:6 are the cited sources.
- **Chapter 7, burial.** Printed `ipso eodemque die` means “on that very same day”; manuscript 4 reads `ipsoque die`, “and on that very day.” Manuscript 1 omits `quam ipse construxerat`, “which he himself had built.”
- **Chapter 8.** Manuscripts 3 and 4 omit `supradicti`, “aforesaid.” Manuscript 2 reads `venit`, “came,” for `perrexit`, “proceeded”; manuscript 4 omits `filius eius`, “his son.” At the next verb manuscript 2 omits `venit`, manuscript 4 reads `et venit`, “and came,” and manuscript 3 `veniensque`, “and coming.” Printed present `suscipit`, “takes possession,” becomes past `suscepit`, “took possession,” in manuscripts 2–4. Manuscript 1 spells “opposition” `contradicione`. Manuscript 3 reads `magna`, “great,” for `maxima`, “greatest”; manuscript 2's `magna` was corrected to `maxima`. Manuscript 1 omits `earum`, “their,” while manuscript 3 reads `regalem`, “royal,” for `legalem`, “lawful.” “Orphans” appears as `et orphanis` (3) and `orphanisque` (4). Manuscripts 2 and 4 read `in medio`, “in the middle,” for `in modum`, “in the form/manner.”
- **Chapter 9.** Manuscript 2 reads `factum`, “when it was done,” for `facto`. At “foreign nations,” manuscript 3 reads `et ceteris`, “and the other,” and manuscripts 2 and 4 `et ex ceteris`, “and from the other.” Manuscript 2's full alternate clause reads: “Those who had been under his father's authority announced peace, observed loyalty toward him, and offered spontaneous service without compulsion.” Manuscripts 2 and 4 read `eos`, “them,” for `inter quos`, “among whom.” Amalarius appears as `Almaharius` (2, 3), and Trier as `Trevirensi` (4). Manuscripts 2, 3, and 5 read `bonae memoriae`, “of good memory,” for `piae memoriae`, “of pious memory.” The envoys had been sent to Michael; compare Einhard's *Annals*. Manuscripts 4 and 6 omit `modo memoriae`, “now to mind,” while manuscript 1 omits the whole span `ad ... occurrit`, “to ... comes to mind.” Manuscript 4 reads `Deus`, “God,” for `Dominus`, “the Lord”; manuscript 1 reads `bene`, “well/kindly,” for `benigne`, and manuscripts 2 and 4 `accipiens`, “accepting,” for `suscepit`, “received.” Manuscripts 2–4 read `multis autem dies`, “but after many days,” for `multos dies`; manuscript 3 reads `nuncios`, “messengers,” for `missos`. Manuscript 2 supplies “whatever was necessary for them until they came into their own region”; manuscript 3, “whatever things were necessary for them until they were in his kingdom.” Manuscript 4 reads `forent`, “might be,” for `fuissent`, “had been,” and omits `in regno eius`, “in his kingdom.”
- **Chapters 10–11.** Printed `cum subscriptione`, “with his signature/subscription,” becomes `cum conscriptione`, “with a written record,” in manuscript 3. In Louis's authentic charters the emperor personally drew the transverse line forming H in the monogram. In manuscript 3 chapter 11 follows this chapter. `Beneventorum` is expanded to `Beneventanorum`, “of the Beneventans,” in manuscript 4. Manuscript 5 corrects `multa`, “many,” to `septem`, “seven,” thousand gold pieces; compare Einhard's *Annals*. Printed `perfecerunt`, “fulfilled/completed,” becomes `fecerunt`, “did/carried out,” in manuscripts 2 and 3.
- **Chapter 12.** Manuscript 3 reads `sibi`, “to himself,” for `ei`, “to him.” Printed `ad procerem` is “as/to the prince”; manuscript 2 instead reads `ad obsequium`, “for service.” Manuscripts 2–4 expand `fidelitatem cum iuramento` to `fidelitatem ei cum iuramento`, “loyalty to him with an oath.” Manuscripts 3 and 4 have the compressed `eum et p.`, “honored him and permitted [him]”; manuscripts 2 and 4 omit `incolumem`, “safely/unharmed.”
- **Chapter 13.** Printed `super`, “through/over,” becomes `supra`, “above,” in manuscripts 2 and 4; manuscript 2 omits `omnia regna`, “all kingdoms,” and also omits `inquirere et`, “to inquire and.” Manuscript 4 reads `esset`, “had been/was,” for `fuisset`; manuscript 1 omits `aliqua iniustitia perpetrata fuisset et si`, “any injustice had been committed, and whether.” Manuscripts 2 and 4 read singular `hoc`, “this,” for plural `haec`, “these matters.” Manuscript 1's corrupt `iurissimus vestibus`, literally “with most lawful garments,” stands for `verissimis testibus`, “most truthful witnesses”; manuscript 4 has `probare`, “prove,” for `comprobare`, “prove fully.” `cum eis` means “with them,” namely the envoys; manuscript 4 instead reads `provinciam`, “province,” for `in praesentiam`, “into [his] presence.” `locopositi`, “local officials,” appears as corrupt `compositi` (1) and `locispositi` (5). Manuscripts 3 and 4 omit `Haec`, “these things.” Manuscript 3 reads `impiorum`, “impious,” for `iniquorum`, “wicked,” and manuscripts 3 and 4 `ingenia`, “schemes/devices,” for `manus`, “hands.” Printed `cum conscriptione`, “with a written record,” becomes `subscriptione`, “with his signature,” in manuscripts 2 and 4. Manuscript 4 omits `Fecit enim`, “for he did”; manuscripts 3 and 4 read `tempore`, “for a time,” while manuscript 2 has corrupt `hoc longo temporeme`, evidently “this for a long time.”
- **Chapter 14.** “Danes” appears as `Danorum` in manuscripts 2–4. The editor notes that below, chapter 33 and manuscript 2 call them `Danai`; this is the same empty learning by which later centuries called them `Daci` even in public documents. Manuscripts 3 and 4 read feminine `paganarum`, “of pagan [nations],” while manuscript 2 reads nominative `nationes`, “nations.” Bernard's name appears without h as `Bernardus` in manuscript 2. `illis partibus` is reordered as `illis in partibus` (4) and `in illis partibus` (2), “in those regions.” Printed past `rediit`, “returned,” becomes present `redit`, “returns,” in manuscripts 2 and 3. Manuscripts 2–4 read `Aquis ibique`, “at Aachen and there,” for `Aquisgrani palatio, ibique`, “at the palace of Aachen, and there.”
- **Chapters 15–16.** Printed `direxit`, “dispatched,” becomes `misit`, “sent,” in manuscript 4. Manuscript 2 reads `Suavos`, “Suevi,” for `Sclavos`, “Slavs.” Manuscript 1 omits `et Stephanus post eum successit`, “and Stephen succeeded him.” Louis appears as `Ludowico` in manuscript 1 and `regi Hludowico`, “to King Louis,” in manuscript 2. At the pope's message, manuscript 2 reads `mandat`, “orders,” manuscript 3 `nuntiat`, “announces,” and manuscript 4 past `nunciavit`, “announced,” for present `nuncians`, “informing.” Manuscripts 2 and 4 read `sibi`, “to himself,” for `ei`, “to him,” referring the choice of place to the pope. Manuscript 2 expands `Quod audiens` to “when Lord Louis heard this”; manuscript 4 reads `confestim`, “at once,” for `statim`, “immediately,” and manuscripts 2–4 `maximis`, “greatest,” for `magnis`, “great.” At the meeting, manuscript 4 reads `obvians ei`, “meeting him,” and manuscript 2 `qui cum obviasset sibi`, “when he had met him.” Manuscript 4 omits `cum`, “with,” before “his whole body”; manuscript 2 reads `toto`, “whole,” for `omni`, and manuscripts 3 and 4 accusative `terram`, “onto the ground,” for `in terra`, “on the ground.” Manuscripts 2 and 3 omit `Benedictus sit`, “blessed be.” Manuscript 2 reads `ergo`, “therefore,” for `enim`, “for”; manuscript 4 has `osculantes pacifice`, “kissing peacefully.” Prayer is pluperfect `orassent`, “had prayed,” in manuscript 2 and indicative `oraverunt`, “prayed,” in manuscript 4.
- **Chapter 17.** Irmingard appears as `Ermengardam` in manuscript 2. Manuscripts 2–4 omit `et uncxit eum`, “and anointed him”; manuscripts 2 and 4 omit `cum`, “with,” before the precious gems. Manuscript 2 reads `asportare fecit`, “had [it] carried,” manuscript 3 `assportaverat`, “had carried,” and manuscript 4 `apportaverat`, “had brought,” for `adportaverat`. Manuscripts 3 and 4 read `supra`, “above/upon,” for `super`. At the pope's stay, the manuscripts read `mansit`, “remained,” for `erat`, “was”; manuscript 4 spells `cottidie` as `quotidie`. Printed `Postquam`, “after,” becomes `Ergo postquam`, “therefore after,” in manuscript 2 and `post quod`, “after which,” in manuscripts 3 and 4.
- **Chapter 18.** After `Postmodum`, “subsequently,” manuscript 4 reads `dies supra modum`, “an excessive number of days”; the intervening or middle words are missing (`media desunt`) in the manuscript tradition. The final note directs the reader to Einhard's *Life of Charlemagne*, chapter 22 and following.

### 19

Returning from there, the lord emperor came to the palace at Aachen, to his seat. For day by day he excelled in sacred virtues—[Note: Col. 0413: lacking in 2–4.] matters too extensive to enumerate. He was of medium height, with large and bright eyes, a radiant countenance, a long and straight nose, lips [Note: Col. 0413: “and lips” 4.] neither too thick nor too thin [Note: Col. 0413: “thin” 4, 9; “long” 3.], a powerful chest, broad shoulders, very strong arms, so that [Col. 0413C] no one could equal him in shooting with a bow or casting a spear [Note: Col. 0413: lacking in 9.] [Note: Col. 0413: “equal” 3; “be equaled” 2, 4, 9.]: long hands, straight fingers, long shins proportionately slender [Note: Col. 0413: “slender” 4, 9; “thick” 2.], long feet, and a manly voice.

He was highly learned in the Greek and Latin languages, but he could understand Greek better [Note: Col. 0413: “more” 4.] than he could speak it [Note: Col. 0413: “understand” 2–4, 9.]; Latin, however, he could speak as fluently as his native language [Note: Col. 0413: “but he spoke Latin as though it were his native language, with equal fluency” 9; “he spoke” 2.]. In all the Scriptures he understood the spiritual and moral sense, as well as the anagogical sense [Note: Col. 0413: “anagogical” 4; “anagogic” 5.] extremely well [Note: Col. 0413: “he possessed the spiritual and intelligible sense” 2.].

He rejected the pagan poetic songs that he had learned in his youth, and no longer wished either to read, hear, or teach them [Note: Col. 0413: “to learn” instead 2.]. He was strong in his limbs, agile and energetic [Note: Col. 0413: “energetic” 1.], slow to anger and [Note: Col. 0413: lacking in 4.] quick to show mercy. Whenever, on weekdays, he went to church in the morning [Col. 0414A] for the sake of prayer, he touched the pavement with his forehead on bended knees, praying humbly for a long time, sometimes with tears; and he was always adorned with every good habit.

He was so generous that previously neither in ancient books nor [Note: Col. 0413: “nor in” lacking in 2–4.] in modern times had it been heard that anyone had handed over royal estates—which had belonged to his father, grandfather, and great-grandfather—to his faithful servants as perpetual possessions [Note: Col. 0413: “perpetual properties” 4.], and had issued charters [Note: Col. 0413: “confirmed” 2; “constructed” 3; “constructed” 4, 9.] and strengthened them with the impression of his ring and his own handwritten subscription [Note: Col. 0413: “inscription” 2, 3; “subscription” 4, 9.]. For he had been doing this for a long time [Note: Col. 0413: “for a long time” 2–4, 9.].

He was temperate in food and drink and moderate in his clothing [Note: Col. 0413: lacking in 3, 4]. He never shone in a golden garment [Note: Col. 0413: “garment” 4], except only on the greatest feast days, as his fathers had been accustomed to do. Then [Note: Col. 0413: lacking in 4, 9.] on those days he wore nothing [Note: Col. 0413: lacking in 1.] except a shirt [Note: Col. 0413: lacking in 2, 3, 4, 9.; “camisa” 9.] and breeches [Col. 0414B] [Note: Col. 0413: “breeches” 1; “underwear” 4, 9.] woven with gold; he was girded with a golden border [Note: Col. 0413D: That is, a border, a military tunic.], with a golden belt [Note: Col. 0413: “belt” 2, 3, 9.] [Note: Col. 0413: “golden” lacking in 4.] and a sword gleaming with gold [Note: Col. 0413: “golden” 1.], and wore golden greaves and a cloak woven [Note: Col. 0413: lacking in 2, 3, 4.] with gold, a golden crown [Note: Col. 0413: “a golden crown gleaming with gold” 4.] on his head, and held a golden staff in his hand.

He never raised his voice in laughter [Note: Col. 0413: “in laughing” 2–4, 9.], not even when, on the greatest feast days, the stage musicians [Note: Col. 0413: “stage musicians”; that is, theatrical musicians. Isidore, *Etymologies*, book XVIII, chapter 47.] came forth for the people’s amusement—clowns and actors with flute-players [Note: Col. 0413: “choraule players” 2–4, 9.] and lyre-players—at table before him, and the people then laughed in moderation before him. He himself never displayed even his white teeth in laughter.

Every day before eating he gave alms to the poor [Note: Col. 0413: “giving of alms” 1; lacking in 4.], and wherever he was, he maintained hospices [Note: Col. 0413: “hospices” 1.]. In the month of August, when deer are at their fattest, he devoted himself to hunting [Note: Col. 0413: “to the hunt” 4, 9.] until the season of [Col. 0414C] the trees [Note: The reading *abrorum* is uncertain; literally, “of the trees.”] arrived.

### 20

Doing everything prudently and cautiously, and nothing indiscreetly [Note: Col. 0413: “he did nothing indiscreetly except that” 4.], except that he trusted his counselors more than was necessary; this resulted from his being occupied with psalmody and continual reading [Note: Col. 0413: Here the annalist of Metz omits our text.], and from another matter, which he did not initiate.

For a long-standing and very evil custom existed [Col. 0414D] [Note: Compare the Monk of Saint Gall, *Deeds of Charlemagne* I.3.], namely, that the highest pontiffs were made from the most worthless slaves [Note: Col. 0413: “and this” 4.]. He did not prohibit this [Note: Col. 0413: “which nevertheless” 4.], although it is the greatest evil among the Christian people, as the histories of the Kings testify [Note: Col. 0413: “testifies” variously; “history” 2–4.] concerning Jeroboam son of Nabad [Note: Col. 0413: “Nadab” 1, 3; “Nabath” 2, 4, 6.], who had been a servant of King Solomon and afterward held authority over the ten tribes of the sons of Israel.

For Scripture reports this about him [Note: Col. 0414D: 1 Kings 13:33]: “After [Col. 0415A] these words Jeroboam did not return from his exceedingly evil way, but, on the contrary, he made priests of the lowest of the people for the high places.
