Whoever wished, he filled his hand, and he became a priest of the high places” [Note: Col. 0415: “Concerning him, in these words: ‘He did not…’” 4; the whole passage from “Whatever…” to “high places” is lacking in 4.]. And because of this the house of Jeroboam sinned, and was overthrown and destroyed from the face of the earth.

After such men seize the summit of government [Note: Col. 0415: lacking in 4.], they are never afterward so gentle and so domesticated [Note: Col. 0415: “so domestic” 1.] that they do not immediately become angry, quarrelsome, abusive, obstinate, injurious, and promise threats to all their subjects; and through such dealings they desire to be feared and praised by everyone [Note: Col. 0415: “and” 2, 4.].

They strive to free their most disgraceful relations from the yoke of their deserved servitude and to impose freedom upon them [Note: Col. 0415: “to impose it” 4.]. Then they instruct some of them in the liberal studies [Col. 0415B], join others to noble women, and compel the sons of nobles to take their female relatives in marriage [Note: Col. 0415: “to take in marriage” 4; “in marriage” is lacking in 4.].

For no one can live with them peacefully except those alone who have such a connection with them [Note: Col. 0415: lacking in 4.]; the rest lead out their days with the greatest sadness, groaning and [Note: Col. 0415: lacking in 2–4.] weeping. But the relatives of the aforesaid men, once they understand something of the situation, mock and despise the noble elders; they are arrogant, unstable, incontinent [Note: Col. 0415: lacking in 4.], immodest [Note: Col. 0415: lacking in 4.], and shameless. Nevertheless, each retains some small good quality.

But after they cast away from themselves holy reverence for their Lord [Note: Col. 0415: “cast away” 2, 3; “cast away” singular 4.] [Note: Col. 0415: “of their Lord” lacking in 3.], they refuse to understand the canonical Scripture called the Council of the Apostles. For there he commanded, saying: “But if a bishop has poor relatives, let provision be made for them [Col. 0415C] as for the poor, so that ecclesiastical property may not perish.” They refuse to accept the book of Saint Gregory [Note: Col. 0415: “Pope Gregory” 2.], entitled *The Pastoral Rule*.

No one can comprehend how they conduct themselves, except those alone who suffer this evil without any interruption. But their relatives, once they understand something of the matter—which is a very great danger for both givers and recipients—are dragged into the sacred order. And although some may be learned [Note: Col. 0415: “although some are learned” 4.], nevertheless the multitude of their crimes surpasses their learning.

It generally happens [Note: Col. 0415: “generally” 1.] that, in the church, a pastor does not dare to challenge certain negligent and harmful men with canonical justice because of the crimes of their relatives [Note: Col. 0415: “and that matter” 4.]. That sacred ministry is often despised by many because it is exercised by such men.

And therefore may almighty God deign to eradicate and suppress this most evil custom from now and henceforth among kings [Col. 0415D] [Note: Col. 0415D: That is, among kings and princes; here *cum* means the German *bei*, “among/with.”] and princes [Note: Col. 0415: “with their kings” 2–4.] [Col. 0416A], so that it may no longer occur among the Christian people. Amen.

### 21 (817)

The aforesaid emperor designated his son Hluthar [Note: Col. 0415: “Hluthar” 2; “Lothar” 3, 4; “Hludhar” 5.] so that, after his death, he might receive all the kingdoms that God had handed over to him through his father’s hand [Note: Col. 0415: “through the hand of his father” 2–4, 6.] and bear the name and empire of his father [Note: Col. 0415: “and therefore the father…” 4.]. For this reason his other sons were indignant.

### 22

In that same year Bernhard, Pippin’s son born of a concubine [Note: Col. 0415: “and born of” 4.], encouraged by evil men, lifted himself up against his paternal uncle [Note: Col. 0416D: That is, his uncle.] and wished to expel him from the kingdom. For he had impious counselors here and there [Note: Col. 0415: The words from “For he had…” to “here and there” are lacking in 1.].

When the lord emperor heard this, he departed from the palace at Aachen [Note: Col. 0415: lacking in 4; “and arrived” 2, 4.] and reached the city of Chalon [Note: Col. 0415: “Davilon” 2.], where Bernhard came to meet him with his impious counselors and presented themselves and commended themselves [Note: Col. 0415: the words “and presented themselves” are lacking in 2–4; “and commended themselves” is lacking in 1.]. The emperor celebrated the Nativity of the Lord there [Note: Col. 0415: “and from there” 4.].

Returning from there, he came to his seat at Aachen [Note: Col. 0415: “Aachen” 2–4.]. After Easter (818), he held a great assembly of the peoples and investigated all the wicked conspiracies of the unfaithful concerning this matter. Some were found to have fallen into this rebellion [Note: Col. 0415: “seduction” 4.] from both the Franks and the Lombards [Note: Col. 0415: “Lombards” 1, 3, 4.]. All were sentenced to death, except the bishops, who were afterward deposed when their confession had been made.

These were Anshelm of Milan [Note: Col. 0415: “Ansselmus” 2.], Theodulf of Orléans [Note: Col. 0415: “Thedulful” 1; “Thiedolphus” 3.], and Wolvold of Cremona [Note: Col. 0415: “Wolvodus” 4; “and Wolvold of Cremona, and Theodulf of Orléans” 2–4.]. The emperor did not wish to carry out against them the death sentence that had been imposed on the others [Note: Col. 0415: “had been imposed” 4.]; [Col. 0416C] but the counselors deprived Bernhard of his eyesight, and likewise his instigators, Egittheus [Note: Col. 0415: “Eggitheus” 2, 3; “Egittheus” 4.], Reginhard [Note: Col. 0415: “Reginhard” 2; “Reinhard” 4.], and Reginharius [Note: Col. 0415: lacking in 3.], who was the son of Hardrade’s daughter [Note: Col. 0415: “Hardard” 2; “Hardrat” 3, 4.]. Hardrade was that most faithless duke who had long ago wished to rise up against the lord Charles and diminish his kingdom; he himself was subjected to the same punishment that his daughter’s son suffered with his associates.

### 23

On the third day after the loss of his eyesight, Bernhard died. When the emperor heard this, he wept for a long time in great sorrow [Note: Col. 0415: “for a long time” 2, 4; “him” 4.], and made confession before all his bishops, accepting penance at their judgment for this one reason: that he had not prevented his counselors from carrying out this mutilation [Note: Col. 0416D; Col. 0415: “mutilation” 2, 3, 5; “cruelty” 1, 4.] [Note: Col. 0415: “doing” 3.]. For this reason he gave much to the poor [Col. 0417A] for the purification of his soul.

### 24

At the same time he ordered his brothers tonsured [Note: Col. 0417: “to be tonsured” 2–4.], Drogo [Note: Col. 0417: “Drogon” 4.], Hugh [Note: Col. 0417: “Hugh” 2–4.], and Theodoric [Note: Col. 0417: “Theodric” 1; “Theoderic” 2.], in order to mitigate discord, and ordered them to be instructed in the liberal disciplines [Note: Col. 0417: “he instructs” 1.]. Later he established them honorably: he gave Drogo a bishopric and Hugh monasteries [Note: Col. 0417: “monastic establishments” 3, 4; “many monasteries” 2.].

### 25

Then the lord emperor went with an army into the region of Britain [Note: Col. 0417: “into the regions” 4; “Britain” 2–4.]. There Murcomannus, their duke [Note: Col. 0417D: Other copies read “Murmannus.”], was killed, and he brought that whole land under his rule. Returning from there, he found Queen Irmingard suffering from fever; she died in peace a few days later [Note: Col. 0417: “rested” 2.].

### 26

In the following year (819), he took as wife the daughter of his duke Hwelf [Note: Col. 0417: “Hwuelf” 1; “Welf” 4.] [Note: Col. 0417: lacking in 4.], who was of the noblest lineage [Col. 0417B] [Note: Col. 0417: “stock” 4.] of the Bavarians [Note: Col. 0417: “Baiovarians” 2, 3; “Bavarians” 4.]. The maiden’s name was Judith; on her mother’s side—whose name was Eigilwi [Note: Col. 0417: “whose name was Eigilwi” is lacking in 2, 3, 4, 5.]—she was of the noblest Saxon family, and he made her queen. For she was exceedingly beautiful.

In the same year he held his general assembly at Ingilenheim [Note: Col. 0417: “Ingilheim” 1; “Inguleheim” 2; “Ingulenheim” 4.] in the royal estate [Note: Col. 0417: lacking in 4–.].

### 27

In the following year (820), he sent his army against the eastern Slavs, whose duke was called Liduit [Note: Col. 0417: “Liudewit” 3.]. They put him to flight [Note: Col. 0417: “into flight” 2–4.] and devastated that land [Note: Col. 0417: the words “and devastated that land” are lacking in 1.]. Returning from there, they came home.

### 28

In the following year (821), he held his general assembly. There Hluthar, his firstborn son by the queen [Note: Col. 0417: “by the queen” lacking in 3.], took in marriage the daughter of Count Hugh [Note: Col. 0417: “of Hugh” 3, 4.], who was descended from a certain duke named Etih [Col. 0417C] [Note: Col. 0417: “Edic” 2; “Edig” 3; “Edith” 4; “Edit” 5.], who was timid beyond all men.

For his household servants sang such things to him that at times he would not have dared to set one foot outside the hedge [Note: Col. 0417: “hedge” 4; lacking in 2.]. Even then disloyalty was threatening him; through the instigation of the aforesaid father-in-law [Note: Col. 0417: “of his father-in-law” 1, 3.] and many other wicked men, he displayed it against his father [Note: Col. 0417: “against his father” 2–4.]. Returning from there [Note: Col. 0417: the words from “Returning from there” through “with his wife” are lacking in 3.], Hluthar came to Worms with his wife.

### 29

In the following year (822), he held his general assembly at the palace of Attigny [Note: Col. 0417: “Attigny” 1.]. From there he sent his son Hluthar with his wife Irmingard to Italy [Note: Col. 0417: “Irmingar” 2; “Irmingard to Italy” 1.]. The lord emperor then departed from there [Note: Col. 0417: “and came” 2–4.] and came to Frankfurt [Note: Col. 0417: “Franconovurd” 3; “Franconofard” 2; “Franconofurt” 4.], where he celebrated the Nativity of the Lord.

### 30

Afterward (823) he sent his legates, the venerable abbot and priest Adalung and Hunfrid, who was duke over Rhaetia [Note: Col. 0417: “Reddica” 1; compare chapter 35; “Rhaetia” 4.] [Note: Col. 0417D: Rhaetia, or the duchy of Chur. Compare Eginhard’s *Annals*.], to Rome because of a certain outrage that the Roman people had alleged against Pope Paschal [Note: Col. 0417: “Roman” 2–4.], accusing him of having been the murderer of certain men.

The aforesaid pontiff cleared himself under oath in the Lateran patriarchal church before the aforementioned legates and the Roman people, with thirty-four bishops and five priests and deacons (824). After those legates had departed, the aforesaid pope immediately died. The Roman people did not wish his funeral to be buried in the church of the blessed apostle Peter until Pope Eugene succeeded him; Eugene then ordered his body to be buried in the place that Paschal himself had built while alive.

### 31

In the following year the emperor went once more into Britain [Note: Col. 0417: “Britain” 2–4.] and devastated that entire land with a great scourge because of their disloyalty.

### 32

The following year (825), he was at the palace at Aachen [Note: Col. 0417: “Aachen” 2–4.] with a great army. There envoys of the Bulgars [Note: Col. 0417: “bringing” 4; “Bulgarians” 1; “Vulgarians” 5.] came bearing gifts. He received them kindly and dismissed them to return to their own country.

### 33

In the following year (826), he was at the royal palace at Ingilenheim [Note: Col. 0417: “Ingilheim” 1; “Inguleheim” 2; “Ingulenheim” 4; likewise frequently.]. There Heriolt came to him from the Danes [Note: Col. 0417: “Danes” 3, 4.]. The lord emperor raised him from the sacred baptismal font [Note: Col. 0417: lacking in 4.], and the lady Judith Augusta raised his wife from the font [Note: Col. 0417: “his wife” lacking in 1.].

Then the lord emperor gave him a large part of the Frisians’ land [Note: Col. 0417: “Frisians” 4.], adorned him with honorable gifts, and dismissed him with his legates to depart in peace [Note: Col. 0417: “into” 4.].

### 34

The following year (827), he sent his army against the Saracens [Note: Col. 0417: lacking in 4.]. In the following year (828), he departed from Ingilenheim; after his general assembly he reached Commercy [Note: Col. 0417: “Commerciacum” 4.] [Note: Col. 0418D: Commercy on the Meuse.].

### 35

The following year (829), he came to Worms. There, in the presence of his sons Hluthar and his namesake [Note: Col. 0417: “his namesake Louis” 4.], he assigned to his son Charles, who had been born of the Augusta Judith [Note: Col. 0417: lacking in 1.], the land of Alamannia [Note: Col. 0417: “Alamannia” 1; “Alemannia” 2.], Rhaetia [Note: Col. 0417: “Rhaetia” 4; “Rhaetia” 5.] [Note: Col. 0418D: Rhaetia of Chur.], and a certain part of Burgundy. His sons Hluthar and his namesake, together with their brother Pippin, were indignant at this [Note: Col. 0417: lacking in 1; lacking in 4.].

### 36

In the following year (830), the lord emperor departed from the palace at Aachen and reached Compiègne [Note: Col. 0417: “and reached” 2, 4.]. There Pippin his son came to meet him with his father’s principal magnates [Col. 0419A]: Hilduin the archchaplain [Note: Col. 0419: “Archchaplain” should be written *archicappellano*, according to the usage of his age.], Jesse, bishop of Amiens [Note: Col. 0419: “Ambiens” 1.], Hugh [Note: Col. 0419: “Hugh” 2; “Hugh” 3, 4.], Matfrid [Note: Col. 0419: “Mathfrid” 2, 4.], Elisachar the abbot [Note: Col. 0419: “Elisachar the abbot and Gotefrid” are lacking in 4.], Gotefrid [Note: Col. 0419: “Godefrid” 2, 3.], and many other traitors. They wished to expel the lord emperor from the kingdom, but his beloved namesake son prevented this.

The aforesaid wicked men, bringing many accusations against him—things impious either to say or believe [Note: Col. 0419: the words “things impious either to say or believe” are lacking in 2, 4.]—said that Queen Judith had been violated by a certain duke Bernhard [Note: Col. 0419D: Son of Saint William, duke and monk of Gellone. Bouquet.], who was of royal stock and the lord emperor’s son from the sacred baptismal font. They were lying about everything.

They took Queen Judith, veiled her by force, and sent her to a monastery; and they tonsured her brothers Chuonrad [Note: Col. 0419: “Cunrad” 2; “Counrad” 3; “Conrad” 4, 5.] and Ruodolf [Note: Col. 0419: “Ruodulf” 2; “Rudolf” 4, 5.] and sent them to a monastery [Note: Col. 0419: “monastery” 2–5; “sent them” 2, 3; “sending them, etc.” 4.].

### 37

In that same year [Note: Col. 0419: lacking in 4.] the lord emperor reached the fortress of Nijmegen [Note: Col. 0419: “Niuuimagun” 1; “Novium Magnum” 2; “Noviomagum” 3, 4.], which is situated [Note: Col. 0419: the words “which is situated” are lacking in 3.] on the river called the Waal [Note: Col. 0419: “Val” 2, 4; “Wal” 3.].

A multitude of men from all his kingdoms came to him. Among them came his aforesaid adversaries, and the lord emperor overcame them, divided them up [Note: Col. 0419: “after he overcame them, he divided them” 2; “he overcame them” 3, 4; “he dismissed them” 4.] and assigned them to custody [Note: Col. 0420D: That is, he distributed them to be guarded.].

His son Hluthar promised fidelity under oath, so that afterward he would never again commit such acts [Note: Col. 0419: “after these things” 2; “henceforth” 4.]. There also Jesse was deposed by the just judgment of the bishops. His namesake son was there, the one who had been his father’s helper in all his labors.

From there the lord emperor came to Aachen, to his seat. His aforementioned wife came there to meet him, and he received her honorably, at the command of Gregory the Roman pontiff and by the just judgment of the other bishops [Col. 0419C] [Note: Col. 0419: “just” lacking in 3.].

### 38

In the following year (831), the emperor was in the palace at Thionville with his sons Hluthar and Hludowic. There the aforesaid duke Bernhard came and cleared himself of the alleged adultery [Note: Col. 0419: “of the alleged offense” 4.], since no one was found who had dared to bring that charge against him with weapons [Note: Col. 0419: “the matter already mentioned” 4.].

### 39

In the following year (832), after Easter, it was heard that his namesake son, with Hluthar’s counsel, had wished to visit his father with an army [Note: Col. 0419: “dishonorably” 2, 3, 4.]. He came as far as the monastery of Saint Nazarius and, remaining there for a short time [Col. 0420A], stayed until his father, coming to Mainz [Note: Col. 0419: “Mainz” 2–4.], assembled an army and followed him.

His aforesaid son, returning home, [Note: Col. 0419: lacking in 2–4; “but, returning home, he waited” 2.] awaited his father’s arrival and wished to defend himself. But when the father arrived, he ordered him to come to him. Receiving him kindly, they held a peaceful conversation, and a few days later they separated with great affection [Note: Col. 0419: “with great joy and affection” 4.]. The son remained at home, and the father returned to Francia.

### 40

When he came to the palace at Frankfurt, Hluthar his son came to meet him there, asking his father to allow him to clear himself, since his brother had caused his father no trouble either by his will or at his instigation. That this is true is known to some [Note: Col. 0419: “that this is true” is rendered “it is truly known to some” 2.].

### 41

While the king was staying there [Note: Col. 0419: “there” 2, 4.], it was heard that his son Pippin wished to cause a disturbance against his father [Note: Col. 0419: “some disturbance for his father” 2–4.]. He hurried to the city of Limoges [Note: Col. 0419: “Limodiam” 4.] to meet him [Note: Col. 0419: “him” 2–4.] and ordered his son, with his wife and children, to go to Francia.

At first, hearing his father’s command, he began to go as far as the palace of Théoduad [Note: Col. 0419: “Theohtuad” 2; “Theotwad” 4.]. Returning from there, he went into Aquitaine [Note: Col. 0419: “and the emperor” 4.] (833). Returning from there [Note: Col. 0419: “returning” 4.], the emperor came to Aachen, to his seat [Note: Col. 0419: “to Aachen” 4.], and remained there for not a long time. Departing from there [Note: Col. 0419: “going out” 3; “departing” 4.], he came to the city of Worms [Note: Col. 0419: lacking in 4.] before the holy season of Lent [Note: Col. 0419: “Lenten” 4.].

### 42

After Easter he heard that his sons wished to come to him again, not peacefully [Note: Col. 0419: “that” 2, 4.]. He assembled an army and went to meet them as far as the great field between Strasbourg [Note: Col. 0419: “Argentaria” 2, 4; “Argentoratum” 5.] and Basel [Note: Col. 0419: “Basel” 4.] [Col. 0420C], which to this day is called the Field of Lies, where the fidelity of very many was extinguished [Note: Col. 0419: “because there” 4; “was extinguished” 4.].

His sons went to meet him with Gregory, the Roman pope [Note: Col. 0419: “pope” 2, 3; “Roman pontiff” 4.]. Whatever they requested, their father consented to nothing [Note: Col. 0419: “nothing was granted to them” 3, 4.]. A few days later the emperor and the aforesaid pontiff came to a conference. After they had spoken for a short time, the pontiff first honored him with great and innumerable gifts.

After each had returned to his tent, the emperor sent royal gifts to the aforesaid pontiff through the venerable abbot and priest Adalung [Note: Col. 0419: lacking in 3 and 4.]. Then some men took counsel to abandon the emperor and go over to his sons [Col. 0421A], especially those who had previously offended him [Note: Col. 0421: “had offended him earlier” 4.]. With the others following, the greater part of them abandoned him one night and, leaving their tents [Note: Col. 0421: “abandoning” 4.], went over to his sons.

On the following day [Note: Col. 0421: “but on the following day” 4.], some who had remained came to the emperor. He ordered them, saying: “Go,” he said, “to my sons. I do not wish anyone, on my account, to lose life or limb.” But they departed from him, overcome with tears [Note: Col. 0421: lacking in 2, 4.].

By then they had separated his wife from him [Note: Col. 0421: the words “By then they had separated their wife from him” are lacking in 1.], confirming under oath [Note: Col. 0421: “confirming” singular 4.] that they desired neither her death nor her mutilation [Note: Col. 0421: “debilitation” 2–4.]. They immediately sent her to Italy, to the city of Tortona [Note: Col. 0421: “Dartona” 4.], where they kept her.

Not long afterward they received their father and led him away with them [Note: Col. 0421: “led him away with them” 2, 3; “having him with them. Not many days later they received him” 3.]. Having done this [Note: Col. 0421: “this having been done” 2.], they separated there: Pippin went into Aquitaine and Hludowic into Bavaria.

### 43

Hluthar, however, took his father with him to the palace at Compiègne and there afflicted him severely with the bishops and several others [Note: Col. 0421: “severely” lacking in 1.]. They ordered him to go into a monastery [Note: Col. 0421: “for they ordered him to go into a monastery” 4; “they ordered him, therefore, to go” 3; lacking in 4.] and to remain there for all the days of his life [Note: Col. 0421: lacking in 1.]. But he rejected this and did not consent to their will [Note: Col. 0421: “pleasure” 1.].

For all the bishops were hostile to him, especially those whom he had honored from the most worthless servile condition, together with those who had been raised to this dignity from barbarian nations.

### 44

Then they chose one shameless and most cruel man, who was called Ebo [Note: *hebo*, witness 4], bishop of Rheims, who was descended from the stock of hereditary slaves, so that he might cruelly afflict him together with the contrivances of the others. They spoke unheard-of things and did unheard-of deeds, insulting him every day. They took the sword from his thigh [Note: *de*—“from”—witnesses 3 and 4], clothing him in sackcloth by the judgment of his own servants. Then the epilogue (*epilogium*) of Jeremiah the prophet was fulfilled [Note: *i. est*—“that is”—witness 3; *epilongium* in witness 1, *epylogium* in witness 3, and *elogium* in witness 4]: “Servants have ruled over us” [Lamentations 5:8].

O, what a recompense you have rendered him! He made you free [Note: witness 1 reads *feci te*, “I made you”], not noble—which is impossible after freedom [Note: after *libertatem*, witness 4 reads *est. Vestivit*, “is. He clothed”]. After freedom he clothed you in purple and a cloak [Note: witness 1 reads *vestivi te*, “I clothed you”]; you clothed him in sackcloth [Note: witness 4 reads “and you”]. He dragged you, undeserving as you were, to the pontifical summit; you wished by a false judgment to expel him from the throne of his fathers.

Cruel man, why did you not understand the Lord’s command [Note: *domini*—“of the Lord”—witness 4] [Matthew 10:24]: “A servant is not above his master” [Note: “his” is added in witnesses 3 and 4]? Why did you despise the apostolic command [Note: witness 1 has *apostolice*, an adverbial or misspelled form, in place of the adjective *apostolica*] of him who had been caught up to the third heaven [Note: witness 4 omits “up to”], so that among the angels he might learn what he should command human beings [Note: witness 4 reads “what he should command human beings”; witness 3 reads *impararet*, “might prepare/provide,” instead of *imperaret*, “might command”]? He thus commands, saying [Note: “for thus he commands: ‘to all …’” in witness 3] [Romans 13:1]: “Be subject to all higher authorities. For there is no authority except from the Lord” [Note: witness 4 omits “for there is”; witnesses 3 and 4 read “from God”].

And again another says [Note: “elsewhere” in witness 3] [1 Peter 2:17]: “Fear God, honor the king. Servants, be subject in all fear to your masters” [Note: witness 4 omits “to your masters”], “not only to the good and gentle, but also to the difficult; for this is grace” [Note: witness 4 reads *hoc*—“this,” instead of *haec*—“this”]. But you did not fear God, nor did you honor the king. If anyone can obtain God’s grace by doing such things, surely he will have God’s anger by despising such things.

Cruel man, who was your counselor or your guide [Col. 0422B]? Was it not he who is king over all the sons of pride, who said to God his creator [Matthew 4:9]: “All these things I will give you, if, falling down, you will worship me” [Note: *adoraveris*—“you will worship”—in witnesses 3 and 4]? [Note: That is, *adoraveris*; *v* and *b* are interchanged.]

O Lord Jesus Christ [Note: omitted in witness 4], where was your angel who easily destroyed all the firstborn of Egypt in one night [Note: omitted in witness 4]? And he who, in the camp of the Assyrians under Sennacherib, that wicked king, extinguished in one night one hundred and eighty-five thousand faithless men [Note: “in one night” is omitted in witness 4], as the prophet Isaiah testifies [Isaiah 37:36]? Or he who struck the younger Herod [Note: witness 4 reads “the young man Herod”] while he was haranguing [Note: witness 1 reads *concinantem*—“singing”], so that he immediately began to swarm with worms [Note: witnesses 3 and 4 read “and” instead of “so that”]? And you, earth, which bore him [Note: witnesses 3 and 4 read “sustained him”; the editor notes that the same meaning is intended by *sustulisti* and *sustinuisti*] at that time, why did you not open your mouth to devour him, just as long ago you did with Dathan and Abiram?

You did not understand your threefold law, which says [Ecclesiasticus 33:25]: “Food and a rod and a burden for the ass” [Note: *onus*—“burden”—corrected from *honus* in witnesses 1, 3, and 4] [Note: that is, “burden”]; “bread and discipline and work for the servant” [Col. 0422C].

The prophet Zechariah prophesied against you, saying [Note: omitted in witness 4] [Zechariah 13:3]: “You shall not live, because you have spoken falsehood in the name of the Lord.”

God revealed your wickedness and preserved his kingdom and his glory for him [Note: witness 1 reads “consecrated” instead of “preserved”]. Through greed and falsehood you have destroyed yourself in great wickedness [Note: the words from “Through greed …” to “rises” are all absent from witness 4]. Fall now into disgrace throughout all the days of your life. Through the precipices of greed and falsehood [Note: witness 1 omits “and falsehood”], let your shame increase from day to day, just as a small number rises by the art of arithmetic to become a great one [Note: witness 2 reads “thus” instead of “just as”].

Cruel man, your canonical judgment is still incomplete. It is necessary that the judgment be completed for your greater disgrace. Your fathers were goatherds, not counselors of princes. With the judgment of the others you deposed Lesse from the priesthood; now you have recalled him to his former rank [Note: witness 1 omits “you have recalled him”]. Either then or now you produced a false judgment. You were an imitator [Note: witness 1 reads *immitator*—“imitator”] of him about whom the poet sings in Book Six of the *Aeneid* [Note: witness 4 reads *Aeneidorum*] [verses 617–621]:

> Unhappy Theseus; and Phlegyas, most wretched, [Note: witness 3 reads *Feguasque* and witness 4 *Fegrasque*, variant spellings of “and Phlegyas”],  
> Warns all and bears witness in a great voice through the shades [Note: witness 3 reads *admonet*, “admonishes,” for *ammonet*, “warns”]:  
> “Learn justice, being warned, and do not despise the gods.”  
> This man sold his country for gold and imposed a powerful master;  
> He enacted laws for a price and repealed them.

What more can I say to you? [Note: witnesses 3 and 4 read, “For if …”] If I had had a tongue of iron and bronze lips [Note: witness 4 reads *labra*—“lips”], I could not have explained [Note: witnesses 3 and 4 read *explicare*, “to unfold/explain,” for *explanare*, “to make plain”] or enumerated all your crimes.

But if there had been someone willing to probe all your misdeeds in poetic song [Note: witness 3 omits “there had been someone who”; witness 4 omits “all”], perhaps he could have surpassed the Smyrnaean poet [Note: witnesses 1 and 3 read *Smirmanum*; witness 4, *Smyrnaeum*], ancient Homer, and Mantuan Maro together with Ovid [Note: witness 1 reads *Minciarumque* instead of *Mincianumque*].

Yet the temptation of the most pious prince, which he endured from the most wicked men, is believed to have occurred for no other reason than that his goodness might be proved, as was also the patience of blessed Job. There was, however, a great difference between the persecutors of the two [Note: witnesses 3 and 4 read “among” instead of “between”]. Those who insulted blessed Job are said in the Book of blessed Tobit [Note: witness 4 reads *Thobiae*; witness 3 omits “in the Book of Tobit”] to have been kings; but those who afflicted this man most severely were his own legal servants and those of his fathers [Note: witness 4 reads “were” instead of “have been”].

### 45

Afterward they led the most pious prince from Compendium to the palace at Aachen. Hearing this, his namesake son withdrew from Bavaria [Note: witness 3 reads *Baioria*], driven by great grief because of the injury done to his father. When he came to the palace at Frankfurt, he immediately sent his envoys from there: Gozbald, abbot of Niederaltaich and archchaplain [Note: of Lower Altaich; the note refers to Eckhard, *Frankish History of the East*, II, 246], together with a presbyter [Note: omitted in witnesses 3 and 4] and Morhard, count of the palace. They requested and commanded that a more humane sentence be shown toward his father [Note: witnesses 3 and 4 read “that he should show”]. His brother Hlothar did not receive this kindly [Note: witness 3 reads “did not receive it”].

After those envoys had returned [Note: omitted in witness 3], he immediately sent others to his father, but they were forbidden to see him.

### 46

Afterward Hlothar departed from the palace at Aachen [Note: witnesses 3 and 4 add “and reached”] and reached Mainz, where his brother came to meet him. There they held an unequal conference, because all those whom Hlothar had with him were unjustly opposed to his father, whereas those whom Louis had with him were faithful to both his father and himself.

Returning from there, Hlothar came to the palace at Aachen and celebrated the Lord’s Nativity there [Note: “celebrated it there” in witnesses 3 and 4] while his father was still confined.

### 47

After the holy day of the Epiphany (834), Louis again sent his envoys to his father: Grimald [Note: witnesses 3 and 4 spell the name *Grimoldum*], venerable abbot [Note: of Weissenburg; the note refers to Eckhard, *loc. cit.*, II, 198], together with a presbyter [Note: omitted in witness 3], and Gebhard [Note: witness 3 reads *Gebahardum* and witness 4 *Gebehardum*], a most noble and most faithful duke [Note: omitted in witness 1].

When they came to Aachen, Hlothar agreed that they should see their father together with the conspirators, one of whom was called Othogar [Note: witnesses 3 and 4 read *Otgarus*], bishop [Note: of Mainz], and the other the treacherous Richgard [Note: witnesses 3 and 4 read *Richardus*].

When the envoys came into the presence of the prince [Note: witnesses 3 and 4 add “and humbly”], they humbly prostrated themselves at his feet [Note: witnesses 3 and 4 read “at their feet”]. Afterward [Note: omitted in witness 4] they greeted him on behalf of his namesake son. They did not wish to disclose the private message to him because of the conspirators who were present, but by certain movements and signs they made him understand [Note: witness 4 reads “make him understand”] that his namesake son did not wish to consent [Note: witness 1 reads “wished that he should consent to this”] to his father’s punishment [Note: witness 4 specifies “to the punishment of his father”].

### 48

When those men had departed, Hlothar immediately compelled his father to go with him [Note: witness 4 reads “to go with him to”] again to Compendium [Note: omitted in witness 3]. The father agreed with his son and went with him.

Hearing this, his namesake son [Note: witness 4 says explicitly “Louis, hearing this”], having gathered a multitude, followed them. When he was not far from them [Note: witness 4 reads *abesset ab eis*, “was away from them,” for *non longe esset ab eis*, “was not far from them”], Hlothar dismissed his father and withdrew from him with his wicked counselors. His namesake son [Note: witness 4 reads “Louis”] then reached him, received him honorably [Note: witness 4 reads *honeste suscepit et*, “received him honorably and”], led him back again to Aachen, to his own seat, and, by God’s command, restored him to his kingdom and his position [Col. 0424C; witness 4 omits the preposition *in*, “to/in,” before “his position”]. There they celebrated the holy Easter of the Lord together [Note: witness 4 reads “they celebrated”].

When Ebo heard this [Note: witness 4 spells the name *Hebo*], he immediately fled. After he had been captured [Note: witness 4 reads “he fled, but was captured”], he was compelled and brought into the presence of the prince [Note: witness 3 reads “emperor”], who committed him to custody [Note: witness 3 reads “thanks be to God”].

In that same year, which was the twenty-first year of his reign, he granted pardon to all those who had been compelled to abandon him [Note: witness 3 reads “who abandoned him”]. This was neither burdensome [Note: witness 1 reads *honerosum*; witnesses 3 and 4 read *ornerosum*; the word is absent in witness 4] nor grievous to him [Note: witness 3 reads “may it not be grievous to him”; witnesses 3 and 4 omit “and”], who was the most pious of emperors, because he had previously spared his enemies [Note: witness 1 reads “commanded”], fulfilling the evangelical command [Note: omitted in witnesses 3 and 4] that says [Note: witness 1 reads “which says”] [Luke 6:37]: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven.”

A good and great reward is prepared for him [Note: witness 4 adds “by God”] by the one who established this command [Note: witness 3 reads “fulfills”] [Hebrews 12:6]: “For whom the Lord loves [Note: omitted in witness 4], he chastises; and he scourges every son whom he receives” [Note: witness 4 reads “and scourges every son”]. Anyone who does not willingly accept the Lord’s corrections [Note: witness 4 reads “his corrections”] cannot become his son [Note: witnesses 3 and 4 read *potest*, “can,” for *poterit*, “will be able”].

### 50

But one must take the greatest care that it not happen again that servants become his counselors. For, if they can, they chiefly contrive to oppress the nobles and strive to exalt themselves together with their most base relations [Note: “that is, themselves”].

This is not fitting for his holy dignity [Note: witnesses 3 and 4 read “when this happens” or “because this happens”]. In the time of his holy father of blessed memory, it had rarely happened that anyone of such men rose to honor. He instructed such a person with the strictest discipline [Note: witnesses 3–4 read: “lest he should ascend; indeed, he ruled him with the greatest discipline”], lest he begin to grow proud. This example must now be put into practice with the greatest firmness [Note: omitted in witness 4].

When the gentlest of princes was in his trial [Note: omitted in witness 4], such men were so troublesome to him [Note: witness 4 reads “if such men”], although he had shown them every kindness despite their unworthiness. What they do to their subjects needs no one to ask [Note: witness 4 reads “no one needs to ask”].

### 51

After the emperor had prevailed, he sent his faithful envoys to Italy to bring back his wife, who had often been afflicted by false accusations [Note: witness 1 reads *mendiciis*—“beggings” or “petitions,” rather than *mendaciis*—“falsehoods”]. When they came, they received her honorably and led her with joy and gladness into the presence of the prince, who was at that time in the palace at Aachen [Note: omitted in witnesses 3 and 4].

### 52

Hlothar, meanwhile, was staying in the city of Chalon [Note: witness 4 reads *Cabilonum*], where he had committed many evils [Note: witness 3 reads “there”]. He despoiled the churches of God and exhibited the emperor’s faithful men as martyrs wherever he had been able to seize them [Note: witnesses 3 and 4 omit “wherever he had been able to seize them”], except only the envoys [Note: omitted in witness 3].

Moreover, he ordered a religious woman [Note: witnesses 3 and 4 read accusative *sanctimonialem* for nominative *sanctimonialis*, both meaning “religious woman”], who was the sister of Duke Bernard, named Gerbirch [Note: witness 3 reads *Gerbire* and witness 5 *Gerberg*], to be shut in a wine-vessel and thrown into the river Saône, of which the poet sings [Virgil, *Eclogues* 1.63]:

> Either the Parthian drinks the Saône [Note: Pith. reads *Pardus*, “leopard,” for *Parthus*, “Parthian”; Chesn. reads *Partus*, a spelling variant of *Parthus*. Pith. and Chesn. both read *bibat*, subjunctive “may drink,” for *bibet*, future “will drink”],  
> Or Germany the Tigris [Note: witnesses 3 and 4 read *tigrim*].

There he afflicted her for a long time, until he killed her [Note: omitted in witness 3], at the urging of the impious wives of his counselors [Note: in witness 4 the words “until,” “her,” “wives,” and “his” are absent], fulfilling the psalmic prophecy [Note: witness 3 reads *psalmiotam*] [Psalm 18:27]:

> With the holy you will be holy, and with the perverse you will be perverse [Note: witnesses 3 and 4 read *perverteris*—“you will be perverted”—instead of *perversus*—“perverse”].

### 53

After this the emperor sent his envoys to him [Note: witness 4 explicitly reads “to Hlothar”]: Marachward [Note: witness 3 reads *Marcuardum* and witness 4 *Marcwardum*], venerable abbot [Note: witness 3 omits “venerable”; the abbot was of Prüm], together with his other faithful men, carrying letters of exhortation. In them he first admonished him to remember almighty God and his commandments, to turn away from his evil path [Note: witnesses 3 and 4 read “and” instead of the second “so that”], and to understand how strict a judgment it is to despise the Lord in his commandments [Note: witness 4 reads “God” instead of “the Lord”].

For God says, among other commandments [Exodus 20:12; 21:17]: “Honor your father and mother,” and: “Whoever curses father or mother [Note: witnesses 3 and 4 read “curses”] shall be put to death.” God did not give this command through prophets or apostles, but himself commanded it to be observed by writing it down. He later showed in the Book of Deuteronomy [Note: witness 4 reads “of Deuteronomy”] how serious it is to neglect this command [21:18–21], saying:

> If a man has begotten a disobedient and stubborn son who does not listen to the command of his father or mother, and, when corrected, scorns obedience, they shall seize him and lead him to the elders of that city and to the gate of judgment, and they shall say to them: “This son of ours is stubborn and disobedient; he scorns listening to our warnings [Note: witnesses 3 and 4 read “despises”]; he devotes himself to revelries, luxury, and banquets [Note: witness 4 has the singular “banquet”].” Then the people of the city shall overwhelm him with stones, and he shall die, so that you may remove the evil from your midst [Note: witness 3 reads “and”]. And all Israel, hearing this [Note: the words from “And” through “shall fear” are absent in witness 4], shall fear [Note: witness 3 reads “shall fear” in a future form].

### 54

After Hlothar had spoken with the envoys mentioned above, he received their embassy harshly [Note: witness 4 reads *graviter*—“harshly,” rather than *grave*—“harsh”] and severely [Note: omitted in witness 3] and promised them threats which have not yet been fulfilled, nor will they be fulfilled afterward [Note: witness 1 reads: “which have not been fulfilled and will not be fulfilled afterward”].

They returned from him [Note: witness 4 reads “departing”] and came to the emperor, reporting to him everything they had heard [Note: witness 3 adds “and seen”; witness 4 reverses the order, “seen and heard”]. His father then groaned, gathered a large multitude, and went after him wherever he had heard that he was.

His sons came to meet him: Pippin from the west, and his namesake from the east [Note: witness 3 reads “and Louis”; witness 1 omits “and from the east”], each with a great multitude to serve their father. As they approached the city of Orléans [Note: witnesses 3 and 4 read “the city” in the accusative], near which Hlothar was staying with his impious seducers, already mentioned above, he refused to heed [Note: witnesses 3 and 4 read “to heed”] his father’s exhortations. Instead, one night he withdrew from him as though fleeing.

Then the emperor sent his envoys after him [Note: witnesses 3 and 4 read “after him” rather than “after that man”]: Badarad [Note: witnesses 3 and 4 read *Baradadus*; witness 6 reads *Baduradus*], a Saxon bishop [Note: of Paderborn], Gerard [Note: witnesses 3 and 4 read *Gebehardus*], a most noble and faithful duke [Note: “and faithful” is absent in witnesses 3 and 4], and the wise Berengar, his kinsman.

When they came to him, the bishop mentioned above [Note: witness 4 reads “the aforesaid”] immediately commanded him [Note: witness 4 reads “commands him”], under the edict [Note: witness 4 reads “edict”] of almighty God and all his saints [Note: witness 4 reads “and his saints”], to separate himself from the company of his wicked seducers [Note: omitted in witnesses 3 and 4], so that the emperor’s faithful men might show whether it was God’s will for their discord to continue or not [Note: witness 3 reads *fidelitates*, “allegiances,” for *fideles*, “faithful men”; witness 1 has the final *an no*, “or not,” in italics].

After the embassy of the bishop named above [Note: witnesses 3 and 4 read “of the aforesaid bishop”], the dukes delivered what had been commanded to them. Hlothar immediately asked them to withdraw outside for a short time, and then called them back again [Note: the words from “asked” through “again” are absent in witness 1], begging them to give him counsel concerning all his actions [Note: witnesses 3 and 4 read “acts”].

They instructed him to come to his father’s mercy [Note: witnesses 3 and 4 read “presence”] together with the other seducers [Note: witnesses 3 and 4 read “his seducers”], promising peace. He promised that he would come with them [Note: witnesses 3 and 4 read “with them”].

The envoys then returned [Note: witness 4 reads “departing”] and came to the prince, reporting what had happened [Note: witness 4 reads “whatever had happened to him”].

### 55

After them [Note: witness 2 reads “afterward”; witness 4, “after”] Hlothar came to the place where the emperor, his father, was sitting in his pavilion. It had been stretched very high in a great field [Note: the editor remarks: “Here again one hears German; *das Zelt* is neuter in our language”], where the entire army could observe him [Note: witness 4 reads “was observing him”], and his faithful sons stood beside him.

Then Hlothar came and fell at his father’s feet [Note: witness 3 reads “at his feet”], followed by his frightened father-in-law Hugh [Note: witnesses 3 and 4 read *Hugo*]. Then Matfrid [Note: witnesses 3 and 4 read *Macfridus* and *Mathfridus*] and all the others who had been foremost in that crime rose from the ground and confessed that they had greatly sinned.

After this Hlothar swore fidelity to his father [Note: witnesses 3 and 4 add “and that”]: he was to obey all his commands [Note: witness 1 reads “he wished to obey”], go to Italy, remain there, and not leave it except by his father’s order [Note: witnesses 3 and 4 read “except by his permission”]. The others also swore.

Afterward the most pious prince granted them pardon, provided they kept this oath [Note: witness 3 reads “preserved it”]. He allowed them to retain their estates and everything they possessed, apart from what he himself had personally given them.

There they separated. Hlothar went to Italy with his utterly wicked associates [Note: omitted in witness 4], and immediately Matfrid, who had been the greatest instigator [Note: witness 1 reads “plotter”] of all those evils, died, along with several others. Those who remained were struck down by fever.

### 56

The emperor, returning from there, came to the palace of Theodon and spent the entire winter there.

After the Nativity of the Lord, in the following year (835), he held a great assembly of the peoples. There the most disgraceful rustic Ebo [Note: witness 4 reads *Hebo*] appeared. The bishops there did not dare firmly to remove him [Note: witnesses 3 and 4 read “expel”], fearing that he might prove their betrayer. Therefore they persuaded him [Note: witnesses 3 and 4 read “him” as “to him”] to acknowledge that he could by no means possess the priestly office [Note: witnesses 3 and 4 read “show” instead of “entrust himself”]. He did so, and for that reason he was plainly dismissed.

This still requires complete correction, because it is better to exercise upon him the just judgment of the holy fathers than to display false clemency under the pretext of religion [Note: witnesses 3 and 4 read “it is better”].

### 57

In that very same year [Note: witness 4 omits “very same”], the emperor went into the region of Lyon [Note: witness 4 reads *ad partes*, “to the region,” for *partibus*, “in the region”]. His sons Pippin and his namesake son came to meet him—“who is still an imitator of the aforesaid sons”—who were younger by birth. [Note: witness 1 reads *mitator*, a defective spelling of “imitator.” Witness 6 reads *imitator est supradictorum qui natu iuniores erant*, “he is an imitator of the aforesaid, who were younger by birth.” The editor says that these words may have been added after the work was completed, when Louis later rebelled. Witness 3 reads *natu*, “by birth,” for the printed *natum*. Witness 4 reads *Pippinus est Lodewicus qui natu iuniores erant*, approximately “Pippin is Louis, who were younger by birth,” with the middle words missing; the printed note explicitly marks a lacuna in this witness.]

There the emperor sat with his sons until his envoys came to Hlothar in Italy and, returning from there, reached him. [Note: witness 4 reads *quoadusque*, “until,” for *quousque*; adds *sui in*, “his … into,” after “envoys”; has *venirent*, “should come,” for *venerunt*, “came”; and reads *et inde … pervenerunt ad eum*, “and from there … they reached him,” with the intervening words missing.]

The emperor then returned and came to Aachen, to his own seat [Note: witnesses 3 and 4 read “and came”]. Pippin returned to Aquitaine, while the emperor’s namesake son went into the region of Austria [Note: witness 4 reads *Aquitaniam; Lodewicus perrexit ad partes [Austriae]*, “to Aquitaine; Louis went to the region [of Austria].” Witness 6 reads *Aquitaniam et Ludowicus perrexit Austrie*, “to Aquitaine, and Louis went to Austria.” Witness 3 spells *Austriae* as *austrae*].

### 58

In that same year, while on the journey, Berengar [Note: witness 1 reads *Berngarius*] died, a faithful and wise duke. The emperor and his sons mourned him for a long time.

This is the twenty-second year [Note: witness 3 reads “twenty-fifth” and witness 4 “twenty-third”; the editor observes that Thegan has elsewhere been seen to count the emperor’s years from 814, so the year 835 must necessarily be called his twenty-second year] of the reign of Lord Louis, the most pious emperor. May he who is blessed forever and ever [Note: witness 3 reads *est benedictus Deus*, “is blessed God”; witnesses 3 and 4 are also reported with the order *est Deus benedictus*, “is God blessed”] graciously preserve and protect him, happily dwelling in this world for a long time [Note: witnesses 3 and 4 omit “may he graciously” before “preserve,” and omit “blessed forever and ever” at the end], and after these passing times grant that he may be brought into the fellowship of all his saints [Note: witnesses 3 and 4 read *dignetur*, “may he graciously grant,” for *concedat*, “may he grant”]. Amen.

#### Complete supplementary textual apparatus for §§44–58

The running notes above translate the apparatus attached directly to their clauses. The following register restores every remaining reading whose exact form, witness, scope, or meaning is not otherwise fully visible in the English text.

**§44.** Witnesses 3 and 4 omit *aut ductor tuus*, “or your guide”; witness 1 reads *dicet*, “will say,” for *dicebat*, “was saying”; witnesses 3 and 4 omit *Deo*, “to God.” Witness 1 has the corrupt *magne ate* for *magna te*, “you with great”; witness 1 spells *praecipitia*, “precipices,” as *praecipia*. Witness 4 reads *fuerunt*, “were,” for *erant*, also “were” but in a different tense. Witness 3 reads accusative *beatum Iob*, “blessed Job,” where the printed text has dative *beato Iob*, “to blessed Job.” Witnesses 3 and 4 read *discretio*, “discernment/distinction,” for *discrepatio*, “difference,” and *in persecutoribus*, “among the persecutors,” for *inter persecutoribus*, the printed mixed construction. Witness 1 has *smirmanum* and witness 3 *smirmanum*, variant spellings of “Smyrnaean”; witness 4 has *smyrnaeum*. Witness 1 has *minciarumque*, a corrupt form, for *Mincianumque*, “and the Mantuan.”

**§45.** Witness 3 omits *inde*, “from there,” before the sending of the first envoys. Witness 3 reads *suus*, “his own,” for *eius*, “his,” before Hlothar. Witnesses 3 and 4 read *suscepit*, “received,” for *non susceperat*, “had not received,” reversing the printed negation and tense.

**§47.** Witnesses 3 and 4 spell Grimald *Grimoldum*. Only witness 3, not witness 4, omits *atque presbyterum*, “together with a presbyter.” Witness 4 omits the whole phrase *secreta vero verba*, “the private words, however.” Witness 4 reads *quod*, “that,” for *ut*, “so that”; witness 6 expands *aequivocus* to *aequivocus filius eius*, “his namesake son.” Witness 1 has the corrupt *hoc essentire voluisset*, approximately “wished to assent to this,” for *hoc consentire noluisset*, “did not wish to consent to this.”

**§48 and the following paragraph.** Witness 4 reads *compulit*, “compelled,” for the participle *compellens*, “compelling.” Witness 4 omits *in* before *locum suum*, so that the phrase lacks “to/in his place”; it reads *simul*, “together,” for *pariter*, likewise “together,” and *celebrarunt*, “they celebrated,” for *celebraverunt*. Witness 4 spells Ebo *Hebo*. Witnesses 3 and 4 read *reliquerunt*, “abandoned,” for *coacti relinquerunt*, “were compelled to abandon.” Witness 1 reads *non sit ei*, “may it not be for him,” for *non fuit ei*, “it was not for him”; witnesses 3 and 4 omit *et*, “and.” The printed apparatus gives *ornerosum* in witnesses 3 and 4 for *honerosum*, “burdensome,” and also marks the word absent; the report is internally compressed, so both the corrupt spelling and the stated omission are retained here. The Wratislav manuscript reads *nec*, “nor,” for *vel*, “or.” Witness 1 repeats *antea*, “previously”; witness 1 reads *praecepit*, “commanded,” for *pepercit*, “spared.” Witnesses 3 and 4 omit *illud*, “that,” before “evangelical command.” Witness 1 reads *quod dictum*, “which was said,” for *quo dictum*, “by which it was said.”

**§50.** Witness 4 reads *cavendum*, “care must be taken,” for the stronger *summopere praecavendum*, “the greatest care must be taken.” Witness 4 omits *maximum*, “greatest,” from “the greatest task,” and omits *in temptatione sua*, “in his trial.” Witnesses 3 and 4 repeat *exhibuit*, “showed,” without changing the translated sense.

**§51.** Witnesses 3 and 4 omit *in*, “in,” before “the palace at Aachen.”

**§52.** Witness 3 omits *tantum in*—“only” and the transmitted *in*—around the exception for the envoys. Witness 3 reads *Gerbire* and witness 5 *Gerberg* for the woman’s name *Gerbirch*. In witness 4 the omission is precisely the four source words *quousque*, “until,” *eam*, “her,” *coniugum*, “wives,” and *eius*, “his.”

**§53.** Witness 3 omits *venerabilem*, “venerable.” Witness 4 reads *recordaretur*, “that he should remember,” for *recordatus fuisset*, “that he had remembered.” Witnesses 3 and 4 read *et*, “and,” for the second *ut*, “so that.” In the commandment, witnesses 3 and 4 have present *maledicit*, “curses,” for perfect-subjunctive *maledixerit*, “shall have cursed”; they also read *contemnit*, “despises,” for the spelling *temnit*, with no change in meaning. Witness 4 has singular *convivio*, “banquet,” for plural *conviviis*, “banquets.” Witness 3 reads *et*, “and,” for *ut*, “so that.” For “remove the evil,” witness 3 reads future *auferetis*, “you will remove,” while witness 4 reads passive *auferatur*, “let it be removed,” in place of *auferatis*, “that you may remove.” Witness 3 reads future *pertimescet*, “will become afraid,” for present-subjunctive *pertimescat*, “may become afraid.”

**§54.** Witness 4 reads *appropinquarent ad Aurelianensium civitatem*, “they were approaching the city of Orléans,” for *properarent Aurelianensium civitati*, “they were hastening toward the city of Orléans.” Witness 4 has *edicto*, ablative “by/under the edict,” for *edictu*, the same case and meaning in a different declensional form. Witnesses 3 and 4 omit *se*, “himself,” from “separate himself.” Witness 4 omits the second *iterum*, “again,” when the envoys are recalled; it reads *darent*, “that they give,” for *dedissent*, “that they had given.” Witnesses 3 and 4 read *actibus*, “acts,” for *actis*, likewise “acts” in another form, and *illis*, “those men,” for *eis*, “them.”

**§55.** Witnesses 3 and 4 read *qui erat extensus*, “which was stretched,” with masculine *qui* for neuter *quod*. Witness 3 reads *Macfridus* and witness 4 *Mathfridus* for Matfrid. Witness 4 omits *cum consentaneis suis pessimis*, “with his utterly wicked associates.” The chronological note dates this to autumn 836 and compares the Annals of Saint-Bertin, the Fulda Annals, and the *Life of Louis*. Witness 1 reads *intentor*, “one who strives or directs,” for *incentor*, “instigator.”

**§56.** Witnesses 3 and 4 read *alii episcopi*, “the other bishops,” for *ibi episcopi*, “the bishops there.” Witness 4 reads *quod*, “that,” for *ut* after “fearing”; witnesses 3 and 4 read *ei*, “to him,” for accusative *eum*, “him,” and *sibi*, “to himself,” for *se*, “himself.” Witness 4 reads *ostenderet*, “that he should show,” for *concrederet*, “that he should acknowledge/entrust,” and omits *et*, “also,” from “which he also did.” Witnesses 3 and 4 read adverb *melius*, “better,” for adjective *melior*, “better”; witness 3 reads *esset*, “would be,” for *est*, “is.”

**§57.** The divergent and lacunose readings are given in full in the translated paragraph above. They preserve witness 1’s defective *mitator*; witness 6’s complete “he is an imitator of the aforesaid, who were younger by birth”; witness 4’s corrupt “Pippin is Louis, who were younger by birth,” with its explicitly reported middle lacuna; witness 4’s additions, altered moods, and lacuna in the embassy sentence; and the distinct witness-4 and witness-6 forms of the final itinerary.

**§58.** Witness 1 spells Berengar *Berngarius*. Witnesses 3 and 4 omit *dignetur*, “may he graciously,” before “preserve and protect”; witnesses 3 and 4 omit the concluding words “blessed forever and ever.”

In the manuscript of the Imperial Library of Vienna the following is appended.

In the twenty-third year of his reign (836), the emperor held a conference with his faithful men at the royal estate of Theodon in the month of May. There came envoys of Hlothar from Italy [Note: the manuscript reads *o*, “from/by” in an anomalous form, for *a*, “from”]: Walah, who was an abbot, the treacherous Richhard, and the faithful Eberhard, together with several others. They reported that Hlothar was willing to come to his father if he could do so peacefully.

Then some bishops and the other leading men promised him their faith with an oath, provided that illness did not prevent him. Lord the emperor then announced beforehand that he would hold his general council in the city of Worms and ordered Hlothar to come there in the middle of September [Note: the manuscript reads *ovi­am*, apparently for *obviam*, “to meet him”].

When the appointed day arrived, the emperor reached Worms with a great multitude, and his sons Pippin and Louis with their armies. The envoys of Hlothar came again and announced that Hlothar was meanwhile suffering severely from a double fever [Note: the note asks whether the reading may mean “while he was suffering from fevers”] and had been completely unable to come.

In that same year the aforesaid Walah died, together with several other faithless men.

In that same year the blessed Hetti, archbishop of Trier [Note: according to Regino, he died in 847], moved by divine command, carried the body of Saint Castor from the place where it had previously rested, called Caradona [Note: Carden on the Moselle, in the district formerly called Maienfeld], to the place called Confluentes, where the Moselle enters the Rhine. He brought it to the monastery that the archbishop himself had built from its foundations, as Saint Maternus, the third archbishop of Trier, had commanded him in a vision.

On the feast of Saint Martin the holy body arrived at Confluentes with great honor. On the following day, Sunday, the aforesaid bishop consecrated that church in honor of Saint Castor and all the holy confessors. After the consecration he received the holy body and honorably placed it in the church, as was fitting.

On the eighth day after the consecration—that is, on the Sunday falling on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of December—the lord emperor came with his wife and children. After the solemn celebration of Masses, he offered there very great gifts in gold and silver. He remained there for two days and as many nights, and the aforesaid bishop honored him, his wife, his children, and his entire household with countless gifts.

The lord emperor returned to Aachen, to his own seat, and remained there throughout the winter.

In the twenty-fourth year (837), the emperor announced that he intended to go to Rome with his entire army, together with his sons and Louis. He established military stations in several places against the Danes [Note: “stations of soldiers or countrymen”].

But the Danes came by ship to one of the stations and killed there an uncountable multitude of Christians. There fell Hemming, who was of Danish stock [so the text says], a most Christian duke, and another duke, Eckihard, along with many of the emperor’s leading men. Some were captured and later ransomed.

Hearing this, the emperor abandoned the journey he had announced. Returning to the estate of Gundulf, he came with his whole army to the fortress of Nijmegen, which is situated above the river Waal.

**Here ends *The Origin of the Kings and Their Deeds*.**

## In the Year of Our Lord 842: Agnellus, Also Called Andreas, Abbot of Saint Mary at Blachernas and of Saint Bartholomew at Ravenna

## Historical Notice on Agnellus

*(From Fabricius, *Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis*.)*

Agnellus, also called Andreas, abbot of Saint Mary at Blachernas and of Saint Bartholomew at Ravenna, around the year of Christ 842 wrote the *Book of the Pontiffs*, or *Lives of the Bishops of Ravenna*, from Saint Apollinaris up to Petronacius, and George, who succeeded him around the year 836.

Benedict Bacchini, abbot of Saint Mary of Lacroma of the Order of Saint Benedict, Cassinese Congregation, first published it from a manuscript of the Este Library and illustrated it with dissertations, observations, and an appendix of ancient monuments, at Modena in 1708, in quarto. It was also published in volume II of the *Scriptores Rerum Italicarum* of the most learned Muratori, Milan, 1723, in folio. See the *Journal des savants*, November 1710, p. 563; *Neven Bucher-Saal*, vol. I, p. 216; the *Acta eruditorum*, 1710, p. 330, and 1724, p. 49, and elsewhere. The life of Saint Apollinaris is also included in the *Acta sanctorum*, vol. V for July, p. 350.

## The *Book of the Pontiffs*, or *Lives of the Pontiffs of Ravenna*, by Agnellus, Also Called Andreas, Abbot of Saint Mary at Blachernas and of Saint Bartholomew at Ravenna

These lives were recovered from the Este Library by the Reverend Benedict Bacchini, abbot of Saint Mary of Lacroma of the Order of Saint Benedict, Cassinese Congregation, and illustrated and enlarged by him with dissertations and observations, as well as an appendix of monuments. Everything in the present edition has again been collated with the Este manuscript, and is corrected and enlarged.

*(From Muratori, *Scriptores Rerum Italicarum*, vol. II.)*

## L. A. Muratori’s Preface

Paulus Diaconus, a man of great renown, composed the *Lives*, or *History*, of the bishops of Metz around the year of Christ 784. Although he was not the first to commit this kind of history to writing, I am persuaded that his example served as a stimulus to Italian intellects to undertake comparable works.

Indeed, Agnellus, born only a few years after Paul’s death, undertook to compose the lives of the archbishops of Ravenna, which we are once again placing before the press for the benefit of scholars.

Concerning their author, know the following. Agnellus, also called Andreas, a native of Ravenna, appears to have been born around the year of Christ 805. In the *Life of Aurelian* he says: “Today I have completed six lustra, with two years besides, and twice five months.” Since, as we shall see below, he affirms that the *Pontifical* was written by him in the year 839, we accordingly infer his year of birth.

He himself sufficiently reveals that he descended from an illustrious family, since among his ancestors on his great-grandmother’s side he lists Joannicius, once a famous secretary of the emperor of Constantinople:

> Joannicius begot Agnes; Agnes produced Andreas. From Andreas, Basil begot Andreas the presbyter, the editor of this *Pontifical*.

Having adopted the clerical state and been enrolled among the presbyters, Agnellus himself also enjoyed the income of the Church. For in that city he was abbot of Saint Bartholomew, as he testifies in the *Life of Ursicinus*.

The thirty-eighth archbishop of Ravenna, Felix, had formerly presided over this monastery. In recounting his tribulations in Felix’s life, Agnellus adds:

> The same thing happened to me concerning the aforesaid monastery. For several years I was deprived without cause of this monastery by Bishop George.

Then, in the *Life of Martin*, the forty-fifth archbishop, he writes that he presided over another monastery, in these words:

> He granted to Andreas the presbyter the monastery of Saint Mary, which is called at Blachernas; and at that time he was still a boy.

He confirms the same thing in the *Life of Peter*, the seventeenth archbishop, writing:

> While I was residing in my monastery of blessed and ever-virgin Mary, which is called at Blachernas.

From these words, as also from other statements of Agnellus himself, we learn that not only monks but also secular clergy were assigned to abbeys, or that secular churches were given the name “monastery,” perhaps because they had formerly served monks. Consequently, those who once bore the title of abbot should not immediately be counted among the monks.

Finally, our Agnellus states in the *Life of Sergius* that his “father’s grandfather,” because he was believed to have consented to the killing of Pope Paul of Rome, was summoned to Rome together with several other noble Ravennates, “and there they were all confined until they died.”

At what particular time Agnellus flourished, and in what year he undertook this work, he himself reveals in more than one place. In the *Life of Saint Maximian, Archbishop*, he relates that the body of Maximian was translated “in the fifteenth year of Archbishop Petronax, and in our own times.” When the coffin was being excavated, Petronax “said to the tenth presbyter in the order of his see, named Agnellus, who was called Andreas (and at that time he was full of ingenuity in every kind of craft): ‘Stand near; instruct the craftsmen how they ought to proceed,’” and so forth. I do not know whether Agnellus himself added this note about himself, or whether someone else inserted it in praise of him. If Rubeus is to be followed, Petronax was elevated to the archbishopric of Ravenna in 817. At least, a diploma of Pope Paschal granted to him in the twelfth indiction and mentioned by Rubeus seems to establish that this office was conferred upon him in 819; hence I do not know why Bacchinius, to be praised below, assigns his consecration only to the year 821. Accordingly, Petronax’s fifteenth year falls in the common era year 832 or 834, when Agnellus took part in the translation mentioned.

Again, in the *Life of Saint Peter the Elder*, he writes:

> “Now nearly thirty-eight years have passed since Charles, king of the Franks, had subjugated all the kingdoms and had received the empire of the Romans from Pope Leo III, after he had offered the sacrament at the body of blessed Peter; returning to France, he entered Ravenna and, seeing a most beautiful image, such as he testified he had nowhere seen like it, had it transported to France.”

In the year 801 Charlemagne, having been proclaimed emperor of the Romans, returned to France. Therefore Agnellus was writing this in the year 839.

Again, let us hear him in the *Life of Archbishop Maurus*, where he relates the removal of a marvelous porphyry stone placed at Ravenna:

> “But nearly twelve years ago, in the time of the pontiff Petronax, Lothair Augustus ordered it to be taken away and transported it to France.”

Since Lothair received the imperial crown at Rome in the year 823, it follows that Agnellus wrote this approximately in the year 836. These statements differ somewhat from the calculation given above, but Agnellus did not complete his work in a single year. In the *Life of George* as well, he recounts the most terrible battle fought in the year 841 between Lothair and the other sons of Louis the Pious. Thus you see how far Agnellus carried his work.

Let us now turn from the author to the book itself. At first sight you may despise it, when you encounter in it so many barbarisms and solecisms—although you may wish to shift some of them, however barely, onto an incompetent copyist; the greater part, certainly, seems attributable to Agnellus himself, who had spent little time in Priscian’s school. Then intolerable anachronisms appear, along with little tales that that age readily embraced but that we either laugh at or find difficult to accept. Moreover, when he can no longer navigate because his water has run out, he still cannot remain silent; that is, he detains the reader with tasteless sermons and fills empty spaces with embellishments, lest the *Lives* of certain archbishops appear too meager.

What is more, he reveals in more than one place that he is ill-disposed toward the bishops of his own time, while conversely he bestows the title of saint upon certain bishops of Ravenna who were tainted either by attempted schism or by depraved conduct. Indeed, he sometimes applauds their audacity so extravagantly that this writer rises with a slanderous tooth against the Roman pontiffs themselves and against their most ancient rights. Yet these considerations did not deter the most illustrious Benedict Bacchinius from bringing this book, which had never previously been published, into the light of day in our own times. For it is equally certain that, however rude and barbarous a writer one may judge Agnellus to be—even, let us say, a writer worth three oboli—he nevertheless preserved for us many things of great value from antiquity, things that are useful not only for greatly enriching the history of the most celebrated Church of Ravenna, but also for placing in a clearer light the customs of ancient times and certain events of secular history, and will be of no small assistance.

Agnellus himself ought to be heard, for he says the following about his work in the *Life of Exuperantius, nineteenth Archbishop*:

> “I, Agnellus, also called Andreas, a humble presbyter of this holy Church of Ravenna, composed the aforesaid *Pontifical*, having been asked and compelled by the brothers of that see; and wherever I found what they had done with greater certainty, I have brought it before your eyes. But where I did not find a history, or how their life had been, neither through aged and ancient men, nor through buildings, nor through any authority whatsoever, lest there be a gap in the succession of the holy pontiffs, I composed their *Life*, and so forth.”

In any case, Italy can display so few historians of the unlearned centuries that this one ought to be welcomed with both arms, and we should give thanks that it has not yet wholly perished.

And indeed it was in grave danger. Jerome Rubeus used it in weaving together his excellent *History of Ravenna*. Yet in book V, page 238, he writes the following about Agnellus:

> “He not only witnessed these events but presided over them, and, learned in the highest degree, left behind a volume written with great seriousness about the archbishops of Ravenna. After it had long remained in the archiepiscopal library, it was removed in past years along with many others and is now found nowhere—a very great loss indeed.”

Thus Rubeus. Agnellus would therefore have been lost to us, unless the Estense Library had preserved one parchment manuscript, written approximately in the year of Christ 1340. Learned men desired that this book should be made public; and the recently praised Benedict Bacchinius, Benedictine abbot, a man of solid and refined learning, was in fact the first of all to publish it at Modena in the year 1708, from the press of Antonio Capponi. At the same time he dedicated it to the most serene Rinaldo d’Este, duke of Modena, and so forth.

Even then Agnellus was not sufficiently known; hence our Collection called for a reissue of his work. Here, therefore, is that edition—complete indeed, in the form in which Bacchinius published it, that is, together with the dissertations and the appendix of documents by which that most learned man corrected, illustrated, and adorned Agnellus. But in order that this edition of ours might win the favor of the learned through new distinctions, I once again collated Bacchinius’s edition with the manuscript codex of the Estense Library, and discovered many passages either not transcribed with sufficient accuracy or omitted through haste. I think that this fault should be assigned not to Bacchinius, a man highly skilled in ancient writing, but to the copyist whom he employed. You will find all these matters noted at the foot of each page.

[Note: We have inserted these into the text within brackets, according to our custom. — Editor.]

I undertook this labor again all the more willingly so that I might remove from learned men the suspicion that Agnellus had been mutilated by Bacchinius himself. Certainly, several lacunae occur in the Bacchinian edition, especially in the final *Lives* of the archbishops, in which, nevertheless, the curious reader expected more from Agnellus as an eyewitness. But now I present myself as guarantor that nothing in Agnellus’s text has been altered, nothing added or removed. Whatever Bacchinius found in the Estense codex, he published intact; and therefore those lacunae must be attributed to earlier times. Later, however, we learned that another manuscript of Agnellus is also preserved in the Vatican Library. Whether it is by a more recent hand or older than the Estense manuscript, I do not know.

Finally, let me add this: Bacchinius published the *Life of Saint Barbatianus* from an ancient Ravenna Lectionary in the Appendix. It is surprising that he did not also cite the Agnellus codex preserved in the Estense Library, where, after his *Pontifical*, that same *Life* is read together with those of other earlier bishops of Ravenna—and in a more corrected form than that published from the Ravenna codex. I have added these corrections. But now let Bacchinius himself be heard, as he discusses Agnellus and his errors at greater length.

[Col. 0435A]

## DEDICATORY LETTER

of the Most Reverend Father Abbot Bacchinius to the Most Serene Rinaldo d’Este, Duke of Modena, Reggio, and so forth.

Most Serene Duke,

Nearly ten full years have now passed since, while examining the codices of Your Highness’s completed library, Most Serene Duke, I came upon Agnellus of Ravenna’s *Pontifical*. I immediately resolved to bring into the light, illustrated as far as my limited ability permitted, what had once been transmitted by that author. This is not the place to explain the reasons that moved me to undertake it; only this should be recalled: during that long interval many events occurred that delayed both my work and the publication of the book.

In particular, it was necessary to await the most fortunate moment when, after the cities of your dominion—and above all Modena—had been restored by the foreign soldiery, I might be permitted to congratulate you on your return with these laurel-crowned letters. This was indeed a favorable omen for my labor: it permits us to hope that the work came forth later into the air so that, as an attendant to the fame and immortality of your glory, it might emerge more successfully from the printer’s hiding places than I had been prepared to enter them.

It will scarcely be possible, while sacred Philology, prostrate at the steps of the throne before the most magnificent trophy erected for you by well-earned achievements, offers you this book, for it not to be overshadowed by the crowns with which Victory honors you. Nevertheless, since the purpose of our studies is to cultivate religion and integrity firmly, the virtues to which you owe your victories and which stand constantly at your side will bring to this work, consecrated to your name, a reputation and fame by which the minds of its readers may be instructed to preserve the holiness of faith and the discipline of morals amid adversity.

This, indeed, is no contemptible reward gained from meditation upon sacred history. But the most illustrious examples of steadfastness amid adversity, energy, justice, and prudence that you have displayed in these most difficult times benefit us in place of a brilliant history, and will benefit the later descendants of your subjects.

The readers of this work will have something from which to learn when, on the very title page of the book, they read the name of the most serene Rinaldo d’Este—namely, the name of one who, with religion and integrity as his guides, obtained and accomplished more than others through arms and wars, and who showed by his deeds that immortality is earned by merit, and that the path to true glory through difficulties is shorter and safer when virtue points the way.

I have said these things because of their connection with the subject, by which they are joined to my purpose. I humbly beg you to regard them with fairness and goodwill—for I know well how much you deserve to be praised, and how much you do not wish to be praised.

For the rest, to return to Agnellus’s work: this very book, which learned men desired because it was found nowhere, and upon which all who have written about the history of the Church of Ravenna built and preserved their accounts, was transmitted unharmed to us by your most serene predecessors. In keeping with the inborn love of the d’Este family for good letters, they preserved this codex, together with many others, both Greek and Latin, through the vicissitudes of times and affairs.

You, Most Serene Duke, not only granted, with the supreme kindness by which you bless us, that it should be illustrated and published through me, but, so that the illustrated work might appear more easily and promptly, you freely and without being asked most generously ordered that the expenses of publication be supplied. Why, then, should what was yours by so many titles not be returned to you through me?

Yet not only is Agnellus of Ravenna’s *Pontifical* yours; my own little work, whatever it may be, employed in illustrating Agnellus, is also yours. For since you have conferred incredible benefits upon me, and since I am wholly yours, whatever is produced through my authorship must also be yours. These things, born in your household in place of household servants, are owed to you; from this they also acquire a value that otherwise they would lack, both for themselves and for their parent.

Would that, with you safe and flourishing, it might fall to me to experience this more often through Nestor’s years! Would that you might long survive for your most serene offspring, as an example and guide to every virtue—you who to this day have displayed through your actions the complete formation of a Christian ruler. This I earnestly and repeatedly pray of the good and great God, and, prostrating myself as a sign of my most obedient spirit, I subscribe myself:

Your Most Serene Highness’s most humble, most devoted, and most obedient client,

**D. Benedict Bacchinius**

[Col. 0435D]

## BACCHINIUS’S PREFACE

### 1

It is customary for those who bring unpublished works into the light to celebrate them with the highest praises. You will therefore wonder, reader, that I immediately proceed by an entirely different path: I undertake to describe Agnellus, now appearing for the first time, as he is—horrid, squalid, barbarous.

Why should I not do so, when from the very reading of the book anyone, even if not especially learned, will ultimately recognize the author’s uncultivated nature? That this is so is attested by Agnellus in his entirety: he observes none of the laws of grammar and is everywhere covered with an inelegant rasping harshness.

Barbarous language might nevertheless be tolerated in a ninth-century writer, although he had been raised from childhood in the Ursian Church, if he did not also suffer from incredible ignorance of everything, both sacred and profane. I would be excessive if I enumerated here all the passages in which he sins absurdly. He confuses times, events, and persons; mingles trifles, madness, and improbabilities; forgetful of himself, relates contradictions; most ineptly joins boots to the head and squares to circles. He piles up whatever he has read, seen, or heard without discrimination, and mixes empty rumors of the common people with truths.

When he has learned little or nothing about a particular bishop of Ravenna that he can relate, so that he may make each portion of his work equal in length, he occupies himself with foolish meditations, from which it is more difficult to extract anything good than to draw liquid from a flint. You will often see the man, when he attempts to explain certain passages of Scripture, entangling them in ridiculous and badly arranged words so thoroughly that even the gravest reader can scarcely restrain laughter.

Meanwhile, he swells with bile against the bishops of his own time.
