He attacks both their simoniacal stain and their vices so fiercely that one who reads him can scarcely believe that the bishops of that age were infamous for so many crimes, and instead may well begin to doubt the writer’s reliability in similar matters on other grounds.

When occasion is given, he commends himself more than once, greedy for petty glory on account of the nobility of his family, the offices conferred upon him, and his skill in the arts; he suffers from an insane disease of self-love, while pretending to humble himself with words composed for modesty.

### II

It was worthwhile to warn you of these matters at the outset, so that you might understand beforehand another especially detestable fault of this Agnellus, and know what credibility such a writer deserves when he attacks the most holy pontiffs of the Roman See and reports things that cast doubt upon the rights of the First See over the bishops of Ravenna and transfer them to the emperors.

This was the stone he pushed and attempted to move, both because he still harbored in his heart the poison of the pernicious schism that had preceded him, and because he was driven against the Roman pontiffs by the goads of vengeance: his grandfather’s father had been taken to Rome and died in prison together with other nobles of Ravenna who had plotted unspeakable things against the supreme pontiff Paul. He relates this in the *Acts of Sergius, Archbishop of Ravenna*.

Hence his anger, and hence also the fact that this man, who elsewhere possessed little judgment, repeats the popular fables born during the time of the schism—especially that concerning the elevation of the metropolitan see of Ravenna by Valentinian III and the pallium allegedly granted at that time, as well as on other occasions, by the emperors—and celebrates a diploma in support of the claim.

Hence he praises the unjust mystery of *autokephalia*—αὐτοκεφαλαία, “autocephaly”—and its author Maurus. For this reason one may also strongly suspect that he attacks with insults the bishops of Ravenna who were properly disposed toward the Roman pontiff, as well as Theodore, who ultimately brought the schism to an end, thereby increasing the rumors of the rebels and pursuing the bishop all the more fiercely for having acted well and piously.

These matters are so important that I cannot consider the issue at all secure unless, after making certain preliminary remarks, I expressly endeavor to show, before you begin reading Agnellus himself, that neither any lay authority nor the emperors possessed the power either to establish ecclesiastical metropolitan sees or to grant the ornament and rights of the pallium. Thus the metropolitan of the patriarch of the West attempted, wholly unjustly, to make himself autocephalous.

### III

Yet you who read this, turning to me, may say: “Was it really such a great undertaking to bring a writer of this kind into the light, and not merely that, but to adorn him with no small labor? Would it not have been better either to leave him to be consumed by moths and dust or, after obtaining permission from the most religious prince, whose jurisdiction it is, to condemn the manuscript codex to flames and oblivion?”

Alas, the excessive abundance of foolish books weighs upon us, ever since the art of printing opened an altogether too easy path for multiplying writings. But this author is not merely foolish: he is also impious, insulting the most holy See of Peter and its rights, and therefore ought to be proscribed on several counts.

Will you not think it ridiculous that, by adding dissertations and notes and using the power of the press, I bring into public view a writer whom I condemn in extended prose as swollen, foolish, unworthy of belief, and impious?

Pause for a moment, benevolent reader. I have arguments to offer on my own behalf by which what at first sight appears *ἄτοπον*—“absurd”—may ultimately be approved by your judgment. When I read the codex, the considerations that had been clearing my mind of any desire to publish Agnellus did indeed immediately occur to me. But after weighing the matter more carefully and consulting my friends, I adopted the opposite view. Accept the force of the reasons that moved me, and the whole matter.

### IV

The dignity of the city of Ravenna is such that it scarcely needs to be commended by me. Yet I may say this: through its vicissitudes, the destinies not only of Italy but of Europe, and even of the East, were linked by a certain bond over several stretches of time, so that the history of a single city embraces the affairs of many kingdoms and distant provinces.

When the emperors first decided to have their seat in the West, Ravenna became the seat of rule; from there, as though from a metropolis, rights were granted and laws prescribed throughout Africa, Spain, Gaul, and Germany. From there the majesty of the Gothic kings shone forth. After these had been subdued by the emperors of Constantinople and Italy recovered, the seat of the exarchs at Ravenna became preeminent. Nor did it lose its ancient glory when afflicted by the disasters of the later age. Even when it seemed to suffer eclipses, it drew the eyes of all toward itself and increased the fame of its name through the very dangers it endured.

Moreover, since ecclesiastical affairs had been established under the most favorable auspices from the time when Apollinaris was ordained bishop by the very prince of the apostles, they grew through an unbroken succession of the most celebrated bishops until the age of Honorius. Later they reached such greatness and power that some of the bishops of Ravenna, having suffered attacks of vertigo, deserved to be restrained by the Roman pontiffs.

### V

Amid all this, however—and it is truly remarkable—there are very few monuments of Ravenna’s history. If any credence may be placed in the author of the verses prefixed to Agnellus’s book, Agnellus himself, also called Andreas, was the very first, in a rude and barbarous age, to dare to write the *Acts of the Bishops of Ravenna*.

Afterward, none of those who took upon themselves the task of adorning the same field undertook it without using Agnellus, for as long as his work remained available. This was done not only in the memory of our fathers by Ferretus, Spretus, and Rubeus, whom I shall mention shortly, but also by all the ancients who wrote either chronicles of Ravenna’s affairs or the *Lives* and discourses of the holy bishops of the Church of Ravenna.

This can be seen from the narratives quoted or praised in the documents that I present as an appendix at the end of the entire work. It would perhaps be easy to prove that more sanctified ancient narratives about the holy bishops of Ravenna, written after Agnellus, were copied from Agnellus’s *Pontifical*.

This happened because no more suitable or more trustworthy writer of Ravenna’s affairs was available; Agnellus alone was regarded as such. While Agnellus himself was extant, all danger of deception was absent, for the faults that most often infect a writer could easily be recognized by sensible men.

The danger began only when Agnellus was lost and the writings of later authors appeared. In them, Agnellus was praised as an entirely trustworthy and learned authority, and accounts were narrated under his guarantee that he had neither skillfully nor truthfully written. Even more, many things that could be pressed out of the mud like gems for the illumination of antiquity were narrated against the truth and in opposition to Agnellus himself, yet gained acceptance.

### VI

Among all writers, the author who sinned in this way most conspicuously was the famous Jerome Rubeus, although he wrote the history of Ravenna with such distinction that the judgment of all learned men has praised him.

He did so with the utmost purity of Latin expression and in such a careful style of writing that he is called a rival of Livy’s glory. But as regards chronology and the critical examination of events and writers, he wrote many things according to his own judgment, as the times encouraged, and often adorned the truth with digressions so elaborately that, once simplicity had been removed, he concealed deception.

More importantly, disregarding what Agnellus truthfully related, he inserted certain falsehoods—falsehoods that readers could easily have recognized as such if Agnellus himself had been read—in such a way that, because Agnellus was praised as a grave authority, hardly anyone could deny that these matters were both his and true.

The leading place in this catalogue of errors belongs to the celebrated fiction concerning the privilege granted by Valentinian III. According to it, the emperor subjected twelve bishops to the Church of Ravenna and also granted the archbishop the use of the pallium in sacred rites.

Rubeus does say that the pallium granted by Valentinian was not the one that the supreme pontiff customarily provides, taken from the body of Saint Peter, but rather something like a military cloak, and so forth. Nevertheless, he is rightly censured for this by the most learned Baronius, who rejects and corrects the apocryphal document.

How much more easily and effectively, however, would the eminent father of the *Annals* have overturned the entire story if he had seen Agnellus, from whom Rubeus—and not only Rubeus, but also Blondus and Sabellicus—had borrowed it! By showing the original source of the fable, and that it deserved no belief, he would have given great force to his other arguments. But since this could not be done while Agnellus’s book lay hidden, this story was believed by many because Rubeus and the others commended Agnellus himself, through whom they often confess that they had advanced, as a trustworthy authority.

Why would the others not also commend, and earnestly desire, the author whom Rubeus praises at length in book V? He says:

> “We transcribed these things from Andreas Agnellus, who not only witnessed them but presided over them, and, learned in the highest degree, left a volume written with great seriousness about the archbishops of Ravenna. After it had long remained in the archiepiscopal library, it was removed in past years together with many others and is now found nowhere—a very great loss indeed.”

The result was that, although the falsity of the document exhibited by Rubeus exposes itself, it is recognized as wholly spurious, while there are nevertheless people who, without having read Agnellus, but seeing him magnificently praised by Rubeus, believe the narrative.

For this reason, when Peter de Marca discusses the matter in *Concordia*, book VI, chapter 6, number 11, he readily grants to Baronius that the aforesaid diploma is wholly “spurious and excellently refuted by the most illustrious cardinal.” Yet, he says, “I am compelled to disagree with Baronius in this: he insists strongly that the pallium cannot be granted to a bishop by an emperor, because it is an ecclesiastical garment.”

Because they likewise did not know Agnellus’s source—the source from which Rubeus drank the fable—pious writers did not hesitate to assert what Baronius had refuted: namely, that Valentinian had bestowed the pallium as a sign of dignity.

For this matter it will suffice to transcribe a passage from the book by Marcus Paulus of the Roman Society of Jesus, *On the Authority and Use of the Papal Pallium*, published at Rome by the press of Ludovicus Grignanus in 1649, quarto, chapter 1, number 12. He says:

> “That the pallium, insofar as it is a sign and ornament of dignity, also includes profane ornaments, Gretserus observed in his commentary on Codinus from the *Turcograecia*, when he asserts that the pallium was granted to patriarchs and bishops—as Liberatus affirms of Anthimus, patriarch of the Church of Constantinople, in his *Breviary*, chapter 21. He also asserts that Valentinian III, in the manner of an emperor, granted the pallium to the archbishop of Ravenna, as Charles of Saint-Paul, abbot of Fuliensis, asserts in his *Sacred Geography*, book IX, concerning the Patriarchate of Constantinople.”

Ferdinand Ughellus must be added to these, in his account of the bishops of Ravenna, under Saint John, surnamed Angeloptes. Both before and after the spurious diploma of Valentinian, he repeats the same things that Rubeus had said.

### VII

It was therefore important that Agnellus be published. Once the opinion that Rubeus had imposed against the truth had been removed through such testimony, this would be the way to recognize that the narrative, from its original source, rested upon a weak and unstable foundation; that it had arisen during the time of the schism; that it had been committed to writing by a single ninth-century author, an enemy of Roman dignity and an incompetent judge in such matters; and that it had scarcely been handed down by any more ancient witness.

Once Agnellus was published, we would have the strongest remedies from the very source of the evil. The same author who reported that the pallium had been granted by the emperor Valentinian, and that the metropolitan see had been established with twelve bishops subject to it, overturned the fiction concerning John Angeloptes.

For what Agnellus wrote about these matters cannot possibly be true if it is compared with what is related in the *Life of Saint Peter Chrysologus*, the immediate successor of the aforesaid John. Peter was consecrated bishop of Ravenna by the Roman pontiff at the divine command, although the nobles of Ravenna resisted. They had elected another man, issued a decree of election, and gone to Rome seeking confirmation and the consecration of their chosen candidate.

Agnellus says nothing here about Valentinian’s authority. If Valentinian had recently founded the metropolitan see and had granted the pallium to John, he would also have claimed some right for himself in defending the earlier election and in the consecration of Peter Chrysologus by the pontiff, carried out against the wishes of the people of Ravenna. He would have asserted the right he had acquired by intervening and handing the pallium to the newly elected bishop.

Nor does Agnellus testify to the subjection of the metropolitan of Ravenna to the Roman pontiff only in that passage; he does so most clearly elsewhere as well. Above all, he does so in the *Life of Archbishop Ecclesius*. There, after explaining the disagreements that had arisen between the bishop and the clergy, he says not only that they were settled by the authority of the Roman pontiff, but also offers us a notable document of that matter, previously unpublished—namely, a letter of Pope Felix IV.

Could stronger arguments be found elsewhere by which both the false traditions about the beginnings of the metropolitan rights of Ravenna and the wholly unjust attempt of the schismatic Maurus to establish *αὐτοκεφαλαία*—“autocephaly”—with the aid of the emperor and the exarch, might be disproved?

Agnellus therefore had to be rescued from darkness, especially because matters that had been falsely transmitted by later writers and adopted by them under the praise of Agnellus, though he himself was lost, were regarded as having some authority. He also had to be rescued because of those things that he records in many places, without being led by preconceived opinion, to the considerable benefit of truth and history; and finally because of those things that he does not record, but which later writers, with great verbal display, impose upon the world.

### VIII

Moreover, if we love truth, although Agnellus is barbarous, ignorant and careless regarding events and times, it cannot be denied that many things may be obtained from his work that can benefit both sacred and secular history.

I omit the matters praised above—things that it resembles a prodigy for a schismatic and impatient opponent of the most holy Roman rights to have said. Yet he said them, although favoring his own side, and he said them to the great advantage of truth.

But in most of the matters that in no way retained the flavor of the vessel in which he had been steeped, why should he not be believed? And if he is to be believed, why should a work that was almost lost not be published for our use?

If you find anything good in the chronology of the bishops of Ravenna, which I have attempted to adorn with dissertations; if anything commends itself to you, learned reader; if Agnellus has held out a torch to you, then remember that he examined ancient diptychs, copied inscriptions, reported the mosaics of basilicas, and also arranged—though without discrimination—what his elders had related to him.

He was the first of all to praise the holiness of the bishops of Ravenna, especially those whom the Catholic Church venerates through public prayers, and he made it possible for us to know their *Acts*, which otherwise would have perished. Above all, no one will deny that those who later honored the saints Apollinaris and Severus in encomia had Agnellus as their herald.

He described the sacred buildings and their ornamentation, and taught who had built them, when they had first been constructed, and at whose expense. He also often published their artistic panels and inscriptions word for word, matters that we would otherwise not know. He preserved for us much ancient information about sacred rites and liturgy belonging both to his own time and to earlier periods, information that is almost unknown to us.

To mention a few individual examples: we know from him the verses of Saint Peter Chrysologus placed in the oratory of Saint Andrew, which attest to the practice of auricular confession. We know the complete letter of that same holy bishop to Eutyches, which Gerhard Vossius found abridged in two more recent codices of the Vatican Library. From this, later critics took occasion to accuse the final words, which establish the infallibility of the Roman pontiff when defining, of having been added by recent embellishment.

We know the structure of the Ravenna clergy both from the aforementioned letters of Felix IV and from several other passages, as well as the manner in which revenues were distributed and the offices and duties of distinguished clerics.

We know these and many other things from Agnellus. Although they are transmitted without order and ineptly, they should not therefore be held in low esteem by sensible men. Far be it from cultivated students of literature to reject documents of later antiquity because they were not composed according to the laws of criticism and grammar, or because they did not have a skillful writer.

If we were so excessively delicate, we would be deprived of the benefit of much knowledge by which we have until now been enriched through the *Acts* of so many saints and through the volumes of *Miscellanies*, *Analecta*, *Libraries*, and ancient readings published by the most learned men.

But “it is altogether better to enjoy even uncorrected authors than to be entirely without them,” as Fabrottus says most truly in the Preface to his extensive edition of Anastasius the Librarian.

### IX

I have, I think, sufficiently set out the force of the reasons by which I judged that Agnellus not only could but ought to be published by me. I now think that certain matters concerning the author of the book, beyond what has already been said, should at last be prefaced.

He is therefore called by two names, namely Agnellus and Andreas. In writing the *Life of Saint Felix the Bishop*, he teaches us something about the family of his father and mother, and shows that he was born at Ravenna in an honorable station. Elsewhere he says that he was raised from childhood in the bosom of the Ursian Church.

In the time of Petronax he held the tenth place among the presbyters of Ravenna, and while still a young man he was abbot of Saint Mary at Blachernas and of Saint Bartholomew. Those are therefore mistaken who confuse him with Agnellus the archbishop, who flourished in the final years of Justinian.

The famous author Gerhard Johannes Vossius is also mistaken when, in *On Latin Historians*, book III, chapter 4, he writes:

> “Andreas Agnellus was archbishop of the Church of Ravenna in the time of Louis the Pious, tenth in order in that see, outstanding in virtue, and endowed with a keen intelligence in all matters, as Jerome Rubeus related about him in book V of his *History of Ravenna*.”

It is not surprising that Vossius was deceived by Rubeus in what concerns Agnellus’s intelligence. It is surprising how this distinguished man extracted from Rubeus—who nowhere says so—that Agnellus was archbishop of Ravenna in the time of Louis the Pious, and by what method of counting he said that Agnellus held tenth place, when from Rubeus himself it is clear that at least forty-five bishops of Ravenna preceded that period.

Rubeus said that Agnellus was the tenth priest in the order of his see, not the tenth archbishop.

What follows in Vossius is this:

> “He also mentions him once and again in book II, as well as in book III, and John Peter Ferretus is fond of transcribing him word for word, as the same author states. Baronius also mentions him in volume IX, under the year 824, but from Rubeus; this is an indication that he does not survive even in the Vatican Library.”

It should be added that, as mentioned above, a codex of Agnellus existed in the time of Blondus. He used it in Decade I, books III, IV, VII, VIII, and X; Decade II, book II; and elsewhere.

### X

The Church of Saint Mary at Blachernas stood outside the walls of Ravenna, at the place where, because the palace of King Odoacer had once existed there, though not a very large one, the name Palatiolum continued into more recent times.

Agnellus obtained building materials from the ruins of that ancient palace, with which he built himself a house at Ravenna on his paternal estate.

Saint Mary of Palatiolum belonged in the tenth century to the abbot and the renowned monastery of Saint Paul in Rome, as is clear from the distinguished cartulary of that same monastery. Today everything lies in ruins within the pine grove belonging to our monks of Saint Vitalis.

Regarding the other Church of Saint Bartholomew, of which Agnellus was likewise abbot, see Faber. From him, Lubinus observed in his *Notice of the Abbeys of Italy* that there were two churches under the name of that same saint, one inside and the other outside the city.

Several passages of the *Pontifical* establish that Agnellus was abbot of Saint Bartholomew outside Ravenna.

### XI.

What I judged ought to be done by me in publishing Agnellus himself, learned reader, you can easily understand from what has been said. I undertook the task in the spirit of an active hunter, eager for his prey, who enters thickets and bushes while opening a path for his companions to follow safely and pleasantly. It was often necessary to point out places full of danger, although the more conspicuous of them were so open and free of bushes that even a blind man could have avoided them. Nevertheless, I thought it worthwhile to indicate these as well. In some places I had to halt more laboriously, where, suspecting that an entirely smooth path promising a little sunlight might lead into the lair of a savage beast, I proceeded with caution.

Having exercised this careful circumspection, I thought that my labor had not been fruitless in discovering several things not to be despised in this forest, so densely overgrown and obstructed. Perhaps I am mistaken; but we grant and request this indulgence in turn. There will be others who will excavate better things.

By carefully comparing the chronological evidence and the indications supplied by Agnellus—or rather, by the monuments to which he himself refers—I recognized that the chronology of the bishops of Ravenna, as transmitted by Rubeus (whom nearly all the others followed), diverges from the truth in very many respects. I therefore thought above all that it had to be brought back, as far as I was able, to critical examination and calculation. I did this in seven Dissertations, which I prefixed to the Lives of particular bishops, so that the reader might approach the history that follows prepared for it.

I divided the entire work into two parts. The first contains the Lives of those pontiffs who flourished from Saint Apollinaris to Ecclesius; the second, those who flourished from Ecclesius to George, at whom Agnellus ends. I divided the Lives of the individual pontiffs into chapters and prefixed arguments to each chapter. Finally, I added my observations to the Life of each bishop, in which I explained what was more difficult, corrected what had been wrongly stated, and noted what was useful.

The codex was copied by an unlearned scribe from an exemplar that was mutilated in places, around the beginning of the fifteenth century. He rendered Agnellus’s barbarous writing, already obscure, remarkably more obscure through his monstrous errors. Consequently, I found what had been written barbarously copied in the most corrupt fashion. I therefore devoted an extremely disagreeable, though necessary, labor to correcting the copyist’s errors. For the task was not merely to erase defects of some kind; rather, this had to be done in such a way that everything was restored to its original deformity.

Whenever I doubted that I had correctly identified a corrupt reading, I retained the reading and noted in the margin what I guessed had perhaps been written or understood in the author’s mind. Certain marginal notes seem, I think, to belong to the copyist. They could have been omitted without loss; yet there may perhaps be some for whom even these are useful, although they are foolish, barren, and full of errors.

Finally, I added several ancient monuments as an appendix, concerning which I shall speak in their proper place.

### XII.

Here, then, I am finally obliged to discharge the trust that I undertook in section 2 of this Preface, and I must demonstrate two propositions—which nevertheless amount to the same thing: first, that no secular power ever possessed the right to confer the pallium upon the bishops of Churches, whether at the original establishment of metropolitan sees or when succeeding metropolitans were ordained; second, that neither the emperors nor the kings ever carried their ambition to enlarge their own authority so far as to alter the rights of the Churches by establishing ecclesiastical metropolises.

When these points have been proved precisely against Agnellus, a third matter will arise: the attempt of the Ravenna metropolitan Maurus, contrary to divine and human law, to become **αὐτοκέφαλος**—“autocephalous”—although he was subject to the Roman pontiff in so many respects.

### XIII.

As for the conferral of the pallium, since the matter has been extraordinarily clarified by the most learned men, it is altogether difficult not to go over ground already covered. I frankly admit, therefore, that I am pursuing a matter already completely clear with superfluous labor. But since this author is only now emerging into the light, and since he alone among the ancients explicitly reports that Valentinian III and Justinian granted the pallium to the archbishop of Ravenna, those who have not been ashamed to follow the perverse and impious system of Marcus Antonius de Dominis may perhaps seize upon this as an opportunity to insinuate their dreams more deeply into the minds of the less cautious. It seemed to be my duty to show that Agnellus’s account is entirely false and opposed to all antiquity.

Nevertheless, I thought it empty and superfluous to begin the matter *ab ovo*, as they say, and to compose a servile and spiteful patchwork of what has already been written with the greatest learning. I therefore set myself limits within which I would refute Agnellus alone and bring forward arguments relating precisely to the period of the bishops of Ravenna from John Angeloptes to Maximian.

Agnellus himself immediately cuts the throat of the story that Valentinian III granted the pallium to John Angeloptes and subjected the bishops to the Church of Ravenna, as I noted above, when he relates the election of Chrysologus; enough has been said about this matter.

As for the story of Maximian’s promotion by Justinian to the see of Ravenna, Agnellus himself unwillingly admits that it is infected with the refuse of schismatics. He testifies that he is reporting what was commonly said about a treasure having been discovered and about other matters inconsistent with Maximian’s sanctity, and foolishly declares these things certain: “I shall make it publicly known,” he says, “just as I heard it from those who related it over the long course of time.”

But, my good man, who would fail to recognize periods so deeply suspect, in which truth was disfigured into falsehood? Who could believe that the excellent and holy man whom the Catholic Church venerates among the heavenly saints, after discovering a treasure, resorted to tricks in order safely to obtain its principal portion by defrauding the emperor of his right, and that by using ambiguous language he paved his way by such devices from the humblest station to the summit of the archbishopric?

Could there be anyone so perverse in judgment that, while daring to doubt the truth of what occurred at Chrysologus’s election—as Dupin does—he would swallow these crude and foolish stories, and on that basis even be able to affirm as true Agnellus’s interpolations about the men of Ravenna traveling to Constantinople to request the pallium for a new candidate, and about Justinian’s giving that pallium to Maximian, the man who had presented him with the gold he had found?

I shall believe none of these things, but only what befits Maximian’s sanctity and what the reliable monuments of those times teach me. I shall discuss these in my observations on the Life of Maximian himself.

### XIV.

Agnellus, therefore, refutes Agnellus quite adequately. But how clearly is the matter established by so many other certain arguments? I think I should select the more decisive of them, lest I abuse your patience too greatly, learned reader.

To remain in the age of Justinian: once all the surviving evidence of the sixth century that speaks clearly and bears unquestionable authority has been examined, it is certain that, going backward from the time of Gregory the Great, the supreme pontiffs bestowed the pallium upon metropolitans.

No one will deny that Gregory himself did this, especially anyone who has read the letters of that most holy pontiff to the bishops of Ravenna. Yet John, the archbishop of Ravenna himself, asserts in a letter preserved in book II, no. 55, near the end, of Gregory’s *Register*, that the same thing had been done by Gregory’s predecessors. He writes:

> “Since, therefore, I have submitted all the privileges granted to the holy Church of Ravenna by your predecessors, for the sake of greater satisfaction, you will nevertheless find them in the venerable archives, arranged according to the times of the consecration of my predecessors.”

Here John plainly asserts both that his predecessors had been consecrated by the Roman pontiffs and that, on the occasion of their consecration, the pallium had been conferred upon them by those same pontiffs.

The preceding letter of Gregory the Great, which is letter 54 of the same book, is clearly a reply to the one numbered 55, especially because Gregory says that the privileges sent by John had once been granted to the bishops of Ravenna by earlier supreme pontiffs:

> “And because you know well this custom of the universal Church, you have made it most clearly known to us in your letters, in which you transmitted to us, attached among the documents, the decree of our predecessor of blessed memory, Pope John, containing all the customs granted to you by the privilege of our predecessors and stating that they ought to be observed by you and by your Church.”

The privilege of Pope John mentioned here, which John of Ravenna had sent together with those of other pontifical predecessors, had been granted to Peter, surnamed the Elder, John’s predecessor. According to the calculations I have made in their proper place, Peter was ordained in the year 568, during the reign of Justin the Younger.

Baluze published it from a manuscript codex of Saint Remigius of Reims, in which it had been written after the praised letter of John of Ravenna, in *Miscellanea*, book V. Since it is relevant to the present matter, I think it should be transcribed here. It reads as follows:

> **Copy of the decree.**
>
> “To John, most beloved brother.
>
> “We recognize that it accords with reason that we adorn with the pallium those whom, in those cities where the honor of the priesthood shines forth by the inspiration of divine mercy, we know to have been granted this same privilege by the apostolic see to the pontiffs who held office there in former times. Therefore, by the authority of the present document, we grant to your Charity the use of the pallium, as your predecessors are known to have possessed it, and we wish all those privileges connected with your honor to remain in force which are known to have been preserved for your Church in earlier times, so that you may suffer no diminution whatever of its privileges.
>
> “And the subscription of the Lord Pope: May God keep you safe. On the tenth day before the Kalends of October, in the reign of the lord Justinian [read: Justin] Augustus.”

According to the calculations mentioned above, this was issued on the fifth day after the consecration of Archbishop Peter.

### XV.

The documents thus demonstrate that, during the reign of Justin the Younger, the pallium was bestowed upon metropolitans by the Roman pontiff, including, among others, the bishops of Ravenna. From the letters praised above it is evident that John sent Gregory the Great the privileges of other pontiffs who had preceded him.

From another source, we know from a letter of this pontiff that Symmachus sent the pallium as early as the year 501 to Theodore, bishop of Lorch. Likewise, Vigilius testifies that it had been granted by the same pontiff to Caesarius of Arles, when he sent it to Auxanius in a letter issued in the year 543. Garner noted this in his commentary on the third title of the *Liber Diurnus* of the Roman pontiffs, where the third formula for sending the pallium is almost identical with the cited letter of Symmachus.

It is therefore certain and evident that, during the period between Symmachus and Gregory the Great, the pallium was granted by the Roman pontiff, not by Justinian or by any emperor. Symmachus preceded Justinian in time and granted it; Vigilius, his contemporary, granted it; and after him came John III, who also granted it. We would be utterly obtuse if we did not hold with complete certainty that the intervening pontiffs did so as well.

What force against these facts can there be in the circumstance that Vigilius once or twice awaited Justinian’s consent before sending the pallium to the bishop of Arles? This does not establish that the granting of the pallium belonged to the emperors, but only that the exceptionally difficult circumstances required such a dispensation, so that the pious and prudent pontiff might protect himself and the Church and avoid incurring the emperor’s suspicion. At that time the emperor was master of Rome, while the barbarians occupied Italy and peace between the emperor and the king of the Franks was by no means secure; rather, causes of disagreement and war were growing. This is drawn from the letter itself of Pope Vigilius, found in volume VI of Labbe’s *Councils*, column 330.

But what will the defenders of the opposing view do with so many documents of unquestionable authority, from which it is evident that the Roman pontiffs granted the pallium without seeking the consent of any emperor? To put it mildly, it is certainly frivolous to resort to the document of the Donation of Constantine in order to obtain an argument—one drawn from a source far too remote—for the claim that the emperors granted the pallium to the Roman pontiff. We rely on certain evidence, not on spurious documents or on things that require an Oedipus to understand them.

### XVI.

To return to the path of the argument: John’s letter to Peter the Elder belongs to the year 568, while Justin began to reign as November of the year 565 was ending. Justinian, therefore, had died shortly before. How, then, could it have happened that, after Justinian had exercised the right of giving the pallium to metropolitans, his successor, immediately upon assuming the throne, should with such extraordinary liberality have refrained from giving it?

Moreover, how could John, in granting the pallium to Peter of Ravenna, have written that it was fitting for it to be granted to those “to whom it is known to have been granted by the apostolic see in former times” if Vigilius, John’s almost immediate predecessor, had not given the pallium to Maximian?

Agnellus’s later assertion therefore collapses on every side, and in its ruin it drags down the earlier one as well: namely, that Valentinian III granted the pallium to the first metropolitan of Ravenna.

### XVII.

The following points, noted by Garner, are relevant here: the expressions in the formula belonging to the age of Symmachus—or rather, in Symmachus’s own letter—the words “according to ancestral custom” and “according to the custom of your Church.” These show that Symmachus was not the first of all pontiffs to grant the pallium to the metropolitans of the West, although some have maintained this on the basis of a mistaken understanding of Vigilius’s letter to Auxanius.

Why should the pontiff’s statement that something was done “according to ancestral custom” not imply an antiquity of at least half a century? It should plainly be believed that this is what the expression means—especially in a pontiff who could not have foreseen the controversies that were to arise in our own age and whose legitimate document we possess—rather than Agnellus, a schismatic writing long afterward, when rumors concerning ancient rights had already gained currency in the Church of Ravenna without any basis in truth.

Certainly, once partisan interests have been set aside, anyone who weighs the force of both accounts will believe Symmachus, not Agnellus.

### XVIII.

Since the question of the granting of the pallium has importance because, by a necessary connection, it signifies the authority conveyed through the pallium, our lack of older documents teaching that the pallium was granted by a pontiff will be a small loss, provided that we are certain of the authority bestowed and of the metropolises established by those same pontiffs.

On this point the evidence is so clear that no lover of truth can cast it into doubt. Of all the ancients, Agnellus alone cast a cloud over a matter so evident. Rubeus, believing him too readily, enabled those who seek a knot in a reed to think they had sufficient support for imposing upon the world something unknown to all antiquity—namely, that the pallium was bestowed upon metropolitans by emperors, together with metropolitan authority.

Here one cannot help wondering at Rubeus’s judgment. When speaking of the pallium, he thought he had to proceed cautiously, saying that the pallium had been granted—not the pallium that the supreme pontiff grants to metropolitans, but a certain imperial garment. Yet, absolutely and without any distinction, he accepted from Agnellus and transmitted to posterity the claim that Valentinian had subjected twelve or fourteen bishops to the archbishopric of Ravenna.

Marcus Antonius de Dominis eagerly seized upon the matter and used the story in *De Republica Ecclesiastica*, book VI, no. 136, writing:

> “It was also within the power of the emperors to take metropolitan right away from other Churches, or at least to diminish it, and to divide, enlarge, or contract dioceses. The emperor Valentinian wished the Church of Ravenna to be archiepiscopal and metropolitan over all Aemilia. Rubeus records the privilege, although Baronius makes every effort to diminish it and charge it with imposture . . . . . The objections of Baronius himself and Rubeus’s hesitation concerning the granting of the pallium are not of great importance.”

After this, seeking support from the common system that I attacked in my Dissertation *On the Origin of the Hierarchy*—namely, that metropolises were established from the beginning according to the pattern of the empire—he adds:

> “Consequently, Valentinian established by his privilege that the archbishop of Ravenna should both use the pallium and possess the full privileges of the other metropolitans.”

This is what he wrote. Some Catholics have not been ashamed to present it in a somewhat softened form, at great cost to religion. Meanwhile, that apostate from Spalato, twisted by the cords of truth, sufficiently recants his statements at the end of the paragraph, so that we understand that he is not consistent with himself, in a way that Catholic authors certainly do not imitate. He writes:

> “If, however, the pallium is ecclesiastical in every respect, we must understand Valentinian in this privilege of Ravenna to have wished and ordered that the archbishop of Ravenna should receive the pallium from his patriarch, while possessing the remaining authority from the Church, although Valentinian himself thus commanded and ordained it.”

### XIX.

But on this point the universal and manifest consensus not only of the entire Church but also of the emperors of that age is wholly opposed to him. This consensus applies not only to the Western and Latin Church, which belonged to the jurisdiction of the Roman patriarch, but also to the Eastern Church. The Acts of the Council of Chalcedon, which belong to approximately the same period in which the twelve bishops are said to have been subjected to the Church of Ravenna by imperial authority, make this absolutely clear.

After peace had been restored to the Church by Constantine the Great, a new form of empire was introduced. The bishops, wrongly interpreting a canon of the Council of Nicaea, claimed that whenever the emperors newly designated civil metropolises, they thereby obtained from the canons a title by which they could assume parishes detached from their ancient metropolitan.

The matters must nevertheless be carefully distinguished. The emperors did not intend to alter the condition of the Churches or to grant jurisdiction to bishops. They merely established, within the limits of their authority, the civil arrangement of the empire, taking account of cities that had grown in population and splendor and of those that had become distinguished because the emperors happened to reside there.

Nor did the bishops go so far as to think that any right could be transferred to them by the emperor. Once a civil metropolis had been established, they considered all their rights to derive from the canons. This is what the ninth canon of the Council of Antioch sets forth, explaining the apostolic and Nicene canon.

Nevertheless, the canons and the rights of the ancient metropolitans were thereby violated. For this reason the Roman pontiffs resisted that Eastern abuse, among them Innocent I, who wrote to the bishop of Antioch in Letter 18, and the African Church, which insisted on the ancient custom in order to guard itself especially against that abuse, so that metropolitan bishops would not be attached to any particular city.

Two things are most clearly evident from the Council of Chalcedon cited above.

First, the supreme Roman pontiff took the greatest care that the abuses which had arisen from the civil glory of cities should be removed. The apostolic legates, steadfastly resisting canon 28, read from a written document what they had received as instructions from Pope Leo the Great. Its tenor was as follows:

> “You must not allow the constitution of the holy Fathers to be violated or diminished by any rashness. You must preserve in every respect the dignity of our person in you, whom we have sent in our place; and if anyone, relying perhaps on the **δύναμις** (*dynamis*, “power”) of his city, attempts to usurp anything for himself, you must repel it with the firmness it deserves.”

Second, although the Fathers of that council, in canon 28, yielded excessively to the ambition of the bishop of Constantinople, they nevertheless resolved to remove the abuses that had grown excessively through the establishment of new civil metropolises, whose bishops had violated the rights of others.

In the dispute over metropolitan right asserted by Eustathius, bishop of Berytus—who claimed it after Phoenicia, all of which had obeyed the metropolitan of Tyre, was divided into two parts by Theodosius the Younger—the situation was restored to its former state, and the following acclamation was made:

> “Against the imperial regulations, let nothing prevail; let the regulations of the Fathers stand, and let all imperial regulations cease; let the regulations stand.”

Finally, canon 12 expressly decreed as follows:

> “It has come to our attention that certain men, after approaching positions of power contrary to ecclesiastical customs, divided one province into two by imperial regulations, so that there would consequently be two metropolitans in the same province. Therefore the holy synod decrees that no bishop shall henceforth dare to do such a thing, since anyone who attempts it falls from his rank. Whatever cities have been honored with the name of metropolis by imperial letters shall enjoy that honor alone, while the bishop who administers its Church shall preserve the rights belonging to the true metropolis.”

It is also worth observing that, at the end of the sixth session, when the emperor Marcian had declared the city of Chalcedon a metropolis in name only, while preserving the proper dignity of Nicomedia, the Fathers acclaimed the emperor’s judgment as just. They added, in answer to the safeguard that had been provided lest anything be taken away from Nicomedia’s dignity:

> “You have prevented the **παραστάσεις τῶν ἐπισκόπων**—‘the evasions [or circumventions] of the bishops.’”

Nothing was decreed concerning the matter in the canons.

### XX.

Here one cannot help marveling at the intellectual acumen of the most learned Thomassin, *De nova et veteri disciplina*, part I, book I, chapter 39, who sees in these Acts of the Council of Chalcedon an exchange of mutual honors by which the emperor and the Fathers honored one another. He writes:

> “The Fathers of the council cry out openly and with the greatest freedom: ‘Against the imperial regulations, let nothing prevail; let the regulations of the Fathers stand.’ Yet they dare to do this only after the imperial judges had referred to the council’s wishes the question whether these ecclesiastical disputes should be settled by canons or by laws, and after the Fathers had made clear to the emperor himself that it was their wish that everything be settled according to the prescriptions of the canons.”

Thus that most skillful writer softened what the Spalatensis had expressed more harshly in the passage cited above, no. 137—namely, that the Fathers had recanted what the emperor had determined. For, he says, they would certainly not have dared to do so unless the emperor had ordered it.

Indeed, we are not permitted to be so perceptive as to see what these exceptionally sharp-eyed men see. The first person to speak about the distinction between the two criteria for settling the dispute was Eustathius, who was acting for the interested party. After the judges had read Photius’s written statement and asked, “What does the most reverend Eustathius, bishop of Berytus, allege in response to these points?” he replied:

> “Order him to say whether he is proceeding according to the canons or according to the laws.”

Before the judges added anything, Photius immediately insisted that he wished the matter to be decided according to the rules of the Fathers and defined by the Fathers of the council:

> “Let the lords and most holy bishops be asked whether the most reverend bishop Eustathius has attempted to overturn the ancient custom. For I do not depart from the rules, nor do I wish to overturn the Fathers’ norms; rather, I demand that those rights not be overthrown.”

Thus, after the petitions of the plaintiff and the defendant, the judges asked the Fathers to decide whether the dispute should be settled according to the laws or according to the canons. They did indeed repeat what Photius had said earlier: that the emperor’s judgment was the one favorable to the canons. But what follows from that? They commend the emperor’s piety; they do not restrict the Fathers’ authority to decide.

Since the defendant had raised an objection and the plaintiff had contradicted him regarding an incidental point, the Fathers had to decide the matter. The judges indicated the question on which a judgment had first to be rendered. But this is not, with due allowance, the same as defining the principal matter; and who could believe that the matter principally at issue had been defined when those same judges said in the fifth session:

> “Dioscorus said: ‘I accept “of two natures”; I do not accept “two natures.”’ But the most holy archbishop Leo says that two natures are united in Christ, without confusion, without change, without division, in the one-begotten Son, our Savior. Whom, then, do you follow—the most holy Leo or Dioscorus?”

Clearly, when we are too eager to appear as sharp-sighted as lynxes, we become blind.

### XXI.

Canon 28 of that same council, the very canon at issue, itself clearly demonstrates that the emperors in no way thought that jurisdiction over bishops belonged to them. The synod of Constantinople, in canon 3, had decreed for the bishop of that city **τὰ πρεσβεῖα τῆς τιμῆς**, “the prerogatives of honor.” Hence, in the canon mentioned above, this was understood to mean that the bishop of Constantinople should hold second place after the Roman patriarch.

Holstenius observed in his notes on the Roman Council of Pope Boniface II that Binius and the most learned Baronius had doubted without justification the canon of the earlier synod, although the Chalcedonian canon bears witness to it.

What lesser bishops had claimed for themselves on the basis of the splendor of cities, the bishop of New Rome thought he ought to claim for himself: Constantinople, the seat of the emperors, to which cases were brought from the entire world. The bishop of that city did not belong to the patriarch of the West, nor to the patriarch of Alexandria or Antioch; consequently, the patriarchal right of the Roman bishop was in no way harmed.

The emperors Valentinian and Marcian desired the glory of the Church of Constantinople. Yet observe the route by which they proceeded. They did not think that they possessed any authority to decide the matter; nor did they consider the decree of the council sufficient unless Leo’s consent were added.

This is clear from their letters to Leo the Great, issued around the year 451 and reproduced in the aforementioned Roman Council of Boniface. In requesting that the bishop of Constantinople be regarded as second after the Roman patriarch, they recognize that this could not be done by imperial authority. They produce the decrees of both ecumenical councils in support of their request and earnestly ask that the Roman pontiff confirm what had been decreed:

> “Since it has also been established that what the one hundred and fifty most holy bishops under the Lord Theodosius the Great decreed concerning the honor of the venerable Church of Constantinople, and what has now been decreed by the holy synod concerning the same matter, should remain firm—namely, that after the apostolic see the bishop of the see of Constantinople should hold the second place, since that most splendid city is now called New Rome—may Your Holiness deign to give your own consent to this part as well.”

The most holy Leo, bishop of Old Rome, resisted. The most pious emperors, who knew the limits of their authority very well, consequently abandoned their undertaking to such an extent that Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, wrote to Leo that what had been done at the Council of Chalcedon should not be attributed to him but to the clergy of his Church.

What Valentinian thought he was not permitted to do beyond the boundaries of the Roman patriarchate—even when the see of Constantinople was concerned, and even though the matter had been decreed by an ecumenical council—he supposedly did within the ecclesiastical jurisdiction of the Roman patriarch, indeed within the diocese of the Roman metropolitan, thereby violating the sacred right of the Roman see on two separate grounds. Such a claim is utterly beyond credibility.

### XXII.

To omit nothing that might enable us to understand the opinion of those times concerning the authority to confer metropolitan rights, it cannot be concealed that abuses from the East occasionally crept into the Western Church as well.

We have one example of this, and we also know that the idea of establishing a new metropolis on the basis of a city’s civil splendor was by no means approved by the Roman pontiff.

The bishop of Arles was claiming for himself the ordinations of the bishops of the province of Vienne, supposedly on the pretext that the city of Arles, having increased in distinction through the residence of emperors, had become a metropolis. This is what Peter de Marca—or Baluze—thinks can be inferred from the constitution of Honorius, cited by Sirmond in his notes on Sidonius.

The Council of Turin in the year 397 maintained the opinion that the bishops of civil metropolises enjoyed the rights of ecclesiastical metropolitans. Yet it was uncertain which city was the civil metropolis, Arles or Vienne, and the council decreed:

> “Whichever of them”—that is, whichever bishop—“shall prove his city to be the metropolis shall possess the primatial honor of the entire province.”

Patroclus of Arles, however, thought he had to pursue another course in order to retain what he had once seized. He brought his case before the Roman pontiff, knowing that nothing could safely be said to him about the glory of a city. He therefore wished to defend himself solely by the weight of ecclesiastical antiquity, on account of which he obtained from Pope Zosimus confirmation of his right to consecrate the bishops of the provinces of Vienne and Narbonne.

The pontiff writes in Letter 70:

> “Since Trophimus, once a priest sent by the apostolic see to the city of Arles, was the first to display in those regions the reverence due to so great a name.”

The pontiffs who followed judged that the same rules had to be maintained when disputes arose concerning the same matter.

Around the year 462, Pope Hilary sent a rescript to the bishops of the various provinces of Gaul in Letter 8, when Leontius of Arles complained that parishes belonging to his Church had been transferred by Hilary’s predecessor to others, although this had not been permitted. He referred the complaint to the bishops, “so that they might decide what accorded with the ecclesiastical rules.”

In the following letter, against Mamertus of Vienne, who had improperly ordained the bishop of Die, he expressly asserts that rulers approved what the Roman pontiff decreed in such matters:

> “For nothing established by my predecessor of holy memory could be taken away from our brother Leontius; nothing owed to his honor could be removed, because it has also been decreed by the law of Christian rulers that whatever the bishop of the apostolic see, after examination, has pronounced concerning the Churches and their rulers for the peace of all, for the priests of the Lord, and for the observance of discipline itself in removing disorders, your Charity should know is to be received with reverence and firmly preserved, together with its peoples.”

### XXIII.

All these points sufficiently demonstrate that the opinion prevailing under Valentinian, certainly in the Western Church but also in the Eastern Church, among bishops as well as rulers and Valentinian himself, was that the authority to alter the rights of metropolitans, establish new metropolitans, provide them with the pallium, and perform other acts of this kind belonged to ecclesiastical power, not imperial power.

This was especially strengthened by the favor shown to the patriarchal rights and metropolitan rights of the Roman pontiff, who was a vigorous defender of such rights against the abuses that had arisen.

If the bishop of Ravenna had possessed metropolitan right and the pallium through Valentinian’s grant, then, by force of canon 12 of the Council of Chalcedon, he would have retained only **τὰ πρεσβεῖα τῆς τιμῆς**, “the prerogatives of honor,” as the Fathers had decreed. But it is established with the greatest certainty that the bishop of Ravenna enjoyed metropolitan rights even after the Council of Chalcedon.

He therefore attained both metropolitan right and the pallium not because of the splendor of the city, nor through Valentinian’s grant, but through the liberality of the Roman pontiff.

### XXIV. [Col. 0449C]

There are also matters that prove this most clearly and decisively. The exercise of fullest jurisdiction, the threat of penalties, and especially the threat to remove metropolitan authority are certainly the prerogatives of the one who granted the metropolitan’s authority and the pallium, by which that authority is signified. We have these matters clearly expressed in the letter of Simplicius, the supreme pontiff, belonging to the year 482 and directed against John, bishop of Ravenna—apparently, as I think, the immediate successor of Peter Chrysologus—who had ordained a certain Gregory, bishop of Modena, against his will. Let the principal statements of that letter be considered:

“For he deserves to lose the privilege who abuses the authority entrusted to him.”

And at the end:

“But we declare that if hereafter you presume to do anything of this kind, and should venture to ordain anyone—whether bishop, presbyter, or deacon—against his will, you are to know that the ordinations of the Church of Ravenna or of Emilia will be taken away from you.”

Thus the one who had granted this authority to his predecessors could threaten to withdraw metropolitan authority. Otherwise, this threat by the pontiff would have been an empty scarecrow, if secular power could have restored what the pontiff removed.

We have, moreover, a most evident proof that metropolitan authority was conferred upon the bishops of Ravenna by the Roman pontiff in that celebrated letter of Gelasius I to the bishops of Dardania, which is number 13 in the Labbe collection and belongs to the year 495. [Col. 0449D]

“We laughed,” says Gelasius, “that they wish Acacius to be compared on the ground that he was bishop of a royal city. Was there not for many years an emperor at Ravenna, at Milan, at Sirmium, and at Trier? Did the priests of those cities ever usurp for their dignities anything beyond the measure anciently assigned to them? For,” as the same pontiff says below, “one authority belongs to secular affairs, another is the distribution of ecclesiastical dignities.”

These words of the most holy pontiff must be considered very briefly. It is certain that Peter Chrysologus was the first of all the bishops of Ravenna to exercise metropolitan rights. Nevertheless, let it be—as I think—that those rights were conferred upon John Angeloptes, Peter’s predecessor, in the final years of his life. From that time Gelasius was separated by scarcely fifty-five years.

If Valentinian, son of Galla Placidia, had subjected the bishops of twelve cities to the bishop of Ravenna and had delivered the pallium to him, without this having been obtained from the Roman pontiff of that period, Gelasius would not have been unaware of it. Therefore Gelasius would not have written these things, which are such a great honor to the bishops of Ravenna of that age; and Acacius, or those who supported the memory of Acacius and adhered to his party after his death, could have defended themselves by the example of the Ravennates. [Col. 0450A]

Valentinian may have transformed Ravenna into a civil metropolis—for he had the power to do that. He may also have asked the pontiff to confer metropolitan rights and the pallium, and may have granted privileges and favors—for he had the power to do so, and I do not begrudge him having done it. But to subject bishops who belonged to the diocese of either the Roman or Milanese bishop and to the patriarchate of the West, and who required spiritual authority, was entirely beyond the emperor’s power.

It must again be impressed upon us: “One authority belongs to secular affairs, another is the distribution of ecclesiastical dignities.” No sane person will place greater trust in Agnellus, an incompetent author of the ninth century attached to schism, than in the supreme pontiff, a most expert authority on canons and affairs, who lived very near the age of Valentinian. [Col. 0450B]

### XXV.

Once all these points have been established, it will be superfluous to add anything against the rashness of Maurus, who did not blush to attempt autocephaly—αὐτοκεφαλαία—in the West and almost within the very boundaries of the Roman diocese, at a time when even the exarchs of the Eastern Church, who had been such from the earliest apostolic times, had finally come to obey another.

What of the obedience of all his predecessors toward the Roman pontiff, and the proofs—known from the memory of their fathers—of the complete subjection of the bishops of Ravenna, both when they were consecrated, when they received the pallium, and when they were summoned to synods? Above all, what of the acts of Gregory the Great, whose surviving letters are read by us, separated by so long an interval from that age, as testimony to this matter?

Nor was Maurus himself unaware that he and his Church were subject to the Roman pontiff. He had been ordained by him, adorned with the pallium, and had provided, on the occasion of the Monothelite heresy, the clear proof of this fact by presenting the formula of security—which they then called a *cautio*—that had by that time become customary. [Col. 0450C]

Yet this proud man, impatient of subjection, finding the times exceedingly difficult and an emperor and an exarch who were the most wicked of all two-legged creatures, attempted by arts suited to his character to withdraw himself, against law and right, from the jurisdiction of his patriarch; and from there he plunged headlong into the terrible crime of schism.

The one thing Agnellus properly accomplished in the Life of Maurus was to indicate, not obscurely, his cunning and greed, or his squandering of the Sicilian patrimony.

It is pleasing to conclude with the learned words of Bertherius, *Pithanon*, Dissertation II:

“I say nothing—using, as Anastasius does in the Life of Donus, the word—of autocephaly, an utterly unworthy deed, by heaven, and one to be buried in eternal silence.”

### XXVI. [Col. 0450D]

With these points laid down beforehand, anyone may safely traverse the rough stretches of Agnellus’s book. For you, learned reader, these matters would not have been a cause of scandal; nevertheless, I considered it my duty not only to preface the foregoing remarks, but also to point out the danger wherever anything not at all pious lies hidden.

Meanwhile, judge my labor fairly and generously. Before you approach Agnellus, receive the chronological series of the bishops of Ravenna whose acts Agnellus wrote, as I have thought it necessary to restore them in my dissertations.

Farewell.

## SERIES OF PONTIFFS

Of the holy Church of Ravenna, whose lives are narrated by Agnellus.

Saint Apollinaris, ordained in the year 50, on 19 June. Crowned with martyrdom in the year 78, on the Kalends of July, after having sat for 28 years, 5 months, and 4 days.

Aderitus. Eleucadius. Martianus. Calocerus. Proculus. Probus. [Col. 0451A] Dathus. Liberius. Agapetus. Marcellinus. Severus began to sit around the year 346 and died around 391. Liberius II. Probus II. Florentius. Liberius III. Ursus, created around the year 400; died in 412, on 13 April, toward evening. Peter, created in that year, died in 425. Neo, appointed in the same year, died around 430, on the third day before the Ides of February. Exuperantius died in 432, on the fourth day before the Kalends of June. John Angeloptes, created in the same year, died around 439. Peter Chrysologus, ordained around 439, died around 450. [Col. 0451B]

John II, ordained in that year, died around 496. Peter III, created around that time, flourished during the time of the supreme pontiff Symmachus. Aurelian, appointed in succession to Peter, died around 523. Ecclesius, created near the beginning of 524, died around July of 534. Ursicinus, ordained in the same year, around August, died around April of 538. Victor, ordained on 4 March 540, died on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of March 546. Maximian, ordained by Pope Vigilius at Patras in Achaea, on the day before the Ides of October 546, died in 552, on the eighth day before the Kalends of March. Agnellus, ordained in 553, on 22 June, died in 566, on the Kalends of August. Peter IV, called Senior, elected in 567, on 28 May; ordained in 568, on 15 September; died in 575, on 16 August.

John III, ordained in 575, on 23 November, died in 595, on 2 January. Marinianus, ordained before 5 July 595, died on 23 October 604. John IV, ordained around the beginning of 605, died around September 610. John V, ordained around the end of 610, died around 629. Bonus, ordained around 630, died in 642, on 25 August. Maurus, ordained in September 642, died around July 671. Reparatus, ordained on 4 October 671, died on 30 July 677. Theodore, ordained on 29 September 677, died on 18 January 691. Damianus, ordained on 24 December 691, died on 12 March 708. Felix, ordained on 4 April 708, died in 716, on 25 November. [Col. 0452A]

John VI died around 752. Sergius, ordained around 752, died around the end of 769 or the beginning of 770. Leo, ordained at about that time, died around 779. John VII began to sit around 779; died in 786, after the feast of Saint Apollinaris. He sat for 7 years, 1 month, and 3 days. Gratiosus, ordained in 786, died around 794, on 23 February. Saint Valerius, ordained around 794, died around 809. Martinus began to sit around 810, died around 819. Petronacius, ordained after 821, died before 837. Georgius, ordained after the aforementioned year, prolonged his life beyond 841.

[Col. 0451C]

## OBSERVATIONS ON CERTAIN VERSES PREFIXED TO AGNELLUS’S *BOOK OF THE PONTIFFS*

### PREFATORY NOTE

The barbarism of the verses prefixed to Agnellus’s work is so great that, while preparing to write the rest, I considered omitting them. Since no grammatical rules have been observed in them, and consequently the order of correct syntax is everywhere disturbed—not to mention the neglect of syllable and verse quantity—it seemed scarcely possible to extract anything worthwhile from them. Indeed, I had little hope that anywhere I would grasp the meaning of the most incompetent scholastic versifier, since he rashly takes one tense for another, one mood for another, and one case for another; hence, being ambiguous (*ἀμφίβολος*) and exceedingly intricate, he requires an Oedipus rather than an interpreter—an exegete (*ἐξηγητὴς*).

Although the barbarism of the ninth century is known from other sources, so that we need be less surprised if we discover the utmost corruption of the Latin language in the surviving writings of that period—a corruption which also commends their genuineness and authenticity—the deformity and scribbling of these verses is nevertheless so great that I scarcely believe one could find a comparable specimen of such characteristics in the writers of that century or the next: a specimen that reveals the genuineness of the writing while concealing the writer’s mind. [Col. 0451D]

Nevertheless, I did not wish to omit anything. I thought that everything relating to Agnellus’s work should be made public in full, lest scholars should miss anything that could be supplied from the Este Codex. I therefore transcribed the most incompetent series of verses and, after examining it more attentively, seemed to have extracted from it certain points that illuminate both the work of the *Book of the Pontiffs* and the life of its author, Agnellus. For this reason I decided to place the verses first, interspersing my observations.

I freely confess that there were some passages whose meaning I had little hope of understanding; I therefore thought it better to leave them untouched rather than, by guessing, impose upon the reader something arbitrary instead of something that could be approved.

The verses are prefixed by the following title:

> Here begin the little verses of a certain least among the scholastics, giving the title of the work of the following book.

### FIRST OBSERVATION

The author of these verses calls himself a *scholasticus* in the title. By this term he means a learned man, as opposed to an uneducated person. Although this word acquired various meanings among writers of Middle and Late Latin—as the most learned Ducange teaches us in his *Glossary*—none appears more suitable or convenient to the time and occasion.

Thus Amalarius of Trier, cited by Brouwer from the aforementioned Ducange, says:

> Whoever you may be—whether powerful in the world, poor, a scholastic, or an uneducated person.

I know that the name *scholasticus* came to signify in churches the office of the man placed over the school, so that he might direct and teach either languages and the liberal arts alone, or these together with theology and subjects pertaining to liturgical and divine matters. But these meanings belong to the period after the time of Charles the Bald.

Moreover, this was the one appointed over the school of a particular church; in later centuries the theological office succeeded to it. On this subject see the most learned Thomassin, *On the Old and New Discipline of Benefices*. [Col. 0452D]

The author of these verses, however, calls himself one of several men who possessed the same title or office when he calls himself “the least of the scholastics.” I seem therefore to perceive an order of men active at Ravenna as the ninth century progressed. In an age otherwise shrouded in the greatest darkness concerning the liberal arts, they appeared to have made some progress beyond others in the art of speaking and in the use of the Latin language, and they were called scholastics. A man regarded as such could use the title without boasting, since, in due proportion, it anticipated the later designation of master or doctor.

Ravenna may have received such an order of scholastics from the Greeks, who distinguished eloquent men with the same title as an honor. This was rightly done in the case of Zacharias, honored with the surname “Scholasticus” in the age of Justinian, as Tarinus maintains in his notes on Zacharias’s *Dialogue on the Creation of the World*, against Genebrard’s view. [Col. 0453A]

That an eminent magistrate at Ravenna was also called a *scholasticus* in the age of Gregory the Great is indicated by the letters of that pontiff. Whether this least of the scholastics was an ecclesiastical man or not, the evidence is insufficient to decide. Nevertheless, if anyone wishes to regard him as devoted to the ecclesiastical life because he lent his hand to the illumination of this work, I do not object. [Col. 0453B]

> In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, a breath,  
> Having studied on account of the sure sign of the age,  
> And Jesus, the Redeemer of humanity, at his birth,  
> Many masters wrote of kings and pontiffs:  
> Whatever time each one had sat, whether an imperial  
> Ruler upon the imperial throne, or an eminent shepherd upon the pontifical  
> Seat. They wrote of the iron reigns of the emperors,  
> Whose lofty empire at last shone forth  
> In the western regions, where abundance of waters rises;  
> And men renowned for holy life, like the age of the apostles,  
> In whatever manner, shone by word and deed.

### SECOND OBSERVATION

To approach the verses themselves and extract their meaning as conveniently as possible, I understand the first eleven verses transcribed above in such a way that they may be explained paraphrastically as follows.

After invoking the most holy Trinity, the author says that many masters—that is, learned men—had considered writing histories beginning with the Redeemer’s birth, on account of the clear sign of the age, that is, for the knowledge and instruction of posterity. They would write about both kings and pontiffs, and especially about the period during which each had sat, whether an emperor on the imperial throne or a pontiff on the pontifical seat. There were also men who wrote the deeds of both groups: of emperors, including those whose power had shone forth in the western regions “where abundance of waters rises,” namely at Ravenna; and of pontiffs, who in speech and works imitated the examples of the apostles.

The basis of this praise was drawn from the feature by which the city of Ravenna was commended: all the waters of the entire region situated on both sides of the Po, from the river’s source to the more celebrated mouths through which it discharges into the Adriatic Sea, as well as the waters flowing down from the mountains bordering Flaminia, converged around Ravenna. We know this from other passages of this *Book of the Pontiffs*. [Col. 0453C]

Let us continue the explanation of the verses once begun.

> And the pen of the Ravennate writers, for roughly  
> Eight hundred years, was long idle and neglected  
> To narrate everywhere the illustrious lives  
> Of their supreme pontiffs, who governed the blessed Church throughout the world.

### THIRD OBSERVATION

Here he says that the pens of the Ravennates neglected to do what others had done: they left the lives and deeds of their own pontiffs, who had governed the Church for approximately eight hundred years, consigned to oblivion. [Col. 0454A]

> Although in the evening—for faith and hand had nevertheless begun—  
> Agnellus, the charming priest, happily began to write  
> This little work of the patriarchs.  
>   
> **[Note: He foolishly calls them patriarchs, although they were merely metropolitans. BACCHINIUS.]**  
>   
> In the time when the apostolic Gregory, exalted and salutary,  
> Held the authority to loose and bind, and when the nourishing Augustus  
> Held the imperial scepters, the mighty son of great Charles,  
> Louis, the peaceful, and his son Lothair,  
> Fierce, holding the warlike kingdoms of Italy, and Rome, having obtained power,  
> Chosen by kings and peoples for the imperial throne,  
> The archbishop Petronacius, rejoicing under the nourishing [*almus*] one,  
> Governed your clergy and people of the Church of Ravenna,  
> The second after the eleventh, whom that supreme pontiff,  
> With good reason, blessed as a presbyter in the rich seat of the city.

The printed variants are: *acer* (“fierce”) for *acre*; *Itala* (“Italian”) for *Italia*; *potitus* (“having obtained power”) for *pontus*; *almus* (“nourishing”) for *almis*; and *tumque* (“and then”) for *tuoque*.

### FOURTH OBSERVATION

At last Agnellus adds that, although late—that is, belatedly—he had devoted himself to undertaking this desired work as a presbyter. He expresses the time when this occurred in several ways: Gregory IV was supreme pontiff, holding Peter’s life-giving gifts—the power to loose and, conversely, to bind; Louis, son of Charles the Great, and Lothair were ruling; and Petronacius was governing the Church of Ravenna as archbishop. The supreme pontiff had consecrated him as the eleventh archbishop after that Church of Ravenna, recovering from the time of Theodore, had submitted itself to the obedience of the Roman bishop. [Col. 0454C]

These matters deserve to be examined somewhat more carefully in determining the designated chronology.

It is clear, moreover, that the chronological markers employed by the scholastic versifier to indicate the time when Agnellus wrote this pontifical book cannot stand unless they are understood as referring to the interval during which Agnellus resumed the writing after an interruption. For Agnellus himself makes clear that the greater part of the work was written not only after the episcopate of Petronacius but even after that of Georgius.

We read the Life of Georgius recorded last; he is also mentioned in the Life of Felix as an archbishop who was certainly no longer among the living. Agnellus says:

> “It also happened to me concerning the aforesaid monastery of Saint Bartholomew. I was deprived of it by Bishop Georgius for a few years without cause. For before he had ascended to such a height, we were to one another as two true brothers born from a single stock. After he received the archiepiscopal dignity, he offended God and destroyed all the priests, seizing all the monasteries and all the treasures of the Church that his predecessors had acquired, and spending them for the guilt of his own body.”

The death of Georgius, as appears from his Life, occurred several years after Charles the Bald’s victory over Lothair at Fontenoy, which took place on the seventh day before the Kalends of July in the year 841.

From this it is also evident that the other chronological marker derived from the reign of Louis and Lothair cannot stand. Louis had died in 840, and the writing can scarcely be maintained to have taken place while Gregory IV was seated, since Gregory died in 843.

The Life of Archbishop Maximian was also written after the time of Petronacius. In it Agnellus says that in the fifteenth year of Petronacius’s archbishopric the body of Maximian was raised, with the priests laboring earnestly at the task, while Agnellus himself performed the work at the command of the pontiff who was present.

Finally, in the Life of Archbishop Maurus, Agnellus shows that Petronacius had died several years earlier, mentioning that the translucent stone of Petronacius’s tomb had been transported into Gaul by the emperor Louis twelve years previously, during Petronacius’s time.

A clearer argument is furnished by the Life of the bishop Peter Senior. There the author, narrating the transfer by the emperor Charles of a bronze horse that once stood at Ravenna, says:

> “And now almost thirty-eight years have passed since Charles, king of the Franks, had subdued all the kingdoms and received the imperial power from Pope Leo III. After offering the sacrament at the body of blessed Peter, he returned to Francia, entered Ravenna, and, seeing a most beautiful image—one like which, as he himself testified, he had never seen—had it carried to Francia and fixed it in his palace, which is called Aachen.”

According to the Frankish Annals reported by Baronius, Charles returned from Rome around the beginning of June in the year 801 and remained at Ravenna for several days. Therefore, when Agnellus wrote the words just quoted, the year was 839. He had written the Life of Archbishop Maximian shortly before; Archbishop Petronacius had raised the body of the aforementioned Maximian in the fifteenth year of his archbishopric; and Petronacius himself had died, as the author’s manner of narration clearly indicates. [Col. 0455A]
