The copyist of this codex, who says that he made it from an exemplar, discovered that the Life of Petronacius was missing. Supplying it from other chronicles and inserting it here, he says that Petronacius swore allegiance to the emperor Charles. But the chronology in no way permits this. Charles died in 814, while Leo III, who did not die until 816, was still alive. Leo was succeeded by Stephen V, called IV. When Stephen returned from Gaul to Rome and celebrated Mass at Ravenna, Martinus, Petronacius’s predecessor, was occupying the see, as Agnellus relates in Martinus’s Life.

Since much is missing from that Life, it is reasonable to believe that Martinus lived for several years after Stephen’s death, who held the see for only seven months and left it to his successor Paschal in the year 807 [**Note: Read 817.**]. Nevertheless, the consecration of Petronacius cannot be postponed beyond the third year of Eugenius, A.D. 826, when Petronacius himself subscribed first among the sixty-three bishops at a council held in Rome. [Col. 0455B]

His episcopate therefore began in the later years of Paschal, who sat after Stephen and before Eugenius for seven years and several months; it should consequently be placed around 822. Once this chronology is established, the raising of Maximian’s body must be referred to 837. Agnellus wrote about it around 839, as he did about the deeds of Peter Senior, by which time Georgius had already been consecrated archbishop of Ravenna by Gregory IV.

The Lives preceding these, however, must necessarily have been written several years earlier. I recognize this from the fact that, in the Life of Aurelian, where the author laments that he was harassed shamefully by many of his fellow priests to bring the *Book of the Pontiffs* to completion, he says among other things of his age:

> “Today, finally, I have completed six lustra, with two additional years and twice five months, since I received the light and emerged from my mother’s womb.”

This cannot be fitted to the year 839. For in the Life of Martinus he says that Martinus gave him the monastery of Saint Mary at Blachernae. Nor is it consistent with his narrative to suppose that this happened during the final years of Martinus, since after the sequence of those events he adds several matters—the death of Pepin, king of the Lombards, and of Charles the Great, as well as other events pertaining to the Life of Martinus—that can be assigned only to the pontificate of Leo.

Since Leo died in 816, Agnellus would have obtained the Church of Saint Mary at Blachernae when he was scarcely seven years old. But if we place this around the year 812, when Agnellus was entering his fourteenth year—for he himself calls himself still a child—it follows that he wrote the Life of Aurelian around A.D. 829, while in the thirty-third year of his age and in the tenth month of that year. [Col. 0456A]

All the chronological markers given by the scholastic fit this year: Gregory IV was Roman pontiff, Louis and Lothair were emperors, and Petronacius was governing as archbishop of Ravenna.

It follows that these verses were written at precisely that time. The work had only been begun and would not be completed for several years; the verses were therefore intended to spur on the author, who was proceeding more slowly than his fellow priests wished.

I understood the following verses—

> The second after the eleventh, whom that supreme pontiff  
> With good reason blessed as a presbyter in the rich seat of the city—

as referring to Petronacius, the eleventh bishop of Ravenna, counting from Theodore, who submitted himself to the Roman pontiff after the schism of that Church.

But, to confess the truth, I am not at all satisfied with this explanation: “the second after the eleventh” is not the eleventh. Nevertheless, no more convenient interpretation is available. [Col. 0456B]

> Who among all priests was wiser than this holy man,  
> Renowned for intelligence and nature? He was called by name  
> Agnellus from childhood, and Andreas in youth,  
> Well-born and sprung from a very proud lineage.  
> Ravenna gave him birth, second to no one,  
> Handsome in face, brilliant in speech, eloquent in mouth,  
> Small in body and limbs, but capable in mind—  
> He whose great understanding, although his body was like Paul’s—

### FIFTH OBSERVATION

Here Agnellus is praised for his priesthood, his intelligence, and his nature, which corresponded to his name; for the nobility of his lineage and parents; and he is compared with Paul, small in body but great in mind.

> As the nightingale, singing sweetly, is found  
> In flower-bearing spring woods, with curved throat  
> Crying out, filling the lofty sky with its calls,  
> Sitting upon a green branch beneath its throne,  
> A mistress and musician, modulating beneath the open sky,  
> Joyfully making melody—traveler,  
> Shepherd, and watchful rider, desiring to hear  
> Its sweetness, all wish freely everywhere  
> For its songs and diligently seek them,  
> And no other can ever surpass it in prolonged song—  
> So this man, seated beneath roofs exceedingly splendid,  
> Which his tall father had ceded to him by hereditary right,  
> In the suburban seat of Ravenna, called  
> Blachernae, built in those ancient places,  
> In honor of the Mother of God and of the Lord’s Mary,  
> The charming writer of the aforementioned *Book of the Pontiffs*,  
> Sighing and burning as he touched what had long been neglected,  
> Labors, with open mouth, freely to devote himself  
> To so great a burden of work.

### SIXTH OBSERVATION

This passage says that just as the nightingale, singing a sweet melody in the woods during spring, sits upon the green ground beneath the open sky and freely delights the ears and minds of passing travelers, shepherds, and riders with a song whose sweetness cannot be surpassed, so Agnellus, seated beneath exceedingly splendid roofs—that is, highly elegant ones—which his tall father had ceded to him by hereditary right in the suburban district of Ravenna, where the Church of Saint Mary, called Blachernae from its ancient name, is located, freely meditates on satisfying the wishes of those who desire a history, weaving together, in place of song, the long-neglected history of the pontiffs of Ravenna.

What should have been said here concerning Agnellus’s ancestry and life, and concerning the Church of Saint Mary at Blachernae, I prefixed to the preface of the entire book and therefore need not repeat. [Col. 0457A]

> [Lacuna], recalling the monuments of fathers and elders,  
> Not a deaf listener to what was born, but with willing mind,  
> Skillfully following the precepts of Moses as he spoke:  
> “Ask your fathers, for they will tell you; your elders  
> Will announce to you”—always seeking and asking  
> For the deeds of former times, and the ancient miracles  
> Of your God and Lord; they will remind you, speaking the truth,  
> By sight and hearing.  
>   
> Then he gathers together the deeds of the earlier patriarchs;  
> He published this work in the time of those whose names,  
> Painted upon a wall, he extracted in their order,  
> And part of whose lives and distinguished governance  
> He gathers partly by what he hears, accustomed to heap them together in books.  
>   
> Beginning with Aderitus and ending with Petronacius,  
> Joining the body of the little work between the two,  
> He wisely writes eleven times four  
> Men’s offices—or hands—regulating each one’s  
> Magnificent governance by tongue, and leaving what he heard and read,  
> Certain through vigilant observation, but uncertain through  
> Alert attention and study.  
>   
> Acting like an eager seeker upon the curved shore  
> Of the earth-bearing Po as it flows back, seeking golden metals,  
> Who vigorously tramples the sand, selecting  
> Certain particles, pouring black liquid onto the page,  
> Revealing to the common people the holy miracles of the blessed,  
> He nobly set them out in sonorous language,  
> In whose ear, as much as there was of manifold report,  
> He was full of truthful testimony; but, wavering over the accounts of others,  
> He preferred to instruct them briefly in polished speech,  
> Like a man sitting joyfully at the benches, drinking cups  
> Brought on platters, stuffed with food, and belching out songs,  
> Looking up at the calm sky, while the sailor with tranquil mouth  
> Gives his sails in eager succession to favorable winds  
> And runs across the glassy waters,  
> When he fears no reef, sees no shoals,  
> And the tenacious anchor, lowered into the deep, does not touch the sandbanks.  
>   
> But when, sorrowful, he sees the sky dark with thick clouds  
> And the winds rushing everywhere through the empty air,  
> Or looks upon a reef or sees one close at hand,  
> Then, drawing his course with the oars, lowering his sails,  
> He anxiously binds and drives the ship with ropes,  
> And, lowering his lead into the sea with a single rope and hook,  
> Eagerly desires to reach a place of refuge.  
>   
> So, conscious of his subject, he likewise wished to set it out in speech,  
> More richly and abundantly in varied passages, adorning his language,  
> Joyful in the grand sound and fame of former men;  
> But, ignorant of how to guide the loosened reins of his glorious speech,  
> He fitted together a few words,  
> Having laid aside arrogance, with tightened and talkative mouth,  
> To bring forth their deeds briefly in truthful speech.

The printed variants include: *nuntii erunt* (“they will announce”) for *erant*; *partim* (“partly”) for each occurrence of *partem*; *manus* (“hands”) for *munus* (“offices”); *vigilans* (“being vigilant”) for *vigili*; *demissisque* (“and with lowered [ropes]”) for *demissoque*; *imo vestibus* (“with the lowest garments”) for *restibus*, although the latter reading is materially uncertain; *conscius* (“aware”) for *suis* (“his own”); *passim* (“everywhere”) for *passu* (“with a step”); and *coram* (“before, in the presence of”) for *eorum* (“of them”).

### SEVENTH OBSERVATION

The remaining verses aim, for the most part, to set forth the method Agnellus followed in composing the *Book of the Pontiffs*.

First, the scholastic opens up the sources from which the historian drank the material of his history. These were chiefly the testimony of elders, in accordance with Moses’ admonition in Deuteronomy 32: “Ask your father, and he will tell you; your elders, and they will say to you.” The earlier verses attempt to explain this. He also used paintings and mosaics, which he diligently investigated, extracting from them not only the likenesses of the bishops but also their names and succession as painted on the wall; and finally, books. He continues in this vein to approximately the sixty-fifth verse.

In the next four verses he briefly summarizes the contents of the whole book, saying that it begins with Aderitus and ends with Petronacius, and that its middle section will contain the lives of forty-four pontiffs. For the bishops between Aderitus and Petronacius themselves make up the number forty-four.

This, then, is what the scholastic believed would happen. But Agnellus added another Life, that of Petronacius’s successor Georgius. Since the Life of Petronacius has been lost, we possess the surviving Life of Georgius, preserved from the injuries of time; this partly compensates for the loss not only of the Life of Petronacius but also of those of Valerius and, in part, Sergius, Leo, John, and Martinus, which we lament as either headless or footless. [Col. 0458B]

If, however, to the forty-four produced by multiplying eleven by four, one adds both terminal figures, namely Aderitus and Petronacius, and also, together with the final Georgius, the first of all, the most holy apostolic man and martyr of Christ, Apollinaris, the complete number of all the Ravennate bishops whose lives Agnellus wrote will be forty-eight.

The verses that follow concern the commendation of Agnellus’s trustworthiness and judgment. Yet Agnellus used little judgment, and when he wrote about matters belonging to the Roman see, he often wrote in bad faith.

He explains what the scholastic had said by means of two comparisons. The first is:

> The eager seeker upon the curved shore  
> Of the earth-bearing Po as it flows back, seeking golden metals.

The Po is praised here because, according to Metrodorus, it not only carries an abundance of pitch at its source, because of a tree called *pades* in Gaul, from which the river takes its name, as Pliny relates in Book III, chapter 16; it also carries with it, when swollen by its waters, a deposit of gold, which it lays down on the shore mixed with sand and mud as it recedes. [Col. 0458C]

The verses quoted prove that this occurred around Ravenna in Agnellus’s time, although in our own time it has either long since ceased or is unknown to occur. The Po is certainly enriched by those rivers whose waters are suited to this activity. To say nothing of the others descending from the mountains of the territories of Modena and Reggio, the not insignificant indications of mines situated in various places around us—and tested even in our own time—prove that they are enriched by deposits of metals and even gold.

The second comparison presents a sailor who, when the sky is calm and everything around him appears safe, happily gives his sails to favorable winds and sits at rest; but when the sea becomes stormy or fear of a hidden reef intrudes, he gathers in his sails, directs the oars, tests the depth with a lead, and ensures that the anchor holds and is fixed in safety. [Col. 0458D]

The scholastic says that the author of this *Book of the Pontiffs* acted in the same way. When much material, and material that was certain, was available to him, he spread out all his sails, so to speak, in a rich and varied discourse. But when he was at a loss—as the proverb says, when the water fails—he fitted together a few words and, speaking with compressed expression, professed at least to say what was plausible.

## BRIEF OBSERVATION

On the verses added to the preceding ones in the same codex.

If anyone wishes to understand the subject or character of the following verses from the prefixed title, he will certainly waste his effort. It is therefore better to leave both the title and the verses to the reader. They are arranged so as to present a dialogue between the Ravennate clergy, who make a request, and Agnellus, who first excuses himself modestly and then accepts upon himself the burden of writing the codex of the *Book of the Pontiffs*. [Col. 0459A]

There is no time to guess what meaning the dactylic verses that follow may have, nor is the matter important enough to delay me from considering the work itself. It is sufficient, therefore, to reproduce the verses themselves with their title.

> Here begins a dactylic six-foot *pempticon*, that is, a thing sent; but first a *detracticum*, then a monastic distich, whose great intentions [lacuna].

> Once, by chance, a crowd of Ravennate priests  
> Came together, among whom there was one  
> Called Andreas. The brothers begged him  
> In humble speech to write his pontifical book.  
> Then he answered them humbly, but with shrewd voice.

**Agnellus:**

> What understanding do I possess, or what learning, that I could  
> With such little sense comprehend the course of eight hundred  
> Years (*vita*; variant *vitam*), or the deeds of those who came before?  
> While I am accustomed, deceiving myself, to face such matters  
> With a confused brow, since all the inward things  
> Seem closed to us in hearing, to uncover them by asking [*petendo*; variant *patendo*, “by opening”].

**The Presbyters:**

> We grieve exceedingly, cruel friend!

**Agnellus:**

> Since I am overcome, then I ask you: pray to the Thunderer,  
> Who turns the stars and restrains the sea’s waters.

Life, swiftly turn your course toward its rising,

And grant me the understanding to write the Pontifical Book.

**The Presbyters:**

Thus, surely, in our great eagerness we shall do it; and since he remains firm in his entreaty,

Let the work answer his words continually;

Although this labor is difficult, nevertheless he undertakes it willingly.

**Agnellus:**

I shall recount the deeds of the pontiffs and the names of those who came before.

**The Presbyters:** [Col. 0460B]

Agnellus once, now Andreas: everlasting greetings.

**Agnellus:**

Greetings, priests, throughout all the ages.

Clear and faithful poems, though small,

Published for you:

Offer them, you who,

With royal inspiration,

Faithfully speak

Praises always

To your friends.

[Col. 0459B]

# AGNELLUS’ PONTIFICAL BOOK (C)

## FIRST PART

Containing the Lives of those who flourished from the time of Saint Apollinaris up to Ecclesius.

## THE PROLOGUE BEGINS

He discloses the sources for writing history and establishes their reliability; he magnifies the difficulty of the work; the author implores divine assistance.

[Col. 0459C]

Since you asked for it, I have arranged this little book concerning the order of the pontifical succession of those pontiffs who nurtured the see of Saint Apollinaris, insofar as the truth and the investigation of your Agnellus—who is Andreas—of that orthodox see of Ravenna, were able to discover and ascertain. It is necessary for me to give thanks to God the Father, and to his Son, and likewise to the Holy Spirit, to the Triune Majesty and single Power, because he has restored me, with my polluted lips, and, insofar as it pleased him, has made my dry tongue eloquent.

For I trust that, through your prayers, God will grant the grace of speech to my words, so that I may recall to memory, insofar as I am able—and because you have compelled me by your words—how each of the holy Fathers, the bishops who preceded one another in the see of the Church of Ravenna, performed his deeds in his own time. I shall disclose to your ears not only what I myself observed of their deeds, but also what I learned by hearsay, which our elders related to me. [Col. 0459D]

For Moses, that most excellent man, wrote the Book of Genesis under God’s inspiration. He himself says: “Ask your fathers, and they will tell you; your elders, and they will say to you”; and Job says: “Ask the former generations, and diligently investigate the memories of your fathers.”

For Moses descended from the stock of Abraham, and it is recorded that, before Abraham was born, the whole structure of this world had been made by God. Mark too, the disciple and baptized son of the apostle Peter, did not follow the Lord’s footsteps bodily, nor did he see any miracles performed by him; rather, he wrote the Gospel as Peter narrated it. Luke, however, the minister of the apostle Peter [Paul], instructed by him in doctrine, opened the source of the Gospel.

Many others too composed books from what they had heard, as is read in the *Lives of the Fathers*: “A certain old man related to me,” and so forth. Did not Gregory, bishop of the Roman Church, report in many passages of his *Dialogues*, saying, “That man or that man related to me,” [Col. 0460D] and the rest?

Yet I cannot possibly claim to be like them. For I confess that, just as a small spark placed in the sight of the sun is overshadowed and its light is not seen, so my page is extinguished [Col. 0461A] before the sight of such great philosophers. How much this is! I can extend these and similar matters in speech, but I spend paper and ink.

For I am like those who are placed in forests or deserts and, seeing dense trees around them, shady and dark places, and impassable thickets of many brambles, do not know which direction to seek or in which to proceed until the entire road has been made and they have emerged from the wilderness. So I too, for this reason, have entered upon the account of the holy pontiffs of this see of Ravenna, as though into the dangers of the sea, and as though a storm from the whole abyss were struggling against me, or the tumult of the blue waves would [perhaps: rage within me]. [Note: [Col. 0461A] Perhaps, “would rage within me.” BACCH.]

Nevertheless, I do not tremble, because through your supplications I have almost [perhaps: forgotten, that is, the danger] [Note: [Col. 0462A] Perhaps, “having forgotten,” that is, “the danger.” BACCH.], and the Lord is with me, who is blessed forever.

Through your charity, let me proceed to the undertaking mentioned above, which I once began at your urging. For some time ago I made known to your ears that I ought to produce something concerning the aforesaid see, about which I had been informed. Perhaps, if I have misled you, forgive me. An exactor ought not to be troublesome when the debtor is about to make repayment.

But in all these things let us bless God the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

**The prologue ends.**

# FIRST CHRONOLOGICAL-HISTORICAL DISSERTATION

Concerning the age of the first twelve bishops, and especially concerning the time of the see of Agapitus, Marcellinus, and Severus, and concerning their succession.

[Col. 0461B]

Nothing is more difficult in ecclesiastical matters than arranging the periods of time that are defined for the earlier centuries. Hence the condition of each Church is such that the age of its ancient bishops can scarcely be assigned within certain limits, their deeds are unknown, and their succession is often confused.

The very distinguished and ancient Church of Ravenna has the good fortune that matters have been handled somewhat more favorably there. Concerning its earlier bishops, Agnellus testifies, on the authority of the elders, to their names, holiness, and order of succession; the rest, as unverified, he conceals in silence.

More recent and highly distinguished men have nevertheless appeared who wished to confine the years of each bishop within definite numbers—apart from several matters committed to writing that were unknown to Agnellus, about which elsewhere—and who have also in some places increased or altered the number and sequence of the most ancient pontiffs. The age and succession of Agapitus, Marcellinus, and Severus have suffered this especially. I therefore thought it worthwhile to illuminate the chronology of the Ravennate pontiffs from Agnellus’s work and from the other documents of established truth, and to determine which matters should be counted uncertain and which probable, if not certain.

Once this has been accomplished, it will give me strength and courage to undertake, successively and as far as my abilities permit, the restoration of the remaining chronology of the Church of Ravenna, arranging similar dissertations in their respective places.

I would have this one point, however, be understood as stated here once and for all, as though repeated everywhere: whenever I am compelled to deny or challenge the statements or opinions of others with arguments, I shall do so while preserving the respect that I wholeheartedly profess toward distinguished writers whose works circumstances will compel me to submit to critical examination.

I would scarcely otherwise have thought of publishing Agnellus, had I not recognized that new light could thereby be brought to history. But this can scarcely be done without repeatedly subjecting to examination matters recently brought to light by later writers. I use the right enjoyed by every writer, when reading the works of others, to approve or reject them. Let others also use their right when reading mine; and if they do so with a sole regard for truth, I shall be grateful.

# CHAPTER ONE [Col. 0461D]

The disagreement between Hieronymus Rubeus and Baronius concerning the question. The arguments of both are set forth. The opinions of Bollandus and his associates. Summary of the statements.

## I

In the earlier edition of his *History of Ravenna*, after relating the death of Bishop Agapitus around the beginning of the reign of Alexander Severus, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of April, Rubeus had added:

“Some believe that, while Constantine and Constans were reigning, around the year of Our Lord 341, Agapitus was bishop under Julius I, Roman pontiff, and sat in the Roman council; but they were deceived because there were several archbishops named Liberius.”

He had placed Marcellinus after him around the two hundred and thirtieth year after the birth of Christ, while Urban was still seated as Roman pontiff, and had said that Marcellinus presided over the Church of Ravenna for forty-seven years. He therefore placed his death around the time when Aurelian, having been raised to the imperial power, began to rage against the Christians.

From this he had derived the beginning of Severus’s episcopate and had placed his death around the beginning of the reigns of Constantine, Constans, and Constantius. He had indeed inserted Liberius as his successor, but added the following:

“There are nevertheless some who place another Archbishop Agapitus after Severus and say that he attended the Roman council celebrated by Julius I, supreme pontiff, together with Benedict of Aquileia, Rufus of Carthage, Julius of Milan, Lucian, bishop of the Moors, and the other one hundred and sixteen bishops. Others place this Agapitus after Liberius. But wherever he is placed, it is established both that he attended that council and that he lived only a very short time in the archbishopric, as did Liberius, who . . . . . after he had died . . . . . received Probus as his successor.”

Rubeus had written these things when Baronius, while publishing notes on the Roman Martyrology and undertaking to refute the asserted date of Severus’s pontificate, attacked the aforementioned writer on the first day of February with arguments substantially as follows.

Since Severus, bishop of Ravenna, is found to have attended and subscribed to the Council of Sardica, held under the consuls Rufinus and Eusebius, as is clear from the acts of that council and from Athanasius’s second *Apology*, if Severus’s episcopate began in the time of Aurelian and Gaius, it follows that he lived as a bishop for at least sixty-four years. For Pope Gaius was created in the year 283, while the Council of Sardica was held in the year 347.

The period of Severus’s see, bounded by these dates, seems excessively long, especially since it includes the dangers of the persecutions. Baronius therefore rejects the claim that Severus succeeded Marcellinus, because the synodal acts show that Agapitus sat in the Roman council under Pope Julius in the fourth year of Constantius and Constans, seven years before the Council of Sardica. This could not have happened if Severus began to hold the see during the reign of the emperor Aurelian and the pontificate of the Roman bishop Gaius.

He adds that, although these facts clearly establish when Severus held the see and which bishop immediately preceded him, they acquire still greater force from the *Life of Severus* cited by Mombritius, in which Severus is said to have been created bishop under the consuls Constantius IV and Constans III.

Finally, he decides that, if it is nevertheless maintained that Severus succeeded Marcellinus, it is necessary either to recognize another person of the same name as Marcellinus or to say that another Marcellinus held the see after Agapitus—something which, he claims, the advocates of the former opinion would not admit.

## II

Thus harassed by Baronius, Rubeus, while preparing a new edition of his *History of Ravenna*, which he published in Venice from the press of Francesco Francisci of Siena in the year 1590, enlarged by more than half, thought that he ought to cling stubbornly to his earlier opinion. To support it and blunt the opposing weapons, he decided to state openly that Severus died on the day he returned from the Council of Sardica, and that Agapitus II succeeded him in due succession.

Having introduced this second Agapitus, and wishing to satisfy the objection concerning the Roman council, he asserted that the council itself had been held after Sardica. He says that he was driven to this opinion for many reasons.

First, according to the unanimous agreement of all Ravennate writers, and also from the paintings of the Ursian church and of the temple now dedicated to the Holy Spirit, it is evident that Archbishop Marcellinus immediately preceded Severus and lived for a sufficiently long time. Therefore, it was not Agapitus but Marcellinus who attended the Roman council.

Moreover, since the council at which Agapitus is remembered to have been present numbered 121 bishops, he argues that it was different from the council that preceded Sardica, which he says consisted of only fifty bishops.

He then turns to the chronological indicators of the same council at which Agapitus was present and relies upon the indiction recorded in the acts as the sixth, which, he says, corresponds only to the year 348. He says that the most reliable method of all for dating public acts is that derived from the indiction, which the Council of Nicaea therefore prescribed should be observed, and which was used not only by Saint Gregory but also by Cassiodorus, who preceded him by a long time, and indeed by Athanasius when recording the dates of the councils of his own age.

He says that Marcellinus Comes, although he writes the consuls, nevertheless places the indiction first, and that the matter appears more certain through this indicator, since the years of emperors and consuls are frequently disputed.

He also turns to another kind of argument, derived from the series of the archbishops of Milan, which he says was arranged by men most learned and well versed in all antiquity. In that series Protasius is placed before Julius. This seems wonderfully to confirm his hypothesis, since Protasius is known to have attended the Council of Sardica with Severus, whereas Julius attended the Roman council held after Sardica with Agapitus.

He therefore believes that, just as Sylvester, after suddenly convening a council at Rome, confirmed the acts of Nicaea, so Julius convened a Roman synod to confirm the Sardican decisions [Col. 0463D] that had recently been issued, by which Athanasius had indeed been acquitted.

He adds that Damasus later did the same after the Council of Constantinople, and that Julius himself praised this custom of the Roman Church in his letter to the Eastern bishops, preserved among Athanasius’s writings. He thinks that Julius’s words concerning Athanasius allude to this, when Julius says: “He was received not only by us but by the entire synod.”

When Rubeus noticed that it could be objected against him that Fortunatianus of Aquileia and Gratus of Carthage are mentioned at the Council of Sardica, although it is known that they survived that council by many years and therefore ought to have attended the alleged Roman council, where Rufus and Benedictus are expressly listed in their place, he met the objection by saying that Gratus is mentioned in the Roman council merely as a bishop, and so could have been bishop of another Church rather than of Carthage.

As for the Fortunatians, he says that there were two bishops of Aquileia named Fortunatianus, with Benedictus occupying the intervening episcopate. Besides this, he asserts that in several ancient and manuscript books not Fortunatianus but Fortunatus is read.

He further says that it is not unusual for two bishops of the same name to have succeeded one another in the same see, citing examples from the series of pontiffs of Rome and of other Churches, where different bishops have been conflated into one because of similarity of name.

Nor, he says, is the Sardican council mentioned in the Roman council, as the Council of Nicaea is, both because mention of it was unnecessary in that place and because the matters treated at Sardica had been taken from the Nicene synod.

As for the age of Severus, which seems to have been extended beyond what is reasonable, he replies that it ought not to seem surprising to anyone who accepts longer lifespans for many other bishops of different sees.

As for those who date the beginning of Severus’s episcopate to the consulship of Constantius IV and Constans III, he says that they speak neither truly nor plausibly. For, if this were admitted, Severus would have lived in the see of Ravenna scarcely one year, since, following Panvinio, he believes that the aforementioned emperors entered that consulship in the year preceding the Council of Sardica, around the middle of that year.

He therefore believes that there were two Agapiti: one who preceded Marcellinus and another who succeeded Severus. He says that this second Agapitus, like his successor Liberius, held the see for a very short time, and that both died while Julius was still alive, “sent into exile,” he says, “by Caesar Constantius.”

## III

Unmoved by these arguments of Rubeus, Baronius, when publishing in Rome in 1594 the third volume of his *Annals*, to the year 337, to which he attached the disputed Roman council under Julius, attacked Rubeus himself with greater effort than before. He says that Rubeus ought to have been privately admonished to correct what he had written in the first edition of his *History of Ravenna*.

He therefore judges that, among the one hundred and sixteen bishops who attended that council, the following should be counted: Benedict of Aquileia, who preceded Fortunatianus; Rufus of Carthage, who succeeded Caecilianus and preceded Gratus; Agapitus of Ravenna, who preceded Severus; and Julius of Milan, who, after Eustorgius, had Protasius as his successor.

He attempts to prove this from the fact that most of the named successors of the celebrated bishops who attended the Roman council are known to have subscribed to the Council of Sardica, and that Gratus subscribed to the later council of Carthage. He also argues from the fact that the sixth indiction was recorded only once during the pontificate of Julius of Rome, in the same year in which the Council of Sardica was held.

He severely reproves Rubeus for relying on the sixth indiction, because that indiction falls in the year 348—which Rubeus himself had conceded—and because the same indiction began in the preceding year, from September, as no one denies to be customary in indictions.

Therefore, since that Roman council is said to have begun on the eighth day before the Kalends of October, it follows that Rubeus must either say that the synod was held in the seventh indiction or, if he continues to defend the sixth indiction, concede that it was held in the sixth indiction of the preceding year, 347.

If he asserts the first alternative, he must withdraw from the chronological indicator that he himself had approved, which is the principal foundation of his opinion. If he asserts the second, he must admit that Agapitus, whom he says was appointed in the year 348 in place of Severus, attended the Roman council in the preceding year, 347.

In that same year he will likewise be compelled to concede that the Sardican and Roman synods were held, at which bishops bearing different names but belonging to the same sees met almost at the same time.

He further says that there was no good reason to doubt the see of Gratus, since the Sardican acts show that the African bishops were subject to him, and that in the following year he presided over the Carthaginian synod, in whose fifth canon mention is made of the Council of Sardica.

He adds that Protasius of Milan was incorrectly placed by Panvinio before Julius. For, contrary to the acts of the Council of Sardica, Panvinio places Dionysius as bishop at that time, preceded by Eustorgius, the successor of Maternus, whose predecessor Protasius had lived in the time of Diocletian.

Finally, he says that it is wrong for Fortunatianus to be called Fortunatus on the basis of some manuscripts. If errors are to be taken into account, he argues, as many bishops would appear to have held office at the same time as there were errors by which the name of the true bishop had been distorted by unskilled copyists.

This is roughly what Baronius says. I do not know whether Rubeus replied to him.

## IV

Bollandus and his associates next laid their hands upon this same rope, each pulling it according to his own purpose, in their outstanding and celebrated work, distinguishing the genuine acts of the saints from the spurious and displaying to the Christian world an incredible abundance of ecclesiastical learning.

They treat the question in various places, but especially on the first day of February, which is devoted to the feast of Saint Severus and also to that of Saint Vincentia, his wife, and Saint Innocentia, his daughter.

After praising the cult of Saint Severus on the basis of manuscript martyrologies, they observe that in the ancient calendars they had seen, the memory of Saint Severus the bishop was recorded on the first day of January, [Col. 0465B] and that in some places one reads: “Saint Severus with his companions.”

They therefore argue that this resulted from confusing Severus the bishop with another martyr of the same name from Ravenna. Rubeus himself, in Book Two, says that this martyr suffered under Maximian Herculeus and that his body was preserved at Orbito, which he says was believed by most people to be the ancient Herbanum. There he accuses Maurolycus of calling this Severus a bishop as well, and Ferretus of identifying him with the other Severus, who was Archbishop Ecclesius’s nephew through his brother.

Bollandus therefore says:

“May it not be permissible to suspect that he was a bishop, but that, since his acts lay hidden, the more celebrated memory of the later confessor Severus was preserved? Yet Ughellus, in the second volume of *Italia Sacra*, sternly declares that it is false to assert that there were several Severuses. We do not indeed assert this, but we do not sufficiently understand by what argument so learned a man supports his severe judgment.

“That there was certainly, from long ago, a widespread opinion that Saint Severus, bishop and martyr of Ravenna, was a celebrated figure will become clear below from the *Life* by Luidolphus. In chapter 2, section 5, a Ravennate monk answers Luidolphus as follows: ‘Severus, whose life you desire to know, was not a martyr but a confessor.’ Therefore Luidolphus had questioned him specifically about a bishop whom he believed to have been a martyr, since the answer fits the question.”

As for the age of the bishop Severus whom we are now discussing, the learned associates believe that it can be determined as follows.

He was created bishop, as stated in one of the two Lives of him that they present—which they judge to have been written in the tenth or eleventh century—in chapter 2, section 6, under the consulship of Constantius IV and Constans III, the Augusti, that is, in the year of Christ 346.

He was consecrated at Rome by Saint Pope Julius, whose tenth year this was. In the following year he attended the Council of Sardica, under the consuls Rufinus and Eusebius, as is clear from the subscriptions.

Finally, he attended the funeral of Saint Geminianus, bishop of Modena, many years later, since Geminianus was still alive in the time of Pope Siricius, who was elevated to the pontificate in the year 385, as they demonstrated on the thirty-first day of January.

They therefore rightly say that Haraeus inferred that Severus died around the year 390.

## V

Having established these points, they expressly attack the arguments of Rubeus. The acts of the alleged Roman council at which Agapitus is said to have been present are dated by three chronological indicators, and two of them contradict Rubeus’s opinion: the year of the emperors corresponds to the year 340, while the consuls correspond to the year 337.

They ask what authority supports most of Rubeus’s assertions. As for his claim that Severus succeeded Marcellinus, they say that it does not follow that Agapitus was not present at the Roman synod or that Marcellinus ought to have attended it:

“For how,” they ask, “is it established that Marcellinus, as Rubeus writes, lived for a sufficiently long time in the episcopate? Agapitus could certainly have died after that first Roman synod under Julius, and Marcellinus, his successor, could likewise have died not long afterward.”

They add other arguments on this matter, saying that there may have been an earlier Marcellinus, succeeded by another Severus, perhaps the martyr Severus mentioned above. They do not, however, consider this necessary in order to establish the age of Saint Severus.

## VI

They make substantially the same arguments on the sixteenth day of March, in their discussion of Saint Agapitus. They accuse Rubeus of gratuitously multiplying the number of Agapiti and of assigning periods of time to the episcopates of the Ravennate bishops without any witness. They assert that these matters will remain uncertain until Rubeus—or Ferretus, whom they say supplied him with the material—produces the evidence for them.

They object to the more recent catalogues and accuse Faber, who agreed with Rubeus on these matters. Nevertheless, they admit that the mosaic work of the Ursian church carries great authority among them, since it places Marcellinus after Agapitus and Severus after Marcellinus.

They say that this can be reconciled even if Marcellinus’s episcopate must be reduced to a few months; alternatively, it could have extended for five, six, or seven years, without prejudice to the Roman council at which Agapitus attended in the year 337.

## VII

The same argument also concerns what they write on the thirty-first day of January, in their treatment of Saint Geminianus, bishop of Modena.

They say that, if the reports concerning Saint Geminianus and the miracle involving Attila are true, there must have been two Geminiani, whom the writer of the Life they present conflated into one.

“The first,” they say, “seems to have been the man who is found to have subscribed through a presbyter to the letter of Ambrose, bishop of Milan, Bassianus of Lodi, and the other bishops assembled at Milan in synod against Jovinianus and his heretical followers, a letter addressed to Pope Siricius and numbered seventh in the first book of Saint Ambrose’s letters:

“‘At the command of the lord Bishop Geminianus, with him present, I, the presbyter Aper, have subscribed.’

“Saint Severus of Ravenna could have attended this man’s funeral, as is reported both here and in the Life of Severus on the first day of February.”

They accuse Rubeus of having incorrectly established the beginning of Saint Severus’s episcopate, though they state the charge cautiously.

They present the Life of Saint Geminianus, which they infer was written after the time of Liutprand, on the basis of the words: “But woe to you, wretched Ravenna, neighbor to the destroyed fleet.”

Yet these very words establish that the writer of that Life lived after the time of our Agnellus. For he copied not only those words but the entire account of Saint Severus caring for the funeral of Saint Geminianus word for word from Agnellus himself, as will be clear to anyone who compares the two accounts.

## VIII

I thought it useful to set forth all these matters concerning this involved question for the benefit of the learned reader, so that the force of the arguments and the grounds of the conjectures might be weighed more easily, and so that, as if in a single view, all that has been more learnedly published up to the present concerning the earliest times and succession of the Ravennate bishops might be known.

Since, however, the responsibility of the undertaking I have assumed also requires me to set forth my own judgment, I shall continue according to this method: I shall weigh the hypothesis of each of the opinions presented in such a way that I do not conceal the difficulties that compel me to depart from them.

Proceeding from there, I shall show that there is one point which certainly ought to have been considered but was not, although nearly the whole hinge of the matter rests upon it. Finally, I shall set forth what I judge must be proposed as a necessary conjecture.

In the meantime, I think it worthwhile briefly to gather into one place the opinions of Rubeus, Baronius, and Bollandus and his associates, which I believe can be reduced to the following summary.

## IX

Rubeus, having defined the age of each bishop within fixed limits, says that, after Agapitus died around the time of Alexander Severus, Marcellinus succeeded him. Marcellinus held the see until the beginning of the reign of the emperor Aurelian and the pontificate of Gaius. Severus’s episcopate therefore began shortly after the Council of Sardica, and he died in the year 348.

Agapitus II succeeded Severus, and Liberius succeeded Agapitus; both, he says, died while Julius was still pontiff.

He says that the Roman council otherwise assigned to the year 337 was held in the year 348, and that Agapitus II attended it.

Baronius maintains that Agapitus immediately preceded Severus and that Severus probably began his episcopate under the consuls Constantius IV and Constans III.

He dates the Roman council at which Agapitus was present to the year 337.

Bollandus and his associates agree with Baronius concerning the beginning of Severus’s episcopate and the date of the Roman council at which Agapitus was present.

They believe that Marcellinus preceded Severus and Agapitus preceded Marcellinus.

They place the death of Severus around the year 390.

They believe that another Severus may have held the see before the time of Agapitus and Marcellinus—namely, the man whom the Church of Ravenna venerates as a martyr—and that this Severus may have succeeded another, earlier Marcellinus.

# CHAPTER TWO [Col. 0467B]

The difficulties in each of the opinions presented. Three bishops alone are insufficient to fill a period of 142 years. The deeds of the ancient bishops were almost unknown to ancient writers. Churches dedicated to saints, and very frequent gatherings of Christians: could these have existed in the time of Aurelian? Agapitus II unknown to all writers before Rubeus. The Roman council incorrectly postponed to the year 348. Marcellinus held the see between Agapitus and Severus. The same difficulty in Bollandus’s opinion. Agnellus asserts that Marcellinus lived a sufficiently long time.

## I

Rubeus’s opinion certainly suffers from several difficulties. Unless he produces the most ancient witnesses for the matter, he will scarcely persuade a sensible reader to believe that a period of nearly 142 years was occupied by only three bishops—Agapitus, Marcellinus, and Severus—especially since the greater part of that period endured savage persecutions, including the persecution under Diocletian, longer and more cruel than the others.

If similar things are related about other genuinely long-lived saints, they are believed when suitable witnesses are produced to support such a matter; otherwise, they are not.

But how could Rubeus, writing in the sixteenth century, have known the period during which each ancient bishop of Ravenna held office, when Agnellus, writing in the ninth century, did not know it? Agnellus therefore supplies the dates only of Saint Apollinaris and, in addition, of a few others whose time was less remote from his own.

He does indicate that some lived to an advanced age, but almost everywhere he refrains from determining the number of years, months, and days.

That this information was unknown in Agnellus’s age is established by the fact that he says everything he relates about Severus was not read by him but reported to him by the elders. From this it is recognized that no written acts of either Severus or his predecessors yet existed at that time, and that the one fact which could be established from records was that one bishop had succeeded another in a definite sequence and that Severus had subscribed to the Council of Sardica.

## II

Another difficulty is added by the fact that a scholar of more refined judgment would much more readily accept the solemnity of the election and the character of the place where it occurred, as described by Agnellus and, following Agnellus, by Rubeus at the beginning of Book Two, if such a history were said to have occurred in the time of Constantine’s sons than if it were reported to have happened under Aurelian or, as in that same place, under Probus or under Carus with his sons Carinus and Numerianus as emperors.

Those who hold that, before the time of Constantine, even when the Church was enjoying relief from persecutions, Christians had places where they assembled for synaxes—but that these places were located in private houses and in upper rooms, which were called by no other name than that of the master of the entire house—will scarcely believe that a temple fortified with three gates was erected and dedicated to Saint Theodore, although I do not approve their opinion.

They say that gatherings were held there with as much frequency as such buildings, which were not sufficiently large, could accommodate, and with the prudent caution that the manner of meeting should not disturb the minds or religion of the pagans.

Therefore, in elections of bishops, it is reasonable that the people came together with the clergy, but only the leading men were admitted, since they were believed able to provide weighty testimony concerning the worthiness of the candidate.

As for the form and public character of temples or churches, those who maintain that no sacred building was anywhere called by the name of a saint gather many arguments from ancient ecclesiastical history, especially from the Titles in Rome of Equitius, Pammachius, Callistus, and Pastor. Just as these names designated the patrimonies of the faithful, so they also designated the places where gatherings were held.

They will therefore expressly cite what Nicholas I wrote to the emperor Michael in Letter 7:

“The Church of the Savior, which was called Constantinian after its founder, was the first that was constructed in the whole world.”

See the learned treatment of this matter by Daniel Papebrochius in his responses to the presentations of errors by Father Sebastian of Saint Paul, Part II.

## III

Anyone who knows that Agapitus II was unknown to all who wrote before Rubeus, and that nothing about him was written or remembered by earlier generations, will also judge that he was invented gratuitously.

Yet, in the familiar phrasing of his first edition of the *History*, Rubeus writes that some say Agapitus succeeded Severus and others that he succeeded Liberius. They will ask him to produce at least one trustworthy person among those “some,” whom he ought to have produced in the second edition of his *History* in answer to Baronius’s criticism, since he had finally decided to subscribe to the opinion of the witness he produced.

## IV

They will scarcely understand how Rubeus could have postponed the Roman council until the year 348, since none of the chronological indicators corresponds to that year among those produced above by Baronius and Bollandus—namely, those by which the circulating acts are said to date that council. These acts contain nothing relating to the Council of Sardica or to the acquittal of Athanasius, but do contain several matters relating to the confirmation of the Nicene synod.

This is of such importance that, because of it, Rubeus’s entire line of reasoning, although ingeniously devised, collapses.

## V

Baronius’s opinion that Severus immediately followed Agapitus scarcely seems capable of being maintained, since the Ravennate paintings and Agnellus’s *Pontifical Book* prove that Marcellinus stood between Agapitus and Severus.

Moreover, if Severus began to hold the see in the year assigned by Baronius and had Agapitus as his immediate predecessor, he will necessarily assign too long a period of episcopate to the preceding bishops, and will thus fall into the very fault with which he accuses Rubeus.

This will occur especially in his assertion that in the year 75 Eleucadius succeeded Aderitus in the episcopate during the time of Vespasian. For from the year 81, the final year of Vespasian, to the year 337, in which he claims Severus was elected, there are exactly 256 years.

If this number is divided by nine—for there were that many Ravennate bishops between Eleucadius and Agapitus—the result is twenty-eight years, five months, and ten days, which means that, by an equal distribution, each of Severus’s predecessors would have lived that long.

This will seem at least as improbable during those times, which were full of persecutions, as the length of the episcopates assigned by Rubeus to Marcellinus and Severus.

## VI

Substantially the same difficulty follows from Bollandus’s opinion, since they recognize that Marcellinus’s tenure of the see can scarcely be extended beyond seven years.

This difficulty could be avoided if it were established that the Severus who was the Ravennate martyr had also been a bishop and had had another Marcellinus as his predecessor. But no suitable witness supports these claims; the authority of the martyrologies cited scarcely suffices to establish an empty conjecture.

It also follows that there can scarcely be doubt about the longer tenure of Marcellinus, and on this matter Rubeus had an excellent witness, although he neglected to cite him: namely, Agnellus, whom we are now illuminating and rescuing from obscurity.

In praising Marcellinus, Agnellus concludes with these words:

“And after the passage of many [or: of a great many] years, he lost both the pontificate and his life.”

Such words would not be said of a man who had completed seven years in the pontificate.

# CHAPTER THREE

Several Roman Councils under Julius. Controversies concerning their number, occasion, and date. The Acts of the earlier Roman synod rejected as spurious by Pagi, Labbe, and the critics. The succession of the bishops of Milan. Julius Firmicus Maternus not a bishop of Milan. Passages from the work *On the Mysteries of Profane Religions* elucidated.

## I

Baronius recognizes three Roman councils celebrated under Pope Julius. The first is this one, which we are now investigating. He says that Julius summoned it so that, at the very beginning of his pontificate, he might confirm the Council of Nicaea, and that it was celebrated in the same year in which the great Constantine died, namely A.D. 337. The second was held in 340, in the case of Athanasius, who had long awaited there the judgment of the bishops and who immediately returned to Alexandria after the council. The third was held in 342, after the Alexandrian disaster and the intrusion of Gregory into that see; for these reasons Athanasius again returned to Rome.

Peter de Marca recognizes another Roman council from fragments of Saint Hilary and from a letter of Hosius to Constantius. He says that it was held two years after the Council of Milan of 347, that is, in 349, in which Photinus, bishop of Sirmium, was condemned. At that council Ursacius and Valens, concerning what they had done at Milan, “assented to the consubstantial faith in a written statement of repentance, and, in letters sent to Athanasius, acknowledged that henceforth they would communicate with him,” as Socrates says in Book II, chapter 19. Sozomen, however, in Book III, chapter 22, while presenting the written statement itself, says that it was given by the aforesaid Ursacius and Valens before the letters to Athanasius were written, when they were journeying together with Theognis to Mareotis. Athanasius also produces the same document in his *Apology II*.

It is not worthwhile here to say anything about this third alleged Roman council. [Col. 0469C] If desired, see Baluze, in the new *Collection of Councils*, p. 27.

The second council asserted by Baronius is disputed by scholars who deny that Athanasius came to Rome twice, as Baronius maintains, and admit that this happened only once, when the Arians, after decreeing his expulsion, had installed Gregory in his place. See the whole matter treated at length by Pagi, from Valesius, under the year 342 in his *Historical-Chronological Criticism of Baronius*.

Others nevertheless maintain that Valesius is mistaken in asserting that the Roman synod—whose existence, they say, is in no way open to controversy—was held in 342. Certain arguments appear to establish that it was held toward the end of 341: Pope Julius explicitly testifies that the bishops were present on the appointed day, while the legates of the Arians were detained until they returned long after the synod had been summoned.

And although Athanasius says in his second *Apology*: “When the synod at Rome had written these things through Julius, the Roman bishop,” and so forth, and although the letter itself was written after the legates’ return, they nevertheless say that the synod entrusted Julius with the task of writing what had been done at the synod and of replying to the earlier letters. Julius later fulfilled this task, replying to the Arians’ letters after both the earlier and later legates had returned.

Otherwise, they add, it would be improbable that the bishops, assembling on the appointed day, should have waited until the following year and only then celebrated the synod after the legates’ arrival.

But, to speak frankly, the matter is exceedingly complicated. For if Athanasius’s arrival at Rome is postponed until Gregory had already been appointed bishop of Alexandria by the Arians, and if Julius’s letters show—and Athanasius himself likewise testifies—that Athanasius waited in Rome for a whole year and six full months, the synod seems not to have been celebrated before the final months of 342.

I know that some hold that nothing concerning Athanasius was done at that synod except to decree that he should rightly be received into communion. But if they deny that the earlier synod took place, they must admit that Julius had already been in communion with Athanasius before such a council. For in their letter to Julius the Arians complained about nothing more than Athanasius’s having been received into communion; Pagi proves this from the passage of Valesius cited above.

But let others judge that question. I have touched on these matters only briefly and in summary, so that it may be clear how controversial are the Roman councils held under Julius at Rome. Consequently, scarcely any certainty can be expected from them for establishing the history of any particular year.

## II

We must now address what is most important in this matter: the earlier Roman synod, which is the foundation of the Baronian view concerning the date on which Agapitus was bishop. Since Rubeus felt himself pressed by it, he found no more suitable course than to transfer it from the year 337, in which Baronius asserts that it was celebrated, to 348.

Bollandus and his associates followed Baronius in this respect and did not think it necessary to investigate the authenticity of that synod. But after seriously weighing the matter, I have thought that, whatever may be said about the synod—which I do not wish to deny was celebrated, since I know that councils were held very frequently in those times, even twice each year according to the Nicene canons—the Acts said to belong to it are nevertheless spurious and unworthy of belief.

Some say, in a marginal note appended to the same work in Labbe’s *Collection of Councils*, vol. II, p. 527, that the document is a patchwork collected here and there by the same Isidore who attached two letters to Julius, and that it was the action which deceived Baronius. Pagi, in the criticism cited above, under A.D. 337, § 8, writes:

> “The Roman synod under Pope Julius is nothing other than a certain patchwork collected by Isidore Mercator from the *Tripartite History* and other sources, and recast in the form of a council. Certainly no mention of it occurs in the synodal document.”

This is why the more recent critics pay it no attention. Among them, Doviatus deserves particular praise for his excellent work *Canonical Preliminary Notices*.

## III

If we now pass from the authority of learned men to the matter itself, it seems evident to me that, if the error in assigning the consuls was considered by Binius such a sign of forgery that, on this ground alone, he rightly judged the letters attributed to Julius in Labbe’s *Collection*, vol. II, pp. 475 and 485, to be illegitimate, then—assuming nothing else were available—this at least makes it impossible not to judge the Acts of this council spurious.

For the same person who tried to present the aforesaid letters as having proceeded from a decree of the synod, relying on the corrupt text of Anastasius, attached to the Acts of the synod and to the letters the same consuls: “Felicianus and Maximianus, most illustrious men, being consuls.”

But if the letters attributed to Julius are considered fictitious on this account, how much more must the Acts of the synod themselves be so considered, since they bear no plausible mark of authenticity! The named college of consuls is found nowhere in the entire series of the *Fasti*. It was therefore just as useless for establishing Baronius’s opinion and assigning the council to the year 337 as was the sixth indiction adopted by Rubeus in order to transfer that same council to 348.

Moreover, as Baronius correctly observes, this would most absurdly make the council appear to have been celebrated in the very year of the Council of Sardica, 347; and from this there would arise a monstrous consequence: in that same year the same sees would have had different bishops subscribing to two councils.

Nor does the fourth year of the reign of the emperors Constantius and Constans stand, since this chronological designation began at the start of the year 340. We know that a council was summoned in that year in the case of Athanasius, but not celebrated, as stated above.

How, then, can we call such Acts legitimate when they cannot in any way be assigned to the years during which Julius was bishop?

## IV

Indeed, when the other monuments of those times are compared with this patchwork, and its dreadful barbarism of thought and style—of which it is full from beginning to end—is recognized, it will clearly appear that nothing in it is genuine.

It is said that Pope Julius spoke to “the holy and apostolic synod of God, gathered in the ancient and venerable city of Rome, by the will and grace of God, consonantly and unanimously in the undivided communion of the Holy Spirit, for the sacred confirmation and correction of our faith and of the immaculate discipline of Christians.”

What could be read that is more dreadful than this? What useful meaning does “the correction of our faith” or “the immaculate discipline of Christians” convey?

After the Creed copied from the Council of Nicaea, the compiler adds:

> “Concerning these things we affirm that they are so and believe that they are so, or even that they formerly were so and were formerly believed so; and that we will stand by this faith unto death, anathematizing every heresy without God.”

A little later those are condemned who “say that the Son of God is capable of free choice, wickedness, and virtue.”

It would be worthwhile to describe the whole work of this foolish man, if it were useful to expose all its barbarisms.

We must now consider the stated reason for this council, which is presented as twofold: first, the confirmation of what the Council of Nicaea had defined concerning the consubstantiality of the Son; second, assistance to oppressed brothers.

The first purpose is fulfilled with sufficient ineptitude. Regarding the second, these few words occur at the end, closing the entire story:

> “And likewise on behalf of us all and of the other oppressed brothers, so that they may be rescued unharmed and preserved immaculate; so that the things which have been well approved may remain firm, through our Lord Jesus Christ, having been done according to the good will, as we believe, of God the Father in the Holy Spirit, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.”

Are these the decreed aids for oppressed brothers?

## V

Baronius bases himself on the first alleged occasion for convening the council: namely, the confirmation of the Acts of the Nicene synod, which Pope Julius supposedly believed had been entrusted to him at the very threshold of his pontificate.

Let this be as the most learned father of the *Annals* wishes: Roman pontiffs may indeed have been accustomed, after convening a synod in the city, to confirm in person councils in which they had participated only through legates because they were far away. Julius may likewise have done this, and may have done it at the time in question.

But the central issue is whether authentic Acts of that council survive. That they do not is shown both by what we have already established and by what we shall add.

Once such Acts fall, nearly the principal argument on which Baronius’s criticism of Rubeus rests also collapses. Rubeus had asserted that during the period in which such a synod was said to have been celebrated, Agapitus had been bishop of Ravenna.

From this preconceived opinion, supported by Baronius’s authority, panic seized all who have written about the succession of the bishops of Ravenna down to the present day. They consequently decided that Agapitus, Severus’s predecessor, must certainly have lived in the year 337, and they adopted various methods to establish this.

Of them all, however, none, in my judgment, went farther astray than Ughellus. Where Rubeus made two Agapiti out of one, Ughellus multiplied them into three, arranging the succession as follows:

> Agapitus, elected in 206, died in 237.  
> Marcellinus, died in 238.  
> Agapitus II, who attended the Roman council in 337.  
> Severus, died in 348.  
> Agapitus III, died in 349.

Thus, although he was scrupulous about multiplying the Severuses—authoritatively declaring anyone who did so to be a liar—he did not fear being accused of falsehood when multiplying the Agapiti, contrary to the faith of the most ancient tradition of the Church of Ravenna and its records.

## VI

Finally, I shall also demonstrate the spuriousness of the Acts examined thus far from the fact that the names of five bishops, among the one hundred and sixteen allegedly listed in them, betray the deception.

Let us grant that, as a matter of honor, the bishops of the most famous churches of Italy were selected for mention: namely, those of Ravenna, Aquileia, and Milan, although it is not established that this was done in other Roman synods. Let us also grant that when bishops subscribe in later centuries, the bishop of Ravenna generally signs first, as we shall see elsewhere. Let us further grant that Rufus of Carthage attended this council.

But why is that Lucian of Mauriana, or Mauritania, listed—a see whose discovery would have required a vain and vexatious disturbance of ecclesiastical geography—and why should one read either “of Mariensis” or “of Maranensis”? Even now, no see of that name is known that could be compared with the other four, although we might suppose that this refers to Saint John of Mauriana in Savoy.

Furthermore, Benedict of Aquileia rests on no other document than one taken from the fabricated council. Ughellus produced nothing else, nor did he learn that anything else could be produced from Dandulus, whom he cites. He shows that he was badly instructed by him when he says that Benedict was made bishop in 332 and governed the Church for twenty years, and immediately adds that Fortunatianus attended the Council of Sardica in 347.

If Benedict, having begun the years of his episcopate in 332, held the see for twenty years, it follows that he died at least in 351. Therefore, in 347 either Fortunatianus was not bishop, or two bishops were occupying the same see at the same time.

That Agapitus was bishop of Ravenna, as the compiler of the alleged council wishes, is so doubtful that it is supported by no certain argument. Perhaps, in order to make the number of bishops correspond to the period between the episcopates of Saint Apollinaris and Saint Severus, it is necessary to measure the years of Marcellinus’s episcopate—whom Agnellus and the Ravennate mosaics, wrongly rejected by Baronius, establish—as more extensive than Bollandus and his associates measured them.

Lucius of Mauriana is altogether either unknown or obscure, together with his see. And although another see is sufficiently famous—namely, Milan—the bishop is nevertheless unknown to the whole of antiquity.

## VII

Papebrochius subjected the ancient catalogue of the bishops of Milan to his customary most careful examination. He prefixed it, together with highly learned observations, to the first volume of the May *Acts of the Saints*, after examining the succession of the bishops of Tongeren.

In the earlier part of that work, he arranges the older series of bishops for the period in dispute as follows:

> Maternus, from 282 to 303.  
> Myrocles, until 315.  
> Eustorgius, until 331.  
> Protasius, until 352.  
> Dionysius, until 362, with the years of exile included in the reckoning.

But the distinguished author demonstrates by evident arguments that the disturbed succession must be restored in this order:

> Myrocles held the see for 22 years.  
> Maternus held the see for 12 years.  
> Protasius held the see for 22 years.  
> Eustorgius held the see for 17 years.  
> Dionysius held the see for 14 years, or 4 years before his exile.

As you see, reader, Papebrochius was not at all intimidated by Baronius’s criticism. Under the year 337 Baronius says:

> “We are certainly astonished that this very man—namely Julius—was omitted by the same author, Panvinio . . . . . . For if the bishops of any ancient Church are sought, those supplied by the Acts of the ancient councils will be more certain.”

This would indeed be so if authentic Acts of that council truly existed; but the case is otherwise, since they are found to have been fabricated.

I know that Baronius inclined toward the opinion that Julius, bishop of Milan, was surnamed Maternus, and that he was the very man whose notable work we possess under the name of Julius Firmicus Maternus, a man of distinguished rank, *On the Mysteries of Profane Religions*.

But apart from the fact that this is proved by no suitable witness, the work itself shows that the author of the commentary was different from the Milanese bishop Maternus. Consequently, the name Julius cannot be attached to him as a second name.

For Baronius could have recognized, from the very passages he quoted from that work, that its author wrote at least in the year of the Council of Sardica, when Protasius was certainly bishop.

Among other passages, he reports from chapter 29 the following words, in which the author addresses Constantius and Constans:

> “In winter—for such a thing has neither ever happened nor will ever happen—you trod the swelling and raging waves of Ocean beneath your oars. The wave of the sea, almost unknown to us by then, trembled, and the Briton was terrified at the emperor’s unexpected face.”

He adds other words from chapter 30:

> “Proud peoples were sent beneath the yoke, and Persian hopes collapsed; nor could cruelty armed with its own evils long stand against you. You both experienced the power of God, though with different outcomes,” and so forth.

Baronius says that these passages ought to be mentioned because, as he claims, they commemorate victories of which no writers make any mention. Since he thinks that this work was written at the beginning of the reign of Constantine the Younger and Constans—although in reality it was written while Constantius and Constans were ruling—he supposes that the victories occurred while their father Constantine was still alive. As evidence of this he produces a coin of Constantine the Younger bearing an Alamannic victory, although it certainly contains nothing that can be related to the Britons or Persians.

## VIII

Maternus, however, is not alluding to just any victory of Constantine the Younger, but to Constans’s British victory, achieved in the depth of winter in the year 343, and to Constantius’s Persian victory, which some, on the basis of the chronicles of Jerome and Idatius, place in 348, while others place it in 345, on the basis of Julian’s first speech to Constantius.

For the former victory Mediobarbus produces two coins from Ducange’s *Christian Constantinople*: one gold and the other bronze. On the reverse of the latter is a trireme with rowers amid the waves; on its prow Victory holds a laurel in her right hand and a palm in her left; at the stern are two military standards; in the middle of the ship is a helmeted emperor, holding a spear in his right hand and a shield in his left. In the waves is a nude figure with the inscription:

> BONONIA OCEANUS

Pagi, in his *Historical-Chronological Criticism* under this year, thinks that Ammianus alludes to the same event in Book XXVII, and Ducange elucidates it in the work cited.

As for the nocturnal battle at Singara and the victory won over the Persians, Julian recounts the matter at greater length in the passage cited. But since he adds that the slaughter of Magnentius occurred “the sixth year after the war” (*ἕκτον μετὰ τὸν πόλεμον ἔτος*), and since this is clearly to be referred to the year 350, marked by the consulship of Sergius and Nigrinianus according to the Chronicle of Idatius, Jacobus Gothofredus took this as a reason, in his *Chronology of the Theodosian Code* and in his notes on the same Code, on law V, to depart from the chronicles of Jerome and Idatius and assign that battle to the year 345. It is certain that in that year the law in question was issued at Nisibis.

Hardouin, in his notes on Themistius’s first speech, and Pagi, in his criticism under the year 345, followed this view.

Ezechiel Spanheim, however, in his notes on Julian’s first speech, after instructing the reader most learnedly about all these matters, honestly observes that Libanius supports the opinion of Petavius and Valesius. The latter indeed thinks that Julian’s text contains an error and that *τρίτον ἔτος* (“the third year”) should be read instead of *ἕκτον ἔτος* (“the sixth year”).

Libanius, in his *Basilicus*, speaks of the matter in such a way as to suggest that the battle had occurred very recently and that the flight of the Parthians, or Persians, had followed it. Accordingly, this battle may appear to have been fought either in 348, according to Idatius, or even in 349, according to Jerome. Gothofredus had assigned the composition of the *Basilicus* to that year in his *Chronology of the Theodosian Code* and in his notes on Book II of that Code, concerning the abduction of virgins; he adds other points that seem to favor this opinion.

## IX

All these considerations wonderfully elucidate the passages quoted from Julius Firmicus Maternus. It is clear that the words “You both experienced the power of God, though with different outcomes” are to be referred, in the case of Constantius, to the Persians who were put to flight at Singara, and, in the case of Constans, to the victory won in Britain.

Just as it appears that this work was written by Maternus before the year 350, in which Constans was killed in Gaul, so it is clear that it was written either after 348, or at least after 345, when that battle and the flight of the Persians occurred while Constans was conducting the war.

Since the author speaks of these victories in such a way as to show—what alone seems truly probable—that they had been won some time earlier, it can scarcely be the case that he wrote the commentary before 348, when Protasius, bishop of Milan, subscribed to the Council of Sardica.

Thus the Maternus who wrote this commentary is different from Maternus, who, according to Papebrochius’s view, was bishop of Milan and predecessor of Protasius. Nor is there any basis for assigning the name Julius to him.

Consequently, for this reason as well, the Acts of the alleged Roman council collapse, together with the argument drawn from them for making Agapitus bishop of Ravenna in 337, immediately before Severus, as Baronius claims.

# CHAPTER FOUR

Severus’s age established from the *Life of Geminianus*. No necessity for multiplying the Agapiti or Severuses. The succession of the bishops of Ravenna certain, the rest obscure. Agnellus’s reliability and sincerity.

## I

First of all, I believe that there can be no doubt whatever about the age of Severus. For the Acts establish that he outlived the death of Saint Geminianus of Modena.

It is true that one should properly say that, through the intercessions of that same Geminianus, who had already been translated to heaven, the eyes of another Geminianus were so dazzled when Attila passed through Modena that he did not see the place where he was. This event was wrongly attributed to Geminianus himself, the earlier saint, while he was still alive, contrary to the chronology.

Nevertheless, there is no reason to doubt the account concerning Saint Severus, who attended the funeral of Saint Geminianus. Agnellus explicitly transmits it from the tradition of his ancestors; the author who composed the *Life of Saint Geminianus* copied it word for word from Agnellus. There is no basis on which anyone could deny it except Rubeus’s preconceived opinion.

Severus, therefore, according to the evidence presented above in chapter 3, no. 6, extended his life until the year 390.

## II

It consequently seems reasonable that he began to serve as bishop in 346, as the aforementioned Bollandus and his associates thought. Otherwise, someone who died in the aforesaid year 390 would have extended his life and episcopate beyond what is credible.

## III

It is clear, however, that we are compelled by no necessity either to multiply the Agapiti, as Rubeus and Ughellus did, followed by others, or to compress Marcellinus’s episcopate into five, six, or seven years. Agnellus, as we have shown, says that Marcellinus died after the passage of a very long period of time.

Nor are we compelled to multiply other Severuses or Marcellinuses.

Moreover, in this matter the *Pontifical Book* of Agnellus should possess the highest authority, along with the mosaic work of the Ursian basilica. For we know that in ancient times the succession and names of the pontiffs were sufficiently known from the diptychs, in which they were recited in order during the solemn celebration of Mass.

It is reasonable that Agnellus, or the elders who supplied him with information, collected the succession of the bishops of Ravenna from these diptychs—or from the Ursian church, where he says elsewhere that he was brought up from childhood.

I therefore consider it exceedingly dangerous to depart from Agnellus and to place oneself in the position of asserting things for which there is altogether no evidence.

## IV

Just as I believe that the succession of the bishops of Ravenna is sufficiently and more than sufficiently established, so I see that there are no arguments by which the dates of those who sat before Severus can be fixed within probable limits.

Since the diptychs contained nothing but the bare names, even of those who had been crowned with martyrdom, nothing concerning their Acts and nothing concerning their ages reached Agnellus’s knowledge.

For the epitaphs with which he defined the life of each one he generally composed from mere probabilities. He sincerely admits this himself below, in the *Life of Saint Exuperantius*, chapter XIX.
