Nevertheless, he believed that in doing so he had not lied at all, because, he says, those bishops about whom he found nothing had been exhorters, chaste men, and givers of alms who won human souls for God.

Nor, therefore, did those who copied the same epitaphs from Agnellus lie. Yet they departed from the reliability of history when they assigned the number of years each bishop had held the episcopate, something Agnellus did not do.

These are the matters I thought should be noted and discussed, so that the preconceived opinion concerning the Acts of the Roman synod might be removed—a preconceived opinion on account of which otherwise highly learned men wished to overturn and completely reverse the succession of the bishops of Ravenna.

# BRIEF NOTICE

Concerning the verses prefixed to the *Life of Saint Apollinaris*.

[Col. 0475]

I thought that these verses should by no means be omitted. Anyone who reads only them will find them alien to Agnellus’s style, although their corrupt Latinity and remarkable hyperbaton in syntax show that they belong to the same period, or to one only slightly later.

It should also be added that they relate that Boniface of Classe recovered his sight through the aid of Saint Apollinaris, of whom Agnellus says nothing. The earlier verses likewise say that Tecla was freed from illness, whereas Agnellus omits her and instead asserts that an unnamed blind son of Hereneus received sight.

The meaning of the first word of the seventh hexameter, “Plamone,” is obscure. Since, however, the verse lacks a syllable for completeness, and since we know that the river Lamone flowed not far from the city of Ravenna into the Padusa, it seems that the copyist should have placed the letter P by itself. Marked with a transverse line, it would, according to the custom of the age, have expressed in abbreviated form the preposition *post*, indicating time. The sense would then be: “After this, at the Lamone,” that is, at the river Lamone, Saint Apollinaris was crowned with martyrdom.

In the following hexameter the same particle, *post*, appears with the same meaning. From this it would follow, according to the author’s intention, that the place where Saint Apollinaris died was at the river Lamone. Others commonly place it outside Classe, toward a village known by the name of the Lepers.

> Here begins [Begin] the verse(s) of metre [metrical], and the designation (*pronomen*)  
>   
> “of blessed Apollinaris” is likewise read.
>
> The gracious (*almis*; *almus*, Bacch.) apostle and steadfast chief of the others,  
> Whom he taught as a disciple by holy admonitions,
>
> Giving to each the supreme seat of bishops—Ravenna—  
> And sending the people rightly to call upon God.
>
> He gave light to the bereft and raised Tecla,  
> Who had long lain sick in her limbs upon her bed.
>
> Joyful, he [so the text] came to the lofty Capitol;  
> In the Lord’s name he overthrew the demonic throngs.
>
> Breaking the snares of greedy death, he restored  
> Rufus’s daughter to life through the Lord.
>
> Through God [the Lord] he restored the gift of light, by [his] tongue,  
> To the Classensian whose name is Boniface.
>
> Crowned with martyrdom at Plamone [perhaps *P. Lamone*].  
> Before this he endured many wounds from scourging.
>
> At heaven’s summons calling him back, thereafter his spirit seeks  
> The heavenly assembly and angelic choirs.
>
> No one, however capable, can comprehend his merit [or: metre].  
> I humbly ask that this not be displeasing.
>
> But, undertaking a journey through *set* [Bacch.: *iter prenset*], through passable places,  
> May he direct his steps and, rejoicing, keep peace with me [or, idem: “may peace be borne”].
>
> The metre—pentameter and hexameter—ends; whoever cannot understand it should turn it into prose.

# LIFE OF SAINT APOLLINARIS

## CHAPTER ONE

Saint Apollinaris’s homeland, worship, and ordination. He comes to Ravenna, preaches the faith of Christ, and performs miracles. The conversion of the patrician Rufus and his tomb.

Saint Apollinaris, an Antiochene by nationality, learned in Greek and Latin letters, a disciple of the apostle Peter, came with him to the city of Rome. After a very long time Peter ordained him bishop and, through the laying on of hands, gave him the Holy Spirit and bestowed a kiss upon him. From the city of Rome he traveled with him for about thirty miles.

There stands the monastery of blessed Peter called “at the Janiculum,” where the apostle prayed to Christ. When he placed his knee there, a stone appeared as soft as wax before a fire, and a hollow was made in the stone in the shape of his knee.

They likewise slept together that night at another monastery of the same apostle called “at the Elm.” In that stone there appear hollows where their heads, backs, buttocks, and legs rested, and they remain there to this day.

Afterward Peter sent him on to Ravenna. Before the most blessed man entered the city of Ravenna, he gave sight to the blind son of Hereneus. For Hereneus is understood to mean “peaceful,” and outside [variant: inside] this city he performed very many miracles.

He overturned the temples of the gods and shattered their images; he ordained priests and deacons; he healed the sick; he drove out demons; he cleansed lepers; and in the river Bedente and in the sea he baptized many people.

He first performed a baptism in the basilica of blessed Euphemia, which is called “at the Ram.” Where he stood with his feet, the stone melted, and footprints were impressed in it like a mark.

He also raised from the dead the daughter of the patrician Rufus. In the patrician’s house we see to this present day the episcopal residence of the Church of Bologna. The house remains intact and unharmed, just as it was in ancient times.

Only about five years ago, Theodoric, bishop of Bologna, removed the stone coffin in which the patrician Rufus had been placed with his daughter and carried it to his church at Bologna, intending to be buried there after his death.

But what did this accomplish for him? He expelled others from it, and he himself was not placed in it, for he was too slow to have it firmly installed.

## CHAPTER TWO

Saint Apollinaris’s imprisonment, exile, deeds after his return, and martyrdom.

The most blessed Apollinaris was therefore cast into prison under a great weight of iron, not far from the Capitol of this city of Ravenna. While the guards watched around him, angels ministered heavenly food to him.

Again they seized him and expelled him from the city, not far from the sixth milestone, where the ancient church of blessed Demetrius was built.

After this he was led captive into the regions of Illyria. Then, through Salona, Pannonia, along the bank of the Danube, and through Thrace, and there on the shore of Corinth, the Lord performed many miracles through him.

Having returned [variant: Again], after three years he came back to Ravenna. His faithful sons and priests received him with great joy.

The enraged pagans later beat him severely, made him stand barefoot upon burning coals, and inflicted many other tortures upon him.

By his prayers he demolished the temple of Apollo, which stood before the gate called the Golden Gate, beside the amphitheater.

Such was his blessedness and gentleness that, while he was suffering, he never injured or rebuked anyone—except when he was being cruelly tortured, when he said to the vicar:

> “Most impious man, why do you not believe in the Son of God, so that you may escape eternal torments?”

Because of the great fullness of his days, he became bent with age.

He was crowned with martyrdom in the time of Caesar Vespasian. He lived on the episcopal throne for twenty-eight years, one month, and four days.

# OBSERVATIONS ON THE LIFE OF SAINT APOLLINARIS

Pseudo-Dexter and Bivarius refuted. Churches mentioned by prolepsis. The Bedente River. Certain dedications of churches to Saint Apollinaris later than his age. The Ravennate patrician Rufus distinct from his namesake, the bishop and martyr of Capua. The Capitol of Ravenna. The inventions of later writers disproved. The time when Saint Apollinaris was crowned with martyrdom. His encomium from an ancient martyrology.

## I

The first matter worthy of observation is that, among the things which Agnellus neither read nor heard from his elders, is the very claim that Bivarius, the defender and commentator of the Pseudo-Dexter fabrications, attempts to establish from Metaphrastes under the first year.

Peter says:

> “When he had not remained long among the Romans—only three or four years, that is—and had ordained Linus bishop, as his suffragan or co-bishop, and so forth . . . . . . . . . . in the forty-seventh year, or at the beginning of the fortieth, he left Rome for Jerusalem, accompanied by Mark, Marcellus, Eugenius, Epaphroditus, Epaenetus, Rufus, Crescens, and others. With these companions, Peter, passing through Ravenna, took Apollinaris with him and finally reached Jerusalem, where that year he attended the Assumption of the Virgin and, in the following year, held a council concerning the non-observance of the legal prescriptions by converts from paganism.”

This, together with what follows, is intended—if God so wills—to support the fables of Pseudo-Dexter, who writes under the first year:

> “Peter, as Christ’s vicar, went to the Spains; he brought images from Antioch; he left Epaenetus of Sexifrim in Baetica, accompanied by many bishops—Mark, Marcellus, Eugenius, and Apollinaris of Ravenna. On his return to Italy Calocerus, Barnabas, and Judas followed him. From there he proceeded to Africa and Egypt.”

Agnellus knew nothing of this, nor did the Ravennates who were Agnellus’s elders, including Archbishop Maximianus, from whose histories Agnellus would have drawn such highly celebrated deeds.

To omit the other considerations that destroy such devices, it is amusing to observe Bivarius’s clever argument. He attempts to prove that Apollinaris first traveled with Peter to Jerusalem and then to Spain on the ground that, according to Metaphrastes’s account, Peter left Rome to go to Jerusalem—as though, in order to complete that journey, he had to pass through Ravenna, and on that occasion take Apollinaris as his companion.

If he had instead said that Peter came to Ravenna precisely to associate Apollinaris with himself, what statement would have been less contrary to the logic of the journey?

But why did Peter not rather summon him so that they might leave Rome together, either by sea from the ports of Ostia, Antium, or Tarracina, or by the same route by which they had come, traveling along the Appian Way as far as Puteoli?

Metaphrastes, as quoted by Surius and misused by Bivarius, says:

> “When he had not remained long among the Romans . . . he came to Tarracina . . . he came to Sirmium, a city of Spain . . . he came to Carthage, a city of Africa . . . to Egypt . . . . . . again to Jerusalem,” and so forth.

This journey is entirely different from Bivarius’s account. The fabrication reveals itself everywhere.

Agnellus reports that Peter, when coming from Antioch to Rome, brought Apollinaris with him, “whom after a very long time he ordained bishop,” and sent him to Ravenna.

He therefore means that Peter did not do this immediately after arriving at Rome. It would necessarily have happened immediately if Peter had not remained long at Rome, but had set out for Jerusalem and, passing through Ravenna, taken Apollinaris—already ordained and already sent—as his companion.

Thus, having once been unwillingly expelled from the Church of Ravenna, he remained away, as will be explained below.

## II.

As Apollinaris was leaving Rome, he relates that he joined Peter as his companion for nearly thirty miles. Along the road he marks the point from which they departed—namely, the Janiculum—and another place where they spent the night, which he calls *ad Ulmum*. At both places he records impressions in the flint: those of Peter praying and of the two men sleeping. He also records monasteries later dedicated there, by a kind of anticipation, to the honor of Peter, the prince of the apostles; by the name “monasteries,” which is familiar to him, he understands private oratories. Thus, indeed, Agnellus’s account should be understood.

Now, just as no one doubts that Peter stopped and prayed at the Janiculum in Rome, and that basilicas were later dedicated to him there after peace had been granted to the Church, so it is extremely difficult to discover from itineraries and maps a station at *ad Ulmum*, thirty miles distant from Rome, although the testimony of Agnellus confirms that a church dedicated to Saint Peter existed there in his own time. If they proceeded along the Via Flaminia, as is reasonable, the calculation of the miles may suggest that such a stopping-place and church existed near Ocriculum.

## III.

He relates that light was restored to the blind son of Hereneus; he is silent about Thecla’s deliverance from illness and about the conversion of the tribune to the faith of Christ, which later writers affirm on Agnellus’s authority. It may be believed that these and other signs are meant by the concluding statement, “He performed very many miracles,” and so with the other statement, “He ordained presbyters and deacons,” he understands what he will later relate in the Lives of the succeeding pontiffs.

Moreover, when he says, “In the Bedens River and in the sea he baptized many,” he shows that one river was called by that name. Later writers call it the Montone, just as Rubeus—who will shortly be cited—observed that it was also called the Arietes, since these names correspond approximately with the Italian meaning of *Montone*, and with the words *aries* (“ram”) and *bedens*, or *bidens* (“two-toothed”).

Faber also testifies that the same river was called the Vervecis, in the first part of his account of the church of Saint Euphemia. Rubeus, in the 1590 edition, testifies that another river was called by the inhabitants the Bedens, and elsewhere is designated by the name Ronchi; this is believed to be the river mentioned in the *Lives of the Ancients*.

Rubeus says the following in Book I:

> They say that the first baptismal font in that part of the city which was called “at the Ram,” taking its name from the river near which it lies—the river which we now call by the common name Montone—was established in the house of the tribune himself, which he made into a temple and consecrated.

As for Rubeus’s final assertion, Agnellus has this:

> In the basilica of blessed Euphemia, which is called “at the Ram,” he first administered baptism.

Rubeus says that after his return Apollinaris dedicated to Saint Euphemia the same building that had previously been a temple, after he had learned from Hermacora, bishop of Aquileia and a disciple of Saint Mark, about the worship and sacred relics of the virgin and martyr, who had suffered shortly before, and had brought them back.

Rubeus derives this from the Acts of Saint Hermacora; Peter, in the *Catalogue*, Book VIII, chapter 29, derives it from the same source, as Baronius observes under 3 September; and Faber derives his account of the church of Saint Euphemia from Rubeus. Yet, however the Acts may stand in every respect, and although Saint Apollinaris may have brought the body of that same holy virgin and martyr to Ravenna, no one will persuade me that a temple or basilica was constructed at that time, since it is well known that Apollinaris must have conducted the sacred rites elsewhere, in huts and private houses.

Agnellus, however, identifies the place where the faithful were first baptized and intends, as is his custom, to indicate that a church was erected there after the passage of time—and nothing more.

## IV.

What follows concerning the patrician Rufus deserves the closest attention. For now that Agnellus has at last been rescued from obscurity, it is established that Rufus the patrician died at Ravenna and was buried there with his daughter, once recalled from the dead by Apollinaris, in a marble sarcophagus. Theodoric, bishop of Bologna, removed Rufus and his daughter from it and transported the sarcophagus to Bologna, while Agnellus was himself present and alive, so that, having adapted it, he might prepare a tomb for himself.

It follows, therefore, that this Rufus was different from the Rufus who until now has been believed to be the same person as the man whom the prince of the apostles, Peter, is said to have consecrated bishop of Capua, and who during that period died at Capua crowned with martyrdom.

Rufus, bishop of Capua, was not a Roman patrician, but perhaps the very man whom Baronius observes Epiphanius to have numbered among the seventy disciples of Christ, and whom he lists among the companions of Peter when Peter came to Rome in the forty-fourth year. Baronius says that this man had already become bishop of Capua, although Apollinaris, Peter’s companion on the same journey, had not yet been sent to Ravenna as bishop.

It is truly astonishing that Baronius, who examined matters of this kind with such learning, should have failed to perceive this, so that in the Martyrology under 27 August he did not correct the confusion caused by the similarity of the name of this Rufus with the other. Yet Baronius may in some measure be excused, since Agnellus did not provide him with a torch in this matter. Rubeus, however, deserves no excuse: he read Agnellus, transferred better material into his own history, and nevertheless says that Rufus was not only converted from paganism to the faith but—something quite unheard of—that while Peter was alive he was made bishop of Capua by that same Apollinaris. He connects this with the martyrdom of Apollinaris narrated below, saying that it occurred

> shortly after Rufus, his disciple, had been killed at Capua for the religion of Christ, while he was bishop of that city.

The Baronius cited above, in his notes on the Martyrology under 27 August, says:

> He is treated in the Acts of Saint Apollinaris, which Surius recites in volume IV under 23 July; from there the others also took their accounts, including Peter in the *Catalogue*, Book VII, chapter 119; Hieronymus Rubeus, *History of Ravenna*, Book I; and others.

But in Surius there is nothing about a Capuan episcopate and nothing about the martyrdom of Rufus. Therefore each of the earlier writers confused one Rufus with the other, considering only the name and chronological coincidence; they did not regard Surius as the authority for this matter.

Faber, in the *Sacred Memoirs of Ravenna*, says that there was a third Capuan bishop named Rufus, who was converted to the faith at Ravenna. If this were true, he would not be the Rufus whom Peter brought from the regions of the East into Italy and made the first bishop of Capua; in this matter Ughelli is not entirely his supporter. Ughelli places Priscus first and Sinotus second, but adds that nothing is found concerning him in the ancient diptychs, and that Michael the monk was the first to assert this from a certain Capuan mosaic.

Then, speaking of Rufus in third place, he explicitly affirms that Rufus governed the see second. The monk himself, as Ughelli likewise observes, recognizes two Rufuses: one, he says, was bishop of Thebes and the other bishop of Capua.

Whatever may be made of these matters, Agnellus nevertheless shows that Rufus—whether the third or the second bishop of Capua—was entirely different from the patrician Rufus buried at Ravenna with his daughter in the same sarcophagus. The house of the latter continued to exist in Agnellus’s time and was used as an episcopal residence by the bishops of Bologna when they were staying at Ravenna with their metropolitan.

The oldest Martyrologies published by Papebrochius, which will be discussed below, have under 27 August:

> At Capua, the natal day of Saint Rufus the martyr.

But here too Ughelli must be corrected in his list of the bishops of Bologna. Where, in the thirty-eighth place, he names Theodore, who lived in the year 855, he must insert Theodoric before Christopher; from this passage of Agnellus it follows that Theodoric died around the year 825, as stated above in the notes prefixed to this work.

## V.

The Capitolium at Ravenna is mentioned by all who wrote the Acts of Saint Apollinaris. Agnellus, however, does not say that Apollinaris was brought by the magistrates to the Capitolium to sacrifice to Jupiter, as Rubeus says in the same book; he says only that Apollinaris was sent to prison not far from the Capitolium.

The prisons situated near the Capitolium, as well as the Capitolium itself, the golden milestone, and other features, show Ravenna to have rivaled Rome in grandeur. Ricquius nevertheless observed that it was customary for the most celebrated cities to possess a Capitolium, in his *Commentary on the Roman Capitolium*, chapter 47, throughout. In chapter 45 he had argued with Baronius concerning the true location of the Mamertine and Tullian prisons, one or the other of which the prison at Ravenna imitated.

## VI.

There is profound silence among Ravenna’s historians concerning the church of Saint Demetrius, six miles from the city. I believe that it was founded and survived into Agnellus’s time after peace had been granted to the Church under Constantine, at the place from which Apollinaris was cast out by the pagans.

Agnellus adds that Apollinaris was led captive into the regions of Illyria, and from there travelled along the bank of the Danube through Pannonia and Thrace, illuminating those places with miracles. He omits the remaining matters asserted by later writers, or concludes them with a general statement.

I do not, however, believe that this should be understood of the revolt which later writers claim was stirred up by Christians against Messalinus and the pagans, in which they say that Apollinaris recorded two hundred of the latter killed by the former—a story rightly rejected by Rubeus. For it is contrary to the gentleness of the early Christians. Accordingly, with good reason, both on this account and for a similar reason, the most learned Papebrochius found an argument for rejecting, among other things, the recent inventions of the Brescia Martyrology.

## VII.

Agnellus does not specify the kind of martyrdom by which Apollinaris was finally crowned and died, nor does the author of the verses prefixed to the Life. There is no mention of Taurus’s conversion or of the assistance he rendered to Apollinaris, whom he sheltered on his suburban estate.

Agnellus nevertheless identifies him as crowned with martyrdom during the reign of the emperor Vespasian, and gives the length of his episcopate as twenty-eight years, one month, and four days. Later writers expand this into a full twenty-nine years and, with Rubeus in Book I, assert that he died in the year 80 of the Christian era, on the tenth day before the Kalends of Sextilis.

Baronius, under the year 75, discussing the succession of Eleucadius after Aderitus and having quoted the words of Saint Peter Damian, who measures the martyrdom—or episcopate—by a period of twenty-nine years, briefly repeats what Rubeus had related about rescripts extorted from Vespasian against Apollinaris.

Yet he must depart from Rubeus concerning the year of the martyrdom. Assigning one year to the pontificate of Aderitus, he should place it at the year 74, as Faber did, following Baronius in his conjecture. How different Rubeus is from these writers, postponing the pontificate of Aderitus to the year 100!

Everything is obscure. Nevertheless, Agnellus in no way supports the opinion that fixes Apollinaris’s death in the year 74. Agnellus says that Apollinaris came to Rome with the apostle Peter and, after a very long time, was ordained bishop and sent to Ravenna. If Peter came to Rome in the year 43 of the common era and Apollinaris died in the year 74, Apollinaris must have been sent in the second year of Peter’s pontificate. But this does not agree with Agnellus, who says that he was sent after a very long time had passed since Peter’s arrival in Rome.

That Apollinaris’s episcopate lasted longer is suggested by the fact that, when near his martyrdom, he walked “bent over because of the excessive fullness of his days.” Since the stricter chronological tables show that Vespasian died in the common year 79, it would be wrong to place Apollinaris’s martyrdom after that year, as Rubeus does. I think it more correct to place the death of Saint Apollinaris around the year of Vespasian’s death. Since, however, Suetonius says that Vespasian died on the eighth day before the Kalends of July, Apollinaris’s death could have occurred only in the preceding year.

If this chronological calculation is accepted, the beginning of Apollinaris’s episcopate will be fixed by counting backward, while preserving the date on which his natal day is marked in all the oldest Martyrologies: 23 July—19 June in the year 50 of the common era.

Since the Martyrologies have now been mentioned, it is appropriate to bring forward, as a conclusion to these remarks, what the oldest Martyrology attributed to Bede says about Saint Apollinaris. It was brought to light by the distinguished Daniel Papebrochius and prefixed to the first volume of March, together with additions successively made by different hands and recovered from the repositories of celebrated libraries. From it will be evident how closely the ancient monuments agree with Agnellus’s simplicity; and although they all agree that Apollinaris was crowned with martyrdom under Vespasian, these ancient documents nevertheless conflict greatly in assigning the years of his episcopate.

The Martyrology cited above has the following under the tenth day before the Kalends of August:

> The natal day of Saint Apollinaris, bishop, at Ravenna. He was ordained at Rome by the apostle Peter and sent there; he also preached in Emilia, in the regions of Corinth [D.: *Thorithiorum*; perhaps *Carinthiorum* (“the Carinthians”). BACCH.], in Mysia, and on the bank of the Danube, and in the regions of Tarachia [T. L.: *Thraciae* (“Thrace”); Tornacense and Letiense. BACCH.], in which places he was sent into exile. Wherever he was able, he performed innumerable miracles and endured sufferings. For he was slaughtered with excessive bloodshed, and again for a long time was placed upon burning coals and beaten with rods; he was hung upon the rack and stretched, his mouth was crushed with a stone, and he was shut in a terrible prison with a very heavy iron weight; he was stretched upon wood, where, neglected by men, he was publicly fed by an angel. Then he was chained and sent into exile; there again he was beaten with rods for a long time, and again, bound at Ravenna, he was beaten and wounded by pagans, then again sent to prison and beaten. Thus he completed his martyrdom under the emperor Vespasian and the patrician Demosthenes. He governed the Church for twenty years and eight days.

Thus the D. manuscript reads. But the Barbarinian, Saint Cyriac’s, Arras, and Tournai manuscripts have twenty-eight years and four days; the Vatican manuscript, thirty-eight years; and the Liège manuscript, eighteen years and four days.

Although the stated measure of years is expressed differently in different manuscripts, you nevertheless see that Agnellus’s assertion is confirmed by several of them. Therefore, just as the copyist of the Vatican manuscript could easily have written thirty for twenty, so the D. manuscript and the Liège manuscript scarcely deserve consideration, since the others disagree with them and Agnellus may have relied upon more reliable documents than those who wrote the Martyrologies far from Ravenna. Moreover, in the Liège manuscript the numeral X could easily have fallen out.

# LIFE OF SAINT ADERITUS

## Chapter One

### The ordination and preaching of Aderitus. His uncertain tomb.

Aderitus I, a holy and devout man, was ordained presbyter by the most blessed Apollinaris. Like a wise architect, he built upon the foundation of his master and teacher. He incessantly entreated God on behalf of his sheep, that they might abandon the worship of idols and confess the living God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. In his time many received baptism after the storm of persecution.

Afterward he brought many into fellowship with God. He died in the city of Classis, as some say, on the last day before the Kalends of October. He was buried in the basilica of blessed Probus, not far from the Church of Saint Apollinaris, about one stade away.

He held the see for . . . years, . . . months, and . . . days.

## OBSERVATIONS ON THE LIFE OF SAINT ADERITUS

With Rubeus, the others extend Aderitus’s episcopate to the common year 100. It may be argued that Aderitus prolonged his life into the time of Trajan because the text says that after the storm of persecution he initiated many people through baptism. This must be understood of the period following the persecution of Domitian; Aderitus therefore survived him by several years.

Accordingly, since Domitian died in the year 96, I have no objection to supposing that Aderitus, during the sufficiently brief and peaceful reign of the emperor Nerva, diligently devoted himself to converting the pagans, and that at the beginning of Trajan’s reign, around the Christian year 100, he passed to the better life, after having held the see of Ravenna for more than twenty years.

The observations that will be made on the subsequent Lives will contribute something toward illustrating the Acts of Aderitus.

# LIFE OF SAINT ELEUCADIUS

## Chapter One

### The name, ordination, wisdom, and writings of Saint Eleucadius. His tomb.

Eleucadius II, whose name is understood in Latin as “Candidus” (“Bright” or “White”), was gentle and prudent, and the most holy Apollinaris consecrated him a deacon. His philosophical learning was so great that he composed many books on the Old and New Testaments and wrote volumes on the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ and on his passion. Hence, in the passion of Apollinaris, the athlete of Christ, we read: “He made Eleucadius the philosopher a deacon.”

He truly preached to the nations and, anointed with the oil of piety in his Church, shone like the light of a lamp. He died on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of March and was buried outside the walls of Classis. There, even to this day, a church has been built and consecrated to God in honor of his name.

He held the see for . . . years, . . . months, and . . . days.

## OBSERVATIONS ON THE LIFE OF SAINT ELEUCADIUS

*The Acts of Saint Apollinaris existed in Agnellus’s time. The body of Saint Eleucadius was not transferred to Pavia. Saint Eleucadius should be numbered among the apostolic ecclesiastical writers.*

### I.

The first point that seems especially worth noting is that the Acts of the passion of Saint Apollinaris certainly existed in Agnellus’s time. From them he took what he related above about Apollinaris, and he would have said more if he had read more.

There is no room for doubt that Agnellus’s account rests upon reliable testimony: above all, that Eleucadius, originally a pagan philosopher, was converted to the faith of Christ and honored with the office of deacon by Apollinaris.

Saint Peter Damian, in his sermon on this Eleucadius, says only what he had learned from Agnellus, as becomes clear to anyone who reads the entire sermon; the rest belongs to later writers.

### II.

The chief point, however, is what Rubeus reports on the authority of a certain book of the Church of Saint Michael at Pavia. He says that the following can be read there:

> On the right-hand side, in the corner of the same temple, is the body of Saint Eleucadius, archbishop of Ravenna. Because he was an exceedingly skilled philosopher and most zealously opposed the faith of Christ, he was at last overcome and converted by blessed Apollinaris, disciple of Peter, prince of the apostles and heavenly key-bearer. After his conversion he wrote and argued wondrously concerning the faith of Christ, so that in his own time he was called “the terror of heretics.” He was also the first in Italy to establish solemnly both the nocturnal and diurnal office, distinguishing the books of the New and Old Testaments, as they are read today throughout the Church at Matins. His body was transferred here from Ravenna by the most Christian emperor Constantine, son of Saint Helena, who founded this basilica in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 325, on account of the glorious triumph he then obtained over the Gauls, who did not respect the empire, through the prayers of the standard-bearer Saint Michael.

Bollandus and Henschenius also report these statements from Rubeus under 14 February. After examining the matter, they add the words of Carlo Sigonio, *On the Western Empire*, Book III, under the year 314, concerning the temple of Saint Michael at Pavia built by Constantine and the body of Saint Eleucadius transferred there.

They further add the same account, given together with Sigonio by Stefano Breventano in Book IV of his *History of Pavia*, although Breventano gives the year as 325 rather than 314. They also add Spelta, in his account of Thomas, bishop of Pavia, confirming what was said about the church constructed by Constantine; Saccus, who asserts only that the temple was built before the Gothic settlement; and finally Guala, in Book IV, chapter 1, of the *Sanctuary of Pavia*. Guala says that the temple was not built by the first Constantine but by a later ruler of Italy, and asserts that the body of Saint Eleucadius was transferred there, as is established by the monuments of Pavia.

After reporting these matters, the distinguished Bollandus and Henschenius express a desire to know more precisely what such monuments are, if any exist, besides the one cited by Rubeus, which attributes the foundation to Constantine, son of Helena. They then cautiously ask, on Rubeus’s authority, who those people are who hold that the sacred body of Eleucadius was transferred by King Aistulf, who reigned in the eighth century during the time of Pippin and Charles.

For Rubeus, who in the first edition of his history had stated the matter categorically, moderated it in the later edition, saying:

> Most people have thought that the body was transferred by Aistulf.

Thus not only the learned collectors but Rubeus himself showed that they doubted the truth of the matter.

### III.

I myself have the gravest doubts about this matter, on the authority especially of Saint Peter Damian and of Agnellus’s silence. How could Agnellus, who wrote without hesitation—as was otherwise his custom—that Eleucadius was buried outside the walls of Classis, where a church in honor of his name had been built and still existed in his own time, and which was still standing in Peter Damian’s day, have added nothing about his transfer to Pavia by Constantine?

If the transfer is attributed to Aistulf, as Rubeus maintains, or to Liutprand, as Faber wrongly does while citing the writers mentioned above, the force of the argument increases. For it seems incredible to me that Agnellus would have concealed an event that occurred almost in his own time.

Here he says nothing, nor does he say anything in the Life of Bishop Sergius, where he relates much about Aistulf. There he says that Aistulf placed the cloak he was wearing upon the holy altar of the Ursian Church and considered building the Petriana Church, which had been utterly destroyed, although the changing circumstances prevented him from doing so.

Agnellus also speaks of the Church of Saint Michael at Pavia in the Life of Bishop George, but nowhere has he a word about the alleged transfer.

### IV.

Besides these considerations, the inconsistency with which the authors mentioned above relate so significant a matter also causes me to doubt its truth. We do not possess two witnesses—“concordant witnesses,” as they say—giving the same account; therefore the truth cannot be extracted from their statements.

The one monument that Rubeus cites suffers from many defects. First, he says that he took the statement from “a certain book in which mention is made of the relics of the saints deposited there,” and offers nothing else to commend the book’s antiquity or authenticity. Indeed, Rubeus himself is found to doubt the reliability of such a monument, since he departs from its assertion and claims that Aistulf, king of the Lombards, carried out the very act which the document attributes to Constantine, son of Helena.

That book was unknown to the writers of Pavia’s history and was evidently the work of some recent sacristan. This is shown by what it says about lessons from the Old and New Testaments being arranged—if it please God—by Saint Eleucadius for the prayers of the Matins office, of the kind recited in the writer’s own time. For it is clear that such lessons were not arranged until at least after the eleventh century; before then they were read according to the direction of the superior in the choir.

Nor was the arrangement of the office, as it is called, the same “throughout the Church,” as the author of the book claims, until later centuries. And what was that glorious triumph which Constantine is said to have obtained at that time—that is, in the year 325—“over the Gauls, who did not respect the empire,” on the occasion of which he built the temple of Saint Michael at Pavia?

We know of no war against the Gauls, or against Gaul, conducted in Constantine’s time. On the contrary, around that period the Theodosian Code and Justinian’s Code represent Constantine, while he was acting in Gaul, as being received with favorable acclamations. The passages are in Book II, *On Veterans*, and in the first book of Justinian, *On Veterans*, where Constantine issued an edict concerning veterans’ immunity; Baronius discusses it under the year 320.

The history of the alleged transfer therefore remains unstable until legitimate monuments are produced, although I am quite willing to believe that the body of another saint of the same name is preserved at Pavia.

### V.

Finally, from Agnellus’s testimony, as well as that of other ancient writers known to Agnellus and of later writers, it is clear that Eleucadius must be numbered among ecclesiastical—and indeed apostolic—writers, although he is omitted by all the authors of bibliographical works who composed catalogues of writers of this kind.

His works have certainly perished, to our great loss. He wrote:

> Several books on the Old and New Testaments.

> On the Incarnation and Passion of the Lord.

# LIFE OF SAINT MARTIANUS

## Chapter One

### The lineage, ordination, life, and death of Saint Martianus.

Martianus III, a distinguished bishop, was born of noble stock. He remained in the holy Church, fruitful in the Holy Spirit. Learned in sacred doctrine, he enlarged the clergy and consecrated very many deacons and presbyters.

He was ordained deacon by the most blessed Apollinaris together with the most prudent Eleucadius, as is found in the passion of his ordainer, where it says: “He consecrated Martianus, a most noble man, and Eleucadius as deacons.”

After many miracles, he surrendered his soul in peace to God the Creator. I therefore suppose that he was buried in the church of blessed Eleucadius.

He held the see for . . . years, . . . months, and . . . days.

## OBSERVATIONS ON THE LIFE OF SAINT MARTIANUS

*Martianus of Ravenna wrongly confused with Martianus of Tortona. Rubeus corrected in his second thoughts.*

Faber, in the *Sacred Monuments of Ravenna*, says that some people confuse Martianus, archbishop of Ravenna, with Martianus, bishop and martyr of Tortona; he rightly corrects them.

Henschenius, in the *Acts of the Saints* under 22 May, says the following:

> Hieronymus Rubeus, otherwise a diligent and accurate writer, deceived by the similarity or identity of the name, combined the two Martianuses into one from certain apocryphal manuscripts in Book I of his *History of Ravenna*, page 55,

as though Saint Martianus, bishop of Ravenna, had suffered martyrdom at Tortona for the Christian faith and his holy body had been brought back to Ravenna, to his own church.

> But it is established that the body of Saint Martianus, bishop and martyr of Tortona, is kept in his own church and honored there as that of a martyr; whereas the body of Saint Martianus, bishop of Ravenna, was buried among his own people. We have shown above—from the rite of the office and the Mass, that is—that he was regarded not as a martyr but as a confessor.

Henschenius then praises Faber and, from him, describes the locations of Saints Peter Chrysologus and Damian, which prove precisely this point.

In the first Aldine edition of his *History of Ravenna* (1572), Rubeus had written only the following about Saint Martianus:

> Martianus was appointed by God, in the form of a descending dove, as successor to Eleucadius in the archbishopric of Ravenna. Born of an exalted family, he lived a life above all devout, just, and temperate. He was driven by such ardor of spirit that, while preaching Christ, he aroused in the hearts of the people of Ravenna a burning love of every virtue. Many were unable to be broken by any blows of adversity or cast down from the path of piety by the assaults of the wicked; instead, they willingly endured every calamity and at last death for Christ. He initiated very many into the sacred rites and, renowned for the glory of his astonishing deeds, departed to the heavenly homeland on the eleventh day before the Kalends of June. As we gathered from very ancient writings, he was committed to the tomb of Saint Eleucadius in the one hundred and thirty-seventh year of the Lord, while Aelius Hadrian was emperor.

This is all that the learned author had written, relying almost entirely on Agnellus. But in his second thoughts, departing from Agnellus, he admitted what Faber, Henschenius, and the other writers rightly refuted.

# LIFE OF SAINT CALOCERUS

## Chapter One

### The etymology of the name, preaching, and death of Calocerus.

Calocerus IV is interpreted as “good time”; and if the *C* is perhaps changed into an *I* and *ieros* is read, it is understood as “elder,” or “priest,” or “lord.” He was indeed a very old man, advanced in age.

During his episcopate the Lord worked many graces and great miracles among the people through him. His preaching was so great, and he exercised such pastoral care, that he not only instructed the sheep already acquired but also tore souls away from the habitation of the pagans and from the stronghold of the devil, restoring them to the heavenly Lord through the sacred baptismal font.

He died and was buried, as some say, on 3 February in the basilica of blessed Probus the confessor.

He held the see for . . . years, . . . months, and . . . days.

## OBSERVATIONS ON THE LIFE OF SAINT CALOCERUS

*Who Calocerus was. Whether he acted as vicar for the preceding bishops. The fabrications of Tamaius de Salazar and Pseudo-Dexter refuted.*

### I.

Bollandus and Henschenius, under 11 February, express some doubt as to whether Calocerus was Greek, a claim that others assert solely on the basis of his name. From Agnellus’s *Pontifical* it is clear that even the ancients believed this; hence Agnellus himself later says in the Life of Saint Peter:

> From the time of blessed Apollinaris, his predecessors, together with this man, were from Syria.

By “Syria” he means the regions of the East. This assertion nevertheless seems to be challenged by the names of several bishops who preceded Peter, since their names are purely Latin; this objection does not apply to Calocerus.

### II.

Later writers add that it can be inferred from the Acts of Saint Apollinaris that Calocerus acted as vicar for his predecessors whenever circumstances required them to be absent. It seems much more probable that, while Saint Apollinaris was alive, this function was performed by the four men who successively occupied the episcopal seat after him. Agnellus says nothing about them.

### III.

The learned collectors cited above report the inventions of Tamaius de Salazar in the *Hispanic Martyrology*. Tamaius offered them to the world according to the assertions of the chronicle of Pseudo-Dexter, and Faber incorporated them all into his own work. They say that these accounts are as suspect to them as those of Mariana had previously been.

I judge that they deserve no credence, since Agnellus found nothing about the matter among the ancient writers whom he heard or read. The fragment attributed to Flavius Marcus Dexter that we possess was published at the end of the *Ancient Hispanic Library* of the once most learned Nicolaus Antonius, through the generosity and love of humane letters of the most learned and most pious Cardinal de Aguirre, who brought the distinguished posthumous work into public circulation.

That fragment records the arrival of Saint James in Spain in this manner:

> James came to Spain, XXXVI.

If, therefore, one maintains that the figures attached to this brief account signify the year 36 from the birth of the Savior—others may judge the matter—how can we believe Pseudo-Dexter’s claim that Calocerus sailed from Syria to Spain with Saint James, preached there, and then, after holding the bishopric of Ravenna for a long time, migrated to heaven in the year 130, although he was more than a hundred years old?

Nor is it established that Calocerus reached such an age. When Rubeus read Agnellus writing, “This Calocerus was indeed a very old man, advanced in age,” he believed himself entitled to measure his age on a larger scale and said:

> After Calocerus had passed his hundredth year in vigorous old age, he exchanged death for life.

Pseudo-Dexter of Higuera adopted this statement and ineptly adapted it to his own purpose, failing to notice that Calocerus would have died many years beyond his hundredth if he had come to Spain as the companion of Saint James.

It is astonishing that Faber did not notice this. He professes to follow Baronius and ought to have carefully considered what Baronius himself had written with great seriousness under 25 July in his notes on the Martyrology: namely, concerning the time when Saint James could have come to Spain and concerning what, according to the testimony of Sacred Scripture and ancient writers, it is reasonable to believe that he did there.

# LIFE OF SAINT PROCULUS

## Chapter One

### The character and death of Saint Proculus. His uncertain tomb.

Proculus V was devout, like a father toward his children. He frequently embraced many people with ecclesiastical affection, and by the sweetness of his preaching he offered himself to the people like honey, just as he supplied cups of milk to those thirsting for it.

Placed in old age and filled with the grace of white hair, he completed both his priesthood and his life. I do not know where his tomb is. I am uncertain whether he was buried in the basilica of blessed Probus or in that of Saint Eleucadius the confessor [Gloss.: on the first day of December. BACCH.].

He held the see for . . . years, . . . months, and . . . days.

## OBSERVATIONS ON THE LIFE OF SAINT PROCULUS

*The day of Saint Proculus’s death is uncertain.*

Agnellus knew nothing of the year or day on which Proculus began or ended his pontificate. The note in the margin of the Codex concerning the first day of December is an addition by a later hand.

Rubeus also attests to the uncertainty of the burial and adds:

> It is established that he died at approximately the time when Hyginus, who had succeeded Telesphorus in the pontificate, was beheaded, and that Pius of Aquileia was appointed his successor, just as Probus was appointed successor to Proculus among the people of Ravenna.

He does not say, however, how this is established. Faber, in Part II, has the following, rendered here in Latin:

> After completing ten years in the pontifical office, when his age was at last declining, Proculus exchanged life for death in the year 142, while Telesphorus was sitting in the Roman pontifical see, having been substituted that same year for Xystus, the first of that name, and while Antoninus Pius was emperor, on the first day of December.

Nor does Faber explain where he obtained this. Everything is therefore uncertain.

# LIFE OF SAINT PROBUS

## Chapter One

### The miracles, death, and burial of Saint Probus. The church held in special honor.

Probus VI was gentle and devout, distinguished in appearance, radiant in his works, wise in speech, prudent in heart, and full of the grace of the Holy Spirit. Whoever, sick, was able to come to him returned healed through his prayers, whatever illness had afflicted him; he also drove out unclean spirits and restored the wounded or broken bodies of groups [Note: [Col. 0487D] Perhaps *catervatim* (“in bands” or “in crowds”). BACCH.]. When, at the setting of his life, he saw the angelic hosts, his holy soul immediately departed from the body on the fourth day before the Ides of November. Then the entire grieving people buried his body with the greatest reverence, and his tomb is venerated among us to the present day; his church is situated in the eastern quarter. No Mass over the people is celebrated in any church within the city of Ravenna or Classis except in this one. The aforesaid basilica was built beside the portico of blessed Euphemia, which is called “at the Sea,” and which we now see demolished. He held the see for . . . years, . . . months, and . . . days.

## OBSERVATIONS ON THE LIFE OF SAINT PROBUS

[Col. 0488]

### The Chronicle of Pseudo-Dexter refuted. Rubeus attacked on many fronts. What is “Mass over the people”?

I. Here too, above all, the monsters of fable must be overthrown. Although Gelasius seems to deny that the apostle Paul came to Spain, as he had promised when writing to the Romans in chapter 15, nevertheless many ancient and highly authoritative men affirm it; Baronius gathered their testimonies under the year of Christ 61. Metaphrastes, in Surius under 25 June, presenting the account as reported by Eusebius in the second book of his *Ecclesiastical History*, adds what follows: Xantippe, the wife of Probus—who was known to Nero and lived in Spain—having seen written upon Paul’s forehead, “Paul, herald of Christ,” was converted to the faith; afterward Probus himself, together with the prefect Philotheus and all who inhabited that region, believed in Christ.

Surius notes not only that the name Probus is elsewhere written *Procus*, but also that, as Baronius had observed, since nowhere is Eusebius found to have written these things, the rest too may be regarded with suspicion. The author of the Chronicle of Pseudo-Dexter built further upon all this, embellishing Probus’s name with additions, calling him Lucius Sabinus Probus and making him bishop of Ravenna. Tamaius of Salazar, under 10 November, spun his own tale in the *Hispanic Martyrology* from Dexter, in these words:

“Saint Probus of Laminium, at Lybisosa in Spain, who, while still a secular man, successfully administered the office of governor in the territory of Laminium, where he married Xantippe, a most holy woman. Together with her he received the Catholic faith there from Saint Paul, the apostle of the nations. Later he returned to Italy and became bishop of the people of Ravenna; there, renowned for miracles and teaching, he departed gloriously into heaven as a confessor.”

He presents the remainder under 23 September, adding a charming epigram as though composed by Eugenius, Xantippe’s brother, in which the matters related about Probus are set forth. Faber, knowingly and willingly, transferred all these things into his own work, adding this especially conspicuous statement, wholly contrary to the evidence: namely, that Probus, after occupying the see for thirty-three years, died in the year 175 of the common era, while Soter was supreme pontiff and Marcus Aurelius Antoninus was reigning.

But how could these things have happened unless Probus had lived for one hundred and thirty years or more? For anyone who follows Baronius’s chronology could not place Probus’s conversion later than the year 67, since Paul is held to have returned to Rome in the following year. If Probus was then known to Nero, had already married Xantippe, and had been governor of the territory of Laminium for at least thirty years, it follows that he was made bishop at the age of 105, in the year of Christ 142, and died at the age of 138—he who is said to have died in the year of Christ 175. Who will believe such things?

Nor would the difficulty be any less for one who trusted the chronology of Pseudo-Dexter, Tamaius, Bivarius, and the other assertors of such matters. For, given Probus’s premature arrival at Ravenna, and the stated time of his episcopate and death, either one of the preceding bishops would have to be erased from the diptychs, or others would have to be inserted to fill the intervening span. But once the development of such fables has been narrated, and once it has been seen upon what utterly flimsy foundations they rest—foundations which the praised Nicolaus Antonius calls, by an allusion to the author’s name, *ficulnea* (“fig-wooden”)—the fables themselves collapse.

II. Rubeus says that Probus was buried “in the church which he himself had founded in the town of Classis, . . . not far from the sea.” Agnellus, however, indicates that he was buried where his church was afterward built; for Probus could not have built a church for himself. It was built at Classis, which he designates by the name “the eastern quarter,” beside the portico—namely, of the church of blessed Euphemia at the Sea—which, he himself testifies, had been demolished by the time he wrote.

III. Rubeus adds that Probus, “after he had honorably placed the bodies of those bishops”—namely, Aderitus and Calocerus—“established that divine worship should continually be conducted there.” Agnellus says nothing about the bodies of the praised bishops being placed there. Of the sacred mysteries he says this: “No Mass over the people is celebrated in any churches within [understand: inside] the city of Ravenna or Classis, except in this one.”

By “Mass” he means a solemn Mass, at which the entire people were present and the archbishop, celebrating the sacred rites with all the clergy, prayed for the people, especially on the more solemn days. Agnellus shows below, in the Life of Theodore, that this was performed in the Ursian church. When all the clergy had seceded from Theodore and gone to the church of Saint Apollinaris, the archbishop moved every stone to make the priests and deacons return; at last, when the matter had been settled in the Ursian church, and the day was already declining, Mass was celebrated.

The priests and clergy gathered at Saint Apollinaris imply the same thing when they cried out: “Arise, Saint Apollinaris; celebrate Mass for us on the day of the Lord’s Nativity.” Thus, while the people were waiting in the Ursian church, once the exarch had settled the dispute, the priests, deacons, and clerics finally came “and celebrated Mass and Vespers at the same hour.” In the other churches within the cities of Ravenna and Classis only private Masses were celebrated; in the church of Saint Probus there was also a solemn Mass, that is, a Mass over the people. This is the same rite which authors of the later period and papal diplomas elsewhere call a public Mass. An opportunity to discuss this church of Saint Probus will arise below.

# LIFE OF SAINT DATHUS

[Col. 0489]

### CHAPTER ONE. The piety and death of Saint Dathus

**Dathus VII.** This religious and exceedingly devout man was also watchful in nightly prayers and an outstanding gatherer of souls, frequently preaching to men and to the people; and, like a brighter mirror, his countenance shone above all others. For when he was called to heavenly grace, his holy soul departed from the body. And, as some maintain, he was buried in the church of Saint Probus. He held the see for . . . years, . . . months, and . . . days.

## OBSERVATIONS ON THE LIFE OF SAINT DATHUS

### The age of Saint Dathus is uncertain

Rubeus says that Probus flourished in the time of Marcus Aelius Aurelius Antoninus, during the pontificates of Pius, Anicetus, Soter, and Eleutherius, down to approximately the year 175 after Christ’s birth. He says that Dathus, after administering the Church for nine years, died on the fifth day before the Nones of July. Faber, determining the matter more precisely, says that Probus died in the year 175, and Dathus, to whom Rubeus assigns nine years of episcopacy, in the year 175 as well. Both assert this without citing any witness or offering any reason.

# LIFE OF SAINT LIBERIUS

[Col. 0489]

### CHAPTER ONE. The piety, wisdom, and death of Saint Liberius

**Liberius VIII.** A great man, full of charity, an abundant spring, outstanding in faith, gentle in mind, he increased the honor of the Church in his own time. With immense humility he guarded the soul of his own life, and held the primacy of every philosophy. After this he died and was buried, as some suspect, with his predecessor. He held the see for . . . years, . . . months, and . . . days.

## OBSERVATIONS ON THE LIFE OF SAINT LIBERIUS

### What philosophy did Liberius possess? The Lives of the following two bishops were considered in the preceding dissertation

Agnellus says of Saint Liberius that “he held the primacy of philosophy.” Rubeus therefore thought it necessary to assert that this bishop was “a most eminent philosopher, highly learned in Greek and Latin.” The other matters that needed to be observed concerning both this bishop and the following two were discussed in the preceding historical-chronological dissertation and therefore need not be repeated here. Everything else handed down either by Agnellus or by more recent writers is obscured by darkness and entirely unknown. Since, then, there is nothing to be annotated, I have judged that these matters should be presented to the reader untouched.

# LIFE OF SAINT AGAPITUS

[Col. 0491]

### CHAPTER ONE. The generosity, death, and tomb of Saint Agapitus

**Agapitus IX**, whose name in Latin is rendered *charitosus* (“gracious” or “full of charity”). He daily held love-feasts with strangers. Indeed, he continually distributed little gifts to the poor, and within the temple of his body he daily wore down his soul, as a sacrifice before the almighty Lord, upon the altar of his heart, in goodness. Afterward, when the divine command came, his holy soul was released from the flesh. He was buried, as some suspect, with the others mentioned above. He held the see for . . . years, . . . months, and . . . days.

# LIFE OF SAINT MARCELLINUS

[Col. 0491]

### CHAPTER ONE. Saint Marcellinus’s vigilant care of the flock. His advanced age. The glory of his tomb

[Col. 0491C] **Marcellinus X**, just and God-fearing, overthrew the armies of demons by his prayers and diligently guarded the sheep entrusted to him by the Lord, so that the most savage wolf, who rages and roars daily, might not tear apart the camp of his Church and snatch prey from his sheep, lest he devour with a beast’s throat the souls of Christians whom the holy man had won for the almighty Lord, or enslave them under his dominion, bound by the infernal chains of Gehenna. After a very long course of years he lost both his episcopate and his life; and his body gave off such a fragrance that those who buried him perceived through their nostrils the most precious perfumes of myrrh and incense. He was buried, as others acknowledge, in the basilica of Saint Probus. He held the see for . . . years, . . . months, and . . . days.

# LIFE OF SAINT SEVERUS

[Col. 0491]

### CHAPTER ONE. His election indicated by the apparition of a dove. He subscribes to the Council of Sardica. He attends to the funeral of Saint Geminianus, bishop of Mutina

**Severus XI**, whose name is understood as the compound *Saevus verus* (“fierce [that is, strong] and true”). This does not refer to savagery but to strength: *saevus*, that is, “strong”; [he is] a true supreme pontiff, whose priesthood was so completely predestined by the almighty Lord that, at his election, the Holy Spirit was sent in the form of a dove, which the whole people saw with bodily eyes and which came to rest upon his head. Hence, to this day, each nation repeats the proverb: “Blessed is that land where, at the election of a pontiff, the Holy Spirit descends in the likeness of a dove and is ordained upon the head on which it rests.”

But woe to you, unhappy Ravenna, neighboring the ruined city of Classis, because now, amid excessive dispute and controversy, a pontiff is ordained in you. Woe to you, unhappy Ravenna. The holy man was present at the Council of Sardica with the legates of the Roman Church.

This blessed Severus, mentioned above, was celebrating Mass and had ascended the pulpit with his deacons, reading the Epistles of the blessed apostle Paul in order to refresh the assembly of the people with spiritual words. Suddenly the holy man fell into an ecstasy, as though held by sleep, neither fully asleep nor awake. His companions, thinking that he had been seized by sleep, began striking his sides. He, however, as if rising from a very deep sleep, raised himself and said to them sorrowfully: “Oh! What have you done? Why did you disturb me? Although I appeared to you here, I was in another place.”

But they continued questioning him and saying: “Tell us, Father, where were you?” He replied: “May the Lord forgive you, beloved sons, for waking me, because I was in the holy church of Mutina. There I commended to the almighty Lord the soul of my brother and fellow bishop Geminianus, the bishop of that church, and I remained there until the aforesaid holy body was placed in the tomb.”

For this reason, in order that the truth might be tested, the citizens of Ravenna and Classis sent horsemen to the city of Mutina mentioned above, so that they might verify the holy man’s words. When they asked on what day or at what hour the holy soul of blessed Geminianus had departed to the Lord, the people there said: “Did not your bishop, Lord Severus, commend his soul to him, and remain here until his body was enclosed in the tomb? Once it had been closed, he suddenly vanished from our sight.”

Those who returned reported to their fellow citizens everything in the order in which it had been told to them. From that day onward they began to venerate his holiness even more.

### CHAPTER TWO. At Severus’s command, his deceased wife turns to the other side to make room in the tomb for their daughter. He dies praying between his wife and daughter

The written history of this man’s blessed life is not found among us; but some say that through him the Lord performed many miracles and wonders among the people, which our pen has not been able to disclose. His holiness, however, is said to have been so great that, after a long period, his deceased wife turned over onto her side.

When the daughter of the most blessed confessor of Christ Severus, named Innocentia, had lost the breath of life, everyone came to place the little body inside the tomb of her mother Vicentia. They saw that the tomb was too small and said: “Two bodies cannot rest here, because the chamber is narrow.”

With tears, Lord Severus said: “Oh woman, why are you troublesome to me? Why do you not make room for your daughter? Receive the one whom you bore; she was taken from your flesh, so do not hesitate to receive her. Behold, I return to you what you gave me; do not be sluggish. She has returned from where she came. Make room for burial; do not grieve me.”

At his voice the bones of his wife were moved to the other side with such speed that even living human bodies could scarcely have been moved so quickly, and she made room for her daughter’s burial.

After this it happened that the holy soul, which men had loved on earth, was to be received by the holy angels at the divine command into a pleasant place. As I heard the account of the blessed man’s passing, so I shall relate it to your ears. On a certain day, after he had celebrated Mass and received the sacred body and blood of the Lord, he ordered his tomb to be opened. Clad in his pontifical stole, he entered it alive, lay down between his wife and daughter, and ordered himself to be enclosed there; then, while praying, he gave his precious soul back to God.

He died in such peace and tranquility on the day before the Kalends of February. The Lord displayed many miracles at his tomb in his church, which is situated in the city formerly called Classis, not far from the district known as Salutaris, down to the present day.

### CHAPTER THREE. A sick boy restored to health at Saint Severus’s tomb

Again I shall tell you what we have seen happen in our own time. I recall it so that you may remember it. There was a man who is alive today, and who, when he was a little boy, had been laid down with his mother at the tomb of the blessed confessor of Christ, Severus, because of an illness of the body. When everyone had been overcome by sleep, that sick boy alone was terrified by the untimely hour of the night and uttered a cry that awakened them all. They saw the candles, which had previously gone out, shining with a suitable brightness.

When they all saw the immense light, terrified in spirit they gave glory to God and to his confessor Severus. When the boy had been brought into their midst, his mother began to question him: “What happened to you, son?” He said before everyone: “I saw a man coming out of this tomb, dressed in episcopal clothing, adorned with white hair, and with an angelic face. He touched me, and I was terrified.”

The boy’s illness immediately left him, and he no longer suffered from fever. These things happened in our own time, and not this alone, but many others as well.

### CHAPTER FOUR. Saint Severus’s election to the episcopate through the appearance of a dove

I shall complete what I began above concerning the election of this holy man, as it was related to me by many elders. One day, when he and his wife were heavily occupied with the work of wool-making—working, as I have said, at the craft of spinning—he said to his wife: “I shall go and see a marvelous vision: how a dove will come from the height of heaven and ascend upon the head of the one who has been chosen.”

His wife began to mock and rebuke him, saying: “Sit here and work; do not be idle. Whether you go or do not go, the people will not ordain you pontiff. Return to your work.”

But he said to her: “Let me go.” And she replied: “Go, for at the hour when you go, you will immediately be ordained pontiff.”

He rose and went to the place where the people were gathered with the priests. Because of the ugliness of his clothing—for he was dressed in shabby garments—he hid himself behind the door of the place where everyone had assembled and was praying. When the prayer had ended, a dove whiter than snow immediately came from heaven, in full view of all, and came to rest upon the head of blessed Severus, the confessor of Christ, who was hiding behind the doors.

When he drove it away from him, it flew through the air and again came to rest upon him, a second and a third time. The entire body of dignitaries [*potemptatus*, corrected to *potentatus*] who were standing there was astonished; giving the greatest thanks to God, they ordained him pontiff.

When his wife heard this—she who had shortly before mocked him—she afterward rejoiced over him. Then the evangelical saying written in Scripture was fulfilled: “With men this is impossible, but with God all things are possible.” And in accordance with Paul’s saying: “God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong.”

Some say that blessed Heraclianus, bishop of the city of Pensaurum, was a disciple of this confessor Severus and, instructed by him in sacred doctrine, held the episcopal see.

Let what you have now heard concerning the Life of blessed Severus suffice, I beg you, so that with God’s support we may speak of the deeds of the others, and so that you may read with desire rather than weariness and give immense thanks to God, who is blessed forever.

He held the see for . . . years, . . . months, and . . . days.

### CHAPTER FIVE. The author’s meditations on the Life of Saint Severus

But I ask you, beloved, to consider more attentively how many powers almighty God grants to his faithful, so that not only the living, through their flesh, but also the dead, through their bones, might obey; for the Truth itself says: “If you have faith like a grain of mustard seed, you would say to this mulberry tree, ‘Be uprooted and transplanted into the sea,’ and it would obey you.”

Why, among the other herbs, did he mention only the grain of mustard? Unless the grain of mustard is crushed, its power is not recognized; but once it has been crushed, strength and sweetness immediately proceed from it. So too, when the saints came to martyrdom, wisdom and humility enabled them to endure severe torments, and they did not fear the words or assaults of their executioners, whether by remaining silent or by speaking [some things are missing].

To call all those whom he had drawn away from the worship of idols sons, in gentleness—does this not seem to be a kind of martyrdom, though not equal in every respect? One kind is public, another hidden. In public martyrdom a man is brought before the governor, dragged, beaten, wounded, mocked, derided, bound in chains, thrust into the entrance of a prison, and after all this beheaded [Note: Perhaps “beheaded.” BACCH.]. And that martyr does not deny the name of Christ.

The hidden martyrdom of a man is practiced within himself: abstaining, fasting, keeping vigil, avoiding evil vices, renouncing carnal desires, not doing to another what he does not want done to himself, retaining no worldly desire, distributing from his own resources to the crowds of the poor, preaching insistently to unbelievers and infidels, rescuing them from blind error, and showing them the way of truth and light, according to what is written: “Be wise in what is good and innocent in what is evil.”

Again it is written: “Be wise as serpents and innocent as doves.” And if the serpent is wise, to which the Truth says through Solomon, “There is no head more wicked than the head of a serpent”; and if it is wise, why is it written: “The serpent was more cunning than all the animals of the earth”? And if it is wise, why is it so cursed among all the animals of the earth? “Upon your breast and your belly you shall crawl, and you shall eat earth all the days of your life.”

Why is this? Because it drew man away from the forbidden apple by making him eat. The devil entered the poisonous throat of the serpent and expelled the first-formed man from paradise. Why was it not said that it should crawl upon its tail, or in some other place, but that it should crawl upon its breast and belly and eat earth all the days of its life? This means: Do not raise yourself toward heavenly things, but toward earthly, filthy pollutions and pleasures.

But the Lord teaches the saints to be prudent and wise for this reason: when a serpent is struck by someone, it offers its body to be beaten and hides only its head. So too the saints are beaten in body, while the head of us all, which is Christ, is hidden beneath the veil of the heart and prayer.

“And innocent as doves.” While the other birds have bile, this bird is free from it . . . from all bitterness; it is a sweet animal, a gentle bird. Indeed, the dove received its name from the clapping of its wings; among the Greeks, the beating of wings is called *περιστερα δονέα* [Greek: “the dove’s wing-beating,” apparently]. *Launum* is interpreted as “dove” . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . many things are missing.

## OBSERVATIONS ON THE LIFE OF SAINT SEVERUS

[Col. 0496]

### The apparition of a dove in the election of the holy bishops who preceded Severus. In Agnellus’s time the Acts of Saint Severus were lacking. Translation of the bodies of Saints Severus, Vicentia, and Innocentia to Mainz

I. First of all, what Agnellus relates about the miraculous election of Saint Severus must be noted, especially this passage:

“His priesthood was so completely predestined by the almighty Lord that, at his election, the Holy Spirit was sent in the form of a dove, which the entire people saw with bodily eyes and which came to rest upon his head; hence also the proverb,” and so forth.

These words seem to indicate that, by relating this story, the author intended to explain a particular mode of divine providence by which God showed, through the form of a dove, that Severus’s election was pleasing to him.

The same seems to have been the intention of Luidolphus, who, in the *Acta Sanctorum* of the Bollandists under 1 February, introduces a monk of Ravenna speaking thus about Saint Severus:

“While the people were praying, behold, suddenly a certain dove flew down from above and, in the sight of all, settled upon his head. Taking this as a sign, they judged him worthy of the priesthood. Others, however, indignant that a man dressed in such wretched garments had dared to stand among the city’s leading men, drove him dishonorably out of the church, just as his wife had wished would happen to him. On the following day, when he wished to hide in the church, he was again exposed by the dove, which stirred the hearts of those who saw it. On the third day, when they had gathered in the church and were awaiting some sign, he who sees and judges not by the face but by the heart, as if rebuking their hardness, publicly demonstrated through the dove, as before, that he was worthy of the priesthood.”

The learned compilers judge that this Life was written after the year 846, when the attacks of the Agarenians reached Classis according to Rubeus, and consequently after Agnellus had written his *Book of the Pontiffs*. These matters seem to establish that, as the ninth century was drawing to a close, what was peculiar to Saint Severus at Ravenna came to be attributed to all those who had preceded Severus after Apollinaris.

This seems to be suggested both by Agnellus’s silence on the matter and by the form of his narrative, in which he implies that the event happened for the first time. Luidolphus speaks still more clearly against the common interpretation: when the dove descended upon Severus’s head, some considered him worthy of the priesthood, while others thought otherwise and even expelled him from the church; nor did they obey the dove’s second descent, but waited for a sign to be shown.

For how could these things have happened if it had been established among the people of Ravenna, from the elections of preceding pontiffs, that a man was designated by God as pontiff whenever a dove appeared over his head?

II. Agnellus himself, however, seems to indicate that the matter was customary: he has Severus say to his wife, “I shall go and see a marvelous vision, how a dove will come from the height of heaven and ascend upon the head of the chosen one.” Unless Agnellus intended Severus to have spoken these words prophetically of his own future election, they must be understood of something that had long been customary in the elections of pontiffs.

At the very least, these words may have sufficed for the opinion gradually to gain strength that all the Ravennate pontiffs from Aderitus to Severus had been elected by the sign of a dove. Among the earlier evidence for this matter must be counted the mosaic work of the Ursian church, praised above in the earlier Dissertation. As we said there, Henschenius and Papebrochius regard it as a venerable testimony of antiquity; nevertheless, we know it to have been made only in the year 1112, under the direction of Jeremiah, the bishop of that time.

The Life of Saint Severus copied in an old Lectionary belongs to the same period. The earlier Lives of the saints in it were written by an older hand, namely, in the eleventh century. I had the manuscript most courteously lent to me by the most illustrious and most reverend lord Cavallo, archdeacon of the principal church of Ravenna, through the care of Lord Francesco Nigri. It belongs to the nuns of Saint Andrew in the same city. It is regrettable that the leaf containing the Life of Saint Severus is missing.

Saint Peter Damian is earlier than all these. But it must be carefully considered that this holy writer has scarcely anything more about the apparition of the dove than Agnellus does; indeed, he seems to have copied Agnellus’s very words when he too has Saint Severus say to his wife:

“I shall go and see a marvelous vision, namely, how a dove will come from heaven and, according to its customary manner, settle upon the head of the chosen one.”

You see that Agnellus’s History lacks the words that touch the heart of the matter: “according to its customary manner.” If Peter Damian supplied them, they show that he held the opinion that the pontiffs who preceded Saint Severus had been elected by the sign of a dove.

Certainly, that tradition was common in the twelfth century is shown by the Life of Saint Severus presented by Bollandus after the previously praised, older Life of Luidolphus, and by the mosaic work of the Ursian church. This claim has more recent proponents in marvelous agreement, although Baronius is silent.

Faber assembled all the materials that could support such a history in the work already cited and frequently to be praised, *On the Sacred Monuments of the Church of Ravenna*, p. 346.

For my part, I think that the pious tradition of the Church of Ravenna should not be abandoned. Nevertheless, I cannot agree with Faber in the matters which he there relates together with Rubeus concerning the time when the church now called by the title of the Holy Spirit was built.

Nor does Agnellus say anything about the matter reported by Rubeus in Book II: that Severus, once consecrated bishop, “was immediately changed into another man, endowed by a divine miracle with the highest wisdom, and, having at once climbed the platform, delivered a sermon full of piety and doctrine, in which he foretold that thereafter the divine ministry of the dove should no longer be awaited in the creation of the bishops of Ravenna.” Agnellus says nothing of this; the earlier documents say nothing; nor does the Life of Saint Severus copied in the aforementioned manuscript.

[Col. 0497D] III. We learn two things from Agnellus a little farther on. First, that in the author’s time the Acts of Saint Severus had not been written, but that everything rested upon the tradition of the elders. He says: “The written history of this man’s blessed Life is not found among us.” Agnellus was therefore the first of all to accomplish this task.

Second, Severus held the see for many years, since he survived his wife for a long time and also attended to his daughter’s funeral “after a long interval,” joining her miraculously to her mother in the sarcophagus at the bishop’s command.

[Col. 0498A] IV. Luidolphus, praised above, relates that the bodies of Severus and the saints Vicentia and Innocentia were stolen from the Ravennate treasury by a certain cleric named Felix, carried to Pavia, and from there taken to Mainz by Archbishop Otgar, who after some time transferred them to Erfurt.

No one should be troubled by Agnellus’s silence concerning so important a matter.
