He not only failed to relate it but treated Saint Severus as though no one had doubted that his body was preserved at Ravenna when he was writing, since he relates a miracle that occurred in his own time at the tomb of that same saint.

These facts, I say, do not in the least conflict with Luidolphus’s History. For although Agnellus wrote the last Lives of his *Book of Pontiffs* around the year 480 of the common era, he wrote the earlier ones, up to Aurelianus, before the year 829, as I proved in the observations on the verses prefixed to the work, Observation IV, at the end.

At that time Otgar had not yet come to Italy, sent by the emperor Louis to his son Lothair to establish peace; on that occasion he obtained the saints’ bodies and soon transferred them to Germany. Baronius indeed followed Sigebert of Gembloux, who assigns such a translation to the year 824, and conjectured that Otgar came to Rome with Lothair, sent by his father to Pope Eugenius, who was then staying there.

But these claims collapse because, in that year, Otgar was not yet archbishop of Mainz, while Aistulf was still alive; Aistulf died in the following year. Moreover, Luidolphus expressly states that the sacred bodies were transferred by Otgar when he was sent by Louis, together with Hildi, bishop of Verdun, and the counts Warinus and Adalgis, to Lothair, who was staying at Pavia in Italy, “to restore peace and friendship between them.”

According to the *Annals of Bertin*, this mission belongs to the year 836, when it seemed possible to settle the disagreements of the preceding years between Lothair and Louis. Those disputes, which had begun in 830, broke out into mournful wars in 833; there is no need for me to assemble more about them, since accounts of those times are readily available.

In the year 836, therefore, the bodies of Saints Severus, Vicentia, and Innocentia were transferred, with the agreement of Lambert of Schafneburg and the priest Siffrid, and thus at least seven or eight years after the time when Agnellus wrote the Life of Saint Severus. Agnellus’s silence, therefore, does not injure the truth.

V. As the edition of Agnellus’s work was finally hastening toward completion, I opportunely learned that the most reverend P. D. Peter Cannetus, abbot of the monastery of Classis, a man highly distinguished for piety, learning, and courtesy and bound to me by the rights of friendship for many years, had obtained from the most eminent and most reverend archbishop and elector of Mainz a notable portion of the body of Saint Severus. Through this relic, the most holy bishop of the Church of Ravenna seems, after so many centuries, to have returned to his own people.

I cannot refrain here from congratulating my very dear friend on obtaining such a treasure and restoring it to the Church of Ravenna. Nor do I see what more distinguished benefit could have been conferred upon that celebrated church, whose memory of this event, I confidently hope, will certainly be preserved forever.

VI. The digression that follows the Life of Saint Severus contains nothing requiring observation, although barbarism resounds throughout it. The Lives of the following three bishops likewise contain nothing worthy of observation apart from matters concerning chronology. Let this suffice.

# SECOND HISTORICAL-CHRONOLOGICAL DISSERTATION

## On the age of the bishops of Ravenna who flourished from Severus to Peter

[Col. 0499]

### CHAPTER ONE. The opinions of Rubeus and Faber concerning Liberius II, Probus, Florentius, and Liberius III. The age of Bishop Ursus concealed in Agnellus. Rubeus corrected in many respects
## I. Rubeus, after that Agapitus whom he brought onto the stage so that he might have a bishop of Ravenna of that name subscribing to a fictitious Roman council, supplies Liberius as Severus’s successor. Concerning him he has only the following brief account:

> “He [Agapitus, that is] is scarcely mentioned at all (indeed, not at all by reliable authorities), and he lived for a very short time in the archiepiscopate, as did Liberius II, who was appointed in his place. Liberius deserved exceedingly well of the Church of Ravenna and performed the duties that seemed appropriate to an outstanding bishop. When he died on the day before the Ides of July, he was buried in the church of Saints Peter and Paul. Probus succeeded him, an old man most richly endowed with every kind of virtue.”

Further below, concerning Probus:

> “At about that time Probus, archbishop of Ravenna, died on the day before the Nones of March, and was buried in the tomb of Liberius. Florentius succeeded him at approximately the time when Julian Caesar, having become sole ruler, …”

Of this Bishop Florentius he relates that he asked Pope Damasus for relics of the saints, which Damasus would place in an honorable location at Rome and adorn with verses. He says that Florentius died during the pontificate of Damasus, under the emperors Flavius Valentinian, Valens, and Gratian, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of December, and was buried in the church of Saint Petronilla at the church of Saints Peter and Paul. He says that the inscription on his tomb was *Liberius Florentius*, and adds several conjectures.

Finally he says:

> “Liberius III was appointed as Florentius’s successor in the archiepiscopate of Ravenna. Some call him Liverius, others Oliverius. He was a man of the greatest holiness, pouring forth a river of eloquence when he preached to the people.”

Concerning Liberius’s death he writes:

> “This occurred [namely, Theodosius’s admission to a share in the empire] not long after Liberius, archbishop of Ravenna, departed this life. He died on the third day before the Kalends of January and was given a place of burial in the church of Saint Pullio, which had been built in his time. Ursus was appointed in his place.”

He had previously related that Valentinian died during Liberius’s time and was succeeded by Gratian; when he reports Liberius’s death, he writes the year 378 in the margin.

## II. Fabrius says that Liberius II was the one whom the Church of Ravenna venerates with the worship due to the saints. He says that Liberius held the see for two years, died in the year 351 on the twelfth day of August, and was buried in the church of Saints Peter and Paul. He adds that his feast is celebrated every year on the third day before the Kalends of January, although his death had been recorded as occurring on the fourteenth day of July because he had been confused with Liberius III, who truly died on the aforementioned thirtieth day of December.

He says that Probus occupied the see for ten years and died in the year 351, on the sixth day of May, and was buried with his predecessor. When Liberius’s body was later raised, ashes found in the same sarcophagus were believed to be those of this Probus.

He reports that Florentius died on the sixteenth day of November in the year 374 and was buried in Saint Petronilla’s church. He gives the epitaph:

> *Liberius Florentius.*

This is the epitaph cited by the aforementioned Rubeus.

He grants Liberius III four years in the see and says that he died in the year 377, on the thirtieth day of December, and was buried in the church of Saint Pullio. Ferretus says that his body was later transferred to the church of Saint Peter Major and placed in the tomb of his predecessor.

## III. There is no need to prove at greater length that the chronology is entirely uncertain, since above we examined the beginning and end of Saint Severus’s episcopate. For when we showed that his life extended to the year 391, after the Council of Milan at which Geminianus of Modena subscribed, it follows that the bishops mentioned above held office after that time.

For how long they held office, however, is uncertain and cannot be established from legitimate documents. The following may properly serve as an argument: Liberius III held the see for a longer period because Agnellus preserved almost nothing worth recording about Liberius II, Probus, and Florentius. For what Rubeus relates concerning relics of the saints requested from Damasus, Roman pontiff, cannot be proved in any way, since Damasus, when the cemeteries at Rome were being excavated, had an abundance of sacred relics with which both to exercise piety and to indulge in sacred poetry.

Concerning the first two bishops, Agnellus knows neither the day of death nor the place of burial. This compels me to believe, contrary to Fabrius’s opinion, that the Liberius whom the Church of Ravenna venerates as a saint is not Liberius II but rather Liberius III. From the most ancient times his feast day was assigned to the third day before the Kalends of January, as the author of the marginal notes to Agnellus’s text observes; moreover, Agnellus himself says that Liberius III’s tomb was known to him and to the people of Ravenna.

In addition, the letters inscribed on Florentius’s tomb—*Liberius Florentius*—indicate that two bishops were buried in the same tomb. If the difference of locations asserted by Agnellus did not stand in the way, one might conjecture that the ashes found in the same coffin of Liberius belonged not to Probus but to Florentius, whose body, in later centuries, together with that of Liberius III, may have been placed in the same sarcophagus and transferred to the church of Saints Peter and Paul.

Neither Rubeus nor the others explain the meaning of the aforementioned inscriptions, and perhaps they did not provide the complete epigraph. Nor is the other inscription adequately explained, which Fabrius says was carved on the ancient tomb of Liberius II:

> *D. N. LIVERIUS A. R. S.*

The name *Liverius*, used for Liberius III, seems to settle the dispute, if—as Rubeus and Fabrius report—he was also called Liverius.

But if we wish to interpret the letters *A. R. S.*, as I indeed think we should, as *Archiepiscopus Ravennas Sepultus*—“the buried archbishop of Ravenna”—it will be clear that the inscription belongs to a later age. In the century of the bishops just mentioned, the bishops of Ravenna were called bishops, not archbishops.

## IV. It is surprising—and Rubeus himself rightly found it surprising—that during the time of Liberius III it was reportedly said among the people of Ravenna that Valentinian the Elder, or Valentinian Major, Augustus, had been murdered at Ravenna, and that a great popular uprising had consequently broken out. For it is established by the common reckoning of the ancient writers that the death of the elder Valentinian, or Valentinian Major—as Agnellus likes to call him in the manner of Paul the Deacon and Jordanes—occurred elsewhere and at another time.

Rubeus asserts that the name belonged to a patrician of Ravenna who was killed in a riot during the time of this Liberius; that Felix succeeded him and met the same fate; and that Felix died in the year 430, although in the same passage Rubeus says that Felix had been elevated to the dignity of patrician by Placidia in the preceding year.

I refuse to believe this, however, since Rubeus is far from consistent with himself concerning Felix’s succession. Moreover, the interval of fifty-three years asserted between the death of the patrician Valentinian, placed around the year 377, and the death of Felix, reported in the year 430, seems excessively long, since an office of this kind was entrusted to men of proven excellence and outstanding experience in public affairs.

If it were established that a patrician named Felix had existed at Ravenna as Valentinian’s predecessor, it would be more suitably assigned to the beginning of the fifth century, under Arcadius and Honorius. From what has been said and what will shortly be said, I believe that Liberius III held office at that time.

Rubeus himself reports that in the year 408, after the killing of Stilicho, some sort of uprising was attempted at Ravenna by Stilicho’s servants and associates, and he testifies that most authorities transmit this account. But what connection does this uprising have with Agnellus’s narrative?

## V. In this matter nothing seems more probable than that Liberius II, Probus, and Florentius could have held the see for a short period of only a few months during the year 391, so that Liberius III was appointed bishop around the beginning of the year 392.

Consequently, when Valentinian—the son of Valentinian the Elder and Justina—was killed and perished at Vienne in Gaul by order of Arbogast, some disturbance may have arisen among the people of Ravenna. From these events a tradition could have arisen through *parachronism*—παραχρονισμός—by conflating events that occurred at different times and places into a single narrative and attaching the name of Valentinian Major to Valentinian the Younger.

I find that the name Valentinian Major was also given to Valentinian III in a privilege of the Church of Ravenna that was inserted by a later imposture. I discussed this in the dissertation *On the Origin of the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, part III.

The fact that Agnellus says that the fortunes of the Christians increased and the number of the pagans declined during the time of Theodosius the Elder supports this view, for that account fits especially well with the age of that most devout emperor.

## VI. With regard to the date of Saint Ursus, the first difficulty obstructing the establishment of the succession of the bishops of Ravenna is this: Agnellus expressly says that Ursus exchanged life for death on the Ides of April, on the very day of the holy Resurrection on which he had formerly dedicated the church he had built. Yet the thirteenth day of April cannot be reconciled with any of the Easter years counted from 396 through 469.

Just as the death of Ursus cannot be postponed until the latter year, so it cannot have occurred in the earlier one. Even if we were to say that Liberius III, whose difficult election in 392 we have found it barely possible to sustain from the conjectures above, held the see for a very short time, the period assigned to Ursus would still have been far too brief. It would not have been sufficient for the construction and dedication of a notable church, and Ursus would also have had to survive its dedication by at least a year if he exchanged life for death when the holy Easter day returned.

Nevertheless, since sound arguments have compelled me, as shown above, to extend the life of Saint Severus beyond the year 390, I do not think we should in any way abandon the earlier conclusion. For this reason I cannot agree with Rubeus or Cajetanus. The former, in book II of his *History of Ravenna*, and the latter in volume I of *The Sicilian Saints*, place the death of Ursus in the year 385, with lunar cycle 6, solar cycle 2, and Dominical letter E.

Nor can I agree with the most learned Henschenius and Papebrochius, who unfairly express doubt as to whether Ursus could have died in the year 396, with lunar cycle 17, solar cycle 13, and Dominical letters F E, on 13 April. They ought to have remembered what they said concerning 1 February in their treatment of Saint Severus: they believe that Severus died around the year 390, together with Haereus, whom they cite. Six years cannot suffice for the episcopates of four bishops, the last of whom accomplished works for which such a period would scarcely have been sufficient.

## VII. It must therefore be considered whether Agnellus’s words can in any way be understood so that we are not forced to alter the *Acts of Saint Severus* and of Saint Geminianus, thereby throwing everything into doubt.

It ought to seem preferable to depart to some extent from the strictness of the words of a writer who was barbarous in accordance with the spirit of his age than to depart from the transmitted chronology, which is openly contradicted by the sequence of what precedes and follows.

Since I see that in the year 412 the feast of Easter fell on 14 April, with solar cycle 1, lunar cycle 14, and Dominical letters G F, I would believe that Bishop Ursus died in that year, namely on the thirteenth day, when the Easter feast was beginning, at the beginning of that same night in which the mysteries of the holy Resurrection were celebrated.

For among the Fathers and the councils, nothing else is understood by the name of Easter when the conferral of baptism is under discussion than Holy Saturday, although they prescribe that it must be performed at Easter. Among others whom it would take too long to enumerate, this is stated by Tertullian in *On Baptism*, by Siricius in letter 1, chapter 2, by Gelasius I in letter 9, by Leo in letter 4 to the bishops of Sicily, and repeatedly by Gregory the Great. In their writings baptism itself is also called “Easter baptism.”

The day of Easter, or of the Resurrection, therefore began according to ecclesiastical custom on Holy Saturday at the third hour, when the blessing of the font and the initiation of the candidates took place, together with the other rites, which continued until finally, during the following night, the blessing of the candle and the solemn celebration of Mass were performed.

This is shown by the most ancient Roman Ordines, published for public use by Menardus, Thomasius, Mabillonius, and others. That these were very ancient rites of the Church is demonstrated by Ennodius, whose two blessings of the Paschal candle are extant, although scholars know that Prudentius did not mention this matter in his hymn.

Thus Holy Saturday is called “the Saturday of Easter” in an old manuscript sacramentary in the library of His Eminence Ottoboni. Before the exorcism of those about to be baptized it contains the following:

> “Prayer on Holy Saturday of Easter for those who are returning. The Lord Pope says after the *pisteusis* (profession of faith): Likewise, for catechizing infants: ‘Nor are you unaware, Satan,’ etc.”

This all the more establishes that Ursus died on the holy day of the Resurrection, even if he died on Saturday evening, since the solemn rites of the Resurrection themselves did not begin until evening. Many of his Masses and ceremonies proclaim this.

It is useful to add the blessing with which the bishop blessed the people before Communion, taken from an old manuscript codex of the Olivetan monastery at Naples. The codex records the blessings assigned to each feast of the year; Cardinal Bona discusses their use in book II of *Liturgical Matters*, chapter 16.

The blessing bears the following title:

> **On Holy Saturday:**  
> “May God, who brings forth new peoples from the undefiled womb of his Church and, while she remains in virginity, continually makes her fruitful with new offspring, fill you with the gift of faith, hope, and charity, and pour into you the gifts of his blessing. Amen.
>
> “And may he who wished to illumine this most sacred night by the Resurrection of our Redeemer cause your minds, cleansed from the darkness of sins, to shine with the rays of virtues. Amen.
>
> “May he grant that you strive to imitate the innocence of those who have just been reborn and, by the example of these present lights, illumine the vessels of your minds, so that with the lamps of good works you may enter with the wise virgins into the bridal chamber of that Bridegroom whose Resurrection you celebrate. Amen.
>
> “He himself, etc.”

Yet in a matter so clear I see myself seeking further light. For Leo the Great, who flourished shortly after these times, removes every doubt. Concerning the sacred ordinations of bishops, he says in letter 89:

> “Ordination must be celebrated not indiscriminately but on the appointed day; and no one should consider the stability of his state assured if he has not been ordained on the evening of Saturday, which dawns into the first day of the week, or on the Sunday itself.”

Accordingly, in accordance with the ancient rite of the Church, both evenings of every Sunday, and therefore of Easter Sunday as well, closed the ecclesiastical day.

This explains what he intends in what follows when, in accordance with the understanding of the Fathers, he asserts that the day of the Lord’s Resurrection was worthy of that honor.

More could be added concerning a matter sufficiently clear, but I believe this is enough. Let it therefore stand that Ursus died in the aforementioned year 412, on 13 April, in the evening.

## VIII. If it were established that the dedication of the Ursian Church took place on 13 April, just as it is established from Agnellus that it was celebrated on the day of the holy Resurrection, we would have an argument that would bring us back almost to the year immediately preceding the beginning of Ursus’s pontificate.

For Easter was celebrated on 14 April in the year 407, with solar cycle 24, lunar cycle 9, and Dominical letter F. Thus, if we understand Liberius III’s episcopate to have ended in the year 400 and Ursus to have been elected around that time, the Ursian Church could not only have been completed but also begun to be built; finally, it could have been dedicated on that same Easter feast and on the same recurring ecclesiastical day on which Ursus eventually departed this life.

In the same codex from which I transcribed Agnellus—a codex copied from an older exemplar around the time of the Council of Constance—there is a list of the days on which, according to the ancient custom of the Church of Ravenna, the anniversary of each church’s dedication in that city is celebrated. In it the dedication of the major church is recorded, as now, on 13 April.

From this it appears that there is an ancient tradition concerning that very day, 13 April: when the Easter solemnity returned, Ursus died and the basilica was dedicated.

This cannot be made to fit the evidence more conveniently than by turning to Easter, celebrated on 14 April: Ursus would then have died in the night following 13 April, which preceded Easter, while the church had been dedicated on the preceding Saturday of the Resurrection in 407. Otherwise, if we sought a year in which Easter was celebrated on 13 April, we would be forced to move much farther back from the time of Ursus.

At that time, therefore, we may place the construction of the notable church. Since the emperor Honorius constantly resided at Ravenna—as appears from the Theodosian and Justinianic Codes and from the laws issued there, which Rubeus carefully dated according to his years—he could have advanced the work through imperial generosity. I consider this more probable than the unsupported assertion that Ursus built the church from his exceptionally wealthy Sicilian inheritance, by which he allegedly appointed the Ursian Church his heir when he died.

For the solemn custom of the emperors was to adorn and enrich the church of the city where they resided. Other considerations likewise suggest that we should believe Honorius, rather than Ursus, both bequeathed the Sicilian revenues to the Ursian Church and provided the expenses by which the notable church was built and dedicated.

## IX. I can scarcely conjecture what caused Rubeus, who—as did all those before him who found this historical field available for cultivation—derived almost the entire sequence of Ravenna’s history from Agnellus, nevertheless to neglect Agnellus so frequently.

He had read that Ursus died on 13 April, the holy day of the Lord’s Resurrection, on which he had formerly dedicated the Ursian Church; accordingly, he judged that it should be called *ἅγιαν ἀνάστασιν*—“Holy Resurrection.”

How, then, could Rubeus have reported that this same Ursus died after holding the see for twenty years from the year 378, in which, according to Rubeus himself, Ursus had been elected—namely, in the year 398, when Easter was celebrated on 21 March, with solar cycle 15, lunar cycle 19, and Dominical letter C?

Fabrius derived the error from Rubeus and increased it by asserting that the Ursian Church was dedicated on 13 April 384, “on which day, he says, the solemnity of Easter fell in that year.” Yet in that year Easter was not celebrated on the stated day but much earlier, on 24 March, with solar cycle 1, lunar cycle 5, and Dominical letters G F.

Octavius Cajetanus, following Rubeus and Fabrius, repeats these same errors; departing from them, he falls into other errors noted by the most learned collectors of the *Acts of the Saints*, when they present the Life composed by him from Rubeus and from a certain monument of Ravenna.

Thus, in historical matters, once an error has been admitted, it grows through further errors.

I certainly see no reason why Rubeus, who arbitrarily lengthens and shortens the lives and episcopates of the bishops of Ravenna, should not at least have extended the life of Ursus to the year 396 in order to preserve Agnellus’s Easter notation. Had he done so, he could have reported that the Ursian Church was dedicated eleven years earlier, namely in the year 385, the seventh year after Ursus’s election, if Rubeus indeed says that Ursus was elected in 378.

I myself would gladly have accepted this, had the considerations stated above and those to be stated below not stood in the way.

## X. But the end has not yet come of the matters presented by Rubeus that cannot be sustained.

He reports—and Fabrius, Cajetanus, and the others follow him—that Bassianus of Syracuse, divinely warned at Rome, came to Ravenna to Ursus, bishop and his relative. Bassianus was later made “bishop of Lodi by Exuperantius, archbishop of Ravenna—or by this Ursus, as others believe,” as Rubeus often likes to phrase it.

Rubeus, who had said that Rufus, bishop of Capua, had been ordained by Apollinaris, could likewise report that Bassianus, bishop of Lodi, a city belonging to the Church of Milan, had been ordained by a bishop of Ravenna.

Whatever the truth of these matters, Henschenius and his associates long ago observed, in connection with 13 April, that the chronology does not hold together. Their observation was based on the *Acts of Saint Bassianus* transmitted by Bollandus under 19 January.

Leaving aside the fact that Bassianus is indeed said in his Acts to have been at Ravenna, but that they contain no mention whatever of Bishop Ursus or of any relationship between Bassianus and Ursus, they also report that Bassianus died at Lodi at the age of ninety in the year 411 or 413, after having occupied the see for thirty-five years.

It follows that Bassianus was consecrated bishop either two years before Ursus or at least in the same year in which Ursus was appointed bishop, if, as Rubeus prefers, Ursus himself began to hold office in the year 378.

These are nearly all the points concerning chronology that needed to be noted about the Lives of the four bishops mentioned above. In the remaining matters, scarcely anything worth observing occurs.

# Life of Saint Liberius II

[Col. 0503]

## Single Chapter. Liberius’s eulogy. Everything uncertain.

Liberius XII, an eminent man, a father to orphans and generous in almsgiving, governed the pontificate in peace. He guarded the evangelical preaching with complete fidelity, in accordance with what is written: “In your patience you will possess your souls.” He stole or seized nothing belonging to anyone else; from his own rightful labors he honored God.

After his death he was most dutifully buried, and he possesses eternal rest. For concerning the Life of the aforementioned Liberius, insofar as I have retained it, I have spoken to you.

This most blessed man held office for … years, … months, … days …

# Life of Saint Probus II

[Col. 0503]

## Single Chapter. Saint Probus’s eulogy and death.

Probus XIII, rich in divine grace and handsome in appearance, decrepit with age, weighty in body, cheerful in countenance, and suffused with heavenly grace, continually sought God with renewed strength.

He never ceased admonishing his sheep, but proved an outstanding preacher. So great was the excellence of divinity in him that he surpassed the learned in spiritual wisdom and refreshed the unlearned by the grace of the Holy Spirit.

When he was near death, he joyfully contemplated the hosts of angels; exulting and stretching his hands toward the stars, he closed his flaming eyes and gave up his spirit. This most blessed man was buried, as I suspect, with his predecessor.

He held office for … years, … months, … days …

# Life of Saint Florentius

[Col. 0505]

## Single Chapter. Saint Florentius’s eulogy, death, and tomb.

Florentius XIV, a just man, father of the poor, and protector of widows, was a great preacher, humble, gentle, and devout. Every day he exhorted his sheep to hasten more quickly to the harbor of salvation and to the fruits of repentance.

This holy man was buried in the monastery of Saint Petronilla, adjoining the walls of the church of the Apostles.

He governed his Church for … years, … months, … days …

# Life of Saint Liberius III

[Col. 0505]

## Single Chapter. Saint Liberius’s pastoral care. The alleged death of Valentinian. The bishop’s tomb.

Liberius XV was a holy man, handsome in appearance and even more distinguished in understanding. He possessed broad-flowing (*latiflua*) eloquence—or, according to the variant reading, “lactiferous” (*lactiflua*) eloquence. For he was a true worshiper of God, a guide of pagans toward good, and a destroyer of idols.

During his time, the number of pagans began to diminish and the holy Church to increase through the Christian people. His gentleness was so great that he was not called “lord” by his priests; rather, he was surnamed as one of their fellow priests. Among them he held precedence only by occupying the throne of the pontifical title.

Every day he exhorted those who blushed at repentance, so that they might approach with confidence.

Finally, during his time, Valentinian Augustus Major was killed outside the Artemetorian Gate, not far away, at the stadium of Tabula, near the Field of Corianthrus. A great uprising then arose among the people, and many were wounded at the place called Benedict’s Well. The Augustus was sent outside the walls of Ravenna and ended his life at the hands of his murderers.

He was buried in the monastery of Saint Pullio, which was built during his time, not far from the gate called the New Gate. His tomb is known to us.

> **[Note: [Col. 0505B] Marginal note: His feast is celebrated on the third day before the Kalends of January. Bacch.]**

The aforementioned bishop held office for … years, … months, … days …

# Life of Saint Ursus

[Col. 0505]

## Single Chapter. The construction of the Ursian Church. Saint Ursus’s death, tomb, and image.

Ursus XVI was most chaste in body and most holy in his works. He had a broad and handsome face and was moderately bald.

He was the first here to begin constructing a temple of God, so that, as a most devout shepherd, he might gather into one fold the Christian people who wandered about in separate huts. He never polluted his church, never sold the Holy Spirit, and never extended his right hand to receive any gift in return for the laying-on of hands.

Accordingly, this most blessed bishop built within this city of Ravenna a holy Catholic church, to which we all continually come, and which he named Ursian after himself. He founded it during his own time and, with God’s help, brought it to completion.

He surrounded the walls with precious stones, and across the vault of the entire temple he arranged various figures in varied tesserae. All the people, as if one man, worked willingly, happily, and joyfully, and praised God together with heaven: *qui* (“who”) [or *quia*, “because”] made salvation prosper in their hands through the intercession of their priest and confessor.

Cuserius [Euserius, according to Bacch.] and Paul adorned one wall on the women’s side near the altar [*altarium*, variant] of Saint Anastasia, which Agatho made. This is the wall where the columns are arranged in a row up to a number greater than the *de positis* [or *postis*, “doorposts”]. On the men’s side Janus [Satius, according to Bacch.] and Stephen decorated the other wall as far as the aforementioned door. Here and there they engraved in plaster and metal various representations of human beings, animals, and quadrupeds, and composed them very skillfully.

The church mentioned above is situated in the Herculanean district. It is called Herculanean because it was consecrated by Hercules, not far from the small Vinceleon Gate, since Vincilius built it.

The most holy man lived within the episcopal residence, which stands beside the ditch of the stream that flows from the place called Organaria, running beneath the Bridge of the Bakers. It was of remarkable size and wholly constructed with a building framework [the printed reading is *madico*]; where it stood, a ruined stable now seems to be located.

After all these things had been completed and the buildings fully constructed, he felt a slight bodily illness and, as though belching, gave up his spirit on the Ides of April. He ended his life in such peace and tranquility on the holy day of the Resurrection.

On that same day the church itself was dedicated by him and called *ANASTASIS*.

Some say that he was buried in the aforementioned Ursian Church, which is Anastasis, the church he himself built, before the altar beneath a porphyry stone, where the bishop stands when he sings Mass.

Therefore, not long afterward, his holiness became renowned, and in the mosaic of the apse of blessed Apollinaris his name, together with his image, was depicted:

> **Saint Ursus.**

He held office for 26 years, … months, … days …

# Observations on the Life of Saint Ursus

[Col. 0507B]

## Whether churches existed at Ravenna before the time of Saint Ursus. Saint Ursus first known from a portrait. His origin. A copyist’s error.

### I

It should be noted in this Life of Saint Ursus that Agnellus says that until the time of Saint Ursus “the Christian people wandered in separate huts” for the sake of prayer, and that he was the bishop who “first began to build a temple of God.”

These statements must be understood in such a way that they do not conflict with what was previously narrated in the Life of Saint Severus. There it is said that a church existed at Ravenna and that the people assembled in it, where the sacred synaxis was celebrated and where a gathering of bishops and people assembled to elect a new bishop.

The point, therefore, is only to show that the churches of Ravenna were crude and inelegant works—namely, those that had been built at Ravenna before the time of Saint Ursus, who was the first of all to conceive the idea of erecting an elegant temple.

The names of the craftsmen who adorned the walls of the temple are probably corrupt in the text. I rejected the word *madicho*, whose meaning is unknown, and restored *machina* in its place.

### II

Ursus is the first of all the bishops whose face Agnellus presents from an ancient mosaic. Since that ancient artwork has perished, many people will certainly wish that at least its rough outline, expressed by the author who saw it, had survived.

Ursus’s origin remains uncertain, and there is nothing to support the opinions of Cajetanus or others. Indeed, if Agnellus is to be trusted, we must affirm that Ursus came from the regions of Syria. For the author expressly says below, in the Life of Peter, as I have noted elsewhere:

> “From the time of blessed Apollinaris, his predecessors, together with this man [namely Peter], were Syrians.”

Just as I believe that, through the generosity of the emperor Honorius, estates in Sicily were added to the Ursian Church and came to be called the patrimony of the holy Church of Ravenna, so I also believe that for this reason the worship of the Sicilian saints Agatha, Lucy, and Eupulus began to be practiced at Ravenna.

### III

The notation of twenty-six years should not delay or trouble us, since it is plainly evident from what was said above in the dissertation that such a period cannot be assigned to the see of Saint Ursus.

It follows that this must be a copyist’s error. Anyone who weighs the matters discussed and considers the succession of the preceding and following bishops can easily begin to think about correcting it.

Moreover, I consider it beyond all doubt that the period of Saint Ursus’s episcopate scarcely completed a cycle of twelve years and did not extend beyond the year 413.

# Third Historical-Chronological Dissertation

## On the period of the bishops of Ravenna who flourished from Peter I of that name to Ecclesius

[Col. 0507]

# First Part

[Col. 0507C]

## The difficulties arising from Agnellus and other documents that impede the history and chronology are set out.

### I

We have reached the most complicated passages in Agnellus, in which there is scarcely any hope of arranging the chronology properly except by conjecture.

To this day all scholars who have written about the bishops of the Church of Ravenna have relied upon the *History of Ravenna* by Hieronymus Rubeus. Although he claims that he arranged everything on the basis of reliable documents, it nevertheless appears that he often built only upon conjectures what necessity itself seemed to demand.

Since I too am compelled to overcome the difficulties by the same method, I ask those who read my efforts to judge them fairly and favorably. I have therefore first decided to set out all the difficulties together, so that, by displaying the difficulty of the matter, I may make the critics more charitable toward the arguments I shall add for dissolving this most intricate knot.

### II

Agnellus lists the bishops of Ravenna in the following order: Peter, Neo, Exuperantius, John, Peter surnamed Chrysologus, Aurelianus, and Ecclesius.

He says that the earlier Peter of that name founded the celebrated church called Petriana after him, although he also says that Peter left it to his successor to complete.

Concerning the time of his death he says:

> “When Valentinian had begun to reign, at the very beginning of his reign this blessed Peter was deprived of life and ended his life.”

This can apply only to Valentinian III, who began to reign in the year 425 of the common era, together with Theodosius the Younger, who was then in the eighteenth year of his reign.

Agnellus then says:

> “During his time Galla Placidia Augusta offered many gifts in the church of Ravenna.”

Galla Placidia, the mother of the aforementioned Valentinian, began to reign in Italy with her son in that same year after the tyrant John had been killed.

Agnellus says that Peter died on the day before the Kalends of August. He adds Neo as Peter’s successor:

> “He was the builder of the aforementioned Petriana Church, part of which his predecessor had constructed from the foundations.”

After these works had been completed, Agnellus says that Neo died on the third day before the Ides of February.

When he had reported that during the time of Exuperantius the patrician Felix was killed in the month of May, he adds:

> “And Lady Eudoxia Augusta was made at Ravenna on the eighth day before the Ides of August.”

Valentinian took Eudoxia, the daughter of Theodosius, as his wife around the year 436. Marcellinus reports in his *Chronicle* that, after wintering at Aquileia, Valentinian brought her to Ravenna in the year following their marriage; Socrates also mentions the matter in book VII, chapter 43, although he gives different consuls.

Exuperantius is said to have died on the third day before the Kalends of June.

### III

Everything would proceed conveniently up to this point if one matter did not stand in the way: among the letters of Pope Leo, surnamed the Great, there is one that in earlier editions was numbered thirty-seven but is now placed as number 135 in Quesnellius’s edition.

Baronius believed that it had been written during the consulship of Marcianus and assigned it to the year 451. Quesnellius, however, thinks that *Majoranus* should be substituted for *Marcianus* and that the letter should be referred to the year 458.

The title of the letter presents it as having been written to Leo, bishop of Ravenna. Baronius and the others who followed him believe that there is an error in the bishop’s name and that *Neo* or *Neone* should be read in place of *Leo*.

For this reason Rubeus displaced Neo and made him the successor of Peter Chrysologus in book II, page 109. In my opinion, he thus anticipated the conjecture of Baronius.

IV. Yet Agnellus increases the difficulties astonishingly in the *Life of Saint John*, surnamed Angeloptis. At the outset one encounters this remarkable point: although he relates that the church of Saint Laurence was built by Lauricius, who, prompted by piety, mocked the emperor Honorius—Lauricius being the emperor’s chief chamberlain and the person to whom, by imperial command, the construction of the palace had been entrusted—and although he says that Lauricius died at more than ninety years of age “during the lifetime of that emperor,” whose funeral Augustus himself attended “with the grieving soldiers,” he nevertheless adds the following mosaic inscription [Col. 0509B], from which we learn that the church of Saints Gervasius and Protasius was founded by Lauricius himself after the death of Honorius:

> To Stephen, Protasius, Gervasius, the blessed martyrs, and to himself, for eternal remembrance, Lauricius dedicated this on the third day before the Kalends of October, in the consulship of Theodosius XV and Placidius Valentinianus . . . [lacuna].

Thus, at least, it is read in the Este manuscript, although Rubeus, book II, page 94, reads:

> To Stephen, Protasius, Gervasius, the blessed martyrs, and to himself, for remembrance, Lauricius dedicated this on the third day before the Kalends of October, in the consulship of Theodosius XI and Placidius Valentinianus.

So Rubeus reads it; yet even by changing the consulship of Theodosius XV to XI he does not remove the difficulty. For it is established that the eleventh consulship corresponds to the year in which Valentinian was first proclaimed Augustus, according to Socrates, Prosper, and Marcellinus. Consequently, Honorius had died in the consulship of Mariniana and Asclepiodorus. Rubeus himself does not deny this, since he assigns the death of Honorius to the year 423. What Agnellus relates to have happened to Lauricius on account of the construction of the church of Saint Laurence [Col. 0509C], he assigns to the period when John held the episcopate, although he had previously stated that Bishop Peter died in the very year in which Valentinian began to rule.

V. But what follows is exceedingly perplexing. For Agnellus reports that this same John went out to meet Attila when Attila was threatening Ravenna. More remarkably still, after the Pons Apollinaris at Ravenna had burned on the night of Easter, on the fourth day before the Nones of April, he says that John himself opened the gates and went out to meet Theodoricus, who had defeated Odoacer, when Theodoricus entered Ravenna, carrying crosses, censers, and the holy Gospels.

Attila, however, could not have come to Ravenna before approximately the year 452, and he died shortly afterward. Theodoricus, on the other hand, took possession of Ravenna after defeating Odoacer in the year 493. After recounting these events, Agnellus again expressly states that John was beloved by Valentinian and that the same Augustus granted the church of Ravenna a most extensive privilege, although it is certain that Valentinian died in the year 455. He further adds that Galla Placidia and Singledia built churches with the greatest magnificence. He then mentions the capture of Aquileia [Col. 0509D], and finally says that John died on the Nones of June, assigning to his episcopate sixteen years, ten months, and eighteen days. Yet, if all the events mentioned are to be taken into account, John would have had to remain bishop for more than seventy years.

VI. Despite these difficulties, Agnellus makes Peter, surnamed Chrysologus, John’s successor. He records that Peter was elected by Sixtus III, with a miraculous vision intervening. Sixtus, however, began to sit in the year 432 and continued until 430. Agnellus partly reports Peter’s letter to Eutyches, and says that Peter, together with Galla Placidia, arranged the funeral of Saint Barbatianus, whom he says died on the third day before the Nones of December.

VII. He makes Aurelianus Peter’s successor. Since he has nothing to report about Aurelianus, however, he complains at length of the burden imposed upon him by his brothers—namely, the writing of the *Lives of the Bishops of Ravenna*. He declares himself unequal to bearing it, and strings words together from words.

VIII. Finally, he shows that Ecclesius was bishop of Ravenna at the time when, by order of Theodoricus, John, the Roman pontiff, went to Constantinople. He says:

> “The beginning, however, of the construction of the church of Saint Vitalis was prepared by Julian after the aforesaid Bishop Ecclesius had returned with Pope John from Rome to Constantinople, together with the other bishops sent on an embassy by Theodoricus, as you heard above.”

Agnellus had discussed that journey of John, the Roman pontiff, Ecclesius, and the other bishops, as well as other matters relating to Theodoricus, in the *Life of Saint John*, surnamed Angeloptis. He also speaks there of a dispute between the bishop and the clergy of the church of Ravenna, settled by agreement, which Felix, the Roman pontiff, confirmed by his signature and letters. Felix began to sit in the year 530. Agnellus concludes by assigning Ecclesius an episcopate of ten years, five months, and seven days. During the time of his successor Ursicinus [Col. 0510B], he adds that King Athalaricus died at Ravenna on the sixth day before the Nones of October, an event which is known to have occurred only in the year 805.

IX. The knot becomes even more entangled, through the complications which Agnellus creates for himself, not only concerning the matters disputed about the age of Saint Peter Chrysologus. Learned men, following Domenico Mita, who elucidated Peter’s sermons and wrote his life, had believed—even before Rubeus wrote his *History*—that Peter had lived down to the time of Pope Symmachus, because they had observed that Peter had subscribed the Acts of two councils held under that pontiff.

There is also the celebrated letter of Pope Simplicius, placed second among the others and written on 29 June of the year 482, in which he severely reproves John, bishop of Ravenna, because he ordained Gregory bishop against his will. From this letter there is no room for doubt that John was bishop of Ravenna in the time of Simplicius and in that year.

These are, broadly speaking, the matters which so disturb the history of the church of Ravenna [Col. 0510C] and its chronology over an entire century that it is scarcely possible to hope to escape from so many mazes and from the darkness of the chronological dislocations.

## PART TWO

**A probable method for arranging the succession of the bishops. Rubeus’s anomalies reported. Agnellus’s probable statements distinguished from the improbable. Neon’s place restored. The remaining succession arranged.**

I. I therefore judge first that what Agnellus reports should be retained insofar as it can reasonably be maintained. It is not preferable to destroy the whole body because one part of it suffers from an ulcer. Rubeus seems to have done this when he arranged the succession of the bishops whom he records in the following manner.

He assigns the beginning of the episcopate of Ursus to the year 328 and his death to the year 398. He says that Exuperantius became bishop in that year and died in 418. He then begins the episcopate of John who saw the angel, assigning his death to the year 432, when he presents Peter Chrysologus as having been elevated to the episcopate; Peter, he says, died in 450. Next he recognizes Neon as bishop and places his death in 454. In that same year he places the beginning of the episcopate of another John, whom he says died in 494. In the following year he places the beginning of the episcopate of a second Peter, whom he calls the Younger, and assigns his death to the year 503. In that same year he says that Aurelianus began to sit; Aurelianus died, he says, in 514, when Ecclesius was elected and continued in life and in the episcopate until the year 542.

Having arranged the succession, Rubeus places the death of Ursus in a year in which Easter could in no way have fallen on 13 April, as we noted above in the second dissertation, together with the other matters pertaining to that question. Although he makes Exuperantius bishop for many years, he neglects to synchronize his episcopate with the arrival of Eudoxia, Valentinian’s betrothed. He discusses her under John Angeloptis in the year 424, and says that during John’s time the chapel built by Lauricius was dedicated. He adds:

> “Nor can this dedication be understood of the whole church of Saint Laurence, since the times do not agree; for Honorius, during whose lifetime it was dedicated, did not live down to this date.”

He reports the inscription under a year of Theodosius’s consulship different from the one read in our manuscript, as was seen above, and suppresses Agnellus’s statement that Lauricius died while Honorius was still alive.

He presents the privilege granted to John by Valentinian. He transfers to John’s period the murder of Felix, which Agnellus had said occurred under Exuperantius, and says that Felix died on the Nones of Quintilis. He adds several details from another *Life of John* circulating concerning this John, including, among other things, the miracle of an infant restored to life because the child had died before the anointing with sacred chrism, as its mother had anxiously desired. Agnellus relates this story below concerning Bishop Damianus.

During Peter’s episcopate, Rubeus says, Eudoxia, Valentinian’s wife, was brought to Ravenna in the year 438. He believes Agnellus when Agnellus asserts that the funeral of the deceased Saint Barbatianus was arranged by Galla Placidia and Peter Chrysologus. He maintains that letters were written by Leo to Neon in the year 452 [Col. 0511B], and reports that Neon built the larger church of Saint Peter. He adds:

> “There are nevertheless some who write that Peter Chrysologus began the larger church of Saint Peter and that Neon completed it.”

He further says that Peter began to construct, and in part founded, the churches of Saint John at the Fountain and at Tricolis, although he assigns him a very brief period in office.

To John II he attributes what Agnellus had attributed to Angeloptis, namely the events concerning Attila and Theodoricus; he also says that a letter was written to him by Pope Simplicius of Rome. He reports that the Council of Ravenna concerning the schism was held under Symmachus while Peter was bishop, and says that Peter also took part in the Roman synods.

From this point he relates that the Petrian church at Classe was begun, and assigns to Peter the matters which Agnellus had attributed to Peter’s predecessor Neon, including the story of Peter’s discovery and recognition of the latter’s body. He attributes little to Aurelianus. Concerning Ecclesius he reports what Agnellus reports, except for the number of years which Agnellus assigns to his episcopate. Those who wrote after Rubeus followed Rubeus [Col. 0511C].

II. Of all these matters, I believe that those supported by reliable witnesses and legitimate documents should be retained; the rest should be corrected in such a way that, insofar as possible, faith may be preserved in Agnellus. If all his statements are overturned, the entire history of Ravenna, which rests almost wholly upon Agnellus as its author, will necessarily be called into question.

I therefore consider it firmly established that Peter was bishop of Ravenna in the time of Symmachus, since the legitimate Acts of the councils in which he took part make that certain. I also hold it certain that Peter Chrysologus was a different person from the Peter praised by Agnellus, and that he lived in the time of the heretic Eutyches and of Pope Leo. This is established by the history of that heresy, by several of Chrysologus’s sermons—including the one hundred and forty-fifth—and by his letter, which will be discussed in its proper place.

It can also be concluded from this that Peter Chrysologus could not have lived into the time of the second Peter, since, while Simplicius was bishop, John flourished as bishop of Ravenna.

On the other hand, Neon’s having sat as bishop after Peter Chrysologus does not seem conclusively proved against Agnellus’s testimony by the alleged letter of John. Quesnellius’s arguments strongly indicate that the notation of the consulship is corrupt, whatever C. V. Pagius may argue to the contrary in *Dissertatio Hypatica*, part III, chapter p., number 6 and following. For all the other letters of Leo from the year 451, in the consulship of Martianus and Adelphius, mention only Adelphius, in accordance with the custom of the writer, who, when naming one of the consuls, chooses the Western consul and omits the Eastern. This letter, however, records the Eastern consul and neglects the Western.

Moreover, the manner of recording the consul differs from Leo’s practice. Leo generally writes not *consulatu*, as here, but *consule* or *consulibus*. Finally, the letter was written on the occasion of the return of people from barbarian captivity, whose baptism was in question, although in that year the barbarians had not yet given occasion for such a question in the regions around Aemilia or Flaminia.

If these points are admitted, and if, with Quesnellius, we insist that Majorianus should be written in place of Martianus, it plainly appears that the letter was written in the year 458, while John was bishop of Ravenna. Yet John had met Attila, and Attila’s death cannot be postponed beyond the year 454; nor could Attila have approached Ravenna after the year 453.

It follows that Neon cannot have died in the year 454, as Rubeus says. Indeed, there is scarcely any place where Neon can be inserted between Peter Chrysologus and John if we agree with Baronius, who maintains that the letter to Eutyches was written in the year 449 and that Attila was compelled by Leo the Great to withdraw in the year 452. John would therefore necessarily have been elected in the year 451, in the very consulship of Martianus.

Since this is so, and since the title of the letter has proved corrupt—it presented the letter as having been written to Leo of Ravenna—I judge that the designation of the Ravennate recipient attached to that Leo, or Neon, is likewise corrupt, or has been corrupted from another similar name. Why should not the name of Ravennius, bishop of Arles, lie corrupted there? We know that other letters were sent by Pope Leo to him during the period when the writers report that Gaul was miserably devastated by Attila.

Whatever may be thought of this method of emendation [Col. 0512B], I believe that this inscription is insufficient evidence for establishing the period of Leo, bishop of Ravenna. Therefore, if it can reasonably be done, the place assigned to Neon by Agnellus should be preserved.

III. I therefore judge that a John distinct from Angeloptis sat immediately after Peter Chrysologus and held the see for a long time, so that his memory remained down to Agnellus’s age.

Since only Peter Chrysologus sat between the earlier and the later John, and since both were distinguished for holiness and were dear to Valentinian and the empress Placidia, I believe that this gave rise to the confusion and confused transmission of the Acts of both men as though they were one.

Nor do I think it sufficient to regard the John to whom Pope Simplicius wrote as different from the John who appeased Attila merely because the conduct of the former seems inconsistent with that of the latter. It might seem unworthy of a man renowned for holiness that he ordained a bishop against his will and deserved to be corrected for this by a severe reprimand from the Roman pontiff.

Moreover, the same letter of Simplicius shows that the predecessor of the John to whom the letter was written had committed a similar error: he had ordained a priest against his will. Thus one or the other of these acts must be attributed to that John who was distinguished for his reputation for holiness.

I therefore hold that this same John was elected around the year 450 and died around the year 496. He was succeeded by a second Peter, who flourished in the time of Symmachus; Aurelianus succeeded him and died in the age of Hormisdas; Ecclesius then succeeded Aurelianus. These points are remarkably confirmed by the verses which are to be read below in Agnellus, in the *Life of Bishop Maximianus*.

IV. I judge that the remaining matters, for the rejection of which no arguments from contemporary witnesses or legitimate documents are available, and which were transmitted by Agnellus, should be retained in such a way that contradictions among them are corrected while the succession of bishops is preserved. I believe we must adhere to that succession as far as possible, because I think Agnellus knew it from the diptychs. It could indeed have happened that identical names were conflated, but it is hardly probable that the succession itself, composed of names entirely different from one another, was inverted.

I do not think that Agnellus necessarily omitted the Peter who flourished in the time of Symmachus; rather, I believe that his *Life* has been lost.

Following the rule stated above, I therefore think Agnellus should be trusted when he asserts that Bishop Peter, successor of Ursus, died in the year in which Valentinian was proclaimed Augustus, namely in the year 425, and that he “laid the foundations of the Petrian church, building a wall around it but not completing everything,” to use Agnellus’s own words.

I am uncertain whether the body discovered by the author in Saint James at the Font of the Petrian church was the body of that first or of the second Peter. I have no doubt, however, that the image which Galla Placidia ordered to be made and decorated with tesserae on the wall of the church of Saint John the Evangelist was an image of the first Peter of that name, since the second died long after Galla’s death.

The gifts dedicated to God by Galla belonged not to the Petrian church but to the Ursian church. For Agnellus says:

> “In the time of this Peter, Galla Placidia Augusta offered many gifts in the church of Ravenna.”

V. I judge that Neon succeeded Peter in the same year, 425. He lived long enough, with the assistance of Valentinian and Galla Placidia, to complete the Petrian church, adorn the fountains of the Ursian church, decorate its vaults with mosaic work, construct the house of the Five Dagubitae, and bring to completion the other works which Agnellus relates.

I therefore think that Neon died around the year 430, on the third day before the Ides of February. In the same year Exuperantius was elected. His obscure Acts lead me to believe that he held the see only briefly.

Nevertheless, during his episcopate the church of Saint Agnes could have been built by Gemellus, subdeacon and governor of Sicily, although Gemellus may have completed it only after Exuperantius’s death. Felix the patrician could also have been slaughtered at the steps of the Ursian church.

Idacius says in his *Chronicle* that Felix was made patrician in the same year in which Valentinian was made Caesar. Marcellinus, however, reports that Felix was killed at Ravenna in the consulship of Theodosius XIII and Valentinian III, which proves that Exuperantius was bishop in the year 430.

His episcopate cannot in any way be prolonged to the year 437, when Eudoxia, Valentinian’s wife, came to Ravenna.

The statement that Exuperantius “built a silver city in the procession” has an ambiguous meaning. What precedes and follows indicates rather that the reference should be to some offering presented to blessed Agnes than to a building constructed at Argenta, as more recent writers have understood it, together with the author of the marginal notes.

I therefore judge that Exuperantius died on the fourth day before the Kalends of June in the year 432, and that the celebrated John, surnamed Angeloptis, succeeded him. John dedicated a chapel to Saints Stephen, Gervasius, and Protasius, built by Lauricius in the consulship of Theodosius XV and Valentinian IV [Col. 0514A], although the church of Saint Laurence had been erected more than twenty years earlier.

Saint Augustine’s testimony establishes that, when he was writing the books *On the City of God*, around the year 413, a memorial to Saint Laurence existed at Ravenna. Thus the church of Saint Laurence and the chapel of Saints Stephen, Gervasius, and Protasius were built at very different times. The former was built while Augustus Honorius was still alive. This confirms the history transmitted by Agnellus, but it provides no support for the other details concerning the time of Lauricius’s death.

Agnellus must be mistaken in saying that Lauricius died during the time of Honorius, since Honorius died in 423, whereas, as the inscription shows, Lauricius dedicated the chapel in 435.

What follows seems to refer not to the chapel but to the church of Saint Laurence—namely, that the inscription on the arch of the greater apse stated that its construction had been completed in four years and six months. It is incredible that so much time was spent constructing the chapel alone [Col. 0514B].

VI. Peter, known to everyone by the surname Chrysologus, then succeeded Neon. Everything that Agnellus relates about him is appropriate to this Peter. He was elected in the final year of Sixtus III and held the see until the period when Attila threatened Ravenna.

In this way, it seemed possible to restore the Acts and chronological succession of the bishops of Ravenna, preserving Agnellus’s reliability insofar as possible. Whenever his other statements do not conflict with the evidence, I have judged him more worthy of belief than the more recent writers, who would scarcely have dared to write a history of the church of Ravenna had Agnellus’s *Liber Pontificalis* not supplied them with its order and material.

I do not, however, wish to excuse the contradictions which he transmits in many places. I maintain only that the truths recognized by comparison with true evidence should be extracted from the midst of the contradictions and should not be disregarded.

# LIFE OF SAINT PETER

[Col. 0513]

## CHAPTER ONE

**Peter’s homeland and that of his predecessors. The Petrian church founded. The image of the Savior praised. The approach and death of a certain hermit.**

Peter, the seventeenth bishop, was a most holy man, slight in body, tall in stature, lean in appearance, and he had a long beard.

From the time of blessed Apollinaris, all his predecessors, together with this man, were Syrians. He was the founder of the Petrian church, building walls around it but not yet completing everything.

[Note: [Col. 0513D] Marginal note: The Petrian church and its founder. No church was comparable to it in construction; it is said to have had three hundred altars. BACCH.]

No church was larger than it in construction or comparable to it, either in length or in height. It was richly adorned with precious stones, decorated with various tesserae, and abundantly furnished with gold, silver, and sacred vessels, which he himself ordered to be made.

They say that an image of the Savior was present there, painted above the royal doors—so beautiful that no human being could ever have seen its equal among paintings. It was exceedingly lovely and resembled the form which the Son of God himself did not disdain to assume in the flesh when he preached to the nations.

Nevertheless, I want you to know what I heard concerning the sacred image of our Lord mentioned above from each of the elders, both laymen and priests, just as they themselves had received it from their predecessors.

This was not communicated only to me, who wish to record this pontifical history, but also to my other fellow students and brothers, who were nourished in the bosom of the holy Ursian church.

There was, they said, a certain spiritual father in the desert who daily asked the Lord to show him the form of his incarnation. After he had grown weary through many years of such prayer and his soul had become exhausted, a man in white garments, dressed in angelic fashion, appeared to him at night and said:

> “Behold, your prayer has been heard, and I have looked upon your labor. Rise, go to the city called Classe, and seek there the Petrian church. When you have entered it, look above its doors, beneath the arch. There you will see me painted in lime on the wall, as I was in the world in the flesh.”

Then, filled with great joy, delighted and exultant at hearing these words, he left the desert. Two lions accompanied him. He traveled over long stretches of land and reached the city of Classe.

When he had entered the aforesaid church with the lions, he wept for a very long time and prayed, beginning to search the walls for the holy image. When he did not find it, he came to the place which had been revealed to him while he slept—the place where the image was said to be painted. When he saw it, he fell face down upon the ground, worshiped it with tears, and gave thanks because he had seen it just as it had been revealed to him in his dream.

Gazing at it for a very long time, he said:

> “I give you thanks, God who hears all, who do not reject those who seek you and do not desire the death of sinners, but are present to those who call upon you. With you there is no need of a mediator, messenger, or intermediary; with you there is no delay for faithful suppliants, according to what you promised us through the prophets: ‘While you are still speaking, behold, I am here.’  
>   
> “Behold, not according to my merits but according to your mercy, my desire has been fulfilled. I am now satisfied with your holy riches; I have now been enriched from the heavenly treasury. Receive my soul into your holy palace, so that, invited to the supper of the Lamb, I may be found worthy to enter your kingdom and sit at your table.”

After saying these things, he prayed and rejoiced for a very long time. Surrounded by the two lions, which roared around him, he gave up his spirit.

Then the people, learning of this, came running. Taking digging tools with great fear and reverence, while the lions licked the holy man’s limbs and footprints and shed tears, they buried him with profound mourning.

One lion then prostrated itself at his head and the other at his feet. They roared loudly at one another, rushing back and forth beside the holy man’s body and making a great tumult, wishing to thrust their necks beneath his tomb. The people wept bitterly together with the lions, and both lions died.

The people buried them in the grave on either side of the holy man’s body, one on each side. Then, overcome with excessive fear, the people returned to their homes and recounted the wonders which the Lord had performed among human beings and beasts.

## CHAPTER TWO

**The death of Saint Peter and the indication of his tomb. His body discovered by Agnellus.**

He lived in the time of Valentinian. For when Valentinian began to rule, at the very beginning of his reign this blessed Peter was deprived of life and went to the stars.

Some say that he was buried in the Petrian church which he had founded. You must know with complete certainty—for I shall tell you the truth and no falsehood—that while I was residing in my monastery of blessed and ever-virgin Mary, which is called at Blachernas and is founded not far from Guandelaria, and while I wished to investigate the Lives of all the bishops of Ravenna, my soul was uncertain about the tomb of this holy man.

As I was thinking about this, one of the boys who stood daily in my presence announced to me that George, a priest of the church of Classe, had arrived. At that time he was in charge of the church of Saint Severus, confessor of Christ. He was a most venerable man, steadfast in all things, firm and without weakness.

When he had entered my presence and sat down, I immediately began to ask whether he knew anything about the *glossochion* [the precise sense of this word is uncertain] of this blessed bishop, either from what he had heard from ancient men or from what he had seen.

With a cheerful face he said to me:

> “Come, I shall show you what you desire most: where the most precious treasure rests.”

When we had mounted horses, we hastened to Classe. I ordered my men who accompanied us to withdraw farther away, approximately half a stadium. We entered the monastery of Saint James, which is founded within the font of the aforesaid church.

We saw a tomb of precious Proconnesian stone. We raised it with difficulty and slightly lifted the cover. Inside the same chest we found a cypress coffin. When we had raised its lid, both of us saw the holy body lying there as though it had been buried at that very hour. It was tall in stature, its skin pale, and all its limbs intact. The chest and belly were whole; no part was missing, except that the small pillow beneath the head had diminished.

So great was the fragrance that came from it that we perceived it as though burning incense mixed with myrrh and balsam. A horrible and most intense terror fell upon us, together with such sadness that although we had opened the tomb cheerfully before, we could scarcely close it even with sighs and groans.

The fragrance overcame us entirely, and for more than a week the smell never left our nostrils.

Above the coffin there was an image of him, wonderfully painted, bearing the inscription:

> “Lord Peter, archbishop.”

## CHAPTER THREE

**The image of Saint Peter dedicated through the care of Galla Placidia. The gifts of the same Placidia. Other works performed through Saint Peter.**

Within the church of Blessed John the Evangelist, Galla Placidia ordered his image to be decorated with tesserae, on account of his holiness, on the wall of the apse behind the bishop, above the seat where the bishop sits.

The image was made in this fashion: it had a long beard and outstretched hands, as though he were celebrating Mass; a host was placed above the altar, as it were; and, behold, an angel of the Lord was depicted at the sight of that altar, receiving the prayers.

During Peter’s time, Galla Placidia Augusta offered many gifts in the church of Ravenna. She had a lamp made entirely of pure gold, together with candles. Some say that it weighed seven pounds according to the public standard. It was made with her own image in the art of *scenofactoria*, placed within a circle, and the following words were written around it:

> “I shall prepare a lamp for my Christ.”

This most blessed man also made Gospel covers of the finest gold and gleaming gems. His image was made there as well, and these objects remain to the present day. The letters written above his head display the following:

> “Lord Bishop Peter offered this on the day of his ordination to his holy church.”

He died on the day before the Kalends of August. He sat for . . . years, . . . months, and . . . days.

# OBSERVATIONS ON THE LIFE OF SAINT PETER

[Col. 0516]

**The truth of Peter, the first bishop of that name, affirmed. Whether the body discovered by Agnellus was his or that of Peter III is uncertain. What were the Gospel covers? The most ancient image of the Savior. The royal doors of the churches. The hermit—an Egyptian or not? The church of Classe and its clergy.**

I. The reasons explained in the preceding dissertation persuaded me to accept this Peter, against Rubeus and those who followed Rubeus, so that I would not invert the succession of the bishops of Ravenna transmitted by Agnellus. I now wish to add what is suggested by the same *Life*.

First, it is unlikely that Agnellus was deceived by the elders when they placed Peter, who flourished in the time of Symmachus, far back, almost to the beginning of the fifth century. For they clearly relate matters concerning an older Peter which can belong neither to Chrysologus nor to that Peter called the Younger.

Our author expressly states that this Peter came from the regions of Syria together with his other predecessors. This would be said falsely either of Peter Chrysologus, whom no one to this day has doubted to be Italian, or of the later Peter, who had several Italian predecessors.

The long beard also provides an indication by which the one may be distinguished from the other. It appears from this that Peter flourished in the period when the church of Ravenna seemed especially to be adopting Greek customs, namely while the emperors were residing there and the clergy were conforming themselves in many matters to the practices of the Greek church.

After the Western Empire had been destroyed and the Goths had taken control of Ravenna and its affairs, the bishops of Ravenna seem to have shaved their beards. Evidence for this may be found in the very ancient image of Saint Ecclesius displayed in an old mosaic at Ravenna.

I believe that the following gives this matter a degree of certainty: at the end of the *Life* it is related that, because of his holiness, Galla Placidia ordered his image to be formed with tesserae in the basilica of Saint John the Evangelist. The place of the image and its features are described so distinctly that it is scarcely believable that Agnellus could have been deceived or that he failed to distinguish between the image of the earlier Peter and that of Peter Chrysologus.

The image cannot have belonged to Peter III: the beard itself proclaims this, and the chronology makes it clear. The image of Peter III could not have been made at Galla Placidia’s command.

What compelled me entirely to recognize this earlier Peter was the lack of other arguments—apart from mere tradition—by which we can prove that Peter III was honored among the saints. From this passage of Agnellus, however, we know of the holiness of the earlier Peter from the time of Galla Placidia.

Therefore the bishop Peter whom the church of Ravenna venerates as a saint is not the third Peter but this earlier one [Col. 0517C].

Of the third Peter we know only that he sat at Rome in many councils during the age of Symmachus, the Roman pontiff. Through a chronological displacement, this has been attributed to the other Peter, who was called the Elder down to Agnellus’s time, although he was later than the first three Peters; Agnellus himself makes this attribution.

II. In the preceding dissertation I expressed doubt whether the body discovered by Agnellus was that of the earlier Peter or of Peter III. I remain uncertain about the matter.

The inscription in which the title of archbishop is assigned to Peter increases the doubt, since it sounds as though it belongs to a later century. The location of the tomb also raises an objection, since the oratory of Saint James was founded after Peter’s time.

Nevertheless, it could have happened that the body was transferred in a later age from the old Petrian church, where most people believed it had first been buried, to the oratory of Saint James, and that the epitaph of archbishop was added at that time.

The inscription on the Gospel covers, being marked with an epigraph, agrees very well with Peter’s period. Nor can it reasonably be doubted that by the barbarous name *alapae*, unknown to the writers of glossaries, the outer boards were meant with which the Gospel book had been bound.

Rubeus, book III, page 133, where he attributes such a gift to Peter III—whom he calls the second—explains Agnellus as saying that Peter “adorned with the finest gold and gems the books of the divine new law delivered by Christ God, books written on tablets.”

III. Agnellus strongly commends here the image of our Lord and Savior at the greater doors of the Petrian church. From the context it is also clear that these doors are designated by the name *regiae*, a term of corrupted Latin familiar to similar writers.

He presents a popular tradition concerning that image, which wonderfully represented its prototype, and concerning a man devoted to the hermit’s life who had been divinely instructed and approached it, then died there with two lions as his companions.

As I believe, the lions’ companionship led Rubeus, in recounting Agnellus’s story—which says that the man arrived by land—to add that he had come from the deserts of Egypt.

Although I judge that many elements in this story bear the mark of the credulity of the century in which Agnellus flourished, I have no doubt that the image of the Savior was extremely ancient. It had already been destroyed in Agnellus’s own time and in the time of the elders of the Ursian clergy. From the beginning it had been placed not merely for decoration but for worship, adoration, and *proskynesis* (προσκύνησις).

IV. From this *Life of Peter* we learn that Agnellus was enrolled in the canon of the Ursian church and was nourished there from his earliest age. We also learn that he was abbot of the church of Saint Mary at Blachernas; these matters will be discussed elsewhere.

We further learn that at that time not only the Ursian church but also the church of Classe had men belonging to the ecclesiastical order. George the priest, for example, governed the church of Saint Severus, which was likewise at Classe.

Thus we learn that the clergy of Classe were distinguished from the clergy of Ravenna. Indications of this matter also appear in the letters of Pope Felix, which are to be read in the *Life of Bishop Ecclesius*.

# LIFE OF SAINT NEON

[Col. 0517]

## CHAPTER ONE

**Buildings constructed by Neon in the church of Ravenna.**
[Col. 0517D] **Neon XVIII.** He had a beautiful appearance and led a most holy and spiritual life. He was the builder of the aforementioned Petriana church, part of which his predecessor had constructed from the foundations; hence it was necessary for his successors to complete the work of their predecessor. Thereafter, when all the buildings had been erected and the roofs of the temple repaired, he had them painted in various colors. He very beautifully decorated the fountains of the Ursian church. In mosaic and with gilded tesserae he surrounded the vault with images and names of the apostles, and he encircled the walls with stones of various kinds. His name was inscribed in letters of stone:

> Yield, ancient name; yield, antiquity, to renewal;  
> Behold, more beautifully shines the glory of the renewed fountain.  
> For the great-hearted and supreme priest Neon  
> Paid for this, arranging everything in beautiful adornment.

[Col. 0518C] Finally, beneath the episcopal residence of the Ursian church, which is called the Five-Dagubita, he constructed a building from its foundations, [Col. 0518D] and brought it to completion. On either side of the dining hall he built marvelous windows, and there he ordered the floors of the dining hall to be adorned with different stones. On the wall, in the part of the church, he ordered painted the story of the psalm that we sing every day, namely, “Praise the Lord from the heavens,” together with the Flood; and on another wall, situated above the river, he had the story of our Lord Jesus Christ embellished with colors—when, as we read, he satisfied so many thousands of people with five loaves and two fish.

On one side of the front below the dining hall he embellished the structure of the world, in which we read every day the following hexameter verses:
