> In the beginning, at the world’s first origin,  
> When the high power of the Father and the might of the Son  
> Made the sea, the earth, and heaven’s shining realms;  
> And when the new sun, moon, day, and dawn gleamed,  
> [Col. 0519A] And heaven, bearing the stars, shone with that light,  
> One man, a man of earth, sprang forth in the new world  
> From virgin soil, innocent in body and servant-like.  
> He alone deserved to be called the image of God,  
> For the love of the heavenly Father produced in the world  
> A human being like himself and established him as lord.  
> The almighty Creator himself, most sweet,  
> Enriched him for a long age with abundant resources.  
> To him he yielded all the rewards of the forests together.  
> He commanded the earth to produce its maternal offspring.  
> His were the snow-white sheep, with their clear voices, amid shining meadows;  
> His too the high-crested horse and tawny lions;  
> His everywhere the branching-antlered deer;  
> His the winged flocks of birds and the fish through the waters.  
> For whatever God had prepared for man,  
> He handed over to him and compelled all things alike to serve him by his word.  
> Yet at the outset, in heavenly instructions, he commanded him  
> To observe his law and the life-giving precepts,  
> And not dare to eat the forbidden fruit.  
> Disregarding the command, he thus lost everything along with himself.

On another front was painted the story of the apostle Peter, and the following metrical verses were inscribed beneath it:

[Col. 0519B]

> Receive gladly, holy one; do not despise this little poem,  
> These few words spoken in our language to your praise.  
> Rejoice, Simon Peter; accept the office entrusted to you.  
> Behold [reading: *En quod*], the great King from on high wished you to undertake it.  
> Receive from heaven the hanging sheets filled with creatures,  
> Sent to you, Peter, bearing various animals.  
> God soon commanded you to slaughter and eat them.  
> There can be no doubt in any respect [Latin: *in nullo*; variant: *nullis*] concerning what the almighty Father,  
> To whom supreme power over creation belongs, created as clean.  
> Rejoice, Simon Peter, whom the golden mind [reading: *mens aurea*] of Christ rejoices  
> To adorn with apostolic light through all the years.  
> In you the holy Church of God, flourishing, shines;  
> In you the Prince of the heavenly choir, born for eternity,  
> Established the firm foundations of his house.  
> Your virtue, authority, and faith are renowned among all.  
> Among the twelve brothers you stand first,  
> Yourself in the foremost place; new laws are given to you from above,  
> You who tame the savage hearts of men and soothe their breasts,  
> And teach [*tu*] all Christ-worshipers to be throughout the world [or: the City].  
> Now, through your merits, the glory of Christ prepares the kingdom.

## CHAPTER II. The death of Neon and the translation of his body. What does “the Strong Arm” mean?

After all these things had been completed, he died on the third day before the Ides of February [Note: [Col. 0519D] Marginal note: “This was in the time of the orthodoxy of the mother Galla Placidia.” BACCH.]. Formerly he had been buried in the Basilica of the Apostles before the altar of the blessed apostle Peter, beneath a porphyry stone. We have now removed him from there and buried him beside the seat of that basilica; and he was transferred through the place called “the Strong Arm.” But you do not know where it is called the Strong Arm, or for what reason it received that name. Since there are few veterans who know, I therefore wish you to know where and for what reason it was so called.

When you go to the region of the Apostles, not far from the wall of Ovilio, enter beneath the arch of the blessed apostle Peter, where an image of our Lord Jesus Christ is painted with his arm extended; and on one side there is an image of the chosen vessel, Paul, and … [lacuna] … and these too are painted. I have told you where it was called so; now I shall tell you why.

Two men, wishing to bind themselves to each other by a pact, said one to the other, who had a child: “I beg a small favor of you; I ask that my entreaty not return in vain.” The other replied: “I shall not burden you; let what pleases you be done.” He said: “Give me your son, so that I may be his father through holy baptism; I shall take him from the sanctified font. Let us be fathers together—you his natural father, and I his spiritual father.”

The other replied: “In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, let it be so.” And it was done. From that day, after the child had been baptized, they were fathers together and held affection for one another in the Holy Spirit and with the kiss of peace—for this is fitting for those who do such things with one another, since they place not human beings but the Holy Spirit as mediator between them.

And so that you may know that the spiritual father is greater than the natural father: the natural father begot his son from sin, and the son was born to him in sin, and the son himself remains in sin. But this spiritual father, after receiving him from the waters of baptism, when the devil and his pomps had been removed, begot a spiritual son from the holy font; he received as sanctified the son newly born through water and the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0519D] Marginal note: “How much more, then, was he who had previously been born in sin from sin afterward sanctified through the Holy Spirit.”].

It happened at that time that one of these aforesaid co-fathers lent three hundred solidi to his fellow co-father. When they had arrived at the place that you heard mentioned above, the Strong Arm, one said to the other: “I beg you, lend me secretly three hundred gold solidi.” The other replied: “Let us meet here tomorrow morning, and I shall bring it between you and me.”

When the following day dawned, they came to the place where they had agreed to meet. After the money had been counted, the lender said to his co-father: “Here, co-father, take what you requested; only consider between yourself and me how you are to repay me. Will you not give me a guarantor? Will you not summon mediators? Will you not give a pledge? Nor do you want anyone to know, out of fear of disgrace; and in all this I agree with you.”

The debtor replied: “A term has been firmly established between you and me, which we cannot transgress. Give me this money merely as a loan; you will lose nothing. In God’s presence I tell you: where I stand, there I shall repay you.”

The lender replied to his co-father: “Let almighty God be mediator between us, whose image is painted here; and let this arm of the Savior, strong and terrible, himself be our guarantor, and let these two great princes and apostles, Peter and Paul, be witnesses between you and me. This right hand that brought the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt, and this strong arm, shall today be my guarantor, because I shall repay you your money.”

Then, looking upon the three hundred solidi that had been counted, he said to the face of the Savior: “Lord almighty God, in accordance with the very words we have spoken, I give these solidi to this co-father of mine; be yourself the guarantor. Through your holy arm I hand them over to him, so that you may stand as guarantor: if he does not return them to me, you return them to me.”

This pleased him, and having established the term, they firmly appointed the strong arm of the Savior as guarantor between them. The debtor received the money and immediately departed to conduct business. When he began trading here and there, he made four times as much. He entered the city of Constantinople, and, seeing that his money was multiplying in his hands, he did not want to return to Ravenna. Behold, the appointed time for repaying the sum arrived, but he did not come.

The co-father who had lent the money came to the image of the Savior, saying: “Lord God, the appointed day has now passed; you were my guarantor for my co-father. Watch over my case, lest I suffer loss; return to me my solidi, which I gave through your strong arm.”

That very night the Savior’s arm appeared in a dream to the debtor and said to him: “Go, return the money that you received to your co-father, for I am your guarantor, since he troubles me every day.” When he had not come, the lender went again [reading: *iterum*] to the image of the Savior and complained as before. That same night the holy arm appeared to him and issued the warning you have just heard.

One day the man who had given the money came and began to utter words of reproach before the holy image of our Lord, saying: “O Lord, why do you not give me justice? You are my guarantor. Through your strong arm I gave the money. You rule heavenly things, govern earthly things, command the sea—and do you not constrain one man? You gave me that money, and if you wish to take it away, who can prevent you? No one, because everything is subject to your power.

“If an earthly man had been my guarantor, I would have compelled him through a judge, or I would have used force against him through a citizen of Fecicus [*ei vim fecissem*; the reading is uncertain], or I would have recovered my money by one means or another. You, who are Lord of heaven and earth—unless you command its return, what am I to do? The heavens are not pure before you; the sun and moon do not shine; angels and archangels tremble; the earth melts; mountains flow down; all the elements fail. What am I, that I should dare to speak to you? Let only your mercy be upon me: defend my case and restore what is mine. Behold, the two apostles chosen by you are both witnesses before you. In their presence your strong arm [reading: *tuum*] became my guarantor. If I speak otherwise, let them themselves bear witness, for they are most truthful, and you have made their tongues the keys of heaven.”

After saying this, he groaned and departed. That very night the image of our Savior appeared in a dream to the debtor, his co-father, and said: “Return quickly to Ravenna and repay your co-father the solidi, for this arm of mine became your guarantor. He has reproached me, and I cannot endure his complaint. And know that if you do not go quickly, and he troubles me further [reading: *mihi*, “me”], you will lose everything you have acquired here; I shall hand your body over to the scourges, and you will be in the greatest tribulation all the days of your life, and there you will perish. I myself will pay your co-father double the solidi from my treasures.”

Then, rising at dawn, he conducted business as best he could, boarded a ship that very day, and returned to Ravenna. When his co-father, the man who had given the money, heard this, he went joyfully to his house, as though to visit him. Among other matters he began to inquire about the money he had lent. The other replied that all his business had prospered and that the solidi had quadrupled.

The creditor said to his co-father: “If that is so, blessed be God; return my solidi to me.” The other replied: “I shall gladly do so, but not today, for it is late. Tomorrow morning let us go before my guarantor, that is, the Strong Arm, which has driven me so forcefully these past days. There I shall repay you, in the presence of our two princely witnesses.”

The next day the debtor brought four hundred gold pieces. They went to the place where he had borrowed the money, and he handed it over. After counting the four hundred solidi again, the debtor said to his creditor and co-father: “You have treated me well, because you raised me from poverty, and almighty God blessed my business and quadrupled the money. Take now the three hundred solidi that you lent me in the presence of my guarantor and our two witnesses, and in addition I give you these other hundred, both because I was not ready on the appointed day and as a gift.”

The other replied to his co-father: “Far be it from me to receive more than I gave. May that strong arm, which is mediator between you and me, not permit me to take interest even up to the strap of a shoe.”

The debtor replied: “I swear to you by this strong arm—and I declare the truth [reading: *et veritatem manifesto*]—that as my money was multiplying in my hands, if this arm had not compelled me three times, I would not have returned to Ravenna this year. On those nights, and on the days that followed them, it came to me in dreams and warned me, saying: ‘Go and repay your creditor the money you took, because your co-father troubles me; today he has disturbed me as your guarantor.’ Thus it warned me twice.

“On one night of this month, however, the holy image of our Lord came to me and began to rebuke me, saying: ‘Why do you not return to repay the money to your creditor and co-father, which you promised to repay through this arm of mine? That man has troubled me greatly today and moreover said to me that if he had had an earthly man as guarantor, he would already have repaid him. Rise quickly, go, and repay it, for I cannot endure further complaints. They are harsh to me; lest perhaps through harshness he blaspheme, you will have to render an account not only for the money but also for that. Do not delay; rise and go.

“‘Know that if you delay, I shall give the solidi from my treasury, while you will remain here, lose everything, and suffer harm in your body.’”

“On the following day I entered a *cymba* [*cumbum*, variant *cumbam*; a small boat] and, with favorable winds, hastened to this God-protected city of Ravenna to return everything to you, as I have done. Now I ask you to take these hundred gold pieces, because I wronged you, so that no harmful liability may remain attached to me.”

The other replied: “I have sworn to you by the Lord and by this strong arm, which brought you back here, that I shall accept nothing—not even a handful of dust—except your affection, which I possess every day. And so that you may understand my words: when at night this arm was pressing me concerning my [variant: *mea*] justice, I was interceding on your behalf; and blessed be God, who brought you back safe and sound to your own.

“Now be innocent of this matter before the eternal God and before me. May almighty God permit our affection, as it has been established here, to remain forever. Let us see and act carefully, so that neither of us defrauds the other, since we appointed this strong arm as mediator between us.”

Saying this, they wept for joy and kissed one another. They departed in peace. From that day, because of this event, the place was called the Strong Arm, down to the present day; but few know the reason. From there the body of the blessed Neon, archbishop, was transferred and buried, as we noted above.

You have seen the house that he built, and in that house, where the images of the apostles Peter and Paul were made in tesserae on either side beside the cross, you observed and read one line of verse containing the words: “Lord Bishop Neon, may he grow old for us.” He sat [ruled] for … years, … months, … days …

# OBSERVATIONS ON THE LIFE OF SAINT NEON

[Col. 0523] What are the Five-Dagubita and the dining hall? The term *co-father* and its meaning. The formalities of contracting a loan. What is a citizen of Fecicus? *Cumbum*, *cumbe*, *cymba*.

### I

Among the buildings that Neon took care to construct, one seems especially worthy of observation: the one that our author says was called the Five-Dagubita, a part of which—namely, the dining hall—he describes with sufficient precision. *Dagubita*, I think, means nearly the same as *accubita* in writers of corrupt Latin, and *ἀκούβιτον* among authors of corrupt Greek. Anastasius, in his account of Gregory III, says: “Likewise he restored anew from the foundations and decorated the *accubita* that are situated in ruins at St. Peter’s.” See Ducange in both Glossaries.

Agnellus distinguishes the building called the Five-Dagubita from the dining hall as a whole from a part, and the building as though it were *διὰ πέντε τὰ ἀκούβιτα*—“because of five *accubita*”—from the dining hall, namely the particular place where the bishop reclined at banquets with the principal clergy and laymen on specified solemn occasions.

Regarding such places, the aforementioned Ducange asks that one consult his *Constantinopolis Christiana*, book II, chapter 6, where he discusses the tribunal of the Nine *Accubita*, which can indeed help to illuminate this passage of Agnellus. Learned men also think that the *Tribunalion of the Nineteen Accubita*, with its *silentiarius* or secretary, was the same institution. There the *symbouloi*—the συμβούλοι—assembled, men bound to silence who carried out some business; therefore, in Theophanes, they interpret *Σιλέντιον ἐκράτησεν* as “he held a synod,” or “he held a consultation.” On this subject, see the aforementioned Ducange in both Glossaries.

As for the *accubita* intended for the banquets of ecclesiastics, the supreme pontiffs at the Leonine Basilica in Rome possessed such a place near the Lateran buildings. There, on the feast of Easter and on other more solemn occasions, they received the clergy at a banquet according to established ceremonies; and when kings and princes residing in Rome were present, they were received there as well. I saw this place, still elegantly adorned with mosaic work.

In the Roman Order of Benedict, canon of St. Peter, which our Mabillon published in the second volume of the *Museum Italicum* and which, as he conjectures, was written before the pontificate of Celestine II, the rite is described by which the pontiff received the cardinals at a banquet on Easter Day. Since it distinguishes *cubitus*, or *accubitus*, from *cubitorium*, or *cubitorum*, and sets forth the splendor of the banquet, it deserves to be described here:

> “The judges lead him—the pope—on that day into the great Leonine Basilica, into the chamber where eleven benches and one seat have been prepared around the table of the lord pontiff, and where his bed is properly prepared in the figure of the twelve apostles around Christ’s table when they ate the Passover. There five cardinals and five deacons, together with the *primicerius*, recline at the banquet, after the presbyterium has first been given in the chamber with the hands, as on the day of the Nativity of the Lord. From there he rises and comes to the place called the *Cubitorum*, where the roasted lamb is blessed. He blesses it [Col. 0524A] and returns to the prepared bed of the table. Then the lord pontiff takes bread from the lamb and first offers it to the chief basilicarius, saying: ‘What you do, do quickly; as he received it to his condemnation, so receive it for forgiveness.’ He puts it into his mouth, and the man receives and eats it. He gives the rest of the lamb to the eleven reclining guests and to the others whom he wishes, and so all eat. When half the banquet has passed, by order of the archdeacon a certain deacon rises and reads a lesson. By order of the lord pontiff, the singers sing a sequence appropriate to Easter, with instruments playing. When it is finished, they go and kiss the feet of the pontiff, who gives them a cup full of drink, and they receive one Byzantine coin from the sacellarius.”

Thus the aforementioned Order, no. 48; nearly the same account is found in the Roman Order of Cencius the Chamberlain, no. 35, where the reading is more correctly *Cubitorium* instead of *τὸ Cubitorum*.

You see that the verses inscribed on the dining hall are sufficiently elegant and reflect credit on their author. I have corrected several errors that must be attributed to the copyists; [Col. 0524B] some, however, in which I could not conveniently determine what error lay concealed, I have left for the reader to correct.

### III

Having noted Neon’s death, Agnellus indicates that the translation of his body took place in his own time, and on this account too he commends everything he had related about him. He then proceeds to explain the reason why that image of the Savior was called the Strong Arm.

That image may perhaps be the one mentioned at the beginning of the synod celebrated by Archbishop Gerbert in the second year of the reign of Otto III, in the eleventh indiction, beneath the image of the Savior below the doors of the greater church of Ravenna. Ughellus published this synod from a manuscript in the Vatican Library in his *Ravennate Bishops*, volume II, page 351.

In Agnellus’s narrative, one first observes the bond and pact by which the father and the sponsor of the baptized child were joined. Hence the name *co-father* was regarded as a sign of the closest relationship, not only between the sponsor and the baptized person, but also [Col. 0524C] between the sponsor and the baptized person’s parents. From this arose the canonical bond of spiritual kinship, concerning which see the canons and, finally, the Council of Trent, session 24, *On Reform*, chapter 2.

The term sometimes appears to have been used to signify an exceptional degree of friendship. Thus Ducange notes that among the letters of Stephen III there is one with the inscription: “To Pippin, king and our spiritual co-father.” Perhaps, however, by this form of address the pontiff intended to encourage Pippin to protect the Church, calling him father together with himself with respect to that same Church. A pact of friendship and a relationship of co-fatherhood is found in Peter Damian, book II, letter 17.

### IV

Here you have the formalities and parties involved in contracting a loan. A guarantor is employed, who is also called a mediator, as are witnesses; the fixed time at which the borrower promises to return the loan is called the *constitutum*. On all these matters, the aforementioned Ducange has treated the subject learnedly in the appropriate places of his Glossary of Latin. I decline to copy him, lest I seem to plunder another’s work.

It is more difficult to determine who is meant by the name “Citizen of Fecicus,” where Agnellus introduces the man who had given the loan speaking to the image of the Savior in this manner:

> “If an earthly man had been my guarantor, I would have compelled him through a judge, or I would have used force against him through a citizen of Fecicus [*ei vim fecissem*; the reading is uncertain], or I would have recovered my money by one means or another.”

From the context it appears that a citizen is meant who, either by office or because of the reputation he had acquired among the citizens in such matters, could compel a debtor or guarantor to make repayment. Otherwise, the matter remains obscure.

Elsewhere he mentions the *cumbum* as a kind of ship, by which the borrower returned from Constantinople to Ravenna; others take *cumba* as equivalent to *cymba*, “small boat.” See the often-mentioned Ducange. The remaining points are clear and require no further examination.

# LIFE OF SAINT EXUPERANTIUS

[Col. 0525]

## CHAPTER I. The church of the blessed Agnes built. The Silver City constructed during a procession. Patrician Felix killed. The arrival of Eudoxia. The Tricolos built.

**Exuperantius XIX**, an elderly man, humble and gentle, prudent in good works. What his predecessors had built, he preserved intact. During his episcopate, the church of the blessed Agnes was built by Gemellus, subdeacon of this holy church of Ravenna and governor of Sicily; he greatly enriched it with gold and silver and sacred hangings. He also constructed the Silver City during the procession of the nativity of that martyr, and it endured down to our own times.

In his days Patrician Felix was killed at the steps of the Ursian church in the month of May, and the lady Eudoxia Augusta was made lady at Ravenna on the eighth day before the Ides of August. Our elders and long-lived men told me nothing more about his life. He has no noteworthy history. He was the builder of the Tricolos, but he did not complete it.

## CHAPTER II. The reason for the history is explained. The death and tomb of Saint Exuperantius.

If any hesitation should arise among you who read this *Pontifical*, and you should wish to ask why he did not narrate the deeds of this pontiff as he did those of the other predecessors, listen to the reason.

I, Agnellus, also called Andreas, a humble priest of this holy church of Ravenna, composed this aforesaid *Pontifical*—from the time of the blessed Apollinaris, after his death, nearly eight hundred years and more having passed—at the request and under compulsion of the brothers of this see. Wherever I found what they had done with greater certainty, I brought it before your eyes; and whatever I heard from elders and long-lived men, I did not deprive your eyes of seeing.

Where I found no history, nor any account of what their lives had been, neither through aged and ancient men, nor through buildings, nor through any other authority, I composed their lives, with God’s help and through your prayers, so that there might not be a gap [variant: *Et ubi*, “And where”] among the holy pontiffs, but that the sequence might show how one after another they occupied this see. I believe that I have not lied, because they were men of prayer, chaste, charitable, and gainers for God of human souls [variant: *animas / animarum hominum*, “souls / souls of men”].

If any of you should perhaps wonder how I could know their true appearance, know that painting taught me, because images were always made in their own times in their likeness. And if an argument should arise from the paintings, on the grounds that I ought not to have asserted that these were their portraits, Ambrose, bishop of Milan, sang of the likeness of the blessed apostle Paul in the Passion of the blessed martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, saying: “His face had been taught to me by a painting.”

He who completed his pontificate by divine command died on the fourth day before the Kalends of June and was buried in the aforementioned Basilica of Saint Agnes the Martyr, before the altar, beneath a porphyry stone. Others say that he was buried behind the altar beneath a porphyry stone. He sat [ruled] for … years, … months, … days …

# OBSERVATIONS ON THE LIFE OF SAINT EXUPERANTIUS

[Col. 0526] What is the Silver City, and what is a procession? Agnellus’s reliability. The other matters related about Exuperantius were unknown to Agnellus.

### I

In the second part of the preceding dissertation, section 5, while engaged in another matter, I prefaced a few observations that may nevertheless sufficiently teach the reader what I think about the common opinion of those who, in more recent centuries, have written about the affairs of Ravenna and who believed that, from this passage of Agnellus, they possessed adequate evidence for writing that Exuperantius, bishop of Ravenna, built the town of Argenta.

The matter now requires more careful examination. Agnellus’s words are these:

> “During his [Exuperantius’s] time, the church of the blessed Agnes was built by Gemellus, subdeacon of this holy church of Ravenna and governor of Sicily; he greatly enriched it with gold and silver and sacred hangings, and constructed the Silver City during the procession of the nativity of that martyr, and it endured down to our own times.”

I confess that here I see nothing solid upon which the alleged construction of Argenta can be built. For from what other ancient or more recent writer can we recognize that town being called a *civitas*? Agnellus himself, below, in the Life of Bishop Agnellus, calls Argenta itself a *rus*, a rural estate. He says:

> “He acquired the estate in the Church of Ravenna called Argentea, and within that estate he built the monastery of the blessed George from its foundations.”

How could the same man who had previously called Argenta a *civitas* later call it a *rus*?

Moreover, those words that certainly refer to the Silver City, and which say that it was constructed “during the procession of the nativity of that martyr,” followed by “and it endured down to our own times,” seem clear enough, I think, to show that they cannot possibly refer to the city or town of Argenta. The latter words would mean that Argenta had perished by the time the author was writing—for that is what the words themselves signify—and Agnellus uses the same phrase in similar circumstances when speaking of things that had fallen into ruin during his lifetime.

Thus, below, in the Life of Maximianus, he says: “And the aforesaid episcopal residences of the Arians remained down to our own times”; and elsewhere he likes to speak in the same way.

But what does it mean that the Silver City was constructed during the procession of the Martyr’s nativity? I shall say what I think. The passage concerns gifts offered by Gemellus, subdeacon and governor of Sicily, to the holy Church of Agnes, which he himself had built. Among these gifts was the Silver City, intended for use in the procession customarily held on the recurring holy day of Saint Agnes’s nativity. This gift had perished by Agnellus’s time through the extravagance of later bishops, whom he will discuss in their proper place.

Thus explained, the sentence coheres properly. Since there were various ancient kinds of processions, I have no doubt that this passage concerns the procession connected with the martyr’s worship.

The Byzantines were said to hold or perform a *πρόκενσον* or *πρόκεσσον* when they proceeded with solemn pomp to the palaces near Constantinople or remained there. On this subject see Ducange, learnedly, in *Constantinopolis Sacra*, book IV, section 11, no. 2, and in his Greek Glossary.

From the material assembled by that author, however, it appears that the same name was applied to the ecclesiastical rite of proceeding in which bishops, with clergy and people, proceeded on designated solemn occasions. Perhaps it was called *πρόκενσον* because the emperor too was accustomed to appear with pomp and ceremony.

This is supported by the Council of Constantinople under Menas, Acts III, where it says:

> Ἐν συνάξει τῆς δεσποίνης ἡμῶν τῆς θεοτόκου, καὶ ἁγίας Μαρίας, τῆς διακειμένης ἐν Βλαχέρνης, προκένσου ὄντος βασιλικοῦ

> “At the assembly of our Lady, the Mother of God, and of Saint Mary, which is in Blachernae, when the imperial procession was being held.”

I think Anastasius is speaking of processions of this sort, specifically called so because of the emperor’s participation, when in his Life of Agatho he reports that, at the pope’s insistence, the emperor forbade a certain bishop to come to the procession.

That processions of this kind, with the emperor’s participation and pomp, were held at Ravenna during the time of Exuperantius and several of his successors is suggested by Valentinian’s residence there; it also gives room for the conjecture that the customs and rites of Constantinople were in many respects cultivated by the Church of Ravenna. Thus churches were called by the same names as the most famous churches of Constantinople, such as Saint Mary in Blachernae; the writer of that work was Abbot Agnellus.

### II

In these processions, I would rather believe that celebration and rejoicing in honor of the martyrs’ nativity were intended than penitence or expiation, which were otherwise the primary purposes of litanies, processions, and rogations. I think Jerome speaks of processions of this kind, celebrated with a large crowd, in his letter 22 to Eustochium, excluding that woman from processions:

> “Let martyrs be sought in your chamber; there will never be a reason for going out if you are always going out whenever it is necessary.”

The same is suggested by letter 12 to Gaudentius and letter 7 to Laeta.

I think we should also include among processions the pomp with which, on feast days throughout the year, the bishop or Roman pontiff proceeded to the mysteries of the Mass. These are described in the Roman Orders, in which, while the pontiff was proceeding, disputes and cases were settled, as appears from the First Order published by Mabillon, no. 2. Mabillon himself notes there:

> “Thus cases were sometimes concluded during the procession itself; hence some learned men think that the word *processus* in our French language—and indeed also in Italian—came to mean a lawsuit.”

Moreover, the distinction between processions held for the sake of joy and celebration and those held for the sake of expiation and penitence appears from the rite itself. In the latter, a gathering was held in one church and a station in another; in the former, however, they proceeded without gatherings.

See the Index of Stations published by Mabillon himself in volume II of the *Museum Italicum*, where gatherings are noted for each day during Lent, but not for the other days.

I know that Mabillon himself taught something almost opposite. Deterred by his authority, I had nearly withdrawn from writing what I have just stated. He calls the stations preceded by a solemn gathering “private” in his preliminary Commentary, no. 5. But the distinction of the days and occasions on which they were held seems to suggest otherwise.

Hence even now that prayer, which is improperly called a gathering and is made for the sake of expiation, is always added to the prayers of the day. Moreover, I think it can scarcely be doubted from reading the Orders that both kinds were solemn, since they describe the solemn pomp of proceeding. Thus in the First Order, no. 2, and elsewhere.

### III

What sort of gift, then, was the Silver City? Unless there is a scribal error here—which I strongly suspect—we may infer that an image of a city was represented on a panel, covered with silver leaf, and displayed as an ornament during the more solemn processions, especially on the nativity of Saint Agnes. For the objects carried in processions otherwise belonged to the *ἀκολουθία*, the liturgical accompaniment of the Mass.

This finally proves that Agnellus is not speaking here of the town of Argenta: that city was called a *civitas* because it had a bishop, whereas other places were called *castella*. See the evidence for this in Ducange under the word *Castrum* and in the appendix to the first volume under *Civitas*.

This also shows that the construction or building of the Silver City should rather be attributed to Gemellus than to Exuperantius. It is therefore astonishing that the beginnings of the town of Argenta should have been so neatly inferred from this passage and attributed to Exuperantius.

### IV

The words “builder of the Tricolos, but not its completer” seem to have intruded here from elsewhere, since below Agnellus says that this building was founded by Peter Chrysologus, and the added verses prove the same thing. What immediately precedes and follows strongly suggests to the reader that these words can scarcely be separated from their proper context.

V. What follows strongly supports Agnellus’s credibility; for he candidly admits that he committed to writing what he learned either from documents, buildings, or the tradition of his episcopal predecessors, but that, when all such evidence was lacking, he said what seemed true to him on probable conjecture, so as not to interrupt the succession of pontiffs. Many therefore have wrongly thought that they possessed sufficient grounds, from eulogies conveying only general information, for assigning certain facts to particular bishops. But the pseudo-Dextrine tales praised by Faber are refuted even more decisively, as is the conjecture that Jerome wrote a letter to this Exuperantius. Agnellus knew none of these things, nor did the men of Ravenna who lived before Agnellus. Would that Agnellus had everywhere preserved the good faith which, as we acknowledge, he observed to some extent in recounting earlier matters, and had maintained it also in more recent affairs, indulging less in the fables of his fellow countrymen and in his hostility toward the Roman See!

# LIFE OF SAINT JOHN ΤΟΥ ΑΓΓΕΛΟΠΤΟΥ [THE ANGEL-SEER]

[Col. 0527]

## CHAPTER ONE. A brief eulogy of John. The building of the Basilica of Saint Lawrence and the Chapel of Saint Stephen. The deeds of Lauricius.

[Col. 0527C] John XX [the first, Bacch.] was greatly venerable for his virtue, nourisher of the poor, adorned with chastity, a lover of purity, at whose prayer angelic hosts descended. He was of medium height, thin-faced, emaciated by fasting, and a provider of food for the needy.

In his time the Church of Blessed Lawrence the martyr, situated in Caesarea, was built by Lauricius, chief of the bedchamber of the emperor Honorius. We see it furnished with the utmost care and with buildings of remarkable size. Nevertheless, I shall not be silent about the said church, or about how I heard of it from those who related the story.

The emperor Honorius ordered this Lauricius to build him a palace in Caesarea. Taking the money, he arrived in Caesarea and there built the aforesaid basilica of the blessed martyr. When everything had been completed, he returned to his master to report that the palace entrusted to him had been finished. He immediately found him disturbed; seated in imperial dress, Honorius began angrily to ask the architect Lauricius whether the entire royal palace which he had ordered him to build had been completed in all its parts.

An ancient and envious deception had brought malicious men to whisper to the emperor that blessed Lauricius had built not an imperial residence but a church. In reply, Lauricius said that he had honorably constructed a great palace, supported courtyards, lofty towers, and common sleeping chambers along the sides of the house. The emperor’s anger subsided. When the emperor Augustus Honorius arrived at Caesarea after a long journey and saw the lofty buildings, he was greatly pleased. When he had entered inside, Lauricius fled at full speed behind the holy altar, so that he might escape.

When Honorius ordered him to be seized, he fell prostrate on his face upon the ground and, falling into ecstasy, the most precious jewel which he wore in the crown on his head became fixed in one of the stones. Raising his head upward, and after his clouded eyes had regained their sight, he saw behind the altar of blessed Lawrence—which the most blessed pope John had consecrated—the aforesaid Lauricius standing, while Lawrence, the athlete of Christ, held his hand upon Lauricius’s neck.

Then the emperor judged Lauricius more righteous than himself. Abandoning his anger, he began to honor him as a father, and kept him among all the others in the palace as a second [reading uncertain]. He lived in this world [or: in this light] for ninety-six years. In the time of that emperor he died in a good old age.

[Col. 0529B] The king followed the bier with his grieving soldiers, and Lauricius was buried in the monastery of Saints Gervasius and Protasius, beside the aforesaid church, wonderfully adorned with golden mosaic, various kinds of stones, and different metals joined to the walls.

That chest in which his most distinguished body rests was so translucent, some say, that passers-by could see the body beneath it. Why it does not appear today as it did in ancient times, I recently learned. I do not know the man’s name, but an emperor wished to remove it for his own use. One night blessed Lauricius appeared to the church’s custodian and said: “Bring ashes and water, and wash my tomb from here onward carefully.” When this had been done, the brightness disappeared.

On another day, when the masons had come to remove it, they saw that it had deteriorated. They reported this to the administrator who was in charge of the revenues, and then, after reporting it, they left for the imperial courts.

To this day the chest itself is supported neither by earth nor by stone. Before you enter the chamber of the chest, look to your right, beside the place where the figures of the Three Children are depicted in mosaic. There you will find golden letters containing the following:

> “To Stephen, Protasius [Gervasius], the blessed martyr, and to himself, Lauricius dedicated this eternal memorial on the third day before the Kalends of October, in the fifteenth year of Theodosius and [the consulship of] Placidius Valentinianus.”

[Note: [Col. 0529D] Marginal note: “This Theodosius was the son of Arcadius, son of Theodosius I. This Valentinian was the son-in-law of this Theodosius II and the son of Placidia and Constantius, who rest at Ravenna.” BACCH.]

[Col. 0529D] … And on the arch of the greater apse, insofar as we were able to read part of it, we found the following inscription: that they had completed the construction in four years and six months, and that everything had been finished. At the entrance to the church we found it written that Opilius adorned it greatly with silver and gold [or: had adorned its façade, Opilius himself].

And if you investigate more carefully, much of the foreign ornamentation [Note: [Col. 0529D] *Faralitius.* I think *foralitius* should be read, that is, brought from outside the Ursian Church, from which it was transported.] of the larger vessels—both crowns and hanging chalices [Note: [Col. 0530D] Hanging chalices were the same as handled chalices.]—which we see in the Ursian Church among its ornaments, was taken from this basilica of the martyr. Opilius himself was buried on the women’s side, around the middle of the lower section.

That jewel of which we spoke above was so superior to other gems that by its light a person could walk through the church at night. Some also say that it shone outwardly, and the mark of the stone where it was fixed remains visible to the present day.

## CHAPTER II. Attila’s arrival. John’s encounter with him. Attila appeased.

[Note: [Col. 0530D] These matters concern John, the successor of Chrysologus.]

At that time, when the blessed John already mentioned held the episcopal chair of the Church of Ravenna, it happened that Attila, king of the Huns, ravaged the borders of Italy and slaughtered the bodies of peoples with his swords. When he had hastened toward the Ravenna region, intending to overthrow it and kill its inhabitants with weapons, his enemies came toward Ravenna for one day and another, wearing cuirasses and carrying shields, lying scattered across the sandy places like a swarm of locusts.

The king himself, clad in armor and surrounded by weapons of war, walked with his army, protecting his chest with a shield-boss and wearing a crested helmet. When the most holy bishop John perceived this, he prostrated himself, face to the ground, and devoted himself entirely to prayer with great lamentation and abundant tears before almighty God. He asked for the death of his own soul, so that he might not see his sons or daughters, the citizens of Ravenna, dragged away or dispersed into destruction or annihilation; so that his Church might not be defiled by wicked and most cruel men; and so that he might not see the destruction of the city delivered into the plunder of marauders.

He prayed that he might not see those souls whom he himself had won from pagan superstition for God alone subjected to pagan hands, that they might not return again to the error of paganism, and that the most deceitful devil might not enslave those souls to his dominion.

While the holy man remained awake throughout the whole night, unceasingly entreating the Lord for his sheep on bended knees, beating his breast with blows and stretching out his hands, he prayed to God in these words:

> “Almighty God, whose wonders are indescribable, hear me, your humble and sinful servant; receive my prayer, most merciful Father. May my tears come before the sight of your mercy. Stand by me, my God, who made heaven from nothing and established the earth by your word; who set the peaks of the mountains upon the mass of the earth; who formed humanity from the liquid element, and in whose creation you delighted, commanding humanity to fear you alone.
>
> “Under your command, Lord, all things tremble. Before your presence the heavens flee, the earth trembles, the mountains are shaken, the streams are disturbed, the angels tremble, the archangels fear, dominions and principalities tremble, and powers fall. Clouds and the air are scattered; the sun obscures its rays; the moon grows dark; and the brightness of the stars is diminished by gloom.
>
> “Have mercy on us, creator of the human race. Deliver us with a strong hand and an exalted arm; save us by your holy and victorious right hand. You are God in heaven above and on earth below, who plunged Pharaoh with his chariots and armies into the depths of the sea and protected the Israelite camps; who overthrew Amalek and crushed the Amorites; who by your holy angel struck down one hundred and forty-five thousand of the Assyrian army.
>
> “I beseech you, almighty God, to grant us help from your holy heavens, for you shatter wars. ‘The Lord’ is his name, through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns as God with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.”

After completing his prayer, he rose from the place drenched with the dew of tears.

Very early the next day, the most blessed man went forth as though for the solemnities of Mass. He was dressed in angelic vestments [that is, ornaments, Bacch.], and with priests and clerics, with censers offering incense before them, proceeding amid great light, singing and praising God, they hastened together toward the aforesaid king Attila.

For divine mercy exerted such power that the king’s heart seemed not merely to have abandoned the allurements of ferocity or to have laid aside his glittering garments; rather, on behalf of the most holy man, the king would have fought with his armies against another king, if necessary, and would afterward have defended those whom he had recently come to destroy.

The king was seated on his royal throne, clothed in gold-woven garments and purple. Seeing the bishop approaching him from a distance with his priests singing psalms, he said to his men:

> “Who are these exceedingly white men singing psalms? From where have they come, and what do they want? I have never seen such men with my own eyes—whiter than snow, more beautiful than all others, and most distinguished. And this man who leads them—is he like an angel of God?”

Those present answered the king:

> “Most invincible lord, triumphant king, the man whom you see standing and weeping in the midst of these white-clad men has come to implore your powerful arm to spare them. He asks for mercy and seeks your compassion.”

The king said to them:

> “For what reason?”

They replied:

> “So that you may not deliver flourishing Ravenna to destruction, but restore the city’s citizens to joy.”

Again the king asked:

> “And where is he from?”

They said:

> “He himself governs the seat of its episcopate.”

The king said:

> “Ask him what he wants, what consolation awaits him, and for what reason he has prostrated himself before our sight.”

They answered the king:

> “Having heard of your great power, your mighty hand, your most powerful arm, and your strong phalanxes, this man has come to you. For the sake of his sons he wishes to offer his life to death, lest he see the overthrow of his city. For your victorious fame has spread throughout the whole world and has been especially widely proclaimed.”

The king said to them:

> “What are you saying—an unheard-of matter? With your harsh words you have tested my ears. Has not the law of the world decreed that whoever brings useless news to a king’s ears should be struck down by the sword? Tell me, all of you who know this matter—and I shall listen carefully and inquisitively—how could this one man have fathered so many sons?”

The bystanders answered the king with great fear and reverence, terrified by dread:

> “It is not as our lord supposes. Yet, if you wish to hear who his sons are, we shall make it clear through truthful assertions and most certain statements. They are not sons conceived through the flesh or through the pollution of lust, but spiritual sons, whom he has acquired for almighty God and drawn away from the worship of the pagans. For their sake he desires to die; for their sake he offers himself as a sacrifice. Before even one of his sheep is killed, he desires to be slaughtered by your flashing sword.”

Hearing these words, the king trembled within himself for about an hour. His face changed; his countenance was pale; his heart was shaken by a great storm [or: in a great storm], and various thoughts followed one another.

His mind wandered, his plans were carried in different directions, and he was utterly astonished in body; he fell into an ecstasy. He reflected that before him stood such a most holy man, worthy to behold an angelic face, one whose mind was daily raised toward heavenly things, whose most holy praises resounded to the stars, who had been likened to the holy prophets and had imitated the proclamation of the holy apostles. He had even imitated the Lord Christ, who gave himself up for his sheep.

Christ, God the Son of God, gave up his soul for us wretched human beings in the fixing of his body to the cross, and restored from the jaws of the Dragon the human being whom he had earlier fashioned from clay; afterward he returned to his heavenly seat.

When these matters had been accomplished, the king’s senses returned to him. He who had recently seemed to people to have lost his mind was restored, through the intercession of the holy man, to his own understanding.

He cried out:

> “O good Father, who offered himself to death for his sons! O indescribable gentleness! O blessed endurance [and most abundant wisdom]! He has given himself up for all, and carries the fidelity of his Lord uncorrupted, so that he may die before any of the sheep entrusted to him is led away in chains. A good shepherd, a most holy man, worthy and proven in faith before his God.”

The king said to blessed Pope John:

> “Father, everything is granted to you. Behold, I shall not raise my spear against your people, nor shall I send my flashing sword against them, nor shall the trumpet of my army sound any longer in your ears.
>
> “There is only one thing which you must do. Your citizens are very clever and resourceful; let them not say of me that I expelled him by deceit, so that disgrace might thereafter cling both to me and to my armies. Your holiness has softened my heart.
>
> “Go quickly, lay your gates flat upon the ground, open the square opening in the wall, and let me pass through the middle of the city. Let the hooves of my horses trample your gates. We shall harm no one, lay no ambush, and you shall suffer no other injury.
>
> “Do this so that people from other towns may not say: ‘He could neither destroy nor subjugate Ravenna. There he and his army were crushed; he turned his back and was put to flight; his strength brought him greater shame than that suffered by the other kings who preceded him and ruled long ago.’
>
> “Now the day is at its end, and, as night brings on the stars, I shall spend the night here; but in the evening, when the first light of day rises, I shall depart from your territory.”

Then the most holy John returned to his city with great haste. The city gates were shaken from their hinges and thrown to the ground, and the entrances remained open, with their thresholds exposed. His troops went around the streets of Ravenna throughout the night, and the army passed through the city from one side to the other.

Very early the next day, as the sun rose with its crimson light, King Attila entered Ravenna. Seated upon a swift, hoofed animal, he trampled the gates of the aforesaid city. Bars with their keys and locks were brought before him, but he wished to steal nothing from them.

The citizens were terrified and struck with great fear. At once all their bodily strength was overturned; they became weak, trembling and groaning, and invoked the heavenly Lord with great sighs.

When the king went out of the city, they went before him with great praises. The city, adorned throughout all its streets and decorated with various flowers, afterward became filled with immense rejoicing [Note: [Col. 0533D] That is, joy; the word is used in this sense frequently elsewhere. BACCH.], among great, small, and middling alike, because when the king had surveyed the great city with his own eyes, his fury was calmed from heaven, and he left Ravenna unharmed behind him.

From that day onward he did not continue in such cruelty. He returned to his own kingdom without engaging in battle, and he was not merely stronger in force but fought with intelligence. Hence this is said of him in proverbs:

> “King Attila fought by strategy before taking up arms; afterward, having been stabbed with a knife by a most contemptible woman, he died.”

Let it suffice for you to hear today about the life of this holy man. For the time is near; the sun is already doubling the shadows, the day is darkening, and the hour is failing.

Yet whoever wishes to compel me to say more about how I wrote above that this holy man, while still in a mortal body, had looked upon an angelic spiritual form—if, by the powerful help of God, I am not too weak after three days—I shall bring before your sight the ancient words which once resounded in my ears, written by my pen in great letters like various vegetables placed in large baskets.

## CHAPTER III. Odoacer is defeated by Theodoric, who takes Ravenna. John appeases the king and makes him favorable to the people of Ravenna. Other matters concerning Theodoric.

[Note: [Col. 0534D] These matters likewise concern the other John.]

On the following day, constrained by a slight bodily illness, I was not able to relate to you all the miracles of the holy man mentioned above. Nevertheless, by the merciful kindness of God, through your prayers, … [lacuna] … what I heard from very old men who related it, I shall explain today, if I remember the words.

In his time, after the Pons Apollinaris at Ravenna had been burned on the night of Easter, on the fourth day before the Nones of April, near Strovilia Peucodis, Theodoric arrived not far from the city of Ravenna with his enemies in the field called Candiani, after he had twice defeated Odoacer, who at that time held the kingdom of Ravenna.

Then Odoacer went out to the aforesaid field with his army, was defeated a third time, and turned his back before Theodoric’s face. He shut himself inside the city, then went away to Ariminum, and from there came with dromons to the harbor of Lione. There he later ordered a small palace to be built on an island not far from the seashore, where the monastery of Saint Mary now seems to stand, below the bathhouse, six miles from Ravenna.

In our own time I ordered my servants to demolish that palace and brought it to Ravenna for the construction of my house, which I built from its foundations by right of my mother. It is called the presbyteral house, in the district known as the Nymphaeum, beside the church of Saint Agnes the martyr, and on the other side, in the district called Bando the First, not far from the Golden Mile.

Theodoric’s army was so subdued by hunger that it was forced to eat hides and other unclean and disgusting things, and hunger killed many bodies which had been spared by the sword.

A very great earthquake occurred at cockcrow on the seventh day before the Kalends of January. Odoacer gave Theodoric his son as a hostage on the fifth day before the Kalends, and after four months he entered the city of Classe.

After this, the most blessed man, Archbishop John, opened the city gates which Odoacer had closed. He went out with crosses, censers, and the holy Gospels, seeking peace with the priests and clerics, singing psalms and prostrating himself upon the ground. He obtained what he sought.

He invited the new king, who was coming from the East, and peace was granted by him not only to the citizens of Ravenna but also to all the Romans, on whose behalf blessed John had petitioned. The king entered Ravenna on the third day before the Nones of March.

A few days later the king killed Odoacer in the palace at Lauro, together with his companions. After Odoacer had been killed at Theodoric’s command, Theodoric alone and securely ruled in the Roman manner.

In the thirtieth year of his reign, after all his adversaries had been defeated, he sent the army of Ravenna into Sicily, ravaged it, and subjected it to his dominion.

In his time, on the northern side, the sky was seen by everyone to burn. The patricians Symmachus and Boethius, kinsmen by blood and Roman citizens, were beheaded with axes at Theodoric’s command.

Pope John the Roman, after his embassy from the East, was brought to Ravenna with Bishop Ecclesius at the king’s order. He was confined by Theodoric and detained as though dead, and was buried in a marble chest inside the public prison.

The aforesaid patricians were buried in another chest [or: another chest was buried for them], which remains to the present day.

After thirty-four years of his reign, Theodoric began to close the churches of God and oppress Christians. Suddenly afflicted with a flux of the bowels, he died and was buried in the mausoleum which he himself had ordered to be built outside the gates of Artemetorus, a place which to this day we call “at the Lighthouse.” There is the monastery of Saint Mary, called “At the Memorial of King Theodoric.”

But, as it seems to me, he was thrown from the tomb, and the porphyry sarcophagus in which he lay has been placed before the entrance of that monastery. But I have wandered sufficiently through various matters; let us return to our subject.

## CHAPTER IV. The spurious privilege of Valentinian for the Church of Ravenna. Valentinian adorns and fortifies Ravenna.

There was much holiness in the aforesaid man John. When his fame reached the ears of the Emperor Valentinian, he had desired for a long time to see him. But the matters which I ought to have explained above are not harmful; so that we do not omit them, let us record them below.

Accordingly, the most serene Valentinian, son of Constantius and Galla Placidia, hastened to the holy pontiff John. Removing the diadem from his head, he greeted him with fear and reverence in his voice; after receiving his blessing, he departed with a cheerful face.

[Note: [Col. 0535D] “Reader, recognize as falsely written by Agnellus, a schismatic man, these matters concerning the metropolitan Church of Ravenna being established by the Emperor Valentinian Augustus and the pallium being granted. Read what has been said about this in the preface; I trust that it will suffice to refute Agnellus and those who believed Agnellus.” BACCH.]

Not many days later, under the consecration of Blessed Bishop John, that Augustus bestowed fourteen cities with their churches by archiepiscopal authority. To the present day fourteen cities with their bishops have been brought under the Church of Ravenna.

One episcopal city, destroyed, is missing; its name is said to be Brintum, not far from the city of Bologna. John was the first to receive from the Augustus a pallium of white wool, which, as is the custom of the Roman pontiff, he wore doubled over, and which he and his successors have used to the present day.

At that time Valentinian held Ravenna as a lofty citadel and ordered a royal palace to be built in the place called Laureta.

[Note: [Col. 0535D] Marginal note: “A house in Ravenna named Laureta.” [Col. 0536D] “Beside this house is a road, or district, called Laureta, in which blessed Eustachius suffered, as you have in the Roman Martyrology on the fourth day before the Ides of October.” BACCH.]

It is called Laureta because a triumphal victory once took place there. The ancient custom was that whoever triumphed over enemies or foes had a laurel crown bound around his head; hence among the ancients they were called men of praise. Later, when the letter *d* was removed and *r* added, the tree itself was called *laurus*, laurel.

Valentinian lived for a long time in that royal house. On both sides he adorned the streets of the great city with great walls [or: with massive walls] and ordered iron bars to be enclosed within the body of the wall.

His foresight was so great that the iron bars would appear not only as decoration, but also so that, if at any time some people wished to fight against this city, and sufficient weapons were not available, they could make arrows, spears, or other swords from the bars themselves, or expend the iron of the walls for whatever purpose was required, as we have said. He also greatly enlarged this city wall.

Previously the city had been enclosed as though it were merely one of the towns, and because it had been narrow in ancient times, that same Augustus made it immense and ordered and decreed that, apart from Rome, Ravenna should be the capital of Italy.

## CHAPTER V. The Church of the Holy Cross built by Galla Placidia. Singleida builds another church of Saint Zacharias. Further matters concerning Galla Placidia.

Meanwhile, while at that time Galla Placidia Augusta, Valentinian’s mother, was building the Church of the Holy Cross, our Redeemer’s church, her niece, named Singleida [Singledia], was warned one night in a vision. A man appeared to her dressed in white garments, with gray hair and a beautiful beard, and said:

> “At such-and-such a place, not far from this Church of the Holy Cross which your aunt has ordered to be built, at the distance of an arrow-shot, build me a monastery, just as you find it marked out in the ground, in the likeness [or: with the shape] of a cross. Let an altar be consecrated there, and give it my name, Zacharias, the father of the Forerunner.”

As soon as she awoke, she quickly ran to the place where the marking had been shown to her. She found what appeared to be a foundation hollowed out by human hands.

She hastened back and reported this joyfully to the Augusta, asking her for workmen. The Augusta granted her thirteen builders. She immediately began to build, just as she had found it marked out, and in twenty-one days, with one additional day, she constructed and completed everything. She consecrated it and enriched it with gold, silver, golden crowns, and most precious gems.

The golden chalices which are carried in procession at the Nativity of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0536D] Here too there is mention of the gifts carried in processions. BACCH.], and from which we carry [or: drink] the Lord’s blood in the holy Ursian Church, came from there. Beside the rim of the chalice we found this inscription:

> “Galla Placidia Augusta offers this to Saint Zacharias.”

Singleida [Singledia] herself rests there. Her tomb is known to us.

The Augusta Galla built the Church of the Holy Cross, constructed of the most precious stones and with sculpted plasterwork. On the curve of the arch are metrical verses containing the following:

> John washes Christ in the fountain at the seat of paradise,  
> He who grants blessed life shows the martyr [Note: [Col. 0536D] There is an error here. BACCH.].

And on the façade of that temple, as one enters, above the doors are painted the four rivers of paradise. If you read the hexameter and pentameter verses, you will find them there:

> Christ, Word of the Father, harmony of the whole world,  
> Who know no end, just as you likewise know no beginning.
>
> Around you stand, saying three times: “Holy, holy, holy,” and “Amen,”  
> Winged witnesses whom your right hand guides.
>
> Before you the rivers flow, poured forth throughout the ages:  
> The Tigris, the Euphrates, Phison, and Geon themselves.
>
> Since you conquer, and beneath your feet throughout the ages are trampled,  
> The savage crimes of kindred death fall silent.

Some say that Galla Placidia Augusta herself ordered fixed candles, with hand-cloths of the proper measure, to be placed upon four red marble wheels which stand before the aforesaid royal doors [Note: [Col. 0537D] *Regiae*, *rogae*, about which Anastasius and the ecclesiastical Orders often speak. BACCH.]. At night she threw herself down in the middle of the pavement to pour out prayers to God, and remained awake in tears, praying for as long as those lights continued to burn.

If you wish to investigate the chronology of Archbishop Maximianus, read the Chronicle. There you will find more about her and about many emperors and kings.

After the Augusta herself had been abandoned by a certain Athulf, the Emperor Honorius gave her in marriage to the count Constantius. After him, the emperor left him as, so to speak, his successor. Constantius ruled the nations for one year after the death of Honorius, then, overcome by illness, lost the breath of life.

He left a young son of Galla named Valentinian.

[Note: [Col. 0537D] Marginal note: “Valentinian, successor of Constantius in the empire; and, as it appears here, this Valentinian died at Ravenna. It should be read: at Rome.” BACCH.]

When Valentinian was six years and four seasons of a year old, he succeeded his divine uncle Honorius in the empire. He remained in power for thirty-one years and was killed at Rome, in a place called “at the Laurel.”

## CHAPTER VI. The death of Galla Placidia. Aquileia captured by the Huns. The Basilica of Saint John the Evangelist is built.

Galla did not see the death of her son, for she died earlier at Rome, on the fifth day before the Kalends of December.

After this, a star appeared burning in the sky for thirty days, and Aquileia was captured and destroyed by the Huns. Ravenna burned on the Ides of March, and much wealth was consumed by the fire.

Galla Placidia was buried, as many say, in the monastery of Saint Nazarius, before the altar and within the railings which had been of bronze and now seem to be of stone. She built the Church of Saint John the Evangelist.

While she was traveling through the dangers of the sea, a storm arose and the ship was shaken by the waves. Thinking that she was about to sink into the depths, she vowed a vow to God concerning a church of the apostle. She was delivered from the fury of the sea.

Inside the apse of that church, above the heads of the emperors and empresses, one reads:

> “Confirm, O God, what you have accomplished in us; from your temple at Jerusalem kings shall offer gifts to you.”

[Col. 0537D] Above this I found another verse, reading as follows:

> “To Saint and most blessed John the Apostle and Evangelist, Galla Placidia Augusta, together with her son Placidius Valentinianus Augustus and her daughter Justa Grata Honoria Augusta, fulfilling a vow for deliverance from the peril of the sea.”

She also built the Church of Saint Stephen at Ariminum.

What more? It is better for me to pass over these matters in silence than to wander through remote and ancient subjects. Let us return to the course already mentioned and speak without delay about our pontiffs; for his successor should now be introduced.

But who could suffice to narrate your deeds, O blessed Peter Chrysologus? Even if my voice grew adamantine, my breast brazen, and my hundred verses were bound in chains, I still could not recount all the deeds of you all.

## CHAPTER VII. Saint John sees an angel during the solemnities of Mass. His death and tomb.

Accordingly, the most blessed pope John, already mentioned above as bishop of Ravenna, was singing the solemnities of Mass in the basilica of blessed Agatha. When he had completed everything according to the rite of the holy pontiffs, after the reading of the Gospel and after the dismissal [or: proclamation], the catechumens witnessed marvels—those to whom it was granted to see them.

When the most blessed man began to offer the canonical words with supplications to God and to imprint the sign of the cross upon the host, suddenly an angel came from heaven and stood on the other side of the altar before the bishop.

After the consecration had been completed and he had received the Lord’s body, the deacon wished to perform the ministry of the levite. He had not seen what he was to do in presenting the chalice. Suddenly he was removed by the angel, and the angel handed the holy chalice to the bishop.

Then all the priests and the people began to fear and tremble, seeing the holy chalice incline of its own accord toward the bishop’s mouth and then return through the air to the holy altar.

Great excitement arose among the people. Some said that the levite was unworthy; others insisted that it was not so, but that it was a heavenly visitation. The angel stood beside the holy man for a very long time, until the solemnities of Mass had been completed.

Not long afterward, having blessed his sons, the citizens of Ravenna, he ended his days with a cheerful face, as though inviting them to a feast, on the Nones of June.

[Note: [Col. 0538D] Marginal note: “He died around the year of the Lord 569.” BACCH.]

He was buried in the aforesaid holy basilica of the martyr behind the altar, at the place where he had seen the angel standing. We see his image painted above the seats there every day. He appears to have been of slender build, with black hair and a few gray hairs. Yet in holiness he surpassed his age, because the heavenly Lord tests minds more than years. Faith is found in the senses, not in age.

Before his image, beneath the vault inside the Ursian Church, a candle of bright light burned throughout every night, until the church, having been damaged, was restored.

Brothers, as I promised, I have brought the life of this man to an end, insofar as I was able, with God’s favor. Now I shall introduce Saint Peter Chrysologus, his successor.

## CHAPTER VIII. The author’s meditations on the Life of Saint John.

Yet with whom can we compare the life of the most blessed John, if we seek a comparison among the many Fathers? If it pleases you, do not reject this from your consideration; and if I should perhaps mislead you, pardon me. For I say these things for the edification of your minds. We are human beings and subject to human misfortunes. Therefore the Prophet, seeing us clothed in fragile flesh and tossed about in the whirlpool of this offense, exclaimed: “Every human being is a liar.” But openly I ask pardon of you—not with arrogant insolence, but with complete humility.

Could I perhaps compare this man with the patriarch Jacob? When Jacob held the angel and would not let him go, the angel said to him: “Release me; dawn has come.” He replied: “I will not release you unless you bless me”; and in that same place the angel blessed him. But the angel did not bless this man: he gave him the Lord’s body together with his blood. Oh, if only someone had given me, at the end of my life, such a sanctified body and blood of Christ, so that what I am not worthy to receive in life I might, I hope, have received at the departure of my soul!

This man imitated David [as you will hear. When David saw the angel who was striking down the people stretch out his hand over Jerusalem, he said: “I beg you, Lord, let your hand be turned against me.”] And when this man was questioned by the king about what he wanted, he made himself known and desired death in place of his own sheep. Then the king granted the peace which the bishop had requested. David did so because of his own sins, since he had rashly sought to obtain a census of the people whom God had multiplied like the sand of the sea [lacuna]. But this king was about to conquer the city because of the people’s sins, since some of them were lukewarm in faith; whereas through the prayers of this holy man he both softened the king and turned God’s mercy toward himself.

He may also be compared with a man named Tobiah, to whose wedding the angel Raphael was sent, both to imitate his father and to restore his sight. [Col. 0539C] But this man the angel both visited and served in the capacity of his minister.

Finally, that great priest Zacharias, whose son at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ not only equaled the prophets but surpassed them all, and whom the holy Gospel calls righteous before God: when he looked upon the angel, he became mute. This man, however, after contemplating an angelic figure, remained cheerful and joyful.

Why was this? Because Zacharias believed that he would have a son only doubtfully, since his blood had grown cold and he had advanced far into old age. And if he doubted the heavenly messenger, how does the Evangelist call him righteous? For he says of Zacharias and Elizabeth: “They were both righteous before God.”

What does this mean? How can it be? Let David speak: “No living person shall be justified in your sight.” Hear also Job: “Behold, even the heavens are not bright, and the stars are not clean in his sight. How much less man, who is rottenness, and the son of man, who is a worm?” Peter, moreover, to whom the power of binding and loosing was given in heaven and on earth, and to whom the keys of the kingdom of heaven were entrusted, says: “Depart from me, for I am a sinful man.”

And if the chief of the apostles recognized himself as a sinner, how does the Evangelist call the married priest [the priest joined in marriage] righteous before God? Let Manasseh come and say with the Evangelist: “Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob [and their offspring: righteous Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob], who did not sin against you.” In this passage he said “offspring”—that is, Christ—not “offsprings,” in accordance with what was said to Abraham: “In your offspring all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed.” “Offspring” in the singular, “offsprings” in the plural.

For before God’s eyes no one is found free from guilt, as Solomon says: “There is no human being upon earth who does good and does not sin.” Before the sight of the divine majesty there are terrifying visions: there the angels tremble, the archangels fear, the thrones are afraid, the dominations are terrified, the powers fall, the principalities are fearful, the virtues of heaven are shaken, the righteous are filled with dread, the earth flees, and the elements are convulsed. How, then, is a human being justified who is born from impurities and, moreover, is a slave of sin?

Hear Job: “Who can appear clean before him, having been born of a woman?”

I ask your charity to grant me pardon [Col. 0540B], or even a little forgiveness, because today I am exhausted by human affairs and, weighed down by sleep, have not refreshed my body. Let these questions not seem burdensome to you, because, if the Lord grants it and life remains with me, I shall explain them tomorrow. And if some delay should intervene, and I do not quickly untie the knot of the question, imitate the holy Gospel, which says: “Have patience with me, and I will repay you everything.”

Do not judge me as ignorant—only as a procrastinator. But how was Zacharias righteous? Or how could David cry out: “No living person is justified before God”? Or how could Manasseh say: “Abraham and the others, who did not sin against you, Lord”? Or how could Moses thunder forth: “Sovereign Lord, merciful and gracious God, and no one is innocent before you by his own power”?

In what follows I shall explain this. Why is it necessary to speak at such length about the man who led the people out of Egypt, who made the swollen sea stand like a massive wall, who fed the people with manna in the wilderness, who brought water from the rock, by whose heavy hand Amalek perished, who crushed the king of the Canaanites, who dried up the river Ethan, who made bitter and forbidden water drinkable through wood, who received the words of the Law on two stone tablets at Sinai, whose face surpassed the sun’s radiance, who raised up the bronze serpent in the wilderness for Israel’s affliction, whose enemies the earth swallowed, who broke the golden calf, who spoke face to face with God as with a friend, who protected the Israelite army by a pillar of cloud by day and of fire by night, and above all of whose other honors an angel was appointed as minister, the Lord saying: “Behold, I send my angel, who will go before you and guard you always.”

Thus he also sent an angel from heaven as guardian of the body of this holy man John. But all these matters, which above I have left laboriously bound together in knots, namely, how a human being is justified, or how he remains in sin or is condemned, I shall gladly announce in the following discourse, so that no weariness may arise, in the Life of another holy man, if the Lord grants it.

This most blessed John ruled his Church for sixteen years, ten months, and eighteen days. [Note: [Col. 0539D] See the preceding dissertation. BACCH.]

## OBSERVATIONS ON THE LIVES OF SAINT JOHN ANGELOPTES AND JOHN II

[Col. 0541A]

Chronological recapitulation. The office of the chamberlains. The location of the *Subdita* in the basilicas. What does Agnellus mean by the name “monastery”? Were the bodies of the dead buried inside basilicas? Certain matters relating to the chronology of the age of Attila and Theodoric. Their deeds elucidated. Valentinian’s privilege for the Church of Ravenna a forgery. The paternal and maternal genealogies of Galla Placidia. Certain liturgical matters.

### I

From what was presented above in the preceding dissertation, it appears that here the deeds of at least two bishops of the same name have been combined into one. Those things that concern Angeloptus are readily distinguished, and they are almost all the matters attributed to Valentinian; some, however, belong among those attributed to the Augusta Galla Placidia. The dedication of the chapel constructed by Lauricius cannot in any way belong to the time of Honorius, on the basis of the consular notation of Theodosius, which will be discussed in its proper place. It should also be observed that our author here reports several things about Theodoric and others that have been anticipated by *prolepsis*.

### II

Agnellus presents the church dedicated to Saint Laurence as built from its foundations and adorned through the labor of two most distinguished men. The first was Lauricius, the second Opilio. At first he calls Lauricius the senior chamberlain of the emperor, and later an architect. Of Opilio he reports that he adorned the façade of the same church and offered precious gifts to the basilica.

As for Lauricius, scarcely anywhere else among the offices of the imperial household—whether of the Eastern or Western emperors—does mention occur of a senior chamberlain. Perhaps, however, this office was identical with that of *praepositus sacri cubiculi*, concerning which there is a discussion in the Theodosian Code, book VI, title 8, and in the penultimate law of the title *On the Superintendent of the Sacred Bedchamber*, in the year 422, under the consulship of Honorius XIII and Theodosius X.

The cited law of the Theodosian Code shows that Macrobius, an illustrious man, was advanced to the honor of this office while Lauricius was still alive; Lauricius had therefore held the dignity earlier. The law itself shows what rank those who had served as superintendents held:

> “Those who have been superintendents of our sacred bedchamber, whether they have now begun to hold that office or whether fate may later summon them to ascend to this lofty degree, shall enjoy the dignity possessed by those who have earned the most eminent praetorian and urban prefecture, or at least military command, so that after they have laid down their administrations there shall be no distinction among them.”
