That the superintendent was also called, by way of eminence, a *cubicularius* is indicated by the acts of the Council of Ephesus against Saint Cyril, where a chamberlain is called, as an honorific title, “most magnificent and Christ-loving.” The letter of Count Irenaeus to the Easterners says:

> “They persuaded the most magnificent and Christ-loving chamberlain Scholasticius, who was confessing…”

These matters concern the time of Lauricius and help determine his dignity. Thus it follows that the eunuchs who formed the chamberlains’ corps had a path open to the highest honors, and Lauricius was evidently one of them.

Our author calls him an architect because he supervised the construction of the building and prescribed its plan. I think nothing further need be determined concerning Opilio, who took care to adorn the façade of the basilica, contributed costly gifts to it for religious purposes, and wished to be buried there after his death.

### III

Our author identifies the location of this tomb, but the barbarous form of the term casts darkness over the passage and makes what he explains require further explanation:

> “Opilius himself,” he says, “was buried in the women’s section, near the middle of the *Subdita*.”

That the basilicas had a women’s section is sufficiently and abundantly established, and there is no need to add more concerning a matter so well known. But what part of the basilica’s buildings was called the *Subdita* has not been possible to discover to this day.

Since the ancient Christian basilicas, both Greek and Latin, were divided into inner and outer parts, it seems that, at least to determine whether the part called *Subdita* by Agnellus belonged to the inner or outer sections, one must turn to that celebrated question which has occupied many writers: namely, whether the bodies of deceased faithful were buried inside basilicas. On this subject the learned Ludovico Muratori, bound to me by a close friendship, most recently defended the affirmative position in Dissertation 7, addressed to the distinguished Joannes Ciampinius and published in the first volume of his *Anecdota*.

On this matter I seem to see great light shining from Agnellus’s work. It is his regular practice to distinguish between basilicas or churches and monasteries. By the term “basilicas” or “churches” he understands what the words themselves signify, requiring no further explanation. But he calls “monasteries” buildings that were indeed dedicated to divine worship but served, in a certain sense, private use and were not open to the public assemblies of Christians of both sexes, which was the jurisdiction of basilicas. Others called them oratories or chapels.

The distinction between a basilica and a monastery can be seen throughout the entire work. A notable passage occurs below in the Life of Saint Maximian, where, speaking of the basilica of Saint Stephen, he says:

> “At the sides of that very basilica he added small monasteries, all of which appear wonderfully adorned with new gilded tesserae and with various other pieces set into the plaster; and the name of Maximian himself is carved above the capitals of all the columns of the same basilica. The monasteries, however, on the men’s side…”

It could easily be demonstrated that such monasteries or oratories, although they were sometimes constructed farther away from basilicas, were originally built only around basilicas. This was done frequently. An example is not only the old Vatican basilica, represented among others by the most learned Ciampinius in his work on the ancient buildings of Constantine, and more recently by Bonanus in his book on the coins of the supreme pontiffs, presented as a preliminary work concerning the world-famous Vatican church; it is also shown by the present appearance of the basilica of Saint Felix at Pincis near Nola.

Indeed, that this practice continued more recently among monks is proved by the church of the monastery of Cava. There, around the central body—which may be called a *capsum*, using Gregory of Tours’ terminology—chapels appear attached to the walls of the *capsum* itself. Among them is one situated on the side of the *Odaeum*, in which the sacred relics of the monastery’s most ancient Fathers are preserved. There is also another, reached by descending several steps, where, according to the most ancient custom, the bodies of the dead are buried; it is accordingly filled with bones and skeletons.

We must seek the origin of this practice in the fact that, although it was not permitted to bury the bodies of the dead inside basilicas, it was lawful to establish cemeteries around them. Gradually, whether individual inclination led to it or the devotion of bishops brought it about, chapels were founded there—chapels which Agnellus calls monasteries.

Hence I think that the basilicas themselves were sometimes called by the name of the cemetery surrounding them, derived from the name of the martyr to whom they were dedicated. Thus Pope Innocent, in his first letter to Decentius, says:

> “The sacraments are not to be carried a long distance, nor do we assign them to priests established in different cemeteries.”

For this reason the aforementioned basilica of Saint Felix at Nola was called by the name of a cemetery because of the smaller buildings surrounding it, dedicated to the burial of the faithful. In them, even now, chests and sarcophagi can be seen, and in addition a great quantity of collected bones. The name eventually passed into the corrupted form *cimitini*.

Paulinus, in Letter 12 to Severus, quoted by Muratori, explains the place most aptly, though in a style of expression that could easily mislead anyone who had not seen the arrangement of the basilica itself and the chambers around it. For the chambers were not inserted in the manner of the chapels of later basilicas—that is, in such a way as to form part of the basilica—but were separated from the body of the basilica by walls like an enclosure. Of one of them Paulinus speaks in these verses, which gave Muratori the occasion for his discussion:

> A little chamber among many, which, attached on every side  
> To the great roofs, offers secure lodgings  
> To the buried.

All these chambers formed, as it were, one building with the central basilica, protected by the surrounding enclosures of its walls. From one of them the thief whom Paulinus describes had intended to escape at daybreak:

> One of these a thief conceals himself in; and when at dawn  
> He sees the barriers of the hall opened, he leaps out through the unlocked chamber.

By “the entire hall” he means the whole building. Thus the faithful were buried, as they had desired, near the memorials of holy martyrs. In this manner the body of the youth Cynegius was placed in the basilica of the most blessed Felix by Paulinus; Augustine discusses the matter in Book II of the *Retractions*, chapter 64, as quoted by Muratori.

### IV

Although bishops were permitted to depart from the common practice, and we consequently read that some of them were buried within the basilica’s enclosure and even at the altar itself, we nevertheless know that many were buried either in one of the surrounding chapels or in a part of the church adjoining the four-sided portico, which our author calls an *ardica*, a term unknown to other writers:

> “Florentius was buried in the monastery of Saint Petronilla, attached to the walls of the Church of the Apostles. Liberius in the monastery of Saint Pullio. Peter in the monastery of Saint James at the fountain of the Petriana Church.”

Of the bishops who follow these, Agnellus says that they had a place in basilicas, except for Chrysologus, who, having designated the place of his tomb while still alive, was buried behind the bishop’s seat and behind the bema of the church of Saint Cassian at Imola.

John, around the time of Gregory the Great, was buried “in the monastery of Saints Mark, Marcellinus, and Felicula, which he himself built from its foundations,” beside the Church of Saint Apollinaris in the city of Classe.

“Marinianus in the *ardica* of Saint Apollinaris. John in the *ardica* of Saint Apollinaris.”

The same, I think, was done with his successor, who bore the same name, although the name basilica is often used.

### V

The more distinguished laymen, however, who were devoted to some martyr and desired after death to be as close as possible in body to the sacred remains of that martyr’s basilica, arranged for such little chambers—or, as our author calls them, monasteries—to be constructed against the walls of the basilica. They adorned them at their own expense and enriched them with very lavish gifts.

Thus Lauricius, after constructing the basilica of Saint Laurence, added to it a chapel of Saints Stephen, Gervasius, and Protasius, where he was to be buried, and prepared a sarcophagus for it from translucent stone.

Singleida, the niece of Galla Placidia, built a chapel of Saint Zacharias not far from the Church of the Holy Cross, where she was also buried. Galla Placidia herself, the Augusta, constructed at the very basilica of the Holy Cross, at magnificent expense and for the purpose of burial, a chapel of Saints Nazarius and Celsus.

From all this it finally follows that the section which Agnellus calls the *Subdita* was outside the basilica, where Opilio was buried, and perhaps formed part of the four-sided portico belonging to the inner women’s section. Enough has been said about a matter sufficiently obscure.

### VI

We noted above that Attila’s arrival at Ravenna, which our author places here, could not have occurred in the time of John the *Angeloptus*. Agnellus himself sufficiently indicates that it took place during the final years of this John’s life, when he says:

> “From that day onward he did not persist in such cruelty, but returned to his own kingdom without engaging in battle.”

And shortly afterward:

> “After all these things he was stabbed to death by a most base woman with a knife.”

Paul the Deacon, in Book XV addressed to Eutropius, says that after Attila had conquered and burned Aquileia:

> “From there the Huns ravaged all the cities of Venetia—that is, Vicenza, Verona, Brescia, Bergamo, and the others—without meeting resistance. They plundered Milan and Ticinum in the same manner, but refrained from fire and the sword. Then, after the cities of Emilia had likewise been stripped, they finally encamped at the place where the river Mincius flows into the Po.”

He then relates the embassy of Pope Leo, Attila’s alarm, and his retreat.

It therefore follows that, after devastating the cities of Emilia and crossing the borders of Flaminia, Attila approached Ravenna. Having departed from there with his mind pacified, as Agnellus reports, and wavering over whether he should proceed to Rome—for Alaric had not long survived the sack of that city—he was finally frightened by the embassy of Leo, the most holy pontiff, and returned to Pannonia.

These events could have occurred only in the year 452, in which, as has been demonstrated above, the other John, later than Angeloptus, flourished.

Jordanes, however, in Book I of *The Succession of Kingdoms*, seems to suggest that Attila approached Ravenna much earlier. After recounting the suppression of John the usurper and the prosperity of Valentinian, who was reigning at Ravenna, he adds:

> “His sister Honoria, while she was being compelled to preserve her virginity for the honor of the court, secretly sent a servant and invited Attila, king of the Huns, into Italy. When Attila came and she could not fulfill her desire, she committed with her steward Eugenius the deed which she had not committed with Attila.”

He then relates that Valentinian went to Constantinople to receive in marriage Eudoxia, the daughter of Theodosius.

Marcellinus, with Baronius agreeing, records Honoria’s adultery under the consulship of Theodosius XV and Valentinian IV—that is, in 435. If this were true, and if Attila, as Jordanes says, had been invited by Honoria to Ravenna, then what Agnellus relates concerning John Angeloptus would, in this respect, agree with the truth.

But however Honoria’s adultery occurred at that time, it cannot be maintained that Attila was then invited to come to Ravenna. All other writers are entirely silent about the affair at the time indicated by Jordanes. Moreover, the account is contradicted by the fact that Valentinian was then living at Ravenna in complete peace during that year, and that Attila did not trouble Italy until much later, after he had begun to reign alone, following the murder of his brother Bleda. This occurred, according to the *Chronicle* of Cassiodorus, under the consulship of Theodosius XVIII and Albinus.

Paul the Deacon, after relating the embassy of Leo the Great and Attila’s retreat, adds:

> “Thus Attila, restrained in this way from his savagery, abandoned Italy and returned to Pannonia. To him Honoria, the sister of the emperor Valentinian, while she was being strictly guarded by her brother for the sake of her chastity, sent her eunuch, so that he might extort from her brother that he give her to Attila in marriage.”

He relates that Attila ordered Valentinian to give him Honoria together with part of the kingdom, adding threats that he would soon inflict worse things upon Italy if Valentinian did not comply. Thereafter, when Attila had added the girl to his other wives, he met a fatal death.

These events occurred during the final years of Valentinian, after Theodosius had already died. If Honoria was sent to Constantinople to be guarded after the crime had been committed, she must have suffered the violation much earlier; then, after returning to Ravenna, she must have attempted to summon Attila back from his retreat to Pannonia. Jordanes has combined events that occurred at different times into a single account.

Let it therefore stand that Attila came once to afflict Ravenna, when, after conquering Aquileia, he devastated the cities of Venetia and the regions of Liguria and Emilia, and, threatening Flaminia, determined to attack Ravenna, the seat of the emperor in the West. Repulsed from there, he first returned from the mouth of the Mincius and then to Pannonia. These events therefore belong to the time of the other John.

As for Attila’s death, Marcellinus agrees with Agnellus, although others, as Marcellinus himself testifies, report that he died by vomiting blood.

### VII

From Attila we must now make a very great leap to Theodoric, so that we may follow our author step by step. The burning of the bridge at Ravenna on Easter, the fourth day before the Nones of April, is presented as a prelude to Theodoric’s arrival.

Easter was celebrated on 2 April in the year 489, with the solar cycle 22, the lunar cycle 15, and the Dominical Letter A. In that same year, under the consulship of Eusebius and Probinus, Marcellinus writes:

> “Theodoric, king of the Goths, occupied the Italy he desired. Odoacer, likewise king of the Goths, terrified by fear of Theodoric, entered Ravenna. Thereafter, enticed by Theodoric through perjuries, he was killed.”

Marcellinus combines the deeds of different years into one account. Cassiodorus records them in their proper chronological order: in that year Theodoric defeated Odoacer at the Isonzo and at Verona; in the following year, under the consulship of Faustus the Younger, he defeated him again at the Adda and besieged Ravenna; under the consulship of Olybrius the Younger, he defeated him at the Candian Bridge; and finally, in the year 494, under the consulship of Albinus, a man of consular rank, he entered Ravenna and killed Odoacer, who was plotting an ambush against him.

Baronius omits the consulship of Faustus and compresses the events of two years into one. We must follow Cassiodorus as the witness to those times, and explain Agnellus as follows: in the year 489, at Easter, fire consumed the bridge at Ravenna; in the following year Odoacer withdrew into Ravenna and was besieged; in the year 491, when the sortie of the Heruli also occurred, Theodoric prevailed.

What follows—“and he went to Ariminum, etc.”—concerns Theodoric. After proceeding to Ariminum, where Rubeus says that he conquered the cities of Flaminia, he returned by means of dromons to the Port of Leo. There he later built a “small palace,” six miles from the city of Ravenna, near the church of Saint Mary. Agnellus himself shows that it ultimately became his property; accordingly, from its ruins he built himself a house on his maternal estate at Ravenna.

The appearance of the place has changed so greatly that it is now very difficult to conjecture where Theodoric’s palace, or the Port of Leo, was located. Nevertheless, just as the name of Candian Field—the place where our author says Odoacer was defeated for the third time—still survives, so we know that the name *Palatioli* has continued to our own time.

Rubeus, drawing on an old chronicle, lists the certain places where he knew Theodoric had encamped: Palatiolum, the Candian Bridge, and Pinetum. Paul the Deacon also mentions the last of these, but contradicts Rubeus when Rubeus says that, during the conflict at the Candian Bridge, Theodoric was frightened and fled to the camp, where his mother repulsed him. Paul asserts that his mother had been left at Ticinum.

Our author reports that Ravenna was shaken by an earthquake during the last days of the year 493, though the others are silent about it. At the same time, he says, Odoacer gave a hostage and, after four months, surrendered Ravenna to Theodoric.

I have thought it useful to note these things, since up to now they have been sought in vain in the published sources. Moreover, Agnellus’s account that the bishop of Ravenna, together with the clergy, obtained terms of peace from Theodoric has Procopius as its supporter in Book I of *The Gothic War*. Procopius also supports the other details concerning Odoacer’s murder, which was carried out through perjury on the occasion of a banquet.

Once he had begun, our author continues his account of Theodoric’s deeds up to his death and praises his remarkable tomb, which still survives: a sarcophagus of porphyry transferred to the Church of the Holy Apostles. For further information, if desired, consult Rubeus and Faber.

The former, when he relates under the year 1509 that Theodoric’s porphyry urn was thrown down by a cannonball from the remarkable marble vault of Saint Mary Rotunda, departs from Agnellus’s history. Agnellus explicitly states that in his own time the sarcophagus, empty of the corpse, lay thrown before the entrance of that monastery or chapel. The more recent author of the chronicle confirms the same.

As for our author’s statement that in the thirtieth year of his reign Theodoric “sent an army into Sicily, devastated it, and subjected it to his dominion,” I confess that I have read this in no other writer. On the contrary, it is established elsewhere that Sicily was subdued in the very beginnings of Theodoric’s reign more by the counsels of Cassiodorus than by force of arms.

Having related the murder of Symmachus and Boethius, as well as the death of Pope John in a confused manner, as though all these things had occurred at Ravenna—although it is known that Boethius was beheaded at Ticinum—the matters that follow concerning their tombs must be understood according to what is certain from other sources: Boethius was buried at Ticinum, where he is still venerated as a martyr, whereas the body of Pope John was transferred to Rome.

### VIII

After gathering together several matters concerning Theodoric’s life and death, our author returns to John. He then presents matters that can belong to no other man of that name than the first John, famous by the surname *Angeloptus*, and, having dealt with Theodoric, proceeds to recall the deeds of the younger Valentinian and Galla Placidia. For he compresses the events of many different years into what is, as it were, a single bundle.

The first and chief matter concerns the metropolitan jurisdiction of the Church of Ravenna and the decree of the emperor Valentinian. If Agnellus is to be believed, by virtue of this decree the bishops of fourteen cities began to be subject to the bishop of Ravenna as metropolitan, and the use of the pallium was granted to him. The pallium was made of “white wool, as is customary for the Roman pontiff, to be worn over the *duplum*,” and John—that is, the bishop in question—and his successors used it.

While investigating the antiquity of the metropolitan see of Ravenna on this occasion, and considering how truthfully it is asserted that this jurisdiction began from the very times of the apostles, I was led to a somewhat lengthy dissertation on the origins of the ecclesiastical hierarchy, which has since been published. I also thought it worthwhile to examine more closely in the preface to this book the matters reported here by Agnellus.

I believe I demonstrated clearly that all these claims are false and contradict both the age of Valentinian III and Agnellus himself. The diploma cited by Rubeus is evidently a forgery, as is the document that Agnellus saw.

I would not deny, however, that Valentinian could have favored the Church of Ravenna and obtained from the Roman pontiff, through his prayers, that John, a bishop of acknowledged holiness, be made metropolitan and adorned with the pallium. Several considerations encourage this view, especially the piety of Valentinian and Placidia, which is known from other sources.

Certainly Peter Chrysologus was the first to exercise metropolitan rights, and he was consecrated by the Roman pontiff. For the rest, see the preface.

Here it is enough to say a few words about the form of the pallium, on which several writers have written. It is well established that among the Latins its form changed around the beginning of the tenth century. Before that, they used the same garment as the Greeks, the *omophorion*.

Baronius says that he did not fully understand the ancient form of the pallium under the year 336, where he confuses the old pallium with the *phrygium*, that is, a head ornament. But the monuments of the Church of Ravenna teach us that from approximately the time of Theodoric until the age of Gregory the Great the pallium retained the same form.

At Ravenna, in the celebrated basilica of Saint Vitalis, renowned throughout Europe, there are two remarkable mosaic works. In one, Bishop Ecclesius is shown together with the architectural representation of the same basilica; the other depicts Bishop Maximianus near the emperor Justinian, both in their ecclesiastical and imperial ceremonial dress. Each bishop wears a pallium of the same form.

I had the earlier image of Ecclesius copied from the mosaic; the other, of Maximianus, I took from an intact icon reproduced by Nicolaus Alemannus in his edition of Procopius’s *Anecdota*. I have wished to place both before the reader’s eyes in the accompanying Plate A.

From these images it can be understood what Agnellus means by “doubled,” and the form of the ancient pallium can be recognized. The *duplum* is the *casula*, so called from its many folds and wrinkles, for these necessarily arose whenever the priest wished to withdraw or move his hands in any way.

For this reason Ducange believes that *διπλὰ διπλωμάδα* in the Greek-Barbarian Glossaries signifies “a wrinkle” or “a fold.” In the same way, I think that the *clanis*, or *laena*, or rather the *paenula*, was called by the name *διπλοΐς*, not because it was double but because, when in use, it abounded in folds and wrinkles.

The form of the pallium in the images just mentioned is the same as that which we know Gregory the Great wore, according to the description of John the Deacon in Book IV, chapter 84, of the Life of that holy pontiff:

> “John says that he wore a moderate-sized pallium, drawn from the right shoulder beneath the breast and in a circle across the stomach, then carried upward over the left shoulder and dropped behind the back; another part of it, coming over the same shoulder in a straight line—not across the middle of the body but from the side, namely the left—hung down.”

I therefore think that Roman and Ravennate bishops used the same form of pallium in ancient times, and that this custom persisted longer than is generally believed.

The distinguished D. Abbot Domenico Passionei, remarkable for his learning and gentleness of character—how much my studies owe to him cannot be explained here—showed me an accurate description of that chapel. It had once been constructed by Pope Saint Paul I in the eighth century at the foot of the Palatine Hill and had been accidentally discovered approximately three years earlier.

In it several figures can be seen wearing a pallium of the same form as that visible in the earlier images of the Ravennate bishops. Multiple crosses appear on the Greek *omophorion*, and its manner of being worn is almost the reverse of the Latin fashion. From the left side and left shoulder it is folded around the neck toward the right shoulder; from there it is reflected over the region of the breastbone back to the left shoulder and then lowered behind the back, so that the front portion hangs almost down the middle of the body, as shown in the accompanying Plate B, taken from Ducange.

[Col. 0547B]

To what many writers have recorded about the use of the pallium I would finally add this: although the ornament of the pallium or *omophorion* appears, in paintings, writers, and ecclesiastical orders, to have been worn only over the *casula*—or, if we are speaking of the Greeks, over the *phenolion* or *polystaurion*—we must nevertheless believe that those bishops who were entitled to wear it sometimes wore it over other sacred vestments as well.

Gregory the Great, in Letter 54 of Book IV, prohibits John, bishop of Ravenna, “from presuming to wear the pallium in the streets.” I would not think that the *casula* was worn in the streets.

In the ancient mosaic of the Lateran basilica, among other figures, there is an image of Saint Sylvester baptizing Constantine. The pontiff is represented wearing a long, square garment, with the pallium placed over it. V. C. Ciampinius bears witness to this in his work entitled *On the Buildings of Constantine the Great*.

Furthermore, in the chapel of Saint Nicholas at the same Lateran basilica, among several pontiffs dressed in *sacci* and *omophoria*, Saint Nicholas himself is seen in the middle wearing a *pluviale*, which is a more recent sacred vestment of the Latins, together with the more recent Latin form of the pallium.

If desired, see an image of this monument in Papebrochius, in the second part of the *Propylea*, together with the prefatory commentary concerning the pallium.

## IX.

The following is written about what Valentinian brought to Ravenna for its benefit, followed by what concerns Galla Placidia Augusta and her acts, which deserve commendation for their nobility and piety. Rubeus and the other writers who praised Singleida derived their knowledge of her solely from Agnellus. Since Galla Placidia is called Singleida’s paternal aunt, it follows that Singleida was the daughter of Arcadius, the father of several daughters, since Jornandes and Paul the Deacon report that Honorius’s two wives, Stilicho’s daughters, died without children—namely Maria and Thermantia, or Hermantia.

Yet certain matters transmitted by Agnellus concerning the chronology of the Emperor Valentinian must either be explained or corrected. He says:

> “When Valentinian was three years and four seasons old, he succeeded his divine uncle Honorius in the empire; Honorius, who had remained in power for thirty-one years, was killed at Rome in a place called *ad Laurum*.”

Prosper records that Valentinian, son of Constantius and Placidia, was born in the consulship of Honorius for the twelfth time and Theodosius for the eighth time—that is, in the year 418—on 2 July; Marcellinus, however, gives 3 July of the following year, when Monaxius and Plinta were consuls. Honorius, Valentinian’s uncle, died at Ravenna on 15 August, in the consulship of Asclepiodotus and Marinianus—that is, in the year 423—according to Hydatius and Socrates. Theophanes assigns his death to 28 August, while Olympiodorus assigns it to 27 August.

From this most diligent writer of that age, praised by the eminent Noris in *Pelagian History*, book II, chapter 13, we learn that, “while Honorius was still alive,” Valentinian was called “most noble.” But he was proclaimed Caesar only after Honorius’s death, namely in the following year, 424. The first of the constitutions issued under that Caesar bears the date 16 October and appears in book 14 of the *Theodosian Code*, under *De murilegulis*; the last was issued in the following year, 425, on 17 November, and is the final law *De palatinis* [S. L.]. The earlier constitutions, in which he is called Augustus, were issued on 3 January and include law 3, *De conductoribus domorum Augustae*, law 23, *De petitionibus*, and law 14, *De senatu et glebis*.

The common opinion of chronologers places his death in the year 455, on 1 April. From these facts it is clear that when Agnellus says that Valentinian “remained in power for thirty-one years,” he understood the title of emperor to include the dignity of Caesar. For he died at the beginning of his thirty-first year, reckoned from the year 424, in which he had been proclaimed Caesar before 16 October.

When Agnellus says that this dignity was conferred upon him when he was six years and four months old, he agrees with Prosper’s chronology and indicates that he was born in 418. Placidia could have been given in marriage to Constantius on 1 January 417; during the eighteen-month period between that date and 2 July 418, Valentinian’s birthday, she could first have borne Honoria and afterward Valentinian himself. No sufficiently firm argument therefore seems available for preferring Marcellinus, who assigns the birth to 419, over Prosper, who assigns it to 418. This is especially so because, if Valentinian was called Augustus at the age of seven after 17 November 425, and if he had been born on 2 July 419, his seventh year would have begun only a few months earlier. Yet when he is called seven years old, this seems more appropriately to mean that he had completed his seventh year.

Thus it follows that Valentinian died in the thirty-seventh year of his age, beginning with the preceding July, after thirty years and nearly seven months had elapsed from the assumption of his Caesarian dignity.

C. V. Pagi, in his dissertation on the consuls for the year 424, writes:

> “Valentinian was born to Constantius and his mother Galla Placidia on 3 July, in the consulship of Monaxius and Plinta, says the same Marcellinus; therefore in this year he was scarcely seven years old.”

But if he was born in 419, how could he have been scarcely seven years old in 424? He would scarcely have been five, since he would have completed his fifth year on 2 July. I therefore accept the more accurate calculation, together with Agnellus and Prosper: Valentinian was born on 2 July 418 and, after six years and with the fourth month already running, was clothed in the Caesarian dress.

It is also worth observing that although Prosper’s Chronicle assigns the death of Galla Placidia to the year 450, the coin presented by Baronius under the year 425, number 4, seems to show that she prolonged her life considerably longer. For on its reverse, around the likeness of Placidia herself, there is an inscription reading:

> **VOTIS XXX. MULT. XXXX.**  
> “With thirty vows, multiplied to forty.”

This indicates that she celebrated, together with her son, the thirtieth vows reckoned from his Caesarian dignity.

The same Pagi, in the prolegomena to his dissertation on the consuls, number 30, recognizes that the coin was struck for the aforementioned thirtieth vows; nevertheless he maintains that Placidia died in 450, although in part II of the same dissertation, chapter 14, he assigns Valentinian’s thirtieth imperial vows to the year 453, when Vincomalus and Opilio were consuls. But both statements plainly cannot be true: namely, that Placidia died in 450 and that she celebrated the thirtieth vows with her son in 453.

Agnellus writes that she died on 27 November, but says nothing about the year. Our author, however, falls into an incurable error when he says:

> “Constantius ruled the nations for one year after the death of Honorius; then, seized by illness, he lost the breath of life and left a little son of Galla named Valentinian.”

Constantius was taken from this life “before seven months had yet elapsed,” as Paul the Deacon writes in book XIV, in the consulship of Eustachius and Agricola—that is, in the year 421. Honorius died in the consulship of Asclepiodotus and Marinianus, in the year 423.

## X.

Jornandes, book I, and Cassiodorus and Marcellinus in their Chronicles report that Valentinian was killed at Rome, in the Campus Martius, through the treachery of the patrician Maximus. In Victor’s Chronicle, *Campus Maximus* is mistakenly written in place of *Campus Martius*. Our author says that he was killed in a place called *ad Laurum*. Although those who described the City are silent about it, I believe that this was some part of the Campus Martius.

The events that follow concerning the destruction of Aquileia preceded Valentinian’s death and therefore also the death of Placidia. Marcellinus reports that a comet appeared in the same year in which Bleda and Attila ravaged Illyricum and Thrace, when Eudoxius and Dioscorus were consuls—that is, in the year 442. I have found nothing in any writer concerning the memorable fire of Ravenna; consequently the year in which such a disaster occurred is uncertain.

Nevertheless, Agnellus has rashly gathered into one bundle both this event and those that follow, although they belonged to different years and the chronological order was disregarded. As for the churches and chapels—or, as our author calls them, monasteries—magnificently built and dedicated by Galla Placidia, it is extremely difficult to determine the dates at which this was done, although Rubeus attempts it. If it were possible to follow C. V. Pagi’s rules concerning the Caesarian consulships and assign these events to the years in which Valentinian either entered upon a consulship or, together with his mother, celebrated the thirtieth, tenth, or fifth anniversaries, we might obtain some light in a most obscure matter. But there is no point in illuminating uncertainties with uncertainties.

## XI.

For a complete knowledge of the families of Theodosius and Constantius, it is worth noting what Agnellus relates about the inscription placed, at Galla Placidia’s direction, in the apse of the church of Saint John the Evangelist. Lovers of antiquity have taken the inscription from Agnellus and used it to illustrate the same matter. It reads:

> “To the holy and most blessed apostle John the Evangelist, Galla Placidia Augusta, together with her son Placidius Valentinianus Augustus and her daughter Justa Grata Honoria Augusta, has fulfilled a vow for deliverance from the danger of the sea.”

Here you see that Galla Placidia’s children were Valentinian and Honoria—no one besides them. It is therefore astonishing that Honorius should repeatedly have been made from Honoria through an erroneous reading by ancient copyists, especially by those who, while calling Honorius Augustus in the last year of his reign and because of a preconceived suspicion against Galla Placidia, say that she sent herself to Constantinople to Theodosius with her children, listing their names according to the scribal error and naming Honorius instead of Honoria, together with Valentinian.

Although Rubeus noted this at the beginning of book III, I know of no one who attended to it before the eminent Noris, who, using this inscription as transmitted by Rubeus and the testimony of Olympiodorus, corrected the error of learned writers.

From this we learn that Honoria was known by several names. Placidia, her mother, gathered these names into the single daughter so as to preserve the memory of two grandmothers, namely Justa and Grata, the sisters of her own mother Galla, who had been born from the elder Valentinian and Justina together with the other Valentinian and Gratian.

In this matter I recognized the error of C. V., the count Francesco Mediobarbus, who was extremely dear to me while he lived. In collecting and enlarging Occon’s coins, he confused Galla, daughter of the elder Valentinian, with Galla Placidia, daughter of that Galla and mother of Valentinian III; or else he called the latter by the name of her daughter and assigned to her the coins of the daughter. Since all those coins bear the surname Placidia, they ought to have been attributed to her, not to Galla.

A third and especially learned collector might have been warned most effectively by the fact that the reverse of one of the coins bears the inscription:

> **VOTA XX. MULTIPLICATA XXX. R. V. CONOB.**  
> “Twenty vows, multiplied to thirty.”

(Pagi, *Hypatic Dissertation*, part II, p. 283, reads **R. M.** from Jacques Chifflet.)

This cannot be applied to Galla, the second wife of the elder Theodosius, since she died in childbirth shortly after her marriage and could celebrate neither her own nor her husband’s tenth anniversary, much less multiply it to thirty.

I believe that the final inscription on the reverse, **VICTORIA. AUGGG. R. V.**, should be referred to the very year in which Galla Placidia saw Constantius, whom she had married, raised by Honorius to a share in the empire; and that it indicates the numerous victories of that same Constantius.

In the same year, when Eustachius and Agricola were consuls, Pagi noted four constitutions in the *Theodosian Code* which bear the names of the three Augusti:

> **Imppp. Honor., et Theod., et Constant. A. A. A.**  
> “The emperors Honorius, Theodosius, and Constantius, Augusti.”

He therefore concludes that Constantius was proclaimed Augustus in 421, correcting Baronius and the others who place this event in 419 or 420.

This inscription on the coin also recalls a sermon of Peter Chrysologus, sermon 130, delivered before the Augusti on the anniversary of his consecration. Speaking of Galla Placidia, he says:

> “There is also present the very mother of the Christian, enduring and faithful empire, who, while through faith, works of mercy, and holiness she pursues and imitates the blessed Church in honor of the Trinity, deserved to bring forth, embrace, and possess the august Trinity.”

Dominicus Mita understands this to mean that Constantius completed the Trinity of Augusti brought forth by Galla Placidia: Constantius, who was proclaimed Augustus because of his marriage to Galla; Valentinian, whom she bore by Constantius; and Galla herself, whom Honorius declared Augusta “so that,” as he says, “he would not seem to have bestowed his sister upon Constantius contrary to her dignity.”

But Constantius was not made Augustus because of Galla Placidia’s merits, but because of his own. Sozomen, book IX, chapter 16, says:

> “The emperor honored Constantius as a reward with his sister, with the crown, with the purple, and with partnership in the empire.”

Therefore Galla could not be said to have brought forth this Augustus. Nor was she proclaimed Augusta until Valentinian was declared Caesar.

Chrysologus must therefore be understood according to the proper force of his words. The dignity of the Augusti that Galla brought forth is related to her in three ways: she bore Valentinian; she embraced Constantius through marriage; and she possessed the honors of an Augusta.

## XII.

This passage of Saint Peter Chrysologus should be noted, since it contains nothing that could be referred to Honoria, who in some manner would have completed a fourfold company of Augustae. Yet the evidence already cited, and especially the coins reported by Ducange in *Byzantine Families* and by Mediobarbus, leave no doubt that she was adorned with the honor of Augusta.

I believe this omission occurred because Peter, after the sexual offense committed by Honoria, refused to mention her to her most pious mother, who had in no way deserved such a misfortune. I therefore think that the church dedicated to Saint John the Evangelist was dedicated around the beginning of John Angeloptus’s episcopate, and that Honoria’s sexual offense, while she was pregnant, was duly recorded in the year 434.

Rubeus therefore erred when he reported that the church was dedicated while Peter Chrysologus was seated in the episcopal chair. Peter had been elected and ordained by Sixtus III, certainly in the first year of his pontificate, 432. It was therefore almost necessary that the basilica be dedicated in that same year, that Peter be ordained, and that Honoria’s sexual offense be acknowledged.

## XIII.

Rubeus relates that in the vault of the same basilica there were images of the Augusti: five on the right—Constantine, Theodosius, Arcadius, Honorius, and Theodosius *nepos* (“grandson”)—and five on the left—Valentinian, Gratian, Constantius, Gratian *nepos* (“grandson”), and John *nepos* (“grandson”). Near the benches, on the right, were Theodosius and Eudoxia; on the left, Arcadius and Eudoxia.

Rubeus does not say where he obtained this information. Agnellus records only the following:

> “And beneath the apse of the church, above the heads of the emperors and Augustae, it is written: ‘Confirm this, O God,’ and so forth.”

I do not see what Constantine had to do with Galla. Nor can any mention of John *nepos* be found in the family of Galla or of her mother. It is therefore permissible to doubt the account transmitted by Rubeus.

On this occasion I am pleased to set out two genealogical tables, one showing Galla’s family and the other the family of Galla Placidia.

Jornandes, book I, writes:

> “Valentinian made his son Gratian emperor at Amiens; he had him by his first wife Severa.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Thus, deceived by Justina, Valentinian had by her four children: the emperor Valentinian, Grata, Justa, and Galla. From Galla came Galla; afterward the emperor Theodosius, when Flacilla, who had borne Arcadius and Honorius, had died, begot Placidia, who was the mother of the present younger emperor Valentinian.”

Paul the Deacon, book II, says that the father of the elder Valentinian and of Valens was “Gratian, sprung from an undistinguished family at Cibalae.”

These facts concerning Placidia’s maternal ancestry are certain and generally known. I have nevertheless thought it useful to note them, since they help establish the genealogy of her father and of her agnatic and cognatic relatives; yet nowhere are the names Constantine or John found.

We know from Agnellus that Singleida was Galla Placidia’s niece through her brother, and from the Chronicle of Marcellinus and other sources we know the remaining daughters of Arcadius.

## XIV.

What our author relates about Saint John’s ecstasy, on account of which he earned the surname *of Angeloptus*—**τοῦ Ἀγγελόπτου**, “of the one who saw the angel”—exhibits several parts of the sacred synaxis. These are listed as follows: “the reading of the Gospel and the protestation of the catechumen” before the appearance of the angel; then the canonical words, with supplications and the sign of the cross over the host; the sanctification of Christ’s body; reception of the Lord’s body; and the presentation of the chalice by the deacon to the pontiff, which the angel performed in the deacon’s place.

All this, together with the other matters belonging to the ancient Mass, was sufficiently and more than sufficiently explained by the once most learned and pious cardinal Bona. The editors of the liturgical orders also elucidated it: Menardus, Pamelius, Thomasius, and Mabillon.

The chalice presented by the deacon, from which the pontiff received the Lord’s blood—not through a tube, as elsewhere, and especially at Rome—seems to have been a distinctive feature. Thus, it is said:

> “Therefore the priests began to fear and shudder with the people, seeing the holy chalice incline itself by itself from the pontiff’s mouth and then return through the air to the holy altar.”

Micrologus, chapter 19, says:

> “The pontiff himself is confirmed by the archdeacon in the holy chalice.”

Thus, also with respect to the bishop, it was the deacon’s function to distribute the holy sacrament:

> “For just as consecration belongs to the priest, so distribution of the sacrament belongs to the minister. The priest sanctifies the offerings; the minister distributes what has been sanctified.”

Rabanus, *Institutions of the Clergy*, book I, chapter 7.

These words must be understood as referring only to the distribution of the chalice, since it is otherwise clear that the bishop or the assisting priests distributed the Lord’s body. In the Roman Church this was done by the bishops assisting the pope.

The aforementioned Cardinal Bona explains the entire matter in *Liturgical Matters*, book II, chapter 17, number 8:

> “The order of communion was as follows: first the celebrant communicated himself; then the bishops, if any were present, or the priests celebrating the synaxis with him; then the deacons, subdeacons, and clerics; the monks, deaconesses, and consecrated virgins; and finally the people, assisted by the priests—first the men, then the women. The same order was observed in the distribution of the chalice, except that the priests received it themselves, the deacons received it from the priests, and the others from the deacons, as is clear from the Roman Order and from the Greek Euchologion.”

It is not useful here to investigate Greek practice. In the Latin Church, however the distribution of the bread may have been carried out, as the most learned cardinal reports, the Roman Orders and others certainly state that it was the deacon’s duty to confirm the celebrant himself with the chalice.

In the first Roman Order, published by the very learned Mabillon, number 20, page 14, we read:

> “When he—the pontiff—has communicated from the holy portion which he has bitten, he places it in the hands of the archdeacon, saying into the chalice: ‘May there be a mixture and consecration of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ for us who receive them unto eternal life. Amen.’ ‘Peace be with you.’ ‘And with your spirit.’ And he is confirmed by the archdeacon.”

The final words are explained by the aforementioned Mabillon in his preliminary commentary, chapter 8, number 11:

> “Then, in the first Order, the pontiff is confirmed by the archdeacon, namely by receiving the blood as the completion of communion, as Micrologus says.”

He repeats the same point in the notes attached to the Order itself:

> “This is surely a remarkable example of the general communion even of priests and bishops.”

But I plainly do not see what can be extracted from this passage to establish a general communion, since it concerns only the celebrating bishop.

The second Order seems to give a different account. In number 14, after the holy portion that the bishop had bitten has been placed in the chalice in almost the same words, the words “and he is confirmed by the archdeacon” are absent. Below, however, after the reception of one species has been described, the following is added:

> “The bishop first receives the chalice from the hand of the archdeacon and stands at the horn of the altar so that he may confirm those in the following ranks. Then the archdeacon, having received the chalice from his hand, pours it back into the bowl mentioned above and gives the chalice to the regional subdeacon, who gives him the small vessel with which he is to confirm the people, and so forth.”

The matter was performed differently according to the difference of times. The aforementioned Mabillon draws this conclusion from the Orders he himself edited, in his preliminary commentary, chapter 8, number 15.

In the third Order, from a Colbertine manuscript nearly eight hundred years old, the following passage is especially pertinent:

> “But the pontiff himself is confirmed by the archdeacon in the holy chalice, from which the archdeacon pours a little into the larger chalice, or bowl, held by the acolyte, so that the people too may be confirmed from the same sacred vessel.”

Our author calls it the holy chalice because the consecration had taken place in it, distinguishing it from the ministerial chalices or bowls. In these, the archdeacon “confirmed with the Lord’s blood, mixed with unconsecrated wine, all whom the pontiff had communicated with the Lord’s body,” as is stated in the Order just mentioned.

Likewise, in a fragment of the third, more recent Order, it is said:

> “The apostolic lord is confirmed from the chalice, the archdeacon holding the chalice.”

And in the following, from Saint Gall:

> “The deacon, having received the chalice from the acolyte, shall present it to the bishop and confirm him.”

Similarly, in another Order that follows:

> “The deacon himself, holding the chalice and the tube, shall stand before the bishop until he has taken as much as he wishes of the blood and body of Christ.”

The words “and body of Christ” seem to have entered a place that is not theirs.

A distinctive rite is described in another Order, presented as the tenth, which Mabillon conjectures was written in the eleventh century. It concerns the pontifical Mass at the Lateran church on Thursday of Holy Week, where we read:

> “After the sacrifice had been completed, the pontiff alone communicates upon the altar without ministers, and on that day and on Friday he confirms himself not with the tube but with the chalice alone.”

These passages, drawn from the Orders made public by a man of the greatest learning and one whom I especially honor, are sufficient to illuminate the deacon’s office in this matter.

## XV.

These points confirm that not all the deeds transmitted by Agnellus can belong to the same Bishop John, as though they were the actions of one and the same bishop. After recounting the place and day of his deposition, Agnellus adds the following concerning the age and appearance of Angeloptus:

> “He appears, he says, to have been of slender build, with black hair and a few gray hairs; but through holiness he surpassed his age, because the heavenly Lord approves minds more than ages.”

He also asserts that this bishop received very ancient veneration in the church at Ravenna, because a candle burned for a long time every night before his image, which stood in the Ursian basilica.

But why could Agnellus not have taken the image of one John for that of another? The matters that follow contain nothing deserving notice. They could have been omitted without loss; nevertheless I wished to publish Agnellus’s work complete, lest omissions should come to seem more important than they ought.

# LIFE OF SAINT PETER CHRYSOLOGUS

## Chapter One. Peter’s birthplace and church. The heresy of Eutyches. Chrysologus’s letter written on that occasion.

Peter XXI [Note: [Col. 0553D] Marginal note: He was elected around the year of the Lord 429. BACCH.], handsome in appearance and pleasing in form. [Col. 0554D] Before him no pontiff was equal to him in wisdom, nor did one arise after him. He composed many books and volumes, and divine Wisdom flowed into him daily like a well-watered spring. Therefore, because of his eloquence, he was called Chrysologus, that is, “golden speaker.”

He was born, by origin [*natione*], in the territory of Cornelium, and was brought up and taught by Cornelius, the bishop of that see. Because of his love for his foster-father, this blessed Peter himself [*ipse* is lacking in the text] renamed Cornelian, from that time onward, the territory formerly called Imola [the text has *quod ... vocabat*; the correction is *quod ... vocabatur*, “which was called”]. Others, however, say that it was called Cornelium because it had been the Forum of Cornelius.

This man governed the see of the Church of Ravenna during the time of the first Leo, the most holy pope. In those days the exceedingly savage presbyter Eutyches, incited by an evil spirit, began, through his most wicked thoughts, to stir up a malignant heresy concerning the holy and indivisible Catholic faith.

The holy Leo admonished him by letter before many holy bishops of God. He could never recall his superstitious belief to a sound purpose. Therefore Saint Leo quickly made the matter known to blessed Peter, bishop of Ravenna [Supplement: “of the city.” Bacch.]. Peter wrote and sent a letter to that heretic; by it he was cast down at the Council of Chalcedon, having refused to assent.

The most holy Leo himself repeatedly sent to Constantinople, by means of his epigrams (*epigrammata*), communications not only to Galla Placidia but also to Valentinian, Honorius, and the other steadfast defenders of the faith, and separately to the divine Gratian [Martian] and Eudoxia—various letters, as we have said, against the aforementioned presbyter Eutyches. The matter remained under discussion for so long that it extended to the time of the emperor Marcian.

Thus, as we have said, after there had been much disputation for many days concerning the holy, undefiled Catholic faith, it happened that, when the aforementioned heretic had been brought before a council of bishops, Bishop Theodore began to debate with him in the presence of all the priests. He displayed individual volumes of the Holy Scriptures and various testimonies showing that the holy Trinity is indivisible and that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one coequal God; and that Christ remains in two natures, divine and human. [Note: [Col. 0555D] This is appropriately to be understood of Christ the Lord. BACCH.] Eutyches did not consent.

Then, when apostolic authority had been demonstrated, he did not repent. The letter of blessed Peter Chrysologus was then produced, containing in part the following:

> “Human laws settle within thirty years all contentious disputes among us; and you presume, after nearly five hundred years, to heap so many insults upon Christ in your speech? Truly, you ought to humble yourself before the holy Roman pontiff and diligently observe his commands. Do not suppose otherwise than that blessed Peter the Apostle himself is alive and, in the flesh, holds primacy over the apostolic chair of the Roman see.”

After this, that most savage Eutyches fell in the very council. The other priests, after the council had been dissolved, went away rejoicing, together with all the Christian people, giving immense thanks to God and offering the greatest praises to the emperor who observed the Catholic and certain [correct] faith [the text has *observantis*; read *observantibus*, “to those observing”].

## Chapter II. Peter Chrysologus’s ordination commanded from heaven.

Therefore, dearest brethren, let us bring forward what remains of Chrysologus’s life and inquire how or in what manner, in such an orthodox see, the citizens of Ravenna ordained as their bishop a man not from their own flock but from the subordinate Church of Cornelium.

At that time, after the blessed bishop John mentioned above had died, the entire assembly of the people gathered with the priests, according to the custom and rite of the Church, and chose a shepherd for themselves. Then they hurried with him [the variant adds *omnes cum*, “all with”] to Rome, to the holy pope of the apostolic see, so that he might ordain their chosen man and so that such a church would not remain deprived of a bishop for many days.

On the following day they were all prepared to present the man [*virum*] whom they had chosen before the holy apostolic presence. That same night blessed Peter the Apostle, the key-bearer of Christ, appeared in a vision to Saint Sixtus, bishop of the city of Rome, together with his disciple Apollinaris. Blessed Peter Chrysologus stood between them. Blessed Peter the Apostle took a few steps forward and said to Saint Pope Sixtus:

> “See this man, whom we have chosen, who stands in the midst of our men [*nostrorum*; read *nostrum*, ‘us’]. Consecrate him, and no other.”

Therefore, when he awoke, the pope ordered the entire people and the man who was to be ordained to be brought in at dawn. The holy pope looked at him for a long time and said:

> “Go and remove him from among them. I do not know this man. Unless you bring me the one who was shown to me, I shall ordain no other.”

They began to inquire among themselves what this could mean, and, after everyone had been expelled, they were saddened.

On another day he ordered that the people, together with all the elect [clerics]—great, middling, and lowly—be brought before him. When he did not see the appearance of the man who had been shown to him, he said:

> “Search among yourselves; perhaps you have not all come, and you are very numerous.”

They replied:

> “You will find no one among us, lord pope.”

“Go and depart,” he said. “I do not yet see the chosen man.”

On the third day, finally, the prince of the apostles again appeared to the same pope, who was neither fully awake nor fully asleep, with his disciple as before. They held the most holy Peter Chrysologus between them and said to him:

> “We have already told you not to lay hands upon anyone except this man, because for many years the Church of Ravenna, like the richness of oil illuminating a lamp when it has been brought near the flame, will grow rich and be illumined by his teaching.”

On the following day everyone was brought in, but the man was not found. Then the holy pope of the Roman see said to the bishop of Cornelium, who at that time had gone to Rome with the citizens of Ravenna:

> “Bring in all your priests and clerics. Perhaps there I shall find the man who was shown to me.”

He answered him submissively:

> “I have no such man, except one deacon who presides over all my affairs and upon whose hands I, your servant, depend. If you command him to come forward, let him be brought.”

The most blessed pope replied:

> “Let not only him come, but all the others as well. If I see the one I desire, I shall gladly receive him.”

When they had all entered, as soon as the holy pope saw the man who had been shown to him in the vision, he looked upon him as upon a shining jewel. By the Spirit he recognized on either side of him the faces of the blessed Apostle Peter and of Bishop Apollinaris, who were holding Peter Chrysologus by his right and left hands.

When the holy pope had seen all this, he immediately rose from his seat and went halfway across the atrium to meet him. With willing hearts they greeted one another down to the knees. When Saint Peter Chrysologus tried to withdraw from the pope, the most blessed pope did not permit him to do so.

The people immediately began to murmur among themselves and to raise a great outcry toward heaven. Some said:

> “We do not receive a novice. He was not from our own flock, but suddenly he seizes the episcopal chair like a robber. Take him away, take him away from among us! We do not receive him, because it is not permitted to transfer someone from a subordinate church to [*in*] a greater one.”

Others replied:

> “This man is just; you are speaking wrongly. Let us receive him, so that he may be beneficial to our city, for he is exceedingly prudent, chaste, a good teacher, and worthy of every honor. He is of our own kindred; we perceive no evil in him. He is full of the fear of the Lord. You wish to destroy him without cause.”

When Saint Sixtus III, the Roman pontiff, saw the people divided in this dispute, some this way and some that, he publicly told everyone of the vision, as we related above, and explained how he ought to consecrate him by apostolic command:

> “If you do not want this man as your father, depart from me, and let all of you be separated from the holy Catholic Roman Church.”

Then, as though with one voice, they began to cry out:

> “Let him be ordained! Let him be ordained!”

They quickly drew up a decree. Through the imposition of hands he received the Holy Spirit, was ordained bishop, and returned in glory to the see of Ravenna. From that day onward everyone began to venerate him as an angel of God.

## Chapter III. Buildings constructed under Peter’s direction. The contemporaneity of Peter and Projectus of Cornelium. The burial of Saint Barbatianus.

This most blessed man built a fountain in the city of Classis beside the church called Petriana, which Bishop Peter founded. This fountain was of marvelous size, constructed with double walls and lofty ramparts according to the art of arithmetic.

He also founded a building within the episcopal complex of the see of Ravenna called Tricoli, because it contains three *cola* (sections). This very ingenious building was constructed below [Note: Buildings. BACCH.]. Not far from the same building he made a monastery of Saint Andrew the Apostle. His image was painted below the gates of that monastery in mosaic tesserae.

On the outside he adorned the walls with Proconnesian marble, and at the entrance, on the outer threshold, he placed the following verses:

> Either light was born here, or, captured here, reigns free.  
>
> Light is here; whence comes the new glory of heaven [the sense of *ante venit* is uncertain].  
>
> Or private dwellings have brought forth the shining day,  
>
> Or a radiance enclosed here shines forth from a heaven shut away.  
>
> See the marbles blooming with rays beneath serene skies,  
>
> And all the stones struck with serene [starry] purple.  
>
> The gifts of Peter shine through the worth of their author.  
>
> To him honor, to him merit, has granted this adornment of small things,  
>
> So that within confined spaces they may surpass what is vast.  
>
> Nothing is small for Christ. He rightly possesses narrow dwellings,  
>
> Whose temples stand within the human breast.  
>
> Peter is the foundation, Peter the founder, and the hall.  
>
> What the house is, the Lord is; what was made, the maker also is,  
>
> In character and in work. Christ is held to be its possessor,  
>
> Who, joining the two, as mediator makes them one.  
>
> Let one who comes here pour forth tears that will give birth to joys,  
>
> Strengthening the contrite mind in the stricken breast.  
>
> Let it not lie prostrate, but cast itself upon the ground and disclose  
>
> Its hidden diseases before the physician’s feet, while care hastens;  
>
> Often the fear of death becomes the cause of blessed life.

He composed many volumes and was exceedingly wise.

He and Projectus were consecrated together as deacons by blessed Cornelius of the Church of Imola, at the same hour. Later, by divine providence, both held an episcopal throne: Peter the Church of Ravenna; Projectus was retained by the Church of Imola.

After Peter had been ordained bishop, the other man was afterward consecrated by him as bishop of the Church of Cornelium [in the Church of Cornelium], during the time of Galla Placidia Augusta, as we find written.

Peter Chrysologus and the aforementioned Augusta embalmed the body of blessed Barbatianus with spices and buried it with great honor not far away, at Posterula Ovilionis. He also consecrated the church of Saint John the Baptist, which Baduarius built.

## Chapter IV. Peter foresees and foretells his death. He goes to the Forum of Cornelius and dies there. The place of his tomb.

After these events, blessed Peter learned through the Spirit the end of his life. He went to the Church of Cornelius and, entering the basilica of blessed Cassian, offered gifts: one golden bowl, another silver cup, and large golden diadems adorned with very precious gems. He imbued all these things from the body of Saint Cassian, placed them upon the altar of that church, and, standing on the step beside the altar with hands outstretched, blessed the entire populace, priests, and people, and prayed, saying:

“You, Lord God, gave a soul to this body; mercifully receive it again, because I am your creature. May the most wicked devil not confront me, but may your holy angel receive it, and command that it be placed in the bosoms of the patriarchs, where light endures and immense joy is.

“And now, Lord, I confess you with lips and heart: you who fashioned all things from nothing, who alone know the things of old, the present, and the future, give this people a teachable heart, so that they may fear you and acknowledge that you are God in heaven above and on earth below; you who, through your holy Son, restored the salvation of the whole human race, in whom we believe as God and Lord of the angels, who are blessed for ever and ever.

“Send them, Lord God, a true shepherd who will gather your sheep—not by scattering them, but by assembling them into the folds of the Church. May he not sleep like a hired servant; may he not be like the keeper of another’s sheep, but a true shepherd who will present the sheep entrusted to him, together with the lambs, spotless before your gaze. May that fierce and most monstrous wolf, who seeks to snatch prey from you, not stir up shepherds’ hearts; may ravenous desire be driven away; may he not tear the fleeces of the faithful sheep, lest the holy Church groan with bleatings.

“Grant this people a good shepherd (*bonum pastorem*; variant *bonus pastor*); send a shepherd who is not a striker but a nourisher; not one who strikes down but one who defends; not one who despises but one who calls back; not a robber but a giver; not one who rends but one who restrains; not greedy but a distributor; not haughty but humble; not fierce but gentle. Guard them: they are your people and the sheep of your hands. You are blessed for ever.”

To the grieving people he said: “Most beloved children, listen to me. I am going away and entering upon the way of all the earth, where the house of every living person has been appointed. Now, children, take courage and be prudent men. The Lord God will give you a shepherd and ruler, as it is written: “The Lord will not reject his people for ever, nor abandon his inheritance.” Listen to him. He will teach you. He will lead you through pleasant pastures; he will refresh you with the nourishment of his word. Listen to him; do not be troubled.

“And do not let your inward affections rise up against him in an outburst of anger. Do not choose a shepherd amid tumult and quarrelling. Let no father of this homeland obtain this see for money; instead, love the one whom the Lord chooses. Be perfect sons; keep yourselves from every heresy. Beware of the Arian doctrine. Hold fast the holy and undefiled catholic faith. Preserve your bodies without pollution, because they are living temples of God. Guard these things and act so that you may deserve to prepare a way for yourselves, together with your shepherd, to the heavenly Lord of all decrees. Guard his commandments carefully; obey him, so that he may pray for the sheep [Note: “For you.” MUR.], because almighty God does not desire what is cheerful, but receives a contrite heart and a humbled spirit.

“May the blessing of the Lord God almighty be upon you and upon your children, in generation and progeny, now and always, and for ever and ever.’”

When all had responded, “Amen,” he turned toward the altar of blessed Cassian and said: “I beseech you, blessed Cassian: intercede for me. I was like a servant of your household, nourished by Cornelius, the bishop of this see, in the bosom of the Church. Now, having returned to you, I entrust my soul to almighty God; but I commend my body to you.”

While he was saying these and similar things, as though pouring forth words, rejoicing and exulting, he gave up his spirit on 3 December, while all who were present wept. The masons, behind the apse of that church, quickly prepared a tomb in the place where he had ordered it, and there his holy body was received; it remains there to this day. He sat [as bishop] for . . . years, . . . months, . . . days, . . .

# Observations on the Life of Saint Peter Chrysologus

[Col. 0559]

The length of Peter’s life. His election, said to have been made by divine impulse, defended against Dupin. Agnellus acknowledges the Church of Ravenna as subject to the Roman Church. Peter’s Letter to Eutyches. Whether he wrote another. Whether he wrote its final sections. Whether the building at Tricoli was constructed by Chrysologus. The Petriana church. Whether the chapel of Saint Andrew was built by Chrysologus. Gifts presented to the Church of Cornelius.

## I.

In the preceding Dissertation we indicated the age of the holy Peter Chrysologus, insofar as this was sufficient to remove the confusion of dates. Now we must determine the matter explicitly, as far as possible. Concerning the beginning of his episcopate, I maintain the view that he was ordained either in the year 440, the last year of Sixtus III’s pontificate, or in the preceding year, 439. The year of his death can be placed neither before 448 nor later than 451.

The truth of the latter assertion is clear from the fact that the cities of Emilia suffered devastation and plundering in 452, while Attila was raging widely; and, when he hastened toward Ravenna, John was sitting as bishop. Perhaps that was not the first year of his episcopate, but it had begun in the preceding year, 451.

The former assertion is established by the Acts of Saint Germanus of Auxerre, faithfully and accurately written by Constantius. From them the most eminent Cardinal Noris has drawn, by certain demonstration, that Germanus died at Ravenna in that same year, 448, on 31 July (*Historia Pelagiana*, book II, chapter 12). It is established, moreover, that Peter Chrysologus arranged that holy man’s funeral.

The same most eminent and learned cardinal says the following concerning the year of Peter Chrysologus’s death:

“Peter Chrysologus died in that year [450], or perhaps the preceding one, on 2 December, the day on which his memory is commemorated. This is clear from Letter 35 of Leo, addressed to Leo of Ravenna and dated 24 October, during the consulship of Marcian—that is, in the year 451. For in 448 Chrysologus sent a letter to Eutyches, who was already in ill repute because of his heresy; but Eutyches was still regarded favorably in Italy in that same year, up to the Kalends of June, according to Leo’s letter to him, dated on that very day, in which Leo praises Eutyches’s zeal in fighting against the Nestorians. This is Letter 6. I thought this should be inserted in order to correct those who write that Peter Chrysologus died around the year 440, an opinion held by Jerome Rubeus and the common body of Ravenna’s writers. If that were true, Germanus of Auxerre would have died at Ravenna, while Chrysologus was bishop, before the year 440.”

Rubeus does not assign Peter Chrysologus’s death to 440 but to 450 (*History of Ravenna*, book II), and therefore he is refuted unjustly.

Furthermore, since Eutyches was still well regarded in Italy up to the Kalends of June 448, the letter of Peter to Eutyches that survives could not have been written in that year. When it was written, Eutyches was in ill repute in Italy, as is clear from the tenor of the letter itself. Therefore Chrysologus’s letter could not have been written before 449.

The letter of Saint Leo said to have been written to Leo or Neon, as was shown above in the Dissertation, does not prove the point, even though, with Pagi against Quesnel, it is assigned to the year 451. Because of the conjecture presented in the Dissertation—that the name *Ravennius* may lie hidden in a scribal error in the inscription—I would add that it may perhaps have been written to John, whose name was changed into Leo through the fault of copyists.

Even if this is admitted, it contributes nothing to the argument, since Quesnel’s arguments compel the same letter to be assigned to 458. Above all, the question there concerns those returning from barbarian captivity, which cannot refer to the exiles who were forced to leave their homeland because of Geiseric’s persecution, since those people were not returning from the barbarians, as the question itself presupposes.

What proves that John was seated before 452 is Attila’s invasion, which occurred in that very year and which John himself encountered, as our author relates. Having considered all these matters, we conclude that Peter Chrysologus died in 450 or 451, and that John succeeded him in the same year. There is no place between them for Neon, who, on account of the many distinguished deeds related in his Life, must have occupied the see for several years.

## II.

To preserve the order of dates, which Agnellus neglected, we must consider Peter’s election to the episcopate, accomplished by the will of God and through the appearance of Saints Peter and Apollinaris.

Ferretus was the first of all to bring this matter from our source into public view; Rubeus then related it explicitly, as is his custom, in his *History*, followed by Baronius and others. But just as the waters of rivers acquire different flavors according to the nature of the soil from which they flow, so that they are no longer as they were when they poured forth from the spring, anyone who has tasted Agnellus’s sources will easily detect that the same thing has happened to this narrative, although its substance has been preserved.

It is astonishing that some people are so constituted that they readily believe everything, while others, by contrast, cast everything into doubt. Dupin, in his *Bibliotheca of Ecclesiastical Authors*, gives the following account of this story, translated from French into Latin:

“But this kind of historical narrative cannot be believed, since no author worthy of trust presents it.”

Whether Agnellus, now brought to light, will be an author worthy of Dupin’s trust, I do not know. I affirm only this: from the story as Agnellus relates it, the tradition of the event is shown to be especially commended by antiquity.

## III.

The privileges granted by Valentinian to the Church of Ravenna deserve notice, if there were any such privileges, and if John, Peter’s immediate predecessor, obtained them—as Agnellus himself testifies. Although Agnellus was otherwise hostile to Roman primacy, these privileges in no way exempted the bishops themselves from the authority of the Roman pontiff.

For if those privileges could have produced such an exemption, it ought to have occurred when Valentinian himself was emperor. Since Valentinian had shortly before granted the privilege, the death of the person to whom it had been granted would have made it necessary to ordain a new bishop.

Thus the writer who says that the people and priests—by which I also think the provincial bishops are to be understood—made a decree concerning the election of a certain man and hastened with him to Rome, to Sixtus, the holy pope of the apostolic see, “so that he might ordain their elected candidate”; and who later adds that, when the people of Ravenna disagreed and caused a tumult, Sixtus, when the vision had been reported, said:

“And if you do not want this man as Father, depart from me, and let all of you be alienated from the holy Catholic Roman Church”—

and that therefore all cried out with one voice, “Let him be ordained,” and, after the decree had quickly been written, Peter “received the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands and was ordained pontiff”—clearly shows that Valentinian granted whatever privilege he ever granted (for he may have granted one unknown to us) in such a way that it in no respect violated the rights of the holy see or the canons of the Church. Nor did it make the bishops of Ravenna autonomous in any sense.

These and similar matters, which we shall examine in their proper places when appropriate, are related by Agnellus. They make me wonder greatly how it came about that he, who in one place, while writing his *Pontifical*, shows himself properly and rightly disposed toward the primacy of the Roman see, elsewhere—and here, after prefacing the matter with a foul invention—betrays himself as a follower of schismatic factions. But such is the condition of falsehood and a bad cause that it destroys itself with its own sword.

## IV.

We must now return to what Agnellus relates earlier concerning Saint Peter, although these events occurred in the final years of his life and concern the heresy of Eutyches, abbot of Constantinople.

Our author has infected the matter with such a harshness of expression and confusion of events that one must divine what he had in mind. The sequence of events in the case of Eutyches must be considered so that the facts may be restored to their proper dates, if anything can be extracted from Agnellus’s *History*. This will also shed light on what we said in the first section concerning the final years of Chrysologus.

After Nestorius’s heresy had been condemned at the general Council of Ephesus, factional zeal caused those who wished to depart from it as far as possible to fall into an equally impious opposite error. Eutyches sinned more absurdly than all the rest: he stubbornly denied the distinction of natures in Christ and accused those who held the opposite view of Nestorianism. He sent letters to Leo, the supreme pontiff, to which Leo himself replied on 1 June 448.

In that same year, at a council held in Constantinople in November by Flavian, bishop of that city, Eutyches was repeatedly summoned. At last he appeared and, asserting his heresy with insolence, was condemned.

Immediately afterward he wrote again to Leo, lamenting that he had been condemned unjustly, and appealed to the emperor so that a general council might be summoned. Meanwhile, the emperor further entangled the matter when a gathering of thirty bishops was held at Constantinople on 1 April 449.

On 18 February Leo had written to Flavian and to Theodosius, asking the reasons for Eutyches’s condemnation. Once he learned them from Flavian, he commended Flavian’s zeal and piety in a letter dated 21 May of that same year. Before that date Chrysologus could not have written his letter to Eutyches, in which he expressly censures the heresy; otherwise he would have recognized what the supreme pontiff himself did not know.

A new synod was then convened at Ephesus. Leo himself sent legates of the holy see and supplied them with letters, among which one was praised by everyone and with the common consent of the Church—the letter numbered 24 in the Quesnellian edition, dated 13 June and addressed to Flavian. In it the mystery of the Incarnation is explained with such elegance, purity, and clarity that in all antiquity it would be difficult to find a more illustrious monument for confirming orthodox doctrine.

The synod at Ephesus began on 8 August of that same year, 449. Because of the predatory crimes committed there, it was afterward called the “Robber Synod,” and it placed the Catholic faith in the greatest danger. Eutyches was acquitted and Flavian condemned; shortly afterward, worn down by hardships and injuries, Flavian died while being led into exile.

For these reasons Pope Leo acted through several letters before Theodosius, asking that the Catholic cause be restored through a general council. Two letters to the emperor survive, dated 13 and 15 October, along with others addressed to different persons. He also dealt with the matter with Valentinian, Placidia, and Eudoxia, and sent legates to Constantinople. Yet he obtained nothing from Theodosius in so grave a matter.
