After Theodosius died and Marcian succeeded him, with Pulcheria, Marcian’s wife, taking action, a council was first held at Constantinople under Anatolius. Legates of the apostolic see attended. Leo’s letter to Flavian was read there and confirmed by the subscriptions of the bishops; Nestorius and Eutyches were both condemned.

Then, at the general Council of Chalcedon, which began to be celebrated on 8 October of that same year, the same letter of the great Leo served as the standard by which the doctrine of Christ’s two natures was established against Eutyches’s heresy. The council subscribed to it in its second and fourth sessions.

## V.

Having briefly touched upon the history of the Eutychian heresy, let us return to Agnellus’s confusions.

First, he says that Eutyches did not repent when warned by the most holy Leo through a letter, and he says that the letter was read in a gathering of many bishops. No letter of Leo addressed to Eutyches was read at any council. Indeed, at none of the preceding councils was the famous letter to Flavian read at the Council of Constantinople under Anatolius, the letter discussed above. Therefore this is the letter to which Agnellus must be referring. But Eutyches was not present at that council, and the matter was no longer open.

He adds an exceedingly confused paragraph:

“Therefore Saint Leo quickly made the facts known to blessed Peter, pontiff of this city of Ravenna. He wrote a letter and sent it to the heretic himself, through which he did not consent at the Council of Chalcedon, and was overwhelmed.”

From this, as I think, some have believed that they possessed an argument for saying that Peter Chrysologus’s letter was read at the Council of Chalcedon. Yet this conflicts with the Acts of that council, in which nothing is said about it. Nor could it have happened that a letter of the bishop of Ravenna was read there as a rule of faith, among men who initially insisted that only the Creeds of the Councils of Nicaea, Constantinople, and Ephesus should be followed. They admitted the second letter of Saint Cyril to Nestorius and another of Cyril’s letters to John of Antioch; and for that reason they accepted the letter of Saint Leo to Flavian, because it did not depart from the meaning of those documents and clearly explained what should be believed concerning Eutyches’s heresy.

Dominicus Mita thinks the matter can be resolved in this way in his *Responses to the Objections to the Life of Chrysologus* that he himself composed, numbers 5, 6, 7, and 8. He proposes that Saint Leo, having learned from Flavian about Eutyches’s heresy and case, summoned Peter to Rome; and that Peter, at the pope’s command, composed that most famous letter in the pope’s own name to Flavian. It was then read first at the Constantinopolitan council under Anatolius and afterward at the general Council of Chalcedon as the rule of what must be believed against both Nestorius and Eutyches.

To evade the objection that could be raised from the difference of style between this letter and Peter’s other writings, Mita limits his conjecture by holding that Leo “transcribed in his own style” the letter written by Peter and added certain passages “on his own authority.”

He attempts to confirm the whole matter from Sermon 75 of Chrysologus, where Peter says that he returned to Ravenna from a journey during Lent and was therefore extremely tired. Mita might perhaps have believed that he had attained the truth if he had read our author, since the passage cited seems to imply that Peter, summoned by Leo, wrote the letter that destroyed Eutyches’s heresy at the Council of Chalcedon.

But from what follows it is clear that Agnellus was speaking of a letter written by Peter with everyone’s agreement. For he says that “the letter of blessed Peter Chrysologus was displayed,” and he also gives part of it, which we shall discuss shortly.

Mita’s conjecture therefore cannot in any way be supported by this passage. It also collapses for another reason: Leo’s letter under discussion was written after Lent in the year 449, specifically on 13 June, while the preceding letter to the same Flavian was likewise written after Lent, specifically on 21 May. How could there be any doubt about the matter, when the style and the very words sound like Leo?

## VI.

Agnellus next discusses other letters of Leo, written to obtain the assistance of the emperors so that the Catholic cause, badly treated at the false Council of Nicaea, might be restored by a new general council.

He falls into a shameful error—unless, through the fault of copyists, the names of the emperors and empresses have been altered—when he mentions Honorius and Gratian, who had died long before the time of the Eutychian heresy.

I wondered whether Honoria might have been substituted for Honorius. But since no letter of Leo to her survives, and since she was also burdened with an extremely bad reputation because of her adultery, I recognize that such an emendation cannot be maintained.

I also suspected that Gratian had been inserted in place of Marcian through an easy scribal slip. But this is opposed by the fact that, in the same period, Agnellus says that the matter was prolonged up to Marcian.

Furthermore, the whole sequence of the ancient Acts of the council convened by Flavian knows nothing of the Theodorus whom our author says fought against Eutyches at the holy council and, by displaying volumes of Sacred Scripture and testimonies of the holy Fathers, established the Catholic faith concerning the two natures.

Thus everything in this passage of our author departs from the truth.

## VII.

No one will deny that an important point concerns the integrity of the letter discussed above. Agnellus’s passage provides abundant proof against certain people who maintain that the final words concerning the supreme authority of the supreme pontiff in matters of the doctrines of faith do not belong to Chrysologus but were added later by someone devoted to and attached to the Roman see.

They rely on the authority of Gerardus Vossius, who published Peter Chrysologus’s letter in Greek and Latin, together with several works of Gregory Thaumaturgus, printed at Mainz in 1604. Vossius noted that those final words were absent from two Vatican manuscripts.

From this, the aforementioned Dupin says the following in his *Bibliotheca*, which I give here in Latin translation:

“Furthermore, the letter seems to end before those words, and what follows was added to commend the authority of the holy see.”

But, as we have noted, Agnellus was not well disposed toward the holy see, as will be evident in its proper places; nevertheless, he reports words from the letter, or at least their meaning. No serious textual critic will oppose this.

It is certain that, down to Agnellus’s time, the complete letter of Chrysologus existed in the manuscripts of the Church of Ravenna, although that church had been afflicted by a long schism. Later, those who attacked the authority of the holy see in defining matters of faith shortened it. This should be attributed especially to those who, sharing the Greek faith, translated the Latin letter into Greek.

I therefore thought it worthwhile to set out the Latin version itself, as published by Baronius and others, and alongside it the text that I found in the Estense manuscript, adding in their proper places the passages reported by Agnellus, so that the reader may judge what should be thought about a matter of this kind.

### [Note: The two versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

## The Commonly Received Latin Letter of Saint Peter Chrysologus

To Eutyches, my most beloved and deservedly honored son, a priest: Peter, bishop of Ravenna.

I read your sorrowful letters with sorrow, and I reviewed your mournful writings with the grief that was their due. For just as the peace of the Churches, the harmony of priests, and the tranquility of the people fill us with heavenly joy, so fraternal dissension afflicts and casts us down, especially when it arises from such causes.

Human laws extinguish human disputes after thirty years; yet the generation of Christ, which divine law declares to be ineffable, is after so many centuries subjected to rash disputation? You know well what Origen, the investigator of first principles, encountered, and how Nestorius fell when disputing about the natures.

The Magi confess Jesus as God in the cradle through their mystical gifts, while priests investigate, with a mournful question, who he is who was born through a virginal birth from the Holy Spirit. When Jesus uttered his cry in the cradle, the heavenly host proclaimed, “Glory to God in the highest”; and now, when every heavenly, earthly, and infernal being bends the knee in the name of Jesus, is the question of his origin stirred up?

We, dearest brother, say together with the Apostle: “Although we have known Jesus according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him.” Nor can we scrutinize with curiosity the one whom we are commanded to honor, to render fear, and to await—not to investigate—the one whom we confess as Judge.

I have replied briefly to your letters. I would write more if our brother and fellow bishop Flavian had sent me something in writing concerning this matter. For if what you write displeases you, although you yourself chose the judgment, how can we judge those whom, because of their absence, we have not seen, and whose understanding we do not know because of their silence?

A mediator is not just if he hears one side in such a way that he reserves nothing for the other side.

[Note: Agnellus’s paraphrase: “You truly ought to humble yourself before the holy Roman pontiff, carefully observe his commands, and judge nothing otherwise than that blessed Peter the Apostle himself is alive and holds in the flesh the primacy of the apostolic chair of the Roman see.”]

In every respect, however, we exhort you, honorable brother, to attend obediently to what the most blessed pope of the Roman city has written, because blessed Peter, who lives and presides in his own see, grants the truth of faith to those who seek it. For, in the interests of peace and faith, we cannot hear cases without the consent of the bishop of the Roman city.

May the Lord deign to preserve your affection safe for the longest time, dearest and most honored son.

## VIII.

Since the same meanings are expressed in very different words in the common versions and in the passages that Agnellus chose to report, this is evidence that he took the meaning, not the words, from Chrysologus’s letter. It is also clear that the wording was corrupted by Agnellus’s characteristic confusion.

As for the earlier passages, where an argument against Eutyches is drawn from the thirty-year limitation established by human law, these were taken—or were spoken by Chrysologus himself in both places—from Sermon 145, section 15:

“Human laws, within thirty years, put an end to all contentious disputes; and Christ, after nearly five hundred years, still provides the causes of his birth, endures disputes about his origin, and bears questions concerning his status? Heretic, cease judging your Judge, and adore in heaven the God [lacuna] whom he adored on earth.”

Although Chrysologus delivered that sermon after the law enacted under the consuls Acturus and Protogenes, on 17 June, concerning the thirty-year limitation, and around the feasts of the Lord’s Advent in the year 449, an attentive reader nevertheless sees that the principal target of attack there is the heresy of Nestorius and those who “attempted to cloud Latin purity with a Greek whirlwind,” blasphemously using *anthrōpotokos* (*ἀνθρωποτόκος*, “bearer of a man”) and *Christotokos* (“bearer of Christ”) in order to remove *Theotokos* (“bearer of God”).

From this a by no means insignificant argument is drawn for assigning the *Life* to a date after the year mentioned above and for dating Chrysologus’s letter later than is commonly supposed.

## IX.

Among the buildings erected under Chrysologus’s direction and at magnificent expense, the second listed is a house within the episcopal complex of the Church of Ravenna called Tricoli. Our author says it was so named because it contained three *cola*, that is, because it was divided into three distinguished members, which the Greeks called *ta kōla* (*τὰ κῶλα*). Hence *trikōlon* (*τρικῶλον*) means something that has three members.

Those therefore deserve no credence who wish the building to have been called Tricoli because it resembled three hills.

That Agnellus attributed to Peter Chrysologus what should have been attributed to the third Peter of that name is clearly recognized from the verses that Agnellus himself says were read in the Tricoli building completed by Bishop Maximian. In them the succession of Ravenna’s pontiffs is set out, namely those who devoted their labor to constructing Tricoli. Peter, surnamed Junior, is called the founder of the building, to distinguish him from the Elder and from Chrysologus.

It is worthwhile to transfer some of these verses here:

> This Peter Junior, following what he had conceived of Christ,  
> As he taught, set it forth in sacred conduct.  
>   
> He also founded this citadel with wondrous structures,  
> And himself gave these monuments to his own name.  
>   
> After his death, Aurelianus held the honors;  
> After him, Ecclesius became bishop.

The Peter who laid the foundations of Tricoli was therefore the Peter who preceded Aurelianus, not Chrysologus, whom another John succeeded. Thus Agnellus corrects Agnellus himself: he may perhaps have found here the occasion for his error and for placing Peter surnamed Chrysologus immediately before Aurelianus, although Chrysologus preceded him by nearly half a century.

## X.

Nevertheless, it is rightly attributed to Chrysologus, among the other buildings, as the first item, a baptismal font of extraordinary size enclosed by double and lofty walls.

Since Agnellus explicitly states that this font was built “beside the church called Petriana, which Bishop Peter founded,” and since Rubeus could not have obtained knowledge of this work from anywhere other than this passage of Agnellus, it is surprising that Rubeus attributes the construction of the font to Chrysologus on page 105, while, after erasing the earlier Peter from Ravenna’s diptychs, he attributes the Petriana basilica to the Peter who flourished during the pontificate of Symmachus and preceded Aurelianus in the Ravenna see.

From this passage it is therefore clearly established that another Peter sat as bishop before Peter Chrysologus, since we are compelled to recognize that the font attributed to Chrysologus was added to the Petriana basilica, to which a font had originally been attached together with a small chapel of Saint James. That chapel still existed in Agnellus’s time, and the body of a bishop Peter was found in it; Agnellus judged that it was the body of the elder Peter.

The other building attributed to Chrysologus is the monastery, or chapel, of the apostle Saint Andrew, not far from the house of Tricoli. Agnellus says that both Peter’s image and verses were inscribed there.

I nevertheless have some doubt whether these should be attributed to Chrysologus or to Peter Junior. The building seems to have been constructed for the convenience of his Tricoli house, and the verses themselves do not appear to bear Chrysologus’s style or reflect his age; rather, they sound more recent.

The final expression of the second verse, *τὸ modernum* (“the modern [thing]”), reflects the age of Cassiodorus, and the phrase itself is not unlike Cassiodorus’s phrasing.

In the passage cited above, Rubeus calls this chapel elegant, “but supported by wooden columns.” The verses assigned to it establish no such thing. They describe a small chapel, scarcely accessible to daylight through narrow windows, but splendid with costly marbles adorned with purple; external light was shut out, while the chapel itself shone with its own light, as the earlier verses say:

> Either light was born here,  
> Or, captured, it reigns here free,

together with the other verses that follow.

The final verses reveal the expiation of sins through secret confession, as Rubeus rightly noted.

Since these verses were written after the time of Nectarius, patriarch of Constantinople, it is evident that they have nothing to do with the famous and controversial event in the histories of that patriarch, by which the heterodox believe that auricular confession was abolished. On the contrary, it is manifest from this evidence that the practice continued even after Nectarius.

I also think that the image which Agnellus believed to have been Chrysologus’s, represented in mosaic above the doors, should rather be attributed to Peter Junior, like the chapel itself.

## XI.

What follows concerning Saint Projectus of Cornelium is clear, as is the account of the Church of Saint John, which Saint Barbatianus, dear to Placidia, held and which Baduarius had built; these matters borrow their light from the Acts of Saint Barbatianus.

The statements our author makes about the death of Saint Peter Chrysologus are also clear and contain nothing to delay the reader.

One point should be added: among the gifts that Chrysologus offered when he came to the Church of Cornelius, a silver cup was preserved with the greatest reverence. Dominicus Mita presented an engraved bronze copy of it before his edition of Saint Peter’s Sermons. Along its rim are engraved verses of a more recent style, which I think should be attributed to it. They are as follows:

> The Lamb whom the beloved people then fastened upon the altar of the cross  
> Becomes the offering of the race, for the sin of the first parent.

The same Mita prefixed to his book what he believed to be a true portrait of Peter Chrysologus, taken from one that he says exists in mosaic at Ravenna, in the vault of the choir of the metropolitan church.

Yet that image could have been made only after the eleventh century from the birth of Christ, since that part of the church was restored only after that time; the form of the pallium is also more recent.

I hear that a learned study of the aforementioned cup is expected from the distinguished Abbot Pastrizio. Perhaps it will be possible to read it before this work of mine is published. But these matters are sufficient for the Life of Chrysologus.

## The Same Text from the Estense Manuscript

To Eutyches, my most beloved and deservedly honored son, a priest: Peter, bishop.

I read your sorrowful letters with sorrow, and I reviewed your mournful writings with grief and lamentation. For just as the peace of priests and the tranquility of the people fill us with heavenly joy, so fraternal dissension afflicts and casts us down, especially when it arises from such causes.

Human laws extinguish human disputes after thirty years; yet the generation of Christ, which divine law declares to be ineffable, is after so many centuries subjected to rash disputation? You know well what Origen, the investigator of first principles, encountered, and how Nestorius fell when disputing about the natures.

The Magi confess Jesus as God in the cradle through their mystical gifts, while priests run about in mournful questioning as to what he is who was born through a virginal birth from the Holy Spirit. When Jesus uttered his cry in the cradle, the heavenly host proclaimed glory to God in the highest; and now, when every heavenly, earthly, and infernal being bends the knee in the name of Jesus, is the question of his origin stirred up?

We, brother, say with Paul: “Although we have known Jesus according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him.” Nor can we examine him with curiosity, since we are commanded to render honor and fear and to await—not investigate—the one whom we confess as Judge.

I have replied to all these matters, brother, in your letters . . . The rest is missing.

# Life of Saint Aurelianus

[Col. 0567]

## Single Chapter

A few matters concerning Aurelianus. Complaints about the work that presses upon him. Interpretation of the verse from the Psalm, “You broke apart,” etc. Aurelianus’s death and his tomb.

Aurelian XXII. An eminent man, young in age but old in understanding, and more refined than all others in every grace, withdrawn from every evil work; gentle among the people, mild among the sheep. He himself enlarged above the foundation the church which the most blessed Peter had founded at the place already mentioned as Tricoli, though he too did not complete it. And so that you may know, beloved, you have placed very great burdens upon my neck. Concerning this man, finally, I could find no deeds, except only the properties which the Ursiana church holds (*detinet*), which he himself acquired in the Comacchio territory, at the place called Ignis, and Bajas—these being likewise names of idols—not far [Col. 0567B] from where the church of Blessed Mary is situated on the old Po. In his time also the aforesaid monastery was built.

But, because of your prayer, lest his history should appear too brief, let us recount without any hesitation what the very human understanding, with the help of heaven, may disclose to our knowledge, while the Lord inspires you as you pray. May that Maker and lover of humankind, who gives the breath of life and strengthened the spirit in my inward parts, who gave me understanding, arguments, and teachable hearts, and who loved his own creation, increase such understanding in us that we may fulfill your request, and that you may receive it, so that you may read with greater desire and love rather than with weariness or negligence.

Now we wish you to repeat your request. But I, being immediately weak in part of my body, can scarcely complete it today [Col. 0567C]; nevertheless, insofar as I am able, with the Creator of all things assisting, let us begin. Do not act as you did the other day. Your eloquence has driven me hard enough. See that you do not burden me too much, for, in Solomon’s words, “Whoever presses words too forcefully draws out blood.” Thus let your prudence take account of me. Consider this: it is not my gift but that of the Almighty. Oh, miserable me, who am daily scourged by you with such harsh questions! Do not act so.

Yet if you wish to break me further with speeches, so that, compelled, I may complete this *Pontifical* more quickly and deliver it into your hands, first consider your own frailty and afterward recognize mine. Today, finally, I have completed six lustra, and in addition two years and twice five [Col. 0567D] months. Since I received the light and came forth from my mother’s womb, I have never endured such scourging, never been so constrained, as I was by you the other day. And if it is such a pleasure for you to make me yield to you, to tug at my ears this way and that, to lead me bound with my hands tied behind my back, and, moreover, to scourge my back and chest and lay blows upon my shoulders, I shall consent. Do what you wish; and after all this, leave me and desist from me, grant me patience, and remove yourselves from me; and retain what has been written about [Col. 0568A] the lives of the pontiffs. You will hear nothing more from me.

But I will complete the Life of this Aurelian, and afterward I shall be silent. What more benefits me, except patience alone? Why do you accuse me? Unless the Lord gives me a learned tongue, let what pleases him concerning me be done. Through Ezekiel, thundering, he says: “I will make your tongue cleave to your palate, and you shall be mute”; and to Moses: “Who made the mouth of man? Is it not I?” And David the Son: “All wisdom is from the Lord God”; and Daniel: “His are kingdom, wisdom, and strength.” Behold the mouth: why have you raged? As much as that craftsman permits me, who formed me from clay with his own hands, so much shall I speak; I cannot do otherwise. I have suggested all this to you. Keep it in your settled minds.

I wish you therefore [Col. 0568B] to know that a time will come when, if I abandon this *Pontifical* because of your tearing me apart, and you read it and find only half of it completed up to this point, you will afterward recall with groaning what I told you. But it will do nothing then; and if afterward you wish to ask me to complete it, I shall not listen. I desire that, through the dispensation of Almighty God, my labor should reach its conclusion; you, because of excessive haste, want me to abandon it. I will not.

For I remember your words, beloved: in the Life of blessed John I professed that I was your debtor, and, cunningly fleeing, hid myself from you before your blazing eyes. Since you immediately found me, I cannot hide myself; and if you are ignorant of my debts, after you have compelled me, before you examine me, I shall [Col. 0568C] reveal them most truthfully. I am your debtor for this question concerning the river Ethan. For it is written: “You broke open springs and torrents; you dried up the rivers of Ethan” [*fluvium* here and below]. Behold my debt. But let us see why he dried up the rivers of Ethan.

Hear the prophet saying: “Behold, I have made a new thing, says the Lord: in the desert, a way, and in the watercourses, rivers.” And if the Lord made all rivers, and even the seas, why then did he dry up the river Ethan alone, when the prophet says: “You broke open springs and torrents; you dried up the rivers of Ethan”?

Alternatively, Ethan was intended to be understood allegorically as another river, namely the stock of Esau, because he did not propagate offspring among the sons of Jacob, when Isaac their father said to Jacob: “May you grow into a thousand thousands, and multiply like the sand of the sea and the stars of heaven; like the dust of the [Col. 0568D] earth may you put forth shoots; like green herbs you shall spread to the east and west and north and south.” But to Esau: “What shall I do for you, my son? For I have made him your lord. You shall live by the sword, and you shall serve your brother.”

Nevertheless, we must inquire very carefully, in the historical sense, what kind of river this Ethan was. We read in Exodus that, when the children of Israel had been led across the Red Sea, after not many days they came to the place called Mara. There the waters [Col. 0569A] were exceedingly bitter. For Mara is interpreted as “bitter.” Because of their excessive bitterness, the people did not drink from them. But, parched with thirst, they found the river Ethan, drew and drank its water, and their bodies were turned into swelling. Some say that the waters of Ethan were not only bitter but also caused those who drank them to swell, and their entrails burst. Then they cried out to Moses, and Moses prayed with them to the Lord, and the Lord dried up the river Ethan.

Another interpretation is also possible. The river Ethan is understood as the devil, who is true poison and, in swelling pride, raises his neck. With an arrow full of poisonous juices he always shoots the servants [or: fellow servants] of God with the goads [of self-indulgence]. But Christ the Word, coming through the Virgin, dried up the river Ethan—[Col. 0569B] that is, he bound the devil, the prince of death, restored the world, and took pity on the human race.

And if God made man, as we read, and alone fashioned the whole world, why was it then necessary to come to man’s aid and restore the world once more? First he made man from the mud of the earth in the flesh and gave him the breath of life; after many ages he regenerated him through grace. Not because God could not rescue man from the snare of death unless he assumed virgin flesh. He could—and without doubt, I believe, he could. And why did he not do so? You have already heard above: “Who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?”

But insofar as I am able, I shall speak truthfully and with great fear. There was a man earthly, from the earth, placed in the flesh in paradise; everything was subjected beneath him [Col. 0569C], and he was prince of every creature. The spiritual devil, seeing such riches entrusted to him, swollen with pride and inflamed with fury, seemed to say: “I have been cast down from heaven; I have lost angelic dignity; and although I am spiritual, having lost the heavenly delights of the outside world, I have nothing. This one, as soon as he was created, was immediately given every good thing, and even the joys of paradise. What shall I do?”

With this envy, beloved, the devil daily burned against the first-formed man. Therefore, having devised his wickedness, he entered the serpent’s beastlike throat and, through its mouth, persuaded the man. After Adam despised the commandment, he lost everyone along with himself; and the devil not only exulted but also deceived him. Behold the trespass of death in Adam.

If you consider with great prudence the question [Col. 0569D] that has been placed before you, I shall solve it with the Lord’s help. The devil had conquered the son of the virgin earth; it was necessary that he be conquered by the Son of the Virgin Mary. From the mud and substance of the earth a carnal, earthly man was made. From the Word of God and the Virgin Word a carnal and spiritual man was made. The devil had tested the earthly man and led him astray; he tested the heavenly man and departed confounded.

Therefore it was necessary that he who had conquered the virgin’s son should be conquered by the Virgin’s Son; that the Virgin should again restore him whom the Virgin had previously generated through God. Why did he cast down the prince of demons not through angels or some heavenly army, but through himself? The devil did not see a spiritual form in Adam, but a carnal one. Therefore Christ permitted himself, in the flesh, [Col. 0570A] to be tempted, so that the cunning seducer could not say that Adam had one form and Christ another. Seeing Christ’s form, he thought of Adam. The form was equal, but the powers were not equal [or: “equal in power”]. Christ had the form of a man, but divine power.

We can find this in many places in Holy Scripture. Where Adam sinned, Christ restored. Adam sinned through the throat; Christ conquered the devil through abstinence. Adam was from virgin earth; Christ was from the Virgin Mary. Earth is so called from being trodden by the feet; Mary is interpreted as “lady,” or “star of the sea,” or “enlightener.” And if you produce Maria in another way, that is, shorten it, you say *Maria*, and fullness is understood. Adam, persuaded by a woman, … Christ, restoring the Church, was born of a woman. Adam was deceived through a tree; Christ restored [Col. 0570B] the world through a tree. Adam was cast out of paradise; Christ brought the Thief into paradise on the cross. Adam was cast into hell; Christ drew him back from hell. Behold what kind of likeness there is between the two.

Man lost himself, and the Son of God freed everyone. He is blessed forever.

This man Aurelian, however, died in peace after a few years, on the seventh day before the Kalends of June. Observing the precepts of blessed Peter Chrysologus, he did not deviate from them. He left the buildings of the church unfinished. He was buried in the church of the Apostles beside the ambo, not far from the tomb where blessed Neon rests, before Neon’s body had been transferred by us to its seat. He sat [as bishop] for [lacuna] years, [lacuna] months, [lacuna] days, [lacuna].

[Col. 0570C]

## OBSERVATIONS ON THE LIFE OF SAINT AURELIAN

Whether the beginnings of the monastery of Pomposa are indicated here. The age of Agnellus, who wrote this and deferred the remainder to another time. Aurelian contemporary with Hormisdas.

### I

Our author gives a brief account of Aurelian, successor of Peter the Younger; more recent writers also have a little to say. Nevertheless, we possess one item that assists the history: namely, the beginnings of the celebrated monastery of Pomposa, as the author of the notes believes.

I would not, however, dare confidently to affirm that the monastery was built in Aurelian’s time, since I know from passages elsewhere that Agnellus understands by the name “monastery” a church lacking a parish. I rather think that a church was then built, to which a monastery was later added, after the age of Saint Benedict.

It is also uncertain whether Agnellus is speaking of the Comacchio territory as it existed in his own time or as it had been in Aurelian’s [Col. 0570D] age, when the places Bajas and Ignis were situated there. Moreover, he calls the Po “the old Po,” which they call the Volana. Rubeus calls Comacchio “Cymacchio” and praises it as a most ancient city founded by the Pelasgians. Agnellus notes that Ignis and Bajas are names of idols, but such idols are otherwise unknown to me. Some further remarks on the monastery of Pomposa will be added below, in the continuation of Agnellus.

### II

From what our author says concerning his age, I recognized above, in the observations on the poems prefixed to the work, that he committed the Life of Aurelian, together with the preceding material, to writing around the year 839. He deferred the remainder to a later time, as is clear from the notes there; and he did what he had threatened when pressed by his fellow priests: namely, he left the work unfinished.

Meanwhile, lest the Life of Aurelian should appear shorter than the others, he added a sufficiently long and rather crude exposition of the psalm verse: “You dried up the rivers of Ethan.”

### III

As for Aurelian’s age, he held office during the time of the supreme pontiff Hormisdas. The remaining matters are uncertain [Col. 0572A], though they will be considerably clarified in part by what will be said below.

# AGNELLUS’S *PONTIFICAL*

## PART TWO

Containing the Lives of those who flourished from the time of Ecclesius to George.

[Col. 0571]

# A CHRONOLOGICAL-HISTORICAL DISSERTATION

## On the Times of Ecclesius, Ursicinus, Victor, Maximian, and Agnellus

Chronology transmitted by Rubeus. Matters in Agnellus relevant to the reckoning of the times considered. Chronology arranged. The acts and dates of Silverius and Vigilius examined. The sequence of years investigated.

[Col. 0571B] As, in the preceding sections, I have done my best to clarify the chronology of the bishops of Ravenna, this dissertation on the next five bishops must be placed before the following material.

Rubeus, whom later writers followed, disregarding in part what Agnellus relates concerning the matters relevant to determining the times of these men, fixes the tenure of each prelate in the following manner. He places Aurelian’s death in the year 510, on the seventh day before the Kalends of June, and begins the episcopate of Ecclesius from that same year. He records Ecclesius’s death in 542 and substitutes Ursicinus, whom, following Agnellus, he says held office for three years and died in 545. In that same year he appoints Victor, whom he likewise says died in the following year, 546, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March, and that Maximian was appointed in his place. He believes Maximian’s life to have ended in 556, on the eighth day before the Kalends of March, on the basis of the manuscript Life of that pontiff preserved among the nuns of Saint Andrew at Ravenna.

Finally, after speaking of Agnellus’s ordination, he assigns it to the year 558 and, on the following page, although he gives him thirteen years of episcopate, says that he died “in the year 566 from the [Col. 0571C] Virgin’s birth.”

In some matters he agrees with Agnellus; in others he departs from him. The following points from our author must be noted.

Regarding Ecclesius, Agnellus says that the church of Saint Mary, which they called the Major Church, was begun by him “after he returned to Rome with Pope John from Constantinople, together with the other bishops sent by Theodoric on an embassy.” This implies that Ecclesius had begun his episcopate before that embassy. He concludes the Life by adding that Ecclesius sat for ten years, five months, and eight days.

Of Ursicinus he relates that he held office when “King Athalaric died at Ravenna on the sixth day before the Nones of October, and on the next day Theodahad was elevated,” and that he acted as pontiff for three years, six months, and nine days.

Although he says that Victor ruled the Church for a short time, he nevertheless reports that he raised many great and magnificent works, and finally, after sitting “six years, eleven months, and eleven days,” died on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March.

He says that Maximian was “consecrated bishop by Pope Vigilius [Col. 0571D] in the city of Patras in Achaea, on the day before the Ides of October, indiction 10, in the fifth post-consular year of Basilius the Younger, in the forty-eighth year of his life.” The copyist foolishly interpreted *P. C.* as *pacifici*.

He reports the following inscription, placed in the basilica of Saint Stephen:

> In honor of the holy and most blessed first martyr Stephen, Maximian, servant of Christ and bishop, with his assistance, built this basilica from its foundations and dedicated it on the third day before the Ides of December, indiction 14, in the ninth post-consular year of Basilius the Younger.

[Col. 0572B] He gives another from the basilica of Saint Apollinaris:

> At the command of the blessed Ursicinus, bishop, Julianus Argentarius built, adorned, and dedicated from its foundations this basilica of blessed Apollinaris the priest; the blessed bishop Maximian consecrated it on the ninth day of May, indiction 12, in the eighth post-consular year of Basilius.

And another from the *ardica* of Saint Vitalis:

> At the command of Ecclesius, the most blessed bishop, Julianus Argentarius built and adorned from its foundations the basilica of the blessed martyr Vitalis, and dedicated it; the most reverend bishop Maximian consecrated it on the thirteenth day … [lacuna] in the sixth post-consular year of Basilius the Younger.

He gives the day of Maximian’s death as the eighth day before the Kalends of March, but says nothing about the duration of his episcopate. This makes it necessary to determine or seek it from the age of the succeeding bishop.

Accordingly, Agnellus’s epitaph, reproduced by our author, must be transcribed here exactly as it stands in the manuscript I use:

> Here rests in peace Agnellus, archbishop, who sat for thirteen years, one month, and eight days; he lived eighty-three years and was laid to rest on the Kalends of August, indiction 3.

### II

It would be very easy to assign each event to its proper year from the tomb of Bishop Agnellus, were it not that the text transmitted by Rubeus is troublesome. It reads as follows:

> Here rests in peace Agnellus, bishop, who sat for thirteen years, one month, and eight days. He lived ninety-four years and was laid to rest on the Kalends of August, indiction 14.

The reading of the manuscript I use cannot be maintained; it has been corrupted by a more recent copyist, who, not content with writing “bishop” in place of “archbishop” for Agnellus, also imposed the false indiction 3 instead of the true 14.

For it will be clear from what is said below in the chronological dissertation concerning the age of the bishops who succeeded Agnellus that Agnellus’s life cannot be extended to the year 570, when indiction 3 was current in August. The indiction 14 cited by Rubeus must therefore be accepted. I admit that I have some doubt only on this point: perhaps what was written as 14 was followed by 15, considering the longer interregnum of two years which must be admitted between Agnellus and Peter if [Col. 0572D] indiction 14 is retained.

Perhaps, too, the copyist added one X to the years of Agnellus as read by Rubeus, since the age of eighty-one years, at which he was made bishop, might have seemed too advanced.

Despite these considerations, let us retain indiction 14, which is supported by other arguments, as will become clear from what follows. Bishop Agnellus therefore died on the Kalends of August in the year 556, when indiction 14 was current. Counting backward thirteen years, one month, and eight days, we find the year in which [Col. 0573A] he began to sit: 553, specifically 22 June, a Sunday, with solar cycle 2, lunar cycle 3, and Dominical Letter B.

In the same year Maximian died, according to the manuscript of the nuns of Saint Andrew cited by Rubeus, on the eighth day before the Kalends of March. The authority of the manuscript makes the day certain, but it is silent about the year. I would believe that he died in the preceding year, 552, solar cycle 1, lunar cycle 2, Dominical Letters G and F, for two reasons.

First, since during that period Pope Vigilius was being harassed in Constantinople in various ways over the question of the Three Chapters, and the emperor was unwilling, a considerable length of time was needed before a new bishop could be ordained.

Second, since I see Maximian’s death marked in the Martyrology on the ninth day before the Kalends of March, I believe that, because it occurred in February of a leap year, one day was added by the writers of the Martyrologies, and that the day of Maximian’s death was marked as 9 March instead of the eighth day before the Kalends.

I would, moreover, gladly agree with Rubeus in postponing his death to the year 556, considering the great buildings and all the other magnificent works completed by Maximian, as well as his journeys to Constantinople [Col. 0573B], and also considering Rubeus’s own authority. But the characters of Agnellus’s tomb make this impossible. Rubeus himself therefore speaks inconsistently and relates incompatible things: for if he says that Agnellus died in 566, when indiction 14 was current, and admits that he sat for thirteen years, one month, and eight days, he should not have asserted that he was ordained in 556. The duration of his episcopate would then have been only ten years, one month, and eight days.

The calculations having therefore been correctly applied, Agnellus’s ordination must be moved back to the year 553.

### III

Indiction 10, the fifth post-consular year of Basilius, was current in October of the year 566, when, as our author relates, Maximian was ordained by Vigilius at Patras, a city of Achaea, on the day before the Ides. Everything agrees perfectly: in that year, solar cycle 23 and Dominical Letter G, the fourteenth day of October, the very day of his ordination, occurred as stated, which wonderfully confirms the matter.

Maximian therefore lived in the episcopate for five years [Col. 0573C], six months, and eight days.

Victor died in the same year, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March. When he is said to have sat for six years, eleven months, and eleven days, this indicates that he was consecrated in the year 539, on 4 March. But 4 March in that year was a Friday, plainly unsuitable for episcopal ordinations.

It follows that an error has entered the numbers given: either a day is missing and XII should be written instead of II; or a day is missing and the year is excessive, so that it should read that he sat for five years, eleven months, and twelve days, having been ordained on 4 March of the leap year 540, when solar cycle 17 and Dominical Letters A and G were current—that is, on a Sunday.

Of Ursicinus, who preceded Victor, we know only that he sat for three years, six months, and nine days, and that he began to sit before Athalaric died, which occurred in the year 534, on the Nones of October. He must therefore have been ordained a few days before Athalaric’s death, in the last days of September, and died in the year 538, around April.

[Col. 0573D] Anyone unwilling to admit a longer interregnum between Ursicinus’s death and Victor’s consecration must assert that Victor was ordained in 539, on 5 March, namely in the evening of Saturday.

No one will deny that an interval of at least several months intervened if he observes the vicissitudes suffered by the Apostolic See in that same year 538, when Ursicinus also died and Silverius, the supreme pontiff, was expelled, Vigilius being intruded by Belisarius.

Ecclesius therefore died in the aforementioned year 534. Since, according to our author, he had sat for ten years, five months, and five days, it follows that he was ordained around the beginning of the year 524. Thus, in the following year, 525, he could have gone to Constantinople with Pope John of Rome and the other bishops, as Agnellus himself relates.

### IV

With the dates arranged in this way, so that what has been asserted under the guidance of our Agnellus may be more firmly established, it is necessary to turn our discussion to matters concerning the acts of the Roman pontiffs, especially Silverius and Vigilius, with whom the ordinations of the bishops of [Col. 0574A] Ravenna, and above all that of Maximian, are necessarily connected.

Anyone who has considered the matter somewhat carefully will admit that it remains obscured by much darkness to this day. Anastasius, who is usually of great assistance in such matters, presents it confusedly and obscurely. Baronius undertook to distribute the history chronologically on the basis of Anastasius, Liberatus, Victor of Tunnuna, the letters of Silverius and Vigilius, and the acts of the councils.

Nevertheless, in the judgment of learned men, Baronius appears to have assigned matters of greater importance to definite years on the basis solely of documents of suspect reliability. Anastasius was also rejected because he did not support the system once preconceived, as were the silence of Liberatus and Procopius, who say nothing of what Anastasius relates because it lies outside the scope of their narratives.

For this reason Baronius transfers Silverius’s death to the year 540: he accepts a letter attributed to Silverius and addressed to Vigilius, in which the pontiff is made to write:

> And when I have been driven out—although, [Col. 0574B] with the Lord’s favor, I have now continuously presided over it [that is, the Apostolic See] for three full years—you strive to invade my time.

The letter is said to have been dated on the eighth day before the Kalends of July. Since Anastasius reports that Silverius died and says that he was deposed on the twelfth day before the Kalends of June, Baronius concludes that he could not have died before the year 540, when he had begun his fourth year as pontiff.

But since that letter is judged spurious by the common calculation of scholars, it can provide no assistance in determining the matter. Nor, in fact, would Silverius merely have begun his fourth year; he would nearly have completed it. For if, as Baronius himself says, the cited letter was written by Silverius “after the completion of the third year of his see,” and if it was dated on the seventh day before the Kalends of July of the following year, 540, on 21 May, only a few days could have been lacking to complete the fourth year of his see. The date of his ordination would therefore have had to be placed, as Baronius himself would have to admit, after 21 May and before 25 June of the year 536.

[Col. 0574C] Moreover, if the entire tenor of that letter is weighed, it proves the opposite of what that distinguished man wished. Since the letter appears to have been written against Vigilius, who was then recently invading the Roman See, it follows that Vigilius did this while Silverius’s fourth year of pontificate was expiring. This is established by the words quoted above:

> And when I have been driven out—although, with the Lord’s favor, I have now continuously presided over it for three full years—you strive to invade my time.

Yet Baronius himself, who accepts a letter of Vigilius addressed to Eutherius and dated on the Kalends of March, in the consulship of John and Volusianus, says that Vigilius was intruded before March of the preceding year, 538.

It must nevertheless be observed that the dates of this letter have been corrupted. In it Vigilius says that the coming Easter will be celebrated on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May. But in the year 538, to which John’s consulship is assigned—better chronologists do not recognize Volusianus—Easter was celebrated on 4 April, solar cycle 15, lunar cycle 7, Dominical Letter C.

Nor do I think that the letter can be assigned to any neighboring year except 562, provided that the date is read with one unit added, as the twelfth day before the Kalends of May. [Col. 0574D] Easter in that year fell on that very day, when solar cycle 19, lunar cycle 11, and Dominical Letter E were current.

No support, therefore, can be obtained from such letters for assigning Silverius’s deposition and Vigilius’s intrusion to a definite time.

### V

Anastasius relates that, after Silverius had been ordained, the tyrant Theodahad was destroyed two months later by divine will, and that “Vitiges was elevated.”

Nothing useful can be extracted for these matters from the Chronicle of Victor of Tunnuna, since everything is assigned to years that are not its own.

Marcellinus, as usual, heaps together several events under indiction 14 and the fifth post-consular year of Belisarius, the most illustrious man, which is the year 536. Among the events proper to that year he has the following, which agree with what Anastasius relates:

> After Agapetus died at Constantinople, King Theodahad substitutes Silverius in the episcopate and, remaining there, sends him to Ravenna. Vitiges kills Theodahad at the place called Quintus, near the river Salernus, and then proceeds through Tuscany, plundering all the wealth of Theodahad, which he had gathered on the island and in the city of Venice. [Col. 0575A] Having entered Ravenna, he takes Metesuintha, the granddaughter of Theodoric, who had been driven from the kingdom, as his wife. For this reason Belisarius, with the Lord’s favor, enters Rome.

Evagrius, in Book IV, chapter 18, drawing on Procopius’s Gothic History, relates that Belisarius entered Rome through the efforts of Silverius, who for that reason had sent to him Fidelis, the curator of Athalaric:

> Rome, which had again been subjected to the Romans after sixty years during which it had been occupied by the Goths, on the ninth day of Apellaeus—that is, on the fifth day before the Ides of December—in the eleventh year of Justinian’s reign.

Baronius observes that the same is related by Nicephorus, although Anastasius says that Belisarius took possession of Rome on the fourth day before the Ides of December.

Justinian’s eleventh year of imperial rule began on the Kalends of April in the year 537, since he had been admitted to a share in the empire by Justin precisely on the Kalends of April and had begun to reign alone after Justin’s death on the Kalends of August of the same year, with Mavortius alone as consul, as Marcellinus likewise relates. There is no room for doubt on this point, for there exists a constitution of Justinian issued on the Kalends of September in the second consulship of Belisarius, which Baronius reproduces under the year 527.

Textual-variant register: *detinet*, “holds”; *Mora/Mara*, “Mara,” interpreted “bitter”; *tamen*, “nevertheless”; *pontificum vita*, “the life of the pontiffs”; *Sed istius*, “but of this one”; *adhaerere/adhaerescere*, “to cleave / to become attached”; *insinuare/insinuavi*, “to communicate / I have communicated”; *vestris*, “yours”; *flammantis/flammantibus*, “blazing / blazing ones”; *fluvios/fluvium*, “rivers / river” (here and below); *servos/conservos*, “servants / fellow-servants”; *stimulīs/incontinentiae*, “with goads / of incontinence”; *extra/ex terra*, “outside / from the earth”; *seduxerat/seduxit*, “had led astray / led astray”; *aequales virtutes/aequalis virtute*, “powers not equal / equal in power”; *alio modo*, “in another way”; and the corrupt *suam/suasus*: the latter means “persuaded,” while the former is materially uncertain in this context.

When these matters are compared, they appear not to cohere. For the beginning of Silverius’s pontificate cannot be placed before 8 August of the year 536. The acts of the Council of Constantinople under Menna, which were not completed until the month of July, and Justinian’s constitution, which is read as dated “on 8 August at Constantinople, in the second consulship of Belisarius [Col. 0575B], the most illustrious man,” mention Agapetus through Theophanes and the deacon Pelagius but make no mention of his successor Silverius. Silverius therefore had not yet been created.

If Theodahad’s death occurred two months after Silverius’s ordination, it must have taken place toward the end of the year, perhaps in December itself, as Agnellus has it in the Life of Ursicinus. Therefore, if Rome was recovered on the fifth or fourth day before the Ides of December, in the sixtieth year after its capture, Belisarius must have entered it at approximately the same time that Vitiges began to reign, in the year 536.

[Col. 0575C] This seems to be confirmed by the aforementioned letter of Vitiges to Justinian, number 32 of Book X of Cassiodorus’s *Variae*, if the words

> And lest, because of its smallness, it should be neglected, it has been proved to have been inflicted not merely upon the provinces but upon the very head of the world

are to be referred to Rome, recovered by Belisarius, as Baronius believes. For it is easy to conjecture that the letter was written before December of the year 537, indeed shortly after Vitiges had acquired royal dignity.

But if this is admitted, Rome was recovered not in Justinian’s eleventh year but while his tenth year was expiring, since the eleventh year must be counted from the Kalends of April of the year 537, as will be clear to anyone calculating backward from the year 526, in which Justinian had been admitted by Justin to a share in the empire on the Kalends of April.

[Col. 0575D] One of the two alternatives must therefore be rejected: either Belisarius recovered Rome in December 536, in the sixtieth year since it had been occupied by the Goths, in which case Justinian’s eleventh year had not yet begun; or, if it happened in December 537, while that eleventh year was expiring, Rome was not recovered in the sixtieth year calculated from the Gothic occupation.

### VI

[Col. 0576A] Although, amid these difficulties, the opinion of learned men is that Belisarius took possession of Rome in December of the year 536, lest they exceed the sixtieth year from the barbarians’ entry into it, I find it more probable that this happened in December 537, during the eleventh year of Justinian’s reign and the sixty-first year after the Heruli entered the city. Writers expressed this period with the rounded number of sixty years, as learned men know was often done in similar cases.

This is plainly more credible than the eleventh year of Justinian’s reign having been written in place of the tenth. Moreover, all the events related by Marcellinus in the Chronicle at the place cited above can scarcely be understood as having occurred within the very brief interval of only a few days. Yet they must be compressed within those limits if Theodahad was killed by Vitiges two months after Silverius’s election, around the beginning of December, and Belisarius took possession of Rome on the fourth or fifth day before the Ides of that same December in the year 536.

This becomes even less probable because, as is reported by the cited Evagrius and Procopius, Belisarius entered Rome through Silverius’s efforts. Since Marcellinus makes clear that Silverius was sent by Theodahad to Ravenna, where he remained as long as Theodahad lived, this is just as plausible as anything could be.

Many things, therefore—indeed, everything except Silverius’s election and Theodahad’s death—that Marcellinus assigns to indiction 14, that is, to the year 536, must be assigned to the following year, 537. This includes Vitiges’s return to Tuscany, his departure from there for Venice, and his plundering of the wealth which his predecessor had gathered there; afterward, his entry into Ravenna and marriage to Metesuintha. To these must be added his writing to Justinian to arrange peace and his waiting at Ravenna for a reply to the letter.

For it is wholly uncertain whether those words should be referred to the affairs and condition of the City, as discussed in the preceding paragraph.

It is also worth observing that, when Theodahad was killed, indiction 14 had passed into 15. The latter had already begun [Col. 0576B] to be counted from September of the year 536; and if he had been killed around December, the year 535 ought to have been recorded.

These matters, begun in the final days of 536, therefore transfer Belisarius’s entry into the Roman city to December of the following year, 537.

VII. Since Belisarius entered Rome no earlier than 9 or 10 December 537, the siege of the city by Vitiges likewise did not take place before 21 February, as Anastasius says, and as Procopius indicates by presenting a certain Sibylline oracle in Book I, chapter 24, of *The Gothic War*. From the impending siege arose the opportunity to introduce false witnesses against Silverius, as Procopius indicates in these words:

> “When there was a suspicion that Silverius, the bishop of the city, was plotting treachery with the Goths, he immediately sent him to Greece; shortly afterward he caused another pontiff, Vigilius by name, to be created.”

Silverius was therefore driven from his see in this manner around 20 February 538 and immediately deported to Greece. [Col. 0576C] From there, by Justinian’s order, he was soon commanded to depart for Rome, to be restored to his own see. But, while Rome itself was surrounded by the siege and Vigilius was acting with Belisarius, he came to the island of Palmaria and, after four months there—that is, on 20 June—departed to the heavenly realm.

These facts are entirely suitable for reconciling the dates in the better catalogues. Most assign to Silverius a pontificate of one year; some count five months, up to 20 February, when he was expelled from his see; others count nine months, up to 20 June, when he died, reckoning the whole intervening period. The catalogues themselves may be consulted in C. V. Papebrochius’s *Propylaeum*. The second catalogue, as it is called, and likewise the third, the Palatine-Vatican catalogue, assign Silverius one year, five months, and nine days. In an old parchment manuscript collated by the aforementioned Papebrochius with a second Corbie manuscript, the tenure of the same pontiff is extended to one year, nine months, and eleven days.

While Theodahad was still acting, Silverius served as pontiff from 9 September 536, although, with the clergy’s consent, he was not ordained until the following Sunday. [Col. 0576D] To this period belong what Liberatus records concerning Theodora and Vigilius, who was staying at Constantinople after Agapetus’s death:

> “The empress Theodora summoned Vigilius, the deacon, and secretly required him to promise her, etc. Vigilius therefore willingly accepted the promise, etc.; and after making his undertaking he departed for Rome. When he arrived there, he found Silverius ordained pope, and also Belisarius at Ravenna” [*Neapolis* should be read instead of *Ravenna*].

To the following year, however, belong what Anastasius records:

> “Theodora, having taken counsel with Vigilius the deacon, sent a letter to Rome to Pope Silverius, asking and entreating him: ‘Do not hesitate to come to us, or at least restore Anthimus to his position.’ When the blessed Silverius had read this, he groaned and said: ‘Now I know that this matter brings about the end of my life.’ But the most blessed Silverius, placing his confidence in the Lord and in blessed Peter, wrote back, saying: ‘Lady Augusta, I shall never do this, namely, restore a heretical man condemned in his wickedness.’ Then the Augusta, enraged, sent her orders to the patrician Belisarius through the deacon Vigilius, as follows: ‘Find some pretext against Pope Silverius and depose him from the episcopate, or at least send him to me without delay. Behold, there you have Vigilius, our dearest archdeacon and *apocrisiarius*, who has promised us that he will restore Patriarch Anthimus.’”

When Vigilius, who had come to Rome while Silverius occupied Peter’s see, proceeded from there to Naples, and then returned to Rome and from there went to Constantinople in the office of *apocrisiarius*, he had to negotiate with Theodora concerning the restoration of Anthimus, await a reply to the letters Theodora had written to Silverius, and return to Belisarius with the empress’s letters. All this must therefore have taken place over several months. Consequently, when the city’s siege finally began, Silverius was driven from the pontifical see by Belisarius, and Vigilius was intruded in his place.

VIII. When Ursicinus, bishop of Ravenna, died around April of the aforesaid year 538, not only the exile of Silverius, the legitimate pontiff, but also the siege of Rome—which was not lifted until the following year, 539—prevented a new bishop of Ravenna from being ordained in the place of the deceased. Since the affairs of the Roman Church had still not been settled, I think Victor’s ordination was postponed until 4 March 540, when Vigilius finally wished to defend not only himself but also the doctrine of the true faith and the privileges of the Roman Church. We have testimony to his proper exercise of the pontificate in a letter sent to Justinian, and likewise in another sent to Menna on 17 September.

There are ecclesiastical historians who profess that they cannot understand how Theodora, a woman of unrestrained temper and fury, could have postponed taking revenge on Vigilius, who had not at all kept his promises concerning the restoration of Anthimus; consequently, they find it difficult to assign the abduction of that pontiff from Rome to the later years. Yet this could not have occurred earlier than 545.

C. V. Papebrochius, in the first part of his *Chronico-Historical Conatus* concerning the catalogue of the supreme pontiffs—contained in that volume called the *Propylaeum*, which is otherwise extremely useful for pontifical chronology—modestly proposes a conjecture by which a double journey of Vigilius to Constantinople may be believed: the first immediately after he denied the restoration of Anthimus that he had promised, and after Silverius’s death, which he himself assigns to 538, when Vigilius was still especially detested by the Romans because of the crimes he had committed and was consequently accused before the Augusta of various offenses, as Anastasius relates; the second in 546, on account of the question of the Three Chapters.

On the first occasion, Theodora, ordering him to do so, afflicted him with exile, in addition to the other exceedingly wicked acts committed against him. On the second occasion, although we know that he took refuge in the basilica of Saint Euphemia because he feared for himself, the circumstances were different. Papebrochius therefore extends the earlier tribulation from the end of 538 into the year 540, distinguishing it from the events that took place again at Constantinople in the seventh year after his earlier return.

This conjecture of C. V. would resolve many historical complications and would consequently advise postponing Victor’s ordination for a longer period. Nevertheless, there are reasons that compel me to depart from the opinion of that most learned man.

First, neither in the whole of Vigilius’s letter to Justinian, sent through Flavius Dominicus, former consul and patrician, nor in the other letter sent to Menna on 17 September, in the consulship of Justin, that is, in the year 540, does any indication of the events conjectured by Papebrochius appear. Indeed, while Vigilius clears himself of the accusation of a certain malicious person and explains why he had delayed writing until that day after assuming the pontificate, he shows that he had previously been neither at Constantinople nor elsewhere in exile.

Furthermore, from the chronology of the years of the Gothic War corrected by the most learned Cardinal Noris in his dissertation *On the Fifth Synod*, chapter 6—where it is established in what year Belisarius truly proceeded to Constantinople with Vitiges after defeating him—an argument is derived that overturns Papebrochius’s conjecture.

Anastasius relates that when Belisarius came to Constantinople, the emperor questioned him:

> “How were matters with the Romans, or how had Vigilius been installed in the place of Silverius?”

The emperor and the Augusta then thanked him for his reply. Since Vigilius had not yet gone there when Belisarius came to Constantinople, the Augustus was asking Belisarius about Vigilius’s affairs. But in the very year in which Papebrochius conjectures that Vigilius returned from Constantinople to Rome, namely 540, Belisarius had come to Constantinople with Vitiges. Vigilius therefore had not been at Constantinople before that time.

Procopius assigns that journey of Belisarius to the fifth year of the Gothic War; but it must be assigned to the sixth, since the aforementioned cardinal has taught us that Procopius counted the second and third years of the Gothic War as one year. Hence arose the continuous anticipation of the years that led even very learned writers astray.

Cardinal Baronius correctly reports that Ravenna was captured and Vitiges defeated in 540. He then adds:

> “Moreover, you will know with certainty, reader, that the fifth year of the Gothic War was the fourteenth year of the emperor, from the fact that the same author assigns the second year of the Gothic War to the eleventh year of that emperor.”

The eleventh year of Justinian is not the second year of the Gothic War, but the third; the second year, however, is the same as the third according to Procopius.

IX. These matters had to be clarified so that it might be recognized that, while Vigilius was residing in Rome, Victor could have been ordained bishop of Ravenna on 4 March 540. I must now examine the remaining matters concerning Vigilius, in order to establish that Maximian was initiated on 14 October 546.

Concerning the place and time, Agnellus does not allow us to remain in doubt; his words must therefore be transcribed here again. He says:

> “Justinian, having devised a plan, ordered the blessed Maximian, a deacon of Pola, to be consecrated bishop by Pope Vigilius in the city of Patras in Achaea, on the day before the Ides of October, in the fifteenth indiction, in the consulship of Basil the Younger, in the forty-eighth year of his life; and, having given him the pallium, he sent him to Ravenna.”

Rubeus, following Agnellus’s footsteps, writes in Book III, page 158:

> “Accordingly, when the people of Ravenna requested the pallium from the Caesar through legates, he ordered Maximian to be consecrated archbishop of Ravenna by Vigilius, the supreme pontiff. At that time the pontiff was living in exile at Patras, a city of Achaea, by order of Theodora, Justinian’s wife. … Thus Maximian was consecrated archbishop of Ravenna by Vigilius on the day before the Ides of October, in the fifth consulship of Basil the Younger, in the tenth indiction, which falls in the year 546 from the Virgin’s birth, when he was in the forty-eighth year of his age.”

Everything is correct and appropriate, except the exile, if it is accepted on Agnellus’s authority that Vigilius was sent into exile by order of Theodora. For all the surviving records of those times are silent concerning Vigilius’s exile, with the exception of Anastasius. Nor could he have been in exile except during that brief interval between the Acts of the Fifth Synod, in which the Three Chapters were condemned, and the confirmation of that same synod by Vigilius himself—namely, from 3 July to 8 December 553.

At that time the proceedings of the Eighth Synod were issued, together with Vigilius’s letter, which the celebrated Petrus de Marca published from the royal manuscripts, along with a highly learned Latin translation and dissertation. By then Theodora had died, and the controversies concerning the restoration of Anthimus had ceased.

Although Vigilius was therefore not in exile in that year, he was nevertheless staying at Patras on the day before the Ides of October, although the common opinion is that he was not abducted from Rome until Saint Cecilia’s day in that same year.

Those who assign this date to the abduction believe Anastasius, who reports that Vigilius was detained “in the church of Saint Cecilia on 22 November, on whose feast day he was presenting himself to the people,” and was placed on the Tiber and carried away from Rome by ship; “when he entered Sicily, he was permitted to conduct an ordination in the city of Catana during the month of December.” But Anastasius shortly afterward relates that he reached Constantinople on the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord, while the people were singing, “Behold, the Lord, the ruler, has come.” They unanimously withdraw from this view because navigation from Catana to Constantinople in that winter weather could not have been completed in the very brief span of only a few days that elapsed from the Saturday devoted to the ordinations to the vigil of the Lord’s Nativity. That year, 546, the vigil fell on Monday, in solar cycle 23, with the Dominical Letter G. They therefore think that Marcellinus should rather be followed, since he records that Vigilius arrived at Constantinople on 25 January of the following year, 547.

X. Yet even this account does not make the matter probable, since a period of one month is neither long enough to deserve the name of an extended interval nor sufficient for Vigilius to have accomplished all the things that contemporary writers report.

Procopius, *The Gothic War*, Book III, chapter 16, writes:

> “Vigilius, the Roman bishop, summoned by the emperor from Sicily, came to Byzantium, ἐτύγκανε γὰρ πολὺν τινὰ χρόνον διὰ τοῦτο ἐν Σικελίᾳ τρεβὴν ἔχων—‘for he had, on this account, spent a considerable length of time staying in Sicily.’”

The same author indicates that Vigilius had remained longer in Sicily by recording that he sent grain purchased in Sicily to Rome, which was besieged by Totila and suffering from famine; the Goths intercepted it.

“Vigilius likewise,” says Petrus de Marca in the aforementioned dissertation, “in letters sent to Menna while on the journey, criticized the condemnation of the Three Chapters and asked, through legates sent to Justinian, that he permit it to be rescinded.” These letters are transcribed from Facundus, Book IV, chapter 4.

For the remaining matters, see Cardinal Noris, *Dissertation on the Fifth Synod*, chapter 4. There, in his usual manner—that is, with the greatest learning—he confirms the opinion of the celebrated Carlo Sigonio, Book XIX *On the Western Empire*, namely, that Vigilius departed from Rome in 545, contrary to Holstenius, Sirmondus, and other most distinguished scholars.

Noris, however, thinking that Anastasius must be rejected in every respect, says that Vigilius departed from Rome at the beginning of the aforesaid year 545 and did not arrive at Constantinople until 25 January 547. He derives the reason for the first assertion from Vigilius’s encyclical of 5 February 552: in it the pontiff says that he left Rome seven years earlier, whereas the seventh year would scarcely have begun two months earlier if he had departed Rome on 22 November 545.

The same claim is also asserted from Victor of Tunnuna, from whom it is shown that Justinian summoned Vigilius to Constantinople in 544. Noris further adds that this is proved by a letter of the Italian clergy—or rather by a petition to the envoys of the king of the Franks—written in 551, in which it is said that Vigilius had departed from Rome six years earlier.

Yet these arguments do not appear suitable for refuting Anastasius. The petition of the Italian clergy was written, as the most learned cardinal himself admits, at the end of 551; thus six years had elapsed from 22 November 545. The fact that Justinian summoned Vigilius in 544 does not mean that Vigilius set out at the beginning of 545. Indeed, it is more consistent with the evidence that he delayed, since when he finally left Rome, he departed unwillingly and was led away almost by force, as the Italian clergy testified, in agreement with Anastasius.

Nor is it so implausible that Vigilius’s encyclical should indicate that the seventh year had begun but was not yet complete—only two months into it—that we must therefore depart from Anastasius. It is customary in chronological questions to resolve such complications by this remedy; I see no reason why it may not be used here.

The *Auctuarium* of Marcellinus reports that Vigilius arrived at Constantinople on 25 January in the sixth consulship of Basil, that is, in the year 547, and the eminent cardinal follows it. But why might “eight days before the Kalends of January” not have been corrupted into “eight days before the Kalends of February”? Moreover, the circumstances transmitted by Anastasius point to the vigil of the Nativity.

Gregory, surnamed the Great, in Book II, letter 36, to the bishops throughout Ireland, or throughout Istria, does indeed bring together Vigilius’s opinion against the Acephali and the calamity of Rome, which was captured by Totila. But, apart from the fact that a difference of one month is not so significant that it compels us to conclude that the date was January 547, it seems possible to infer from Marcellinus’s *Auctuarium*, if we trust the tenth indiction, that Totila gained possession of Rome on 17 December 546. For the tenth indiction had been running since the preceding December.

Certainly the sixth consulship of Basil cannot properly be combined with the tenth indiction in December 547, since by then the eleventh indiction had begun. If this is accepted—namely, that Totila gained possession of Rome in December 546 and that Vigilius entered Constantinople at the same time, on the vigil of the Lord’s Nativity, where he immediately issued his decree against the Acephali—then Gregory the Great more suitably wrote that both events had occurred at the same time than if we say that Vigilius came to Constantinople on 25 January and that Rome was captured on 17 December 547.

XI. The exact day, or the kind of day, on which Vigilius came to Constantinople is not relevant to the present argument. What agrees with Agnellus’s chronology is that he was abducted from Rome in 545, and that consequently, in October of the following year, while living at Patras in Achaea, he ordained Maximian bishop of Ravenna.

Yet when we recognize from this chronological indication that the pontiff was already staying at Patras at the beginning of October, from which place he had decided to proceed to Constantinople by land through Achaea, the end of this journey appears to be postponed too far if it is extended beyond the Nativity of the Lord in that same year, since nearly three months elapsed from Maximian’s ordination to that year’s Nativity.

Moreover, since Agnellus appends years, days, and months to events in Maximian’s *Life* more carefully than he usually does elsewhere, he plainly shows that he derived many of his statements from the legitimate records of the Church of Ravenna, and perhaps from Maximian’s own *Annals*, which he praises. He is therefore a source of no little value for arranging the chronology of the acts of Pope Vigilius.

As for Patras, it is the celebrated city of the Peloponnese praised by Strabo in Book VIII and also distinguished in many respects by Pausanias in his *Achaica*, especially because Augustus granted autonomy among the Achaeans to the people of Patras alone. It still flourishes near the promontory of Rhium.

XII. What remains is to discuss only the time at which Agnellus of Ravenna was ordained; the matter can be settled briefly.

Since, after applying the calculations, we have seen that his ordination cannot be transferred beyond 22 June 583, there is no reason to repeat here what was said in the second paragraph. The exile of Vigilius to Proconnesus, asserted by writers of great renown, would indeed disrupt the entire sequence of events. But the most learned Cardinal Noris has shown with such certain arguments in his *Dissertation on the Fifth Synod*, chapter 8, that the pontiff was in no way sent into exile, that to add further arguments against the older opinion would be to carry wood into a forest.

A new bishop was therefore ordained at Constantinople on the aforesaid day, scarcely two weeks after the end of the synod.

As a conclusion to this dissertation, it seemed appropriate to arrange in three separate tables a distinct sequence of years corresponding respectively to secular affairs, the affairs of the Roman bishops, and those of the bishops of Ravenna, so that everything discussed up to this point might be visible, as it were, at a single glance.

# LIFE OF SAINT ECCLESIUS

[Col. 0583]

## CHAPTER ONE

The church and image of the Blessed Virgin. The times of Ecclesius. The basilica of Saint Vitalis praised. The death and tomb of Ecclesius.

Ecclesius XXIII, the holy vessel. Of average stature, neither tall nor short. His head was full of hair and shaggy; above the eyebrow [the transmitted text reads “ear”] there was a little gray, and he was handsome in appearance.

In his time the church of the blessed martyr Vitalis was founded by Julian the banker together with the bishop himself. This pontiff also built, under his own proprietary right, the church of the holy and ever-virgin undefiled Mary, which you see, of wondrous size, and, in the vault of the apse [and a front adorned with gold, and in that apse-vault], an image of the holy Mother of God, such as no human eye had ever been able to behold.

If anyone dared to gaze for a long time at that image, which contained the following metrical verses beneath its feet:

> The Virgin’s hall shines forth, she who received Christ from heaven;  
> An angel, a messenger, had first come from heaven.  
> A mystery! Mother of the Word, perpetual virgin,  
> And mother of her own Creator, the Lord.  
> The magi, the lame, the blind, death and life confess the truth.  
> Ecclesius dedicates these sacred heights to God.

The beginning of the church’s construction was prepared by Julian after the aforementioned pontiff Ecclesius returned with Pope John from Constantinople to Rome, together with the other bishops sent on an embassy by King Theoderic, as you heard above. He built the Tricolim [Tricollem], but left it unfinished.

Woe to you flocks—what shepherds they had! How greatly you have changed from them! They were true lamps in the Church, whose lamp-light shone every day for those who were in the house of God, as the Lord says: “The lamp of your body is your eye; if your eye is sound, your whole body will be full of light”; and elsewhere: “If your eye is evil, your whole body will be full of darkness.”

Let these things suffice for today, so that, after removing this man, we may introduce another pontiff. But, as I said above, in his time the church of the blessed martyr Vitalis was built by Julian the banker. No church in Italy is comparable in its buildings and mechanical workmanship.

As for the expenses of the aforementioned church of the martyr Vitalis, we find in the eulogy of the holy memory and remembrance of Julian, its founder, that 26,000 gold solidi were spent.
