[Note: [Col. 0583B] Marginal note: “26,000 gold solidi were spent on the church of Saint Vitalis. No church in Italy is comparable. Since in the monastery of Saint Vitalis itself, in the chapel called the Holy of Holies, there is a certain chest on which certain Greek letters are written, whose meaning is commonly unknown, and since I found them explained, I decided to set them down, together with their meaning and interpretation. It is:

> Here lies Strategius, who kept Rome and the West unharmed;  
> conqueror of the Gallic lords, and of Isaac, who was an assailant of the empire,  
> and of Armenia—the great king of Armenia of the vast world [the wording is corrupt].  
> For this illustrious lord was laid to rest here by his wife Susanna, who mourned him piously;  
> for thirty years she often sighed, bereft of her husband,  
> at her husband’s tomb [the construction is corrupt], through her kindly work, to God,  
> who is blessed at the rising and at the setting of the sun.  
> For he began military service, proceeding from the West toward the East.”

BACCH.]

Thus this most blessed man died and was buried in the church of the blessed martyr Vitalis, beneath the monastery of Saint Nazarius, before the altar in the central place, beside the body of the blessed bishop Ursicinus on one side and that of the blessed Victor on the other; and in the middle was this man.

## CHAPTER TWO

The disturbances between the Ravenna clergy and the bishop are settled. The letter of Pope Felix. Again, some matters concerning the death of Ecclesius.

It happened at that time that a dispute arose between the blessed pontiff Ecclesius and the priests concerning various matters of the Church. They went to the holy Pope Felix of the city of Rome so that he might establish just regulations between them. He summoned the bishop of Ravenna together with all the clergy, immediately issued a decree between them, and confirmed it as follows:

## LETTER OF POPE FELIX

[Col. 0585B]

> “Felix [IV], bishop of the city of Rome.
>
> The concern of our predecessors for ecclesiastical peace and quiet is worthy of praise, because a shepherd who must keep watch and restrain disputes either condemns or corrects them. As we walk along this same path, we ought to be seen as like them, because, by God’s mercy, we hold their place and ought to follow their examples.
>
> Through envy, such things have occurred among the priests of the church of Ravenna as are known to have saddened the minds of all Catholics: quarrels, seditions, and wickednesses that sought to tear apart the whole of ecclesiastical discipline. We again … keeping the true fear of God before our eyes, so that we neither give boldness to unlawful excesses nor reject … [lacuna] by our decree to establish what is just, according to Solomon, who says: ‘Do not give passage to water.’
>
> Therefore, after reviewing the petitions submitted by our brother Ecclesius [*our brother* is absent], and by the priests, deacons, clerics [clergy], and notaries of the church of Ravenna, in the presence of our brother and fellow priest Ecclesius and of the clergy designated below, we judge what we have seen to be reasonable: they ought to undertake the office of the clergy, provided that the authority of the sacred canons cannot impugn their life and conduct.
>
> As for clerics, wishing only that they be properly appointed and publicly announced, we order that, so far as priests and deacons are concerned, they be solemnly promoted at the appointed times. Regarding the church of Ravenna and of Classis, let the ancient custom be preserved.
>
> Clerics and monks seeking to obtain an order or position to which they are not entitled shall not seek the patronage of powerful men, through which the bishop might appear either ungrateful when he does not comply or unjust when he does.
>
> The fourth part of the patrimony of the church of Ravenna, namely three thousand solidi, shall be completed by the customary distributions to all the clergy, or to those to whom it is customary to distribute them. If, however, by the will of our Lord, something should accrue from rents or inheritances, then, with the same Lord’s help, it too shall be added to the fourth portion [shall contribute to it]. Yet this must be done in such a way that, once written accounts have been arranged, what is distributed to each person cannot remain hidden … [lacuna] according to merit and according to rank, since God has established everything according to justice and measure … [lacuna] so that each person, except in the necessity of illness or for a legitimate reason connected with the altar, may vigilantly observe everything belonging to his office.
>
> We decree that the revenues of estates [the variant reading is *excepta*], as well as additions for household expenses, gifts offered to various persons, and banquets which it is necessary to provide for them, whether on account of their position, merit, or the reception of visitors, should accrue to the bishop.
>
> Let no one from the clergy attempt to form any conspiracy or private gathering that could not remain unpunished even among laypeople in the Church of God. For just as we hope that heavenly mercy will not allow such things to be admitted, so, if anyone attempts them, let him experience the authority of the canons and ecclesiastical discipline, according to the Apostle’s saying: ‘Correct those who offend in the presence of all, so that the rest may have fear.’
>
> Let the good, who keep watch over God’s works, deserve praise. Let those who appear to adorn their purpose through their obedience experience the affection of their own priest. Let those who do not cease from works pleasing to God in their offices and services glory in the love of their pontiff, as the divine words say: ‘The laborer is worthy of his wages.’
>
> As for the patrimony of the Church, by the judgment of their bishop … [lacuna] let selected persons from the clergy, with the assistants whom the bishop shall appoint for the purpose of keeping accounts, be sent under suitable surety; their fidelity and diligence must first have been proved, so that the sustenance of the poor may not suffer fraud, the amount of the Church’s patrimony may not remain hidden, and each cleric, under fear of God and of his own priest, may faithfully render an account of what has been entrusted to him.
>
> But there is something that must be utterly detested with a devout purpose. We ought not even to speak of it or set it out in words. It has come to our attention that some members of the clergy attend spectacles. This is so cruel a matter that it disturbs the souls of Catholics by its abomination: those whom one has heard reciting the divine words in the house of God, one sees gathering at spectacles contrary to the commandments. In these things discipline is brought to shame and divine precepts are trampled underfoot.
>
> Therefore the bishop must also take care concerning this matter, so that, if they do not do it, they may not do it in the future, and, if they do, they may be corrected according to ecclesiastical discipline.
>
> If any members of the clergy hold urban or rural estates belonging to the Church, we decree that these be assigned to them by written leases at a fair assessment of the rent, so that they may retain what they customarily receive according to their customary arrangements, but transfer what remains to the ecclesiastical revenues for the benefit of the Church.
>
> Concerning urban or rural estates and other movable property left by the faithful by name to various basilicas for the sake of their souls’ salvation, let the ancient custom be preserved.
>
> As for the notaries, according to the order of the register—first notaries, second notaries, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh—let them, on their own responsibility and in the presence of the priests and deacons, receive the ecclesiastical documents described in faithful written summaries, so that whenever the occasion requires they may produce and return them faithfully. Nevertheless, we order them to do everything with the command and arrangement of their bishop.
>
> For this reason all ecclesiastical documents must be recorded: so that in no way may those received perish, or be unable to be produced for ecclesiastical needs when they are required.
>
> Yet those notaries who are diligent and energetic in observing their office shall obtain, without diminution, the benefits assigned to them and to their predecessors from ancient times.
>
> They too, as reason requires and antiquity has ordained, shall return to those concerned, signed by the bishop’s hand, the leases and securities of the entire ecclesiastical patrimony.
>
> Whenever ecclesiastical estates, whether urban or rural, have been given to secular persons who have no need to support a household, let the bishop, through the clerics whom he orders, recall them to the ownership of the Church; and thereafter let him presume to give them to no one except for the reason stated above.
>
> Mastalus, archdeacon of the church of Ravenna, shall receive without diminution the benefits assigned to that office according to ancient custom, just as it is clear that those who held it before him obtained them.
>
> Let monasteries of men and of women servants of God be organized by the bishop, so that reason, justice, peace, and discipline may be preserved for all.
>
> The order of our position requires us not to remain silent about these matters; our brother Ecclesius is bound to guard them, because justice preserved with the canons generates peace. From justice proceeds charity, through which we see God and by whose grace we are able to observe these precepts.
>
> Therefore it is fitting for us to be negligent in nothing, but watchful in all things, so that we may return to the giver of all good the talent entrusted to us, increased by good works.
>
> We have acknowledged this.
>
> Coelius.”

[Col. 0587C]

> “I, Felix, bishop of the Catholic Church of the city of Rome, have subscribed to this decree between the parties.”

Names of the priests, deacons, and clerics of the church of Ravenna who came to Rome with the bishop:

Patritius, priest. Stephanus, priest. Constantinus, priest. Servandus, priest. [Honorius, priest.] Exuperantius, priest. Clemens, deacon. Ursus, deacon. Felicissimus, deacon. Vigilius, deacon. [Col. 0587D] Neon, deacon. Johannes, deacon. Stephanus, deacon. Gerontius, subdeacon. Honorius, subdeacon. Petrus, subdeacon. Vitalis, subdeacon. Julianus, acolyte. Faustinus, acolyte. Romanus, acolyte. Severinus, acolyte. [Andreas, acolyte. Petrus, lector. Marcus, lector. [Col. 0588A] Asterius, lector. Another Petrus, lector. Andreas, lector. Marinus, defensor. Majoranus, notary-defensor. Hermolaus, primicerius-defensor. Honorius, cantor. Tranquillus, cantor. Antonius, cantor. Melitus, cantor.]

Names of the priests and deacons who came to Rome with the priest Victor and the deacon Mastalus:

Laurentius, priest. Rusticus, priest. Victor, priest. [Col. 0588B] Thomas, priest. Mastalus, deacon. Magnus, deacon. Paulus, deacon. Agnellus, deacon. Maurus, subdeacon. Stephanus, acolyte. Vincemalus, acolyte. Thomas, lector. Laurentius, lector. Florus, lector. Reparatus, lector. Luminosus, lector. Calunnius, lector. Ysaac, lector. [Col. 0588C] Laurentius, granary keeper. Petrus, dean. Stephanus, dean. Vendemius, acolyte. Colos, acolyte. Cassianus, acolyte. Laurentius, acolyte. Stephanus, acolyte.

After these events the blessed Ecclesius came to his senses, and thereafter was like a father to his sheep, as a father with his sons. He bestowed everything upon his clergy, once he had been corrected by the Roman pontiff; indeed, he became even more generous. After this he governed his Church in peace, and heard no word of complaint from his clergy, but only praises. [Col. 0588D] These statutes remained in force for his successors for many generations.

He was buried, as we said, in the church of Saint Vitalis. In the forecourt of its façade he ordered the following metrical verses to be written in silver tesserae:

> The lofty temples rise with venerable summit,  
> Sanctified to God by the name of Vitalis.  
> Gervasius and Protasius likewise hold this fortress,  
> Whom their lineage, faith, and temples unite.  
> Their father, fleeing the contagions of the world,  
> Was an example of faith and martyrdom to his sons.  
> Ecclesius first entrusted this fortress to Julian,  
> Who wondrously fulfilled the work committed to him.  
> He also commanded this to be maintained by perpetual law:  
> Let no one be permitted to bury bodies in these places.  
> But since the monuments of earlier pontiffs stand there,  
> Let it be lawful only to place there those who are like them.

He sat for ten years, five months, and seven days.

# OBSERVATIONS ON THE LIFE OF SAINT ECCLESIUS

[Col. 0589]

Was the basilica of Saint Vitalis built with Justinian’s money? The Augustus did not attend its dedication. The monogram does not concern Narses. Julian the Banker: an office, not a surname. The inscription of Isaac Strategius. Analysis of the Constitution of Felix.

I. First, the enormous work of Ecclesius and Julian the banker presents itself—namely, the basilica of Saint Vitalis. On account of its excellent and remarkable construction in an age that was not especially cultivated, and in an Italy afflicted by incredible calamities, the story—which Rubeus rightly refutes—deserves a somewhat less severe criticism. For it is scarcely credible that a private individual, or even the bishop of a city subject to Arian kings, could have supplied the expenses, which our author testifies rose to 26,000 gold solidi.

From the time of Valentinian and Valens, when previously eighty-four gold solidi made one pound of gold, and seven solidi made one ounce, the external valuation of the solidus was increased, and it was decreed that six solidi should equal one ounce and seventy-two solidi one pound of gold; this pound was called the Western pound. On this subject we possess the learned and highly useful Dissertation of Jacobus Gothofredus on the Theodosian Code, book I, *De Oblatione votorum*, title XXIV; it also elucidates book II of the Justinian Code, *De veteris numismatis potestate*. Thus 26,000 gold solidi were valued at 4,333⅓ ounces of gold, which corresponded almost exactly to 34,664 of our gold shields, eight of which are reckoned to one ounce of gold.

Moreover, from Agnellus it is clear to whom the glory of founding the basilica belongs, and the tale does not deserve a more extensive refutation—although the common people have obstinately continued to defend it to this day, as though the dignity of the building would perish unless, with the story added, it were declared to have been founded by the Emperor.

Agnellus appropriately informs us that “the beginning of the construction of the church”—understand this not only of the church of Saint Mary Major, but also of Saint Vitalis—“was completed by Julian after the aforementioned Bishop Ecclesius returned with Pope John from Constantinople to Rome, together with the other bishops sent by Theodoric on an embassy.” For while the Arian king was raging against the Catholics, and even threatening to overthrow the Catholic churches, it would not have been possible to consider such a project freely.

Yet no one who knows the sound counsels of the excellent woman Amalasuntha, and her harmony with Justinian, will wonder that this could have been done under her rule. The church was not completed during the lifetime of Ecclesius, however, but only under Bishop Maximian, after the efforts of Theodahad and Vitigis had been overcome and Ravenna had been recovered by Justinian.

At that time, too, the crowns were placed upon it, and Justinian’s favor and the gifts bestowed upon the church were commemorated in mosaic work. I believe that these are represented by the mosaics still surviving, which Rubeus, Alemannus in his notes on Procopius in part, Octavius Ferrarius in *De re vestiaria*, Ducange in *Byzantine Families*, and also Ciampinus in the second volume of *Ancient Mosaics*, have published in engravings. I do not believe that the solemnity of the church’s dedication is represented by them, since nothing corresponds to the ceremonies appropriate to such an event, and since neither Justinian nor Theodora was ever at Ravenna.

The gifts offered for completing or enriching the church are therefore being represented: each of them displays an urn, basket, or something similar indicating an offering. Hence it is also permissible to attribute this distinction to the famous basilica: with the munificence of the Emperor Justinian added, what Ecclesius and Julian had begun was completed and enlarged, while those elements that cannot be maintained are relegated to the realm of fable, since the entire history of that period contradicts them.

Thus both statements will be true which our supreme authority among scholars, Mabillon, wrote with a qualification in his *Italian Journey*:

> “Among the Ravennates there is no basilica of greater dignity than Saint Vitalis, made illustrious by the monastery of our Cassinensians. It is the work either of the Emperor Justinian, as more recent writers prefer, or of Julian the banker, commissioned by Bishop Ecclesius, as Rubeus proves from an ancient inscription.”

Rubeus, book III, p. 152, writes:

> “Meanwhile, at Ravenna, the temple of the blessed martyr Vitalis began to be built by Julian the banker, at the command, as they say, of Justinian Caesar, who had already, three years earlier, constructed and dedicated at Constantinople, with the greatest expense and skill, the sacred church of Saint Sophia.”

On p. 560, after elegantly describing the church and noting the buildings that the care of our contemporaries had adorned with their present elegance, Rubeus adds the verses copied from Agnellus and the complete inscription, which we possess partly mutilated in the Este manuscript and which is also found in the *Life of Maximian*. I therefore think it should be reproduced here. It is as follows:

> “Julian the banker built the basilica of the blessed Vitalis at the command of Bishop Ecclesius; it was consecrated by the most reverend Bishop Maximian on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the sixth year after the consulship of Basil the Younger, a man of consular rank, in the tenth indiction.”

At this point Rubeus continues:

> “Since no mention is made of Justinian, and since Procopius the rhetorician, a contemporary of those times, in the little book he published on Justinian’s buildings—where he treats even the smallest matters with the greatest care—says nothing about these buildings at Ravenna, I have nothing certain to write. Let belief rest with those authors who report that Justinian and Theodora adorned the consecrated temple with splendid gifts . . .”

Earlier, however, Rubeus had said that Justinian and Theodora were present when the basilica was consecrated. Alemannus denied that this could be maintained in his notes on Procopius’ *Secret History*, chapter 9.

Some have also said that Narses contributed labor and money to the construction of the church of Saint Vitalis, and for no other reason than that a monogram is visible on the capitals of the enormous columns, composed of intertwined letters that seem to form the name of Narses. Others, however, believe that Justinian’s name can be read there. I recognize neither interpretation. Certainly, before Narses assumed responsibility for affairs in Italy on Justinian’s behalf, the basilica of Saint Vitalis had not only been completed but also dedicated, as is clear from the preceding Dissertation.

Our most learned Montfaucon, in the first volume recently published in which he describes his Italian Journey, believes that the monogram indicates the name of the craftsman, who was called Nepos. The monogram is of the following form:

[The monogram is not represented in the supplied text.]

There is also, on the capitals of certain columns in the same basilica, a monogram in which Julian’s name appears to be written in abbreviated form. Hence it seems highly credible to me that the other monogram, together with the sign of the cross, presents the name of Bishop Ecclesius in a similarly intertwined form.

## II.

Two matters seem worthy of special investigation. The first is whether Julian is called *argentarius* as a surname, or rather by virtue of his office; the second is what he himself contributed to the construction of the basilica.

To add further arguments demonstrating that the use of surnames for distinguishing a family or clan is much more recent than the time of this Julian—and could not even properly be applied to the time of Agnellus, who was writing then—would be to spend good hours establishing a point that is perfectly clear, although some people obstinately cling to their preconceived opinions even to this day.

The word, therefore, is the name of an office by which this Julian is distinguished. He was otherwise a man of great reputation among the Ravennates, and Bacauda was his son-in-law. Agnellus praises him and calls him a man “of holy memory.”

Those bankers were people with whom money was deposited at interest and who exchanged money itself. They were also called money-changers, *nummularii*, *trapezitae*, or ἀργυρομοίβοι (*argyromoiboi*, “silver-exchangers”). Such a man is the one who:

> “Made himself a merchant in both kinds of metal,  
> and always changed one into the use of the other,”

as the verses of Manilius read after Salmasius corrected them in his *Plinian Exercises*.

We can learn about their guild and their methods of contracting in the period of Ecclesius, bishop of Ravenna, from Justinian’s Novel 136, *On Transactions with Bankers*, issued “on the Kalends of April, in the consulship of Our Lord Justinian, perpetual emperor, and Basil, a man of consular rank.”

We know of a certain John the banker at Ravenna in the time of Saint Gregory the Great. When he had acted as surety for a certain Palatine named Importunus, he came to Rome and remained for a long time in a church, accused of having stood surety for the sake of his own advantage—namely, profit. He cleared himself of the charge at the most sacred body of the blessed chief of the apostles. For this reason Saint Gregory acts as his advocate before the exarch, in letter 23 of book IX, addressed to John of Ravenna, in January of the fourth indiction.

But what common relationship did such an office have with the revenues of the church? It seems impossible to doubt that the church of Saint Vitalis was built with the bishop’s money, while Julian the banker, or money-changer, was placed in charge of properly disbursing those funds and supervising the construction of the basilica. This is the second question proposed.

This seems to me to be indicated by the words of the inscription: “Julian built it at the command of Bishop Ecclesius,” and by the verses that were read in the church’s atrium:

> “Ecclesius first entrusted this citadel to Julian,  
> who marvelously completed the work entrusted to him.”

I therefore believe that this Julian was the banker of the church of Ravenna, entrusted with keeping ecclesiastical revenues deposited with him. In accordance with the bishop’s instructions—or with agreements made with the clergy, as will shortly be explained—he would distribute the money, after keeping the accounts, to the archpriest, archdeacon, and chief clerk, for them to distribute further.

It is known that the guardian of the bishop’s treasury was counted among the ecclesiastical offices. He was called the *sacellarius*, from the treasury, which they called the *saccus*, “bag.” Thus John the Deacon, in the *Life of Saint Gregory*, book II, chapter 23, praises a *sacellarius* whom “the holy pontiff had customarily ordered to invite twelve pilgrims to dinner.”

Gregory himself, speaking in book IV, letter 34, of the enormous distributions made in the Roman Church during the Lombard period, says:

> “Just as in the regions of Ravenna the piety of our lords has a *sacellarius* with the first army of Italy, who provides daily expenses as circumstances arise, so in this city I am their *sacellarius* in such matters.”

Here, however, by the word *sacellarius* he means not a person holding an ecclesiastical office but anyone responsible for public money, just as the public treasury is called the *fiscus*, the public bag.

Nevertheless, a *sacellarius* was also a minister of the church, to whom the church’s bag, or treasury, was entrusted, although, as they say, he was entirely different from the treasurer. Isidore describes his office:

> “To the treasurer belongs the appointment of the doorkeepers of the basilicas”—

Thomasinus counts these among the laymen, like the *basilicarii*, in *Ancient and Modern Ecclesiastical Discipline*, part I, book II, chapter 103—

> “the preparation of incense, the care of preparing the chrism”—that is, the care of preparing whatever is required for making chrism—“the care of arranging the baptistery, and the preparation of lamps in the sacristy and for the sacrifices.”

I therefore believe that Julian was the *sacellarius* of the church of Ravenna, also called a banker or *argentophylax*, whose responsibilities in constructing Saint Vitalis and in other matters undertaken at the bishop’s command included receiving money, supplying it from the church’s bag or treasury, and supervising the work.

## III.

The inept author of the marginal notes, who reproduced here a corrupt ancient inscription of Isaac the *strategos*, compels me to print the Greek text again together with its Latin translation, although Rubeus long ago, in book IV, and most recently our learned Montfaucon, have each published a copy transcribed at Ravenna in the first volume of his Italian Journey mentioned above.

The Greek text is as follows:

> Ἐνταῦθα κεῖται ὁ στρατηγήσας καλῶς  
> Ῥώμην φύλαξας ἀβλαβὴ, καὶ τὴν Δύσιν  
> Τοῖς γαλήνοις τρὶς δεσπόταις ἕξ ἐνὶ αὐτοῖς  
> Ἰσαάκιος, τῶν βασιλέων ὁ σύμμαχος.  
>   
> Ὁ τῆς ἁπάσης Ἀρμενίας κόσμος μέγας,  
> Ἀρμένιος γὰρ ἦν οὗτος ἐκ λαμπροῦ γένους.  
>   
> Τούτου θανόντος εὐκλέως, ἡ σύμβι  
> Σώσαννα σώφρων, τρυγόνος τρόπῳ σεμνῆς  
> Πικρῶς στενάζει τοῦ ἀνδρὸς ἐστερημένη.  
>   
> Ἀνδρὸς λάξαντος ἐκ καμάτων εὐδοξίαν  
> Ἐν ταῖς ἀνατολαῖς ἡλίου, καὶ τῇ δύσει·  
> Στρατοῦ γὰρ ἦρξε τῆς Δύσεως, καὶ τῆς Ἐῶ.

> Translation of the Greek: Here lies Isaac, who exercised military command well,  
> preserving Rome and the West unharmed,  
> for three times six years under tranquil sovereigns,  
> the ally of the emperors.  
>   
> He was the great ornament of all Armenia,  
> for he was an Armenian of illustrious descent.  
>   
> When he had died gloriously, his wife,  
> Susanna, prudent and chaste in the manner of a turtle-dove,  
> bitterly laments, deprived of her husband—  
>   
> a husband who won glory through his labors  
> in the lands of the rising sun and in the West;  
> for he commanded the army of the West and of the East.

The accompanying Latin version reads in translation:

> Here lies Isaac, who rightly acted as a military leader,  
> preserving Rome and the West unharmed,  
> for three times six years under tranquil princes,  
> Isaac, the comrade-in-arms of kings.  
>   
> The great ornament of all Armenia,  
> for he was an Armenian of illustrious descent.  
>   
> When he had died gloriously, his spouse,  
> the prudent Susanna, in the manner of a chaste turtle-dove,  
> continually groans, deprived of her husband—  
>   
> a man who obtained glory through his labors  
> in the east of the sun and in the West;  
> for he increased the army of the East and of the West.

Rubeus learnedly records in the appropriate places the deeds of this Isaac, exarch of Ravenna. It is useful to add here a fragment of an unpublished inscription, excavated at Cymaclum and preserved at Ravenna in the house of a certain citizen. In it the son of this Isaac is praised after his death, as on the tablet marked A.

## IV.

When discord arose among the clergy of Ravenna, Felix IV issued a constitution, which our Agnellus preserved, to the great benefit of ecclesiastical scholarship. We now publish it for the first time. It is nevertheless regrettable that, through the ignorance of the copyists, it is in places so corrupt and mutilated that, having despaired of correcting it suitably, I thought it preferable to transcribe even the errors themselves, although they destroy the entire sense, exactly as they stood.

This difficulty is encountered especially at the beginning of the constitution. As it proceeds, everything coheres reasonably well. It was headed: “Felix IV, bishop,” and so forth. I have deleted the numerical notation, since it appears to have been added arbitrarily by the copyist. This warning is sufficient.

It is uncertain whether we possess any other constitutions of this pontiff. Of the three circulated under his name, the first two were stitched together by an impostor from letters of other pontiffs. The third, although Sirmond attributed it to this Felix on the basis of its consular notation, was formerly believed to belong to Felix III and to have been addressed to Caesarius of Arles.

The value of this constitution is therefore enhanced by its rarity, but there are also several reasons for recognizing its usefulness. First, it easily dispels the statements made elsewhere by Agnellus against the authority of the Roman See. For he himself admits that the dissenting bishop and clergy “went to the holy Pope Felix of the city of Rome, so that he might establish just regulations between them,” and he presents documents from which it is clear that the bishop of Ravenna and the clergy acknowledged the Roman pontiff as judge of the church of Ravenna and its legitimate governor.

Second, the tenor of the decree and the matters established in it show that the central issue in the preceding dispute was disagreement concerning the ordination of sacred ministers, the proper distribution of the church’s revenues—especially those that came in addition through the piety of the faithful—and the accounts that had to be rendered by stewards, notaries, and others of this kind. The principal authors of the dispute were Victor the archpriest and Mastalo the archdeacon. From the appended list of the clergy it also becomes known who adhered to the bishop and who adhered to Victor and Mastalo.

Since 3,000 solidi amounted to one quarter of the revenues of the church of Ravenna in the time of Bishop Ecclesius, it follows that 12,000 solidi constituted the entire revenue of the Ravennate church. According to the valuation mentioned above, this corresponded to 16,000 of our gold shields, eight of which make one ounce of gold.

That the revenues of the church of Ravenna increased in later times will be clear especially under Bishops Maximian and Agnellus, when, at Justinian’s command, the churches of the Arian bishops and of the Goths were added to it.

Benedict the deacon, in the time of Bishop Maurus, is said to have received from the Sicilian patrimony alone, “in addition to 50,000 *modii* of wheat, without any other grain or legumes, red-dyed and hyacinth-colored ram skins, silk-adorned *casulae* and cloaks, and other vestments, and vessels of brass and silver,” 31,000 gold solidi, of which he transported 15,000 to the imperial palace at Constantinople and 16,000 to the church archive.

I believe, however, that these were revenues from several years, not from one year alone.

## V.

From this we can also recognize that the clergy of the church of Ravenna consisted of nine priests, eleven deacons, five subdeacons, eleven acolytes, twelve readers, four singers, two deans, one defender, one notary-defender, one chief defender, and one granary keeper.

Although I believe that not all who were listed in the register went to Rome, and consequently acknowledge that there were others besides them, I nevertheless think that persons of each order were sent.

That there were several notaries is clear from Felix’s constitution itself. Since they had been entered on different occasions in wax, or in the register, they were called the first, second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh chief notaries. It is also established elsewhere that these belonged to the class of laymen serving the church—a matter on which Thomasinus should be consulted in the place cited—and it is plainly inferred from this same decree, where it is provided that ecclesiastical property must not be left in the hands of men of secular conduct, after the notaries of this kind had been permitted to receive it “without diminution of the privileges assigned to them or to their predecessors from ancient times.”

Among the clerical order, however, we have the notary Majoranus, who is also called a defender. Ducange believes that in the Roman Church, as elsewhere, notaries were chosen from among the clergy.

He also learnedly explains the office of the defenders. Here we have three of them, including the senior, or chief, defender.

Here we read of two deans, listed among the lower clergy and almost at the end of the list. The office of a dean in this period was therefore entirely different from that of deans in later centuries, who in canonical or collegiate churches held the position that a prior held in monasteries.

Ducange deals with this subject as well. In his *Glossary of Greekness*, from the Alatian manuscript, he recognizes deans among the church’s minor officials, whose office is described as follows:

> Ὁ δεκανὸς τάσσει τοὺς ἱερεῖς ἐν τοῖς ἐρκομένοις αὐτῶν δικαιώμασι·

> “The dean assigns the priests to the rights due to them.”

And again:

> Ὁ δεκανὸς ἵνα κᾶλη τοὺς ἱερεῖς εἰς τὰ αὐτῶν δικαιώματα καὶ προσφερέματα.

> “The dean is to summon the priests to receive their rights and offerings.”

The most learned author adds:

> “His”—that is, the dean’s—“office is to summon the priests by name when they are to receive their monthly distributions or allowances.”

I believe that this very office belonged to the deans in the church of Ravenna, since they are listed here in the lowest position.

The granary keeper also has a place before the deans. I do not remember having read anything about him anywhere. From the name, however, it seems to indicate a man entrusted with the care of public grain, which was to be distributed or sold to the clergy and the poor.

This office may have been peculiar to the church of Ravenna, because an enormous quantity of grain was collected from its estates in Sicily. We shall touch on this matter below from the *Life of Archbishop Maurus*.

From the entire list of the Ravennate clergy reproduced here it appears that the names “priests,” “deacons,” “subdeacons,” “acolytes,” and “readers” denote ranks, while the other terms signify particular offices.

## VI.

As for the quarter of the revenues from the patrimony of the Ravennate church, which the pontiff decrees should be used to “complete the customary distributions to all the clergy, or to those to whom distributions were customarily made,” this was done according to the letter of Gelasius, Roman pontiff, to the bishops of Lucania. In that letter he prescribed that all the revenues of the Church should be divided into four parts:

> “One part the bishop retained for himself; another the clergy received for the diligence of their offices; the third was assigned to the buildings; and the fourth was distributed to the poor and pilgrims.”

Felix distinguishes three classes of other ecclesiastical revenues.

The first consisted of revenues that came through “expenditures and inheritances” in addition to the customary income. He orders these to be added to the clergy’s quarter and distributed according to each person’s merit and labor.

The second consisted of revenues drawn from estates newly acquired by the church. He decrees that these should belong to the bishop, who was to use them for household expenses or for providing gifts and banquets to guests, in accordance with the dignity of his position and with the merit and status of those for whom these things were prepared.

The third comprised “urban or rural estates, or movable property” that the faithful had “left by name to different basilicas as payment for their souls.” Regarding these Felix establishes nothing new but orders the ancient custom to be preserved, since such properties were added to the remaining patrimony of the church.

From these points, and from what follows, I believe it becomes clear that even then, when these matters were being regulated, there had been a retreat from the strictness of the old discipline—a discipline that Ecclesius wished to preserve. Formerly everything had been done at the bishop’s direction: from the church’s revenues he provided, through the archpriest and archdeacon, whatever was necessary and proper to the priests, deacons, and clergy, who shared a common table and household.

Gradually, however, it came to be accepted that a fixed portion of money and goods should be given to each of them according to merit, rank of office, and other circumstances. Pope Gelasius prescribed a definite arrangement for this, and Felix IV settled the disputes of the Ravennate clergy according to it.

Hence there was not one uniform custom among all churches, although the Gelasian arrangement was the more common; some trace it back to the time of Pope Silvester. For the Council of Orléans, cited by Gratian in 10, q. 1, *Antiquos canones*, assigns half the revenues to the bishop and half to the clergy.

The Council of Mérida, canon 14, assigns one third to the bishop and one third to the priests and deacons:

> “The third, however, is to be assigned to the subdeacons and clergy, so that the chief clerk may distribute it to each according to the zeal with which he sees them devoted to their office.”

This indicates that the strictness of common life was no longer being preserved, but that each person was managing private resources, although all the revenues were first collected into one common bag.

These distributions were also called the clergy’s allowances and the clergy’s stipends in the synods of sixth-century Spain. Thus the way was gradually prepared for the division of ecclesiastical estates, individual portions of which bishops assigned to individual clergy as benefices according to rank and office.

The beginnings of this practice in the church of Ravenna can be seen in this very letter, or constitution, of Felix IV, where he decrees:

> “If anyone from the clergy is holding urban or rural estates belonging to the church, we decree that they be assigned to him by written leases drawn up according to a fair assessment of the rent, on this condition: that he retain what he customarily receives in his own right, and that he contribute what remains to the ecclesiastical revenues for their benefit.”

Some members of the clergy had therefore already begun to hold church estates. In this matter the pontiff provided that they should not merely hold them under a written lease after paying a fixed rent, but that, after retaining from the annual revenues what would otherwise have been distributed to them according to the measure of their order and office, they should return the remainder to the common treasury.

The matter subsequently advanced farther and finally became law, although from the beginning it was certain that this had been done contrary to law.

Archbishop Theodore attempted to restore the ancient custom but provoked the hatred of the Ravennate clergy. He compelled the archdeacon, the archpriest, and the clergy to renounce their quarter and place themselves under the bishop’s provision.

Agnellus recounts this below with great indignation. After first saying that, during a severe grain shortage, Theodore deprived the entire region of grain through monopoly, he adds:

> “When the priests could not find where to buy grain, they went to him and begged him to give them assistance. He summoned the archdeacon named Theodore and said to them: ‘Tell the priests of the church and the entire clergy: Why are you being consumed by the want of hunger? If you relinquish the entire quarter of the church and receive only a gift for the quarter throughout the year, according to the bishop’s provision, I will immediately relieve your poverty.’ They, long chastised and with the famine worsening, consented; and from that time the quarter was taken away from the clergy of this church, down to the present day. He also abolished and burned the custom of Ecclesius, which had been written in separate volumes for each office.”

## VII.

This constitution of Felix finally reveals that spectacles were frequently held at Ravenna, and that the clergy were accustomed to attend them contrary to the canons of the Church. On this matter the pontiff adds a serious complaint and takes care that it not happen in the future, ordering that transgressors be punished.

Rubeus observed that this is indicated by Salvian in the sermon he delivered on the vanity of spectacles, in which he says that many people were accustomed to go to Rome and Ravenna for the sake of seeing them. He relates it to the period of King Theodoric, p. 134.

We know, however, that Leo Augustus prohibited such events on Sundays in the final law of the Code, *De feriis*. Theodoric himself tolerated the bloodiest contests—those in which men fought with beasts—rather than permitting them, as is clear from his letter to the consul Maximus, letter 42 of book V of Cassiodorus’ *Variae*.

These points had to be noted concerning the constitution of Felix IV, now brought to light for the first time.

## VIII.

From the verses written by Ecclesius in the atrium of the church of Saint Vitalis, we possess an excellent piece of evidence for the matter on which we have discussed elsewhere: namely, that it was not permitted to bury the bodies of the faithful within basilicas. Ecclesius also prohibits it here, while nevertheless noting that an indulgence had already been granted for the bodies of pontiffs, whom we have previously observed to have been buried in porticoes or in the *ardicae*.

# LIFE OF SAINT URSICINUS

[Col. 0597]

## CHAPTER ONE. Analysis of secular history. The church of Saint Apollinaris completed by Julian the banker.

[Col. 0597A] Ursicinus XXIV. A humble man, with a ruddy face, large eyes, tall in stature, and slender in body; holy, engaged in holy work. Builder of Tricoli, but he did not complete it.

Finally, during the time of this pontiff, King Athalaric died at Ravenna on the sixth day before the Nones of October. On the following day Theodahad was elevated, and he deposed Queen Amalasuntha from the kingdom. Theodahad sent her into exile at Vulsinii on the day before the Kalends of May. Some say that she herself ordered, by her own authority, the house to be built where the monastery of Saint Peter was constructed, which is called the Trophy of the Orphan.

[Col. 0597B] Not many days later King Theodahad went to Rome and, as he was returning, was killed by the Goths at the fifteenth milestone from Ravenna in the month of December.

In the month of May of that same year, Belisarius, the patrician, entered the city of Classis and entered Ravenna. Thereafter he returned to Sicily and ravaged it.

The Empress Theodora died at Constantinople on the twenty-seventh day of July.

Narses the *chartularius* entered Ravenna with a large army in the aforementioned month, on the fifth day of the week. He fought King Totila and was killed, and a great number of his army fell by the sword; the survivors departed wounded.

The Goths then raised up for themselves a king named Teia at Ticinum, and there was a brief respite.

Let these matters suffice for today. It is already time for us to return to the church and explain the life of the pontiff; whatever remains, when we have leisure, we shall narrate steadily.

[Col. 0597C] This holy man also ordered and instructed that the church of the blessed Apollinaris should be founded and completed by Julian the banker. Julian promptly fulfilled the commands and, by God’s will, built it from precious stones in the regions of Italy.

No church is like this one, because at night it almost shines as brightly as in the day.

This holy man therefore daily broke the sacred body of the Lamb with his hands upon the Lord’s altar and expiated the sins of the people with tears.

## CHAPTER II. Agnellus’ meditations on the sacred assembly. The death and tomb of Ursicinus.

[Col. 0597D] But because today you have wished, in your nobility, to turn aside into my house, what shall I do, since I am the guardian of a poor dwelling and lack food? My table is not such, nor is the storehouse of my heart such, that it can refresh your bodies.

Nevertheless, I have a very fat Lamb, whose eaten body is never diminished but always remains whole. For it would be shameful, after you have entered the entrance of my monastery, the house of the blessed Bartholomew, for you not to receive a blessing from the apostle himself and to return fasting.

Let four feet be brought, and place the table upon them. The four stable feet are the four Evangelists, who contain the whole square world in their preaching. The table above them is the holy altar, that is, the cross upon which Christ died and was offered as a sacrifice to the Father for the salvation of the world.

Like the four feet, the table also has four horns.

Have you reclined? Eat the bread. The bread set before you is he who said: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven.” Eat not carnal food but heavenly food; not earthly bread but angelic bread.

That is the bread of which David sang: “He gave them the bread of heaven; man ate the bread of angels.”

How will angels eat, since they are incorporeal? Are they clothed in flesh? They do not eat with bites; they are satisfied from the fullness of divinity, which is the living bread unto ages of ages.

Let this Lamb, placed upon the dish and wrapped as he was placed in the holy tomb, come to us. He was brought near to the fire but was not burned.

He descended likewise to the underworld; he extinguished the flames of Gehenna, destroyed death, slew the lion, shattered Tartarus, carried away the righteous, destroyed the bronze gates, and cast down the adamantine bars, according to the prophet’s saying: “I shall be your death, O death; I shall be your bite, O underworld.”

He rose from the tomb and left us his flesh. Walking upon the wings of the winds, he trod upon the heads of the clouds. He was received into heaven and sits at the right hand of the Father.

Eat that flesh of the immaculate Lamb. If you eat his flesh and drink his blood, you will remain in him and he in you, as he himself says: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him.”

Did not the law given through Moses command that no animal blood should be eaten, because it is the animal’s soul? It commanded this, and truly commanded it.

But this Lamb is nothing common, nothing earthly. He alone is unique, immaculate, from the One, true from the True; he does not have what is his own, but takes away what is ours.

Thus also the people of the Hebrews, when they departed from Egypt, smeared the doorposts with the blood of the lamb, so that they would not be killed by the destroying angel. Where there was no blood of the lamb, the house was struck, because the Lord, passing through the middle of Egypt, separated the chosen from the rejected.

Behold the flesh of the Lamb that we eat all day long: it is not diminished, but rather increases, and it bestows eternal life upon those who eat it.

[Col. 0598D] Now let drink follow the food. Drink the clearest wine from the vine that said: “I am the true vine, and my Father is the cultivator.”

Let this wine come with songs and organs, with lyres, dances, songs and psalteries, horns and cymbals, and symphonies, with great honor and much dignity, because it is worthy.

These songs signify spiritual praise. The organs are our throats. The lyre is the human breast, which we strike daily before God; for just as a lyre is struck by the heart, so we strike our breasts with the beating of the heart.

The chorus signifies the ranks of priests. The trumpet is our voice, because through it we render praises to the Father.

The psaltery derives its name from the singing of psalms, which represents the whole Trinity and the inseparable unity.

The cymbals and symphony signify the voice of those singing psalms in the chorus with a great sound, through which the readings resound throughout the whole Church, and they do not cease to invoke God day and night.

While blessed Ursicinus performed these things at their appointed times, by divine command his soul was separated from his body. The body went to its proper place and was buried in the basilica of the blessed martyr Vitalis before the altar of Saint Nazarius.

He sat for three years, six months, and nine days.

# OBSERVATIONS ON THE LIFE OF SAINT URSICINUS

Agnellus’ historical statements are corrected or explained.

A few points relating again to chronology must be noted here. It is in no way tenable that Theodahad, as is stated, went to Rome “not many days” after Amalasuntha’s murder, and that, while returning from there, he was slaughtered; for it is clear from Procopius that Peter was sent from Constantinople to Ravenna, where he negotiated peace with Theodahad and brought matters to the point that Theodahad himself promised to abdicate the kingdom and wrote to Justinian about it. A few days were insufficient for handling these matters through envoys sent back and forth [Col. 0599C], nor did Theodahad go to Rome before he had despaired of peace.

I think these events should be referred to May of the year 536, when Belisarius could first have attempted Ravenna. Our author reports—though Procopius and the others are silent—that he then proceeded to Naples, which Agnellus indicates by writing that Sicily was devastated by Belisarius [Col. 0600A]. Hence perhaps Liberatus’s statement, which all have judged in need of correction, can be maintained: he reports that Vigilius, coming from Theodora, found Belisarius residing at Ravenna; that he proceeded with him from there to Sicily; and that, entering Rome alone in September, he found Silverius already ordained.

Although Liberatus himself seems to suggest that Vigilius came to Rome and found Silverius ordained before he approached Belisarius, I think this certainly did not happen. Before setting out for Rome with Belisarius, Vigilius had to deal with him according to Theodora’s instructions. Liberatus’s words readily allow this interpretation, when he says that “Vigilius, coming to Rome, found Pope Silverius ordained, and also Belisarius at Ravenna.” Thus a more probable explanation emerges for the delay by which Vigilius came to Rome later than he should have: he had to conduct negotiations with Belisarius, who was to advance Vigilius’s election in some way, while Theodahad, meanwhile, by force forestalled the designs of Vigilius and Belisarius and compelled Silverius’s election [Col. 0600B] and ordination to be expedited.

What follows is narrated proleptically. Procopius reports that Theodora died in the twenty-second year of Justinian’s reign, corresponding to the year of Christ 549. From Agnellus her day of death is fixed as the twenty-fourth day, namely of July; since Procopius likewise states that she reigned for twenty-one years and three months, it follows that Justinian took her as his wife before 27 April 528. Similarly, it appears from the continuation of Marcellinus that Narses did not come to Italy until the year 552; therefore he could not have been residing at Ravenna in the same month in which Theodora died. By the more probable reckoning Totila was killed in the following year, 553, since, according to the prophecy of Saint Benedict, he had reigned ten complete years and had entered upon the eleventh, as Procopius likewise relates.

## II

What is added here concerning the completion, at the command of Bishop Ursicinus, of the basilica of Saint Apollinaris by Julian the argentarius confirms what was noted above concerning Julian’s office [Col. 0600C]. To add more would be, as it seems to me, to seek light where the matter is already perfectly clear. The remaining material, piously treated by Agnellus, concerning the most holy sacrament of the Eucharist will not be altogether useless to the reader for illuminating the sacred liturgy of that age.

# Life of Saint Victor

[Col. 0599]

## Chapter One. The silver ciborium of the Ursian Church. An endothis offered. Baths constructed for the clergy.

[Col. 0559C] Victor XXV. What does “Victor” mean? By divine providence it had been given to him as a cognomen in accordance with his parents’ wish; by his own action it was also his name [agnomen], because through many virtues, especially prayer and fasting, he very often conquered the camp of the devil. He was handsome in face and cheerful in expression. He was the builder of Tricoli, but he did not complete it.

He also made a silver ciborium over the altar of the holy Ursian Church, which is called after the name of its builder, with marvelous workmanship. Some say that he made it together with the people; others say that, in the time of Justinian the elder, the orthodox emperor, he had requested through a petition that he be allowed to make such a work, so that he might provide assistance. Moved by compassion, Justinian granted the blessed Victor the entire tax-revenue of Italy for that year. After receiving it, he constructed the work that you see: subsequently, after the old wooden structure had been removed, it was built with a proper weight of two thousand pounds of silver [literally, “a hundred times twenty”] [Col. 0600C]. The following verses were inscribed upon the arches [arcos] of the ciborium:

> Victor the priest, together with the people, pays this vow to Christ,  
> He who increased faith among the peoples through love.
>
> A band of winged beings, encircling these holy places,  
> Ministers to the bishop as he pays his vows to Christ.
>
> The removal of age causes the excellent work to be admired;  
> It returns improved, in nobler adornment.
>
> If any lover of the Catholic law comes [lacuna],  
> Soon restored by your body, O Christ, he departs.

Of what remained, he constructed various vessels for the bishop’s table, some of which survive in part to the present day.

He also made an endothis over the altar of the holy Ursian Church, of pure gold woven with silk threads, extremely heavy, having a central *cocca* [the term is obscure, as the commentator below acknowledges]. Among five images we see his own there, and beneath the represented feet of the Savior a purple inscription is woven:

> Victor, bishop and servant of God, offered this adornment for the day of the Resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the fifth year of his ordination.

He also restored the bath adjoining the church residence and attached to the walls of the bishop’s house, where he lived. To this day it is marvelously used for bathing. He joined the walls with the most precious marbles, composed various figures in golden tesserae, and arranged diverse designs. He also set up a panel written in gold tesserae, which we took pains to read, and found the following catalectic hexameter verses written upon it:

> Victor, the priest protected by apostolic power,  
> Took down the little baths, formerly old through ancient workmanship,  
> And restored them with marvelous novelty,  
> So that more beautiful in adornment and greater they might rise again from the foundations.
>
> He also decreed that this custom be observed perpetually:  
> That the clergy of this city bathe there freely on two days:  
> The third day and the sixth day, when bathing was permitted.

## Chapter II. The adornment of the fountain at the Petrian Church. Attack on vices. Victor’s death and tomb.

He ruled his Church for a short time, but the amount of work evident from his labors during the period in which he held the see is great.

He adorned the tetragonal fountain which the most blessed Peter Chrysologus built in the city [civitate] of Classis beside the Petrian Church. In the middle, on the side of the men, beneath the arch, there was a small circular space in which the following inscription remains to this day: “With the lord safe” (*Salvo Domno*). On the other side, on the women’s side, there was another small circle, similarly arranged; the gilded letters facing one another are read by those who inspect them as follows: “Pope Victor” (*Papa Victore*). [Together: “with Lord Pope Victor safe.”] As I have said, he adorned this very beautifully [that is, he decorated it, Bacch.], but now it is being destroyed by wicked men, because the devil so constricts their hearts that the temple of God, constructed by holy priests [Col. 0601C] and most faithful Christians, is being destroyed by false Christians.

Why is this happening? Because the end is near, the limit is near, and the destruction of the world. But, according to the Apostle, these are perilous times, and people are lovers of themselves. The world is ending amid evils. However great the joy was at the beginning of the world, so much greater will be the weeping at the consummation of the world.

Before the world is consummated, according to the Gospel, there will be pestilence, famine, terrors from heaven, anger, quarrels, dissensions, and swords. Nation will rise against nation, and kingdom will rage against kingdom. The young will take precedence over the old, and those who come after will show no honor to their predecessors. Sons will also despise their fathers; they will not merely mock them but will even subject them.

These things are according to the holy Gospel: “Woe to us, wretched ones! [Variant: “to you” (*vobis*) for “to us” (*nobis*); the supplied bracket is unclosed.] We have witnessed everything. But you, immortal God, exalted and terrible, save us by your great power. We have witnessed all these things, earthquakes in various places, and signs in the sun and moon. But since it speaks of the consummation itself and of the hour, which has not been revealed even to the holy angels, we do not know it. Yet we know that it is near, and we understand that the old man is soon to die and that we see in him the sign of death. We do not know on what day or at what hour he will depart. Thus all the signs which the Truth foretold are coming to pass, but the day and hour are hidden from us. Yet to you, knower of sinners [perhaps ‘of breasts’], and searcher of hearts, all things are known and possible.”

Here, after the most blessed man completed his life on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March, he was honorably carried to the bier and then buried, after his shroud had been torn, in the Church of Saint Vitalis, beneath the monastery of Saint Nazarius, beside his predecessor. He sat for six years, eleven months, and twelve days.

[Note: [Col. 0601D] Marginal note: Victor, archbishop, died around the year of the Lord 563. BACCH.]

# Observations on the Life of Saint Victor

[Col. 0602]

Rubeus errs knowingly and willingly. The use of the ciborium. What is an endothis? The building of the Petrian fountain.

## I

It is immediately astonishing that Rubeus, in Book III, page 157, knowingly and willingly went astray by assigning Victor a very brief episcopate of only a few months. For although Agnellus himself says that Victor governed the Church of Ravenna for “a short time,” he nevertheless testifies that he sat for six years, eleven months, and eleven days.

Among other things, Rubeus himself relates that, under Victor’s direction, an endothis woven of gold and silk was made for the adornment of the church [Col. 0602B], “with letters inscribed around the endothis which, at Victor’s command, testified that it was his gift.” Yet he refrains from reporting the wording of the letters or inscription, because the fifth year of Victor’s episcopate was stated there; consequently, he would have been exposed as responsible for a badly arranged chronology.

Certainly a period of only a few months could not have sufficed for the works which Victor contributed to the adornment and convenience of the church, as Rubeus himself writes. The learned writer could also have recognized that, if Justinian granted the entire tax-revenue of Italy for one year for the construction of the silver ciborium, that year could not have passed without at least the lapse of the year whose revenue the emperor had donated.

It is reasonable that this occurred in the very year in which Victor was ordained, 540. Ravenna had been recovered by Belisarius and Vitiges had been taken to Constantinople; for these reasons Augustus could, in obedience to the divine will and in gratitude for the recent victory, grant the revenue of that year to the Church of Ravenna as a token of pious and grateful feeling.

Rubeus asserts that, according to Agnellus, the entire revenue amounted to two thousand pounds of silver [literally, “a hundred times twenty”]. But Agnellus’s wording is different: he says that the ciborium was “built, after the old wooden structure had been removed, with a proper weight of two thousand pounds of silver [literally, “a hundred times twenty”],” and he adds that “from what remained various vessels were constructed for the bishop’s table.”

I think that, instead of *centies viginti* (“a hundred times twenty”), *centum viginti* (“one hundred and twenty”) should be written, and that this cannot be referred to the tax-revenue of Italy. Agnellus reports a rumor preserved in the memory of certain people, although he clearly indicates that he himself does not accept the story that Augustus donated the revenue of one year. Moreover, the inscription placed by Victor says that the vow was made by the bishop and the people, which sufficiently demonstrates that Justinian contributed nothing to this undertaking.

## II

What a ciborium was would be evident from the cited verses, even if it were not otherwise sufficiently and abundantly known, especially from the final two verses. They show not merely that it served to cover the altar—hence Rubeus substituted the word “vault”—but chiefly that it was made so that the sacred mysteries of the Eucharist could be stored in it for use [Col. 0602D]. The following words cannot be understood in any other sense:

> If any lover of the Catholic law comes [lacuna],  
> Soon restored by your body, O Christ, he departs.

Ducange discusses ciboria at greater length in both of his Glossaries and in his description of Saint Sophia addressed to Paul the Silentiary, no. 57, where he treats of ciboria and their form and use.

## III

In discussing the endothis, Ducange cites passages from Rubeus in which ornaments of this kind, offered by Maximian, are drawn from ancient monuments, especially from Agnellus. In one of them, the entire history of Christ appeared to be represented; in another, the succession of the bishops of Ravenna with their portraits.

He notes that learned men believe that *ἐνδύτην* should either be read or understood, since the Greeks also use this term for the larger altar-cloth, as Goar explains in his discussion of the Greek Euchologion. He adds, however, what seems certain from the material of which the endothis of the Ravennate Church was composed: that it signified rather a veil by which the front part of the altar was adorned.

He also notes that he discusses the same subject in his description of Saint Sophia, no. 65, and that *ἐνδύτην* is construed in the masculine gender. It is also apparent from an anonymous author after Theophanes, page 439, cited by the same Ducange in his Glossary of Greek, that the Greeks embroidered sacred histories with a needle on such coverings or hangings. The passage reads:

> Καὶ προσεκύνησεν τὴν ἐνδύτην τὴν ἐχούσαν τὴν ἁγίαν γένεσιν τοῦ Κυρίου.

> And he venerated the *endytē* which bore the holy birth of the Lord.

The same is supported by several passages in Anastasius.

The endothis of which our author speaks is said to have been made of pure gold, woven with a silk warp, on which five images were represented, one of them depicting Victor. At the bottom, beneath the feet of the Savior, he added a votive inscription. From this we learn that the gift was offered on the very day of Holy Easter, which in the year 545—namely, the fifth year after his ordination, as was demonstrated in the preceding dissertation—fell on 16 April, with solar cycle 22, dominical letter A, and lunar cycle 14.

What the words “having a central *cocca*” signify [Col. 0603B], I confess that I do not know, and I willingly leave the matter to those devoted to the study of ancient textiles to guess.

The construction of the baths built by Victor, together with the decree that the clergy should bathe there freely on the third and sixth weekdays, although it provides useful information, requires no further investigation.

## IV

The account handed down concerning the baptismal fountain of Classis is somewhat obscure. Our author seems to distinguish the fountain itself, which he describes as tetragonal, from a chamber—namely, a building surrounding the fountain itself. On the arch or higher gable of its vault, words were arranged here and there in circular spaces [Col. 0604A] and could be read as follows: “With the gift safe, Pope Victor” [the wording here, *Salvo dono papa Victore*, is uncertain; the earlier text has *Domno*, “lord,” rather than *dono*, “gift”].

In the same chamber he distinguishes the men’s and women’s sections, which we recognize from the order in which they are to be read as arranged from left to right, as in basilicas. The fountain itself, enclosed by its own tetragonal wall in the middle of the chamber, we recognize from the Life of Peter Chrysologus, where the fountain is said to have been built “with marvelous size, double walls, and high fortifications.”

By “fountain” he understands the whole building; the walls refer to the central tetragonal fountain, and the fortifications to the surrounding chamber.

Concerning buildings of this sort, called “fountains” by earlier writers but “baptisteries” by writers of the later age, Ducange writes learnedly and at length in both Glossaries and in his description of the Church of Saint Sophia, nos. 82 and 83.

Among the more recent centuries, he rightly praises the fountains or buildings of this kind constructed by our fathers, where everyone was baptized, and he commends in particular the splendid Church of Saint John the Baptist at Florence, situated beside the cathedral, as the distinguished writer cited above praises it.

Allow me, in obedience to my love for my homeland, to praise the remarkable baptistery constructed at Parma toward the end of the thirteenth century. The whole building consists of enormous marbles wonderfully joined together, in a round form terminated by a vast vault. In the middle is a large stone set upon arches, into which the water was led after the baptismal rite; that the rite was performed by immersion is shown by the structure itself.

Now, in the corner of the building beside the door facing west, a vessel raised according to the more recent custom holds the water with which infants from the whole city are baptized by sprinkling.

# Life of Saint Maximian

[Col. 0603]

## Chapter One. Maximian’s homeland. A treasure discovered, part of which is shown to Justinian and another part concealed by clever planning. He is ordained bishop. Through gentleness of character and conduct he reconciles the Ravennates, who were hostile toward him.

Maximianus XXVI was tall, slender-bodied, thin-faced, bald-headed, with little hair, gray eyes, and adorned with every grace.

He was not from this fold, but was a foreign sheep, a deacon from the Church of Pola, ordained and honored by his own bishop. But why did a foreigner hold the episcopate of this city? I shall explain it; I shall not conceal it, but make it publicly known, just as I heard it from those who recounted it through the long course of time—and it is true beyond all doubt.

One day, while digging the earth in order to sow seed, after first cutting the crop [the transmitted *cesalis* is uncertain; Bacch. suggests *cerealis*, “cereal”], he immediately found a large vessel full of gold, together with many other kinds of riches. After devising a plan by himself, since the matter could no longer remain hidden, he ordered a large ox to be brought and slaughtered. He commanded that its emptied belly be filled with gold coins [from gold coins].

Similarly, he summoned shoemakers and instructed them to make large boots from goatskins; he filled these too with solidi of gold. The remainder, when he had gone to the city of Constantinople [Col. 0604C], he carried with him.

He offered it to the emperor Justinian. When Augustus saw it, he gave thanks and then carefully asked him whether there had been more. Maximian replied under oath: “By your safety, Lord, and by the safety of your soul, I have no more of it except what I spent on the belly and on the boots.”

He was speaking of what he had concealed, while Justinian thought that he meant food for the body and footwear for the feet. Justinian was considering what reward he should give him for such loyalty, which Maximian had shown toward him.

At that time Victor, bishop of this city of Ravenna, died. The citizens of Ravenna went with the priests and the entire people to the emperor, requesting the pallium for the election [Note: [Col. 0603D] Here, pious reader, read carefully: this is infected with schismatic darkness. The pallium was requested not from the emperor but from the pope, whose office it was also to approve the bishop’s election and to ordain the elected candidate. See the Preface. BACCH.].

Afterward Augustus ordered the petitioners to delay. Having devised a plan, he ordered the blessed Maximian, a deacon of Pola, to be consecrated bishop by Pope Vigilius in the city of Patras in Achaea, on the day before the Ides of October, indiction 10, in the fifth year after the consulship of Basil the Younger, in the forty-eighth year of his life. He then sent him to Ravenna with the pallium.

When the citizens of Ravenna refused to receive him so quickly, he remained outside the Gate of Saint Victor, not far from the river called the Fossa Sconti, in the basilica of Saint Eusebius, in the episcopal residence which Bishop Uvimundus had built during the reign of King Theodoric.

Likewise he remained in the episcopal residence of Saint George, which had been built in the time of the Arians. These episcopal residences survived until our own time and were demolished almost twenty-six years ago at the command of Bishop Valerius, who ordered the construction of the house that is now called the New House, or rather the Valerian House.

As we have said, the people refused to receive him. Therefore, men on the bishop’s side wanted to send envoys to him, announcing that his commands had been profane and that the Ravennates, persisting in terrible arrogance, had refused to receive their ordained bishop; with the Church left widowed, the flock wandered here and there [the flocks wandered].

The most blessed Maximian, however, did not agree with them. He restrained them with his words, saying:

“Stop, brothers. Do not accuse others; do not rejoice in another’s ruin [ruin]. What kind of shepherd am I if I do not spare my sheep? Do you want me to slaughter them? This is not good counsel. Let them be; they will suffer no annoyance from me. Let the Lord’s will be done. I beg you to grant them a brief delay.”

Not many days later he sent a trusted messenger from among his own men and summoned one of the priests and the leading men of the city. He asked them to dine with him. When they came, he made merry with them; after food and drink he offered them gifts of the gold which he had formerly discovered.

Having been reconciled with them, he sent them back into the city of Ravenna with his blessing and asked them to visit him frequently. On the following day he sent for other leading men and did as before, and likewise a third time.

Then they discussed these matters among themselves and said:

“What is this that we are unwilling [willing] to do? This man is good; he is prudent. We devised harm against him, but he did not wish to repay us evil for evil. We cannot be without a bishop and father. Look, the priests are wandering, the people are limping, and the Church is declining. Let us rise at dawn, bring him into the city, and venerate his footsteps.”

At sunrise they all went together, as one man. Opening the city gates with crosses, banners, standards, and praises, they honorably brought him into this city of Ravenna. They kissed his feet and adorned the city streets with various decorations.

All the buildings were crowned with ornaments; there was joy among the soldiers, gladness among private citizens, and both small and great rejoiced, while those of middling rank celebrated. They asked him to sit upon the seat of the Church [Col. 0605D], heard Mass from him, and kept that day of solemnity with great joy and everlasting gladness.

## Chapter II. The Church of Saint Stephen is built. Monasteries or small chapels beside the basilica. Materials miraculously prepared in the space of one night.

After this he lived among his sheep like a father among [Col. 0606A] his sons. He built the Church of the blessed Stephen, deacon and martyr, here at Ravenna [Note: [Col. 0605D] Marginal note: The Monastery of Saint Stephen. Since there is now only one monastery of Saint Stephen in the city of Ravenna, in which nuns live, and since from what can be seen there appears to be no trace of such a great structure of buildings and precious objects, this monastery is near the Church of Saint Andrew of the Goths, commonly called the Gothic Church. I believe that the monastery mentioned here in this history was near the Church of Saint Barbatian, which is not far from the monastery and Church of Saint Zachariah, as I saw and as can be seen in a certain public document written by the notary Morandus, which is in his registers, dated 1296, on the day . . . of the month . . . , folio . . . , and is in the chartulary of the lords cardinal of the Church of Ravenna. BACCH.].

Not far from the small sheepfold gate, he adorned it from its foundations on a marvelous scale and decorated it most beautifully. His likeness was set into the vaults of the apse in various tesserae, and the circuit was constructed with marvelous glasswork. He also deposited there many relics from the bodies of saints, whose names you will find written as follows:

> In honor of the holy and most blessed first martyr Stephen,  
> Maximianus, servant of Christ and bishop, built and dedicated this basilica from its foundations, with Stephen’s assistance, on the third day before the Ides of December, indiction 14, in the ninth year after the consulship of Basil the Younger.

And he rejoiced in the Lord, who had granted him such great blessings that no human being could worthily recount them.

Here he placed the relics of the apostles and martyrs: Saint Peter, Saint Paul, Saint Andrew, Saint Zachariah, Saint John the Baptist, Saint John the Evangelist, Saint James, Saint Thomas, Saint Matthew, Saint Stephen, Saint Vincent, Saint Laurence, Saint Quirinus, Saint Florian, Saint Aemilianus, Saint Apollinaris, Saint Agatha, Saint Euphemia, Saint Agnes, and Saint Eugenia. May they pray for us.

On the upper part of the arch of the apse you will find metrical verses containing the following:

> The temples shine with the merits and name of Stephen,  
> Who first performed the glorious work of a martyr.
>
> One palm is granted to all for sacred blood,  
> Yet he enjoys more, because he was the first in time.
>
> He himself, O great priest Maximian, assisting you,  
> Has now completed this work, your faith and vow.
>
> For such a hall, raised suddenly upon foundations,  
> No human hand alone could have made:
>
> While the shining moon renews its eleventh return,  
> The work begun and brought to a beautiful completion gleams.

Beside the basilica he added small monasteries, all of which appear marvelously adorned with new gilded tesserae and with various other tesserae set in plaster. The name of Maximian himself is sculpted above all the capitals of its columns.

In the men’s section of the monastery you will find six letters set in mosaic. Those who do not know their meaning are led into error; those who understand know that the letters MU. SI. VA are written there.

Some say that one day the bishop summoned the chief overseer of the work [Note: The head of those who press on the work. ID.] and asked him why he was not completing the building of the aforesaid church. He replied:

“Because you, our lord, had sailed to the regions of Constantinople, the cement and bricks ran out, and we do not have enough stones to continue the work.”

Then, at the bishop’s command, in a single night the carriers prepared and brought all the materials—lime, small bricks, stones and *bisalos* [an uncertain building-material term], stones and timber, columns and slabs, sand and gravel—so great a quantity in one night, as I have said, that they could scarcely have prepared it by laboring for eleven moons [months, Bacch.].

## Chapter III. The forest in Istria secured for the Church of Ravenna. Crowns placed upon the building of Tricoli.

During the time of this most holy bishop, a dispute arose concerning the forest called Vistrum, situated in the regions of Istria. He traveled to Constantinople twice so that, in the presence of the emperor Justinian Augustus, he might settle such a dispute.

Both men, adorned with gray hair at the same time, remembering how they had been separated in youth [joined together in old age], began to mourn together most affectionately. Then the pious emperor Justinian Augustus issued a permanent legal decree concerning this forest, establishing that it belonged to the holy Church of Ravenna, whose rightful and reasonable claim to it he had recognized.

In his own time he completed all the buildings of Tricoli. Where he himself is depicted with his predecessors, if you wish to read while looking at them, you will find the following inscription:

> Here Peter the Younger, following Christ’s commands [“conceptions”],  
> Displayed them in sacred conduct, as he taught [Rub., “as was fitting”].
>
> He also founded this stronghold with marvelous structures;  
> He gave these monuments of his own name.
>
> After his death Aurelian held the honors;  
> After him Ecclesius became bishop.
>
> Then came Ursicinus; next in order came Victor;  
> In his time the younger Maximian appears.
>
> He was a profound Levite of Christ from Pola,  
> Compassionate according to God’s law and good in piety.
>
> God himself adorned this man with the sacred dignity  
> And appointed him bishop of his Church.
>
> He himself knows by his own deeds that he did not deserve  
> The apostolic dignity, but received it through God’s mercy.

## Chapter IV. The Church of Saint Mary at Pola. The Church of Saint Andrew restored. Saint Andrew’s body at Constantinople. The apostle’s beard. Crowning and dedication of various buildings.

He built the Church of the Blessed Mary at Pola, called Formosa, from which he had been a deacon, with marvelous beauty, and adorned it with various stones.
