He also built the house in which the rector of this Church lives in that city, and he transferred all his possessions to the Church of Ravenna, which we possess to this day.

Here at Ravenna he supported the Church of the blessed apostle Andrew with marble columns, with every care, not far from the district of Herculanea [Herculana]. He removed the old wooden structures made of walnut and decorated them with Proconnesian marble.

Then he attempted to bring the apostle’s body to Ravenna. When the emperor at Constantinople learned of this, he ordered the blessed Maximian to come to Constantinople and bring the holy body of the apostle with him.

The emperor rejoiced and said to him:

“Let it not trouble you, Father, that Rome, the first sister, possesses one, while the second possesses this one. They are two sisters, and these are two brothers. I do not wish to give him to you, because, since the imperial residence is here, it is fitting that the apostle’s body also be here.”

The most blessed Maximian replied:

“Do as you command. I ask only that tonight I may perform psalmody with my priests before this holy body.”

The emperor immediately granted his request. They then kept vigil throughout the whole night. After everything had been completed, Maximian seized a sword and, after praying, cut off the apostle’s beard as far as the chin. He also carried away many relics from the relics of other saints, with the emperor’s approval, and afterward returned to his own see.

[Note: [Col. 0607D] A schismatic vow, which will be discussed in the observations. BACCH.]

And truly, brothers, if the body of Andrew, Peter’s brother and chief apostle, had been buried here, the Roman pontiffs would never have subjected us in this way.

He consecrated the Church of the blessed Bishop Apollinaris situated at Classis, the Church of the blessed martyr Vitalis at Ravenna, and the Church of the blessed archangel Michael here at Ravenna, which Bachauda built together with Julian the argentarius of blessed memory, in the district called ad Frigiselo.

There you will find the following inscription in the vault of the apse:

> Bachauda and Julian, having received the benefits of the archangel Michael, built and dedicated this church from its foundations, on the Nones of May (7 May), in the fourth year after the consulship of Basil the Younger, most illustrious man, in the eighth indiction.

Some say that this Bachauda was the son-in-law of the aforementioned Julian, and that Bachauda rests in a stone coffin not far from the Church of the Archangel, beneath a tower.

In the apse of Saint Vitalis, the image of Maximian, together with those of the emperor and empress, is beautifully represented in tesserae [perhaps “well adorned,” Bacch.].

How long could we continue recounting the great goodness of this holy man? The time available for narration fails me. He labored more than all the other bishops who preceded him.

In his time the neighboring building near my house was constructed, called the first *banchus* [read *bandus*, Bacch.], not far from the Golden Milestone. We also find his name inscribed on the tiles as follows:

> Maximianus, bishop of Ravenna.

I saw and read this inscription.

In the *ardica* of the Blessed Apollinaris and Vitalis you will find panels inscribed in large letters, containing the following.

In the *ardica* of Saint Apollinaris:

> At the command of the most blessed man Ursicinus, bishop, Julian the argentarius built, adorned, and dedicated the basilica of the blessed priest Apollinaris from its foundations; and the blessed bishop Maximian consecrated it on 9 May, in the twelfth indiction, in the eighth year after the consulship of Basil.

In the *ardica* of Saint Vitalis you will find:

> At the command of Ecclesius, the most blessed man and bishop, Julian the argentarius built, adorned, and dedicated the basilica of the blessed martyr Vitalis from its foundations; and the most reverend bishop Maximian consecrated it on the thirteenth day, in the sixth year after the consulship of Basil the Younger.

This holy man embalmed the body of the blessed Probus with spices, together with the bodies of the other holy bishops, and placed it properly. On the front of the Church of the blessed Probus, Eleuchadius, and Calocerus he adorned their images with various tesserae, and beneath their feet you will find [Note: [Col. 0608D] The inscription is missing. ID.] [lacuna].

## Chapter V. Maximian’s writings, with a fragment from his *Annalogia*. Some secular history.

He had previously traveled through the eastern regions, as he himself says in his writings:

> “[Col. 0609A] In Alexandria, however, there was no external cause of evil; rather, because the people are fierce, seditious, and always restless, civil war broke out among them—not for the sake of virtue, nor for defense, but for the slaughter and destruction of citizens. The entire population, stirred up, killed its prefect inside the church; previously, some had similarly killed their own bishop after accusing him of being a heretic. When the emperor learned this, he became enraged and ordered the city to be utterly destroyed. Finally, having sent another prefect named Laudicius, he hanged forty men on timber in each of the city’s districts. But then Dioscorus, the bishop of that city, exerted himself and openly gave his life for his sheep. Monks chosen from the desert hurried to the emperor and begged pardon for the citizens’ excesses. Then the emperor yielded to the priests and thereafter ordered precautions to be taken against such things. This bishop was succeeded at Alexandria by Timothy, whom I saw, while sailing to the East, governing his own city well.”

A little earlier he says:

> “The city of Nazarba in Cilicia collapsed when an earthquake occurred; they say that more than thirty thousand people perished there.”

These are the words of the bishop. After Saint Jerome, Orosius, and other historians, he worked on a chronicle. Following them, he wrote his own chronicle in several books concerning the more distinguished rulers—not only the earlier emperors themselves, but also kings and prefects.

In his time a battle took place between the Goths and the soldiers. Narses went out in Campania on the Kalends of October; the Goths were defeated, and many Gothic bodies lay dead. Their king Theja was killed by Narses. Narses returned in peace and came to Lucca, [Col. 0609C] and expelled the Goths from there in the month of September. The city of Forum Cornelii was restored by the prefect Antiochus. The aforesaid Narses came again to Ravenna with a great victory; then he went to Rome and proceeded into Campania, to the fortress of Cumae, where he remained.

After this, the heresy of the Manichaeans arose in the city of Ravenna. Orthodox Christians refuted them and drove them outside the city; at a place called Fossa-Sconii, beside the river, they stoned them, and they died in their sins. Thus the evils were removed from Ravenna.

In the third year thereafter, a red sign appeared in the sky on the eleventh day of the month of November, and Pope Pelagius died on the third day of March. Then Narses the patrician proceeded with his army to Rome. At that time many signs and prodigies occurred around Ravenna, [Col. 0609D] so that many people marked their possessions, houses, and vessels in order that they might be recognized; and many saw visions by day, as though people were speaking face to face with them.

They fought against the citizens of Verona, and the city of Verona was captured by the soldiers on the twentieth day of July. Another great and terrible sign was seen: behold, in the air there appeared something like a battle of men fighting one another, as in combat, on the eighth day before the Kalends of August, at the third hour of the day, on the second day of the week. Many were terrified by it.

It is now time to close this reading, so that tomorrow we may hear what follows.

## CHAPTER VI. Chrism-vessels; several *endothae*; a golden cross; ecclesiastical books corrected by Maximian; denunciation of vices

He made two chrism-vessels. One of them weighed fourteen pounds and was executed with remarkable *anagrifa* [*anaglyphtica*, Bacch.] workmanship; but shortly before this time it perished, during the episcopate of Archbishop Petronax. The other remains to the present day, beautifully wrought, and bears the inscription:

> “The servant of Christ, Maximian, archbishop, ordered this chrism-vessel to be made for the uses of the faithful.”

He himself commissioned a most precious linen *endothe*, such as we have never been able to see its equal, made with needles [perhaps “small needles”], containing the entire history of our Savior. On the holy day of the Epiphany it is placed upon the altar of the Ursian Church, [Col. 0610B] but he did not complete it all. His successor completed one part. Who could have seen anything like it? One cannot judge the images, beasts, or birds made there in any other way than by saying that, in the flesh, they all seem alive.

Images of Maximian himself were splendidly made in two places, one larger and the other smaller; yet there is no difference between the larger and the smaller. On the smaller one letters are inscribed as follows:

> “Magnify the Lord with me, who raised me from the dungheap.”

He also made another *endothe* of gold, on which all his predecessors are represented; he ordered their images to be made in woven gold. He made a third and a fourth with pearls, on which one reads:

> “Spare, Lord, your people, and remember me, a sinner, whom you have raised from the dungheap into your kingdom.”

He himself ordered a larger golden cross to be made and adorned it with the most precious gems and pearls—hyacinths, amethysts, sardstones, and emeralds. Beneath the gold, in the middle, he concealed a piece of the wood of the holy cross of our redemption, on which the Lord’s body hung. Its weight in gold is enormous.

He had all the ecclesiastical books—that is, seventy-two—written out with the greatest care. He read them for a long time and with the utmost caution, and left them to us without reproach; we still use them today, including, at the end, the Gospels and the apostles’ letters. If you wish to seek his own words, you will find them written as follows:

> “I corrected them with the greatest care against the versions of Augustine and according to the Gospels that blessed Jerome sent to Rome and directed to [his parents], so that they might not be corrupted by ignorant or bad scribes.”

He also published Missals for the entire cycle of the year and for all the saints. For the daily and Lenten seasons, and for whatever pertains to the rite of the Church, you will find everything there without doubt. It is a large volume, wonderfully written.

We possess only a small portion of them, namely, the sayings [or: the books containing his sayings] that were carried across to Rome; and the Romans who saw twelve books written in a single volume know how highly they were regarded there. We have said little out of much; you will find more about him than what you have read here.

He never tore his sheep, never bit them, never struck them; rather, he refreshed them with words, nourished them with food, admonished those who wandered, recalled those who strayed, gathered those who were scattered, ministered to the needy, and shared the grief of the afflicted. I marvel that this man, who came from another see, so ordered himself with his sheep that they never uttered a single word against him.

Now, having a shepherd from among ourselves, once they obtain the see they wish to devour us with their teeth and know no mercy. They seek worldly elevation more than heavenly glory. They do not share with the sheep, but alone swallow the Church’s possessions; and, nourished by those very resources, they become such that they do not serve the Church but rather lay it waste, nor do they pour out prayers to God for the soul of the benefactor [*dimissor*, one who bequeathed ecclesiastical property; note at Col. 0611D].

Then the sheep themselves cry out daily to the Lord in mourning, saying:

> “Deliver us, Lord, from the captivity of our shepherd’s teeth, for he holds not the place of a hireling but the cruelty of a wolf; in his arrogance he consumes us all.”

But this most blessed Maximian never acted in such a way. Rather, with gentleness he humbled the hearts of his enemies, so that what is written might be fulfilled:

> “Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.”

And elsewhere:

> “In your patience you will possess your souls.”

## CHAPTER VII. The death of Saint Maximian and his tomb; the translation of his relics

He died on the eighth day before the Kalends of March and was buried in the basilica of Saint Andrew the Apostle, beside the altar where he had deposited the apostle’s beard. In our own time, however, he was buried beside the apostle’s seat in that church.

In the fifteenth year of Archbishop Petronax, while each of us was urging him in words to draw the body of blessed Maximian from beneath the earth and place it in an elevated location, one day, coming to his senses, he ordered all of us priests to hurry with him to the church of Blessed Andrew. After prayer had been offered in our hearts, he ordered the masons to raise the *plathonia* above it. But, because this was done carelessly, it broke. The bishop became somewhat angry and began to threaten the masons.

Then he said to the tenth priest in the order of the see, named Agnellus, who was called Andrew—and who at that time was full of skill in every kind of craft:

> “Stay here nearby and instruct the craftsmen how they must proceed, so that neither the coffin nor the stone placed over it is broken.”

Thereupon the craftsmen prepared everything according to the priest’s command. When the stone with which the coffin had been sealed was lifted, the bones of blessed Maximian appeared beneath water; the vessel, moreover, was full of water.

When we saw this, we began to weep bitterly with our bishop, and while we wept we said to one another:

> “Where are your sheep now, shepherd Maximian? Where is your flock? Where is your people, whom you acquired for the Lord? Where are your admonitions, your sweet words, your holy preaching, your teaching? If we say that you are our shepherd, how are we to reject this man who is present? Behold, you are both shepherds in one place: you who lie here speechless and lifeless, and this man who weeps, whom we must obey. Your example constrains our innermost being. Behold, we seek you and love you; how much more lovable must you have been to all those who knew you?”

After we had all wept for a very long time and with the deepest bitterness, and had been sated with mourning, a small bronze vessel was brought to us, which in the common tongue we call a *siclus*. One hundred and fifteen *sicli* full of water were poured out from within the coffin, over the bones of blessed Maximian. I myself counted them aloud for everyone with my own mouth.

When all the bones had been brought out [variant: removed], they were wrapped in the shroud that had been on the altar of Blessed Andrew the Apostle. After the shroud had been tied, the bishop sealed it on its side with his ring.

After this, the coffin was drawn out without any damage, and we carefully lifted it and placed it above. We found all the bones intact. They were delicate, but long, and arranged at their joints as though they had been removed from the flesh almost a year earlier. There was no deficiency except that one tooth was missing on the right side.

Therefore, after the bones had been washed with choice wine, arranged with spices in due order, in the presence of those singing psalms and of the bishop, they were all placed in the same coffin and, amid immense mourning, reverently enclosed in the tomb.

For many days we who had seen this were seized by such fear and trembling that it seemed as though blessed Maximian himself stood before our eyes.

He sat for . . . years, . . . months, . . . days.

# OBSERVATIONS ON THE LIFE OF SAINT MAXIMIAN

How could the pallium have been requested from the emperor? Which church was Saint Stephen’s? Did Maximian come to Constantinople once after obtaining the see? Was Saint Andrew’s building an oratory or a church? Which Vitalis is meant, to whom the poems of Venantius Fortunatus are addressed? When were Saint Andrew’s relics brought from Constantinople? What was a *bandus*? Maximian’s account of the Alexandrian Church’s riots. Some matters of secular history. What were the chrism-vessels? Books intended for the Church’s use: the Missals.

## I

Rubeus, reporting Maximian’s election from Agnellus, says that after Victor’s death the Ravennates “requested the pallium from Caesar through envoys.” Henschenius, in his notes on the first chapter of the Life derived from Rubeus, writes:

> “Perhaps the writer meant, or ought to have said, only this: because Ravenna was the seat of the exarchs, whom the emperor appointed over the lands of Italy, the emperor was informed of the bishop’s death—if he customarily claimed for himself some right to name the successor, just as Baronius shows that he claimed such a right in the confirmation of the Roman pontiff, under the year 554, numbers 1 and 2.”

Regarding the nature and use of the pallium granted by the emperor to the bishops of Ravenna, Henschenius cites Baronius, who argues against the apocryphal privilege of Valentinian; we shall discuss this in its proper place.

Concerning Henschenius’s observations, I think this should first be noted: during the time of Pope Vigilius, Justinian could not have claimed anything for himself in the election of the bishop of Ravenna on the grounds of the exarchs, since such a prefecture did not yet exist in Italy and did not begin before the age of the Lombards, by which time Justinian had already died.

I have no doubt that Justinian claimed for himself not only the right to give consent to the election of the bishop of Ravenna but also to that of the Roman pontiff, since the Gothic kings had claimed the same right. The electors had to endure the calamity of their times and circumstances.

It is certain that Pope Vigilius granted the pallium by his own right to those whom it suited, but he did so with Justinian’s consent. The letters of that same pontiff to Auxentius and Aurelian, bishops of Arles, appear to prove this. In the letter dated the tenth day before the Kalends of September, in the fifth year after the consulship of Basilius, the pontiff says that Belisarius, by sending a man, had “removed the necessity of undertaking the journey to the most merciful prince,” but that as soon as he received a reply, he “indicated it to him in his own letter.” It seems, therefore, that someone was being sent to the emperor in order to obtain his consent for the pallium to be received from the pontiff.

We know that sharp disputes over this right arose from the facts of the case among the most learned men of our own age. On this subject see Peter de Marca, Christianus Lupus, Thomassinus, and others.

I would briefly note that the two examples mentioned above can scarcely be regarded as instances of consent sought from Vigilius. They establish that the pontiff granted what was being requested, namely, the sending of the pallium to that province in which, at that time, the emperors of Constantinople believed that they possessed some legal right. What they call the reasoning of the state may have suggested that this was possible; otherwise, the emperors did not believe that they possessed any right by which they could grant the pallium. On this matter see our preface, where we refute Agnellus.

## II

Faber, in the first part of the work so often cited, believes that the church of Saint Stephen built by Maximian was the one called *in Olivis*, as the ancient monuments of the Church of Ravenna testify. Nuns lived there long ago, as they do today.

The author of the marginal notes denies this. He is led to that conclusion by the argument that the nuns’ church in his own time—namely, at the time of the general Council of Constance—was not as elegant as Agnellus praises it, and he believes that another church must be meant, one surviving in his day near the church of Saint Barbatianus and the monastery, or oratory, of Saint Zacharias.

He proves this from an old document of the notary Morandus, dated 1296, preserved in the Cartulary of the canons of Ravenna.

Agnellus says that the church was built not far from the small gate of the sheepfold. Rubeus incorrectly reproduced the first verse, which was inscribed on the brow of the apse-arch, and Faber, following Rubeus, did the same. Henschenius corrected the error in the Life of Maximian, volume III of the February collection, page 295, in his notes on chapter 3 of the Life.

The reading should therefore be, as in the Este Codex, instead of “martyris, meritis”:

> **Templa micant Stephani meritis, et nomine sacra.**  
> Stephen’s shrine shines with his relics and is holy by his name.

That “merits” here signifies the saint’s relics is proved by other passages of this Life written by Agnellus.

The inscription also differs in some copies from the reading of our Codex. From what our author adds, however, it is clear that Maximian traveled once to Constantinople, around the year 548, as will be said below, while the basilica of Saint Stephen was being founded. For this reason bricks and mortar were lacking and the work was interrupted; the holy bishop repaired the damage of the delay by a miracle, preparing in a single night what would have been sufficient for many days’ labor.

At that time Justinian was about sixty-eight years old, while Maximian was approximately fifty-five. They could therefore converse with one another quite well despite their advanced age, as our author says.

Maximian eventually completed the church of Tricoli. He ensured this with verses that removed from posterity any opportunity for doubt about the succession of several bishops.

## III

The sacred building of Saint Andrew, which had originally been an oratory constructed by Saint Peter Chrysologus, became a church after Saint Maximian restored it. There is no difficulty in this.

What our author relates about the relics of Saint Andrew the Apostle cannot, however, be maintained, as Rubeus and Henschenius have observed. Nevertheless, it cannot be doubted that Maximian restored Saint Andrew’s building on a larger scale and deposited the apostle’s relics there together with the relics of other saints, just as the bishops of Ravenna of that period are all well known to us.

Nevertheless, there survive poems by Venantius Fortunatus addressed to a certain Vitalis, a bishop of Ravenna otherwise entirely unknown, in which these same acts are attributed to Vitalis. Rubeus discusses the matter more fully in book III, page 172. It will not be useless to copy the verses here, if possible, in order to solve the difficulty.

### TO VITALIS, BISHOP OF RAVENNA

> O bishop of the Lord, living through your merits forever,  
> You who possess the joys of Christ as shepherd of his flock;  
> When antiquity wished to call you Vitalis,  
> It knew that you had deserved eternal life.  
>   
> Worthy priest, resplendent with an apostolic mind,  
> You who place the sacred and most holy limbs of Andrew.  
> How well, in accordance with his merits, he has taken his seat in the Lord’s hall,  
> Through whom a house worthy of God has been built!  
>   
> You received your height from the Lord, for whom you build heights;  
> He gave you worthy gifts, and you return the favor with honor.  
> The mighty hall shines, perfected in solid metal;  
> There, day continues unbroken through the night.  
>   
> The place itself invites God beneath perpetual light,  
> So that he may enter the home with loving, peaceful steps.  
> You provide places for the peoples in which they may always adore the Lord;  
> In order that they may receive forgiveness, you yourself prepare the way.  
>   
> Grace, understanding, spirit, goodness, love of the people,  
> Rank, piety—these have made you a father.  
> Your prosperity proves itself, for, supplying joys,  
> It brought distinguished men to your prayers.  
>   
> Here a commander shines in arms; there a prefect in laws;  
> They have come, through whom festivals commonly increase.  
> So that honor might not be lacking to you, God increased your prosperous people,  
> Who saw that you had willed this with understanding.  
>   
> He fulfilled the mystery of faith for the one who made the request.  
> Happy is he for whom the Lord himself brings about what he desires!  
> Celebrate many solemn rites by the divine gift,  
> And, flourishing, cultivate temples to be dedicated to God.

### ON THE CHURCH OF SAINT ANDREW BUILT BY VITALIS, BISHOP OF RAVENNA  
[Variant: “Ravennensis,” Bacch.]

> Whoever hastens to these thresholds of the holy temple,  
> If you come as a suppliant, here you receive help through prayer.  
> The sacred bishop Vitalis founded this citadel,  
> Raised to the roof, which was brought to completion in a short time.  
>   
> He founded it, built it, endowed it, and then dedicated it,  
> And deserved to fulfill the vows of his temple.  
> Here rest the venerable remains of the devout Peter,  
> Who alone deserved to bind the heavens with the key.  
>   
> Paul too is held in this apostolic hall,  
> Once a deceiver, now triumphing as a teacher.  
> Holy Andrew claims this citadel as his own,  
> And governs it in shared possession with his pious brother.  
>   
> Lawrence fills these roofs with his serene fire,  
> To whom sacred flame granted enduring daylight.  
> This house pleases Vitalis, who, while alive,  
> Deserved, buried in the sand, to lose the path of death.  
>   
> These are the places of Martin, who clothed the Thunderer;  
> So that he would not suffer greater cold, Martin gave his own clothing.  
> Behold, this is the citadel of Vigilius, whom the rustic crowd killed;  
> From the place where he wished to die, death itself fled all the more.  
>   
> Martyrius and Sisennus likewise inhabit it,  
> United by lineage, faith, and the one salvation.  
> Holy Alexander and blessed Cecilia are mighty here;  
> One crown awaits them all according to their merits.  
>   
> The good bishop John, at the urging of Vitalis,  
> Placed these holy remains in an excellent location.  
> O exceedingly happy man, destined to enter eternal light,  
> Whose life advances this work before its God!  
> [Variant: “in devotion,” Bacch.]

## IV

Some certain facts emerge from these passages that entangle the difficulty; one certain fact appears to resolve it.

The facts that create the difficulty are these: that this Vitalis, of whom Venantius speaks, was a bishop; that the bishop’s name cannot be doubted; that Andrew’s church was constructed in a short time; that a military commander and the prefect of the province were present at its dedication; and that most of the relics correspond with those listed by our author.

From these facts it seems to follow that Vitalis, bishop of Ravenna, carried out everything that is related about Maximian.

The fact that appears to resolve the difficulty is that this Vitalis was indeed a bishop, but under a metropolitan bishop. John, therefore, is introduced as the one who deposited the sacred relics at Vitalis’s urging. The verses name that bishop John:

> “The good bishop John, at the urging of Vitalis,  
> Placed these holy remains in an excellent location.”

I therefore think that Vitalis was a native of Ravenna and a bishop of one of the dioceses subject to the metropolitan of Ravenna. He himself had built and dedicated the splendid church of Saint Andrew and had obtained from the metropolitan the relics described above, together with their solemn translation into their own shrines, while the leading men of the people of Ravenna and a great multitude of neighboring inhabitants were present.

John, bishop of Ravenna, during whose episcopate these things occurred, was the man who flourished immediately after Peter the Elder, of whom more will be said below.

It should also be observed that the relics of the saints praised by Agnellus were deposited in the church of Saint Stephen, whereas those of which Venantius speaks were in the church of Saint Andrew built by Vitalis.

For the present, these observations are sufficient.

## V

It is worth noting concerning the body of the apostle Andrew that Justinian rebuilt the building once dedicated to that saint by Constantine, as Eusebius reports in *Life of Constantine*, book IV, chapters 50 and 60, and Socrates in book I, chapters 12 and 26. Procopius relates this in book I of *Buildings of Justinian*.

When the rebuilding was taking place, “the stonecutters and craftsmen found three wooden coffins with letters carved on them, indicating that they contained the bodies of three apostles—Andrew, Luke, and Timothy.”

Baronius, citing Nicephorus, book XVII, chapter 26, says that these holy relics were solemnly brought to the Church of the Apostles in the year 552, on the twenty-ninth of June.

Pagius, however, in *Dissertatio Hypatica*, part II, final chapter, page 303, argues from Theophanes that the consecration of the basilica and the solemn translation of the relics took place on Tuesday, the twenty-eighth of July, in the year 548. After recounting the games held in April, Theophanes adds:

> “On the twenty-eighth day of July, a Tuesday, the consecration of the church of the Holy Apostles took place, together with the deposition of the holy relics of Andrew, Luke, and Timothy, the holy apostles. Bishop Mennas proceeded with the holy relics, riding in a golden imperial carriage adorned with gems; he carried the three shrines of the holy apostles upon his knees, and thus celebrated the dedication.”

From this the year in which Maximian came to Constantinople can be determined: namely, 548. Since he did not obtain from the emperor the discovered body of blessed Andrew—perhaps because the emperor had arranged to retain it for other purposes—he obtained at least permission to keep vigil with his own clergy beside the sacred body. Seizing that opportunity, he cut off the saint’s beard, which he later brought to Ravenna along with other relics.

I believe these facts can be reconciled in this way.

It is certain, moreover, that the relics of Saints Andrew and Luke had been transferred to Constantinople from Achaia long before this, although it is disputed whether this occurred under Constantine the Great or under Constantius. Baronius discusses the matter in his notes on the Martyrology for 9 May.

The following words breathe the horror of schismatic soot:

> “And indeed, brothers, if the body of blessed Andrew, the brother of Peter the prince, had been buried here, the Roman pontiffs would never have subjected us in this way.”

But what new right would have accrued to the Church of Ravenna from possessing the body of Saint Andrew, so that it might thereby be exempted from the authority of the Roman pontiff?

The Church of Constantinople itself, which had previously been under Heraclea, in order to cloak its more recent claims with some appearance of legitimacy and to assert for itself an equality with Rome from the beginning, eventually did not hesitate to say that, because Andrew’s body had been preserved there, it had been founded from the beginning by Andrew, the brother of the apostle Peter.

Our author perceived that this would provide support for the Church of Ravenna.

## VI

Agnellus does not state in what year the church of Saint Michael was consecrated by Maximian. An inscription shows that it was completed and dedicated on the Nones of May in the year 545; [Col. 0615D] but Maximian did not begin to occupy the see until October of the following year. Therefore the church’s dedication festival could not have been celebrated before May of the year 547.

Thus the building and dedication are distinguished from the consecration in the inscription of the basilica of Saint Vitalis.

The lineage, relationship, and piety of Bachauda and Julian are illuminated by this.

## VII

A “*numerus*” is said to have been built in Maximian’s time near the house where Agnellus wrote. It was called the first *bandus*—I have printed *bandum* for *bancum*, as it was corruptly read—not far from the Golden Milestone. Agnellus says that he read the name of Maximian inscribed on its tiles, together with the title of bishop of Ravenna.

This agrees with his account and with what is related in the Life of Saint John, surnamed Angeloptis. There he says that, from the ruins of the old palace built by Theoderic, he constructed a house for himself at Ravenna on property belonging to his mother:

> “It was called the presbyteral house, in the district called ad Nymphaeos, beside the church of Saint Agnes the martyr, and on the other side beside the first *bandus*, not far from the Golden Milestone.”

Agnellus’s house therefore stood at the boundary of the district of the Nymphaeos and the Golden Milestone.

Rubeus and Faber say that the basilica of Saint Agnes stood in the Herculanean district. Rubeus, however, divided Ravenna into seven districts: the Asian or Aetian district, the Herculanean district, the Golden Milestone, the Upper Street, the Forum of the Hippodrome, the Marcia, and the district of the Ram. Faber divided it into fourteen.

What, then, do the names *numeri* and *bandi* mean in military terms? Later, in the Life of Felix, Agnellus relates that, during very difficult times, an army of citizens prepared for the defense of their homeland was distributed within the city by Georgius, son of Joannicus, who had been elected supreme commander, approximately as follows:

> “He divided the people of the city into eleven parts; the twelfth part was reserved for the Church. Let each soldier proceed according to his military unit and number, namely: Ravenna, the first *bandus*, the second *bandus*, the new unconquered *bandus*, the Constantinopolitan, the Firmans, the Laetus, the Mediolanese, the Veronese, the Classensian, the pontiff’s division with the clergy, with those worthy of honor, and with the household and the *stratores*, or with the other subordinate churches. This arrangement remains to the present day.”

By the name *bandi*, therefore, were understood—as they still are in the cities of our Italy—groups of citizens gathered under a particular commander. We call them *bande*, perhaps from the banner of each group, which they called a *bandum*, and which we call a *bandiera*.

A building had been constructed for each *numerus* or *bandus*. There the soldiers of each group, assigned to a specific number, kept watch when necessary, or their commanders met to conduct business. We recognize this from the passage just cited, as well as the buildings of the first *numerus* or *bandus* and their location.

But why was the name of Maximian the bishop inscribed on its tiles? I believe that Maximian extended his magnificence to public works of this kind as well.

## VIII

This also dissipates the little story about the body of Saint Eleucadius having been transferred by Constantine the Great from Ticinum to Saint Michael’s. Maximian is praised for having “seasoned with spices the body of blessed Probus together with the bodies of the other holy bishops, placed them properly, and set images of blessed Probus, Eleucadius, and Calocerus on the front of that church.”

Agnellus knew of no other translation of Eleucadius, even one later than the time of Constantine; if he had known of such a translation, he certainly would not have omitted it here.

See what I have observed in its proper place.

## IX

Agnellus preserved from Maximian’s historical work a fragment by which we learn not only that Maximian must be numbered among ecclesiastical writers, but also that, in the prime of his life, he sailed to Alexandria while Timothy, the successor of Dioscorus, occupied that see. According to Baronius’s calculation, this began in the year 519.

Thus Maximian was then in the twenty-first year of his life. Born in 498, he was forty-eight years old when he was ordained, in the year 546.

The civil war of the Alexandrians mentioned here by Maximian arose on the occasion of Dioscorus II, who had been substituted, by order of the emperor Anastasius, for the deceased John. The Alexandrians tried to exclude Dioscorus because he was neither an Alexandrian nor elected by the Alexandrian clergy according to the canons. Matters proceeded so far that, when a riot broke out, Theodosius, the son of Calliopius Augustalis, was killed.

The emperor was enraged by this. Acacius, the *magister militum*, killed as many people as he was able to capture. Baronius reports these events from Anastasius under the year 516; he also says there that Dioscorus intervened with the enraged emperor on behalf of the Alexandrians.

From Maximian’s fragment we learn that Anastasius, after sending the prefect Laudicius, hanged forty men from each district of the city of Alexandria, and that monks from the desert came with Dioscorus to Constantinople to beg pardon.

Maximian praises Dioscorus and Timothy, elsewhere heretics, for qualities deserving praise in any person. Matters that do not concern doctrine, but are otherwise sound in heterodox people, should not be deprived of the honor due to them when the opportunity to write about them presents itself spontaneously rather than being deliberately sought.

The bishop who had previously been killed by the Alexandrians was Proterius; see Baronius under the year 457.

Anazarbus, the principal city of Cilicia Minor, is said to have been shaken by earthquakes four times in different years. While Justin was reigning, Augustus himself restored the city after it had been shaken and called it Justinopolis.

The history composed by Maximian, which our author says was compiled from Jerome, Orosius, and other writers and divided into several books, is elsewhere cited under the name *Analogia*. He uses it especially, as he also uses Paul the Deacon, when writing about matters belonging to secular history.

Here he says that it was a *Chronicon* not only of emperors but also of kings and prefects.

## X

Among the matters that follow, some relate to secular history and also to ecclesiastical history; others, as is customary, are stated anticipatorily [Greek: προληπτικῶς].

The matters concerning the victories of Narses mentioned here after the death of Theja—namely, the siege of Cumae, the recovery of Lucca, and the remaining triumphs over the Goths and Franks—must be sought in Agathias’s *History*, book I.

Everything that Agnellus relates about Narses occurred after Maximian’s death. From the fact that he says Forum Cornelii was restored by the prefect Antiochus, we learn this.

I think that the events mentioned here concerning the discovery and suppression of the Manichaean heresy at Ravenna occurred after Maximian had been transferred to a better life.

The death of Pope Pelagius I occurred only after Maximian’s time, when Agnellus was bishop. The distinguished Papebrochius, in his *Conatus*, states that Pelagius died after occupying the see for four years, ten months, and eighteen days, eleven years after his initial election—that is, in the year 561, on the second of March.

Our author gives the third as the day of his death. He says that this occurred three years after the slaughter of the Manichaeans; therefore they were punished around the year 557.

The fourth year of Bishop Agnellus is intended, for the portent of the red sign appearing in the sky belongs to the eleventh of November in the year 560.

The other aerial portent must be assigned to the year 567, from the indication of the second day of the week coinciding with the twenty-fifth of July, with solar cycle 16 and Sunday letter B.

Theophanes mentions that Verona was occupied by the army of Narses together with Brescia under the eleventh indiction, that is, in the year 563, as follows:

> “In that same year, in the month . . . . . . . victorious announcements reached Constantinople from Rome: namely, that the patrician Narses had recovered from the Goths two extremely well-fortified cities, Verona and Brescia.”

## XI.

The two chrism containers donated to the church by Maximian—certainly larger than the small vessels now used for storing sacred chrism—are shown by the weight of one of them, namely fourteen pounds. The inscription attached to one proves only that it was made “for the uses of the faithful”; what that use was, however, can scarcely be guessed. Ducange, drawing on Rubeus, noted the name of the vessel in his *Glossary of Latinity*, but said nothing further about its use. Perhaps the use of chrism in baptism and in the final anointing of the faithful was then [Col. 0618A] more extensive than it is now.

The other gifts bestowed on the church by Maximian commend his munificence, while the inscriptions engraved upon them display his humility and moderation of spirit: everywhere he professes that he was raised up by the Lord from the dungheap. It is not known where in Pola he was born, but his acts and writings attest to his liberal education. I believe that the stories told about the treasure discovered by Maximian and partly offered by Justinian were most unfortunately fabricated by the Ravennates infected with schism. Such things are unworthy of the most holy bishop whom the Catholic Church venerates as numbered among the heavenly citizens. Moreover, the end of their fiction was that it might be said that the pallium had been requested from the emperor by the Ravennates and bestowed by him. See what we noted in the preface.

We have said enough above about the *endothys* in the Life of Saint Victor. From this passage we learn what books the church of Ravenna used in those times for ecclesiastical liturgy and psalmody: the Old Testament, translated by the Seventy, and the New Testament from Jerome’s version, [Col. 0618B] with the scholarly works of Augustine employed, together with Missals—this being the oldest name for them that I have read—covering the entire annual cycle. These books contained the rites of the Mass proper to each day. Thus, approximately until the eleventh century, Missals did not contain readings from the Gospels and Epistles, as they did later, but the rite of the Mass proper to each day. Learned men have observed this, and an old Missal preserved in the library at Cassino confirms it.

The same is true of the ancient codices containing the Gelasian Order, which the most learned Father Thomasius made public from the library of Queen Christina and which are now kept in the Vatican, where the most courteous D. Zaccagnius, now custodian of that library, kindly displayed them to me for examination. The other enormous volume, composed of twelve books, whose removal to Rome Agnellus laments, I do not at all believe was assigned to ecclesiastical offices; rather, it seems to have been some other distinguished work of Maximian, as is suggested by the fact that it was divided into books.

[Col. 0618C] ## XII.

Taking occasion from Maximian’s integrity, Agnellus attacks the corrupt morals of his own times and passes to the age of Petronax, in order to relate how the bones of the holy bishop were transferred from a humble place to a more distinguished one. From this and from other passages of the work it is evident that Agnellus wrote after the time of Petronax, bishop of Ravenna. We noted this in the observations on the poems prefixed to the entire work, no. 5, where we also discussed the date of his translation.

Here he sufficiently commends himself by saying that he sat tenth among the priests of the Ravennate Church and by displaying his expertise in architecture on the occasion of narrating that translation. The word *sicli*, used to signify a flask or vessel customarily used for drawing water, still survives among us, altered into *secchio*. It is easy, therefore, to call it Gothic in origin.

# LIFE OF SAINT AGNELLUS

[Col. 0617]

## CHAPTER ONE

Agnellus first a married man and soldier, then a deacon. At his death he appoints his niece as heir.

Agnellus was twenty-seven years old. He had a ruddy face, a full figure, scant hair on his eyebrows, a red scalp, staring eyes, and a double chin beneath his beard. He was of medium height, handsome in body, perfect in conduct; but after losing his wife, he abandoned the military belt [*militiae*], offered himself wholly to God, and devoted himself to him.

During the episcopate [archiepiscopate] of Ecclesius he was ordained a deacon, [Col. 0618D] served in the church of Saint Agatha, and was therefore a levite; he held that church as his title, and his house was attached to the wall of the aforesaid church, which we knew down to the present day. Born of noble stock, he was wealthy in various properties and animals and abundant in riches.

When, toward the end of his life, he was near death, he left as heir his niece, the daughter of his daughter [variant: daughter], after the death of her mother. Among her other riches he left her five pieces of silver tableware and many other things whose wealth it is unnecessary for us to enumerate in detail. Death intervened [perhaps *diutius*, that is, “later”; Bacch.].

But we must ask why this married man obtained so eminent a see. If you understand the Apostle as saying that a bishop should be the husband of one wife and have children, then this was proper by divine providence, since the canons also prescribe it. But let us return to the order of events, and discuss women later.

## CHAPTER TWO

The churches and property of the Goths are donated by Justinian to the Church of Ravenna. Several are listed. Particulars concerning the church of Saint Martin. A mystical interpretation of the paintings within it.

In the time of this man, Justinian, the Augustus of orthodox faith, granted all the property of the Goths to this church and to the blessed Bishop Agnellus—not only in [Col. 0619B] the cities but also in suburban estates and villages, as well as temples, altars, male and female slaves, and everything that could have belonged to their jurisdiction or pagan rites. He donated and granted all these things to the church, confirmed them by privileges, and caused them physically to be handed over by letter. The letter contained, in part, the following:

“Holy Mother Church of Ravenna, truly a mother, truly orthodox, for many other churches introduced a false doctrine through fear and the terrors of rulers. This church, however, held the true and only holy Catholic faith; it never wavered or endured fluctuation, but remained unmoved, shaken though it was by the storm.

“Therefore this most blessed man reconciled all the churches of the Goths that had been built in the time of the Goths or of King Theodoric, and that were held by Arian perfidy and the sect, doctrine, and belief of heretics [Col. 0619C] [perhaps *saeva*, ‘savage’; editor]. He reconciled the church of Saint Eusebius, priest and martyr, situated not far from the Campus Coriandri outside the city on the Ides of November, which Bishop Unimund built in the twenty-third year of King Theodoric, without foundations.

“Likewise he reconciled the church of the blessed George in the time of Basil the Younger, as is read on the tribunal itself. He reconciled the church of the blessed Sergius, situated in the city of Classis beside the garden, and that of the blessed Zeno in Caesarea.

“Within the city of Ravenna itself he reconciled the church of Saint Theodore, not far from the house of Droedo. That house, together with its bath and the monastery of Saint Apollinaris—which was built above the house—was the episcopal residence of that church. Where the monastery of holy and ever-virgin, undefiled Mary now stands, there were formerly the fountains of the aforesaid mother church.

“But concerning the name *Cosmedim*, I hold that it is Latin—a matter over which not only Latins but also Greeks have had some disagreements—for *cosmi*, that is, ‘ornamented’; hence the world is called *cosmos* among the Greeks.

“Therefore the most blessed pontiff Agnellus reconciled within this city the church of Saint Martin the Confessor, which King Theodoric founded and which is called the Golden Heaven. He decorated the tribunal and both walls with images of advancing martyrs and virgins in mosaic tiles; he fixed golden metal plates over them with gypsum, attached various stones to the walls, and fashioned the pavement wonderfully in stone mosaic.

[Col. 0620A] “If you look at the interior front of the building, you will find an image of the Emperor Justinian, together with that of Pontiff Agnellus, decorated with gilded mosaic tiles. No church or house is comparable to this one in its ceilings or beams. After consecrating it, he feasted in the episcopal residence of that confessor [there].

“If you inquire carefully at the tribunal, above the windows you will find the following words engraved in stone letters:

‘King Theodoric made this church from its foundations in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.’

“Concerning the aforesaid church, we shall now tell why it is fortified with broad pavement slabs, as we have heard. At that time there was a not entirely orthodox king of the Vandals who wished to remove the pavement from this church and carry it away to his own seat. When everything had been prepared [Col. 0620B] for tearing up the slabs, suddenly, through a whirlwind, the day became dark. During the night that followed, a powerful wind rushed through the church, carrying with it loud howls. A great sound arose throughout the entire church. Then all the marble slabs resounded as though they had been broken and crushed by hammermen. Nevertheless, you can see this on the wall.

“There, as I said, two cities have been represented. From Ravenna the martyrs go forth, the men proceeding toward Christ; from Classis the virgins advance toward the holy Virgin of virgins, while the Magi go before them offering gifts. Yet they are depicted in various garments, and not all have one kind of clothing, because the divine painter followed Scripture itself.

[Col. 0620C] “For Gaspar offered gold in a hyacinth-colored garment, and in that garment marriage is signified. Balthasar offered frankincense in a yellow garment, and in that garment virginity is signified. Melchior offered myrrh in a variegated garment, and in that garment repentance is signified.

“The one who went ahead was dressed in a purple cloak; through him the King himself is signified, both born and having suffered. The one who offered a gift to the newborn while wearing a variegated cloak signifies that in the same way Christ heals all the sick and is scourged by various injuries and by the diverse blows of the Jews. It is written of him: ‘He himself took up our infirmities and bore our illnesses, and we considered him as though he were a leper [etc.],’ and afterward: ‘He was wounded because of our sins and fastened because of our crimes.’

[Col. 0620D] “The one who offered the gift in white signifies that after the resurrection he is in divine glory. For just as those three precious divine gifts contain mysteries within themselves—through gold, royal wealth; through frankincense, the figure of the priest; through myrrh, death is understood—so that all these things might show him to be the one who took upon himself the iniquities of human beings, that is, Christ, so likewise, as we have said, these three gifts are contained in their cloaks.

“Why did not four, or six, or two come from the East, but only three? So that they might signify the perfect fullness of the entire Trinity. Out of love for them, this most blessed Agnellus completed a portion of the linen *endothys* [variant: *endothym byssinam*] mentioned above, which his predecessor Maximian had not completed. This man perfectly adorned the story of the Magi, and his own image was set before the eyes by mechanical workmanship.”

## CHAPTER THREE

The fountain at Saint Martin’s is reconciled and adorned. A silver cross. The estate of Argenta acquired; the church of Saint George founded. Certain secular events. Agnellus’s death. His epitaph.

He himself reconciled the fountains in the church of blessed Martin and decorated them with mosaic tiles. But the tribunal of that church, violently shaken by a great earthquake, was broken and collapsed during the time of Archbishop John the Fifth the Younger. Later he adorned the chamber with colors.

The most blessed Agnellus made a large silver cross in the Ursian church, above the seat behind the bishop, in which his image prays with outstretched hands. He also acquired [Col. 0621B] an estate in the Church of Ravenna called Argentea, and within that estate he built the monastery of blessed George from its foundations.

But when he was advanced in age, his image was wonderfully painted on a panel, and before the entrance of the monastery there were metrical verses, which I could not clearly read.

In the days of this man the Franks were expelled from Italy by the patrician Narses. After this a comet appeared in August and remained until the Kalends of October. The Emperor Justinian died at Constantinople in the fortieth year of his reign, and there was great mourning everywhere and excessive grief for such an orthodox man. Red signs appeared in the sky; the city of Fano was consumed by fire and a multitude of people were destroyed by the flames; the fortress of Cesena was also devoured by fire.

In the third year of the Emperor Justin the Younger, the patrician Narses was summoned from Ravenna and departed with all the wealth of Italy. He had been governor for sixteen years, defeated two Gothic kings, and slaughtered the Frankish leaders with the sword.

In the time of this prelate there was great abundance and good order among the people of Italy. In the city of Classis he ordered the monasteries adjoining the walls and fountain of the Petriana church—the monasteries of the Apostle Matthew and of James—to be decorated with mosaic tiles.

In the chamber of the tribunal of the Apostle Matthew you will find the following inscription:

“While Pope Agnellus is safe. From the gifts of God and of his servants, which they offered for the honor and adornment of the holy apostles, and the remaining portion from the sum of the deer that perished and, by God’s providence, were found. This apse has been adorned with mosaic.”

[Col. 0621D] It is time to close the mouth and bar it with bolts. Let us seal the keys with the cross, lest a thief come and find the door open; let him not sow tares at the bottom of the heart, mock, and destroy. Therefore, “Place, O Lord, a guard over my mouth, and a door around my lips; do not incline my heart to a word of evil [to evil], but help me, so that I may be able to finish the Life of Agnellus himself.”

He died on the Kalends of August and was buried in the church of Saint Agatha the martyr before the altar. Above his body, on marble letters, you will find the following epitaph:

“Of the bishop’s rest, by heavenly gift . . .”

“Agnellus, by the virtue of God, did not lose it,

Who deserved to know the desired peace of the light,

That the temple of his own body might be preserved.

The just man, together with the saints, will rise through Christ [through the Physician].

Thus also, according to his merits, he rejoices who accomplished such things.”

“Here rests in peace Agnellus, archbishop [read: bishop; Bacch.], who sat for 13 years, 1 month, and 8 days; who lived 83 years [rubric: 94]; he was laid to rest on the Kalends of August, indiction 3 [read: indiction 14; Bacch.]; he sat 13 years, 1 month, and 8 days.”

# OBSERVATIONS ON THE LIFE OF SAINT AGNELLUS

The age of Bishop Agnellus. His letter to Armenius. The title to which he was ordained. Transfer from one title to another. The churches of the Arians. The Arians’ two baptismal fountains at Ravenna. An inscription in Rubeus differing from Agnellus’s. Secular matters reserved for examination in the following dissertation.

[Col. 0622B] ## I.

We discussed the age of Bishop Agnellus at greater length in the preceding dissertation, where we said that the epitaph should be corrected according to the reading described by Rubeus. Nevertheless, I wondered whether the years of his age were more faithfully recorded in our Codex, and whether the eighty-three years rather than ninety-four should be retained.

If he died at the age of eighty-three, he would have been ordained a deacon after passing his forty-second year. For in the year 524, when Ecclesius became bishop, he was in his forty-first year. In the list of the clergy appended to the constitution of Pope Felix, he is recorded last among the deacons who had adhered to Mastalo. Thus, around the year 527, after abandoning his military belt and his wife having died previously, he had been enrolled among the clergy and distinguished by the order of the diaconate.

According to this hypothesis, he became bishop at the age of seventy, in the year 553, still vigorous and healthy, as is proved by his image described by our author.

## II.

In the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, volume VI, there is a letter [Col. 0622C] to Armenius concerning the faith of this Agnellus. Those are certainly mistaken who confuse Bishop Agnellus with the Agnellus whom we are now discussing.

We learn, moreover, that Agnellus, bishop of Ravenna, was formerly ordained deacon by Ecclesius, “served in the church of the blessed Agatha, and was therefore a levite, and held that church as his title.” Rubeus says that Agnellus was “prefect of the Church of Saint Agatha.” Faber conveys the same meaning in Italian, saying that he was appointed “custodian” of that church.

Certainly, “to hold a church as one’s title” means the same as to be ordained to the title of that church. Yet those ordained to the title of a particular church did not thereby become prefects or custodians of that church. For not only deacons and subdeacons but also lower-ranking clergy—acolytes, readers, and singers—were ordained to the title of a particular church.

In an old codex of the Cassino library, no. 451, I read approximately what Hitorpius made public concerning the sacred rites. In the order “How presbyters, [Col. 0622D] deacons, and subdeacons are to be chosen in the Roman Church,” before the antiphon at the introit, “the pontiff announces among the people, saying: ‘With the help of the Lord our God and Savior Jesus Christ, we choose for the order of subdeacon, deacon, or presbyter this acolyte, subdeacon, or deacon, from that title; this man to the title of Saint Mary; to the church which is in that village; or to that monastery. But if anyone,’” and so forth.

All those ordained were therefore attached to particular churches in which they were to serve. A presbyter, however, was placed over each of these churches to conduct sacred affairs and instruct the people, assisted by the ministry of the lower orders. Deacons, subdeacons, acolytes, and the others promoted to a higher order were transferred from one title to another.

## III.

It is clear that, after the Goths had been subdued, the Arians departed from Ravenna with their bishops, and that their property and churches, by Justinian’s command, passed under the jurisdiction of the bishop of Ravenna. This was effected by the emperor’s so-called imperial letter, from which our author extracted several words praising the Church of Ravenna for having preserved the integrity of the Catholic faith under an Arian king. Spretus, Blondus, and Rubeus copied the same words from our author, though they differ in some details.

The cult of the saints whose names are assigned to the churches that had once belonged to the Arians and are now said to have been dedicated to God is indicated by their reconciliation. Otherwise, how can one believe that the Arians dedicated their churches to God under the names either of Martin of Tours, or of Saint Eusebius the priest and martyr—whether he was Eusebius of Samosata or of Vercelli?

Faber says that such churches were destroyed, except for Saint Mary in Cosmedim and Saint Martin in the Golden Heaven. He describes the former but is silent about the latter. Rubeus wrote that the mosaics of this church were already falling in his own time and would last only a short while [Note: They still exist. See Ciampini, *On Mosaics*, p. 2. Bacch.].

I do not see to what period the story told here by our author can be assigned, or how much it rests on truth: namely, the story of a not entirely orthodox king of the Vandals who ordered the marble pavement slabs to be carried away and was prevented by a miracle.

It is clear from this that the Arians had two baptismal fountains at Ravenna. One was at Saint Theodore, where the house of Driedo served as the episcopal residence together with its bath, and where the oratories of Saint Apollinaris and Saint Mary in Cosmedim were later built. The other was at Saint Martin, which Bishop Agnellus reconciled and decorated with mosaic tiles, and whose tribunal, or tribune, collapsed after being shaken by an earthquake during the episcopate of John V of that name.

The magnificent gifts presented to the Ursian church receive further illumination from the observations on the Life of Saint Maximian. The estate of Argentea was discussed in the Life of Saint Exuperantius. Beside the fountain of the Petriana church, two chapels—or, as he calls them, monasteries—are said to have been decorated with mosaics; one was called by the name of Saint James, the other by that of Saint Matthew.

What the inscription of the latter signifies in its final words can scarcely be guessed. Perhaps it indicates that property and houses recovered after the expulsion of the Arians were used for the worship of God. Rubeus copied this inscription, but in abbreviated form and with differences in some places, as where he has, “This has been adorned beneath the apse in bones,” in place of what is read in our Codex: “This apse has been adorned with mosaic.”

## IV.

The matters relating to secular history reported in this Life of Agnellus are to be examined in the following dissertation. They have this peculiar feature: from the author’s perspective, everything seems to have happened while Agnellus was sitting as bishop. This is conveyed by expressions such as “in his days,” “in the time of this prelate,” and similar phrases. How true this is will become clear from what follows.

# CHRONOLOGICAL-HISTORICAL DISSERTATION

## On the Age of Peter the Elder, John, Marinianus, and Both Johns

[Col. 0623]

## CHAPTER ONE

Rubeus and Agnellus give different accounts of the age of the bishops under discussion. The argument must be divided and treated in definite sections.

### I.

Since what was done in the preceding dissertations is to be done here as well, Rubeus’s opinion must be presented, from which later writers have considered it wrong to depart. After stating that Bishop Agnellus died in the year 566, on the Kalends of August, Rubeus says that Peter was elected in the year 568, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of October. He says that Peter died around the year 575, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of September.

Since he gives no certain information about the time when the following bishops were ordained, he merely specifies their deaths: John in the year 595, on the third day before the Ides of January; Marinianus in the year 606, on the tenth day before the Kalends of November; and he extends the age of John—believing that the two Johns were one man—down to the year 630.

### II.

Our author gives approximately the following account. Agnellus was laid to rest on the Kalends of August, indiction 3, which, as we have shown, must be corrected and replaced by indiction 14, [Col. 0623D] in the year 566. Peter was “consecrated at Rome without fasting” in the second indiction, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of October; he died on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of September, and sat for eight years, two months, and nineteen days.

John died on the eleventh day of January, after having worn the episcopal insignia for sixteen years, one month, and nineteen days. Marinianus died on the tenth day before the Kalends of November. John, the successor of Marinianus, sat for five years, ten months, and eighteen days. The other John sat for eighteen years, six months, and eight days.

In the Life of each one he adds several matters relating to secular history, copied largely from the books of Paul the Deacon that we possess on the deeds of the Lombards. We must examine these matters in order, so far as possible, to arrange the chronology relating to these bishops. Otherwise it can scarcely be hoped that so many tangled matters will be disentangled, since Agnellus himself has points on which he is confused or deceived, and many numerical figures are incurably corrupted through the fault of copyists.

At the outset it is worth noting that Agnellus made a shameful error in confusing this Peter with Peter the Roman pontiff’s contemporary Symmachus and reporting that he sat in a synod of the city. To arrange the remaining matters clearly, in so far as possible, and in some kind of order, I think we must treat the age of each bishop separately and section by section.

## CHAPTER TWO

The ordination of Peter the Elder must be distinguished from his election. The cause of the longer interregnum. The beginnings of Bishop John. The restoration of the basilica of Saint Severus. The inscription concerning it. John’s death assigned to a definite time.

### I.

Peter the Elder’s ordination is explained by such definite indications that there can be no doubt about it. “This man,” says our author, “was consecrated at Rome in the second indiction, without fasting, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of October.”

The second indiction had begun on the first day of September in the year 568, and the fifteenth day of that month was a Saturday, with solar cycle 17, Dominical letters A and G. He is said to have been ordained without fasting, that is, before the fast of the seventh month, which was to occur on the days of the following or incoming week.

Peter was therefore ordained on the evening of that Saturday. I believe that the custom had already become established which the old Roman Order, edited by Mabillon, describes in “The Degrees of the Roman Church,” namely, that bishops “should be blessed at night,” specifically during the night preceding the Lord’s Day. We shall note more suitably below, in the Life of this Peter, certain matters concerning this practice.

Since we possess the definite day, month, and year of Peter’s ordination, and it is established that his predecessor died in the year 566, we are compelled to admit an interpontificate of more than two years and one and a half months. We are consequently driven to investigate how he could have sat for eight years, two months, and nineteen days, as our author writes.

“The same man founded the church of the blessed Severus, confessor of Christ, but death intervened and left it unfinished,” says Agnellus. Likewise, in the Life of his successor: “After the accession of the blessed Peter, he completed the unfinished work that Peter had left behind, namely the church of Saint Severus, and brought it to completion.”

Rubeus, moreover, gives an old inscription that once existed and must be reproduced here, for it expresses the year in which the church was crowned:

“Through divine worship, the shining construction of many things

Reveals itself to be the work of a priest.

The excellent shepherd Peter had begun to build this,

But death did not allow that man to remain with it.

Yet what the old man left roofed but not yet completed,

A man born at Rome finished as this work.

The prudent successor of Peter, and shepherd John,

Who bore away the honor that lies in so great a thing.

That Father of the people, coming from the city of Rome,

Gave these monuments worthy of his merits.

This is the ancient house renewed for holy Severus,

In whose honor true songs are sung to God.

In the five-hundredth year of the Lord, with seven times ten,

Add five more to these, good reader, in due order,

From the Virgin’s birth, who bore without guilt,

While the second Justinian retained the empire,

Living in the world and ruling for eleven years.”

[Note: This verse has been restored from the final position to this one. Bacch.]

### II.

It is worth observing here that this is not one inscription, but two on a single stone, the second being considerably more recent than the first. This is shown by the slight Leonine flavor in it, the method of counting from the Virgin’s birth, and the awkwardness inserted into it by which, to make the verse scan, Justin is called Justinian among other things.

Nevertheless, despite these features, I believe that everything relating to chronology agrees with itself. For C. V. Pagius demonstrated by incontrovertible arguments in *Hypatian Dissertation*, part III, no. 1 and following, that the beginning of Justin’s reign falls in the final days of November 565.

Thus the eleventh year of his reign had begun to be counted after the fourteenth day of November in the year 575. Therefore, in the final days of that year, the basilica of Saint Severus had been completed by John, who was consequently already sitting as pontiff, Peter having been transferred to a better life.

I therefore believe that Peter died in that same year 575, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of September. But in order for the years during which he is said by Agnellus to have sat to stand, his election must be distinguished from his ordination.

Thus, elected in the year 567 on 28 May, ordained in the year 568 on 15 September, and dying on 16 August 575, he sat from the date of his election—as Agnellus counts—for eight years, two months, and nineteen days; from his ordination, however, for six years and eleven months.

The reason why almost sixteen months elapsed between his election and ordination must be sought in the fact that Peter’s election and the death of his predecessor Agnellus occurred at a time when Longinus, the first of all the exarchs, was soon to be sent to Ravenna in that very year 575.

After the election, a messenger was sent to Constantinople concerning it, and the ruler’s command had to be awaited. For this reason, not only this interpontificate but also those preceding it was longer than those that followed. For once the seat of the exarchs residing at Ravenna had been established, the emperor’s consent no longer had to be awaited from Constantinople; it was granted by the exarch himself.

Learned men have also observed this in the chronology of the supreme pontiffs, although they hold that the consent requested from the Ravennate exarchs was sought only later. Consider what is related about the election of the great Gregory in his Life by John the Deacon, as well as in the fourth letter of the first book of that pontiff to John, bishop of Constantinople, and in other letters to be read in the Register.

In the Church of Ravenna, however, the ruler’s command was supplied by the exarch as soon as the exarchs began to reside at Ravenna. This first occurred when Peter died and John was elected.

That by this time the ruler’s command was required not only for the ordination of the bishop of Ravenna but also for that of the Roman pontiff is clear from Anastasius, who notes concerning Pelagius II that he was “ordained without the ruler’s command, because the Lombards were besieging the city of Rome.”

This was indeed to be expected in those times, when Italy had begun to be occupied by the Lombards, so that the emperor was extremely solicitous about his rights. After Peter had been elected, and a messenger had been sent to Constantinople concerning the matter, his ordination was delayed until, when the Lombards began to press in on every side, Longinus, the first exarch, was sent with the necessary authority. Coming in that same year 568, he provided consent in the emperor’s name, and Peter was consecrated at Rome.

### III.

To establish the beginnings of John, who succeeded Peter the Elder, on a definite day, no more suitable or probable method can be found than to investigate the year and day on which he died.

From Agnellus we have the day, namely the eleventh of January; the letters of Gregory the Great indicate the year. For it is entirely certain that John died in indiction 13, in the February of which year we possess letters 64 and 65 to John, bishop of Squillace, and to the clergy, order, and people residing at Ravenna.

The following words are written in the latter:

“Having learned of the death of your bishop, we took care to entrust solemnly the visitation of the abandoned Church to our brother and fellow bishop Severus Paulinus. We gave him instructions not to allow anyone to usurp anything concerning the promotions of clergy, revenues, [Col. 0626B] adornment, or ministries.”

John had therefore died on the eleventh day of the preceding January, in the year 595, when indiction 13 was running.

Having established this, we must convert the statement of the length of his episcopate given by Agnellus. Its figures are easily recognized as having been corrupted by copyists. For the years counted from 575 to January 595 are not sixteen but nineteen.

Retaining the nineteen days and one month, and substituting nineteen years for the sixteen years, then counting backward from John’s day of death, the eleventh of January 595, without including that day, we arrive at 23 November of the aforesaid year 575. This was suitable for the ordination of bishops, being a Saturday, with solar cycle 24 and Dominical letter F.

Thus, when John was ordained, the basilica of Saint Severus had nearly been restored; within a month, and before the end of the year, it was completed according to the wording of the inscription cited above. These matters will receive clear illumination from the examination of the secular events that Agnellus relates in the Life of each bishop.

## CHAPTER THREE

The entry of the Lombards into Italy. The death of Narses. The different epoch of the Lombard kingdom and the epoch of their entry into Italy. Sigonius defended against the criticism of Camillo Pellegrini.

## I. Matters concerning the time of Peter the Elder

Agnellus relates the following matters concerning the time of Peter the Elder. In the year in which he was ordained, Venice was invaded and occupied by the Lombards. In Justin’s fifth year, the destruction of the oxen, Tuscany overwhelmed by arms, Ticinum surrounded by siege, and Caesarea fortified with palisades by Longinus the exarch. Narses died at Rome. Alboin was killed through the treachery of his wife. These matters must all be investigated.

Paul the Deacon relates the Lombards’ entry into Italy “in the month of April, in the first indiction, on the day after Easter, whose feast in that year, according to the reckoning, fell on the Kalends of April, when 568 years had already elapsed from the Lord’s Incarnation.” All this plainly belongs to the common era of 568 from Christ’s birth, in which year Easter was celebrated on the Kalends of April, with lunar cycle 18, solar cycle 17, and Sunday letter A, G. The calculations begun by Rubeus and Baronius from Gregory’s letters to the empress Constantina and to the emperor Phocas agree with this.

Yet Agnellus conflicts with Rubeus, who says that “Longinus came into Italy as exarch the previous year, in order to receive and rather to impede the Lombards’ attacks.” For Agnellus relates in the preceding Life that, when Longinus came to Ravenna, Narses had departed from it. This occurred in Justin’s third year, which began in November 567; and the order of events makes it consistent that, upon Longinus’s arrival, Bishop Peter was ordained, as we observed above.

Our author reports: “In Justin’s fifth year Tuscany was devastated by the Lombards, and they besieged Ticinum.” Justin’s fifth year began in November 569. Paul the Deacon, book II, chapter 25, says that Alboin entered Liguria “in the third indiction, on the third day before the Nones of September,” and immediately afterward, in chapter 26:

> “At that time the city of Ticinum, having endured a siege for more than three years, held out bravely, while the Lombard army remained not far from it on the western side. Meanwhile Alboin, with selected soldiers, invaded everything as far as Tuscany, except Rome and Ravenna, and certain fortresses constructed on the seacoast.”

The third indiction began in that September on whose third day before the Nones the Lombards entered Liguria. Therefore, in the following November, the fifth year of the Emperor Justin began; in December of that same year, 569, the siege of Ticinum began. Once the siege had begun, and while the year 570 was running, still within Justin’s fifth year, Alboin advanced as far as Tuscany and devastated the region extensively.

Paul adds in chapter 27:

> “But the city of Ticinum, after enduring the siege for three years and several months, finally surrendered to Alboin and the Lombards, who were besieging it.”

And in chapter 28:

> “After this king had reigned in Italy for three years and six months, he was killed by his wife’s plot.”

Below, in chapter 31, he says that Cleph reigned for one year and six months, and finally, in chapter 32, he states:

> “In the seventh year after Alboin’s arrival, through these Lombard leaders, after churches had been plundered, priests killed, cities destroyed, and peoples—who had multiplied like crops—slain, Italy was captured and subjugated by the Lombards for the most part, except for the regions which Alboin had conquered.”

From all this it follows that Ticinum was captured by the Lombards around the earlier months of 573. Our author says that Alboin was murdered at Verona through his wife’s agency “on the fourth day before the Kalends of July,” and Paul agrees, saying that Alboin reigned in Italy for three years and six months. The years of his reign must therefore be counted from the beginning of the siege of Ticinum, on 29 December 569.

But the numeral indicating Justin’s year has been corrupted in Agnellus, and VIII must be written instead of VI, for that year had begun in the preceding year, 572. After Alboin’s death, Cleph was immediately proclaimed king. Having reigned for one year and a half, he died around the end of the following year, 574.

In 575, on the day after the Kalends of April, the seventh year from the Lombards’ entry into Italy was completed. Italy was then extensively devastated by the dukes, and on the sixteenth day of June of that year Benedict was ordained Roman pontiff.

Agnellus indicates these events when he says that, “after the foundations of the church”—namely, of Saint Severus, laid by Bishop Peter—“had been set, the whole of Italy was afflicted by the greatest devastation,” and that the exarch Longinus fortified Caesarea with “palisades” driven in like a wall.

Thus, before the beginning of 575, while Cleph was reigning, the foundations of the church of Saint Severus were laid. In the first months of 575, says our author, “the Lombards went forth,” and “crossed Tuscany as far as Rome; and, setting fire to it, they burned Petra Pertusa in the conflagration. The aforesaid Lombards constructed Forum Cornelii, and the city was completed by them.”

## II. The death of Narses
