Our author places the death of Narses around the year 574. He says that Narses died at Rome, in the palace, in the ninety-fifth year of his age; Anastasius agrees, saying that Narses died in the same year as Pope John.

More could be added on this matter against Baronius’s opinion, which assigns the event to 567 or 568, but we would stray too far from our purpose. It should nevertheless be noted in passing that, if Narses was in his ninety-fifth year when he died, he cannot have been the same man who, famous for military service, lived under Maurice.

Narses is praised by the poet Corippus; he was living at Constantinople in 566 and the following years and was different from the other Narses who at that same time was renowned as an elder in Italy. Nevertheless, Greek writers of a later age treated the two as one.

Agnellus says nothing about Narses’s having summoned the Lombards. Yet the statement that the honors of the Romans were thereby destroyed and their wealth plundered is hardly favorable to Narses’s glory. But enough on this matter for the present.

## III. The two Lombard eras

From what has been said, I think the necessity of establishing two distinct eras is clear: one beginning with the Lombards’ entry into Italy, the other with the beginning of Alboin’s reign in Italy. The first is fixed to 2 April 568; the second to 29 December 569. Otherwise everything would be reported confusedly.

For example, it is not surprising that, because this distinction between the eras was neglected, Baronius assigns Alboin’s death to the year 571, although in the same place he acknowledges from Paul the Deacon’s words that Alboin was killed after Ticinum had been recovered, after three years and several months of siege and three and a half years of Alboin’s reign, while in the preceding year Alboin and the Lombards had entered Liguria on the third day before the Nones of September, in the third indiction.

The celebrated light of the people of Modena, Carlo Sigonio, must nevertheless be defended. Because he praised this distinction between the eras, another most learned writer, Camillus Peregrinus, censures him, following Baronius’s calculations in comparing the years of the Beneventan dukes, from Zotto, the first of all, to Arichis II, on page 262.

Peregrinus says that Sigonio, in his *Kingdom of Italy*, is mistaken when he states that King Authari was acclaimed in 585,

> “because, having wrongly interpreted Paul and Landulf, whom he himself cites, he thought that Alboin’s three and a half years had to be reckoned from 570, whereas they had to be reckoned from 568.”

But the points we have noted above are so clear—the time when Paul says that Alboin entered Liguria, the fact that the city of Ticinum was besieged for three years and several months, and Alboin’s death after Ticinum had been occupied and three and a half years of his reign had elapsed—that they could extract agreement even from an unwilling opponent. They clearly show that the era of the reign was entirely different from the era of the Lombards’ entry into Italy. They consequently prove that Sigonio understood Paul perfectly, although Peregrinus unjustly censures him together with Paul himself.

Moreover, it is established from a letter of Gregory the Great, in the ninth indiction, that Authari died in 591: the letter shows that the king had completed his sixth year of reign, which had begun in 585, as Paul reported. Thus, when the calculation is begun from the start of Alboin’s reign, one arrives by counting backward at the final days of December 569, when the siege of Ticinum began.

Since Paul therefore agrees accurately with Gregory the Great, who was his contemporary, there is no reason to depart from his account. He also says that Agilulf was made king in the same year in which Authari died, namely in November, and that he was confirmed at Easter of the following year.

The same conclusion can be drawn from Gregory, who, in book I, letter 17, written in December, says that Authari had died—whereas Paul records the event under the Nones of September. Gregory himself, in book II, letter 32, to John, bishop of Ravenna, in the tenth indiction, in the month of July, that is, in the year 592, indicates that Agilulf, approaching Naples, was called Arogis. “Arogis,” “Agilulf,” and “Arnulf” have been corruptly written there, as learned men have established.

[Note: In section IV, the sections of text comparing Bacchinius with Peregrinus are printed in parallel in Migne.]

## IV. Comparison of the two chronological systems

I think it must be demonstrated clearly that these eras must be distinguished entirely if Peregrinus’s method of arranging the years of the Beneventan dukes is considered. For if the era of the kings is not distinguished from the other era, that of the Lombards’ entry into Italy, it is impossible, while preserving the intervals assigned by Paul to each king, to reach the year 663, in which Peregrinus believes Grimoald began to reign.

This will, I think, become evident from the comparison written below: Paul as I understand him, and Paul as Peregrinus must understand him, with the two eras confused into one.

### The era of the Lombard kingdom fixed at the end of 569 or the beginning of 570, as Sigonio maintains

### The era of the Lombard kingdom fixed at 568, when the Lombards first entered Italy, as Peregrinus maintains

Authari begins to assume the kingship around the beginning of 585. He dies on the Nones of September 590.

Authari begins his reign around April 583. He dies on the Nones of September 588.

Theodelinda raises Agilulf to the kingship in September of the same year.

Agilulf becomes king in September of the same year.

Agilulf is confirmed at Milan at Easter of the following year, 591, namely on 15 April, with lunar cycle 3, solar cycle 12, and Sunday letter G.

He is confirmed as king by the Lombards in April 589.

Paul the Deacon, book III, chapter 36.

After completing twenty-five years of reign, Agilulf dies in September 615.

After completing twenty-five years, Agilulf dies in September 613.

Paul, book IV, chapter 43.

Adoald, still a very young boy, reigns in the same year, 615, immediately after Agilulf’s death, with his mother Theodelinda.

Adoald begins to reign with his mother in the same year, 613.

When Adoald became insane, after reigning with his mother for ten years, he was expelled and Arioald was substituted for him around October 626, namely at the beginning of Adoald’s eleventh year.

Adoald is expelled in 623, at the beginning of the eleventh year of his reign, around October.

Paul, book IV, chapter 43, appears to count ten full years of Adoald, as well as the following twelve years of Arioald; otherwise the chronology could not stand with what is immediately said below.

But the ordination of Pope Honorius would disrupt the calculation if it had to be assigned to 28 September 626, as the distinguished Papebrochius argues in his *Conatus*. For a letter of that same pontiff to Isaac the exarch survives concerning Adoald’s expulsion and Arioald’s election.

Sigonio therefore more suitably refers these events to 625, in whose September Honorius was elected or ordained. This is demonstrated by another letter of the same Honorius to the bishops of Epirus, written on the Ides of December in the fourteenth indiction.

The pontiff’s ordination cannot in any way be moved back to September 623, as would be necessary if the years of the Lombard kings were to be reckoned from 568.

Arioald is therefore made king around October 625.

Arioald is made king in 623.

After completing twelve years, or at least when they were soon to be completed, he dies in October 637.

He dies in 635.

Paul, book IV, chapter 44.

Rothari reigns around the end of October 637.

Rothari reigns in 635.

He publishes the Edict in November 644.

He dies after completing sixteen years and four months, at the beginning of March 654.

He dies after completing sixteen years and four months, at the beginning of March 652.

Rodoald dies at almost the same time, having reigned together with his father for five years and seven days. Aripert succeeds him in the same year.

Paul, book IV, chapter 44, writes that Rothari published the Code, which he called an Edict, in the seventy-seventh year from the Lombards’ arrival in Italy, that year running from the preceding April.

Peregrinus himself gives the Edict’s chronological notices as follows: “in the eighth year of his reign, in the twelfth indiction”—without doubt “second” should be read—“in the month of November,” extended, namely, to the Kalends of January, as often elsewhere, “and in the seventy-seventh year after the arrival of King Alboin.”

He agrees that this refers to November 644. But according to the preceding calculations, Rothari’s eighth year would have begun in November of the preceding year, 642, and Rothari’s death would belong to the year 652, since Peregrinus admits that he reigned sixteen years and four months.

In determining the years of Rodoald’s and Aripert’s reigns, Sigonio departs from Paul and presents Rothari’s Edict with chronological notices that conflict with Paul’s history. I have thought it worthwhile to note this, lest we appear to be swayed by partisan interests.

The reasoning presented makes it impossible to separate Rodoald’s reign from his father’s. While Rodoald was reigning, therefore, the events reported by Paul occurred—events that might otherwise appear to have taken place after Rothari’s death.

I nevertheless believe that Rodoald reigned several months after his father, at the time when he married Gondiberg, who, accused of adultery, was acquitted in a duel by Carellus; after her husband was killed, she built the basilica of Saint John the Baptist at Ticinum. Rodoald should therefore be understood to have died around September of that same year, 654.

Aripert begins to reign around September 654.

Peregrinus records all these events accurately under their proper years. But if he had applied the calculations while confusing the era of the Lombards’ entry into Italy with the era of the kingdom, he would have anticipated everything by at least one year. For:

Aripert would have begun to reign in the final months of 652.

He dies toward the end of 661, with the eighth year of his reign in progress.

He would have died in 659.

Bertarid and Godepert, his sons, succeed him at the same time.

One year and three months after Aripert’s death, Grimoald, duke of Beneventum, seizes the kingdom, namely in the first months of 663.

Grimoald would have begun to reign in the first months of 662.

In the sixth year of his reign, in July, in the eleventh indiction, Grimoald enlarges Rothari’s Edict, namely in 668. He dies in 671.

He would have supplemented the Edict in 667.

He would have died around 669.

There can be no doubt about the year in which Grimoald began to reign, since Peregrinus himself acknowledges that Rothari’s Edict was supplemented in 668, on the basis of the notes inscribed in the laws of the Lombards in the Basel edition of 1557—namely, in Grimoald’s sixth year, in July, in the eleventh indiction.

## V. Conclusion concerning the two eras

I have thought it worthwhile to make these observations so that it might be recognized that Paul was correctly understood by Sigonio and that the twofold era was properly established. If this distinction is neglected, the years of Rothari and Grimoald cannot be correctly established. Because the chronological notices preserved in the laws of the Lombards leave no room for doubt, the intervals which Paul assigns to the preceding kings must be extended, although Peregrinus had said that he did not wish to depart from them.

Certainly Landulf cannot be understood otherwise than on the assumption that the two eras have been established and accepted, when he says:

> “In the year 568, in the first indiction, on the Kalends of April, the Lombards departed from Pannonia; in the second they began to plunder in Italy; in the third they established their dominion.”

These observations concern roughly the matters which our author relates from secular history in the Life of Peter the Elder. In the Life of John, whose beginning and end of tenure we have already established above, he did not mix in any of these matters.

Nevertheless, events concerning John’s age are mentioned below in the Life of Marinianus: namely, the destruction of the monastery at Cassino by the Lombards. We shall add something about this shortly.

# CHAPTER IV. Marinianus sits in the Roman council of 595. The year of Gregory the Great’s death. Rubeus corrected

## I. The date of Marinianus’s episcopate

Having established the chronology of Peter the Elder and John, bishops of Ravenna, we must now clarify the time during which Marinianus held the see.

On 11 January 595, after a comet had been visible for a considerable time, as our author reports from Paul, book IV, chapter 11, John died. Agnellus nowhere says on what day Marinianus was elected or ordained, when he died, or how long he held the episcopate. He records only that Marinianus departed this life on the tenth day before the Kalends of November.

Nevertheless, it is established that Marinianus occupied the episcopal see on 5 July of that same year, 595, at the synod held at Rome by Gregory the Great, for he is the first of all the bishops to subscribe.

The following date is given:

> “In the perpetual reign of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the time of the most pious and serene lords Maurice, Tiberius, and Theodosius, Augusti, in the thirteenth year of the same lord, the emperor Maurice, in the thirteenth indiction, on the fifth day of the month of July, Gregory the pope, and so forth.”

We learn that a considerable interval elapsed between John’s death and Marinianus’s consecration from the fact that the election was changed twice, although an order had originally been issued by the exarch residing at Ravenna. Gregory’s letter 89 in book IV, addressed to Andrew the scholasticus, demonstrates this.

In it the pontiff says that, at the command of the exarch Donatus, the archdeacon had been presented for ordination. John the presbyter was then presented. He says that he refused to consecrate the first because he had found many reprehensible matters in his conduct, and the second because he did not know the psalms.

Thereupon the people of Ravenna, by common and unanimous vote, elected Marinianus, who had formerly lived for a long time in the monastery together with Gregory himself and who was a presbyter. Although he resisted, he was ordained.

Since the letter just mentioned is placed in the *Register* immediately after the synod, it seems to follow that Marinianus sat in the synod immediately after his ordination and therefore that his ordination belongs to the first days of July.

As for Marinianus’s death, Agnellus appears to record it in the same year in which the death of Gregory the Great occurred. For, after narrating Gregory’s death, he immediately adds:

> “Therefore, as we have said, this most blessed man died on the tenth day before the Kalends of November.”

He had said nothing previously about Marinianus’s death. Thus the Greek expression τὸ “as we have said” has the same meaning as “in the year which we have mentioned.”

He narrates Gregory the Great’s death in almost the same words as Paul, book IV, chapter 30, namely, in the second year of the emperor Phocas, in the eighth indiction, that is, in 605.

But if Phocas’s second year was running when Gregory died, and if he died on 12 March, the eighth indiction was not running, but the seventh, as John the Deacon and Bede state. Baronius rightly corrected Paul on this point under the year 604.

Marinianus therefore must have died in the eighth indiction, which had already begun in the preceding September of 604, while Phocas’s second year was still in progress and would not end until 25 November of the following year. I say that he died on 23 October, as our author reports.

## II. Rubeus’s calculation corrected

Rubeus, who assigns Marinianus’s death to the year 606, offers nothing that would move me from my opinion. Yet he is inconsistent both with himself and with the truth when he says that Marinianus held the see for eleven years and one month and died, as Agnellus says, on the tenth day before the Kalends of November.

If these statements are accepted, Marinianus’s consecration would fall on 23 September, a Friday, with the solar cycle at 26 and Sunday letter C—almost three months after the Roman synod to which Rubeus himself noted that Marinianus had subscribed, on page 189.

Furthermore, there are letters numbered 89 in book IV, addressed to Andrew the scholasticus, and 98, addressed to Marinianus himself. Since they are dated in the thirteenth indiction, they prove that his consecration cannot in any way be transferred to September, when the fourteenth indiction began.

The period of Marinianus’s episcopate has therefore been wrongly calculated by Rubeus, and there is no reason for me to depart from the conclusions discussed above.

Gregory the Great’s final letters to Marinianus, who was suffering from spitting blood, were written in the sixth indiction. It therefore seems consistent that Marinianus survived Gregory by only a few months and died in the eighth indiction.

He consequently held the see for nine years and nearly four months.

# CHAPTER V. The inguinal plague. Again concerning Alboin’s era. Battles among the Frankish kings. When the monastery of Cassino was destroyed. The daughter of King Agilulf captured by Gallinicus. Her restoration around the time of Marinianus’s death

## I. The plague

Agnellus here includes several matters belonging to secular history, taken for the most part from Paul. It must be considered whether all of them should be assigned to Marinianus’s time.

The inguinal plague, which first filled Rome with funerals when Gregory began to hold the see after Pelagius had died of the same disease, and which then spread throughout Italy, Gaul, and Spain, afflicted Ravenna and the coastal regions after Marinianus’s ordination, and afterward Verona.

Similarly, Paul the Deacon, book IV, chapter 15, after narrating in the preceding chapter the death of John, bishop of Ravenna, says:

> “Afterward, a very severe pestilence again devastated Ravenna and those who lived along the coast. In the following year, a severe mortality also consumed the population of Verona.”

Baronius, speaking of this plague under the year 590 and assigning Authari’s death to September of that same year, overturns his own position that Alboin’s death should be assigned to 571.

For since it is established from Paul that Cleph reigned for one year and a half after Alboin, that the Lombards then remained under dukes for ten years, and finally that Authari ruled for six years, the sum of the years amounts to seventeen years and six months. Added to the year 571, these bring Authari’s death to after Easter, or to September 588, although Baronius himself says that he died in the aforementioned year 590.

## II. The wars among the Franks

Several years after Marinianus’s ordination, war was waged among the Frankish kings Theudebert and Theodoric, who were brothers, and their paternal uncle Chlothar.

But our author here speaks of the earlier conflict between Theudebert and his paternal uncle Chlothar. Paul discusses this in book IV, chapter 4. On that occasion, as our author does, he mentions meteorological phenomena.

The appendix to Gregory of Tours, chapters 19 and 20, and Regino, book III, chapters 87 and 88, compare these phenomena with the later battles between the two brothers and their uncle, whom Paul wrongly calls their father.

Camillus Peregrinus had noted these matters in his *Chronology of the Beneventan Dukes*; they shed light on this passage of Agnellus.

Aimoinus also narrates the later war in book III, chapter 87 of his *Deeds of the Franks*. When the dates are calculated, it belongs to the year 603, which preceded the year in which Marinianus died.

## III. The destruction and restoration of the monastery of Cassino

Learned writers have made a celebrated effort to reconcile Paul the Deacon with Leo of Ostia, and Leo of Ostia with himself, concerning the Lombards’ destruction of the monastery of Cassino and the interval between its desolation and its restoration through Petronax’s work.

Our author, who copies Paul, follows Paul and appears to place the destruction of the monastery around the final year of Marinianus. Yet I believe it cannot be disputed that, while Pelagius was pope, the monks of the monastery of Cassino moved to Rome and obtained a monastery near the Lateran.

This is stated both by Leo of Ostia, *Chronicle of Cassino*, book I, chapter 2, and by Anastasius the Librarian in the Life of Pelagius.

Leo’s words are:

> “The brothers went to Rome … and, with the permission of the Roman pontiff Pelagius, who was then presiding over the apostolic see, they built a monastery beside the Lateran patriarchate; and there they lived for one hundred and thirty years, for as long as the monastery of Cassino remained destroyed.”

Anastasius says:

> “The brothers, fleeing from the monastery, went to Rome … and, with the permission of Saint Pelagius II and of the emperor Tiberius Maurice, they built a monastery beside the Lateran patriarchate.”

Camillus Peregrinus, so often praised, was the first to demonstrate that Petronax lived at Cassino in the restored monastery in the year 720, on the basis of Saint Willibald’s itinerary.

The monastery was therefore restored shortly after the ordination of Pope Gregory II, who began to hold the see in 714. These facts are clear.

But how did it happen that Leo, who in the passage cited counts 130 years from the destruction to the restoration of the monastery, appears in the preface to his *Chronicle* to follow Paul’s opinion by counting only 110 years?

Adrevaldus of Fleury, in book I, chapter 113 of *The Miracles of Saint Benedict*, and the Abbot of Ursperg in his *Chronicle* also adopted the shorter number of years of desolation.

Camillus Peregrinus, a man of keen judgment, in his list of the abbots of Cassino, believes that the altered number should not be attributed to Leo of Ostia, but either to Peter the Deacon or to another writer who, as elsewhere, substituted 110 in the preface on the basis of Paul the Deacon.

Angelo de Nuce, in his dissertation on chapter 2 of Leo’s *Chronicle*, and Bollandus, in the *Acts of the Saints* under 13 February, pages 695 and following, retrace Peregrinus’s steps.

Bollandus, however, places Saint Willibald’s arrival later, under Pope Gregory III. Nuce maintains that the monastery began to be repaired while Gregory II was seated, around the year 718, and that the years of its desolation must be counted backward, bringing one to the year of its destruction, 688 or 689.

He believes that Leo consistently wrote 130 years of desolation, as he thinks can be shown from the corresponding passages of the same *Chronicle*, but that Peter the Deacon, following Paul’s calculation, substituted 110 for 130 in the preface.

I consider these conclusions properly established. But did Paul the Deacon, who was close in time to those events, err by nearly twenty years in reporting the true period of the monastery’s desolation? This is the common opinion.

Yet we may observe that Paul did not calculate the 110 years from the destruction of the monastery, but from the time when “that place began to be deprived of human habitation.” These are his words in book VI, chapter 40.

The monastery’s destruction and plundering may therefore have occurred in 589, causing the monks to flee; but perhaps one or two years later some of them returned and lived there for a time, until finally they were compelled to leave altogether around 604. Thus nearly 110 years would have elapsed by the time the monastery was restored under Gregory II.

But, to confess what I think, I am not at all satisfied with this explanation. Paul himself acknowledges that during the intervening period “some simple men remained” at Cassino, whom Petronax found when he arrived. Therefore, by “human habitation” he means the monastery itself.

The monastery had been destroyed and plundered by the Lombards, while the monks, unharmed, fled according to the prediction of the holy Father. Gregory the Great testifies to this in *Dialogues*, book II, chapter 17:

> “Theopropus then heard his voice, but we see its fulfillment, for we know that his monastery, now destroyed by the Lombard nation…”

These words, together with what follows, clearly establish that the monastery was destroyed around the final year of Pope Pelagius.

## IV. The capture and restoration of Agilulf’s daughter

The events that follow concern the capture of King Agilulf’s daughter at Parma by the exarch Gallinicus, who broke the truce, and her removal to Ravenna. Sigonio assigns them to the year 601.

Paul, book IV, chapter 21, says:

> “In those days the daughter of King Agilulf, together with her husband, named Godescalc, was captured from the city of Parma by the army of Gallinicus the patrician, and they were led to the city of the Ravennates.”

In chapter 29 he relates that Cremona, Mantua, Padua, and other places were conquered because of this. Our author indicates that these events belong to the beginning of Phocas’s reign, while Saint Gregory and Marinianus were still alive.

Smaragdus had left the exarchate in 597, and Gallinicus had succeeded him. After Gallinicus was removed—or recalled by the emperor, as our author says, because of the rash act by which he had recklessly provoked the Lombards, according to Sigonio—Smaragdus again became exarch.

Under Smaragdus, after Gregory the Great had died and in the same month in which Marinianus died, the king’s daughter was restored and a truce was made until the following April.

This is clear from Paul, who in book IV, chapter 29, says:

> “The king’s daughter was restored by Smaragdus, and peace was made in month 10”—I understand November—“until the Kalends of April, in the eighth indiction.”

This peace, or truce, belongs to November 604.

# CHAPTER VI. Two bishops named John. The years of both bishops. Agnellus supplemented from Paul. The secular matters related by Agnellus examined

## I. The two bishops named John

After Marinianus, two bishops of Ravenna appear with the same name. Rubeus therefore thought that they should be joined into one. Yet nothing in what moved Rubeus induces me to abandon the distinction between them.

I can readily believe that several persons bearing the same name have elsewhere been combined into one; it is more difficult to believe that one person has been divided into several. Agnellus distinguishes one John from the other and defines the duration of each episcopate by exact years, months, and days.

It is incredible that a writer who elsewhere says nothing about such periods invented this here arbitrarily.

In the Life of the second John, Agnellus does indeed confuse the chronology and reports many events that ought to be assigned to the earlier John’s time. But this is not important enough to make us abandon our conclusion, since he repeatedly neglects chronology in these matters—not only here, but elsewhere—and in the Life of one bishop often relates events belonging to the Life of another.

## II. The duration of John’s episcopates

The first John’s episcopate is therefore said to have lasted five years, ten months, and eighteen days.

He could not have been ordained except around the beginning of 605, since we have established that Marinianus died on 23 October of the preceding year, 604. John therefore died around September 610.

The second John is said to have held the see for eighteen years, six months, and eight days. He may therefore be believed to have died around July of 629 or 630.

Carlo Sigonio disagrees, saying that the second John succeeded the first in 618, in book II of *The Kingdom of Italy*. But I must not depart from Agnellus’s meaning without the testimony of an older witness, especially since Sigonio himself often goes astray in assigning the dates of other bishops of Ravenna.

## III. Agnellus supplemented from Paul

To bring the events narrated in the Life of the later John into chronological calculation, we must first observe that Agnellus transcribed here, with only slight changes, material from Paul the Deacon. Two passages, however, were mutilated by the copyist and must be supplemented from Paul, book IV, chapter 37.

The first passage occurs where certain events concerning the time of Phocas’s accession are narrated. The number of years of his reign is missing, and the passage must therefore be restored as follows:

> “Therefore, as we have said, Phocas, after killing Maurice and his sons and invading the rule of the Romans, held the principate for the course of eight years.”

The second passage is mutilated where the disturbances of the Greens and Blues are narrated. What is missing is the distinction between the event itself and the Persians, on the one hand, and the Greens and Blues, on the other.

When the missing words are supplied from Paul, the complete sense should be restored in this manner:

> “Meanwhile war was stirred up in the regions of the East and of Egypt. The Greens and the Blues, inflicting the most grievous slaughter upon one another in civil conflict,” hurled each other down in mutual killing. “The Persians too, waging the most serious wars against the commonwealth, devastated many Roman provinces, even Jerusalem itself, and so forth.”

## IV

Having supplied what was lacking in Agnellus, we must determine whether the matters he relates belong to the time of the earlier John or of the second John as bishop.

After recounting the death of Saint Gregory, and stating that in the summer of that same year, in July, Adaloald was hailed as king at Milan in the presence of his father Agilulf, and that the daughter of King Theudebert was betrothed to him and peace was established with the Franks, Paul adds little else and continues:

> “Finally, in the following month of November, King Agilulf made peace with the patrician Smaragdus for one year, receiving twelve thousand solidi from the Romans.”

But if, as was observed above, a truce was made in November 604 until the following Easter, or somewhat later, either that truce was extended for one year, or this later truce was made in November of the following year, 605, with the agreed payment of money. The latter is perhaps more likely, for in the following year, after the truce—namely, at the next Easter—the king’s bathhouse and the old city were invaded by the Langobards. Nevertheless, in the following April and May peace was again concluded between the Langobards and the Romans for three years. These events, therefore, belong to the time of the earlier John.

The incursion of John Consinus into Naples belongs to the time of Heraclius. Anastasius will shed light on these matters. In the Life of Pope Deusdedit he writes:

> “At that time the patrician and chamberlain Eleutherius came to Ravenna and killed all those who had been involved in the death of John the exarch and judge [others: ‘of the judges’] of the republic. He came to Rome and was received by the most holy Pope Deusdedit, very favorably [others: ‘very favorably’]. The pope, having gone out from Rome, came to Naples, which was held by John Compsinus [or Consinus], being under siege [perhaps *arctata*, ‘hard-pressed’]. The patrician Eleutherius entered Naples by force and killed the tyrant. He then returned to Ravenna, and when a military donative had been given to the soldiers, peace was made throughout Italy.”

Again, in the Life of Boniface:

> “At that time, before the days of his ordination, the patrician and eunuch exarch Eleutherius entered and assumed the kingdom. When he came to the Roman city, he was killed by the soldiers of Ravenna in the fortress called Luceolis. His head was carried to Constantinople to the most pious emperor.”

The more probable calculations place the beginning of Deusdedit’s pontificate in the first days of January 616, and the ordination of Boniface V in April 620. It follows that the killing of John the exarch took place in 615; that in the following year, 616, Eleutherius punished the men who had killed John at Ravenna; that from there, after several months, he went from Rome to Naples, where he extinguished the tyranny of John Consinus; and finally that, before April 620, Eleutherius himself was killed at the fortress of Luceolis.

All these events, therefore, belong to the time of the later John. What follows in Paul and Agnellus plainly belongs to the earlier period; indeed, some events occurred while Gregory and Marinianos were still alive, such as the slaughter of Maurice and his sons and the beginning of Phocas’s reign.

It should be noted that Boniface is credited with establishing that the Roman Church should be honored as the head of all the Churches, and with obtaining the dedication to God, in honor of the Blessed Virgin and all the martyrs, of the ancient Roman Pantheon. Yet Anastasius makes it clear that the first measure was undertaken under Boniface III, while the second was granted to Boniface IV.

The remaining events can readily be assigned to their proper periods. There is only one matter whose year I do not know how to determine: namely, the celebrated deed of the later John, who, as the account says, “bought the city of Classis three times from the hostile people, at great expense from the resources of the Church, and redeemed not only the city but also its inhabitants, together with all their suburbs, and redeemed his own achievement.”

Rubeus says that the city was liberated from Saracen incursions; but at that time the Saracens had not yet reached the shores of Ravenna. I rather think that money was paid to the Langobards from the resources of the Church, since it is otherwise known that this people could customarily be appeased with money, as several letters of Gregory the Great show. It is also established that not only did the exarch pay out a vast amount of gold, but that, for the army stationed at Ravenna, there were treasurers who kept money ready for extraordinary expenditures. See Gregory’s Letter 34, indiction 13.

I therefore believe that what is called the Church’s “redemption” was the purchase, three times, of relief from oppression with money, when the property and safety of the citizens were in danger, through the agency of Bishop John. For this reason he should be compared with Gregory the Great and is most worthy of praise.

# THE LIFE OF PETER THE ELDER

### Chapter I

**The repair of the Basilica of Saint Severus begun. Peter ordained at Rome. The people of Ravenna come to meet him with acclamations.**

## Peter the Elder XXVIII

He was advanced in age, senior in understanding, and adorned in body and head with gray hair. He led a holy and gentle life. He was truly Peter, because he built the temple of his body upon a firm rock.

In the time of Symmachus he sat in council near Rome and founded the church of the Blessed Severus, confessor of Christ, in the district called Vicus Salutaris.

[Marginal note: “He founded the church of the Blessed Severus around the year 578. BACCH.”]

[Marginal note: “But, death intervening, he left it unfinished, in the city formerly called Classis.”]

He was consecrated at Rome in the second indiction without a fast, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of October. Returning in peace, he was received by the citizens of Ravenna with extraordinary enthusiasm. The people of Classis, however, came out to meet him at the Ninth Mile.

Then, as they all rejoiced, they sang praises:

> “God has given you to us; may the Divinity preserve you.”

Then boys went before him with songs of praise, so that not only the adults but also the little ones might be endearing.

### Chapter II

**The Langobards enter Italy. Ticinum besieged. The statue of Theodoric that had stood at Ravenna is described. Charlemagne carries it away to Aachen.**

In that year Venetia was occupied and invaded by the Langobards, who were expelled without a battle.

In the fifth year of the emperor Justin II there was pestilence among cattle and death everywhere. Afterwards, having ravaged Tuscia, the Langobards besieged Ticinum, the city called Papia, where Theodoric built a palace. There I clearly saw, in the chambers of the tribunal, his image seated upon a horse, executed in ornamented mosaic.

There was also a similar image in the palace that he himself built, in the tribunal of the dining hall called “at the Sea,” above the gate, and on the façade of the royal palace called “at Calchi” in that city. There was the first gate of the palace, at a place called Sicrestum, where the church of the Savior appears to have stood.

At the pinnacle of that place was an image of Theodoric, wonderfully adorned in mosaic, holding a spear in his right hand and a shield in his left and dressed in armor. Around the shield stood Rome, executed in mosaic, with spear and helmet. Ravenna, holding the weapon, was depicted in mosaic with her right foot upon the sea and her left upon the land, hastening toward the king.

Wretched city! She suffered envy on every side.

The citizens, among themselves, with the greatest zeal ...

[Marginal note: “Some material is missing here. BACCH.”]

... before their eyes a pyramid of square stones, six cubits or so in height, and a base. Above it stood a bronze horse covered with yellow-gold plating, and its rider, King Theodoric, carried a shield on his left shoulder and held a spear with his right arm raised.

From the horse’s open nostrils and mouth birds emerged, and in its belly they built nests. Who could ever have seen anything like it? Whoever does not believe it should travel to Francia, and he will see it.

Others say that the aforesaid horse had been made out of love for the emperor Zeno. Zeno was an Isaurian by nationality, and because of his extraordinary agility [or speed] of foot the emperor Leo took him as his son-in-law and granted him the highest honor at the imperial court.

This man had no kneecaps, and he ran so powerfully that, once he had begun running, he could overtake chariots on foot. After the death of his son, who had succeeded his grandfather Leo in the kingdom, this Zeno was made emperor. He ruled the peoples for sixteen years.

For his sake that most excellent horse was made of bronze and adorned with gold; but Theodoric decorated it with his own name.

Now, nearly thirty-eight years ago, when King Charles of the Franks had subjected all the kingdoms and had received the imperial dignity of the Romans from Pope Leo III, after taking an oath at the body of Saint Peter, he returned to Francia. Entering Ravenna and seeing this most beautiful image—which, as he himself testified, he had nowhere seen equaled—he had it transported to Francia and set it up in his palace called Aachen.

### Chapter III

**Italy is laid waste. Ravenna is thrown into alarm. Narses dies after destroying the glory of the Romans.**

Let us return to the ancient history said by some to have occurred in the time of this bishop Peter.

At that time, after the foundation of the church had been laid, all Italy was shaken by the greatest affliction. In those days, at Caesarea near Ravenna, a stockade [variant: an abundance of stakes] was constructed by the prefect Longinus in the form of a wall, out of fear of the people. Then the Roman senate gradually declined, and afterwards Roman liberty was taken away with triumph.

From the time when Basil was serving as consul until the time of the patrician Narses, the Roman provincials were reduced to nothing. After this the Langobards went forth and crossed Tuscia as far as Rome. Setting fire to the perforated rock, they burned it completely.

The aforesaid Langobards built Forum Cornelii, and the city was completed by them.

In those days the people of the Avars arose, and they came into Pannonia. The patrician Narses died at Rome. After winning many victories in Italy, with all the Romans stripped bare, he rested in the palace of Italy. He died in the ninety-fifth year of his life.

### Chapter IV

**Alboin is slain through the agency of his wife Rosmunda. Rosmunda is honorably received at Ravenna by Longinus. She dies there by poison. The death and tomb of Bishop Peter.**

Accordingly, in the sixth year of the reign of Justin II, the grandson of Justinian, Alboin, king of the Langobards, was killed by his own men in his palace at the command of his wife Rosmunda, on the fourth day before the Kalends of July.

I will not omit the cause of his killing, which we know, but will bring it openly before you, so that you may take warning.

One day, while he was happily passing the hour of the meal, and royal food had been brought to him, and drunkenness from wine had followed, among the other cups he ordered the head of his father-in-law, Rosmunda’s father, to be brought. When it had been brought, he ordered it to be filled to the top with wine, and drank all of it.

All drank together, made merry by the wine. Then the king ordered the cupbearer to fill the head to the top and give it to his wife Rosmunda. The head had been mounted in the finest gold and set with pearls and various precious gems.

When it was offered to her, the king said: “Drink it all.”

As soon as she received it, she groaned, but with a serene expression said: “I will eagerly fulfill my lord’s command.”

After she drank, she returned it to the cupbearer, but doubled her grief in her heart, preserving hardness in her breast.

Let us not wander through many details; let us disclose the killing.

In those days there was a strong man in the king’s palace named Helmegis, who enjoyed intercourse with the queen’s wardrobe attendant. The queen summoned him and urged him to kill the king.

He refused her wish and said: “Far be it from me to raise my hand against my lord the king. You know that he is a very powerful man, and I cannot overcome him.”

She said: “Even if you do it, no one will know.”

He replied: “Certainly this word will never leave my mouth. Get another killer; I will not do it. When you wanted to do this, you should not have joined yourself to him; but once you have become queen, keep faith.”

Then she withdrew, furious, to her chamber and began to consider how she could kill her husband.

Having devised a plan, she summoned her wardrobe attendant and said to her: “Swear to me that you will not betray me or disclose my plan, and whatever I tell you, do it.”

After the woman had promised, as you have heard, the queen said: “My mind is daily overcome by love for this young man who has slept with you. Arrange secretly for him to sleep with you at a certain time, and say to him: ‘Enjoy intercourse quickly, because I am in a hurry and cannot linger.’ I will put on your clothes, which you will place in hiding, so that I will not be recognized.”

One day, when he wished to sleep with the wardrobe attendant as he usually did, she, having been instructed, said: “Unless you come at such-and-such an hour to such-and-such a hidden place, we cannot embrace one another, because, being frequently summoned, I cannot be absent from the queen’s sight.”

He agreed and said: “Let it be so.”

She did as she had been instructed and reported all these words to the queen.

When the appointed hour had grown dark, Rosmunda put on the clothes of her servant girl and stood in the place where the iniquity was to be completed.

When he came and had begun to kiss her, she said to him in a subdued and gentle voice: “It is already time; I will return to my mistress, lest the trouble already sought should increase for me.”

Then he remained with her in the same place, and she lay down. After the crime had been completed, she said to him: “Who am I?”

He replied: “The queen’s wardrobe attendant.”

She answered: “Am I not Queen Rosmunda? Did I not tell you that what you refused to do willingly, I would force you to do unwillingly?”

When he realized that she was the queen, he began to weep and say: “Alas for me! Why have you brought this sin upon me? Why have you killed me without any sword? Who has ever polluted the king’s bed or violated a queen as I, wretched man, have done?”

Then she began to speak consoling words and said: “Be silent. This has been done for your salvation. Yet such a dispute has arisen between you and King Alboin that either you will punish him or he will cut you down with his sword. Before this becomes known, attack him first. When the day is suitable, I will send for you; come to the appointed place and kill him.”

One day, after a royal meal had been prepared, the king enjoyed himself as the banquet continued, and, urged on by his wife, drank as much wine as he had ever drunk in his life.

After he withdrew to his bed, Rosmunda entered and began to part the king’s hair from side to side and stroke his scalp with her fingernails, as though it gave him pleasure.

Suddenly overcome by sleep and compelled by the wine, he touched her two or three times to determine whether perhaps he was not sunk in heavy slumber, and sent for his accomplice in the crime to come quickly.

Then she removed the double-edged sword that lay at his head and that he used at the king’s side—the weapon we call a *spatha*—and tied it firmly beside the headboard of the bed with the same strap by which the king girded his loins and which was fastened into the scabbard.

When the killer came, wishing to escape such a crime and not lay his hand upon the king, she reproached him, saying that if he claimed that he was weak and lacked the strength to kill him, she herself would extend her hand.

“Only say that you are weak in courage,” she said, “and now you will see what the weaker sex can do.”

This dispute between them lasted almost an hour. When it became burdensome to her, and she was forcing him to kill the king, she added:

“The sword whose power you fear most is wrapped up and firmly tied.”

He replied: “You know that he is a warrior, strong in bodily strength and extremely powerful in his hands. He has won many wars, subdued very many men, overthrown the camps of his enemies, and, after devastating them, joined the cities of one people to the territory of another. He who has shaken all these things without fear of anyone else—how can I alone cut his throat?”

Then she said sadly: “You cannot charge me with any crime. Remember the crime you committed. If he is exposed, you will die; for everyone except the king loves me. If anyone learns of this deed, I will have you secretly killed.”

At these words he was perplexed, but entered the chamber where the king lay, partly recovered from the wine. He approached the king’s bed and drew the sword in order to kill him.

The king, sensing this, awoke and rose from sleep. He wished to draw his sword, but could not, because it had been firmly tied by his wife’s hands.

Then, taking the footstool on which he usually rested his feet, he used it as a shield and defended himself as best he could. He shouted, but no one was there to hear, because, at his wife’s command, all the palace doors had been closed, ostensibly so that the king might rest.

The king was overcome and killed.

The Langobards wished to kill the murderer and the queen with him, but, when the plan became known, she went to Verona until the fury of the people should subside.

But the Langobards angrily quarreled against her. After plundering the palace, she came with a multitude of Gepids and Langobards to Ravenna in the month of August and was honorably received by the prefect Longinus with all the royal treasure.

After several days the aforesaid man sent word to her, saying:

“If she is joined to my affection, if she wishes to cleave to my side and unite herself with me in marriage, she will be greater than she is now as queen. Is it not better for her to hold the kingdom and sovereignty of all Italy than to lose this and forfeit the kingdom?”

She sent him word, saying: “If he wishes it, it can be done within a few days.”

One day, when she had ordered a bath to be prepared, and the man who had killed her husband had entered the bath, after he came out, while the heat of his body was still intense, Rosmunda brought him a cup full of drink, supposedly for the king’s use; it had been mixed with poison.

He took the small vessel from her hand and began to drink. But when he realized that the drink was deadly, he moved the cup away from his mouth and gave it to the queen, saying: “Drink with me.”

She refused. He drew his sword, stood over her, and said: “If you do not drink from this, I will strike you.”

Willingly or unwillingly, she drank, and they died in that same hour.

Then the prefect Longinus took away all the treasures of the Langobards and all the royal wealth that Rosmunda had brought from the kingdom of the Langobards, together with the daughter of Rosmunda and King Alboin, and sent them to the emperor Justin at Constantinople. The emperor rejoiced and greatly rewarded the prefect.

[Marginal note: “The author’s admonitions.”]

Therefore, all you men who are married, flatter your wives, lest you suffer worse things than this man did. Mitigate their fury, and keep silent during quarrels.

There are men who say: “Whatever I command will stand; whatever you say will not happen.” If you inflame her, you will turn her against yourself. “I care nothing about it. I cannot believe you did not taste such a cup, but that out of shame and embarrassment you kept silent and were ashamed before another.”

Then you immediately say: “That woman is my wife, the one for whom you mock me and make sport of me. She does not seek harm for my household; she keeps my affairs well, and I approve of her management.” You cannot say otherwise except in peaceful words.

But if the wife does not hear this, the husband, inflamed and quarreling for a long time, becomes perplexed and wanders here and there in fear of his wife.

This man, who obtained the kingdom, crushed his enemies, won battles, laid cities waste, shed blood, overthrew towns, and humbled his foes—see how gently he was killed, and how his body was struck with wounds.

What man could devise such a destructive plan? What a malicious mind!

There are some who will not even receive a friend or relative into their house without their wife’s consent, because the wife holds primacy over the husband. Willing or unwilling, they obey the woman’s will.

In crime, consider the Egyptian woman; in falsehood, Jezebel; in sedition, Delilah; in death, Jael; in contempt for her husband, Vashti; in merriment, Herodias; in fury, the woman of Shunem; in anger, the maidservant who was doorkeeper to the ruler.

I tell you this because we have found many such men, and have especially mocked and grieved over them.

Brothers, we are human beings; we fall like grass. But if we can, before death comes, let there be no evil reputation in us, for your holy preachers taught this, and with them the great Bishop Peter, in whose time these events occurred.

He died in a good old age on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of September and was buried, as some assert, in the *ardica* of the Blessed Probus the confessor in the city formerly called Classis.

He was placed in a great stone sarcophagus there beside the church of the Blessed Euphemia, called “at the Sea,” which the pontiff Maximianus wonderfully adorned with various mosaics. It has now been demolished.

Afterwards the sarcophagus itself was torn out and placed elsewhere.

He sat for eight years, two months, and nineteen days.

# OBSERVATIONS ON THE LIFE OF PETER THE ELDER

**The ordination of Peter the Elder without a fast. Statues erected for Theodoric. What is meant by the name Venetia. The history of Alboin’s murder differs in certain respects from Paul’s account.**

## I

We noted above that Peter’s ordination, which Agnellus says took place “without a fast,” must be understood as having occurred before the fast of the seventh month was imminent.

After Morinus, Menardus, and others, our celebrated Mabillon published two Roman Ordines concerning sacred ordinations, in which, he says, many matters relevant to this subject are contained; he is an excellent judge of such matters.

In the first, it is noteworthy that the ordination of bishops is assigned to Sunday, in the words: “on another day, which is Sunday,” and so forth. In the second, it is moved back to the preceding night, even outside the customary times of the lower orders, in the words: “Bishops, however, may be blessed at any time, but now it is customary for them to be blessed at night.”

From this I do not know whether one should rightly argue that the later Ordo is more recent than the earlier, or whether episcopal ordinations were conducted in different ways while preserving the tradition mentioned by Leo the Great: that ordinations should take place “on Saturday evening, which dawns into the first day of the Sabbath, or on the Sunday itself.”

At least this is certain: even in Leo’s time bishops were ordained on the night preceding Sunday. Leo himself shows that the Saturday fast—which is otherwise known to have been extremely ancient in the Roman Church—was to be taken into account in ordinations, in Letter 12 of the Quesnellian edition, at the passage cited by Mabillon in his commentary, chapter 16.

But I think this applies above all to the ordinations of the others, which took place during the times of fasting. I believe that bishops were ordained either on Saturday evening or on the morning of the following Sunday, even when Saturday was not observed as a fast.

That this practice prevailed certainly in the time of this Peter is shown by this passage of Agnellus.

## II

Our author praises the statues erected for King Theodoric at Ticinum and Ravenna and relates what was commonly said about the emperor Zeno, to whom the honor of an equestrian statue at Ravenna was first attributed.

Suidas says that in the time of Leo, who succeeded Marcian, a certain Indacus flourished, possessing such swiftness of foot that he covered a long distance by running in an extremely short number of hours, so rapidly that he could ascend and descend the steep slopes of mountains with great speed.

I think that the popular rumor arose from this, namely, that the same distinction was attributed to Zeno, whom Leo therefore took as his son-in-law, and who, as our author says, lacked “the kneecaps.”

This is certainly an amusing explanation of the fastest possible running, which even less capable osteologists will admit with laughter, since, if those bones are missing, a man would become unfit for running.

Agnellus adds here that the statue was taken away from Ravenna by Charlemagne thirty-eight years before he wrote this, after Charlemagne had been inaugurated as the new emperor at Rome by Pope Leo III. From this I have determined, in the material prefixed to the poems of the entire work, the period in which Agnellus was writing.

## III

What he says about Venetia being occupied and invaded by the Langobards must be understood not of the famous city of the Venetians but of the region of the Venetians.

Agnellus learned this from no source other than Paul the Deacon. Paul writes in Book II, chapter 14:

> “Accordingly, Alboin captured Vicenza, Verona, and the remaining cities of Venetia, except Padua, Monselice, and Mantua. For Venetia does not consist only of the small islands that we now call the Venetias, but its boundary extends from the borders of Pannonia to the river Adda. This is proved by the annalistic books, in which Bergamo is said to be a city of Venetia. For in histories we also read the following about Lake Benacus: ‘Benacus, a lake of Venetia, from which the river Mincius flows.’”

The name Venetia therefore signifies a region, not a city.

This city, situated among lagoons, was able to withstand the first assault of the Langobards more easily than Padua, Monselice, and Mantua.

What follows—“They were expelled without a battle”—does not in any way fit the historical account, unless it is applied to those cities of the Venetian region that Paul says were spared from the incursions of the Langobards.

## IV

Our author relates the history of Alboin’s murder through his wife’s treachery somewhat differently from Paul’s account, which he committed to memory in Book II, chapter 28.

There it is related that Rosmunda plotted to overthrow the king with Helmigis, the king’s *schilpor*, or armiger, who advised Rosmunda to employ Peredeus, a powerful man, in carrying out the deed.

When the queen had arranged this, Peredeus is said to have denied that he would commit so great a crime. Therefore she secretly slept with him while disguised as the wardrobe attendant, and by this means compelled him to carry out the king’s murder.

Paul himself then says that Helmigis acted as Rosmunda’s husband until both of them died at Ravenna after taking poison.

Our author relates everything about Helmigis and says nothing at all about Peredeus. It is indeed strange if Peredeus, who had slept with the queen and had committed a great crime for that reason, patiently tolerated Helmigis’s being preferred to him.

One thing seems certain to me in this matter: Agnellus derived the history of this deed from a source other than Paul. He also assigns Alboin’s death to a precise day, namely the fourth day before the Kalends of July, and states that Rosmunda and Helmigis arrived at Ravenna in the month of August. Paul is silent about this, although it is highly useful for establishing the time when Alboin first began to reign.

# THE LIFE OF JOHN THE ROMAN

### Sole Chapter

**John’s birthplace. The Basilica of Saint Severus completed and the body of Saint Severus transferred. John’s death. His tomb and epitaph at the oratory of Saints Mark, Marcellinus, and Felicula.**

## John the Roman XXIX

John is interpreted as “the grace of God.”

He was not of this flock but was Roman by nationality. He was of medium height, neither particularly tall nor short. He had an excellent physique, being neither thin nor very fat. His hair was curly, mixed with gray.

After the death of the Blessed Peter, John completed the unfinished work that Peter had left behind—namely, the church of the Blessed Severus, confessor—and brought it to completion. In the middle of the church he dedicated the body of the Blessed Severus the confessor and adorned it with extraordinary magnificence.

He took the holy body from the monastery of Saint Rophilus, which was supported alongside that church on the side reserved for men, and placed it in the middle of the church.

In the time of this John, in the month of January, a comet appeared in the morning and evening. In that same month the aforesaid pontiff died, and the star disappeared.

As I have said, he was born at Rome. Sent from that same see, he earnestly preached the teaching of the Apostle and urged everyone to turn away from sin.

After this most blessed John died on the eleventh day of January, he was buried in the church of the Blessed Apollinaris of the city of Classis, outside the walls, in the monastery of Saints Mark, Marcellus, and Felicula. He himself had built it from its foundations, adorned it with mosaics, and completed everything.

Above the doors of the said monastery you will find verses in meter, containing the following:

> The illustrious thresholds of the saints shine forth in the temple  
>   
> Of Mark, Marcellinus, and Felicula together.  
>   
> Rome gave these pontiffs their beginning; this woman is held a martyr;  
>   
> Pope Gregory grants the relics of these saints.  
>   
> The bishop John, seeking them by merit and by spirit,  
>   
> Prepares to return small gifts for great ones.  
>   
> Filled with such power, he established the shrine.  
>   
> From whose auspices its grace is known  
>   
> [Rubricator: “and the work stands.”]  
>   
> He who, in the fourteenth year of the sacred diadem,  
>   
> By watchful administration governs the Church,  
>   
> Also fixed this citadel, ruled by the summit  
>   
> Of reverence [or: reverend dignity], and brought its completion to its appointed end.  
>   
> Suspending the summit suddenly by wondrous art,  
>   
> He restores the bent side from both directions.  
>   
> To these merits fortunate Smaragdus is added for all time,  
>   
> Whose work shares in these inscriptions.

He sat for sixteen years, one month, and nineteen days.

# OBSERVATIONS ON THE LIFE OF JOHN THE ROMAN

**Certain matters concerning the use of the pallium. What were the *mappulae*? Andreas, to whom Saint Gregory’s letter was addressed, was not a bishop. Monks were numerous at Ravenna. The apocrisiarius of the Roman see at Ravenna. Bishop John defended against the charge of schism, against Rubeus, Blondus, and Sigonius. The year in which the church of Saints Mark, Marcellinus, and Felicula was consecrated.**

## I

There are many matters that made the name of this John famous, all of which Rubeus collected carefully and excellently. It is almost astonishing that Agnellus omitted nearly everything: he says nothing about the relationship between them and nothing about the disputes concerning the use of the pallium that took place between John and Gregory the Great.

I have treated this subject briefly in the dissertation on the Origin of the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy and above in the Lives of John Angeloptis and Maximianus, but more fully in the preface. All of it is learned from the Register of Saint Gregory’s letters, from which more recent writers derived their material concerning the use of the pallium, each wishing to support the cause he had once chosen.

I believe the following: since the piety of John and Marinianos is sufficiently established by the letters of the Lord Gregory himself—especially that of Marinianos, whom the same holy pontiff, against his will, transferred from the monastic life and placed over the Church of Ravenna—and since the same question also prevailed in his case, I readily suppose that the pallium had in fact been used by earlier bishops during the Litanies, that is, when they proceeded with clergy and people associated with them to the churches of Ravenna for prayer.

Moved by the religious scruple through which every honorable man protects the dignity of his office, they therefore tried, as far as they were permitted, to retain this praised custom of wearing the pallium.

But Saint Gregory, who, even in the most difficult times, defended the supreme authority of the Roman Church and sought to ensure that one rule of ecclesiastical discipline should prevail throughout the world, found no documents in his archives by which this custom could be defended. He was also informed that it had never been customary among the representatives of the Holy See, and therefore judged that it ought to be prevented.

Yet, so that a right once acquired by another should not be violated, Gregory acted with great and serious moderation.

Indeed, in Book IV, Letter 11, he grants this John permission “until something more precise and reliable is learned, to use the pallium during the solemn Litanies, that is, on the feast of the Nativity of Blessed John the Baptist, of Blessed Peter the Apostle, and of Blessed Apollinaris the Martyr, and at the celebration of the bishop’s ordination.”

For the remaining feasts he prescribes:

> “He should put on the pallium in the secretarium, according to the former custom, after receiving and dismissing the sons of the Church.”

Finally, he himself sent the formula of the oath to be sworn before witnesses, by which the truth might become clear. It is found in Book V, Letter 33, and bears the title:

> “To Castorius the notary, concerning restoring the use of the pallium to Andreas, bishop of Ravenna, according to ancient custom.”

The title “bishop of Ravenna” is inappropriately attached to this Andreas, since no one of that name is known to have held that office in the Church of Ravenna.

In the text of the letter, which was written while Marinianos was bishop, Andreas is adorned by Gregory the Great with the titles “Magnificent” and “Lord.” These titles present him as an illustrious man, but a layman, who had earnestly petitioned Gregory for the restoration of the use of the pallium.

Another dispute also arose concerning the *mappulae*. Since the clergy of Ravenna commonly used them, the Romans, who maintained that their use was permitted only to themselves, sought to prohibit their use by the clergy of Ravenna.

Nevertheless, the most holy pontiff granted that the deacons of the bishop of Ravenna might use *mappulae* when they proceeded with the bishop, and then only as part of their service to him, not at other times.

Lantmeterus notes in Book I of his work *On Clerical Dress*, chapter 18, that these *mappulae* were coverings spread over horses, on which the Roman clergy sat when the pontiff proceeded. Ducange confirms this in his *Latin Glossary*, citing Anastasius’s Life of Constantine.

## II

The friendship that, as we have said, existed between John and Gregory is commended by the gift of the relics of Saints Mark, Marcellinus, and Felicula. Rubeus discusses this at length in Book IV and transcribed from Agnellus the verses placed above the doors of the oratory that John himself built from its foundations and which is called a monastery.

That a monastery of monks stood beside this oratory is established from Book X, Letter 9, addressed to the notary Castorius and cited above. Matters concerning certain things belonging to the legacy or testament left to that monastery were entrusted to Castorius.

It therefore seems that a community of monks was added by John to that oratory, since the letter was written in the fifth indiction, that is, in the year 602, while Marinianos was bishop.

From various letters of Gregory, written for the protection and discipline of these monks, it is also clear that in the time of John and Marinianos there were many monks at Ravenna and several monasteries at Classis.

This gives rise to two things that one cannot help wondering at: first, that two exceptionally pious bishops—one of whom had himself been a monk and the father of monks—were not especially well disposed toward them, so that the most holy pontiff had to admonish and restrain them more than once; and second, that our Agnellus wrote absolutely nothing anywhere in the entire *Book of the Pontiffs* about the monks of Ravenna or Classis.

### III

Since Rubeus has noted many noteworthy matters from the letters of Gregory the Great relating to the Church of Ravenna, I think I must not omit the fact that an apocrisarius of the Holy Roman See resided at Ravenna. This is established most clearly by the aforementioned letter to Castorius, since the following words occur in the formula of the oath:

> “But this I know, and I have learned through my own experience: before the time of John, former bishop of Ravenna, the bishop of Ravenna had the customary use of the pallium in the presence of this or that apocrisarius of the Apostolic See, on this or that day; and I have not learned that he had usurped this secretly or in the absence of the apocrisarius.”

We know from various letters of the same pontiff that, during Gregory’s pontificate, Castorius first and then John, a subdeacon, fulfilled this office. I had conjectured that an apocrisarius of the Holy Roman See began to be sent to Ravenna when the exarchs first exercised there what was virtually the delegated authority of the emperor. But since this concerns testimony to an ancient custom, and the question is not merely whether John or his predecessor Peter had used the pallium, but whether earlier bishops of Ravenna had done so while “that one or that one” apocrisarius was present at Ravenna, it follows from Gregory the Great’s testimony that, according to an ancient practice which had prevailed before the exarchs, the city had been granted the privilege of having an apocrisarius reside there. Why should this custom not have arisen in the time of the Gothic kings?

### IV

For the sake of clearing this John’s reputation of every suspicion, it is worthwhile here to expose and refute the error of the most distinguished Ravenna writer, as well as of Carlo Sigonio in Book I of *On the Kingdom of Italy*, on whom Rubeus seems to have relied too heavily in this matter.

What Paul relates in Book III, chapter 27—and Blondus after Paul—Rubeus improperly understood and asserted in Book IV, page 180, that this John had been the leading example among the bishops of Ravenna who suffered from insolent pride. He says that he is reporting not merely Paul’s opinion but that of most writers who believed that John was the first of all the bishops of Ravenna to withdraw from the obedience owed to the Roman pontiff, “and who openly attempted this, having brought many bishops of the cities of Italy over to his position.

> “But while he was testing this course upon Severus, bishop of Aquileia, and entertaining no doubtful hope that he would easily obtain everything from him, since he was his fellow citizen and was thought to desire the dignity of his homeland, he found, contrary to what he had expected, that Severus absolutely refused; nor could he be persuaded by any arguments to perpetrate so impious a deed against divine law and against the Roman Church itself, the mother and teacher of all the Churches.”

He then says that, after force had been applied by Smaragdus, Severus was dragged to Ravenna with three other bishops and compelled to communicate with John. When they returned to their own sees, their provincial colleagues, uncertain whether they ought to receive them into communion, decided to await the judgment of the Roman pontiff, “whose office it is to judge concerning heretics.” After that judgment had been obtained, a synod of ten bishops was convened, and Severus and the three other bishops, having renounced their “heresy,” were restored to their sees.

“When Gregory was then made pontiff,” he says, “John the archbishop appeared to have come to his senses and to have assented to the three chapters of the Council of Chalcedon, from which he had previously recoiled.”

He continues, and asserts that Blondus related that the matter had turned out otherwise: Severus had become a “heretic,” had been converted through the efforts of Gregory and John, and had then fallen back again into “heresy.” He adds that “he preferred to agree with Blondus, who writes the foregoing, rather than with Paul.”

It is astonishing how greatly Rubeus errs in these matters, deceived because he did not recognize Paul the Aquileian deacon as an adherent of the defenders of the Three Chapters. Consequently, Paul tells the story in a more hostile manner and favors Severus—not as a heretic, but as a schismatic. Yet how could Rubeus have failed to hear Paul himself explicitly relating that John had been a condemner of the Three Chapters?

Who, indeed, ever wrote that John, bishop of Ravenna, was the first to attempt to withdraw from the authority of the Roman See and to bring the bishops of the Italian cities over to his own opinion—so that Rubeus implies that they were numerous, by asserting that most writers affirm this?

Paul the Deacon says nothing of these matters, nor of an awaited reply from the pontiff before the synod was convened. On the contrary, he records that Severus, who had communicated with John at Ravenna and had assented to the condemnation of the Three Chapters, returned to his own territory and, together with John of Parenzo, another Severus, and Vindemius, bishops, and Antonius the defender, was received by the synod assembled at Marano. There, Paul says, “he presented a written statement of his error, because he had communicated at Ravenna with the condemners of the Three Chapters.”

The schismatic bishops themselves relate the same thing in a letter sent to the emperor Maurice, when they were summoned by Gregory the Great to the Roman synod and refused to come. Baronius presents this letter under the year 590, communicated by Nicolaus Faber from what he believes to have been the Pithoean library. I have thought the following passage should be transcribed here:

> “After this, when our most blessed archbishop Severus had been ordained in the holy Church of Aquileia, the insults inflicted upon him, the injuries and bodily violence of blows, and the force by which he was brought and taken to the city of Ravenna and reduced to custody, and the hardships by which he was oppressed and crushed, could undoubtedly have reached the merciful ears of our Lord.”

Thus the opinion of “most men”—although none of them are found—falls utterly to the ground; it is excessively defamatory of John. It is established that he worked with the exarch Smaragdus to restore the schismatics to unity, and that he considered nothing more important than submission to the Roman See. Rubeus himself acknowledges this, even though a controversy with the Roman pontiff was then active concerning the use of the pallium and the *mappulae*.

Rubeus is, as the saying goes, completely mistaken when he says that John was foolish because he recoiled from the Three Chapters, but came to his senses when he assented to them. He does not seem sufficiently acquainted with the history of the Three Chapters, which is treated elsewhere. Once the Roman Church had finally added its vote to the condemnation of the Three Chapters, when Vigilius approved the Fifth Synod, the person who recoiled from the Three Chapters was the one who held the sound opinion, whereas among the schismatics it was the person who assented to them who was foolish.

### V

In the year 589, when John was completing the fourteenth year of his episcopate, we know from the ninth verse appended to the life of that bishop that he completed and dedicated the church of Saints Mark, Marcellus, and Felicula. I believe, however, that it had been largely constructed two years earlier, since the exarch Smaragdus is said to have supplied part of the final expenses of the work. Smaragdus had yielded his place to the new exarch Romanus in the year 587. These matters, which relate chiefly to chronology, are clarified by what was said in the preceding dissertation.

# LIFE OF MARINIANUS

## Chapter One

### Marinianus’s family and homeland. The *Pastoral Book* of Saint Gregory. His attack on simoniacal bishops.

### Marinianus XXX

He was a Roman by nationality. He had a ruddy complexion, a long, drawn face, a gray-blue eye, and was in every respect very handsome. He was the nephew of the aforementioned John, his predecessor.

> [Note: [Col. 0645D] Marginal note: “He was consecrated by the blessed Pope Gregory around the year of Our Lord 548.” BACCH.]

Consecrated at Rome by the most blessed Gregory, he was sent here by him. When he wished to escape from this see so as not to become a bishop, he said that he could not bear the burden of so great an honor.

Then the most blessed Pope Gregory began to refresh him with words of consolation, saying:

> “For your sake alone I shall make a little book. Keep it constantly in your hands; always direct your attention to it; observe the words of that book, and be free from every fear.”

And, writing the *Pastoral Book*, he sent it to him, saying:

> “Dearest brother, I have made this book for your sake. Guard it carefully, and instruct your flock as it is set forth here. Remain with your priests and with all your people, so that on the day of judgment you may confidently say: ‘Here am I, Lord, and my people with me.’”

> [Note: [Col. 0645D] Here Agnellus truly attacks the clergy and bishops of his own time. Read it, therefore, with the caution taught in the preface, §1. BACCH.]

And blessed Marinianus received it, reading it every day and observing its teaching.

He was not like the others, who devour the property of the Church in exchange for the honor of the episcopate. They also take gifts from others and become indebted; and if a dispute should arise between two persons, they bargain for the dignity of their office as though they were selling a person. They send spies among themselves to find out how much money the other man wishes to offer. When it is reported that perhaps five hundred solidi are being offered, he laughs because the sum is small: “I,” he says, “shall give a thousand.”

I ask: when my ordainer says to me . . . . . . . . it is better for him to accept a thousand solidi than the small sum offered by the other.

Wretched men, they do not know that they are following the simoniacal heresy. And how can they fail to know it, when the pontiff protests, saying: “See to it that, through payment or promise, you do not become a simoniac”?

And when he forbids it, do they not consent to the evil of both parties? They give and receive secretly, and publicly deny everything before all.

Why do you not remember, wretched men? What you deny before human beings will be revealed before the divine eyes, before angels and archangels, before principalities and powers, before thrones and dominions. Before the heavenly hosts and virtues, every hidden secret will there be made public.

Do you wish to reach the summit of dignity? Look to the labors of the contest. What good does it do you to put on an expensive garment when your soul is caught in the devil’s snare?

Does it seem a small thing to you to govern the Church? If you are willing to consider it, a bishop is greater than a king. A king, clothed in purple and gold and seated on a royal throne, is always thinking about death; conscious of the sword, he is continually weighing how he may shed blood. A bishop, however, is concerned with the salvation of the soul, with the punishment of the impious, and with the joy of paradise.

Consider the difference between the two: the king acts so as to destroy bodies, the bishop so that the soul may be crowned. The king leads rebels into captivity, while the bishop purchases, redeems, and absolves captives. The one sleeps peacefully at night; the other persists throughout the whole night in divine praises.

And what more need be said? The king himself also asks the bishop to pray to God on his behalf.

Let this suffice; I have said enough about you. It is not a matter of warning but of recalling to memory. Consider how this man, who was not from our flock, duly held the hieratic see when instructed in apostolic doctrine.

## Chapter Two

### Contemporary events from the history of Marinianus. His death and epitaph.

In his time, the inhabitants of the sea-coasts, especially in this city of Ravenna, were devastated by a very severe plague. When the year had completed its circuit, the citizens of Verona were consumed by a powerful death.

After this, a terrible sign appeared in the sky, as though bloodstained enemies were fighting throughout the entire night, and a very bright light illuminated everything.

In that same year, King Theudebert of the Franks engaged in war with his cousin Lothar, and his army was severely defeated.

After some time had passed, the monastery of the Father Benedict, situated in the fortress of Cassino, was plundered at night by the Lombards during the abbacy of Boniface.

> [Read: Bonitus, Bacch.]

Meanwhile, the daughter of King Agilulf was captured with her husband Gudeschalc by the army of the patrician Callinicus from the city of Parma, and they were brought as captives to this city of Ravenna.
