Here, too, Smaragdus, previously a private citizen, was appointed patrician. Later Callinicus removed him from the dignity of the patriciate, and Callinicus assumed the dignity for himself. Then the citizens of Ravenna, indignant, expelled the rash Callinicus and restored Smaragdus to his former position.

Maurice Augustus, after holding the imperial power for twenty-one years with his sons Theodosius, Tiberius, and Constantine, was killed by Phocas, his own *strator*, who had been the servant of the patrician Priscus.

Thus, as we have said, there was always war between the people of Ravenna and the Lombards, and there was great discord because of the king’s daughter, who had been captured by the people of Ravenna. Because of her, the city of Cremona was captured and destroyed by the aforesaid king, while Mantua was grievously harassed and laid waste.

In the second year of Phocas’s reign, indiction 8, blessed Gregory departed to the Lord, and Savinianus succeeded him. At that time there was a severe cold; the crops were ravaged by mice, and others were struck by blight. In the same year there was a severe famine among the people, because every form of food was found in small quantity and rarely, as is now the case in our own times.

This happened so that God might show through that severe famine an indication of the preaching that had been lost through the death of blessed Gregory. For divine preaching is food for the soul, whereas every kind of food is food for the body.

Thus, as we have said, this most blessed man died on the tenth day before the Kalends of November and was buried in the church of blessed Apollinaris outside the walls of Classe, amid much lamentation. An epitaph was inscribed there as follows:

> O holy priest, ever mindful of counsels and worthy of remembrance,  
>   
> Marinianus, you lie placed in this tomb.  
>   
> Though dead in body, your fame nevertheless survives;  
>   
> Your limbs pass to earth; your light endures [the reading after “light” is uncertain].  
>   
> Coming here from the walls of Rome, the bishop  
>   
> Guarded holy Ravenna by your prayers.  
>   
> Disposing all ages in saving time,  
>   
> Pious Christ gave you to the people as they prayed.  
>   
> That you deserved to receive burial in these temples—  
>   
> Such great tombs prove that you pleased God.  
>   
> And since, as Christ’s representative, you duly served as priest,  
>   
> May holy rest be yours in his own places.  
>   
> He sat for . . . years, . . . months, . . . days . . .

# OBSERVATIONS ON THE LIFE OF MARINIANUS

### Marinianus a monk and presbyter. Whether abbot of the brothers’ cell. The *Pastoral Book* written to John, not to Marinianus. The occasion of its composition. Summary of all the letters of Gregory the Great written to John and Marinianus.

### I

Agnellus calls Marinianus the nephew of John, his predecessor, something that is otherwise unknown. He says nothing about his having been a monk with Gregory the Great, although this is certain from the testimony of the holy pontiff.

In Book IV, Letter 45, to Andrew the scholastic, he is called a monk, then a presbyter from a monk, and one who avoided the office of bishop. “At last,” Gregory the Great says, “when these men”—namely Donatus and John—“had been rejected, they sought the venerable man, brother and presbyter Marinianus, whom they had long known to have lived with me in the monastery . . . . . . . . . He, though reluctant, could only with difficulty and after various approaches finally be persuaded to consent to their request.” Much else follows there in praise of Marinianus.

I once considered whether this Marinianus might have been the same man who is named prefect of the brothers’ cell at Rome, concerning whom Gregory himself writes in Book I, Letter 54, to the subdeacon Peter. But he appears to have been a different person, since the man who was abbot, or prefect, of the aforesaid cell seems to be the very man to whom Gregory writes concerning the restoration of the church of Saint Gregory.

Moreover, what our author reports—that Gregory wrote the *Pastoral Book* to raise Marinianus’s spirits—cannot be accepted, since in both the published and unpublished copies the book is addressed to Bishop John. In the preface, the occasion for writing is said to have arisen because John reproached Gregory for attempting, by hiding himself away, to escape the burden of pastoral office.

Gregory says that he wrote the book so that a person who lacks the burdens of dignities would not recklessly seek them, and that one who recklessly sought and obtained them might fear that he had done so. This is plainly an argument better suited to restraining an ambitious man than to drawing Marinianus toward undertaking the burden of office.

Our author therefore betrays himself here: he is entirely a stranger to the reading of Gregory’s book and has been deceived by popular reports.

### II

Rubeus gathered many materials for illuminating the life of Marinianus from the Register of the letters of Gregory the Great, in Book IV, and Carlo Sigonio gathered still more in that outstanding work *On the Kingdom of Italy*. I think these materials could serve in place of a complete commentary on the lives of John and Marinianus if a brief summary were supplied here of the letters that the great pontiff wrote to both men. This is all the more appropriate because, in composing the lives of these bishops, our author behaved rather negligently; from these letters he ought otherwise to have extracted much more for the instruction of posterity.

## Series of the letters of Gregory the Great to John and Marinianus, bishops of Ravenna, and of those letters which in any way relate to their acts

### From Book I, Letter 35, indiction 9, after March of the year 591

Maurilius, a distinguished and innocent man and former prefect, was staying within the precincts of a church because of accusations brought against him. Gregory strongly commends him to John the bishop, so that he may be able to render an account before the prefect Georgius without danger of oppression.

### From Book II, Letter 22, indiction 10, in July of the year 592

Bishop John is praised because he had not only visited Castorius, bishop of Rimini, when he was ill, but had also received him within the city of Ravenna. The pontiff says that he had ordained him because of the importunity of those who had requested it.

He orders that, if possible, Castorius be sent to Rome. He commends to the bishop of Ravenna those bishops belonging to his metropolitan jurisdiction who, because their routes were blocked, were unable to come to him. He stipulates, however, that they should not be summoned to Ravenna on their account, lest their distress be increased in these very difficult times. If there are matters deserving reprimand, the bishop of Ravenna should admonish them by letter; more serious matters should be referred to Gregory.

### From Book II, Letter 28, same indiction

In this letter to John, Gregory orders that the dispute between Viuland and the deacon Gavimianus be settled briefly.

### From the same book, Letter 32, same indiction

Gregory says that he had not replied to John’s letters because the hostile fury toward the Romans of Agilulf, whom he calls Arnulf, king of the Lombards, had afflicted him with such sorrow that he had fallen into colic.

He acknowledges the love of the bishop of Ravenna toward him and his desire to come to his aid, though he is entirely unable to do so. He praises the actions and writings directed against the schismatic bishops of Istria, and says that, when Maurice ordered him to cease compelling those men, he wrote with apostolic freedom.

He advises that the patrician Romanus be tolerated and that efforts be made to establish a truce with Agilulf, at least for a short time, since the small number of soldiers made this advisable.

He warns that a person once ordained ought not to be ordained again, just as a baptized person ought not to be baptized again. But if someone entered the priesthood with a minor fault, he should remain in the order conferred upon him after penance has been imposed.

He says that Agilulf, together with Aroges, was threatening Naples.

He declares that alms should not be sent to the schismatic Severus, whose city had been burned, because Severus was defending his position before the emperor by means of gifts. Rather, assistance should be given to the city of Fano by sending Abbot Claudius with money, the amount of which he leaves John to determine.

He rejoices that Bishop Natalis has come to his senses, and orders Bishop Malchus likewise to render an account before departing.

### From Book II, Letter 54, indiction 11, May 593

John had taken badly the warning given by Castorius, the notary of the Roman Church, when Castorius came to Ravenna, that the pallium was to be worn only on certain days.

For this reason Gregory again admonishes him by letter and gives detailed instructions that the custom of the other metropolitans be observed, unless John produces a special privilege obtained from the Roman Church. He impresses upon him the need for a moderate disposition.

Gregory says that he had searched for such a privilege in the archives and had not found it; rather, there were certain documents that opposed John’s claim. Nor, he says, was the claim supported by custom.

He forbids John to wear the pallium during public litanies or to use it in the sacristy before the dismissal of the brothers.

The cases of criminal priests are either to be settled by John at Ravenna, or those priests are to be compelled, under prohibition from exercising sacred orders, to come to Rome.

Concerning the use of the *mappulae*, Gregory grants that the deacons attending the bishop as he proceeds may use them.

### From Book II, Letter 55, same indiction

A letter from John, bishop of Ravenna, in which he defends himself with the greatest moderation. He had believed that the use of the pallium was owed to him, not through proud arrogance, but out of zeal for his Church and in accordance with the custom of his predecessors.

He nevertheless says that he is guided by the greatest obedience, as was fitting, toward the Roman See, in whose bosom he had been nourished and on whose behalf he had incurred the hostility and indignation of many.

He had attempted nothing new, he says, but had done what the custom of all the people of Ravenna commended. He complains and laments that, because of his sins, this had happened to him: after so many labors and hardships endured within and outside the city for the Roman Church, such treatment was being repaid to him.

He nevertheless hopes that the pontiff will act like a father: after applying a sharper correction, he will soothe him and not only confirm the privileges but increase them.

He adds that the people of Ravenna also used *mappulae* at Rome, and calls the Romans themselves as witnesses to this matter.

He again asks that the privileges of the Church of Ravenna, which it had sent to Rome, be preserved. Meanwhile, he would abstain from using the pallium until he learned what the pontiff judged should be decided concerning these matters.

### From Book III, Letter 37, indiction 12, July 594

This letter was written to Constantius, bishop of Milan. Among other things, it says that, since many people found it astonishing or scandalous that Constantius recited the name of John of Ravenna during the solemn celebration of the Mass, he was admonished not to do so. The bishop of Ravenna did not name the bishop of Milan, and the practice could not be continued without causing scandal to some.

### From Book IV, Letter 1, indiction 13, before January 594

Since certain clerics and laymen were coming to the monasteries of monks under the influence of a spirit that led them to be placed over the others, the pontiff warns John in this letter that this must not happen and that what had happened should be corrected.

### From Book IV, Letter 11, same indiction, October 594

Gregory consoles John, who was grieving because he had been prohibited from using the pallium during the litanies. This was done at the request of the exarch and the leading men of Ravenna.

He grants that, according to the testimony produced by the deacon Adeodatus, John may meanwhile use the pallium on the feast days of blessed John the Baptist, blessed Peter the Apostle, and blessed Apollinaris, and on the anniversary of his own ordination. In the sacristy, however, he may use it after the dismissal of the children of the Church.

### From the same book, Letter 15, same indiction

Gregory reproaches John because he says one thing and writes another, imposes upon his servants, and brings accusations; because he does not devote himself to promoting ecclesiastical discipline; and because he presumes to use the pallium outside the church.

He adds that he is favoring the Church of Ravenna: he has increased the rank of a Ravenna deacon and has written to Constantinople so that he may be informed what the other metropolitans customarily do concerning the use of the pallium.

He admonishes him again.

### From the same book, Letter 18, same indiction, December of the same year

The presbyter Speciosus, relegated to a monastery by Bishop John, resisted, relying on the power of the exarch.

Gregory warns the exarch to allow the bishop to exercise his right freely and not to offer assistance to nuns who had returned to secular life.

### From the same book, Letter 20, same indiction, February 595

The pontiff says that John’s death had been reported to him. He therefore entrusts the visitation of the Church of Ravenna to Severus of Ficulensis, instructing him to conduct it in such a way that nothing is taken from either the Church or the clergy.

### From the same book, Letter 22, same indiction

This letter was sent to the people of Ravenna and has the same subject as the preceding one.

### From the same book, Letter 23, same indiction

Gregory warns Castorius that, after John’s death, which he laments, the election of a new bishop must not be made on account of money but after consideration of merit.

Whether one or two candidates are elected, he orders five of the senior presbyters and five deacons to come together to him at Rome. Of the other clergy, apart from those who decide to come, Castorius is to send any others whom he considers necessary.

### From the same book, Letter 44, on the fifth day of June, same indiction

The acts of the Roman synod, in which Bishop Marinianus of the city of Ravenna subscribes immediately after Gregory.

### From the same book, Letter 45, same indiction

The pontiff tells Andrew the scholastic that the exarch had commended the archdeacon Donatus, while John, a presbyter, had been elected. Gregory rejected both: the former because of actions that could not be approved, and the latter because he did not know the Psalter.

He says that the presbyter Marinianus, formerly his companion in monastic life, had been requested but had resisted; nevertheless, he approved him and strongly commends him as bishop of Ravenna.

### From the same book, Letter 54, same indiction, August

Gregory grants the pallium to Marinianus on the following conditions: he may use it in his own church, proceeding from the reception hall to the solemn celebration of the Mass after the children have been dismissed; once the Masses have been completed, he is to lay aside the pallium in the reception hall.

Outside the church he grants its use on four days of the year, as he had granted it to John. He confirms the privileges of the Church of Ravenna.

### From Book V, Letter p. [as printed], indiction 14, year 595

The clergy of Ravenna had complained that, after John had made his will, he had wronged that same church.

Although the rejection of the inheritance had removed every prejudice, Gregory nevertheless decrees that whatever belonged to the church, and whatever the testator had acquired during his episcopate, should be assigned to the church. Whatever he had possessed before becoming bishop, however, was to belong to those to whom it had been bequeathed.

The letter was written to Marinianus. Gregory adds that the legacy to the monastery of Saint Apollinaris, built by John, ought to take effect; John had requested while alive that it be confirmed.

### From the same book, Letter 2, same indiction

Gregory asserts to the people of Ravenna that Marinianus stands for the holy Council of Chalcedon and venerates the preceding ecumenical councils.

### From the same book, Letter 24, same indiction, November

The clergy of Ravenna had complained about a dispute between the Church and Abbot Claudius that had been brought to Rome.

Gregory considers this properly done, since Claudius said that he had been wronged by John, Marinianus’s predecessor, and the dispute had consequently been duly brought before the Roman See.

Likewise, in the imperial city, the presbyter John had appealed to the Roman See against John, bishop of Constantinople, in accordance with the canons, and the case had been judged at Rome.

Gregory orders Marinianus to send to Rome, through Secundinus and Castorius, the sword that the deacon Peter had left at Ravenna.

### From the same book, Letter 28, same indiction, March 596

When Marinianus requested measures that would prejudice the monasteries of monks, Gregory refused what he had asked and warned him to support and defend those monasteries, and not to allow them to be troubled in any way by clerics or laymen.

He grants Marinianus authority to release the clerics Romanus and Dominicus, who had dared to leave Rome without a blessing.

### From the same book, Letter 29, same indiction, April

Writing to Secundinus concerning peace with Agilulf, Gregory orders him to reprimand Marinianus because he had provided no alms, and complains that Marinianus had not replied to his letters.

### From the same book, Letter 30, same indiction

Sent to the people of Ravenna. Anyone who had secretly posted at night written accusations against Castorius was bound by excommunication.

### From the same book, Letter 33, same indiction

Andrew, honored with the titles *Magnificus* and *Domnus*, had insisted that, in accordance with ancient custom, the bishop of Ravenna should use the pallium during public litanies.

The pontiff decrees that Castorius should hear sworn witnesses on this matter at the body of blessed Apollinaris, and he prescribes the form of the oath.

### From Book VII, Letter 39, indiction 15, July 597

Gregory warns Marinianus to ordain a bishop for the Church of Cornelium in place of the one who had fallen.

### From the same book, Letter 40, same indiction

He orders that clerics not remain in monasteries under any pretext. If a monk is promoted to the clerical state or to a sacred order, he is thereafter to have no authority in the monastery.

He asks that someone come to Rome and that Marinianus entrust to him the monks who were to remain in the monasteries of Ravenna.

### From Book VII, Letter 18, indiction 1, April 590

This was sent to Marinianus, as related above, and contains privileges for the monastery of Saints John and Stephen at Classe.

### From the same book, Letter 19, same indiction

He commends Abbot Claudius to Marinianus.

### From the same book, Letter 21, same indiction

He commends to Marinianus the wife of John, whose legal status had been brought into dispute.

### From Book VII, Letter 9, indiction 2, after September 598

Gregory writes to the exarch Callinicus that he had informed Marinianus what had been decided concerning the island of Capritana.

### From the same book, Letter 10, same indiction

A certain John, who had come from Pannonia to the fortress of Novas, to which the island of Capritana was attached as though by diocesan jurisdiction, had been ordained. He had nevertheless been violently expelled from his see by the bishop of Istria, who ordained another in his place, and had been permitted to live on the island.

Unwilling to adhere to the schism, he had requested, together with his people, to be united to the Catholic Church. Later he had withdrawn, while the people persisted in their request.

Gregory orders Marinianus to determine whether the bishop wishes to return to unity. If he does not wish to return, Marinianus is to ordain another and retain the island within his diocese until the bishops of Istria renounce the schism.

He is also to arrange for Callinicus to report these matters to the emperor. Gregory says that he himself had done so through Anatolius.

He entrusts to Marinianus the case of Maximus and, if the matter requires it, orders him to associate Constantius, bishop of Milan, with himself as judge, so that it may be determined whether Maximus had been properly ordained or had fallen into the simoniacal heresy.

### From the same book, Letter 50, or 84, same indiction, after January 599

As the election of the bishop of Rimini approached, Marinianus was entrusted with investigating the merits of the candidate and the election itself.

### From the same book, Letter 51, elsewhere 85, same indiction

He orders the clergy and people of Rimini, because of the bishop’s illness, to elect another bishop and bring the man elected to Ravenna before Marinianus. Marinianus, coming to Rome himself, is to provide testimony on behalf of the candidate.

### From the same book, Letter 69, elsewhere 103, same indiction

He entrusts to Constantius, bishop of Milan, the case of Maximus, bishop of Salona, which he had previously committed to Marinianus.

### From the same book, Letter 77, elsewhere 111, same indiction

Florentius, a deacon of Ravenna, had testified that the bishops of Ravenna customarily used the pallium at all litanies.

In this letter to Castorius, Gregory says that he had learned the opposite. He says that the same thing could be inferred from the letters of John, once bishop, in which it is stated that, according to ancient custom, the metropolitans of Ravenna had worn the pallium at the more solemn litanies, and that the deacon Adeodatus had said that this occurred at four or five solemn litanies.

Gregory therefore wishes to be informed in writing how many solemn litanies—those called the greater litanies—it was customary to celebrate.

He nevertheless warns Castorius not to investigate this among the clergy, but among others who were attached to neither side, so that, once the truth had been discovered, he might console Marinianus.

### From the same book, Letter 80, elsewhere 114, same indiction

This matter was entrusted to Marinianus, who had requested it through Castorius: if Maximus, bishop of Salona, should clear himself at the shrine of Saint Apollinaris of the charge of simoniacal corruption and of the other charges, by taking an oath and undergoing penance if necessary, he was to be absolved.

The pontiff says that he will regard as valid whatever Marinianus decides in these matters.

The two following letters to Castorius and Maximus have the same subject.

### From the same book, Letter 99, elsewhere 133, same indiction

Schismatics who had returned to the unity of the Church are commended to Marinianus.

### From the same book, Letter 100, elsewhere 134, same indiction

Gregory informs the inhabitants of Caprea, or the island of Capritana, that he had entrusted to Marinianus the decision about what should be done if their schismatic bishop refused to return to unity.

Since this letter has the same subject as Letter 10 of indiction 1, either this letter belongs to the preceding year or that one belongs to this year.

### From the same book, Letter 130, elsewhere 164, same indiction

He sends the pallium to Maximus of Salona, who had fully cleared himself of the charges brought against him.

### From Book VIII, Letter 8, indiction 3, year 600

He commends to Marinianus the prefect John and his wife, who is to be brought to Rome.

### From the same book, Letter 9, same indiction

A certain wicked man named Peter had abducted a nun from her monastery and was keeping her with him.

The pontiff urges Marinianus to punish the crime, promising to provide assistance and, if necessary, to write to Constantinople.

### From Book IX, Letter 2, indiction 4, in the aforementioned year, before December

Marinianus had sent Florentius, or Florentinus, a deacon, to Constantinople so that he might restore the property of the Church of Ravenna in Sicily, which had suffered the greatest losses.

Gregory informs Marinianus that he will commend Florentius to Anatolius. He grants Marinianus authority to promote a certain man to sacred orders. He indicates that Marinianus had neglected something entrusted to him.

### From the same book, Letter 3, same indiction

He commends the deacon Florentius to Anatolius.

### From the same book, Letter 4, same indiction

He strongly commends to the presbyter Alexander the Sicilian property of the Church of Ravenna, for the restoration of which he had sent the deacon John to Sicily.

### From the same book, Letter 28, same indiction, year 601

Gregory urges Marinianus, who was suffering from vomiting blood, in a letter filled with expressions of affection and esteem, to arrange the affairs of the Church and come to Rome, where he could be treated for his illness. Meanwhile, he should abstain from fasts, vigils, and other practices of this kind.

### From Book X, Letter 5, indiction 6, year 602

He commends to Marinianus the people of Maurentius. A following letter to Theodore, the curator, has the same subject.

### From the same book, Letter 9, same indiction

He orders Castorius that, if anything had been donated to the monastery of Saints Mark, Marcellinus, and Felicula, the donation should stand.

### From the same book, Letter 22, same indiction

After Abbot Claudius had died, discussion was taking place concerning the election of another. Gregory therefore orders John the subdeacon that Optimus be approved and ordained by Marinianus. The burden of eradicating from the monastery the particular vice of favoritism rests upon Optimus.

### From Book XI, Letter 27, indiction 6, February 603

He orders that Boniface arrange for John, a cleric of Ravenna, to be sent to him.

### From the same book, Letter 34, same indiction, March
He instructs Marinian to take care of himself during his consumption, and, once he knows that he has recovered, grants him permission to fast once or twice a week. He nevertheless warns him not to place too much confidence in his health, and foresees that the illness has been suppressed, not cured.

From Book XII, Letter 1, indiction 7, in October of the same year.

Fortunatus had been appointed abbot of Saints Laurence and Zeno at the fortress of Cesena by the former bishop Natalis. Natalis’s successor Concordius had removed him from office without any cause. The pontiff therefore orders that, after the matter has been investigated, he be restored by Marinian to his former dignity. [Col. 0654D]

Besides these matters, collected here for convenience from the Register of Gregory the Great, there exists in the collections of the councils a Roman, or rather Third Lateran, council, in which a decree is recorded on behalf of the monks, issued on the Nones of April, indiction 3—elsewhere 4—in which, from a manuscript of the monastery of Flavigny in the duchy of Burgundy, “Marinian, bishop of Ravenna,” subscribes. In that decree, however, almost the same matters are contained as those read above, Book XVII, Letter 18, indiction 1. In any case, it seems improbable that Marinian was at Rome in indiction 3 or 4, or indeed during almost the whole period of his episcopate, as is clear from the sequence of the preceding letters.

## LIFE OF JOHN

[Col. 0655]

### ONLY CHAPTER

[Col. 0655A] Perpetual denunciation of the vices of his own time. John’s tomb is indicated, together with the length of his episcopate.

John [the Third] XXXI. He was full-bodied, handsome in appearance, with a plump face, large eyes, a cheerful expression, and an attractive presence. [Note: [Col. 0655D] Marginal note: He flourished about the year of the Lord 568, during the reign of the emperor Phocas. BACCH.]

This man was not like a master, but like a devoted father to his sheep. He lived gently with them, beloved by all, a blameless man, father of orphans, comforter of widows in their tears, defender of orphans, giver to the needy, raiser of the oppressed, liberator of the imprisoned, and follower of every good work, more glorious in the praises of God. Oh, what a man he was—and what men there are now! He did not tear the sheep apart; rather, his table was always replenished from the produce of the flock, and he ate joyfully, exulting with the priests [Col. 0655B] and the whole people.

[Note: [Col. 0655D] Here Agnellus attacks the bishops of his own age with excessive bitterness. Whether the vices he denounces are real, let the prudent reader determine from elsewhere, and consider what is said in the Preface, § 1.]

But men of this kind do not exist today. What, then, are they like? Are they not bishops, like those men, receiving the Holy Spirit at the hour of their ordination, just as those men did, and likewise bishops sanctified in the same way? Yet they are far more unlike them, because those earlier bishops offered the greater part of their possessions to their churches for the sake of their own souls, and ennobled the churches. Every day they offered prayers to God with lamentation, and redeemed captives; and by such benefactions sins were expiated, while daily in their prayers they entreated the merciful Lord.

But these men now are not like those men. There are some who, from the gift once granted to the Church, feed dogs, cast out the poor, manage bird-catchers, cherish hawks, and delight in buffoons [or: delight in buffoonish songs]. They cast out priests, repel the officials of the Church, and stifle every gathering of the Church. Worse still, they sell the Church’s grain, oil, pulses [legumes and], and wine, turning them into measures of silver and gold; and they give these to princes and rulers so that they may destroy their own priests, and even the whole people.

Those earlier bishops, as you heard above, gave in order to redeem; these men now give in order to kill. They do not remember the saying of that prophet who declares: “Your princes in your midst are like roaring lions, even devouring souls by their power.” Who are these princes if not wretched bishops, who swallow up the Church’s possessions, despise their priests, take away their goods under various pretexts, and offer them no assistance? Indeed, they take away what belongs to them, [from the resources] of the Church they do not [share], but they ruin their own affairs. [Col. 0655D]

Hear your reproach in Solomon’s words: “A roaring lion and a hungry bear is a proud ruler over a poor people.” Why do you not remember, bishops who inspect and oversee, prelates of the Church, what is said in the Gospel: that your Lord will come at an hour when you do not know? Why do you not live piously and offer an example to those who see [or: to those who live], [Col. 0656A] so that they may receive instruction from you and live piously in Christ?

But if we wish to rebuke someone, they immediately hurl at us a voice full of mockery: “Who are you? Are you better than this bishop or that?” “I saw such-and-such an overseer giving bread from his table to dogs. I saw another running with his horse beside dogs and hares. I saw that man holding a hawk in his own hands. And you preach to me?” Behold, when we hear such things and others like them, we fall back from them in confusion.

Tell me, overseers, where do you get your wealth? Is it from your parents? No; it is from the bequests of dead people that the churches have been enriched. For what reason, then, did those people make their bequests, unless so that God might cleanse and wash their souls through your intercessions? Why do you transgress the rule of the holy Fathers and abandon what they commanded, saying: “Bishops are to use the Church’s possessions as entrusted goods, not as their own”?

Tell me, when you have departed from your bodies, if they themselves do not bring accusations against you, will God forgive you this sin? Even if you give them alms from those very possessions, what reward will you have? It is not from your own substance, but from the soul of your predecessors.

For just as a master calls his steward and orders him, at the expense of his household, to give one hundred measures of grain, and the steward keeps some portion for himself and does not expend all of it, while those outside report to his master that he did not give the whole amount but fraudulently retained it—whereupon the master scourges him, removes him from his stewardship, casts him out, or sends him to prison for failing to complete through negligence what he had not fulfilled—so the Evangelist has pronounced a similar judgment upon you, saying:

“But if that servant says in his heart, ‘My master is delaying his coming,’ and begins to strike the boys and the maidservants, and to eat and drink and become drunk, the master of that servant will come on a day when he does not expect him and at an hour he does not know, and will divide him and cut him asunder and appoint his portion with the unbelievers.”

Wretched men! These words have been spoken about you, who have undertaken the governance of the Church, who ought to be blameless and without any stain. And when you are seized by death in such negligence, what destruction there will be, when a bishop is carried off to punishment while the common people are invited to the kingdom?

But, my fathers, act cautiously, because the day of the Lord will come like a thief. Take the place of the apostles; you occupy their chairs; travel along their paths, [Col. 0656D] so that you may be counted among them.

But this most blessed John, who governed the episcopal office humbly, led all the days of his life in joy. He governed his Church in peace, fulfilling the divine commandments. He died bodily and was buried, as I suppose, in the atrium of Saint Apollinaris. He sat for five years, ten months, and eighteen days.

## LIFE OF JOHN

[Col. 0657]

### CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0657A] Classis purchased with the Church’s resources on three occasions. Moral exhortations once more addressed to the bishops.

John [the Fourth] XXXII was a gentle and humble man, wise in heart, prudent in speech. He possessed eloquent words, led an honorable life, and had good manners accompanied by honeyed speech. He preserved intact and unharmed the admonitions of his predecessors.

Now, some citizens say that he bought the city of Classis from a hostile people three times, at great expense to the Church; [Note: [Col. 0657D] Marginal note: The city of Classis was bought by John, archbishop of Ravenna; it was destroyed by Liutprand, king of the Lombards, through the betrayal of its citizens. BACCH.] and he purchased not only the city but also its inhabitants, together with all their suburbs, as his own possession. For, observing the Gospel saying, he attended daily to the words: “Learn what this means: ‘I desire mercy, and not sacrifice.’”

Hear, then, through the prophet: “Shall I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats?” Hear [or: Hear also] the other prophet, Isaiah son of Amos: “When you stretch out your hands, I will turn my eyes away from you; and when you multiply your prayers, I will not hear.” Why? Where is the glory of the Lord? “You will call upon me [or: But David: ‘Call upon’] in the day of your tribulation; I will deliver you, and you will glorify me.” And certainly another prophet says: “In the day of tribulation they will cry out, and I will hear them.”

What then? Where, therefore, is Isaiah’s prophecy, in which you said: “Thus says the Lord: When you entreat him, while you are still speaking he will say, ‘Behold, here I am’”? [And on the contrary he says:] “I will turn my eyes away from you.” One voice gladdens us; another troubles us. And why will the Lord [God] not hear us when we call upon him? Indeed, he will hear us—but we shall die.

Listen: “Why are your hands full of blood? Wash yourselves, be clean; remove the evil of your thoughts from my sight. Seek justice, assist the oppressed, defend widows, and come and argue your case with me, says the Lord.”

And again: “Woe to those who justify the wicked for a bribe and condemn the righteous for a gift. Woe to those who call evil good and call good evil, because it is not for the wicked to rejoice, says the Lord.”

But if you remove from yourself every bond of iniquity and every murmuring word, and give your bread to the hungry from your heart, you will satisfy the humbled soul. And Isaiah says: “Your God will be with you always and will not turn away from you. Then you will cry out, and the Lord will hear you; while you are still speaking, he will say, ‘Behold, here I am.’”

See how quickly God will hear those who observe his commandments? Hear David again concerning the righteous: “I was young, and now I am old, and I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his offspring seeking bread.”

But what is written concerning sinners? “But to the sinner God said: ‘Why do you recite my justice and take my covenant upon your lips?’” and so forth up to: “Understand this, you who forget God, lest he seize you and there be no one to deliver you.”

O dearest ones, this saying ought to stand before your eyes every day, so that however much we are concerned about fear, it may profit us for salvation. Woe to that soul which is snatched away just as a hawk snatches birds. At the hour when the soul departs, we take nothing away with us except the sins we have committed. We are mocked by evil spirits, derided by them, and confined without mercy.

When we are harshly handled, they say: “This man claimed to be a Christian, but we find no works of Christ in him.” [Note: [Col. 0657D] Here too Agnellus attacks the bishops of his own time; read this, therefore, with the same attitude and caution with which I advised you to read the Life of the preceding bishop. ID.] Behold, this judge has been captured; behold, this king has fallen. Not like an ordinary guilty person, but like this priest, he has been hurled into the depths.

Before human eyes the body lies quietly, but it is not seen how his soul is dragged by evil spirits to punishment. And the overseers of the Church are examined not only on their own account, but also for their sheep and for the whole people entrusted to them. A layman perhaps suffers punishment for his own soul; overseers suffer for the whole flock.

If the man who did not draw a soul to Christ is to be sent into outer darkness, where will the one who destroyed Christian souls be sent? You did not preach; you kept silent; you did not acquire. Those whom you had acquired and who were serving God—why did you harass or afflict them? Why were you guilty of perjury at the judgment-seat where you sat? Why were you the author of crime? Why were you an accomplice in murder?

Does not the canon command that a bishop personally undertake no secular concern, but devote himself to nothing except reading, and continually read and teach the Gospel? If you do not wish to follow this, imitate this holy man; make yourself equal to this blessed John. Redeem captives; rescue, as the prophet says, those who are being led to death; preach; teach; raise up the suffering sheep; do not allow yourself to be separated from your brothers, so that you may be blessed together with them and the grace of God may not be empty among us.

### CHAPTER TWO

Wars and truces between the Lombards and Romans. The revolt and fate of John and Eleutherius. Phocas becomes emperor. The Roman Church, mother of all the churches. The Pantheon is dedicated. Wars in the East. The beginnings of the emperor Heraclius. The death and tomb of John.

In his time, then, Agilulf, king of the Lombards, made peace with the patrician Smaragdus and remained at peace for one year. After that year had been completed, the king’s bath and the Tuscan city called Orvieto were invaded by the Lombard army. In the months of April and May a comet appeared in the sky, and once again the Romans made peace with the aforesaid king for three years.

After this, Naples was invaded by John, and Eleutherius, after expelling him some days later, killed him. When Eleutherius was returning in victory, he disdained the insignia of the patriciate; and although he had been a eunuch, he assumed the rights of imperial rule. When he had left Ravenna and wished to go to Rome, he was killed by soldiers with a sword at the fortress of Luceoli. His head was enclosed in a sack and carried to the emperor at Constantinople.

At that same time the aforesaid king Agilulf sent his notary Stabilianus as an envoy to the emperor Phocas. He then returned with the emperor’s envoys, and peace was made between the two. Italy remained quiet for several years.

Then, as we have said, Phocas, after killing Maurice and his sons, invaded the Roman realm and held the imperial office for the course of eight years. At the request of the blessed Pope Boniface, he decreed that the Roman Church should be the head and see of all the churches, whereas previously the Church of Constantinople had been called first.

[Note: [Col. 0659B] Observe that these words are perversely stated from a schismatic standpoint. The disputes that arose between Gregory the Great and the bishop of Constantinople are well known, as is the firmness with which the pontiff restrained the presumption of that patriarch. Phocas acted so that the patriarch would desist from his undertaking and affirm the Roman primacy. Agnellus is lying when he dares to say that this was granted by Phocas, whereas previously the see of Constantinople had been called first. BACCH.]

Again the aforesaid pope asked him that, in the ancient shrine which the Romans called the Pantheon, after the filth of the idols had been destroyed, a church should be established and consecrated to the holy and undefiled Virgin Mary and to all the holy martyrs and confessors of God. There, where all the assemblies of demons were gathered, the memorial of all the saints and elect of God was to be venerated.

Meanwhile war was stirred up in the regions of the East and of Egypt. The Greens and the Blues, slaughtering one another in the most grievous civil conflict, struck each other down in mutual slaughter. [Note: [Col. 0660B] See the preceding dissertation, chapter 6. ID.]

The Persians, too, waging the most severe wars against the Roman state, captured many Roman provinces, even Jerusalem itself; they plundered the churches and reduced them to nothing, carrying away the wealth and ornaments of the Church. They also took away and ravaged the very standard through which we were redeemed, the cross [the holy object by which we were redeemed], and carried it off with them.

Heraclianus, who governed Africa in those days, rebelled against this Phocas. He came with an army and deprived him of both kingdom and life. Heraclius and his son assumed responsibility for governing the Roman state.

After these events, this most blessed man died and was buried, as I suppose, in the atrium of Saint Apollinaris. He sat for eighteen years, six months, and eight days.

# CHRONOLOGICAL-HISTORICAL DISSERTATION

## On the age of the following bishops of Ravenna: Bonus, Maurus, Reparatus, Theodore, Damian, and Felix

[Col. 0659]

## PART ONE

[Col. 0659C] Rubeus’s chronological arrangement is explained. Several matters reported without testimony cannot be maintained. Agnellus is compared with Anastasius. The sees are arranged chronologically.

I. Since I have found nothing worthy of notice in the Lives of the last two bishops, I thought it worthwhile to pass on to the chronology of those who follow. Accordingly, in accordance with the custom of the distinguished Ravenna writer Rubeus, his chronological arrangement must be explained.

He committed the acts and deeds of all these bishops to memory in Book IV of his History. He says that Bonus died shortly before the battle fought at the Scultenna, in which the exarch Theodore was defeated by the Lombards, with seven thousand Ravennates lost; he reports that this battle took place in the year 650. He says that the bishop in question died in the preceding year, 648, on the seventh day before the Kalends of September.

Concerning Maurus, after reporting the matters relating to the Roman synod under Martin, he writes that Maurus sat for approximately twenty-four years and died around the year 672 from Christ’s birth.

He asserts that Reparatus died on the third day before the Nones of August, after presiding for five years, eight months, and twenty-six days, during the pontificate of Donus at Rome and the exarchate of Theodore.

He relates that Theodore of Ravenna went to Pope Agatho in the year 680, on the basis of the acts of the Roman council and of the Sixth Synod: “While Conon was still pontiff,” he says, “and had not yet completed a year of his pontificate, the exarch Theodore died, at almost the same time as Theodore the archbishop, when he had already presided over the Church of Ravenna for eleven years,” and so forth.

He writes that Damian died on the third day before the Ides of March, after sitting for sixteen years, two months, and sixteen days, and that after his death Felix was substituted for him in the year 702 from the Virgin’s birth.

Finally, concerning Felix himself, he writes: “Felix the archbishop, after displaying an outstanding example of holiness and becoming distinguished by divine gifts, finally departed from this tearful lodging to his heavenly homeland on the seventh day before the Kalends of December, having been enrolled among the saints,” and so forth. “He governed the Church for approximately eighteen years.”

So writes Rubeus. Departing from Agnellus, and without stronger testimony, he leaves room elsewhere for determining the matter. There are also reasons that urge us to depart from his chronological arrangement.

For although he explicitly says that Damian sat for sixteen years, two months, and sixteen days, and died on the third day before the Ides of March—as Agnellus likewise relates—and similarly says that Felix was substituted for the deceased Damian in the year 702, it follows that Damian was ordained toward the end of December in the year 685, namely on the twenty-seventh day of that month, a Thursday, in solar cycle 12 and with Sunday letter G.

But if Damian’s predecessor Theodore died at almost the same time as the supreme pontiff Conon, and if Conon, according to Baronius, whom Rubeus follows, died on 13 October 687, it follows that Damian was ordained at least a year and several months before Theodore’s death, especially since, according to Baronius’s reckoning, Conon was not ordained until 686.

These matters will refute Rubeus’s assertion even more decisively if the reasons that compelled the distinguished Papebrochius to assign Conon’s dates later are considered, so that Conon was ordained on 8 September 687 and died on 30 August 688. For then Damian would have been ordained almost three years before Theodore’s death, or Theodore would have died not around the time of Conon but around the time of Leo’s death, if Papebrochius’s reckoning is retained.

Ughellus explicitly assigns the beginning of Damian’s episcopate to the aforesaid year 685. Yet, more absurdly, he does not recognize the error, although from Anastasius he had learned that Damian was consecrated by Pope Sergius. Nor did he see that this could not have happened in 685, when, according to Baronius, John V was seated at Rome, or when, according to Papebrochius’s reckoning, Benedict II was ordained on 14 March—precisely the year and month in which Ughellus says that Damian was consecrated by Sergius.

Nor does he more suitably assign Damian’s death to the year 707, both because of what will be said below and because, following Rubeus in this matter, he says that Damian sat for sixteen years, two months, and sixteen days. For if, disregarding the months and days, sixteen years are subtracted from the year 707, we go back to the year 691, not to 685; yet twenty-two years intervene between 685 and 707.

II. Moreover, it is most clearly established from Anastasius’s Life of Pope Constantine that Felix was not ordained as Damian’s successor until the pontificate of Constantine. On this matter Anastasius presents several details, which Rubeus does not conceal, although he suppresses the pope’s name lest it expose the ulcer of his badly constructed chronology.

According to Baronius’s view, Constantine was not created pontiff until 7 March of the year 708. Felix therefore could not have been consecrated bishop in 707, as Ughellus says, and much less in 702, as Rubeus reports.

Since Rubeus writes that Felix presided over the Church of Ravenna for approximately eighteen years, if those years are counted from 702, when he is said to have been created, his life would have extended almost to the year 720. He therefore could not have died before 718, the year in which John’s subsequent creation appears to be recorded, while he assigns numbers in the margin. Ughellus, considering the matter too carelessly, took these numbers as an opportunity for error and said that Felix died on the seventh day before the Kalends of December in the year 717.

These conclusions, then, arise against Rubeus from Rubeus himself. Yet he will become entangled in many other difficulties if he thinks that the matters narrated by Agnellus must be taken into account, and if the chronology of those matters is to be arranged here.

III. Our author offers certain chronological indicators on which the method of arranging these times depends, and which must therefore be examined and compared with Anastasius.

The creation and sufferings of Felix, the last of all the bishops, are especially useful for the present argument. For from Agnellus and Anastasius we learn that Felix was fraudulently taken from Ravenna to Constantinople by order of Justinian, the successor of Constantine Pogonatus. Anastasius also teaches us that he was ordained by the aforesaid Pope Constantine:

“This man,” says Anastasius, “ordained Felix, archbishop of Ravenna, who, following the customary practice of his predecessors, refused to provide guarantees in the scrinium.”

The chronologers agree on the year in which Constantine was created pontiff, although they disagree about the day, and they assign it to the year 708. Felix therefore could have been consecrated only in March of that year, in which they say that the pontiff was elected, either on the fourth or on the seventh day of that month.

Baronius and Pagius also agree—Baronius in Volume VII, Pagius in the dissertation on Hypatius, page 353—that Justinian, after ruling for six years following his restoration to the imperial power according to Theophanes, was murdered at the end of the year 711 by Philippicus, together with his son Tiberius.

Felix, therefore, was certainly ordained before that year. Since several events narrated by Agnellus took place while Justinian was ruling after his restoration, and since these require a considerable period of time, it follows that Felix’s ordination must be assigned to the earlier acts of Constantine’s pontificate.

Agnellus indicates that Felix’s abduction, torture, and blinding occurred during the last years of Justinian. He relates that Justinian was slaughtered on the day after the cruel and savage killing of Joannicius.

Moreover, at Felix’s very ordination those disturbances and complications occurred which Anastasius narrates. After them Felix sat peacefully throughout the period required by the works performed at the bishop’s command by Joannicius. Agnellus writes of these:

“The most wise Joannicius flourished in this man’s time. When the pontiff asked him to expound all the antiphons which we now sing on Sundays at the cross—whether of the holy apostles, or martyrs, or confessors, and likewise of virgins—he did so not only in Latin expressions, [Col. 0662A] but also in Greek words, because he was a most accomplished orator in both languages.”

These works seem to have required at least two years. After them, the disaster at Ravenna and the sufferings of the pontiff and Joannicius began in the year 710 and ended in 712, with Justinian murdered around the end of 711.

It follows from these facts that Felix was ordained in the very year 708, immediately after the consecration of Constantine the supreme pontiff.

Although Rubeus disagrees with Agnellus about the number of years Felix sat, he nevertheless retains the day of his death, 25 November. Since our author, from whom there is no reason to depart except by adding a small number of days, says that Felix sat for eight years, seven months, and nineteen days, it follows that, reckoned backward from 25 November, his ordination fell on 6 April.

But this date was unsuitable for episcopal ordinations in the year 708, when the solar cycle was 15 and the Sunday letter C. It follows that, instead of nineteen days, twenty-one days must be written, and Felix’s ordination must be moved back to 4 April of the aforesaid year 708. [Col. 0662B] Felix therefore died in the year 716, on the aforementioned day, 25 November.

The ten years added by Rubeus to the years reported by Agnellus, besides being supported by no witness, do not appear capable of being assigned to Felix after he had been worn down by his earlier sufferings.

When Agnellus says that, after returning to his see from the calamities of exile, Felix “built a house within the episcopal residence after three years, and named it the House of Felix after his own name,” this should be understood to mean that the house was completed in the third year after his return.

IV. Once the period of Felix’s episcopate and death has been established, a brighter light shines upon the preceding events. Agnellus says that Damian sat for sixteen years, two months, and sixteen days, and died on the third day before the Ides of May. Rubeus agrees, except that he replaces May with March—and rightly, as will be clear from what follows.

Thus Damian died on 12 March of the same year, 708. He had been ordained sixteen years, two months, and sixteen days earlier, namely on 27 December 691. Since, however, in that year the solar cycle was 28 and the Sunday letter A, and the feast of the Nativity then fell both on a Saturday and on a Sunday, I think that here too an error entered the number of days, and that nineteen days should be written instead of sixteen. His ordination should therefore be moved back to 24 December.

He was ordained by Sergius the supreme pontiff, as Anastasius testifies in this bishop’s Life.

Theodore, Damian’s predecessor, died at the beginning of the year, namely on 18 January, after completing thirteen years, three months, and twenty days in the episcopate, as Agnellus relates, although, as we observed above, Rubeus confines his episcopate to only eleven years.

According to Agnellus’s account, if we count backward from 18 January 691 by the stated years, months, and days, Theodore’s ordination falls on 29 September 677. But since in that year the solar cycle was 14 and the Sunday letter D, two days must be added to the stated number, and twenty-two days must be written instead of twenty. The ordination therefore falls on 27 September.

Reparatus had accordingly died on the third day before the Kalends of August—that is, on 30 July of the same year—after holding the episcopate for five years, nine months, and twenty-six days. Rubeus agrees with all this and supplies the twenty-six days omitted by the copyist of our manuscript. He had therefore been ordained on 4 October, a Saturday, in the year 671, solar cycle 8, Sunday letter E.

The date of death of Maurus, the bishop notorious for the disgrace of schism, is nowhere recorded, nor does Rubeus himself report anything about him, although elsewhere he is extremely careful in determining days and moments.

Considering the state of affairs in those times, however, when, according to the privileges obtained by Maurus from the emperor, the new bishop had to put on the pallium at the emperor’s command and had to be ordained by his three suffragan bishops, I think that at least three months intervened between the death of Maurus and the schismatic ordination of Reparatus. During that period, I suppose, someone was sent to Constantinople to request the pallium and then returned. An even longer and more protracted delay would have been required by the efforts of the pontiff defending his rights, unless his death occurred at approximately the same time; that death may have favored the people of Ravenna in securing victory for their bad cause.

We know that all this was arranged through the efforts of Maurus, both from the privilege of that same man, which will be described below in the Life of Maurus, and from Agnellus, who says that it was obtained “that the future shepherd of the Church of Ravenna . . . should be consecrated here [that is, at Ravenna], his chosen candidate by his three bishops, and that he should bring the pallium from the emperor at Constantinople.”

I therefore suppose that Maurus died around July of that same year, 671. This is also suggested by the following calculation: if we seek the date of his ordination from Agnellus’s data, subtract from the year 671 the twenty-eight years, ten months, and eighteen days during which he sat, we arrive at September of the year 642. We must exclude from Maurus’s period the day 25 August, which Agnellus records as the date of death of his predecessor Boninus.

It follows that Bonus, whom our author says died in a good old age, held the see from the year 630 until August 642.

## PART TWO

[Col. 0663B] The established chronology is disturbed by Papebrochius’s chronology of the Roman pontiffs. It is reconsidered.

I. The chronology of the Roman pontiffs arranged by the distinguished Papebrochius appears in part to disturb the foregoing account, especially where he attempts to establish the period of Pope Donus, who succeeded Adeodatus.

This eminent man believes that Adeodatus, who succeeded Vitalian, was ordained on 14 March 672, sat for five years, two months, and five days, and died on 18 May 677. Donus, he says, was ordained on 4 October of the same year, sat for one year, five months, and ten days, and died on 13 March 679.

If these dates are accepted, then in the chronological arrangement of the bishops of Ravenna explained above, the death of Bishop Reparatus would wrongly be assigned to that very year 677, on 30 July—namely, two months and four additional days before the ordination of Pope Donus.

But Anastasius explicitly relates the following in the Life of Donus:

“During his time the Church of Ravenna, which had separated itself from the Roman Church on account of autocephaly, again subjected itself to its former apostolic see. Its bishop, named Reparatus, immediately, as it pleased God, ended his life.”

Reparatus’s death would therefore have to be postponed to the following year, and at the same time the entire calculation of the sees assigned to the bishops of Ravenna would have to be reversed against Agnellus’s calculations; or else the creation of Bishop Felix would likewise have to be postponed, contrary to the considerations above that persuaded us to assign his ordination to the year 708.

These matters therefore compel us to investigate more closely the dates of the celebrated Roman pontiffs and Papebrochius’s own view.

He admits that all the copies of Anastasius, and the authors who followed Anastasius, assign only four years to Adeodatus. The same is also recorded in a catalogue written approximately eighty years after Adeodatus’s death, which he presents in the same volume of the Propylaeum, page 72, and which the distinguished scholar believes Anastasius followed.

Nevertheless, because he thinks that an error occurred either in this pontificate or in the two that followed—for only a year and a half is assigned to Donus, and two and a half years to Agatho, although Agatho himself is considered to have survived until the end of 681—he believes that Adeodatus’s period must be extended beyond four years.

But since the deeds of the latter pontiff, namely Agatho, induced Baronius to assign him a seven-year pontificate, Papebrochius thought it better, leaving one year to Agatho, to reduce the seven years assigned to Adeodatus by Baronius to five:

“Yet,” he says, “on the condition that, if one year could be added to either of his predecessors beyond the number of years assigned to that predecessor in Anastasius himself—namely, thirteen to Vitalian and two to Eugene—Adeodatus could be content with four years. In that case he would have been ordained in the year 673, on 8 March, the third Sunday of Lent, and would have died on 17 May, so that the episcopal see would have been vacant for four months and seventeen days. Meanwhile, as I have already said, an evident necessity appears for adding at least one year by conjecture around this time, something I otherwise do not willingly do, so that the remainder of the chronology drawn from the catalogues and Anastasius may be preserved.”

But the “sacred imperial decree,” prefixed to the Sixth Ecumenical Council and “addressed to Donus, the most holy pope of Elder Rome, but delivered to Agatho, the most holy and blessed pope of that same ancient Rome,” appeared to contradict this method of establishing the chronology of the pontiffs. It states that Donus “had departed from the present life,” and is recorded as having been issued “on the day before the Ides of August, at Constantinople, indiction 6”—that is, in the year 678.

The candid scholar admits that this document moved him, just as it moved Baronius, to bring Donus’s death and Agatho’s succession forward by one year:

“Although,” he says, “there appeared to be an error in the name of the month—for on whatever day of the year the death is placed, it must nevertheless have preceded the Ides of August by at least four months, during which it was unknown at Constantinople. This is as impossible as it is incredible that Agatho should have been ordained without the command and knowledge of the imperial exarch.”

He adds that he later recognized that the words “issued, etc.” deserved no credence, since they are found neither in the Greek nor in the old Latin Paris edition of 1524, based on the most ancient manuscript of Beauvais. He therefore believes that the imperial decree should be dated to the year 679, indiction 7, at the boundary between February and March.

## II.

Despite these considerations, I favor arranging the periods of Adeodatus, Donus, and Agatho differently from Papebrochius: assigning Adeodatus, in accordance with all the manuscripts of Anastasius and the very ancient catalogue cited by Papebrochius, only four years of pontificate, beginning on the day of his ordination, 14 March 672, and ending in 676, his pontificate extending to 18 May; assigning Donus, ordained on 5 October of that same year, one year, five months, and ten days—namely, until 14 March 678; and assigning Agatho, who began his pontificate in that same year on the day of his ordination, 30 May, three years, six months, and three days, dying on 3 December.

In this method of calculation, retaining Sundays for the ordinations and retaining Papebrochius’s calculation for Eugenius and Vitalianus, only one year is added to Agatho’s pontificate, making three years what Anastasius calls two. The acts of the Sixth Synod compel this, together with the following evidence, which it is useful to set out here.

In Labbe’s *Collection of Councils*, volume VI, page 579, there is a council held at Rome under Agatho, beginning as follows:

> “In the name of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, under our most pious lords and Augusti, Constantine the greater, emperor, in the twenty-sixth year, and the tenth year after his consulship, and also Heraclius and Tiberius, new Augusti, his brothers, in their twenty-second year, in the seventh indiction, in the month of October, with Agatho, most holy and thrice-blessed apostolic universal pope, presiding.”

The seventh indiction, with October in progress, corresponds to no year except 678. Thus, in October of the aforesaid year, Constantine Pogonatus was in the tenth year of his reign, or consulship, since his father Constans was killed at Syracuse in 668 not merely after 16 September—as Pagi observed in his *Dissertation on the Hypate*, part III, chapter 3, page 349—but only after October.

I therefore think it plainly established that Agatho was pope in October 678. The title of the council in the same edition was incorrectly put together, stating that such a council was held in the Constantinian basilica called that of Our Savior in the year of Christ 680, or, as others maintain, in the preceding year—that is, in October, indiction 7. The seventh indiction, however, corresponds only to October 678, not to 679 or 680; nor can Constantine’s tenth year of imperial rule correspond to either of those years. In the first act of the Sixth Synod, on 7 November, indiction 9—namely, in 680—he was reckoning the thirteenth year of his reign, or consulship, as is clear from the chronological markers of that act, which perhaps designate the very day on which his reign had formerly begun and on which he wished the synod to open.

It is certainly erroneous to infer, from the seventh indiction and the tenth year after Constantine’s consulship, his twenty-sixth year of empire and the twenty-second year of Heraclius and Tiberius. Yet since the imperial date of Constantine does not support the view assigning that council to 680, I believe that a scribal error entered the text, and that, in accordance with the two mutually consistent markers—the indiction and the post-consulship—the reading should be restored as Constantine’s twenty-fifth year and Heraclius and Tiberius’ twentieth year.

A fragment of the same council is added according to the Malmesbury manuscript. From it one concludes that Wilfrid was acquitted at that synod. Baronius thinks this occurred in the following year, 679, a matter to be discussed shortly.

Baronius likewise reports that John was sent to Britain so that, among other things, he might summon Theodore to the Roman synod. John was more likely sent to convey to Theodore what had been decreed at Rome concerning the British Church, and to instruct him that a synod was to be convened in Britain concerning the heresy of the Monothelites, as Bede teaches in book IV, chapter 18.

It follows, therefore, that Theodore was summoned to Rome—as the fathers of the Roman council say in the letter preserved in act 4 of the Sixth Synod—when, immediately after receiving from Agatho the imperial letter that had been sent to Donus, who had already died, plans were made to convene a Roman synod. But once the divisions in Britain were understood, it was judged preferable for Theodore to remain in his own diocese and for a synod of all the British bishops to be assembled there.

## III.

From the whole course of this discussion it is therefore evident that one year must be added to Agatho’s pontificate, which Anastasius limits to only two years, and that Donus’s pontificate must likewise be brought forward by one year, assigning it an earlier date than C. V. Papebrochius judged.

The chronology of the Ravennate pontiffs will thus be placed on the firmest footing. Although the month may perhaps be erroneous in the imperial letter prefixed to the Sixth Synod, the sixth indiction must nevertheless be retained, so that it may be understood as having been issued in 678.

Even if some Latin writer added this to the Greek text—perhaps something that passed from the margin into the text—it should by no means be rejected, since it is confirmed by certain arguments from elsewhere. The month of August could indeed have been written by the author of this addition in place of another month, in order to adapt the letter to Agatho’s pontificate and to indicate the time when it was delivered, rather than when it was written.

While the letter was being sent from Constantinople to Rome, Agatho may have obtained authorization from the exarch; news of Donus’s death may have reached the emperor; and, at the same time, the election of Agatho may have become known. Thus the letter originally addressed to Donus may have been addressed to Agatho in the registers, and the date of the month altered.

Whatever the truth may be, I do not think anything can be set against the argument supplied by the Roman synod held under Agatho before the disputes of the British Church, which plainly shows that Agatho was pope in October 678, when the seventh indiction had begun in the preceding September.

While Donus was pope at Rome, Reparatus of Ravenna could therefore properly have considered subjecting his Church to the Roman Apostolic See, in accordance with Anastasius’s account. Donus began his pontificate on 5 October 676; Reparatus died on 30 July of the following year, 677.

Further confirmation is supplied by Agatho’s apology in the letter written on the occasion of the synod, indeed repeated in the name of the entire synod in another letter of the same subject and written on the same occasion, preserved with the former in act 4 of the Sixth Synod. In these letters, arguments are carefully assembled to excuse the long delay in arranging what was necessary for sending the delegation to the aforementioned Sixth Synod.

Agatho explains that a lengthy period was required in order to obtain the opinions of the Western bishops, which had to be given in provincial synods; that responses from the most distant Britons had to be awaited; and that there were other causes of delay, including his illnesses and the scarcity of learned men. The fathers also mention the latter circumstance when writing in the name of the synod.

These considerations demonstrate that a lengthy delay had intervened, extending beyond a year, as C. V. Papebrochius himself acknowledges in his dissertation 15, *On the Pontificate of Agatho*—and perhaps beyond two years, since so many excuses were needed to justify it.

## IV.

In the same place, the learned man denies that any credence can be given to words which, he says, are absent from the Greek text and from the old Latin edition. These words were added to another imperial letter, written after the arrival of the legates at Constantinople and addressed to George, bishop of Constantinople. They are as follows:

> “Issued on 10 September at Constantinople, under our most pious lord, perpetual Augustus Constantine, emperor, in the twenty-eighth year and the twelfth year after his consulship. Since the synod began under the divinely crowned and most serene lords Flavius Constantine, most pious and, by divine decree, great prince, perpetual Augustus and emperor, in the twenty-seventh year of his reign and the thirteenth year after his consulship, by the divinely instructed gentleness of his rule, and Heraclius and Tiberius, his brothers, consecrated by God, in their twenty-second year, on 7 November, indiction 9, and since all the acts of the synod are consequently dated in this manner, it is necessary to conclude that an error entered the work of the person who added the date to the aforementioned imperial letter when he composed the years of the reign and of the post-consulship.”

He therefore says that it is wrong to maintain that the legates came to Constantinople one year earlier than the synod itself took place, thereby extending the date of the synod by almost six months.

He also observes that throughout the entire council nothing is changed in the designation of the years of so many eras. The first and second of these eras refer to the imperial rule shared by Constantine’s father Constans with his eldest son around the year 654 and, five years later, with his two other sons. The third era, he says, “is reckoned from the abandonment of the perpetual consulship after the father’s death on 15 July 668, so that the emperor appears, for the sake of greater convenience, to have reduced all those eras to one common epoch fixed in October, lest their multiplicity produce confusion in public acts.”

He nevertheless admits that he does not know why October was chosen, unless it was because in that month, by paternal decree, the years of Constantine’s reign began to be recorded, with the years of his consulship omitted.

Finally, he acknowledges that the Latin version of act 9, beginning on 8 March, records Constantine’s twenty-eighth year and proceeds accordingly, thereby distinguishing the eras. Yet he says that he suspects such precision, because nothing is changed in the reign of the brother Augusti or in the years after the consulship, whereas he thinks the year after the consulship ought to have been changed in act 16, held on 10 August.

He says that it was rightly done that the change from indiction 9 to 10 was observed in act 17, on 11 September, so that we need not rely on those earlier considerations.

## V.

From the uniformity with which the years after the consulship are marked under Constantine Pogonatus, son of Constans, the learned Pagius argues, in his *Dissertation on the Hypate*, part III, chapter 4, no. 2, page 351, that the formula marking the post-consulship should not be understood as in the preceding passages, namely, as excluding the year of the consulship. Rather, Constantine himself introduced a new method of reckoning, in which the consulship functioned like tribunician power. Consequently, to count the years after the consulship is the same as counting the years of the reign.

Once this observation is applied, all Papebrochius’s conjectures fall away, the chronological markers cited above are properly understood, and it is recognized that they fit together most appropriately.

The year of the imperial era of Constantine is itself 654, when he was proclaimed Augustus by his father before 26 April. This is indicated by act 15 of the Sixth Synod, in which the imperial year changes from 27 to 28, as the aforementioned Pagius maintains. But if the Latin version is followed, that change occurs in act 9, on 8 March, and in this respect we are compelled to depart from Pagius and place the beginning of Constantine’s empire before that day—precisely on the seventh day, when act 8 was held.

It must nevertheless be noted that where the Latin texts write “twenty-eighth,” the Greek texts write ἔκτους εἰκοστοῦ ἑβδόμου, “twenty-seventh year.” For this reason the aforementioned Pagius judged that act 9 should not be taken into account in multiplying the years of the empire, nor should the subsequent acts up to act 15, on 26 April 681.

The fact that neither in that act nor in the subsequent acts up to act 16 is the imperial year of Heraclius and Tiberius changed is explained by their having entered the imperial succession—or, rather, been declared Caesars—in a different and later month, in the year 659.

When, finally, in act 16, held on 9 August, their twenty-second year is increased to the twenty-third, it becomes clear that they had been declared Caesars before that day, as Pagius observed.

The years after the consulship likewise continue, because, functioning like tribunician power, they designate the very year of the empire. Since Constantine began to rule alone, they indicate that on 16 September, when the final act was held, the thirteenth year had not yet been completed. That year had begun before 10 November of the preceding year, 680, when the first act of the council was celebrated.

From this it follows that Constantine succeeded his father later than C. V. Papebrochius judged in 668. As noted above, Pagius has supplied the guiding light in this matter, against Anastasius, who assigns the death of Constans to 15 July.

I nevertheless see that the dates of the imperial letter addressed to George of Constantinople are corrupt: they mark the twenty-eighth year of the reign together with the twelfth year after the consulship on 10 September. I recognize that this cannot be maintained, for reasons to be given shortly.

## VI.

While I am writing this, C. V. Pagius has opportunely sent, through the care of the most illustrious Magliabechi—whose services to students of humane letters are known to all—a most learned letter to Nicasius, abbot and French canon of Dijon. In it he sets out several of the more select points from his chronological criticism of the later volumes of Baronius’s *Annals*, which scholars eagerly await and which are soon to be published; thus he increases our appetite to taste the entire work.

On page 5 of that letter, after the middle, he holds that Wilfrid was elected to the bishopric of York in 664 but was not ordained until the following year, 665. Thus, he says, the author of the catalogue of the bishops of York, published by Labbe in volume I of the *Bibliotheca*, rightly states that Wilfrid was expelled from the episcopate in 677, in the twelfth year of his episcopate, which he considers consistent with Bede’s account.

He says that Wilfrid went to Rome in the following year, wintering on the journey in 678 in Frisia, where he devoted himself to the conversion of the pagans, and arriving in Rome before October. There he attended the council held, he says, in that same year, not in the following year, to which it is assigned in all collections of councils.

At that council Wilfrid was restored to his episcopate, and he returned to England in the following year, 679.

There is something in this last assertion that compels me to differ from C. V. He understands the council at which he says Wilfrid was acquitted to be the council discussed above, which we assigned to 678 on the basis of certain indications. I am glad to find so learned a man agreeing with me on this point. Yet I do not see how this can be the council at which Wilfrid was both acquitted and seated among the fathers, since his acquittal at one synod resulted in his sitting at the other Roman synod.

Nor can we doubt which council this was, since, while he was present at it—the council whose letter is read in act 4 of the Sixth Synod—Wilfrid himself subscribed as follows:

> “Wilfrid, humble bishop of the holy Church of the island of York in Britain, legate of the venerable synod constituted throughout Britain, have likewise subscribed to this petition, which we unanimously composed on behalf of our apostolic faith.”

The Malmesbury author therefore most appropriately distinguished the two Roman synods in these words:

> “Glorying in these decrees, the bishop was also ordered, by command of the pope, to sit among the 150 holy bishops who were conducting a council against those who proclaimed one operation in the two natures of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

It is therefore clear that this Roman synod, at which Wilfrid sat and to which he subscribed as legate of the British synod, could not have been held before the beginning of the year 680. The synod of Hatfield, presided over by Theodore the archbishop and held against the heresies of Eutyches and the Monothelites, is said to have been held:

> “Under Ecgfrith, king of the Northumbrians, in the tenth year of his reign, on 17 September, indiction 8; and under Æthelred, king of the Mercians, in the sixth year of his reign; and under Æthelwald, king of the East Angles, in the seventeenth year of his reign; and under Lothair, king of the Kentish people, in the seventh year of his reign.”
