That synod therefore began on 13 September 679, when the eighth indiction had begun. It was only after several months that what had been decreed there, and that Wilfrid had been appointed its legate, could have been heard at Rome. By virtue of these decisions he sat as legate of the same British synod at the Roman council in 680, after which he returned to England.

It is worth observing that the British synod was prolonged for some time after Wilfrid had been designated as legate, since the fathers of the Roman synod, in their synodical letter to the emperor Constantine, imply that it had not yet been dismissed. In explaining, among other things, the cause of the lengthy delay, they write:

> “We were also hoping to bring from Britain to our humility Theodore, our fellow servant and fellow bishop, archbishop and philosopher of the great island of Britain, together with the others who have remained there up to the present, and so forth.”

The second Roman synod must therefore be assigned to the beginning of the year 680, the synod at which Wilfrid sat as legate of Britain.

To this same period must also be referred the sound counsel of Theodore, bishop of Ravenna, and of his suffragan bishops. By this counsel he restored himself and his Church to Catholic unity, something his predecessor, prevented by death, had been unable to complete. He enjoyed such honor among the other metropolitans that he alone sent a legate of his Church to Constantinople. This legate attended the Sixth Synod and sat immediately after the legates of the Roman synod, as is proved by the acts of that Constantinopolitan synod.

These matters had to be examined carefully in order to establish the dates of Reparatus and Theodore. Once this chronological knot is untied, everything else presents no difficulty and fits together properly.

As a conclusion to all these matters and to the entire dissertation, I had intended to subject here to examination the decree issued by Constans, father of Constantine Pogonatus, in favor of Bishop Maurus, and to submit its dates to critical scrutiny. I think, however, that these matters should more appropriately be reserved for discussion in the observations appended to the Life of Maurus, where the text of that decree will also be given.

# Life of Bonus

## Single Chapter

Images of the bishops of Ravenna. A second exhortation to the bishops. The death and tomb of Bonus.

### Bonus XXXIII

This man was Bonus both in name and in deeds: gaunt and ruddy in appearance, with a head smooth of hair, adorned with grayness, and full of every grace.

And if someone should perhaps reflect privately, or ask others, how this man could know what the appearances of these holy men had been—whether they were gaunt or fat—let no doubt arise from this, because painting reveals their faces to me.

From his time the afflictions of the nations began to increase and their waves to dash against one another. But this man, accustomed to prayer, did not cease continually to offer prayers to God. He prayed for the faithful, that they might be perfected; for the unbelievers, that they might attain grace, because before the world is destroyed, all will hasten to Christ.

Hear David:

> “Let all the tribes of the earth remember and turn to the Lord, and they shall worship before the sight of the nations.”

See how, before the day of judgment, the whole world will follow Christ and will worship the one living God for ever and ever.

Speak also the rest, O king:

> “And all the kings of the earth shall worship him, and all kings shall serve him.”

And the apostle Paul cries out:

> “Until the fullness of the nations has entered, and thus all Israel will be saved.”

And why do they not believe now? Because their hearts have been hardened and their inward parts closed. The veil that Moses had over his face has been fixed upon their hearts.

And if they have a veiled heart, how then does Ezekiel cry out:

> “I will take the stony heart from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh, and you shall know that I am the Lord”?

They have been given hearts of flesh, but that hardness continually increases in them.

Hear the Apostle:

> “But according to your hardness and impenitent heart, you are treasuring up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of the just judgment of God, who will repay each according to his works.”

Hear the Truth itself concerning their hardness:

> “God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham.”

With God all things are possible. And why did he not raise them up? If he wished to do so, who contradicted him? When, as the sole giver [or: ruler] of all, he raised up the holy apostles, who were descended from Abraham, you became their imitators and bear their likeness.

Remember carefully, I beg you, inspectors of the holy Church: although you occupy an exalted seat, you are nevertheless mortal—always anxious, always fearful.

Hear through the prophet:

> “You shall die like men, and fall like one of the princes.”

And the son of the aforesaid prophet says:

> “Blessed is the man who is always fearful; but he whose mind is hard will fall into misfortune.”

This most blessed prelate died on 26 August, in a good old age, and was buried in peace in the basilica of Saint Apollinaris the priest and martyr at Classe. He sat [as bishop] for [lacuna] years, [lacuna] months, [lacuna] days.

## Observations on the Life of Bonus

Images of bishops customarily placed in churches. Likewise, images of the Augusti. The beginning of the incursions of the Saracens.

### I.

There is scarcely anything in the Life of this pontiff that deserves observation. Since our author has nothing to narrate about Bonus, he turns, as is his custom, to the vices of his own times.

The author’s credibility is supported to some extent by the fact that, lest anyone doubt the bodily appearance of each bishop whom he habitually describes, he says that he learned it from their likenesses expressed in paintings.

Although—as we learn from this *Pontifical Book* of Agnellus—at least from the time of Valentinian and Martianus, the predecessors of Bonus, images of bishops were customarily painted in basilicas and their porticoes as a mark of honor, this practice seems to have become more solemn around the time of Bonus. At that time orthodox bishops, just as they were inscribed in the diptychs, also occupied a place in sacred buildings through their painted images.

Hence Anastasius, in the Life of Agatho, says that at the Sixth Synod, after the Monothelites had been condemned, the fathers:

> “Removed from the diptychs of the churches the names of the patriarchs, and from the church paintings their figures, removing them also from the doors where they might have been—namely, those of Cyrus, Sergius, Paul, Pyrrhus, and Peter, through whom the error against the orthodox faith had until then continued to sprout.”

Concerning John VII he likewise says:

> “He also made images throughout various churches, and whoever wishes to know them will find their likeness painted there.”

Honor of this kind was also paid to the Augusti of both sexes. This is shown in various places, both elsewhere and at Ravenna, by the many examples reported throughout this *Pontifical Book*, beginning with the times of Valentinian and Placidia, and later by the acts of Bishop Damianus.

These matters are also readily illuminated by the history of the Iconoclast heresy, which disturbed the Church in the eighth century.

### II.

When our author says that “from the time of this bishop” the afflictions of the nations began, it is plainly evident from what follows that he is referring to the beginnings of the Muhammadan sect and to the armed incursions of the Arabs against the Roman Empire, bringing destruction upon Spain and Italy.

These attacks, however, afflicted Ravenna later. See Baronius under the year 630 and following years.

# Life of Maurus the Schismatic

> [Note: Here, pious reader, you must detest the unspeakable crime of the bishop of Ravenna, than which nothing more unjust can be found in ecclesiastical history. But observe also Agnellus’s perverse mind, since he recounts these matters in such a manner that he himself displays his schismatic character and hostility toward the Roman See. Learn from this how much credence he deserves, whether when he praises Maurus, or when below he attacks and persecutes Theodore and assails the most holy pontiffs with calumnies. It will be useful for me to have warned you of this briefly. BACCH.]

## Chapter I

Maurus the deacon and abbot of Saint Bartholomew. Having become bishop, he contends with the Roman pontiff.

### Maurus XXXIV

This man was strong in bodily power. He was a deacon of this Church, its steward [*oeconomus*], and abbot of the monastery of Saint Bartholomew. There, as you see, I now am, by God’s favor, having received it after the resignation of Sergius, my paternal cousin.

This man, as I have said, after becoming pontiff, had many troubles with the Roman pontiff, many conflicts, many upheavals, and many disputes. He went to Constantinople many times in order to turn his Church away from the yoke or authority of the Romans.

And so it happened: the Church of Ravenna was withdrawn from that authority, so that thereafter the pontiffs of the See of Ravenna would never go to Rome for consecration. The future pastor of the Church of Ravenna would neither have that government imposed upon him nor ever be under the authority of the Roman pontiff. Instead, his own three bishops would consecrate the man he had elected, and he would receive the pallium from the emperor of Constantinople.

If we were to travel through many distant regions and narrate in order how this happened, or for what reason and by what devices, then, if we wished to recount everything, I would expend paper and ink, while you, waiting, would grow weary.

He was a deacon and steward of this Church. He held the monastery of Blessed Bartholomew the apostle, where I seem to be abbot, [lacuna].

## Chapter II

Benedict the deacon, administrator of Sicily. The wealth of the Sicilian patrimony belonging to the Church of Ravenna. The steward sent again to Sicily and returning rich.

He therefore sent to his administrator in Sicily, named Benedict, a deacon who at that time managed the affairs and possessions of the Church of Ravenna, his steward, wishing to appoint him administrator of Sicily by letter, saying:

> “Your service has pleased us sufficiently. You have grown old; return to the holy mother Church where you were raised. It is now time for me to see you. Appoint this steward of ours as administrator after you. If possible, do not let this admonition of ours be burdensome to you; but if this matter is burdensome, see how you can send him back to us.”

But he, knowing the pontiff’s wishes, honored him with various gifts and presents: gold, silver, desirable vessels, and many other things. When they had been escorted to the ship, they kissed one another, and, bidding farewell, he gave him three hundred gold pieces and sent him back wealthy to his pontiff.

Then the aforesaid deacon Benedict returned to Sicily. From there he sent fifty thousand *modii* of wheat in laden ships, without any other grain or legumes; red-dyed ram skins; hyacinth-colored chasubles and silk-decorated copes; other garments; vessels of brass and silver; and thirty-one thousand gold solidi.

Of these, he carried fifteen thousand to the palace at Constantinople and sixteen thousand to the church treasury. This payment was made every year, while the pontiff always consumed the wheat at his table.

When the steward returned, he told the pontiff everything that had happened, reported the gifts that had been bestowed upon him, and gave thanks for the absent man.

After the third year, he again sent the man who had previously gone to Sicily to the aforesaid deacon, taking the opportunity to have him make an addition to the garden he possessed, so that he might reward him again. He also sent word that, if he could not settle the matter, lest anyone encroach upon it, he should even proceed to Constantinople and appeal to the emperor.

But after reading the letter sent to him, he received him honorably and said to him:

> “As for the garden in question, tell my lord that we have it. Tomorrow let us go there, and I will arrange the matter for which you were sent in such a way that you will never wish to come to Sicily again.”

He gave him much silver and very many weights of gold. Thereafter, once he reached Ravenna, he had no need to sail back to Sicily.

## Chapter III

Maurus, summoned by the pontiff to Rome, refuses to go. Punished with an anathema, he dares to pronounce an anathema against the Roman pontiff. The death of both.

At that time it happened that the Roman pope sent a delegation to him, asking him to go to Rome, since he wished to subject him to his authority.

He received the letter, read it, and folded it, saying to the legates of the Apostolic See:

> “What is this that you are attempting to do? Has it not been established and confirmed by oath between us that neither he against me or my Church, nor his future successors against my successors, would trouble us? He has my signed document, and I retain his, together with everything written between us and confirmed by the hands of my priests and his. The page containing the decree was confirmed in his own hands. You yourselves also wrote letters there. I do not consent to these commands. Return to the one who sent you and report what you have heard.”

They returned and reported in order what had happened.

Then the pope, enraged, ordered a letter to be written, binding him with the bonds of an anathema. He subscribed it with his own hand, declaring that, if Maurus the archbishop did not come to the Apostolic See, he would not have permission to celebrate Mass, no one would be permitted to enter into communion with him, no cleric would adhere to him, he would not approach the holy altar with him, and no offering would be made with him or on his behalf.

Whoever was so rash as not to observe these commands would be bound by Jewish bonds and excluded from the kingdom of God.

The legates of the Roman See carried all these provisions in the letter and presented them to Maurus, pontiff of the city of Ravenna.

When Maurus the bishop received it, he read the most sorrowful letter. He too, filled with anger—not, perhaps, with the appearance of madness, but as though seized by an irreversible fury—ordered a similar letter to be written, imposing an anathema, so that that pope would have no permission to celebrate Mass, just as he himself did not.

He ordered his letter to be written in imitation of the Roman letter and sent it to the aforementioned pope at Rome. After reading it, the pope threw it away from him, then ordered it to be collected again.

After this he wished to send legates to Constantinople to the emperor, so that he might compel Maurus the archbishop to go to a council at Rome, and so that he might learn how Maurus had dared to send his master a letter of anathema.

In such a state of mutual condemnation both men died.

From that day, offerings were made for him neither at Rome nor here for this man. Instead, every week, on Thursday, after the evening office had been completed, the priests, deacons, subdeacons, and clerics gathered, entered the sacristy, and divided among themselves a morsel of bread, a single sausage each, and a cup of wine.

The priest, or whoever was first in rank, said:

> “May the Lord God grant eternal rest to the soul of him in whose memory we have taken these things.”

The others replied:

> “May God command it.”

After these words they departed.

Some say that, after their deaths and after much time had passed, this case was discussed at Rome in a council. By the providence of the bishops, as though for their deposition, the tips of their right feet were cut off. So it happened to that one, and so to this one.

At the hour of his death he summoned all his priests, weeping before them, asking forgiveness, and said to them:

> “I am entering the way of death. I charge and warn you: do not place yourselves under the Roman yoke. Choose a pastor from among yourselves, and let him be consecrated by his own bishops. Ask the emperor for the pallium, for on whatever day you are subjected to Rome, you will no longer be whole.”

After saying these things, he died and was buried in the portico (*ardica*) of Blessed Apollinaris.

## Chapter IV

The tombstone. Lothair Augustus carried it away to Gaul. The body of Saint Apollinaris transferred from the chapel to the middle of the basilica. The epitaph of Maurus.

There was there a stone of wondrous burial, a most precious and exceedingly bright porphyry stone, like glass, before the aforementioned tomb.

When the doors facing the church of Saint Severus were opened, anyone who looked at that stone could see in it, as in a mirror, whatever passed before it—human beings, animals, birds, or any other things—as though in a mirror containing an enigma.

But nearly twelve years later, in the time of the pontiff Petronax, Lothair Augustus ordered it to be removed. He enclosed it in a wooden chest upon wool, carried it to Francia, and placed it above the altar as the table of Saint Sebastian.

The pontiff commanded me to go there, lest the stone be broken through the careless actions of the masons. But, with my heart filled with grief, I withdrew to another place.

This man then took the body of Saint Apollinaris, which had long before been buried in its portico (*ardica*) by Bishop Maximianus together with Julian the silversmith, and placed it in the middle of the church. He also attached the history of that martyr to silver plates.

Above it you will find an epitaph written as follows:

> First Faith—and the Father had long promised to our people—  
>   
> that Christ would be seen by their eyes and called by the voice of the law.  
>   
> Celebrating Christ, he sounds forth Christ; everything is Christ.  
>   
> O exceedingly sweet name of Maurus the pontiff, light and glory,  
>   
> and our protection, certain rest from our labors!  
>   
> A pleasant taste upon the lips, fragrant odor, irrigating fountain,  
>   
> chaste love, beautiful appearance, sincere pleasure [or: will].  
>   
> If a deaf people denies you so many praises,  
>   
> you have seen so many voices and elements of things [or: such great things],  
>   
> high, accompanied by angelic hosts,  
>   
> where the final, immeasurable expanse extends.  
>   
> For, running [lacuna] by steps and bringing worthy rewards to the seated king,  
>   
> [lacuna] which carried you so joyfully,  
>   
> you rightly failed to be among the first followers of those eloquences.  
>   
> As lofty as your lineage is, so lofty is the glory of your speech.  
>   
> Untainted love, praises of a chaste life.  
>   
> Gracious in speech, good in character, eloquent in word.  
>   
> Vows approved by God and favorable to the holy through your merits—  
>   
> all that you wished for, prosperous, which [lacuna], and likewise.  
>   
> Whatever you desired [lacuna] happened, as you wished.  
>   
> Believed to restore human lives by the art of healing,  
>   
> therefore this reverence for your completed life remains.  
>   
> By your virtues you raised your seat to the summit,  
>   
> and, holding apostolic wreaths, you placed it in its proper rights.  
>   
> Even now you remain peaceful, withdrawn into pious care,  
>   
> and now you are continually felt beneath the honor of the tomb.  
>   
> The turbid corruption of the father, of the flesh being born [fragment; syntax uncertain].

You will find Christ, the offspring; [you will find] the parent from the heart [sense uncertain]. And before that ark you will find, engraved in mosaic on the pavement, the following inscription:

> Here rests in peace Maurus, archbishop, who lived approximately sixty-seven years and, in the time of the Lord Emperor Constantine, freed his Church from the yoke of Roman servitude. He sat [as bishop] for 28 years, 10 months, and 18 days.

[Note: [Col. 0673D] *P. M.*, that is, “more or less.” BACCH.]

# Observations on the Life of Maurus the Schismatic

The steward of the church, called *vicedominus* in Latin. Abbots among the clergy. The abbey of Saint Bartholomew at Ravenna. The sees of the bishops of Ravenna in synods. The decree obtained from Constantine by Maurus. The chronology is corrected; the succession of exarchs is supplemented from it. Autocephaly arose and passed into schism. Agnellus refuted.

## I

Maurus, whom Agnellus himself—although sufficiently impatient of Roman authority—plainly indicates to have been a man of exceedingly crafty intelligence, had been steward of the Church of Ravenna before becoming bishop. The Greeks called such a man an *oikonomos*, the Latins a *vicedominus*: one who, at the bishop’s and clergy’s direction, was appointed to administer the church’s revenues and distribute them according to the canon, and who was required to render accounts of them.

It is established that this office was instituted only after churches began to possess, in addition to the offerings of the faithful, extensive estates and immovable property, whose revenues seemed scarcely manageable by the clergy without distracting them from the ministries of divine things. Accordingly, by decrees of several councils—the earliest being the Council of Chalcedon, canon 25 and 26—it was established that in each church this office should be entrusted to a layman chosen by the clergy, who was afterward appointed by the bishop.

On this subject see Jacobus Gothofredus on the title *De bonis clericorum* in the Theodosian Code, where the law of Theodosius and Valentinian, issued on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of January during the consulship of Ariovindus and Aspa[r], calls the stewards of churches *oeconomi*. Thus, when that law was promulgated, namely in the year 434, an office of this kind was already in use.

From the time of Bishop Ecclesius, however, the office of steward in the Church of Ravenna was already divided among several members of the clergy. That the bishop entrusted it to them is shown by the letter of Pope Felix; their office is explained in the following terms:

> “As for the patrimony of the church, according to the judgment of their bishop, [lacuna] persons chosen from the clergy, together with the allowances which the bishop shall assign for their support, are to be sent under suitable surety, their fidelity and diligence having been proved, so that the provision for the poor may suffer no fraud, the amount of the church’s patrimony may not remain concealed, and each cleric, in the fear of God and of his own priest, may faithfully render an account of the things entrusted to him.”

## II

Maurus was not only steward of the Church of Ravenna but also abbot of Saint Bartholomew; Agnellus himself was honored with that office after his uncle’s resignation, as we learn from this passage.

Moreover, it is more widely known than would require Sarnellus’s efforts to establish it in his Italian treatise entitled *On the Common Life of Clerics* that the name “abbot” did not always designate a monastery and monks, and that many churches enjoyed the title of abbey although from their beginning they had belonged to clerics.

Several monuments of a later age remind us of this fact. We also know that the name “abbot” passed in many different ways not only from monks to clerics but also to laymen. See Ducange in his *Glossary of Latinity*.

In any case, I think that this abbey of Saint Bartholomew, like the other abbey of Saint Mary at Blachernae, over which Agnellus likewise presided, contained clerics rather than monks, although it is called a monastery; for it has already been noted what the word “monastery” signifies in our author.

The historians of Ravenna say nothing about the abbey of Saint Bartholomew, nor about the title bestowed upon Maurus and our Agnellus. Faber, in his *Sacred Monuments of Ravenna*, identifies two churches at Ravenna consecrated under the name of Saint Bartholomew. One of them still survives, though it is not of great renown, despite being known from the year 1262, when Pope Urban IV, by a charter, confirmed it to the canons of Ravenna and confirmed their right over it.

Saint Mary at Blachernae, whose abbot was Agnellus, was the church now called Saint Mary of Palatiolum, joined to the monastery of Saint Vitalis of the Cassinese monks, not far from Ravenna. Agnellus himself indicates this fairly clearly in the Life of John Angeloptus, chapter 3.

The other church of Saint Bartholomew stood where there is now the elegant church dedicated to Saint Romuald, together with the distinguished monastery of Camaldolese cenobites. Which of these two churches of Saint Bartholomew should be commended as the one whose abbots were Maurus and Agnellus is difficult to determine.

I would more readily give my vote to the first, since it lies about a mile outside the city walls. For I do not think that abbots of this kind administered churches within the city of Ravenna in those times; nor do I doubt that this church had anciently belonged to the rights of the canons.

But enough of these matters, which we have also discussed in the preface.

## III

It is remarkable that Agnellus omitted the earlier deeds commendably performed by Maurus during his episcopate. But the writer who judged that bishop worthy of praise for the very act by which he earned universal hatred among posterity—namely, his attempted autocephaly—did not see that the earlier deeds agreed with the later ones, nor that the later ones answered to the former, since Maurus had previously acknowledged his Church’s subjection to the Roman Church and then knowingly and willingly attempted to make it independent.

The acts of that council testify to the outstanding service rendered by Maurus in the Lateran Council under the most holy pontiff Martin for the suppression of the Monothelite heresy, through Maurus, bishop of Cesena, and Deusdedit, presbyter of the Church of Ravenna. Rubeus discusses these matters at length in Book IV, under the year 649.

From the first secretary of that synod, which has been praised above, it is clear that Maurus’s legates were counted third in the list of bishops, namely after Maximus, bishop of Aquileia, and Deusdedit, bishop of Cagliari; yet, when the sentence was being delivered, they spoke first of all.

No one, however, can fail to see that the order of precedence should more reasonably be inferred from the place in which each person delivered his sentence—a fact certain from the surviving acts—than from the list of subscribing bishops, which could have been altered through the fault of copyists.

Rubeus treats the matter explicitly and learnedly in his *History of Ravenna*, Book V, pages 283–284, under the year 1040. There he reports that Clement II held a celebrated council at Rome, whose acts have nevertheless perished. At that council, on the advice of the Fathers, it was decreed in what they call a contradictory judgment against the bishops of Aquileia and Milan that the bishop of Ravenna should sit on the right hand of the pontiff when the emperor was absent, but on the left when he was present, by virtue of the ancient right of the Church of Ravenna.

This right, he says, was not compromised by the fact that the former bishop Peter, in the age of Pope Symmachus, had sat after the bishop of Milan at Roman synods, since Pope John, the successor of Symmachus, left written testimony that this had occurred because of Peter’s moderation.

Rubeus says that he saw Clement’s charter in the archive of Saint Vitalis at Ravenna. Ughellus reproduces it from the Ravenna archive, and Cardinal Noris includes certain portions of it in his dissertation on the Fifth Synod. An exemplar of the charter also exists in the Estense Codex, which contains Agnellus’s book, and is followed by the testimonies of the notaries:

> “I, Ubaldus, Ravenna notary and notary of the Church of Ravenna, having seen and read it in the original, have written it accordingly.”

> “I, Artusinus, and Bartolinus, and Camelius of the Artusini, have seen the original privilege, sealed with the seal of the Lord Pope Clement.”

> “And I, Paulus Scordili of Candia, doctor of decrees and provost of the Church of Ravenna, have seen and read that privilege in the original, and have seen it sealed with an apostolic lead seal, though not in the manner of the other apostolic seals.”

Paulus Scordili is the very man to whom we owe the Lives of several bishops of Ravenna, to be added in an appendix. On the different forms of leaden seals, see Mabillon, *On Diplomatics*, Book II, chapter 14, no. 10.

## IV

But, to return to our subject: after reporting the offices held by Maurus before his episcopate, Agnellus immediately proceeds to the quarrels he had with the Roman pontiff. Although he does not praise that pontiff, chronological calculations show that he was Vitalian.

He indicates that Maurus devoted several years to conducting and advancing these affairs. Having found in the impious emperor Constans a ruler much like himself—one who, after recently perpetrating many outrages against Saint Martin, the Roman pontiff, was nevertheless tolerated by the Romans in many matters of prudential policy—Maurus brought to completion the plan he had conceived for the autocephaly of his Church, and ultimately achieved his desire, to his own destruction and that of his people.

In the same Estense Codex that contains Agnellus’s book there is a decree of Constans, as it was called. I think it worthwhile to transcribe its text here, since from it a not insignificant light shines upon our understanding of the Ravenna schism and upon the elucidation of Agnellus.

It is regrettable that, through the fault of the copyist, the document is deformed in many places, so that in some passages scarcely any convenient meaning can be extracted; I have despaired of restoring all the corrupt readings. Here it is, exactly as it stands.

### Privilege of the Emperors Constantine [Constans, Bacch.] Eradius [and Heraclius, same source] to Maurus, bishop of Ravenna

> “The perceptive and faithful mind of Your Holiness, which, in relation to our pious empire, [Note: [Col. 0675D] Something is missing.] has hitherto displayed the work itself, has often demonstrated [has deserved, same source] our piety; and because it exercises its purpose toward our service with greater and still greater vigor, not only through the report of our glorious exarch, by which he indicates the assistance granted to him, but also through the report of Your Holiness, sent by Reparatus, the priest beloved of God and steward, by which you also ask that we should become much greater protectors of the province of Italy, beloved of Christ, and of its holy Church of Ravenna.

> “Therefore, just as it is the duty of a good shepherd who cares for the flock entrusted to him, so also for this reason we have ordered, by our pious command, that a suitable arrangement be made for the welfare of our province of Italy, beloved of Christ, and we exhort Your Holiness in all things for our service [lacuna] to maintain.

> “But since he has also requested protection for his Church, we believe that he has now been satisfied, because nothing has been neglected that pertains to the welfare, stability, or increase of honor of yourself and your Church. We have fortified it with privileges by which we decreed that it should be removed from the jurisdiction of every greater see and belong to its own jurisdiction, together with its holy Church after it; and we ordered that it remain perpetually firm, stable, and unshaken.

> “Even now, for the sake of greater readiness [clarity, same source] of mind, through this our present pious command we decree that it remain still more secure and free from every superior episcopal condition, and devote itself solely to prayer for the entreaty of our empire; and that it not be subject in any way to the patriarch of the ancient city of Rome, but remain *αὐτοκέφαλον* [*autokephalon*, ‘autocephalous’], together with its holy Church after it, with everything belonging to it throughout its diocese and parishes, with their ordinators, like the other metropolitans remaining in the various provinces of the state, who are consecrated by their own bishops—namely, by yours—and with the honor of the pallium, just as has been abundantly granted by the sanction of our divinity through heavenly inspiration.

> “For it is necessary that we honor with exceptional devotion those who have devoted themselves earnestly to our service with the whole attention of their minds. What, indeed, is more honorable than those things which we have piously arranged in this way, pertaining to the honor of a priest devoted to us and appearing exceedingly so [a parent, same source]? [The text is corrupt.]

> “We exhort Your Paternal Beatitude to pray unceasingly to Almighty God for the expansion of the Roman state entrusted to us by His majesty.

> “So be it. The emperor’s letter. Given on the Kalends of March at Syracuse; while our most pious and perpetual Augusti, our lords, Constantine [Constans, same source] the elder was emperor in the twenty-fifth year of his reign and in the fourteenth year after his consulship, and the new Constantine, Heraclius [Heraclius, same source], and Tiberius, sons preserved by God; Constantine indeed in the fourteenth year, and Heraclius and Tiberius in the seventh.”

## V

The first matter requiring correction in the document just quoted was the series of chronological indications, corrupted by the copyist.

Since it is said to have been issued at Syracuse, it must belong to one of the three years between 664 and 668, during which Constans remained in Sicily. For from Paul the Deacon, Book V, chapter 11, we know that “he entered Sicily in the seventh indiction” and lived at Syracuse.

Although Theophanes, when calculating the period during which Constans conducted the war against the Lombards in Italy and was at Rome, says that he remained six years in Sicily, he also explains why he left Constantinople: namely, because, fearing for himself, he had considered transferring the imperial residence to Rome.

Paul, in the same passage, reports that Constans remained at Syracuse until the twelfth indiction. This is correct, for he was killed around November of the year 668, when the twelfth indiction had already begun to be counted. Nor does this conflict with Anastasius or Theophanes, as it seemed to Baronio.

For Anastasius extends the eleventh indiction to the next Kalends of January, and this fits well with the twenty-seventh year of the emperor’s reign, marked by Theophanes under the twelfth indiction.

I believe that the charter belongs to the year 666, since of the four chronological indications given, two agree with that year, and according to them the other two must be corrected.

The twenty-fifth year of Constans’s reign and the seventh year of the reigns of Heraclius and Tiberius agree with that year. Therefore the post-consular year must be corrected to 23, and in place of the fourteenth year of Constantine must be restored the twelfth year, which was still in progress but would end in the following month.

The calculations should be undertaken according to the principles set out in the preceding dissertation. Constans’s name has been mistakenly changed to Constantine; this is a common blunder in documents of those times, as appears from the collection of the councils by Labbe.

## VI

From this charter we learn that Gregory was exarch at Ravenna in the year 666 mentioned above, and that the tenure of office of Theodore Calliopas had ended.

We were astonished that the period of this exarch should have lasted from the year 650 to 686, namely thirty-six years. To determine the periods of these men, one must observe that Maurus appears in this charter to have been striving to make himself agreeable to the emperor, and to have arranged matters so that he would make the exarch well disposed toward him, seizing the opportunities supplied by those times.

Among these opportunities, I have no doubt that the most favorable was the Romans’ hatred of Constans because of his impious abduction and deportation of Saint Martin. Maurus could therefore undertake measures that contributed greatly to keeping his extensive diocese of Ravenna in its duty.

It is also probable that Constans, in order to avert the unpopularity of the deed, not only ratified the election of Vitalian, who succeeded Eugene as pope, but, as Anastasius reports, renewed the privileges and sent back the legates who had been courteously received. At the same time, he wished them to carry to Saint Peter as a gift “golden Gospels adorned around the circumference with white gems of marvelous size.”

It is probable, I say, that he removed Theodore Calliopas, of whom no further mention is found, from the exarchate and substituted Gregory.

I infer that this occurred during the pontificate of Eugene, when Constans recognized that the Romans were sufficiently hostile both to himself and to the exarch, from their unanimous persistence in rejecting the synodical letter of Peter, patriarch of Constantinople, “which,” says Anastasius in his Life of Eugene, “was cast out from the Holy Church of God with great uproar.” They did not permit the pontiff to celebrate Mass in the basilica of the Blessed Virgin before he had promised that he would never receive that letter.

Thus I think that Calliopas was recalled around the year 658 and Gregory substituted in his place. Maurus would immediately have led Gregory to prepare himself for Maurus’s wishes, taking advantage of the emperor’s hostility toward the Roman pontiffs and his fear of Lombard power, which caused him to consider crossing into Italy with an army.

After this Gregory, Theodore—another man besides Calliopas—was appointed. He was at Ravenna while Theodore was bishop, as will be shown below, and remained in office until the year 686.

The fact that a new exarch was sent after the death of Constans leads me to believe that, generally speaking, whenever the Augusti began to rule alone, they recalled the man who had administered the province under their predecessor and sent another into the province. Thus Smaragdus was sent by Maurice; Smaragdus again by Phocas; John Demiges, or Remiges, by Heraclius; and Theodore Calliopas by Constans.

For these reasons I believe that this younger Theodore held better counsels than Calliopas and Gregory. While he was in office, the Church of Ravenna acknowledged the right of the Roman pontiff and returned to his unity.

## VII

My first duty here is to refute as contrary to the truth what Agnellus relates, when he falsely suggests that a written agreement was once concluded between Maurus and the most holy Roman pontiff.

> “Was it not established,” he makes Maurus say to the legates of the Apostolic See, “and confirmed by oath, that neither he should trouble me or my Church, nor his descendants [should trouble] my successors?”

Now Vitalian was one who deserved to be recorded among the saints in the ecclesiastical registers. It is therefore certain that in defending the rights of the Roman Church he possessed a steadfastness corresponding to that reputation—something only an impious man could deny.

We have a particularly notable proof of this virtue in his first letter to Paul, archbishop of Crete. There he severely rebukes him for having attempted to restrain John, bishop of Lappa, who had appealed to him, contrary to the canons. He also absolved John, who had been unjustly treated by that metropolitan, in a synod convened at Rome.

A pontiff of such virtue and holiness, who wished so nobly to defend the right of appeal against the metropolitan of the Eastern Church, and whom Anastasius praises for having “entirely preserved ecclesiastical rule and rigor, as was customary,” could not have neglected his right over the bishop of Ravenna or—something unworthy of belief—consented to such an agreement to the detriment of his Church.

He resisted, indeed, and, driving the sword of excommunication into Maurus’s throat, undertook with great courage to remove the beginnings of the autocephaly unlawfully established by the emperor Constans. Agnellus himself bears witness to this.

Constans, although unanimously regarded as an impious Monothelite, pretended to be Catholic in order to win the favor of the pontiff, as the circumstances of those times and of Italy required. Although for that same reason, through the agency of the exarch Gregory, he granted the decree of autocephaly in order to bind the archbishop of Ravenna to himself, he did not attempt to force Vitalian to consent. He feared that, for this reason, Vitalian would become alienated from him.

I think this can be inferred from the very decree of Constans that we have presented: it would not have been issued if Vitalian had surrendered his right in his own cause through a written agreement and oath, or if, after the pontiff’s surrender, the emperor had nevertheless thought that the same arrangement needed to be confirmed by his own edict. In that case, he would have mentioned the pontiff’s consent.

I believe that this sort of decree is indicated by Anastasius under the name of the *typos*, when, under Leo II, during the reign of Pogonatus, it was finally “restored for the removal of scandals from the Apostolic See; for, when the imperial command of the most merciful prince had been circulated, the Church of Ravenna was restored under the authority of the Apostolic See.”

This is further confirmed by the fact that we know the term *typos* was commonly used to signify imperial constitutions; on this point Ducange cites this very passage of Anastasius in his *Glossary*.

From this and other statements of Anastasius we understand what Maurus dared to do and from whom he obtained what he obtained: namely, autocephaly. It was granted not by the pontiff but by Constans, and by it Maurus was not exempted from that right by which the pontiff presides over the whole Church, but from patriarchal jurisdiction—that is, the ancient metropolitan jurisdiction under which, from the beginning of the Church, there had been one metropolitan in the West. I believe this has been sufficiently established in my dissertation *On the Origin of the Hierarchy*.

Maurus considered himself to have achieved his desire through the power of the secular authority, and, hoping that he could defend himself by the same means, immediately felt the pontiff as an avenger when he was summoned to obedience under threat of anathema.

But, a proud and obstinate man, he dared with horrible audacity to pronounce anathema against the pontiff himself and fell into schism.

Theodore completely rescued the Church of Ravenna from the schism, and under Leo II every pretext for autocephaly was removed when the *typos*—that is, the decree of Constans—was restored.

## VIII

Nevertheless, in the Church of Ravenna there remained something of the old obstinacy: the clergy believed that account had to be taken of the anathema which Maurus, in the utmost wickedness, had hurled against the Roman pontiff.

For this reason they did not believe that Vitalian’s name should be recited in the sacrifice at the altar. Agnellus rightly relates that in the secretarium,

> “every week, on Thursday, after the evening service had been completed,”

the clergy assembled and, having received

> “a morsel of bread, a sausage for each, and a cup of wine,”

prayed well for the soul of the deceased, asking the Lord to grant it eternal rest.

I certainly see in this something that I condemn with horror. I do not think that the Roman pontiff could, without error, have been struck by anathema through any prelate whatsoever, regardless of his dignity.

For the rest, if anyone regards these actions as having been performed in contempt of pontifical dignity for some cause other than the one mentioned above, he will certainly have reason to join me in blaming the rashness of the clergy of Ravenna.

But if anyone thinks that these matters too were falsely reported to Agnellus from the rumors of wicked men, he will find me most willing to agree with him, since I would wish the reputation of the most noble Church of Ravenna to be defended everywhere from such accusations.

As for the rumor that a certain council decreed something concerning censures of this kind, imposed on both sides, though with unequal effect, and what is meant by “with the shoe of the right foot cut off”—just as I willingly and deliberately confess that I do not understand it, so I believe it should be counted among old wives’ tales and the distorted rumors of the common people.

Since I despaired of correcting the epitaph transcribed at the end of the Life, I copied it as it lay in the manuscript. The rest is sufficiently clear, especially what concerns the Sicilian patrimony. It would be desirable to know by what name the enormous annual payment of fifteen thousand gold pieces to the court of Constantinople was made.

# Life of Reparatus

[Col. 0679]

## Single Chapter

The offices of Reparatus. He obtains many things from the emperor. A safeguard that an elected bishop of Ravenna should not remain at Rome for more than eight days. The images of Reparatus and the emperors. Complaints against the bishops of his time.

### Reparatus XXXV

He was already advanced in age, and his emaciated likeness was in the Church of the Blessed Peter. He was ordained bishop at Ravenna by three of his suffragan bishops, as is the Roman custom for consecrating a pontiff.

He was taken from the monastery of Saint Apollinaris here at Ravenna, not far from the shepherd’s wicket, in a place called Public Mint. From there he became abbot. He was also steward of this church, and after the pontiff likewise held the chief office during the reign of Constantine, the elder brother of Heraclius and Tiberius.

He went to Constantinople and obtained everything he requested from the emperor. Among other matters, they ordered the following decree to be drawn up as a confirmation: no priest, or any cleric who had paid any tax into the public treasury, should have any tax demanded from him—neither a riverbank tax, nor a gate tax, nor a siliquatic tax, nor a toll [no one could or should demand any of these from them].

Again, he established and decreed that neither a church nor a monastery, nor the founder [the commendatory patron] of that church, nor its builders or cross-bearers, should be subject to any judge, tax collector, or other authority, except only the pontiff or the rector of the church.

He also decreed that, at the time of consecration, an elected bishop should not remain at Rome for more than eight days.

He ordered that their likeness and his own be painted in the apse of the Blessed Apollinaris and decorated with various mosaics, and that beneath their feet two metrical verses be written, containing the following:

> Since Reparatus was to be the emperor’s companion in merit,  
> The hall caused its new vestments to shine throughout the ages.

Above the emperor’s head you will find the following inscription:

> Constantine the elder, emperor of Heraclius and Tiberius, [lacuna] emperor.

> A true shepherd, he lived piously with the sheep. [Note: [Col. 0679D] See the Observations, § 2. BACCH.] He did not subject himself to the Roman See. He raised priests from poverty, enriched them, and enlarged the clergy. He did not take away from them, as they do now, but distributed from the lesser resources of the church and increased the greater ones.

> The sheep of the church rejoiced; doctrine flourished. By day and night he kept vigil. He was not filled with greed, not swollen with pride, not exalted, not envious, not a lover of gluttony, not filled with love of money. He rejected *xenodoxia* [*cenodoxia*: vainglory], fled sloth, and despised arrogance.

> Such was he as the Lord said: a true Israelite, in whom there was no deceit.

How can we remember our elders saying such good things about the goodness of the pontiffs, while now we see many evils in them? Those who ought to have repaired a broken vessel themselves break what is sound.

Alas, how many lamentations cover us! How many griefs, and how many tears, weeping, and sobs impede us! Those who ought to pray to God in simplicity of heart blaspheme most of all, and, leaving their sins aside, ask to be delivered from evil shepherds.

That prayer is itself in sin, according to the saying: “And let his prayer become sin.” Yet it is better to be delivered by calling upon God daily than, by remaining silent, to be brought under the hands of the impious.

For it is written: “In tribulation you called upon me, and I delivered you”; and elsewhere: “Call upon me in the day of your tribulation, and I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me.”

Let us hold these promises firmly, because God hears and delivers those who seek him in the time of distress.

Moses was delivered from the hand of Pharaoh by crying out. Hezekiah, by crying out, obtained from heaven an angel who struck down one hundred and eighty-[five] thousand men from the Assyrian camp. Peter was rescued from the hand of Herod by prayer.

Who has implored God, not deceitfully but with all his strength, and has not been rescued from the hands of the enemy?

Hear the Lord saying in the Gospel: “There was a judge in a city who did not fear God and had no regard for man.” A certain widow troubled him every day, saying: “Vindicate me against my adversary,” and so forth.

But the Lord himself said: “Yet will not God avenge his elect, who cry out to him day and night?”

Therefore one must always pray and not grow faint, just as this holy pontiff obtained everything through prayers more than through money.

He died, therefore, and was buried in the Church of the Blessed Apollinaris. His epitaph has been erased. He died, as we have said, on the third day before the Kalends of August. He sat [as bishop] for five years, nine months, and [lacuna] days.

# Observations on the Life of Reparatus

Reparatus worked under Maurus to obtain autocephaly. Taken from a monastery. Which monastery was it from which he was taken? He obtains a privilege from Pogonatus, supporting concord more than autocephaly.

## I

Accordingly, in the first ordination under autocephaly, Reparatus, bishop of Ravenna, was consecrated by three suffragan bishops and received the pallium not from the Roman pontiff but from the emperor.

There was no one among the clergy of Ravenna more suitable than Reparatus to be substituted for Maurus and to continue the undertaking already begun, since he had been the man who had helped Maurus entangle it. He had acted as legate for the bishop under Constans, so that autocephaly might be confirmed by an imperial command; the emperor himself appears as a witness to this matter in the document presented above.

“First he was taken from the monastery of Saint Apollinaris,” says our author. By the word “monastery” he does not here mean what he sometimes means elsewhere, but a monastic cenobium.

It remains uncertain whether he was taken from the monastery of Saint Apollinaris at Classe, since, according to Rubeus, monks were settled there only around the year 755.

Yepesius, however, in *tom. p.*, under the year 595, holds that in the age of Gregory the Great that building was given to monks by Marinianus. If this were established by reliable documents, it would become highly probable that Reparatus had been a monk there from the beginning.

I say, however, that it remains uncertain whether he was taken from the other monastery of Saint Apollinaris, which was at Ravenna, beside that famous basilica which Theodoric built, which Bishop Agnellus reconciled, and which was dedicated to Saint Martin. It is described by our author in the Life of Bishop Agnellus and by Blondus in *Decades*, Part *p.*, Book IV.

Yet this basilica does not seem to have been called by the name of Saint Apollinaris until the time when, around the year 856, the body of Saint Apollinaris was transferred into it from the basilica at Classe.

Faber testifies that monks had lived there from a time beyond memory, and our author seems to indicate which monastery he means by the following words: “at Ravenna, not far from the shepherd’s wicket, in a place called Public Mint.” These words seem to designate a basilica situated within Ravenna.

He rose to the episcopate by the same steps as his predecessor, namely as abbot among the clergy and steward of the Church of Ravenna. Thus the administration of public revenues and ecclesiastical money provided an easy ascent to higher offices.

He became bishop during the reign of Constantine Pogonatus. Since in Agnellus’s Codex “father of Heraclius and Tiberius” had been written corruptly, I judged that “brother” should be read instead, since it is beyond dispute that Pope Vitalian died during the reign of Pogonatus, and therefore Maurus did too.

## II

Agnellus reports that Reparatus was commended to the emperor in the highest esteem and obtained everything he requested; Rubeus and others likewise derive this account from Agnellus.

Among other things, Rubeus says that Reparatus obtained “the liberation of the archbishops of Ravenna from the domination of the Roman pontiff, and that his image, together with the book of their privileges being presented by Caesar Constantine to Reparatus, could be seen in mosaic work in the apse of the church of Saint Apollinaris at Classe.”

This is what he says in Book IV, page 207. On his authority, Baronius gives the same account under the year 669, and Ughellus and Faber repeat it from both writers.

Our author, however, relates something entirely different. The privilege granted by Constantine was one of very extensive immunity from taxes for the bishop and the clerics of the Church of Ravenna, and from lay jurisdiction. Among these clerics the *staurophoros*, or “cross-bearer,” is expressly numbered.

It deserves notice that the emperor’s decree established that an elected bishop of Ravenna should not remain at Rome for more than eight days at the time of his consecration.

The matter therefore concerned the restoration of the Roman pontiff’s original right of consecrating the bishops of Ravenna, on the condition that the consecration could not be delayed beyond the eighth day after the elected bishop’s arrival at Rome and presentation of the decree of election. For this reason it was obtained that the emperor should restrict the period of delay to a fixed number of days.

## III

Whatever may be said about Agnellus’s account, it is certain from Anastasius that, while Reparatus was bishop, the Church of Ravenna was restored to the Roman See. For under Pope Donus we read:

> “During his times the Church of Ravenna, which had separated itself from the Roman Church because of autocephaly, again subjected itself to its former Apostolic See; and the bishop of that Church, Reparatus, immediately afterward, as it pleased God, ended his life.”

Agnellus was wrong, however, to write that what the pontiff had perhaps graciously granted—namely, that an elected bishop of Ravenna should remain at Rome for no more than eight days for the sake of his ordination—had been decreed by the emperor.

Below, in the Life of Theodore, he more appropriately relates this same matter as an agreement between the Roman pontiff and the bishop of Ravenna, with the pontiff certainly consenting out of the greatest generosity and with no mention of the emperor.

But if the matter occurred as Anastasius relates, what do Agnellus’s words about Reparatus mean?

> “A true shepherd, he lived piously with his sheep; he did not subject himself to the Roman See.”

I would seem excessively indulgent toward Agnellus if, in order to make the accounts agree, I attributed the matter to a copyist’s error, saying that when *non* had been written it was copied as though it were absent.

Therefore, if those who are displeased by this explanation accuse Agnellus of openly contradicting himself and reporting mutually incompatible accounts, I will not oppose them.

Although Reparatus returned to obedience and to his senses, his successor Theodore nevertheless wished to be ordained under the pretext of autocephaly by three suffragan bishops. In the end, however, he completely subjected himself and his Church to the Roman pontiff. In this matter Agnellus agrees with Anastasius in the Life of Agatho.

# Life of Theodore

[Note: [Col. 0681D] Here, indeed, Agnellus vents all his fury against Theodore. You should know its cause: namely, Theodore’s return to obedience toward the Roman pontiff. When the bishop wished also to correct the corrupted morals of the clergy of Ravenna, it is not surprising that he gave offense. We should therefore commend Theodore for the very reasons on account of which Agnellus, gnashing his teeth with envy, harasses him with calumnies.]

[Col. 0681]

## Chapter One

The fourth of the ecclesiastical revenues customarily given to the clergy is abolished. Documents favorable to the clergy are collected and consumed by fire.

Theodorus XXXVI. This man was young in age, terrifying in appearance, hideous to behold, and full of every kind of deceit. In the Church of the Apostles at Ravenna he was consecrated by his fellow bishops. Our elders recounted many of his wicked deeds. I wonder how he managed to retain his position for even one day amid his evil actions! Until this man’s accession, the statutes of Ecclesius, established in the time of Pope Felix between the priests and the clergy, remained in force. Let us bring his cruelty into the open. He stole the fourth-part from the clergy. He ordered the written statutes of Ecclesius, which contained these provisions, to be burned. He fixed the weight of loaves and reduced the measures of wine. Thereafter he added many other burdens, which, while I try to proceed to the rest, I cannot set down here with my tearful pen.

In those days, therefore, a severe famine arose throughout this entire land, and he swallowed up the grain of the whole region. When the priests could find no means by which to buy grain, they went to him, begging him to provide them assistance. He summoned the archdeacon, named Theodorus, and likewise the archpriest, also named Theodorus, and said to them:

“Tell the priests of the Church and the entire clergy: Why are you being consumed by the want of famine? If you relinquish the whole fourth-part belonging to the Church and receive for the fourth-part only a gift each year, according to the bishop’s provision, I shall now relieve your want.”

After being long chastised and with the famine growing worse, they consented; and from that time the fourth-part was taken away from the clergy of this church, down to the present day.

He also removed and burned the custom of Ecclesius, which had been written in the individual volumes for each office. One day, while he was sitting in the seat of authority, the priests and clergy were murmuring against him about the custom of Ecclesius, wondering how anyone from the office could have possessed it. Seeing that he had been defeated, he said openly before them all:

“Believe me, sons, for I do not usurp your custom in anything; rather, I increase it.”

And after an undertaking had been given in the assembly of the Church that anyone who found the customs written anywhere should bring them before him, many sheets were brought before him. This pleased him according to the evil contrivance of his heart. He received them as though with joy and, with a serene expression before everyone—but with a most savage wound in his heart—said to them again:

“Search still further, so that you may find them, and let such confirmation be made between me and you that no disputes may ever increase between us [you] and my successors.”

They went away again and searched carefully; as soon as they were able to find the documents, they brought them to him. He deceitfully pretended to examine all the sheets and said to them:

“Go now, so that I may consider with myself how I should confirm this, so that the dispute may never be repeated.”

Then, gathering everything together into separate volumes, he burned it all in the furnace of this bathhouse [fire]. Thus did this bishop commit such perjuries against his own sheep and deceive them by wicked trickery. Would that he had held neither the shepherd’s chair nor even the place of a hired servant! In his seat he was a wolf among the flock, a lion among four-footed beasts, a hawk (*gerax*) among flying creatures, and a storm among ripening fruits.

What benefit did the episcopate bring him, when even to this day the clergy, whenever they falsely speak of his tomb, utter curses and insults—though perhaps, after the passage of 180 years, [Col. 0684A] his body lies buried and destroyed [lacuna]? Even the others, who do not know, angrily say: “Show us where that most wicked bishop lies.”

## CHAPTER II. The monastery, or oratory, of Blessed Theodorus, built by Theodorus the exarch. The piety of the same exarch. Joannicius flourishes. Further details about him.

At that time the monastery of Blessed Theodorus the deacon was built by Theodorus the patrician, not far from the place called Calchi, beside the church of Saint Martin the Confessor, which is called the Golden Heaven and which King Theodoric built, but which was recorded under the authority of this bishop [lacuna].

The aforementioned patrician and exarch made three golden chalices for this holy Church of Ravenna; they are still there to the present day. Every day he also went to the monastery of Saint Mary called at Blachernae, where, by God’s will, I am now abbot; he is buried there with his wife Agatha. He also made a reliquary over the altar of the Virgin from the most precious *blatta alithina*, bearing a depiction of how God made heaven and earth, the creatures of the world, Adam, and his descendants. Who has ever seen anything like it? By God’s favor, it remains to this day.

He himself, together with this bishop, raised up and enlarged the church of Blessed Paul the Apostle, situated near Wandalaria, because previously it had been described as a synagogue of the Jews.

In the time of this patrician, a man named Joannicius began here at Ravenna to make wisdom flourish in his palace. Let us set forth the reason [variant: *causam*, “the reason”] for this, and not leave it so great [variant: *nec tacitam*, “nor unspoken”]. It happened at that time that the notary of the aforementioned exarch died by divine command. The patrician mourned him, not only because of his death but even more because he had no comparable and most learned man who could compose imperial letters or complete in the palace the other writings that had to be put onto tablets.

When he had made his grief known to his attendants, they said to him:

“Our lord should have no doubt on this account. There is here a young man named Joannicius, a most skilled scribe, learned in the Scriptures, eloquent in wisdom, prudent in counsel, truthful in speech, cautious in expression, and full of every kind of knowledge; he was born of very noble parents. If you immediately order him to come and stand before you, he will please you, because he is learned in Greek and Latin letters.”

When he heard this, the patrician was cheered and ordered Joannicius to come. He stood before him, but the patrician despised him in his heart because he was short in stature and unattractive to behold. He recoiled from visible things but afterward loved invisible ones. God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong.

The patrician then turned to the leading men of this city and said:

“Do you think that this man will be able to protect this palace by his learning? I do not think so.”

They replied:

“Let our lord order him to be questioned; if he is unable, let him withdraw.”

He ordered a letter that had come to him from the emperor, written in Greek, to be brought, and the patrician said to him:

“Read.”

But Joannicius, having prostrated himself at his feet, rose, unfolded the letter, and said:

“Do you order me, my lord, to read it in Greek, as it is written, or in Latin words? For he used Greek and Latin, and he handled Latin as though it were Greek.”

Then the patrician, together with the leading men and the assembled people, was astonished. He ordered a document written in Latin letters to be brought, and said to him:

“Take this document in your hand and read the same thing in Greek words.”

He took it and read the whole of it in Greek. The patrician was then pleased with the judgment of Joannicius and glorified God, who had taken away the soul and restored the animated body. He ordered that Joannicius should never set foot outside the palace except on account of his learning, but should stand before him every day.

After these events, in the third year the emperor of Constantinople ordered a letter to be written to this patrician, containing the following:

“Send me that man who composes such writings as those you sent me and who composes verses.”

The patrician loaded a sturdy ship with various provisions and sent Joannicius to Constantinople. When the emperor had seen him, his learning seemed incredible to him. After a few days his education became renowned, and the emperor counted him among the leading men.

## CHAPTER III. At the Nativity of the Lord the clergy withdraw from Theodorus. The disagreement is settled through the exarch. The clergy are restored to their former condition.

Theodorus, the bishop of this city, did not cease from the boundless wickedness that he had begun. Whenever he embraced the priests, he rejected all the deacons; after exercising his vengeance, he again favored the deacons and cast aside the priests. The utterly wicked sower sowed such dissensions among them, mocking each one. Finally, he reduced them all to poverty and afflicted them severely with want.

Because of their great need, they were all indignant with the utmost anger. On the day of the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord, the priests went unanimously to Theodorus the archpriest and Theodorus the archdeacon and said to them:

“Tell our lord the bishop: He acts badly toward us; he oppresses and goads us excessively; he imposes many burdens upon us which we cannot endure. He has taken away our fourth-parts on various pretexts, broken the apostolic statutes, burned the customs of the Church, removed the registers, driven us from the bosom of the Church, disregarded the Gospels, afflicted our bodies, seized our possessions, taken away our resources, and tried to make us his dependants. We cannot endure his anger.”

They went and repeated the words of the clergy in the bishop’s ears. When he had heard all their words, as though receiving a missile or a spear, he immediately turned to anger and said to them:

“You are provoking the clergy; you are putting these words into their mouths. Those who said this will certainly never improve.”

Then he turned to the archpriest and said:

“You are the author of this criminal speech; you are the head of the priests’ sedition; you are completely their fiercest enemy; you are the agitator of the people. You are an utterly hostile adversary on every side. After this festival I shall ensure that you never again challenge another man with your voice.”

In that anger they all went to the church of Blessed Mary Ever-Virgin to celebrate the vigils. After the service had been completed, they repeated the bishop’s words to the entire clergy. They were indignant, took counsel together, and each went to his own place.

Then Theodorus the archpriest went to Theodorus the archdeacon, his cousin, at the monastery of Saint Andrew the Apostle, founded not far from the church of the Goths, near the house called Mariniana. When he knocked at the door, the household servants came to find out who was striking the wood. He announced:

“It is I.”

They quickly went away and reported:

“Theodorus the archpriest is knocking at the door and wants to come in to you.”

Another servant came swiftly and said that he was in the monastery. The archdeacon said:

“What benefit is there in our speaking, since we have not brought anything to completion?”

His household servants said to him:

“Why are you angry? He is your own flesh, your cousin. Speak with him; do not separate yourselves. If the bishop rages against you, how will he speak on your behalf?”

He entered the monastery, and they spoke together. Before they separated, they said to one another:

“How will these plans of ours, which we have discussed, remain firm?”

The archpriest said:

“May almighty God be mediator between us, and this apostle of his, and may he stand between you and me on the day of judgment. Whoever transgresses, let God demand an account of the deceit.”

The archdeacon replied:

“May it be so; so be it.”

Such an agreement was firmly established between them that we cannot transgress it. All the priests of this church are coming together to me; summon all the deacons and the rest of the Church. Let us go to the church of Blessed Apollinaris, enter the house of the Antiochene, and remain there to hear Mass. Let no one minister with him today. Let us reject him, since he is not our shepherd.

After saying this, he departed.

That same night they all went to the church of Blessed Mary the Virgin to celebrate the solemn Masses. They spoke secretly with the officials of each office, reached agreement, and said:

“Would that this had been done earlier, and that we had not fallen into such poverty!”

When the Mass had been completed in the Church of the Apostles and dawn had arisen, when the lights of Phoebus had illuminated the earth, they all went unanimously to the church of Blessed Apollinaris, which was situated in the city formerly called Classis, and, crying out, wept bitterly.

After the sun’s ray had shone forth upon the world, the aforementioned bishop sent a notary, according to custom, to summon the priests to proceed to the church and celebrate Mass. When the notary arrived, he found none of them and returned to report this to the bishop.

The bishop said:

“Perhaps they are sleeping because they were tired during the night and have therefore been overcome by slumber.”

After waiting for about an hour of the day, he sent the notary again. He found none of them and reported that they were all absent.

The bishop said:

“What is this? What hour is it now? If they have not all come, let at least however many there are come.”

One of those standing nearby replied:

“Let our lord not suppose anything other than what I say. You will find none of your priests today who will approach the altar with you on this solemn feast.”

He said:

“Why?”

The man replied:

“Because they have all crossed over to Caesarea [Reponius reads *Classis*; Bacch.]. They have gone to Saint Apollinaris, and there the priests, deacons, subdeacons, acolytes, doorkeepers, readers, and singers, together with the entire clergy, are celebrating Mass. Not one of them has been left behind. There is only the church; there is no custodian.”

They declared that they were greatly afflicted and had departed.

Then the bishop rose from the seat where he was sitting, struck his forehead with his hand, and said:

“Alas! I am defeated.”

Drawing deep sighs from his heart and mourning for himself, he entered his chamber. The people in the church were astonished, unaware of the cause of this event.

When these things had been done, the bishop immediately sent noblemen with the swiftest horses to bring them back to the church by offering satisfaction. When they saw them coming toward them, they all immediately rose, bowed their faces to the ground, and, before the bishop’s envoys had spoken, said in a loud voice:

“Go away, because we have no bishop [shepherd], but a murderer. When he entered this fold, he did not make the promise that he now makes. Rise, Saint Apollinaris; celebrate Mass for us on the day of the Nativity of the Lord. Saint Peter gave you to us as our shepherd; therefore we are your sheep. We run to you; save us.

“You did not receive consecration here, but the apostle himself blessed you with his own hands, gave you the Holy Spirit, and sent you to us; and we received your preaching. You were sent to govern, not to destroy. You stand before the most just Judge; fight for us. Break the bloody jaws of the wolf, so that you may lead us through the pleasant pastures of Christ.

“If you do not rise and celebrate Mass today, on this Nativity, we shall all immediately leave your house together, set out for Rome to Blessed Peter your master, prostrate ourselves before him with lamentations, and say with immense mourning, abundant tears, and great sighs:

“‘We went to your disciple, our bishop and preacher, whom you gave us, and he refused to celebrate Mass on this most important day, the Nativity of the Lord. Either avenge us against him or give us a new shepherd who will defend us from the mouth of the dragon that lies within our walls and will grieve over our afflictions.

“‘Behold, you yourself, good shepherd, know that many of your sheep have departed because of excessive burdens and the want of famine. They have withdrawn from your holy commandment and teaching because the most wicked bishop has suffocated them.

“‘If he does not hear us, we shall then proceed to Constantinople to the emperor and seek there a father and shepherd.’”

As these words were spoken, such immense lamentation and mourning arose on both sides that those who returned to the bishop, because of the uncontrolled tears and the murmuring of all those clergy, were scarcely able to speak or complete their embassy.

Then Theodorus the archbishop, fearing this, went sorrowfully and with great haste to the palace. He reported everything that had happened to the patrician, saying in grief:

“My sheep have abandoned me; I have been stripped of pastoral honor, rejected, and despised. The Lord’s flock entrusted to me is seeking another shepherd. They have hurried to Classis, entered the church of Blessed Apollinaris, accused me before God, and mocked me.”

The patrician immediately sent noblemen to recall the entire clergy and restore all their customs to their former condition. But they, still indignant, began to weep and said:

“If we reach Constantinople, we shall also complain about this exarch, because earlier he refused to correct him. We are not coming [we shall not come]; but we shall wait until the ninth hour for this Blessed Apollinaris, our bishop. If he delays, we shall go to Rome.”

They returned, shedding abundant tears, and reported to the bishop and the patrician what they had heard and how they had lamented. They added that such mourning and bellowing resounded within the church itself as had never before been heard or seen throughout all Classis. Even when we heard the voices of those who were mourning, we wept bitterly with them.

Then the archbishop, deeply afflicted by grief, wanted to prostrate himself at the patrician’s feet. He said in profound mourning:

“I beg your clemency: do not hesitate to go there and undertake this labor on my behalf, so that you may give your pledge for me. Promise them that I shall do everything according to their wishes and that, in the possessions of the Church, I shall have no greater share than any one of them.”

The patrician ordered trappings to be put on a horse, mounted it, and came to the aforementioned martyr’s tomb. He summoned them all to him, spoke gentle and peaceful words, and led them back with him, promising to correct everything, just as you have recently heard.

They came back, and at the approach of evening celebrated Mass and Vespers together with the gentle bishop.

On the following day the exarch came to the church-house and sat with the archbishop. All the priests were there, with the deacons standing behind them; the entire clergy stood in opposition. After much controversy and an exchange of words between them, the bishop was convicted. All were immediately restored to their honors and dignities and allotted the Church’s revenues. There was no one among them who did not receive some portion of the Church [perhaps “the fourth-part,” according to Bacchus], together with the agents and *prastias* withdrawn from the household-members of this church; and they all went joyfully to their monasteries, blessing God.

Some things [variant: “which”] that the bishop alone had previously enjoyed were afterward allotted to everyone. From that day such an agreement was established between the bishop and the priests, before his consecration and by formal promise, that the household members of the Church should have more careful authority and supervision.

## CHAPTER IV. Theodorus submits to the Roman bishop. Leo II confirms the statutes under Agatho, with certain conditions accepted. The death of Theodorus and the duration of his episcopate.

After a short time, this bishop, still harboring in his heart the desire to harm his priests and remembering the injury they had inflicted upon him—and because he was entirely unable, as he wished, to enrich his relatives from the possessions of the Church—secretly sent to Pope Agatho at Rome, asking him to order Theodorus to come there, ostensibly to confer with him concerning the cause of the holy churches of God and the Catholic faith.

Agatho immediately wrote a letter ordering Bishop Theodorus to hasten to Rome on behalf of the holy and undefiled Catholic faith. Theodorus read it before all his priests and replied, saying to them:

“What do you think? You have seen the apostolic letter and know what it contains. What do you think? I shall do nothing without your will. We have one counsel, brothers; let there be one will and one mind among us. Shall we go, or shall we remain?”

They, replying in simplicity and unaware of the hidden plan, said:

“We must all submit to the danger of death for the orthodox faith and the holy Church of God.”

When he reached Rome, he subjected himself and his Church to the Roman bishop. The Roman bishop rejoiced, having obtained what his predecessors had lost; he received Theodorus gladly, consented to everything he requested, and granted whatever he asked according to his will.

After Pope Agatho died, he fulfilled all the agreements with his successor Leo. It was established between them that whichever man the priests brought from Ravenna to Rome as their chosen candidate, Leo would consecrate; that he should remain in Rome at the time of his consecration no longer than eight days; and that he should not come there again except on the feast of the Apostles’ Nativity, when he was to send a representative from among the priests. Thus the bishop of Ravenna would remain undisturbed. Many other chapters were also confirmed by Leo’s hand together with the priests, but we cannot write them all down.

This most ferocious man died on the eighteenth day of January. Amid great rejoicing by the priests and universal celebration, he was buried in the ground; he lies beneath the portico of Blessed Apollinaris. I was unable to read his epitaph clearly. He occupied the see for thirteen years, three months, and twenty days.

# OBSERVATIONS ON THE LIFE OF THEODORUS

Theodorus defended against Agnellus’s calumnies. Theodorus the exarch distinguished from Calliopa. Some matters relating to discipline and to the autocephaly of the bishop of Ravenna are indicated.

### I
