What Agnellus committed to posterity in this Life of Bishop Theodorus is summarized by Rubeus in Book IV, page 208. He then adds:

> “From this history, which we have copied from the Lives of the Archbishops of Ravenna, it can easily be inferred—both from what all the other most serious authors have transmitted and from the merits of the matter itself—that it departs far from the truth. It was written by men of that age who, lifted up by arrogance against the Roman Church, endured that subjection only with difficulty. For Theodorus is said to have been exceedingly devout and most generous toward the poor, and to have corrected with just severity the morals of the priests of Ravenna, which, amid the great license of all things, were declining into worse conduct and becoming corrupt.”

I thought it worthwhile to excerpt these passages from several sources and add them to Agnellus’s account, so that whatever might assist Theodorus’s reputation could be set against the curses and insults. Although Agnellus is wholly occupied with pursuing the memory of Theodorus with denunciations, he nevertheless does not omit certain matters that redound to the bishop’s praise. Among these are the matters relating to the church of Saint Paul, which he built or transformed into a better and larger structure and which was called Vandalaria. In earlier times it had either been a synagogue of the Jews or had been despised as though it were a synagogue; for the phrase in which our author relates this is ambiguous to me.

### II

On this occasion the piety of Theodorus the exarch is especially commended. He built an oratory for Blessed Theodorus the deacon, offered three golden chalices and a precious reliquary to the Church of Ravenna, and regularly visited the church of Saint Mary at Blachernae, situated outside Ravenna’s walls, where he also ordered that he and his wife Agatha be buried.

These actions are entirely unlike the character of Theodorus Calliopa and show that this man differed from him, as was indicated above in the Life of Bishop Maurus. The matters reported in this bishop’s Life also show him to have been a man of gentle disposition: he settled the clergy’s disagreement with great prudence, refrained from correcting the refractory clergy (which, with Rubeus, I believe true), and from settling the matter with a bishop’s temper by the use of force; he left all judgment to the Church, as the canons required.

I also have no doubt that this same man assisted in deed the plan of Reparatus, by whose negotiation Theodorus restored the Church of Ravenna to the Roman bishop. It is plainly impossible that such an action could have accorded in any way with Calliopa’s character and disposition.

In mentioning the oratory of Blessed Theodorus built by the exarch, our author refers to the church of Saint Martin in the Golden Heaven. This weakens the conjecture by which I suspected that Reparatus had served there as a monk, unless in the Life of that bishop the same basilica is called by the name of Saint Apollinaris, while here it is praised under the older name of Saint Martin. Agnellus contradicts this, however, for he always calls it Saint Martin.

I therefore acknowledge the matter to be uncertain, and willingly admit—as I have always done—that in our author the name “oratory” may refer to the monastery in which Reparatus served and from which he was raised to the episcopate.

### III

Readers may extract from this Life of Theodorus many matters concerning discipline and ecclesiastical practice—for example, the method of distributing ecclesiastical revenues, the offices of the archpriest, archdeacon, and notary, the manner of announcing and celebrating solemn Masses on the chief festivals of the year, and many similar matters. It would be superfluous to recount them.

In the story of Joannicius, moreover, a public exarchal notary is found, a position that indicates his distinction. Agnellus will deal with this same man below in the Life of Felix and will add matters concerning his family, lineage, and death.

Above all, it deserves notice that the clergy of Ravenna gave their consent when, during a controversy of faith—while the Monothelite heresy had not yet been overthrown and the matter was being brought into question—the bishop was summoned to attend the Roman synod. This clearly amounted to renouncing the autocephaly of the synod.

It could, however, have happened that the bishop said that he was summoned, or that the matter was to be conducted either outside the Roman synod or in a general and ecumenical council to be convened; in either case he could have attended, not as a subject of the Roman metropolitan or patriarch, but as an *acephalus*.

With the clergy consenting, Theodorus subjected himself and his Church—although the clergy had not wished this—to the Roman bishop, both in the matter of ordination and in that of the synod, and renounced the autocephaly that Maurus had recently obtained by fraud.

# LIFE OF DAMIAN

[Col. 0691A]

## CHAPTER I. A boy is restored to life and dies again after being signed with chrism. Joannicius returns to Ravenna.

Damianus XXXVII. Short in stature, not sufficiently stout, from this flock, consecrated at Rome: a humble, gentle, and devout man. While he occupied the see, there was great peace among the priests and the people, as our elders reported to us. Listen.

It happened at that time, as I heard it recounted, that a certain woman came with a small infant so that the bishop might give the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands and anointing with chrism. The bishop, however, was being tonsured. Those attending him said to the woman:

“Wait until he has been tonsured.”

But she cried out, saying:

“Oh, what madness, men! The child is dying, and you do not wish to help the soul that is departing; you do not even wish to announce it, and I remain silent? Run and tell our lord the bishop to sign this little child, because he is at the point of death, before he dies, so that after the child’s funeral you may not be held guilty.”

While they went away and delayed, the child died. Then the woman began to cry out and shout in a loud voice, raising a commotion like a theater and spreading the lamentation of trumpeters among the crowd.

Hearing this, the bishop began to ask what had happened. They tried to conceal the facts and turn the bishop away from anger, but they could not.

The woman cried out:

“Behold, I have waited here for many hours, and none of your men was willing to announce that you should sign the child. Now there is no soul in him. How can a dead body receive the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete? You must decide, excellent bishop.”

Then the bishop took the child into his arms, groaning and weeping deeply. He went behind the apse of the church, threw himself face down upon the ground with the child, and wept and prayed for a very long time, calling upon the heavenly Lord.

While he was praying, the child’s soul returned to its body; and after the bishop had signed him, the child gave up his spirit.

At that time the aforementioned Joannicius returned from Constantinople to Ravenna, and his wisdom became renowned throughout all Italy.

## CHAPTER II. The citizens of Ravenna customarily fought among themselves. Factions took their names from the city gates. A great slaughter of men, followed by the treacherous and secret killing of many others. A public prayer was proclaimed; the authors of the crime were discovered and punished.

We, brothers, are always on watch, like soldiers in battle array; and whenever we hear of the miracles of our almighty God, we rejoice, because he has deigned to raise those who are falling up to the kingdom. And whenever we hear that the devil has harmed someone and ensnared him in his traps, we grieve, because that captive did not fight bravely against the invisible enemy. Yet no one will be able to fight against him unless he has been fortified with a heavenly shield. He is that deceiver who wished to be most high and mocked the Son of God. If you are not weary of standing, you shall hear what works of his cunning he sowed in this city during the time of this bishop.

In ancient times, therefore, a custom arose which has remained until now—horrible, to be avoided, and to be condemned as wicked. Every Sunday, or on the day of the Apostles, the citizens of Ravenna—not only the distinguished, but men of every age: youths and ephebes, men of middling age and little boys, of both sexes, as we have said—after eating, would go out in groups through the various gates and proceed to battle. Madmen and lunatics! They subjected themselves to death for no reason.

It happened at that time, as we have said, that the Tiguriensis Gate entered into combat with Pusterula, which is called the Upper Village, beside the Lamis trench. When those who had entered the battle line were pursued by slingers, the Pusterulenses turned their backs. The Tigurienses, following them, struck many bodies down upon the ground, came to the aforesaid Pusterula, threatened the remainder within, broke their mallets and saws, and returned to their homes victorious.

Eight days later, on Sunday, both groups went out from their respective gates. The boys, as was their custom, abandoned their game with a small discus and rushed upon one another, breaking one another’s heads with sticks. Others killed one another from a distance with their hands and by throwing stones; others, terrified by the bellowing of the *rumboli*, fled in different directions; others, armed here and there with youthful weapons, sent slaughter against their own peers. There was no respite anywhere. From the side of Pusterula, people fell dead by the sword throughout the crowd; others were left half alive, and a warm, bloody stream flowed from their breasts; others lay with open mouths, blood like roses pouring from them; many poured out a copious flood of gore from wounds in their bodies and, biting the earth with their mouths, breathed out their lives.

But whenever anyone asked his enemies for life, saying, “Alas, my soul, my soul!” the blows ceased and he was not killed. Even now, when someone trusts that he will not die and asks for the life of his soul, they allow him to live and strike him no further.

A great slaughter occurred in that district, such as had never before happened there in ancient times, so far as our elders could remember. Behold the first destruction in that district, and mourning, and woe. The second destruction and killing, however, was the greatest lamentation of all.

After these events there was a brief respite from the slaughter. But the most destructive devil, the invisible enemy who is hostile to the human race, stirred the hearts of the Pusterulenses. As though someone were knocking at a door, so their hearts burned every day; and, with every plan frustrated, they considered how they might subject the Tigurienses to death and eradicate them utterly.

Then each man said to his companion, his fellow-lodger, and his friend:

“What [variant: ‘Why’] life remains for us? Behold, the Tigurienses have killed all our comrades; they are plotting to kill us alive on Sunday. [lacuna] We shall leave our children orphaned; we do not know whom they will serve. Our wives will remain widows; our enemies will swallow up all our property. Why should life remain for us? Let us be most courageous in battle.”

They all raised their voices and wept. After laying aside their mourning, they said: “Come, let us ambush them. Let us secretly prepare deceitful falsehoods against them and invent wicked words; let us deceive them under the appearance of false humility.”

On the following Sunday, beneath the Ursiana church, the men of Pusterula secretly asked the Tigurienses to dine with them and requested that no one should know. When the divine words had been completed, each man went to the one who had invited him; and, scattered through the individual dwellings, they served death in various dishes.

Some were killed with daggers and committed to the earth. Others, struck in the head with axes, were buried in a stable beneath horse dung, so that no signs of the killing might be found. Some were pierced through the thigh by a missile weapon. Others [lacuna], stripped of their garments, were thrown into a sewer. Others, rushing upon them with a swallow-shaped blade, ended their days and their lives. Many, struck by flying iron, were thrown into a pit and covered with mud.

The wretched Tigurienses were killed by the Pusterulenses through various punishments. The deed was carried out so secretly that no one could discover any sign either of the killing or of the burial, nor could any of their friends learn what had happened.

On the following day there was great mourning, and the whole city remained everywhere steeped in sorrow. The baths were closed; public spectacles ceased; merchants withdrew from the streets; innkeepers shut their taverns; market sellers abandoned their business; priests groaned in the churches; the elders mourned; all the young men were grieving in the streets; every husband took up lamentation; matrons mourned beside the marital bed. Widows dressed themselves in mourning clothes; the beauty of the virgins was changed; little children were shaken by excessive sobbing; all were afflicted in the bitterness of their souls.

Some wept for a father whose death was unknown; others awaited their sons, not knowing whether they were fugitives; others, ignorant of the danger to their brothers; others waited for their husbands, knowing nothing certain. Each person went about by different paths, here and there, searching, but they found them nowhere.

The words of the mourners were these:

“If the earth truly swallowed them, surely someone would have seen them. If they had been submerged in the depths of the sea, the waves would have returned their bodies to us. If beasts had devoured them, they would not have swallowed their bones. If someone had killed them with a sword, their blood would have revealed their death to us.”

The grieving people imagined many other things. They lay prostrate on the ground, tore out their hair and beards, disfigured their faces with their fingernails, and ripped their garments and their breasts [or: “their clothing from the breast”]. Weeping for brothers and relatives, sons and grandsons, and searching for their lost kinsmen, the citizens spent the entire week in lamentation.

Then the holy man Damianus, seeing this city remaining in such great mourning, gave himself over to the greatest tears. On Sunday he proclaimed a fast, so that on Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday they might pray to God without ceasing, asking that, fortified from heaven by divine assistance, this destruction might be revealed to someone.

The bishop ordered the people to proceed in groups. He himself went with the clergy and monks in one section; the laymen—old men, adolescents, and boys—formed another choir. Married and unmarried women, widows, and girls went in another section, while the band of the poor proceeded separately. They did not all go together, but separately, at approximately a stone’s throw from one another.

The priests, having laid aside their sacred garments, put on sackcloth, sprinkled ashes on their heads, and walked barefoot. All the noble and common people covered themselves with haircloth; with unkempt heads and shaggy beards, they went along mourning. The matrons, laying aside their cheerful clothing, put on garments of mourning. Everyone shaved the crown of his head and exposed the skin. The beauty of the virgins was taken away.

They removed from themselves their changing garments and cloaks; they cast away their earrings and rings, their bracelets, *pereselidae*, necklaces, scent-boxes, pins, mirrors, crescent ornaments, little lilies, ornaments, and *laudosiae*; they threw away everything pleasant and desirable, and were steeped [variant: ‘clothed’] in a song of lamentation.

Little children hung from their mothers’ breasts. The entire city resounded with the lamentation of men, the wailing of little children, the weeping of mothers, the lowing of cattle, the neighing of horses, the bleating of sheep, and the cries of all the other animals.

When the three days of affliction had been completed, before sunset the almighty God—who reveals the depths from darkness and brings hidden things into the light—performed wonders such as had never been heard among the nations. From the Amphitheater, which in ancient times stood beside the gate called the Golden Gate, to the aforesaid Pusterula, there arose something like a cracking and a great sound. Smoke rose like a mist, and the gaping earth displayed within its bosom all the dead whom it had held shut beneath itself—those whom the Pusterulenses had destroyed in their excessive fury.

When the people heard the sound, they ran toward the stench and found, each in the individual houses, his own dead, with worms feeding within their wounds. Then they seized the murderers, judged them according to their deeds, overturned that district together with its buildings, reduced it to nothing, and called the district “of the Robbers” [Note: [Col. 0693D] Marginal note: “Posterula, or the district of the robbers.” BACCH.], down to the present day.

Not only the murderers themselves, but also their wives and children, suffered various forms of punishment. No one wished to take anything from their possessions; rather, their possessions were consigned to the pyre at the bridge called the Milvian Bridge, which was recently destroyed. That bridge stood in the same district, the district of the Robbers, beside the tribunal of the monastery of the blessed confessor of Christ, Severinus [perhaps Severus, Bacch.].

## CHAPTER III. Various matters are related concerning a certain anonymous man living in Damianus’s time. Damianus himself is praised.

There was in this city of Ravenna a most religious man, of good reputation. Whenever he came to the Ursiana church, his shoulders touched the upper part of a column of the church. Before the entrance of the Masses he sang psalms; he never conversed there with anyone; and after the entrance of the Masses he always gazed into the bishop’s face.

One day the bishop ordered him to come to the blessing of Saint Apollinaris, so that he might share the bishop’s table. After his belly had been stretched with food and the fibers of his breast filled with wine, though his mind remained sober, the bishop asked him why he always looked upon his face in the church.

He replied: “I do not look upon you, excellent bishop, so much as upon the one who stands behind your back, whose beauty I cannot fully endure. And when you celebrate the sacred rite [variant: ‘you sanctify’], his countenance stands beside you. He is not present now, but he is always with you at the solemn celebrations of the Mass and never abandons you.”

After some days he departed in peace. Some people heard him say, before his death, that on a certain Sunday, while everyone was singing the antiphon at the Benedictions [Note: that is, the Song of the Three Young Men. BACCH.] during the night and saying, “Mountains and hills shall sing praises before God,” he testified that even the stones of the church—the columns and slabs, the bricks and tiles, and also all the metal objects—were singing that antiphon together with everyone else.

After the man had been buried, the bishop ordered a small railing to be made around the aforesaid column, lest anyone’s unworthy feet touch the base of the column where the saint’s feet had stood. He also ordered a small cross to be fixed there as an everlasting memorial, which remains to the present day.

## CHAPTER IV. John, abbot of Saint John’s beyond Caesarea. He conducts the business of his church at Constantinople. He comes to Ravenna in one night through the power of demons. He repents of what he has done.

Nor should we pass over John, abbot of the monastery of Saint John situated beyond Caesarea, formerly at Classis, which is called “at Titus.” This man lived during the time of this bishop Damianus: a priest named John, abbot of the monastery of Saint John, which is called “at Titus,” though country people, not knowing better, call it “at the Pine.”

Since the aforesaid priest had many disputes and lawsuits with various men concerning the property of his monastery of the blessed John, and no conclusion had been reached, while many were especially eager unjustly to swallow up the monastery’s estates, he reached Constantinople. After remaining there many days, he did not see the emperor’s face.

As he turned various plans over in his mind, one day he stood below, beside the wall of the chamber where the emperor was seated, reciting the invitatory for the Advent of the Lord: “He who is to come will come and will not delay; the kingdom, power, and empire are in his hand.”

Hearing this, the emperor was pleased and listened attentively. One recruit [manuscript: *tironos*, BACCH.] came and wanted to remove him from that place, but the emperor ordered from above that no one should trouble him until he had finished. When he had completed the entire invitatory, the emperor called him up. He stood before the emperor and set out in an orderly fashion the case for which he had come.

The emperor ordered a writ to be drawn up declaring that the property should belong perpetually to that monastery and that the document should serve as an everlasting legal protection.

After this, the aforesaid priest John prostrated himself for a long time at the emperor’s feet, weeping and saying: “Let my lord order a letter to be written to the exarch, so that my guarantor may not be seized, since tomorrow the hearing is scheduled at which I was to stand in conflict with my adversary.”

The emperor yielded to his petitions and ordered a letter to be written to the exarch, instructing that no distinction should be made in this case, that no one should bring him before the court, that his guarantor should not be seized, and that he should not be troubled in any way.

When the letter had been written, secured with a seal, and handed to him—specifying the month, day, and hour—he withdrew. As evening fell, he came to the gate of the city of Constantinople, hoping that he might find a ship traveling to Ravenna or Sicily. But after inquiring about all the *carabi*, *chelandia*, and *dromons*, he found none.

He then set out along the seashore. Night spread its black wings and brought him hostility. But in proportion as the darkness oppressed him, the Selenite [Note: [Col. 0696B] That is, the moon. BACCH.] bestowed the benefit of its scattered rays upon him; and the higher it rose in the heavens, the brighter the earth appeared.

As he walked along the shore, considering what he should do, three men in black clothing appeared before his eyes and said to him: “Why, Abbot John, are you wandering along this shore with a troubled mind?”

He replied: “I obtained everything I asked of the emperor. I have remained here a long time. There is no ship for my return to Ravenna, and therefore I am surrounded by sadness.”

The wicked men said to him: “If you do what we tell you, tomorrow you will be in your own house among your people.”

He said to them: “I will do what you wish.”

They said: “Take a staff in your hand and draw the outline of a ship in this sand, then draw the sails, oars, boats, and sailors.”

He did as he had been ordered. Again they said to him: “Lie down in the ship’s *catalecta*, beneath the bilge, beside the keel. You will hear the roaring of the winds after you have entered the open sea; you will hear the voices of those in danger; you will hear the storms and be terrified; you will hear the sounds of the waters pouring over you. Therefore close your mouth, so that your hand may not even make the sign of the cross.”

He lay upon the ground, looking toward the sea beside him. Suddenly there arose everywhere a sound like the crash of clouds, like a stormy tempest. The wind roared; the sea beat its waves against itself. Oars were broken, masts were cut down, boats were torn apart; the sailors uttered the blackest and most dreadful lamentations. The abbot forced himself to remain so silent that no one could have heard his breath.

At cockcrow he was found upon the roof of his monastery. Seeing himself alone, he cried out in a loud voice to his people to lower him from the roof. They, thinking that he was a phantom, did not want to obey their master’s orders.

Then he shouted even more loudly, calling each of them by name and saying: “Lower me, and you will know that it is I. You know that I went to the city of Constantinople for the interests of this monastery, and now I have returned. So that you will not be afraid, know that I was thrown here by powerful winds.”

When they heard these words, they quickly placed a ladder, and he descended. His people recognized him, and after he had kissed them all in turn, he ordered them to strike the wooden board, saying that it was now the hour of Matins and that, after the Work of God [completed] had been completed, he desired rest.

The next day, after touring Caesarea, he departed. From the Vandalaria Gate, which is near the Caesarean Gate, he left the palace of Laurence, entered the Theodoric Palace, and ordered that he be presented to the exarch.

The exarch received him gladly, ordered the writ to be read, and returned it folded to the priest who had presented it. He said to him: “Let this writ be a perpetual protection for you and your descendants. I shall release your guarantor, because you were negligent in dealing with your adversary.”

He replied: “Our lord the emperor gave his order by letter, declaring that all my obligations should be invalid in court.”

Then the patrician, becoming angry, took the letter from the priest’s hand. As he read it, he found it written exactly as we have stated above. He kept the letter and, turning toward *achemenia* [text uncertain], burst out, saying: “Tell me, author of falsehood, when was this letter written?”

The priest John replied: “Yesterday, at the ninth hour.”

The patrician said: “And how could you have come here so quickly? No one can go to Constantinople and return within three months.”

“How I returned,” the priest replied, “I shall report to my bishop. Let my business and my repentance remain with me this morning. Yet if you press me with an accusation of falsehood, send your envoys with me and let us go there. If this is found to be false, let the matter be settled according to [our] paternal agreements” [Note: [Col. 0697D] Perhaps: “let me hear the agreements between us.” BACCH.].

Then, withdrawing from there, he came to the bishop’s residence of this church. He entered before Pope Damianus, prostrated himself at his feet, and told him everything that had happened. He explained how phantoms had carried him through the dangers of the sea, set him upon the roof of his monastery, and left him there alone.

At the bishop’s exhortation he performed true repentance and ended his days in peace.

## CHAPTER V. The conversion of a certain Jew. Damianus’s homeland and education. The burning of the Ravenna archives. The bishop’s death. His epitaph.

I beg you, brothers, do not be weary of standing; one more miracle remains.

One Sunday, after the Lord’s Prayer had been completed, the aforesaid bishop was breaking the Lord’s Body with the priests, as we customarily do. A certain Jew, who was accustomed to stand among the virgins in the place called Ermolas, quickly ran toward the holy altar and said to the bishop:

“I beg you, excellent bishop, give me a portion of the body of the Lamb, which is now being torn apart by your hands.”

The high priest replied: “You are not permitted to share in the Lord’s body, because you have not been washed in holy baptism.”

Again the Jew said: “Father, I am not asking you for sacred bread [from you], but for the flesh of the Lamb that you are tearing apart with your hands, whom I see with my human eyes as you handle him upon this altar. I ask for the Lamb whom I see; I do not desire the bread that I do not see.”

The holy man replied: “We cannot give the Holy One to the unclean until the one who is defiled has been cleansed with holy water. Receive the sign of the Lamb, and eat with us from that Lamb.”

At once, when he saw this, the Jew gave his name. After being instructed by the bishop, he received immortal baptism and was changed from unbelieving to faithful.

This bishop came from the region of Dalmatia, but his parents offered him to this church. Instructed in sacred letters, he rose to the summit of this church [Note: [Col. 0698D] Marginal note: “For he lived in the time of the Emperor Constantine.”].

At that time the archives of this church were consumed by fire. The flames destroyed many documents there, and many others were stolen and hidden by wicked men. Then, after all the priests had assembled, the aforesaid bishop sat with them in the *propina*. He pronounced anathemas of condemnation against anyone who possessed any of the aforesaid documents and did not return them: let him be accursed. Whoever returned them, however, was to be innocent of guilt.

This most blessed man died on the third Ides of May. You will find his epitaph above his tomb, containing these words:

> Ever remembered for your holy merits, venerable priest,  
> You, Damianus, lie placed within this tomb.  
> Though dead in body, your fame nevertheless survives;  
> Your limbs have died on earth, but your light endures.  
>   
> The blessed bishop, coming from the fields of Dalmatia,  
> Ravenna, made holy, was protected by your prayers.  
> Laying aside all things at the saving time [lacuna]  
> The devout one gave you among the people, Christ interceding [variant: “Christ praying”].  
>   
> Yet that you deserved to receive burial in these temples,  
> These great tombs prove that you pleased God.  
> And just as you rightly performed the office of the priest  
> Whose place you held, so may holy rest be yours in his places.

We found these words written within the church of the blessed Apollinaris above his tomb. He held office for sixteen years, two months, and sixteen days.

## OBSERVATIONS ON THE LIFE OF DAMIANUS

What is related here about the boy restored to life is told elsewhere and differently by Rubeus. The rite of confirmation is illustrated from certain unpublished sources. The abuse of civil combat at Parma ceased a few years ago. What is said of another person has been wrongly attributed to Damianus. The story related about the abbot John is fabulous. The rite was borrowed from the monks. The barbarism of that age is apparent from the epitaph.

### I

The first event encountered in this Life of Damianus is the restoration to life of a boy who died before receiving confirmation and who died again immediately after receiving it. Concerning this matter Rubeus, book IV, page 212, has the following brief statement:

> “They say that he restored a man who had already died to life by pouring out prayers to God.”

In the Life of John surnamed Angeloptis, book II, page 99, he had related a similar story. He had prefaced it as follows:

> “I should by no means omit here what is written concerning John, bishop of Ravenna, although he was another person than the one we now have in mind. Where he should be placed, since many archbishops of this name followed one another, remains uncertain to me.”

He added that it was related how, when John was anointing boys with sacred chrism in the temple of Saint Vitalis, a certain widow could not approach through the crowd so that the boy whom she carried in her arms, languishing near death, might be anointed with sacred chrism. She therefore followed the bishop as he returned home. When she was shut out at the doors and was seeking someone who might arrange her access to the bishop, she saw that the boy had died.

As she lamented with cries the loss of the boy taken from her before confirmation, the bishop ran to her, took upon himself the blame for what had happened, and, pouring out prayers to God, restored the boy to life and returned him, confirmed, to his mother.

Rubeus praises the memorial of that miracle, said to remain in the chapel of the archiepiscopal house. He says that it was also related that, as that John became more celebrated each day because of the fame of the miracle he had performed, he withdrew from the sight of everyone and shut himself away in the Alps of Mount Pirchinnian and Caprasius.

Everyone can see that the story has been displaced from its proper setting and stuffed with various fables. Accordingly, if the memorial said to exist in the archiepiscopal house records only the sequence of the infant’s restoration to life and confirmation by the bishop, it must be referred to Bishop Damianus, not to some John. The other details are absurd and do not accord with the facts or the times, as Rubeus himself astutely observes.

### II

It is surprising that a boy baptized by Damianus could have been left without being confirmed with sacred chrism, since the newly baptized were accustomed to be confirmed immediately and then strengthened by participation in the sacred synaxis—that is, to receive communion from the Lord’s body—as is stated by Alcuin in *On the Office of Holy Saturday*, by Rabanus in *On the Institution of Clerics*, and by others in many places.

That the sacrament of confirmation was delayed in some parts of Gaul is established from Jonah of Orléans, book I of *On Lay Instruction*, chapter 7, where he censures such a delay. But that it was customarily administered immediately after baptism in the churches of Italy is proved by several works already published.

From unpublished sources I have the following. In the sacramentary codex of the most eminent Ottoboni, first written out in the eleventh century, the final prescriptions in the conferral of the sacrament of baptism are these:

> “He baptizes him, and the priest anoints him on the head with chrism, and says: Almighty God, etc.  
>   
> Prayer for confirming the infants: Almighty and everlasting God, who have deigned to regenerate these your servants and handmaids from water and the Holy Spirit, and who have given them remission of all sins, send upon them from heaven your Holy Spirit, the Paraclete: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety. Fill them with the spirit of your fear, and, in your mercy, mark them with the sign of the cross of Christ for eternal life. Through, etc.”

Among the most precious books of the most eminent Casanata—whose memory will never fade among the devout and among students of sacred letters—there were two excellent parchment volumes. When I was in Rome in 1698, he took them from a chest with his own hands, showed them to me, and most courteously allowed me to copy them.

In one of them are described the rites for blessing the font and administering baptism; in the other are the ceremonies and prayers of sacred ordination. Both volumes are adorned with many figures, painted with an art not unworthy of the age, which place the rites and mysteries themselves before the eyes. Musical notation is also visible, with words added in some places.

Litanies are appended to the volume that presents the rites of baptism; in them Saint Benedict and his sister Saint Scholastica are invoked. Everything is written in Lombard script, and the final verses added from the same volume, transcribed here, prove that the book belonged to the Beneventan Church and to the eleventh century:

> You see the golden-haired images which [lacuna] reader,  
> Gleam in heavenly modes and sparkle with plates of gold;  
>   
> If you look within, the limbs shine white with light;  
> If cautiously you descend by the straight path to the depths,  
>   
> Our spirit is given many things, rejoicing to love them:  
> Lilies with violets, cassia with its flower, and amomum—  
>   
> All mixed together adorn the appearance most beautifully.  
> Perhaps you seek the author who ordered the poems  
> To be adorned; if you read the name, [lacuna] itself supplies it.  
>   
> The outstanding bishop Landolphus, another holier man,  
> In whose time the Virgin’s hall was enriched.  
>   
> For his praise we all ask you yourselves  
> To pray with devoted heart to the Virgin’s Son,  
> That he may deem him worthy to possess the splendid places of the saints.

For the present subject, however, the passages in the same volume concerning the administration of confirmation and communion after baptism should be noted. After the rite of baptism has been set out, the following is added:

> “Then let the little vessel be brought outside [that is, let those who have been baptized come out of the font], and let them remain in the church until Mass is celebrated and they are confirmed with the Lord’s sacraments. Before receiving the Lord’s body, let these prayers be said, etc.”

Finally, after the prayers, everything is concluded with these words:

> “Then let the Eucharist be given with these words: May the body of our Lord Jesus Christ preserve you unto eternal life. Amen. This must be guarded against above all, lest it be neglected, because then every legitimate baptism is confirmed in the name of Christianity.”

But these observations, set down here by way of occasion, are sufficient.

### III

Several matters related in Chapters II and IV display the ancient appearance of the city of Ravenna—its gates, districts, and roads. Agnellus himself testifies that the factional form of combat which gave rise to the horrifying and clandestine slaughter perpetrated by the Pusterulenses against the Tugurienses continued down to his own time.

It should certainly be observed that this practice had only recently ceased among the Parmenses. It is clear that, a few years ago, the practice described here was still customary among citizens of neighboring city gates, though they belonged to the lowest class: on feast days after dinner, armed bands would meet one another outside the city walls with slings and stones, and many of them would return with their heads shattered by stones.

When matters finally reached the point at which they began to fight not merely with stones but also with swords, clubs, and firearms, producing numerous killings, it seems that this sort of conflict—whose suppression had often previously been attempted—was at last completely abolished through prescribed and inflicted punishments and through the piety of the most serene Duke Francis. The attempts of the assembled populace to bring about its own destruction can now easily be prevented by the soldiers enlisted to defend the city on the occasion of the present wars in Italy.

Abuses once admitted thus endure for many centuries and are removed only with difficulty and the greatest exertion.

### IV

Among the matters related here concerning the anonymous Ravennate renowned for holiness in Damianus’s time, there is one that the writers on Ravenna attribute to Damianus himself. Namely, before he died, he is said to have told someone that, while a certain antiphon was being sung, the entire building seemed to sing praises to God.

Agnellus himself, however, shows that this was wrongly understood. After the man’s death, he immediately adds that the bishop ordered the place to be enclosed by an iron railing, where the man had been accustomed to stand while hearing the divine offices.

The title “Benedictions” refers to the Song of the Three Young Men, by which it is also called in chapter 12 of Saint Benedict’s Rule.

### V

The account that follows concerning John, abbot of the monastery of Saint John, who returned from Constantinople to Ravenna through the aid of demons in less than one complete night, was omitted by Rubeus and by the other writers who wrote after Rubeus, perhaps because they considered what was related wholly unworthy of belief.

I too hold this opinion, knowing that such things are the dreams of the common people. I think that John went to Constantinople, vindicated the rights of his church, and returned when his return was least expected; but I believe that the remaining details should be relegated to popular fantasy.

Nevertheless, this account was not entirely without value. The location of Caesarea, by which it was connected with Ravenna, is explained; and we learn that abbots lived in such monasteries with their clergy, who at fixed hours—not only by day but also by night—performed the appointed task of divine psalmody.

A wooden board gave the signal by which they rose for Matins at cockcrow. I have no doubt that this came from monastic practice. Ducange noted in the *Glossary of Latin* the board called by Palladius the *σφυρίον ἐφυπναστικόν* (“waking hammer” or “wake-up instrument”) in the *Historia Lausiaca*, chapter 104; he adds other material relevant to the matter under the same heading.

### VI

The history of the converted Jew has been properly copied from Agnellus in the books of the Ravennate writers; there is therefore no reason to linger over its elucidation.

What is surprising in what follows is the great barbarism of that age: when the clergy decided that an epitaph should be written in memory of Damianus, the excellent bishop, they copied, with only a few alterations, the epitaph that had once been placed for Marinianus, and even introduced errors into the few things they changed, such as the line:

> “The blessed bishop, coming from the fields of Dalmatia.”

Agnellus transcribed the epitaphs of Marinianus and Damianus as nearly identical, just as he had read them.

Moreover, why was that Joannicius who had returned from Constantinople to Ravenna before Damianus’s death—a man learned in both Greek and Latin—not employed at all to write the bishop’s epitaph?

The following brief inscription still exists in the basilica of Saint Apollinaris at Classis:

> D. N. DAMIANUS ARCHIEP. FECIT.  
> “Our Lord Damianus, archbishop, made this.”

# LIFE OF SAINT FELIX

## CHAPTER I. Felix’s appearance, character, and writings. He is both abbot and steward. Some matters concerning Bishop Georgius.

Felix XXXVIII [Note: [Col. 0701D] Marginal note: “He was archbishop around the year 693.” BACCH.].

He was short in stature, thin of face, with small eyes and a meager appearance, but full of the spirit of wisdom and a well-watered spring, an excellent father, an outstanding preacher, and the author of many volumes. In his holy church he was fruitful. He composed the exposition that we still possess concerning the Day of Judgment, where the Gospel says, “When you see the abomination”; he dictated this himself. He alone was spared by the priests, for he burned all his other books with his own hands.

He governed the monastery of the blessed Bartholomew, where, by God’s favor, I was abbot, and he held the vice-domestic administration with the greatest distinction. Yet after the many tribulations he endured at Constantinople, as you shall hear, the Lord brought him back to his own see with the crown of victory.

The same thing happened to me concerning the aforesaid monastery. I was deprived of it without cause by Bishop Georgius for a few years, and I was removed from this monastery [or: “I was deprived of this monastery”]. Before Georgius had risen to such a height, we were toward one another as two true brothers from a single womb. But after he received the archiepiscopal dignity, he offended God and destroyed all the priests, seizing all the monasteries and spending for the sinful indulgence of his own body all the treasures of the church that his predecessors had acquired.

## CHAPTER II. Justinian, here called Constantine, has his nose and ears cut off and is driven out. He returns to imperial power. His vengeance upon the Ravennates. Felix is captured and blinded.

Therefore, in the time of this Constantine [read: Justinian], the emperor’s own soldiers, together with certain citizens of Ravenna, cut off his nose and ears. They reduced his body, once most distinguished, to a pitiable state; expelled from the palace, he was thrown onto the shore, while they wished to mutilate him completely. But after his limbs had been weakened, he begged for his life, asserting that he had forgotten the whole empire. After these events, while he was walking sick along the shore, he made an agreement with the Bulgarians, was restored to his own seat, and regained the empire. He had a nose and ears made for himself out of gold [or: gilded metal]. Remembering the people’s anger, he ordered the nobles to be mutilated with the sword.

A tremendous outcry arose among the afflicted; the young were destroyed, and many beat their heads against the thresholds; others, pierced through, with the hilt [of the weapon] shrieking against their entrails [text corrupt]; some were thrown into the open sea in a sack and drowned; many were consumed by flames on pyres penetrating to their marrow. Other wretched men, with their entrails dissolved, sought their last meals; some suffered tyrannical punishments of lead. Many of them were received by poverty, and cities were everywhere consumed.

Turning his thoughts back toward Ravenna, he withdrew and, pondering many things through the night, said within himself: “Alas! What shall I do, and what beginning shall I make against Ravenna?” And as he considered the matter, his mind, wandering through many plans, was drawn now one way, now another.

Soon he summoned his faithful *straticus* [military official] secretly, ordering him to prepare a vessel, take his companions to the shore, and make provision for expenses; but he did not reveal what the whole matter was. He ordered him to conceal himself until the proper time came [read: until the opportunity was revealed]. Then he addressed him in this manner and gave him these instructions:

“Be steadfast in obeying my commands; act resolutely. You shall go as my messenger, speak to the people of Ravenna, and report my words to me as quickly as possible. That hostile people, by treacherous plans, cut off my nose and ears. Set up your tent on the bank of the Eridanus, compose flattering words, and cover your anger with a calm expression. Speak words of greeting to them on my behalf. Give gifts, distribute them, and invite them to a formal banquet. In their eyes be pleasant; in your heart be their enemy.”

He left the city, reached the vessel, ordered the sails to be given to the winds, sat upon the bench, and cut through the salt waves with the ship’s keel. After surveying the harbor of Drepanum, he was carried to Pachynus along the Sicilian coast. With the sea raging and a black cloud over the dark waters, the rainy Orion [or: “the watery Trion”] filled the unyielding sky. Against his will he remained in that place.

Seeing the waves calm and the sea peaceful, he entered the Adriatic gulf. He looked ahead joyfully toward Ravenna, and his deceptive tongue burst forth in these words:

“O unspeakable, wicked, cruel Ravenna, whose countryside is exposed outwardly, while within it lies the sharpest poison! You appear level with the ground, yet you touch the clouds with your head.”

While he was speaking, the ship came near the shore. With the oars extended, it cut across the bank of the Eridanus, and all the people came out with great rejoicing.

When they had come out from the city, the *ministraticus* [official] of the Greeks ordered seats to be prepared in a splendid hall upon the greenest grass. Inviting all the elders to him, he received them as though with a willing and gracious spirit. On the following day he ordered various coverings and curtains to be stretched out on both sides, for nearly the length of a stadium. He invited all the nobles who came to the threshold, two by two, and had them brought in to him [read: had them brought in two at a time]. Once they had been seized, he drove wooden hooks [read: wedges] into their mouths; their heads were tied behind their backs, and they were thrown beneath the ship’s deck.

By such treachery all the nobles were captured. Felix, the bishop of that city, was deceived there; there Joannicius, the wisest man, was captured; and many ordinary people were bound there as well. None of the citizens was able to recognize the trick beforehand. But after they had entered through the hollow beams of oak [Note: [Col. 0703D] Perhaps read, “in the hollow beams of oak.” BACCH.], and sought to flee, their ruin—and likewise the treachery—became clear.

Then the survivors entered within the city walls and set fire beneath the citizens. The people were in an uproar and raised a roar up to heaven. A great lamentation arose everywhere. Everyone was thrown to the ground. The sea’s waves do not make sounds like these, nor clouds thunder, nor does a great mass fall from the Alpine heights, nor do cypresses in a mountainous forest shake in a powerful wind. Trumpeters went through the streets, raising enormous cries, and the earth resounded.

With salty tears they poured forth their fear of the present disaster: excessive weeping, no consolation, and no restoration of life. Cries came from every side, sighs from every side, and the earth itself now gave a lowing sound in response to their cries.

One day, while the marauders and exiles—fifty in number—were running through the glassy fields after the city’s destruction, Joannicius said to his brother: “Bring paper and black ink, and write this: ‘Today, at the third hour, your kinswoman, my wife, has died; I have avenged her, and you will return with the greatest riches.’”

Accordingly, when they entered Constantinople, they found the emperor Justinian seated upon a golden emerald [or: an emerald-colored golden throne], with his head encircled by a diadem which his royal consort had distinguished with gold and pearls. He ordered all of them to be placed under guard until he could inflict various punishments upon them.

All the more important senators were killed and destroyed, and he bound himself by an oath to kill the bishop. On that very night, before the day had come, before the Ocean had given forth the dawn and the lamp of Phoebus had illuminated the world, while the divine Augustus was taking peaceful sleep upon his breast, a most distinguished young man, adorned with every glory, appeared before him together with Bishop Felix and said to him: “Spare the man of the single sword.” Immediately he vanished.

Again, looking in his sleep, he saw above the same bishop’s head what seemed to be a human right hand, shining with brilliance on either side. When the emperor awoke, he reported the matter to his attendants. Yet, because of the oath he had sworn, he did not wish to appear to have lied, nor did he wish the citizens to kill him. He therefore ordered a great dish of [uncertain: “false”] and very pure silver to be brought in; it was placed in an enormous fire, and, after it had been heated intensely, he ordered the sharpest vinegar to be poured over it. The bishop was compelled to gaze upon it there for a very long time, and he lost the sight of both eyes.

## CHAPTER III. A New Crisis for the People of Ravenna. Georgius, Son of Joannicius, Elected Duke with Supreme Authority. He Arranges Everything for War Outside and Within the City.

Meanwhile the people of Ravenna, also called the Melisenses, uncertain about their allies, exchanged various reports among themselves and, grieving over the accursed day, remained in deep mourning.

One day, at dawn, before the subdued night had snatched away its wings and the chariot had arisen from the dampness, while armed men were watching the sea, they suddenly saw in the distance an enormous ship moving across the glassy fields and forcefully cutting through the glasslike waters.

When the helmsman saw the city walls, he twisted the rudder and began to turn the ship’s course. He passed the harbor, keeping close to the bank of the Eridanus. Then, at the man’s arrival, everyone came out from the city with armed hands, their bodies clothed in iron.

Fear struck their hearts. They all recognized themselves as captives by their pallor and began to shed tears among themselves. They questioned one of the men, who was foremost among them, and said:

“We appeal to your head and your life: do not fabricate lies, because faith is not safe in this present hour; fraud and perjury rule in this present age.”

Then he stretched his palms toward the stars and turned his eyes to heaven. With a great groan he raised his voice:

“I call heaven and earth to witness, by undefiled faith and the inviolable heavenly kingdom: I shall not fabricate lies; I shall say nothing false or empty. A liar and a wicked man always loves lies.”

He spoke, and all remained silent, intent upon him. Their faces hung over him, and, seeing all the assembled ranks around him, he explained to them everything they had witnessed. They wept over all the deadly words with raised voices. Their cry struck the heavens, the earth groaned, and the mountains resounded.

Then the people of Ravenna chose for themselves a man of distinguished name [read: “a man more distinguished”], Georgius, son of Joannicius [Hymenaeos]. At that time he was prudent in speech, foresighted in counsel, truthful in conversation, and more elegant than all in grace. They all bound themselves alike to obey his commands, and whoever was disobedient was to be punished.

He mounted a mouse-colored steed, surveyed Italy outside the city, and returned at the sixth hour. He said to his companions:

“Let us station watches in those cities through which we have traveled. I declare that, from the serpent’s mouth—the serpent carried here from the sea of Byzantium—we have all drunk one poison, and gifts with swollen hearts. Let us not turn our backs upon the Danaans. Be confident; for the sake of our household gods, a spirit prepared for battle is necessary.

“Present the strongest and most iron-like breasts; summon allies, and sound the terrible trumpet. Go swiftly; impose a dark night upon the citizens. Let allied men come from the mountainous regions. Equip the bows; bend the deer-hide string, so that you may shoot arrows like seed and hurl the flying wood.

“Let the first youth move the camp with youthful weapons. Let the weapons ring; let shining shields brighten upon the shoulders. Sharpen the spears [the text is corrupt]; let the sea’s waters gleam.

“Leave the mature bodies of your parents and the most wretched old men in their old age. Let the church be their resource for prayer. Let them go with the priests, seek heavenly aid, burn incense at the altar, and bring a sacrifice to the holy altar.

“By day, in the fortifications, the purple, firelike adversary rises for us; but when, borne through the sky, it leaves the Ocean, hides itself beneath the pole, and exhales its fiery rays, when it has returned its chariots to the earth, seek poplar wood and cut it with naked iron. Let some take double axes; keep the untrimmed viburnum; weave rods from the shrubs and mix them with oak.

“Attend to the making of tents; protect your heads from the heat. Let no one be cowardly when he first hears the signal; let neither fear nor any judgment betray him.

“Let all the assemblies and all the contests of Ravenna be established. Let him who is strong in running on foot, and he who is bold in the strength of his breast, not tolerate the sluggish. But with a warm javelin, the arrows . . . . . . [lacuna].

“When our companions see this, let them prepare their spirits for battle. Do not be afraid; defend your walls with your right hands. Companions will join you from every suburb, to defend our citadel and save the city.

“Let the shores be secure, and let there be watches throughout all the harbors. Let Sarxena keep watch; Cervia of the sea, toward Nonae; Flavia Papia with arms. Let Cesena, which is called ‘the Curved,’ stand ready. Let the men of Popilienses cling to the harbor of the Sapis, near where they climb the sea waves. Let the decuman colonists keep watch beside the harbor of Candianus. Let the inhabitants of Livia stand ready on the curved shore. At the old bed of the river Bedente, let the camp of Faventia inspect the region beyond the harbor of Lachernum and the bank of the Eridanus.

“Let the Cornelian force survey the fields of Coriander, and let armed phalanxes occupy all the surrounding places. Let the people of Bononia, after crossing the Eridanus on the side of the Lion, serve . . . . . . [lacuna].”

After these things had been done, they all sent their voices up to the stars, blessing God; heaven and earth resounded with praises. Then Georgius raised his hand and ordered the powerful voices to fall silent.

After this, the religious men of Melisena asked him that, just as the city was enclosed all around by a crown, so he should establish watches within it. He consented to their request and divided the city’s people into eleven parts. The twelfth part was reserved for the Church.

Let each soldier proceed according to his military unit and number, namely: Ravenna; the first *bandus*; the second *bandus*; the new *bandus*; Invictus; Constantinopolitanus; Firmans; Laetus; Mediolanensis; Veronensis; Classensis; and the bishop’s divisions, with the clergy, the persons worthy of honor, the household, the *stratores*, and the other subordinate churches.

This organization remains to the present day.

## CHAPTER IV. Joannicius Put to Death by a Savage Butchery. Justinian Is Killed. The Sister of Joannicius Dies after Seeing the Head of Justinian, Which She Had Desired.

Let us turn our pen toward another city and recount in order the loss of our fellow citizens.

Justinian, having been transformed into an Achaemenid [or: “in the Achaemenian manner”], ordered Joannicius to be brought before him. Pretending not to know him, he asked about him, saying: “Is this the secretary of Joannicius?”

When he was told that it was indeed he, the emperor’s divine anger rose higher. He ordered a reed to be brought and, in fury, commanded it to be driven beneath all the nails of the man’s fingers, as far as the second joint.

He ordered paper and a pen to be given to him, so that he might write. When Joannicius received them, he forced the pen between two of his fingers. He did not wish to write with ink, but with the blood flowing from his fingers. He traced these words:

“God, attend to my help; Lord, hasten to help me. Deliver me from my enemies, my God, and from the hand of this wicked emperor.”

He threw the little sheet into the face of the emperor, who was sitting in the audience chamber, saying: “Take this, most wicked man, and sate yourself with my blood.”

The emperor threatened him for a long time, saying: “What are you doing, you who are about to die? Your boldness will perish.”

He ordered the attendants to take him to a place where his life would be punished, and he ordered the herald to proclaim:

“Joannicius of Ravenna, that eloquent poet, because he opposed the unconquered Augustus, shall be deprived of life by a mouse-trap death between two arches.””

They thrust seven [uncertain] beams through iron rings around his neck and harshly raised a stone above him. But he turned his blazing eyes toward heaven and stretched his bloodstained hands toward the stars.

When his prayer was finished, he said to his executioners: “Tomorrow, at this same hour as now, you will kill your emperor, and he will be with me before the most righteous Judge. Tell him this.”

They released one stone from above, and another slab [the text is corrupt] was let down upon his living neck. It crushed his body, and they left him dead. In such torment and martyrdom he ended his life.

On the following day, at the hour he had foretold, the people, unable to endure their emperor’s wickedness, attacked him and killed him. Some thrust spears between his side and his flanks; others pierced his groin with a weapon. His loins vomited blood. With his hair scattered and his feet bound with tow, his mangled, cold body was dragged down the slope to the depths, and dark death rushed upon him [read: “in darkness”].

While various people looked on, one man seized a sword, grasped his hair in his hand, tore off the emperor’s head, and, with the iron flashing and shrieking, pierced the body and cast it upon the ground. After taking counsel among themselves, they placed it in a sack and sent it throughout all Italy.

When the sister of the aforesaid Joannicius heard this, she begged the heavenly Lord with tears that she might see Justinian’s severed head, as the report had said, and immediately die.

It happened that, when the said head was being carried through the various streets fixed upon the tip of a spear, word was brought to the aforementioned woman that the severed head was to be carried past. She quickly climbed to the upper part of the house and, looking through the windows, asked the bearer to stop. After gazing at it for a very long time, she filled her breast with tears and gave thanks to God because she had seen what she desired. As she was about to turn away from the window, she fell backward, was shattered by the fall, and died.

## CHAPTER V. Philippicus Frees Felix and Gives Gifts to Many. On His Return to Ravenna, Felix Shines through Miracles. For These Deeds He Is Laden with Honors and Privileges by the Emperor and Restored to His See. He Builds a House Called Felix’s House.

After the death of Justinian, the Pelasgians raised Philippicus up as a new emperor and established him as lord of the whole earth; the empire was confirmed in his hand.

He said to Bishop Felix: “Return to your land and to your see.”

The bishop replied: “Where shall I return? Or where shall I go?”

The emperor said to him: “Why not? For what reason?”

The bishop answered: “I have lost the sight of my eyes. All my church’s possessions have been consumed here. What your pious predecessors, the emperors, had given and brought for the adornment of the Church has been carried away to this city, and nothing remains except the circuit of the walls.”

The emperor said to him: “And who took them? If they are not yours, take even some of our possessions.”

Bishop Felix replied: “My own possessions are sufficient for me, if you order them to be returned, since different people carried off different things.”

Moved by compassion, the emperor then ordered a herald to proclaim throughout the whole city that whoever possessed anything from the church of Ravenna should bring it quickly to the palace.

Vessels, coverings, and all the church’s ornaments were brought, and the bishop received them. He lost only one candelabrum from among them.

After this the emperor asked the bishop to accept some gift from his palace. He replied:

“Your favor alone is sufficient for me. Yet if, for the remedy of your soul, you wish to offer gifts to my church, you have crystal gems in this place and that within the treasury of this palace. They could be wonderfully and suitably fashioned for the adornment of a church.”

When he heard this, the emperor sent most trustworthy men from among the *Myrmidons* to verify on the spot whether the things were there as the bishop had said. They found them. He ordered all the vessels discovered there to be brought and given to Felix.

An inventory was made:

One large crystal crater of gold, decorated with gems; two other craters of onyx gem, likewise of gold and gems; one large basket containing figures of men and various birds made of clear glass resembling crystal; one *amas*, also finely carved; a water pitcher resembling a hand, and above it a hand-basin of such silverwork that no human likeness visible in our time could compare with it; two crystal ladles; and one crown of modest gold, yet possessing extremely precious gems.

So valuable was it that, in our own time, when a Jewish merchant was asked by Emperor Charles for what price it could be sold, he replied that even if all the possessions of this church, together with all its ornaments and coverings, were sold, they could not equal its value. It has not appeared since the time of Georgius.

After these events, when Felix wished to leave the city, a man at the gate pretended to be lame and to have all his limbs disabled, so that he might receive gifts. He cried out:

“Fortunate Felix, help an invalid body!”

The most blessed pope stopped and said to him:

“My son, why do you pretend to be what you are not? Why do you mock me? Although I have been deprived of outward sight, the inner lights nevertheless shine within me through the grace of Christ.”

Taking him by the hand [read: “his hand being taken”], he said: “Rise, stand up, go, and do not mock God’s servants again.”

The citizens who were with him beside the gate began to cross themselves. Terrified, they said among themselves: “This man is righteous.”

When he had left the city walls and was only a little distance from the ships, some *dromides* [couriers or mariners] were waiting for him, hoping to receive something from him. They took wicked counsel among themselves and said:

“They say that this prophet of Ravenna is a charitable man and has generous hands. Let us test whether this is true. Let one of us lie on the ground pretending to be dead; let us ask for gifts for his burial, and whatever he gives us, we shall divide by lot.”

They carried this out. As the bishop passed, they raised howls and fabricated cries, feigning tears and saying:

“Help us, good shepherd; give us something so that we may bury our dead companion.”

He removed the cloak with which he was clothed and gave it to them, saying: “Take it; if you truly have a dead man, bury him.”

They pretended to weep, but, rejoicing even more than those who celebrate victory, they took it.

After the bishop had gone a short distance, the aforementioned *dromides* thought that their companion, who was pretending to be dead, was lying on the ground. They said to the man who lay there lifeless:

“Rise, stand up; look, we have the bishop’s cloak.”

But the death which he had invited to himself by mockery and pretense came upon him in reality. They struck his sides from one direction and another, but he did not move. They wept false tears, yet he did not look upon their tears; they rolled him over, but he remained motionless.

The report of this quickly filled the imperial city. When the divine emperor heard it, he ordered blessed Felix to return from the ship. He received him in a house made of magnificent marble, asked his blessing, and offered him many gifts: two large crystal dishes, vessels made from the same material, and other small vessels for the adornment of the church.

He ordered all the privileges to be written according to the bishop’s request. Whatever Felix asked of him, he obtained. The emperor ordered ships and all necessities and desirable goods to be prepared and loaded. He kissed Felix, bade him farewell, received his blessing, and withdrew. He ordered the privileges to be written as he wished, exalted Felix far more than he had been before, and sent him back to his own see joyful and glad.

Meanwhile, after leaving the imperial city, Felix ordered the sails to be given to the winds and the oars to spread their wings as they cut through the sea. The treacherous ship is sought [the sense is uncertain]. He surveyed the harbor of Drepanum and reached the Sicilian shores.

After remaining there for several days while arranging the affairs of his church, he was received at Palermo and stayed there a few days. He reached Tyndaris; from there he crossed over and came to the shores of Pachynus. While the sun was scattering new rays over the earth, he ordered the aligned fleets to proceed. They left the abandoned harbor without a rower; the foam twisted, and the blue waters moved on, running across the glassy fields.

With a gentle breeze breathing, he crossed the Adriatic gulf and reached the harbor of the Eridanus. Entering the city, the see itself joyfully received its rider, crying out [the text is uncertain].

Three years later he built a house within the episcopal residence and named it Felix’s House after himself.

## CHAPTER VI. Before the Disaster Recounted Above, Joannicius Had Arranged the Sacred Offices. His Genealogy. His Piety Proved by a Miracle. Other Matters Concerning Him.

Before such slaughter and destruction had taken place, the wisest Joannicius flourished in this period. The bishop asked him to explain all the antiphons which we now sing on Sundays at the cross, whether those of the holy apostles, martyrs, confessors, or virgins—not only in Latin expressions but also in Greek words, because he was a most accomplished speaker in both languages.

From that same family tree and from his nobility we have little branches and great-grandchildren. Joannicius begot Agnes; Agnes gave birth to Andrew; from Andrew Basil was born; and Basil begot Andrew the presbyter, the editor of this *Pontifical*.

But let us bring forward what his notary, Hilarus by name—who afterward became a church archivist, instructed by him in this holy church—reported concerning him to his grandson, the son of his daughter, Andrew, as we have said, my grandfather, my mother’s father [or: my father’s father].

Each night, Joannicius used to walk through the various churches of God and return to his own house late. His notary, whom we mentioned above, wishing to penetrate unlawful matters which he had no right to know, rose silently in the quiet hour of the night from his soft bed and set out for the church of Saint John the Evangelist.

His notary went with him in order to see what he was doing. He said within himself: “I shall see whether this man secretly consults with the exarch at night, or perhaps takes pleasure with prostitutes, or for what reason he walks alone.”

When the aforesaid Joannicius reached the *pila* of that church [that is, the gate, Bacch.], the doors were immediately opened; the bars and bolts were silently torn away and moved to another side. After praying for a very long time before the presence of the Savior, he entered the *ardica* [porch or atrium] of that church of the apostle. When all the barriers had been opened, he prayed prostrate upon the ground.

After the prayer he withdrew, and the doors closed; all their fastenings moved back into place, each to its own position.

When Hilarus saw all this, he was struck dumb with astonishment. He withdrew into a corner of the entrance, where he ordered his body to be placed beneath the marble as a lifeless testimony to the event. When Joannicius reached the place, he gently uttered his voice, saying:

“Hilarus, why do you rush away and wish to hide? What you have seen, tell no one as long as I live. But if you tell it while I am alive, death will immediately seize you.”

He also testified another thing about him: whenever, during winter, Joannicius saw a poor man during the day, or whenever he saw sick people, he ordered a meal to be prepared for himself. When it had been brought before him so that he might taste it, he pretended to be weighed down by illness and ordered the entire meal to be put away until the next day.

At night he visited the sick, brought the meal which he had ordered to be put away, and gave it to the sick person. After the sick man recovered his strength, Joannicius would walk secretly through the churches of God and afterward return to his own dwelling.

The monastery of Saint Andrew the Apostle, called Jerichomium, was his own house. He left there five hundred pounds’ weight of bronze vessels for the monastery’s use. Above the altar, where a crown hung by bronze chains, there hung a thread of gold such as the most noble virgins of Ravenna use. He placed it on the front.

Where the crowns hung, women’s golden belts hung from bronze chains, and he ordered them to be suspended there.

In speaking of this man—not merely for the glory of his descendants, but so that we might make his deeds known—we have wandered far from the bishop through many lengthy digressions. But what we have once begun, we cannot abandon until we finish it.

I inquired about his tomb and found the matter firmly and certainly established, just as the deacon Maurus reported to me over nearly thirty days. Returning from Constantinople, he said: “At the gate called the Golden Gate there is a small church belonging to him. I was there, and in that same temple I poured out prayers to almighty God.”

## CHAPTER VII. The Deeds of Felix. The Relics of the Saints Deposited by Him. He Orders His Writings to Be Consumed by Fire. He Collects the Sermons of Saint Peter Chrysologus. His Death, Tomb, and Epitaph.

After this blessed Felix had entered the church, he deposited many relics and constructed silver panels [or: pages], and beneath the arch of the brow [read: “verses”] containing the following . . . [lacuna].

He deposited many relics of the saints there, and a reliquary made of cypress wood was placed upon the altar. It remained there until the time of Bishop Petronax. Later Sergius the deacon, abbot of the monastery of Saint Bartholomew the Apostle—where the aforesaid bishop had been abbot, deacon, and administrator of this see, and where, by God’s help, after the aforesaid Sergius the deacon, I now am abbot by divine providence through his generosity—removed the aforesaid altar from its place. It was made of *proconnesian* stone and wonderfully adorned with various marbles, among which I too decorated the work.

This blessed Felix made a reception hall, from which bishops proceed to the entrance of the Mass even to the present day, openly before the sight of the people. Above its doors I found an inscription containing these words:

> The form of this place, once . . . [lacuna]
>
> Was squalid, yet it was open to the people.
>
> After it seemed to grow young again through the merits of the bishop,
>
> It thereby received a day neighboring the Church.
>
> The company of priests proceeds better from here into the hall;
>
> It does not know how to leave its shepherd behind in forgetfulness [bishop].
>
> As he advances through the midst of the people, reverence increases,
>
> When he pours forth above them the words of God that they know.
>
> Let every priest who comes preserve this rite;
>
> For the way that lies in the middle is accustomed to remain fixed.
>
> Felix, this worthy priest, restored these things through his merits.
>
> And let the pontifical office have no end.
>
> A loquacious reputation will never conceal such great honors,
>
> For [Note: [Col. 0709] Marginal note: “For previously the departure to the evening reception hall was from here.”] . . . [lacuna]

When he was near death, he adjured the priests and clergy that whoever possessed anything from his homilies or any of his writings should bring it before him. When everything had been brought before him, he immediately ordered a pyre to be prepared and burned them all in the fire.

When the priests asked him why he had done this, he said:

“I am deprived of my sight and can see nothing; nor can I revise the books I composed. Perhaps I added something, or the scribe deceived me, lest anyone after me bring forth errors from my words. You have the books of Peter Chrysologus, which you see and will find, and which he wrote most brilliantly. Keep them and use them as you wish.”

After completing these things, he died on the twenty-fifth day of November and was buried in the church of Saint Apollinaris, not far from the monastery of Saint Felicula. You will find his epitaph containing these words:

> Amid holy praises and the triumphs of virtues,
>
> By which bishops worthy of God are crowned,
>
> Felix was a lover of supreme patience;
>
> He ordered his honorable life according to distinguished morals.
>
> He flourished magnanimously at the summit of the pastoral office.
>
> With one mind the bishop regarded all the people,
>
> Nor could he bear to see anyone sorrowful.
>
> Subtle in intellect, acute, prudent, and grave,
>
> Comparable to his predecessors.
>
> He knew supremely how to honor the apostolic dignity,
>
> Relying upon whose aid, he drove out profane doctrines [the printed reading *polet* is corrupt; read perhaps *pellit*, “drives out”].
>
> Fluent in speech, accustomed to dictate with abundant eloquence [the printed reading is corrupt],
>
> Learned and educated, he saw memorable words in cultivated style [the printed reading is uncertain].
>
> As bishop he endured excessive hardships for his country:
>
> In exile, losses, hunger, nakedness, slaughter, dangers,
>
> Contempt, banishment, terrors, chains, and blows.
>
> It was the highest honor for the pontiff to endure mockery.
>
> Removed from his territory, deprived of his own see,
>
> Lacking bodily sight, he was adorned with divine light.
>
> He was carried upon a narrow crag of the earth in Pontus,
>
> Where food was lacking, but Christ, the bread, was present,
>
> In whom he was buried in his whole body and strength.
>
> The bishop was consoled by the supreme grace of God,
>
> And raised from the heavy confinement of the island of Pontus.
>
> Heaven [F.: *caecus*, “blind”] carried him to the harbor of his beloved homeland.
>
> Drawn forth [the printed reading is corrupt; perhaps “born again”], he was adorned with all his former see.
>
> There, with pure heart, offering sacrifices to the Lord,
>
> He extends a double period of years over the earth [the text is uncertain].
>
> Here, therefore, he is buried by sacred funeral rites,
>
> And his lamentation is not to be remembered among gifts [the line is corrupt].
>
> He occupied the see for eight years, seven months, and nineteen days.

## Observations on the Life of Saint Felix

Agnellus passes over Felix’s disputes with the Roman pontiff in silence. Later writers give accounts that are by no means true. The causes of Justinian’s anger against the people of Ravenna. Other matters omitted by Agnellus. Certain matters narrated by Agnellus were neglected by Rubeus. Agnellus’s genealogy from Joannicius. Felix among the saints. An ecclesiastical writer.

## I.

Of the otherwise most distinguished bishop, Agnellus judged that matters should be passed over in silence which he foresaw might in any way damage his reputation among posterity. Accordingly, he says nothing of the disputes that arose between him and the Roman pontiff. He therefore praises Felix because, like several of his latest predecessors and successors, he had been abbot of Saint Bartholomew’s and steward of the Church of Ravenna; but he entirely omits what concerned his consecration at Rome by the pontiff. Anastasius records the following about these matters in his account of Constantine:

> “He ordained Felix archbishop of Ravenna, who, following the custom of his predecessors, did not wish to make the customary written declarations in the archive, but, relying on the power of the judges, set them forth as he preferred. His declaration, which had been placed by the pontiff in the most sacred confession of Blessed Peter the Apostle, was found many days later filthy and as though burned by fire.”

The same author says of Felix’s return:

> “At the same time Felix, archbishop of Ravenna, removed from exile, moved to repentance; although deprived of the light of his eyes, he nevertheless returned to his own see, and here too he confessed the customary memoranda and statements of faith that are made by all in the bishops’ archive, and thus earned absolution through reconciliation.”

In his account of Nicholas, the same author reports of John, archbishop of Ravenna, that he
