> “falsified the declarations and memoranda which it is customary for the archbishops of Ravenna to make in the archive at the beginning of their consecration, following the practice of his predecessor Felix; and he composed some barbarous writings and others that were false.”

Later writers built much upon what Anastasius relates here—material, as I think, unknown even to Anastasius himself. Platina, in his *Lives of the Supreme Pontiffs*, among the other arguments by which he proves that Justinian, after recovering the empire, showed the highest reverence and the most devoted obedience toward Pope Constantine, adduces the following [Col. 0712B]: when Felix, at his ordination, was compelled according to custom to promise and undertake in writing obedience and a guarantee concerning money to be sent to Rome, and refused to do so out of arrogance, Justinian, learning of the bishop’s rebellious attitude toward the pontiff, sent the patrician Theodore to Ravenna with a fleet. After defeating the Ravennates, Theodore brought Felix in chains to Constantinople, where, by order of the emperor, he was blinded and banished to Pontus:

> “Nevertheless,” Platina adds, “Constantine by no means approved this cruelty; for he wanted to bring the man back to sanity, not to afflict him with such great sufferings.”

Later, concerning Felix’s return, he writes:

> “Felix, whom we have said was banished to Pontus by Justinian, abandoning his former heresy, returned to his homeland and reclaimed the see from which he had been expelled.”

From Platina, Rubeus, in book IV, pages 213–214, composed a very elaborate and, as usual, highly embellished history. He says that Felix, “relying upon the power of the Roman judges,” returned to Ravenna and, according to his own discretion, refused the “financial payment” that was owed “by ancestral custom, ancient institution, and the recent testimony of the preceding archbishops.” He further reports that Felix summoned the Ravennates and urged them to withdraw from obedience to the Roman prelate and not to pay the tribute customarily rendered.

Accordingly, when Constantine had admonished the Ravennates as a father and achieved nothing, he informed Justinian of all these matters. Justinian then sent in a fleet, inflicted a defeat upon the Ravennates, carried Felix away, blinded him, and punished him with exile.

I am certain, however, that much of this was invented at the author’s discretion and has no basis whatever in truth. Who could doubt that Ravenna was under the jurisdiction of the emperor of Constantinople when Felix was ordained? I therefore will not believe that the Ravennates customarily paid a tribute to the Roman pontiff until this has been proved by a competent witness. Everything indicates that Anastasius misunderstood the word *cautionum*; for it does not signify a promise to pay a definite sum of money, but an affirmed and sincere profession of faith expressed in fixed verbal formulas. By this profession the newly ordained bishop also swore that he wished to remain subject to the pontiff, both in that general obedience by which all bishops were subject to the Roman bishop and in that particular obedience by which the metropolitans of Ravenna were subject to him.

It would be exceedingly difficult to demonstrate that, “by ancestral custom, ancient institution, and the recent testimony of the preceding archbishops,” any sum of money was paid to the pontiff during the time of this Felix. The judges upon whose support Felix relied when he made his declaration according to his own discretion—or, as Anastasius says, “as he preferred”—were not Roman judges, but judges of the exarchate; and if they exercised jurisdiction at Rome, they did so in the emperor’s name and depended upon his will. The emperor therefore ought first to have been enraged against them, not against the bishop; and, if against the bishop, not against the Ravennates on that account.

## II.

I therefore judge that Felix, archbishop of Ravenna, sinned in refusing to make the customary declarations to the Apostolic See, such as those contained in the *Book of the Day*, perhaps because he wished to add or remove something in favor of his own Church. The pontiff, however, rightly demanded that he use the formula employed by the other bishops and metropolitans—and especially by those who, from the beginning of the Church’s age, by synod and ordination, had been immediately subject to the Roman pontiff. Felix, relying on the exarch’s authority, made the written declaration “as he preferred,” while the pontiff bore this with difficulty and entrusted the matter to God and to the protection of Saint Peter.

But the claim that the Roman pontiff sought Justinian’s favor so that Felix might be compelled to do what he owed—and that Justinian therefore ordered Ravenna to be overthrown and Felix to be carried away—is wholly inconsistent with the truth, since Agnellus makes clear that Justinian had an entirely different reason for issuing these commands.

Justin­ian’s fury, as against all the others who were in any way believed to have participated in the crime of his deposition and mutilation, blazed forth. Writers of those times unanimously testify that he cruelly butchered, drowned, and slaughtered them, both at Constantinople and elsewhere. He was similarly inflamed against the Ravennates, who are said to have conspired with the soldiers to murder Justinian. The emperor called them “a people hostile to him, who by treacherous counsels had cut off his nose and ears.”

Among them, above all, the emperor believed that Joannicius, a man of great authority, had added oil to the fire. He therefore took savage vengeance upon him, with the herald proclaiming:

> “Joannicius of Ravenna, that eloquent poet, because he opposed the invincible Augustus, is to be deprived of life by a mouse-like death between two arches.”

The bishop was ill-treated not because of disputes with the Roman pontiff, but because Justinian, in his outrage against the injury done to his own person, grew more savage in the vengeance exacted from the Ravennates. These conclusions are easily gathered from the whole context of Agnellus’s narrative, which in this part is not at all suspect. Consequently, the other matters repeated by later writers deserve no credence.

For anyone who wishes to read more about Justinian’s fury against the patricians, the bishop of Constantinople, and even the friends through whose support he had recovered the empire; about his murder; and about his severed head, which was exposed to public insult in the cities of Italy—as our author relates happened in the case of the murdered sister of Joannicius—let him consult Theophanes, Cedrenus, Anastasius, and the others.

## III.

Besides the matters relating to Felix’s ordination, Agnellus also omitted other things: for example, that Felix was banished to Pontus. Agnellus could not have been unaware of this, since it is expressly mentioned in the epitaph.

As for the name of the *strategus*, or military commander—as Agnellus calls him, the man employed to bring disaster upon the Ravennates and Felix—Anastasius writes that he was called Theodore and had been placed “first in command of the armies of Sicily.”

Agnellus is silent about Justinian’s stay in the Chersonese after he had been driven from the throne and mutilated in his ears and nose, namely from the year 695 to 705. He is also silent about the death inflicted at Ravenna upon John, surnamed Rizocopus. Anastasius records the following in his account of Constantine:

> “Accordingly, when Pope Constantine came to Naples, he found there John the patrician and exarch, surnamed Rizocopus. When John came to Rome, he slaughtered Paul the deacon, Peter the *vicedominus* and treasurer, Sergius the abbot and priest, and Sergius the ordinator; then, proceeding to Ravenna, he met his death there by the judgment of God, dying a most shameful death for his abominable deeds.”

Since I am nevertheless certain that Agnellus’s text is mutilated, and that in his account of the landing of some unknown person on the shore of Ravenna not only the man’s name but also his office and the purpose for which he had landed armed soldiers have dropped out, I think that something about Rizocopus’s death was written there as well. The election of George as commander, and the other matters described there, show that the Ravennates, having shaken off the exarch’s yoke, asserted jurisdiction for themselves against everyone. That these events occurred during the period of Justinian’s death is proved by the fact that Rizocopus was killed at Ravenna after the pope’s return, and that three months after this return news of the emperor’s death was brought to Rome, as the aforementioned Anastasius relates.

When Philippicus had seized power, matters with the Ravennates were settled, and not only an exarch but also a bishop was sent and restored to his see. Peter, however, who had been sent to perform in Italy not only the office of exarch but also that of commander, did not come to Ravenna. Nor can it easily be demonstrated that the scholasticus exarch sent by Artemius, who was also called Anastasius, remained at Ravenna for any length of time.

## IV.

Conversely, it is remarkable that many matters narrated by Agnellus in this Life were either passed over or reported very briefly by the most eloquent historian of Ravennate affairs, who had read Agnellus. These include the fact that Justinian became enraged against the Ravennates because they had either participated in, or were believed to have participated in, his deposition and mutilation; that, although he had sworn to put Felix to death, he was deterred by a nocturnal vision and refrained from killing him, contenting himself with blinding him; and that George, the son of Joannicius, was elected commander and organized the army in an orderly fashion both at Ravenna and throughout the exarchate, arranging the frontier guards, along with other matters of lesser importance.

Yet the major and extraordinary matters narrated by our author about Joannicius certainly ought not to have been omitted. Rubeus includes them all in this brief clause, book IV, page 216:

> “At this time Joannicius of Ravenna flourished. He arranged the sacred books, the antiphons, and all the rites that the Church of Ravenna uses in the performance of divine services; concerning him, some remarkable matters were recorded in our *Annals*.”

At the very least, the following should have been transmitted to posterity: that, while Theodore was seated, Joannicius was appointed exarchal notary; that afterward, while Damianus was seated, he was summoned by the emperor to Constantinople; that, after Justinian had been driven from the throne, he returned to Ravenna; and that, when Justinian was restored to the kingdom, Joannicius was carried to Constantinople with Bishop Felix and the leading men of Ravenna and committed to prison. He remained there until the day preceding Justinian’s death, when he was slaughtered by a cruel death, which he endured with steadfast courage, and buried in a certain church at the Golden Gate.

The day on which Justinian was killed and died is uncertain. From Anastasius, however, Baronius established that it should be assigned to the end of the year [Col. 0714C] 711. Joannicius therefore perished at the same time as the emperor who, while dying, foretold that he would be slaughtered on the following day.

Since Bishop Felix was consecrated by Pope Constantine, whose pontificate began in 708, and since Felix, together with Joannicius, organized ecclesiastical offices—a task requiring several months—it follows that Justinian conceived the plan of inflicting disaster upon the Ravennates at approximately the same time as he became enraged against the inhabitants of the Chersonese, namely toward the end of the year 710.

The matters concerning the descendants of Joannicius ought not to have been omitted, both because of the man’s outstanding virtue and because Agnellus, the author of this *Pontifical Book*, is numbered among them. This token of gratitude ought surely to have been given to the memory of the author—though otherwise far from pious and foolish—to whom Rubeus owes the older parts of his History; and likewise by Rubeus and by anyone who undertakes to preserve or illuminate the history of the Ravennates.

Here is the genealogical stemma collected from Agnellus’s accounts.

From the frontier watch-posts arranged by George, it might perhaps be possible to recognize what the boundaries of the exarchate were at that time, extending from Sarcina to Bologna. It would also be easy to recognize the appearance of the surrounding territory of Ravenna, and the fact that the Eridanus flowed not far from the city through the intervening plain which they called Coriander. At the mouth of that river there was a harbor where merchandise and soldiers were regularly landed.

## V.

Baronius, together with the others, shows that Felix was numbered among the saints by the long-standing consensus of times and peoples. Under the year 711 he records the following inscription from Rubeus, which was written on the tomb:

> “This tomb preserves the enclosed body of the lord Felix, most holy and three times blessed archbishop.”

A later inscription still exists in the basilica of Saint Apollinaris in Classe, on the marble platform of Saint Mary Major; Rubeus likewise reproduces it. Faber gives another from the campanile of the cathedral of Comacchio, as follows:

> +TEM. DN. FELI. TR. B. ARCP. SCE.  
> ECC. RAV. F. D. F. VINCENTIUS RIMU. EP. C.  
> ECC. SCI. CASSIANI. CI. CUM. PRIMI. EDIFIC.  
> P. IND. VI. +FELICIT.  
>
> “[In the time of] Lord Felix, thrice-blessed archbishop of the holy Church of Ravenna, … Vincentius …, bishop of the Church of Saint Cassian, … first built [this] in the sixth indiction. Felicity.” The expansion of several abbreviated words is uncertain.

This belongs to the year 708, when Felix was first ordained.

That this Felix should be included among ecclesiastical writers is proved by what is related here about his writings, although not only the works that he ordered to be handed over to the fire while he was alive, but also the homily that survived into Agnellus’s time, have entirely perished.

His moderate disposition is commended by the fact that, since blindness prevented him from reviewing, correcting, and revising his own writings, and since he feared that through his own or his copyists’ fault something might have slipped in that could harm readers, he preferred to have everything consumed in the flames rather than preserve it at the risk of others.

We possess his works—and, through the labor of Peter Chrysologus, the sermons—which he declared should compensate for the loss of his own writings by being found, collected, and arranged by him.

## VI.

As a conclusion to these observations on the Life of Felix, it is useful to present to those skilled in chronology the chronological indicators under which the diploma of John, as I think John VII, Roman pontiff, is read in the celebrated and outstanding Codex of the monastery of Farfa.

It is said to have been issued as follows:

> “On the day before the Kalends of July, while our most pious lord, the emperor Augustus Tiberius, was reigning, in the eighth year of his reign, in the sixth year of his principate, and also under Theodosius and Constantine.”

I see that the diploma belongs to the year 705, and that by the day before the Kalends of July the eighth year of Tiberius Absimarus had begun to run. The seven years during which Theophanes says that Tiberius reigned must therefore be understood as completed; and Justinian was not restored to the throne until after the month of June in that year.

These matters are clear and admit of no doubt. What is unknown is what the epoch of this same principate signifies, beginning in the year 700 and differing from the epoch of the imperial reign. Does it signify a consulship begun by him two years after he seized the empire? Who were Theodosius and Constantine, admitted into partnership in the empire? These matters are certainly unknown from other sources. Let the most learned chronologists of our age examine and decide them.

The diploma is addressed to Thomas, abbot of Farfa, and in it the origin and fortunes of his monastery are related. Thomas flourished from 680 to 715 and died on the fourth day before the Ides of December, as can easily be determined from the same Codex and from the catalogue of the dukes of Spoleto, which Mabillon published from the aforementioned Farfa archive in his *Italian Itinerary*, together with appended documents.

# Chronological Excursus

## On the dates of the remaining Ravennate pontiffs about whom Agnellus writes

The mutilated and meager Lives of the succeeding bishops. What Rubeus and Ughellus report. The periods of Liutprand, Aldeprand, Rachis, and Aistulf. The names of the pontiffs Stephen and Paul transposed by Agnellus. Other matters relating to the chronology of the Ravennate pontiffs.

## I.

The Lives of some of the pontiffs who follow are entirely missing; most of the others are mutilated and extremely meager. Moreover, almost everywhere Agnellus’s accounts are corrupted by the author’s ignorance and hostility: by ignorance, because he confuses the order of events and periods; by hostility, because he serves up to posterity, as though they were history, tales born from popular rumors during the time of the schism.

I would not dare to promise the reader any certainty concerning the truth of the narratives here, since many things are plainly false. I have nevertheless been able to extract a few details concerning chronology. In this brief chronological excursus, therefore, I have decided to note only a few matters that may in some way help establish the periods of these pontiffs and shed some light upon the chronology.

For the most part, Rubeus does not determine the beginnings and ends of the sees here; instead, by using the word *circiter* or *circa*, “approximately” or “around,” he prudently leaves the matter undecided.

Ughellus fixes the period of each bishop as follows. He says that Felix died on the seventh day before the Kalends of April in the year 717; that John was consecrated in 718 and died in 748; that Sergius was ordained in the same year and died on the eighth day before the Kalends of September in 770; that Leo was consecrated by Stephen in the aforementioned year and died on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of March in 777; that a second John succeeded him in 777, occupied the see for seven years, and died in 784; and that Gratiosus was consecrated in that same year and died in 788, on the seventh day before the Kalends of March.

After Gratiosus, Rubeus and Ughellus add another John, whom they say died in 807 or 809. Since this John was unknown both to Agnellus and to the person who revised Agnellus’s Codex, in my judgment he has no place in the succession of the Ravennate bishops.

Ughellus therefore reports that Saint Valerius was ordained in 809 and died on the Ides of May 812, when Martin was elected. When Martin died on the Ides of September, Petronacius was ordained in 817; he died on the sixth day before the Ides of March in 835, and finally George was consecrated, remaining in office until 846.

Ughellus gives no explanation of the evidence on which he based these dates. I myself have no evidence more certain than what I shall shortly present.

## II.

John, who succeeded Felix, lived longer than all the others. Agnellus reports that while John was seated Ravenna was captured by Liutprand through the treachery of its citizens. After the exarch recovered it with the assistance of the Venetians, Anastasius, in his account of Zacharias, states that several years later it was again attacked, and that John himself, archbishop of Ravenna, together with the exarch and the people, sought assistance from the Roman pontiff.

Ravenna was captured by Liutprand around the year 725. Gregory II, in his first letter to Leo the Isaurian in defense of the veneration of the holy images, writes the following about this affair:

> “The Lombards ravaged unhappy Decapolis with their incursions, seized Ravenna itself, the metropolis, expelled your magistrates and appointed their own magistrates, and determined to treat the neighboring royal seats near us, and Rome itself, in this way, since you are quite unable to defend us.”

These words indicate that Ravenna was occupied by Liutprand for a considerable, though not necessarily very long, period before the exarch recovered it.

Anastasius, in the passage mentioned above, reports that Ravenna was again thrown into alarm while John was still archbishop, when Liutprand moved against it:

> “In the eleventh indiction,” he says, “when the aforesaid king was oppressing the province of the Ravennates exceedingly, and had prepared to make his move and besiege the city of the Ravennates, Eutychius, the most excellent patrician and exarch, learning of the movement of that king, together with John, archbishop of the Church of Ravenna, and the whole people …”

The eleventh indiction belongs to the year 743, when these events took place.

It is almost certain that John continued to live after Liutprand’s death; but since no definite year is indicated, the matter remains uncertain. As a conjecture, one might suppose that he lived into the time of Aistulf. After relating the ordination of Sergius at Rome, our author immediately adds:

> “At that time this city was being harassed by the Lombards and Venetians.”

This may refer to the period of Aistulf, since there was no Lombard movement against the Ravennates under Rachis, who succeeded Liutprand after the brief reign of Ildeprand. Aistulf did indeed attack Ravenna with determined effort, and actually captured it as soon as he became king after Rachis had assumed the monastic habit.

To approach as closely as possible the year in which Sergius began to occupy the see, it is worthwhile to establish the date when Ravenna was captured by Aistulf. This is also of great importance because at that time, when Eutychius fled to Greece, the exarchate came to an end.

Baronius assigns the beginning of Aistulf’s reign to the year 750. Rubeus says that, immediately upon being elected king, he marched against Ravenna and captured it around the year 752.

In the highly esteemed Farfa Codex mentioned above there is a confirmation by King Aistulf of the monastery’s possessions and privileges:

> “Given at Ravenna in the palace, on the fourth day of the month of July, in the third year of our most fortunate reign, in the fourth indiction.”

The fourth indiction was running in July of the year 751. Aistulf had therefore occupied Ravenna before July of that year and had begun to reign before July of 749.

From this point we can move back with complete confidence to the beginning of Rachis’s reign. Before the July just mentioned, Rachis had assumed the monastic habit. Since he reigned for five years and six months, as the *Chronicon Casinense* of Ostia, book I, chapter 8, reports, it follows that he began to reign around the end of the year 743, and that Liutprand died six months before the period assigned to Ildeprand—contrary to the common opinion, which places his death in the year 744.

As for the eleventh indiction mentioned by Anastasius, when Ravenna was attacked by Liutprand, I think this should be referred to the final months of the year 742, when that indiction began to run from September.

## III.

All these conclusions, however, would entail that Sergius was ordained while Rachis was still reigning if John died in 748, as Ughellus says. Since it is certain that Rachis became a monk while Zacharias was seated, it would follow that Sergius too was ordained by that same Zacharias. There are reasons why I strongly doubt this.

Agnellus’s history must here be subjected to serious examination. In the Life of this Sergius, after first stating that Aistulf was already residing at Ravenna, Agnellus relates that, because Sergius had failed to go out to meet Pope Paul when Paul was traveling to France, Paul, on his return from France, tore the Valley of Gallia from the jurisdiction of the archbishop of Ravenna and wished to bring Sergius himself to Rome and strip him of his dignity.

When the Roman bishop objected that Sergius’s ordination was invalid because he had entered the episcopate as a married man, our author says:

> “To this the pontiff of Ravenna replied: ‘I was not appointed through my own presumption, but the entire clergy and people elected me. You questioned me in due order according to canonical custom, and everything about me was disclosed to you: how I was a layman, how I had a bride, and how I entered the clergy. This was made known to you, and you said that none of these things could be an obstacle to me. After you had formed such an opinion about me, why did you consecrate me?’”

Agnellus then adds that, while Sergius was in great anguish of mind, the pontiff died that same night, and Stephen, the brother of the deceased pope who succeeded him in the pontificate, promised Sergius his freedom.

He further says that this Stephen, while traveling to France, stopped at Ravenna and carried away many things, along with the other matters related there. Whether these accounts deserve credence is not for this place to investigate. What touches chronology, however, must be brought back to the anvil.

## IV.

It is absolutely certain that Pope Paul was succeeded by his brother, who is listed in the succession of the supreme pontiffs under the name Stephen III, and not the reverse. The Roman pontiff who succeeded Paul was indeed called Stephen, but he had no connection with his predecessor Paul. Furthermore, after Paul’s death, an intruder named Constantine occupied the Roman see for a year and a month before Stephen IV of that name was consecrated.

These facts do not at all fit the history of Sergius. In his own case Sergius replies to the pontiff that he had been ordained by him, and that the very man who was then accusing him and threatening to strip him of the episcopate had questioned him according to the canons concerning his status. Although Sergius could have been ordained by Stephen III, he certainly could not have been ordained by Paul.

A diploma shows that the monastery of Gallia was restored to Sergius by Paul in the year 759. In the diploma it is said to have been taken away by Stephen, Paul’s predecessor; whereas Agnellus says that Sergius was deprived of that monastery by Paul.

Furthermore, Paul never went to France, and therefore could not have become angry with Sergius for failing to go out to meet him on that occasion, as our author relates.

All these matters, when weighed together, show that Agnellus confused everything, not only in his history but also in chronological matters. In my view, because certain unfortunate events had occurred to the Church of Ravenna under Stephen IV, and because these events had been attributed to the pontiff through clerical hostility, the similarity of the names caused them to be attributed to Stephen III. Thus, as is the custom of dreamers, several truths were confused into a single, solemn, and exceedingly foul falsehood.

Hence the periods of the two pontiffs were transposed, and Stephen was wrongly made Paul’s successor, although Paul in fact succeeded Stephen.

Once these matters have been observed, the chronology of the Church of Ravenna emerges, as it were, from dense darkness. It follows that Sergius was ordained by Stephen III and correctly replied, when accused concerning the status from which he had been taken into the episcopate, that he had disclosed everything to that same pontiff, who was considering bringing him back into the proper order and who questioned him at his consecration according to the canons: everything concerning his lay status and his marriage, neither of which, in the judgment of that pope, had been an obstacle to his ordination.

Thus Sergius was ordained around the year 752, when Aistulf had already occupied Ravenna. In 757 he feared for himself at Rome, when Stephen died on the sixth day before the Kalends of March. While Paul was seated, he recovered the monastery of Gallia in 759.

The year of his death will be discussed shortly. Two letters of Pope Paul must now be examined; they establish with near certainty the sequence of events that has so far been arranged.

Baronius, under the year 767, gave an index of their contents from Panvinius, after having searched for the letters in vain. The Magdeburg Centuriators had already given one in volume 8, page 725. Gretser first published the collected volume of the letters at the command of Charlemagne from manuscripts; Francis Duchesne reprinted it in volume III of the *Scriptores of Frankish History*.

The content of the letter numbered 29 by Baronius and 27 by Gretser is identical in both editions; at the end it says that Paul was “working to have Sergius restored to his own see.”

But the summary and letter numbered 14 by Baronius and 28 by Gretser present a different matter from the summary cited by Baronius. Baronius’s version reads:

> “He sends the letters of Sergius, the traitor and bishop of Ravenna, and requests assistance.”

Gretser’s summary, however, together with the letter itself, says that the pontiff sent Pippin letters written by Sergius, bishop of Ravenna, asking that the pontiff request assistance from Desiderius—whose peace had been settled with him—for the defense of Ravenna and the Pentapolis.

Once Gretser corrected the summary of this letter and presented the letter itself, it became clearer than midday light, from the tenor of both documents and from the restoration by the same pontiff of the monastery of Gallia, for which Rubeus supplies documentary evidence, that Paul was not only never hostile to Sergius but loved and supported him exceedingly. At one point, after Sergius had been driven from his see, Paul did everything in his power to restore him.

It is therefore clear that the common error must be corrected. Rubeus, failing to observe in Agnellus that what ought to have been attributed to Stephen III had been attributed to Paul, and vice versa, said—and Baronius, Faber, Ughellus, and the others followed him—that Sergius was ill-treated under Paul. In fact, this occurred under Stephen, Paul’s predecessor, while Sergius always experienced Paul’s benevolence toward him.

## V.

Anastasius, in his account of Stephen IV, relates the death of Sergius and the beginnings of Leo, which were made disastrous by a grievous schism. Although these events cannot be assigned to a definite year, it is nevertheless certain that they occurred some time after the Roman synod held concerning the preceding pseudopontiff Constantine, in April of the seventh indiction, namely in the year 769.

When Anastasius is about to relate the death of Sergius, archbishop of Ravenna, and the ordination of Leo, he says:

> “After these synodal proceedings had been completed, it happened, after some time, that Sergius, archbishop of the city of the Ravennates, departed from this life …”

It follows that Sergius died around the end of that year or the beginning of the following year, 770. Leo’s peaceful occupation of the see could not have been delayed beyond the year 771, once Stephen had extinguished Michael’s schism, since Stephen himself died on the Kalends of February in the year 772.

As for the death of this same Leo, according to Ughellus’s calculations he died on the Kalends of March in the year 777, and John, whom they call the sixth of that name, was substituted for him. Rubeus had reported nearly the same thing, writing the aforementioned year 777 in the margin.

Among the letters of Pope Adrian are some whose summaries Baronius and the Magdeburg Centuriators provide and which concern Ravennate affairs.

The fifth explains to King Charles that he had ordered the Venetians to be expelled from Ravenna, or the Pentapolis, and that the duke Germanus had invaded the property and possessions of the Church of Ravenna.

The twelfth grants King Charles the mosaics and marbles of the city of Ravenna, both those situated in the churches and those in the walls and pavements.

The twenty-eighth accuses Leo, bishop of Ravenna, on account of his disobedience.

The twenty-ninth indicates that he is sending the letter of the patriarch of Grado. He complains that Leo, archbishop of Ravenna, had previously opened and read it. He again accuses Leo.

The thirtieth states that he is pleased that Leo, archbishop of Ravenna, had gone to Charles.

The thirty-first again vehemently accuses Leo, archbishop of Ravenna, because he had become disobedient and insolent after returning from Charles. He asks Charles not to allow anything to be taken from Saint Peter that had been offered to Blessed Peter by Charles himself and by his father Pippin.

The thirty-ninth accuses Leo of lying and rebukes him because he had sent his envoys to Ravenna for the election of a new pontiff.

The following letters relating to Ravennate history are also preserved in the *Codex Carolinus*, and we give their summaries.

**Letter 50.** The pontiff writes to Charles that the Lombards and Ravennates, because the king had detained his envoy, were saying that the king himself no longer remained in apostolic charity. He therefore asks that the envoy be sent back.

**Letter 51, in the postscript.** He accuses Leo of Ravenna because, after returning from Charles, Leo refused to obey and retained Imola and Bologna. Furthermore, because Leo had sent the pontiff’s envoy Dominic to Ravenna in chains with an armed force and would not allow anyone from the cities of Emilia to come to the pontiff—namely Faenza, the duchy of Ferrara, Comacchio [read: Comaclo, Bacch.], Forlì, Forlimpopoli, Cesena, and Bobbio, or the tenth tribunate—he asks that Leo be brought back into order.

**Letter 52, in the postscript.** It contains much the same concerning Leo as the preceding letter.

**Letter 53.** He says that Leo of Ravenna’s journey to Charles was not unwelcome to him.

**Letter 54.** The pontiff again accuses Leo on account of the matters recounted in the preceding letters 51 and 52. Particularly noteworthy is the statement that Leo defended himself by retaining the cities of Emilia, following the example of Sergius. The pontiff says that Sergius had been deprived by Stephen of the administration of the exarchate “while he was striving, in a spirit of arrogance, to act against Stephen’s will.” From this we recognize that Sergius had fallen from Stephen’s favor.

**Letter 67.** The pontiff grants Charles the mosaics and marbles of the palace of Ravenna.

**Letter 71.** The pontiff explains how the bishop of Ravenna is elected. He says that when Sergius died, the matter proceeded amid disagreement because of the schism of Michael. He adds that the new archbishop is elected with the approval of the Apostolic See by the clergy and people, and not by an envoy sent by kings—either in the election of John or in that of Gratiosus.

**Letter 82.** It mentions John, a monk and abbot of Ravenna, sent by the pontiff to Charles.

**Letter 84.** The pontiff tells Charles that he had ordered the Venetian merchants to be expelled from the city of Ravenna and from the Pentapolis. He asks that the duke of Germanus be restrained, since he had seized certain lands belonging to the Church of Ravenna.

## VI.

Of the letters mentioned above, letter 71 provides the light necessary for arranging the chronology. We know not only that Leo’s election took place while Stephen was seated, but also that before Adrian’s death Leo, John, and finally Gratiosus had died, and that the election of the successor—who proved to be Valerius—is discussed in that letter.

Since, according to our author, Gratiosus occupied the see at the time when Charles came to Ravenna while Adrian was still alive, it necessarily follows that Gratiosus had already been ordained by the year 786. For Charles came against the Beneventans during the winter at that time and celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Florence, as Einhard relates.

John, Gratiosus’s predecessor, may have died shortly before from the illness he contracted soon after cursing a young man around the feast of Saint Apollinaris, on 23 June. If, as Agnellus reports, John occupied the see for seven years, one month, and three days, he had died around the year 776, when Leo began his episcopate.

The life of Bishop Gratiosus, however, cannot be extended beyond the year 795, the year in which Adrian died. Since Adrian’s letters were collected without chronological order, they provide no illumination from which I could conclude that Gratiosus lived into Adrian’s final years. This is suggested by the fact that, among all Adrian’s letters, none says anything about the successor of Gratiosus, the bishop of Ravenna.

VII. Thus St. Valerius was ordained by Hadrian around the year 794. Concerning Martin, who succeeded Valerius, Agnellus writes the following in his Life:

> “He attained nearly eighty years of this see, having been consecrated at Rome by the hands of Pope Leo III.”

The number eighty must refer to Martin’s age when he was ordained bishop. Since he is said to have been consecrated by Leo III, he must have begun his episcopate before the year 816, for Leo III died in that year. [Col. 0720D] But Martin was consecrated even before 811; for our author says in his Life:

> “During his time Pippin, king of the Lombards, died; and after some time the emperor Charles died on the thirtieth day of January.”

Pippin died shortly after concluding his war with the Venetians, which is assigned to the year 810; Charles died in 814. There are also indications that Martin began to sit before the aforementioned year 811—namely, several events that occurred while Leo III was still alive and that seem to have required a span of several years: the rebuilding of the church of St. Apollinaris in Classe through the generosity of the Roman pontiff, and the disputes between Martin himself and Leo.

Thus St. Valerius’s episcopate is nearly confined between the years 794 and 809. It is also almost certain that Martin outlived Pope Stephen, for he received Stephen himself when he came to Ravenna, as we learn from our author, who had written more about Martin than what survives; these additional passages perished together with the complete Life of Bishop Petronacius. [Col. 0721A] It therefore becomes almost certain that this pontiff died, more than ninety years old, during the early years of Pope Paschal.

He was therefore mistaken who supplemented the Life of Petronacius when he wrote that Petronacius swore an oath of allegiance to the emperor Charles, since Charles had died several years before Petronacius began to sit. To these points should be added what I noted concerning the age of Agnellus in the observations on the verses prefixed to the *Liber Pontificalis*, observation four.

Baronius assigns the beginning of Pope Paschal’s pontificate to 28 January 817. Petronacius’s beginning must be placed before 819, as is concluded from a privilege of that same Paschal, issued in July, indiction 12, as it is read in Rubeus, who copied it from the original—written, as he himself says, on the bark of a tree, or more truly on Egyptian papyrus. [Col. 0722A] Petronacius signed the acts of the Roman council under Eugenius in 826 and lived down to the time of Gregory IV, by whom his successor Georgius was ordained, as our author relates. Gregory began to sit around the year 827. Georgius lived beyond the year 841, in which, on 25 June, Charles the Bald won a victory over Lothair at Fontenay. To add more about the chronology of these pontiffs would be to indulge in dreams.

# THE LIFE OF JOHN

[Col. 0721]

## CHAPTER ONE

Ravenna captured through the treachery of its citizens by Liutprand. John goes into exile. He is restored through the efforts of the scriniarius Epiphanius. The same Epiphanius takes vengeance on John’s enemies.

### John [the fifth], XXXIX

He was exceedingly patient, humble, and gentle. During his time the Petriana church collapsed in an earthquake after the solemn rites of the Mass had been completed on a Sunday.

While the kingdom of the Lombards was governed by King Liutprand, the aforementioned city was surrounded and devastated by his army like a crown. It was betrayed by its own citizens through a feigned stratagem at the gate called Vicus Salutaris, which stood beside the river Pantheum. All the citizens ran there. One of them, however, hostile to his fellow citizens, brought the keys after money had been promised him; he secretly removed the mechanisms of the gate leading to Vicus Leprosus, where there was a bridge made from squared stones, opened the barriers, and laid all the gates open. The enemies entered the city and overthrew it. [Note: That is, the gate. BACCH.]

[Note: [Col. 0721D] The marginal note says: “This appears to have been the city of Classe.” BACCH.]

For by God’s judgment, the very man who had plotted against his fellow citizens and opened the barriers of the gate was immediately killed when he was pierced by a wooden beam [variant: timber]. He did not receive the money that had been promised him, but gave his own blood before everyone else, and was not committed to the earth.

Therefore the citizens of Ravenna, enraged against this pontiff, banished him into exile in the regions of Venetia, and he remained an exile for one year. Then Epiphanius the scriniarius, seeing the destruction of this holy church and the father of his country in distress and held in deep affliction, recalled him through the exarch of this city to his own see.

After he had been restored to the pontifical throne, the aforesaid Epiphanius the scriniarius said to him one day:

> “Lord Father, do not hesitate to go to the exarch in the palace, offer him a large *palvita* [variant: *palarea*] of silver, and ask him to compel those men who sent you into exile to stand trial. Let us take vengeance on them, and I will restore to you ten times what you give. You maintain the conduct proper to a pontiff; I shall litigate with them, and, with the Lord’s help, I know that I shall carry away a triumph over your enemies.”

And it happened as you have heard above. As soon as the aforesaid pontiff John had been received again into the maternal bosom of the Church, on the following day the author of the plan, Epiphanius the scriniarius, standing in conflict with each of the men, said:

> “You have a written injunction concerning these matters, that you must never act against this holy Church or against the pontiff of this see on any account, nor mutter against him with your lips. Tell me: what sort of sheep are you, that, while your shepherd was cherishing you and leading you through grassy fields, you struck him with your horn and wrote documents against him?”

He collected *jugies* from those convicted in the judgment and gave them to the exarch. [The precise sense of *jugies* is uncertain.] After these things had been done, all of them came humbly and unanimously to him, asking mercy, and no one afterward led him into bitterness.

## CHAPTER TWO

Battle between the Ravennates and the Greek *ministraticus*, accompanied by a portent. The day of Saints John and Paul made a festival for this reason. John’s death.

[Col. 0722C] During John’s time the *ministrategus* [variant: *ministraticus*] came again to Ravenna to lay it waste, thinking that he would escape as before. When the Ravennates learned this, they went out against him in battle to the field of Coriander. They pretended to flee and gave their backs; but when they reached the stadium of Tabula, where a stone boundary had been fixed as a marker, they turned back toward the Greek front and began to fight bravely. There was no respite anywhere for those striking one another; great slaughter was inflicted on the Greeks by the sword.

The priests, together with the pontiff and the elders, lay prostrate on the ground, clothed in sackcloth, ashes sprinkled on their heads, and entreated almighty God. The elders were covered with sackcloth, their heads unkempt and their appearance squalid; with tearful eyes they cried out to heaven. Likewise, all the males and females who had been left within the city awaited the help of the Almighty. The rest, girded with iron and taking up the weapons of youth, struck down the enemy without interruption.

Then, as we heard from those who told the story, an image resembling a great bull appeared between the two armies. It began to scatter dust with its feet against the Greek army, and immediately a voice resounded—no one recognized where it came from or whose it was—and cried in the ears of all:

> “Come, Ravennates, fight bravely; victory will be yours today.”

When the Pelasgians saw that their horn had been broken, they began to flee, thinking to save themselves within their *dromones*. Then the Melisenses—that is, the citizens of Ravenna—surrounded them with boats and *carabi*, attacked the Byzantines, killed them all, and hurled their bodies into the Eridanus. Thus for six years no one from Patheremum [variant: Patherenum] ever ate a fish from that place.

This happened on the day of Saints John and Paul. They began to celebrate that day as a festival like Easter, decorating the city’s streets with various cloths and proceeding with litanies to their church, blessing God forever and ever. Amen.

He died and was buried in the basilica of Blessed Apollinaris. You will find an epitaph over him containing the following:

> [lacuna] sat for eight years, [lacuna] months, [lacuna] days.

[Note: [Col. 0723D] “The epitaph is missing here; I did not find it in the original.” BACCH.]

# OBSERVATIONS ON THE LIFE OF JOHN

[Col. 0723B] This John was the sixth of that name. Why was he called the fifth? Particulars concerning Ravenna’s capture. Classe destroyed. John went into exile, not on account of the Iconoclasts. The office of the scriniarii. The date of the events related concerning the Ravennate victory is uncertain. Which river was the Pantheum, or Patheremum?

## I

Rubeus cites public records engraved on marble that commend the generosity of this John; from them it is clear that around the year 731 he donated several things to the monks living at St. Apollinaris in Classe. He is called:

> “John, the bountiful pontiff, junior, fifth in name.”

Hence the distinguished historian of Ravennate affairs considers it certain that the two Johns who succeeded Marinianos, of whom Agnellus speaks, must be counted as one.

> “This,” he says, “is the reason for what we stated: that those two archbishops named John, who succeeded one another without an intervening bishop according to Agnellus, and those who followed him in later times, were one and the same, the fourth of this name; but this man was the fifth.”

Rubeus’s argument, however, although it seemed decisive to him, is not so at all. At the time when that monument was erected, the Ravennate opinion was the same as Agnellus’s: namely, that there was one John of that see, also distinguished by the surname Angeloptis, who encountered Attila when he invaded Italy and lived during the reign of Theodoric. Those two Johns who succeeded Marinianos were therefore distinguished from that John; otherwise this man would have been the fourth, not the fifth.

For these reasons, and because of what I noted in its proper place, I judged that one should not depart from Agnellus’s opinion concerning two bishops of the same name—especially since I saw that Rubeus had gratuitously and without witnesses added another John after the episcopate of Bishop Gratiosus. He seems to have inferred that this had occurred because, from the sequence of the succeeding Ravennate pontiffs and from the numbers added to those called John in public documents, he saw that one John, distinguished by the number five, was necessary to continue the sequence.

[Col. 0723D] Thus this John is the sixth of that name, although he was called the fifth; the seventh preceded Gratiosus, and the eighth sat after Deusdedit, the successor of Georgius.

## II

It is certain that Ravenna was captured by Liutprand’s army during the early years of this John’s episcopate, but the more recent accounts disagree among themselves about the event. Our author gives a detailed account of the matter: a certain citizen betrayed the city. While the citizens were rushing to the gate called Vicus Salutaris, against which the enemy was chiefly advancing according to the plan, he handed over undefended the other gate, at Vicus Leprosus, through which the Lombards burst in.

The author of the marginal notes wondered whether this should be understood as referring to the city of Classe, which was destroyed on that occasion—perhaps because the gate of Vicus Leprosus provided an entrance into the city of Classe. I myself clearly see that Ravenna was captured by a Lombard soldier of Liutprand, although Classe may have been occupied first and may have suffered the greater damage. Thus, when Agnellus writes that Classe lay almost in ruins, this is evidence that, by adding the word “formerly” when he names Classe, he implies that scarcely anything of it remained in his own time.

Others nevertheless write that Classe was occupied by Faroald, duke of the Spoletans, before Ravenna was captured by Liutprand’s soldiers. Our author says nothing about this.

## III

After recounting Ravenna’s capture and the death of the man who betrayed his country, the narrative turns to Bishop John, who was in exile among the Venetians and was restored through the efforts of the scriniarius Epiphanius. I infer that this happened on the occasion of Ravenna’s occupation by the Lombards.

Rubeus says:

> “They do not give the cause of the exile; nevertheless, most people believe that the exarch Paul inflicted it, because the archbishop did not assent to the heresy of the Iconoclasts.”

Since Agnellus’s account conveys something else, I do not believe this. Epiphanius, having recalled through the exarch the pontiff who had been driven into exile by the hatred and calumnies of the citizens, compelled the authors of the calumnies, brought before the court, to sing a recantation and imposed a substantial fine upon them. This could have happened if John had been in exile because Paul had expelled him for rejecting the Iconoclast heresy by his dissent.

It seems more probable to me that, while Paul himself was staying among the Venetians after fleeing when Ravenna had been captured by the Lombards, John was attacked by calumnies before the new rulers, brought under suspicion, and expelled from the city. When affairs had been settled and Ravenna had been recovered through the cooperation of the Venetians and the Roman pontiff, he was easily restored by the exarch to his own see.

## IV

I recognize that this Epiphanius, who deserved well of John by arranging his recall to his own see and by standing in court with the bishop’s calumniators, was a layman from the fact that he suggested to the prelate that he wished to act as the accuser in the case, while the pontiff should “maintain the conduct proper to a pontiff”—that is, refrain from accusing the citizens. This scriniarius, therefore, belonged to the exarch, not to the bishop, and still less was he a *quaestor*, as others have thought.

*Scrinia* were places in which the public documents of the state were preserved in an orderly arrangement; those who worked at copying and storing these documents were called *scriniarii*. It is nevertheless clear that there was also a scriniarius in the Ravennate Church, just as the Roman Church had scriniarii. Anastasius, in his Life of Stephen IV, praises “the scriniarius of the Ravennate Church.”

Among other duties, the office of such scriniarii was to compose the letters sent by the pontiff. This is clear both from the records of the pontiffs and from Letter 27 of Nicholas I, in which the pontiff says that he had not had his letters written in the usual manner because:

> “On account of the Paschal celebrations, he had not been able to have his scriniarii at his disposal as he ought, since they were occupied with their proper duties.”

It is probable that the scriniarii of the Ravennate Church performed the same office—

## V

It is extremely difficult to determine when that *ministrategus*, as Agnellus calls him, attempted to attack Ravenna, and when the Ravennates celebrated the recurring anniversary of their victory with festive honors.

Agnellus plainly describes him as a Greek accompanied by Byzantine troops, and says that he had previously come to destroy the city—under Bishop Felix, namely—and had escaped after inflicting a defeat through trickery. But how could it have happened that, while the emperor’s exarch was residing at Ravenna, the Ravennates rose against a commander at Classe, armed themselves, met him as he came, and, after defeating him, celebrated the memory of the victory every year?

I know that during the episcopate of this John the minds of the Ravennates were divided among conflicting causes; indeed, the exarch Paul and his sons were handed over to death amid a tumult, while the Constantinopolitan emperor was raging against the pontiff and the Catholics because of the Iconoclast heresy. On that occasion, the same man who had nearly destroyed Ravenna under Bishop Felix may have been sent to Classe, and the Ravennates may have overwhelmed him.

Once the disputes and disturbances had been settled, however, and Eutychius was residing at Ravenna, it is scarcely credible that the anniversary of the victory could have been celebrated every year with the greatest pomp without provoking the indignation of that same exarch.

The river which is here said to have flowed not far from the mouths of the Po is called *Pantheum* in the first account, although corruptly, and *Patheremum* in the second. I think it was a ditch flowing from the nearby lagoon of Padusa, which was as rich in fish for the Ravennates as Padusa itself, of which Virgil writes:

> “Or the fish-filled river of Padusa.”

The Petriana church is said to have suddenly collapsed in an earthquake on a Sunday, after the solemn rites of the Mass had been celebrated. This may serve as a conjecture that the disaster occurred during the early years of this bishop’s episcopate.

# THE LIFE OF SERGIUS

[Note: [Col. 0725D] Reader, recognize that the following Life of Sergius has been polluted by the rumors of schismatics. You also have Agnellus, who, driven by the goad of vengeance, relates unworthy things about the Roman pontiff. Accordingly, this author deserves no credence in these matters; he also grievously strays from historical truth, as has been noted in its proper places. See below in the Observations.]

[Col. 0725]

## CHAPTER ONE

Sergius, a married layman, becomes bishop. His wife Euphemia becomes a deaconess. The clergy are hostile to the bishop. The bishop creates new priests and deacons. When matters are settled, these ministers serve in different clothing and in a lower rank.

### Sergius, XL

He was young in age, short in stature, smiling in face, handsome in appearance, blue-eyed, and born of the noblest parentage. He was a layman and had a betrothed woman. After he assumed the government of the Church, he consecrated his betrothed, Euphemia, as a deaconess, and she remained in the same habit.

But during his time, because of zeal among the priests and those who did not possess true [virgins?], and because they were not united in spirit, the multitude was divided. After he had been consecrated at Rome, the priests despised him, the ministers separated themselves from him, and there was no one who would approach the holy altar with him.

At that time this city was being harassed by the Lombards and the Venetians. We cannot go through everything in detail, because it is tedious; nevertheless, for the sake of brevity we shall present the reason. The pontiff sent to the deacons and to the other ministers of the Church, asking them all to gather together into the bosom of the Church. But they, persisting in the sting of their grief, refused.

Then, having devised a plan, he consecrated priests and deacons. When those hard-hearted men heard this, they came, and on Sunday proceeded with him to the solemn rites of the Mass. But the new sheep, who had thought themselves to stand in a lofty place, were repelled by the old priests, and, ashamed, closed their mouths.

Then the pontiff gently and kindly comforted the former priests, pouring soothing words upon them until he recalled them from anger to gentleness. After they had deliberated much among themselves, they established a peace agreement concerning the new consecration: the deacons were to put on a *superhumerale* over the dalmatic in the Greek manner and stand beside the altar. From that day the number of Levites began to increase, although the canons prohibit this, safeguarded by apostolic authority.

## CHAPTER TWO

The arrival at Ravenna of Pope Zacharias, who had anointed King Pippin. He celebrates Mass and gives an *endothim*. Aistulphus offers gifts both at Rome and at Ravenna. He restores the Petriana church. Other matters concerning the same man.

At that time Pope Zacharias of Rome departed from Rome and reached the borders of Francia, seeking protection and aid to drive the Lombards from Roman territory, because King Aistulphus was harshly oppressing Italy.

But after another king had been expelled from the Frankish throne, Pippin received the scepter of the kingdom, was blessed by the hands of the pope, and was anointed with sacred chrism. He then returned to Rome.

Before returning to Rome, Zacharias celebrated Mass in the church of Blessed Apollinaris and offered an *endothim* of *blatta alithena*, magnificently adorned with pearls; his name was written there. When King Aistulphus saw that troubles had grown heavy upon him from every side, he sought help from the Italians, since circumstances were not favoring him. He went to the threshold of Blessed Peter the Prince, offered gifts and many presents, and then returned to Ravenna. He placed upon the holy altar of the Ursian church the gold-embroidered cloak that he had been wearing.

He wished voluntarily to rebuild the Petriana church, which had been utterly destroyed by the earthquake. He erected pyramids around it and set up columns, which remain to this day, but he did not complete the work.

Concerning the aforesaid king, who was called by the name Aistulphus: shall I speak, or remain silent? Nevertheless, I shall tell the story. Five infants were born to one mother, in one hour and in one birth, from one womb. When this was reported to the king and the astonishing matter became known, he formed a new plan and ordered them to be brought before him in a single large basket. When he saw them, he did not wish to throw them into a dung heap. He was horrified to be the father, although he had been their begetter.

He ordered a royal staff to be brought and said to his men:

> “Whoever among them grasps the staff with his hand shall live.”

As soon as the staff was placed in the middle, this one held it among his brothers with an outstretched arm. Then his father named him Aistulphus.

Let us return to the foregoing account.

## CHAPTER THREE

Sergius, ordained contrary to the canons by the Roman pontiff, is brought to trial. A new pontiff restores Sergius to his see. He gives thanks to St. Nicholas.

When this Bishop Sergius was in office and Pope Paul [variant: Stephen] of Rome was traveling through Francia [variant: “Franciae: traveling through Tuscany”], he did not go to meet him. The pope, angered, departed with great anger from the valley called Calle Collata, which in rustic speech is called Galliata; he surveyed the Lombard kingdom, crossed the lofty heights, and passed over the ridge of Mount Jove. Then he took the road to Francia and obtained from King Pippin everything he had requested. Afterward he returned and began to harass Archbishop Sergius.

Sergius, trusting in the king that he would give him support, was deceived. He was brought to Rome by his fellow citizens and overcome by fraud. When the bishops had been assembled at the pope’s command, they wished to deprive him of his dignity and cast him out of the pontifical rank.

The Apostolicus pronounced this sentence against him:

> “You are a neophyte. You were not from the sheepfold, nor did you serve according to the canons in the Ravennate Church. Instead, you suddenly invaded the cathedra like a thief, expelled your priests, who were worthy to enjoy these things of the Church, and, through the favor of secular men, although with authority, obtained the see.”

To this the pontiff of Ravenna replied:

> “It was not through my presumption, but the clergy and the entire people chose me. You questioned me in due order according to canonical custom; everything about me was disclosed to you—how I was a layman, had a betrothed woman, and reached the clergy. This became known to you, and you said that no obstacle could stand in my way. After you had learned these things about me, why did you consecrate me?”

The bishops expressed different opinions among themselves, and within each chamber of the heart a great storm was shaken. For they all said:

> “How can we, since we are disciples, judge our master?”

When the pope heard this, he became furious and declared that on the following day he would tear the *orarium* from Sergius’s neck with his own hands.

That same night Sergius, Bishop of Ravenna, threw himself with tears before the altar of Blessed Nicholas and surrendered himself wholly to profound lamentation. Lying prostrate, he poured out tears for so long that the place where he mourned became thoroughly wet and produced little streams.

By God’s judgment, that night Pope Paul [variant: Stephen] suddenly died: he was abruptly taken away, rested, and his attendants secretly kept the matter hidden until morning. At dawn, before a ray of sunlight shone and illuminated the earth with Phoebus’s beam, Stephen [variant: Paul] the deacon of the city of Rome, brother of the aforesaid pope, came to him in the very custody where Bishop Sergius was held.

He said to him:

> “What will you give me if you return in peace to your home, increased in every honor and dignity?”

When the bishop heard this, as though freed from a noose, he came out and said:

> “I promise you no small gifts; whatever you hear, I will do.”

[Note: [Col. 0727D] Read this cautiously and consult the notes. BACCH.]

> “Come yourself to Ravenna, enter the bishop’s residence in that church, and diligently search all the treasures of that household: gold, silver, vessels, and coins. Let everything be given to you, and whatever you wish to leave as a blessing, leave.”

Upon these terms they swore mutually to one another. That very day the aforesaid brother of the dead pope was elected to the apostolic throne. He immediately released all captives and granted pardon to all the guilty. Then he ordered Sergius, the pontiff of Ravenna, to come with every honor and glory.

When he saw him, he rose from the chair where he was sitting, lifted him from the ground as he lay prostrate with his face lowered, raising him with uplifted hands, and rushed upon his neck, kissing him. He ordered Sergius’s seat to be placed beside his own. They spoke peaceful and gentle words to one another, and he permitted Sergius to return to his see with great joy and eagerness.

After three years he entered Ravenna. Those who received him with his party offered only moderate rejoicing, and there was only moderate peace. Bishop Sergius went to the monastery of the Blessed Virgin Mary called Cosmedin. After celebrating Mass, he prostrated himself before the altar of Blessed Nicholas, praying for a very long time and shedding tears, which are visible even to the present day.

## CHAPTER FOUR

The pontiff comes to Ravenna. The clergy plot abominable things against him. The deacon Uviliaris offers the sounder counsel. The pontiff carries away many things. Sergius exercises authority over the region like an exarch. Those implicated against the pontiff are taken to Rome. Other matters concerning Sergius. Some things are missing. Everything must be read cautiously.

At that time Pope Stephen [Paul, BACCH., here and below] of Rome departed from Rome, took the road to Francia, and hurried from there to Ravenna. He lodged in the bishop’s residence.

The priests knew and saw that he would search the treasures and swallow all the wealth of the Church. Among them there were troubling words. Some said:

> “Let us suffocate him.”

Others said:

> “No; let the Church’s resources be preserved.”

There were conflicting voices among the people.

Then the deacon Leo, the lord’s vicedominus, said to the priests:

> “When he begins to lay everything waste, let us secretly call him, as though there were something to show him, and throw him headlong, so that, submerged in deep water, he may never appear again.”

This was the plan among them, accompanied by disturbing words, as well as by useful measures and concluded arrangements; others, as though the deed had already been done, were considering how to remove the charge.

When Uviliaris, archdeacon of this see of Ravenna, heard this—he was at that time abbot of the monastery of St. Bartholomew, where, by God’s favor, I am now the fourth abbot after him—he ran with the utmost speed to the bishop’s residence. He saw all the priests engaged in such plots and conversations, turning various plans over among themselves. Recognizing that his own view was contrary to theirs, he clapped his hands and cried out against them:

> “What madness, brothers, if you have been considering such things! To destroy the pontiff? You carry no equitable counsels in your hearts. Listen to me, so that the pope may depart honorably from here; keep your hands innocent, and let us preserve inviolate the sacred bond of our bishop.”

> “When black night begins, and the Romans’ bodies have been filled with food and bright wine, and they lie in their first sleep as though buried, let all the lamps of the courtyard be extinguished, so that the candle flames may not offer them comfort during the night. Whatever we can secretly remove, let it all be hidden away [variant: concealed in the crypts], without our pontiff knowing. Once the places containing the riches that the Roman pope will find have been opened, let him take them.”

This plan pleased everyone, and they decided that Uviliaris’s proposal was better than the opinion put forward by the others. The priests entered the individual places where the treasures were kept and hid as much as they could.

At an untimely hour of the night the aforesaid Pope Stephen arrived. All the keys were brought before him from the Church’s wardrobes, and every door was opened for him. He took away the relics that they had not been able to hide so quickly, nine *balantiae* full of gold, many silver vessels, one fourfold set of silver spoons, and various other objects of gold and silver. Thus he departed for Francia, while he sent one [variant: “one with its locks”] to Rome.

When the citizens of Ravenna learned, after the pope had departed, of the Church’s plundering, they wished to pursue the wagon carrying the silver. But they were afraid; the drivers were taken to Ariminum, and the Ravennates returned to their city.

This man then governed the entire Pentapolis from the borders of Pertica as far as Tuscany and as far as Uvalanus’s table, like an exarch, arranging everything as the Romans now customarily do.

After Pope Stephen returned from Francia to Rome, he had first reached an agreement with the archbishop and then sent to several noble Ravennate judges, with excessive flattery and peaceful letters, urging them to go to Rome—those who had consented to the death of the pontiff. Among them was also my paternal grandfather. They were kept under restraint at Rome until all of them died there.

After this the pontiff made a treaty with the Venetians, so that nothing worse might happen to him or happen again, since the king of the Lombards had deceived him and he no longer trusted him. He distributed money among those who assisted him [possibly: “those who helped,” BACCH.], spending seven *balantiae* of gold through the noblest men.

He built a cell of Blessed Apollinaris from the men’s portion, established monks there, and left many possessions there. [lacuna]

[Note: [Col. 0729D] The following is written in the margin:

“Concerning Archbishop Sergius I find the following account of his death. After these events had taken place, some time later it happened that Blessed Pope Stephen departed this life. Then Michelius, a scriniarius of that Church who held no priestly office, immediately rose up and went to the duke of Ariminum, Mauritius. This most wicked Mauritius gathered an army together with the support of the Lombard king, hastened forth, entered Ravenna, and with strong force chose the aforesaid Michelius and introduced him into the bishop’s residence of the Ravennate Church. He took Leo the archdeacon, who had been elected in the bishop’s residence, to Ariminum, and there Mauritius had him held in strict custody.

Thus the aforesaid Leo was taken to the monastery of St. Agatha, where, after three days, he ended his life through the gouging out of his eyes, because of the pain. Sergius was taken to the monastery of Clivus Scauri and afterward brought to the Lateran, where he remained until the death of the aforesaid pontiff.

At the first hour of the night, Calventinus the chamberlain came with Rusius the presbyter and Leonatius the tribune, inhabitants of the city of Anagni. While Lord Pope Stephen was still alive, eight days before he departed this light, Calventinus took Sergius himself away and handed him over to the aforesaid Campanians, that is, the Anagnians, on the orders given to him by Paul the chamberlain, surnamed Africa, otherwise Arsiaca, and Gregory the regional defender, and John the duke, brother of Lord Pope Stephen, together with Calvillus the chamberlain. These men had been ordered to take away and kill the aforementioned Sergius.

He immediately sent to the Campanians, namely the Anagnians, his most faithful ministers. They killed the aforesaid Sergius and buried him with a rope tied around his throat; his body had been wounded by blows.

This is sufficient concerning Sergius, Archbishop of Ravenna.”]

# OBSERVATIONS ON THE LIFE OF SERGIUS

[Col. 0729] The truth of the narratives in the Life of Sergius concerning the Roman pontiffs. The new clergy ordained by Sergius. The deacons’ *superhumerale*. The monastery of St. Hilary of Galliata. The period during which Sergius was detained at Rome. The boundaries of Ravennate territory. The foolish supplements of the scribe of this codex.

## I.

Here, indeed, Agnellus wrote down what was commonly circulated among the people of Ravenna—equally irreligious and inept—in an irreligious and inept manner. The acts of various persons, which occurred at different times, were distorted by the Ravennates, with persons and dates altered, so that they might maliciously disparage the two most holy Roman pontiffs, Stephen III and Paul I—the latter being numbered among the saints both in the Roman Martyrology and by Peter de Natalibus on 28 June. Clearly, the Ravennate had not entirely cast off the poison of schism, nor did the fierce populace willingly endure the rule of the Roman pontiff.

Here I shall briefly indicate a few true facts, from which I think the falsehoods that were fabricated and gained currency among the Ravennates arose. Agnellus, who readily recorded them as his own because of his ignorance of events and his hostility toward Roman authority, preserved them.

First, it is certain that Stephen III occupied the papal see in exceedingly difficult times, when Aistulf, king of the Lombards, was cruelly harassing the Roman Church and had occupied Ravenna together with the exarchate. It is also certain that this pious and vigorous pontiff went to Gaul to Pippin, through whose assistance Aistulf was compelled to restore Ravenna and the exarchate. This occurred in the ninth indiction, that is, in the year 756. After Stephen’s death in the tenth indiction, on the sixth day before the Kalends of May, his brother Saint Paul I was elected pope thirty-two days later. Stephen IV succeeded him after the lamentable schism of Constantine, in the year 768.

While this Stephen was seated on the papal throne, the Church of Ravenna also suffered a schism after the death of Archbishop Sergius. Michael, the scriniarius of that Church, had been intruded through the influence of the Lombard duke Maurice of Rimini. The steadfastness of the supreme pontiff was tested by abundant promises of gifts, so that he might consecrate Michael; but in vain. Mindful of his office, he rejected the intruder and defended Leo, the legitimate elect.

These facts are found for the most part in Anastasius. The following passage from him, concerning the plundering of the Ravennate Church, should be noted:

> “In no way did Michael, the intruder, wish to submit to the apostolic admonitions. He gave very many gifts to Desiderius, king of the Lombards, as well as the vessels, ornaments of that Church, and various other objects; and by force of arms he occupied and retained the episcopal residence for the course of one year and more, stripping it bare and reducing it to great poverty.”

Once these facts have been observed, we possess the materials from which, by placing them incorrectly, the monstrous narrative of Agnellus was assembled. Since this plundering of the Ravennate Church occurred while Stephen IV was Roman pontiff, they attributed to Stephen both what the intruder Michael gave to Desiderius and what he had offered to Stephen when Stephen rejected it. They invented the claim that these things were given to Stephen by Sergius on the occasion when Sergius was required to give an account of himself, because he had passed from the lay state to the archbishopric. This indeed occurred under Stephen III, but Sergius was acquitted by his successor, Saint Paul.

Since, however, the name of Paul was incompatible with their story, and since the Church of Ravenna was plundered by Michael under Pope Stephen, the dates and names were altered, and various phantoms of persons and events were fused into something resembling a single dream.

Agnellus therefore deserves no credence here, nor does any benefit come to us from him except that we learn the opinions by which the clergy and people of the Ravennate Church were troubled in those times. This should not be considered useless to history. It is highly beneficial to recognize and preserve, for definite periods, the opinions and sentiments of peoples, both right and wrong, in order to discern the truth. Much more could be brought forward on this matter if it belonged to the present subject; perhaps it will at some time be worthwhile to do so. It would certainly be very useful to write a history of preconceived opinions according to the diversity of regions and times. From such a history we would gain the greatest assistance in judging many matters that perplex us when we read the ancients.

Here I wish to note one matter concerning Paul I, the most holy pontiff. It is sacrilegious to call his holiness into question, since it is recorded in the public registers of the Church. Yet someone who happened to read in a writer of that period something that seemed in any way to damage Paul’s reputation might be led astray, not knowing that the pontiff, although most holy, had nevertheless been held in a perverse opinion by the Roman people. Constantine declared this in the Roman synod under Stephen IV:

> “He had suffered violence from the people, had been elected through the arm of the people, and had been compelled to be led to the Lateran patriarchate because of those grievances and prejudices which the lord Pope Paul had inflicted upon the Roman people.”

Clearly, holy men have also deserved to be enrolled among the saints because they were ill-regarded and hated by the people of their own age. Recognizing this and seeing it clearly from reliable documents is highly useful for strengthening and confirming the reputation for holiness that they acquired among later generations.

I have thought it appropriate to make these observations so that, if what Agnellus narrates here should seem in any way to touch Saint Paul, it may instead serve to establish the virtue and steadfastness of that most holy pontiff, who suffered the condition both of the saints and of Christ: hated by the wicked and harassed by slanders.

## II.

When the priests and deacons of the Ravennate Church refused to minister with the bishop at the solemn celebration of Mass because of hostilities and disagreements whose origin is unknown, Sergius unexpectedly ordained several others. Thus he brought it about that those who had refused to minister out of obstinate dissension should demand the office of ministering as though it were due to them by right, through the fault of envy by which they excluded the newly ordained.

The dispute is said to have been settled on these terms:

> “The new deacons, having laid aside the dalmatic, were to put on the *superhumerale* in the Greek manner and stand around the altar.”

Learned men have observed that the deacons of the Roman Church used the dalmatic as their proper vestment, while the deacons of other distinguished Churches used it by concession from Rome. Accordingly, this privilege of the Ravennate deacons was retained by those who defended themselves by the right of their ancient ordination. The newly ordained were forbidden to use dalmatics, and in place of the dalmatic they were granted the *superhumerale*, which they were to wear according to Greek custom.

I think that *superhumerale* here should be understood not in its usual sense, but as what the Greeks call the *ὠράριον* (*ōrárion*), namely, a long band hanging down on both sides from the left shoulder. Yet it is clear from ancient monuments that the deacons of the Latin Church also wore this over the dalmatic. I suppose that the difference between Greeks and Latins was that the Latins wore the *orarium* over the dalmatic, contrary to present practice, whereas the Greeks wore it over a long, ankle-length tunic, as may be seen in plate 10 of the material presented by Ducange before his *Glossarium Graecitatis*.

Thus it was decreed that the newly ordained Ravennate deacons, having removed the dalmatic, should wear the *orarium* immediately over the alb. In this way the number of deacons was increased, and they became of two kinds: some wore dalmatics, while others proceeded without dalmatics. It was also provided that the new deacons should not stand close to the celebrating bishop, but farther away around the altar, and should not touch the sacred things, as the earlier deacons did.

Agnellus, when discussing these matters, calls the *orarium* by the name *superhumerale*. In this same Life he uses *superhumerale* to mean the *orarium* when he says that the pope “asserted that on the following day he would tear the *orarium* from his neck with his own hands.” He means the pallium, the principal ornament of a metropolitan.

## III.

What Agnellus writes about Pope Zacharias coming to Ravenna he has related in the wrong place, since, as was shown above, Sergius was ordained by Stephen III.
