While that same Stephen was active, Aistulf was compelled to abandon Ravenna and the Pentapolis. Our author says that Aistulf came to the threshold of the Apostles with the gifts he offered. This must have happened when Stephen was leaving for Gaul to summon Pippin, since the king of the Lombards could then have feared for himself. For this reason, too, he may have undertaken the restoration of the Petriana Church at Ravenna.

Agnellus falsely reports that Sergius incurred Stephen’s anger because he did not go out to meet the arriving pontiff, and that, when Stephen returned from Gaul, he therefore took away the monastery of Galeata. Saint Paul teaches us the true reason in the diploma by which he restored that monastery to Sergius:

> “It happened,” he says, “that, on his return—that is, Stephen’s return—his journey led through the monastery of Blessed Hilary, situated in the territory of Populonia. When the fury of his rivals had ceased, he was received with the greatest humility and honor by Anscausus, formerly bishop of Populonia and abbot of that venerable monastery.”

Moved, it is said, by such services, he “granted the aforesaid monastery to Bishop Anscausus for his enjoyment during the days of his life, thereby conferring upon him a return for the benefit he had generously bestowed.”

Lubinus, in his *Notice of the Abbeys of Italy*, under the letter G, says that in the *Codex of the Chamber’s Assessments* this monastery is called at one time Saint Hilary’s and at another Saint Ellary’s of Galeata. He says that it was built by Saint Hilary beside the river Bidente and enriched with estates by Olibrius, whom Saint Hilary had healed. He adds that Camaldolese monks were introduced there in 1448, and that the monastery stands on a lofty mountain from which both seas can be seen.

The pontiff therefore traveled by an exceedingly difficult route when he returned from Gaul to Rome. He could consequently write the following entirely truthful words to Pippin concerning his journey:

> “For we entrusted our body and soul to great labors. Trusting greatly in your faith, we set out by God’s will upon a broad and distant road and province, afflicted by snow and cold, heat and floods, mighty rivers and most savage mountains, as well as various dangers.”

Perhaps the pontiff crossed into Tuscany more safely from the Lombards by way of the mountains of Galeata than by proceeding through Emilia and along the Flaminian route.

## IV.

Sergius spent three years in Rome among the accused and returned to his own country when Stephen died and Paul was seated on the papal throne. Stephen died on the sixth day before the Kalends of May, and Paul was ordained around the beginning of June in the year 757. Sergius therefore remained in Rome for several months after Paul’s accession. In the latter part of 754, as soon as Stephen returned from Gaul, Sergius had been brought to Rome through the treachery of his fellow citizens.

At that time Aistulf was raging, not only refusing to restore the territory he had promised to return, but also threatening Rome after assembling an army. I believe that Sergius procured from the king a safeguard against the pontiff and perhaps won the support of the people through the king’s favor. For these reasons, after Ravenna had been recovered, he deserved to be punished by the pontiff.

Aistulf was soon compelled to abandon Ravenna together with the Pentapolis. Anastasius lists the cities that Abbot Fulrad received from Desiderius in the name of Pippin and offered to Saint Peter:

> “Ravenna, Rimini, Pesaro, and Fano; Cesena, Senigallia, Jesi, Forlimpopoli, Forlì, with the fortress of Sussubium; Montefeltro, Acerra, Monte Lucario, Serra, the castle of Saint Marino, Bobbio, Urbino, Cagli, Luceoli, Gubbio, and Comacchio.”

The dukes of Spoleto had seized the city of Narni; on this occasion it was restored together with the territories previously surrendered by Aistulf.

While Paul, who was most devoted to him, occupied the papal see, Sergius ruled widely, as Agnellus says:

> “He governed from the borders of Pertica throughout the whole Pentapolis and as far as the Mensa of Walani. Like an exarch, he arranged everything just as the Romans now customarily do.”

I do not doubt that this occurred at first with the indulgence of the Roman pontiff and with Pippin’s consent. For this reason, under Hadrian it happened that Leo, who succeeded Sergius against the will of the pontiff, dared to exercise dominion over several cities, claiming that he had received this authority by concession from King Charles, as is clearly apparent from several arguments in Hadrian’s letters.

I understand the boundaries of the whole Ravennate territory over which Sergius is said to have ruled as follows: to the east, the boundaries of Pertica, now called Pergola; to the west, Mensa—that is, the territory belonging to Mensa, or the jurisdiction attached to the Church of Ravenna—of Walani, where the port now called Volana is situated; to the south, Tuscany; and to the north, the sea. These matters acquire and shed light when compared with the passage from Anastasius cited above.

# LIFE OF LEO

## Single Chapter

He draws Charles into Italy and shows him the route through Martin. Desiderius is captured. Adelgisus flees.

### Leo XLI

This man came from this fold. He was not very tall in stature, excessively thin, but strong in body. He was the first to show the Franks the route into Italy through his deacon Martin, who afterward governed the Church as its fourth bishop. Invited by him, King Charles came to Italy, devastated the kingdom of the Lombards, and their king Desiderius, his father-in-law, was carried captive into Francia.

Adelgisus, the son of the aforesaid king, together with his army, turned his back before him and fled into the regions of the Chaonides. After remaining for several days at Salerno, when Charles came to Rome he proceeded fearfully with a few of his faithful followers to Constantinople . . .

The rest is missing.

## OBSERVATIONS ON THE LIFE OF LEO

Leo is discovered to have been a man of exceedingly bad character. How he was the first to show the route to the Franks coming into Italy. No bishop intervened between Gratiosus and Valerius.

### I.

A great loss to ecclesiastical history has resulted from the disappearance of this bishop’s Life. It is easy to infer that many events of the greatest importance occurred during his time, events that it would have been worthwhile to know, from the matters scarcely indicated in the letters of Pope Hadrian cited in the preceding chronological excursus and in the Life of Hadrian written by Anastasius.

Meanwhile, if any credence were to be given to Agnellus—which deserves none whatever—we would have a cruel example of Leo’s wicked character in the preceding Life of Sergius. For, while serving as a deacon, he is said to have advised the Ravennate clergy to destroy the pontiff and throw him from a steep place into the river below.

It is better, however, to judge all of this false. During the schism of Michael, who, relying on Lombard power, had invaded the see despite being a layman, Leo was elected. After the pseudo-bishop had been expelled, Leo was duly and canonically ordained by Stephen IV, who had allowed himself to be induced neither by threats nor by promises to ordain Michael. Thus the apostolic see returned good for evil; Leo, however, returned evil for good.

Under Hadrian, that same pontiff complained to King Charles that Leo had widely seized territory and had made his letters to the patriarch of Grado public and had them read aloud. From many other charges, it becomes as certain as anything can be that Leo sinned against Hadrian, although most of the details are unknown.

### II.

Our author reports that Leo showed Charles the route into Italy through his deacon Martin and himself invited Charles to attack the Lombards. As for showing the route, Leo is said to have been the first to teach it. Those who have written this account from Agnellus have observed that it should be understood as referring to the first Frankish invasion, when the Franks, seeking Italy, subsequently ruled there.

The matters concerning Charles, Desiderius, and Adelgisus are straightforward. This is useful for arranging the succession of the Ravennate bishops: Martin, who was a deacon under Leo and who, at the bishop’s command, showed the approaching Charles the route, is said to have been the fourth bishop of Ravenna.

After Leo, John occupied the see; after John, Gratiosus; after Gratiosus, Valerius; and Martin came fourth after him. No John can therefore be admitted between Gratiosus and Valerius, although Rubeus preferred to do so. Agnellus, who was certainly alive while Martin occupied the see, recognized no intervening bishop; neither do I recognize one.

# LIFE OF JOHN

## Chapter I

A headless Life. Some disagreement with the bishop. The ecstasy of Abbot John.

### John [the sixth] XLII, the Younger

. . . When the pontiff heard these harsh words, his expression changed, and his heart became like the roar of a lion. He said to his archdeacon:

> “What madness you are nourishing in your body! Help him, if you can.”

Then, as anger rose against anger, like a mist lifting into the heights, or like swelling waves raised aloft and striking the shore, so the hearts of the priests were shaken in different ways.

After this the archdeacon said to the archpriest:

> “Do you want us to go and drive him out?”

And they said to the other priests:

> “Come, brothers; let us visit our brother and trouble him over this matter. He is our member and our flesh; we belong to one fold. We have one father and an incorrupt mother, and we were washed in one font.”

They all went to the door of Cuthina. The archdeacon and the archpriest, both with knees raised, broke down the door of his lodging by kicking it. They dragged him outside, and all went with him into the church and sat in the sacristy until a messenger came from above, asking that they all go up, as was customary.

They found the pontiff quarreling and making a great uproar, but his priests were not frightened by his threats.

One day, while the aforesaid pontiff was sitting behind the tribunal of the church with the priests and many people from the populace, John, abbot of the monastery of Saint Donatus—which is called at Monterione, outside the Gate of Saint Lawrence, beside Vandalaria, not far from the monastery of Saint Mary called at Blachernae, where, God willing, I am abbot—suddenly fell to the ground and entered into an ecstasy. His sight vanished. When he returned to his normal senses, those standing around asked him what had happened.

He rose and said to them:

> “If I tell you, death will consume me.”

The pontiff then questioned him openly before everyone:

> “What is the reason this has happened to you?”

He replied:

> “Leopatus died at that very moment, and I saw his soul being carried into heaven by an angel in a shining linen cloth, with a joyful countenance.”

All those present were astonished and wondered. To establish the truth, the pontiff immediately sent one of his chamberlains. He found that Leopatus had died at that very hour.

That abbot himself died eight days later.

## Chapter II

The disastrous effects of an unjust curse cast upon an innocent man. The unhappy death of John.

I hasten to tell you about the death of the pontiff. Stand and behold the divine and just judgments of God.

There was in this city the son of a very noble man who, after his father’s death, held possession of the monastery of Saint Martin, called at Aqua Longa. He was my mother’s maternal uncle. Every day the pontiff plotted how he might seize the aforesaid monastery. Since he could not use force against him because of the nobility of his family, he killed him with the sword of his tongue, through curses and blasphemy.

On the feast day of Saint Apollinaris, the very boy whom he was cursing offered him an offering. The aforesaid pontiff refused it but cursed him, saying:

> “After this curse, may I see your death—and may I die immediately.”

The boy went away, rejected and distressed, weeping. After completing the solemnities of Mass, he went to his mother, who had been widowed by her husband’s death, and reported everything to her in tears. He told her:

> “He would not even give me the body of the Lord.”

After this, by divine command, God afflicted the pontiff with a stomach illness. Worn down by it, he died in a village called Aureliacus, twelve miles from the city, beside the aqueduct near Hercules.

His entire household was thrown into confusion. After they had washed his body, they placed it on a cart, where it lay like a corpse. Many [the printed text has *multi*] who were bereaved were filled with tears. His mother lay prostrate on the ground by day; some beat their breasts, others disfigured their faces with their fingernails, others wove wicker frames from willow branches, others cut willow branches that covered the bier; others spread fresh green grass above it; others pulled up elder plants, *fagineos* [*faginos*]; [the text is corrupt: they “adhaerebant saxos”], so that the wheels might roll more swiftly.

Some went ahead on every side with various willow rods. Others drove the oxen forward with a goad. Some spread grassy flowers beneath the body. Men from Hercules led the burden-bearing animals. The *camarini*, who were also bearers of the litter, struck the flanks of the bulls with rods. The young oxen went along the Aqueduct road with their nostrils wide [the variant reads: “the milk-white horns of the aqueduct”]. They came as far as the Bridge of Odio.

Then Andrew, a kinsman of the dead man, ordered the body to halt and commanded the adult men to stand in a circle around it. They adorned the corpse and bier with various cloaks. A *limbus* [*loibum*], tied from the beard to the head, had been sent to him by his mother from Basil’s own gold.

Then everyone came out of the city, from the greatest to the least: noblemen and commoners, old women and unmarried girls. There was immense wailing and mourning everywhere. They mourned not only the buried body but also the mother, deprived of her son.

Then, carried on the shoulders of men, he was brought to the monastery of Saint Euphemia and Saint Callinicus, where they buried him.

When the weeping crowd reentered the city, they raised lamentable cries in the pontiff’s ears. He asked what this was. The messenger who had seen it told him:

> “Deusdedit, son of Peter the Tribune, has died.”

He sent another messenger to learn the truth more certainly. The man returned and said the same thing. While the pontiff was sitting at table behind the tribunal of the church, above the fishpond, he lifted his hands upward, looked toward the face of the Savior, and said:

> “I give thanks to you, Lord Jesus Christ, and to you, Blessed Apollinaris, because you have heard me. I have always desired this day.”

He said to his cupbearer:

> “Mix it, for, thanks be to God, you have heard me.”

The cupbearer then took a vessel from the *calicodimia* [read: *calicotheca*], filled with unmixed wine, and handed it to the pontiff. The pontiff took it and drank half the cup. Suddenly he was struck by a stab in his left side. He quickly handed the cup to the servant and ordered the table removed. The joy of the banquet was turned into sadness, and he took to his bed.

On the seventh day after the young man’s death, he himself died. The bereaved mother rejoiced, just as he had rejoiced over the young man’s death.

Behold the divine vengeance!

He was buried in the basilica of Blessed Apollinaris the Confessor. You will find an epitaph engraved above his tomb.

He sat for seven years, one month, and three days.

## OBSERVATIONS ON THE LIFE OF JOHN

The disagreement between the bishop and the clergy indicated. What is related about John by Rubeus. What is *calicodimia*?

### I.

The earlier part of this Life indicates a certain disagreement between the clergy and the bishop, during which one of the clerics, after the doors had been forced open by the archdeacon and archpriest, was released from prison.

Rubeus, Book V, page 229, has briefly and, as is his custom, elegantly summarized the remaining events narrated here. After praising the holiness of John, abbot of Saint Donatus, he says nothing about the death of Leopatus.

The monastery over which the author of this Pontifical book presided as abbot he calls Saint Mary at Blachernae. In the manuscript I use, however, it is consistently written everywhere as *ad Blachernas*.

He commends Bishop John because he covered the great vault of the Ursian Church with sheets of lead, on which an inscription recorded the memory of the work; because he adorned the great altar of Saint Apollinaris in Classe with silver, gold, and a vault fashioned like a pyramid; and because he donated enormous metal crowns to the same basilica.

Among the relatives of Deodatus, Agnellus praises his father Basil and his grandfather Andrew, who is said to have been a kinsman of the deceased. Andrew’s wife, the mother of Basil and, as I think, the sister of Deodatus, had sent a golden *limbus*, or band, with which the dead man’s face was to be bound—the final memorial of her love for her brother.

Deodatus is said to have been buried not in the basilica but in an oratory, which our author customarily calls a monastery. Elsewhere we have shown that such oratories were built over cemeteries.

### II.

Among the barbarous words used by our author, *calicodimia* occurs here. It is sufficiently clear that it designated the place from which the cupbearer took the cup and handed it to the pontiff filled with wine. I think the word was written *calicotheca*. But these matters are not important enough to detain us longer.

# LIFE OF GRATIOSUS

## Chapter I

King Charles at Ravenna. He dines with the bishop. The simplicity of Gratiosus, for which Charles praises him.

### Gratiosus XLIII

[Marginal note: He lived around the year 810, and at that same time he prophesied. BACCH.]

This man was humble and gentle, handsome in appearance, somewhat bald, with a long neck, large eyes, attractive features, and pleasant speech. He had been abbot of the monastery of Blessed Apollinaris, founded not far from the Church of the Holy Redeeming Cross at the Old Mint. From there came Saint Reparatus.

[Marginal note: Truly Gratiosus, because he was filled with the grace of God. He was archdeacon of this see.]

During his time a terrible sign of a deadly plague appeared. On the clothing or any garment of a person, or on a *cherumanica* [a term of uncertain meaning], or on footwear, three blue drops [perhaps: poisonous drops] would appear; on the third day the person would be carried off by death. Bodies lay strewn upon the ground, and the living could scarcely manage to commit them to burial.

In those days King Charles of the Franks came to Ravenna. When invited to dine there, he came gladly. The priests said to their pontiff:

> “My lord, retain your simplicity and take care not to say anything inappropriate.”

He replied:

> “No, my sons, no—but I shall keep my mouth shut.”

As they ate and drank, the pontiff began to urge the king, saying:

> “Eat, my lord king, eat.”

The king was astonished and asked:

> “What is this expression that the prophet is using—‘Eat, eat’?”

Then the priests standing around him said:

> “Let our lord the king pay no attention to these words as though they were insulting or mocking; they are words of persuasion. This man is your servant and spokesman, a man of great simplicity. But just as a mother caresses her children and, out of excessive love, urges them to eat something, so he, with great kindness, asks your clemency to eat and enjoy yourself.”

Then the king ordered silence openly before everyone and cried out:

> “Behold a true Israelite, in whom there is no deceit.”

After this, whatever the bishop requested from him, he obtained.

I shall now explain another horrible sign that appeared in the sky. At the time when Charles took possession of Lombardy, many people saw in the heavens, after sunset, horses with their riders fighting among themselves, and there was movement everywhere.

## Chapter II

The author’s prophecy attributed to Gratiosus. The death and tomb of Gratiosus.

[Note: [Col. 0738D] Marginal note: Archbishop Gratiosus prophesies, not the author of this work. BACCH.]

Therefore, dearest ones, do not be sluggish, but stand firm and listen to what the Lord will speak through me, so that you may know what is to come. I am not a prophet; but the Spirit himself who spoke through the prophets can likewise pour himself into our hearts. The Holy Spirit himself cries out through Joel: “I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh”; and he says to Jeremiah: “Behold, I have given my words into your mouth.” The patriarch Jacob also says: “Gather together, sons of Jacob; listen, Israel, to your father, that he may announce to you what is to come.” And the Son himself of the eternal Father says: “I will give you a mouth and wisdom.”

What wonder is it, then, if before the Incarnation the Holy Spirit filled the hearts of the prophets so that they might foretell what was to come, and now, after he has become a companion of our flesh, has bestowed upon it the fullness of grace through his word, as the Evangelist says: “We have all received from his fullness”? If, therefore, that same Spirit spoke through the mouths of Gentiles and unbelievers—through the cruel tyrant King Nebuchadnezzar, through the Gentile poet Virgil, and through the prophetess Sibyl—and foretold the future, why should that same divine majesty not now speak through a Christian man redeemed by blood? For if the Spirit himself dwelt in the fragile sex, namely in Anna and the Sibyl, then do not doubt the Gospel words which say: “The Spirit breathes where he wills.”

But I tell you, my brothers, my fellow soldiers, citizens of Ravenna, that a time will come upon it such as none of those dwelling there will be able to recall. It will be diminished in all its possessions and will be utterly consumed by its own citizens; there will be wars among them and various disputes, as they envy one another and conceive wicked designs, speaking peaceful words with their mouths while holding a sword in their hearts.

Its head will be under siege, and its enemies will trample it. Ruin will be everywhere within it; they will rise against their enemies, and, terrified, will turn back [and, seeing them, will return in fear]. They will seize the spoils of neighboring cities, trample the churches of the saints, and plunder those of the apostles. Men from the western regions, their beards shaven in its defense, will come, but they themselves will inflict the greatest harm.

At that time there will be a very great famine and widespread destruction. Severe pestilences will arise around the seacoasts, and the sea, with swollen waves, will fiercely devour its own shore; the sea will aid in attacking its own creation, and the fish that it then gladly finds in the waters it will cast upon the shores. Every species will corrupt its own seed.

Even the sky itself will obscure its serenity and, at the season of need, withhold the dew. The clouds will restrain the rain through their moderation, but the gathered rays will display a darkened day. That prophecy will come to pass which says: “The sun has gone down upon them at midday”—as though Christ, the Sun of righteousness, had said it, who ascended the cross at midday. Yet this is understood both spiritually and bodily.

And the moon will be diminished in brightness; that is, my holy teaching in the Church will be diminished by wicked and ignorant priests. For a most wicked time will come upon this Church. Young men will take precedence over old men, and they will mock the teaching of the elders and the holy Church. Claiming to be wise, they will be fools; and, according to the Apostle’s words, they will always be learning but never attain knowledge of the truth. These are ignorant and exceedingly wicked men, hard of heart, who do such things. They are entirely unable to suck the milk of the Church. They are not true sons but stepchildren.

Ravenna will gradually and continually fall into opposition. Four men of one mind will not be found in it; and if three of one mind are found in a single house, they will bite one another in jealousy. There will be a cruel and most evil wound among men and among all creatures.

The earth will not yield its fruit, and she who is the mother of all will herself become a stepmother. Desirable fruits will fail, and all joys will be turned into mourning. What is now the Roman Empire will be laid waste, and kings will sit upon the imperial throne. Christians will become tributary subjects to other Christians, and no one will show mercy to his neighbor.

This will be the beginning of the signs, when priests begin to be proud and greedy and show no honor to their predecessors. Through wicked bishops, the Church of Ravenna will gape open and, for the sake of its own honor, will give away the Church’s treasures and scatter gifts. After they have consumed all the ornaments of the Church, they will give away its estates.

A time will come when they will serve at the Church’s table with wooden vessels. They will kill the shepherds and their sheep; they will not shear them, and will love the world more than the things of God.

Unknown peoples will come around the shores of the sea. They will kill Christians and plunder their regions, and those who remain will become tributaries to them. Christians will rise against Christians and oppress them most cruelly; they will seize their possessions and afflict their bodies. In their extreme weakness they will blaspheme against heaven. The whole world will rise up, each part against the other.

The people of the Hagarenes will rise from the east and plunder the cities situated on the seacoasts, and there will be no one to rescue them. For in every region of the earth there will be impoverished kings, lovers of gifts, who will oppress the peoples subject to them. The Roman Empire of the Franks will perish, and kings will sit upon the imperial throne. Everything will be diminished; servants will surpass their master. At these things the earth will bellow, the elements will gape open, everyone will trust in his sword, and all the hearts of the earth will tremble.

The elders will fail, and the young will be exalted. They will not remember the ancient commandments, but each will walk in the way of his own wickedness. The stars will be shaken from heaven, and there will be a blow upon creation, upon cattle and upon beasts of burden. Many will groan under the burden of extreme poverty, and the bodies of many will waste away because of the scarcity of food. Roman nobles will go into captivity in foreign lands.

Because of its riches, Rome will be plundered by its own people and will lie burned in a conflagration. The whole earth will be barren, and there will be no fruit upon it. Whoever loves peace or authority will be abominable. Justice will not be remembered; judgments will be perverse. Gifts will blind their eyes, and they will stifle the cases of the poor and delight in the suffering of widows.

Monasteries will be torn apart, and churches will be destroyed. The devil will harry the holy churches so greatly that they will be demolished by faithful Christians. The house of God will be darkened, and the ministers will remove incense from the holy altar but will not offer it. Many sacrifices will be troubled, because priests will not be honored by men; when they wish to admonish anyone, they will be mocked by them.

The sacrifice will not be pleasing to God if the desire for this world is not entirely cast aside [perhaps: by the priests]. But if anger is not removed from the heart, the offering will not be pure.

In those days, slaves will marry the daughters of their masters, and commoners will marry noblewomen. They will beget sons and daughters through fornication, and those born of them will become judges and leaders and will overturn the earth.

Many, unable to bear disgrace, will leave their cities and their homes and dwell in a foreign land. The fortresses of the churches will be overturned, and the priests will also be scattered. Nuns will be oppressed by individual men of the world; unwillingly and against their will, they will kill their offspring, lest the fruit of the womb become a witness and betrayer.

These things, brothers, I have drawn in small measure from the depths, because I am consumed by the pain in my head. Yet, according to the words of blessed Job, who can restrain the word he has conceived? Stand firm, most prudent men, and fight against the most destructive enemy, lest the head ache, lest the eyes grow dim, lest the ears become deaf, lest the mouth be silent, lest the tongue cease speaking, lest the spirit rest from the sign of the cross, lest the arms wither, lest the heart swell, lest the fibers of the breast stretch out with agitation, lest the belly be distended by food, lest the knees grow stiff—not with backs unbent, not with inflexible knees, nor with sluggish feet, but with the whole body standing firm.

Be perfect, God willing, as this most blessed Gratiosus was throughout all the days of his life. He died on the twenty-third day of February and was buried in the church of Blessed Apollinaris, priest and martyr of Christ, in the city of Classis. He occupied the see for three years, ten months [supplied by Bacch.], and eleven days.

## OBSERVATIONS ON THE LIFE OF GRATIOSUS

### I. The Monastery of Saint Apollinaris at Veclum

The prodigies reported here do not belong to the age of Gratiosus. What Agnellus appends to the Life of Gratiosus is wrongly attributed to Gratiosus.

What is related in the Life of Bishop Reparatus about the monastery of Saint Apollinaris receives illumination from this passage, since Reparatus too was abbot of that place. It is said to have stood not far from the church of Saint Crucis. If the church of Saint Crucis was the one erected and dedicated by the Empress Placidia, then, in Faber’s view, it is the church which is now parochial and belongs to our Cassinese Saint Vitalis. The same Faber discusses this monastery of Saint Apollinaris and testifies that it was called by this name in the bulls of Alexander III and Urban IV, just as Agnellus calls it in the Life of Reparatus: namely, the monastery of Saint Apollinaris situated near the Pusterula of Opilio [Col. 0741A].

The present parish church of Saint Apollinaris at Veclum is now called by a more recent designation, to distinguish it from the basilica of Saint Martin in the Golden Heaven, after the latter began commonly to be called Saint Apollinaris the New. Thus the Pusterula of Opilio, or Ovilio, gave its name to a district of the city near the walls of Ravenna, where both the churches of Saint Apollinaris and Saint Crucis stood.

### II. The Prodigies

The prodigies related here, some of which are said to have been seen when Charles received Lombardy, are mentioned as an incidental digression, and I am not certain that they belong to the times of Gratiosus; rather, they seem to belong to the preceding period of Leo. No one should therefore doubt the chronological dates assigned to these bishops. Agnellus himself sufficiently shows that he is relating events from another period when he says, “at the time when Charles received Lombardy”; for he distinguishes that time from the age of Gratiosus.

### III. Gratiosus and Prophecy

It is truly astonishing that the Ravennates should have seized upon the foolish jumble appended by Agnellus to the Life of Gratiosus as an occasion for numbering Gratiosus himself among the prophets. The author of the notes impresses this upon the reader twice, and all who have written histories of Ravenna have repeated the same claim.

But who does not see that these things should be attributed to Agnellus? Whenever he had only a few facts available from the deeds of some bishop, he was accustomed to add similar material so that he would not write a shorter Life. Agnellus himself described Gratiosus adequately, yet says nothing about his prophetic spirit.

He is called a “prophet” by Charles when he asks: “What is this speech that the prophet is speaking?” But here “prophet” means the same as bishop, old man, or something similar. Certainly, whether the additions made here to the Life of Gratiosus belong to Agnellus or to Gratiosus as author, they contain nothing suggestive of the gifts of prophecy. Rather, they should be referred to the schismatic and seditious mind of Agnellus, who, indirectly and as though engaged in another matter, foretells—though falsely as a prophet—that the temporal and ecclesiastical authority of the Roman see will prove destructive to the Ravennates.

[Col. 0742A] The Life of the following bishop is missing. In its place the copyist of the manuscript has written:

“Here too there ought to have been the history of Archbishop Valerius, but it is missing. These few things written here about him are not by the aforesaid Agnellus; I found them in other chronicles, and therefore placed them here.”

## ON SAINT VALERIUS XLIV

Valerius XLIV. The feast is celebrated in the church of Classis on the fourth day before the Kalends of February.

Rubeus, Book V, p. 235, supplements the Life of Saint Valerius from various passages of Agnellus as follows:

> “Valerius, finding Pippin most devoted to the Christian religion, greatly restored divine worship and adorned the churches, as the monuments testify in the church of Saint Apollinaris of Classis, especially at the marble steps of the high altar and at the altar dedicated to Saint Eleucadius, Archbishop, on the left beside the Holy Tower, with the priest Peter providing particular assistance.
>
> “He also arranged for the demolition of the basilicas of Saints George and Eusebius, built outside the Gate of Saint Victor in the age of the Arians, as we have written. From all those demolished churches he constructed splendid buildings, called the Valerian buildings, as Agnellus testifies. When Archbishop Valerius had given the Ravenna church a silver abacus in the form of a plane tree, together with many other silver vessels, he died and was buried in the church of Saint Apollinaris of Classis on the Ides of March.”

The same Rubeus, in Book VI, relates that in the year 1222, on the ninth day of May, under the direction of Archbishop Simeon, the bones of Saint Valerius were transferred from the church at Classis to the Ursian church, in a solemn procession announced by the bishops of Faenza, Cesena, and Ficocle. The very ancient cult of this bishop is therefore sufficiently established by the evidence cited, although the memory of his deeds has been lost through the injuries of time.

# LIFE OF MARTIN

[Col. 0741]

## CHAPTER ONE

Martin’s age when he was ordained by Leo III. His tall bodily form. He grants the author the monastery of Saint Mary at Blachernae. He fortifies the church of Saint Euphemia. Pippin and Charles die. The basilica of Saint Apollinaris at Classis is repaired at the expense of the Roman pontiff. Martin is summoned to Rome after offending him. John of Arles is honored at Ravenna with gifts.

Martin XLV. He was tall in stature, with a large, bald head, and a body full of great bulk. He was archdeacon of this see, from the monastery of Blessed Andrew, which lies not far from the church of the Goths. He had nearly reached eighty years of age when he obtained this see, having been consecrated at Rome by the hands of Pope Leo III.

When he had returned from Rome, he sent his messengers to the Emperor Charles in Francia, and the Augustus was thereby pleased. Martin granted the monastery of Saint Mary, called at Blachernae, to the presbyter Andrew, who was still a boy; and the aforesaid pontiff received from him two hundred gold solidi for the benefit of his church. From these he made a golden vessel, adding more gold, in the shape of a marine shell, and it remains in use for the chrism to the present day.

Thus great was he in bodily form, as I have said, that the two hundred gold pieces which I handed to him in a pair [or: a double handful] he enclosed in his left hand alone. The leading men of this city of Melessus [Melessans, that is, Ravennates], together with the priests who saw this, were astonished.

This bishop fortified the church of Blessed Euphemia, which is called at the Ram, and which had once been dominated by water.

During his time Pippin, king of the Lombards, died. After some time the Emperor Charles died on the thirtieth day of January, and his son Louis succeeded him in the Empire.

At that time Leo, bishop of the Roman Church and city, sent his chamberlain, named Chrysaphus, and the other masons, and restored the roofs of Saint Apollinaris. Everything was made of fir beams and coffered ceilings, and all the coverings of that martyr were provided at his own expense.

All the suburban cities came, bringing all the materials, roof tiles, roofing timbers, and all the fir wood that was needed. The citizens of Ravenna transported them by forced labor to the boundaries, and [supplied] the rest of the necessary materials. The masons arranged the beams upon the walls, and everything was completed. This bishop alone ordered the hypocausts to be fixed [or: built in].

Not long afterward, Pope Leo, angry with Bishop Martin [against Bishop Martin], sent his legate to Francia [Col. 0743A] to Emperor Louis, wishing to proceed against the aforesaid Bishop Martin. Emperor Louis consented to his will and sent John, bishop of Arles, commanding him to go with Bishop Martin to Rome and deal with Pope Leo.

The aforesaid John, bishop of Arles, came to Ravenna and, after taking counsel with the archbishop, compelled him, through a guarantor, to go to Rome. They guaranteed him for two thousand gold solidi, except in the event of bodily illness.

After ten days he left his see and set out to hasten to Rome. Coming to a place about fifteen miles from Ravenna, at Novae, where there had once been a city but which was now ruined, he stayed for fifteen days in the church of Blessed Stephen.

He sent his legate to Rome to say that he had left the city intending to come but had fallen ill. He was unable to ride because his body was weak. In part he was pretending illness. When the Roman pontiff heard this, he was very distressed, because he could not summon Martin to himself and compel him forcefully.

He then settled the matter with him and ordered him to return to his own see together with the emperor’s legate.

After the legation had been completed, the priest of Arles entered Ravenna. Bishop Martin received him with great joy and much eagerness. When they had been filled with food, the Ravennate attendant [Ravenna scedulus; text corrupt] brought forth silver vessels: an entire table fashioned in the form of a plane tree, which had been in his palace as a bequest of Archbishop Valerius, who had made it in his own time; and golden covers for the Gospels, fashioned with rather unskilled workmanship.

## CHAPTER TWO

Leo III dies. Stephen succeeds him and celebrates Masses at Ravenna, displaying the Savior’s sandals. Emperor Louis offers the Ravenna church a silver table.

At that time Pope Leo died, and Stephen succeeded him in the see. This aforesaid pope went to Francia to Emperor Louis and obtained from him everything he requested. He came to Ravenna, and the two bishops—the Roman and the Ravennate—kissed one another.

The Roman bishop celebrated Masses in the Ursian church and displayed the Savior’s sandals, which the whole people saw. Rejoicing, he left the city and returned to his own see.

During the time of this Martin, Emperor Louis, from the bequest of his father Charles, sent Bishop Martin of this Ravenna see a silver table without wood, with the whole of Rome engraved beneath it in relief, together with four square silver feet and various silver vessels, as well as one golden cup. This cup was placed in a holy golden bowl, which we use every day . . . The rest is missing.

## COPYIST’S NOTE

[Col. 0743]

Much is missing from this Martin. After him came Archbishop Petronacius, but his Life is missing, and I did not find it in the original. These few things written here about Archbishop Petronacius who followed him are not by the aforesaid Agnellus; I found them in other chronicles, and therefore placed them here.

## OBSERVATIONS ON THE LIFE OF MARTIN

[Col. 0744A] Martin’s age and some of his deeds. The time of John of Arles. The silver table bequeathed by Charles to the Ravenna church. The Savior’s sandals.

### I

In the year 775, when Charles came into Italy, Martin, who showed him the route, was approximately forty-four years old. Around the year 811 he succeeded Valerius in the bishopric of Ravenna, when he was eighty years old; and, as Ferretus transmitted in his manuscripts, according to Faber’s report, he was designated by that same Valerius.

Agnellus writes that Charles was pleased by Martin’s consecration. Since the bishop had rendered him services when he was coming into Italy, it is reasonable to believe that Charles showed his approval for that reason. We learn from Agnellus that the monastery of Saint Mary at Blachernae was then granted to our Agnellus while he was still very young; this matter was discussed in the Observations on the verses prefixed to the work.

The great size of this bishop’s body is indicated by the fact that he enclosed in his left hand the two hundred gold solidi that had been offered to him. Concerning the church of Saint Euphemia, which this bishop restored, Rubeus and Faber provide further information, which may be consulted in their works.

From our author we learn that it had originally been built surrounded by water, but that in Martin’s time it stood on dry land, since the sea had already been pushed away by the growth of the soil through alluvial deposits.

Anastasius also records that, under Pope Leo and at his expense, the basilica of Saint Apollinaris at Classis was repaired. In reporting this, our author envelops the whole matter in a barbarous style of composition. We understand clearly enough that the cities subject to Ravenna supplied labor for the repair of the church and were obliged to transport fir timber by forced service.

### II

The accounts of Leo, the Roman pontiff, who was angry with Martin and acted through a legate with Louis so that Martin might be brought to Rome for punishment, together with the subsequent events concerning Martin and John of Arles, are omitted by Rubeus and the other historians of Ravenna.

From the context of the Life it appears that these events occurred near the end of Leo’s life, when a fierce conspiracy of the Romans was formed against him. I would suppose that the bishop was dismissed to his Ravenna see when the conspiracy against Leo began to grow. We do not know the reason why the archbishop of Ravenna incurred Leo’s anger.

Rubeus found here something concerning Valerius, Martin’s predecessor: a table ingeniously constructed in the shape of a plane tree. From this corrupt passage of Agnellus it is scarcely possible to determine whether it was given to John or merely used when that bishop was received at Martin’s banquet.

We recognize from this passage that John occupied the chair of the Church of Arles during the time of Martin and the earlier years of Louis’s reign. Elsewhere it is known that this same John, together with Nebridius, archbishop of Narbonne, was ordered by Emperor Charles, who was still alive, to ensure at the Council of Arles in the year 813 that the assembled Fathers restore ecclesiastical affairs and discipline. The acts of that council still survive. Theodulf succeeded John, and is well known from the records of those times.

### III

Eginhard, and later writers following him, provide further information about the silver table offered to the Ravenna church by Louis from the will of Charles. They likewise provide more information about the journey of Pope Stephen to Gaul.

Returning from there, the same pontiff came to Ravenna and, celebrating Masses in the Ursian basilica, displayed the Savior’s sandals to the people. Agnellus does not say what these were, nor does he mention them anywhere else in the entire work. In his Life of Nicholas, however, Anastasius records that John, archbishop of Ravenna, after returning to the right path, placed “deeds and writings concerning the life-giving cross of our Lord Jesus Christ and his sandals.”

# LIFE OF PETRONACIUS

[Col. 0745] Some material collected by the Copyist

Petronacius XLVI, who swore fealty to Emperor Charles. In his time Andrew, also called Agnellus, abbot of Saint Mary at Blachernae and of Saint Bartholomew, composed this Pontifical Book, as is evident above, at the beginning of this book, in the verse that begins: “In the Father and the Son.”

Likewise, in his time the body of the most blessed Maximian, archbishop of Ravenna, was discovered, as you have above in the chapter on Maximian. This Agnellus, Andrew, was a cardinal presbyter of the Church of Ravenna.

## OBSERVATIONS ON THE FOREGOING, CONCERNING PETRONACIUS

[Col. 0745] He could not have sworn allegiance to Charles. Agnellus wrote part of the book while Petronacius was seated. The designation “cardinal presbyter” is later than Agnellus in the Church of Ravenna. Some supplementary material.

### I

It has already been observed above in the Chronological Excursus that Petronacius could not have sworn fidelity, or allegiance, to Emperor Charles, since he occupied the see for several years after Charles’s death. Either the statement is entirely false, or “Louis” ought to have been written in place of “Charles.”

The remaining details sufficiently show that the Copyist was extremely inept in history, and consequently it is unsafe to trust him. The statements concerning the time when this book was written by Agnellus are likewise only partly true, as we observed in connection with the verses cited here.

The Copyist also calls Agnellus a cardinal presbyter, following his own rather than Agnellus’s usage. For it is by no means evident from Agnellus himself that, in Agnellus’s time, the leading presbyters of the Ravenna Church were accustomed to be designated “cardinals,” that is, placed upon the hinge [in cardine], as they called it.

When Petronacius undertook the transfer of Maximian’s body, Agnellus says that he was tenth among the presbyters. Whenever occasion permits, he calls himself both presbyter and abbot, but never cardinal. I therefore consider this usage in the Church of Ravenna later than Agnellus.

Rubeus argues that Gregory the Great used this designation in a charter which he presents in Book IV, p. 189, addressed to Marinianus. But, apart from the fact that it contains no explicit mention anywhere of Ravennate cardinals, the charter could easily be shown to be either spurious or certainly unrelated to Gregory the Great or to Marinianus. Among the strongest indications is that it has Gregory confirming privileges granted to the Ravenna Church by the Lombard kings. For those times, it is wholly improbable that the Lombard kings granted privileges to the bishops of Ravenna.

### II

The Copyist, utterly incompetent as he was, omitted matters concerning Petronacius: namely, the privileges granted by his predecessors to this archbishop and to the Ravenna Church, confirmed in the year 819 by Pope Paschal in a charter from the Ursian archive, reported by Rubeus in Book V, p. 236, and copied from Rubeus by Ughellus.

Also omitted is the fact that, when Eugenius II of that name was seated, Petronacius signed in the Roman council of sixty-three bishops in the year 826 in the first place after the Roman pontiff.

# LIFE OF GEORGE

[Col. 0745]

## CHAPTER ONE

Gregory IV consecrates George. George plunders the Church’s treasures. At Pavia he lifts the daughter of Lothar from the sacred font. Prodigies. The death of Louis the Pious. Wars among his sons.

George XLVII. He was young in age, with curly hair and large eyes. He was consecrated at Rome by Gregory IV [the Roman pope]. But after he had sworn an oath upon the body of blessed Peter, he left Rome and immediately became hostile to his consecrator.

After he assumed the government, he broke open all the Church’s treasures, disrupted the crypts, and extracted the treasures of his predecessor bishops. In order to lift Lothar’s daughter from the font, he spent great wealth on the occasion.

That year he went to Pavia. After all the customary gifts had been presented to the Augustus, he bought from the palace of that emperor baptismal garments for five hundred gold pieces, white linen decorated with gold. He received the daughter of the aforesaid Augustus, named Rotruda, whom he handed to me; I clothed her with my own hands and adorned her feet with shoes decorated with gold and hyacinth stones. Afterwards he celebrated Masses before the Augustus.

Likewise, the Empress Ermengard, accompanied by maidens, was dressed in a shining garment bordered with gold. Her hair was bound with hyacinth-colored ribbons, her face was veiled with gems [prosobsi—uncertain], and she wore a stole adorned with sardius and emeralds set in gold [the text is corrupt]. Before the beginning of the Masses she confessed that she was burning with thirst and secretly drank a full phial of foreign wine. Afterward she partook of the heavenly table [or: heavenly table’s sacrament] within the palace of that city, in the monastery of Saint Michael.

At that time, on the seventh day of May, the day of the dedication of the basilica of Saint Michael, blood rained at Ravenna. On the eighth day of the same month, during the night watch, a marvelous sign appeared in the sky: stars running against one another from east to west; and again another extremely swift movement from east to west, with the moon twenty [the reading is uncertain].

Likewise, on the fifth day of May, in the third indiction, the sun became exceedingly dark at midday throughout the whole world until the ninth hour. A fiery star also appeared in the sky, like a torch surpassing the power of the sun, and some smaller stars beneath it, about two paces away, moved from east to west. After the power of the sun’s ray had passed, their brightness again appeared in the stars themselves.

Emperor Louis died, as some say, on that very day. His son Lothar succeeded him. Before the Augustus died, he divided his empire among his royal sons: the largest portion to Augustus Lothar, the kingdom of Aquitaine to Pippin, and Bavaria to Louis. These were the sons of Ermengard.

To Charles he granted the more fertile and prosperous portion, and he gave his daughter Gisela in marriage to a man named Conrad, a most devout man. The Empress Judith bore this son and daughter.

After Louis died, there was always war among the brothers. There was peace, but it was unstable.

## CHAPTER TWO

George obtains permission to be sent to Gaul with legates by the pontiff for the sake of peace. The pomp and extravagance with which he traveled. The battle at Fontenay. George is captured and subjected to insults. Charles’s wife intercedes for him. On his return he is cruel toward his priests. He dies.

After these events, Archbishop Georgius learned that legates of the Apostolic See were to go to Francia to obtain peace between the brothers. He sent his messengers to Lotharius Augustus to ask Pope Gregory that he himself should proceed to Francia with the Roman legates. And so it was done; he went with the apostolic curse upon him. Believing that he himself held the apostolic office, Georgius went with three hundred horses carrying various loads. He took with him much gold [Col. 0747B] and silver, having plundered the church’s treasury, as well as golden crowns made by the blessed Bishop Peter, chalices, golden patens, various silver and golden vessels, gems from the cross, and the crowns that he had dismantled. He carried these things with him so that he might distribute them all with a generous hand.

Thinking that through these gifts he could turn the emperor’s heart so that he would withdraw from the authority of the Roman pontiff, he also carried away all the privileges that Maurus and the other bishops of Ravenna had obtained from the sacred rulers. He reached the emperor with the Roman legates, and they found him on the battlefield at a place called Fontaneam [Fontaneum], fighting against Carolus. The army of Lotharius was so immense, they say, that no four-footed creature or small flying thing could have escaped or flown across it. When the battle was joined on the Saturday immediately after the feast-day of Saint John the Baptist, bright weapons clashed with one another. Arms rang out; splendid shields were swung upon shoulders; the soldiers trembled in spirit and, their hearts afraid, turned their backs; bodies fell beneath the iron amid immense groans.

Lotharius, armed, plunged into the midst of the enemy. Seeing his men defeated and fleeing everywhere in all directions, he found no respite. Limbs were severed by swords. As I have said, having entered the midst of the enemy, he was not at the side of those who could offer assistance [“he was not at the side of one who could offer assistance”], but alone and fierce he cut down many corpses. Alone he won the battle with his spear, but all his men turned their backs. Sitting upon a long-haired charger, adorned with painted trappings, he struck the horse with his face and heel, devastating the enemy with its bites. [Col. 0747D] If there had been ten men like him alone among the enemy, the empire would not have been divided, nor would so many kings have occupied their thrones.

Meanwhile, victory passed into the hands of Carolus. His brother Ludovicus, king of the Bavarians, was helping him. But after Pippinus, son of Pippinus and nephew of Lotharius, king of Aquitaine, arrived, Lotharius’s army was strengthened, and the battle was joined again. Some on Carolus’s side fell, because they were scattered through the countryside; but when they gathered themselves and the battle was renewed, more than forty thousand men fell on the side of Lotharius and Pippinus.

Archbishop Georgius was captured there. They forcibly pulled him from his horse, stripped off the cloak with which he was covered, and compelled him to walk before his own horse, like one of the animals. When he was unable to walk on foot, they struck him with a lance or spear. Then one of them, in mockery, placed him on the back of a broken-down beast without bedding; its ears and tail had been cut off, and it was exceedingly ugly. Georgius went along mourning. Again another man came, removed him from that animal, and made him sit upon another beast, with a worn saddle-cloth, flasks and a sitacium [sitarcium] tied to the saddle. They led him to King Carolus, who ordered him to remain under guard for three days.

All his priests were scattered, and the church’s possessions were dispersed by the hands of plunderers. The three Roman legates who were bishops, however, took flight and went to the city of Auxerre. Then Carolus, moved by mercy, ordered that wherever priests [Col. 0748B] or clerics of the Church of Ravenna were found, they should be brought before him unharmed, safe, and with honor.

Judith, the mother of Carolus, gave those same priests one small silver tribilium [tribilion], declaring that she had no more, and saying: “Take this vessel and restore your strength in your poverty.”

Carolus and Ludovicus, brothers born of the same father, hearing of Georgius’s wickedness, since he was savage and most evil, wished to send him into irrevocable exile. But although he had been wicked, his priests pleaded for him for a long time. When Augusta, the mother of King Carolus, saw this, she was moved exceedingly to mercy and quickly asked her son and her stepson to send Georgius back to his see.

Then Carolus ordered him to come before him. Georgius prostrated himself on the ground and fell at the king’s feet. The king stood wearing youthful armor, dressed in purple and girded with a golden brooch. From his left side hung a golden bulla fastened with a chain, shining with emeralds and hyacinth-colored gems. His shoulder was covered by a shield; he was clad in a cuirass and held a spear in his hands, with the lance joined to its iron point. Fierce in arms, he stood there with his crested head raised among the ranks, and his voice burst openly from his chest:

“Ho, you shepherd—if this name justly remains yours—why did you abandon the Church entrusted to you, and fail to recover your people whom you afflicted? If you came on account of the long journey, to see the battle, why was it necessary for you to plunder your Church and, in a single hour, discard what had been bestowed by Christian princes or emperors and acquired by your predecessors? [Col. 0748D] Even if you live a hundred years, you will not recover it.”

Then Georgius the prophet, groaning as he heard such a command, turned his eyes sideways toward the ground. At once he became speechless and bewildered; he stood helpless from confusion and could not answer the purple-clad king. With abundant tears and his face lowered toward the ground, he said: “We came to seek peace, not to take up arms against you.”

To this Carolus added: “As I see it, you are irreverent and senseless. Tell me now, face-to-face in battle: did you not, on the day before yesterday, while you were in your own tent, say that once Carolus had been defeated and his arms bound with straps, after his hands had been stripped, you would make him a cleric and carry him away to your own parish? Why do you deny your own words? Behold two evils, both without remedy: one because you spoke thus, the other because, through fear of a man, you dishonor God and provoke the living God in heaven, who delivered you from our hands. When he comes, he will repay you according to your own words. Behold, as my mother commanded, I shall release you. Return to your own see.”

Then, by order of the kings, the relics of the saints, the holy wood of the Lord’s cross, and the holy Gospels were brought in. After everyone else had been put outside, men not yet fully mature in body were brought in, and Georgius, bishop of the see of Ravenna, gave the oath as he had been commanded. Immediately he was released. Wherever any of the Church’s possessions were found in his possession, Carolus ordered that they be returned at once.

One of the clerics had the Gospels with golden covers in the fold of his garment. Pretending to be in pain, he lay face-down upon them for five days and nights and thus saved them. The ancient privileges by which Georgius had trusted that he could withdraw from the authority of the Roman pope were thrown into the mud and shattered by spears and lances. A golden crown from the church of the blessed martyrs John and Paul was captured there; it had the most precious gems. Likewise, a golden basket, chalices set with gems, and many other objects were taken there.

The priests and other common people who were not found in Carolus’s hands lost everything through the excessive violence of the enemy. They were left with nothing but linen garments. Those who had previously been mounted became pedestrians, and, like pilgrims, all begged for alms along the roads.

That very hour, when evening had begun, Georgius promised his companions in the presence of the impoverished priests and before God that he would firmly correct everything and repent of the evils he had previously committed. When some solidi had been found among those who had escaped by flight, and after he had restored himself with food and drink, he returned under the burden of an evil conscience. After they had crossed the cloud-covered Mount Jovis and were making their way back along the roads of that region, he denied everything he had said and did not remember the oath he had made to the Lord.

The priests, ruined and worn out by hunger, said to him: “Lend us some money with which we may live. We shall go to Ravenna; demand double in return.” But he refused to comply with their request and persisted still further in his cruelty.

In his time [on Sunday], bread crackled in the oven of a certain judge, and all the loaves were found to have become mud, while all the offerings were black like soot. The same thing happened in the bishop’s own oven. Many nobles borrowed bread from their neighbors, and mourning arose in that city.

“But what else,” my brothers, “is shown by this except the priest’s dark deeds, so that what kind of man he had been and what sort of sacrifice he ought to offer might be revealed? The offerings themselves prove this. Although his sheep had not dared to speak against their shepherd on account of his wickedness, the offerings, which he was accustomed to tear apart sluggishly, cried out against him and drove their sacrificer away from themselves. Such signs are wondrous and tearful, my brothers, when creation is changed into various forms because of our crimes. For when we do not turn back in order to amend our ways, and do not heed the holy Scripture protesting to us, nor the evangelical command, creation threatens us so that we may repent.”

Meanwhile, he fell ill with a most grievous illness. Some say that he surrendered his soul badly; there is no need for us to say anything about this, since it is better to pass over the deeds of the wicked than to be silent about the praise of the just. He died on the twentieth day of January and is now buried, as is customary, by his priests, but as he was being carried away . . . [lacuna]

The Pontifical of the Church of Ravenna ends here, edited by Andrea, called Agnellus, abbot of the Church of Saint Mary at Blachernae. It contains the lives and the ends of these most holy prelates. Amen.

## Observations on the Life of Georgius

Rubeus says many things about Georgius that are not true. The daughter of Lotharius was called Rotrudis, not Geltrudis. Her mother was Irmingardis. The prodigies are considered in relation to their chronology. What is singularly demonstrated by the episode of the bread and the offerings.

### I

Rubeus mixes many falsehoods with the truth in this life of the pontiff, which Faber copied. Rubeus writes that Georgius was sent by Gregory IV as a legate to Francia to arrange peace among the sons of Ludovicus. Agnellus says rather that, with the Roman legates, he was permitted to go by a reluctant pontiff, because, while acting before Lotharius, he had secured that assignment for himself.

According to Rubeus, Georgius escaped by flight from the battle at Fontanas, then, following wiser counsel, successfully negotiated peace and, coming into Italy with Ludovicus, the son of Lotharius, was restored to his own see at Ravenna despite the opposition of the Ravennates. Agnellus, who committed to memory what he had seen, reports that Georgius was subjected to insults and, through the intervention of Judith, the mother of King Carolus, was permitted to return to his own see. Agnellus should be trusted here rather than Rubeus.

There can be no doubt about the year in which the memorable battle of Fontaniacum occurred; it is rightly assigned to the year 841, although Eginhard places it in 842. The Saturday immediately following the feast of Saint John the Baptist falls in the preceding year, 841, when the solar cycle was X and the Dominical Letter was B. As the battle approached, writers say that Lotharius, delaying and entering into negotiations for peace, waited for the forces of his nephew Pippinus; when they arrived, he engaged in battle with his brothers.

Agnellus, however, reports that the battle was fought before Pippinus’s arrival and that, when matters had gone badly for Lotharius, it was renewed after Pippinus arrived. Here too he relates that more than forty thousand men from the armies of Lotharius and Pippinus fell. Others, reckoning the losses of both armies, say that one hundred thousand men fell.

### II

Rubeus calls the daughter of Lotharius, then king of Italy, whom Georgius received from the sacred baptismal font at Pavia, Geltrudis [Col. 0750D]. Our author calls her Rotrudis, daughter of Irmingardis. Lotharius had received Irmingardis as his wife from his father; she was the daughter of Count Hugo, in the year 821, as Eginhard and others report. By her Lotharius fathered not only Rotrudis but also the sons Lotharius, Ludovicus, and Carolus.

Rotrudis was baptized after the year 830, as may readily be inferred from the chronology of the period in which Georgius began to occupy the see. Irmingardis, the mother of Rotrudis, died in the year 850, according to the Saxon Chronographer published by the most learned Leibniz.

As for the eclipse of the sun, which our author says occurred on the fifth day of May, in the third indiction, Eginhard records the same event, saying that it occurred on the third day of the Greater Rogations. That third day fell on the fifth of May in the year 840, when the solar cycle was IX, the Dominical Letter D, C, and the lunar cycle V; Easter was celebrated on 28 March. Eginhard, however, incorrectly refers these events to the year 841.

The other prodigies are mentioned by several writers of those times. [Col. 0751A] It is distinctive that blood is said to have rained at Ravenna in the second indiction, namely in the year 839, around which time the baptism of Rotrudis appears to have taken place.

### III

Our author relates another great prodigy seen at Ravenna, which certainly deserves attention: loaves were turned into mud in the ovens, offerings were stained with soot, and this occurred especially in the bishop’s ovens.

No one will deny that by the name “offerings” Agnellus understands the hosts that we call offerings, prepared for the sacrifice of the Mass. He calls these same objects “offerings,” and says that the pontiff was supposed to tear them—that is, break them in the sacred liturgy—for himself and the people; yet they “cried out against the pontiff” and “drove their sacrificer away from themselves.”

Offerings, therefore, were baked in the ovens at Ravenna. From this I believe two conclusions can be established. First, the offerings prepared for the sacrifice of the Mass were of a different shape and made by a different process from ordinary bread, for Agnellus distinguishes between the two. Second, although the offerings were made from unleavened dough, they were thicker, in the manner of cakes, than our unleavened breads, which are baked in an iron mold rather than in an oven.

Relevant to this matter is what Hincmar of Reims says in the Chapters issued in 852 to the priests of his diocese. In article 7 he decrees:

“Let the priest take suitable portions, cut and placed in a clean and appropriate vessel, from the offerings presented by the people and left over after consecration, or from the loaves which the faithful bring to the church, or certainly from his own loaves, so that after the solemnities of the Mass those who were not prepared to receive communion may receive eulogiae from them every Sunday and on feast days.”

Likewise, the following is read in the Rite of the Monastery of Athanacum, reported by our Martène in *Treatise on the Antiquity of Ecclesiastical Discipline*, and elsewhere:

“When the Mass on the Lord’s Supper has ended, unconsecrated but blessed hosts are to be given to the poor in place of blessed bread.”

Let those who are more learned weigh these matters in relation to the present question.

## Appendix to Agnellus’s Pontifical

### Notice to the Reader

In the same Estense-library codex from which I copied Agnellus’s *Pontifical*, there was read the brief series written below of all the bishops of Ravenna, composed anonymously and carried down to Opizo Sanvitalis, and from that point continued more fully by Paulus Scordilla, provost of the Church of Ravenna, down to his own times.

It seemed appropriate to append it to Agnellus, although in part it is exceedingly meager, because it may have been useful to writers on Ravenna, while the continuation by Paulus contains several things not unworthy of attention. At the appropriate places I also thought it useful to insert certain passages from manuscripts, which may shed light upon a fuller history of the affairs and bishops of Ravenna. The whole text of these materials follows.

## Here Begins the Chronicle

[Col. 0751B]

The reverend fathers and archiepiscopal prelates of the Church of Ravenna, transmitted in abbreviated form in succession. Until 1286 this was the work of one man; down to the present day, the work of another.

## May It Begin Happily

These are the reverend fathers, the lords archbishops of Ravenna, who existed from the time of the apostles, the blessed Peter the prince and his disciple Apollinaris, who was the first archbishop of this see, down to the present day, when the venerable Father, the lord Opizo of Saint Vitalis of Parma, by the grace of God and of the Apostolic See, presides as archbishop of the aforesaid holy see. At that time the fifty-first year of the Lord was running; it is now 1286, in the ninth indiction.

Among the twelve aforesaid men who presided over this Church at various times, twelve served in the likeness of the twelve apostles. They were not chosen by human skill but rather called by heavenly mercy, and upon their heads rested a dove sent down from heaven.

## Of Saint Apollinaris, First Archbishop

Apollinaris, the first, was Antiochene by birth [nation], educated in Greek and Latin letters, and a disciple of the apostle Peter and of the Lord himself. Ordained bishop by him, and receiving the Holy Spirit and a kiss from him, he was sent to Ravenna. He came with him from the city of Rome for approximately thirty miles, as people generally say, and there the aforesaid man dedicated the holy Church at Ravenna and the city itself through martyrdom.

He lived in the episcopal chair for twenty-eight years, one month, and four days.

## Of Saint Aderitus, Second Archbishop

Aderitus, the second, a holy and God-fearing man, was ordained priest by the most blessed Apollinaris and consecrated archbishop through the choice of the Dove. When he died, he was buried in the city of Classis on the fifth day before the Kalends of October.

## Of Saint Eleucadius, Third Archbishop

Eleucadius, the third, was consecrated deacon by the most blessed Apollinaris. He too, like a philosopher, was educated in Greek and Latin letters and composed many volumes. He died and was buried on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of March outside the walls of Classis. Through his teaching the holy mother Church of Ravenna flourishes in her service. His body now rests in the city of Pavia.

## Of Saint Martianus, Fourth Archbishop

Martianus, the fourth, was ordained deacon by the most blessed Apollinaris and was buried together with the aforesaid [saint] Eleucadius in the church of the aforesaid blessed Eleucadius.

## Of Saint Calocerus, Fifth Archbishop

Calocerus, the fifth. Through him the Lord performed great wonders, and his preaching was useful and powerful. He died and was buried in the basilica of the blessed confessor Probus, on the third day before the Ides of February.

## Of Saint Proculus, Sixth Archbishop

Proculus, the sixth, distributed to the peoples the sweetness of his preaching like the taste of honey. He died and was buried in the basilica of the blessed Probus, or of the aforementioned Eleucadius, on the first day of December.

## Of Saint Probus, Seventh Archbishop

Probus, the seventh. Whoever was ill and could come to him returned healthy through his prayers. He was buried in the church that he founded within the city of Classis, on the third day before the Ides of November.

## Of Saint Dathus, Eighth Archbishop

Dathus, the eighth, an outstanding gatherer of souls, died and was buried, as some say, in the church of the blessed Probus.

## Of Saint Liberius, Ninth Archbishop

Liberius, the ninth, full of charity, an irrigating fountain, held the foremost place in every branch of philosophy. He was buried, as some say, with his predecessor.

## Of Saint Agapitus, Tenth Archbishop

Agapitus, the tenth, giving small gifts to the poor, departed from the flesh as a holy soul when the divine command came upon him. He was buried with those named above.

## Of Saint Marcellinus, Eleventh Archbishop

Marcellinus, the eleventh, just and God-fearing. Such fragrance issued from the arrangements of his body that those who buried him perceived the incense of the most precious myrrh. He was buried in the basilica of Saint Probus.

## Of Saint Severus, Twelfth Archbishop

Severus, the twelfth, a man of wondrous simplicity. He died on the Kalends of February and was buried in the church situated in the city formerly called Classis, not far from the district known as Salutaris. All the men named above were wonderfully chosen through the Holy Spirit.

## Life of Saint Severus

### Brief Notice Concerning the Following Life of Saint Severus

It seemed worthwhile to append here a life written by a monk around the time of Blessed Peter Damian, taken from an ancient Lectionary of Ravenna. I obtained this through the efforts of the most illustrious and most reverend lord Cavalli, archdeacon of the Church of Ravenna, from the nuns of Saint Andrew in that city.

A folio was missing from the original manuscript, but all the historical material can easily be extracted from the allegorical and moral passages that the author of the life added in accordance with the spirit of his age.

## Here Begins the Life of Saint Severus, Archbishop of Ravenna

Whenever the deeds of courageous men and their praiseworthy achievements are recited in the churches—men who, burning with desire for heavenly rewards, left a level road of faith for their weaker neighbors—it is undoubtedly believed that this is done so that the ardor of divine love, which each day, as iniquity increases, is accustomed to grow cold even in holy men under the action of some hostile breath, may again be kindled as though by a deep inhalation.

Hence the Church says in the *Canticles*: “Rise, O North Wind, and come, O South Wind.” For this reason we, almost uneducated and sluggish men, desiring with whatever sort of style to set forth the life, ordination, and most sacred death of the most precious lily of Christ, the blessed archbishop Severus, have decided simply to disclose to the ears of the faithful whatever about so great a man has been able to reach the knowledge of our littleness. We have looked more to their edification and salvation than to the pompous elegance of the curious.

For whoever speaks sophistically, according to Solomon, is found hateful to God in every respect: he kills himself with the weapon of boasting and, in addition, does nothing at all for the weakness of his hearers. But because, following the customary manner of historians, it is necessary to attach the anchor of faith to the account of what happened, we place three things at the beginning of the narrative as instruments for the composition of the work: namely, the person, his homeland, and his condition.

To touch briefly upon the truth about his person: Severus was not called by his parents without a certain divine omen. For if we examine the etymology more closely, it does not signify “severity” or “savagery,” but rather paternal gravity, concerning which the Psalmist says: “Among a grave people I shall praise you.” And not without reason, since he was destined to be an exceedingly stern eradicator of vices and an exceedingly eager gatherer of virtues.

His homeland is sufficiently clear to everyone, since he was a citizen of Ravenna; and, as it was said of the blessed Pope Gregory, “From the place where he drew his origin, he ascended to the highest honor.”

What his condition was is demonstrated by the whole of his most holy life, since he was truly a Christian and led a dove-like life in simplicity of heart. He lived a poor life with Tobias, because he feared the divine presence and always considered the vigilance of the Almighty. Yet he possessed all good things, because he possessed charity, which is God, in every way.

As far as worldly luxury is concerned, he led a poor life because, as the most truthful reporters relate, together with his wife, to whom he had long before been joined in a most chaste marriage, he obtained his daily expenses only through the work of wool-making. For, as a religious and orthodox Catholic, he lived by the labor of his hands with the Apostle and inflicted neither force nor fraud upon anyone. Nor did he pass by with deaf ears the Psalmist’s proclamation: “For you shall eat the labors of your hands; blessed are you, and it shall be well with you.”

At this point, if some proud man, with a rusted mind and foolish objection, disparages the blessed man because he came as a married man to the archbishopric of Ravenna, let him hear the Apostle answering on his behalf: “All things are clean to the clean.” Just as a man is not polluted by eating food unless treacherous desire comes first, so a Christian is not defiled by lawful marriage if he has not bound himself by a vow of virginity or continence—unless deceitful lust first corrupts him with the ferment of obscene love.

Otherwise, if someone is bound by a vow, he is compelled to fulfill it, because it is written: “Vow and repay.”

But since, for the sake of defending the truth, we have spoken at some length as though going beyond our subject, let us return to what we began.

After the preeminent champion of truth, Apollinaris, had been ordained bishop by the prince of the apostles to preach the word of the Lord everywhere, just as divine Providence had predestined before the ages, and had received the keys of the kingdom of heaven as a suitable and wholly approved vicar, he immediately took into his apostolic care the most noble city of Italy and the metropolis of many cities, as though it were a second Rome.

For that most clement and pious king so distinguished the city by honoring it with the exceptional merits of his triumphant servant that, after this fortunate soldier, crowned with the crown of martyrs, entered into the joy of his Lord, the city supplied twelve successors over the course of many years, in the likeness of the twelve apostles. They were not chosen by human skill but rather summoned by divine mercy, and upon their heads rested a dove sent down from heaven.

In the time of the blessed Severus, already mentioned and always to be mentioned, it happened that the Church of Ravenna was left without its own shepherd. When many bishops assembled, both neighboring and more distant, so that they might ordain a bishop for so great a city according to the customary practice, and when the prayer had ended and everyone together was joyfully awaiting the spectacle—namely, for someone to be indicated from heaven through a dove—the same man of God, the blessed Severus, happened to be busy at home with his work.

As he was simple and a friend of the dove, he addressed his wife in these words: “If it pleases you, I shall go quickly and see the wondrous vision, how a dove comes from heaven by divine agency and settles upon the head of the chosen man.”

She answered him: “Stay here and work; do not waste your time, because it is not good for us. Whether you go or remain here, the people will not ordain you bishop.”

To this he replied: “Let me go.”

And she said: “Go, if it pleases you, for at whatever hour you enter, you will be ordained bishop.”
