While his wife continued in this ironic manner, he immediately arose and hastened to the church, where the people and priests were assembled. Because of the poverty of his clothing, for he was dressed in a filthy garment, he hid himself behind the doors of the church.

When the prayer had ended, a dove whiter than snow came down from heaven and settled upon the head of the blessed Severus, who wished to remain hidden. But whenever he tried to drive the dove away, and it flew here and there, again and again it returned to the beloved head of that blessed man, as though the Holy Spirit were revealing in visible form what was actually the case, saying: “Upon whom shall I rest, if not upon the humble, the quiet, and the one who trembles at my words?” And again: “I love those who love me.”

Hence this venerable proverb has long been circulated throughout the whole world: “Blessed is that city where, at the election of a bishop, the Holy Spirit descends in the likeness of a dove, and the man upon whose head it rests is ordained.”

All the authorities and clergy, and everyone present at this divine spectacle, were astonished at it and gave thanks to God, the giver of every good and every dignity. In this manner the blessed Severus was ordained bishop of the Church of Ravenna, and he was anointed with the oil of gladness and with the ointment of sacred chrism according to the custom of bishops.

Then what the Lord said in the Gospel was fulfilled in him: “With men this is impossible, but with the Lord all things are possible.” And in Paul’s words: “God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong.”

Behold what the apostle Peter says: “God is not a respecter of persons, but in every nation whoever fears the Lord and works righteousness is acceptable to him.”

But, oh, the change of the times, and oh, the wickedness of the trafficking! Our Redeemer, wishing to show his faithful how damnable the business of trafficking is, entered the temple and violently drove out all who were selling and buying in it. Having made a whip of cords, he most powerfully expelled from the temple those who were selling doves.

But the ancient enemy of the human race, who, according to the Apostle, already works the mystery of iniquity in his members, and who sits with the rich in secret places to kill the innocent, once again, through his own Simon, makes the dove available for sale with the gall of bitterness. Through his moneychangers he does not cease to imitate the coins of iniquity, by which he may plunge them more deeply into the pit of destruction.

Behold, no bishop is now elected anywhere, because the Churches are not permitted to elect them. What is more horrible than every monstrosity, and the worst form of adultery, has taken first place. While a city’s bishop is still alive, someone unlearned and depraved desires his honor, seeks it, promises it, strengthens the hope with an oath, and shamelessly gives money, so that later what he acquired by such a wicked attempt may be sold still more disgracefully.

But since the logic of this matter has now brought in the dove for the sake of ecclesiastical vigor, let us pursue, as we began, its ill-deserving sellers. Do you see how, after Simon, the first heresiarch—whose wretched head was cut off by the apostolic sword amid the very cradles of the infant Church, and who was then buried under perpetual anathema by so many Fathers favoring justice in ecclesiastical councils—other heads, as it were of a hydra, grow up again?

It is therefore necessary that the bishops of our own time be either few or none before the Almighty Lord. Hence the prophet also says: “They became princes, but not through me; they reigned, and I did not acknowledge them.”

What do certain young and unlearned men mutter in response—men who know how to speak but do not understand? “Monks,” they say, “do not have permission to preach, even though they are filled with divine authority.” It is no wonder, because flesh does not know the spirit.

The truth is bitter, and those who strive to teach it are filled with bitterness. Behold, the blessed Severus, almost uneducated and without letters, touched by the Spirit of truth, becomes a most fruitful teacher, while a monk who has studied the divine letters from his earliest beginnings is obliged to remain silent.

The apostle Paul obtained this special privilege: because he learned the sacred letters at the feet of Gamaliel, he deserved both to be called and to be the Chosen Vessel. Hence he is called the special Teacher of the whole world . . . [lacuna]

Here an entire folio is missing.
his own, which he had foreseen long before through a revelation of the Holy Spirit, he fortified with the most salutary reception of the sacraments. Having summoned to himself the clergy of the whole city, as well as people of both sexes according to ecclesiastical custom, he delivered a lengthy sermon, in accordance with the wisdom granted him, concerning the integrity of the catholic faith and the attainment of unanimity and brotherly charity. When this was finished, peace and blessing having been confirmed, he—clad as he was in the pontifical vestment and surrounded on every side by the assembled people—ordered his own tomb to be opened. Entering it alive, he placed himself with remarkable authority between his wife and daughter; with a clear voice and a very vigorous countenance, he gave himself over to his final sleep in the Lord and ordered the marble to be gently closed over him. There, after praying for some time, he joyfully returned his precious soul to God, perfected in the nest of the Church; and thus, stripped of the burden of the flesh, he attained the Capitol of the heavenly kingdom.

In this manner, then, he died in the peace of the Church, full of days, on the day of the Kalends of February. From that time to the present, our pious and merciful Christ the Redeemer, to display the singular merits of his confessor, has worked innumerable miracles exceeding human measure at his tomb. There now stands in his honor a basilica, tastefully adorned with marble paneling, in the city formerly called Classis, not far from the district called Salutaris, and it remains there to this day.

Of the innumerable signs of benefits which almighty God has deigned to reveal through his beloved blessed Severus toward the sick, we faithfully relate one that shone forth in our own times, so that through it the others, which remain unknown to our insignificance, may be commended.

A certain woman of Ravenna, whose name escapes us, had a little son suffering more than he should from a daily recurrence of fever. Because of the excessive continuity of his pain, she resolved to offer him to God at the tomb of blessed Severus, archbishop and confessor, in the hope of his speedier recovery. When she had arrived with her son, accompanied by the assistance of friends, she prostrated herself humbly before God and his holy servant Severus, praying with earnestness for the child’s health. Since they were encouraged by good hope, they decided to spend the night in the church. Partly because the night was long and partly because of their perseverance in prayer, all of them, overcome by weariness, fell asleep.

At the dead of night, while everyone was sunk in sluggish sleep, the sick boy alone, suddenly overcome by astonishment, uttered a plaintive cry and awakened them all. Looking around, they saw the lamps, which had previously been extinguished, shining with an appropriate brilliance. When they recognized the miracle of the light sent down from heaven, they were shaken in mind and gave glory to God and to Saint Severus.

When the boy had been brought into their midst, his mother began to question him, saying, “What happened to you, my son?” He replied before them all: “I saw an old man coming out of this tomb, dressed as a bishop and adorned with snow-white hair, with an angelic face. He touched me, and I was terrified.”

The illness immediately withdrew from the boy, and thereafter the burning fever was extinguished in him.

But why mention these things? Because there can be no doubt that whatever he wishes to ask of almighty God, he obtains without delay and beyond all doubt.

For the present, let these remarks about so great a prelate of the Church suffice—of whose [lacuna] history, as we believe, no pen is adequate, even if a Ciceronian one were added. Behold, as we promised, we have avoided the adornment of novel expressions, although other things too might have been supplied, had it pleased us to pursue display rather than goodwill. For we have written for little ones about little things; indeed, we read that “little things suit the little.” Moreover, the Apostle teaches us not to think lofty thoughts but to associate with the lowly; and certainly the Law forbids anyone to place a stumbling-block before the blind. The kingdom of God is not, to be sure, in speech but in power.

But since, with Favonius now blowing, we have somehow swum across the pond of this history with our merchandise safe, let us pause briefly to see whether some precious pearl of allegory lies hidden in it as in a shell.

Are we to suppose that a dove descended easily and without great authority from the heavenly hinge all the way to earth? Certainly not. The arrival of a dove is nowhere recorded except as a testimony to the presence of the Holy Spirit. No room for reproach is left to the heretics who think that Saint Severus of the Lord was bound by marriage to the disgrace of the Church; wrapped as they are in the filth of their own uncleanness, they are wholly ignorant of the grace of the Holy Spirit.

If someone has never tasted honey, it is no wonder that he does not know what flavor it has. But those who use only wormwood at all times, neglecting every other herb, naturally find sweetness bitter and think that the other herbs share the same bitterness, because they lack experience of that flavor. Of such people it is written: “Woe to those who call good evil and evil good.”

If, therefore, something appears evil to anyone, he himself is a witness that he is evil; and what he himself has become through privation, he thinks that all others possess indiscriminately by nature. But whoever regards everything simply, and with incorrupt eyes believes that every creature of God is good, is himself a witness that he is good.

Let the good person therefore rejoice that he was created by God; but let the evil person know that he is without the Creator and therefore nothing. For nothing except the Lord is uncreated. If, then, something were evil, what, I ask, would it be except good? Scripture says: “And God saw everything that he had made, and it was not only good but very good.” From this it is permissible to define that the things that exist are good, and that they do not exist at all if they are not good. All things, therefore, are good, though not all are just.

Blessed Severus, then, looked upon all the works of the Lord with dove-like eyes. He saw marriage as very good if a person uses it lawfully, since, if it were not good, woman would never have been created as a help for the first-formed man. The son of the Dove had the eyes of a dove, by which the Holy Spirit is signified—not that any of the faithful can rightly be called a son of the Holy Spirit, but rather a son of God the Father and of Mother Church through the grace of adoption. Hence the Bridegroom addresses the Bride in the Song of Songs, saying: “Your eyes are like those of doves.”

Our first parents lost these eyes when, because of their transgression, they were abandoned by God, and “the eyes of both of them were opened.” After they had lost their dove-like eyes, they immediately became ashamed by the just judgment of God, because death had already entered through the window of their carnal eyes.

For example, so long as a child has not grieved the Holy Spirit, he is said to possess the eyes of a dove, because he looks simply upon all that exists in the world. He is not ashamed of his limbs, is angry with no one, plots against no one, thinks of nothing immodest, and desires nothing unlawful, because the indwelling Spirit, who guards him with an incorrupt mind, knows none of these things.

But if, through the divisions of vices, he slips into the exile of life and into carnal desire, he is rightly ashamed, because what the Psalmist says has been fulfilled in him: “Man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared with foolish beasts and became like them.”

The Spirit of adoption, whom blessed Severus received in holy rebirth, nourished, like a dove in a cleft of the wall, the nestlings of the virtues in the little nest of his heart, and did not depart from him until, when he was chosen as bishop, it became known to human beings that he would remain [the source text is uncertain here].

Behold how Christian people set aside the heavenly life after they fall from the lofty summit of innocence, their conscience corrupted, into an earthly and bestial existence.

Blessed Severus, then, a simple and upright man, had a wife, and he also had a daughter—but before his episcopate. Was he for that reason unworthy of the episcopate because he had a little wife? Far from it. Was not the blessed prince of the apostles, to speak more boldly, legally married? Certainly he was, but before his calling.

Accordingly, by the same reasoning, blessed Severus was joined in marriage when the novelty of the Gospel was already shining everywhere, because he had not taken a vow of continence, nor had Paul, the teacher of the world, forbidden him; rather, Paul gave his assent. Behold Peter, called to the apostolate and chosen, leads his wife about with him, but does not make use of her. His wife, indeed, was transformed into a sister, because, when the Sun of the world had risen, the order of the times was changed.

For he who formerly commanded by the Law concerning those who remained without offspring among the people of Israel now thunders terribly through his Gospel: “Let your loins be girded.”

Blessed Severus too, chosen for the episcopate by the dove, simply led his wife about with the teacher Peter and raised a virgin daughter. Yet thereafter he in no way used his wife, because he had been appointed shepherd and vicar of the Church of Christ.

Let those who invent evil withdraw far away—those who understand neither what they say nor the subjects about which they make assertions.

That the holy man sought his daily livelihood from the work of wool-making commends his holy simplicity. For it was fitting that the sheep of the Lord, clothed in the fleece of that Lamb who takes away the sins of the world, should sustain his own life and that of his household from nothing other than the covering of sheep, that is, of clean animals.

He was one of these sheep, and not an ordinary one. The true and eternal shepherd Christ commends such sheep in the Gospel with these words: “My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me, and I give them eternal life.” And again: “I have other sheep that are not of this fold; I must bring them also, and they will hear my voice.”

For, as tradition has it, the sheep is naturally above all animals very clean and gentle, and devoted to simplicity. If there is any meaningful comparison between rational and irrational things, made incidentally, then we rightly compare like with like in such matters.

For it must not be believed that so great a man happened by mere chance to choose such a way of life. Rather, it appears to have been a certain indication of his future office, since he was to be entrusted with pastoral care, by which, in evangelical obedience, he would have to feed both lambs with Peter and sheep.

Thus too we read in the Acts of the Apostles that Paul, the teacher of the whole Church, lived by the labor of his own hands so that he would be a burden to none of his hearers. He was a worker in the tent-making trade.

Could Paul, who was full of every skill, not have lived by some other means? Certainly he could. But we believe that this was done for the sake of a certain mystery: since that outstanding preacher commended by his works everything that he preached to the faithful, lest he himself should become disqualified, it was altogether necessary that the labor of his hands should bear witness to his life and preaching.

And because the work by which he lived was necessary to migrants and travelers, it was fitting that, by a certain prophetic tongue, he should already then speak symbolically of what he would later write while persuading people to despise the world: “We have here no lasting city, but we seek the one that is to come.”

It was fitting that, in a figurative manner, the very awnings should then speak, as though they were openly saying to those who use them by human reason:

“See, O sailors and foreign travelers, the equipment and cheap material of your huts; and from the nature of us, which you know, consider the height of your dignity, which our maker and joiner Paul teaches you without ceasing. We took our origin from waters, and we are born on the banks of ponds. We are so light and easily transported that we can readily be carried away by travelers, and yet through our service they obtain a desired shelter.

“But you, who are able to use reason and have been reborn from water and the Holy Spirit, do not burden yourselves with earthly pleasures and the enticements of the world, so that, freed and unencumbered, you may traverse the short road of this pilgrimage and return as quickly as possible to reach your eternal homeland.”

Behold in what words the work of the Apostle addresses its possessors, whence to spend the life of their present exile . . . [lacuna]

The same may suitably be understood of the blessed Severus’s domestic work, insofar as, through the fleeces of sheep, they admonish his followers to maintain gentle and simple hearts.

Now the order of the exposition demands that we also try, with lynx-like eyes, to penetrate what is meant by his being caught up in the Spirit at the hour of the divine office and being said to have attended the funeral of the blessed priest Geminianus.

In this miracle of a special gift, we may rightly judge that Saint Severus, archbishop of the Lord, is in all things to be compared with blessed Ambrose. For just as that most blessed bishop attended the feast of the death of the holy and glorious bishop Martin, so this man attended that of blessed Geminianus.

If someone should wish, in friendly contention, to argue that the miracle ought in some way to be considered different because the distances of land between Milan and Tours are greater, let him know for certain that almighty God, who exists everywhere without being confined to any place, is neither enlarged in the greatest places nor compressed in the smallest. For the centre of heaven, which is the earth, is not his kingdom; he is difficult to find where he is, and more difficult to find where he is not.

But since, because the writers neglected to establish the exact date of blessed Severus, we do not know which of the two was earlier in age, the matter does not directly concern us. Nevertheless, no one of sound mind is permitted to doubt that one and the same gift was bestowed upon both in every respect.

Perhaps someone objects to us in this way: “How, you will say, can someone from the company of priests be compared with Ambrose, a teacher of the Church?”

We quickly resolve this little objection, as though it were an opening for a new slander, if we take a more subtle view of the moral praise of the Holy Spirit. For it is established in writing about the Holy Spirit that he is both manifold and one. He is manifold because of the multiform grace distributed to all the faithful, but simple because of the indivisible unity of the divine essence.

The Holy Spirit is found as manifold because of the gift of manifold knowledge in Ambrose, who after the Vessel of Election, Paul, obtained primacy in the word of the Lord. Yet he is found no less authoritative in blessed Severus, who was content with the simplicity of unity, because it is one and the same Spirit who works all things in all.

The similar gift bestowed in this event testifies that the glorious Fathers Ambrose and Severus possessed one and the same merit.

It is also pleasant to consider what the reason may be for the great authority by which the man of God ordered that, at his daughter’s burial, the body of his wife, who had died long before, be turned onto its side.

Just as this miracle is found to be rarely customary, so it is not explained by us without difficulty. Nevertheless, whatever it may be that shines through to our understanding, we judge that it ought by no means to be concealed in silence.

It seems, moreover, that our ignorance should understand in every respect that this holy man was by no means unequal to raising his wife’s body, since he was able to obtain from almighty God that, by a mere command, it should so quickly turn onto its side.

There is also another point that seems useful to understand. Above, we fought sufficiently—and more than sufficiently—with a crescent-shaped sword against the heretics and adversaries of the Church who claimed that the holy man of the Lord had labored for no purpose because of the disgrace of his wife. Therefore it was necessary that the devil, through his accomplices, should be exposed in the open as the crafty and deceitful one he is, and that the holy Church throughout the world should obtain, in so great a [lacuna], the glory of the herald of God.

To speak the truth about the chastity and continence he possessed before his episcopate, the Holy Spirit himself clearly displayed it at his election through the dove. The dove flew over so many persons of the secular order and, assigning the beloved inner chamber to him, revisited him.

And it should be noted that the Holy Spirit, who is the friend of the number twelve, made the mode of his bodily presence correspond to that number in blessed Severus, since according to the catalogue of the Church of Ravenna he is the twelfth after his holy predecessor Apollinaris.

But so that nothing may remain unexplained among us from which false men might obtain an occasion for shouting, it seems that the most sacred pontiff secretly makes satisfaction to his Church concerning the reputation of the wife once joined to him.

For the fact that he is said to have wept before performing the miracle should be understood as his recalling his former life, since he is read to have been bound by the marital bond with Christian liberty.

But the fact that he gave the command with such imperious authority, ordering the body itself to incline so quickly onto its side, clearly shows how free he had been from any attachment to her after he became bishop.

Finally, let us turn to consider his passing, and let us see, with what may be called eagle eyes, how full of virtues the most holy man was.

“He descended alive,” it says, “into the excavated place of the tomb, in which his holy wife had formerly rested together with his daughter; and, placing himself between them, he fell asleep in peace.”

Whom did this man imitate in his death, if not that most brilliant ray, John the Theologian, who, as ecclesiastical history testifies, likewise rested in extreme old age?

After his fellow apostles, we can compare no one with John, since the whole world is compelled to acknowledge this. Nevertheless, in this wondrous virtue we assert that this man shared something with John.

John is believed to have been blessed, chosen by the Lord with a special prerogative, beloved, and taken up. But the man of the Lord, Severus, is held among us more fully under his own title.

He is therefore present on earth synecdochically (*συνεκδοχικῶς*, “by synecdoche”); in heaven he peacefully awaits the time of the general resurrection (*ἀνάστασις*, “resurrection”).

For this reason, with every effort of devotion, let us strive to venerate so great and such a Father and patron. Let us regard his absence as present, as though he were still dwelling among us in the flesh, because, to make the truth plain, he is believed to stand more present beside us than if he were alive in the flesh.

Indeed, joined in heaven to the highest and eternal Sun, who dwells in inaccessible light, nothing occurs among creatures that does not appear naked before his eyes.

Therefore let us rejoice. Let us rejoice, I say, and exult and be glad in the Lord, because today, amid the alternating hymn-singing choirs of the angels, he entered the pastures of the eternal inheritance, where there is one fellowship of all the blessed, where, after the labors and hardships of this age, there is a happy and sweet refreshment for holy souls.

Let us all rejoice; let each of us rejoice, because our hierarch, blessed Severus, now secure in his imperishable glory, has today reached the palace of heaven.

In him we have a most sweet patron, a most merciful defender, who daily offers our vows and prayers, whatever they may be, to the supreme pontiff, Christ Jesus the Lord, and who, as a devoted advocate, interposes himself on behalf of his clients by pledging himself for them.

Let us disclose to him in every way the secrets of our conscience, so that on the day of the dread judgment he may defend us beneath the shield of his fatherhood and strive to place us at the Judge’s right hand.

Praise and thanksgiving be to him who predestined him before the ages for the kingdom, inscribed him in the book of life, chose him for the episcopate through the dove, the creature of the Holy Spirit, received him in peace, and introduced him into the citizenship of eternal Jerusalem, where he is forever to be congratulated; he lives and reigns in the name of the Trinity and in the power of unity, for ever and ever. Amen.

## The Chronicle Follows

### Of Liberius, the Thirteenth Archbishop

Liberius XIII, an outstanding shepherd of orphans and generous in almsgiving, was buried with the greatest care after his death.

### Of Probus, the Fourteenth Archbishop

Probus XIV, enriched by divine grace and handsome in appearance. Placed near his final death, he contemplated the ranks of angels and, joyful and exultant, made his way to the stars. He was buried with his predecessor.

### Of Florianus, the Fifteenth Archbishop

Florianus XV. A just man, father of the poor, protector of widows, and great preacher. He was buried in the monastery of blessed Petronilla beside the walls of the Apostles.

### Of Liberius, the Sixteenth Archbishop

Liberius XVI, a holy man possessing eloquence flowing like milk. In his time the Emperor Valentinian was killed, and many were wounded. He was buried in the monastery of Saint Pullio; his feast is celebrated on the third day before the Kalends of January.

### Of Ursus, the Seventeenth Archbishop

Ursus XVII, who founded the church called Ursiana and ended his life on the Ides of April, the day of the Resurrection. On that same day it was dedicated by him and called Anastasis (*ἀνάστασις*, “Resurrection”), and he was buried in it beneath a porphyry stone, where the pontiff stands when he sings Mass. He held office for twenty-six years.

### Of Peter, the Eighteenth Archbishop

Peter XVIII. The bishop who founded the Petriana church, but did not complete it. No church was comparable to it in construction; it is said to have had three hundred altars. He died on the day before the Kalends of August.

### Of Neom, the Nineteenth Archbishop

Neom XIX. Founder of the church of Saint Peter Major and founder of Tricolis, but not its completer. He lived in the time of the orthodox mother Galla Placidia. He died on the IN Ides of February [the numeral is uncertain in the supplied text]. In former times he was buried in the basilica of the Apostles before the altar of Saint Peter the Apostle.

### Of Exuperantius, the Twentieth Archbishop

Exuperantius XX, an aged, humble, and gentle man. In his time the church of Saint Agnes was built. He died on the third day before the Kalends of July. He was buried in the aforementioned basilica before the altar, beneath a porphyry stone.

### Of John, the Twenty-First Archbishop

John, first of that name, XXI. A most holy man who saw an angel. He acquired fourteen cities for this Church, under episcopal authority, from the Catholic King Valentinian. He died on the Nones of June and was buried in the church of Saint Agatha at Ravenna on the Nones of June. He held office for sixteen years, ten months, and eighteen days.

### Of Peter of Ravenna, the Twenty-Second Archbishop

Peter XXII, bishop of Ravenna, also called Chrysologus. Before him no one among the pontiffs was his equal in wisdom, and after him none arose. His body was buried at Imola in the major church; his feast is celebrated on the third day before the Nones of December. He was elected and confirmed as archbishop around the year of the Lord 429.

## Annotation

There is a chapel in the upper part of the old archiepiscopal palace, elegantly decorated in mosaic work. By common opinion, it is believed to have been built by Saint Peter Chrysologus, on the basis of the monogram expressing the name of Peter. In several places the mosaics have fallen away, especially above the altar, where verses were written by the painter’s work. Agnellus, and Rubeus on the authority of Agnellus, attest that these verses were once read in the oratory of Saint Andrew constructed by Chrysologus.

I thought it would be useful to the reader if the ornaments of the little chapel, engraved on three bronze tablets, were given here. Among the saints whose images adorn the four sides of the vault is Saint Cassian, to whom Peter Chrysologus is known to have been especially devoted; for, having once been ordained a deacon to the title of his church, he ultimately wished to die beside his body. This provides a substantial argument for assigning the work to Peter Chrysologus himself.

There is no need to add more here on this subject, since the learned and erudite friend, the lord abbot Ferrus, patrician of Forum Cornelii, will illuminate that work more fully in his excellent composition written for the glorification of his native city and soon to be published. The tablets to be joined at this point are marked with the letters A, B, and C.

## To the Following Life of Saint Barbatianus

### Notice

I have judged that the following Life of Saint Barbatianus, copied from an ancient Lectionary of Ravenna, ought to be inserted here, since it is lacking in the printed editions. There are certain matters with which the chronology conflicts, such as the settlement of the schism between Boniface and Eulalius being connected with the arrival in Rome of Valentinian, the son of Galla Placidia; for when that schism arose, he may not yet have been born.

Rubeus, under the year 425, praises the piety of Placidia and Valentinian, who, while dwelling in Rome, visited Barbatianus and escorted him honorably from Rome to Ravenna. But this, I think, he narrated by conjecture.

For the rest, I have no doubt that everything Rubeus illustrates in the same eloquent discourse about Saint Barbatianus was taken from this old Life. It is worth noting the frequent mention of offerings brought to the Mass of Saint Barbatianus, by which private vows were fulfilled—something that one might otherwise suspect belonged to a later age than the period in which this saint flourished. Saint Peter Chrysologus is praised together with Librificus. But enough of this.

## The Life of Saint Barbatianus the Confessor Begins

I rightly believe that, when undertaking a narration of miracles, I should first set forth those native to the imperial cities, where the wonderful contest of the saints was completed and their venerable miracles arose. The miracles that form the beginning of this narrative, having been attested in our own days as true by so great a people and so great a city, should also provide credibility for what is about to be related.

Accordingly, when Pope Zosimus, by God’s command, had completed the episcopate of his life in the city of Rome, dissension arose among the clergy of the apostolic see, and they chose two bishops, one named Boniface and the other [variant: “another”] Eulalius. They ordained Boniface in the Constantinian basilica.

When Galla Placidia Augusta heard this, while she was seated at Ravenna with her son Valentinian Augustus, they reported it to Honorius Augustus, who was seated at Milan. Both Augusti immediately issued an authoritative order that both men should leave the city of Rome.

After both had been expelled, when the holy day of Easter was approaching [variant: “with the holy day of Easter approaching after they had been expelled”], Eulalius then entered the city of Rome with presumptuous boldness, baptized, and celebrated Easter in the Constantinian basilica. When this was heard, the Augusti sent orders and expelled Eulalius from the city of Rome, sending him to Campania [variant: “they expelled Eulalius from the city of Rome and sent him”], where he ended his life. They recalled Boniface and appointed him pontiff.

At the same time, Galla Placidia Augusta, together with the Augusti Honorius and Valentinian [variant: “Valentinianus”], came [variant: “coming”] to Rome to the thresholds of the holy apostles, where they offered many gifts. Then word spread among them that two men had come to the city of Rome from Antioch, one named Timothy and the other Barbatianus [variant: “the other”], both holding the honor of the priesthood, fearing God, performing miracles, and healing the sick through their holy prayers [variant: “performing healings”]. For this reason they were especially venerated by everyone.

But when the Augusta had summoned them, the most holy priest Timothy had already migrated to the Lord four days before her inquiry. A certain most noble widow had buried his body, embalmed it with spices, and carefully arranged it with great joy and honor, as is fitting for saints, on the Vatican Mount called Aureus. At his tomb, sick people were made well and demons were driven out; and many miracles are performed there daily to the praise and honor of our Lord Jesus Christ.

The most holy priest Barbatianus, confessor of Christ, had withdrawn to the cemetery of Callixtus and was living there secretly. When the Augusta conducted an inquiry concerning the holy man, because he did not wish to show himself to princes, they found him hiding quietly in his cell and brought him to the Augusta with great honor.

When she saw him, the Augusta gave thanks to God because she had been deemed worthy to find him [variant: “Seeing him, the Augusta rejoiced and gave thanks”]. The most holy man Barbatianus greeted her in these words:

“Peace to you, Galla Placidia Augusta, servant of Christ, and victory to your son Augustus” [variant: “to your Augustan sons”].

When everyone had replied, “Amen,” the Augusti approached and greeted one another. When they asked him from what country he had come to Rome, the confessor of Christ declared that he had arrived from Antioch with Timothy, the most holy man.

After offering a prayer, the Augusta then asked him to help her handmaid, who was afflicted by a most grievous pain of the eyes—not only for that purpose, but also so that he might confirm the reputation that had spread about him.

He answered nothing other than that he wished good things to prosper in her eyes. When he had departed from her, he reached his cell [variant: “having reached it”] and, prostrating himself, prayed to the Lord. Rising from prayer, he directed toward the girl his face-cloth, soaked with water, so that she might wipe her eyes with it.

When she obeyed his command and wiped her eyes, the swelling of blood and the dimness were displayed before everyone present, so that [variant: “they ceased, and she was immediately made well, as if”] she had never had any blemish in her eyes, and she did not cease continually to give thanks with hymns and praises to our Lord Jesus Christ.

But we shall also relate the remaining miracles that the same most holy man performed to illuminate the hearts of all who believe in the Lord [variant: “in Christ”].

There was a man named Gallogenes, a Greek by nationality. When he had been ordered by Augustus Valentinian to descend quickly by a ladder, he was shackled and fell to the ground from above. His foot was crushed, and he was in danger because his feet, shins, and bones had been shattered.

When he saw that the aid of the physicians was powerless to help him, and that nearly the bones of his feet and shins were gradually falling apart, while his flesh, dissolved by an abundant discharge of pus, was wasting away, he was carried to the most holy man Barbatianus and took refuge with him, imploring him to find health for him in this condition.

When the holy confessor of Christ saw him, he looked toward heaven and, prostrating himself with tears, prayed to the Lord. Rising from prayer, he ordered the lame man to be carried to him. After praying over him and making the sign of the holy cross [before him], the shattered bones were restored [variant: “and at that hour he was made well”].

After this astonishing cure had been performed, there was a man named Isidore, who had been grievously afflicted in the lungs. For this illness none of the physicians could provide him with a remedy for recovery; everything they did to him instead proved harmful. When he had already become putrid, he gradually wasted away, coughing up phlegm and blood, and he expected the end of his life to come from this.

Because of this, Isidore despised himself and recognized that he had received no hope of recovery [variant: “from human beings”]. He went quietly in the morning to blessed Barbatianus, so that he might receive a blessing from his hands and recover the remedy of health.

When the holy man questioned him [variant: “and heard from him the illness he had described”], his face fell into tears [variant: “he wept for a very long time”], and, prostrating himself on the ground, he besought the Lord to restore to him the former health of his body.

Rising from prayer, he handed him a small piece of citron. The sick man gratefully received what he had been given and willingly ate it. While he was still chewing the last portion of citron that he was eating [variant: “while he was still chewing the final part of the citron”], he was suddenly moved to vomit and, together with the food, expelled a worm that had been consuming his lung or internal organs.

By expelling it, he expelled the illness as well, and immediately recovered the strength of health.

After the remarkable healing of Isidore, let us bring forward the illness of Minas, so that, hearing of it with your ears, you may glorify our Lord Jesus Christ with praises and hymns. This Minas, whom we have mentioned, was gravely ill; his illness was a violent fever, which attacked him persistently [or: urgently] and fiercely, and, extinguishing almost his entire body with moisture, reduced him to a state of exhaustion and dryness. To remedy this dryness of the belly, the disciples of physicians brought medicines and foods that would loosen the bowels, but nothing they had given him benefited him; rather, he became worse, and they harmed him severely.

After he had endured the danger for twice seven days and was no longer able to bear it, he fled to the most holy man Barbatianus, in the cell where he had withdrawn, entrusting his life and death to him. When he came to him, he did not come on foot or in the carrying-chair in which the sick are transported—he could neither sit nor walk—but, lying on a small bed, he was carried in relays by sixteen men. When they came to the most holy man Barbatianus, the bearers fell prostrate on the ground and begged him to make the sick man well.

As soon as he saw him, the confessor of Christ [variant: the most holy man] took pity on him. Raising his eyes to heaven, he prayed for a very long time. After completing his prayer, he took a single fig, made the sign of the holy cross over it, and brought it to the sick man to eat. When the latter immediately received and ate it with great joy, he recovered his health at once and obtained complete healing. The faithful herald sent by him praised the grace of the most holy man and, taking upon his shoulders the little bed on which he had been carried to him, carried it away. In this action he imitated the man who had lain sick in the Pool of Bethesda, whom Christ saved after thirty-eight years, saying: “Take up your pallet and walk.” He had commanded him to take up his pallet and walk, thereby revealing the ineffable power and the remarkable deed that the saint had performed for him [variant: the ineffable power and remarkable work that he had experienced in him].

At the same time there was a certain man named Geddeus who had a fistula in his groin. This spectacle draws us to consider it. The affliction of the fistula that he had in his groin arose from this: after suffering scourges, and with drops of fluid flowing out and collecting there from his entire body, he was hindered by this torment and eagerly desired to be entirely freed from it [variant: humors gathered there from the whole body in flowing drops; wishing to be completely freed from this torment]. He frequently clung to the vestibule of physicians and was continually brought before them. But after he had experienced the skill of them all, spent everything, and had not been freed from the fistula, he came by night to the most holy man Barbatianus. He had no physician who would continue his treatment, nor did he possess gold or silver; instead, he came to that man who did not require payment, but rather nourished the poor and bestowed benefits upon the sick.

When he had come to him, he immediately showed his wound to the most holy Father and, falling prostrate in prayer, begged the Lord. Rising from prayer, Barbatianus extended to him from his own hand a prepared poultice, which he received both to eradicate the fistula and to fill the wound itself. When it had been applied, the fistula dried up, the cavity was immediately filled, and he was made healthy, to the honor and praise of the holy confessor of Christ.

But let us also bring forward the other miracles that the Lord worked through the most holy confessor of Christ, Barbatianus. While praising the discipline of the divine physician and the grace of power granted to him by God, we shall pass to Minas the lame. This Minas, with Barbatianus’s martyrdom providing the occasion for the praise [variant: having this as the subject of Barbatianus’s praise], had once been swift-footed, as though he were a she-goat in the field, according to holy Scripture, which speaks of Asahel, who was remarkable in Scripture for the speed of his feet. But although he had once been exceedingly swift in running, he became lame instead of swift-footed [variant: he fell into a long illness in which he became lame instead of swift-footed]. After finally emerging with difficulty from his long illness, he did not escape its harm, but remained motionless on his bed and was not restored from his sickness.

When the physicians predicted a long illness and despaired of him because of the disease that had arisen from that ailment, a vision appeared to him in sleep [the vision is lacking], telling him that he would be freed through the prayers of the most holy man Barbatianus. He awoke suddenly and, carried by the feet of others, was brought to his cell during the night. When he had confidently made his way there, the confessor of Christ saw him, prayed to the Lord, and cast away that weakness [perhaps “hernia”; perhaps “sluggishness”]. He recovered his former speed in Christ Jesus our Lord.

After this miracle, let the healing of Theodore also be brought forward. Theodore himself was ill with blindness of the bodily eyes. Theodore suffered greatly from this and, finding no adequate care [variant: suffering from pain and finding no suitable care], developed dark scars [variant: darkness] over both eyes. When he had gone to physicians and learned that his condition was incurable, he ordered himself to be carried to Saint Barbatianus, declaring his one hope of faith: “For if I can be joined to him, I shall be saved.” But when he had hastened to his cell, he begged the most holy man [variant: on the road he declared his hope of faith, saying, “If I can be joined to him, I shall be saved. When he reached his cell, he begged] to let him remain for some days in that same cell.

The most holy Father did not refuse him, but consented that he should remain there. Thus the sick man, praying there [variant: the same man praying there], soon obtained the fruit of salvation. Saint Barbatianus, the confessor of Christ, then ordered him to go out to the fountain and bring water in a bucket [variant: have water brought to him]. He replied: “I am blind; I cannot see. How can I go to draw water?” Blessed Barbatianus answered him: “Go, nevertheless.”

When he had gone out, he still could not see where he was going. Meanwhile the most holy confessor of Christ fell prostrate in prayer and entreated the Lord on behalf of the man, asking that he recover the light of his eyes. But through the mercy of the one who had inspired him and taught him to come, he brought a bucket filled with water to the saint. After blessing it and giving it to him, he ordered him to wash his face. When he had washed, immediately things like fish-scales [the text is defective: “such things”] were removed from his eyes. He raised his voice loudly with tears, giving thanks to God, who had enlightened him through the prayer of the most holy man. This was proclaimed throughout the whole region of the city of Rome, to the honor of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

At the same time Galla Placidia Augusta and her son Valentinian Augustus proceeded to Ravenna, and they brought the most holy presbyter Barbatianus with them in great honor. The emperor Honorius, however, returned to Milan. When they had entered the city of Ravenna and the palace, she immediately granted that venerable man an ergastulum of her own, in which the servant of God constructed a building from its foundations [variant: and dedicated it in honor of blessed John the Baptist]. There he also established the rule of the monks, with whom he never ceased serving the Lord day and night through fasts and prayers.

After these events there was a man named Julianus, born of noble family. Hearing that the most holy man bestowed benefits upon all, he went with offerings to obtain from him the celebration of solemn Masses for himself, so that his son might be freed through the saint’s prayers. Scrofulous swellings had surrounded the boy’s throat; because of the great masses of flesh he could scarcely raise his neck, so much so that ulcers had already appeared externally and pus was giving off corruption.

When Barbatianus had completed the prayer of the Masses [variant: the solemn prayer of the Masses], Julianus fell at the feet of the most holy man and began to beg him with tears to provide healing for his son, since neither the medicine of any physician nor the advice of others had been able to free him. At this the blessed man raised his eyes to heaven, offered a prayer, and entered his cell. Taking in his hand a plaster mixed with wax [“plaster” here and below], together with a small piece of bread mixed with oil, he ordered the boy to be brought to him. After making the sign of the cross over the plaster, he placed it upon the very hard wounds. Immediately they burst, and before all who were standing there more than sixty-seven little worms fell out, as was reported by those who counted them. The boy’s father collected them all and, for many days, hung them up and displayed them to everyone as evidence of the event, which had occurred for the praise and glory of our Lord Jesus Christ through this most holy man.

At the same time, when by divine inspiration a church of blessed John the Evangelist, the disciple beloved of Christ, had been built by Augusta Galla Placidia, the Augusta fell into great anxiety with her son because no relics of the apostle’s body could be found. Then the most holy confessor of Christ Barbatianus was summoned, and they took counsel that, through vigils and prayers, they should prevail upon the Lord to reveal the relics of that holy disciple of Christ. This was done, and they did not cease spending the nights in prayer and entreating the Lord.

When the prayer had been completed, they withdrew for a little rest. As sleep, as it were, approached the most holy confessor of Christ, he, neither fully asleep nor completely awake, saw a man walking in splendid clothing, with an angelic face, carrying in his hand a thurible containing incense to be offered to the Lord. When he awoke, he thought that he had seen a vision. But when, with open eyes, he looked at the man clearly [variant: eagerly], he went silently to the place where the Augusta was sleeping and gently touched her to awaken her.

When she had awoken, the most holy man Barbatianus pointed out with his finger to the Augusta the man whom he had seen, for she too was fervent in spirit [variant: she herself was ardent in the Lord]. She rose from the place where she had been lying and ran toward him with great joy, falling at his feet and wishing to hold him. But he was suddenly taken from her sight and left in her hands the sandal that he had worn on his right foot.

When the Augusta saw this wonderful mystery, she raised her voice with great joy, praising the Lord Jesus Christ, who had worked such holy wonders through his apostle [the printed text has “Sanctus,” apparently anomalous]. Her son the Augustus was filled with immense joy, as were all who heard of it and who lived in that God-beloved city of Ravenna [the phrase “of the mystery” is defective]. After this sacramental mystery, the holy church itself was consecrated to the praise of our Lord Jesus Christ, in honor of the most blessed John the Evangelist. The most holy Barbatianus was thereafter revered by all, and the Augusta herself recounted to everyone the miracle and all that had been done through the confessor of Christ. The venerable man then returned to his cell.

Not long afterward, while the servant of God was staying in his monastery, there was a very noble woman in the city of Ravenna named Theodora. She suffered a severe illness and fell into great weakness [variant: through which she came into great debility], having a flow of blood. Physicians and all others who attempted cures provided her no help; rather, everything proved harmful to her, so that she could scarcely raise herself or walk.

When she heard of the miracles of the most holy man Barbatianus, and that many had been healed through him, she placed her hope and confidence in the Lord and said within herself: “What shall I do? I believe in almighty God that, if I go to him, I shall be saved.” She therefore called her relatives so that they might carry her to the door of the cell of the monastery of blessed Barbatianus.

When she had gone there, the blessed man Barbatianus was informed of the arrival of the sick woman. Rising from prayer, he went to the monastery gate with the other servants of that venerable place. When he saw her, he offered a prayer and said to the woman:

“Our Lord Jesus Christ, who granted health to the woman Veronica and freed her from the flow of blood, in his name and with confidence I tell you: rise and go to your home.”

[Editorial note: This is the oldest reference to Veronica as a matron that I have seen. BACCH.]

When these words had immediately resounded in her ears, she was made well and went home completely healthy, as though she had never possessed any affliction [variant: blemish]. She blessed the Lord, who had worked such wonders through the most holy man.

When the people heard this, they held the servant of God in great admiration. From that day onward Theodora continually came with offerings, asking that the solemn rites of Mass be celebrated for her and seeking the blessing of the most holy man. While she remained for a long time, diligently fulfilling this worthy duty, her husband Ursicius, a violent and wicked man, was stirred by a diabolical spirit and became jealous of his wife.

When Barbatianus went in the morning hours to the church [of blessed John the Baptist], distributing to the poor the alms he had received from the Augusta, and approached a point not far from the bridge over the river, Ursicius secretly took his position beside the wall of a house, behind a stone column, intending to strike the holy man as he passed with his sword drawn.

He raised his arm but was unable either to strike or to lower it. His arm dried up, his hand remained rigid, and his mind was changed. The blessed man passed by, completing what he had begun.

At first light the people came and found that obstinate man standing as though mute, holding his rigid arm and the sword in his hand. Everyone was amazed, and no one knew why this had happened to him. When the third hour of the day had already passed and the servant of Christ God was returning to the church, he learned of what had happened. Raising his tearful eyes toward heaven, he groaned and prayed. Immediately Ursicius returned to himself and his tongue was released. He at once fell at the feet of the most holy man Barbatianus, asking that this sin be forgiven him.

The holy man gave him his blessing and went to his cell. Ursicius himself made known to the people everything concerning the evil he had committed, and the whole people gave praise to God, who had worked such wonders in his servant. News of this therefore reached the palace and was reported to Galla Placidia Augusta and her son Valentinian Augustus, who likewise gave thanks to God.

From that same day onward Barbatianus did not leave the cell of his monastery, but remained in that holy monastery and never ceased giving thanks to the Lord through vigils and prayers. Many who came to him secretly received benefits and the grace of healing. At that time, desiring to have his blessing, the Augusta daily partook of the blessing through the sanctification of that man.

While the church of blessed Stephen, the first martyr, was being built by the Augusta in the fortifications outside the walls of the city of Ariminum, and she herself was staying there with her son the Augustus to complete it, the most holy man and confessor of Christ awoke during the night and, while keeping vigil, fell ill. When the end of his life was approaching [variant: when he saw that his end was approaching] by the command of the Lord God almighty, the most holy Father, Bishop Librificus Peter of Ravenna, was informed—he himself being in his vigils within the holy church—that the same most holy confessor of Christ Barbatianus had departed [variant: was departing] to the Lord.

He immediately sent a messenger to the Augusta to announce the event. The Augusta herself and her son hurried there as quickly as possible and entered the cell in which the servant of God and confessor of Christ lay. When the holy man saw them, he offered a prayer and blessing for them and for all who believed in the Lord. Then, as best he could, as though belching three times, he departed to the Lord.

The most holy Father Peter the bishop washed his body and carefully seasoned it with priceless spices, as had been the ancient custom for the burial of the saints, together with Galla Placidia Augusta and her son Valentinian Augustus. They buried him in the best place, in a new monument that she had recently ordered to be magnificently carved in marble, beside the altar of the most blessed John the Baptist.

They buried him on the second day before the Kalends of January. Many noble and humble people came there, and many sick persons obtained healing through his sacred prayers. The servant of God Galla Placidia Augusta and her son the Augustus went out [variant: returned] to the work of constructing the holy church, which they knew they would complete [variant: had vowed to complete] for the Lord, to the praise of our Lord Jesus Christ, who reigns with God the Father in heaven in the unity of the Holy Spirit, now and always and throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## Note

The memory of the consecration of the church of Saint John the Evangelist, which is narrated in this Life of Saint Barbatianus, is famous among the people of Ravenna. The history of the event still exists represented in marble relief above the principal door of the façade of that same basilica.

I wish to praise here, with every expression of honor and respect, the Reverend Father Thomasius, on account of his piety and especially his sacred learning, as well as the signs of affection that he has shown toward me. He most courteously gave me a drawing of that work, which I have been pleased to append here, engraved on copper in two plates. Moreover, from the two impressions of the other plate that were sent to the same Reverend Father at Ravenna, I have chosen to present here the more accurate one.

# Example of the Ravennate Documents Concerning the Sicilian Estates

## Notice concerning the following documents

The very ancient monument transcribed below belongs to these same times, and I wish to preface it with a few remarks.

I prepared this copy from an original written on Egyptian papyrus. The distinguished and illustrious gentleman Joannes Gallianus de Coccapanis, secretary of the Most Serene Duke of Modena, most courteously arranged for me to see it; Count Andreas Sora produced it from the treasures of the noble Sanbonifacian family.

The papyrus on which the document is written has the structure described by Allatius in *Animadversiones*, no. 66, and belongs to the type that, according to Pliny, was called amphitheatrical, *Natural History*, book XIII, chapter 12.

Since the papyrus is mutilated and corroded in many places, I could scarcely grasp the sense of the documents. I recognized that they concern estates and their revenues, customarily administered in Sicily through a tribune and various lessees, whose management was entrusted to a certain Sisinnius after the departure of the tribune Pyrrus. The first letter appears to have been written to Sisinnius himself. The second was addressed to the people living on those estates. The third was addressed to Eleutherion and Zosimus, the principal lessees; all of them are ordered to obey Sisinnius, and instructions are given for sending the revenues to Ravenna.

The name of the writer prefixed to the third document is mutilated. From the history of Ravenna we know of a famous Lauricius in the age of the Emperor Theodosius, whom our Agnellus calls the emperor’s master of the household. Could he perhaps be the man who wrote these documents? The office of tribune, placed in charge of the revenues of Sicily, seems to suggest that an imperial matter is being treated here. Yet from elsewhere it is known that at this time the church of Ravenna possessed extensive estates in Sicily, which were administered through a rector.

The consular notices, in which the names of the debtors and the accounts are recorded, belong to the years of the common era 443 and 444. These, therefore, are the oldest documents on Egyptian papyrus that have survived and that the most learned investigators of such matters have observed to the present day; among them, see Mabillon, *De Re Diplomatica*, book I, chapter 8.

The form of the letters is the same as that of the so-called will of Julius Caesar; concerning it, see the work cited above, pages 344 and 460.

While I was writing this, the learned Mabillon published these same documents in an appendix to his excellent work *De Re Diplomatica*. I therefore considered omitting them. But after comparing my original—which I myself transcribed from a copy—with Mabillon’s printed version, I saw that several things were lacking in Mabillon’s text. Having obtained from that most courteous man, by letter, permission to reprint them, I decided that it was worthwhile to give both versions here.
