## FREDERICUS, Archbishop LXII

[Col. 0794C]

Fredericus LXII. In the year in which he died, King Henry, the greatest king, first came to Italy.

## ARNALDUS, Archbishop LXIII

Arnaldus LXIII, bishop.

## ERIBERTUS, Archbishop LXIV

Eribertus LXIV, bishop.

## GEBEARDUS, Archbishop LXV

Gebeardus LXV. His election was presented to the emperor Conrad in the year of the Lord 1026 and was subscribed by the suffragans, clergy, and people of Ravenna. This man [Col. 0794D] built the church of blessed Andrew the Apostle in Ravenna, as is recorded in other Chronicles, and did many other good works.

The aforementioned Gebeardus, archbishop of Ravenna, died in the year of the Lord 1044. He lies in the monastery of Saint Mary of Pomposa, in the Old Po, in the diocese of Comacchio, in the chapter of the brothers, beneath a marble stone with mosaic work, on which these verses are inscribed:

> Here lies the body of the great bishop Gebeard,  
> through whom the holy house and this place grew.  
> He gave very many things, which he bequeathed under this condition:  
> what Judas suffers, let the robber himself suffer as punishment.  
> Pour forth prayers to Christ, reader; say, “Have mercy.”

He died in the year of the Lord 1044. Note that he greatly enlarged the aforesaid monastery of Pomposa, as is recorded in its Chronicles.

## HIMFRIDUS, Archbishop LXVI

[Col. 0795A]

Himfridus LXVI, bishop.

## HENRICUS, Archbishop LXVII

Henricus LXVII, bishop.

## GIBERTUS, Archbishop LXVIII

Gibertus [Note: [Col. 0795D] The barbarous author of the Chronicle is mistaken, confusing Gibertus with Gerbertus and following vulgar and unworthy rumors about Sylvester II. The reputation of that learned and pious pontiff has been securely defended by the most eminent Baronius, by Ciacconius, and most recently by the most reverend Father and Abbot Andrea Rainerius in his learned historical panegyric of Saint Anselm; it does not require me to add more here. BACCH.] LXVIII.

He was first archbishop of Rheims, then of Ravenna, and afterward was named pope Sylvester II. He paid homage to the devil and met a bad end, as you find in full in the Martinian Chronicle [in the chapter on Sylvester II].

After this, the following is properly added in the form of a note—not that he was not the man of whom mention was made. Guibertus of Parma, formerly chancellor of the emperor in the Italian kingdom, was elected in that Church after the death of the archbishop of Ravenna through the [influence] of the empress. Later, through the insistence of many, he obtained consecration from Pope Alexander, although the pope was unwilling. After that pontiff had laid the hand of consecration upon him, he is said, filled with the prophetic spirit, to have spoken as follows:

> “I am already being offered up, and the time of my release is at hand. But you will henceforth experience the whole [bitter] vengeance of this most holy Church.”

## NOTE
[Col. 0795]

At this point Rubeus inserts Richard, Otho, and Jeremiah. The first of these is said to have been lawfully consecrated by Gregory VII; he is called Richard by conjecture, because in certain letters of Pope Gregory he is indicated by the capital letter R. For this reason Ughellus calls him Richard. Otho and Jeremiah are believed to have been intruders. In place of Jeremiah, Rubeus substitutes Walter; Ughellus, however, inserts Philip as archbishop on the authority of a certain charter. He says that it is “no slight argument” that Philip sat beside Queen Matilda, “since it is scarcely credible that a woman most devoted to the Apostolic See would have wished to admit a schismatic, chosen in violation of canonical procedure, into her company. But how do we know that this Matilda was so devoted to the Apostolic See? Take care that similarity of names does not deceive you. The charter is said to have been issued in the year 1118. But Matilda, daughter of Boniface, who was most devoted to the Apostolic See, had died in the preceding year, 1115. Since, then, he too has been omitted by the author of this Chronicle, I readily believe that he should be numbered among the intruders. This is clearly confirmed by the letters of Gelasius to Walter, reported by Rubeus.”

## OF WALTER, ARCHBISHOP LXIX

[Col. 0795D]

Walter LXIX. A religious and most eloquent man, who governed the Church of Ravenna for twenty-four years, six months, and eight days. He died on the Ides of February in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1144.

## OF MOSES, ARCHBISHOP LXX

Moses LXX. A native of Vercelli, a very well-educated man and a good rector of the Church, who governed the Church of Ravenna for ten years, three months, and twenty-four days. He died on the seventh day before the Kalends of November, a Wednesday, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1154, during the pontificate of Pope Anastasius IV, in the second year of King Frederick, in the third month, when he first came to Italy.

[Note: [Col. 0796D] Marginal note: “Concerning this Moses, archbishop, I find the following in other chronicles. Around the year of the Lord 1184, Pope Lucius III, a Tuscan by nation, confirmed Moses of Vercelli as archbishop of Ravenna; his body rests in the Ursian Church at Ravenna.” BACCH.]

No one among our pontiffs was more learned than he. He was instructed in both divine and human laws and adorned with many other sciences. He contributed very many benefits to this Church. He spent seven hundred pounds redeeming the possessions of the Church of Ravenna from pledge. Concerning this archbishop I found the following in an old document:

“In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1144, in the time of Pope Lucius II [Lucius III] and King Conrad, in the seventh indiction, Moses, the elected archbishop of the city of Ravenna, entered on the first day of June, which was then a Thursday. He was received by everyone with the greatest honor. In the following month he was consecrated in the city of Faenza [Ferentina] by the aforesaid apostolic, on the feast day of Saints Processus and Martinianus, whose feast then fell on a Sunday.”

Finally, this was recorded in a certain chest of the Church of Ravenna. Concerning this archbishop I find the following, which I set down here.

### Letters of Pope Eugenius to the elected bishop of Piacenza

Eugenius, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son John, elected bishop of Piacenza: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It has not escaped our knowledge, nor do we believe that it has escaped your memory, that both by our letters to the Church of Piacenza and orally, in your presence, we instructed you to appear before us at the most recent feast of Saint Luke, to answer our venerable brother Moses, archbishop of Ravenna, and to carry out whatever justice should dictate, and to make preparations . . . [having made them]. But because you evaded coming into our presence at the appointed time or sending a letter of response that might offer any reasonable explanation, after carefully examining the privileges and writings of our predecessors and our own, and after consulting with our brothers, we have judged that you and your successors elected bishops of Piacenza shall receive consecration without objection from the archbishop of Ravenna as your proper metropolitan, and shall offer him obedience and reverence without troublesome resistance.

Therefore, by these present writings [issued by us], we command and enjoin that, by the octave of Epiphany, you go to our aforesaid brother, the archbishop of Ravenna, and receive consecration from him as your proper metropolitan. If you do not do so, from this moment we suspend you from the administration of the Church of Piacenza.

Given at Pisa, on the fifth day before the Ides of November.

### Another letter of the same Eugenius to the clergy and people of Piacenza

[Note: [Col. 0796D] The Church of Piacenza is subject to the Church of Ravenna.]

Eugenius, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the clergy and people of Piacenza: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Just as the obedient, through obedience, preserves the guardianship of the virtues, so the disobedient, through disobedience, introduces an accumulation of sins. To resist is like the sin of divination, and to refuse to obey is like the crime of idolatry. Therefore, by these present writings [issued by us], we command and enjoin that you offer obedience and reverence to our venerable brother, the archbishop of Ravenna, as your metropolitan, lest a complaint against you, aroused by anger, reach our ears and we be compelled to punish your disobedience more severely.

Given at Pisa, on the fifth day before the Ides of November.

## OF ANSELM, ARCHBISHOP LXXI

[Col. 0798]

[Col. 0797B]

Anselm LXXI, bishop of Hamelburg. He succeeded Moses and received the pallium on the day when Frederick was crowned by Adrian IV in the Church of Saint Peter. He died at the beginning of the siege of Milan, on a Monday—namely, the second day after the feast of Saint Lawrence—in the year of the Lord 1227.

## OF GUIDO, ARCHBISHOP LXXII

Guido LXXII. A prelate.

## OF GERARD, ARCHBISHOP LXXIII

Gerard LXXIII. In his time the body of the most blessed martyr of Christ, Apollinaris, was discovered by Cardinal Hildebrand, the apostolic legate, as we have it in the account of the translation of Blessed Apollinaris.

## OF WILLIAM, ARCHBISHOP LXXIV

[Col. 0797C]

William LXXIV.

[Note: [Col. 0797D] He is omitted by Rubeus and Ughellus. BACCH.]

## OF GUIDOTUS, ARCHBISHOP LXXV

Guidotus LXXV.

[Note: [Col. 0797D] Rubeus calls him Gerard, while Ughellus calls him Uvido; concerning him there is more in Saint Antoninus and Vincent of Beauvais. [Col. 0798D] The same.]

## OF WILLIAM [GUGELMO], ARCHBISHOP LXXVI

William LXXVI.

## OF ALBRETUS [ALBERTUS], ARCHBISHOP LXXVII

Albretus [Albertus] LXXVII.

## OF GILES, ARCHBISHOP LXXVIII

Giles LXXVIII.

## OF UBALD, ARCHBISHOP LXXIX

[Col. 0797D]

Ubald LXXIX.

[Note: [Col. 0798D] After him Rubeus and Ughellus mention Archbishop Picininus. The same.]

## OF SIMEON, ARCHBISHOP LXXX

Simeon LXXX. He died around the year of the Lord 1227.

## OF THEODORIC, ARCHBISHOP LXXXI

Theodoric LXXXI. A man handsome in body and soul, he lived in the time of the Emperor Frederick II. He received the investiture of the archbishopric from the Emperor Frederick II. He died in the year of the Lord 1230, on the fifth lunar day, at the end of December, at Forlì. His body was brought to Ravenna and buried beside the great doors of the church, in the chest in which Archbishop Moses, of blessed memory, had been buried, in the year of the Lord 1248, on the eighth day, at the beginning of June.

Lord Archbishop Theodoric returned to Ravenna [the reading is *Ravennae*; *Ravennam*], with all the citizens of Ravenna who were *exteri sui* [*extrinseci*], and Ravenna returned to allegiance to the Church.

## OF PHILIP, ARCHBISHOP LXXXII

Philip LXXXII. Elected to the Church of Ferrara. A vigorous man, adorned with varied wisdom. Because of that vigor, he often served as legate for the Roman Church. In that office, among his other achievements, he captured Padua with the army he commanded from the hands of Ezzelino da Romano, the treacherous tyrant in the Trevisan March.

Around the year of the Lord 1256, this archbishop, while serving as legate at Brescia, was captured and delivered to Ezzelino, who held him in prison. He arranged for the *arca* [*arcam*], the chest of the saints that is in the Ursian Church, to be transported. He died around the year of the Lord 1270. He belonged to the family of the Fontana, citizens of Ferrara.

## OF BONIFACE, ARCHBISHOP LXXXIII

Boniface LXXXIII, of the Order of Preachers, an enlarger of the Church’s possessions and very diligent, a native of Lavagna, a handsome orator. By Pope Gregory X, of blessed memory, he was sent as nuncio to King Philip IX of France; afterward, by the same pope, he was legate of this Church at the Council of Lyons.

[Provision was made for this Church. He was also legate in France.] He was in France, in Gascony, together with the archbishop of Monreale—who later became archbishop of Capua and finally patriarch of Aquileia—to procure the release of the illustrious Charles, prince of Taranto, later king of Jerusalem and Sicily, who was being held prisoner by the king of Aragon.

He greatly increased the Church’s temporal goods. He occupied the archiepiscopal see for twenty-two years, or approximately that long. He died on the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord at Oriolo in 1295 [on 25 December]. He was carried by men on a litter, wearing the habit of the Order of Preachers, almost as far as Ravenna, and was buried in the Ursian Church beside the altar of Blessed Mary Magdalene. He had caused that altar to be founded in a very beautiful mausoleum, which, while he was alive, he had brought from Saint Lawrence outside the walls of Ravenna.

This Archbishop Boniface held a council at Ravenna concerning the affairs of the city of Acre, which had been captured by the Saracens and is called Accon.

## OF OPIZO, ARCHBISHOP LXXXIV

Opizo LXXXIV, of Parma, from the lineage of Saint Vitalis. Previously he had been bishop of Parma; he was a good courtier and generous, broad-bodied and fat. His father was a knight, while his mother was Genoese by birth and the sister of Pope Innocent IV, of blessed memory.

He was learned in various sciences and experienced in practical affairs. He was very magnanimous and a great distributor of temporal goods; he was compassionate toward the poor. First he was a canon of the Church of Parma, and afterward he was elected to govern the Church of Tripoli for five years. Through his aforementioned uncle, Innocent IV, he was transferred to the Church of Parma, where he governed for forty-four years with great secular power and reputation. Finally, after forty-four years, Pope Boniface VIII transferred him to the see of Ravenna in the year of the Lord 1296.

Up to this point this Chronicle preserves a record of these archbishops—namely, up to Archbishop Opizo of Saint Vitalis, who lived around the year 1286 [1296], as appears at the beginning of this work.

## CONTINUATION BY PAUL SCORDILLA

[Col. 0799]

### The rest concerning Opizo

While he was in that see—namely, the see of Ravenna—and was worn out by old age and burdened by debts, especially those incurred through the service he had rendered to the Roman Church, he gained no advantage from it. Indeed, he handed over silver to Azzo, Marquis of Este, which afterward he was completely unable to recover. For this he was severely reproached by the Roman See, and on that account he was summoned to the Roman Curia. Harassed by various tribulations and weighed down by illnesses, he ended his life in extreme poverty in the old city in the year of the Lord 1300, in the third indiction, on 12 September, and was buried in the church of the Friars Minor beside the high altar.

[Note: [Col. 0799D] Others give 1303, on the feast of Saint Agnes, in the month of January. BACCH.]

## OF RAYNALD, ARCHBISHOP LXXXV

Raynald LXXXV, of Milan, from the family of Corrigio [Others: Concoregio; BACCH.]. Previously he had been bishop of Vicenza, a man of holy and upright life who performed many miracles.

Around the year of the Lord 1314, in the month of August, during the time of Lord Archbishop Raynald, the entire nave of the Ursian Church was newly constructed. In his time a whale was found on the shore near Ravenna.

He died in the year of the Lord 1321, on 18 August. He was buried in the major church of Ravenna, in a chest beside the altar of Saint Mary in the middle of the church.

## OF RAYNALD, ARCHBISHOP LXXXVI

Raynald LXXXVI, of Polenta. He was killed by his kinsman Ostasius.

## OF AIMERIC, ARCHBISHOP LXXXVII

Aimeric LXXXVII, from the castle of Luci, chaplain of the lord pope. He was count of Romandiola; he was transferred to the bishopric of Chartres and subsequently became a cardinal of the Holy Roman Church.

## OF GUIDO, ARCHBISHOP LXXXVIII

[Col. 0800A]

Guido of Tripoli of Reggio. A learned man who lived only a short time. He was buried at Bologna in the church of the Friars Minor, before the choir screen, in the year of the Lord 1333, in the month of September.

## OF FRANCIS, ARCHBISHOP LXXXIX

Francis LXXXIX, of Venice, from the family of Ca’ Michele, later transferred to the archbishopric of Candia on the island of Crete.

## OF NICHOLAS, ARCHBISHOP XC

Nicholas XC, of Canale of Pergamum, later transferred to the archbishopric of Patras.

## OF FORTUNATUS, ARCHBISHOP XCI

[Col. 0800B]

Fortunatus XCI, of the Order of Friars Minor, a native of Cahors. He held the archiepiscopal see for nearly seven years and four months; afterward he became patriarch of the Church of Grado and administrator of Ravenna, and subsequently a cardinal of the Holy Roman Church.

## OF PETROCINUS, ARCHBISHOP XCII

Petrocinus XCII, of Ferrara, a great and profound doctor, a great orator and good counselor, a man of great justice and truth.

He was a monk in the monastery of Saint Bartholomew near Ferrara, born of a rather humble family. Later he became abbot of Saint Cyprian of Torcello near Venice; afterward he was appointed bishop of Torcello, and then elected and consecrated archbishop of Ravenna in the time of Urban V.

As I heard, he had certain human bones taken from a stone chest near the bell tower of the Church of Saint John the Baptist, at the entrance to the church on the left hand. These bones were popularly believed to be the relics of saints. Since no inscription had been found [was found] in the aforesaid chest, he had a certain companion of his, named John de Porcellinis, who had died, placed inside it.

After this, every night great noises and cries were heard in that church. It is said that an image of the devil, as it is painted by a certain nun named Virginula, who often visited churches, was seen above that chest on many different occasions. Consequently, the body of the aforesaid John and his bones had necessarily to be removed from there, and the earlier bones were placed in the chest again, just as they had been at first.

This Petrocinus reformed the constitutions of the cardinal and cantor chapters, although those reforms later fell into contempt and are not observed at all. He also established four benefices in the Ursian Church, called mansionaries; their holders sing Mass on non-festal days in alternate weeks. This was a very excellent institution.

For the Roman Church he was rector in Romandiola, an office popularly called the countship of Romandiola. He held that rectorship for a long time. When he aspired to the dignity of cardinal, the members of the Roman Curia whom he trusted—although, in courtly fashion, they were not a little jealous of him—advised him to resign the rectorship of Romandiola, so that the pope might more easily promote him to the cardinalate. He did so.

When the supreme pontiff had decided to make Lord Petrocinus a cardinal, his rivals finally appeared, saying: “How will he be capable of governing in the Roman Church, when he has resigned the rectorship of Romandiola, judging himself incapable?” When the pope heard this, he postponed the matter and did not promote him to the cardinalate.

When Petrocinus wished to see the body of the prophet Elisha, which rests in the monastery of Saint Lawrence in Caesarea, he had the chest of that Elisha opened, together with certain prudent clerics and laymen, masons, and bricklayers. What he saw I did not hear clearly, except that I learned from the jurist Peter de Zabaronibus that Petrocinus saw the body of Elisha clothed in a white stole, holding a scepter in his hand, with his head adorned by a round tiara and his face bearded with a rather long, very white beard.

After this opening of the tomb, Archbishop Petrocinus and the others who had assisted him did not live long, except for one mason named Remesinus, whom I saw and employed in my works. I regret that, having forgotten, I did not question him about the body of the blessed Elisha and the other matters.

Petrocinus held the see for seven years, five months, and twenty-two days. He was buried in the Ursian Church in a large and artistically carved chest, where the body of the excellent Archbishop Boniface of Lavagna rests; it stands beside the altar of the blessed martyr Apollinaris.

## OF PILEUS, ARCHBISHOP LXXXXIII

Pileus LXXXXIII, noble by birth, from the Forum of Julius, descended from the noble family of Prata and originating from the castle of Prata. He was sufficiently learned in grammar, but had no education at all in the other liberal arts or in canon or civil law. He was a deceitful man, [and full of every kind of trickery, a great spender and] a great squanderer.

Previously he had been bishop of the Church of Padua; afterward he was transferred to the holy Church of Ravenna, and finally Pope Gregory XI made him a cardinal in the Roman Church.

At the request of Jacopo de Alpinis of Parma, archdeacon of the Church of Ravenna, and others, he removed the ancient office of our Church of Ravenna, although no cleric at least publicly opposed him, and was the first to introduce the office of the Roman Curia, which we still use today.

That archdeacon Jacopo was an excellent administrator of divine affairs in the aforesaid Church. The gout by which he was oppressed did not hinder him at all, however severe it was [had been] in his youth. Yet, when burdened by old age, with the aforesaid archbishop abandoning him [or: he abandoning the aforesaid archbishop], he served as that archbishop’s vicar and administrator of his affairs in the Ursian Church. He resided there in the district of Gazzi, beside the square of the church popularly called the Cattle Market.

At last he ended his life in the year of the Nativity of the Lord 1412, when there was also a severe plague everywhere. He was buried peacefully in front of the Ursian Church, in the place called *le Laste*, in a stone chest.

At first Pileus was a household retainer and close associate of Lord Guido, formerly Lord Bernardino da Polenta, lord of Ravenna and general vicar for the Roman Church in that city and its district. Later, claiming rights in the name of the Church of Ravenna and of the archiepiscopal dignity in that city, he turned their former friendship into enmity.

When he came from the castle of Luci and wished to enter the city of Ravenna, he was not permitted to enter by the guards at the Adriana Gate. He was told to wait until permission had been obtained from Lord Guido. The archbishop was astonished at these words, since previously he had entered the city without permission. Disdaining the treatment, he turned his horses around and returned to Luci. He never again resided with his bride, the Ursian Church, although he had visited it briefly for the consolation of residence.

When he was in need of money, he sent messengers to Lord Guido to ask him to lend him one thousand ducats, offering the castle of Luci as security. When Guido kept the archbishop’s messengers waiting for a long time with verbal evasions, Pileus sent messengers concerning the same business to Lord Nicholas, Marquis of Este, a man most illustrious in wisdom, virtues, and power.

When the aforementioned marquis heard this, he quickly lent him the money and accepted the castle of Luci as a pledge. The Church of Ravenna never recovered it afterward; it remained in the possession of the marquises until the time of Nicholas the Younger, Marquis of Este, whose governors carelessly lost it, as will be related below in the History of Archbishop Cosmas.

The same archbishop made a similar alienation of the castle of Ariolo to Sinibaldus, a knight of the Ordelaffi family and lord of the city of Forlì. He also committed many other acts of dishonest alienation concerning the castles of the Church of Ravenna. There is no doubt that, in the strict judgment of the Judge, his soul was punished for these deeds.

After the death of Pope Gregory XI, Pileus, a cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Praxedes, conspired with other cardinals against Pope Urban VI. Urban captured seven of them and, taking them with him in chains, killed them at Genoa under the enormous weight of iron and stones in a certain stable. He ordered other archbishops and prelates who were aware of the conspiracy to be slaughtered and killed by various kinds of punishment. He would have done the same to Pileus and the other cardinals, had he been able to capture them.

Pileus, however, abandoned the Church of Ravenna in desolation and fled with the other cardinals of the Roman Church to Anagni, carrying away with him many books and treasures belonging to that Church. Finally, when they arrived at the city of Fondi, there, on the advice and urging of Nicholas of Naples—a most infamous man, a famous doctor of both laws and consistorial advocate—they elected Robert, cardinal-priest of the Twelve Apostles, of Geneva, as antipope. Together with the elected man, they all moved to the city of Avignon.

For this reason Urban deprived Pileus and the other cardinals of their cardinalitial dignity and all their benefices, restoring only one: Bartholomew de Mezzavachis of Bologna, Cardinal of Rieti. Even so, in the sight of everyone, he publicly dishonored him by placing him shamefully at the last seat during sessions, behind even the most insignificant persons. Bartholomew always bore this peacefully, uttering no evil word, and nothing profane was ever heard from his mouth.

The aforesaid schism in the Church of God lasted for thirty-three years and more, and still continues.

As I have heard, the cause of so great a schism was that Urban, when he had been conditionally elected on the understanding that he would resign, began, after being incited by the cardinals, to treat them badly. He deprived some of their benefices and imposed restrictions on others concerning their horses and household servants. Therefore the indignant cardinals began to plot Urban’s death, and this led to their deprivation and the election of the antipope mentioned above.

So that the truth may nevertheless not be lacking for readers, in the time of Gregory XI, who was residing at Avignon, the Roman Church was in turmoil throughout the regions of Italy and was losing all its cities and castles. Gregory came to Rome, desiring to restore everything, and believing that he would end his days there, died there.

After his death, the Roman people, taking up arms and unwilling that the papal dignity should pass any longer into French hands, cried out for an Italian pope, and ran to the palace of Saint Peter. The cardinals elected as pope a cardinal of Saint Peter, who, remaining in the papal see for three days, never wished to accept the office.

When the Roman people continued to insist, the cardinals elected Urban—then called Bartholomew of Prignano, archbishop of Bari and chancellor of the Roman Church—as pope, under the aforesaid condition that he should resign once the people’s fury had ceased. They accepted and enthroned him, and afterward, as though he were pope, they entreated him and offered him every reverence.

[lacuna]

[Note: [Col. 0803C] The following is restored from the Este manuscript:

“Urban, however, if it is permissible to tell the truth, after obtaining the papacy turned to folly and inflicted many insults upon Queen Joanna of Apulia, refusing assent to any of the queen’s petitions. He treated the cardinals and all the members of the Curia badly. All these things were the driving causes of the horrible schism. I did not wish to pass over some of them briefly, but shall relate them.

He had the aforesaid cardinal of Saint Peter served at dinner with liver and lung seasoned with fennel, as a gift, saying that because the cardinal did not see well, the pope was assigning him fennel, an herb excellent for sight. The cardinal replied: ‘I do not see well; he speaks the truth. Yet I saw worse, because I did not hold the papacy. Had I done so, Urban would not be pope.’

To the Cardinal of the Twelve Apostles, the man of Geneva, he served a chicken with its wings cut off, saying: ‘We shall cut off the wings of him and his associates.’ The cardinal replied: ‘I and my associates have wings, and we shall fly not only through this city but throughout the whole world, if necessary.’

As for Nicholas of Naples, who had been seated at table above Otto of Brunswick, the husband of the aforesaid Joanna, Queen of Apulia, Urban publicly rebuked him, saying: ‘Lord Nicholas de Spinellis, do you not see that Lord Otto, the queen of Apulia’s husband and your lord, is sitting below you? Rise, in an evil hour.’ He did the same thing to Nicholas three times concerning other noblemen.

Nicholas did not eat a bite at that dinner. Instead, he thought and turned over in the secrets of his angry mind how he might take revenge on Urban—and he did so. For he advised the cardinals to elect another pope, which they did, as I said above.

But woe to you, Nicholas! Why did you tear apart God’s seamless tunic? You will not escape punishment: undoubtedly your soul will finally be tortured in the depths of hell, and at the very end below, if such a thing may be said.

When Brother Thomas of Ghifono, minister general of the Order of Friars Minor, had been designated by the aforementioned Queen Joanna as her ambassador to Urban, and had come with great pomp, with many attendants and knights, Urban undertook another dishonorable act.

He asked Brother Thomas, pretending not to know: ‘Who are you?’ And he replied: ‘Most blessed Father, I am Brother Thomas of Ghifono, minister general of the Friars Minor, ambassador of your daughter Joanna, Queen of Apulia.’

Urban said to him: ‘It is not fitting for the cord of Saint Francis to pass with such pomp. By . . . by—’ Urban cried publicly, ‘I shall humble you. What do you seek?’

The friar then prudently presented the queen, his lady’s, embassy, asking that the pope deign to crown Lord Otto, the queen’s husband, king of Apulia.

The pope replied: ‘What does that woman want, devil? I do not wish it, nor shall she have what she asks.’ Let us return, and so forth.

This Paul Scordilla, who professes to have written these things while the schism was still in force, was excessively hostile to Pope Urban—perhaps because his own archbishop, Pileus, had been deprived of the priesthood and cardinalitial dignity, or because his mind leaned toward the schismatics. He mixes into his account many things that perhaps arose from partisan invention and that must be read with caution.”]

[Col. 0804A]

Let us return to our Pileus. Pileus remained for a long time with Robert, who called himself Clement VII. Finally, after the death of Pope Urban, Robert sent him as legate to Rome to make an acquisition for the Church against Boniface, who had succeeded Urban.

Pileus spent large sums of money in his usual manner, and finally, after many evil deeds had been carried out by him and his supporters, he reached an agreement with Pope Boniface IX, Urban’s successor. Boniface restored him to the honor of the cardinalate and again made him cardinal-priest of Saint Praxedes—he is now called bishop of Tusculum.

At last, already weakened by old age, he died. I saw his tomb in Rome, in the Church of Saint Mary the New, together with two other cardinals buried there. I am now told that his bones were transferred to the Church of Padua and that his body was honorably buried there.

## OF COSMAS, ARCHBISHOP XCIV
Cosmas XCIV, a native of Sulmona, born of a lowly family, from the lineage of the Meliorati, of fairly handsome appearance, bald at the forehead, cheerful in countenance, a doctor of canon law and skilled in civil jurisprudence, although he had not held a magistracy, learned through experience in worldly affairs, and a man of good counsel.

At the time when he was studying at Bologna in the lower grades, he lived in the period of Giovanni da Legnano, the most renowned doctor of both laws and of the seven liberal arts. When Giovanni da Legnano was sent as envoy to Pope Urban VI on behalf of the community of Bologna, Cosmas traveled with him to the Roman Curia. Giovanni da Legnano warmly commended him to the aforesaid supreme pontiff. When Urban heard this, he kept Cosmas with him and, as time passed, appointed him apostolic collector in England. When the persecution of the schism against Urban intensified—of which I spoke above in the history of the preceding pontiff—Cosmas very frequently visited the pope by letters [and with money]. Urban, considering this most pleasing, reflected within himself on how he might honor Cosmas with some reward.

When our holy mother, the Church of Ravenna, which is called Hagia Anastasis (“Holy Resurrection”), became vacant because of the deprivation of the aforementioned Pileus, he promoted Cosmas to its governance. Cosmas could not take possession of it here at Ravenna, because Guido da Polenta, a knight and lord of the city of Ravenna, adhered to the aforementioned schismatic Robert and was allied with a certain Louis, duke of Anjou, who had come with forty-five thousand armed men in Pileus’s time in order to make himself king of Apulia.

Nevertheless, Louis, while passing through the territory of Ravenna at the request of the queen of Apulia, brought the aforesaid Guido back to his way of thinking. Because of this, a very great quarrel arose between Galeotto Malatesta, knight and lord of Rimini, and Lord Guido. Under the pretext of the Roman Church and in the name of Pope Urban, he secretly and forcibly took from Guido the city of Cervia, the castle of Polenta, and Cuglianello, which were governed under Guido’s jurisdiction and authority, and inflicted much harm upon this city of Ravenna.

While he was planning to invade the city of Ravenna by means of ladders at night, the entire population lay stricken by violent attacks of fever. Nevertheless, many of Galeotto’s subjects climbed the city walls and entered the city. When Lord Guido da Polenta heard this, he sent his firstborn son Bernardinus to defend the city. But Bernardinus, terrified by no small fear, fled and announced to his father that the enemy had entered the city.

Guido, however, enraged, beat his son with a stick and attacked the enemy with as many men as he could gather; he drove them from the city. The repulse was bravely pressed by Leonardus of Fossola, provost, and Laurentius of Luderano, cardinal of this Church, in the tower of the Priests.

At last, five of the enemy were captured. Placed under examination and asked why they had not fulfilled their purpose, they replied:

“We heard that the city was buried beneath the disease of sickness; but when we were entering by the ladders, we saw thousands of armed men inside the city of Ravenna, with white banners marked with the sign of a red cross. Therefore we delayed, being not a little afraid.”

The five were finally hanged near the tower of the Priests, where formerly there had been the citadel, or Roman fortress, of the Church, and where they had made their entrance.

The aforementioned Lord Galeotto Malatesta, having encamped with his army not only in the monastery but also in the church of Saint Lawrence in Caesarea, was struck by illness. Departing from there and heading toward Rimini, he ended his final day. Thus that Gospel saying came upon him: “Why have you made my temple a den of thieves?” Let laymen, therefore, not touch the anointed of the Lord, although it is the custom of the people of Ravenna to act contrariwise in the churches of that same city.

During Cosmas’s time, Urban died in the city, and Peter of Tomacelli of Naples was ordained as Boniface IX. A few days later, he made Cosmas a cardinal priest of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem and entrusted the Church of Ravenna to him. Cosmas sent messengers to Lord Guido da Polenta, after Guido had been deposed from the lordship of the city of Ravenna, concerning its retention.

The sons of the aforementioned Lord Guido, who shortly before had obtained the vicariate of the said city from Boniface through the intervention of their maternal uncle, Lord Alberto, marquis of Este, permitted the possession of the Church to be maintained for only ten years [promised to maintain possession of the Ravennate Church].

Thereupon Cosmas sent Barnabas of Leonessa, a doctor of canon law, as vicar to Ravenna—a man distinguished in judgment and bodily courage, as well as in military skill. Barnabas bravely recovered by armed force the castles of the Church of Ravenna from Ubaldino and Antonio degli Ubaldini and Astorgio Manfredi. He did so, however, with the help of Charles and Malatesta Malatesta, brothers of the Malatesta family, with whom Cosmas was on very familiar terms.

Nevertheless, at the request of certain rivals and of low-born men who ate broth, Cosmas removed Barnabas, insofar as it lay within his power, from the office of vicar and viscount of the said castles. Barnabas, however, did not intend to depart. Instead, he inhumanely tortured and tormented a certain envious abbot, Antonio of Loratino, a canon of Capua and his detractor, and hung him by the testicles.

At last Barnabas entered into arbitration with the aforementioned Cosmas. They condemned the cardinal by their judgment to pay large sums of money. Then Barnabas, relying on letters from the aforesaid Charles and Malatesta, hastened to Rome, where he was thrown into prison.

Let those who devote themselves to the service of lords remember this example, I beg you. For the love of a lord, and wine left overnight in a vessel that was excellent until morning, shamefully vanish.

During Cosmas’s time, after Lord Alberto d’Este, marquis, had died, Azo d’Este, marquis, invaded the territory of Modena with hostile intent. Departing from there, he personally transferred himself to the castle of Barbiano, in Romagna, then under the jurisdiction of Count Giovanni da Cunio.

Fearing the arrival of the marquis Azo, Lords Filippo de Robertis and Giovanni da Sale sent a certain Giovanni of Saint George as envoy to the aforesaid Count Giovanni. They asked him to kill Azo or consent to his death; if he would do this, they promised him the castles of Luci and Consilicis.

Giovanni promised to do so, but informed Azo of the matter. They killed a certain member of Azo’s household, named Theotonius, dressed in Azo’s clothing and very much resembling him. Giovanni then handed the castles of Luci [Lugi] and Consilicis over to the aforesaid Count Giovanni.

When the affair was uncovered, Giovanni of Saint George was captured, and all the mercenaries of the younger Nicholas, marquis, were stripped by force of their arms and all their possessions.

But what concern is this to the ravaged Church of Ravenna, whose goods everyone invades as far as he can?

After this, a few days later, Cosmas resigned from the Church of Ravenna and urged and arranged for Giovanni, his nephew—who perhaps was his son—to be ordained by Boniface.

After Boniface’s death, Innocent VII was elected pope. Before his election, the Roman people violently took control of the city from Innocent and governed it as a popular regime. A few days later, when thirteen Roman citizens insistently requested Ponte Molle from the pope, Louis, his nephew, slaughtered and butchered all thirteen and threw them from the windows of the houses of the Holy Spirit in the city down to the ground.

The people, enraged by this, stripped all the members of the papal household. The pope fled to Viterbo, but eventually returned to his seat and voluntarily released the rule of the city and of Campania to Ladislaus, king of Apulia, and left them under his authority.

A few days later he died and was buried in a small chapel near the chapel of the auditors in Saint Peter’s Church at the Vatican, on the right hand as one enters that chapel. His body is covered by the earth, as is likewise that of Boniface VIII [IX], his predecessor.

## On Giovanni, Archbishop XCV

Giovanni XCV, [by nation] a native of Sulmona, was the nephew of his immediately aforementioned predecessor Cosmas. Small in stature, with small eyes, a large mouth, and large teeth; pockmarked in the face; white in complexion; a doctor of laws, although he had only slight knowledge of them; simple with a simplicity that was not, however, dove-like but went beyond it, so that it could rather be called a vice than a virtue; a great spender of the goods of the Church, more through the negligence of those serving him and his own negligence than through the impending vice of prodigality.

Like his uncle or paternal uncle, he never personally visited his Church, but remained either at Ferrara, Bologna, or Rome.

During his time, a great dispute arose between the singers and the cardinals of the Church of Ravenna. The singers asserted that, just like the cardinals, they ought and could celebrate at the silver altar where there is the ciborium of Archbishop Victor, where the body of [lacuna] archbishop rests.

The sower of this tares was Servideus, formerly the first cantor [of this church], but now abbot of the monastery of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, called by the surname “el Bagatella,” either because of his shadowy and childish quibbles or because he knew the art of performing tricks.

Servideus went to the aforesaid Archbishop Giovanni at Bologna and obtained a privilege for the singers, permitting them to celebrate in the same way as the cardinals. When the cardinals heard this, they hastened to Bologna. The archbishop, hearing of their arrival, revoked the privilege he had previously granted and ordered the singers not to dare to celebrate there in future. This order was carried out by Luca of Cantarelli of Reggio, the vicar of the said Giovanni.

Servideus, acting with a mind more frantic than guided by solemn deliberation, became an object of universal laughter.

After he became abbot—a promotion in which I, Paul Scordilli, doctor of canon law and provost of this venerable Anastasis, played a large part—behold the repayment he offered me, most gratefully, in the ironic sense of “Bagatella.”

On the day after his blessing, he sowed new tares against me and against the singers, whose position had been [confirmed], and incited the abbots against the singers together with the canons, so that they might stir up a dispute against them. He said that in processions the singers ought to follow the abbots, and then the cardinals.

When this was done, the singers were distressed, since they had always been accustomed to walk together with the cardinals. The aforementioned Archbishop Giovanni referred the dispute for hearing to Angelarius of Montefano, doctor of canon law and his vicar. After receiving the testimony of certain ancient witnesses, Angelarius declared by his letters that the singers were in something like possession of the right to follow the abbots.

Thus Servideus, otherwise called Bagatella, became an object of ridicule to everyone, as before. Later he sowed other disputes and, like an ignorant and incompetent man in everything, fell and was defeated.

At last Giovanni was made cardinal priest of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem through the intervention of his uncle or paternal uncle and was released from the bond by which he had been held to the Church of Ravenna.

When the clergy and people of Ravenna heard this, they unanimously and without any dissent elected Bertrando of Arnasano, a doctor of canon law, a man of eminent learning and auditor of the Apostolic Sacred Palace, as archbishop. He had been a cardinal priest of this Church of Ravenna.

Innocent, moved by family affection, delayed confirming his election. To give the aforesaid Bertrando an opportunity to remain silent, he made him a subdeacon and conferred many [benefices] upon him.

This Giovanni attempted to seize the castle of Argenta from Lord Nicholas, marquis of Este, and the castle of Luci from Louis and Manfred, counts of Cunio, by litigation. His efforts, however, eventually came to nothing. Afterward [after these events] he transferred himself to the Roman Curia, where he remained until Innocent’s death.

After Innocent died, Gregory XII was substituted for him. He had previously been cardinal priest of Saint Mark, Angelo Correr of Venice by name. He had promised and sworn to the other cardinals and to God that he would renounce the papacy, so that unity might thereafter follow.

He solemnly sent messengers to Benedict, the antipope [Benedict XII, actually Peter of Luna], and, insofar as could be seen from outside, worked for union at the beginning. He was ready to resign at Savona, where the antipope likewise was prepared to do so.

In the end, however, at the urging of his relatives Antonio Correr and Gabriele Condulmer, and of Giovanni Dominici of the Order of Preachers, and having been seduced by their suggestions, he created and appointed the same Gabriele and Giovanni Dominici, as well as Giacomo of Udine, cardinals, contrary to the form of his vow, promise, and oath. He abandoned so great a holy work of union and thereby morally made clear the saying of the psalm-writing prophet:

“If they had not ruled over me, I would have been blameless, and I would have been cleansed from a very great offense.”

Because of this creation of new cardinals, the other cardinals fled from Gregory in the city of Lucca and appealed from him to Christ, to the future council, and to a future pope who was to be newly elected, and from a pope who had been badly informed to one who would be better informed.

Gregory did not heed their appeal. On the contrary, he secretly deprived them all, except Cardinal Antonio of Todi, cardinal priest of Saint Praxedes, who alone remained with the said Gregory.

Gregory hastened to Siena, and from Siena to Rimini.

When the clergy and people of Ravenna heard [lacuna] Giovanni, formerly commendatory administrator of the Church of Ravenna and previously its archbishop, they unanimously elected me, Paul Scordilli, doctor of canon law and provost of this church, as archbishop of the Church of Ravenna, at the request, however, of the magnificent Lord Opizone da Polenta.

Gregory delayed confirming the election, which had been sent to him at Rimini through the agency of Giovanni de Refellis, doctor of laws. The delay was due to the negligence of the said Giovanni, who sought the abbey of the monastery of Classis for Benedict, his son, mindful of the saying: “When one’s own fields are thirsty, those of another are not to be irrigated.”

Gregory, departing from Rimini, hastened to Udine. Against him Antonio, patriarch of Aquileia, waged a great and vigorous war. Gregory then departed and hastened to Gaeta.

The cardinals, including Cardinal Antonio of Todi, cardinal of Saint Praxedes, convened a council against Gregory. Having cited Gregory and the antipope Benedict, they declared both of them and each of them deprived. At Pisa they elected Alexander V, previously Peter XII, a cardinal priest of the Apostles.

Alexander was a Cretan by nation, from the lineage of the Filardi, and of the Order of Friars Minor. He came to Bologna, enjoyed the papacy at Bologna for a short time, and there ended his final day. He was buried in the Franciscan church of Saint Francis, where he remains to the present day.

After this, the cardinals shut themselves in conclave and elected Baldassare Cossa of Naples, cardinal deacon of Saint Eustace, as Pope John XXIII.

After his election, our Cardinal Giovanni, previously archbishop and then commendatory administrator, entered the way of all flesh. He was buried in the [new] sacristy of the principal church of Bologna, with funeral rites that were sufficiently meanly prepared [performed] for the commendation of his soul.

After his death, Malatesta Malatesta, lord of Cesena, seized the castle of Ripa Urriani [Ursiana], Trideroni, and Surcinola [Tuderani and Surivola], as well as other places. The viscount of the Church of Ravenna was then removed.

This Giovanni and his uncle or paternal uncle Cosmas benefited the Church very little and obtained very great revenues, though in a manner different from the way in which they now render an account of their administration before the strict judge.

Nevertheless, I wish that their souls, and those of the other dead, may in Christian fashion fly upward to the heavenly Jerusalem.

During Giovanni’s time, Apollinaris of Gracchis [Gnacobis], abbot of the monastery of Saint Apollinaris Nuovo, inspired—as he himself asserted—in a dream by the blessed Apollinaris, most glorious martyr of Christ, to excavate and make known his body, broke [the ground] beneath the principal altar of the said monastery and made a certain opening. There he found a wooden chest, in which a body or corpse was found. Its occiput was broken, and the whole body was covered with a certain shroud.

Under the head of the said corpse was a leaden tablet, very ancient in appearance, on which the following letters had been skillfully engraved and hollowed out:

“In this sarcophagus rests the body of the most holy and blessed martyr of Christ, Apollinaris, deposited by Archbishop Giovanni.”

This matter was discussed above in the history of the translation of the blessed Apollinaris himself.

The matter was reported to Brother Gualterio of Galeata, of the Order of Hermits, bishop of Bologna and general vicar of the said Giovanni. He inspected the matter. I, Paul Scordilli, doctor of canon law and provost of the said Church of Ravenna, was with him, as were many other clergy.

Brother Gualterio reported the matter to Giovanni, his lord. Giovanni, however, promised by letter that he would provide for it most carefully. In the end he did nothing, and so the affair remained unfinished.

## On Thomas, Archbishop XCVI

At last, as a conclusion to this Appendix, I wished to add here the see of the bishops of Ravenna, depicted on four bronze plates, which I saw in the archive of the archiepiscopal church.

It is made of wood and decorated with images in relief work, from a material that, being whitish, can easily imitate ivory. The images are enclosed by bands and surrounded by various figures of animals and birds.

The first plate, marked E, represents the entire seat with its dimensions.

The second plate, marked F, displays the outer convex part. Of the images, those remain that are contained in three recesses. In the upper one, Christ is baptized by John in the Jordan; in the other two, he multiplies loaves and fishes and, after the resurrection, eats with his disciples. I conjecture that this part of the seat represented the life of Christ the Lord, the rest of it having fallen away.

The third plate, marked G, contains the two sides of the seat, on which the history of Joseph is represented in sections.

The fourth plate, marked H, has the lower part of the seat, and in the middle Christ the Lord, who blesses with his right hand and holds with his left a small sphere containing a lamb. He bears the appearance of a shepherd and priest.

On either side of him are two evangelists on one side and two on the other. Above the Savior’s head is a monogram from which I seem easily to see letters that could be carved to form:

**MAXIMIANUS EPISCOPUS**

If experts believe that the character of the entire work can be referred to the age of that bishop, I shall congratulate myself for having struck the matter precisely.

The innermost part is quite clearly visible in the first plate. It shows that figures have perished and that those remaining should be referred to the Nativity of Christ. This brief sketch may whet the appetite of learned readers to investigate more closely the period in which a seat of this kind was made.

# Calendar of the Church of Modena

## Notice

There exists in the distinguished archive of the cathedral of Modena a parchment codex in which, in Lombard script, are written the Salic, Lombard, and Roman laws, together with certain Capitularies.

At the end of the same codex there is a calendar for the divine offices, along with certain rules for the seasons of the year by which those seasons were arranged according to the calculations of the computists.

Since the Church of Modena was subject to the Church of Ravenna as its metropolitan church, it seemed likely to be very agreeable to the Reader if the same calendar were added, from which it might become clear what saints’ offices were customarily celebrated in the churches subject to Ravenna.

I believe that this calendar belongs to the beginning of the eleventh century. The learned Reader may perhaps find here other things that are not useless.
