## Rules for finding the Kalends in the calendar

January, August, and December have one rule: namely, thirty-one days, the fourth day before the Nones, the eighth day before the Ides, and the nineteenth day before the Kalends.

March, May, July, and October have one rule: namely, thirty-one days, the sixth day before the Nones, the eighth day before the Ides, and the seventeenth day before the Kalends.

April, June, September, and November have one rule: namely, thirty days, the fourth day before the Nones, the eighth day before the Ides, and the eighteenth day before the Kalends.

February has its own rule: namely, twenty-eight days, the fourth day before the Nones, the eighth day before the Ides, and the sixteenth day before the Kalends.

When a leap year occurs, it is calculated with twenty-nine days.

## Method for finding the Kalends

If you wish to know how the day of the Kalends is to be found, take the concurrents of that year and add them to the regular numbers of the Kalends of whatever month you wish. Divide by seven; whatever remains below or above seven is the day of the Kalends.

## Chapter on finding the moon

If you wish to know the age of the moon on the Kalends, take the epact of that year and add it to the regular numbers of the moons of whatever month you wish. Whatever remains below or above thirty is the moon on the Kalends.

## Regular numbers of the Kalends

March: 5.  
April: 1.  
May: 3.  
June: 6.  
July: 1.  
August: 4.  
September: 7.  
October: 2.  
November: 5.  
December: 7.  
January: 3.  
February: 6.

## Concurrents

B: 1, 2, 3, 4.  
B: 6, 7, 1, 2.  
B: 4, 5, 6, 7.  
B: 2, 3, 4, 5.  
B: 7, 1, 2, 3.  
B: 5, 6, 7, 1.  
B: 3, 4, 5, 6.

These are the concurrents of the Kalends.

## Regular numbers of the moons

September: 5.  
October: 5.  
November: 7.  
December: 7.  
January: 9.  
February: 10.  
March: 9.  
April: 10.  
May: 11.  
June: 12.  
July: 13.  
August: 14.

## Epacts of the moons

None; 11; 22; 3; 14; 25; 6; 17; 27; 9; 20; 1; 12; 23; 4; 15; 26; 7; 18.

These are the epacts of the moons.

## Method for finding the term of Septuagesima, Lent, Easter, and Rogationtide

January has the regular number 32 for finding Septuagesima. Therefore subtract from the 32 regular number the epact that runs in that year. If seventeen or more remain, you will have the term of Septuagesima on that day within January; if fewer than seventeen remain, the term of Septuagesima will not be in January but in February.

Likewise, as above:

For finding Septuagesima, February has the regular number 31. Subtract the epact of the year being examined from it; however many remain, on that many days in February will be the term of Septuagesima. Take care not to forget to add one in both January and February in a leap year. +

### Another

Add twenty-one to the days of Septuagesima. From this sum, when Septuagesima falls in January, subtract the days of January; when Septuagesima falls in February, subtract the days of February; and you will find the beginning of Lent.

If both Septuagesima and the beginning of Lent fall in February, so that not enough remains to subtract an entire month, the number of days you find within February will be the beginning of Lent.

### Another

Add forty-two to the days of Lent. From this sum, if the beginning of Lent falls in February, subtract the days of February; if the beginning of Lent falls in March, subtract the days of March.

If the beginning of Lent falls so near the end of February that the days of February and March—that is, fifty-nine without a leap day, or sixty with one—can be subtracted, the number of days left over will be Easter in April.

If the beginning of Lent falls in March, subtract the days of March; however many remain, on that many days in April will be Easter.

### Another, as above

Add five to the March days of Easter. If the result is less than thirty or exactly thirty, that many days into April will be Rogationtide. If it is more than thirty, subtract thirty; however many remain, on that many days in May will be Rogationtide.

## Chapter on Easter

Add six to the April days of Easter; however many result, on that many days in May will be Rogationtide.

## Chapter on Pentecost

Add thirteen to the days of Rogationtide. If the result is less than thirty-one or exactly thirty-one, Pentecost will fall on that many days in May. If it is more than thirty-one, subtract thirty-one; however many remain, Pentecost will fall on that many days in June.

## Chapter on the moon

Subtract eight from the moon of Septuagesima; in a leap year subtract nine. You will find what the moon is at the beginning of Lent.

### Another

Add twelve to the Lenten moon, and you will find the Paschal moon.

Add seven to the Paschal moon, and you will find the moon of Rogationtide.

## Method for finding Lent alone

For finding Lent, February has the regular number 32. Know the age of the moon on the Kalends of February, and subtract that number from the regular number. If seven or more than seven remain, the term of Lent will be on that many days into February; if fewer than seven remain, the term of Lent will not be in February. In a leap year, do not forget to add one.

## Term of Lent

For finding Lent, March has the regular number 24. Subtract from it the epact of the year being examined, and you will find how many days into March the term of Lent will fall.

The term of Lent must in no way be before the eighth day before the Ides of February, nor before the day before the Nones of March.

However many days before the day before the Ides of April Easter falls, that many days before the Kalends of March will be the beginning of Lent.

However many days before the day before the Ides of April Easter falls, that many days after the [day before the] Kalends of March will be the beginning of Lent; and if Easter falls on the day before the Ides of April, the beginning of Lent will fall that many days after the Kalends of March; and if Easter falls on the Ides of April, the beginning of Lent will be on the Kalends of March.

March has the regular number 36 for finding the fourteenth moon. Therefore subtract from the 36 regular number the epact that runs in that year. If thirty-one or more remain, you will have the fourteenth moon on that day of March; if fewer than twenty-one remain, the Paschal moon will not be in March but in April.

# Associates of the Palatine Household

## On the Bull of Pope Paschal I to Petronacius, Archbishop of Ravenna
[Col. 0829A] When, among the many monuments of venerable antiquity which Cardinal Federicus Borromeus had gathered for the adornment of his library—which, with the ancestral humility of his family, he preferred to have called Ambrosian—we came upon a copy of the bull of Pope Paschal addressed to Petronacius, archbishop of Ravenna, which the distinguished Ludovico Antonio Muratori mentions in his preface to the *Pontificale Ravennatis*, and D. Benedictus Bacchinius on the preceding page 184 (this volume, col. 745), we thought that it would not be unwelcome to scholars if we published it here just as it is read in our copy. We undertake this all the more willingly because we observed that in Hieronymus Rubeus, who presents it in *Historia Ravennatis*, p. 237, and in Ughellus’s *Italia Sacra*, vol. V, as well as in all the others who copied it in full from Rubeus, it has been transmitted so corrupted by errors that a reader acquainted with the diction of that age is repeatedly struck and brought to a halt by the unfamiliar novelty of the wording.

From the aforesaid Rubeus we learn that the original was written on the bark of a tree, or, as is more probable [Col. 0829B]—as Bacchinius also observed on the preceding p. 170 (col. 721)—on Egyptian papyrus. In the passage cited above, after setting out the text of the bull, Rubeus says:

> “These letters still exist in the library of the archbishopric of Ravenna, written on the bark of a tree two cubits long and one cubit wide. They are written in the Lombard script, the most beautiful of all the documents kept there (and there are many), in lines separated from one another by two transverse fingers. Since, however, they have been eaten away in several places, Cardinal and Archbishop Julius Ruvereus, a lover of antiquity, so that such an ancient monument might not perish—for it is thought to be an autograph (Greek αὐτόγραφον, “written by one’s own hand”)—had it glued to a thin supporting cloth. From this it may be understood that the archbishop of Ravenna was accustomed to have his own intermediary, or *apocrisiarius*, as we have called him, at the imperial courts. These letters were given in the year 819 from the birth of the Virgin.”

Thus far Rubeus, who on the same page assigns Petronacius’s election to the year 817. The most distinguished Bacchinius, however, asserts on the preceding p. 16 (col. 451) that Martinus, Petronacius’s predecessor, died around the year 819 and that Petronacius was ordained after the year 821; on p. 19 (col. 455) he thinks that it should be placed around the year 822, but after reconsidering the matter more carefully he later abandons this opinion. For on p. 170 (col. 721) he says:

> “Baronius assigns the beginning of Pope Paschal’s pontificate to 28 January 817; and it follows from the privilege of that same Paschal, given in July in the twelfth indiction, that the beginning of Petronacius must be placed before the year 819.”

He confirms this again on p. 184 (col. 745). We, however, have no hesitation in accepting the testimony of the aforementioned Rubeus, a most careful writer.

As regards the diplomatic matter, its characters are precisely of the same type as those in which the bulls of Popes Benedict III and Nicholas I were written. Mabillon presents specimens of them in *De re diplomatica*, table XLVII—marked XLVIII through a typographical error—and the following tables XLVIII and XLIX. From this we learn that this kind of script was used chiefly by the Roman curia in the ninth century. It is not sufficiently clear when it began or ceased. Certainly the diplomas of John V and Sergius I, the first written in 685 and the second in 697, although they agree in the form of some characters, differ so greatly in most respects that they appear to belong to another kind of script. We therefore think that the beginning of our script does not go back beyond the beginning of the eighth century. That it had already disappeared near the end of the tenth century is shown by the bull of Pope John XIII, given in the year 972; it may be seen, together with the preceding examples, in the aforementioned Mabillon, tables XLVI and L.

The formula *in perpetuum*, which our document contains, is extremely common in papal bulls of the ninth and tenth centuries, although it also frequently occurs before the ninth and even in the eleventh century, as is found throughout the Cluniac, Cassinese, and Roman bullaries and elsewhere. The *Bullar. Cassinense*, vol. II, also contains another bull of the same Paschal I addressed to Ingoaldus, abbot of Farfa, with the same formula *in perpetuum*. Nevertheless, not all pontiffs of that age used it consistently. Indeed, we believe that some pontiffs reserved it for bulls of greater importance and those extending over a long period, while reserving the alternative *Salutem et apostolicam benedictionem* (“Greeting and apostolic blessing”) for lesser rescripts that were to be carried out immediately, as is clear from the bulls of Gregory VII and Urban II.

[Col. 0830B] The salutation expressed in the words *Bene valete* (“Farewell”) generally occurs in bulls of the ninth and tenth centuries. In the eleventh century, however, Pope Leo IX reduced the same words to a monogram, as Mabillon repeatedly observes in *De re diplomatica*.

Before Leo IX, chronological notes were used in a twofold order. The first indicated the time when the document was written; the second, the time when the diploma was issued. Between them stood the salutation mentioned above, *Bene valete*.

The first chronological note contained the month and the indiction, but never, so far as we have seen, the day. (We are speaking of bulls whose inscription closes with the words *in perpetuum*; the arrangement of later bulls, on whose front appears *Salutem et apostolicam benedictionem*, is different.) The second assigned the day of the month, the years of the emperor together with the repeated indiction, and sometimes, though not always—as one sees in our bull—the years of the pope. This is found throughout the authors cited above. Here too, with the most learned Mabillon, *De re diplomatica*, “it should be observed” (these are his words, book II, chapter 25, no. 2):

> “In bulls that contain both *scriptum* and *datum*, the *datum* is often written by another hand, or at least in another character, and sometimes indeed several days after the text, as the difference in ink proves. For *scriptum* indicates the time when the document was written by the notary; *datum* expresses the time when the diploma was delivered to the petitioner by the librarian or chancellor, whose notary had prepared the written text.”

This appears particularly clearly in our example. The *datum* differs from the text not only in the distinct form of its characters but also, notably, in its thinner letters.

As for the material, our specimen consists of ordinary paper made from fragments of linen, which was subsequently smeared with oil, so that the characters superimposed upon the autograph could more easily be copied while preserving their size and form. This was carried out by the work of some learned man who attempted in this way to renew, as it were, the autograph, which was decaying day by day. [Col. 0830D] Its dimensions equal the measure reported by Rubeus, but it is now cut transversely into nine equal pieces and bound together for more convenient use as a book. It is preserved among the manuscript codices in folio, letter E, no. 106. We determine nothing certain concerning its antiquity, since it contains no chronological notation. Nevertheless, that it is ancient is apparent from this very fact: it contains some readings which Rubeus, who inspected the autograph before the year 1571, omitted as obliterated. This is made even clearer by the fact that our specimen, although preserved with the greatest care, displays many characters—as though cut out with a knife—corroded by the sharpness of the ink. The experts in ancient codices are now convinced that this is unquestionably an indication of great antiquity.

Finally, we wish to warn readers that the lacunae which we encountered in our copy, and which, since the autograph had already been obliterated, could plausibly not have been copied from it, have been restored by us. We have nevertheless used a different form of script, so that we might not appear to deceive our readers. This was especially necessary near the end of the bull, in the second chronological note beginning *Datum*. Since it was written, as we indicated above, in a thinner character, it suffered more severely from the ravages of time and became for the most part so faint that it escapes the eye. Yet lest we appear to have restored it without basis, or to have assigned to letters and sigla a meaning shaped not by the true reading but by our own ingenuity, consult bulls issued in the same and preceding centuries, especially those of Pope Benedict III, in Mabillon, part II, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis S. Benedicti*, century IV, [Col. 0831B] which he reproduces again in *De re diplomatica*, p. 439. There one finds:

> “Given on the Nones of October, by the hand of Theophilactus, subdeacon of the holy apostolic see, while our lord, the most pious and perpetual Augustus Lothair, crowned by God, great emperor, was reigning, in the thirty-ninth year, and in the thirty-ninth year after his consulship, and while his son Louis, the new emperor, was in his seventh year, in the fourth indiction.”

See also another bull of Pope Honorius I addressed to his namesake, the bishop of Dorchester, in Bede, book II, chapter 18, which, following the corrections of Chifflet and Mabillon, should be read as follows:

> “Given on the fourth day before the Ides of June, while our most pious lords, the Augusti Heraclius, in his twenty-fourth year, and, after his consulship, in his twenty-third year, and Constantine, his son, in his twenty-third year and in the third year of his consulship, were reigning, and also while Heraclius Felix Caesar, that is, his son, was in his third year, in the seventh indiction.”

Observe here that the clause “that is, his son” may have been inserted by Bede. See also one of the same Paschal I, pope, addressed to Bernard, bishop of Vienne, in Mabillon, century IV, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis S. Benedicti*, part II, p. 567, which he corrects in *De re diplomatica*, p. 183, as follows:

> “Given while our lord, the perpetual Augustus Louis, crowned by God, great and pious emperor, was reigning, in the fourth year, and in the fourth year after his consulship.”

See also the others in the bullaries mentioned above and in Sirmond, Ughellus, Dublet, Baluze, and the others. If you compare them with our correction, no room for doubt will remain. But why delay any longer over so clear a matter, unknown even to those who have merely crossed the threshold of learning? Let us therefore come to the bull itself, which we have arranged to print in such a way that Rubeus’s text is placed opposite the corresponding portion of our text, so that the difference between the two may more easily be recognized. We thought it right to retain throughout the orthography of the Ambrosian copy, although it is less accurate.

## PASCHAL I, POPE, TO PETRONACIUS, ARCHBISHOP OF RAVENNA

[Col. 0831]

[Note: [Col. 0831] The sections of text headed “Manuscript copy of the Ambrosian Library” and “From Rubeus’s *Historia Ravennatis*, p. 237” are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0831C] Manuscript copy of the Ambrosian Library

Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the reverend and most holy brother Petronacius, archbishop of the holy Church of Ravenna, and through you to that same Church, in perpetuity.

Since the desires of a pious will and the intention of praiseworthy devotion must always be assisted by apostolic efforts, diligent care must be taken that what is lawfully carried out and accords with the equity due to a person cannot be disturbed by any opposition, but may remain permanently secure by inviolable right before God; and therefore, through apostolic sanctions promulgated for this purpose, whatever is supported by reason and permitted by law must be confirmed as something that ought to be possessed.

Therefore, since your fraternal holiness has sent to us through Sergius, a religious deacon of your holy Church of Ravenna, the privilege of the former lord Adrian, our predecessor the pope, in which he confirms [Note: [Col. 0831D] *Confirmabit* occurs for *confirmavit*, with *v* changed into *b*, just as below *postulabit* should be read *postulavit*. Conversely, in other words *b* is changed into *v*, and we read *inrefragavile* for *inrefragabile*, *perturvare* for *perturbare*, *corovorationis* for *coroborationis*, *veneravilis* for *venerabilis*, *juvemus* for *jubemus*, and so forth. This was extremely common in that age.] the privileges of the former emperor Leo, issued by Epiphanius, formerly a religious notary [Note: [Col. 0831D] The rank of notaries varied according to differences of time and place. The notaries of bishops were their scribes, generally taken from the clerical order. It may be inferred from the *Book of the Sacraments* of St. Gregory that they also performed other duties in the churches: “And then two candles are lit, which two notaries hold,” and so forth. On these matters see Ducange in the *Glossary*, Mabillon, and others.], and by the scrivener [Note: [Col. 0832D] Scrivener-clerks were those who worked in the archives and acted in the place of writers. See Cujas, Gothofredus, and others. Archives were repositories of public writings, as in the Scholiast on Julian the Antecessor, *Code of Theodosius and Justinian*, and elsewhere.] and the *apocrisiarius* [Note: [Col. 0832D] *Apocrisarius*, or *apocrisiarius*, is not the name of one office alone. Sometimes it means the chancellor, who keeps the prince’s seal and signs royal diplomas, as in John of Genoa: “*Apocrisiarius*, secretary, counselor, or he is also called chancellor, because he himself is the secretary of the king or emperor and knows his secrets.” It can also mean a referendary, as Carolus Dufresne argues in the *Glossary*. In this place, however, it is to be understood as the intermediary of the archbishop of Ravenna at the court of Leo, the emperor of the East. This practice was especially customary among pontiffs and patriarchs at that time. Their duty was to conduct the affairs of their churches and report them to the prince if any difficulty arose in ecclesiastical matters relating to public administration which the prince ought to decide. See Justinian, *Novels* 6, chapters 2 and 3; St. Gregory the Great, *Dialogues*, book III, chapter 36. The term was also a title of rank at the courts of kings and emperors, whose office concerned ecclesiastical affairs. Hence Hincmar, in *On the Order of the Palace*, chapter 13, calls him the “representative of ecclesiastical affairs.” He performed the office which the apocrisiarius of the Roman Church performed at Constantinople, after whose model he was appointed—not by the apostolic see, however, but by the king. The same work, chapter 16, says: “The apocrisiarius, whom our people call the chaplain or guardian of the palace, governed the whole clergy under his care and authority. He was assisted by the chief chancellor, formerly called the secretary; and subject to him were prudent, intelligent, and faithful men who would write the royal commands without the excessive venality of greed and guard his secrets.”] of the holy Church of Ravenna, who was sent by Damianus, archbishop of venerable memory, so that the preceding formulas might be confirmed as sacred: the privileges granted by the emperor Leo, of divine memory, by the ancient Justinian as well as by the other most pious emperors to your holy Church, in which, among other pious provisions, its boundaries were granted so that they might not be violated by sacrilege or the harshness of plunder; and your holiness has also requested from us that these same provisions receive stability through our apostolic letters.

Therefore, assenting, we more fully decree and confirm that all privileges issued in your holy Church of Ravenna—those of our predecessors, namely Adrian and Leo, of holy memory, and of their predecessors, as well as those of emperors; and gifts from kings or offerings made by Christian people through donations, sales, or wills—shall, in due order, generally and specifically, possess the full strength of confirmation of every kind of generosity bestowed upon your holy Church in perpetuity. We decree and confirm that no place or right subject to the jurisdiction of your holy Church may, by any contrivance whatsoever, be judged or usurped, withdrawn, violated, or subjected to any new construction by any power that dares to act, whether supported by civil or military authority.

But if anyone should attempt to restore or rebuild a damaged or fallen church, he shall not have permission to do so before the holy and venerable cross has first been set up there through the customary blessing by your paternal holiness. Nor shall clerics beloved of God who come from another episcopal jurisdiction or city and reside there presume to perform priestly ministry in the churches subject to you without your priestly authorization. Rather, your holiness shall hear and regulate all the affairs and boundaries of the most religious clerics who come from elsewhere, and shall impose upon them the appropriate effect according to the tenor of the divine laws and most sacred rules.

The monastery of your holy first martyr Stephen, which is so called and lies beside the palace, together with all the religious monks belonging to it; all the venerable oratories and monasteries; and the other venerable places existing within the parish shall be subject to your holiness, under your jurisdiction and power, and through you to your holy Church. Whatever sacred privileges belong to them shall be preserved in their entirety. In these matters no one shall impose any molestation, forced services [Note: [Col. 0834D] *Angariae*, which the common people now understand as unjust exactions, coercions, and compulsions, were among the ancients services which a person was obliged to perform either personally or with property. We would now call them burdens. It would take too long to specify how many there were and of what kinds, since they varied according to different periods and according to the differing avarice or clemency of princes. Usually, however, this name denotes services which each person was obliged to provide with wagons, horses, mules, asses, and persons during the passage of kings and Caesars, and especially during the transport of armies and military equipment. See more in the *Capitularies* of Charlemagne, book I, chapter 81; book VII, chapter 367; the *Capitularies* of Charles the Bald, title XXIII, chapter 14; in Goldast, *Charters of Alemannia*, chapter 42; the *Code of Theodosius*, “On the Public Post,” and in the Visigothic law, book V, title 5, § 3, and passim elsewhere. Gunther also mentions *angariae* in the *Ligurinus*, book II:

> “For long ago, within the boundaries of the city,  
> Guido of Blandrate, under the protection of Liguria,  
> alone held the county almost free from the burdens of the Italians.”]

or exactions, or guard duties [Note: [Col. 0835C] *Excuvias* occurs for *excubias*. Here it is to be understood not as the watches of guards, as the word ordinarily signifies, but as any unjust burden, molestation, or service, as Ducange correctly observes and as is known from the Lombard Law, book III, title 952, concerning men who had alienated their property: “Wherever they reside upon them, let the count constrain them through the public *excubiae*, as the law provides.” The gloss says: “That is, service for restoring bridges.”], upon any portion of your holy Church. Nor shall anyone remove the colonists, tenant-sharers [Note: [Col. 0835D] *Partiarii*: a class of slaves, discussed more fully elsewhere.] or slaves subject to the property of your holy Church for military service. But if they have been enlisted, we shall order them to be released from military service and returned to your venerable property.

If anyone should rashly attempt to violate such provisions, then, for these things piously sanctioned by us, rightly requested from us, and contained in the present apostolic document of ours, not only shall his action be entirely ineffective, but for such atrocious boldness he shall also be made to suffer the loss of all his possessions; nor shall he be able to avoid the peril of the punishment of his soul, with all this sufficiently established by the mere display of this apostolic document of ours.

But if anyone should act against this apostolic command of ours, let him pay five pounds of refined gold [Note: [Col. 0835D] *Obriti*, or *obrizi*, signifies pure, excellent, and tested gold. Ducange, under the word *obryzum*, gives the following: “*Auribricum*, corruptly also in the Lombard diploma of Paschal I, concerning the Church of Ravenna.” If he is speaking of our bull, it is not clear to us where he took this reading. Rubeus, who first published it, has *auribriti* in the Venetian edition of 1589; in the preceding Venetian edition of 1572 there is no mention of the bull, and many passages are absent which he later added or corrected, including, among other things, Petronacius’s election, which he had said occurred after Pope Paschal’s death. Ughellus, both in the Roman edition and in the recent Venetian edition, has *auri boni*, certainly corrupt, as also in the other diplomas which, usually spoiled by scribal error, we have found otherwise when consulting the autographs. In our copy, at any rate, the reading *auri obriti* is clear. The mention of *aurum obritum* occurs, to omit published examples, in a diploma of Berengar in favor of the Ticinense Parthenon of St. Mary Theodota (now commonly called “at Pusterula,” perhaps because it was built beside the ancient walls of the city and near one of the smaller or later gates, which at that time were called *pusterulae* or *posterolae*), given on the fifth day before the Ides of March “in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 899, in the thirteenth year of the lord Berengar, most glorious king, in the third indiction.” And in another diploma of the emperor Louis, son of Boso, king of Provence, for the same Parthenon, given at Pavia “on the fifth day before the Ides of March, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 981, in the first year of the lord Louis, most glorious emperor, in the fourth indiction.” This word is frequent in diplomas, especially imperial ones, as are also *aurum coctum*, *aurum purum*, *aurum purissimum*, *aurum perfectissimum*, *aurum probatissimum*, and *aurum optimum*. Meanwhile, it should be noted that a monetary fine against transgressors, extremely common in the diplomas of the Caesars and kings of Italy in the ninth and following centuries, occurs more rarely in papal bulls and other ecclesiastical monuments, perhaps only in those which were to be enforced within the dominion of the Holy See, such as this bull of Paschal I and the Roman council under Pope Sylvester, in which the immunity of the monastery of Perugia is asserted and it is decreed: “Whoever attempts to renew this defined dispute, let him pay ten pounds of the purest gold to the Lateran palace,” in Labbe, *Councils*, vol. IX, col. 1247. For the most part, however, pontiffs used only curses against violators, while praying to the Lord for eternal life for those who obeyed their commands. We deliberately omit examples of these, which are found throughout the authors, so as not to become too lengthy.] and moreover be bound by the bonds of anathema and subjected to everlasting condemnation.

We have ordered this decree of confirmation made by us to be written by Timothy, notary and scrivener of our see, in the month of July, in the twelfth indiction. + Farewell. +

Given on the fifth day before the Ides of July, by the hand of Sergius, librarian of the holy apostolic see, while our lord, the perpetual Augustus Louis, crowned by God, great and peace-bringing emperor, was reigning, in the sixth year [Note: [Col. 0836D] Louis’s sixth imperial year in the month of July is the year of the Lord 819. For the authorities agree that he was invested with the imperial diadem by his father Charles at the assembly held at Aachen and declared his associate in the empire in the year 813; they dispute only the month. The Chronicler of Moissac reports that this occurred in September:

> “He [namely, Charles] ordered that whatever they had determined in each synod should be reported at the assembly of the appointed emperor. This was done, and in that same year, in the month of September, the aforementioned Charles held a great assembly of the people at the palace of Aachen from throughout his kingdom or empire. Bishops, abbots, counts, and the senate of the Franks came together with the emperor at Aachen. There he established forty-six chapters concerning matters that were necessary for the Church of God and the Christian people”—

Pagius thinks that *twenty-six* should be read in his *Critica* on Baronius’s *Annals*—

> “After this he held council with the aforementioned bishops, abbots, counts, and the Frankish nobles, so that they might appoint his son Louis king and emperor. They all agreed together, and so forth.”

The Imperial Annalist, edited by Lambecius, reports under the forty-fifth year of King Charles that Louis was proclaimed emperor in August, in these words:

> “Richulf, archbishop of the Church of Mainz, died on the fifth day before the Ides of August, and a great assembly was held at Aachen in the month of August. Charles the emperor appointed his son Hlodoveus—that is, Louis—to reign together with him, placing the diadem upon his head, and so forth.”

Pagius, in his *Historical-Chronological Criticism on the Annals of Cardinal Baronius*, argues that Louis was inaugurated in November:

> “The inauguration of Louis and Bernard took place in November, as will be clear from what will be said concerning Bernard’s death in the year 817, no. 15.”

Under the year 817 he writes:

> “Bernard was buried at Milan in the church of Saint Ambrose, where there is an inscription cited by Baronius under no. 18, which reads: ‘He reigned four years and five months; he died on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the eleventh indiction.’”

Therefore, in the following year of Christ—that is, 818—and since he had entered upon his reign in November of the year 813, as these words demonstrate. You now see the arguments by which Pagius attempts to prove that Louis was summoned by his father to share the empire not in September, as the Chronicler of Moissac reports, nor in August, as the Imperial Annalist has it, but in November. For when he saw that at one and the same time, namely at the assembly held at Aachen, Louis had been raised to the imperial dignity and Bernard placed over the kingdom of Italy, and that Bernard had departed this life on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May after reigning four years and five months, he calculated that, subtracting four years and five months from the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, the election of both fell in November of the year 813. He therefore thought that their inauguration must be reckoned from that month alone.

Pagius, however, took this opinion from Carlo Sigonio, *On the Kingdom of Italy*, book IV; Sigonio in turn borrowed Bernard’s royal inscription from Tristano Calco, book V, who seems to indicate that the stone was excavated around the year 1498, at the time when Ludovico Sforza, duke of Milan, laid the foundations of the magnificent monastery beside the basilica of Saint Ambrose, as it is seen today. Since the inscription itself, which is still preserved in the aforesaid basilica, is worth presenting here especially because Baronius, as also Sigonio under the year 818 and Pagius under the year 817, count the indiction as the eleventh, whereas anyone can still see the marble tablet itself marked only with the tenth indiction, we thought it appropriate to give it. Although this does not agree as well with the ordinary calculation as the eleventh indiction, we do not for that reason think that Bernard’s death should be moved back to the year 817 against the judgment of so many authors, nor that the stonecutter should be accused of error. Rather, we believe that the discrepancy arose because a distinctive indiction was in use among the ecclesiastics of Milan in that age, as Puricellus observes in *The Monuments of the Ambrosian Basilica*, and that this practice was not always consistent, as we may perhaps demonstrate elsewhere. The inscription runs as follows:

> **BERNARD, MARVELOUS IN CIVIC STATUS AND ILLUSTRIOUS IN THE OTHER VIRTUES, KING, RESTS HERE. HE REIGNED 4 YEARS AND 5 MONTHS. HE DIED ON THE FIFTEENTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF MAY, IN THE TENTH INDICTION. SON OF THE MOST PIOUS LORD PEPIN.**
From this inscription, therefore, we learn how long Bernard reigned and when he closed his final day. But whether he began his reign on the day when, at the assembly held at Aachen, he was proclaimed king of Italy by the emperor Charles, or on the day when he received the crown of the Italian kingdom at Monza, we can determine only by conjecture. It will therefore still be doubtful whether, in the month of November, his inauguration [Col. 0838B] or his coronation took place. Nevertheless, we are rather persuaded that the coronation is meant by what Pagius himself says under the year 813, no. 17:

> “The author of the *Life of Louis the Pious* reports that he spent the entire summer in his father’s company, was then crowned with the imperial diadem, and finally returned to Aquitaine in the month of November.”

Therefore, if the inauguration of Louis and Bernard occurred at one and the same time, and Louis had already been crowned before the month of November, it is permissible to believe that Bernard too had been proclaimed king before that time. We thought it not inappropriate to pursue this matter at somewhat greater length. In any event, in July of the year 819 no one can certainly reckon any year other than the sixth of Louis’s empire, whether one dates its beginning from August, September, or even from November itself.

But whether Louis himself reckoned the years of his empire only from his father’s death—that is, from 28 January [*V Kalends of February*] 814—or also from the day on which he was called co-ruler of the empire [Col. 0838C], remains doubtful. Pagius, in the passage recently cited, asserts that both eras were used by him:

> “In his diplomas Louis generally reckons the years from his father’s death, but sometimes also from the day on which he was called co-ruler of the imperial name; these two eras therefore must not be confused.”

Although that most learned man cites no examples there by which to support his opinion, we believe that he did not lack them, since we too have encountered several diplomas of Louis published by various writers whose chronological notes could by no means be referred to the time when he succeeded his father in the empire. Whether an error has always crept into their numerical notes, however, we dare neither assert nor deny. Nevertheless, that this occurs frequently—especially in books that have been reprinted several times—will easily become clear to anyone who consults the autographs or examines the diplomas themselves more carefully.

Du Chesne gives a diploma of Louis the Pious in favor of the Christians [Col. 0838D] who, fleeing the tyranny of the Saracens in Spain, had taken refuge in Gaul. Its subscription is as follows:

> “Given on the Kalends of January, in the second year, Christ being propitious, of the empire of our lord Louis, most pious Augustus, in the eighth indiction. Done at the royal palace of Aachen.”

The eighth indiction corresponds only to the Kalends of January of the year 815. Therefore the second year of the empire cannot be reckoned from Charles’s death; for, as we said above, he had died on the fifth day before the Kalends of February in the year 814, and consequently the first year of the empire had not yet been completed. Someone might therefore confidently conclude that the second year of the empire must be reckoned from Louis’s inauguration.

But if one compares with the foregoing another privilege of the same Louis for the monastery of Saint-Denis, which Mabillon gives in *De Re Diplomatica*, p. 394, and for which he also supplies a specimen of the script in plate 26, one will find that an error lies in its numerical note designating the year of the empire. For the Dionysian privilege [Col. 0839A] reads as follows:

> “Given on the Kalends of December, in the first year, Christ being propitious, of the empire of our lord Louis, most serene Augustus, in the eighth indiction.”

You now see that the Kalends of December in the eighth indiction fall in the last month of the year 815. Thus this privilege precedes the one mentioned above by only a single month, yet it is marked with the first year of the empire. Why, then, should we believe that Louis began his empire from his inauguration on the Kalends of December, but on the following Kalends of January began counting the years from his father’s death? Certainly nothing occurred during this brief interval that could have caused a change of era.

Nevertheless, Baluzius in volume I of the *Capitularia of the Frankish Kings*, and Pagius under the year 815, no. 4, also noticed the error and corrected it, replacing the first year of the empire with the second. We readily believe that they would have corrected several other diplomas bearing this notation in the same way, had they been able to inspect the autographs or compare them with others issued at the same or a nearby time.

For our part, in all the autographs of Louis that we have so far seen, we have observed that the years of his empire are consistently reckoned from the fifth day before the Kalends of February in the year [Col. 0839B] 814. His five statuses must nevertheless be distinguished: while his father was alive, he was first king of Aquitaine; then, after his father’s death, sole emperor; afterward emperor together with Lothair, but subsequently separated from him; and finally, after his deposition, restored to the throne.

] and in the sixth year after his consulship [Col. 0837A] [Note: [Col. 0838D] The year after Louis’s consulship must be restored. We thought that the sixth should be replaced, moved by the example of the often-cited Mabillon, who, in *De Re Diplomatica*, book II, chapter 25, no. 3, when reporting a bull of Pope Paschal I to Bernard, bishop of Vienne—a bull that we too mentioned above—assigns both the fourth year of Louis’s empire and the fourth year after his consulship; indeed, he replaced the third, which had mistakenly entered the fourth *saeculum* of the *Acts of the Saints of Benedict*, part II, p. 567. For, as I suppose, the learned man believed that Louis’s consulship—which he had observed elsewhere that the Caesars customarily entered only on the Kalends of January following their coronation—should be reckoned from the year 814, chiefly because he had already been crowned by his father at Aachen in the preceding year and admitted to partnership in the empire. Unless, perhaps, one prefers to agree with Pagius under the year 817, no. 2, that at that time it had become customary for Caesars to assume a perpetual consulship on the very day on which they entered upon the empire.

It should nevertheless be noted that in another bull of the same Pope Paschal I, reported by Cornelius Margarini in volume II of the *Cassinese Bullarium*, constitution 16, no note after the consulship is found. We believe, however, that it was not absent from the original example, but was overlooked through the copyist’s negligence. For, besides the fact that it is clearly read in our copy, it is also appended to the aforementioned bull of the same pontiff to Bernard, bishop of Vienne. We therefore find it difficult to believe that in the bull just cited it was deliberately omitted, contrary to the practice of that pontiff and of others of his time. We infer, after examining many bulls, that this practice continued at least until the beginning of the tenth century.] but also in the year . . . . . . of Lothair, the new emperor, his son [Col. 0838A] [Note: [Col. 0839D] The year of Lothair’s empire must likewise be restored: certainly the second or the third must be supplied. For it is known to all that he was summoned by his father Louis to share the empire at the assembly held at Aachen in the summer of the year of the Lord 817.

The opinions of the writers nevertheless differ regarding the month. The imperial annalist edited by Lambecius reports that this occurred in June:

> “In the fourth year”—that is, of Louis Augustus—“the emperor Louis held his assembly with the Franks at Aachen in the month of June, and, after a fast had been proclaimed”—add “according to the Hildesheim chronicler, a fast”—“his son Lothair was appointed emperor, so that he might become co-ruler of the kingdom with his father. In that year Pope Stephen died, and Paschal succeeded him in the pontificate,” and so forth.

The annalist of Moissac does not indicate the month, although he describes the other matters with the greatest precision in these words:

> “The emperor Louis celebrated Easter at the palace of Aachen. And at that season”—perhaps “in the summer”—“he ordered an assembly of the people from the whole of his kingdom, or empire, to be held there at Aachen, the royal seat: bishops, abbots, counts, and the leading men of the Franks. He revealed to them the plan of his counsel, which he had conceived, namely, to make one of his sons emperor. For he had three sons by his wife, Queen Ermengard: the first was named Lothair, the second Pippin, and the third Louis. Then it pleased all the people that, while he was still alive, he should appoint one of his sons to rule as emperor, just as his father Charles had done with him. Then all the people fasted for three days, and litanies were celebrated. After this the aforementioned emperor chose Lothair, who was the eldest, as emperor, and bestowed the empire upon him through a golden crown, while the people acclaimed him, saying: ‘May the emperor Lothair live!’ Great joy arose among the people on that day. The emperor himself blessed the Lord, saying: ‘Blessed are you, Lord our God, who have today given me, before my eyes, one of my offspring seated upon my throne.’

> “When Bernard, son of King Pippin and king of Italy, heard what had happened, he conceived a most wicked plan. He wished to rise against the emperor and his sons and to usurp the empire by tyranny.”

Baluzius, in his notes on Agobard [Patrologia, volume CIV], asserts, on the basis of an unpublished author of the *Annals of Aniane*, that Lothair was proclaimed emperor on the third day before the Kalends of August. Pagius, however, although he does not deny that he was proclaimed emperor on that day—which in the year 817 fell on a Thursday—asserts that he was not crowned then, since at that time the practice had become established that such ceremonies were performed only on Sundays or solemn feast days.

Since our bull is dated the fifth day before the Ides of July in the year 819, if one reckons Lothair’s years of empire from June, the second year had already been completed and the third had begun. If, however, one begins from the third day before the Kalends of August, the second year of the empire was still running.

But we shall not linger over this matter any longer. On this occasion it is preferable briefly to touch upon his other eras, omitting that of the kingdom of Bavaria. They are as follows: from his confirmation in the empire at the assembly held at Nijmegen, that is, from May of the year 821; from the assembly at Attigny, at which he was sent into the kingdom of Italy, in the year 822, in the month of August, according to Einhard; from 5 April of the year 823, a day consecrated to the solemnity of Easter, when he received from Pope Paschal at Rome the crown of the Italian kingdom and of the empire; and finally from the death of his father Louis, which occurred on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July in the year 840, as Nithard, the annalists of Metz and Fulda, and the others agree.

After his father’s death, however, he began to use two eras. The first began on the twentieth day of June, which, as we recently said, was the day of Louis’s death, and from it he reckoned the years of his empire in Francia. Mabillon, in *De Re Diplomatica*, book II, chapter 26, no. 15, asserts that the other began from the year 820. There he produces several examples by which he proves that the years of the Italian empire in Lothair always precede the Frankish years by twenty years.

How Lothair could have begun the Italian empire, after his father’s death, from the year 820, the learned man honestly admits in the passage cited that he has not yet been able to determine. He merely doubts whether it should be reckoned from Bernard’s death, if that death could be extended to the end of the year 819, or perhaps from his confirmation in the empire, which, as we have already said, took place in May of the year 821 at the assembly of Nijmegen.

As for Bernard’s death, we proved in the preceding note from his tomb inscription that it occurred on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May. As for the confirmation, we demonstrated that it conflicts with the truth on the basis of the subscriptions of the diplomas that Mabillon himself cites in the passage mentioned above to prove that the eras of the Italian and Frankish empires differ by twenty years.

Among the other diplomas, Mabillon cites one dated:

> “6 October, in the year, Christ being propitious, of the empire of our lord Lothair, pious emperor, in Italy 21 and in Francia 1, indiction 3.”

He refers this formula to the year 840. But if the assembly at Nijmegen took place in May of the year 821, as he and the others agree, then on 6 October 840 the first year of the Frankish empire had indeed begun, while the Italian year was not the twenty-first but only the twentieth.

He also gives another:

> “Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of November, in the year, Christ being propitious, of the empire of our lord Lothair, pious emperor, in Francia 10 and in Italy 30, indiction 13.”

He refers this to the year 850. But on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of November, the thirtieth year of the Italian empire was indeed in progress, whereas the eleventh Frankish year had already begun on the twentieth day of June.

We omit the other formulas that he produces in the passage cited. From them the same conclusion is clearly established as from the preceding examples. Lothair’s empire in Italy, therefore, can be reckoned neither from the death of King Bernard nor from the assembly at Nijmegen, but certainly from the year 820.

Pagius, under the year 821, no. 2, infers that this era had already begun before the final day of May in the year 820 from the second part of the *Cassinese Bullarium*, constitution 30, where we read:

> “Done in the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 841, in the twenty-second year of the empire of the most Christian emperor Lothair, indiction 4, on the day before the Kalends of June.”

We do not think that much reliance should be placed upon a single example, especially one taken from the *Cassinese Bullarium*, in which the carelessness of printers or scribes has introduced so many errors into the numerical notes. It should also be added that this constitution contains not a diploma of Lothair but a donation by Rampert, bishop of Brescia, of certain goods in favor of the monastery of Saints Faustinus and Jovita. It was issued before the death of Louis the Pious, as is clear from the formula itself. Someone might therefore doubt whether it reckons the years of the Italian empire from the same era that Lothair used only after his father’s death.

In the passage already cited, Pagius assigns yet another era. He argues that it began from the year 838, when Louis Augustus made a new partition between his sons Lothair and Charles. He supports this with a single example, namely, the confirmation of a donation made to the monastery of Grandval, which Mabillon, in *De Re Diplomatica*, book II, chapter 26, no. 15, reports from the Acherian *Spicilegium*, volume VII, p. 184, as follows:

> “The eighth day before the Kalends of September, in the twelfth year of the empire of our lord Lothair”—read “pious”—“emperor, in Italy 30 and in Francia 10, indiction 12.”

Mabillon assigns this to the year 849, as does Pagius. Pagius nevertheless reckons Lothair’s twelfth year from the aforesaid era of the year 838, whereas Mabillon, recognizing that the numerical note XII was a scribal error, believed that the copyist had read the letter P, which had been obliterated in the autograph, as the numeral X for ten; he therefore corrected it by adding *lege pii* in parentheses.

Whatever may be believed concerning this era, it is certain that in so many diplomas of Lothair issued after the year 838 that we have seen, we have nowhere found any consideration given to it. Indeed, we have never found his diplomas marked with three eras in addition to the indiction.

It is meanwhile worth observing that even the most learned men have often erred in interpreting the chronological notes of Lotharian diplomas. We believe that this happened chiefly because they had not sufficiently understood the various eras that he used.

Our Puricellus, in the monuments of the Basilica of Saint Ambrose, reports two diplomas of Lothair. The first, on p. 182, reads:

> “Given on the third day before the Nones of May, in the eighteenth year, Christ being propitious, of the empire of the lord Emperor Lothair, indiction 13. Done at the royal palace of Pavia, happily in the name of God, amen.”

The second, on p. 185, reads:

> “Given on the eighth day before the Ides of May, in the eighteenth year, Christ being propitious, of the empire of our lord Lothair, pious emperor, indiction 13. Done at the royal palace of Pavia, happily in the name of God, amen.”

He refers these notes to the year 841, but incorrectly, since they correspond to the year 835, with the era taken from the year 817, as the indiction clearly demonstrates. Yet that most learned man, who was otherwise extremely diligent, candidly admits that he took no account of the indiction there. Without considering it, however, one can scarcely ever arrive at a correct reckoning of time in the diplomas of those Caesars who used various eras.

But we have no time now to pursue all matters of this kind. We shall omit only one point: Cornelius Margarini, in volume II, constitution 32 of the *Cassinese Bullarium*, cites a confirmation by Lothair of the possessions of the monastery of Bobbio under these chronological notes:

> “In the year, Christ being propitious, of the empire of our lord Lothair the emperor, in Italy 28 and in Francia 17. Done at the villa of Gandolfo, in the royal palace, happily in the name of God, amen.”

We ourselves recently saw this document in the exceptionally well-equipped archive of the monastery of Bobbio and observed that it bears the year 27 of the Italian kingdom, not 28, and year 7 of the Frankish kingdom, not 17. This agrees exactly with the eras that he used after his father’s death, as we have already said.

From Rubeus, *History of Ravenna*, p. 237.

[Col. 0832B]

[Col. 0832C]

Paschal, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to the reverend and most holy brother Petronacius, archbishop of the holy Church of Ravenna, and, through you, to that Church in perpetuity.

Since the intentions of pious desire and the purpose of praiseworthy devotion should always be assisted by apostolic efforts, diligent care must be taken that those things which are lawfully done and are fitting to equity may not be disturbed by any opposition, but may remain secure by inviolable right, and that, for this reason, the apostolic sanctions promulgated for the purpose may confirm as lawfully possessed those things which the requirements of reason [lacuna] supply.

For it is written that your fraternal holiness sent to us through Sergius, a religious deacon of your holy Church of Ravenna, [lacuna] the same document of our predecessor Pope Adrian, in which he confirmed the privileges of Leo, made by the emperor through Epiphanius, the religious notary, keeper of the archives, and apocrisiarius of the Church of Ravenna, who had been sent by the late Damian, archbishop, [lacuna] confirmed [Col. 0832D] the sacred preceding formulas of the pious Emperor Leo, both those of the divine memory of the ancient Justinian and those privileges that the other most pious emperors had generously granted to your holy Church, among which were also other pious provisions; and so that without sacrilege [lacuna] or you may bear [lacuna], the boundaries of their plunder have been generously granted, and your holiness has also requested that our apostolic [lacuna] receive firmness.

Therefore, assenting, we establish and confirm all privileges that have been issued for your holy Church of Ravenna, whether by our predecessors the pontiffs—namely, by Adrian of holy memory and by Leo, his predecessor—or by emperors, or by royal gifts, or by donations, sales, or wills made by Christian persons. We order that all such grants, generally and specifically, according to the whole arrangement of the generosity shown toward your holy Church, should possess the firmness of perpetual confirmation, and we confirm them.

No place, right, or possession subject to the jurisdiction of your holy Church may, under any pretext whatsoever, be judged, supported by civil or military power, usurped, withdrawn, or violated, nor may anyone introduce [lacuna] through the innovation of construction. But if anyone should attempt [lacuna] to restore a temple that has fallen, or to build one, he shall not have permission to do so before, by the customary blessing of your paternal holiness, the holy and venerable [object uncertain] is first set there, lest [lacuna] clerics beloved of God, coming from another episcopate or city and dwelling there, presume to exercise their ministry in the churches subject to us without our priestly authorization [Col. 0834C], but rather all the most religious clerics who come from elsewhere, [text corrupt], are to obey your holiness and be regulated, and the effect of the divine laws and most sacred rules is to be applied to them.

As for the monastery of the holy first martyr Stephen, whose foundations are so named and which lies beside the palace, and all the religious monks belonging to it, all venerable oratories or monasteries, as well as the other venerable places existing under its parish, let them be subject to your holiness’s jurisdiction and power, and through you to your holy Church. Whatever privileges they possess must be observed in their entirety. No one shall inflict upon any part of your holy Church any molestation, forced service, burden, or watch-duty; nor shall anyone withdraw from the portion subject to your holy Church the tenant farmers or [lacuna] in order to make them serve as soldiers. If they have been enlisted, we order that they be released from military service and restored to our venerable portion.

If anyone should rashly attempt to contravene such provisions, then, for the things that we have piously sanctioned and that you have rightly requested from us, as this present apostolic document provides, not only shall he accomplish nothing, but on account of such reckless audacity he shall suffer the loss of all his property, nor shall he be able to escape the danger of punishment to his soul, all this being sufficiently contained in the grant of this sole apostolic document of ours.

If anyone should act against this apostolic command of ours [lacuna], let him pay five pounds of refined gold [Col. 0836B]; moreover, let him be bound by the chains of anathema and subjected to perpetual condemnation.

We ordered this instrument of confirmation, made by us, to be copied by Timothy, the notary and keeper of the archives of our see, in the month of July, indiction 12. Farewell.

Guidus Julius, by the hand of the royal [lacuna], librarian [lacuna] of the apostolic see. Emperor Augustus, Louis [lacuna], Bondo.

# In the Year of the Lord 844. Gregory IV, Roman Pontiff.

[Col. 0841A]

# Historical Notice on Gregory IV

(Mansi, *Amplissima Collectio Conciliorum*, volume XIV, p. 503.)

[Col. 0841]

[Col. 0841A] [Note: [Col. 0842] Gregory. On 24 September 827, Gregory, adorned with the crown of every virtue, was elected pope by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit and by the unanimous agreement of the entire people and all the clergy, as the successor of Valentine. He began the pontificate that he had vainly attempted to evade from the translation of Saint Gregory, so that, strengthened by the intercession of that most holy father, he might carry upon his shoulders to the end the exceedingly burdensome pontifical office without harm to his own salvation or injury to the entire flock of the Lord.

When Michael died of dysentery, Theophilus the most cruel Iconoclast succeeded him in the East [Col. 0843C]. To settle the disturbances that had arisen between the emperor Louis and his sons, about which more will be said below, the pontiff—most devoted to peace and concord—came into Germany. He accomplished nothing among the criminal sons except to make them more hostile to himself and to the whole Roman Church, since he refused to lend his support to the efforts of the most impious sons against their father. On this occasion Louis, deprived of the empire, soon recovered his scepter; I shall discuss this below in the notes on the council held at Compiègne.

After Louis had been restored to the empire, Gregory, according to Sigebert, admonished him that in Gaul and Germany the feast of All Saints should be celebrated on the Kalends of November. Until then the Romans had been accustomed to celebrate it according to the institution of Pope Boniface. At Pope Gregory’s urging, all the bishops of Gaul and Germany obeyed Louis with remarkable unanimity.

Of these matters Alcuin [Col. 0843D]—the most celebrated writer of this age, who had already died by the year 804 [Mansi]—says the following in his commentaries on the divine offices:

> “It has been established that throughout the whole world all the people should strive to assemble at the church on the Kalends of November, as on the day of the Lord’s Nativity, for the solemn celebration of Mass in honor of all the saints, so that whatever human frailty may have performed less fully through ignorance or negligence on the solemnities of the saints might be remedied in this holy observance.”

In the eleventh year of Gregory’s pontificate, King Pippin of Aquitaine died. His kingdom, divided by Louis between Lothair, whom he had taken back into favor, and Charles, the son of his later marriage, generated new conflicts. For Louis, king of Bavaria, resuming against his father the arms that he had once been compelled to lay down, brought upon his parent troubles of such a kind that they contributed to his death, in the twenty-seventh year of his empire.

Lothair succeeded his father in the empire. Since he desired sole rule, he waged war against his brothers, not without great loss to his own affairs. Louis and Charles, by repeated embassies, could not induce him to establish peace and concord; but at last, defeated and put to flight in a bloody battle, with justice as their guide, they deprived him of the kingdom of Francia by the just judgment of the bishops, and divided it among themselves, as Nithard, a most noble Frank and grandson of Charlemagne through his daughter Berta, testifies. Later, when he humbly requested that the kingdom be restored to him, he was admitted by the counsel of the bishops, through favor, to receive a portion of the kingdom.

After the death of the emperor Theophilus, through the efforts of Michael and the empress Theodora, the heresy of the Iconoclasts was utterly destroyed in the East, and orthodox religion was restored through Methodius, the Catholic bishop of Constantinople. — SEV. BIN.]

Gregory IV, a Roman by birth, son of John, sat for sixteen years. He was a vigorous and most benevolent man, filled with holiness and piety, adorned with learning, pleasing in speech, more modest than all in conversation, most steadfast in the Catholic faith, just in his deeds, and a most diligent investigator of the divine Scriptures. He was also an indefatigable visitor of the holy churches, a father to the poor, and a nourisher of all widows. Desiring nothing earthly and abandoning the worldly gains of this present life, he acquired for himself eternal rewards in heaven through worthy merits.

This most blessed pontiff, blessed by God, illustrious by birth but still more illustrious in holiness, handsome in appearance and more beautiful in faith, did not display all these praises only during the time of his pontificate. Even while he was still in the vigor of youth, he tirelessly strove to perform such deeds. This did not remain hidden from the Romans for long, as it is written:

> “No one lights a lamp and puts it under a bushel, but on a lampstand, so that it may give light to all who are in the house” (Matthew 5).

His holy activity began to resound more fully from day to day throughout the whole city of Rome, as the Gospel teaches:

> “Nothing is covered that will not be revealed, and nothing hidden that will not be known” (Matthew 10).

For these innumerable good works, Paschal, the most holy lord of this sacred see and pope, made him not only a subdeacon but also a priest [Note: [Col. 0844D] That is, a cardinal presbyter. Mansi].

He remained established in the rank of the priesthood, chastely and modestly, recalling what Sacred Scripture says:

> “Let the priests of God be clothed with righteousness” (Psalm 131),

that is, let them occupy themselves with nothing else except prayer, reading, and fasting.

While he was devoted to these things, the aforementioned pontiff Paschal was taken from this light according to the human condition, and Eugenius, a bishop chosen by God, attained the dignity of the sacred office. After remaining in this life for only a short time, he too died. After him, Valentine obtained the summit of the episcopal office for tending the flocks, but was taken from this present life with the utmost speed.

At last all the Romans began to consider more earnestly not only the pontiffs who had been lost so suddenly, but also the future, so that they might recognize someone illumined by the grace of the Holy Spirit, under whose teaching and rule the entire nobility of the senators could live properly [Col. 0843C].

The Creator of all things, their helper in times of need and in tribulation, kindled the hearts of all those nobles with his inexhaustible holy light and turned their minds toward the pious deeds of the most blessed Gregory IV.

They all agreed in the same spirit and with one heart, and the man elected by them was brought into the Lateran patriarchate. They had dragged him there by force from the Basilica of the blessed martyrs Cosmas and Damian, for he said that he would be unfit for such a ministry. But since he could not resist so immense a multitude, they led him to the place already mentioned with hymns and spiritual songs.

But since we cannot investigate all that he accomplished in a rapid account, let us nevertheless bring briefly to everyone’s knowledge what he offered, with a sound mind and devout dedication, to holy and venerable places.

Moreover, after his election and consecration, he began to devote the greatest care to the saints and their churches, so that, with the Lord’s protection, he might quickly restore them to their former condition through renewed adornment. This was indeed done. At that time he had the church of the blessed martyr Saturninus, situated outside the Salarian Gate, which through extreme antiquity and long decay had already fallen from its foundations, rebuilt with new structures and decorated with various paintings. There also he offered one brocade garment.

When he had completed these works mentioned above, his pontifical mind began to attend most diligently to other memorials of the saints. Since he was then inflamed by the divine fire of love, he removed the body of blessed Gregory, pontiff of this universal Church, through whom the grace of the Holy Spirit had brought throughout the whole world the imperishable gift of wisdom, from the place where it had previously been buried, and transferred it with the highest honor to another place newly constructed within the church of the blessed apostle Peter, not far from the former site. He adorned its sacred altar on every side with silver panels and dedicated an oratory in his holy name. He also painted the apse of the same oratory with gilded mosaic.

In that oratory he brought the bodies of the blessed martyrs Sebastian [Note: [Col. 0844D] Sebastiani. Ado of Vienne testifies in his Chronicle that a part of the body of Saint Sebastian, removed from the City through Hilduin’s agency, was brought to Gaul and deposited in the monastery of Saint Medard. SEV. BIN.], Gorgonius, and Tiburtius from the cemeteries where they had previously lain. He placed each of them at a separate altar. Finally, during his pontificate he decreed that the monks appointed to perform the office in the church of the blessed apostle Peter should not cease to sing praises there to almighty God every day.

He offered in the same oratory eighteen larger and smaller silk curtains; three altar cloths above the altar beneath which the body of the most holy Pope Gregory rests; one with a gold-thread border, bearing a scene …; and one brocade garment upon each of the aforementioned martyrs’ altars. He also offered three silver-plated and gold-covered images above them, bearing the face of the Lord and images of those whose particular bodies, buried there, abound in miracles and virtues.

[Col. 0845A] When these works had been completed, the venerable pontiff suddenly turned his attention and mind to other matters.

[Note: [Col. 0845D] “For at that time the church of the blessed confessor …” Gregory brought into this title of Saint Mark, which he had adorned with a most noble structure, the body of Saint Hermes the martyr. By what miracles the relic of this martyr was transferred to Gaul, Eginhard relates in book IV, chapter 24. SEV. BIN.]

At that time he demolished from its foundations the church of the blessed confessor and pontiff Mark, which he had undertaken to govern during his priesthood and which remained under his authority and jurisdiction until he attained the grace of the pontificate; because of its extreme antiquity it seemed repeatedly on the point of collapse. With the help of almighty God, he then brought the whole building, through new construction, to greater dignity and beauty. He painted the apse of the aforesaid basilica with mosaic overlaid with gold-colored pigments, with great rejoicing. He made all its roof-work new and preferred that whatever he had previously recognized as poor in it should afterward be made precious.

After completing all these things for the remedy and future recompense of his soul, he offered in the aforesaid church the following objects, to remain there for future times:

One golden crown, which still hangs above the altar, with very fine gems and a golden cross in the middle, likewise adorned with precious gems. Also, three bowls of the purest gold hanging before the aforementioned altar; twelve incised silver bowls made by angelic workmanship; and five other incised bowls, with their bases.

In the same place he offered three incense vessels covered with gold-colored decoration and twelve silver baskets; nine larger and smaller silver crowns; three silver crosses, each weighing one pound; and four silver-plated candle stands.

He also made a ciborium, for the praise and adornment of the confessor so often mentioned, of the purest silver, weighing one thousand pounds. He likewise adorned his altar with silver panels, wishing through the performance of temporal works to attain eternal rewards in heaven.

The aforementioned venerable pontiff also offered, in the same place, one brocade garment with points around its border. He made another garment of holoseric silk, having gems and golden apples in the middle and a gold-thread border around it. Indeed, the most holy pontiff offered a holoseric-silk garment with griffins and unicorns. He also offered another garment with a gold-thread border around it and, in the middle, the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ.

The venerable pope mentioned so often offered in the aforesaid church a garment with griffins and a gold-thread border around it, having in the middle the nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ. He also offered another garment with a gold-thread border, having four gold-thread wheels through the middle, and the nativity and baptism of our Lord Jesus Christ.

The aforesaid pontiff also offered another garment with lions, having the Lord’s resurrection worked in gold thread. He offered eight smaller brocade garments, which are placed over the altars and are known to extend around the same church.

He offered four white silk curtains: one having Tyrian material all around, with a cross and gold-thread *gammadia* in the middle; another of *stauracium*, having in the middle a cross of holoseric silk and *gammadia* of Tyrian holoseric silk; and the third and fourth similarly.

He offered four rose-colored curtains surrounding the sacred altar, one of which has a cross of gold thread. He offered twenty-six brocade curtains, and an equal number of linen curtains, hanging from the arches of the church.

He offered three Alexandrian curtains hanging before the main doors, bearing human figures and horses; one Alexandrian curtain; four other curtains with brocade points; one curtain of octaphyllum; eight other brocade curtains having a purple *periclysis* around them; and six other curtains with eagles, having a Tyrian *periclysis* around them.

He offered five additional brocade curtains bearing lions and having a Tyrian *periclysis*. He also offered Alexandrian curtains, one of which had wheels and roses in the middle and another trees and wheels; these hung before the doors of the church.

He offered one small holoseric-silk curtain having in the middle a man with a horse; fourteen curtains with Spanish silver decoration; and ten small holoseric-silk curtains, each having ducks.

Protected here by divine inspiration, he offered in the aforesaid basilica one silver *aquaemanile*.

He also made in the church of the blessed martyrs Cosmas and Damian one brocade garment having in the middle a painted scene with a gold-thread border.

At the church of the blessed Abbacyrus [Abba Cyrus], and of the archangel at Alefantum. This elect and renowned pontiff of God offered in the basilica of the blessed martyr Eustachius one brocade garment having in the middle a scene worked in gold thread.

The pontiff mentioned so often made another brocade garment in the church of the blessed martyrs Sergius and Bacchus. In the same way he made another brocade garment in the church of Saint Sylvester situated on Mount Soracte.

[Col. 0846B] After all these things had been completed and carefully carried out, he made in the church of the blessed apostle Peter fourteen curtains with gold-thread decoration, bearing various Gospel scenes and the passions of the blessed Peter and Paul, as well as of the apostle Andrew. They hung between images cast in gold and silver on a beam plated with silver, before one approached the sacred confessio; they were exceedingly beautiful to human eyes and especially splendid.

The magnificent pontiff also made porticoes on both sides of the church of the blessed martyr of Christ, George, and adorned them with various paintings for the adornment of that basilica. With the Lord’s help he also rebuilt the apse of the same diaconia from its foundations, with the greatest care.

This most beloved pontiff, observing carefully that the sacristy of the same venerable diaconia was decaying through excessive age, newly raised it to greater dignity, out of love for it and for the benefit of others. Accordingly, the most holy pope offered the following gifts in the same place:

One brocade garment with a gold-thread border, bearing an image of the Savior and of the martyrs Sebastian and George; two larger brocade curtains and eighteen smaller ones. In the confessio of that basilica he made silver *rugae* covered with gold. In the same way he newly restored the roof-work of the basilica of the blessed martyr Hadrian, situated on the Sacred Way, which had decayed through excessive age.

He also made in the Lateran patriarchate a dining hall of remarkable size, decorated with a mosaic apse, and two other apses, situated on the right and left beneath the *paracellarium*, painted with various scenes.

The most holy pope also made in the church of the blessed confessor Clement one brocade garment with lions and a *periclysis* of octaphyllum.

Similarly, in the diaconia of the blessed martyr Theodore he made a brocade garment bearing lions, with a *periclysis* of octaphyllum.

In the church of the blessed martyr of Christ, Lawrence, situated outside the walls, he made a gold-thread garment bearing the story of Zacchaeus. He also made another brocade garment with griffins in honor of the holy Mother of God, *Ad Martyres*. Likewise, in the church of the blessed protomartyr Stephen on the Caelian Hill, he made a brocade garment with *gammadia*. In the diaconia of the blessed Mother of God on the Via Lata he made a *stauracium* garment with a *periclysis* of purple.

Similarly, in the church of the blessed Mother of God, ever-virgin Mary, our Lady, *Ad Praesepe*, he made a gold-woven garment bearing the nativity, baptism, presentation, and resurrection. At the head of these scenes it had 380 white gems, fifty hyacinth-colored gems, twenty-two green gems, and around it *alvavira* [a type of gem or ornament] bearing the name of Lord Pope Gregory IV.

[Col. 0847A] He also made in the diaconia of the blessed martyr Hadrian, *In Tribus Fatis*, one brocade garment.

The aforesaid pontiff made in the church of the blessed apostles *Ad Vincula* one brocade garment bearing lions and griffins. He also made another brocade garment in the church of the blessed confessor and pontiff Martin, bearing lions with trees.

Likewise, in the basilica of the blessed martyr Eusebius he made a holoseric-silk garment bearing eagles, with a *periclysis* of quadruple cloth.

The aforesaid pontiff also offered in the basilica of the blessed Mother of God Mary, across the Tiber, a Tyrian garment bearing a scene of the Lord’s nativity and the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Indeed, in the diaconia called Cyrus he likewise offered a brocade garment. Likewise, in the diaconia of blessed Mary on the Via Lata he offered a brocade garment.

This renowned and venerable pontiff, relying on divine inspiration, made in the church of the blessed confessor and pontiff Mark an octagonal, gilded paten, bearing in the middle the face of our Lord and, on two sides, the face of the blessed Mark. It weighed six pounds.

In the same way he offered there an octagonal cast chalice, gilded and adorned with leaves, weighing six pounds. He also had a silver cup offered there weighing six pounds.

The aforementioned pontiff also offered two *ennephodia* baskets, together weighing fourteen pounds.

In the church of the doctor of the nations, the blessed apostle Paul, the pontiff mentioned above offered a gold-thread garment bearing a scene of our Lord God, and, in his service, on the right and left, archangels and apostles, in a worthy number, of remarkable size and beauty, most beautifully adorned and woven with various stones and pearls.

This most kind and renowned pontiff, acting as a good and true shepherd and exercising the greatest care and vigilance everywhere for the condition of the holy Church of God, considered the poverty of the Romans: when they ground wheat for food, they had no place at all in which to do so. Relying on divine assistance, he therefore undertook, with devoted labor, to rebuild and reconstruct the structure called the Sabbatina, which had seemed for many years already to be broken and ruined, just as it had been built in ancient times, so that it might flow without interruption, as before, toward the church of the blessed apostle Peter and toward the Janiculum.

He also made in the diaconia of the blessed ever-virgin Mary at *Cosmedin* a Tyrian garment bearing the scene of the Lord’s nativity and the resurrection of Christ, our true God.
