For the honor and glory of the blessed virgin of God Susanna, the most holy pontiff offered in her church a brocade garment with a Tyrian *periclysis*.

In the church of the blessed martyr and deacon Cyriacus he made a brocade garment bearing a *periclysis* of *stauracium*. Similarly, in the church of the blessed virgin Pudentiana he made a brocade garment with a *periclysis* of quadruple cloth.

He offered to the blessed martyr Vitalis a brocade garment bearing eagles and a *periclysis* of quadruple cloth.

The aforesaid pontiff made in the church of the blessed martyr Anastasia a brocade garment bearing eagles and a *periclysis* of holoseric silk.

Indeed, the pontiff mentioned above offered in the basilica of the blessed martyr Lucia, called *Orfea*, a brocade garment with a *periclysis* of octaphyllum.

Finally, the most holy pontiff made in the title of the blessed martyr Chrysogonus a Tyrian garment bearing the story of Daniel, with a *periclysis* of *stauracium*.

The most blessed pope offered in the title of Pammachius a *stauracium* garment with a *periclysis* of quadruple cloth.

He also made in the church of the blessed martyr Cecilia a brocade garment bearing eagles and griffins, with a *periclysis* of holoseric silk.

[Col. 0848A] Similarly, in the title of Aemiliana he offered a brocade garment bearing eagles and a *periclysis* of Byzantine purple.

Likewise, in the church of the blessed martyr and pontiff Sixtus he made a Tyrian garment bearing the story of Daniel, with a *periclysis* of holoseric silk.

He made in the basilica of the blessed martyr Balbina a brocade garment with a *periclysis* of holoseric silk.

In the title of Damasus he made a *stauracium* garment bearing a *periclysis* of Byzantine purple.

He also made a brocade garment in the church of the apostles James and Philip. Likewise, in the church of the blessed confessor and pontiff Marcellus he made a brocade garment.

Similarly, in the basilica of the blessed Lawrence at Lucina he made a *stauracium* garment. In the church of Saint Valentine he made a brocade garment with *gammadia* of octaphyllum.

When all these things recorded above had been more freely completed and perfected by the fourth pope of this undefiled see, Gregory, with God’s favor, he did not wish to be idle. After caring for the flocks, he began without distinction to attend to the cultivation and improvement of venerable places, so that in his time they might be strengthened with a new form of cultivation. This was accomplished, through the intercession of the prince of the apostles, Peter, in accordance with the wish of his desire.

While he was turning such matters over in his pontifical mind and considering them hesitantly, it suddenly came back to his memory that it would not be right for the church of the holy Mother of God, which to this day, according to ancient custom, is called Callistus, across the Tiber, to remain without the service of monks—especially since miracles of no small importance and various acts of power frequently occur there.

At last, divinely moved in heart and strengthened and supported by the help of almighty God, he established a monastery from its foundations beside the aforementioned basilica and adorned it with new buildings. He also gathered canonical monks there, who were to perform the office in that place and, day and night, sing thanks and praises to almighty God with the inward breath of their hearts.

As we now see, the outstanding shepherd greatly enlarged and firmly established this work with great struggle and great zeal. Where previously there had been no notable cultivation, there are now, by God’s ordering, beautiful dwellings for monks. In places that recently appeared full of brambles and filth, cells have now been built in which the sheep of Christ, together with all that benefits them, dwell and sleep abundantly after the offices of praise.

At that time the aforesaid church was broken down in certain places around it by long decay, but he restored it on every side with very strong fortifications. He also made in it a holy manger after the likeness of the manger of the holy Mother of God called Major, and adorned it with gold and silver sheets.

In it, for the remedy and forgiveness of sins, he offered these gifts: a golden image bearing a scene of our Lady and various precious gems; thirteen larger hyacinths; ten green gems; twenty-nine larger white gems; twenty larger almandines; and small white gems around the crown of the head, of various *philopares*.

[Note: [Col. 0847D] A very corrupt passage.]

There are two pairs of *cercelli*, having eighteen precious white gems, eight green gems, and four hyacinth-colored gems.

The same image also has two extremely precious green *murenae*, from which eleven pendants hang. It also has a three-stranded golden *murena*, bearing seventy-three various white gems and thirty-three small knobs.

It has a *murena* from which thirteen hyacinth-colored gems hang; nine golden finger-shaped ornaments hang from a golden thread. It also has a threaded *murena*, from which fourteen hyacinth-colored gems hang.

The image of Christ has two little ships and three *murenae*, all the *murenae* with their comb-like ornaments.

It has the purest gold, incised *gabathae*, of the *philopare* type.

It has a sign of Christ hanging on three lily-shaped chains, and a hook … bearing an inscription about the gifts of God and of holy Mary, called the Manger across the Tiber, of Lord Pope Gregory IV, who willingly offered three stone-inlaid *gabathae*.

The sign of Christ bears a scene in the form of an unmaned lion, with various works in the purest gold hanging on four chains and one hook.

It also has a stone-inlaid *gabatha* in the form of Leo IV, with various scenes of serpents, and a pine tree standing in the middle, gilded, with four little lions hanging on three chains and one hook.

It also has stone-inlaid *gabathae*. From each of them gilded works hang on three chains, with four hooks; one of them has glass gems. Lord Pope Gregory IV offered these willingly.

Indeed, the pontiff mentioned above offered in the church of the doctor of the nations, the blessed apostle Paul, a brocade curtain hanging from the triumphal arch, having in the middle the annunciation and nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ.

He also offered one holoseric-silk curtain hanging from a horizontal rod beneath a silver image, bearing a scene of an emperor. There he also made two other small brocade curtains, hanging around the altar and having twenty-five straps.

He made twenty-four curtains hanging in the presbytery and forty brocade curtains hanging from the larger arches. In the ciborium of the same church he made four curtains.

Similarly, in the church of the blessed martyr of Christ, George, he made six brocade curtains having *gammadia* of octaphyllum around them.

This God-protected and renowned pontiff made in the monastery of Saint Sabas a holoseric-silk garment with lions, having a *periclysis* of octaphyllum.

He also made, in the same way, in the monastery of the martyr Saint Anastasius a *stauracium* garment with a *periclysis* of quadruple cloth.

Likewise, in the monastery of Saint Andrew, called *in Clivo Scauri*, he made one *stauracium* garment with a *periclysis* of octaphyllum.

In the monastery of the martyr Saint Agatha, situated above the Subura, he made one holoseric-silk garment with a *periclysis* of octaphyllum.

He also made in the monastery of Saint Erasmus one *stauracium* garment with a *periclysis* of octaphyllum.

In the diaconia of Saint Lucia, situated at the Seven Ways, he made one holoseric-silk garment with a *periclysis* of octaphyllum.

In the oratory of Saint Lucia, situated in the monastery of Serenatus, he made a holoseric-silk garment with lions, having a *periclysis* of octaphyllum.

Similarly, in the monastery of Saint Sylvester he made one holoseric-silk garment with a *periclysis* of octaphyllum. There he also made a brocade garment with griffins, having a *periclysis* of purple.

Likewise, in the monastery of Saint Praxedis he made one holoseric-silk garment with a *periclysis* of *stauracium*.

This God-protected and renowned pontiff made in the basilica of the doctor of the world, the blessed apostle Paul, curtains of gold thread across the arches of the presbytery, bearing a scene of the blessed apostle Paul himself and, around them, a gold border, twenty-seven in number.

This elect and renowned pontiff of God offered in the church of the blessed Mother of God, ever-virgin Mary, our Lady, which we call that of Callistus and Cornelius, two silver crowns, each having twelve dolphins, together weighing twelve pounds.

Likewise, in the diaconia of the blessed martyr of Christ, Gregory, he made one silver crown with twelve dolphins, weighing six pounds.

This God-protected and renowned pontiff made in the basilica of the blessed Mother of God, ever-virgin Mary, our Lady, which we call that of Callistus and Cornelius, four silver baskets bearing the inscription “Holy Mother of God, Pope Gregory IV,” weighing twenty-four pounds.

He also made on its altar silver panels weighing 113 pounds.

The same venerable pope made in the same holy place, within the precinct of the church, a laborious and beautiful raised structure.

Previously the altar had stood in a low place, almost in the middle of the vault. Around it the people of both sexes gathered, while the pontiff celebrated the sacred mysteries with the clergy confusedly mingled among the people.

Moreover, the holy bodies of the blessed Callistus, Cornelius, and Calepodius, buried in the middle part of the church and lying behind the people, were not being honored suitably.

The same most religious pope did not endure this lightly. Applying himself with his customary carefulness and deepest diligence, he began and successfully completed a marvelous work.

Having excavated a hidden chamber, he lifted the aforesaid holy bodies with the highest reverence and honorably placed and concealed them in the western part of the same church, that is, in the circuit of the apse. Around them he raised a massive mound, building and adorning a platform for the ministers with dressed stones.

Above the confessio, facing the rising sun, he fitted together a structure decorated with carvings of wondrous fragrance and ornament.

Beneath the rising base of the altar, he raised, in honor of the holy Mother of God, ever-virgin Mary, a structure plainly made of silver, of wondrous proportion and adornment, higher than the former one, between ascending steps of beautiful workmanship.

Before it he constructed the spacious presbytery completely, with elaborate workmanship. On its northern side he added stones around the enclosure of the matrons.

Adding beauty to the altar and honoring the Mother of the Lord with worthy gifts, he made there a gold-thread garment with Byzantine purple, bearing scenes of the nativity and resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ. Above it he also placed an image of the blessed Mother of God Mary, embracing an image of her donor.

This God-protected and renowned pontiff made six silver *amae*, which precede all the stations, weighing thirteen pounds. He made two cups, each weighing ten pounds, and eight *gemmiliones*, each weighing two pounds.

After all these things had been suitably completed by the oft-mentioned pontiff, with God’s favor, he restored to their former condition and adornment those things in the church of the blessed apostle Peter outside the walls that seemed already ruined through long age.

He newly adorned almost the whole portico above the oratory of the holy Mother of God Mary, called *Mediana*, with beams and other timbers, for the beauty of the basilica.

He also completed, in a new manner and with special adornment, another portico before the silver doors.

Furthermore, on the front of the paradise of the aforementioned church he decided to paint and restore with great speed, in the principal mosaic, all the things that had been destroyed on that wall since ancient times.

He also renewed the portico of the same basilica that is visible above its steps, by which the people freely ascend in fulfillment of their vow of prayer.

Near the *acolitus*, for the pontiff’s rest, he also made a small but honorably constructed lodging, where, after the morning prayers or the offices of the Mass, his limbs might rest, and he decorated it with outstanding paintings.

Among the other examples of good works, he also made in the Lateran patriarchate, for the benefit and use of the pontiff, near the oratory of the holy martyr of Christ Lawrence, a sufficiently suitable dwelling where there was excellent rest and from which the pontiff, departing with his clergy, could offer due praises to almighty God.

After all the works mentioned above had been built—works that had already been ruined or, through the passage of time, were nearly collapsing, and that the ancient fathers had evidently constructed below the palace—the most blessed Pope Gregory, so often mentioned, rebuilt and arranged them from their foundations with new adornment and workmanship.

He newly reformed the descent facing the *paracellarium*, by which people previously went up and down as though at night, so that thereafter no darkness could obstruct those passing through it as before.

From that place all the way to the oratory of Saint Lawrence he restored everything that was old, and he added other new structures, among which he ordered three heated rooms to be made.

He also entirely renewed from its foundations the bathhouse situated beside the *paracellarium*, and decorated it with marble and other suitable works. Previously it seemed destined to collapse through the long persistence of age, unless the mind and excellent zeal of so great a pontiff had decided to restore it to its former condition.

Similarly, in the church of the Savior, which is called Constantiniana, he made a gold-woven garment bearing scenes of palm branches and the Lord’s Supper.

In the venerable monastery of the holy Mother of God, ever-virgin Mary, and of Saints Cornelius and Callistus, which they call *Trans Tiberim*, he made six baskets, together weighing eighteen pounds; one cup weighing eight pounds and four ounces; a *cantharum* with an incense vessel, weighing three pounds; and one *siclon*, weighing three pounds.

When all these works had been completed and carried out exactly, since, as has already been said, his holy, venerable, and memorable simplicity was always intent upon the service of almighty God, he was likewise unstintingly concerned for the future safety of the people and the liberation of his homeland, lest they should in any way, with God’s permission withheld, be captured by enemies.

[Note: [Col. 0851D] “For during the times of this most holy pope …” For the same reason, Gregory, as Sigebert testifies, laid the foundations of another new city, so that he might make safe the basilica of Saint Peter situated outside the City. He adds that it was called Leonine because Gregory began it and Leo IV completed it. Sigebert’s words are these: “Pope Gregory, grieving that the suburb of the Roman city around the church of the blessed prince of the apostles, Peter, was harassed and devastated by frequent incursions of the Saracens, intended to build a new city there. Encouraged for this purpose by the counsel and assistance of the emperor, he made a new structure but did not complete it; for Leo IV of that name finished the work he had begun.” This is Sigebert. SEV. BIN.]

In the times of this most sacred father and pope, the impious, wicked, and God-hated race of the Hagarenes rose from its own regions, traversed nearly all the islands and the regions of every land, and cruelly carried out the plundering of people and the desolation of places; nor has it in any way ceased to do so to this day.

The most merciful pontiff, greatly fearful of these unusual dangers, and anxious lest the people entrusted by God to him and to the blessed apostle Peter—those who lived in the cities of Portus and Ostia—should suffer loss through tribulation and plunder at the hands of the most wicked Saracens, drew sighs from the depths of his heart and began prudently to inquire how he might assist and liberate the city of Ostia.

Immediately almighty God placed this counsel in his heart: that he should build there from the foundations a new city in which he might preserve the people, since the city built in earlier times, shaken by long decay, now appeared to lie in ruins.

He acted according to the divine inspiration given to him. In the aforementioned city of Ostia he built another city from the ground, exceedingly strong, fortified on every side with higher walls, gates, bars, and portcullises. Above them he constructed, with noble skill, stone-throwing machines for attacking enemies should they come. Outside, not far from those same walls, he surrounded the city with a deeper ditch, so that they might not easily reach the walls.

When the aforesaid city deserved the beginning of its new construction, the most holy pope himself remained there for many days and, taking as his allotted share a substantial section of the walls with his own men, raised it from its foundations.

Until, with God’s favor, the oft-mentioned city was brought to the lawful completion of its entire construction, he unceasingly endured many labors and struggles in his holy heart.

He also established that the newly built city should bear this name forever: that it should be called by all, whether Romans or members of other nations, by the name proper to it, namely Gregoriopolis.

And it rightly took its name from its founder, because—something we read of no other pontiff—this man, with the help of almighty God and fortified by his power, built and arranged the work already named, for the people and the liberation of his homeland, with marvelous architectural beauty.

With these things remaining in their proper places, the same angelic and outstanding pontiff made in the basilica of the Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ, beside the Lateran patriarchate, a garment with a gold-thread border, bearing on the front of the altar a scene of the most blessed Baptist and evangelist John.

Around the altar he likewise made a continuous unified covering, as though curtains of gold thread, with certain paintings in the form of griffins, whose horns were painted on their heads.

He also made in the monastery of the most blessed martyr of Christ Lawrence, called *Pallacinis*, six silver baskets, two silver-plated candle stands, one silver cup, and likewise one silver *ama*.

He also made in the oratory of the most holy Pope Gregory, situated within the church of the blessed apostle Peter, four small silver columns containing forty pounds of silver.

After all this, the venerable pontiff ordered a sufficiently worthy house to be newly built from the ground in the court called *Draconis*, surrounded on every side by porticoes and upper galleries. In it both he himself and future pontiffs, together with all who serve them, could remain spaciously for as long as they wished.

Likewise, in another court called *Galeria*, he made another broad and spacious house, sufficiently distinguished for the work and use of the pontiffs, where, whenever it should be convenient, they might lodge most amply with all who serve them.

The same nourishing and renowned pontiff, burning with heavenly love, made in the basilica of the holy, undefiled virgin and Mother of God, our Lady Mary, called *Ad Martyres*, a ciborium of the purest silver, weighing four hundred pounds altogether. He also made one crown of the purest silver, weighing ten and a half pounds.

Similarly, in the basilica of the blessed confessor and pontiff Marcellus he made three crowns of the purest silver, together weighing … pounds.

Indeed, in the diaconia of the blessed martyr George he made an Alexandrian curtain bearing twelve pheasants, and one linen, feathered curtain before the doors.

When this most blessed pontiff had ruled the Roman and apostolic see most gloriously for sixteen years, he was taken from this light and departed to eternal rest.

He held five ordinations in the months of March and December, or seven; [he ordained] priests …, deacons …, and bishops in various places, 185 in number.

He was buried in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter.

[Col. 0853]

## LETTERS OF POPE GREGORY IV

### FIRST LETTER. TO ALL BISHOPS

On accusing Aldric, bishop of Le Mans, nowhere except before the apostolic see, and on the power of the Roman pontiff.

To our most beloved brothers, all fellow bishops established throughout Gaul, Germany, Europe, and all the provinces, Gregory, [the Roman edition adds: “bishop,”] servant of the servants of God.

We are stirred by divine commandments and most salutary apostolic admonitions to keep watch with unflagging concern [Edit. Rom. omits: “unflagging”] for the condition of all the Churches. And since, by divine dispensation, we bear responsibility for all the Churches, we desire to assist all who seek our apostolic support. For it is a decree of divine power and human frailty that the affairs of all the Churches should tend toward the concern of our restoration. [Col. 0853B] [Note: 2, question 6, *Decr. nostro*; Ivo, part V, chapter 349.]

Therefore we send this letter to you, in which, by our decree, we ask your charity and command that, if anyone—which we do not desire—should wickedly attempt to accuse Aldric, bishop of the Church of Le Mans, at the instigation of his rivals, then, in order that the memory of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, the privilege of the Roman Church over which he presided, and the authority of our name may be honored, he shall be permitted, after the hearing before the primates of the diocese, if need should arise, to appeal to us; and, by our authority, either before us or before legates sent from our side, in accordance with the decrees of the Fathers, to conduct and conclude his proceedings. No one is to judge him, or presume to judge him, before this has taken place. [Col. 0853C] [Note: Ibid., chapter 11.]

But if—God forbid—some grave and intolerable charge should be brought against him, our decision must be awaited, so that nothing may first be decreed concerning one who has fled to the bosom of the holy Roman Church and implored its aid, until it has been commanded by the authority of that same Church. It has so distributed its functions among other Churches that they have been called to share in its solicitude, not in the fullness of its power.

Therefore let your affection, in whose devotion we rejoice, join its care to our arrangements, and take pains that, through the presumption of anyone, nothing whatsoever be decreed concerning the aforesaid brother—whether by your provision or that of your successors, should he himself survive—otherwise than has been inserted here. Rather, let these provisions, which have been set forth here by authority for his protection and defense and salutarily established, be fully carried out without any excuse. [Col. 0853D] [Note: Ibid., section “But if.”]

But if—which we do not suppose—anyone should presume otherwise, and he should be removed from clerical office and judged guilty of wrongs by everyone, let not wolves who have entered in the guise of sheep dare to tear people apart with beastly savagery [Col. 0854A] and presume to inflict on others what they do not want done to themselves.

Nor should anyone frivolous, contentious, or obstinate contend that we prescribe these things irrationally, since both the authority of the canons and the decrees of our predecessors have sanctioned that an accused bishop, if he wishes, may appeal to the Roman pontiff and, if he chooses, flee to him; either his case may be heard by him, or he may send legates from his side to hear it, who, together with all the bishops of his province, may judge it justly by his authority.

It is unnecessary to insert all these provisions here, lest we appear to be traitors rather than instructors. Our predecessor, Innocentius, of holy memory, said among other things as follows: “If greater cases have arisen, let them be referred to the apostolic see, as the Council of Nicaea determined and ancient custom has required.” And there are many other such provisions, which are found in full in their own authors.

Nor should these things appear burdensome or useless to any brother. For just as we come to the aid of the aforesaid brother by the authority of Saint Peter and our see, so we both ought and wish to assist all who require it, without delay. And just as each person wishes help for himself, so he ought to help another, and not resent another’s assistance, since the Apostle urges everyone: “Rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep” (Romans XII).

We direct all our purpose and care toward this end: that nothing pertaining to the exaltation of the holy Church of God, or to the protection and advancement of priests, be violated by dissension or neglected through indolence. [Col. 0854C] [Note: 2, question 7, “If anyone should accuse.”]

If anyone wishes to criticize us [Edit. Rom. adds: “us”] concerning these matters, or attempts to act outside our authority, let him come to the apostolic see, to which all ecclesiastical affairs in dispute have been commanded to converge, so that there, before the confession of Saint Peter, he may contend justly with me, and one of you may there receive his sentence.

We exhort and admonish you, brothers, not to disturb by any dispute what we have piously commanded you concerning the aforesaid brother and what has been salutarily established and enjoined for the defense of his simplicity. For temerity of presumption is absent where there is diligence. Let none of you seek what is his own, but what belongs to another, and what the Apostle says: “Let each of us please his neighbor for his good,” and the rest (Romans XV). [Col. 0854D] [Note: Distinction 12, “By apostolic commandments.”]

Therefore, apostolic commandments must not be resisted with harsh pride; rather, what has been commanded by the holy Roman [Edit. Rom. adds: Church] and apostolic authority must be beneficially fulfilled through obedience, if you desire to remain in communion with that same holy Church of God [Edit. Rom. omits: of God], which is your head. [Col. 0855A]

Those who know that they have been placed over certain people should not resent someone’s being placed over them; rather, they themselves should uphold the obedience they demand [Edit. Rom.: *dependant*, “they depend”]. Hence it is clear that, with every effort of devotion, you must unanimously obey divine and apostolic commands and, God forbid, become disobedient in nothing. [Note: Distinction 45, “Although very often.”]

For although matters deserving correction often arise among priests, benevolence accomplishes more toward those who must be corrected than severity, exhortation more than threat [Edit. Rom.: *commotio*, “agitation”], charity more than power, since none of us lives without reproach or sin. [Note: Ivo, part V, chapter 368.]

For if the Lord had judged the blessed apostle Peter, our teacher, immediately after his threefold denial, He would not have received from him so great a fruit as He did. Therefore the rulers of the Churches must rather be awaited and corrected than judged immediately and without consultation with us. For the canons of the holy Fathers, composed by the Spirit of God and consecrated by the reverence of the whole world, command that greater affairs and more difficult outcomes of cases be suspended while our sentence is awaited and be brought to an end under our guidance [Edit. Rom.: “preserved”].

It is therefore necessary that these and all other ecclesiastical affairs be examined more carefully and guarded more diligently after the experience of many cases, so that, through the spirit of charity and peace, every source of scandal, the presumption of the envious, and the oppression of the simple [Edit. Rom.: “of simple brothers”] may be removed from the Churches of the Lord.

And just as none of the brothers wishes to be weighed down by another’s judgment, so let no one dare inflict upon others what he does not wish done to himself, remembering the command of the Lord and Savior, who says: “Do not judge, and you will not be judged” [Edit. Rom.: “so that you may not be judged”]; “For with the judgment with which you judge, you will be judged” (Matthew VII), and the rest.

Therefore we must not, through our leniency, detract in anything from the tribunal of the exalted Judge, since those things are valid which are pious, true, and just; and the consideration of necessity must be treated in one way, that of intention in another. For the enemy has left no one untouched; therefore those caught in his snares must be helped. The hunter’s snare must therefore be crushed, so that, when lamentations have been driven away, the sun of justice may shine in the eyes of those who are falling, both through just moderation and through the compunction of mercy, by apostolic authority. [Note: Ibid., chapter 11.]

Nor should it perhaps displease or shame you to obey our commands or observe the precepts of the apostolic see, since God gives grace to the humble, not to the proud. [Note: Distinction 19, “No one is permitted.”] For no one is permitted either to wish or to be able to transgress the precepts of the apostolic see, nor the ministry of our disposition, which your charity ought to follow.

Therefore let anyone who wishes to oppose apostolic decrees lie prostrate in grief at his own ruin. Let him henceforth have no place among priests, but be exiled from the holy ministry; and let no one afterward concern himself with his judgment, since he has already been condemned by the holy and apostolic Church by this authority, and it is not doubted that, by this authority, he has already been condemned by the holy and apostolic Church for his disobedience and presumption. For he must be expelled by the greater excommunication of deposition, to whom the discipline of the holy Church has been entrusted, since he ought not only to have obeyed the commands of the aforesaid holy Church but also to have instructed others not to disregard them. Let him who refused to obey apostolic commands be excluded from divine and pontifical offices.

Let the aforesaid Aldric therefore remain, by this apostolic authority, always a bishop until he appears before the apostolic see. Before he comes here, let him pay no attention to the harmful words of such people or others, submit to their judgment, or receive any harsh sentence; nor let him be disobedient to us, as they are—which we by no means suppose he will be.

Let him appeal, if he wishes and if necessity requires, to the holy bishop of the aforesaid apostolic see, and let him go freely to him without any impediment. If certain bishops supported by apostolic authorities cannot be bound, judged, or condemned, how much less can this be done by those who—if the deed has occurred, which we do not believe—have already been condemned by the authority of those bishops for their disobedience and insolence?

For we cannot correct or govern persecutors of their brothers except by the commands of the holy see, before which the whole world bows as before its head, in accordance with the examples of the Fathers who preceded us, unless we pursue them with zeal for the Lord’s faith and cut them off from sound minds, with whatever severity we can, lest this plague spread farther.

Whoever attempts what has been forbidden will feel that the censure of the apostolic see will by no means be lacking. And whoever refuses to obey apostolic admonitions must necessarily be punished by the rule of severity, lest anyone do or permit something by which he may deceive another by seizing him and create for himself causes through which he may become liable under the decretal statutes.

Beware, brothers, of neglecting what has been stated; beware of attempting what has been forbidden, lest you become entangled in the aforesaid restraints. Do not judge, condemn, or burden the often-mentioned brother without our presence or authority, as has been stated. Rather, just as he has been fortified by apostolic protections, so let him be supported by your assistance, and let him remain untouched and free from every snare, oppression, or human judgment of the entire priestly order until our judgment, as has been said—he who has merited the aid of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. [Col. 0856D]

Therefore do not raise yourselves against the head. Do not despise the see of blessed Peter the key-bearer, whose legation we discharge in Christ’s place, or the authority of his see, lest you suffer his offense or generate scandal for the Church. Rather, be especially concerned for the salvation and liberation of your brothers, and labor with the greatest zeal for the welfare of the holy Church of God.

Arm yourselves with charity, not severity. Let charity meet each one of you individually, and let it rejoice with you forever in the Lord, joined with you by the bonds which Christ releases in a thousand ways.

Moreover, you must restrain and instruct by ecclesiastical discipline the persecutors of their brothers: those who, not maintaining the standing [Edit. Rom.: “statutes”] of their forebears, often attempt, by their presumption, to violate God’s priests and the holy Church—which consists chiefly in its priests—while following the favor of rulers and peoples and not fearing God’s judgment.

You must give them no consent, whether by deeds, counsels, open actions, or secret ones, as the Lord says: “You saw a thief, and you ran with him” (Psalm XLIX). Not only those who do these things, but also those who consent to those who do them, are held guilty.

This alone ought to arouse your minds most forcefully: that you may be found immune from every stain of this world and secure before God’s sight; that, without losing charity, you may be supporters of your brothers, so that, in accordance with the Apostle, you may remain united, pursuing one thing, in Christ, claiming nothing through contention or empty glory, but pleasing in all things not human beings but God our Savior (Philippians II).

Therefore, by this bond of charity, I beg you, restrain them from the aforesaid brother. If you learn of the plots or rivalry of any persons whatever, do not in any way give your consent to them—something we judge harder than all other harsh things [Edit. Rom.: “harder than harsh matters”].

Even if he does not have agreeable conduct in some respect, he must nevertheless be held dear out of reverence for Saint Peter, by whose authority he is fortified. We do not command anything new by this present order [Note: Distinction 12, “By apostolic commands,” section “Not a new thing.”]; rather, we confirm those things that appear to have been granted long ago. No one can doubt that not only every episcopal case but also every matter concerning holy religion must be referred to the apostolic see, as to the head of the Churches, and receive its rule from the place from which it received its beginning. Otherwise the head of the institution would appear to be disregarded; and all priests who do not wish to be torn away from the solidity of the apostolic rock, upon which Christ founded the universal Church, must uphold the sanction of its authority.

If anyone does not observe these precepts of the apostolic see, he must unquestionably be regarded as an enemy of the honor he has received. Perhaps you and your predecessors have not resisted until now. And lest it ever happen that you resist, we repeat our admonitions again and again, so that those who seek to disturb such brothers may be avoided and prevented from sowing anything other than what our farmer has commanded.

For how can those who disturb the minds of the elect fail to grieve us, when no one wishes anyone to perish? The Lord’s word in the Gospel bears witness. The Savior himself says that it would be better for one who causes scandal to one of the little ones to be plunged into the depths of the sea, and the other things that pertain to this meaning (Matthew XVIII).

All Christians, not only priests, must beware of such people, since priests, who are called the thrones of God, ought to be at peace and free from every disturbance. Nor was it without reason that the Savior himself overturned the tables of the money-changers with his own whip and drove the sellers of doves from the temple (Matthew XXI). Hence it is clear that the chief priests await his judgment. To confirm this, what he says elsewhere is of great force: “God stood in the assembly of the gods, but in the midst he distinguishes the gods” [Edit. Rom.: “the Lord”] (Psalm LXXXI), and other such passages, which are found in their own sources.

Therefore we cannot excuse those who do not wish to be watchmen if we permit brothers, whom we ought to protect and assist to the best of our ability, to be defiled by wicked contagion. Accordingly, we exhort, entreat, and admonish your affection to watch over these matters with the diligence you ought [Edit. Rom.: “you ought and can”], because you ought to be on the watchtower, lest the audacity of those who attack break forth.

Resist such people with all your strength, because it is impious to burden the religious [Edit. Rom.: “to preach against the religious”] and to tolerate the suffering of brothers, whose affliction ought also to torment us, since they are our members. We must bear the cross in accordance with the word of the Lord and Savior, who says: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Matthew XVI).

Yet blessedness remains promised to those who are proved to endure persecution for the sake of justice. The Savior’s following discourse declares what he promises them in the future.

Let us understand that these things displeasing to us are also displeasing to you. We shall be able to prove this only if you extend your hand with us to those to whom we extend ours, so that we may extend ours with you to anyone to whom you extend yours. For we are not one flock and one shepherd in any other way than as the Apostle teaches, saying: “Let us all say the same thing, and let us be perfected in the same understanding and in the same judgment” (1 Corinthians I).

May God preserve you unharmed, most beloved brothers, mindful of us.

## Letter II. To the Bishops and Orthodox Faithful

[Note: Codex Laudunensis: “This compiled letter, compiled in part from Gregory—how false it is, the evidence itself clearly shows. For in Gregory’s time—the time of the man in whose name this was written—the emperor Louis had been expelled from the empire, and after the emperor’s restoration Ebo was deposed by his own judgment and that of the bishops, and was condemned by Sergius, Gregory’s successor, to lay communion alone.”]

He restores Ebo, archbishop of Reims, who had been deposed, to his former rank.

Gregory, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to his most reverend and holy brothers in Christ, his fellow bishops, and also to all orthodox princes and all the faithful of the Catholic Church.

Since, by divine prompting, we must always keep careful watch over the Lord’s flock, in prosperity, how much more in the excessive adversities that have come upon our days because of sins? Just as those who persist with wicked intention amid God’s scourges and perish are to be mourned, so those who, corrected by such great chastisement, make themselves ready to be corrected with contrite and humbled hearts are to be congratulated rather than cast off. Above all, those are to be magnified who, tested in distress with a perfect and excellent heart, unwillingly bring the fruit of life to their lesser brethren by salutary examples.

Therefore, dearest brothers, we rightly give immense thanks to our Lord God for your great triumph: amid the world’s battles and excessive diabolical temptations, He tested you and preserved you unharmed. By turning neither to the right nor to the left and avoiding offense against God, you overcame worldly dangers with the greatest caution and discernment.

Among your many other great struggles, the case of our brother Ebo, archbishop, was certainly not the least [Forte: “was not the least,” Hard.]. As we have often learned through many faithful informants, he was neither canonically summoned but was violently dragged away from the Church, endured various exiles, and was thrust into close confinement. Convicted of no definite crime and having made no voluntary confession, he was held under another’s power in the absence of his Church and was thus brought before you by secular power to be examined or deposed.

You therefore appeased, with marvelous circumspection and compassion, the irrational violence that had arisen among the people, and so softened the fury of his persecutors by humble satisfaction that you escaped both divine and human offense. Thus, by prudent care, you preserved the brother unharmed so that he might be restored at a more suitable time, just as it is written concerning the true members of Christ: “When one member suffers, all the other members suffer with it” (1 Corinthians XII).

Your kindly intention also became clear when, as soon as you had obtained even a small measure of ecclesiastical peace, he was restored to his rightful see by imperial and episcopal authority—the see from which he had been violently dispossessed—and there, by public consent, he received and discharged the customary pontifical office, as he ought, until the disputes of the princes were again inflamed. Then, in order to pacify the dreadful sedition, he offered himself with the other faithful of the kingdom.

When that disturbance had been calmed, he was immediately sent by an unexpected imperial command to the eastern regions, for the sake of the concord and unity of the Christian people, and he willingly obeyed his commanders to the best of his ability.

After all these things had been carried out so praiseworthily, worn out by many labors and making his way to the apostolic see, he faithfully fulfilled the vow of visitation that he had made to the Lord and to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, in his distress. Trusting in the intercessions of the holy prince of the apostles, to whom the power of binding and loosing had been divinely given, he was rescued from bodily dangers; and that prince, in his mercy, would also absolve him from all the bonds of sin.

Therefore, having carefully considered all these matters, we received the confession that he made privately with you, and he communicated it fully to us. He also satisfied the holy Roman Church by showing it the written subscription that, terrified, he had composed in order to escape.

In all these matters we found no certain crime warranting deposition or legitimate absolution. Therefore we confidently entrust him to your inviolable charity. If it can be done without cruel persecution, we desire that he be restored with you to his rightful see. Otherwise, however, bishops ought not to neglect a fellow bishop divinely joined to them, in whom we have recognized not merely a similar but a renewed spirit of his sacred dignity through penitence, restored after the example of David.

David, renewed and strengthened by a right or princely spirit, promised with complete confidence that he would afterward teach and recall even the impious for the sake of the Lord his God, and he faithfully endeavored to fulfill this through perpetual examples of kindness.

The chief of the apostles himself, whose place we unworthy men occupy, denied his discipleship in danger, but was not cast off; rather, he was mercifully recalled and regained his former dignity, learning in himself how mercy ought to be shown to others.

Moreover, that evangelical father, in his abundant kindness, did not reject the prodigal son but joyfully received him when he was lost and restored him with honor to his former status. He himself also instructed his true followers, saying: “Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful” (Luke VI; Matthew III). For the same Lord of lords, abundant in mercies, has declared throughout all the regions of the world that the merciful are blessed.

Instructed by these and many other testimonies of the Old and New Testament, we faithfully carry out the evangelical and ecclesiastical order if we grant bishops who have suffered persecution and fled to another city the free ability to minister in vacant places.

How much more should we do this for the aforesaid brother of ours, who was once joined to us with the consent of the glorious Caesar and the whole empire, and confirmed to the holy Roman Church by an unbreakable bond of charity through apostolic privileges?

Having received there the mission of preaching, let him always strive with all his strength to labor wherever he can accomplish more, so that he may in no way fall away from the divine work he has begun or from gaining the talent entrusted to him. For just as we pronounce divine offense against him for neglecting so great an office, [Col. 0860C] so we announce heavenly vengeance against those who impede him. And just as we implore divine grace for his helpers, so we denounce to those who harm him the terrible punishment of condemnation, which we do not desire.

Finally, having fortified him on every side with the highest authority, following the custom of our predecessors, we rightly enroll him in our sacred order and decree that he is to remain adorned with all his former episcopal office. By apostolic right, through these public writings, we duly strengthen this by inviolable confirmation, as is contained in his earlier privileges.

## Letter III. To the Bishops of the Kingdom of the Franks

(See this letter among the works of Saint Agobard, volume CIV of this *Patrologia*, column 297.)

## Letter IV. To Rabanus Maurus

[Note: It exists in the Codex of Udelricus, no. 15, in Eccard, *Corpus Historiae*, volume XI, page 31.]

Pope Gregory, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved son in the Lord, Rabanus, pious and venerable abbot.

The care of our pontificate urges us to favor the interests of all the holy Churches of God and, according to the condition in which each is to remain, to grant them appropriate assistance. For from this we undoubtedly earn the greatest reward of profit from God, the creator of all, if venerable places, suitably ordered, are without doubt brought to a better condition.

Therefore, because you have requested this from us, we decree by our apostolic command to grant back and reconfirm perpetually to you and your successors the monastery of Fulda, which flourishes under the name of Saint Boniface, situated in the place called Bochonia beside the bank of the river called the Fulda, together with all its cells, estates, jurisdictions, and all movable property belonging to it, which it now possesses and, with God’s help, will possess in the future.

We also grant and give to you, dearest and most beloved son, and perpetually to your successors as abbots, out of the great love and extraordinary affection that we have for you and desire henceforth to have, the monastery of Saint Andrew the apostle, called Exajulum, situated at Rome beside the church of holy Mary, ever-virgin Mother of God, which is called at the Crib, together with all its dwellings, heated rooms, cells, wine cellar, and kitchen, with vineyards, gardens, and various kinds of fruit trees, with an estate and well, and with an entrance through the principal gate from the public road, together with everything belonging to that monastery, situated both within and outside the city, which is rightly and properly recognized as belonging to it.

Let no bishop, archbishop, patriarch, or anyone constituted in the clergy in any capacity presume rashly or arrogantly, unless he has received permission from you, to celebrate the solemn rites of Mass upon the principal altar of your monastery or to exercise any jurisdiction or authority over your monastery of Fulda—apart from our apostolic see. Even the bishop in whose diocese it appears to be situated may not, unless he has been invited by the abbot of the monastery, presume there to celebrate the solemn rites of Mass.

We confirm and strengthen, with perpetual security, the gifts, offerings, and tithes of the faithful to your monastery itself, without opposition from any person, according to the privileges of your predecessors.

We also decree that no person, great or small, may inflict any force or controversy upon that monastery concerning its possessions or dependents, nor presume in any way to subject all or part of it to any mortal person or to give it under the name of a benefice. Rather, at all times it shall serve only our holy Roman Church freely and securely.

When necessary, the brothers shall also have the power to choose an abbot for themselves from among their number, according to the rule of Saint Benedict, without opposition from any person.

Furthermore, after deliberation, we decree that at appropriate times we shall imitate the care of our ecclesiastical responsibility, so that monastic religion may be directed in the regular habit and devoted to concord through suitable ecclesiastical discipline, lest, God forbid, under the pretext of this privilege, the disposition and steps of our rectitude should at some time be turned away from the norm of justice.

We also grant you, dearest son, whom we know to be a well-educated and eloquent man, permission to preach the word of God by the authority of Saint Peter the apostle and of us, his unworthy vicar. We further grant that both you and your successors may, before all the abbots of the whole of Gaul and Germany, hold the primacy of seating in every place and assembly, whether in judicial judgment or in all councils and orders, by our apostolic authority.

The abbot is to be blessed only by our apostolic see, by which he ought to be blessed; nor is he ever to await consecration from any bishop except the Roman pontiff. Nor is an abbot consecrated for another monastery to be introduced into, or set over, the monastery of Fulda.

We also grant you the use of the dalmatic, leggings, and sandals, according to what was granted by our predecessors.

And lest any woman ever presume to enter there, we forbid it by our apostolic authority. We also forbid anyone ever to hold a public court there or in its other places, or to compel servants or tenants to any service, except one to whom the abbot has given his consent for the useful fulfillment of his needs.

Therefore we have judged it worthy to add this general provision: whatever is known to have been granted to the monastery of Fulda by the authority of any of our predecessors, kings, or emperors shall also be confirmed and strengthened by our apostolic authority through this privilege.

By apostolic censure, under invocation of divine judgment, we establish that none of our successors among the Roman pontiffs, kings, emperors, dukes, margraves, counts, or, moreover, archbishops, patriarchs, or persons of any dignity or condition, may ever dare to attempt anything against this privilege.

Whoever therefore observes this privilege of ours, preserves it out of reverence, and ensures that it is not violated in any respect, may be filled with every blessing and merit from God, the giver of all good things, the remission of his sins, so that he may rejoice in the heavenly seat.

But whoever—God forbid—presumes to violate this command of ours, unless he repents, shall incur the wrath of the indivisible Trinity, be excluded from the company of all the saints, and be overwhelmed by the curse of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles. He shall be condemned by the sacred council of the 318 Fathers and, lost under the *anathema maranatha* (“accursed until the Lord comes”) on the final day of judgment, shall not know the brightness of light but shall groan forever in outer darkness with the devil and his companions. Amen.

Given by the hand of Benedict, notary and archivist of the Roman Church, on the Ides of May, in the fourteenth indiction (in the year 836).

## In the Year of Our Lord 844. Frotharius, Bishop of Toul

[Col. 0863B]

## Historical Notice Concerning Frotharius

(Fabricius, *Library of Medieval and Late Latin Literature.*)

[Col. 0863]

[Col. 0863A] Frotharius, formerly abbot of Saint Aper, was bishop of Toul in Gaul from the year 813. He died after the year 837. Andreas Duchesne published twenty-five of his letters from an ancient manuscript of Chartres in volume II of the *Writers of the History of the Franks*, pages 712–723. They were addressed to the emperor Louis the Pious; to Judith, his wife; to Aglemar the abbot; to Drogo, Eginhard, and Gerung, chief usher of the sacred palace; [Col. 0864A] to Hetti the archbishop, Hitto the bishop, Hilduin the father and master, Hugo, Sichard the master, Teutderic and Ragenard, venerable men, and to Wighard the abbot. Six letters addressed to Frotharius by Wicard or Wighard the abbot, by Aldric or Alberic, by Jeremiah, and by Hetti, archbishop of Langres, are added.

[Col. 0863B]

## The Letters of Frotharius

(In Dom Bouquet, volume IV, *Collection of Historians.*) [Note: [Col. 0863C] Andreas Chesnius first published Frotharius’s letters from ancient Chartres manuscripts, volume II of the *Frankish Writers*, page 712.]

## Letter I. To Hilduin

[Col. 0863B]

To the distinguished man, to be named with the highest reverence, Hilduin [Note: [Col. 0863C] Hilduin was chief chaplain of the palace and abbot of Saint-Denis, Saint-Germain of Paris, and Saint-Médard. He is believed to have died in the year 840.], chosen by God as father and master, Frotharius [Note: [Col. 0863C] Frotharius, formerly abbot of Saint Aper, was ordained bishop of Toul in the year 813. He died around the year 847. In Calmet’s proofs for the *History of Lorraine* there are two charters granted by Frotharius to the monastery of Saint Aper. In one of them Frotharius wishes certain things to be rendered to him in return for the gifts he had bestowed on the monastery: “We have determined that for these gifts there should be presented to us each year on the feast of Blessed Aper, namely, a banquet to be held there, a horse worth thirty solidi . . . also a shield and a lance, as well as two hides and an equal number of hair-shirts (*cilicia*), and, moreover, at the time of military service, a forced transport.””], humble bishop, wishes you everlasting blessedness and salvation in the Lord.

With the fullest effort of our mind, with the whole understanding of our spirit, and with all the strength of our heart, we desire, wish, and ask that your exalted dignity may continually possess health of body and soul, and that by happy elevation you may long increase both in the heavenly radiance of spiritual gifts and in the splendor of earthly dignity.

We also desire to behold the face of your dignity and to enjoy in the Lord the words of your diligence; indeed, we desire to contemplate the temples of your most devout religion, from which we may receive spiritual admonitions and take up the salutary ornaments of holiness.

For although I cannot contemplate with bodily sight the most splendid beauty of your order, I nevertheless contemplate it continually with spiritual eyes and ineffable joy. Indeed, I do not fail frequently to impress upon myself and my people, through exhortation, the traces of such things that ought to be followed.

For I cannot fail to retain in memory the deeds of such great joy and the pious services of divine worship that I recently witnessed in the presence of your most devoted fatherhood. Who, after seeing them once, would not paint them deeply in his mind for his salvation, since their remembrance strengthens the highest piety and their performance brings the attainment of perpetual peace?

May divine command look favorably upon me and all who behold the exercises of your devotion, so that we may worthily follow them; and may it happily grant you the rewards of everlasting recompense for the example of the work you have displayed for imitation. Amen.

I, together with Smaragdus [Note: Smaragdus, abbot of Saint Michael’s on the Meuse (Saint-Mihiel), in the diocese of Verdun], make known by letter to the lord emperor how Abbot Ismundus [Note: Hismundus, secular abbot of the monastery of Medianus. See Letter III for the cause of the quarrel between him and the monks of Medianus] and his monks are divided from one another by a certain dispute. May your pious concern act so that those monks may be able to fulfill the vow they promised to God, and may your Humility convey this same letter to his presence.

## LETTER II. TO GERUNGUS, CHIEF DOORKEEPER OF THE SACRED PALACE

To the most illustrious man, Gerungus, worthy of honor and love with all affection, chief doorkeeper of the sacred palace [Note: The palace doorkeeper was called by another name, *scarion*, by the ancient Franks [Col. 0865C]; among the ancient Romans this office was reckoned under the title of *aedile*, as the monk of Saint Gall testifies in Book I of *The Deeds of Charlemagne*: “The palace doorkeeper was first among the palace officials, who were subordinate to the greater ministers,” as Hincmar teaches in *On the Order of the Palace*, chapter 7. In 822 Gerungus, as Einhard testifies in the *Annals*, became administrator of Lothar, king of Italy; afterward he was a monk of Prüm. Wandalbert, in the book he wrote about the miracles of Saint Goar in the year 839, calls him “the most illustrious man, formerly an aedile of the palace, now a monk.”], Frotharius, by the grace of God bishop, eternal salvation in Christ.

We are always mindful of your prosperity and advancement. Therefore we frequently implore divine mercy for your salvation, that it may continually inflame you to fulfill His commandments and preserve you for a long time for the advancement of many; and that, living piously, soberly, and justly, He may enable you, with His aid, to cross the sea of this present shipwreck, so that afterward, brought to the harbor of eternal rest, He may happily crown you with everlasting recompense.

Know, then, that we continually remain in this intention, and that during these days our brothers have sung so many Masses and so many psalters for your life and health. Finally, know that we are sending letters to the lord emperor by our present messenger. We therefore ask that, if the lord Hilduin is absent, you send our messenger before the lord emperor.

Farewell always in the Lord, and remember us.

## LETTER III. TO LOUIS THE EMPEROR

We bring to the ears of your mercy, most pious emperor—I, Frotharius the bishop, and Smaragdus the abbot—that in the time of Fortunatus, abbot of the monastery of Mediolacus [Note: Correction: Medianus. This monastery, commonly called Moyen-Moutier, was situated in the Vosges and belonged to the parish of Frotharius, bishop of Toul; the monastery of Mediolacus, Medeloc, or Mithlac, in the diocese of Trier, lay far away. After Madalvinus, abbot of Medianus, died, the monks disagreed among themselves about choosing a successor. To reconcile them, Charlemagne sent Fortunatus, whom the monks elected abbot [Col. 0866C–D]. Fortunatus of Grado was the patriarch who, harassed by the Venetian dukes, fled to Francia to Charlemagne in 803. At the beginning of Louis the Pious’s reign, a dispute arose between Fortunatus and the monks over the portion that belonged to each. Fortunatus claimed for himself, by the strictest right, the administration of the entire property; but the monks argued that, since he belonged to another flock and institution, a fixed portion ought to be assigned to them. When the matter was brought before Louis, he entrusted its care to Smaragdus, abbot of Saint Michael’s on the Meuse, who “gave the monks a portion of the abbey, so that they might live according to the rule.”], Smaragdus, at your command, gave the monks of that monastery a portion of the abbey, so that they might live according to the rule.

Accordingly, they lived well and according to the rule until Fortunatus withdrew [Note: This occurred either in 821, when Fortunatus withdrew to Constantinople, or in 825, when, while on his way from that city to Rome, he died in Francia]. But when Hismundus took over the monastery, he reclaimed their portion and promised that he would regularly provide them with everything necessary. They testify that afterward matters repeatedly turned out otherwise for them. Thus they have now come to us, protesting and saying that they neither live inwardly according to the rule nor receive the necessities of bodily sustenance outwardly according to the rule.

We therefore went there together, found that this was so, and learned that the negligence was partly theirs, the monks’, and partly that of their abbot. He then promised again that he wished to correct in every respect whatever had hitherto been negligently handled on his part. We consented to this and worked to persuade the monks to agree. But they feared that, as had often happened, his promise would be frustrated either by him or by his ministers. They therefore said that they could neither trust his promises any longer nor accept his correction unless their portion were restored to them, as you had formerly ordered it to be given to them.

Since he said that he would in no way do this without your command, they all together, with a common purpose and common prayer, asked that we grant them permission to return to the presence of your Piety and implore your mercy. They said that they would rather be expelled from that monastery and live in pilgrimage and begging than trust false promises any longer and serve under the false name of monks.

For this reason we gave them permission to come to you. We have made these matters known to your Wisdom so that, before they come to you, you may understand the causes of their complaint.

## LETTER IV. TO N. . . . [Note: Perhaps Gerungus, as above]

[Col. 0866B]

To the most excellent and noble man N., lofty and most worthy of honor, chief doorkeeper of the sacred palace, Frotharius, humble bishop, and the whole Church of Toul—that is, the company of canons, monks, virgins, and all the other faithful—wish eternal salvation in Christ.

We remember you in our sacred prayers and frequently beseech the God of heaven and earth for the safety of your body and soul: namely, that in this life He may preserve you unharmed for a longer time, for our advancement and that of other faithful people, and afterward grant you happily to share in eternal life.

Let your Eminence know, then, that after I recently sent our messenger to you, I fully convened the synod of our parish and had Masses and psalters sung for your salvation. We both ought and desire to do this more frequently for your prosperity.

You, for your part, remember us always, and do not hesitate to labor for the needs and advancement of our Church. I mean especially the matter concerning which I sent to you our vassal Catallo [Catalaunis], and concerning which we are now sending letters to the lord N.; we beg your goodwill that, together with him, you will settle this matter and persuade N. himself to agree with you concerning it, because the same small property belongs to his administration.

Let your concern here keep watch in such a way as we, your faithful servants, trust in you.

Farewell always in Christ.

## LETTER V. TO N. . . .

To the most noble man N. . . ., worthy of mention with every honor, Frotharius the bishop wishes eternal salvation in the Lord.

Let your affection know that we always remember you in our sacred prayers and continually desire that your health remain secure. For this reason, too, I have now had Masses and psalters sung for you.

You also should always remember us, and take care to do whatever this messenger of ours tells you. Farewell in the Lord three, four, and a hundred times.

## LETTER VI. TO SICHARDUS THE ABBOT

[Col. 0867B]

To the most noble man Sichardus [Note: Sichardus was elected abbot of the monastery of Acutianus, or Farfa, in 829; he died in 843], a venerable teacher by divine providence, worthy of honor because of the affection of our profound love, Frotharius, the most humble bishop, wishes present and perpetual happiness in the Lord.

Both the gaze of divine knowledge knows how greatly we continually desire your high station to flourish with every kind of prosperity and to overflow everywhere with all good fortune, and your own discernment will be able to recognize it as soon as an opportunity for service arises. Indeed, we believe that He now truly recognizes it, because He wisely understands that charity, though obstructed by every kind of obstacle, is held inviolate in the heart but often is not displayed in the exercise of works.

But if we have hitherto done less than we should in your service, let your command admonish us henceforth, so that, as is fitting, we may serve you with diligent devotion.

Furthermore, we beseech the clemency of your Piety to introduce this boy, your servant, the son of Count Haudulf, before our senior, the lord Lothar, and to obtain from him, through worthy intercession, the necessities that he has made known to you. Thus, just as with many others, your almsgiving and reward may be increased through this man as well, so that in the present time you may have service from us and from him, and receive from God the reward of eternal recompense.

## LETTER VII. TO JUDITH THE EMPRESS

I make known to your Clemency, most serene empress—I, Frotharius, humble bishop—that your agents have committed certain injustices in our parish. That is their designation, because they reorganized in another way and removed from certain churches what rightly and reasonably belonged to them, although those churches had been ordered by us according to ecclesiastical arrangement.

They also took half a *mansus* from the church of this priest of yours, together with half of his tithe, and gave it to a layman, contrary to canonical statutes and contrary to our office and will.

We know, however, that your command and will were that they should act with rectitude and justice and presume nothing against the sacred ministry. Therefore, if it is your will that the matter be corrected, command us, and according to your order we shall correct all these things in such a way that your almsgiving may thereby increase and your eternal reward grow.

Always defend the Church of God and exalt ecclesiastical law, so that the Almighty Lord may defend you from every evil and happily lead you to the exaltation of the heavenly kingdom. Amen.

## LETTER VIII. TO DROGO, BISHOP OF METZ

To the most noble man Drogo [Note: Drogo, son of Charlemagne, became bishop of Metz in 823; he died in 857], bishop of the see of Metz by the cooperation of divine grace, worthy of honor with all my affection, I wish perpetual salvation in Christ.

I greatly desire to contemplate the desirable person of your dignity with a fruitful gaze and to speak with you in salutary conversation about matters that are useful and appropriate to our ministry. Indeed, in your words, since they are gracious and sweetened, the grace of friendship will certainly be found, and on your lips will resound a sweetness of the highest delight; through them, a salutary drink will be offered to the hearer’s inmost being, as well as life-giving nourishment.

A little later, if life accompanies us, I shall attain the fulfillment of this desire and intention—namely, when we begin to set out for Hesperia because of the military expedition that has been announced, or when, after the military campaign has been completed, we gather at the palace for the general assembly.

Having explained these matters, we make known to your affection that Leufredus, the bearer of this letter, has approached us, asking that we inform you about the circumstances of his marriage, which he is said to have contracted between us. At present we have been unable to investigate the certainty of this matter fully; we shall be able to explain it to you more clearly when we have reached the palace mentioned above.

I wish you to prosper happily in Christ.

## LETTER IX. TO HILDUINUS

To the man of most excellent nobility, Hilduinus, elected by God as father and teacher, worthy of mention with the highest veneration, Frotharius, the humblest of bishops, and the entire Church of Toul—that is, the company of canons, monks, virgins, and all the other faithful—send greetings of everlasting happiness in Christ.

It is clear to us that your fatherhood has been ordained from heaven by divine providence for the benefit and advancement of the holy Church: namely, so that through your patronage many may be supported both temporally and spiritually and preserved for a very long time in holy religion.

For this reason, it is evident that you undertake various people’s cases and bring the cases you have undertaken to the imperial ears, so that through such labor and zeal your eternal reward and recompense may increase.

Accordingly, we too humbly entreat that you may be preserved for a long time as an adornment of the holy Church and may continually provide fruitful joy to the Christian community.

Let your Highness know, then, that during these days we convened the assembly of our subjects and had Masses and psalters sung for the health of your heart and body. We both ought and desire to do this more frequently for your happiness.

You, however, remember us with your customary piety, and do not disdain, when a suitable opportunity arises, to mention to the lord emperor the matter concerning the need and benefit of our Church that was recently made known to you—namely, the matter of two *mansi* belonging to the basilica of Saint N. . . ., formerly removed from the possession of Saint Stephen.

He holds them who, weighed down by bodily weakness, is unable to go out on military service or to serve at the palace. If it pleases your Clemency that this small property be restored to its rightful possession, then, according to your constitution, it can be restored to the aforesaid possessor either by *praestaria* or by benefice.

Thus the house of God will not lose what is justly owed and belongs to it.

There are also, in another place, six *mansi* adjoining another basilica built in honor of Saint N. . . ., and forty others belonging to the church of Saint N. . . ., likewise formerly removed from the right of our Church. Because of the ancient constitution’s having fallen into disuse, no census is paid for them.

Therefore let your pious concern keep watch, so that what was once justly assigned to ecclesiastical right may, through your foresight, be restored there at an appropriate time for perpetual possession—provided, of course, that neither the Church is defrauded of the goods owed to it nor their possessors deprived of that same possession.

For now, however, so that the petition of our smallness may not burden the ears of your Highness, deign to labor only on behalf of the aforesaid two *mansi*. As for the rest, when I come to your Sublimity and make the contents of the same documents clearer to your diligence, you will be able to act here and there as it seems best to your Serenity.

Moreover, when it pleases you to speak with me about these matters, if you take with you that faithful man of yours, our friend, he will in every respect assist your service in this matter.

Let your Wisdom act here in such a way as we, your sons, trust in your protection. May heavenly protection fortify and guide your fatherhood everywhere, as you continually support our advancement, and grant you prosperous health with everlasting strength.

## LETTER X. TO DROGO, BISHOP OF METZ

[Col. 0869D]

To the man of most noble dignity and most worthy of lofty honor, Drogo, by the favor of divine grace bishop of the Church of Metz, Frotharius, likewise a lowly bishop, wishes perpetual salvation in Christ.

Preserving love and affection for you in pious devotion, we rejoice that you lead a happy life through long courses of years, and we earnestly beseech that this may be granted by heavenly will.

I humbly ask that the rights of that same affection be returned to me by you and preserved inviolate, so that, joined to you by this spiritual bond, I may be refreshed by your conversation and profitably instructed by salutary pursuits and examples.

Furthermore, let your affection know that I am deeply displeased about certain monks of your monastery, whose rector appears to be Erlefredus [Note: Erlefredus was in charge of the abbey of Senones (Senone in the Vosges). The abbots of this monastery received temporal authority from the bishop of Metz and spiritual authority from the bishop of Toul, as the monk Bicherius testifies in the *Chronicle of Senones*, in Acherius, *Spicilegium*, vol. III, p. 303].

Since that place lies within our parish and its inhabitants, by God’s favor, ought to be protected under our guardianship, some of them leave our parish without our permission and authorization, supposedly because of certain complaints; where they are going, I do not know at all.

Furthermore, if they come to you or bring a grievance to your ears, canonical order ought to have been preserved toward us, so that their complaints might be made known to me and suitable correction might be given them by our joint counsel.

Since this has hitherto been negligently omitted, your diligence ought henceforth to correct it with a worthy remedy, so that neither your ears may be troubled further in this matter nor our canonical right and due reverence taken away from us.

There is also another cell belonging to your lordship situated in the village of Warengissi (Warengeville), which the monks likewise are known to inhabit without my permission. But because I grew up among them, namely in the monastery of Gorze, my smallness tolerates this to some extent.

Finally, I do not conceal from your fatherhood that certain basilicas belonging to your jurisdiction are entrusted to our care, yet are supported neither by the subjection of *mansi* nor guarded by the presence of priests. For all these matters, let your administration send a representative to us, through whose intervention they may be corrected.

Until suitable correction has been made in the aforesaid cells or churches, we must presume nothing concerning their ecclesiastical appointments or arrangements. For even in the aforementioned Vosges monastery, certain representatives of yours were sent there to establish rectitude; yet, unless I am mistaken, they accomplished nothing useful there. Rather, by multiplying discord, they made those same brothers worse in every respect.

It is fitting that in monasteries, churches, and all things subject to your authority such order and rectitude should be maintained that both we and all your neighbors may be instructed by your examples and, through you, in some measure be led to the pursuit of true religion, as though by the supreme shepherd and most noble ruler of the people.

May your fatherhood prosper happily in Christ for a long time. Amen.

## LETTER XI. TO HILDUINUS

[Col. 0870D]

To Hilduinus, a man of most excellent nobility and exalted by the summit of glorious dignity, elected by God as father and teacher, Frotharius, the least of bishops, and the entire Church of the city of the Leuci, humbly wish perpetual salvation in Christ.

With the most frequent petitions of our prayers, we ask the divine Clemency, both with mouth and heart, that your fatherhood may remain strong with happy vigor and a prosperous course through long years.

Since the grace of God has ordinarily permitted the protection of your governance to preside over us, we recognize by true experience that the defense of heavenly protection is present for our advancement.

Now, therefore, may your mercy, as it has always been accustomed to do, deign to labor for our need, because a service of great burden is imposed upon us, which our strength cannot possibly perform without difficulty.

For we are ordered to work at the palace of Aachen and to apply ourselves to the labors to be carried out there. But other services and necessities recall us from this work; and, if it pleases your Piety, they also provide a sufficiently suitable excuse.

Your fatherhood can certainly remember that when the lord emperor was staying this year at the palace of Gundumvilla [Note: Correction: Gundulfi-Villa, whose site is placed where the town now commonly called Gondreville still stands, one league below Toul of the Leuci, by the lord Michael Germanus in Book IV of *On Diplomatic Matters*, p. 285], he held your hand and ordered me to construct, at the front of that palace, the work of a raised structure by which one could enter the chapel. He also added that he had often allowed someone to remain there, silently indicating your person.

He likewise ordered me to add another wall of stonework above the wooden wall of that house. Although such works are to be completed quickly, a third task still remains to be undertaken on our begun basilica; we have done nothing concerning it since you departed from here, because the laborers have hitherto been hindered by the winter season and the season of sowing.

To these labors has been added, against our will, a necessity and the adversity of miserable misfortune. For a certain servant of sin and of ours, envious of his fellow servant, our cellarer, because he was preferred to him in office, secretly placed a destructive fire in the barn where the grain had been stored in the countryside and whose consumption we expected to sustain us until harvesttime. At once he consumed everything that was there: an unhappy servant, an ungrateful servant, one deserving to be condemned by a savage anathema, who deprived us in an instant of such great resources for living.

Moreover, famine in past years has so destroyed the household of Saint Stephen and brought it to such miserable poverty that they can scarcely in any way support the expenses of their frail lives. Consequently, I cannot demand from them the census they owe except in return for the work of their hands, for which I in turn feed them; and even in this way the debt cannot usefully be recovered.

Deign to weigh these matters and those mentioned above with pious consideration, and do not hesitate to free us from the aforesaid service. Otherwise, I shall personally come before the lord emperor and before you, and humbly beseech you to remove this burden of pastoral care from me, because my smallness cannot bear it in this way. It is far more useful for me to be relieved of such care than, through confidence in my authority, for so many of the Lord’s sheep to perish in the danger of destruction.

Therefore, let my Lord act toward me in this petition as He has always acted, and may He prosper happily in Christ through many cycles of years. Amen.

## LETTER XII. WICARDUS TO FROTHARIUS

[Col. 0872A]

To the reverend lord and father Frotharius, most gentle of bishops and most worthy of every honor, Wicardus [Note: It is not clear over which monastery Wicardus presided. It is inferred from Letter XIX that his monastery was not far from the town of Bonn. At that time there was an abbot named Wicardus in the monastery of Inda near Aachen], the least of abbots, together with my brothers, wishes perpetual glory.
