What thanksgiving shall we render to you, best of men, for the benefits that you bestow upon our smallness solely with regard for heavenly reward? For you deign to provide not only for our inmost spiritual needs through pastoral care, but also, through pious concern, for the external affairs of our property.

Moreover, to demonstrate the fullness of your charity toward us, you have now deigned to send to our humility the relics of Saint Aper, as well as the deeds of his blessed way of life—what could be richer for us than gold?

But for all these things, He for whose love you do this will certainly not forget to restore to you the fruit of abiding recompense. Let us nevertheless remember that we can offer our most humble prayers to the heavenly Majesty for your salvation; and in temporal matters, wherever your Dignity wishes to command us, we shall strive to be most devoted and ready.

Therefore let your kindness act, as it has begun to do kindly, not only concerning the goods and the people dwelling upon them who are readily available to us, but also concerning those goods that these same people of ours, who appear to live everywhere freely and without restriction, have purchased. Thus they may always be subject to the regard of the Lord and Savior, together with those very people who possess them.

How this should be handled is clearer to your Wisdom. Nevertheless, it seems to us that, if you judge it useful, you should have whichever of those bondsmen are attempting to withdraw themselves from our authority give formal surety acknowledging their servitude before you, so that thereafter, once subjected by justice, they may be unable to perpetrate this fraud.

We are sending to your Dignity a copy of the gift of those goods, together with a copy of the lord emperor’s charter of grant, by which he granted our monastery exemption from the toll so that it would nowhere be demanded from us throughout his kingdom; likewise, a copy of the immunity charter.

We greatly wish you, lord and father, to prosper happily in Christ.

## LETTER XIII. ALDRICUS TO FROTHARIUS

[Col. 0872]

To Frotharius, my excellent and dearly beloved bishop, Aldricus sends eternal greetings.

(See below, among the works of Aldricus of Le Mans.)

## LETTER XIV. TO HILDUINUS

To Hilduinus, most excellent and most worthy of the highest honor, elected by God as father and teacher, Frotharius, the humblest of bishops, and the entire company of the Church of Toul, wish perpetual blessing in Christ.

Concerning all our needs and deficiencies we always turn to you, as to our one father and most pious defender, whose patronage we continually need and by whose aid we are frequently relieved. For it is clear that your protection is the door of salvation and your governance the harbor of the most solid peace.

Therefore, may your Clemency help us as usual and come to our aid with fatherly affection. We are importunate because we plead with you so frequently, but may the serenity of your Highness in no way disdain us on account of this importunity; rather, may it deign to consider the need arising upon us.

For the lord emperor, at my suggestion, returned a certain estate to the basilica of Saint Aper (in the year 836), which his grandfather Pippin had given to that same church. A certain Spaniard named Joseph had hitherto held it by our benefice. While still alive, he left it desolate and reduced it to nothing, and by oppressing the servants of that place he destroyed them.

He himself has now departed this life. His wife remains, together with their small son, and they are members of the lord emperor’s household. Nevertheless, out of charity and affection, or by way of the lord emperor’s almsgiving, I wished to give her ten *mansi* and a vineyard worth nearly forty measures of wine from that same benefice; I arranged to restore the remaining twenty *mansi* for the use of the brothers of the aforesaid church.

But the aforesaid woman despised my gift, and now, coming to the palace, is attempting secretly and against our will to seize the entire benefice. May your Wisdom now deign to act according to the custom of your former piety, so that the aforesaid properties may remain in the possession of Saint Aper and provide the brothers with the food supplies owed to them.

Thus may both the merits of Saint Aper and the pious petitions of those brothers benefit you unto eternal life.

We always wish you to prosper, holy and most reverend father.

## LETTER XV. TO THE SAME

[Note: From this letter and the two following it is evident that, after the death of Jeremiah—which occurred at the beginning of the year 828—the see of Senones remained vacant for some time.]

To Hilduinus, most worthy of the honor of excellent veneration, the truly most holy lord of the people of Senones, the most humble devotion of the Church, wishes eternal prosperity in the Lord.

Because, through the inspiration of divine mercy, you have often deigned, my lord, to sympathize with the cries of our wearisome importunity, we have now again, compelled by extreme necessity, presumed to trouble the ears of your Highness.

For we know, most reverend lord, how kindly and mercifully you deigned to assist our earlier petitions, and how, despite none of our merits—and something we had never hoped would happen—you worked to obtain and grant us a second election.

But because, as we believe, our sins required that the vows and desires with which we have so often dared to appeal to your Holiness should be greatly hindered and not be permitted to reach fulfillment, we have therefore been compelled on this occasion also to report to you the causes of our misery.

My lord, we have now made a second election, and have found one of our own number, well known to us from childhood, not disgraced in birth or conduct, teachable in age, suitable for this office, not wholly ignorant of literary studies, and not entirely without knowledge of divine learning; he also possesses some portion of certain other arts [Note: That man is Aldricus, or another person in whose place Aldricus was elected].

When we presented him, not at all thinking that he would be rejected, we did not deserve to obtain what we desired because the lord’s agents intervened. Therefore, prostrate in spirit at the feet of your Piety, we tearfully ask you to deign to suspend the matter until we hurry to your Highness with the man in writing and explain our situation more fully to you in person.

Although the person of whom we speak may be less or more capable of bearing this burden, let him be accepted or rejected according to the judgment of your Dignity. Thus certain persons will no longer torment us, the most wretched, by seizing upon pretexts, nor will your most gentle Sublimity be troubled any longer by us.

Having laid these matters before your Clemency—and would that we might obtain it—we pray the heavenly mercy to grant you prosperity in many forms and eventually permit you to attain the joys of eternal blessedness.

To the excellent lord and truly most holy Hilduinus, appointed by God over sacred affairs of the city of Senones, the lowly and humble Church sends perpetual greetings.

## LETTER XVI. TO EINHARD

[Col. 0874C]

To the illustrious and exceptionally noble lord Einhard, the most holy lord, the most humble devotion of the Church of Senones.

We have presumed, my lord, humbly to make the causes of our need known to the ears of your Clemency, so that through your piety we may quickly deserve to receive consolation in these matters.

We believe that you know that the lord emperor had granted us, most unworthy as we are, permission to make an election from among ourselves. But when we had elected the man whom you know, and he had not been fully accepted by the serenity of the lord emperor, we were again permitted, if we could, to find another among ourselves suitable for this office.

When such a man had been found, and, as we believe, was capable of serving God and the lord emperor, we do not know for what reason he was not received with full goodwill by the lord’s agents.

Therefore we ask your kindness to deign to be our helper in this matter, so that we ourselves may lead the man of whom we speak into the presence of the lord emperor; the matter may be examined according to his command, and it may be tested whether he can be of benefit to us and whether he is capable of serving God—or not.

We wish you always to be fortified by divine protections and eventually to rejoice in the crown of immortality, most pious and reverend lord.

To the most holy and pious lord Einhard, deservedly venerable, the worthless and lowly congregation of the city of Senones.

## LETTER XVII. TO JUDITH THE EMPRESS

To Judith, illustrious and most renowned for every nobility, glorious empress, the most humble devotion of the Church of Senones.

We have presumed, my lady, humbly to make the causes of our need known to the ears of your Clemency, so that through your piety we may quickly deserve to receive consolation in these matters.

We believe that you know that the lord emperor had granted us, most unworthy as we are, permission to make an election from among ourselves. But when we had elected the man whom you know, and he had not been fully accepted by the serenity of the lord emperor, we were again permitted, if we could, to find another among ourselves suitable for this office.

When such a man had been found, and, as we believe, was capable of serving God and you, we do not know for what reason he was not received with full goodwill by the lord’s agents.

Therefore we ask your kindness to deign to be our helper in this matter, so that the case may be suspended until we ourselves lead the man of whom we speak into the presence of the lord emperor and into yours; the matter may be examined according to your command, and it may be tested whether he can be of benefit to us and whether he is capable of serving you—or not.

We wish you always to be fortified by divine protections and eventually to rejoice in the crown of immortality, most pious and serene lady.

To the most excellent and most renowned Judith, empress, the most humble devotion of the people of Senones.

## LETTER XVIII. TO HETTI, ARCHBISHOP OF TRIER

To the most blessed lord Hetti [Note: Hetti, formerly abbot of Mediolacus, became archbishop of Trier in 814], worthy of honor through the affection of unique love, archbishop of the Church of Trier by the supreme gift of providence, Frotharius, the least of bishops, sends greetings in Christ.

I burn with such ardent longing to behold and address the sublimity of your fatherhood, as though many years had already passed during which I had been unable to enjoy your presence or conversation. For I confess that I am distressed in every way by this also: when I recently returned from the palace, I lacked the opportunity to speak with you. Hence, with insatiable longing, I desire to visit your sweet presence here in these regions as soon as possible. Therefore I ask that you inform me by letter when you are to come here on the embassy entrusted to you, or when you are to convene the synodal council according to the present constitution. I remain especially concerned about these matters because, in accordance with the imperial command, I myself must go from Mont-Joux to the palace at Aachen to provide lodgings in which the envoys are to be received; and, departing during the month of October, I wish to return home before the feast of Saint Andrew. But if I learn that you are setting out for these regions during that same month, I shall make every effort to be present, so that, serving and assisting you in all things, I may once again deserve to receive from you suitable support in spiritual matters. I wish you, mindful of us in all things, to prosper in Christ.

## LETTER XIX. TO WIGARD, ABBOT OF INDA

Frotharius, bishop by the mercy of God, sends greetings to Wighard, a venerable abbot worthy in merit and holiness, and to the entire congregation.

Know that I continually have concern and care for your progress and welfare, and that, concerning the matters you recently reported—including the ordination of your cleric—I wish to fulfill whatever we can reasonably and suitably accomplish. Furthermore, I ask that, with your assistance, you arrange for three cartloads of wine from Bonn to be brought to us at the palace at Aachen; and whatever you again require from our service, send word to us. Farewell always in the Lord.

## LETTER XX. TO AGLEMAR, ABBOT

Frotharius, by the grace of God bishop of the Church of Toul, wishes perpetual salvation in Christ to Aglemar, the venerable abbot.

Let your affection know that I am, in some measure, enjoying bodily health, and that I frequently implore the clemency of heavenly mercy for the soundness of your heart and body. For I desire that you may possess enduring happiness and, after the completion of this life, be perpetually refreshed by the gift of heavenly rest. Furthermore, let your fraternity know that, in the new buildings of our church, we need your assistance. Therefore I ask you to send us, for decorating the walls, the various colors that are available: namely, gold pigment, Indian leaf, vermilion, lapis lazuli, and blue-green pigment, as well as quicksilver according to your means. Send these things to us, and in turn demand from us the service that is due. For, bound to one another by the indissoluble bond of charity, we are compelled to serve one another in turn and to repay brotherly services. Farewell always in the Lord.

Your most generous providence, granted by God long ago, entrusted the sheepfold of the holy Church to my hands in such a way that I might withstand the bites of the invading wolves and, with whatever strength I wished, restrain and kill them as well. But since the time for rendering an account of that same struggle has not yet come, I shall meanwhile report to your diligence how I contended in the killing of bodily wolves. After you entrusted that episcopal estate to me, I killed 240 wolves in your forests. I say “killed,” because they were captured at my command and through my contrivance. Finished. Amen.

## LETTER XXI. TO HUGO

Frotharius, humble bishop by the grace of God, wishes eternal salvation in the Lord to Hugo, a most devoted servant of Christ, revered with the affection of exceeding love.

[Note: Hugo, son of Charlemagne and brother of Louis the Pious and of Drogo, bishop of Metz, was abbot of Sithiu and Quintin; he held the office of archchancellor under Louis the Pious. He was killed during the siege of Toulouse in the year 844.]

Because, through the recent messenger of your highness, I was permitted to learn that you were well and safe, I rejoiced with the greatest gladness of heart. For I always desire that you possess happiness in heart and body, and I ask this with every prayer. Yet I rejoiced less because we are so soon deprived for a time of the presence of your dignity. Until now we had both believed and desired that at least two lamps might remain to us from so pious and exalted a lineage, whose brightness and merits would gladly illuminate and improve us and our neighbors.

[Note: He means Hugo and Drogo.]

But I am greatly saddened by this, because I have neither rendered you the service I ought to have rendered, nor am I now able to serve you as I should, with various cares pressing upon me. For, in meeting the hardships of the journeys that we have either just undertaken or are about to undertake, and in sending royal gifts to the palace, we have been compelled to distribute almost everything we possessed among our best horses. The few that remain have until now been kept with the mares for breeding. Hence, now that they are emaciated, they cannot be assigned with dignity to their customary services.

Therefore, since at present we did not have one suitable for conveying you, let your kindness know that, when by God’s help I have returned from the journey mentioned above, I shall prepare one that can be given without embarrassment either to you as you return to these regions or to your messenger. But that which was dearer and more precious to your diligence—the relics of Saint Aper, confessor of Christ—we are sending to you. We implore the assistance of Saint Aper, so that you may return here quickly and safely and receive from our devotion the benefits of worthy service. We wish you to prosper happily in Christ.

## LETTER XXII. TO ***

Frotharius, bishop by the grace of God, wishes salvation in the Lord to that most reverend and wholly devoted venerable abbot, and to the entire congregation serving God under your rule.

Let your affection know that I am in some measure strong in body and desirous of your welfare. Furthermore, we return immense thanks to your affection because you sent us a faithful man skilled in sacred crafts. His expertise in the art is exceedingly pleasing, and the dignity of his religious character is gratifying to those who behold him. When he has completed his duty of obedience, we shall send him back to you; by the Lord’s consenting grace, we set before your eyes the matter arising from it [the reading *ex illa rem* is uncertain]. May your dignity prosper in the Lord.

## LETTER XXIII. TO GERUNG, CHIEF DOORKEEPER OF THE SACRED PALACE

To Gerung, an excellent and most noble man, worthy of the highest honor, chief doorkeeper of the sacred palace, Frotharius, humble bishop, and the entire Church of Toul—the whole company of canons, monks, virgins, and other faithful—wish eternal salvation in Christ.

We remember you in our sacred prayers and frequently beseech the God of heaven and earth for the health of your body and soul: namely, that he may preserve you safe for a long time in this life, for our advancement and that of other faithful people, and after death grant you happily to share in eternal life.

Furthermore, let your highness know that I, your petitioner, am pressed by many necessities, by which I am compelled to come into the presence of our lord the emperor and humbly fall at his feet, so that through your assistance I may obtain his mercy and comfort amid the necessities now pressing upon me. [Note: The passage is mutilated.]

Therefore I beseech the greatness of your clemency to deign to inform me secretly by your letters, or through our present messenger, when I may come to you, so that by your counsel and assistance I may be able to explain my necessities to him. I wish you to prosper in Christ.

## LETTER XXIV. TO THE SAME

To the most noble man, to be named with every honor, Gerung, Frotharius, bishop by the grace of God, sends eternal salvation in the Lord.

We always remember you in our sacred prayers, asking that health and long life be granted to you against the enemy, and that afterward eternal rest be bestowed upon you. Know, therefore, that after I recently spoke with you at the palace, we had one hundred Masses and fifty psalters sung for your welfare.

But we ask you, as usual, to remember me, and, if our senior should wish to send me to the regions of Spain during the coming winter for their protection and supervision, deign to excuse me from that service. For you know that our lord the emperor himself wishes to visit our region in the following year, and then I shall not be able to serve him as I desire unless I have been released by you from the service mentioned above. Farewell very much in the Lord.

## LETTER XXV. HETTI TO FROTHARIUS

[Col. 0876]

In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, Hetti, archbishop by the mercy of God of the diocese of Trier, and also envoy to Louis, the most serene emperor, sends eternal salvation to the venerable brother Frotharius, bishop of Toul.

[Col. 0878D] Let it be known to you that a terrible command of our lord the emperor has reached us, ordering us to make known to all who appear to remain within our embassy that everyone should prepare himself, so that all may be able to set out for war in Italy, since, with Satan lying in wait, King Bernard is planning to rebel against him.

[Note: Bernard, king of Italy, was born to Pippin the elder, son of Charlemagne. At the instigation of the nobles, he attempted in the year 817 to plot a revolt against Louis the Pious, intending to seize, if he could, the empire which he believed was owed to him by hereditary right. Louis imposed punishment the following year on those involved in the conspiracy.]

Therefore we command and order you, in the name of our lord the emperor, to act with vigilant care and the utmost speed toward all the abbots, abbesses, counts, royal vassals, and all the people of your parish who are required to provide military service to the royal authority, so that everyone may be prepared. If the announcement is made to them in the evening, they are to depart in the morning; and if in the morning, in the evening, without any delay, toward the regions of Italy, because our lord the emperor is preparing his journey so that, as soon as he can, he may proceed there together with his faithful.

## LETTER XXVI. FROTHARIUS TO TEUTDERIC

Frotharius, bishop and prelate of the Church of Toul by the grace of God, wishes perpetual blessedness in the Lord to Teutderic and Ragenard, venerable men, together with the entire flock entrusted to you.

[Note: Theodoric is believed to have been abbot of Sens. Ragenard, or Reginard, governed the monastery of Moyenmoutier after Ismund.]

Whenever I learn that your dignified person, together with those subject to you under our governance, is flourishing well and safely, I give abundant thanks to divine mercy. But whenever I hear that either you or your people, belonging to our diocese, are in any way weakened or endangered, I am afflicted by great grief and anxiety of sorrow, and I lament on every side as though for dearly beloved sons and my own sheep.

I confess that this has happened in these days, when I happened to learn of the deadly pestilence raging with great violence. For it was reported to me that some of your people had been overcome by the devastation of wolves and had been utterly destroyed from this life by sudden disasters. I do not doubt that this wound was inflicted everywhere through diabolical deceit, with divine judgment permitting it. For, because our sins demand it, we suffer many adversities with God’s permission, which would by no means befall us if we served him daily with our whole mind as was fitting.

For—as must be said with profound lamentation—iniquity abounds and the charity of many grows cold. For this reason, as heavenly judgment arranges that so many blows should descend, our misery endures so many adversities caused by demonic instigation and hostile to the human race. In past years we suffered various forms of famine because of the dryness of the crops or the onslaught of hail; in the present year we see the abundance of the harvests and the richness of the vineyards consumed by the devastation of mice. Finally, what must be said with mourning, we see Christian human beings suddenly killed by the rabid attacks of wolves.

I am astonished in every way that you did not earlier report these events to our presence. I would have come to you and endeavored to strengthen the hearts of the wavering both through preaching the word and through the laying on of hands and confirmation. I shall indeed do this soon, if life accompanies me.

For now, however, I advise you to order all the priests living in those places to gather together at your monasteries and for three days to devote themselves to fasts and litanies; to wrap themselves in haircloth and sackcloth, sprinkle themselves with ashes, and earnestly beseech the Lord’s clemency with a common supplication, so that his overflowing mercy may not judge us according to our merits or exact vengeance from us according to the crimes of our iniquities, but rather, having been appeased, may wait for us and mercifully deign to receive those who return to repentance.

Let the priests therefore urge all the people to confession and repentance for their sins, and let the offenses unknowingly committed by the people be remedied by suitable correction, lest a deadly disease suddenly consume us and the voracity of hell swallow us forever to be tormented. And if our mind refuses, through love of charity, to serve in the sight of God, then at least let fear of death withdraw it from evil and strengthen it in acts that bring salvation.

## LETTER XXVII. JEREMIAH TO FROTHARIUS

[Col. 0880B]

“Jeremiah, servant of Christ,” and so forth. For the remainder, see Patrologia, volume 105, column 733, among the Works of Jeremiah.

## LETTER XXVIII. HETTI TO FROTHARIUS

[Col. 0880]

Hetti, archbishop by the grace of God, earnestly implores health in the Lord for the venerable Frotharius, bishop of Toul, worthy of the highest reverence.

We wish your sagacity to remember the admonition that you received this past year, expressed in very similar words. For you are not unaware with what caution we received this command of our lord the emperor: that we in our diocese, and each bishop in his own parish, should attend to the rule for increasing religious observance and thereafter to the workshops and service-buildings of the canons, so that, if they were well arranged in any places, they might henceforth be adorned with the greatest diligence.

Now a meeting is imminent, at which the Lord who issued the command will undoubtedly inquire about obedience to his order. Therefore examine carefully in your parish, in your own monasteries and in those of others, whether the aforesaid rule is being properly observed in every respect, and whether the workshops constructed and renovated according to its decrees are maintained, so that when we are presented before the imperial diligence, the truth concerning everything may be reported to him by us together, with the deficient undertakings of others cast far away.

For this admonition has been given for three years. Therefore no excuse can be found. Consequently, the more imperfect anything is for each person, the more fragile it will also be. Farewell in the Lord, and do not forget our smallness. May the God of peace and love be with you. Amen.

## LETTER XXIX. THE BISHOP OF LANGRES TO FROTHARIUS

[Col. 0880]

Alberic, bishop of Langres by divine permission and appointment, wishes eternal salvation in the Lord Jesus Christ to the most reverend and most desired lord, father and brother Frotharius, bishop of the Church of Toul.

[Note: This bishop of Langres was Alberic, as he names himself in the following letter.]

[Col. 0881A] We think it necessary and proper always to exercise due care and concern for those whom divine dispensation has wished us to govern, so that they may obtain from us by either prayers or services whatever appears necessary and useful to them. Therefore we have sent our cleric named Bertigang to your dignity and devotion, so that, as is your custom and practice, you may not disdain to ordain him to the priesthood.

Indeed, because we have such confidence in your humanity and kindness, deign nevertheless to hear us willingly. And if something prevents you, so that it is not appropriate for you to ordain him, may your letter grant us leave to ordain him ourselves. For your part, do not doubt that we are always ready and most devoted, both in service to God and in every office by which so exalted a person ought to be honored. May you always prosper exceedingly in the Lord, most reverend and most desired father, lord, and brother.

## LETTER XXX. ALBERIC TO FROTHARIUS

[Col. 0881]

Alberic, unworthy and useless, a bishop in name only, invokes happiness for Frotharius, his lord, father, and fellow bishop, revered with the affection of unique love.

If you are enjoying success in every respect, you are as we continually desire and pray. For the rest, we inform your affection that we have a certain village in your parish called the Monastery of Boso. But now it is losing both its name and its privilege and census, because of the new chapels dedicated by you for Teuderic.

Therefore I beseech your brotherly affection to act according to episcopal sincerity and ecclesiastical ordinance, so that, because of new chapels, the ancient Church may not lose what it has held for so many years, and so that I may not be compelled to summon an episcopal assembly over this matter. For you may not be without blame, and I may be liable, if through us it loses what it has always possessed.

But whatever your fatherhood decides concerning this, communicate it to us through the bearer of this letter. I wish your holiness to be governed by the Lord; remember me.

## LETTER XXXI. FROTHARIUS TO HITTO

[Col. 0882]

Frotharius, humble bishop of Toul, wishes eternal salvation to Hitto, bishop by the grace of God, revered with the highest honor and complete affection.

[Note: Hitto, or Hetto or Heyto, was bishop of Basel and abbot of Reichenau. He died in the year 836.]

We desire that the state of your fatherhood may flourish happily everywhere and that you may prosper in all things. For this reason we frequently implore divine clemency with complete attention, entreat it with every prayer, and beseech it with all our effort and all our heart, so that it may continually increase the progress of your good devotion, while safely reserving the fruit of your reward.

May it preserve you for a long time, in the course of passing time, with abundant health, so that here you may be adorned with the glory of many sons and in heaven joined to the fellowship of very many saints. We also earnestly ask you and those subject to your rule, as faithful people, to repay our remembrance in your sacred prayers and never cease to fortify and protect our frailty through prayer.

Leaving these matters aside, we inform your affection that we have been told that a dispute has arisen between you and Bertarius, our faithful vassal, because one of his servants concealed for some time and retained in his power your female servant, whom he had carried off by theft. The rest is missing.

## IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 845. ELDEFONSUS THE HISPANIC BISHOP

[Col. 0881D]

### NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING LITTLE WORK OF ELDEFONSUS

*(In Mabillon, Vetera Analecta, Appendix, p. 548.)*

[Col. 0881D] Although I do not doubt that, for some people, little credibility will attach to the title of “Revelation” and to the crude and mystical method of treatment employed by the author in the following little work, it nevertheless did not seem to me that it should be rejected entirely: first, because of the author’s antiquity; second, because of certain unusual matters explained in it; and finally, because of the scarcity of ancient authors who have written on this subject.

The date of the Incarnation, 845, in which the Revelation is said to have occurred, establishes its antiquity. The practice of celebrating three Masses at Easter, Pentecost, and the Transfiguration confirms it, as does the method of explaining the weight of a pound by twenty-five solidi, a custom especially common among the Franks in the age of Charlemagne. The author’s words occur at the end of the little work: “And three hundred such coins make a pound according to twenty-five solidi.”

This method of reckoning the pound agrees with what was established in the Council of Aachen of the year 817, chapter 57, “On the Pound of Bread”: that it should weigh thirty solidi before it is baked, as the heading of the chapter itself states. The text then follows, prescribing that a pound of bread be measured at thirty solidi by twelve denarii. Just as a numerical pound is still used among our people, so formerly a pound of weight consisted of twenty asses. But because the Council of Aachen defined the weight of raw bread according to the intention of the Rule of Saint Benedict, it consequently required thirty solidi for the pound.

Why, however, Eldefonsus requires twenty-five solidi for the ancient pound may perhaps be explained by the fact that the Spanish pound then consisted of fifteen ounces. From this method, I say, of calculating the pound by asses, it may be inferred that Eldefonsus lived at the time he himself indicates. Finally, a parchment codex about five hundred years old from the Vatican Library—[Col. 0883A] from which the following little work was copied by the most eminent Cardinal Bona and generously sent to me—supports this dating.

I have been unable to discover in which place Eldefonsus was bishop. He lived approximately two hundred years after the great Ildefonsus, bishop of Toledo. The lists of the Spanish bishops are empty in Tamius for the middle of the ninth century, when Eldefonsus lived, doubtless because of the ravages of the Moors. Rodrigo, bishop of Toledo, lists many bishops in book 4, chapter 18, of his History who attended the dedication of the church of Oviedo after the middle of the ninth century, but Eldefonsus is not among them. This is what concerns the author.

There are seven matters altogether explained in this little work: the inscription of the hosts, their quantity, number, weight, round shape, the quality of the unleavened bread, and baking within iron. The first four conditions seem to fall under the revelation, but not the last three. From this it is understood that the revelation was not intended to introduce the use of unleavened bread, but to define, once its use had already been accepted, its prescribed markings, quantity, number, and weight.

The author discusses the weight of the hosts at the end of his little work. He says that the larger host, while still raw, has as much weight as three coins placed on a balance, and that after being baked by fire it is reduced by one-sixth; the smaller host, however, weighs no more than one coin. He then says that three hundred coins make one pound. Thus each pound consisted of twenty-five solidi, and each solidus of twelve coins, just as among the Franks even in ancient times it consisted of twelve denarii.

From these facts I draw three conclusions. First, the larger hosts of the priests and the smaller hosts of communicants, as now, already existed at that time. Second, raw hosts could be placed on a balance and weighed, and therefore they were then made from a solid mass, even though they were baked within iron. Thus among the Cluniacs, “one man kneaded flour and pressed it together very vigorously upon a most polished board, having a rim all around it slightly higher than its surface, so that the water could not run off,” as stated in book 3, chapter 13, of the Customs of Cluny.

Third, one hundred larger raw hosts could be made from a single pound, a weight very different from that of our larger hosts. To test this, I weighed thirty of our larger hosts after baking and found that their weight amounted to one solid ounce. Multiply this number and weight of hosts by four: you will have one hundred twenty hosts weighing four ounces. Subtract one-sixth of the hosts in proportion to the baking, and one hundred hosts will remain; raw, they will weigh four ounces, whereas Eldefonsus’s one hundred hosts would weigh one pound—that is, twelve ounces, or perhaps fifteen. From this you may understand that, if Eldefonsus’s calculation is not mistaken, the weight of our hosts has decreased by at least two-thirds since that time.

Concerning the quantity or size of the hosts, Eldefonsus makes clear to us that five hosts were formed by a single impression of the larger iron: one larger host and four smaller ones. The larger host had the measure of three fingers from the center outward in the roundness of the unleavened bread—that is, if I understand correctly, three fingers from the center to the circumference—whereas our larger hosts, which we use at Paris, scarcely measure one finger and ten lines, as I have learned by experiment. Hence it is clear how much our more recent hosts have also diminished in this respect. Moreover, among the Cluniacs, six hosts could at the same time be placed in the iron in the eleventh century, as Udalricus, cited above, testifies.

As for the number of hosts, it varies with Eldefonsus according to the solemnities. There are five on Sundays and feast days; at Easter, forty-five at each of the three Masses; and the same number at Pentecost. But at each of the three Masses of Christmas and the Transfiguration of the Lord, and at the Ascension, there are seventeen; on weekdays, one.

Here a doubt troubles my mind: whether this rite of Eldefonsus was different from the rite of the Mozarabs, according to whose prescription the consecrated host is divided into nine portions, called the Corporatio, Nativity, Circumcision, Epiphany, Passion, Death, Resurrection, Glory, and Kingdom. All of these are consumed by the priest, with the two called Glory and Kingdom being placed in the chalice.

Furthermore, in representing the hosts, consideration was given not so much to geometric proportions—which are not accurately rendered in the manuscript—as to the figures that express the hosts. It is enough to have noted these matters concerning the present little work, whose title in the Vatican manuscript is as follows.

## REVELATION THAT WAS SHOWN TO THE VENERABLE ELDEFONSUS, A HISPANIC BISHOP, IN THE HOLY SPIRIT, IN THE SEVENTH MONTH

[Note: In the text, “the tenth.”]

[Col. 0883]

[Col. 0883C] In the year 845 of the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, this design—that is, the measure of three fingers from the angle in the roundness of the unleavened bread—arranged in this way and written according to this measure, appeared to me through a revelation of the Most High God in the tenth month, at dawn on the seventh day of the week, after the customary work had already been completed.

[Col. 0884C] Therefore these two wheels, engraved on two irons, always belong to a single bread, formed between their two sides. If the coin of an earthly king, valid everywhere, circulates, why should the ever-valid coin of the heavenly King not circulate everywhere even more effectively?

Behold the points painted on the wheels: the wording *retro quinque acta* is uncertain; the wheels and points show that God, who stands in the middle, has neither beginning nor end, just as neither the points nor the wheel has a beginning or end in its circuit. Look at the prophet Ezekiel struggling and conversing beside the river Chebar, among five wheels and four living creatures. Each creature had, on each head, four faces set on four sides, while one wheel stood within another in the central place.

For beneath the three points, within which are two things resembling columns above all others, is the Trinity, holding all things beneath itself, although it sits in the center while all are offering gifts around it. If there is a way of the feet on earth, there is truth of the head in heaven; the life of the breast remains in the middle and is to be restored to the saints.

Let us recall briefly what we earlier sought in Aaron’s breast, when we affirmed that the unleavened breads had been made to signify eternal life. If Andrew and James are companions on earth, and are joined together, so are Peter and Paul with the Most High Almighty God and all the saints in heaven. The four evangelists give testimony to Jesus together with all the saints on every side.

Just as a man’s thumb ought to cover an entire coin, so three coins, under the governance of God in this Trinity, touching one another, arranged in a triangular form, ought together to cover the whole host beneath them, in such a way that no one of the three coins can take an entire coin within itself while the other parts remain uncovered—so that the bread below is neither narrower nor wider outside by more than the circular white mark of a human fingernail.

[Col. 0885C] And what more need be said? “Whoever is ashamed of me and of my words,” says the Lord, “the Son of Man will be ashamed of him”—that is, he will be ashamed to hear, look upon, and assist him—“when he comes in his majesty, and that of the Father and of the holy angels.” And “whoever despises you despises me; whoever hears you hears me.” And if they have kept my word, they will keep yours also. And I will do the will of those who love and fear me.

Let us now return to the order. At Christmas, in the first, second, and third Masses, breads are to be offered in equal number and form: always twelve around the circumference, that is, in a circle, to signify the angelic choir; and in the middle, five in the form of a cross, to signify the evangelists and the one Son of God whom they attest, as though indeed supporting the one who was once crucified for the redemption of the human race.

Consider these seventeen together, since there are nine orders of angels, and you will find that the Holy Spirit is always sevenfold. The tenth is Man-God, created by generation in the flesh and formed in human appearance by being created in the Virgin Mary.

As for the three offices, join all the breads together; they amount to forty-one. But you will find, my friend of God, in the divine significance, that although God is one, the number fifty signifies every fullness in God, as does one hundred; and likewise ten, and also one thousand.

This is signified by the tenth month of Christmas, in which, in God Christ and man bodily, the fullness of all divinity is not merely dwelling but always remaining, as the apostle Paul himself testifies.

At Easter, namely on the Lord’s Resurrection, which is the subject of our discussion, one hundred thirty-five breads are to be offered in the form of a cross over the services of the three Masses: forty-five at each Mass, as follows:

[Col. 0886C] At the Ascension of the Lord Jesus Christ and at his Transfiguration, manifested to certain disciples on a high mountain—which took place on the sixth day before the Kalends of August, in the fifth month—the breads are to be offered in one and the same number and form. The same applies in every respect at Christmas, as is shown.

[Note: Yet it is now celebrated on the eighth day before the Ides of August; that month was called Sextilis by the ancients, or the sixth month.]

[Col. 0886D] Let us consider attentively in our minds the significance represented by the one hundred fifty-three fish. Or, following Athanasius, let us contemplate it more deeply: not three, but one. Such as the Father is, such is the Son, such is the Holy Spirit. And behold, the whole fullness is both hidden and manifest, signified in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit by John in heaven.

Nor is the Son seen without the Father and the Holy Spirit in the river Jordan. Nor is the Holy Spirit seen without the Father and the Son, flying through the expanse of this air. Christ bears witness to this when he says to the apostle Philip, who sought to see the Father: “Whoever sees me,” he says, “sees the Father also, because the Father, remaining in me, himself performs the works.”

Understand, therefore, O man, who yourself possess three persons distinct from one another within you: a living soul, an apparent flesh, and a spirit continually going forth from you. For the Father is eternal life itself; the Son is eternal speech itself; and the Holy Spirit is, like a ray of the sun, the splendor of eternal light that goes forth and returns.

Therefore do not think that the Most High God the Father is confused with the one proper Son himself. Saint Sedulius defines this wonderfully, saying:

> Not because the Supreme Father is, and this one is the Son:
>
> But because whatever the Supreme Father is, this the Son is.

Let us speak of the mystery. At Pentecost also, under a square form, yet with a cross in the middle—the figure of the heavenly city of Jerusalem—all the breads are to be offered in every respect, that is, over the services of the Masses, as many as at the Lord’s Resurrection, as appears in the following figure.

[Col. 0887D] On Sundays and on the feasts of God’s saints, no more breads are to be offered, and in particular no fewer than five in the form of a cross. For that middle bread ought often to be larger and more honorable than all the others; concerning it we read in a certain passage: “The Lamb signified in the middle.”

[Col. 0888B] On ordinary days, neither more nor fewer than one alone, because there is one God who is always one above all.

[Col. 0888C] And since, in so small a space of this book—unless it were as extensive as a very large library—I cannot display the loaves themselves made whole and painted with letters, as they ought to be and as they ought to be placed upon the altar, nor the actual figures of those solemnities, as written above, nor their quantities, that is, their sizes, at least I wish to indicate this by points. And just as we marked it above by way of prefiguration, so we repeat it again for remembrance of heart.

At the Nativity of the Lord, as you have heard, seventeen [loaves], three times. At the Resurrection of the Lord, forty-five loaves, three times. Likewise at Pentecost, forty-five loaves, three times. Likewise at the Transfiguration, which is at the time written above, seventeen loaves, three times, similarly to the Nativity. On Sundays, however, and at the festivals of the saints, only once, that is, in one serving, five loaves in this manner.

If it perhaps seems impossible to anyone, whose mind is filled with disgust, to offer all so many loaves to God at once with equal size, at least let one middle loaf of these five—that is, the Lord’s loaf—be this large, and so ornamented with writing on both sides, as was shown above in the two circles. Let each of the others have one-third of its size, and let only one name from these three names be written on it: either XPC, or IHC, or DS. Let no one assume any other name, if he wishes to write that name upon the Host, except one of these three. For not only one without the other, but also, truly, without several others, almost all the remaining names, as it has been revealed to me by the Holy Spirit, ought not to be written on the Hosts, except one of these three, whichever you wish: either XPC, or IHC, or DS. Not DNS, not REX, not PAX, not OMNIPOTENS, not VITA, not PANIS, as certain apocryphal writers suppose; except only that on one side there be XPC, and on the other a cross with two letters, thus:

[Col. 0889B] In one iron mold, although a large one, five Hosts can be formed together in such a manner that the middle one, which was written above first, is larger, while the other four are smaller, having one-third of its size, at the four corners of that mold: so that one has XPC written above, another IHC below, and REX on the left. But it is never to be offered alone, without some largest one, or without one of the other three; and in the fourth place, toward the south, [let there be] DS.

But so that you, faithful servant of God, may know the exact measure of such Hosts, which will not allow you to err in any way, hear what weight the bread first shown above in the larger circles has; hear, and discern it in the smaller ones, just as, through the revelation and governance of the indivisible Holy Trinity together, I learned with complete truth.

Three modern coins have as much weight as 153 largest blue grains, which are called wheat. And that larger Host, while still uncooked, has as much weight as three coins weighed in a balance; when cooked by fire, its weight is reduced by one-sixth. The smaller Host, too, should have no more than the weight of one coin; or each of the smaller Hosts should weigh one coin; or three together should weigh three coins—this also not without a great mystery, under the governance of the Holy Trinity.

For when I consider the number of fish, namely 153, and likewise the same number of wheat grains given in the weight of three coins, and the bread Host, which, if weighed with perfect exactness, is neither larger nor smaller than—as it is written—the measure of three fingers at the corner, just as was shown above by the space of three coins, I marvel, exceedingly astonished, at the truly divine dispensation, foreordination, and arrangement.

Let no one doubt this: although the Hosts have different and dissimilar forms in the book—that is, one is larger here and another smaller there—when each one has been expressed in the molds according to its exact weight, its most certain form will immediately be recognized in the circle, without ambiguity.

Let us speak about the weight. And behold, three such coins, whose weight contains neither more nor less than the larger Host, if it has been made with the most exact weight, receive neither more nor less, according to the ancient custom, than what is contained in 153 larger grains of wheat. And 300 such coins, through twenty-five solidi, make a pound. And twelve such pounds, which are made from 3,600 coins, make one sextarius of wheat; from this, seven loaves can be formed, by which one person can live for an entire week—or seven in a single day. Indeed, a fair and exact modius ought to consist of seventeen such fair sextarii, and it can, with the Lord’s protection, sustain 119 men hired for their daily food.

Thus far, with Christ assisting and effecting the work, we have discussed weight, form, and measure; and, as was heard above, we have defined them in writing as best we could.

**The End.**

**In the year of the Lord 846. Joseph the priest.**

[Col. 0889D]

## Historical Notice

(From Fabricius, *Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis.*)

[Col. 0889]

[Col. 0889C] Joseph the priest, whose *History of the Translation of the Bodies of Saints Ragnobertus and Zeno*, carried out in the year of Christ 846, was published by Dacher at volume XII of the *Spicilegium*, p. 600 (new folio edition, volume II, pp. 127–133).* The same *History of the Translation of the Bodies*, etc., was published by the Bollandist Fathers from two different manuscript codices, volume XIV, p. 618, but with frequent interpolation from another source. They believe, however, that the author of this same History was not Joseph, but Erveus, who is often mentioned in that History, never without praise. Nevertheless, the writers of the *History of French Literature* rightly attribute it to Joseph. See the same History, volume V, p. 91.

[Col. 0891A]

## History of the Translation of the Bodies of Saints Ragnobertus and Zeno, by Joseph the Priest

Former chancellor of the king of Aquitaine and tutor of King Louis.

(From Acher, *Spicilegium*, volume II, p. 127.)

[Col. 0891A] Here begins the account of the Translation of the bodies of the blessed Ragnobertus and Zeno, and of the miracles which the Lord deigned to display through them.

## Chapter One. On the Warning, or Translation, of the Body

In the year of the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 846, in the tenth indiction, in the seventh year, while King Charles was reigning—namely, the son of the Emperor Louis—and while Sergius was governing the Roman Church (having received the honor of the apostolate in the first year, at which time the church of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, was captured), while the venerable Bishop Baltfrid was governing the Church of Bayeux, the most blessed pontiff Ragnobertus of the Church of Bayeux appeared in a vision to a certain venerable man named Erveus [Col. 0891B] and addressed him in gentle words:

“Arise, man of God; go to the city of Bayeux, and climb to the place called Montem Ecclesiae, where the bodies of the bishops of that city were formerly buried. There you will find a basilica built in honor of blessed Exsuperius, the first bishop of that see. But now it has been almost stripped of its ornaments, so that it has no beauty, and no divine office is celebrated there; rather, it is cracked, abandoned, and solitary, displaying the ruin of its collapse. In it the bodies of the blessed confessors, the pontiff Ragnobertus and his minister Zeno, lie neglected, without any reverence for dignity or honor. Therefore I command you, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, to exhume them from there with the utmost religious reverence, transport them by carrying them to the proper places of your authority, and become their guardian for all time. Also provide suitable places, adorned with their own splendor, for burying their bodies, where they may remain honorably.”

When he had said this, they immediately vanished. Erveus arose and, recalling the vision he had seen, was shaken in mind and horrified by the unbelievable sight. For he thought that he had been deceived by a phantasmal illusion; therefore he told no one and consigned the whole matter to oblivion. He considered himself burdened by the weight of many crimes [Note: [Col. 0891D] *Illatum*: read *illigatum*, “bound”], and entangled in the secular affairs of the laity; he believed himself in no way worthy to enjoy heavenly visions, to lift the bodies of the saints from their tombs, or to dare to carry them to their proper places.

After some time had passed, the same venerable man appeared a second time to Erveus, who was lying on his left side. In the sleep of night it seemed to him that the same saint struck him with his fist on the right side, sternly rebuking him for neglecting the command of the earlier vision, which the Lord had deigned to show him through His servants. For this reason he was seized by fever and afflicted by three months of torment. This second-order vision was shown to him on the eighth day before the Kalends of July; like the first, he completely concealed it through disbelief arising from consideration of his own frailty.

## Chapter Two. On the Terrible Apparitions and on the Garments of Blessed Ragnobertus, Which Appeared Unharmed at His Translation

As the celebration of the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ approached, on that most solemn night, after the crowing of the roosters, two men visibly came to the aforementioned Erveus. One of them appeared to be dressed in episcopal garments. The *planeta* [Note: [Col. 0892D] *Planta*: Acher emends it to *planeta*, “chasuble”] which he wore above shone with a saffron radiance; we saw him wrapped in it at the translation of his body, and we affirm that it still remains with the body in the tomb today.

The same venerable man was terrifying in appearance and lofty in stature; his white hair gleamed beneath his well-groomed head of hair, and his reddish face was suffused with extraordinary brightness. Standing before Erveus, he addressed him in terrifying words:

“I am Ragnobertus, together with my companion Zeno, and we have been sent by the command of almighty God. Jesus Christ has sent us to you for the third time and has revealed to you through us the secret of His mercy. But you, being disobedient, have in no way wished to obey His commands; stubbornly, you have refused to fulfill the orders of your teacher. And because, treating lightly what we announced to you for the third time, you have not merely consigned it to oblivion, failing to understand that the mysteries of heaven are being revealed to you, but because you have been unwilling to let these things penetrate within you, scorning the authority of our embassy, behold, what the Lord speaks through the voice of the Prophet will be fulfilled against you, saying: ‘He who did not desire blessing, it shall be far from him; and he clothed himself with cursing as with a garment,’ etc. (Psalm 103:16–17).

“Know, then, that if from this day you do not strive to fulfill the commands of your teacher, because you have remained disobedient for so long, you will be consumed for a very long time by the greatest sickness and suffer such loss to your body that, apart from the servant of God Job, no human being would have returned to the gifts of life after paying such penalties in his body. Therefore, once chastised, do not again, after being instructed by the persuasions of so great a divine gift, regard the secrets of these gifts as unbelievable.

“Moreover, if even now, with the most stubbornly arrogant mind, you attempt to delay and refuse to fulfill the commands of almighty God, may you die of elephantiasis, and may you perish with your entire body struck by leprosy. The discharge from ulcers shall gush forth through your most protected extremities, even to the destruction of your body, so that scarcely any of your loved ones will be able to endure the scars of your most foul-smelling body. Having undergone such a death, you will be buried in damnation in hell.

“Since you are considering these things in your mind, whether the Lord grants you the power to act, or whether you can effectively accomplish what you have received, a period of fifteen days is granted to you.”

Saint Zeno, who was present with the blessed confessor Ragnobertus—he appeared to be covered in exceedingly white deacon’s garments, which nowhere appeared at the translation of his body, unlike the garments of blessed Ragnobertus [Note: [Col. 0893D] *Comparuerunt*: perhaps it should read *computruerunt*, “rotted,” or the word *putrefactae*, “having decayed,” should be supplied]—departed from the man’s sight after these words.

“Now, man of God, remember and ponder in your mind the vision sent to you from heaven. Since two things have been offered to you which are rather remedies for your health, do not neglect to decide that they must be carried out; for by divine judgment you will either pay the penalties of the present life or those of the future eternally.”

Then, suddenly terrified, Erveus awoke, rose from the bed on which he was lying, and with a mind full of terror penetrated the meaning of what he had seen. He hurried to the church to which he had gone in the evening to celebrate the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ. After completing the office of the festive night in the praises of God, he also fulfilled the ministry of the most sacred day by listening to the daytime office.

Thus, on the very day of the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ, on which he had gone in terror to that same city, he wished to disclose what had been named to the aforementioned Baltfrid, the city’s own bishop. But when he could not find him there in any way, he returned as quickly as possible from the city of Lindis [Note: [Col. 0893D] *Lindis*: that is, Lisieux, says Acher]. There he found Freculfus, the venerable bishop of that city, and told him everything he had seen.

When the prelate heard this, he encouraged him to carry it out, saying:

“If what you say appears to have been truly announced to you, act, man of God, as quickly as possible, so that you may accomplish what, with the Lord’s consent, has been entrusted to you. For the Lord who commanded you to announce these things will be your companion, and you will have Him as the strongest helper of your work. He will direct His angel of peace with you, who will guard you and make your steps proceed along the way of salvation, so that you may strive to do everything according to the Lord’s command. But if, deceived by some illusion and caught, like a dreamer, by fantasies, you rashly attempt and endeavor to do this, without doubt you will incur danger to your present life, your soul, and your possessions, and you will be punished with eternal penalty.”

Furthermore, instructed by the counsel of the most religious prelate Freculfus, Erveus took with him two venerable priests, Guinemarus and Harduinus, and hastened to the city of Bayeux, where the bodies of the saints rested. Nevertheless, he approached the city secretly because of the devastation of the Britons, who at that time had occupied the same land and were crushing the region with great slaughter.

## Chapter Three. On Entering the Church When Their Monuments Were Translated, and on the Fog Which Covered the Whole Region on the Following Day

He entered the church of that city and, having lit lamps, prayed there for the Lord’s help. As day was declining and the signal for the office of Compline sounded, he entered with the priests of God the church in which the bodies of the saintly confessors were located.

They began to dig up the tomb of the blessed confessor Ragnobertus. There, with devoted care and under the protection of the divine gift, the venerable priests, filled with great joy, gathered the bones of blessed Ragnobertus the pontiff. Lifting him from the tomb with every mark of devotion, they bound him in a cloak and placed him in a new vessel.

After this they turned to the tomb of Zeno, formerly his disciple. Laying hands upon him, they removed him from the grave in which he lay and enclosed him in another vessel. Finally, when day began to dawn, they carried the bodies of the saints out of the city with hymns and divine praises.

That day there was such a dense fog of the air throughout the entire region that they could scarcely see one another, which, by the Lord’s permission, proved extremely helpful for their journey.

At that time Baltfrid was bishop of that city. He had been accused before the glorious King Charles of a shameful crime and died [Note: [Col. 0893D] “He died.” This narrative is badly corrupt in many places. The intention is to cleanse as many blemishes as possible; here, since the text as it stands cannot be understood, it can be restored with some certainty if one reads: “and therefore, because … in the synod, however, he received the office,” etc.], because he had hurried to the holy synod convened by the king. He was absent from the city; at the synod he recovered the office into which he had fallen [or: from which he had been suspended], because he had been suspended by the king, and he was even adorned with many gifts.

Meanwhile, the aforementioned men, traveling with the bodies of the saints, turned aside at evening to rest in a village called Nogerolas. Resting there that night, they spent the night in vigil at the divine offices.

## Chapter Four. On the Woman Blind from Birth Who Received Sight, and on the Unquenchable Light Carried Before Them

When morning came, they lifted the bodies of the saints onto their shoulders and began the journey which, with the Lord’s favor, they had undertaken. A very large crowd of people and religious priests of God came to meet them from every side. As they proceeded on the second day with a great multitude of people, it happened that they reached a place where certain criminals had killed a man that same night.

While they were giving the man burial, Erveus, out of his charity, began to urge the people to implore the Lord’s mercy for his soul.

It happened that a certain woman blind from birth, named Bedenigga, came there and received the light which she had always lacked. By the Lord’s mercy she obtained health before the funeral procession of the saints. This occurred on the fifth day before the Ides of January.

Their lights—for although at that season the days commonly abound in heavy rains and showers—never failed, but remained continuously unquenchable. Then, lifting the bodies of the saints from the place where they had paused for a little while, where the woman blind from birth had also received sight, they reached a basilica consecrated in honor of blessed Victorius, built on the property of Erveus’s mother. There they placed the bodies of the saints upon an altar constructed in the same basilica.

As the dawn of day rose and the fame of the confessors spread throughout the region, a certain man came whose hand was withered and useless for every task; he could not even bring it to his mouth. He was restored to health.

## Chapter Five. On the Woman Afflicted by Quartan Fevers Who Was Freed, on Many Others, and on the Healing of Many People’s Toothache

On the eighth day, a certain woman named Savenildis, afflicted with quartan fevers, hurried to the tombs of the holy confessors and immediately obtained the grace of health and was freed from the illness by which she was held.

Many others afflicted by these fevers came from the neighboring regions on every side to the bodies of the blessed men mentioned above, with vows of devotion, and obtained the fulfillment of their requests. Others, tormented by various illnesses and diverse bodily afflictions, came bearing their vows and, by the Lord’s favor, returned healed of them all at that same place.

I do not think that the miracles which the Lord deigned to perform through His servants should be left unmentioned. For when the sick hear of these things, they are restored to faith, and the healthy are strengthened toward better things. When the deeds of diligent men are committed to the writings of the saints so that they may be preserved in memory through the ages, they summon those who hear them to a great contest of devotion. When they behold the saints’ good zeal in action, they recognize where they ought to advance toward better things.

They contemplate themselves as though in a mirror of their own vision, and when something deformed appears, they strive to cleanse it by God’s will. There each person sees how he ought to imitate Christ amid the various afflictions of his body, despise the present world, and hasten as quickly as possible toward eternal happiness.

When the torments of persecution, blows, and excessive fasts of the saints are recounted, men of good will are pierced with compunction. Enlightened by divine grace, they are summoned to the contest of battle, so that they too may obtain, through the service of devotion, the same grace of the Holy Spirit which the saints attained through the contest of labor. Thus, by imitating them through the diverse torments of their sufferings, those who devoutly imitate them may also receive the palm which the saints won as victors and may reign in eternal happiness.

The reward of heavenly recompense comes to those who persevere; therefore those who persevere pursue the payment for their labor. [Col. 0896A] He rightly awaits the promise of God who carries out His command, whose judgment depends upon the outcome of our examination. What we sow, we reap; what we give, we receive.

When we see that the saints endured the evils of the world for a long time and recall their examples to mind, we are made stronger for enduring kinds of suffering, since we have seen that they went before us, already triumphing with the Lord. And if we remain steadfast in these same hardships for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, we too shall deserve to attain the glory of everlasting life.

The examples of the saints are of great benefit, especially to those who imitate them. Very many of the saints’ good works are shared by many people, and therefore those who delight in them more freely raise their spirit amid labors, vigils, prayers, and fasts, and are compelled with complete dedication to complete the contests of a better life.

If some such poison has slipped into anyone’s inner chambers and ensnared the marrow of his mind, he has the purest medicines to which he must hasten, so that before the wound is brought to the rottenness of a scar, it may be healed by the prayers and examples of the saints.

Those who refuse to follow the footsteps of the saints, walking along precipitous paths, are worn down by a double constraint and in the future are crushed by a double condemnation: they did not do the good things they were able to do, and they did the evil things they ought not to have done. Therefore the deeds of the saints, and also their miracles which our Lord Jesus Christ deigns to perform through them, must be drawn upon for our advancement, entrusted to memory, and always meditated upon, because there it is found fully how they pleased and served God.

But since we have digressed a little, let us return to the matters above that remain to be completed. We have, as it were, turned our style toward writing about other things; nevertheless, we remained there, since we are speaking about them.

Moreover, at the same time there was a certain blind man from the region of Le Mans named Hildegarius. He was warned in the sleep of night to go to the bodies of the saints in order to receive his sight. Immediately supported by the hands of a servant, he was led by him to their monument. There, by the grace of the Lord, he received the use of the sight which he had long ago lost and obtained his former health.

## Chapter Six. On the Paralytic Woman Who Was Healed, and on the Warning Concerning the Construction of the Church

Nor should this be passed over: a certain paralytic woman named Gislildis had lain for five years with her body paralyzed and could not use any limb for its strength or service. While she was being carried by the hands of her maidservant, she rested prostrate before the bodies of the saints. There the most blessed pontiff Ragnobertus and his companion Zeno appeared to her in an ecstatic state and said:

“Rise and go to Erveus, and tell him to build a church in honor of the holy Savior in a clean and undefiled place, because God in no way wishes us to rest in this place or be buried here.”

[Col. 0897A] It is always the custom of the saints that, seeking purity of mind and body, they deserve to see the pure God. Without doubt, whoever strives to see God should endeavor to seek cleanliness and purity of mind and body, because God is seen by no one except the pure in heart, as He Himself says: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8). And elsewhere someone says:

> You who desire to be good and seek an honorable life,  
> Love the cleanliness of body and soul.  
> A clean house will be able to retain a clean Lord.  
> For you will always be such a guest of such a host.

If a clean place is sought for the burial of the body, how much more must purity be maintained with the splendor of cleanliness? It does no good to keep the body clean and clad in splendid garments while holding the soul below, defiled by the filth of its sins. But it does no harm for the body outwardly to be covered with certain scars and wounds, provided that inwardly the mind is kept vigorous in health.

When the aforementioned woman heard the warning, she replied:

“Who am I, that we should be able to believe these things when I announce them? For I will in no way be believed.”

Blessed Ragnobertus the confessor replied:

“Do as I command you, and I will make in you a sign of belief, by which they will unquestionably believe your words. Rise,” he said, “in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, and be freed from the illness by which you are held. Let your flesh receive its health, so that by this you may affirm in faith whatever you say.

“There is still another indication revealing the truth of the matter. From this present day until the translation of our body, the Lord Jesus Christ will deign to display no sign of a miracle through us His servants as long as we remain in this church, where the bodies of the dead lie buried, whose spirits are tormented in hell. We cannot come here in any way. What have we to do in the heavenly Jerusalem, in the homeland of life with the Lord, with those who are imprisoned and tormented in the confines of hell?

“We were once in this pilgrimage through which the just and the unjust alike run. Although the conduct of the saints in this life is always in heaven because of the performance of good works, nevertheless they are joined together on the road by the equal condition of their bodies. After departing from this sorrowful captivity, they are divided from one another, because the just proceed to the homeland of happiness, where they enjoy the vision of God alone with angelic choirs, while the impious and sinners are led to the savage torments of Tartarus, where they are tortured with the devil and his angels.

“And this is the misery of supreme unhappiness: to dwell together in this world and enjoy this life together, but not to live equally. For this reason we can no longer come here, now that we have revisited our bodies. Therefore let a new place be chosen for our burial, where our bodies may rest, where also the glorious assembly of angels may be present, and acceptable vows may be offered; where daily praises may be given to the Lord with divine offices by day and by night; where those who come together may obtain forgiveness of sins and be healed of various illnesses; and toward which the eternal Lord may look with a merciful and serene countenance through heavenly illumination.”

After these words they vanished completely. The woman immediately rose healthy from the bed on which she had lain and announced to Erveus what she had seen and heard, and what she had been commanded.

## Chapter Seven. On the Dedication of the Church and on the Miracles Which the Lord Displayed Through His Servants on That Day

When the religious man Erveus heard this, he began to consider in his mind where, from what source, and at whose expense he should found a church in honor of the holy Savior. With the Lord’s consent, he found a place most worthy of God because of the illustrious merits of the saints. At his own expense—not as he had wished and hoped, but as he was able—he founded a church in honor of our Lord Jesus Christ, raised it to the roof despite his poverty and limited means, and adorned it with various decorations as he was able. Thus, under the Lord’s guidance, he brought the whole work to completion.

The time for the dedication of that church and the festive day of the translation of the blessed bodies had now arrived. Present were venerable and distinguished prelates, namely Freculfus, bishop of Lisieux in the same region [Note: [Col. 0897D] *Lixogensis*: Acher emends it to *Lexoviensis*, “of Lisieux”], as well as Baltfrid, prelate of the city of Bayeux, and Ansegaudus, bishop of the Church of Avranches. Invited by Erveus, they arrived at the village of Suiacum on the tenth day before the Kalends of April. Coming together, they exhorted the crowds of people to celebrate the praises of the divine gift and solemnly completed the vigil of the entire night with the appropriate offices.

At dawn they rose and put on the holy vestments, together with a multitude of priests of the same order, to transfer the bodies of the saints. They prepared the purest place in which to put them. Almost the whole province was represented there by a multitude of people, offering due praises to God, and every order of venerable priests had gathered for that most festive day. With them an innumerable common people also rejoiced, offering praises and vows to the one God with exultant joy, filled with every happiness and awaiting the festive solemnity of the day.

When about the third hour of that day had passed, the aforementioned prelates entered the church of Saint Victor [Note: [Col. 0898D] *Victoris*: above, in chapter 4, it reads *Victorii*. Not long afterward, *arcae* should be restored to *arae*, “altar”], where the bodies of the blessed confessors were located.

They lifted the bodies of the blessed confessors with hymns and divine praises and carried them to the newly built house. Three arks of almighty God had been constructed there, with a place prepared in the middle for burying the bodies of the saints. One was buried at the right wall, namely the holy pontiff Ragnobertus; another was buried on the left; those who inhabit the holy house venerate them there to this day.

Before they were carried by the aforementioned prelates, the house of God was consecrated inside and out through the grace of sanctification. Three altars were consecrated there by the consecrations of three prelates. The venerable Freculfus, bishop of Lisieux, consecrated the first in honor of our Lord Jesus Christ. Baltfrid, bishop of the Church of Bayeux, consecrated the middle one in honor of Saint Ragnobertus and all the saints, together with Zeno; it appeared to have been founded at the heads of the confessors. Finally, Ansegaudus, bishop of the city of Avranches, blessed the third in veneration of holy Mary, Mother of God, and Saint John the Baptist.

When these things had been properly arranged according to custom, the bodies of the blessed confessors were buried. Under the Lord’s guidance, they placed each one in his own location with praises and divine honors.

There was rejoicing throughout the entire city, praises rang out in a voice of exultation, and to this day an enduring, unspeakable joy remains there. What a multitude of monks was present, and what a great crowd of canons! Almost the entire multitude of the people from the neighboring regions had gathered there. Until the bodies were committed to burial, they accompanied them with hymns and praises and with every kind of spiritual exultation.

Nor does it seem that what happened for joy on that same day should be passed over. Rain had occupied the whole land of that region and watered everything like rivers. But in the very place where the people had gathered to celebrate the feast, it did not rain at all. In a marvelous manner the watery moisture coming from elsewhere failed to reach them there, and while they celebrated the feast in that place, not even dew touched them. Thus the priests of God, who had gathered with all the people wearing priestly garments for the funeral rites of the blessed, began to return joyfully to their own homes without rain showers, once the bodies had been committed to burial.

Moreover, what almighty God deigned to accomplish on the day of the translation and dedication of the church through the merits of His servants must be entrusted to memory for the benefit of many in future times.

A certain mute woman named Hildeburgis, mute from birth, began to speak. Because the day of the new translation and the new consecration of the church had dawned, the Lord wished to illumine that day with a new sign of miracles, showing that many signs were being performed in those times.

We also saw another miracle on that same day which must not be concealed. A certain woman named Bertinda, afflicted by a demon, was freed there on that same day. Furthermore, a certain blind woman, sitting near the bodies of the saints at the place where they had previously rested before the translation and seeking the gifts of the Lord’s mercy, was given sight on the very day of the festival.

Thus this day is seen to have been illumined by these three signs of the Lord. And since three altars had been built inside, signs of three miracles were effected there. This most solemn festival is celebrated on the eighth day before the Kalends of April.

## Chapter Eight. On a Man Blind from Birth Who Was Given Sight

A certain blind man named Hermenricus, blind from his mother’s womb, received the sight which he had always lacked and deserved to be restored to his former health. Thus, having received the brightness of his sight, he returned joyfully to his own home.

## Chapter Nine. On the Priest’s Arrogance and His Broken Leg
While he was returning with joy, by the road along which he had come, giving thanks to God, he encountered a certain priest named Gulfuido, seated on a horse. The priest said to him: “Where are you coming from, and where are you going? Are you not the man who, having long ago lost his sight, used to walk across the level roads with a guide?”

The blind man replied: “I am the one who, before today, never deserved to see the sight of heaven, but always went along the roads by which I had to travel with a guide, led by the hands of others.”

“But,” said the priest, “whose merit do you think brought this about, so that you received the light you had lost?”

He replied: “I have been freed through the merits of the holy confessors, and have been restored to complete health.”
