Then the aforementioned priest, mocking him, struck his own leg with the staff he was carrying and said: “Indeed, the Lord performed this miracle through these servants just as you claim—just as I am now going to break these very legs of mine.” And when he struck his legs with the staff, immediately, as he spoke these words, pain afflicted the leg; he fell from his horse to the ground, and the leg appeared to be broken. By this sign it was made clear both that the blind man had been freed through the merits of the saints and that the priest’s leg had been broken through his own fault, because of the incredible mercy of almighty God toward his servants.

The report spread throughout that entire region, and there was nowhere where the name of the Lord was not invoked, or where the glorious merits of Saint Ragnobert the confessor and of Zeno, his companion, were not remembered with veneration.

## CHAPTER X. Of a woman freed from a flow of blood, by the Lord’s favor.

There was a woman born in a village called Baliola who had suffered from a flow of blood for a long time. She came to the bodies of the saints and brought her vows; there she was freed from this illness and, having recovered her health, returned home.

But because there precede many miracles of signs that the Lord deigned to perform through the merits of his servants, and because he also commanded them to be brought to this place, while many more events occurred in the same place afterward, we judge it worthwhile to insert a few from among the many. For who could count how many sick people are healed there every day, by the Lord’s favor, from various ailments? No sick person who comes devoutly for the sake of his illness to be cured fails to deserve to be heard and healed there. Accordingly, people afflicted with various illnesses come from every direction, and, with our Lord Jesus Christ always propitious, deserve to be healed.

From this it is clearly understood that, while they are visibly healed outwardly, inwardly, through the most hidden mercy of the omnipotent Lord, they are released from many bonds of sin; offenses are lifted, crimes washed away, and various kinds of sin are healed when they are enlightened by the grace of the Holy Spirit. Therefore, while people suffering from various ailments hasten to that same holy place for remedies of health,

## CHAPTER XI. [Col. 0901A] Of sight restored to a blind man.

A certain blind man also came from the aforementioned village of Baliolas, from which the woman who suffered from the flow of blood had come. His name was Odricus. When he reached the bodies of the blessed confessors, he made a prayer and deserved to receive the light of his sight. He had come blind, but returned seeing and filled with joy.

## CHAPTER XII. Likewise, of a daughter blind from birth, who had no light and received light.

His daughter too, who had formerly lacked the sight that she had been unable to have, on the day of their feast, through the Lord’s mercy, deserved to receive sight. Thus, like her father, having received the vision of her brightness, she returned from there rejoicing to her home.

## CHAPTER XIII. Of a lame woman healed.

Furthermore, a certain lame woman named Regnoara was carried by the hands of others to the place of healing. There she recovered the health of her weakened limbs, and, guided by the Lord, returned on her own feet without anyone’s assistance.

## CHAPTER XIV. Of Herveus’s obedience and of his illness.

It seemed worthwhile to insert the account of how the blessed confessor foretold what was to come upon Herveus, who was disobedient to his admonitions. For, on the third occasion of his vision, he rebuked him and foretold that he would suffer many adversities because he had not believed his admonitions and, in his disbelief, had not fulfilled the Lord’s commands, but had consigned everything to forgetfulness and paid no attention to the instructions of the saints.

Thus the saints’ word was fulfilled: although it came late, the predicted blow fell upon Herveus—an unbearable affliction of the heart and a dissolution of all his limbs—so that for eighteen continuous months pain afflicted his heart and body. By then nearly wasted away in the flesh, so that scarcely anyone could live in such bodily weakness except by the Lord’s support, he endured torments that can neither be spoken nor believed. Finally, he felt no relief in his body, neither by day nor by night. His only food and drink was water. He could neither turn onto the other side nor bring his hand to his mouth. Thus, consumed by such torments, he was afflicted for the aforesaid lengthy period.

But when the time of the Lord’s mercy was approaching, so that he might in some way receive relief from such great pain, he remembered the permission previously granted to him by our Lord Jesus Christ through the merits of the saints. He was therefore carried to the tombs of the saints; there, by the Lord’s favor, he deserved the aid of healing and received the preservation of his health.

O ineffable divine goodness and merciful compassion, which makes sinners be punished in the present life so that you may have them purer in the life to come; which chastises the negligent through your mercy and inflicts every kind of diverse scourge upon them, lest they remain bound by the chains of sins; so that, recognizing the evil of their wicked deeds, they may strive to perform the good works of their way of life, through which, with Christ’s gift, they may be able to reach the homeland of life.

## CHAPTER XV. Of his wife, freed from fevers.

Finally, his wife, a woman of good religious character named Milesendis, was afflicted by fevers for three days. She came to the holy place and was cured, healed of her affliction. Very many possessed by demons are brought there and are healed daily through the saints’ merits. Many who come to the tomb of Saint Zeno and fulfill their vows are also freed from toothache. For all who are tortured by various painful afflictions and ask for mercy before the tombs of the blessed confessors deserve to receive health of body and soul.

## CHAPTER XVI. Of the rash presumption of robbery. [Col. 0902B]

Indeed, it is not shameful to write what happened to a certain most wretched man because of his reckless presumption in robbery, what great disasters of misery followed him, and with what torment of death he miserably lost his life, suffering a punishment worthy of his vengeance.

There was a certain wretch who practiced the cruelty of robbery like a beast. He was one of the tyrants’ associates, belonging to a certain most wretched Martin. Following his customary will, he shamelessly attacked the holy place, bound together bundles of grain with their ties, began to steal them, and carried them away from that same holy place.

When one of God’s servants named Gothardus came out of his cell and saw him acting in this way, he addressed him with gentle words, saying: “Why, brother, have you entered the holy place so irreverently? And why are you trying to carry away with you the heap of ears of grain from which the brothers of this place must live?”

The man, filled with an unclean spirit and eager to heap malice upon malice, said: “Even if Ragnobert himself were a bundle of ears of grain, I would certainly give him to my horse to eat.”

When Brother Gothardus heard this, he hurried back to his little cell, shut the door, and began to implore the Lord’s mercy and invoke the merits of the saints.

Then the aforementioned man went with the sheaves of grain to a village named Promerendum. When he entered a certain house there, he gave the bundles to his horse to eat and told the owner of the house where he had found the sheaves and how he had taken them by force; he also told him what he had said to the servant of God.

The man said to him: “May you repent of having acted against your own soul, wretch. Go back to the holy place and return what you presumptuously carried away from there. Moved to repentance, humble yourself before God and his saints, lest the Lord’s fury and indignation come upon you and you perish, consumed by a demon.”

But he replied: “By my salvation, I will certainly not do that. Even if that saint himself were a sheaf, I would surely give him to my horse to eat.”

Then the horse suddenly collapsed and died. The wretch, seized by a demon, put his fingers into his own eye, tore out the first one, and said: “Receive, Saint Ragnobert, the eye that has been taken from me in payment for your sheaves.” In the same way, when he had torn out the other, he added: “Receive this one also, in punishment for my cruelty, for your bundles.”

He then turned to his tongue, and, having cut it with his own teeth, drew from his mouth with his hand the piece of tongue he had severed, together with the blood. Thus, by the penalties exacted from the three [members] of his own body [Note: [Col. 0903D] “Penalties exacted.” Acherius says that perhaps it should read “with the punishments inflicted”; I see no need for correction here.], he paid the vengeance for three bundles. Finally, miserably tearing out the hair of his head, he immediately ended his life.

Indeed, no one doubts that infernal torments gnaw at the man who was not afraid to say that he wanted to give a saint to his horse to eat. Saints must be treated with reverence, honored, and venerated by all. For with how many terrifying torments are those afflicted who hunger after the spoils of robbery, when they are also shaken by torturous pains and descend to the prison of hell to be tormented forever? There, without any respite or end, they are punished with torments; there, their worm will not die and the fire will not be extinguished, but whoever is burned there will pay eternal penalties in everlasting corrosion.

But you, whoever you are who read these things or hear them read, recall them and bring them back to memory through diligent meditation, so that you may take heed of what must be avoided in such matters. Flee from such acts as you would flee from poison, lest, by imitating such deeds, you come to the same punishments. Let it be enough for you to live from what is your own, or to seek your livelihood through good ingenuity or a craft, so that you may complete this life far from such things.

## CHAPTER XVII. Another similar miracle.

Moreover, it seems necessary to add another similar sign of miracles: namely, the case of a certain criminal who, because of the detestable deeds of his presumption, received the punishment he deserved, so that the audacity of his wickedness was demonstrated and the vengeance of damnation followed him as well.

There was a certain servant named Modingus, himself the servant of Herveus’s brother, whose name was Crelion. Stirred up by the devil, he boldly approached a certain house full of grain for the purpose of theft. Because he could not find the key to the door, he struck it three or four times with his foot and broke the door of the house into three parts.

Then, secretly and fraudulently, he stole a purse full of three modii. On the third day, punishment and death followed him. For his body was divided into three parts. Since he had divided the door of the house into three parts, and had carried away three modii of grain by theft, his body was cut apart in three sections. Thus, by such a death, he ended a life worthy of it.

Let every hearer tremble at this and be afraid to approach this place where the bodies of the holy confessors are venerated unless humbly; to conduct himself there unless reverently; or to do anything there unless it is honorable and chaste, contributes to the usefulness of the place, or suitably accords with the place’s holy religion. For if he acts otherwise, or does anything there or in the surrounding area that is improper, he will by no means remain there, because the vengeance of his damnation will immediately follow him.

But you, human being, attend to the conduct proper to this most holy religion, and embrace the good works of mercy that follow.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Of King Charles’s toothache and of the gift he bestowed upon the saints. [Col. 0904A]

Finally, the most glorious Charles, king of France, Aquitaine, and Neustria, was afflicted by toothache. He sent vows to the bodies of the blessed confessors and immediately obtained relief.

His most noble wife, Hermentrudis, the venerable queen, then asked the magnificence of the aforementioned most magnificent King Charles, on account of the merit of her munificent devotion, that he deign to bestow something of his own upon the holy confessors. With God’s favor he granted her request and, for the sake of the merit of his most venerable wife, bestowed upon those same blessed confessors a gift of his devotion. By a command of his authority, he confirmed that the property which he appeared to possess there as a legal benefice should be held and retained there perpetually in its entirety.

That magnificent King Charles was exceedingly devoted to places consecrated to divine worship. None of his predecessors—whether emperors, parents, or kings—had bestowed such abundant gifts on the churches of God or adorned them with such munificence as he did.

Therefore, when he came to the villa called Veteradomus, Hilispogius, prince of the Britons, came to him there with the son of the aforementioned most exalted King Charles, named Hludovicus. There, with the counsel of the noble Frankish nobles, Hilispogius gave the kingdom of Neustria to his son Hludovicus and established him to reign in that part of the kingdom. At that same assembly, in response to the petition of his most noble and devoted wife Hermentrudis, he bestowed upon the blessed confessors—as he had upon many other holy places—resources for the support of the servants of God serving God there. Thus, by God’s generosity, together with whatever other goods the God-fearing had contributed there, the brothers of that church were able to live.

The greatest of queens, Hermentrudis, not only prompted the king to do this but also sent a pallium to the bodies of the blessed confessors, saying: “May I deserve to obtain forgiveness for my sins unto eternal life from the goods I have secured, and by the pallium sent I now seek to experience the unremitting pain of my breast.”

We have found that this was indeed her faith: for already in the first year of the glorious King Hludovicus—that is, the son of the great King Charles and of Hermentrudis, his most noble wife and glorious queen—they bestowed gifts for the love of almighty God and in veneration of the blessed Ragnobert the confessor and bishop and his companion, Saint Zeno the confessor.

I, Joseph, a sinner, a priest and the least of all Christ’s servants, once chancellor of the king of Aquitaine, now, though unworthy, teacher of the liberal arts to the illustrious King Ludovicus, and formerly serving in the office of chancellor of that same sacred palace, once studied letters at Tours under the instruction of Amalricus, archbishop of Tours, together with Paul, archbishop of Rouen.

When I, Joseph, a sinful and unworthy priest, was moved to take up my pen for this writing, I did not take care to write these things as I ought, although the aforementioned bishops were, as it were, bodily alive and present in mind. For I was not competent in the eloquence of antiquity, but was covered by the error of rustic ignorance. [Col. 0906A] Therefore, lying prostrate at the feet of all the faithful, I humbly ask that you not disdain my words.

**In the year of the Lord 847. Pope Sergius II.**

[Col. 0905B]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE

*(Mansi, The Most Extensive Collection of Councils.)*

[Col. 0905]

[Col. 0905B] Sergius—after the death of Gregory IV, the deacon John had violently seized the see; but when the legitimate authorities deposed him as a schismatic, Sergius was elected by common consent, the second of that name, on the fourth day before the Ides of February, in the year of the Lord 844. He did not change the name he had before the pontificate, as more recent historians fabulously relate. What they falsely attribute to this pontiff happened in the case of Sergius III. He was called Peter and afterward named himself Sergius II, not because of any disgrace attached to the name, but out of reverence. For he thought it unworthy that he should be called by the name with which Christ had named the first pontiff of the apostolic see, the prince of the apostles, from Simon—Peter. The first after the Apostle Peter to change his name was Octavianus, son of the patrician Albericus, who was called John XI. Hence it is clear that the story told by more recent historians is an invention: that Sergius was previously called “Pig’s Snout,” and, because of the disgrace of the name, first wished to be called something else and imposed another name upon himself.

During his time occurred that remarkable victory against the sacrilegious and shameless Saracens, celebrated by writers of every kind, who were demanding an infamous tribute. It was won through the aid of Saint James, who, as he had promised the king in a vision, was visibly seen by all fighting before the battle line against the barbarians. **SEV. BIN.**

He was a Roman by birth, the son of Sergius of the fourth region, and he sat for three years.

Since he had been born illustrious from his mother, she began to educate him with great zeal in chaste nourishment, so that no one could hear or see anything obscene or lustful from him. He did not shrink from despising childish amusements, so that he appeared to excel before all in pious conduct and began to shine in the character of noble elders, fortified and instructed by his mother’s pure admonitions.

Accordingly, his mother rejoiced daily and eagerly gave thanks to almighty God, who by heavenly assistance had granted her such offspring. In the twelfth year of his age, however, his mother died and departed to the Lord. After being left by his mother—for his father had already been deprived of the light of life—he lived with his brothers among his relatives in the family house.

At that time, blessed and distinguished Pope Leo III held primacy over the church of the city of Rome. Remembering the nobility of this outstanding boy and recalling the nobility of his parents, he ordered him to be brought to his presence with great affection. When he had been brought, he began to observe him with a cheerful countenance and serene mind, and the boy pleased his heart beyond measure.

Then the bishop entrusted him to the school of singers to be educated in the common letters and to be instructed in the honey-sweet melodies of song.

The same distinguished and diligent boy quickly acquired the whole skill of literary discipline, so that he surpassed all the boys of that school. When the excellent pontiff heard these things, he was daily filled with inexhaustible joy at the boy’s kindly progress. Then he appointed him an acolyte in the holy Roman Church.

In the twentieth year of his pontificate, when Leo had died, Stephen assumed the priesthood of the Roman Church. Sergius himself loved him with a broad affection of the heart. When Stephen observed that Sergius was vigorous and nobly quick in the divine Scriptures, he immediately granted him the office of subdeacon.

After he had administered the episcopal government for a short time, Paschal assumed the governance of the Church. Paschal consecrated this man, prudent in all things and adorned with life, learning, and character, as priest of the titular church of blessed Silvester the confessor and pontiff. There he shone above all in mercy, zeal, vigilance, and every excellent discipline.

After Paschal’s death, Eugenius received the height of the pontificate. When Eugenius had remained in the pontificate for three years, Valentinus was consecrated pontiff of that see. After his fall, Gregory assumed the summit of the Church. Because the aforementioned man was loved by him with particular care, he ordained him archpriest in the holy Church.

After he had governed the Church most diligently for sixteen years, he was brought to his end and died. Then, when the nobles, the leading men of the city of Rome, and the whole people of the Church had gathered together to choose a pontiff, and, as usually happens in such circumstances, each was shouting for a different candidate, suddenly, pierced by divine providence and moved by God’s will, they began to discuss more carefully the religious character of the aforementioned archpriest Sergius, so that all cried out that he was worthy to obtain the governance of the pontificate.

Once the decision had been confirmed in favor of this same man, each person returned to his own place. Then suddenly a certain deacon of that Church, John, gave way to such madness and insanity that, having persuaded a certain inexperienced and rustic people, he gathered a band of turbulent and seditious men and entered the Lateran patriarchate with weapons of war, breaking through the doors by force and transgressing the established law and order.

As a result, everyone who was inside the walls of the patriarchate was filled with astonishment and fear. After that gathering of ignoble people had remained with him for about an hour, seized by fear and abandoning him, it disappeared without a trace.

When these things had happened, all the leading men of the Romans were indignant. By common counsel they gathered together in the basilica of blessed Martin the confessor and pontiff, hastening there with a large mounted force. They brought out the archpriest Sergius, a man proven in every virtue, whom we mentioned above, from the church. With great honor and accompanied by a great crowd of people, amid resounding praises, hymns, and spiritual songs, he was elected and led to the Lateran patriarchate.

On that same day so much snow fell upon the city that everything appeared white. Many said that this was a sign of joy and brightness.

The leading men of this Roman city expelled the aforementioned deacon John from the patriarchate with great disgrace and ordered him to be thrust under strict guard into confinement, because of the great rashness, impiety, and dreadful presumption that the aforesaid deacon John had repeatedly dared to commit. The princes also wished to condemn him in a council of bishops and deprive him of his honor. Others even wished to tear him limb from limb with swords and kill him. But the kind and diligent bishop Sergius prevented this, unwilling, in accordance with the evangelical saying, to return evil for evil to anyone (Romans 12).

At last, while all the priests, nobles, leading men, and peoples of the Church rejoiced, this most holy man was ordained and consecrated pontiff in the most sacred apostolic see of blessed Peter.

He was distinguished by birth, pure in faith, free in preaching, humble before God, renowned among human beings, cheerful in countenance and even more cheerful in mind; a governor of churches, a cultivator of peoples, a supporter of the poor, a shelter and comforter of widows, a generous giver to the needy, a gatherer and preserver of the scattered, a despiser of empty and worldly things, eager for and a lover of the riches of wisdom alone.

When news of this most sacred consecration reached the ears of the unconquered Augustus, the emperor Lotharius, he sent Drogon, archbishop of the Church of Metz, to Rome with his most excellent son Ludovicus. [Note: [Col. 0907D] “Lotharius sent Drogon to Rome with his son Ludovicus.” Addo of Vienne recounts why this happened in the year 841 in these words: “Lotharius sent his son Ludovicus, whom he had made king in Italy, to Rome through Drogon, his uncle, so that he might receive the name of emperor. Sergius, already pontiff at that time, placed the crown upon him; and, with the whole people acclaiming him, he was hailed emperor and Augustus.” From this the impudence of the schismatic Sigebert is refuted: in favor of the schismatic emperor whom he supported, he writes according to his own whim that Ludovicus was sent by Lotharius to Rome to confirm the election of Sergius as pontiff. **SEV. BIN.**]

He also ordered several archbishops and bishops, abbots, and counts to set out with them. From the moment they entered the borders of the city of Bologna with their warlike armies, they inflicted such slaughter and carnage upon the people that those who were in the cities and countryside, terrified by tyrannical cruelty, abandoned their own places and hid themselves in remote locations and hiding places.

While they were carrying out this savage wickedness everywhere, through individual cities, villages, and fields, they came to the bridge of Capella. At that time the sky was so clear that no one could see any sign of clouds or rain anywhere in the air. Suddenly, however, a considerable mass of black clouds formed, and, surrounded by storm clouds and flashes of lightning, certain leading men among Drogon’s counselors were struck and killed by lightning.

When the Franks saw this horrible sign, they were all seized by exceedingly great fear. Yet they did not at all lay aside the ferocity of their minds; with savage intent they hastened rapidly toward the City.

When the most blessed Pope Sergius learned that their arrival was drawing near, he sent all the judges to meet his most excellent King Ludovicus nearly nine miles from this Roman city.

They received him with standards and great resounding praises. When he had approached to within almost a mile of the City, he sent out all the military companies together with their patrons. They all sang praises worthy of the most noble king, while other highly skilled Greek soldiers sang imperial praises. With the sweet-sounding voices of those praises they gloriously welcomed the king.

His Holiness sent venerable crosses and standards to meet him. As is customary when receiving an emperor or king, he had him welcomed with immense honor. When King Ludovicus saw the most sacred crosses and standards coming to meet him, he became cheerful and greatly rejoiced. Then, with all his people, all the Roman judges, and the military companies preceding him, he hastened toward blessed Peter.

The aforementioned life-giving pontiff awaited the same king, together with his clergy, on the steps of that apostolic hall, on the Sunday after Pentecost. When the king joined him and ascended all the steps of that most sacred church of blessed Peter, he approached the aforementioned pontiff, who was standing in the courtyard above the steps near the doors of the church with all the clergy and the Roman people.

Then, embracing one another, King Ludovicus took the right hand of the aforementioned pontiff, and they entered the inner courtyard and came to the silver doors. In that courtyard, one man from the army, seized by a demon, was violently tormented in the sight of all the Franks.

Then the life-giving bishop had all the doors of blessed Peter closed and ordered them locked. Prompted by the Holy Spirit, he said to the king: “If you have come here with a pure mind and sincere intention, for the welfare of the commonwealth, of the whole world, and of this Church, enter these doors at my command. Otherwise, neither through me nor by my permission will these gates be opened to you.”

The king immediately replied that he had come with no evil intention, perversity, or malicious design. Then, at the bishop’s command, they laid their hands upon the aforementioned doors and opened them. Thus they entered that venerable hall of blessed Peter, praising God and his majesty. The entire clergy and all the devout servants of God acclaimed in full voice: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord,” and so forth.

With that same pontiff, the king, all the bishops, abbots, and judges, and all the Franks who had come with him approached the confession of blessed Peter. There they prostrated themselves and gave thanks to our almighty God and to that prince of the apostles. After the aforementioned blessed pontiff had given a prayer over the people, they all left the church together.

In the following days, they ravaged all the suburbs with continuous devastation and tore up the fields, crops, and meadows as if struck by a bolt of lightning. While these things were happening, the pontiff, protected by God, heard from certain people that they wished to enter this famous city for the sake of hospitality; but since the gates were fortified and closed, he by no means allowed it to happen.

On the following Sunday, all the archbishops, all the abbots, all the Franks who had come with him, and all the Roman nobles and distinguished men gathered in the same basilica of the prince of the apostles.

Then the life-giving pontiff anointed Ludovicus, the son of the emperor Lotharius, with holy oil, crowned him with a royal and most precious crown, and placed him in authority over the Lombards. Giving him a royal sword, he ordered him to gird himself with it there. [Note: [Col. 0909D] Platina in his account of Sergius says that Ludovicus was created and crowned emperor at Rome, not king of the Lombards; this is established by the testimony of several writers. The only point disputed is whether Sergius, or rather Leo IV, placed the imperial crown upon him at his request. Leo of Ostia in his *Chronicle*, Addo of Vienne in the passage cited above, and certain diplomas in Sigonius, *On the Kingdom of Italy*, book one, assign the first year of Emperor Ludovicus to the time of Pope Sergius and to the year of the Lord 844. The records of the Roman council, however, assign the beginning of Ludovicus’s empire to the second year of Leo IV, which is the year 848 of our Redeemer. This is because, according to the cited acts of the council, the fifth year of the emperor is joined with the seventh year of Leo IV, namely 853 of Christ our Redeemer. Since the matter is exceedingly uncertain, I suspend my judgment. For the recently discovered epitaph of Pope Sergius the Younger, see Cardinal Baronius’s *Annals*, year 847, number six. **SEV. BIN.**]

When the celebration of the Mass had ended, everyone returned from the church with the king, rejoicing. Thereafter, day after day, the archbishop Drogo of the Church of Metz, whom we mentioned above, stirred up a new conflict against the most holy pontiff and all our bishops, leading men, and nobles. He did so together with all the archbishops and bishops who had gathered with him against this universal Church, the head of all the churches of God, without the consent or summons of its metropolitan.

These were: Gregory, archbishop of the Church of Ravenna; Angilbertus, archbishop of the Church of Milan; Joseph, bishop of the Church of Ivrea; Aginus, bishop of the Church of Verona; Almaricus, bishop of the Church of Camos; Northaudus, bishop of the Church of Vercelli; Sigifridus, bishop of the Church of Reggio; Toringanus, bishop of the Church of Concordia; Odelbertus, bishop of the Church of Acqui; Ambrosius, bishop of the Church of Lucca; Joannes, bishop of the Church of Pisa; Petrus, bishop of the Church of Volterra; Gausprandus, bishop of the Church of Pistoia; Lantio, bishop of the Church of Siena; Lupus, bishop of the Church of Textina; Sigismundus, bishop of the Church of Teramo; Ricco, bishop of the Church of Ascoli; Fratellus, bishop of the Church of Camerino; Gisus, bishop of the Church of Fermo; Racipertus, bishop of the Church of Nocera; Amadeus, bishop of the Church of Penne; Donatus, bishop of the Church of Fiesole; and others.

The counts Boso, Adalgisus, Joannes, Vuldo, Vernandus, Winfridus, and Maurinus, together with the others, also contended with them.

But, through the inspiration of divine grace, they were unable to overcome either the words or the prudence of the life-giving pontiff. Such heavenly power attended him that they could not confine or constrain him by any speech.

Overcome by him, they departed in shame and covered with confusion. When they saw this, they entirely laid aside all the anger and ferocity they had harbored in their minds.

When these matters had been completed, they asked the aforementioned pontiff that all the Roman primates might promise fidelity by oath to King Ludovicus. The most prudent pontiff by no means permitted this, but began to say to them:

“I consent and permit this oath only if you wish them to swear it to the lord Lotharius, the great emperor. For neither I nor all the Roman nobility consents that it be sworn to Ludovicus, his son.”

Then at last, seated in that same church, the most blessed pontiff, the great king, and all the archbishops and bishops, while the remaining priests and the nobles of the Romans and Franks stood, promised fidelity to Lotharius, the great emperor, forever Augustus.

After this, two archbishops, Ebbo and Bartholomaeus, who had been deprived of their honors and expelled from the Church because of their crimes, asked the most holy pontiff to deign to reconcile them to the Church and grant them the pallium. The same bishop said that they were not worthy even to receive communion among the clergy, but that they should have permission to communicate only among the common people. [Note: [Col. 0911D] Platina, in his account of Sergius.]

At that time, while King Ludovicus himself was staying at Rome, Siconulfus, prince of the Beneventans, came to Rome with a large army. When the aforementioned king had received him honorably, Siconulfus explained everything for which he had come. The king, with a grateful heart, granted and conceded whatever he had asked.

When the Franks, Lombards, and Beneventans had gathered together, an enormous multitude of people was formed, so that Rome appeared to be surrounded on every side. By their multitude all the crops were destroyed.

Siconulfus himself ardently desired to see the pontiff and receive his blessing. When the bishop received him, Siconulfus prostrated himself on the ground and humbly kissed his precious feet. Having received his blessing, he returned from his presence joyfully, giving thanks to God.

When all these things had been brought to completion, the most excellent king Louis returned with great rejoicing to Pavia, where from the beginning of his reign he had held the summit of power. Then everyone rejoiced: the Roman Senate and people, together with their wives and children, having been freed from so great a plague [Col. 0911C] and redeemed from the yoke of tyrannical savagery, venerated the most holy bishop Sergius as the author of their salvation and the restorer of peace. He, however, attributed the deed not to his own virtue but to the divine gift.

Now, since the tongue cannot explain in order everything that he accomplished, let us pass to what he offered in the holy places and begin to recount it briefly. At the very beginning of his pontificate, burning with heavenly love, he completed a work of marvelous beauty in the basilica of the Savior, which is called Constantinian. For the circuit of the sacred altar, which had once been constructed there in a narrow form, he marked out with his own finger, enlarged it, and completed it from the foundations; he splendidly adorned it with beautiful columns and with marble sculptures set above in a circle [Col. 0911D]. There the sacred clergy now stands in abundance for the administration of the holy office.

When this had been completed, that life-giving pontiff offered in the same basilica, for the beauty and adornment of this splendid work, twenty white silk curtains, ornamented around the edge with *fundatus*. Likewise, twenty other very fine *fundatus* curtains, ornamented around the edge with *blatteus*. There also, with Christ’s assistance, he constructed a marvelous confession and splendidly adorned it with silver panels overlaid with gold. After consecrating it with his own hands, he placed relics in it. He also completed another very fine work before the doors of this venerable basilica. For he made the sacred doors, which had previously lain hidden from the people [Col. 0912A], manifest to everyone with the greatest care, constructing there from the foundations arches of beautiful design, which he also brightly decorated with various paintings.

This distinguished pontiff, protected by God, made, for the remedy and future recompense of his soul, the chamber of the manger of our Lord Jesus Christ, which is joined to the basilica of the blessed Mother of God, our Lady, commonly called Major. He magnificently and especially adorned it with silver and gilded panels bearing the history of the blessed Mother of God, Mary—a work which none of the pontiffs, throughout so many years, had thought to bring to such a splendid appearance.

This bishop, while carefully overseeing all the churches [Col. 0912B], also completed from the foundations the basilica of the holy Archangel, situated on the summit of Mount Fajani [perhaps Gargani], making it more spacious than it had previously been. He ordered it to be brightly painted with radiant pictures and newly restored its damaged roofing. There he also offered four garments of *mizilo*, and likewise four curtains. This life-giving and most blessed pope also newly restored from the foundations, through God’s merciful favor, the school of singers—which had formerly been called the orphanage and, because of extreme age, seemed almost ruined and broken down—to a better condition than it had formerly possessed. He also completed from the foundations the basilica of the blessed Roman martyr, situated not far outside the city at the Salarian Gate, and decreed that it should be the parish church under the title of Saints Sylvester and [Col. 0912C] Martin. He also built the basilica of the holy martyr Theodore, which appears to stand in the territory of the Corani, at the thirtieth milestone from the city of Rome; he splendidly decorated it with gleaming paintings.

In the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter he made a garment of *chrysoclavus*, bearing in the middle an image of the Savior and, to his right and left, shining figures of all the holy apostles. He also adorned it with the most precious green and hyacinth-colored gems. When these things had been completed with the greatest care, the pontiff, protected by God and most blessed, devoutly concerned for the desired honor of Saints Sylvester and Martin, rebuilt from the foundations, through God’s merciful favor, the church consecrated in their name. From the beginning of his priesthood [Col. 0912D] until he was raised to the summit of the pontificate, he had diligently governed it; but over many years its exposed age had caused it to decay, and it had remained shattered and torn by long antiquity. He painted its apse with great devotion, overlaying it with golden mosaic colors. For the honor of almighty God and of the same most blessed bishop Sylvester, he dedicated and placed beneath the sacred altar the body of Sylvester together with the most blessed Fabian, Stephen, and Soter, martyrs and pontiffs; the martyr Asterius together with his most holy daughter; Saint Cyriacus; Maurus, Largus, and Smaragdus; Anastasius and Innocent [Col. 0913A], pontiffs; Saints Quirinus and Leo, bishops; the martyrs Artemius, Nicander, and Crescentianus; the blessed Soteris and Paulina; Memmia, Juliana, and Quirilla; the virgin martyrs Theopiste and Sophia; and the blessed widow Cyriaca, with many others whose names are known to God alone.

After magnificently completing these works, with a grateful spirit and attentive mind he offered in the same church the following objects, to remain there perpetually: a very precious golden *regnum* with green, hyacinth-colored, and white gems, which may still be seen hanging above the altar, bearing in the middle a cross of the purest gold likewise set with precious gems. Also four *gabathae* of the purest silver overlaid with gold, hanging before the vestibule of the sacred altar; and gilded, engraved *gabathae* with two bosses. Two very fine golden crosses with gems, and one other silver cross likewise. In the same basilica he offered three censers overlaid with gold, two patens of the purest silver and gilded, one gilded silver strainer for use in the sacred office, and one silver *regnum* with little bells, bearing in the middle a cross with a dove.

This most blessed pope, burning with heavenly love, offered at the place mentioned above three pairs of silver washbasins. Also two silver *sextaria*. Four large silver crowns with dolphins, weighing … pounds [Col. 0913C]. Two large silver chalices, likewise gilded. A large silver paten overlaid with gold, bearing in the middle an image of our Lord Jesus Christ. Three pairs of silver-plated *cerostrata*. Three silver baskets. One paten with a gilded chalice. One silver bowl weighing … pounds.

For the honor of that venerable basilica he offered twelve *canthari* of *aurichalcum*, and likewise six pairs of *rugae* of *aurichalcum*. This distinguished man also made, for the glory and honor of the holy confessors whom we mentioned above, a ciborium of the purest silver weighing … pounds.

[Col. 0914A]

He also magnificently adorned the confession of the sacred altar with silver panels overlaid with gold, weighing … pounds, so that through the holy intercession of those saints he might possess the joys of the heavenly kingdom.

This most merciful and kindly bishop offered at the place mentioned above three images overlaid with silver and gold. One of them bears the image of our Lord Jesus Christ; the other two show Saints Sylvester and Martin, seated [*sedentium*: perhaps “of those seated”] above the vestibule of the sacred altar.

In the basilica mentioned above he offered a garment of *chrysoclavus*, bearing the history of the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ, with green, hyacinth-colored, and white gems. He also made another very precious *fundatus* garment with *chrysoclavus*, bearing in the middle an image of our Lord Jesus Christ the Savior and, to his right and left, images of Saints Sylvester and Martin [Col. 0914B], likewise with green, hyacinth-colored, and white gems. Indeed, the most holy bishop offered three Alexandrian curtains woven with the most precious workmanship; twenty *fundatus* curtains ornamented around the edge with *blatteus*, hanging in the arch of the basilica; fifteen other *fundatus* curtains with a *periclysis* of *blatteus*; and four white silk curtains surrounding the sacred altar, one of them bearing in the middle a cross and *gammadia* of *chrysoclavus*, with other ornaments around the edge of *blatteus*.

This renowned and most blessed pope, protected by divine inspiration, constructed from the foundations beside that basilica, for the praise of the Creator, a monastery in honor of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, and of Saints Sylvester and Martin [Col. 0914C]. In it he established a community of monks serving God, praying day and night to our Lord God in the aforesaid church through their daily praises.

This most blessed pontiff, after governing the Roman and apostolic see with the greatest glory for three years, departed from this light and passed into eternal rest. He held one ordination in the month of March: eight priests, three deacons, and twenty-three bishops in various places. He was buried in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter.

[Col. 0913D]

[Note: [Col. 0913D] Letter of Pope Sergius. That it should be attributed to Sergius II was established by the authority of Hincmar, since the letter was without a superscription; Hincmar writes in Letter 6 that Drogo obtained this precedence from Sergius [Col. 0914D]. It may be understood as having been acquired in the year 844 from chapter 11 of the Synod of Verneuil. JAC. SIRM.]

## LETTER OF POPE SERGIUS II TO THE BISHOPS BEYOND THE ALPS

[Col. 0913] Concerning the precedence of Drogo, vicar of the apostolic see.

[Col. 0913D]

Indeed, dearest brothers, I had wished to present my bodily presence at so glorious a contest and to labor in every way for the recovery of the glory of so excellent an order. But since concern for all the churches weighs upon us, wherever we ourselves cannot be present, following the moderation of our predecessors we appoint vicars of our authority. Therefore, in place of our humility, we have appointed throughout all the provinces situated beyond the Alps, after prudent deliberation, Drogo, archbishop of Metz, son of the once-glorious emperor Charles, whose most blessed governance united the empire of the Romans and the Franks [Col. 0914D].

Since he is the uncle of our most serene and devout son, the great emperor Lothair, and of his dearest brothers, our sons Louis and Charles, kings, and since he is distinguished by holiness and learning, we desire that, having received authority from this most holy see of the prince of the apostles, he may everywhere serve as a capable minister on our behalf for your needs. And because we have commanded him to bear concern for all of you, we wish him to be accompanied by the obedience of all. It is fitting, brothers, that he who labors for everyone should be supported by everyone’s assistance.

To him, therefore, in convening general synods, we lend our authority throughout all parts of the aforesaid regions, and whatever shall have been defined by a provincial synod we order to be brought to his knowledge without delay [Col. 0915B]. If anyone from those regions should need to appeal to this holy see and should request to be heard in our presence, we admonish him first to submit himself to Drogo’s hearing. When the ecclesiastical acts of his region have been reasonably arranged and presented, if the judgment of the bishops concerning one who is perhaps accused of crimes should be divided—so that some judge him guilty while others judge him innocent—then, once those acts have been brought to us and he has been commended by a letter from our aforesaid brother, to whom we have granted our place, let him come safely either to us or to the see of blessed Peter, and let no delay hinder him on his journey.

We have also granted to our appointed brother Drogo, archbishop, this permission and authority, under the following terms, to examine and investigate bishops and abbots [Col. 0915C], while preserving in every respect the primacy of this universal Roman see, the honor and power of our episcopate, and the dignity and exaltation of our dearest spiritual son, Lord Lothair, the great emperor. For it has greatly pleased us, because of the various disturbances of the churches of God, to complete this necessary and entirely fitting work.

But if, disregarding this admonition, anyone thinks that by sheer wickedness he can free himself from accusations [Col. 0916A], let him know that he will by no means obtain a rash absolution from our gentleness unless his case has first been examined by the provincial synod and afterward by a general synod in the hearing of our aforesaid brother. For a case is examined more closely there where the offense is recognized to have been committed. Nevertheless, if he requests to come to us, as we said above, he shall not be detained.

But if, having been summoned, he refuses to attend the provincial synod of his metropolitan, or disdains to come to the assembly of the aforesaid vicar and our legate for the general synod, and then decides to report these matters to our apostolic ears by letter, let him know that he will be judged by the authority both of us and of the whole Catholic Church.

If any bishop complains that violence has been inflicted upon him by our religious sons, the kings, so that he cannot observe the decrees of the canons [Col. 0916B], we believe, with the Lord’s approval, that this refuge can be removed by letters sent to them. For it is utterly intolerable to hear that the threefold fellowship of the brothers united in the faith of the Trinity should depart from mutual affection and the common equity of law. If any one of them should prefer to follow the author of discord and refuse to be content with Catholic peace, we shall endeavor, with God’s help, to chastise him by canonical authorities as best we can.

For the rest, brothers, I address your holiness as constituted under one sphere of charity, so that you may all think alike and there may be no schisms among you; nor, through the winding paths of empty arguments, should you conceal the truth either from yourselves or from the people entrusted to you. Truth proceeds without turning aside from contradiction and says: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matthew 5). By contrast, it is openly understood that those who desire wars are sons of the devil. But we trust in him who conquers the world, through the intercession of the blessed apostle Peter, that your authority will not yield to any arrogance of worldly boldness. Even if such forces prevail for a time, there is no doubt that they will be condemned forever.

But you, even if you suffer persecution for the sake of justice, are blessed. May God preserve you unharmed, brothers. Amen.

## IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 850. FRECULPHUS, BISHOP OF LISIEUX.

[Col. 0915D]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE ON FRECULPHUS

*(Fabricius, Bibliotheca medii et infimi Latini.)*

[Col. 0915]

[Col. 0915D]

Freculphus, formerly a monk of the Benedictine order and abbot of Fulda, was bishop in the Gallic church of Lisieux from the year 823 to 851. He wrote two volumes of Chronicles [Col. 0916D]. [Note: [Col. 0915D] Only the first volume was seen by Sigebert, ch. 90, and Trithemius, ch. 259.] The first of these, divided into seven books, he addressed to Elisachar, his teacher, whom he calls a venerable priest [Note: [Col. 0916D] In the hexameter poem prefixed to the same Elisachar.]. It extends from the creation of the first human being [Col. 0917A] to the birth of Christ the Lord, or the year 5129 of the world.

The second volume, dedicated to Judith, the second wife of Louis the Pious, consists of five books, extending from the birth of Christ the Savior to Boniface III, who held the papacy from the year 607. The twelve books of Freculph’s Chronicle that now exist were published at Cologne in 1539, in folio, from the press of Egenolph; in a more corrected form from the Commelinian press in 1597, in octavo; and also in the Paris supplement to the Library of the Fathers in 1639, in volume IX of the Cologne Library of the Fathers, and in volume XIV of the Lyon edition, page 1061.

The anonymous writer of Melk, chapter 64, says: “This is Freculph, a bishop distinguished in knowledge and learning” [Col. 0918A]. He says that, besides truthful histories from the beginning of the world to the times of the Northmen, Freculph wrote Explanations on Genesis. But Freculph did indeed encourage Rabanus Maurus to compose explanations of Genesis, as is clear from a letter of Freculph to Rabanus, prefixed to the second volume of Rabanus’s Works, to which Rabanus sent and dedicated, with the prefatory letter, four books of his Expositions on Genesis for Freculph to reread and examine.

[Col. 0917B]

# TWO VOLUMES OF THE CHRONICLES OF FRECULPH, BISHOP OF LISIEUX

The first extends from the beginning of the world to the time of Caesar Octavian and the birth of our Savior Jesus Christ; the second thereafter contains a history of events down to the kingdoms of the Franks and Lombards.

*(From the Library of the Ancient Fathers.)*

[Col. 0917]

## PREFACE

### By the author himself to Elisachar, his teacher, concerning the first volume of this work

[Col. 0917B]

Since the industry of prudent men usually rouses the sluggish minds of some people, lest, weighed down by the sleep of idleness, they waste away uselessly in languid leisure, but, with the darkness of their drowsiness removed, awaken so that they may diligently perform whatever they can accomplish by writing or teaching—for fear that one day they may hear the Lord’s terrible sentence pronounced concerning a talent wickedly buried—you, my dearest Elisachar, venerable teacher, insatiable in your love of wisdom, after the others whom you habitually spur earnestly with the goads of charity so that, faithfully watchful, they may distribute at the proper time to their master’s servants what has been entrusted to them, at last turned to my littleness and commanded me to labor at carefully examining the volumes of the ancients, whether hagiographers or even pagan [Col. 0917C] writers, and briefly and clearly gathering whatever pertains to historical truth.

You commanded me to begin from the creation of the first human being and continue to the birth of Christ the Lord—namely, to explain more carefully whatever our Christian or pagan writers have thought concerning the first age, which existed before the universal catastrophe, and the second, which followed the Flood and continued to the birth of Abraham and the reign of Ninus, king of the Assyrians. You also instructed me not to neglect disentangling, insofar as it concerns historical truth, the difficult questions found in the writings of the Lawgiver during these periods.

From there, through the kings of the Assyrians, Medes, Persians, and Greeks, down to the monarchy of Caesar Octavian—through the peoples to whom, by successive ages, the Assyrian kingdom passed by transmission [Col. 0918B]—you directed me to observe carefully the number of years. Among the people of God, I was likewise to trace the years through the patriarchs, judges, kings, and priests, and again through kings; and I was to note the deeds throughout the ages and regions of the world that deserved remembrance, so that I might show when and where the things that are perpetually recounted through the successive ages occurred, who at that time achieved distinction in the greater kingdoms, and who ruled over the people of God.

Moreover, from the destruction of the temple of Jerusalem to the birth of Christ the Lord, you urged me to gather in summary and orderly fashion the events that took place among the Jewish people, since they appear confused because of the disasters that befell them. Showing all these matters to my littleness as though depicted briefly on a tablet, you left me no opportunity for excuse [Col. 0918C], but rather commanded me to undertake the work.

Therefore, aided by God, who makes the mute speak, I have begun to navigate so vast a sea in a small boat, an inexperienced sailor—not through presumption, but out of obedience. But if the calm of the sea changes and the waves swell, you who gave the command extend your hand to the shipwrecked man.

Although bound by ecclesiastical and secular affairs, hindered in speech and dull in understanding, I, an unlearned beginner, have undertaken this great work, which ought to have been entrusted to the wise. Yet because I could not refuse your kindness, I send it to you for examination; and if you judge it useful, it will be no less acceptable to the writer than to the critic.

I have not everywhere inserted the names of the authors from whom I gathered the material contained in the seven books [Col. 0919A], as you advised, because, where they appeared to agree, I strove to express briefly the sense of what I had selected, compressing their views into a concise account. But I have decided to record the names of both our own and pagan writers and have adopted their opinions as they are found in their books whenever they seem to depart from the others by varying from them.

I therefore ask the candid reader not to attribute to presumption rather than obedience anything in these books that displeases him because of my weakness. Let him not criticize rashly before he has read more carefully the authors from whom we have excerpted these things and to whose authority we likewise refer them.

## A HEXAMETER POEM BY THE SAME AUTHOR TO THE SAME PERSON

[Col. 0919]

[Col. 0919A]

With you as guide, Christ, the road is easy as we pass through all things;

You grant us power to overcome varied and wearisome labors,

Which nature denies; you grant us, with fragile courage, the strength to conquer great things.

[Col. 0919B]

The little human mind trembles to touch difficult matters;

It marvels that it has touched them, and rejoices to have overcome them.

For if anything has been worthy of praise and worthy of remembrance,

Let it attribute what appears accomplished not to itself but to the Lord:

To him who gave understanding to the dull, who governs all things,

In heaven, on earth, and throughout all ages forever.

With his help, though not with equal strength,

[Col. 0920A]

I undertook to climb beyond the lofty hills of the age.

I shall paint with my pen what took place through ancient times:

I shall recount the enduring days and the great deeds of kings,

[Col. 0920B]

At what time and where such things occurred throughout the world;

The brave men, the portents, the famines, the world’s evils;

The disasters civil wars inflicted upon peoples;

The unspeakable desire that wore down foreign nations;

The accidents that reckless care bestowed upon kingdoms.

These things I have sung briefly, venerable priest, in remembrance,

Singing not unknown matters concerning the ancients, but the sayings of those before me.

# HERE BEGINS THE FIRST VOLUME OF THE CHRONICLES

Containing a history of events from the beginning of the world to the Birth of our Savior Jesus Christ.

## BOOK ONE

### CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0919C] On the fact that nearly all historians began to weave their histories from Ninus, king of the Assyrians

As I sought to gather, in a varied form of discourse, a sequence of ages from the learned works of both sacred and secular historians, tasting a few small flowers from many of their books—or plucking blossoms from various flourishing meadows—so that the reader might easily discern what had happened in each period among the more celebrated deeds of kings and kingdoms, my own weakness was struck by the fact that nearly all historians, especially the Greeks and Latins, began their accounts of events with Ninus, son of Belus, king of many peoples. They chiefly related the misfortunes of wars, the overthrow of kings and regions, and the misery of human beings; and, as we learn from their assertions, they described wars as nothing other than evils inclining toward one another.

They left untouched the ages that had passed before, as though they had been without fault—as some of them preferred to believe—and as though human beings had previously lived like irrational beasts. Therefore, supported by the help of almighty God and relying on the authority of divine Scripture, I resolved to begin my account with the first-created human being [Col. 0920C], who was the first parent and author of mortal humanity and was the last of God’s works to be created, on the sixth day. For there is no doubt that after creating him the Lord ceased from new acts of creation, though not from governing creatures. For this reason Scripture records that the Lord rested on the seventh day from all his works.

### CHAPTER TWO

Why the human being was created last among creatures

It may nevertheless be asked why the human being was created last in the order of creation, on the sixth day, although it is clear that humanity is nobler than the other creatures because of its superior understanding—those creatures whose creation is recorded on the preceding days. The reason may be that the world was first made as a house, and only afterward its lord, that is, its inhabitant, was brought into it [Col. 0920D].

### CHAPTER THREE

How the human being was created in the image and likeness of God

He was also created in the image and likeness of God. We know that this image and likeness exists in the understanding of the rational soul, not in the form of the body, according to what the Apostle says: “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new human being, who was created according to God.” And elsewhere he says [Col. 0921A]: “Putting off the old human being, put on the new, who is renewed in the knowledge of God according to the image of him who created him.”

Our body itself, too, has been fashioned in such a way as to show that we are better than the other animals. For all those animals are inclined toward the earth, whereas the human body is upright, so that it may show that our soul ought always to be upright toward things above, toward spiritual realities.

The difference between image and likeness is therefore this: the image of God exists in the immortality of the soul. Hence even a sinful soul does not cease to be the image of God; likeness consists in moral character. For this reason only a holy soul possesses the likeness of God, since it is like its Creator in that in which it will be equal to the holy angels.

### CHAPTER FOUR

[Col. 0921B] On the obedience given to the human being by God

The sower of the human race was also established as the cultivator of paradise, so that he might live there happily, enjoying eternal joys without any calamity or fear of death, if he preserved the commandment by obeying it. But if he proved disobedient, he would be deprived of eternal happiness and subjected to the miseries of death—which he experienced when he touched the forbidden tree, which he had been prohibited from touching.

Thus the first parent was driven from the delight of paradise together with his wife. The Apostle says that she was deceived by the devil’s fraud, whereas Adam himself was not deceived but transgressed for the sake of his companion.

### CHAPTER FIVE

[Col. 0921C] On the tree of the knowledge of good and evil in paradise and on the tree of life

There was indeed physically in paradise a tree called the tree of life, just as there was the rock which, when struck, supplied water in the wilderness to the people of God, although both mystically signified Christ. It was called the tree of life because, while those human beings tasted from it, they would not fail through disease or old age.

In the other trees there was nourishment; in this one, a sacrament. The tree of the knowledge of good and evil was not called so because the tree itself was rational by nature or possessed knowledge of good and evil. Rather, it was called the tree of the knowledge of good and evil because, through experience of it, the human being learned what the evil of disobedience was.

If anyone wishes to know more fully about these matters, let him read the books of Father Augustine on The City of God [Col. 0921D].

### CHAPTER SIX

On Abel, killed by his brother Cain, and on the punishments Cain suffered

Two male children were born to Adam in the region to which God transferred him after his transgression, when he left paradise. The elder was called Cain, and the younger Abel. They were brothers, but they delighted in different pursuits.

Abel, the younger, cultivated righteousness and considered the Lord present in everything he did; his way of life was that of a shepherd. Cain, however, was exceedingly wicked in other matters and was always intent solely on profit; he was the first to begin cultivating the earth. For this reason he killed his brother [Col. 0922A].

When they wished to offer sacrifice to God, Cain offered gifts from the fruits of the earth, while Abel offered from the firstborn of the sheep and their milk. God was more pleased with the sacrifice that had arisen spontaneously and naturally than with that which appeared to have been produced by the invention of a greedy man.

Therefore Cain grew angry because Abel had been preferred by God. He recognized this because God’s fire consumed his brother’s sacrifice but left his own untouched. Provoked by jealousy, he killed his brother Abel.

### CHAPTER SEVEN

On the origin of the two cities

For this reason the Lord said to Cain: “Where is Abel your brother?” He replied: “I do not know.”

The Lord does not ask as one who is ignorant, but as a judge questioning the guilty man whom he is about to punish. Cain, thinking that God did not know what he had done, replied: “I do not know.”

God said to him: “Do you suppose that I do not know what you have done? I saw your thought, which you had wickedly conceived, and warned you beforehand not to complete it in deed. But lest you complain that I pronounce an unjust sentence against you, I do not bring the accusation against you; there is a witness who accuses you—the voice, namely, of your brother’s blood, which cries to me from the earth.”

Cain replied to the Lord: “My iniquity is greater than that I may deserve pardon.” From the frenzy of his mind and the trembling of his body, by which he was shaken, he understood that he deserved to be killed, and said: “Behold, you drive me away today from your presence, and I shall be hidden from the face of the earth; I shall be a wanderer upon the earth, and everyone who finds me will kill me” [Col. 0922C].

But God, unwilling to end his torment through the shortcut of death or to hand him over to the punishment by which he had condemned himself, said: “Not so”—that is, “You will not die as you think, nor will you receive death as a remedy. Rather, you will live until the seventh generation and will be tormented by the fire of your conscience, so that whoever kills you, according to a twofold understanding, will either do so in the seventh generation or free you from great torment.”

This does not mean that the person who struck Cain would be subjected to seven punishments. Rather, the slayer would bring to an end the seven acts of vengeance that had continued against Cain for so long, killing the one who had been left alive for punishment.

To make what we are saying clearer, let us give an example from daily life. A servant says to his master amid beatings: “Because I burned your house and destroyed all your property, kill me.” The master replies: “You will not die as you wish and end your punishments by death. Rather, you will be kept alive for a long time, and you will live so unhappily in this light that whoever kills you will confer a benefit upon the one killed, since he will free you from so many torments” [Col. 0922D].

### CHAPTER EIGHT

How God spoke to the first human beings, and concerning what is written: “If you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, you have sinned.”

It is commonly asked how God spoke to the first human beings: he spoke with them through a subordinate creature, as their companion, in a form suited to them.

But what benefit did this bring Cain? Did he not complete the crime he had conceived of killing his brother even after the divine word?

The statement, “If you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, you have sinned,” has produced many interpretations because its obscurity makes it unclear why or from where it was spoken. Each interpreter of the divine Scriptures attempts to explain it according to the rule of faith.

A sacrifice is offered rightly when it is offered to the true God, to whom alone sacrifice ought to be made. But it is not divided rightly when the places, times, or things offered are not properly distinguished; or when the one who offers, the one to whom it is offered, or those to whom what has been offered is distributed for eating are not properly distinguished. Thus we should understand “division” here as discernment.

This may occur when something is offered where it ought not to be offered, or when something is offered there that ought to be offered elsewhere; when it is offered at a time when it ought not to be offered; when something is offered that should never have been offered at all; when a person keeps for himself the better things of the same kind rather than offering them to God; or when a profane person or anyone else who ought not to do so participates in what has been offered. It cannot easily be discovered which of these displeased God in Cain’s case.

But since, as John says, Cain was “of the evil one,” and killed his brother out of envy, while his brother’s works were good, it is understood that the Lord did not look upon his gifts because Cain himself divided them wrongly: he gave something of his possessions to God, but gave himself to himself. This is what all do who follow not God’s will but their own, dividing wrongly—that is, living wrongly.

For the Lord, giving him a just and good commandment, said: “Rest; for its turning is toward you, and you shall rule over it” [Col. 0923C]. Surely he did not mean his brother? Certainly not. What, then, unless sin? For he had said, “You have sinned.”

Then he added: “Rest; for its turning is toward you, and you shall rule over it.” This may indeed be understood as meaning that sin’s turning ought to be toward the human being, so that he may know that he must attribute to no one but himself the fact that he sins. This is the healing medicine of repentance and the proper request for forgiveness.

But when he says, “Its turning is toward you,” we should not supply “will be,” as though he were merely predicting something. Rather, it should be understood as the command of one giving orders. Each person will then rule over sin if, instead of defending it, he subjects it to himself through repentance.

### CHAPTER NINE

[Col. 0923D] On what is written: “Cain knew his wife, and she bore him Enoch,” after whose name he called the city he had built; and on how it can be reconciled with the fact that only three human beings then existed to build a city.

It follows: Cain knew his wife, and she conceived and bore Enoch; and he built a city and called its name Enoch, after the name of his son Enoch. Hence a question may be raised: since at that time there seemed to be no more than four men—or rather three afterward, because one brother had killed another—on the earth, how is Cain said to have built a city by himself?

But those whom this troubles give too little consideration to the fact that the writer of this sacred history did not need to name all the human beings who could then have existed, but [Col. 0924A] only those whom the purpose of the work required—namely, those through whom the genealogy would be woven down to Noah and afterward to Abraham. Nor does it follow that Cain should be thought to have fathered this son first merely because it is said, “he knew his wife,” as though he had intercourse with her for the first time then. For this is said of Adam himself not only when Cain, his firstborn, was conceived, but also later: “Adam,” it says, “knew Eve his wife, and she conceived and bore a son, and called his name Seth.” From this it is understood that Scripture commonly speaks in this way, although not always.

For it could have happened that, although he had other sons, he loved this one more than the others for some particular reason. For Judah was not Jacob’s firstborn, although Judaea was named from him and the Jews were so called. Therefore, [Col. 0924B] if Enoch was Cain’s firstborn, he should not for that reason be thought to have given the city its name immediately upon the birth of his son, since it could not at that time have been founded by one man. A city is nothing other than a multitude and community of human beings. But when the family of that man had grown so numerous that it already constituted a population, it could then have happened that a city was founded and named after the firstborn.

Therefore, if one considers that people in those times lived so long that even those who lived the shortest lives are found to have lived seven hundred and fifty years, and that they did not have only the children whom Scripture mentions—for it adds, “he fathered sons and daughters”—it may be understood that they had exceedingly numerous offspring. From this one may infer that, if from Abraham’s grandson, namely Jacob, [Col. 0924C] so great a multitude could multiply in Egypt within three hundred years that there were six hundred thousand when they went up from Egypt, what wonder is it if people, over a period of nine hundred years or more, could have established a large family capable of building many cities?

But it is credible that Cain’s city is mentioned with reference to the earthly city, which took its beginning from the founder who established it. From this point two cities arose: that of the impious and that of the righteous. The foundation of the righteous city began its pilgrimage in Abel, then in Seth and his descendants, and thus, laboring, it makes its pilgrimage down to the present time.

Therefore, in the earlier ages, although the city of God was multiplied with abundant fertility through the seventh generation in the sons of Seth [Col. 0924D], it was nevertheless built among the few in comparison with the wicked, until the Lord Christ, God the Son of God before the ages, came forth in our time as man from the womb of the most holy virgin Mary. He, true God and true man, from two substances and one person, shone forth as a new light upon the world. Thereafter, throughout the whole world, this holy city has been built more fruitfully in his members, and is daily gathered to its citizens, namely the angels of God, whose protection continually assists it in this pilgrimage.

But in Cain and his kin the city of the impious was built on an extremely broad scale. The historian Josephus of antiquities does indeed report of him that, after he had received a sign so that he would not be killed by whatever beasts might find him, but might wander without fear throughout the whole earth, [Col. 0925A] a sign having been placed upon him by which he could be recognized, he was cast out of the region where he had killed his brother and where he had lived with his father. After traveling through a great extent of land with his wife, he eventually reached a place called Naida, and remained there; there sons were also born to him.

Yet he did not regard that punishment as correction. Rather, he nourished it in his body for its increase and for lust, although he possessed it at the cost of injury to those who lived with him. He increased his wealth through a multitude of riches amassed by robbery and violence, and also invited his household to luxury and brigandage, being their teacher in criminal pursuits. He exchanged the simplicity with [Col. 0925B] which people had previously lived for the invention of measures and weights, and led their entire life from ignorance of such things into cunning and corruption.

He was the first to establish boundaries of land, to found cities, and to fortify them with walls; there he compelled his household to gather. He named this city Enoch, after his elder son Enoch, as we have said.

## CHAPTER X. How the Greek and Latin philosophers held a different opinion from the Hebrews concerning the first age

The philosophers of the Greeks and Latins, therefore, thought very differently about the first age from what Josephus reports. They call it the Golden Age, and maintain that at that time people devoted themselves only to leisure, were content solely with the [Col. 0925C] crops that the earth produced of its own accord, drank only simple water, and did not partake of any meat. According to their opinion, one of our own writers composed the following poem, which I have wished to insert into this little work:

> Extremely happy was the former age,  
> Content with faithful fields,  
> And not ruined by slothful luxury;  
> An age that was accustomed, at evening,  
> To break its fast with the easy acorn.  
> They did not know Bacchus’s gifts,  
> To mingle them with liquid honey,  
> Nor to dye shining fleeces from Seres  
> With Tyrian poison.  
> The grass gave them healthful sleep,  
> The winding stream gave them drink,  
> And the lofty pine gave them shade.  
> As yet no one had cut the high seas,  
> Nor had a traveller, with merchandise gathered from everywhere, seen new shores. [Col. 0925D]  
> Then the savage trumpets were silent,  
> Nor had blood, poured out amid bitter hatreds,  
> Stained the dreadful fields.  
> For what would hostile fury have wanted  
> To be the first to move weapons,  
> When people saw savage wounds  
> And no rewards for bloodshed?  
> Would that our times might now return  
> To the ancient ways!  
> But a love of possession, fiercer than the fires of Etna,  
> Burns hot.  
> Alas! Who was that first man  
> Who dug up the weights of hidden gold,  
> And the gems that wished to lie concealed—  
> Precious dangers?

For Sallust, briefly praising earlier times, says: “When human life was conducted without greed, and each person was content with what was his.” Later, [Col. 0926A] he says, “after Cyrus began in Asia, and the Lacedaemonians and Athenians in Greece, to subjugate cities and nations, they made the desire to rule the cause of war, and considered the greatest glory to lie in the greatest empire,” along with the other matters that he himself set forth.

## CHAPTER XI. Concerning Seth, Adam’s son, who pleased God, and concerning his sons and grandsons, who wonderfully discovered wisdom down to the seventh generation and finally wrote it on columns

Adam, who was first formed from the earth, after the murder of his son Abel and the expulsion of Cain, when he was two hundred and thirty years old, fathered Seth. When Seth grew up, he devoted himself to virtue and began to invoke the name of the Lord; and, being an outstanding man, he left behind [Col. 0926B] sons who imitated him. For from his lineage the city of God grew.

Josephus reports the following concerning his sons:

> Since they had all been born good in that same land, they lived there most happily and without any hardship, and nothing cruel befell them until the end of their lives. They were the first to discover the study of heavenly matters and their adornments. Their kinsman Jobal invented music and praised the psaltery and the lyre. And lest what seemed to have been discovered by him should slip away from human beings, or perish before coming to their knowledge, Adam having foretold that the destruction of all things would come, once through the power of fire and again through the force and multitude of waters, they made two columns—one of bricks [Col. 0926C] and the other of stones—and inscribed upon both whatever they had discovered. Thus, if the brick structure were destroyed by the rains, the stone one, remaining, would enable human beings to know what had been written. The stone column, moreover, remains to this day in the land of Syria.

Thus Seth, when he was two hundred and five years old, fathered Enos. Enos lived one hundred and ninety years and fathered Cainan. Cainan lived one hundred and seventy years and fathered Malaleel. Malaleel lived one hundred and sixty-five years and fathered Jared. Jared lived one hundred and sixty-two years and fathered Enoch.

## CHAPTER XII. Concerning Enoch, who was taken away and who also left written prophecies

Enoch lived one hundred and fifty-five years and fathered Methuselah; [Col. 0926D] afterward he walked with God for three hundred years. Hence he disappeared, because God took him. He also wrote certain things, as the apostle Jude testifies. He says:

> Enoch, the seventh from Adam, prophesied, saying: “Behold, the Lord will come with his holy thousands to execute judgment against all and to convict all the ungodly,” and so forth.

It is perfectly clear that the beginning of letters originated with the first man, who was still alive when his sons and grandsons were ardently pursuing wisdom. Thus the sons of Seth, together with their kinsman Jobal, wrote on columns what they had wisely discovered concerning the study of heavenly matters, along with their other [Col. 0927A] arts, as was made clear above from Josephus’s words.

## CHAPTER XIII. Concerning the sons of Seth, who displeased God after the seventh generation
