The sons of Seth remained for seven generations, judging the Lord to be the Lord of all and always looking toward virtue, to use Josephus’s words. Then, as time went on, they advanced from their ancestral religious observances into evil. They no longer rendered legitimate honors to God, nor practiced justice toward human beings; rather, through their subsequent deeds they displayed in doubled measure the zeal that they had previously possessed, now turned toward wickedness. For this reason they provoked the Lord against themselves.

## CHAPTER XIV. [Col. 0927B] Concerning the sons of God, who took the daughters of men as wives

It follows. Moses says:

> “The sons of God, seeing the daughters of men, because they were beautiful, took wives for themselves from all whom they chose.”

Thus these same men were called angels of God. Hence many think that they were not human beings but angels. Yet it is in no way considered credible that holy angels could at that time have fallen in such a manner, nor that the apostle Peter spoke of these when he said that God did not spare the angels who sinned, but rather of those who fell together with their prince, the devil.

For in sacred language [Col. 0927C] human beings are called angels, as it is written concerning John: “Behold, I send my angel before your face.” The prophet Malachi was also properly called an angel.

Therefore, leaving aside the opinions of many, here we understand the sons of God to be the sons of Seth, and the daughters of men to be the daughters of Cain. From these, giants are reported to have been born; and history shows that they existed even earlier, when it said: “For there were giants in those days.” We also learn from historical tradition that certain giants existed after the Flood, although more existed before it. Thus Nebroch and others arose from the lineage of Noah; scorning every good thing because of their confidence in their strength and the beauty of their bodies, they provoked the Lord and perished.

## CHAPTER XV. Whether the people of the first age lived without wives through so many successive years, since we read that they fathered sons only after many years

Methuselah lived one hundred and eighty-seven years and fathered Lamech, [Col. 0927D] and afterward lived seven hundred and eighty-two years.

Here the question may be raised whether people at that time remained without wives for so many successive years, or, if they took wives earlier, what the reason was that they remained without children for so long. This question is solved in two ways.

Either people who possessed such great longevity remained free from the bond of marriage for a longer period, or—and this is most true—the truthful historian Moses includes only those from whom Noah and his sons derived their ancestry, through whom the world was to be restored after the destruction of the other human beings in the Flood.

Thus Matthew, when listing the genealogy of Christ, does not include only firstborn sons, but those from whom the Lord’s birth according to the flesh was derived. Isaac was not Abraham’s firstborn, [Col. 0928A] but Ishmael; Judah was not Jacob’s firstborn, but Reuben; nor was David Jesse’s firstborn.

## CHAPTER XVI. Whether Methuselah lived fourteen years after the Flood, as seems to be contained in Genesis

Lamech lived one hundred and eighty-two years and fathered a son, and called his name Noah. When Noah was six hundred years old, the Flood came upon the whole earth, destroying the entire human race except Noah, his sons, and their wives, whom the Lord preserved in the ark in order to restore the human race.

Now a very famous question arises concerning Methuselah, one that has often been debated in the churches: according to a careful calculation, he is said to have lived fourteen years after the Flood. But since he is said above to have lived nine hundred and sixty-nine years, [Col. 0928B] how can it be true that only eight persons were saved in the ark if he lived after the Flood?

It follows, therefore, that here, as in many other cases, there is an error in the number. For this is how it is found written in both the Hebrew and Samaritan books:

> “Methuselah lived one hundred and eighty-seven years and fathered Lamech. Methuselah lived seven hundred and eighty-two years after he fathered Lamech. All the days of Methuselah were nine hundred and sixty-nine years. Lamech lived one hundred and eighty-two years and fathered Noah.”

From the day of Methuselah’s birth to the day of Noah’s birth there are therefore three hundred and sixty-nine years. Add Noah’s six hundred years, because the Flood occurred in the six hundredth year of his life. Thus it follows that Methuselah died in the nine hundred and sixty-ninth year of his life, in the same year in which the Flood began.

## CHAPTER XVII. [Col. 0928C] Concerning the statement that vengeance would be taken sevenfold upon Cain, but seventy-sevenfold upon Lamech

Lamech said to his wives Adah and Zillah:

> “Hear my voice, wives of Lamech; listen to my speech, for I have killed a man for my wound, and a young man for my bruise. Sevenfold vengeance shall be taken upon Cain, but seventy-sevenfold upon Lamech.”

Lamech, therefore, who confesses to his wives that he committed murder, was the seventh from Adam. In the sons of this murderer, the sevenfold vengeance upon Cain was discharged through the waters of the Flood, since Cain’s entire offspring was destroyed in him. For it is credible that the savage death, avenger of human crimes, found the murderer Lamech himself among the rest who were destined to perish.

“But seventy-sevenfold upon Lamech.” [Col. 0928D] We have already related part of what pertains to the resolution of this question. According to the truth of history, however, seventy-seven generations are found from Adam to Christ. In these, the sin of Lamech—that is, the sin of the whole world—was dissolved through the shedding of Christ’s blood.

Among the Jewish people also, seventy-seven acts of vengeance were established because of the killing of Christ, in accordance with the Gospel passage in which the apostle Peter was told: “Not seven times, but seventy-seven times,” if he repents, forgiveness is to be granted to his brother—that is, the returning Jew is to be received into Christ’s forgiveness through the seventy-seven acts of vengeance that have been established.

## CHAPTER XVIII. [Col. 0929A] Concerning the wrath of God and the statement in Genesis, “It repented me that I had made man,” although there is no repentance in God, in whom foreknowledge is certain

“The Lord God,” it says, “seeing that the wickedness of human beings had multiplied upon the earth, said: ‘I will destroy the human being whom I have made from the face of the earth, from man to beast, and from creeping things to the birds of the air, because I am angry that I made them.’”

The wrath of God is not a disturbance of his mind, but a judgment in which punishment is inflicted upon the sinner. His thought and reconsideration concerning the changing of things is an unchanging ordinance. For the Lord does not repent of any deed of his as a human being does; his decision concerning all things is as fixed as his foreknowledge is certain. But if [Col. 0929B] Scripture did not use such expressions, it would not, in a certain sense, make itself familiar to every kind of human being, whose welfare it wishes to provide.

## CHAPTER XIX. Concerning God’s statement, “Their days shall be one hundred and twenty years”

When God said, “Their days shall be one hundred and twenty years,” this should not be understood as though it had been foretold that from then onward human beings would not exceed one hundred and twenty years of life, since we find that even after the Flood some lived beyond five hundred years. Rather, it should be understood that the Lord said this when Noah was approaching the end of his five hundredth year—that is, when he was four hundred and eighty years old—which Scripture, according to its custom, calls five hundred, often designating the whole [Col. 0929C] sum by its largest portion.

For the Flood occurred in the second month of Noah’s six hundredth year, and thus the aforementioned one hundred and twenty years were foretold as the future span of life allotted to the human beings who were to perish: when they had elapsed, they would be destroyed by the Flood.

Jerome, however, translated the passage from the Hebrew as follows:

> “My spirit shall not judge these human beings forever, because they are flesh.”

That is: because the human condition is fragile, I will not preserve them for eternal punishments; rather, here I will repay them according to what they deserve.

Thus, instead of the severity found in our books, the Lord’s clemency is expressed, since the sinner is punished here for his crime. Moreover, lest he seem cruel because he had not granted sinners an opportunity for repentance, he added: “But their days shall be one hundred and twenty years”—that is, they shall have one hundred and twenty years in which to practice [Col. 0929D] repentance.

Human life, therefore, was not shortened to one hundred and twenty years, as many believe. Rather, that generation was given one hundred and twenty years for repentance. For we find that after the Flood Abraham lived one hundred and seventy-five years. The Lord, however, did not wish to wait until the appointed time had elapsed; instead, cutting short twenty years of the period, he brought on the Flood in the hundredth year designated for repentance.

## CHAPTER XX. How Noah became the tenth ruler of his people from Adam

Noah held the leadership that his fathers had possessed through ten successions of generations—that is, from Noah back to the first parent, with sons succeeding their fathers. [Col. 0930A] Being the tenth from Adam, he was deeply distressed by human conduct and found their counsels exceedingly displeasing; he strove to turn their minds and actions toward better things.

When he saw that they would not heed such admonitions, but were held fast by an intense desire for evil, he feared that they might kill him also, together with his wife and sons, and he departed from that land.

God therefore loved Noah’s righteousness, but condemned not only their wickedness, but the whole human race. When he resolved to destroy it and establish another race free from wickedness, he commanded Noah to build an ark having four compartments, three hundred cubits in length, fifty in width, and thirty in height. Protected by it, Noah remained with his sons and wives as the only human beings left after the Flood, [Col. 0930B] together with his household, as we have stated above.

These remarks concerning Noah’s deeds, according to Josephus’s understanding, are sufficient.

## CHAPTER XXI. Concerning the size of the ark and its compartments

Some people therefore thought it impossible for the ark to contain so many kinds of animals and creeping things, together with the necessities required for the comfort of life over so long a period. They do not consider that Moses was educated in all Egyptian wisdom, [Col. 0930C] or that the cubit used by the Egyptians in geometry was worth as much as six cubits of the kind not used by us.

Those who say that a structure of such magnitude could not have been made by human ingenuity should consider the span of one hundred years that Noah had received for its construction, as well as the strength of human beings who flourished in the first age. They know that immense cities were built. Unless, perhaps, stone can adhere to stone, joined only by mortar, so that a wall may extend for many miles, while wood cannot be joined to wood, fastened with nails, and connected by bitumen so that an ark may be built—not curved, but extended far and wide in straight lines—which no human effort would launch upon the sea, but which the waves would lift when they came, according to the natural order of weights and, even more, through divine providence than human prudence.

It is also written that this ark had upper rooms and a third story. Another translation chose to call it “two-storied” and “three-storied,” so that we understand it to have contained five distinct habitations.

The [Col. 0930D] lower spaces were assigned to dung and to adjacent two-storied compartments that preserved the animals’ fodder. The lower sections, they say, were divided for these purposes. The upper sections, called three-storied, were first assigned as a dwelling for beasts, savage animals, and creeping things. Next, the adjoining upper spaces served as stalls for gentler animals. Above all, at the highest level, a place was allotted to birds and human beings, so that, just as humanity surpasses all animals in honor and wisdom, it might also surpass them all in position.

Thus five dwellings are understood to have existed in the same ark: the first for dung, the second for stores, the third for savage animals, the fourth for tame animals, and the fifth for human beings.

## CHAPTER XXII. [Col. 0931A] Concerning the statement that two of the unclean animals and seven of the clean animals were in the ark

As for the fact that two and two of the unclean animals were brought in, but seven and seven of the clean animals, they give the following reasons: more of those animals that would be useful to human beings were preserved in the ark, and Noah would have animals from which, after leaving the ark, he could offer pleasing sacrifices to the Lord.

## CHAPTER XXIII. Concerning the smallest and useless creatures, whether they were in the ark

A question is also often raised with great minuteness concerning the smallest creatures—not only mice and geckos, but also locusts, beetles, [Col. 0931B] flies, and finally fleas: whether more of them were in that ark than the number specified when God gave the command.

Those who are troubled by this should first be advised that the statement “the things that creep upon the earth” should be understood in such a way that it was not necessary to preserve in the ark those creatures that can live in water—not only those submerged, such as fish, but also those that float upon it, such as many birds.

Next, when it says, “There shall be male and female,” this is plainly understood to refer to the restoration of the species. Consequently, it was not necessary for those creatures to be there that can be born without sexual union from various substances or from the decay of things. Or, if they were present—such as those accustomed to live in houses—they could not have been included under any fixed definition of number.

Alternatively, if the most sacred mystery being enacted, and the figure of so great a matter through an actual event, could not otherwise be fulfilled unless [Col. 0931C] everything that cannot live in water, by nature’s prohibition, were there in that fixed number, this was not the concern of that man or those men, but of God. For Noah did not capture and bring them inside; he allowed those that came and wished to enter to do so.

This is the force of the statement, “They shall enter to you”: not by human action, but by divine command. In any case, we should not believe that creatures without sex were there, nor those that are produced from different kinds, such as mules.

## CHAPTER XXIV. How the animals that are thought unable to eat anything but meat lived in the ark

Some are also accustomed to be troubled by the question of what kinds of food animals that are thought to eat nothing but [Col. 0931D] meat could have had there. Were animals included beyond the appointed number, contrary to the command, because the necessity of feeding others required them to be confined there? Or rather—and this is what ought to be believed—were there, besides meat, certain foods that were suitable for all?

For we know how many animals for which flesh is food also eat grains and fruits, especially figs and chestnuts. What wonder, then, if that wise and righteous man, instructed by God as well, prepared and stored food suitable for every kind without meat?

What is there that hunger would not compel an animal to eat? Or what could God not make pleasant and healthful, since by divine power he could even make them live without food?

## CHAPTER XXV. [Col. 0932A] Concerning Noah’s entry into the ark, where the ark came to rest after the Flood, the number of years from Adam to Noah, and what the philosophers of the nations thought about the ark

Noah was six hundred years old when the Flood began upon the earth. From that time back to the creation of the first human being, two thousand two hundred and forty-two years had elapsed.

Therefore, having briefly touched upon certain matters as we indicated above, this is how the first age unfolded. Noah entered the ark with his sons Shem, Ham, and Japheth, and with their wives, in the second month, on the seventeenth day of the month. He was lifted upward by the violent force of the waters.

When the ark came to rest on the summit of a mountain in Armenia, Noah left it at the Lord’s command in the second month, on the twenty-seventh [Col. 0932B] day of the month. The Armenians call the place of departure “the place of exit,” for there the inhabitants of the province display the customary remains of the ark.

We still see evidence of this Flood in stones that we often find in remote mountains, rough with shells and oysters and hollowed out by water. Nevertheless, I shall briefly report what the historians and wise men of the nations wrote about this ark and this Flood.

One of them, Berossus the Chaldaean, speaking of the Flood, expressed himself as follows:

> “It is said that his ship came to Armenia, near Mount Cardicus, and that part of it still exists. Some people still take bitumen from it, which they chiefly use for purification rites.”

Jerome the Egyptian, who is known to have written the antiquities of Phoenicia, also mentions these matters. Manasseas of Damascus [Col. 0932C] likewise says the following about this Flood in the ninety-sixth book of his Histories:

> “There is also in Armenia, above the city of Muniadas, a lofty mountain called Baris. It is said that many fugitives were saved upon it at the time of the Flood, and that someone carried there in an ark came to the summit of a mountain in Sicily. They say that the remains of the wood were preserved there for a long time.”

This was the ark about which Moses, the lawgiver of the Jews, also wrote.

## CHAPTER XXVI. Concerning what seems impossible to certain people: that human beings lived for nine hundred years

Noah lived three hundred and fifty years after the Flood. All the days of Noah were therefore nine hundred and fifty years.

If such a long span of life among the ancient people [Col. 0932D] seems incredible to anyone, let him consider Josephus’s assertion. He says:

> “Let no one, comparing their life with modern life and with the short number of years in which we now live, think that what has been said about the ancients is false, or, because life is not now conducted for so long a period, believe that they did not attain the length of that life. For since they were devout and had been made by God himself, and since more suitable nourishment had been prepared for them for a longer time, they rightly lived through such great cycles of years. Moreover, because of the virtues and glorious benefits that they continually pursued—that is, astronomy and geometry—God granted them longer spans of life, which they could not have fully expounded unless they lived six hundred years. For through so many cycles of years the great [Col. 0933A] year is completed.”

All those who chose to record antiquity among the Greeks and barbarians bear witness to this. Manetho, who composed a history of the Egyptians; Berossus, who excerpted Chaldaean history; Mochus; Aetius; and also Jerome the Egyptian, who arranged the Phoenician history—all agree with these statements. Hesiod, Agathaeus, Hellanicus, Acusilaus, Ephorus among them, and Nicolaus likewise mention in their histories ancient people who lived for a thousand years.

## CHAPTER XXVII. How the whole human race was propagated from Noah’s three sons, and what regions of the earth they occupied
The sons of Noah were Shem, Ham, and Japheth. For from these, after the Flood, peoples were scattered throughout all the lands and islands of the sea. But which nations each one founded, and which regions of the world they occupied, I have chosen to extract from the books of Josephus and Jerome.

The sons of Noah had descendants whose names, in their honour, they bestowed upon the nations they founded and upon the lands they were able to seize. Japheth, therefore, the son of Noah, had seven sons. They inhabited the region beginning at the Taurus and Amanus Mountains and extending through Asia as far as the river Tanais.

In Europe, however, the land of the Gazzim, since none of those mentioned above was dwelling there, its peoples called themselves by various names. They are now called Galatians by the Greeks, but formerly they were called Gomanicae, whom Gomer established. Magog established the Magogites, named after himself. [Col. 0933C] These were called Scythians by the Greeks.

Among the sons of Japheth were also Madeus and Janus. From Madeus came the peoples whom the Greeks call Medes; from Janus came all the Ionians. From them descend the Hellenic peoples, who are also the Greeks; hence the Ionian Sea is so called.

Jobel founded the Jobeli, who in our time are the Iberes, that is, the Spaniards; from them the Celtiberians were later named. Moga was originally so called; later it was Cappadocia, and now the Romans give it the name Caesarea, that is, “from Caesar.” The Moscini were planted by Mosoch; they are now called Cappadocians. A sign of their ancient name is still displayed, for among them there is a city called Moscha to this day, showing to those capable of understanding that at one time all the peoples of that region [Col. 0933D] were so called.

Thyras called his people Thyrenses. He was their prince, but the Greeks altered their name to Trachii. Such, then, were the peoples established through the sons of Japheth.

Gomer had three sons. Astinegas established the Astinegans, who are now called Regini by the Greeks. Riphath established the Riphaeans, who are called Paphlagonians. Tygram established the Tygraneans, who are called Phrygians by the Greeks.

Janus, the son of Japheth, also had three sons. Helisa called his people the Helisaeans; he was their prince, and they are now the Aeolians. Tharsis established the Thyrsi—for Cilicia was so called in ancient times. Among them Tharsus is called the greatest metropolitan city, with the letter *tau* substituted for *theta*. Cythim possessed the island of Cythima, now called Cyprus; from it all islands and coastal regions are called *Cythym* in Hebrew. One of the cities in Cyprus bears witness to my statement, having been able to retain the ancient name. It is called Cythis by those who gave it a Greek name, and thus the name Cythi has not disappeared.

The sons or grandsons of Japheth therefore possessed these nations, as well as others that are perhaps now unknown. Nevertheless, we read that nearly all the islands, the shores of the whole world, and the lands near the sea were occupied by Greek settlers. As we said above, they possessed all the coastal regions from the Amanus and Taurus Mountains as far as the British Ocean.

The sons of Ham were Cush, Mesraim, Put, and Canaan. Cush is now called Ethiopia by the Hebrews; Mesraim is Egypt; Put is Libya. From him the river of Mauretania is also called Put to the present day, and the entire surrounding region is called Putensis. Yet only in one part of that climate does the ancient name Libya remain; the rest of the land is called Africa.

Canaan, moreover, occupied the land that the Jews later possessed. After the Canaanites had been expelled, the sons of Cush were Saba, Evila, Sabatha, Regina, and Sabatacha. Sabatacha—that is, Saba—gave rise to the Sabaeans; Evila to the Getuli, dwelling in the desert adjoining the more remote part of Africa. Sabatha gave rise to the Sabatheni, who are now called Astavari. Regina and Sabatacha gradually lost their ancient names, and it is unknown what they are now called in place of the former names.

The sons of Regina were Saba and Dadan. This Saba is written with the letter *sin*, whereas above we said that the Sabaeans were named with *samekh*. Saba is now interpreted as Arabia. For in the seventy-first Psalm, where we have, “The kings of the Arabians and of Saba shall offer gifts,” the Hebrew has “the kings of Saba.” Dadan is a people of Ethiopia, in the western region.

Mesraim, however, fathered Ludim, Anamim, Laabim, Neptuim, Petrusim, and Cesluim. From these came the Philistines and the Chapturim, except for the Labaim, from whom the Libyans were later named; they had previously been called Putei. The Casloim were later called Philistines, whom we correctly call Palestinians. The remaining six peoples are unknown to us, because they were destroyed in the Ethiopian war and their former names passed into oblivion. They possessed the land of Gaza as far as the remotest borders of Egypt.

Canaan fathered his firstborn, Sidon, [Col. 0934D] and Heth, Jebus, Amorrah, Gerges, Hivah, Arach, Sima, Arad, Samarith, and Matthaeus.

Sidon was the firstborn of Canaan; from him the city of Sidon in Phoenicia is named. The Arachite founded the town of Archas, situated at the foot of Lebanon. The Aradians are those who possessed the island of Arad, separated from the Phoenician coast by a narrow strait. Samaria was a renowned city of Coele-Syria. The Macedonians who ruled after Alexander’s death called it Epiphany.

The boundary of the Canaanites extended from Sidon to Gerara, and onward to Gaza, Sodom, Gomorrah, Adama, and Seboim, as far as Letzem. The other cities—namely Sidon, [Col. 0935A] Gerara, Sodom, Gomorrah, Adama, and Seboim—are known by their own names.

Thus all the sons of Ham—that is, of Noah’s middle son—number four, together with five grandsons. From one of his sons came two great-grandsons, and from one grandson the total becomes eleven. After these have been enumerated, the account returns to another Ham, who was called Mesraim. Those whom he fathered are mentioned not as individual men but as seven nations; and from the sixth, as though from a sixth son, a people is said to have emerged called the Philistines. Thus there are eight.

The account then returns again to Canaan, in whose son Ham was cursed, and eleven descendants whom he fathered are named. After certain cities have been mentioned, together with the territories to which they extended, it is stated that, counting sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons, thirty-one descendants were born from the line of Ham.

Shem, Noah’s third son, had five sons, who inhabited Asia separately as far as the Ocean, beginning at the Euphrates. Elam left the Elamites, who are the rulers of the Persians. Assur founded the city of Nineveh; his people are now called Chaldeans. Arphaxad named the Arphaxadites, while he himself was their prince. Aram established the people whom the Greeks call Syrians. Those whom they now call Lydians were named by Lud—then called Ludas.

Aram had four sons; to these he assigned Trachonitis and Damascus, which is joined to Media, Palestine, and Syria. Otrus established Armenia; Geter, the Bactrians; and Mes, the Mesaneans, whose land is now universally called Arax.

Arphaxad was the father of Sala, [Col. 0935C] from whom Heber was born; from him the Jews were formerly called Hebrews. Heber fathered Joktan and Peleg. Joktan, who was the son of Heber, had the following sons: Elmodad, Saleph, Asarmoth, Jare, Aduram, Uzal, Deda, Ebal, Abimael, Sheba, Ophir, Evila, and Jobab. These inhabit certain places in Syria situated near the river Cophena of India.

Such, then, are the generations of Shem. When Shem was one hundred years old, he fathered Arphaxad, two years after the Flood. Arphaxad lived thirty-five years and fathered Sala; Sala likewise lived thirty years and fathered Heber. Heber lived thirty-four years and fathered Peleg.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

### On the interpretation of Peleg as “division,” because in his days the division of languages took place; concerning the building of the tower, its Nimrod, and what the learned among the nations have thought about it

This Peleg was so called because he was born at the division of the nations. The Hebrews call *peleg* “division,” because, although until then humanity had possessed one language, it was divided into several languages; and what had previously been called the human language thereafter, because of the demand of pride, received different names.

When God commanded the sons of Noah after the Flood to increase and multiply, and, inhabiting different regions of the earth, to enjoy an abundance of fruits, they were uneducated and therefore disobedient. Falling into calamities, they came to feel the weight of their sins. Inflamed by the vigor of youth and believing that they possessed good things through their own strength rather than through God’s favor, they proceeded to become disobedient to God’s will.

Nimrod, the son of Cush, who was the son of Ham, the son of Noah, made them arrogant toward God and contemptuous of him. Since he was especially bold and powerful in hand, he persuaded them not to attribute human prosperity to the Lord, but to believe that it was supplied by human strength. He alone presumed to turn people away from the fear of God and to place their hope in their own power.

For this reason he urged them to build a tower of such height that water could not reach it, and that it might even touch heaven. The multitude was eager to obey Nimrod’s commands, thinking it a burdensome service to obey God, and they built the tower, abandoning none of their efforts. Its height therefore advanced with ease, beyond what anyone might have expected. Built by many hands, it continued to grow.

Hence the Lawgiver testifies that the Lord descended to see the tower that the sons of Adam were building, saying: “Behold, one people and one language belong to all; they have begun to do this, and they will not desist from their plans until they complete them in action. Come, therefore, let us descend and confuse their language there, so that each one may not hear the voice of his neighbor.” And thus the Lord divided them from that place throughout all the lands. They ceased building the city, and therefore its name was called Babel, because there the language of the whole earth was confused.

From there they migrated everywhere and took possession of the land, [Col. 0936C] each one of the region that God had allotted to him. Thus the entire earth was filled by them, both the inland regions and the maritime ones. Some also crossed by ship and inhabited islands. Hence certain peoples still preserve the names bestowed by their founders, as was explained above; others changed the names they preferred.

History declares that the divisions of languages numbered seventy-two—not in the sense that there were then only that many people and no more, but that this number represents the heads of families already born from the sons of Noah, who founded peoples and nations. Scripture says: “This is the family of Noah according to their peoples and nations, and from these the nations were divided on the earth after the Flood.”

The Sibyl also mentions this tower and the different human languages, saying: “When all human beings possessed one language, certain people built a lofty tower, as though intending through it to ascend to heaven. But the gods, sending winds, overturned the tower, divided each person’s speech, and for this reason it happened that the city was called Babylon.”

Aetius mentions the plain called Shinar in the region of Babylon, saying: “Those who escaped from among the priests, taking up the sacred rites of Jupiter, came to Shinar of Babylon.”

Nimrod, therefore, the son of Cush and grandson of Noah, whom we have already mentioned, was the one who first became powerful on the earth. He was a mighty hunter before the Lord. From him arose the proverb: “Like Nimrod, a mighty hunter before the Lord.” This should be understood to mean that this giant was against the Lord. The meaning is indicated by the word “hunter”: he was a deceiver of souls and an oppressor of human beings. Because he drew people away from the worship of God, he was given this name.

The beginning of his kingdom was Babylon, together with Erech, Accad, and Calneh in the land of Shinar. Erech is the city of Edessa. Accad is now called Nisibis. Calneh, after its name was changed, was called Seleucia by King Seleucus.

Nimrod seized an unprecedented tyranny. He was the first to rule over peoples and in Babylon. It appears that this most powerful tyrant ruled in the very place where languages were divided to confound human pride. The Syrians report that he also wrote about astrology and geometry and made maps of the world.

## CHAPTER XXIX

### On the statement that Assur came out of the land of Shinar and built Nineveh

The statement that Assur came out of the land of Shinar, which belonged to Nimrod’s kingdom, and built Nineveh and the other cities that the Lawgiver lists, refers to an event that occurred much later. The Lawgiver touched upon it on this occasion because of the renown of the Assyrian kingdom, which Ninus, son of Belus, greatly expanded. Ninus was the founder of the great city of Nineveh, whose name was derived from his own, so that it was called Nineveh from Ninus.

Assur, from whom the Assyrians derive their name, was not among the sons of Ham but is found among the sons of Shem, who was Noah’s eldest son. It therefore appears that the one who later possessed the kingdom of that giant arose from the line of Shem, [Col. 0937C] and that from there he proceeded to establish other cities as well.

## CHAPTER XXX

### Why, when Ham sinned, his son Canaan received the sentence of punishment

Why, when Ham sinned, did his son Canaan receive the sentence of punishment? Why is he struck not in his own person but in his posterity, unless it is because the wickedness of the reprobate, though it often prospers in the present, is punished in the future?

Or perhaps it is because he prophesied that the sons of Israel, who came from the seed of Shem, would receive the land of Canaan after the Canaanites had been expelled and defeated, foreseeing and perceiving what was to happen long afterward.

## CHAPTER XXXI

### How the statement “May God enlarge Japheth, and may he dwell in the tents of Shem” is to be understood

“May God enlarge Japheth, and may he dwell in the tents of Shem.”

Although God is the God of all nations, nevertheless, in a certain manner and by a proper name, even among those nations he is called the God of Israel. And from what did this come, except from the blessing of Japheth? For among the people of the nations the Church has occupied the whole world. This was plainly foretold when it was said: “May God enlarge Japheth, and may he dwell in the tents of Shem.”

Shem, from whose seed Christ was incarnate, is interpreted as “name-giver.” What is more renowned than Christ, whose name now burns everywhere, so that even in the Song of Songs, in a prophecy that preceded him, he is compared with poured-out perfume?

In his houses—that is, in the churches—the breadth of the nations dwells, for Japheth is interpreted as “breadth.” Behold how God enlarges Japheth and dwells in the tents of Shem—that is, in the churches that the apostles, the sons of the prophets, built. Accordingly, the Apostle Paul says to the faithful from the nations: “At that time you were without Christ, alienated from the fellowship of Israel, strangers to the covenants and to the promise, having no hope and without God in this world.”

These words show that Japheth did not yet dwell in the houses of Shem. But let us observe how he concludes shortly afterward: “Therefore,” he says, “you are no longer strangers and sojourners, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household, built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the chief cornerstone.”

## CHAPTER XXXII

### On the statement: “From Shem were born, the father of all the sons of Heber, the elder brother of Japheth”

“From Shem were also born, the father of all the sons of Heber, the elder brother of Japheth.”

Here he begins to weave the genealogy of Shem, Noah’s eldest son, since he had begun with Japheth, the younger, and thus finally reached Shem.

There is some difficulty in the very beginning of the account, when it says: “From Shem were born, the father of all Heber, the elder brother of Japheth.” The order of the words is: “Heber was born from Shem; Shem is the father of all the sons of Shem.” Thus he wished Shem to be understood as the patriarch of all who arose from his stock, [Col. 0938C] whether sons, grandsons, or great-grandsons, whom he is about to mention.

For we know that Heber was not Shem’s son but his great-grandson. Nor is Heber, his great-grandson, introduced after the sons without reason, except that among the descendants of Noah’s sons he is found pleasing to God. He had not joined the sons of pride in building the tower as an affront to God; they belonged to the city of the impious and deservedly suffered the injury of confusion through the destruction of their own language. For this reason they were scattered throughout the whole world, abandoning the work whose completion they had hastened with the greatest zeal.

In the house of Heber, because he remained free from the punishment of the proud earth-dwellers, the ancient language remained. At first it was called human because it was common to all; later, after his name, it was called Hebrew, to distinguish it from the others. Through successive generations it reached Abraham, and then, through the patriarchs descended from Abraham’s stock, it was spread among the people of God.

Yet neither Heber nor Abraham himself was able to spread it through all his descendants, but only among those who appeared to belong to the city of God, from whom Christ was born according to the flesh.

## CHAPTER XXXIII

### Since Genesis makes no mention of anyone righteous from Noah to Abraham, whether there was any such person

After the two sons of Noah had been blessed and one in their midst had been cursed, there is silence down to Abraham concerning any righteous people who might have worshiped the Lord devoutly. Nevertheless, whether the city of the devout did not exist, or remained hidden, or rather continued among the two blessed sons of Noah and their descendants, while the impious city existed in the one who was cursed and in his offspring, from whom the giant hunter against the Lord also arose—this is not easy to determine.

Perhaps—for this is certainly more credible—there were already, among the sons of those two blessed men, even before Babylon began to be established, people who despised God; and among the sons of Ham there were worshipers of God. In any case, we must believe that neither kind of human being was ever absent from the earth.

Just as, when one language belonged to all, the sons of pestilence were not thereby absent—for before the Flood there was also one language, yet all except the one righteous household of Noah deserved to be destroyed by the Flood—so after the Flood I would not believe that the righteous were absent.

But if all of them were mentioned, the account would become excessively long, and this would represent historical diligence more than prophetic foresight. The sacred writer—or rather the Spirit of God through him—therefore follows those matters in which past events are not merely narrated but future events are also foretold, matters that pertain to the city of God.

Thus, leaving aside the other sons of Noah, who do not pertain to this purpose, he joins together in the sequence of generations those through whom the line could reach Abraham, just as before the Flood the generations were linked through those by whom the line would reach Noah, generations descended from that son of Adam who was called Seth.

## CHAPTER XXXIV

### How the statement that the Lord descended, and that they would not desist from their plans until they completed them in action, is to be understood; and how seventy-two languages began throughout the lands from the three sons of Noah

Some people are troubled by the statement: “The Lord descended to see the city,” since God does not move from place to place, but is always wholly present everywhere.

It is to be understood in this way: “The Lord descended to see the city and the tower that the sons of Adam were building”—that is, not the sons of God but the sons of human beings, the society living according to humanity, which we call the earthly city.

God did not descend locally, since he is wholly present everywhere and fills all things. Rather, he is said to descend to earth whenever he works miraculously, beyond the ordinary course of nature. Nor does he learn something by seeing it at a particular time, since nothing conceived in anyone’s mind can be unknown to him. He is said to see and know something at a particular time because he causes what he disapproves to be seen and known.

That city was not seen in the way God caused it to be seen when he revealed how displeasing it was to him. Nevertheless, it may be understood that God descended to that city because his angels descended, and he dwells in them; thus he descended through the descending angels, in whom he was present.

He did not say, “Come, and, descending, confuse their language,” but, “Let us confuse their language there,” showing that he works through his ministers in such a way that they too are fellow workers with God.

The statement, “They will not desist from their plans until they complete them in action,” was not spoken as a confirmation but as though in the form of a question, as threatening speakers commonly express themselves. It should therefore be understood as though he had said: “Will not everything they have attempted to do fail?” Yet if it is phrased in this way, the threatening force is not expressed, because we cannot write down the tone of the speaker.

“Come, therefore, let us descend and confuse their languages there, so that each one may not hear the voice of his neighbor.” And thus the Lord divided them from that place throughout all the lands. They ceased building the city, and therefore its name was called Babel, because there the language of the whole earth was confused; and from there the Lord scattered them over the face of all the regions.

The evil intention is rightly punished even when the intended result does not follow. What, then, was the nature of this punishment? Since the authority of one who commands lies in language, pride was condemned precisely there: the one who had refused to understand in order to obey God’s command could no longer be understood when commanding another person. Thus their conspiracy was dissolved, as each person departed from the one whom he did not understand and joined himself only to one with whom he could speak.

Through the languages the nations were divided and scattered throughout the lands, as God wished, in ways hidden from us and beyond our comprehension. From those three men, the sons of Noah, seventy-two languages therefore began throughout the lands and, increasing, reached the islands. The number of nations, however, grew much greater than the number of languages.

## CHAPTER XXXV

### On the number of years from the Flood to the birth of Abraham, and on how Josephus, the Seventy Translators, and Eusebius differ from the Hebrew text

As we began to mention above, the sequence of years from the Flood to the birth of Abraham is as follows.

Shem was one hundred years old when he fathered Arphaxad, two years after the Flood. Arphaxad, being thirty years old, fathered Sala. In the thirtieth year of his age Sala likewise fathered Heber. Heber, being thirty-four years old, fathered Peleg. Peleg lived thirty years and fathered Reu. Reu lived thirty-five years and fathered Saruch. Saruch lived thirty years and fathered Nahor. Nahor lived twenty-eight years and fathered Terah. When Terah was seventy years old, he fathered Abram, Nahor, and Haran.

Therefore, from the birth of Abraham, who was the tenth from Noah, as has now been shown, if you calculate the number of years from the birth of each father to the birth of the succeeding son, you will find 292 years—that is, from the birth of Abraham back to the Flood.

However, blessed Jerome in the *Chronicle* of Eusebius, and Orosius at the beginning of his books—while Josephus does not differ from them by much—hold a different view of the number of years. By counting backward, they say that from the birth of Abraham to the Flood of the whole world there are 942 years.

Thus the second age of the world proceeded as has been stated, insofar as knowledge of it could reach our small understanding on the authority of the ancients. This age they call childhood.

## CHAPTER XXXVI

### How Terah departed from Chaldea with Abraham, Lot, and Haran and came to the land of Canaan

Terah took Abram his son, Lot the son of his son Haran, and Sarai his daughter-in-law, the wife of his son Abram, and led them out of Ur of the Chaldeans to go to the land of Canaan. They came as far as Haran and settled there.

Josephus says that Ur was a city of the Chaldeans. From there Terah departed with the members of his household and came to Haran, which another translation usually calls Carrhae.

Jerome explains this passage of the history as referring to the death of Haran before the death of his father and to Ur of the Chaldeans: “Haran died before Terah his father in the land of his birth, in Ur of the Chaldeans.” In place of what we read, “in the land of his birth, in Ur of the Chaldeans,” the Hebrew has “in Ur cestim,” that is, “in the fire of the Chaldeans.”

The Hebrews relate the following story on this occasion: Abraham was thrown into the fire because he refused to worship fire; surrounded by a Babylonian conflagration, he was rescued by God’s help and escaped from the fire of idolatry.

The statement later written that Terah departed with his offspring from the region of the Chaldeans corresponds to the Hebrew wording “from Ur,” that is, “from the conflagration of the Chaldeans.” This is the meaning of the statement now given: “Haran died before Terah his father in the land of his birth, in the fire of the Chaldeans”—namely, that because he refused to worship the fire, he was consumed by fire.

## CHAPTER XXXVII

### On Abraham’s departure after the death of his father Terah; on the statement that the Lord said to Abraham, “Go out from your land and from your kindred,” although he had first departed from it with his father; on Nahor, Abraham’s brother; and on matters pertaining to this question

After the death of Terah, Abraham’s father, the following is read: “And the Lord said to Abraham: Go out from your land, from your kindred, and from your father’s house,” and so forth.

When blessed Stephen was recounting this in the Acts of the Apostles, he said, among other things: “The God of glory appeared to our father Abraham when he was in Mesopotamia, before he lived in Carrhae, and said to him: Go out from your land, from your kindred, and from your father’s house.”

According to Stephen’s words, God did not speak to Abraham after his father’s death. Terah died in Carrhae, where Abraham too lived with him as his son. Rather, God spoke before Abraham lived in that city, that is, while he was still in Mesopotamia. He had therefore already left the Chaldeans.

When Stephen adds, “Then Abraham went out from the land of the Chaldeans and lived in Carrhae,” this does not mean that it happened after God spoke to him. Abraham did not leave the land of the Chaldeans after those words of God, since Stephen says that the Lord spoke to him in Mesopotamia. Rather, the word “then” refers to the whole period beginning when he left the Chaldeans and lived in Carrhae.

The following statement likewise says: “And from there, after his father had died, he settled him in this land in which you now dwell, and your fathers.” It does not say, “After his father had died, he departed from Carrhae,” but, “From there he settled him here after his father had died.”

We should therefore understand that the Lord spoke to Abraham while he was in Mesopotamia, before he lived in Carrhae; but that Abraham reached Carrhae with his father, retained the Lord’s command within himself, and departed from there in his seventy-fifth year, while his father was in his one hundred forty-fifth year.

He says that Abraham’s settlement in the land of Canaan, not his departure from Carrhae, occurred after his father’s death, because his father was already dead when Abraham purchased the land and began to possess it as his own.

When the Lord says to Abraham, already established in Mesopotamia—that is, already departed from the land of the Chaldeans—“Go out from your land, from your kindred, and from your father’s house,” this does not mean that he should remove his body from there, since he had already done so, but that he should detach his mind from it.

He had not departed from it in spirit, but was held by the hope and desire of returning. That hope and desire had to be cut off at God’s command and with his help, while Abraham obeyed.

It is not implausible to suppose that, after Nahor had followed his father, Abraham then fulfilled the Lord’s command by leaving Carrhae with his wife Sarah and Lot, the son of his brother.

Earlier passages of this sacred history relate how Terah left the region of the Chaldeans with his household, came to Mesopotamia, and lived at Haran. But one of his sons, named Nahor, is not mentioned, as though Terah had not taken him with him.

Later, when Abraham sent his servant to obtain a wife for his son Isaac, we find the following written: “The servant took ten camels from his master’s camels, together with all his master’s goods, and rose and departed for Mesopotamia, to the city of Nahor.”

This and other testimonies of the sacred history show that Nahor too left the region of the Chaldeans and established a dwelling in Mesopotamia, where Abraham had lived with his father.

Why, then, did Scripture not mention him when Terah departed from the Chaldean land with his household and settled in Mesopotamia, where not only Abraham his son but also Sarah his daughter-in-law and Lot his grandson are mentioned as having accompanied him? Perhaps it was because Nahor had departed from filial and fraternal devotion and adhered to the superstition of the Chaldeans, and later, either in repentance or because he suffered persecution—which is the more suspected explanation—he too migrated from there.

“All the days of Terah were 205 years, and he died in Haran.” This should not be understood as though he spent all those days there, but because he completed all the days of his life there—the total of 205 years.

It is unknown how many years Terah lived in Carrhae, since it is not stated in what year of his life he came to Carrhae. It is absurd to suppose that in this genealogical sequence, where the number of years each person lived is carefully recorded, the number of years of this one man’s life alone was omitted.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

### Why Genesis is silent about the years of some people while counting those of others

It is customary to ask why the years of certain people mentioned by the same Scripture are omitted, while those of others are counted.

The answer should be that they do not belong to the sequence in which the reckoning of times is woven through the death of those who beget and the succession of their begetters; for this reason the years of their lives are not counted.

But the sequence that runs from Adam to Noah and from Noah to Abraham contains no one without a number of years.

## CHAPTER XXXIX

### Whether the father of Milcah is also the father of Iscah, and who Iscah was

The statement in Genesis that the father of Milcah is also the father of Iscah, or the question of who Iscah was, should be understood as follows:

Terah fathered Abraham, Nahor, and Haran. Haran fathered Lot and Milcah, as well as Sarai, also called Iscah. They took wives: Abraham took Sarai, and Nahor took Milcah.

At that time marriage between paternal uncles and their brothers’ children had not yet been forbidden by law.

## CHAPTER XL

### How Sarah, although she was abducted by Pharaoh, is not believed to have been violated by him

The question is how Sarah, although she was abducted by Pharaoh, can be believed not to have been violated by him.

The answer is that, according to the Book of Esther, among the ancients any woman who pleased the king was anointed for six months with myrtle oil, and for six months was treated with various perfumes and women’s preparations; only then did she enter [Col. 0943C] before the king.

It may therefore have happened that, after Sarah had pleased the king, while her entrance to the king was being prepared for a year, Pharaoh gave many gifts to Abraham, and afterward Pharaoh was struck by the Lord while Sarah still remained untouched by intercourse with him.

## CHAPTER XLI

### Who the “unencumbered men” were whom Abraham is said to have counted

It is also asked who the “unencumbered men” were of whom Genesis says: “He counted his unencumbered home-born servants.”

By “unencumbered men” he meant young men prepared for war who were not married. Later he said of them: “Except for what the young men had eaten.” And he pursued them as far as Dan.

Dan is a town of Phoenicia, now called Paneas, where one of the sources of the Jordan rises; it is called Dan, while the other is called Jor. When these two sources, which are not far from one another, join into a single stream, it is called the Jordan.

Thus, just as one river comes from two sources, so one name is produced from two names.

## CHAPTER XLII

### Who Melchizedek was, the king of Salem who received tithes from Abraham
Melchizedek, king of Salem, brought out bread and wine for Abraham. He was a priest of God Most High, and he blessed him. They also relate that he was Shem, Noah’s first son, who, after changing his name, was called Melchizedek—a name that in our language is interpreted as “king of righteousness.” At the time Abraham was born, he was 390 years old, as follows from this reckoning.

In the second year after the Flood, when Shem was 100 years old, he fathered Arphaxad. After his birth he lived 500 years, making 600 years in all. Arphaxad, at the age of 35, fathered Shelah. Shelah, himself also thirty years old, fathered Eber, whom we read to have fathered Peleg at the age of 44. Again, after thirty years had elapsed, he fathered Reu. Reu, likewise, after the thirty-fifth year of his life, produced Serug. When Serug had reached the age of thirty, Nahor was born. Nahor, at the age of 29, fathered Terah, whom we read to have fathered Abraham, Nahor, and Haran at the age of seventy. Add up the years of each successive generation, and you will find 390 years from the birth of Shem to the generation of Abraham.

Abraham died in the 175th year of his life. By calculation, it is found that Shem, Abraham’s great-grandfather, outlived him by 35 years. They also report that, down to the priesthood of Aaron, all firstborn sons were priests, sacrificed victims to God, and that this was the birthright which Esau sold to his brother Jacob.

It is therefore not surprising if Melchizedek came out to meet Abraham after his victory, and brought bread and wine for the refreshment both of Abraham himself and of his warriors, and blessed him, since he owed this duty to his great-grandson, and received from him tithes of the spoils and the victory—or, as the ambiguous wording has it, whether he himself gave Abraham tithes of his own possessions and displayed generosity toward his descendant. Both interpretations are possible, according to both the Hebrew text and the Septuagint translators: that he himself received tithes of the spoils and gave Abraham tithes of his possessions. Nevertheless, the Apostle in the Epistle to the Hebrews most clearly determines that Abraham did not receive tithes of Melchizedek’s wealth, but that the high priest received a portion from the spoils of the enemies.

Salem, however, is not—as Josephus and all our people supposed—the name of Jerusalem, composed from Greek and Hebrew, an absurdity demonstrated by the mixture of a foreign language. Rather, it is a town near Scythopolis that is called Salem to this day. There Melchizedek’s palace is shown, and the greatness of its ruins reveals the magnificence of the ancient structure.

Elsewhere in Genesis it is written concerning this place: “Jacob came to Succoth,” that is, “to tents,” “and made houses and tents for himself there, and he crossed over into Salem,” a city of the region of Shechem, which is in the land of Canaan.

It must also be considered that, when Abraham was returning from the slaughter of the enemies whom he had pursued as far as Dan, now called Paneas, his route was not from the direction of Jerusalem, but from the town of the metropolis of Shechem. Concerning this place we also read in the Gospel: “John was baptizing at Aenon near Salim, because there was much water there.” It makes no difference whether it is called Salem or Salim, since the Hebrews very rarely use the same vowels in the middle of words, and according to the preference of readers and the variety of regions they pronounce the same words with different sounds and accents.

The Apostle also says that this Melchizedek was “without father, without mother, without genealogy.” He said this either because Holy Scripture does not recount his genealogy, or because, according to the legal tradition, he did not offer the sacrifices which the Lord commanded priests of the Levitical line to sacrifice, or because, as stated above, being from the tribe of Levi, he had neither father nor mother.

You need not, however, trouble yourself greatly over these omissions, since they are generally of such a kind that you can readily establish them from your reading of the sacred Scriptures.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0945]

## CHAPTER I. On Joseph’s exaltation, and on the partly incomplete and partly false account given by pagan historians of the reason why the children of Israel departed from there

Pagan historians also wrote something about our Joseph. The historian Pompeius, and his epitomator Justin, say among other things as follows:

“Joseph was the youngest in age among his brothers. Fearing his exceptional intelligence, his brothers intercepted him and sold him to foreign merchants. Brought by them to Egypt, and having there acquired magical [Variant: magnificent] arts through his skillful intelligence, he soon became exceedingly dear to the king himself. For he was especially astute in interpreting prodigies and was the first to establish an understanding of dreams; nothing concerning divine or human law seemed unknown to him. So far did this extend that, foreseeing many years in advance the future barrenness of the fields, he gathered and stored the crops, and his achievements were so remarkable that his answers seemed to come not from a human being but from a god.

“Joseph’s son was Moses, whom, in addition to inheriting his father’s knowledge, the beauty of his appearance also commended. But when the Egyptians were suffering from scabies and vitiligo, they were warned by an oracle and expelled him, together with the afflicted, beyond the borders of Egypt, lest the disease spread to more people.”

This is what Justin says. But since this same Moses, whom they testify to have been wise and learned, recorded more fully and more truthfully, both personally and through his people, what happened, their ignorance must first be remedied by his testimony and authority—which even they approve. Next, the deceptive stratagem of the Egyptian priests must be refuted. Either by cunning—as is more evident—they attempted, through a confused and piecemeal account, to remove from memory the manifest wrath and mercy of the true God, lest they show that he deserved to be worshiped, since by his counsel these disasters had been announced and by his aid they had been avoided; or, if we interpret the matter more leniently, they simply forgot.

For the Egyptians themselves, like priests, abound in the grain of that Joseph of ours, who was a servant of the true God and, through his provision, piously and attentively concerned for the work of his Lord. Yet because they were false priests, they did not grieve together with the other hungry people. Indeed, whoever is pleased forgets; whoever grieves remembers. Nevertheless, although the histories and official records are silent about the evidence of that period, the land of Egypt itself declares itself a witness, for when it was then brought under royal control and restored to its cultivators, it has continued to pay a perpetual tax of a fifth part of all its produce down to the present day.

There was therefore this great famine under the Egyptian king Diopolites, whose name was Amoses. At that time Baleus ruled the Assyrians, and Apis the Argives. Before this, there had been seven preceding years of abundance, whose plenty our Joseph, with his prudence, gathered and stored—lest it perish all the more negligently because it had arisen so abundantly—and thus preserved all Egypt. He acquired all the money for Pharaoh, while rendering glory to God, according to the most equitable distribution: taxes to whom taxes were due, honor to whom honor was due. He collected all their livestock, lands, and assessments. He also distributed seed to them under an established tax, so that they might repay the land of Egypt which they had purchased and give the king a fifth part of the produce.

## CHAPTER II. The patriarch Jacob’s clear prophecy concerning Christ’s coming; and the time when Greece began to use grain

Altadas, the tenth Assyrian king, reigned for 32 years. It was the 315th year from Abraham’s birth and the 240th year of the promise. Eratus was the tenth king of the Sicyonians. Argus was the fourth king of Argos. In Egypt it was the eighteenth dynasty. At that time Amoses was the first king of the Diopolites.

When Jacob had reached the 147th year of his life, he prophesied about Christ and the calling of the nations, saying in his blessing of Judah: “The ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor the leader from his loins, until the things reserved for him come, and he himself shall be the expectation of the nations.” As he was about to die, he blessed his sons and his grandsons through Joseph, and he died in Egypt. Joseph brought his body back with great honor to the land of Canaan.

Thus, while Argus was reigning, Greece began to use grain and to possess cultivated fields, after seeds had been brought from elsewhere. After his death Argus was also regarded as a god and honored with a temple and sacrifices. This honor, while he was still reigning, had previously been transferred to a private individual, a certain Gyros who had been struck by lightning, because he was the first to yoke oxen to a plow. At that time Sparta was founded by Spartacus, the son of Phoroneus.

## CHAPTER III. Joseph’s death, and the affliction of the children of Israel that immediately followed

Manitus, the eleventh Assyrian king, reigned for 30 years. It was the 347th year from Abraham’s birth and the 272nd year of the promise. Plemneus was the eleventh king of the Sicyonians. Among the Egyptians it was the reign of Ammenophis, succeeded by Neeges.

While these kings were reigning, Joseph died. After his death the people of God, growing wonderfully, remained at peace until those who had known Joseph had died. Then, because his increase was envied and regarded with suspicion, the Egyptians oppressed the Hebrews with slavery. They endured this most severe servitude for 144 years, until they were divinely delivered.

The total number of years which the Hebrews spent in Egypt is 215, counted from the time when Jacob descended into Egypt with his sons. According to the opinion of some, Prometheus lived during these times. They relate that human beings were made by him from clay. In truth, since he was wise, he transformed their savagery and extreme ignorance into humanity and knowledge, although it is not shown who the wise men of his time were.

## CHAPTER IV. Callithias, the first to exercise the priesthood at Argos; and the time when Atlas was a distinguished astrologer

Machaleus, the twelfth Assyrian king, reigned for 30 years. It was the 377th year from Abraham’s birth and the 302nd year of the promise. Criasus was the fifth king of Argos. Under him Callithias, son of Pirantus, was the first to exercise the priesthood at Argos. Orthopolis was the twelfth king of the Sicyonians; among the Egyptians it was Nuspharmitos, succeeded by Tumosis.

In these times Atlas, the brother of Prometheus, was a preeminent astrologer. Because of his learning in the discipline, he was even said to support the heavens. Euripides, however, asserts that he was a very high mountain called Atlas.

## CHAPTER V. From where Syria received its name

Iphraeus, the Assyrian king, reigned for 30 years. It was the 407th year from Abraham’s birth and the 322nd year of the promise. Among the Egyptians it was the reign of Amenopis. This is the Amenopis whom some consider to be Menon, the speaking stone.

While these kings were reigning, a native named Syrus is said to have lived; Syria was named from his name. At that time the Ethiopians also, advancing from the river Indus, settled near Egypt.

## CHAPTER VI. At what time and with which contemporaries Moses learned Egyptian philosophy

The fourteenth Assyrian king was Mamilus, who reigned for thirty years. It was the 427th year from Abraham’s birth and the 352nd year of the promise. Phorbas was the sixth king of Argos, and Orus was king of Egypt.

While these kings were reigning, Moses, as a young man, learned the whole of Egyptian philosophy. The city of Epidorus was then founded. Emon was the first king in Thessaly. Phorbas took possession of Rhodes. Hercules, as the story goes, defeated Antaeus in a wrestling match. Trochilus was the first to yoke a four-horse chariot. Xanthus founded Triopalesbus. Cidon ruled in Crete.

Some write that Prometheus, P[h]iemetheus, Atlas the brother of Prometheus, Argus the all-seeing, and Io the daughter of Prometheus lived in these times; others place them in the age of Cecrops, while some place them sixty or nine hundred years before Cecrops.

## CHAPTER VII. The time when the Athenian kingdom began; and the contest between the gods Neptune and Minerva over the name of Athens

Sparetus, the fifteenth Assyrian king, reigned for forty years. It was the 457th year from Abraham’s birth and the 382nd year of the promise. Marathius was the thirteenth king of the Sicyonians, and Troipas the seventh king of Argos. Aceneres ruled among the Egyptians.

At this time the Athenian kingdom began. Cecrops, also called Diphyes, was the first to rule in Acte, which is now called Attica, and he ruled for fifty years. From Cecrops to the first Olympiad fourteen kings are counted. Twelve of them were rulers whose reigns ended only with death; under them many marvelous events are said to have occurred among the Greeks.

Cecrops was called Diphyes either because of the length of his body or because, although he was an Egyptian, he knew both languages. This Cecrops founded Athens in Euboea, a city which they also call Diadar. The Euboeans called the city Corcomenon.

The supposed judgment of the gods, Neptune and Minerva, concerning their contest over the region, is said to have taken place before Cecrops in the following manner. As for the reason Athens was called Athens—for the name certainly comes from Minerva, who is called Athena in Greek [Ἀθήνη]—Varro gives this explanation:

“When an olive tree suddenly appeared there, and water burst forth in another place, the king was moved by these portents and sent to consult Apollo at Delphi about what they meant and what ought to be done. Apollo replied that the signs indicated the goddess Minerva and Neptune, and that it lay within the power of the citizens to decide after which of the two gods, whose signs these were, the city should be called.

“After receiving the oracle, Cecrops consulted all the citizens of both sexes. For it was then the custom in those places that women also participate in public deliberations. He summoned everyone to cast a vote. When the multitude had been consulted, the men voted for Neptune and the women for Minerva. Since the women were found to outnumber the men by one, Minerva won.

“Then Neptune, enraged, devastated the lands of the Athenians with raging sea waves, since it is not difficult for demons to scatter waters wherever they wish. To appease his anger, the same author says that the Athenians imposed a threefold penalty upon the women: that they should no longer cast votes, that none of those born should receive the mother’s name, and that no one should call them Athenians.”

Thus that city—the mother or nurse of liberal learning and of so many great philosophers, than which Greece possessed nothing more illustrious or noble—received the name of Athens from a woman, while demons mocked the quarrel between their gods, the sea-god and the female god, and the victory won through women.

The Areopagus is also said to be in that same city, where the Apostle Paul disputed with the Athenians. It was named from Mars, who is called Ares in Greek, because when he was accused of homicide, he was acquitted by six votes when twelve gods judged him in that place. Whenever the number of votes was even, an acquittal was the result rather than a condemnation.

Varro, however, maintains that the Athenians’ Neareonpagon [sic] [Note: Something appears to be missing here.] was named from Mars and the place, as though he believed it to mean “the place of Mars.” For the Areopagites are the municipal officials of that same city.

## CHAPTER VIII. The history of Moses’ birth, exposure, upbringing, and life, and of his deeds in Ethiopia and Egypt

Aschatades, the sixteenth Assyrian king, reigned for forty years. In the eighth year of his reign, Moses, after performing remarkable deeds and prodigies in Egypt, led the Hebrew people out of Egypt to the desert of Sinai at the Lord’s command. He was then 505 years from Abraham’s birth and 430 years from the promise. In the wilderness he expounded the law to them for forty years.

Thus, from the departure of the Israelite people from Egypt to Solomon and the construction of the Temple, 479 years are counted—according to the lower figure contained in the Third Book of Kings; for according to the Book of Judges the total is reckoned as 600 years.

Maratus was then king of the Sicyonians, succeeded by Echireus. Among the Argives Erotophus was the eighth king, and he had Sthenelus as his successor. During these times the Castors arose among the Argive rulers. But when Danaus expelled Sthenelus, he held Argos, and his descendants continued there until Eurystheus, son of Sthenelus and grandson of Perseus. After him the Pelopids assumed power, with Atreus the first of them to reign.

At that time Aaron, Moses’ brother, was appointed the first high priest among the Hebrews at God’s command.

I shall briefly explain who this Moses was. He was the seventh descendant of Abraham, the son of Amram, who was descended from Kohath, who was born from Levi; Levi was descended from Jacob, who was descended from Isaac, the son of Abraham.

After Joseph’s death, while the Egyptians were oppressing the children of Israel with the harshest servitude, one of their sacred scribes foretold by prophecy that a child would be born among the Hebrews who would greatly afflict and humble the Egyptians and free Joseph’s descendants from their yoke of servitude. For this reason the king, together with his Egyptians, was armed with counsels to kill all the male children of the Hebrews who were born; and they attempted to carry this out.

Oppressed by these misfortunes, the Hebrew Amram was tormented by no small anxiety. God appeared to him in a vision at night and foretold that a son would be born to him who would free his own people from such great misery, overcome the afflicted and despoiled Egyptians, and finally defeat them by drowning them in the sea, leaving the most celebrated memory of his name throughout all ages. The outcome of events proved the vision true.

Therefore, when Moses was born, his birth was concealed from the midwives with the Lord’s approval. He was thus nourished at home for three months. When his father no longer dared to conceal him, he placed him in a vessel made of papyrus and coated with bitumen, and exposed him on the river, commending him to the Lord who had foretold that he would be born.

God caused Termuth, the king’s daughter, to be at the riverbank for amusement. When she saw the vessel on the river’s edge, she ordered it to be brought to her. When she saw the child and noticed his handsome appearance, she was greatly pleased. She ordered him to be cared for and, since she had no offspring of her own, adopted him as her son.

He was handsome in appearance and ardent in intelligence, so much so that many people, admiring him, hurried to see him, abandoning their own business because they took greater pleasure in looking at him. There was great grace in him as an infant.

Termuth, who had adopted him as her son, frequently brought him to his grandfather. One day the king took him, held him to his breast, and, out of affection for his daughter, placed the crown on his head. Moses, playing like a child, seized it, threw it to the ground, and trampled it underfoot.

When that sacred scribe saw this, he cried out that this was the one whom, by God’s will, he had foretold would be born—the one who would hasten to overthrow the rule of the Egyptians unless death should overtake him first. He attacked him and decided that he must be killed. The king was slow to consent to his death, however, lest he offend his beloved daughter. Termuth scarcely managed to rescue him from their hands and save him from death.

After some time, a fierce war broke out between the Egyptians and the Ethiopians. Since they were known to be neighbors, merchants carrying goods back and forth provoked the Egyptians to quarrels and disputes. For this reason the Ethiopians, indignantly bearing these things, took up arms, ravaging Egypt and raging through it. Capturing their cities and meeting no resistance, they advanced in a frenzy as far as Memphis, the famous Egyptian city.

Driven to this extremity, the Egyptians resorted to divinations and oracles. After receiving the oracle that a Hebrew should be appointed commander of the army, with whose aid the Ethiopians would not only be driven from their borders but also subjected to Egyptian rule, Moses was chosen as commander. His superior prudence and exceptional appearance commended him.

Planning to fall upon the enemy in such a way that they would have no foreknowledge of his arrival, he led the army through the trackless regions of the desert. The difficulty of the route was increased especially by the attack of serpents, not only creeping but also flying, in the pathless parts of the desert.

Having received divine advice, Moses took ibises shut up in cages with him, for serpents greatly fear these birds. This animal is hostile to serpents. When they approach, the serpents flee; and when they attempt to hide, the ibises seize and devour them as though carried away by the breath of stags. With their aid he freed the army from the plague of poisonous creatures.

Advancing against the Ethiopians, he defeated them in the first engagement, routed them, and killed them as they fled. Since they could resist him nowhere, they withdrew to their most famous city, Saba. While they were being besieged there, and Moses was repeatedly afflicting the besieged by fighting bravely and intelligently, the daughter of the Ethiopian king fell in love with him.

Unable to withstand the force of her love, she sought his marriage through trusted attendants. Moses did not refuse, on the explicit condition that the allied citizens surrender themselves into his hands. Through the advice of the young woman this was quickly accomplished, and after celebrating the marriage Moses joined her to himself as his wife. Thus, after Ethiopia had finally been conquered, he returned in triumph to Egypt.

This success inspired his own people with confidence in their freedom and instilled greater fear in the Egyptians. They therefore sought an opportunity to hand him over to death. Moses, understanding this, considered how he might evade their ambushes. After killing an Egyptian, he was sought for execution and, scarcely escaping, fled through the most difficult parts of the desert to Midian. There he lived with the priest Jethro, whose daughter he married. While tending Jethro’s flock on Mount Sinai and enjoying communion with God, he was sent by God to Egypt for the liberation of the children of Israel.

We have excerpted these matters from the History of Josephus.

Gentile historians also wrote certain things about the same Moses, and we have thought it useful to excerpt some statements from their accounts. Pompeius, or Justin, says of him as follows:

“When the Egyptians were suffering from scabies and vitiligo, they were warned by an oracle and expelled Moses, together with the afflicted, beyond the borders of Egypt, lest the disease spread to more people. Made leader of the exiles, he stole the sacred objects of the Egyptians. When the Egyptians attempted to recover them by force of arms, they were driven by storms to return home.”

Cornelius, however, writes concerning the same matter:

“Many authorities agree that, when a plague arose throughout Egypt which disfigured bodies, King Bocchoris, after consulting the oracle of Ammon and seeking a remedy, was ordered to purify his kingdom and to send this class of people, as hateful to the gods, into other lands. After the crowd had been searched out and gathered together and abandoned in the wilderness, while the rest lay helpless and wept, Moses, one of the exiles, warned them not to expect assistance from gods or human beings, but to trust themselves to a heavenly leader, since by his aid they had driven away their present miseries.”

Thus Cornelius says that the Jews were driven into the desert because the Egyptians compelled them; afterward he carelessly adds that, through the aid of Moses their leader, they had driven their miseries from Egypt. This shows that certain deeds bravely performed by Moses were concealed.

Justin likewise asserts that Moses, expelled together with the people, stole the sacred objects of the Egyptians, and that when the Egyptians attempted to recover them by force of arms, they were compelled by storms and driven back to return home. Here he disclosed something more, even if not everything, than the other author concealed.

Therefore, if both men bore witness to that great leader Moses, their testimony is better presented from the man himself, just as the deeds and words were accomplished and spoken through him.

The historian Orosius says the following:
