“When the Egyptians oppressed the people of God—that is, the race of Joseph, by whose aid they had been saved—with servitude and tormented them by labor, and in addition compelled them by cruel authority to kill their own offspring, God ordered his people to be released as free men to serve him, through Moses as his messenger. When they resisted, he drove them on through the harshest punishments.

“Overburdened and crushed by ten plagues, they finally compelled those whom they had refused to release even to hasten away: after the waters had been turned into blood, with burning thirst bringing remedies of punishment more severe than the punishments themselves; after the loathsome filth of frogs, creeping through every clean and unclean place; after the fiery gnats, nowhere avoidable as they vibrated through the whole air; after the dog flies, running even through the inner parts of the limbs with horrible bites and inflicting tortures as grievous as they were shameful; after the sudden destruction and general slaughter of all the cattle and beasts of burden; after the boiling blisters and running ulcers, or, as they themselves preferred to say, the scabies and vitiligo erupting over their entire bodies; after the hail mixed with fire, striking down men, herds, and trees everywhere; after the clouds of locusts, which, having consumed everything, pursued even the roots of the seeds; after the darkness, dreadful in its phantoms, tangible in its thickness, and deadly in its duration; finally, after the uniform death throughout Egypt of the firstborn and the equal calamity of bereavement everywhere, those who had not yielded to God’s command yielded to his punishment.

“But soon, in the worst repentance, they dared to pursue those whom they had released and to pay the final penalties of their wicked obstinacy. Their king drove the entire Egyptian army, equipped with chariots and horsemen, against the wandering people. We can infer its number from this one argument above all: six hundred thousand men feared and fled from it.

“But God, protector of the oppressed and avenger of the obstinate, suddenly divided the Red Sea. Stretching apart its shores, he raised and suspended the sides of the rigid waters like mountains, so that the pious, drawn forward by the hope of a pathway where salvation seemed impossible, entered safely, while the impious entered a pit of unexpected death.

“Thus, while the Hebrews walked safely across the dry ground, the masses of standing water, released behind them, overwhelmed and killed the whole Egyptian multitude, together with its king. The entire province, previously tormented by the plagues, was emptied by this final slaughter.

“Even now the most certain memorials of these events remain. For the tracks of the chariot wheels are visible not only on the shore but also in the deep, as far as sight can reach. If they are temporarily disturbed by accident or by someone’s curiosity, they are immediately restored by divine power to their original appearance through winds and waves, so that whoever is not taught the fear of God by the zeal of revealed religion may be terrified by the example of his completed vengeance.”

Cecrops, whom we mentioned above, is also said to have been highly educated during the time of Moses, the leader of the Hebrew people. Moses was the first of all the prophets before the coming of the Lord and Savior to explain the divine laws in sacred writings.

Moses is found to have been older than all those whom the Greeks consider most ancient: Homer and Hesiod, the Trojan War, and, much earlier still, Hercules, Musaeus, Linus, Chiron, Orpheus, Castor, Pollux, Asclepius, Liber, Mercury, Apollo, and the other gods of the nations, as well as their sacred rites and seers, and even the deeds of Jupiter himself, whom Greece placed at the summit of divinity.

All those whom we have listed lived after Cecrops Diphyes, whom we have established as the first king of Attica. Thus, without any ambiguity, Moses and Cecrops, the first king of the Athenians, lived at the same time.

This Cecrops Diphyes was a native, under whom an olive first arose on the citadel and the city of Athens received its name from Minerva. He was the first of all to invoke Jupiter, invent images, establish an altar, and sacrifice victims—things never before seen in Greece.

The other marvels loudly celebrated among the Greeks are also found to have occurred after Cecrops. For after him came the flood under Deucalion, the conflagration under Phaethon, Erichthonius, son of Vulcan and Earth, and Dardanus, who founded Dardania. Concerning him Homer writes:

> Whom Jupiter first fathered in the heavenly citadel.

The abduction of free-born Europa also occurred, as did the rites of Ceres, the shrine of Isis at Eleusis, the grain of Triptolemus, and the kingdom of Troy, whose Ganymede, born on Ida, they wished to carry off to the stars so that he might pour the wine of the god at the great banquets.

At this time Tantalus and Tityus also lived, and Apollo was born. Latona was the wife of Jupiter in the time of Tityus, and Apollo, as they relate, was the son of Latona and Jupiter.

After these events Cadmus came to Thebes, and fathered Semele. From her came Liber, a most beautiful offspring, who, brought forth in a fitting birth, produced the appropriate fruit.

Liber and the others whom we shall soon mention lived after the two-hundredth year of Cecrops: namely Linus and Cethus, Amphion, Musaeus, Orpheus, Minos, Perseus, Asclepius, the twin Castors, and Hercules, in whose time Apollo served Admetus. After them came the destruction of the city of Troy, which Homer follows at a long interval and which occurred much later.

Homer himself is found to have lived much earlier than Solon, Thales of Miletus, and the others who with them were called the Seven Wise Men. Then came Pythagoras, who wished to be called not “wise,” as his predecessors had been, but “philosopher,” that is, “lover of wisdom.” He was followed by Socrates, who educated Plato, by whom philosophy was famously divided into its various branches. We shall insert each of these, in the order of the ensuing history, in its proper place.

In these same times such a continuous and oppressive heat blazed forth that the sun, carried along an unaccustomed path, is said to have scorched the whole world not merely with heat but with fire. The Ethiopian, who was accustomed to heat, could not endure the intensified burning, nor could the Scythian bear what was unfamiliar. From this some people, unwilling to grant God his ineffable power, devised empty rationalizations and spun the ridiculous fable of Phaethon.

Thus, as I mentioned above, in the eighth year of Scatades’ reign among the Assyrians, 430 years of the promise had elapsed, and 505 years from Abraham’s birth. Moses, now eighty years old, became leader of the Hebrews’ journey from Egypt. He governed God’s people in the wilderness for forty years, handing on to them the law given to him by God.

At that time Cradovus was the second king of the Athenians, and Amphition succeeded him. During this period the Curetes and Corybantes founded Gnoson and invented a measured, harmonious dance in arms. A musician is recognized as the son of Evethaeus and a nymph.

At this time Corinth was founded; it had previously been called Epira. According to some, Io went to Egypt and was there called Isis. Later, after marrying the Egyptian king Telegonus, she gave birth to Epaphus.

## CHAPTER IX. The murders committed by the sons of Danaus and Aegistus, the first name of Egypt, and the tyranny of Busiris in that land

Amnites, the seventeenth Assyrian king, reigned for 45 years. In the ninth year of his reign Moses died, and Joshua son of Nun led the people for 26 years, distributing the land of the Philistines by lot among the Jews. At that time Eleazar was the second high priest of the Hebrews.

Thus, from the first creation of the world to the death of Moses, the five books of his work contain 3,730 years, according to the translation of the Seventy Elders.

Danaus was then reigning as the tenth king of Argos, and Corax as the sixteenth king of the Sicyonians. Erichthonius ruled the Athenians; he was the first in Greece to yoke a four-horse chariot, although it had long existed among other nations.

While these kings were reigning, fifty murders were committed in a single night among the sons of the brothers Danaus and Aegistus. Only Lynceus escaped, and he later ruled after Danaus.

Danaus himself, the architect of so many crimes, was driven from the kingdom he had acquired through such atrocities and withdrew to Argos. There, shamefully persuaded to commit a crime, he expelled from the throne at Argos Sthenelus, who had received him as an impoverished exile, and ruled in his place.

The number of sons should not seem incredible among barbarians, since they have such innumerable marriages. Egypt received its name from the Egyptian king mentioned above; previously it had been called Aeria. At the same time Dardanus founded Dardania.

The temple at Delphi was burned by Phlegyas. At that time Busiris also lived in Egypt, the son of Neptune and Libya, the daughter of Epaphus. While exercising tyranny in the regions near the Nile, he cruelly murdered passing guests. His hospitality was that of the most bloodthirsty tyrant, and his religion was even more cruel: he offered the blood of innocent guests to the gods as participants in his crimes.

During these times—that is, from Israel’s departure from Egypt to the death of Joshua, through whom God’s people received the land of promise—the kings of Greece instituted rites for false gods. By solemn celebration they recalled the memory of the Flood and of humanity’s deliverance from it, as well as of the wretched life of those who moved sometimes to the heights and sometimes to the lowlands.

They interpret the ascent and descent of the Luperci along the Sacred Way in this manner: they say that these rites signify human beings who, because of the inundation of the waters, sought the mountain summits and, when the waters receded, returned once more to the lower places.

## CHAPTER X. Progne and Philomela, and Cathmus, king of Thebes
The eighteenth Assyrian king was Belochus, who reigned for twenty-five years. His daughter Tosa, also called Semiramis, reigned with her father for eight years. From the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt, seventy-seven years had passed. Gothoniel, the first judge of the Jews, had already been judging the people for eleven years. Thereafter he ruled for twenty-nine years, which, together with the preceding years, make forty.

The seventeenth king of the Sicyonians was Epopeus; the fifth Athenian king was Pandion; and the eleventh king of Argos was Lynceus. During their reigns, foreigners held the Hebrews subject for eight years, which, according to Jewish tradition, are joined to the period of Gothoniel. Gothoniel was a judge from the tribe of Judah.

At that time Phinees assumed the high priesthood among the Hebrews. Among the Argives, Hypermestra, daughter of Danaus, exercised the priesthood. Jupiter then united himself with Europa, the daughter of Phoenix. Afterward she was carried off by the Cretans in a ship whose emblem was a bull. Asterius—whom others call Exanthus—later took her as his wife and fathered by her Minos, Rhadamanthus, and Sarpedon.

At that time also occurred the crime of Tereus against Progne and Philomela: incest was joined to parricide, and a banquet more abominable than either was added through unspeakable food. Because the chastity of her sister had been violated and her tongue cut out, the mother killed her little son, and the father ate him. Progne and Philomela were daughters of Pandion, who was the son of Erictheus.

At that time Cathmus also ruled the Thebans. From his daughter Semele was born Dionysius, that is, Liber Pater. Under him Linus the Theban was a musician. The cities of Melus, Paphus, and Tharsus—or Thasus—as well as Calista and Bithinia, were founded.

Linus the Theban, Zethus, and Amphion became famous in the art of music; at that time they ruled the Thebans after Cathmus. In Dardania Ericthonius, son of Dardanus, reigned. They represented this Ericthonius as the son of Neptune and Minerva because he was found exposed, wrapped in a serpent, in the temple of Vulcan and Minerva, which the two possessed jointly at Athens. The serpent signified that he would become great; and because of the shared temple and his unknown parents, they declared him the son of the gods.

The events reported concerning Diana, whom they say was Isis, and concerning Danaë, from whom Perseus was born, occurred during these times. Ephira, now called Corinth, was founded by Sisyphus. Armenia was captured by Cathmus. Phoenix and Cathmus, having departed from the Thebans of Egypt for Syria, ruled at Tyre and Sidon. At this time, they say, the Idaean Dactyls were the people who discovered iron.

### CHAPTER XI. The games instituted in honor of Apollo, at the time when Hercules flourished and Dionysius revealed the vine; likewise concerning the flood under Deucalion and the conflagration under Phaethon

The nineteenth Assyrian king was Bellespares, who reigned for thirty years. From the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt, one hundred and two years had passed. Aod, from the tribe of Ephraim, was judge of the Hebrews for eighty years. Foreigners held the Hebrews subject for eighteen years; these years are counted under the same judge.

At that time musical games were instituted for Delphic Apollo, so that his anger might be appeased. They thought that the regions of Greece had been afflicted with sterility because they had not defended his temple, which King Danaus burned when he invaded those same lands in war. They were instructed by an oracle to establish these games.

In Attica, Ericthonius, son of Cecrops, first instituted games for him and built a temple. He judged that games should be held not only for Apollo but also for Minerva, where oil was first placed for the victors. They relate that Minerva was the discoverer of its fruit, just as Liber was the discoverer of wine.

Hercules, called Desanaus, is held to have been famous in Phoenicia. From that time down to our own memory, he is still called Desanaus by the Cappadocians and Elians. Yet this was certainly another Hercules, not the one whose immense and innumerable deeds are recounted.

At this time Dionysius, who was also called Liber Pater and was regarded as a god after his death, is said to have revealed the vine in the land of Attica to his host. Ericthonius, likewise the son of Vulcan and Earth, whom Homer calls Erictheus, lived during the reign of these men.

At that time Arcas, son of Jupiter and Callisto, having brought the Pelasgians under his rule, called their region Arcadia. Thus, from Deucalion, Hellen, and Pyrrha, those who had formerly been called Greeks were then called Hellenes, and Actea was called Benactica.

Regarding the flood that occurred at that time under Deucalion in Thessaly, the conflagration that occurred under Phaethon, and also the various plagues of Ethiopia that then took place, Orosius writes as follows:

Eight hundred years before the founding of the City, Amphiction, third after Cecrops, ruled at Athens. During his reign a flood of waters destroyed the greater part of the peoples of Thessaly, with a few survivors escaping to the mountain refuges, especially Mount Parnassus. Around this mountain Deucalion then held the kingship. He received those who fled to him on rafts and, once they had reached the two ridges of Parnassus, protected and nourished them.

For this reason, Greek myth relates that the human race was restored from stones, because of the innate hardness of the human heart.

At that time, Plato testifies, very many plagues and dreadful diseases raged in Ethiopia, almost to the point of desolation. And lest anyone think that the anger of God and the fury of war occurred at separate times, in that same period Liber Pater subdued India, drenched it with blood, filled it with slaughter, and polluted it with lust—although it was a people that had never been subject to any human being and was content only with its native peace.

### CHAPTER XII. Troy and Achaea founded; Triptolemus distributes grain among the cities; Hercules brings Theseus back from the underworld

The twentieth Assyrian king was Lamprides, who reigned for thirty-two years. From the departure of Israel from Egypt, one hundred and thirty-two years had passed. The eighteenth king of the Sicyonians was Laomedon. Under him Apollo, son of Latona, served Admetus in the care of flocks, and Neptune laid the foundations of the walls of the Trojans. Laomedon deceived both of them, however, because he defrauded them of the payment for their labor.

The twelfth king of Argos was Abbas. Pelops ruled in Greece, and from him the Peloponnese was named. He was the son of Pandion, and under him the mysteries of the Greeks began.

At this time Triptolemus, whom Philochorus says approached the cities in a long ship and distributed grain, gave rise to the suspicion that his ship had been a winged serpent as its emblem. Others invent that, at Ceres’ command, he was carried by winged serpents and brought grain by flying to lands in need.

Achaea was then founded by Achaeus. The story of Proserpina, whom Aidoneus—that is, Orcus, king of the Molossians—carried off, also belongs to this period. His dog, Cerberus by name and of immense size, devoured Perithous because he had come with Theseus to carry off his wife. Hercules, arriving when Theseus himself was already in danger of death, rescued him; for this reason Theseus is said to have been received, as it were, from the underworld.

At that time Boreas, son of Astreus and a Thracian, carried off Orithyia, daughter of Erictheus; myth falsely represents her as having become the wind.

According to the opinion of some, Phrixus also lived in this age. Fleeing with his sister Helle from the plots of his stepmother, he was seen to be carried through the air by a ram with a golden fleece. A ship had in fact been prepared for his flight, and its emblem was a ram. Palaephatus, moreover, asserts that the ram was the name of the man who had nourished him and through whom he was rescued.

### CHAPTER XIII. The abduction of Ganymede; Medea’s slaughter of her little children; and the beheading of the courtesan Gorgon

The twenty-first Assyrian king was Sosares, who reigned for twenty years. From the departure of the Hebrews from Egypt, the one hundred and sixty-fourth year had passed. Aod, the same as above, was judge of the Hebrews. At the same time, Erictheus was the sixth king of the Athenians; the nineteenth king of the Sicyonians was Sycion, from whom the Sicyonians received their name, whereas they had previously been called Aegialeans. The thirteenth king of Argos was Protheus, who had Acrisius as his successor.

During the reigns of these men, Melampus was recognized as a seer. In Dardania Tros ruled, from whom the Trojans were named. At Phithia the prophetess Phemonoe is said to have first sung the future in hexameter verses.

At that time Tantalus ruled the Phrygians, who had previously been called Maeonians. For Tantalus, king of the Dardanians, having carried off Ganymede, son of King Tros, in the most shameful manner, kept him in a still more disgraceful contest of rivalry, as the poet Phanocles confirms. He records that a very great war arose for this reason—or because Tantalus himself, whom the poets wish to appear as a favorite of the gods, had prepared the abducted boy for Jupiter’s lust by familiar pandering, and did not hesitate to offer even his own son Pelops at Jupiter’s banquets.

Pelops himself, who took Hippodamia as his wife, endured great struggles against the Dardanians and Trojans. Because such matters are customarily celebrated in myths, they are heard with too little attention.

At that time also occurred the hatred, adulteries, and parricides of Atreus and Thyestes, deeds hateful even to heaven. Oedipus is likewise said to have lived then: the murderer of his father, the husband of his mother, the brother of his children, and his own stepfather.

At that time Eteocles and Polynices perished in mutual attacks, so that each became a parricide.

At that time Medea, wounded by savage love, proceeded to slaughter her little children. Perseus was transported from Greece to Asia. There he subdued barbarian peoples in a severe and prolonged war and finally, as victor, gave his name to the subjected people. For the Persians were called after Perseus.

I pass over as well the matters that Palaephatus reports concerning Perseus, Cathmus, the Thebans, and the Spartans, through the inextricable recurring alternation of disasters.

The Lemnian crimes and the lamentable flight of Pandion, king of the Athenians, are also thought to have occurred at that time. The head of the courtesan Gorgon was likewise cut off. Because of her extraordinary beauty, she rendered those who looked at her incapable of reason, so that she was thought to turn them into stones; hence they invented for her a head covered with serpents.

### CHAPTER XIV. The prophetess Deborah and the transfer of the kingdom of the Argives to Mycenae

The twenty-second Assyrian king was Lampares, who reigned for thirty years. From the departure of Israel from Egypt, the one hundred and eighty-fourth year had passed. After Aod, foreigners brought the Hebrews under their authority for twenty years. According to Jewish tradition, these years are joined to the period of Deborah and Barak, who judged the people for forty years.

Deborah was a prophetess. Her prophecy concerning Christ is not very clear and requires a lengthy exposition. Deborah, of the tribe of Ephraim, and Barak, of the tribe of Naphtali, ruled the people.

The king of the Sicyonians was Polybus, while the seventh king of the Athenians was the younger Cecrops.

During their reigns, the kingdom of the Argives came to an end. It had lasted 544 years, until the time of Pelops. Thereafter, when the rule was transferred to Mycenae, Eurystheus reigned after Acrisius; he was the son of Sthenelus.

After the power of the Argives had been transferred to Mycenae, these kings succeeded one another: Perseus, Sthenelus, Atreus, Thyestes, Agamemnon, Aegisthus, Orestes, Thysamnus, Pentilus, and Cometes, down to the departure of the Heraclids.

### CHAPTER XV. The time when Ilium and Troy were founded; the golden age of Saturn

The twenty-third Assyrian king was Pannias, who reigned for forty-five years. From the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt, 214 years had passed. The eighth king of the Athenians was Pandion.

During their reign, Gideon, of the tribe of Manasseh, judged the Hebrews and served as judge for forty years. Under him the foreigners were brought under his authority for seven years.

Ilium was founded by Ilus. Amphion was ruling the Thebans; they say that by the singing of his lyre he moved rocks. His hearers, however, were hard-hearted and, so to speak, stony.

According to others, Cathmus was then ruling the Thebans.

What is recorded concerning the Spartans, as Palaephatus wrote it, since they were from neighboring regions, is that they suddenly stood against Cathmus and, because they seemed to have been gathered from every side as though drawn out of the earth, were called Sparti.

[Note: The passage at [Col. 0957D] is corrupt.]

At that time a temple was built at Eleusis, and Troy too was founded.

At that time the Laurentes ruled everywhere in Italy. Their first king was Picus, son of Saturn. They called Saturn “lord” because he taught people to cultivate the earth and to enrich it with manure so that it might produce more abundant crops; for this reason he was called Stercutius, or Sterticus.

Under him Virgil and the other learned men of antiquity write that there was a golden age, because he recalled to the plains human beings who had fled to the mountains, established them in an orderly way of life, gave them laws, and preferred to call the region Latium because, while fleeing his son, he had safely hidden there.

They also included his successor Picus among the gods because he is said to have been a distinguished augur and a warrior.

### CHAPTER XVI. Liber and his Bacchic rites; likewise Daedalus and the Sphinx, the Argonauts, and finally the Scythians, Amazons, and island of Scanza

The twenty-fourth Assyrian king was Sosarmus, who reigned for nineteen years. He was succeeded by Mitreus, who reigned for twenty-seven years. At the beginning of Mitreus’ reign, 278 years had passed since the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt.

Abimelech and Thola judged the people of the Hebrews for twenty-five years at that time. In Sicyon Inachus was king; Chareus and Thyestes ruled at Mycenae.

At this time some attribute to Liber Pater the deeds and the events reported concerning Lycurgus, Athenaeus, and Pentheus: how he stood against Perseus and was killed in battle, as the poet Dinarchus relates.

Anyone who wishes may inspect the tomb of Liber Pater himself at Delphi, beside the golden Apollo. Liber is painted in the form of a woman and with a delicate body because women served in his army when he conquered India. These women were called Bacchae, not so much renowned for their courage as for their madness.

Some writers indeed say that this Liber was defeated; others say that he was both defeated and killed in battle by Perseus. Nor do they conceal where he was buried. Nevertheless, under the name of this supposed god, Bacchic rites—or rather sacrileges—were instituted through unclean demons.

The Senate later became so ashamed of their frenzied indecency that it prohibited their celebration in the city of Rome.

During this period Perseus and his wife died. People believed that they had been received into heaven in such a way that they were not ashamed to call their images divine beings.

At that time Pandion is also said to have suffered an ambush while fleeing from the Ionians. Europa, daughter of Agenor, was likewise carried off while the kings mentioned above were reigning.

Philammon of Delphi was then held in high esteem. He was the first to establish a chorus at Pythia.

Palaephatus also records the myths concerning Daedalus, who was thought to have made moving images. He was the first of all, he says, to separate the feet of statues from one another, whereas others fashioned them joined together. Palaephatus also records how Daedalus fled from Minos by ship with his son Icarus, and, because his flight could not be traced, was thought to have flown away on wings.

At that time Orpheus of Thrace was also famous; his pupil was Musaeus, son of Eumolpus. Linus, the teacher of Hercules, was likewise renowned.

Palaephatus writes that the events related concerning the Sphinx, Oedipus, and the Argonauts—among whom were Hercules, Asclepius, Castor, and Pollux—occurred at that time. He says that the Sphinx was the wife of Cathmus and that, out of jealousy for Hermione, she withdrew from her husband and took a stand against Cathmus.

Let us now say something more about the Argonauts.

There is a river called Aquilis. Tradition relates that the ship Argo was carried to it and brought onward to the Tyrrhenian sea. The Argonauts, avoiding a powerful wind, did not use the same ship on their return voyage. Instead, crossing the sea above the Scythians, they came by these rivers to the borders of Italy and, wintering there, founded a city called Hemona.

When summer arrived, with the help of the inhabitants of the region, they dragged the Argo almost 400 stades by mechanical skill overland to the river Aquilis, which joins the Eridanus. The Eridanus has its mouth in the Italian sea. Thus they returned to their homeland.

At the same time Vesozes, king of Egypt, attempted to unite in his kingdom the southern and northern regions, which were divided almost by the whole extent of the sky and sea. He was the first to declare war on the Scythians, sending ambassadors beforehand to announce to the enemy the terms on which they must submit.

The Scythians replied to the ambassadors:

“Foolishly, an exceedingly wealthy king has undertaken war against the poor. In the reversal of fortune, this will be more fearful for him, because of the uncertain outcomes of war: there will be no rewards, but the losses are obvious. We should not wait until he comes to us; we shall go out to meet the booty ourselves.”

There was no delay, for deeds followed their words. First they compelled Vesozes himself, terrified, to flee back to his kingdom. Then they attacked his abandoned army and seized all its military equipment. They would also have devastated the whole of Egypt had they not been repelled by the marshes.

Returning immediately from there, they made Asia, which they had subdued through countless slaughters, tributary. After remaining there for fifteen years without peace, they were finally recalled by the demands of their wives, who threatened that, unless they returned, they would seek children from neighboring peoples.

Meanwhile, among the Scythians, two royal youths, Plinius and Scolopetius, were expelled from their homeland by a faction of the nobles. They led a large number of young men with them and settled on the coast of Pontic Cappadocia, beside the river Thermodon, after bringing the Themiscyrian plains under their authority. After ravaging the surrounding lands for a long time, they were slaughtered by a conspiracy of their neighbors in an ambush.

Their wives, moved by exile and widowhood, took up arms. To give everyone courage from their shared condition, they killed the men who had survived and, inflamed against the enemy, avenged the blood of their slain husbands by destroying the neighboring peoples.

Having sought peace by means of arms, they entered into relations with foreigners. They killed the male children born from these unions, but carefully raised the females, burning away the right breasts of the infants so that they would not hinder the shooting of arrows. Hence they were called Amazons.

They had two queens, Marpesia and Lampeto. Dividing their army into two parts, they alternated responsibility for warfare and the guarding of their homes.

After they had conquered most of Europe and captured a number of cities in Asia, and after they themselves had founded Ephesus and other cities, they sent home the greater part of their army, laden with the richest booty. The remainder, left to defend their rule in Asia with Queen Marpesia, was slaughtered in an encounter with the enemy.

Sinope took Marpesia’s place. She crowned her exceptional reputation for courage with perpetual virginity.

The fame of these women aroused such admiration and fear among the peoples that when Hercules was ordered by his master to bring back the queen’s arms, as though destined for unavoidable danger he gathered the entire chosen and noble youth of Greece and prepared nine long ships. Yet, not content merely to examine his forces, he preferred to attack unexpectedly and surround the women when they were unsuspecting.

At that time two sisters ruled the kingdom, Antiope and Orythia. Hercules arrived by sea and overwhelmed them while they were unprepared, unarmed, and careless because of the peace.

Among the many women who were killed or captured, the two sisters were retained: Antiope and Melanippe by Hercules, and Hippolyte by Theseus. Theseus took Hippolyte in marriage; Hercules returned Melanippe to her sister and accepted the queen’s arms as the price of ransom.

After Orythia, Penthesilea obtained the kingdom. In the Trojan War we have received the most distinguished examples of courage among men from her.

We have already shown, on the testimony of distinguished historians, that the Scythians—who were also Goths—were stirred up by the Egyptian king Nesozes not only to the misery and confusion of himself and his people but also to that of other nations. I have therefore decided briefly to clarify from which nation they first derived their origin and what settlements they inhabited.

For Claudius Ptolemy, that outstanding geographer, reports in the second book of his work:

“There is a large island in the Ocean called Scanza, situated in the Arctisalian Ocean. It stretches lengthwise like a cedar leaf, spreading broadly at its sides and enclosing itself. Pomponius Mela likewise reports that it lies in the Codanian Gulf, whose shores are washed by the Ocean.

“It lies opposite the mouth of the river Vistula, which rises in the Sarmatian mountains and, with three branches, flows into the Northern Ocean in sight of Scanza, separating Germany from Scythia.

“On the east, therefore, it has a vast lake in the bosom of the earth’s sphere, from which the river Vagus, as though generated from a kind of womb, rolls in waves into the Ocean. On the west it is surrounded by an immense sea, and on the north it is likewise enclosed by the same vast, unnavigable Ocean.

“From this Ocean, as from a kind of arm extending outward while retaining a gulf, the German Sea is formed.

“Because of the excessive cold, no swarm of honey-making bees is found there.

“In one part of the island lives the Arcthoan people, said to derive their name from Dogit. They are said to have continuous daylight for forty days and nights in midsummer; and in winter, for the same number of days and nights, they are said not to know clear light, alternating sorrow with joy.

“This occurs because, in their more extended settlements along the edge of the axis, they see the sun returning to the east. In their shorter settlements it is not seen in the same way as those living in the south are accustomed to see it. For to us the sun seems to rise from below, whereas to them it circles the edge of the earth.

“No one should regard this as incredible. Pliny, that most learned author of secular literature, testifies that the same thing occurs on the island of Thile.

“Although many and diverse nations dwell on this island, Ptolemy mentions the names of seven nations. Among them is a people called the Suchans. They use excellent horses.

“Then follows a multitude of other nations: the Theutes, the Vagoths, and the rest. Of these, the Ostrogoths are the outermost.

“From the stock of these peoples the Danes have indeed sprung. Among all the nations of Scanza, they claim for themselves the chief name because of their extraordinary height.”

From this Scanza, then, like a workshop of nations or certainly like a sheath of nations, the Goths are once said to have departed with their king, whose name was Berich. As soon as they came out from their ships and touched the land, they immediately gave the place its name. For even today, it is said, that place is called Gothi-Scanza.

Moving forward from there, they encamped near the settlements of the Ulmerugi, who at that time occupied the shores of the Ocean. They drove them from their own settlements in battle and then subdued their neighbors, the Vandals, adding them to their victories.

When the population had greatly increased, and nearly the fifth king after Berich, Philuner, son of Gadarig, was reigning, he decided that the Gothic army should move onward with its families.

While seeking suitable settlements and appropriate places, he reached the lands of Scythia, which in their language were called Oium. Delighted by the great fertility of the region, he moved half of the army across. But, it is said, the bridge by which they had crossed the river collapsed irreparably, and thereafter no one could go forward or return.

That place, as they relate, is enclosed by a whirlpool surrounded by trembling marshes; nature has made it impassable through this double confusion. Nevertheless, even today, it is possible to believe the reports of travelers that the voices of cattle can be heard there and traces of human beings detected, though those who hear them are far away.

That part of the Goths which crossed the river into the land of Oium under Philuner, having obtained the desired soil, immediately came to the people called the Spali. After engaging them in battle, they gained the victory.

From there, now as victors, they hastened to the furthest part of Scythia, which lies near the Pontic Sea. This is also recalled collectively in their ancient songs, almost in the manner of historical writing.

Ablaunis, an outstanding recorder of the Gothic people, bears witness to this in a most truthful history, and some of the ancients have agreed with his account.

Their settlements in the land of Scythia were as follows, according to the historians: first beside the Maeotian swamp, second in Mysia, Thrace, and Dacia, and third above the Pontic Sea.

While they lived in the first settlement beside Maeotis, they are known to have had Philuner as their king. In the second settlement—that is, in Dacia, Thrace, and Mysia—they had Zalmoxes, whom the historians testify to have possessed extraordinary philosophy and learning.

Most writers of annals say that they first had an educated man named Zeutes, and afterward Diceneus. This Diceneus came to Gothia when Sulla held supreme power among the Romans. Boscurta, king of the Getae, received him and granted him almost royal authority.

On his advice the Goths ravaged the lands of the Germans that the Franks now occupy.

Caesar, who was the first of all the Romans to claim imperial power for himself and who subjected almost the entire world to his authority, subduing every kingdom so completely that he even seized islands situated in the Ocean beyond our world, repeatedly attempted to subjugate the Goths but could not do so.

Gaius Tiberius, already the third ruler, was reigning over the Romans, yet the Goths remained unharmed in their own kingdom. For them it was beneficial, suitable, and desirable that whatever Diceneus, their counselor, commanded should be judged in every respect to be sought after and useful.

By introducing them to almost the whole wisdom of the philosophers, he restrained their barbarous customs. He soothed their minds with poems and various songs and made them devoted to study. Hence many poems composed by them still exist in their own language.

After Diceneus died, they had Comosicus as their wise man. Because of his skill, he was regarded among them both as high priest and king. Then they had Zalmoxes as their fourth, nor did there fail to be others who instructed them in the pursuit of wisdom.

Thus the Goths became wiser than almost all the barbarians and nearly equal to the Greeks, as Dio relates; he composed their histories and annals in the Greek style.

The Getae were praised so highly that they even say that Mars, whom the deceit of poets declares to be the god of war, arose among them. Hence Virgil says:

> “And the aged father who presides over the Getic fields.”

In the third settlement, above the Pontic Sea, they had already become more civilized and, as we said above, wiser. Their people, divided into families, were called Visigoths, who are also called Getae.

Their first concern among neighboring peoples was to bend the bow with Getic sinews, as Lucan testifies, more as a historian than as a poet. He says:

> “And string the Armenian bows with Getic bowstrings.”

They sang the deeds of their ancestors in this song, with melodies and lyres. They are likewise said to have been such men as those whom antiquity scarcely declares to have been heroes, men of astonishing renown.

As we have already indicated, Vesozes brought a disastrous war upon them. They are said to have been the husbands of the Amazons.

Eusebius in his Annals and Orosius in Book I Against the Pagans call them Scythians because they inhabited part of Scythia.

At that time there was also a most savage conflict between the Cretans and Athenians. After both peoples had been defeated, the Cretans unfortunately inflicted the bloodier victory. They cruelly dedicated the sons of noble Athenians to the Minotaur.

Whether this Minotaur was truly savage, inhuman, and cruel, as Philochorus writes in the second book of his *Attica*, is uncertain. He says that Minos’ teacher was a man named Taurus, or an unformed monster whose eyes the Greeks gouged out and whom they fattened.

Gnosius testifies that Androgeon, son of King Minos, was treacherously killed at Athens. Because of the death of his son Androgeon, Minos established a contest, offering Athenian boys as the prize. Taurus defeated everyone in the contest.

At last it happened that Theseus defeated him in the wrestling school, and for this reason the Athenians were freed from the tribute imposed upon them.

Theseus gathered the Athenians, who had previously been scattered throughout the region, into a single city. He also carried off Helen, whom her brothers later recovered after capturing Theseus’ mother.

Finally Theseus, having fled, abandoned Athens.

During those same days the Lapiths and Thessalians fought in exceedingly famous conflicts. Palaephatus, in the first book of *On Incredible Things*, reveals that the Lapiths were believed and called centaurs because, when horsemen raced about in battle, they seemed to be one body made of horses and men.

At that time Priam reigned after Laomedon. There were also then the seven strong men who fought against Thebes, and Thamyris, son of Amon, was celebrated as a distinguished figure.

### CHAPTER XVII. Carthage founded by Dido; Hercules institutes the Olympic contest and kills Antaeus, son of Earth; the ten-year Trojan War begins. When it finally ends, Aeneas, seeking other settlements, comes to Latium, and so forth.

Assyrian XXVI: Thaitthanes, for 32 years. Accordingly, from the Exodus of Israel out of Egypt there are 306 years. Airus, from the tribe of Manasseh, judged the Hebrew people and ruled over them for 22 years. After him, the Ammonites reduced the Hebrews to submission for eight and ten years, which are joined to the periods of the judges who followed—namely, Jepthah, who ruled for six years; Essebon, for seven; and Lapdon, for eight. After Essebon, according to Jewish tradition, Calabon is said to have ruled the people for ten years; he is not mentioned by the Seventy translators.

Adrastus ruled the Sicyonians, and was succeeded by Polipedes. Agamemnon was king of Mycenae, and Menestheus of Athens. At the same time Minos established laws and legal institutions. Eventually, taking up arms in Sicily against Daedalus, he was killed by the daughters of Cocalus.

Carthage was founded in Africa by Dido. At that time Hercules also established the Olympic contest; from his time until the first Olympiad 430 years are reckoned. During the same period Hercules killed Antaeus in Libya. Antaeus is called the son of Earth because he was exceedingly skilled in the art of wrestling and in contests practiced on the ground; for this reason he appeared to be aided by his mother Earth. After the death of his son, Hercules was purified with water at Athens in the rites of Ceres. After killing Iphitus, whom he unjustly slew as a foreigner and friend, Hercules fell into a wasting illness. To relieve his suffering, he threw himself into the flames on the mountain called Oeta, after accomplishing many brave and extraordinary deeds, and thus met his end at the age of fifty-two. Some, however, say that he was thirty. Among the great deeds of this Hercules they count twelve especially distinguished achievements.

While the rulers mentioned above were in power, Alexander, son of Priam, carried off Helen. The ten-year Trojan War began, and at last Troy was captured and destroyed. We read that this happened in the history of Dares and others.

Pelias was regarded at that time as the greatest of the kings of Greece, and the other kings obeyed his counsels. He had a nephew named Jason, the son of his brother. When he recognized that Jason was fierce in spirit, prudent in counsel, and vigorous in body, he became jealous of him. Therefore he sent him with an army against the Colchians, a very brave and warlike people, promising that, if Jason conquered them and brought him the golden fleece which he knew the Colchians possessed, he would make him his successor in the kingdom.

He instructed his leaders that Jason should proceed first to war with his companions, while they, leaving Jason in mortal danger, should withdraw by sea. But Jason, being exceedingly shrewd, recognized this treachery. After gathering an army, he entered the open sea with triremes and a great array of ships. As the north wind was blowing, he departed from the direct route and reached the harbor of the Trojans, where the river Simois flows into the sea.

When Laomedon, king of the Trojans, heard that the Greek army had reached his territory, he sent against them his son Priam with a strong force. Jason begged that passage be granted him so that he might travel through their territory to the Colchians without conflict with their people. They refused to agree, however, and drove him from their borders with great insult.

The Greeks, having regained a favorable wind, reached Colchis and found the inhabitants unprepared and unaware. Jason attacked them with his army, yet compelled the leaders of his grandfather Pelias to go before him into battle. He overthrew and defeated the Colchians, captured and ravaged their cities, found the golden fleece, and carried it back to Greece to his grandfather with great spoil.

When King Pelias learned what his army had suffered at the hands of the Trojans, he was enraged. He sent a strong force to afflict the kingdom of Laomedon. The Greeks then came upon the Trojans unexpectedly, laid waste their land far and wide, and carried away to Greece as a captive, together with much booty, Laomedon’s daughter Esiona, a woman of extraordinary beauty and distinction.

After some time, the kings of the Greeks gathered in Macedonia, their metropolis, for a certain festival. There were present men who had assembled there from every part of Greece: Pelias and his nephew Jason; Agamemnon and his brother Memnon; Ajax and Palamedes; Achilles, Triptolemus, Menelaus, and Polypus; Castor and Pollux; Alea, who first invented the game of tables; and the other lesser kings. They had gathered for the festival mentioned above to sacrifice to Jupiter.

When Alexander, son of Priam, heard of this, he departed from Troy, gathered a large army, boarded great ships, crossed the Mediterranean Sea, and came to the island of King Agamemnon. He approached Agamemnon’s palace, where Helena, his queen and wife, was celebrating a festival of the goddess Minerva.

Alexander, son of Priam, immediately attacked the aforementioned Helena, a queen of extraordinary beauty, and carried her off together with all her treasures and those of her husband, in revenge for his aunt Esiona, whom the Greeks were holding captive and refused to return.

When the Greek kings learned this, they took it very hard. After deliberation, they gathered from every quarter with all their equipment, crossed the sea with a prepared fleet, and came to Ilium. They asked that Helena be returned and that they be allowed to depart. The Trojans replied that they would by no means do this unless they first received Esiona, the sister of King Priam.

Since both sides were enraged, they waged extremely severe war for ten years. Priam had the following sons by his wife Hecuba: Hector, the firstborn, most distinguished and a very brave warrior; Alexander, who carried off Helen; Troilus, the third; Deiphobus, the fourth; and Achimachus, the fifth. He also had two daughters, Polyxena and Cassandra, both very beautiful.

Thus fifteen kings of the Greeks fought against King Priam, his sons, and his people, and the two sides clashed most fiercely. Hector, the bravest of the Trojans, fought four battles with his people against the Greek kings and their army. In these battles, as we read in Dares, 258,204 Greeks fell, according to the enumeration made by the Greeks themselves. Of the Trojans, 134,422 fell. Among the Greek kings, Ajax fell with three leaders.

The enormous slaughter mentioned above occurred in three battles. In the fourth, Hector killed King Palamedes. While he was stripping off Palamedes’ golden cuirass, Achilles unexpectedly arrived and, finding Hector heedless and intent upon stripping the dead man, killed him. I have not found the number of the other dead in that battle.

Thereupon Troilus armed himself to avenge the death of his brother Hector. After fighting two battles, he proved himself most courageous. In the first, Polypus, king of the Greeks, fell with two leaders, together with 40,023 of the remaining army. Of the Trojans, 25,026 fell.

Agamemnon, wiser than the other kings, was about to return to Greece with the undertaking unfinished, unless Achilles had opposed him. Achilles preferred to die rather than withdraw without avenging his people and without victory.

Accordingly, they again encouraged one another to war, and Troilus met them with the Trojans. As they fought bravely for three continuous days and nights, an innumerable multitude fell on both sides: 145,000 Greeks and 112,000 Trojans. In addition, Troilus was struck by Achilles and died. Achilles dragged his body around the city, bringing great mourning upon the Trojans.

When Hecuba, Troilus’ mother, saw this, she wished to ransom him with a great quantity of gold so that he might receive burial. Achilles, seeking Polyxena, daughter of Priam, in marriage, said that, if she were given to him, he would return the dead man’s body and make the Greeks withdraw from Troy.

While she had been promised to him, he returned Troilus’ corpse to his parents. But when Achilles went to the temple of Diana, as though he were about to receive Polyxena, Alexander ambushed him near the palace and killed him.

When Agamemnon learned of Achilles’ death, he again urged the people, with a great outcry, to withdraw from Phrygia. Triptolemus opposed him, saying, “I will not leave this place alive unless I have avenged my father’s death.”

Battle again broke out. Deiphobus, with the Trojans, met the Greek army. In that battle 115,054 Greeks fell, and 70,603 Trojans, as the people reckoned. Deiphobus was wounded by the enemy and soon died after returning to the city.

Then the king’s household members, Aeneas and Ulysses, advised their lord Priam to return Helena, adding gifts, so that the enemy might withdraw from them, since they saw themselves weakened and almost defeated. When Agamemnon heard this, he readily agreed.

Alexander, however, refused to return Helena, and his brother Achimachus further incited the people to war. When Aeneas and Antenor heard this, they were indignant. They secretly sent to the kings of the Greeks and made a pact with them: the Greeks were to spare them and everything that appeared to belong to them, while they themselves would deliver the city into the Greeks’ hands.

After receiving a pledge from the Greeks, they devised at midnight an unheard-of signal in the likeness of a horse’s head and placed it above the wall. Through their treachery the Greeks entered the city and fell upon Priam and his children, sparing none of them. They recovered Helena.

Aeneas concealed Polyxena and Cassandra in a tower of the city. Triptolemus sought Polyxena, on whose account her father Achilles had died. But when Aeneas claimed that he did not know where she was, and was caught in this lie, he was expelled from Phrygia.

Agamemnon handed Polyxena over to Triptolemus, and he slaughtered her upon her father’s tomb. Thus, after Troy had been utterly destroyed by fire and sword, Aeneas was driven from the territory of the Trojans with all his people. Seeking other settlements, he came to Latium and lived there.

Since he was a savage and exceedingly cruel warrior who spared no one, he perished, struck by a thunderbolt from God because of such great impiety.

Others, however, say that Phrygas and Aeneas were brothers: Aeneas ruled in Latium, and Phrygas in Phrygia. After Aeneas, Ascanius abandoned the kingdom of his stepmother Lavinia, founded Alba Longa, and raised with the greatest devotion his posthumous brother Silvius, the son of Aeneas and Lavinia.

Ascanius also fathered a son, Julius, from whom the family of the Julii arose. But because he was still a child and not yet capable of governing his citizens, Ascanius left his posthumous brother Silvius as heir to the kingdom.

From Phrygas there arose a people who wandered through many regions with their wives and children. They chose one of their own as king, named Francio, from whom they are called Franks, since Francio is said to have been exceedingly brave in war. After he had fought against many peoples, he directed his journey toward Europe and settled between the Rhine and the Danube.

After Francio died there, they fought many battles, in which they were worn down until only a small band of them remained. From among themselves they then appointed leaders, yet they always refused to bear another’s yoke. This, they think, is how matters stood concerning the origin of the Franks.

Others, however, assert that they originated from the island of Scanza, which is the “womb of nations,” from which the Goths and the other Teutonic peoples emerged; their language also bears witness to this. On that island there is a region which, they say, is still called Francia.

With the Lord’s favor, we intend to recount these matters more fully in the work that follows.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Samson, judge of the Hebrews; Aeneas, first king of the Latins; and after him Ascanius, etc. The story of Ulysses fleeing from Scylla is also assigned by tradition to this period as a fable.

Assyrian XXVII: Teuteus, for 40 years. From the Exodus of the children of Israel out of Egypt there are 330 years.

Samson, that exceedingly strong man, was judge of the Hebrews for 20 years—so strong that some compare his deeds with those of Hercules. They were almost contemporaries, although Hercules lived somewhat earlier.

The foreigners reduced the Hebrews to their power for 11 years. After Samson, Eli the priest succeeded him and ruled the Hebrews for 40 years, according to Jewish tradition, but only 20 years according to the Seventy translators.

At Athens Demophon, the son of Theseus, was then reigning; he was succeeded by Oxyntes. Ceuxippus was king of the Sicyonians.

While the rulers mentioned above were reigning, after the capture of Troy, the first king of the Latins—who were later called Romans—was the exile Aeneas, as we explained somewhat more fully above. From the destruction of Troy he held the kingdom of the Latins for seven years and reigned for three years.

What wars he stirred up in Italy, what battles he provoked for three years, and with what hatred and destruction he afflicted the peoples, the works of literary education attest, and the memory of our discipline also preserves these matters in common use.

He took as his wife the daughter of the Latin king, named Lavinia. By this marriage he joined the Phrygians to the Latins; and once the Phrygians and Italians had been united, they called the peoples Latins. From that time onward they ruled, although in a very poor kingdom and a narrow territory called the land of the Laurentes.

After Latinus came Aeneas and his successors, who were called Silvii and Albani—Silvii after the posthumous Aeneas and Albani after the city Alba. This posthumous Aeneas was called Silvius because, after Aeneas’ death, Lavinia, fearing the jealousy of Ascanius, secretly gave birth to him in a forest and named him Aeneas Silvius.

Ascanius, who reigned in Italy after Aeneas, abandoned his stepmother Lavinia’s kingdom and founded the city of Alba, in which he also reigned; he gave the name Albans to its people. With the greatest devotion he instructed his posthumous brother Silvius, the son of Aeneas and Lavinia, and left him as heir to the kingdom, although he had a son named Julius, from whom the family of the Julii arose. But because he saw that his young son was not yet capable of managing the government, he made his brother his successor in the kingdom.

Before Aeneas, Italy had been ruled by Latinus, by his father Faunus, by his grandfather Picus, by his great-grandfather Saturn, and by his great-great-grandfather Janus, for approximately 150 years; others assert that they ruled for 180 years.

At this time, Palefatus writes in the first book of *On Incredible Things* the matters that fables relate about Ulysses—how he escaped Scylla of Triger, who was accustomed to rob guests—and also that the Sirens were prostitutes who deceived sailors.

At this time Pyrrhus was also killed by Orestes in the temple at Delphi through the treachery of the priest Machareus. Some also say that the poet Homer was already living at that time.

## CHAPTER XIX. After the death of Eli the priest, the prophet Samuel succeeds him, and Saul is appointed the first king of the Hebrews.

Assyrian XXVIII: Thineus, for 30 years. From the Exodus of Israel out of Egypt there are 377 years.

The Athenian king was Thymoetes, who had Melanthus as his successor. Among the Latins, Posthumus Silvius, son of Aeneas, was king.

In the eighteenth year of Thineus’ reign, Eli the priest, having heard of the death of his sons and of the capture of the Ark of the Covenant by the Philistines, fell from his seat, broke his neck, and died. The prophet Samuel succeeded him and judged the Hebrew people. Under him Saul, the first king of the Hebrews, was appointed. He was from the tribe of Benjamin and reigned for 40 years.

While the rulers mentioned above were in power among the nations, the line of the Sicyonian kings came to an end. They had reigned for 862 years, from Aegialeus to Ceuxippus. After them priests of Carnius were appointed, and they ruled for 33 years. Then Caridemus was appointed priest; because he could not endure the superstitious expenses of the pagans, he fled.

Thisamenus, son of Orestes, ruled at Mycenae. At that time the sons of Hector recovered Ilium, having expelled the descendants of Antenor, while Helenus provided them assistance.

At that time, according to some accounts, the Amazons burned the temple of Diana at Ephesus. At that time also the kings of the Athenians surnamed Ericthidae ceased to rule. Their entire period, from Cecrops Diphyes to Thimothes, is found to comprise 429 years.

After them, Melanthus, the Pylian son of Andropompus, assumed the kingdom, and his son was Codrus. Together they ruled for 58 years.

When the rule of the Ericthidae had been destroyed, the kingdom of the Attic leaders was transferred to another family. This happened as follows. Xanthus the Boeotian challenged King Tymetes to single combat. When Tymetes refused, Melanthus, the Pylian son of Andropompus, undertook the combat and thereafter became king.

For this reason the Apaturia is celebrated, that is, the festival of deception, because the victory had arisen through fraud.

## CHAPTER XX. David, the first king of the Hebrews from the tribe of Judah, is appointed. Some think that Homer also flourished at this time. Codrus, king of the Athenians, and how he freed his country.

Assyrian XXIX: Dercilus, for 40 years. From the Exodus of Israel out of Egypt there are 407 years.

Samuel was prophesying among the Hebrews while Saul was reigning. In the twenty-eighth year of Dercilus’ reign over the Assyrians, David, the first king of the Hebrews from the tribe of Judah, was appointed. Under him Abiathar was renowned as high priest.

Codrus, son of Melanthus, was king of the Athenians. Among the Latins was Aeneas Silvius, although in another history it is found that the fourth Latinus Silvius was the uterine brother of Posthumus, the son of Lavinia and Melampus, and that the fifth—here placed as the fourth—was Silvius Aeneas, son of Posthumus.

In those days Theuris first ruled at Lacedaemon; similarly, Aleces first ruled at Corinth. According to some opinions, Homer also lived in these times.

How great the disagreement among the ancients concerning Homer was will become clear from what follows. Some place him before the departure of the Ericthidae. Eratosthenes places him 100 years after the capture of Troy; Aristarchus places him at the time of the Ionian migration, or 100 years afterward. Philochorus places him at the time of the Ionian emigration, during the archonship of Archippus at Athens, and 180 years after the capture of Troy. Apollodorus of Athens thinks that he lived 240 years after the destruction of Ilium.

Others held that he lived shortly before the beginning of the Olympiads—that is, 400 years after the capture of Troy—although Archilochus thought that he lived after the thirteenth Olympiad and in the five-hundredth year after the destruction of Troy.

At that time the Ionians, as exiles, withdrew to Athens, while the Peloponnesians fought against Athens. Through this Peloponnesian war the rule of the Ericthidae, that is, of the Athenians, was destroyed.

Codrus, king of the Athenians, deliberately exposed himself to be killed, unknown to the Peloponnesians, the enemies of his city. It is said that he liberated his homeland in the following way. The Peloponnesians had received an oracle that they would finally overcome only if they did not kill their king.

Codrus deceived them by appearing in the clothing of a poor man and provoking them to kill him during a quarrel. Hence Virgil says, “and the quarrels of Codrus.” The Athenians afterward honored him as a god with sacrificial rites.

## CHAPTER XXI. Two calculations of the years from Adam to Solomon and the building of the Temple: one according to Eusebius and Saint Jerome, the other according to Josephus.

Assyrian XXX: Cupales, for 38 years. From the Exodus of Israel out of Egypt this was the 342nd year.

During his reign Solomon, the glorious king of the Hebrews, was appointed. He began the Temple of the Lord and completed it with uniquely splendid magnificence in the world over a period of seven years.

The entire period from Moses and the departure of Israel out of Egypt to Solomon and the building of the Temple is calculated as 480 years, as the Third Book of Kings testifies. From the Flood to Moses there are 1,447 years; from the Flood to Adam, 2,242 years. These figures, added together—480, 1,447, and 2,242—make 4,169 years from Solomon back to Adam.

We have taken care to reconcile this calculation of the years with the *Chronicle* of Eusebius and the statement of Jerome.

Josephus, the author of the *Antiquities*, calculates the years from the building of the Temple back to Adam as follows. He says:

“Solomon began to build the Temple in the fourth year of his reign, in the second month, in the 502nd year after the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt. After 1,030 years came Abraham from Mesopotamia into Canaan; from the time of the Flood, 1,400 years had passed; but from Adam, the first-created man, to the building of Solomon’s Temple, a total of 3,102 years had elapsed.”

This little book contains the sequence of years from Abraham’s birth to the building of the Temple. I preferred to divide it—that is, from the first year of the promise to the departure of Israel from Egypt, and from that point to the building of the Temple—so that the reader may more easily retain what is narrated as having occurred in the times of each person.

Now, wearied after the immense labor of such a long journey, and turning aside into byways while the sun was moving toward the western hours, as the lengthening shadows were already advancing from the mountains, we at last came to the Temple of the Lord and obtained our desired resting place. Here we bring the second book of our work to its conclusion.

# BOOK THREE

## CHAPTER ONE. How David advanced from the life of a shepherd to the kingship and greatly enlarged it.

Because in the preceding book we marked out in their appropriate places only the names of the judges of the Israelite people or of the kings, together with the number of years during which they ruled the people, while passing over in silence the other things they did—matters repeatedly recalled to memory through continuous reading—we thought it unnecessary to repeat what is known to everyone.

David, the mightiest of the kings of this people, was chosen by the Lord from the pastures of sheep and raised to greatness through immense and varied labor. After killing the outstanding giant whom he slaughtered with youthful weapons, and after many routs of the enemy, he was soon confirmed in the kingdom. Gathering a strong band of companions, hitherto unconquered, and possessing the Lord’s strength and experience in war, he boldly attacked the city of the Jebusites.

Although the citizens, confident in the strength and height of their walls, treated him with mockery, he nevertheless immediately captured the city. He also took the citadel that towered above it, bravely and remarkably, by making the proposed leadership of the army the reward of the exploit.

Because of this courage and daring, Joab, who had first surmounted the height of the citadel, was made commander of the army. After slaughtering and driving out the Jebusites, the ancient inhabitants, David named the city Jerusalem and made it the capital of the kingdom.

After he had enlarged his kingdom with the aid of his remarkable and very brave companions, from the great river Euphrates to the river of Egypt, and had become exceedingly rich through the spoils of many kings and cities—in gold, silver, bronze, and precious stones—after many wars and the slaughter of powerful enemies, he wished to build a Temple for the Lord in Jerusalem, at the very place where Abraham had once offered his son Isaac to God for sacrifice and, by offering victims, had turned away from his city and people the sword of the destroying angel.

But God forbade him, because his right hand had been stained by wars and the blood of many. Nevertheless, God foretold that his son, who was to succeed him in the kingdom, would accomplish this work.

## CHAPTER II. The expenditures, arrangements, and order of the priests that David prepared for building the Temple of the Lord.

We shall briefly recount the expenses that he had prepared for his son’s building project, so that the son, being young and inexperienced, would not have to struggle with such matters at that time, but, finding everything prepared, might more quickly bring his father’s intention to completion.

He appointed 83,000 stonecutters and placed 500 men over the laborers. He designated 96,000 to transport the stones. He prepared much iron and bronze for the works, and cedar wood, supplied by the Sidonians whom he had commissioned; also 10,000 talents of gold and 100,000 talents of silver.

He divided these resources for the service of the Temple according to the variety of the vessels and the quality of their weights, and distributed them according to the measure of each candelabrum and lamp. He also gave gold for the table of the Presence according to the variety of its measure, and similarly silver for the other silver tables and for the other vessels, whether gold or silver, which he judged should be made individually for the work of the Temple and for whatever would be necessary.

David said: “All these things that I command to be made came to me written by the hand of the Lord, so that I might understand all the works through such models.”

In addition to these things that he had prepared, he offered 3,000 talents of gold from Ophir and 7,000 talents of the purest silver for gilding and adorning the walls.

The heads of families and nobles of the tribes, together with the king’s ministers, gave for the work of the house of God 5,000 talents of gold, 10,000 solidi, and 10,000 talents of silver, besides abundant bronze and iron. They also gave precious stones for the treasury of the house of the Lord, of which the king had previously offered a large and costly supply.

David therefore summoned all the leaders to Jerusalem, together with the priests and Levites. When he counted them, he found 38,000 Levites between the ages of thirty and fifty. Of these he appointed 12,000 as overseers of the construction of the Temple; 6,000 as judges of the people and their scribes; 4,000 as doorkeepers of the house of God; and an equal number to sing hymns to God, singing with instruments which David, a most accomplished psalmist, had instituted.

He also divided them by families. Separating the priests from the tribes, he found among them twenty-four families: sixteen from the house of Eleazar and eight from Ithamar. He commanded that each family serve God for eight days, from Sabbath to Sabbath.

Thus all the families received their lots in the presence of David, Zadok and Abiathar the priests, and all the leaders. The first family to come up was written first, the second second, and the third third, and so on through the twenty-fourth. This division continued until the destruction of the Temple under Vespasian and Titus.

He honored those descended from Moses with exceptional distinction. He made them guardians of God’s treasures and of the vessels that kings might happen to dedicate to God, and he ordered all those of the tribe of Levi, together with the priests, to serve God day and night, as Moses had commanded them.

## CHAPTER III. Solomon, how nobly he was raised to the kingdom and how richly he buried his father; as became clear when Hyrcanus, after a long time, opened his tomb and carried away countless sums of money, and Herod later did the same.

After these things he divided the army into twelve cohorts, with their commanders, centurions, and tribunes. Each cohort had 24,000 men, whom he ordered to keep watch for 300 days, from the first hour to the last, over King Solomon, together with the chiliarchs and centurions, and over the other arrangements that he had prudently and very wisely established.

While he was still alive, he appointed his son Solomon king and instructed him to serve God with a perfect heart and willing spirit. David also addressed the whole assembly that he had gathered in Jerusalem, urging them to keep the laws of the Lord with a perfect mind and to remain faithful to the commandment.

The people rejoiced with great joy, offering many victims to the Lord. They ate and drank before the Lord with great gladness, and they anointed Solomon a second time as their king.

King David also blessed the Lord in a wondrous and spiritual manner before the entire multitude. Then, full of days, he died. How worthy he was of praise and how endowed with righteousness are sufficiently shown by the Book of Chronicles and by Josephus in the seventh book of his *Histories*.

Anyone can recognize the extent of his wealth from the following. After 1,300 years, when the city was being besieged by King Antiochus, surnamed the Illustrious, son of Demetrius, Hyrcanus the high priest wished to give Antiochus money so that he would withdraw from the siege and remove his army. But since Hyrcanus had no means of accomplishing this, he opened one of the burial chambers of David’s tomb, took out 3,000 talents, and gave part of them to Antiochus. In this way he removed the severity of the siege, as we shall also indicate elsewhere.

After a long period of years had passed, King Herod likewise opened another burial chamber and carried away very large sums of money.

Accordingly, Solomon sat upon the throne of the Lord as king in place of David his father. Everyone was pleased with him, and all Israel obeyed him. All the leaders and powerful men, all the sons of King David, also gave their allegiance and submitted to King Solomon.

While David was still alive, he instructed his sons with the greatest care to obey Solomon as their lord, saying to them:

“I tell you, then, that our father Jacob had twelve sons. You know that Judah was king, and that I too had brothers, yet none of them took offense that I became king. Although the kingdom is great, if all the sons and grandsons of a king with a numerous offspring attempt to reign, they will become not kings but tyrants, not counselors of the kingdom but its destroyers.

“Therefore I urge my sons not to stir up rebellions against one another when their brother assumes the kingdom. Let them willingly accept him as their lord, since they are not serving a stranger; rather, let them rejoice in the honor of imperial authority belonging to their brother. It is an outstanding glory to be the king’s brother, when all cannot reign together.”

Thus the Lord magnified Solomon over all Israel and gave him the glory of a kingdom such as no king of Israel before him had possessed.

## CHAPTER IV. Assyrian XXXI: Laustenes, during whose time Solomon completed the Temple of the Lord with the assistance of Hyram, king of Tyre; and what writers of the two peoples have related about them.

Assyrian XXXI: Laustenes, for 45 years.

Solomon, likewise the wisest and richest of all the kings of the Hebrews, now held the Israelite kingdom, nobly enlarged by his father David. At the Lord’s prompting, he undertook to build the Temple in Jerusalem, with the remarkable support of his father’s preparations, and in the eleventh year of his reign completed all the work of the Temple. He was assisted by the friendship of Hyram, king of Tyre, especially with cedar wood and many other things.

Menander, who translated the antiquities of the Syrians from the Phoenician language into the Greek tongue, mentions these two kings, saying:

“After Abibaal died, his son Hyram succeeded to his kingdom. Although he lived for 53 years, he reigned for 34. He excavated a broad area of ground and built a golden column, which is in the temple of Jupiter. In addition, he cut timber from Mount Lebanon for the roofs of the temples. After destroying ancient sanctuaries, he built a temple of Hercules and Astarte, and first erected this temple to Hercules in the month Peritius. He also led an army against the Eucheans, who were not paying tribute; after subduing them, he returned again to Tyre.

“In his time there was a young man, the son of Abdemon, who always solved the problems proposed by the king of Jerusalem, whatever he ordered.”

The historian Dio also mentions these matters, saying:

“When Abibaal died, his son Hyram reigned. He destroyed the eastern part of the city, enlarged the city, and, demolishing the temple of Olympian Jupiter, joined the central area to the city and adorned it with golden offerings. He also climbed Mount Lebanon and cut down a great forest for the construction of sacred buildings.

“He adds that Solomon, king of Jerusalem, sent certain puzzles to Hyram, king of Tyre, and asked him to solve them, agreeing that, if Hyram could not distinguish their solutions, he would pay money. When Hyram declared that he could solve them, although he was about to suffer a considerable loss of money, the proposed problems were solved by a certain Tyrian named Abdimus. Hyram then proposed other problems; if Solomon could not solve them, he was to give Hyram a large sum of money.”

At that time Latinus Silvius held the chief power in Italy, and Alba Silvius was his successor. Ion was king of Corinth and had Egilon as his successor. Archippus then ruled the Athenians.

At the same time Ephesus was founded by Andronicus. Some also hold that Carthage was founded at that time by Chalcedon the Tyrian; others say that it was founded by Dido, his daughter. Some also say that Homer and Hesiod lived in these times.

At that time Zadok was renowned as priest of the Hebrews.

## CHAPTER V. Assyrian XXXII: Piritiabes, during whose time the Hebrew kingdom was divided and Shishak, king of Egypt, plundered the Temple of the Lord; what an educated writer among the nations also related about this.

## Chapter V

Assyrian XXXII: Piritiades, for 30 years. The forty-fourth year from the completion of the temple had now come. Here, indeed, a discrepancy arises among the historians concerning the years of Solomon’s reign: in the Books of Kings he is read to have reigned for 40 years, whereas Josephus asserts that he reigned for 80 and that the whole span of his life was 94 years.

After Solomon’s death, the kingdom of the Hebrews was divided between Rehoboam and Jeroboam. From that time onward some of the Hebrews were called Judeans, and others Israelites. Israel retained its former name, while those descended from the kings who arose from the tribe of Judah from David’s time onward were called Judeans. Hence the whole nation also received the name of Judah.

Concerning Jeroboam, Solomon’s servant, who was appointed king over the ten tribes—how he turned the people away from God and made them worship images, establishing altars on the high mountains and instructing the people to sacrifice there—and concerning Jaddun, the prophet of Jerusalem, who foretold what would happen to Jeroboam and his descendants; and also how Jeroboam was deceived by an evil old man and false prophet whom he greatly honored because he frequently told him what pleased him: anyone wishing to know these matters more fully will find them in the eighth book of Josephus.

In the fifth year of the reign of Rehoboam, Solomon’s son, Shishak, king of Egypt, fought against the Judeans and plundered the temple of Jerusalem. Herodotus of Halicarnassus also mentions this devastation. For he says:

> Since he also left behind the statues of those who surrendered without a battle, and concealed in them the sexual organs of women.

Rehoboam, however, surrendered the city without a battle. He also said that the Ethiopians had learned the circumcision of the sexual organs from the Egyptians, although it is clear that among those living in Palestine no people except the Judeans practice circumcision.

When Rehoboam died—he had reigned in Jerusalem over the tribe of Judah and Benjamin—Abijah succeeded him, and Asa succeeded Abijah. When Jeroboam, who had ruled over the ten tribes in Samaria, died, his son Nadab succeeded him.

At that time, among the Latins, Aegyptus Sylvius—also called Athis Sylvius—son of the king of Upper Alba, was king. Prunis was king of Corinth, Doristus of Lacedaemon, and Tersippus of Athens. During this period Samos was founded and Smyrna was enlarged to the form of a city. In Judea Azias, Amos, Joel, and Azariah were prophesying.

## Chapter VI

### Assyrian XXXIII: Ofrateus, during whose time the wicked king Ahab reigned over part of Israel, under whom there was Elijah. What Menander wrote about the drought of that time.

Assyrian XXXIII: Ofrateus, for 20 years. The seventy-fourth year from the founding of the temple had now come. Under him, Josaphat held the government among the Judeans; while among the Israelites, Nadab, Baasha, Elah, and Omri died in rapid succession, and Ahab held the power. With Jezebel, he was the most wicked of kings, surpassing all the wicked kings who had ruled Israel before him. His wife was far more savage and audacious than he, and she reached such extravagance and madness that she filled the cities of Israel with images and altars, polluted everything according to the rites of the nations, and, in addition, slaughtered the Lord’s prophets.

Then a certain prophet of the Most High God, named Elijah, came from the city of Tishbe in the region of Gilead and said to Ahab:

> Because God says that he will send neither rain nor dew upon this land during those years, unless he himself appears again.

After saying these things, he departed, and the Israelites suffered an extreme drought for three years and six months.
