Menander also mentions this drought in his account of the deeds of the king of the Tyrians, saying:

> And drought came upon them from the month Hyperberetaeus until another month.

When he prayed to God, many streams were poured forth. By saying this, Menander indicates that the drought occurred under Ahab.

At that time Capis Sylvius was king of the Latins—the son of Aegyptus, that is, of Athis the Elder. Carpentus Sylvius succeeded him in the kingdom. Phorbas was king of Athens, and Megacles succeeded him; Bachis was king of Corinth, and Agesilaus of Lacedaemon. In Israel Elijah and Elisha, Obadiah, Azariah, and Micah were prophesying.

## Chapter VII

### Assyrian XXXIV: Ofratenes, under whose reign Tiberinus was king of the Latins. Homer is also said to have lived at that time. Likewise Lycurgus the lawgiver, and Jehoiada, the righteous priest of the temple, who, according to sacred history, lived 130 years after Moses.

Assyrian XXXIV: Ofratenes, for 50 years. The ninety-fourth year from the founding of the temple had now come. Under him Joram, Ahaziah, Athaliah, and Joash reigned in Jerusalem. In Israel, Ahaziah, Joram, and Jehu succeeded one another in the government.

Among the Latins, Tiberis Sylvius, son of Carpentus, was ruler. The river Tiber was named after him; it had previously been called the Albula. His son Agrippa thereafter obtained the kingdom.

While he was reigning among the Latins, the poet Homer flourished in Greece, as Apollodorus the grammarian and Euphorbius the historian testify: according to them, this was in the 124th year before the founding of the city and, according to Cornelius Nepos, in the 100th year before the first Olympiad.

At the same time Elijah was taken up, and Lycurgus the lawgiver was held in high esteem as an eminent servant of Apollo. Jehoiada was also then priest of the temple. According to sacred history, he is said to have lived 130 years after Moses. He was righteous and worthy of all reverence, and he was buried in Jerusalem among the royal tombs because he restored the rule of David’s house.

At that time the Thracians also gained control of the sea.

## Chapter VIII

### Assyrian XXXV: Acrazapes, during whose reign Zechariah, the prophet and son of Jehoiada the priest, was killed between the temple and the altar. At that time Sylvius Romulus also established a stronghold among the hills where Rome now stands.

Assyrian XXXV: Acrazapes, for 42 years. The 164th year from the construction of the temple had now come. Joash reigned over the part of Judea, and Amaziah succeeded him. In Israel, after Jehu’s death, Jehoahaz and Joash reigned one after another. Diognetus was king of Athens, Eudaemon of Corinth, and Aremulus Sylvius of the Latins.

While these were kings of the nations, Zechariah was priest and prophet. The Lord mentions him in the Gospel. By the command of King Joash, he was killed between the temple and the altar. After the death of the priest Jehoiada, Zechariah had saved Joash from death, secretly raised him in the temple, and made him king.

That same king abandoned concern for divine religion, and with him the leaders of the people were likewise corrupted with respect to the lawful rights of the Law. Therefore the Lord sent prophets to them to testify that they should turn away from the wickedness of such deeds. Joash, however, not only failed to repent and turn from his iniquity; he even ordered Zechariah, the son of the high priest Jehoiada, to be stoned to death in the temple, forgetting his father’s benefactions.

When the Lord appointed that Zechariah as a prophet, he stood in the midst of the crowd and urged both the people and the king to practice justice, warning that they would suffer great punishments if they refused to obey God’s commands. As he was dying, he called upon God as witness to his sufferings, because he was cruelly and violently put to death for giving good counsel and for the services his father had rendered to King Joash.

The prophet Elisha also died at that time. Some say that Carthage was founded during this period. Sylvius Aremulus, or Remulus, son of the preceding king Agrippa, established a stronghold of the Albans among the hills where Rome now stands; he was struck by lightning because of his impiety. His son was Julius Proculus—the Julius Proculus who, migrating to Rome with Romulus, founded the Julian family.

## Chapter IX

### Assyrian XXXVI: Thonos Concoloros, whom the Greeks call Sardanapalus, who was more corrupt than a woman. For this reason he was despised and overthrown by Arbaces, commander of the Medes, and the Assyrian kingdom collapsed together with him.

Assyrian XXXVI: Thonos Concoloros, whom the Greeks call Sardanapalus, for 20 years. The 186th year from the founding of the temple had now come. Azariah, also called Uzziah, was king of the Judeans, and Roboam was king of the Israelites. Phereclus was king of Athens, succeeded by Ariphron. Aristemedes was king of Corinth, and Aventinus Sylvius king of the Latins.

Aventinus was the elder son of Aremulus, and he gave his eternal name to the hill that is now part of the city. During this period the poet Hesiod flourished, and Pheidon discovered the standards of measures and weights for the Argives. The first Olympiad was established by the Greeks, and a lamb spoke in Egypt. In Judea Hosea, Amos, Isaiah, and Jonah were prophesying.

Sardanapalus, king of the Assyrians, was a man more corrupt than a woman. Among crowds of prostitutes, dressed as a woman, he worked purple wool with a distaff. His prefect Arbaces, who at that time governed the Medes, saw him and regarded him with disgust. Soon Arbaces summoned the peoples of the Medes to war against him. Sardanapalus was defeated and threw himself into a burning pyre.

From that point the kingdom of the Assyrians passed to the Medes. History reports that until then there had been kings of the Assyrians. From Abraham’s birth to the end of this kingdom there are altogether 1,197 years. The total years of the Assyrian kingdom, counted from the first year of King Ninus, are 1,240.

After destroying the Assyrian empire, Arbaces transferred the kingdom to the Medes. It is said that in the intervening period—that is, until Dejoces became king of the Medes—affairs were conducted without rulers, and that during this interval the Chaldeans in particular prevailed. Separate successions of their kings are also reported. The remaining peoples likewise used their own kings.

## Chapter X

### Median I: Arbaces, during whose reign Hosea, Isaiah, Amos, and Jonah prophesied. Like springs, they burst forth into prophecy when the first Babylon fell and the second began to arise—that is, Rome, under whose rule Christ was born.

Arbaces was the first to reign over the Medes, for 28 years. The 206th year from the construction of the temple had now come. Under him Azariah, also called Uzziah, was still reigning over part of Judea.

In Israel, after Roboam, there had been Zachariah for a few days, and then Shallum, whom Menahem succeeded. Tespicus, son of Ariphron, was king of Athens when the Assyrian kingdom was destroyed. Procas Sylvius was king of the Latins; he was the son of the previously mentioned King Aventinus. Alexander was king of Corinth, Talchamenes of Lacedaemon, and Catanus was at that time the first king of the Macedonians.

Hesiod was also held in high esteem at that time, as Porphyry maintains.

## Chapter XI

### Median II: Sosarmus, during whose reign the first Olympiad began, the kings of Lacedaemon and Corinth died out, and the kingdom of Lydia began. At that time the tyrant Phalaris justly punished the originator of a most wicked invention in Sicily. The holy prophets also began to preach the salvation of the nations.

Median II: Sosarmus, for 30 years. The 234th year from the founding of the temple had now come. Joatham reigned over part of Judea, and Pekah over the Israelites. In Pekah’s fifteenth year the first Olympiad also began to be named. From it until the captivity of Troy, 405 years are reckoned.

Iphitus, son of Praxonides, or of Emon, first established that Olympiad, in which Coroebus of Elis was victorious. The Eleans were accustomed to hold a five-year contest, with four intervening years completed, during which they appointed those annual rulers.

Aeschylus, son of Agamestor, was then ruler of the Athenians. From this time the history of the Greeks is believed to be reliable, for earlier writers produced differing accounts according to their individual opinions.

Amulius was king of the Latins. After expelling his brother Numitor, he held power over the kingdom, which he had wrongly acquired. Agamestor was king of Athens, and Aeschylus succeeded him. Cyrus was king of the Macedonians.

At that time Bogorus established laws for the Egyptians; some say that under him the lamb also spoke. The Lacedaemonians adopted the laws of Lycurgus. In those same days the kings of the Lacedaemonians and Corinthians died out. The kingdom of Lydia began, with Ardis as its first king.

At that time the Sicilian Phalaris was ravaging the Agrigentines after seizing the tyranny. Cruel in mind and even more cruel in his inventions, he committed every outrage against the innocent, yet eventually found someone whom he could justly punish despite his own injustice.

A certain bronze-worker, seeking the tyrant’s friendship, thought that a gift suited to his cruelty would be appropriate. He made a bronze bull and fitted a door into its side, through which condemned people could be confined. When the prisoner inside was roasted by fires placed beneath him, the hollow bronze amplified the sound of his voice and produced a fitting, deathly murmur from the image, so that in that wicked spectacle the bellowing seemed to be that of an animal rather than the groaning of a human being.

Phalaris embraced the work but hated its maker, and turned it into an instrument both of vengeance and of cruelty. He punished the craftsman with his own invention.

At that time the greatest war between the Peloponnesians and the Athenians was also fought with all their strength and determination. Mutual slaughter finally forced them to withdraw from one another as though defeated and to abandon the war.

At the same time the peoples of the Amazons and the Cimmerians produced great and widespread slaughter in Asia through sudden incursions.

In those days the Lacedaemonians fought the Messenians for twenty years with unremitting fury because the Messenians had rejected their maidens during a solemn Messenian sacrifice. In doing so, they entangled all the strength of Greece in their own ruin.

After they had been exhausted by a ten-year siege, and after hearing the complaints of their wives, who protested against their prolonged widowhood and the danger of childlessness and threatened to seek intercourse with neighboring men unless their husbands returned, the Lacedaemonians were moved to action. Yet, so that they would not be recalled, they sent back to Sparta certain men chosen from the army and permitted them promiscuous intercourse with all the women.

It should nevertheless be understood that Sparta is the same city as Lacedaemon, and that the Lacedaemonians are therefore called Spartans.

While fighting the Messenians with cruelty, although victory often hung in the balance, they eventually overcame them. They then turned their weapons against the Athenians. For a long time the battles were varied and severe, and victory remained uncertain; at last, with the outcome still undecided, both sides withdrew.

Such was the fury of the Spartans that, although involved in two wars, they did not refuse to undertake a third.

At that time, after the innumerable kings of the Laurentian region in Latium—the Sylvii and the Albans, who had ruled in that part of Italy for 300 years, though in great poverty—King Amulius made his brother Numitor’s daughter, named Rhea and also called Ilia, a Vestal virgin.

When she was found to be pregnant, she tried to excuse her crime by falsely claiming that she had been violated by Mars. After she gave birth to twin boys, the king ordered them to be exposed.

The infants were exposed, crying, beside the bank of the Tiber. Faustulus, the king’s shepherd, carried them to his wife Laurentia. Because of her beauty and her sexually rapacious and profitable body, she was called Lupa, “the she-wolf,” by her neighbors. Hence the bedrooms of prostitutes are called *lupanaria*.

The twins were raised among the other shepherds. When they grew up, they gathered a band of robbers and shepherds, killed Amulius at Alba, restored their grandfather Numitor to the kingdom, and avenged their mother, who had been buried alive according to the law as punishment for sexual misconduct.

Thus, as kingdoms passed away and arose, a new order came into being.

## Chapter XII

### Median III: Madidus, during whose reign the ten tribes called Israel were transferred to the mountains of the Medes, and the Cuthaeans, who are called Samaritans, were settled in their place in their region. Romulus, after killing his grandfather and his brother, founded Rome. The Erythraean Sibyl also lived at this time and prophesied openly about Christ.

Median III: Maditus, for 40 years. The 264th year from the founding of the temple had now come. While Maditus ruled the Medes, Achar reigned over the Judeans, and his son Hezekiah succeeded him. Among the Israelites, another Pekah reigned, and Hoshea succeeded him.

During those times the prophets mentioned above were active, namely Amos, Isaiah, Micah, and Hosea. Jonah and Joel are added to them when Joatham, who succeeded Uzziah, was already reigning. I have not been able to find the dates of these two prophets in the canonical books.

These prophets burst forth together like springs of prophecy when the Assyrian kingdom came to an end and the Roman kingdom began. Just as Abraham appeared at the beginning of the Assyrian kingdom, when the promises were made most openly—namely, that in his seed all the nations would be blessed—so, at the beginning of the Western Babylon, under whose imperial rule Christ was to come, those promises foretold through the mouths of the prophets were to be fulfilled, not only through those who spoke but also through those who wrote.

Although prophets had almost never been lacking among the people of Israel from the time when kings first began to exist, they had served only their own people and not the nations. When prophetic Scripture began to be composed more openly, so that it might one day benefit the nations, it was appropriate that this should begin when the city that would rule the nations was being founded.

Alemeon was then king of the Athenians, Thyrimmas of the Macedonians. Hesiod and Aristotle are also remembered as having lived at that time.

In the fifteenth year of Maditus’s reign, the first captivity of the ten tribes of Israel took place under Sennacherib, also called Salmanassar, king of the Chaldeans. They were transferred to the mountains of the Medes.

Samaria was ruled for 240 years, seven months, and seven days from the time when the other tribes separated from the house of David and the tribe of Judah. From the time when they obtained that province under the leadership of Joshua, 947 years had passed.

Some also report that the Erythraean Sibyl prophesied at that time. Varro states that there were several Sibyls, not one. This Erythraean Sibyl composed certain clear verses about Christ, which blessed Augustine translated from Greek into Latin. He showed that the order of the letters at the beginnings of the verses formed the words **JESU CHRISTE, THEOS, SOTER**, that is in Latin, “Jesus Christ, Son of God, Savior.” These verses, whose initial letters produce the meaning just mentioned, were translated as follows:

> The sign of judgment: the earth will grow wet with sweat.  
>   
> From heaven the King will come, destined to remain through the ages,  
>   
> Present in the flesh, assuredly, to judge the world.  
>   
> Hence the unbelieving and the faithful will behold God,  
>   
> The Most High, with the holy ones, at the end of the age itself.  
>   
> Then souls will be present with the flesh, which he himself will judge,  
>   
> When the uncultivated world lies in dense thorns.  
>   
> They will cast away images of men and all wealth as well.  
>   
> Fire will burn up the lands, the sea, and the heavens.  
>   
> Seeking out the gates of gloomy hell, he will break them open.  
>   
> For to all holy flesh a free light will be given,  
>   
> But the guilty he will consume with eternal flame.  
>   
> Then, revealing hidden deeds, each person will speak,  
>   
> And God will disclose secret hearts to the light.  
>   
> Then there will also be mourning, and all will gnash their teeth.  
>   
> The sun’s radiance will be taken away, and the chorus of stars will perish.  
>   
> The heavens will be dissolved, and the moon’s splendor will pass away.  
>   
> He will cast down the hills and raise the valleys from below.  
>   
> Nothing among human affairs will remain lofty or high.  
>   
> The mountains will already be level with the plains and the blue waters of the sea.  
>   
> All things will cease; the shattered earth will perish.  
>   
> Likewise the springs will boil, and the rivers with fire,  
>   
> And then the trumpet will send forth a mournful sound from above,  
>   
> Across the world, lamenting the wretched crime and its varied sufferings.  
>   
> And the earth, splitting open, will reveal Tartarean chaos,  
>   
> And here, before the Lord, all kings will be brought to stand together.  
>   
> Fire and a river of sulfur will fall from heaven.

Some writers, however, have said that the Erythraean Sibyl lived not under these rulers, as we have stated, but at the time of the Trojan War.

Eumeleus was then recognized as a Corinthian versifier. In Sicily Syracuse was founded, and likewise Catana. As we mentioned, the Lacedaemonians were waging war against the Messenians, and Messene was captured by them.

Thales of Miletus, a natural philosopher, was then recognized. He is said to have been one of the Seven Sages and to have been the first among the Greeks to investigate natural philosophy. Thales also produced successors. He investigated the nature of things and strengthened his arguments by committing them to writing. He was especially admired because, having mastered the calculations of astronomy, he was able to predict eclipses of the sun and moon.

Nevertheless, he thought that water was the principle of things, including all the elements of the world, the world itself, and whatever appears to exist within it. Yet, after contemplating the world, he placed nothing in this work above the divine mind, which we behold as so marvelous.

At that time the magistrates who had governed the Athenian state until their deaths also ceased to exist, and for ten years the Athenians maintained the customary system of magistracies. After the aforementioned magistrates, Carobs, son of Aeschylus, was the first to rule with them.

The island of Aradis was then inhabited, and Gizaecus was founded.

In the ninth year of Maditus, and the 414th year after the destruction of Troy, during the sixth Olympiad—which was customarily celebrated at Elis, a city of Greece, in its fifth year after four intervening years had been completed—Romulus and his brother Remus, whom we have said were raised among shepherds, gathered a multitude of shepherds and robbers and began the buildings of the Roman city. The younger brother, who had killed his brother, ordered that the city be called after his own name.

Romulus immediately stained the kingdom of the city with fratricide. With a similar success of cruelty, he endowed the Sabine women, whom he had seized and joined to the Romans in disgraceful marriages, with the blood of their husbands and parents.

Thus Romulus first killed his grandfather Numitor, then his brother Remus; he seized power and established the city. He dedicated his grandfather’s kingdom, his brother’s walls, and his father-in-law’s temple with blood, and gathered a band of criminals by promising them immunity.

For the protection of the new city, a rampart seemed sufficient. When Remus criticized its narrowness, he leaped over it and was killed at his brother’s command. He was certainly the city’s first victim.

Romulus had made an image of a city rather than a city, but inhabitants were lacking. There was, however, a nearby place, and he made it an asylum. Immediately an extraordinary multitude of people flowed together: Latins and Etruscan shepherds, Phrygians from overseas who had come under Aeneas, and Arcadians who had come under their leader Evander. From these various elements he gathered one body and thus formed the Roman people.

When marriages with neighboring peoples were requested and could not be obtained, they were taken by force. During a simulated equestrian festival, the Sabine maidens and women who had come to watch became booty. This immediately became the cause of war.

The gates were betrayed to the Sabines by the maiden Tarpeia. Once the enemies had been admitted within the walls, a savage battle took place in the forum, so that Romulus could scarcely stop the shameful flight of his men.

At last the women who had been carried off intervened, their hair torn loose from mourning, and peace was made with Tatius and a treaty concluded. Yet as soon as Romulus had taken the aged Tatius into partnership in the kingdom—Tatius was occupied with honorable and dutiful concerns—Romulus killed him.

The Veientes were then driven away and put to flight; the town of the Cennenses was captured and destroyed; and the king carried off rich spoils from the king Argon Feretrius. The maiden Tarpeia, mentioned above, was crushed beneath the shields of the Sabines. From this the Tarpeian Hill received its name; the Capitol now stands there.

From that time onward there were ceaseless struggles, and both foreign and civil conflicts, always severe in proportion to the available strength.

Romulus established the following constitution for the state. The young men were divided into tribes and, mounted and armed, kept watch against sudden wars. The conduct of the state, however, was entrusted to the elders, who, on account of their authority, were called “fathers,” and on account of their age formed the senate. From the people he selected a thousand men to stand ready and armed at his side. Hence they were called *milites*, “soldiers,” from *mille*, “a thousand,” just as *senatores*, “senators,” came from the elders, and *Quirites* from the *curiae*.

Romulus himself was lifted up by the head of a goat near a marsh and disappeared without ever being seen again. At the urging of Proculus, he was named Quirinus; nevertheless, some say that he was deceived by the Senate because of his harsh disposition.

At the same time Sennacherib, king of the Chaldeans, sent Assyrian settlers to guard the territory of the Israelites. They became imitators of the Judaean law and were called Samaritans—a term expressed in Latin as “custodians.” More precisely, they are called Euthaeans (*Euthaei*; cf. the heading’s *Cuthaei*), from a certain river Eutha, which is in the province of Pesida, from which the king had made them migrate to Samaria.

## Chapter XIII

### Median IV: Cardicas, during whose reign Numa was king of the Latins and established many vain and superstitious practices.

Median IV: Cardicas, for 13 years. The 304th year from the construction of the temple had now come. Under him Hezekiah reigned in Judea. The ten tribes called Israel had already been led into captivity.

Perdiccas was king of the Macedonians, Hippomenes of Athens, and Leocrates succeeded him. Numa, also called Pompilius, became king of the Romans after Romulus. He waged no war against neighboring peoples.

He added two months to the year, January and February, whereas previously only ten months had been established among the Romans by Romulus. He also built the Capitol from its foundations. He was a man especially devoted to religious rites, and he taught the sacred ceremonies and the entire worship of the gods. He set down the offices of the pontiffs, augurs, and other priests, as well as certain secret pledges of imperial power, and established Janus with two faces.

He was the first to entrust the hearth of Vesta to virgin women for tending, so that, as an image of the guardianship of the empire, a flame might keep watch over the heavenly stars.

He was so deceived by vanity that, at the devil’s prompting, he wrote down many things which he later recognized would cause great harm if they became known to humanity. Because he feared burning them, he secretly hid them underground beside his own tomb, where he believed no one would come.

In the course of time, while a certain countryman was farming in that place, his plow tore up the writing. He brought it to the praetor, and the praetor brought it to the Senate. When the Senate saw it, it recoiled in extreme horror and disgust, and committed it to the flames, burning it so that such a great diabolical crime would not come to human knowledge through curiosity.

The war fought at Tyria between the Lacedaemonians and the Argives is also now believed to have occurred. The Sibyl who is also called Erophila was held in high esteem at Samos. Nicomedia was founded at that time; it had previously been called Astacus. Isaiah and Hosea were prophesying during this period.

## Chapter XIV

### Median V: Dejoces, under whom Manasseh was led captive to Babylon and, through repentance, deserved to be released. Tullius was king of the Romans, and established many institutions contributing to the state’s dignity. Cities were also founded at that time.

Median V: Dejoces, for 54 years. The 317th year from the founding of the temple had now come. While Manasseh was reigning over part of Judea, he was led captive to Babylon and bound in iron chains. He is said to have repented, and his song of repentance is also read.

Afterward he returned to the kingdom. Condemning his former sins and repenting, he gave thanks to God, who heard his prayers and rescued him from the greatest afflictions. He then led an exemplary life, yet left his extremely wicked son Amon as his successor.

At that time Absander was king of Athens, and Erixias succeeded him. After the kings had ceased and magistrates had been established, nine noblemen were chosen to preside over the city of Athens and conduct the state. Argacus was king of the Macedonians.

Tullius Hostilius was king of the Romans; the kingdom was voluntarily granted to him in honor of his virtue. He established the whole system of military discipline and the art of warfare. He was the first of the Roman kings to use the purple and the fasces. By encompassing the surrounding valley, he enlarged the city and added the Caelian Hill.

After training the young men, he brought war against the Albans. For a long time the opposing sides endured uncertain hope and defeat; at last, through the brief encounter of the three pairs of twins, there came a most disastrous conclusion and a doubtful outcome.

When peace was again broken, Mettius Fufetius of Fidenae, who was plotting war and had also been suspended because of his treachery, paid the penalty for his double-mindedness with a divided body, as chariots dragged him in opposite directions.

At that time Cyzicus was founded, and Locri in Italy. In Lacedaemon, barefoot performances are said to have been held for the first time. The musicians Archilochus, Simonides, and Aristoxenus were held in high esteem. The lawgiver Zaleucus was celebrated with frequent praise, while Cypselus exercised tyranny at Corinth. Byzantium was then founded, as was the city of Histria in Pontus.

## Chapter XV

### Median VI: Phraortes, under whom Josiah was king of the Judeans, and Ancus Martius of the Romans.

Median VI: Phraortes, for 24 years. The 371st year from the founding of the temple had now come. Under him Josiah began to reign over part of Judea. He cut down the sacred groves, expelled the idols of the nations from his kingdom, and worshiped the God of heaven with complete devotion.

He also burned human bones upon the altar that the wicked Jeroboam had built for the subversion of Israel. Thus he fulfilled what had been prophesied about him by Jaddun, the man of God from Judah, when Jeroboam was offering sacrifice.

Philip was then king of the Macedonians, and Ancus Martius of the Romans. Ancus was Pompilius’s grandson through his daughter. He added the Aventine and Janiculum hills to the city, enclosed the city with walls, and built a bridge over the Tiber where it flowed into the city.

On the seacoast, thirteen miles from the city, at the very boundary between the river and the sea, he founded the city of Ostia.

According to some, Thales of Miletus, the celebrated natural philosopher, lived in those days. In Judea Jeremiah, the woman Huldah, and Zephaniah were prophesying.

The musician Terpander was also held in high esteem. Greece first made use of the oracle at Dodona. The Athenian poet Myrtheus was then known, and Draco is also said to have been a lawgiver at that time. The city of Epidaurus was founded; it was later called Dyrrhachium.

## Chapter XVI

### Median VII: Cyaxares, during whose reign Josiah, king of the Judeans, was killed, the Judeans were oppressed by various calamities, and their kings suffered an unhappy fate between the Egyptians and Babylonians. Tarquinius Priscus was king of the Romans; he increased the Senate and devised many distinguished and honorable institutions through which the dignity of imperial power is displayed.

Cyaxares VII of the Medes, [reigning] 32 years. From the building of the Temple, however, 395 years. At that time Josiah was king of the Jews. When he engaged Necho, king of the Egyptians, he was killed. He was succeeded by Jehoahaz, whom Necho bound and led away to Egypt. [Col. 0984D] After the wars against the Babylonians, Necho appointed his elder brother by the same father, named Joakim, in his place as king; he was also called Eliakim, and imposed tribute upon the province.

Accordingly, when Joakim was entering the eighth year of his reign, Nebuchadnezzar came with a great army against the Jews. He had taken all Syria from the hand of Necho, king of Egypt, whom Nebuchadnezzar had also defeated in battle near the Euphrates and had driven from Assyrian dominion, subjecting it to himself. Fearing this Nebuchadnezzar and his threats, and desiring to maintain peace, Joakim paid him the tribute he had ordered for three years. In the third year, however, he did not pay it, deceived by the hope of an Egyptian war. For he had heard that the Egyptians were going to fight against the Babylonians again, but the Egyptians did not dare undertake this at all.

Nebuchadnezzar therefore came again with a great army against the Jews, and Joakim received him under the terms of the treaty. When the king of Babylonia had entered the city, however, he in no way kept faith: he killed the strongest young men of Jerusalem together with King Joakim, whom he also ordered to be thrown unburied outside the walls. Others who held positions of honor he led captive to Babylon. Among those taken away was the prophet Ezekiel, still a boy.

He appointed Joakim’s son king over the entire province, a decision of which he soon repented. For he feared that, remembering the wrong done in the killing of his father, he might invade his province. Sending an army, he besieged King Joakim in Jerusalem. The latter obtained from them an oath that neither he nor the city would suffer any harm. The king of Babylonia did not keep it, however, but ordered his commanders to take captive all the young men who were in the city, together with the craftsmen, and to bring them bound to him. All of these numbered 10,832, along with Joakim, his mother, and his friends, whom he kept in custody after they had been brought to him.

He appointed Joakim’s uncle, named Zedekiah, king, taking an oath from him that he would guard the province for him, undertake no hostile action, and not support the Egyptians.

We have reported these matters according to Josephus’s account. Eusebius and the writers of our own times, however, relate them as follows: In the third year of Joakim, Nebuchadnezzar captured Judea and made it tributary. After bringing many Jews under his authority, and having seized part of the Temple vessels, he made Eliakim tributary and returned victorious to his own people. He took boys of royal descent with him to Babylon and, after making them eunuchs, handed them over to the school, together with the other nobles whom he had plundered from various nations, so that they might learn all the wisdom of the Chaldeans. Among them Daniel, Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael were held in high renown.

At that time Philip was king of the Macedonians, Sadyattes of the Lydians, and Tarquinius Priscus of the Romans. Although he was of overseas origin, Tarquinius sought the kingship and received it voluntarily because of his ability and refinement, since, being descended from Corinth, he mingled Greek intelligence with Italian practices.

He also enlarged the majesty of the Senate in number and increased it by three centuries, although Accius Naevius, a most eminent man in augury, forbade the number to be increased. The king asked him, as a test, whether something he had conceived in his mind could be accomplished. Having examined the matter by augury, Naevius replied that it could. The king said to him: “This is what is at issue: whether a razor can cut that skin.” The augur replied, “It can,” and cut it. From that time the augurship was sacred among the Romans.

Nor was Tarquinius more ready in peace than in war. With frequent campaigns he subdued the twelve peoples of Etruria. From them came the fasces, the trabeae, the curule insignia, the rings, the phalerae, the military cloaks, and the bordered togas; from them came the practice of celebrating a triumph in a golden chariot drawn by four horses, the embroidered togas, and the palm-embroidered tunics. In short, all the honors and insignia by which the dignity of imperial power is conspicuous were adopted from them.

He also built the Circus at Rome, increased the number of senators, established the Roman games, constructed the walls and sewers, and was finally killed by the sons of Ancus, the king whom he had succeeded.

## CHAPTER XVII

Astyages VIII of the Medes: during his reign Jerusalem was captured and the Temple burned. The Jews were led captive to Babylon. The great courage of Nebuchadnezzar, and the remarkable deeds he accomplished by valor and action, are briefly recorded. What writers among the nations also said about him. Accordingly, since the kings of Babylon were men of extraordinary courage, the question arises why the number of years is reckoned according to the kings of the Medes. Also concerning the sufferings of the prophet Jeremiah; why he went unwillingly down to Egypt; and how he foretold the devastation of Egypt. Also concerning Pythagoras and the seven wise men of the Greeks who lived in those times.

Astyages VIII of the Medes, [reigning] 38 years. From the building [Col. 0986B] of the Temple, however, 427 years. Acropus was king of the Macedonians, and Alyattes of the Lydians.

In the eighth year of Astyages, the Jews were taken captive from Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Babylonians. The city was captured in the eleventh year of King Zedekiah, in the fourth month, on the ninth day. The Babylonian commanders captured it; the siege seemed to have been entrusted to them by King Nebuchadnezzar, who himself was staying in the city of Arabatha.

When the city was captured, Zedekiah immediately escaped by flight. The Babylonian commanders, pursuing and capturing him in the desert together with his wives and sons, brought him to the king at Arabatha. When Nebuchadnezzar saw him coming to him, he began to call him impious and unfortunate, and forgetful of his oath, because, after receiving from Nebuchadnezzar the kingship that he had taken from his brother and given to him, Zedekiah seemed to have acted hostilely toward his generous benefactor.

Using these words, he ordered that Zedekiah’s sons and friends should immediately be put to death, while Zedekiah himself and the other captives looked on. Then, having put out Zedekiah’s eyes and bound him, he led him away to Babylon.

Everything else was proclaimed in agreement by the prophets: how the city would be devastated and Zedekiah himself led captive to Babylon. Ezekiel, however, differed on this point, saying that Zedekiah would not see Babylon, whereas Jeremiah had said that the king of Babylon would lead him there in chains.

These things that Jeremiah and Ezekiel prophesied came to pass: Zedekiah was captured and brought to the king of Babylon; he would speak to him with his own mouth and see the king’s eyes, as Jeremiah said; but after being blinded and led to Babylon, he did not see it, as Ezekiel had foretold.

The Babylonian king then sent the commander of his army, Nebuzaradan, to Jerusalem to plunder the Temple. He ordered him to burn it, to level the royal buildings and the city to the ground, and to lead the people away to Babylon.

When Nebuzaradan came to Jerusalem in the eleventh year of King Zedekiah, he overturned the Temple and carried away the golden and silver vessels of God, as well as the great cup that Solomon had placed in the Temple, and also the bronze columns and their capitals, the golden tables, and the lampstands. After taking these things away, he also burned the Temple, at the beginning of the fifth month, in the eleventh year of King Zedekiah, in the eighteenth year [Col. 0987A] of Nebuchadnezzar. He burned the royal buildings as well and destroyed the city.

The Temple was thus burned 370 years, six months, and ten days after it had been built; from the departure of the people from Egypt, 1,062 years, six months, and ten days had passed. From the Flood to the devastation of the Temple, the entire period was 1,957 years, six months, and ten days.

From the creation of Adam to the events that befell the Temple, there were 3,513 years, six months, and ten days. Such, therefore, was the total number of years.

This people remained under kings—from Saul and David and those who first assumed rule over the Jewish nation—for 532 years, six months, and ten days. Under the judges it remained for more than 500 years after the death of Moses and the leader Joshua.

This is how matters stand according to Josephus’s account. According to the reckoning of others, however, the Temple was burned in the 435th or 442nd year from its construction.

Nebuchadnezzar was therefore a man of such great courage that Magestenes, in the fourth book of his *Indian History*, attempts to demonstrate that this king surpassed Hercules—who was eighth in courage and greatness. For he says that Nebuchadnezzar devastated the cities of Libya and Iberia.

Diocles, moreover, mentions this king in the second book of his *Colonial Histories*. Philostratus, in his histories of India and Phoenicia, says that this king besieged Tyre for three years, when Joathabula was king of Tyre. From the spoils of his enemies he lavishly adorned the temple of Bel and the other buildings, bestowed further additions upon the ancient city, and surpassed what had existed before, so that the besiegers were in no way able to divert the river or prevail against the city.

He erected three colonnades within and three outside, strengthening them suitably with baked brick and adorning them with great magnificence. Near his father’s royal buildings he constructed other royal structures, whose extent and remaining beauty I believe it unnecessary to describe. Yet this should be known: although these buildings were great and exceedingly splendid, they were completed in fifteen days.

In these royal buildings he set stones resembling a mountain, planted various trees, and made a gate that was called hanging. In this way various peoples preserved the memory of this king.

Since the Babylonian kings were so powerful and famous, the question arises [Col. 0987D] why they are not included among the number and succession of illustrious kings. We know that the Assyrian kingdom, founded in Babylon by Semiramis, the wife of Ninus, remained there for a long time, down to Sardanapalus. After Sardanapalus was killed, the Assyrian kingdom was transferred to the Medes by Arbaces, prefect of the Medes, and the kings of the Medes are transmitted by historians in the succession and number of kings until the kingdom was transferred to the Persians.

Therefore, if the Assyrian kingdom was transferred to the Medes and retained with them, as the histories make clear, anyone who wishes to know what the Babylonian kingdom was should recall that Ninus occupied Asia and the entire East as far as the borders of India, while his wife also subjected the Ethiopians and other nations to the Assyrian kingdom.

From this it is evident that when Arbaces descended upon the Medes, he seized the greater part of the kingdom and its dignity and retained them in Media. The Chaldeans, however, claimed Babylon for themselves against the Medes. Thus the power of Babylonia belonged to the Medes, but the ownership of the kingdom belonged to the Chaldeans.

Because of the ancient dignity of the royal city, the Chaldeans preferred to call the kingdom not by their own dignity but by that of the city. Hence it happened that Nebuchadnezzar and the other kings after him, down to Cyrus and Darius—who destroyed the kingdom of the Chaldeans and the city of Babylon—are read of as famous under the name of Babylonia, although they were powerful through the strength of the Chaldeans.

Indeed, I now recall that the blessed apostle Peter rightly called Rome “Babylon” in his writings, since at that time Babylon in the East had become the first capital of the world and remained unshaken down to Sardanapalus. After his death it lost most of its power, but the Chaldeans retained part of the kingdom and claimed Babylon for themselves against the Medes.

At that time Proca, the grandfather of Rhea Silvia, who was the mother of Romulus, began to reign. The histories of the Latins begin with him. From him the seed of Rome was sown, although its shoot had not yet appeared. Babylon, however, was finally overthrown by King Cyrus at the time when Rome was first freed from royal domination by Tarquinius.

Under one and the same correspondence of times, the one fell in the East and the other rose in the West. The former, as though dying, left an inheritance after suffering the domination of foreigners; the latter, reaching maturity, recognized itself as heir and even rejected the arrogance of its own people. Then the power of the East died, and the empire of the West arose. For this reason Rome is rightly called Babylon by the Apostle.

Nebuzaradan, the commander of Nebuchadnezzar’s army, who burned the Lord’s Temple and caused its vessels and the great cup made by Solomon to be carried away from Jerusalem to the king of Babylon together with the people, left certain remnants of the people in Judea to cultivate the land and pay tribute to the king. He placed Godoliah over them.

At that time Godoliah was killed by Ishmael, who was of royal descent. The Jews who had remained, fearing the Babylonians because of the killing of Godoliah, who had been appointed governor by the Babylonians, took the prophet Jeremiah—unwilling and protesting—and, together with his disciple Baruch, dragged him down with them to Egypt.

Vaphres was then king of the Egyptians. The prophet Jeremiah, who had begun to prophesy in the thirteenth year of King Josiah, continued until the city and Temple were devastated, proclaiming through prophecy what was going to happen to that people. He gave his prophecies, written in a book, to the people to read.

For this reason he suffered many evils from the Jews: he was beaten and afflicted with chains. With King Zedekiah’s permission, the princes also brought the prophet out of prison and lowered him into a certain pit full of mud, so that he might be suffocated and die there. He remained sunk in the mud up to his throat and lived in these hardships. He was freed, however, by one of the king’s servants, a man honored with high office who was of Ethiopian birth.

While Jeremiah was staying in Egypt, at God’s command he foretold to the people the captivity that would come upon Egypt, how captives would be led away to Babylon, and how others would be slaughtered by them in their own country.

These things were indeed fulfilled in the fifth year of the captivity of Jerusalem. After Nebuchadnezzar had subdued the Ammonites and Moabites, he proceeded to Egypt and overthrew it. He killed the king who was then ruling and appointed another in his place; he again led the Jews captive to Babylon.

Thus the people of the ten tribes fell through the Assyrians from Samaria, when Uzziah was reigning over them. Then the multitude of the two tribes, after Jerusalem had been captured by Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Babylonians and Chaldeans, was devastated.

For when Salmanasar transported the Israelites, he established in their country a people that had previously lived in the inner region of Persia and Media. At that time they were first called Samaritans, taking their name from the province in which they appeared to live, whereas previously they were called Euthaeans, after the river beside which they dwelt.

When the Babylonian king led the two tribes into captivity, he did not cause another people to inhabit their province. Therefore all Judea, Jerusalem, and the Temple remained desolate for seventy years.

The entire period from the captivity of the Israelites to the transportation of the two tribes was 130 years, six months, and fifteen days.

No faithful person can doubt that the remarkable events we read of Daniel and his companions before King Nebuchadnezzar took place at that time, nor that the things that happened to Nebuchadnezzar were foretold to him by the holy Daniel.

In those times, when contestants competed in the games, a *tragus* was awarded as the prize—that is, a goat—from which, they say, tragedians received their name.

Alcman and Stesichorus were held to be distinguished poets. Pittacus of Mytilene, who was one of the seven wise men, engaged in combat with Phraenon of Athens, formerly a Phoenician, and killed him.

Solon established for the Athenians, over whom he presided, new laws based on the old laws of Draco, except for those concerning bloodshed.

The seven whom antiquity celebrates as wise were these: Thales of Miletus, Pittacus of Mytilene, Solon of Athens, Chilon of Lacedaemon, Periander of Corinth, Cleobulus of Lydia, and Bias of Priene.

All seven were called wise. They became famous after the theological poets because they expressed certain nobler moral precepts in concise sayings.

They left no literary monuments for posterity, except that Solon gave certain laws to the Athenians, as I have said, while Thales was a natural philosopher and left books containing his doctrines.

Pythagoras of Samos, from whom they also say that the name of philosophy arose, and who is said to have been the inventor of the art of arithmetic, is reported to have flourished at the same time. For previously those who seemed to excel others were called “wise men”; but when this man was asked what profession he followed, he replied that he was a philosopher—that is, a student or lover of wisdom—because to profess oneself wise seemed excessively arrogant.

At the same period the woman Sappho became famous in a different kind of poetry. Pherecydes, a writer of histories, and Xenophanes, a natural philosopher, are held to have been inventors of tragedy [the printed wording is uncertain]. Simonides was renowned as a lyric poet. Anacreon of Bericus was then held to be a distinguished poet.

Hipparchus and Hippias exercised tyranny at Athens. At that time Harmodius and Aristogiton killed the tyrant Hipparchus. When Leena, a prostitute and their companion, was tortured in order to force her to betray her associates, she cut out her own tongue with her teeth.

At that time Pythagoras, a distinguished natural philosopher and philosopher, was celebrated.

The Roman Servius Tullius took over the reins of government at this time. His low birth did not prevent him, although he had been born to a slave mother. For Tanaquil, the wife of Tarquinius, had generously educated him because she had perceived his exceptional character, and a flame appearing around his head had promised that he would become famous.

After Tarquinius’s death, with the queen’s support, Servius was substituted in the king’s place. Although the kingship had been obtained by deceit, as though only temporarily, he managed it so skillfully that he seemed to have acquired it lawfully.

Under him the Roman people were entered into the census, organized into a military class, and then distributed among curiae and collegia. Through the king’s supreme prudence the state was so ordered that all estates, dignities, ages, and distinctions of trades and offices were recorded in registers; thus the greatest state was contained with the diligence of the smallest household.

In those days there was also an eclipse of the sun, which Thales had previously predicted. At that time Alyattes and Astyages fought.

Anaximander of Miletus, a natural philosopher whose teacher was Thales of Miletus, was also recognized then. He investigated the nature of things and was especially admirable because, having grasped the principles of astronomy, he was able to predict eclipses of the sun and moon. Nevertheless, he thought that such was the principle of things, and that from it came all the elements of the world, the world itself, and what is described in the corrupt text as existing [reading uncertain]—that is, from moisture.

His student Anaximander succeeded him and changed his teacher’s opinion concerning the nature of things. He did not think that each thing arose from one substance—that is, from moisture, as Thales held—but from its own proper principles. He believed that the principles of individual things were infinite, that they generated innumerable worlds, and that whatever arose in them, as well as the worlds themselves, was sometimes dissolved and sometimes generated anew.

[Note: [Col. 0989D] The passage is corrupt.]

How much each was driven by the Argives, after the one who had been under Archemerus. For the gymnastic contest, which they call the *pantathene*, was then held.

## CHAPTER XVIII

How Cyrus the Persian destroyed the empire of the Medes and defeated his uncle Astyages in war; how he overthrew Babylon, divided the river Gyndes into 460 channels, and, marching against Lydia, captured King Croesus. Finally, after accomplishing many brave deeds, he perished in Scythia with his entire army. Under him the Jews were released from captivity. At that time Tarquinius, surnamed Superbus, ruled as king of the Romans; and how he was expelled because of his tyranny and arrogance, and the Romans at the same time cast off royal power with him.

Cyrus the Persian destroyed the empire of the Medes, which had stood for approximately 258 years. After overthrowing Astyages, his maternal uncle, he was the first to reign over the Persians, for 30 years.

How the kingdom passed from the Medes to the Persians should, I think, be explained. Astyages, the last king of the Medes, lacking male offspring, had Cyrus, his grandson, born among the Persians. As soon as Cyrus grew to adulthood, he assembled a Persian force and challenged his uncle to battle.

Astyages, having forgotten the crime he had earlier committed against Harpalus—when he killed Harpalus’s only young son, served him to his father at a banquet, and, so that fortunate ignorance might not conceal anything from the most wretched bereaved man, insulted the father by displaying the child’s head and hands as the meal—entrusted the supreme command of the war to Harpalus himself. Harpalus immediately handed over the army he had received to Cyrus through treachery.

When Astyages learned this, he seized his forces and marched against the Persians himself, renewing the battle with greater intensity. He declared to his men that anyone who attempted to withdraw from the battle would be put to death by the sword.

Because of this necessity, the Medes fought resolutely. When the Persian line was again put to flight and began gradually to retreat, their mothers and wives came out to meet them and begged them to return to battle. When they hesitated, the women lifted their garments and exposed the shameful parts of their bodies, asking whether the men wished to flee into the wombs of their mothers or wives.

Ashamed by this deed, they returned to battle and, making an attack, compelled those whom they had been fleeing to flee themselves. Astyages was then captured. Cyrus took nothing from him except his kingdom and placed him in command of the Hyrcanian people. He himself did not wish to return to the Medes.

This was the end of the empire of the Medes. The cities that had been tributary to the Medes, however, defected from Cyrus, and this became the cause and origin of many wars for him.

At that time the captivity of the Jews was in progress, lasting seventy years. Daniel and Ezekiel were prophesying in Babylon.

After Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Babylonians, had died, his son Evilmerodach assumed the empire. He was succeeded by his brother Belshazzar. Daniel interpreted for this Belshazzar the writing that had appeared on the wall, signifying that his empire would be transferred to the Medes during his lifetime. It is not burdensome to explain how this occurred.

Cyrus, king of the Persians, whom I mentioned above for the purpose of explaining the history, was then ranging through Asia, Scythia, and the entire East with arms. At the same time Tarquinius Superbus, whether as king or enemy of Rome, was oppressing Rome either by servitude or by war.

Cyrus, as I have said, after subduing all those against whom he had marched, attacked the Assyrians and the Babylonian people, and their city, then the wealthiest of all. His attack, however, was intercepted by the river Gyndes, the second greatest in size after the Euphrates.

One of the king’s horses—[variant: horsemen]—outstanding in whiteness and beauty, had been persuaded to cross with confidence. The river, whose whirlpools rose above the obstructing shallows, seized, swept away, and drowned it.

The angry king decided to take revenge upon the river, declaring that the river which had now swallowed a splendid horseman should be left passable even to women, with the water scarcely reaching their knees.

Because this task delayed him, he spent an entire year diverting the river Gyndes through great trenches and cutting it into 460 channels. By this work he also diverted the Euphrates, far more powerful and flowing through the middle of Babylon, through the channels dug by the excavators. He made it passable by fords and by broad sections of its bed, and captured the city.

That a city could have been built by human labor or destroyed by human strength was almost equally incredible to mortals. Many have reported that Babylon was founded by the giant Nimrod and restored by Ninus or Semiramis.

The city, visible from every side across the level plain and situated in an exceptionally fertile region, was laid out like a camp, with equal walls forming a square. The strength and size of its walls are scarcely credible to describe: they were fifty cubits wide and four times that height, while their circuit extended for 300 stadia.

The wall was joined with baked brick and intervening bitumen. A broad ditch outside, flowing around it like a river, surrounded the front of the walls. There were 100 bronze gates.

The width of the city, extending to the completion of the battlements, contained on both sides, equally arranged, dwellings for its defenders, separated by an intervening space and divided into squares. Within were houses in four double rows, remarkable for their threatening height.

And yet that great Babylon, that first city founded after the restoration of the human race, was soon overcome, captured, and destroyed with scarcely any delay.

At that time Croesus, king of the Lydians and famous for his wealth, came to aid the Babylonians. He was defeated and hastily fled back to his kingdom.

After Cyrus invaded Babylon as an enemy, overturned it as a victor, and organized it as king, he transferred the war to Lydia. There he easily defeated the army, already terrified by the previous battle, and captured Croesus himself. After capturing him, he granted him both his life and his property.

These matters have been reported partly according to Orosius’s history.

According to Josephus’s tradition, however, the following account is given concerning the successors of Nebuchadnezzar and the destruction of Babylon. After Nebuchadnezzar’s death, his son Almilmapadachus succeeded him in the kingdom. He released Jeconiah, king of the Jerusalemites, who was also called Joakim, from his chains, received him among his close friends, and granted him many gifts.

For his father had not kept faith with Jeconiah, who had voluntarily surrendered himself, together with his wives, sons, and entire family, for the sake of his city.

When Amilmapadachus died after eighteen years of reign, his son Egesarius held the supreme power for forty years. After Egesarius’s death, the empire passed to his son Naborsadachus. When Naborsadachus had held it for nine months, he died, and it passed to Belshazzar, who was called Naboar.

Against this king, Cyrus, king of the Persians, and Darius of the Medes encamped. While they were besieging him in Babylonia, a remarkable portent is said to have occurred.

Belshazzar had not used the vessels of God which his father had carried from the Jerusalem Temple to Babylon and placed in his own temple. Belshazzar, however, driven by pride, decided to use them as drinking vessels while, cheerful at a banquet with his concubines and royal friends, he was heated with wine. In this way he blasphemed God.

Then he saw a hand coming from the wall and writing certain letters on the plaster. The rest, exactly as it happened, is truthfully written in the Book of Daniel.

While the city was being besieged, Belshazzar himself and the city were captured by Cyrus, king of the Persians, who fought against him with the greatest determination.

The same Belshazzar, grandson of King Nebuchadnezzar, reigned eighteen years. We understand that this was the end of Nebuchadnezzar and of Babylon.

Darius, the son of Astyages, who destroyed the rule of the Babylonians, was sixty-two years old when Babylon was invaded together with his kinsman Cyrus. He was known by another name among the Greeks. Taking the prophet Daniel with him, he brought him to Media and raised him to the highest honor [variant: celebrated him].

Daniel was one of three satraps whom Darius appointed over 360 satraps. There is no doubt that under Darius the events Daniel left in his writings took place: namely, what he suffered from the envious, and what he was permitted to know in advance, at the Lord’s prompting, concerning the kingdom of the Greeks or Persians and other matters.

According to Josephus, in the first year of the reign of Cyrus, king of the Persians, the seventieth year of the captivity of the Jews was completed.

When Cyrus read the prophecies of Isaiah and learned among the prophet’s proclamations what the Lord had foretold about him, and when he marveled at the name of the Lord God, a certain impulse seized him to fulfill the generous prophecy.

For he found it written that the Lord had said: “I desire Cyrus, whom I have appointed king over many great nations, to send my people back to their own land and rebuild the Temple.”

Isaiah had proclaimed these words 170 years before the destruction of the Temple.

Cyrus released nearly 50,000 Jews from captivity and sent them back to Judea. They built an altar and laid the foundations of the Temple. When neighboring peoples hindered the work, it remained unfinished until the time of Darius; only the altar remained standing.

The entire period of the captivity of the Jews is reckoned as seventy years. According to some, these years are counted from the third year of Eliakim to the twentieth year of Cyrus, king of the Persians.

According to others, they extend from the thirteenth year of Josiah, king of the Jews, under whom Jeremiah began to prophesy, to the first year of the aforesaid King Cyrus. The seventy years of the Temple’s desolation, however, were completed under King Darius.

Among the Hebrews who then went up to Judea from captivity, the high priest Jesus, son of Josedech, and the leader of the nation, Zerubbabel, were held in high renown.

The aforesaid Cyrus, elated by the successes of his recent campaigns, waged war against the Scythians. Their queen, Thamyris, who then ruled the people, could have prevented him from crossing the river Araxes, but allowed him to cross, first because of her confidence in herself, and then because of the advantage provided by the river, in which the enemy could be enclosed.

Cyrus therefore entered Scythia and pitched his camp some distance from the river he had crossed. Moreover, he prepared a stratagem: he abandoned the camp, furnished with wine and provisions, as though he had been terrified and fled.

When the queen learned this, she sent one-third of her forces and her adolescent son to pursue Cyrus. The barbarians, as though invited to a banquet, were first overcome by drunkenness. Soon Cyrus returned, and all of them, together with the young man, were slaughtered.

Thamyris, having lost her army and son, prepared to soothe the grief of a mother or queen with the blood of her enemies rather than with her own tears. She feigned distrust and despair because of the disaster inflicted, and by gradually withdrawing lured the proud enemy into an ambush.

There, after arranging an ambush among the mountains, she destroyed 200,000 Persians together with the king himself. Above all, the event was made remarkable by the fact that not even a messenger survived to report so great a disaster.

The queen ordered Cyrus’s head to be cut off and thrown into a wineskin filled with human blood. She rebuked him without any womanly softness, saying: “Satisfy yourself with the blood for which you thirsted, you who for thirty years remained insatiable.”

At that time the Carthaginians were sacrificing utterly impious victims—human beings—and consequently experienced the Lord’s anger severely.

After they had long fought unsuccessfully in Sicily, they transferred the war to Sardinia and were defeated there even more disastrously. For this reason they ordered their commander Mazeus and the few soldiers who had survived to go into exile.

When the exiles sought pardon through ambassadors and were rejected, they surrounded their homeland with war and siege.

At that time Mazeus, the leader of the exiles, encountered his son Cartalo, a priest of Hercules, who came toward him dressed in purple as though mocking him. Mazeus hung him on a cross before the eyes of his country, just as he was, in his purple robe and priestly fillets.

A few days later he captured the city itself. After killing many senators and ruling with bloodshed, he was killed.

## CHAPTER XIX

Cambyses, the second king of the Persians, forbade the rebuilding of the Temple in Jerusalem and conquered Egypt in war. Magi succeeded him; Darius exposed their audacity, destroyed their deceptions, and himself became king. He ordered the Temple of the Lord to be built, a work begun under Cyrus, and by his command it was completed.

Cambyses, son of Cyrus and the second king of the Persians, [reigned] seven years. They say that this Cambyses was called the second Nebuchadnezzar; under him the history of Judith was written, in which she killed Holofernes.

Cambyses prevented the rebuilding of the Temple and city of the Jerusalemites, a work that had already been hindered by the neighboring peoples. After conquering Egypt, he abominated the entire religion of the Egyptians and abolished its ceremonies and temples.

[Col. 0994D] After him two brothers, both prominent, reigned for one year, according to Josephus; others say that they reigned for seven months.

These men, who were magi, ruled under the name of their king, whom they had killed. They had dared to usurp the kingdom, but were soon discovered and overthrown. Their audacity was revealed by this fact: the magi were found with their ears cut off, although in all other respects they resembled the son of Cambyses whom they had killed. Cambyses, who hated the magi, had ordered their ears to be cut off.

In these days Hyppicus, a writer of poems, and Xenophanes, a natural-philosophical writer of tragedies, were recognized; Simonides was renowned as a lyric poet, and Phocylides was held in high esteem. At that time Anacreon of Bericus was regarded as a distinguished poet.

Hipparchus and Hippias exercised tyranny at Athens. At that time Harmodius and Aristogiton killed the tyrant Hipparchus. When Leena, a prostitute and their companion, was forced by torture to betray her associates, she bit off her own tongue.

At that time Pythagoras, a distinguished natural philosopher and philosopher, was celebrated.

Darius was one of those who had restrained the audacity of the magi by the sword. By the unanimous consent of all, he was made king of the Persians, and reigned for 36 years.

In his second year the captivity of the Jews was completed, as had been foretold through the prophets. The prophet Zechariah is a contemporary witness to this, saying: “Lord almighty, how long will you not have mercy on Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, which you have scattered?” This is the seventieth year.

Thus permission to build the Temple had its beginning under Cyrus. Because of the obstacles that existed, as we have said, it remained unfinished until the reign of King Darius. In the second year of his reign, it was built by Zerubbabel and Jesus, and in the fourth year the work of construction was completed by them.

Josephus says that the Temple was completed in seven years by the aforesaid men. This was the ninth year of the reign of King Darius. The last prophets were then prophesying: Haggai, Zechariah, and one of the Twelve who is called Malachi among the Jews.

This will be the end of the third book of our work, which contains the period from the first building of the Temple under Solomon to its second rebuilding under Darius: according to some, 512 years; according to Josephus’s account, 440 years.

# BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0995]

# CHAPTER ONE

**Darius, the fourth Persian king, made war on the Scythians, subdued Asia and Macedonia, and fought the Athenians on the plain of Marathon, where he lost two hundred thousand of his army and, defeated, fled back to Persia.** [Col. 0995B]

Darius, therefore, son of Hydaspes, who was the third Darius among the Persians, reigned for thirty-six years. He brought this war chiefly against Antyrus, king of the Goths dwelling in Scythia, because he had not obtained the marriage with his daughter that he had sought for himself. Clearly, for the desire of one man, an immense necessity exposed seven hundred thousand men to the danger of death. For, entering Scythia with an unbelievable apparatus and six hundred thousand armed men, and with the enemy refusing to grant a regular battle, while sudden attacks tore apart the rear of his forces, he feared that his return might be blocked by the destruction of the bridge over the river Hister. Having lost eighty thousand soldiers, he fled back in panic, although he did not count this number of the dead among his losses; and what scarcely anyone would have dared to seek as an acceptable possession, he did not perceive as lost. From there he attacked and subdued Asia and Macedonia. He also defeated the Ionians in a naval engagement. Then, when the Ionians had helped his opponents against him, he attacked the Athenians and directed his arms against them.

Moreover, when the Athenians learned that Darius was approaching, although they had requested assistance from the Lacedaemonians, they knew that the Persians were being detained by the leisure of a four-day religious observance. Taking hope from this opportunity, they marched out onto the plain of Marathon with only ten thousand citizens and one thousand auxiliary Plataeans, against six hundred thousand enemies. [Col. 0995D] Miltiades commanded them in that war. Relying more on speed than on strength, he advanced with sufficiently lively haste and closed with the enemy before they could repel him with the unhindered discharge of their arrows. There was such a difference in the manner of fighting in that war that on one side men seemed prepared to kill, while on the other they seemed like beasts prepared to die.

Two hundred thousand Persians fell at that time on the plain of Marathon. Darius felt this loss, for, defeated and put to flight, he seized his ships and fled back to Persia. When he was preparing to renew the war and planning to take vengeance on the victors, he collapsed amid the preparations themselves.

# CHAPTER II

**During his reign, Brutus and Collatinus were established as the first consuls among the Romans after the expulsion of the kings; and the events that took place among the Romans in those days are described, as well as the fact that the laws of the republic were administered for two hundred and forty-three years under kings, then for four hundred and sixty-four years by consuls, tribunes, dictators, and again consuls.**

At that same time, after the expulsion of the kings, the Romans had Brutus and Collatinus as their first consuls; the dying matron Lucretia had entrusted her vengeance to them. Immediately they transferred authority to those same champions of their liberty, though with a change of law and title, and from a single power a double authority was established, lest it be corrupted by isolation or delay. They called them consuls instead of kings, so that they would remember that they ought to consult for their fellow citizens.

But the magnitude of the evils that the Romans endured through that uninterrupted domination of kings for two hundred and forty-three years was shown not only by the expulsion of one king, but also by their hatred of the royal name and power. Brutus, therefore, the first consul among the Romans, who strove not only to equal Romulus, the first founder and king of Rome, in parricide but even to surpass him, brought forward his two adolescent sons and an equal number of young brothers of his wife, the Vitellii, accused of favoring the recall of the kings. He had them beaten with rods and struck with the axe, so that he plainly seemed, as a public father, to have adopted the people in place of his children. [Col. 0996D]

From that point the free Roman people first took up arms against foreigners for liberty, then for their borders, afterward for their allies, and finally for glory and empire. Thus Porsenna, king of the Etruscans and a most powerful supporter of the royal name, was bringing Tarquin back by force. He appeared before the city with immense forces and pressed hard against its very entrances. Having occupied the Janiculum for three continuous years, he terrified, enclosed, and besieged the trembling city. [Col. 0997A] Had the enemy Mucius not driven him away by his steadfast endurance in burning his own hand, he would soon have captured the city, or, with the king restored, it would have been subjected to perpetual slavery.

That same Mucius, the bravest of the Romans, attacked the king by ambush in his own camp. But when, having missed his blow, he was seized near the king’s head, he thrust his hand into the burning fire and increased the terror by deception: “O,” he said, “so that you may know what sort of man you have escaped: three hundred of us have sworn the same oath.” Having done this, he remained undaunted, while the king trembled as though it were his own hand that was burning.

Indeed, one of the maidens given to the king as a hostage, Cloelia [Al.: Clylia], escaped her guards and boldly crossed her native river. Thus, terrified by so many and such great examples of courage, the king withdrew. The Tarquins nevertheless continued fighting until Brutus killed the king’s son Arruns with his own hand, and then died over him from a mutual wound. [Col. 0997B]

After the kings had been driven from the city, Rome scarcely maintained its authority as far as the fifteenth milestone. For after the kings, consuls began to exist under Brutus; afterward tribunes of the plebs and dictators held the public authority, and again consuls, for approximately four hundred and sixty-four years, until Julius Caesar, who first seized sole power.

At that time Valerius, the colleague of Brutus, died so poor that he was buried at public expense. When a census was conducted at Rome, one hundred and twenty thousand persons were found. Thus, in the ninth year after the expulsion of the kings, a new dignity was created: the dictatorship, together with a master of the cavalry who would obey the dictator. The first dictator was Largius [Al.: Marcus Valerius], and the master of the cavalry was Spurius Cassius. [Col. 0997C]

At that time the historiographer Hellanicus, the philosopher Democritus, Heraclitus, surnamed “the Obscure,” and Anaxagoras the natural philosopher were held in renown. Pythagoras died, and Aeschylus was recognized as a writer of tragedies. At that time also occurred the war fought at Marathon, as I mentioned earlier, and the deeds recorded concerning Miltiades and Aristides are said to have taken place.

At Rome the maiden Pompilia [Al.: Porphyria], caught in adultery, was buried alive. Anaxagoras, therefore, a student of Anaximenes, perceived a divine mind as the maker of all the things we see, and said that everything consists of infinite matter, composed of particles similar to one another, through which each individual thing was made from its own proper particles, but by the action of a divine mind.

Diogenes, his associate, likewise said that air was the matter of things, from which everything came into being, but that it was possessed of divine reason, without which nothing could be made from it. [Col. 0997D]

# CHAPTER III

**On Melcho, king of the Carthaginians, who fought unsuccessfully in Sicily and, returning home, killed himself with his own hand.**

When Melcho, king of the Carthaginians, was waging war in Sicily, he suddenly lost his army to a terrible plague. Nor was there any delay: as the people fell in groups from the disease, each person was quickly seized, soon died, and was no longer even buried. When news of this calamity, filling Carthage with sudden grief and consternation, had spread through the city as though it had been captured, the state was thrown into confusion.

Everything resounded with wailing. All the doors were closed everywhere, and both private and public duties were abandoned. Everyone hurried down to the harbor, and, as the few survivors of the disaster came out of the ships, asked them about their countrymen. When the wretched people learned of the destruction of their own men—while the survivors remained silent or groaned—then, along the entire shore, the voices of mourners and the wails and lamentations of unhappy mothers could be heard.

Amid these events the commander himself came forward from his ship, wearing a filthy, servile tunic and ungirded. At the sight of him the mourning crowds gathered around him. He too raised his hands to heaven, now accusing and lamenting his own misfortune, now the public calamity.

At last, crying out through the city, he entered his house and dismissed with a final address all those who followed him weeping. Then, after bolting the doors and excluding even his sons, he ended both his grief and his life with a sword. [Col. 0998B]

# CHAPTER IV

**On Ezra: how, having gained the favor of King Xerxes, he returned to Jerusalem with a great crowd of Jews and very many gifts.**

Xerxes succeeded his father Darius in the kingdom and ruled for twenty years, according to Josephus’s history, twenty-five. It was the twenty-seventh year from the rebuilding of the temple in Jerusalem.

Ezra, having gained the favor of Xerxes, was sent to Jerusalem with the king’s most generous largesse and that of his friends. Through him the king sent many gifts to the temple. Moreover, the king granted that any Jews living in his kingdom who wished might return with Ezra to Jerusalem and to their ancestral land, with no one preventing them, and might return with all the possessions they appeared to own. He also sent a copy of the letter containing these provisions to the Israelites living in Media.

When these people learned of the king’s piety toward God and of the favor he had for Ezra, many of them brought their possessions and came to Babylon so that they might ascend with Ezra to Jerusalem. Priests and Levites also came, together with gatekeepers, singers, and sacred servants.

Gathering them from the captivity, Ezra remained beyond the Euphrates for three days and imposed a fast upon them, so that they might offer vows to God for their safety and suffer no adversity on the journey. These two tribes, which had undergone captivity under Nebuchadnezzar, returned to Judea under the rulers mentioned above. From the time when they set out from Babylon, both they and the province have been called Jews.

The ten tribes, however, which had earlier been led into captivity and were called Israel, are demonstrably still dwelling beyond the Euphrates. After Ezra and those returning with him had fulfilled their vows, they rose from the Euphrates and reached Jerusalem on the twelfth day of the first month, in the seventh year of Xerxes’ reign, in the fifth month of that same year.

They brought with them sacred funds: six hundred and fifty talents of silver, silver vessels weighing one hundred talents, gold vessels weighing twenty talents, and bronze vessels better than gold, weighing twelve talents. The king, his counselors, and the Israelites living in Babylonia donated these things, which Ezra handed over to the priests and guardians of the temple. [Col. 0999A]

The king also ordered Ezra—whom he had found to be exceedingly wise in the law of God—to instruct the Jews, so that through ignorance they would not transgress the ancestral laws in any matter.

# CHAPTER V

**On Nehemiah, who rebuilt the walls of Jerusalem and gathered inhabitants into it.**

At that time, when Joachim, the high priest, died, his son Eliasib succeeded to the high-priesthood. Nehemiah, Xerxes’ cupbearer, with the Lord’s help deserved to obtain permission to return to his homeland with great honor and rebuild the ruined city.

When he came to Jerusalem with a large crowd of his people, he restored the city’s destroyed walls and, gathering the people into it, made them dwell there through his goodwill. He was a kindly man toward his own nation. [Col. 0999B]

At this time the maiden Pompilia [Al.: Porphyria], on account of the crime of adultery, was buried alive at Rome. Aeschylus, Pindar, Sophocles, and Euripides were celebrated as distinguished writers of tragedies; Herodotus was recognized as a writer of histories, and Zeuxis as a painter.
