# CHAPTER VI

**How Xerxes is said to have had seven hundred thousand armed men from his kingdom, three hundred thousand auxiliaries, twelve hundred ships equipped with beaks, and three thousand cargo ships in his army; how Leonidas, commander of the Spartans, opposed him with four thousand men and nearly defeated him; and how afterward Themistocles, commander of the Athenians, overcame his army in a naval battle. Xerxes, defeated and having lost his forces, disgracefully fled back to his homeland.**

Xerxes is said to have had six hundred thousand armed men from his kingdom and three hundred thousand auxiliaries, as well as twelve hundred warships and three thousand cargo ships. Thus it is rightly recorded that for an army so unexpected and a fleet so immense, rivers scarcely sufficed for drinking, lands scarcely for entry, and seas scarcely for passage.

Against this incredible host for those times—whose number is now harder to establish than it was then to defeat—Leonidas, king of the Spartans, opposed four thousand men in the narrow pass of Thermopylae. Xerxes, however, despising the small number presented against him, ordered battle to be joined and hand-to-hand combat to begin.

Those whose relatives and fellow soldiers had fallen on the plain of Marathon were the first to engage, both in the battle and in the disaster. Then a larger and more sluggish crowd followed. Since it was now neither free to advance, nor equipped for battle, nor ready for flight, but was being subdued only by death, for three continuous days there was not a battle of two sides but the slaughter of a single people.

On the fourth day, when Leonidas saw the enemy surrounding him on every side, he urged the auxiliary allies to withdraw from the battle, climb to the summit of the mountain, and preserve themselves for better times. He said that another fate had to be undertaken by him and his Spartans, and that he owed more to his fatherland than to his life.

After dismissing the allies, he reminded the Spartans at length of glory, but told them to expect nothing from life. They should await neither the enemy nor the day, but should break into the camp by night, mingle the weapons, and throw the ranks into confusion. Nowhere, he said, would victors die more honorably than in the camp of their enemies. [Col. 1000A]

Persuaded, therefore, that they would rather die, they armed themselves to avenge their future death, as though they themselves were both exacting and avenging their own destruction. Incredible to relate, six hundred men broke into the camp of thousands.

A tumult arose throughout the entire camp. The Persians themselves also helped the Spartans by killing one another. The Spartans, seeking the king and not finding him, cut down and overthrew everything. They roamed through the whole camp and, among dense heaps of bodies, scarcely pursued the few surviving men. Without doubt they were victors, unless they had chosen to die.

The battle, begun at the start of the night and lasting through most of the day, was prolonged until at last, exhausted by victory, each of them seemed satisfied with the vengeance exacted for his own death as his limbs failed. There, slipping and dying amid the corpses, in thick and half-congealed blood, they finally fell. [Col. 1000B]

Xerxes, twice defeated on land, prepared a naval battle. But Themistocles, commander of the Athenians, understood that the Ionians, who had previously helped him in war, had turned the attack of the Persians against him and were now bringing a fleet prepared to aid Xerxes. He decided to win them over to his side and withdraw them from the enemy.

Because the opportunity for conversation was denied by the battle signals, he ordered signs to be displayed and attached to rocks at the places where he thought the Ionians would bring their ships. By a suitable reproach he addressed those who had once been allies and sharers in danger but were now unjustly inactive, and by an exhortation he urged them to remember their ancient rights and sacred treaties. Above all, he warned them that, once battle had been joined, they should check the stroke of their oars and withdraw themselves from the war.

The king, therefore, keeping part of the ships for himself, remained on the shore as a spectator of the battle. On the other side, Arcemidora, queen of Halicarnassus, who had come to Xerxes’ aid, entered the battle fiercely among the foremost commanders. Thus, in a reversal of roles, feminine prudence was seen in a man and masculine boldness in a woman.

When the battle was uncertain, the Ionians, following Themistocles’ instructions, began gradually to withdraw from the engagement. Their defection persuaded the Persians to flee on that side. In the resulting panic many ships were sunk and captured. Most of the others, fearing the king’s savagery as though it were the ferocity of an enemy, slipped away to their homes.

Mardonius then approached the king, who was distressed by so many disasters, advising him that he should return to his kingdom before adverse rumor stirred up revolution at home. If the remaining forces were entrusted to him, Mardonius said, he would exact vengeance from the enemy and avert the domestic disgrace; or, if the fortunes of war continued unfavorable, he would yield to the enemy, but without the king’s dishonor.

The plan was approved, and the army was handed over to Mardonius. The king departed with a few men for Abydos, where, as though victor over the sea, he had constructed the bridge. But when he found that the bridge had been destroyed by winter storms, he crossed anxiously in a fishing boat.

It was surely something for the human race to behold and grieve over, as it contemplated the changes of fortune in so great a reversal: the man who had once had the whole sea lying hidden beneath him was now content to shelter beside a small boat; the man who had carried the yoke of his captivity on a bound bridge now needed the wretched service of a single lowly servant. For his power had caused mountains to be cut down, valleys to be filled, rivers to be drained, and nature itself to yield. [Col. 1001A]

The infantry forces entrusted to the commanders also wasted away from toil, hunger, and fear. As the disease grew more violent, such plague and such foulness arose among the dying that the roads were filled with corpses. Savage birds and shameless beasts, attracted by the lure of food, followed the dying army.

Mardonius, to whom Xerxes had entrusted the remaining wars, was first inflated by brief success and soon afterward cast down into the depths. He captured Olynthus, a city of Greece. After attempting, through various inducements, to lead the Athenians to hope for peace, when he saw that their liberty could not be overcome, he burned part of the city and moved all his war preparations into Boeotia. [Col. 1001B]

One hundred thousand Greeks followed him there. When battle was joined without delay, they destroyed Mardonius’ forces and compelled him, stripped bare as if from a shipwreck, to flee with a few men. They captured the camp, filled with royal riches, at no small cost to ancient discipline. For after the division of this booty, Persian gold was the first corruption of Greek virtue.

Thus the disaster begun presses the wretched toward utter destruction. For, by chance, on the same day that Mardonius’ forces were destroyed in Boeotia, part of the Persian army was fighting in Asia in a naval battle beneath Mount Mycale. There, a new report suddenly filled the ears of both fleets and peoples: Mardonius’ forces had been destroyed and the Greeks had been victorious.

Wonderful is the ordering of divine judgment: a battle was fought in Boeotia at sunrise, while in Asia, at the hours of midday on that same day, the news was announced across such vast intervening spaces of sea and land. [Col. 1001C]

That report greatly contributed to the outcome. When the Persians heard of the disaster suffered by their allies, they were first seized by grief and then by despair. They were rendered neither fit for battle nor capable of flight, and a more steadfast enemy, encouraged by the success of fortune, attacked them while they were thus terrified and routed.

Xerxes, having conducted the war unsuccessfully and become contemptible to his own people, was surrounded and killed in the palace by his prefect Artabanus. At that time Diogenes and his followers, the natural philosophers, were recognized. Themistocles fled to the Persians. Pindar was held in renown. Sophocles, a writer of tragedies, and Euripides were held in renown. Herodotus was recognized as a writer of histories. [Col. 1001D] Bacchylides and Diagoras were celebrated in much discussion.

# CHAPTER VII

**During the reign of Artaxerxes, the books of Pythagoras were burned by the Athenians. A memorial of the philosophers who existed at that time, namely the Milesians, Hippocrates the physician, and Socrates.**

Artaxerxes, who was called Machir, reigned for forty years, after Artabanus, who had reigned for seven months. It was the forty-seventh year from the rebuilding of the temple.

During his reign Ezra the priest was held in renown among the Hebrews, for he was the teacher of all in the sacred laws who had returned from captivity to Judea. Nehemiah completed the walls of the city of Jerusalem. The high priest of the temple was Joachim, son of Eliasib, whom Josephus calls Judas. After his death, his son John assumed the priestly honor.

At that time Aristarchus the writer of tragedies, Cratinus and Plato, writers of comedies, and Zeno and Heraclitus were recognized. Pherecydes was regarded as a second writer of histories, and Sophocles and Aristophanes as writers of tragedies.

When Herodotus had read his books at Athens before the council, he was honored. The Athenians, however, burned the books of the sophist Pythagoras by public decree because they had found magical arts and necromancy in them.

The philosophers Empedocles and Parmenides, and also the Milesian natural philosopher, were held in renown. This Thales, wishing also to propagate successors, investigated the nature of things and committed his disputations to writing. He was especially admirable because, having mastered the calculations of astrology, he was able to predict even eclipses of the sun and moon.

Nevertheless, he thought water was the principle of things, and that from it all the elements of the world, the world itself, and the things joined within it came into existence. Yet he placed no divine mind before this work, which, when we contemplate the world, we behold as so marvelous.

Zeuxis was recognized as a distinguished painter. Some think that the bathhouse of Byzantium was named from one of his paintings, of which he had made very many for various people.

In those days, according to the Hebrews, the seventieth jubilee began. [Col. 1002B]

At that time a stone fell from heaven into the river Aegis. Hippocrates the physician and Socrates the philosopher were also held in renown; Sophocles the tragic poet and Democritus were recognized, and Pindar also became known at that time. [Col. 1002C]

# CHAPTER VIII

**On Mamilius, the Tusculan commander, who subdued the Latins; on the first contest held at Rome; on the great plague that almost consumed the Roman strength; and on the other events that took place among the Romans at that time.**

In those days, under Mamilius, the Tusculan commander, the Latins were defeated, conquered, and subjected at Lake Regillus. The spoils won there remain, though the text reads *deontia* [sic]. At that time the first contest was also held in renown at Rome.

At Rome, therefore, when the war had been suspended for a short time, a severe plague followed. It spread violently throughout the entire city, so that, in view of the preceding portent, heaven may rightly have seemed to burn when the head of the nations was aflame with such a fire of disease. For that year the plague consumed both consuls, Ebutius and Servilius; it destroyed most of the military forces and wiped out many nobles, especially the common people, with a loathsome wasting disease. Yet the sickness had already arisen in the preceding fourth year and had ravaged that same people.

In the following year, citizens in exile and runaway slaves, under the leadership of Herbonius, a Sabine man, invaded and burned the Capitol. There, under the consul and commander Valerius, battle was fought with great courage. But the danger of the battle was so fierce and grave that the consul Valerius himself was killed there and, by his own death, further stained the unworthy victory over slaves.

The following year the consul was besieged with a defeated army. For the Aequi and Volsci overcame the consul Minucius when he joined battle and surrounded him, as he fled, with hunger and the sword at Algidus. The outcome would have been disastrous had Quintius Cincinnatus, that distinguished dictator, not broken the close siege by crushing the enemy.

Found in the countryside, he was summoned from the plow to the fasces. Having accepted the office and assembled an army, he soon became victorious, placed the yoke of oxen upon horses, and, holding victory as though it were a plow handle, led the subjected enemies before him. [Col. 1003A]

# CHAPTER IX

**On the seventy weeks foretold by Daniel, which were completed in the last year of Nero’s reign.**

Ezra records that Nehemiah, who built the walls of Jerusalem, completed the work in the thirty-second year of Artaxerxes, king of the Persians. [Col. 1003B]

If anyone counts seventy weeks from that time, as written by Daniel—weeks which amount to four hundred and ninety years—he will find that they were completed in the reign of Nero. Under Nero the siege of Jerusalem began; afterward, in the second year of Vespasian, the city was captured.

# CHAPTER X

**During the reign of Darius, surnamed Nothus, the wise men who flourished at that time. The Romans then requested laws from the Athenians and wrote them on the Twelve Tables. [They] expelled the consuls and established decemvirs; how great an evil arose from this; and what happened to them in those days.**

Darius, king of the Persians, surnamed Nothus, reigned for nineteen years. He was preceded by Xerxes II and Sogdianus, who reigned for only nine months. Thus, from the second dedication of the temple, eighty-seven years had passed.

Bacchides, a writer of poems, was recognized at that time, and Pherecydes died. Eupolis and Aristophanes, writers of comedies, were recognized. At that time the Romans, through envoys, sought Solon’s laws from the Athenians, wrote them on the Twelve Tables, expelled the consuls, and transferred authority to the decemvirs for the purpose of establishing Athenian laws.

This brought great ruin upon the republic. For when the other decemvirs withdrew, the first of them, Appius Claudius, alone prolonged the authority for himself. Immediately a conspiracy of the others followed, as they resented the fact that power which had been common to them was in the hands of one man. A band of tyrants emerged from the new beginning of this wicked arrangement.

Moved by the cruelty of their necessity and warned by the danger to their liberty, the people seized the Aventine armed. They did not cease defending their liberty with weapons until the conspiracy of the conspirators renounced even the offices they themselves held.

At that time, throughout nearly an entire year, earthquakes were so frequent and so severe in Italy that Rome was wearied by continual reports of countless shocks and the destruction of farms and towns. Then there was such prolonged and burning drought that it destroyed hope of producing the fruits of the earth.

Finally, in those days, when the enemy Fidenates threatened the Roman citadels, terrifying them with a force that destroyed the greatest auxiliary troops, the dictator Aemilius, the third of that name, drove away and relieved the great burden of evil, scarcely capturing Fidenae itself. So great was the struggle among the evils and passions involved that wars poured in from outside either obscured domestic disasters or, after the losses of war had brought a relaxation of truces, different plagues, blazing in heaven and on earth, destroyed everything with unceasing harassment.

At that time Sicily, which from the beginning had been the homeland of the Cyclopes and afterward the nurse of tyrants, [and had often itself been the captive of slaves]—the first of whom fed on human flesh, the middle ones on tortures, and the last on deaths—endured many misfortunes from its own people and from outsiders. There the recurring fires of war begin, but they nearly consume and destroy the exhausted and burned-out strength of the Greeks. [Col. 1004A]

# CHAPTER XI

**On the discord of the Sicilians, that is, between the Catanians and Syracusans, who sought assistance from the Lacedaemonians and Athenians; on how, through this occasion, not only Sicily but all Greece was worn down by the gravest wars.**

While the Sicilians were suffering from discord within their kingdom, the Catanians requested aid from the Athenians against the Syracusans, whom they found oppressive and hostile. The Athenians sent a fleet prepared for battle to Sicily.

Those who had been sent began successfully, having defeated the enemy. From there they returned to Sicily with larger forces and a stronger army, under the commanders Miceas and Lamachus, with such strength that even those who had requested their assistance began to fear their support.

The Athenians immediately fought two successful land battles. They confined the enemy, exhausted in the city and surrounded by the fleet stationed against them, on land and sea.

But when the Syracusans’ fortunes were broken and exhausted, they sought help from the Lacedaemonians. The Lacedaemonians soon sent Gylippus with supporting forces. As soon as he reached Sicily, he was defeated in two battles, but was not frightened. In a third engagement he killed Lamachus, routed the enemy, and freed his allies from the siege. For Gylippus defeated Nicias and Demosthenes in Sicily.

The Athenians therefore fought for two years in Sicily, not without inflicting losses on the Lacedaemonians. Alcibiades, their commander, fled from the Athenians and went to Lacedaemon. He persuaded the Spartans to continue against the Athenians with a new war, and together with them stirred up all Greece against Athens.

Darius, king of the Persians, mindful of the hatred inherited from his father and grandfather, sent forces and the expenses of war against that city through his prefect of Lydia, Tissaphernes [printed: Partissafernem]. [Col. 1004D]

Incredible to relate, the resources of the Athenians were so great at that time that, although the forces of Asia, Greece, and the entire East attacked them—against one city alone—they seemed, by fighting often and never yielding, to have been exhausted rather than defeated.

If anyone wishes to know more fully the discord of the Athenians, the grievous wars they endured, and the actions and exiles of Alcibiades, let him read the second book of Orosius *Against the Pagans*.

Nevertheless, the Athenians, wisest of all and sufficiently instructed by their own misfortunes that the smallest things grow through concord and the greatest are shaken by discord, and that all good or evil accomplished abroad is rooted in and sent forth from internal beginnings, wiped away their hatreds at home and restrained the wars abroad. They left to their descendants an example from their own ruin and advice for their restoration—provided that, because of the extreme mutability of the human mind, what is counseled in adversity might also be preserved in prosperity. [Col. 1005A]

But this same resolution was corrupted almost while the words of the resolution were being spoken, so that scarcely two years later that most renowned of philosophers, Socrates, driven by misfortunes among them, forced life from himself by poison.

# CHAPTER XII

**How Artaxerxes fought against and defeated his brother Cyrus; concerning the earthquake in Sicily and the severe eruption of Mount Etna; concerning the plague that afflicted the Athenians; and concerning the hardships of the Romans.**

Artaxerxes, also surnamed Mnemon [printed: Mennon], son of Darius and Parysatis, reigned for forty years. From the restoration of the temple, one hundred and five years had passed. He is the one whom the Hebrews call Ahasuerus, under whom the Book of Esther was completed.

In those same days civil war among the Persians was scarcely ended without parricide. After King Darius died, when his sons Artaxerxes and Cyrus disputed the kingdom, they eventually fought with great preparations and with great destruction of provinces and peoples on both sides.

In this conflict, when the two brothers rushed against each other from opposite directions and chance brought them face to face, Artaxerxes was wounded first by his brother but escaped death through the speed of his horse. Cyrus, however, was soon overwhelmed by the royal cohort and brought the battle to an end.

Artaxerxes, therefore, gaining both the spoils of his brother’s expedition and the army, secured the power of the kingdom through fratricide. [Col. 1005C]

Afterward, in those times, Sicily was shaken by a most severe earthquake. Moreover, with the fires of Mount Etna boiling over and hot ashes pouring forth, it was devastated, causing enormous damage to fields and farms.

At that time the city of Atlante, adjoining Locris and situated on land [Al.: contiguous to it], was suddenly torn away by a violent movement of the sea and broken apart into an island.

The wretched remnants of the Athenians were also attacked by a plague and ravaged for a long time. At that time the Romans, often shaken by sudden eruptions of enemies and, in addition, forced to wage war in winter quarters, had to spend the winter under hides. Finally, compelled to endure hunger and cold in the sight of the enemy, they captured the city only at the end through tunnels and secret infiltration, without any worthy testimony to Roman courage.

They achieved this victory over the Veientes, useful rather than glorious, through the skill of the former dictator Camillus. Then the invasion of the Gauls and the burning of the city followed. Who, if able, would dare compare any events of this time with that disaster, although past misfortune and present injury cannot be weighed equally? [Col. 1005D]

# CHAPTER XIII

**On the Gauls who burned and devastated Rome and finally sold it.**

The Senonian Gauls, therefore, under the leadership of Brennus, with a very large and exceptionally strong army, were besieging the city of Clusium, which is now called Tuscia. There they saw Roman envoys, who had come to arrange peace between the parties, fighting against them in the battle line.

Moved to indignation by this, they abandoned the siege of Clusium and hastened with all their forces toward Rome. Fabius, the consul, met them with an army as they rushed upon the city, but he could not withstand them. Rather, that hostile assault cut down, scattered, and passed through them like a dry crop.

The river Allia bears witness to this disaster of Fabius, just as the Cremera bears witness to the disaster of the Fabii. No one could easily recount a similar collapse of the Roman army, even if Rome had not also been burned.

The Gauls entered the exposed city. They slaughtered the senators, who sat rigid in their seats like statues, and, after burning them in the fires of their houses, buried them beneath the collapse of their own roofs.

They enclosed the entire remaining youth, which is known to have consisted then of scarcely one thousand men, hidden in the citadel of the Capitoline hill, with a siege. There they wore down, subdued, and sold the unfortunate remnants through hunger, plague, despair, and fear. For they agreed on one thousand pounds of gold as the price of their departure—not because Rome had been of little account among the Gauls, but because they had already so thoroughly worn it down that it could not then be worth more. [Col. 1006B]

When the Gauls departed, what remained within the former circuit of the City was an unsightly heap of shapeless ruins. Everywhere, amid the impediments and the voices of those wandering about, with an answering echo sounding among unfamiliar surroundings, their frightened ears were held in suspense. Horror shook their minds; silences terrified them. For in spacious places the very rarity of sound is a source of fear.

Thus they began to consider, approve, and attempt changing their dwelling, inhabiting another town, and even being known by another name. [Col. 1006C]

# CHAPTER XIV

**The days in which Socrates and Plato flourished.**
When Archelaus, Amintas, Pausanias, Argeus, and then again Amintas ruled among the Macedonians, succeeding one another, Dionysius was exercising tyranny in Sicily. Socrates also at that time attained distinction among the Athenians as Plato’s teacher.

Socrates, therefore, is remembered as the first to turn the whole of philosophy toward correcting and disciplining conduct. Before him, everyone had devoted his greatest effort chiefly to physics—that is, to investigating natural things—and he taught that the good end could not be achieved except by living well. He therefore did not want minds polluted by earthly desires to stretch toward divine things and attempt to investigate their causes, since he saw that they were inquiring into causes which he believed to be first and highest only in the will of the one supreme God. Hence he thought that these could be grasped only by a pure mind; and for that reason he judged that one must persevere in purifying life through good conduct, so that the mind, freed from the burdens imposed by lusts, might raise itself by its natural vigor toward eternal things and, through the purity of its understanding, behold the nature of the incorporeal and unchangeable light, in which the causes of all created natures abide securely. [Col. 1006D]

Nevertheless, when the Athenians had been stirred up by the envy of the ignorant, he was condemned on the basis of a slanderous accusation and punished with death.

But afterward the very city of Athens, which had publicly condemned him, publicly mourned him. [Col. 1007A] The people’s indignation turned so violently against his two accusers that one of them perished, overcome by the force of the crowd, while the other escaped a similar punishment through voluntary and perpetual exile.

Socrates therefore left behind, through the illustrious reputation of his life and death, very many followers of his philosophy. Their zeal was directed, in rivalry with one another, toward debating moral questions, in which the highest good is discussed, without which a human being cannot become happy. Plato, accordingly, was more eminent in glory and reputation than all the disciples of Socrates—and not undeservedly, since he had determined that the end of the good was to live according to virtue, and that happiness could be attained only by one who possessed knowledge of the one God and imitation of him, and that there was no other reason for being happy. [Col. 1007B]

Plato, who had been born at Athens in an honorable position among his people and whose remarkable intellect far surpassed that of his fellow students, was not content with Socratic instruction. He traveled far and wide, wherever the reputation of some distinguished body of knowledge drew him in the hope of acquiring it. Thus, in Egypt, he learned whatever great teachings were held and taught there; and from there, coming into those regions of Italy where the reputation of Pythagoras was celebrated, he readily grasped everything that belonged to Italian philosophy. And because he loved his teacher Socrates with singular devotion, he made him the speaker in nearly all his dialogues, blending with Socrates’ charm and moral discussions even those things that he had either learned from others or had himself discerned with as much understanding as he could muster.

Thus, since the pursuit of wisdom is concerned with action and contemplation—whence one part of it may be called active and the other contemplative—the active part pertains to conducting life, that is, to instructing one’s morals, while the contemplative part pertains to beholding the causes of nature and the purest truth, Socrates is remembered as having excelled in the active part, whereas Pythagoras devoted himself more intensely, with whatever powers of understanding he possessed, to the contemplative. [Col. 1007C]

Plato, therefore, is praised for having perfected philosophy by joining the two together. He divided it into three parts: one moral, which is chiefly concerned with action; another natural, which is assigned to contemplation; and a third rational, which distinguishes truth from falsehood. Although this last part is necessary for both action and contemplation, contemplation above all claims the discernment of truth. [Col. 1007D]

This threefold division is therefore not contrary to that distinction by which it is understood that the whole pursuit of wisdom consists in action and contemplation. The Athenians also began to use twenty-four letters, whereas previously they had only twenty-two. Xenophon and Thisias were regarded as distinguished. Diogenes was known, as was Eudoxus the astrologer; Plato and Xenophon, as well as other Socratics, were also held in distinction. When Evagoras was reigning in Cyprus, he went mad. Moreover, when a great earthquake occurred, Helice and Bura, cities of the Peloponnese, were swallowed up. At that time also occurred that most famous war of the Carthaginians.

## CHAPTER XV

**During the reign of Artaxerxes, who was also called Ochus, John, the high priest of the Jews, killed his brother Jesus in the temple. For this crime the Jews suffered many severe punishments.** [Col. 1008A]

Artaxerxes, who was also called Ochus, ruled for twenty-six years. From the rebuilding of the temple, it was the one hundred and forty-fifth year. The Macedonian kings were Alexander, Ptolemy, Perdiccas, and Philip, succeeding one another at short intervals. The Jewish priest was John, son of Judah, who killed his brother Jesus in the temple when Jesus was disputing his claim to the priesthood.

Because of this crime, Bagoses, commander of King Artaxerxes, who loved Jesus, entered and profaned the temple; and for this reason he reduced the Jewish people to slavery. He also no longer permitted the daily sacrifices to be offered in the temple, while exacting a tax of fifty drachmas for each year. Taking advantage of this opportunity, he afflicted the people for seven years because of the murder of the priest Jesus, saying: “Never before, either among the Greeks or among the barbarians, has such a thing been done so cruelly or wickedly.” Therefore God did not leave this unpunished. [Col. 1008B]

## CHAPTER XVI

**How Artaxerxes proclaimed peace to the Greeks and joined conquered Egypt to his empire** [Col. 1008B]

After Artaxerxes had brought to an end the great and prolonged war in Egypt, he led many Jews into exile and ordered them to live in Hyrcania, beside the Caspian Sea. Meanwhile Artaxerxes, king of the Persians, ordered all the peoples of Greece through envoys to withdraw from arms and submit to peace—not because he was mercifully concerned for the weary, but so that, while he was occupied with wars in Egypt, no incursion against his kingdom might be attempted.

All the Greeks therefore relaxed into the most desired quiet and domestic leisure. They could certainly have despised him as steadfastly as they had often defeated the greatest Persian forces, if, at the mere announcement of peace, the war-weary purpose of all had not melted away in their hearts. For the peace itself, willingly accepted by brave men, bears witness to how many grievous and intolerable wars the Lacedaemonians and Athenians had waged against one another, the Arcadians against the Lacedaemonians, and how Conon the Athenian, commander of the Persian army, afflicted the Spartans; it also bears witness to how he fought against Agesilaus, the lame but keen-minded commander of the Lacedaemonians, and finally defeated him. It is also shown by the judgment that scarcely a hundred old men were found among the Lacedaemonians. But whoever wishes to know these matters more fully will find them in the third book of Orosius *Against the Pagans*.

Artaxerxes, who was also called Ochus, destroyed Sidon and joined Egypt to his empire, after driving Nectanebus into Ethiopia, where the kingdom of the Egyptians was destroyed. [Col. 1008C–D]

## CHAPTER XVII

**During these days a great pestilence cruelly devastated Rome; the earth opened in the City and swallowed alive Curtius, a man of equestrian rank. At that time the Gauls also, conspiring against the Romans, were defeated three times.** [Col. 1009A]

At that time a great pestilence seized all Rome—not, as usually happens, a disturbance of the weather more or less than is normal for the seasons, that is, an untimely winter drought, a sudden spring heat, an unsuitable summer dampness, or the unassimilated luxuriance of a rich autumn. In addition, a corrupting breeze breathed out from the Calabrian groves brought sudden attacks of acute illnesses. The severe and prolonged disease, differing from no sex and unlike in no age, consumed everyone by a general wasting over two continuous years, so that even those whom it did not carry to death it left weakened and afflicted, emptied by shameful emaciation. [Col. 1009B]

In the following year this wretched plague was followed by a sufficiently grim portent and by an even more wretched expiation of it. Suddenly, in the middle of the City, the earth split apart, and, after a vast rupture, the underworld gaped open. For a long time an indecent cavern remained open, an object of terror and spectacle to all, and, with the gods as interpreters, it demanded the accursed burial of a living man. M. Curtius satisfied those wicked jaws by hurling himself into them. He was an armed equestrian [Note: [Col. 1009D] The word *vir* (“man”) should be deleted.] and cast an unexpected fullness into the cruel earth, which would have found it insufficient to receive the dead through the graves after so great a pestilence unless, once split open, it also swallowed the living. [Col. 1009B–C]

After this, a second terrible flood of Gauls settled beside the river Anio, at the fourth milestone from the City. There is no doubt that, by the weight of their numbers and the vigor of their courage, they would have seized the disturbed city, had they not grown sluggish through idleness and mildness. There Manlius Torquatus began the most savage battle single-handed, and T. Quintus the dictator brought it to an end in the bloodiest engagement. After being routed in this battle, many Gauls rushed back into war with their forces restored, but they were defeated by Gaius Sulpicius the dictator.

Shortly afterward a battle against the Etruscans also took place under C. Marcius. From this one may infer how great the number of those killed was, since eight thousand Etruscans were captured. On the third occasion during these same days, the Gauls spread themselves through the coastal regions and the plains below the Alban hills, offering themselves as prey. Against them, after a new levy of soldiers had been held and ten legions enrolled, sixty thousand Romans advanced, the Latins having denied them assistance. Marcus Valerius brought this battle to an end, aided by a raven, from which he was afterward called Corvinus. After the Gallic challenger had been killed, the terrified enemies fled in scattered groups and were slaughtered mercilessly.

The Romans were not content merely to drive them from their own walls. Since the Gauls were spreading the wreckage of their defeat more widely through Italy, the Romans pursued them so relentlessly that, several years later, the consul Dolabella destroyed all their remaining forces in Etruria, at Lake Vadimon, lest anyone of that people survive to boast of having burned the Roman City.

Manlius Torquatus, the consul, who afterward defeated the Latins following the slaughter of the Gauls, had his own son—because he had, against his command, attacked and defeated the enemy, killed Metius of Tusculum, a most distinguished equestrian, and slain enemies who challenged and insulted him—beaten with rods and struck with the axe. [Col. 1009D–1010A]

## CHAPTER XVIII

**Concerning the fact that the night became longer than usual and that true stones falling from heaven battered the earth severely. This also occurred when Alexander the Great of Macedon was born. During these days Aristotle was renowned, and Plato died.** [Col. 1010A]

At the same time the night appeared to extend over most of the day, and hail as hard as stone descended from the clouds and struck the earth with genuine stones. During these days Alexander the Great was born—truly that vortex of misery and most savage storm of the whole East. [Col. 1010B]

At that time the orator Demosthenes became known, Aristotle the philosopher was celebrated by everyone, and Plato died. After him Speusippus held the Academy.

## CHAPTER XIX

**That, during the reign of Arxes, Roman matrons were discovered engaged in a criminal poisoning; and that Philip, king of the Macedonians and father of Alexander the Great, waged very many wars, overthrew cities, and subdued countless peoples**

Arxes, son of Ochus, reigned among the Persians for four years. From the rebuilding of the temple, it was the one hundred and seventy-first year. Jaddus, after his father John had died, assumed the leadership of the Jewish priesthood.

During these days the Roman matrons burned with incredible frenzy and love of crimes. It was indeed a foul and pestilential year, and everywhere slaughter was already being carried out in crowds. Yet everyone still held the simple belief that the cause was corrupted air, until a certain maidservant came forward as informer and witness. First, many matrons were compelled to drink the poisons they had prepared; then, as soon as they had swallowed them, they perished. So great was the number of matrons implicated in these crimes that three hundred and seventy of them are said to have been condemned at once. [Col. 1010C]

At that time Alexander, king of the Epirotes and uncle of that Alexander the Great, crossed into Italy with his forces. As he prepared for war against the Romans, seeking to strengthen his army around the cities neighboring Rome and either acquire allies for himself or deprive his enemies of them, he was defeated and killed in Lucania in a great battle by the Samnites, who were supporting the Lucanian people.

Others say that this man was Pyrrhus, who had been summoned by the Tarentines to provide them with aid against Roman arms. Tarentum was a foundation of the Lacedaemonians, formerly the chief city of Calabria, Apulia, and all Lucania in wealth and size, remarkable for its walls, harbor, and very site.

Pyrrhus, therefore, wishing to vindicate the half-Greek city founded by the Lacedaemonians, came with all the forces of Epirus, Thessaly, and Macedon, together with elephants previously unknown in that region, by sea and land, with men, horses, and weapons, and with the added terror of wild beasts. Their size, ugliness, unfamiliar smell, and shrill cries so terrified the Roman horses in the first battle, under the consul Laevinus, that, imagining the unknown beasts to be larger than they were, they fled and spread slaughter far and wide. [Col. 1010D–1011A]

The war was fought more successfully in Apulia and afterward at Asculum, under the consuls Curius and Fabricius. The terror of the beasts had by then faded, and Gaius Municius, a spearman of the Fourth Legion, had shown that the animals could die by cutting off the trunk of one of them. The Romans therefore hurled spears at the elephants, and torches were thrown against their towers; flaming destruction covered the entire enemy host. The slaughter ended only when night separated the combatants, and finally the king himself, wounded in the shoulder, fell in his armor from the hands of his guards as he fled.

In the battle of Lucania, under the same commanders as above, Roman courage proved itself in every respect, in war and peace, abroad and at home. When that terrible Pyrrhus, after his victory in the first battle, understood Roman courage and, although victorious, wished by treaty to be received into friendship, the senate refused him. No event displayed the strength of the Roman people, the wisdom of the senate, and the greatness of the commanders more than the Tarentine triumph; nor did any more beautiful or splendid triumph enter the City.

Before that day, the Romans had seen nothing except the cattle of the Volscians, the flocks of the Sabines, the wagons of the Gauls, and the broken weapons of the Samnites. But then, if you looked at the captives, there were Molossians, Thessalians, Macedonians, Bruttians, Apulians, and Lucanians; if at the procession, there were gold, purple, statues, paintings, and Tarentine luxuries. Yet the Roman people looked with greatest pleasure upon those beasts which they had feared, together with their towers, now following the victorious horses with lowered necks, not without some awareness of their captivity. [Col. 1011B–C]

Since I have decided to review the actions of different peoples by touching on them only in part, I shall now, prompted by the fall of that Alexander, briefly retrace some years and gather, as far as I can, the great matters in small summaries concerning Philip, king of the Macedonians, who had Olympias, the sister of this Alexander of Epirus, as his wife and by her fathered Alexander the Great.

Philip, son of Amyntas and father of Alexander, obtained the kingdom of the Macedonians and held it for twenty-five years. During that time he constructed this whole heap of cruelties and this entire mass of evils. First, after being given as a hostage to the Thebans by his brother Alexander, he was educated for three years under Epaminondas, a most vigorous commander and supreme philosopher. When that same Alexander had been killed through the crime of his mother Eurydice—although she had also committed adultery and had first killed another son, while having deprived her daughter of her husband by arranging a marriage with her son-in-law after the death of his wife—Philip was compelled by the people to assume the kingdom, which he had been protecting for the young son of his murdered brother.

Since he was wearied at home by fear of repeated plots discovered there and abroad by the attacks of enemies rising everywhere, he first waged war against the Athenians. After defeating them, he transferred his arms against the Illyrians and, after killing many thousands of the enemy, captured Larissa, a most famous city. From there he invaded Thessaly, not so much from love of victory as from ambition to possess the Thessalian cavalry, whose strength he wished to combine with his own army. Thus, having taken the Thessalians by surprise and reduced them to his power, he made his army invincible by joining together strong and numerous bodies of cavalry and infantry.

After defeating the Athenians and subjecting the Thessalians, he married Olympias, sister of Auruchas, king of the Molossians. Auruchas thought that, by establishing an alliance with the Macedonians through the king’s marriage, he would enlarge his own power; deceived in this hope, he lost it and grew old in exile as a private man.

Then, while Philip was besieging the city of Methone, he lost an eye to an arrow. He soon stormed and captured the city itself. From that point he subdued almost all Greece, having first forestalled it by his schemes. The cities of Greece, each wishing to rule, all lost their rule; and while they rushed without restraint toward mutual destruction, they finally realized, crushed and enslaved, that everything which each had lost had perished for all.

Philip watched their mad rivalries like a spectator and, by continually supplying assistance to the weaker side, cunningly fostered their disputes, the fuel of wars. A skilful contriver of deceit, he subjected both the defeated and the victors alike to himself. He afflicted all Greece with such miseries [Note: [Col. 1011D] Something is missing.], and he attacked in a hostile manner others by whom he had been received in peace, cruelly plundered them, and, entirely abolishing every sense of fellowship, sold the wives and children of all at auction and overturned every temple.

After this he crossed into Cappadocia and waged war there with equal treachery. He killed neighboring kings captured by deceit and subjected all Cappadocia to his authority. Then, after the massacres, fires, and plunder that he had carried out in allied cities, he turned to parricide and killed or put to death the brothers whom he feared as coheirs of the kingdom. After laying waste to the cities and territories of all, he made his bloody presence cause him to be feared even when absent.

He tore some peoples away from their homes and placed them opposite the borders of their enemies; others he settled at the farthest limits of his kingdom. Some he divided into reinforcements for exhausted cities, through rivalry of strength, so that they could not achieve what they were believed capable of achieving. Thus that once glorious body of flourishing Greece, its freedom first extinguished, collapsed into many torn and scattered fragments.

Moreover, when two brothers, kings of Thrace, had by common agreement preferred him as judge, Philip, following the custom of his character, entered the judgment as though it were a war, with an army drawn up, and deprived the unsuspecting young men of life and kingdom. He also crossed into Scythia with his son Alexander intending to plunder. When battle was joined and the Scythians were superior both in number and in courage, they were defeated by Philip’s treachery.

In that battle twenty thousand boys and women of the Scythian people were captured, and a great quantity of livestock was carried away; no gold or silver was found. This fact first gave credence to the poverty of the Scythians. Twenty thousand noble mares, sufficient for breeding, were sent to Macedonia.

As Philip was returning, the Triballi met him in battle, in which Philip was wounded in the thigh so severely that the horse beneath him was killed by the wound passing through his body. As soon as he recovered, he brought war against the Athenians. Placed in such danger, they invited the Lacedaemonians, once their enemies but then their allies, and wearied the cities of all Greece with embassies, urging them to attack the common enemy with common forces.

Some cities therefore joined the Athenians, while fear of war drew others to Philip. When battle was joined, although the Athenians had a far greater number of soldiers, they were defeated by the hardened courage of the Macedonians, seasoned through continual wars. The outcome itself showed that this battle had been far more terrible than all the previous wars. For that day brought to all Greece the end of the glory of acquired domination and of the condition of its most ancient freedom.

Afterward Philip exercised a most bloody victory over the Thebans and Lacedaemonians. He struck some leaders of the cities with the axe, drove others into exile, and deprived them all of their property. Those who had long before been expelled by their fellow citizens he restored to their homeland. Of these he appointed three hundred exiles as judges and governors; and, so that they might heal their former pain through their new power, they did not allow the unfortunate peoples whom they oppressed even to breathe in hope of liberty.

Moreover, after a great selection of soldiers had been made throughout Greece to support the royal policy, he organized two hundred thousand infantry and fifteen thousand cavalry, apart from the Macedonian army and the countless barbarian forces, intending to send a Persian expedition into Asia. He chose three commanders—Parmenion, Amyntas, and Attalus—to be sent ahead against the Persians.

While the forces mentioned above were being assembled from Greece, he decided to celebrate the marriage of Alexander, who was the brother of his wife Olympias and who, as we have mentioned above, was later slain by the Sabines in Lucania. Philip had made him king of Epirus in payment for the sexual outrage committed against him, and now he intended to marry him to his daughter Cleopatra.

The day before he was killed, when he was asked what end was most desirable for a human being, he is said to have replied: “The best is that which, after a brave man has gained the glory of his virtues and is reigning in peace, can come upon him suddenly and swiftly, without bodily struggle or disgrace to the soul, by an unexpected weapon.”

This very end soon befell him. Thus for twenty-five years one king’s deceit, savagery, and domination stirred up the burning of cities, the destruction of wars, the subjugation of provinces, the slaughter of human beings, the seizure of wealth, the plundering of livestock, the sale of the dead, and the enslavement of the living. These deeds of Philip, committed to our memory as examples of misery, would be sufficient even if Alexander had not succeeded him in the kingdom. [Col. 1013C–D]

## CHAPTER XX

**Concerning the most serious battles fought between the Samnites and Romans during those days. In these battles the Romans were defeated by the Samnites and sent beneath the yoke of servitude; then the Romans, victorious again under their commander Papirius, defeated the Samnites and removed the yoke.**

After twenty thousand Samnites had already fallen in battle, with Fabius, master of the cavalry, commanding the engagement, the Samnites, taking more careful precautions and making more elaborate preparations, encamped at the Caudine Forks. There, when they had shut in the consuls Q. Veturius and Postumius, together with all the Roman forces, by the narrowness of the place and by their weapons, Pontius, their commander, was so carried away by the security of victory that he thought it necessary to consult his father Herennius whether he should kill the trapped Romans or spare them after placing them under the yoke. He chose to preserve them alive for disgrace.

It was well known that the Romans had often been defeated and killed, but had never been captured or forced to surrender. Therefore the Samnites, having gained the victory, ordered the entire Roman army, shamefully captured and stripped even of its weapons and clothing—except that each man was granted a cheap covering to conceal his private parts—to be sent beneath the yoke and subjected to servitude in a long and ostentatious procession. After taking six hundred Roman cavalry as hostages, they sent back the consuls burdened with disgrace and empty of all else.

The following year the Romans broke the treaty established with the Samnites and compelled them to war. The battle was begun under the command of the consul Papirius and produced great slaughter of both peoples, since the anger of recent disgrace drove one side to fight and the glory of an imminent victory urged on the other. At last the Romans won by dying stubbornly. Neither side stopped killing or being killed until, after the Samnites had been defeated and their commander captured, the Romans restored the yoke of servitude.

Papirius then stormed and captured Sutricum, after expelling the Samnite garrison from it. This Papirius was then regarded among the Romans as so warlike and energetic that, when Alexander the Great was said to be planning, after departing from the East, to seize Africa by force and from there cross into Italy, the Romans considered that, among all the best commanders in their republic, Papirius would be the one most capable of withstanding Alexander’s assault.

During these days a certain man named Hanno, whose private wealth exceeded the resources of the state, conceived a desire to seize power. He judged it a useful plan to pretend that he was arranging the marriage of his only daughter and, during the drinking, kill with poison all the senators whose authority he believed would obstruct his undertakings. The plot was exposed by his servants and avoided without punishment, lest, in the case of a powerful man, the discovery of the plot cause more trouble than its conception.

Foiled by this plan, Hanno prepared to undertake the crime through another device. He stirred up the slaves so that they might suddenly overwhelm the unwary city. But when he realized that he had been betrayed and forestalled before the appointed day of slaughter, he seized a certain fortress with twenty thousand armed slaves. While he was there inciting the Africans and the king of the Moors, he was captured. First he was beaten with rods; then his eyes were gouged out and his hands and legs broken, as though punishment were being exacted from each of his limbs; finally he was killed in the sight of the people. His body, torn by blows, was fastened to a cross. All his sons and relatives were handed over to punishment, lest anyone of the same family ever contemplate either imitating or avenging him.

These events took place during the time of Philip. During that period the philosopher Xenocrates was renowned. [Col. 1014A–1015A]

## CHAPTER XXI

**During the reign of Darius, whom Alexander killed, Jaddus, leader and priest of the Jews, expelled his brother Manasseh from the priesthood because he had married the daughter of the satrap of Samaria. On this occasion a temple was built on Mount Garizim, modeled on that of Jerusalem.**

Darius, son of Arsames, ruled for five years [alternative reading: six]. From the rebuilding of the temple, it was the one hundred and seventy-sixth year. Jaddus was the high priest of the Jews.

His brother was Manasseh, to whom Sanballat, a satrap sent by Darius to Samaria and a Cuthaean by descent, gave his daughter in marriage. The Cuthaeans, from whom the Samaritans also descend, and the leaders of the priesthood with the people, took offense at this. They thought that the former captivity had also arisen from such wicked marriages, because many had sinned in these matters by marrying provincial women.

They therefore ordered Manasseh to separate from his wife or not to enter the sanctuary. Manasseh, forbidden by his brother to approach the altar, went to his father-in-law Sanballat. Sanballat promised to give him not only the priesthood but also the chief authority of the priesthood, together with power and honor over all the places subject to him.

Accordingly, taking advantage of a suitable opportunity, he built for him a temple modeled on that of Jerusalem on Mount Garizim, which appeared broader than all the mountains of Samaria. He did this because he knew that Alexander was angry with Sanballat, the high priest, since Sanballat was not sending provisions to the army and was withholding from Alexander what he had previously supplied to Darius while Alexander was besieging Tyre.

For, having already despaired of Darius, Sanballat selected eight thousand of his own men and set out to join Alexander. He won Alexander’s favor and obtained from him permission to build the temple already mentioned. This also seemed useful in dividing the power of the Jews into two parts, lest the united nation rebel.

That temple remained, and whenever anyone had incurred guilt among the people of Jerusalem, whether through illicit food or transgression of the law, he withdrew to the Shechemites. The Jerusalemites who settled there lived among them. [Col. 1015B–C]

## CHAPTER XXII

**During these days Alexander, having obtained the kingdom of the Macedonians after the death of his father, carried out great and remarkable deeds among his own people, first defeated the Parthians in war, then, after subjugating Egypt and Syria, reached Jerusalem and left the temple unharmed and honored with gifts; afterward, destroying the forces of the Parthians in two battles, he finally killed Darius, being most cruel toward foreigners and impious toward his own relations.** [Col. 1015D]

Alexander, king of the Macedonians, succeeded his father Philip in the kingdom. He first displayed his spirit and courage by swiftly suppressing the disturbances of the Greeks. Their instigator, urging them to revolt from Macedonian rule, had been the orator Demosthenes, corrupted by Persian gold. Thus, when the Athenians begged for peace, he spared them and even relieved them of their great fear [Al.: of their fines]. He destroyed the Thebans, razing their city [Col. 1016A] [Al.: their city], and sold the survivors under the crown. He made the other cities of Achaea and Thessaly tributary. Then, transferring the war elsewhere, he subdued the Illyrians and Thracians. As he was preparing to depart for the Persian war, he killed all his relatives and close associates.

His army consisted of thirty-two thousand infantry, four thousand five hundred cavalry [Al.: two hundred], and one hundred eighty ships. With so small a force he conquered the whole world; whether it is more astonishing that he won, or that he dared to undertake the attempt, is uncertain. At his first encounter with King Darius, six hundred thousand Persians stood in battle array. They were defeated no less by Alexander’s skill than by the valor of the Macedonians, and turned their backs. There was therefore a great slaughter of the Persians. In Alexander’s army, however, only one hundred twenty [Col. 1016B] cavalry and nine infantry were lost.

Next he besieged, stormed, and captured Gordium, a city of Phrygia now called Sardis, and gave it over to plunder. Then Darius’s arrival with a large army was announced to him. Fearing the narrowness of the region in which he was situated, he crossed Mount Taurus with astonishing speed and, traversing five hundred stades in a single day’s march, came to Tarsus. There, while sweating, he descended into the very cold river Cydnus, became stiff with cold, and, through the contraction of his sinews, came close to death.

Meanwhile Darius advanced to battle with three hundred thousand infantry and one hundred thousand cavalry. This multitude of enemies alarmed even Alexander, especially when he considered the smallness of his own forces, although he had already learned, after defeating six hundred thousand enemies with the same small force, not merely not to fear battle [Col. 1016C] but even to hope for victory. Accordingly, when the two armies had taken their positions within missile range, and the commanders, running among the peoples intent upon the signal for battle, sharpened them with various exhortations, the battle began on both sides with immense courage. In it both kings—Alexander, of course, and Darius—were wounded, and the contest remained uncertain until Darius fled.

A slaughter of the Persians followed. Eighty thousand infantry and ten thousand cavalry were killed, and forty thousand were captured. Of the Macedonians, one hundred thirty infantry and one hundred fifty cavalry fell. In the Persian camp a great quantity of gold and other wealth was found. Among the camp prisoners were Darius’s mother, his wife, who was also his sister, and his two daughters. Although Darius offered even half his kingdom, he could not obtain their ransom. For a third time, therefore, having gathered all the Persian forces and the aid of their allies, he renewed the war.

While Darius was occupied with this, Alexander sent Parmenion with troops to attack the Persian fleet, while he himself set out for Syria. There, when many kings came voluntarily to meet him wearing their fillets, he adopted some, changed others, and destroyed others. From there he advanced toward Judaea and went up to Jerusalem. Jaddus, the high priest, came out to meet him wearing a hyacinth-colored and golden robe, with a turban and a golden plate upon his head. The other priests wore linen robes, and the rest of the multitude wore white garments.

For the Lord had shown the high priest in a dream that he could escape the king’s anger in this way [Col. 1017A]. Alexander alone approached, worshiped the name of God written on the golden plate, and was the first to honor the high priest. All the Jews greeted Alexander with one voice. The surrounding kings of Syria and the others were astonished to see him do this and thought that the king’s mind had been corrupted.

Parmenius alone asked him, saying: “Why, when everyone was worshiping him, did you yourself worship the high priest of the Jewish nation?”

He replied: “I did not worship him, but the God whose priestly office he administers. For, while I was still in the Macedonian city of Dium, I saw him in such a garb in a dream. And while I was considering whether I could conquer Asia, he urged me [Col. 1017B] not to hesitate but to advance boldly. He said that he would lead my army and deliver the power of the Persians into my hands. Therefore, when I saw no one else wearing such a robe and recognized this man, remembering the vision and the nocturnal confirmation, I greeted him. From that moment I believe that I was chosen with divine assistance, defeated Darius, and broke the power of the Persians. Moreover, I trust that everything I hope for in my heart will come to pass.”

After speaking with Parmenion, he honored the high priest and, with the other priests coming forward, proceeded as far as the city. He went up to the Temple and sacrificed to God, according to the high priest’s revelation. To the high priest himself and to the other priests he gave many generous gifts.

When a scroll of Daniel was presented to him, in which it was written that a certain Greek would destroy the power of the Persians, he supposed that he himself was the one whom Scripture signified. He summoned the Jews and ordered them to ask for whatever gifts they wished to receive. The high priest requested permission for them to live according to their ancestral laws and that the seventh year should be free from tribute. He granted everything.

Then, proceeding to the other cities, he attacked and captured Tyre, a most ancient and flourishing city that resisted him because it trusted in its Carthaginian kinsmen. Next he swept through Syria, Rhodes, and Egypt with stubborn fury. From there he went to the temple of Jupiter Ammon, intending, by arranging a lie for the moment, to erase the disgrace of his uncertain father and the infamy of his adulterous mother. For, having summoned the priest of the shrine, he secretly instructed him what answer he wished to receive as one consulting the oracle, as their historians relate [Col. 1017D].

Thus Alexander became certain—and revealed to us—that, with the gods themselves deaf and mute, either the priest has it in his power to invent whatever he wishes, or the consulter may choose whatever he prefers to hear.

Returning from Ammon, and preparing for a third war against the Persians, he founded Alexandria in Egypt. Darius, however, having abandoned hope of peace, brought forty-four thousand infantry and one hundred thousand cavalry into battle against Alexander as he returned from Egypt, near Tarsus.

There was no delay before the battle: all rushed blindly and furiously upon the weapons. The Macedonians were emboldened by the enemies they had so often defeated; the Persians, preferring death unless they won. Rarely in any battle was so much blood shed. But when Darius saw his men being defeated, although prepared to die in battle [Col. 1018A], he was compelled by the persuasion of his followers to flee.

In this battle the power and kingdoms of Asia collapsed, and the whole East passed under the authority of the Macedonian empire. The confidence of the Persians was so crushed in this war that afterward no one dared to rebel. The Persians patiently accepted the yoke of servitude after so many years of empire.

For thirty-four continuous days Alexander inspected the spoils of the camp. He invaded Persepolis, the capital of the Persian kingdom, a most famous and densely populated city, rich in the wealth of the whole world. When he learned that Darius was being held bound in golden fetters by his own relatives, he decided to pursue him. He therefore ordered the army to follow, while he himself set out with six thousand cavalry. On the way he found Darius abandoned, pierced by many wounds, breathing out the last breath of life through those wounds [Col. 1018B].

He ordered that the dead man be carried back and buried in the tombs of his ancestors, in an empty show of pity. Yet he held in cruel captivity not only Darius’s mother and wife, but even his little daughters.

Amid such a multitude of calamities, it is exceedingly difficult to believe that in three battles and as many years fifteen times one hundred thousand cavalry were destroyed—and indeed that these came from the kingdom and peoples from which, not many more than ten years earlier, nineteen times one hundred thousand are reported to have been routed. Besides these disasters, during those same three years many cities of Asia were crushed, all Syria was ravaged, Tyre destroyed, Cilicia emptied, Cappadocia subdued, and Egypt brought under control. The island of Rhodes, shaken into voluntary servitude, likewise submitted; many provinces beyond Taurus were subjected; and Mount Taurus itself, long refusing the yoke, was subdued, defeated, and forced to accept it.

And lest anyone should then [Al.: now] suppose that only the East had been subdued by Alexander’s strength, or that only Italy had been wearied by Roman unrest, at that same time war was also being waged in Greece by Agis, king of the Spartans; in Lucania by Alexander, king of Epirus; and in Scythia by Zophyrion, the governor.

Agis the Lacedaemonian, having stirred up all Greece to rebel with him, engaged Antipater with very strong forces. Amid the great slaughter on both sides, he too fell. Alexander, however, aspiring to rule the West in Italy and imitating Alexander the Great, was defeated by the Bruttians and Lucretians [Lucanians] after waging many serious wars there, and his body was sold for burial [Col. 1018D], as I mentioned above.

Zophyrion, governor of Pontus, gathered an army of thirty thousand and dared to make war upon the Scythians. He was slaughtered to the last man and utterly destroyed with all his forces.

After Darius was killed, as we have already stated, the Persian kingdom collapsed. The kingdom of the Alexandrians, that is, of Egypt, arose. Alexander the Macedonian ruled for five years. These five years are counted last in the sequence of the years during which he held the world’s monarchy; his first seven years are reckoned under the Persian kingdom. From the rebuilding of the Temple, it was the one hundred eighty-first year.

## CHAPTER XXIII

After Alexandria was founded in Egypt and the Persian empire destroyed, Alexander held the monarchy of the world for five years. He subdued very many peoples, invaded and conquered India, and crushed and captured the other inaccessible nations situated along the shores of Ocean. At last, returning to Babylon, he died after drinking poison.

Accordingly, after Darius’s death, Alexander the Great subdued the Hyrcanians and Mardi. While he was still intent upon war, Halestris, or Minothea, a shameless Amazon, came to him with three hundred women, stirred by the desire to bear offspring by him. After this he attacked the Parthians, who resisted him for a long time; he nearly annihilated them before he conquered them.

Then he attacked the Trancae, Evergetae, Parimae, Parapemeni, Adarpii [Col. 1019B], and the other peoples who lived at the foot of the Caucasus. He subdued them and founded there a city called Alexandria, situated on the river Danai [Tanais].

His cruelty toward his own people was no less than his fury toward the enemy. This is shown by the killing of his cousin Amyntas; the murder of his stepmother and brothers; the slaughter of Parmenion and Philotas; the destruction of Attalus, Eurylocus, Pausanias, and many other Macedonian leaders. Clitus too, advanced in years and an old friend, was wickedly killed.

At a banquet, relying upon the intimacy of royal friendship, Clitus defended the memory of Alexander’s father Philip, whose deeds he placed before those of the king. The offended king, in vain anger, pierced him with a spear and stained the common banquet with blood.

But Alexander was insatiable for human blood, whether that of enemies or even of allies, and always thirsted for fresh gore. Thus, rushing headlong into war, he accepted the submission of the Chorasmi and Dacae, an untamed people. He killed the philosopher Callisthenes, who had been his fellow student under Aristotle, along with many other leaders, because Callisthenes had abandoned the custom of greeting him and refused to worship him as a god [Al.: because he did not worship him as a god].

After this he invaded India, intending to extend his empire to the Ocean and the farthest East. He came to the city of Nysa, conquered Mount Daedalus and the kingdom of Queen Cleophilis. When she surrendered, she redeemed her kingdom by intercourse with him.

After traversing and conquering India, Alexander came to a rock of astonishing roughness and height, where many peoples had taken refuge. He learned that Hercules had been prevented by an earthquake from conquering that same rock. Moved by rivalry, and wishing to surpass the deeds of Hercules, he seized the rock with supreme toil and danger [Col. 1019D], and accepted the submission of all the peoples of the place.

He waged a most bloody war against Porus, the strongest king of the Indians. Alexander engaged Porus in single combat; when his horse had been killed and he was thrown from it, he escaped imminent death through the rush of his bodyguards. Porus, pierced by many wounds, was captured. Restoring him to his kingdom as a testimony to his valor [Al.: restoring him to the kingdom], Alexander founded two cities there, Nicaea and Bucephala, which he ordered to be called after the name of his horse.

Whoever wishes to know more fully what Alexander suffered in India, in inaccessible regions among monstrous beasts and serpents, and to learn about the golden house of the aforesaid King Porus, supported by golden columns of astonishing size [Col. 1020A], as well as the other marvels found there, should read through Alexander’s letter sent to his mother and to his teacher.

From there the Macedonians stormed the Adrestae, Cattheni, Persidae [Praesidae], and Candaridae after slaughtering their armies. When they came to the Chosidae, they joined battle there against two hundred thousand enemy cavalry. Although already worn down by old age, distressed in spirit, and exhausted in strength, they achieved a difficult victory and built a camp there, more magnificent than usual in memory of it.

Afterward Alexander proceeded to the river Agesines. He was carried along it into Ocean, where he crushed the Gressones and Siboi, whom Hercules had founded. From there he sailed past the Mandri and Subagri. These peoples came against him with eighty thousand armed infantry and sixty thousand cavalry. After battle was joined, the contest remained uncertain and bloody for a long time, and at last yielded the Macedonians a sorrowful, almost ruinous victory [Col. 1020B].

For after the enemy forces had been routed, Alexander led his army to the city. Having first climbed the wall, he thought the city empty and leapt inside alone. When hostile enemies surrounded him on every side, it is incredible to relate that neither the multitude of the enemy, nor the great force of their missiles, nor the uproar of those attacking him terrified him: alone, he killed and put to flight so many thousands.

But when he perceived that he was being overwhelmed by the surrounding multitude, he protected his rear with the barrier of the wall and held off his opponents more easily until, at the danger and outcry surrounding him, the entire army burst in through the breached walls.

In that battle an arrow pierced him beneath the breast. With his knee fixed, he continued fighting until he killed the man by whom he had been wounded [Col. 1020C].

Then, boarding ships and sailing along the shores of Ocean, he reached a city ruled by a certain King Ambira. During the attack on the city, he lost a large part of his army to arrows smeared with the enemies’ poison. Later, after a plant shown to him in a dream had been given as a drink to the wounded and they had been helped, he stormed and captured the city.

After what was almost a circuit had been completed [Al.: after the turning-point had been completed], he entered the river Indus from Ocean and quickly returned to Babylon. There envoys from the provinces terrified throughout the entire world were awaiting him—namely, from Carthage and all the cities of Africa, as well as from the Spaniards, Gauls, Sicily, and Sardinia, and from a very large part of Italy.

So great was the fear of the commander established in the far East that it had seized the peoples of the farthest West that one could see an embassy from the whole world arriving from there, though one could scarcely believe that the report had reached so far [Col. 1020D].

At Babylon, while still thirsting for blood, Alexander drank poison through the treachery of a servant, after his greed had been badly restrained, and died.

## CHAPTER XXIV

On the wars waged between the Romans and the Samnites and Gauls at the time when Alexander was ravaging the East, and on the manifold miseries produced by their mutual conflicts.

At the same time the following events were taking place among the Romans. When Fabius Maximus and Quintus Decius Mus were consuls, four of the strongest and most flourishing peoples of Italy joined together in a single army and alliance. The Etruscans, Umbrians, Samnites, and Gauls, conspiring in one force [Col. 1021A], attempted to destroy the Romans.

The Romans’ courage was shaken by this war and their confidence weakened. Not daring to rely wholly upon their strength, they divided the enemy by strategy, judging it safer to become involved in several wars than in great ones. Thus, after sending some of their own men ahead to devastate the hostile fields in Umbria and Etruria [or: in Etruria], and forcing the Umbrian and Etruscan army to return to defend its own territory, they hastened to engage the Samnites and Gauls.

In this war, when the Romans were hard pressed by the attack of the Gauls, the consul Decius was killed. Fabius nevertheless finally won after a great slaughter of Decius’s side. In that battle forty thousand Samnites or Gauls were killed, while seven thousand Romans fell; the destruction is reported to have been only among the contingent of Decius, who himself had been killed [Col. 1021B].

Livy reports that, apart from the Etruscans and Umbrians, whom the Romans summoned to the war by this stratagem [OCR uncertain], there were one hundred fifty thousand three hundred thirty Gallic and Samnite infantry, forty-seven thousand cavalry, and one thousand charioteers standing armed against the Roman battle line.

Pestilence burdened this bloody and sorrowful victory for the state, and the funeral processions of the dead that met them polluted the triumphal pageants. No one could be persuaded to rejoice in a triumph when the entire state either sighed over the sick or mourned the dead.

The following year the Romans, after the Samnites renewed the war, were defeated and fled into their camp. Later the Samnites adopted a new appearance and spirit: their weapons and garments were silver-plated, and they presented themselves to war with the resolve that, unless they won, they would die [Col. 1021C].

Against them the consul Papirius was sent with an army. When the pullarii augurs tried to prevent him from engaging on the basis of their empty predictions [Al.: the augurs who interpreted the sacred chickens], he mocked them and completed the war as successfully as he had undertaken it resolutely. Twelve thousand of the enemy were reportedly killed in this battle and three thousand captured.

The following year Fabius Gurges, as consul, fought unsuccessfully against the Samnites. After losing his army and being defeated, he fled back to Rome. When the Senate was therefore considering removing him, his father Fabius Maximus pleaded against his son’s disgrace and offered to go as his son’s lieutenant, provided that the son were granted the opportunity to remove the disgrace and wage the war again.

After this was granted and battle had been joined, the old and dutiful father saw his son the consul suddenly engaged in combat, surrounded by Pontius, the Samnite commander [Col. 1021D], and hemmed in by the enemy’s weapons. He rode into the middle of the battle line. Moved by this act, the Romans threw themselves into the entire battle until they captured Pontius himself, the enemy commander, after destroying and defeating his army.

Thirty thousand Samnites [Al.: thirty-five thousand] were killed in that battle, and four thousand, together with their king, were captured. At last the Samnite war, which had dragged on for forty-nine years with great Roman losses, was ended by the capture of the commander.

In the following year war was waged against the Sabines, with Curio as consul. There the consul himself displayed how many thousands of men had been killed and how many captured. When he wished to report in the Senate the extent of the Sabine land acquired and the multitude of the people [Col. 1022A] [Al.: add “of captives”], he was unable to state the number.

Then, when Dolabella and Domitius were consuls, the Lucanians, Bruttians, and Samnites, having formed an alliance with the Etruscans and Senonian Gauls, were preparing to revive the war against the Romans. The Romans sent envoys to appease the Gauls. When the Gauls killed them, the praetor Caecilius was sent with an army to avenge the death of the envoys and suppress the enemy’s uprising. He was overwhelmed by the Etruscans and Gauls and perished.

Seven military tribunes were also killed in that battle, many nobles slaughtered, and eighteen thousand Roman soldiers [Al.: fourteen thousand] fell in that war. Thus, whenever the Gauls rose up, Rome was worn down with all her resources.

## CHAPTER XXV

How Alexander obtained the monarchy, and among whom he cruelly divided the kingdom he had acquired; and what portion fell to each man.

Accordingly, in three battles Alexander routed fifty times one hundred thousand of the Persian forces. After killing Darius, he obtained Asia, subdued the Hyrcanians and other peoples, captured the rock of Ornus, and crossed the river Indus. He engaged in battle with Porus and Axile, the strongest kings of the Indians; gaining the upper hand, he conquered them and subdued India.

After he had been called lord of diverse nations, he died at Babylon in the thirty-second year of his life. For twelve years he had pressed the trembling world beneath him by the sword.

After Alexander’s death, the Macedonian commanders received different provinces by lot and consumed one another in mutual wars. Thus, throughout the entire Macedonian kingdom—that is, throughout all Asia, most of Europe, and the greater part of Libya [or: Libya and the greatest part of it]—suddenly terrifying storms of war converged.
