Although these wars ravaged the chief regions in which they broke out, they disturbed all the rest with a darkness of terror and rumor, like smoke. Thus the princes of Alexander tore apart in fourteen years the world that he had acquired swiftly and bravely. Like eager cubs tearing at a rich spoil brought down by a great lion, they destroyed one another, goaded into quarrels by rivalry over the prey.

Although I have also resolved from this point to trace the number of years and the succession of the kings of the Alexandrian—that is, Egyptian—kings down to the monarchy of Caesar Octavian, I shall now make clear which portions of Alexander’s empire his commanders obtained.

The first portion, Egypt, Africa, and part of Arabia, fell by lot to Ptolemy. Syria, adjoining this province, went to Laomedon of Mytilene; Cilicia to Philotas; Illyria to Philo. Acropatus was placed over Greater Media, and Perdiccas’s father-in-law over Lesser Media. The Susianian [Susiana] people were assigned to Scynus, and Greater Phrygia to Antigonus, son of Philip.

Nearchus received Lycia and Pamphylia; Cassander, Caria; Menander, Lydia. Leonnatus received Lesser Phrygia. Thrace and the regions of the Pontic Sea went to Lysimachus; Cappadocia with Paphlagonia was given to Eumenes.

The supreme command of the camp fell to Seleucus, son of Antiochus [Col. 1023A]. Cassander, son of Antipater, was placed over the king’s bodyguards and attendants. In Further Bactria and the regions of India, the former governors who had begun serving under Alexander remained in office.

Taxiles held the Seres, situated between the two rivers Hydaspes and Indus. Phytagon, son of Agenor, was sent to the colonies founded in Syria [Al.: India]. Oxyarches received the regions of the Caucasus. The Arachosians and Chedrosians were assigned to Sybirtus. Statanor received the Drangae and Arii; Amyntas, the Atrians [Bactrians]; Scytheus, the Sogdians; Itachanor [Nicanor], the Parthians; Philip, the Hyrcanians; Fratrafernes, the Armenians; Thlepolemus, the Persians; Peucestes, the Babylonians; Archoas, the Pelasgians; Archelaus, Mesopotamia.

## CHAPTER XXVI

After the death of Alexander, king of the Macedonians, his commanders consumed one another in mutual wars.

The cause and origin of the wars was a letter of King Alexander, in which he ordered all exiles to be restored to their country and liberty. The powerful men of the Greek cities, fearing that the exiles, once restored to liberty, would plan revenge, revolted from the Macedonian kingdom.

The Athenians were the first. They assembled an army of thirty thousand and two hundred ships and waged war against Antipater, to whom Greece had fallen by lot.

After this a very serious war arose between Antigonus and Perdiccas. Many provinces and islands were torn apart according to whether assistance was refused or supplied, and for a long time it was debated whether the war should be transferred to Macedonia or fought in Asia [Col. 1023C].

At last Perdiccas himself marched against Egypt with a huge army. Thus Macedonia, while its commanders moved in two directions, armed itself against its own vitals. Ptolemy, equipped with the forces of Egypt and the troops of Cyrene, prepared to meet Perdiccas in war.

Perdiccas engaged Ptolemy with the utmost bitterness. After losing his forces, he too was killed. Olympias, Alexander’s mother, was killed by Cassander, who had taken possession of Macedonia, after the slaughter of many leaders. Hercules, Alexander’s son, was placed in custody with his mother Roxana and, when he was already fourteen years old, was killed by the same Cassander.

Antigonus, however, engaging through his son Demetrius against Ptolemy, Cassander, and Lysimachus, who were supported by the alliance of Seleucus, was defeated in battle [Col. 1023D]. Ptolemy later fought Demetrius in a naval battle. After losing almost his entire fleet and army, he was defeated and fled to Egypt.

Elated by this victory, Antigonus ordered that he and his son Demetrius be called kings. All the others followed this example and assumed the royal name and dignity for themselves.

Ptolemy, Cassander, and the other commanders of the opposing faction, seeing that Antigonus was deceiving them one by one, confirmed one another by letters and agreed upon a time and place to meet together. They organized a war against Antigonus with their united forces.

Cassander, entangled in wars with neighboring peoples, sent Lysimachus, the most distinguished of all the commanders, with a large force to aid his allies on his behalf. Seleucus too, descending from Greater Asia, joined the war as a new enemy of Antigonus.

This Seleucus had indeed waged many wars throughout the East among the allies of the Macedonian kingdom. At the outset he stormed and captured Babylon by war. He subdued the Bactrians [Al.: Bactrian peoples], who were rising with new customs, and then crossed into India, which after Alexander’s death, as though its yoke had been removed and shaken from its neck, had killed his governors.

The forces of Ptolemy and his allies were therefore joined, and battle was begun. The more powerful their array, the heavier the ruin. For at that time almost all the strength of the Macedonian kingdom collapsed into that battle. Antigonus himself was killed in the fighting.

But the end of this war became the beginning of another. When the victors could not agree about the spoils, they were again divided into two agreements [Col. 1024B]: Seleucus joined Demetrius, and Ptolemy joined Lysimachus.

After Cassander died, his son Philip succeeded him. Thus new wars of Macedonia arose, as though from the beginning. Demetrius, son of Antigonus, elated by the enlargement of Greece and all Macedonia, planned to cross into Asia.

Ptolemy, Seleucus, and Lysimachus, having learned in their earlier struggle how great were the forces of concord, renewed their alliance. Joining their armies, they transferred the war to Europe against Demetrius.

King Pyrrhus of Epirus joined them as companion and ally in the war, hoping that Demetrius could be driven from Macedonia. His hope was not in vain: when Demetrius’s army was corrupted and Demetrius himself put to flight, Pyrrhus invaded the kingdom of Macedonia.

Lysimachus, who ruled the Hellespont, was stained by repeated acts of kin-murder after the killing of his son-in-law and the death of his son. He was abandoned by his own soldiers. They went over to Seleucus and urged him to make war on Lysimachus.

It was a spectacle of the foulest kind: two kings, Lysimachus seventy-four years old and Seleucus seventy-seven, meeting to seize one another’s kingdoms, standing in battle array, and bearing arms. This was the last war of Alexander’s fellow soldiers, preserved as an example of human misery. Although, after the death of thirty-four of Alexander’s commanders, they alone possessed the world, they did not look to the narrow limits of old age and their own lives. They imagined that the limits of the entire world were narrow for their empire.

In that war Lysimachus was killed last, after he had already lost or had killed fifteen children before the battle [Col. 1024D]. Thus the death of Lysimachus was the end of the Macedonian wars.

But Seleucus did not enjoy even so great a victory with impunity. After seventy-seven years he did not find rest in a natural death; instead, he brought his unhappy life to an end as though by premature death. Ptolemy, whose sister Lysimachus had married, pursued him; Seleucus was surrounded by treachery and killed.

Such were the dealings among parents, sons, brothers, and allies, in their exchanges of kinship and partnership.

In those same days, while the Carthaginians were waging continual and never sufficiently successful wars against the Sicilians and had surrounded Syracuse, then the most flourishing city of Sicily, with a siege, they were brought to the extremity of despair by Agathocles, king of Sicily, who outmaneuvered them with remarkable ingenuity.

While Agathocles was being besieged by the Carthaginians at Syracuse, and saw that he was neither a match for them in battle with the forces at his disposal nor able to endure the siege because his funds for pay were insufficient, he formed a well-planned and even better-concealed design. He crossed into Africa with his army. There he revealed what he was undertaking and then explained what had to be done.

Immediately, with one accord, they first burned the ships in which they had arrived, so that there might be no hope of retreat. Then he overthrew everything he encountered, burned farms and fortresses, and met a certain Hanno with thirty thousand Carthaginians. He killed Hanno with two thousand of his own men, while losing only two men himself in that war [Col. 1025B].

By this battle the courage of the Africans was astonishingly broken, while that of his own men was immensely increased. He stormed cities and fortresses, carried off immense spoils, and slaughtered many thousands of the enemy.

Then he established his camp at the fifth milestone from Carthage, so that the Carthaginians could watch from the walls of the city itself the losses of their extraordinarily wealthy possessions, the devastation of their fields, and the burning of their farms.

A still more grievous report was added to their present misfortunes: it was announced that an army with its African commander had been destroyed in Sicily. In fact, Andro, Agathocles’ brother, had overwhelmed it when it was careless and almost inactive.

When this news was spread throughout Africa, not only the tributary cities but also allied kings revolted from the Carthaginians. Among them, King Asellas of Cyrene agreed with Agathocles to share the war, while eagerly aspiring to the kingdom of Africa. But after they joined their armies and camps, Agathocles surrounded him with blandishments and treachery and killed him.

The Carthaginians gathered their forces from every direction and rose up for war. Agathocles, with Asellas’s forces beside him, engaged them and defeated them in a severe battle, with great bloodshed on both sides.

This crisis of battle brought such despair upon the Carthaginians that, if a mutiny had not broken out in Agathocles’ army, Hamilcar [Bomilcar], the Carthaginian commander, would have gone over to him with his army. For this offense he was fastened to a gallows in the middle of the forum by order of the Carthaginians and provided a cruel spectacle for his own people.

After Agathocles’s death, when the Carthaginians ravaged Sicily with a fleet, they were repeatedly defeated by land and sea by King Pyrrhus of Epirus, summoned from Italy; finally, they turned their attention to war against the Romans.

## CHAPTER XXVII

How Ptolemy, the successor of Alexander, captured Jerusalem by deceit and led many of the Jews captive with him into Egypt.

After Alexander, Ptolemy, son of Lagus, ruled Alexandria, as we have already stated, for forty years. He also captured Jerusalem by trickery and deception. He entered the city on the Sabbath under the pretext of offering sacrifice; the Jews did not resist him, because they considered nothing hostile to be intended and were therefore idle, unsuspecting, and sluggish [Col. 1026A].

After seizing the city without effort, he ruled them cruelly. Ovid Sabatarcides is a witness to my statement. In writing the deeds of Alexander’s successors, he reproached the Jews for the superstition on account of which they had lost their freedom, saying:

“There is a nation called Judaea, holding a fortified and great city, Jerusalem. It attempted to take up arms against King Ptolemy and, because of its excessive superstition, suffered the burden of having a most savage rule.”

Sabatarcides wrote these things about the Jewish nation.

Ptolemy, however, taking many captives from the mountainous regions of Judaea or from the neighboring areas around Jerusalem—that is, from Samaria or Agarizin—migrated to Egypt [Col. 1026B]. But when he learned that those whom he had led away from Jerusalem were steadfast in their oaths and worshipers of God, and that, when Alexander sent an embassy to them, they had replied that they would in no way take up arms against him while Darius lived, he assigned many of them to garrisons after Darius’s defeat. He established them as citizens of Alexandria alongside the Macedonians and received their pledge that they would preserve their alliance with his descendants.

Many other Jews also came voluntarily to Egypt, attracted by the wealth of the region and Ptolemy’s generosity. Their descendants raised disturbances against the Samaritans while striving to preserve the ancestral offering of their own people.

The Jerusalemites defended themselves by saying that their Temple was holy and that sacrifices ought to be sent there [Col. 1026C]. The Shechemites, however, ordered that they be directed to Mount Garizim.

At Jerusalem the high priest was Jonias, son of Joaddi. After his death, his son Simeon succeeded him.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

On the battles fought by the Tarentines against the Romans together with Pyrrhus, king of the Epirotes, who was the first to bring elephants with him into Italy, and on the various portents that occurred at that time; and how all Italy was then subjected to the Romans.

At this same time, when the Tarentines saw a Roman fleet passing by while they were attending a theatrical spectacle, they attacked and routed it. They dragged the damaged fleet into the harbor. The naval commanders were slaughtered; all who were fit for war were killed, and the rest were sold for money. For these reasons a great war broke out between the Romans and the Tarentines. This final necessity compelled the Romans to enlist even the proletarians—that is, those who in the City had always remained free for the purpose of producing offspring—and to enroll them for military service; for concern about offspring is futile unless provision is made for present circumstances. Accordingly, a Roman army under the consul Aemilius invaded the whole territory of the Tarentines, ravaged everything with fire and sword, captured very many towns, and cruelly avenged the outrage insolently inflicted upon it.

Immediately Pyrrhus greatly strengthened the Tarentines, who were supported by the garrisons of many neighboring peoples; indeed, because of the magnitude of his forces and plans, he transferred to himself the chief command and title of the war. Tarentum was a foundation of the Lacedaemonians, formerly the capital of Calabria, all Apulia, and Lucania—a city marvelous for its wealth, size, walls, harbor, and very location. Thus, wishing to vindicate the half-Greek city founded by the Lacedaemonians, Pyrrhus came with all the forces of Epirus, Thessaly, and Macedonia, bringing elephants previously unknown in that region, by sea and land, men, horses, and weapons, and adding to these the terror of wild beasts. Because of their size and ugliness, as well as their unfamiliar smell and trumpeting, the Roman horses were thrown into confusion in the first battle, under the consul Levinus. Suspecting that the beasts, unknown to them, were more terrifying than they really were, they fled and caused widespread slaughter.

This war was fought in Apulia; afterward the battle was fought more successfully at Asculum, under the consuls Curius and Fabricius. By then the terror of the beasts had worn off, and Gaius Numitius, a spearman of the Fourth Legion, having cut off the trunk of one elephant, had shown that the beasts could be killed. Accordingly, the elephants were assailed with spears, and torches hurled into their towers covered so many enemy ranks with blazing destruction. The slaughter ended only when night intervened; and, last among the fugitives, the king himself, wounded in the shoulder by his guards, fell in his armor. The commanders in the battle in Lucania were the same as above; but in war and peace, abroad and at home, Roman valor then proved itself in every respect. After that battle, when the terrifying Pyrrhus had understood the valor of the Romans, he concluded a treaty and, although victorious, wished to be received into their friendship; but the Senate refused him.

No other victory displayed more clearly than the Tarentine victory the courage of the Roman people, the wisdom of the Senate, and the greatness of its commanders; nor did any more splendid or magnificent triumph enter the City. Before that day the Romans had seen nothing except the cattle of the Volscians, the flocks of the Sabines, the wagons of the Gauls, and the broken weapons of the Samnites. Then, however, if one considers the captives: Molossians, Thessalians, Macedonians, Bruttians, Apulians, and Lucanians; if the procession: gold, purple, statues, paintings, and Tarentine luxuries.

But nothing did the Roman people look upon more gladly than those beasts which they had feared, together with their towers, now following the victorious horses with lowered necks, not without an awareness of their captivity. Thus, only in the fourth year after he had come, Pyrrhus fled defeated from Italy. At Argos, a most flourishing city of Achaea, he was misled by his desire for the Spartan kingdom and was killed in battle by a blow from a stone.

When the Tarentines learned of Pyrrhus’s death, they again stirred up a new war against the Romans. Through ambassadors they requested aid from the Carthaginians and received it. After battle was joined, the Romans were victorious. At that point the Carthaginians, although they had not yet been declared enemies, realized that they could nevertheless be defeated by the Romans. This development provided the occasion for wars and conflicts between the Africans and the Romans. Both peoples experienced these wars, which were prolonged for a long time and were exceedingly savage, although in the end the Romans emerged victorious after immense exertion.

After the disaster at Tarentum, the Picentes were defeated under the consul Sempronius; the Sallentines, added to the Picentes, were also defeated. Finally, the Volsinians, the wealthiest of the Etruscans, came under Roman allegiance. They implored aid from the Romans against their former slaves, who, after being granted freedom by their masters, had risen against them and, having transferred the state to themselves, exercised dominion. But these people too, by decree of the Senate and under the command of Fabius Gurges, suffered the penalties they deserved. Thus at last Italy was subjected and subdued by the Romans.

Although, while the events related above were taking place abroad, the Roman people was being afflicted at home by prolonged illnesses and various disasters, they were also terrified at that time by different prodigies. Blood, indeed, gushed forth from the earth, and gore flowed from the springs. Milk fell from the sky like rain. The earth also trembled when the Romans had drawn up for battle against the Picentes, standing within a spear’s throw of them. At that same time, when the census was held at Rome, 270,000 Roman citizens were found. Envoys from Alexandria, sent by Ptolemy, first obtained friendship at Rome. The cities of Ariminum and Beneventum were also founded by the Romans.

[Col. 1028C] Appius Claudius Caecus was renowned at Rome; he brought the Aqua Claudia into the City and paved the Appian Way. Serapis entered Alexandria. Sostratus of Cnidus also built a forum in Alexandria. Seleucus founded the cities of Antioch, Laodicea, Seleucia, Apamea, Edessa, Beroea, and Pela; he built Antioch in the twelfth year of his reign.

Accordingly, after Alexandria had been founded, as the capital of the Egyptian kingdom, Alexander the Great of Macedon reigned for five years, during which he obtained the world monarchy. The preceding seven years during which he had reigned before breaking the power of the Persians are not counted in the sequence.

Here, having shown the end of the Persian kingdom and Italy subjected to the rule of the Romans, I shall bring this book to an end. It contains approximately 186 years, from the rebuilding of the Temple to the death of Alexander the Great.

# BOOK FIVE

[Col. 1029]

## CHAPTER ONE

The narrative of how Ptolemy Philadelphus honored Eleazar, the high priest of the Jews, with gifts and honored the Temple; how he also released more than one hundred thousand Jewish captives; and how he summoned seventy of the wisest elders to come to him and ordered them to interpret the divine laws.

Ptolemy, also called Philadelphus, reigned for thirty-eight years. From the rebuilding of the Temple, 226 years had elapsed. The high priest of the Jews was Eleazar, who assumed this honor of the high-priesthood for the following reason.

When Onias, the high priest, died, his son Simon succeeded him. He was called “the Just” because of his devotion toward God and the favor he appeared to enjoy with the king. When Simon died, leaving behind a young son named Onias, his brother Eleazar assumed the office of the priesthood.

Ptolemy honored him generously with gifts. This happened as follows. Demetrius of Phalerum, placed in charge of the king’s library, was striving to collect and acquire every volume discovered throughout the world, whenever he heard of anything worthy of his own diligence or the king’s desire—since he knew that the king was generously devoted to the collection of books. When Ptolemy asked him how many volumes he possessed, he replied that he already had twenty thousand, but that within a short time they could reach fifty thousand. He also reported that many writings concerning the Jews’ laws existed among the Jews themselves, worthy of the king’s scholarly interest and royal library.

“Nothing prevents you,” he said, “from having them translated at your own expense, so that their laws too may be contained in your library.”

The king, therefore, delighted by Demetrius’s excellent proposal, wrote to the high priest of the Jewish people, ordering that this be done.

Aristeas, a close friend of the king, beloved by him because of his modest character, had often previously tried to ask Ptolemy to release the Jewish captives who were under his rule. Considering this a favorable time for his request, he first spoke to the chief bodyguards, Sosibius of Tarentum and Andreas. Strengthened by their approval, he approached the king and said:

“By no means, O king, should we be carelessly deceived by a vain hope; rather, we should disclose the truth. If, out of your favor, we wish not merely to transcribe the law of the Jews but also to interpret it, you have the means by which this can be done: so many Jews are serving in your kingdom, and the kindness of your magnificence requires that they be released from their present yoke of slavery and sent to the God who gave them their laws, for the protection of your kingdom.

“For, after investigating the matter many times, I have learned that they worship the God who made all things, whom we call Zeus—*Zena*—that is, Jupiter, because he grants *zen*, that is, life, to all. Therefore, in honor of the God whom they appease with the greatest devotion, restore them to freedom, to their homeland, and to their ancestral customs.

“Know, however, O prince, that I am neither related to them nor born from the same nation, so that I might be making this proposal on their behalf. Rather, knowing that God is the creator of all human beings, I have come to this request because I gladly embrace you as a benefactor.”

After Aristeas had spoken, and the king had looked upon him with a cheerful and smiling face, he said: “How many thousands do you think can be released?”

Andreas, who was present, replied: “A little more than one hundred thousand.”

“You are asking a substantial gift from us, Aristeas,” he said.

When Sosibius too, in the presence of the others, declared that it would be worthy of the king’s generosity to offer this act of thanksgiving to the God who had granted him his kingdom, the king gladly ordered that provisions be supplied as payment to the soldiers and that 120 drachmas be given for each captive held among them. He also promised to issue written instructions confirming both his generosity and Aristeas’s request.

Moreover, the will of God was present, by which he granted release not only to those who had been transferred by the king’s father or by his army, but also to those who were under his own rule. If any others had subsequently arrived, the king bestowed more than four hundred talents for their redemption. Of the captives and enslaved persons, he sent more than one hundred thousand back to Judaea. Those strong in body and of military age he assigned to military units; he also placed in the palace many who could be trusted to remain loyal to the court.

Therefore he sent Andreas, chief of his bodyguards, and Aristeas, his most beloved servants, to Jerusalem. Through them he presented the first offerings of his vows to the Temple of the Lord: twenty golden bowls, thirty silver bowls, five mixing bowls, and a table of marvelous workmanship inlaid with the most precious gems. He sent these vessels to be offered to God, together with one hundred talents for sacrifices and other necessities of the Temple.

He instructed Eleazar, the high priest, to select from every tribe six elders distinguished by wisdom and character—men who would bring him the law of God and, interpreting it carefully and prudently, translate it into the Greek language.

When the king’s letter had been delivered to Eleazar, he rejoiced exceedingly at the benevolent generosity expressed in it. He selected seventy elder men carrying the law and sent them quickly to the king, asking that, after the law had been copied, he return it carefully with the bearers.

[Col. 1030D] Thus they arrived at Alexandria. When Ptolemy heard that those whom he had sent, together with the seventy elders, were present, he immediately ordered the envoys Andreas and Aristeas to be brought in. They came, presented the letters they had brought from the high priest, and delivered the message he had instructed them to state orally.

When the elders arrived in the presence of Ptolemy with the gifts that the high priest had given them to bring to the king, and with volumes containing the laws written in letters of gold, the king questioned them about the books. When they unrolled and displayed the thinness of the parchment and its incomprehensible construction, the king marveled that the volumes had been assembled in such a manner.

After he had examined them for some time, he said: “I give thanks to you for coming, and even more to the one who sent you; but above all to God, whose revered laws these are shown to be.”

The elders and those who were present cried aloud, praying that prosperity might come to the king from God. The king was so delighted that he burst into tears. For nature often permits this in the case of supreme joy, just as it can also occur to those who are grieving.

He then ordered the books to be entrusted to the chief officials. After kissing the men, he said that it was proper first to address them concerning the matters for which they had been summoned. He also promised to celebrate every year, throughout the whole span of his life, the day on which they had been brought to him. It happened that the day of their arrival was also the day of his victory over Antigonus in a naval battle.

He ordered them to dine with him and announced that all accommodations in the citadel should be assigned to them. Nicanor, who was in charge of receiving foreign visitors, summoned Dorotheus, who had responsibility for them, and ordered him to prepare whatever each one required.

The king had arranged that the foods customary in the several cities should be provided, out of consideration for the habits of visitors who came to him, and that everything should be prepared for them so that they might take greater pleasure in their usual foods and perhaps not be troubled by unfamiliar ones.

This was also done for these men. Dorotheus, whom the king had appointed over the matter because of his integrity of life, prepared everything suitable for such banquets. He ordered them to recline in two groups: one group, half of them, on his right, and the remainder beyond his couch. He omitted nothing that could contribute to their honor.

After they had reclined in this fashion, he ordered Dorotheus to serve the customary foods used by all Jews who came to him. He then declined the sacred heralds, sacrificers, and other persons who perform vows, and asked one of the elders, a priest named Heliseus, to offer the prayer.

Standing in the midst, Heliseus prayed for good things for the king and his subjects. Applause arose amid the joy and acclamation of all. The king then ordered them, seated and engaged in feasting and enjoyment, to dine together with him.

Moreover, when the king thought the time appropriate, he began to philosophize, questioning each of them about natural matters and stimulating them to contemplate the questions. They answered and explained everything put before them carefully. Delighted, he continued the banquet for twelve days.

Anyone who wishes to know each of the things prepared at the banquet should read the volumes of Aristeas, which he wrote for this very purpose, and will learn them there. When the king saw that not only he but also the philosopher Menedemus marveled, he brought the banquet to an end.

The king said that their presence had brought him the greatest benefits, for it had profited him to learn from them how he ought to conduct himself.

He ordered talents to be given to each of them and appointed men to escort them to their lodging.

After three days had passed, Demetrius gathered them together and, crossing the bridge, went toward the northern districts. He held a meeting in a house standing near the shore and suitable for private consideration of affairs. Having brought them there, he asked that everything they required for interpreting the law be provided in their presence, so that they might complete the work without interruption.

They carried out their careful translation generously and laboriously, sitting at the task until the ninth hour, after which they turned their attention to the needs of the body. Dorotheus invited them and provided abundantly the wholesome things suitable for their way of life. In the morning they came to the palace, bringing many of the things prepared for the king, greeted Ptolemy, and returned again to the same place. There they washed their hands in the sea and purified themselves, and so devoted themselves to the interpretation of the law.

When the law had been transcribed, and the work of translation had been completed after seventy-two days, Demetrius gathered all the Jews together at the place where the translated laws had been produced. In the presence of the translators, he read them aloud.

The multitude praised the law and its elder interpreters, and also praised Demetrius, since he appeared to be the discoverer of great things. They further requested that copies be given to their rulers for reading. All the priests, interpreters, elders, and leaders of the people also asked that the translation remain well established and unaltered.

When everyone had approved the decision, they ordered that if anything appeared in the law to be superfluous or excessively expressed, they should examine it and, making the matter clear, correct it. They did this so that what had once been judged sound might remain sound in perpetual memory.

The king rejoiced, seeing that his desire had been brought to completion for a useful purpose. Delighted by the laws that had been left to him, and astonished at their meaning, wisdom, and the labor involved in producing them, he began to speak with Demetrius. He said that, although the legislation was so extraordinary, no historian or poet had ever remembered anything like it.

Demetrius replied that no one had dared to touch the written form of these laws because they were divine and venerable. He explained that Theopompus, wishing to write something about them in his history, had become mentally disturbed for more than thirty days and had humbly begged God’s forgiveness, suspecting that mercy had been shown him for this reason.

He had also seen in dreams that this had happened to him because he had examined the divine laws and wished to disclose them to impure men. When he stopped writing about them, he recovered his understanding.

Demetrius also told of Theotectus, the poet of tragedies. He said that, when Theotectus had tried to recall in a drama some of the things contained in the divine book, his sight became obscured. He recognized the cause of his blindness, and so, when God granted him forgiveness, he was released from his affliction.

The king received these accounts sincerely and asked that the interpreters frequently come from Judaea to him, saying that this would bring him honor and that gifts from him would benefit them. For the present, however, he said it was right to release them. If they came to him of their own accord, he promised to grant whatever it was proper for their wisdom to request and to give generously in accordance with his majesty.

At that time the king released them, giving each man the finest robes, two talents of gold, a cup worth one talent, and the entire furnishing of the banquet couch.

Through them he sent to Eleazar the high priest ten couches with silver feet, suitable furnishings, and a cup worth thirty talents; in addition, ten robes, purple cloth, a splendid crown, and one hundred linen garments made of byssus. He also sent two golden bowls, a ladle, libation vessels, and two golden mixing bowls, to be dedicated as vows to God.

He also asked him by letter that, if any of these men wished to return to him, he should permit it, since he took great pleasure in always conversing with learned men and gladly sharing his wealth with such people.

Such royal magnificence, to the honor and glory of the Jews, was displayed by Ptolemy, called Philadelphus.

They also obtained honor from the kings of Asia, since they camped with them. For Seleucus, called Nicanor, in the cities he had built throughout Asia, in Lower Syria, and in Antioch itself, the capital, granted them civic status and assigned them an honor equal to that enjoyed by the Macedonian and Greek inhabitants.

## CHAPTER II

The various battles fought by land and sea between the Romans and the Carthaginians, with countless numbers of men killed on both sides; these continuous wars of the wretched peoples lasted twenty-five years.

While the events described above were taking place under Ptolemy in Judaea and Egypt, the Romans sent the consul Appius Claudius to aid the Mamertines, who were requesting assistance against Hiero of Syracuse, a most powerful king, and against the Carthaginian forces that the king himself had hired.

He defeated the Syracusans and Carthaginians so quickly that the king himself, terrified by the magnitude of the events, declared that he had been defeated before he had even engaged in battle. When he begged for peace with his strength broken, he obtained it after being fined two hundred talents of silver.

The consuls had besieged Hannibal, the Carthaginian commander, in Agrigentum, a city of Sicily. Lack of supplies would have reduced him to the utmost poverty and destroyed him, had not Hanno, the new Carthaginian commander, intervened unexpectedly with 1,500 cavalry, 30,000 infantry, and thirty elephants, briefly delaying the capture of the city. But the city was captured soon afterward.

The Carthaginians were defeated and routed in a great battle; eleven elephants were brought under Roman control, and all the people of Agrigentum were sold under the auctioneer’s crown. The elder Hannibal escaped with a few companions.

When he later ravaged the Italian coast with a fleet of seventy ships, the Romans too ordered a fleet to be built and equipped, and the consul Duilius quickly fulfilled the order. For within forty days of the trees being felled, a fleet of 130 ships had been launched and stood at anchor.

The consul Cornelius Asina, having reached the island of Lipara, was captured by Hannibal through Punic treachery and killed in chains. When the other consul, Duilius, heard that he had been killed, he avenged him by engaging in a naval battle. Hannibal, seeing the destruction of his army, abandoned the ship on which he had been sailing and escaped in a boat. Hanno, who had been appointed in his place, was later killed by the consul Scipio.

From there, the Roman consul Calatinus, while advancing against Camarina, a city of Sicily, rashly led his army into narrow defiles that the Carthaginian forces had long since fortified. When he could neither resist nor escape, he was freed through the valor of Calpurnius Flamma.

The cities of Sicily were subjected to the Romans. When the consuls tried to transfer the war to Africa, they sailed toward Sicily with 330 ships. Hamilcar, the Carthaginian commander, and Hanno, commander of the fleet, met them. After a naval battle was joined, the Carthaginians were put to flight and lost sixty-four ships. The victorious consuls crossed into Africa and first of all received the city of Clupea into surrender.

From there, advancing toward Carthage, they ravaged 300 or more forts and carried hostile standards around Carthage. The consul Manlius, withdrawing from Africa with the victorious fleet, brought back to Rome 27,000 captives and enormous spoils.

Regulus, to whom the Carthaginian war had been assigned, marched with his army and established a camp not far from the river Bagradas. There, when a serpent of astonishing size was devouring many soldiers who had gone down to the river because they needed water, Regulus set out with his army to destroy the beast.

But when he saw that the arrows striking its back accomplished nothing, and that the impact of every weapon was futile—since the missiles slid across the dreadful lattice of its scales as if across an oblique shield-formation—and that the creature miraculously repelled them from its body without injury, while at the same time seeing a great multitude crushed by its bite and assault, and others killed even by its poisonous breath, he ordered ballistae to be brought forward. These, striking its spine with stones of the size used against walls, broke apart the structure of its entire body.

Thus the beast, which for so long had resisted so many arrows unharmed, was weakened by the blow of a single stone; soon surrounded by weapons, it was easily overcome. Its hide was carried to Rome. They say it measured 120 feet, and for some time it was a marvel to everyone.

Regulus waged a most savage war against three commanders: two Hasdrubals and Hamilcar, summoned from Sicily. In that battle 17,000 Carthaginians were killed, 5,000 were captured, eighteen elephants were brought in, and eighty-two towns surrendered to the Romans.

The Carthaginians, broken by wars and exhausted by disasters, asked Regulus for peace. But when they heard the intolerable and harsh conditions of peace, they judged it safer to die armed than to live in misery. Without paying the required price, they decided to obtain not only the Spanish and Gallic auxiliaries whom they had already had in great numbers, but also Greek forces.

Accordingly, they summoned Xanthippus, king of the Lacedaemonians, with auxiliary troops and placed him in command of the war. After inspecting the Carthaginian forces and leading them onto the plain, Xanthippus greatly improved their arrangements and engaged the Romans in battle.

There was an immense destruction of Roman strength. Thirty thousand Roman soldiers were struck down in that engagement. The commander Regulus, a man of noble birth, was captured with 500 men and thrown into chains. In the tenth year of the Punic War, he provided the Carthaginians with a famous triumph.

Xanthippus, conscious of having accomplished so bold a deed and fearing the instability of fortune, immediately departed from Africa for Greece.

Therefore, when the consuls Aemilius Paulus and Fulvius Nobilior heard of Regulus’s captivity and the defeat of the Roman army, they were ordered to cross into Africa with a fleet of 300 ships. They advanced against Clupea.

The Carthaginians immediately came there with an equal fleet. A naval battle could not be postponed. One hundred and four Carthaginian ships were sunk, and thirty were captured with their crews. In addition, 35,000 of their soldiers were killed. Of the Romans, nine ships were lost with all hands, and 1,100 soldiers perished.

The consuls established a camp near Clupea. The two Hannos, commanders of the Carthaginians, came there again with a large army; after battle was joined, they lost 9,000 soldiers.

But among the Romans prosperity was never lasting, for successes of any kind were immediately overwhelmed by great masses of misfortune. When the Roman fleet was returning to Italy laden with spoils, it was destroyed in a disastrous shipwreck. Of 300 ships, 220 were lost; only eighty were saved, and those barely, after their cargoes had been thrown overboard.

Then Hasdrubal, the new Carthaginian commander, came from Africa to Lilybaeum with 130 elephants and more than 30,000 cavalry and infantry. He immediately engaged in battle with the consul Metellus at Panormus.

Metellus, however, fearing the great force of the beasts, first—using great skill—drove them either to flight or to destruction, and thus easily overcame the enemy’s considerable strength. Twenty thousand Carthaginians were killed in that battle. Twenty-six elephants were also killed, and 104 were captured and led through Italy, providing the Italian peoples with a magnificent spectacle.

Hasdrubal fled to Lilybaeum with a few companions and, while absent, was condemned to death by the Carthaginians.

After this, exhausted by so many disasters, the Carthaginians decided that peace must be sought from the Romans. For this purpose they thought that Attilius Regulus, the Roman commander whom they had already held captive for five years, should be sent above all among the other envoys. When he returned from Italy without having obtained peace, they cut off his eyelids, bound him to a machine, and killed him by cutting his throat [variant: by keeping him awake].

Meanwhile Lutatius crossed to Sicily with a fleet of 300 ships. When he had engaged in battle near the city of Drepanum, he was pierced in the thigh and, when he was already being overwhelmed, was rescued after fighting most fiercely [variant: with the greatest difficulty].

The Carthaginians, for their part, came to Sicily with 400 ships and large forces under the command of Hanno. Lutatius was no less energetic; indeed, with astonishing speed he anticipated the Carthaginians’ plans.

After the two fleets had remained near one another by the Aegates Islands throughout the night, their anchors almost touching, at daybreak Lutatius was the first to give the signal for battle. As the battle grew fiercer, Hanno was defeated, turned his ship away, and was the first leader to flee. A considerable part of his army sailed with him toward Africa; others took refuge at Lilybaeum.

Sixty-three Punic ships were captured, 125 were sunk, 32,000 men were captured, and 14,000 were killed. Twelve Roman ships were sunk.

Lutatius then came to the city of Eryx, which the Carthaginians held, and there killed many Carthaginians in the battle that followed—[variant: 2,000].

Then the Carthaginians, in desperate haste, sent envoys to the consul Lutatius and afterward to Rome, begging for peace. They immediately obtained it on the conditions previously proposed. The conditions were that they should withdraw from Sicily and Sardinia and pay, for the expenses of the war, 3,000 talents of pure Euboean silver in equal installments over twenty years.

This peace settlement was concluded in the twenty-third year after the First Punic War had begun.

## CHAPTER III

The time when extraordinary fire and flooding nearly destroyed the City.

At that same time, various disasters of fire and water nearly consumed the City. The Tiber, swollen by unusually heavy rains and overflowing beyond expectation either in duration or in volume, destroyed all the buildings of Rome situated on low ground.

A fire also, whose origin was unknown, spread through many parts of the city and caused a pitiable destruction of people and houses. Then, after devastating everything around the Forum, it seized the temple of Vesta. The temporary fire extinguished the fire that was thought to be eternal.

During these days the silver coin was first minted in the City.

Antiochus, also called Soter, was then reigning in Syria and Asia after Seleucus. For Seleucus, after Demetrius had been captured in Sicily and the kingdom of Asia destroyed, had made one empire out of the two kingdoms, Asia and Syria.

## CHAPTER IV

During the reign of Ptolemy Euergetes, Jesus composed the Book of Wisdom, while Josephus so greatly won King Ptolemy’s favor that he was appointed commander not only of Judaea and Samaria but also of Syria and Phoenicia.

Ptolemy Euergetes reigned for twenty-six years. From the rebuilding of the Temple, 264 years had elapsed. Under him Jesus, son of Sirach, composed the Book of Wisdom.

After Eleazar’s death, his uncle Manasses assumed the office of the priesthood. When Manasses died, Onias succeeded him; he was the son of Simon, surnamed the Just. This Simon was Eleazar’s brother, as we said above.

Onias was childish in understanding and greedy for money. The royal tax for the people, which his ancestors had paid from their own resources—namely, twenty talents of money—he failed to deliver, and thereby provoked King Ptolemy to anger.

Through an envoy, the king accused Onias of withholding the taxes and threatened that, unless the customary payments were immediately made, he would measure out the land of the Jews by the yoke and send soldiers there to settle.

This caused the Jews great fear, although it did not at all move Onias, who was devoted to greed.

When Josephus, the son of Onias’s sister, learned of these events, he voluntarily offered himself as an envoy on behalf of the people. He was a very shrewd man and noble among his own people.

He won such favor with Ptolemy through his many services and acts of familiarity that he not only rescued his people from the impending danger but was also appointed commander of Judaea and of Lower Syria, or the neighboring regions. For twenty-two years he administered the taxes of Syria, Phoenicia, and Samaria.

He led the Jewish people from poverty and weakness to the most distinguished prosperity.

After Josephus died, the Jewish people suffered civil discord because of his sons. The elder sons, stirred by jealous resentment against Hyrcanus—the youngest of Josephus’s sons, because of his intelligence, energetic character, and the favor he had obtained with King Ptolemy—went to war against him, and the people became divided against one another.

Many supported the elder sons, together with Simon the high priest, who was their relative and kinsman. This Simon had assumed the office of the priesthood after the death of his father, Onias.

Hyrcanus therefore went down from Jerusalem across the Jordan. There he built an extremely strong tower, constructing it of white stone and carving it all the way down to the ground. He fortified the place with various animals and other marvelous structures and called it Tyre.

## CHAPTER V

At this time the Parthians withdrew from the yoke of the Macedonians, and the Romans lived peacefully for one year without war—something that had not happened to them for 450 years, that is, since the time of King Numa.

After this came the great and severe wars fought between the Romans and the Gauls, the Histri, and the Illyrians.

The Parthians, at that time, withdrew from Macedonian rule; their first king was Arsaces, from whom they were also called Arsacids. In Macedonia, Demetrius reigned after Antigonus. Among the Romans, after [Col. 1037D] the First Punic War, the Romans rested for a year without armed conflict, and the gates of Janus were closed—namely, after 450 years, that is, from the time of Numa, the successor of Romulus, under whom they had lived peacefully, until the aforesaid period.

In the following year, Roman envoys were killed by the Illyrians, and afterward a most savage war was waged against them. After many towns and peoples had been destroyed, the survivors surrendered to the consuls Fulvius and Posthumius. Then the Senate, greatly alarmed, learned of the revolt of Cisalpine Gaul and was also informed that a huge army was approaching from farther Gaul, especially the *Gestatores*—a name not of a nation but of Gallic mercenaries. Accordingly, the consuls, deeply shaken, concentrated the forces of all Italy [Col. 1038A] for the defense of the empire. It is reported that, once this had been done, there were 800,000 armed men in the armies of the two consuls, as the historian Fabius wrote, who took part in that war. Of these, 348,200 were Roman and Campanian infantry, and 26,600 cavalry; the rest were allied forces.

When battle was joined near Arretium, the consul Atilius was killed, and 8,000 Romans [alternatively, 7,800] were killed. They fled, although not even so large a part of their forces had been slain as ought to have terrified them. For historians report that 3,000 of them were killed on that occasion. This is all the more shameful and disgraceful because, after losing so few men, such great columns scattered in flight; for they showed that in their other victories they had prevailed not through strength of spirit but through the advantages gained from experience in war. Who, indeed, would believe that this [Col. 1038B] number had been present in the Roman army, let alone that it had fled?

After this, a second battle was fought with the Gauls, in which fully 40,000 Gauls were slaughtered. In the following year, the consuls Manlius Torquatus and Fulvius Flaccus were the first to lead Roman legions across the Po. There they fought the Insubrian Gauls: 23,000 were killed and 5,000 captured.

In the year immediately following this one, dreadful omens terrified the wretched city. Wretched indeed was the city that was frightened on one side by the roar of enemies and on the other by the wickedness of demons. In Picenum, a river flowed with blood; among the Etruscans, the sky appeared to be on fire; at Ariminum, a great bright light shone at night; and three moons appeared to have risen in different regions of the sky. At that time Caria and [Col. 1038C] the island of Rhodes were also so violently shaken by a great earthquake that, as roofs generally collapsed, that immense colossus too fell.

In the same year, the consul Flaminius, disregarding the auspices that forbade him to fight, engaged the Gauls and defeated them. In that war 9,000 Gauls were killed and 17,000 captured. After this, the consul Claudius destroyed 30,000 *Gestatores*. There he also killed their king, Judomar, who had advanced into the front line; and among the many Insubrian towns that he had compelled to surrender, he captured Mediolanum as well, a most flourishing city.

Then the Istri, new enemies, arose. The consuls Cornelius and Minucius subdued them, though at the cost of much Roman blood. In those days the poet Quintus Ennius flourished. Brought to Rome, he lived on the Aventine Hill, with very modest means and content with the service of [Col. 1038D] a single maidservant. The Stoic Zeno died, while Antigonus, the successor of Demetrius and king of the Macedonians, restored liberty to the Athenians.

## CHAPTER VI

During the reign of Ptolemy Philopator, 60,000 Jews were killed by Antiochus, and they suffered the events recorded in the Third Book of Maccabees.

Ptolemy Philopator, for 17 years. From the rebuilding of the temple, 290 years had passed. Under this ruler the Jews were likewise defeated, and 60,000 of them were killed by Antiochus, king of Syria. The events written about in the Third Book of Maccabees are also reported to have taken place.

At that time, therefore, the Jews happened to endure many misfortunes at the hands of Antiochus the Great, who ruled Asia, while their land was subject to various [Col. 1039A] calamities together with those who seemed to inhabit Lower Syria. When Antiochus fought against Ptolemy Eupator and his son Ptolemy, surnamed Epiphanes, the Jews suffered hardship; while Antiochus was victorious, they endured the same things, so that they were like passengers in a storm-tossed ship, since they were jointly caught between Antiochus’s prosperity and disaster.

After Antiochus had defeated Ptolemy, he captured Judaea and cruelly afflicted it. The high priest of the Jews was Onias, the son of Simon. To him Arius, king of the Spartans—that is, the Lacedaemonians—sent an embassy and letters stating that the Jews and the Lacedaemonians were descended from one lineage and had shared a bond of friendship with Abraham; [Col. 1039B] that it was therefore right for them to be brothers; and that they should request through envoys whatever was necessary and regard one another’s possessions as common.

The king of the Macedonians was Philip.

## CHAPTER VII

In those days Hannibal, the most hostile enemy of the Romans, set out from Spain with a large army and came into Italy. Remaining there continuously for thirteen years, he waged wars of such gravity and magnitude against the Romans and battered them almost to the point of utter despair. He was later recalled from Italy to Africa and defeated there by Scipio, although previously he had very often been victorious. While the Romans were being oppressed by a domestic enemy whom they could not endure in their homeland, they also undertook wars against various foreign peoples.

The Romans therefore suffered Hannibal, an enemy most hostile and intolerable [Col. 1039C], at that time. This came about as follows. The Carthaginians deeply resented that they had long been paying tribute to the masters of peoples and islands, although they had previously been accustomed to receive it. They burned with resentment that the sea had been taken from their noble people and the islands seized. Thus, as a boy, Hannibal swore vengeance at the altar of his father Hamilcar.

Saguntum, a noble and wealthy city of Spain and a friend of the Roman people, was chosen as the pretext for war. Hannibal, seeking causes for new disturbances, first attacked it in war, then surrounded it with a siege, tormented it with hunger, and finally destroyed it in the eighth month. He also most outrageously drove from his sight the envoys whom the Romans had sent on behalf of their allied city.

Then he crossed the Pyrenees and cut a path by the sword among the fiercest Gallic [Col. 1039D] peoples. On the ninth day he reached the Alps from the Pyrenees. There, while he defeated in battle the mountain Gauls who resisted his ascent, and cut through impassable cliffs with fire and iron, he remained for three days. Only on the fifth day did he reach the level ground with the greatest labor. His army is said to have then consisted of 100,000 infantry and 20,000 cavalry.

The consul Scipio was the first to meet Hannibal. When battle was joined near the Ticinus, Scipio himself was seriously wounded and escaped death at the hands of the Carthaginian commander through the intervention of his son, still wearing the *praetexta*—the man later surnamed Africanus. Almost the entire Roman army was killed there.

A battle was then fought under the same consul at the Trebia River [Col. 1040A], and again the Romans were defeated with equal disaster. The consul Sempronius, learning of his colleague’s misfortune, returned from Sicily with an army. Engaging the enemy similarly at the same river, he lost his army and escaped almost alone. Hannibal too was wounded in that battle.

Later, when Hannibal crossed into Etruria in early spring, he was overtaken by a storm on the summit of the Apennines. For two continuous days he and his army remained immobile, shut in and weighed down by snow, and froze. There a great number of men, many pack animals, and almost all the elephants perished from the severity of the cold.

Meanwhile the other Scipio, the consul Scipio’s brother, fought many battles in Spain. He also defeated and captured Mago, the Carthaginian commander.

At that time Rome was terrified by dreadful omens. The disk of the sun [Col. 1040B] appeared to diminish; at Arpi shields were seen in the sky; the sun seemed to fight with the moon at Capena; two moons rose during the day; in Sardinia two shields sweated blood; at Faleri the sky appeared to split open as though by a great chasm; and at Antium, while the people were harvesting, bloody ears of grain fell into the basket.

Hannibal, knowing that the consul Flaminius was alone in the camp and wishing to overwhelm him before he could prepare himself, set out in early spring and took the nearer but marshy road. At that time the Sarnus, swollen far beyond its banks, had left the fields hanging and broken apart. Of this it was said:

> … and the Sarnus, which waters the plains.

When Hannibal advanced with his army through these places, the mists—especially those exhaled from the marsh—prevented them from seeing ahead, and he lost a large part of his allies and pack animals [Col. 1040C]. He himself, riding the only elephant that had survived, barely escaped the difficulty of the journey. He also lost an eye, which had already been diseased for some time, through the violence of the cold, sleeplessness, and toil.

When he was near the camp of the consul Flaminius, he provoked Flaminius to battle by ravaging the surrounding regions. This battle took place at Lake Trasimene, where the Roman army, most disastrously surrounded by Hannibal’s stratagem, was utterly slaughtered.

The consul himself was also killed. It is reported that 25,000 Romans were killed in that battle and 6,000 captured. Of Hannibal’s army, 2,000 fell.

This was a famous contest at Lake Trasimene, especially because of the magnitude of the Roman disaster. The determination of the combatants [alternative: “the spirit of the combatants”] was so intense [Col. 1040D] that they did not notice at all the most violent earthquake, which happened at that very time and is said to have been so powerful that it destroyed cities, shifted mountains, split rocks, and forced rivers to flow backward.

After this, the consuls Lucius Aemilius and Terentius Varro were sent against Hannibal.

But because of the rashness of the consul Varro, almost all the forces of Roman hope perished most disastrously at Cannae, a village of Apulia. In that battle 44,000 Romans were killed. Although a large part of Hannibal’s army was also slain, the Romans were never brought to such utter destruction in any Punic war. For the consul Aemilius Paulus perished in that battle; twenty men of consular or praetorian rank were killed [Col. 1041A]; thirty senators were captured or slain; 300 noblemen, 40,000 infantrymen, and 3,500 cavalrymen also perished. The consul Varro fled to Venusia with fifty horsemen.

There is no doubt that that would have been the final day of the Roman state if Hannibal, immediately after his victory, had hastened to invade the city. As a token of his victory, Hannibal sent to Carthage three *modii* of gold rings, which he had stripped from the hands of slain Roman knights and senators.

So great was the final despair of the republic among the Romans who remained that the senators thought they should deliberate about abandoning Italy and seeking new settlements. This would have been approved at the urging of Caecilius Metellus had not Cornelius Scipio, then a [Col. 1041B] military tribune—the same man who was later called Africanus—deterred him with a drawn sword and instead compelled him to swear allegiance to his words in defense of his country.

The Romans, daring as though to breathe again from the underworld and recover hope of life, appointed the tenth dictator, Junius. He gathered four legions from every quarter, choosing men from the age of seventeen onward, for an immature and disorganized military force.

At that time he also compelled slaves of proven strength and willingness—or, if necessary, those purchased at public expense—under the title of liberty, to take the military oath [alternative addition: “those who offered themselves”]. They removed from the temples the weapons that were lacking, and private wealth was poured into the impoverished treasury. Thus the equestrian order and the trembling plebs, forgetting their private interests, acted together for the common good.

Accordingly, the dictator Junius, recalling an ancient measure adopted in Rome’s distress, issued, by edict, a levy to replenish [Col. 1041C] the army. As though an asylum had been opened, he promised immunity to all who were burdened by crimes or debts and enrolled them in military service. Their number was 6,000 men.

Campania—or rather, all Italy—revolted to Hannibal, since all hope of restoring the Roman state had completely been abandoned. After this, the praetor Lucius Posthumus was sent to fight the Gauls and was killed with his army.

Then, when Sempronius Gracchus and Quintus Fabius Maximus were consuls, Claudius Marcellus, designated proconsul after having served as praetor, defeated Hannibal’s army in battle and was the first, after such great disasters to the republic, to give hope that Hannibal could be overcome.

In Spain, the Scipios crushed Hasdrubal, the Carthaginian commander, in a most severe battle while he was preparing an army to march into Italy. They reduced his army by 35,000 men [Col. 1041D], either through slaughter or capture. They also won over the Celtiberian soldiers by payment; these were the first foreign troops whom the Romans began to keep in their camp, and they led them from the enemy alliance into their own camp.

The proconsul Sempronius Gracchus was led into an ambush by a certain Lucanian who was his guest and was killed. Centennius Paenula, a centurion, voluntarily requested that war be assigned to him against Hannibal. He was killed by Hannibal together with the 8,000 soldiers whom he had brought into battle. After him, the praetor Gnaeus Fulvius was defeated by Hannibal and, having lost his army, barely escaped.

At that time, when they were unable in any way to withstand one domestic war, three additional overseas wars were undertaken [Col. 1042A]: one in Macedonia against Philip, the most powerful king of Macedonia; another in Spain against Hasdrubal, Hannibal’s brother; and a third in Sardinia against the Sardinians and another Hasdrubal, commander of the Carthaginians. In addition to these there was the fourth war, that of Hannibal, by which they were being oppressed in Italy. Yet, through courageous perseverance amid mutual despair, they advanced toward better things. For in all these wars they fought in desperation, and by fighting they conquered.

In the tenth year after Hannibal had come into Italy, when Gnaeus Fulvius and Publius were consuls, Hannibal moved his army from Campania. After inflicting enormous devastation everywhere, he proceeded by way of the Sedicine and Suessan territories along the Latin road and encamped at the Anio River, three miles from the city. The whole city was seized by incredible fear. The Senate and people trembled with anxiety; matrons [Col. 1042B], maddened by terror, ran along the defenses, carried stones onto the walls, and eagerly desired to fight before the walls.

Hannibal himself advanced threateningly with his light-armed cavalry as far as the Colline Gate. Then he drew up all his forces for battle. The consuls Fulvius and the proconsul likewise did not refuse the fight. But when the opposing lines had been deployed and stood facing one another, with Rome before them as the prize of the victor, such a heavy rain mixed with hail suddenly poured from the clouds that the ranks were thrown into confusion and, scarcely able to retain their weapons, withdrew to their own camps.

Afterward, when clear weather returned and the forces and battle lines had gone out again onto the field, a violent storm once more restrained the courage of mortals with even greater fear and forced the terrified armies to flee back into their tents. Then [Col. 1042C] Hannibal, turning toward the region, is said to have remarked that sometimes the will, and sometimes the power, to take Rome was denied him.

In Spain, however, both Scipios were killed by Hasdrubal’s brother. In Campania, Capua was captured by the proconsul Quintus Fulvius. The leading men of Campania took their own lives with poison; and although the Roman Senate forbade it, Fulvius Sulpicius killed the entire Senate of Capua.

After the Scipios had been killed in Spain, while everyone hesitated in fear, Scipio, still a very young man, offered himself for the command. Since the treasury was short of money, and since Claudius Marcellus and Valerius Laevinus were then consuls, all the senators openly brought coined gold and silver into the public treasury before the quaestors. They left themselves and their sons nothing except one ring each and one *bulla* [Col. 1042D] each; and for their daughters and wives, only one ounce of gold and no more than one pound of silver apiece.

Scipio Africanus, at the age of twenty-three, received the proconsular command in Spain. With his mind especially intent on avenging his father and uncle, he crossed the Pyrenees and, in his first assault, captured New Carthage, where the Carthaginians kept enormous pay funds, strong garrisons, and great quantities of gold and silver. There he also captured Mago, Hannibal’s brother, and sent him to Rome with the others.

The consul Laevinus, returning from Macedonia, stormed Agrigentum, a city of Sicily. There he captured Hanno, commander of the Africans, accepted the surrender of forty cities, and stormed twenty-six. In Italy, Hannibal killed the proconsul Gnaeus Fulvius [Col. 1043A], eleven military tribunes, and 14,000 soldiers.

The consul Marcellus fought Hannibal for three successive days. On the first day they withdrew after an evenly matched battle; on the next, the consul was defeated; on the third, he was victorious, killed 8,000 of the enemy, and forced Hannibal himself, together with the survivors, to flee to his camp.

The consul Fabius Maximus stormed and captured Tarentum again, after it had revolted from the Romans. There he destroyed the enormous forces of Hannibal together with their commander, Carthalo, sold 30,000 captives, and paid the proceeds into the treasury.

In the following year, in Italy, the consul Claudius Marcellus was killed by Hannibal together with his army. In Spain, Scipio defeated the Carthaginian commander Hasdrubal and stripped his camp. In addition, he brought eighty cities under his power, either by surrender or by war. He sold the Africans under the crown [Col. 1043B] [as slaves], but released the Spaniards without payment.

Hannibal killed both consuls, Marcellus and Crispinus, after surrounding them in an ambush. When Hasdrubal, Hannibal’s brother, came from Spain through Gaul into Italy, having been ordered by the Carthaginians to join his forces to his brother’s and bringing with him substantial Spanish and Gallic auxiliaries, he descended from the Alps after hastening his arrival. The consuls learned of his approach, and before Hannibal knew what had happened, the Roman army intercepted and killed him with his entire army.

There 58,000 men from Hasdrubal’s army were killed and 5,400 captured. Among them, 3,000 Roman citizens were found and recovered. This was a consolation to the victorious consuls, for 13,000 [Col. 1043C] men from their army had also fallen. Hannibal’s brother Hasdrubal’s head was thrown before his camp.

When Hannibal saw it and learned at the same time of the Carthaginian defeat, in the thirteenth year after he had come into Italy, he fled to the Bruttians.

After this, a year appeared to pass in quiet between Hannibal and the Romans, without the tumult of war, because the camps were troubled by disease and both armies were being ravaged by a severe pestilence.

Meanwhile Scipio, having reduced all Spain from the Pyrenees to the Ocean into a province, came to Rome. He was elected consul with Lucius Crassus and crossed into Africa. There he killed Hanno, the son of Hamilcar and commander of the Carthaginians, and destroyed his army partly by slaughter and partly by capture. In that battle he killed 11,000 Carthaginians.

The consul Sempronius engaged Hannibal and was defeated, then fled. In [Col. 1043D] Africa, Scipio attacked the winter quarters of the Carthaginians and those of the Numidians, both of which were not far from Utica, and set them on fire at dead of night.

The Carthaginians, terrified and thinking that the fire had occurred by accident, rushed out unarmed to extinguish it. They were therefore easily overwhelmed by armed troops. In both camps, 40,000 men were consumed by fire and sword; 5,000 were captured. The commanders themselves were miserably burned and escaped only with difficulty. Hasdrubal, the commander, fled to Carthage.

Thus Syphax and Hasdrubal soon rebuilt a very large army. They again engaged Scipio, but were defeated and fled. Laelius and Masinissa captured the fleeing Syphax; the rest of the multitude fled to Cirta. Masinissa besieged and received it into surrender [Col. 1044A], then led Syphax, bound in chains, to Scipio. Scipio handed him over to Laelius to be led away, together with enormous spoils and very many captives.

Hannibal was sent back to Africa to aid the exhausted Carthaginians. Weeping, he left Italy, after killing all the Italian-born soldiers who were unwilling to follow him. When he was approaching the African shore, he ordered one of the sailors to climb the ship’s mast and look out to determine which land they were approaching. The sailor replied that he saw a ruined tomb.

Hannibal, horrified by the omen, changed course and landed his forces near the town of Leptis. After immediately restoring his army, he came to Carthage. Then he requested a conference with Scipio.

When the two most distinguished commanders had gazed at one another for a long time, astonished and mutually admiring, the negotiations for peace failed and battle was joined [Col. 1044B]. It had been arranged through the great skill of the commanders, conducted with the great masses of their armies, and brought to completion through the great strength of the soldiers; it brought victory to the Romans.

Eighty elephants were either captured or killed there. Twenty thousand Carthaginians were killed. Hannibal, experienced above all in war and in battle, escaped amid the tumult with a few men—scarcely four horsemen—and fled to Rumetum [place-name uncertain in the supplied text].

Afterward, thirty-six years after he had left Carthage as a small boy with his father, Hannibal returned there. He persuaded the deliberating Senate that no hope remained except to seek peace.

When Gaius Cornelius Lentulus and Publius Eliopetus were consuls, peace was granted to the Carthaginians through Scipio, with the consent of the Senate and the Roman people. Nevertheless, more than 500 ships were taken out to sea and burned in sight of the city.

Scipio, already [Col. 1044C] surnamed Africanus, entered Rome in triumph. Terence, who later became a comic playwright, a noble Carthaginian captive wearing the cap—the emblem of the liberty granted to him—followed his triumphal chariot.

The comic poet Naevius died at Utica, driven from Rome by the faction of the nobles, especially the Metelli. Plautus died at Rome. Because of the difficulty of obtaining grain, he had hired himself out to a baker to turn the hand-mills. Whenever he was free from work, he used to write plays and sell them.

## CHAPTER VIII

King Ptolemy Epiphanes, through his commander named Scopas, brought Lower Syria, Judaea, and Samaria under his rule—regions that Antiochus had recently taken from his authority. Again, after defeating Scopas, Antiochus subjected those same regions to his own [Col. 1044D] rule.

Ptolemy, also called Epiphanes, for 24 years. Under Ptolemy the martyrs of the Maccabees were crowned. During his reign the events contained in the history of the Second Book of Maccabees took place. From the rebuilding of the temple, 307 years had passed. The high priest of the Jews was Onias, the same man mentioned above.

When Ptolemy Epiphanes’s father Philopator died, Ptolemy sent a powerful army under a commander named Scopas against Lower Syria and captured many of its cities. Among them he conquered the Jewish people in war and received them under his rule, although Antiochus had recently allied them to himself after defeating Ptolemy Philopator.

Not long afterward, Antiochus defeated Scopas, engaging him near the source of the Jordan and striking down many of [Col. 1045A] his army. Later, when Antiochus captured Samaria and the cities of Syria that Scopas had held, the Jewish people voluntarily transferred their allegiance to him. They received his entire army into the city, supplied abundant provisions for his elephants, and willingly assisted him as he besieged the garrison left by Scopas in the citadel of Jerusalem.

Antiochus therefore judged that the Jews’ devotion toward him ought to be generously rewarded. He wrote to the magistrates and his friends, bearing witness that he had been well treated by them. He also openly informed them of the gifts that he intended to grant them as a favor: namely, that they should rebuild the ruined city and gather its scattered inhabitants into it.

For sacrifices, offerings of wine and oil, and incense, he ordered 20,000 [Col. 1045B] silver pieces to be provided; for fine flour, 1,475 *modii* of wheat; and for salt, 375 *modii*. For the temple porticoes and the other buildings that had collapsed, he granted timber from Lebanon.

He permitted the entire Jewish people to live according to their own laws. He released the priests, scribes of the temple, and sacred singers from the taxes that they paid for their own persons. Those who had been enslaved from the city itself, together with their children, he gave their freedom, and he ordered their possessions to be restored to them.

He sent an edict throughout his empire for the adornment of the temple. It declared that no foreigner was permitted to enter within the temple walls; that no Jew might enter unless purified according to the ancestral law; and that the meat of animals forbidden to the Jews [Col. 1045C] was not to be brought into the city. They were permitted to use the customary practices of their ancestors, which divine law had judged appropriate for sacrifice to God.

Concerning these events among the Jews at that time, Polybius of Megalopolis says the following in Book XI of his history:

> Scopas, the commander of Ptolemy, advancing into the upper regions, defeated the Jewish people in winter. In the same volume he also says how Antiochus, after conquering Scopas, captured Bathania, Samaria, Abella, and Cedar. Shortly afterward, the Jews who lived around the temple surrendered to him. Later, when Ptolemy made friendship and a treaty with Antiochus, he gave him his daughter Cleopatra in marriage and granted him Lower Syria, Samaria, Judaea, and Phoenicia as her dowry.

## CHAPTER IX [Col. 1045D]

An account of how Philip, king of the Macedonians, was defeated by the Romans and gave his son Demetrius as a hostage. Likewise, how Nauides, commander of the Athenians, was defeated by the Romans and gave his son Armenes as a hostage. Various nations were subjected to the Romans together with these. Antiochus, king of Syria, was also twice defeated with all his forces and compelled to pay tribute by land and sea.

Among the Romans, in those same days, the Second Punic War ended. The Macedonian War immediately followed it. The consul Quintus Flamininus received command of it and, after many very serious battles in which the Macedonians were defeated, granted peace to their king Philip.

Then he fought against Lacedaemon. After defeating their commander, Nauides, he led the noblest hostages before his chariot: Demetrius, Philip’s son, and Armenes, Nauides’ son.

The Roman [Col. 1046A] captives who had been sold throughout Greece under Hannibal were all recovered. With their heads shaved as a sign that their servitude had been removed, they followed the triumphal chariot.

At that time the Insubrian Boii and the Cenomani, having united their forces with Hamilcar, the Carthaginian commander who had remained in Italy, ravaged Cremona and Placentia. They were defeated in a very difficult war by the praetor Lucius Fulvius.

Afterward, the proconsul Flamininus defeated King Philip in battle, together with the Thracians, Macedonians, Illyrians, and many other peoples who had come to his aid. The defeated Macedonians lost their camp. Livy writes that 8,000 of the enemy were killed that day and 5,000 captured. Valerius says that 40,000 were slaughtered, while Claudius records that 32,000 were killed.

King Antiochus of Syria, therefore, preparing war against the Roman people, crossed from Asia into Europe. At that time Hannibal, because rumors were circulating among the Romans that he was fomenting war, was ordered to appear before the Roman [Col. 1046B] Senate. He secretly departed from Africa and went over to Antiochus.

When Scipio Africanus, who had been sent among the other envoys to Antiochus, found Hannibal at Ephesus, he also held a friendly conversation with him. But when the negotiations for peace had failed, Hannibal withdrew from Antiochus.

In both Spains, the praetors Flamininus and Fulvius waged wars that were extremely savage and bloody for both peoples.

When Publius Cornelius Scipio and Marcus Acilius Glabrio were consuls, Antiochus occupied Thermopylae, hoping that its fortifications would make him safer amid the uncertain outcomes of war. Nevertheless, when battle was joined, he was defeated by the consul [Col. 1046C] Glabrio and barely escaped from the battle with a few men, reaching Ephesus.

He is said to have had 60,000 armed men; of these, 40,000 were killed and more than 5,000 captured.

The other consul, Scipio, engaged the Boii. In that battle he killed 20,000 of the enemy.

In the following year, Scipio Africanus, assisted by Eumenes, son of Attalus, fought a naval battle against Hannibal, who at that time was in command of Antiochus’s fleet. Antiochus was defeated, Hannibal was put to flight, and his entire army was lost. Antiochus requested peace and obtained it on these terms: every year he would pay the Romans 1,000 talents as tribute, and he would voluntarily return Africanus’s son, whom it is uncertain whether he had captured while scouting or in battle.

At the same time, Africanus, living in prolonged exile from the city that had shown him no gratitude [Col. 1046D], died of illness near the town of Amiternum. In those same days, Hannibal killed himself with poison at the court of Prusias, king of Bithynia, when the Romans were demanding that he be handed over.

At that time, in Sicily, an island of Vulcan suddenly rose from the sea, an island that had not existed before. To everyone’s amazement, it remains there to this day.

Titus Livius, the writer of tragedies, was considered distinguished in those days. Because of his talent, he was granted freedom by Livius Salinator, whose children he was educating.

## CHAPTER X
