How Antiochus occupied Egypt but, terrified when the Romans warned him, withdrew from it; how he then went to Jerusalem, plundered the temple, set up an altar there, and polluted it with unclean sacrifices; how he devastated and destroyed the city [Col. 1047A], built a citadel in it to house Macedonian guards, led part of the people away captive, and put another part to the sword; how he compelled the survivors to live according to the customs of the nations and ordered those who resisted to be subjected to various punishments; and from what source this evil was believed to have begun [the supplied source ends here].

Source preparation: Embedded foreign-language text recovered from the supplied local archive where present; translated as part of this section.

Ptolemy Philometor reigned for 35 years. From the rebuilding of the Temple, however, 331 years had passed. Perseus was king of the Macedonians.

When Seleucus, king of Syria, died, his brother Antiochus took over the reins of the kingdom; he was called Epiphanes. Ptolemy, king of the Egyptians, who was likewise called Epiphanes, also died, leaving two sons who were still under age. One of them, the elder, whom we have just mentioned, was called Philometor; the younger was called Physcon.

Antiochus, [Col. 1047B] planning to lead an army into Egypt for the successful advancement of his power, was drawn by his desire for that kingdom and by the fact that Ptolemy’s sons were weak and entirely incapable of managing so great an affair. Accordingly, he reached Pelusium with a powerful force and, deceiving Ptolemy Philometor by trickery, seized Egypt. When he had reached the district of Memphis, he captured it and proceeded toward Alexandria, intending to besiege Ptolemy and capture him.

He was expelled, however, not only from Alexandria but also from the whole of Egypt, when the Romans ordered him to withdraw from the province.

At about the same time, when Onias, the chief priest, had died, Antiochus granted the chief priesthood to his brother. For the son whom Onias had left was still an infant. But the king, angered against Jesus, who was Onias’s brother, removed the chief priesthood from him and [Col. 1047C] gave it to their younger brother, whose name was Onias. Thus, as we have already said, the chief priesthood passed to the three sons of Simon.

Jesus, for his part, called himself Jason. Onias, however, was called Menelaus. The chief priest Jesus therefore stirred up a revolt against Menelaus, and when the people were divided between the two, the greater part supported Jason. Consequently, Menelaus and those who agreed with him, being hard pressed, withdrew to Antiochus.

They also informed him that they wished to abandon the laws of their ancestors and to observe the way of life and customs of the Greeks. They asked him to permit them to build a gymnasium in Jerusalem. When he granted this, they concealed their circumcision so that, [Col. 1047D] when naked, they would not appear different from the Greeks. Abandoning everything else that their ancestral custom imposed upon them, they followed the practices and rites of other nations.

Thus these revolts, which were disgracefully carried on among the brothers mentioned above because of ambition and the dignity of the highest priesthood, and the dissensions that were cruelly enacted between Hyrcanus, the son of Josephus—whom we mentioned above—and his brothers, produced among the Jewish people the greatest seeds of calamity. While calling the arms of foreigners against themselves, they tore apart their own entrails; while some summoned Seleucus and his officials, and others Antiochus, his successor, for the desolation of the Temple and the ruin of the people, as we have already related.

Accordingly, King Antiochus, returning from Egypt because of fear of the Romans, led his army against [Col. 1048A] the city of Jerusalem. When he arrived there, he captured it in a certain engagement, since those who consented to his will opened the gates to him. After entering the city of Jerusalem, he killed many who held opinions contrary to his own; he also killed those who had opened the gates and handed the city over to him, because of the Temple’s wealth. Carrying off large sums of money from the Temple, he returned to Antioch.

After he had stripped the Temple—so that he carried away the vessels of God, the golden lamps, the golden altar, the table, and the sanctuary—and had not even spared the curtains, which were made of fine linen, purple, and scarlet, he also emptied the treasuries, leaving absolutely nothing behind. In this way he brought the Jews into the deepest mourning on account of what had happened.

[Col. 1048B] He also prohibited the daily sacrifices that they offered to God according to the laws from being celebrated. Plundering the whole city, he killed some and led others into captivity with their wives and children, so that the number of captives was said to have reached 10,000. He also burned its finest places and, demolishing the walls, built a citadel in the inner part of the city. It had previously stood high above the Temple and was more elevated than it; therefore he fortified it with high walls and towers and stationed a Macedonian garrison there.

Impious and morally corrupt men also remained in the citadel, and from them the citizens repeatedly suffered many bitter afflictions. He built an altar in the sanctuary as well, and sacrificed pigs upon it—victims that were unlawful and contrary to the ancestral religion of the Jews.

[Col. 1048C] He also compelled them to abandon their ancestral religion, worship an idol, and build Jewish temples in every city and village. He ordered them to set up altars and sacrifice pigs upon them every day, and he forbade anyone to be circumcised. He also threatened the severest tortures if anyone were found carrying out such practices. He therefore appointed officials to compel them to fulfill the imperial commands.

Many Jews followed the king’s orders willingly; others did so because of fear of the threatening king. But the most upright and noble, abhorring the detestable crime, adhered to the laws of their ancestors. For this reason they were afflicted with punishments day after day; they endured bitter tortures and were killed. Beaten and exhausted by various torments, they were fastened alive to the cross.

[Col. 1048D] Their wives and children likewise, whom they had circumcised, were strangled because of the king’s command, being bound by their necks to those of their parents. Moreover, if a sacred scroll or a copy of the Law were found in anyone’s possession, that person died a cruel death.

## CHAPTER XI

In these days the Romans slaughtered countless multitudes of people in Spain and destroyed more than 300 towns. The Macedonian War, which deservedly must be counted among the greatest wars, was also fought at that time. The Third Punic War likewise arose. When it was concluded, Carthage was utterly destroyed by fire and sword, in the six hundredth year after its foundation.

[Col. 1049A] At that time, among the Romans, Fulvius Flaccus, praetor in Hither Spain, defeated 23,000 men in a great battle and captured 4,000. After him, Sempronius Gracchus in Further Spain forced 105 towns, emptied and shaken by wars, to surrender. Then Lucius Postumius killed 40,000 enemies in battle in Hither Spain, while the praetor Gracchus again stormed and captured 200 towns there.

In those same days the Macedonian War was fought, deservedly to be reckoned among the greatest wars. Perseus, son of Philip, whom the Macedonians followed, had the Thracians as auxiliaries, with their king Cotys, and all the Illyrians, with their king Gentius.

The people of the Bastarnae, enticed by the hope of plunder and hastening to his aid, were destroyed without any battle or enemy. While crossing the Danube with their entire army over the ice, the ice, cracking beneath the enormous weight, split apart. The frozen crust, unable to bear the whole army that it had long supported, collapsed and broke up, abandoning them in the midst of the waters; then, when fragments blocked their way, it closed over them again and submerged them. Only a few of all the people barely escaped, with their entrails torn, to either bank.

[Col. 1049B] On the Roman side, first all Italy, then Ptolemy, king of Egypt, Ariarathes of Cappadocia, Eumenes of Asia, and Masinissa of Numidia provided assistance. When Crassus arrived, Perseus confronted him, and in the ensuing battle the Romans were miserably defeated. In the following battle, after almost equal losses on both sides, the armies withdrew into winter quarters.

Afterward Perseus, having routed the Roman army in many battles, crossed into Illyricum. By fighting, he captured the town of Sulcium, which was defended by Roman garrisons. There he killed many of the Roman garrison, sold some under the crown, and took others with him to Macedonia. Later the consul Aemilius Paulus fought against him and won. He killed 20,000 infantry in that war. The king fled with his cavalry, but was soon captured and led in triumph before the chariot with his sons. Later he died in confinement at Alba.

His younger son learned the craft of metalworking at Rome in order to endure poverty, and there he perished. Many other wars, with very different outcomes, were fought everywhere among numerous peoples; I have omitted them for the sake of brevity.

[Col. 1049C] When a great fear of the Celtiberians had seized all the Romans, and no one among them—neither soldier nor legate—dared to go to Spain, P. Scipio, who was later called Africanus, voluntarily offered to serve in Spain, although he had already been assigned by lot to Macedonia. He therefore departed for Spain and inflicted great slaughter upon the peoples. He more often performed the duty of a soldier than of a commander. He even killed a barbarian who challenged him to single combat.

The praetor Sergius Galba, however, was defeated by the Lusitanians in a great battle. After losing his entire army, he himself barely escaped with a few men.

[Col. 1049D] At that time the censors decreed that a stone theater should be built in the city. Scipio Nasica opposed this with a most forceful speech, saying that it would be utterly hostile to a warlike people, encouraging idleness and serving as an invention of wantonness. He so influenced the Senate that it ordered not only that everything acquired for the theater be sold, but also that benches for public games be prohibited.

The Third Punic War then arose. When the Senate had voted that Carthage must be destroyed, the consuls set out for Africa, and Scipio, then a military tribune and, as they say, the son of the elder Africanus, established a camp near Utica.

[Col. 1050A] There, summoning the Carthaginians, he ordered them to surrender their weapons and ships. Without delay, such a quantity of weapons was handed over that all Africa could easily have been armed from them. But after the Carthaginians had surrendered their weapons and had been ordered to withdraw from the city to a place 10,000 paces from the sea, they were driven by grief to desperation. They resolved either to defend their city or to be buried with it and through it. They chose two commanders, both named Hasdrubal.

They first began to manufacture weapons, making up for their lack of bronze and iron with supplies of gold and silver. The consuls decided to attack Carthage, whose location is said to have been as follows.

[Col. 1050B] The city extended for 22,000 paces along its walls and was almost entirely surrounded by the sea, except for an inlet 3,000 paces wide. At that point the wall was 30 feet thick and 40 cubits high, built of squared stone. The citadel, called Byrsa, occupied somewhat more than 2,000 paces. On one side the wall overlooked the sea, which they call a lagoon because it is constricted by the projection of an extended tongue of land.

Although the consuls had demolished part of the wall by battering it with siege engines, they were nevertheless defeated and driven back by the Carthaginians. When they fled, Scipio protected them after forcing the enemy back inside the walls. Censorinus returned to the city, while Manilius, abandoning Carthage, turned his arms against Hasdrubal.

[Col. 1050C] After Masinissa died, Scipio divided the kingdom of Numidia among Masinissa’s three sons. Thereupon Manilius returned to Carthage, stormed and plundered the city of Degaza: 12,000 Africans were killed there and 6,000 were captured.

Hasdrubal, commander of the Carthaginians and grandson of Masinissa, was killed in the senate-house by his own men with fragments of benches, because they suspected him of treachery.

The praetor Juventius, engaging in Macedonia against Pseudo-Philip, was killed with the greatest disaster suffered by the entire Roman army, in the six hundredth year from the founding of the City.

[Col. 1050D] After the Second Punic War, during the consulship of Gnaeus Cornelius Lentulus and Lucius Mummius, Scipio, the consul of the preceding year, undertook the final destruction of Carthage and entered Gothon. After fighting there continuously for six days and nights, the Carthaginians’ ultimate despair drove them to surrender. They asked that, since the disaster of war had left some of them alive, they might at least be permitted to serve.

First a sufficiently pitiable procession of women descended, followed by one more wretched still of the men. For tradition records that there were 25,000 women and 30,000 men. King Hasdrubal surrendered voluntarily.

The deserters who had occupied the Temple of Aesculapius consumed themselves by a voluntary leap into the fire. Hasdrubal’s wife, together with her two sons, threw herself into the midst of the flames, with a man’s grief and a woman’s fury, giving herself the same end in death that the first queen of Carthage had once given herself. She was the final queen of Carthage.

[Col. 1051A] The city itself burned for seventeen continuous days and offered its conquerors a wretched spectacle of the varying condition of human affairs. Carthage was destroyed, every piece of its wall-stone being crushed into dust, in the seven hundredth year after its foundation. The entire multitude of captives, except for a few leading men, was sold.

Thus, in the fourth year after the war had begun, the Third Punic War was brought to an end.

The wars that were also fought at that time in Hither Spain, the manner in which Baebius was surrounded by the Ligurians and perished with his entire army, how the consul Fulvius fought a most bitter war with the Galatians around Mount Olympus, and the other wars that the Romans were then waging in various places—whoever wishes to know more fully may read the books of Orosius and the other historians.

Statius Caecilius, a writer of comedies, was famous in those same days. He was a Gaul by nationality; some say that [Col. 1051B] he was from Milan. He was first the associate of Ennius, and in the following year after Ennius’s death he too died and was buried beyond the Janiculum.

Ennius, however, the poet, died at the age of seventy from an arthritic disease and was buried in the monument of Scipio on the Appian Way, within the first mile from the City.

[Col. 1052A] At that time the poet Lucius was also born. When a census of Rome was conducted, 334,000 people were found.

At that time the philosopher Aristobulus wrote commentaries on the books of Moses and presented them to King Ptolemy. After killing Pseudo-Philip, the Romans made the Macedonians, formerly rulers of nations, tributaries, and the Macedonian kingdom came to an end.

For Carthage, as we have related, was utterly destroyed by fire and sword. Antiochus, as we mentioned above, polluted the Temple of the Lord and placed in it an image of Olympian Jupiter.

In Samaria, on the summit of Mount Gazirim, where Sanballat had once built a temple modeled on that of Jerusalem, Antiochus ordered a shrine of Jupiter Pegrinus to be consecrated in the name of the Most High God, [Col. 1052B] at the request of the Samaritans themselves.

Now that we have shown the pollution and devastation of the Temple, and that two very powerful kingdoms—the Macedonian and the Carthaginian—have come to an end, we have decided to bring this volume also to its conclusion.

# BOOK SIX

[Col. 1051]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 1051B] How Mattathias, resisting the edicts of Antiochus, defended the ancestral laws, appointed Judas leader over the people, and how Judas himself attained the chief priesthood.

[Col. 1051C] At the time when Ptolemy Physcon was reigning in Alexandria, while Antiochus was cruelly raging against the Jews and afflicting them with various punishments, as we briefly recalled in the preceding book, there lived in the village of Modin in Judaea a certain Mattathias, son of John, a priest from Jerusalem. He had five sons, whose names were these: John, who was also called Gaddis; Simon, who was called Mattathias; Judas, who was called Maccabaeus; Eleazar, who was called Apphus; and Abraham, who was also called Jonathan.

This Mattathias therefore mourned before his sons the plundering of the city, the stripping of the Temple, and the calamities of the people. He judged it better to die for the laws of his ancestors than to live without glory.

[Col. 1051D] When those sent by King Antiochus came to the village of Modin to compel the Jews to do what had been ordered by the king, and when the officials appointed there commanded them, according to the king’s order, to sacrifice to idols, Mattathias—who surpassed the others in teaching and reputation for glory—not only abstained from sacrilege and from obeying the royal edict, but also, when he found one of his fellow citizens sacrificing victims to the idols, pierced him through with a sword.

Then, gathering a band of men, he and his sons killed those who violated ancestral custom and the ordinances of the Law, and drove out many others. He was also the first to authorize attacking in battle on the Sabbath, so that they themselves would not be deceived by the same stratagem. For many of their people had already fallen when they refused to undertake battle on the Sabbath and enemies attacked them.

He persevered in what was right until the end of his life, devoted to defense and piety. But when he realized that his final day was approaching, he summoned the citizens and his children who stood beside him. He urged them to defend their homeland and the religion of the Temple, and he left Judas Maccabaeus as the successor to his care and responsibility.

[Col. 1052B] Judas was brave in war, wise in counsel, and more ready than the others in faith. It is not appropriate to relate here how often he routed countless enemy forces with a small band. Because of his outstanding merits, he obtained the chief priesthood, although the people opposed him, and governed as high priest for three years. This happened as follows.

Onias, the chief priest, who was also called Menelaus, was the son of Simon, who had incited Antiochus Epiphanes against the Jews and had become a traitor to his own law, as we related in the preceding book. He was killed by the younger Antiochus, at the urging of Lysias, who said that he had been the beginning of the evils: he had induced his father to compel the Jews to abandon their ancestral religion, and, when he himself held the chief priesthood, he had driven the Jews to transgress their own laws.

[Col. 1052C] [Col. 1052D] After his death, Achimus, also called Joachim, who belonged to another family, obtained the priesthood by fraud. For this reason Onias, the son of the chief priest Onias whom we mentioned above, who had been left still a small child when his father died, saw that the king had killed his uncle Menelaus and had given the chief priesthood to Achimus, who was not of priestly descent. He fled to Ptolemy, king of Egypt, and received honor from him and from his wife Cleopatra. He requested a place in the region of Heliopolis, where he built a temple resembling that of Jerusalem.

Joachim, however, after doing many things against the laws and against his fellow citizens, refused to demolish the ancient wall of the sanctuary, which had been built by the ancient prophets. He was suddenly struck by a plague from God; as a result he fell speechless to the ground and, tortured for many days, died in a detestable manner. He had held the chief priesthood for four years.

[Col. 1053A] After his death, the people handed the priesthood over to Judas. This Judas nobly restored the Temple that Antiochus had destroyed and cleansed it from the filth of idols. It had been polluted and desolate for three years. In celebration of the Temple’s restoration, he glorified God with praises and psalms and, together with his fellow citizens, celebrated sacrifices for eight days.

When he also heard of the Romans’ power, he formed a treaty of friendship and alliance with them. Later, after waging many successful battles against Bacchides, he fought after being abandoned by his own allies. Unwilling to flee, he was surrounded by the enemy; after killing many of his opponents, he himself was struck down and died.

## CHAPTER II

[Col. 1053B] During the reign of Ptolemy Euergetes, Simon obtained the chief priesthood after Jonathan’s death.

Ptolemy, also called Euergetes, reigned for 29 years. From the rebuilding of the Temple, it was the 366th year.

Jonathan was high priest of the Jews. He had succeeded his brother Judas and was his equal in valor, not only by natural kinship but also by likeness of virtue. After accomplishing many deeds in war and performing religious services that were recognized and approved in connection with the purification of the Temple, he strengthened his power by friendship with the Romans.

[Col. 1053C] He was reconciled with the son of Antiochus, but this did nothing to help him escape danger. For the tyrant Tryphon, guardian of the son of Antiochus, plotted to capture him and, wishing for this reason to strip him of his allies, seized Jonathan by treachery when he had come to Ptolemais accompanied by a few men. After binding him, Tryphon moved an army against Judaea.

He was driven back by Simon, Jonathan’s brother. Angered at having been defeated by him, Tryphon then killed Jonathan. Simon, intent on governing affairs with strength, was not inexperienced but tested by the triumphs of fraternal partnership—if only he had been as perceptive in avoiding deceit as he was powerful in his hand and distinguished in the conduct of war!

He captured and destroyed Gaza, Joppa, and Jamnia. He also supported Antiochus against Tryphon, but could not satisfy the king’s greed, although he had also contributed his own efforts to Tryphon’s death. Not long afterward, Antiochus sent Cendebaeus, one of his commanders, with an army to ravage Judaea and reduce Simon to servitude.

[Col. 1053D] Although Simon was an old man, he conducted the war with youthful vigor. He sent his sons, together with the strongest men, ahead; accompanied by part of the army, he attacked from another side. He also placed many ambushes in the mountains and, prevailing everywhere, won a most glorious victory. He was declared high priest and, after 170 years, freed the Jews from Macedonian domination.

He too died at a banquet, caught in an ambush by his son-in-law Ptolemy. After confining Simon’s wife and two sons in prison, Ptolemy sent trusted messengers to kill John III, who was also called Hyrcanus.

[Col. 1054A] When the young man learned of the murder being prepared, he hurried toward the city, relying on the support of many people, both because of the memory of his brother’s virtue and because Ptolemy’s wickedness was hated by everyone.

Ptolemy also wished to enter the city by another gate, but the people rejected him, having received Hyrcanus sooner. Ptolemy immediately withdrew to a fortress beyond Jericho called Dagon. Hyrcanus, however, soon assumed his father’s honor of the high priesthood.

## CHAPTER III

On the destruction of the most wealthy city of Tyre and how Achaia was subjected to the Romans by the consul Metellus. At this time Androgeus was seen at Rome, and a great pestilence followed the portent. Viriathus, a Lusitanian shepherd, also defeated and routed the Romans in various battles. Finally he was killed by his own men.

[Col. 1054B] At that time the destruction of Corinth followed the ruin of Carthage, and the miserable conflagration of two very powerful cities shone forth in different parts of the world within a short interval.

When the praetor Metellus had defeated the Achaeans and Boeotians, who had joined together, in two battles—first at Thermopylae and again in Phocis—the first war is reported to have killed 20,000, and the second 7,000. After the defenses of all Achaia had been destroyed, and while Metellus the praetor was planning the overthrow of the abandoned cities, the consul Mummius suddenly came to his camp with a few men. After immediately displacing Metellus, he stormed Corinth without delay.

[Col. 1054C] At that time Corinth was by far the wealthiest city in the whole world. For many centuries it had been, as it were, a workshop of every kind of craftsman and of every art, as well as the common marketplace of Asia and Europe.

The captives were also cruelly given permission to plunder. Everything was so filled with slaughter and fire that the flames poured out from the circuit of the walls, as though narrowed from a furnace into a single peak. A great part of the population was consumed by sword and flames; the rest were sold under the crown.

[Col. 1054D] After the city had been burned, its walls were utterly demolished, the wall-stone reduced to dust, and immense booty carried away. Because the multitude and variety of statues and images were mixed together in that conflagration of the city, all the gold, silver, bronze, and other metals flowed together into one mass, producing a new kind of metal. Hence, whether made from that substance itself or in imitation of it, bronze of Corinth, as tradition records, and Corinthian vessels are still so called.

Under these same consuls, Viriathus, a Lusitanian by birth in Spain, a shepherd and brigand who first attacked the roads, then devastated the provinces, and finally defeated, routed, and subdued the armies of the praetors and Roman consuls, became a source of the greatest terror to all the Romans.

He defeated the praetor Vitellius in war; afterward he routed the praetor Plautius, whom the same Viriathus had broken in many battles. Later Claudius was sent against Viriathus with a great military force, as though to erase the previous disgrace, but he himself increased the infamy in an even more shameful way. For when he engaged Viriathus, the Roman army lost all the immense forces that Claudius had brought with him.

[Col. 1055A] Viriathus set up Roman cloaks, fasces, and other insignia as trophies in his mountains.

At that time an androgyne was seen at Rome and, by order of the haruspices, was plunged into the sea. Such a sacrilegious expiation was followed by so great a plague among the people that the houses of the great remained empty of the living and full of the dead. Finally, the possibility was denied not only of living in the city but even of approaching it, because of the foul stench of the corpses.

The consul Pompey then entered the territory of the Numantines and withdrew after suffering a great defeat. After Viriathus had worn down the Roman commanders and armies for fourteen years, he was killed by a plot arranged by his own men.

[Col. 1055B] Afterward the consul Mancinus, having received the army from Popilius at Numantia, conducted all his battles so unsuccessfully and was driven to such utter desperation that he was forced to make a most disgraceful treaty with the Numantines, although Pompey had shortly before already concluded an equally infamous treaty with those same Numantines.

The Senate ordered that the treaty be dissolved and that Mancinus be handed over to the Numantines. With his body stripped naked and his hands bound behind his back, he was placed before the gates of Numantia. Remaining there until evening, abandoned by his own people and not accepted by the enemy, he offered a spectacle that drew tears from both sides.

## CHAPTER IV

How the king of the Parthians subjected Babylon and various nations to his rule. At that time Brutus defeated in battle the Gallicians in Hither Spain who were bringing aid to the Lusitanians. Lepidus the proconsul attempted to storm the harmless Vaccaei in Spain, but, having lost his army, was defeated by them. At the same time, slaves conspiring at Rome were soon killed.

[Col. 1055C] At that time, in the East, the sixth [king] of the Parthians after Arsaces, having defeated the commander of Demetrius, victoriously invaded the city of Babylon and all its territories. He also subdued all the nations lying between the rivers Hydaspes and Indus and extended his bloody rule as far as India.

He defeated and captured Demetrius himself when Demetrius confronted him in a second war. In this way a certain Diodorus, together with Alexander the son, usurped his kingdom and royal title. Later, so that he would not have Alexander—whom he had had as a partner in danger while invading the kingdom—as a partner in possessing it, he killed Alexander himself.

[Col. 1055D] Meanwhile, Brutus in Hither Spain crushed 40,000 Callaeci who had come to the aid of the Lusitanians, in a very harsh and difficult war, although he had caught them off guard. Of these, 50,000 are reported to have been killed in that battle and 6,000 captured; a few escaped by flight.

In Hither Spain, Lepidus the proconsul obstinately attempted to attack the Vaccaei, a harmless and suppliant people, despite the Senate’s prohibition. Soon, however, he paid the penalty for his wicked obstinacy by suffering a most grievous defeat. Six thousand Romans were justly killed in this unjust war; the rest escaped after abandoning their camp and losing their weapons.

At that time, too, a four-footed, four-handed child was born at Rome to a slave woman, with four eyes, the same number of ears, and a double male nature. Mount Etna in Sicily vomited and poured forth vast fires.

[Col. 1056A] A servile war then broke out in Sicily. It was severe and savage because of the number of slaves, the organization of their forces, and the magnitude of their strength—so much so that it terrified not only the Roman praetors, whom it utterly routed, but even the consuls. For it is reported that 70,000 slaves then conspired to take up arms.

## CHAPTER V

In these days Numantia was destroyed by Scipio Africanus, and King Attalus of Asia, by his will, made the Roman people his successor; but his brother seized the kingdom, to the destruction of the Roman people and his own annihilation.

[Col. 1056B] Scipio Africanus, chosen consul with everyone’s approval, was sent to Spain to wipe away the disgrace of the treaty that Mancinus had made with the Numantines. He did not immediately attack the Numantines as though they were unaware and unprepared—he had always known them to be ready—but first exercised his soldiers in the camp, as though in schools. This nevertheless proved useful.

When battle was joined, although the Romans had initially begun to flee because they could not withstand the Numantines’ attack, the general’s skill and daring sharply restrained them and compelled them to flee from those whom they had fled. Scipio, rejoicing in this unexpected victory, fortified the city with a ditch, built a rampart reinforced with stakes, and thus crushed the Numantines by siege.

[Col. 1056C] The Numantines, shut in for a long time and tormented by hunger, offered to surrender themselves if tolerable terms were ordered. Often they also begged for the opportunity of a fair fight, so that they might be permitted to die like men. Finally, they all suddenly burst out through two gates, having first taken a large quantity of drink—not wine, for that region does not produce it, but a juice made from grain by a special process. Because it is heated, they call this juice *celia*.

After recovering their strength from the long famine through this drink, they offered themselves for battle. The fierce contest lasted a long time and reached the point of danger for the Romans. Once again the Romans would have proved themselves capable of fighting the Numantines only by fleeing, had they not fought under Scipio.

The Numantines, after their bravest men had been killed, yielded in battle. Yet, maintaining their ranks, they neither prevailed nor returned to the city as fugitives. They refused to accept the bodies of the slain when offered for burial.

[Col. 1056D] At the last extremity of despair, all of them resolved upon death. They entered the closed city, set it on fire from within, and were all consumed together by sword, poison, and fire. The Romans gained absolutely nothing from their victory over them except their own security. Even after Numantia had been destroyed, they said that they had conquered the Numantines less than they had escaped them.

Not one Numantine was held captive in the victor’s chains, and therefore Rome saw no triumph. It saw neither gold nor silver that could have survived the fire, for there was none among a poor people; fire consumed their weapons and clothing.

After Numantia had been destroyed, when Scipio was arranging peace with the other cities of Spain, he consulted a certain Celtic leader named Tyresus about how Numantia, which had previously resisted so bravely, had endured while 4,000 Numantines fought against 40,000 Romans for a long time and often defeated them.

He replied: “Unbroken concord accomplished this.”

At that time, Attalus, son of Eumenes, dying, ordered by his will that the Roman people should succeed him as heir to the rule of Asia.

[Col. 1057A] Thereupon the consul and chief pontiff Licinius Crassus was sent with a fully equipped army against Aristonicus, the brother of Attalus, who had invaded Asia bequeathed to the Romans by the will. He was also supported by great kings and their immense forces: Nicomedes of Bithynia, Mithridates of Pontus and Armenia, Ariarathes of Cappadocia, Philomene of Paphlagonia, and their armies.

Nevertheless, when battle was joined, he was defeated. After the army had been put to flight with extensive slaughter, Crassus himself was surrounded by the enemy and nearly captured. He struck the eye of a Thracian with the staff he had been using for his horse. The barbarian, inflamed with anger and pain, pierced Crassus’s side with his sword. Thus, by devising the manner of his death, Crassus escaped disgrace and slavery.

[Col. 1057B] The consul Perpenna, who had succeeded Crassus, heard of Crassus’s death and the Roman army’s defeat. He hastened into Asia and attacked Aristonicus, who was resting after his recent victory and was unprepared for war. Stripped of all his forces, Aristonicus was put to flight.

When Perpenna had surrounded the city of Stratonicea, to which Aristonicus had fled, he compelled him, exhausted by hunger, to surrender. The consul Perpenna died of illness at Pergamum. Aristonicus was strangled in prison at Rome by order of the Senate.

## CHAPTER VI

At this time the conspiracy of the slaves broke out far and wide, and soon they were destroyed after being driven to punishment by their masters or by the Roman consuls. At this time Etna vomited fires of unusual magnitude beyond all measure, and in Africa a multitude of locusts, plunging into the sea and being rolled back onto the shore, corrupted the air excessively and inflicted a pestilence upon mortals.

Therefore, the conspiracy of the slaves in Sicily stirred up no small disturbance far and wide. In Sicily, indeed, while the slaves were arrogantly exercising authority, Piso the consul fastened 8,000 of them to the gallows for having gained their power wickedly. His successor Rutilius slaughtered more than 20,000 of the rebellious slaves. Yet, after they had first been surrounded by a siege, they were driven by such desperate necessity that they devoured the corpses of their comrades. At Minturnae, moreover, 450 slaves were crucified, and at Sinuessa about 4,000 slaves were crushed by Quintus Metellus. The same slave uprising was also suppressed in the mines of the Athenians by the praetor Periclitus. At Delos, too, the slaves, swelling with a new revolt, were checked by the townsmen who came against them.

At the same time Cicero was born, his mother being Helvia and his father belonging to the equestrian order, from the noble lineage of the Volsci. The comic poet Turpilius died in old age. In those same days Mount Aetna, violently shaken by a vast tremor, overflowed with fiery globes. On another day the island of Lipara and the sea around it grew so violently hot that it dissolved even huge rocks, tore the ship-planking away with the wax melted from its fastenings, boiled the lifeless fish that floated upon the surface, and suffocated human beings—except those who were able to flee farther away—by repeated inhalation of the hot air, their vital organs burned inwardly.

There was also such a vast swarm of locusts in Africa that they consumed not only every green plant but even gnawed bitter bark and dry wood. Suddenly seized by the wind, however, baked into masses, and carried for a long time through the air, they were plunged into the African sea. When waves driven far inland had pushed their submerged heaps along the broad stretches of shore, the decaying and putrefying mass again exhaled an excessively foul and, beyond all expectation, pestilential odor. From this there followed such a plague among all living creatures alike, and the birds, cattle, and wild beasts were so destroyed by the corruption of the air, that the rotting corpses scattered everywhere increased the infection.

But as for the extent of the human pestilence, I myself shudder throughout my body as I recount it. In Numidia, where King Micipsa was then ruling, 800,000 people died. Along the coastline, however, especially adjoining the shores of Carthage and Utica, more than 200,000 soldiers—who had been assigned to protect all Africa—were extinguished and swept away. The disaster came upon them so suddenly and violently that it is said that at Utica, in a single day and through a single gate, more than 1,500 of those young men were carried out dead.

At the same time Antiochus, not content with Babylonia and Ecbatana and the whole empire of Media, engaged King Phraates of the Parthians and was defeated. Although he seemed to have 100,000 armed men in his army, he mixed with the cohorts more than 200,000 camp-followers and sutlers, and handed them over to prostitutes and actors. Thus, easily crushed by the strength of the Parthians and by his entire army, he perished.

At the same time the wretched life of Ptolemy, king of the Alexandrians, came to a more wretched end. He had dishonorably known his own sister and then taken her in marriage, but finally cast her away in a manner still more shameful than that in which he had married her. He took his stepdaughter—that is, the daughter of his sister and wife—as his wife; he killed his own son, whom he had fathered by his sister, and also his brother’s son. For this reason, entangled in such great parricides, he became detested by the Alexandrians and was driven from the kingdom.

## CHAPTER VII

On John, son of Simon, who was called Hyrcanus: how he captured many cities of Syria, the Samaritans, and the Idumaeans in wars successfully conducted, and grew old in complete peace and prosperity. Also, how his son Aristobulus, who first after the return of the Jewish people from Babylonia assumed the royal title, killed his mother and his brother Antigonus, and himself, scarcely after completing a year, died detestably in the kingdom.

Ptolemy Physcon, also called Soter, [reigned] 17 years. From the rebuilding of the Temple, however, 567 years.

John, son of Simon, was leader and high priest of the Jews. Waging war against the Hyrcanians, he was called Hyrcanus. As soon as he had obtained his father’s office and had offered sacrifices to God, he quickly attacked Ptolemy, who was keeping his mother and brothers bound with him and had treacherously handed over their father Simon to death at a banquet. When John had attacked the fortress, he was superior in other respects but yielded to righteous grief.

Whenever Ptolemy was hard pressed, he brought John’s mother and brothers out onto the wall, where they could be plainly seen, beat them, and threatened to throw them down unless John withdrew at once. Thus fear and pity moved Hyrcanus more than anger. His mother, however, terrified neither by the blows nor by the threatened death, stretched out her hands and begged her son not to spare the impious man, even though he was broken by the injuries inflicted upon his own family. Indeed, she herself considered the death Ptolemy had prepared for her preferable to immortality, provided that he paid the penalty for the unlawful deeds he had committed in her household.

John, now considering his mother’s steadfastness and hearing her pleas, was driven to attack. But whenever he saw her being beaten and torn apart, he became faint-hearted and was filled entirely with grief. Because the siege was thus prolonged, the sabbatical year arrived. The Jews customarily allowed this year to cease every seventh cycle, following the example of the seven days. Ptolemy therefore obtained a respite from the siege and, after killing John’s brothers together with their mothers, fled to Zeno, surnamed Cotylas, the tyrant of Philadelphia.

Antiochus, angry because of what he had suffered at Simon’s hands, led an army into Judaea. There, sitting before Jerusalem, he besieged Hyrcanus. Hyrcanus, however, opened the tomb of David, who had been the wealthiest of kings, and removed more than three thousand talents of money from it. Having given Antiochus three hundred talents, he persuaded him to withdraw from the siege. To lessen the odium of his deed, Hyrcanus is said to have been the first to establish hospices, where he could receive poor travelers.

Yet when Antiochus later undertook war against the Medes and thereby gave Hyrcanus an opportunity for revenge, Hyrcanus immediately marched against the cities of Syria, judging—and rightly—that they were empty of defenders. He himself captured Medaba and Samaga with their surrounding territory, as well as Sicima and Angariza. In addition, he captured the Cuthaean people, who inhabited the places adjoining a shrine built in imitation of that at Jerusalem. He also captured no small number of other Idumaean cities, as well as Adoreon and Maresan.

Advancing as far as Samaria—which is now the city of Sebaste, founded by King Herod—he surrounded it on every side and placed his sons Aristobulus and Antigonus in command of the siege. As they relaxed nothing of the pressure, those inside the city were driven by such a shortage of food that they were even forced to consume their own flesh. They therefore summoned Antiochus as an ally, surnamed Spondion. When he had readily complied with their request, he was defeated by Aristobulus and Antigonus and fled as far as Scythopolis, pursued by the aforementioned brothers.

They returned to Samaria, again forced the multitude inside the wall, captured the city, destroyed it, and led away its inhabitants as captives. Since success followed success in this way, they did not allow their eagerness to cool. They advanced with their army as far as Scythopolis, captured it as well, and divided among themselves all the fields within the region of Carmel.

The prosperity of John and his sons aroused the envy of the gentiles and provoked a revolt. Many gathered against them and did not cease until they were defeated in open war. John lived out the remainder of his life in the greatest prosperity, having administered affairs most successfully for thirty-two years. He died leaving five sons, plainly most blessed and having given no one any reason to complain about Fortune on his account.

In the end, he alone possessed three especially distinguished offices: he was ruler, high priest, and also prophet. God conversed with him in such a way that he was completely ignorant of nothing that was to come. Indeed, he foresaw and foretold that two of his elder sons would not remain in possession of the Lord’s affairs.

It does not seem unworthy to relate what became of their lives, however far they departed from their father’s happiness. After their father’s death, the elder Aristobulus transferred the leadership to the monarchy and was the first to place a diadem upon his own head, 475 years and three months after the people had entered that land, having been freed from the slavery they had endured among the Babylonians.

He brought forward his second brother, Antigonus—for he seemed to love him—in equal honor. He handed the others over to custody in chains, and likewise bound his mother, who had dared to dispute some matter of power. For John had left her as the mistress of affairs, and Aristobulus advanced to such a degree of cruelty that he killed her by starvation.

He paid the penalty for these crimes through the death of his brother Antigonus, whom he loved most and had made a partner in the kingdom. He killed him as well, led on by accusations maliciously fabricated by enemies of the kingdom. Aristobulus, after the murder of his mother and his brother Antigonus, was tortured by the most fitting and cruelest pain of the viscera and died detestably, having reigned no more than a year.

His wife, releasing his brothers from their bonds, established as king Alexander, who was older in age and seemed to excel in moderation.

## CHAPTER VIII

On the rebuilding of Carthage, and on the revolt of the slaves that arose at Rome in hope of freedom; also, how the Allobroges and the Gauls of the Arverni were defeated and destroyed by the Romans. At that time, too, the eruption of Aetna afflicted the Catinians.

At this time also, by order of the Senate, Carthage was rebuilt once more. In the twenty-second year after its destruction, Roman citizens were settled there with their families, and the city was filled and restored.

A revolt also arose at Rome, which the tribunes Gracchus and Flaccus stirred up by promising to grant freedom to the slaves and distribute public lands. In that disturbance more than three thousand people were killed in the City, including the authors of the revolt.

In those days Metellus, campaigning throughout the region, subdued the Balearic Islands. At that time Domitius, the proconsul, defeated the Gallic Allobroges in a very severe battle near the town of Vindalium, especially because both the enemy’s horses and the enemy themselves were terrified and fled at the unfamiliar appearance of the elephants. Twenty thousand Allobroges are reported to have been killed there, and 3,000 captured.

At that time Mount Aetna burned more violently than usual. Its fiery torrents poured over the surrounding area and flowed widely around it, overwhelming the city of Catina and its territory, so that the roofs of buildings, scorched and heavily burdened by the ashes of the disaster, collapsed. To alleviate this calamity, the Senate remitted ten years’ taxes to the Catinians.

Meanwhile the consul Fabius went against Bituitus, king of the Arverni, a Gallic people, who was preparing for war with a very large force. He met him with so small an army that Bituitus boasted that the Romans were scarcely numerous enough to provide food for the dogs he had with his army.

When Bituitus realized that a single bridge over the Rhône was too small to transfer his forces, he built another bridge by fastening together boats with chains and laying planks over them. Battle was joined and fought fiercely for a long time. The Gauls were defeated and turned to flight. While each man was anxious for himself, they crowded their columns together without thought, broke the chains of the bridge in their hasty crossing, and soon were submerged along with the boats themselves.

Bituitus’s army is said to have contained 180,000 armed men, of whom 150,000 were either killed or drowned. After the consul Martius was defeated, he attacked in war a Gallic people settled at the foot of the Alps. When they saw themselves surrounded by the Roman forces and realized that they would be unequal to the war, they killed their wives and children and threw themselves into the flames. Those who had not been able to carry out their intended death because the Romans forestalled them, and who had been captured, destroyed themselves—some with the sword, some by hanging, and others by refusing food. No one survived at all, not even a little child, who out of love of life would endure the condition of slavery.

With matters standing thus, the Senate declared war on Jugurtha, king of the Numidians.

## CHAPTER IX

On Jugurtha, king of the Numidians, and on the consuls who fought against and defeated him.

Jugurtha, the adopted son of Micipsa, king of the Numidians, and made heir alongside his natural sons, first killed his fellow heirs, namely Hiempsal, and drove Atherbal, defeated in war, out of Africa.

Then he corrupted the consul Calpurnius, who had been sent against him, with money and brought him to the most disgraceful terms of peace. Moreover, when he himself had come to Rome, after corrupting or attempting to corrupt everyone with money, he mixed seditions and dissensions together. As he was leaving, he marked the city with a sufficiently infamous saying, declaring: “A purchasable city, and one soon to perish if it finds a buyer!”

In the following year he killed Aulus Postumius, the brother of the consul Postumius, whom the consul had placed in command of an army of 40,000 armed men, and united almost all Africa, which was defecting from the Romans, to his own kingdom.

Then, restrained by the discipline of Metellus and defeated in two battles, he returned 3,000 deserters and gave 300 hostages. Failing to observe the terms of peace, he was defeated again by the consul Marius, who was no less astute than Metellus. Distrusting his own strength, he brought Bocchus, king of the Moors, over to his side as an ally. Strengthened by Bocchus’s forces, he repeatedly afflicted the army of Marius.

Finally, near the ancient city of Cirta [Cirtam], he came against the Romans equipped with 400,000 cavalry [F., *millibus* for *militibus*]. Fighting them continuously for three days, he so crushed them that, when everything seemed hopeless, the Romans were killed in great numbers, hemmed in on every side, weakened by thirst and the intense heat of the sun and by dust, and no longer hoped for any safety, while they endured every intolerable hardship.

The cavalry of the Numidians and Moors, as though they had captured the Romans almost without effort and surrounded them, slaughtered them. Suddenly help was sent to the Romans from heaven. A violent rainstorm poured down, and a powerful tempest arose. It refreshed the Romans and restored their strength, but rendered the Moors and Numidians almost defenseless: their javelins, which had no thongs, became slippery, while their shields, made from elephant hides, absorbed water like sponges and became unusable. Through this turn of Fortune Marius gained the advantage and won.

Bocchus and Jugurtha lost 90,000 of their men while fleeing. Therefore Bocchus, losing confidence in fighting the Romans, sued for peace. He captured Jugurtha by treachery, bound him in accordance with the peace terms, and sent him to Marius. Marius led him in triumph before his chariot and ordered him to be strangled after he had been placed in prison.

Moreover, during the wars of the Jugurthine period, the consul Cassius pursued the Tigurini in Gaul as far as the Ocean, but was again surrounded by the same ambush and killed.

## CHAPTER X

On the Roman consuls who fought unsuccessfully against the Gauls, were defeated, and were killed. Against those Gauls, Marius was appointed consul for the fourth and fifth time and sent forth to avenge the consuls and defend the frontiers. He killed 440,000 Gauls, besides the women and children, who killed themselves. In Asia and Syria, those who were then ruling were as follows.

From this point the consul Mallius and the proconsul Scipio were sent against the Cimbri and Teutones, and against the Tigurini and Ambrones, peoples of Gauls and Germans who at that time had conspired to destroy the Roman Empire. They divided the provinces between themselves along the Rhône River. While they contended with one another in bitter envy and rivalry, the Romans were defeated with great disgrace and danger to the Roman name.

Indeed, in that battle Marcus Aemilius, a former consul, was killed; 80,000 Romans and allies were slaughtered at that time, and 40,000 camp-followers and sutlers were killed, as Athias records. Thus it is reported that scarcely ten men from the entire army survived to bring back the wretched news and increase their misery.

The enemy gained possession of twenty-two camps and, with a novel and extraordinary act of execration, destroyed everything they had captured. Clothing was torn apart and thrown down; gold and silver were cast into the river; the cuirasses of the men were ripped apart; the horses’ ornaments were scattered; the horses themselves were plunged into the whirlpools; and men were hanged from trees with nooses placed around their necks, so that neither victor nor vanquished could recognize anything as booty.

At that time there was the greatest mourning at Rome, and not mourning alone but also fear that the Cimbri might immediately cross the Alps and destroy Italy.

Therefore Marius was sent against the Gauls for the fourth time. Fighting the Tigurini and Allobroges in two battles, he defeated them, not without great danger to his own men. Two hundred thousand armed men among them were killed in battle, 80,000 were captured, and scarcely 3,000 are reported to have escaped. Their women, after dashing their children against the rocks, all killed themselves with the sword or by hanging.

The Teutones and Cimbri, with their forces intact, crossed the snowy Alps and invaded the plains of Italy. There, while they were being softened by cups, food, and baths, Marius, consul for the fifth time, and Catullus were sent against them. Following Hannibal’s strategy, they postponed battle in the fog and deployed in the sunlight. For the sun rose with the wind directly in the enemy’s face; the dust obscured their sight, and the brightness dimmed their vision. Thus it happened that so great and terrible a multitude was slaughtered with minimal loss to the Romans but with their own complete destruction.

It is reported that 140,000 of them were killed in that battle and 60,000 captured. Their women, through many pitiable forms of death, gave themselves and their children over to destruction. Thus, in these two battles, 340,000 were killed, apart from the countless multitude of women who, in womanly fury but with manly courage, tore themselves and their children to pieces.

In those same days Publicius Malleolus committed a deed previously unknown among the Romans. He killed his own mother with the assistance of slaves. For this crime, condemned for parricide, he was sewn into a sack and thrown into the sea.

At that time Antiochus, also called Orfus, ruled in Syria and Asia. He was succeeded by Antiochus Crippus, who was driven from the kingdom by Antiochus Cytinus; then Crippus Antiochus defeated Cytinus and recovered the kingdom. Thus they ruled Syria and Asia while fighting against one another in succession.

In those days the philosopher Marcus Terentius Varro and Cicero were born. The poet Marcus Furius, surnamed Babylus, was born at Cremona.

## CHAPTER XI

On the various battles and seditions, or parricides, which Alexander II, king and priest of the Jews, waged against foreign peoples and against his own people.

Ptolemy, also called Alexander, ruled for ten years after Ptolemy Physcon had been expelled from the kingdom and withdrawn to Cyprus through the agency of his mother Cleopatra. Ptolemy, who had been expelled by his mother, returned from flight, regained the kingdom, and ruled for eight years, since the citizens had expelled Alexander, who had preceded him, because of his killing of native citizens.

From the rebuilding of the Temple, however, 412 years had passed.

As stated above, after John’s death Aristobulus had assumed the high priesthood and kingdom of the Jews. After Aristobulus’s death, as we have mentioned earlier, his brother Janneus, also called Alexander, likewise obtained both the kingdom and the priesthood of the Jews and ruled his citizens with extreme cruelty.

When he was released from the bonds in which he had been bound at his brother’s command—for he was older than his other brothers and seemed to excel them in merit—he was proclaimed both king of the Jews and high priest. Once he had obtained power, he killed one brother who was seeking the kingdom; another, who was content with life, he kept with him after stripping him of his possessions and depriving him of his property.

He also fought Ptolemy and killed many of the enemy, but victory inclined more strongly to Ptolemy’s side. He fought repeatedly with the son of Zeno, Theodorus; after gaining the upper hand, he added to his kingdom fortresses and fortified places belonging to Theodorus, although his army is reported to have lost as many as 10,000 men to Theodorus.

After he had subdued Gaza, Raphia, and Anthedon, he suffered revolts from the Jews. On a certain festival day the people were stirred up against him. Banquets often kindle seditions, and he seemed unable to suppress the ambushes unless he obtained the aid of foreigners. Thus, after winning repeated battles against his own people, he killed no fewer than 50,000 Jews over six years.

Yet he did not rejoice in his victories, because he had exhausted the strength of his kingdom, and therefore attempted to be reconciled with the Jews. They hated his fickleness and variability of character so deeply that, when he asked them how he might calm them, they replied: “If he were to die.” They said that they would scarcely pardon him even after his death for having committed so many crimes.

He also fought Demetrius, whom the Jews had summoned to their aid. Defeated by him, he withdrew into the mountains. But when Fortune changed, his own men, moved by pity for him after having previously deserted him, abandoned Demetrius and joined Alexander, as many as 6,000 of them. Strengthened by their valor, he restored himself for war.

Demetrius, broken by this reversal and loss of support, soon withdrew from the region. Yet the remaining multitude did not lay aside its hostility because its allies had departed. It continued to fight Alexander in a prolonged war until, after most had been killed, the victorious Alexander led the rest as captives to Jerusalem.

But, carried beyond measure by anger, he acted so that his cruelty advanced even to impiety. He crucified 800 of them in the middle of the city, killed their wives and children before their eyes, and watched the scene while drinking and reclining with his concubines.

Such terror seized the people that even the supporters of the opposing party fled the following night, 7,000 of them, beyond the whole of Judaea. Alexander’s death put an end to their exile.

After he had finally secured with difficulty such a period of peace for his kingdom, he rested from arms. Therefore, whoever wishes to know his deeds more fully should read the thirteenth book of Josephus’s *History of Antiquities*.

The beginning of illness followed the cessation of war. He died in the thirty-seventh year of his reign. He left the reins of the kingdom to his wife Alexandra, certain that the Jews would be especially obedient to her, since, being very different from his cruelty and resisting his injustice, she had won the goodwill of the people. Nor was his hope disappointed.

## CHAPTER XII

On the Social Wars endured by the Romans, when all Italy defected from them, and on the dreadful and wondrous portents that preceded these disasters.

In those days, too, many calamities disturbed the Romans, although they were already called masters of many nations. For the sake of concise brevity, I have decided to pass over them quickly. But if anyone wishes to know them more fully, let him read the fifth book of Orosius.

Saturninus, tribune of the plebs, became the author of the disturbance stirred up in the City. He conspired with Marius, consul for the sixth time, and Glaucia, the praetor. First, through the criminal actions of judges who belonged to the same faction, they sent Metellus Numidicus, a most vigorous and innocent man, into exile, to the grief of the entire City.

Fearing that Memmius, a vigorous and upright man, might become consul, Saturninus killed him. Then, while promoting a dispute in his own house, he was called by some “commander” and by others “king.” The Romans, indignant at such recklessness, killed Saturninus and the leaders of his faction, with the consul Marius as the instigator. They decreed that all their property should be confiscated. Thus, after the seditious men of so great a conspiracy had been killed, the people had peace.

Afterward Rutilius, a man of the highest integrity, was condemned through the perjury of judges. He moved to Smyrna and grew old devoted to literary studies.

Then, in the consulship of Julius Caesar and Marcus Philippus, the Social War, arising from internal causes, stirred up all Italy. Livius Drusus, tribune of the plebs, had enticed all the Latins with the hope of freedom; when he was unable to fulfill what had been agreed, he roused them to arms. Drusus, anxious amid such great evils, was killed in his own house, though the author of the deed is uncertain.

The Picentes, Vestini, Marsi, Paeligni, Marrucini, Samnites, and Lucani, while they were still secretly planning their defection, killed Gaius Servilius, the praetor sent to them as a legate, at Asculum. Immediately closing the city gates, they slaughtered all the Roman citizens in an unproclaimed massacre.

The most atrocious disaster was immediately preceded by infamous portents. Animals of every kind that were accustomed to tolerate the touch of human beings gently and to live among them abandoned their stalls and pastures and fled to the forests and mountains with pitiful bleating, neighing, and lowing.

Dogs as well, whose nature it is to be unable to exist apart from human beings, wandered about with tearful howlings like wolves. At sunrise a fiery globe also flashed from the northern region with a tremendous crash of the sky.

Among the Arentines, while loaves were being broken at banquets, blood flowed from the middle of the loaves. Moreover, for seven continuous days a storm of stones, mixed also with fragments of pottery, struck the earth over a very wide area.

Among the Samnites, a flame burst forth from a vast chasm in the earth and seemed to extend all the way to heaven. Many Romans also saw, while traveling, a golden-colored globe roll down from the sky toward the earth, grow larger, then be carried upward again from the earth toward the east, and with its size cover the sun itself.

Therefore the praetor Gnaeus Pompeius fought against the Picentes by order of the Senate and was defeated. The Samnites had then appointed Papias Mutilius as their commander, while the Marsi had preferred Agamemnon, their chief pirate.

Julius Caesar, defeated in battle by the Samnites, fled after his army had been cut down. The consul Rutilius chose as his legate Marius, his relative. Marius repeatedly restrained him, judging that delaying the war would be useful and that the inexperienced soldiers ought to be trained for a while in camp. Rutilius, thinking that Marius was doing this deliberately, despised him and carelessly threw himself and his entire army into an ambush of the Marsi. There the consul himself and many nobles were killed, and 8,000 Roman soldiers were slaughtered.

The Tolenus River carried along the weapons and bodies of the slain in the sight of the legate Marius and raised them up as evidence of the disaster. Marius immediately gathered his forces, unexpectedly overwhelmed the victorious enemy, and killed 8,000 Marsi himself.

Caepio, led into an ambush by the Vestini and Marsi, was slaughtered along with his army. Lucius Julius Caesar, after fleeing when defeated at Aesernia, gathered forces from every direction and fought against the Samnites and Lucani, killing many thousands of the enemy.

When he had been hailed as commander by the army and had sent messengers to Rome with news of the victory, the Senate laid aside the *saga*—that is, the garment of mourning—which it had assumed when the Social War began, encouraged by this hope, and recovered the ancient dignity of the toga.

Marius then killed 6,000 Marsi and stripped 7,000 of their weapons. Sulla was sent with twenty-four cohorts to Aesernia, where Roman citizens and soldiers were being hard pressed by a very close siege. In a great battle, with a vast slaughter of the enemy, he saved the city and its allies.

Gnaeus Pompeius routed the Picentes in a severe battle. Because of this victory, the Senate resumed its broad-striped togas and the other insignia of rank, after having worn only ordinary togas while first recovering its breath from Caesar’s victory [Al., “while first breathing again from Caesar’s victory”].

The praetor Porcius Cato, and again the legate Plotius [Al., “the praetor Porcius Cato defeated the Etruscans, and so forth”], defeated the Umbrians at the cost of much blood and with the greatest difficulty.

In the consulship of Gnaeus Pompeius and Lucius Porcius Cato, Pompeius besieged the city of Asculum for a long time. Yet he would not have captured it if he had not defeated the people, who had burst out into the field, by a very severe assault.

In that battle 18,000 Marsi were killed together with their commander Franco. On the same day the Picentes also engaged in battle and were defeated. At that time Sulla likewise overcame and defeated the Samnites in war; 18,000 Samnites were killed in that battle.

Therefore the Marrucini and Vestini were pursued and devastated by Sulpicius, Pompeius’s legate. By the same Sulpicius, the Italian commanders were also crushed and killed in a dreadful battle.

Pompeius entered Asculum and beat all their prefects, centurions, and leading men with rods and struck them with the axe. He sold their slaves and all their booty at auction, and ordered the rest—free, but naked and destitute—to depart.

## CHAPTER XIII

On the civil wars that were waged between Sulla and the Marians and continued for ten years, in which 150,000 of the finest men were killed.

Therefore, while the Social War had not yet ended, the first civil war was set in motion at Rome. In that same year the Mithridatic War also began—though less infamous, no less grave. Accordingly, Marius aspired to a seventh consulship and to undertake the war against Mithridates. When this became known in Campania to the consul Sulla, who was about to depart for Asia with an army against Mithridates, he was immediately moved by anger and indignation and returned to Rome. Indeed, before the City he killed Marius’s legate, as though the first victim of the civil war, and soon burst into the City.

Marius, however, after unsuccessfully attempting to stir up the nobility, inflame the commons, and arm the equestrian order fully against Sulla, finally withdrew to the Capitol. [Note: [Col. 1065D] The words “but after the Sullan party had been severely crushed here,” inserted into the text at this point from an unknown source, are not recognized by the text of Orosius which Freculphus follows. [Col. 1066D] EDIT.] But after the Sullan party had been severely crushed there, he fled from him amid the great slaughter of his followers; and there Sulpicius, Marius’s colleague, was then killed. Marius too, while fleeing, when he had been surrounded by the pressure of his pursuers, hid himself in the marshes of Minturnae. From there he was disastrously dragged out, covered with mud, and brought in disgraceful fashion to Minturnae amid a shameful spectacle, then thrust into prison. The executioner sent against him was terrified by his mere appearance.

Afterward, slipping his bonds, he fled across to Africa. Having freed his son from Utica, where the young man was being held under guard, he immediately returned to Rome and joined himself to the consul Cinna through a partnership in crimes. Accordingly, in order to destroy the entire state, they divided their army into four parts. Three legions were assigned to Marius; Gaius Carbo was placed over one part of the forces; Sertorius took another part—that Sertorius, namely, who was already the instigator and participant in this civil war and who, after it had ended, also stirred up another war in Spain, which he prolonged for many years amid the greatest disasters of the Romans. The remaining portion of the army followed Cinna.

Moreover, Gnaeus Pompeius, who had been summoned by the Senate with an army to assist the state and had long held himself in suspense by seeking revolutionary opportunities, was despised by Marius or Cinna and betook himself to Octavius, the other consul. Soon afterward he clashed with Sertorius. The intervention of night brought the unfortunate battle to an end. Six hundred soldiers were slaughtered on either side.

Marius, having entered the colony of Ostia, exercised there every kind of lust, greed, and cruelty. Pompey, struck by lightning, perished. His army, however, seized by pestilence, was almost entirely destroyed. For eleven thousand men from Pompey’s camp died, while six thousand from the side of the consul Octavius were lost.

Marius burst into the cities of Antium and Aricia like an enemy and killed everyone in them except the traitors; he permitted their property to be plundered by his own men. Later, the consul Cinna entered the City with his legions, and Marius with the fugitives, and killed all the most noble men of the Senate and very many former consuls.

But what proportion is this of the misery displayed? Who could define in a single statement the slaughter of the good, whose number was so great, whose duration so long, whose cruelty so severe, and whose forms so diverse? Even posterity, hearing of these things, should shudder.

Accordingly, when Marius piled up the heads of murdered citizens—presented at banquets, brought to the Capitol, and placed upon the Rostra—and had seized a seventh consulship together with Cinna as third-time consul, he was finally carried off by a belated death at the beginning of his consular authority. Cinna compensated for the slaughter of the good by the killing of the wicked. For when the band of fugitives introduced by Marius had become insatiable in plundering and supplied no share of the booty to the consuls, its leaders were summoned into the Forum as though for pay and, surrounded by soldiers, killed while unarmed. On that day eight thousand fugitives were slain in the Forum of the City. Cinna himself, in his fourth consulship, was killed by his own army.

Meanwhile, the remaining senators who had escaped by flight the power of Cinna, the cruelty of Marius, and the madness of Fimbria and the audacity of Sertorius crossed over to Greece and compelled Sulla by their entreaties to bring aid to their endangered—indeed, already utterly ruined—homeland.

Accordingly, as soon as Sulla reached the Campanian coast, he defeated the consul Norbanus in battle. Six thousand Romans were then killed by the Romans, six thousand of the same force were captured by them, and one hundred and twenty-four fell on Sulla’s side.

Fabius Hadrianus, who held command as propraetor, while seeking the kingdom of Africa by means of slaves, was burned alive at Utica with his entire household after bundles of brushwood had been piled around him.

The praetor Damasippus, at the instigation of the consul Marius, summoned Quintus Scaevola, Gaius Carbo, Lucius Domitius, and Publius Antistius into the Senate-house as though for consultation, and murdered them with the utmost cruelty. The bodies of the slain were dragged by the executioner’s hook and thrown into the Tiber.

At the same time, Sulla’s commanders fought several battles against the Marian party with most disastrous success. Quintus Metellus defeated the forces of Carinas and overran his camp; Gaius Pompeius severely slaughtered Carbo’s cavalry. The greatest battle at that time between Sulla and the younger Marius took place at Sacriportus. In it, as Claudius records, twenty-five thousand of Marius’s army were killed.

Pompey also stripped Carbo of his camp and, pursuing him in flight, at one time by slaughtering and at another by compelling surrender, deprived him of a very large part of his army. Metellus crushed Norbanus’s column, where nine thousand of the Marian party were killed.

Lucullus, when besieged by Quintus, broke out and, in a sudden battle, destroyed the besieging army. More than ten thousand are reported to have been killed there at that time.

Then Sulla, together with the Samnite commander Campanius [variant: Lamponius] and the remaining forces of Carinas, brought his standards before the very gate of the City, the Colline Gate, at the ninth hour of the day. After a most severe battle he finally won. Eighty thousand men are said to have been slain there; twelve thousand surrendered; and the victors’ unappeasable rage consumed the remaining multitude when it had been put to flight.

As soon as Sulla entered the City in triumph, he killed three thousand men who had surrendered through envoys, contrary to divine law and contrary to the pledge that had been given, although they were unarmed and unsuspecting. Very many others were also killed at that time—not to mention the innocent, even men belonging to Sulla’s own party. They are said to have numbered more than nine thousand.

Thus slaughter was carried on freely throughout the City, with executioners wandering about and attacking anyone whom either anger or the prospect of booty incited. When everyone was now openly muttering what each had feared individually, Quintus Catulus said publicly to Sulla:

“With whom, then, are we finally going to live, if we kill armed men in war and unarmed men in peace?”

After men of consular rank, praetors, and senators had been destroyed indiscriminately and without consideration throughout the City—those whom Sulla had most cruelly entered on the lists—Sulla departed from there for Praeneste. He ordered all the leaders of the Marian forces—that is, legates, quaestors, prefects, and tribunes—to be killed.

Pompey captured and killed Carbo, the Marian commander, while he was attempting to flee to Egypt. The same Pompey crossed over into Africa and, making a sortie near Utica, killed eighteen thousand men. In that war Domitius, the Marian commander, was killed while fighting among the foremost.

[The same Pompey], pursuing Hiarbas, king of Numidia, and finding him stripped of all his forces in flight, killed him.

Finally, Sulla was created dictator, so that the lust for condemnation and cruelty might both be armed and concealed by the reverence due to an honorable title. At last Sulla was deprived of power.

Thus ended two most disastrous wars: the Italian Social War and Sulla’s Civil War. Drawn out over ten years, they consumed more than one hundred and fifty thousand Romans. Rome lost in this civil war as many of its finest men and native soldiers as the census, without distinction of age, had found in earlier times, when it was already preparing itself against Alexander the Great.

In addition, thirty-four men of consular rank, thirty-six praetorians, and nearly sixty senators were killed, apart from the countless peoples of all Italy who were destroyed indiscriminately and without consideration.

After Sulla’s death, Lepidus, champion of the Marian party, rose against Catulus, Sulla’s commander, and rekindled the revived ashes of the civil wars. [Readings: *Bistucatiae*; *Bis tunc acie* (“then twice in battle”); the text is corrupt.] A battle was fought. Very many Romans were killed—men already wretched because of their very small number and still raging with that former madness.

The city of Alba, attacked by siege and tormented by the extremity of famine, was spared through the surrender of its pitiful survivors. There Scipio, Lepidus’s son, was captured and killed. Brutus, fleeing into Cisalpine Gaul, was killed at Regium while Pompey pursued him.

Thus this civil war, no less because of Catulus’s clemency than because of weariness with Sulla’s cruelty, vanished as quickly as it had flared up, like a fire in straw.

In those same days Terentius Varro was born in the province of Narbonese Gaul. Later, at the age of thirty-five, he learned Greek literature with the greatest zeal.

Cicero, indeed, advances to Athens, Rusticus having been defended against Chrysogonus [corrupt transmitted wording: Cicero namque Athenas succedit Rustico, defenso contra Chrysogonum; the construction is uncertain, and succedit Rustico could also mean “succeeds Rusticus”]. [Note: [Col. 1069D] The passage is corrupt. It should be restored from Eusebius’s Chronicle in Saint Jerome as follows: “After defending Roscius against Chrysogonus, Cicero withdrew to Athens, and from there, etc.” EDIT.]

After three years he returned to Rome; in the twenty-sixth year of his age he also defended Quintius. At that time Plotius Gallus was the first to teach Latin rhetoric at Rome. Cicero reports of him as follows:

“I remember that, when we were boys, a certain Plotius first began to teach in Latin.”

At that time Lucius Pomponius of Bononia, a celebrated writer of *Catillanorum* [variant: *Attellanarum*, Atellan] plays, was held in high repute. The poet Lucretius was also born. After drinking a love potion, he was driven mad and wrote several books during intervals of his insanity; Cicero later corrected them.

## CHAPTER XIV

### Under Ptolemy Dionysius; Alexandra Salina, wife of King Alexander, ruled the Jews; and the events that occurred among them in those days

Ptolemy Dionysius [reigned] thirty years; from the rebuilding of the Temple there had been four hundred and thirty years. Alexandra Salina, wife of King Alexander, as we have said, held the kingdom of the Jews.

Since she had two sons born to her by Alexander, she appointed the elder, Hyrcanus, high priest because of his age, and made him king because of his modesty. She preferred that the younger, Aristobulus, live as a private citizen, because he was of a more passionate disposition.

Alexandra herself detested from the beginning those who violated the sacred laws, yet she served the divine religion with superstitious devotion. For this reason the Pharisees, a certain Jewish association, attached themselves to this woman. They were thought to practice piety more than others and to interpret the laws with greater expertise. Because of this, she regarded them with special favor.

But they gradually despised the woman’s simplicity and, removing and deposing everyone according to their own pleasure, binding and releasing whomever they wished, completely disrupted the orders of the state, so that they themselves enjoyed royal privileges while Alexandra bore the expenses and difficulties.
