Nevertheless, she was remarkably skilled in administering greater affairs. Accordingly, always intent on increasing her forces, she assembled a double army. She also secured no small number of foreign auxiliaries, by which she not only strengthened the position of her people but also made herself feared by foreign powers. She commanded others, but willingly obeyed the Pharisees herself.

Finally, they killed a certain prominent man, Diogenes, who had been a very close friend of Alexander, accusing him of his counsels, so that the eight hundred whom I mentioned above might be crucified by order of the king. Nevertheless, they urged Alexandra to kill others as well, those at whose instigation Alexander had been stirred up against them.

Since, in her excessive superstition, she considered that nothing should be refused them, they slaughtered whomever they pleased on that pretext—until each of the nobles whose danger was at stake fled to Aristobulus. He persuaded his mother to spare them out of regard for their dignity, but to expel from the state those whom she considered guilty. They, once permission had been granted them, dispersed through the countryside.

Meanwhile, while Alexandra was suffering from illness, her younger son Aristobulus, with his servants—of whom he had many, and all exceptionally loyal because of the fervor of their youth—seized all the fortresses. With the money he found there, he hired auxiliaries and declared himself king.

Moved by the complaints over this, Hyrcanus’s mother confined Aristobulus’s wife with her sons in the fortress adjacent to the Temple on the north. As we have said, it was formerly called Baris; later it was called Antonia, under the emperor Antonius, just as, in accordance with the names of Augustus and Agrippa, cities were called Sebaste, Agrippas, and others.

Alexandra died before she could avenge upon Aristobulus, Hyrcanus’s brother, the insults he had inflicted and whom she had arranged to be deposed from the kingdom. She had administered it for nine years, and Hyrcanus became heir to everything; indeed, while still alive, she had entrusted the kingdom to him.

## CHAPTER XV

### On the various crashes of wars by which Rome was terrified: one in Spain, another in Macedonia, a third in Pamphylia, and a fourth in Dalmatia

Meanwhile these events were taking place among the Romans. With the crash of wars resounding everywhere—one in Spain, another in Pamphylia, a third in Macedonia, and a fourth in Dalmatia—the Roman state, still bloodless and exhausted from its internal destruction, like a body afflicted by fevers, was compelled to repel by arms the strongest peoples of the West and the North.

Sertorius, a man powerful in deceit and audacity, had belonged to the Marian party. Fleeing Sulla, he slipped away from Africa into the Spains and incited the most warlike and savage peoples to take up arms.

To oppose him, as I shall state briefly, two commanders were sent, Metellus and Domitius. Domitius was defeated with his army by Hirtulegius, Sertorius’s commander.

Manilius, proconsul of Gaul, crossed into Spain with three legions and fifteen hundred cavalry and joined battle with Hirtulegius under unfavorable conditions. Stripped by him of his camp and forces, he fled almost alone into the town of Ilerda.

Metellus, worn down by many battles and wandering through byways, exhausted the enemy through delay until he could join Pompey’s camp. Pompey, having assembled an army near Palantia, attempted unsuccessfully to defend the city of Lauron, which Sertorius was then attacking; defeated, he fled.

Sertorius, having overcome and routed Pompey, devastated the city of Lauron with the utmost bloodshed. The remaining column of the Lauronites, which had survived the slaughter, he led away into Lusitania in pitiable captivity.

He boasted that Pompey—that Roman commander—had been defeated by him, although Rome had sent him to this war with great confidence, not as proconsul but as though he were acting in place of consuls.

Galba writes that Pompey then had thirty thousand infantry and one thousand cavalry; he records that Sertorius had sixty thousand infantry and eight thousand cavalry.

Afterward Hirtulegius, having engaged Metellus near Italica, a city of Baetica, lost twenty thousand soldiers. Defeated, he fled with a few men into Lusitania.

Pompey captured Belgida, a distinguished city of Celtiberia. Then Sertorius engaged Pompey and killed ten thousand of his soldiers; from the other wing, where Pompey was victorious, Sertorius himself lost nearly the same number. Many further battles were fought between them.

Memmius, Pompey’s quaestor and also his sister’s husband, was killed. Hirtulegius’s brothers were killed. Perpenna, who had joined Sertorius, was crushed.

Finally Sertorius himself, in the tenth year after the beginning of the war, was killed by the treachery of his own men—the same kind of treachery by which Viriathus had been killed—and brought the war to an end, giving the Romans a victory without glory.

Although afterward part of his army followed Perpenna, Pompey defeated him and killed him together with his entire army. Pompey also received all the cities of Spain voluntarily and without delay through surrender, and then overthrew them.

Meanwhile, having drawn Macedonia by lot, Claudius subdued the various peoples who surrounded the Rhodope Mountains and were then devastating Macedonia with the utmost cruelty. Among the other horrors, dreadful to tell and hear, that they inflicted upon captives, whenever a drinking cup was needed they eagerly and without revulsion used human skulls as though they were genuine cups—skulls still bloody and hairy, smeared with brains that had been poorly scraped out from their inner cavities. The most bloody and savage of these peoples were the Scordisci.

As I have said, Claudius attempted to drive them from the boundaries of Macedonia by war and exposed himself to great masses of evils. Thus, when he was sick in spirit, surrounded by anxieties, and additionally seized by illness, he died.

His successor Scribonius, avoiding the force of the peoples attacked in the earlier war, turned his arms toward Dardania and conquered it.

Publius Servilius, a former consul, attacked Cilicia and Pamphylia with the utmost cruelty. While striving to subjugate them, he nearly destroyed them. He captured Lycia and its cities after besieging and crushing them.

Moreover, after traversing Mount Olympus, he overthrew Phasidem [variant: Phaselim] and destroyed Corycus. He also explored the sides of Mount Taurus facing Cilicia and brought the Isaurians, broken by war, into submission.

He was the first of the Romans to lead an army across the Taurus and made it the boundary of his route. After three years, during which the war was conducted, he assumed the name Isauricus.

The proconsul Cosconius, having drawn Illyricum by lot, crushed and subdued Dalmatia and finally stormed and captured Salonae, a most flourishing city, after two years.

## CHAPTER XVI

### On the gladiators who, escaping from the training school, stirred up many extremely destructive wars against the Romans, their masters

In the consulship of Lucullus and Cassius, seventy-four gladiators escaped at Capua from the training school of Gnaeus Lentulus. Immediately, under the leadership of the Gauls Crixus and Inomaus and the Thracian Spartacus, they occupied Mount Vesuvius.

From there they considered making a breakout. [Note: Orosius reads: “Breaking out from there, they stormed the camp of the praetor Clodius, who had surrounded them with a siege, and, after putting him to flight, turned everything into plunder. From there, etc.” EDIT.]

Afterward, being led around through Consentia and Metapontum, they quickly gathered enormous forces. Crixus is said to have had a multitude of ten thousand, while Spartacus had three times that number. Inomaus had already been killed in the earlier war.

Thus, while mingling everything with slaughter, fires, rapine, and sexual violence, at the funeral of a captive matron who had killed herself from grief at the violation of her chastity, they presented a gladiatorial show from four hundred captives. They, of course, who had formerly been a spectacle for others to watch, were now themselves to watch it—as lanistae, leaders of gladiators rather than soldiers.

Then the consuls Gellius and Lentulus were sent against them with an army. Gellius defeated Crixus, who was fighting most fiercely, in battle; Lentulus, overcome by Spartacus, fled. Later, after both consuls had uselessly joined their forces, they fled after suffering a severe defeat.

Next, the same Spartacus defeated and killed Gaius Cassius, the proconsul.

Accordingly, when the state was terrified by almost as great a fear as that with which it had trembled under Hannibal roaring near the gates, the Senate sent the consul Crassus with legions and a new supplement of soldiers.

As soon as he joined battle with the fugitives, he killed six thousand of them and captured nine hundred. Then, before he attacked Spartacus himself, who was encamped at the headwaters of the Silarus River, he defeated his Gallic and German auxiliaries. Thirty-three thousand men among them, together with their commanders, were killed.

Finally, he engaged Spartacus himself in an arranged battle and routed the greatest forces of fugitives with him. Sixty thousand of them are reported to have been killed and six thousand captured; three thousand Romans were recovered. The rest, who had escaped from this war and were wandering about, were crushed by repeated searches under several commanders.

## CHAPTER XVII

### On the various battles fought in the East—that is, those which Mithridates first conducted successfully and later unsuccessfully—and on what Sulla, Lucullus, and the other commanders of the Roman army accomplished at that time

Mithridates, king of Pontus and Armenia, after attempting to deprive Nicomedes, king of Bithynia and a friend of the Roman people, of his kingdom, was warned by the Senate that, if he attempted this, war would be waged against him by the Roman people.

In anger, he immediately overran Cappadocia. After expelling King Ariobarzanes from it, he devastated the entire province with fire and sword. Then he attacked Bithynia with equal destruction. He afflicted Paphlagonia with a similar end, driving out its kings Philomenes and Nicomedes.

When he came to Ephesus, he issued a cruel edict that throughout Asia all Roman citizens who were found should be killed on a single day. And it was done.

No words can in any way explain or encompass the multitude of Roman citizens who were then killed. What grief there was in so many provinces, what lamentation among those who were being killed and those who were killing, when each person was compelled either to betray innocent guests and friends or to endanger himself by the punishment of his guests.

Archelaus, too, Mithridates’ commander, having been sent ahead to Achaea with one hundred and twenty thousand infantry and cavalry, seized Athens and the whole of Greece, partly by force and partly through surrender. [Variant: “Greece, partly by force, partly by surrender.”]

Sulla, to whom the Mithridatic War had fallen after his consulship, besieged Archelaus at the Piraeus, the port of the Athenians, fortified by a sevenfold wall, for a long time. He captured the city of Athens itself by force and afterward engaged Archelaus in a regular battle.

One hundred and ten thousand of Archelaus’s army are reported to have been killed, with scarcely ten thousand left alive.

When the disaster became known, Mithridates sent seventy thousand elite soldiers from Asia to Archelaus as reinforcements. In a second battle, fifty thousand [variant: fifteen thousand] of them were killed, and there Diogenes, Archelaus’s son, was slaughtered.

In the third battle, all the forces that Archelaus possessed were destroyed. Twenty thousand of his soldiers, driven into a marsh, pleaded for Sulla’s protection but were killed by the victor’s insatiable rage. An equal number were forced into a river and killed; the rest of the wretched men were slaughtered indiscriminately.

Meanwhile, Mithridates resolved to kill the leading men of the most distinguished cities in Asia and confiscate their property. After he had already killed one thousand six hundred in this way, the Ephesians, fearing their example, shut their gates against him after expelling his garrison.

The Smyrnaeans, Sardians, Colophonians, and Trallians did likewise.

Mithridates, thrown into confusion, made peace with Sulla through his commander Archelaus.

Meanwhile Fimbria, an accomplice in the Marian crimes and the boldest of all men, killed the consul Flaccus, whose legate he was at Nicomedia. Soon afterward, having seized his army, he drove Mithridates’ son from Asia to Militopolis, attacked the king’s station, and drove Mithridates himself from Pergamum. Pursuing him, he besieged him at Pitane.

He would certainly have captured him if Lucius Lucullus had placed the care of the state above civil disagreements and wished to hem him in by sea with a fleet.

Then Fimbria, angry with the Ilians, by whom he seemed to have been repulsed through the closing of the gates because of their support for Sulla’s party, destroyed the city itself—the ancient parent of Rome—utterly by slaughter and fire. Sulla immediately rebuilt it.

When the same Fimbria was besieged with his army at Thyatira by Sulla, driven to despair, he killed himself in the temple of Aesculapius.

Fannius and Maius, deserters from Fimbria’s army, joined Mithridates. At their urging Mithridates made a treaty with Sertorius through envoys sent to Spain.

Sertorius sent Marcus Marius to him to strengthen the treaty. The king kept him with himself and soon made him commander in place of Archelaus, who had gone over to Sulla with his wife and children.

Marius and Eumachus, commanders sent by Mithridates against Lucullus, quickly assembled a large army and engaged Publius Rutilius near Chalcedon. They killed him together with a very large part of his army.

Lucullus surrounded Mithridates, who was besieging the Cyzicenes, with a trench and compelled him to suffer what he was inflicting.

Accordingly, he sent a message to the Cyzicenes urging them to remain confident, using a soldier skilled in swimming. Suspended from two inflated skins, holding a small rule in his hands, and paddling with his feet, the man crossed seven thousand paces.

Mithridates, suffering from want, ordered part of his forces, equipped for battle, to return home. Lucullus intercepted and completely destroyed them. He is said to have killed more than fifteen thousand men at that time.

Then Fannius, who had joined Mithridates, and Metrophanes, the royal praetor, were defeated by Mamercius. They fled with two thousand cavalry into Mysia. From there, turning toward Maeonia, they came upon hills and sandy plains, where not only burned mountains and rocks blackened as though by a kind of soot are visible, but also fields, barren from scorched soil, extending for fifty thousand paces [variant: *quinginta millia*, “fifty thousand paces”], with no sign of fire or furnace, and rotten ash hanging and lying in the depths.

Three places also display burning chasms, which the Greeks call *physae*. After wandering about in them for a long time, they were finally rescued from unexpected dangers and secretly reached the king’s camp.

Deiotarus, king of Gallograecia, killed the king’s commanders in battle.

Meanwhile, Mithridates, at Cyzicus, was besieged by the same delay with which he had been besieging the city, and reduced his army to great want and pestilence. For he is said to have lost more than three hundred thousand men from hunger and disease during that same siege. He himself, with a few companions, seized a ship and secretly fled from the camp.

Lucullus, with no bloodshed among his own soldiers, gained a new kind of victory as a spectator of another’s disaster.

Soon afterward he attacked Marius, defeated him, and put him to flight. More than eleven thousand Marian soldiers are reported to have been killed in that battle.

Later Lucullus engaged the same Marius in a naval battle and either sank or captured thirty-two royal ships and several cargo vessels. Many of those whom Sulla had proscribed were killed there.

On the following day Marius was dragged out of the cave where he was hiding and paid the deserved penalty for his hostile spirit.

In the same advance Lucullus devastated Apamea and, beneath Mount Olympus, captured and sacked Prusa, a very strongly fortified city, after taking it by assault.

Mithridates, sailing toward Byzantium with a fleet prepared for battle, was caught by a storm and lost eighty ships with beaks. When he himself was already sinking with his shattered vessel, he leapt into the *meoparon* [variant: *myoparon*] of the pirate Seleucus, with the pirate himself assisting him.

From there he reached Sinope and afterward Anison with great difficulty. Lucullus had besieged Sinope in order to storm it. Seleucus, the chief pirate, and the eunuch Cleochares, who was in charge of the garrison, left it plundered and burning.

Lucullus, moved by the internal destruction of the wretched enemy, arrived swiftly and extinguished the fire that had been set. Thus the unfortunate city, by a reversal of circumstances, was destroyed by those from whom it should have been defended—its allies—and preserved by those from whom it should have been destroyed—its enemies.

But Marcus Lucullus, who had succeeded Curio in Macedonia, attacked the entire people of the Bessi in war and received them into submission.

Moreover, Lucullus crossed the Euphrates and the Tigris and engaged Mithridates and Tigranes near the city of Tigranocerta. With a very small force of his own, he killed a great number of the enemy. Thirty thousand men are reported to have been killed in that war.

Tigranes fled accompanied by scarcely one hundred and fifty cavalry, throwing away his diadem and tiara so that he would not be recognized.

Then envoys from nearly the whole of the East came as suppliants to Lucullus. With winter approaching, he returned through Armenia into Mesopotamia and stormed and captured Nisibis, a city then renowned in those regions.

In those same days pirates, scattered across all the seas, were increasing without measure. They no longer merely intercepted the transport of ships but also devastated islands and provinces, joining themselves publicly through impunity in crime and greed for plunder.

Gaius Pompey suppressed them with astonishing speed, after the great devastation they had inflicted for a long time by land and sea.

At the same time Metellus overthrew the island of Crete for two years and, after subduing it in a prolonged war, brought it under his authority. He exchanged the laws of Minos for Roman laws.

In those same days, Armenia and Mesopotamia having been conquered by Lucullus and Nisibis captured, Syria passed into Roman control. Until then it had been held by the kings of the Macedonians from Alexander onward.

At that time the satiric poet Horace Flaccus was born at Venusia to a freedman father. Apollodorus of Pergamum, a Greek orator and teacher of Galidius and Augustus, was held in high repute.

Accordingly, the events that Sallust writes about Catiline and Lentulus, or Cicero, took place at this time.

The orator Marcus Callidus was also held in high repute. Later, during the civil war, he followed Caesar’s party and, while governing Cisalpine Gaul, died at Placentia.

Now I have decided to bring the sixth book to an end, so that the wars of the Romans—both their civil wars mingled everywhere with foreign wars—and also the wars of the Jews, both those that have been recounted and those that follow, may, since they are linked to one another in an uninterrupted sequence of times and successive misfortunes, at least be separated by the boundary of a book.

# BOOK SEVEN

[Col. 1075]

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 1075C] When Hyrcanus and his brother Aristobulus contend for control of the kingdom, they call upon Pompey as judge; as a result, they are subjected to the Romans.

[Col. 1075D] Accordingly, Hyrcanus, who was high priest of the Jews, had also assumed the reins of the kingdom, although his mother opposed him, as we have stated above. His brother Aristobulus, however, surpassed him in strength and influence. When they had engaged in a conflict near Jericho over supreme authority, most of the people, abandoning Hyrcanus, went over to Aristobulus. Hyrcanus, with those who remained, fled in advance to the fortress of Antonia, where he secured hostages for his safety. Aristobulus’ wife and sons were being held there in custody, as we have stated above. Before anything serious occurred, however, he returned to an agreement on these terms: Aristobulus was to have the kingdom, while Hyrcanus was to withdraw, content as the king’s brother and with the other honors. Thus reconciled in the temple, after they had most kindly wished each other well in the sight of the surrounding people, they exchanged homes: Aristobulus withdrew to the royal palace, while Hyrcanus went to Aristobulus’ house.

Fear also seized the other enemies of the ruler, contrary to their expectations, and especially Antipater, who had long been hated by Aristobulus. He was an Idumaean by birth, and in nobility, wealth, and abundance of other resources was the leading man of his people. Accordingly, he urged Hyrcanus to flee to Aretas, king of Arabia, and with his aid reclaim the kingdom; and he himself persuaded Aretas to receive Hyrcanus and restore him to the kingdom, making many disparaging remarks about Aristobulus’ character and praising Hyrcanus with many commendations. At the same time, he reminded Aretas that one said to rule a most illustrious kingdom ought to extend a hand to those oppressed by injustice, whereas Hyrcanus was suffering wrong because he had been deprived of the principate owed to him by right of succession.

Having thus instructed and prepared them both, Antipater fled by night from the city with Hyrcanus and, traveling at a rapid pace, reached safety in the town called Petra, which was the seat of the kingdom [Col. 1077A] of Arabia. There, after placing Hyrcanus under the protection of King Aretas, he prevailed upon the king, by many words and many gifts, to provide him assistance so that he might be restored to the kingdom. Accordingly, the king gathered an army from every direction and led it into Judaea. There were fifty thousand infantry and cavalry. Aristobulus was wholly unable to withstand them; defeated at the first assault, he was forced to flee to Jerusalem. He would have been completely captured had the Roman commander Scaurus not lifted the siege that threatened him.

Scaurus had indeed been sent by Pompey the Great from Armenia into Syria, where Pompey was waging war against Tigranes. But when Scaurus came to Damascus and found it held and captured by the consuls Metellus and Lollius, he drove them out. Learning what was happening in Judaea, he hastened there as though to seize an opportunity for profit. [Col. 1077B] Finally, when he entered the territory of the Jews, envoys came to him from each brother, asking him to give assistance preferably to himself. But justice was set aside for the four hundred talents Aristobulus had sent. After receiving as many more, Scaurus sent envoys to Hyrcanus and the Arabs, threatening them with the name of Rome and Pompey unless they withdrew from the siege. Accordingly, Aretas, struck with fear, withdrew from Judaea to Philadelphia, and Scaurus returned to Damascus.

Hyrcanus and Antipater, deprived of Arab assistance, placed their hope in their opponents. When Pompey had crossed Syria and reached Damascus, they took refuge with him and, after presenting him with many gifts—citing only those by which they had previously approached Aretas—strongly urged him to regard Aristobulus’ violence [Col. 1077C] as deserving hatred and to restore Hyrcanus to the kingdom, to which he was entitled both by age and by character.

Aristobulus, relying on Scaurus’ support, did not fail to appear before Pompey. But when he realized that he had not at all gained Pompey’s favor, he withdrew angrily to Jerusalem and was already considering engaging Pompey in war. Pompey, however, thought that Aristobulus should not be given time for preparations and immediately followed him. His eagerness had been greatly increased by the news, received near Jericho, of Mithridates’ death. After spending the night there, he hastened in the morning toward Jerusalem.

Terrified by this advance, Aristobulus went to meet Pompey as a suppliant, promised money, and offered to place himself and the city in Pompey’s hands. In this way he calmed Pompey’s anger, but none of the promises was fulfilled. [Col. 1077D] Even Gabinius, who had been sent to receive the money, was not admitted into Aristobulus’ town by Aristobulus’ supporters. Angered by this, Pompey placed Aristobulus under guard.

When Pompey had gone to the city and was making a circuit of it to inspect from which side the ascent would be easiest, a revolt broke out within the city. Aristobulus’ supporters declared that it was more honorable to wage war and free the king; those who sided with Hyrcanus wanted the gates opened to Pompey. At last, the defeated party withdrew into the temple. They cut down the bridge that joined it to the city and prepared to resist to the very end.

When others had admitted the Romans into the city and handed over the royal palace to them, Pompey introduced Piso, one of the commanders obedient to him, with soldiers, in order to secure these positions. After distributing garrisons throughout the city, Piso was unable to persuade any of those who had taken refuge in the temple to make peace. He therefore prepared everything around it for an assault, while Hyrcanus and his friends were eager to deliberate and carry out whatever he ordered.

Pompey himself surrounded the temple with a siege. He placed towers against it and brought up siege engines, attempting to break through the walls, but the defenders drove the Romans back with stones and by force of arms. In the third month of the siege, when scarcely one tower had been thrown down, the sanctuary was stormed. The first to dare to climb the wall was Faustus Cornelius, son of Sulla; after him came two centurions, Furius and Fabius, with their columns.

After surrounding the sanctuary on every side, they killed those who fled there or offered even brief resistance. Some zealous supporters of the opposing party slaughtered many of their own countrymen. Many threw themselves headlong from the cliffs; others, driven mad, set fire in despair to everything around the wall and were consumed in the flames along with it. Thus twelve thousand Jews were killed, while only a very few Romans fell, though many were wounded.

Nothing in that disaster seemed more grievous to the Jewish people than that the sacred mystery, previously seen by no outsider, had now been revealed to foreigners. Pompey, entering the temple with his companions—where no one but the high priest was permitted to be present—examined everything inside: the lampstands with their lamps, the tables from which it was customary to pour libations and burn offerings, and all the vessels of gold. He also saw the great mass of spices and nearly two thousand talents of sacred money. Yet he touched neither these things nor anything else among the sacrosanct treasures or implements. On the following day, after the destruction, he ordered the temple attendants to cleanse the temple so that it would contain no filth, and he ordered the customary sacred rites to be celebrated.

He himself, having appointed Hyrcanus high priest—because Hyrcanus had also shown himself energetic in other matters and had recalled from Aristobulus a large force of country people ready for war—won the goodwill of the populace, as befitted a good commander, by benevolence rather than fear. Among the captives was Aristobulus’ father-in-law, who was also his uncle. Pompey struck down with the axe those who had been chiefly responsible for the war; but he rewarded Faustus and those who had fought bravely with him with splendid prizes, and imposed tribute upon Jerusalem. [Col. 1078D]

Pompey entrusted Scaurus with the supreme affairs of the regions from the Euphrates River to the borders of Egypt, together with two [unspecified units], and himself hurried to Rome by way of Sicily, taking Aristobulus captive with his family. Aristobulus had two daughters and an equal number of sons. One of them, Alexander, escaped on the journey; the younger, Antigonus, was carried to Rome with his sisters.

Meanwhile Alexander gathered a band of men, threatened Hyrcanus more seriously, and ravaged Judaea. He believed that he could quickly defeat Hyrcanus, and fortified suitable towns with walls—Alexandrium, Hyrcanium, and Macherus—not far from the mountains of Arabia. He took care to gather an army from every direction, until he had ten thousand infantry and fifteen hundred [Col. 1079A] cavalry.

Gabinius, who had been sent to Syria and had succeeded Scaurus, advanced against Alexander with a strong force of soldiers and a large number of Jews. Alexander was defeated in the battle, losing six thousand men, three thousand of whom were captured alive and three thousand slain. He himself took refuge in the fortress of Alexandrium. When he was surrounded by a siege and saw that the enemy was pressing him ever more fiercely, Alexander, terrified and despairing of everything, sent envoys to Gabinius. He begged pardon for his offenses and did not hesitate to surrender the fortresses he controlled, Macherus and Hyrcanium; he even placed Alexandrium under Gabinius’ authority.

Gabinius completely demolished all these fortifications, following the advice of Alexander’s mother. Afterward, having brought Hyrcanus to Jerusalem, he entrusted him with care of the temple, placed the optimates in charge of the other departments of government, and divided the entire Jewish people into five judicial districts: one at Jerusalem, another at Doris, a third at Amathus, a fourth at Jericho, and a fifth at Sepphoris, a city of Galilee. Freed from the singular rule of one man, the Jews willingly allowed themselves to be governed by the optimates.

## CHAPTER II

How Crassus plundered the temple and was soon afterward killed in the Parthian war; also concerning Herod’s father and mother, his brothers and sister; and how the historian Africanus held a different opinion from Josephus about Herod’s father; concerning Lucullus, who defeated Mithridates and Tigranes in war; and concerning Pompey, his successor, who subjected most of the East to Roman rule.

[Col. 1079C] After these and other events had taken place, Crassus, Gabinius’ successor, meanwhile assumed command of Syria. As he was departing for the Parthian war, he removed all the gold that was in the temple at Jerusalem, and in addition ordered two thousand talents to be taken from the inner sanctuary, which Pompey had left untouched. He did not long enjoy his success. When he crossed the Euphrates, he lost a very large army, and he himself was killed by the Persian forces.

Made more confident by this success, the Parthians believed that they should cross into Syria. Cassius vigorously met them with an ambush and drove them back from the borders of the province entrusted to him, not without heavy loss to the enemy. They had advanced in a disorderly manner, thinking that no one would dare oppose them, while Cassius, having anticipated them, occupied positions narrowed by the terrain. Finally, after most of their bravest men had been routed, the Parthians abandoned the war.

After repelling the enemy, Cassius, secure in the province, invaded Judaea. He destroyed Taricheae and sold thirty thousand Jews into slavery. He also ordered Phitalaus, suspected of treachery because he supported Aristobulus’ party, to be put to death. Antipater was not without a share in this plan, since he wished above all to exclude a rival to his power.

Accordingly, Antipater took a wife named Cypros, born in the most distinguished station among the women of Arabia, and had by her four sons and one daughter. Their names were as follows: the first was Phasaelus, the second Herod, the third Josephus, the fourth Pheroras, and the only daughter was Salome. By gifts and services he had earned Gabinius’ favor to the highest degree, and he also gained Cassius’ friendship. [Col. 1080A]

Made a distinguished man by having so many sons, he sought, through gifts and friendship, to purchase an alliance with powerful men. Above all, he had secured the goodwill of the king of the Arabs, because he claimed a relationship arising from the region of Arabia from which his wife had come.

We have excerpted this account from the writings of Josephus. Africanus, who is himself also regarded as a leading historian, gives a different account:

“They say,” he writes, “those who investigated the matter more carefully, that a certain Antipater was the father of Herod the Ascalonite, and that this Antipater himself was the son of a certain Herod, an attendant of the temple of Apollo. This Antipater, captured as a very young boy by Idumaean bandits, remained with the robbers because his father, being reduced to poverty, was unable to ransom his son. The boy, however, raised in the life and ways of brigands, later became a close associate of a certain Hyrcanus, the high priest of the Jews. From him was born this Herod who lived in the time of the Savior.”

This is Africanus’ account.

## CHAPTER III

Concerning Lucullus, who defeated Mithridates and Tigranes in war; and concerning Pompey, his successor, who subjected most of the East to Roman rule.

At that time the following events were taking place among the Romans. After Lucullus had defeated the kings Mithridates and Tigranes and subjected the greater part of the East to Roman authority, Pompey became his successor.

Accordingly, in Lesser Armenia, near Mount Dastracum, Pompey surrounded the camp of King Mithridates with a siege. The king made a sortie by night with all his forces and decided also to repel his pursuer in battle. Pompey set out to pursue the fugitives. Thus the battle was joined at night. The moon had then risen behind the Romans. Taking the royal [variant: of the king’s] length of the shadows to indicate the enemy’s proximity, the Romans discharged all their weapons to no purpose. Later, attacking as though unarmed, they won without difficulty. Forty thousand of the royal army were killed or captured; one thousand Romans were wounded, while scarcely forty were killed.

The king escaped amid the confusion of the battle, aided by the dim light of the night. Abandoned by all his companions—philosophers, writers of histories or poems, and physicians—he alone, leading a horse by the hand and trembling at every nocturnal noise, turned aside into a certain fortress and from there proceeded into Armenia.

While pursuing the king, Pompey founded the city of Nicopolis between two rivers that rise from one mountain through separate caves, namely the Euphrates and the Araxes. He founded it for the veterans, camp-followers, and sick who wished to remain there. He granted Tigranes’ request for pardon. He defeated in battle three times the army of Herod, king of the Albanians, and his commanders; afterward he willingly accepted Herod’s letters and gifts to renew an alliance with the Albanians.

He routed Artaces, king of Iberia, in war and received all Iberia into submission. After organizing Armenia, Colchis, Cappadocia, and Syria, he advanced from Pontus into Parthia and afterward reached Bathana [Ecbatana], the capital of the Parthian kingdom, on the fiftieth day.

At that time, while Mithridates was celebrating the Cerealia in the Bosporus, a very severe earthquake suddenly occurred, and it was reported that a great destruction of cities [Col. 1081A] and fields followed from it. At the same time Castor, Mithridates’ commander who governed Phanagoria, killed the king’s friends, seized the citadel, and sent four of Mithridates’ sons to the Roman garrisons.

Mithridates, inflamed with anger, broke out into crimes. He then killed several of his friends and his son Exipodras, having already murdered another, Aliomachares [another named Machares], by parricide. Pharnaces, another of his sons, terrified by the example of his brothers, won over the army that had been sent to pursue him and soon led it against his father.

Mithridates long pleaded with his son in vain from the top of a very high wall. When he saw that Pharnaces was implacable, he is said, as he was about to die, to have cried out: “Since Pharnaces commands me to die, I pray you, ancestral gods—if you exist—that he too may one day hear these words from his own children.” He then descended and gave poison to all his wives, concubines, and daughters.

When he himself drank last of all, the poison could not kill him because of the antidotes with which he had often fortified his vital organs against harmful substances. He therefore summoned a certain Gaulish soldier who was running about after the wall had been breached, and offered him his throat. Such was the end of Mithridates’ life.

When Pompey received news of Mithridates’ death, he attacked Coele-Syria and Phoenicia in war. He first subdued the Ituraeans and the Arabs, and captured their city, which they call Petra. From there, as we have stated above, he hurried to the Jews and ordered Jerusalem to be destroyed and leveled to the ground. After striking down several Jewish leaders with the axe, he restored the priesthood to Hyrcanus and led Aristobulus captive to Rome. Pompey himself declared before the assembly that he had waged this eastern war against twenty-two kings.

## CHAPTER IV

How the provinces of Gaul were assigned to Caesar by the Senate; and concerning the various battles fought in Gaul.

Meanwhile, the consul Gaius Caesar was given three provinces with seven legions for five years: Transalpine Gaul, Cisalpine Gaul, and Illyricum. The Senate afterward added Gallia Comata.

The Helvetii, therefore, the bravest of all the Gallic peoples, had been roused to war by a certain Orgetorix, a leading man of the nation, chiefly because they were almost continually engaged in war with the Germans, from whom they were separated only by the Rhine. He had inflamed them with the hope of invading all Gaul. [Col. 1081D] The other optimates seized him and compelled him to die, but they were nevertheless unable to restrain the populace, which had once been aroused by the prospect of plunder. After forming a conspiracy and setting a date, they burned their villages and homes so that no desire to return might remain from the hope of recovering them, and then departed.

When Caesar encountered them near the Rhône River, he defeated them only with difficulty in two major battles and forced the defeated people to surrender. When they first set out, their entire multitude—Helvetii, Tulingi, Latobriges, Rauraci, and Boii, of both sexes—numbered 157,000 people. Of these, 47,000 fell in the war; the rest were sent back to their own lands.

Afterward Caesar defeated Ariovistus, the king who was stirring up and bringing with him an incredible multitude of Germans, at the Sequani. He had recently boasted that he had subjected all the peoples of Gaul to himself. After Caesar’s army had long refused battle, terrified by the number and valor of the Germans, Ariovistus seized a small boat, crossed the Rhine, and escaped into Germany. Two wives and an equal number of daughters were captured.

The peoples in Ariovistus’ army were the Harudes, Marcomanni, Triboci, Vangiones, Nemetes, Eduri, and Suebi. The Germans’ great phalanx was especially formidable in the battle. They had formed themselves into a single column and, interweaving their shields above their heads, had constructed a protective formation on every side for breaking through the Roman line.

But after some Roman soldiers, distinguished for agility and courage, leapt onto the shield-covering testudo and, tearing away the shields one by one as though scales, pierced from above the exposed shoulders of the men whom they had uncovered and discovered, the terrified enemy, faced with this new danger of death, broke up the fearsome formation. Then they turned to flight and were slaughtered without respite for fifty thousand paces. It was impossible to determine the number of Germans who had been present in the battle or the number who had been killed.

After this, the nation of the Belgae, which is a third part of Gaul, rose up against Caesar. Their forces were distributed as follows. The Bellovaci, who seemed to surpass the others in number and valor, had forty thousand chosen armed men [Alternative: sixty thousand]. The Suessiones, from twelve towns, had fifty thousand. The Nervii, whose savagery was said to be so untamed that up to that time they had never admitted merchants among them bringing wine or other goods—things whose introduced pleasures might bring lethargy to their valor—likewise had fifty thousand. The Trebatians and Ambiani had ten thousand; the Morini, twenty-five thousand; the Menapii, nine thousand; the Caleti, ten thousand; the Bellocassi and Veromandi, likewise ten thousand; the Atuatuci, eighteen thousand; and the Condrusi, Eburones, Caerosi, and Cemanni, who are called Germans by one name, forty thousand.

Thus, it is reported, there were 272,000 chosen armed men. When they suddenly burst out of a forest, Caesar’s army was thrown into confusion and put to flight, with many of his men lost. At last, encouraged by the commander, it rallied, attacked the victors, and almost annihilated them.

## CHAPTER V

How Julius Caesar, after believing that Gaul had been subjected to surrender and wishing to return to Italy, was drawn back by the attack of the Gauls, became involved in various battles, crossed from Gaul into Britain, and subjugated it, not without great danger to his men.

[Col. 1082D]

Accordingly, after accomplishing great things in Gaul, Caesar, when he had decided to depart for Italy, sent Galba with the Twelfth Legion against the Veragri and Seduni. Galba had settled for the purpose of wintering in a village of the Veragri called Octodurus, and had assigned to the inhabitants the half of the town separated by a torrent. One day he saw that they had withdrawn by night and occupied the neighboring hill.

They despised the small number of barely half a legion and believed that booty would fall to them without any difficulty. They called their neighbors to share in the killing and plunder. Galba, surrounded by such immediate dangers and terrified, uncertain of a definite plan amid various deliberations, suddenly saw the Gauls pour down from the mountain, surround the unfinished camp, and bombard the few defenders along the rampart with stones and missiles.

When the camp was already being stormed, at the advice of Pacuvius, the chief centurion, and the tribune Volusinus, all the Romans burst out through the gates. They suddenly attacked the unsuspecting enemy, first throwing them into confusion and then scattering them in flight with a pitiful slaughter. More than thirty thousand barbarians are reported to have been killed at that time.

Caesar, who now thought that all the peoples of Gaul had been pacified, was drawn back into a new and very great war. While the young Publius Crassus was wintering with the Seventh Legion near the Ocean among the Andicavi, the Veneti and their neighboring peoples suddenly conspired to take up arms. They seized the Roman envoys and announced to the Romans that they would release them only if they received back their own hostages.

They brought the Osismi, Lixovii, Namnetes, Ambivaritae, Morini, Menapii, and Diablintes in as allies for this war, and summoned auxiliaries from Britain. Caesar, informed by Crassus of the revolt of these peoples, understood how difficult it would be to undertake the war, but nevertheless judged that so important a matter must not be neglected, lest an example of this kind open the way for the others to attempt the same thing.

He therefore tried in vain to pursue the enemy by land. Since the enemy was protected by the waterways extending inland from the Ocean and by inaccessible retreats, Caesar ordered long ships to be built on the Loire River. They were brought down it into the Ocean, and as soon as the enemy saw them, their 220 ships, prepared and fully equipped with every kind of weapon, advanced from the harbor and took up position opposite them.

Brutus, looking around and seeing that the naval engagement was greatly unequal, found that the barbarians’ ships were built of solid timber and reinforced with massive beams, so that, like rocks, they blunted the blows of the beaked ships that struck them. His first advantage was that he had prepared very sharp sickles, not fixed rigidly to poles but attached by ropes. Whenever necessary, these could seize the rigging from a distance; then, by lowering the poles and drawing back the sickle along the rope, they could cut it down.

After quickly putting these devices into operation, he ordered the enemy’s yardarms and rigging to be severed. As the yardarms fell, several ships were immediately rendered motionless, as though captured. Others, terrified by this danger, raised their sails and tried to flee wherever the wind carried them; but when the wind soon ceased, they were left helpless and became an object of derision to the Romans.

Accordingly, after all the ships had been burned and those who had fought had been killed, the remaining Gauls all surrendered. But Caesar, especially because of the injury done to the envoys and in order to brand the nation with a terrifying example that would deter it from every such plan, had all the leaders killed by torture and sold the rest under the crown.

During these same days, Titurius Sabinus, after the Alverni, Eburovices, and Lixovii had killed their own leaders because they refused to be the authors of reviving the war, made a sortie and destroyed them in an incredible slaughter.

Publius Crassus, however, was met by war when he reached Aquitania. The Sotiates [Sontiates], attacking the Romans with a large cavalry force and very strong infantry troops, greatly harassed them for a long time. After they had been defeated, driven into the town of the Sotiates [Sontiates], and surrounded by a siege, they saw that the town was being stormed, surrendered their weapons, and were accepted into submission.

The Aquitani, shaken by this defeat, gathered an army from every direction and summoned auxiliaries from inner Spain as well. They appointed as commanders in the war chiefly those who had served with Sertorius. While these men were preparing to besiege Crassus, Crassus overwhelmed them in their camp and destroyed them all. Of the Aquitani and Cantabri, fifty thousand of whom had then come to their aid, twenty-eight thousand are reported to have been killed.

Caesar attacked in war the Germans who had crossed the Rhine with immense forces and were preparing to subject all Gaul to themselves. He slew them almost to the point of annihilation. Their number is said to have been about 440,000.

Then Caesar crossed into Germany over a bridge. He freed the Sicambri and Ubii from siege, terrified the Suebi—a very large and fierce nation, of which many have reported that there were one hundred districts and peoples—and terrified all Germany by his arrival.

Soon afterward he dismantled the bridge and withdrew into Gaul. From there he went to the Morini, from whom the nearest and shortest crossing to Britain lies. After preparing about eighty transport and light cargo ships, he crossed into Britain.

There he was first exhausted by a fierce battle; then, overtaken by a storm, he lost most of his fleet and a considerable number of soldiers, while almost all his cavalry was destroyed. Returning to Gaul, he sent the legions into winter quarters and ordered six hundred ships of both types to be built.

At the beginning of spring he crossed again into Britain in these ships. While he himself advanced against the enemy with the army, the ships lying at anchor were caught by a storm; some were dashed against one another, others struck the sandbanks, and they were wrecked. Forty of them perished; the rest were repaired only with great difficulty.

Caesar’s cavalry was defeated by the Britons at the first encounter, and the tribune Labienus was killed there. In a second battle, Caesar turned the Britons, after defeating them at great cost to his own men, and put them to flight.

From there he proceeded to the river Thames, which is said to be fordable at only one place. On the farther bank, an immense multitude of the enemy had assembled under their commander Cassivellaunus. They had fortified the riverbank and almost the entire ford beneath the water with very sharp stakes.

When this was detected and avoided by the Romans, the barbarians, unable to withstand the attack of the legions, hid themselves in the forests. From there they repeatedly burst out and grievously wounded the Romans again and again.

Meanwhile, the very strong city of the Trinovantes, under their leader Androgorius, surrendered to Caesar after giving forty hostages. Following this example, many other cities entered into alliance with the Romans. When these cities pointed it out to him, Caesar at last captured the town of Cassivellaunus in a fierce battle. It lay between two marshes, was additionally fortified by the cover of forests, and was abundantly supplied with everything.

After this, Caesar returned from Britain to Gaul. [Col. 1085A] Once he had sent the legions into winter quarters, he was suddenly surrounded and harassed everywhere by the turmoil of war. Ambiorix, conspiring with the Eburones and Atuatuci and encouraged by the advice of the Treveri, ambushed and killed Cotta and Sabinus, envoys among the Eburones, together with their entire legion.

Elated by this victory, Ambiorix hastily gathered the Atuatuci, Nervii, and many others to arms, and marched against the legate Cicero, who at that time likewise commanded a legion in winter quarters.

The size of the enemy force may be inferred from the fact that, when Roman prisoners informed them that a rampart had to be built around the camp, and they had no agricultural tools, they cut up the earth with swords and carried it away with hoes [or: cloaks], and scarcely within three hours completed a rampart ten feet high and a ditch fifteen feet deep around a circuit of fifteen miles. In addition, they built 120 towers of extraordinary height.

For seven successive days and nights, columns of the enemy fought, and when a very strong wind suddenly arose, they hurled burning pots with slings and cast fire-tipped missiles from their hearths. Once the missiles had caught fire and were glowing, they threw them into the camp. The wind, rushing rapidly over the roofs, fanned the scattered flames.

Yet even then the Romans did not yield, though they were overwhelmed on every side by wounds, hardship, sleeplessness, fasting, and fire. At last Caesar was informed that one legion had been destroyed and another was almost spent.

When Caesar approached with two legions, the enemy abandoned the siege and all rushed against him with their forces hastily gathered. Caesar deliberately shut himself in a very small camp. He sent cavalry ahead and ordered them to pretend to flee, so that, by contempt for him, they might lure the enemy toward the crossing of the valley that lay between them and seemed dangerous to him.

When the enemy approached, he also ordered the gates to be blocked. Seeing this, the Gauls, as though they had already won, turned to throw up a rampart from the outside. Caesar suddenly poured his prepared army out through all the gates and, routing the Gauls, destroyed them in an immense slaughter. They are reported to have numbered sixty thousand; only a few escaped through the impassable marshes.

Induciomarus, leader of the Treveri, possessed a large armed force. After learning of the agreement of all Gaul, he decided that it would be easy to destroy Labienus’ camp and the legion under his command. He then intended, joined with the Eburones and Nervii, to proceed against Caesar and overwhelm him.

Labienus used every stratagem at his disposal to pretend fear. He thereby made Induciomarus less cautious while he was roaming with his attacking forces before the rampart, and in a sudden sortie he struck him down. By this victory Labienus checked the remaining efforts of the Gauls, and Caesar enjoyed somewhat greater quiet for the rest of the winter.

But Caesar understood that greater burdens of war still lay before him. A large part of his army had been lost and others had been seriously wounded, so that he seemed scarcely fit to withstand the enemy, much less to suppress the attack of the Gauls. He therefore asked the proconsul Gnaeus Pompey to levy legions and send them to him as reinforcements. Thus, before winter had ended, three legions arrived in his camp.

[Col. 1086A] Accordingly, before the enemy forces could unite, Caesar prepared, at the beginning of spring, to attack the terrified and overwhelm those scattered through their own territories. First he ravaged the territory of the Nervii and allowed the very abundant booty to the army.

Then he invaded the Menapii, who seemed to him strongly protected by their immense marshes and extremely dense forests, with three columns. After great slaughter had been spread everywhere, he accepted the survivors, who came as suppliants, into submission.

In the following battle Labienus killed the entire force of the Treveri, whom he had drawn into war by stratagem before they could join the Germans who were approaching, and immediately captured the city itself.

Caesar wished to avenge the death of the envoys Sabinus and Cotta. After learning that Ambiorix and the Eburones, the authors of the destroyed legion, had taken refuge in the forest of the Ardennes, he surveyed it. This is the largest forest in all Gaul; it extends from the banks of the Rhine and the borders of the Treveri as far as the Nervii, and stretches for more than five hundred miles in length.

Caesar considered it extremely dangerous for his men to be divided in an unknown region amid obstructed and vast forests while searching for an enemy thoroughly familiar with the terrain. He therefore invited all Gaul by messengers to seek out and plunder, each according to his own inclination, whatever booty was hidden in the Ardennes forest.

As a result, while Gauls were dying on both sides, he avenged the greatest wrongs done to the Romans without danger to any Roman. Thus, secure in this safest method of victory, he returned to Italy.

## CHAPTER VI

After Caesar’s return to Italy, the Gauls again conspire to take up arms; Caesar quickly returns against them, crushes them in various battles, and hands them over to eternal slavery.

Therefore, when Caesar had returned to Italy, Gaul again conspired to take up arms, and many peoples joined together at once. Their leader was Vercingetorix. At his advice, all the Gallic communities immediately burned their own towns of their own accord; the first was Bituricum, burned by its own inhabitants. From there they attacked Caesar, who had secretly hurried back to the army by forced marches through the province of Narbonensis.

Caesar had then shut up a town called Cenabum under siege. After it had long been assaulted, it was finally captured and destroyed, following many Roman losses, on a rainy day [variant: in rainy weather], when the additions to the enemy’s siege engines and their sinews had weakened. Towers were brought up against it, and the town was taken. It is reported that forty thousand people were there; scarcely eighty escaped by flight and reached the nearest camp of the Gauls.

Moreover, the Arverni and the other neighboring peoples, having also persuaded the Aedui to join them, fought many battles against Caesar. When, exhausted by fighting, they had withdrawn into a certain fortress, the soldiers, eager for booty, resolved to storm the town, although Caesar vainly warned them of the unfavorable nature of the place. Thus Caesar, hard-pressed when the enemy burst out from above, lost a large part of his army, was defeated, and fled.

While these events were taking place at Alesia, Vercingetorix, whom all had unanimously chosen as king, urged that from the whole of Gaul all who were capable of bearing arms should be present for this war. For this was a single war in which either perpetual freedom, or eternal slavery, or the death of all would result. Accordingly, in addition to the countless number whom he had previously gathered, approximately eight thousand cavalry and two hundred fifty thousand infantry were assembled.

Afterward, the Romans and Gauls occupied two hills facing one another. Fighting there in frequent sorties and with varying outcomes, the Romans at last prevailed, chiefly through the valor of the German cavalry whom they had long since made their allies and whom they had now summoned to their aid.

On the following day Vercingetorix, having gathered all those who had escaped by flight, said that he had acted in good faith as the defender of liberty and the breaker of the treaty; and that he was now prepared either for all of them to offer themselves to the Romans unto death, or for him alone to surrender on behalf of them all. Accordingly, the Gauls, as though adopting the decision at their king’s command, immediately begged pardon for themselves and surrendered him alone, as the author of a great crime.

The Bellovaci were considered, in their own judgment, stronger than all the Gallic peoples. Under the leadership of Correus they renewed the war, and joined to themselves in this alliance of the war they had undertaken the Ambiani, the Aulerci, the Salii, the Bellocassi, and the Atrebates. They seized a certain place surrounded and obstructed on every side by marshes. Having joined battle, they slaughtered a large force of the Remi who were aiding the Romans.

Then, when they had occupied a place suitable for an ambush, and when the Romans, having learned of this, came equipped and formed up at the place of the ambush, battle was joined. The Romans enclosed the fleeing Gauls within the same fortifications of the place by which they themselves had been shut in, and slew them all. There Correus, refusing either flight or surrender, compelled the Romans, who were pressing to take him alive, to kill him by killing them.

Therefore, when Caesar thought that all Gaul was pacified and would not dare to attempt any further disturbances, he dismissed the legions into winter quarters. Yet he himself devastated the territory of Ambiorix, who had stirred up so many wars, with a terrible slaughter of its inhabitants.

But the legate Gaius Caninius encountered war among the Pictones, where a great multitude of enemies surrounded a legion delayed on the march and brought it to the utmost danger. Fabius, however, after receiving a letter from the legate Caninius, set out for the Pictones. There, having been informed by captives about the suitability of the terrain, he overwhelmed the unsuspecting enemy and, after inflicting great slaughter, carried off immense booty.

Then, when he had given Caninius a signal of his arrival, Caninius suddenly burst out from the entire camp and threw himself upon the enemy. Thus, with Fabius pressing them on one side and Caninius on the other, innumerable Gallic forces were slaughtered in a great and prolonged war.

From there Fabius went to the Carnutes. He knew that Domnacus, a very old commander and the instigator of the entire rebellion, had escaped from this war; if he joined the Aremorican peoples, he would again stir up the greatest disturbances in Gaul. But he subdued these peoples, still trembling from the novelty of the uprising, with extraordinary valor and speed.

Meanwhile Draptes and Lucterius together, seeing that Caninius and the legions had arrived in their territory, gathered forces from every side and occupied a town, or perhaps Uxellodunum [editorial correction]. This town hung upon the highest summit of a mountain; on two sides it was enclosed by precipitous slopes and by a river of considerable size. Then, halfway down the slope, it was made secure by a very abundant spring; protected by a plentiful supply of grain within, it looked down from afar upon the fruitless movements of the enemy.

Caninius, using the only measure available to Roman foresight, drew both leaders out into the open field with the greater part of their forces and defeated them in a very great battle. For one of the leaders was killed, while the other fled with very few followers. No one returned to the town, but Caesar was needed to besiege it.

Accordingly, when he had been informed by messengers [*fuit* should be deleted], Caesar hurried there. After examining everything, he saw that if he attempted to take the town by force, his army would be destroyed as a game and spectacle for the enemy; there was only one means of defense: to cut the enemy off from water by whatever method was possible.

But even this could have been accomplished by no one but Caesar, since the spring from which they obtained drinking water flowed out halfway down the steep side of the mountain. Caesar ordered covered approaches to be brought up near the spring and a tower to be built.

A great sortie was made from the town on every side. Since the defenders could fight without danger, the Romans, although they resisted stubbornly and came forward again and again, nevertheless lost many men. Accordingly, an embankment was constructed, together with a tower sixty feet high, whose summit could be raised to the level of the spring, so that missiles could be thrown from equal height and the defenders would not need to fear rocks hurled down from above.

But when the townspeople saw that not only their animals but also the weaker classes of human beings were being exhausted by thirst, they filled casks with pitch, tallow, and shingles. Then, after setting them on fire, they rolled them down the slope, and they themselves followed them in a mass from the whole town.

When Caesar saw that the burning engines made the battle heavy and dangerous for his men, he ordered cohorts to move rapidly around the town by a concealed route and suddenly to raise a vast shout from every side. The townspeople were thrown into confusion by this. While they wished to rush back to defend the town, they withdrew from attacking the tower and from demolishing the embankment.

Meanwhile, those who, under the protection of the embankment, were digging tunnels to cut the channels of the spring caused the hidden passages of the water, once discovered, to be divided into many branches, weakened, and consumed within themselves.

When the spring had been dried up, the townspeople, seized by the utmost desperation, surrendered themselves. Caesar cut off the hands of all who had borne arms, but left them alive, so that the punishment of the wicked might be a more conspicuous warning even to posterity. For the proposed example of punishment is highly effective in restraining boldness: the visible condition of the miserable man who continues to live both reminds those who know of it and compels the ignorant to inquire.

After the Gauls had been exhausted and their defenses demolished, Caesar returned safely to Italy with the legions, fearing no further Gallic uprising behind him, since he knew for certain that there were scarcely any who would dare to stir, or who, if they did stir, would need to be feared.

## CHAPTER VII. The death of Crassus and the Roman army among the Parthians

Now, when Caesar had returned victorious from Gaul, civil wars followed him, together with other very serious disasters, among which came the killing of Crassus among the Parthians and the slaughter of his army.

Crassus, the colleague of Pompey in the consulship, had obtained by lot the province directed against the Parthians. He was a man of insatiable greed. Having heard of the wealth of the temple at Jerusalem, which Pompey had left untouched, he turned aside into Palestine, went to Jerusalem, entered the temple, and plundered its riches, as we have mentioned above.

From there, advancing through Mesopotamia toward Parthia, he demanded auxiliary forces and exacted payments from the allied cities wherever he passed. As soon as he had crossed the Euphrates, he encountered Baias, whom Orodes, king of the Parthians, had sent to him. Baias vehemently rebuked him for crossing the Euphrates, driven by greed and contrary to the treaty of Lucullus and Pompey. For this reason, he said, it would soon happen that, in exchange for Parthian gold, Crassus would be loaded with Serican iron.

When they had come near Carrhae, the Parthians suddenly attacked the Romans, overwhelming them with arrows under their commanders Surena and Silaces. Many senators fell there, including several men who had been consuls or praetors. The son of Crassus also, a young man of outstanding distinction, was killed in the battle.

Moreover, four cohorts with their commander Barguntius were caught in the middle of the plain and killed. Surena, having hastily seized the cavalry, set out to pursue Crassus. After surrounding him and killing him when he vainly sought a conference, Surena nevertheless would have preferred to take him alive.

A few, saved by the protection of night, took refuge at Carrhae. The greed of a single man also completed the crime, so that twelve Roman legions were either captured, with only a few escaping, or slaughtered together with their commanders.

Crassus’ head, together with his right hand, was carried to the king. This became a spectacle for those watching. The king therefore ordered molten gold to be poured into his mouth, saying:

> “Let Parthian gold now burn you, as it burned you while you were alive.”

When the Roman disaster became known, and many eastern provinces had abandoned the alliance or loyalty of the Roman people, Cassius [OCR: *Nicasius*; variant: *pressisset*, “had restrained”] gathered the few soldiers who had escaped and, with outstanding courage and moderation, restrained the swelling power of Syria.

He defeated and killed Antiochus and his enormous forces in battle. He also drove out the Parthians whom Orodes had sent into Syria and who had already entered Antioch, and he killed their commander Osages.

Meanwhile Rome, seized by a sudden fire, was burned. It is uncertain how the conflagration began; the fire consumed a very large part of the City, and they say that no city had ever before been damaged and devastated by so great a blaze. For tradition records that fourteen districts, together with the district of the Jugarius, were consumed.

## CHAPTER VIII. The civil wars that arose between Caesar and Pompey because Pompey incited the Senate to deny Caesar a second consulship

From this point the civil war was begun, although it had long been prepared by great disagreements and undertakings. For Caesar, returning victorious from Gaul, demanded that a second consulship be decreed for him while he was absent. The consul Marcellus opposed this, with Pompey supporting him.

Then the Senate decreed that Caesar should not enter the City unless he had first dismissed his army, and that Pompey should be sent with imperium from the authority of the consul Marcellus to the legions stationed at Luceria.

Caesar withdrew to Ravenna. Marcus Antonius and Publius Cassius, tribunes of the plebs, interceding on Caesar’s behalf but being excluded from the senate-house and the Forum by the consul Lentulus, went to Caesar; Curio and Coelius accompanied them.

After crossing the Rubicon, Caesar soon arrived at Ariminum. There he explained to the five cohorts—which were then all he possessed, and with which, as Livy says, he attacked the whole world—what needed to be done. Lamenting his wrongs, he declared that the cause of the civil war was the restoration of the tribunes to their country.

Then, through Antonius, he received from Lucretius the seven cohorts that were staying at Sulmo. He brought over to his side the three legions that were staying with Domitius at Cornificium [Corfinium].

Pompey and the entire Senate, alarmed as Caesar’s strength grew, crossed over into Greece as though driven from Italy and chose Dyrrachium as the base from which to conduct the war.

Caesar came to Rome. He broke open the doors of the treasury and seized the money that had been denied him, removing from it 4,136 pounds of gold and nearly 900,000 pounds of silver.

From there he departed for Ariminum, to join the legions, and soon crossed the Alps and came to Massilia. Since the city did not admit him, he left Trebonius there with four legions to besiege it and hastened to Spain, which the Pompeian commanders Lucius Afranius, Marcus Petreius, and Marcus Varro held with their legions.

There, after defeating Petreius and Afranius in many battles, he dismissed them under an agreed arrangement. In Further Spain he received two legions from Marcus Varro.

Likewise, his commanders acted elsewhere: Curio drove Cato from Sicily; Valerius drove Cotta from Sardinia; Varus expelled Tubero from Africa.

When Caesar returned to Massilia, he conquered it by siege. He granted its inhabitants only their lives and freedom, stripping them of everything else.

Dolabella, one of Caesar’s partisans, was defeated in Illyricum by Octavius and Libo and, deprived of his forces, fled to Antonius. Basilius and Sallustius, each with the single legion under his command, and Antonius and Hortensius, coming from the lower sea with a fleet, all set out together against Octavius and Bibulus [Libo] and were defeated.

When Antonius surrendered himself to Octavius with fifteen cohorts, all were led by Libo to Pompey. Curio crossed from Sicily into Africa with an army; King Juba immediately met him and slaughtered him together with all his forces.

While Octavius was attempting to besiege Salona, he lost almost all the troops he had brought. Coelius revolted from Caesar and joined the exiled Milo. When the two attempted to attack Capua with a force of slaves, they were killed.

## CHAPTER IX. The battles fought between Caesar and Pompey, Caesar’s victory and Pompey’s death; the other civil wars fought over four years; and finally the assassination of Julius Caesar

Meanwhile, many kings of the East came to Pompey at Dyrrachium with auxiliary forces. When Caesar arrived there, he unsuccessfully surrounded Pompey with a siege, building a ditch fifteen miles long across the land, while the sea remained open to Pompey.

Pompey overthrew a certain fort near the sea, which Marcellinus was defending, and killed Caesar’s garrisons stationed there. Caesar therefore attacked Torquatus and one legion in order to storm the fort. When Pompey learned of the danger threatening his allies, he drew all his forces there.

Caesar immediately turned against Pompey, abandoning the siege. Torquatus burst out at once and pursued Caesar from behind. Thus Caesar’s soldiers, terrified by the twofold danger, fled despite Caesar’s vain efforts to hold them back.

Pompey, victorious even according to Caesar’s own testimony, recalled the pursuing army. Four thousand of Caesar’s soldiers, twenty-two centurions, and several Roman knights were killed in that battle.

Caesar then marched rapidly through Epirus into Thessaly. Pompey followed with the greatest forces, and battle was joined.

The two armies were accordingly drawn up. Pompey placed eighty-eight cohorts in three lines. His infantry numbered forty thousand; there were six hundred cavalry on the left wing and five hundred on the right. In addition, there were many kings, senators, and a very large number of Roman knights, besides a considerable force of light-armed troops.

Caesar likewise arranged eighty cohorts in three lines. He had no fewer than thirty thousand infantry and one thousand cavalry.

It was a sight to witness and lament: the assembled strength of the Romans stood ready on the plains of Pharsalus for mutual slaughter. If harmony had governed them, no people and no king could have withstood them.

At the first engagement Pompey’s cavalry was driven back and exposed his left flank. Then, after the fighting had for a long time hung in the balance on both sides, Pompey, on one side, said while urging his men, “Spare the citizens,” though he did not do so; while Caesar, on the other side, did what he was pressing them to do, saying:

> “O soldier, strike the face.”

[Note: In Orosius: “Soldier, strike the face.” The word *intuere* should be deleted. Editor.]

At last Pompey’s entire army fled, and his camp was plundered. Fifteen thousand Pompeians and thirty-three centurions were killed in that battle.

This was the outcome of the battle at Palaeopharsalus. Pompey, fleeing, found a merchant ship at the mouth of the Peneus River and crossed into Asia. From there he went through Cyprus to Egypt. As soon as he reached the shore, he was killed by order of the young Ptolemy, who wished to win the favor of Caesar the victor.

Pompey’s wife and sons fled. The rest of the Pompeian fleet was plundered, and everyone aboard it was cruelly slaughtered. Pompey of Bithynia was also killed there. Lentulus, a former consul, was killed at Pelusium.

After settling affairs in Thessaly, Caesar came to Alexandria. When Pompey’s head and ring had been brought to him and he had seen them, he wept.

When he withdrew into the royal palace, the guardians deceived him to prevent him from receiving money. They cunningly stripped the temples of their treasures both to show that the royal treasuries were empty and to stir up the people against Caesar.

The praetor Achillas, the royal commander, already stained with Pompey’s blood, was also plotting Caesar’s death. For when he was ordered to dismiss the army under his command—twenty thousand armed men—he not only disregarded the order but also drew up his battle line.

During the battle itself, the royal fleet, which happened to have been drawn up on shore, was ordered to be burned. When the flames spread into part of the city as well, they consumed four hundred thousand books, stored by chance in nearby buildings: a remarkable monument to the diligence and care of earlier generations, who had collected so many works of so many distinguished minds.

Afterward Caesar seized the island where the lighthouse stood. Achillas came there with Cabinian troops, and a great battle was fought. A large number of Caesar’s soldiers fell there; all the assassins of Pompey were also killed.

Pressed by the force of the enemy’s attack, Caesar boarded a small boat. Soon, when the boat became overloaded and sank beneath the weight of those following him, he reached the ship by swimming for two hundred paces, holding one hand above the water because it contained his papers.

Then, after being attacked in a naval battle, he either sank or captured the royal fleet with great success. When the Alexandrians asked for their king, Caesar returned him to them, warning them that they should strive to test Roman friendship rather than Roman arms.

Yet as soon as the king was free, he made war. He himself was immediately destroyed together with his entire army. It is reported that twenty thousand men were killed in that war, while twelve thousand surrendered together with seventy long ships. Fifty of the victors are said to have fallen.

The young king himself, taken aboard a small boat while attempting to flee, was drowned and killed when many others leapt into it. His body was carried to shore and identified by his golden breastplate.

Caesar sent it ahead to Alexandria, and by driving the Alexandrians to despair compelled them all to surrender; he then gave the kingdom of Egypt to Cleopatra.

From there he traversed Syria and defeated Pharnaces in Pontus. Afterward, when he came to Rome, was made dictator and consul, and crossed into Africa, he fought Juba and Scipio at Thapsus. He killed a very great multitude there, plundered both camps, and captured sixty elephants.

Cato killed himself at Utica. Juba offered his throat to an executioner after giving him money to perform the deed. Petreius pierced himself with the same sword. Scipio, who had attempted to flee to Spain in a ship but had been forced by the wind to return to Africa, cut his own throat. Titus Torquatus was also killed on that same ship.

Caesar ordered the grandsons of Pompey the Great, Pompeia his daughter, and along with them Faustus and Sulla, as well as Afranius and Petreius, to be killed.

Then he entered Rome in four triumphs. After arranging and restoring the state, he immediately set out for Spain against the Pompeii, the sons of Pompey. On the seventeenth day after leaving the City, he reached Saguntum and immediately fought many battles, with varying fortune, against the two Pompeii, Labienus, and Attius Varus.

The final battle was fought at the river Munda [variant: “at the city”]. There the combat was so fierce and the slaughter so great that Caesar himself, when he saw his line being cut down and driven back, and when even his veterans were not ashamed to yield, considered that it would be better to anticipate by death the disgrace of defeat. Suddenly, however, Pompey’s army turned and fled.

Indeed, this battle was fought on the very day on which Pompey’s father had fled from the City to wage war; and for four years this civil war had thundered without interruption throughout the whole world.

Titus Labienus and Attius Varus were killed in the battle. Gaius Pompey fled with one hundred cavalrymen. His brother Sextus Pompey, having quickly gathered a considerable force of Lusitanians, engaged Cesonius, was defeated, and was killed while fleeing.

The city of Munda was captured by force, with immense slaughter of its inhabitants, while Caesar besieged it.

Caesar returned to Rome. There, while he was restoring the condition of the state with clemency, contrary to the examples of his ancestors, he was stabbed to death in the senate-house with twenty-three wounds, through the agency of Brutus and Cassius and with the knowledge of a very large part of the Senate.

They say that more than sixty men were involved in the conspiracy. The two Brutuses, Gaius Cassius, and their other associates withdrew to the Capitol with drawn daggers. For a long time it was debated whether the Capitol, together with the authors of the murder, ought to be burned.

The people, seized by grief, snatched up his body and burned it in the Forum with fragments of tribunal platforms and benches.

But while the events I have related were taking place among the Romans, the following events meanwhile occurred in Judaea.

## CHAPTER X. How Antipater won Caesar’s favor; how, when accused by Antigonus, he displayed the wounds he had received on Caesar’s behalf after stripping his body; and how he divided the authority he had received over Judaea between his sons Herod and Phasael

Julius Caesar—briefly to repeat what had happened earlier—found Aristobulus imprisoned at Rome and soon released him. After removing him from custody and even rewarding him with military gifts, he sent him into Syria to bring Judaea over to his side and press Pompey from the rear.
