But at the beginning of his attempt, when he reached the place, he was killed by poison and left the undertaking unfinished. When Pompey learned this, because Aristobulus had attempted to prepare a renewed war against him in Judaea, he also ordered Aristobulus’ son Alexander to be beheaded.

Afterward, when most of Pompey’s close associates were seeking Caesar’s friendship, Caesar granted it especially to Antipater, who had sought his friendship in an extraordinary manner. This happened as follows.

Ptolemy, king of Egypt, had violated the pledge he had given and was being hard pressed by Caesar in very serious wars. As we have already said, the Pergamene Mithridates, with the entire force he had brought with him to provide assistance to Caesar, had been repulsed by the defenses at Pelusium and had withdrawn to Ascalon, despairing of passage and having failed in his attempt.

He no longer dared to risk battle, since the terrain was unfavorable and his forces were inferior. Antipater first summoned Arabs to his aid, and then brought with him three thousand Jews with a strong force equipped with arms.

He also stirred up the powerful men of Syria to assist Mithridates; strengthened by their alliance, other peoples too were roused to war. Relying on these added forces, Mithridates approached Pelusium. When he was prevented from crossing, he undertook a siege.

At this point Antipater gave a distinguished demonstration of military skill. While the townspeople resisted and the struggle was being waged with the greatest force on both sides, he was the first, together with his men, to burst into the city after the section of the wall where he was fighting had been breached, and he captured it.

Nor was this the end of his labors or assistance. When the army advanced farther inland and the Egyptians wished to resist near the region called Onias, so as to block the route, Antipater not only drove back the attack but also arranged for whatever supplies were necessary to aid the army to be furnished by the very men who had prepared to fight against it.

As a result, the people of Memphis too were recalled from battle and willingly offered to join Mithridates’ alliance.

Mithridates passed by the more suspect positions and judged that battle should be joined with the remaining Egyptians. He fought vigorously in more open terrain, but against the stronger men of the region itself, whose inhabitants were called the Jewish army.

He exposed himself to such extreme danger and came so near to destruction that he would certainly have perished if Antipater, seeing that the entire right wing in which Mithridates stood was being pressed by a cohort and was also enclosed by a river, with no means of escape, had not bravely charged from the left wing against those who were pursuing Mithridates as he retreated. Antipater pursued them until the entire enemy force had been destroyed.

In that battle Antipater lost eighty of his own men, while Mithridates lost more than eight hundred, although Mithridates himself escaped unexpectedly.

This disaster followed immediately. Antipater, having received many wounds in his body, found in Caesar an outstanding witness to his valor; Mithridates especially praised him not only as the interpreter of his own acquittal but also as the herald of his courage.

Caesar was greatly pleased by these deeds. He therefore received Antipater, as was fitting, among his friends, honored him with distinctions of the Roman state, and, regarding him as a man approved by himself, granted him other pledges of his favor.

At Antipater’s recommendation he also confirmed Hyrcanus in the office of high priest.

When Antipater was accused before Caesar by Antigonus, the son of Aristobulus, on the charge that he favored Pompey’s party too strongly, he did not answer Antigonus with words. Instead, he tore open his clothing and, stripping off his garments, displayed his body full of wounds. With his torn cloak and the evidence of his courage before the eyes of those standing around, he said:

> “Behold the proofs of my alleged ill will toward Caesar. Let the wounds that shine like the lights of the soul defend the accused. To you, Caesar, I offer these scars as hostages of my inward loyalty. These are the pledges of my faith, and I bear upon my body written testimony. If citizens are not believed, let the enemies be questioned on whose account I received those wounds. What else were they pursuing in me except the loyalty that I was bringing to you?
>
> “But he charges me with Pompey’s favor. I admit it, Caesar: I was a friend not of the man but of the Roman name, and I worked earnestly so that my services might be devoted to your state. I therefore served not one man but all. Pompey may have been dear to me, but he became my friend before he became Caesar’s enemy. He was your son-in-law, and you were his father-in-law. When he was in the regions of Judaea, I helped him as a Roman commander.
>
> “Yet I did not receive on his behalf the wounds that I received on yours. For you I offered pledges of death and received the blows of enemy weapons.”

When Antipater had finished speaking, Caesar declared that Hyrcanus appeared more worthy of the priesthood. To Antipater, however, he granted the choice of authority.

Antipater, seeking him as arbiter of honor and moderator of his power, and placing the measure of honor in the hands of the one who granted it, returned the distinction and increase of authority with considerable tact and modesty. He was also made procurator of all Judaea.

He requested permission to rebuild the walls of Judaea, which had been destroyed in the war. Confident in the pledge given to him, he both asked for and obtained this considerable concession. In accordance with the custom of Roman commanders, these matters were written in the Capitol at Caesar’s discretion, so that the honors Caesar judged appropriate to confer upon Antipater might remain as evidence both of Caesar’s justice and of the man’s merits, as well as for the knowledge of posterity.

After returning to Judaea, Antipater first restored the wall that Pompey had destroyed to its former condition. Then he suppressed the disturbances of the Jews and entrusted the affairs of the province to his sons.

He appointed Phasael, the elder of his children, governor of Jerusalem and commander of the army. He also placed Herod, the younger and still very much a youth, over Galilee with equal authority.

As soon as Herod obtained power, his naturally vigorous disposition for conducting affairs immediately found an opportunity to display itself. Syria was suffering from the raids of the bandit Hezekiah, who, as the leader of a predatory force, was ravaging the whole province and appearing as an enemy in every region. Herod seized him and ordered him to be beheaded, and he killed many of the bandits. This won him the greatest glory for courage and abundant favor among the Syrians.

## CHAPTER XI. The death of Antipater, Herod’s father; and how Herod and his brother Phasael won the favor of Antony

At the same time war broke out among the Romans. Caesar, who had gone beyond the condition of a private citizen, was killed by the treachery of Cassius and Brutus and paid the severe penalty in the Senate.

Cassius therefore set out to seize Syria. While the young Caesar and Antony were waging war with Brutus and Cassius, Marcus and Cassius raised an army in Syria. Since Herod supplied a large part of it when the need arose, they appointed him procurator of all Syria.

Cassius also promised that, if the war ceased, he would confer the kingdom of Judaea upon Herod.

It happened, however, that Antipater’s hope and his son’s courage became the cause of his death. Malichus, who had aspired to kingship, feared the power of Antipater, which was strengthened by Herod’s valor. Fearing that Antipater would obstruct his attempt, Malichus bribed a certain royal youth and persuaded him to give Antipater a cup mixed with poison.

Antipater died after the banquet. He was a man vigorous in other matters, capable of administering affairs, and one who had preserved the kingdom recovered for Hyrcanus.

After Herod had celebrated the most distinguished funeral rites for his father, he feared that Malichus, whom he believed to be the author of his father’s death, would rouse the Jewish people against the Romans and, after overthrowing Hyrcanus, easily become king.

Acting on Cassius’ advice and relying on his assistance, Herod surrounded Malichus by treachery and killed him, piercing him with many wounds.

While Hyrcanus was present, he was thrown into such terror by this that he lost consciousness and became numb in every power of mind and body. After recovering a little, however, he asked Herod who had ordered Malichus to be killed.

When he learned that Malichus had been killed by order of Cassius, the Roman commander, as Herod had explained, he immediately replied:

> “Then Cassius has been the salvation both of me and of my country, since he killed the plotter against us both.”

Whether he said this from fear or truly thought it, however, is not clearly apparent.

Antigonus, whom we mentioned above, the son of Aristobulus, had escaped from custody at Rome and had repeatedly attempted to stir up disturbances in Judaea. He was supported by the forces of Ptolemy, for his father-in-law Ptolemy, the son of Mennai, who lived at Chalcis beneath Lebanon, supplied him with everything.

When Antigonus had seized some of the Jewish fortifications, Herod met him, equipped and stationed at the entrance to Judaea. After killing Malichus and driving his brother Felix from the territory of Judaea, Herod engaged Antigonus in battle and defeated him.

From there, after putting Antigonus to flight, Herod returned to Jerusalem. Because of the merit of what he had accomplished, everyone loved him, so that even those who had formerly despised him then placed themselves among his close associates, partly because of his relationship with Hyrcanus.

Herod had long had a wife from the native population, a woman of no low standing named Doris, by whom he had a son, Antipater. At that time he had also married Mariamne, the daughter of Alexander, whose father was Aristobulus; she was Hyrcanus’ granddaughter through his daughter. Through this marriage Herod had become close to King Hyrcanus.

Even so, Herod did not escape envy. When Caesar and Antony had defeated Cassius and the Brutuses in the Macedonian war, Caesar hastened to return to Italy, while Antony hurried to Syria.

Herod immediately presented himself before Antony and won his favor by offering many gifts. Antony therefore appointed Herod and Phasael tetrarchs and entrusted them with the administration of all Judaea, although many Jewish envoys vainly accused them before Antony.

## CHAPTER XII. Antigonus handed the young Hyrcanus over to his father, deceitfully obtained the priesthood, and was captured and killed by the Romans and Herod after the capture of Jerusalem; Herod was made king
[Col. 1096D] Therefore Brazafanes, satrap of the Parthians, occupied Syria after two years, together with Pacorus, the king’s son. Antigonus approached him and promised a thousand talents and five hundred women if he would depose Hyrcanus and hand the kingdom over to him. Attracted by these gifts, the Parthians treacherously surrounded Hyrcanus and Herod’s brother Phasael. While they were setting out from Jerusalem to seek an audience with the king, the Parthians soon violated their oath and bound both Hyrcanus and Phasael. After devastating Jerusalem and the neighboring cities, they installed Antigonus as king. Not only this, but they also handed the bound Phasael and Hyrcanus over to him to be scourged.

Antigonus, however, bit off Hyrcanus’ ears with his teeth, so that, if he were released and circumstances changed, he could never again receive the high priesthood; for sacred rites ought to be celebrated by those who are physically whole. But Phasael’s courage thwarted Antigonus. [Col. 1097A] Since he had neither iron available nor his hands free, he died by smashing his head against a rock, and thus proved that he was truly Herod’s brother.

Although the Parthians lacked the women they desired, nevertheless, having settled matters for Antigonus at Jerusalem, they led Hyrcanus, bound, into Parthia. Herod, however, anticipating the barbarians’ plots and trusting them in nothing, seized his mother, his brothers, and the betrothed girl together with her mother, and, escaping by flight during the night, hastened by the shortest route toward the fortress of Masada. While he was fleeing, many people joined him. But after he reached the region of Didyma, his brother Joseph met him and persuaded him to reduce the crowd of followers: Masada could not contain so great a multitude, which numbered more than nine thousand.

[Col. 1097B] Herod therefore followed his advice and dismissed those who were unequal to the emergency through Didyma, supplying them with provisions for the journey. He retained the strongest and most necessary men and was thus received into the fortress. Then, leaving nine hundred men there to protect the women and arranging a retinue sufficient for those under siege, he himself proceeded to the city of Petra in Arabia. Yet he did not find the friendship of the Arabs reliable. Finally, their king Malichus sent men to order him to return from his territory as quickly as possible.

Then Herod, discovering that the Arabs whom he had considered his closest friends were hostile to him, made for Egypt. When he reached the city of Alexandria, Cleopatra received him honorably, intending that he should be her military commander in the enterprises she was preparing.

[Col. 1097C] Encouraged by the queen’s entreaties, he did not fear either the severity of winter or the dangers of the sea sufficiently to prevent him from sailing to Rome. Accordingly, he immediately set out from there for Rome and first went to Antony, because of the friendship Antony had shared with his father. He related to him both his own disasters and those of his entire family, and explained that, leaving his relatives in the fortress and surrounded by siege, he had sailed to Antony as a suppliant in winter.

Moved by compassion for so pitiable a misfortune, and also mindful of the right hand joined with Antipater,

[Note: [Col. 1097D] The passage is corrupt, as are very many passages in what follows. EDITOR.]

—therefore, out of regard for Antipater’s own virtue, Antony proposed even then to make Herod king of the Jews, although he had previously made him tetrarch. Antigonus, moreover, was hated no less than Herod was favored. Antony considered him both seditious and hostile to the Romans.

[Col. 1097D] Antony commended Herod to Caesar, recalling far more readily than Herod himself the campaigns of Antipater, which he had endured in Egypt with Herod’s father, as well as their hospitality and goodwill in every matter. When he also observed Herod’s own effectiveness, he nevertheless summoned the senate. There Messala, and after him Atratinus, with Herod present, praised his father’s services and Herod’s loyalty toward the Roman people. At the same time they pointed out that Antigonus was an enemy—not only because he had begun to quarrel within so short a time, but also because previously he had sought to obtain the kingdom while disregarding the support of the Parthians and opposing the Roman people.

The senate was moved by these arguments. When Antony declared that a war against the Parthians would be advantageous, all agreed that Herod should be created king.

After the council was dismissed, Antony and Caesar went out with Herod between them, while the consuls and the other magistrates went ahead to deposit in the Capitol the victims decreed for Caesar and the decree of the senate. On the first day of Herod’s reign, a banquet was held at Antony’s house.

From there Herod was carried by ship from Italy to Ptolemais. Having gathered a considerable force of foreigners and Gentiles, he hurried through Galilee against Antigonus, supported by the assistance of Ventidius and Cilo. Antony sent Dellius to them to escort Herod, and Dellius persuaded them to do so. Herod then hastened toward Masada with a strong force of both native and Roman soldiers. From Masida he easily recovered his relatives and possessions [Col. 1098A] from the fortress,

[Col. 1098B] and proceeded to Jerusalem. Both Solon’s soldiers and the rest of the city’s inhabitants joined him, terrified by his strength. After establishing a camp around the city, they attacked it with arrows and javelins. But since they were quite unable to break through, the Jews inside the city resisting because they favored Antigonus’ faction, the defenders of the walls stood firm, although the fighting had been so intense that the archers and javelin-men had driven everyone from the towers.

Then winter arrived, and the siege was lifted. The soldiers withdrew to suitable places for winter quarters. At the same time Antony was vigorously besieging Samosata, a very strong city beside the Euphrates. Herod went there to demonstrate his courage and to win Antony’s favor still more.

[Col. 1098C] As soon as he arrived, he brought the siege to an end, killing many barbarians.

While these events were taking place with Antony, Herod’s affairs in Judaea were collapsing. He had left his brother Joseph in charge of everything, with instructions not to begin war against Antigonus before Herod’s return. But when Joseph learned that his brother was far away, he forgot the instructions and set out for Jericho with five cohorts sent with him by the Roman commander Machera, intending to seize the grain when the crops were ripe.

Overtaken by the enemy in mountainous and rugged terrain, Joseph himself fell; nevertheless, he won great glory in that battle as a brave man. All the Roman soldiers who were with him also perished, since the cohorts had recently been levied in Syria and contained none of the veteran soldiers who could assist inexperienced men.

[Col. 1098D] Antigonus was not satisfied with this victory. So greatly was he inflamed by anger that he scourged the dead Joseph as well and had his head cut off.

Herod, who was staying at Daphne near Antioch, received clear indications of his brother’s death in a dream. When he sprang up in agitation from his bed, messengers announcing the disaster entered. He therefore lamented briefly from grief, but, postponing most of his mourning, hastened against the enemy, pressing forward beyond his strength.

Each day a great multitude of Jews joined him. Some were moved by hatred of Antigonus, while others were driven by a desire for change. [Col. 1099A] Before reaching Jerusalem, he repeatedly fought bravely against Antigonus’ soldiers and defeated them.

Finally, in battle, he beheaded Pappus, the commander of Antigonus’ troops, and sent the head to his brother Feroras, the army’s commander, in vengeance for their slain brother. Pappus was the man who had killed Joseph.

When the severity of winter had ended, Herod set out for Jerusalem. He brought his troops up to the walls, for it was now the third year since he had been proclaimed king at Rome. Having assigned the army to the work, closed the suburbs, and gathered the entire force, they established a camp near the northern wall with eleven legions of infantry and six thousand cavalry, apart from the Syrian auxiliaries.

[Col. 1099B] He ordered three embankments to be raised and towers to be built upon them. Herod himself, relying on the decree of the senate by which he had been proclaimed king, cheerfully directed everything. Antony had sent Sossius, a military commander, with a strong force to Herod’s aid.

The warriors inside the wall, becoming more resolute, prevented the embankments from being brought against the walls and continually devised some new obstacle against the attackers’ equipment. In nothing did they prevail more than in countermining. They lacked neither courage nor engines, for they had determined to resist to the very end.

At last, with so large an army surrounding them, they endured the siege for five months, until some of Herod’s chosen men dared to cross the wall and burst into the city, followed by Sossius’ centurions.

[Col. 1099C] First of all, the areas near the temple were seized, and, once the army had poured in, there was extensive slaughter everywhere. The Romans were angry because of the delays of the siege, while Herod’s forces were intensely determined that none of their opponents should remain at all.

Very many were slaughtered. Driven through the narrower streets and districts into their homes, or even if they had taken refuge in the temple, they received no mercy because of age or feminine weakness. Although the king repeatedly went everywhere asking that they be spared, no one restrained his right hand; like maddened men, they pursued people of every age.

At that time Antigonus, considering neither his former nor his present fortune, came down from the house and fell at Sossius’ feet. Sossius, however, showed him no pity despite so great a reversal of fortune. He mocked him immoderately and called him “Antigona,”

[Col. 1099D] yet did not release him from custody as a woman. Thus Antigonus was kept bound.

Since Herod had conquered his enemies, he took care to bring even the foreign auxiliaries under his yoke. He firmly promised that he would distribute pay to each man from his own resources. He rewarded every soldier generously and according to his merit, and he also presented Sossius himself with a royal gift, so that no one would depart lacking money.

After this, Sossius returned from Jerusalem, carrying the bound Antigonus to Antony, after dedicating a golden crown to God. Antigonus, desirous of life and clinging to the single hope of survival, was ultimately met with a death by the axe suitable to his cowardice.

Herod, now king, separated the city’s population. He treated those devoted to his own faction honorably, so as to make them more favorably disposed toward him,

[Col. 1100A] but he handed the Antigonian party over to execution. Antony had already been corrupted by love for Cleopatra and had surrendered himself to every desire.

If anyone wishes to know these matters more fully, let him consult the thirteenth book of Josephus.

## CHAPTER XIII

**When Herod, a foreigner, was made king, the prophecies that had foretold Christ’s coming then were fulfilled, and the kingdom of the Jews was to be destroyed.**

Hyrcanus, as we said above, was captured by the Parthians. Then Antigonus, his successor, whom the Parthians had made priest, was captured and killed by the Romans. Thus the kingdom and priesthood of the Jews came to an end.

For Herod, a foreigner with no connection whatsoever to Judaea—the son, namely, of Antipater the Ascalonite from the region of Idumaea, and of his Arab mother Cypros—

[Col. 1100B] assumed the leadership, kingship, and priesthood of the Jews, despite the opposition of the Romans. What had previously been maintained through successive inheritances—that is, the succession of judges, kings, priests, and again kings and priests—was then destroyed.

The prophecy was therefore fulfilled which speaks through Moses as follows:

> “The ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor the leader from his thighs, until he comes to whom the promise was made; he is the expectation of the nations.”

For until Herod, judges, priests, and kings had governed the Jewish people through hereditary succession. From that time onward, high priests were by no means appointed through priestly succession. Nor were men chosen to serve God according to the law of Moses with lifelong tenure. Instead, men of low status, one after another at different times, some for the span of a single year or a little longer, bought the priesthood from the Roman emperors.

[Col. 1100C] Herod therefore appointed a certain Ananel, summoned from Babylonia, as high priest of the Jews. After a short time he appointed Aristobulus, the brother of his wife Mariamne and the grandson of Hyrcanus, as his successor. After Aristobulus was killed a year later, Herod restored the priesthood to Ananel.

The prophet Daniel had foretold all these circumstances long beforehand, saying:

> “And after seven weeks and sixty-two, the anointing shall perish, and there shall be no judgment, and the holy temple shall be corrupted by the people, when the leader comes.”

And later:

> “The temple,” he says, “shall be an abomination of desolations, and until the consummation of time, consummation shall be imposed upon desolation.”

Thus the seven and sixty-two weeks, which together make sixty-nine weeks and amount to four hundred and eighty-four years, were the period during which the “Christs”—that is, priests consecrated by anointing—reigned, from the restoration of the temple under Darius until Hyrcanus, in whom the final anointing and priesthood of the Jews came to an end.

Therefore, while Herod was reigning in Judaea and Augustus among the Romans, Christ, the Son of God, was born. He confirmed the worship of the true God through many apostles and believers.

Whatever was done afterward in the temple, after the Lord’s Passion, was not a sacrifice to God but worship of the devil, while all were crying out together:

> “His blood be upon us and upon our children.”

And:

[Col. 1101A]

> “We have no king except Caesar.”

That from the completion of the temple until the tenth year of the emperor Augustus, when Herod obtained Judaea after Hyrcanus had been killed, seven and sixty-two weeks—that is, four hundred and sixty-four years—are reckoned, can be demonstrated as follows. In the third year of the sixty-sixth Olympiad, that is, the tenth year of Augustus, Herod assumed power over the Jews. These periods amount to four hundred and eighty-four years when each Olympiad is reckoned as four years.

At that time Virgil, having assumed the toga, crossed to Milan and after a short time went to Rome. Cicero was killed at his Formian [Phormian] estate by Herennius and Publius, in the sixty-fourth year of his life. His head and right hand were placed before the Rostra beside the crowned image of the soldier Publius who had killed him.

[Col. 1101B] In those days three suns rose simultaneously at Rome, but gradually joined into a single disk, as we said above. Across the Tiber, oil burst forth from an oil merchant’s shop and flowed all day without interruption. Among the other portents that then occurred throughout the world, an ox spoke in a suburb of Rome, saying to the plowman that it was being driven in vain, because soon it would not be grain but human beings that would fail.

Ovid Naso was born among the Pelignians. The poet Cornificius, abandoned by his soldiers, died; he often used to say that the soldiers fleeing were hares wearing helmets. His sister was Cornificia, whose distinguished epigrams are extant. Cornelius Nepos was regarded as a famous historical writer. Sallust died four years before the Actian War. M. Vanius

[Col. 1101C] [Jerome: Bavius], the poet whom Virgil censures in the *Bucolics*, died in Cappadocia.

## CHAPTER XIV

**Octavian, taking up his uncle’s name and kingdom, and how, by waging civil and foreign wars, he reached the point at which the senate decreed that he should possess tribunician power in perpetuity.**

[Col. 1101D] While affairs were being conducted in Judaea as we have partly related, the order of the narrative requires us to return to the sequence of events among the Romans.

After Julius Caesar was killed in the senate house at Rome, a great increase of evils immediately followed. Bands of conspirators were drawn into his murder. For it was certain that Caesar, unjustly slain, might have many avengers.

Octavian, who by the will of his uncle Julius Caesar had assumed his inheritance and name, and who was afterward called Augustus, had scarcely arrived at Rome as a young man returning from Apollonia when he devoted his youthful energy to civil wars.

To explain briefly the accumulation of disasters, he waged five civil wars: the Mutinensian, Philippian, Perusine, Sicilian, and Actian. Of these, he conducted the first and last against Mark Antony; the second against Brutus and Cassius; the third against Lucius Antony; and the fourth against Sextus Pompey, the son of Gnaeus Pompey.

Antony, declared an enemy by the senate, had shut Decius Brutus up under siege at Mutina. The consuls Hirtius and Pansa, together with Caesar, were sent to free Brutus and attack Antony.

[Col. 1102A] Pansa, arriving first, was caught in an ambush. Amid the losses of his men, he himself was severely wounded by a javelin and died several days later from that wound. Hirtius, bringing aid to his colleague, destroyed Antony’s large forces in a great slaughter. Caesar remained in charge of the camp.

In the second battle against Antony, great slaughter occurred on both sides. The consul Hirtius was killed there; Antony was defeated and fled, while Caesar gained the victory. Decius Brutus, who had confessed his part in the conspiracy that killed Julius Caesar, poured out prayers of repentance before him.

Dolabella killed Trebonius, one of Caesar’s assassins, at Smyrna. The senate declared Dolabella an enemy. The armies of both slain consuls obeyed Caesar.

Later Decius Brutus was captured and killed in Gaul by the Sequani.

[Col. 1102B] Vasillus, a knight [another reading: likewise], one of the assassins, was killed by the hands of his own slaves. Through Lepidus’ efforts, Caesar restored Antony to favor and, as a pledge of the reconciliation, took Antony’s daughter in marriage.

When they approached Rome and rumors arose of a future proscription, Gaius Thoranius, a former praetor, fearing nothing of the kind, was killed in his own house by an attack of soldiers. Many others were also slaughtered.

Therefore, so that the killings might not be extended more broadly and without restraint,

[alternative reading: so that an unbounded massacre might not be carried out],

the names of one hundred and thirty-two senators were posted on a tablet—first at Lepidus’ command and under his name, then under Antony’s, and third under Caesar’s.

There Antony proscribed T. Cicero, his enemy; there he proscribed L. Caesar, his maternal uncle; and, adding to the enormity of the [Col. 1102C] crime, he proscribed him while his mother was still alive. Lepidus cast L. Paulus, his own brother, into the same company of the proscribed.

Thirty Roman knights were later added to the number of the proscribed. Many prolonged and varied killings followed, and the houses of the proscribed were destroyed after everything in them had been plundered.

Dolabella waged many wars against Cassius in Syria. After being defeated by him, Dolabella killed himself. Brutus and Cassius, having assembled large armies, met at Athens and devastated the whole of Greece.

Cassius attacked the Rhodians by land and sea and forced them to surrender, leaving them nothing except their lives.

[Col. 1102D] Caesar and Antony therefore pursued them into Macedonia with great preparations for war and drove them to death. Yet it was quite evident that this battle was decided not by the courage of Antony’s side but by Caesar’s good fortune.

Caesar was ill at the time. When he had decided to remain in the camp to obtain rest, a physician urged and entreated him, claiming that he had been warned in a dream to lead Caesar out of the camp that day for the sake of his safety. Caesar therefore went out into the field among the troops while ill [another reading: with difficulty], and soon his camp was captured by the enemy.

[Col. 1103A] But the Caesarian soldiers in turn captured Cassius’ camp.

Thus driven to despair, Brutus and Cassius brought about their premature deaths before the end of the war. They summoned their assassins: Cassius offered his head, and Brutus his side.

At Rome, however, Fulina [variant: Fulvia], Antony’s wife and Caesar’s mother-in-law, exercised domination like a woman. She attacked Caesar, who had returned to Brundisium, with insults, factions, and plots. Repulsed by him, she withdrew to Antony in Greece.

Sextus Pompey, after discovering that his name had been included among the proscribed, turned to banditry and devastated the whole coast of Italy with slaughter and plunder. After seizing Sicily and obstructing the grain supply, he afflicted Rome with famine.

Soon the triumvirs—or, rather, the tyrants—Lepidus, Caesar, and Antony made peace with him. But when Pompey immediately began taking fugitives contrary to the agreement, he was treated as an enemy.

Mena, Pompey’s freedman, defected to Caesar with a fleet of sixty ships, and by Caesar’s order he himself was placed in command of that fleet. Together with Statilius Taurus, he immediately waged a naval battle against Menecrates, Pompey’s commander.

Then Caesar himself fought the most bloody naval battle against the same Pompeians. But immediately afterward he lost almost the entire victorious fleet in a shipwreck at Scyllaceum.

[Col. 1103B] Ventidius defeated the Persians and Parthians, who were invading Syria, in three great battles, and killed their king Pacorus in battle—on the very day on which Crassus had been killed by the Parthians.

Antony, after scarcely capturing one fortress, made peace with Antiochus so that he might appear to have completed so great an undertaking. He placed Ventidius in charge of Syria and ordered him to make war on Antigonus, who at that time had conquered the Jews, plundered the temple after capturing Jerusalem, and given the kingdom to Herod [another reading: taken it away from him]. Ventidius immediately defeated him and received his surrender.

Mena the freedman returned to Pompey with six ships. Pompey received him kindly, and Mena burned Caesar’s fleet, although Caesar had recently lost another fleet in a second shipwreck.

Later, after being surrounded by Agrippa in a naval battle, Mena crossed over to Caesar with six triremes. Caesar, however, left him as an inactive man after his third defection, granting him only his life.

Then Agrippa fought and won a naval battle between Mylae and Lipara against Demochares and Pompey. There he either sank or captured thirty ships, damaging the rest. Pompey fled to Messana.

Meanwhile Caesar had crossed to Tauromenium. Pompey attacked and defeated him by a sudden assault. Caesar, having lost many of his ships and a great number of his soldiers, fled to Italy. Without delay he returned to Sicily, where he met Lepidus arriving from Africa. Lepidus was claiming the highest power for himself through terror, threats, and arrogance.

[Col. 1103D] A few days later Agrippa, by Caesar’s order, engaged Pompey in a most savage naval battle from the shore, where Caesar watched with his line drawn up, and defeated him. He either sank or captured one hundred and sixty-three ships. Pompey barely escaped with seventeen ships.

Lepidus, swollen with the arrogance of twenty legions, had plundered Messana after allowing it to his soldiers. When Caesar himself came to him, Lepidus twice spurned him and instead ordered that he be attacked with weapons. Caesar avoided them by gathering his cloak over his left arm and using it to ward them off.

Soon he mounted a horse and returned to his men. Advancing with an army drawn up against Lepidus,

[Col. 1104A] he compelled many of Lepidus’ legions to cross over to his side, with only a few men killed.

At last Lepidus understood where his vanity was leading. He laid aside his military cloak, put on a girl’s garment [variant: a dark garment], and became a suppliant before Caesar. He obtained his life and property, but was permanently corrected by exile.

Taurus, Caesar’s commander, brought almost the whole of Sicily, tested and crushed by the sword, into submission.

At that time forty-four legions were under Caesar’s single command. The soldiers, made fiercer by their numbers, stirred up disturbances to obtain lands. But Caesar, great in spirit, discharged twenty thousand soldiers, restored thirty thousand slaves to their masters, and crucified six thousand whose masters could not be found.

He entered Rome in an ovation. The senate decreed that he should possess tribunician power in perpetuity.

[Col. 1104B] In those days, across the Tiber, a fountain of oil burst from an oil merchant’s shop, and flowed all day in a very abundant stream.

After Antony crossed the Araxes, he was surrounded by every kind of disaster and at last barely returned to Antioch with a few men. He repeatedly attempted several battles, but was always defeated and escaped with a large force of cavalry and archers. In addition, he was hindered in regions whose locations were uncertain and unknown. Driven by the most severe famine, he was forced to eat abominable foods, and many of his soldiers surrendered to the enemy.

He crossed into Greece and ordered Pompey, who had been defeated by Caesar and was rebuilding his army and war effort, to come to him with a few men. Pompey, fleeing, was repeatedly defeated in land and sea battles by Titus and Furinus, Antony’s commanders,

[Col. 1104C] and was captured and killed shortly afterward.

Caesar subdued and brought under control Illyricum, Pannonia, and part of Italy through war.

## CHAPTER XV

**Antony, elated by certain successes, declares war on Octavian Caesar. He is defeated three times by Caesar and finally captured and killed.**

Antony therefore captured Arthabanes, king of Armenia, through treachery and deceit. He bound him with a silver chain and forced him to reveal the royal treasures. After storming the town in which Artavasdes had said the treasures were stored, Antony carried away a great quantity of gold and silver.

Elated by this wealth, he ordered war to be declared against Caesar and a divorce to be announced to Caesar’s sister Octavia, his own wife. He commanded Cleopatra to meet him from Alexandria.

He himself set out for Actium, where he had assembled his fleet. When he found that hunger had carried off nearly a third of the rowers, he was unmoved. “Let the oars be safe,” he said, “for there will be no lack of rowers as long as Greece has men.”

Caesar set out from Brundisium for Epirus with two hundred and thirty beaked ships.

Agrippa, sent ahead by Caesar, captured the cargo ships, laden with grain and weapons, that were coming from Egypt, Syria, and Asia to support Antony. After sailing around the Peloponnesian gulf, he stormed Methone, a very strong city fortified with an Antonian garrison. From there he captured Corcyra. Pursuing and routing those who fled in a naval battle, and carrying out many bloody operations,

[Col. 1105A] he came to Caesar.

Antony, distressed by the desertion and hunger of his soldiers, decided to hasten the war. He suddenly drew up his forces, advanced toward Caesar’s camp, and was defeated.

On the third day after the battle, Antony moved his camp to Actium, prepared to decide the matter in a naval battle. Caesar had two hundred and thirty beaked ships and thirty triremes without beaks, equal in speed to the Liburnian vessels. Eight legions were stationed aboard the fleet, apart from five praetorian cohorts.

Antony’s fleet consisted of one hundred and seventy-five ships. It fell short in number by as much as it surpassed the other in size, for its ships rose ten feet above the sea.

This was the famous and great battle at Actium. From the fifth hour until the seventh, with victory uncertain, the slaughter on both sides was extremely severe. During the rest of the day and the following night, the outcome inclined toward Caesar’s victory.

[Col. 1105B] Queen Cleopatra was first [Latin: Priorum; variant: Prior] to flee, with sixty very swift ships. Antony, removing the standard from his flagship, also followed his fleeing wife.

At daybreak Caesar completed the victory. Twelve thousand of the defeated are reported to have fallen, and six thousand were wounded; of these, one thousand died while receiving treatment.

Antony and Cleopatra decided to send their children, together with part of the royal treasury, ahead to the Red Sea. They themselves placed garrisons around the two extremities of Egypt, Pelusium and Paretonium, and prepared their fleet and forces for renewed war.

Caesar, called imperator for the sixth time [variant: sixth imperator], and consul for the fourth time together with Marcus Licinius Crassus, came to Brundisium.

[Col. 1105C] There he distributed the garrisons of the world by dividing the legions among them. From there he set out for Syria and soon reached Pelusium, where the Antonian garrison voluntarily welcomed him.

Meanwhile Cornelius Gallus, sent ahead by Caesar, received into his allegiance the four legions that Antony had stationed at Cyrene as a garrison. From there, after defeating Antony, he captured Paretonium, the first city of Egypt on the Libyan side, and soon defeated Antony himself near Pharos.

Antony began a cavalry war against Caesar, but was miserably defeated in that encounter as well and fled.

On the Kalends of Sextilis, at first light, Antony descended to the harbor to arrange his fleet. Suddenly all the ships crossed over to Caesar. Deprived of his single remaining support, Antony withdrew in panic with a few men into the palace.

The queen fell at Augustus’ feet and tried to captivate the commander’s eyes, but in vain.

[Col. 1105D] For her beauty found its limit in the prince’s chastity. She was not struggling for the life that was being taken from her, but for a share of the kingdom.

When she despaired of this from the prince, and learned that she was being reserved for the triumph, she found her guards less vigilant and withdrew into the royal mausoleum. There, dressed in her finest attire, as was her custom, she placed herself beside Antony on a couch filled with perfumes. After applying serpents to her veins, she was released from life as though from sleep.

Caesar took possession of Alexandria, by far the wealthiest and greatest of all cities, as victor. Rome, too, was increased by his public works to such an extent that, because of the abundance of money, the prices of estates and other goods for sale were set at twice what they had previously been.

By Caesar’s order, the elder son of Antony was killed, as was Publius Canidius, always a most hostile enemy of Caesar but disloyal to Antony; Cassius of Parma, the final victim of the violated party of Caesar

[alternative reading: of Caesar, the violated father];

and Quintinus Ovinius, chiefly notorious because he, the first Roman senator, was not ashamed to preside over the queen’s wool-working and weaving establishment in the most obscene manner.

Then Caesar came with his infantry forces into Syria. Afterward he withdrew to winter quarters in Asia and later proceeded through Greece to Brundisium.

## CHAPTER XVI

**How Caesar Octavianus personally subjugated the whole of Spain; how the glory of Alexander the Great was reflected in him through envoys from the Indians and the other peoples of the East; and how, both personally and through his own envoys, he subjected the entire world to himself.**
[Col. 1106B] Returning victorious from the East, Caesar entered the City in a triple triumph on the seventh day before the Ides of January; and then, for the first time, he himself closed the gates of Janus, when all civil wars had been quieted and brought to an end. On that day he was first hailed as Augustus. This title, formerly inviolable for all and, until this man [Al.: now], not ventured by other rulers, lawfully assumed as that of the whole world, declares the summit of imperial power. From that day onward supreme authority and power began to lie with one man and remained there—a condition the Greeks call monarchy.

Moreover, this was the very same day, namely the eighth day before the Ides of January, that we observe as Epiphany, that is, the appearance or manifestation of the Lord’s sacrament. Caesar, realizing that little had been accomplished in Spain over two hundred years, opened the gates of Janus and himself set out with an army for the Spains. The Cantabrians and Asturians are part of the province of Gallaecia, through which the extended chain of the Pyrenees descends northward, not far from the nearer Ocean. They were prepared not only to defend their own liberty but also dared to seize that of their neighbors. Although Caesar attacked them repeatedly without success because of the difficulty of the Pyrenees, at last he ordered a fleet to approach by sea from the Gulf of Aquitaine and land troops while the enemy was off guard. He defeated and captured them by this sudden attack.

After the victory over Cantabria, Gallaecia, and all Spain, Claudius Drusus, Caesar’s stepson, having received Gaul and Raetia as his command, subdued by arms the greatest and strongest peoples of Germany. At that time, it was as though all the nations were hastening toward an appointed day of peace: everywhere the peoples were stirred either to accept the terms of peace if they were defeated, or to enjoy untroubled liberty if they were victorious. The Norici, Illyrians, Pannonians, Dalmatians, Moesians, Thracians, and Dacians, as well as the Sarmatians and the numerous and mighty peoples of Germany, were either defeated or restrained by various commanders, or shut off by the barrier of the greatest rivers, the Rhine and the Danube.

Drusus first subdued the Sosipetes [Al.: Usipetes], then the Tencteri, and the Acathi [and Chatti]. He nearly destroyed the Marcomanni. Later he overcame in a single war the bravest nations—those to whom nature had given strength and habit had given experience in using it—the Cherusci, Suebi, and Sicambri; he also defeated the Susi and Persians. [Col. 1107A] Their courage and savagery may be judged from the fact that their women too, whenever they were hemmed in among their wagons by a sudden Roman attack, would throw their little sons, battered against the ground, into the faces of the enemy when their weapons were exhausted or when they lacked anything else that frenzy could use as a weapon. In killing each son, they were twice murderers: both of their children and of themselves.

At the same time in Africa, Cossus, Caesar’s commander, confined the Musulami and Gaetuli, who were ranging widely, by narrowing their boundaries, and compelled them through fear to keep away from the Roman frontiers.

And, to demonstrate the savagery of the peoples by reaching farther back, one of the commanders of Moesia, after requesting silence before the battle, asked: “Who are you?” The answer was: “Romans, lords of the nations.” But he replied: “That will come to pass if you defeat us.” Soon afterward, however, they were defeated by the Romans.

The Thracians, who were subdued by Piso, displayed their fury even in captivity. For, gnawing with their teeth at the chains by which they were bound, they punished their own savagery. Lentulus also conquered, expelled, and subdued Dacia beyond the Danube. He drove the Sarmatians beyond the Danube as well; because of their excessive barbarism, they do not even understand what peace is. Caesar, through Quirinus, subdued the Marmaridae and the Caramantes in the eastern region.

The Germans, Gauls, Britons, Spaniards, Iberians, Austurians, and Cantabrians, lying beneath the western sky, Augustus himself, by coming to them, compelled to serve Roman laws. Meanwhile, at Tarragona, a city of Nearer Spain, Caesar was at last found by ambassadors of the Indians and Scythians, who had crossed the entire world and could search no farther. They reflected upon Caesar the glory of Alexander the Great. Just as an embassy of Spaniards and Gauls had approached Alexander in the middle of the East at Babylon to seek peace, so, at the farthest limit of the West, the Eastern Indian and the Northern Scythian approached Caesar in Spain as suppliants, praying to him with gifts characteristic of their peoples.

After the Cantabrian war, which lasted five years, and after all Spain had been laid down and restored to an everlasting peace, as though taking breath from its exhaustion, Caesar returned to Rome. During those same years he conducted many wars himself and many others through commanders and envoys. Among the rest, Piso was sent against the Vindelici. After subduing them, he came as a victor to Caesar at Lyons.

Tiberius, Caesar’s stepson, destroyed the Pannonians, who were swelling with a renewed uprising, in an extremely bloody slaughter. He immediately took up war against the Germans as well, and returned victorious with forty thousand captives. [Col. 1107D] This was truly a great and terrifying war, waged with fifteen legions for three years; as Suetonius testifies, scarcely any greater war had taken place after the Punic War.

At the same time Quintilius Varus, acting with extraordinary arrogance and greed toward his subjects, was utterly destroyed by the rebellious Germans together with three legions. Caesar Augustus bore this disaster to the state so heavily that, often overcome by the violence of his grief and striking his head against the wall, he cried out: “Quintilius Varus, give me back my legions!”

Agrippa defeated the Bosporans and, recovering in war the Roman standards that they had once taken under Mithridates, compelled the defeated to surrender.

The Parthians, as though marked out in the sight of all by the fact that the entire world had either been conquered or pacified and that all the strength of the Roman Empire would now have to be turned against them alone—for they were stung by the memory of their duty to avenge the slaughter of Crassus—of their own accord sent back to Caesar the standards that they had taken after Crassus was killed. They also handed over royal hostages and, through a loyal supplication, earned a firm treaty.

Thus, in the seven hundred and fifty-second year from the founding of the City, Caesar Augustus, with all peoples settled under a single peace from East to West, from North to South, and around the entire circuit of the Ocean, himself closed the gates of Janus for the third time. From then on, they remained shut in the most peaceful leisure for nearly twelve years, and rust itself sealed them. They were never opened again until Augustus’s extreme old age, when they were forced open by the uprising of the Athenians and the disturbance of the Dacians [Dracones].

After closing the gates of Janus, Augustus strove to nourish and enlarge by peace the state that he had acquired by war. He established many laws by which the human race might live, in free reverence, according to the discipline of custom. He avoided being called “lord,” as though he were merely a man. Once, while he was watching games, the following line was spoken in a mime: “O fair and good lord!” Everyone applauded joyfully, as though it had been spoken about him. Immediately, by gesture and expression, he restrained the unbecoming flattery; on the following day he rebuked it in a very stern edict and thereafter would not allow himself to be called “lord,” not even by his children or grandchildren, whether seriously or in jest.

At that time, therefore—that is, in the year in which, by God’s arrangement, Caesar established the firmest and truest peace—Christ was born. This peace served his coming, and at his birth the rejoicing angels sang before human hearers: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will.”

At that same time, the man to whom supreme authority over all things had passed did not permit himself to be called “lord”; indeed, he did not dare to do so, while the true Lord of the whole human race was born among human beings. In that same year, for the first time, Caesar himself—the man whom God had predestined for these great mysteries—ordered a census to be conducted everywhere in each province and all people to be registered, at the very time when God deigned to be seen and to exist as man.

This was that first and most illustrious declaration which, by the individual registration of every person, marked Caesar as ruler of all and the Romans as masters of the world; in it, he who made all human beings also wished to be found and registered as a human being among human beings. Nothing of this kind had ever been done from the founding of the world and the beginning of the human race. It had not been granted even to Babylon or Macedonia, much less to any lesser kingdom.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the battles waged by Herod against the king of the Arabs, and how he gained the favor of Octavian Caesar

Herod had been confirmed in the kingdom of the Jews by a decree of the Senate and through the favor of Antony and Caesar, as we related above. While he was equipped with every preparation for war and was hastening to the war at Actium with Antony, Cleopatra cunningly intercepted him so that he would not share Antigonus’s dangers. She set a trap for the kings—that is, Malichus of Arabia and Herod—and persuaded Antony to entrust the war against the Arabs to Herod. If the mistress of Arabia conquered, she would be established as the ruler of Arabia; if she were defeated, Herod would be established as ruler of the Jews; and one powerful man would destroy the other.

But Octavian Caesar anticipated her intention. As soon as Herod arrived in Arabia, he was met in battle, prevailed, and won the victory. When the Arabs had been defeated, however, they rose in a still greater uprising. With a strong force they renewed the battle, and, after routing Herod’s troops around rocky and inaccessible places, drove them into flight. After many had been struck down, they captured those who had fled together with the camp.

After this defeat, another calamity befell Herod. In the seventh year of his reign, while the war at Actium was raging, an earthquake killed an immense number of animals and thirty thousand human beings. Herod’s army, however, remained unharmed because it was living under the open sky.

When the Arabs learned of this misfortune of the Jews—for sad reports add something even more grievous to what has happened—they immediately rushed into Judaea with their entire army. When Herod heard of their arrival, he is said to have consoled his men as follows:

“They are not coming relying so much upon their hands and weapons as upon our misfortunes. But hope is deceptive when it rests not on its own strength but on the adversities of others. Neither favorable nor unfavorable circumstances among human beings are certain; rather, you see fortune wavering alternately in either direction. Your own examples will demonstrate this to you. In the preceding battle we were victorious, but afterward we were defeated by the enemy. Now, therefore, insofar as it is possible to judge, they will be captured while believing that they themselves will be victorious. Excessive confidence makes a man careless, whereas fear teaches foresight.

“Let nothing terrify you in the movements of lifeless things, and do not think that the shaking of the earth is a portent of some future disaster. The elements too have natural defects, and they cause no harm unless harm arises from them. A sign of pestilence, famine, or earthquake may perhaps precede it by some time; but when these things themselves occur, they come to an end through their own magnitude.”

By examples such as these he encouraged his soldiers. Herod attacked the enemy, overcame them, and won. As long as they stood their ground, not many of them were killed; but when they turned their backs, many were trampled by the Jews and many by one another. Herod killed or captured nearly all of them.

Yet anxiety over Antony’s friendship after Caesar’s victory at Actium darkened this victory. Therefore Herod entrusted himself to danger and crossed over to Rhodes. He approached Caesar without a diadem, in private clothing and dress but with royal bearing, and, without concealing the truth, said openly:

“Caesar, I confess that, having been made king by Antony, I was useful to King Antony. I would not hesitate to say that he found me grateful to him in every way and even in arms, had the Arabs not prevented it. Nevertheless, I sent him all the assistance that my strength allowed, and many thousands of measures of grain.

“For I gave him excellent counsel, saying that Cleopatra’s death was the one remedy against his adversaries. If he had killed her, I promised him both money and walls for defense, an army, and myself as an ally in the war against you. But in truth, Cleopatra’s love and the God who granted you victory closed his ears. Thus I was defeated together with Antony and laid down the crown of my kingdom together with his fortune.

“I have come to you, presuming upon the hope of safety from your virtue, and hastening to prevent an inquiry into what sort of friend I was and whose friend I was.”

To this Caesar replied:

“Rather, be truly safe, and now reign with greater certainty. For you deserve to rule many, since you have protected friendship with such loyalty. See to it, however, that you remain loyal even to those who are more fortunate. I indeed place an excellent hope in your greatness of spirit. Antony nevertheless acted rightly in obeying Cleopatra rather than you. We have gained you through his friendship.”

With this courteous speech he encouraged Herod as king, so that he would have no doubt about Caesar’s friendship. He placed the diadem upon him and confirmed his kingdom.

From there Herod followed Caesar’s journey into Egypt. By supplying everything that would be useful either to Caesar himself or to his army, he won the commander’s greatest favor through his own efforts—especially because, in the more arid regions as far as Pelusium, he provided an abundant supply of water with royal generosity.

Through these services he so infused everyone with love for him that he seemed to have earned more than he had received, and the power of his kingdom was judged less than the generosity of his humanity. Therefore, when Caesar had successfully completed his affairs in Egypt and Antony and Cleopatra were dead, he restored to Herod not only what had been taken from him but also, in addition to what Cleopatra had seized, granted him Zadora, Hippos, Samaria, and the coastal cities Gaza, Anthedon, Joppa, and the Tower of Strato. He also granted the king four hundred bodyguards from Gaul, with whom Cleopatra had been accustomed to surround herself, and many other things.

The king rejoiced in all these gifts, but even more because Caesar loved him above everyone except Agrippa, and Agrippa loved him below Caesar alone.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the more outstanding works accomplished by Herod, and on the killing of his sons, wife, and friends, and finally on his execrable death

After Caesar had subjected to Herod’s authority the region of Trachonitis, Batanea, and the whole land of Galilee, and had appointed him procurator of all Syria, Herod’s spirit rose to greater undertakings.

In the fifteenth year of his reign he restored the temple. Around the temple he enclosed with a wall twice as much land as had previously been enclosed, at enormous expense and with extraordinary generosity. The great porticoes around the precinct and the fortress connected with them on the north gave evidence of this; he built these from their foundations.

He also renewed, with lavish resources, a place that was in no respect less than a royal residence, and called it Antonia in honor of Antony. Moreover, after constructing a royal palace for himself in the upper part of the city, he built in it two immense and beautiful buildings, with which not even the temple could have been compared. He named one Caesarium and the other Agrippium, after his friends.

Nor did he confine their memory and names to buildings alone; he extended his zeal for generosity to entire cities as well. In short, he left no suitable place in his kingdom without the honor of Caesar. After filling his own territories with temples, he also spread their honors through the provinces and established temples called Caesarea in many cities.

His other works were all constructed with great generosity. Those who wish to know about them in detail should turn to the books of Josephus. I shall, however, describe the harbor and works of a single city that he completed.

When he saw a city already worn out by age, called the Tower of Strato, he entirely rebuilt it on the seashore with white stone. The adjoining coastline was so lacking in harbors that all who sailed the sea were forced to ride the waves, fearing the winds of Africus, which blow from Phoenicia toward Egypt. Even a moderate breeze raises such masses of waves against the rocks that, when the tide returns, the violence of the waters increases for a considerable distance out to sea.

But the king, overcoming the nature of the place through generosity and expense, constructed a larger harbor and in its interior made very high berths for ships. Although the entire site opposed him, he contended with the difficulty so successfully that the solidity of the construction yielded in no way to the sea, while its beauty was so great that it appeared as though no obstacle had hindered its ornamentation.

Having measured out the harbor for the distance described, he sank stones twenty cubits deep. Most of them were fifty feet long, fifteen feet high, and ten feet wide; some were even larger. After completing the space that concealed the waves, he extended a wall for two hundred feet. Of these, one hundred feet were constructed to repel the waves; the rest were placed beneath the stone wall enclosing the harbor, with great towers interposed. The largest and most beautiful of these was named Drusium after Caesar’s father, Drusus.

There were also frequent arches for draining away whatever the harbor collected, and in place of or around the arches were broad stone piers to receive ships as they departed. The entrance was on the north, since Boreas is the gentlest wind according to the position of the place.

At the mouth of the harbor stood statues, or Colossi, supported on each side by three columns. On the left as one entered, a solid tower supported them; on the right, two tall stones joined together exceeded in size the tower on the opposite side.

Buildings connected with the harbor, likewise made of white stone and extending toward it in the manner of the city, were constructed according to equal measurements. Opposite the harbor’s entrance, on a hill, stood a temple of Caesar, outstanding both in size and beauty. In it was a statue of Caesar, or a Colossus, no smaller than the statue of Jupiter at Olympia, after whose model it had been made.

He therefore named this city Caesarea in honor of Caesar. Out of love for his parents—Antipater, Cypros, and Phasael—he built cities, fortresses, and towers as an everlasting memorial. He also restored, at his own expense, the Olympic games and gymnasia in various cities.

His physical abilities too corresponded to the greatness of his spirit. He was an outstanding hunter, a brave warrior, a highly accurate archer, and extraordinarily fortunate in times of crisis; his pride diminished the fortune that otherwise favored him.

As soon as he obtained royal power, he repudiated the wife he had previously possessed, whose name was Doris, and married Mariamne, the granddaughter of Hyrcanus and daughter of Alexander, the son of Aristobulus, born of royal stock. He drove away his former wife from the royal household, together with her son Antipater, whom he had had by her.

He himself loved Mariamne with immense affection, but he was not at all loved by her; rather, he was hated by her. Her reason was that he had treacherously killed her grandfather Hyrcanus after the Parthians had returned him from exile. He had also ordered the killing of his wife’s brother Joathan, to whom he had granted the dignity of the high priesthood, because envy had been aroused by the popular favor shown to him.

These grievances, together with the nobility of her blood, stirred the woman against her husband. The extraordinary love of her husband, which she knew he bore toward her, and the fertility of her offspring gave her confidence. She had borne him three sons and two daughters. One son was called Alexander, the second Aristobulus, and the third, who had been sent to Rome for a liberal education, died there.

Mariamne therefore reproached Herod for the killing of her family and insulted King Herod’s sister Salome and his brother Pheroras with still harsher abuse. The king, however, was silent out of love for his wife. The women, on the other hand, raged with intense indignation and, besides many other charges that they invented, accused her of adultery—an accusation by which they could most strongly move Herod.

Stirred by this hatred, Herod ordered his wife to be killed. As for his sons Alexander and Aristobulus, because they were supposedly indignant over their mother’s death and plotting his own death, he requested from Caesar Octavian that they be put to death.

The emperor received Alexander’s defense—for he was exceptionally forceful in speaking—and reconciled the sons to their father. He instructed them to obey their father with sincere affection, as their lord, and told Herod to recognize his sons with paternal affection. He then sent them, reconciled, back to the kingdom.

As soon as Herod returned to Judaea, he was ensnared by the plots of Antipater, who desired his father’s kingdom. Doris, his former wife, whom he had brought into the bed of the murdered Mariamne, again armed him against his sons. The father’s hatred and indignation toward his sons increased day by day until he handed them over to death.

After they had been killed, Antipater did not rejoice with impunity, for he had been the cause of his brothers’ death. By the just judgment of God, and through the wickedness of the parricidal Herod—who always regarded all his friends with suspicion—Herod discovered that Antipater, whom he had designated before Caesar as successor to the kingdom, was plotting his death. He kept him bound and tormented him for a long time, and finally ordered him to be killed.

He also killed the husband of his sister Salome. After giving her to another man in marriage, he killed that man as well. He had also cruelly killed his mother-in-law, the mother of Mariamne. Thus his kingdom was filled with the most bitter injustice.

Whenever he suspected anyone, he immediately slaughtered them. Many people used the king’s anger, eager as it was for bloodshed, against their adversaries, and lies were instantly believed. Punishments were swifter than accusations themselves. In the end, the man who had just accused another was accused himself and was led to punishment together with the man who had previously been convicted.

He brought questions concerning the king’s life and safety to their conclusion by the shortest possible process. He had advanced so far in cruelty that he would not look upon any of the accused with humanity; indeed, he showed himself most merciless even toward his friends.

His sons Alexander and Aristobulus, whom he had killed, left the following offspring. Alexander’s sons by Glaphyra, the daughter of Archelaus, king of Cappadocia, were Tigranes and Alexander. Aristobulus’s sons were Agrippa, Herod, and Aristobulus. Beronice, the daughter of Herod’s sister Salome and therefore his niece, bore these sons to him.

Herod himself had, besides those whom he had killed, the following sons: Herod Antipas, Archelaus Herod, Philip, and Phasael; and the daughters Bosam, Salome, and Olympias. In addition to these, he had two daughters of Alexander and Aristobulus by Mariamne, the wife whom he had killed. He fathered this offspring by various wives, of whom he had many.

Herod, as rumor had it, killed his brother Pheroras with poison.

After the immense slaughter of his household and the insatiable oppression of his subjects, Herod learned from those who proclaimed it that the Lord Christ had been born. He immediately turned to cunning measures and sought to destroy him. When this did not happen as he wished, he revealed the fury that he had concealed in his heart by killing the children of Bethlehem.

By a decree more cruel than that of all barbarians, he ordered all boys from the age of one night up to the span of two years to be slaughtered. The Lord terribly avenged upon him this massacre of the innocent, although Herod had also burned alive two sophists highly learned in the law together with their disciples, and had ordered others who agreed with them to be slaughtered, because they had resolved to remove from the temple the golden eagle that he had established contrary to the laws.

He also killed the scribes and interpreters of the divine law, whom I suspect had been involved with Herod in plotting the death of the little children.

Herod’s body was afflicted by illness and worn down by various pains. He had a severe fever, while an intolerable itching covered the entire surface of his body. He was tormented by continual disorders of the colon; his feet had swollen as though from an accumulation of fluid beneath the skin; his belly was distended, and his testicles had rotted, producing worms. By this time he was also seized by black bile and seemed almost to threaten death itself.

He therefore devised a wicked act. He ordered the leading men of every village throughout Judaea to be gathered and confined in a place called the Hippodrome. Then he summoned his sister Salome and her husband Alexas and said:

“I know that the Jews will celebrate my death with festive rejoicing. But I can be mourned by others and obtain splendid honors at my burial if you do what I command. As soon as I breathe my last, kill these men who are being held in custody, surrounding them with soldiers, so that while I am still alive the whole of Judaea, the whole nation, may weep for me.”

Because Herod was swollen by the combined violence of starvation and coughing, he tried to anticipate his fate. After taking an apple, he also asked for a small knife. He was accustomed to eat it cut up. Then, looking around to ensure that no one was present to prevent him, he raised his right hand as though he were about to stab himself.

But when his cousin Aciabus rushed up and restrained his hand, thereby delaying his death for a little while, Herod revised his will. He named Archelaus, the eldest son and brother of Antipater, as his successor, and Antipas as tetrarch.

Herod therefore died forty-four years after he had killed Antigonus and taken possession of the kingdom of the Jews, but thirty-two years after he had been declared king by the Romans. In all other matters he had enjoyed favorable fortune, but in domestic affairs he had been most unfortunate.

Augustus appointed Archelaus in Herod’s place and made his four brothers tetrarchs.

## CHAPTER XIX. That Christ was born during the reign of Octavian, as the prophets had foretold and the angels had announced; and which illustrious men worthy of remembrance lived at that time

In those days the kingdom of the Egyptians, which had existed in Alexandria, was destroyed. It had stood for 240 years, until Cleopatra. Egypt thereafter became a province of the Romans. Its first governor was Cornelius Gallus of Forum Julii, a poet who, in the forty-third year of his age, killed himself with his own hand; Virgil mentions him in the *Bucolics*.

At that time, when a census had been conducted at Rome, four million and forty-three thousand Roman citizens were found.

The philosopher Marcus Terentius Varro died when he was nearly ninety years old. Nicopolis was then founded near Actium, and the Actian games were established.

Arctoricus, Augustus’s physician, perished in a shipwreck after the victory at Actium. He had advised Octavian to hasten from the camp into the open field, although he was ill, against Antony’s soldiers; he said that he had learned in a dream that this would benefit him. When Augustus did so, he escaped the danger of death, for the camp was immediately captured by Antony’s forces.

The Larissaean, a magician and Pythagorean, was expelled by Augustus from the city and from Italy. Augustus also made the Gauls and Calabria tributary.

M. Gnatius Plautius, a disciple of Cicero, was regarded as a distinguished orator. While governing Transalpine Gaul, he founded Lyons.

M. Lollius made Galatia a province. Quintilius of Cremona, a friend of Virgil and Horace, died.

Tiberius, sent by Augustus, occupied Armenia. The poet Virgil died at Brundisium when Saturninus and Cinna Lucentianus were consuls. His bones were carried to Naples and buried at the second milestone from the city, beneath the following inscription, which he himself had repeatedly dictated at the time of his death:

> Mantua gave me birth; the Calabrians took me away; now  
> Parthenope holds me. I sang of pastures, fields, and leaders.

Verrius and Tucax, companions of Virgil and Horace, were also regarded as distinguished poets. They later corrected the books of the *Aeneid* under the condition that they add nothing.

The poet Aemilius Macer of Verona died in Asia. Augustus adopted Agrippa as his son.

Tiberius made the Vindelici and those who bordered Thrace Roman provinces; afterward, after ravaging Germany, he was called emperor.

Gaius Julius, surnamed Polyhistor, was regarded as a distinguished grammarian. Horace died at Rome in the fifty-seventh year of his age.

Tiberius Caesar celebrated a triumph over the captured Pannonians. Augustus condemned his daughter to exile after discovering her in adultery.

Marcus Tullius Tiro, Cicero’s freedman and the first to compose shorthand signs, grew old on his estate at Puteoli until he reached one hundred years.

Augustus presented a gladiatorial spectacle and a naval battle. He adopted Tiberius and Agrippa as sons.

Judas the Galilaean encouraged the Jews to rebel. Asinius Pollio, a consular orator who triumphed over the Dalmatians, died at his villa in Tusculum in the eightieth year of his age. His son was Asinius Gallus, an orator who was killed by Tiberius with dreadful punishments. Virgil also mentions him.

Thus, as we announced above, we have reached the birth of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God and man. As it had been foretold by the prophets, proclaimed by the angels, guided by the star, and attested by the priests and teachers of the law, it was celebrated at Bethlehem of Judaea in the five hundred and fifteenth year from the rebuilding of the temple, which took place under King Darius; in the one thousand and twenty-seventh year from Solomon and the first construction of the temple; and in the one thousand five hundred and sixth year from Moses and Israel’s departure from Egypt.

From Abraham and the kingdom of Ninus and Semiramis, 2,011 years had passed; from the Flood, 2,921 years; from Adam, 5,129 years. According to the account of Genesis and the reckoning of Africanus, 128 additional years are found.

We have therefore taken care to recount this succession of years, from the first-created human being down to the Lord’s coming, by the several kingdoms and according to our ability, using the more celebrated events. Now, after immense waves of the sea, we have at last escaped the Scylla-like barking [Col. 1116B], and, having reached the desired harbor, have come through the long darkness of the ages to the true light. Sprinkled with that light at the coming of the Lord Christ, we have brought the books to an end.

# PREFACE OF THE AUTHOR TO JUDITH AUGUSTA FOR THE SECOND VOLUME

Most fortunate Judith, lady of the Augustae, since nothing higher can be found among human affairs by which you may increase your rank: if the matter concerns a husband, who among emperors is nobler, or wiser in divine and secular disciplines, than the unconquered Caesar Louis? Nor is it surprising that he produced such offspring for Charles, the most excellent Augustus of the age.

If the matter concerns bodily beauty, then, to speak the truth without the cosmetic of flattery, you surpass in beauty all the queens whom the sight or hearing of my smallness has encountered. If it concerns offspring, is not Charles the glory of the world and the delight of humanity? By the elegance of his body and his excellent character, and by the swift pursuit of wisdom, he surpasses his immature age by conquering it, so that his grandfather seems not to have died but rather, having wiped away the darkness of sleep, to illuminate a new world. In his grandson, his immortal genius shines together with his name, adorned by virtue.

Therefore, since you lack nothing in temporal affairs by which you might be increased, you enlarge yourself through your devotion to wisdom, so that you may be found more excellent than the empresses of earlier ages.

The wisdom given to you by God and the knowledge of your natural intellect make me astonished among your other assistants. When I came to know the eloquence of your learning in divine and liberal studies, I was amazed, and immediately began to consider what little gift, gathered by my labor, I might offer to the ardor of your graciousness.

Accordingly, I undertook to write a second work beginning with Octavian Augustus and the birth of our Savior, the Lord, and completed it through the kingdoms of the Franks and Lombards, when the Roman emperors and rulers had disappeared from Italy and Gaul, as had also the Gothic kings who had succeeded them, after those rulers too had been expelled.

I divided this work into five books. In them, as in a mirror, my lord Charles—the most glorious son of your excellence—will be able, through the reminder and command of your most holy devotion, to see what ought to be done and what ought to be avoided.

For it is fitting that you, venerable lady, should instruct your only son, the king of our joy and of the new age, just as Bathsheba instructed Jedidiah, the wisest king of former ages. As he himself says concerning this:

> For I too was a tender son to my father,  
> and the only one before my mother;  
> and he taught me and said:  
> “Let your heart receive my words;  
> keep my commandments, and you shall live.  
> Acquire wisdom; acquire prudence.  
> Do not forget, and do not turn away from the words of my mouth.  
> Do not forsake her, and she will guard you;  
> love her, and she will preserve you,” and so forth.

As we trust in the Lord’s mercy, he will obey your sacred commands and will not disdain to entrust these little books to his memory among the other admonitions of his motherly affection. Enlightened by the deeds of emperors, the triumphs of saints, and the splendid teachings of doctors, he will discover more cautiously what ought to be done and more subtly what ought to be avoided.

The love of your affection, therefore, my lady, ever Augusta, compelled me to write these little books. They await the judgment of your graciousness and immortal wisdom. If, through your judgment, they obtain praise, it will be credited eternally to your memory, since your most sacred name, Judith, is interpreted as “judging” or “praising.”

# HERE BEGINS THE SECOND VOLUME OF THE CHRONICLES

Containing the history of events from Octavian Augustus and the birth of Christ our Savior through the kingdoms of the Franks and Lombards.

## BOOK ONE

[Col. 1117]

### CHAPTER ONE. What histories of the various kingdoms the earlier books contain, from the beginning of the world to the birth of Christ
