In the preceding books, with the Lord’s support, I took care, after laboring with no little exertion over many short works both of hagiographers and of pagan authors, to excerpt whatever seemed useful to my small abilities and likely to benefit readers, beginning with the first father who propagated the mortal race. At last, after the many darknesses of the ages, we reached the birth of the new man, namely our Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God and man. There I decided to bring the preceding books to an end, so that they might conclude with the legal ceremonies, shadows, and former errors.

## CHAPTER II. [Col. 1117B] On the birth of Christ, announced by angels and prophets, which consecrated the sixth age of the world

Now that the Savior has been born and, by his rays, the darkness has been removed and the world illumined, another road must be traveled. The pen will no longer, as before, be wearied by writing the histories of the kingdoms of various nations, since the ferocity, rage, and boundless desire of individual peoples to rule—which we briefly touched upon in the preceding books—have all alike fallen under the authority of a single dominion. And this was prepared not by human strength or wisdom, but by the omnipotence of God, something that had never previously occurred. Foreseeing this from afar, the prophet says: “Nation shall not lift up sword,” and what follows.

It was therefore fitting that, at the birth of him who is the one God, in the substance of the Father and [Col. 1117C] the Holy Spirit, the whole world should be subjected under a single census. Thus this birth was celebrated with the prophets proclaiming and the angels announcing: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will,” when the whole world was resting under one peace, in a marvelous manner unheard of in earlier ages. This birth and peace were foretold long beforehand not only in the writings of divine revelation but also by the oracles of the pagans, as is contained in the Sibylline poems and those of others.

Accordingly, after Octavian Caesar began to rule—he was the first to obtain the monarchy of the world, although his uncle Julius Caesar had existed before him more as the measurer-out of imperial power than as emperor—when nearly forty-two years had passed, the Lord Christ was born, [Col. 1117D] bringing true light to the world, which had been numb in darkness from age to age. For it happened that, [Col. 1118A] just as the holy Abraham was born in the forty-third year under Nimrod, the first king of the nations, to whom the promises were given and from whose seed Christ had been promised, so Christ’s birth corresponded with the end of the forty-second year, so that it would no longer be in a part of the third year, but rather the third year itself would be beginning.

I think it is sufficiently understood how greatly, how newly, and how extraordinarily that year abounded, even without my setting it forth. Throughout the whole world there was one peace for all, brought about not by a cessation but by the abolition of wars. The gates of Janus Geminus were closed, the roots of wars having been eradicated rather than merely restrained. There was the first and greatest census, when the entire great creation of the nations swore allegiance to the single name of Caesar, and through participation in one census became a community united [Col. 1118B] in one association.

Thus, in the seven hundred and fifty-second year from the founding of the City, Christ was born, bringing the world saving faith. Truly he was the stone placed in the midst of events: whoever stumbled against it would be shattered, while whoever believed would be saved. Truly he was the burning fire: whoever follows it is illumined, while whoever tests it is consumed. He is Christ, the head of Christians, the savior of the good, the punisher of the wicked, and the judge of all. For by his coming this Jesus Christ, Son of God, consecrated the sixth age of the world.

## CHAPTER III. On the foreigner Herod, under whom Christ was born, and on the prophecies that were then fulfilled which foretold this birth

As we showed in the preceding books, after leaders and princes from the seed of Judah had been removed from the kingship or leadership of the Jews while they were bitterly contending for supreme power, Herod was appointed ruler by the Romans—a foreigner with no connection whatsoever to the Jews. He was the son of Antipater the Ascalonite and Cypros the Arabian. When he received from the Romans the leadership of the Jews, he indicated that Christ’s birth was near and that the priesthood and kingdom of Judea, formerly held through successions of lesser rulers, were to be destroyed. The prophecy spoken through Moses was now fulfilled: “A prince shall not fail from Judah, nor a judge from his loins, until he comes to whom it has been reserved; and he shall be the expectation of the nations.”

At this point the “Christ,” of whom the book of Daniel speaks beforehand, also came to an end. For until Herod, the *christs*—that is, the priests—were kings of the Jews; they began to rule from the restoration of the Temple, [Col. 1118D] under Darius, until Hyrcanus, with 483 years having elapsed in between. [Col. 1119A]

Daniel also signifies these rulers when he says: “Know therefore and understand: from the beginning of the word concerning the return and rebuilding of Jerusalem until the rule of the Christ, there shall be seven weeks and sixty-two weeks.” These make sixty-nine weeks, or 483 years, during which the *christs*—that is, the priests—consecrated by anointing, ruled until Hyrcanus.

When this last of them had been captured by the Parthians, Herod, the son of Antipater, received from Caesar and the Senate the leadership of Judea, which had no connection with him. His sons ruled after him until the final captivity of Jerusalem. They were not appointed from the succession of the priestly line as high priests, nor did they serve God with the perpetuity of life prescribed by the law [Col. 1119B] of Moses. Instead, certain obscure men, some at one time and others at another, and some for a single year or little more, purchased the priesthood from the Roman emperors.

The prophet Daniel also foretells all these things, saying: “And after the sixty-nine weeks the anointing shall perish, and judgment shall not be in it; and the people, with a leader who is to come, shall corrupt the Temple and the sanctuary.”

## CHAPTER IV. On Octavian, who did not allow himself to be called lord, and on the kind of life he led and the end that overtook him

Octavian, who—as we have already stated—was the first of all emperors to obtain the monarchy of the world, did not permit, nor even dare to allow, his own children [Col. 1119C] to call him lord, much less foreigners, because while he was emperor the true Lord of the entire human race was born among human beings.

While he was watching games, a line was spoken in a mime: “O fair and good lord!” Everyone approved it enthusiastically, as though it had been said about him. Immediately, however, he restrained the disgraceful flattery with a gesture and expression, and on the following day rebuked it in a very stern edict. From then on he did not permit himself to be called lord, not even by his children or grandchildren, whether seriously or in jest.

Nevertheless, I shall briefly explain his origin, the life he led, and the end that overtook him—he who, after closing the gates of Janus, nourished by peace the republic he had acquired through war and strove to enlarge it. He was born to his father Octavian, a senator. Through his mother he derived his lineage from Aeneas by way of the Julian family. Through the adoption of his maternal great-uncle, Gaius Caesar, he was called Gaius Caesar; afterward, because of his victory, he received the surname Augustus.

Once placed in power, he exercised the tribunician authority himself. He reduced Egypt, a region made difficult of access by the flooding of the Nile and impassable because of its marshes, to the form of a province. To make its grain supply abundant for the City, he had ditches closed by the mud of long neglect reopened through the labor of soldiers. In his time, twenty million units of grain were brought annually from Egypt to the City. He added the Cantabrians and Aquitanians, the Rhaetians and Vindelicians, and the Dalmatians to the Roman people as provinces; he destroyed the Suebi and Chatti. He transferred the Sugambri to Gaul and added the Pannonians as tributaries. He compelled the peoples of the Getae and the Bastarnae, provoked by wars, to make peace. The Persians offered him hostages and entrusted to him the choice of their king. The Indians, Scythians, Garamantes, and Ethiopians sent ambassadors to him with gifts.

Finally, he so detested disturbances stirred up by wars that he never declared war against any people except for just causes. He used to say that the eagerness for triumph and for the laurel crown—that is, for fruitless leaves—was characteristic of a boastful and frivolous mind, and that it was madness to cast the security of citizens into danger through the uncertain outcomes of battles. Nothing was less fitting for a good commander than rashness. Whatever was conducted advantageously was accomplished quickly enough, and arms should never be taken up except in hope of a greater gain, lest a victory sought at the cost of a small profit and a great loss resemble those who fish with a golden hook: if it is broken off and lost, no profit from the catch can compensate for the damage.

Finally, he behaved with the greatest clemency toward his citizens and proved faithful to his friends. The foremost among them were Maecenas, distinguished by his silence, and Agrippa, by his endurance of labor and modesty.

He also loved Virgil. He was slow to form friendships but extremely constant in preserving them. He devoted himself so intensely to liberal studies, especially eloquence, that no day passed—even when on campaign—without his reading, writing, or practicing declamation. In his own name he issued some new laws and revised others. He increased and adorned Rome with many buildings, boasting in these words: “I found a city of brick; I leave one of marble.”

He was, it is said, gracious, possessed of a civil disposition, and witty; handsome in his entire body, but especially in his eyes. Their gaze, flashing like the brightest stars, willingly accepted the fact that those who looked intently at him turned their eyes away, as though from the rays of the sun. When a soldier turned his eyes away from his face and was asked why he did so, he replied: “Because I cannot bear the lightning of your eyes.”

Yet so great a man was not free from vices, since he served dominating greed and lust. After divorcing his own wife, Scribonia, he married Livia, as though her husband had handed her over to him. He loved her so greatly that he adopted her sons, Tiberius and Drusus, his stepsons, as his own children, setting aside his own offspring. Of these, he designated Tiberius as his successor in the empire.

He ruled for fifty-six years: twelve with Antony and forty-four alone. Certainly, he would never have drawn the power of the republic to himself, nor possessed it for so long, unless this had happened for the sake of the Lord’s birth. It would take too long to recount the honors with which the Senate exalted him after his death. For, as we have said, he was the first to obtain the unique principate, and he left to his successors the same power of empire together with his own name, Augustus.

Near the end of his life, because the Jews could not endure the arrogance of Archelaus, the son of Herod, who had ruled in Judea for nine years after him, but instead accused him voluntarily, Augustus banished that same Archelaus from Vienna, a city of Gaul. To diminish the power of the Jewish kingdom and subdue its insolence, [Col. 1121A] four of his brothers were created tetrarchs in his place: Herod Antipater, Lysias, and Philip. Philip and Herod, who was previously called Antipas, had also been appointed tetrarchs while Archelaus was still alive.

## CHAPTER V. Under Tiberius, John preaches and baptizes; the Lord Jesus comes to his passion by preaching and performing miracles

Tiberius, Augustus’s stepson, ruled for twenty-four years. In the twelfth year of his reign, Pilate was sent to Jerusalem to govern Judea. Herod the tetrarch, who held the leadership of the Jews for twenty-four years, founded Tiberias and Livias in honor of Tiberius and his mother Livia.

Thus, in the twelfth year of Tiberius’s reign, John, son of Zechariah, preaching in the wilderness beside the streams of the Jordan, testified that Christ the Son of God was present among them. The Lord Jesus Christ himself then announced to the peoples the way of salvation, confirming through signs and mighty deeds that what he said was true. Jesus Christ, the Son of God, performed the miracles written in the Gospels and instructed his disciples in divine mysteries, commanding them to proclaim conversion to God among all nations. According to the prophecies that had foretold him, Jesus Christ came to his passion in the eighteenth year of Tiberius.

## CHAPTER VI. On the earthquake and darkness that occurred during the Lord’s passion, and on what pagan writers—and Josephus the historian—thought about them

At that time we also found the following written word for word in other pagan records: “An eclipse of the sun occurred; Bithynia was shaken by an earthquake; in the city of Nicaea many buildings collapsed.” All these things correspond to what had happened during the Savior’s passion.

Phlegon, who is an outstanding reckoner of Olympiads, also writes about these events in his thirteenth book, saying:

“In the fourth year of the 202nd Olympiad, a great and remarkable eclipse of the sun occurred, greater than all those that had taken place before it, at the sixth hour of the day. The sun was completely darkened, and a dreadful night suddenly covered the earth,” and, as it has been said:

> And the impious ages feared everlasting night.

It is also clear that neither the moon obstructed the sun’s light nor clouds did so, since it is reported that on that day, the fourteenth, the moon was present very far from the sight of the sun, although it stood across the whole region of the sky, and that the stars shone throughout the entire sky during the daytime—or rather, during that dreadful night.

And, as we mentioned above, an earthquake in Bithynia overturned many buildings in the city of Nicaea. When the other cities of Asia had likewise been destroyed by that earthquake under the same emperor, their tributes were remitted.

So much for the aforementioned writer. The Gospel of John provides evidence that the Savior suffered in that year: it says that, after the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, the Lord preached for three years.

Josephus, a native Jewish writer, also testifies that around this time, on the day of Pentecost, the priests first perceived a shaking of the places and certain sounds. Then, he says, a voice suddenly burst forth from the inner sanctuary of the Temple, saying: “Let us depart from these places.”

The aforementioned writer also records that in the same year, Pilate, the governor, secretly placed images of Caesar in the Temple at night, and that this became the first cause of sedition and disturbances among the Jews.

From this point one must consider how many disasters subsequently overwhelmed the Jewish people. After the above-mentioned sedition, which had been stirred up because of Caesar’s images, Pilate spent the sacred treasury—which the Jews call the *corban*—on an aqueduct for Jerusalem, thereby providing the seeds of a second sedition. [Col. 1122B]

Sejanus, Tiberius’s prefect, who possessed very great influence with him, urged him most insistently to destroy the Jewish people, as Philo recalls in Book II of his *Embassy*. Tiberius therefore removed their young men to provinces with harsher climates under the pretext of military service, and expelled the rest of that same people, or those who followed similar practices, from the City under penalty of perpetual slavery if they did not obey.

## CHAPTER VII. On the appointment of James and the seven deacons; also on the conversion of King Abgar through Thaddaeus

At that time, after Christ’s ascension, the apostles who were about to preach throughout the regions of Judea appointed James, the brother of the Lord, bishop at Jerusalem. They also appointed seven deacons. After Stephen was stoned, [Col. 1122C] the Church was scattered throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria.

It is pleasing to write more fully about these matters. First, therefore, Matthias, who was one of the Lord’s disciples, was chosen by lot among the apostles in place of Judas the betrayer. Seven deacons were also appointed through the prayers and laying on of the apostles’ hands, for the ministry of widows. Among them was Stephen, who was also the first to be stoned after Christ by those who had killed the Lord; through this, Christ gave Stephen the crown of his name.

Afterward, the ancient historians record that James who was called the brother of the Lord—this very James, I say, who was also surnamed Just—because of the merit of his virtues and the distinction of his life, was the first to receive the seat of the Church that is in Jerusalem, as Clement asserts in Book VI of his *Outlines*, saying:

“Peter, James, and John, although they had been preferred above almost everyone by the Savior after his assumption, did not claim for themselves the glory of primacy. Instead, they appointed James, who was called Just, bishop of the apostles.”

In Book VII of the same work, he adds the following about him:

“To James, who was called Just, and to John and Peter, after the Lord’s resurrection, he entrusted all knowledge; and they entrusted it to the other apostles. Those apostles entrusted it to the seventy disciples, one of whom was Barnabas.”

It is clear that there were two Jameses: one was this James the Just, who, after being thrown down from the pinnacle of the Temple, was struck with a fuller’s club and handed over to death. [Col. 1123A] The other was the one who was beheaded by Herod.

Paul also remembers this James the Just when he writes: “I saw none of the other apostles, except James, the brother of the Lord.”

At this time, Thaddaeus was also sent to King Abgar according to the Lord’s command. He freed Abgar himself from bodily illness, but joined the entire city of the Edessenes to Christ the Lord through a sufficiently faithful belief, so that even to the present day that city, having deserved to receive writings of the Lord and our Savior himself, appears to have been dedicated to Christ by a special devotion.

Eusebius also decided to write about these matters at greater length. In Book I of his *Ecclesiastical History* he says:

“Finally, after the Lord’s resurrection and ascension into heaven, the apostle Thomas, in response to a divine command, sent to the city of Edessa an evangelist and preacher of the word of God, a certain Thaddaeus, one of the seventy disciples, who was also to fulfill the promises made by the Lord.

“We found these things written in the public archive of the city of Edessa, in which the aforementioned Abgar then ruled, in documents that had preserved from ancient times the deeds of King Abgar. To make the truth of what has been said evident, copies of the letters from Abgar to the Savior and from the Savior to that same king, together with an account of how these events occurred, are fully contained in Book I of Eusebius’s *Ecclesiastical History*.”

## CHAPTER VIII. On the first persecution of the Church, through which the word of God reached the nations; among them, Ethiopia was the first to receive it

Meanwhile, the first persecution against the Church of God, which was in Jerusalem, scattered—or rather, as holy Scripture indicates, sowed—all the disciples throughout Judea and Samaria, except the eleven, under Stephen, the first martyr. Some of them reached as far as Phoenicia, Cyprus, and Antioch. They did not yet dare to proclaim the mystery of the faith to the gentiles, but they preached to the Jews.

Meanwhile Paul was still ravaging the Church, entering houses and dragging away men and women to hand them over to prison. But Philip, who had been appointed one of the seven deacons together with Stephen, went down to Samaria, filled with the power of the Lord, and [Col. 1123D] was the first to preach the word of God to the Samaritan people.

The efficacy of divine grace was so great in him that through his preaching he even overwhelmed Simon the magician. At that time Simon enjoyed a celebrated reputation among the Samaritan peoples, so that he was thought to possess the great power of God. But when he saw the signs and miracles performed by Philip through the power of divine grace, he was astonished and frightened. He pretended to believe in Christ, even to the point of receiving baptism.

As the preaching of the divine word increased day by day, through God’s providence a certain man came from the regions of Ethiopia, as though to fulfill vows in Jerusalem. He was an official of the queen of that nation. [Col. 1124A] It is indeed the custom of that nation even now to be ruled by women.

At the command of the Holy Spirit, Philip entrusted to this man—the first from among all the nations—the mystery of the faith and the sacrament of baptism, consecrating him as a kind of first-fruits of all the nations to God. Tradition holds that, after returning to his native land, he preached to its indigenous peoples the knowledge of the Most High God and the salvation of our Lord, just as it had been handed on to him.

In this man the prophecy was fulfilled in reality which says: “Ethiopia shall hasten to stretch out her hands to God.”

While these things were taking place, Paul, the vessel of election—not from human beings nor through a human being, but through a revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ and of God the Father, who raised him from the dead—was called to the apostolate by a heavenly voice addressed to him.

## CHAPTER IX. [Col. 1124B] How Pilate reported to Tiberius and the Senate the Lord’s resurrection, his miracles, and that he was God

Meanwhile, when throughout every place the joyful report of the resurrection and miracles of our Lord Jesus Christ, and of his ascension into heaven, was already being proclaimed, and the report of this blessed event was circulating in everyone’s ears—and since it was an ancient custom among the Romans that the governors of provinces should report to the emperor or the Senate anything new that might occur in the provinces they administered, so that they would not appear to be ignorant of anything that was happening—Pilate reported to Tiberius, the emperor, the resurrection from the dead of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, which had already become known everywhere. He also reported his other miracles and that, after his death and resurrection, very many people had come to believe that he was God.

Tiberius reported what he had learned to the Senate. The Senate is said to have rejected it because no indication of the matter had first been brought to it, but the judgment of the populace had preceded its authority. For an ancient law had been established among the Romans that no one should be regarded as a god unless confirmed by a decree and decision of the Senate.

Yet what was happening was true, and divine power did not need human defenders. Although the Senate rejected the matter, as we have said above, Tiberius nevertheless maintained his own decision and threatened the accusers of the Christians with the danger of death, so that he would undertake nothing contrary to the teaching of Christ.

This is what Tertullian says. Divine providence had clearly placed this conviction in Caesar’s mind at that time, so that, without any obstacle, the word of the Gospel might spread everywhere from its very beginnings. Hence it also came to pass that, as though a heavenly light had suddenly been displayed or a ray of the sun had burst forth, the entire world was illumined by the radiance of heavenly light, so that the prophecy too might be fulfilled which had said: “Their sound has gone out through all the earth”—namely, the sound of the evangelists and apostles—“and their words to the ends of the world.”

From that time, in every city and village, immense crowds were gathered into the Church like grain to threshing floors at harvest time.

## CHAPTER X. [Col. 1125A] On the life and deeds of Tiberius, and how the Church of Christ then flourished wondrously at Antioch; where Christians were first so called, and on other events that occurred at that time

Tiberius Caesar, under whom the events we have recounted took place, was sufficiently skilled in warfare and sufficiently fortunate before assuming the empire under Augustus. He possessed extensive literary knowledge and was more distinguished in eloquence, but of the worst and most treacherous character. He pretended to want what he did not want, appearing hostile to those whose interests he wished to promote, and benevolent toward those whom he hated. He was better at sudden replies and decisions than at those formed after deliberation.

Once emperor, he himself waged no wars, but in several places he quickly suppressed, through his legates, disturbances among nations that he had foreseen. In the fourth year of his reign, Germanicus, son of Drusus and father of Caligula, triumphed over the Germans, against whom he had been sent by the aged Augustus.

For much of his reign Tiberius governed the republic with great and serious restraint. When certain governors advised that the provincial tributes be increased, he wrote to them that it was the duty of a good shepherd to shear the flock, not flay it. Thus Tiberius Caesar’s highly praised restraint gradually changed into punishment of those who opposed the Senate, and from the gentlest of princes he blazed forth as a savage beast.

For he proscribed many senators and compelled them to die. He had selected twenty patrician men as his council; scarcely eleven of them did he leave unharmed, killing the rest for various reasons. He killed his prefect Sejanus when he was plotting revolution—deservedly, because he had most stubbornly opposed the Christian religion.

He destroyed his sons Drusus and Germanicus, of whom Drusus was his natural son and Germanicus his adopted son, with unmistakable signs of poisoning; and he killed the sons of his son Germanicus. It is abhorrent and shameful to recount his deeds one by one. He raged with such frenzy of lust and cruelty that those who had refused to be saved by Christ the King were punished by Caesar the king.

While he was emperor, Agrippa, surnamed Herod and the son of Aristobulus, son of King Herod, went to Rome to accuse Herod the tetrarch, but Tiberius threw him into chains. There he won many people over to his friendship, especially Gaius, the son of Germanicus.

At this same time, as divine favor was being poured out more abundantly everywhere among all the pagan peoples, Cornelius was the first in Caesarea of Palestine to be brought to the faith of Christ, together with his entire household, through the ministry of Peter.

From then on many others from the nations also came to the faith at Antioch, drawn by the preaching of those whom, as we explained above, the persecution stirred up against Stephen had scattered everywhere. Through them a flourishing Church was assembled at Antioch. There were also many men of prophetic rank, among whom were Barnabas and Paul. While all of them lived together in the grace of God and in harmony, it was there first that the disciples, taking their name from the everlasting fountain, were called Christians.

In those days the poet Ovid died in exile. He had been condemned by the aged Augustus because of the books of the *Art of Love* that he had composed. The historian Livy died at Patavium. Philip called the tetrarchy of Paneas, where he had built many structures, Caesarea Philippi, and another city Julia.

Tiberius then summoned many kings through flattering promises, but never sent them back to their own lands. Among them was Archelaus of Cappadocia. After converting his kingdom into a province, Tiberius ordered that its most distinguished city, Mazaca, be called Caesarea.

He also killed many senators and Roman knights; finally, he himself died in Campania.

## CHAPTER XI. On Philo, who adorned the Church with praise of Gaius, and on the great evils the Jews suffered under that same emperor [Col. 1126B] in punishment for the cross

After Tiberius, Gaius Caligula assumed the empire. He immediately handed the leadership of the Jews to Agrippa, who was also called Herod, releasing him from chains, and gave him the tetrarchies of Philip and Lysanias.

As for Herod himself, who had either been responsible for John’s death or had been present at the Lord’s passion, Gaius tortured him in many ways and condemned him to perpetual exile, as Josephus writes.

In his time Philo, the most distinguished of writers, flourished. He was regarded as foremost among the foremost not only in our own philosophy but also in that of the Greeks. By ancestry he was descended from Hebrew forebears; at Alexandria he was more distinguished and noble than all its eminent and noble men.

Everyone can see what sort and degree of knowledge he possessed of the divine laws and ancestral institutions from the memorials he handed down in his books. Who could adequately explain how thoroughly he was trained in the liberal arts, how thoroughly in philosophy, and especially how greatly he excelled in the Platonic and Pythagorean disciplines, surpassing nearly all who flourished with him and even many who came before him?

This same man sets out in five volumes the great evils that befell the Jews in the time of Gaius. He also recalls Gaius’s madness of mind: he was so swollen with pride that he wished to be called God.

In the passages where he reports the disasters of the Jews, he also describes his own embassy, which he undertook on behalf of his fellow Jews to the city of Rome, and how, when pleading before Gaius for the ancestral laws, he brought home nothing more than ridicule, indeed nearly incurred the danger of death.

Josephus also mentions these matters in Book XVIII of his *Antiquities*. Among other things, he says that Philo was immediately driven from Gaius’s presence with insult. After leaving, Philo said to the Jews who stood beside him: “We must keep our courage. Gaius is angry with us because divine help must be present when human assistance ceases.”

He clearly reveals the divine vengeance inflicted upon the Jews for the sacrileges they had wickedly committed against Christ.

It is also reported that, when Philo came to Rome a second time to bring the embassy of his people to Claudius, he spoke in that city with the apostle Peter and formed a friendship with him. For this reason, they say, he adorned the Church of Peter’s disciple Mark at Alexandria with his praises. He also wrote a book on the conduct and life of our people.

In it he says that this sect existed not only in Alexandria but also in many provinces, among both men and women, and that their dwellings were called monasteries. From this it appears that the Church of those who first believed in Christ was like the communities that monks now imitate and desire: nothing belonged to anyone individually; no one among them was rich and no one poor; their estates were divided among the needy; they devoted themselves to prayer, psalms, teaching, and self-restraint. He asserted that they were like those whom Luke reports to have been the first believers at Jerusalem.

Thus divine vengeance was condemning the Jews for the crime they had committed against the Savior, as the same author and Josephus relate in their histories. They show in clear words that from the time of the sacrilege they had committed, the frenzy of seditions, wars, and deaths never ceased among them, until the final and fatal disaster enclosed them under siege in the time of Vespasian.

First, under Tiberius—concerning whom, during the Lord’s passion, they cried, “We have no king but Caesar”—they suffered countless disasters. As the aforementioned writers report, it was impossible to write down all the evils that had befallen them from that time onward. They had turned to sedition because of the money taken from the treasury called the *corban*, which Pilate spent on the aqueduct. The ways in which they were afflicted and crushed, as well as the fact that Pilate ordered Caesar’s images to be brought into Jerusalem and set up there at night under cover, have also been recorded.

When day dawned, this caused great disturbance among the Jewish people, who were astonished and troubled by the unprecedented situation. They inferred from this that their laws and all the institutions of their ancestors were now being despised and trampled upon, although nothing of this kind was permitted within the walls of that city.

But this is precisely the matter for which the swift vengeance of their impious possession condemned them.

Gaius, therefore, hated the Jews above every kind of people. With a particular cruelty, beginning at Alexandria, he ordered their places consecrated for divine worship to be plundered and profaned contrary to the religion and customs of the nation, filling them with his statues, standards, and images.

He even dared to transform the Temple of the holy city, which alone had remained untouched by every profane contamination and had endured as a refuge for their ancestors, into a temple of his own name, so that it would be called the temple of Jupiter, the most noble new god Gaius.

Moreover, countless other disasters and griefs beyond all tragic lamentation were inflicted upon the Jews at Alexandria under Gaius. As Philo and Josephus write, throughout the Roman world statues, images, and altars of Gaius Caesar were consecrated in the synagogues of the Jews.

## CHAPTER XII. On Herod and Pilate, who paid the just penalties for their deeds, and on the wicked acts of Gaius Caligula

Herod the tetrarch, himself seeking the friendship of Gaius, came to Rome at the urging of Herodias. But when Agrippa accused him, he also lost his tetrarchy. Fleeing to Spain with Herodias, he perished in grief.

Pilate likewise, who had performed the office of an unjust judge against the Savior, was tortured in the same period of Gaius by disasters of such magnitude and kind that he is said to have pierced himself with his own hand and violently ended his wicked life.

The agent of so great a sacrilege could not escape unpunished, as we find in the histories of the Greeks, specifically those who write the Olympiads and compose annals of events for the memory of posterity.

Gaius, surnamed Caligula, ruled for four years. Before his principate he was beloved and well received by everyone; as emperor, however, he was such that it was rightly said that no lord had been more savage than he.

Finally, he dishonored his three sisters through sexual relations and then condemned them to exile on islands. In the palace he subjected noble married women to public lust. He was the first of the Caesars to put on a diadem, order himself to be called lord, and demand that he be worshiped as a god.

He also married the wife of Memmius Regulus, forcing him to write that he was the father of his own wife and to hand over his property to Gaius.

Then he ordered all exiles to be killed, as well as many Roman nobles. But the result was not what he wanted; for he is said to have exclaimed: “Would that the Roman people had a single neck!”

He himself was killed by his protectors in the palace in the twenty-ninth year of his age.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the arrival of blessed Peter at Rome under Claudius, and on the deeds of Claudius; and on events that occurred during his reign
[Col. 1128C] Claudius Titus, the son of Drusus, the brother of Tiberius, and the uncle of Caligula, reigned for slightly fewer than fourteen years. At the beginning of his reign, Peter, the apostle of our Lord Jesus Christ, came to Rome. There he held the episcopal chair for twenty-five years, teaching all believers the saving faith in faithful speech and confirming it by the most powerful miracles. From that time many Christians began to be present in Rome.

Rome recognized this benefit of the faith. For when Caligula had been killed, and the Senate and consuls had resolved many measures for abolishing the imperial power, restoring the republic to its former order, and utterly destroying the entire family of the Caesars, Claudius, as soon as he had secured the empire, displayed a clemency previously unknown at Rome. So that vengeance might not rage against so great a multitude of nobles, he pardoned everyone for whatever evil the Senate or consuls had done or decreed should be done against him or his supporters. [Col. 1128D]

At the same time there occurred a great miracle of God’s present grace. F. Camillus Scribonianus, governor of Dalmatia, plotted civil war and had enticed many very brave legions to change their oath. Accordingly, when a day had been appointed for men to assemble from every direction around the new emperor, neither could the eagles be drawn up nor could the standards in any way be moved or carried away. The army, shaken by faith in so great and unprecedented a miracle and converted to repentance, immediately abandoned Scribonianus on the fifth day and killed him, while remaining bound by its former military oath.

It is sufficiently well known that nothing has ever been more grievous and destructive to the city of Rome than civil wars. Therefore, because of the arrival of the apostle Peter and the tender shoots of the Christian faith—still very few, yet already breaking forth into confession of the holy faith—this rising tyranny and the civil war that was emerging were restrained by divine action.

Accordingly, Claudius undertook an expedition against Britain, which seemed to have been thrown into revolt because it had not returned the fugitives. He crossed over to the island, which no one had dared to approach either before Julius Caesar or after him. There, to use the words of Suetonius Tranquillus, “without any battle or bloodshed, within a very few days he received a very large part of the island into surrender.” He also added to the Roman empire the Orkney Islands, situated in the Ocean beyond Britain, and returned to Rome in the sixth month after his departure. [Col. 1129B]

At the same time, during his reign, an exceedingly severe famine occurred throughout Syria and, in addition, throughout the whole world—a famine that our prophets had also foretold. But Helena, queen of the Adiabenians, who had been converted to faith in Christ, supplied abundant aid to the needs of the Christians at Jerusalem by transporting grain from Egypt.

Nevertheless, in the following year there was such a famine at Rome that, after the emperor had been seized by the people in the middle of the Forum and most disgracefully attacked with insults and pieces of bread, he barely escaped the fury of the aroused crowd by taking refuge in the palace through a postern gate. Shortly afterward he killed thirty-five senators and three hundred Roman knights simultaneously, for the most trivial reasons.

## CHAPTER XIV. [Col. 1129C] Of James, beheaded by Herod, and of the tortures inflicted upon that same Herod by an angel

At that time Herod, who was also called Agrippa, laid hands upon some members of the Church in order to afflict them, and killed James, the brother of John, with the sword.

Concerning this James, Clement of Alexandria also records in the seventh book of his *Outlines* a memorable account, handed down to him through the tradition of earlier generations:

> “Since even the man who had brought him before the judge for execution—James, that is—was himself moved and confessed that he was a Christian, both of them,” he says, “were led together to punishment. As they were being taken along the road, he asked James to forgive him. After a brief deliberation, James said, ‘Peace be with you,’ and kissed him. Thus both were beheaded together.” [Col. 1129D]

But then, as the divine Scripture says, when Herod saw that the killing of James pleased the Jews, he went further and also cast Peter into prison, undoubtedly intending to punish him, had divine assistance not intervened. An angel came to him by night, miraculously released him from the bonds of his chains, and ordered him to go free to the ministry of preaching.

Such were the events concerning Peter. But the king’s crime committed against the apostles did not await a delayed punishment; divine vengeance immediately appeared, as the history written in the *Acts of the Apostles* teaches us.

Josephus, however, says of him in the nineteenth book of the *Antiquities*:

> “When he happened to arrive at Caesarea—which had previously been called Strato’s Tower—he was presenting spectacles for the citizens in honor of Caesar. On what appeared to be the emperor’s appointed festival of well-being, when men of distinction from the whole province had assembled there with their wealth and honors, on the second day of the spectacles he came into the theater at daybreak, wearing a splendid garment wonderfully woven from gold and silver. When it received the first rays of the sun in the folds of its silvery fabric, the reflected brilliance poured forth a doubled light upon the spectators from the flashing metal, so that it dazzled the eyes of those looking at it. By this means the craftsman’s arrogance falsely represented something greater of him than belonged to human nature. [Col. 1130A]
>
> “At once the voices of the flattering crowd resounded, proclaiming honor but bringing destruction. From every side, from the tiers of seats, he was hailed as a god and entreated as a beneficent deity. The people said, ‘Until now we feared you as a human being; but from this moment we confess that you are above human nature.’
>
> “The king did not restrain the acclamation, though it violated divine law, nor did he recoil from the impiety of the unlawful flattery. Then, looking up shortly afterward, he saw an angel threatening and looming over his head, and immediately recognized him as the agent of his destruction—the very one whom he had previously known as the provider of his benefits. Suddenly agonizing torment seized him, accompanied by unbearable pain and swelling of the abdomen. Looking at his friends, he said: ‘Behold, I am that god of yours; behold, I am immediately driven away and expelled from life, since divine power has now exposed as false the voices recently directed toward me. I, whom you were just calling immortal, am already being hurried headlong to death.’ [Col. 1130B]
>
> “Thus, swarming with worms, he brought this life to its miserable end. He had reigned seven years—four under Gaius and three under Claudius—and left his son Agrippa as successor to the kingdom. Agrippa remained in it until the overthrow of Jerusalem and the destruction of the Temple.”

## CHAPTER XV. Of Theodas, the false prophet mentioned in the *Acts of the Apostles*, and of Claudius, enslaved to vices, and his death

At that same time Theodas appeared, claiming to be some kind of magician; he himself and all who followed him perished. Josephus gives a full account of this deceiver, explaining how, through his lies and false promises, he persuaded a multitude of people, after they had abandoned their possessions, to leave the cities and occupy the banks of the Jordan, and thereafter how he perished, along with all who followed him.

At the same time, while the apostle Paul was ministering the preaching of the Lord’s word from Jerusalem throughout the surrounding regions and as far as Illyricum, the emperor Claudius expelled the Jews from the city. Aquila and Prisca, expelled from the city with the other Jews, then came to Asia and joined the apostle there, laying the foundations of the Church in that region for the first time, as the book written concerning the *Acts of the Apostles* teaches.

While Claudius was still emperor, during the very festival of Passover, such disturbance and devastation befell the Jews at Jerusalem as a result of a revolt that had broken out that, of those alone who were killed at the Temple gates by the crush of the crowd, thirty thousand Jews were counted, and their festival day was turned into mourning.

Josephus also describes many other evils inflicted upon the Jews in these words. Afterward, having inserted certain intervening material, he added the following:

> “More grievously than all this devastation, however, a certain Egyptian false prophet afflicted the Jews. When this magician came to Judaea, he won confidence for himself as a prophet by magical art. Immediately gathering and leading about thirty thousand men through the desert, he came with them to the mountain called the Mount of Olives. From there he was prepared to burst into Jerusalem, seize the city by force and power, and subject the Roman garrison and the people alike to his tyranny, relying entirely upon the followers whom he had brought with him as his armed attendants. [Col. 1131A]
>
> “But Felix forestalled his attempt. He promptly went out to meet him with armed men, while the rest of the populace joined him in the undertaking. When battle had been engaged, he put the Egyptian to flight with a few companions; some of the others were killed and others captured, and he easily checked the rash enterprise.”

Josephus reports this in the second book of his *Histories*. It is nevertheless worthwhile to compare what he writes concerning the Egyptian with what is recorded in the *Acts of the Apostles*. There, the tribune who was in Jerusalem, speaking to Paul during the sedition that the Jews had stirred up against him, says under Felix:

> “Are you not the Egyptian who, some days ago, stirred up the people and led four thousand assassins out into the wilderness?”

That is sufficient concerning Felix.

Accordingly, when a census was conducted at Rome under Claudius, 6,944,000 Roman citizens were found. Water was brought into Rome, and it was called the Claudia.

This ruler, obedient to his belly, wine, and shameful lust, was subject to the commands of his freedmen and his wife. His wife was called Messalina. At first she openly consorted with adulterers; afterward, inflamed with even more atrocious desire, she determined to keep the most distinguished married women and virgins with her in the manner of prostitutes. Thus his freedmen acquired supreme power.

From among these men he appointed Felix commander of the legions in Judaea. Before him the apostle Paul was accused and delivered his defense.

Afterward Claudius took Agrippina, the daughter of his brother Germanicus, as his wife. While securing the empire for her son, she first killed her stepchildren through various intrigues and then destroyed her own husband with poison.

He lived for sixty-four years. His funeral, as had once happened with Tarquinius Priscus, was concealed for a long time, while guards corrupted by a woman’s cunning pretended that he was ill. [Col. 1131D]

## CHAPTER XVI. Of Nero’s most criminal deeds, and of the killing of Seneca, his teacher, and of the poet Lucan

Nero, his stepson, assumed the rights of empire and remained in power for not quite fourteen years. A follower—and indeed a transgressor—of his uncle Gaius Caligula in every vice and crime, he practiced wantonness, lust, luxury, greed, and credulity, and polluted himself with every crime.

Driven by wantonness, he visited nearly all the theaters of Italy and Greece. He even adopted the disgrace of varied costumes and often imagined that he had surpassed actors, lyre players, tragedians, and charioteers.

He was so agitated by lusts [Col. 1132A] that he is said not to have abstained even from his mother, sister, or any respect owed to blood relationship. He took a man as his wife and was himself received by the man as a wife.

His luxury was so unrestrained that he fished with golden nets drawn out by purple cords and bathed in cold and hot perfumes. It is also reported that he never traveled with fewer than a thousand carriages.

Finally, he made the burning of the city of Rome a spectacle for his pleasure. For six days and seven nights the blazing city fed the eyes of royalty. The granaries built of squared stone, and those great ancient structures which the spreading flame could not reach, were undermined and set alight with great machines once prepared for foreign wars.

The wretched populace was driven into the tombs and burial chambers, while he himself gazed from that lofty tower of Maecenas, rejoicing—as he said—in the beauty of the flames and singing the *Iliad* in tragic costume. [Col. 1132B]

His greed was so headlong that after this burning of the City—which Augustus had boasted of transforming from brick into marble—he permitted no one to approach the remains of his property. Everything that had survived the flames in any way he himself seized.

He ordered 100 million sesterces annually to be paid to him for the expenses of the Senate. He deprived very many senators of their property without any cause being apparent. In a single day, even employing torture, he stripped all merchants completely of their entire assessed wealth.

This Nero was the first to persecute the Christians; he also killed the apostles Peter and Paul.

Driven by such a frenzy of cruelty [Col. 1132C] that he killed most of the Senate and nearly annihilated the equestrian order, he did not even abstain from parricide. Without hesitation he struck down his mother, brother, sister, wife, and all his other relatives and kinsmen.

He also killed Seneca, his instructor in the liberal disciplines and his guide, because Seneca sought to advise him concerning the welfare of the state and the uprightness of life. Seneca was a nobleman and a friend of the apostle Paul.

Likewise he killed the poet Lucan, Seneca’s maternal uncle. Seneca of Cordoba had lived a life of the strictest self-control. As stated above, the letters commonly read as those of Paul to Seneca and Seneca to Paul declare him to have been Paul’s friend. In them, although he was Nero’s teacher and the most powerful man of that time, he says that he wished to hold among his own people the position Paul held among the Christians. [Col. 1132D]

Nero killed him two years before Peter and Paul were crowned with martyrdom.

## CHAPTER XVII. Of Paul’s release and his second preaching before he was crowned with martyrdom under Nero

Meanwhile, while Nero was emperor, Festus was sent to Judaea to succeed Felix. Before him, as we read in the *Acts of the Apostles*, Paul pleaded his case and, by the governor’s decree, was sent in chains to Rome.

There he spent two years preaching the word of God, with no one forbidding him. After he had made his defense before Nero, he was released from custody. Then he set out again for the ministry of preaching, confirmed by the authority of the ancients. [Col. 1133A]

This apostle Paul, previously called Saul, was from the tribe of Benjamin and the town of Giscala in Judaea, and was outside the number of the twelve apostles. When the Romans captured Giscala, he migrated with his parents to Tarsus in Cilicia. Because of his devotion to the Law, they sent him to Jerusalem, where he was instructed by Gamaliel, a very learned man whom Luke mentions.

When he had witnessed the death of the martyr Stephen and, having received letters from the chief priest of the Temple, was traveling to Damascus to persecute those who believed in Christ, he was compelled by the revelation recorded in the *Acts of the Apostles* to embrace the faith and was changed from a persecutor into a chosen vessel.

When Sergius Paulus, proconsul of Cyprus, first believed through his preaching, Paul received this name from him, because he had brought Sergius under the faith of Christ. Taking Barnabas as his companion, he traveled through many cities and returned to Jerusalem, where Peter, James, and John appointed him apostle to the Gentiles.

Since his conduct is described at great length in the *Acts of the Apostles*, I shall say only this: in the twenty-fifth year after the Lord’s Passion, during Nero’s first year, when Festus succeeded Felix as governor of Judaea, Paul was sent in chains to Rome. Remaining for two years in unrestricted custody, he disputed daily with the Jews concerning the coming of Christ.

It should be understood that during his first defense, before Nero’s imperial power had become firmly established and before he had erupted into the crimes that histories recount about him, Paul was released by Nero so that the Gospel of Christ might also be preached in the regions of the West. Paul himself writes this in the Second Epistle to Timothy, composed at the time when he had also suffered and was writing from his chains:

> “At my first defense no one stood by me, but everyone deserted me; may it not be charged against them. But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me, so that through me the preaching might be fulfilled and all the Gentiles might hear; and I was delivered from the mouth of the lion.”

By “the lion” he most clearly signifies Nero, on account of his cruelty. [Col. 1133C]

And later:

> “I was delivered from the mouth of the lion.”

Immediately afterward:

> “The Lord delivered me from every evil work and saved me for his heavenly kingdom.”

He says this because he knew that martyrdom was already threatening him. For in the same Epistle he had stated earlier:

> “I am already being poured out, and the time of my release is at hand.”

Thus, in Nero’s fourteenth year, on the same day as Peter, Paul was beheaded at Rome for Christ. He was buried on the Ostian Way, in the thirty-seventh year after the Lord’s Passion. [Col. 1133D]

## CHAPTER XVIII. Of the death of James the Just, bishop of the apostles, and what the histories report concerning him

Under Nero, James, who had been appointed bishop of Jerusalem by the apostles, was also brought to completion through martyrdom. He was called the brother of the Lord because he was the son of the sister of Mary, the mother of the Lord, although some thought that Joseph had fathered him by another wife.

The very reliable historian Hegesippus, who lived immediately after the first successions of the apostles, reports the following about him in the fifth book of his *Commentaries*:

> “The Church was received together with the apostles by James, the brother of the Lord, who was surnamed the Just by everyone. He had continued from the Lord’s own time until our day. Many men were called James, but this man was holy from his mother’s womb. He drank neither wine nor strong drink, ate no animal food, and no iron came upon his head. He was anointed with oil and did not use baths. To him alone it was permitted to enter the Holy of Holies. He did not wear woolen clothing but only linen. He alone entered the Temple and lay upon his knees, praying for the people’s forgiveness, so that through praying he developed calluses on his knees like a camel, constantly bending his knees and never ceasing from prayer. Therefore, because of this incredible self-restraint and supreme justice, he was called the Just.” [Col. 1134B]

When a very great multitude of both Jews and Gentiles everywhere believed in Jesus, the scribes and Pharisees, moved and disturbed by envy, said to one another:

> “We accomplish nothing. Behold, the whole world believes in Jesus.”

They then took counsel and approached James, the brother of the Lord, saying:

> “We beseech you, therefore, to persuade all those who assemble on the day of Passover concerning Jesus. For we all obey you, and both we and the people bear witness concerning you that you are just and show partiality to no one. You, therefore, persuade the people concerning Jesus, so that they may not go astray, because we all obey you. Ascend, then, to the highest point of the Temple’s pinnacle, so that, standing on high, you may be visible to everyone and your words may be heard by all.”

Since crowds assembled during the days of Passover—not only of Jews but also of Gentiles—the scribes and Pharisees mentioned above set him upon the pinnacle of the Temple. Then, shouting loudly, they said to him:

> “Most righteous man, whom we must all obey, since the people are going astray after Jesus who was crucified, tell us what the door of Jesus is.”

Then James answered them in a very loud voice:

> “Why do you question me concerning the Son of Man? Behold, he himself sits in heaven at the right hand of the Supreme Power, and he himself will come upon the clouds of heaven.”

When many had been satisfied by James’s reply and testimony, and had gladly listened to what James had proclaimed, they began to glorify God and say:

> “Hosanna to the Son of David.”

Then the scribes, Pharisees, and priests became indignant and, turning to fury, threw him from the pinnacle of the Temple and killed him by stoning while he prayed for them. [Col. 1134D]

Josephus also relates this about him in Book XX of the *Antiquities*. Clement, in Book VII, says that after the death of Festus, who governed Judaea, Nero sent Albinus as his successor. Before Albinus had reached the province, Annianus, he says, the high priest, a young man and the son of Annas, of priestly descent, seized the opportunity and convened the council. He publicly compelled James to deny that Christ was the Son of God, and when James contradicted him, ordered him to be stoned.

Thrown from the pinnacle of the Temple, James drew up his legs. Still half alive, he raised his hands toward heaven and said:

> “Lord, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.”

Then he was struck on the head with a fuller’s club, the implement used for beating out clothing, and died.

The same Josephus records that James possessed such holiness and standing among the people [Col. 1135A] that it was believed that Jerusalem had been overthrown because of his death.

He is the one concerning whom the apostle Paul writes to the Galatians:

> “I saw none of the other apostles except James, the brother of the Lord.”

The *Acts of the Apostles* also frequently bears witness to this.

Jerome reports the following concerning him:

> “The Gospel that is called according to the Hebrews—which was recently translated into Greek and Latin, although Origen often bears witness to it and uses it—contains the following account after the Savior’s resurrection:
>
> “‘The Lord, after he had given the linen cloth to the servant of the priest, went to James and appeared to him. For James had sworn that he would not eat bread from that hour in which he had drunk the Lord’s cup until he saw him risen from the dead.’
>
> “Again, shortly afterward:
>
> “‘Bring a table,’ says the Lord.
>
> “Immediately it adds:
>
> “‘He took bread, blessed it, broke it, gave it to James the Just, and said to him: “My brother, eat your bread, for the Son of Man has risen from the dead.”’” [Col. 1135B]

For thirty years, therefore, he governed the Church at Jerusalem—that is, until the seventh year of Nero. Near the Temple, where he had been thrown down, his tomb remained famous until the siege of Titus and the final phase of Hadrian’s reign.

## CHAPTER XIX. Of Jude, the brother of James

Jude, the brother of James, preached the Gospel in Mesopotamia and the inland regions of Pontus. Through his holy teaching he tamed savage and untamed peoples, whose natures were like those of beasts, and subjected them to the Lord’s faith. He was buried in the Armenian city of Nerito.

He left a short Epistle, one of the seven catholic Epistles. [Col. 1135C]

## CHAPTER XX. Of Simon Peter, how he fought against the magician Simon, and of Nero’s most criminal death

Simon Peter, son of John, from the Galilean province and the village of Bethsaida, brother of the apostle Andrew and chief of the apostles, preached the Gospel in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, Bithynia, and Italy, after his episcopate over the Church of Antioch and his preaching to those of the circumcision who had believed.

He shone forth through the following miracles: with uncertain, wavering steps he walked upon the boiling sea; by passing along, he restored the dead to life through his shadow; he restored to the lame their former use of their limbs; and he returned the weakened limbs of the paralytic to their proper condition.

Among these deeds he raised a dead widow, condemned Ananias and Sapphira to death for their crime of faithlessness, and struck Simon down to the earth when he was ascending into heaven by magical arts.

It is pleasing to discuss at greater length something concerning Peter, the chief of the apostles.

Meanwhile, as faith in our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ increased throughout the minds of all and the growth of religion spread day by day, the enemy of human salvation did not remain at rest. Instead, he went ahead to the greatest city, which is the capital of all things, and summoned that Simon of whom we spoke earlier. Supplying greater assistance to his wicked arts, he cast many citizens of that city into the bonds of his error.

Justin, a distinguished writer who arose not long after the time of the apostles, reports the following about him in the *Apology* that he wrote to the emperor Antoninus on behalf of our faith:

> “After the Lord’s ascension into heaven,” he says, “the demons incited certain men to say that they were gods; we drove them away. Finally, a certain Samaritan named Simon, from a village called Gitta, was raised up under Caesar Claudius by magical arts and the aid of demons. In your city, which is the capital of every kingdom, he deceived very many through apparitions and was declared a god by the Senate. A statue was set up for him among you with the honor of a god, in the river Tiber between the two bridges, bearing an inscription in Latin letters: *Simoni deo sancto*—‘To Simon, the holy god.’ Nearly all the Samaritans, and some people of other nations as well, worship and confess him as the supreme god. [Col. 1136B]
>
> “They also consecrated with him a certain prostitute named Selene, his companion in error and deception. She had previously worked in a brothel at Tyre, a city of Phoenicia, and they consecrated her as a kind of First Mind (*Nous*).”

This is what Justin says.

Irenaeus writes similarly in the first book of *Against Heresies*. In it he gives a fuller account of who Simon himself was, how impure his works and teaching were, and how he deceived and seduced people through various tricks and diabolical frauds. It would take too long to insert these matters here, since anyone who wishes may learn each detail from the books of the aforementioned Irenaeus, concerning Simon and the other authors of various heresies and their poisonous doctrines.

We therefore understand that the head of all depravity and the beginning of every heresy originated with Simon. At that time the devil raised up this father and author of such evils, Simon, from among his attendants, and compelled him to go to Rome, the greatest city, so that he might resist there the most powerful athletes of the Lord and our Savior Jesus Christ—the apostles whom God had appointed for this very purpose.

But divine power and grace never abandon their own in the greatest and most important contest. With complete speed it extinguishes the flame kindled by the wicked one and destroys every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God.

Therefore neither Simon nor anyone else who then engaged the Lord’s apostles could obtain victory, because the light of truth and the brightness of the divine word, which had recently shone forth for the salvation of humanity, drove the darkness of ignorance from human minds through the apostles, dispersing all the gloom of falsehood. [Col. 1136D]

Finally, the magician, struck by the brilliance of the true light, immediately fell into the blindness of an unsound mind. For after the apostle Peter had already refuted him in Judaea concerning the crimes he was committing, he attempted an overseas flight and proceeded from East to West, hoping nowhere to preserve his life except through the aid of flight.

He entered Rome and, using the assistance of Selene, the prostitute who accompanied and clung to him, advanced to such a degree of wickedness that the Roman citizens even honored him as a god with a statue.

But divinity acquired through fraud does not last long. Immediately, during the very time of Claudius, divine providence’s mercy brought to Rome Peter, the most proven of all men and the greatest of the apostles, distinguished by the magnificence of his faith and the merit of his virtue. He came like a commander and teacher of God’s army, one who knew how to wage divine battles and lead the camps of virtue, to resist the common destruction of the human race.

Arriving from the regions of the East like a heavenly merchant, he brought a supply of divine light for anyone prepared to purchase it. He was the first in the city of Rome to open, through the saving words of his preaching, the gate of the heavenly kingdom with the keys of the Gospel.

When the bright light of God’s word had dawned upon the city of Rome, Simon’s darkness was extinguished together with its author. The word of truth and light preached by Peter peacefully illuminated the minds of all who heard it, so that those who listened were never satisfied by hearing him only once.

Therefore hearing alone was not enough for them. They earnestly begged Mark, his disciple, to commit to writing what Peter preached orally, so that they might possess it as a permanent reminder and remain at home and abroad in meditation upon such teaching. They did not cease their entreaties until they obtained what they had requested.

This was the reason for writing what is called the Gospel according to Mark. When Peter discovered through the Holy Spirit that he had been deprived by a religious theft of what belonged to him, he rejoiced as he considered their faith and devotion, approved the deed, and entrusted the written work to the churches to be read forever. [Col. 1137C]

After Peter had founded the Church of Antioch under Caesar Claudius, he went to Rome against that same magician Simon. There he preached the Gospel and held the bishopric of that city for twenty-five years.

In the thirty-sixth year after the Lord’s Passion, he was crucified upside down in Rome by Caesar Nero, as he himself wished. He wrote two Epistles, which are called catholic, and also the Gospel according to Mark, as we have said, since Mark was Peter’s hearer and interpreter.

The books of which one is entitled *The Acts of Peter*, another *The Gospel*, a third *The Preaching*, a fourth *The Apocalypse*, and a fifth *The Judgment* are reckoned among the apocryphal writings.

After his remarkable deeds and teachings, accomplished through signs and virtues, and after the triumphs by which he repeatedly defeated Simon when, at the devil’s instigation, Simon renewed his contests and attempted to rise again, the most criminal of all men—Nero—then sought the deaths of the apostles themselves, who were leaders and standard-bearers among God’s people, so as to show openly that he was an enemy of divinity and piety.

He condemned Paul to be beheaded in the city itself and Peter to the punishment of crucifixion. Yet he soon experienced the sentence of divine vengeance against himself.

While he was devising other unbelievable crimes aimed at disturbing—or rather destroying—the state, he was declared an enemy by the Senate. Fleeing in the most disgraceful manner, he killed himself at the fourth milestone from the city, and with him the entire family of the Caesars was destroyed.

## CHAPTER XXI. [Col. 1138A] Of the tyrants who arose after Nero’s most disgraceful death and were quickly extinguished, up to the reign of Vespasian

Galba, who had been proclaimed emperor by the army in Spain, came to Rome upon hearing of Nero’s death and usurped the imperial power.

Since he offended everyone through greed, cruelty, and sluggishness, he adopted Piso, a noble and energetic young man, as his son and successor to the kingdom. Before assuming supreme power, Piso had governed many provinces admirably and had treated the soldiers with the utmost severity, so that, as soon as he entered the camp, the saying immediately spread:

> “Learn to be a soldier, soldier; Galba is here.”

He reigned for seven months and as many days, and was killed by Otho’s faction.

Otho, after Galba and Piso had been killed at Rome, seized the empire amid tumult and slaughter. Soon discovering that Vitellius had been proclaimed emperor in Gaul by the German legions, he plotted civil war. He first engaged the Vitellian commanders in three minor battles and emerged victorious; but in the fourth battle, near Bedriacum, when he saw that his men were being defeated, he killed himself in the third month after beginning his reign. [Col. 1138B]

Vitellius, victorious, came to Rome. There he committed many cruel and wicked acts and burdened human life with disgrace through an incredible appetite for gluttony.

When he learned of Vespasian, he first attempted to lay down the empire. Then, encouraged by certain men, he drove Sabinus, Vespasian’s brother, who suspected no evil at the time, into the Capitol with the other Flavians. After the Temple had been set on fire, and flames and ruin had been mingled together, he consigned them all alike to one death and tomb. [Col. 1138C]

When his own army subsequently deserted him for Vespasian’s cause, and the enemy was already approaching, he was terrified and withdrew into a small chamber near the palace. Dragged out of it in the most disgraceful manner, he was led naked along the Sacred Way, while people everywhere threw filth into his mouth. Taken to the Forum, in the eighth month after he had seized the throne, he was flayed alive at the Gemonian Steps by repeated punctures and innumerable tiny blows. From there he was dragged with a hook and thrown into the Tiber, and was denied even an ordinary burial.

For many days Vespasian’s soldiers raged against the Senate and the Roman people, slaughtering indiscriminately in many criminal and abominable ways.

Thus, after that brief but turbulent season of tyrants had been dispersed, a peaceful serenity returned under the leadership of Vespasian. At that time he was on the eve of the war he had directed against the Jews, having been sent by the emperor Nero. The army with which he was besieging Judaea appointed him emperor. He immediately hastened toward Rome and entrusted his son Titus with the conduct of the war and the siege of Jerusalem.

## CHAPTER XXII. Of unheard-of deaths among other peoples and of the assaults of brigands during the siege of Jerusalem
Verum post ascensionem Domini Salvatoris nostri, because of the sacrilege committed by the Jews against him, the persecution of the apostles, the killing of Stephen, [Col. 1139A] and also the beheading of the apostle James, as well as the crime committed against James, likewise the brother of the Lord, who is called Justus, and against all the others whom they had ensnared because of their faith in Christ by ambushes, deceit, and every kind of wicked fraud—for all these evils, I say, punishment was being exacted from them by divine judgment.

The apostles, indeed, after first being driven away by them and scattered throughout every place, as we said above, continued in the power of Christ, who had commanded them, saying: “Go and baptize all in my name.” But the Church that had been gathered in Jerusalem, having received a response from God, was ordered to emigrate and cross over to a certain town called Pella, beyond the Jordan. Thus, once the holy and righteous men had been removed from the city, a place would be left for heavenly vengeance, both upon the sacrilegious city and upon the [Col. 1139B] impious people, through the destruction and overthrow of their homeland.

How great, then, were the evils with which the whole nation was punished; how the land of Judaea itself was devastated by war, famine, fire, and slaughter; how many thousands of people—fathers together with their wives and countless children—were massacred without number or distinction; what sieges were laid against the various cities, and also against Jerusalem itself, that magnificent and most famous city; what devastation there was, and how great the slaughter by various forms of death; what the course of the wars was in each case; how, in accordance with what the prophets had foretold, “the abomination of desolation” was placed in that once most famous temple of God; and how at last fire ravaged everything and flame consumed it—whoever wishes to know these things more fully should read the Histories of Josephus.

We, however, [Col. 1139C] shall take from them only what suffices for the explanation of the work we have undertaken. In them he reports that people from all Judaea had gathered in Jerusalem on the solemn day of Passover, as though compelled by some fatal hand. He says that there were three million persons. It was plainly by a just judgment of God that this time was chosen for vengeance, so that the whole multitude, which during the days of Passover had violated its Savior and the saving Christ the Lord with bloodstained hands and sacrilegious cries, might during those same days, as though shut up in a single prison, receive the destruction of the dreadful punishment it deserved.

I shall pass over the task of describing what was inflicted upon them by the slaughter of the sword and by the other engines of war. I shall set forth only what the aforesaid historian reports that they endured in the destruction brought by terrible famine, so that those who read these things [Col. 1139D] may understand how great a sacrilege it is to dare anything against Christ, and by how severe punishments such daring is expiated.

Let the fifth book of Josephus’s Histories, therefore, be placed before us, from which their entire sorrowful tragedy may be thoroughly learned. “For the rich,” he says, “to remain or to perish was one and the same thing. If they remained in the city, they were killed because of their property, on the charge that they were planning to desert. The necessity of famine, however, made the possessors of wealth insolent, and on both sides hunger and recklessness increased together.

“There was nowhere any grain available publicly; but the brigands who rushed through the city searched the houses. If they found anything, [Col. 1140A] they inflicted punishment as though upon people who had deceived them; if they found nothing, they tortured them all the same, as though they had hidden it more secretly and carefully. They regarded the appearance of bodily nourishment as evidence against them: since the people still seemed to be alive and their bodies still endured, they assumed that they would certainly already have died unless they were concealing food somewhere. If they saw anyone wasting away from emaciation, they passed him by with permission to live, considering it pointless to kill those whom famine would soon consume.

“Many nevertheless, in hiding, purchased for all their possessions one *metretes*—if they were rich, of wheat; if they were poorer, of barley—and, shutting themselves in the innermost recesses of their houses, some did not even eat the grain after it had been made into bread. Others, as necessity or fear allowed, cooked it. No one sought to have a table set, but snatching the food from the half-burned fire, they devoured it as though it were stolen.

“It was a pitiable spectacle of their own misery when the stronger seized whatever had been found, while nothing remained for the weaker except grief and tears. For although famine surpasses all the bitterness of human circumstances, nothing so overturns and destroys modesty as famine. Whatever, when conditions are safe, is worthy of shame is despised in this necessity. Finally, wives snatched food from the hands of their husbands, children from those of their parents, and—most grievous of all—mothers snatched food from the hands and mouths of their little children.

“And while their sweetest children were wasting away in their hands and before their eyes, no one spared them the effort of tearing the small supports of life from their very teeth. Yet these unhappy people did not even conceal the tiny morsels they took. A brigand was always at hand, and as soon as he saw someone’s doors closed, he considered this evidence that the people inside were eating. Suddenly breaking down the doors, they rushed in headlong and, squeezing the food from their very throats, so to speak, forced back whatever had already been swallowed.

“Old men were beaten if they attempted to defend their food; women were dragged by their scattered hair when they tried to conceal anything that had been discovered in their hands. No respect was shown to the old for their white hair, no pity to children. When the little ones clung to a small fragment of bread, the brigands lifted them from the very object to which they clung and dashed them to the ground.

“Against anyone who had forestalled the robbers by consuming the food, they raged more cruelly and devised terrible punishments: they blocked the unfortunate victims’ natural outlets of digestion, while against others they drove sharpened stakes through the same shameful parts. I shudder to recount what was done. By such means they forced the wretched to confess to a single loaf or a *cyathus* of flour. For the torturers themselves did not suffer hunger. It would in some way have been more tolerable if they had seemed compelled to do these things by starvation; but they acted either to prepare food for themselves for the future or so that cruelty might grow strong through practice.

“Among these people, if anyone had slipped out secretly through the enemy posts to gather herbs, those who encountered them as they rejoiced that they had escaped the enemy’s hands seized whatever they had brought back. When the victims begged and invoked the once-terrible name of God, asking them to grant at least some portion of what they had sought at the risk of death, they gave them absolutely nothing. It was counted as a kindness if the person who had been captured was allowed to escape alive.

“After some further remarks he adds the following: ‘For the Jews every hope of safety through leaving the city was likewise cut off. As the cruelty of famine grew stronger, it devastated houses, families, and the nation at once, so that in the inner chambers the corpses of women and children lay stretched out, while through the streets lay the bodies of unhappy old men, consumed more by hunger than by age.

“‘Young men and everyone of stronger age wandered about in the roads and at the exits like phantoms, falling wherever starvation caused their steps to fail. Neither the multitude of the dead nor the weakness of their strength allowed them to bury the corpses of their relatives, while each person was at the same time uncertain of his own life. Finally, some gave up their lives above those whom they were burying.
