“‘Many also, while escorting funerals, expired before they reached the tomb. Nor was the customary lamentation or mourning offered to the dead, because famine had claimed all these things for itself. The dryness of starvation had left no one moisture for tears. Deep silences had besieged the city, and a night full of death covered everything.

“‘The brigands alone flourished more grievously than all these evils. They did not consider it unlawful even to strip the unburied corpses, seeking not so much plunder as to heap crime upon mockery, and testing the sharpness of their swords by cutting up corpses. At times the blade was even applied to some who were still breathing, to test its edge.

“‘When others, half-dead, saw this, they stretched out supplicating hands, asking that the crime might be turned into a favor toward them also, so that they might be released more quickly from the tortures of famine. But in a new form of cruelty, they refused, when asked, to inflict the death they themselves willingly dealt out. Yet each of the dying, while turning his eyes toward the Temple with a groan, grieved not over his own death but over the impunity of the brigands whom they were leaving alive.

“‘At first the intolerable stench had led him to order the dead to be buried at public expense. But when the multitude of those dying began to exceed every expense, they threw the corpses down from the wall.’”

[Col. 1141D] But when Titus, making the rounds, had seen the ditches filled with the corpses of the dead and the native land drenched with the decay of human bodies, he raised his hands to heaven with a great groan and called God to witness that this was not his doing.

A little later he continues with something of the following kind:

“I shall not hesitate,” he says, “to state what I think. For I believe that even if the Romans had for a short time ceased their arms against the impious citizens, the city would have paid the penalty either by the opening of the earth, or by a flood of water, or by Sodomite fires and lightning hurled from heaven. It had produced a present generation much more unfortunate than those who endured these things, and more wicked than they. For their sake the whole nation would deserve to be utterly destroyed.”

But in Book VI he writes the following about the same people:

“Of those who were being destroyed by the famine throughout the city there was an innumerable multitude, whose misery cannot be described. In every house, if any food happened to be found, wars and murders immediately arose among relatives and parents and children dear to one another, while they struggled to snatch food from one another not only from their hands but even from their very throats.

“Trust was not granted even to the dead. The brigands searched even those who were already breathing out their spirit, lest some morsel of food might remain hidden in their bosom. Others, gasping from starvation like rabid dogs, were driven here and there and, as though impelled by a kind of madness, rushed into the same houses again and again within a moment.

“Necessity turned everything into food, even those things which custom has not allowed dumb animals themselves to eat. At last they did not abstain even from leather straps, belts, or their very shoes. Tearing away the coverings of doors, they put them into their mouths to be ground by their teeth. Some ate even strands of old hay. They sold the smallest weight of refuse collected from every source for four drachmas.

“But why should I explain the magnitude of that famine through these details, when a deed was committed there such as no one has ever heard of among Greeks or barbarians—a deed dreadful to speak of and incredible to hear? I would indeed have kept silent about that monstrous crime, lest anyone think that I was telling tales of the impossible, had I not had many men of our own memory as witnesses to the crime committed. Moreover, I do not think I would be doing anything worthy for my homeland if I withheld the words describing the evils whose deeds it endured.”

## CHAPTER XXIII. Concerning Mary, who ate her own son and thereby forced the confused brigands to depart

A certain woman from those who lived beyond the channel of the Jordan, named Mary, daughter of Eleazar, from the village of Beth-Ezob—which is interpreted as “house of hyssop”—noble in birth and wealth, was found among the rest of the multitude that had flowed together into Jerusalem and was enduring with everyone else the common disaster of the siege.

The tyrants seized the remainder of her possessions, which she had brought from home into the city. If anything remained from the great wealth by which she had maintained her daily sustenance, however scanty, the brigands’ attendants rushed in from time to time and snatched it away. The loss of these things tormented the woman with an immense indignation that had almost become madness, so that at times she provoked the brigands to kill her with curses and insults.

But since no one, whether angered or moved to pity, killed her, and if she had sought any food, it was sought by others as well, with no opportunity now remaining to find anything anywhere, while terrible famine pressed upon her very entrails and marrow, and starvation and anger, those worst advisers, drove her toward madness, she now armed herself against the laws of nature.

For she had a little son at her breast. Holding him before her eyes, she said:

“Unhappy mother—O still more unhappy son! In war, famine, and the plundering of brigands, for whom shall I preserve you? For even if life could be hoped for, we are oppressed by the yoke of Roman servitude. But now famine has itself forestalled servitude, while the brigands will press upon us with a double force. Come, then, my son; become food for your mother, madness for the brigands, and a tale for future generations—the one thing still lacking from the disasters of the Jews.”

When she had said this, she immediately killed her son. Then she placed him over a fire and roasted him. She consumed half, but kept the other half covered.

And behold, the brigands suddenly rushed in, drawn by the smell of the roasted flesh. They threatened her with death unless she immediately showed them the food they sensed had been prepared.

Then she said: “I have reserved the finest portion for you.”

At once she uncovered the remaining limbs of the infant. Suddenly an immense horror seized them; though their savage hearts were hardened, they froze, and their voice was blocked in their throats.

But she, with a grim expression, more savage now than the brigands themselves, said:

“This is my son; he is my offspring, and the deed is mine. Eat. For I have already eaten the child whom I bore. Do not prove yourselves more religious than a mother or more tender than a woman. But if pity conquers you and you abominate my food, I—who have already fed upon such things—shall feed upon them again.”

After this, terrified and trembling, they departed, having left this single food among all her possessions to the wretched mother.

At once the whole city was filled with the report of the unspeakable crime, and each person, bringing before his eyes the deed that had been committed, shuddered as though he himself had committed it. [Col. 1143C] All those whom the necessity of famine pressed hurried more eagerly toward death, calling blessed those to whom it had fallen to die before they were polluted by hearing of such evils.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the final destruction of Jerusalem and the number of those killed according to Josephus’s reckoning

Thus far Josephus.

The historian mentioned above, adding up the total number of those killed either by famine or by the sword, reported it as eleven hundred thousand. He states that the remaining robbers, assassins, and brigands died from wounds inflicted upon one another after the city’s destruction.

He says that the most distinguished young men, whose beauty and stature commended them, were preserved for the triumph; but the rest, who were over seventeen years of age, were bound and sent to labor in the mines of Egypt, or were scattered through the other provinces. Some were delivered to gladiatorial games, others to wild beasts.

Those who were found between the seventh and tenth years of age were ordered to be dispersed into slavery throughout the various provinces. Their number reached ninety thousand.

All these things took place in the second year of Vespasian’s reign, in accordance with what the Lord and our Savior Jesus Christ had foretold. For he already saw the things that were to happen when, according to the testimony of the Gospels, he saw the city and wept over it, and, as though speaking beforehand in its hearing, said these words:

“If you too had known on this day—for days will come upon you when your enemies will surround you with a rampart; they will surround you, press upon you from every side, bring you down to the ground, and kill your children.”

And again, speaking as though about the people, he said:

“There will be great distress upon the earth and wrath against this people. They will fall by the edge of the sword and will be led captive into all nations, and Jerusalem will be trampled by the nations until the times of the nations are fulfilled.”

And again:

“When you see Jerusalem surrounded by an army, then know that its desolation is near.”

Let everyone now compare the words of our Lord and Savior with the historian’s account of the war that was waged and of the city’s destruction. Seeing the wondrous power of the divine presence, let him acknowledge the divinity of the one who foretold it.

These things came upon the Jewish nation after the Savior’s Passion as a just vengeance, because the whole nation cried out that the author of life should be taken away from them.

Thus, counting from the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar and from the beginning of the preaching of the Gospel, there were forty-two years until the second year of Vespasian’s reign, when this destruction of the city of Jerusalem was accomplished.

From the captivity that they suffered under Antiochus there were 238 years. From the second year of Darius, under whom the Temple was rebuilt, there were 590 years. From the first building of the Temple under Solomon until its final destruction under Vespasian there were 1,102 years.

Here I have decided to bring the first book of the work begun to an end. There the legal sacrifices fell irrecoverably together with the Temple and the most wicked Jewish people.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 1143]

## CHAPTER I. Preface to the preceding book

In the preceding book, therefore, I undertook, in concise discourse drawn from the books of various authors, to gather together events from the birth of Christ through his Passion, and then through the destruction of the Temple of Jerusalem and the dispersion and destruction by various deaths of the Jewish people through God’s just vengeance for the Passion of Christ, God and man, and for the persecutions and killings of his servants—both the deeds of the emperors and the actions of ecclesiastical men.

## CHAPTER II. On the good deeds of Vespasian

Vespasian, then, as we stated earlier, learned of Nero’s death and, at the urging of many kings and commanders—especially Josephus, the leader of the Jews, who, when captured [Col. 1145A] and being thrown into chains, had declared with complete confidence that he would soon be released by that same emperor—and gained the imperial power.

Leaving his son Titus to conduct the siege of Jerusalem, he traveled through Alexandria toward Rome. But when he learned of Vitellius’s death, he remained for a short time at Alexandria.

Titus, meanwhile, pressing the Jews with a great and prolonged siege, with engines and every kind of military apparatus, and not without much bloodshed among his own men, at last captured the city, leveled the walls of Jerusalem to the ground, and destroyed the Temple, the most famous throughout the whole world.

The emperors Vespasian and Titus, therefore, celebrating a magnificent triumph over the Jews, entered the city. Among the 320 triumphs that had been celebrated from the founding of the city up to that time, this was a beautiful and previously unknown spectacle to all mortals: father and son carried in a single triumphal chariot, bringing back the most glorious victory over those who had offended the Father and the Son.

Having immediately suppressed all wars and disturbances at home and abroad, he proclaimed peace throughout the whole world, and at last, the sixth time since the founding of the City, they decreed that the twin temple of Janus should be kept closed with its gates shut.

For rightly the same honor of vengeance was paid to the Lord’s Passion as had been attributed to his birth.

After this, without any disturbance of war, the Roman state advanced to immense greatness. For Achaea, Lycia, Rhodes, Byzantium, Samothrace, Cilicia, and Commagene, then first reduced to provinces, obeyed Roman judges and laws.

In the ninth year of his reign, three cities in Cyprus collapsed in an earthquake, and there was a great pestilence at Rome.

Vespasian died in the ninth year of his principate, at his own villa near the Sabines, from a flux of the bowels.

Among his other good qualities, he possessed this singular one: he could forget enmities. Thus he gave the daughter of Vitellius, his enemy, a very rich dowry and joined her to a distinguished husband.

He restored the world, long drained of blood and exhausted, in a short time. First, he preferred to bend the satellites of tyranny—unless some had gone much further in cruelty—rather than destroy them after torturing them, wisely judging that wicked services were maintained by many through fear.

He repaired Rome, disfigured by fires and abandoned to ancient ruins: the Capitol, the Temple of Peace, and the monuments of Claudius, where owners willing to rebuild lacked the means to do so. He also established many new works throughout all the lands subject to Roman law.

Cities were renewed with splendid adornment, and the roads were strengthened by immense works. At that time mountains were cut through along the Flaminian Way for easier passage; this is commonly called the “pierced rock.”

He brought a thousand nations into order, although he had found only two hundred with the greatest difficulty. After most had been extinguished by the savagery of tyrants, Vologases, king of the Parthians, was compelled by fear alone to make peace.

The desire to say more compelled me to speak of a good emperor whom the Roman state, drained by the savagery of tyrants after the death of Augustus for fifty-six years, obtained lest it should collapse altogether.

And so, while he was being pressed more heavily by the evacuation of his bowels, he rose and said: “An emperor ought to depart from this world standing.”

## CHAPTER III. On the magnificent works of the emperor Titus

Titus, son of Vespasian, assumed the rights of imperial power after his father’s death. Born to a freedwoman named Domitilla, he ruled for two years and two months.

He was highly skilled in both languages and educated in the liberal disciplines through a passion for reading. When he assumed responsibility for his country, it is incredible how greatly he surpassed the father whom he imitated, especially in clemency, generosity, magnificence, and contempt for money.

For when he had obtained the praetorian prefecture while his father was emperor, he was suspected, because of certain actions, of being an imitator of Nero if he gained the imperial power. But these qualities were so thoroughly transformed for the better that they brought him such immortal glory that he was called “the delight” and “the love of the human race.”

Finally, when he assumed the imperial burden, he ordered Berenice, who hoped to marry him, to return home, and ordered the bands of emasculated men to depart.

During his reign Mount Hebius in Campania began to burn. From its summit such a fire burst forth that it consumed the neighboring regions and cities together with their inhabitants.

Titus also built the amphitheater at Rome and, at its dedication, killed five thousand wild beasts.

He completed and splendidly adorned the city of Aventicum, which his father Vespasian had begun to build, in Cisalpine Gaul. Because that region bordered a lake and, as they say, resembled Galilee of the Palestinians—which he had conquered with no little toil and blood—he decreed that it should be called Galilee.

During his principate also, a fire raged at Rome for three days and nights without respite, and there was a plague as great as any that had scarcely ever occurred before. Yet, without troubling anyone, he relieved these evils from his own funds, employing every kind of remedy: at one time personally restoring the sick, at another comforting those afflicted by the deaths of their loved ones.

He lived forty-one years and died of fever in the same Sabine region where his father had died.

His death brought such grief to the City and the provinces that, as we said, they called him the public delight and mourned the world as though it had been deprived of an everlasting guardian.

He was a ruler of such goodness that, when during a dinner he remembered that he had done nothing for anyone that day, he said: “Friends, I have lost this day.”

When he was preparing to storm the inner fortification of the Temple at Jerusalem, which the multitude of priests and leaders defended from within, he persisted with greater force and delay.

But after he had brought the Temple under his power, he admired its workmanship and antiquity and deliberated for a long time whether he should burn it as an incitement to the enemy or preserve it as a testimony to victory.

But since the Church of God was already flourishing abundantly throughout the whole world, this Temple, as empty and useful for no good purpose, was to be taken away by the judgment of God.

Therefore the emperor Titus, having been acclaimed by the army, burned and destroyed the Temple at Jerusalem.

During the times of these aforementioned rulers, after Christ’s ascension, I shall endeavor to set forth briefly which illustrious doctors of the Churches flourished, which authors produced books handed down for use in reading, which regions of the world the apostles received by lot for preaching, and in which places they gained the eternal palm as victors through their struggles.

Thus, in the preceding book we discussed Peter and Paul and both Jameses at greater length.

## CHAPTER IV. Which parts of the world the apostolic men and the other holy teachers who flourished under the aforementioned rulers undertook to evangelize, and in which places they gained the palm of martyrdom, set forth in order

Matthew, who was also called Levi, an apostle from a tax collector, first composed the Gospel of Christ in Judaea, for those who had believed from the circumcision, in Hebrew letters [Col. 1147B] and words.

Who later translated it into Greek is not sufficiently certain. The Hebrew text itself is preserved to this day, as Jerome says, in the library at Caesarea, which the martyr Pamphilus most diligently assembled and organized.

It should be observed in this work that whenever the evangelist, whether in his own person or by quotations from the Scriptures spoken in the person of the Lord and Savior, makes use of scriptural testimonies, he does not follow the authority of the translators of the Septuagint but the Hebrew text. Two such passages are: “Out of Egypt I called my Son,” and: “He shall be called a Nazarene.”

He first preached the Gospel in Judaea and afterward in Macedonia. He rests in the mountains of the Parthians.

Andrew—whose name means “beautiful”—the brother of Peter, first according to John and second according to Matthew, received Scythia and Achaea as his assigned field of preaching. In the city of Achaea he was also suspended on a cross and died.

James, son of Zebedee and brother of John, fourth in order, wrote to the twelve tribes that are scattered among the nations. He preached the Gospel in Spain and the western regions and poured the light of preaching into the western part of the world.

He was killed by the sword by Herod the tetrarch and died; he was buried within Marmarica.

Thomas, called Didymus of Christ and, according to the Latin language, “the twin” of Christ and like the Savior—unbelieving through hearing but faithful through seeing—preached the Gospel to the Parthians, Medes, Persians, Hyrcanians, Bactrians, and Indians. He occupied the eastern region and penetrated the land of the nations, carrying his preaching there even to the title of his Passion.

For he died after being pierced with lances in the Indian city of Calamina, where he was also honorably buried.

The apostle Bartholomew, whose name is taken from the Syrian language, received Lycaonia as his assigned field of preaching and translated the Gospel according to Matthew into the language of the Indians.

At last, while living in the city of Albanum Major in Armenia, he was flayed by barbarians and thus buried in the earth.

Judas, brother of James, preached in Mesopotamia and the inner regions of Pontus. By his holy teaching he softened savage and untamed peoples, as though they possessed the nature of wild beasts, and subjected them to the Lord’s faith.

He was buried in the Armenian city of Neritus.

After the martyrdom of James, the destruction of the city of Jerusalem immediately followed. It is reported that the apostles and the other disciples of the Lord who still remained at that time gathered together from every place, along with those who were called the Lord’s relatives according to the flesh—for many of these were still alive at that time—and held a common council to decide whom they should judge worthy to succeed James.

With one accord they appointed Simon, son of Cleopas, whose mention is made in the Gospels, to receive the episcopal see.

This was Simon the Zealot, who was first called the Cananaean, burning with zeal for the Lord. Equal to Peter in surname and similar to him in honor, he received the leadership of Egypt and, after James the Just, held, as we said, the chair of Jerusalem.

After 120 years of life, he was granted under Trajan to endure the suffering of martyrdom by the cross. He lies in Bosporus.

Philip was from the city of Bethsaida, as was Peter. The Gospels and the Acts of the Apostles frequently preserve worthy memories of praise concerning him. His daughters also became prophetesses and, as ecclesiastical history relates, were women of extraordinary holiness and perpetual virginity.

He preached Christ to the Gauls and brought barbarian peoples, neighbors of darkness and joined to the swelling Ocean, to the light of knowledge and the harbor of faith.

Then he was crucified and died in Hierapolis, a city of the province of Phrygia, after being stoned. His body was buried upright, and he rests there together with his daughters.

Matthias was one of the seventy disciples and was substituted among the twelve apostles in place of Judas Iscariot. Chosen by lot, he alone had no surname, and the preaching of the Gospel in Judaea is assigned to him.

Barnabas the Cypriot, appointed with Paul as an apostle to the Gentiles, composed one Epistle pertaining to the building up of the Church; it is counted among the apocrypha.

Afterward, because of John the disciple, who was also called Mark, he separated from Paul. Nevertheless, he carried out the work of evangelical preaching entrusted to him.

Luke the physician from Antioch, whose writings show that he was not ignorant of the Greek language, was a follower of the apostle Paul and his companion throughout all his journeys.

He wrote the Gospel concerning which Paul himself says: “We sent with him the brother whose praise in the Gospel is throughout all the Churches.”

Likewise, in the Epistle to the Colossians: “Luke the most beloved physician greets you.”

And to Timothy: “Only Luke is with me.”

He also published another distinguished volume, entitled the Acts of the Apostles. Its narrative reaches Paul as he remained in Rome for two years—that is, until the fourth year of Nero.

From this we understand that his book was written in that same city.

Let us therefore count the work concerning Paul and Thecla, and the entire household of Leo that was baptized, among the apocryphal writings. For it is absurd that Paul’s inseparable companion should have been ignorant of this alone among all the apostle’s affairs.

Tertullian also, who lived near those times, reports that a certain presbyter in Asia named Paul was convicted before John of being the author of the book. He confessed that he had done this out of love for Paul and had been removed from office.

Some suppose that whenever Paul says in his Epistles, “According to my Gospel,” he means that Luke learned it from Paul. Luke was not with the Lord in the flesh but learned from the other apostles.

Luke himself declares this at the beginning of his volume, saying: “Just as those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and ministers of the word delivered them to us.”

Thus he wrote the Gospel as he had heard it, but composed the Acts of the Apostles as he himself had seen them.

He was buried at Constantinople. In the twentieth year of Constantius, his bones were transferred together with the relics of the apostle Andrew.

The evangelist Mark, concerning whom we spoke in the preceding book, is said to have cut off his thumb so that he would not be compelled to enter the Jewish priesthood.

Nevertheless, he first held the episcopal chair at Alexandria and first founded the Churches of Egypt. He flourished with such virtues of teaching and self-restraint that all the disciples of Christ followed his example.

He died in the eighth year of Nero and was buried in peaceful repose.

Timothy, bishop of the Ephesians, was from the city of Lystra. His father was a Greek—that is, a pagan—but his mother was Jewish, as the apostle reports, saying: “The faith that dwelt first in your grandmother Lois and in your mother Eunice [Alternative: Eutice], and, I am certain, in you also.”

He was Paul’s disciple and spiritual son. Paul himself took him with him as a boy. Timothy remained chaste and a virgin, and he lies buried with great honor near Ephesus, on the mountain called Pion.

Titus was Paul’s disciple and his son in baptism. He was Greek by nationality and was the only Gentile whom Paul circumcised after the Gospel.

The aforesaid Apostle left him to establish the Churches of Crete. There he died in peace and was buried. Hermas, whom Paul also mentions in writing to the Romans—“Greet Phlegon, Hermas, Patrobas, and the brothers who are with them”—is said to have been the author of the book called The Shepherd. It is publicly read in certain Churches of Greece and is in truth a useful book; many ancient writers have used testimonies from it, but it is almost unknown among the Latins.

Thus, although the disciples of the Lord, preachers of the faith and teachers of the nations, were all one body, each received a particular region in the world for preaching.

To repeat this briefly: Peter received Rome; Andrew, Achaea; James, Spain; Thomas, India; John, Asia; Matthew, Macedonia; Philip, Gaul; Bartholomew, Lycaonia; Simon the Zealot, Egypt; Matthias, Judaea; James, the brother of the Lord, Jerusalem; Judas, the brother of James, Mesopotamia.

No particular lot was assigned to Paul together with the other apostles, because he was chosen as teacher and preacher among all the nations. For just as the apostleship of the circumcision was given to Peter and the others, so that of the uncircumcision among the nations was given to Paul.

Nevertheless, he evangelized seven Churches and three disciples.

## CHAPTER V. On Josephus the historian and what he related about the Savior
At that time Josephus, son of Matthias, a priest from Jerusalem, was captured by Vespasian and then spared by his son Titus. Coming to Rome, he presented the emperors, father and son, with seven [Col. 1150A] books of *The Jewish War*, which were both deposited in the public library, and earned him, on account of the distinction of his talent, a statue at Rome. He also wrote twenty other books of the *Antiquities*, from the beginning of the world down to the fourteenth year of Caesar Domitian, and two against Apion, the Alexandrian grammarian. Apion had been sent under Caligula on behalf of the Gentiles against Philo, who had also written a book containing an indictment of the Jewish nation. Another book of his, entitled [title not supplied], is also considered highly elegant; in it the martyrdoms of the Maccabees are arranged.

In Book XVIII of the *Antiquities* he most plainly acknowledges that Christ was killed by the Pharisees because of the greatness of his signs, that John the Baptist was truly a prophet, and that Jerusalem was destroyed because of the killing of the apostle [Col. 1150B] James. He wrote about the Lord in these words:

> At that time there was Jesus, a wise man—if indeed one ought to call him a man. He was a worker of astonishing deeds and a teacher of those who gladly receive the truth. He had many followers, both among the Jews and among the Gentiles. He was believed to be the Christ. When Pilate, because of the envy of our leading men, condemned him to the cross, nevertheless those who had loved him did not cease to do so. For he appeared to them alive on the third day. Many other wondrous things were told about him by the prophets, who had foretold these and countless other marvels concerning him; and even to this day the people named after him has not disappeared.

The same historian also reports a certain oracle found in the sacred writings, which at that very time was understood to designate a man who would arise from their [Col. 1150C] religion and acquire dominion over the whole world. He suspects that the prophecy of this oracle pointed to Vespasian. But Vespasian ruled no peoples other than those alone who appeared to be subject to the Roman Empire, nor did he arise from the lineage or religion of the Jews. Therefore these responses are more rightly referred to Christ, to whom the Father says:

> Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance,  
> and your possession to the ends of the earth.

And at that same time, through his apostles, their sound had gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.

## CHAPTER VI. On the Arrogant Deeds of Domitian

Domitian, son of Vespasian and the freedwoman [Col. 1150D] Domitilla, and brother of Titus, ruled for fifteen years. At first he pretended to clemency and did not appear so utterly inactive, either at home or in war, but rather capable of endurance. For this reason he defeated the Chatti and the Germans, administered justice with complete fairness, and either began many buildings at Rome or constructed them from their foundations. He restored the libraries destroyed by fire, obtaining copies from everywhere, especially from Alexandria. He was so skilled with the bow that arrows shot at a distance passed through the open fingers of a man whose hand was extended.

From that point he gradually advanced through every degree of wickedness, until he dared to attack the Church of Christ, firmly established throughout the whole world, by issuing everywhere edicts of the most savage persecution. He fell into such arrogance that he ordered himself to be called, written of, and worshiped as a [Col. 1151A] god and lord. Out of envy and at the same time for the sake of plunder, he openly killed some of the noblest senators, drove others into exile, and ordered them to be slaughtered there. In the intemperance of his lust he did everything that can be imagined. He built very many houses in the city, destroying the property of the Roman people.

He waged war against the Germans and the Dacians through his generals, with equal ruin to the state: in the city he himself was continually rending the Senate and the people, while abroad the army, badly led, was constantly being destroyed by the slaughter inflicted by the enemy. For I would unfold at length how great were the battles between Diurpaneus, king of the Dacians, and the commander Fuscus, and how great were the Roman disasters, were it not that Gaius Tacitus—who composed this history with the greatest care—said that he had bound both Sallustius Crispus and very many other authors to silence concerning the number of those killed, and that he [Col. 1151B] himself had especially chosen to do the same.

Domitian, lifted up by this most perverse boastfulness, celebrated a triumph under the name of the conquered enemy over legions that had been destroyed. Inflamed by the same arrogance through which he wished himself to be worshiped as a god, he ordered persecution to be carried out against the Christians, becoming second after Nero in this command.

## CHAPTER VII. On the Lineage of David and the Relatives of Christ Sought Out by Him

Among the Jews, too, an order was given that the lineage of David should be sought out amid the severity of tortures and the bloodiest interrogation, and that its members should be killed, because the holy prophets were viewed with jealousy and it was believed that someone would still arise from the seed of David who might obtain the kingdom. He himself feared being deprived of his earthly kingdom by the Lord Christ, just as Herod [Col. 1151C] had feared this when he heard of Christ’s birth. Therefore he ordered that the royal lineage of David, or the relatives of Christ according to the flesh, be sought out and put to death.

At that time certain descendants of David were brought before Caesar. When Domitian asked them whether they were of the family of David and relatives of Christ, they confessed that they were. Then he asked how many possessions or how much wealth they had. They replied that the property of both of them amounted to no more than nine thousand denarii. Each possessed half of this amount in due proportion; and even this was not held by them in money, but in the assessed value of land, consisting of thirty-nine *jugera*. They cultivated it with their own hands, supporting themselves from it or paying their taxes. At the same time they displayed hands hardened by the labor of rural and daily work, stiff with toil and callused. [Col. 1151D]

When they were asked about Christ—what sort of kingdom was his, who he himself was, from where he came, and when he would come—they replied that his kingdom was not a kingdom of this world, nor was dominion over this earth assigned to him. Rather, a heavenly kingdom was being prepared for him through the ministry of angels at the consummation of the age; that is, when he would come in glory and judge the living and the dead, restoring to each person according to his deeds and merits.

When Domitian found no crime in them and held their lowly condition in the utmost contempt, he ordered them to depart free. He also checked, by issuing further edicts, the persecution that he had ordered to be carried out against the churches. Released by him, they became leaders of the churches, either because of the merit of their martyrdom or because of the privilege of such [Col. 1152A] kinship with Christ, and remained so until the time of Trajan.

This is what Hegesippus reports. Tertullian also relates similar things about Domitian, saying:

> Domitian once attempted something similar, being a portion of Nero in cruelty; but, like a human being, he soon abandoned it, even recalling those whom he had sent into exile.

Thus Domitian’s wife was called Augusta by decree of the Senate. Titus was enrolled among the gods. This same Domitian built a temple without the use of timber. He was also so arrogant that he ordered golden and silver statues of himself to be set up in the Capitol. Under him Bruttius put very many Christians to death. Among them he ordered F. Domitilla, niece through his sister of the consul F. Clemens, to be deported into exile on the island of Pontia [Col. 1152B] because she had declared herself a Christian.

At that time the apostle John, banished to the island of Patmos, saw the *Apocalypse*. Many signs and portents also occurred at that time in Rome and throughout the world. Nevertheless Domitian was soon cruelly killed by his own people in the palace. His corpse was carried away and buried in the most disgraceful manner.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the Good Deeds of Nerva and the Remarkable Deeds of Trajan

After Domitian, Nerva assumed the principate. Under him all the titles of honor that had been conferred upon Domitian were removed. All those whom Domitian had driven into exile were ordered, by decree of the Senate, to be recalled and to recover their property. Those who wrote the deeds of those [Col. 1152C] times bear witness to each of these matters.

At that time, therefore, our writers state that the apostle John returned from the island to Ephesus, as though to his own school. Nerva adopted Trajan in place of a son and made him a partner in the empire. While Nerva was shouting angrily at a certain petty king, he was seized by sweat. When this subsided, a chill affected his body and brought on a severe fever, and not long afterward he died, in the sixty-third year of his life. His body was buried in the tomb of Augustus, after the Senate had conferred upon him the honor once given to Augustus. On the same day on which he died there was an eclipse of the sun. He ruled for one year and four months.

He remitted many taxes and relieved afflicted cities. He ordered girls and boys born to impoverished parents to be supported at public expense in the towns of Italy. [Col. 1152D]

After Nerva, Trajan assumed the empire at Agrippina, a distinguished colony of Gaul. He possessed diligence in military affairs, gentleness in civil matters, and generosity in relieving cities. Since two qualities are expected of excellent princes—uprightness at home and courage in war—and prudence in both, he possessed such moderation in the greatest affairs that he seemed to have blended his virtues by a kind of balance, except that he was somewhat devoted to food and wine. He was generous to his friends and, as though equal to them in the conditions of life, enjoyed their company.

As soon as he had obtained the insignia of empire, he restored Germany beyond the Rhine to its former condition and subdued many peoples beyond the Danube. He made the regions beyond the Euphrates [Col. 1153A] and Tigris into provinces; he seized and held Seleucia, Ctesiphon, and Babylon. In the Red Sea he established a fleet in order that it might lay waste the borders of India. Thus Trajan made Armenia, Assyria, and Mesopotamia into provinces.

Under him the Jews rose in rebellion and, as though driven mad, erupted at one time through various parts of the world. They also waged the most savage wars against the inhabitants throughout all Libya. Libya was then so utterly desolated by the killing of its inhabitants that, unless the emperor Hadrian later brought colonies there from elsewhere, the land would have remained completely empty, its inhabitants wiped out.

They disturbed all Egypt, Cyrene, and the Thebaid with bloody rebellions. After a battle had been joined at Alexandria, they were defeated and crushed. When the rebels in Mesopotamia [Col. 1153B] also revolted, war was brought against them by order of the emperor. Thus many thousands of Jews were destroyed in a vast slaughter. Indeed, they destroyed the city of Salamis in Cyprus after killing all its inhabitants.

Trajan, deceived by error, therefore stained all his good qualities through the persecution of Christians. He was the third after Nero to persecute Christians, ordering those who were found to be compelled to sacrifice to idols and those who refused to be killed. Under him many nobly attained the palm of martyrdom, and many more would have been killed had he not been warned by the report of Pliny Secundus, who had been appointed a persecutor among the other judges.

While governing a certain province and having killed very many Christians during his magistracy, Pliny was frightened by their number and wrote to Trajan asking what should be done. He reported [Col. 1153C] to him that, apart from their obstinacy in refusing to sacrifice and their assemblies before dawn for singing to a certain Christ as God, and their confession of him, they did nothing contrary to Roman laws. Moreover, in order to bind their discipline together, they were forbidden by their rules to commit murder, theft, adultery, perjury, robbery, or anything similar. They possessed such confidence in their innocent confession that they did not fear even death as something grievous or frightening.

The emperor immediately moderated the edict by a more lenient rescript. He decided that this class of people should not be sought out, but that those who were brought before the authorities should be punished.

This Pliny Secundus is regarded as a distinguished orator and historian, and many works of his talent survive. Nevertheless, the Golden House at Rome, which Nero had built at enormous expense from the property and possessions of private citizens, was suddenly consumed [Col. 1153D] by fire, so that it might be understood that the persecution sent by another was being punished especially in the monuments of the man from whom it had first arisen, and in the very author of it.

Four cities of Asia were overthrown by an earthquake: Elaea, Myrina, Pitane, and Cyme. Two cities of Greece, those of the Opuntians and the Orites, were likewise destroyed; three cities of Galatia were ruined by the same earthquake. The Pantheon at Rome was burned by lightning. An earthquake almost entirely overthrew the city of Antioch.

Trajan therefore died at the city of Selucia in Isauria from a flux of the bowels, in the sixty-third year of his life. He had ruled for twenty years. His bones were carried back in a golden urn and placed in the forum beneath a column bearing his name. Of all the emperors, he alone was buried within the City.

## CHAPTER IX. [Col. 1154A] On the Miracles and Death of John the Evangelist

The apostle and evangelist John, son of Zebedee and brother of James, remained alive in the body until Trajan’s time. Chosen as a virgin by the Lord, he was loved more than the others. Reclining upon the breast of his teacher, he drank the streams of his Gospel from the fountain of the Lord’s sacred breast itself. Like one of the rivers of paradise, he spread the grace of the word of God throughout the whole world. At Christ’s command he succeeded to Christ’s place, when, by taking the teacher’s mother into his care, the disciple himself was in a sense left as another son in Christ’s place.

While preaching the Gospel of Christ in Asia, he was banished by Caesar Domitian to the mines on the island of Patmos, where he also [Col. 1154B] wrote the *Apocalypse*. After Domitian was killed, the Senate released him from exile, and he withdrew to Ephesus. There, at the urgent request of the bishops of Asia, he published the last Gospel in order to refute the cunning arguments of heretics.

He is said to have preached the Gospel almost until the final period of his life without any written record. But when knowledge of the three Gospels reached him, he is said to have approved the faith and truth of what they contained, yet to have seen that certain things were lacking—especially those that the Lord had done at the beginning of his preaching.

For it is clear that in the earlier three evangelists only those events appear to be contained that occurred in the year in which John the Baptist was either imprisoned or punished. Finally, if one observes the beginnings of the narratives, after [Col. 1154C] Matthew reports the forty-day fast and Christ’s temptation, he immediately adds:

> When he heard that John had been handed over, he departed from Judaea and came into Galilee.

Mark likewise says:

> After John had been handed over, he came into Galilee.

Luke, even before he begins to report anything about Jesus’ deeds, says that Herod added this to all the evils that he had committed: he shut John up in prison.

Because these matters appeared to have been omitted by the others, the apostle John is said to have been asked to write down what the earlier evangelists had passed over—what the Savior had done before John was handed over. Therefore he says in his Gospel:

> This was the beginning of Jesus’ signs.

And again, in another place, he indicates this by saying:

> For John had not [Col. 1154D] yet been sent into prison.

From this it is clear that he describes what Jesus had done before John was handed over. Therefore, if anyone considers these things more carefully, he will plainly find that the Gospels do not disagree with one another, but that John writes of events belonging to one period, while the others write of events belonging to another.

Since either Matthew or Luke had described the Savior’s birth according to the flesh, John passed over this and took his beginning from theology and from Christ’s very divinity. This part was undoubtedly reserved for him, as an exceptional writer, through the Holy Spirit.

Among the other virtues of this John, the greatness of his signs was as follows. He changed wild branches into gold [Col. 1155A] and rocks from the shore into gems. He also restored fragments of gems to their proper nature. At the people’s request he raised a widow and restored to life the body of a young man. After drinking a deadly potion, he not only escaped its danger but restored to life the people who had been struck down by it.

He had entrusted a certain handsome young boy to a bishop. But the boy did not at all submit to the bishop’s instruction. As his wickedness increased, he became so depraved that he made all those who had previously been his teachers in crime into his disciples, and became the leader and violent chief of thieves and robbers.

As Eusebius reports, the apostle miraculously brought this man back to the Church. He continually offered prayers for him, undertook frequent fasts together with him, and sought from God the pardon that had been promised to him. Through various consoling speeches, [Col. 1155B] like spells of persuasion, he softened the man’s savage and terrified mind. He did not desist until he had reformed him in every respect and placed him over the Church, thereby offering great examples of true repentance, a powerful demonstration of new regeneration, and visible signs and trophies of resurrection in that man.

In the sixty-seventh year after the passion of the Lord and Savior, under the emperor Trajan, John was worn out by the long old age of his life. Sensing that the day of his departure was approaching, he is said to have ordered a grave [Col. 1155C] to be dug for him. After bidding farewell to the brothers and offering a prayer, he entered the tomb while still alive. Then he rested in it as though in a bed.

As a result, some say that he is still alive and suppose that he lies in the tomb not dead but sleeping—especially because earth rises from below and bubbles up to the surface of the tomb, as though dust were being stirred upward by the breath of one resting below.

He rested at Ephesus on the Kalends of January.

## CHAPTER X. On Clement and His Virtues; He Suffered under Trajan

At that time the ancient enemy, hostile to all good things and jealous of the salvation of humanity, grieved that faith in the truth and the worship of religion had illuminated the whole world. For this reason he incited the aforementioned ruler Trajan to pursue and destroy the preachers and worshipers of the true light.

Under Trajan, throughout the Roman world, many were crowned [Col. 1155D] with a glorious confession of Christ. I have therefore wished to insert into this work the memory of some of them.

Clement, then, is the one about whom the apostle Paul, writing to the Philippians, says:

> Together with Clement and the rest of my fellow workers, whose names are written in the book of life.

He was the fourth bishop of Rome after Peter, since Linus was second and Anacletus third. Nevertheless, there are many Latins who think that Clement was second after the apostle.

In the name of the Roman Church he wrote a very useful letter to the Church of the Corinthians, one that is also publicly read in certain places.

It seems to me that this letter corresponds in style to the Epistle that is circulated under Paul’s name as addressed to the Hebrews. He also makes use of many passages from that same epistle, not only in meaning but [Col. 1156A] even according to the order of its words. The resemblance between the two is altogether considerable.

A second letter is also circulated under Clement’s name, but it is rejected by the ancients, as is the *Disputation of Peter and Appion*, written in an extended discourse, which Eusebius refutes in the third book of his *Ecclesiastical History*.

The most blessed Clement faithfully followed apostolic teaching. After he occupied the episcopal seat of the Roman Church, he was loved by everyone—not only by Christians, because of his outstanding virtues, the excellence of his teaching, and the gentleness and generosity of his excellent character, but also by pagans and Jews.

Rich in many flowers of preaching and in virtues, he consecrated Domitilla, a virgin and granddaughter of the emperor Domitian, betrothed to Aurelian, Aurelian the emperor, a friend of Nerva, who believed [Col. 1156B] in Christ, with the sacred veil so that she might persevere in purity. Because of this confession she was condemned to exile.

He also taught Theodora, wife of Sisinnius, a powerful and noble man, who had turned away from images, to profess before God her resolve to chastity. Through her, in accordance with the apostle’s words, Sisinnius himself was converted to faith in Christ and became a faithful husband, although previously, through jealousy of his converted wife, he had become blind and deaf.

Through the woman’s faith and the intercession of the blessed Clement, all the functions of his body were restored to him, and he received the grace of baptism. Those baptized with him—men, women, and children—numbered 423. Through this Sisinnius many nobles and friends of the emperor were converted to [Col. 1156C] Christ.

The guardians of the idols, seeing an innumerable multitude believing in Christ, were moved by great envy. They stirred up the patrons of the districts, giving them money, and incited sedition against the Christian name.

For this reason Blessed Clement was driven into exile across the Pontic Sea, to a desert adjoining the city of Cherson, in the province of Lycia. There he found about two thousand Christians condemned to prolonged exile and forced to cut stone. After he had addressed many words of consolation and patience to them, he learned from them that they carried water on their shoulders from the sixth milestone.

Then Saint Clement said:

> Let us pray to the Lord Jesus that he open in this place the veins of a spring for his confessors; and may he who struck the rock on Mount Sinai, and waters flowed forth in abundance, open for us a plentiful [Col. 1156D] stream.

When he had finished praying and was looking around in every direction, he saw a lamb standing there. Raising its right foot, it seemed to point out a place to Saint Clement.

Then Saint Clement, understanding that it was the Lord Jesus Christ—whom he alone could see, while no one else saw him—went to the place and said:

> In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, strike this place.

When everyone was digging around the area with mattocks without touching the exact place where the lamb stood, Saint Clement took a short twig and, striking lightly at the spot beneath the lamb’s foot, opened a spring furnished with abundant veins of water. It immediately burst forth with such force that it formed a river.

Then, while everyone rejoiced, blessed Clement recited the responsory:

> The rushing of the river [Col. 1157A] makes glad the city of God.

At this report the whole province gathered. Everyone who came to hear the teaching of Saint Clement was converted to the Lord Jesus Christ, so that in a single day five hundred souls or more were baptized in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, and departed perfected in the Christian faith.

Throughout the province, within one year, seventy-five churches were founded by the believers, all the temples were destroyed, and all the idols were broken.

After three years, however, when the pagans persisted, an ambitious report reached the emperor Trajan. They claimed that an innumerable Christian population had increased there through Clement.

A certain man named Arsidianus was sent, and he killed many [Col. 1157B] Christians by various punishments. When Arsidianus saw everyone approaching martyrdom with joy, he yielded to the multitude and compelled only Clement the bishop to sacrifice.

When he saw that Clement was so firmly fixed in the Lord that he could not be moved at all, he said to his men:

> Take him to the sea, tie an anchor around his neck, and throw him into the middle of the sea, so that the Christian people cannot worship him as a god.

When this had been done, the whole multitude of Christians wept. As they wept, his disciples Cornelius and Phoebus said:

> Let us all pray with one accord, that the Lord may show us the remains of his martyr.

As the people prayed, the sea withdrew into itself for nearly three miles. The people entered on dry ground and found in the middle, inside a stone chest, the body of Saint Clement [Col. 1157C], with the anchor by which he had been thrown lying beside him.

It was revealed to his disciples that they should not remove his body from there. It was also made known to them that every year, on the day of his passion, the sea would withdraw for seven days for those who came, providing a dry path. The Lord causes this to happen for the praise of his name down to the present day.

When this had occurred, all the peoples around believed in Christ. The same most blessed Clement himself relates in his writings how he came to the faith of Christ and remained Peter’s disciple and inseparable companion. Among other things he says:

> Since I was possessed by an excellent desire for immortality—a desire whose truth was later demonstrated by the outcome of events and shown by the grace of almighty God—this intention of my mind led me to the investigation of truth and to the recognition [Col. 1157D] of the true light.
>
> While I was being troubled by these agitations of thought, a report gradually reached us at the beginning of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, having originated in the eastern regions. Growing stronger in every place, like a good messenger sent by God, it filled the whole world and did not allow the divine will to be concealed in silence.
>
> Thus it spread throughout every place that there was in Judaea someone who proclaimed the kingdom of God to the Jews. He said that those who observed the institutions of his commandments and teaching would receive it. To make his message worthy of belief and full of divinity, he performed many wonders and signs.
>
> Finally, gatherings began to take place throughout the city, and [Col. 1158A] people began to discuss this message: who the man was who had appeared, and who, as though sent by God, had brought a message to humanity.
>
> Then, in that same year, a certain man standing in a very crowded place in the city proclaimed to the people:
>
> “Hear me, Roman citizens! The Son of God is present in the regions of Judaea, promising eternal life to all who are willing to hear him—provided that they direct their actions according to his will. Therefore turn from evil to good, and from temporal things to eternal ones. Recognize that there is one God, ruler of heaven and earth, in whose sight you stand, you who unjustly possess his world. But if you turn and repent, when you come into the age to come and are made eternal, you will enjoy his ineffable blessings.”
>
> The man who spoke these words was a Hebrew by [Col. 1158B] nationality, named Barnabas. He also said that he was one of Christ’s disciples and had been sent for the purpose of making these things known to those who wished to hear them.
>
> After hearing this, I began, together with the rest of the multitude, to follow him and listen to what he said. I understood that he explained simply and without any rhetorical artifice what he had heard from the Son of God or had seen himself.
>
> I then followed Barnabas from the City and came to Caesarea. There I found Peter, by whom I was kindly received. Delighted by his preaching, his great miracles, his integrity, and his holiness, I became his companion in every respect as he went through each city preaching, until, during the days of Caesar Claudius—that is, in the second year of his reign, after Peter’s episcopate over the Church of Antioch—I came with him from Antioch to the city [Col. 1158C] of Rome to overthrow Simon Magus.
>
> For the present, this account of the beginning of my conversion is sufficient for this work.

## CHAPTER XI. On Simeon, Son of Clopas, and Ignatius, Bishop of the Church of Antioch, Who Suffered under Trajan

At that time Simeon, son of Clopas, whom we have already shown above to have been ordained the second bishop of Jerusalem, was released from the bonds of the flesh through martyrdom. His guarantor in this matter is that same Hegesippus whom we have already brought forward as a witness.

He reports that the aforementioned man was accused by certain heretics as a Christian and afflicted with many tortures for many days. Even the judge [Col. 1158D] himself, together with his friends, marveled at his endurance. Finally, the judge ordered him to end his life by a death like the passion that the Lord had endured. He was 120 years old under Caesar Trajan, in the presence of Atticus, the consular governor.

That Simeon was one of the Lord’s own helpers is indicated either by his longevity or by the truth of the Gospels, where his mother is also said to be Mary, the wife of Clopas.

At that time Ignatius, the third bishop of the Church of Antioch after Peter, was condemned to the beasts when Trajan stirred up persecution, and was sent to Rome in chains. While sailing, he came to Smyrna, where Polycarp was a disciple of the apostle John. There he wrote one letter to the Ephesians [Col. 1159A], a second to the Magnesians, a third to the Trallians, and a fourth to the Romans.

After leaving there, he wrote to the Philadelphians, to the Smyrnaeans (printed: Phinerneos), and separately to Polycarp, commending to him the Church of Antioch. There, from the Gospel translated by Jerome, he gives testimony in Christ’s person, saying: [Col. 1159B]

> I know and believe that he was in the flesh even after the resurrection; and when he came to Peter and those who were with Peter, he said to them: “Behold, touch me and see, for I am not an incorporeal demon.” And immediately they touched him and believed.

Since we have mentioned so great a man, it seems appropriate to me to include a little from his letter to the Romans:

> From Syria to Rome I fought with beasts, on sea and land, by night and day, bound among ten leopards—that is, soldiers who guard me. Even when one does good to them, they become worse; their injustice is my instruction. But for this reason I have not been justified.
>
> May I enjoy the beasts prepared for me! I pray that they may be swift for my destruction and that I may entice them to eat me, so that, as happened with some other martyrs, they may not dare to touch my body. And if they are unwilling to come, I myself will compel them; I will force myself upon them so that I may be devoured.
>
> Forgive me, little children. I know what benefits me. Now I am beginning to be a disciple of Christ, desiring none of the things that are seen, so that I may find Jesus Christ. May fire, cross, beasts, the breaking of bones, the severing of limbs [Col. 1159C], the crushing of the entire body, and the torments of the devil come upon me, provided that I may enjoy Christ.

When he had already been condemned to the beasts and, in his fervor to suffer, heard the lions roaring, he said:

> I am Christ’s grain; let me be ground by the teeth of the beasts, so that I may be found pure bread.

He suffered in the eleventh year of Trajan. His bodily remains lie at Antioch, outside the Daphne Gate, in the cemetery.

Hegesippus therefore reports that down to these times the Church remained a pure and undefiled virgin, with corrupters of the truth and violators of the divine word either nowhere to be found at all or, if there happened to be any, hiding in the earth’s secret and remote places.

But when the choir of the apostles and that whole generation which had received the living voice [Col. 1159D] from the Lord had departed from this light, then, as though into an empty house, impious error in the form of false doctrine poured itself. As though no defender of the divine treasury remained, they bared their heads, seized the weapons of falsehood, and attempted to attack apostolic truth.

This war was waged within, while from without the burden of persecutions pressed upon the Church. Therefore immense crowds of martyrs were slaughtered every day.

## CHAPTER XII. On the Emperor Hadrian and What Happened under Him. At That Time Quadratus and Aristides, or Agrippa, Were Teachers

Aelius Hadrian, son of Trajan’s cousin, the twelfth [Col. 1160A] after Augustus to obtain the principate, ruled for twenty-two years. He was deeply educated in Greek literature and absorbed the studies and customs of the Athenians. Trained in every discipline, he possessed knowledge of singing, chanting, medicine, and painting, and of fashioning from metal and marble anything he wished.

Being a musician, arithmetician, geometrician, and exceedingly sharp both in provoking challenges and in answering them, he traveled through all the provinces. He restored Alexandria, which had been overthrown by the Romans, at public expense.

He relaxed many of the cities’ taxes, having publicly burned the records, and freed very many from tribute. When the Athenians requested laws, he compiled a body of law from the books of Draco, Solon, and the others. At that time the Jews took up arms and ravaged Palestine, while Timo Rufus held the province; Hadrian sent him an army to crush the rebels. This Hadrian, instructed and educated through Quadratus, a disciple of the apostles, Aristides of Athens, a man full of faith and wisdom, and the legate Serenus Granius, by means of books composed on the Christian religion, ordered in a letter sent to Minucius Fundanus, proconsul of Asia, that no one should be permitted to condemn Christians without an accusation or proof of crime. He was immediately and continually called “Father of his Country” in the senate, beyond the custom of his ancestors, and his wife was called Augusta.

Yet this emperor, though so highly educated, was not without vices: he was hardly restrained in his love of boys. Accordingly, he loved the boy Antinous, of extraordinary beauty, to such an extent that he established temples and priests for him and named a city after him. Envious also of Trajan’s glory, he recalled the armies from Assyria, Mesopotamia, and Armenia, provinces which Trajan had made subject. Indeed, after constructing distinguished and numerous buildings at Athens, he founded a public contest and built a library of marvelous workmanship.

Hadrian organized the state under the most just laws, waged war against the Sarmatians, and defeated them. The Jews, agitated by the disturbance caused by their crimes and ravaging the province of Palestine, once their own, he subdued by a final slaughter, and he avenged the Christians. For Cochba, leader of the Jewish faction, killed the Christians who refused to provide assistance to him against the Roman army with every kind of torture. The Jewish war being waged in Palestine came to an end, with Jewish affairs completely crushed.

[Col. 1160D] From that time they were also deprived of permission to enter Jerusalem: first by God’s will, as the prophets had foretold; then by the Romans’ prohibition. The city was granted to Christians alone, and Hadrian restored it to an excellent condition by constructing its walls. He ordered it to be called Aelia, from his own name. On the front of the gate by which one goes out toward Bethlehem, a boar was carved in marble, signifying that the Jews were subject to Roman power.

Thus, up to this time of the destruction, when the Jews again revolted, were once more subdued by the Romans in great battles, and were nearly annihilated, fifteen successions of bishops are said to have passed in Jerusalem. They were taken away very quickly by the swiftness of death and each held the priesthood only for a very brief time. They all, it is said, were Hebrews of ancient origin and had faithfully received the teaching; therefore, without hesitation, those who were able to judge their merit in the faith considered them worthy of the priesthood as well. At that time the whole Church seemed to have been gathered and established from faithful Hebrews, beginning with the apostles and continuing until that time of destruction.

Since at approximately that time the appointment of bishops from the circumcision ceased, it seems necessary to enumerate together all the priests from the first up to that point. The first, therefore, was James, who is called the Lord’s brother; after him Simeon was chosen; the third was Justus; Zacchaeus was fourth; then Tobias was fifth; Benjamin sixth; John seventh; then Matthias, whom Philip succeeded; after him Seneca was appointed tenth; then Justus; Levi twelfth; after him Ephrem; then Joseph was fourteenth; and Judas was the last of all.

These are nearly all those who, from the apostles until the times designated above, presided as bishops in Jerusalem over that people from the circumcision. Then Mark was appointed the first bishop from the Gentiles in Jerusalem, when those who had been from the circumcision had ceased.

Hadrian, therefore, died at Baiae from dropsy, being more than sixty years old. Under the emperor Hadrian just mentioned, Quadratus, a disciple of the apostles, was appointed in the place of Publius, bishop of Athens, who had been crowned with martyrdom for Christ. By his faith and zeal he gathered the Church, which had been scattered in great terror.

When Hadrian had spent the winter in Athens visiting Eleusis and had been initiated into nearly all the sacred rites of Greece, he gave an opportunity to those who hated Christians to harass believers without an imperial order. Quadratus presented him with a book composed in defense of our religion, very useful, full of reason and faith, and worthy of apostolic teaching. In it, while also demonstrating the antiquity of his own time, he says that he himself had seen many people who, oppressed by various calamities in Judaea under God, had been healed, and that he had seen people who had died rise again.

Aristides of Athens, a most eloquent philosopher and, while still wearing his former philosophical dress, a disciple of Christ, composed a volume containing an account of our doctrine at the time when Quadratus also gave his work to the emperor Hadrian—namely, an *Apology for the Christians*. It survives to this day among scholars as evidence of his talent.

In those days Granius Serenus, a highly distinguished man and legate, sent a letter to the emperor, saying that it was unjust for the blood of innocent people to be surrendered to the outcries of the mob and for them to be made guilty merely on account of their name and sect, without any crime. Moved by this, Hadrian wrote to Minucius Fundanus, proconsul of Asia, that Christians were not to be condemned without an accusation of crimes. A copy of this letter survives to our own time.

At that time Basilides, the founder of a heresy, lived in Alexandria; from him the Gnostic sect takes its name. During this period Agrippa, surnamed Castor, a very learned man, argued with great force against the twenty-four volumes that the heretic Basilides had composed on the Gospel. He exposed all his mysteries and enumerated his prophets—Barchaban and Barchon, and others who had never existed—names he had invented to terrify his hearers, along with other barbarous names. He also taught his followers to remain silent for five years, after the Pythagorean custom.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the deeds of Antoninus Pius and on Justin, a teacher of his time

Antoninus, surnamed Pius, created emperor as the thirteenth after Augustus, governed the state with his sons Aurelius and Lucius for twenty-three years less a fraction. Adopted as a son by Hadrian, whose son-in-law he had been, he displayed such goodness in his rule that he undoubtedly lived without equal precedent. His age may be compared with that of Numa: for twenty-three years he ruled the whole world by authority alone, without any war, so greatly did all kings, nations, and peoples fear and love him that they considered him a parent or patron rather than a master or emperor. Like the heavenly powers, they all prayed for his favor and asked him to judge their disputes. Indeed, when they had learned of the justice of so great an emperor, the Indians, Bactrians, and Hyrcanians sent ambassadors to him.

He lived in power with such tranquility and holiness that he was rightly called Pius and Father of his Country. In his time Valentinus, founder of a heresy, and Cerdo, the teacher of Marcion, came to Rome and were declared heretics and enemies of the holy religion. But the philosopher Justin presented Antoninus with a book composed in defense of the Christian religion and made him well disposed toward Christians. Antoninus died after being seized by illness at the twelfth milestone from the City.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the deeds of Marcus Antoninus and his brother Aurelius Commodus, who ruled together for a time

Marcus Antoninus Verus, the fourteenth after Augustus, assumed the kingdom together with his brother Aurelius Commodus and remained in it for nineteen years. These were the first to protect the state under equal authority. They then waged war against the Parthians with admirable courage and success.

Marcus Antoninus Verus set out for that war. For Vologeses, king of the Parthians, was devastating Armenia, Cappadocia, and Syria with a violent invasion. But Antoninus, through very able commanders and after accomplishing great deeds, captured Seleucia, a city of Assyria situated on the river Hydaspes, together with four hundred thousand people, and triumphed with his brother in celebration of the Parthian victory. Not long afterward, while sitting in a carriage with his brother, he was suffocated by a sudden illness, which the Greeks call *apoplexy*, and died.

After his death Marcus Antoninus alone presided over the state. During the days of the Parthian war, however, the fourth persecution of Christians after Nero arose, by his order, in Assyria and Gaul; many of the saints were crowned with martyrdom.

A plague followed, spreading through many provinces, and devastated all Italy with such pestilence that villages, fields, and towns everywhere, deprived of cultivators and inhabitants, were abandoned to ruins and forests. The Roman army and all the legions stationed in widely scattered winter quarters were reportedly so depleted that the Marcomannic War, which arose immediately afterward, could be conducted only through a new levy of soldiers, which Marcus Antoninus continually held for three years at Carnuntum.

That this war was administered by God’s providence is established by many proofs, but especially by a letter of the most serious and restrained emperor. For when barbarous peoples, innumerable in their multitude, had risen up—namely the Marcomanni, Quadi, Vandals, Sarmatians, Suebi, and nearly all Germany—and the army, advancing as far as the territory of the Quadi and surrounded by the enemy, was suffering the danger of thirst more than of the enemy because of the lack of available water, certain soldiers suddenly called upon the name of Christ, openly pouring themselves out in prayer with great steadfastness of faith. So great a force of rain poured down that it abundantly refreshed the Romans without harming them, while terrifying the barbarians with repeated strokes of lightning—especially since many of them were killed—and drove them to flight.

The Romans cut down their fleeing backs to the point of annihilation and carried away a most glorious victory, one to be preferred above nearly all the titles of the ancients, with a small and inexperienced number of soldiers but through the most powerful assistance of Christ.

Even now, it is said, letters of the emperor Antoninus survive in which he acknowledges that, through the invocation of Christ’s name by Christian soldiers, both that thirst was driven away and victory was granted.

The same Antoninus took his son Commodus into the kingdom. He also remitted the taxes throughout all the provinces for the preceding period and ordered all the accumulated and defamatory records of fiscal proceedings to be burned together in the Forum. He moderated the harsher laws with new enactments. Finally, while stationed in Pannonia, he died of a sudden illness.

The writers of the annals say of this emperor that, had he not been born for those times, everything in the Roman state would surely have collapsed as if in a single fall; he was set before the public calamities as their defender. For there was nowhere any rest from war: throughout the entire East, Illyricum, Italy, and Gaul, wars were raging; there were earthquakes not without the destruction of cities, floods of rivers, frequent plagues, and kinds of locusts utterly hostile to the fields. In short, nothing that can be said or imagined as a cause by which mortals are worn down by the greatest anxieties failed to rage during his reign.

From the beginning of his life he was exceptionally tranquil, so much so that from childhood he never changed his expression either from joy or sorrow. He was devoted to philosophy and Greek literature. He permitted men of higher rank to provide banquets with the same furnishings and similar attendants as his own.

When the treasury had been exhausted and he had no money for the gifts he wished to distribute to the soldiers, and was unwilling to impose anything on the provincials or the senate, he sold the objects of imperial luxury after setting up a sale in Trajan’s Forum. He sold golden vessels, crystal and murrine cups, his wife’s and his own silk and gold clothing, and many jeweled ornaments; the sale continued for two full months.

After the victory, however, he returned the prices to the buyers who wished to return what they had purchased. He troubled no one who preferred to keep what he had bought. Yet this emperor, deceived by error, stained many of the good qualities of his character when he initiated by his edict the fourth persecution of Christians after Nero. It is therefore fitting briefly to touch upon those who flourished most notably in our doctrine during his reign or were crowned with martyrdom among the better known.

## CHAPTER XV. On Polycarp, the disciple of the apostle John and bishop of Smyrna

Polycarp, therefore, the disciple of the apostle John and ordained bishop of Smyrna by him, was the leading man of all Asia. For he had teachers who had seen some of the apostles and those who had seen the Lord, and he himself had seen them.

Because of certain questions concerning the day of Easter, under the emperor Antoninus Pius, while the Church at Rome was being governed by Anicetus, he came to Rome. There he brought back to the faith many believers who had been deceived by the persuasion of Marcion and Valentinus. When Marcion himself met him and said, “Recognize us,” he replied, “I recognize the firstborn of the devil.”

Later, under Marcus Antoninus and Lucius Aurelius Commodus, during the fourth persecution after Nero, while the proconsul was seated at Smyrna and the whole population was shouting against him in the amphitheater that he was, as it were, the father of the Christians, the greatest teacher of that sect, and an overturner of the gods, he was handed over to the fire after his glorious confession.

When a great flame had blazed up and, curving like a vaulted chamber, had stood above the martyr’s body in the form of a ship’s sail billowed by the wind, the officers of the crimes saw that the fire could not consume the body. They ordered the executioner to come closer and pierce with a sword the body from which the fire had recoiled.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the philosopher Justin, how greatly he labored in defending Christianity and how distinguished a legacy he left

Justin the philosopher, who also walked in the dress of philosophers, was from Neapolis, a city of Palestine, and his father was Priscus Bacchius. He labored greatly for the religion of Christ, to such an extent that he presented to Antoninus Pius, his sons, and the senate a book written against the Gentiles. He was not ashamed of the disgrace of the cross. He also presented another book to the successors of that same Antoninus, Marcus Antoninus Verus and Lucius Aurelius Commodus.

Another volume of his against the Gentiles survives, in which he also discusses the nature of demons; and a fourth work against the Gentiles, whose title he prefaced with *The Psalmist*; another on the monarchy of God; another book whose title he prefaced with *The Psalmist*; another on the soul; and a dialogue against the Jews, which he held with Trypho, a leading Jew.

He also wrote distinguished volumes against Marcion, which Irenaeus mentions in the fifth book of his *Against the Heresies*. There is also another book against all heresies, which he mentions in the *Apology* that he gave to Antoninus Pius.

While Justin was in Rome and was refuting Crescentus the Cynic, who blasphemed greatly against Christians, calling him a glutton, afraid of death, a betrayer of philosophy, and a follower of luxury and lust, he was eventually accused through Crescentus’s zeal and plots on the charge that he was a Christian, and shed his blood for Christ.

## CHAPTER XVII. On Hegesippus, the writer of ecclesiastical history, and the period in which he flourished

Hegesippus lived near the times of the apostles. He wove together histories of ecclesiastical events from the Passion of the Lord up to his own age, gathering here and there much that was useful to readers, and composed five books in simple language, so that in his speech as well he might portray the lives of those whose way of life he followed.

He asserts that he came to Rome under Anicetus, who was the tenth bishop after Peter, and remained there until Eleutherius, bishop of the same city, who had once been a disciple of Anicetus.

Moreover, while arguing against idols and explaining by what original error they had arisen, he added a history from which he shows in what period he flourished. For he says:

“They made tombs for the dead and temples, as we see to this day. Among these is Antinous, the slave of Caesar Hadrian; in the city of Antino, which he founded from that man’s name, a gymnastic contest is held in his honor, and he established prophets in his temple. Caesar Hadrian is said to have kept Antinous among his favorites.”
