Melito, an Asian from Sardis and bishop of that city, gave the emperor Marcus Antoninus Verus a book in defense of Christian doctrine.

He also wrote other works, of which the following are those we shall list: two books on Easter; one book on the life of the prophets; one on the Lord’s Day; one on faith; one on the creation; one on the senses; one on the soul and body; one on baptism; one on truth; one on the generation of Christ; one on his own prophecy; one on love of gifts; one on hospitality; another book entitled *The Key*; one on the devil; one on the Apocalypse of John; and six books of selected testimonies and excerpts.

Tertullian mocks his elegant and declamatory talent in the seven books he wrote against the Church on behalf of Montanus, saying that many of our people considered him a prophet.

Theophilus, the sixth bishop of the church of Antioch, composed a book against Marcion under the emperor Marcus Antoninus Verus; it survives to this day. Four volumes addressed to Autolycus are also attributed to him, as well as one book against the heresy of Hermogenes and other brief and elegant treatises concerned with the edification of the Church.

I have read, under his name, a Gospel and commentaries on the Proverbs of Solomon, but these do not seem to me to correspond with the elegance of the works mentioned above.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On Apollinaris of Hierapolis and Dionysius, bishops of Corinth

Apollinaris, bishop of Hierapolis in Asia, flourished under the emperor Marcus Antoninus Verus and gave him a distinguished volume in defense of the Christian faith. Five other books of his *Against the Gentiles* survive, as well as two books *On Truth* and a work *Against the Cataphrygians*, at the time when Montanus first began, together with Prisca and Maximilla, mad prophetesses.

Dionysius, bishop of the church of Corinth, possessed such eloquence and energy that by his letters he instructed not only the people of his own city and province but also those of other provinces and cities. Among these letters are one to the Lacedaemonians; another to the Athenians; a third to the Nicomedians; a fourth to the Erethrians; another to the church of Amastris and to the other churches of Pontus; a sixth to the Gnosians and to Philetus, bishop of that city; a seventh to the Romans, written to Soter, their bishop; and an eighth to Erisophora, a holy woman.

He flourished under the emperor Marcus Antoninus Verus and Lucius Aurelius Commodus.

Pinitus, bishop of Gnosia, a city of Crete, wrote to Dionysius, bishop of the Corinthians, a very elegant letter in which he teaches that the people should not always be nourished with milk, lest, like infants, they be overtaken by the final day, but that they should also eat solid food, so that they may advance toward spiritual maturity. He too flourished under Marcus Antoninus and Lucius Commodus.

## CHAPTER XIX. On Tatian, founder of the heresy of the Encratites

Tatian, who first taught rhetoric and acquired no small glory for himself through that rhetorical art, was a follower of the martyr Justin. He flourished in the Church as long as he did not withdraw from Justin’s side.

Afterward, puffed up by the swelling of his eloquence, he founded a new heresy called that of the Encratites. Severus later enlarged it, and from him the heretics of that same party are called Severians to this day.

Tatian wrote countless volumes. Among them, one book entitled *Against the Gentiles* survives as a work of great distinction and is said to be outstanding among all his writings. He too flourished under the emperor Marcus Antoninus Verus and Lucius Aurelius Commodus.

## CHAPTER XX. Catalogue of certain orthodox writers who published books against the heresy of the Marcionists

Philip, bishop of the Cretan city of Gnosia, whom Dionysius mentions in his letter written to the church of that same city, published a distinguished book against Marcion. He flourished in the time of Marcus Antoninus Verus and Lucius Aurelius Commodus.

Musanus, not undistinguished among those who wrote on ecclesiastical doctrine, composed under the emperor Marcus Antoninus Verus a book addressed to certain brothers who had turned from the Church toward the heresy of the Encratites.

Modestus, who likewise lived under the emperor Marcus Antoninus Verus and Lucius Aurelius, wrote a book against Marcion in the same manner; it survives to this day. Many other works are also attributed to him, but scholars reject them as spurious.

[Col. 1167A] Bardesanes was held in renown in Mesopotamia. At first a follower of Valentinus, and later his refuter, he founded a new heresy. His intellect was ardent; he was most eloquent in the language of the Syrians and a forceful dialectician. He wrote countless works against nearly all the heretics who had sprung up in his age.

Among them is that famous and powerful book which he published to Marcus Antoninus *On Fate*, as well as many other volumes written during the persecution, which his followers translated from Syriac into Greek. If such force and brilliance are found in the translation, what should we suppose was present in the original language?

## CHAPTER XXI. When the heresy of the Cataphrygians arose

Under the aforementioned emperor, many in Gaul were gloriously put to death for the name of Christ; their struggles, recorded in books, continue to the present day.

At that time the false prophecy called the heresy of the Cataphrygians also began, under the leadership of Montanus and the mad prophetesses Prisca and Maximilla.

In those same days Lucius, king of Britain, sent a letter to Eleutherius, bishop of Rome, and obtained that he might be made a Christian.

At that time, therefore, Fronto was considered a distinguished orator. He instructed the aforementioned Marcus Antoninus in Latin literature.

## CHAPTER XXII. On the unfortunate deeds of the emperor Commodus and on the teachers who flourished under him

Lucius Antoninus Commodus, the fifteenth after Augustus, succeeded his father in the kingdom and remained in it for thirteen years. He waged war successfully against the Germans.

For the rest, he was corrupted in every way by the disgrace of luxury and obscenity. He very often fought with gladiatorial weapons and frequently exposed himself to wild beasts in the amphitheater. He also killed very many senators, especially those whom he observed to excel in nobility and ability.

The punishment of the king’s crimes overtook the City. For the Capitol was struck by lightning, and the fire that resulted burned in a devouring whirlwind that library, constructed by the care and zeal of the ancestors, as well as other buildings standing nearby. Later another fire broke out at Rome and razed the temple of Vesta, the palace, and a very large part of the city to the ground.

Commodus, harmful to all, is said to have been strangled and killed in the house of Vestilianus. Even while alive he was judged an enemy of the human race. He showed what he would become at the very beginning. For when, as his father lay dying, he was warned not to allow the barbarians, already weakened, to recover their strength, he replied that affairs could be completed by the living, even if gradually, but that nothing could be done by the dead.

Among his other actions, the emperor Commodus ordered the head of the Colossus to be removed and the head of his own image placed upon it. Yet he did not decree that persecution should be carried out against Christians. Under him peace spread to the churches throughout the whole earth, and the word of the Lord gathered souls from every kind of people to the knowledge and worship of the supreme God.

Finally, in the city of Rome he brought many distinguished and very wealthy men, together with their children, wives, relatives, and the whole household alike, into fellowship in the faith. But that ancient enemy of human salvation did not look upon this with impartial eyes. He immediately attacked our people with various devices and consequently raised up many heretics.

Under this emperor Victor, the fourteenth bishop of the city of Rome, ruled the Church for ten years, writing certain short works on the question of Easter.

Irenaeus, a disciple of Photinus, who governed the church of Lugdunum in Gaul, was sent as an envoy to Rome by the martyrs of that place concerning certain questions of the Church. He brought Eleutherius, the bishop, an honorable letter concerning his own name. Later, when Photinus was nearly ninety years old and had been crowned with martyrdom for the name of Christ, Irenaeus was appointed in his place.

It is established that he was a disciple of Polycarp, the priest and martyr mentioned above. He wrote five books *Against the Heresies*, a short volume *Against the Gentiles*, another *On Discipline*, a work addressed to his brother Marcion *On Apostolic Preaching*, a book of various treatises, a work to Blastus *On Schism*, and one to Florinus *On the Monarchy*, or *That God Is Not the Author of Evils*. He also wrote an excellent work *On the Eighth*, at the end of which, indicating that he had lived near the times of the apostles, he adds:

> “I adjure you who transcribe this book, by our Lord Jesus Christ and by his glorious coming, at which he will judge the living and the dead, that after you have transcribed it you compare it and carefully correct it against the exemplar from which you copied it. You must likewise transfer this adjuration exactly as you found it in the exemplar.”

Letters of his to Victor, bishop of Rome, concerning the question of Easter are also circulated. In them he admonishes him that he ought not easily to sever the unity of his colleagues. For Victor had believed that many bishops of Asia and the East, who celebrated Easter with the Jews on the fourteenth day of the moon, ought to be condemned.

By this decision he brought many churches that had withdrawn from him back into peaceful concord. Irenaeus flourished especially under the emperor Commodus, who succeeded Marcus Antoninus Verus in the empire.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On Helvius Pertinax and Julian, his slayer

After Commodus, the aged Helvius Pertinax was created emperor by the senate. He was the sixteenth after Augustus and was killed in the palace, through the crime of Julian the jurist, in the sixth month after he had begun to reign.

He was a teacher of the literature transmitted by grammarians, more pleasant than beneficent. For this reason they called him by the Greek name *Chrestologon*. He was never moved by an injury he had received to seek revenge. He loved ordinary simplicity. After his death, the title “Divine” was decreed for him.

In his praise they repeatedly acclaimed him with applause until their voices failed:

> “While Pertinax ruled, we lived in safety; we feared no one—with a pious father, the father of the senate, the father of all good men.”

While he was emperor, the senate begged him to call his wife Augusta and his son Caesar, but he refused, declaring that it was enough that he himself ruled unwillingly.

After killing Pertinax, Julian seized the empire, but soon was defeated and killed by Severus in a civil war near the Milvian Bridge, in the seventh month after he had begun to reign. Thus one year was consumed between Pertinax and Julian.

Julian himself was a noble man, highly skilled in law, partisan, headstrong, and greedy for power.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the virtue and deeds of Severus, and on the fact that honors were not sold during his reign

Severus, an African by origin, from the city of Lepcis in Tripolitania, wished to be called Pertinax, after the name of the emperor whose death he had avenged. He was the seventeenth after Augustus. He obtained an abandoned empire and held it for seventeen years.

By nature harsh and constantly challenged by many wars, he ruled the state with great courage but with immense labor. He defeated and killed Pescennius Niger, who had aspired to tyranny in Egypt and Syria, at Cyzicus.

He either suppressed or restrained the Jews and Samaritans when they attempted rebellion by force of arms. He defeated the Parthians, Arabs, and Adiabenians.

In the fifth persecution of Christians after Nero, he tortured Christians, and very many of the saints throughout the various provinces were crowned with martyrdom.

God’s heavenly vengeance immediately followed this profane presumption of Severus against Christians and the Church of God. For Severus was immediately carried—or rather dragged—back to Gaul from Syria for a third civil war. He had already waged one war at Rome against Julian and another in Syria against Pescennius. A third was being stirred up by Clodius Albinus, Julian’s associate in the killing of Pertinax, who had made himself Caesar in Gaul. In this war much Roman blood was shed on both sides.

Albinus, however, was overwhelmed and killed near Lugdunum. Severus, victorious, was drawn into Britain because nearly all his allies had fallen away. There, after many great and serious battles, he thought that the part of the island he had recovered should be separated from the remaining unconquered peoples by a rampart.

Accordingly, he drew across the land a great and very strong wall, further fortified with frequent towers, for a distance of one hundred and thirty-two thousand paces from sea to sea. There, near the town of Eboracum, he died of illness.

The writers of the annals say of him that he was the sharpest in intellect of all who had preceded him, pressing to completion everything he had undertaken; that his benevolence was remarkable and enduring toward those to whom he inclined; that he was diligent in seeking and generous in giving; and that he was equally forceful toward friends and enemies.

He permitted no one during his rule to sell honors. He was adequately instructed in Latin literature, educated in the Greek language, and more fluent in Punic eloquence. He left two sons, Bassianus and Geta. Geta, declared a public enemy, died. Bassianus, surnamed Antoninus, assumed and obtained the kingdom.

## CHAPTER XXV. On Aurelius Antoninus and his deeds

Aurelius Antoninus Bassianus, also called Caracalla, obtained the principate as the eighteenth after Augustus and remained in it for seven years less a fraction.

He lived more harshly than his father. He was more immoderate than any man in lust and even married his stepmother Julia.

He killed his brother Geta, and for this crime he paid the penalty in a frenzy and under the pursuit of the Furies, who are rightly called avengers; afterward he recovered from his madness.

When he saw the body of Alexander of Macedon, he ordered himself to be called Alexander the Great. He was led to this by the deceptions of flatterers, so that he walked with a grim expression and his neck turned toward his left shoulder, a feature he had observed in Alexander’s manner.

He was called Caracalla from the ankle-length garment—*caracalla*—which he ordered the common people who came to greet him to wear.

While preparing to wage war against the Parthians, he was surrounded by enemies and killed between Edessa and Carrhae.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the emperor Macrinus

After Bassianus, the nineteenth after Augustus was Ophilus Macrinus, who had been prefect of the praetorian guard. Together with his son Diadumenian, he seized the empire. But after a year had passed, he was killed immediately in a military revolt at Archelais.

Since Severus and his son Antoninus had decreed the fifth persecution of Christians after Nero, I shall briefly note which distinguished men flourished in our doctrine under them or attained the palm of martyrdom, insofar as I have been able to discover their memory.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the teachers who flourished under the aforementioned emperors
Panthenus, a philosopher of the Stoic school, possessed, in accordance with an ancient custom in Alexandria—where, ever since Mark the evangelist, there had always been teachers of the Church—such wisdom and learning in the Scriptures as well as in secular literature that, when requested by the people of that nation, he was sent to India as an envoy by Demetrius, bishop of Alexandria. There he discovered that Bartholomew, one of the twelve apostles, had preached the coming of Christ according to the Gospel of Matthew, written in Hebrew letters; returning to Alexandria, he brought it back with him. Many commentaries of his on Holy Scripture survive. But he benefited the churches much more by his living voice, and he taught under the emperor Severus and Antoninus, surnamed Caracalla.

Rhodo, an Asian by birth, was instructed at Rome in the Scriptures by Tatian, whom we mentioned above. He published many works, especially three treatises against Marcion, in which he explains how the Marcionites themselves disagree among one another. He also relates that he had once discovered Apelles, an old heretic, and, having engaged him in debate, convicted him of teaching many things that were evil. Finally he asked him what he believed about God; Apelles replied that he did not know the God whom he worshiped. In the same book, which he wrote to Coelestion, Rhodo mentions that he had been Tatian’s assistant at Rome. He also composed elegant treatises on the Hexaemeron, and a notable work against the Cataphrygians. He flourished in the times of Commodus and Severus.

Clement, presbyter of the Alexandrian church and a pupil of Panthenus, whom we mentioned above, took charge of the ecclesiastical school at Alexandria after Panthenus’s death and served as its teacher. His distinguished volumes are in circulation, full of learning and eloquence, concerning both the divine Scriptures and the instruments of secular literature. Among them are the following: seven books Against the Nations; one book of the Instructor; three books On Easter; one book On the Question of Fasting; and another book entitled Who Is the Rich Man Who Is Saved from Detraction?; one book On the Ecclesiastical Canons; and Against Those Who Follow the Error of the Jews; and one book which he wrote specifically to Alexander, bishop of Jerusalem.

In his Stromata he mentions Tatian’s volume Against the Nations, which we discussed above, and the chronography of a certain Cassianus, although I was unable to find that little work. He also mentions Aristobulus, Demetrius, and Eupolemus, Jewish writers against the nations, who, in the manner of Josephus, uphold Moses and the Jewish people.

There also survives a letter of Alexander, bishop of Jerusalem, who later governed the church together with Narcissus, concerning the ordination of Asclepiades the confessor. It was addressed to the Antiochenes as a congratulatory letter, in which he writes, saying:

> “I have sent this letter to you, brothers of the Lord, through the blessed presbyter Clement, an illustrious and approved man, whom you also know and now know more fully.”

When he came, in accordance with the wisdom and visitation of the Lord, he strengthened and increased the Church of the Lord. It is agreed that Adamantius was his disciple.

In the times of Severus and his son Antoninus, Miltiades flourished. Rhodo mentions him in his work composed against Montanus, Prisca, and Maximilla. He wrote a distinguished volume against those same persons, as well as other books against the nations and the Jews, and he presented the emperors of that period with an *Apologeticus*.

Apollonius, a most eloquent man, wrote against Montanus, Prisca, and Maximilla a distinguished and lengthy volume. In it he asserts that Montanus and his mad prophetesses perished by hanging, and he reports many other things concerning Prisca and Maximilla:

> “If they deny that they received gifts, let them admit that they are not prophets. If they do receive them—and I shall prove this by a thousand witnesses—are prophets shown not to be prophets by their other fruits? Tell me: Does a prophet dye her hair? Does a prophet paint her eyes with antimony? Is a prophet adorned with clothing and jewels? Does a prophet play at the board and with dice? Let them answer whether these things may be done or not. It is my task to prove that they did them.”

In the same book he says that forty years had elapsed up to the time when he himself wrote the book, counting from the beginning of the Cataphrygian heresy.

Tertullian, after publishing six volumes against the Church, which he wrote on ecstasy, prepared eight against Apollonius, in which he attempts to defend everything Apollonius had attacked. Apollonius flourished under the emperors Commodus and Severus.

Serapion was ordained bishop of Antioch in the eleventh year of the emperor Commodus. He wrote a letter to Caristus and Pontius concerning the heresy of Montanus and added the following:

> “But so that you may know that the madness of this false doctrine, that is, of the new prophecy, is rejected by the whole world, I have sent you the letters of the most blessed Apollinaris, who was bishop of Hierapolis in Asia.”

He also composed a volume To the Lord, concerning the one who had withdrawn to the Jews during the persecution, and another book on the Gospel circulated under the name of Peter, addressed to the church of Rhossus in Cilicia, which had turned toward that heresy through reading it. Brief letters of his are also read here and there, consistent with the character and life of their author.

Apollonius, a senator of the city of Rome under the emperor Commodus, was betrayed by a slave because he was a Christian. When the emperor ordered him to give an account of his faith, he composed a distinguished volume. After he read it in the senate, he was nevertheless condemned by the sentence of the senate and beheaded, since an old law among them provided that Christians who had once been brought before their tribunal were not to be released without a trial.

Theophilus, bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, formerly called the Tower of Strato, under the emperor Severus composed, together with the other bishops, a synodal and very useful letter against those who celebrated Easter with the Jews on the fourteenth day of the moon.

Bachylus, bishop of Corinth, was regarded as eminent under the same emperor Severus. He wrote an elegant book on Easter, representing all the bishops who were in Asia.

Polycrates, bishop of the Ephesians, together with the other bishops of Asia who, in accordance with an ancient custom, celebrated Easter with the Jews on the fourteenth day of the moon, wrote a synodal letter against Victor, bishop of Rome. In it he declares that he follows the authority of the apostle John and of the ancients. We have excerpted the following brief passages from it:

> “We therefore celebrate the day without violation, neither adding nor taking away. For in Asia great luminaries have fallen asleep, and they will rise on the day of the Lord, when he will come from heaven in glory and raise up all the saints: I speak of Philip, one of the twelve apostles, who fell asleep at Hierapolis; and his two daughters, who grew old as virgins; and another daughter of his, who, filled with the Holy Spirit, fell asleep at Ephesus; and John, who reclined upon the breast of the Lord and was his priest, bearing the golden plate upon his forehead, a martyr and teacher, who fell asleep at Ephesus; and Polycarp, bishop, following the ecclesiastical rule. I too, Polycrates, the least of all, according to the teaching of my relatives, whom I followed—for seven of my relatives were bishops in succession, and I am the eighth—have always celebrated Easter when the Jewish people were eating unleavened bread. Therefore, brothers, being sixty-five years old in the Lord and instructed by many brothers from throughout the world through the grace of all Scripture, I shall not fear those who threaten us.”

> “For my predecessors said: ‘We must obey God rather than human beings.’”

I have included these words to show, from this brief work, the man’s character and authority. He flourished in the time of the emperor Severus.

At the same time in which Narcissus was present at Jerusalem, Heraclitus, under the rule of Commodus and Severus, composed many commentaries on the Apostle.

Maximus, under the same emperors, discussed in a distinguished volume the famous question: “Whence comes evil, and was matter made by God?”

Candidus, during the reigns of the emperors mentioned above, published very fine treatises on the Hexaemeron.

Apion likewise composed treatises on the Hexaemeron under the emperor Severus.

Sixtus wrote a book On the Resurrection under the emperor Severus.

Arabianus, under the same emperor, published some little works relating to Christian doctrine.

Judas discussed at great length the seventy weeks in Daniel and carried the succession of earlier times down to the tenth year of the emperor Severus. In this he is shown to have been mistaken, because he predicted that the coming of the Antichrist would occur around his own time. He did so because the magnitude of the persecutions threatened the present world with its end.

Tertullian, a presbyter, is placed first among the Latins after Victor and Apollonius. He belonged to the province of Africa and the city of Carthage, and his father was a centurion in the proconsular service. A man of sharp and forceful intellect, he flourished especially under the emperor Severus and Antoninus Caracalla. He wrote many volumes, but since they are known to very many people, we pass them over.

Jerome reports the following about him:

> “I myself saw a certain Paul, an old man from Concordia, which is a town in Italy. He said that, when he himself was still a young man, he had been the secretary of the blessed Cyprian, already advanced in age. When he came to Rome, he used to say and report that Cyprian never let a day pass without reading Tertullian, and that he often said to him, ‘Give me the teacher,’ clearly meaning Tertullian.”

Tertullian was a presbyter in the Church until middle age. Later, because of the envy and insults of the clergy of the Roman Church, he fell into the doctrine of Montanus and mentions the new prophecy in many books. In particular, he composed volumes against the Church: On Persecution, On Modesty, On Fasts, and On Monogamy; six books On Ecstasy; and six which he composed against Apollonius. He is said to have lived into extreme old age and to have produced many little works that no longer survive.

In the tenth year of Severus Pertinax, when persecution had arisen against the Christians, Adamantius was left poor, with six brothers and his widowed mother, after his father Leonides had been crowned with the martyrdom of Christ. He was about seventeen years old. The treasury had seized his family property because of his confession of Christ.

In the seventeenth year of his age, at Alexandria, when the Church was scattered, he began his work. He was appointed in place of Clement the presbyter by Demetrius, bishop of that city, and flourished for many years.

At that time Perpetua and Felicitas suffered for Christ on the Nones of March at Carthage in Africa, being assigned to the beasts in the military camp. Alexander also became distinguished because of his confession of the Lord’s name.

During these times Narcissus, bishop of Jerusalem, became distinguished and exceedingly famous. We have already mentioned him above. We shall recall only one event concerning him, by which credible belief may rightly be given to the other things reported about him.

Once, on the solemn day of the Paschal vigil, oil was lacking for the lamps. When the ministers reported this, the people were overcome with great sorrow. But Narcissus, trusting in faith, ordered the ministers to draw water and bring it to him. When they had brought it, he prayed over the water and blessed it, then commanded that it be poured into the lamps. Suddenly, by a wondrous kind of power unheard of in the ages, the nature of the water was changed into the richness of oil, and it gave forth a light even brighter than usual.

As proof of the event, some of the religious brothers preserved from that same oil which had been changed from water, so that for many years it continued to provide evidence of the miracle.

How great his courage was will likewise be shown by one other deed of his.

Among his other virtues, he was a man of very steadfast character and unshakably devoted to justice and uprightness. Certain wicked little men, conscious of their own evil and fearing that, if they were accused, they would be unable to escape punishment for their crimes, acted in advance through conspiracy and sought to circumvent the judgment they feared.

Accordingly, they fabricated against him a disgraceful and harmful charge. They gathered informers and produced witnesses from among themselves, who under oath confirmed the accusations brought forward. One of these witnesses testified that he was speaking the truth, lest he be consumed by fire; another, lest he be afflicted with jaundice; a third, lest he be deprived of his sight.

Although no faithful and God-fearing person believed anyone on the basis of such oaths, since Narcissus’s life, conduct, and chastity were known to everyone, he himself, unable to bear the indignity and annoyance of the proceedings and at the same time always desiring to live a secluded and philosophical life, withdrew from the crowds of the Church and hid for many years in deserted places and more remote little fields.

But that great eye of divine Providence does not rest for long. Through the very curses they had invoked in their perjuries, it brought punishment upon the wicked.

The first witness’s house was set on fire at night by a small spark, and he himself, together with his entire household and family, was consumed by avenging flames. The other was suddenly filled and destroyed by jaundice from the soles of his feet to the crown of his head—the very disease he had called down upon himself.

The third, seeing the destruction of the others and perceiving that the divine eye had not overlooked him, came forward and, in the hearing of everyone, disclosed, in belated repentance, the whole sequence of the crime they had devised. He wept over the enormity of the deed committed with such abundant tears, yet day and night he continued in his weeping until he was deprived of his sight.

Thus these men suffered punishments of this sort for their fabrication.

Narcissus therefore led a solitary and philosophical life until three successions of bishops had been appointed in his place. Since Narcissus had withdrawn into the wilderness and hidden himself in such remote places that no one knew where he lived, the bishops considered it necessary to appoint another in his place, whose name was Dius.

After Dius had presided over the Church for a short time, Germanus succeeded him, and Nigordius succeeded Germanus. Then suddenly, as though restored to life and returned from heaven, Narcissus appeared unexpectedly. The brothers again begged him to preside over the Church.

Their love for him had been stirred all the more strongly, both because he had yielded to the criminals despite his innocence, because he loved a secluded and philosophical life, and because the Lord had fulfilled in him the saying: “Vengeance is mine; I will repay.”

We have reported these things about Narcissus because in certain Chronicles another bishop named Narcissus is said to have been the fourth after him at Jerusalem. This is asserted by those who fail entirely to consider his return, after three intervening bishops, to his former see.

Now, since we have mentioned many teachers under the emperors named above and the deeds of those same men, our stomach growing weary and our pen failing, we here bring the second book to an end.

# BOOK THREE

[Col. 1175]

## CHAPTER I. On the Crimes and Wicked Deeds of the Worst Emperor, Marcus Aurelius Antoninus

At this time of persecutions I have taken care to note, in part, how many and what kind of teachers of the churches and strong defenders of our faith there were, so that, seeing the wondrous providence of God, we may strive, as he grants it, to praise more earnestly and give thanks for his omnipotence and for his clemency toward the human race.

For he graciously and wondrously enlarged the Church redeemed by his blood, while the whole world rose up against it. The proud ancient enemy did not cease to bring against it terrors from outsiders, deaths from our own people, and various doctrines of schisms, grieving as he saw human salvation and his own stripping and expulsion. But the more the Church was pressed on every side by the faithless and by schismatic men deceived through the devil’s fraud, the more nobly it spread, grew, and was strengthened among very many people.

Now, beginning the third book, let us return to the work we began.

Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, the twentieth emperor after Augustus, obtained the imperial power and held it for four years. He had been a priest of the temple of Heliogabalus and left behind no respectable memory of himself, but only the infamy of sexual crimes and every kind of obscenity.

When he came to Rome amid the great expectation of the soldiers and senate, he defiled himself with every disgrace. Since, through a defect of nature, he could not yet attain the sexual gratification he desired, he turned his desire upon himself and ordered that he be called Bassiana by a woman’s name instead of Bassianus. He joined a Vestal virgin to himself as though in marriage, and, after having his genitals cut off, dedicated himself to the Great Mother.

Then he made his cousin Marcellus, later called Alexander, Caesar. He himself was killed in a military uprising.

His body was dragged through the streets of the city by the soldiers like a dog’s corpse. In a military jest they called him the little bitch of untamed and greedy lust. Finally, when the narrow opening of the sewer could not receive the body, it was taken as far as the Tiber and thrown into the river. He lived for sixteen years.

## CHAPTER II. On the Emperor Aurelius Alexander, What Happened During His Reign, and Origen, the Distinguished Teacher

Aurelius Alexander, the twenty-first emperor after Augustus, was made emperor by the will of the senate and the soldiers. He was a model of worthy justice for thirteen years. His mother, Mammaea, was a Christian and arranged to hear the presbyter Origen.

After immediately undertaking an expedition against the Persians, he defeated and crushed their king Xerxes in a great war. With Ulpian as his assessor, he displayed the highest moderation in governing the state; but he was killed in a military uprising at Mainz.

During his reign, the baths called the Alexandrian Baths were built at Rome, and at Nicopolis Actiaca—that is, in Epirus—the edition of the divine Scriptures called the sixth edition was found in a jar.

Urbanus, bishop of Rome, brought many nobles to faith in Christ and to martyrdom.

Origen was regarded as distinguished at Alexandria—indeed, throughout the world. Finally, as I mentioned above, Mammaea, the mother of Alexander, arranged to hear him, and summoned him to Antioch, where she held him in the highest honor.

Since we have mentioned above this same Origen, who was also called Adamantius, and have now mentioned him again, let us discuss him more fully.

When he had already reached middle age, and was passing through Palestine under the testimony of an ecclesiastical letter on behalf of the churches of Achaea, which were being troubled by very many heresies, he was ordained presbyter by Theotistus and Alexander, bishops of Caesarea and Jerusalem. This offended Demetrius, who raged against him with such madness that he wrote throughout the whole world concerning his name.

It is established that, before he moved to Caesarea, Origen had been at Rome under the bishop Severinus. Immediately after returning to Alexandria, he made Heraclas, a presbyter who continued in the dress of a philosopher, his assistant. Heraclas later governed the church of Alexandria after Demetrius.

How great his glory was is evident from the fact that Firmilianus, bishop of Caesarea, invited him, together with all Cappadocia, and kept him for a long time. Later, when Firmilianus came to Palestine under the pretext of visiting the holy places, he was instructed by Origen for a long time in the Holy Scriptures.

It is also evident from the fact that Origen came to Antioch at the request of the religious woman Mammaea, the emperor Alexander’s mother, and was held there in the highest honor. He also wrote letters to the emperor Philip, who was the first of the Roman emperors to be a Christian, and to Philip’s mother; these letters still exist today.

Who does not know that he devoted himself so intensely to the Holy Scriptures that, contrary to the character of his age and nation, he learned the Hebrew language and, apart from the translators of the Seventy, gathered together the other editions into one collection: those of Aquila, the Pontic proselyte; of Theodotion; of Bebioneus; and of Symmachus, who belonged to the same doctrine?

He also wrote a commentary on the Gospel according to Matthew, in which he attempts to affirm his own doctrine. Moreover, he found the fifth, sixth, and seventh editions, which we too possess from his library, through extraordinary labor, and compared them with the other editions.

And, not to remain entirely silent about his immortal intellect, he also learned dialectic, geometry, music, grammar, arithmetic, rhetoric, and every school of philosophy. He had many followers among students devoted to secular literature, to whom he lectured daily; and crowds came to him in a remarkable manner.

He received them for this reason: that under the pretext of secular learning he might instruct them in the faith of Christ.

Therefore, if anyone wishes to know the condition of Adamantius and what happened to him, he can learn it clearly, first from his letters sent to various people after the persecution, then from Book VI of Eusebius of Caesarea’s *Ecclesiastical History*, and from the volumes of Adamantius himself.

He lived until the time of Gallus and Volusianus—that is, until the sixty-ninth year of his life—and died at Tyre, where he was buried.

Some report about him that, because of his great eloquence, he attempted to establish certain perverse doctrines in books entitled *Periarchon* (*On First Principles*). In these books, besides many things contrary to sound doctrine, he also asserts concerning the transformation of the whole rational creation that not only the souls of wicked human beings but even the devil himself, after a long purification, will be restored and return to the dignity of his origin. There will always be successive revolutions from good to evil and from evil to good, because this alternation cannot fail to be perpetual, so that in turn the blessed become wretched and the wretched become blessed.

At that time Geminus, a presbyter of Antioch; Hippolytus; and Berillus, bishop of Bostra in Arabia, were also regarded as distinguished writers.

## CHAPTER III. On Maximinus the Persecutor and His Successors, Gordian the Father and the Grandson, Who Were Killed After Succeeding One Another Within a Short Interval

Maximinus, the twenty-second emperor after Augustus, of Gothic origin, was made emperor by the army without the consent of the senate after successfully waging war in Germany. He carried out the sixth persecution against the Christians after Nero. But immediately, in the third year of his reign, he was killed by Pupienus at Aquileia and brought an end to both his persecution and his life.

His son was torn apart with him, while everyone shouted in the military camp that, because he came from so evil a stock, he was not even fit to be kept as a puppy.

Maximinus had sent the persecution against priests and clerics—that is, teachers—especially because of the Christian household of Alexander, whom he had succeeded, and of Alexander’s mother Mammaea, and especially because of the presbyter Origen. He also persecuted the wealthy, the innocent, and the guilty alike, driven by greed.

After his reign, the two Gordians, father and son, seized the imperial power, and one after the other perished. Likewise Pupienus and Balbinus, seizing the kingdom, were killed under the aforementioned Maximinus, and Antherus, bishop of the city of Rome, was crowned with martyrdom.

Gordian, the grandson of Gordian, was made emperor, the twenty-third after Augustus, and remained in power for six years.

Gordian, still a very young boy and about to depart for the East to wage war against the Parthians—as Eutropius writes—opened the gates of Janus. I do not remember reading that anyone had closed them after Vespasian and Titus, although Cornelius Tacitus reports that Vespasian himself opened them again after one year.

Gordian therefore, after winning great battles successfully against the Parthians, was killed by the treachery of his own men not far from Roman territory—as some report, through the conspiracy of Philip, the prefect of the praetorium.

The soldiers built a tomb for this Gordian overlooking the Euphrates, after his bones had been carried back to Rome.

## CHAPTER IV. The Period in Which Julius Africanus Flourished

At this time Julius Africanus was regarded as distinguished among ecclesiastical writers. In the *Chronicles* which he wrote, he reports that he hurried to Alexandria, summoned by the exceedingly celebrated reputation of Heraclas, who, according to what fame declared, was most learned in both divine and philosophical studies and in every branch of Greek learning.

During those days, at Caesarea in Palestine, Origen imbued with divine philosophy the young brothers Theodore, surnamed Gregory, and Athenodorus, later the most distinguished bishops of Pontus.

## CHAPTER V. On Philip, Father and Son, the First Christian Emperors

Philip, the twenty-fourth emperor after Augustus, was made emperor and made his son Philip his colleague in the reign. He remained in power for seven years.

He was the first of all the emperors to be a Christian. After the third year of his reign, the thousandth year from the founding of Rome was completed.

It was celebrated with such magnificent games, the most splendid of all those previously held, that innumerable beasts were killed in the great circus, theatrical games were held in the Campus Martius for three days and nights while the people kept vigil, and a contest marking a thousand years was conducted. This anniversary was celebrated under a Christian emperor.

There is no doubt that Philip attributed the grace and honor of such great devotion to Christ and the Church, since no authority shows either that he ascended the Capitol or that he sacrificed victims according to custom.

Nevertheless, both father and son were killed in different places by a military uprising and through the treachery of Decius.

During these days Origen responded in eight volumes to a certain philosopher, Celsus the Epicurean, who had written books against us. To put it briefly, he was so diligent in writing that Jerome records in one place that he had read five thousand of Origen’s books.

## CHAPTER VI. On Decius, Persecutor of the Christians

Decius, the twenty-fifth emperor after Augustus, seized the imperial power after killing the Philips. He held it for one year and three months. He had been both the instigator and suppressor of civil war.

Immediately, after teaching by this act that he had killed Philip for that very reason, he issued savage edicts for persecuting and killing Christians—the seventh persecution after Nero—and sent very many saints from their tortures to the crowns of Christ.

Eusebius reports on this persecution in Book VI of his *Ecclesiastical History*, and the records of the martyrdoms of very many sufferers bear witness to it.

In this persecution Fabianus was brought to completion by martyrdom in the city of Rome. Alexander, bishop of Jerusalem, was killed at Caesarea in Palestine, and Babylas at Antioch.

But, as Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria, reports, this persecution did not begin from an imperial command. Rather, a full year before the imperial edicts, the minister of demons—who was called divine in our city—anticipated the official decrees and stirred up a superstitious mob against us.

Decius made his son Caesar, a man equipped with deeds and virtues, gentle and approachable at home, and most ready for military service. But because he carried out persecution against the Christians, he received this reward: in barbarian territory he was drowned in a swamp amid confused crowds, so that even his body could not be found. His son, however, was killed in battle when the Goths fought against him.

## CHAPTER VII. On Gallus and Volusianus, and What Happened During Their Rule Among Teachers and in Other Matters Worth Remembering

Gallus Hostilianus, the twenty-sixth emperor after Augustus, obtained the kingdom and lived for two years in power with his son Volusianus.

Retribution for the violated name of the Christians arose. For as long as the edicts of Decius continued in force for the destruction of the churches, the plague of extraordinary diseases extended itself, so that scarcely any Roman province, city, or household remained that was not corrupted and devastated by that general pestilence.

The blessed Cyprian’s book, written concerning this mortality, bears witness to it. As Dionysius reports, Gallus and Volusianus, notorious even for this one calamity, were killed while undertaking civil war against Aemilianus, who was attempting a revolution.

Aemilianus, however, was killed in the third month after seizing the tyranny.

Yet Gallus could neither avoid nor even foresee the evil of Decius; he stumbled against the same stone of offense. Although at the beginning his reign flourished and everything proceeded according to his wishes, he persecuted the holy men who were praying to the supreme God for the peace of his reign. With them he drove away both his prosperity and his peace.

Origen died before completing his seventieth year and was buried in the city of Tyre, as we stated above.

At the request of a certain matron named Lucina, Cornelius, bishop of Rome, lifted the bodies of the apostles from their tombs at night and placed that of Paul on the Ostian Way, where he had been beheaded; and that of Peter near the place where he had been crucified, among the bodies of the holy bishops, in the temple of Apollo on the Golden Mount in the Vatican, at the palace of Nero, on the third day before the Kalends of July.

Under the emperors just mentioned, Cornelius was crowned with martyrdom. Cyprian’s letters to him survive.

At this time Novatus, a presbyter of Cyprian, came to Rome and joined himself to Novatian and the other confessors, because Cornelius had received repentant apostates.

Inflated by a certain arrogance, Novatus entirely deprived them of the hope of salvation, even if they had repented worthily. Thus he became the founder of the heresy of the Novatians. Separated from the Church, they called themselves, under a proud name, *Cathari*, that is, “the pure.”

For this reason a very celebrated council of priests was assembled in the city of Rome, numbering sixty bishops and an equal number of presbyters, together with very many deacons. Moreover, after careful deliberation had been held throughout the individual provinces concerning this matter, the decrees indicate what needed to be done.

It was therefore determined that Novatus, together with those who followed him in his mental arrogance and those who had turned aside to this inhuman judgment that preserved nothing of brotherly love, should be regarded as alien from the Church. Those who had fallen in the struggle, however, were to be cared for with brotherly compassion and healed with the remedies of repentance.

Dionysius, the remarkable teacher of Alexandria and author of many books, flourished at this time. Concerning the lapsed, he refutes Novatus’s error in the following manner:

> “These divine martyrs, therefore, who sit with Christ in the heavenly places and share in his kingdom and judgment, who judge with him concerning the fallen brothers—these very men, he says, received the fallen into repentance and did not reject their conversion, knowing that our God, whose martyrs they were, does not at all desire the death of one who dies, but seeks his conversion and repentance. If, therefore, they received certain people, restored them to the Church, and shared with them in prayer and food, what do you wish us to do, brothers? What do you think we ought to do? Should we not follow their judgment and agree with their decision?”

Cornelius likewise refuted this madness with the strongest arguments.

Cyprian, who wrote much about the lapsed and the penitent, maintained that the penitent should be received to such an extent that even if, at the final moment of life, they lamented their sins with groaning, one ought not to despair of their salvation.

The teachers who flourished under the emperors mentioned above and distinguished themselves by writing and struggling, although we have already mentioned some of them, we shall nevertheless briefly note again their deeds worthy of remembrance.

Ammonius, an eloquent man and highly learned in philosophy, was regarded as distinguished at Alexandria during this same period. Among the many illustrious monuments of his intellect, he also composed an elegant work On the Harmony of Moses and Jesus and devised the evangelical canons, which Eusebius of Caesarea later followed.

Porphyry falsely accuses him of having been a pagan after being a Christian, whereas it is established that he remained a Christian until the end of his life.

Ambrose, at first a Marcionite and afterward corrected by Adamantius, was a deacon of the Church and distinguished by the glory of confessing the Lord. For Ambrose, together with the presbyter Protheotistus, Adamantius wrote a book on martyrdom.

Through Ambrose’s industry, expense, and persistence, Adamantius dictated innumerable volumes. Ambrose himself, being a nobleman, was also a man of elegant intellect, as his letters to Adamantius show. He died before Adamantius and is criticized by many on this account: that, although wealthy, he did not remember his aged and poor friend.

Triphon, a pupil of Adamantius, to whom some of Adamantius’s letters survive, was highly eloquent in the Scriptures. Many of his little works, scattered here and there, demonstrate this; especially the book he composed on the red heifer in Deuteronomy and on the spices, dove, and turtledove mentioned by Abraham in Genesis.

Minucius Felix, a distinguished advocate at Rome, wrote a dialogue between Christians and pagans entitled *Octavius*. Another work is also circulated under his name, *On Fate*, or *Against the Mathematicians*. Although this too is the work of an eloquent man, it does not seem to me to accord with the style of the earlier book. Lactantius also mentions this Minucius in his books.

Gaius composed a very distinguished volume containing a disputation against Proculus, a follower of Montanus. He accused Proculus of rashness in defending the new prophecy. In the same volume he enumerates only thirteen letters of Paul, saying that the fourteenth, which is circulated as the letter to the Hebrews, is not Paul’s, although among the Romans it is regarded as Paul’s.

Berillus, the last bishop of Arabia, after governing the Church religiously for some time, finally fell into the heresy that denies that Christ existed before the incarnation. Corrected by Adamantius, he wrote various little works, especially letters in which he gives thanks to Adamantius. Letters from Adamantius to him also exist.

There is also a dialogue between Adamantius and Berillus in which the heresy is refuted.

Berillus flourished under Alexander, son of Mammaea, and under Maximinus and Gordian, who succeeded Alexander in the imperial power.

## CHAPTER VIII. On Certain Orthodox Teachers Who Flourished Under Gallus and Volusianus
Hippolytus, bishop of a certain church (for I have not been able to learn the name of the city), in his exposition of Easter [Col. 1181C] and in the calendar of the seasons which he composed, carries his account down to the first year of the emperor Alexander. He discovered a sixteen-year cycle, which the Greeks call a *cycle*; and Eusebius, who composed a nineteen-year cycle concerning the same Easter, writes on this occasion:

“He published commentaries on some of the Scriptures, among which he found the following: on the Hexaemeron, Exodus, the Song of Songs, Genesis, Zechariah, the Psalms, Isaiah, Daniel, the Apocalypse, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, Saul and the Witch of Endor, the Antichrist, and the Resurrection; also against Marcion, on Easter, and against all heresies; and on the praise of the Lord and Savior, concerning which he indicates that he spoke in the presence of Adamantius.”

In rivalry with him, Ambrose—whom we have said was corrected from the heresy of Marcion to the true faith—urged Adamantius to write commentaries on the Scriptures. He provided him with seven or more stenographers, together with their expenses, and an equal number of copyists; and, greater still, he demanded work from him every day with incredible zeal. Hence, in a certain letter, he also calls him “Adamantius.”

When Alexander, bishop of Cappadocia, was traveling to Jerusalem out of a longing for the holy places, and Narcissus, bishop of that city, already advanced in age, was governing the church, it was revealed then to Narcissus and to many of his clergy that Alexander would enter the city the following morning as bishop, destined to be an assistant to the episcopal or priestly see. And so, when everything had happened as foretold, all the bishops of Palestine having assembled together, and Narcissus himself, bishop of the Jerusalem church, exerting himself above all, Alexander assumed the governance with him. At the end of a certain letter which he wrote to Adamantius and on behalf of Adamantius, Alexander speaks as follows concerning the peace of the Church:

“Narcissus greets you—the old man who held this episcopal office before me and who now governs it with me through his prayers, being about one hundred and sixteen years old—and he prays with me that you may hold one and the same judgment.”

He also wrote another letter to the Antiochenes through Clement, the presbyter of Alexandria, whom we mentioned above; likewise to Adamantius and on behalf of Adamantius against Demetrius, and stating that he had appointed Adamantius presbyter in accordance with a good testimony. Other letters of his to various persons are also reported.

During the seventh persecution, under Decius, at which time Babylas suffered at Antioch, Alexander was brought to Caesarea and confined in prison, and he was crowned with martyrdom on account of his confession of Christ.

Julius Africanus, whose five books *On the Seasons* are extant, lived under the emperor Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, who had succeeded Macrinus. He had received from the emperor the commission to restore Emmaus in Judaea, which was thereafter called Nicopolis. His is a letter to Adamantius concerning the question of Susanna, since he says that it is regarded as a story in Hebrew and does not correspond with the Hebrew text. Against this letter Adamantius wrote a learned response. Another letter of his to Aristides is extant, in which he argued at full length concerning the apparent discrepancy in the genealogy of the Savior according to Luke.

Geminus, a presbyter of the Antiochene church, composed a few monuments of his talent. He flourished under the emperor Alexander. Sebennus, bishop of his native city, flourished especially at the time when Heraclas was ordained bishop of the Alexandrian church.

Thus Valerian, the twenty-seventh emperor after Augustus, was made emperor by the army in Raetia.

## CHAPTER IX. On the deeds of the emperors Valerian and Gallienus, and on the teachers or martyrs who lived at that time

At Rome his son Gallienus was proclaimed Augustus by the senate and remained in power for fifteen years, although misfortunes were pressing upon him from every side. It is therefore remarkable what happened with Valerian: above all those who had preceded him, he showed himself humane and kind toward the servants of God, so that at the beginning he even seemed much kinder to them than those who were at least called Christians by name. He revered the servants of the Lord so greatly that his entire household was a church of God.

But he was corrupted and cast down from the truth by a certain exceedingly wicked teacher, the master and prince of the Egyptian magicians, so that he ordered just and holy men to be persecuted and killed, as though they opposed the magical arts to which he had subjected himself. For there really were—and still are—men who, by the power of their merits, can extinguish the deceits of demons.

Therefore, when the perpetual and grievous plague afflicting the human race had briefly drawn breath beyond its usual measure, he summoned his punishment through forgetful wickedness. Impiety indeed feels the scourges with which it is tortured, but, hardened, does not perceive by whom it is scourged.

As soon as Valerian seized imperial power—the eighth emperor after Nero—he compelled Christians by tortures to deny their faith and ordered those who refused to be killed, so that the blood of the saints was poured out across the entire breadth of the Roman realm.

Valerian, the author of the wicked edict, was immediately captured by Sapor, king of the Persians. With his eyes gouged out, he grew old in the most disgraceful slavery among the Persians as emperor of the Roman people. He received this perpetual condemnation for his infamous service for as long as he lived: bent toward the ground, he was obliged to raise upon his back the king, who was always mounting a horse—not with his hand, but with his back.

Gallienus, terrified by so manifest a judgment of God, as though moved by the example of his wretched colleague, restored peace to the churches with anxious repentance. But the punishment of one impious man does not compensate for the measure of the injury and vengeance, although his perpetual and excessively abominable captivity, together with the blood of so many tortured saints and righteous people crying out to the Lord, begs to be avenged in that same land where it was shed.

For judgment did not demand punishment only of the one who issued the command; it was also just that the executors, informers, accusers, spectators, and judges—and finally all who, even by silent consent, approved such utterly unjust cruelty—should be struck by the same blow of vengeance, since the Lord is the knower of hidden things. A very large portion of the population throughout all the provinces was involved in this.

Suddenly, by God’s permission, the peoples who had been placed and left around the empire for this purpose were released on every side; with the reins loosened, they poured into all the borders of the Romans. The Germans penetrated the Alps, Raetia, and all Italy, reaching as far as Ravenna. The Alamanni ravaged Gaul and also crossed into Italy. Greece, Macedonia, Pontus, and Asia were destroyed by the inundation of the Goths. Dacia beyond the Danube was permanently lost. The Quadi and Sarmatians devastated the Pannonias, while the farther Germans, having laid waste to it, took possession of Spain. The Parthians seized Mesopotamia and plundered Syria.

Ruins of great cities still contain, throughout the various provinces, small and impoverished buildings preserving signs of misery and traces of their names. Of these, Orosius says, “In Spain we point out Tarraco as a consolation for the recent misery.”

And lest any part of the Roman body fail to be torn apart by this devastation, tyrants conspired within; civil wars arose; and Roman blood was poured out everywhere, while Romans and barbarians alike raged.

But God’s anger soon turned into mercy, and the greater pattern of the vengeance that had begun was reckoned as a measure of fulfillment rather than punishment. Thus the first, Genuus, who had assumed the imperial purple, was killed at Mursa.

Posthumius seized tyranny in Gaul, though with considerable benefit to the state. For ten years, exercising great courage and moderation, he expelled the hostile rulers and restored the ruined provinces to their former condition. Nevertheless, he was killed in a soldiers’ mutiny.

Aemilianus was suppressed at Mainz while attempting a revolution. After the death of Posthumius, Marius seized the empire there, but was immediately killed. Then Victorinus was freely chosen by the Gauls and shortly afterward killed [Col. 1184A]. He was succeeded by Tetricus, who at that time was administering the office of governor of Aquitaine and endured many mutinies among the soldiers.

In the East, meanwhile, a certain Odaenathus gathered a peasant force; the Persians were defeated and driven back, Syria was defended, and Mesopotamia recovered. The peasants of Syria, with their Odaenathus, advanced victoriously as far as Ctesiphon.

Gallienus, however, after abandoning the state and devoting himself to his pleasures at Milan, was killed.

At this time Cyprian the African first taught rhetoric with distinction. Then, at the urging of the presbyter Caecilius—from whom he also received his surname—he became a Christian, distributed all his property to the poor, and, after not much time had passed, was advanced to the presbyterate and also appointed bishop of Carthage. It would be superfluous to pass judgment on his talent, since his works are clearer than the sun.

He suffered under the emperors Valerian and Gallienus, during the eighth persecution, on the same day as Cornelius, though not in the same year. Pontius, Cyprian’s deacon, enduring exile with him until the day of his passion, published an excellent volume on the life and passion of Cyprian.

Theodore, later also called Gregory, bishop of Neocaesarea in Pontus, while still very young, moved from Cappadocia to Berytus because of his devotion to Greek and Latin literature, and from there to Caesarea in Palestine, taking his brother Athenodorus with him.

When Adamantius saw their outstanding natural gifts, he urged them toward philosophy. Gradually instructing them in it, he introduced them to the faith of Christ and made them his own followers. After being educated by him for five years, they were sent back to their father.

As he was departing, Theodore wrote a panegyric and expressions of gratitude to Adamantius. After gathering a large audience, he recited it in the presence of Adamantius himself; it remains extant to this day. He also wrote a short but very useful volume on Ecclesiastes. Other letters of his are commonly circulated.

Most notable, however, are the signs and miracles which he performed as bishop of Neocaesarea in Pontus, to the great glory of the churches. Among them is the following: when there was not enough space for building a church because of an overhanging cliff and the bank of a river, he moved the mountain by his prayers and made a spacious site available to the builders.

He also so stilled battles, the deaths of men, and raging brothers.

There was a certain lake situated in the regions of Pontus, full of fish, whose capture provided exceedingly rich revenues. This property fell by lot of inheritance to two brothers, but greed concerning it violated the rights of brotherhood.

The blessed Gregory summoned them, with paternal affection, to the edge of the deadly lake and said to them: “I shall now, by the power of the Lord, free you from every bloody contest of strife.”

After saying this, in the sight of everyone he fixed the staff he was holding into the first waves along the shore. Then, kneeling, he stretched his palms toward heaven and prayed to the exalted God.

As soon as he finished praying, the wave immediately withdrew and rapidly fled away, ordered to depart from the heavenly presence; it returned to its depths and left the dry field to the brothers, who had by then been reconciled.

Dionysius, whom we mentioned above, bishop of Alexandria, held the school as a presbyter under Heraclas and was Adamantius’s most distinguished student. Agreeing with the position of the African Cyprianic synod, he sent many letters to various people concerning the rebaptism of heretics; these remain extant to this day.

He also wrote to Fabius, bishop of the Antiochene church, on repentance; to the Romans through Hippolytus; another letter to Sixtus, who had succeeded Stephen; to Philemon; to Dionysius, a presbyter of the Roman church; to that same Dionysius, later bishop of Rome; and to Novatian, who complained that he had been ordained bishop of Rome against his will. His letter begins as follows:

“Dionysius sends greetings to his brother Novatian. If, as you say, you were ordained against your will, you will prove it when you withdraw willingly.”

He has another letter to Dionysius and Didymus, as well as many rhetorically composed writings on Easter. There is also a letter to the Alexandrian church concerning exile; one to Heraclas, bishop in Egypt; and other writings on mortality and on the Sabbath to Hervia [reading uncertain].

He also wrote another work on the persecution of Decius, and two books against Nepos, a bishop who asserted in his writings a bodily reign of one thousand years; in these he discusses the Apocalypse of John with great care.

He wrote against Sabellius and Hermammon, bishop of Berenice; to Telesphorus; four books to Euphranor; to Dionysius, bishop of Rome; to the Laodiceans on repentance; likewise canons on repentance and on the order of sins; a work on nature to Timothy; on temptations to Euphranor; and many letters to Basilides. In one of these he asserts that he had also begun writing commentaries on Ecclesiastes.

A distinguished letter of his against Paul of Samosata is also reported to have been written a few days before his death. He died in the twelfth year of Gallienus.

Novatian, a presbyter of the city of Rome, attempted to seize the priestly see against Cornelius. He established the doctrine of the Novatians—called *Cathari* in Greek—unwilling to receive apostates who repented. Its originator was Novatus, a presbyter of Cyprian.

Novatian wrote on Easter, the Sabbath, Circumcision, the Priest, Jewish Foods, Perseverance, Attalus, and many other subjects, as well as a substantial volume on the Trinity. He made it an epitome of Tertullian’s work, claiming equality and likeness for himself; because many do not know this, they consider it a work of Cyprian.

## CHAPTER X. On the emperors Claudius and Quintillus

Claudius, the twenty-eighth emperor, assumed power by the will of the senate. He immediately attacked the Goths, who for fifteen years had been ravaging Illyricum and Macedonia, and destroyed them in an incredible slaughter. The senate decreed for him a golden shield in the senate house and an equally golden statue on the Capitol.

But shortly afterward, at Sirmium, before completing two years in power, he died of illness.

After Claudius’s death, his brother Quintillus was chosen emperor by the army. A man of uniquely great moderation, and the only one who could properly be preferred to his brother, he was killed on the seventeenth day of his reign.

During these days, in Alexandria, the Bruchium, which had been under siege for many years, was finally destroyed.

## CHAPTER XI. On the triumphs of Aurelian, the persecutions of Christians, and those who flourished under him

Aurelian, the twenty-ninth emperor, assumed power and held it for five years and six months. He was a man of outstanding military ability. Having undertaken an expedition to the Danube, he drove the Goths to flight in great battles and restored Roman authority to its ancient boundaries.

Then turning toward the East, he brought Zenobia—who, after the killing of her husband Odaenathus, claimed Syria, which had been recovered for herself—under his power more by the terror of battle than by battle itself.

In Gaul he easily overcame Tetricus, who was quite unable to withstand the mutinies of his soldiers and who was even writing:

> “Rescue me, unconquered one, from these evils.”

Through this traitor to his own army, Aurelian conquered without difficulty.

Thus, as recoverer of the East and the North, he celebrated a triumph with great glory and surrounded the city of Rome with stronger walls.

Finally, when he issued a decree instituting a persecution against the Christians, the ninth after Nero, a thunderbolt fell before him amid the great terror of those standing around him. Not long afterward he was killed on the road, reportedly through the treachery of his servant. The servant had carried to certain military men, friends of Aurelian, a written list of their names, falsely imitating Aurelian’s hand and giving the impression that Aurelian was preparing to kill them; they therefore killed him.

For this reason, they say, he accomplished something greater than Alexander the Great or Julius Caesar the dictator. He recovered the Roman world from its invaders in three years, whereas Alexander reached India through immense victories in thirteen years, and Gaius Caesar subdued the Gauls in ten years and fought against his fellow citizens for four.

Under Aurelian, the mint workers rebelled in the city of Rome; he suppressed them after defeating them with extreme cruelty.

He was the first among the Romans to fasten a diadem to his head and to use gems and an entirely gilded garment, which until then had seemed almost unknown in Roman customs. Thus he was savage, bloodthirsty, and grim throughout his life, even killing his sister’s son.

During his persecution, the most blessed virgin Columba was crowned with martyrdom at Sens, the metropolitan city of Gaul.

Thus, as Aurelian celebrated his triumph at Rome, Tetricus and Zenobia preceded him. Tetricus later became governor of Lucania, since Aurelian decided that it was better for him to be placed in an elegant and elevated position, governing some part of Italy, than to reign beyond the Alps.

Zenobia grew old in the city in the highest honor; from her the family of Zenobia at Rome is still named.

Aurelian built a temple to the Sun, and the Games of the Sun were instituted by Aurelian.

In his time Malchion, a most eloquent presbyter of the Antiochene church—who also taught rhetoric with great distinction in that same city—held a debate, with stenographers taking it down, against Paul of Samosata, who was bishop of the Antiochene church and had revived the doctrine of Artemon. This dialogue remains extant to this day.

Another substantial letter, written by him in the name of a synod, was also sent to Dionysius and Maximus, the bishops of the Roman and Alexandrian churches.

He flourished under the emperors Claudius and Aurelian.

Eutychianus, bishop of Rome, was then crowned with martyrdom and buried in the cemetery of Callistus. He himself buried three hundred and thirteen martyrs with his own hand.

## CHAPTER XII. On the emperors Tacitus and Probus

After Aurelian, Tacitus assumed power. He was an outstanding man in character, but died of a fever at Tarsus on the two-hundredth day of his reign.

Florian succeeded him. But when a large part of the army chose Probus, an experienced soldier, Florian exercised imperial power as though in play for sixty days; then, having cut his own veins, he died from the loss of blood.

Probus, born to a peasant father, a Dalmatian by name and devoted to gardening, became the thirty-first emperor and held the throne for six years and four months.

He finally liberated Gaul, which had long been occupied by barbarians, after destroying the enemy in many difficult and severe battles.

He then fought two civil wars, at the cost of much bloodshed. In the first, in the East, he defeated and captured Saturninus, who had been sent to restore the city of Antioch and had supported his tyranny. In the second, he defeated and killed Proculus and Bonosus in great battles at Cologne.

He allowed the Junii, the Gauls, and the Pannonians to depart.

Through military labor he planted the mountain Alma near Sirmium and Mount Aureus in Upper Moesia with vines, and gave them to the provincials to cultivate.

He was killed at Sirmium in an iron tower.

During these days the insane heresy of the Manichaeans arose, founded by a certain Persian called Mani. It would take too long in this work to explain their impieties, sacrileges, and shameful practices.

Archelaus, bishop of Mesopotamia, composed in the Syriac language a book containing the debate which he had held against the Manichaean as he was coming from Persia. Translated into Greek, it is possessed by many.

He flourished under the same emperor Probus.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the emperors Carus and his son Carinus, and on those who were considered distinguished in their time

Carus of Narbonne, the thirty-second emperor, assumed power and held it for two years. After making his sons Carinus and Numerian co-rulers, he waged war against the Parthians, ravaged their territories, and captured the two most celebrated Parthian cities, Coche and Ctesiphon. He was then struck by lightning in his camp above the Tigris and died.

Numerian, who had been with his father, was suffering from an eye ailment and was being carried in a vehicle. Through the treachery of Aper, who was his father-in-law, he was secretly killed.

His death was concealed until Aper could seize the empire, but the crime was revealed by the stench of the corpse.

Then Sabinus Julianus, attempting to seize the empire, was killed by Carinus in the Veronese plains.

Carinus stained himself with every crime. He killed many innocent people on fabricated charges, violated the marriages of noblewomen, and was also destructive toward schoolmates who, when they were attending lectures with him, had reproached him for weariness in speech.

In the end he was slaughtered, chiefly by the hand of a tribune whose wife he was said to have violated.

Anatolius of Alexandria, bishop of Laodicea in Syria, flourished under the emperors Probus and Carus. He was a man of remarkable learning in arithmetic, geometry, astronomy, grammar, rhetoric, and dialectic. The greatness of his talent is shown by the volume he composed on Easter and by the ten books of instruction in arithmetic, which we can scarcely understand.

Victorinus, bishop of Poitiers, knew the refinements of the Greek language better than those of Latin. Hence his works seem grand in meaning but inferior in verbal composition.

His commentaries are on Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Isaiah, Ezekiel, Habakkuk, Ecclesiastes, the Song of Songs, and the Apocalypse of John; he also wrote against all heresies and many other works. At last he was crowned with martyrdom.

Pamphilus, presbyter of Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea in Neocaesarea, burned with such love for the divine library that he copied a very large portion of Adamantius’s works in his own hand. These are still preserved in the library at Caesarea.

Concerning him Jerome says:

“But among the twelve prophets I also found twenty volumes of Adamantius written out by his hand. I embrace these with such love that I rejoice and believe that I possess the riches of Christ. For if it is a joy to possess one letter of a martyr, how much more so to possess so many thousands of lines, which seem to me to have marked their traces with his own blood?”

Before Eusebius wrote his *Apology for Adamantius*, Pamphilus had written one. He suffered at Caesarea in Palestine during the persecution of Maximinus.

Pierius, a presbyter of the Alexandrian church, taught the people with great distinction under the emperors Carus and Diocletian, at the time when Theonas was governing that same church. He attained such elegance in his sermons and various treatises, which remain extant to this day, that he was called “the younger Adamantius.”

He was an extraordinary lover of voluntary poverty and extremely learned in the art of dialectic. After the persecution, he spent the remainder of his life at Rome.

His is a very lengthy treatise on the prophecy of Hosea, delivered during the Easter vigils, as he himself demonstrates in plain speech.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the emperor Diocletian, Maximian, and the other Caesars whom he appointed; on their battles and the persecutions of Christians

Diocletian, the thirty-third emperor after Augustus, was a Dalmatian, the freedman of the senator Anulus. His mother and his town alike bore the name Diocles. From these names he was called Diocles until he assumed imperial power; when he acquired authority over the Roman world, he converted his Greek name into Roman usage.

He ruled for twenty years. As soon as he possessed the opportunity to exercise power, he personally killed Aper, the murderer of Numerian.

He then overcame Carinus, whom Carus had left as Caesar in Dalmatia, although Carinus was living disgracefully; the war was extremely difficult and required immense effort.

Afterward, when Amandus and Helianus had gathered a force of peasants—whom they called the Bagaudae—and had stirred up dangerous disturbances in Gaul, Diocletian made Maximian, surnamed Herculius, Caesar.

He sent him into Gaul, where Maximian easily restrained the inexperienced and disorganized band of countrymen by military valor.

Then a certain Carausius, low-born but quick in judgment and action, was stationed to watch the shores of the Ocean, which the Franks and Saxons were then troubling. Since he was acting more to the detriment than to the advancement of the state, he aroused suspicion by taking booty recovered from the pirates and restoring none of it to its owners, but claiming it all for himself. It was suspected that through calculated negligence he was also allowing the enemies themselves to make incursions into the borders.

For this reason Maximian ordered him to be killed. Carausius assumed the purple and occupied Britain.

Thus, throughout all the borders of the Roman empire, the uproar of sudden disturbances resounded: Carausius was in revolt in Britain; Achilleus in Egypt; the Quinquegentiani were troubling Africa; and Narseus, king of the Persians, was pressing the East with war.

Moved by this danger, Diocletian elevated Maximian Herculius from Caesar to Augustus. He chose Constantius and Maximian Galerius as Caesars.

Constantius took Theodora, the stepdaughter of Maximian Herculius, as his wife; by her he fathered six sons, the brothers of Constantine. Constantine, however, was born to him by his concubine Helena.

Carausius, after vigorously claiming and retaining Britain for seven years, was finally killed through the treachery of his associate Allectus.

Allectus then seized the island from Carausius and held it for three years. The praetorian prefect Asclepiodotus pressed him and recovered Britain after ten years.

In Gaul, Constantius Caesar suffered a defeat in his first battle against the Alamanni, and barely escaped alive himself. In the second, however, a sufficiently favorable victory followed. For it is reported that sixty thousand Alamanni were killed in a few hours.

Augustus Maximian conquered the Quinquegentiani in Africa.

Diocletian, moreover, besieged Achilleus for eight months, captured him at Alexandria, and killed him. But he used his victory without restraint: he gave Alexandria over to plunder and polluted all Egypt with proscriptions and slaughter.
