Furthermore, after Maximian Galerius had already fought against Narseus in two battles, he engaged him for a third time between Callinicum and Carrhae and was defeated. Having lost his forces, he fled to Diocletian.

Diocletian received him with extreme arrogance, so that it is reported that Galerius, wearing the purple, ran before his vehicle for several miles.

Nevertheless, humbled by this insult, he applied himself to valor, through which he sharpened the edge of his mind after scraping away the rust.

Accordingly, he soon gathered forces from every side through Illyricum and Moesia, hastily returned against the enemy, and defeated Narseus through great strategy and strength.

After destroying the Persian forces and putting Narseus himself to flight, he invaded his camp, captured his wives, sisters, and children, seized an immense quantity of Persian treasure, and carried away very many Persian nobles as prisoners.

Returning to Mesopotamia, he was received by Diocletian with the greatest honor.

Later, under the same commanders, they fought energetically against the Carpi and the Bastarnae. Then they defeated the Sarmatians and dispersed their extremely numerous captives among the garrisons of the Roman borders.

Meanwhile Diocletian in the East and Maximian Herculius in the West ordered the churches to be laid waste and Christians to be afflicted and killed—the tenth such persecution after Nero. This persecution was longer and more savage than almost all those that had preceded it.

For ten years it continued without interruption through the burning of churches, the proscription of innocent people, and the slaughter of martyrs.

An earthquake followed in Syria; at Tyre and Sidon, roofs collapsing everywhere brought down many thousands of people.

In the second year of the persecution, Diocletian compelled Maximian, against his will, to lay down the purple and the imperial power with him, so that younger men might be substituted in the administration of the state and they themselves might grow old in private leisure.

Thus, on the same day, Diocletian at Nicomedia and Maximian at Milan laid down both imperial power and its insignia.

Diocletian therefore grew old on his own estates. When Herculius and Galerius asked him to resume the empire, he detested it as though it were some plague and replied in this manner:

“If only you could see at Salona the vegetables planted by our hands; surely you would never judge that undertaking worth attempting.”

At last, fearing Constantine and Licinius, as though they had favored the factions of Maximinus and Maxentius, he died after swallowing poison in terror.

## CHAPTER XV. On Galerius and Constantius, who first divided the Roman world, and on the many emperors who sprang up and perished in those days; and on the teachers or martyrs who lived at that time

Galerius and Constantius were the first Augusti to divide the Roman empire into two parts. Galerius Maximian ruled Illyricum, Asia, and the East; Constantius ruled Italy, Africa, and Gaul.

But Constantius, a most tranquil man, was content with Gaul and Spain alone. While the churches in other parts of the world were suffering various persecutions, Constantius alone—the father of Constantine—allowed Christians freely to remain in their religion.

Indeed, we know that he performed a certain memorable miracle. Wishing to test whether some Christians in his palace were good and steadfast men, he summoned them all and ordered them, saying that if they came to sacrifice and worshipped his gods, they should remain around him and retain their positions in his household; but if they refused, they should leave the palace, giving thanks that they were not punished.

When they had shown themselves in both ways—some abandoning their religion, others, after deliberation, placing divine things before present advantage—he decided to use as friends and advisers those who had remained faithful and steadfast in what was better. He rejected the others as effeminate and expelled them from his presence, believing that those who had been such ready traitors to their God would never be devoted to an emperor.

For this reason, while Constantius was still alive, Christianity did not seem to be illegal among those who lived within Italy, Gaul, and Britain, and around the Pyrenees, as far as the Western Ocean.

Galerius then chose two Caesars: Maximinus, whom he appointed in the East, and Severus, to whom he entrusted Italy, while Galerius himself remained in Illyricum.

Constantius Augustus, a man of the greatest gentleness and civility, died at York in the sixteenth year of his reign.

Nevertheless, the devastation of the churches and the shedding of Christian blood continued to rage in various places until the seventh year of Constantine.

This persecution burned so cruelly and so frequently that within one month seventeen thousand martyrs are found to have suffered for Christ.

Crossing the shore of the Ocean, it condemned Alban, Aaron, and Julius of Britain, together with many other men and women, to a blessed death by blood.

At this time Pamphilus, the presbyter of Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea in Neocaesarea, suffered. Eusebius himself included his life in three books; we mentioned him above.

In the third year of the persecution, the year in which Constantius also died, Maximinus and Severus were made Caesars by Galerius Maximian. Maximinus added his sorceries and sexual outrages to the persecutions of the Christians.

At that time Peter, bishop of Alexandria, suffered together with many bishops of Egypt.

Lucian also suffered, a presbyter of Antioch distinguished in character, self-control, and learning.

Timothy also suffered at Rome, on the tenth day before the Kalends of July.

I shall now recount, repeating briefly what was said above, what happened in the Roman world during those days on account of the innocent blood of Christians that was shed, almost all at one time, when the emperors were appointed.

Constantius, the father of Constantine, and Armentarius were called Augusti, with Severus appointed Caesar over Italy and Maximinus, the son of Galerius’s sister, over the East. At the same time Constantine was made Caesar.

Maxentius became emperor at a villa six miles from the city on the Lavican Way. Then Licinius was made Augustus, and in similar fashion Alexander became emperor at Carthage.

Valens was likewise made emperor.

Their ends were as follows:

Severus Caesar was destroyed at the Three Taverns near Rome by Herculius Maximian. His funeral was brought to the tomb of Gallienus, nine miles from the city along the Appian Way.

Galerius Maximian died after his genitals had wasted away.

Maximian Herculius was besieged by Constantine at Marseille and then captured and paid the penalty of death.

Finally, with his neck broken by the noose, Alexander was slaughtered by Constantine’s army.

When Maxentius engaged Constantine in battle and hastened to enter the Milvian Bridge, which had been constructed from boats, from the side, his horse slipped and he was submerged in the depths. His body, swallowed by the mud and weighed down by his breastplate, was recovered only with difficulty.

Maximinus died at Tarsus a natural death.

Valens was put to death by Licinius.

I shall now recount, from among the many, the memory of a few of the teachers or martyrs who lived during the reigns of these emperors.

Lucian, a most eloquent man and presbyter of the Antiochene church, labored with such devotion to the Scriptures that certain copies of the Scriptures are still called “Lucianic.”

Booklets on the faith and brief letters to various people are attributed to him.

He suffered at Nicomedia for confessing Christ during the persecution of Maximinus, and was buried at Heliopolis in Bethany.

Phileas, from the Egyptian city called Thmuis, of noble birth and possessing no small wealth, undertook the episcopate and composed a most elegant book in praise of the martyrs.

After a discussion of the authorities had been held, he was beheaded for Christ in opposition to the judge who compelled him to sacrifice. The author of the persecution in Egypt was the same as the one under whom Lucian suffered at Nicomedia.

Arnobius taught rhetoric with great distinction in Africa under the emperor Diocletian and wrote the volumes *Against the Nations* that are commonly available. Firmianus, also called Lactantius, was Arnobius’s pupil; under the emperor Diocletian he was summoned together with the grammarian Flabo, whose works on medicine composed in verse are extant. He taught rhetoric at Nicomedia; but, because of the scarcity of pupils, he withdrew from there to Greece, specifically in order to write. We possess his *Symposium in Brief Pieces* (*commatum Symposium*), which he wrote as a young man for the schools, composed in hexameter verse from Africa to Nicomedia. We also have another book entitled *The Grammarian*, and the very fine work *On Anger*, as well as seven books of the *Divine Institutes Against the Nations*; one book *On Equalities* and an *Epitome* of the same work; two books *To Asclepiades*; one book *On Persecution*; four books of letters *To Probus*; two books of letters *To Severus*; two books of letters *To Demetrius*, his pupil; and one book *To the Same Person, On the Workmanship of God, or the Formation of Man*. In extreme old age he was tutor in Gaul to Caesar Crispus, the son of Constantine; Crispus was later killed by his father.

According to Eusebius, this persecution under Diocletian and the other emperors of the same period began with the soldiers themselves and, like a small spark, set almost the entire Roman world ablaze—especially Egypt, Africa, and Mauretania. They diligently sought out Christians among themselves, and, when they found them, compelled them to sacrifice; those who refused they deprived of military service and life.

Among these, at Nicomedia, while Augustus Caesar was present, Dorotheus, superintendent of the imperial bedchamber, and his associate Gorgonius—who had made nearly all the chamberlains under their authority Christians through teaching and faith—saw the steadfastness of a certain Peter, a most noble man. He had publicly seized and torn to pieces the unjust laws promulgated against Christians. For this reason he had endured every kind of torture in the presence of Augustus, and finally, placed upon a gridiron over burning embers, he joyfully breathed out his life in faith.

Then the men mentioned above said: “Why, emperor, do you punish in Peter the judgment of his mind, which lives in all of us? Why is that counted as a crime in him which all of us confess? This is our faith, this is our worship, and this is our unanimous and common conviction.” When the emperor nevertheless ordered them to come forward publicly, he subjected them to punishments like those inflicted on the others and finally ordered them to be killed by hanging from a noose.

At that time Anthimus, bishop of that city, persevering in the confession of our Lord Jesus Christ, received the glory of martyrdom by decapitation. Almost the entire multitude of his flock followed him as a truly good shepherd leading the way along the path of martyrdom. Thus it cannot be explained how many tortures were devised for God’s holy martyrs at that time, or how many thousands of saints were killed by new and unheard-of instruments of torture. Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea and author of the *Ecclesiastical History*, was present among them; what he learned in truth and saw with his own eyes he endeavored partly to disclose in the eighth and ninth books of his *Histories*.

## CHAPTER XVI. How Constantine was raised to imperial power, and which emperors persecuting Christians he overthrew

Constantine, the thirty-fourth emperor, received the reins of government from his father Constantius and held them most successfully for thirty-one years. After Constantius died in Britain, as I have said, Constantine was made emperor. He was the first Christian emperor, except for Philip, who was a Christian for a very few years and seems to me to have been appointed for this sole purpose: that Rome’s thousandth year might be dedicated to Christ rather than to idols.

From Constantine onward, all emperors who have been created down to the present day have always been Christians, except Julian, whom an accursed life abandoned while he was, as they say, plotting impious schemes. At that time, when Crispus and Constantine were Caesars and consuls, Sylvester presided over the Roman Church, Alexander over the Alexandrian Church, and Macarius over Jerusalem. At Antioch, the city on the Orontes, no one had yet been ordained after Romanus, since the persecutions prevented it. Not long afterward, those who had assembled at Nicaea, admiring his eloquence, judged Eustathius worthy to preside over the apostolic see. Since he was bishop of nearby Beroea, they transferred him to Antioch.

At that time the eastern Christians who lived around Lespia, as far as the borders of Egypt, did not dare to gather openly in churches, because Licinius had exchanged the favor he had previously shown them for hostility. Nor did the Helladic, Macedonian, and Illyrian Christians in the West freely persist in their religion, because Constantine was the Roman ruler in those regions.

We later learned that many things happened to this man by which he was turned toward reverencing Christian doctrine, but above all because of the sign shown to him by divine power. Since we have reached this point, let us recount the matter at somewhat greater length.

When Diocletian and Maximian Herculius had chosen a private life, and Maximinus Galerius, who had ruled with them, while holding Italy, appointed two Caesars—Maximinus in the East and Severus in Italy—Constantine, after his father’s death in Britain, was appointed emperor in the first year of the two hundred and first Olympiad, on the twenty-seventh day of July. At Rome, meanwhile, Maxentius, the son of Maximian Herculius, was made emperor by the praetorian soldiers. His father, from a desire to rule, did not wish to deprive his son of the kingdom, which he had been unable to do himself.

Severus, advancing from Rome against Maxentius, was killed through the treachery of his soldiers. Accordingly, Maxentius was regarded at Rome as a tyrant: he shamelessly practiced adultery and killed the husbands of the women involved. Constantine wished to crush him and free the Romans from their disasters. He considered which god he might have as an ally in war, knowing that the gods whom Diocletian worshiped were of no help, and that his own father had lived successfully while despising the religion of the pagans.

While he was occupied with these anxieties, he saw in sleep the sign of a cross brilliantly set in the sky. As he gazed in wonder at the vision, angels appeared and said: “O Constantine, conquer by this.” It is also reported that Christ himself appeared to him, showed him the sign of the cross, and commanded him to make a figure like it and to use this aid in battles, so that he might obtain the rights of victory.

Eusebius Pamphili reports that he heard the emperor himself declare under oath that, when the sun was already declining around midday, he had seen, together with the soldiers who were then with him, a sign of the cross formed from light, accompanied by an inscription saying: “By this conquer.” He was traveling with his army along a road when this miracle, he says, was shown to him. As he wondered what it meant, night came on. While he slept, Christ appeared to him with the sign he had seen in the sky and ordered him to make an image of that sign, which would serve as an aid in the clashes of battle.

To repeat, then, what has already been mentioned in part and on several occasions: after Severus was killed, Galerius made Licinius emperor. Licinius had intensified the persecution begun by Diocletian and Maximian through even more savage edicts. After exhausting the provinces of every kind of person for ten years, his inner organs having putrefied and his vital powers dissolved, he not only experienced the horror of human misery but even vomited worms. The physicians could no longer endure the stench and were repeatedly killed at his command. At last, rebuked by a certain physician who found courage in despair, he was told that his punishment was the wrath of God and that therefore he could not be cured by physicians. He then sent edicts throughout the empire recalling the Christians from exile; but, unable to endure his sufferings, he took his own life.

Thus the state was then under four new rulers: Constantine and Maxentius, the sons of Augusti, and Licinius and Maximian, men newly risen to power. After ten years during which the persecutors had afflicted the churches, Constantine granted them peace.

Then civil war arose between Constantine and Maxentius. Compelled by this crisis, Constantine anxiously considered which god he might have as his helper in the approaching battles. Hence the heavenly signs were shown to him, as we mentioned above.

Maxentius, worn down by many battles, was finally defeated and killed at the Milvian Bridge. Maximinus, the instigator and most relentless executor of the persecution of Christians, died at Tarsus while preparing a civil war against Licinius. Licinius, suddenly roused to madness, ordered all the Christians to be expelled from his palace.

Soon war flared up between Licinius and Constantine. Constantine first defeated Licinius, his sister’s husband, in Pannonia, and then crushed him at Cibalae. After gaining possession of the whole of Greece, he repeatedly fought Licinius, who rose against him and was checked by land and sea, and finally forced him to surrender. But, following the example of his father-in-law Maximian Herculius, and fearing that Licinius might once again take up the purple he had laid down to the ruin of the state, he ordered him, though a private citizen, to be killed. Although all the ministers of the wicked persecution had already been removed, Licinius too deserved fitting punishment for having carried on the persecution as far as he could.

Constantine’s sons Crispus and Constantine, and the young Licinius, son of Licinius Augustus and Constantine’s nephew through his sister, were made Caesars.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the madness of Arius, the synod assembled at Nicaea, and what was done there

In those days Arius, a presbyter of Alexandria, deviated from the truth of the catholic faith and established a destructive doctrine for many. As soon as he became either known or marked out at Alexandria, he became the object of attack among the confused followers and opponents of the common people, and was expelled from the Church by Alexander, then bishop of that city.

Since he had not only led the people whom he had seduced into error but had also incited them to rebellion, a gathering of three hundred and eighteen bishops was held at Nicaea, a city of Bithynia. Through them the Arian doctrine was most clearly recognized as destructive and wretched, publicly exposed, and rejected.

It is established that Syrians, Cilicians, Phoenicians, Arabs, and Palestinians came to the council, along with Egyptians, Thebans, Libyans, and those who came from Mesopotamia; Persians also attended. Nor was a Scythian absent. From their assembly, Pontus and Asia, Phrygia and Pamphylia supplied highly distinguished men. Thracians, Macedonians, Achaeans, Epirotes, and peoples living farther inland were present as well.

Only one Spaniard attended, the very famous Hosius, who also sat among many others. Thus Constantine, the one and only emperor of his age, adorning Christ’s crown with the bond of peace, dedicated to his Savior God a fitting offering for victory over his enemies and foes.

He therefore prepared a very large hall and took his imperial seat there, ordering benches to be set up sufficient for the rank of the priests. Having thus prepared suitable honors for them, he invited them to enter and deliberate about the matters before them.

The emperor himself entered last, accompanied by a few men. His stature was worthy of praise, his appearance remarkable, and the dignity he displayed was even more remarkable, with modesty upon his countenance. A smaller seat than those of the others was placed for him in their midst, but he first asked that the bishops grant him this privilege. Then that most sacred assembly sat down with him.

For when bishops had gathered from almost every region and, as commonly happens, had brought with them quarrels arising from various causes, each repeatedly appealed to the emperor. Petitions were presented and accusations brought forward, and they devoted their attention more to these matters than to the business for which they had come.

Seeing that the principal matter was being frustrated by such quarrels, he appointed a fixed day on which each bishop who seemed to have a complaint would submit it. When he had taken his seat, he received the petitions from each of them, held them all together in his bosom, and did not disclose what they contained. He said to the bishops:

“God appointed you priests and gave you authority to judge even us; therefore we are rightly judged by you, but you cannot be judged by human beings. For this reason, await judgment among yourselves from God alone, and let all your quarrels, whatever they may be, be reserved for that divine examination. For you have been given to us by God as gods, and it is not fitting that a human being should judge gods, but only the one of whom it is written: ‘God stood in the assembly of the gods; in the midst he distinguishes among the gods.’ Therefore, setting these matters aside, distinguish without any discord among yourselves the things that pertain to the faith of God.”

After saying this, he ordered all the petitions of complaint to be burned together, so that the pretended holiness of the priests might not become known to anyone, and so that they might all devote themselves unanimously and diligently to the ecclesiastical business for which they had come.

From the memory preserved of only a few men one may infer how many great and beloved servants of God were present at this venerable council—men who established the ecclesiastical laws that we call canons and who condemned the perverse doctrine of Arius, anathematizing both it and its author.

Among those present at the council was Paphnutius, a man of God and bishop from Egypt, a confessor from the number of those whom Maximian had condemned to the mines after gouging out their right eyes and cutting through their left knees. Yet such was the abundance of virtue in him that signs were performed through him no less than formerly through the apostles. He drove out demons by a mere word and cured the sick by prayer alone. He is also said to have restored sight to the blind and returned paralytics to the stability of their bodies.

Constantine held him in such great reverence and affection that he often summoned him into the palace, embraced him, and kissed with eager affection the eye that had been torn out in the confession of the faith.

From the same company, and said to have been even more distinguished, was the bishop Spyridon of Cyprus, a man from the order of the prophets. He had been a shepherd of sheep and remained one even after becoming a bishop.

One night, when thieves came to the sheepfolds and stretched out their criminal hands to make an opening through which they could lead out the sheep, they were bound by certain invisible chains and remained until daylight as though handed over to torturers.

In the morning, the old man came to lead the sheep to pasture and saw the young men hanging in the folds, held fast without any human bonds. When he learned the cause of their offense, he released by his word those whom their deeds had bound. And, so that their nighttime occupation would not prove fruitless, he said: “Take, young men, one ram for yourselves, so that you may not seem to have come here for no reason. It would have been more fitting for you to seek it by prayer than by theft.”

They also relate this remarkable event about him. He had a daughter named Irene, who, after serving him well, died a virgin. After her death, a certain man came saying that he had entrusted a deposit to her; the father knew nothing of the matter. The entire house was searched, but what was being sought was nowhere found.

The man who had entrusted it persisted, pressed him with weeping and tears, and declared that he would even bring about his own death unless he received what had been entrusted. Moved by his tears, the old man hurried to his daughter’s tomb and called her by name.

Then she answered from the tomb: “What do you want, father?”

He said: “Where did you place the deposit entrusted to you by that man?”

Pointing out the place, she replied: “There you will find it buried.”

He returned home, found the object just as his daughter had answered from the tomb, and handed it over to the claimant. Many other miraculous deeds of his are also reported, celebrated at that time by the mouths of everyone who was alive.

Thus, even in those times, many such men shone forth in the churches of the Lord, and very many of them were present at that council.

Athanasius was also present at the council. At that time he was a deacon of Alexander, bishop of Alexandria, and assisted the old man in many deliberations. The great Eustathius was also present, distinguished in merits and virtues and appointed to preside over the church of Antioch.

Likewise present was Eusebius Pamphili, bishop of the church of Caesarea, who had nobly persevered in the faith during the persecution and was a most diligent author of many distinguished little works. Many other highly respected men were there as well, whose intellectual gifts, wisdom, and spiritual virtues shone forth both before the emperor and in the other offices of dignity.

Whoever wishes to know in detail what was done at this council should set aside the works of others and read the *Ecclesiastical History* of Eusebius of Caesarea, which Rufinus translated into our language, as well as the histories of the three distinguished men Sozomen, Socrates, and Theodoret. Whoever wishes to know more fully the deeds and life of this emperor Constantine should read the works of the aforementioned Eusebius devoted specifically to this subject.

Let us now return our writing to the task of the abridgment we have begun.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On Helena, the mother of Constantine, and how she found the Lord’s cross

At the same time Helena, the mother of Constantine, a woman incomparable in faith, religious devotion, and singular magnificence, whose son Constantine both was and was believed to be, was instructed by divine visions and went to Jerusalem. There she inquired of the inhabitants about the place where the most holy body of Christ had hung affixed to the cross.

The place was difficult to find because the ancient persecutors had set up an image of Venus there, so that if any Christian wished to worship Christ in that place, he would appear to be worshiping Venus. For this reason the place had become neglected and almost forgotten.

But when the devout woman, as we said above, hastened to the place indicated by heavenly judgment, she removed from it everything profane and polluted, cleared away the accumulated rubble, and found three crosses lying in confused order.

The indiscriminate identity of the crosses disturbed the joy caused by the discovery. The inscription that Pilate had composed in Greek, Latin, and Hebrew letters was indeed present, but even it did not sufficiently reveal which cross was the Lord’s cross.

Thus, uncertain in the midst of human ambiguity, she demanded a divine testimony. In that principal city, a certain woman of high rank from that place was lying half-dead, wasted away by a grave illness. At that time Macarius was its bishop.

When he saw the queen hesitating, together with all the others who were present, he said: “Bring here all the crosses that have been found, and God will now reveal to us which one carried the Lord Christ.”

Then he entered with the queen and the people and, kneeling before the woman who lay there, poured out this prayer to God:

“You, Lord, through your only-begotten Son, deigned to grant salvation to the human race through the suffering of the cross. Now, in these final times, you have inspired the heart of your handmaid to seek the blessed wood on which our salvation hung. Clearly show which of these three was the cross destined for the Lord’s glory and which were intended for the punishment of slaves, so that this woman, who lies here half-alive, may at once be touched by the saving wood and be recalled from the gates of death to life.”

After saying this, he first applied one of the three crosses, but it did no good. He applied the second, and nothing happened then either. But when he brought the third near, the woman suddenly opened her eyes, rose, and, having recovered the strength of her limbs, became much livelier than she had been when healthy. She began to run throughout the house and to glorify the power of the Lord.

Thus, by this clear sign, the queen obtained what she had desired and, with royal magnificence, built a splendid temple on the spot where she had found the cross.

She also carried to her son the nails with which the Lord’s body had been fastened. From some of them he made bridles for use in war, and from others he is said to have fashioned a helmet likewise suitable for warfare.

She brought part of the saving wood itself to her son, while she left another part enclosed in silver cases at the place, where it is still preserved with reverent care as a memorial.

Her son Constantine founded a city in honor of his mother and named it Helenopolis after her.

## CHAPTER XIX. At what time the peoples of the Iberians and Armenians were converted to the faith of Christ

At that time a certain philosopher named Meropius was traveling through Outer India, exploring it as he went. This region is separated by a long distance from Inner India, is inhabited by different languages and nations, and, because it was considered so remote, had not been touched by the plowshare of apostolic preaching.

Meropius was captured and killed by barbarians. Two boys whom he had trained in the liberal disciplines were spared out of the barbarians’ compassion and brought before the king. When he discovered that they were capable and noble, he took a great liking to them. He entrusted his accounts and treasuries to Frumentius, whom he had found the more perceptive, while he made Edesius his cupbearer.

They were held in great honor while the king lived, and in even greater honor after his death under his son, whom he had left as heir to the kingdom. They were raised so high that they built churches there and held Christian gatherings in various places.

When they returned to the Roman world to visit their relatives and reported what had happened to their bishops, Athanasius, who had recently been appointed bishop of Alexandria, chose Frumentius for the office of preaching and sent him back to India.

Through him, as the grace of the Lord shone forth, many apostolic miracles were performed, and countless multitudes of barbarians were converted to Christianity. Thus the seeds of the faith began to sprout in Outer India.

At the same time, among the people of the Iberians, who lived beneath the northern sky, there was held captive a highly devout Christian woman. Through the merits of her perseverance in vigils, fasts, and prayers, many miracles shone forth. Finally, the queen of that people, who was afflicted by a serious illness and had been given up by the physicians, went down to the room of this foreign woman and lay upon her sackcloth.

Having received health through the woman’s prayers, she returned to her own residence. On this occasion the king of that people believed in Christ and built a magnificent church. He also sent envoys to the emperor Constantine, at the exhortation of the foreign woman mentioned above, asking him to send bishops who would instruct both him and his people in the sacred religion.

When the emperor learned of this request, he rejoiced, and the king of the Iberians obtained from him what he had asked.

At that same time, as I have already indicated, the peoples of India and the Iberians received the beginnings of Christian doctrine. We also learn that the Armenians were then first made Christians.

For they say that Tiridates, the king of that people, was converted to Christianity because of a remarkable sign of God that occurred near his palace. He ordered all those subject to his rule, by a single command, likewise to bow their necks to God. Hence Christian doctrine also passed to the neighboring peoples and spread widely among them.

## CHAPTER XX. On the concern of the devout emperor Constantine, which he showed not only for his subjects but also for foreigners on behalf of the faith of Christ

I believe that Christianity began among the Persians at the time when certain Persians, coming to Osroene and Armenia for the sake of trade, as is customary, conversed there with holy men and experienced their miracles.

As time passed, their numbers increased, and they already had churches, priests, and the other ministers of the faith. This greatly grieved the magi, who are known to possess the religion of the Persians as a kind of priestly tribe, entrusted to them from the beginning through hereditary succession.

It also grieved the Jews, who are in a certain natural sense enemies of Christian doctrine. Therefore they accused before Shapur, then king, Simon, archbishop of the royal cities of Seleucia and Ctesiphon in Persia, alleging that he was a friend of the Roman Caesar and disclosed Persian affairs to him.

For this reason the king of Persia not only had Simon arrested, but also the other bishops of his kingdom, men worthy of God, and had them thrown into chains. He also handed over to various deaths priests of proven good life, deacons, monks, holy virgins, and countless multitudes of the common people, as well as many of his own beloved and intimate household members, together with his tutor and foster-father.

He did this on account of Christian doctrine, because they refused to worship the sun, a creature of God, as God.

It is reported that nearly sixteen thousand men and women in the kingdom of Shapur were crowned with martyrdom during that persecution, while the magi and Jews incited the king to this sacrilege.

When the calamity that had befallen the Christians in Persia became known to the devout emperor Constantine, and while he was concerned for the true religion, he wrote to the king of Persia through the envoys who were then present. He offered warnings of piety and asked that the worshipers of God among the Persians might enjoy fitting honor.

As the letter he sent to that king on behalf of our faith states, he included many fearful reminders of the disasters that had befallen persecutors of this doctrine. He also wrote that Valerian, the Roman emperor who had preceded him, had been captured by the Persians and had grown old among them in the greatest disgrace because he had decreed that Christians should be subjected to various deaths.

Thus this excellent emperor, adorned with piety, acted with concern not only for his subjects but also for those who lived under another ruler.

For this reason he himself also enjoyed divine protection. He held all Europe, Libya, and, in addition, the greater part of Asia. He not only had devoted subjects, but some barbarians served him willingly while others had been conquered. Everywhere triumphs were seen, and the emperor was recognized as victorious among men.

Since he had three sons, he called them Caesars and appointed each of them to rule for ten-year periods of his reign. He made his first son, Constantine, who bore his own name, ruler of the western regions for the first decade; he appointed his second son, Constantius, named after his grandfather, Caesar in the East during the second decade; and he appointed the younger Constans during the third decade.

While Constantine was residing at Nicomedia, weighed down by illness and aware of the uncertainty of this life, he received the grace of holy baptism. He had postponed it until that time, desiring to obtain it in the Jordan River.

He left his three sons as heirs to the empire and ordered the great Athanasius to return to Alexandria, although Eusebius was present and tried to persuade him otherwise. Having made his will and established his three sons as heirs, he died.

He lived seventy-five years and reigned thirty-one. Meanwhile, the reasons why so great a man turned the avenging sword and the punishment destined for the wicked even against his own affections remain hidden. For, as they say, he killed his son Crispus and Licinius, his sister’s son.

I shall not be silent about those who, by writing under him, left monuments for later generations.

## CHAPTER XXI. On the various teachers who flourished under the emperor Constantine

Arnobius was held in high repute as a rhetorician in Africa, although this was already the case earlier under the emperor Diocletian. While he trained young men at Sicca in declamation and, still a pagan, was driven by dreams toward belief, he could not obtain from the bishop the faith that he had always attacked. He therefore labored through the nights over brilliant books against his former religion and at last obtained a pledge of faith through certain guarantees of his devotion.

Firmianus, also called Lactantius, the pupil of Arnobius, was summoned under the emperor Diocletian together with Flabo the grammarian, whose books on medicine composed in verse are extant. He taught rhetoric at Nicomedia, but because of the scarcity of pupils he withdrew from there to Greece, specifically in order to write.

We possess his *Symposium in Brief Pieces* (*commatum Symposium*), which he wrote as a young man for the schools of Africa; and his *Hodoeporicum*—that is, his *Journey*—written in hexameter verse from Africa to Nicomedia; and another book entitled *The Grammarian*; the very fine work *On the Anger of God*; seven books of the *Divine Institutes Against the Nations*; one book of the *Epitome* of the same work; two books *To Asclepiades*; one book *On Persecution*; four books of letters *To Probus*; two books of letters *To Severus*; three books of letters *To Demetrianus*, his pupil; and one book *To the Same Person, On the Workmanship of God, or the Formation of Man*.

In extreme old age he was tutor in Gaul to Caesar Crispus, the son of Constantine; Crispus was later killed by his father.

Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, was exceptionally devoted to the divine Scriptures and, together with Pamphilus the martyr, a most diligent investigator of the divine library. He published innumerable volumes, among which are these: twenty books of *Harmony and Variance*; ten books of the *Ecclesiastical History*; the *Complete History of the Chronological Canons* and a work on their authors; a work on the interpretation of the Gospels; ten books on Isaiah; twenty-five books *Against Porphyry*, who was writing at the same time in Sicily, as some believe; six books *For Adamantius*; three books *On the Life of Pamphilus*; works *On the Martyrs* and other brief writings; learned commentaries on the one hundred and fifty Psalms; and many other works.

He flourished especially under the emperor Constantine and Constantius, and received his surname from his friendship with the martyr Pamphilus.

Rheticius of the Aedui—that is, the bishop of Augustodunum—was held in Gaul under Constantine to be a man of the highest reputation. His commentaries on the *Song of Songs* are read, as is another substantial volume *Against the Novatians*. Apart from these, I have found no other work of his.

Methodius, formerly bishop of Lycia and later of Tyre, composed in polished and well-ordered language a book in brief pieces *Against Porphyry*; the *Symposium of the Ten Virgins*; an outstanding work *On the Resurrection Against Adamantius*; another work *Against the Same Person, On the Pythoness*; commentaries on Genesis and on the *Song of Songs*; and many other works commonly read.

At the end of the final persecution—or, as others maintain, under Decius and Valerian—he was crowned with martyrdom at Chalcis in Greece.

Juvencus, a Spanish presbyter of very noble birth, composed four books by transferring the four Gospels almost word for word into hexameter verse, together with some other works in the same meter concerning the order of the sacraments. He flourished under the emperor Constantine.

Eustathius, a Pamphylian by birth, first governed the church of Beroea in Syria and then that of Antioch. He composed extensively against the Arian doctrine and, under the emperor Constantine, was expelled into exile at Trajanopolis in Thrace, where he was also buried. His works *On the Soul Against Adamantius* and innumerable letters are extant, though it would take too long to enumerate them.

Marcellus of Ancyra, a bishop, flourished under the emperors Constantine and Constantius. He wrote many volumes on various subjects, especially against the Arians. Books by Aristeus and Apollinaris are circulated against him, accusing him of the Sabellian heresy.

Hilary too, in his seventh book *Against Arius*, mentions Marcellus by name as though he were a heretic. But Marcellus defended himself against the doctrine of which he was accused and obtained communion with Julius and Athanasius, the bishops of Rome and Alexandria.

Eusebius of Emesa, a man of elegant and rhetorical talent, composed innumerable books intended for popular applause and followed history more closely. Those who are devoted to declamatory writing read him with the greatest enthusiasm. Among his works, the principal ones are *Against the Jews, the Nations, and the Novatians*; ten books *To the Galatians*; and numerous short homilies on the Gospel.

He flourished during the reign of the emperor Constantine, under whom he also died and was buried at Antioch.

At that same time Porphyry, after sending Constantius a distinguished volume, was released from exile. At that time also Athanasius was appointed the nineteenth bishop of Alexandria.

In those days Constantine, together with his sons, also sent honorable letters to Antony; with God’s help, we shall discuss them at greater length in what follows.

At that time, too, the daughter of the rhetorician Nazarcus equaled her father in eloquence, and Tyberianus, an eloquent man, governed the prefecture of the Gauls.

Eustatius of Constantinople is also known, a presbyter through whose efforts a martyrium was constructed in Jerusalem.

Moreover, under Constantine it was not only those whose memory we have recorded who shone in wisdom and virtues, but also many others whom we pass over in silence. Constantine, therefore, was accustomed to call Trajan “the wallflower,” because of the inscriptions bearing his name on many buildings. Trajan constructed a bridge over the Danube, wore royal dress adorned with gems, and decorated his head with a perpetual diadem. Yet in many respects he was especially useful: he was most severe in suppressing calumnies, in fostering the good arts—above all, literary studies—and he diligently practiced reading, writing himself, reflection, and the sagacious hearing of embassies and the complaints of the provinces. After subduing many peoples in various wars, he founded a city bearing his name, a city of the Roman emperors, either alone or as the first to do so. This city alone, free from idols, was founded and advanced by a Christian emperor in so short a time that, in its form and power, it can rightly be compared with Rome, which was advanced over so many centuries and through so many miseries.

Then, in due and pious order, Constantine was the first to alter the edict, since he decreed that the temples of the pagans should be closed without any killing of human beings. In this, too, the omnipotence of our Lord Jesus Christ is worthy of praise and wonder: whenever he willed it, then, by the edict of a single religious ruler, the shrines and temples of idols, constructed through the skill of the most powerful kings and emperors and of men strong and wise in past ages, were closed without any worshipper resisting, almost throughout the whole world, and were reduced to nothing. Since these deeds were successfully accomplished, I have decided to bring this third book to an end.

# BOOK FOUR

[Col. 1203]

## CHAPTER ONE. How, after Constantine’s death, the Roman world came into the possession of his three sons, and what portions each of them obtained

Meanwhile the state was being afflicted by accidental disasters. We therefore consider it not inappropriate to touch upon certain matters summarily and briefly. It has already been related in the preceding books that, when the founder of the city of Constantinople died, his three sons assumed the imperial power. It should also be known that their cousin, named Dalmatius and bearing his father’s name, ruled together with them; but after he had held power for a short time, he was killed by the soldiers—not by Constantius’s order that he should be killed, yet also without Constantius preventing it.

Thus dominion over the Roman world was divided into three parts among Constantine, Constantius, and Constans, the sons of Constantine. Each of them received these regions for administration: Constantine the Younger, everything beyond the Alps; Constantius, Asia and the East from the strait of the Propontis; Constans, Illyricum, Italy, and Africa; Dalmatius, Thrace, Macedonia, and Achaea.

Meanwhile Constantine and Constans immediately began to quarrel over possession of Italy and Africa. Constantine, under the pretext of suppressing brigandage, while off his guard and disgracefully drunk, made an incursion into another’s territory. He was cut down by the commanders of Constans, and thrown into the river called the Alsa, not far from Aquileia.

## CHAPTER TWO. How the Arian heretics, through a certain presbyter, gained access to Constantine’s intimacy

Meanwhile the devil’s ever-malicious persecution of the true God—this persecution which, from the beginning of the world until now, has disturbed the slippery hearts of human beings by spreading clouds of error and turning them away from the sincere path of faith and religion—after it had ceased to persecute Christ’s Church through the zeal of idolatry, when Christian emperors were turning the highest royal power toward better things, devised another scheme by which it might trouble the Church through those same Christian emperors.

Thus a ready entrance and easy path to the familiarity of the emperor Constantius was opened for Arius, the author of the new error, and for his other disciples; and this came about as follows. After the mother of the religious ruler, Helena, who had been honored with the highest dignities of the Roman realm, had departed this life, Constantia, the widow of Licinius, enjoyed the consolation of her brother Augustus.

It happened that a certain presbyter came to her notice, secretly favoring the party of Arius. At first, however, he disclosed nothing at all about these matters to the emperor’s sister. But when great familiarity gave him the opportunity, he gradually began to introduce the subject, saying that envy had been stirred up against Arius and that, because of private hostilities, his bishop had attacked him contentiously, pierced by the goad of rivalry because Arius was sufficiently dear to the populace.

By suggesting these and similar matters more and more frequently, he won over Constantia’s mind. When she was visited on the day of her death by her brother Constantius, and he addressed her gently and reverently, she is said to have asked him for this final favor: that he receive the presbyter into his confidence and listen to what he offered her concerning hope and salvation. She herself, she said, now departing from this life, cared for nothing; but she was anxious about her brother’s position, lest perhaps he should suffer the destruction of his kingdom for the punishment of the innocent.

Having accepted these admonitions from his sister, and believing her sisterly concern to be faithful, Constantius lent his ear to the presbyter. When Constantius himself was departing this life, and, in the absence of his children, he had written a testament concerning the succession to the Roman world for his heirs, he is said to have secretly summoned the presbyter whom we have said was commended to him by his sister. Under oath, he entrusted to him what he had written, since the presbyter had gained access to his intimacy on the occasion mentioned above, charging him not to place it in anyone’s hands except those of Constantius when he should arrive.

Because the eunuchs who were in the palace favored him, and because they had craftily marked the emperor’s death, the documents remained intact and preserved until Constantius’s arrival, while many who attempted new schemes were suppressed. When Constantius arrived, the presbyter returned the deposit to him.

In gratitude for this service, the emperor, who desired the kingdom, became so bound to him that he who had sought to rule everyone patiently allowed himself to be ruled by that man. Once the emperor had been bound to him, the presbyter began to suggest the restoration of Arius and to persuade him to compel the priests who were unwilling to comply.

Then he made Eusebius, bishop of Nicomedia and a supporter of Arius’s party, together with the other associates of Arius, especially familiar to the emperor, with the palace eunuchs supporting him—eunuchs whose minds he had bound to himself by diabolical deceit. They persecuted Athanasius, defender of the Catholic Church, with false accusations, to such an extent that the ruler Constantius repeatedly wished to kill him, had not God’s pious providence protected and preserved him for the restoration of his Church.

The ecclesiastical history called the *Tripartite History* recounts by what marvelous means he was repeatedly snatched from the hands of those seeking his life. He himself, as one who suffered these things, reports them in order in his own works, as does Rufinus, the writer of the ecclesiastical history of the aforementioned period.

## CHAPTER THREE. Concerning the various synods at which the Arians attempted to overthrow the decrees of the Catholic Council of Nicaea

Accordingly, the supporters of the perverse doctrine—Eusebius of Nicomedia [Col. 1205A], together with the other satellites and enemies of God’s Church—having found an opportune moment, gradually and craftily attempted to overturn the Catholic decrees of the Council of Nicaea. They first assembled at Antioch under the pretext of dedicating the church there, begun with great magnificence by the father of the Augusti and completed by Constantius. Nearly ninety Eastern bishops gathered.

There they enacted measures against the Catholic faith of the Council of Nicaea, though not as openly as in the other councils. Later, as time passed, they held various councils, desiring to abolish the faith of the Council of Nicaea concerning the one substance of God the Father and the Son, with the emperor himself supporting them. They carried out these actions repeatedly, emboldened by his presence.

But after the death of Constans, when Constantius had decreed that a synod should be held at Milan, at which he would make the Eastern and Western bishops agree in Arian madness, he was unable to bring this about. He therefore ordered the Westerners to assemble at Ariminum, and the Easterners at Tyre.

At these synods the Homoousians, refusing to communicate with the Arians, held different councils elsewhere concerning this matter and generated an even more turbulent storm against the Catholics. Constantius, urged on by the treacherous, now pressing with blandishments and now with threats, nevertheless could not bring the bishops to unanimity. His efforts were frustrated, and greater discord arose here and there in the churches.

As the Arians persisted, Constantius reached such madness that he believed there were degrees within God. He who had once left error through the door of idolatry was again led into its bosom, as though through a false door, while seeking gods within God.

Thus, with zeal perverted, deceived power was armed, and the force of persecution was set in motion under the name of piety. They contended over the choice of a new name, so that the churches might belong rather to the Arians than to the Catholics.

## CHAPTER FOUR. Concerning the persecution of Athanasius and the other Catholic bishops

Therefore the king, inflamed at the instigation of the Arians, first persecuted Athanasius. When he was being sought for punishment, he was honorably received by Maximinus, bishop of Trier, who at that time was held in considerable renown.

He ordered Paul, the successor of Alexander as bishop of Constantinople, a man worthy of praise, to be driven into exile, and substituted Macedonius, a cruel heretic, in his place. But when Hermogenes, the master of the soldiers, attempted, by the king’s command and through the faction of the Arians, to deport Paul into exile, the Catholic populace dragged him through Constantinople and killed him.

Paul, however, was later ensnared by the treachery of the prefect Philip, driven into exile, and strangled there by that same man, because Philip was a supporter of Macedonius and the Arians. From this point Liberius, bishop of the Roman see, was condemned to exile because he refused to communicate with the heretics and to subscribe to the condemnation of Athanasius.

But when Constantius came to Rome, accepting the petition of the noble Roman matrons on Liberius’s behalf, he restored him to his own see. Nevertheless, some suspected him of having subscribed because he had been overcome by weariness of exile. He had also learned that the clergy and people of the city avoided communion with Felix, that successor of his, as though he were a heretic, and did not attend his solemn services at all.

At that same time Eusebius of Vercelli, Hilary of Poitiers, and the other religious and Catholic bishops and presbyters were sent into various exiles. From that point the Arians persecuted, through different forms of affliction, all the bishops who did not belong to their party, with the emperor’s consent. Civil wars broke out, churches were plundered, and in many places people of different condition, age, and sex suffered slaughter and death.

A horrifying earthquake followed these wicked persecutions; it threw many cities of the East to the ground. But these matters may suffice for this brief work.

## CHAPTER FIVE. [Col. 1206B] Concerning the battles of Constans against the Parthians and Franks, and his death. Where the Franks lived at that time

Now let us return to the sequence of the history we began. Constans fought nine battles, with little success, against the Persians and Sapor, who had devastated Mesopotamia. Finally, compelled to engage in battle at night by a mutiny and the intemperance of his soldiers, he lost, after an almost complete victory, what he had won and was himself defeated.

Constans also fought against the Franks with varying results. At last the Franks were subdued by Constans, and peace was made with them.

The blessed Jerome, in the *Life of Hilarion*, mentions the Franks and where they lived at that time. For he says:

“For the candidate of the emperor Constantius, red-haired, and by the whiteness of his body indicating his province—for his people are a race between the Saxons and the Alamanni, not so extensive as it is powerful; among historians, Germania is now called Francia—was possessed by an ancient [lacuna] demon, and so forth.”

After Constans had surrendered himself to intolerable vices and had almost won the favor of the provincials and soldiers, he was killed through the plots of Magnentius in a town called Helena, near Spain.

## CHAPTER SIX. Concerning the tyrannies of Magnentius and Nepotianus, and those who killed them

Magnentius seized the imperial power at Augustodunum and immediately extended it through Gaul, Africa, and Italy. In Illyricum, the soldiers created Vetranio, an old man, emperor for themselves—a man simple by nature and pleasing to everyone, but one who had never learned even the first elements of letters.

Thus, while the aged emperor sometimes unwillingly practiced the alphabet and the syllables of letters, Constantius, who was then preparing war against Magnentius, inflamed by the desire to avenge his brother, ordered him to lay down the imperial power. Vetranio cast off the purple together with his letters, content with private life, and abandoned both the palace and the school.

Nepotianus, the son of Constantine’s sister, then invaded the imperial power at Rome, relying on a band of gladiators. Since he was wicked and therefore hated by everyone, he was later overthrown by the commanders of Magnentius.

Then came the horrible war between Constantius and Magnentius, fought near the city of Mursa. In it, the Roman forces suffered such heavy destruction that the loss harmed them even afterward. In that war the strength of Rome was almost never recovered, and the fortune of the whole empire was ruined.

Magnentius, however, was defeated and fled; not long afterward, at Lugdunum, he killed himself with his own hand. His brother Decentius, whom he had appointed Caesar over Gaul, ended his life by hanging at Sens.

## CHAPTER SEVEN. Concerning Gallus, made Caesar by Constantius and soon afterward killed; and concerning the battles of Julian, Gallus’s brother, against the Germans and Franks, and how he seized the imperial power

Constantius immediately chose Gallus, the son of his paternal uncle, as Caesar. After creating him, he killed him not long afterward because Gallus was acting cruelly and tyrannically. He also took care to surround and suppress Sylvanus promptly, since Sylvanus was aspiring to revolutionary action throughout Gaul.

After Sylvanus had been killed, Constantius appointed his cousin Julian, the brother of Gallus, Caesar, and sent him to Gaul. Julian Caesar restored Gaul, which had been overthrown and oppressed by its enemies, to its former condition with the greatest energy. In the Silver Fields of Gaul, with only a few soldiers, he destroyed countless enemy forces.

Mounds resembling mountains stood there, and blood flowed like rivers. The noble king Nodomarius was captured; all his nobles were routed; the frontier was restored to Roman possession. Later, when he fought against the Alamanni, he captured their most powerful king, Badomarius.

Elated by these successes, he usurped the rank of Augustus. Soon afterward, invading Italy and Illyricum, he deprived Constantius, who was occupied with wars against the Parthians, of part of his kingdom.

Constantius then pressed him through embassies and advised him to return to his former status and title. Julian replied in milder terms that, under the name of the exalted empire, he would obey much more dutifully.

When Constantius learned of Julian’s crime, he abandoned the Parthian expedition. While returning to the civil war, he died on the road between Cilicia and Cappadocia.

Thus that man, who had torn apart the members of the Church by breaking peace and the unity of the Catholic faith, arming Christians against Christians in a civil—or, so to speak, ecclesiastical—war, spent, exhausted, and expended the entire troubled period of his reign and the most grievous span of his life in civil wars stirred up even against his relatives and kindred.

He ruled for twenty-four years and five months together with his brothers Constantine and Constans. After they had died, and Magnentius and the other tyrants had been destroyed, the reins of the whole Roman world were submitted to his authority.

## CHAPTER EIGHT. A remembrance of distinguished writers and of those who performed wondrous deeds and flourished at that time

During his reign there flourished learned men whose monuments survive in writing.

Antonius the monk, whose life Athanasius, bishop of the Church of Alexandria, set forth in a distinguished volume. He sent seven letters in Egyptian to various monasteries, written in an apostolic spirit and style; these were translated into Greek. The most important of them is addressed to Arsetas. He flourished especially while Constantine and his sons were ruling. He often reported to those who came to him many things about a certain Paul of Thebes, a man of extraordinary blessedness, whose death Jerome explained in a brief book.

Basil of Ancyra, a bishop skilled in the medical art, wrote a book against Marcellus on virginity, as well as certain other works. Under the emperor Constantius, he belonged to the Macedonian party with Eustathius of Sebaste.

Theodore, bishop of Heraclea in Thrace, was a man of elegant and lucid speech and of a particularly historical intelligence. Under the emperor Constantius he published a book, as well as commentaries on Matthew and on the Psalter.

Triphilus, bishop of Cyprileda, or Leocotheon, was the most eloquent man of his age and was also highly renowned under King Constantius. His commentaries on the *Song of Songs* are read, and he is said to have composed many other works, which have not come into our hands.

Donatus, from whom the Donatists derive their name, lived in Africa under the emperors Constantine and Constantius. He asserted that our people had handed over the Scriptures to the pagans during the persecution, and by his persuasion deceived nearly all Africa, especially Numidia. Many of his works concerning his heresy survive, including a book on the Holy Spirit agreeing with Arian doctrine.

Asterius, the philosopher of the Arian faction, wrote, during Constantine’s reign, commentaries on the Epistle to the Romans, the Gospels, and the Psalms, along with many other works, which the members of his party read with great enthusiasm.

Lucifer of Cagliari, a bishop, together with Pancratius and Hilary, clerics of the Roman Church, was driven into exile by the emperor Constantius under Bishop Liberius because of his faith. He refused, under Athanasius’s name, to condemn the faith of Nicaea and was banished to Palestine. A man of extraordinary steadfastness and prepared for martyrdom, he wrote a book against the emperor Constantius and sent it to him to read. Not long afterward, under the emperor Julian, he returned to Cagliari and died during the reign of Valentinian.

Eusebius, a Sardinian by birth and, from a reader of the city of Rome, bishop of Vercelli, was banished by the emperor Constantius to Scythopolis and from there to Cappadocia because of his confession of faith. Under the emperor Julian he returned to his church and published commentaries on the Psalms by Eusebius of Caesarea, which he had translated from Greek into Latin. He died while Valentinian and Valens were ruling.

Fortunatus, an African by birth and bishop of Aquileia, wrote, under Constantius, commentaries on the Gospel, arranged according to its headings, in brief and rustic language. In this respect he is detestable: at that time, when Liberius, bishop of Rome, was going into exile for the faith, Fortunatus was the first to pressure and break him and to compel him to subscribe to the heresy.

Acacius, whom, because he was one-eyed, they called Avonioraon, was bishop of Caesarea in Palestine. He composed seventeen volumes on Ecclesiastes and many additional and diverse treatises. He became so prominent under the emperor Constantius that he appointed Felix bishop of Rome in Liberius’s place.

Serapion of Thmuis, a bishop who earned the surname “the Scholastic” because of the elegance of his intellect, was dear to the monk Antonius. He published an excellent book against Mani, another on the headings of the Psalms, and useful letters to various people. He was distinguished under the emperor Constantius.

At that same time there was also James of Nisibis, a bishop who became renowned for many miracles. Among the miracles he performed was the following. When Nisibis, after Mesopotamia had been devastated, was besieged by Sapor, king of the Persians, with enormous forces for seventy days and afterward, a wall collapsed under the force of a river which the army had skillfully held back and forced to assault it, once the intervening sluices had been removed and it could no longer withstand the force of the water. The man of God restored it completely through his sacred prayers during the intervening night.

The following day Sapor believed that he would invade the city through the riverbed and the ruin of the walls. But he saw that the wall had been restored together with its battlements. Not only did the restoration of the wall terrify him and those with him, but another vision also disturbed him. For he saw standing above the wall a figure clothed in imperial form, shining with both purple and a diadem.

He supposed that this was the Roman emperor and threatened death to those who had reported that the emperor was not present there. When they insisted that they had spoken the truth and that Constantius was staying at Antioch, he recognized from the face he saw that their words were true and said that God was fighting for the Romans.

Nevertheless, even after recognizing these signs, he did not withdraw from the siege. Accordingly, at the urging of the besieged, the aforementioned bishop approached the wall so that, by looking upon the Persian camp, he might curse it. But he pronounced no other curse against them except that he asked the Lord to send gnats and mosquitoes upon them, so that through small creatures they might recognize heavenly power.

Such a cloud of gnats and mosquitoes followed his prayer and filled the Persian camp, so that the elephants and horses, unable to endure their force, threw the battle lines into confusion and disrupted the camp. They ran off in different directions and sought the wilderness.

Terrified by such things, the most powerful king, with his innumerable army, withdrew in confusion after lifting the siege.

This James was one of the confessors who became renowned under the persecutor Maximian and who condemned Arian doctrine at the Council of Nicaea. He wrote twenty-six books in the Syriac language: against all heresies; on universal charity; on fasting; on prayer; on love of neighbor; on the resurrection; on life after death; on humility; on repentance; on satisfaction; on virginity; on the soul’s understanding; on circumcision; on the act of blessing—that is, concerning what is read in Isaiah, “the cluster was not destroyed”; on Christ, that he is the Son of God and consubstantial with the Father; on chastity; against the pagans; on the construction of the tabernacle; on the conduct of the nations; on the kingdom of the Persians; and on the persecution of Christians.

He also composed a chronicle which, though less concerned with the curiosities of the Greeks, is more trustworthy because it is constructed solely on the authority of the divine Scriptures. It silences the mouths of those who, with presumptuous speculation, idly philosophize about the coming of Christ our Lord.

This man died in the time of Constantius and, at the command of his father Constantine [Col. 1210A], was buried on the wall of Nisibis, evidently to protect the city. This happened according to Constantine’s faith. For many years later, when Julian entered Nisibis, either begrudging the glory of the buried man or because of hatred for the faith of Constantius, whose house he was persecuting for this reason, he ordered the body of the saint to be removed from the city. A few months later, although it was done for the sake of the state, the emperor Jovian, who had succeeded Julian, handed the city over to the barbarians.

From this point Sapor, king of the Persians, persecuted the Christians.

To return to the sequence of the history: while Constantius was emperor, Gallus Caesar crushed the Jews who, after killing soldiers during the night, had taken up arms in rebellion. Many thousands of people were killed, even those of harmless age, and he delivered their cities—Diocaesarea, Tiberias, and Diospolis—and many other towns to the flames. Some nobles were killed by Gallus at Antioch.

At that time the eloquent Titianus was administering the prefecture of the praetorium in Gaul. Victorinus the rhetorician and Donatus the grammarian, Jerome’s teachers, were renowned at Rome; Victorinus even earned a statue in the Forum of Trajan.

During those days the relics of the apostle Timothy were brought to Constantinople. When Constantius entered Rome, the bones of the apostle Andrew and of Luke the Evangelist were received by the people of Constantinople with extraordinary enthusiasm.

Hilary, after presenting a book on his behalf to Constantius at Constantinople, returned to Gaul. Once back, he condemned in Gaul the deceit of the Ariminian perfidy.

## CHAPTER NINE. How Julian was converted from Christianity to idolatry and at last paid the just penalty

When Constantius’s death became known, Julian alone obtained the supreme imperial power for one year and eight months. He attacked the Christian religion by strategy more than by force. To make the faith of Christ be denied and the worship of idols accepted, he sought to entice people through honors rather than compel them by tortures.

Nevertheless, he openly decreed by edict that no Christian should be a teacher of the liberal studies. Yet, as we have learned from our forefathers, almost everyone everywhere embraced the conditions of the decree and preferred to abandon office rather than faith. Many Christians at that time also fell voluntarily while seeking honors.

This Julian, who had formerly been a Christian and afterward became a traitor, while still a young man, had his hair cut and pretended to live a monastic life. In secret he practiced philosophy, while openly reading the sacred books of the Christians. At last he was appointed a reader in the church of Nicomedia, and under this disguise he avoided the emperor’s fury.

He did these things out of fear, because he was afraid of the emperor Constantius, who had killed his brother Gallus, and he knew that Constantius regarded him with suspicion.

He therefore read the books of the pagan philosophers, at whose instigation he began to desire the imperial scepters. For this reason he traveled throughout all Hellas seeking prophets who would give answers, asking whether he would attain the imperial power. He found a man who claimed that he could tell him what he desired.

The man led him to a certain place of idols and introduced him into the inner shrine, where he summoned deceptive demons. When they appeared in due ritual, Julian was compelled by terror to form the sign of the cross upon his forehead.

Then the demons, seeing the figure of the Lord’s trophy and remembering their defeat, suddenly disappeared. When the magician realized this, he began to blame Julian. Julian, however, explained his terror and said that he had been astonished by the power of the cross, since the demons had vanished when they saw that sign.

But the magician said: “Do not suppose this, good man, that they were afraid, as you say. Rather, they departed because they detested this sign.” Thus he deceived the wretched Julian and filled him with hatred for the Christian sign.

After this, the emperor summoned Julian and appointed him Caesar. He gave him his sister Constantia as wife and sent him to Gaul against the barbarians, as we have said above.

When Julian first obtained sole authority, as though condemning Constantius’s wrongful actions, he ordered the bishops to be released from exile. Later, however, he rose against our people with every art of doing harm.

Since he was a crafty and cunning deceiver, he ordered the Jews, out of hatred for the Christians, to gather from everywhere at Jerusalem. He commanded that expenses be supplied to them from the public treasury so that they might rebuild the temple and offer the lawful sacrifices there, hoping at least in this way to abolish Christianity.

But by a wondrous dispensation, the greater part of the Jews who had gathered there were killed by an earthquake, while the rest were consumed by avenging flames. Those who survived also saw the sign of the cross both in the sky and on each person’s clothing—a sign which, even if they wished, they could not erase from themselves. Thus, compelled against their will, they were forced to confess Christ as the Son of God; terrified by these signs, they departed.

The emperor, who had long endeavored to spread paganism throughout all his dominion, was deeply distressed when he saw that Christians were instead being approved. He concluded that the state was sustained by a good life and Christian conduct. He therefore tried everywhere to adorn pagan temples according to the structure and order of the Christian religion, with seats and processions. He appointed readers of his superstition according to the model of clerics, instructing them to observe solemnly fixed hours, days, and prayers.

He likewise commanded that men skilled in philosophy should take care of the dwellings of travelers and the poor, and that other forms of provision for the needy should be arranged according to pagan religion, so that it might acquire the name of piety. If anyone sinned willingly or unwillingly, he established, following Christian practice, that the person should undergo correction after a moderate penance.

By doing these things the emperor sought the destruction of the Christians, yet he could not persuade his subjects, and he was openly ashamed to employ force.

Julian was greatly afflicted by the vice of vainglory. In the speech he wrote about the Caesars, he tore apart all the emperors who had preceded him, and after Julius Caesar he was the first emperor to recite in the senate what he had composed.

Moved by this arrogance, he also wrote books against the Christians. In order to expel cooks and barbers from the palace, he acted as a philosopher, though not as an emperor; but in attacking and vilifying them, he acted neither as a philosopher nor as a ruler.

After he had distributed throughout the Roman world all the arguments he could devise against the Christians through the devil’s agency and his own cunning, he became excessively desirous of glory—vanity had inflamed him—and, preparing for war against the Parthians, he gathered Roman forces from everywhere and took them with him on the expedition. He vowed the blood of Christians to his gods, intending to persecute the churches openly if he should obtain victory.

He also ordered an amphitheater to be built at Jerusalem, in which, after returning from the Parthians, he would throw the bishops, monks, and all the holy men of that place to beasts—beasts made still more savage by some artifice—and watch them being torn apart.

After he moved his camp from Ctesiphon, he was led into the wilderness by the treachery of a certain deserter. As the army was perishing from the violence of thirst, the heat of the sun, and, in addition, the labor of crossing the sands, the emperor, anxious amid such dangers, wandered carelessly through the vast wilderness, separated from his troops. He was struck in the side by the spear of an enemy cavalryman whom he encountered and died.

After receiving the mortal wound, he scattered his own blood into the air and cried: “You have conquered, Galilean; you have conquered!” For he was accustomed to call Christians Galileans.

Thus the merciful God dissolved the wicked plans of the wicked man through his death. Julian had voluntarily abandoned God, the author of all things, trusting in wicked magical arts through the insolence of his frivolity, as though, more daring than everyone else, he had surpassed them all; and he paid the deserved penalty.

For it is not fitting for an emperor to be distinguished from others by daring, but by moderation and wholesome counsels. His personal safety must always be preserved for the security of everyone, and especially in war.

## CHAPTER TEN. Concerning the Christian tutor and Julian Saba, who foretold the destruction of the impious Caesar Julian in Persia

At that same time, a very good tutor of young men lived at Antioch. There was also a famous and impious sophist there, Libanius, who was awaiting Julian’s victory and had his threats before his eyes.

He therefore asked the tutor, mockingly addressing our religion: “Now, what do you think the son of the carpenter is doing?”

But the tutor, filled with divine grace, foretold what happened shortly afterward. He replied: “O sophist, the Creator of all things, whom you have called the son of a carpenter, is preparing a little burial place for Julian.”

A few days later, Julian’s death was announced, and he was brought and placed in the little burial place; the fear of his threats was emptied of its force.

At that time Julian, surnamed Saba, a most holy man, when he heard the threats of that impious man, immediately began to groan and weep and beseech the merciful Lord. Suddenly the river of his tears stopped, and he was filled with joy; his face became radiant.

When his attendants saw this change of spirit, they asked him to reveal the cause of his sudden joy. He then said: “The savage destroyer of the sacred vineyard has paid the penalty for his devastation. He lies dead, deprived of his terrors and threats.”

When everyone learned this, they rejoiced and offered grateful hymns to God. Later, messengers reported that it was the very same day and hour of Julian’s death that the most holy old man had recognized and foretold.

## CHAPTER ELEVEN. How Jovian was made emperor by the soldiers and led the army back from Persia
The soldiers, therefore, being plunged into the greatest turmoil, without any further delay placed the imperial diadem upon Jovian the following day. For he was a brave and noble man, and at that time a commander of a thousand, when Julian had proposed to the soldiers by law that they sacrifice or leave the army. He chose rather to lose his military belt than to obey the impious commands of the emperor. Julian therefore kept him among the military men at that time because of the necessities of war [Col. 1213B].

When the soldiers were forcibly dragging him to the imperial office, he cried out that he did not wish to rule pagan men, since he himself was a Christian. When all the soldiers together proclaimed that they too were Christians, he accepted the imperial power.

Jovian, therefore, was considering the common welfare and how he might bring the army safely out from among its enemies. He needed no grand strategy, but from the seeds of piety he reaped a most useful harvest. For God suddenly revealed his providence and brought Jovian’s wavering to the harbor of tranquility. When the king of the Persians learned of his distress, he sent an embassy and sought peace. He then sent provisions to the soldiers and ordered a market for the sale of goods to be prepared for them in the desert [Col. 1213C]. After the treaties had been concluded, he brought the army back unharmed.

These agreements were disgraceful as far as Roman glory was concerned, but they suited the necessities of the time.
