For Jovian withdrew after Syria had been lost and the Mesopotamian city of Nisibis had been handed over to the Persians. These events strengthened the Christians and brought grief to the pagans.

Moreover, the soldiers strongly condemned Julian’s reckless ardor and attributed to him the cause of the loss of Roman territory: seduced by the Persian as though by a traitor, he had burned the ships that were to transport grain by river and had inflicted famine upon the soldiers. Pride therefore deceived him, and boastfulness, as he was puffed up with sophistic disciplines. By these the superstitious worshiper of idols gloried, saying that the times would be happy when he himself possessed imperial power.

But when Jovian, at the age of twenty-nine, had arranged peace and returned to Roman soil, and a brighter light arising from the East spread itself over our world, he undertook to restore the state with every moderation, as though after excessive storms. He did not, however, make the care of the Churches his secondary concern; yet he did not act rashly, as Constantius had done, but was warned by the downfall of his predecessor. His first written order was that the bishops should return from exile, and he declared that the Churches ought to be restored to those who had inviolably preserved the faith set forth at Nicaea.

## CHAPTER XII. The recall of Athanasius, and how Jovian used his counsel in handling ecclesiastical affairs

With honorable and most dutiful letters he summoned Athanasius [Col. 1214A] and received from him the pattern of the faith and the method by which the Churches were to be organized. Athanasius sent back a complete exposition of divine doctrine, consistent with the apostolic teachings, by which the emperor, instructed, might avoid the most wicked deceits of the heretics and restore peace to the catholic Churches.

After a short interval, the great Athanasius, desiring to see the emperor beloved by God, came to Antioch and instructed the prince concerning what was necessary. Some say that the emperor himself had summoned him more insistently, so that he might set forth what seemed necessary for religion and the true faith; and, arranging the affairs of the Church as was fitting, he was considering the restoration of the Churches.

Moreover, he sent Athanasius, who had become his closest friend, to Egypt, so that he might arrange the affairs of the Churches and the peoples as seemed best to him [Col. 1214B], threatening those who disparaged him with punishments appropriate to their offense, since he knew that Athanasius had suffered many hardships undeservedly through unjust accusations.

The emperor’s purpose, however, was to cut short the contentions of those who disagreed by kindness and persuasive words. He said that he would in no way trouble any of the believers, but that he loved and greatly honored those who preserved the decrees of the Council of Nicaea for the unity of the Church, in which ecclesiastical unity is contained.

But death, before its time, seized these beginnings, so pious and so joyful. While returning to Illyricum and traveling through Galatia, he hastened toward Constantinople but died at Dadastena, in the eighteenth month after he had begun to rule and in the thirty-eighth year of his age.

## CHAPTER XIII. Valentinian made emperor by the soldiers, and a memorable event during his reign [Col. 1214C]

After Valentinian had been created emperor at Nicaea with the consent of the soldiers, he remained in power for eleven years. Since he was a Christian of sound faith and served under the military oath, he had been tribune of the Scutarii under the emperor Julian. When that sacrilegious emperor ordered him either to sacrifice to idols or to leave the army, Valentinian, knowing faithfully that God’s judgments were more pleasing and his promises better, withdrew of his own accord.

Thus, after a brief interval, Julian was killed and soon afterward Jovian died. Valentinian, who had lost his tribunate for the name of Christ, received the imperial power in the place of his persecutor, Christ repaying him. For he excelled not only in courage but also in prudence, temperance, justice, and bodily stature. He was at once kingly and civil, so that when the army attempted to associate another colleague with him, he replied:

“Yours it was, O soldiers, when there was no emperor, to give me the government of the empire; but once I had accepted it, it was now my concern, not yours, to think about matters of common interest.”

The soldiers, astonished by his words, followed his will. Later he made his brother Valens a partner in the empire and killed the tyrant Procopius and many of his supporters.

An earthquake occurred throughout the whole world and so shook the sea, which was likewise thrown into confusion, that the sea, pouring back over the neighboring flatlands, is said to have destroyed many island cities after they had been shaken and undermined [Col. 1215A].

Valens was baptized by Eudoxius, the bishop and defender of the Arian doctrine, and was persuaded by him; he turned aside into the most savage heresy. For a long time, however, he concealed his malevolent persecution and did not join power to his will, until he was restrained by the authority of his living brother. He considered how much force an emperor who, once a soldier, had shown such steadfastness in defending the faith might exercise in avenging it.

In the third year of their imperial reign, Gratian, the son of Valentinian, was made emperor. In that same year, at Atrebates, true wool mixed with rain fell from the clouds. Furthermore, Athalaric, king of the Goths, persecuted the Christians among his people with the utmost cruelty and raised many Barbarians who had been killed for their faith to the crown of martyrdom.

Many of them, nevertheless, fled to Roman territory for the confession of Christ, not trembling as though toward enemies, but confident that they were going to brothers [Col. 1215B].

Valentinian crushed the Saxons at the very borders of the Franks. This people, settled along the shores of the Ocean and amid impassable marshes, terrifying in courage and agility, had been planning a massive and dangerous incursion into the Roman territories.

He also subdued the Burgundians, a new name for new enemies. They are said to have numbered more than seventy thousand armed men and to have occupied the bank of the Rhine. After Lower Germany had once been conquered by Drusus and Tiberius, the adopted sons of Caesar, these people had been distributed in forts and had grown into a great nation. They had also taken their name from this activity, because the frequent settlements established along the frontier were commonly called *burgi*. Their powerful and destructive force is attested even today by the Gauls [Col. 1215C].

They remain settled in the possession they had taken, although by God’s providence they have all now become Christians, accepting the catholic faith and our clergy, whom they obey. They live gently, peaceably, and innocently—not as though among subject Gauls, but truly among Christian brothers.

In the eleventh year of his reign, when the Sarmatians had spread throughout the provinces of Pannonia and were laying them waste, Valentinian prepared war against them at the town of Prigition. There he was suddenly suffocated and died through an outpouring of blood, a condition called *apoplexis* in Greek.

## CHAPTER XIV. The sons of Valentinian, who ruled the western regions after him, and Valens, Augustus of the East [Col. 1215D]

After him, his son Gratian held the empire in the West, while his uncle Valens was established in the regions of the East. He also made his very young brother Valentinian a partner in the empire, although they were not born of the same mother.

For Severa, the former wife of the elder Valentinian and the mother of Gratian, saw in the baths the beauty of Justina, a young woman whom she had brought into her own circle, and fell in love with her. The empress disclosed the girl’s bodily beauty to her husband, who immediately took Justina as his wife. He did not, however, cast off his former wife, and on their account he enacted laws permitting all men who wished to do so to enter into two marriages with impunity.

After Valentinian had therefore taken Justina, as we have said, he had by her the younger Valentinian and three daughters: Justa, Grata, and Galla [Col. 1216A]. Later the elder Theodosius, the emperor, married Galla, by whom he is known to have had a daughter, Placidia. For it is known that he had Arcadius and Honorius by his former wife, Placella.

While these princes were ruling, Athanasius was living peacefully at Alexandria in true doctrine and religion and was held in great renown. Under the emperors Constantius and Julian he had endured many hardships for our faith.

He is said to have written two books *Against the Nations*, one book *Against Valens and Ursacius*, one book *On Virginity*, and many books *On the Persecutions of the Arians*. He also wrote on the titles of the Psalms, letters containing the life of the monk Antony, and many other works too numerous to list.

Hilary, bishop of the city of Poitiers in Aquitaine, was exiled to Phrygia from the Council of Biterrae through the faction of Saturninus, bishop of Arles [Col. 1216B]. He composed twelve books against the Arians, another book *On Synods*, which he wrote to the bishops of Gaul, and commentaries on the Psalter—namely, on the first and second Psalms; on Psalms 50 through 72; and on Psalm 118 through the final Psalm.

In this work he imitated Adamantius and also added some material from his own understanding. He also wrote a short book to Constantine, which he presented to him while he was alive at Constantinople; another against Constantius, which he wrote after Constantius’s death; and a book against Valens and Ursacius containing a history of the Councils of Ariminum and Seleucia. He wrote also a work to the prefect Sallustius, or against Dioscorus; another book of hymns and mysteries [Col. 1216C]; commentaries on Matthew; and treatises on Job, which he translated from the Greek of Adamantius according to its sense.

There is also an elegant short book of his against Auxentius, as well as several letters to various persons. Some say that he wrote a notable volume on the Song of Songs, but this work is unknown to us.

After returning from exile, he illuminated Gaul like a splendid light and freed the other provinces from the Arian plague through his sacred teaching. He died at Poitiers while Valentinian and Valens were ruling.

Titus of Bostra, a bishop, wrote vigorously against the Manichaeans under the emperors Julian, Jovian, and Valentinian, producing books and several other short works. He died under Valens.

## CHAPTER XV. Ambrose and the other teachers who flourished under the aforementioned emperors [Col. 1216D]

Meanwhile, when Auxentius, the heretical bishop, had died at Milan, the people of both parties were carried along by divergent zeal. A serious dispute and dangerous sedition were preparing a timely destruction for their own city, since neither side, desiring a different outcome, could obtain what it sought.

Ambrose at that time held the consular office of the same province. When he saw destruction threatening the city, he immediately entered the church, in accordance with his position and office, intending to calm the people’s sedition. After he had delivered a lengthy speech there, according to the laws and public discipline, for peace and tranquility, a sudden cry and a single voice rose from those who were fighting and disagreeing among themselves, demanding Ambrose as bishop [Col. 1217A].

People immediately cried out that he should be baptized—for he was a catechumen—and that he should be given to them as bishop. They declared that the people could not otherwise become one people and one faith unless Ambrose were given to them as priest.

When the emperor Valentinian learned of this, he suddenly ordered both that Ambrose be baptized and that he be ordained bishop as a worthy man. For he knew that Ambrose’s will was more reliable than any weight of authority and that he possessed the subtler secrets of the whole rule of faith. He also judged that a divine decree was at work in him, since even the opposing party had agreed in his election.

Thus, after receiving the gift of holy baptism, Ambrose also received the grace of the episcopate. When this had been done, the excellent emperor is said to have offered the following hymn to the Savior and Lord—for he had been present during these events:

“I give thanks to you, almighty Lord and our Savior, because I entrusted bodies to this man, while you entrusted souls to him, and you have shown that my choice accords with justice.”

Let this suffice here concerning Ambrose.

At that time Photinus, from Galatia, a disciple of Marcellus, was ordained bishop of Sirmium. He attempted to revive the heresy of Ebion, and afterward was expelled from the Church by the emperor Valentinian. He wrote many volumes, including a particularly important work against the nations and one book addressed to Valentinian.

Optatus Afer, bishop of Milevis, wrote from the catholic side under the emperors Valentinian and Valens. Against the accusations of the Donatian party he composed seven books, in which he asserts that the crime of the Donatians is falsely turned against us.

Acylius Severus, a Spaniard descended from that Severus to whom the two books of Lactantius’s letters are addressed, composed a volume resembling a travel narrative, containing the course of his entire life, in both prose and verse. He called it *Cintacipoiam*, or “the Rock,” and died under the emperor Valentinian.

## CHAPTER XVI. The evil deeds of Augustus Valens against the Catholics, and his persecution [Col. 1216D]

When Valens was summoned by his brother Valentinian to share the empire, he was being instructed in the apostolic doctrines. But when the Goths had crossed the Danube and were traversing Thrace, he gathered an army and planned to fight against them.

He decided that he should not fight without the protection of sacred grace, but armed with holy baptism. This decision was good and very wise. What he did afterward, however, signified great weakness of spirit and betrayal of the truth. For he suffered the same misfortune as his forefather Adam.

He was seduced by his wife’s conversation and ensnared by feminine words. She had first been caught in the snares of the Arian deception, and she persuaded him also to fall with her into the pit of blasphemy. Eudoxius was the author of this seduction. He still held the reins of the Church of Constantinople—not governing it, but rather sinking his own ship.

At the time of his baptism, therefore, Eudoxius bound the wretched man by an oath, so that he would remain in the impiety of the doctrine and expel from everywhere those who held contrary opinions. Thus, abandoning the apostolic teaching, Valens took the opposing side [Col. 1218A]. What he had concealed through fear while his brother was alive, he shortly afterward fulfilled as he had sworn.

Valens held the empire for four years after Valentinian’s death. While he was acting impiously, he immediately, with the reckless boldness of unrestrained power, issued a law that monks—that is, Christians who, having abandoned the manifold activities of worldly affairs, devote themselves to the single work of faith—should be compelled to enter military service.

At that time the vast deserts and widespread sands of Egypt, unknown to human habitation because of thirst, sterility, and the extremely dangerous abundance of serpents, had been filled by a great multitude of monks. Tribunes and soldiers were sent there to drag away the holy and venerable soldiers of God under another name for persecution. Many bands of saints were killed there [Col. 1218B].

What was done for a long time throughout the various provinces by similar orders against the catholic Churches and the peoples of the true faith is sufficiently shown in ecclesiastical histories. For Valens drove bishops into exile, and he brought presbyters, deacons, and monks even to torture and handed them over to the flames. He plotted many wicked and cruel acts against the Church of God, devised in various parts of the Roman world under the impious emperor—other forms of suffocation and countless tortures by which the Lord’s vineyard was devastated.

The historians, whose purpose was to transmit these things in writing to posterity, were unable to record them fully because of the multitude of different deaths. We have taken care to include one account from among many in this concise work.

## CHAPTER XVII. How the people of Edessa avoided Valens’s fury through a woman dragging her son to martyrdom [Col. 1218C]

It must also be related what is known to have happened at Edessa in Mesopotamia. In that city there is a very famous and splendid basilica of the apostle Thomas, in which assemblies are frequently held out of reverence for the place.

The emperor wished to inspect it, and, learning that all those hateful to him were gathering there, is said to have struck the prefect because he had not expelled all the orthodox. Although the prefect, having suffered this insult, unwillingly tried to serve the prince’s anger—for he did not wish to inflict slaughter upon so many people—he secretly ordered that no one should remain in the basilica.

But no one heeded either his command or his threat. For the next day they all gathered together at the place of prayer. When the prefect was hurrying to the basilica with a large force of soldiers to carry out the emperor’s order, a certain poor woman interrupted his task as she hurried toward the basilica, dragging her son by the hand.

The prefect, angered, ordered that the woman be brought before him and said to her:

“Unhappy woman, where are you running so indecently?”

She replied:

“Where the others are hurrying to go.”

Then he said:

“Have you not heard that the prefect will kill everyone he finds there?”

“I have heard,” she replied, “and that is why I am hurrying to be found there among them.”

“And where are you dragging this little infant?”

Then the woman said:

“So that he too may deserve to receive martyrdom” [Col. 1219A].

When the man heard this woman’s expression of the resolve of those gathering, he immediately returned to the emperor and reported that they were all prepared to accept death for their faith. He said that it was unreasonable to kill so many people in a short time. After hearing this, he recalled the emperor from his anger.

In this way, therefore, the people of Edessa escaped the emperor’s fury. During the same period, the Church, as though burning in the fire of persecution, shone forth purer than gold. For faith is tested not in everyone’s words but in exiles and prisons, since to be catholic was not a matter of honor but of punishment.

## CHAPTER XVIII. The holy men who flourished at that time in Egypt and elsewhere [Col. 1219B]

At that time Egypt flourished not only with men learned in Christian philosophy but also with those who lived throughout the vast desert and performed signs and wonders through the apostolic simplicity of their lives and the sincerity of their hearts.

There were Macarius of the Upper Desert and another Macarius of the Inner Desert; Isidore in Scythia; Pampus in the Cells; Moses and Benjamin in Nuria; Scyrion, Elias, and Paul in Apoliote; and another Paul in Focis.

There were also Pæmen and Joseph in Pispiri, which is called the Mountain of Antony. We have learned through reliable report that many other men of this kind were living in the regions of Egypt at that time, so that the Apostle’s saying might truly be fulfilled: “Where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more.”

For Egypt had once served, more superstitiously than all other nations, various monstrous forms of idols. At the same time Mesopotamia also had distinguished men, accomplished in the same pursuits, at Edessa and Carrhae and in other places.

But Cappadocia was no less fertile than either of these regions; indeed, it produced something more joyous, for it brought forth Gregory and Basil. Both were noble, both educated at Athens, both fellow students, and both having left the lecture hall to teach rhetoric. But by God’s will they turned to divine philosophy, in which they flourished wonderfully.

Cappadocia itself therefore produced a very rich harvest of many saints. Because of their number, I have postponed recording their miracles in this work, since several learned men had left written works of their own concerning the merit of their lives and the example of their conduct.

## CHAPTER XIX. The battles fought in Africa by Theodosius, father of the emperor Theodosius, and the battle fought in Gaul by Gratian against the Alamanni [Col. 1219D]

Meanwhile, in the regions of Africa, Firmus, having stirred up the Moorish peoples and made himself king, devastated Africa and Mauretania. He captured Caesarea, a most distinguished city, by deceit, then filled it with slaughter and fires and handed it over to the Barbarians as plunder.

The comes Theodosius—the father of the emperor Theodosius, who later ruled—had been sent there by Valentinian. He broke the forces of the Moors in many battles and compelled Firmus himself, afflicted and overcome, to die.

Afterward, with the most experienced prudence, he restored all Africa together with Mauretania to a condition better than before. But under the emperor Valens, when many other distinguished men had also been killed, envy gradually arising and insinuating itself, Theodosius was ordered to be killed at Carthage.

He preferred to be baptized for the remission of sins. After obtaining the sacrament of Christ, which he had sought, he abandoned the glorious life of this world, secure also concerning eternal life, and willingly offered his neck to the executioner.

Meanwhile Gratian, a very young emperor, saw an immeasurable multitude of enemies pouring into Roman territory. Trusting in Christ’s power, he threw himself against the enemy with a greatly inferior number of soldiers. Immediately, near the town of Argentaria, he brought to an end a most terrifying war in Gaul with astonishing success. More than thirty thousand Alamanni are said to have been killed in that battle, with minimal loss to the Romans [Col. 1220B].

## CHAPTER XX. The Goths, who defeated the erroneous emperor Valens in war and eventually burned him alive [Col. 1220C]

In the thirteenth year of Valens’s reign—that is, shortly after Valens had carried out the devastation of the Churches and the slaughter of the saints throughout the entire East—the root of those miseries produced a luxuriant growth of branches all at once.

For the nation of the Huns, long secluded behind inaccessible mountains, suddenly flared up in violent fury against the Goths and expelled them, thrown into confusion everywhere, from their ancient settlements.

The Goths crossed the Danube in flight and were received by Valens without any treaty being made. They did not even surrender their weapons, so that the Romans might more safely trust the Barbarians. Later, driven to take up arms by the intolerable greed and mistreatment of the commander Maximus, they defeated the army of Valens and spread throughout Thrace, pouring slaughter, fires, and plunder over everything at once.

When Valens had left Antioch and was being drawn toward the final outcome of his unfortunate war, he was prompted by the late repentance of the prefect Maximus and ordered the bishops and the other holy men to be recalled from exile.

Thus, in the fifteenth year of his reign, he fought that grievous war in Thrace against the Goths, who by then were thoroughly equipped through the growth of their strength and resources. At the very first assault, the Roman cavalry squadrons were thrown into confusion by the Goths and abandoned the infantry supports on every side.

Soon the infantry legions, surrounded everywhere by the enemy cavalry and first overwhelmed by clouds of arrows [Col. 1220D], were then driven, mad with fear, in scattered groups through trackless places. They were utterly slaughtered by the swords and spears of their pursuers.

The emperor himself, wounded by an arrow and turned to flight, was with difficulty carried away and hidden in the hut of a little farmstead. He was discovered by the pursuing enemy, placed in the fire, and consumed. To make the testimony of his punishment and of divine indignation an even more terrible example for posterity, he was also deprived of common burial.

He was extinguished in this manner in the fiftieth year of his life. He had reigned thirteen years with his brother and three years after his brother.

The Goths had previously asked through suppliant ambassadors that bishops be sent to them, from whom they might learn the rule of the Christian faith. The emperor Valens, with destructive perversity, sent teachers of the Arian doctrine [Col. 1221A]. The Goths retained the first rudiments of the faith that they had received.

Therefore, by God’s just judgment, they themselves burned alive the man because of whom they too, even when dead, will burn through the fault of error.

## CHAPTER XXI. Didymus and the other teachers of that time

At that time Didymus of Alexandria, blind from early childhood and for that reason ignorant even of the elements of learning, offered so great a miracle to all who knew him that he learned even dialectic and geometry—which depend above all upon sight—to perfection.

He wrote many distinguished works: commentaries on all the Psalms; commentaries on the Gospel of Matthew and on John; works on doctrines; two books against the Arians; one book on the Holy Spirit, which Jerome translated into Latin; eighteen commentaries on Isaiah; three books of commentaries on Hosea; five books on the prophet Zechariah; commentaries on Job; and countless other works, the arrangement of which must be left to the judgment of the individual reader.

Ephrem, a deacon of the Church of Edessa, composed many short works in the Syriac language. He attained such renown that, after the reading of the divine Scriptures, his writings were publicly recited in certain Churches.

He published a Greek volume on the Holy Spirit, which someone had translated from the Syriac language. From this translation, too, the sharpness of his lofty intellect is evident. He died under the emperor Valens.

Under the emperor Valens, therefore, such a storm arose at Constantinople that hailstones of extraordinary size, falling like stones, killed many people [Col. 1221C]. The Lord’s indignation became evident to all because of the exiles and persecutions inflicted by the emperor and the Arians upon God’s servants.

In those days Melania, the most noble of Roman women and the daughter of the former consul Marcellinus, leaving behind her only son, the praetor Urbanus, sailed to Jerusalem. There she displayed such a remarkable example of virtues, especially humility, that she received the name of Thecla.

## CHAPTER XXII. Gratian, who recalled the bishops from exile and appointed Theodosius emperor of the East

Gratian, the fortieth emperor after Augustus, held power for six years after Valens’s death, although he had already long been reigning with his uncle Valens and his brother Valentinian.

After Valens died, the Barbarians again came as far as the walls of Constantinople and devastated its suburbs. Consequently, the citizens carried whatever weapons they found and resisted the enemy as best they could.

The wife of the emperor Valens, named Dominica, provided the soldiers who fought well with rewards from the public treasury, according to custom. The Saracens offered them assistance, which their queen, named Mavia, an ally of the Romans, had sent.

Gratian, the son of Valentinian, had long held the scepter of Europe after his father’s death. When Valens also died without offspring, he took possession of the kingdoms of Asia and Libya as well. He soon demonstrated through his deeds the piety that he had conceived in his mind and dedicated the beginnings of his reign to the Lord of all things [Col. 1222A].

He therefore issued a law ordering that the expelled shepherds should return to their own sheepfolds and that the sacred basilicas should be restored to those who followed the communion of Damasus. Damasus, bishop of the city of Rome, was a praiseworthy man and a remarkable defender of the apostolic doctrines. He had promptly taken up the governance of the Church after Liberius.

Together with this law, the emperor sent a certain Sapor, then a very famous military commander. He ordered that the preachers of Arian blasphemy should be expelled from the divine enclosures like pestilences, while everything should be restored to the best shepherds and the sacred sheepfolds.

He decreed that this be observed throughout all the provinces.

Gratian, therefore, having obtained the empire together with the younger Valentinian, recalled everyone from exile and enacted a law that every religion might celebrate its sacred rites freely. He prohibited only the Eunomians, Photinians, and Manichaeans from the Churches.

When he saw that the condition of the state was afflicted and almost collapsing, he himself selected Theodosius, just as Nerva had once chosen the Spaniard Trajan, through whom the state had been restored. Theodosius was a Spaniard and a man necessary for the restoration of the state. Gratian clothed him in the purple at Firmum and appointed him at the same time to rule the East and Thrace.

## CHAPTER XXIII. The deeds of Theodosius, and how he attained the imperial office [Col. 1222C]

Theodosius therefore believed that the afflicted state could be restored from God’s anger through mercy. Placing all his confidence in the help of Christ, he fearlessly attacked the great Scythian peoples, feared by all their predecessors and avoided even by that Alexander the Great—as Pompey, Cornelius, and others have testified—but now, after the Roman army had been destroyed, most fully equipped with Roman horses and weapons: the Alans, Huns, and Goths.

He defeated them in great and numerous battles, entered the city of Constantinople as victor, and, lest the small Roman army itself be worn down by constant warfare, concluded a treaty with the Gothic king Athanaric.

As soon as Athanaric came to Constantinople, he died. All the Gothic peoples, after the death of their king, observing Theodosius’s courage and kindness, surrendered themselves to the Roman empire.

At the same time the Persians, who, after Julian had been killed and the other emperors repeatedly defeated, and now after Valens had also been put to flight [Col. 1222D], were belching out the satisfaction of their most recent victory in savage mockery, sent ambassadors beyond Constantinople to Theodosius and suppliantly sought peace. A treaty was then concluded, and the entire East enjoyed profound tranquility.

I shall briefly explain how Theodosius attained the imperial office.

When Gratian learned that the Barbarians were devastating Thrace, he left Italy and came to Phoenicia. At that time Theodosius was very famous both because of the nobility of his parents and because of his own courage. For this reason, worn down by the envy of judges, he was staying in Spain, where he had been born and raised.

While the emperor was uncertain what to do—for the Barbarians, elated by victory, appeared invincible—he believed that the war could be brought to an end under Theodosius’s command. He therefore suddenly summoned him from Spain, proclaimed him master of the soldiers, and sent him with an expedition against the Barbarians [Col. 1223A].

Strengthened by faith, Theodosius confidently set out for Thrace. When he arrived and saw the Barbarians, he drew up his army for battle. When the engagement took place, the Barbarians, unable to withstand the attack, abandoned their battle lines.

They fled, while the Romans bravely pursued them. An immense slaughter of the Barbarians then took place. After many had been killed and only a few had secretly crossed the Danube, the excellent commander dispersed his army through the neighboring cities and himself returned swiftly to the emperor, so that he became the messenger of his own victories. Even the emperor, amazed, thought that this could not have happened.

The envious said that Theodosius had fled. But he asked that men be sent who could see the multitude of enemy dead. Moved by these words, the emperor sent men to inspect what had happened and report to him.

For Theodosius had seen in a dream that Saint Meletius, bishop of the city of Antioch, clothed him in an imperial cloak and adorned his head with a crown. When he had seen this during the night, he reported it to one of his friends. The friend said that the dream was clear and contained no riddles or uncertainty.

Only a very few days passed before those who had been sent to inspect the victory returned and reported that many thousands of the enemy had been killed. Therefore the delighted prince made Theodosius emperor.

Meanwhile, when one hundred and fifty bishops had assembled at Constantinople [Col. 1223C], the emperor ordered that no one should point out which of them was the great Meletius. He wanted that man to be identified to him from the memory of his dream.

When the entire company of bishops had entered the imperial residence, Theodosius left all the others and ran to the great Meletius. Like a son who loves his father and, after a long time, obtains the sight of his father, he embraced and kissed him—his eyes, lips, breast, head, and right hand, the hand that had crowned him in the dream—and told him the vision he had seen.

After greeting the others appropriately, he asked them, as fathers, to consider the present circumstances.

After Theodosius had defeated the Barbarians in war and they had begged to be counted among the friends of the Romans, he accepted hostages as the basis of the treaty and came to Thessalonica. There, when he fell ill, he was baptized by Acoleus, the bishop of that city, although he had followed the Christian doctrine and the faith of the Council of Nicaea from his parents.

## CHAPTER XXIV. The Arian empress Justina, who, while ordering Ambrose to be dragged into exile, herself suffered exile
At the time when synods were being discussed at Constantinople, while Theodosius was attending to the unity of the faith and the condition of the Church, such events occurred in the West. Maximus rose up from the regions of the Britons against the Roman empire and brought war upon Gratian, who was engaged in fighting the Alamanni. In Italy, while Valentinian was still quite young, the former consul and prefect Probus administered affairs.

But Valentinian’s mother Justina, since she was an Arian, was unable to harm the orthodox while her husband was alive. After his death, and when her son was still very young, she came to Milan and became hostile to Bishop Ambrose, so much so that she ordered him to be sent into exile. When he was ordered to leave the church, Ambrose said:

“I shall do this willingly, lest I appear to hand the sheepfolds over to wolves, or to blasphemers against God. If it pleases you, kill me here; in this place I willingly submit to death.”

When the people, who loved Ambrose deeply, resisted strongly as they dragged him into exile, Justina, becoming still more indignant, summoned Benivolus, then quaestor, and ordered him quickly to introduce a law confirming the faith promulgated at Ariminum. When he declined to do this—for he was orthodox—she invited him to accept greater honors. But Benivolus removed his belt and threw it at the feet of the empress, saying that he wanted neither that honor nor a greater one as the reward for impiety. When he absolutely refused to do this, others were found who would serve the commands of wickedness.

Meanwhile it was announced that Gratian had been killed by the treachery of the tyrant Maximus. For Andragathius, the commander of Maximus, carried in a litter in order to kill Gratian, spread the following rumor among the people: that Gratian’s wife was hurrying to meet her husband at Lyons, a city of Gaul, as he crossed the river. Gratian, believing that his wife—whom he had recently married—was truly coming, did not guard against the ambush, and, like a blind man falling into a pit, ran into the hands of his enemy.

When Gratian had come as though to his wife’s carriage, Andragathius suddenly leapt out and craftily killed him. He died in the fifteenth year of his reign and the twenty-fourth year of his life. After this deed, Justina’s anger against Ambrose subsided for the time being.

When Maximus heard what was being done against Ambrose, the eloquent preacher of truth, he wrote to Valentinian that the war being waged against the churches should be brought to an end, warning him not to abandon his father’s piety. He also added threats of war, saying that, unless Valentinian ceased, he would fulfill his words by deeds. Accordingly, he took an army and came to Milan, where Valentinian was then residing.

Valentinian, recognizing his invasion, fled into Illyricum, learning by experience what evils he had endured through his mother’s counsel. But by the just judgment of God, Justina suffered exile during her lifetime—the exile which she had unjustly attempted to inflict upon Ambrose, the man of God.

When Theodosius heard what Justina had done and what had been written by the tyrant, he replied to the fleeing Valentinian that it was not surprising if terror increased in the emperor while power increased in the tyrant, since the emperor had rebelled against piety whereas the tyrant was providing him assistance; and therefore the one was fleeing naked while the other was arming himself against a naked man.

## CHAPTER XXV. How Theodosius killed the tyrant Maximus, the murderer of Gratian

Theodosius, the forty-first emperor, after Gratian had been killed by Maximus, obtained the rule of the Roman world and remained in it for eleven years, having already reigned for four years in the eastern regions while Gratian was still alive.

Thus, moved by just and necessary causes to civil war, since, as one of two Augusti, he sought both vengeance for the blood of his murdered brother and the restoration of the other unfortunate brother who was living in exile, he placed his hope in God and set out against the tyrant Maximus, greater in faith alone but far inferior in comparison with the whole apparatus of war. Maximus was then established at Aquileia, watching the outcome of his victory. His count Andragathius directed the entire war.

With very large forces, and with outstanding skill having secured all the approaches through the Alps and across the rivers, he had made them extraordinarily difficult for anyone to pass. Yet, by God’s ineffable judgment, while preparing by a naval expedition to forestall and overwhelm the unwary enemy, he voluntarily abandoned the very barriers that he had established. Thus Theodosius crossed the empty Alpine passes without anyone noticing—or, I should say, without anyone resisting—and, arriving unexpectedly at Aquileia, shut in, captured, and killed, without treachery or dispute, that great and savage enemy Maximus, who by the mere terror of his name exacted tribute and military service even from the most savage German peoples.

Valentinian, having recovered Italy, took possession of the empire. When Count Andragathius learned of Maximus’s death, he threw himself headlong from a ship into the waves and was drowned.

## CHAPTER XXVI. How the bodies of the martyrs Protasius and Gervasius were revealed to blessed Ambrose

At that time, while blessed Ambrose was being harassed by the madness of Justina and the plots of the other Arians, the Lord revealed to him the bodies of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius. They were shown to him as though they had just then been placed there, exuding a wondrous fragrance.

At their head he found a small book containing the following:

“I, the servant of Christ Philip, buried within my own house the bodies of the saints, which I carried away with my son. Their mother was called Valeria, and their father Vitalis. She bore them as twins in a single birth; one they called Protasius, the other Gervasius. Their father Vitalis, while serving as a soldier, was a consul and an Arian. They themselves became soldiers of Christ, of whom it may rightly be said:

‘These are the conquerors and friends of God, who, despising the commands of princes, earned eternal rewards; now they are crowned and receive palms.’”

By their virtues, the venerable bishop, supported by wisdom and uprightness of life and adorned with distinguished examples, strengthened the Church of Milan and freed Italy from the Arian plague.

## CHAPTER XXVII. How Theodosius, rebuked by Ambrose, earned forgiveness through repentance

At the same time Ambrose heard that, by order of the emperor Theodosius, in Thessalonica—a very populous city—perhaps as many as seven thousand people, innocent together with the guilty, had been killed indiscriminately by soldiers sent there to avenge the judges whom the people of the city had stoned and dragged away.

Ambrose deeply deplored this unjust anger. When the emperor came to Milan and solemnly wished to enter the holy church, Ambrose went out to meet him at the doors and prevented him from entering the sacred threshold, rebuking him at length with words such as these:

“Do you not know, emperor, how great is the magnitude of the slaughter you have committed? How will you extend those hands from which unjust blood is still dripping? Go away from here, go away, lest you try to increase your former wickedness by a second sin. Accept the bond with which you are now bound, for it is the greatest medicine of health.”

The emperor obeyed these words. He had been nourished by divine instruction and clearly knew what belonged to priests and what belonged to kings. Groaning and weeping, he returned to the imperial residence.

When eight months had passed continuously, the feast of the Nativity of our Savior drew near. The emperor, remaining in the palace amid continual lamentation, shed unceasing tears.

Accordingly, when the emperor came humbly to Ambrose, asking that he be permitted to enter the church, Ambrose granted him communion on the condition that he write and confirm a law by which decrees of anger would be invalidated, the sentence of death would be suspended for thirty days, and the judgment of reason would be awaited.

The emperor gladly accepted this admonition and, confident that it was excellent, immediately ordered the law to be written and confirmed it in his own hand. When this had been done, Ambrose released him from the bond. This law is still observed.

Enlightened by these and other rebukes from the venerable bishop, the most sacred emperor Theodosius declared above all that he had recognized Ambrose truly as a bishop.

After restoring the youthful Valentinian to the empire, Theodosius, coming as an elder to Rome, corrected, added to, and altered many laws and had them written under his own name. Whatever he observed in the city that was still harmful or superfluous through ancient custom, he decreed should be removed; and whatever was necessary to strengthen the commonwealth, he took care to add. With peace nearly established through these achievements, he left Valentinian in the West and returned to Constantinople with his son Honorius.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Concerning the war that Theodosius waged against the tyrants Arbogastes and Eugenius, and concerning the remarkable deeds of his wife

After Maximus and his son Victor had been destroyed—the latter having been left by Maximus as emperor over Gaul—the younger Valentinian was restored to the kingdom and himself crossed into Gaul. While he was living there in peace, with the state tranquil, he was, as is said, strangled at Vienne through the treachery of his count Arbogastes, after the guards had been corrupted. He was then hanged by a noose, so that it might be believed that he had voluntarily inflicted death upon himself.

After Augustus Valentinian’s death, Arbogastes immediately dared to create the tyrant Eugenius. He chose a man upon whom he could impose the title of emperor, intending himself to increase his power: a barbarian in spirit, and excessive in judgment, skill, audacity, and power. He gathered countless and unconquered forces from every side, relying in one place on Roman garrisons, in another on barbarian auxiliaries, elsewhere on authority or on kinship.

Arbogastes had obeyed Theodosius when Theodosius was equipped with such great defenses. He himself, though the smallest of men, had captured Maximus; and now, when he poured forth against that same Theodosius with the gathered forces of the Gauls and Franks, relying also on an especially elaborate worship of the gods, he nevertheless fell with great ease.

Eugenius and Arbogastes had therefore deployed their battle lines across the plains and, by cleverly placing ambushes in advance, occupied the narrow Alpine slopes and impassable passages, so that even if they were inferior in numbers and strength, they might nevertheless be victorious through the arrangement of the war alone.

But Theodosius, stationed on the highest Alps, deprived of food and sleep, knowing that he was abandoned by his own men but not knowing that he was enclosed by the enemy, prayed to the Lord Christ alone—the only one who could do all things—with his body stretched upon the ground and his mind fixed upon heaven.

After passing the sleepless night in continuous prayer and leaving behind almost palpable pools of tears, which he had offered as the price of heavenly protection, he confidently took up his arms alone. Knowing that he was not alone, he gave the signal for battle with the sign of the cross and entered the war, ready to be victorious even if no one followed him.

The first avenue of salvation was opened by Arbitio, a count of the enemy faction. He had surrounded the emperor in ambushes and received him without knowing who he was; but, turning out of reverence for the Augustus who stood before him, he not only freed him from danger but also supplied him with assistance.

When they reached the nearby spaces where the battle was to be joined, a great and ineffable whirlwind of winds immediately rushed into the faces of the enemy. The missiles thrown at the enemy were carried through the air beyond the measure of human range and, borne across the vast emptiness, were scarcely allowed to fall anywhere before striking their targets.

The unceasing whirlwind now battered the faces and breasts of the enemy with shields violently dashed against them; now, with shields pressed upon them, it shut up those who stubbornly held their ground; now, after violently tearing their shields away, it exposed those left defenseless; now, with shields set against them, it continually drove them backward.

The weapons that they themselves had hurled with great force were caught by the winds, turned back in their course, and driven backward, unhappily piercing the very men who had thrown them.

The fear born of human conscience then looked to its own safety. For immediately, after a small portion of their forces had been scattered, the hostile army surrendered itself, prostrate, to the victorious Theodosius.

Eugenius was captured and killed. Arbogastes struck himself with his own hand. Thus civil war was extinguished by the blood of these two men, apart from the ten thousand Goths whom Arbogastes is said to have utterly destroyed after Theodosius sent them ahead. Their loss was in any event a gain, and to be defeated was to conquer.

Theodosius, therefore, having restored and settled the state, died while established at Milan, leaving both empires to both his sons, Arcadius and Honorius. His body was transferred to Constantinople and buried in the same year. He lived sixty years, of which he reigned for sixteen.

It happened that John had sent him word concerning the outcome of the war to which he was departing against the tyrant Eugenius, and concerning Eugenius’s future death in Italy. John was then leading a monastic life in the Thebaid, full of the grace of God and possessing foreknowledge of future events. Theodosius sent to him the eunuch Eutropius, his most faithful servant, either to bring John, if he wished to come, or, if he refused, to ask him about the outcome of the war.

Eutropius was unable to bring John, but he brought back his message: Theodosius would win the war, kill the tyrant, and die in Italy after the victory.

When Theodosius came to the imperial purple, he had Placella as his wife. She frequently admonished him concerning the divine laws, having first instructed herself perfectly. She was not lifted up by the heights of royal power but rather inflamed by divine love. The greatness of the benefit she had received produced in her an even greater desire for the benefactor.

As soon as she came to the imperial purple, she took care of the lame and the weak. She used neither servants nor other attendants but acted herself, going to their dwellings and providing each person with whatever he needed.

She also went through the hospices of the churches and ministered to the sick with her own hands: wiping their pots, tasting their broth, offering spoons, breaking bread, serving food, rinsing the cup, and performing all the other tasks that servants and attendants customarily carry out.

To those who tried to prevent her from doing such things, she would say:

“To distribute gold is the work of the empire. But I offer this work for the empire itself, which confers all good things upon me.”

She often said to her husband:

“You must always consider, husband, what you once were and what you now are. If you always consider this, you will not prove ungrateful to your benefactor; instead, you will govern the empire you have received lawfully and will appease the author of these blessings.”

## CHAPTER XXIX. Concerning the teachers and wonder-workers who flourished under Theodosius

While Theodosius was emperor, it seemed fitting to insert the memory of those divine men who became distinguished in the Scriptures.

Damasus, bishop of the city of Rome, possessed an elegant talent for composing verse. He published many other short works in heroic meter and died under the emperor Theodosius when he was nearly eighty years old.

Apollinaris, bishop of Laodicea in Syria, the son of Probus, devoted himself in his youth especially to grammatical studies. Later, after writing countless volumes on the sacred Scriptures, he died under the emperor Theodosius. Thirty books of his against Porphyry are extant and are especially esteemed among his other works.

Pachianus, bishop of Barcelona in the Pyrenees, chaste in eloquence and distinguished both in life and speech, wrote various short works, among them *Certus* and a work against the Novatians. He died under the emperor Theodosius, already in extreme old age.

Cyril, bishop of Jerusalem, was often expelled from the Church and restored; finally, under the emperor Theodosius, he held his episcopate undisturbed for seven years. Some short works that he composed in his youth are extant.

Cuzoius, a rhetorician at Ephesus, was educated as a young man at Caesarea together with Bishop Gregory of Nazianzus. Later, as bishop of that same city, he attempted with great labor to restore on parchment the library of Adamantius and Pamphilus, which had already been corrupted. Finally, under the emperor Theodosius, he was expelled from the Church. Various and numerous treatises are attributed to him, and they are very easy to identify.

Bishop Gregory of Nazianzus, a most eloquent man, composed all his works in approximately thirty thousand verses. Among them are the following: *On the Death of His Brother Caesarius*; *Praises of the Maccabees*; *Praises of Cyprian*; *Praises of Athanasius*; *Praises of Maximinus the Philosopher after His Return from Exile*, whom some falsely label with the name *Heron*—for there is also another book containing criticism of that same Maximinus, as though it were not permissible to praise and criticize the same person according to circumstances; a book in hexameter verse concerning *Virginity and Marriage Arguing against Each Other*; two books against Eunomius; one book on the Holy Spirit; and two books against the emperor Julian.

He followed the style of Polemon in speaking. While still alive, he was ordained bishop in his own place; he practiced the life of a monk in the countryside and died under the emperor Theodosius.

Lucius, an Arian bishop after Athanasius, held the Church of Alexandria until the emperor Theodosius, by whom he was also expelled. His solemn letters on Easter, together with a few little books of various treatises, are extant.

At that time many among the bishops shone forth—not only in philosophical learning, leaving monuments through their writings for our posterity, but also because certain among them became distinguished by remarkable virtues. Of the many, I have chosen to insert the praiseworthy deeds of only three, who are less well known among us.

Donatus of Euaria Heperi, through whom the provincials testify that many miracles were performed, accomplished one especially notable deed concerning a dragon. It lay near a bridge on a public road, seized and devoured sheep, goats, horses, cattle, and human beings, and made them its food.

Donatus came to this beast without a sword or any weapon. When it raised its head as though it were about to swallow the man, he traced the sign of the cross in the air before its face with his finger and spat into its mouth. The beast immediately received the spittle in its mouth and died. It was then, as is reported, dragged into a nearby field by eight pairs of oxen and burned after a fire had been lit, lest it corrupt the air with its stench.

The burial place of this Donatus is distinguished; there is an oratory there called by his name, possessing a spring of water which he is said to have discovered through his prayers. For when the place was without water and he had come there from a journey, they say that, because those who were with him were weary, he prayed, and immediately a flood of water burst forth. It has continued there from that time until now.

At that time Thothimus governed the Church of Tomi and Scythia, a man trained in philosophy. The barbarians living beyond the Danube, who loved his virtue, declared that he was the god of the Romans.

Once, while he was traveling, the barbarians of that land came upon him. While those who were with him were terrified and disturbed, as though they were about to die immediately, he dismounted from his horse and prayed. The barbarians, however, could see neither him nor his followers nor the horses from which they had dismounted, and they remained there.

As he frequently crossed among the naturally fierce Scythians and softened them by feasts and gifts, a certain barbarian, thinking that Thothimus was wealthy, began plotting how to seize, bind, and drag him away. When he had prepared this and extended his right hand for the purpose of casting a noose around him, his hand was immediately bound in the air, and the barbarian was fettered by invisible bonds.

Then, when others pleaded on his behalf, Thothimus entreated God that the barbarian might be released, and he was immediately freed through his prayers.

At that time there was also Epiphanius, bishop of Cyprus, at whose tomb demons are expelled to this day. He had distributed his own possessions to those suffering need and, when many people also offered him money, gave it out with the greatest generosity. It happened that, when the money ran out, the church steward began to complain.

After this, someone who was present in the house where the steward was staying gave him a bag of much money and then disappeared, so that it was impossible to determine either who had given it or who had sent it. Everyone judged that this event was divine.

It is also worthwhile to report another miracle of his. Certain poor men tried to deceive Epiphanius by their artifice so that he would give them something. While he was traveling, one of them threw himself flat on the ground, while another stood nearby mourning him as though he were dead, claiming that he had nothing with which to bury him.

When Epiphanius arrived, he prayed that the man might sleep peacefully and supplied what was necessary for burial. He also consoled the one who was weeping, saying:

“Cease your tears, my son. He cannot be raised to life by weeping; what has happened is unavoidable.”

After Epiphanius had departed, the man began to prod his companion so that he would rise. When he had done this once and a second time, saying, “Rise; today let us feast on the fruits of your labors,” and the other did not respond at all, he realized that he was truly dead. He ran back to Epiphanius weeping and asking him to raise his companion.

Epiphanius consoled him so that he would not grieve excessively over what had happened, but he did not raise the dead man again. I believe that this occurred so that the ministers of God might not easily be deceived.

In those days Damasus presided over the Roman Church; Theophilus over Alexandria; John over Jerusalem; Flavian, after the Arian bishops had been expelled, held the see of Antioch; and Nectarius held that of Constantinople.

## CHAPTER XXX. Concerning the overthrow of temples and the destruction of idols

Theodosius had decreed that the temples of idols should be overthrown, that wooden gods should be handed over to the flames, and that metal ones should be melted down.

While these things were being carried out in various places, especially in Alexandria, where superstition concerning idols had taken deep root, the prefect of Alexandria and the commander of the military order assisted Bishop Theophilus in executing the emperor’s command.

The idols of the gods were melted down to make pots and for various needs of the Alexandrian church. The emperor had donated the gods to it for the expenses of the needy.

When Theophilus had overthrown all the gods, he left only one image, that of Syrmis, ordering it to be preserved publicly and openly, lest later generations of pagans deny that they had worshiped such gods.

They had already overthrown the temple of Serapis, which was held in the greatest honor among the Alexandrians, not without immense labor. They cut the god Serapis himself into pieces and handed him over to the fire; they also ordered his genitals and those of the other gods, objects of ridicule, to be carried through the streets.

Confounded by these most shameful spectacles, some of the pagans rushed to slaughter Christians when a sedition arose. They were likewise stirred by the destruction of the other temples and by the exposure of their impious mysteries, when the rites of Metria—where they committed murders—were publicly revealed among their other filthy ceremonies. Others among the pagans, abandoning their former errors, turned to the true religion of the Christians.

In the preceding book, where the temples of the pagans were closed under the emperor Constantine, we brought our account to an end. Let this book, however, conclude with the destruction of the false gods and the overthrow of the temples.

# BOOK FIVE

## CHAPTER ONE. Concerning the accession of Arcadius and Honorius to the empire after their father’s death, and the persecution of John, bishop of Constantinople, who was unjustly condemned and died in exile

As we have already stated, after the elder Augustus Theodosius died, his sons Arcadius and Honorius began to hold the two empires, divided only by their places of residence. Together they administered the state as the forty-second rulers after Octavian. Arcadius governed the East, while Honorius, still very much a boy, governed the western regions.

The soldiers who had gone out with the emperor against the tyrant Eugenius returned to Constantinople a short time after Eugenius’s death. When the emperor Arcadius, according to custom, had gone out to the gates to meet the returning army, the soldiers killed Rufinus, the emperor’s prefect. He was suspected of being capable of seizing the tyranny.

It was also said that he himself had summoned the Huns into the Roman provinces; they were then devastating Armenia and the eastern regions and laying ambushes for the emperor.

His head, together with his right hand, was cut off and carried around Constantinople as an object of ridicule. After his wife had been sent into exile, the eunuch Eutropius acquired all his wealth.

A short time later Nectarius, the bishop of Constantinople, also died. Accordingly, by common agreement, it pleased the emperor that John, a presbyter from Antioch, a man of admirable conduct and especially well trained in philosophical disciplines, should become bishop of the see of Constantinople.

This greatly displeased Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, because he was trying to entrust the same see to a presbyter whom he loved very much. But the judgment of the majority prevailed.

When John became bishop, he spared no one, and what is contained in the ancient proverb happened to him: “Truth produces hatred, and compliance produces friends.” For on various occasions he offended both the clergy entrusted to him and the empress, and especially Theophilus and his followers, by whose attacks he was repeatedly harassed.

The plots of his enemies, especially those of his wife, prevailed so greatly with the emperor Arcadius that John was driven into exile. The people, however, loved him fervently out of reverence for his holiness and because of his preaching.

Through their intercession, and also at the urging of the empress, he was recalled from exile, lest a popular uprising occur. But when he returned, he did not remain quiet; rather, if it is lawful to say so, he showed himself even more intolerable to his rivals.

Therefore, stirred up again by his wife, the emperor ordered councils to be held against John the bishop, although Theophilus had previously plotted against him in various places.

Finally, driven into exile a second time, he was led as far as the boundaries of the Roman empire. He died in exile. A large part of the people of Constantinople followed him—not by walking, but in affection—and held separate gatherings, refusing to share communion with his opponents or with his successor Acacius.

As a result, many disturbances arose between the opposing parties, and very many people suffered various evils.

Meanwhile Innocent, the Roman bishop, heard about John and was distressed. Wishing to convene a general council, he wrote to John and to the clergy of Constantinople that no successor ought to be given to John and that his clergy ought not to obey another bishop.

They say that, when John was being led into exile, he learned through a vision the day on which he would die. The bishops of Europe especially abhorred the causes of this injustice. They withdrew themselves from communion with those who had consented to his condemnation, and all the bishops of Illyricum likewise joined them.

Many of the Eastern bishops avoided the injustice, but they did not wish to divide the body of the Church. Yet when that teacher of the whole world died, the Western bishops did not accept communion with the Egyptians, the Easterners, the Bosphorenians, or the Tharatenians until the name of that most holy man had been placed among the bishops who had preceded them. They did not consider Acacius, who had been ordained after him, worthy of mention in any discussion.

At that time a violent hailstorm descended upon Constantinople and the suburbs around it. They said that this had occurred because of God’s anger, since John had been condemned without a judgment. The death of the empress, which immediately followed, gave credence to their words. For she died on the fourth day after the hailstorm.

## CHAPTER II. Concerning the tyrants destroyed by the power of God, and the great king of Scythia under Arcadius

Gainas was Celtic by birth, barbarian in counsel, and greatly puffed up with tyrannical ambition. At that time, while he was master of the soldiers and had many of his own people and many Romans under his command, he brought terror even upon the emperor himself through his contemplation of tyranny. He was an Arian.

When he wished to seize the imperial insignia and sought to kill the emperor, he sent a strong band of his men to set fire to the imperial residence at night. But the barbarians saw angelic forces around the palace in the appearance of armed soldiers and, having failed in their undertaking, returned to him.

He did not believe their report at all. Knowing that the army had been dispersed from the imperial city, he sent more men the following night. When those whom he had sent approached the imperial court, they too saw on every side ranks protecting the imperial residence. Terrified by this vision, they withdrew.

When Gamas learned of this, he threw the whole city into confusion with fire and sword. Fleeing across the Hellespont, he lived as a pirate. A naval battle was fought against him; many of his Goths were killed, and although he himself escaped the battle, he was soon afterward punished by decapitation.

After his suppression, the Isaurians, roaming through Mount Taurus, inflicted enormous damage upon the state. Narbazaicus was sent against them, but immediately brought an even greater calamity.

At that time Roilus, commander of the Scythians, crossed the Danube with an innumerable army and ravaged Thrace with great violence. He threatened to besiege and destroy the imperial city itself. But divine majesty struck him and his entire army from above with arrows and lightning and burned them all together.

Something similar was also done by the Lord, their consoler, in the Parthian war. When the Parthians learned that the Romans were unprepared, they attacked the cities situated on the frontier and violated the terms of peace. Their territories were devastated, and no one brought assistance.

For the emperor, relying on the peace, had sent his commanders and soldiers to other wars. Then God, sending exceedingly heavy rain and hail, did not allow the enemy to advance any farther. He restrained their march so completely that for twenty days they were unable to travel even as many stades as there were days.

The commanders came and gathered their army. At the first battle, while besieging the city named after the emperor, they proved ineffectual.

When King Gororanus had besieged that city for more than thirty days and had constructed many siege engines and built tall towers against the city walls, only Eunomius, the most holy bishop of that city, resisted. He destroyed their assault and their machines.

Although our commanders had yielded to the enemy in battle and the besieged citizens dared not resist, he alone, by praying, restored the city without devastation.

Not long afterward, John died, and the emperor Arcadius also died. He was a gentle and peaceful man, but he showed himself blameworthy in this respect: he did not avoid the attacks that were stirred up against the ministers of Christ.

Together with his father Theodosius he reigned for thirteen years, and after his father’s death for fourteen. He lived forty-one years.

## CHAPTER III. Concerning the teachers who became distinguished through their writings under Arcadius and Honorius
Therefore, before we speak of the disasters and calamities which, because of their sins, occurred at that time in the regions of the West—namely, Gaul, Spain, and Africa—we have judged it appropriate to commemorate the illustrious men who, while Arcadius and his brother Honorius were emperors, still shone in the Churches like glittering stars.

Gregory the Baetican, bishop of Iberia, composed various treatises in a moderate style, continuing into extreme old age. Taebadius, bishop of Agen in Gaul, published an elegant book on the faith against the Arians. He is also said to have written other short works.

Epiphanius, bishop of Salamis in Cyprus, [Col. 1234B] wrote books against all heresies, as well as many other short works, which learned people continue to read because of their subject matter, though simpler readers find them difficult because of their unfamiliar language.

Diodore, bishop of Tarsus, became especially distinguished when he was a presbyter at Antioch. His commentaries on the Apostle are extant, together with many other works belonging more to the style of Eusebius of Emesa. Although he followed Eusebius’s meaning, he could not imitate his eloquence because of his ignorance of secular literature.

Eunomius, bishop of Cyzicus on the Arian side, burst forth into open blasphemy concerning his heresy, so that he publicly confessed what others conceal; he also dared to write many things against the Church. Apollinaris, Didymus, Basil of Caesarea, Gregory of Nazianzus, and the man of Emesa replied to him.

Priscillian, bishop of Ávila, who was put to death at Trier by the tyrant Maximus through the faction of Hydatius and Ithacius, published many short works. Some accuse him of the Gnostic heresy—that is, the heresy of Basilides or of Marcus, about whom Irenaeus wrote—while others defend him, saying that he did not hold the views of which he is accused.

Latroianus, a man of great learning from the province of Spain and comparable with the ancients in poetic composition, was himself put to death at Trier, together with Priscillian, Felicissimus, Julian, and Eucrocia, the leaders of the same faction. Works displaying his talent, composed in various meters, are extant.

Tiberianus the Baetican, in defense against the suspicion of heresy under which he was accused together with Priscillian, wrote an Apology in inflated and elaborate language. But afterward, overcome by weariness of exile following the execution of his associates, he changed his purpose and, like the dog returning to its vomit [Col. 1234D] according to Holy Scripture, gave his daughter, a virgin devoted to Christ, in marriage.

Ambrose, bishop of the Church of Milan, whom we mentioned above, nobly published many short works. Since they are well known through the constant reading of them, I think it unnecessary to recapitulate them here.

At that time Ambrose of Alexandria, a pupil of Didymus, died. He wrote against Apollinaris a volume of many verses on doctrinal matters, as well as commentaries on Job.

Sophronius, a man of outstanding learning, composed, while still a young man, praises of Bethlehem and a remarkable book on the destruction of Serapis. He also translated into Greek, with great elegance, Jerome’s short works On Virginity, addressed to Eustochium, and The Life of the Monk Hilarion.

Jerome, son of Eusebius, born in the town of Stridon, wrote the following:

The Life of the Monk Paul; one book of letters to various persons; an exhortation to Heliodorus; the dispute between a Luciferian and an Orthodox Christian; a Chronicle of universal history; twenty-eight homilies of Adamantius on Jeremiah and Ezekiel, which he translated from Greek into Latin; On the Seraphim and the Hosanna; On the Frugal and Prodigal Son; On Three Questions of the Old Law; two homilies on the Song of Songs.

Against Helvidius, one letter on Mary’s perpetual virginity. To Eustochium, On the Preservation of Virginity. To Marcellus, one book of letters. A consolatory letter to Paula on the death of her daughter.

Three books of commentaries on the Apostle Paul’s Epistle to the Galatians. Likewise, three books on Paul’s Epistle to the Ephesians. One book on Paul’s Epistle to Titus, and one book on Paul’s Epistle to [Col. 1235B] Philemon; commentaries on Ecclesiastes.

One book of Hebrew Questions on Genesis. One book of Didymus’s On the Holy Spirit, which he translated into Latin; thirty-eight homilies on Luke. Seven treatises on the Psalms from the tenth through the sixteenth. On the Captive Monk. The Life of Blessed Hilarion.

He restored the New Testament to the Greek standard and translated the Old Testament according to the Hebrew text; also the letter to Paula and Eustochium.

He wrote two books of explanations on Micah; one on Nahum; two on Habakkuk; one on Zephaniah; one on Haggai. He produced substantial volumes by profitably explaining Isaiah. He also expounded Jeremiah and explained Daniel, and composed a commentary on Matthew, along with very many other short works.

In those days the most blessed Martin, bishop of Tours and a confessor, after performing many distinguished miracles, was released from the bonds of the flesh and departed to the Lord. Noble by birth, he had served in the army under Constantius and Julian. Eventually, at the Gallic city of the Wangiones, under the emperor Julian, he laid aside his military belt and devoted himself to the most devoted service of Christ. Sulpicius Severus ennobled his life and deeds of wonder by his eloquence.

## CHAPTER IV. On the Tyranny of Gildo in Africa

When Arcadius was dying, he entrusted the supreme authority of the Eastern Empire to his very young son Theodosius.

Now let us turn our pen toward the regions of the West. Honorius, whose father Theodosius had died, had assumed the empire while still a very young boy. Meanwhile Count Gildo, who governed Africa at the beginning of his reign, as soon as he learned that Theodosius was dead, attempted to unite Africa with the territories of the Eastern Empire—either, as some report, moved by a certain envy, or, as another account relates, because he judged that little hope was to be placed in children, especially since scarcely anyone formerly left a child in imperial power had attained the maturity of manhood without them. These two are found almost alone to have been advanced by Christ’s protection, though divided and abandoned, because of their father’s royal fidelity and their own.

Gildo dared to seize Africa, detached from partnership in the commonwealth, content with the license of a pagan more than inflated by the ambition of royal pretension. His brother was Mascezel, who, horrified by his brother’s attempts at revolution, returned to Italy after leaving two adolescent sons serving in the army in Africa.

Gildo, suspecting both his brother’s absence and the presence of his sons, ensnared the young men by deceit and killed them. Mascezel the brother was then sent to pursue him in war as an enemy. The recent grief of his own bereavement promised that he would be well suited to administer the commonwealth.

Mascezel therefore, having already learned from Theodosius how much a person’s prayer, through faith in Christ, could obtain from God’s mercy in the most desperate circumstances, went to the island of Capraria. From there he took with him, stirred by his prayers, certain holy servants of God. Continuing with them in prayers, fasts, and psalms day and night, he earned victory without battle and vengeance without slaughter.

The Ardalio is the name of a river that flows between the cities of Tenes and Mercia. There, with a small force—that is, with five thousand soldiers, as they say—he pitched camp against seventy thousand enemy troops. When, after a delay had been imposed, he wished to leave the place and cross the narrow passages of the valley lying before them, night fell. He seemed in a dream to see the blessed Ambrose, bishop of Milan, who had died shortly before, pointing with his hand and striking the ground three times with his staff while saying: “Here, here, here.”

By prudent interpretation Mascezel understood that the faith of victory was being announced deservedly: by the word, the place; by the number, the day. He halted, and only on the third day, after keeping vigil through the night in prayers and hymns, did he advance against the enemy, having been strengthened by the very mysteries of the heavenly sacraments.

When he was addressing those who first came to meet him with pious words of peace, he struck a standard-bearer who was insolently resisting and already provoking battle on the arm with his sword. By the wound he forced the man, whose hand had been disabled, to lower the standard downward. When the remaining cohorts saw this, they thought that the first troops had already surrendered and, vying with one another, handed themselves over to Mascezel with their standards turned toward him.

The barbarians, whose great multitude Gildo had led out to war, deprived of their soldiers, fled in different directions. Gildo himself, attempting flight, seized a ship and put out to sea. He was then recalled to Africa and, after several days, died by strangulation.

## CHAPTER V. On Alaric, King of the Goths, Who Laid Waste Rome, and on Another Gothic King Who Entered Italy with a Great Army and Perished with All His Forces

[Col. 1236D]

At that time Radagaisus, by far the most savage of all the enemies of ancient and present times, invaded the whole of Italy in a sudden assault. They say that there were more than two hundred thousand Goths among his people. In addition to this incredible multitude and its untrained courage, he was a pagan and a Scythian; and, as is customary among barbarians of this sort, he had vowed to offer all Roman blood as a libation to his gods.

Two Gothic peoples, with their two most powerful kings, were then raging through the Roman provinces. One of them was Christian and closer to the Romans and, as events proved, restrained by fear of God in slaughter. He was Alaric, who had served with the Goths under Theodosius.

[Col. 1237A] When Theodosius died and his sons became emperors, they withdrew the paternal gifts from the Goths, who had voluntarily submitted to the commonwealth. Compelled by this necessity, the Goths conspired against the Romans. Although they were Christians and grieved that they had been despised by the emperor, they made Alaric their king.

Leaving Pannonia, they entered Italy. The emperor Honorius was residing in the royal city of Ravenna. By his will and command they were hastening toward Gaul without harming Italy, but because of Stilicho’s actions, they became savage: they not only plundered Italy but also invaded Rome.

The other king, the pagan barbarian and true Scythian Radagaisus, armed himself not so much for glory or plunder as for slaughter born of insatiable cruelty. Having already received Italy into his bosom, he was shaking Rome, which trembled nearby, with terror.

Uldin and Sarus, commanders of the Huns and Goths, arrived as a Roman reinforcement. Thus, by God’s providence, fear drove Radagaisus, terrified, into the mountains of Faesulae. Two hundred thousand people were enclosed on the rugged ridge of the mountain: the columns which had lately found Italy too narrow were driven together, by a hidden providence, onto one summit and through a single passage. There, while hungry, parched, and exhausted, those monstrous enemies were killed.

King Radagaisus alone, placing his hope in flight, secretly abandoned his men and fell among our troops. They captured him, held him for a short time, and then killed him.

So great, it is reported, was the multitude of captive Goths that, like the cheapest livestock, groups of human beings were sold everywhere for a single gold coin.
