Meanwhile Count Stilicho, to whom Honorius had entrusted the supreme affairs of the West—and whose appointment the dying Theodosius had decreed—was lifted up by arrogant pride. Disregarding the fact that he ruled under an emperor, he determined to make his son Eucherius emperor.

For this reason, when Alaric, king of the Goths, was humbly and straightforwardly asking for peace and for any settlement whatsoever, Stilicho corrupted him by a secret treaty while publicly declaring war, so that, by denying the possibility of peace, he might provoke him to terrify the commonwealth.

Stilicho summoned not only the Goths but also the Alans, Suevi, Vandals, and even Burgundians to arms, wishing to strike Gaul. The wretched man hoped that, under this necessity, he could hand the empire over to his son and that barbarian peoples could be suppressed as easily as he had stirred them up.

When this scheme of such great crimes was revealed to the emperor Honorius and to the Roman army, the army was most justly stirred, and Stilicho was killed. In order to clothe one boy in the purple, he had sacrificed the blood of the entire human race.

Eucherius was also killed.

Alaric arrived, besieged and disturbed trembling Rome, and broke into the city. Nevertheless, he ordered that if anyone had fled to holy places—especially to the basilicas of the holy apostles Peter and Paul—they should first of all be left unharmed and secure; then, afterward, that those who were greedy for as much booty as possible should abstain from bloodshed.

It also happened that the city’s invasion might be shown to have been brought about more by God’s indignation than by the enemy’s strength. The blessed Innocent, bishop of the city of Rome, like the just Lot removed from Sodom by the hidden providence of God, was then staying at Ravenna and thus did not see the destruction of the sinful people.

As the barbarians moved through the city, one of the Goths, a powerful Christian, found an aged holy virgin of God in a certain ecclesiastical house. When he honorably asked her for gold and silver, she steadfastly affirmed that she possessed a great deal and promised to bring it at once; then she produced it.

When he saw the treasures laid out, the barbarian was astonished by the weight and beauty of the vessels, as well as by the unfamiliar quality of their workmanship. The virgin of Christ said to the barbarian: “These are the sacred mysteries of the Apostle Peter. Take responsibility for what you do, if you dare. You will see the result yourself. Since I cannot defend them, I dare not retain them.”

Moved by reverence for religion, by fear of God, and by faith in the virgin, the barbarian reported these things by messenger to Alaric. Alaric immediately ordered all the vessels to be carried back, just as they were, to the basilica of the Apostle, and commanded that the virgin, together with all the Christians who joined her, be escorted there under protection.

The house was, as is said, at a considerable distance from the holy sites, with much of the city lying between them. Accordingly, to the great spectacle of all, the vessels were arranged one by one and carried openly, the gold and silver vessels raised above the bearers’ heads. Swords were drawn everywhere to provide protection, guarding the pious procession, while hymns to God were sung publicly by Romans and barbarians alike.

During that invasion, Placidia, daughter of the emperor Theodosius and sister of the emperors Arcadius and Honorius, was captured by Ataulf, a relative of Alaric, and taken as his wife. It was as though Rome, by divine judgment, had handed her over as a special pledge and hostage. Her union with this most powerful barbarian king nevertheless brought considerable benefit to the commonwealth.

By the wondrous dispensation of God, Alaric invaded and devastated the city and corrupted the Roman people, who had offended God in many ways, more through terror than through slaughter. After three days he departed from Rome.

When he died, Ataulf, who had soon been made king of the Goths and had married Placidia, the sister of the emperors, left Italy with the approval of Honorius and hastened toward Gaul, which various barbarian peoples had occupied.

## CHAPTER VI. On the Various Peoples Who Poured into Gaul

Meanwhile, two years before the invasion of Rome, the peoples stirred up by Stilicho—the Alans, as I have said, the Suevi, the Vandals, and many other peoples with them—crossed the Rhine [Col. 1238D], invaded Gaul, and advanced in a direct assault as far as the Pyrenees. Repelled for a time by that barrier, they poured back through the surrounding provinces.

While these peoples were raging through Gaul, Gratian, a native of the island of Britain, was made tyrant there and killed. In his place Constantine was chosen from the lowest ranks of the army, solely because of the hope attached to his name and without any merit of valor.

As soon as he had seized the empire, he crossed into Gaul. There, often deceived by the barbarians through uncertain treaties, he proved more a source of damage to the commonwealth.

He sent judges into Spain. Through their agency, the barbarians betrayed the guard of the Pyrenees and opened its barriers, allowing all the peoples wandering through Gaul to enter the provinces of Spain; the barbarians themselves joined them there.

[Col. 1239A] After spending some time in great and bloody movements, and after severe devastation of property and people, they settled down once they had drawn lots and distributed the land among themselves.

## CHAPTER VII. On the Tyrants Who Emerged under Honorius and Were Quickly Destroyed; on Constantius and His Faithful Consul, Whom He Eventually Made Consul

Accordingly, when the emperor Honorius saw that nothing could be done against the barbarians while so many tyrants opposed him, he ordered that the tyrants themselves be destroyed first, entrusting the supreme command of this war to Count Constantius.

Count Constantius therefore set out for Gaul with an army. He shut up Constantine the emperor in the city of Arles, captured him, and killed him. His son Constans was killed by Gerontius at [Col. 1239B] Vienne, and Gerontius put a certain Maximus in his place. Gerontius himself was then killed by his own soldiers.

Maximus, stripped of the purple and abandoned by the Gallic soldiers, fled. Later Jovinus, the most distinguished man of Gaul, rose into tyranny and soon fell. His brother Sebastian chose only this: to die as a tyrant. For as soon as he was appointed, he was killed.

Attalus, however, chose to die among the tyrants. After obtaining the consulship of Africa, he was lifted up by pride. He chose as his son-in-law Sabinus, his household officer, a man clever in intellect and skillful in diligence, who would have been wise if he had devoted his mental powers to peaceful pursuits. Because of suspicion concerning certain dangers, Attalus killed him.

After Africa had for some time been deprived by him of its grain supply beyond the customary measure, Attalus himself eventually set out for Rome with a fleet enormous and, in the circumstances of our own time, sufficiently incredible. For it is said that he then possessed 3,700 ships. Histories report that this number was possessed neither by Xerxes, that famous king of the Persians, nor by Alexander the Great, nor by any other king.

As he was proceeding toward the city with his army, he disembarked on the shore. Terrified by the arrival of Count Marinus and put to flight, he seized a ship, returned alone to Carthage, and was immediately killed there by military force.

This entire catalogue, as I have said, of either manifest tyrants or disobedient commanders, the excellent emperor Honorius was enabled to know through his piety and good fortune. Count Constantius completed it with great diligence and speed. Justly so, because in those days, by the command of Honorius and with the assistance of Constantius, peace and unity were restored to the Catholic Church throughout Africa.

Accordingly, while Count Constantius was stationed at Arles, a city of Gaul, he expelled the Goths from Narbonne with great efficiency and forced them to depart for Spain. At that time King Ataulf ruled the Gothic peoples. After the invasion of the city and the death of Alaric, he had succeeded Alaric, having taken Placidia, as I said, the captured sister of the emperor, as his wife.

As had often been heard and was proved by his final fate, Ataulf was a sufficiently devoted follower of peace. He preferred faithfully to serve the emperor Honorius and to restrain the strength of the Goths for the defense of the Roman commonwealth.

He was killed at the city of Barcelona in Spain [Col. 1240A] through the treachery of his own people. After him, Segeric was made king of the Goths, but he too was killed by his own men.

Next Valia succeeded to the kingship. He concluded an excellent peace with the emperor Honorius, giving him highly distinguished hostages. He honorably and properly returned the emperor’s sister Placidia to her brother.

Honorius married her to Constantius, who had brought her back, and made Constantius emperor at Ravenna.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the Tyranny of John and His Timely Death

Honorius, who had ruled for thirteen years with his brother Arcadius and afterward for sixteen years with Theodosius the Younger, the son of his brother Arcadius, departed from human affairs.

[Col. 1240B] After his death, the tyrant John seized the empire of the West. Against him Ardaburius was sent by the emperor Theodosius as patrician. He had often fought against the Parthians and had defeated them successfully.

But as he was sailing with his army toward Aquileia, a contrary wind suddenly arose, disturbing the fleet and driving him toward the enemy. Captured by the tyrant, he caused the emperor great anxiety.

The emperor, following his customary practice, turned to the mercy of the Lord and persisted in prayers and tears for the liberation of his homeland and of his most faithful commander. What the emperor’s prayer accomplished then, I think, should be related.

An angel of God, appearing in the guise of a shepherd, led Aspar, the son of Ardaburius, and all who were with him through the marsh beside Ravenna to the places they hoped to reach—places through which, it is said, no one had ever passed.

Then God made passable a land that could not be traversed. As they crossed through the dry marsh, they encountered no water; and, finding the gates of the city of Ravenna open, they also captured the tyrant.

The tyrant was staying in that city and had an army there. The most devout emperor then displayed the reverence he held toward the Divinity. While he was looking around, word was brought to him that the tyrant had been killed.

For this reason he addressed the people, saying: “Come, if it pleases you, leaving behind this pleasure and going to the Church, let us offer hymns of thanksgiving to God, whose hand has confronted the presumption of the tyrant.”

When he had spoken, the spectacle ended. Everyone went with him through the middle of the city, joining together in thanksgiving, and gathered at the church. Thus the whole city seemed to be a single church, and those who came to the place of prayer offered continual thanks to the Lord throughout the day.

After the tyrant had been killed, the emperor Theodosius considered to whom he ought to entrust the kingdoms of the West. At that time Valentinian was very young. He was born to Placidia, his mother and the emperor’s paternal aunt, who was the daughter of the elder Theodosius and the sister of Arcadius and Honorius; his father was Constantius, who had received the authority of the empire from Honorius and had reigned with him for a short time.

The emperor therefore made this Valentinian, his cousin, Caesar, and sent him to the regions of Italy. He sent his mother Placidia with him and entrusted to her the entire administration of the empire.

## CHAPTER IX. On Events Worthy of Remembrance in the East under the Emperor Theodosius; Also on Bishop Atticus

When Valentinian assumed the imperial crown at Ravenna and ruled the western regions together with his mother, let us briefly gather, as though plucking a few items in passing, some of the events that occurred in the East under the rule of Theodosius and that are considered worthy of remembrance.

At that time Atticus was bishop of Constantinople, a remarkable man, outstanding in learning, religion, and generosity.

Among other events, when a certain Jew lay paralyzed and, after all the physicians’ treatments and the Jews’ superstitious purifications had been applied, found that nothing benefited him, he finally turned to the healing of Christ when all the others had despaired.

This was quickly [Col. 1241B] reported to Bishop Atticus. He ordered the man, who had become a catechumen and was promising hope in Christ, to be carried on his bed to baptism.

The Jewish paralytic, however, received baptism with true faith and, when he had been lifted from the font, was suddenly freed from his illness and remained healthy thereafter. Thus the power of Christ demonstrated this healing at that time as well. For this reason many pagans, believing, were baptized.

Atticus was so generous that he sent large sums not only to the poor of his own dioceses but also to neighboring cities for the relief of the needy.

To Calliopius, a presbyter of the Church of Nicaea, he sent three hundred gold pieces, giving him these instructions: “Spend these three hundred solidi as you wish, especially on those who are ashamed to ask, and not on those who make a business of their belly. From such people observe only one thing: that you nourish those in need.”

He foretold his own death to this same Calliopius long beforehand, and in saying this he did not lie.

Atticus had also baptized a certain Jew. Yet this Jew, for the sake of sordid gain, repeatedly baptized people among various heresies and accumulated money by this practice.

At last he came again to the Church of the orthodox. After the period of fasting, baptism and a suitable garment were prepared for him. Once the font had been filled, the Jew was led in to be baptized.

Then a certain invisible power of God commanded the water to disappear. Those present, failing to consider God’s power, suspected that the water had drained away through its own channel. They carefully sealed the font on every side and filled it again. When the Jew was led in a second time, the water disappeared again.

Then the priest said: “What evil have you done, man? Or have you perhaps already received baptism without knowing it?”

When various people gathered because of this event, someone recognized the Jew whom he himself had received after Bishop Atticus baptized him. In this way the man’s fraud became apparent to everyone.

## CHAPTER X. On Bishops Maruthas and Atticus, and on the Battles Undertaken against the Parthians for the Sake of Christians

At that time Maruthas, a distinguished bishop of Mesopotamia, was held in high regard. The emperor Theodosius sent him as an envoy to the king of the Persians.

When he arrived in Persia, he found King Sigerdes suffering for a long time from an extremely severe headache. He could not be cured by any incantations of the magicians, by the purifications of his priests, or even by the skill of physicians.

The venerable bishop healed him by prayer alone and drove a most troublesome demon from his son. For this reason Christianity spread among the Persians, and the frauds of their magicians were exposed.

In those same days the Jews living in Crete were deceived by a certain man who claimed that he was Moses the lawgiver, sent down from heaven to them again. He urged them all to abandon their possessions and money, because under his guidance they would cross the sea on dry land and reach the joys of the Promised Land.

Captured by this hope, they gave up everything they owned. When the day appointed by the deceiver arrived, he led them to a certain cliff that sloped sharply downward and ordered them to hurl themselves down in the guise of *thaumarum* [sic]. This is what the first ones did; and when they reached the rocks, they suddenly died, torn apart by the sharp rocks just as people drown in water.

More of them would have died if, by God’s providence, certain Christian fishermen and merchants had not arrived. They rescued and revived some of those who were being killed.

Those who escaped wanted to kill the deceiver, but he suddenly disappeared. They suspected that he had been a demon.

Because of this disaster, many of the Jewish inhabitants of Crete were then converted to the Christian faith.

The emperor Theodosius therefore broke the treaties with the Persians on behalf of the Christians whom Bishop Atticus, and others throughout the Roman world, had taken under their protection. These Christians had fled from the Persian king when he persecuted them; but when the same king demanded them back, the devout ruler refused to return them.

He considered it preferable to undertake wars, which were vigorously conducted by Ardaburius, the master of the army. Entering Persian territory through the borders of Armenia, Ardaburius devastated one of its provinces, Azazene, very severely.

Narseus, a commander of the Parthians, met him with a very large army; battle was joined, and Narseus was defeated.

In other battles as well, with the Lord’s help, the commanders and armies of the most devout prince were found superior and victorious. Angels proclaimed to them that they should have confidence, pray, and believe in God, because victory would follow the Romans, saying that they had been sent by God as mediators of the war.

At last, in a battle fought on the frontier of Mesopotamia, the very powerful Persian army—called by the Persians “immortal”—was slaughtered by the Romans.

The king of the Persians, recognizing the causes of his misfortune and receiving the Roman embassy, made peace with them. In this way the war that had arisen on behalf of the Christians came to an end in the land of the Parthians.

## CHAPTER XI. On the Excellent Life of Theodosius and of His Wife

The emperor had a daughter by Eudoxia, named Eudocia. Valentinian, his cousin, whom Theodosius had made emperor of the western regions, asked for her in marriage.

When Theodosius consented, Valentinian, having secured the West, came to Constantinople for the wedding. After the celebration, he took his wife and returned.

The emperor Theodosius therefore gave thanks to God for the benefits bestowed upon him, repaying his vows to Christ with many honors, and sent his wife Eudoxia to Jerusalem. She too had made this vow, if she should see her daughter married.

She honored both the churches established at Jerusalem and those situated in each of the cities, both while she was traveling there and when she returned to Theodosius.

Born and raised in royal circumstances, Theodosius possessed nothing lukewarm. He was so wise that, among those engaged in conversation, he was thought to possess practical knowledge of affairs.

He endured cold and heat alike. He frequently fasted, especially on the fourth and sixth days of the week, out of Christian devotion, and otherwise than as a monastery he did not appear to be a palace.

In the morning he went to his sisters and recited the divine praises. For this reason he could recite the sacred writings without a book.

When bishops were speaking, he responded from the divine reading as though he had formerly been made a priest. He gathered sacred books and all manner of interpreters and commentators on them.

He surpassed all people in patience and clemency, overcoming anger, sadness, and lust by his actions and desiring to avenge himself on no one.

When one of his attendants asked him why he did not condemn to death anyone who harmed him, he replied: “Would that it were possible for me even to restore the dead to life!”

He was so merciful that whenever anyone committed an act deserving death, the condemned person did not even reach the city gates before a reprieve immediately followed from the emperor’s clemency.

## CHAPTER XII. On the Relics of Blessed Stephen, Conveyed to the West through Orosius

[Col. 1243C]

When Theodosius was ruling with his uncle Honorius, and afterward with his cousin Valentinian, the son of Constantius, let us briefly recall the events that we passed over.

Lucian, the presbyter to whom God revealed the location of the tomb and relics of blessed Stephen, the protomartyr, wrote the revelation in Greek for all the churches.

Avitus, a presbyter of Spanish origin, translated this revelation into Latin prose and, adding his own letter, sent it through the presbyter Orosius to the western peoples.

When Orosius reached the holy places—the purpose for which Augustine had sent him to Jerome to learn about the nature of the soul—he received the relics of blessed Stephen and, returning to his homeland, was the first to bring them to the West.

The miracles that the Lord performed in Africa through the venerable relics of blessed Stephen were many and extremely remarkable. The outstanding teacher Augustine, who knew that they had certainly occurred, recorded them in his books On the City of God.

So many volumes composed by Augustine’s talent, with sound meaning and irreproachable reasoning, remain extant that one of the learned is said to have remarked about him: “He lies who claims to have read all of it.”

At his command, his aforementioned disciple Orosius also composed, nobly and usefully, seven books against the pagans.

## CHAPTER XIII. On Various Events in Africa and Britain, and on the Death of Augustus and Thereafter of the Emperor Theodosius

[Col. 1244A]

At that time the province of Africa was handed over to the Vandals by the count Boniface and was withdrawn from Roman authority. When Boniface had incurred Valentinian’s displeasure, he wished to defend himself by means of a public calamity. He invited Gizeric, king of the Vandals, from Spain—the man who had killed Ermengarius, king of the Suebi—and, as though unwillingly, took vengeance through him for the wrong done to Saint Eulalia. The Vandals had settled in Baetica, a region of Spain, for fifty-four years. From there they crossed into Africa with all their families, joined by the Alans and the Goths, and defiled everything alike with the sword, fire, plunder, and Arian impiety.

Then blessed Augustine, bishop of Hippo and teacher of all the Churches, so that he might not see the ruin of his own city, departed to the Lord in the third month of its siege, on the fifth day before the Kalends of September, having lived seventy-six years. At that time the Vandals, after capturing Carthage, also ravaged Sicily.

In those days Aetius, commander of both armies, was called patrician. He subdued the Burgundians, who had rebelled against the Romans: twenty thousand Burgundians were killed, as well as nine thousand Goths who had provided them with assistance.

At that time the Britons, unable to endure the attacks of the Scots and Picts, sent to Rome. Promising their submission, they requested assistance against the enemy. A legion was immediately sent to them; it slaughtered a great multitude of barbarians and drove the rest beyond the borders of Britain. As this legion was preparing to return home, it ordered its allies to build a wall across the island, between the two seas, to keep out the enemy. Constructed without an architect or master, chiefly of turf rather than stone, it proved of no benefit to those who worked on it. For as soon as the Romans had departed, the enemy, transported by ships, overran everything in its path like a ripe harvest: it cut down, trampled, and devoured all before it.

Again they hastened to Rome to seek assistance. Having obtained it, they drove the defeated enemy beyond the sea. Joining the Britons to themselves, they built a solid wall—not of earth and dust as before, but of stone—between the cities that had been established there out of fear of the enemy, extending from the wall to the sea. On the southern shore as well, because the enemy was feared from that direction, they erected towers at intervals to keep watch over the sea. Thus they bade farewell to their allies, as though they would never return.

At that time Palladius was sent by Pope Celestine as the first bishop to the Scots who believed in Christ. Accordingly, when the Roman army withdrew from Britain, the Scots and Picts, learning of this, returned and seized the whole northern part of the island, displacing the native inhabitants as far as the wall. Before long, after the wall’s guards had been killed, captured, or put to flight, and the wall itself breached, a savage plunderer began to rampage even within it.

A letter filled with tears and anguish was sent to Aetius, a man of Roman authority and three-time consul, in the twenty-third year of the reign of the emperor Theodosius, requesting assistance; but it was not obtained. Meanwhile a dreadful and notorious famine afflicted the refugees. Compelled by it, some surrendered to the enemy; others fought bravely from the mountains, caves, and forests and inflicted slaughter upon the enemy.

The Scots returned home, though they would return again after only a short time. The Picts took possession of the farthest part of the island, intending to inhabit it then and thereafter. The famine mentioned above was followed by great abundance of crops; abundance by luxury; luxury by negligence; negligence by a most severe plague; and soon afterward by the still more grievous blow of new enemies, namely the English.

When these events had thus taken place in the eastern and western regions, Theodosius died at Constantinople, in the twenty-sixth year after the death of Honorius, in the forty-eighth year of his age. After him Martian, acclaimed Augustus by the soldiers and the army, was elevated to the throne.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the battles of Attila, king of the Huns, against the Romans and other peoples.

Meanwhile Attila, king of the Huns, having with him the subjected Gepids under Ardaric, the Goths under Valamir, and various other nations with their kings, ravaged all Illyricum and Thrace, both Dacias, Moesia, and Scythia. Against him Argenisdus, commander of the army of Moesia, marched out and fought bravely near Marcianopolis. When his horse fell beneath him, he was thrown down; but he did not cease fighting even then, and was killed.

Attila, therefore, elated by many triumphs over different nations and by the submission of numerous kings whom he had brought under his authority, and puffed up by the subjection of the Ostrogoths as well, prepared to invade Gaul and crush the Visigoths. He therefore sent ambassadors to the emperor Valentinian, pretending peace and declaring that he was hastening westward to avenge an injury done by the Romans, so that, after destroying the Visigoths and the other peoples who held parts of Gaul and Spain, he might restore those regions to the empire.

He also attempted to persuade the king of the Visigoths to invade the Roman Empire together with him, so that they might perhaps possess it equally. But the deception did not escape the emperor. Through Aetius, the patrician who at that time governed Gaul, he quickly induced Theodoric, king of the Goths, to support his side.

By then the exceedingly savage king Attila had overthrown cities and strongholds throughout Gaul far and wide and was hastening to destroy the city of Orléans. At that point, through the agency of the most blessed Anianus, bishop of Orléans, both Aetius, the Roman patrician, and Theodoric, king of the Goths, together with his son Thorismund, formed an alliance and hastened to meet the Huns, gathering warriors from every direction against the fierce king.

Their auxiliaries were the Franks, Sarmatians, Armoricans, Burgundians, Saxons, Ripariolibrians—formerly Roman soldiers—and also some Celts and Germans. Attila, meanwhile, had with him many nations and many kings whom he had subjected to his authority, and the army of the Ostrogoths was preeminent among them.

The first encounter, as they say, took place near the Loire. But the war was prolonged, and on the Catalaunian Plains, called Mauriacus, a savage and stubborn battle was joined, such as is rarely found in the records of antiquity. King Attila judged that the battle should begin around the ninth hour of the day, so that, if his men were victorious, they could pursue the enemy farther and return to their camp before nightfall; but if they were defeated, they could take refuge in the protection of night and recover their strength.

In this most celebrated battle, 165,000 are reported to have been killed on both sides, apart from the 15,000 Franks and Gepids who fell from wounds inflicted by one another. Thus Theodoric, king of the Goths, died there. King Attila, defeated, withdrew into the camp he had prepared from wagons.

Aetius, however, urged Thorismund, the son of the slain King Theodoric, not to allow his brothers to seize the kingdom of their murdered father, and immediately compelled him to go to Toulouse, which was the seat of the Visigothic kingdom. Through ambassadors Attila then sent him a warning, while pretending friendship, that he should quickly return to his own kingdom before the new enemies surrounding him inflicted greater harm upon him.

Aetius himself, however, regarding both sides as enemies of the empire, withdrew after leaving the matter unresolved. Attila, taking advantage of the opportunity and now secure because the Visigoths had departed, left Gaul and turned his forces toward the oppression of the Romans.

In his first assault he besieged the city of Aquileia for a long time. After capturing it, he destroyed it so completely that scarcely any traces of its ruins remain. From there, made more audacious, he seized Milan, a metropolitan city, and likewise Ticinum, royal cities, and with equal violence cast down and demolished the neighboring places.

When he was intent on attacking Rome, Pope Leo personally approached him and made him more merciful. Laying aside his fury, Attila withdrew beyond the Danube after promising peace.

## CHAPTER XV. On the death of Aetius and the plundering of Rome by the Vandals.

The patrician Aetius, the great salvation of the Western Empire, returned to Italy after Gaul had been freed from its enemies. At length, through the faction of the eunuch Heraclius, he was killed by the emperor Valentinian; and with him the kingdom of the Western lands fell.

Valentinian himself was murdered by a stratagem of Maximus, being stabbed by the soldiers of Aetius whom he had chosen for himself. Maximus then seized his empire. Although everyone believed that he would in every respect benefit the state, he soon demonstrated by a revealing act what he had in mind. He received Valentinian’s murderers into his friendship, forbade his wife, the empress, to mourn the loss of her husband, and compelled her to marry him within a very few days. Yet he did not long enjoy this unrestrained conduct.

For after the second month, when the arrival of Gaiseric, king of the Vandals, was announced from Africa and many nobles and commoners were fleeing the city, Maximus himself also wished to depart in panic, after granting everyone permission to leave. But he was torn apart by servants, thrown limb by limb into the Tiber, and even denied burial.

After Maximus’s death, the Roman captivity, deserving of many tears, followed immediately. Gaiseric took possession of the city, which was entirely without defenses, while Saint Leo the bishop came out to meet him beyond the gates. His supplication, by the Lord’s agency, so softened Gaiseric that, although everything had been handed over to his power, he nevertheless spared the city from fire, slaughter, and torture.

For fourteen days, therefore, Rome was emptied of all its wealth through unrestricted and undisturbed search. Gaiseric returned victoriously to Carthage, taking with him many thousands of captives, together with the empress Eudoxia, who, as they say, had invited him, and her daughters.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the restoration of the Eastern Empire under the emperor Marcian and the deeds of the bishop Germanus among the Britons.

Accordingly, Marcian, emperor of the East, restored by divine permission the kingdom that his predecessors and their forebears, ruling in succession for nearly sixty years, had diminished, so that great rejoicing increased among all who were subject to him.

He established a treaty of concord with Avitus, emperor of the Western lands, whom the Romans had made Caesar after the death of Maximus the tyrant and the plundering of the city. Governing both empires harmoniously, they ruled them together. At length, in the sixth year and sixth month of his reign, Marcian died in peace.

Leo succeeded him on the throne. Avitus, however, withdrew from Italy into Gaul, where, abandoned by the army and the Gothic auxiliaries, he returned to Italy and became bishop at Placentia. At his instigation Theodoric, king of the Goths, led an army against the Suebi, because they were ravaging the regions that they had restored to the Romans.

A battle was fought against the Suebi in the Campania of Tarragona, where very many of the Suebi were killed. Their king Richarius, fleeing, was finally captured and thrown into custody. After their kingdom had been destroyed, the Suebi surrendered themselves to Theodoric, king of the Goths.

At that time the people of the English, or Saxons, arrived in Britain in three longships. When news of their successful journey was brought home, a stronger army was sent. Joining the first arrivals, it initially drove away the enemy. Then, turning its weapons against its allies, it subjected almost the entire island, from its eastern region to its western, by fire and sword, inventing the excuse that the Britons, who were fighting on their behalf, had not provided the promised payment in sufficient measure.

At that time the Pelagian heresy disturbed the faith of the Britons. Seeking help from the Gallic bishops, they received as defenders of the faith Germanus, bishop of the Church of Auxerre, and Lupus, likewise a prelate of apostolic grace at Troyes. The bishops confirmed the faith by the word of truth and by signs of miracles.

They also, at that time, defeated by divine power the war undertaken by the Saxons and Picts against the Britons, when Germanus himself became commander of the army. Not with the sound of a trumpet, but with the cry of “Alleluia,” raised heavenward by the voice of the entire army, he put the savage enemies to flight.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the frequent changes of emperors, and how the Romans lost the empire of the West.

As we have said, Leo became emperor of the East after Marcian, while Majorian was appointed Caesar at Ravenna. Majorian made a treaty through ambassadors with Theodoric, king of the Visigoths. Theodoric was recalled to Gaul from Emerita, a city of Spain that he was then ravaging, not, however, without great slaughter and devastation among the Suebi and other peoples living in various parts of Spain, whom Theodoric had ordered his commanders to crush and plunder.

After concluding peace with King Theodoric, the emperor Majorian set out for Spain and ordered ships to be prepared so that from there he might cross against the Vandals in Africa. But when he had reached Carthagena, the Vandals attacked and plundered the fleet that he had ordered to be prepared. Thus, frustrated in his undertaking, the emperor returned to Italy and was killed at Tortona. Severianus took his place, but he himself died at Rome scarcely three full years into his tyranny.

At that time a battle was fought at Dijon between the Franks and the Burgundians. Gundeiflus had deceitfully contrived it against his brother Gaudebaudus. Accordingly, Gundeiflus and his followers fought against his brother together with the Franks; after putting his brother to flight, he held his kingdom for a short time.

Gaudebaudus fortified himself at Avignon. In the same year, having recovered his strength, he besieged Vienne, captured and killed his brother Gundeiflus, condemned many other Burgundians to death, and joined his brother’s kingdom to his own and retained it.

Then the emperor Leo appointed Artemius, the son-in-law of the blessed Marcian, Caesar from the rank of patrician and sent him to the West as emperor. Through Ardabur, son of Aspar, he killed Bigen, king of the Goths. He also sent Basiliscus, the brother of his empress, with an army to Africa against the Vandals. After repeatedly attacking Carthage in a naval battle, Basiliscus withdrew when bribed with money.

As soon as Artemius came to Rome, he sent his son-in-law Ricimer against the Alans, an outstanding man who routed a multitude of Alans and killed their king Beorgus after defeating him in the very first engagement.

Theodoric, king of the Visigoths, therefore, seeing the frequent changes among the Roman emperors, attempted to occupy Gaul as his rightful possession. When the emperor Artemius learned of this, he requested the assistance of the Britons. Their king Riotimus came with 12,000 men to provide aid. Against them Theodoric, king of the Visigoths, led an innumerable army and, fighting for a long time, drove the Briton king Riotimus to flight before he could join the Romans.

Having lost a large part of his army, Riotimus fled with those whom he could gather and came to the neighboring people of the Burgundians, who at that time were allied with the Romans.

Theodoric, king of the Visigoths, then occupied the city of Clermont in Gaul after the death of the emperor Artemius. Artemius had ravaged Rome in an internal war while fighting against his son-in-law Ricimer, and had himself been killed by his son-in-law. He left the kingdom to Olybrius.

At that time in Constantinople Aspar, first among the patricians and renowned for his Gothic ancestry, was killed in the palace by the swords of the eunuchs, together with his sons Ardabur and Patriciolus. Their father had formerly been called patrician; the latter had been called Caesar and son-in-law of the emperor Leo. Olybrius himself died before he had completed eight months on the throne.

Glycerius was made Caesar at Ravenna more through presumption than election. After scarcely a year had passed, Nepos, the son of the sister of the former patrician Marcellinus, ejected him from the throne, ordained him bishop at the port of Rome, and himself seized the kingdom.

Seeing such great variations and changes among the Roman emperors, Theodoric—as we stated above—occupied the city of Clermont, where Cedicius, the most noble of the senators, was then commander of the Romans. Cedicius was the son of the emperor Avitus, who had seized the throne for only a few days. After capturing Clermont, the Goths also seized Narbonne.

Against them Nepos, the emperor, sent Orestes, master of the soldiers. Orestes, having taken command of the army, came to Ravenna and, remaining there, made his son Augustulus emperor. When Nepos heard this, he fled to Dalmatia; there he was deprived of the kingdom and died, in the place where Glycerius, formerly emperor, already held the bishopric of Salona.

After Augustulus had been appointed emperor at Ravenna by his father Orestes, Odoacer, king of the Torcilingi, soon afterward occupied Italy, bringing with him Sciri, Heruli, and auxiliaries of various peoples. After killing Orestes, he drove his son Augustulus from the throne and condemned him to exile in the fortress of Lucullanum in Campania.

Thus the Western empire of the Roman people—which Octavian, the first of the emperors, had obtained in the 709th year after the founding of the City—perished with this Augustulus, in the 522nd year of the reigns of his predecessors and forebears. From then onward the Roman state in the regions of the West, which had until that time ruled over nations, groaning, submitted to kings of foreign peoples.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On Theodoric, king of the Goths, how he obtained Italy through the gift of the emperor Zeno, and on his deeds.

At that time the emperor Leo sent to every orthodox bishop throughout the world separate but concordant letters concerning the Chalcedonian Tome, asking them to write back what they believed about it. He received replies from all of them concerning the true incarnation of Christ, so harmonious that one might have thought they had all been written at the same time and dictated by one person.

In those days Theodorus, bishop of the city founded by Cyrus, king of the Persians, and called Cyria after him, wrote concerning the true incarnation of the Lord and Savior against Eutyches and Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria, who denied that Christ possessed human flesh. He also wrote an Ecclesiastical History from the conclusion of Eusebius’s books up to his own time—that is, up to the reign of this Leo, under whom he also died.

At that time Victorius, at the command of Pope Hilary, wrote the date of Easter for a period of 532 years.

Leo crowned his grandson Leo with his own hands. After making him emperor, he died in the sixteenth year of his reign. Since Leo was still very young and had only a short time remaining, he appointed his father Zeno emperor and then departed this life.

Zeno ruled the Eastern Empire for seventeen years. When he learned of Theodoric’s fortunate success—that he had settled in Illyricum with an army of Ostrogoths after departing from Pannonia with his father Theodomir in search of other homes, and that they had subdued and subjected the neighboring peoples whom they had encountered—Zeno sent an embassy to him and ordered him not to delay coming to him. He also reminded Theodoric of the great honors bestowed upon him by the emperor Leo, when, after having been a hostage with him for nearly ten years, he had been sent back to his native land and to the presence of his father.

Theodoric therefore came without hesitation and hastened to the royal city. There he was kindly received and magnificently honored by the emperor Zeno, and he was made ordinary consul. Not only this: he also received from the emperor an equestrian statue, which was set up before the imperial palace.

Meanwhile Theodoric, allied under the rule of Zeno, enjoyed every good thing in the city, but heard that his people, settled in Illyricum as we have said, were not entirely prosperous or well supplied. He therefore preferred to seek a livelihood through the customary labor of his people rather than enjoy in idleness the wealth of the Roman kingdom while his people lived in moderate circumstances.

After deliberating with himself, he said to the emperor:

“Although nothing is lacking to us who serve your empire, nevertheless, if your piety considers it worthy, may it willingly hear the desire of my heart.”

Since he had been granted permission to speak familiarly, as was customary, he continued:

“The Western region, which was formerly governed by the rule of your predecessors and forebears, and that city, the capital and mistress of the world—why does it now fluctuate beneath the tyranny of the king of the Torcilingi and the Rugi? Send me with my people, if you command it, so that here you may also be free of the burden of expense; and there, if I prevail with the Lord’s help, the fame of your piety may shine forth.

“For it is better that I, who am your servant and son, should possess that kingdom if I prevail by your gift, than that an enemy should oppress your senate and a part of the state under the yoke of tyranny and servitude. If I prevail, I shall possess it through your gift and favor; if I am defeated, your piety loses nothing—indeed, as we have said, it gains the expenses.”

When the emperor heard this, although he was distressed by Theodoric’s departure, he nevertheless did not wish to grieve him. He granted what he requested, dismissed him richly endowed with gifts, and entrusted the Roman senate and people to his care.

Accordingly, Theodoric left the royal city and returned to his people. With the entire Gothic nation, which nevertheless gave its consent to him, he headed toward the Western lands. Proceeding by the direct route, he ascended through the lands near Pannonia by way of the Sirmian region; then, entering the territory of Venetia, he pitched his camp at the place called the Bridge of the Sontius.

After remaining there for some time to restore the strength of men and animals, Odoacer sent an armed army against him. Theodoric destroyed it with a great slaughter on the Veronese plains, broke up and plundered its camp, and entered Italy with greater confidence. After crossing the river Po, he established his camp before Ravenna, the royal city.

In the third year, therefore, he compelled Odoacer, who had been besieged, to surrender and killed him after stripping him of his kingdom. From that time all Italy was subject to Theodoric. In the third year after his entry, with the emperor’s approval, he laid aside the private clothing of his own people and assumed royal dress, as though he were now ruler of both Goths and Romans.

After these successes, wishing to have the nation of the Franks as an ally, he sent an embassy to their king, Louis, requesting his daughter. Having obtained her, he joined her to himself in marriage, as the historian Jordanes reports. He also married his daughters to neighboring kings: one to Alaric, king of the Visigoths, and another to Sigismund, king of the Burgundians. He gave his niece Amalaburga to Ermenfrid, king of the Thuringians, and his sister to Trasamund, king of the Vandals, desiring in this way to extend his family nobly.

At that time John, bishop of the Roman Church, came to Constantinople. At the gate called the Golden Gate, while crowds of people came out to meet him, he restored sight before everyone to a blind man who asked him to do so.

When John returned and reached Ravenna, Theodoric killed him and his companions by imprisoning them, moved by jealousy because Justin, the defender of Catholic piety, had received John honorably.

Theodoric also had the patrician Symmachus murdered at Ravenna, although no cause for his execution existed. Struck by divine anger, Theodoric himself died there by a sudden death in the following year, in the thirtieth year of his Italian reign. His grandson Atalaric succeeded him.

For we read in the Dialogue of Saint Gregory that a certain priest visibly saw Theodoric bound and dragged by Pope John and the patrician Symmachus to a cauldron of Sicilian fire.

## CHAPTER XIX. On the emperor Zeno, how he recovered the empire he had lost, and on his successor Anastasius.

Accordingly, while the emperor Zeno was living at Chalcedon, his mother-in-law, the empress, proclaimed her own brother Basiliscus emperor in the city. When Zeno heard this, he withdrew to Isauria, lest some misfortune arise in civil wars on his account.

When Basiliscus learned of Zeno’s flight, he rejoiced, but not for long. Zeno returned to the throne and was received by his own people, while Basiliscus was condemned to exile.

A certain man named Illus, who had been Zeno’s closest friend during his private life, secretly disparaged the empress Ariadne and provoked the emperor to jealousy. The emperor, deliberating on killing her, quietly entrusted the matter to one of his men.

When that man attempted to carry it out, he disclosed the plan to a chamberlain. When the empress learned of it, she escaped to the bishop Acacius. On the following day, Zeno, believing the deed accomplished, received no one, as though he were mourning. Bishop Acacius entered, accused the emperor of what had happened, and cleared the empress of suspicion. After receiving a pledge of safety, the empress returned.

Illus, however, departed from the city after assuming tyranny. He was killed by the emperor’s army, while Zeno rested in peace.

Anastasius was suddenly elevated by the empress and became known as both emperor and husband. He ruled for twenty-eight years, but so unhappily that, surrounded by various forces of enemies—both external enemies and tyrants—he often mourned and groaned and never succeeded in hearing that any of his enemies had been avenged. He himself did not preserve the rights of the Church; rather, favoring the heresy of Eutyches, he persecuted the Catholics. He himself perished by a divine thunderbolt.

## CHAPTER XX. On the persecution of Catholics by the Vandal kings, and on what took place in various regions.

At that time Huneric, the Arian king of the Vandals, closed the Catholic churches and subjected the people to various tortures. Indeed, although he cut off the hands and tongues of countless people, he could not deprive them of the power of speech for their Catholic confession.

Thus Trasamund, Huneric’s successor and king of the Vandals, also closed the Catholic churches and condemned many bishops to exile, sending them to Sardinia.

At that time Pope Symmachus, among his many works for the churches—some of which he built from their foundations and others of which he restored from antiquity—constructed dwellings for the poor near the basilicas of Saints Peter, Paul, and Lawrence. Every year he also supplied money and clothing throughout Africa and Sardinia to the bishops who were in exile.

In those days Hilderic, king of the Vandals, recalled the bishops whom his predecessors had condemned to exile and ordered the churches to be restored. He removed the profanations of the heretics.

The abbot Benedict, distinguished by the wonders of his life and character, also flourished at that time. Blessed Pope Gregory wrote of his virtues in the book of the *Dialogues*.

At the same time Sigismund, king of the Burgundians, was handed over by his own people to the Franks. The Franks led him away with them in the clothing of a monk, together with his wife and children, and eventually killed them by throwing them into a well.

After his death, King Chlodomer of the Franks fought against the Burgundians and, as is reported, was killed in battle.

Boethius the patrician, who had nobly published two books on arithmetic in the Latin language and had written other little books with great elegance, was finally condemned to exile. After composing the books of the *Consolation of Philosophy* in an exceptionally eloquent metrical and prose style, he was killed in the territory of Milan.

## CHAPTER XXI. On Belisarius, consul of Justinian, who destroyed the Vandals in Africa and crushed the Goths in Italy, and who also fought against the Persians.

At that time the emperor Justin died after, in the interests of the state, designating as his successor in the empire his nephew Justinian, the son of his sister.

Justinian held the Eastern Empire for thirty-eight years. After prolonged wars and many labors undertaken against the Persians, a treaty was established with the Persian king through ambassadors.

When peace had thus been secured, Justinian [recalled] the Roman army from the borders of the Persians. He then chose Belisarius as consul and sent him with an army toward the southern region against the Vandals.

With the Lord’s favor, Belisarius overcame the Vandals as easily as he had advanced against them and joined Libya to the body of the entire empire, destroying the Vandal nation. Carthage was also recovered in the ninety-sixth year after its loss. The Vandals were driven out and defeated, and their king Gelimer was captured and sent to Constantinople. Presented to the emperor in the royal city before the people, he enabled Justinian to celebrate a triumph over the Vandals through Belisarius.

In Italy, after the death of King Theodoric, his grandson Atalaric succeeded him by his own appointment. Although living in a childish manner, he remained in power for seven years while his mother Amalasuntha ruled. At that time he restored to the Franks Gaul, which they had long sought to recover.

After Atalaric’s death, his mother made her cousin Theodahad a partner in the kingdom. Not long afterward, she was killed at his command.

Because she had previously commended herself and her son to the emperor Justinian, when he heard of her death he was grieved and did not allow it to go unavenged. Instead, he immediately placed at the head of an army of various nations the same commander who had conquered the Carthaginians and was still in office, triumphing over the wealth of the Vandals, and sent him to the Western regions.

At his first arrival he quickly overran Sicily, defeating its commander Sinderith. While he remained there for some time to organize the province, he learned that civil wars and internal battles were raging in Africa.

For Stotzas, almost the last among the soldiers, a client of Marcianus, the master of the soldiers, had seized tyranny and become the leader of the rebels. After treacherously killing Cyrillus, Marcellus, Pharas, and various other judges, he raged against the commander Solomon and devastated the whole of Africa in tyrannical fashion.

Belisarius therefore crossed by sea from Sicily to Africa and, with his customary success, put the rebels to flight, liberated the province, restored Solomon to Carthage, and returned to Sicily.

There Evermund, the son-in-law of Theodahad, king of the Goths, who had come against him with an army, saw the consul’s success and voluntarily surrendered to the victorious side. He urged Belisarius to come at once to Italy, which was already panting and fearful at his arrival.

Belisarius therefore assembled an army and blockaded Naples with both a naval and a cavalry force. After besieging it for a few days, he invaded it at night through an aqueduct. Having killed both the Goths who were present and the rebellious Romans, he thoroughly plundered the city.

When Theodahad perceived this, he appointed Vitigis, one of his commanders, over the others and sent him against Belisarius. When Vitigis entered Campania and soon reached the barbarian plains, the army immediately proclaimed him king with one voice.

Elevated to the throne, he sent men from among his companions to destroy Theodahad as the latter was returning to Ravenna. Thus securing his own kingdom, he abandoned the expedition and, rejecting his private wife, joined himself to the royal maiden Mathesuentha, granddaughter of King Theodoric, more by force than by love.

While he was delighting in his new marriage at Ravenna, the consul Belisarius entered the city of Rome. He was received by that people, once Roman, and by the senate, whose very name had almost been buried along with its power. Immediately he occupied the neighboring places and the defenses of the cities and strongholds.

In the first Gothic engagement, with Hunnila leading the army through Usinum [Perusium] to a stronghold, Belisarius defeated the Goths. After slaughtering more than 7,000, he drove the rest in confusion as far as Ravenna.

In the second engagement, he fought against Vitigis himself as he was blockading the Roman fortifications. After burning with fire his engines and towers, by which he had attempted to approach the city, Belisarius outwitted him for a year, although suffering from famine.

Afterward he pursued him as far as Rimini. From there, having driven him away and shut him up in Ravenna, he received his surrender.

The same consul also triumphed against the Goths in a nearly equal struggle against the Franks, who had come with their king Theudebert in a force of more than 200,000. But because he was occupied with other matters elsewhere and did not wish to become entangled in another conflict, he granted peace at the request of the Franks. Without loss to his own men, he expelled them from Italian territory and brought the king, the queen, and the palace treasures to the emperor who had sent him.

Thus, within a short period, the emperor Justinian, through his loyal consul, subjected two kingdoms and two states to his authority.

While these events were taking place in the southern and western regions, the Persians broke the treaty and invaded Roman territory. Ravaging Coele-Syria and defiling everything with the sword and slaughter, they reached as far as Antioch.

Finding it without a Roman garrison, they plundered everything. They did not withdraw burdened with booty, nor did they pursue the fleeing Romans, because, when he heard of their arrival, the consul Germanus abandoned Antioch and fled.

The emperor sent several commanders against them, but, defeated and terrified, they were unable to resist the enemy. Belisarius was therefore sent once more against the Persians. He did not subdue them as he had other nations; he merely compelled them to withdraw from the Roman borders and return to their own settlements. After arranging peace, he returned to the emperor.

Then, as usually happens, a change of circumstances and the differing will of rulers caused the senators and patricians to burn with jealousy. They advised the emperor to expel Belisarius from the rank of patrician, as though he were aspiring to the throne, and to deprive him of his dignities.

This action gave no small encouragement to the Goths as they recovered their breath and to the other nations hostile to the Romans. Not long afterward the emperor himself regretted what he had done. When the courtiers attempted to deprive Justinian of the kingdom and to make a certain Florian emperor, Justinian, aided by the strength of Belisarius, was restored to the throne, although the innovators were undeservedly slaughtered.

## CHAPTER XXII. Under the reign of Justinian, the Franks fought against the Goths and expelled them from the kingdom of Gaul. They also fought against the Saxons and defeated them, and subdued the Britons.

At that time, war arose in the regions of Gaul between Alaric, king of the Goths, and Clovis, king of the Franks, although previously many conflicts had taken place between them with varying outcomes. At last an engagement occurred in Campania Voglavensis, ten miles from the city of Poitiers. There Clovis, king of the Franks, killed Alaric, king of the Goths, and slaughtered the greater part of his army. He took away the kingdom that the Goths had long held—from the River Loire to the Rhône, across the Pyrenees as far as the Ocean—and subjected it to Frankish rule.

This came about through God’s wondrous providence: when the stipends of the Roman consuls had been withdrawn because of avarice, those who were compelled by hunger and poverty conspired against the Romans and took up arms, laying waste to Illyricum, invading Italy, and plundering Rome, the mistress of nations [the reading *docuinam* is evidently corrupt], so that Alaric, whom the Goths had made king, raised up his people and kingdom, celebrating success after success. At length Alaric and the Gothic people and kingdom failed, just as the Roman power in the West had failed under Augustus Caesar, when it was mistress of other peoples, and finally failed under Augustulus, as we have related above, becoming subject to other nations.

Thus, while Justinian was emperor, the body of Saint Antony the monk was discovered by divine revelation, carried to Alexandria, and buried in the church of the blessed John the Baptist. Dionysius also wrote the Paschal cycles, beginning with the year 532 from the Lord’s Incarnation, which is the 258th year of Diocletian. At that time the book of laws called the Justinian Code, established by the emperor himself, was promulgated throughout the world. Victor, bishop of Capua, likewise wrote a book on Easter and refuted Victor’s errors.

At that time Chramn presumed to rebel against Chlothar, king of the Franks, who was his father. When he would not desist from the rash undertaking he had begun, he withdrew to Brittany and armed that people, together with its king, against his father. Chlothar pursued him with his other sons and the Frankish army. After the Breton king had been killed, Chramn was captured, shut up alive in a house with his wife and sons, and burned. Chlothar, triumphing over the spoils of the Bretons, subjected that people to the Franks and made it tributary. He also crushed the rebellious Saxons in very severe battles and defeated them, though not without the shedding of much of his own men’s blood.

Thus Justinian, after holding the empire of the East for thirty-eight years, departed from human affairs, and Justin succeeded him in the kingdom.

## CHAPTER XXIII  
### Concerning Narses the Patrician, who destroyed the Goths in Italy and later, as they say, summoned the Lombards to possess it

Justin the Younger was emperor for eleven years. At that time, after the consul Belisarius had departed from Italy and had transported to the emperor Justinian the Gothic king Vitigis, the queen, and the treasures of the palace, as we stated above, the Goths who were settled beyond the Po in Liguria, recovering their courage, rose again for war. They appointed Hildebad as their petty king, but he was killed after barely a year had elapsed. Eraric succeeded him, but he too was killed before the year had ended.

Then they made Totila, also called Baduila, their king. Recovering his strength, he fought against Rome, defeated and overthrew its commanders, and invaded the city. Advancing from there, he captured Sicily and, harrying the Romans, devastated almost all Italy.

Against him the emperor Justin sent Narses the patrician. Coming into Italy, Narses fought against the Goths with manly courage and strength, killed Totila their king, and struck down the Gothic people in slaughter. When they had again recovered their breath, they appointed Teia as their king; Narses the patrician killed him also and utterly destroyed the Goths. He freed Italy from their yoke.

Afterward he fought against Bucellinus, commander of the Franks, when they met in battle, and, as is said, killed him together with his entire army. Having now freed Italy from the attacks of its enemies, he restored it to the body of the commonwealth. He rebuilt Milan, the royal city, which had been demolished by the Goths and Burgundians, and restored other cities throughout Italy that had been destroyed.

Later, because of the jealousy of the Romans, for whom he had endured much labor against the Goths, he was accused before Justin and his wife Sophia of oppressing Italy. He withdrew to Naples in Campania and wrote to the Lombard people, inviting them to come and possess Italy.

At that time John, pontiff of the Roman Church, completed and dedicated the church of the apostles Philip and James, which his predecessor Pelagius had begun.

## CHAPTER XXIV  
### Concerning the blessed Gregory and his deeds

While Tiberius was emperor, having succeeded Justin, the blessed Gregory was serving as an envoy at the imperial court. In the presence of Tiberius, he demonstrated by Catholic arguments that Eutychius, bishop of Constantinople, had erred concerning our belief in the resurrection, and convicted him of error. Consequently the emperor himself decreed that the book which Eutychius had written about the resurrection should be burned in the flames.

For Eutychius taught that our body would be immaterial in the glory of that resurrection, subtler than winds and air, contrary to the Lord’s words: “Touch and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me have.”

After Tiberius, when Maurice was reigning, the same blessed Gregory—now pontiff of the Roman Church and its greatest teacher—gathered a synod of twenty-four bishops at the body of the blessed apostle Peter and issued decrees concerning the needs of the Church.

He also sent Augustine, Mellitus, and John, together with many other God-fearing monks, to Britain and converted the English to Christ. Ethelbert, having soon been converted to the grace of Christ together with the people of Kent over whom he ruled and with the neighboring provinces, granted episcopal sees both to his bishop and teacher Augustine and to the other holy pontiffs.

The peoples of the English north of the River Humber, situated under the kings Aelle and Ethelfrid, had not yet heard the word of life. Gregory therefore wrote to Augustine and decreed that the bishops of London and York, having received the pallium from the apostolic see, should be metropolitans.

By divine inspiration he composed the *Moralia on Job*, and also produced with great clarity the *Pastoral Book*. Dictating the books of the *Dialogues*, so that later generations might imitate the venerable men who had distinguished themselves in those times, he handed them down for us to read. He composed an outstanding work on Ezekiel. His book of homilies supplies extremely salutary and spiritual nourishment to those who taste it. Many of his letters also remain, useful to readers for the affairs on which they were composed.

While Phocas was emperor, he departed to the Lord.

## CHAPTER XXV  
### Concerning the Lombards invading Italy, and the martyrdom of Hermenegild, son of the Gothic king

At that time Alboin, king of the Lombards, invited by Narses, as we have already stated, left and burned Pannonia, where he had lived. Coming with all his people, accompanied by famine and pestilence, he invaded Italy.

At the same time Hermenegild, son of Leovigild, king of the Goths, was stripped by his Arian father of the insignia of kingship because of his steadfast confession of the Catholic faith, bound in chains, and thrown into prison. At last, on the holy night of the Lord’s Resurrection, he was struck on the head with an axe and entered the heavenly kingdom as king and martyr in place of an earthly kingdom.

As soon as his brother Reccared received the kingdom after their father, he converted to the Catholic faith the entire Gothic people over whom he ruled, under the urging of Leander, bishop of Hispalis, who had also instructed Hermenegild.

## CHAPTER XXVI  
### Concerning the deeds of Pope Boniface

Therefore, at the request of Pope Boniface, the emperor Phocas, the successor of Maurice, decreed that the see of the Roman and apostolic Church should be the head of all Churches, because the Church of Constantinople was writing that it was the first of all Churches.

The same Phocas, at the petition of Pope Boniface, ordered that the ancient shrine called the Pantheon, after the filth of idolatry had been removed, should become the church of the blessed ever-virgin Mary and of all the martyrs. Thus, where once the worship had been offered not to all gods but to demons, there afterward the memory of all the saints would be celebrated.

## CHAPTER XXVII  
### Concerning the six universal synods

Let us briefly repeat what we passed over above and show which are the six universal synods, received and jointly celebrated by the whole East, by those who retain the Catholic faith with a sound mind.

The first universal synod was assembled at Nicaea against Arius, with 318 Fathers, during the pontificate of Pope Julius and the reign of the emperor Constantine.

The second was held at Constantinople, with 150 Fathers, against Macedonius and Eudoxius, during the pontificate of Pope Damasus and the reign of the emperor Gratian, when Nectarius was ordained bishop of that city.

The third was held at Ephesus, with 200 Fathers, against Nestorius, bishop of the imperial city, under the emperor Theodosius the Great and Pope Celestine.

The fourth was held at Chalcedon, with 630 Fathers, under Pope Leo and during the reign of the emperor Marcian, against Eutyches, leader of the most impious monks.

The fifth was likewise held at Constantinople, during the pontificate of Pope Vigilius and the reign of the emperor Justinian, against Theodore and all heretics.

The sixth universal synod was celebrated at Constantinople and written in the Greek language, during the pontificate of Pope Agatho, with the most pious emperor Constantine presiding and conducting the proceedings within his palace, while the legates of the apostolic see and 150 bishops were seated together.

From the Nativity of the Lord Jesus Christ, out of love for my lady, the empress Judith, I undertook the work that I brought down to the death of Gregory, that outstanding teacher. I also briefly touched upon certain matters concerning the deeds of Pope Boniface, after the Roman rulers and the Goths had been driven from Italy and Gaul and the Franks and Lombards had succeeded them in the kingdoms. Here I have judged it right to place an end to my books.

## In the Year of the Lord 850  
### Columbanus, abbot of Saint-Trond

## A Mournful Poem on the Death of King Charlemagne

*(In George Colvenerius, works of the blessed Rabanus Maurus.)*

From the rising of the sun to the western shores of the sea,

lament strikes every breast.

Alas for me, wretched man!

Beyond the sea, sorrow has touched the ranks

with immense grief.

Alas for me, wretched man!

Franks, Romans, and all the faithful

are pierced by mourning and great distress.

Alas for me, wretched man!

Children, old men, glorious bishops,

and matrons lament the loss of Caesar.

Alas for me, wretched man!

Now, now the rivers of tears do not cease,

for the world laments Charlemagne’s death.

Alas for me, wretched man!

The common father of all orphans,

of foreigners, widows, and virgins.

Alas for me, wretched man!

The tomb inscribed with titles covers

the serene emperor Charlemagne.

Alas for me, wretched man!

Christ, who governs the hosts of heaven,

grant Charlemagne rest in your kingdom.

Alas for me, wretched man!

All the faithful and believing ask this;

the holy elders, widows, and virgins ask this.

Alas for me, wretched man!

May the Holy Spirit, who governs all things,

raise his soul to rest.

Alas for me, wretched man!

Woe to you, Rome, and to the Roman people,

having lost the supreme and glorious Charlemagne.

Alas for me, wretched man!

Woe to you, beautiful Italy alone,

and to all your noble cities.

Alas for me, wretched man!

France, having suffered a terrible injury,

has never yet endured such grief.

Alas for me, wretched man!

When she delivered the eloquent Augustus, Charlemagne,

to the earth in the soil of Aachen.

Alas for me, wretched man!

A dreadful night has now brought me dreams,

and the bright day has brought no light.

Alas for me, wretched man!

Which carried the venerable ruler of the Christian peoples of the whole world to death. [The antecedent of *quae* is uncertain in the supplied text.]

Alas for me, wretched man!

O Columbanus, restrain your tears;

pour out prayers to the Lord for him.

Alas for me, wretched man!

The merciful Lord, father of all,

may grant him the most splendid place.

Alas for me, wretched man!

O God of the entire human host,

and Lord of heaven and of hell,

Alas for me, wretched man!

Receive the devout Charlemagne, O Christ,

in the holy seat with your apostles.

Alas for me, wretched man!

## In the Year of the Lord 850  
### Christian Druthmar, monk of Corbie

## Historical Notice from Fabricius

*(Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis.)*

Christian of Aquitaine [Note: Sigebertus, chapter 72], a monk of Corbie, of the Benedictine order [Note: Trithemius, chapter 280, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, and II, 67, *On Illustrious Benedictines*], of the congregation of Fleury, is distinguished by Cangius, without justification, from the grammarian Christian Druthmar. He wrote a *Commentary Worthy of Reading* [Note: See Richard Simon, book III of the *Critical History of the New Testament*, chapter 26, pp. 370 ff.] on the Gospel of Matthew, divided into sixty-one chapters, for the monks of the monasteries of Stavelot [Note: Stavelot in the Ardennes, in the diocese of Liège. See Labbe, volume I, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, p. 753] and Malmedy, the monasteries of Saint Peter, situated under one abbot in the diocese of Liège.

Jacob Wimpheling first published his epitomes on Luke and John from manuscript codices, with a privilege of the emperor Maximilian prefixed and the insignia of Leo X placed on the first page, at Strasbourg in 1514, folio. The edition also included the judgment of Jacob Oessler, Doctor of Both Laws, censor and general superintendent of the printing art throughout the Roman Empire.

This edition was by no means fabricated by Edmund Albertinus [Note: See Albertinus, *On the Holy Eucharist*, pp. 933 and 861], but is found in libraries: in France, in Dallaeus [Note: Johann Rudolph Westenius, p. 79, on Origen *Against the Marcionites*, testifies that he compared the Wimpheling edition from beginning to end with the Molther edition, and that Molther had corrupted nothing, but had used another manuscript and presented certain variant readings to the reader, while altering nothing in the substance]; in England, in John Tenison [Note: Cave, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under the year 480]; and in Germany, in Johann Ludolph Tunemann [Note: *Acta Eruditorum*, volume ten, Supplement, p. 382].

It has also been discovered and attested that the same material is found in that older edition published at Haguenau in 1530, octavo, by Menard Molther and Johann Secerius. Although Sixtus of Siena, book VI of the *Sacred Library*, note 112, cites certain passages from a Franciscan manuscript at Lyon that are read differently from the Haguenau edition, it is established that the same material was reproduced in the Paris, Cologne, and most recent Lyon *Libraries of the Fathers*, volume XV, p. 165. Labbe attributes that edition to Johann Oecolampadius, volume I, p. 222, but retracts this on p. 751.

The same printer’s error causes him to call Molther “Moltser” and Secerius “Senerius.”

Druthmar declares that he strove “to follow the historical sense more than the spiritual; for it seems unreasonable to me to seek a spiritual interpretation in some book while completely ignoring the historical sense, since history is the foundation of all understanding and must first be sought and embraced, and without it one cannot pass perfectly to another [sense].”

He also devoted himself to brevity and clarity, since, in his judgment, “it is foolish talk in the exposition of a book to speak in such a way that it becomes necessary to seek an expositor for the exposition itself.”

He says that he wrote on Matthew because he saw that Jerome had passed over many words as though they were insignificant. “If it pleases you,” he says, “I shall turn my hand to the Gospel of John,” which Augustine, following the eagle—that is, blessed John—approached as he walked above the clouds, leaving many things untouched as though they were known to all. “For in Mark it is not necessary to turn my hand to the work after blessed Bede. In Luke also, I hear that the same Bede worked after Saint Ambrose. But so far I have been unable to find in his exposition anything except certain homilies. If I do not find it, and if the encouragement of all of you is present, I shall attempt to labor on this also.”

It is useful to mention the date of this Druthmar. Learned men commonly place him after the middle of the ninth century, because in chapter 56 he mentions the Bulgarians as having been brought to the rites of Christ and being accustomed to be baptized daily [Note: Chapter 56 on Matthew, volume XV of the *Library of the Fathers*, p. 158: “We no longer know of any nations under heaven among whom there are no Christians. For even among Gog and Magog, peoples of the Huns whom they call Khazars, there are Christians. One nation among those whom Alexander had led, the stronger of them, has been circumcised and observes the whole of Judaism. The Bulgarians too, who are likewise among the nations, are baptized daily.”]. Cedrenus says that this occurred from the year 845; Leo the Grammarian, p. 462, from the year 857; and the author of the *Life of Basil the Macedonian*, chapter 65, p. 164, more plausibly around the year 870.

This passage of Druthmar should also be noted, volume XV of the *Library of the Fathers*, p. 169, on Matthew 27:7, “the potter’s field”:

> “It was then used for the burial of foreigners, and now that same place is called the hospice of the Franks, where in the time of Charles he possessed estates, that king granting it out of love for Charles. Now they live solely from the alms of Christians, both the monks themselves and those who come.”

But Druthmar himself seems to have to be assigned altogether to the waning eleventh century and to the time of Gregory VII [Note: Learned men who have dealt with our Druthmar unanimously disagree with this assertion of Fabricius: Sigebertus, Trithemius, Sixtus of Siena, Cave, and finally the authors of the *Literary History of France* judge him to be nearly two centuries earlier, that is, to be assigned approximately to the middle of the ninth century. We follow them. EDITOR.].

For if he is the same person as our Christian Druthmar, the anonymous writer of Melk identifies him with Guidmundus in chapter 102, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*:

> “Guidmundus, also called Christian, was first a monk in the monastery of Stavelot. When he was about to be made abbot and sent to govern another place, he fled. Seeking an unknown province so that he could not be recognized, he changed his name for the better, taking the name of Christian, which is common to all the faithful. At last, when he was sought and found under Gregory VII, he was made bishop of Aversa [Note: Compare Ughelli, volume I of *Sacred Italy*, p. 488], and he wrote for the brothers of the monastery mentioned above an outstanding explanation of the Gospel according to Matthew. In the prologue of that explanation he also promises to write on John. But whether he did not write it at all, or whether he did write it but it has not reached us, is still unknown to us. He nevertheless wrote an explanation of the Gospel according to Luke.”

From this it is clear that he is the same person whom the same anonymous writer of Melk mentions in chapter 90:

> “Christian, bishop of the Apulians”—that is, bishop of Aversa in Apulia—“a man distinguished for learning and holiness, argued most vigorously against the same heresy”—that of the Berengarians.

For this Guidmundus, called Christian by others [Note: See the old writers on the Catholic faith, edited by Peter Francis Chiffletius, p. 365. Another Guidmundus, who was made a cardinal in 1088, is mentioned by Latinius, *Sacred and Profane Library*, volume I, p. 81b], wrote three books against Berengar, *On the Truth of the Body and Blood of Christ in the Eucharist*, addressed to Roger the monk. They were first published by Erasmus in 1530—see his *Letters* XXVIII, 10, London edition—and were afterward reprinted several times in the *Libraries of the Fathers*, including the most recent Lyon edition, volume XVIII. Following those three books, on p. 465, there is also his *Confession concerning the Holy Trinity, the Humanity of Christ, and the Truth of the Lord’s Body and Blood*; and on p. 468, *The Prayer of One Refusing the Episcopate*, addressed to William I, king of England.

Finally, Arnoldus Wion notes that several homilies of Christian Druthmar exist in the *Library of Homilies*, volume I of the *Tree of Life*, p. 410.

## Commentary of Christian Druthmar, Monk of Corbie, on Matthew the Evangelist

*(From the *Library of the Ancient Fathers*, part II of the ninth century.)*

## The Prologue Begins
