To the venerable Fathers in Christ, namesakes of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, in the monasteries of Stavelot, serving God with diligent devotion and striving toward better things: your faithful servant, Christian, an unworthy priest, wishes peace and prosperity in the present age, and in the splendors of the saints fellowship in future eternal blessedness with the King of kings and Judge of the ages.

All words pass away when spoken, and in passing they perish. Therefore words that seem to possess some usefulness must be bound in letters, so that when the idle and frivolous wish to strive toward perfection, they may cast away vanity and again find something by which they can be admonished—something that, in the manner of youth, they once passed over with hurried and deaf ears.

Since I have observed that our young men, after the text of Matthew’s Gospel had been expounded twice, had consigned it to oblivion, I resolved that the exposition itself should be committed to writing in the same form in which I had arranged it in words before you.

If someone asks why I dared to undertake this after blessed Jerome, I reply that I saw blessed Jerome pass over many words as though they were insignificant and make difficult the understanding of simple minds. Therefore what had once seemed difficult to me he made easy for those able to understand.

Moreover, a manner of speech is better understood from those who come from the same province than from someone whose usage has been corrupted. Each province has its own manner of speaking, which another does not possess, and for that reason it is heard more pleasantly.

I also arranged the text itself in clear language, because it is foolish talk in the exposition of a book to speak in such a way that it becomes necessary to seek an expositor for the exposition itself. One ought to speak to another in the way one wishes his words to be understood by the person to whom he speaks, just as the blessed apostle Paul says: “If you were Greek, I ought to speak Greek to you.” To one person, a Greek word; to another, a Latin word.

I strove to follow the historical sense more than the spiritual, because it seems unreasonable to me to seek a spiritual understanding in a book while completely ignoring the historical sense. History is the foundation of all understanding; it must first be sought and embraced, and without it one cannot pass perfectly to another understanding.

I shall compel no unwilling person either to read or to possess this book; let whoever wishes do so. If someone detests it, let him arrange something better, and I shall willingly accept it. For this work harms no one.

In this undertaking I obeyed my friends; by my own choice my enemies will not touch it, lest rivalries arise concerning a good work.

If, therefore, I see that this first work pleases you, I shall turn my hand to the Gospel of John, because Augustine, following the eagle—that is, blessed John, who was compared to an eagle—walks above the clouds, while John walks near the clouds. For this reason a humble expositor, proceeding close to the earth, is necessary for those of simple understanding, so that they may understand what the other leaves untouched as though it were known to everyone.

For in Mark it is not necessary to turn my hand to the work after blessed Bede. In Luke also, I hear that the same Bede worked after Saint Ambrose. But so far I have been unable to find in his entire exposition anything except certain homilies of his. If I do not find it, and if the encouragement of all of you is present, I shall attempt to labor on this also, provided I hope that it will be pleasing to you.

Above all people, your fellowship is dearer to me, because it is sincere and without deceit, and because it was taught by God and preserved by his holy apostles and handed down by them for posterity to preserve. There is no gall of bitterness among you, nor the jealousy of iniquity, but firm faith and inviolable charity toward God and neighbor.

Although you lack earthly possessions, you are nevertheless filled with virtues, so that whoever has known you perfectly cannot afterward be separated from you in affection. If someone has stayed with you for even a short time, he will certainly understand that God dwells with you and that the Holy Spirit governs your works.

For an evil man will not dwell long among you, nor will he remain in your fellowship. Just as gold and silver cast off impurities in the furnace of testing, so whoever comes among you will either cease from evil works or certainly be excluded from your fellowship.

Those who live among you should not be greatly surprised that very many saints have been found worthy in these monasteries. They will certainly discover that whoever is not good among you will undoubtedly be good nowhere else, since you are those who have truly heard the voice of the Lord saying: “Be wise as serpents and simple as doves.”

And if kings and princes and the common people had truly recognized you and loved you as true disciples of Christ, you would be honored and loved above all men.

May Christ, your guardian, who began to guard you forever, grant that you remain steadfast in the good work you have conceived until the end of your life.

## CHAPTER I  
### The Commentary of Christian Druthmar on the Gospel According to Matthew Begins

The evangelist did not give this title—that is, the interpreter who interpreted the book itself. Matthew gave his book the title *Book of the Generation*, according to the custom of the Jews, for whom he was writing and who were accustomed to give their books names from their beginnings.

Thus there is *Genesis*, that is, “generation,” because it is written there: “These are the generations of heaven and earth.” Likewise there is *Exodus*, that is, “departure,” and *Numbers,” and the remaining books.

Similarly, because blessed Matthew first wrote about the Lord’s generation, he gave his book the name *Book of the Generation*. “Begins” means “commences.” It is a compound word formed from the preposition *in* and the verb *capio*, “I take,” with *a* changed into *i*.

“Gospel” is a Greek word and is said in Latin to mean “good news”: *eu*, “good”; *angelion*, “message.” Hence the word “angel” is also used. It must nevertheless be understood that among the Greeks it is written with two gammas: “angel” likewise with two gammas, as Priscian also says. But because this seemed harsh among us, in Latin the first syllable is written with *n* and the second with *g*. The *u* is not to be joined with *a*, but with *e*, because *eu* means “good.”

At the beginning of every book three things must be sought: time, place, and person. The same three things must be observed concerning this Gospel.

The place was Judea, where it was written in the Hebrew language for the Hebrews who believed in Christ.

The time was that of the emperor Gaius, who held the sole monarchy of the entire world at Rome.

The person was Matthew. By birth he was a Levite, and by dignity he was a priest. His name, interpreted in our language, means “given.” He was called this by a worthy prophecy, because he was appointed and given in God’s presence to recount the deeds of Christ, who many ages earlier had been shown by the prophets in the form of a man.

Since he was going to narrate the deeds that our Lord performed in the flesh according to his human nature, he therefore appeared in the likeness of a man.

Mark also appeared in the form of a lion, because he began his Gospel with the action characteristic of a lion, whose nature it is to roar in the desert. For he said: “The voice of one crying in the wilderness.”

Luke likewise appeared in the likeness of the face of a calf, because he began with the one who was accustomed to offer calves frequently, namely the priest Zechariah.

John, however, flying in the manner of an eagle, sought in the Word the one who sits above the stars, saying: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word,” and so forth.

It must also be asked why, although we read that many Gospels had been arranged and written in the names of two apostles and also of other teachers, as Luke relates, God chose none of them to be read or received in his Church except these four—neither more nor fewer.

These four Gospels were ordained by God on account of the four regions of the world and were shown by the prophets many ages earlier. They were called living creatures because the Gospel is preached for the soul of man.

They were therefore foretold as full of eyes before and behind, within and without, because they narrated both the deeds of the Lord in the present and the future judgment to come.

They are said to have straight legs because nothing crooked is found in the Gospels.

There was a wheel within a wheel because the Gospel is supported by the Old Testament. Whatever the Gospel announces was foretold in the Old Testament, and the two agree with one another.

When it says, “Wherever the impulse of the spirit was, there they went,” it shows that the Evangelists narrated nothing other than what the Spirit poured forth in their hearts.

The forms of these living creatures also correspond to the Lord: he became a man by being born, a calf by dying, a lion by rising again, and an eagle by ascending.

Because these four Gospels were so ordered by God and shown long beforehand, the Catholic Church rejects the ravings of other false teachers and receives these four, in the likeness of the four rivers that flow from one spring in paradise—just as these four flow from the mouth of the Lord Jesus Christ.

By Gihon, which is said to mean “earthly,” Matthew is signified, because he narrated Christ’s earthly deeds.

By Tigris, which is interpreted as “swiftness,” Mark is signified, because he set forth the Lord’s deeds rapidly.

By Euphrates, which is interpreted as “fruitfulness,” Luke is signified, because he recounts the Lord’s deeds more fully and broadly.

By Pishon, which may be called “breathing” or “inspiration,” John is signified, because, more excellently inspired by the Holy Spirit, he touched upon the Lord’s dignity.

Just as these four rivers water the whole world, so the four Gospels water the whole Church.

Many mysteries are found in Holy Scripture that make this number sacred. There are four elements by which the world subsists: heaven, earth, fire, and water.

By water, Mark is signified, who said: “The voice of one crying in the wilderness.”

By earth, Matthew is signified, who said: “The book of the generation.”

By fire, Luke is signified, who says: “Was not our heart burning within us?”

By heaven, John is signified, who passed beyond all creatures, saying: “In the beginning was the Word.”

Man consists of the four elements mentioned above.

Adam has a name composed of four letters, which are the beginnings of the four regions of the world. In the Greek language, *a*, alpha, *anatolē*, that is, “east”; *d*, delta, *dysis*, that is, “west.” Likewise *a*, *arktos*, that is, “north”; *m*, *mesēmbria*, that is, “south.”

Noah’s ark is read to have been made square from wood.

The Ark of the Testament was carried by four golden rings, and by four poles covered with gold. The four Gospels are signified by these. The ark signifies the Church; the poles signify the teachers.

Just as the poles were surrounded by rings, so priests learned in the Old and New Testaments and in the four Gospels defend the Church against heresies.

The linen vessel that Peter saw signifies the Church. The four corners by which it was lowered signify the four Gospels. It contained clean and unclean animals because the Church is gathered from all nations.

This number four was also sacred among the pagans, because it stands solid on every side, or because of the four virtues: prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice.

Why did it please the Lord that two apostles should be evangelists and two disciples of disciples? So that he might show himself to be the one who chose the sons of Jacob as a people specially belonging to him, gathered and born from two wives and two concubines.

As they are arranged, so they were published.

The first is Matthew’s Gospel, because it was produced in the time of Gaius.

The second is Mark’s, which was written at Rome in the Greek language during the time of Claudius.

The third is Luke’s, in Achaea, in Greek expression.

The fourth is John’s, in Asia, in the city of Ephesus, likewise in Greek, during the time of the emperor Nerva.

Because the Romans, who ruled the whole world, spoke Greek, and because among all nations they had Romans who held the lands, those three therefore wrote in Greek. Greek itself is also considered more sonorous than all languages.

The order of the Gospels may perhaps be arranged this way so that one apostle stands at the beginning and another at the end, and so that the two placed between them receive authority from those two.

Nevertheless, I saw a book of the Gospel written in Greek that was said to have belonged to Saint Hilary, in which Matthew and John came first and the other two afterward. I asked Euphenius the Greek why this was so. He said to me: “It is in the likeness of a good farmer who first yokes the stronger oxen that he has.”

Each Gospel has three titles. The first shows which canon it is, and the canons rise to ten, no higher.

The second contains the harmony of the Evangelists. Of these, Matthew has 300 and 55; Mark, 200 and 34; Luke, 300 and 42; John, 100 and 31.

The third is proper to each Gospel and shows in what order the sayings are found in that Gospel. Of these, Matthew has 81, Mark 47, Luke 79, and John 14.

Three kinds of philosophy existed among all wise men, and these too are found in divine Scripture: namely, physics, ethics, and logic—that is, natural, moral, and rational philosophy.

In physics, that is, in natural science, there is the order of inquiry through the nature and constitution of things. The wise men also divided physics into four disciplines: arithmetic, geometry, music, and astronomy. They are called numerical, mensural, cantilene-bearing, and sidereal, because these arts are natural to us, and without them the world cannot exist, nor can we know anything good.

They likewise divided ethics, that is, moral philosophy, into four virtues: prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance. The wise men instructed each person to shape his conduct according to these virtues and to strive, as far as possible, to be prudent concerning divine and human matters. Within prudence there should be justice, and first there should be strength of spirit, so that whether adversity or prosperity befell him, he would always remain tranquil in the same manner: adversity would not cast him down, nor prosperity lift him into pride. After all these things, and in all these things, he should maintain temperance—in prudence, justice, and [Col. 1266D] fortitude—so that he exceeded the proper measure in none of them.

They also divided logic, that is, rational philosophy, into three divisions: grammar, rhetoric, and dialectic. Thus a person would first seek natural and moral causes through reason, and then, by learning and disputing, would be able to know more about moral and heavenly causes. All these definitions are also found in the divine Scriptures.

Physics, that is, natural philosophy, is found in Genesis: each person should, according to the law of nature, do for his neighbor what he would wish done for himself, and should not do to another what he would not wish to suffer. Moral philosophy is found in Proverbs: “Fear the Lord and observe his commandments”; for this is the whole human being. Logic is found in the Song of Songs, because everything said there about the bridegroom and bride is rationally and logically interpreted as referring to the Lord and his Church.

There is also a place in Scripture where each of these kinds of wisdom is found separately, a place where only two are found, and a place where all three are found. To give one example, so that it will be enough to seek the others in the same manner from what we said above: in the case of Adam sleeping, according to history and physics this happened as it is written; but according to logic we must understand Christ sleeping on the cross, that is, dying, since the dead are also called “sleeping,” as Paul says: “We do not want you to be ignorant concerning those who sleep.” And just as Adam’s wife was formed while Adam slept, so the Church was formed while Christ was dying.

An example of all three is found in Noah. According to physics, because he did the Lord’s will, the Lord rescued him from the destruction of the ungodly. According to ethics, whoever strives to order his conduct in this way will be delivered from the future destruction that will overtake the ungodly. According to logic, that is, rational interpretation, Noah signifies Christ and the ark signifies the Church. In Noah’s three sons are represented the whole human race—those who believed in the Trinity and strove to belong to its number. Therefore, wherever these interpretations occur, we shall explain them and bring them to knowledge insofar as the Lord grants this.

The word *liber* (“book”) is used in two ways. A free person is called *liber* from freedom, that is, released from servitude; and something free from another thing is also called *liber*, which in Greek is *eleutheros*. The inner part of the bark of a tree is also called *liber*. Among the ancients, before parchment was invented, books were made from this material; from that usage it descended that books are called by this name even when they are made of another material, parchment or papyrus. Hence Virgil says of it: “The bark adheres to the elm.” This word is also a synonym: a *volumen* is so called from *volvere*, “to roll,” and a *codex* is so called as if from *caudex*, “trunk.”

“Generation.” This word is derived from the Greek [the supplied text is corrupt here: “ι, η”]. From it come *genus* and the expression “the generation of Judah,” because those who are generated are from the earth.

“Jesus.” *Jesus* is a Hebrew name and is rendered in Latin as “Savior” or “one who will save.” Moses first gave this name to Joshua when he returned victorious from battle. Yet it is written with all the letters, whereas this form is written with three letters—iota, long eta, and sigma—to signify that the Trinity cannot be contained or explained by letters, but is ineffable. Alternatively, it is written with iota, sigma, and an accent above, to indicate what we have said above. If it is in the nominative case, it is written in this way; if it is in another case, a *u* must be written at the end. The Greeks do not join the iota to the eta, but pronounce them separately, so that the iota is always a vowel; for it is pronounced *Iesus*.

“Christ” is a Greek name and is interpreted in Latin as “anointed”; in Hebrew it is called *Messiah*. Latin did not formerly possess this name, although it could have possessed it. Among the Jewish people priests and kings were called by this name, because they were anointed with chrism when they were ordained. Hence it is said concerning them in the Psalms: “Do not touch my christs.”

Just as in the Roman empire everyone was called Caesar or Augustus after Julius and Octavian, who were the first to bear those names, so all those Jewish kings are called christs. Hence David said concerning Saul: “I will not lay my hand upon the Lord’s christ.” When the term refers to the Lord, it is written with chi, rho, sigma, and an accent above, so that here it signifies what we said concerning the name Jesus: that it is ineffable.

The same applies to *God* and *Lord*: when the word refers to a human being, it is written out in letters; when it refers to God, it should be written in contracted form, because no name can properly be applied to God that is capable of displaying his majesty. Christ our Lord was not anointed with bodily oil or chrism, but spiritually, as it is written: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness.” He did not wish to possess an earthly kingdom except in the manner in which he now possesses it with the Father in power; therefore he did not wish to be anointed with temporal oil.

“Sons of David.” Sons are spoken of in four ways: first, by nature, as Isaac was the son of Abraham. Second, by imitation: the Jews are called sons of the devil because they imitate him, as the Lord says to them: “You are from your father the devil”; and again: “Whose works you do, his son you will also be called.” Third, by adoption, as Esther was called the daughter of Mordecai. Fourth, by teaching, as Paul says: “Through the Gospel I begot you.”

“David.” David is said to mean “strong of hand,” because he overcame Goliath. Abraham is said to mean “father of many,” with “nations” understood—one who would become the father of many nations through faith. Why, then, is he called the son of these men? Because the promise concerning Christ was made to them. To Abraham it was said: “In your seed all the nations will be blessed.” To David: “I will place upon your throne the fruit of your womb.”

Why did he place David first and Abraham afterward? Because among that people no one was more excellent than David. And because he was going to narrate and repeat Abraham in the order of the genealogy, he therefore placed David first and Abraham afterward, so that he could say: “Abraham begot Isaac.” He is called their son because not only those begotten by a father are called sons, but also those who belong to the same lineage. Thus all Jews are called the sons of Israel, and all Saracens the sons of Ishmael.

“Sons of Abraham.” There is no need to say anything about Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, because you know who they were, how justly they lived, and how they prefigured the Lord in their actions.

“Abraham begot Isaac.” Abraham signified the Lord the Father; Isaac, the Lord Jesus Christ. Just as Abraham offered his son, so the Lord offered his Son to be sacrificed for us. And just as Isaac was not sacrificed, but a ram was offered in his place, so it was not the divinity that suffered, but the humanity—the body, namely, which dwelt among sinners like a ram among thorns.

Isaac is interpreted as “laughter,” because his mother laughed when it was promised that he would be born.

“Jacob begot Judah and his brothers.” Jacob is interpreted as “supplanter,” and he himself bore the figure of the Lord, having twelve sons just as the Lord afterward had twelve disciples, as though twelve sons.

“Judah begot Phares and Zarah by Tamar.” Judah is interpreted as “confessor” or “one who confesses,” because his mother said when she gave birth to him: “Now I will confess to the Lord.” Therefore he is called one who confesses or a confessor. He and his brothers also prefigured the Lord.

“Judah begot Phares and Zarah by Tamar.” It must be asked why sinful women are mentioned in the Lord’s genealogy, while righteous women such as Sarah and Rebecca, and the many others who were there, including the mother of David and Jehoshaphat, are not. Those sinful women are included so that it may be shown that the one whose genealogy is being given came because of sinners, just as he himself said: “I did not come to call the righteous, but sinners,” and so that no sinner would despair of turning to the Lord.

Nevertheless, those women should not be excessively blamed if someone carefully considers their circumstances. Tamar, considered according to the literal sense, preserved excellent fidelity to her deceased husband: she waited for his brother for a long time and did not marry another. When she saw that he was not given to her, she did not seek a son from another family, but from the very one from whom she had had her husband. She did not do this with Judah until after Judah’s wife had died.

At that time everyone desired to have children, because the world was empty, and each person wanted peoples and kingdoms to be called his own, since virginity and widowhood had not yet been commanded. She sought nothing further than to conceive; therefore she is not as despicable as many judge her to be.

Tamar is interpreted as “palm” or “bitterness.” “Palm” refers to the saints who arose from her lineage, concerning whom it is written: “The righteous will flourish like a palm.” “Bitterness” suits her because she quickly lost her husband. She also bore children who mystically prefigured the peoples, namely the Jewish and gentile peoples.

Zarah is interpreted as “rising” or “dawn,” because many saints came from her. Phares is interpreted as “division,” and from him the Pharisees received their name.

“Phares begot Esron.” Esron is interpreted as “he saw an arrow,” that is, he foretold Christ’s coming in the flesh. The devil was wounded by that arrow.

“Esron begot Aram.” Aram means “exalted,” signifying in his name the Lord Jesus Christ, of whom the prophet says that he was regarded as exalted. The Psalmist likewise says: “The Lord is exalted above all nations, and his glory is above the heavens.” And again: “Who is like the Lord our God, who dwells on high?” and so forth.

“Aram begot Aminadab.” Aminadab is said to mean “my spirit is spontaneous,” and in this name the Lord Jesus is signified, who was born in the world by the spontaneous will of his spirit.

“Aminadab begot Naason.” Naason is interpreted as “serpentine,” and the Lord was prefigured by him, as he himself said: “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so it is necessary for the Son of Man to be lifted up.”

“Naason begot Salmon.” Salmon is said to mean “peace,” and in his name he manifests the Lord, who is our peace and who reconciled the things that were in heaven and on earth, destroying enmity in himself.

“Salmon begot Boaz by Rahab.” Rahab is interpreted as “ascending.” In her the Church from the nations is prefigured, the Church that would ascend from the washing of baptism, made clean and immaculate from its former errors. She should not be excessively blamed, but praised, because through receiving the spies she foresaw salvation for herself and strove to unite herself to the people of God, just as the Church afterward came from the nations.

This Salmon was a prince of Judea, who was commanded, with the others, to number the people in the wilderness.

Boaz means “in whom there is strength,” or “in fortitude.” By these names, who is more fittingly expressed than our Lord Jesus, who is the power of God the Father? He also acted in strength, because he rose from the dead like a lion and broke the bars of hell.

“Boaz begot Obed by Ruth.” Here Ruth, a foreigner, is mentioned, because although she was a foreigner, she nevertheless possessed good faith. She abandoned her gods, sought the God of the Hebrews, and served him. For love of her husband she left her parents and clung to her husband’s parents. She did not join herself to worse people or wander about, but joined herself legitimately to better people, without acting wantonly. Hence she was called a woman of virtue.

Ruth is also interpreted as “hastening,” so that by her name she signifies the Church. Boaz prefigures Christ, who was to receive a bride from the nations.

“Obed begot Jesse.” Obed is said to mean “serving,” in whom the one who said, “The Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve,” is signified.

Jesse had two names; he was also called Isai. Jesse means “opening,” announcing in his name the one of whom it is written: “He opened their understanding, so that they might understand the Scriptures.” Isai is also said to mean “sacrifice” or “incense,” plainly showing that the one would come who would make himself a sacrifice for many, as a fragrant offering.

“David the king begot Solomon by her who had been Uriah’s wife.” Here too a sinful woman is mentioned, to show that he was born from human beings for the sake of sinners. Uriah was a foreigner; he was not one of the Jews. Although he was good, he expressed the type of the devil, to whose marriage the Church had previously been joined, before Christ desired her when he saw her washing—that is, cleansing herself from the filth of the world through the water of the bath.

There is no need to say anything else about those who are now inserted in the middle, because their history—who they were and what they did—is known from the Books of Kings. It is enough to give the interpretations of their names.

David is interpreted as “strong of hand,” because he threw a stone from a sling with his hand and killed Goliath. In this deed he signifies the Lord Christ, who conquered the devil through his endurance. David suffered Saul’s persecutions, just as Christ suffered those of the Jews. Just as David was abandoned and betrayed by his counselor, so Christ was betrayed by his disciple Judas. And just as David was driven from the kingdom by his son, so the Lord was expelled by the Jewish people: he was called his son by adoption, cast outside the city of Jerusalem, and killed. This is also said because the same Lord Christ proceeded from David’s stock.

Solomon is interpreted as “peaceful.” He prefigured the Lord by the peace he possessed in his kingdom, because the Lord is our peace and our peacemaker. It was said of him: “In his days justice will arise, and abundance of peace, until the moon is lifted up.” And because Solomon built a house for the Lord, so the Lord built the heavenly Jerusalem from living stones.

“Roboam begot Abia.” Roboam is interpreted as “breadth of the people,” but by antiphrasis, that is, by contrariety. Among grammarians there is a mode called antiphrasis, when a thing is other than its name sounds—for example, something is called “fair” because it is anything but fair. Thus here too “breadth” is said by contrariety, because ten tribes defected from him, and the kingdom of Judah was thereby narrowed under him.

Abia is interpreted as “the Father is Lord.” The *b* must not be joined to the *i*: *ab* stands by itself, and *ia* by itself, the latter being the name of the Lord. He was rightly called by this name because he recognized that the Lord was the Father of his creation and salvation.

“Abia begot Asa.” Asa is interpreted as “grieving” or “lifting up.”

“Asa begot Jehoshaphat.” Jehoshaphat means “the judgment of the Lord,” and he clung to the Lord.

“Jehoshaphat begot Joram.” This is the Jehoshaphat who joined himself to Ahab, the wicked king, and went with him to war, where he ought to have died, because against the Lord’s will he was his ally. For this he was rebuked by the prophet, because he offered Ahab assistance. He also made ships to go to Ezion-geber with Ahab’s ships, but by the Lord’s will they were broken. Understanding this, Jehoshaphat thereafter wished to join his ships with Ahab’s.

“Joram begot Uzziah.” He was not his son but his grandson; nevertheless, those who come from a distant lineage are called someone’s sons. Joram begot Ahaziah; Ahaziah, Joash; Joash, Amaziah; Amaziah, Uzziah. But because Joram had taken Jezebel’s daughter—she who killed Naboth and persecuted Elijah, the prophets, and the priests of the Lord, as well as his worship—therefore, because they were born from her offspring, they are removed from the Lord’s genealogy up to the third generation.

The evangelist also intended to set out three orders: one before the Law, in the time of the patriarchs; another under the age of the prophets; and a third under the rule of the priests. Thus there are three groups of fourteen. This is expressed by the printed Greek phrase τρὲς τέσσαρες καὶ δέκαδες, followed by the Latin *tres tessares et tres decades*, “three fours and three tens”; the text continues, “that is, four, and ten, and seven.” The intended sense appears to be three groups of fourteen, although the transmitted wording is corrupt, because of the number seven, which belongs to the Sabbath: seven and seven make fourteen.

Just as the children of Israel came to the promised land under Moses through forty-two encampments, so we too, under the leadership of the Lord who comes to us through these stages, will reach eternal life.

Matthew, who narrated the Lord’s earthly genealogy, shows how he descended from heaven through an earthly genealogy. Luke, following a distinctive order, shows how all those who strive to be incorporated into his members will ascend into heaven.

Therefore this is presented through fifty generations, which signify the rest of the Jubilee; or through seventy-two generations, the number in which the nations are read as having been divided at the beginning, so that it might be shown that believers in Christ from all the nations would ascend into heaven; or, if you wish to count seventy-seven generations, which extend from Christ to Adam, this is the number the Lord established for the remission of sins when he said: “I do not say to you, Peter, seven times, but up to seventy-seven times,” to show that he would forgive all our sins in baptism.

And just as no generation was passed over without being counted from Adam to Christ himself, so there is no sin that is not forgiven in baptism. Under this example we are instructed to forgive those who sin against us seventy-seven times.

Matthew, however, shows the labor of the struggle that the Lord and his saints would have through the forty-two generations, which prefigured the labors in the wilderness.

Joram means “exalted.” This too is by antiphrasis, because he was cast down on account of Ahab and Jezebel.

Uzziah means “the strength of the Lord,” and he was rightly called this because he trusted in the Lord and did what pleased him, except that he wished to offer sacrifices by himself, which was a sacramental matter. For this he was struck with leprosy and lived apart from himself, in a house separated from the city and the people. He had two names.

“Uzziah begot Jotham.” Jotham means “perfect.” The etymology is beautiful and fitting for him, since he was perfect before the Lord and built the gate of the temple.

“Ahaz begot Hezekiah.” Ahaz means “grasping,” with “all wickedness” understood, because he abandoned the Lord, saw the altar in Damascus, worshiped it, and ordered a similar one to be made in Jerusalem. Behold: a wicked father begot a good son.

Hezekiah is called “the strength of the Lord,” because he was seen to be in the Lord. In his days the Lord killed 185,000 Assyrians, and Sennacherib fled from his land with ten men. He was killed by his sons while worshiping Nesroch, his god, and saying: “Why did you let me flee in this way from Judea? I would even have sacrificed my sons to you if you had commanded it.” When his sons heard this, they killed him, fearing that he would kill them for such a vow, and they fled to Mount Ararat.

“Hezekiah begot Manasseh.” Manasseh means “forgetful,” because through many crimes he forgot the Lord, to such an extent that he passed his son through the fire to demons. Once again a good father begot a wicked son. Nevertheless, afterward the Lord accepted his prayers because of his father and freed him from Babylon, where he had been led captive because of his sins.

“Manasseh begot Amon.” Amon means “faithless.” *Ammon*, with two *m*s, means “son of my people”; with one *m*, it means “faithless.” He is called faithless because he departed from the way of the Lord.

“Amon begot Josiah.” Josiah means “where is the incense of the Lord.” He was rightly called this because he served the Lord worthily, destroyed idols and the worshipers of idols, and celebrated the Lord’s Passover magnificently.

“Josiah begot Jechoniah.” Jechoniah means “the preparation of the Lord.” Here Jechoniah is understood as the first father; the Jechoniah after the transmigration was his son. He is also called Joachim: the first is written with *c*, *h*, and *m*; the second with *c* and *n*. The first Joachim means “the preparation of the Lord”; the second means “the preparation of God.”

If we count only one Jechoniah, there will be only thirteen generations. But the correct account is this: the first Jechoniah was the one whom the king of Egypt appointed king. Then Nebuchadnezzar came against him and exacted an oath and tribute from him. Because he lied to him, Nebuchadnezzar killed him and ordered his body to be thrown into the street.

But the son of this man was the one whom Nebuchadnezzar encountered before he came to Jerusalem, together with his mother and wife. Nebuchadnezzar granted him benefits in his land and handed him over to his brother Zedekiah. Because Zedekiah lied concerning the oath he had sworn to Nebuchadnezzar, Nebuchadnezzar came again to Jerusalem, seized him, killed his sons before his eyes, tore out his eyes, and put him in a cave like a wild beast, because his prophets had told him that he should be like a lion. He took him to Babylon, put him in prison, and left him there until Nebuchadnezzar himself died. There he also had his nephew Evil-merodach with him, whom he had found in the kingdom when he himself returned from among the beasts.

It is also written of him that Evil-merodach lifted Joachim’s head from prison, spoke kindly with him, gave him estates, and established food for him at his table, because they had been companions in prison.

When it says “his brothers,” this refers to one whom the king of Egypt, Necho, joined to him and took to Egypt. Another was Eliakim, who reigned in Judea when Nebuchadnezzar first came to Jerusalem, when he plundered that land three times and removed three kings from it: the one I have just mentioned, Eliakim, whom Necho had appointed after killing his brother; another whom he led out with his mother; and the third, Zedekiah.

The transmigration took place in Babylon because they were compelled by Nebuchadnezzar to migrate from their own land to Babylon.

“Salathiel begot Zerubbabel.” Salathiel means “the petition of the Lord.” He is rightly called the Lord’s petition, to show that all the ancient fathers petitioned the Lord to come for the redemption of the human race.

“Zerubbabel begot Abiud.” This is the Zerubbabel who guarded King Ahasuerus while he was sleeping, together with two others. They said to one another: “Let each of us state an opinion, and it will become clear who gives the better opinion.” One said: “The king is strongest under heaven.” Another said: “Wine is strongest under heaven.” The third, Zerubbabel, said: “Truth is stronger, and women.”

The king rose and approved this answer before his men, because Zerubbabel had spoken the better opinion. Then he gave him authority over all the Jews who were in his kingdom and permission to return to Jerusalem with all the Jews.

Thus *zo* means “this,” *ro* means “teacher,” and *Babel* means “of Babylon”: “this teacher from Babylon.” He signifies the Lord Christ, because Babylon is called “confusion” and signifies this world. The Lord Christ is its author and teacher, and he leads his people out into the promised land, that is, into eternal life.

Of those who come in the middle and were in captivity, we have no written account of what they did. We shall only give the interpretations of their names.

“Abiud begot Eliakim.” Abiud means “strength of the father.” Through him the Lord Christ is shown, who is the power of God through which all things were made. The *ab* must stand by itself, because *ab* means “father.”

Eliakim is interpreted as “resurrection,” because he signified the one through whom the whole world will rise again.

“Eliakim begot Azor.” Azor is interpreted as “helper,” prefiguring the one of whom it is written: “A helper in times of need, in tribulation.”

“Azor begot Zadok.” Zadok means “just,” plainly prefiguring the one who is just beyond comparison, of whom the Psalm says: “The Lord is just; he has loved righteousness.”

“Zadok begot Achim.” *Achis*—the form printed in the explanatory sentence, while the heading has *Achim*—means “my brother.” He too prefigures in his name the one who says: “I will announce your name to my brothers.” He who was God in majesty became a brother to the Christian people through humility and resurrection.

“Achim begot Eliud.” Eliud means “God is helper”: *el* stands by itself, and *iud* follows afterward. His name also announces the future Savior, who would be called Emmanuel, that is, “God with us.”

“Eliud begot Eleazar.” Eleazar means “the help of the Lord,” prefiguring the one of whom the Psalm says: “Our help is in the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth.”

“Eleazar begot Nathan.” Nathan means “sweetness” or “satisfying.” It signifies sweetness, prefiguring the one of whom the evangelist later said: “All marveled at the things that were spoken about him.” “Satisfying” also pertains to him, of whom it is written: “The Lord satisfied five thousand men.”

“Nathan begot Jacob.” Jacob means “supplanter,” and by his name he foretells the Lord, who supplanted vices and raised up virtues.

Concerning those who are placed at the end of the genealogy, we must consider why Matthew says, “Jacob begot Joseph,” while Luke says that Heli begot Joseph. We must know that the Law prescribed that when a brother died without leaving a son, another brother should take his wife, in addition to his own wife, and beget children through his deceased brother’s wife; those who were born were called the sons of the dead brother.

This, then, is the reason for the difference among the evangelists. Matthew, following the natural order, says that Joseph was the son of Jacob. Luke, following the ancient law, says that he was the son of Heli.

Heli means “ascending”; Jacob means “supplanter”; Joseph means “increase.” He too announces the one who was to come, who increased his people, saying: “I have other sheep that are not of this fold; I must bring them also, and they will hear my voice, and there will be one flock and one shepherd.”

“The husband of Mary.” When you hear the word “husband,” search and you will find in Scripture that bridegrooms are also called husbands, and brides wives. It is also the custom of historians to write history according to how something was thought to be at the time when it occurred. Thus it is said of Herod that he was saddened at the request for John’s head—not because he was truly saddened, but because this was what those who saw him thought.

In the third order of the genealogy Christ is the fourteenth, because this genealogy was arranged as a means of catching the devil, like a hook used to catch fish. Just as the hook is hidden at the end in the bait, so the divinity of Christ was hidden beneath the flesh. God the Father sent the hook when he commanded that the Son become incarnate. The devil bit, and was pierced by his divinity—that is, he caused the flesh to be crucified—and he was seized and bound by the very divinity that lay hidden beneath the flesh.

The rod into which the hook was inserted is Abraham, who was the origin of this genealogy.

We have already said why he divided this genealogy into three orders: namely, because of the three periods—before the Law, under the Law and the prophets, and under the priests—or because of the Trinity. The number fourteen is due to the sacred number seven among the Jews because of the Sabbath: seven and seven make fourteen.

“From whom Jesus was born, who is called Christ.” As you know, Matthew wrote the Lord’s Gospel after his ascension into heaven, in the time of Gaius Caligula. Therefore he says that he is called by both names, that is, by those who believe in him.

Why was Joseph’s genealogy narrated, since Christ was not his son? There were four reasons.

First, so that Mary’s origin might be known through Joseph’s genealogy, since they are understood to have belonged to one lineage. It had been commanded that each man take a wife from his own tribe, and Joseph, who was righteous, observed this. This was also apparent from the declaration made during the census. When it was commanded that each person return to his own land and homeland, declare his name and occupation there, and pay the census tax, Joseph and Mary went up from Galilee to Bethlehem to declare their names in their homeland.

Nor is it the custom of Scripture to construct histories around women. Although Adam had many daughters, and Noah and others likewise, Scripture does not report concerning any of them as it does concerning Abel and Cain, Shem, Ham, and Japheth, or, in the Book of Kings: “There was a certain man from Ramathaim Zophim.” The same is true in other histories.

The second reason was that Mary would not be stoned by the Jews if she were without a husband and had a son. The unbelieving Jews would all have stoned her if Joseph had separated himself from her. He preferred that some people doubt the origin of the child rather than that his mother be disgraced by false suspicions or tortured, since she was both delicate and of the weaker sex.

The third reason was that, when going to Egypt or returning from it, the man who was her husband would provide the necessities required by a woman—fire and food—and would carry and bring back the infant on so long a journey.

The fourth reason was that the devil might not know of her birthgiving. If he had known that Christ was born from a virgin, he would never have persuaded the Jews to crucify him. Hence he also investigated this through temptations, to determine whether he was the Son of God. He knew through the Scriptures that he would be born, but he was deceived in this: he thought that he had been born from a woman.

The generation of Christ was therefore as was said above. But why “of Jesus Christ”? Let the angel explain it.

“You will call his name Jesus,” he says. *Christ* is a Greek name, rendered in Latin as “anointed,” and in Hebrew as *Messiah*. Latin did not formerly have this name, although it could have had it, as is now evident.

This name was celebrated among the Jews for as long as their kingdom endured. Just as among many peoples there are titles of dignity that kings and princes possess by succession—for example, among the Egyptians they are called Pharaohs and Ptolemies, and among the Romans Caesars and Augusti—so among the Jews this name also existed.

Thus, from Julius, who was first called Caesar because he was brought forth from his dead mother’s womb after being cut out, all the rest were called Caesars. And from Octavian, whom the Romans, after he had subdued the world, met with a golden shield and precious stones and named Augustus because he had increased their empire, all the rest were called Augusti.

In the same way, because Aaron was anointed priest by Moses at the Lord’s command, all priests are called Messiahs. Likewise, all kings descended from Saul, their first king, who was anointed king by Samuel, are called Messiahs, that is, christs. Hence David said: “I will not lay my hand upon the Lord’s christ,” and in the Psalm: “Do not touch my christs.”

The interpretation of *Messiah* and *Christ* is one and the same. Nevertheless, because the Greek language is more sonorous and more elegant than all the languages under heaven, and also more widely known—especially because of the Romans, who ruled throughout the world, and because the Greeks were wiser than other peoples—the evangelists and interpreters decided to leave that name in the language that was more familiar and more pleasing.

*At the vigil of the Nativity.*
When she was betrothed. “Betrothed man” and “betrothed woman” are derived from *spondere*, “to pledge,” because formerly they pledged to one another guarantees concerning the marriage, gave sureties, and were also formally pledged with a ring. Thus Mary had been betrothed to Joseph, though she had not been joined to him in desire. Why she had been betrothed has been explained above.

His mother. Whose mother? The mother of the immaculate one, the mother of the only-begotten one, who in heaven was born without a mother and on earth without a father. She is called “mother” because something is brought into being from her. Mary is called “illuminer” or “star of the sea,” for she bore the light of the world. In the Syrian language she is called “lady,” and rightly so: she bore the Lord, Savior of the world and ruler of the whole earth.

Before they came together. That is, before the union by which a betrothed man and woman ordinarily come together.

She was found. Clearly, she was found by Joseph himself, who, with what was thought to be the marital authority of a future husband, knew all the secrets of his future wife. It was customary among that people for the man who was to take a wife to betroth her at the temple; afterward, if he was wealthy, he would have his servants remain with her, or, if he was poor, he himself would keep watch over her together with her father and mother until the appointed time.

Accordingly, in this condition she was found by Joseph: pregnant by the Holy Spirit, because he knew for certain that no man had been joined to her in such a way that she could have conceived. Of this woman alone it is written that she had the Holy Spirit in her womb. But she had him both in mind and in her womb. When the expression refers to the Holy Spirit, it is called *ἅγιος πνεῦμα* (*hagios pneuma*, “holy spirit”); when it refers to another spirit, it is called *ὅσιος πνεῦμα* (*hosios pneuma*, “devout” or “sacred spirit”).

Being righteous. This is the Evangelist’s testimony concerning Joseph: he was righteous and established in the perfected law. We may also infer this from the angel’s appearance and from his words: “Do not be afraid.” For if Joseph had regarded her with an evil suspicion, neither would he himself have been righteous, nor would the angel have said, “Do not be afraid,” but rather, “Do not despise her.”

And unwilling to expose her. That is, to defame her, or to bring her forward publicly—literally, to lead her out into the condition in which she then was—and thus to deliver her over to blasphemy.

He wished to dismiss her secretly. If he was righteous and had no evil suspicion of her, why would he wish to dismiss a holy and righteous woman? But he knew that her conduct would be holy, and he considered himself unworthy to approach her, just as blessed Peter acted when he saw the miracle of the fish and said: “Depart from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man.” Or as the centurion, sending messengers to the Lord, said: “I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof, nor did I consider myself worthy to come to you.” So this man too was saying: “Keep her far from me and from my family, because I perceive in her a great mystery.”

While he was considering these things. That is, while he judged himself unworthy to approach her. For if he had been considering something else wickedly, the angel would not have appeared to him. God withdraws from the proud rather than drawing near to them; therefore it is evident that what kept Joseph at a distance was not the contempt of pride but the withdrawal of humility.

Behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream, saying. There are seven kinds of visions through which almighty God spoke before the Incarnation to those to whom he wished to speak.

The first kind is through the bodily ears, as when Moses saw the bush burning and heard the voice of God with his bodily ears, and the whole host of the people of Israel heard the Lord speak the ten words of the law.

The second kind is ecstasy, as happened to Peter when Cornelius sent for him: “A trance fell upon him,” and he saw a linen vessel being lowered from heaven.

The third kind is like that experienced by Nebuchadnezzar when he saw a statue made of metals, or a tree cut down from its roots, and understood nothing.

The fourth is through a cloud, as when God spoke to Job after the affliction.

The fifth is in the heart, as with many holy people, and also with Balaam, when God placed a word in his mouth and Balaam spoke after taking up a parable.

The sixth is the filling of the Holy Spirit, as when he filled the seventy elders in the wilderness.

The seventh is when they saw in dreams and understood in their minds.

Others—and this is more accurate—have said that there are three kinds: one through bodily eyes, as when Abraham and Lot saw angels and spoke with them; another in the heart, as when God spoke to Daniel in his heart about what Belshazzar had seen with bodily eyes but had not understood; and a third in dreams and in the heart, as with Isaiah, all the prophets, and this Joseph. This vision is more excellent than the others.

For it is of no benefit to see with bodily eyes, as Belshazzar saw, unless one also sees with the mind, as Daniel saw the same vision. Similarly, it is of no benefit to see in a dream, as Pharaoh and Nebuchadnezzar saw, unless there is someone who sees in the manner in which Daniel and Joseph saw.

In the same way, therefore, in which God spoke from the beginning to perfected men, he also spoke to this Joseph, because he understood and believed what he saw in the dream. For just as almighty God appointed Gabriel among the other archangels to announce the mystery of our Savior—Gabriel is called “the strength of God”—and we believe that he also spoke to this Joseph, so God appointed perfected men to expound the Incarnation of our Lord. He did not choose to accomplish this through the wealthy, who are usually full of vices, but through the poor, who were full of virtues and perfected in them.

Thus this man alone was judged worthy to become God’s foster-father and the guardian of his mother. And it was fitting that the one who held all human beings under his power should bring the holier and more perfect men near to himself.

Joseph, son of David. He is called a son not only because he belonged to David’s lineage, but also because he imitated David’s faith.

Do not be afraid to take Mary as your wife. Do not tremble; do not judge yourself unworthy to serve him or his mother, because she had been found worthy and appointed to give birth to him, while you were chosen to raise him.

Your namesake Joseph also was found chaste and good, but you are not inferior to him: to you the virginity of his mother and the carrying of the one who was to be born were entrusted. For the present, let her be called your wife, so that you may free her from the persecutions of the Jews. Yet she will be better for you than if you had possessed as many wives as Solomon had.

The one who will be born from her will for a time be called your son, but he is also your Creator, and he will be better for you than if you had had forty sons, as Abdon had. Therefore serve him as Lord of lords and King of kings.

Call her your wife, so that the devil and the Jews may not know that the one who is to be born is born of a virgin. If she is not your wife in the manner of other men, she will nevertheless be your wife so that you may receive a reward: she will receive one for giving birth, and you will receive one for raising the child, in eternal life.

They are called “wives” because of the yoke imposed upon those joined in marriage, or because of the betrothal based on the first pledge, when one still does not know marital intercourse.

For what has been conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit. Joseph is instructed more clearly about what he had previously thought concerning holy Mary—namely, that what he saw in her was from the Holy Spirit.

And she will bear a son. Although what has been conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit, she will nevertheless bear a son—something you have never heard of, that a woman should bear a son from the Holy Spirit.

And you will call his name Jesus. I tell you his name, which existed before the ages. You shall not give him a name according to your own inclination, nor shall his mother do so; instead, call him by the name he possessed before the ages.

Bear witness that he is Savior, because from the beginning he himself saved the whole world. Jesus is a Hebrew name, and the angel of God expressed its etymology and interpretation when he said: “For he himself will save his people from their sins.”

Among us, Jesus is written with iota, eta, and sigma, with a diacritical mark above. In Greek books, however, it is written only with iota and sigma, with a diacritical mark above. And, like the other names of God, it ought to be written in an abbreviated form, because the name of God cannot be fully expressed by letters. When it signifies an ordinary human being, it is written with all the letters.

We ought also to know where this name was first found. It was first given by Moses to the son of Nun, when he returned victorious from the battle against Amalek, into which Moses had sent him with part of the people. Then the rest of the people came out to meet him together with the priests, and gave him this name, so that he was called Joshua—that is, “Savior”—because he had saved the people from Amalek.

Both in his name and in his deed, that Joshua prefigured the Lord. Amalek, whose name is interpreted as “the licking people,” signifies the devil, from whose licking—that is, seduction—he continually frees his people. He is the one who hastens to belong to his own people in mouth and deed, and from whose name Christians are called.

He did not simply say “the people,” but added “his,” meaning those who placed their faith and hope in him.

Now all this took place so that what had been spoken might be fulfilled. That is, these things were foretold because they were going to happen; and they happened so that events might correspond to the words, so that he might be shown to be the true Lord in the prophets and in all his works.

“All this took place” means that the angel was sent, that Mary conceived, and that she gave birth: all these things had been foretold by the prophets. Isaiah said of him, “She will conceive,” because Isaiah spoke of the future; this text has “she will have,” because it was already recounting past events.

And they will call his name Emmanuel. The Evangelist explained what Emmanuel means when he said: “God with us.” *Emmanu* means “with us”; *El* is one of the ten names by which God is called among the Hebrews.

God was with the patriarchs and the fathers, but he was with those of whom the prophet spoke in another way: he lived among them in the flesh, and they heard him speaking with a living voice and saw him performing miracles. What many prophets and kings desired to see and hear—this then occurred among them.

Joseph, rising from sleep, did as the angel of the Lord had commanded him. From this action it is evident both that Joseph had been perfectly instructed by the angel concerning the matter and that he was a wise man, since afterward he sought neither advice nor an interpreter concerning it, but immediately did as the angel had commanded him.

He took his wife in order to guard her. “Wife” is derived from *coniungere*, “to join together.”

And he did not know her until she had borne her firstborn son. From these passages heretics arose who said that the words “until she had borne” mean that he knew her afterward. Yet this is not the meaning of the expression in divine Scripture, as it is in ordinary human speech.

For Scripture says in the Psalm: “Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet.” Will the Lord Christ therefore no longer sit at the right hand of the Father after his enemies have been placed beneath his feet?

And in another passage Scripture says: “Until you grow old, I am the Lord.” Will he therefore no longer be Lord after those to whom he spoke these words have grown old?

But in divine Scripture “until” is used to mean eternity, so that the sense is: “Sit at my right hand forever, and I will make your enemies your footstool.” Likewise in another passage: “I am the Lord forever, both while you live and while you grow old, and even when you die”—that is, forever.

From another word heretics arose who said that he would not be called “firstborn” unless other brothers followed him. But this is not so. Read the Old Testament, and you will find that all who first open the womb are called firstborn, even if they have no brothers; they are called both only-begotten and firstborn.

Whoever wishes to know more about this should read the book of Saint Jerome which he wrote against Helvidius on this subject.

## CHAPTER II. On the Epiphany of the Lord

When Jesus had been born in Bethlehem of Judah in the days of King Herod. Because the Evangelist, under the direction and governance of the Holy Spirit, narrates the deeds of the Lord by distributing them among themselves, the reader ought to recall what another Evangelist says about the same matter.

Luke narrates how the angel Gabriel came to Mary, and how blessed Mary conceived by hearing and believing. Matthew narrates how she was betrothed to Joseph. Then Luke again narrates how they went up from Galilee because of the registration for the census. Matthew, in turn, narrates how, after his birth, he was worshiped by the magi.

He says: “When Jesus had been born.” It was customary for historians, when writing history, to record the time, as is still done—not only in accounts of events but also in documents. For this reason Matthew also gives the time of Herod, who was reigning in Judea.

Luke, going back farther and higher, recorded the emperor’s name, the names of the consuls, and the time of the registration for the census, saying: “A decree went out from Caesar Augustus,” namely Octavian. Christ was born in the forty-second year of Octavian’s reign, and the census was conducted.

And just as Abraham, who preceded the Lord as a figure, was born in the forty-second year of Ninus, who was the first king in the world, so Christ was born in the forty-second year of Octavian, who was the first to be called emperor. On that very day many portents occurred which showed him to be the Creator of the world.

On that day, from a tavern or wine-shop, an exceedingly abundant spring of oil flowed throughout the entire day, to show that the one was being born who would be called Christ—that is, anointed with spiritual oil—and that his Church would be called Christian.

On the same day the angels sang: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will.” And, so that this voice might be fulfilled, such peace was established throughout the world for twelve years as no king had been able to establish in a single province. Thus, as the prophet said, they “beat their swords into plowshares and their spears into pruning hooks,” and as the Psalmist had said: “In his days abundance of peace shall arise.”

At that time Octavian, to whom supreme authority over all affairs had fallen, did not allow himself to be called lord of men—indeed, he did not dare to do so—at the very time when the true Lord of the entire human race was born among human beings.

For one day, while games were being performed as he watched, a certain mime declared: “O fair and good lord!” When everyone joyfully applauded, Octavian immediately restrained the flattery with his hand and expression. By a very severe decree he afterward forbade himself to be called “lord” even by his children, grandchildren, or slaves.

In Bethlehem of Judah. Bethlehem is interpreted as “house of bread”; previously it was called Ephratha, that is, “fruitful.” But after Jacob pastured his flocks there, he called it Bethlehem.

The second letter among the Hebrews is called *beth*, and it means “house.” Both names are appropriate to the Church. It was fitting that the house in which Christ was born should previously have been called by these names, because in his Church the true bread and eternal satisfaction are found by all who seek in truth.

It should not, however, be written “of Judea,” but “of Judah,” because no other people outside the Jews is found to have had a city called by the same name.

Nevertheless, there are two cities in Judea called Bethlehem. One is in Galilee, in the territory of the tribe of Zebulun. The other is Bethlehem, the city of David, in the territory of the tribe of Judah, six miles from Jerusalem toward the south, beside the road leading to Hebron. There are also the tomb of David and that of his father, the tomb of King Archelaus, and near it the tower of Adder, belonging to the flock, where the angel of the Lord spoke to the shepherds.

It was in this city that our Lord was born.

In the days of King Herod. This is Herod, son of Antipater. When he had been plundered by brigands, he was so poor that he could not ransom that same Antipater. This Herod was his son.

After Herod had joined himself to Hyrcanus, king of the Jews and grandson of Simon Maccabaeus, Hyrcanus sent Herod as an envoy to Pompey. Because he benefited from the mission and through its favor received a share in the kingdom, the Senate decreed under Antony that he should rule the Jews.

Behold, magi came from the East. The magi are those commonly called sorcerers, because they perform evil, shake the elements, and disturb minds. The peoples from whom these men came were learned in this art.

These three kings were of the race of Balaam. They came from three kingdoms in the land of Havilah, where, as Moses says, the finest gold is mined, and they were neighbors of the Persians. Hence Juvencus says:

> “The Persians delight to extend their step.”

In the prophecy of Balaam they learned that the one who had been born was both king and man. From the words “A star shall arise,” they understood that he was the Lord, because at his rising a more wondrous and greater star was appearing.

When Balaam said, “A rod shall rise from Israel,” they understood that he would be a man, because he would be born from Jerusalem. From the words “He will shatter the leaders of Moab,” they learned that he would be a king.

And for a certain further period he was permitted to practice divination in the stars, so that they might recognize Christ there; afterward no one there was able to discover the truth.

The mathematicians likewise said that they could know from the stars the births, character, qualities, and deaths of human beings. Christ was indeed born in Judea, but the magi, positioned in the East, saw the star and recognized whom it indicated.

The star led them for several days. But when they approached Judea, the star then left them by God’s command, so that, abandoned by the star, they would come to the royal city and speak with their fellow king Herod, since they had one emperor, Caesar. Thus Herod would question the Jews, and they would be without excuse, because they had heard this from the Gentiles and would become more certain when they heard that it had indeed been prophesied.

They came to Jerusalem. This city was first built by Shem, son of Noah. He was called Melchizedek, that is, “righteous king,” and his city itself was called Salem, that is, “peace.”

In Abraham’s time it was called Solyma. Homer later called it Hierosolyma, because *ieron* in Hebrew means “fortification.” The Jebusites later held it and called it Jebus; from these two names it was called Hierosolyma. From Solomon onward it was called Jerusalem—that is, “Jebus of Solomon,” meaning “peaceful.”

In it is the tower of Zion, whose name is interpreted as “mirror.”

We saw his star in the East and came to worship him. They call it “his star” because they believed that each person was born under the destiny of the stars and that each person had his own star.

Nevertheless, this star had existed neither before nor afterward; it was created at that time for the purpose of instructing and leading the nations to Christ. Some people say many things about this star, but because they do not possess the source of truth, I have preferred to pass them over.

We came. This may be understood in the present tense, as though they were saying, “We have just arrived and are still on the journey,” with the penultimate syllable lengthened; or in the past tense, with the same penultimate syllable shortened, as though they were saying: “We saw him and came this far.”

To worship him. Not so that, abandoning our emperor, we might pay tribute to him, but so that together with the earthly lord we might recognize and venerate the heavenly God, the Creator of the world and of ourselves.

When King Herod heard this, he was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him. Herod was troubled because he knew that he did not belong to the royal lineage of David and that he had sought the kingdom by fraud. He had even once ordered the Scriptures to be burned, lest any question arise for his descendants from the ancient written tradition, thinking that if he removed the public records, no other testimonies could make clear from what stock of patriarchs or ancient proselytes he had descended.

“All Jerusalem was troubled with him” is an instance of synecdoche, in which the container is used to signify what it contains: that is, the city is used to signify its inhabitants.

They too were troubled because when a king changes, some people usually fall and others are exalted, as Daniel says of Nebuchadnezzar: “Those whom he wished he exalted, and those whom he wished he humbled.”

And gathering together all the chief priests and scribes of the people, he inquired of them where Christ was to be born. Since Herod was not a Jew and did not believe or use the Scriptures, he therefore questioned the Jews.

To inquire means to ask. Indeed, God commanded that the priests be consulted about the law, and he had determined that whenever the people went astray, the matter should be referred to the priests.

The scribes were so called from the Scripture that they used.

But they said to him: In Bethlehem of Judah. It is evident that they had the Scriptures in regular use, since they were able to answer so quickly and produce from memory the testimony concerning the place in which the ruler was to be born.

Similarly, the apostle Peter commands us: “Ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you concerning the hope that is in you.”

For it is written through the prophet: “And you, Bethlehem, land of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah, for from you will go forth a ruler who will govern my people Israel.”

Micah said this as though he were saying: “You, Bethlehem, which lie in the territory of the tribe of Judah, are by no means least among the principal and praiseworthy cities of Judah, because you produced David, who ennobled and exalted this kingdom. But again from you will go forth one who will govern my people Israel”—that is, those who wish to see the Lord with the mind, because *Israel* is interpreted as “a man who sees God.”

Who will govern my people Israel. Attention must be paid to the words “my people Israel,” because those who are God’s people are governed by God’s authority and do what belongs to God. Those who do not do such things are not God’s people but the devil’s.

Then Herod secretly summoned the magi and carefully learned from them the time when the star had appeared to them. “Secretly” means privately.

He spoke with them in secret because he feared that the Jews might themselves deliver the child to him. For he knew that the Jews hated him because he was of foreign descent.

Here the narrative is incomplete, because it does not relate what he said to them or what they answered concerning the time of the star. But because Herod ordered the children of two years and under to be killed, some wish to infer that they said that a year had passed since they had seen the star, and that he counted one year for that period and waited another year for their return.

Some say that they came to Christ after a year and twelve days; others say that, traveling with dromedaries, they came in twelve days after seeing the star.

A dromedary is a kind of camel, smaller in stature but swifter, and it gets its name from its speed. For *dromos* in Greek means “running” and “speed”; swift ships are therefore also called *dromones*. A dromedary is said to be able to run one hundred miles or more in a single day.

And sending them to Bethlehem, he said. Because he had heard from the scribes that the new ruler ought to be born there, he sent them so that, when they saw him, the guardians of the child would think that Herod likewise wished to do so after the magi returned.

Go and inquire carefully about the child, and when you have found him, report to me, so that I too may come and worship him. Herod observed and understood that these magi were already faithful to the one whom they were seeking. Therefore he said that he wished to worship him.

He also did not wish to confess this to the Jews, because he knew that they hated the child and eagerly desired that a king should arise from their own people. But although he was hidden from human beings, he was not hidden from the one who was present in a small body and who alone knew human hearts.

For since they were faithful to the child, they would have returned to Herod had they not been forbidden to do so by the child in a dream.

And behold, the star that they had seen in the East. This star was not in the heaven where the other stars are, but closer to the earth and brighter than the rest. It went before them until, coming forward, it stood above the place where the child was.

Herod was not worthy to see the star because of his wickedness, for God does not tempt to evil—that is, he is not the helper of those who act wickedly, but the permitter of wicked deeds, since he allows many things to be done that are contrary to his will. He does not help them; the devil does.

When they saw the star, they rejoiced with exceedingly great joy. People often experience greater joy over something lost when they find it than they did at first when they began to possess it.

And entering the house, they found the child with Mary his mother. Because they had come on account of the child, the name “child” is placed first.

And falling down, they worshiped him. “To worship” is sometimes used for “to bow,” and this may be done both toward human beings and toward God. Thus it is said of Cush: “He worshiped the king, prostrate on the ground.”

Here, however, it does not have that meaning. They worshiped him as God and Lord, for the remission of sins and for the attainment of eternal life. Hence in our prayer we say: “Pour into our hearts what you inspired in the minds of the three magi.”

With this worship Mordecai refused to worship Haman.

And opening their treasures, they offered him gifts. “Treasure” is partly Greek and partly Latin. In Greek, *thesis* means “a placing,” and *thesaurus* means “a placing of gold.”

It is rightly asked whether each of them offered one gift or whether each offered three. We believe that each offered three, because they displayed through their gifts what they believed in their hearts.

Gold was offered to him as king, because gold is the glory of the world, and kings demand it from their subjects.

Frankincense was offered to him as Lord, because both among pagans and among worshipers of the gods this spice was always offered and consecrated to a lord or deity. Indeed, it was customary among the pagans—as Solinus relates—for pure boys in clean garments to gather it whenever it was time to collect it.

It is a tree of Arabia, enormous and spreading, which bears this substance. Its bark is exceedingly smooth, like that of the maple, and it is shaped like an almond; it produces a white aromatic sap, and when broken it crumbles into powder. When placed on fire, it burns easily. Among us it is called “male,” because it is round, resembling testicles. This is the finest kind.

The other kind is flat and rough; it is cheaper and is called so from *tundere*, “to pound” or “strike,” because wherever the tree has been struck, more of it comes forth.

It is also called Lebanon from the mountain of Arabia where the Sabaeans live, because their mountain is called Lebanon, where frankincense is collected.

They gave myrrh because they recognized that he would die for the salvation of the world. It was customary among many people, and especially among the Jews who believed in the resurrection, that when someone dear had died—particularly someone noble or powerful—the intestines were removed, and myrrh was pounded together with aloe or other spices. The whole body was first anointed inside and out with balsam, and afterward sprinkled with the powder, so that the body might remain intact through the ages.

For this reason Joseph also brought to the Lord’s burial a mixture of myrrh and aloes weighing one hundred pounds, although it was not necessary.

Myrrh also grows in Arabia, in the same manner as frankincense, from a small tree. The larger tree is five cubits high and resembles the thorn called *acanthus*. Its drop is green and bitter, from which it received the name *myrrh*, meaning “bitter.”

The drop that flows naturally is more precious; that extracted by wounding the bark is cheaper. None is more precious than that brought from the island of Troglodyta.

And having received an answer in a dream that they should not return to Herod. Just as earthly kings customarily give answers to embassies, so our Lord gave an answer to the kings who had come to worship him. He gave it himself, even in a dream, as he did to prophets and perfected men, such as these.

He warned them not to return to Herod, because their route had not brought them through him except for the reasons explained above. For Bethlehem lies before Jerusalem for those coming from the East.

Since we have passed rapidly through the historical interpretation as best we could, let us now consider the spiritual one. As we said earlier, all three of the philosophical disciplines of the Greeks are found in divine Scripture. Indeed, every philosophy and every mode of expression existed in divine Scripture before it existed among secular sophists. If the latter possessed anything, they possessed it by God’s gift, since he bestowed it.

When Jesus had been born in Bethlehem. Bethlehem, as we said, is interpreted as “house of bread” and signifies the Church, in which the true bread is found—that is, Christ, who said: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven, and if anyone eats from this bread, he will live forever.”

The three magi signify the Gentile people, who arose from the three sons of Noah, or because they were destined to believe in the Trinity.

They came from the East, either because they came from the paradise of our father to the devil, or because our Lord is called the East and they received from him the means to come to him. For no one comes to the Father except through the Son, because we believe through him, as he gives growth in the heart.

His star is the light of faith, by which we have been inspired so that we ought to believe in him.

Jerusalem may here be understood as sacred Scripture, through which we come to know the Lord.

Herod, whose name is interpreted as “leathery,” that is, “deceitful,” signifies the devil, who seeks to extinguish Christ in the hearts of the elect—that is, to erase him from their memory.

The scribes and Pharisees are the devil’s followers and members, or heretics who suggest Christ to us. For often, when heretics provoke us, we come to know from them what had been hidden from us about Christ.

Or we go around the various sects, and from the abundance of vices that we detect in them we understand the Lord, because he hates vices and loves virtues. Then we recognize that he must be sought in Bethlehem—that is, in the Catholic Church.

If one of them tells us something good, we ought to do as the magi did, for it is written: “Do what they say, but do not do what they do.”
