When we have been separated from the devil, we see the star. The closer we draw to the Lord, the more fully we know the Lord, and from him we receive an answer not to retrace the road by which we came.

We promise that we will renounce the devil and his angels, because, just as the way of the good consists in good works, so the life of the wicked consists in vices. Our homeland was paradise; from it we departed through our first parent by gluttony, avarice, vainglory, and other things like them.

If, then, we desire to return to our homeland, let us not imitate the first Adam, but the second, who departed by doing what had been forbidden to him. This one, by holding to and showing us the way of life, ascended into heaven and now sits at the right hand of God.

Behold, the physical interpretation has appeared to us in the historical account, and the logical interpretation in the spiritual one. An ethical interpretation can also be found if we seek according to the anagogical meaning: namely, if our heart becomes Bethlehem, so that in it spiritual meditation on the Scriptures—the word of God—may abound, and so that, believing in the Holy Trinity, it may also appear before the Lord adorned with the three virtues: faith, hope, and charity.

These are so dear to the King of the ages, to God the Creator of all things, and to the man made at the end of the ages, who is one Lord, that he delights in them more than in gold and topaz when they are found in the minds of his faithful.

If, therefore, we once come before the Lord’s presence with these gifts, let us take care not afterward to return to Herod—that is, to the devil.

Since this Gospel is read among us on the Epiphany, let us briefly explain how sacred this day is considered. In Greece, this Gospel is read on the Nativity of the Lord, while on this day the Gospel concerning his baptism is read.

At Easter, however, “In the beginning” is read, so that just as these solemnities are especially distinguished above the other festivals, so the most distinguished Gospels may be read on those same festivals.

For on the Nativity his bodily birth is read; at Easter, the birth of his divinity.

Since it is customary for this Gospel to be read on this day, let us also speak of the miracles that took place on it.

On this day the Lord not only received the magi as the firstfruits of the nations, but on this day he also chose to be baptized by John in the Jordan. On this day he also chose to turn water into wine, and he fed five thousand people with five loaves—not, however, in a single year, but over the recurring cycles of the years.

On this same day—which the Greeks call *Epiphany*, and which Latins may call “Appearance”—at the third hour, under a clear and cloudless sky, a circle resembling a heavenly rainbow surrounded the city of Rome, as though to show that the one who had been born was the one and supreme and uniquely glorious person in this world, who alone had made and governed the sun itself and the entire world.

Some also call this day *Theophany*, that is, “the appearance of God.” We ought to celebrate it with complete devotion because those magi were the firstfruits of the nations and foreshadowed us who were to believe in Christ. Therefore we must embrace this day with the greatest devotion.

The day on which he appeared manifestly through angels to the Hebrew shepherds may also be called Epiphany, because it is written concerning them: “They came and found it as it had been told them by him.” But this day is especially ours because he was shown to us through the star, through that creature which this nation most greatly worshiped and venerated.

## CHAPTER III. On the Nativity of the Innocents
When they had departed, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph [Col. 1286D], saying:

There are some who wish to say that the magi came to him in Egypt, because the slaughter of the infants is celebrated before the day of the Epiphany. This cannot possibly be so, because the infants were killed after two years from Christ’s birth. Moreover, the magi found the Lord in Bethlehem, so that they might become more certain through Micah’s prophecy concerning Christ. The Gospel plainly says that, when they had departed, the angel of the Lord warned Joseph to take the child away to Egypt.

“Rise, and take the child and his mother.” It should be noted that he does not say “your wife” now, but “the child’s mother.” *Puer* (“child”) is used in three ways: first, for age and purity, because *puer* is derived from purity, as Isaiah says concerning the Lord: “A child is born to us” [Col. 1287A]; *puer* is used simply for age, as in the case of an infant seven years old; and *puer* is used for service and obedience, as when the Lord says to Jeremiah: “You are my servant; do not be afraid.” And in the Book of Kings, David’s servants are called *pueri*.

Behold, the Lord did what he was afterward going to command his own people to do: “If they persecute you,” he says, “in this city, flee into another,” giving an example, so that those who despair of being able to endure the burden of persecution do not sin if they withdraw to another place—provided only that they keep their head, that is, Christ, in their mind, and do what he himself commanded. For his dominions are in every place, he himself is everywhere, and his eyes are upon the righteous and his ears upon their prayers.

Egypt, as you know, after the Jews had lived there, was always familiar to the Jews; and the Egyptians always feared the God of the Hebrews and revered the Hebrews themselves. Therefore, as Josephus and other authors relate, under King Philadelphus the priest Onias, a good and righteous man who had been expelled from Judea, built a temple in Egypt and instituted the practice of burnt offerings, as was done in Judea. For this reason it pleased God more to go into Egypt than into other lands, where there was less religion.

Egypt was called after a certain man named Egyptus. It is a region unaccustomed to the rains of heaven and ignorant of showers. The Nile alone waters it by its inundation. Hence it is fertile in crops and very richly supplied with other commodities.

“For it will happen that Herod will seek the child.” *Futurum* means “going to happen,” that is, “about to come”; it comes from the verb *sum* (“I am”), which has no present participle except this one, *venturus* (“about to come”) [Col. 1287C].

“To destroy him.” This was shown in the children whom he killed on his account.

“He arose and took the child and his mother.” When he fled, night is mentioned; when he returned, nothing of the kind is mentioned.

Eusebius, in his *Ecclesiastical History*, relates that, when Joseph was carrying the Lord into Egypt, they passed through the city of Heliopolis. In its streets there was a terebinth of marvelous size, beneath which the inhabitants of that place practiced divination. When Joseph passed by with the child, the tree bowed itself down before him to the ground and lay there until he had passed; then, rising again, it stood as it had stood before.

When he had entered Egypt, what the prophet had said was fulfilled: “Behold, he will ascend upon a light cloud and enter Egypt, and the idols of Egypt will fall.” When Joseph with the child passed before a temple, all the idols fell to the ground, to show that he was the same God before whose ark Dagon had lain prostrate, with his hands and feet cut off [Col. 1287D].

“Until the death of Herod”—that is, until three years had passed. This is also the period of weaning, during which the ancients weaned their children and thereafter held a feast of separation, as Abraham did for his son Isaac. And the longer an infant or an animal is nourished on its mother’s milk before being weaned, the better it grows.

“So that what was spoken through the prophet might be fulfilled”—namely, through Micah. Balaam also says this: “Out of Egypt I have called my Son.” This may be understood in one way of carnal Israel, which was called out of Egypt through Moses; but more truly it refers to the Lord, who is the natural Son [Col. 1288A].

“Then Herod, seeing how he had been mocked by the magi”—that is, after waiting one year, he realized that he had been mocked. He had been deceived in that they had said they would return but did not.

“And he sent and killed all the children who were in Bethlehem and in all its boundaries.” “In all its boundaries” means in the villages belonging to its jurisdiction. As they relate, he waited for them to come to the solemnity that they were celebrating at that time; and when they were there, he ordered the soldiers to kill them.

“From two years old and under.” *Bimatus* means “two years old,” from *bis* (“twice”), that is, from two years [the transmitted wording is corrupt]. “And under” means those who were less than one year old, or half a year old, or even one night old.

“According to the time that he had ascertained from the magi.” As we have said, he reckoned one year from the magi’s statement, as though the year in which they had come had already passed; then he waited for another year, expecting their return.

“A voice was heard in Ramah.” We should not suppose that Ramah is the name of a place, but rather that *Ramah* is interpreted as “high,” as though he had said: “A voice was heard far and wide.” For the Ramah that we read of in the Book of Kings is near Gibeah.

“Rachel weeping for her children.” How is Rachel said to have wept for those who were not of her own offspring but belonged to another? It should be understood that Rachel was buried in Bethlehem, and that this is said according to prophetic usage—either through metonymy, by showing the container through what is contained, or because the tribe of Benjamin was joined to the tribe of Judah, and those who were killed in Bethlehem were associated with them. For this reason Rachel is said to have wept for her children [Col. 1288B].

“And she refused to be comforted, because they are not.” The implied meaning is “because they are no longer to be recalled into this world”; they had brought the world to an end by a good outcome. Or, in another sense, she refused to receive consolation because she thought that they would be lost.

“For they are dead who sought the child’s life.” This is a figure called by grammarians *synecdoche*, in which more or less is expressed than is literally meant. Here the plural “they are dead” is used although Herod alone was dead. Yet it could also have happened that others who had harbored evil intentions against Christ died during so long an interval.

Concerning this Herod, Josephus and others report that he lived under suspicion and ended most wretchedly. They relate that he killed his wife Mariamne, the daughter of King Aristobulus, whom he regarded as the more noble of his wives, because she had been accused before him of wishing to kill him by poison [Col. 1288D]. By her he already had the sons Hyrcanus and Aristobulus, who had been commended to the emperor Octavian; yet he killed them also in the same way, because they seemed angry with him on behalf of their mother.

Afterward he killed a third son, Antipater, who had consented to the killing of his brothers. Finally, Herod himself fell into a grave illness. He summoned his son-in-law and his trusted friends and said to them:

“I know that the Jews will rejoice at my death, because they hate me. But you can ensure that I have mourners at my funeral if you do what I shall command. I will order all the sons of the nobles to be confined, so that when I breathe out my spirit you may kill them; then, unwillingly, they will mourn my funeral.”

They promised that they would do this, but they did not [Col. 1289A]. As soon as he was dead, they released them.

He suffered, among other tortures, a burning fever in his private parts, which then rotted, so that scarcely anyone could approach him. Therefore he wished to kill himself, unless he had been prevented by the man who guarded him. Thus he who had killed the innocent with many tortures departed from this life to greater torments.

Behold, we have heard about Herod’s death. When we come to the Passion, we shall say which Herod that is. For now, it is enough to have said that you will hear no more of this Herod in this Gospel, but of others.

“He arose and took the child and his mother.” Here also it should be noted that he does not say “his wife,” although three years had already passed since the child’s birth. For this reason Helvidius lied when he said that holy Mary had children by Joseph.

[Col. 1289B] “He came into the land of Israel.” All Jews are called Israel, whereas Judah is only one tribe.

“But when he heard that Archelaus was reigning in Judea in place of his father Herod, he was afraid to go there.” After Herod’s death, the emperor divided his kingdom among Archelaus and his brothers, namely Philip, Herod, and Lysias. He entrusted Jerusalem, the capital of the kingdom, to Archelaus. Archelaus enjoyed it for only a short time, because the emperor, after the Jews accused him at Vienna—which is a city in Burgundy—of the insolence of his conduct, sent him into exile and entrusted his kingdom to Pilate. He did not, however, give Pilate the kingdom or permit him to bear the royal title.

Therefore the Gospel says that Joseph did not wish to go to the place where Archelaus reigned, because God, who warned him to turn aside into another region, foresaw that Archelaus would have the same disposition as his father [Col. 1289C]. His brothers, however, had not loved their father so greatly, because of the killing of their relatives. For this reason Joseph turned aside into Galilee, where Herod reigned.

“So that what was spoken through the prophets might be fulfilled: ‘He will be called a Nazarene.’” Whenever the evangelist says “through the prophets,” using the plural, he does not set down one fixed proof-text. Nevertheless, all the prophets foretold that he would be a *Nazaraeus*, that is, a holy one.

Isaiah, however, says this in Hebrew:

“A branch will go forth from the root of Jesse,  
and a Nazirite will rise from his root.”

There is a difference between *Nazarenus* and *Nazaraeus*. *Nazarenus* derives from a place; *Nazaraeus* from religion.

## CHAPTER IV  
### Christian Druthmar’s Treatise on John’s Preaching

“In those days”—that is, in the days of the king who was then reigning in Galilee, namely Herod, as Luke indicates more explicitly when he says: “In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, when Pontius Pilate was governor of Judea and Herod was tetrarch of Galilee, while his brother Philip …”—John the Baptist came.

*Joannes* is interpreted as “the grace of God.” This name was given to him by the Lord because the grace of God was truly in him, as you have heard in the Gospel.

*Baptista* is a Greek name and is said in Latin as *lavator*, “washer.” It comes from the Greek verb *baptizo*, that is, “I wash.”

John also had an epithet in addition to his name, one that came from the Lord: namely, “sent.” For the angel had said to Zechariah: “He himself will go before him.” And Zechariah had said to his son: [Col. 1290A] “And you, child, will be called the prophet of the Most High; you will go before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways.”

Nor should one think that John did not understand this when he was only eight days old. Even while he had not yet been named, he understood holy Mary speaking and leaped in his mother’s womb.

“Preaching in the wilderness.” Historically, John lived in the wilderness beside the Jordan, near Betharaba, or, as it is called by another name, Ennom, where there was much water. Spiritually, however, Judea was already at that time deserted of the guardianship that it had formerly possessed; deprived and abandoned, it was announcing the consolation of the Redeemer.

“Repent,” he said, “for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near.” Just as John preceded the Lord in his prophecy, so also he preceded him in his preaching and in his baptism, lest the Jews should have an excuse concerning Christ, saying: “He announces and does new things to us; therefore we do not accept his preaching” [Col. 1290B].

“Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near.” No one before John preached these things, except concerning earthly matters, saying: “If you do this or that, you will live for a long time in the land that you are entering to possess.” Now, through the herald of righteousness, it is said: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near.”

The Lord’s herald is honored because he announces concerning the Lord what no one before him had prophesied: namely, that the very way which had been closed to the first human being by sin was soon to be reopened.

In this Gospel the kingdom of heaven sometimes means the present Church, sometimes eternal life, and sometimes the Lord himself. Here both may be understood: the Lord himself, because he is already near, since they hear the voice of him who preaches; or eternal life, because it is soon to be opened to those who seek it through good works.

“This is he who was spoken of through Isaiah the prophet.” The prophets foretold not only what the Lord was going to do in the flesh, but also that he would have a herald. It was fitting that great and innumerable oracles should precede the great Lord.

John was called “the voice” by Isaiah because he was going to precede the Word. You know that the Lord Christ is called the Word of the Father: “For through him all things were made.” In human speech, a sound—that is, a voice—normally precedes the word. Therefore, just as the voice precedes the word, so John, because he went before the Word, was called “the voice” by the prophet.

What that voice was to cry is then added: “Prepare the way of the Lord.” Everyone who proclaims right faith and good works does nothing other than prepare a way for the Lord who is coming into the hearts of his hearers, so that the power of grace may penetrate the heart and enlighten it with the light of truth, and make straight paths for God by forming pure thoughts in the mind through the word of good preaching.

The Lord’s way is directed toward the heart when the truth of the word is humbly heard.

“Make his paths straight.” The paths in human hearts are crooked when pride or other vices have their dwelling there. Those vices are like certain mountains, which the Lord abhors, as he himself said: “Upon whom shall I rest, except upon the humble and quiet one who trembles at my words?” [Col. 1291A]

In this way, therefore, crooked ways are made straight by preachers: if, through the preaching of the Gospel, those who were formerly proud become humble; those who were lustful become chaste; and those who were cruel become merciful.

Then the Lord will not merely come into the hearts of such people, but will also make his dwelling there, as he himself says: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him.”

“John himself had a garment of camel’s hair.” An austere garment is an indication of repentance. Haircloth and garments are made from the wool shorn from camels. Beneath the belly a camel has wool, with which other wool—and also goat’s hair—is mixed; sometimes astonishingly rough and harsh garments are made from it, and John wore one of these [Col. 1291B]. For this very thing he was praised by the Lord.

“And a leather belt around his waist.” Elijah too was girded with a leather belt, because he was like John in every respect. The leather belt signifies the mortification of the flesh, which John had in his own body.

“His food was locusts.” Concerning locusts I heard one man say that these were small birds with red legs. I also heard another say that John lived beside the Jordan and ate sea locusts, that is, fish. Neither statement is true. Rather, they were the locusts that we have seen in the meadows, which are also permitted to be eaten in the Old Testament. Origen says the same.

Nevertheless, larger locusts are found in that land than in ours. Why would John be praised for the rigor of his abstinence if he ate delicacies from the sea, or birds, which the Jews desired?

“Wild honey.” Even today this honey falls more abundantly in that land than in other lands, because the land was also called a land flowing with honey. It is the manna on which the children of Israel were fed for forty years.

But when the children of Israel came out of that land in which they had not seen it fall—for it had never rained there—they said: “What is this?” Thereafter they always called it by that name, namely, *manna*.

We have also seen some brought by people who came from that land. It resembles snow or salt, but has the sweetness of our honey.

“Then Jerusalem went out to him.” John was filled with the Holy Spirit. His father, being a noble priest, had also instructed him in the sacred writings. Abundant preaching flowed from his mouth; they had heard of the wonders that had occurred at his birth, and they saw his austere life according to the custom of the prophets. Therefore the crowds went out to hear him and to consult him about their way of life.

“All Jerusalem”—the city of God and of kings, where there were priests and more extensive learning than in the other cities.

“And all Judea.” He says Judea on account of the royal tribe of Judah, because it always held primacy among the other tribes.

“And all the region around the Jordan.” That land was better because of the irrigation of the Jordan. Jericho and Segor were there, where balsam grows, as we read concerning Sodom that it was like the paradise of God.

“And they were baptized by him in the Jordan, confessing their sins.” He could not baptize for the remission of sins. Nevertheless, as the Lord’s herald, including in his actions, he washed only their bodies with water. He commanded that whoever was baptized with his baptism should believe in the one who was to come after him and should receive another baptism for the remission of sins.

When he baptized them, he said: “I baptize you so that you may believe in him who is to come after me.” For this reason he later said: “This is the one who baptizes, who takes away the sins of the world through his baptism.”

“Seeing many of the Pharisees and Sadducees coming to his baptism, he said: ‘Brood of vipers.’” A viper is so called because it gives birth violently. When the mother’s belly has swollen with childbirth, the young, unwilling to wait for the natural and timely opening, gnaw through her sides and burst out, causing her death.

It is also said that when the male, inserting his mouth, discharges his seed into the viper, she, overcome by lust and turned to rage, bites off the male’s head when she receives it in her mouth. Thus both parents die: the male while mating, the mother while giving birth.

Lozenges are made from vipers, which the Greeks call *theriaca*, “antidotes,” so that whoever eats or drinks them will never again have leprosy; and if he has it, it will not increase further.

There are also other kinds of vipers, one of which seized Paul and which he shook off into the fire.

John says that the Jews were like these vipers, because they killed their fathers: Naboth and Jeremiah; Uzziah and Zechariah [the transmitted name is uncertain]; and King Manasseh cut up his uncle Isaiah. Because of such deeds they are called a brood of vipers.

“Who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath?” The coming wrath is the day of judgment, which will come upon all the wicked who refuse to obey God’s commands.

Whoever is concerned about his sins, so that they may be forgiven through good works, flees from the coming wrath. He hastens to remove himself from the left side of the goats and flees to the right with the lambs: the goats will be tormented, while the lambs will be protected by the Lord.

“Therefore produce worthy fruit of repentance.” To produce worthy fruit of repentance is to punish past evils with tears and to do good instead, so that, just as we presented our members to serve injustice, we may likewise present them to serve righteousness in sanctification.

Or the worthy fruit of repentance is to do good and redeem committed evils through almsgiving.

“And do not wish to say: ‘We have Abraham as our father.’” Do not boast of the nobility of the patriarchs. If you are not imitators of Abraham in faith and works, you will not be called children of Abraham. For God said of you through the prophet: “Your father was an Amorite, and your mother a Hittite.”

“For I say to you that God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham.” By these stones he means the Gentiles, who are called stones because they worshiped stones. For it is written: “Let those who make them become like them, and all who trust in them.”

Or he means any material stones, because the one who created the world from nothing is able to create human beings from stones.

By imitating Abraham’s faith, all nations are called children of Abraham; and by imitating the devil, the Jews are called children of the devil, as the Lord later said to them: “You are from your father the devil, and you wish to do the works of your father” [Col. 1293A].

“Even now the axe is laid at the root of the trees.” This is an allegory through the likeness of a fruitless tree. Just as a fruitless tree is cut down and thrown into the fire, so the soul of a person who does not produce good fruit is uprooted from the body by the angels and will be cast into eternal fire—not so that it may burn up, but so that it may be tormented without end.

Would that an end could have been found in that fire! But what is more bitter is that the person is preserved there so that he may burn eternally.

The axe is the sentence of God, which separates the soul from the body.

“Therefore every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire.” This is a comparison by which the parable proceeds from the lower to the higher and from the inanimate to the animate: from the tree to the human being.

It is said with great certainty and definition that every tree—that is, every human being—who does not produce fruit, namely a good work, will be cut down and thrown into the fire, and will be cut off by the sentence of God forever [Col. 1293B].

“I indeed baptize you in water for repentance.” I am a small human being; I merely wash your bodies with water, but I do not wash your minds through forgiveness. Yet the crowds did this in repentance so that they might bear witness and come to the one who could also wash their minds through forgiveness.

“But the one who is coming after me”—that is, by preaching—“is stronger than I.” He is stronger in divinity, because he created everyone.

John, filled with the Holy Spirit, gradually announced Christ to the crowds in due order. At the end he said: “I have seen and borne witness that this is the Christ.” The uneducated crowds could not grasp that God had become human.

“Whose sandal strap I am not worthy to carry.” Here John humbles himself. In another place the evangelist says: “I am not worthy to loosen the strap of his sandal.”

As I said above, it was the custom among that people that when a brother died, his brother or a relative would take the dead man’s wife and raise up offspring for his brother or relative. If he did not wish to take her, he came before the assembly, and his sandal was removed from his foot because he had refused to take her; then the man who was second in order took her.

John alludes to this mystery, as though he were saying: “I am not worthy to claim for myself the bride of Christ, which is the Church” [Col. 1293D].

Or, in another sense, sandals are made from dead animals; and the Divinity came to us as though shod, when it appeared clothed in the corpse of our flesh. Therefore John seems to say: “I am not fit to unlock the mystery of how the Divinity was clothed in flesh.”

“He himself will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire.” We are baptized in the Holy Spirit not only when we are reborn each day through baptism, but also when we are set on fire by the gift of that same Holy Spirit to perform divine commands, and receive daily remission of sins through seven modes.

We are baptized with fire either because the Holy Spirit is fire, according to the Acts of the Apostles; and just as fire ordinarily destroys wood, so the Holy Spirit destroys sins; or, also, in the future, according to the Apostle’s words, we will be baptized with fire, because we will pass through fire when we depart from this body.

“If anyone’s work is burned, he will suffer loss; but if anyone’s work remains, he himself will be saved—yet as through fire” [Col. 1294A].

“His winnowing fan is in his hand.” The winnowing fan is also called a shovel. He gives, metaphorically, a comparison from the lesser to the greater. This is a figure called *parabola* in Greek, consisting of dissimilar things, and it signifies examination or separation, because the good will be separated from the wicked by the angels; or it signifies the storm that will precede the face of the righteous Judge on the dreadful day.

“And he will cleanse his threshing floor.” That is, his Church.

“And he will gather his wheat into his granary.” By his wheat he wishes the elect to be understood; by the granary, eternal life.

Therefore a certain martyr, when he was being tortured, said: “I am God’s wheat; I am ground by the teeth of beasts.”

“But the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire.” The chaff means the wicked, who have no good works and are found light and easily carried toward every vanity of the world. They will be burned in a fire that will never be extinguished.

## CHAPTER V  
### Treatise on the Lord’s Baptism

“Then Jesus came from Galilee to the Jordan.” “Then” means when the people themselves were going out to John.

According to the Gospels and the chronicles, we find that John went out into the wilderness in the twenty-ninth year of his life, and that the Lord came to baptism at the beginning of his thirtieth year. At the age of thirty the whole world will rise again, whatever the age at which anyone may have died. Thus the Apostle says: “Until we all attain to a perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ.” Adam was also created at such an age.

The Lord came to John’s baptism for three reasons.

First, so that through the water of the Jordan he might sanctify the streams of all waters.

Second, so that he might fulfill the righteousness of the entire Law and provide an example of humility. He did not disdain to be baptized by his servant; thus the Creator was baptized by his creature.

Third, so that he might prove that John’s baptism had been commanded by him and by the Father.

“But John tried to prevent him, saying.” Out of humility, as was fitting, John spoke these words to the Creator. For he knew that the Lord was to be baptized by him, as he himself said: “Upon whomever you see the Spirit of the Lord descending and remaining, he is the one who baptizes.”

It is evident from the words “I must be baptized by you” that he knew him. In the words that he had said above, “This is the one who baptizes,” John knew that the Lord would baptize his faithful. That is, whoever of his faithful performs the baptism, the Lord himself will be the one baptizing through them.

“But Jesus answered and said to him: ‘Allow it now.’” That is: “Permit me to act in this way for the present, so that I may be baptized by you, and afterward you may be baptized by me. Thus, having taken the form of a servant, I may fulfill the humility appropriate to it. Otherwise, know that on the day of judgment you will be baptized by me.”

“Allow” is an imperative verb, derived from *sino*, “I allow.” *Now* is an adverb signifying the present time [Col. 1295A].

“For thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness.” He did not add “the righteousness of his nature” or “of the Law,” but said “all righteousness,” so that we might understand all of these.

“Then he allowed him.” That is, he consented to what he had previously feared.

Just as blessed Peter was terrified that the Creator of all things should humble himself to wash his feet, so John was afraid to place his hands upon the Creator. But Peter was told: “Unless I wash you, you will have no share with me.” Likewise John was told: “Allow it to happen as I wish, and what you wish will happen.” The consequence is: “If you do not do my will, neither will I do yours.”

“When Jesus had been baptized, he immediately came up from the water; and behold, the heavens were opened.” The Trinity is shown here, and everything happens for our sake, so that we may know how we ought to believe in the Lord our Father.

Behold, our Lord is baptized. The voice of the Father giving testimony to the Son is heard. The Spirit appears in the form of a dove.

The heavens are opened not by the physical elements being torn apart, but to spiritual eyes. Ezekiel also relates, at the beginning of his book, that he saw them opened.

“And the dove sat upon him.” So that no one would think that a voice had been produced for John.

Just as that star was created for the purpose of serving the Lord’s mystery at that time and afterward did not appear, so they also say concerning the dove that it was created for the purpose of displaying the Holy Spirit through it and afterward did not appear.

I heard this handed down by the man who first explained the Gospel to me—but neither Jerome nor Bede says anything about it: that it was a real dove, possessing real flesh and a real body.

“This is my beloved Son.” He is not adopted, like Israel, but proper to me, whom I begot before the ages.

“Beloved” in a unique sense.

All these things were displayed for our sake. Almighty God the Father already knew the Son, because he was one God with him. The Holy Spirit was also in him and with him, because the inseparable Trinity—the Holy Spirit with the Father and the Son—is one.

But these things were displayed so that we might recognize the Trinity and believe that it is one.

The fact that the heavens were shown to be opened there signifies that when a human being is baptized, the door of the heavenly kingdom is opened. That door had been closed to the human race after the sin of the first-formed man, with a cherub placed as guardian.

The flame that had been set between us is extinguished when a human being is immersed in the waters of holy baptism. The fact that the Holy Spirit was seen to descend upon him shows that, through baptism and after baptism, through the invocation of the priests, the Spirit descends upon every believer [Col. 1295D].

But when it says that the Spirit remained upon him, this pertains especially to our Lord. It was his distinctive property that, after filling him once, the Spirit never departed from him, because he did not drive the Spirit away through any sin; he was free from sin.

Thus the Spirit comes upon the saints and withdraws for a time. Yet he is always with them for their protection and to preserve love of neighbor, as the Lord said to the disciples: “He will be in you, and he will remain with you.”

## CHAPTER VI  
### On the Lord’s Temptation

“Then Jesus was led by the Spirit into the wilderness.” The word “then,” which is an adverb of time, refers to what he had said: “Jesus came to the Jordan.” At that very time, after his baptism, he went out into the wilderness and fasted.

On that same day, as we hold by the tradition of our elders, he turned water into wine, and some of the disciples believed in him. Then Jesus was led into the wilderness, because Luke says: “Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan and was led by the Spirit into the wilderness for forty days and was tempted by the devil.”

The wilderness was a place beyond the Jordan. It was called wilderness because it was unsuitable for cultivation; and because it was not valued, it had been abandoned. Theudas led four thousand people there from Jerusalem [Col. 1296B].

“Led by the Spirit”—that is, by his Holy Spirit, of whom the evangelist says that he returned from the Jordan full of the Holy Spirit.

It was fitting that his own Spirit should lead him to the place where the evil spirit would find him for the purpose of tempting him.

He also gave us an example, so that after receiving baptism we might flee the pomps of this world. At baptism we gave sureties that we would renounce the devil and his pomps.

“To be tempted by the devil.” After the Lord had become a young man, the devil clung to him through temptation, just as he does to other human beings. But now, with his weapons restored, he began the battle more vigorously, as the teachers relate.

At his baptism he heard the voice saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” He wished to investigate whether he was the true Son of God who had been foretold through the prophets, or an adopted son, as he had heard concerning Israel: “Israel is my firstborn son” [Col. 1296C].

The Lord knew that Satan was very eager to tempt him and was looking for an opportunity. Like a strong combatant, he did not deny him the field in which he could fight with him.

Indeed, the devil did not find in him an excessive love of the serpent’s head, as Eve had; he did not find a love of women, as Solomon had; nor prostitutes, as Samson had; nor did he have a wife, as Job did. Therefore the devil had no means or person through whom he could deceive him.

He resorted to that by which the whole world is endangered: through his suggestion, namely, gluttony, greed, and vainglory.

He took on an aerial form and approached him, so that he could be seen by a human being. But the Lord provided the opportunity by which he knew that the devil wished to tempt him.

“He fasted forty days, and afterward he was hungry.” If he had not become hungry, perhaps, because of the voice he had heard and because he saw him living without sin, the devil would not have approached him to tempt him.

He saw him hungry and judged him inferior to Moses and Elijah, concerning whom nothing of this kind is reported—that they had become hungry. And because he was hungry, the Lord allowed the devil to perceive it through the gesture of his body. For otherwise the devil cannot know the thoughts of human beings.

And when he had fasted forty days and nights. If he had not added “nights,” it might be thought that he fasted during the days and ate at night. But ten multiplied by four makes forty, because the one who carefully keeps the Decalogue joins it with the Gospel, which has been set forth by the four evangelists. This number is always applied in Holy Scripture to repentance and tribulation, as in this passage and in the Old Testament, where the world was destroyed by water for forty days, and the people of Israel were wearied by the labor of their journey in the wilderness for forty days and years. Moses abstained for forty days a second time in order to receive the law; and Elijah did likewise, in order to be freed from the evil of persecution. And if we wish to conquer the devil, or to be freed from the persecutions of this present age, or even to reach the promised land—that is, eternal life—then, following the Lord’s example, let us fast for forty days not only from food but also from every vice, and afflict our flesh fortyfold.

“Say that these stones become bread.” In a similar way, as he had first said to the human being, “Taste, and you will be like gods,” so now he tempts him regarding gluttony, then regarding avarice, and finally regarding vainglory, because he thought that he would conquer in the same way as he had conquered the one whom God had instructed personally. Luke followed the historical order of the Lord’s temptation, whereas Matthew followed the order of Adam’s temptation.

For thus he said to Adam: “Taste”—behold, gluttony. “You will be like gods”—behold, avarice, because avarice concerns not only the acquisition of money but also honor, as Paul indicates when he says of the Lord: “He did not regard equality with the Lord as a thing to be seized.” As though he were saying plainly: If he had not been equal by nature, and had wished to be equal to the Lord, it would have been regarded as robbery. After avarice he persuades him toward vainglory: “knowing good and evil,” because wishing to know evil contributes to no progress except vainglory.

In the same order the devil tempts the Lord: first regarding gluttony, second regarding avarice, when he showed him all the kingdoms of the world, and third regarding vainglory, although Matthew does not narrate them in that order. It should also be noted that the first two temptations took place in the wilderness, whereas the third took place in Jerusalem, upon the pinnacle of the temple.

Jesus answered him: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God.” As though he were saying plainly: Why do you urge me to ask for earthly bread, when body and soul can live by the word of God? Thus Moses, intent for forty days upon the utterances of God and nourished by the utterances of God, did not hunger even in the flesh. Moses likewise said to the children of Israel: “The Lord fed you with manna for forty years, so that you might know that man does not live by bread alone, but can be refreshed by the word of God.”

We must retain in our minds what the Lord said: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God,” so that we may always be more concerned to nourish with the word of God the soul that will live forever than the body that will one day die. For the soul that is not nourished by the word of God plainly lies dead.

Then the devil took him to the holy city. Just as the Lord voluntarily went into the wilderness, so also he went up to the holy city in order to give the tempter an opportunity to approach him. Jerusalem is called holy because of the Lord’s temple and altar, and because of its religious observance and the many good men who were still there. Even after the Lord’s ascension, all the apostles, as long as they remained there, worshiped in the temple.

And he set him upon the pinnacle of the temple. It was customary in that province to make flat roofs, so that people could walk upon them. The temple had been constructed in this manner, and around it there were railings so that no one might accidentally fall to the ground; you frequently hear of this in the Gospels. The priests were accustomed to read the law there and expound it to the crowds standing below. From this place, therefore, the devil urged the Lord to leap down to the ground, so that he might be seen by the crowds and praised if he remained unharmed.

Just as there was vainglory when he said, “knowing evil,” so there would be vainglory in leaping from the height down to the ground, with no benefit in either case.

“If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down.” “Downward” is an adverb of place. Throughout all the temptations he investigates in what manner he might be the Son of God, whether adopted or proper. But the Lord, who had come to give us an example both in words and in deeds, both left the devil uncertain and indicated to us what we ought to do when we are tempted: namely, recall to mind the words of sacred utterance and restrain our temptations by those same words.

The devil, however, urges this not by his own simple word, but with an addition from divine Scripture, saying: “It is written, ‘He has commanded his angels concerning you,’ and ‘They will take you up in their hands, lest you perhaps strike your foot against a stone.’” This entire psalm was written about King Hezekiah, concerning the protection that the Lord gave him against Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians; yet it can be understood of every elect person. But because the devil believed that a mere human being was God, he set before him this example, which had been spoken concerning a righteous man.

Jesus said to him again. “Again” must be joined in this way, because it is an adverb, and these are the evangelist’s words; it has the sense “a second time.” Afterward one must insert, “It is written,” because this is the Lord’s word, not the other. As though he were saying plainly to the devil: For this reason neither I nor any other human being ought to listen to you, because there is a divine utterance that forbids me and everyone else to seek God for vainglory and for things that have no usefulness.

Again the devil took him to a very high mountain. This temptation took place in the wilderness together with the first temptation. By this mountain we understand either Tabor or Hermon, but more truly Tabor. And he showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory. Just as almighty God, according to the purpose of the devil’s temptation, permitted him to show the higher things of which you have heard, so it may be that he permitted him to show the whole world in a single vision, in the manner in which we also read that blessed Benedict saw it.

Or it may be a certain figure frequently found in divine Scripture, called in Greek *synecdoche*, when the whole is stated while a part is understood. That is, he showed him some part and promised him that he would give him the remainder together with the whole.

The glory of the world is gold and gems; this is what the world glories in. And “the kingdoms of the world” means the people inhabiting the world. Whatever worldly people can possess, this is their confidence; yet they do nothing else with it except glory and display. For they do not plow with it or perform any other necessary work; they merely live, while those who carry and guard these things are burdened by them day and night.

He said to him: “I will give you all these things, if you will fall down and worship me.” Just as it was a lie when he said, “I will set my throne in the north and I will be like the Most High,” so this also would have been a lie if the Lord had worshiped him when he said, “I will give you all these things.” But the devil does not care about the progress of those whom he deceives, nor does he care or fear that he will later be found a liar, provided only that he can now deceive whomever he wishes. He did the same with Adam when he said: “You will be like gods.”

It must be understood, according to his own statement, that everyone who worships the devil falls—and not only the one who worships, but also the one who listens to him, because to worship is to venerate. A person venerates him when he prefers his suggestions to God’s commands, listens to him, and abandons the Lord who forbids him.

Then Jesus said to him: “Go, Satan.” In the other suggestions the Lord did not answer the devil with such force as in this one, because he had spoken with excessive pride when he ordered himself to be worshiped either by God or by a mere human being; and as perverse as he was, so perversely he spoke. The Lord said to him: “Go, Satan”—that is, into the abyss or into perdition. He did not refute Peter with a similar answer, for he said to him: “Go behind me”—that is, follow my will.

“You shall worship the Lord your God.” In our language, “to worship” is understood in two ways. We say “to worship” when we mean to incline oneself. Hence it is written: “So-and-so worshiped the king”—that is, he inclined himself. To worship in the higher sense is to offer the worship owed to the Lord, as it is written: “Solomon worshiped the Lord.” In this sense, therefore, the ancients were commanded not to worship foreign gods or anyone except the Lord alone. Hence it is said: “You shall worship the Lord your God.”

To worship means to believe in the Lord with complete faith, to love him with one’s whole heart, to ask him for the remission of sins, and to hope from him for all good things, both present and future. In Greek, however, a distinction is made here: worship directed toward God is called *proskynēsai*, προσκυνῆσαι, whereas worship directed toward a human being is called *klinein*, κλίνειν.

“And you shall serve him alone.” What does the Lord mean by saying, “You shall serve him alone,” when the apostle Paul says that we are to serve one another through charity? Did the Lord command one thing and Paul another? No. There is a service that belongs to God alone and not to human beings, a service that must be offered to no one else but God alone: namely, to believe in him with firm faith, to place all one’s hope in him, to offer sacrifices to him, to render divine worship to him, and the other things that belong to God alone.

In the Greek language also there is a similar distinction concerning this matter. Service directed toward a human being is called *douleusis*, δούλευσις, and a servant is called *doulos*, δοῦλος. But the service that belongs to God alone is called *latreusis*, λάτρευσις. Thus in the song of Zechariah it does not say *douleusate*, δουλεύσατε, but *latreuein*, λατρεύειν αὐτῷ—“let us serve him.”

We must know these distinctions between creature and Creator, so that we do not ask any saint for the remission of sins, but strive through them to obtain that it may be given to us by God. Nor should we believe in anyone except God. We believe the saints, but we do not believe in the saints.

Then the devil left him; and behold, angels came and ministered to him. What the devil had urged God to do, the angels did for him: that is, they worshiped him, to show that he himself deserved to be worshiped, not the devil. The angels ministered so that the dignity of the victor might be confirmed.

The Lord conquered all these temptations by patience, so that he might provide us with an example of patience. If the one who is the Creator, and who could have plunged his tempter into the abyss by a single word, endured him and answered him with the words of sacred utterance, then we too, whenever we are tempted visibly or spiritually, should always recall to mind what God has commanded, because the Creator must be heard, not the devil.

“Devil” is interpreted in Hebrew as “flowing downward,” because he fell from heaven. In Greek it means “accuser,” because he charges the innocence of the elect with fabricated accusations. Hence it is said in the Apocalypse: “The accuser of our brothers has been cast down, who accused them before our God day and night.” “Satan” in Latin means “adversary,” because he is always opposed to the virtues of the saints.

It should be noted, moreover, that all the testimonies which the Lord brought forth in this struggle he took from Deuteronomy. It was right for the Lord to take them from Deuteronomy, for there the law is more perfect, because what is done a second time is done better. *Deuteronomy* means “second law”: *deuteros* in Greek means “second,” and *nomos* means “law.” The *u* must not be separated from the *e*, for then it would seem to have the sense of the preposition *de* and the noun *uterus*; rather, it is *Deuteronomium*, because among the Greeks it is composed of two nouns. It is not feminine in Greek but masculine.

## Chapter VII. That when John had been handed over, the Lord began to preach

When he had heard that John had been handed over, he withdrew into Galilee. Before John had been handed over, the Lord was preaching; but after John’s imprisonment he began to preach more earnestly, so that the people would not lack a teacher of salvation.

He came from the wilderness, where he had been tempted; to Nazareth, where he had been brought up. And leaving that very Nazareth because of its unbelief, he went to Capernaum, in the territory of Zebulun and Naphtali.

In this land Israel was first taken captive by the Assyrians, and it was fitting that the Lord should begin to preach there, where an enemy had once ruled because of sins. Zebulun is interpreted as “dwelling of beauty.” Naphtali likewise conveys the same idea; it is said to mean “of one who dwells,” because before God came into this world everyone sat in the darkness of ignorance. But through Christ there arose a light that enlightens every human being coming into this world.

And we were under the shadow of death, because, in comparison with the second death, death in this age is a shadow; in the future age it will be real, because it will be eternal.

From that time Jesus began to preach and to say. “From that time” means after John had been sent into prison, because when the law ceased, the Gospel succeeded it.

“Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near.” The fact that the Lord preaches the same things as John shows that he is the son of the one by whom John was sent. We explained above how the kingdom of heaven has drawn near. It has drawn near because it was already close at hand, after the completion of the preaching, passion, and ascension of the Lord, when the way to eternal life was to be opened to those who genuinely repent—that is, who punish their former manner of life within themselves and begin a new one. For *poenitentia*—repentance—is so called as if from *punientia*—punishment.

## Chapter VIII. On the calling of the apostles

As Jesus was walking beside the Sea of Galilee, he saw two brothers. The evangelists appear to write differently about this calling, but to those who understand, they are not contradictory.

First occurred what John records: blessed Andrew heard John’s testimony about Christ, came to him, and remained with him. Afterward he brought his brother Simon, and they came to know him; but again they returned to their work.

Then occurred what Luke relates: how Jesus entered Peter’s boat and preached from it; after the preaching he ordered him to let down the nets for a catch and said to Peter: “From now on you will be catching people.” But Peter then brought the boat to shore, followed him for some time, and returned again to the boat. He had brought it to shore for this reason.

Now, however, leaving their nets and the boat, they followed him so that they might always be with him. The same is to be understood of James and John: they had believed in him earlier, when he changed water into wine, but they did not follow him continuously until this moment.

The teachers of the Church say that at that time some manifestation of divinity shone forth in his face and drew them to him, so that from then on they followed him continually. They report that the divinity itself shone in his face three times during his life in the flesh: first when he called the disciples; second when he drove the buyers and sellers from the temple; and third when he was transfigured on the mountain. But at that time the majesty was so great that the disciples could not bear it. Hence it is written: “They fell upon their faces.”

What the Sea of Galilee signifies we shall explain later. Likewise, concerning the apostles, when we have spoken about the others in their catalogue, we shall also speak about these.

“Come after me, and I will make you become fishers of people.” The preaching is appropriately compared with fishing, because just as a net has many meshes, so preaching has many testimonies. Just as the net catches small and large fish, so preaching catches the wise and the foolish. The sea is this present age, in which people continually persecute one another. As Peter began with fish, so afterward he caught people with the word.

Those two disciples were called sons of Zebedee after this Zebedee. Zebedee is said to mean “given” or “flowing.” He was called by this fitting word because he flowed away and withdrew from the Lord’s preaching; for this reason he was also abandoned by his sons.

“Repairing their nets” means mending them, because the nets were old. Leaving their nets and their father, they followed him. Now it becomes clear how they followed him with complete determination. This was not said in the other appearances.

## Chapter IX. On the Lord’s first works of virtue

And Jesus went about all Galilee, teaching. The diligence of the teaching Lord is shown by the fact that he did not wait for the people to come to him; he himself came to them, giving blessed teachers and bishops an example of what they ought to do for the peoples subject to them.

Teaching throughout Galilee. By saying “throughout,” he shows that he taught without respect of persons: teaching those present and preaching to those who came.

In their synagogues. Throughout all the cities, the Jews held synagogues on the Sabbath days and on the other feasts. On those days they did nothing else—apart from food and drink—but devoted themselves to reading and prayer. And *synagogue* means “assembly.”

And preaching the Gospel of the kingdom. The Gospel of the kingdom is the good news of the heavenly kingdom, because all preachers ought to preach this, since Christians ought to labor in order to attain eternal life.

Healing every sickness. That is, of souls. For just as the body is said to be sick when it cannot perform its functions, so the soul that is sluggish in God’s commandments is said to languish.

And every disease. This refers to bodily diseases; and it is a synecdochic figure, in which a part is understood from the whole.

His fame went throughout all Syria. “Fame” means reputation.

…an evil than which none is swifter.

Syria: Tyre and Sidon are understood here, in which Syrians lived.

And they brought him all who were suffering. Those who had lesser illnesses.

Those seized by torments. He wishes to indicate more severe illnesses, because *tormenta* is derived from *torquere*, “to torture.”

And those who had demons. That is, those concerning whom it was certain that they were held without interruption.

Lunatics. They too were demoniacs; but, for the purpose of defaming the Creator, the demons tormented them at one time and released them at another, so that the Creator might be defamed—the Creator who had made the moon good. There are certain illnesses that do more harm under one moon than under another, because the body increases and decreases together with the elements from which it was created. For the human being was made from earth, water, fire, and air.

“Paralytic” is called in Greek *paralyticus* and in Latin *dissolutus*, “relaxed” or “loosed”; it denotes one who, through an effusion of blood, has lost the functions of his body.

And great crowds followed him. For this reason he said to the disciples: “The harvest is great”—from Galilee, where he had been brought up. For there are two Galilees: this one belonging to the Jews, around Tiberias and the lake of Gennesaret, in the tribe of Zebulun; and another Galilee of the Gentiles, near the borders of the Tyrians, where Solomon gave Hiram twenty cities of the kingdom. It belongs to the portion of the tribe of Naphtali and to the Decapolis.

*Decapolis* is a Greek name and means “of ten cities.” For *polis* in Greek means “city” in Latin, and *deka* means “ten”; hence the compound name *Decapolis*. It is a region beyond the Jordan containing ten cities.

And from Jerusalem, the royal city, and from Judea. Judea, a region of Palestine, was named from Judah, from whom that land had its kings. Its length begins at the village of Arpha and extends to the village of Juliad; its width reaches from Mount Lebanon to the lake of Tiberias.

And from beyond the Jordan. That is, from those two and a half tribes to which Moses gave possession beyond the Jordan.

## Chapter X. On the eight beatitudes

When Jesus saw the crowds, he went up onto a mountain. The Lord chose three places of refuge for himself whenever great crowds gathered to hear his words: this mountain, Tabor; the lake of Gennesaret; and the Lord’s temple.

There were also six groups among the crowds who followed him, with different motives: first, the disciples, because of their love, to hear his preaching; others because they desired healing; others because they wished, out of admiration, to see him perform miracles; others because of their need, wishing to be satisfied by him or to receive some alms in coins or in another form; but the Pharisees and their attendants came for the purpose of criticism.

He went up onto a mountain: on the higher part of the mountain, speaking more privately to the disciples; but in the lower places, to the crowds, where he also fed five thousand people.

And when he had sat down. That is, separated from the crowds. God’s sitting means spiritually that he was incarnate, because, as it were, in becoming incarnate he contracted himself—that is, he was not such as he is in his divinity.

His disciples came to him. They came like eager people, like members of his household, like the elect separated from the crowds, worthy to hear the mystery of the kingdom of heaven, which the crowds could not hear.

And opening his mouth. He who had formerly opened the mouths of the prophets.

He taught them. He who had once taught through legislators and prophets now taught through himself, saying:

“Blessed are the poor in spirit.” He does not simply say “the poor,” but adds “in spirit,” because many are poor unwillingly. But he speaks of those who, although they could be rich, pursue poverty for God’s sake, or who have no desire to possess, as did the apostles to whom he was speaking. Or “poor in spirit” means humble, concerning whom it is written: “He will save the humble in spirit.” And concerning them Isaiah says: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me; he has sent me to announce good news to the poor.” For theirs is the kingdom of heaven—that is, eternal life.

“Blessed are the meek.” That is, the gentle. The Lord commanded us to learn this virtue from him, saying: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart.” *Mansuetus*, “gentle,” is said to derive from *manu assuetus*, “accustomed to the hand.” These are those who do not despise others but love and receive everyone as a neighbor; who are not proud and do not disdain the rest.

“They will possess the earth.” Not this earth, which produces thorns and thistles, and which the most savage and proud possess more fully, but that earth of which it is said: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living.” Describing its possessor, the psalmist says, as though speaking of the devil already conquered: “Proceed prosperously, advance, and reign, because of truth and meekness and righteousness,” and so forth. Through these three things that land of the Lord is possessed: truth, meekness, and righteousness.

“Blessed are those who mourn.” There is an evil mourning: to mourn over earthly loss, because the sorrow of this age produces death. And blessed Gregory says: “Far be it that any of the faithful should mourn the destruction of the world; a Christian ought to mourn neither over the world nor over anything worldly.”

But there is a good mourning, which Christians ought to have. Their mourning consists in remembering that they have transgressed God’s commandments or failed to do what belongs to God; or they ought to mourn for their neighbors who deviate from God, as Samuel mourned that Saul had transgressed God’s commands. The mourning of the perfect also consists in grieving over the delay of eternal life and longing for the vision of God.

Therefore those who mourn either in remembrance of their own sins, or of the sins of their neighbors, or because of the future judgment, or because they are pilgrims away from the heavenly homeland, will be comforted with eternal consolation, which will have no end.

“Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness.” Those who always practice righteousness—that is, do what is just—and always desire to do more, suffering, as it were, the hunger to act: they will be filled with eternal goods, which “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the human heart,” which God has prepared for those who love him.

“Blessed are the merciful, for they will obtain mercy.” Mercy is not found only in earthly matters but also in spiritual matters, so that we may help our neighbors wherever we can. Whoever does not help one who is perishing, if he is able, kills him; and the one who does this and the one who consents to the one doing it are equal.

Mercy is called *misericordia*, “mercy,” from a sorrowful heart. If we cannot do something, let us at least grieve in our heart; this applies to earthly losses and to offenses committed against us. But whoever sins against God is not ours to forgive, unless we believe that God has already forgiven him.

The resurrection of Lazarus is an example for us. The disciples did not release him before the Lord had raised him. Nor can the pastor of the Church absolve a sinner from sins until he has been raised—that is, until he has been changed in soul. As long as he remains in will or in deed as he was before, he is promised forgiveness of sins in vain.

Of such people the Lord says: “It is not good to recognize a person in judgment.” And again: “Do not incline your heart to the right or to the left.” Likewise: “If a man sins against a man, God can be appeased on his behalf; but if a man sins against God, who will pray for him?”

“Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God.” Those are pure in heart whose conscience is not troubled by a criminal sin, or who think of nothing except what is good. The pure God will be seen by the pure in heart in this age with the eyes of the heart, and in the future life under a certain image, face to face.

“Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called sons of God.” *Pacifici*, “peacemakers,” is a compound word from *pax*, “peace,” and *facio*, “I make.” Those are peacemakers who first make peace within themselves regarding their vices, so that vices do not fight against virtues, but who have God at peace with them. Then they strive to make peace among their neighbors in what is good, not in what is evil.

For the peace that the wicked possess is not good, and the righteous person ought neither to consent to it nor to share in it, because while we ought to love our neighbor, we ought to hate his vice.

“Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” These are those who do good and receive evil in return for those good things: Saint Lampert, Saint Leodegarius, and countless others. The same applies to those who suffer persecution for Christ, as all the martyrs did.

“Blessed are you when people curse you, persecute you, and speak every evil against you falsely because of me.” He explains this eighth beatitude, showing how persecution for righteousness is to be endured. If they speak evil of us unjustly and lie; if they persecute us unjustly; if they speak every evil while lying—then we are blessed. But if they speak the truth, we will not be blessed.

And if we suffer persecution because of our sins, we will not immediately be blessed; but if we endure patiently and acknowledge that it is just, and yet not as much as we deserve, we will eventually attain blessedness, provided that we do not add further offenses to those that lie ahead.

“Rejoice and exult, for behold, your reward is great in heaven.” If we are struck by adversity while doing good, we can be sure, if we endure patiently, that we will receive a reward in the future. But if we do something good and prosperity smiles upon us, we ought to fear lest we receive our reward here for the good things we have done. If we both do evil and enjoy prosperity, we can be sure of hell. If we are also suffering evil and yet murmur about those very evils, we can be sure that through these evils we will reach worse things.

Christ fulfilled all these beatitudes, because he taught nothing that he had not first fulfilled himself. He was poor both in possessions and in heart, for he said: “The Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.” He was meek, for he said: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart.” He mourned the sins of others, for when he saw the city, he wept over it. He hungered and thirsted for righteousness, for he said: “My food is to do the will of my Father.” He was merciful, for he said: “I desire mercy and not sacrifice.” He was pure in heart, for he said: “Be holy, because I am holy.” He was a peacemaker, for he said: “I leave you my peace.” He suffered persecution, for he said: “If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you.”

For thus they persecuted the prophets who were before you. They expelled Samuel from his position of leadership; they cut Isaiah in pieces; they drove Elijah from the land; they stoned Jeremiah. No one has ever been good in this age who did not suffer persecution in this age. Therefore rejoice in persecutions, if you wish to be companions in the beatitudes.

“You are the salt of the earth.” Salt is so called because it leaps forth from fire. There are many kinds of salt. There is, however, natural salt, necessary for every food. It gives flavor to dishes and arouses eagerness and appetite for all foods; from it comes the pleasure and greatest enjoyment of every meal. All animals are delighted by it once they have tasted it. It tightens and dries bodies; it also preserves the dead from the corruption of decay, so that they endure.

All this nature of salt applies spiritually to teachers. For they create an appetite for the spiritual food of Scripture, which previously seemed worthless to us; through their explanation it becomes delightful to us. It is desired by all living creatures, because the teaching of the apostles is received by all nations. It constricts bodies, as occurs through teaching when the lustful become chaste; it drives away flies, that is, demons.

And therefore the Lord rightly said to them: “You are the salt of the earth”—that is, of those dwelling on earth.

“But if the salt has lost its savor, with what will it be salted?” If a teacher has gone astray, by what teacher will he be corrected? “It is good for nothing any longer except to be thrown out and trampled underfoot by people.” Just as salt is harmful in every field, because every land becomes sterile through it, so we read that it was scattered over destroyed cities, lest anyone afterward wish to dwell there. We read that Abimelech did this; Aelius Arianus writes of Jerusalem.

By this comparison, if a teacher turns to heresy, he is expelled from the Church and held in contempt by all, so that no greeting is even given him; rather, he is rejected by everyone, as Paul says: “Avoid a heretical person after the first and second correction.”

“You are the light of the world.” You are light by participating in that light of which it is written: “He was the true light that enlightens every human being.” For just as all harmful things are driven away by light—thieves, harmful beasts, and the phantoms of demons—so through the preaching of the apostles all things harmful to souls have been exposed and rejected, and the hearts of believers have been enlightened.

“A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden.” By “city” he means the Church, built upon the Lord. The apostles ought to make it known to all nations, so that all his elect may be gathered to it, if not bodily, then in heart, and so that it may be called *catholic*, that is, universal.

“Nor do they light a lamp and place it under a measure, but upon a lampstand”—that is, the evangelical teaching, exalted in the preachers, so that it may be perfectly known to everyone who is in the Church. They ought not to place it under a measure—that is, hide it through some fear or dread of anyone—but so that people may see their good works for the building up and advancement of their souls.

“And glorify your Father who is in heaven.” You should not seek to be praised, but God, whose gift it is if there is anything good in you.

“Do not think that I came to abolish the law or the prophets.” By “think” he means “consider” that he came to loosen, dissolve, or annihilate. “I did not come to abolish but to fulfill”: where it was not properly understood, I came to explain it, as in the matter of sending away a wife. Where perfection was lacking, I wish to add it, as in the matter of murder, because I first wish to cut away anger.

For, as blessed Augustine says: “All things whatsoever were truly commanded to the ancients, apart from the figurative commandments, and those things which the legislator granted them because of the hardness of their hearts, are to be retained.”

From this passage he confirms the point: “Amen, I say to you”—that is, “I tell you the truth.”

“Until heaven and earth pass away, one iota or one apex will not pass from the law until all things are accomplished.” As though he were saying: Until heaven and earth pass away, even the things signified by the iota and the apex in the law will not pass away, but will be fulfilled by my elect.

The iota is both Hebrew and Greek. In Hebrew it is called *Iot*, in Greek *Iota*, and in Latin [it is] *i*. An apex is called a *titulus*, a mark that among the ancients was placed above certain letters, either to distinguish them or to show that a letter was to be doubled.

For example, when *populus* signifies “the people,” the apex was not placed above it; but when it signified a tree, an apex was placed above it, to remind the reader that he should depart from the customary meaning and that the syllable was long. It was also placed to indicate doubling, as in *Alleluia*, because there ought to be two *l*s; one was written, with an apex above it, and from this it was understood that the letter was to be doubled. Likewise, in “Luia” an apex was placed above the *i* to show that the *i* was to be doubled.

The Lord therefore shows that such distinctions are not to be passed over in divine Scripture, because if they were neglected, the meaning too would perish along with them.

In another interpretation, *i*, the iota, signifies ten among the Greeks without an apex, and ten thousand with an apex. From this we can infer that if the ten words of the law are not kept spiritually by us, ten thousand talents will be demanded from us, according to the Lord’s parable about the servant who was brought before the king owing ten thousand talents.

According to the Latins, *i* signifies one; an apex placed above it signifies one thousand. From this we may believe that we will be debtors for a thousand quadrantes and one, and will not depart until we repay that one.

“Therefore whoever loosens one of these least commandments and teaches people to do so will be called least in the kingdom of heaven.” He says plainly: Every teacher who loosens—that is, dissolves—and despises one of these least commandments, or who does not fulfill it, will be called least in the kingdom of heaven—that is, in the present Church. For when a person’s life is despised, it follows that his preaching is condemned.

“But whoever does them and teaches them will be called great in the kingdom of heaven.” For it is fitting that those who build up the Church by word and example should be held in honor, just as Paul says: “Let presbyters be considered worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in the word.”

## Chapter XI. On the fulfillment of the law
I say to you: He now begins to fulfill the Law. Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven. The righteousness of the Pharisees is not to kill, not to commit adultery, not to steal, and to give tithes and firstfruits from everything they possess. The righteousness of Christ and of all Christians is not to hate, not to lust, to love one’s neighbor for God’s sake, and to love persecutors from the heart. The meaning, therefore, is this: The Pharisees regard murders and thefts as crimes; my disciples must also avoid wicked thoughts and words.

But whoever kills will be liable to judgment. “Judgment” means the judgment of death. You have heard that it was said to the ancients: “You shall not kill.” Behold the righteousness of the Pharisees. But I say to you—I, the new man, lay down new commands for you—that everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment. Behold the righteousness of Christians. In the Gospel, the person who hates his brother is held liable to the same punishment as the person who killed someone under the old dispensation.

It must be understood that wherever this book says “to the ancients,” “to the fathers” is implied: God approves that command and wishes it to be observed until heaven and earth pass away. But where “to the ancients” is not added, God did not command it; Moses permitted it to a people still crude and carnal. If he had commanded it to them, he understood that they would not do it. Thus the Lord says concerning the dismissal of a wife: “Moses, because of the hardness of your hearts, wrote this commandment for you; but from the beginning it was not so.” But whoever says to his brother, “Raca,” will be liable to the council.

All this belongs to the righteousness of Christians. He has now removed hidden anger from the heart; now he removes anger expressed in speech by imposing a greater punishment. “Raca” is an interjection among the Hebrews and merely indicates an angry disposition. It may be rendered “empty” or “without a brain.” We use this insult in ordinary speech, since someone who has no brain is not of sound mind. It is as though he said: Whoever is so stirred by anger that he displays it in speech to his neighbor must be punished more severely than the person who, angry in his heart, did not express it in words. Therefore, in his case, deliberation must now be held concerning the punishment by which he is to be chastised.

In the first case there is hidden anger, and death that is quickly ended by the sword. In the second, anger expressed in speech: thought is already being given to the kind of torment by which the person is to die. In the third, anger accompanied by insult, and a determination of how many punishments of hell he must be handed over to. *Rachus* is also said in Greek to mean “ragged” or “clothed in rags,” but the preceding interpretation is better.

But whoever says, “Fool”—“to his brother” is understood here, as in the preceding cases—for we have no other brother except the one who confesses with us that he has the same Father in heaven, that is, every Christian—will be liable to the fire of Gehenna. In the case of the person who burst out in anger against his brother’s fault, there is no longer a council to be held; rather, he is assigned by an open sentence to avenging flames. And why is the name “fool” imposed on a brother? Because he likewise believes in God, as we do, and trusts that he possesses the Holy Spirit. For whoever does not honor his brother wrongs the Holy Spirit who dwells in him, as Peter says to Ananias: “You have not lied to men but to God.”

If, therefore, you offer your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you—“gift” here means not only sacrifice but also every prayer, since in prayer itself we say, “Forgive us, as we also forgive”—and when he says, “because your brother has something against you,” this means that he has some just complaint against you, because you have injured him in some way, leave your gift there before the altar and go first to be reconciled to your brother.

If he is nearby, you must go to him on foot. But if he is far away, you must go to him in spirit and promise the Lord that, as soon as you can, you will go to him bodily as well and make amends for whatever harm you have inflicted on him. Yet many ask forgiveness in words and do not repair the harm they have done to him.
