Such forgiveness is not acceptable to God, because, as blessed Jerome says concerning Judas: “If a man does not destroy or make amends for his deed, he asks for repentance in vain; his sin increases daily, although he himself is dead and wants to obtain forgiveness.”

For example, someone wrongfully acquires a man or takes another person’s landed property, then comes to confession and says: “It is my fault; I sinned in such-and-such an action. Assign me a penance.” And the confessor says to him: “Abstain from wine and meat for such-and-such a period.” O what obvious deception! That man’s grandsons serve him every day, and at the end of the world there will be a hundred or two hundred servants descended from that one man. Yet this deceiver says to him: “You will be saved.” He retains the landed property and gold that he took, and abstains from his own wine; consequently, tomorrow he will have more solidi than he would have had if he had drunk.

O devilish confessor, if you do not know how to save him, why do you know how to destroy yourself? You ought to have said: “Destroy the deed, and then accept a penance. Why did you love gold more than the Lord, who forbade these things to you?” Was not the devil in evil when his soul departed from his body, and does the evil still increase? Does John not say, “There is sin unto death; I do not say that anyone should pray for it”? Fool, in whatever direction a tree falls, there it will remain.

We can understand both expressions: “Be reconciled to your brother,” that is, bring him back to peace with you; and “be reconciled with your brother,” that is, become reconciled to him yourself.

Be well-disposed toward your adversary. Some explain this saying with reference to the devil, so that we should be kind toward him and not do evil, because then he will be tormented more greatly for the evils he has suggested to us than because of our enemies. For above he commanded us to reconcile ourselves with them, and below he will command us: “Love your enemies.” For in Greek he has *eunoun* (εὐνοῦν), that is, “well-disposed,” and it can rightly be understood to mean that we should, insofar as it depends on us, be at peace with all people.

It can also appropriately be understood of the word of the Gospel, which is, as it were, our adversary, because it commands things contrary to our pleasures. Nevertheless, it is better that we should agree with it while we are in the body and on the road of this age, lest perhaps the very Word whom we did not obey despise us, and the judging angel hand us over to the devil’s minister, who will send us into the prison of eternal punishments.

Amen I say to you, you will not come out from there until you have paid the last quadrans. “Until” here also refers to eternity, because whoever enters hell will not thereafter come out. It is as though he said: “You will never come out from there,” and there you will pay the torments even for the smallest sins, which are understood by the quadrans. For the quadrans is a kind of coin that contains two small coins, that is, five denarii, and is likewise called by this name in Hebrew. Hence in one Gospel it is written that a woman put a quadrans into the treasury, and in another that she put two small coins:

You have heard that it was said to the ancients, “You shall not commit adultery.” But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman in order to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart. I, who gave the Law through Moses, complete what was lacking: whoever looks with the purpose of deciding that he wants to do this is already held guilty in the sight of the Lord.

Blessed Jerome says that one thing is passion, another is the first impulse (*propas­sio*), and another is what is tempted by the devil or by the flesh, while the person nevertheless does not decide to act accordingly. Such a person is not held guilty in the sight of God. We can take an example from theft. If someone is touched by the thought that he wants to steal another person’s horse, but does not put the thought into effect, he has been tempted through suggestion, but not through action. If someone thinks about it and decides that he will do it if he can, but lacks the opportunity, he is nevertheless held guilty in the sight of God; of such a person it is said that he has already committed adultery with her in his heart, or stolen her.

And if your right eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and throw it away from you. By the eye, hand, and foot we must understand spiritual desires. When the eye sees and desires, we must cut off that eye—that is, the desire—in the same way with the foot and the hand.

In another sense, by the eye, hand, and foot let us understand parents and friends. If there are people who oppose us on the way of God and whom we cannot convert, it is better to be without them and without their friendship than to incur God’s displeasure. Accordingly, it is commanded concerning the high priest that he not defile himself even for his father or his sons, unless he preserves him undefiled whose worship he has been dedicated to serve.

It was said: “Whoever dismisses his wife, let him give her a bill of divorce.” Here “to the ancients” is not added. Therefore it is clear—as he will say in the later section—that Moses said this on his own, although God did not command it. For the lawgiver knew that, if they lived together, before they were willing to retain their wives they would kill them, and he judged separation better than murder. A “bill” means a written document of divorce, that is, of separation, since *repudiare* means “to reject,” and a *repudium* is something given or sent with the testimony of witnesses.

But I say to you that everyone who dismisses his wife, except on account of fornication, causes her to commit adultery; and whoever marries a dismissed woman commits adultery. The Lord’s command is straightforward: even if a man dismisses his wife because of fornication, neither he may have another wife as long as she lives, nor may she have another husband. But if he has legally put her to death by judicial sentence, then he may have another wife.

A husband has a similar law with his wife as a wife has with her husband. If a husband commits adultery with a woman, he cannot have her killed unless he himself also dies, because he is likewise guilty of adultery. If they wish to withdraw to a monastery, neither may dismiss the other unless both are willing, and neither may have a partner as long as both live.

Again it was said to the ancients: “You shall not swear falsely, but you shall fulfill your oaths to the Lord.” So that the Jews would not swear by the names of idols, the Lord permitted them to swear by his own name. He did not forbid us to do so either, but taught us perfection: such faith should exist among Christians that it is unnecessary to introduce the Lord’s name as a witness. Perjury is forbidden to us and to them.

We ought to say *non pejerabis*—“you shall not swear falsely”—without the *r*, because the verb does not contain an *r* in that form; rather, we say *pejero* and *dejero*. *Pejerare* means “to swear falsely”; *dejerare*, “to swear very solemnly.” *Jurare* is, as it were, *jure orare*, “to pray by right.” When he says, “You shall fulfill your oaths to the Lord,” this means that you shall refer them to him, so that you swear by his name and not by the names of foreign gods.

Some people swear upon an altar and think that this is not perjury. Yet God regards it in the same way as the person to whom the oath is sworn, even if no relics of saints are present there, because the name of the Lord is greater than the bodies of the saints. Indeed, God attributed nothing else to Zedekiah when he swore to Nebuchadnezzar except that he had despised the Lord’s name when he violated that oath, saying: “The oath that he despised I will place upon his head, and I will hand him over to Nebuchadnezzar.” Yet the person to whom the oath had been sworn did not believe in God. But because Zedekiah had despised the Lord’s name and treated it as worthless, he was handed over to the one to whom he had promised faith.

Do not swear—not even by heaven, because it is God’s throne. “Throne” is Greek, and in Latin it is called *sedes*, “seat.” The Jews had the custom of swearing by created things. God forbids this to us because the person by whom someone swears is the one he worships and venerates, as Paul says: “People swear by one greater than themselves.”

Heaven is called God’s seat because the splendor of his divinity is contemplated there more fully by the saints, or because it is inhabited by the saints in whom he dwells. Nor swear by the earth, because it is called the footstool of his feet: for his saints, who are his members, still walk upon the earth. Nor by Jerusalem, because it is the city of the great King. Jerusalem is called the city of the great King, namely, of the Lord, because it was said of it: “Its foundations are in the holy mountains.” And although this earthly Jerusalem is not to be despised, there is another Jerusalem, because true peace and eternal security are there. Of it the Psalmist says: “Jerusalem, which is built as a city.”

Nor shall you swear by your head. By these four examples we are forbidden to swear, so that we may be taught not to swear by the remaining elements or bodily members.

Let your speech be, “Yes, yes,” “No, no.” It is not contrary to the Lord’s command to swear by his name; but when we become accustomed to the practice of swearing, we frequently incur the crime of perjury and falsehood. Therefore, as though addressing the perfect, he commands that truth be maintained among Christians and that each person speak truth to his neighbor.

Whatever is more than this is from evil. “From evil” means from the evil hearer who does not believe; with such a person we must use more emphatic speech, just as the Lord himself did by adding “Amen.” So also the apostle Paul says: “We speak before God in Christ.”

You have heard that it was said to the ancients. Here, however, “to the ancients” is not implied, because Moses also commanded this on his own authority: “An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth.” It is understood that this was to be removed in the old Law.

But I say to you, do not resist evil—that is, do not repay evil with evil. But if someone strikes you on your right cheek, offer him the other also. The ecclesiastical man is described as one who in all things becomes an imitator of the one who said: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart.” David likewise says in the Psalm: “If I repaid those who rendered evil to me.”

Spiritually, we are not commanded to offer the left cheek but another right one, for the righteous person has no left cheek. And to the one who wishes to contend with you in judgment and take your tunic, surrender your cloak as well.

A tunic is so called because it makes a sound when the wearer moves, from *tonare*, “to thunder.” A cloak is the garment with which, among the ancients, the shoulders of servants were covered, so that while serving they could move about freely; it is not in use among us. The garment that we put on with a fastening brooch was called a *chlamys* among the ancients.

Give to the one who asks of you. This cannot refer to an earthly possession; it is better understood spiritually, so that if someone asks us for nourishment in the word, we should not refuse, insofar as it depends on us, whatever may benefit him for edification.

And whoever compels you to go one thousand paces, go with him another two. “One thousand paces”—he is speaking according to geometrical measurement—means one mile, which contains five thousand feet. According to the geometricians, sixteen transverse digits make a foot; two and a half feet make a step; two steps complete a pace. Of these paces the Lord says here, as follows: “Go with him another two miles.”

*Angariare* comes from Greek and means “to compel someone to walk.” The sense appears to be: If someone compels you to walk one mile, go with him so that it becomes two. The word *angariare* may refer either to indicating the route or to urging someone on by compelling him; and this includes what you have gone of your own accord. All these commands pertain to the perfection mentioned above.

You have heard that it was said: “You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy.” The Lord does not acknowledge that he commanded the latter, “You shall hate your enemy.” It was not fitting that God, who created all people equally from one father and mother, should have commanded anyone to hate another. Nor did Moses command this; he indicated what they would do. It is not expressed in the imperative mood but in the indicative. If, then, it had been commanded that they hate their enemies, Samuel, David, and the other saints under the old Law would not have loved their enemies.

But I say to you: Love your enemies—in the heart is understood; do good to those who hate you—in action; and pray for those who persecute and slander you. Behold, through three commands we are ordered to do good to our enemies, by which we customarily confer benefits upon them: love them in the heart, pray for them with the mouth, and do good to them in action. Therefore we will have no excuse if we do not love them.

If, however, they are wicked with respect to the worship of God, we must hate their vices but love the creature.

So that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven. In accordance with his divinity and in accordance with his flesh, he gave us an example. He makes his sun rise upon the good and the wicked, and rains upon the just and the unjust. In accordance with the form of his flesh, he prayed for those who persecuted and slandered him. He gives us an example from the superior to the inferior, and an illustrative form of exhortation.

For if you love those who love you, do not even the tax collectors do this? Tax collectors are called those who lease the revenues of the treasury and public property, or those who collect public taxes, or those who pursue profits through worldly business; hence they received this designation.

And if you greet your brothers, what more are you doing? Do not even the gentiles do this? *Ethnici* is Greek; in Latin they are called *gentiles*, “pagans.”

Be perfect, therefore, just as your heavenly Father is perfect. Here he shows that all the matters included above pertain to perfection.

Be careful not to perform your righteousness before people. Above, in the commands he enumerated, he showed what constituted the righteousness of Christians. Now he commands that we not perform these acts of righteousness before people in order to be seen by them and praised by them. “Be careful” means “take heed.”

In three places in this Gospel the expression “be careful” occurs, and it always has the same meaning: take heed and observe, lest you do something in order to be seen, or wish to be seen, or wish to be praised. For the person who acts so that God may be praised and his neighbor edified acts well; but the person who acts for human praise loses his reward with God.

If we wish, we can punctuate the sentence in this way: “Be careful not to make righteousness”—and then continue, “your own,” that is, not to wish to make our own the righteousness that belongs to God. For no one acts justly or performs righteousness except by God’s gift. Whatever is good belongs to God; whatever is evil belongs to us. Thus Moses shows this at the waters of contradiction by turning God’s power back upon himself, saying: “Can we bring water out for you from this rock?” Yet the power was God’s, which was being exercised, and not that of the man through whom it was exercised.

When, therefore, you give alms, do not sound a trumpet before you, as the hypocrites do in synagogues and in streets, so that they may be honored by people. Here he indicates how we should not perform our righteousness before people, as those hypocrites—that is, those who pretend—do in synagogues, assemblies, and villages.

A village (*vicus*) is so called from its inhabitants, because it has roads like a city but lacks walls. The inhabitants of a city are also called *vici*. At that time they used to sound trumpets, supposedly to gather the poor; but, as is shown here, they did this rather for human praise, so that many would recognize that they were giving a great amount in alms.

Amen, I say to you, they have received their reward. That is, they have received the human praise they sought and for which they acted; they have nothing to expect from God.

But when you give alms, let your left hand not know what your right hand is doing. *Eleemosyna* is a Greek word and means “mercy.” We ought to say *eleemosyna*, with *e*, not *elimosina*, with *i*. In everything we must take care that our left hand does not know the good that we do. The left hand signifies *xenodoxia*, “the desire for human praise,” and is always understood in a bad sense.

And when you pray, do not be like the hypocrites, who love to pray standing in synagogues and at the corners of the streets. Streets are called *plateae* from their breadth—this is a Greek etymology—and they are usually laid out before the city gate so that those entering and leaving can pass through. *Hypocritae* should be written with one *p*, not two.

Amen, I say to you, they have received their reward. If they have received praise from people, let that be enough for them, because all who do anything good under the pretext of hypocrisy have been frustrated in the sight of God.

But when you pray, enter your room and, having shut the door, pray to your Father. He simply instructs the hearer to avoid the empty glory of praying. But this also appears to be a spiritual command: with the thought enclosed in the breast and the lips pressed together, we should pray to the Lord, as Anna is said to have done—only her lips moved, and her voice was not heard at all.

When you pray, do not speak at great length, like the gentiles—that is, the pagans. They worship deaf gods who have ears but do not hear. Christians, however, do not need to speak at great length, because they speak to God, who knows everything before it happens, as he himself says: “Your Father knows what you need before you ask him.” Therefore it is not necessary for us to be narrators but petitioners.

## CHAPTER XII. On the Form of the Lord’s Prayer

Pray, therefore, in this way. The other Evangelists relate that the disciples themselves asked the Lord to teach them the form of prayer: how they ought to entreat him together with the Father and the Holy Spirit. And the Lord poured forth this prayer from the fountain of his breast, filled with every necessary petition. For everything that is necessary for us, both in the present age and in the future, is contained here. There are also seven petitions and eight prayers.

“Our Father.” No mortal would dare to say this unless he himself, in his mercy, had commanded us to do so. God is our Father in two ways: by creation, because he formed and created us; and by adoption, because through his mercy he adopted us as sons. He commanded us to call him Father, provided that we are not made unworthy of so great a Father by degenerating from his only-begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ. He showed us the pattern of perfection through which we can become sons of God and his brothers by good works.

Since, then, we confess that we have one Father in heaven, we ought to be brothers in love. For whoever refuses to recognize all Christians as brothers refuses to have God as Father together with them.

We therefore invoke you who are in heaven. Although you are everywhere, those who dwell with you in heaven contemplate your majesty more splendidly; or you are “in heaven” because you dwell in your saints.

“May your name be sanctified.” Since it is holy in itself, we pray that it may become holy in us, because we are called Christians from your Son Christ. In this way, through good works, we may be yours, and you may deem it worthy to dwell in our hearts.

“May your kingdom come.” May the whole world know you, and may you reign in us, ruling and governing us unto eternal life—not the devil, whose possession we are not.

“May your will be done, as in heaven and on earth.” May we serve you on earth just as your angels serve you without fault in heaven.

“Give us this day our daily bread.” In Greek, *pan* means “all,” and by “bread” every substance necessary for us each day is understood; this is “daily bread.” In Greek, instead of “daily,” it has *epiusion* (ἐπιούσιον), which is translated “super-substantial,” namely, what pertains to our substance—that is, food and clothing.

“Give us this day.” You are our Creator and Lord. Or may one spiritual bread satisfy our soul; or grant us also to receive your body and blood worthily today, that is, always.

“And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.” Whatever we have committed against you because of the weakness of the flesh or at the persuasion of the devil, release us from it, so that the punishments owed to transgressors may not come upon us, because we also, according to your command, forgive those who sin against us.

“And do not lead us into temptation.” Do not permit us to fall into any temptation harmful to body or soul, because you are powerful enough to free us; and you do not lead us into it except in order to free us from it.

“But deliver us from evil.” That is, from both the evil of the present age and the evil that is future and everlasting.

Behold seven petitions, in which everything necessary for us, both in the present age and in the future, is contained. An eighth prayer is added at the end: “Amen.” This means “true,” so that everything for which we have prayed above may come to pass as true.

All who pray this prayer must observe the following: they must guard themselves against all anger, so that they may truthfully say to the Lord, the Creator, “Our Father.” For if they do not love all Christians, they are not brothers; and whoever hates anyone has cast himself out of the Lord’s fatherhood. Whoever did not wish to have a brother in love of the Lord and of neighbor will not have the Father’s protection.

Similarly, they must observe the following words: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive.” They must not lie to the Lord or accuse themselves by asking that they be forgiven on the condition that they themselves forgive their debtors. Nor can they suppress this word, because the one who taught the prayer will not hear it unless it is said as he composed it.

He immediately adds: “For if you forgive their sins, your heavenly Father will also forgive you your offenses.” Forgiveness has been placed in human hands: if people do not count the sins of those who sin against them, neither will God count theirs; but if they retain them, they will be retained. This refers to those who sin against us as human beings, not to those who offend against God.

When you fast, do not become like the hypocrites, gloomy. Throughout, the Lord shows us how we should not perform our righteousness before people, lest we lose our reward with God. We must not act like the Sadducees, who, when they fasted, did not wash their faces or comb their heads.

For they disfigure their faces. That is, they distort them from the appearance in which they were accustomed to walk on other days, or they destroy their appearance in order to pretend sadness. So that they may appear to people—that is, so that they may appear to be fasting.

But when you fast, anoint your head. He speaks according to the custom of the province, whose inhabitants had a prepared ointment made from oil and fragrant balsam, and anointed their heads. We should not pretend to sadness on account of fasting in order to gain the favor of the crowd, but should serve God cheerfully, because our reward will then remain certain if we do everything for God’s sake.

And wash your face, so that you may not appear to people to be fasting. We are commanded to wash our face and comb our head so that we may not appear to fast for the sake of empty glory. Nevertheless, if we go about unwashed because of some other necessity, we do not sin.

Do not store up treasures for yourselves on earth. The word “treasures” is compounded from Greek and Latin. For *thesis* in Greek means “placement” in Latin, that is, “the placing of gold.” Yet this must be understood of all money, because the Lord commands here that from all the things we can possess we should make our treasure in eternal life, for which we may be received into our eternal homeland.

Through the three things named here, the rich of this age most often lose their treasure: rust, which pertains to kinds of metal; moths, which consume clothing; and thieves, who take everything that can be possessed. There is also a spiritual rust: empty glory; a moth: envy; and thieves: demons. Through these a Christian loses the treasure of his soul unless he guards himself with vigilant care.

Store up treasures for yourselves in heaven, as blessed Sixtus and countless Christians did through the hands of the poor. For the Lord himself said: “Whatever you have done for one of the least of mine, you have done for me.” Once something has been given to a poor or good person in the Lord’s name, the giver cannot lose his reward.

Where your treasure is, there is your heart. This can be understood of every pleasure in which someone is excessively absorbed. The treasure of the gluttonous is the belly, that of the luxurious is banqueting, and that of the lover of lust is licentiousness and amusements. A person serves the one by whom he is conquered.

The lamp of your body is your eye. If your eye is sound, your whole body will be full of light. This is an allegory: he wishes something other than what the surface of the words expresses. The Lord gives the example that a person with healthy eyes can see whatever he wishes and walk correctly along the road. A person without light frequently wanders from the path and stumbles on the journey. Likewise, a person who does not have a right intention in his faith or in his love toward God frequently falters in his actions, because a double-minded person is unstable in all his works.

Yet for those who believe in God all things work together for good. Hence what follows: “If your eye is sound, your whole body will be full of light.” The eye is the intention of action. If, therefore, the light that is in you is darkness, how great will that darkness be? That is: if the body, having lost the light of the eyes, suffers darkness—the inward light that ought to govern soul and body—how great will it be? Clearly, how great indeed: greater than the body’s darkness.

## CHAPTER XIII. On Not Serving Two Masters

No one can serve two masters. And how can this be, when he says elsewhere, “I did not come to be served but to serve,” and Paul says, “Through love serve one another in the bond of peace”? Yet it must be understood that, as we said above, there is a service that ought to be offered to God alone and to no mortal: to believe in God with firm faith and worship him; not to have another god; not to take the name of God in vain; to love him with all one’s heart and all one’s inward being; to offer sacrifices to him; and to hope for every good from him.

Other services, however, we can offer both to God and to human beings according to his commands: namely, we should do for our neighbors all the good things we wish others to do for us.

There is a distinction in the Greek language between these two services. The service offered to God alone is called *latreusis* (λατρεύσις); the service directed toward human beings is called *douleusis* (δουλεύσις). This is what Paul says: “Serve one another.” In Greek he has *douleusate* (δουλεύσατε).

Either he will hate the one—that is, the devil—and love the other—that is, God—as is worthy and just; or he will endure the one—that is, the devil, since no one loves the devil but endures him for a short time in order to fulfill his desires—and despise the other—that is, God. He did not say “hate,” because no one can hate God. But many despise him and abuse God’s patience. Thus the Lord also said to Samuel: “Those who honor me I will honor; but those who despise me will be held of no account.”

Who, then, are the two masters whom we cannot serve simultaneously? He continues: You cannot serve God and Mammon. In the Syriac language, *Mammon* means “wealth.” It is one thing to possess riches, another to serve riches. Whoever serves riches cannot serve God.

He did not say, “Whoever possesses riches.” For the person who possesses riches and distributes them, as the Lord said to those who receive him here—that they will be received into eternal dwellings—and who have understanding for the needy and poor, will be in the other life with Job, Abraham, David, and others who possessed riches in this age and purchased eternal life for themselves.

But those who serve riches and give none of those riches to anyone except people from whom they can receive something in this age will be buried with the rich man in an eternal burial, so that there they may lack every good.

The Jews also say that Mammon is the name of a demon who presides over riches. They teach that demons are appointed over each vice, with others placed under them to lead people into this or that vice. Hence the saying: “They were led astray by the spirit of fornication.” Apart from these, they say that each person has two guardian angels, one good and the other evil.

Therefore I say to you—“if you have chosen me as Lord and rejected the other” is understood—do not be anxious about your soul, that is, about your life, concerning what you will eat, nor about your body, concerning what you will wear. I made the soul; I will provide the food by which it can subsist until the appointed time.

Nor be anxious about your body, concerning what you will wear. For I created the body in the stature it now has, and I will clothe it, provided that you obey my commands. For you will be called the sons or servants of the one whose works you perform.

Is not the soul more than food? The one who gave an immortal and rational soul will also give food. “More” means more valuable and more precious, because it is immortal and rational. And the one who gave the body beauty, an upright posture, readiness for every action, and intelligence—much more than the beasts possess—will clothe it.

He says all these things to remove fear and anxiety from our souls, as though we might die of hunger or cold if we did his will. We must, however, perform work by which we may live and be clothed, since this was said to the first man: “By the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread.” And Paul commands, saying: “Rather, let each person labor with his own hands at what is good, so that he may have something to give to those suffering need.”

Look at the birds of the air, how they neither sow—that is, plant—nor reap, nor gather into barns; and your heavenly Father feeds them. He commands us to look at the birds so that we may have confidence that the one who gives food to the birds will give it to us, since they are irrational and mortal and were created for our use—not, however, so that we may be idle and not labor in sowing and reaping, but so that, out of fear, we may not store up treasures of temporal goods and fail to extend a hand to the needy, fearing that we shall suffer want if we give generously in the Lord’s name.

Are you not worth more than they? That is, are you not of greater value, while they exist today and will not exist tomorrow? You, however, will always exist, either for good or for evil. *Pluris* refers to weight, that is, to greater worth; *plures*, on the other hand, is the comparative degree formed from the positive *multus*, and refers to number.

[Col. 1318B] And which of you, by thinking about it, can add one cubit to his stature? Just as no one can add anything to his stature, and yet almighty God made you grow to the form you possess, so surely he who gave the greater thing without your effort will also give the lesser. That is, food and drink.

And concerning clothing, why are you anxious? Just as he removed fear concerning food, so likewise, from what follows, he removes it concerning clothing. Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow: they do not labor or spin. “Spin” means “to weave,” from the verb *neo*, “I spin.” He says this so that we may see how the lilies are clothed in whiteness without their own labor, or that of the roses in their color, since no linen can compare with the whiteness of a lily, no dyed fabric with the color of a rose, and no purple with the hue of a violet.

Therefore, if God so clothes the worthless grass which we are accustomed to send to the marketplace when it has withered, how much more will he clothe you, whom he created in his own likeness? But I say to you that not even Solomon in all his glory was clothed like one of these. He gives the Jews Solomon as an example, because they had no richer king. There were many richer men, such as Nebuchadnezzar, Ahasuerus, Octavian, and their successors, but the Jews did not know them as they knew Solomon. He therefore says that Solomon, with all his glory, was not clothed in linen so brilliant, nor in a more beautiful mantle, than these aforementioned plants.

And if the grass of the field, which exists today—the grass of the field means these very plants; “exists today” means “does not last long”—and tomorrow is thrown into the oven—“tomorrow” means “in the future,” when they have dried; “into the oven” means “into the furnace”—if God clothes it with such beauty, how much more will he clothe you, who possess some faith, which they do not possess? For they are without understanding. In Scripture, “tomorrow” is taken to mean future time, as Jacob says: “Tomorrow my righteousness will answer for me.”

Therefore do not be anxious, and so forth. In every way he wishes to remove anxiety from us while requiring that we work. But concerning spiritual food and clothing, we ought always to be anxious and suffer hunger, because blessed are those who hunger for righteousness.

For all these things the Gentiles seek. That is, they are concerned about these matters because they do not worship the true God. For your Father knows that you need all these things. Therefore he will care for us if we do his will, since he knows all our necessities [Col. 1319A] before we ask him. This is followed by: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you.” That is: do God’s will in those matters which he has commanded you, and these things—understand, “necessities”—will be added, that is, increased for you. They will be added for necessity, not for excess, because no Christian ought to seek any provision for temporal life except what is necessary.

Do not be anxious for tomorrow, that is, for the future. From the adverb *cras*, “tomorrow,” the noun *crastinus*, “of tomorrow,” is derived. Sufficient for the day is its own trouble. By “trouble” he means the labor of the present day, as though he were saying: the concern of the present time is sufficient for us; let us leave the care of the future, which is uncertain.

Do not judge, so that you may not be judged. He forbids judging in uncertain and doubtful cases, so that we may first be investigators before becoming condemners, as Job says: “The case I did not know I investigated most diligently.” Indeed, in judgments no one ought to judge either a cleric or a layperson until he has heard that person’s confession concerning the sin at issue. Accordingly, Paul commands judgment concerning manifest sins, such as sexual misconduct, murder, and theft. For he says: “When you were assembled with me in spirit, I have already judged the one who acted in this way, to hand him over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh.”

For with whatever judgment you have judged—understand, “unjustly”—you will be judged justly, because you judged unjustly. And with whatever measure you have measured, it will be measured back to you. If, he says, you diligently strive to do all the good you are able to do and to commend it to your neighbors, divine mercy will be present, granting you in the present life the understanding to grasp higher things and the ability to accomplish stronger deeds; and in the future it will grant you eternal rewards beyond what you could hope for.

Why do you see the splinter in your brother’s eye? This refers to what he said earlier, not to judging your brother rashly. Why do you consider another person’s fault and forget your own? When you see another sin lightly, you condemn him and judge his sins serious, while you regard your own more serious sins as slight. By the splinter he means a light sin, sudden anger, or an idle word; by the beam, deep-seated hatred, envy, or more serious sins.

We ought to say *festucam* with an *e*, not with an *i*, as Bede instructs. Beams properly are the timbers of ships laid crosswise, where sailors sit; beams are also so called in houses because they support the roof. Here there is an allegory, a comparison in the form of a parable, from an inanimate object to a living one, from a splinter to sin.

Hypocrite, first remove the beam from your own eye, and then you will see how to remove the splinter from your brother’s eye. That is: cleanse yourself from serious sin, and then you will be able to cleanse your brother from a lesser sin. For no one with dirty hands can clean a dirty vessel unless he first washes his hands. *Hypocrita* is Greek; in Latin it means “simulation,” or “a dissembler.”

Do not give what is holy to dogs, and do not throw your pearls before pigs. Here dogs are understood as heretics or apostate Christians who, after acknowledging the faith, return to their former sins. Pigs are understood as pagans, because just as pigs always lie in the mud, so these people always lie in depraved pleasures. [Col. 1320A] The Gospel, therefore, should be entrusted to neither group until we perceive that they have been converted in mind and body.

For concerning the first group the Apostle says: “Avoid a heretical person after the first and second correction.” Why the divine word should not be entrusted to them he adds, saying: “Lest they trample them under their feet and, turning, tear you apart.” That is: lest they mock the word of the Gospel and kill you, who could still have been salvation for others.

That pearls are called the divine utterances is shown both in this Gospel and in many other passages, as in the example of the merchant seeking good pearls. A pearl is the word of God, and it can be pierced from every side.

Ask—understand, “well”—and it will be given to you. Ask with the mind, seek with words, knock through actions. Ask by word, seek through good works, knock by perseverance. Ask for faith, seek hope, knock for love. For everyone who asks—understand, “well”—receives; whoever seeks through good works will find; and to whoever knocks with perseverance, it will be opened.

Which of you is there who, if his son asks him for bread, will give him a stone? According to the literal sense, no one gives his son something bad when he asks for something good; how much more will God, who is good in his very essence, give good things spiritually even if we ignorantly ask for bad things? If we ask for faith, he will not repay us with unbelief; and if we ask for hope, he will not give despair. For just as a fish lies hidden in water, so our hope lies hidden in the present age, but it will appear in the future, when we shall be satisfied with God’s blessings.

If you, then, although you are evil—It should be noted that he calls the apostles evil, because in comparison with God no one is good; in themselves, however, all creatures are good—whatever you wish people to do to you, do also to them. This saying may be understood as referring to what the prophet says: “For the Lord will make a shortened word upon the earth.” This was the natural law which Adam received. For this is the Law and the Prophets: whatever he commanded in the very extensive book of the Law and in the writings of the Prophets, if you have love toward your neighbor, you will keep it all. You wish every good thing to be done to you, and you do it to another; you will do no evil to anyone, since you do not wish it to be done to you.

Enter through the narrow gate. This is an allegory, because by the gate the way of Christ’s commandments is understood. The broad and spacious way leads to destruction; that is, it is the pleasure of the world, which offers itself freely. Since it delights this body, there is no need to seek it or learn it; therefore many are those who enter by it.

How narrow the gate and constricted the way that leads to life! That is, it is exceedingly narrow: one must pass through the world by fasting, patience, and love of enemies, and arrive at eternal life. It is a constricted way. Hence the Psalm also says: “I have kept difficult ways.”

And there are few who find it. He says that few find it; yet not all who find it walk along it, since there are many who know that Christians worship one God and nevertheless do not worship him themselves. There are also many who profess in words that they know God and declare themselves to be Christians, but deny him in their deeds. For this reason they do not walk the narrow way, because, as the Lord says elsewhere: “Many are called, but few are chosen.” The called are those who have become Christians; the few chosen are those who do not deny God by their works.

## CHAPTER XIV. On Avoiding False Christians

Beware of false prophets. “Beware” means: take care, guard yourselves, observe. This word occurs in three places in this book, and it always has the same meaning. Many false prophets appeared among that people even after the Lord’s coming, such as Theudas and Judas the Galilean, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles. Concerning them he instructed the apostles not to follow them and perish, like those who followed them.

Afterward the statement can be understood of all false Christians, who do one thing with their mouths and another in their actions. There were pagans who claimed to be Christians so that they might investigate their conduct and hand them over to death for torture. It can also be understood of heretics.

Who come to you in sheep’s clothing. Sheep are gentle animals, physically defenseless and peaceful in character. Christ commanded his own to be like this: gentle, not resisting evil, at peace with all people, and feeding others with their clothing and food. All these are the works and clothing of sheep belonging to Christianity. Whoever does not do these things is a wolf.

A wolf is called *lucos* (λύκος) in Greek, and its name is derived from its character, because it is always devoted to rapacity and bloodshed. Those are like wolves who always desire to plunder other Christians, either through violence or even as if by worldly law. If they are dependent upon his benefaction, or are his servants, or hold authority over them, they seek opportunities to strip them as though by law. They do not consider that they are descended from one lineage and one father, but treat them worse than their own dogs. They do not consider that God made them all in one way and redeemed them with one blood. What he gave to the emperor entering the world, he also gave to the beggar departing from it. We brought nothing into this world, nor can we take anything away except our works. In the other life there will be no distinction between master and servant except according to merits.

Many are called Christians, but many are wolves in their actions. Not only laypeople but also clerics are wolves in character: they appear among the sheep in the Lord’s fold, but they are wolves and predators.

Whoever associates with a predator is like him. For Paul says: “If anyone is named a brother and is greedy or rapacious,” and so forth, “with such a person do not even eat.” Those who wickedly devour the provisions and money of the poor are ravenous wolves.

It follows: You will know them by their fruits. They say: “They are under my benefaction; according to the law I take what I take.” God says: “Consider whether you would want this done to you; if so, you act rightly. Otherwise, the time will come when he will be in glory and you in hell.” The fruits of human beings are their works, whether good or evil. If they are good, the person is a sheep; if evil, a wolf.

Do people gather grapes from thorns, or figs from thistles? By thorns are meant those who above were called wolves; by thistles also, which are likewise a thorny plant, namely a bramble, the same people are represented. By grapes and figs are meant works worthy of God.

Thus every good tree produces good fruit. For just as every tree is recognized by its fruit and is praised or condemned because of it, so every person will be rewarded or condemned according to his work, which is his fruit. This is an allegorical comparison, in the form of a parable, from a lower thing to a higher one, intended as exhortation. Israel ought to have produced grapes, but produced sour grapes; it ought to have brought forth sweet figs, but produced bitter figs. The vine is so called because it possesses the power of taking root. The fig is named from fruitfulness, because it bears fruit three times a year.

A good tree cannot produce bad fruit, nor can a bad tree produce good fruit. If a good tree cannot produce bad fruit, how did Moses, a good tree, sin at the waters of contradiction? How did David commit adultery and murder, and Peter deny the Lord? Or how did Jethro and Achior, bad trees, give useful counsel?

It should be understood that a person is called a good tree only so long as he does good works. If he begins to do evil, he is called a bad tree. Thus Manasseh became a bad tree when, through many crimes, he forgot the Lord. But when he repented and turned from evil to good, he was changed into a good tree.

God will judge each person according to his present state. If he is found engaged in a good work on the day of judgment, he will be judged according to the good; but if he is found in serious sin, he will be judged as evil. As is stated more fully in Ezekiel. Solomon also says: “The tree will remain wherever it falls.” That is: if a sinner lies down in evil, he will be condemned for evil and punished with it. But if he turns away from evil and is found in good, before the day of infirmity, he will be delivered with that good.

Concerning those who are converted in illness, blessed Jerome says in his exposition of the Psalm verse, “For in death there is no one who remembers you”; in death and in hell he denied that repentance could be carried out in either place.

Every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down. Every human being, whether Christian or pagan, if he does not produce good fruit, will be cut down; his soul will be uprooted from the body. He will not escape through ignorance, because ignorance is not permitted.

He will be thrown into the fire, which will never be extinguished. Therefore you will know them by their fruits. Because you will know them, I say: beware of them.

Not everyone who says to me, “Lord, Lord,” will enter the kingdom of heaven. Let no one trust that he is a Christian if he does not perform the works of Christianity; he will not enter eternal life. For “whoever says that he knows God but does not keep his commandments is a liar.” We also understand here what Paul says: “No one can say, ‘Lord Jesus,’ except in the Holy Spirit,” and in faith we sing: “Those who have done good will go into eternal life, but those who have done evil into eternal fire.”

That fire will be eternal for each person, as God said: “Go into eternal fire,” because whoever has once entered hell will not come out again. Even if he receives his body, without judgment or delay he will return to the place assigned to him.

Many will say to me on that day, “Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and in your name cast out demons?” Even evil people can prophesy and perform miracles, as Balaam did, who spoke many good things when he was summoned to Balak, yet was led astray by greed and killed. Job also [Col. 1323A]—because he himself was Elihu [lacuna]. [Note: Col. 1323D: Something is missing.]

Saul and Caiaphas prophesied; Pharaoh and Nebuchadnezzar saw things to come. Many can also perform miracles, as the magicians did in Egypt, and Simon, and many others through necromancy—that is, the invocation of the dead—as did the pythoness woman in the Book of Kings. Evil people also customarily cast out demons, such as those Jewish exorcists, and the man concerning whom the apostles said to the Lord: “We saw someone casting out demons in your name who does not follow us.” Judas also did this when he followed the Lord.

This is granted to evil people either because of the authority of the name by which the invocation is made, or for the salvation of those who see and hear. This is not a sign of Christ’s disciples. He did not say to his disciples, “Learn from me to perform miracles,” but rather, “Because I am gentle and humble in heart.” And elsewhere: “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.” These are the distinguishing marks of Christ’s disciples. No evil person can possess these three signs and remain evil: gentleness, humility, and love.

It follows: Then I will declare to them that I never knew you. “I will declare”: I will reveal to them the truth which they themselves refused to fulfill. “I never knew you”—understand, “as my disciples,” because you did not possess those three things which I commanded my disciples to possess as distinguishing marks from other disciples. But you said that you were my disciples; you spoke falsely. I never observed the works.

Depart from me, you who practice iniquity. “Go away from me, you who will be practicing it when you are commanded to depart from the body.” He did not say, “you who have practiced it,” lest he take repentance away from those who convert, but “you who practice it,” that is, who still practice it in your will, because while it was still possible to live, you also wished to sin.

Depart from me. There is no need to hand them over to the devil, because he himself knows what he must do with those whom he sees do not belong to God. In that life every person will belong either to God or to the devil. The devil is so cruel that there is no need to command him to torture; he knows that those who are not God’s are his own.

Therefore everyone who hears these words of mine and does them—It should be considered that he says, “who hears my words and does them,” that is, who does good for my sake and for the sake of my words. For there were many philosophers who abandoned all their possessions and abstained from vices to such an extent that, withdrawing to remote places, they lived strictly by the work of their hands; yet this profited them nothing.

Titus was an excellent giver of alms and a doer of good works, so much so that one day he said sorrowfully: “Today we have lost the day, because we did not provide great benefit to anyone.”

Diocletian, although he had the whole world at peace, abandoned the empire without being compelled to do so. He gave it neither to his son nor to his daughter, nor to any relative. He even compelled Maximian, his imperial colleague—whom he had taken as his associate because they had previously been friends—to withdraw. When the same Diocletian was asked by his relatives and friends not to do this, since everything was at peace, he replied: “When all our actions are free from blame, we ought to yield our place to another. Yet if you saw our gardens and orchards planted by our own hands, you would never advise us to retain these things.”

Thus acted a pagan emperor. What do you think? If they had done these things for the love of God, of how great merit would they have been worthy before God?

He will be like a wise man who built his house upon rock. Just as one who lays an earthly foundation must place it in a firm location, so one who wishes to do something good must perform the works of Christ and build upon him who is called the cornerstone, doing them for his love and spending them on those to whom he gave the command: “Whatever you did for one of the least of mine.”

If he does this, what follows will happen: The rain descended, the rivers came, and the winds blew. The rain is the devil with his temptations, as when he came against blessed Job; the rivers are his friends; the winds are the adversities which the devil inflicted upon him through the losses of his possessions. But because he had his foundation upon the rock, it was said of him: “In all these things Job did not sin with his lips.”

Likewise concerning Paul: the rain was, “A thorn of my flesh was given to me”; the rivers were, “A door was opened to me”; but “many adversaries” were the winds: “Five times I received forty lashes less one; three times I was beaten with rods; once I was stoned,” and so forth.

For it was founded upon the rock. Because Paul’s house was founded upon the rock—that is, Christ—after such and so many torments he said: “Who will separate us from the love of Christ?” And at the end: “In all these things we are more than conquerors, through him who loved us.” For all who place their hope in God will not be put to shame.

And everyone who hears these words of mine and does not do them will be like a foolish man. Throughout the Gospel text, figures and tropes from secular literature are found, but to avoid tediousness and because of the book’s length, we frequently omit them. Here too there is a metaphor, a transfer from an inanimate thing to a living one, from a house without a soul to a human being with a soul.

It is a type of metaphor called a parable, whenever we exhort or deter someone by means of an example. The exhortation was given above; the deterrent is what is now said concerning the house built upon sand—that is, concerning the person who places his hope in worldly pleasure. What happened to that person will come upon him, or upon the one who said: “Soul, you have many good things stored up for many years; rest, eat, drink, and feast.” That very night he heard: “Fool, this night your soul will be taken from you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?”

And it happened that when Jesus had finished these words. This finishing pertains to perfection, which is the meaning of the word in this context. In another sense we say, “The food is finished,” because it is ended; in another, “The book is finished,” because it is complete in its writing. Here, therefore, the completion refers to perfection: what God began, he brought to perfection, not to failure.

The crowds were astonished at his teaching. They marveled as though at a fountain of wisdom. If it was said of Moses that he was powerful in deed and word, what must be said of the one who taught him, the Wisdom of God the Father? For he was teaching as one possessing authority, and not as the scribes and Pharisees. They taught as people who had learned from mortals, and they did not fully understand the things they read in the Law and the Prophets. The Lord, however, taught as the one who had given the Law and spoken through the Prophets.

## CHAPTER XV. On the Cleansing of the Leper

When he had come down from the mountain, great crowds followed him. You heard that he went up the mountain and first instructed the disciples in the higher places concerning more secret matters and the eight beatitudes, and afterward instructed the people in a somewhat lower part of the same mountain. When all these things had been completed, he came down from the mountain, and the crowds that had gone up the mountain because of him returned together with him.

And behold, a leper came and worshiped him, saying: Lepers were forbidden to approach people in their houses. Therefore he encountered the Lord neither on the mountain, because of the crowd, nor in a house, but on the road. Leprosy is a roughness of the skin covered with scales, resembling stone. In Greek the leper is called *leprosus*, from the excessive itching of the affliction, which now turns black, now white, and now red.

Although this man was held by such an illness, he was wise in approaching, humble in speaking, and persistent in asking. He fell on his face. This expressed humility and shame. He was not ashamed of his illness, but he showed reverence.

Lord, if you will, you can cleanse me. He worships and invokes God. “Lord, if you will”: I do not know whether I am worthy to be cleansed, because I believe this has happened to me on account of my sins. You know; I place everything in your will. You wished this most unclean leprosy to come upon me so that, being corrected, I might repent—or perhaps for the sake of your mighty works, so that by cleansing me wonderfully you might be magnified by all.

I did not dare say, “If you can do anything, help me,” because I know that you can do everything. I ask only your will: if you will, you can cleanse me.

And extending his hand, he touched him, saying: He extended his hand toward the man whom the priests did not consider worthy to touch. Or he extended his hand to show that he was above the Law, since he had commanded the leper; the leprosy itself did not dare await his hand, but as soon as it saw the hand coming, it fled.

I will. In response to the very words with which the leper had pleaded, saying, “If you will,” the Lord answered, “I will.” To his statement, “You can,” he replied, “Be cleansed.” The words should not be joined so as to mean, “I will cleanse”; rather, “I will” should be said first, followed by the command, “Be cleansed.” Here *mundare* is not the infinitive mood but the imperative. Because the Lord perceived both faith and humility in him, he responded in this corresponding way to his words.

And immediately his leprosy was cleansed. I do not know whether the leprosy feared his word or his touch more. If he had remained silent, the leprosy would not have dared await the Lord’s hand, because it had not been created there. If he had not extended his hand and said, “I will,” it would not have dared remain. For he was within that body who said, and things came to be.

[Col. 1326A] And Jesus said to him: See that you tell no one. He gives this command to show his disciples that when they do something good, they must not publicize it in order to seek praise or money. Indeed, there was no need to tell it in words, since everyone saw that the man whom they had previously seen as a leper was now well.

But go, show yourself to the priest. For three reasons the Lord commanded the cleansed man to present himself to the priests. First, so that he might appear to show reverence to the priests. Second, so that he would not appear to abolish the Law, which they accused him of doing. Third, so that, if they did not believe that the man was cleansed when they saw one whom they themselves had been unable to cleanse according to the Law, they might be condemned more severely.

And offer the gift that Moses commanded. Moses commanded that whoever had been cleansed from leprosy should offer a burnt offering to the Lord, two turtledoves or two young pigeons, as is contained in Leviticus. Indeed, his body and blood had not yet been mystically consecrated, which he accomplished one day before the Passion; therefore he did not wish to destroy the symbolic sacrifice until the new one should come.

For a testimony to them. That is, so that they might offer a burnt offering for one cleansed by me and yet refuse to believe.

In a symbolic sense, this man, who is said to have been full of leprosy, represents the human race, which before the Lord’s incarnation was full of every sin. When the Lord came, he not only restored us to the camp of the Church, but also made us a priestly race, a holy nation, and a people of possession; and we who were far away because of our sins were made near.

He commanded that we, made into turtledoves and pigeons in our manner of life, should offer ourselves to God, so that, imitating the chastity of turtledoves and the simplicity of pigeons, and without the gall of bitterness, we may learn to pass through the snares of this age. Thus we may become not only a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God, but also the temple of God, in which he deigns to dwell and walk, until he brings us to the place where we may rejoice with him without end.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the Healing of the Centurion’s Servant

When he had entered Capernaum. Capernaum was a large village in Galilee where Roman officials were accustomed to reside. When the Lord approached it, a centurion came to him—not bodily, but in faith and devotion. Luke relates that he sent Jews to him, considering himself unworthy to appear before him. A centurion is so called because he is in charge of a hundred soldiers, just as a *quinquagenarius* commands fifty and a *decanus* ten soldiers. He appealed to him through the Jews he had sent, who also said this to him: “He is worthy that you should grant this to him, because he loves our nation, and he built our synagogue for us.”

Lord, my servant lies at home paralyzed. *Paralyticus* means in Greek what in Latin is called “relaxed in all his limbs.” I said above that servants are called by four designations. In the sense in which David’s *pueri* were so called, namely because of obedience, this man also calls him his *puer*, unwilling to say that he was his slave, out of affection for the boy. To express the pain, he says that he is both paralyzed and lying down, since many paralytics walk.

And he added: And he is suffering terribly.

And Jesus said to them—that is, to those he had sent—I will come and heal him. As another Evangelist reports, he immediately began to go, not for any gift, but because of the centurion’s faith, humility, and prudence: faith, because he believed that the paralytic could be healed by the Savior; humility, because he did not consider himself worthy to come to him; prudence, because he knew that God could accomplish whatever he wished by a word, wherever he was.

And the centurion answered and said: Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof. Luke relates that he sent messengers on the road, saying that the Lord should not trouble himself, because he was not worthy for him to enter under his roof.

But only say the word, and my servant will be healed. Although he was a Gentile, he believed that the Lord was the one who said, and things came to be; he commanded, and they were created.

[Col. 1327B] For I too am a man under authority, having soldiers under me. He gives an example, as though saying: If I, who am merely a human being placed under another’s authority—namely, that of the emperor Tiberius—say to my junior soldiers that they should do this or that, and it is done, how much more can you, who have angels under your authority, accomplish whatever you command? If you give an order to Raphael or to his order, it will immediately be done.

“I say to this one” means, understand, “to this soldier.” A soldier is called *miles*, from *mille*, “thousand,” because the first thousand were organized by Romulus, or because one was chosen from a thousand when men were selected.

And to my servant, “Do this,” that is, the task, and he does it. A servant is called *servus* because he was first preserved in war. Every creature obeys you as Lord; therefore you can do whatever you wish.

When Jesus heard this, he marveled. He demonstrated to those who saw and heard that this was faith to be marveled at and imitated. For he himself, who had created him, had already known his faith.

And he said to those following him: I have not found such faith in Israel. He speaks of carnal Israel, which possessed the Law and the Prophets but did not understand his divinity in this way. For he had found perfect faith in the apostles and in Nathanael, but he spoke of the carnal Jews, because the whole nation was called Israel by the general name. It was as though he had said: all Israel, possessing the Law and the Prophets, ought to have known me in the way this man did, but it does not.

A part is understood through the whole by synecdoche, as in another passage: “They are dead,” although only Herod had died.

But I say to you that many will come from the east and the west. Through these two parts the others are also understood, namely the whole world. They will approach God in faith and will be received into that paradise where Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob are, and they will enjoy blessed life.

But the children of this kingdom will be cast into the outer darkness—that is, the Jews, who were born there and received the Law and descended from the patriarchs, will be sent into the outer darkness, that is, into hell, where there is perpetual darkness. The inner darkness is the blindness of the mind, by which we ought to see better. But whoever does not know God possesses this darkness in the present life; for this reason he will be sent into the outer darkness, where he will be tormented together with body and soul.

There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. In the weeping of the eyes and the gnashing of the teeth, the resurrection of flesh and bones is signified. These things will suffer a real punishment, not an imaginary one or one occurring as in a dream.

This centurion represents the first people of the Gentiles who would believe in God, become children of Abraham through faith, and obtain the place of the Israelites in the kingdom of God. The servant for whom he pleads represents that part of the people who are converted to God slowly and are said, as it were, to be servants, because they remain longer in the service of idols. For those who make idols become like them, as do those who trust in them; and whoever commits sin is a servant of sin.

And Jesus said to the centurion: Go; as you have believed, so let it be done for you. Almighty God frequently said this to many people. Thus it is shown that each person will receive from God and obtain what he asks according to his faith, if he believes perfectly, asks in the Savior’s name, and does not hesitate in asking.

And the servant was healed in that hour. From this we can gather that the prayers of some help others, as does perfect faith. Let all of us Christians imitate this centurion in prudence, faith, and humility. Let us strive to be prudent according to God, since God said: “Be prudent as serpents.” Let us fight for righteousness even unto death, prepared to give an answer to everyone who asks us for an account of the hope that is in us.

Let us also possess a firm and upright faith in God, and keep all promises we have made, except insofar as they depart from God’s will. Let us possess humility in mind and body, because God commanded all Christians to learn from him humility and gentleness.

## CHAPTER XVII. On Peter’s Mother-in-Law
[Col. 1328C] And when Jesus had entered Peter’s house, he saw Peter’s mother-in-law lying sick with a fever. Peter’s mother-in-law is said to be the woman whose daughter the blessed Peter had [as his wife]. Another Evangelist says that they pleaded with him on her behalf. And standing over her, he commanded the fever, and it left her. Sometimes the Lord awaits the prayers of those who ask. Sometimes, of his own accord, he heals the sick person, wishing them to give greater thanks to God, for whose sake he acts in response to their prayers; even today, regarding the things he has arranged for us, he wishes us to ask him for them.

And he touched her hand, and the fever left her. Since his two beloved disciples were pleading for her, he drove away the fever by his word and extended his hand to the woman as she rose. And she rose and ministered to them. It is natural for all fever patients, once they have been freed from the fever, to feel the greater discomfort of illness and weariness [Col. 1328D] and to lie as though half-alive. But to show that he healed differently from earthly physicians, he healed all whom he healed in a moment, so that no trace of the former illness remained. Thus, when this woman rose, she immediately began to minister to the Lord. She signifies a person oppressed by some sin—lust or greed, for example. If good friends pray for such a person, he will be healed of that fever, to the point that he will minister to the Lord, whereas previously he ministered to the devil by doing his will.

But when evening came, they brought him many who had demons. Since that day had been the Sabbath, they did not dare to bring the sick before evening because of the Sabbath, especially those possessed by demons—people whom they could bring in no other way [Col. 1329A] except bound and by force. This is figuratively represented as meaning that, when he who was the true sun was about to set on the cross, he would heal the whole world.

Luke says of these that they confessed him to be the Christ, either because they were tempting him, as their master had previously done when he said, “If you are the Son of God,” or because they recognized him through the greatness of his signs.

It follows: “So that what had been spoken through Isaiah the prophet might be fulfilled: ‘He himself took our infirmities and bore our sicknesses.’” This may be understood of both kinds of infirmity: both of those from which, as he has just said, he freed them, and of the infirmities of souls, from which every day he frees many thousands.

## CHAPTER XVIII. The Rejected Scribe and the Lord’s Poverty

When he saw the great crowds around him, he ordered them to go across the [Col. 1329B] strait. Above I said that, because of the crowds pressing upon him, the Lord chose three places of refuge for himself: the pinnacle of the Temple, this lake, and Mount Tabor. When he saw the multitude, he ordered them to cross the strait.

The word *fretum* (“strait”) is derived from *fervere* (“to boil”), because every day they saw signs on land by which they could recognize that he was the creator of lands and human beings. He preferred that they should also know him to be the God of the sea and of all creatures—not, as among the pagans, one god of heaven and earth and another of the sea, but the one God through whom all things visible and invisible were made.

And a certain scribe approached and said to him. This scribe was also a learned man, called in Greek *grammaticus*, “a grammarian.” Having seen the greatness of the signs, he wished to follow the Lord for the sake of profit, like Simon Magus. This is apparent from his words: he calls him neither “God” nor “Lord,” but “teacher,” judging that he would be like other human beings.

And Jesus says to him: “Foxes have dens, and the birds of the air have nests.” It is as though he said to him: “Why do you wish to follow me for the sake of profit, when I am so poor that I lack what even small beasts and the birds of the air possess—namely, a place to make a bed, unless I lodge as a guest in other people’s dwellings? I am content with food and clothing.”

But another of his disciples said to him: “Lord, permit me first to go and bury my father.” This man both believed better and followed with better devotion, since he said, “Lord.” He also possessed the better intention, since he desired to bury his dead father, even though he had died a violent death.

Jesus said to him: “Follow me, and let the dead bury their own dead.” A person is called dead in two ways: dead in body [Col. 1329D] and dead in soul. But woe to those who are dead in both ways, because they are beyond restoration. For those who are dead only in soul can still, if they hasten, be raised again, provided they promise amendment with their whole heart. Solomon speaks of such people: “Better is a living dog than a dead lion.” But of those dead only in body it is written: “Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord.”

The man whom the disciple wished to go and bury was dead in soul and body, while those who were near him were dead in soul. It could happen that, if the disciple went away to those who were dead in soul, he too would die inwardly, because one usually becomes holy with the holy and perverse with the perverse.

“Let the dead in soul bury the dead in body and soul.” And because he says “their own dead,” it may be that they themselves had killed him inwardly through their bad example. Whoever provides someone with a bad example of a grave sin kills that person, if the person follows him.

## CHAPTER XIX. The Storm at Sea

When he had entered the boat, his disciples followed him. In these lakes large ships are not usually built because of the force of storms, but smaller ones, which can scarcely hold twelve men. For this reason he says, “and his disciples followed him.” The crowds would have followed if they had had boats. But they remained outside and saw the miracle from a distance, and they recognized that he did not possess, as someone said of Octavian,

> “Caesar shares the empire with Jupiter,”

[Col. 1330B] but that he held heaven with earth, the sea, and everything in them under his power.

And behold, a great disturbance arose in the sea. Storms usually do more harm in these pools than in rivers, because waters that do not flow, when they are slightly disturbed, develop a more powerful agitation. Thus, unless people quickly fled to the shore, they were endangered.

So that the boat was covered by the waves. It was covered to such an extent that it could not be seen by those standing on land, because of the high waves beside it. But he himself was sleeping. Both natures are indicated in this miracle, the divine and the human: the divine, because he commands the sea and the winds; the human, because he is said to sleep.

Jonah, understanding that the sea had been stirred up on his account, had gone down into the inner part of the ship to sleep, so that when the sea did not see him, it might rest from seeking him as he fled from God. This second Jonah went down to sleep so that he could rebuke the sea and the disciples for their little faith.

The sea seemed to say about Jonah: “The one I am seeking is in this ship.” This sea seemed to say: “The one in whom you place your trust is sleeping. Do you not believe that he is awake by his divinity? Therefore we shall cast you into fear.” If they had been as perfect as they later became, they would have said: “We are not afraid, because you do not dare to drown your Lord and Creator.”

He was sleeping in body, but he stirred up the sea and the winds and cast the disciples into fear. And they approached and awoke him, saying. Jonah caused the disturbance unwillingly, but this man did so willingly. The sailors wanted to flee with Jonah, but the sea did not permit it, as though saying: “Repay him by fleeing, so that I may cast him into prison, and go in peace.” These men wanted to flee, and the sea seemed to say: “Unless you believe that he is our God, you will not escape.”

They resorted to what they were accustomed to, to the body they could see. They were not yet perfect enough to say: “He who created you is awake; he who sleeps is here with us. He was born of holy Mary; nevertheless, you do not dare to drown him.”

“Lord, save us; we are perishing!” Not soberly, but excessively, as when they awoke him in fear, saying: “Save us; we are perishing.” When Jonah rose, he delivered his companions; but this man did so by his power, whereas Jonah did so through his own humiliation.

And he said to them: “Why are you afraid, you of little faith?” A person has little faith who is not perfect in love. Or the apostles are said to have had little faith because, while the Creator was present, they were afraid.

Then he rose [Col. 1331A] and rebuked the winds and the sea, and there was a great calm. He said to the sea, “Be silent,” and to the wind, “Be mute.” He did not pray, as the pagans do, who worship the wind; he commanded it to cease.

And from this it follows: “For the men marveled.” It had happened before that many who suffered storms drove them away by prayer; but no one before him had done so by command. And there was a great calm. In correspondence with what was said above—“a great disturbance arose”—it is again said, “there was a great calm.” He who commanded a great disturbance to arise commanded a great calm to arise, and every creature recognized its Creator.

The “men” who marveled are understood to be the sailors. Or, if you wish to understand them as the apostles, they are called men because they were afraid in the presence of the Lord.

“What sort of man is this?” Supply: “How great a man is he,” since he commands insensible creatures and they obey him.

That lake signifies this world, and the ship signifies the Church. He is always present in his Church, as he said: “I am with you until the consummation of the age.” But sometimes he permitted those who were in the Church to be afflicted by the persecutions of unbelievers, so that they who were in it said: “Rise up; why do you sleep, O Lord? Rise up; do not reject us forever.” But he rose and made great peace for his Church.

## CHAPTER XX. The Healing of Two Demoniacs

And when he had arrived across the strait, in the region of the Gerasenes. Gerasa is a famous city in Arabia, across the Jordan, which was in the tribe of Manasseh, not far from the lake of Tiberias.

Two men possessed by demons met him, coming out of the tombs, exceedingly fierce. Historically, this is what happened; allegorically, they signify peoples devoted to sins who delighted in dead works—that is, in sins.

And they cried out, saying: “What have we to do with you, Son of God? Have you come before the appointed time to torment us?” This confession is not voluntary but compelled. They were testing whether he was the Christ, for they wanted to determine this through the greatness of his signs. And, as some teachers say, the devil did not persuade the Jews to crucify Christ because he did not know that he was the Christ, but because he did not foresee that he would be condemned by his death.

When they say, “You have come before the appointed time to torment us,” they know for certain that on the day of judgment they will be subjected to more severe tortures. Therefore, like runaway slaves anxious about beatings, they are concerned about them and plead for relief.

Now there was not far from them a large herd of pigs feeding. These pigs did not belong to the Jewish peoples but to foreigners, because the Jews abhorred not only eating them but even touching them, as we read in the Book of Maccabees. For this reason they allowed them to be killed, since they were unwilling to eat pork; and because pigs were not offered in God’s sacrifice, they asked that the demons be permitted to enter the pigs.

And because the Romans who lived there with their royal governors could not keep those same pigs together with Jewish livestock, so many had been gathered in one place.

The demons, however, were pleading. Luke says that they begged him not to command them to go [Col. 1332A] into the abyss, knowing that a future judgment would come, when, at the Lord’s advent, they would be sent into the infernal abyss. They pleaded that this condemnation not come upon them too soon—or “into the abyss,” that is, into deep water.

Their request was granted to their condemnation, because what they feared happened to them.
