Some teachers say that each evil angel that fell into water can exercise power in water, while one that fell upon land has power on land. Or they were granted their request so that, through the death of the pigs, the inhabitants of that place might believe; and so it happened.

They found a dwelling suitable for themselves, because no animal lives more filthily than a pig. The devil is accustomed to dwell in such animals, and those who live like pigs are accustomed to dwell with him, because they are always thinking about the belly, whose god is the belly, and they always wish to live in the mire of lust.

And behold, the whole herd rushed headlong into the sea. What the demons feared happened to them. The herdsmen fled and, coming into the city, reported everything.

And behold, the whole city went out to meet Jesus. For the sake of the salvation of these men, the Lord considered it a small matter that the pigs should be killed, since no creature under the sun is dearer to God than the soul, and a person ought to give everything he possesses for his soul.

When they saw him, they begged him to depart from their territory. They did not plead out of hatred, but out of humility, judging themselves unworthy of his presence. That they pleaded for this reason became apparent when he returned: they not only came to him themselves but also invited their neighbors to come to him.

## CHAPTER XXI. The Healing of the Paralytic

And he entered the boat, crossed over, and came to his own city. From the region of the Gerasenes he crossed the lake again and returned to Galilee.

And he came to his own city. His own city is called Nazareth, for no other reason than that he had been raised there. Our Lord and Savior gave preachers an example, so that with all diligence they should announce the word of life to peoples. Thus he was now in Gerasa, now in Nazareth, now in Capernaum, and yet never [“ocsus”; sic].

And behold, they brought him a paralytic. Another Evangelist says that this happened in Capernaum. There is no obstacle to understanding it in this way, because when the Lord crossed over from the strait, he passed through Nazareth and came to Capernaum, and an innumerable multitude of people gathered around him. As a result, this paralytic could not be brought in through the doorway; instead, after the roof had been stripped of its tiles, they lowered him down before Jesus.

“Paralytic,” or *paralysis*, is a Greek name and is called in Latin “dissolution of the limbs,” or “one dissolved in his limbs.” Physicians say that this happens because of an excessive abundance of blood. But I do not think this is so, because this illness scarcely weakens a person before the age of forty, and we know that at that time the blood already begins to diminish in each person. The part weakened by paralysis is regarded as though dead; therefore I think that the blood there dies.

For if this happened because of an abundance of blood, it would occur in young people, in whom the blood increases and is hot. But now it always occurs in old people; and if the blood were abundant, surely the limbs would remain alive [Col. 1333A]. But when the blood fails—for it is the seat of the soul—the soul abandons the limbs and contracts itself where the blood is.

The power [truth] of the literal meaning is clear. Morally, this man represents any sinner weighed down by the burden of sins and despairing, who, because of the excessive enormity of his crimes, does not even ask forgiveness for his sins. If good men take him up and, as it were, carry him back to God through exhortation, and entreat God on his behalf, they will restore him to health.

Hence it follows: “And when Jesus saw their faith, he said to the paralytic.” Seeing the faith of those who brought him, the Lord has mercy on the man who was in despair. If someone ceases to sin and good people pray for him, they will be heard.

“Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven you.” He calls him “son” because his sins are forgiven. Here, however, the Lord shows that many fall into illnesses because of their sins. For we find in divine Scripture that illnesses befall people for three reasons, which some reduce to five. Let us state the five, which are the same.

An illness is given either for the increase of merits, as in the case of Job and Tobit; or for the preservation of virtues, as in the case of blessed Paul, to whom a thorn in the flesh, an angel of Satan, had been given; or for the manifestation of God’s glory, as in the case of Lazarus and the man born blind. Of some people it is said that their illnesses occurred for the manifestation of God’s glory. I say that all these are one reason, because everyone’s merits were increased through the illnesses, although others count three.

Or people are weighed down because of their sins, as this paralytic was, and those who hear from the Apostle that many receive the Lord’s body unworthily: “For this reason many are weak and ill, and many sleep.” Herod and Antiochus were condemned for their sins, both in the present and in the future, as were countless others.

Sometimes their sins are forgiven in the present, and they are healed in the body, as happened to these people and to Mary in the wilderness. Sometimes they pass from a present punishment to a future one, as Herod and Antiochus did. Those who speak of five divide this one reason into two.

I add a third reason: lack of self-control, when someone does not preserve his body according to its nature and reason. This is the only condition that physicians can sometimes cure. In other cases, no one can cure it except the one who permitted it to rule.

And behold, certain scribes said to themselves: “This man is blaspheming.” The scribes thought that he was merely a human being, [Col. 1333D] and they had read in the prophet the words spoken in God’s person: “I am the one who blots out your iniquities.” Therefore they accused him of blasphemy.

And when Jesus saw their thoughts, he said to them. The Lord answered their thoughts as though he had said: “If you have read that no one can forgive sins except God alone, you have likewise read that no one can know human thoughts except God alone, as Solomon says: ‘For you alone know the hearts of human beings.’ Understand, therefore, that he who knows your thoughts can also forgive sins.”

“Why are you thinking evil in your hearts?” Namely, that I cannot forgive sins.

“For which is easier to say, ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say, ‘Rise and walk’? Which do you consider lighter, and which more difficult? Perhaps you consider ‘Rise and walk’ more difficult, because this is seen with bodily eyes.”

“But so that you may know that I have authority to forgive sins”—and that I have forgiven sins—“therefore I can heal him.”

Then he said to the paralytic: “Rise, take up your bed, and go to your house.” Because they did not believe what they could not see with bodily eyes, he said, “Rise,” so that they might see that, just as he was healthy from bodily illness, so he was healthy from spiritual illness.

“Take up your bed,” so that they might know that you have been healed differently from earthly physicians, since no trace of your former illness appears in you, to the point that you can carry the bed on which you had been unable even to turn yourself.

“And go to your house,” you who were carried here on the feet of others.

And he rose and took up what he had lain upon. And he went to his house. Without delay he did three things: he rose, [Col. 1334B] took up his bed, and went to his house. Because he himself had not pleaded for his health, but others had interceded for him, the Lord did not wish him to have a follower until he returned to his own house, recognized the benefits conferred upon him, and returned to him.

For those weighed down by this illness do not usually possess a complete understanding, so that, when others grieve for them, they themselves seem almost not to understand or grieve over their own evil. This is apparent in the fact that, when a part of the body dies, the function that the soul was accustomed to perform through those limbs ceases.

When the crowds saw this, they were afraid. The lesser crowds were afraid because the scribes had dared to disparage him in their thoughts. But those wicked men did not fear, because a mind devoted to evil does not fear the evil it itself commits, as others do who shudder at it.

And they glorified God, who had given such authority to human beings. As imperfect people, they did not understand that the one in that man was the one who had given authority to the human being whom they saw. Yet they did something good if they gave thanks to God, who had permitted one sharing a body with human beings to perform such deeds on earth. If they had been perfect, they would have given thanks with the Father, who had been pleased to perform such things on earth through him.

This man therefore signifies a person weighed down by a mass of sins who, because of the excessive heap of his sins, does not ask forgiveness, judging that he cannot attain pardon for so many evils. If he has good teachers who bring him back and present him to Christ through the hope of forgiveness, and who pray for him, they will obtain for him the help of hope and forgiveness.

They are rightly said to have been four, because through the four books of the Gospel he can be brought back to the hope of forgiveness. They lowered him down by four ropes, because, together with the teaching of the Gospel, it is necessary to preach the four virtues through which each perfect person walks the road of this world without stumbling: prudence, fortitude, temperance, and justice.

“Son, your sins are forgiven you.” You who were previously a son of the devil by doing his will will become a son of God when you have been freed from sin.

And he rose and went to his house. He rose who had previously been lying in sins, and he went to his house—that is, to the Church of God.

## CHAPTER XXII. The Calling of Matthew

And as Jesus was passing on from there, namely from Capernaum, he saw a man sitting in the tax office. “In the tax office” means “at the tax office,” in charge of tax collection. For *telos* in Greek means “tax” in Latin. A tax—a census payment that can be carried—is so called from *vehere*, “to carry.”

He was sitting because he himself was the master and had younger men who went around the marketplace, collected the taxes, and brought them back to him. Or he was sitting inside because the marketplace was over the water, and he collected what was paid from the ships, since that too is called a tax office.

His name was Matthew. Other Evangelists call him Levi, which was not his public name. He had two names. Out of modesty and respect, they kept silent both about his common name and about the occupation he practiced.

But he himself, in accordance with Solomon’s saying that the righteous person in the beginning is his own accuser, not only names himself Matthew but also confesses his occupation, so that he might deserve to be justified, in accordance with the saying: “Declare your iniquities, so that you may be justified.” He also offers an example to all who wish to be converted, since he himself was changed from a tax collector into an evangelist.

And he said to him: “Follow me.” Not only with the steps of the body but also by imitating his conduct.

Understanding this, the blessed Matthew, according to Luke’s Gospel, left everything and followed him. He did not wait to collect the tax or render an account to his master, but abandoned completely what he was doing; he who had been accustomed to seize what belonged to others abandoned what was his own.

Recognizing his guilt—for he himself was of the tribe of Levi, from which he was also called Levi, and ought to have served the Lord at the Temple, but had attached himself to a base occupation out of love of money—the blessed Matthew made known the perfect model of following the Lord. He cared neither about loss nor about the danger that could result from the loss of earthly property, since he abandoned an incomplete account of his taxes.

Nor is it surprising that he followed the Lord with such eagerness at the sound of a single command, since he had both heard and seen him perform many miracles, while a divine inspiration was present within him, invisibly kindling him to follow. There was also the majesty and radiance shining from the face of the Lord who called him.

And it happened, while he was reclining at table in the house, that behold, many tax collectors and sinners were reclining with Jesus. These tax collectors were men who had at that time collected public taxes unjustly with others, or contractors of public revenues, such as Matthew.

These sinners were people who pursued the profits of this world through business, such as merchants or those practicing various occupations. There are, in fact, businesses that cannot be conducted without sin—for example, when someone buys gold, silver, or something similar in one place, contributes no labor to it, undertakes no journey for it, and, when his neighbor comes to buy it, doubles the price. Whatever he receives beyond his expenditure, he defrauds his neighbor of entirely.

Thus those who had been tax collectors and sinners reclined with the Lord, but they had now changed their occupation and been changed in mind. The Lord went to sinners’ banquets so that he might have an opportunity to teach and could introduce spiritual food among the bodily food for his hosts. His humility is also commended to us, as is the place of repentance.

Indeed, wherever he is read to have been invited, it is immediately reported that he taught there or performed some virtuous deed—not that anyone compelled him or conspired to make him drink, or that he himself compelled anyone, even though Luke reports that Matthew made a great banquet for him.

And when the Pharisees saw this, they said to his disciples. Since they did not dare to speak to the teacher out of reverence for his signs and wisdom, they rebuked his disciples: “Why does your teacher eat with tax collectors and sinners?” Because they saw and heard that there was a place for repentance, and they had an example in their teacher Matthew, they flocked to the teacher.

But Jesus, hearing this, said: “Those who are well do not need a physician, but those who are sick.” The Lord gives an analogy: just as the ministry of physicians has no function for a healthy person, so the physician of souls can offer no benefit to one who does not confess that he is sick—that is, a sinner in soul.

He calls himself a physician, since he was wounded because of our sins, and by whose bruise we have been healed. He calls the scribes and Pharisees “healthy,” not because they were truly healthy in soul, but because they themselves claimed to be healthy. He calls the tax collectors sick because they admitted that they were sinners.

There is no evil worse before God than to be a sinner while thinking oneself righteous. If someone is not a sinner, he becomes unrighteous by justifying himself. For where there is no confession, there is no forgiveness.

When David was righteous in his conduct, he began to become proud in his heart. God so abhorred this evil that he allowed him to fall into adultery and murder, manifest crimes, so that, while he recoiled from what was manifest, he might be chastened for the hidden evil in his soul.

“Go and learn what this means: ‘I desire mercy and not sacrifice.’” Go either to yourselves, to one another, or to your books, since you do not believe my teaching. Learn that you still do not understand what you think you understand.

Almighty God says this through the prophet: it is more pleasing to him that someone show mercy to his neighbor than that he offer holocausts for himself. Whoever extends mercy to someone else slaughters himself in that person’s suffering.

The sacrifices once permitted were instituted for no other reason than to prevent them from being offered to demons, as he says: “I did not desire your holocausts.”

“For I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners.” When God came into this world, no one was righteous; we were all held under the condition of sin. Therefore, by “righteous” he means not those who truly are righteous, but those who think themselves righteous.

No one who thought himself righteous and refused baptism attained forgiveness of sins, whether through Christ or through the apostles. The people earlier called “healthy” are called “righteous” here. Both terms are false descriptions.

Then the disciples of John approached him, saying: “Why do we and the Pharisees fast, but your disciples do not fast?” The disciples of John were not yet perfect. They had heard their teacher frequently praise Christ and denounce the Pharisees, calling them “offspring of vipers,” yet they joined them in criticizing the Lord’s disciples.

If the Pharisees had seen the Lord eating at that very time, how would his disciples not also have criticized him, since they even tried to turn the healings of people into something evil?

These fasts had not been commanded in the Law; the Pharisees themselves had invented them, just as they invented other superstitions. The Sadducees did likewise, as Josephus relates.

And Jesus said to them: “Can the wedding guests mourn while the bridegroom is with them?” “Mourn” is used for “fast,” because fasting belongs to mourning.

He gives an analogy about a bridegroom and a bride: when they are joined together, they spend days of joy. He wishes himself to be understood spiritually as the bridegroom and the Church as his bride.

The bridal chamber of this bridegroom was the womb of holy Mary, in which God deigned to become human. When he was speaking these words, that union was taking place, since through his preaching he was gathering that same bride to himself.

Therefore he says, “The wedding guests cannot mourn”—namely, the apostles—because they had been begotten by him through the Gospel.

“But days will come when the bridegroom will be taken away from them, and then they will fast.” He indicates the time when he ascended into heaven. Although he was always spiritually with them, he withdrew from them in bodily presence.

“No one puts a patch of new cloth on an old garment.” Throughout the text of the Gospel there are figures of speech, but because of the tediousness and length of the book we frequently omit them.

By metaphor and its form, allegories and parables make a comparison from the lower to the higher and from the inanimate to the animate. Just as, when garments are mended, if a new patch is sewn onto an old garment, the new material removes from the old whatever has been joined to it and makes the garment worse, so the Lord says that this would happen to his disciples. They were still old because of the teaching of the Pharisees with which they had been imbued. If he suddenly imposed upon them the austerity of his preaching, they would lose even something they seemed to possess.

This is what the seventy disciples did: because they did not understand the word itself, they went back and no longer walked with him.

“Nor do they put new wine into old wineskins.” The new wine is the preaching of the Gospel; the old wineskins are the apostles. New wine not only bursts old wineskins; must also bursts large and sturdy wooden vessels.

Likewise, the preaching of the Gospel, when not properly understood, became a ruin for many. Otherwise, the wineskins will burst, the wine will be spilled, and the wineskins will perish—that is, their hearts will be scattered, they will depart from the faith, and they will be lost.

“But they put new wine into new wineskins.” When they have been made new through my teaching, strengthened through my passion, resurrection, and ascension, and through the coming of the Holy Spirit, then they will observe all that is hard and difficult, and both will be preserved: the disciples and the preaching that has been sown in them.

And so it happened, because afterward they endured crosses, tortures, and scourging, although previously they could not endure even a harsh word.

## CHAPTER XXIII. The Daughter of Jairus Raised

While he was speaking these things to them, behold, a certain ruler approached. While the Lord was speaking to the crowds about the salvation of souls, a certain ruler of the Jews came. Because he was learned in the Law and was an *archisynagogus*, that is, a ruler of the synagogue, he was called this because, on account of his knowledge, he was their teacher in their assemblies. He was also of noble status. His name is given by the other Evangelists, who say: “His name was Jairus.”

And he worshiped him, saying: “My daughter has just died.” She was not yet dead when her father approached, but this was announced to him on the way. Matthew, however, aiming at brevity, narrates it in this way.

Although he was a Jew, he did not say, as the centurion had said, “Speak, and it will happen,” but “Come,” believing that he would be only a prophet, though he did not truly believe. Nevertheless, he was exceedingly wicked, and the Lord consented to act at his request.

“But come, lay your hand upon her, and she will live.” Because he had no other daughter or son, he loved her tenderly. Therefore he himself came, fell at his feet, and wished to return with the teacher to her, like the Shunammite woman who would not let Elisha go until he reached her dead son.

And Jesus rose and followed him, along with his disciples. It should be noted that the disciples are mentioned as being present at all the Lord’s deeds, and they rightly became such men, because the examiner of the heart examined their hidden things.

[Col. 1338C] According to Matthew’s text, seven miracles are now reported as having been performed by the Lord. At the eighth, the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue was about to enter, but the woman with the hemorrhage intervened.

Figuratively, this ruler of the synagogue is understood as Moses, because he is called Jairus, that is, “enlightened,” since he was enlightened by God with the light of faith and knowledge of the Law.

He has one daughter, that is, the synagogue, whom he loved with a singular love and for whom he frequently entreated God. To fall at his feet is to venerate his incarnation. Since God is the head of Christ, his feet can appropriately be understood as his incarnation. To fall at his feet therefore means to confess him to be singularly great above all.

“My daughter has just died.” Shortly before the Redeemer’s coming, she had lost all the righteousness of the Law.

“He rose and followed him.” When God saw that the Jews had perished from true life, he came to restore them. He followed him because, just as Moses had foretold about him, so the Lord did in every respect.

And behold, a woman who had suffered from a flow of blood. This woman signifies the Church gathered from the Gentiles. Just as she had been excluded from houses and crowds for twelve years because of the impurity of her blood, and therefore came to the Lord on the way, so the Gentile people had been excluded from the assembly of the faithful and polluted by the innate flow of carnal desires.

But when she saw that, by the word of God, he was saving the daughter of the synagogue, she seized salvation for herself.

The ruler of the synagogue’s daughter was twelve years old, and this woman had suffered from her illness for twelve years. When the former began to be born according to God in the patriarchs, the latter began to grow distant from God and to become sick in mind.

She approached from behind. When Christ ascended, the Gentiles began to believe. To approach from behind means to follow and imitate him, because he said: “If anyone serves me, let him follow me.” And elsewhere: “You shall walk after the Lord your God.”

And she touched the fringe of his garment. The Lord had commanded that fringes be made at the top of the tunic, so that just as circumcision was a distinguishing mark on bodies, so it might be on garments. The Jews devised the practice of placing thorns there, so that whenever they were pricked they might be recalled to the law of God, and the law of God might be remembered. But this woman did not find thorns there, because the Lord abhorred and detested the superfluous abominations of the Pharisees. Nor is the reason for touching the garment that covered the Lord’s flesh, but rather that which protruded outward. [Col. 1339B] In another sense, to touch the fringe of his garment means to believe in his incarnation. For she was saying within herself: “If I touch only his garment, I shall be saved.” If I believe in his incarnation, I shall be saved. And *primordium* is the beginning of an unclean thought, from which sin is born. The fountain of blood was the origin of sin. And she had suffered much at the hands of many physicians. For there were many philosophers who debated the virtues of the soul and its vices, but nevertheless did not lead the gentile people to true medicine. And she had spent all her substance on them. For the gentile world expended all its labor on the various poems of the philosophers.

But Jesus turned and, seeing her, said. The other evangelists report that he said: “Who touched me?” And Peter said: “Master, the crowds press upon you and [Col. 1339C] afflict you, and you say: ‘Who touched me?’” Others touched him with bodily contact; she touched him with faith. Whoever touches the Lord in this way deserves to be healed. Thus the Church from the gentiles also touched the Lord through faith, because she believed in him with a perfect heart; hence it was said to the other woman, who did not yet believe rightly: “Do not touch me,” because you do not touch me perfectly in faith. But she came and fell before him, and confessed for what reason she had touched him, and how the flow of her blood had immediately stopped.

For the salvation of others the Lord inquired so carefully, so that others likewise might strive to possess good faith, and it might be said of them: “Daughter, your faith has saved you”; you were saved because you believed. This woman is called *aimatosa*, a Greek name, her name being derived from the action. For blood is called *haima* (αἷμα) in Greek, and from it *aimatosa* is derived, [Col. 1339D] that is, “blood-bearing” or “hemorrhagic.” She is healed in the eighth place because of the eighth day of the resurrection, which the entire Church of the gentiles venerates. And the woman was saved from that hour. Whoever strives to be of good faith toward God will also become a son of God, and it will be done for him according to his faith. Likewise, from the time when the Church from the gentiles believed in God, she began to be saved, both in mind and in body.

And when Jesus had come into the ruler’s house and had seen the flute players. *Tibicines* is derived from *tibia*, and *tibia* is so called from the shanks of fawns, from which they were first made in Phrygia; now they are also made from cranes and from *matellae* [small vessels; the reading is uncertain]. The flute players were formerly employed at the funerals of the dead, but now at the journeys of rulers. The sound produced by the instrument is called *tibicen*, as it were, “the song of the flute.”

A tumultuous crowd. [Col. 1340A] Because she was the only child of her father and mother, the household mourned the one whom they had hoped would be their mistress after the departure of her parents. The synagogue still lies dead, and in its house there are the tumult and flute playing of the Jews: the lamentations that they uselessly perform on the Sabbaths. For Jesus has not yet come to them.

He said: “Go away.” For when the Lord Jesus comes to her, the tumults of their teaching and their irrational lamentations will depart. “The girl is not dead, but sleeping.” She was dead to them, but she was sleeping because he could awaken her so quickly. Hence the custom has prevailed among Christians that their dead who have departed in a good confession are called not dead but sleeping, and that their tombs are called not tombs but *koimētēria* (κοιμητήρια), that is, “sleeping places,” in Greek. The synagogue of the Jews likewise appears dead to you, but [Col. 1340B] God will raise it through his faithful witnesses Enoch and Elijah.

And they laughed at him. For they did not yet recognize the power of the speaker. And when the crowd had been put out, he entered and took her hand. Because they preferred to ridicule the Lord’s words rather than believe them, they are put out and do not deserve to see the one who raises the dead. Likewise, unless the synagogue removes from itself the crowds within which it lies dead, it will not rise. And he entered, took her hand, and the girl arose. Unless the Lord takes and cleanses the hands of the Jews, which are full of blood, the synagogue will not rise.

And this report went out through all that land. In the other evangelists it is said that he commanded that they tell no one. He thereby gave his followers an example: if they do anything good, they should not care to proclaim it publicly for the sake of praise, because of vainglory. [Col. 1340C] It is also said in another evangelist that he commanded that food be given to her, evidently to demonstrate her health and resurrection.

We read in the Gospel that three dead persons were raised by the Lord, but it is not without reason that no more and no fewer than three alone are recounted there. For we read in other books that he raised more, and we believe that this is so. Nevertheless, it did not please the evangelists to narrate the raising of more, because the Holy Spirit, who spoke in them, ordered it for the sake of the mystery’s sacramental meaning.

Thus the three dead in the body signify three dead in the soul, because the soul that sins dies, according to the prophet’s saying: “The soul that sins, it shall die.” The three dead, therefore, are three kinds of sinful people. There is a sinner who sins by a grave offense, [Col. 1340D] and his soul dies in the sight of the Lord; yet, because he does not habitually commit that sin, he fears God’s anger and dreads the future judgment. This person is signified by the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, who was still in the house when she was raised by the Lord. Likewise, this sinner still conceals his sin in the chamber of his heart, and it is not known to many concerning him. Therefore his resurrection is, as it were, easier, because although he sinned, he neither set a bad example before many nor made a practice of the sin.

Another dead person raised by the Lord was the son of the widow. He was no longer in the house but in the street and at the gate of the city, and the Lord of life restored him. He signifies the sinful person who frequently kills his soul with a deadly crime and exposes it [Col. 1341A] to the knowledge of many. The Lord will also raise him if the righteous offer frequent and manifold prayer to the Lord on his behalf.

The third person he raised was the dead Lazarus, of whom it is written that he stank. He signifies the most wretched sinner, weighed down by the enormity of his crimes, who has not only made his wickedness known to many but is also hated by everyone because of the stench of his evil reputation. For just as there is a pleasant odor belonging to a good reputation, so there is an evil odor belonging to a bad reputation. He too will be raised if the tears and continual prayers of the righteous are poured out for him.

By these examples, therefore, all of us who are sinners can hope for forgiveness of our sins, if we punish the evils we have committed [Col. 1341B] worthily and earnestly through fasts, almsgiving, and tearful prayers, and do not afterward return to the vomit of sin. May God grant this to us and to all who wish to repent, so that they may accomplish it perfectly.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the Two Blind Men Who Were Given Sight

And as Jesus was passing from there, two blind men followed him, crying out and saying. These blind men signify two peoples, the Jewish and the gentile. They were blind when the Lord, their inner eyes having been blinded, was coming to Jericho. Jericho signifies the world or his incarnation, because Jericho is interpreted as “moon,” and through the moon, decline or the incarnation of our Redeemer is signified.

“Have mercy on us, Son of David.” For unless they believe that the Son of Man also descended from David’s lineage, they will not receive spiritual light. And when he had come into the house, [Col. 1341C] the blind men approached him. For when he ascended into heaven, he illuminated the eyes of their hearts through the apostles.

He said to them: “Do you believe that I can do this for you?” They said: “Yes, Lord.” Teachers likewise, when they give sight to the pagans’ inner eyes, ask them: “Do you believe in God the Father almighty and in Jesus,” and so forth. Then he touched their eyes, saying: “Let it be done for you according to your faith.” For unless someone believes with the heart and confesses with the mouth, he does not obtain the remission of sins.

And their eyes were opened. For if he believes, even if he cannot understand the mystery of the Trinity, through belief he will attain to understanding of the Word. And Jesus sternly warned them, saying: “See that no one knows.” This was for the example of [Col. 1341D] his disciples, as we said above.

## CHAPTER XXV. On the Demoniac Who Was Healed

And when they had gone out, behold, they brought him a mute man who had a demon. As we find in the other evangelists, three general signs occurred in this man. He was mute, deaf, and full of a demon. Indeed, in the Greek language in which the Gospels were written there are many distinctions that do not exist among us. In particular, the word *alalos* (ἄλαλος) in Greek means only “mute,” whereas *kophos* (κωφός) means both “mute” and “deaf.” And blessed Gregory says that everyone who is naturally mute is deaf. Therefore the evangelists mentioned only two ailments, so that [Col. 1342A] deafness might be understood there. In fact, he was freed from the demon and from the two ailments.

And when the demon had been cast out, the mute man spoke, and the crowds marveled. The crowds, who appeared less educated, always marveled at the Lord’s teaching. But the Pharisees and Sadducees disparaged it or turned it to an evil meaning because of envy, since they were distressed on account of the Lord’s teaching, because Christ was believed by the crowds to be both holier and wiser.

Thus Solomon says: “Whoever increases knowledge increases sorrow.” Whoever possesses knowledge, if he does not possess charity and humility, immediately possesses pride. This is what he means when he says that where charity and humility are lacking in great knowledge, there is great indignation. This, therefore, existed in the Pharisees, who said: “He casts out demons by the prince of demons.”

The Jews [Col. 1342B] called the prince of demons Beelzebub. Just as the first idol in this world was called Bel, so they also called that Lucifer who was changed into the devil, the first angel, by his name. In particular, there was Bel, son of Ninus, the first king of the Assyrians in the world, who is also called Belus in Latin. From this name the Jews composed the name Beelzebub, that is, “Bel” or “Baal of flies,” meaning “one who has flies.” In mockery they called the god of the pagans and the prince of the devil by this name; among them he is also called Resep. They also say that he was the one who expelled Adam from paradise. We read of Bel in Daniel, whom the Babylonians worshiped and whom Daniel destroyed.

But they were lying, as though the Lord, having appeased the devil, prayed to him concerning the one whom they held, in order that he might appear to perform miracles. Yet we read nowhere [Col. 1342C] that this happened. Moreover, the Lord showed—as another evangelist reports—that every kingdom divided against itself cannot stand. For just as an earthly kingdom perishes and is annihilated if it is divided, so also among the devils, if one casts another out of his place, Satan’s kingdom cannot stand. This is explained more fully in the other evangelists; Matthew touched on it only briefly. But let us follow what comes next in his account, which we have undertaken to elucidate.

And Jesus went around all the cities and villages, teaching in their synagogues. He shows the Lord’s concern for our salvation when he says that he went around all the cities. And not only the cities, but also the villages and their synagogues, that is, their assemblies. He added that he was teaching and preaching and healing every disease, [Col. 1342D] namely, of souls. For just as the body languishes, so the soul languishes when it grows sluggish in God’s commandments.

And every infirmity among the people. “Infirmity” refers to bodies. It can, however, be understood with the addition “of the good,” because he did not heal every sick person, but those whom he foresaw to be worthy and good, as we read concerning those who lay at the pool of Bethesda: from among many he chose and healed one. Or it is a form of synecdoche, which is characteristic of divine Scripture, when a part is understood from the whole.

And when he saw the crowds, he had compassion on them. This was both in his teaching, so that he might teach them the life of life, and in earthly food, when he satisfied five thousand with five loaves. Matthew, foreseeing that others would narrate this, passed over it himself. For they were harassed [Col. 1343A] by demons and idols and were lying like sheep without a shepherd. He says that they were lying in sins, although they were sheep. Here too a part is understood from the whole, because not all of them were going to become sheep.

He demonstrates the negligence of the priests when he says: “Not having a shepherd.” For God had commanded the priests to proclaim the law to the people and to lead them by the example of good works. Kings and all priests—bishops as well as presbyters—must still do this in the same way, because God placed them over the peoples for this reason. For *rex* (“king”) is derived from *regere* (“to rule”). If he does not rule and defend well, he is called not a king but a tyrant. Solomon, understanding this because he had been instructed by his father, still asked God to increase his wisdom for governing the people.

Bishops are also called by a Greek name *episkopoi*, or “overseers”; that is, in the likeness of shepherds, [Col. 1343B] they must look around carefully lest a harmful beast from any quarter infect or disturb their flock. Let them read Ezekiel, where they are called shepherds; nevertheless, let them hear what the Lord adds here.

Then he says to his disciples: “The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few.” This is a metaphor, and a type of metaphor called allegory: by “harvest” he wishes the people to be understood, and by “laborers,” preachers. The whole world was in error when the apostles began to preach. If divine power had not been present, how could the whole world have abandoned its errors through twelve men?

“Ask the Lord of the harvest to send laborers into his harvest.” The patriarchs and prophets sowed this harvest, but the apostles brought it to maturity through their preaching. The patriarchs and prophets sowed in tears, [Col. 1343C] but these reaped in joy, because the gate of the kingdom of heaven was already open to them, whereas it had been closed to the others.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the Twelve Apostles Sent to Preach

And having summoned his twelve disciples, he gave them authority over unclean spirits. The evangelists report that, when he went up onto a mountain, he called to himself those whom he wished; that is, he chose them from among many and appointed them apostles. The evangelists briefly summarized this, but the seven orders possessed by the rulers of the Church received their beginning there at that time.

For casting out unclean spirits belongs to exorcists; possessing the virtues of discernment belongs to doorkeepers; healing the sick belongs to deacons and presbyters. Concerning these it is commanded that they be [Col. 1343D] brought to the sick and anointed. The apostles are called *apostoloi* in Greek and *missi* (“sent ones”) in Latin, from which *apostolicus* is derived. Indeed, he could not appoint them bishops, or apostles, unless he first granted the other orders; and for this deed they were called apostles.

It must be understood that the one who first made Moses an apostle, when he sent him to liberate the children of Israel, also made these men apostles. The one who then chose twelve tribes also wished to have twelve disciples, to signify that his year consists of twelve months, and that the day likewise consists of twelve hours, as does the night. Moreover, this number is held in high esteem by arithmeticians, because it contains within itself all perfect and sacred numbers; and when resolved, it is not only not diminished but is also increased. Hence they made the pound consist of twelve ounces. They also set forth twelve principal signs in the heavens.

For three times four makes twelve, and the apostles—three times four—were sent to preach, so that they might baptize the gentiles throughout all the regions [Col. 1344A] of the square-shaped world: “In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.” In this sacrament the children of Israel also appear to have encamped in such a way that on every side there were three tribes. And the heavenly Jerusalem is described as having twelve gates: three from the east, three from the west, three from the south, and three from the north. This figuratively shows how the Church will come forth from all the gentiles.

The apostles were also appointed in the twelfth place of the signs, and he gave them authority to cure bodily diseases and infirmities. But there is a great difference between the giver and the recipient. The Lord, who gave the power, said: “I say to you, rise”; they said: “In the name of Jesus, rise.”

[Col. 1344B] These are the names of the twelve apostles. The catalogue of the apostles is set down so that no one might deceive anyone under their names, and so that their dignity and authority might be commended.

First, Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother. Simon was called by this name before his calling; it is interpreted as “obedient.” When he was brought to the Lord by his brother Andrew, the Lord imposed the name Peter upon him, from the firmness of faith; it is the same as Cephas. Peter is Greek and Latin, while Cephas is Syriac; in Greek also Cephas means “head,” because he was appointed head of the Church. You know also the place of his birth and his deeds, which are narrated in the Gospel and the Acts [Col. 1344C] of the Apostles.

He first preached in Cappadocia; afterward, under Claudius, he came to Italy and held the pontificate in Rome for twenty-five years, although he did not possess even five feet of land there in authority. In the thirty-sixth year after the Lord’s Passion he departed to the Lord, crucified upside down. He was buried on the eastern side beside the Triumphal Way, which is otherwise called the Catacombs. When the Greeks were removing the bodies from that place at night, the entire Roman people rushed there and seized them. They buried them in another place on this side of the Tiber, in a place called Lavigana, and Paul on the Ostian Way.

Andrew is a Greek name and is interpreted as “manly,” that is, from manliness, *apo tou andros* (ἀπὸ τοῦ ἀνδρός). “Man” is called *andros* and *aner* in Greek, and therefore Andrew was most appropriately [Col. 1344D] named. After the discipleship of Saint John, he followed the Lord’s footsteps manfully and ascended the cross manfully, as his book of martyrdom shows. He preached in Achaea and was killed at Patras, where he was also buried; but, when Constantine transferred him, he lies in Constantinople.

In Hebrew, however, Andrew is said to mean “beautiful” or “answering.”

James, son of Zebedee, and John his brother. He was surnamed from his father and is interpreted as “supplanter,” because when his name was brought into Latin, an ending was added, as usually happens with barbarian names when they enter our language. He sent the epistle called Catholic to those dispersed for Christ’s name. Killed by Herod the tetrarch, he was buried in Archaia Marmarica.

[Col. 1345A] John is interpreted as “the grace of God,” which rested in him more than in the other apostles. He preached in Greece, so that, just as he was wiser than the others, he might be sent to a wiser people. Under Trajan he rested in Ephesus, but now his body is not found on earth. The sarcophagus in which he lay was opened, but it is empty. They do not know what happened to him, because he was not removed by human beings. These two brothers were finally called Boanerges, that is, “sons of thunder,” because both heard that voice on the mountain: “This is my Son.”

Philip and Bartholomew. Philip is interpreted as “mouth of the lamp,” and rightly so, because as soon as he recognized the Lord, he took care to announce him to his brother, saying: “We have found the Messiah of whom Moses wrote.” He preached in Galicia; [Col. 1345B] he was stoned and crucified in the city of Hierapolis, and was buried there.

There was also another Philip, a deacon, who preached in Samaria, where blessed Peter and John later came to confirm those who had believed. For if Philip had been an apostle, he would have been able to confer the Holy Spirit. Since he could not do so, it is evident that he was not an apostle.

Bartholomew is interpreted as “son of the one who suspends waters,” because through his preaching he kindled the hearts of his hearers toward heavenly things. He preached in India; in the city of Albana he was flayed alive by barbarians, and was buried there.

Thomas is said to mean “abyss.” He was surnamed Didymus, which in Greek means “twin.” Some wish to say that it means “similar,” because he was similar to Christ; but this is not true. Rather, whoever is born a twin is always similar [Col. 1345C] to the one with whom he is born. He preached to the Persians; he was killed with spears at Calamina and was buried there.

Matthew the publican. Matthew is said in Hebrew to mean “given.” Appropriately so, since he was given to write the Gospel. The other evangelists placed Matthew first, before Thomas, and suppressed the name “publican.” He himself put himself last and confessed that he had been a publican, according to the saying of the wise man: “The righteous man at the beginning is his own accuser.” He was of the tribe of Levi, from which he received the surname Levi. He first wrote his Gospel in Hebrew in Judaea; afterward he preached in Macedonia. He was killed in Persia, where he rests.

James of Alphaeus. He is called Alphaeus from his father and received this name from his father. He is the one called the brother of the Lord, surnamed [Col. 1345D] “the Just.” He was said to have been born from the tribe of Judah and to be the Lord’s brother because he was the nephew of Saint Mary through her sister. He was thrown down from the Temple, struck with a club, and killed; he was buried there.

Judas, brother of James, is interpreted as “confessor,” and he had three names: he was called Thaddaeus and Lebbaeus. He is the one whom ecclesiastical history relates was sent to King Abgar. He was killed in the city of Nirata and lies buried there.

Simon the Cananaean was so called from the place; by another name he is called the Zealot. *Cana* is interpreted as “zeal,” where the Lord made wine from water.

Judas Iscariot was of the tribe of Issachar. He was called Iscariot from the place, or from the very tribe from which he arose; by prophetic foreknowledge he was so called because he was going to receive [Col. 1346A] payment for the destruction of his Master. *Iscariot* and *Issachar* are interpreted as “payment.”

Jesus sent these twelve, instructing them and saying. He appointed these twelve as apostles and sent them before his face into every place where he himself was going to come. He also sent seventy others with them, but did not appoint them to any order; he gave them only the authority to heal the sick and cast out demons while they were his disciples. Yet afterward they abandoned him and did not walk with him.

Judas was also an apostle and performed miracles in his name, for they said when they returned: “Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name.” Therefore whoever receives a righteous person in the name of a righteous person will receive a righteous person’s reward. Whoever does good to someone because he considers him a servant of God will receive such a reward from the Lord as though the person were what he believed him to be, because he did it for the name of God.

And he said to them: “Do not go on the road of the gentiles.” This was so that the Jews would not be scandalized if the gentiles were preached to before them. He commanded that they first offer them the divine [Col. 1346B] word, and this before the resurrection. But afterward, when they rejected him and crucified him, he said: “Go, teach all nations.”

“And do not enter the cities of the Samaritans.” The Samaritans appeared to be neither Jews nor gentiles. They were not Jews because they were not descended from Abraham. They appeared not to be gentiles because they were circumcised and possessed the Jewish law. For this reason he specifically commanded them: “Go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.”

They are called sheep according to the Psalmist: “He who shepherds Israel, attend; he who leads Joseph like sheep.” He calls them lost [Col. 1346C] sheep, with “by the devil because of sins” understood. “And as you go, preach, saying that the kingdom of heaven will draw near.” He himself first preached this, and it must be preached before and above all else, because the entrance that had been closed to us through Adam has been opened. Let all hasten to enter eternal life through good works.

And so that you may be believed, heal the sick—sick both in body and in mind. Raise the dead, including the dead in soul, because when the soul sins it dies, and the dead in body, so that through one person dead in body many may be made alive in soul.

Cleanse lepers. Just as there are lepers in body, so there are lepers in soul, entangled in various sins. In the same way they are repulsive in God’s sight as the former are in human sight.

Cast out demons, both from those in whom they are openly named and from those [Col. 1346D] over whom they secretly preside in the mind. Demons are called in Greek *deinoi*, that is, “knowing” or “skilled in matters.” For they foresee many future things, partly through the sharpness of a subtler sense, partly through the very long experience of life, partly by God’s command through angelic revelation, and partly through the active nature of their aerial bodies.

“You have received without payment; give without payment.” You received from me without payment; provide this teaching without earthly payment, lest they think you preach out of mere greed.

“Do not possess gold or silver.” At the end he says why this is unnecessary, saying: “The laborer is worthy of his food,” namely, that he should receive food and clothing from those to whom he preaches.

“Nor money in your belts.” This must be understood in two ways: [Col. 1347A] they should neither place gold and gems in their belts as ornaments, nor fasten purses containing coins to their belts. By “money” he means bronze denarii, which were then used in trade. Hence Peter, together with John, said to the lame man: “Silver and gold I do not have.”

“Nor a bag on the road.” A bag is a shepherd’s pouch for carrying bread. Hence it is said of David: “He took a shepherd’s bag,” which he was accustomed always to carry with him.

“Nor two tunics.” He speaks of one tunic, the one in which he went clothed, so that they would not keep another for themselves out of fear of the future, since they were empowered to receive one from elsewhere.

“Nor sandals.” Mark says that he commanded them to wear sandals. Spiritually, this is to be understood concerning footwear: they should not conceal the evangelical word, nor rely on earthly advantages, nor obscure evangelical preaching for the sake of earthly things.

“Nor a staff.” Mark says that a staff was to be carried. But Matthew speaks of a staff [Col. 1347B] of wood and of the body. Through the staff Mark wishes the authority of evangelical preaching to be understood. The authority of preaching is understood in the staff, so that whoever wishes to live from the Gospel because he proclaims it may do so; it is in his power not to do so. Hence Paul also says: “Do we not have authority to live from the Gospel? But we have not used this authority.”

There are certain things that God commanded, and whoever neglects them will pay the penalty of guilt; but there are other things that he permitted, which we may either omit or do.

“The laborer is worthy of his food.” In this passage Paul accepts what he said: [Col. 1347C] “The Lord ordained that those who proclaim the Gospel should live from the Gospel.”

And into whatever city or village you enter, inquire who in it is worthy, and remain there. The pure Lord wishes to have pure disciples, because with the holy one a person can become holy, and with the perverse, perverse. He does not wish the preacher to lodge from house to house, lest evil conversations corrupt good morals.

And when you enter a house, greet it, saying. By “house” we should understand its inhabitants. We should bless not only the host whom, because of his good reputation, we choose—hence he had earlier said, “Who in it is worthy,” that is, worthy to receive blessing or to hear the words of life more abundantly—but we should also wish peace for all people.

He himself indicates what we should say: “Peace to this [Col. 1347D] house.” By both this command of the Lord and the custom of the Romans, we ought to greet Christians, because this was the custom among our ancestors. In Hebrew and Syriac this is called *salamalech*; in Greek, *chaire* (χαῖρε); in Latin, *ave*.

But through bad custom and teaching it has grown among the palace officials that no one should wish well to his equal when he meets him. Let them read the Book of Kings; there they will find that the Hebrew kings acted in this way. The Romans did likewise, so that not only men among themselves but even emperors were greeted by birds. Hence there is the verse of the parrot:

> “From you I shall learn the names of others;  
> I learned this by myself: Chaire, Caesar.”

What harm would it do a person, when he perhaps encountered one chosen by God, if he said to him: “May the Lord save you”? For the prophet Elisha [Col. 1348A] , in anger, said one word to the boys, and forty-two of them perished. If he had said a good word, the result would likewise have been good.

And if the house is worthy, your peace will come upon it. This means that if the inhabitants who dwell in the house are worthy, then—by indicating the contained through the container—what was wished upon them will come upon them. But if it is not worthy, your peace will return to you. For if the person for whom good is wished or on whose behalf one works is not worthy to receive it, the reward will remain with the one who speaks or does the good.

And whoever does not receive you or hear your words, as you go out shake the dust from your feet as a testimony against them. The dust is shaken off as a testimony to their labor: the apostolic preaching reached them, yet they did not even receive what was necessary [Col. 1348B] for sustenance and rejected the Gospel.

“Amen, I say to you, it will be more tolerable for the land of Sodom in the day of judgment than for that city.” This is because they did not have preachers sent to them. Here it appears that there are different punishments among sinners in hell.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the Persecutions of the Apostles
I am sending you out like sheep among wolves. He calls the scribes and Pharisees wolves. “Among” does not mean in place but in hatred, because when you begin to appear wise and good, they will hate you just as they hate me.

Be prudent, therefore, as serpents, and simple as doves. By your prudence avoid their evil teaching; by the simplicity of the dove avoid their evil deeds. The serpent has this cunning: it exposes its entire body to blows in order to keep its head safe. So must we also act. Our head is Christ. We must give our whole body for Christ, so that we do not deny him. Through the simplicity of the dove—or of the Holy Spirit, who was signified by it—let us strive to maintain peace with all people.

But beware of human beings. “Beware”: observe, watch, guard yourselves. For they will hand you over to councils. “They will hand you over,” that is, they will betray you to be killed, because you believe in me. And in their synagogues they will scourge you. The book of the Acts of the Apostles testifies that this happened: it is written there that, after the apostles had been beaten, they were warned not to speak any longer in the name of Jesus.

And you will be led before kings and governors. Governors were so called from presiding. Consuls, who administered the provinces—such were Pilate [Col. 1348D] and Albinus in Judaea. Kings included both Herods and others whom the books of their sufferings mention. Before these the apostles were brought: some were scourged, others killed. Since he placed governors before kings, it should be understood that the consuls who presided over provinces were superior to many kings and had under their administration four or five provinces together with their kings, as Cyrinus had Syria.

For a testimony to them and to the nations. This means that you will have pressed the preaching of the Gospel upon them so insistently that they will not merely refuse to hear it [the sentence appears incomplete in the supplied text].

But when they hand you over, do not worry about how or what you should say. Let your will alone be upright, and offer it to God; the Holy Spirit will speak for you, dwelling within you. For what you should say will be given to you [Col. 1349A] at that hour. The Holy Spirit knows what is necessary or suitable for each person to say. For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you. Although the voice is heard through the channel of your heart, the Spirit will be within you as the source of goodness, giving growth and boldness to your speech.

A brother will hand over his brother to death. This frequently happened during the persecutions: a pagan brother betrayed his Christian brother to death. And a father will hand over his son. He not only handed him over to death, but many also killed [them]. And children will rise up against their parents and put them to death. There is no question about this, since we have sufficient examples.

And you will be hated by everyone because of my name. Blessed is the hatred suffered for the Savior; all Christians ought to desire it. When he says, “You will be hated by everyone,” “by the wicked” is understood. For the good will not merely refrain from hating them but will love them as brothers.

But whoever perseveres to the end will be saved. It is of no benefit to begin well if one does not persevere in the right faith to the end, or in good works, because the tree remains wherever it falls. Here *hic* is a pronoun in this passage, not an adverb, and has the sense of “that one.”

But when they persecute you in this city, flee to another. He was speaking of the mission then at hand: if they persecuted them, they were to return to him, because he did not wish them to be killed before he himself first died for all. Nevertheless, this is a general command of the Lord. Whoever does not wish to complete his life through martyrdom should yield place to the persecutor and go where he can serve God more peacefully. Yet the more cruelly he suffers for God, the more blessed he will be in the eternal kingdom.

Amen I say to you: you will not finish the cities of Israel before the Son of Man comes. He says this because he himself was going to come to preach where he was then sending them.

A disciple is not above his teacher. That is: do not seek great things. They persecute me, who am your teacher and Lord; how much more will they persecute you, who are disciples and my creatures. It is enough for a disciple to be like his teacher. Then the disciple will be perfect if he is able to equal his teacher.

If they called the master of the household Beelzebub, how much more will they call his household servants Beelzebub. If they said of me, who preside over you like the master of a household, “He casts out demons by Beelzebub,” how much worse things will they say of you [Col. 1349D]!

The ancient genitive form *paterfamilias* descends from Greek; the master of a household is so called because he presides over his household as a father. The Lord is rightly called by this name, since he said to his disciples, “You are my friends,” and commanded them to invoke the Father himself. He calls the apostles household servants because, through faith and action, they belonged to his household.

Nothing is covered that will not be revealed, and nothing hidden that will not be known. The Lord is speaking of the future judgment: at the final examination, each person’s will and work must be made manifest. It is as though he had said: A time will come when both your virtue and their wickedness will be displayed; you will receive good for your good deeds, and they will receive evil for their evils. *Opertum* means something covered over [Col. 1350A].

What I tell you in darkness, speak in the light; what you hear secretly, proclaim more openly; what I teach you in a small place in Judaea, proclaim throughout the whole world. What you hear in the ear, proclaim upon the housetops. He speaks according to the custom of the province, where they were accustomed to stand above the houses and preach from there, since their roofs were flat. This is what James did when he was thrown down from there.

And do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. Do not fear handing over your body for Christ, because although they can destroy the body, they can neither take away the soul’s glory nor prevent the body from rising in glory, however they may burn it or into whatever water they may throw it. Rather, fear him [Col. 1350B] who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna. He is to be feared who in this age can do whatever he wishes with soul and body, now sending the soul into eternal punishments and, after the day of judgment, sending the body with the soul into the same torments.

By Gehenna he wishes hell to be understood. There was, finally, a valley beside Jerusalem called Gehennon, that is, the valley of Hinnom, because in the Hebrew language *ennom* means “valley,” while it was the proper name of its possessor. It was irrigated by the torrent of Siloam and covered with trees. Whenever the people of Israel turned back from the worship of God, they sacrificed idols there and practiced divination. The Lord then threatened that the place itself would be filled with the corpses of the dead, so that it would no longer be called Tophet, that is, “beautiful,” but *Poliandrum*, that is, “a burial place of the dead.” [Col. 1350C] The Lord threatened this through Jeremiah, and it was fulfilled in the time of the Chaldeans.

Thus future punishments are signified by the name of this place. Job indicates that Gehenna is twofold, where sinners will be tortured—namely, excessive cold and excessive heat—when he says: “They pass from waters of snow to excessive heat.”

Are not two sparrows sold for an *as*? There are many kinds of sparrows: some delight in holes in walls, others seek dewy valleys, and some desire barren mountains. The sparrow is so called from its smallness. In the old law they were frequently commanded to be offered for certain observances or purifications. He therefore gives, by metaphor, a comparison from a lower thing to a higher one. It is a form of parable involving things dissimilar in kind, encouraging and demonstrating what divine compassion provides for the human race.

It is as though he plainly said: If small and worthless animals, which you see being sold here for one *as*, do not fall into human snares without God’s will, how much more are you, who were made in the image of God, guarded by God’s providence and protection?

Concerning the *as*, which is a kind of weight—that is, one scruple—or a numerical term, the authors explain it in different ways. The arithmeticians say that when they count, *asse duo, tres*—“two, three by the as”—has the sense of one. Again, in the notation of the arithmeticians, twelve ounces are called an *as*. It may therefore be that at some times they were very expensive because of the various purifications performed with them in the Lord’s temple [Col. 1351A], and at other times cheap.

According to one interpretation, “for an *as*” may mean for one denarius, or one bronze scruple. According to another, it may mean that two were bought for one pound, which is an *as*. Luke also agrees with this when he says: “Are not five sparrows sold for two *asses*?”—that is, for two pounds or two scruples.

The Gospel sense seems to agree more readily with this, as though it said: Those small animals are so expensive that two are sold for one pound, because no one can capture them unless God permits it. Why do you doubt concerning yourselves that anyone can harm you except to the extent permitted by God?

*Veneunt* has a passive meaning and is understood as “are sold”; its active form is *venundo*. When it says that one will not fall upon the ground, this means into anyone’s snare or bird-trap without the will of the Father.

But the hairs of your head have all been numbered. Such is God’s care for you that he even knows the number of your hairs. The numbering signifies knowledge of the number, not preservation of that same number.

Therefore do not fear; you are worth more than many sparrows—that is, you have greater value and are more precious to God. *Melioris* refers to evaluation, whereas *meliores* refers to comparison.

Everyone who acknowledges me before human beings, I also will acknowledge before my Father who is in heaven. Here acknowledgment is understood not only by word but also by deed, because whoever says that he knows God but does not keep his commandments is a liar.

But whoever denies me before human beings, I also will deny him [Col. 1351C] before my Father. Here too denial is understood both through words and through deeds. Not only will the denier of God fail to be acknowledged by God in the life to come, but the one who does not know God will also be unknown by God.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. That the Lord came not to send peace but a sword

Do not think that I came to send peace, but a sword. *Arbitrari* is used for “to estimate” or “to think.”

How can this be, since elsewhere the Lord is said to say, “I leave you peace,” while here he says, “I did not come to send peace”? It should be understood that there is good peace and bad peace. When the Lord came into this world, the world possessed a bad peace in evil. The Lord sent his Gospel, and they began to recognize that they were not rightly in agreement with one another. A good war was sent, therefore, so that the bad peace might be broken.

God is read to have acted in a similar way when the whole world that then existed gathered together to build a tower by which they might investigate what was in heaven and also defend themselves from a flood, should one come again, or from the fire that is destined to destroy the world. In one night he introduced a diversity of languages, and they began to disagree because of this, and abandoned what they were doing.

In the same way, when the world was united in the worship of idols, he sent the word of the Gospel, and those who had previously been united in evil then began to disagree rightly. He calls the sword the separation produced by the word, because just as a sword separates what cannot be reunited, so the word of God separated brother from brother, father from son, and daughter-in-law [Col. 1352A] from her mother-in-law. A mother-in-law is the husband’s mother; a daughter-in-law is the woman who has his son.

And a man’s enemies will be those of his own household. This belongs to the teaching concerning what later happened: a father was pagan and his son Christian, as was the case with the father of Saint Celsus or of Saint Martin, concerning whom it is written that he begrudged his son’s blessed deeds. We read similarly about all parents: some believed and others did not, and in this there was separation.

*Domesticus* is derived from *domus*, meaning one who is accustomed to the household.

Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me. Here is the sword of separation of which he had spoken. Because of this sword, many thousands of saints were separated from their parents, and all who wish to be good and live blessedly in the other life must still act in this way.

Here one must learn the order of love, which the bride in the Song of Songs asks to be established in her when she says: “Order charity in me.” Here is the order: neither father nor mother above God, but God first; then parents; after them, all Christians. But if it should happen that father and mother do not wish to become Christians or good people, and one cannot love both at the same time, love the Creator with all your inward being and abandon wicked parents.

Hence he also said to one of his disciples: “Leave the dead to bury the dead person.” “More than me” means: whoever prefers someone else’s love to my love. “Is not worthy of me”—“disciple” is understood.

And whoever does not take up his cross and follow me. This is an allegory: by the cross he wishes the mortification of vices to be understood. It is as though he said: Whoever does not mortify himself to this age and its desires and keep my commandments—for this is what it means to follow him—is not a disciple worthy of me.

Whoever finds his soul will lose it. By “soul,” human life is understood. Whoever finds his life in all its pleasures will lose it in the life to come. Or, in another way: if you love your soul, lose it for Christ. And whoever loses his soul for my sake will find it. This is evident in the martyrs, because they did not hesitate to lose their souls in the present for Christ, so that they might now be with God himself in glory.

Whoever receives you receives me. Since he had commanded them, if necessity arose, to abandon all relatives for his sake, he tempers the severity of his commands by the authority of his promises. Whoever receives you with honor and obedience, even if he thinks little of me, whom he sees, should know that whoever receives me receives him who sent me, that is, the Father, and [receives] me in divinity, and the Holy Spirit.

Whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward. He gives the example that those who received prophets when they traveled through the land of the Jews teaching—as we read in the Book of Kings—and who had their rooms and utensils prepared for them, received a reward from God because they served them in the Lord’s name.

Thus one woman received her son back, raised from the dead by Elijah, and another deserved to have a son although she had been barren. Micaiah, because he hid a hundred prophets and fed them during the persecution, deserved the spirit of prophecy, and he himself is the twelfth of the prophets.

He does not say that one should receive a reward from a prophet or from a righteous person, but the reward of a prophet and of a righteous person. That is, one will receive the reward that a prophet and a righteous person will receive, even if the person is neither a prophet nor righteous, provided that he comes to us in the Lord’s name, we believe that he is such, and we give him what he needs for the Lord’s name.

If he is lying, he will pay the penalty for his falsehood; but we will not be deprived of the reward that we gave in the Lord’s name. For all who received Judas the betrayer in the Lord’s name at the time when he followed the Lord had the same reward with God as those who received Peter and John, because Judas was then one of the men to whom the Lord was speaking. We must consider not the person of the one sent but the Lord who sends.

And whoever gives one of these least ones a drink—even a cup of cold water in the name of a disciple—amen I say to you, he will not lose his reward. We must certainly believe that whatever good we do in the Lord’s name, whether in word or deed, we shall receive as a reward either in this age or in the future.

Nevertheless, if we do not know that he is opposed to the Lord’s way, but know that he is held in some mortal crime, openly practices it, and does not wish to reform despite the corrections of good people, we must regard him as a pagan and a publican. For so the Lord commanded, and Paul likewise said: “If anyone is named a brother who is greedy, or rapacious, or involved in anything of this kind, and is so, with such a person do not even eat.”

It should be noted that he did not say merely, “if he is named,” but added, “if he is,” because many are called such but are not. He was speaking of those who are publicly called such and actually are.

It should also be noted that he said, “one of these least ones,” that is, my least ones, who are humble in spirit. For Mark says, “In my name, because you belong to Christ.”

And it happened that when Jesus had finished instructing his twelve disciples. “When he had finished” means “when he had brought it to completion.” It is one thing when we say that a fire or a meal has been completed, and another when we say that the speech of a teacher has been completed. In the former case an end is understood; in the latter, perfection is indicated.

“His twelve”: he gave one set of commands separately to the twelve, and another set to the twelve and the seventy-two together. The twelve received more secret teachings; the seventy-two received common teachings.

When he had given the twelve a complete arrangement and instruction, he moved on from there to teach in their cities [Col. 1353D]. Hence the reference is understood to mean Mount Tabor, on which he taught the higher things.

We should carefully observe that, after the Lord began to preach, he did not cease for three and a half years, except when he slept, giving an example that whoever begins a good work should practice it diligently. For whoever is negligent and careless in his work is a brother to one who destroys his own work; and if you are lukewarm, neither cold nor hot, you will be vomited from the mouth of God.

## CHAPTER XXIX. That John sends from prison to the Lord

Now when John heard in prison about the works of Christ. Shortly before John was arrested [Col. 1354A] by Herod the tetrarch, the Lord began to preach, so that the divine word would not be lacking to Israel after John.

John was arrested by Herod the tetrarch, the son of Herod, and was sent to prison and bound, because Herod had taken his brother’s wife. Herod himself had not taken her from him; rather, her father had taken her away from Philip because of certain disputes that had arisen between them and had given her to Herod, since this Herod possessed greater power.

Although Herod was Jewish on one side and not Jewish on the other—for on one side he was descended from Simon and from his son John, since Mariamne, the daughter of Aristobulus the priest, had been the wife of Herod the elder, whom he himself killed—Aristobulus was the grandson of John, the son of Simon, who is mentioned in the Book of Maccabees.

John therefore did not cease to announce to him that he had acted unjustly—although his father had given her to him—by retaining his brother’s wife. The woman, however, loving her second husband more than the first, persuaded him to put John in prison.

While he was in this prison and in these bonds, he heard about Christ’s works. What works of Christ did he hear about? Those whose performance you heard of above: namely, that he was healing every illness among the people.

Sending two of his disciples, he said to him: John knew that Jesus was the true man and the true king of God’s glory, and that he had become incarnate in order to redeem the world through his death. But when he heard that Jesus was performing such great miracles, he began to think, saying: “If he performs such great miracles, who will kill him? Now he will become known to the world; now no one will dare to kill him, but everyone will revere him. I believed that he was to die for us, but now one of two things must be true: either he does not perform as many miracles as I hear, or, if he does, no one will kill him, but they will love and exalt him.”

Because of this doubt he sent two of his disciples and said to him: “Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect another?” That is: “Are you the one who is to come, as I believed, through whose death the human race would be liberated, you who perform such great deeds? Or must you send another who is to die for us?”

This is the more plausible meaning, as we may infer from the Lord’s deeds and sayings, which we shall explain below. We do not ignore that others have understood this passage differently: John sent his disciples to the Lord in order to invite them to become the Lord’s disciples, since some already hated him and slandered his deeds together with the Pharisees.

And Jesus answered and said to them. Another Evangelist reports that he commanded the blind, the lame, and the lepers to come before him, healed them, and then said: “Report to John what you have heard and seen.” The miracles you saw being performed by me: it was as though he were directing that John should know that I do before you what he heard, so that you might be able to report it from sight and hearing.

I perform wondrous deeds, and yet I shall die as he believed, because the hour is coming when he who has no offense against me will be very blessed and rare.

The blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead rise, and the poor are evangelized. How often above have we heard of these miracles being performed by the Lord, and of the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue being raised.

Why does he say, “the poor are evangelized”? Because Isaiah had specifically prophesied that he would do this, saying: “He has sent me to announce good news to the meek of the land.” And the Lord had spoken about these same people: “Blessed are the poor in spirit.”

And blessed is the one who is not scandalized by me. It is as though he plainly said: “There are already chosen and very few people who will not take offense at me and who do not wish to put me to death.” He uses the present tense for the future—“he will be blessed”—because in God’s sight all future things are present.

When they had departed, Jesus began to speak to the crowds about John. God, knowing human frailty—for John was human and pride could steal upon him—did not wish to praise him in the presence of his disciples. After they had gone away, however, for the example and edification of others, he said about him what ought to be imitated.
