Following his example, no one should praise another in his presence, in accordance with the wise man’s command: “Do not praise a person during his lifetime.”

What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind. The reed is so called because it quickly dries out. It is also called *canna* in Hebrew and Latin, and it is abundant in that country just as in Italy, so that hedges and other useful things are made from it. It grows in marshy places in the manner of grass, which among us is called *ros*.

There is an allegory here: one thing is said and another intended. By the reed he wishes unstable people to be understood. It is as though he plainly said: “When you went into the wilderness to hear John’s preaching, did you see him unstable and changeable like a reed against the wind?” For just as a reed turns in another direction when the wind touches it, so a carnal person is bent in another direction either by desire or by fear.

But John was not a reed; he was a cedar. Of him and other chosen people it is said: “The righteous will flourish like a palm tree,” and so forth. The wicked person is one who abandons God’s command because of a gift or some fear of God, or who is one kind of person in prosperity and another in adversity, either toward God or toward his neighbor. Hence Scripture says: “The foolish person changes like the moon.”

John, however, was steadfast in God’s commandments and did not flatter sinners. With a firm heart he said to the Pharisees: “Brood of vipers,” and to King Herod: “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife.” Until death he was not changed either by gifts or by threats, and therefore he was praised by the Lord.

But what did you go out into the wilderness to see? A man dressed in soft garments? Again the Lord praises John for maintaining an austere life both in food and in drink. Although nobly born and delicately raised, in the fervent years of his youth he entered the desert, as you have heard, lived austerely, and was covered with harsher clothing, since he wore a garment made of camel’s hair.

For this reason the Lord now says: “When you went to consult John, did you see him dressed in soft garments?” It is as though he plainly said: “Those who refuse to endure hardship for God serve not a heavenly but an earthly king.”

This may also be understood another way: John is said not to have been dressed in soft garments because he did not indulge the life of sinners with flattering words but rebuked it with harsh denunciation, saying: “Brood of vipers.” The words of the wise ought to be like goads and nails driven deep into the wicked, so that they may understand and remember their sin, as Solomon says: “Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he seem wise to himself.”

Nevertheless, we must observe that the Lord praises John for the roughness of his clothing. If wearing cheap clothing were not a virtue, the Lord would never have praised him for it. Nor would blessed Peter have forbidden women to seek expensive clothing if it were not blameworthy, saying: “Not in costly clothing.”

But what did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet [Col. 1356B]. The Lord continues to praise John. He says that John was not only a prophet but more than a prophet. The ministry of prophets is to proclaim what is to come, but not also to point it out. John not only foretold the Savior but also pointed him out with his finger, saying: “Behold the Lamb of God.”

What John ought to be called he shows deservedly in what follows. For it continues: “This is the one about whom it is written: Behold, I send my angel before your face, who will prepare your way before you.”

Whoever must explain a matter and exalt someone with praise should proceed in this way: first he should establish what the person is not, and then explain what he is. First the Lord said that John was neither a reed shaken by the wind nor dressed in soft garments; then, gradually, that he was not only a prophet but more than a prophet; finally, he calls him an angel.

For “angel” means messenger. He is rightly called an angel who, made the Savior’s trustworthy messenger and herald, openly pointed him out by sight and by his finger. Every believer who is counted by the name of priest is also called an angel, as Zechariah attests, if he carries out the duties of his ministry. For he says: “The lips of the priest will guard knowledge, and they will seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord.”

Therefore, whoever is adorned with that name should strive to be an angel in life and works, so that in deed and word he may announce God to those who see and hear.

It follows: “Who will prepare your way before you.” John prepared the way for the Lord because he preached to many, and also baptized them so that they might believe in him, even as a testimony. Each one of us also prepares the way for the Lord if, after expelling the thorns of vices from the heart, he plants virtues there.

Amen I say to you, among those born of women there has not arisen anyone greater than John the Baptist. The Lord exalted John with a worthy proclamation of praise when he said that he was equal in merit to all the saints. We must not think that he compared him with the Lord Jesus Christ, because our Lord was born not of a woman but of a virgin.

It follows: But whoever is less in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he. Here the Church is understood as the kingdom of heaven. In it Christ was then held in lesser renown, but was greater than John in divinity.

Or in another way: every saint who had already passed beyond the corruption of the flesh was greater than John, because John still stood in battle and was clothed in corruptible flesh. Therefore it can rightly be understood of one who, although small in merits, was nevertheless greater than John because he had already transcended the corruption of the flesh, whereas John, placed in the flesh, could still sin and lose God’s grace. For this reason that person was greater than John.

From the days of John until now the kingdom of heaven suffers violence. John was the first to preach that the kingdom of heaven was drawing near and that access to it would be open to those who wished to repent. From that time publicans and sinners, who because of their frauds were worthy of death, began to repent and aspire to the kingdom of God.

And the violent seize it. Through repentance those who had been worthy of hell become worthy of heaven. Or it is also a great act of violence that a human being, born on earth [Col. 1357B], should wish to possess heaven. Yet this is the mercy of God.

For all the prophets and the law prophesied until John. Whatever the law and the prophets prophesied about Christ was fulfilled after he came; therefore they no longer had an office. For once the king has come, the heralds fall silent.

It follows: And if you are willing to accept it, he is Elijah who is to come. In another passage, when John was asked whether he was Elijah, he answered that he was not; here the Lord says that he is. Are they contradictory? No. John spoke to foolish crowds about his body, saying that he was not Elijah. But our Lord spoke spiritually to his spiritual disciples about John’s spirit and likeness, saying that John was Elijah in spirit and action.

Just as Elijah will precede the Lord’s second coming, so John preceded his first coming. Just as Elijah, leading an austere life in food and clothing, suffered persecution from King Ahab and Queen Jezebel because of his zeal for the worship of God, so John, living in the same manner, suffered persecution from Herod and Herodias because of his zeal for the divine law, even [unto death].

Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear. Whenever the Lord adds this conclusion, he summons attentive hearers to spiritual understanding. All those who heard him had bodily ears, but he sought the ears of the heart, to which he spoke these words, so that they might understand both what came before and what followed spiritually.

It follows: To what shall I compare this generation? He continues to praise John. For he shows that he placed John’s example before that generation, if they had wished to imitate him.

It is like children sitting in the marketplace, who call out to their companions and say: The Jews are compared to children because of their foolishness and perversity. Just as a child, because of youth, frequently acts wrongly, so the Jews, being children in understanding, frequently went astray with regard to God’s law.

We sang for you and you did not dance; we lamented and you did not mourn. These children are the prophets, of whom one says: “Behold, I and the children whom God has given me.” And the Psalm says: “From the mouth of infants and nursing children you have perfected praise.”

They cried out to the Jews sitting in the marketplace, because the place where the Jews were occupied with their commerce could be called a marketplace. “We played the flute for you,” that is, we urged you to perform good works to our song and to dance to our melody, as David danced before the ark of the Lord, but you were unwilling. Hence one of them said: “I will sing to my beloved the song of my kinsman concerning his vineyard.”

We lamented for you, to urge you to repentance, but you were unwilling to do even this, rejecting both the exhortation and repentance for your sins. Hence Jeremiah also said: “Let my eyes pour out tears day and night, and let them not be silent, because the virgin daughter of my people has been crushed with a great crushing, with a very grievous wound.”

The same thing is happening now. John came neither eating nor drinking, and they said: “He has a demon,” giving you an example of abstinence; yet you were unwilling to imitate him.

Then I came eating and drinking with you, so that I might gain you [Col. 1358B]. You not only did not obey me, but also slandered me, saying: “Behold, a glutton and a wine-drinker, a friend of publicans and sinners.”

I ate with publicans and sinners for this reason: while I received bodily food from them, they might receive spiritual food from me. In Greek, *oinopōtlos*—οἰνωπώτλος, or more correctly *oinopotēs*—οἰνοπότης, “wine-drinker,” sounds better than in Latin, because in Greek it means “powerful in wine-drinking,” while in Latin it means “a drinker of wine.”

They did not reproach him for drinking wine, which is not a vice if it is drunk moderately; rather, they reproached him for being capable of drinking wine. Yet they falsely criticized and reproached the Lord in this, as in the rest, because without doubt he exceeded no measure of human flesh either in food, drink, or other necessities.

And wisdom has been justified by her children. That is: I, who am the wisdom of God the Father, have been justified by my children—that is, by my apostles and disciples—in this respect: I offered you every kind of healing and conversion, and you rejected them all.

Then he began to reproach the cities in which many of his mighty works had been performed, because they had not repented. The Lord reproaches the cities that were in Galilee, intending the people who lived in those cities to be understood: although they had seen him conducting himself righteously among them from childhood, they did not imitate him—neither the example of his way of life nor the words of his preaching—while many others, as soon as they heard him preaching, turned from their evils.

Woe to you, Chorazin; woe to you, Bethsaida, [Col. 1358D] because if the mighty works that were performed in you had been performed in Tyre and Sidon, they would long ago have repented in sackcloth and ashes. Tyre and Sidon are therefore preferred to the cities of Galilee, because Tyre and Sidon themselves trampled upon the natural law. These, however, transgressed both the natural law and the law of the written letter, and held the Lord’s preaching in contempt. For we read above that the Lord went around all the cities and villages, healing every disease; he was even brought up among them.

Chorazin was a town of Galilee, two miles from Capernaum. It is now deserted, and its name is interpreted as “my ministry.” This interpretation is therefore fitting for Christ the Lord, since his ministry was entrusted to him by the Father, including the conversion of those who lived there. There are two places called Bethsaida: one, Bethsaida of the pool that was called the Sheep Pool, where the sick lay; the other, Bethsaida in Galilee, the city of Andrew, Peter, and Philip, whose name is interpreted as “house of hunters.” “Hunters,” like “fishers,” can be understood in both a good and a bad sense. Because of those disciples of the Lord who came from there and followed the Lord, it can be taken in a good sense: they hunted some of the Gentiles, just as they also fished for them. Elsewhere, however, “hunters” is always taken in a bad sense.

Sodom is interpreted as “cattle,” because through its sins it acted foolishly like cattle, and for this reason it was [condemned] to the everlasting punishment of the present fire. It is now preferred to the cities of Galilee, although both were extremely wicked, because the word that the Lord placed in making the comparison—“perhaps,” an adverb expressing doubt—indicated the faithlessness of the inhabitants who had been in it. Nevertheless, these words show that there are different punishments in hell, so that the one who sinned more may be tortured more severely, and the one who sinned less may experience lighter torments. It is not necessary to write what Sodom was or what end it met, since its history is known to everyone. Even now, while it is seen, the terror of the dreadful judgment is displayed; therefore its conduct must be avoided by all.

## CHAPTER XXX. The Lord’s confession to the Father, and his yoke, which is easy

At that time Jesus answered. The phrase “at that time” refers to what he had said: “Then Jesus began to reproach,” because in that reproach of those cities the faithlessness of the Jews was foreshadowed—the faithlessness by which they were going to reject Christ; and in the preference given to the Gentile cities, the Gentiles who would believe were signified. The point of this confession is that he is now about to glorify the Father. When it says “answering,” this is understood as referring to the Father.

I confess to you, Lord, Father of heaven and earth. There are two kinds of confession: one by which a sinner confesses his sins; the other is confession belonging to praise and thanksgiving, which in this Gospel we frequently read that Christ the Lord offered to the Father. Concerning this latter kind it now continues: Because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones. He calls the scribes and Pharisees “wise,” not because they truly were wise, but because they appeared wise and prudent to themselves. And you have revealed them to little ones—that is, to the humble, namely, my apostles.

[Col. 1359D] Philosophers distinguish between wisdom and prudence, saying that wisdom is knowledge of divine things, while prudence is recognition of divine and human things. The “wise and prudent” may also be understood as the Jewish people, who appeared wise to themselves because of the law and the teaching of the prophets that they had received. But because they interpreted and understood it badly, they could not comprehend within it the uncertain and hidden wisdom of God. The Gentiles, however, are called humble and little ones because, recognizing their ignorance, they accepted the Lord’s preaching as soon as they heard it.

Yes, Father, because this was pleasing before you. “I give thanks” is understood. This confession is called in Greek *exomologesis* (ἐξομολόγησις). The word has a twofold meaning: one refers to the confession of sins by which we confess our offenses to the Lord—not as though he were ignorant, since nothing is hidden from him, but confession is a profession of error, so that the sin we detest in his sight may come to an end. The other confession belongs to praise and thanksgiving, as in this passage: “I confess to you, Father of heaven and earth.”

Everything has been handed over to me by my Father. He speaks according to the form in which he became human, concerning the elect who would believe in him; where he says “everything,” “the elect” is understood. According to his divinity, these things were handed over when he was begotten from the Father. If this statement appears to contain some difficulty, I think it better to remain silent than to explain it hastily now, until an appropriate time for a fuller exposition is found, because, as the canons prescribe, obscure questions should be kept silent before the people.

And no one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son. This knowledge is understood according to the nature of divinity, by which the Father and the Son are one God; and because the Son proceeded from the Father, or because the Father is eternal, the Son eternal, and the Holy Spirit eternal. That knowledge is always ineffable to human speech, as the Prophet also says: “Who will recount his generation?”

As for what follows—“and the one to whom the Son wishes to reveal him”—we plainly believe that the power does not lie externally in the human teacher, but in the Lord himself, who gives growth inwardly. For elsewhere in this same Gospel we read: “No one comes to me unless my Father draws him.” From these words we understand one operation of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and we firmly believe that unless the Holy Spirit, who is one God, touches someone, no one can believe or understand the divinity. To whomever the Father reveals, the Son reveals, and the Holy Spirit reveals, because the operation of the undivided Trinity is one.

Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. In this passage he calls both the Gentiles to repentance and all who were oppressed under the heavy yoke of the burden of sins. The Jews, who possessed zeal for God, sought their own righteousness and were not subject to God. The Gentiles, however, ignorant of the Creator and worshiping the creature in place of the Creator, served under the burden of demons, becoming like the stones and pieces of wood that they worshiped, according to the Psalmist, who says: “Let those who make them become like them, and all who trust in them.”

It continues: “And I will refresh you”—that is, by removing your sins through baptism, I will make you rest. The Psalmist shows that the burden of sins is heavy when he says: “My iniquities have gone over my head, and like a heavy burden they have weighed heavily upon me.”

Take my yoke upon you. That is: come willingly, believe in me, and submit your necks beneath my easy yoke, because until now your necks have been burdened and worn down beneath the yoke of the law. Hence Peter later complained, saying: “Why do you wish to place upon our necks a yoke that neither our fathers nor we have ever been able to bear?”

No one can believe unwillingly, but only voluntarily. Therefore, “take my yoke upon you,” because the yoke is faith by which each person chooses to believe in God and follow him.

And learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart. This is the yoke that we must take upon ourselves and beneath which we must submit our necks, so that we may be gentle and humble in heart. We must be gentle and meek with all good people, since this same simplicity is what we are commanded to imitate in the form of the dove. For, insofar as it depends on us, we ought to have peace with all human beings.

What virtues did the Lord warn us to learn? He did not say, “Learn from me to raise the dead, drive out demons, or walk upon the sea with dry feet,” but rather what we can imitate: that we should be gentle and humble in heart. Elsewhere also he says: “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.” These are the three signs by which Christ’s disciples are recognized. Whoever is discovered not to possess these three is proved not to be Christ’s disciple, even though in name only he may be called a Christian.

It is not one of those things of which what follows is said: “And you will find rest for your souls.” He promises spiritual things, not temporal ones, because visible things are corruptible and quickly pass away, whereas the things given after death to the righteous are eternal and unfading.

For my yoke is sweet, and my burden is light. How can what the Lord says be true—that his yoke is lighter than the yoke of the law? But if we examine it carefully, we shall find that the commandments of the Gospel are lighter than those of the law. In the law there are many commandments that the apostles testify cannot be fulfilled, because the law requires works, and “the one who does them will live by them.” In the Gospel, however, the will is sought; even if it has not achieved its effect, it nevertheless does not lose its reward. We are commanded to observe things that we are able to observe—namely, that we should not desire wrongly.

Under the old law, if the act occurred but the will was absent, the one who performed it was punished. In the Gospel, each person is judged according to the will. For example, if a woman is assaulted and violated by force, although her will was absent, under the old law she is punished because of the act. In the Gospel, however, because her will was absent and she suffered violence, she is judged a virgin before God.

## CHAPTER XXXI. Concerning the disciples’ plucking the ears of grain

At that time Jesus went through the grainfields on the Sabbath; and his disciples, being hungry, began to pluck ears of grain and eat. “Grainfields” means fields that have been sown. It was the custom and law among that people that anyone who wished to enter the harvest of his neighbor and eat grain could do as much as he wished, provided that he did not reap with a sickle. Likewise, whoever entered a vineyard could eat as many bunches of grapes as were sufficient, provided that he did not carry any out.

Because of this law, while Jesus was walking along the road, his hungry disciples went ahead, plucked the ears, rubbed them in their hands, and ate. For we read in this Gospel that many people were coming and believing, and they did not have time to eat; [Col. 1362A] therefore they were hungry like ordinary human beings and relieved their hunger. This may also indicate an austere life, since they did not have prepared banquets but were content with simple food.

But when the Pharisees saw this, they said to him: Behold, your disciples are doing what is not lawful to do on Sabbaths. Here it becomes clear that they followed the Lord for no other reason than to find grounds for accusation. The fact that they say nothing about damage to another person’s harvest, but only about violation of the Sabbath, relates to the reason he mentioned above. The Lombards also have the same law for this very reason, as do many other peoples: when someone enters a grainfield or vineyard, he may eat as much as he wishes, provided that he carries nothing out.

The Jews had the custom of preparing for themselves on the day before the Sabbath the food that they would eat on the following day. Hence that day, the sixth day, is called *parasceve*, that is, “preparation.” On the Sabbath they neither prepared food nor lit a fire. For this reason they criticized Christ’s disciples, asking why they did this.

The Lord shows that the Sabbath must be observed spiritually, and also that he himself was Lord of the Sabbath and that the Sabbath had been commanded for the sake of human beings.

Jesus said to them: Have you not read what David did when he was hungry, and those who were with him—how he entered the house of God and ate the bread of the Presence, which it was not lawful for him to eat, nor for those who were with him, but only for the priests?

To refute the Jews’ criticism, he recalls an event from ancient history reported in the Book of Kings: David, fleeing from Saul, came to the priest Ahimelech and said, as you know, that the king had sent him; he asked him for bread to eat, or for other food. Since the priest had no other bread, he gave him the loaves that had been on the table of the Presence, which no one was permitted to eat except priests or Levites. He asked him nothing else except whether they were clean from women.

That high priest understood that, in accordance with the prophetic saying, it pleased the Lord more to show mercy to one’s neighbor than to offer a burnt offering. For the Lord commanded sacrifices to be offered for no other reason than so that they would not be sacrificed to idols, as he himself says in the Psalm: “Shall I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats?”

It is as though the Lord were saying to the Pharisees: If that blessed priest is not criticized—in fact, is praised—for preferring mercy to sacrifice, why do you not consider the same reason in the case of my disciples? Nevertheless, there is a great difference between them and David, because David was fleeing during the days of the New Moons, on which no one was permitted to travel more than one mile, and he also ate the consecrated loaves, which lay people were not permitted to eat.

As for his saying “those who were with him,” we do not read that anyone was there with him. But from what he said to the priest—“I have arranged with the young men to meet in this place and that”—we believe that either they followed him or came to meet him by another road.

From the custom by which that blessed man asked whether the young men were clean from women, a command was established in the canons even for those who have lawful wives, who ought to receive the body and blood of the Lord: they are to abstain from them on Friday, and, after washing their bodies and clothes, receive communion on the third day.

Or have you not read in the law that on Sabbaths the priests in the temple violate the Sabbath and are without guilt? For on the Sabbath the priests sacrificed victims, slaughtering rams and bulls and burning them upon a pile of wood. According to another Evangelist, he added that when it happened that an infant was born on the Sabbath, it was circumcised on the eighth day, another Sabbath day, so that the law might be fulfilled which commands circumcision on the eighth day.

Joshua also went around the walls of Jericho with his army for seven days. Understanding and considering this, the Maccabees later decreed that if anyone attacked them on the Sabbath, they would fight against them. They did so, gained victories, and proved that this did not displease God.

He likewise refutes them on another occasion, when they criticized him concerning the woman who had been healed, by pointing out that they watered their own animals on the Sabbath and, if they fell into a well, hurried to pull them out.

But I say to you that here is greater than the temple. In this passage, “here” is not a pronoun but an adverb of place, because the one speaking there was Lord of the Sabbath, since he himself had commanded the Sabbath to be observed. It is as though he were saying: If David, who ate unlawful bread, and the priests, who sacrificed victims for the people, are without guilt both before God and before you, how much more may I, who am king and the true priest, Lord of the temple and of the Sabbath, allow my disciples to be without blame, since for the salvation of human beings it was not previously lawful for them to eat?

If you had known what this means—“I desire mercy and not sacrifice”—you would never have condemned the innocent. Abimelech understood that saying better than you did. He had no previous example, yet he did not hesitate to act, firmly knowing that the things created and commanded in the world, except those pertaining to worshiping and praising God, were made and ordained for the sake of human beings.

This consideration must be applied to all the necessities of human weakness, whether to fasts imposed upon the sick or to abstinence from foods, because care of the flesh is forbidden in its desires, not in its necessities. All superiors, bishops, abbots, and others ought to learn this saying of the Lord: “I desire mercy and knowledge of God more than a burnt offering.”

For the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath. There is a hyperbaton here, a disturbance in the order of the words. The order is: “The Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath,” because the one who was speaking with them was the Creator of all things and the giver of the Sabbath commandment.

Mystically, the disciples pass through the grainfields: the apostles or teachers, when they consider how they can lead each person to salvation, suffer that hunger in accordance with the example of the Lord, who said: “I have food to eat, and my food is to do the will of my Father.”

As they pass through, they pluck the ears of grain because they pluck people away from earthly pleasures in which they had been fixed. To rub them with the hands means, through the examples of the Holy Scriptures, to strip each person of carnal desire as though of husks. To eat the grains [Col. 1364A] means for each person, once stripped, to be incorporated among the members of the Church. The disciples do this as they go before the Lord because they preach before the teachers, and thus the Lord touches the heart so that people may believe.

## CHAPTER XXXII. Concerning the healing of the withered hand

And when he had departed from there, he came into their synagogue; and behold, there was a man who had a withered hand. When the Lord arrived at their synagogue on that same day, a man came before him and begged, saying: Lord, help me, for I used to live by the work of my hands, but now I shall beg unless you help me. For he had been a mason.

The Pharisees, before he said anything, questioned him, saying: Is it lawful to heal on Sabbaths? They asked this in order to accuse him: if he did it, as a transgressor; and if he did not do it, they could say that he was able to help but was unwilling.

The Lord answered them in this way, also wishing to show that, because of their greed, they violated the Sabbath—the very thing for which they reproached him, although he did everything he did out of mercy. The Pharisees extended their hands to their mouths every day in order to eat and drink.

This man spiritually signifies the human race, which, after extending its hand toward the forbidden food, had its arm condemned until Christ came. Christ extended his undefiled hands upon the cross in place of the hands that had been extended incontinently, and afterward taught the human race, by his example, to extend its hands toward almsgiving and good works.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. Concerning the Pharisees’ anger toward the Lord, and Isaiah’s prophecy

But the Pharisees went out and took counsel against him about how they might destroy him. They became worse precisely through the means by which they ought to have become better. They themselves extended their hands to their mouths a hundred times a day, and, stirred by envy, for one extended hand [the hand] of the weak man they plotted death for the Savior.

But Jesus, knowing this, withdrew from there. He withdrew as a human being, because the hour had not yet come when he wished to die, nor was there a place outside Jerusalem where he was to suffer. And they followed him, and he healed them all. Those who seek the Lord with devout faith find him, because, according to the Psalmist, the Lord is near to all who call upon him in truth.

And he healed them all—those who were good—from illnesses of soul [Col. 1364D] and body. And he ordered them not to make him known. According to the historical sense, he acted as a human being, concealing himself from those who were wickedly seeking him in order to destroy him.

This was to fulfill what had been spoken through the prophet Isaiah. What it says, “that it might be fulfilled,” refers to the statement, “and he healed them all,” because it had been prophesied both by Isaiah and by others that he would heal the infirmities of souls and bodies: “Behold, my child.” The prophet says this in the person of God the Father.

“Child” is used in four ways. A child may be so called because of age and infancy, as a seven-year-old child; a child because of obedience, as in “David’s servants”; a child because of foolishness, as in “The hundred-year-old child will die”; and a child because of innocence, as here: “Behold, my child.” For he is called *puer* (“child”) from purity, because he himself was pure from sin.

Whom I have chosen—to become incarnate for the redemption [Col. 1365A] of the world.

My beloved—above all others, as the only-begotten one.

In whom my soul has been pleased—because he will do my will irreproachably.

All these statements are to be understood according to the humanity by which he deigned to become human. In his divinity, however, he is one God with the one who speaks these things through the prophet.

I will place my Spirit upon him—not according to measure, as with my saints, but as much as the body could contain.

He will announce judgment to the Gentiles—the judgment by which the good and the evil will be judged and distinguished, as he himself later testifies that he will do, saying: “When the Son of Man sits upon the throne of his majesty,” and so forth.

He will not contend, nor will he cry out. He will not contend with anyone, because he will bring peace in word and deed.

Nor will he cry out. This “crying out” refers to contempt. For it continues: “Nor will anyone hear in the streets.” That is, in the broad way that leads to death, in which many are found, because they do not hear the voice of the Savior.

He will not break a bruised reed. The bruised reed is the sinner lying beneath the burden of sins, crushed by the devil so that he cannot lift his head. The Lord not only did not crush him further but also extended the hand of his help, saying: “Take heart, son; your sins are forgiven.”

And he will not extinguish the smoking flax. There is allegory both in the reed and in the flax. By the flax is understood the body of a human being; by the smoke, a small awareness of faith. He did not extinguish the smoking flax but instructed it fully, saying: “Do you believe in the Son of God?” And the man said: “Who is he, that I may believe in him?” He replied: “You have seen him, and the one speaking with you is he.” And falling down, he worshiped him.

[Col. 1365C] Until he sends forth judgment to victory. He did this when he conquered the devil by rising again and ascending.

And in his name the Gentiles will hope. This is clearer than daylight, because, so that nearly all might believe in him, he himself read these words of Isaiah in the synagogue of the Jews when he rose to read. Believers and unbelievers in that synagogue recognized that these things had been prophesied about him.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. Concerning the healing of the demon-possessed blind and mute man

Then a demon-possessed man who was blind and mute was brought to him, and he healed him, so that he spoke and saw. Above you heard about the man who had been mute, deaf, and demon-possessed, and who was healed by God. This man was blind, but in the other respects he was like him.

Three general signs occurred in this man: he was freed from the demon, received sight [Col. 1365D], and recovered speech. Historically, this happened in the way described; spiritually, he signifies the human race, which was blind in its spiritual eyes and did not speak of the things that belonged to God because demons possessed it.

All pagans are likewise understood in this way. When they come to faith, the demons are driven out of them; the eyes of their hearts are opened so that they can see God—that is, understand and praise him—which is to recover speech.

And the crowds were astonished and said: Is this the Son of David? The crowds marveled and wished to say that he was of David’s lineage and from Bethlehem, where they knew that Christ was to be born. But the Pharisees contradicted them, as though he were neither of David’s lineage nor from Bethlehem, and as though he did not perform mighty works from God. Since the mighty works were plainly being performed and they could not deny them, they tried to turn them to an evil interpretation, claiming that he performed them through incantations, like the magicians in Egypt.

But those magicians could not perform greater signs; rather, because of Pharaoh’s sin, they were permitted to perform certain ones.

This man does not drive out demons except by Beelzebub, the prince of demons. Beelzebub, as you know, was an idol of Ekron, whose name is interpreted as “man of flies.” For *zebub* means “fly.” Because of the filth of sacrificial blood, or because of uncleanness, the Jews called him by this name, and also called him the prince of demons. As the blessed Bede says, we ought not to read any other letter at the end of the name than *b*.

Demons are called in Greek *daimones*, as though from *demnas*, that is, “knowing.” They possess knowledge of things greater than human beings do, partly through the acuteness of a subtler sense and partly through the experience of a long life, because they were created as good angels but became evil through pride.

But Jesus, knowing their thoughts, said to them. They did not say this in words but in their hearts; he answered their thoughts so that they might be compelled to believe, knowing, according to Solomon’s saying, that no one else knows human thoughts except God alone.

Every kingdom divided against itself will be laid waste, and every city or house divided against itself will not stand. Just as a kingdom, if it is divided within itself, is quickly destroyed and perishes, so also the kingdom of the devil, if it is divided, will quickly fall, because discord has overthrown and annihilated many kingdoms, while concord has made great and exalted things that were small, as we still see today.

O Jews, you know that the devil’s kingdom is divided; why do you wish to belong to his kingdom by doing his will?

And if I drive out demons by Beelzebub, by whom do your sons drive them out? “The sons of the Jews” can be understood in two ways: as the apostles, who drove out demons by the power given to them by the Lord, as we read in this Gospel, since the apostles returned and said to the Lord: “Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name”; or he may call the exorcists of that people the sons of the Jews.

Solomon the king had taught them certain adjurations in the name of God, and by this method they drove out demons. Josephus relates that they did this in the presence of Vespasian.

If you attribute the expulsion of demons in your sons to God, why does the same deed in me not receive the same praise? And if you attribute the expulsion of demons to God, to whom do you attribute the healings of bodies? Therefore they themselves will be your judges.

If he is speaking by comparison with the exorcists, they will judge without possessing the same authority. If you refer this to the apostles, they will sit upon twelve thrones and judge the twelve tribes of Israel.

But if I drive out demons by the Spirit of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon you. There is irony in this passage, understood through the contrary, as in the Psalm: “If they shall enter into my rest”—that is, they shall not enter.

The sense is likewise contrary here: Since I drive out demons by the finger of God, certainly the kingdom of God has not come upon you. You possess the knowledge of God, by which you can recognize the good and distinguish it from evil, but through envy you oppose my good work; therefore the kingdom of God has not come upon you.

I see your faithlessness, by which you have chosen to persist in evil; therefore I say these things with complete certainty. The kingdom of God means either eternal life, or the Lord himself, or even Holy Scripture. Hence the Lord said: “The kingdom of God will be taken away from you.”

Or how can anyone enter the house of a strong man and plunder his possessions, unless he first binds the strong man? Then he will plunder his house. In another Gospel he gives the comparison that, when a strong armed man guards his courtyard, everything he possesses is at peace. But if someone stronger comes upon him and conquers him, he takes away all his weapons in which he trusted and distributes his spoils.

He speaks this parable about himself and the devil, because before the Lord came bodily into this world, this world served the devil. The Lord came and took away his weapons—the unbelieving powerful people through whom he accomplished whatever he wished—or his weapons in which he dwelt. His spoils were the innocent who had been deceived by him; alternatively, his vessels were those from whom he drove out demons, like the man under discussion, or the many others about whom you heard above.

Whoever is not with me is against me. This is to be understood about the devil, since the devil always performs works contrary to the Savior. The devil desires to hold human souls captive; the Lord desires to free them. The devil preaches idols; the Lord, knowledge of the one God. The Lord loves virtues; the devil, vices.

Therefore I say to you: Every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven human beings, but the blasphemy of the Spirit will not be forgiven. And whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven; but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come.

How can this be, since many Arians who blasphemed against the Holy Spirit, when they said that he was lesser than the Father and the Son, nevertheless returned to repentance, were received, and were saved? Yet it is said concerning them: Although they know the truth, they openly surrender themselves to blasphemy through envy.

Even someone who speaks against the Father or the Son will not be forgiven so easily—especially if he has been baptized and is Catholic—unless he repents worthily through persistent tears and prayers and frequent fasts.

Indeed, since the forgiveness of sins occurs through the Holy Spirit, whoever, in imitation of the devil and his angels, does not hesitate to attack the majesty of the Godhead against his own knowledge has no forgiveness forever, but will be guilty of an eternal offense. Alternatively, the one who does not believe in the forgiveness of sins and persists in this may be said to blaspheme against the Holy Spirit.

We can also say that the Lord foresaw that those to whom he was speaking would not believe, and that he was speaking this specifically about them.

When he says that it will not be forgiven either in this age or in the age to come, this implies that for certain sins there is forgiveness in the other life, because when this is denied of one sin, it follows that it can be understood of some others—such as idle speech, desires, and lesser sins.

As for graver sins, we do not dare say anything other than what John says: “There is sin unto death; I do not say that anyone should pray for it.” And Paul says: “Do not be deceived: neither fornicators, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor those who lie with males, nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor robbers will possess the kingdom of God.” This applies to them, however, if they are found to be such at the end, or if they die in that condition.

Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree bad and its fruit bad. He says this about himself, because his works were good—namely, the healings of human beings and the words that proceeded from him. If these were good, how could anything evil come from them? For it cannot happen that good comes from evil or evil from good. Indeed, the tree is recognized by its fruit.

Just as one branch cannot produce different fruit, good and bad, and just as sweet and bitter water cannot flow from a single opening, so one human being cannot be both good and evil. All these things were said concerning that statement they had made: “He drives out demons by Beelzebub.”

Brood of vipers, how can you speak good things, since you are evil? He showed concerning them that, just as they were evil in their deeds, so also they were evil in heart—the heart that ought to govern the members—for the conscience is inward and governs the members outwardly. Why they are called a brood of vipers was said above. For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks. Just as a flowing stream has the same taste as the spring from which it arises, so likewise a person brings forth outwardly, in deed and speech, what abounds within.

And consequently he says: Therefore the good Lord Christ brings forth [Col. 1368C] good things from the good treasure, while the evil man—the devil, who is called “man” because of his envy—and the Pharisees brought forth evil things from an evil treasure.

But I say to you that for every idle word which people speak, they will give an account on the day of judgment. This is added to what he said above about blasphemy against the Spirit, as though he were saying: “Not only will those who blaspheme be tormented in hell on account of blasphemy, but also on account of slander, and indeed on account of every idle word.” An idle word is one that lacks any usefulness. But a malicious word, which leads toward vice, whether toward pursuing drunkenness or enticing someone toward sexual excess, will be judged more severely. Slander is a mortal crime, for “the one who slanders will be uprooted from the land of the living”; that is, he will have no root there if he ends his life in this state.

[Col. 1368D] By your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned. Whoever says “the Lord Jesus in the Holy Spirit”—which the Apostle commanded should be said when he says, “No one can say, ‘The Lord Jesus,’ except in the Holy Spirit”—can be justified by his words. And whoever considers what the apostle James says, “No human being can tame the tongue” (that is, the evil tongue), and what Solomon said, “Death and life are in the power of the tongue,” understands how a person can be condemned through the tongue. Whatever Arius chiefly sinned, he sinned through the tongue. Through the tongue that sin is committed of which he said above that it is not forgiven either in this age or in the age to come.

Then some of the scribes and Pharisees answered him, saying:

[Col. 1369A] Teacher, we wish to see a sign from you.

Another Evangelist states more explicitly what sort of signs they were requesting: namely, they wished either, in the manner of Elijah, for fire to come down from heaven in order to burn some people, just as Elijah did when he killed two captains of fifty together with their fifty men; or, in the manner of Samuel, they wanted thunder and lightning to occur in summer, contrary to the custom of the region.

Among us it thunders in summer because we are in the West and the clouds have been lightened; for that reason they can move. Among Eastern peoples, however, it thunders in winter, because in summer their clouds are so clear that they have no source from which to rain: the sun does not allow them to gather enough rain to produce thunder. It is not true, as people believe, that no one knows what thunder is. Rather, it is that of which [Col. 1369B] John says that the Holy Spirit is in the hearts of believers. For just as mortals are shaken by this thunder, so by that thunder the minds of mortals are terrified and fall away from their thoughts and deeds.

For the sound that is heard in the clouds is produced by the clouds when some of them have water and others do not. Those that have water move, and then the sound is heard as you have heard it; and they kindle the very fire that you see, because every collision creates fire, as you see happening when one piece of iron strikes another, or one stone another.

How, then, can this be the thunder of which John says, “The seven thunders spoke with their voices”? And again: “From the throne proceed flashes of lightning and thunders.” Rather, he speaks of the thunder of the Holy Spirit, which occurs in sevenfold form, not of another kind; for it is impossible to express in words [Col. 1369C] how and in what ways it shakes the hearts of mortals.

## CHAPTER XXXV. On the Request for Signs

An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign. It is called an evil generation not by nature, but by conduct. It is called adulterous because it frequently abandoned God and worshiped idols, as the Lord reproaches it through Ezekiel, or also because at that time it loved other creatures more. For blessed Augustine says, drawing authority from that passage of the Apostle—“and avarice, which is the service of idols”—that every person who abandons God’s justice for gold or for some other creature then commits fornication in soul against God, and at that moment seems to worship and venerate the gold itself, for whose sake he abandons God’s commandment.

[Col. 1369D] And no sign will be given it except the sign of the prophet Jonah. Recall Jonah’s story: when he was sent to preach to the Ninevites, he wished to flee from God’s command. Later, as you know, when he was discovered by lot—because the sea was seeking him—he was thrown into it, swallowed by a sea-monster, and lay there for three days. In a similar way, the Lord says that he will give the Jews a sign.

Jonah prefigured the Lord: just as Jonah himself was sent to convert the Ninevites, who were Gentiles, so the Lord Jesus was sent into this world to preach to the Gentiles. The sea signifies this age, and it was troubled because of Jonah; so this age too was troubled because of his preaching, since he says: “I have not come to bring peace, but the sword of separation.”

[Col. 1370A] The sea-monster signifies the earth, or hell, because the earth received his body, while hell received his soul. As for the fact that four days are mentioned, although in every respect he was not there for a full three days, a part is understood from the whole by synecdoche: for he was placed in the tomb at the eleventh hour on Friday and lay there for twenty-seven hours. And just as Jonah did not wish to go to the Gentiles before being swallowed, so he says to the apostles: “Do not go on the road of the Gentiles”; but after the resurrection he commanded them, saying: “Go and teach all the nations.”

The men of Nineveh will rise in the judgment with this generation and will condemn it. Not by authority, but by comparison: for although they saw no signs from Jonah, and although he preached for no long time but only for three days, those Gentiles believed a foreigner. [Col. 1370B] Now I, who am greater than all, commended by John, and who performed many miracles among you, have not only not been heard, but have been called Beelzebub.

And behold, something greater than Jonah is here. For I am Jonah’s creator. Here the word “here” is an adverb of place, not a pronoun. Jonah is interpreted as “dove” or “one who mourns,” and he prefigured the Lord. Nineveh was a city built by Asshur, the son of Shem, and adorned by the first king of the Assyrians. He named it Nineveh after his own name—that is, “beautiful”—and it was always the seat of the Assyrians.

The queen of the South will rise in the judgment with this generation and will condemn it. The queen of the South had not heard that Solomon performed miracles, raised the dead, or preached the kingdom of heaven; nor had she heard that he knew letters without a teacher. Nevertheless, she came from the East to hear Solomon. Therefore this generation will be condemned more than that one, because, although it has with it the one who gave wisdom, it did not wish to hear him.

[Col. 1370C] Spiritually, Solomon signifies the Lord Christ, because Solomon is said to mean “peaceful.” And this queen signifies the Church, which is to be converted from the Gentiles to our true Peaceful One.

And behold, something greater than Solomon is here. For he was speaking of the one concerning whom Solomon had said: “The Lord possessed me at the beginning of his ways, before he made anything from the beginning.”

When an unclean spirit has gone out from a person, it travels through dry places. This can be understood of a person freed from a demon: if he does not guard himself against evil deeds, he will again be handed over to the one to whom he had previously been handed over. It can also be understood of the Jews, who were perversely resisting the Lord and were destined to become worse after despising the law of the letter and the Lord’s preaching than they had been before receiving the law. [Col. 1370D]

For when they received the law, the devil went out from them and traveled among the Gentiles; but now he has dismissed the Gentiles and returned to the Jews. By the broom with which a house is cleaned is understood the doctrine of the Jews, left empty because it did not possess God, who said, “Let us cross over from these dwelling places,” as Josephus reports. The seven spirits signify the seven principal vices.

While he was still speaking, behold, his mother and his brothers appeared. His brothers were not the children of holy Mary, but nephews or other cousins, who are called “brothers” in Holy Scripture, just as Lot was called Abraham’s brother although he was his nephew.

The man who announced this to him was testing him, to see whether he would prefer heavenly things to earthly things and abandon his preaching [Col. 1371A] for the sake of carnal kinship. But he showed that spiritual brotherhood is better than carnal brotherhood. If both exist together, however, there is a double good, as was the case with holy Mary, because a person becomes a mother when someone is reborn in Christ through that person’s word, just as Paul says: “Through the Gospel I became your father.”

On that day Jesus went out from the house and sat beside the sea, and great crowds gathered to him, and so forth.

Not only the Lord’s sayings but also his deeds are full of mysteries. When the Lord is said to have gone out from that house where the Jews were hurling profane words against him and to have come to the sea, this showed that he would leave Judaea because of the merit of its crimes and profane words and would pass over to the Gentiles, who are signified by the swollen and wave-tossed sea.

[Col. 1371B] For just as the sea was moved by every wind, so the Gentiles were changed by the agitation of every doctrine. It is known to everyone which sea he means: the Lake of Gennesaret, where he was accustomed to enter and teach the crowds from a boat.

It was in the Galilee of the Jews, measuring one hundred forty stades in length and forty in breadth, and containing all kinds of fish that are found outside the sea. It also had cities built upon it, and according to the variety of the neighboring provinces or cities it received different names. Thus it was called the Sea of Galilee after the province and the Sea of Tiberias after the city. In Greek it was called Gennesar, as though “generating gold for itself”; it was said to raise storms on its own. Its water was purer and [Col. 1371C] sweet and suitable for drinking.

The shore is called *litus* because the water is dashed against it—that is, struck as it comes. It was a suitable place for teaching, because he could be seen and heard by everyone and could not be crowded out by the multitude.

And he spoke many things to them in parables. It was customary among those inhabitants to speak frequently by means of comparisons; therefore the Lord followed the custom to which they were accustomed to listen.

Behold, the sower went out. He gives a comparison from earthly sowing, showing that spiritual sowing is carried out in a similar way. The one who sows went out: the Lord Jesus. He went out from the Father and descended from heaven. To sow his seed: the word of the Gospel.

And as he sowed, some seed fell beside the road. That is, it fell upon those whom the devil is accustomed frequently to visit and, as it were, inhabit. Therefore he tramples the seed of the word, because he removes it and [Col. 1371D] introduces other cares.

The demons are called birds because they roam through the air in the manner of birds.

And other seed fell upon rocky ground. The Lord explained the rock as hardness of heart; the soil as steadfast faith; and the sun as the heat of persecution, by which, when adversity arises, they deny the Lord or abandon justice.

But other seed fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up and choked it. The Lord explained the thorns as riches. When the word is preached to those who are rich, they receive it with joy. But when that hour has passed and they have returned to their riches, the suggestions acquired by the person prick him from within; and because they possess the power to do whatever they wish, they do what their pleasures suggest and abandon what they heard in church.

[Col. 1372A] Other seed fell on good soil and produced fruit: one a hundredfold, another sixtyfold, and another thirtyfold. According to agricultural practice, there is found overseas soil that multiplies seed a hundredfold, sixtyfold, or thirtyfold. This is not found in our land, because compared with the land in which the Lord was speaking these things, our land is barren, almost wild.

With regard to spiritual seed, the one who produces a hundredfold is the person who, along with the other virtues, perseveres as a virgin in body and soul, like holy Mary and many virgins. The one who bears fruit sixtyfold is the person who leads a just and good life for a long time in widowhood, as Anna did, who is praised in this Gospel. The one who produces thirtyfold fruit is the person who enters marriage, uses it lawfully, and is adorned with the other virtues, [Col. 1372B] not forgetting the commandments of his Creator, as Zachariah did.

These, then, are the three orders of the elect through whom the Church is constituted. We shall pursue what remains together with the Lord’s interpretation.

And the disciples came and said. It must be asked how the disciples came to the Lord when he was in the boat—namely, they were with him in the boat.

Because it has been given to you to know the mystery of the kingdom of heaven, but to them it has not been given. To you, because of the right faith and charity that are in you, it has been granted to know and understand the secrets of God. But they, because of the envy they possess, are not worthy to know the secrets of God, because wisdom will not enter into a malicious soul.

There were many good and many evil people among them. The Lord touched the hearts of those who were good, so that they might either [Col. 1372C] return or persevere until they understood what they had heard briefly.

For whoever has will be given more, and he will abound. Whoever possesses faith or charity will receive the remaining virtues. But whoever does not have—charity is understood—and what he has, that is, what he appears to have, will be taken away from him.

Therefore I speak to them in parables, because seeing they do not see. That is, they see with the eyes of the body, but because of envy and unbelief they do not wish to have the eyes of the heart. Likewise, although they hear with the ears of the body, they do not wish to hear with the ears of the heart so as to understand. This was also prophesied by Isaiah, because they would reject my preaching.

The heart of this people has grown fat. This is because, just as the soul is nourished by the words of God, so an [Col. 1372D] impious soul grows fat on evil. And because they heard the Lord’s preaching with dull ears, they strove to criticize it. The prophet then follows by saying why this happened to them:

They have closed their eyes. Hardness and an impenitent heart came first, and these did not allow them to turn and be healed.

But blessed are your eyes because they see, and your ears because they hear. The very eyes whose blindness he condemned in the Jews he praises in the apostles, and likewise their spiritual ears, by which they saw and heard the Savior. To see him with the eyes of the flesh and not with the eyes of the heart, as Herod and Pilate saw him, is condemnation rather than salvation.

Amen, I say to you, many prophets and righteous people desired to see what you see, and did not see it. That is, although they saw it in the spirit, as Abraham and David did, they desired also to see it with [Col. 1373A] actual eyes, as the apostles did, both bodily and spiritually. For they knew that their liberation was drawing near, so that they would no longer be held under the power of darkness, just as they had been held for a long time until then.

Therefore suffering Job also said: “If I wait, hell is my house; in darkness I have made my bed.”

Therefore hear the parable of the sower. Hear obscure sayings together with the disclosure of the comparison. The Apostle now explains that some among the crowd were not worthy to hear.

Everyone who hears the word of the kingdom—“of God” is understood—and does not understand it, the devil comes and snatches away what was sown in his heart. [Col. 1373B] For this reason every person who hears the word in church ought to inquire until he understands it and puts it into practice.

This is the one who was sown beside the road: beside the road of demons, which the wicked have formed in his heart by thinking constantly about evil things. Nothing is said here about those who do not even deign to hear with the ears of the body; they are more guilty than these.

But the one who was sown upon rocky ground is the one who hears the word and immediately receives it with joy. Yet he has no root and is temporary. The Lord explains this, so there is no need to explain it; but today such people are like lukewarm Christians who, because of the anger of some powerful person or because of a gift, abandon the truth and turn to injustice.

There is some difference between the person who abandons the truth in tribulation and the person who voluntarily [Col. 1373C] abandons justice without tribulation. Hence it follows:

When tribulation or persecution arises because of the word, he is immediately scandalized. Whoever abandons the truth without tribulation is worse than a pagan.

The one who was sown among thorns is the one who hears the word, but the anxiety of this age and the deceitfulness of riches choke the word. For just as thorns prick, so the cares of the rich frequently touch them: how they may acquire more. The more they have, the more they desire, because:

> The love of money grows as the money itself grows.

Care touches the mind, asking how he may guard his acquisition; care also touches him, asking from whom he may seize these things greedily, like the man who said:

> You have many good things stored up for many years. Rest, eat, drink, and feast.

[Col. 1373D] They are called deceitful because they deceive and mislead those who trust in them, as it was said to that man:

> This night they will demand your soul from you; and the things you have prepared—whose will they be?

But the one who was sown on good soil is the one who hears the word, understands it, bears fruit, and produces one a hundredfold, another sixtyfold, and another thirtyfold.

By the hundredfold is meant virginity, or every perfection of virtues, because one hundred is a perfect number. And just as, in counting, one hundred passes from the left to the right, so the person who preserves virginity and perfection of virtues undefiled will pass from the present age into eternal life.

By the sixtyfold is meant a life of continence, perfected in deed and understanding, because on the sixth day God perfected his works, and sixty arises from six times ten. [Col. 1374A] Hence, in the method of calculation, sixty is expressed by a contracted finger-joint. The unmarried person ought to consider the things of the Lord and not live in pleasures, whether man or woman, lest, being dead, he or she be judged in the sight of God, as Paul says of the widow: “She who lives in pleasures is dead.”

Thirty, too, in its interpretation seems to indicate male and female, since the component parts join together as though by kissing.

He put forward another parable for them, saying: The kingdom of heaven is like a man who is a householder and sowed good seed in his field.

The Lord is going to interpret this parable, but let us take what he himself said: The one who sows the good seed is the Son of Man; the field is this world.

It continues: While the people were sleeping. This means that the teachers of the churches were not diligent [Col. 1374B] in meditating on the divine utterances. Bishops and superiors of churches must beware lest this also be said of them. They ought to devote themselves, both personally and through their subordinates, as far as they can, to announcing the people’s sins, so that they may know what they ought to avoid and how to guard themselves against the coming sword.

The good seed: the Son of God. His enemy: the devil, who is the enemy of God and of human beings, from the time when he saw the man placed in paradise. The weeds: the sons of the devil through their deeds. The grass and the fruit: works. The servants of the householder who came: the angels of the Lord. The enemy who was a man: the devil, of whom it is said, “Arise, O Lord; let not man prevail.”

Lest perhaps, while gathering the weeds. The weed, called *lolium* by another name, is, according to agricultural usage, a harmful seed that grows among spelt, [Col. 1374C] and whoever eats it when it is gathered does not have a sound mind for the moment. Thus anyone who dissents from God is not fully rational. Here, however, as the Lord explains, evil people are meant.

The servants said: Do you wish us to go and gather them? And he said: No, lest while gathering the weeds you uproot the wheat together with them. Let both grow until the harvest.

Here all kings, bishops, and superiors ought to take an example, so that they do not pronounce judgment in uncertain cases before they have truly recognized the crime. Grass signifies either an imperfect age or hidden deeds, all of which must be endured until full knowledge is attained. For when blessed Paul commanded, “Remove the evil person from among you,” he was speaking of open and manifest transgressors. [Col. 1374D]

When he says, “Lest while gathering the weeds you uproot the wheat as well,” both God’s patience and his purpose are shown in this saying. He patiently awaits the wicked so that they may be converted, but condemns those who have not been converted more severely. Moreover, the person who appears to be a weed today can become God’s wheat tomorrow.

At harvest-time I will say to the reapers: Gather the weeds first and bind them into bundles to be burned. Then, clearly, the greedy will be sent with the greedy, the sexually immoral with the sexually immoral; and each person will be joined in punishment to those like him in softness and indulgence.

The wheat: the righteous. The barn: eternal life.

The Son of Man will send his angels, and they will gather out of his kingdom, from the Church, all scandals and those who have caused his elect to stumble, and those who commit iniquity. He does not say “those who committed,” but “those who were still doing so in this life.”

[Col. 1375A] There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. Weeping and gnashing of teeth signify both the greatest torments and the true resurrection of bodies.

Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father. The Lord is the heavenly light, and the sun will be in it; and the saints, sharing in his radiance, will shine like the sun.

The kingdom of heaven is like a mustard seed. In the present Church, let each believer receive the word of the Gospel and store it in his field—that is, in his breast and heart.

It is the smallest of all seeds. But when it has grown, it is greater than all garden plants. Such is the doctrine of the Gospel: it appears small in outward appearance and in hearing, but in power it is more ardent and excellent than all doctrines. To the Jews it seemed a stumbling block, and to the Gentiles foolishness: that God had died for his servants and had risen on the third [Col. 1375B] day.

Nevertheless, no philosophical doctrine filled the world as this one did, nor did any doctrine offer the reward of eternal life except this one.

So that the birds of heaven come and dwell in its branches. The birds are the preachers of the age. Its branches are the examples of the Scriptures, through which faithful souls have become accustomed to fly toward heavenly things and, neglecting desires for temporal possessions, to keep their hearts above.

The kingdom of heaven is like leaven, which a woman took and hid in three measures of flour. Leaven is named from fermenting—that is, from heating—and is made from the lees of wine or beer. A *satum* is a kind of measure containing one *modius* and a half. Three *sata* contain four and a half *modii*. It was said among the Hebrews that whoever measures this same measure should lift it.

He speaks of the first parable as concerning himself and his hearers, [Col. 1375C] and of the other as concerning what the devil introduced after the Lord’s seed. He then praised his own seed by saying that it was like mustard; now he says what all ecclesiastical people ought to do with the word of the Gospel.

By the woman he wishes the Church to be understood. Each person who belongs to the Church ought to hide the word in the faith of the Holy Trinity, until he does everything he does in the name of the Holy Trinity.

Or it may be understood in another way: there are three passions in us—anger, desire, and reason. Let us place the word of the Gospel among these passions and bring all those passions into order through the word of the Gospel, so that we do not become angry or desire wrongly, as the Gospel commands, and so that we shape our reason according to the Gospel.

Jesus spoke all these things in parables to the crowds, and without parables he did not speak to them. Whoever does not wish to be a disciple hears words in the crowd and in parables. Whoever is a disciple worthy of Christ deserves to hear the interpretations of the parables, because God gives him understanding so that he may comprehend the Scriptures.

[Col. 1375D] This was fulfilled which was spoken through the prophet who said: “I will open my mouth in parables.” Through the prophet David, indeed, in the seventieth Psalm: “I will utter what has been hidden since the foundation of the world.” Not everything, but some things; and by the figure called synecdoche, a part is to be understood from the whole.

The kingdom of heaven is like a treasure hidden in a field. In this Gospel “the kingdom of heaven” is spoken of in four ways: the Lord Jesus Christ, eternal life, the present Church, and the breadth of the divine Scriptures. It is understood differently according to the different passages. [Col. 1376A]

Here, in this parable, the present Church is understood as the kingdom of heaven. The field, however, is the breadth of the divine Scriptures. In this field the treasure is found—that is, our Lord Jesus Christ—because he was announced to us through the Scriptures by the prophets and apostles.

Whoever finds him ought to set everything else aside and count worldly things as worthless in his love, so that he may love him before and above all things. Whoever finds him hides him in the secret place of his breast, not out of a desire for avarice; by this is expressed the love of one who wishes to preserve him.

And because of his joy. There can be great joy in discovering and knowing the one through whom a person can be freed from hell and enjoy blessed life.

He sells everything he has and buys that field. For in all his actions and possessions he ought to follow God’s [Col. 1376B] will. Such a merchant was Zacchaeus. When he was in the sycamore tree in order to see the treasure that he could buy, he received it into his house and said: “For this treasure, if I have taken anything from anyone, I restore fourfold, and I give the remainder to the poor.”

Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a merchant seeking good pearls. Here too the Church is understood as the kingdom. In that Church all Christians ought to be such merchants as seek good pearls—that is, the finest understandings in the Law and the Prophets.

When they have found the finest pearl, the Lord Christ, let them despise all the pleasures of this age in order to gain Christ. Such a merchant was the eunuch who had come to worship in Jerusalem and was returning seated on his [Col. 1376C] chariot, seeking pearls in the book of Isaiah. Philip came and showed him that pearl; he placed it in his heart and loved it above everything he possessed.

Such were Nicodemus and Joseph, who asked Pilate for the small chamber in which that pearl had been placed, because he too already possessed that same pearl. All the apostles were merchants of this kind.

Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a dragnet cast into the sea. Everything here is said allegorically, and this is a form of allegory: a parable involving things different in kind. For both the treasure and the pearl are worthless in comparison with God; the spiritual dragnet is inferior to the literal dragnet; and the kingdom of heaven is the Church, as above.

The dragnet means the Lord’s preaching. Cast into the sea, into this age, because, as in the sea, one fish pursues another and either kills [Col. 1376D] it or takes away whatever it can. Sometimes the sea is calm, sometimes troubled; likewise in this age there are sometimes peace and sometimes persecutions.

Fish of every kind were gathered. For people from every nation are converted to God. When the Lord said these things, he was casting the dragnet into the sea and teaching the twelve fishermen how to fish.

The Lord’s net and that of his disciples caught many, and even today it is cast; it catches both good and evil. And when they come—that is, when each person’s end comes—the angels come. They place the good fish in a pool, into eternal life, but the evil in eternal fire, so that they may no longer devour the good fish or make children like themselves, but may burn because they have eaten the good fish.

Such a fish was Julian, [Col. 1377A] who broke through the net and went out. Because he devoured and persecuted many of the Lord’s fish, he was separated from the good and is still being cooked, paying the penalties on their behalf.

So it will be at the consummation of the age. The angels will go out and separate the wicked from the midst of the righteous. Although at the end of the world this will happen to many, the separation also occurs daily: evil Christians and pagans are separated from the good and sent into the furnace of fire.

The shore is the end of the age; the furnace is the fire that will not be extinguished.

Have you understood all these things? They said to him: Yes. “Yes” is an adverb of affirmation; that is, “We have understood.”

He asks only the apostles, and is a perfect teacher, because he was also instructing them as teachers of the churches. Just as a dragnet is made from many meshes, so he was teaching them to arrange preaching from many examples of the Scriptures.

Therefore it follows:

[Col. 1377B] For this reason every scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven is like a householder.

“For this reason” means: “I wish you to understand what I am saying, so that you may be like me, who am the householder, and you may be my scribes. Thus, just as I bring forth new things from myself and old things from the old books, so should you when you begin to preach.”

A scribe is so called from writing: namely, one who exercises himself in the Scriptures.

And it happened that when Jesus had finished these parables. To finish is characteristic of the wise; fools leave their undertakings incomplete. This too is as though proper to him, since it had already been said of him when God completed his work: “And the heavens and the earth were perfected.”

He went away from there, and coming into his own country, he taught them in their synagogue. According to the historical account, you hear that the Lord taught in various places. And if [Col. 1377C] there were people unwilling to come to hear his teaching, he himself came to them, so that they would have no excuse concerning their ignorance.

He returned to Galilee, to the city of Nazareth. It is called his homeland and his city, not because he was from it, but because he had been raised there.

You know what a synagogue is.

So that they were astonished and said: They were astonished because they had seen him raised among them, yet had never seen him learning letters. They heard him, however, bringing forth testimonies from the Law, which he could not have produced unless he had read it.

Nevertheless, they would not have been astonished if they had known him, because he was the one who had taught Adam all natural philosophy, Abraham astrology, Moses grammar, and Solomon wisdom. If many people were amazed at Solomon’s wisdom, what is surprising if the teacher [Col. 1377D] of Solomon spoke marvelous things?

Is not his mother called Mary? Although she is poor among you, she is from the house of David. She bore the one who enriched your exceedingly wealthy king Solomon and permitted Octavian to reign. If he had wished, he could also have enriched her as he enriched Libya. But the one who wished Peter and John, his chief disciples, to say, “We have neither gold nor silver,” had already said: “The Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.”

He was the son of a craftsman, but not of this one. His Father fashioned the chamber of heaven, so bright and arched, through this man whom you despise.

And his brothers were James and Joseph, and Simon and Judas. You also know that James and Judas the apostles, and Joseph and Simon, are called his brothers because they were nephews [Col. 1378A] of holy Mary through her sisters.

I told you above why it pleased God for a time that some people should call Joseph his father, although in truth he was not.

Mary is interpreted as “illuminatrix,” because she bore the true light.

Where, then, did this man get all these things? That is, wisdom in teaching and miraculous powers in the healing of people.

And they were scandalized because of him. They took God in human form as a stumbling block and an occasion of anger, as Paul says: “We preach Christ, a stumbling block to the Jews and foolishness to the Gentiles.”

But Jesus said to them: A prophet is not without honor except in his own country and in his own house. As the Lord said, so it has always been among the Jews and among other nations, as blessed Jerome said: “Citizens envy their fellow citizens.”

Elijah too was fed during a famine by a Gentile woman in Zarephath of Sidon. Jonah had no reputation among his own people, but among the Ninevites he was greatly feared. His own people wished to kill Elisha, lest Naaman the Syrian give his servant boy one hundred pounds of silver and double garments. Isaiah was killed by his own grandson, King Manasseh. Foreigners made Daniel ruler over one hundred twenty provinces. His own people put Jeremiah into a cistern; Nebuchadnezzar held him in great honor, and Nebuzaradan commended him.
