The Lord himself suffered many evils and reproaches from his own people, while Abgarus wished to share his kingdom with him.

And he did not perform many miracles there because of their unbelief. As God, he could indeed do as much as he wished, but he did not do so, leaving them to their condemnation. For the more someone sees of a good example, the more [Col. 1378C] he is condemned if he does not follow it. But if he deliberately avoids seeing it, then he is judged even more wicked and apostate, and is like the devil.

At that time Herod the tetrarch heard the report about Jesus and said to his attendants. This Herod was the son of Herod, the brother of Archelaus, and he is the one who, during the Lord’s Passion, sent him back to Pilate. This Herod, then, was the brother of Philip. Later Philip married the daughter of King Aretas, named Herodias. Afterwards, when certain hostilities had arisen between him and his son-in-law, her father is said to have taken his daughter away from Philip and given her to Herod, because Herod was the more powerful. This woman, moreover, was related to both these kings, since she was born from the daughter of Herod who had killed the infants. Nevertheless, it was customary among the Jews to take close relatives as wives, though not sisters, nor the daughters of one’s paternal or maternal uncle. But because these men were descended from a pagan grandfather and a Jewish grandmother, they imitated their grandfather Herod, who had been a glorious king among the Romans, and retained some things from the old law while rejecting others; for they worshiped the God of heaven and were circumcised.

Herod the tetrarch heard the report about Jesus. “Tetrarch” is a Greek name composed from four, which are called *tetra* in Greek, and *archon*, “rule”; thus a tetrarch is a ruler over four. “The report”—that is, the reputation concerning the miracles he performed. “And he said to his attendants”—that is, to those who served him.

“This is John the Baptist, whom I beheaded; he has risen from the dead, and therefore miraculous powers are at work in him.” Since Herod had not previously known the Lord Christ, he spoke in this way. For it had been customary among the Jews that whoever was to become a prophet should follow an earlier prophet and imitate him in his actions, as Joshua did Moses, Elisha Elijah, Baruch Jeremiah, and Gehazi Elisha. Because Herod had not heard that the Lord had been John’s disciple, he therefore supposed that he himself was John.

They thought correctly about the resurrection when they said, “John has risen; therefore he performs miracles that he did not perform before,” as if they had said: “John now performs miracles because he is immortal and has greater power after the resurrection; therefore he can perform miracles that he did not perform before.” For all the bodies of the saints possess greater power after the resurrection than before.

For Herod had seized John; he brought him from the desert where he had been and bound him in prison at Machaerus, because of Herodias, the wife of his brother. She had already been his brother’s wife, but at that time she was no longer so. John said to him: “It is not lawful for you to have her”—that is, while his brother was alive. He did not wish to kill him, however, but feared the people. He had read in Chronicles that Joash, king of Israel, had killed Zechariah, the son of Jehoiada the priest, and that afterwards the king himself had been killed because of this; so he feared the same thing for himself, since John had been the son of the high priest. He also added this, because they regarded him as a prophet—that is, they revered him as a prophet.

On the day of Herod’s birthday, when he himself had been born. He rightly celebrated that day, since in this world he was going to possess only so many good things. The end of the saints is therefore called their birthday, because then they are reborn into that life where they will live forever in joy, as Mark says: “On that day he made a banquet for the rulers and the leading men of Galilee.” We read that many kings frequently held banquets for their subjects, because all good things abounded for them, such as Ahasuerus, Belshazzar, and Herod, and many others. Many Roman kings did the same; concerning one of them, Titus, it is recorded that at the dedication of the theater he killed five thousand wild beasts. Yet among mortals only Pharaoh and Herod are said to have celebrated the day of their birth, and both polluted it with murder. This Herod, however, was all the more wicked because the victim was a prophet and because the murder followed a prohibition in the law.

The daughter of Herodias danced. Since both Herod and the woman descended from the family of the elder Herod, they therefore bore his name. She is called his daughter, not Herod’s, because she had been born from another husband. Many peoples regard dancing at banquets as an honor, as though it showed who was the more agile. The Basques and the peoples of Spain still retain this practice, whereas among the Franks it is a disgrace. Dancers were named after Salius of Arcadia, whom Aeneas brought with him to Italy and who taught the noble Roman youths to dance.

> [Note: “This Salius, together with Patron, one of whom was an Acarnanian …” (Virgil, *Aeneid* V, 298).]

We read, moreover, that the Sibyl danced ten eclogues of Virgil in the senate.

It pleased Herod. It was not only her dancing that pleased him, but also the Greek-composed metrical piece which she danced. Therefore he promised her with an oath that he would give her whatever she asked of him.

Herod himself, together with his wife, found this way of killing John without causing an uprising. For this reason he kept him confined: so that when he had sworn, he might kill him as though out of reverence for the Lord’s name, lest he appear to violate the Lord’s name by perjury. But she, having been instructed beforehand by her mother—for she feared that Herod might become reconciled with his brother, listen to John’s admonitions, and dismiss her—said: “Give me here on a dish the head of John the Baptist.”

A dish was formerly called *iscus*, from its resemblance to a shield; hence afterward a small dish was called *discus*, because it covers [the wording is uncertain].

And the king was distressed. It is the custom of historians to write the cause as it was thought by those present at the time. Thus Joseph is also called by the evangelists the father of the Lord, although they knew truly that he was not. Likewise here the king is said to have been distressed, although he pretended to be sad and was glad in his heart. Because of the oath and those who were reclining with him, he ordered that it be given.

Since the king was partly Jewish, they nevertheless did not eat from a single vessel, as Joseph did with his brothers and with the Egyptians. He sent and beheaded John in prison. We have it written that “he prayed while standing in the middle of the prison, saying: ‘Lord my God, to you I commend my spirit.’” A prison is a place from which one is forbidden to leave, and *carcer* is said to derive from restraining or coercing.

His disciples came, took the body, buried it, and went and reported to Jesus. Herod is not excused on the grounds that he acted unwillingly, because if the death of his mother or sister had been requested, he would have refused it. What he would have rejected for a carnal relative, he ought to have preserved in the case of a prophet.

We read in Roman history about Flaminius, a Roman commander, that at the request of a prostitute with whom he was lying he had the head of a condemned man, guilty of a capital crime, brought into the banquet. Afterwards he was expelled from the senate because he had mixed murder with a banquet. How much more criminal were Herod, Herodias, and the girl, who asked as the price of her dancing for the prophet’s head, so that she might have his tongue under her control and prevent him from reproving their unlawful marriage!

Spiritually, John’s beheading signifies the diminution of his reputation, by which Christ was believed to be John, just as Christ’s exaltation on the cross signifies the perfection of faith. For he who had previously been thought to be a prophet was recognized as the Christ, because, as John said, Christ had to increase while he himself had to decrease. The distinction of the seasons also signified this, since John was born at the time when daylight begins to diminish, and Christ at the time when that same light begins to increase.

Josephus relates that John, having been bound, was brought to the fortress of Machaerus and there beheaded; ecclesiastical history says that he was buried at Sebaste, that is, Samaria. In the time of the emperor Julian, the pagans, seeing Christians frequently visiting his tomb, are said to have dug him up and scattered his bones through the fields. At that time some monks from Jerusalem happened to be there. When they collected his bones together with other Christians, those same pagans began to gather them up again and burn them in the fire. The monks, however, brought what they had collected to Jerusalem, to their abbot Philip. He sent them to Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, and they were kept there until the time of the emperor Theodosius. Then, after the temple of Serapis had been cleansed, they were placed there, and he dedicated the temple itself in John’s name.

His head, however, was not found at that time. During the reign of the emperor Marcian it was revealed to two monks, who found it near Herod’s palace, where the wretched women had hidden it.

The Herod who killed him and joined Pilate in consenting to the Lord’s Passion went to Rome, urged on by his wife, so that he might obtain the kingdom that his brother Agrippa possessed. Agrippa followed him there and accused him before Caesar, alleging that he was planning to rebel against him and had weapons prepared. Since he could not deny the matter of the weapons, he was deported to Lugdunum, a city of Burgundy, in perpetual exile, and his kingdom was given to Agrippa.

His wife came to the emperor to plead for her husband. The emperor, however, wishing to act on behalf of her brother Agrippa, wanted to keep her with him. But she said to the emperor: “I count all your goods as nothing, nor do I wish to receive them unless you restore my husband to me.” The emperor said to her: “Since you speak in this way, you will see neither your husband nor your homeland.” She too was sent into perpetual exile. By such vengeance the crime that they had committed against the Lord and his forerunner was punished. Even now they are tormented by indescribable sufferings.

And his disciples came and took his body. These were disciples who had once belonged to John but then belonged to the Lord. They reported to the Lord—that is, they told him how John had completed the course of his life and had died while proclaiming the law. The Lord himself was also killed by the Jews for the same reason, because he proclaimed God’s law to them. Whoever dies while zealously upholding or proclaiming the Lord’s law, provided that he has hatred toward no one but charity, will be like John and the martyrs in the other life.

Some ask why John did not perform miracles during his life, although so many things occurred at his birth. John’s father was a man of such power and had such influential relatives that Herod feared they might kill him. How much more, then, if John had performed miracles, would no one have been able to kill him.

When Jesus heard this, he withdrew from there. Either those who had consented to John’s death were unworthy to hear his preaching—the rulers of Galilee who had been present at the banquet—or he acted as a human being: he did not wish to give them an opportunity, lest they should want to add murder to murder. When he says “into the desert,” he means beyond the Jordan.

Crowds on foot followed him from the cities. They demonstrate their love of preaching by following without pack animals, vehicles, or food. Because the Lord saw their eagerness, he acted as follows.

He went out, saw a great crowd, and had compassion on them. He came out to meet them and had compassion on them both in healing their sick and in satisfying their bodily needs. The Lord’s withdrawal from the Jews signifies that, after the Jews had lost the prophets and had dealt wickedly with and misunderstood God’s law, Christ passed over to the deserted nations, so that they might receive the word that the Jews had rejected. To those who abandon their former ways of life for God’s sake, the Lord comes and shows mercy.

When evening came, the disciples approached Jesus. The evening hour indicates the end of the ages, into which the Savior came to save the human race; or it indicates the time when the true sun set on the cross, when he had mercy on the nations through his apostles. The place was deserted, and the hour had already passed. They had neither a marketplace nor villages where they could find food.

But Jesus said to them: “They do not need to go away.” That is, they have here the one who fed the people with manna for forty years, and Moses and Elijah by his word; he has the true bread that descended from heaven.

“You give them something to eat.” The Lord urges his disciples to generosity, so that they may do good to everyone and be willing to assist their neighbors beyond their own strength. He prefers that the need for bread, once recognized by many, should produce greater thanksgiving when abundance has been supplied by him.

They answered him: “We have nothing here except five loaves and two fish.” According to the historical understanding, we believe that this took place on Mount Tabor. According to the higher interpretation, the five loaves signify the five books of Moses. According to another evangelist, the boy who had them signifies Moses; according to this account, he signifies the Jewish people, who had received the law itself from God through Moses.

The two fish are understood as the books of the Prophets and the Psalms, because before the Lord’s coming the Old Scripture consisted of these three divisions, as he himself says: “Everything written about me in the law, the prophets, and the psalms must be fulfilled.”

According to John, those five loaves are reported to have been barley loaves, because only the bare historical sense followed in them: namely, knowledge of God, the creation of the world, and the course of the passing age. Before they were blessed by the Lord, the people were fed, as it were, like brute animals on rougher food.

The two fish appropriately represent the oracles of the prophets and the sayings of the psalms. Through them he added delights to the people’s nourishment from the law, because in them the spiritual sense and the Lord’s coming are already found. And just as fish lie hidden in the waters, so the meaning in the prophets is obscure.

“Bring them here to me,” as if he had said: “Understand me in the law and the prophets.” Then, gradually increasing, the Lord displayed understanding and knowledge to the peoples: first the natural law, second the law of the letter, third the prophets, and finally the grace of the Gospel, which he also signified through earthly food. First he used five barley loaves, then seven loaves, which are not said to have been barley, signifying the teaching of the Gospel and of the Holy Spirit; finally, through bread and wine, he entrusted to them the mystery of his body and blood.

And he ordered them to recline on the grass. Grass commonly grows abundantly on these high mountains in summer, as those who have lived in our Alps have seen. Since the place was far from cities and villages, no one cut it. The grass signifies the pleasure of the flesh, which those who are nourished by foods must trample underfoot, as is related in another Gospel.

They reclined in groups of fifty or a hundred. Although Christians exist throughout the whole world and in different regions, they are nevertheless nourished by one bread, because all must embrace the one Gospel and all must be brothers and love one another. If they do not do this, they are not Catholics and do not belong to the Church, because in our faith we profess that we believe in the catholic Church—that is, the universal Church.

Through the numbers fifty and one hundred, the rest of eternal life is signified. It will be given to those who have belonged to Christ in this desert of the age and have striven to be nourished by his spiritual food.

Taking the five loaves and the two fish. Because the Lord satisfies the crowds not with new foods but with those that the apostles had, he shows that he is the one who gave the law and spoke through the prophets. Therefore he both teaches the same things and indicates how pregnant they are with mysteries, while completing what was lacking.

Looking up to heaven. He looks up to heaven in order to teach us to direct our minds toward heaven and to seek the light of knowledge there.

He blessed them. For all the Old Scripture was blessed by him and given to human beings.

He broke them. That is, he opened the understanding of the apostles so that they might understand the Scriptures; or he explained how they were to understand them.

He broke them. For from one commandment he made two for us when he said: “You have heard that it was said to the ancients: ‘You shall not kill.’ But I say to you: ‘Do not become angry.’” The same applies to the other commandments.

He gave the loaves to his disciples, and the disciples to the crowds. For he himself instructed them directly, and through the apostles he instructed the nations.

They all ate and were satisfied. He showed the apostles’ perseverance and their perfection in his teaching.

They gathered up the fragments that remained, twelve baskets full. By the remnants of the fragments are signified the more sacred mysteries, which the crowds were unable to understand. For, as the canons prescribe, profound questions should not be raised among crowds, nor should they be neglected by the perfect; rather, they should be sought by the perfect.

By the twelve baskets are signified the bodies of the twelve apostles, which were humble on the outside but filled within with great sacraments. A basket is a rustic container made of twigs for carrying things on the ground. Hence the psalm says of Joseph: “His hands served in the basket.”

The question arises: in so vast a wilderness, when only five loaves and two fish had been found, where did so many baskets come from? But it should be understood that the sick came with them and were healed. The sick, as he said above, were cured of their ailments, and the baskets remained empty.

The number of those who ate was five thousand men, besides children and women. By the five thousand are signified those who know how to use the five bodily senses well but are still involved in external works. They are rightly fed with five loaves, because they must be instructed in royal commandments. They do not yet possess the perfection possessed by those who were satisfied with four and with seven loaves.

Women and children are not counted in the number, because the female sex is unstable and changeable. Infants are still in an imperfect age; therefore they too are not worthy of being counted.

Immediately he ordered his disciples to get into the boat and go on ahead of him to the other side of the strait, until he had dismissed the crowds. Why he ordered the disciples to cross the strait after the loaves had been multiplied, the evangelist John explains: the people were going to come and try to make him king. Therefore he withdrew from the place so that they would not find him, because he, the creator of the world, did not desire worldly power. Those who possessed power had it because he had given or promised it. He was the one of whom Solomon says: “Through me kings reign.”

The Strait of Gennesaret. It is called a strait from boiling [*fervendo*].

In the evening he was there alone. He himself went up alone to the summit of the mountain to pray, while the disciples labored at sea, rowing throughout the night. The disciples were not yet perfect; therefore he allowed them to discover what they could do without him, so that they might love him more and firmly believe that he is the God of the elements.

By praying he gave us an example of what we ought to do. We are mere human beings with sins; if he, without sin, frequently devoted himself to prayer, then whenever anyone does something good or excellent, he ought to give thanks to the Lord, from whom he received the ability to do it, and pray that no pride should steal upon him because of the deed.

By refusing earthly power, he showed what his chosen ones ought to do, because no one can possess power without many sins. Therefore whoever wishes to reign gloriously with Christ should not seek power in this age. For if power were to be desired, he would either have possessed it himself, or given it to his mother, or given it to his apostles. Nor should kings contend for kingship.

For the Lord has certainly ordained who are to be kings in this age, just as he showed concerning those whom God revealed to Daniel. Whoever wishes to reign well should wait to receive it from the Lord, as David did. Although he knew that he had been anointed king, he did not seek it through bloodshed by killing the king, even though he frequently had the opportunity; nor did he kill the king’s son after his death; nor did he wage war against his own people. Rather, he fled through foreign lands and was forced to bring his father and mother into a foreign land. He awaited an inheritance alien to himself and his parents until it pleased God. For this reason he obtained not only that kingdom but many others as well.

If someone entered the kingdom by another way, without God’s will, God allowed him to rule either because of his own sin or as a scourge for his subjects, so that he might rule wickedly, as Zimri did, who killed Elah, took his kingdom, and reigned for seven days. Likewise Pekah killed Pekahiah and took his kingdom; but he himself was killed by Hoshea, and Hoshea was captured with all Israel by the Assyrians.

I believe the same concerning bishops: God has ordained those who are to be bishops in this age, not for their own sake but for the sake of their subjects, among whom there are many saints. Therefore no one needs to labor uselessly for a bishopric and enter it in sin. If he has been appointed by God, he will become one; but if he enters without God’s will, he will quickly fall. If death finds him there, he will be in hell without end, because he ended his life by robbery. Hence John says: “There is sin unto death; I do not say that anyone should pray for it.”

The boat was being tossed by the waves in the middle of the sea. The boat being tossed signifies the Church being shaken amid the storms of persecutions. The wind signifies the persecutions themselves, inflicted by unbelievers.

During the fourth watch of the night he came to them, walking on the sea. The Romans, together with their emperors and armies, divided the night into four parts for the watches that soldiers were to observe, assigning three hours to each watch. Thus when he says “the fourth watch,” he means that three had already passed and the fourth was in progress. This is also demonstrated spiritually: when the true Lucifer drew near, tranquility came to his Church, because even the emperors who had shaken the Church came to believe.

They saw him walking on the sea and thought he was a phantom. What the disciples then thought, heretics later thought, saying that Christ had not possessed a fleshly body and had been able to walk over the waters with dry feet. But just as they recognized their own error, so we recognize theirs. For not only did a true body walk on the waters, but Peter’s body did also, until he doubted. Yet just as we cannot explain how he was incorporated in the Virgin’s womb, so we cannot explain how he balanced a fleshly body upon liquid waters; nevertheless, we believe both.

They saw him walking on the sea and thought he was a phantom. They supposed that some deception was being inflicted upon them by the devil, as commonly happens to those who do not believe correctly, especially to those who believe the error of the pagans—that Neptune possesses some power over the waters and is held in hell like the other wicked beings.

They cried out from fear. A demon commonly fears the voice of a righteous man; therefore they cried out.

Immediately he spoke to them, saying: “Take courage.” First he removes fear of himself, so that they may recognize him; second, he stills the threats of the storm. There they saw two outstanding miracles: his walking on the waters, which had never been heard of before, and his calming the storms by a word.

Wind is air in motion, and it receives different names according to the various directions, such as the *subsolanus*, because it is beneath the sun, and similarly the others. There are twelve winds. Wind is so called because it is violent, so that it uproots rocks and trees, shakes the earth, and disturbs the sea.

Peter answered. Peter still did not believe that a fleshly body could walk upon the waters of the sea unless he learned this through his own experience. But just as he acted in his faith, so he acted in his steps. He believed to some extent when he left the boat, but he doubted when he saw the strong wind, and therefore began to sink.

“Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you upon the waters.” Blessed Peter was placed between hope and doubt: he recognized the voice, and yet doubted whether it was truly he.

Then the Lord said: “Come.”

Peter descended from the boat and walked upon the water. Wonderful was blessed Peter’s action: he walked upon the waters, and yet he was afraid. Nevertheless, by the fact that he walked, he recognized the Lord and sought his power against the strength of the wind.

The ship, that is, the Church in this age, was driven by winds upon the sea, because it was wearied by persecutions. This happened when the Lord withdrew bodily from it, so much so that he said: “Why, O Lord, have you withdrawn far away? Do you despise me in times of trouble?”

The Lord came to it during the fourth watch of the night, that is, when the true Lucifer was rising through the aid by which he freed the Church from the persecutions of the powerful. Peter came to him in the person of the Church, because no one can come to him unless he grants it.

But just as Peter sinks when he loses confidence, so every believer sinks when he loses confidence in the Lord. Whoever asks God for something good ought not to doubt, as James says: “Let him ask in faith, without hesitating at all.”

He took hold of him. For he is near to all who call upon him in truth—that is, he comes to their aid through his mercy.

He is rebuked for having had little faith, since he doubted in the presence of the Creator. Or faith is called little because it is thought little in this age, while it is not seen; nevertheless, it possesses great ardor and great reward after the world has been conquered.

When the Lord had entered the boat, the wind ceased. As it pleased the Lord, he gave peace to his Church.

Those who were in the boat, both the apostles and the sailors, came and worshiped him, saying: “Truly you are the Son of God.” For they recognized that no one other than the one who speaks and brings to be whatever he commands could be the creator of the sea and the winds.

When they had crossed over—that is, when they had sailed across—they came to the land of Gennesaret. From that lake, Gennesaret, the region on one side is called the region of Gennesaret in the direction of Tyre. It is evident that these people were of good will, since not only did they themselves come, but they also sent to other places and came to God. Every person ought to do the same: he should do good himself and urge his neighbor to do likewise.

They recognized the Lord because they saw him frequently, since the Lord had often lived there, or because of the fame of the signs that preceded him. They brought to him all who were sick and asked him that they might touch even the fringe of his garment. They had heard that the woman with the issue of blood had received healing from the fringes themselves, without a word from him; therefore they desired to touch the fringes. Earlier I told you that these fringes had been commanded to the Jews in order to distinguish them from other nations.

And as many as touched him were saved. Because these people possessed love of God and of their neighbor, they obtained what they asked. They possessed love of God because they eagerly received him and desired that God’s praise should spread far and wide; they possessed love of their neighbor when they wished others to be saved.

Then scribes and Pharisees came to him from Jerusalem and said: Others came from Jerusalem to hear preaching and to obtain the salvation of their souls, since religion and knowledge ought to have been greater there. The scribes and Pharisees came for the purpose of criticism, and all this was prompted by envy.

“Why do your disciples transgress the tradition of the elders? For they do not wash their hands when they eat bread.” We read in the other evangelists that they had various baptisms, that is, washings, during the day, and that they observed these, on the basis of carnal tradition and the invention of their teachers, more carefully than the things that almighty God had commanded in the law. For this reason the Lord frequently reproved them because they abandoned love of God and of neighbor, which God had strongly commended. They criticized those who observed this practice and insisted on traditions that neither harm nor help if they are not observed.

Whenever they sat in judgment with the Romans, who held that land, they ate nothing unless they had first bathed, and they ate nothing unless they had repeatedly washed their hands.

But he answered them: “Why do you also transgress God’s commandment because of your tradition? For God said: ‘Honor your father and mother,’ and, ‘Whoever curses father or mother must die.’”

“Honor” is to be understood both in speech and in every gift, as in the passage where Paul says: “Let the presbyters who labor in the word be considered worthy of double honor.” There “honor” means a gift. And in another passage: “Honor widows who are truly widows.” Therefore, when God said these things, he intended parents to be honored with food, drink, and gifts.

After fathers grew old, and sons acquired authority in the household, and it became the sons’ burden to support their father or mother, the sons afflicted them concerning food, drink, and clothing, following the tradition of the Pharisees. They told them: “The true Father is God. You do not dishonor your father or mother if you give these things to God.”

By this pretext they made fathers and mothers needy of every good, although God did not eat those things; instead, those who received them stored up useless treasures for themselves.

Or in another way: When they gave their father or mother something to eat and drink, they said to them: “What you are eating I had already devoted to the temple of the Lord.” Then the parents were terrified and said: “It is more bearable for me to die of hunger than to eat these things.”

When they say, “Whatever gift comes from me will benefit you,” it is as though they were saying: “What I give to the temple I offer on your behalf just as I offer it for myself.”

“And you have invalidated God’s commandment because of your tradition.” God did not command parents to be honored in the way you have invented for your profit. And you criticize my disciples, who harm no one if they do not wash their hands.

“Hypocrites, Isaiah rightly prophesied about you, saying: ‘What Isaiah prophesied concerning you, you do: with your lips you profess that you fulfill God’s commandments, but in heart and deed you show yourselves wicked.’”

Thus your fathers said: “Everything that the Lord has commanded we will do.”

“They worship me in vain, teaching human doctrines.” A person worships God in vain if he professes with his lips that he is a Christian but contradicts this in his conduct. Whoever says that he knows God but does not keep his commandments is a liar.

“It is not what enters the mouth that defiles a person, but what comes out of the mouth—this defiles a person.” The commandment is simple, because in God’s sight nothing that we eat causes harm, unless something is done contrary to its created nature. For every creature is good, and nothing is to be rejected that is received with thanksgiving.

In another Gospel it is written, “making common.” This word properly belonged among the Hebrews. They called the foods that the nations ate “common,” foods of which they themselves did not taste, such as hares, swine, oysters, eels, and whatever does not chew the cud or divide the hoof, or does not have scales. Whatever people ate, they called “common.” Hence he says that they make a person “common,” that is, they make him unclean.

In all our books you will find neither God nor the emperor addressed in the plural, although this is customary in our common language. Nevertheless, there is a reason why, in our land, this usage has developed of speaking to one man as though to two.

Then the disciples approached him and said, “Do you know that the Pharisees, when they heard this saying, were offended?” *Scandal* is a Greek word and may be rendered in Latin as “offense” or “stumbling block.” From this it was transferred to an offense of the mind, because just as a person stumbles on his path against some stone or snare, so likewise he stumbles when some contrary word is set against his mind or reasoning. Thus the disciples were telling the Lord that, in that tradition which the Jews held in place of the Law, and which they always observed, a contradiction had been introduced. They thought they had found something by which they could reproach him and convict him of having spoken against the Law.

Yet they investigated and discovered that the patriarchs, before the Law, had eaten many things that these people did not eat. They understood that God had not commanded the Jews to abstain from such foods for his own sake, but for this reason: if he permitted them to eat them, they would say that they were not good, because this was their custom; or they might imitate those same beasts or birds in their practices, doing certain things that do not harm beasts but would harm human beings if they were done by them. Paul confirms this concerning the same people: “Therefore he handed them over to the passions of birds, quadrupeds, and serpents.”

Because the Pharisees had accepted the saying in this way, the disciples came to the Lord as faithful and devout men and reported what they had heard.

Jesus answered and said to them, “Every planting that my heavenly Father has not planted will be uprooted.” If every other planting will be uprooted, what of Paul’s saying, “I planted”? But that planting is God’s, since he continues: “God gave the growth.” Again he says: “You are God’s cultivation; you are God’s building.” If a human being has good will, no one can uproot him from God’s cultivation; yet he himself can do so, for Jeremiah says: “I planted you as my chosen vine; how have you been turned into the bitterness of an alien vine?” No one could uproot it unless it had itself given its consent.

“Leave them: they are blind guides of the blind.” Leave them; let them remain in their errors, and do not attach yourselves to them. This concerns those who, after being frequently corrected by their brothers and by the Church, refuse to return, as he says elsewhere: “Let him be to you as a pagan and a tax collector.” Paul likewise says: “Avoid a heretical person after the first and second correction.”

They are blind in their spiritual eyes, and those who attend to their teaching are themselves blind. “But if the blind lead the blind, both will fall into a pit.” If a blind man wishes to lead a blind man, both fall into a pit. Likewise, if a foolish person wishes to teach another foolish person, just as he himself remains in error, so the other also will be in error, until they fall into hell.

[Col. 1389A] Peter answered and said, “Explain this parable to us.” Peter thought that the Lord’s simple statement was a parable.

Again he said to them, “Do you not understand that whatever enters the mouth goes into the stomach and is expelled into the privy?” The Apostle says: “Every creature is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving.” Some heretics criticized this statement, as though it were not naturally expressed, because the nourishment of food passes through the pores into the limbs of the body. Just as food is digested in the privy, so the bodily fluids are also deposited there. Therefore he spoke in this way as the creator of the body.

“Those things that proceed from the mouth come out of the heart,” that is, murders, adulteries, and the rest.

*Murder* (*homicidium*) is composed of *homo*, “human being,” and *caedes*, “slaughter.” For whoever commits slaughter against a human being is called a murderer.

*Adultery* is the violation of a spouse. It is so called as though “adulterous” were understood, when either a woman or a man, abandoning the lawful partner, seeks another’s bed. It is a greater sin than fornication, because it is a sin against three [parties]. Fornication, however, is committed in many ways; and a man can even fornicate with his own wife if he does not use her lawfully. Every sexual pollution, except with one’s lawful wife, is fornication and a criminal vice.

*Thefts.* Theft is the secret taking of another’s property. It is said to derive from *furtum*, “darkness,” because it is done in obscurity. Sacrilege is also theft.

*False testimonies* occur when someone, either alone or together with others, accuses a brother in order to bring about some condemnation. When several people are involved, the sin is all the worse. Such people resemble Judas, who handed the Lord over to death.

*Blasphemies.* [Col. 1389C] Blasphemies are slanders and evil speeches, when someone attempts to defame God and his neighbor by his evil words.

All these vices are also committed spiritually. Whoever entices someone to sin kills both himself and the other. He commits adultery against the soul who abandons God or God’s justice for gold or some other thing. He commits fornication against the soul when he covets his neighbor’s property. He commits theft against the soul who withholds the truth by remaining silent, or lends an ear to someone slandering his neighbor.

These and similar things defile a person before God and render him abominable to God. In the Lord’s statement, “They come out of the heart,” it is shown that the seat of the soul is in the heart, not in the brain. *Heart* derives from the Greek *kardia* (“heart”), and is said to come from *cura*, “care.” It has two arteries, of which the left side has more blood and the right more spirit. Hence a person who suffers paralysis on the right side lives longer than one who suffers it on the left.

It is also shown that the devil can be an assistant and instigator of our thoughts, but cannot be their author; nor can he know the hidden things of the heart except insofar as he can recognize them from our movements.

And Jesus departed from there and withdrew into the region of Tyre and Sidon. He left the scribes and Pharisees, who always wanted to find fault, and proceeded to the region of Tyre and Sidon.

Tyre was a city of the Phoenicians, founded by Phoenicians; Sidon likewise was founded by them. They were built in the sea, but through continuous siege and the accumulation of an embankment, when the Lord came into the world they were connected with the mainland. For Nebuchadnezzar besieged them and piled up a great embankment with ships, so that he could stand outside the wall, which previously he could not do. He first began with Sidon after capturing Judea; Tyre he besieged for three years. Meanwhile the inhabitants removed everything of value from the city, as Ezekiel says; he too describes its glory.

After Nebuchadnezzar, Alexander besieged them and joined them to the mainland. Tyre is called “narrowness,” because it was surrounded by the sea; Sidon means “fishy,” because fish were abundant there. They had been promised by the Lord to the children of Israel and assigned to them by lot, but the children of Israel were unable to take them.

And behold, a woman came out from those borders. The Lord did not enter the territory of the Tyrians, but walked nearby. She cried out, saying to him—

This woman is called a Canaanite because her ancestry came from the Canaanites. Their land had been promised to the Jews, but because of their sins they were unable to drive them out.

This woman possessed three virtues. She had faith, because she believed that the Lord could do this. She had humility, by which she did not confess herself equal to the dogs, but to the puppies. She had patience, because whenever she was rejected she persevered.

The simple history edifies the hearer, so that we may have right faith in God, believing that we shall obtain whatever we ask, if we ask for what concerns the salvation of the soul. Let us also do this with humility, because God does not despise a contrite and humbled heart. Let us likewise have patience with perseverance.

According to the allegory, this woman signifies the Church from the Gentiles, which was to be converted to the Lord. She came out from her borders, that is, separated from her former way of life and former vices, and entered the Church of Christ.

Her daughter is the soul of each individual among those peoples, who was tormented by a demon before they believed in God.

But he did not answer her a word. He did not do this out of pride, but so as not to give the Jews an opportunity to reject his word and preaching, since he himself had said: “Do not go into the way of the Gentiles.” He also did this to display the woman’s patience and perseverance for the instruction of those who saw and heard.

And the disciples approached and pleaded with him, saying, “Send her away, because she cries out after us.” They urged him because they wished to be rid of her persistence.

“I was sent only to the sheep that had perished from the house of Israel.” This does not mean that he was not sent to the Gentiles, but that he was sent first to Israel because of the election of the patriarchs and the privilege that people had always possessed with God. When that people rejected him, he would then send him to the Gentiles.

But she came and worshiped him, saying, “Lord, help me.” This is how we must be persistent in prayers and persevere. At first she called him the Son of David, but now she calls him Lord and worships him as Lord.

“It is not good to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs.” Now the Lord speaks to her mystically, and that bread is the divine word given through Moses and the prophets. For Scripture is a table, which ought to have supplied the Jews with the bread of life; but crumbs fell from it because the Jews neglected its spiritual meaning. The crumbs of the children are the inner mysteries of the Scriptures, by which the hearts of the humble are accustomed to be nourished.

Therefore this woman was not asking for crusts, but for crumbs from the bread of the spiritual children—the marrow of the meaning that the Jews did not care about.

Thus the Lord says: “It is not right to take the teaching from the Jewish children and give it to you dogs, since, because of idolatry, blood, and the corpses of the dead to which you are devoted, you are dogs.”

But she said, “Yes, Lord.” The Lord had said, “It is not good.” She replied that it was good, and offered the example of human beings: just as, when people eat, crumbs fall from the table for the dogs, so it is right that the Jews should be lords because of the patriarchs and because of you, who were born from them, while we should be not great dogs, using the primitive form of the word, but little dogs, expressed with the diminutive. We do not ask for the whole grace of the teaching or its more secret mysteries, because we are not worthy, but for the more open and simpler commandments.

Then Jesus answered and said to her, “O woman, great is your faith; let it be done for you as you wish.”

O woman worthy of praise, whom the Lord himself praised! The apostles are often criticized as having little faith, whereas you are said to have great faith. Let anyone who can imitate her, and it will happen to him as it was said to her: “Let it be done for you as you wish.” Would that we all might ask worthily and thus obtain what we seek.

And her daughter was healed from that hour. The Church from the Gentiles, praying for her own members, is heard, and souls are daily healed from demonic diseases: pagans are renewed in baptism, and sinners return to innocence through confession, the distribution of alms, and constant prayer.

And when Jesus had crossed over from there, he came beside the Sea of Galilee. From the place where the Lord had previously fled so that he would not be made king, he returned again, understanding that the hearts of those who had been filled with the loaves had changed. Just as an eagle or hen calls its young to fly, he does not cease to preach here and there and to provide the nourishment of the word.

And he went up onto a mountain and was sitting there. This mountain was a beloved place for the Lord, because it was removed from the crowds of cities, secluded, and suitable for teaching and praying.

And great crowds came to him. There was no one in the whole world who taught in this way or did such things; therefore they flocked to him so eagerly, bringing with them the mute, the blind, the lame, the weak, and many others.

The syllable *o* shares a sound with the diphthong *au*, as in *lotus* for *lautus*; similarly, *clo* is used in place of *clau*, as *clodus* for *claudus* [the transmitted reading is uncertain]. We must consider why he says “the weak” and afterward says “many others.” For, as blessed Jerome says, the Latin language does not have a specific name for each infirmity, as the Greeks do; therefore he used *debiles* (“weak”) in our rustic language.

Someone who is called *luscus* (“one-eyed” or “squinting”) in our language is called *killos* in Greek. When the translator encountered this word in Greek, he had no other Latin term and therefore said *debiles*. In the account of the healings he listed mute people speaking, blind people seeing, and lame people walking. He passed over that word because he could not find a term in the proper usage of the Latin language with which to express it.

But Jesus, calling his disciples, said, “I have compassion on the crowd, because they have remained with me for three days.” In this deed both natures of the Lord are shown: the divine, by which he performs the miracle, and the human, by which he has compassion on the crowd.

“And I do not want to send them away fasting, lest they faint on the way.” That he satisfied four thousand people with seven loaves is his clemency: “The merciful and compassionate one gave food to those who fear him.”

Mystically, he shows that we cannot cross the road of this world safely in any other way unless we are filled with the word of our Redeemer. By that earlier event, which you heard about above, in which the five loaves satisfied the crowd, the spiritual nourishment is signified that he provided for his faithful from the Old Testament. This present event signifies the satiety that he produces from his Gospels in those who believe in him. In that letter of the Old Testament, spiritual grace is revealed to believers.

Both nourishments are celebrated on one mountain, because there is one giver, and both nourishments invite us to one banquet, which the same one who gave this has prepared for us.

When he says, “They have remained with me for three days,” this may refer either to his preaching or to the healing of his sick followers. Spiritually, the crowd remains with the word for three days when all believers in the Holy Trinity await forgiveness of sins from him; or the crowd remains with the Lord for three days when, in thought, speech, and deed, they take care not to offend God.

“I do not want to send them away, lest they faint on the way,” because although the peoples believe in him, they stumble on the road amid so many adversities unless they are frequently consoled and refreshed by the admonition of the divine word.

“How many loaves do you have?” He asks about what is not hidden from him, so that others, once they know the miracle, may be edified. He who performed the miracles ordained that there should then be five loaves and now seven, because of the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, with which believers are filled.

They are not said to have been barley loaves, because he proclaimed the revealed glory of the Lord in the Gospel, which the Old Testament had veiled.

“And a few small fish.” These signify the other books of the New Testament: Paul’s Letters, the Acts of the Apostles, their Apocalypse, and the remaining books; or the saints who lived at that time, whose life and passion Scripture contains. Chosen and lifted up, as it were, from the depths of this world, consecrated by heavenly blessing, they provide nourishment when they serve as examples for us in doing good.

And he commanded the crowd to recline on the ground. At the other meal they reclined on grass, because those ancient peoples were commanded only to trample upon carnal pleasures; in the Gospel, those who are perfect are commanded to renounce all earthly things together with their pleasures.

And taking the seven loaves, giving thanks, he broke them and gave them to the disciples, and the disciples gave them to the crowds. The Lord wished to instruct his apostles and, through them, to have the crowds instructed.

His giving of thanks shows how greatly he rejoices in the salvation of the human race, and teaches us to give thanks for all the gifts of life that have been bestowed. From this passage, or from others, the faithful have preserved the custom of blessing food and chanting a verse of a psalm, although that people already had this custom.

The breaking signifies the opening of the mysteries by which the people were to be instructed for eternal salvation.

And they ate and were satisfied. They eat and are satisfied with the Lord’s loaves and fish when they hear the Lord’s words and, looking upon the saints who preceded them, stir themselves to heavenly desires.

And what remained of the fragments they took up, seven baskets. By these fragments are understood the higher commandments of perfection, which the multitude of the people cannot understand or keep, such as many precepts concerning divinity and the preservation of virginity, or the abandonment of everything—things not commanded to the perfect and willing, but displayed as examples.

That there are seven baskets signifies the grace of the Holy Spirit, which the prophet proclaims under the number seven.

By the seven baskets the chosen preachers are represented. For just as baskets are made of reeds and palms, so they firmly and tirelessly preserve the memory of their Creator in their hearts; and they flourish, as it were, when day by day they breathe out a new desire for the love of their Creator. Of them it is said: “The righteous will flourish like a palm tree.”

There are also small baskets, such as those that we see carried in basilicas with offerings; there are large ones, capable of holding three or four measures of grain; and there are also those in which the sick can be carried, as happened there.

Those who ate numbered about four thousand, so that by this number they might show that they had been fed with the nourishment of the Gospel. Likewise, women and children are not included in the number in this account, because of their changeability and imperfection.

He went up into the boat and came to the land of Magadan. Mark says “Dalmanutha.” The teachers say either that it was one place with two names, or that a scribal error occurred in Mark.

And the Pharisees approached and, testing him, asked him to show them a sign from heaven. John relates what sort of sign they were seeking, as has already been said above: after the feeding with the five loaves, they likewise asked him either to feed the people with manna or to make thunder.

But neither of those two signs would come from another heaven, but from this one where the birds fly, from which we speak of “the birds of heaven.” Thunder, however, is produced by wind and water. When the wind has enclosed itself in a cloud, it seeks an opening through which to burst out; when it tears through the cloud, it makes a sound and creates fire. These arise together, but the light is seen first because it is brighter and the sense of sight is keener than that of hearing: we see farther than we hear.

The fire of lightning has greater power to penetrate because it is subtler than ours, that is, than the fire available for our use. Sometimes punishment is inflicted upon human beings through it, just as through the other elements.

They had also seen signs from those elements when the Lord had calmed the sea and the winds. But those who ask for something while testing the Lord do not deserve to receive it, just as those people did not.

“When evening comes, you say, ‘It will be fair weather, for the sky is red.’” This commonly happens. If the evening sun has no rain around it in the cloud, but the cloud is red, there will be no rain the following day.

“And in the morning”—the words “you say” are understood—“Today there will be a storm,” for the gloomy sky glows red. When the eastern clouds are red, there will be rain that day.

In the daytime the Lord says to the Jews: “You know how to judge the face of the sky, but you cannot recognize the signs of the times.” You have the custom of noting rains and fair weather, but from the prophetic oracles you cannot recognize the signs of the coming of the Son of God.

“An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign, and no sign will be given to it except the sign of the prophet Jonah.” This has already been discussed above; it is enough to say here that, in the sign of the Lord’s death, a sign was given from heaven when the sun covered the sky with a dark cloud; a sign was given from the earth when an earthly body rose; and a sign was given from hell when its gates were broken and many thousands of saints came out.

And leaving them, he went away. At that time the Lord was abandoning the unbelievers, and even today he does the same invisibly. He abandons unbelievers and the proud, and rests in those who tremble at his words.

And when his disciples had come across the strait, they had forgotten to take bread. Again, after feeding the crowds, he withdrew from that place, lest the people should have the same intention as before.

That he says the disciples had forgotten to take bread shows that neither the Lord nor the disciples were greatly concerned with earthly food. Or it was because bread was abundant in that land, and the people supplied the Lord and his disciples with what pertained to their nourishment.

How had they forgotten, when it is said that they had taken up seven baskets? They had left that food for the poor. They had only one loaf when they crossed the lake. They had one earthly loaf and another spiritual one, of which he had said, “I am the living bread that came down from heaven.” Therefore they did not need to seek an earthly loaf.

He said to them, “Watch and beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees.” As the Lord always taught his disciples so that they would not remain idle or cease from good works while empty of them, he commanded them to guard themselves against the teaching of the Pharisees, intending “leaven” to mean teaching.

The teaching of the Pharisees was to place the decrees of the divine Law below human traditions, or to preach the commandments of the Lord in words while opposing them by their deeds.

In another Gospel he also commands that they beware of the leaven of Herod. The leaven of Herod is adultery, murder, and a pretense of religion. *Leaven* is named from *fervor* (“boiling” or “fermentation”), because it cannot be contained for more than an hour; as it grows, it exceeds its bounds.

But they were thinking among themselves, saying, “It is because we did not take bread.” The Lord was speaking spiritually, but the disciples understood him carnally. They thought that he knew they had no bread, so that, when they found flour, they would not leaven it with the leaven of the Pharisees.

Knowing this, Jesus said to them, “Why are you thinking among yourselves, you of little faith, because you have no bread? I am speaking neither about that leaven nor about that bread of which you are thinking. Do you not yet understand, nor remember the five loaves for the five thousand people?”

When he says, “You do not yet understand,” he requires spiritual understanding, because everyone who saw the miracle understood it at the literal level. He wants them to understand spiritually those feedings, the bread, the fish, and the leaven. For if leaven is mixed into flour, what seemed small grows into something larger; so bad teaching grows more than good teaching, as the Apostle says: “A little leaven corrupts the whole lump.”

Likewise, if heretical teaching has crept into someone’s heart even to a small degree, it quickly perverts him. For every person is shaped more quickly toward evil than toward good.

Jesus came into the region of Caesarea Philippi. This was the territory of Philip, the brother of Herod whose wife Herod had taken. Jesus came into the region of his kingdom, to a place called Caesarea.

Philip himself rebuilt a certain city in honor of Tiberius Caesar and called it Caesarea Philippi, in honor both of Tiberius, under whom he ruled, and of himself. Another city had already been built there under his own name, Tiberias.

It is a province of Phoenicia at the foot of Lebanon, which has great cedars. There are two springs there, Jor and Dan; they flow together from a distance and form the river Jordan. The city itself is now called Paneas.

There is another Caesarea, which Herod rebuilt in honor of Octavian. He called it Caesarea; it had previously been called Strato’s Tower.

When he came to this place—and, as Luke says, when he was away from the crowds and the twelve disciples had been with him on the way—he asked them, saying, “Who do people say that the Son of Man is?”

I have explained above why he is called the Son of Man: it was customary among that people to call a prophet, a distinguished man, or a man of God “a prophet” or “a son of Adam,” that is, “a son of man.” Hence Ezekiel is frequently called “son of man.”

Therefore he says, “Who do they say the Son of Adam is?” He does not say, “Who do they say that I am?” so that he would not appear to be asking about himself boastfully.

He calls them “people,” those who speak falsely about the Son of God, because “every human being is a liar.” But those who hold the truth about the Son of God are, as it were, above human beings.

And they said—

In this passage the name “Christ” was first applied to the Lord Christ by blessed Peter and the other apostles through the revelation of the Holy Spirit. Just as Joseph was commanded, speaking from the person of God, to call him Jesus, so, speaking from the person of the Holy Spirit, it was ordained that he be called Christ through blessed Peter and the other apostles.

It should be noted that he does not address the Lord in the manner prescribed by secular learning among us, but says, “You are,” as the ancients are found to have used in old books. Romulus and Remus, for example, are said to have been two brothers of such great harmony that neither wished to possess anything without the other, and they called and possessed everything in common, just as monks do now. From this practice the custom grew up in this Gaul of addressing the Lord in the plural.

Some said John the Baptist, as though he himself ought to rise again, because he had preached for only a short time.

Others said Elijah, because it is written in the book of his prophecy: “I have appointed you a prophet among the nations.” Since his death is not read of in Scripture, they said that he would come to preach to the nations.

Finally, their opinion about Jeremiah will prove false, because his book shows how he prophesied to the nations—to Moab, the Idumeans, and the Babylonians. Therefore what had been said to him was fulfilled: “I have appointed you a prophet among the nations.” We also have it written that the Jews stoned him in Egypt because he prophesied that Nebuchadnezzar would come there after the Jews, who had fled there out of fear of him.

Or one of the prophets, any one of those from earlier times.

But he said to them, “And you, who do you say that I am?” As though he were saying plainly: separating them from the people and indicating that they had become children of God by adoption, he says, “You, who are gods, who do you say that I am?”

They were rightly called gods, because God dwelled in them and they heard the word of God every day. The psalmist calls those to whom the word of God came “gods,” saying: “I said, You are gods.”

We must also consider the distinction in the way the Lord, speaking of his humility to the disciples, calls himself the Son of Man and does not call himself the Son of God. In the Gospel he calls himself the Son of Man much more frequently than the Son of God. He does all this to form us in humility.

Peter answered him. Peter answered for them all, because he had already been appointed head of the apostles. His answer was the answer of all the apostles, since they too had been questioned. “Who do you say that I am?” And what the Lord said to Peter, he said to all the apostles.

“You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.”

“You are the Christ.” If others were called *Christs* by designation because they were to govern the people for a time, you are more truly the Christ, because you are the king of the whole earth.

You are the Son of the living God, who are God essentially, unlike those others who are called gods but are not, because they are the works of human hands and neither see nor hear. You are the Son of that God who is worshiped and honored by the Jews, of whom it is said: “God is known in Judah; his name is great in Israel.”

Why should people themselves err concerning you, when I declare what I believe about you? You are the Christ of God and the Son of God, the Son of that God before whose ark Dagon lay with his hands and feet cut off.

Jesus answered and said to him, “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jona.” *Bar* is Syriac for “son”; *Jona* means “dove.” He is blessed because he is a son of the Holy Spirit, simple like a dove and shrewd like a serpent.

And he is blessed for this reason: “For flesh and blood has not revealed this to you.” That is, no living human being composed of flesh and blood has revealed it, but my Father—the very one whom you have confessed. He is the living Father beyond comparison, my Father who is in heaven, and I also am with him, together with the Holy Spirit, whose spiritual son you are.

The Lord Jesus knew what the apostles believed about him, what they thought, and what they would answer. But, in order to teach us humility, he was pleased to be revealed invisibly to the apostles in their hearts together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, to be heard in the world through their confession, and to reward a worthy confession with a worthy recompense. Thus all who, to the end of the world, agree with and confess this confession may be certain that they will share in its reward.

“And I say to you that you are Peter.” You said, “You are the Christ,” and I say to you that you are Peter. I am the Christ, anointed with invisible oil by the Father, the king of Christians, and you are their foundation.

Blessed are you, Simon—that is, “obedient”—because you are the son of the dove; and because you are Peter, that is, “firm.”

“And upon this rock I will build my Church.” Upon this firmness of faith that you have confessed I will build my Church, and upon me I will build you together with my whole Church.

“And the gates of hell will not prevail against it.” Whoever strives to belong to my Church and to those who have confessed in this way will not be overcome by the gates of hell, so that they could drag him to themselves, as he says elsewhere: “No one can snatch my sheep from my hand.”

Or the gates of hell signify sins, vices, or the teaching of heretics, by which deceived people are led to Tartarus. There are many gates of hell, but none prevail against the Church, because whoever holds the faith of Christ perfectly in his heart will, with God as his protector, very easily conquer whatever temptation occurs outwardly.

Whoever has departed from the Church in faith or conduct must be believed to have laid his foundation not upon rock but upon sand.

“And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven.” The keys of the kingdom of heaven signify the knowledge by which one discerns, and the power by which the worthy are to be received into the kingdom and the unworthy excluded.

“And whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven.” We rightly believe that this was granted both to Peter and to all the apostles and their successors who hold the same office in the Church. For after his passion he appeared to them and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them; whose sins you retain are retained.”

Thus, when they have recognized the circumstances of sinners whom they know truly to repent and not to wish to return again to the vomit of sin, they should judge them worthy of absolution and console them against the fear of eternal death. But those whom they see ending their lives in serious sins they should declare destined for everlasting punishments, as the Lord himself indicates, saying: “If he does not listen to the Church, let him be to you as a pagan and a tax collector.”

A comparison is offered from the lepers in Leviticus. Just as the priest was commanded to examine the leper, so that by his judgment it might be decided who was a leper and who was not, so bishops and priests in the Church ought to bind those whom they see to be lepers in soul because of serious sins.

When they see or hear that the leprosy has been removed—that is, that sins have been removed through worthy works of repentance and confession—they should then absolve them.

We have already explained this through the example of Lazarus: he should strive to absolve the one whom the Lord has raised in soul. For if the disciples had loosed Lazarus before the Lord raised him, they would have displayed stench rather than power.

Although this commission appears to be spoken to Peter alone, it is so because he spoke for all, the answer was given to all in him, and he confessed with true faith and followed with true love. It was also done so that all believers might know with certainty that whoever separates himself from the unity of the faith will neither obtain forgiveness of sins nor be able to enter the gate of the kingdom of heaven.

Therefore let us imitate blessed Peter in confessing the true faith, so that we may believe with our heart and confess with our mouth. Let us imitate his simplicity, since he is called the son of the dove. Let us also strive to equal him in steadfastness for conquering worldly pleasures, so that we may deserve to reach the one with whom he now is.

Then he instructed his disciples not to tell anyone that he was the Christ. We read above that he sent his disciples to preach and commanded them to announce his coming to the people; now he commands them not to call him Christ. The distinction must be understood. Above, he ordered them to announce that the one who would proclaim the word of salvation to them and heal their sick had come, so that they might come to him. Afterwards, when he saw who made themselves worthy to know the more hidden mysteries, these mysteries would be disclosed to them together with the apostles; but those who made themselves unworthy would depart empty-handed with the Pharisees, as he himself said: “Do not cast your pearls.”

In the same way, in this passage he commands that they should not publicly announce him as Christ, lest the benefit of the cross be delayed and the world not be redeemed. Or there was another reason: “Christ” was a great name among that people, just as “Caesar” and “Augustus” are among us. He therefore did not wish that name to be publicly proclaimed about him, lest it cause scandal among the Jews because he was claiming royal power. Hence afterwards the Jews accused him before Pilate; nevertheless, by writing it down, Pilate unwillingly confirmed that he was king of the Jews.

This is understood because kings were called “christs,” and he gave his followers an example, so that they would not seek to be called great among the peoples. “Christ” is not the Savior’s proper name, but a common designation of dignity and power. “Jesus Christ” is the Savior’s proper name.

From that time Jesus began to show his disciples that he must go to Jerusalem and suffer many things from the elders, the scribes, and the chief priests. Now he explains why he had commanded that he not reveal himself as Christ among the people. It is as though he openly said: “When you see me rising from the dead after my Passion—for it is of no benefit to preach now that I shall appear for a little while, be mocked, and be crucified and scourged—” He also foretells his Passion, so that they may doubt less concerning his resurrection.

It must also be noted that the one who would suffer these things, the Son of God, is the Son of Man, because the divinity remained impassible during the Passion. The one who was born of holy Mary suffered.

And Peter took him aside and began to rebuke him, saying:

Blessed Peter, because of the excessive faith and love that he had toward our God, when he heard the insults and death that the Lord foretold he would suffer in Jerusalem, took the Lord aside secretly, lest he appear to rebuke his teacher before the others. Moved by his desire for the Lord’s happiness, he began to say to him: “God forbid, Lord; this shall never happen to you.” That is, “May what you are saying be far from you.” Or, as the Greek has it, ἱλεώθητί σοι, that is, “Be propitious to yourself.”

For he did not wish to destroy his confession, and he thought he would lose the Savior’s reward, which he had heard: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah,” and the rest that he had heard. Nor did he think it possible that the Son of God could be killed. “This shall never happen to you”: “My ears cannot receive these things, nor can my heart believe them.”

But turning, he said to Peter: “Get behind me, Satan.” Satan means “adversary.” “Get behind me”: follow my will, and do not be an adversary concerning those things that I have ordained with the Father. You are a disciple; therefore you must follow, not teach.

This sentence is not like the one that the Lord addressed to the devil. To the devil he said, “Go, Satan,” with “into the abyss” understood. To this man, however, he said, “Go behind me,” that is, “Imitate me, so that you may will the same things that I do.”

It is not surprising that the Lord said such things to Peter after the great blessedness he had spoken of above, because blessed Peter was not yet perfect. He was still going to deny him, and all those things had not been granted by God for the present but promised for the future: “I will give you,” not “I give you,” and the rest.

“For you do not understand the things that are God’s.” You do not know God’s plan, because I have determined to redeem the world through my death. You advise me about the things that belong to human beings when you advise me to avoid death, because mere human beings ordinarily fear death.

Then Jesus said to his disciples:

He spoke neither these words nor those described above to the crowds, but to his disciples, because these matters were not to be preached to the imperfect, but to the perfect.

“If anyone wishes to come after me”—that is, if anyone wishes to imitate me, as disciples ought to imitate their teacher. After foretelling his own insults and death, he arms his followers so that they may prepare themselves to endure the same things.

“Let him deny himself.” Let him cease to be what he has hitherto been through an evil way of life under the tradition of the Pharisees, and begin to be new through my admonition. Let him deny in his actions that he is the old man, who is corrupted according to his desires, and begin to be the new Adam, who is renewed day by day in the knowledge of God.

“And let him take up his cross and follow me.” “Cross” derives from *cruciatus*, “torment,” and by the cross the mortification of vices is understood. Just as one who is crucified dies to this world, so one who wishes to follow Christ must mortify the passions of his members.

The cross is taken up in two ways: either when the body is afflicted through abstinence, or when the soul is distressed through compassion for one’s neighbor. Paul cries out the same thing in other words, saying: “Mortify your members that are upon the earth: anger, fornication, avarice,” and the rest.

He showed us an example in himself when he said: “I chastise my body and bring it into servitude, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should become reprobate.”

Behold, we have heard about the cross of his body; let us now inquire about compassion for one’s neighbor. For he says: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not inflamed?”

Whoever wishes to save his life will lose it.

Whoever wishes to save his life in such a way that he is unwilling to give it for Christ will lose it when he ought instead to possess it more fully.

But whoever loses his life for my sake will save it.

Whoever does not fear handing over his life for my sake in this world will save it in the world to come.

It is as though one were saying to a farmer: “If you want to save your grain, lose it in the ground; for if you keep it in the granary, it will perish, but if you cast it into the earth, you will receive twice as much.”

This was then said to those who were living amid the persecutions of the pagans. If we wish to be like the martyrs, we must patiently endure the evils of our neighbors and the persecutions of wicked Christians, because we shall not be companions of the martyrs unless we share in their sufferings, at least in some measure.

But whoever loses his life for my sake—or, as it is written in another Gospel, “for the sake of my Gospel”—will find it, either in the sense that we have stated above, or because our life means the pleasures of this world. Whoever denies himself the delights and pleasures of this world for the love of God will receive in the eternal world things such as “eye has not seen, nor has it entered into the heart of man,” which the Lord has prepared for those who love him.

[Col. 1399D]

For what does it profit a man if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul?

What did it profit those emperors who possessed this world for twenty years—or Octavian for fifty-three years—when for eight hundred years now he has been lying in hell? Would it not have been better for him to be the companion of poor Lazarus than now to be the companion of the devil?

All their honors passed away like shadows and like a dream. Frequently they were received by consuls with golden chariots and golden shields; afterwards they were received naked and guilty by the blackest demons and bound in eternal fire.

What is worse, many Christians will go with them—Christians who ought to know the way of truth.

[Col. 1400B]

Or what exchange can a man give for his soul?

A man ought to give no exchange for his soul. But, what is worse, there are many who prefer the body to the soul, temporal things to eternal things. They do not think about the soul or everlasting life, but about earthly honors and perishable things, and they sell themselves in order to do evil, as is said of Ahab: “He sold himself to do evil.”

They frequently suffer the fate of Balaam. Although God had forbidden him to go and curse the people, he was led by the desire for payment and repeatedly questioned God, even though God is not like a human being who can lie. But because he made his request so importunately, he received what God did not wish, and it did him no good.

So many, when they enter the church, sing the words of another with their tongues, while in their minds they think about honors—and they do so for many days. But God looks upon the heart and sees what the heart prays for. The words spoken by the tongue are another person’s words, unless the tongue sings what the heart conceals out of shame.

When God therefore sees that we more frequently desire something in our hearts and deeds, he angrily grants what is against his will and against our salvation. In this way a person gives an exchange for his soul when he chooses earthly things and neglects eternal ones.

For the Son of Man is going to come in the glory of his Father with his angels.

Because he had foretold exceedingly harsh things about himself and his followers, he now moderates them and shows for what reason they must endure such things: namely, because he is going to come—that is, the Son of Man himself, in the glory of the Father—to judge the living and the dead, because the Father has given all judgment to the Son.

And then he will repay each according to his works.

Then, if you endure bravely and patiently, you will receive eternal reward, while those who trouble you will receive eternal torments.

Amen I say to you: There are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom.

The apostles might have secretly thought and said: “These things he promises us will happen at the end of the world,” and in this way they might have fallen away from hope. Now he promises something nearer at hand: namely, that some of them will not taste death until they have briefly tasted it, as it were in advance.

“Until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom”—that is, in the royal glory in which he will be seen by all the elect after the judgment has taken place. At the judgment he will be seen in the form of a servant, as it was said when he ascended: “He will come in the same way as you saw him going.” Both the good and the wicked will see him whom they despised, as it is written: “Every eye shall see him, and those who pierced him.”

The unjust will see him as terrifying, the just as gentle, although he will appear in one and the same form.

Or his kingdom may be understood as the present Church, which many saw established in the flesh before they had tasted death, as John, who writes to the seven churches, so that it might be a consolation for them to see already in part the world that would believe in him.
