For the disciples were still inexperienced, and it was necessary to promise them something in the present by which they might be strengthened in the present and more powerfully consoled in the future.

Or this may be understood of his Transfiguration, in which those three saw him as though in his kingdom—that is, in the royal dignity in which he will be seen at the judgment.

## CHAPTER XXXVI  
### On the Transfiguration of the Lord

And after six days Jesus took Peter, James, and his brother John.

After six days—that is, after he had spoken the things you heard above, that some would not taste death. Luke says truly eight days, but Luke includes the first and last day, whereas these two count the days that were in between.

The Lord chose these three so that they might strengthen the others during the time of his Passion. The others were not yet sufficiently perfect to be able to see such things. Indeed, even these three fell down and were greatly afraid.

These three were separated from the others for definite reasons. Peter was chosen because he was destined to be the shepherd of the Church and to be sent to the Romans, who ruled the world. John was chosen because he was destined to speak of Christ’s divinity to the world in a loftier manner and to be sent among the Greeks, who were wiser than all the nations. James was chosen because he was destined to be the first of the apostles to suffer martyrdom for Christ. For this reason they were called “sons of thunder”: they were the ones who were to hear the voice of which he now speaks.

This is shown figuratively: many are called, but few are chosen.

He continues:

He leads them up onto a mountain.

That is, Tabor in Galilee, which is interpreted as “coming light.” The interpretation is fitting, because there they were frequently enlightened by the true light, as also on this occasion.

A high mountain.

That is, exceedingly high, like our Alps in Burgundy, where heat can do little harm even in summer, when this Transfiguration took place.

Apart.

That is, apart from the other disciples. It is an adverb indicating separation.

And he was transfigured before them.

He was transfigured into another form. He did not lose his substance, nor did he assume a spiritual or airy body; rather, he made the same substance glorious, as follows.

And his face shone like the sun.

He appeared to the apostles in the form that only the pure eyes of the saints will see after the judgment has been completed. When he said “like the sun,” he could not rise higher in his comparison than what a human being knows with bodily eyes.

And his garments became white like snow.

From this we can know that it was the very same body, because the garments were the same. Of them it is said that they became white like snow, or, as it is written elsewhere, “such as no fuller on earth can make.”

It is evident that they did not lose their substance, but were clothed from above with radiance. The garments of Christ figuratively signify his saints, of whom Paul says: “For all of you who were baptized in Christ have put on Christ.” They shine now in the present, but more brightly in the future, because when he appears we shall be like him.

Of them it is said: “Such as no fuller can make on earth.”

That fuller is the one of whom the Psalmist says: “You shall wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow,” because he cannot grant to the saints what he promised to grant in heaven.

And behold, Moses and Elijah appeared.

Through Moses and Elijah he shows the lawgiver and the outstanding one among the prophets, because the law was given by him and prefigured him; and the prophets prophesied under his inspiration and sang of everything that was destined to happen concerning him.

Figuratively, through Moses are signified the saints who, having already tasted death, were reigning with the Lord. Through Elijah, who is said still to be alive, those elect who will be found in the flesh are represented. For, as Paul says: “The dead who are in Christ will rise first; then those found alive will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet Christ in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord.”

Speaking with him.

That is, announcing beforehand his departure, which he was about to accomplish in Jerusalem.

Origen says that Moses appeared with the tablets on which the written law was inscribed, and that Elijah came with a fiery chariot; from this the apostles recognized them. It was fitting that, appearing with the Lord in charity, they should appear both terrible and splendid, as though they were saying:

“Do not think it harsh to suffer for Christ, because I foretold this through the law, and he through prophecy, at his command.”

Lord, it is good for us to be here; if you wish, let us make three tabernacles here.

Because Peter had seen things delightful, if only for a moment, he wanted to remain there forever, so that he would not descend to the earth, where he knew for certain that Christ would be crucified.

He did not know what he was saying, and he had forgotten that the Lord promised the saints a kingdom in heaven, not on earth, and that no one surrounded with mortal flesh can enjoy immortality unless he has first tasted death.

“Let us make three tabernacles here.”

Three tabernacles are not to be made, but one, because although the Trinity is to be believed, God is one in substance, and Christ has one sheepfold, which is the one catholic Church.

While he was still speaking, behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them.

Because Peter wanted to build tabernacles, the Lord showed him that he could have the same shelter that he had provided for Moses and his people for forty years. Or this may refer to the very common manner in which God speaks to his elect through a cloud, as to Job and to Moses himself, since the cloud signifies gentle consolation.

And behold, a voice from the cloud, saying:

Because Peter had said nothing reasonable, he did not deserve an answer. Instead, the Father answers on behalf of the Son and teaches both the apostles and, through them, the others that he is his Son—not an adopted son, but his own proper Son. The tabernacle must be fixed for him alone; both the apostles, Moses, and Elijah must obey him.

“This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him.”

And this must be retained: just as the Trinity was shown at the baptism, so also it was shown on the mountain.

And when the disciples heard this, they fell upon their faces and were greatly afraid.

It is not surprising that the disciples were greatly afraid, because they saw the Lord glorified beyond human form; they heard the voice of God the Father through a subject creature; and, because the cloud had touched them, they realized that they had still been in error.

And Jesus approached and touched them.

It is customary for human nature, when something beyond itself appears, to be overcome by fear, and then to be restored through voice and touch. We read the same thing in Daniel and in Ezekiel. Thus, because they lay cast down by the heavenly voice and action, they were restored by the familiar human voice and touch.

“Do not be afraid.”

All these things happened for our instruction, not for our destruction. It belongs to the elect to fall upon their faces, and to the reprobate to fall backward, as happened in the Passion to the persecutors of the Lord.

And when they lifted up their eyes, they saw no one except Jesus alone.

When the Father’s voice began to commend the Son, the servants departed. When the disciples arose, they saw no one else except the Lord, lest anyone think that the voice which had sounded had been addressed to someone other than him.

Figuratively, after Christ appeared, there was no longer any need for the shadow of the law or for prophetic prediction.

And as they were coming down from the mountain, Jesus commanded them, saying:

“Tell no one about the vision.”

He did not wish them to proclaim publicly what they had seen on the mountain, lest it not be believed because of the greatness of the event; or lest the disgrace of the cross produce scandal and cause it to be regarded as worthless, until the glory of the one reigning was announced together with the triumph of the resurrection.

And his disciples questioned him, saying:

Why then do the scribes say that Elijah must come first?

We must inquire where this question arose among the Lord’s disciples, because above the Lord had said that some would not taste death until they saw the Son of Man coming in his kingdom. They thought that the glorification of the kingdom itself ought to occur immediately. Therefore they said: “What is the meaning of what the scribes and Pharisees say—that Elijah must precede your coming?”

For, according to what is written by Malachi, the Pharisees held that Elijah would precede the Lord’s coming. But this must be understood of the second coming, not the first. They saw that Elijah had departed, and therefore they were troubled.

But he answered them:

“Elijah indeed is coming, and he will restore all things”—namely, the things that the same prophet Malachi foretold.

As you have heard, Elijah came at the Lord’s second coming according to the truth of the body.

But I tell you that Elijah has already come, namely in the spirit and activity of John, and they did not recognize him—that is, they did not recognize his holiness. But they did with him whatever they wished: they despised him and beheaded him.

“So also the Son of Man is going to suffer at their hands.”

It is asked why the Pharisees are said to have killed John, when Herod killed him. They are said to have consented because they did not oppose the killing. For whoever can help someone about to perish but does not do so kills him.

Similarly, Herod is said to have killed the Lord because, although he could have freed him, he did not wish to do so, but consented with Pilate and sent him back to him.

## CHAPTER XXXVII  
### On the Lunatic

And when he had come to the crowd, a man approached him, falling on his knees.

The Lord’s actions must always be noted, for he never ceases to work for the salvation of human beings. On the mountain he disclosed the secrets of his majesty to the disciples; when he descended from it, he was received by the crowd. On the mountain he healed the doubtful minds of the apostles; on the plain he healed the bodies and minds of the crowds.

“Lord, have mercy on my son, because he is a lunatic.”

Those people thought that the man suffered because of the moon’s decline, but that was not so. Rather, the devil watched for the time of the moon in order to injure people in their souls and seize the man, so that the Creator might be defamed through his creature and the Creator who had made such a creature might be blasphemed, since human beings suffered evils through it.

Mark reports that this man was deaf and mute. According to the historical account, this is what happened. In another sense, he signifies those of whom it is written: “The fool changes like the moon.”

When it says that he often falls into fire, avarice is understood, because avarice burns as though with fire while wealth increases: the love of money grows as the money itself grows. Or anger is expressed through fire.

And frequently into water: into the flood of lust, which through sensual pleasures usually dissolves the mind.

“And I brought him to your disciples, and they could not cure him.”

Frequently the deeds on account of which people pray oppose the prayers of those who ask, when the person for whom they are asking does not turn away from evil. Hence the Lord frequently says: “According to your faith, let it be done for you.”

Whoever is handed over to a demon is handed over either for his own sin or for the sin of his parents, as we find throughout the Gospel narratives.

Jesus answered and said:

“O faithless and perverse generation, how long shall I be with you? How long shall I endure you?”

He did not say this as though he were wearied or turned to anger, for it is written of him that, like a lamb, he did not open his mouth. Rather, Solomon says: “The words of the wise are like goads, and like nails driven deep.”

He wished what he said to remain fixed in their minds, as if a physician were saying to a sick man: “How long shall I come to your house? How long shall I waste my medical skill? I prescribe one thing, but you do another.”

Or through him he reproves the Jews for their unbelief. The following words show that he did not speak from an angry spirit.

It continues:

“Bring him here to me.”

And Jesus rebuked him.

He rebuked not the man but the devil, who had dared to throw him down in the presence of the Creator. For the Evangelist says that at that very hour he troubled him and threw him to the ground.

If we understand the man also to have been rebuked, it is shown that the demon ruled him because of his sins. The reason it tormented him more severely at that moment was either to avenge its anger at being expelled or to instill hatred of virtue.

And the demon went out from him.

Another Evangelist says that Jesus commanded it not to enter him again, because the devil is accustomed to reclaim voluntarily the place of his habitation unless the one who has been freed guards himself against sins. The Lord shows this in the case of the man who had been healed, saying: “When an unclean spirit has gone out from a man,” and the rest.

Then the disciples approached Jesus privately and said: Why could we not cast it out?

Here it is evident that the apostles frequently performed miracles and expelled demons, since they ask only about this case why they had been unable to cast it out.

He said to them: Because of your unbelief.

This is what he said to them elsewhere: “Whatever you ask in my name, believing, you will receive.” Whenever we do not receive, the fault lies not with the one who gives but with the one who asks.

Or, as James says: “Let him ask in faith, doubting nothing.” Or their unbelief consisted in believing that the man was afflicted because of the moon’s decline.

Amen, amen, I say to you: If you have faith like a grain of mustard seed—

Faith is not compared to a grain of mustard seed because it is small, but because it is burning and becomes great when it begins to produce works.

—you will say to this mountain, “Move from here,” and it will move.

This mountain signifies the devil himself, because he was then cast out of that man. Therefore he says, “to this mountain.” Hence it is also said in the Apocalypse: “The devil, like a great mountain, was cast into the sea.” And elsewhere: “A pestilential mountain that corrupts the whole earth.”

Some who wish to understand the passage literally in terms of an earthly mountain ask whether any saint has moved a mountain from one place to another. Yet it must be known that the almighty Lord established all mountains in suitable places, and it is not necessary to transfer them from place to place, although we read that Gregory of Nazianzus did this. We also read of King Alexander that, when he could not destroy by war the nations of Gog and Magog, whose enclosure is now called Gazara, he turned to God and asked him for help. God increased the mountain at their enclosure, and Alexander enclosed what remained of them with his people and placed bronze gates beneath the mountain.

But this kind will not be driven out except by prayer and fasting.

Prayer consists not only in words but also in righteous works, which pray for us, as the Apostle commanded: “Pray without ceasing.”

How can we pray without ceasing, when we cannot live without sleep and food? To pray without ceasing means to perform works that plead for us while we sleep, because it is of no benefit to withdraw the stomach from food while indulging in lust or other vices.

Through such prayers and fasts, let us know that the temptations of unclean spirits and of hostile human beings must be overcome. In the same way, the Lord’s anger can be calmed and forgiveness of sins obtained.

By this gift the children of Israel were freed from the domination of the Philistines when Samuel prayed and fasted with them. The Ninevites also rose from their impending fear. The Jews, together with Esther and Mordecai, obtained victory over Haman. The Maccabees likewise became stronger than their enemies.

As they were moving about in Galilee, Jesus said to them:

“The Son of Man is going to be handed over into the hands of men, and they will kill him, and on the third day he will rise again.”

The Lord frequently foretells these things because this was destined to be like a shipwreck for the apostles. They were destined to lose almost all hope. Since they neither believed nor understood these things, he foretold them so that they might endure them more lightly if they knew them beforehand.

Yet he mingles prosperity with adversity, namely the resurrection of the one who would die. When he says “into the hands of men,” sinners or soldiers are understood, because since he was handed over to them, it was certain that he was being handed over to be killed.

And they were greatly saddened.

They were saddened out of love for their teacher, whom they did not want to suffer any adversity, since they knew that he lived justly.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII  
### On the Stater That Was Given

And when they had come to Capernaum—

Capernaum is clearly a large village in Galilee, which is sometimes called a city because of its size. The Romans were stationed there and were rulers in that land.

When the Lord had come there, those who collected the didrachma approached Peter.

You know that the whole world became tributary under Octavian, except for certain people who earned the privilege through an exceptional friendship, so that the Romans called them citizens. For this enrollment Joseph came with Mary to Bethlehem to register and pay the census tax for their persons.

Because of the reverence that he himself showed toward all people, especially toward the Romans, as the centurion demonstrates, that tax collector did not dare to approach him directly concerning the tribute. They supposed, indeed, that he was a native of Nazareth; therefore Herod’s subordinates demanded the tax from him. For he was under Pilate’s jurisdiction, being from Bethlehem.

A didrachma is two drachmas, that is, six denarii.

Peter did not deny that the tax was unpaid, although the collectors served a pagan power.

And when he had entered the house, Jesus anticipated him, saying:

He anticipated Peter’s statement. He knows all things before they occur, and he did this so that the disciples would not be scandalized when they heard that tribute was being demanded from their teacher.

“What do you think? From whom do the kings of the earth receive tribute: from their own sons or from foreigners?”

And he said: “From foreigners.”

Our Lord showed that he would pay the census tax of his own free will, because if he had not wished to do so, he would not have paid it. According to the flesh he was descended from David; according to his divinity he was the Son of the Most High Father and the Creator of the world.

Nevertheless, to give the example that we should be subject to the higher authorities, he did what he wished to be done by us.

“Go to the sea and cast in a hook.”

That is, into the lake of Gennesaret. In every respect the Lord’s power is wondrous: he knew that a fish had a stater in its mouth and also that it would be the first fish to be caught.

But the one who foretold this also created both the fish and the gold that it had in its mouth. We must not suppose that someone’s money had fallen into the lake, so that the Lord might free himself from another person’s loss. Rather, the gold itself was created for this purpose, and the fish still had it in its mouth, not in its belly.

It should simply be understood that he was so poor that he had nothing to give for himself.

A stater is two didrachmas.

Other people paid the census tax in bronze, four denarii for their own persons alone. But the Lord, to show that he possessed something more precious in his body than other human beings—namely, the hidden divinity—gave gold for himself.

Mystically, the fish signified the Lord himself: namely, the Lord’s body, which he took from Mary. It carried gold in its mouth, that is, wisdom, of which Solomon says: “A desirable treasure is in the mouth of the wise.”

The gold was given for him because, in order that he might have adopted brothers, it came about through the word of his Gospel. And not only was there gold, but also a fish that was killed, because his flesh died for us.

Through Peter, his entire Church is signified—the Church entrusted to that same Peter—for which the Lord gave his blood.

## CHAPTER XXXIX  
### On the Example of the Child
At that hour the disciples came to Jesus, saying, “Who, do you think, is greater in the kingdom of heaven?” The Evangelist’s words, “At that hour,” refer to the time when they saw the tribute paid by Peter together with the Lord, and when they had previously seen him set apart from the others on the mountain and had heard it said to him, “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven.” Now they saw him compared with the Lord in the payment of the tribute, and contention arose among them over which of them seemed to be greater—even to the point of questioning God.

And the Lord, like a compassionate teacher, took care to calm their contentiousness through humility. They seemed to be saying, “Whom do you consider worthy to be made greater in the kingdom of heaven?” And calling a little child, he set him in their midst. He brought forward a certain little child from the crowd, an infant in age, who did not know how to desire either position or gold, or to envy or lie.

And he said to them: “Amen I say to you, unless you turn and become like little children, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven. Unless, through my teaching and by your own will, you become such as this child is by age—so that you do not desire what belongs to another, do not hate anyone, do not seek honor in this world, and do not lie or deceive your neighbors—you will not enter eternal life.”

Origen says that when someone is an infant, he is then the true Adam, and such as God wished Adam to be. Until he is initiated among human beings, he cares only about food and cold; he does not care about luxuries or costly clothing; he does not know what gold is; he loves stones and gems equally; an egg is more pleasing to him than gold; he does not know how to deceive anyone; he does everything with a good disposition, and nothing secretly. This is the simplicity of doves, which we ought to imitate through innocence.

But once the infant begins to grow—namely, when he begins to embrace the things he loves: gold, luxuries, and the remaining evils—then he becomes like us. This may also be understood of the Lord himself, who said this about himself and who was such in innocence. Yet he had long before given himself to them as an example for imitation, and for this reason they followed him, so that they might imitate him.

Therefore, whoever humbles himself like this little child is greater in the kingdom of heaven: what the child is by nature, let that person be through instruction; such a one is greater in the kingdom of heaven.

“And whoever receives one such little child”—that is, one such as I have just commanded him to be—“in my name receives me.” Certainly, whoever becomes such because of God’s command has God dwelling in him. Let those who are received, however, see to it that they are such as the Lord commanded.

For those who receive them, even if the recipients are unworthy, will receive from God the reward they would have received if the recipients themselves had been holy—provided that the recipients are not publicly evil. For they come to them in Christ’s sheep’s clothing, and whatever is given to them is expended for Christ. Thus he himself says: “He receives me who receives him in my name.”

“But whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him if a millstone carried by a donkey were hung around his neck and he were drowned in the depths of the sea.”

He speaks according to the custom of the province, in which those who committed greater crimes were punished in this way: a huge stone was tied around their neck, and they were plunged into the water. A millstone turned by a donkey—that is, one which a donkey carried.

What he says, “it would be better,” means “it is more fitting.” Or: It is better for him to perish temporally than, by increasing his sins, to be assigned to eternal punishments.

From this passage we can gather that all who are punished for murders and thefts, if they recognize their sin and understand that they are justly suffering those same punishments, and confess their sins and beseech God that their sins may be forgiven on account of these punishments, will be saved in the next life. Let them say, as the thief said: “We are indeed being punished justly in this way, because we have sinned against God and against Christians.”

“Woe to the world because of stumbling-blocks.” There was woe for the world because they were at peace in evil, and no opposition was offered to them in worshiping idols. For stumbling-blocks must come. Because the pagans do not wish to acknowledge the God who created them, adversities will come upon them; then they will seek God to help them in their adversities, because those whom they worship, being dead, cannot help them.

Constantine did this when he was about to wage war against Maxentius: he sought which god he might have as a helper, since his own gods were works of human hands.

“Nevertheless, woe to the person through whom the stumbling-block comes.” Whatever evil exists in this world is through the devil, and the devil scourges his own followers, those who do his will. For all of God’s chastisement, both in this age and in the next, is carried out through devils, because God is not the tempter of evils, but evil inflictions are carried out through evil angels.

We can take the example of Nebuchadnezzar. When he and his people had been commanded to chastise the Lord’s people, because he and his people acted cruelly against them, they were afterward handed over to a similar punishment.

Therefore all people ought to guard themselves, lest they become a stumbling-block to anyone.

“But if your hand or your foot causes you to stumble, cut it off and throw it away from you.” By the hand or foot are understood friends, whose help and counsel we need daily. If such people wish to obstruct us on the way of God, they must be abandoned, so that the love of God may be kept firm in the heart. Otherwise, if we wish to share in this life with the lost, we may perish together with them in the future.

“And if your eye causes you to stumble…” By the eye, too, carnal friends are understood. If they are a stumbling-block to us on the way of God, they too must be abandoned. For someone causes a brother to stumble when he becomes the cause of his ruin in word or deed. *Scandalum* is indeed a Greek word and may be rendered in Latin as *offensio* (“offense”) or *ruina* (“ruin”).

**[Col. 1409A]** “See that you do not despise one of these little ones.” Above, he removed all the carnal affections through which we can stray from the way of God, since it is better to endure tribulation in the present age than to lose eternal life. Now, too, he commands that everyone take every precaution not to inflict a stumbling-block on those who, for God’s sake, have chosen to be poor and humble in this world.

“For I say to you that their angels in heaven always see the face of my Father.” From this passage and from others we find that each person has two angels assigned to him from the day of his birth until the day of his death, one good and one evil. For we read in the Apocalypse: “To the angel of Ephesus,” and to the others, “Write this or that.” And the Apostle commands that women’s heads be veiled in churches because of the angels.

For this reason each person must strive not to inflict evil unjustly on anyone, because he both provokes God against himself and grieves the good angels—his own and the other person’s.

“For the Son of Man came to save what had perished.” This is true, because almighty God wills all people to be saved, and he preached so that they might have peace among themselves.

## CHAPTER XL. On the Parable of the Sheep

“What do you think? If someone has a hundred sheep…” Almighty God had a hundred sheep: he created the perfect number of the ten orders of angels, together with humanity, for his praise. For perfection is signified by the number one hundred.

“One sheep went astray” when humanity sinned in paradise. He left the nine orders of angels—not by changing their place, but by showing himself incarnate—“on the mountains,” that is, in the heavenly places. He came to seek the human being who, by sinning, had departed from God, not bodily but through conduct.

“It happened that he found it.” This means that he found a gentile people who voluntarily corrected what they had done wrong.

“Amen I say to you, there is greater joy over it than over the ninety-nine that did not go astray.” Greater joy is produced in heaven over converted sinners than over righteous people who remain standing. For when humanity had been restored and the Lord had ascended into heaven, the joy of the angels was filled, and he who restored humanity, raised above the angels, is the God of archangels.

Or, there are righteous people who daily afflict themselves before God as though they had committed the deeds of the impious; such people too may be called sinners. Over such people joy is produced daily in heaven.

“So it is not the will of your Father that one of these little ones should perish.” That almighty God did not wish to destroy humanity was shown by the redemption and the bitter death which he endured for us.

## CHAPTER XLI. On Forgiving a Brother

“But if your brother sins against you…” Above he taught that humble people who remain Christians with us must not be despised. If they sin against us, we should not therefore alienate ourselves from them until we learn whether we can convert them and remedy the violation of charity.

For in another Evangelist he says: “If your brother sins against you, rebuke him; and if he repents, forgive him.” We must pay attention to the words “against you,” because it is one thing to sin against us and another to sin against God. If someone sins against us, we have the power to forgive. But if someone sins against God, it must be corrected according to what the ancients established in the canons, just as it is said in the Book of Kings: “If a man sins against a man, God can be appeased on his behalf; but if a man sins against God, who will pray for him?”

“Go and rebuke him between you and him alone.” One person should be rebuked privately by another, lest, if he loses his sense of shame, he become worse.

“If he listens to you, you have gained your brother.” For whoever converts a sinner from the error of his way will save his soul from death and cover a multitude of his own sins.

“But if he does not listen to you, take with you one or two more.” Two or three are brought either out of a desire to correct him or so that the matter may be addressed with witnesses.

“But if he does not listen to them, tell it to the Church,” so that the person who did not wish to be converted privately may be converted through the reproaches of many.

“But if he does not listen even to the Church, let him be to you as a pagan and a tax collector.” *Ethnicus* is a Greek term, rendered in Latin as *gentilis* (“gentile”). A tax collector is one who exacts public profits through commerce, theft, and perjury, and who serves the public interest. A person who is a Christian but attacks fraternal peace, or who publicly becomes a stumbling-block to a Christian, is worse than a pagan who has not yet received Christianity.

“Amen I say to you, whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven.” Because he had said, “Let him be to you as a pagan and a tax collector,” lest those who cause scandal to their inferiors regard this lightly, he shows that the person who persists in evil is anathematized by the Church. Divine mercy follows their judgment if they act regularly and according to love of neighbor.

“Again I say to you, if two of you agree on earth about anything that they ask, it will be done for you.” This applies if they ask in the way he stated elsewhere—that is, in the name of Jesus and for the salvation of the soul.

We have an example of this in the blessed Peter and Paul, who petitioned concerning Simon, who was a snare of death to others; they obtained that he should fall and perish, lest he become a stumbling-block to others.

“Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them.” Josephus says of a Jewish sect—whom he nevertheless calls Essenes—that whatever one hundred of them established together was regarded as law. But the Lord speaks of three and tells his faithful that whatever they do in his name, he himself does.

For this reason it has been established that a bishop should not be ordained by fewer than three.

“Then Peter came to him and said…” Since above he had commanded Peter and all his followers to forgive and correct those who sinned against them, Peter asks how often he ought to do this—whether perhaps up to seven times.

Seven was a sacred and customary number among them because of the Sabbath.

“I do not say to you seven times, but up to seventy times seven.” Whether you calculate seven by seventy or seventy by seven, the result is the same, namely four hundred and ninety: a number of times by which no one can sin against another.

That is, as long as he asks, we should forgive him. The calculation is so fixed in every number that whether we multiply the lesser by the greater or the greater by the lesser, the results return to the same meaning.

It was customary in that land to attach parables to all discourses, and therefore the Lord always spoke with parables.

“Therefore the kingdom of heaven is like…” That is, so that we may forgive those who sin against us and ask forgiveness from us. The kingdom of heaven always signifies those who are in the kingdom of heaven—in the Church of Christ, in which he reigns.

“A king…” means almighty God, who wished to settle accounts with his servants—that is, with Christians who are in the Church.

These accounts are settled daily in the Church. When we ask God to forgive our debts, he has made an agreement with us that we should forgive our debtors; then he will forgive our debts.

We are debtors to him for ten thousand talents: these are the more serious sins that each person recognizes in himself, since no one can recount how greatly we sin against God every day—in thoughts, in idle, harmful, and deadly speech, namely through slander, and likewise in idle, harmful, and deadly deeds performed through all our bodily members: through the ears, by hearing idle, harmful, and deadly things; through the eyes; through the nostrils; through the feet; through the hands; and through all the affections of the body.

“But when he had nothing with which to repay, the lord ordered him to be sold, together with his wife and children and all that he had, and repayment to be made.” The law ordered that someone unable to pay a fine should become the servant of those to whom he had been condemned, until he could redeem himself. Herod, however, had added that he should be sold to whomever he wished, and this was practiced in that land.

This is why the Lord says this. For if the Lord wished to condemn us according to our deeds, no one could be clean in his sight. The Lord commands that we be sold, together with our wife and children, when, because of our thoughts, words, and deeds, he commands us to be handed over to eternal torments.

When we are ill and hear through the words of his servants, “Those who have done good will go into eternal life, and those who have done evil into eternal fire,” we are afraid and pray that we may be forgiven. The Lord forgives us if we cease from evil and recover again.

It follows: “But when that servant went out, he found one of his fellow servants”—that is, someone who was likewise a Christian—“who owed him one hundred denarii,” that is, one hundred kinds of offenses and stumbling-blocks.

For it is not a sin to demand a debt that someone justly owes another. But if he sees that the person cannot repay because of poverty, he ought to treat him as he would wish to be treated, or wait until the debtor is better able to repay.

“And seizing him, he was choking him, saying: ‘Pay what you owe.’” When some people are stronger than others, if the weaker have offended them in some way, they rage against them without mercy because they see that they possess greater power. They not only choke them but also kill or destroy them, failing to consider that they can do what they can only through God’s gift.

Therefore they will be tormented without remedy in the next life, unless here they repent worthily and correct what they have done.

“When his fellow servants saw what was happening, they were greatly grieved.” These may be the angels of the Lord, who report our deeds to God, or the priests whom we have between ourselves and God. When we refuse to listen to them and forgive those who have sinned against us, they do not resolve our sins or pray for us.

For if someone dies in discord, no Christian ought to pray for him or make a commemoration for him at the altar of the Lord.

“Then his lord summoned him and said to him…” He commands him to leave the body and come before Christ’s tribunal. Because he refused to show mercy to his fellow servants, he is handed over to the torturing demons until he pays all the sins he committed before God.

“So also my heavenly Father will do to you.” He confirms his judgment and removes every pretense of simulated peace, saying: “If you do not forgive from your hearts…”

For it is of no benefit to forgive with the mouth if we hate the person in our heart. Therefore he says, “from your hearts.”

## CHAPTER LXII. On Not Divorcing One’s Wife

“And it happened that when Jesus had finished these words…” It should be noted that the word “finished” is always used in connection with the work of the perfect.

The Lord moves from Galilee into Judaea. Although the whole province of Palestine was generally called Judaea, to distinguish it from other regions—because Jews inhabited it—one particular part among them was specifically called Judaea, where Jerusalem had been built.

Thus he came from Capernaum into Judaea, and the crowds, who were poor, followed him because of his teaching and healing. The powerful people of Judaea and those who considered themselves wiser followed him in order to find fault, since in his deeds and words they sought a way either to condemn him to death according to the law, or, according to earthly power, to stir up hostile peoples or the Romans so that he might be killed through them.

“Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife for any cause?” They had heard him preach chastity and purity, and they had seen him live as a virgin. So they said among themselves: “See, he lives differently from us. We can trap him in this matter. Let us ask him this question. If he says that the woman should be divorced, he speaks contrary to his own words and deeds, and the women too will hate him. But if he says that she should not be divorced, we have trapped him, because he has spoken contrary to Moses.”

But the Lord, like a fountain of wisdom, always passed through their snares without blame.

He answered them: “Have you not read that he who made humanity from the beginning made them male and female?” Concerning the very one whom they thought to use in bringing an accusation against him, the Lord displayed and confirmed his teaching, as though he were saying:

“The same God who gave us the law through Moses, according to the account of that same Moses, made only one woman for one man, not two, so that when he had cast one out he might take another. And God also prophesied through Adam that a man would leave his father and mother and cling to his wife. Here too he did not say ‘wives,’ as though there were several, but ‘wife,’ one.

“And they will be two.” He does not say three.

“In one flesh.” God is not like a human being, so that it would be necessary for him to change his judgment. For God speaks once and does not repeat the same thing a second time. Therefore he could not then have established one thing and commanded something else through Moses.

“What God has joined, let no human being separate.” If they have become one flesh through love, or even through children, how can they be separated? What God has joined through love—he who permitted love to rule in human hearts—a human being ought not to separate.

They say to him: “Why then did Moses command that a certificate of divorce be given and the woman dismissed?” Here is the snare they concealed when they said: “What is this that Moses commanded—that women be given a document of separation?” They dug a pit, but, as always, they themselves fell into it.

“See: neither is God a liar nor Moses evil; rather, you are hard-hearted and sluggish. Because of your hardness Moses did not command this, but permitted it to you. If he had not permitted it, you would have killed your former wives so that you might take younger and more beautiful, or richer, ones.

“But from the beginning it was not so. We read that Noah and his sons each had one wife in the ark, and no more. Although Abraham had the barren Sarah as his wife, he did not divorce her, and none of the patriarchs divorced his wife except at death.

“But I say to you that whoever divorces his wife, except on account of fornication, and marries another commits adultery.”

From this passage Paul took what he said: that a woman does not have authority over her own body, but her husband does. Likewise, a man does not have authority over his own body, but his wife does. That is, they cannot separate unless both wish to do so by common agreement.

“And whoever marries a divorced woman commits adultery.” Adultery is committed by three persons: by the man who divorces, since he is the cause of his wife’s fornication; by the wife who does not remain continent—for if she cannot remain continent, she ought to return to her first husband; and by the man who takes another’s wife while her husband is alive.

Therefore those who desire to leave the world ought to wait until their spouses too are able to remain continent. One person ought not to enter a monastery while the other takes a partner outside.

His disciples say to him: “If this is the situation of a man with his wife, it is not advantageous to marry.” The disciples who were present with the Lord understood that once a wife had been taken—whether she was gluttonous, quarrelsome, or ill—she had to be kept until the day of death, unless both mutually agreed to leave the world.

Therefore, before taking a wife, a man ought to know her character and health, and he ought not hastily do what he will long have to regret. But if everything must be done with counsel, this matter requires it even more, since he is about to give himself over so that two may become one flesh.

Although many consider seven qualities in taking wives—noble birth, wealth, beauty, health, wisdom, and character—two must be sought above all: wisdom and character. If these two are lacking, the others can be lost.

For we have seen some women nobly born and wealthy reduced, because of lack of self-control in their conduct, to such poverty that they ended their lives by begging. We have also heard of many women killed because of the evil of fornication. Conversely, others born in a more humble condition have risen from poverty to wealth because of their wisdom and restraint of character.

He said to them: “Not all grasp this saying.” Because the disciples said, “It is not advantageous to marry,” the Lord replied that not everyone grasps this saying so as to fulfill it by abstaining from women.

“But it is given to those to whom it is given”—that is, by God, to abstain in virginity.

“For there are eunuchs who were born so from their mother’s womb.” Just as people are born physically disabled in all the other members, so some are born disabled in these members, because the vein from which the semen ought to descend was not open, just as the veins through which hearing penetrates into the interior are closed in those who are born deaf.

“And there are eunuchs who have been made so by human beings.” From the ancient practice of the pagans, it still remains among many peoples to crush the testicles of infants at an early age, to shrivel them, or even to remove them entirely for various reasons: either so that they may be constant in serving their masters, or so that they may not squander the property entrusted to them on women. Before Christianity, some were made eunuchs for shameful service.

Now in Benevento, whenever they intend to make someone a cleric, the father and mother crush his testicles in infancy. Such men appear always to remain young until they begin to grow gray. If this is done at a mature age, however, they are immediately weakened and lose their strength.

**[Col. 1414C]** “And there are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven.” The other two kinds are eunuchs bodily; those who are to become eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven become so in mind, not in body, since no one is permitted to cut off his own limbs on account of any lack of self-control.

If someone does so, he cannot hold ecclesiastical orders; and if he already holds them, he will lose them. But if it has been done unjustly by others, he does not lose his honors.

“Let the one who is able to grasp it, grasp it.” To grasp means to fulfill. Whoever can fulfill this so as to remain a virgin should do so. It is as though he were saying openly: “I command no one unwillingly, but whoever wishes to imitate me will receive a worthy reward. Whoever cannot do so will not for this reason lose eternal life.”

For there are three orders upon which the Church is founded: the married, the continent, and virgins.

And so that the Lord might sanctify both states, he deigned to come to a wedding and perform a miracle there. He wished to be blessed by the prophetess Anna and by the old man Simeon. And to show that the virgin would be mother and queen of all virtues and companion of the angels, he was born of a virgin, and, having deigned to be born of her, he chose to remain a virgin.

Accordingly, he chose among his apostles some who were married, some continent, and some virgins. Nevertheless, he placed the blessed Peter, who was married, over all the orders, so that virgins would not become proud or married people despair of being able to attain the perfection reached by virgins.

The blessed Paul gives a similar instruction when he says: “Concerning virgins I have no commandment of the Lord, but I give advice.” That is, for someone to remain a virgin is not a commandment but an exhortation.

Therefore he adds: “I want all people to be as I myself am”—that is, without a wife.

If someone says, “Why should presbyters and deacons not have wives?” we will answer that many people, in following God’s example, hold to what is better and therefore more pleasing to God. For this reason it is not necessary for the Lord’s ministries to be administered by married men.

But the canons command that those who violate the vows they made to the Lord—that is, to minister in virginity—be condemned as apostates and removed from the ministry.

Then little children were brought to him so that he might lay his hands on them. Because the age of infants was less developed, it was accustomed to suffer demonic apparitions; and the younger the child, the more fiercely—so the midwives say.

For when a child was found alone before nine days had passed, he was killed by a demon. For this reason there was a custom among the prophets of blessing little children. In the same way they brought those who could not yet come on their own, so that they might be blessed by the Lord.

“And that he might pray”—understand, “over them”—just as Jacob blessed Ephraim and Manasseh by laying his hands upon their heads.

But the disciples rebuked them, not out of envy, but because they feared that, like other people, he might become annoyed by their multitude.

Jesus, however, said to them: “Allow the little children, and do not prevent them from coming to me.” Then he received them in the manner you have heard and blessed them.

And always, whoever wishes to approach him with a childlike spirit—that is, in humility, having become a child in wickedness—he receives, as the psalm says: “The Lord will receive the meek.”

“For of such is the kingdom of heaven.” That is, the kingdom belongs to those who are such through innocence as these children are through age. He did not say, “The kingdom of heaven belongs to these,” but “to such,” requiring innocence of mind, not of age.

Likewise the Apostle commands: “Be children in wickedness, but perfect in understanding.” We spoke above about the innocence of infants, and therefore it is not necessary to repeat it here.

“And when he had laid his hands on them, he departed from there.” He saw that the scribes were more eager to find fault than to believe, and therefore quickly left the unbelievers, because he flees a mind that he does not find humble. He went to the humble and to those who trembled at his words.

## CHAPTER XLIII. On the Rich Man Who Tempted Him

“And behold, someone came up and said to him.” Perhaps this man had heard about imitating the innocence of children, and therefore wished each point explained to him: what true innocence itself might be.

“Good Teacher, what good shall I do so that I may have eternal life?” Another Evangelist says: “Why do you call me good?” Because this man believed him to be merely a human being, calling him “teacher” but not Christ or God, he is rebuked for calling him good while not believing him to be God.

The Lord therefore does not deny that he is good, but demonstrates that he is God. He wished the one who called him good to learn in what way he was good. For every human being, however holy, and every creature, in comparison with God, is not good. In itself, however, both a human being and every creature is good if it is as it was created.

Since the Lord wished this man to understand that point, he called himself good elsewhere, saying: “I am the good shepherd.” And concerning the Holy Spirit: “Your Father will give the good Spirit to those who ask him.”

“Why do you ask me about the good? God alone is good.” When “good” is used absolutely in Scripture, God is understood, because he is good by nature, not through an accidental gift. He is not only good, but goodness itself and the fountain of goodness.

Whoever is good is good by participating in him and receiving from him. Every creature, insofar as it is good, is from God; insofar as it is evil, it is evil from itself and through its own defect.

Here is the testimony of the Lord not only concerning the Father but also concerning himself and the Holy Spirit, who are one God, supremely good beyond comparison and beyond expression.

“But if you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments.” From this passage we understand that all who kept the old law without contamination possess eternal life.

He said to him: “Which ones?” Jesus then said to him: “You shall not commit murder.”

Murder is committed in two ways. Murder occurs when someone destroys the dwelling-place of the soul before the appointed time and, as though without God’s command, compels the soul to depart from its exile—whether his own soul or another’s.

It is an exceedingly great evil for anyone to be evil toward himself. And not only is laying hands upon oneself an accursed evil before God and his Christians; among the ancient pagans it was also so hated that the hand which had committed such an act was denied common burial with the body.

But what he says is grievous: even today Christians in name only commit this act. The responsibility for the danger of this evil falls upon bishops, who do not announce to them that they are not ending their sorrows and tribulations but multiplying them, as they pass from these torments to more terrible ones.

Another murder is spiritual: when someone sins unto death, or causes a brother to sin, or sees him sinning and does not call him back, and both die in soul. The first dies because he abandoned God by sinning; the second because he saw and did not call him back, although he could have done so.

“For the soul that sins, it shall die.” The Apostle says: “Not only those who do these things, but also those who consent to those who do them, are worthy of death.”

Let us recall what happened to Eli. He did not rebuke his sons as he ought, and he perished on their account, while they passed from present destruction into eternal destruction.

It follows: “You shall not commit adultery.” To commit adultery is to enter another person’s marriage-bed. Although every fornication is a criminal sin, this is a more serious form of the vice of fornication, because the sin is committed by three people.

This too is committed spiritually, when a soul that ought to have God as its husband, to whom it promised at baptism that it would cling, abandons him for gold, gems, or some bodily pleasure and clings instead to the devil who persuades it.

Ezekiel explains this fornication more fully under the figure of two women, namely Jerusalem and Samaria, intending their inhabitants to be understood through them.

“You shall not steal.” This too is committed in two ways: when someone takes something from his neighbor through any evil deception. To steal is to take secretly, that is, in concealment.

There is a distinction between theft and sacrilege. Although sacrilege is also theft, it is greater insofar as it concerns sacred things. Just as theft may concern a temporal object, so there is also spiritual theft: to take the divine word away from someone who does not know it.

**[Col. 1417A]** “You shall not bear false witness.” Someone bears false witness when he speaks with a meaning different from the one intended by the person who first spoke. The person who consents to another’s lie and keeps silent about the truth he knows also bears false witness.

This is the innocence that we are commanded to imitate in children, through which we can both please God and reach eternal life.

“Honor your father and your mother.” This honor is to be understood not only in words but also in all gifts and honors. There is also the true Father, our Creator, the Lord, whom we must honor before and above all things.

We are likewise commanded to love and honor our mother, the Church, which gave birth to us.

“You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” Our neighbor is every human being, as he himself showed in the parable of the wounded man. Or our neighbor is the person who worships the same God as we do; we are commanded to call him a brother, as the Lord showed in the Lord’s Prayer.

The young man says to him: “I have kept all these things.” He did not question the Lord with the intention of tempting him, as another Evangelist shows, who says that the Lord looked upon him and loved him. Rather, he was concerned about himself and simply confessed his way of life.

For if he had come to him with a divided heart, the one who saw the secrets of the heart would certainly not have loved him. The Lord loves those who keep his commandments, even the least of them, and shows them what perfection they lack.

Therefore he says to this man:

If you wish to be perfect, go, sell what you have, and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven. Whoever wishes to be perfect ought to sell—not in part, as Ananias and Sapphira did—and give to the poor, and follow the Savior; that is, abandon evil and do good. This is not commanded to everyone, nor is it said, “No one can enter the kingdom of heaven unless he has done this,” but only to those who wish to do so; just as virginity is not commanded, but only to those who wish it and to whom it is pleasing. For what he said above is spoken to all who desire to enter into eternal life. This, however, concerns the more perfect. For he himself had twelve apostles who did these things following the Lord’s example. He also had [Col. 1417D] other disciples who by no means did so, such as Nicodemus, Gamaliel, and Joseph, of whom it is written that they were his disciples, but secretly, because of fear of the Jews: they did not wish to abandon everything, but to possess it with justice and goodness.

When the young man heard the word, he went away sorrowful. This is the sorrow that produces death, because godly sorrow produces repentance leading to salvation, whereas the sorrow of this world produces death. And the reason for his sorrow is given: “For,” he says, “he had many possessions.” Behold where the thorns choked the seed of God: that is, riches prevented it from springing up for his salvation. It was not necessary for him to be sorrowful: he could have kept what was his and lived with justice and holiness, and he could have possessed eternal life. And we believe that he did so, because it is written of the Lord: “He will not extinguish the smoking flax.”

Jesus then said to his disciples: “Amen, I say to you, that a rich man will enter the kingdom with difficulty.” There are four kinds of rich people. One is rich who possesses riches, yet his riches are not condemned in him, but he uses them as their master. This person is counted as poor, as David was, who said: “I am needy and poor.” Yet he offered one hundred talents of gold and one thousand thousand [i.e. a million] of silver for the temple of the Lord. He also exhorted others, saying: “If riches increase, do not set your heart upon them.”

There is another rich person who does not possess riches, but could possess them if he wished; they are offered to him, yet he sets his heart upon them in no way. If they should come to him, he distributes them so that he may always remain poor. Such was Julian the monk, and many others who, although riches flowed to them, always chose to be poor; and this person is reckoned poor in the sight of God.

There is also a third rich person who possesses nothing but desires to possess something, and therefore is always thinking how he might acquire riches. Sometimes he considers how he would distribute or increase them if he obtained them. Such was Simon Magus, and the world is full of people like him.

There is a fourth rich person who possesses riches and suffers hunger in order to have more. He thinks of nothing except how he may do the things of this world and rise higher and higher in worldly power. By whatever means he can, he oppresses his neighbors and brings accusations against whatever subjects he is able, in order to increase his riches. Those whom he cannot oppress he envies; he wishes to become superior, and is always in distress, although he is rich. Of this person it is written:

> The love of money grows as the money itself grows.

There are many thousands of such people in this world. Of them it is said here:

> It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven.

The camel is a beast of burden, like a donkey, though larger, and it is said to be named in Greek from its curved shape. For the Greeks call something curved *camon* [Greek term as transmitted], whence also comes *camus*, either because it has a curved neck or because it bends when it is loaded. It has a hump on its back. Arabia, moreover, produces better camels, having two humps on their backs and never wearing down their feet.

The rich man is therefore compared to this animal when he swells with abundant prosperity: he does not comfort the needy, visit the sick, receive guests, or perform the other duties of religion. Let all Christians therefore strive to avoid these latter kinds of rich people, because the Lord said of them: “As long as they remain such and refuse to be Christ’s poor, they cannot enter the kingdom of heaven.”

When the disciples heard this, they were greatly astonished, saying: “Who then can be saved?” When the disciples heard the Lord say that a rich man would enter with difficulty—and he did not say that it was impossible, but difficult—they were astonished, because they understood at once that those who, although they did not possess riches, nevertheless wished to possess them would not enter. They also understood that at that time there were few such people in the world, since there were no others except the Lord’s disciples. Now, however, there are many thousands of Christians who do not wish to possess riches, even if they could.

[Col. 1419A] Nevertheless, the Lord comforts them and says: “With human beings this is impossible, but with God all things are possible.” The almighty Lord, who created the camel, can make it pass through the eye of a needle. Just as he created the world from nothing and created a place that did not exist in which the world might exist, and just as he made a she-ass speak and made a rock travel with the army to provide water, so also from a corporeal animal—and from the one symbolized by the animal, namely, the rich man twisted in his schemes or pleasures—he can make a person upright and pure, so that he may pass along the narrow and confined way that leads to life, along which few of the rich walk, as he did with Zacchaeus.

It must not, however, be thought that the rich will enter the kingdom with their wickedness, [Col. 1419B] but rather that they must be changed for the better while they are still alive, so that they may be placed among the poor. He is called almighty for this reason: because he can do whatever he wishes.

The name “camel” can also be understood of our Redeemer, who humbled himself to bear the burdens of our sins. When he passed through the eye of the needle—that is, through the narrowness of his sufferings, through which, as through a needle, he deigned to mend the torn garments of our nature, that is, to restore them—we, being better reformed, might hear from the Apostle: “All of you who were baptized into Christ have put on Christ.”

Then Peter answered and said: “Behold, we have left everything.” When Peter heard the perfection proposed and praised by the Lord to the young man, he wished to know what reward awaited those who pursued it, and he said to the Lord: [Col. 1419C] “Behold, we have left everything.” How does he say “everything,” when he had nothing except a net and a boat—and even these he took back when necessity required? For we find that he went fishing after the resurrection.

Yet “everything” must be understood as everything that could have been desired, because they also abandoned the desire to possess. If some king had wished to give them many estates and honors, they would not have accepted them.

“And we have followed you.” That is, we have left everything in the way that you have left it, since you do not wish to possess anything in this world. We have followed you not only with the steps of our bodies but also by imitating your conduct.

In the same way, all monks and canons ought to leave things behind, just as the apostles did. From whom should bishops, presbyters, and deacons receive an example, if not from the one from whom they receive their rank? Just as in the old law the priests followed the example of Moses and Aaron, who were the first priests, so in the new law all apostolic men, bishops, presbyters, and the remaining orders ought to take their example from Christ and from the apostles.

Thus Paul also says: “Be imitators of me, as I am also of Christ.” Monks too, although they may appear to do something beyond what is written in the Gospel, ought nevertheless to observe the same standard. And if something more is commanded them, it is commanded for no other reason than that the Lord’s rule may be preserved.

For if we are commanded not to speak after Compline, this is commanded for no other reason than that, when those who have eaten begin to converse, some quarrel might arise and those who have kept too long a vigil might be unable to rise at the proper hour for the praises of God. If we are commanded to abstain from flesh without necessity, this has been done so that chastity may be preserved. For in a situation of necessity it is not prohibited.

We nevertheless believe with certainty that the Lord observed the same rule in food and drink as in other matters, taking only what was needed to sustain the body. Yet bodily necessity is not forbidden to us, just as Paul says: “Do not make provision for the flesh in its desires.” He does not say “in its necessities,” because what is necessary for the body as support is forbidden neither by God nor by any other teacher.

For blessed Benedict was not an imitator of someone else, nor did he wish to do more than the Lord, since it is enough for a disciple to be like his teacher, and then he will be perfect. Those who are called monks are called regulars because they live under a rule; and this is what *canonici* means in the Greek usage of the word.

All, nevertheless, have Christ as their example, and his apostles, whom they ought to imitate. Laypeople, however, have Nicodemus, Gamaliel, and Joseph; and if they are more powerful, they can find in the divine Scriptures someone whom they may imitate both in worldly power and in the gentleness and humility of Christ.

Behold, I shall set before you a rich man and a poor man of God: take an example from the very head, and do as he did. Let us see how Job was righteous. He had never heard the law in written form, yet he possessed worldly power and observed in practice the teachings of the Gospel, which were proclaimed much later.

Let us hear his own words, which he uttered unwillingly, yet not out of vainglory. He says: “Young men saw me and hid themselves; old men rose and stood. Princes ceased speaking and placed their finger upon their mouth. Leaders restrained their voice, and their tongue clung to their throat.” Here is royal power and honor.

Let us see, alongside this, the poverty later proclaimed by the Lord. “The ear that heard blessed me, because I had delivered the poor man who cried out, and the orphan who had no helper. The blessing of the one who was perishing came upon me, and I consoled the heart of the widow. I was an eye to the blind and a foot to the lame; I was a father to the poor. I broke the jaws of the wicked and snatched the prey from his teeth.”

Here is what God said: “I was hungry and you gave me food,” and the rest of the works of mercy.

Let us look further at excellence and humility. He continues: “When I sat like a king, with the army standing around me.” Here is excellence. “Yet I was a comforter of the sorrowful.”

Again: “If I despised judgment when my servant and my maidservant disputed against me; if I denied the poor what they desired and made the eyes of the widow wait; if I ate my morsel alone and the orphan did not eat from it; if I afflicted the souls of my farm laborers—for compassion grew with me from the beginning and came forth with me from my mother’s womb.”

Here is what the Lord said: “Blessed are the merciful,” and the rest.

Do you wish to know what he was like toward his subjects? He says: “If I raised my hand against the orphan, even when I saw myself in the gate in a position of authority. The stranger did not remain outside; my door was open to the traveler.”

Do you wish to know how chaste he was? He says: “I made a covenant with my eyes not to think upon a virgin.” And again: “If my heart was deceived concerning a woman, then let my wife be a prostitute for another man.”

Here are power and riches in one man. Those who do not wish to abandon power in every respect should retain it as this man did, who was richer than any of our kings, yet existed without the law of Moses and without the Gospel. Let anyone who wishes find such a rich man to imitate in both respects.

If I were not afraid of the length of the book, I would show what vigilance he exercised concerning his sons, what firmness he showed toward women, how strong he was in prosperity and adversity—how neither prosperity lifted him up nor adversity cast him down—even though the devil, using the woman who was his familiar vessel, stirred up wars against him with all his strength.

It follows: “Jesus then said to them.” Because Peter had spoken for all the apostles, the Lord answers them all, saying: “Amen, I say to you, you who [Col. 1421B] have followed me.” He does not say, “You who have left everything,” because many pagans and philosophers did this—Socrates and Chrysodemus, who, after selling their patrimonies, bought very precious gems and smashed them for the sake of popular approval. Diocletian too voluntarily abandoned the entire empire of the world.

But he speaks of what was more perfect: “you who have followed me” by imitating me.

“In the regeneration,” that is, in the renewal. Just as the soul is renewed through faith, so our bodies will be renewed on the day of judgment through incorruption.

“When the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty.” To sit is the posture of one judging; that is, when he comes to judgment. The throne is in the air, where the judgment of his majesty—that is, of his terror—will take place.

“You will sit upon twelve thrones.” By the number twelve, the entire perfect number of the saints is expressed. They will judge the wicked by comparison with themselves: why, since they too were clothed in flesh and created by God, did the wicked not keep God’s commandments as these saints did? Thus they will condemn them as worthy of Gehenna, because they refused to do what the saints did.

“Judging the twelve tribes of Israel.” Just as the entire number of the elect is expressed through the twelve apostles, so all the nations and the Jews are understood through the twelve tribes, because the number twelve is perfect and is found both among the pagans and consecrated in the divine Scriptures.

“And everyone who has left house, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or fields for the sake of my name will receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life.” That is, whoever has abandoned earthly things for God will receive spiritual goods, which, in comparison and according to their worth, will be as though the number one hundred were compared with a very small number.

Or, if we wish to speak of what is written elsewhere—that he will receive a hundredfold in this world—we may consider how much glory blessed Peter received in this world. After he came to the Lord, he was able by his word to kill the living, raise the dead, lift up the lame, and even, as is sung, to close and open heaven. How great this good was in comparison with what he had possessed before!

Even now he has a great kingdom of estates and servants throughout the whole world, both he and all the saints, for the love of God.

“But many who are first will be last, and the last first.” This can be understood of Jews and nations, of Judas and the thief, and of the lazy brother and the diligent one: often the slow brother, if nevertheless diligent, attains what the sharp-minded person loses through laziness.

## CHAPTER XLIV. On the Workers Hired for the Vineyard

“The kingdom of heaven is like a householder.” This parable is spoken in relation to the preceding verse: “For many who are first will be last.” The kingdom of heaven is understood as the present Church. The householder is almighty God, who possesses the universal vineyard, namely, the Church, which extends from righteous Abel to the last person who will be born at the end of the world, and which has produced saints as though it had sent out so many branches.

“Who went out early in the morning to hire workers for his vineyard.” For almighty God, at the beginning of the world, sent the patriarchs: Adam, Abel, Enoch, and the others.

[Col. 1422B] “And after agreeing with the workers for a denarius a day.” The Lord made an agreement with humanity when he promised that, in return for keeping the commandments, perpetuity and immortality would be given. Or the agreement may be understood as eternal life.

The first hour was from Adam to Noah; the third hour from Noah to Abraham; the sixth from Abraham to David; the ninth from David to John; and the eleventh, in which the apostles were sent, when those who came late received the full reward.

To them the Lord says elsewhere: “Others have labored, and you have entered into their labors.” In this passage the Gentiles are called, and to them it is also said: “Why do you stand here idle all day?” For they stood idle all day, as it were, because throughout the long period of four thousand years they did not worship the God of heaven.

They say to him: “Because no one has hired us.” That is, no one has preached to us the ways of life.

“Go also into my vineyard.” As though he were saying openly: “You too shall be my vineyard,” because until then the Jews alone had been called the Lord’s vineyard.

We can also understand the same intervals of hours in each individual person. He labors in the Lord’s vineyard from the first hour until evening who, living innocently in the Lord’s Church from childhood, instructs others by the good example of his life, or by example and word.

He labors at the third hour who is changed from wickedness after childhood. Someone is converted at the sixth hour when, in youth, he is recalled from evil works through God’s visitation. At the ninth hour, someone who comes to his senses after youth is changed, through the years of early adulthood, into God’s service.

At the eleventh hour the sinner is converted when he feels himself already near death. Then, through God’s mercy and visitation, he begins to consider what he has done over so long a time. As though God were speaking in his heart, he says: “For so long I have lived in my pleasures; now I am almost being dragged to hell, although I have never labored for the salvation of my soul.” Then he is afflicted with sorrow in God’s service. The later he begins, the more ardently he burns, and often he is rewarded before the one who has labored in God’s service from childhood.

“When evening had come, the lord of the vineyard said to his steward.” Evening is the day of retribution, or the day of judgment. The stewards of the vineyard are the angels of the Lord, or each individual person.

“Call the workers.” We are called every day, because every day we die.

And he gave each one [Col. 1423A] according to how he had labored in the Church, whether for good or for evil. He begins with the last, because he admitted the thief into paradise before Peter.

Therefore, when those who had come about the eleventh hour arrived, they received one denarius each. When the first also came, they thought that they would receive more. But they too received one denarius each.

For those from the Gentiles who believed through the apostles receive the same eternal life as the patriarchs and prophets who belonged to the line of Abraham received.

They are said to have murmured—not because those who were being admitted to life truly murmured, but because the Jews who were living at the time and to whom the Lord was speaking took offense and murmured in their hearts when they heard that God would make sons of Abraham from the Gentiles [Col. 1423B] and make them equal to the Jews.

The same meaning appears in the parable in Luke concerning the two sons, when one refused to enter because his father had received the prodigal son.

“These last have worked one hour, and you have made them equal to us who have borne the burden of the day and the heat.” This is what we read in the Passion of Saint Peter that the Jews said: “We are descended from the patriarchs, to whom God spoke, so that they might display his wonders. You have always worshiped idols; it is not right that you should now be made equal to us.”

To have borne the burden of the day and the heat means to have endured tribulations for God’s laws from the beginning of the world, as they did under Antiochus and other kings.

But he answered one of them and said: “Friend, I do you no injustice.” He calls the Jewish people themselves “friend” because of the prerogative of their fathers; they were also frequently called God’s sons.

“Did you not agree with me for a denarius?” Nothing is diminished for the Jews if almighty God gathers the nations and brings them into life.

“Take what is yours and go.” That is, let whoever among you wishes, through worthy works, receive the eternal life that I prepared for them from the beginning of the world.

“I wish to give to this last one as well as to you.” In his immense clemency, he gives equally to those who live worthily—those who were once called the tail—as to the Jews, who were called the head and the people of God.

“Or is your eye evil because I am good?” By the eye, envy is expressed, which the Jews always had toward the nations, and especially after the apostles’ preaching. Thus they said to Peter: “Why did you enter men who had the foreskin and eat with them?” Because God gathered the nations through his freely given mercy, the Jews took up envy.

“So the last will be first, and the first last.” We offer immense thanks to the clemency of God alone, because we have come to know the one whom we formerly did not know. What was said of the Jews can also be said of us: “God is known among the nations.”

“For many are called.” This refers both to Jews and to the nations.

“But few are chosen.” This is a sentence to be feared: few are those who serve God without defilement, and in many things we offend God without perceiving it. Whenever we do something good, if vainglory (*xenodoxia*) intrudes, we are deprived of our reward with God. For example, if we pray, fast, give alms, and perform other good works while seeking some praise, or wishing someone to see us doing this, we lose everything we do. Whenever we do not help our neighbor in his necessities when we are able, we pass over God’s commandment and lose charity.

What he says, “many are called,” can also be understood of Christians alone: they have been called through preaching, but nevertheless do not follow through in their works. Of these, the greater part walks along the broad way. Hence John says: “Whoever says that he knows God but does not keep his commandments is a liar.”

## CHAPTER XLV. On the Sons of Zebedee

“And as Jesus was going up to Jerusalem.” Because the Lord foresaw that the minds of the disciples would be disturbed by his Passion, he therefore predicted it to them more frequently, so that they might retain it in memory and then be more steadfast.

[Col. 1424B] “He took his twelve disciples aside privately and said to them.” He separated them from the crowd, because the mystery of the cross was not to be preached among the people until it had been accomplished.

“Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem.” “Behold” is an adverb used by one who points something out, because he was on the way as he went up to his Passion.
