He is said to go up from Jericho to Jerusalem, from the east to the south, because Jerusalem was higher than the other cities. It was the capital of that kingdom, situated at the navel of that land, rich in varied resources, fertile in crops, and renowned for its waters.

Shem, the son of Noah, who was called Melchizedek, built it and ruled in it. Later the Jebusites held it and called it Jebus; until then it had been called Salem. From these two names it was called Jerusalem. David later captured it, Solomon restored it, and it was called Hierosolyma, as if “Jebus of Solomon.” Under Aelius Hadrian it was finally called Aelia.

“And the Son of Man will be handed over.” He is called the Son of Man because, insofar as he was the son of holy Mary, he endured these things.

“To the chief priests.” By Judas, who was then with him.

“And they will condemn him to death.” That is, they will adjudge him worthy of death, although falsely.

“And they will hand him over to the Gentiles,” to Pilate and the soldiers, who were Romans.

“To be mocked.” This they did when they covered his head, struck him, and said: “Prophesy!”

“And to be scourged.” For he was scourged at the pillar.

“And to be crucified,” outside the gate.

“And on the third day he will rise.” He adds this for the disciples’ consolation. But, as Luke says, the apostles understood nothing, because they could not believe that the one who had been so exalted among the people could come to such disgrace.

Then the mother of the sons of Zebedee approached him. As what follows shows, the sons urged their mother to make these requests. They had heard the Lord say that he would rise on the third day, and they thought that the Lord’s kingdom would immediately appear—although it will come after the day of judgment. Therefore John and James made these requests through their mother.

He said to her: “What do you want?” He does not ask because he does not know, but so that he may respond more appropriately to what she says. He also gives pure-minded people an example not to answer before they have heard, as Solomon says: “Whoever answers before he hears shows himself to be a fool and worthy of confusion.”

[Col. 1425A] She said to him: “Say that these two sons of mine may sit, one at your right hand and one at your left, in your kingdom.” They had also heard the Lord say above: “You will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.” They wished to be first in that sitting, because they were not yet perfect.

The Lord answered: “You do not know what you are asking.” By saying to the woman who was making this request for her sons, “You do not know what you are asking,” the Lord shows that the mother’s request arose from the suggestion of her sons.

As another evangelist says, before they stated their request they asked him to grant whatever they might ask. But the Lord, in order to give people an example, neither granted nor denied anything until he had heard it. Who should grant something before knowing what he is granting? For if it should be evil, then, if he granted it, he would either be guilty of evil [Col. 1425B] or a liar.

Those who sought a higher place without life and works were still foolish according to God, and they wished to ascend into eternal life neither by the way nor by the door, but by some other route. Such offices, however, do not have guardians who permit anyone to obtain them by evil cleverness, as happens in this world.

“Can you drink the cup that I am about to drink?” By the cup, the Passion is understood. Thus the Lord, when his Passion was near, prayed: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me.” And the Psalmist says: “The cup of salvation.”

They say to him: “We can.” In their reply they speak confidently, just as Peter had said: “Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you.”

He says to them: “You will indeed drink my cup”—that is, “you will endure my sufferings.”

It is asked how these two drank the Lord’s cup. For James, it is certain how he ended his life through the palm of martyrdom: he was beheaded by Herod’s nephew. John, however, ended his life in peace under the emperor Trajan. But if we recall the Scriptures, we will find that he suffered much for Christ.

In the synagogue of the Jews he was scourged with the other apostles; afterward, voluntarily for the Lord, he went into exile in Greece; then he was also banished far away to Patmos; and finally he was lowered into a vessel of boiling oil. He endured many such things for Christ, in which he repaid the Lord what he had first received from him by drinking his cup.

“But to sit at my right hand or at my left is not mine to give you.” This means: “There is no partiality with God. It is not the giver who determines this, but the recipient—the one who prepares himself in such a way that he is worthy to receive it.”

It is not the one who merely says it, but the one who does it, who receives that place. It is not mine to give to the proud, such as you are, but to the humble. If you wish to have it, change your mind. Become humbler than all, and strive to conquer the devil. Then it will be given to you by my Father and by me—not merely by this man whom you thought you could unjustly bend through a woman’s entreaty.

Or it means: “It is not mine to give you in the manner you ask; it has been prepared by my Father from the beginning of the world for the victorious.”

When the ten heard this, they were indignant at the two brothers. They were not indignant at the woman but at the sons, because they understood that she had made this request after being prompted by her sons, who did not yet know their own measure; and therefore they had flared up over a small desire.

Jesus then called them to himself and said: He called them to himself and made them draw near from the crowds, wishing to correct all of them privately: the two for a request that was not fitting for them, and the others for their indignation against their brothers.

He acted like a compassionate teacher. Gently he explained how they all ought to humble themselves and serve their brothers, not rule through positions of power or acquire authority by evil cleverness, as many Christians do.

“You know that the rulers of the nations lord it over them, and those who are greater exercise authority over them.” He gives an example by contrast—something to avoid, not imitate—so that, knowing this, they might strive to act otherwise.

Those who are greater in this world are so through tyranny; and through power they are greater over them, because every rich man is either wicked or the heir of a wicked man.

Among secular people this figure is called “from opposites,” as when someone wishes to show another the right road and says: “There is a pit on the left,” not so that he may fall into it, but so that he may beware.

In the same way the Lord says: “It shall not be so among you.” For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God.

“But whoever wishes to become greater among you shall be your servant.” This is what he said elsewhere: “Whoever humbles himself in this world will be exalted by God in the other.”

Let them not seek greatness through empty words, and do not be indignant if others wish to possess it. Rather, both you and those who wish to be first among you must be your servants. The meaning is one, whether in “servant” or in “minister.”

And so that this might be fixed more deeply in their hearts, he adds his own example, saying: [Col. 1426C] “Just as the Son of Man did not come to be served but to serve.”

Everything the Lord did at his first coming was displayed to us as an example of humility. Although he was the creator of the earth, he did not wish to rule in this world, but to become poor, to travel on foot to preach, to visit the sick, to feed the crowds, to wash the disciples’ feet, and to perform the remaining duties of mercy himself—and finally to give his life for many.

He does not say “for all,” but “for many,” namely, for those who wish to believe. Similarly, in the canon of the Mass it is sung concerning the Lord’s blood: “Which will be poured out for you and for many for the forgiveness of sins.”

## CHAPTER XLVI. On the Two Blind Men Who Were Given Sight

“And as they were going out from Jericho, a great crowd followed him.” It appears that the Lord, coming from Galilee and crossing the Jordan, did not go directly to Jerusalem, but came from Jericho along the Jordan. From there he took the public road that ascends from across the Jordan to Jerusalem, a road on which many robberies occurred between Jericho and Jerusalem, until the Romans built a fort there and sent a military guard.

Because this was a public road, blind men remained there to ask for alms. One of them was so well known that another evangelist gave both his name and his father’s name. Nevertheless, the other evangelists mention only one, who represents the people of the nations, because they wrote for the nations. Matthew, however, who wrote for believing Hebrews, [Col. 1427A] mentioned two, so that Jews and nations might be understood through those two.

The historical truth is clear, as is the Lord’s power. Allegorically, however, Jericho is interpreted as “moon,” and through the moon the decline and mutability of our flesh are expressed.

When the Lord approached Jericho, he gave sight to one blind man. But when he began to depart and ascend to Jerusalem, he gave sight to two, because when he assumed the mortality of our corruption, he healed many from the Jewish people of spiritual blindness. When he became immortal after the resurrection, he gave light to both peoples, for the most part, through his apostles.

They are rightly said to have been sitting beside the way, because they were not on the way. He said: “I am the way.” They were beside it because the Jews knew something about the Creator through the law, and the philosophers of the nations knew the Creator of heaven through natural knowledge. Plato also left this written in his books.

“They heard that Jesus was passing by.” The Jews heard through the prophets; the nations too were not wholly ignorant, but their wise men likewise announced him. Hence there is Virgil’s line:

> Now a new generation is sent down from high heaven.

And the Sibyl says:

> From heaven the King Christ will come, destined to endure through the ages.  
> Present in the flesh, so that he may judge the world, where the unbelieving and the faithful will behold God.

Another man, when he had come near death, called his disciples and said to them: “I am now dying. Write down the dream I saw and had hidden in my mind. Now I know that I will not see that dream fulfilled in reality, but blessed will be those who see it.

“I dreamed that wine rained from heaven, and a mist rose from the earth and from the waters, and mingled with it. And I know that Divinity will come from heaven and mingle with flesh.”

Was he not, as it were, saying: “Truth will spring up from the earth, and righteousness will come forth from heaven”?

Thus, in this manner, Jews and Gentiles were sitting beside the way, and they cried out, saying: “Lord, have mercy on us, Son of David.” Long ago the people of the nations had cried out: “Hosanna, Son of David, have mercy on us.”

But the crowd rebuked them so that they would be silent. This may refer either to the Jews, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles, or to that part of the people which does not believe and which wished to hinder the faithful people from believing in their God. Hence it also produced many martyrs through torments.

Or the crowd may be the tumult of vices that resist our turning to God.

But they cried out even more, saying this, because the Church grew greater through persecutions.

“And Jesus stood still and called them.” He passed by us when he was born, suffered, and rose again. He stood still when, after his ascension, he became unchangeable in heaven at the right hand of the Father. Or he is said to have stood still because of the help he provides to his faithful.

“What do you want me to do for you?” He wishes them to ask for what he already knows he will grant them when they ask. “The Lord is near to all who call upon him.”

They say to him: “That our eyes may be opened.” This is certainly what the people of the elect pray for: that they may be worthy to see with spiritual eyes, without end, the King of the ages in his beauty.

Or they pray that he may open for the rest of the people the ears of their hearts, so that they may understand the hidden things of the mystery. Let us too seek the light that we may be able to see only with the angels.

Moved with compassion for them, Jesus touched their eyes. For if anyone believes, he believes because Christ himself gives the increase.

Immediately they saw and followed him. For whoever sees Jesus with the eyes of the mind follows him by imitating his actions. He sees and follows who practices the good that he understands. He sees but does not follow who indeed understands the good but refuses to practice it. For he follows Jesus who imitates him.

Hence it is said: “If anyone serves me, let him follow me”—that is, “let him imitate me.”

Through these blind men we can understand the Jews, or the Pharisees.

## CHAPTER XLVII. [Col. 1428B] On the Lord’s Reception by the Jerusalemites

And when they had drawn near to Jerusalem and had come to Bethphage, at the Mount of Olives.

Our Lord Jesus Christ dispensed everything orderly and wisely, as the Wisdom of God. He himself truly performed certain miracles to stir the hearts of the elect and the reprobate; and through these the good advanced, while the wicked became worse, until they conspired together over his death. When they desired to kill him before the time appointed by his will, they could not touch him. But when the days of his will drew near, they received permission, and became even more frenzied over his wondrous deeds.

To show that he was the Son of him who once, from the time of Samuel, struck the Philistines together with their gods, and caused his ark to be brought back to its proper place by means of cows that had recently calved, the Lord employed another animal to demonstrate this. For just as those cows, which had never yet borne a yoke, although they had young calves, nevertheless, after receiving the Lord’s ark, went along a road they did not know, proceeding and lowing as if they were saying: “We do not forget our calves, but we fear the Creator, whose ark we are carrying, more”; so also this young donkey, which had never before been separated from its mother and had never had a rider, acted in the same way after receiving the Lord’s body.

When he had come to Bethphage, he sent two disciples, saying:

Bethphage is a small village on the Mount of Olives, near Bethany. It was a little settlement of priests, and its name is interpreted as “house of the mouth” or “of the jaws,” because the heads of rams and goats lay there.

When, therefore, the Lord had come there on the first day of the week, which among us is called the Lord’s Day, he sent two of his disciples, while he himself went on to Bethany and remained there that night in the house of Simon the leper. Mary, Lazarus’s sister, also came there and poured ointment over his head. Meanwhile the disciples brought the she-ass and the colt, and people in Jerusalem heard that he was there. For they had not seen him after he had raised Lazarus.

The Lord had often come to Jerusalem, but he had never entered it with such glory as at that time, so that those who had previously wanted to kill him might then have the opportunity. For at that time he was pleased to die, as if he had said to them through his deeds: “You become worse because of the benefits I have bestowed on you, and you wish to kill me. Now, if you wish, I give you the opportunity. Yet I perform greater wonders than I did before. I raised the dead for you; just now I have raised one who had been dead four days.

“And so that you may recognize me as the Son of that God whom you claim to worship, just as you read that the little cows forgot their nature and their love for their calves because of the Lord’s ark that was upon them, so see here the young donkey forgetting its love for its mother and going along my road without a bridle or halter. As if that brute animal itself were saying to you: ‘I love my mother, but I fear more the Creator whom I have as my rider.’”

Then Jesus sent two of his disciples, saying:

“Go into the village that is opposite you.”

The village is now called Jerusalem, which was once called the city of the great King, that is, of God, because its citizens had conspired to kill their Savior. “That is opposite you,” because they could already see it from the same Mount of Olives. Bethany, however, was fifteen stades from Jerusalem. Yet the Temple was constructed in such a way that from it the olive trees on that mountain could be seen, and from the mountain itself the burning oil in the Lord’s Temple could be seen.

“And immediately you will find a she-ass tied up, and a colt with her.”

This she-ass had been given to the Lord’s Temple and belonged commonly to the priests; any one of them who wished could take her. A colt is called an *asellus*, that is, “a little donkey,” because it is its diminutive. The young offspring of any animal or bird may be called a *pullus* while it is still young, as in “young doves” and “young sparrows.”

“Untie them,” that is, release them from their bonds. “Bring them to me,” because I must perform a work of power with them, so that they may be separated from one another.

“And if anyone says anything to you, say that the Lord has need of them, and immediately he will let them go.”

Because they had many lords, he commanded them to say simply “the Lord,” without identifying any particular one.

It pleased the Lord to perform this work with the priests’ young donkey, so that they would know that it had never before had a rider upon it, since the priests especially opposed his works.

“Now all this took place.”

What does “all this took place” mean? It means that they were to bring the animals so that he might sit upon them. For this had been foretold by the prophet Zechariah. Whatever God was going to do bodily in this world was all foretold by the prophets, and this deed too was announced beforehand as something he would perform.

The Lord also chose to bring the words of the prophets into agreement with his deeds, so that he might be shown truthful both in the prophets’ words and in his own works. For he is truth and cannot lie, as the Psalm says: “The Lord is righteous in all his ways and holy in all his works.” The passage we read in the Book of Kings, where the spirit says, “I will go out, and I will be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets,” refers not to the Holy Spirit but to the devil, who, for a time and because of the king’s sin, deceived the hearts of his prophets.

“Tell the daughter of Zion.”

Tell her with exultation and rejoicing.

It was the custom among the Romans, after their enemies had been defeated, to enter Rome in a triumph. The whole senate, every dignitary, and all the people would come out to meet the victor; they would compose praises in verse and sing them to him. He would throw golden coins over them on one occasion and silver coins on another.

But no one entered so gloriously as our Lord did here. For while lies were sung to those other victors, these people pleaded: “Save, we pray, in the highest.”

“Behold.”

This expresses amazement.

“A King.”

Not a tyrant, because a king’s duty is to rule and govern the people, to free the oppressed, and to defeat the oppressors. Whoever does not do this is not a king but a tyrant, who occupies the position and perhaps himself ravages them and allows others to plunder them.

“Your king.”

The prophetic word is addressed to spiritual Israel: “He will be yours, to save and rule you, if you are willing. But if you are unwilling, he will not destroy you; he will allow you to be destroyed, because God is not the tempter of evil.”

“He comes to you.”

That is, he comes for your benefit.

“Gentle.”

As he later said: “I am gentle and humble in heart.”

“Sitting upon a she-ass.”

The Lord could have had a horse or an elephant to ride, he who could have had lions and griffins to subdue the Egyptians. But just as there he subdued the proud through small animals, so here he wished by means of a lowly and brutish animal to confound the wise of this world.

It is as if the prophet were saying: “Certainly not upon a golden chariot, nor upon a fiery horse, a lover of strife and discord, whose breast is filled with pride, who, when he hears the sound of the trumpet and sees battle, strikes the earth with his hoof and says in his heart: ‘Ha!’ He sits upon a colt upon which no human being has sat.”

It not only does not bite the iron, stain the gold with saliva, or possess a halter; it proceeds along its road and is subject to the yoke because it is a friend of peace.

The disciples went and did as Jesus had instructed. They said, as the other evangelists relate: “Bring them.” They brought them, and they did not sit upon them but led them by the hand. They placed their garments upon them—not a saddle adorned with gold or silver, since these things were required only for the mystery.

A very large crowd spread their garments on the road, so that the young donkey would not fall into a pit. Some spread their garments; others spread branches from the trees.

The crowds that went before him and those that followed cried out, saying:

The crowds that went before him were those who had come from the city to meet him. Those who followed were those who had followed him from Jericho and the other cities, coming to the feast of Passover.

“ Hosanna to the Son of David! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!”

The word *hosanna* is Hebrew, formed from a complete expression that has been corrupted. Among the Hebrews, “save, I pray” is said *hosanna*, an interjection of one who makes a plea. When the words are joined together, the *i* is removed by synaloepha, so that it is not even written, and the form becomes *hosanna*: the *o* is separate, while the *s* is joined with the *a* and *n*.

Thus also in the one hundred seventeenth Psalm, where we have written, “O Lord, save,” the Hebrew has *hosanna*.

“Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.”

He is blessed because he comes in the name of the Father. Another comes in his own name, and therefore he will be accursed.

Since we have said something of the literal sense, let us now proceed spiritually.

The Lord came to the Mount of Olives, that is, to his Church—not a Church that existed at that time, but the Church that he made by seeking his own, in which there is consolation amid labors and sorrows. He remained in Bethany, that is, in the “house of obedience,” because before his Passion the foundations of his Church had already been laid. In it were those of whom it could be said: “Upon whom shall I rest, if not upon the humble and quiet person who trembles at my words?”

He sent two disciples because of the two peoples, or because of the two commandments: love of God and love of neighbor. He commanded the she-ass and the colt to be brought to him: the Jews and the Gentiles, because, according to God’s plan, Judaea is the mother of the nations.

“You will find a she-ass tied up, and a colt with her.”

When the Lord came, the whole world was held bound under original sins.

“Untie them,” through your ministry.

The apostles brought them to him and placed garments upon them, that is, sacred teachings. They made Christ sit above them, so that those who had previously had the devil as their rider might thereafter have God.

The other evangelists, who wrote about the Gentiles, mention only that the colt was brought. Matthew, however, who wrote for believing Jews, also mentions the she-ass, to show that the Jews would receive the faith of Christ. Since the Gentiles were to be gathered completely, while Judaea was to be postponed until the end, Christ is said to have sat upon the colt.

It is rightly said: “Upon which no human being has sat,” because none of the teachers had been sent to them to instruct them to restrain themselves from evil speech or evil deeds.

A very large crowd spread their garments on the road, because many among the Gentiles gave their bodies for the Lord in martyrdom, so that they might provide others with an example of how they ought to love God.

Others cut branches from the trees: the teachers set before them examples of the saints in order to encourage them.

“And those who went before and those who followed.”

The patriarchs and prophets went before, and we follow, worshiping one God and offering one supplication. Although the Jews receive our one Lord Jesus Christ, we too believe in that same one. We believe with the firmest faith that we worship the God of the Hebrews, to whom we say what David said: “O Lord, save us on earth and lead us to possess and inhabit the heavenly Jerusalem.”

According to the anagogical sense, if we keep the Lord’s commandments, Christ dwells and presides in our body. We spread our garments if we discipline our bodies through abstinence, so that we may always prepare a way for him and provide others with a good example of conduct. We pluck branches if we extract from the teaching of truth the judgments of the Fathers. And we confess him as blessed in the name of the Lord, because our one hope and faith belong both to the peoples who went before and to those who follow.

And when he had entered Jerusalem, the whole city was stirred.

His entry into Jerusalem took place on the fifth day before Passover, on the second day of the week. On that day the lamb that was to be sacrificed at Passover was also commanded to be brought into the house and kept until the fourteenth day of the moon. He wished to show that he was coming to his Passion not unwillingly but voluntarily: he went to the place of his Passion and waited through those days until he was seized.

“The whole city was stirred.”

Some were stirred with good will, others with evil.

Those who said, “Who is this?” were the rulers. They seemed to disdain acknowledging the one whom the common people venerated.

But the people said:

The poor proclaimed the Lord as a prophet, because they did not dare say to the rulers, “He is the Christ” or “He is God,” but only, “He is a prophet.” Yet they did not lie, since God himself also called himself a prophet.

“This is Jesus, the Nazarene of Galilee.”

Nazareth is a village in Galilee where the angel Gabriel spoke to holy Mary concerning the Lord’s incarnation. Nazareth is the city where he was brought up, and from it he was called a Nazarene.

And Jesus entered the Temple of God.

He gave an example to everyone: whenever they come into a city or village, they should immediately seek God at the Lord’s Temple, and afterward attend to the matters for which they came.

And he drove out all who were selling and buying in the Temple.

Because the priests did not dare lend money at interest, since this was forbidden in the Law, they devised a way to recover that loss. Many came from distant places who had nothing to offer. The priests took the birds or other things that had already been given for the Temple and put them up for sale. In this way they retained both the things themselves and the money paid for them. Those who did not have the price borrowed from them. Thus they plundered the poor and did not consider what God had said: that he desired mercy more than sacrifice.

Understanding this plunder, the Lord made a whip from cords and drove the whole crowd out of the Temple, provoking great scandal in the two chief men—either because he drove out their sellers or because he took care of the Temple, which seemed to belong to them.

“And the tables of the money-changers.”

The money-changers had tables with coins upon them, for exchanging money if anyone wished.

“And he overturned the seats of those selling doves.”

These birds were frequently commanded to be offered, and they were expensive in many purifications, as we also read concerning sparrows. Therefore men of standing were sellers of those doves, and they had seats on which to sit.

Spiritually, the money-changers are those who ought to proclaim the divine words among the peoples, because “the sayings of the Lord are pure sayings, silver tested in the fire.” Those who have been made watchmen among the peoples and do not announce their iniquities to them, but instead tell them pleasing and flattering things, saying to the wicked, “You are good”—these are the money-changers who exchange silver.

The doves signify the spirit or the gift of the Holy Spirit. Those who sell for money the grace of the Holy Spirit, which they ought to give freely—such things as baptism, the laying on of hands, and ecclesiastical ranks—are called sellers of doves.

If, therefore, Christ finds such people in his Church, people who sell or buy the divine word and sacred mysteries—namely, episcopates, presbyterates, and diaconates—for rewards, they are driven out of the Church of God, and their seats, that is, their teaching authority, will be overturned.

And he said to them:

“It is written: My house shall be called a house of prayer, but you have made it a den of thieves.”

The person who seeks profit from religion or from the divine mystery, attaining it not on account of the merit of his life and wisdom, nor through the election of the elect and the people, but through gain, has turned the Lord’s house into a den of thieves. As long as he lives, he will be regarded before God not as a shepherd but as a hireling and a merchant, because he seeks to recover what he has given: he sought earthly gain, not the profit of souls. This is the Simoniac heresy.

Each one of us ought to be the Temple of the Lord, as Paul says: “The Temple of God is holy, and you are that Temple.” Let us see to it that the Lord finds nothing in our temple except what pleases him: love of God and of neighbor, and the other things that accord with these.

And the blind and the lame came to him in the Temple, and he healed them.

The Psalmist says: “The Lord is exalted and humble; he regards the lowly, but the proud he knows from afar.”

In this deed he appeared so terrifying to the rulers that they did not dare resist him in any way or even look at him. But he was gentle toward the good, so that when the wicked fled from before him out of the Temple, the blind and the lame approached and were healed.

Blessed Jerome says:

Among all the things our Lord did in this world, he performed nothing so astonishing as this: that one man, and at that time a contemptible man—so much so that he was afterward crucified—while the Scribes and Pharisees raged against him and watched their profits being destroyed, could with a single whip drive out such a great multitude, overturn tables, break seats, and do other things that an innumerable army could not have done.

Titus fought a great battle in the Temple after Jerusalem had been captured. But, as that same Jerome says, “Something fiery and star-like radiated from his eyes, and the majesty of his divinity shone in his face.” For this reason they did not dare lay hands upon him or assert their authority against him. Nor did they dare say what they later said: “By what authority are you doing these things?” They said only: “Do you hear what these people are saying?” It was as if they had said: “The things said about you are things said about God.”

But the Lord so moderated his reply that he both showed that this had been spoken about him and ensured that his answer would not expose him to rebuke. He did not say, “I am the God about whom these things were spoken,” although that was true. Instead he said that the prophet had foretold that praise would be perfected for God from the mouths of infants, so that they might inquire of whom this should be understood.

For the other evangelists say: “He said to them, ‘If these people are silent, the stones will cry out.’”

The deed of the children is confirmed from the one hundred seventeenth Psalm.

And leaving them, he went out of the city to Bethany, and remained there.

Mark says that he stayed until evening, looked around at everything, and went out. From this it may be understood that he was so poor that in such a large city he found no lodging. Nevertheless, we believe that the rulers who most intensely envied his deeds were staying in that city, and that the good people who still loved the glory of God more than that of human beings were afraid to receive him because of their anger.

## CHAPTER XLVIII. On the Withered Fig Tree

But as he was returning to the city in the morning, he was hungry.

Just as everything he said was full of mysteries, so nothing he did was without sacramental significance. When he was returning from Bethany, where he had spent that night, to the faithless city of Jerusalem, he was hungry—either because of the reality of human weakness, since he had not indulged in a heavy meal the previous night, or because he hungered for the salvation of the faithless city. For this was also why he returned to it in the morning: so that he might convert someone.

“And seeing one fig tree.”

The fig is so called from its fruitfulness, because it provides a richer yield than all the other trees, both in offspring and in fruit. It bears fruit three times a year. The first two harvests are better; the third is already despised. Its fruits are called *caricae*, named from their abundance. In the Book of Kings it says: “Cakes of figs.”

He therefore came to the fig tree—not because he was ignorant that it had no fruit, since it was not the season; it was before Passover—but to show what would happen to the Synagogue or the city, over which he had wept the previous day.

Just as he came to the tree with leaves and found no fruit at all, so he came to the Synagogue, which possessed the sayings of the Law and the prophets, and found no fruit of works. Every tree is recognized not by its flowers and leaves but by its fruit. Likewise, every person is judged good not by reputation or the display of speech but by the true performance of works. It is useful to say good things, but it is more useful when deeds correspond to what is said.

And just as the fig tree without fruit was condemned, so Judaea, possessing the words of the Scriptures without perfection in works, was condemned and punished. Not all Judaea was without fruit, for the apostles and the primitive Church came from it; but the greater part of it persisted in unbelief.

Similarly, under the figure of the fig tree, the Lord speaks elsewhere of the Synagogue, of the fig tree planted in the vineyard. This fig tree stood beside the road because it possessed the Law and the prophets, but it did not understand among them the one who said, “I am the way.” It saw him but did not recognize him.

He came to it through his incarnation and found nothing in it except leaves. And he said to it:

“May fruit never grow from you again forever.”

The tree itself had committed no sin. But because it had been created for human use, he wished through the tree to terrify human beings, lest anyone, possessing words of righteousness but displaying them without works, should deserve to be cut down and thrown into the fire.

What he says, “forever,” does not signify perpetually but for some period. For *aion* is a Greek word meaning both “age” and “forever.” When *aionas ton aionon* is said, however, it signifies the infinite—“ages of ages.” In relation to the tree, this may be understood to mean that its leaves withered while its trunk remained sound, because Judaea will be converted at the end through Enoch and Elijah and will bear pleasing fruits for God.

If we wish to understand it entirely of the present people, we shall say that it is the people who cried: “His blood be upon us and upon our children.”

Finally, if we wish to understand it simply, the Lord, because he was soon to suffer, wished to strengthen the minds of the disciples, so that, just as he caused the fig tree to wither, he could, if he wished, do similar things to his enemies. Hence it is also said that they were amazed that it withered immediately.

And Jesus answered and said to them:

“Amen, I say to you: if you have faith and do not hesitate, you will do not only what was done to the fig tree; even if you say to this mountain, ‘Take yourself up and throw yourself into the sea,’ it will happen.”

According to the literal sense, this could happen to an earthly mountain. We read of the blessed Gregory of Nazianzus that when he wished to build a basilica, there was a rock on one side and a mountain on the other, narrowing the site. He prayed to the Lord that he might make the mountain withdraw farther away. When he returned in the morning, he found that it had happened as he had prayed. Likewise, we read that Saint Benedict performed similar deeds. Others too could have commanded such things, if they had wished.

In another sense, Scripture sometimes understands the mountain as the devil. The apostles did this not only then, but holy men do it every day when they drive him from the hearts of the good and allow him to remain in the hearts of the faithless, where he exercises the madness of his mind amid bitterness and turbulence.

Of this it is said in the Apocalypse: “And the second angel sounded his trumpet, and something like a great mountain burning with fire was cast into the sea.”

The mountain is cast into the sea when the devil leaves the hearts of the elect at the preaching of teachers and, enraged, turns toward the reprobate.

Paul removed the mountain from its place when he drove the evil spirit out of the pythoness at Philippi.

“And whatever you ask for in prayer, believing, you will receive.”

This is certainly so, provided that the Lord does not lose his name, that is, Jesus, because Jesus means “Savior.” If he were to grant something contrary to salvation, he would no longer be our Savior, which cannot happen. Our Savior often permits things that are contrary to our salvation, but he does not grant them.

## CHAPTER XLIX. The Lord Questioned by the Priests

And when he had come into the Temple, the chief priests and the elders of the people approached him, saying:

Just as they were always accustomed to turn God’s deeds toward an evil interpretation, so they did now. When they say, “By what authority are you doing these things?” they doubt God’s power and intend it to be understood that what he does belongs to the devil. And when they add, “Who gave you this authority?” they deny that he is the Son of God, supposing that he performs signs not by his own powers but by those of another.

Yet on that very day they did not dare to ask these questions.

But Jesus answered and said:

“I will ask you one question. If you answer me, I too will tell you by what authority I do these things. The baptism of John—where was it from: from heaven or from human beings?”

The Lord could have refuted his enemies through simple teaching. But it was fitting that he should answer their question in such a way that either by their silence or by their judgment they would condemn themselves, as indeed happened.

But they were thinking:

“If we say, ‘From heaven,’ he will say to us, ‘Why then did you not believe him?’ For he testified about me when you sent people to him, and from him you heard by what authority I do these things. If we say, ‘From human beings’—that is, that it was composed by human invention—we fear the crowd. For everyone regarded John as a prophet, because at his birth they had seen miracles take place.”

And they answered, saying:

“We do not know.”

Now, in order to conceal the truth, they turned to the way of humility and said that they did not know.

He said to them:

“Neither do I tell you by what authority I do these things.”

You do not wish to admit what you know, and I will not tell you what I know. You will lie; I am truth, and I cannot lie. I know, but I do not tell you.

There are two reasons why truth is to be withheld: when the one who hears cannot grasp it, as the Lord said to the disciples, “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now”; or when we foresee that the person to whom we ought to speak will become worse through our preaching. Concerning this the Lord also says: “See that you do not cast your pearls before swine.”

## CHAPTER L. On the Two Sons Sent into the Vineyard

“But what do you think? A certain man had two sons.”

Because the Pharisees were unwilling to give John a favorable testimony, the Lord himself praises John and those who listened to him, while condemning those who did not listen to the man who was present and were unwilling to bear witness even after his death.

This man is understood as God, who had both good and evil sons among the Jews by creation. Through Moses he commanded them to work in his vineyard by keeping themselves in the way of God and instructing others.

There were some who turned toward evil at the beginning of their lives, such as tax collectors and prostitutes. There were others who said that they ought to keep God’s Law, such as these Pharisees. But when John came and announced their sin to them, the former turned from their evil way and began ardently to do good.

These Pharisees, however, who said that they were righteous, were unwilling to obey him. They even consented to his being killed and plotted against the Lord himself.

Therefore the Lord sets forth the parable, saying:

“John came to you in the way of righteousness—in abstinence, chastity, and the other good things.”

The tax collectors, who at first said through their evil practices that they would not do so, repented. You neither acted then nor are you now willing to proclaim his good deeds.

It can also be understood of the two peoples, the Gentile and the Jewish. The Gentile people at the beginning of the world withdrew from the worship of God, but afterward repented and changed its way of life. The Jew said, “We will do everything that the Lord has commanded,” but neither then did he do so nor does he now; he is worse than the Gentile was when he worshiped idols.

## CHAPTER LI. On the Parable of the Vineyard Workers

“Listen to another parable.”

Because he was soon to depart from them through death, he pressed the words of life upon them all the more, and in his parables disclosed what they themselves were thinking and doing.

“A householder.”

I said above that *paterfamilias* is a compound noun formed from a nominative and an ancient genitive, because among the ancients it was customary, after the manner of the Greeks, for the genitive of the first declension also to end in *-as*. He is called a *paterfamilias* who presides over his entire household like a father.

God governs the whole world as a most loving father. He gives good things to everyone and evil to no one. If someone suffers some evil, the devil causes it. He is ready to do harm, and when he sees that God has abandoned someone because of his crimes, he immediately seizes him. Unless there were a good angel who resisted him and prevented him from doing as much harm as he wished, he would immediately destroy that person.

This householder is God, who planted the vineyard of which Isaiah speaks and at the end says: “For the vineyard of the Lord Sabaoth is the house of Israel.” And in the Psalm: “You brought a vine out of Egypt.”

“And he surrounded it with a hedge.”

Either the wall of the city or the assistance of the angels.

“And he dug a winepress in it.”

The altar of the Lord.

“And he built a tower.”

There is no doubt that this means the Temple, concerning which Micah says: “And you, tower of the cloudy daughter of Zion.”

“And he leased it to farmers.”

Elsewhere he calls them the workers of the vineyard, who were hired for a daily denarius at the first, third, sixth, and ninth hours.

“He went abroad.”

Not by changing his place, since God fills the entire world, but by leaving the farmers to their own will.

“When the time of the fruits drew near.”

He rightly says “the time of the fruits,” not “of progress,” because the Synagogue produced no perfect fruit, although it had been cultivated with care.

“And the farmers seized his servants, and struck one.”

For example, Moses and Aaron, whom they provoked in the camp.

“They killed another.”

For example, Ahimelech together with fifty priests.

“They stoned another.”

For example, Naboth.

“Again he sent other servants, more than the first, and they treated them in the same way.”

Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Zechariah.

“Finally he sent his son to them, saying, ‘They will fear my son.’”

When he says, “They will fear my son,” he is not speaking from ignorance, because there is nothing God the Father does not know. God is always said to deliberate in order that human free will may be preserved.

“But when the farmers saw the son, they said, ‘This is the heir. Come, let us kill him.’”

What they were plotting in their hiding places, the Lord spoke about openly, to show that he knew everything. For he now plainly says that the rulers crucified the Lord through envy, not through ignorance. They were saying: “If we let him go on, everyone will believe in him.”

The son’s inheritance is the Church, which he acquired through his blood. The Jews tried to make this inheritance their own when they crucified him. They sought to extinguish together with the Church the faith that his Church had in him, so that they might establish their own righteousness through the Law and with their own Synagogue.

“And they seized him, threw him out of the vineyard, and killed him.”

This is what they were going to do on the third day after he spoke these words. He speaks of future events as though they were past, because he knew the future with complete certainty; and if he had wished, he could have avoided his Passion.

“They threw him out of the vineyard,” because they led him outside the gate of Jerusalem to be crucified.

“Therefore, when the lord of the vineyard comes, what will he do to those farmers?”

They say to him:

“He will destroy those wicked men wickedly, and lease his vineyard to other farmers.”

Although they were wicked, being descended from priests they nevertheless prophesied the truth. He destroyed them wickedly through famine, than which nothing is harsher; it even compelled those under siege to eat human flesh. He destroyed them and entrusted his Church to Christian teachers.

Therefore let kings and bishops beware of this condemnation of the farmers, lest they too suffer similar things if they do not cultivate the Lord’s vineyard well—that is, the entire multitude of Christians.

Jesus said to them:

“Have you never read in the Scriptures: ‘The stone which the builders rejected’?”

He continues to foretell his Passion and, through a metaphor, compares the action of the Jews to the action performed upon an animate Christ by means of an inanimate stone—a hyperbole.

This is written in the one hundred seventeenth Psalm, which is sung entirely about the Lord’s coming. We have nothing there according to the literal sense; everything is allegory.

The Jews were the builders. While proclaiming their own teachings, they rejected the Lord as the foundation upon which to build their faith.

“This has become the cornerstone.”

Just as a stone at a corner receives two walls coming from different directions, so Christ receives the Jews and the Gentiles who wish to believe in him, and one house is built from stones—just as the Church of Christ is built from worthy people. And just as one stone bears another stone, so those who came before bore us, and we in turn ought by equal right to bear those who come after us.

Paul speaks of the vineyard and the building of the holy Church: “You are God’s cultivation, God’s building.”

That vineyard is the Church, the stones are its people, and the one precious stone laid in the foundation is Christ, whether the Jews wish it or not; and the evil farmers—that is, the builders—are answered: “this has been done by the Lord.”

Finally, unless this had been done by the Lord, the faith of Christ and his Church would not have filled the whole world, although all the rulers wished to extinguish it.

“And it is wonderful in our eyes.”

The whole incarnation of the Lord was accomplished wonderfully. But it is also sufficiently wonderful that all the nations have placed their foundation upon him and desire to hold firm faith and hope in him.

“Therefore I say to you: the kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits.”

Both parables—the one about the vineyard and the one about the stone—are explained in this verse. The farmers did not cultivate the Lord’s vineyard as they ought, and they rejected the cornerstone. Therefore the kingdom of God was taken away from them, namely, knowledge of the Scriptures, and given to the Gentiles who wish to practice what they read.

“And whoever falls upon this stone will be broken; but upon whomever it falls, it will crush him.”

The one who sins falls upon the Lord, yet still has hope of rising again through repentance, because “the righteous falls seven times and rises again.”

But the Lord falls upon unbelievers who refuse to acknowledge the Creator. The one who sins falls, but can rise again. The one who does not believe has already been judged, and eternal destruction will come upon him and crush him utterly.

And when the chief priests and the Pharisees heard his parables, they recognized that he was speaking about them. They knew what they themselves were plotting, and therefore understood that the comparisons were directed against them.

Hence a certain wise man said:

> “Conscious of his own guilt, each person thinks that everything is said about him.”

And while they sought to seize him, they feared the crowds, because the crowds regarded him as a prophet. A crowd is always in motion: just as it is easily moved to conversion, so it is inclined toward despair. The one whom on one day they had exalted with praises as God, on the sixth day they demanded should be crucified as a murderer.

## CHAPTER LII. On the Wedding Feast of the King’s Son
And Jesus, answering, spoke to them again in parables. “Answering” is said in response to their thoughts [Col. 1439A], because they were thinking not only of destroying him but also of destroying all who believed in him. Therefore he addressed to them the parable, saying:

“The kingdom of heaven is like a king who made a wedding feast for his son.”

This refers to Christ the Lord. The Church, gathered from both Jews and Gentiles—the assembly of the righteous—is called the kingdom of heaven. The kingdom of heaven, then, is the Church of the righteous. In this, the Father the King made a wedding feast for the Son, joining the holy Church to him through the mystery of the Incarnation.

“He sent his servants to call those invited to the wedding, and they were unwilling to come.”

These servants are understood as the prophets, David together with the others. For although the Law had been given and God had been announced through the prophets, almost the whole world nevertheless neglected God’s commandments.

“Again he sent other servants, saying: Tell those who were invited, ‘Behold, I have prepared my meal.’”

These other servants are understood as the apostles, who announced to us the delights prepared for those who love God, things “which eye has not seen nor ear heard.” One of them, speaking in the person of the Lord, said: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.”

Alternatively, the meal may mean the divine Scripture in the Lord’s Church.

“My bulls and fattened animals have been slaughtered.”

By metaphor, royal riches are being described; this is a kind of metaphor called allegory. By the bulls are understood the martyrs of the Old Testament, such as Eleazar and the Maccabees, who were permitted, as it were, to defend themselves with their horns and to hate their enemies. By the fattened animals, well-fed birds are understood. *Altilia*—“fattened animals”—is so called, as it were, from *alere*, “to nourish,” and in common speech refers to creatures that have been fed. The prophets are meant: nourished abundantly by the Holy Spirit and the word of God, some of them were lifted up from the earth.

“And everything is ready; come to the wedding.”

Likewise, Peter said: “When you see, you will rejoice with inexpressible and glorified joy.”

But they disregarded it and went away, one to his farm and another to his business.

Someone goes to his farm and scorns coming to the eternal banquet when, possessing sufficient earthly property, he has at hand the means to satisfy his pleasures. He does what pleases him, embraces what currently delights him, and neglects to consider the destination to which he has been called.

Another goes to his business when, having some occupation by which he can accumulate money or other worldly riches, or acquire wealth through commerce, he thinks more about these things than about what he promised at baptism. Let each person reflect on how he has offended God and for what reasons he neglects God’s commandments; then he will understand among whose number he will be counted and with whom he will be reckoned in the other life.

“But the rest seized his servants, treated them shamefully, and killed them.”

There is a distinction between those who, for the sake of their pleasures, refused to come to the eternal banquet—whether they are perfect Christians in the Church—and those who treated the servants sent to them with insults. The latter are judged doubly guilty: they not only did not come, but either insulted or killed the king’s servants.

All this was perpetrated by the Jews to whom these words were spoken. Let all Christians also beware lest they do similar things to them; lest, if they do not wish to come to the meal, they become an offense to those who do wish to go. For it is said to them: “Whatever you did for one of the least of mine, you did for me.”

But when the king heard this, he became angry.

At the beginning, he is called both man and king, because his clemency is narrated there: he invited all who wished to come to his banquet. Here, however, the name “man” is omitted, and he is called king alone when he is said to carry out vengeance:

“Sending his armies, he destroyed those murderers and burned their city.”

Literally, this happened to the Jews. Since they killed the servants of God sent to them, or encouraged those who killed them—formerly the prophets and now the apostles, John, James, the other James, Stephen, and countless others—God’s army was sent against them.

And rightly so, for Vespasian and Titus exercised God’s vengeance. He destroyed the murderers and burned the temple, which had been more magnificent; afterward the city was destroyed by the Romans themselves, and salt was scattered throughout it.

Then he said to his servants:

“The wedding is indeed ready.”

The wedding would have taken place then if they had joined themselves to that banquet. They were not worthy. They did not prepare themselves to be worthy.

“Go therefore to the exits of the roads.”

“Go and teach all the nations.”

At the exits of the roads were the Gentiles, because they had no Law by which they could have reached the one who said, “I am the way.”

“And whomever you find, call to the wedding.”

This happens every day: rich and poor, humble and proud, masters and servants, tax collectors and prostitutes are all called together, and it is said: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is drawing near.”

And his servants went out into the roads.

It says “into the roads,” not “into the road.” The singular number is understood in a good sense; in the plural, pleasures or different sects are meant.

“They gathered both good and bad.”

It must be asked how good people were found among the Gentiles. But it should be understood that they are called good in comparison with the wicked. Nevertheless, many good people were found among the Gentiles, such as Job, Jethro, and Achior. Even among the pagans there was considerable moral discrimination, since many detested vices, rejected riches, and worshiped the God of heaven.

“And the wedding hall was filled with those reclining at table.”

The wedding here is the present Church. We know that the Church is composed of both good and wicked. In heaven there are only the good; in hell, only the wicked. In the present Church there are both good and wicked.

The king entered to see those reclining at table, and he saw there a man not wearing a wedding garment.

The wedding garment is charity, because through love God joined the Church to himself. The wedding garment may also be understood as the garment of innocence that we receive in baptism.

The king will enter to inspect the garments when, on the day of judgment, he examines the merits of each person. But judgment is also carried out daily when someone departs from this body.

“To see those reclining at table”—that is, to recognize them in their faith.

“One who was not wearing [the garment].”

By this one, all the wicked are understood. Just as all the good are said to belong to one generation, so all the wicked are called one people: there is one spiritual Lord, God or the devil; one is either God’s or the devil’s.

“Friend, how did you come in here without a wedding garment?”

Behold, he even calls him “friend,” while rejecting his life, as though he were saying: “Friend according to faith, but not according to conduct.”

But he was speechless.

At that time no one will have an excuse in words, because the judge who rebukes outwardly will see inwardly and outwardly, and our conscience, as witness, will dare to say nothing else. As the apostle Paul says: “Their thoughts accuse one another on the day when God will judge the hidden things of human beings.”

Then the king says to the attendants:

“Bind his hands and feet.”

His hands and feet will be bound because then all our activity will cease.

“Cast him into the outer darkness.”

The inner darkness is blindness of mind; the outer darkness is eternal, where light will be absent. Whoever here did not take care to suffer the inner darkness will there also suffer the outer darkness.

“There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.”

Through the weeping of the eyes and the gnashing of the teeth, both the resurrection of the bodies and the greatness of the torments are expressed: there the eyes will weep because here they wandered through various paths; the teeth will gnash because here they rejoiced in gluttony. Thus each member will undergo the punishment to which it was subjected here while serving its particular vice.

“For many are called, but few are chosen.”

This was said of Christians who have been called through faith and baptism, because they are counted within the Church; yet, while maintaining the faith, they are known to lie to Christ through their Christian profession by their works, which belong to the devil. Therefore each of us must humble himself, because even if he is chosen, he does not know it.

## CHAPTER LIII. On rendering to God the things that are God’s

Then the Pharisees went away and took counsel in order to trap him in his speech.

“Then” is an adverb of time. It means “at that very time,” when they heard him prophesy serious accusations against them through the parables.

They approached and conferred together in order to trap him in his speech, so that whatever he said might be exposed to accusation. You heard this in the Gospel according to Luke, when a registration was made throughout the various regions of the world and in Judea for the payment of tribute and taxes to the Romans under Octavian.

There was therefore great disturbance among the people. Some said that it was not right for a people who paid tithes, firstfruits, and the other things sanctioned by the Law to pay tribute and taxes to the Romans. Others said that they could by no means refuse to pay tribute to the Romans, who held the whole world; and their soldiers also fought wherever necessary on behalf of those same Jews.

So they sent their own agents together with the agents of Herod the tetrarch, in order to question him. If he said that tribute should not be paid to the Romans, Herod’s soldiers would arrest him. But if he said that it should be paid to the Romans and not to God, they would immediately seize him as a transgressor of the Law.

Nevertheless, he did what he usually did: he passed through the snare that had been prepared.

“Teacher, we know that you are truthful, and that you teach the way of God in truth, and that you do not care about anyone. For you do not regard the status of persons.”

All these statements are true, but they were spoken with an evil intention. They were brought forward so that he would disregard Tiberius’ imperial authority and say that tribute should not be paid. They had perceived that he loved the worship of God more than the emperor; then Herod’s soldiers would immediately arrest him as one who contradicted Caesar.

“Is it lawful to pay the census-tax to Caesar or not?”

Jesus, knowing their wickedness, said:

“When you took counsel”—although he was far from you there—“even when you were thinking about it.

Why are you testing me, hypocrites? Whom do you not deceive by your cunning?”

The first virtue is to recognize the questioner’s intention; then one should answer according to the circumstances, as Solomon says: “Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he seem wise in his own eyes.”

“Show me the coin of the census-tax.”

One coin is called a denarius, whether of silver or bronze, and it is named from *nomen*, “name,” because the names of kings are impressed upon it. Alternatively, as some wish, it is named from Numa, the Roman ruler who first ordered this to be made among them.

Sometimes *nummus* is used for a solidus. *Numisma* in Greek is called *inflexio* in Latin, “a turning” or “impression.” This is shown by the fact that when the Lord ordered them to present a coin to him, they understood and offered a denarius.

The denarius is a kind of coin counted as ten bronze coins, and it bore in silver or bronze the image of Caesar. He could have said what he wished without displaying the coin, but it was more fitting to convict them through the coin itself.

“Whose image and inscription is this?”

It was similar to the way the names of emperors are now inscribed, and his figure was represented so that no one would dare adulterate the metal or despise the place where he saw Caesar’s image. Nowhere at all did they dare to despise an image of Caesar once it had been displayed.

They say to him, “Caesar’s”—that is, Tiberius’. Since Julius Caesar, the first so called, all later Roman emperors were called Caesars.

Then he says to them:

“Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s.”

If his image is on the denarius, it is clear that the coin belonged to the one who ordered his own image to be made upon it. What you have been paying for thirty years, do you want me to order you to abandon, when I, who possess nothing of the earth, have paid the tribute for myself and Peter, and have rendered to God the things that were God’s by doing the Father’s will? Rather, I will command you to be subject to the king, as to one who is preeminent.

“Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s”—namely, the tribute, the coin, and the other things you promised when you made your profession, during the days of your profession.

“And render to God the things that are God’s”—tithes, firstfruits, and the things commanded in the Law.

Just as Caesar demands his image from you, so God wishes to possess his undefiled image, which he established in you.

When they heard this, they marveled. Those who ought to have believed marveled because he had found an answer to their cunning.

And leaving him, they went away.

The unbelievers withdrew from the devout one, because different ways of life do not wish for unity. Since they were perverse, they did not wish to turn toward his righteousness; therefore they went away without fruit.

## CHAPTER LIV. On the woman who was married seven times

At that time the Sadducees approached him, who say that there is no resurrection.

There were two sects in Judea, the Pharisees and the Sadducees, yet all were Jews. They nevertheless lived and believed according to different customs.

The Pharisees lived communally, as the apostles later lived, and accepted seventy-two books. They were called Pharisees from Phares, the son of Judah, and the name is interpreted as “divided.”

The Sadducees lived as the prophets had lived. Yet they did not accept the prophets or believe them, nor did they accept any books except the Pentateuch. They did not believe that a future resurrection would occur, nor in an angel or spirit, but only in God. Just as among us there are monks and canons, although they belong to one Frankish people, so it was among them. They were nevertheless at odds with one another.

But at the time of the Lord’s temptation they agreed, just as Herod and Pilate became friends in the Lord’s Passion.

Until then the Pharisees had questioned the Lord—for they were stronger and more numerous—and had thought they could seize him, but they could not. The Sadducees approached, whose name is interpreted as “just,” from a certain Jew called Sadduceus, who had been the founder of this sect. They say that there is no resurrection.

For they said: “Why should we believe in a resurrection, when the Lord gave no command through Moses about it, although through him he commanded all the other good things?”

“Teacher Moses said: ‘If someone dies without having a son, let his brother marry his wife and raise up offspring for his brother.’”

God commanded this so that that people might multiply—the people he loved because of the patriarchs—and fill the earth, since at that time it was for the most part without inhabitants.

“There were seven brothers among us. The first married a wife and died.”

This could have happened among their people. For we read that some among them had twelve wives, and some women had ten husbands—people who did not believe in the resurrection of bodies.

They rightly invent such a fable by which they may accuse those who assert the resurrection of bodies of madness. Likewise the second and third, and so on up to the seventh; finally the woman also died.

They use the shamefulness of the story as an argument to deny the truth of the resurrection.

But Jesus answered and said to them:

“You are mistaken, knowing neither the Scriptures nor the power of God.”

He never answered the Pharisees so severely, because they possessed at least some reasoning, whereas these had none.

“You are mistaken in your sect, knowing neither the Scriptures nor the power of God,” because you have rejected the prophets and do not understand the Pentateuch or the power of God—that is, me, who am the power of the Father and the wisdom of the Father. You are mistaken because you are ignorant of the Scriptures and therefore also do not recognize the power of God, that is, Christ.

For not only can no one be wise concerning God if he does not know the Scriptures; no one can be perfectly wise even concerning worldly matters without knowledge of the Scriptures.

“For in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like the angels of God in heaven.”

The interpreter of this Gospel found in Greek an active and passive verb, although the verb is neutral and applies only to women. The proper expression is: “They will neither marry nor take wives.” For it is the woman’s role to marry, that is, to veil her head. Here, however, *nubere*—“to marry”—is used of women.

It is evident from the statement “they neither marry nor are given in marriage” that the bodies which can marry will rise; but there is another reason why they will not do so.

“But they are like the angels in heaven.”

That is, after they have risen, they will not be subject to bodily passions. They will not eat or drink, and they will not marry; yet they will have bodies, just as the Lord had a body that could eat but did not need or desire food. He ate in order to demonstrate the truth of the resurrection.

They will be like the angels of God in heaven, renewed with the glory of the resurrection. Without any stain of corruption, they will enjoy the perpetual vision of God.

“But concerning the resurrection of the dead, have you not read what was spoken by God, who said to you: ‘I am the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob’?”

They had read it, Lord, but they would not have understood it unless you had explained it.

The Lord could have produced much clearer testimonies concerning the resurrection from the prophets, among which is this: “The dead will be raised, and the dead will rise from the tombs.” And this: “Many of those sleeping in the dust of the earth will rise, some to eternal life and others to eternal disgrace and eternal confusion.”

Nevertheless, as I have said, they would not concern themselves with the sayings of the prophets unless the matter were demonstrated to them from something Moses had said. Therefore the testimony had to be given from the book they accepted, from that very book.

“He is not the God of the dead but of the living.”

When God spoke these words, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob had been dead for three hundred years. If the soul had perished together with the flesh, he would not have said, “I am their Lord,” if they were not still living in soul; rather, he would have said, “I was their God when they existed.”

No one says of someone who does not exist, “I am his Lord.” Since they denied that the soul existed after the death of the body, the Lord showed them that those of whom he said, “I am their God,” were alive.

And because their souls were alive, it is certain that their bodies too will rise and will receive the good or evil things they did while they lived.

When the crowds heard this, they marveled at his teaching.

The crowds marveled because many years had passed without either the Pharisees or the Sadducees understanding anything about the resurrection. For many years the Pharisees had been unable to convince them from those five books that the soul lived after death. But he knew, for he was the one who had spoken to Moses, with what meaning he had spoken that very word.

## CHAPTER LV. How the Pharisees question the Lord about the first commandment

But when the Pharisees heard that Jesus had silenced the Sadducees, they gathered together.

Again they gathered together and chose the wisest of their number. One of them, a teacher of the Law, questioned him, testing him, and said:

“Teacher, which is the great commandment in the Law?”

He wished to learn; for this reason he called him “teacher,” since that is the custom of disciples.

“Which is the great commandment in the Law?”

Let me explain why he wished to ask this. There was a question among the Jews. The priests who wished to receive burnt offerings frequently said that no action was as pleasing to God as offering him a sacrifice. But the wise considered that, without offerings of victims, many patriarchs had pleased God; and, instructed by the prophet, that God prefers each person to have knowledge of him rather than burnt offerings.

No one is ever found to have pleased God through burnt offerings alone, without faith and love. He declared that he held this position. For this reason the man asks which is the greatest and chief commandment, the one in which God takes the greatest delight.

Jesus said to him:

“You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind.”

The first and greatest commandment of all, therefore, is knowledge and confession of the divine unity, together with the practice of good works.

No limit or measure is imposed upon us in the love of God. With all our heart—as much as the soul can contain and the heart and mind can conceive—we must love God in thought, speech, and deed, without comparison to anything else.

This is the greatest and first commandment.

Now he makes clearer what the man had asked: this foundation of piety must be placed before and above all the commandments.

“And a second is like it: You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”

On these two commandments the whole Law and the prophets depend.

The Lord adds this to what he had been asked because the first cannot be fulfilled without the second: God himself commanded that one love one’s neighbor as oneself.

The first is greatest and chief; this second, nevertheless, comes first. For whoever does not love the neighbor whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see? Through love of neighbor one reaches love of God.

Whoever fulfills these two commandments fulfills everything the Law and the prophets commanded.

For whoever loves God does not worship gods, does not take the Lord’s name in vain, and does not violate the other commandments that concern the worship of God. Whoever loves his neighbor does not kill, commit adultery, steal, or bear false witness; he does not covet his neighbor’s property, because all these offenses are committed against one’s neighbors. In this way charity is preserved.

Concerning this it was said through the prophet: “The Lord will make a brief word upon the earth.”

## CHAPTER LVI. The Lord questions the Pharisees

When the Pharisees had gathered, Jesus questioned them, saying:

“What do you think about the Christ? Whose son is he?”

The Pharisees were always ready to raise questions. They had sometimes recognized that he could both solve everything and propose questions that they themselves could not solve.

The Lord questions them about the one whom they said would come—for they did not wish to believe that he was present—and asks whose son he ought to be.

If they had known what followed, they would have said, as they said concerning John, that they did not know.

They say to him, “David.”

For they had written the Lord’s saying to him: “From the fruit of your womb I will place [him] upon my throne.” Therefore they knew.

“How, then, does David call him Lord in the Spirit?”

In the Holy Spirit—not through uncertain error or personal will, but prophesying in the Holy Spirit—he calls him his Lord, saying:

“The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand.”

David prophesied about the ascension of the Lord Christ: the one born from holy Mary, raised above the angels and every creature, was placed at the Father’s right hand and began, through his humanity, to possess the honor of divinity that he had previously possessed through his divine nature.

Because the Jews disdained to believe that Christ was God and man, they could not understand this.

As for the enemies being subjected by the Father, this does not reveal weakness in the Son but demonstrates unity of nature. For the Son also subjects enemies to the Father, who glorifies the Father on earth.

“Sit at my right hand.”

In this sitting we should understand glory and stability. Since the Son, taken from holy Mary, did the Father’s will, the Father rightly said to him at his ascension, “Sit at my right hand.”

Victorious in glory.

“Right hand” does not indicate a location but equality.

“Until”—here it means “forever,” as in: “Until you grow old, I am God.”

It is as though he were saying: “Sit, because your enemies are being placed beneath your feet.” The Lord’s feet are understood either as the Incarnation or as the apostles.

And no one could answer him a word.

Then they were wickedly confounded, because they could not undo the word of the Psalm. After the Lord’s ascension, when others were likewise refuted by this word, they found an explanation that Melchizedek had said this to Abraham when he returned from battle. This cannot be understood in that way, because the following verse contradicts it:

“With you is the beginning on the day of your power,” and what follows.

And no one dared from that day onward to question him any further.

Now the Jews recognized with certainty that no one could trap him with words, because he spoke like a fountain of wisdom and caught the wise in their own cunning.

Afterward, they corrupted his disciple with money so that he might betray him without the crowds and, once they had seized him by force, hand him over to Roman authority.

From this it is understood that the poisons of envy can be overcome, but that it is difficult for envy to become quiet.

The Lord rebuked many things in the Pharisees.

Then Jesus spoke to the crowds and to his disciples, saying:

“The scribes and Pharisees have sat on Moses’ seat.”

Here he calls “seat” teaching authority and doctrine. That is, they claim for themselves the place and teaching authority that Moses once held over the people in the wilderness.

Similarly, we can understand “teaching” where it says, “and in the seat of pestilence.” And he overturned the seats of those selling doves.

“Therefore do and observe everything they tell you.”

Wonderful is the patience of God. They acted toward him as wickedly as they could, yet he nevertheless urged the people, on account of the dignity of the priesthood, to retain the good things they heard from them and to guard themselves from their evil deeds.

“Everything” means, implicitly, everything good. When the Scriptures were read, they did not dare to say anything other than good things because of the people, since they were all educated in the written word.

Thus many benefit by saying what they do not do, but they would benefit much more if they did what they say.

“But they bind heavy and unbearable burdens and lay them on people’s shoulders, while they themselves are unwilling to move them with their finger.”

Here “burdens” means their commandments and customs, which they drew out from their teaching. For this reason we must preserve the implicit qualification stated above: everything good that they say, just as in the apostle’s statement: “Test everything; if you find it to be good, hold on to it.”

Behold, here it says: “They bind heavy and unbearable burdens.” Everything would have to be done if they themselves were the ones binding such burdens. “They bind” means that they order each person to bind them.

Through metaphor and allegory, the burdens, the binding, the shoulders, and the fingers are all mentioned in the manner of a burden. Just as a burden is tied and placed upon the shoulder for carrying, and the person who imposes a burden usually helps the one who is carrying it, so these people impose upon the credulous commandments of their own invention. They themselves observe them neither in word nor for a moment, but command others to keep them—concerning their offerings and observances.

Whoever is a ruler in the Church must first fulfill the things he commands others to fulfill.

“But they do all their works in order to be seen by people.”

They do not seek recompense from God but praise from people. Whoever does something good in this manner, as they do, loses the whole benefit.

“For they enlarge their phylacteries.”

When God gave the Law through Moses, he said to their ancestors: “These things shall be in your hand and before your eyes”—that is, in memory and in action.

They, misunderstanding this, made for themselves on parchment the ten words of the Law and wrapped them around their heads. In Greek they called them *phylacteria*—that is, “safeguards”—because *phylaxe* in Greek means “to guard” in Latin.
