Then the one who most eagerly desired praise made the phylactery larger. Hence the Lord says: “They enlarge their phylacteries and magnify their tassels.”

Similarly, the Lord had commanded that blue tassels be made on the four corners of their cloaks, so that there might be a distinction between the people of Israel and foreigners; circumcision served this purpose on their bodies, and tassels on their clothing.

Thus, if they ever came to battle, they would recognize one another when they saw the tassels and know whom they ought to fight. By the circumcision of the dead they would know whom they should strip, because in battle a dead man frequently loses his head, but never that member.

Those tassels were therefore useful in battle, because a person could easily find them and they did not fall off like the little branches that soldiers customarily carried in battle, a sign that our people likewise make.

The Jews therefore devised a practice involving those tassels: they inserted thorns into them, so that when they were pricked they might remember the observance of God’s Law. Yet the woman who touched the Lord’s tassels found no thorns there.

Likewise, those who wished to be praised more greatly made the tassels larger.

“They love the first places at banquets.”

Among the ancient leaders, places at banquets were arranged in three parts: on the right, on the left, and behind, so that once satisfied, a person could recline in whichever part he wished. This arrangement was called a *triclinium*.

Those who love and seek these seats through hypocrisy are reproved.

“And the greetings in the marketplace”—that is, in public.

He did not condemn those who rightly possess such honors; it is the will and hypocrisy that are condemned.

“But do not be called rabbi.”

This is prohibited in the same manner as the preceding practices. Nevertheless, we must acknowledge the supreme Teacher of all doctrine and the Father of our authority, through whom we were created—the one who is in heaven—for he also commanded these things.

He did not prohibit calling someone “father” in the sense in which he commanded us to honor father and mother. Rather, he wanted each person to acknowledge and direct his mind toward the true Teacher and Father, the source of the human race.

For if we call someone “father,” we give honor to his age, but we do not consider him the author of our life; we consider God to be that author.

The same applies to “teacher” and “son”: such titles are used figuratively, whereas God is so called naturally.

“The one who is greatest among you will be your servant.”

Alternatively, this refers to the Lord himself, who was greater, because God did not come to be served but to serve; or it refers to his command that whoever wishes to become greater should serve the others.

“Whoever exalts himself in this world will be humbled in the next; and whoever humbles himself for God’s sake in this world will be exalted in the next.”

When almighty God sees those whom he loves being irrationally exalted through pride, he humbles them through some tribulation. Thus he acted with David: he permitted him to be driven from his kingdom, and, after he had been humbled, caused him to remain in the kingdom.

He did the same with Hezekiah. When Hezekiah became arrogant, God permitted him to be dominated by the king of the Assyrians, to such an extent that he gave the Assyrian king the doors of the Lord’s temple and the silver plates that he himself had attached. When the king’s messengers were shut up in the city, he did not dare to answer them harshly, although the holy prophet Isaiah was there.

After he had again been humbled, the Lord killed 185,000 of the Assyrian army on his behalf. The king fled from his land with ten men and was killed in his own land by his sons.

In this way God chastised many others whom he loved.

Some he sees loving earthly things entirely and preferring them to eternal things. He permits them to be exalted so that afterward they may be tormented without end. Such were many kings and tyrants of the Assyrians, Greeks, and Romans.

Others, walking in excessive pride, he humbles in this world and in the next, such as Nebuchadnezzar, Sennacherib, and the emperor Valerian, whom Sapor, king of the Persians, humbled so completely that whenever he wished to mount his horse, Sapor would stoop down and mount the horse from his back.

Herod too, because he permitted the peoples to call him lord, breathed his last after being eaten by worms for five days.

Fearing such pride, the ancient Roman emperors, although they were pagans, established that whenever the emperor was adorned with royal ornaments, he should hold in a pouch, in his left hand, dust from the body of a dead man, so that he might remember that he would shortly become ashes and not exalt himself above others.

Let whoever wishes choose one of these three.

I choose to be humbled now with the meek rather than divide spoils with the proud.

“But woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you shut the kingdom of heaven before people.”

“Woe” is the interjection of one who grieves, and here it signifies eternal weeping, in which those to whom he prophesied these things will be found.

By “scribes” the Sadducees, priests, Pharisees, and rulers of the people are also understood. The Pharisees were called after Phares, the son of Judah, because of the tribe of Judah, although all who held the same sect were called Pharisees. Thus Paul says: “Brothers, I am a Pharisee,” even though he belonged to the tribe of Benjamin.

They are called hypocrites—that is, pretenders—because of the matters previously reproved, their false interpretation.

“You who shut the kingdom of heaven.”

That is, you shut divine Scripture, either by concealing what you ought to teach them or by hiding it out of envy, unwilling that they should believe in me.

Every teacher who, together with good doctrine, provides his disciple with a bad example also shuts the kingdom of heaven before him.

Divine Scripture is called the kingdom of heaven because in it is found the knowledge by which the King of heaven and his kingdom are recognized, as well as eternal life.

Therefore, above, the Lord said: “The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits.”

### “For you do not enter”

For you do not enter. Behold, you yourselves are guilty, because you know what is good and do not do it, nor do you permit those entering to enter. The Lord shows that many wished to recognize him through the Scriptures, but they themselves were saying, “The Christ will not arise from Galilee”; yet they heard many calling him the Son of David, who was not from Galilee but from Bethlehem, whence also came holy Mary.

Woe to you. The omitted sense is: “it is impending.” You who travel around sea and dry land in order to make one proselyte. A *proselyte* was called “a newcomer” in Greek, because someone from another nation was converted to their law. Such were Jethro and Achior, and many thousands of men from the nations were circumcised and believed in the God of heaven. The Jews also went through foreign lands preaching the name of the Lord, as many Christians did after the Lord’s coming. These men, however, are blamed because they did this for the sake of profit, not out of love for the Lord, and because afterward they destroyed what they had accomplished by their evil example. By “sea” he also means the islands that are in the sea.

And when he has been made one, you make him a son of Gehenna twice as much as yourselves. For one who had previously gone astray once, when he saw their evil example, returned to his vomit and was then worthy to be beaten with many blows: “For the servant who knows his master’s will and does not act accordingly shall be beaten with many blows.” They are called sons of Gehenna, just as they are called sons of the world, because whoever performs someone’s works will also be called that person’s son.

Woe to you. The omitted sense is: “it is impending.” Blind guides. In terms of earthly and bodily blindness, no one who lacks the light of his eyes wishes to guide another. Yet many are blind in mind, that is, foolish, and wish to become guides, although they do not know how to walk the road itself or show it to others. There are also those who know it, but neither walk it themselves nor show others how to walk it.

Who say, “Whoever swears by the temple is nothing, but whoever swears by the gold of the temple is obligated.” The Jews had also devised this practice in this matter: whoever swore against his neighbor, for the sake of some reconciliation, by the temple—even if he swore falsely—was held guilty of no offense. But if he had sworn by the gold of the temple, he was compelled to pay what he had falsely sworn. Likewise, if he had sworn by the altar, he owed nothing. But if he had sworn falsely by the gift that was upon the altar, he was compelled to pay the priests as much as the gift itself was worth. Because they themselves accepted this, they said that the sin of perjury existed. Concerning perjury by the temple and the altar, which pertained to the restoration of the temple, they said that it was not perjury. The Lord approves this insofar as all things within the temple and altar are sanctified through them. He had already forbidden swearing by heaven above.

### [Col. 1450A]

Woe to you, Pharisees and scribes, hypocrites, because you tithe mint, dill, and cumin, and have abandoned the weightier matters of the law. It is evident that God greatly hates hypocrites, since he reproaches the Jews so often. When he says, “you tithe mint, dill, and cumin,” he shows through these cheaper garden herbs that they expressly collected tithes from everything that was cultivated, while neglecting judgment, mercy, and faith.

He did not threaten them with woe because they tithed even such lesser things, but because they abandoned the things that belonged to God, for the sake of which they collected tithes: namely, administering justice to the oppressed, or demanding it from those who ought to administer it. Likewise, they neglected mercy, as he himself showed in the parable of the wounded man: a priest and a Levite passed by, saw the wounded man, and were not merely unmoved by mercy but left him in an even worse condition, because they knew him and did not help him. Thus they proved themselves like robbers, because whoever does not help one who is perishing, when he can, kills him.

He blames them concerning faith because they did not keep faith with those to whom they owed it: first, with the Lord as God and Creator; then with father and mother; afterward, with all who worship God, since these are called their neighbors. Nevertheless, they are not blamed for receiving tithes, as he says in what follows, but because they abandon the things that belong to God and neighbor—judgment, mercy, and faith—and the weightier matters of the law, that is, its chief requirements.

For it is the duty of priests both to proclaim the Lord’s law among the peoples and to bring those who stray back to the law. They ought to have done this—that is, judgment, mercy, faith, and the things pertaining to them—without omitting those matters, while receiving tithes. Let the teachers of the churches who exercise a similar ministry among the peoples and hold the estates of the churches take heed, lest they become like these men if they remain silent about the people’s vices.

Blind guides, who strain out a gnat but swallow a camel. By the gnat, which is a fly equipped with a sting—for they have a tube in their mouth in the form of a spike, with which they pierce flesh in order to drink blood—lesser commandments are understood. By the camel, a crooked and misshapen animal, the greater commandments are understood. To strain out, in human practice, is to reduce something to such a liquid state that it can pass through hairs. To strain out the gnat means to treat the lesser commandments carefully, that is, tithes or evil words. To swallow the camel means to neglect or forget the greater commandments—judgment, mercy, and faith—or, spiritually speaking, to strain out the gnat and swallow the camel: choosing Barabbas but killing Christ.

Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you cleanse what is outside the cup and the dish. A cup is called a vessel for drinking because a hot drink was given in it; or from the Greek ἀπὸ τοῦ πῶτος [πώματος] καλίνῳ, that is, “from wood” [the etymology is uncertain in the supplied text]. A dish is a four-sided drinking vessel, that is, one with equal sides of an apse. Through these vessels the bodies of the Pharisees themselves are understood: they made those bodies bright on the outside, but inside they were full of vices.

Hence he says: “Inside, however, they are full of plunder and uncleanness.” Plunder is taking away another person’s property by any wicked scheme. Uncleanness is the condition by which someone’s heart is stained with vice.

### [Col. 1451A]

They are the opposite of those about whom it is said: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.” Uncleanness also signifies every kind of fornication.

Blind Pharisee, first cleanse what is inside the cup and the dish, so that what is outside may become clean. Above, he himself showed what defiles a person: evil thoughts proceeding from the heart, murders, perjury, and other things like these. For if these are absent, a person will be clean in the sight of the Lord.

Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you are like whitewashed tombs. A tomb is so called from one who has been buried. At first, each person was buried in his own house; afterward this was forbidden by laws, because the very stench was killing the living. For this reason, burial was likewise prohibited within cities.

He rebukes the Pharisees for hypocrisy in different words. Previously he reproved them through vessels; now he reproves them through tombs, saying that they are like tombs which were whitewashed outside with lime, adorned with marble, and painted with colors, while inside they were full of every kind of filth, that is, uncleanness. Among the ancients, there was great zeal among other peoples for adorning the monuments of their ancestors; this still appears in Roman monuments, and we read of it in the book of Maccabees. But Western poverty, compared with Eastern wealth, is nothing.

Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, who build the tombs of the prophets. The Lord announces that woe will come upon these men—not because they build tombs and monuments for the righteous and the prophets, but because they are so certain that their fathers did evil by killing good men that they know those men must have been good, since they themselves build their monuments. And although they know this for certain, they are held by the same will and are sons of murderers, not merely by flesh but by imitation.

This may also be understood in another way: they built monuments for the righteous so that it might become known to others who had been able and powerful enough to kill them. For when they said, “If we had been in the days of our fathers, we would not have consented to their deeds,” they spoke boastfully and mockingly.

And you, fill up the measure of your fathers. Fill up the very measure that they did not complete but began. They killed servants; you will kill the Lord. They killed prophets; you will kill the Lord of the prophets, or his apostles.

Serpents, offspring of vipers. Just as the viper kills its parents, so they did, and so you will do.

How will you escape the judgment of Gehenna? “How will you escape?”—that is, because you practice such things. “The judgment of Gehenna?” This is what John said: “From the coming wrath,” namely, from hell, where all who practice such things will be sent.

Therefore, behold, I send to you wise men and scribes, and some of them you will kill. The omitted sense of “therefore” is: “I tell you this because you will act in this way.” I will send to you wise men and scribes—learned men in the old law and in the new.

And some of them you will kill, such as James, the brother of the Lord, and Stephen.

And you will crucify them, such as Simon, son of Cleopas, bishop of Jerusalem.

And some of them you will scourge in your synagogues, as you did to all the apostles when they went away from the council rejoicing.

And you will persecute them from city to city, so that all the righteous blood poured out upon the earth may come upon you.

The Jews did not kill all the righteous, since they were not present when Abel was killed. But, as I have already said, all the wicked are said to belong to one generation, just as all the righteous belong to another. Thus, when the Psalmist described many people from different nations who would ascend the Lord’s mountain, saying, “The innocent in hands and pure in heart,” and the rest, he added: “This is the generation of those who seek the Lord.” Likewise, because the Jews killed their fathers, the prophets, they are said to belong to Cain’s offspring, and with him they will suffer eternal punishments—the one who killed his brother.

From the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah. The history of Abel is known to everyone. Zechariah was the son of Jehoiada the priest. Jehoiada took the infant Joash when Queen Athaliah was killing the royal offspring so that she herself might reign. For her husband and her son had died, and she hid Joash for seven years. In the seventh year, he raised him to be king and ordered the queen to be killed.

Thus, while Jehoiada lived, Joash did what was pleasing to God. But after Jehoiada had died, the king accepted evil counselors, abandoned God, and the Lord sent prophets to him, but he did not listen to them. Then this Zechariah, the son of Jehoiada, came to him and said, as it is written in the book of Chronicles: “Thus says the Lord: Why do you transgress the commandment of the Lord, which will not benefit you, and abandon the Lord, so that he may abandon you?”

Those gathered against him threw stones at him, by the king’s command, in the courts of the house of the Lord. King Joash did not remember the mercy that Jehoiada his father had shown him, but killed his son. As he was dying, Zechariah said: “May God see and require it.”

When a year had passed, the army of Syria came against him. It entered Judea and Jerusalem and killed all the princes of the people. When only a small number of Syrians had arrived, the Lord delivered an innumerable multitude into their hands, because they had abandoned the Lord. They also inflicted disgraceful punishments upon Joash and, when they departed, left him in great illnesses. His servants then rose up against him in vengeance for the blood of the priest Jehoiada’s son and killed him in his bed.

In this manner that Zechariah was killed between the temple and the altar, that is, in one of the chambers of the treasuries, or beside the treasury. The fact that the Lord calls him the son of Barachiah is for the praise of that priest, who in every respect strove to be a Barachiah—that is, “blessed by the Lord,” which is what the name signifies. It should also be noted that this Jehoiada, although he was high priest, ordered the queen to be killed.

Amen I say to you, all these things will come upon this generation. It is as though he were saying: all these things deserved to come upon those who did such things.

### [Col. 1453A]

Jerusalem, which kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to you. “Jerusalem, Jerusalem” are vocative forms, although they are indeclinable. The word should not have an aspiration at its beginning, because what occupies the place of a consonant cannot be aspirated; nor does it have an aspiration among the Greeks.

It is as though he said: “O Jerusalem, which kills the prophets sent to you and stones them, because I frequently wished to gather your children beneath the shelter of my wings, as a hen gathers her chicks, and you were unwilling.”

You have ceased from evil works; even those who seemed to have been gathered will be scattered. And your house, in which you have confidence, will be left desolate.

By “Jerusalem” he addresses its inhabitants. This is a case of metonymy, by which he indicates the contents through what contains them.

How often? “Very often”—he shows that he himself sent the prophets.

As a hen. He shows great compassion that he exercised toward the Jewish people, comparing himself to a hen in its concern for its young, because no bird is so solicitous for its offspring as a hen, so that even if you do not see the chicks, you nevertheless recognize the mother. No one can be compared with God’s compassion. For in his compassion alone he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings, and being found in appearance as a human being.

Behold, your house will be left to you desolate. “Behold” is the adverb of one pointing something out, because the time was already approaching when they would kill him, God’s protection would withdraw from them, and that temple would soon be despised, and not long afterward burned, while the city would be destroyed. This happened in the forty-second year after his ascension into heaven.

Earlier, through Jeremiah in the person of the Lord, it had been said: “I have abandoned my house; I have dismissed my inheritance. My inheritance has become for me like a hyena’s cave.” The hyena is a beast that habitually lives always in the tombs of the dead. The Jews are rightly compared with this beast, since they frequently abandoned the Lord and turned to idols. Of them it is written: “There is no hope in their mouth. Let those who make them become like them.”

For I say to you, you will not see me from now on until you say, “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.” This refers back to what he had said: “How often I wished to gather your children.” You will not see me toward you in such a disposition that I wish to gather your children until you repent and recognize that I am the one of whom it was said in the psalm, “Blessed is he who comes.”

They still remain in such a condition. Enoch and Elijah will come, and they will recognize him; then they will be gathered beneath his wings and under the Lord’s protection. For this verse cannot otherwise be properly understood, since he returned to them bodily when he celebrated Passover and again when, bound, he was brought out to be crucified.

### [Col. 1453D]

And he went out from the temple and was going away. He was going again to his lodging, as he was accustomed to do, in Bethany. And his disciples came to him to show him the buildings of the temple.

What reason was there for the disciples to show him the buildings of the temple, which he had already been seeing for thirty-three years? They had taken the opportunity from what he himself had said: “Behold, your house will be left to you desolate.” They wished to know in what sense the Lord had said this—whether it could be that such a building would become desolate.

He said to them: “Do you see all these things?” That is, “Are you amazed at these things?”

Amen I say to you, not one stone will be left upon another that will not be destroyed. This happened not only to the temple but also to the city, because everything was rebuilt in another place by the emperor Aelius Hadrian, and salt was scattered over the place where the city had stood, so that no one afterward would wish to remain there.

If you wish to understand this spiritually as well, the dwelling of God departed from the Jews and came to the nations. And when the head has been removed, all the members fight among themselves.

Now, while he was sitting on the Mount of Olives, his disciples came to him privately, saying—because they were about to ask about more secret mysteries, they rightly approached both bodily and mentally, lest any unbeliever hear and report it to the Jews, providing an occasion for killing him, since they had killed the prophets Isaiah and Jeremiah for lesser statements.

At first, when they did not understand what he had said—“Your house will be left desolate”—they did not dare ask in what frame of mind he had said it. Instead, they showed him the stones and the structure, wishing to give him the opportunity to say what he had said earlier. But when he repeated the same things more openly, they now dared to ask about the more secret matters of his coming and the end of the age.

Tell us, when will these things be, and what will be the sign of your coming and of the consummation of the age? In these questions they wished to learn both about his coming and about the consummation of the age.

And in what follows the Lord answered them concerning all these matters and said to them: “See that no one leads you astray.” The merciful Lord first admonishes them to guard themselves, lest they be led astray by some false prophet.

Many will come in my name, saying, “I am the Christ,” and they will lead many astray. Among them was one Simon, who said that he himself was the Christ, even in Nero’s presence. He also left this written in his books: “I am the word of God; I am beautiful; I am the Paraclete; I am almighty; I am all things belonging to God.”

For you will hear of wars and reports of wars; see that you are not disturbed. They heard of many wars, both among the Romans and among other peoples, and of reports—that is, rumors—of wars. Yet he commanded them not to be disturbed, but to maintain strength of spirit amid adversity and prosperity. They had no reason for grief, nor anything to lose, because they had left everything for God, following the counsel of that philosopher who came by ship from Athens to Rome.

The merchants with whom he had come suffered shipwreck at sea and lost their possessions. But he, who had nothing except a simple garment, had nothing outside himself that he could lose. When the merchants came to Rome, he appeared before the emperor; and when the emperor had tested and found that he was wise, he gave him many estates and honors.

After many days, when the merchants had borrowed money with which to return to their homeland, they asked him what message he wished them to give to his parents and friends. He said: “Tell them that, when they undertake their journey, they should carry a treasure that neither the sea nor thieves can take away, as I did. I lost nothing, and now I am richer than those with whom I came, who departed wealthy and return poor.”

For these things must happen first, but the end is not yet. Whoever reads the words that Orosius collected in his histories concerning wars may be frightened by the extent of such tribulations. For this reason the Lord fortified his own people, so that they would not be disturbed or think that the end of the world was at hand.

Nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom. The Jews also did this in the time of Pilate. The Romans, too, on the very day when blessed Peter entered Rome, were prepared to fight among themselves. But out of reverence for Saint Peter, no one could harm his opponent, because their arms stiffened, and they returned home unharmed. Yet they did not know on whose account they had been saved.

And pestilences and famines. Pestilence is an illness among a people which, once it has seized one person, quickly passes to many, as we read happened in the time of Saint Gregory and in the time of David, when the angel is said to have struck the people; this angel is understood to be the devil.

This plague also frequently occurs in Palestine and in Italy. Hence Saint Gregory rightly says: “We suffer pestilences without cessation.” There were many famines at that time, but one affected the whole world in the tenth year of the emperor Claudius; it is mentioned in the Acts of the Apostles.

Earthquakes in many places: they both occurred then and continue to occur. Sometimes they occur at God’s command as a sign, as when the apostles prayed and an earthquake took place, so that the Lord might show that he terrified unbelievers and defended the faithful. Sometimes they occur through natural causes: a wind finds an opening, enters beneath the earth, and, because it is violent, seeks an exit; in this way it displaces the earth.

All these things are the beginnings of sorrows. We read that all these events occurred in Palestine before the province was overthrown. They were the beginnings of sorrows, because more bitter sufferings came afterward.

Then they will hand you over to tribulation and kill you. This is to be understood of the apostles and the successors of the apostles, since when the province of Palestine was destroyed, very few of the apostles were still alive. None of them had gone out into Judea; Christians, however, were in Judea, and many were even within the city. Yet we do not read that they died there, because the Romans did not prevent anyone from leaving, except those who were themselves inside the city.

And you will be hated by all because of my name. The hatred that is received for God’s sake should be a cause for rejoicing. From what source these tribulations would come is shown when, after the Lord’s death, their future occurrence is also foretold for the disciples.

And then many will be scandalized. Either they will take offense against their neighbors who become Christians, or the Jews will grow angry when they see all nations believing in Christ, because it is a scandal to the Jews to hear that God became incarnate.

And they will hand one another over, and the pagans will hate Christians among themselves.

And many false prophets will arise. *Pseudo* is Greek and is called *falsus* in Latin, “false,” such as Theudas and Judas the Galilean, who led the people after them, saying that they were prophets. But they themselves perished, along with all who agreed with them.

And because iniquity has abounded, the love of many will grow cold. This verse pertains to the times of Antichrist, when the love of Christians will grow cold, many will abandon Christianity, and they will turn to his will.

But whoever perseveres to the end—the omitted sense is: “in faith and love of God”—this one will be saved. “This one” is the pronoun used here. For the one who remains in faith will be saved in the other life.

And this Gospel will be proclaimed throughout the whole world. This is one sign of the end of the age: the end of the age must then come when all nations have heard the Gospel of the kingdom.

As a testimony to all nations. There is no nation beneath heaven that has not heard both of the Lord’s deeds and that he himself is believed to be God by many, whether through preachers or through neighboring peoples.

And then the consummation will come. We do not now know of any nation beneath heaven in which Christians are not found. Indeed, among Gog and Magog—which are the nations of the Huns, called Gazari by them—one nation, which was stronger than those whom Alexander had brought with him, has now been circumcised and observes all Judaism. The Bulgarians also, who likewise belong to those nations, are baptized daily.

Therefore, when you see the abomination of desolation, which was spoken of by the prophet Daniel, standing in the holy place—The abomination of desolation is called an idol in the book of Daniel. He prophesied about it, so that, when they saw it in the temple, they would recognize that the desolation of the temple and the province was near.

This may also be understood of Caesar’s image, which Pilate placed in the temple twenty-five years before the city’s destruction; or of Hadrian’s equestrian statue, which the Romans made for him. For, as he was going to war, he stopped on the road with his horse because a certain widow cried out, until he had rendered her justice against her oppressor. Because of this pious deed, the consuls ordered the statue to be erected throughout all the cities. It stood in the temple of Jerusalem before the destruction of the city, which Hadrian himself brought about. He subdued the rebellious Jews for the second time in a final slaughter, ordered the city to be built in another place, called it Aelia, and forbade the Jews to enter it.

This may also refer to the times of Antichrist, because he will command that he be worshiped as almighty God, as the Apostle says: “He will sit in the temple, displaying himself as though he were God.” The Lord Jesus will kill him with the breath of his mouth and destroy him by the manifestation of his coming.

Then those who are in Judea must flee to the mountains. “Then” refers to this: “When the things I am proclaiming have come.” For Luke relates it in this way: “When you see Jerusalem surrounded by an army, then those who are in Judea must flee to the mountains,” namely, so that they are not enclosed in that siege.

For if those who were enclosed had been able to know with certainty how the matter would end, they would by no means have shut themselves in there. Many Christians, instructed by this Gospel, when they saw the Roman enemy approaching, withdrew across the Jordan into the kingdom of Agrippa and suffered no harm. The apostles also were still living nearby at that time.

If you wish to understand this spiritually, you can refer all these things to heresies and sins. When you see them reigning over those who ought to be teachers of the Church, then those who are in Judea—that is, in the confession of the true faith—should hasten to ascend the mountains of virtues.

And the one who is upon the housetop—that is, the one who has passed in mind beyond carnal things—must not descend to his former acts of worldly conduct.

And the one who works in the field, which is understood as the Church, must not look back toward the things he left for God’s sake, but must always press toward the faith set before him.

Woe to those who are pregnant and nursing. For they will not be able to flee, as we read concerning the nurse of Mephibosheth. When she heard that Saul and Jonathan had died, she hurried to flee with the child, but fell with him, and he became lame.

We also read that during that very siege Mary, a noble and once extremely wealthy woman who previously could scarcely walk upon the ground because of excessive delicacy, ate her son, who was five days old, during the siege itself.

But pray that your flight may not occur in winter or on the Sabbath. To flee in winter would be difficult because of the cold. If she fled on the Sabbath, she would transgress the law; if she remained, she would die, as the Maccabees did.

Nevertheless, when Vespasian came into the province, it was summer, because Titus approached Jerusalem on the very day of Passover. But the siege of Jerusalem continued for two years.

For then there will be great tribulation, such as has not been from the beginning of the world until now, nor ever will be. This may be understood of the siege of the Jews, since they never experienced tribulation such as those who were in that siege endured. Not a dog, nor a piece of leather, remained at the doorway or lying anywhere. People who were alive went into tombs and there awaited death. Troy was besieged for ten years, but its inhabitants did not suffer such great evils there.

This can rightly also be applied to the time of Antichrist, when the tribulation will be indescribable. For he will not only inflict more bitter torments upon the saints, but will also perform many signs and give many gifts in order to lead Christians astray.

And unless those days had been shortened, no flesh would be saved. “Shortened” refers not to their measure but to their number. For this tribulation, the more severe it will be than the others, will be moderated by the brevity of its duration. For, as may be understood from the prophet Daniel and the Apocalypse, it will rage for three and a half years.

The days themselves will always have equal measure, as the Psalmist says: “By your ordinance the days endure.” But they have been fixed in a small number, during which the elect will be tested and the wicked revealed.

Then, if anyone says to you, “Behold, here is the Christ,” or “There,” do not believe it. “Christ” here is to be understood not only as our Lord but also as the king of the Jews, because the Jews called their kings by this name. At that time there were many who called themselves Christs and wished to be kings, if they could then achieve victory. In Jerusalem itself there were three who called themselves kings.

For false prophets and false Christs will arise and will give great signs and wonders, so that, if possible, even the elect may be led into error. These words may be understood of both periods, but we refer them more suitably to the time of Antichrist, in which not only he himself will perform many signs, but also his ministers.

For whose faith will not then waver when he sees a cruel persecutor performing signs?

So that, if possible, even the elect may be led into error. The Lord speaks with the emotion of one who is uncertain, both to indicate the magnitude of the tribulation and to show that freedom of choice exists in human beings. For a faithful person, even if deceived for an hour, will nevertheless quickly rise again, as blessed Peter did.

Behold, I have foretold it to you. In this discourse of warning, he repeats this three times, so that they will not listen to the persuasion of evil men.

Therefore, if they say to you, “Behold, he is in the wilderness,” do not go out. There Theudas, that false prophet, led the people away.

“Behold, he is in the inner chambers,” that is, in some secret places; do not believe it. Spiritually, the catholic Church—that is, the universal Church—is not confined merely to Africa or to some other particular place, nor to the inner chambers of heretics, but is spread throughout the whole world. For this reason it is called catholic, that is, universal.

For just as lightning comes out from the east and appears as far as the west, so will be the coming of the Son of Man. He will not come hidden, since in his first manifestation he appeared concealed beneath a cloud of flesh. Through a figure called *idea*, he describes his coming. There will be no need to seek him in secret, since he will appear openly to everyone and will be terrifying like lightning.

*Fulgur* is a noun of neuter gender. It does not have an *o* in the nominative, but a shortened *u*. There is another noun, *fulgor, fulgoris*, with a lengthened *o*, and it is understood as “radiance.”

Wherever the body is, there the eagles will be gathered. He gives an example from an inferior matter to another inferior matter by way of a parable: just as eagles are said to sense corpses across the sea and gather there, so on that day all the elect will be united with the Lord.

He signifies that he himself will fall into death for his own people, since *cadaver* takes its name from falling (*casus*), and he wishes himself to be understood as the body or corpse. By the eagle he means his saints, whose youth will be renewed like the eagle’s, and who will take wings so that they may fly to the Lord.

Immediately after the tribulation of those days, the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light. Either they will appear darkened in comparison with the brightness of God, or they will truly be darkened, as they were darkened at the time of his death.

For what Joel says has not yet been fulfilled: “The sun will be turned into darkness and the moon into blood, before the great and manifest day of the Lord comes.” But when the judgment has been completed and there is a new heaven and a new earth, what Isaiah says will occur: “The light of the moon will be like the light of the sun, and the light of the sun will be sevenfold, like the light of seven days.”

### [Col. 1458D]

And the powers of heaven will be shaken. What shall we wretched people do if the powers of heaven tremble on that dreadful day? The powers of heaven are the angels, archangels, and the nine orders of angels.

And then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven. He will be seen both by the righteous and by the wicked. Thus John says in the Apocalypse: “Every eye will see him, even those who pierced him.” And as we read in the Acts of the Apostles, it was said when he ascended: “As you saw him going, so will he come.”

Alternatively, by “the sign of the Son of Man” we may understand the standard of the cross, the victorious standard of the triumphant one.

And then all the tribes of the earth will mourn. By “all the tribes of the earth” he means all nations. As they mourn, they will say: “Blessed are the barren who have not borne children, and the breasts that have not nursed.” They will say to the mountains, “Fall upon us,” and to the hills, “Cover us.”

### [Col. 1459A]

And they will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds of heaven with great power and majesty. With power and majesty they will see the one whom they refused to hear when he was in humility. With power and majesty, because all the angels and saints will be with him.

“Fire goes before him, and a mighty storm surrounds him.” If the people of Israel, who heard only a representation of his vision from Mount Sinai, were unable to endure it because of fear, what do we think will happen then?

And he will send his angels with a trumpet and a loud voice. Concerning this trumpet the Apostle Paul says: “For the trumpet will sound, and the dead who are in Christ will rise first.”

[Col. 1459B] “And they will gather his elect from the four winds.” By “the four climates of heaven” he means east, west, north, and south. And lest anyone think that the elect are to be gathered from the four regions of the earth, rather than from all its boundaries together, including its inland regions, he added: “From the farthest reaches of the heavens to their limits.” For on that day no elect person will remain who does not meet the Lord. They will come in the air to the judgment, whether they are found alive—though they will nevertheless taste death—or whether they are dead and to be raised. “In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye.” A moment is a fortieth part of an hour. The twinkling of an eye occurs when it is closed and opened. Whoever has been eaten by beasts or burned will experience neither delay nor difference.

The reprobate, too, will come to judgment, whether they are found alive, destined to die and to be raised with the other dead. [Col. 1459C] There will nevertheless be this distinction: the righteous will come with joy in the Lord, while the wicked will come so that they may see the Lord whom they will lose in blessedness, and so that, once the judgment has been completed, they may perish with the devil and descend into hell with their bodies and souls, just as Dathan and Abiron descended into hell.

“Learn a parable from the fig tree. When its branch has already become tender and its leaves have appeared, you know that summer is near.” How, he says, when the emerging twigs have become tender, summer is already near, because they cannot break forth before the sun approaches. “So also you, when you see these things happening”—that is, when you see these signs preceding which I have foretold—“know that my coming, the consummation of the age, and the joy of the future kingdom have drawn near.” For the comparison with the delight of this age will be such as summer is in comparison with winter, because then the clouds of our sorrow will pass away, and the days of eternal life will shine with the brightness of the everlasting sun.

“So also you, when you see these things happening, know that he is near, at the doors.” Just as worldly people know from the emerging branches of trees that the desired season is approaching, so you also should know from the foretold signs that your desired joys are near. “At the doors”—that is, at the final boundaries. For just as a door is the end of a house, and one who comes out through the door becomes visible to many, so then I and the day of judgment will be “at the doors,” because from that point I will begin to appear to many.

This may also be understood spiritually of the Synagogue: when, through Enoch and Elijah, it begins to believe in God and to produce leaves and fruit through good works, the end will be near, because “when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel will be saved.”

[Col. 1460A] “Amen I say to you, this generation will not pass away until all these things take place.” “Amen,” if it is permissible to say so, is like the Lord’s oath. He strongly commends whatever he adds this to. By “this generation” we may understand both the race of the Jews and the entire human race.

“Heaven and earth will pass away.” In this passage he calls heaven the airy expanse where birds fly; hence they are called “the birds of heaven.” The fire will take up and destroy as much space as the water occupied in the Flood. For the heaven in which the stars are will be renewed into a better form, as John says: “There will be a new heaven and a new earth.” Of the earth, too, only as much will burn as was defiled by human labors; the remainder [Col. 1460B] will be changed into a better form.

“But my words will not pass away.” The implied meaning is: so as to prove false what I have said. Or, in another way: in this world nothing is more enduring than heaven and earth, as though he were saying, “Heaven and earth can pass away sooner, so that they no longer exist, than what I have said will fail to happen,” because I am truth, and it is impossible for truth to be able to lie. Or: “Heaven and earth will pass away,” that is, from the form they now have into another.

“But concerning that day and hour no one knows, neither the angels of heaven, except the Father alone.” The Son, through whom every day was made and who is the wisdom of God the Father, cannot be ignorant; rather, in him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom. Since he is one God with the Father, he himself knows everything that the Father knows. But he is said not to know this in the sense that he causes others not to know it, just as a “blind pit” is called blind not because it itself is blind, [Col. 1460C] but because it makes those who do not know blind.

For when the apostles questioned him after the resurrection about the day of judgment, he said: “It is not for you to know the times or the moments which the Father has placed in his own authority.” By saying, “It is not for you to know,” he shows that he himself knows, but that it is not expedient for the apostles to know, so that they may always live watchfully concerning the Lord’s coming, as though they were to be judged on the following day.

“As in the days of Noah, so will be the coming of the Son of Man.” Just as in the days of Noah they suspected nothing adverse, but each person did what seemed pleasing to him, so it will be at the Lord’s coming, because those wars and disturbances which he narrated above will occur beforehand. Then there will be peace.

Just as we now know what has been foretold about Antichrist, so the Jews knew through the prophets what had been foretold about Christ, and yet they did not recognize him when he was present. Thus we must fear lest the Lord come upon us unaware. Therefore, according to the Lord’s command, it is fitting that we should always be ready. For “when they say, ‘Peace and security,’ then sudden destruction will come upon them, like labor pains upon a pregnant woman, and they will not escape.”

“Then two will be in the field: one will be taken and the other left.” These two are the Jewish and Gentile peoples. Or the two are the good and wicked peoples who, in the field—that is, in Holy Scripture—ought to practice good works, through which they may live forever. One will be taken and the other left, because there are many within the holy Church who read the Scriptures but do not obey them, and who profess themselves Christians, yet will not be taken.

“Two will be grinding at the mill.” These two are the Synagogue and the Church, which in the Law [Col. 1461A] or in Scripture ought to grind the flour of the Word of God for their own nourishment and that of others. But one will be taken and the other left: namely, the Church of the elect will be taken, while that of the reprobate will be left.

“Therefore keep watch.” To keep watch is to practice good works. If she does this, even if she sleeps bodily, those works themselves will keep watch and pray on her behalf. The person who practices in action what he believes is keeping watch. Hence Paul says: “Awake, righteous people, and do not sin.”

“Because you do not know at what hour your Lord will come.” It should be noted that he does not say “we do not know,” but “you do not know.” For this reason he did not disclose it plainly to the apostles: so that they might always believe that he would come on any day and prepare themselves in such a way as to be worthy to receive him.

The Lord therefore wished the final hour to be unknown to us so that it might always be feared; since we cannot foresee it, we may prepare for it without interruption. For according to the tradition of our predecessors, the Lord ought to come at Easter shortly before midnight, just as the destroyer passed through the houses of the Egyptians, striking them, as it is written: “While all things were in quiet silence and the night was in the midst of its course, your almighty Word, Lord, came from heaven, from the royal throne.”

Thus, moreover, they left us written that the world was made on the eighth day before the Kalends of April; the Lord was conceived and suffered, and in a similar manner the world will be destroyed. They established that on that night no one should sleep before midnight, but that they should keep watch in the praises of God according to this admonition of the Lord. Then Easter is celebrated on the eighth day before the Kalends of April.

[Col. 1461C] Later, at the Council of Nicaea, it was established that we should await the Lord’s Day after the spring equinox; and in a cycle of nineteen years Easter does not occur in this same way except once. In this manner, too, that day itself will be hidden from us. Therefore, the more uncertain it is for us, the more ready we ought to be at all times.

Indeed, the Lord comes to each one of us when the end of our days approaches. He knocks when, through the distress of illness, he announces that death is near. We immediately open to him if, by always practicing good works, we receive him with love. The person who trembles at leaving the body and fears seeing as judge the one whom he despised does not wish to open to the Judge who knocks.

To shake off the sloth of our mind, even external losses are introduced by way of comparison, so that our spirit may be stirred to keep watch. For he says: “But know this: if the master of the house had known at what hour the thief would come, he would surely have kept watch and would not have allowed his house to be broken into.”

The thief breaks into the house when the devil weakens the dwelling place of the soul, so that its inhabitant may depart. For all the illnesses of human beings and animals are inflicted by the devil, as he did with Job and his children, Tobias, and Paul—though God permits it and a good angel presides, lest the devil carry out his will according to his wicked desire. Hence the Lord also said to him concerning Job, when he handed over his body: “Nevertheless, preserve his soul.”

This saying of the Lord is understood in two ways: that he should cause no injury to his soul, either to its mind or in any other evil way; and that he should not so destroy the dwelling place of the soul [Col. 1462A] that the soul could not remain. For how can death be understood as a thief, when it lacks substance? It is nothing other than the absence of life, just as darkness is nothing other than the absence of light.

The master of the house is called a man because he ought to rule over his own members, just as a master of a household rules in his house. “He does not allow his house to be broken into.” When a person perceives and rejoices that the day of departure has come, he goes out joyfully, and the body falls asleep, as it is written of John and Stephen that they “fell asleep in the Lord.”

“Therefore you also must be ready, because you do not know at what hour the Son of Man will come.” When the master of the household is unaware, the thief breaks into the house, while he is idle in good works. Any messenger of God who comes destroys the dwelling place of our flesh and compels its inhabitant to depart, [Col. 1462B] because, when the spirit does not foresee the coming losses, death snatches it away to punishment. He could resist the thief if he kept watch through good works, lest he perish unrepentant.

“Who, then, do you think is the faithful and wise servant whom his lord appointed over his household, to give them food at the proper time?” Here the Lord admonishes his own disciples, and through them the teachers of the Church, so that they themselves may keep watch and announce the divine word to others, through which they may know how to keep watch and observe that hour.

Those servants themselves will then be wise and faithful if, at the proper time, they know how to give their fellow servants portions of the Word. That is, at a suitable time they should not conceal it, nor thrust profound and lofty teachings upon ignorant crowds; following the Lord’s example, they should supply more secret things to the more perfect and the nourishment of barley to ordinary people.

“Blessed is that servant whom, when his lord comes, [Col. 1462C] he finds doing this.” The blessed person is so called because he has been made abundantly good. Happy and blessed will be the person who first fills himself with the divine Word, so that he first practices it and afterward supplies nourishment from the Word to others by mouth and deed, because it is written of this same Lord: “What Jesus began to do and teach.” He acted first, then taught. And above he says of teachers: “Whoever does and teaches will be called great in the kingdom of heaven.”

“Amen I say to you, he will appoint him over all his goods.” There is a great difference between good practitioners and preachers. If he finds good hearers keeping watch, he makes them recline—that is, rest in eternal life. “And passing by, he will minister what has been prepared for those who love God.”

But if he finds good preachers who have dispensed things wisely, so that they themselves are satisfied [Col. 1462D] and have ministered sufficiently to others, he will appoint them over all his goods—that is, over all the joys of the heavenly kingdom—not so that they alone may possess them, but so that they may enjoy them more abundantly with the saints and eternally.

“But if that wicked servant says in his heart, ‘My lord delays his coming,’ and begins to beat his fellow servants, while he eats and drinks with drunkards…” This may be understood of every Christian, especially of teachers of the churches, kings, bishops, and counts who imagine that they will live for a long time, beat Christians or commit other injustices against them, devote themselves to feasting and drunkenness, and indulge in other vices.

“The lord of that servant will come.” This means the Lord’s messenger, who will separate their souls from their bodies at a time [Col. 1463A] when they do not expect it, and will assign their portion with the hypocrites, to whom he said above: “Woe to you, hypocrites”; or with those of whom he said: “One will be taken and the other left”—that is, with those who descend into hell. “There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth,” through which they will be brought into the harshest torments.

“Then the kingdom of heaven will be like ten virgins.” In the preceding parable he introduced the apostles and teachers under the figure of the good and wicked servant; he showed what the one who ministers the divine Word well will receive, and what the one who ministers negligently will receive. Now he sets forth a parable generally about the whole Church and the hearers of that same divine Word, still in the prophetic manner by which the apostles and all those hearers had been instructed.

They were accustomed to call those souls virgins which had not worshiped a foreign god, and to call the God worshiped by each soul the bridegroom, and the soul that worshiped God the bride. For just as a woman ought to do everything she does with her husband’s consent, and to devote everything she gives to his work, praise, or benefit, and ought not to consider anyone wiser, more beautiful, or stronger than her husband, so the soul of every person who worships God ought to do everything with God’s will and in the Lord’s name.

It ought not to love father or mother, gems, gold, silver, estates, or any creature under heaven more than God. A person loves God when he does what God has commanded. But if he abandons justice for the sake of something else, then he loves that thing more than God, and his soul commits fornication there.

In this way the whole Church of Christ ought to be a virgin—that is, all Christians. Of such virgins the Lord says: “The kingdom of heaven is like”—that is, the present Church, which is frequently called the kingdom of heaven.

The whole human race is rightly expressed by the number ten, because ten is a perfect and complete number, and beyond it no number exists except one multiplied from it. In this parable there is no one who is not represented here. Every human being consists in the five bodily senses. The doubling of five completes ten. And because a multitude of believers is gathered from both sexes, the holy Church is declared to be like ten virgins.

“Virgin” is a common-gender noun; in the same way one says “the holy virgin Mary” and “the holy virgin John.”

[Col. 1463D] “Who took their lamps and went out to meet the bridegroom and the bride.” The lamps are understood as bodies. They went out to meet the bridegroom and the bride when, through baptism, they entered his Church.

“Five of them were foolish and five wise.” Those who love the world or the things in the world more than God are foolish according to God. A person’s soul commits fornication against God when some reward pleases it more than God’s [reward]—that is, the recompense of eternal life for its deeds.

“But the five foolish, having taken their lamps, did not take oil with them.” They did not have works acceptable to God, either because they did evil or because, if they did anything good, they did it for human praise.

“But the wise took oil in their vessels with their lamps.” They acted solely for the love of God and for the recompense of eternal life. The vessels are the hearts of the elect.

“While the bridegroom was delayed.” This delay is still taking place, because judgment has not yet come. “They all grew drowsy.” They became weak. “And they slept.” They died. This happens daily to believers and unbelievers, but it will happen universally on the day of judgment.

“But at midnight a cry was made.” As we have said, we believe that the end of the world will occur at midnight and unexpectedly. A cry was made by angels with trumpets, by human beings, by flashes of lightning, and by thunder.

“Behold, the bridegroom is coming.” He will come more openly and will not remain silent. “Go out to meet him.” He summoned heaven above and earth below—that is, those who are in heaven and on earth.

“Then all those virgins arose.” The good and the wicked will rise with their bodies. [Col. 1464B] “They prepared their lamps.” They received resurrected bodies.

“But the foolish said to the wise: ‘Give us some of your oil, because our lamps are going out.’” This means: Help us before God.

“The wise answered, saying: ‘Perhaps there will not be enough for us and for you.’” They do not say this out of avarice, but out of fear, because their works will scarcely be able to save each person. For each person will receive a reward according to his works, and on that day the virtues of some will not be able to lift up the vices of others.

Just as during the Babylonian captivity Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Habakkuk, Daniel, Ananias, and Misael could not free others, so on that day the saints will not be able to help others except those whom their own good works have helped. The prayers of the saints will be able to help in conjunction with good works.

[Col. 1464C] “Go instead to those who sell, and buy some for yourselves.” They did not give advice, but condemned the offense, as though they were saying: “Go to the flatterers, for whose vain praises you practiced your works.” The sellers of oil are understood as flatterers. For the person who praises someone’s work in exchange for some gift sells oil, as the Psalmist says: “May the oil of the sinner not anoint my head.”

“But while they went to buy, the bridegroom came.” Because they could not be with the Lord and the elect, they will be with the devils whom they obeyed. “The bridegroom came.” The judgment will be carried out.

“And those who were ready entered with him into the wedding feast.” Those who had perfect works were received, so that they might be with God and his angels—that is, in that heavenly blessedness.

“And the door was shut.” The entrance of mercy was closed. For after the judgment there is no longer a place for prayers or merits. Then the door will be shut, with all the wicked excluded; now it is opened daily to all who repent from the heart.

The blessed Bede similarly laments this in a verse of a certain poem, saying: “There will be no expectation of salvation or remedy when the door of the bridal chamber is shut, the bridegroom’s wedding having been completed.”

“Finally the other virgins also come, saying: ‘Lord, Lord, open to us.’” In vain then will those cry out who refused to hear him here, when he called through his Gospels and his preachers. They repeat, “Lord, Lord,” but in vain, because the time for repentance will then have passed. For repentance is so called as though it meant punishment; the time for punishment will be present, but hope of pardon will no longer exist. [Col. 1465A] For no one who now refuses to repent will then find pardon, as David says: “For there is no one in death who remembers you.”

Great will be the severity after the judgment, because before the judgment he has shown immeasurable mercy. “But he answered and said: ‘Amen I say to you, I do not know you.’” “I do not know you” means, by implication, “I do not know you to have been mine through your works.” For God’s not knowing is his rejection.

Woe to the proud, to whom God will say these things: “Therefore keep watch, because you do not know the day or the hour.” Since he himself often called out in this world that they should keep watch, and they disdained to listen, they will call out repeatedly and will not be heard.

Concerning this woe, the aforementioned Bede continues in the verse already mentioned, saying: “O how unhappy the soul deprived of this feast, which will never again return to the memory of the Lord.”

We must always fear the last day, which we can never foresee. David, fearing it, said: “Make known to me, Lord, my end and the number of my days, so that I may know what I lack.” For if someone must make a journey, he wishes to receive sufficient provisions for the road. “So that I may know what I lack.” He feared that his lamp might be extinguished; therefore he said: “So that I may know what I lack.” Let us continually prepare provisions for the journey, lest on that day we be excluded when the door is shut.

“As a man setting out on a journey.” Since the Lord was soon to pass bodily from the world, and the disciples questioned him about the day of judgment, while he did not wish to reveal a fixed time, he showed through many parables how greatly that day should be feared and guarded against.

Above he spoke of the watchful and prudent [Col. 1465C] servant, and of the negligent one. Again, generally, he spoke of his whole Church, which professes to worship God, under the figure of the ten virgins. Now once more he speaks chiefly of the apostles and teachers, and with them of all human beings.

This man is our Lord Jesus Christ, who, although he was God, in his gratuitous mercy deigned to become man for us. “Setting out on a journey.” “Peregre,” meaning “far away,” comes from the word *pereger*, from which also comes *peregrinus*, “one who travels farther.” “Setting out” comes from the deponent verb *proficiscor*; *proficiscens* is its participle.

The Lord Christ set out on a journey when he ascended into heaven. For although his divinity had been in heaven, that man whom he assumed from holy Mary had not previously been in heaven.

“He called his servants.” To the apostles to whom he was speaking, he handed on evangelical teaching. “And to one he gave five talents, to another two, and to another one.” Although all the apostles departed from the Lord equally instructed, some were more and others less so.

Thomas was less wise, for he said, “Lord, we do not know where you are going,” than Peter. Likewise Philip was less wise, to whom it was said, “I have been with you so long, and you have not known me, Philip,” than John, who said, “In the beginning was the Word.”

Therefore in the five talents we should understand different graces. Or in the five talents the gift of the five senses—that is, external knowledge—is expressed: sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch. A person who is permitted to be vigorous in these five senses is honored sufficiently and abundantly.

In the two talents, understanding and action are signified. In the one talent, understanding alone is signified. We nevertheless believe that the chosen apostles possessed both five and two talents, and that many in Christ’s Church still possess them in the same way.

“According to his own ability.” He gave more to one and less to another not according to generosity or parsimony, but according to the recipients’ capacities. For although the seventy-two elders in the wilderness were filled with the same Spirit as Moses, they were not filled as profusely as Moses.

“And he departed immediately.” He remained with the disciples until he saw that they no longer needed instruction through his bodily presence; afterward he departed from them bodily, though he never abandoned them spiritually.

“But the one who had received the five talents went away, worked with them, and gained another five. Likewise the one who had received two gained another two.” There can be no doubt that the apostles doubled the talents they received from God according to God’s will.

Hence their follower Paul, possessing both five and two talents, said: “Woe to me if I do not preach the Gospel, because a dispensation has been entrusted to me.”

Likewise, concerning external talents: “These hands have ministered to the things that were necessary for me and for those who are with me.” And again: “I have shown you everything, because it is necessary to labor in this way and to receive the weak.”

The person who doubles external talents is the one who acquires eternal life for himself through earthly duties. We can understand this of every human being, but especially of those who hold the place of the apostles in the Church, namely the preachers of the divine Word.

The two talents may also be understood as understanding and charity, because action has been left to human choice. If we understand action there, someone might object that he cannot do good because he did not receive the talent of action. But we know that God has left human beings in the freedom of their will, whether they wish to do God’s commandments or not.

“But the one who had received one talent went away, dug in the ground, and hid his master’s money.” To hide money in the ground is to entangle the intelligence one has received in earthly affairs; it is not to seek spiritual profit and never to lift the heart from earthly desires.

Judas received one talent of understanding, because he was instructed by the Lord in the same way as the others; but he converted everything into earthly profit through avarice. Having the master’s money box, he stole whatever he could until he even sold the Lord.

[Col. 1466D] Let each person examine himself: no one who possesses all the bodily senses sound can claim that he did not receive, or could not have received, a talent. For, since he possessed soundness, he was able to learn how he might live and benefit both himself and others.

No one will be able to excuse himself on the grounds of ignorance, because ignorance is not permitted; the earth is filled with the knowledge of the Lord. Rather, he will be condemned for laziness and for casting away his talent.

Another Evangelist says that he tied the talent up in a cloth. The person who ties the master of the household’s teaching in a cloth is the one who converts the gift of understanding into luxury, feasting, drunkenness, or other pleasures of this age.

“After a long time, the lord of those servants came and settled accounts with them.” There will be a universal examination of all human works on the day of judgment. It also takes place daily, whenever the elect and the reprobate are snatched from this world.

“And the one who had received the five talents came forward and offered another five, saying…” They will not speak in words, but perfect works will be displayed, because on that day each person’s work will be made manifest.

This also happens in the present age, when someone employs the five bodily senses in good works, instructs others by his example, and God sees that his intention is right. God grants him knowledge even greater than that of one endowed with natural intellectual ability.

“His lord said to him: ‘Well done, good and faithful servant.’” *Euge* is a Greek word, and in Latin it is rendered *bene*, “well”; the implied sense is, “Rejoice, good servant.”

A servant is not always called a servant because of fear arising from status, but also because of love. In another passage the Lord says: “I will no longer call you servants.” And elsewhere: “Say, ‘We are unworthy servants; we have done what we were obliged to do.’”

Here, then, the servant is called such in relation to love, not fear, but the love of pleasing God.

“Faithful.” Because he both preserved God’s gifts within himself and increased them in others.

“You have been faithful over a few things.” “Over a few things” means over earthly things, because, however great earthly possessions may be in this world, compared with heavenly things they are few and worthless.

“Enter into the joy of your lord.” Receive what “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man.”

“But the one who had received the two talents also came forward.” If we understand action as the talents, many will say, “I did not receive from the Lord a talent by which I could perform what I understand, and for that reason I cannot accomplish God’s works.” But we know that all human beings possess free will, so that we may perform either the works of God or the works of the devil.

It is therefore better to understand the talents as understanding and charity.

“His lord said to him: ‘Well done, good servant.’” Both servants received a similar joy: the one who made ten from five and the one who made four from two. He did not consider the magnitude of the profit, but the intention of the effort, because God considers the intention in every person, as he himself said concerning the widow who put two small coins into the treasury: “I tell you that this widow has put in more than all the rich.”

What greater gift can be given to a faithful servant than to be with God and to see the joy of his lord?

“But the one who had received the one talent also came forward and said: ‘Lord, I know that you are a hard man: you reap where you did not sow, and you gather where you did not scatter.’” Through this servant all wicked people are understood, or each wicked person individually, because scarcely anyone can be found who has not received a talent from God. Whatever each person lives by will be reckoned as the talent he received.

Even the person who occupies a position with a rich man, if he does not intercede for the poor, will be held accountable for retaining his talent.

“You are a hard man.” Many worldly people consider God’s justice harsh. But just as truth exists by nature, so the just person and justice exist by nature; and the one who is essentially good cannot act unjustly.

“You reap where you did not sow.” For among the Gentile peoples, too, whoever made an effort to perform good works had works acceptable to God, as in the case of the Magi, to whom Christ had not been preached, and of the others whose deeds we do not have written down.

“And you gather where you did not scatter”—namely, the word of preaching. From this it is understood that those who have acted well among the Gentiles will not have torments as severe in Tartarus as those who acted as wickedly as they could.

Or, in another sense: you punish not only those who knew what they ought to do, but also those who did not know you and those who did not listen to you.

“And being afraid, I went away and hid your talent in the ground.” As though he were saying: “When I considered that you punish both those who act through ignorance and those who act through the weakness of frailty, while you receive without blemish those whom you receive, I despaired of being able to attain your grace or your kingdom. Therefore I placed all my effort in earthly things, so that, if I lost the blessed life in the future, I would at least not lose present affection.”

This may also be understood in the present age. When someone does not follow the keenness of understanding he received from God, through his own laziness he loses what he could have known; and frequently the person who seemed to possess dull intelligence attains it through diligence and good will.

“Behold, you have what is yours.” From the time our first parent sinned in paradise, he wished to attribute his own faults to his Lord, saying: “The woman whom you gave me gave me, and I ate from it.” The whole human race strives to turn its faults back upon others.

Thus this servant also says: “Behold, you have what is yours,” as though he were saying: “Even if I did not instruct others, I preserved myself, and you have your talent safe in me.” He ought simply to have confessed his idleness and sin; instead he says that he acted through prudent counsel, so as not to lose the money, when the only thing he ought to have feared was returning to God without profit.

[Col. 1468C] “But his lord answered and said to him: ‘Wicked and lazy servant.’” He is called a wicked servant because he brought an accusation against his lord and wished to turn his sin back upon him. He is called lazy because he did not put the talent out at interest.

“You knew that I reap where I do not sow and gather where I did not scatter. If, according to your own statement, I demand even what I did not give for investment, why, knowing my will, did you not give my money to the money changers?”

Money changers are called *nummularii* from *nummus*, “coin,” because they strike the coins. Moneyers are accustomed to receive silver from some people, mint denarii, and after a full year return what they received, together with half as the profit from their skill.

Divine law forbids this with earthly money, because it is the beginning of greed to demand repayment for something one does not know one has lent. Hence the Psalmist says of the just man: “He has not given his money at interest.”

But concerning spiritual money—that is, divine preaching—the person who has not endeavored to multiply it will pay the required penalties.

“Take the talent from him and give it to the one who has ten talents.” It might seem appropriate that when the talent was taken from him, it should be given to the one who had two rather than to the one who had five. But if we consider the force of the saying, the one who had two—that is, understanding and charity—possessed more than the one who had received the five bodily senses, because the knowledge of God and charity excel all virtues before God.

Therefore we frequently see that the person who administers external matters well, even if he is a simple brother, has greater gifts from God than the person who boasts of his learning and disdains others.

This one wicked servant may also be understood as the Jewish people, who did not wish to multiply among the Gentile people the teaching of the Law that they had received. Its talent was taken away, as the Lord says elsewhere: “The kingdom of God will be taken from you and given to a nation producing its fruits.”

“To everyone who has, it will be given.” To the one who has faith or good will, the remaining good things will be given. But from the one who does not have faith or good will, even what he appears to have through hypocrisy will be taken away.

Or this refers to earthly possessions, which he loved more than eternal life. They will be taken away from him, and then he will have neither.

“And cast the useless servant into the outer darkness.” Above I said that inner darkness is called blindness of mind. Outer darkness will be in hell, where neither God nor the sun will shine upon him. God is light; the one who is distanced from him is placed in darkness.

“There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.” Through weeping and gnashing of teeth, terrible torments are foretold and the true resurrection of bodies is demonstrated.

A talent is the largest kind of weight. There are three kinds: the smallest, of fifty pounds; the middle, of seventy-two; and the greatest, of one hundred and twenty.

When the Son of Man comes in his majestic seat, and all the angels with him. The Lord said many things about what will take place on the day of judgment, but he does not say when that day or hour will be. Yet it is certainly established that he who knows the other, more secret mysteries also knows this one. Above he gave admonitions to everyone; [Col. 1469C] now he shows what he himself will do at the final hour. We know that the Father gave judgment to the Son, and that he who came in the first advent to be judged will come in the second to judge the living and the dead. No tongue can recount how great the terrors will be there, when heaven and earth burn, the sound of thunder and lightning is heard, and angels sounding their trumpets shake the mortal multitude. Why should we not believe that those angels who assume bodies from the air—for they are frequently read to have appeared to the fathers—will sound with an aerial sound, just as they did when the Lord spoke to the crowds through a created instrument? To this day of judgment all nine orders of angels will come, and all human beings, good and evil. Then he will sit in his majestic seat. By “sitting” is meant the authority to judge; by “majesty,” power. Many have thought that judgment would take place in the valley of Jehoshaphat, which is a place in Judea; but this is by no means true, although “Jehoshaphat” sounds like “judgment.” It will be in the air, as Paul says: “We shall be caught up in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord.”

And all the nations will be gathered before him. Whoever has possessed the immortal breath of life, such as angels and human beings, will be present there. And he will separate them from one another as a shepherd separates sheep from goats.
