Since he had already said, “I am the good shepherd,” he continues in the same parable: just as a shepherd at evening separates sheep from goats, sending the latter to one dwelling and the former to another, so God, at the evening of this world, will gather his sheep into the sheepfold and shut the goats away in Erebus [Col. 1470A]. And he will indeed place the sheep on his right, that is, on the good side. But the goats on the left, that is, on the evil side. Let those who still live now see to it that they hasten to be Christ’s sheep: let them clothe the naked and feed the needy; let them live simply, neither by plunder nor harming anyone, because whoever imitates the goats in this life will then be the companion of the impious. They are compared with goats because the goat is a wanton and lustful animal; those who are dissolute in their pleasures, lustful and greedy toward their neighbors, are like them.

Then the king will say to those who will be on his right: “Come, blessed of my Father.” That is: Come with me, with whom you ought to be heirs of eternal life. He blesses them because, having been made in the image of God, they are therefore blessed. “Possess.” That is, without any opposition, “the kingdom prepared for you” [Col. 1470B] through the presence of God. “Kingdom” means a spacious dwelling, which will not be narrowed for you but will be widely extended. “From the foundation of the world”: we believe that this blessed dwelling was created by God in the beginning, to be the receptacle of the righteous.

“For I was hungry in my members”—that is, in my Church—“and you gave me food,” whether earthly or spiritual food. “I was thirsty, and you gave me drink.” Just as there is spiritual food, so there is also spiritual drink. Hence blessed Paul said: “They drank of the spiritual [drink].” “I was a stranger, and you welcomed me.” A *hospes* is both one who receives and one who is received. “I was a stranger; I needed hospitality, and you received me,” because a stranger must not only be received but also drawn in and sought out. Thus blessed Tobias, when he was sitting at table, sent his son to look for someone who might eat with him.

“I was naked, and you covered me” [Col. 1470C]. There is bodily nakedness and spiritual nakedness. Hence it is said: “Blessed is the one who keeps watch over his garments, lest he walk naked.”

“I was sick, and you visited me.” Those who call upon God the Father are to be visited both in bodily sickness and in sickness of soul. For when someone begins to be saddened amid the tribulations of this age, then he becomes sick. Whoever visits him and strengthens him with his word will not lack a reward.

“I was in prison, and you came to me.” *Carcer* (“prison”) is derived from *coercere* (“to restrain”), because the accused are restrained there—that is, confined. Prison may also be understood as distress and faintheartedness of spirit. All these works of mercy may be understood as being practiced both bodily and spiritually, and they pertain to the active life. Whoever diligently fulfills them in this age afterward reaches the [Col. 1470D] contemplative life of God, in which his eyes will see the King in his beauty without end.

“Amen, I say to you: whatever you did for one of these least brothers of mine, you did for me.” It must be noted that he said “for one of these least brothers of his,” that is, those who believe in God the Father, call upon him, and are not proud but humble in spirit.

Then he will say to those who will be on the left. It should be noted that he does not say “on his left,” but merely “on the left,” because God possesses nothing left-handed. Hence it is written: “The ways that are on the right the Lord knows; but those that are on the left are perverse.”

“Depart from me.” Behold a terrifying and fearful voice, even if he had added nothing else, because whoever departs from God is handed over to the devil. Outside God there is nothing but unspeakable evil [Col. 1471A].

“Accursed.” There can be no accursed person where there is a blessed one. Created by God, you were blessed; by your works you have become accursed.

“Into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels.” To depart into the eternal fire means to be commanded to fall disorderly, because from that day onward they will be cruelly treated. The fire will be eternal for them because, although they had an end to their sinning, they nevertheless had the will always to live and always to sin; therefore, because of their will, they will be condemned without end.

“Which has been prepared for the devil and his angels.” Here it is evident that the punishments of hell were prepared not for human beings but for the evil angels. Whoever joins himself to their company through evil works will endure what they must endure.

“For I was hungry, and you did not give me food,” and so forth. In everything [Col. 1471B] by which the righteous are crowned, the impious are condemned, because they did the opposite.

“And these will go into eternal punishment.” Twice in this passage the Lord affirms that the punishments of the impious will be eternal. The impious are said to be in eternal punishments just as the righteous are said to be in eternal life. And if the impious were not always to be tormented, neither would the righteous always be glorified, as the Greeks say. Origen, their eminent teacher, went astray in thinking that the day of judgment would last for a period of a thousand years, so that during this period all the impious, after performing penance, would come to forgiveness—and the devil himself as well. For many years he taught this. But when he heard the two expressions “eternal fire” and “eternal punishment,” he recognized his error, went to a synod, and publicly confessed that he had recognized himself to have been mistaken: the impious, he said, ought to be tormented eternally [Col. 1471C], just as the righteous rejoice eternally in eternal life. He accepted penance and abstained from the office of celebrating Mass until the day of his death. It must also be retained that the one who is said to judge is called the Son of Man, so that we may know that the one who was judged will himself be the judge.

And it happened, when Jesus had finished all these sayings. “Completion” pertains to perfection. For it is characteristic of the good to complete—that is, to bring to perfection. He completed them because he said as much as he wished and what he knew to be necessary.

### Here follows the exposition of Christianus Druthmar on the Passion of the Lord.

He said to his disciples: “You know that after two days the Passover will take place.” Passover is Hebrew, not Greek, and it is not called so from [Col. 1471D] *passion* but from *passing over*, because the destroyer of the Egyptians—who is understood to be the devil—after striking the Egyptians, did not dare to enter the houses of the Hebrews because of the blood of the lamb that he saw on the doorposts. Or, in another sense, Passover is called from *passing over* because the Lord passed through the houses of the Hebrews on that very night when the Egyptians were being struck, in order to save his people.

There is this difference between Passover and Unleavened Bread: Passover was the first day itself, when they ate the lamb; Unleavened Bread was the seven days that followed, during which they did not dare to eat bread contaminated with leaven, and therefore those days themselves were called “unleavened.”

“And the Son of Man will be handed over to be crucified.” *Biduum* (“two-day period”) is a compound word, from the adverb *bis* (“twice”) and the Greek *dio*, that is, “two” [Col. 1472A]. “After two days”—after two [days], with “days” understood. This is what the statement “The Son of Man will be handed over after two days” refers to. For Passover and the following day were celebrated: he was speaking on Wednesday, he celebrated Passover on Thursday—that is, he ate the lamb—and on Friday, which was the two-day interval, he was handed over.

“And the Son of Man will be handed over.” He is rightly called the Son of Man, because the divinity is incapable of suffering and only the flesh suffered. He was handed over by the Jews, because whenever they wanted to kill someone, they condemned him to death and then handed him over to Roman authority, since they were not permitted either to bear arms or to kill anyone.

Then the chief priests gathered in the courtyard of the chief priest, who was called Caiaphas. Since they had already conspired to kill him, they now gather again to deliberate how they might seize him [Col. 1472B] without the crowds. For they believed that he would suffer unwillingly, and they feared that if he escaped from their hands even once, by whatever means, they would not be able to seize him again. They gathered at the high priest’s house because they had no greater man from their own people. Indeed, after the transmigration, priests had always ruled over them with royal honor, until Herod. Thus they gathered, not fearing an uprising of the people, but taking care lest he be taken from their hands with the people’s help.

*Caiaphas* is interpreted as “inventor of evils.” They took counsel to seize Jesus by deceit and kill him. Deceit is cunning of mind, from the fact that it deceives; or deceit is when someone says one thing and thinks another. For they knew that he was not worthy of death, although they said so with their tongues.

[Col. 1472C] When Jesus was in Bethany, in the house of Simon the leper. This happened before the Lord came to Jerusalem, seated on a donkey. But Matthew repeats it because it was done as a foreshadowing of his death. It signifies Mary, the Church of Christ, which spiritually gave the Lord the good fragrance of knowledge and does so daily by announcing his salvation from day to day.

Mary was the sister of Lazarus. She had already washed his feet and wiped them with the hair of her head, as John the Evangelist affirms. By adhering to the Savior through good works, loving him and serving him, she earned this: that she would be worthy to place her hands upon the Savior’s head, holding out hope of forgiveness to all penitents, if they repent from the heart and thereby obtain complete remission.

“Of Simon the leper.” This does not mean that he was then [Col. 1472D] a leper, because no leper lived with other people in a city or village; rather, he had formerly been a leper and had been healed by the Lord. Thus he is designated by his former name, so that the Lord’s power may be remembered.

*Simon* is interpreted as “obedient”; *Bethany* as “house of obedience.”

An alabaster vessel is a kind of white marble marked with various colors. Physicians commonly hollow vessels from it and place substances in them because they are better preserved there; the ointment itself is called by the name of that marble because it is more often preserved in it. By a figure of metonymy, the container is used to indicate what it contains [the text’s wording is corrupt here]. It is called precious because, as the Greek physicians say, it surpasses all other ointments.

Mark identifies the aromatic plant from which the ointment is made [Col. 1473A]. Spikenard is an aromatic shrub with a black, thick, fragile, but rich root. Its smell is close to that of cypress, its taste harsh, and its leaves small and dense. Its tops grow into spikes, which are also called ears. Hence Mark says “spikenard,” that is, nard possessing spikes. Since it was precious, it had been made from its roots, spikes, and leaves.

John, however, writes *nardus pistica*. *Pistis* means “faith” in Greek, and *pisticus* is derived from *pisti*. It is therefore called “faithful nard,” because it was made genuinely and contained no adulteration or mixture of anything bad.

It is asked why this woman then wished to do this for the Lord, when she had not done it before, or why she permitted this precious work to be done for her. After the Lord had [Col. 1473B] raised Lazarus, he had not come to Bethany except then, for the first time, and she could no longer perform service for her resurrected brother.

She bought this ointment and anointed his head. It was the custom of the Jews to anoint the head with prepared ointments, since balsam grew abundantly in their land. Because of this custom, rich and poor alike anointed their heads after washing their faces. Hence the Lord also says: “But when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face.” From this custom, therefore, the Lord’s head was anointed, and for this reason he permitted it to be done to him. Figuratively, the Church of Christ anoints the head when it receives with fitting reverence the mysteries of the humanity he assumed.

But when the disciples saw this, they were indignant, saying. By the figure of synecdoche, many are said to have been indignant for one, since John says that only Judas was indignant [Col. 1473C].

“This could have been sold for much and given to the poor.” Judas took offense against the Lord on this account, although he had always previously been unbelieving. He was angry because he had not been permitted to sell the ointment, and he thought that the Lord was not God, since the one who had always lived in contempt and regarded the glory of this age as nothing was now allowing himself to be anointed with such precious ointment.

There was indeed a custom in that land, and in many lands where people cannot survive because of the abundance of serpents unless they possess medicines, for physicians to make ointments and antidotes, since herbs and spices were abundant there, and to sell them to those who did not have them. Thus your people also purchase scammony [Col. 1473D], which those who sell it prepare from a cheap herb.

But Judas said: “Why this waste? For this could have been sold for much and given to the poor.” “Sold for much,” because it could have been sold for three hundred denarii, that is, twenty-five solidi. Yet John says that it was a pound of ointment—that is, that it could have been bought for one pound. He did not want to give it to the poor but to increase his own greed.

But Jesus, knowing this, said to them: “Why do you trouble this woman?” One who is troublesome is called harsh or angry. “She has performed a good work for me.” Other evangelists explain why it pleased God that this precious work should be done. “She has anticipated,” he says, “anointing my body for burial,” because he was not to remain in the tomb long enough for it to be necessary to embalm his body with aromatics. He allowed [Col. 1474A] this woman to do this for him both to reveal his death through the act and to fulfill the devotion of the woman who had bought the ointment for this very purpose.

“For you always have the poor with you, but you will not always have me.” He was speaking of the presence of his body, because he was about to depart from them. For the presence of his divinity is always with all his elect, just as after the resurrection he said to his disciples: “Behold, I am with you always, until the end of the age.”

“For in pouring this ointment upon my body”—the woman is understood—“she did it for my burial.” That is, she anticipated performing for me the service that would have to be done after my death, inspired by me to do what, because of my swift resurrection, she would not be able to do.

“Amen, I say to you: wherever this Gospel is preached throughout the whole world” [Col. 1474B]. It is as if he said: When my Gospel is preached, what she did will also be told in her memory. Throughout the whole world she too will be praised, and an example of serving the Lord will be taken from her. Spiritually, this may also be understood of the Church.

And, becoming saddened, they began one by one to say: “Surely I am not the one, Lord?” Although they were conscious that they had thought nothing of this kind against their teacher, they nevertheless believed the teacher more than themselves. They were saddened because there was someone among them who had conceived such a plan.

But he answered and said: “The one who dips his hand with me in the dish will betray me.” Gradually and by indications, like a merciful lord and teacher, he wished to correct him. But Judas, having become irreverent, was not only not saddened like the others; he even put his hand into the dish with the teacher. The sin of greed [Col. 1474C] that he harbored in his mind also made him shameless in every other respect.

A *paropsis* is a square, four-sided vessel, that is, one with equal projections.

Then one of the Twelve went away. Since the evangelists say that Judas went to the Pharisees after the anointing of the Lord’s head, and again relate that he went away after the morsel, it should be understood that from that hour he had resolved in his mind to go. For he had heard that the chief priests had decreed that if anyone knew him, he should betray him.

The one called Judas Iscariot. He is called Iscariot from the village in which he was born.

“What will you give me, and I will hand him over to you?” Hence Judas was especially wicked, because he himself first went to the Pharisees and placed the Lord’s price in their power. And whatever Christian [Col. 1474D] conceals the truth for a reward, or unjustly oppresses a member of Christ for the sake of rewards, is like Judas, because Christ said: “I am the truth.” And: “Whatever you did for one of my least ones, you did for me.” The one who destroys the harmony of fraternal peace is like him also, because God is love.

And they fixed for him thirty pieces of silver. It is not unreasonable to believe that Joseph was sold for the same price, although authorities differ on this, since Joseph went before as a figure of the Lord. Joseph was sold into perpetual service, whereas the Lord was manifested only to be handed over without a crowd. They determined that they would give it to him, but did not give it until after the destruction.

From then on he sought an opportunity to betray him. “Without the crowds” is understood: that he might hand him over without the crowds and others, and that he himself might not have [them; the reference is unclear].

Now, on the [Col. 1475A] first day of Unleavened Bread. That is, on the first day when they removed leavened bread; it was the day of Passover, since they also ate unleavened bread then. On Thursday morning they asked, and in the evening he came after them into the city to eat the lamb.

His disciples approached him: Peter and Andrew, who were senior both in age and in wisdom. John, who was younger, was there; Judas, who kept the Lord’s money, was among them.

“Where do you wish us to prepare the Passover for you to eat?” It was both a command and a custom in that land to come to the Lord’s temple for the great feasts, but to eat the lamb with whomever one wished, provided that, if the household in a house was too small, it should take a neighbor of its house. Therefore they asked where he wished to eat the lamb, because Judas’s duty was to buy the lamb and the other necessities [Col. 1475B].

But Jesus said: “Go into the city to a certain man and say to him.” Why was it necessary to give his name, when he himself showed them their guide, saying: “As you enter the city, a man carrying a jar of water will meet you. Follow him into the house into which he enters, and you shall say to the master of the house…” Matthew, directing his attention to other matters, left what was to be said to the other man. Mark similarly speaks of a pitcher. But “amphora” and “pitcher” are used for the same thing, and both names derive from Greek. They signify an earthen vessel with two handles, such as country people commonly use for preserving water.

Mystically, through water the washing that cleanses the world is shown to those wishing to celebrate the spiritual Passover. Through the amphora and the pitcher, our fragility is signified, which was to be washed through baptism.

[Col. 1475C] “The Teacher says: My time is near; I will keep the Passover with you.” When he says “My time is near,” “for celebrating the Passover” is understood. For that man was not so faithful that the Lord should have needed to tell him of his approaching death; if he had been faithful, the disciples would have known his house, and he would have received the Lord more frequently.

And the disciples did as Jesus had appointed them, and they prepared the Passover. That is, they prepared what was necessary and furnished the house.

When evening came, he reclined with his twelve disciples. The lamb was commanded to be sacrificed in the evening, on the very night [Col. 1475D] when the destroyer was to pass through; or because the moon changes at night when the fourteenth day arrives, since the moon’s power is at night; or because the people of Israel fled from the land of Egypt on that very night.

And while they were eating, he said: “Amen, I say to you, one of you will betray me.” He who had foretold the Passion foretold the betrayal as well, so that the guilty man might repent. He does not identify him explicitly, lest, being made reckless, he become worse.

“The Son of Man indeed goes, as it is written of him.” “Goes,” that is, to death. “As it is written.” This has been stated in many places of Scripture, as in Isaiah: “Because of the crime of my people I struck him.”

“But woe to that man through whom he will be betrayed.” This means that the woe is perpetual. Woe threatens that man in hell [Col. 1476A], because he will betray him for his greed. For the Father also handed him over, and the Son handed himself over; but the Father and the Son did so out of love, Judas out of greed.

“It would be better for him if he had not been born.” This does not mean that anyone would possess any good unless he were born, but simply that it would have been better for him not to exist than to exist in evil.

But Judas answered and said: “Surely I am not the one, Rabbi?” Pride appears in his voice, as does unbelief. Whereas the others, who were greater than he, said “Lord,” he, as though he were not God, says “Teacher.” He waited and did not excuse himself with the others, because he wanted God to expose him openly, so that he might have an occasion to say: “Since you reproach me for things I have not done, I ought to abandon you and seek another teacher.” But God, who foreknew his thoughts, knew that he would not find in him an occasion [to abandon him] [Col. 1476B].

He said to him: “You have said it.” As if he were saying: “I am not saying it; you are. You will not find in me an occasion to abandon me.”

And while they were dining, Jesus took bread, blessed it, and broke it. After he had completed the old Passover that had been commanded and brought the old shadows to an end, he began to inaugurate the beginning of the new grace and the new sacrifice.

He took bread, which strengthens the human heart and contains more for human bodies, and placed in it the sacrament of his love. But that spiritual bread strengthens every human being and creature much more fully, because in him we move and exist.

He first [Col. 1476C] blessed it because in that human being he blessed the human race; then, in the one whom he had assumed from holy Mary, he showed that the blessing and power of divine immortality truly dwelt there.

He broke the bread, himself, because he voluntarily offered himself to suffering. There he broke the dwelling of his soul for our satisfaction, as he himself said: “I have power to lay down my soul, and I have power to take it up again.”

And he gave it to his disciples and said: “Take and eat; this is my body.” He gave his disciples the sacrament of his body for the remission of sins and the preservation of love, so that, remembering what he had done, they might always perform in figure what he was about to do for them and might not forget it.

“This is my body,” that is, in the sacrament [Note: [Col. 1475D] Alternatively: “that is, truly subsisting in the sacrament.” See Sixtus of Siena, *Bibliotheca sancta*, book V, note 112.]

And taking the cup, he gave thanks and gave it to them, saying: Since among all the foods of life bread and wine are effective for strengthening and restoring our weakness [Col. 1476D], it rightly pleased him to confirm through these two the ministry of his sacrament. For wine both gladdens and increases the blood. Therefore Christ’s blood is fittingly represented by it, since whatever comes to us from him gladdens us with true joy and increases all our good.

Just as, if someone departing abroad leaves his loved ones some bond of affection, with the instruction that they perform this every day so that they may not forget him, so God commanded us to do this, spiritually transferring the body into bread and the wine into blood [Note: [Col. 1476D] Alternatively: “the bread into the body and the wine into the blood.” See Sixtus of Siena, in the same place], so that through these two we might remember what he did for us through his body and [Col. 1477A] blood and not be ungrateful for such devoted love.

Since water is mixed into the sacrament of his blood, his people are signified through the water, for whom he wished to die. Neither is there wine without water, nor water without wine, because he died for us, and so we too must die for him or for our brothers, who are the Church. Hence blood and water came forth from his body.

When he says, “This is my blood of the new covenant,” he says it to distinguish the new covenant from the old, since the blood of goats could not cleanse sin in those who served sin.

“But I say to you: I shall not drink from this fruit of the vine from now on until the day when I drink it new with you in the kingdom of my Father.” The vine is Judea; the wine is that of the patriarchs, prophets, and the rest of the elect. Until then [Col. 1477B] Judea produced grapes from which wine might flow—that is, works through faith. After the Lord’s death it produces wild grapes, until Enoch and Elijah lead it into the kingdom, into the Church of Christ, at the end of the age.

Or, more simply, from that hour of the supper he did not drink wine until, after the resurrection, he became immortal and incorruptible.

As for the fact that he wished to give his disciples the sacrament of his body and blood after the supper, while we are commanded to receive it fasting, the reason is this: the Lord showed that the figurative covenant commanded by him would remain until the true one came; he set an end to it and gave a beginning to the new covenant. For this reason he celebrated the new before the old. For a long time the apostles likewise did this, taking the Lord’s [sacrament] after another food. Later, when the Hebrews came to receive Communion, it was [Col. 1477C] decreed in a synod that each person—provided he had also been purified from other sins—should first be refreshed with spiritual food and afterward with temporal food.

And when the hymn had been sung, they went out to the Mount of Olives. Either, following the custom of the Jews, he sang that very day before supper the one hundred and twelfth psalm, “Praise the Lord, you servants,” through the middle of the one hundred and thirteenth, “Not to us, Lord, not to us”; and after the meal, the remainder through Psalm 118. Or he sang the prayer that John reports him to have prayed before his arrest.

He went out from the city again and proceeded to the Mount of Olives, in order to give an opportunity to the betrayer and those who would seize him [Col. 1477D].

Then Jesus said to them: “You will all be scandalized because of me on this night.” He foretells what they will suffer, so that when the hour of suffering comes they may bear it more easily. It should be noted that he said “on this night,” because just as those who are drunk are drunk at night, so those who suffer scandal are still in the night—that is, in ignorance. If they were perfect in knowledge, earthly temptation could not cause them to stumble, because it belongs to the perfect to remain even-tempered amid adversity and prosperity.

For it is written: “I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered.” Almighty God spoke this through Zechariah in his own person: he would give his only one over to death for us, and the apostles would abandon him out of fear. But the Lord acted like a good shepherd: when he saw lions and wolves coming, he went to meet them and set himself against death [Col. 1478A] for his sheep. Meanwhile the sheep fled when they saw the shepherd dying. For he said: “If you seek me, let these go.”

“But after I have risen, I will go before you into Galilee.” He mingles joyful things with difficult ones to refresh their spirits. After saying that they would be scattered because of his death, he adds that he will rise and that they will see him in Galilee. Some of the disciples did see him after the resurrection, but fully in Galilee. Of this appearance blessed Paul says: “Then he was seen by all the apostles.”

But Peter answered and said: “Even if all are scandalized because of you, I will never be scandalized.” Peter does not say this out of [Col. 1478B] fickleness but from the most ardent will. Yet the one who knew all things knew what a human being would do, before he had been filled with the Holy Spirit.

Jesus said to him: “Amen, I say to you: on this night, before the cock crows, you will deny me three times.” Behold, Peter too denies the Lord three times in the night, because every sin steals upon a person more easily at night than during the day. Everyone who sins is in the night.

Then Jesus came to the valley called Gethsemane. He descended from the Mount of Olives into the valley of Gethsemane, where there is now a church, at the place where he prayed. Gethsemane is called “valley of the fertile,” instructing us by example that whoever desires to worship should ascend the mountain of light. Let him also possess a fertile valley, that is, humility.

And taking Peter and the two sons of Zebedee, he began to be sorrowful and troubled. Since he had assumed flesh, he necessarily also had the passions [Col. 1478C] of the flesh, except for that one thing which had not been created with the flesh, namely sin. Because he had begun to be sorrowful, lest harmful sadness mingle with good sadness, he took with him those whom he was accustomed to have in private, so that he might always converse with them about divine things.

We too should all do this in a time of sadness: speak with good people and friends, so that sadness, which produces death, may not find a place in us; in this way it will be avoided.

Then he said to them: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death.” He said this according to the flesh, not according to his impassible divinity. He was sorrowful either for the Jewish people, who had been a part and people of God; or for the apostles’ tribulation; or even for the treacherous Judas—not for his own death, which he willingly underwent and had arranged with the Father many ages before.

Even if we say that he was sorrowful according to his humanity, there is no obstacle to understanding this: he was flesh, and sadness is a passion of the flesh, unless it is removed by God’s power.

And going forward a little [Col. 1478D]. Luke says: “He was separated from them by about a stone’s throw.” Whoever sincerely wishes to be heard must seek secret prayers, removed from all the noise and turmoil of vices. As a warning that in every tribulation the Lord is our refuge and wall, let us continually implore him to free us from the impending danger according to his will.

“My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me.” *Mi* is a possessive vocative, coming from *meus*, “my.” He therefore speaks concerning the Jews: “If it is possible for the nations to be saved without the rejection of the Jews, so that they themselves do not bring death upon me, let it be so” [Col. 1479A]. “Nevertheless, let it be,” not according to the human feeling in which I speak, but rather according to what I have arranged with you in divinity.

Here we too should take an example for prayer: whenever we ask God for some temporal thing of ours, we should always at the end ask even more earnestly for his pleasing will, so that if perhaps we are asking for something against our salvation, he who is our Savior may govern and hear us according to his counsel.

And he came to his disciples and found them sleeping. Sorrow for the Lord was weighing them down, and it was also the time when they were accustomed to sleep. Sleep often follows tears and sadness, especially after indulgence in food.

And he said to Peter: “Could you not watch with me for one hour?” To prepare Peter [Col. 1479B] to endure temptation, he rebukes him because of his sorrow. It is as if he said: “If the coming sadness has already oppressed you, what will you do when it arrives? It is evident that you will deny me, since you cannot now watch with me.”

“Watch and pray.” Watch both in body and in spirit. “And pray that you do not enter into temptation.” He did not say, “that you may not be tempted,” which cannot happen, because there was no one who was not tempted. And whoever has not been tempted has not been tested. We should not pray that we may not be tempted, but that we may not be led into temptation. Therefore he says, “that you do not enter into temptation” that you cannot bear.

“The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.” The spirit, that is, the soul, is ready to give its members for the salvation of human beings, but the flesh is terrified, as an earthly thing before earthly torments. What will those who are mere human beings say, if our Lord, so filled with divinity, spoke in this way? [Col. 1479C]

Again, he went away a second time and prayed, saying: “My Father, if this cup cannot pass unless I drink it, your will be done.” “Let it be done” does not mean according to the feeling of a human being, but because I came down to earth by your will. If it can happen that a multitude of nations believes without the destruction of the Jews, I refuse the Passion. But if they must be blinded so that all the nations may see, then not my will, Father, but yours be done.

Again, a third time he went away and prayed. Just as temptation is completed in three ways, so weapons against temptation must be sought three times.

Then he came to his disciples and found them sleeping. The causes mentioned above were weighing down their eyes.

“Sleep now and rest.” This is understood ironically. It is as if he said: “It is not time to sleep [Col. 1479D], because the one who betrays me is approaching.” This is a form of irony. But if, according to Mark, who says “Sleep” and then adds “It is enough,” we understand that they slept for some interval, and that the Lord then said, “You have slept enough.”

“Rise, let us go.” It is as if he said: “Let them not find us appearing afraid and hesitant; let us go willingly to death, so that they may know that we neither avoid nor flee from it.”

While he was still speaking, behold, Judas, one of the twelve, came, and with him a large crowd carrying swords and clubs, sent by the chief priests and the elders of the people. The priests had asked Pilate, and Pilate had given them one cohort—that is, five hundred soldiers—and with these the priests sent their own servants with spears [Col. 1480A] and staves, among whom was Malchus. Now the one who betrayed him had given them a sign, saying: “Whomever I kiss, he is the one; seize him.” Judas was afraid that he might hide himself, as he did when they wanted to throw him down and stone him. Therefore he gave them such a sign that, after he had kissed him, if he should vanish, Judas would not lose his payment.

It is evident that the pious Lord had this custom: when one of his disciples returned from outside, he would kiss him. This is not done among us now except after several days. Cain also had this sign, kissing everyone out of fear—similar in deed, similar in crime, although this man was worse. And immediately approaching Jesus, he said: “Hail, Rabbi.” *Ave* is said in Latin; in Greek, *chaire* (χαῖρε); in Hebrew, as Judas himself said, *Salam lekh* (סלאם לך), a word of greeting by which the whole world, at the command of the Romans, used to greet one another.

And Jesus said to him: “Friend, for what purpose have you come?” This is understood by antiphrasis—that is, by contrariety—as though he were saying, “Not a friend, who brings such enemies.” Or “friend” in knowledge, but not a friend in action. “For what purpose have you come?”—understand, “Complete what you have begun.” Or, as another Evangelist says: “With a kiss you betray the Son of Man.” You turn into hostility the sign of peace that exists among all peoples.

The ancients established this as a sign of peace: that those whom people customarily make friends or enemies should be joined together. This sign was to signify that, just as we join two limbs together, so all the limbs should be one. Then they approached and laid hands on Jesus [Col. 1480C]. What John reports happened first: when he said to them, “I am he,” they went backward, as unwilling men commonly fall, and fell to the ground. And when they had separated the disciples, then they bound him. O wretched men, who ought to have kissed his feet—you bound his hands!

And behold, one of those who were with Jesus, stretching out his hand, drew a sword. Peter did this with the same fervor of faith with which he did the other things. Yet it pleased the Lord that this should happen, so that all might recognize that he did not wish to defend himself and, after the display of power, the disciples might be released.

And striking the servant of the chief priest, he cut off his ear. What did you think, chief priest, when you saw your servant healed and condemned to death the one who had done this? Allegorically, Malchus is interpreted as “king”; and the Jewish people, who ought to have been king by ruling themselves, became the servant of sin. And he lost his right ear, by which he ought to have heard the commandments of God; but the Lord restored it to those among them who wished to believe.

Jesus said to them: “For all who take up the sword”—understand, for doing evil—“will perish by the sword.” If not by a material sword, then by an invisible sword, or by the sword of God’s word. We also frequently see that one who unjustly kills another, unless he repents, often himself dies in the present life. This seems to be the sentence that he himself spoke to Noah, saying: “Whoever sheds human blood, his blood shall be shed.”

Or do you think that I cannot ask my Father, and he will provide me now with more than twelve legions of angels [Col. 1481A]? I do not need the aid of twelve apostles, since, if I wish, I can have twelve legions of angels. Nor ought it to say “twelve,” but “twelve legions.” Among the ancients, one legion consisted of six thousand; thus there would be seventy-two thousand angels, corresponding to the nations into which the languages were divided. Against each nation I could have one legion of angels.

The prophets prophesied in vain unless I do what they themselves prophesied. At that hour Jesus said to the crowds: “You have come out as against a robber, with swords and clubs.” They had come to resist, in case anyone should wish to free him from the crowds. For the disciples had no swords except the two they had bought, since no Jew carried weapons for battle [Col. 1481B].

It is evident that these Romans too had come afterward to the Lord’s preaching, and that he was speaking these words to them. For none of the Jewish leaders was there except their servants, who had come to report to their masters whether the Romans were willing to apprehend him. They were not certain that he would be apprehended.

“This is your hour.” Everyone who does evil hates the light, and all evildoers love the night more than the day. Now all this happened. “Betrayal” means apprehension. Of betrayal the Psalmist says: “He who ate my bread magnified his treachery against me.” Of apprehension: “Like a sheep he will be led to slaughter.”

Then all the disciples, leaving him, fled. The words of the Lord were fulfilled: “You will suffer scandal because of me on this night” [Col. 1481C]. Like a pious teacher, he permitted them to flee and gave himself over to danger.

But they, having seized Jesus, led him to Caiaphas the chief priest, where the scribes and Pharisees had assembled. Matthew narrates this briefly, but John says that he was first brought to Annas, because Annas was on the road for those coming and had been high priest in the preceding year. Then he was brought to the house of Caiaphas, who was high priest that year.

For the Lord had commanded that, as long as the high priest lived, he should retain the office of high priest. But Herod, in order to receive gifts, devised a system by which he would have no authority for more than one year unless he bought it again. The Romans later did the same, for as long as that office endured. Therefore the other leading men gathered to Caiaphas, who was chief priest by purchase [Col. 1481D]; and there he was falsely condemned to death, and from there he was led into the praetorium.

For this reason the Gospel of John should not read, “They bring Jesus to Caiaphas,” with *ad* governing the accusative, but “from Caiaphas,” with an ablative preposition and *Caiapha* in the ablative case. For if the servants were unwilling to enter the praetorium, how much more Caiaphas, who was chief priest? They thought that they would be defiled among pagans, even though those pagans already had the seven days of Unleavened Bread. In Greek also it reads ἀπὸ τοῦ Caipha, with the ablative case.

Peter, however, was following from a distance. He followed from a distance because he was soon going to deny him. Yet he had not seen the tortures being prepared; therefore he followed. But John brought him into the courtyard of the chief priest, as John himself reports, because he was known to the high priest [Col. 1482A]. They say that Caiaphas had John’s sister as his wife, and Annas had Caiaphas’s sister. He entered to see the outcome—namely, what the priests would decide concerning him.

The chief priests and the whole council were seeking false testimony against Jesus in order to hand him over to death. They knew that the Romans would not kill him unless they stated a charge. But they did not find one, although many false witnesses came forward.

The other Gospels say that they accused him of stirring up the people and making them follow him through his preaching, forbidding them to pay taxes to Caesar, and saying that he was Christ the King. All these charges were false. Finally two false witnesses came forward. Because the Lord had commanded that no one should be condemned on the testimony of one person, the leaders themselves arranged for two [Col. 1482B].

One said: “I can destroy the temple of God and rebuild it after three days.” The Lord said neither these words nor this meaning. He said: “Destroy this temple”—that is, the temple of the dwelling of my soul—“and I will raise it up.” “Destroy” means “dissolve,” and “I will raise it up.” These words refer more properly to the body than do “destroy” and “rebuild,” which refer to a stone house.

Here it is evident that every person who says something with a different meaning from the one who first spoke it is a false witness, because he does not speak with the meaning intended by the first speaker. And what harm would it have done them if he had actually said it in that way—or if it had been relevant to his condemnation?

Then the chief priest rose and said to him. Because the priest was hearing neither Christ nor the false witnesses say anything from which he could find grounds for condemning him [Col. 1482C], he rose from his seat and adjured him, so that he might find some opportunity for accusation.

But Jesus remained silent. He knew that they wanted to twist his words into an accusation rather than believe; therefore he was silent. And the chief priest said to him: “I adjure you by the living God to tell us whether you are the Christ, the Son of God.”

This most wicked high priest understood that, when adjured by the name of God, he would not take that name in vain but would answer with the truth. Yet the Lord so tempered his reply that he seemed neither to disregard his own name nor to expose himself to any accusation.

“You have said so. Nevertheless I tell you: from now on you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of God.” That is, good people will see with the eyes of the heart that the one called the Son of Man possesses the same power as God when he has ascended into heaven and all authority in heaven and on earth has been given to him; and they will see him coming on the clouds to judge the whole world—the one whom you have judged.

What would his martyrs have done if he himself had remained silent in this way? Since he had already determined to die for the people, he proclaimed the truth in order to give his martyrs the example that they must proclaim it steadfastly even unto death.

Then the chief priest tore his garments. It was the custom of the Jews, whenever they heard something resembling blasphemy, to tear their garments. We read that Paul and Barnabas did this in Lycaonia when they were being honored with the worship of gods. But Herod, because he did not give honor to God by rejecting as false the divine name being attributed to him, was struck by an angel [Col. 1483A].

That priest understood that the Lord had said he would sit at the right hand of the Father and judge the world—something appropriate to no one except God. But what he considered blasphemy is our firm faith.

They answered: “He is guilty of death.” This is a specifically Roman expression, frequently used among them; *reus* means “guilty.”

Then they spat in his face. It was also the custom of the Jews to spit in the face of those whom they considered worthless. Hence the Lord said concerning Mary, the sister of Aaron: “If her father had spat in her face, ought she not to have been put to shame for seven days?”

And they struck him with fists. *Colaphus* is the Greek word for “fist.” Others struck him in the face with their palms. As the other Evangelists report, they covered his face, because he had called himself a prophet, and in mockery said: “If you are a prophet, tell by prophecy who struck you” [Col. 1483B].

You ought to have wept over that prophecy, because he had already prophesied to you that Jerusalem would be surrounded by an army.

Peter was sitting outside in the courtyard. There was a larger house where those priests sat, while the Lord stood before them. Apart from that house there was another beside it. This is the courtyard mentioned here, where the servants of the chief priest had a fire and could see from there those sitting in council.

Peter was there, brought in by John. Thus the Lord could see Peter, and Peter could see him. But Peter did not dare approach him, lest he be recognized. For those who had brought him entered Pilate’s house and left the Lord with the priests.

The courtyard is called *atrium*, as though from *ater*, “black,” namely because of the smoke. In the Lord’s temple, the courtyards before the main roof of the temple are likewise called *atria*. In that other house, then, Peter waited, wishing to know whether the priests would release him or condemn him to death.

And a maidservant approached him, saying: “You also were with Jesus the Galilean.” Woman is a curious creature, eager for novelty. This woman had heard from the servants of the high priest who were there that he had been present when the Lord was seized. They did not wish to say so—either lest the power he had displayed there become known, or because they did not dare to raise their hand against him, since Roman law prescribed that anyone who struck another in an assembly should lose his hand.

This woman, or the other woman, could not keep silent, but immediately began to reproach him for having been with the Lord at the time of his apprehension. And, what is worse, this sex too was not absent from the Lord’s persecution—although it was redeemed and was the first to announce the resurrection to men.

After a little while, the servants of the priest who were standing there approached, and Malchus’s relative himself said: “I saw you with him.” Others said: “Your speech makes you evident.” This does not mean that Peter’s tongue belonged to another language, as they accused him, but that each province has its own peculiarities and sounds, as other provinces do in which people are recognized.

Thus in the Acts of the Apostles they say: “Are not all these who speak Galileans? And how is it that we hear each of us in our own language in which we were born?” And Peter, preaching, speaks in such a way that the language of the people was called *aceldama*. This statement shows that the inhabitants of Jerusalem and the Galileans called the same place by different names [Col. 1484A].

Then he began to curse and swear that he did not know the man. It would have been better for blessed Peter to flee with the others than to remain and curse and deny the Lord, because when he denied the Lord, he denied that he was his disciple. This is what those do today who yield to tortures and deny that they are Christians.

And immediately the cock crowed. Earlier the Lord had looked at Peter, and then Peter remembered the Lord’s word. And going outside, he wept bitterly. Blessed Peter was still fragile, since he did not even dare to weep in the priest’s courtyard.

Spiritually, this signifies that we cannot perform perfect repentance among the wicked, and that association with the wicked does great harm. Placed among the disciples, he confessed Christ as the Son of God; in the priest’s courtyard he denied knowing the same Christ.

When morning came, all the chief priests and the elders of the people took counsel against Jesus in order to hand him over to death [Col. 1484B]. See the persistence of evil: they stayed awake the whole night so that they might commit murder. Envy and hatred did not permit them to consider what they were doing; indeed, they were putting to death an innocent man who had also performed miracles.

And having bound him, they brought him and handed him over to Pontius Pilate the governor. It was their custom that anyone whom they condemned to death should be handed over bound to Roman authority, because they themselves did not have the power to kill.

*Pontius* was Pilate’s nomen, derived from the province near Constantinople, because he had been born there; from it the Pontic Sea is named. Hence the expression “the Pontic Sea,” sweeter than the other seas. *Pilatus* was his personal name.

*Pontius* is interpreted as “turning aside counsel,” because he said that he would turn aside the counsel of the Jews. But if he had done so completely, it would have pleased them today. *Pilatus* is said to mean “the mouth of a hammerer,” referring to the authority he exercised wickedly over the Lord.

When Judas, who betrayed him, saw that he had been condemned, he was moved to repentance and returned the thirty silver pieces to the chief priests and elders, saying: “I have sinned by betraying innocent blood.”

Because of the magnitude of his greed, Judas did not consider the outcome of the matter, and therefore threw himself into so terrible a precipice. So many act when love of sin persuades them: they forget the punishments of hell and all the great things of God. But once the deed has been done, they understand that desire has wounded them, passed through them, killed them, and departed.

Hence it is also said of the elders in the story of Susanna: “They turned away their sense and lowered their eyes, so as not to see heaven or remember the judgments of the righteous.”

O detestable Judas, for thirty denarii you betrayed the Lord and Master, forgetting his teaching and his benefits—even if he had not been God. When he saw that he had been handed over to Roman authority, he then believed what he had heard from him: that he would be crucified. Before this, he had always believed that the Lord would be favorable to him and would escape from the hands of the Jews; and he would have obtained forgiveness from the Lord if he had not hastened to kill himself.

Behold, wretched Judas is a witness for the Lord that he always lived justly and saw nothing evil in him.

Blessed Jerome says that when someone sins in such a way that he can undo the evil deed, then he can repent. But if he does not undo the evil deed, he cannot repent. He says: “If a brother sins against a brother in such a way that he can correct what he has done, he can be forgiven. But if the deeds remain, repentance is taken up in vain by words.”

Those who unjustly deprive others of their liberty or their allodial property do not consider this. Someone inserts himself into or takes away an allodial holding; children are born to that man; and at the end of the age there will be a thousand who cry out against him. For as the offspring increase, so does his sin. Then, when he comes to an evil confessor, the confessor orders him to abstain from wine or meat for forty days.

O destruction of souls! Have you forgotten what God said? “If you offer your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there and go to be reconciled with your brother; then come and offer your gift” [Col. 1485B].

It is now also said that he repents in vain so long as the sin has flourished and continues to grow.

But they said: “What is that to us?” It concerns you greatly. For if he sinned who betrayed his Master, you, who were the leaders of the people, not only failed to prevent the evil, but by offering money provoked the disciple to do it and, through lies, handed the Lord over to be condemned to death.

“You will see.” Here *videris* is not the present indicative, but the past subjunctive. It is as though they said: “You ought to have foreseen this before accepting the payment, so that you would not do a deed of which you would repent.”

Judas could no longer undo what had been done, but the leaders could have done so if they had wished, because Pilate acted unwillingly and even gave them the opportunity to release him.

Having thrown the silver pieces into the temple, he departed. The leaders did not wish to receive the money, fearing that, if they accepted the silver and did not return the Lord, he would go to the governor and the governor would recognize their wickedness. But Judas, knowing that it had been given to him from the temple, threw it into the temple.

And departing, he hanged himself. For when Ahithophel saw that his counsel had not been followed, he immediately understood that David would return to the kingdom; unable to bear the disgrace that would come upon him, he died by hanging. So this man, when he saw fulfilled what the Lord had said about himself—namely, that he would be handed over to the nations—became certain that the rest would follow: that they would kill him and that he would rise on the third day. Unable to bear his shame, he wrenched life from himself with a noose [Col. 1485D].

Nevertheless, hated by heaven and earth, he perished in the air. Because of the thirty denarii that Judas received, thirty curses are upon him in the Psalter, among which is: “Let another take his bishopric.” Thus it is certainly known that he too was ordained an apostle with the others.

The chief priests, having taken the silver pieces, said: “It is not lawful to put them into the *corbanan*.” *Corbanan* is called in Hebrew; in Greek, *gazophylacium*; in Latin, “the treasury of riches.” “Because it is the price of blood.”

O wretched men! It is not lawful to put the price of blood among the coins, yet you have polluted yourselves with murder! How dare you touch in the Lord’s temple either the sacrifice of God or his vessels? Therefore the Lord said to you that you are like whitewashed tombs.

The silver did nothing, but you polluted yourselves—the disciple and the silver—and now you considered the uncleanness of the money while considering nothing about yourselves.

After taking counsel, they bought with it the potter’s field as a burial place for foreigners. At that time it served as a burial place for foreigners; now the same place is called the hospital of the Franks, where it had estates in the time of Charles, that king having granted them out of love for Charles. Now they live solely on the alms of Christians, both the monks themselves and the newcomers.

For this reason that field was called *Haceldama*, that is, “Field of Blood.” Not only Christian writings but also pagan testimony and the names of places bear witness even to this day to the sacrilege of the Jews, although a basilica exists there on one side.

The name seems to be compounded from the Latin word *ager*, “field,” and the Greek *haima* (αἷμα), “blood.”

Then what was spoken through the prophet Jeremiah was fulfilled. Since everything done by the Lord was foretold by the prophets, we can have little doubt. It was fitting that all good people who came from him should announce this: both that he was to be sold for thirty denarii and that a field was to be bought with them.

Jesus stood before the governor. He is called *praeses* because he presides over the protection of a place. In order to diminish the power of the Jews, the emperor—or the Romans—first sent the foreigner Herod. After Herod’s death, they divided it among triarchs; then among tetrarchs; and finally appointed governors and prefects [Col. 1486C]. If they had not acted in this way, they would not have destroyed them whenever they wished. They proceeded gradually and in stages, like wise men. Thus they subdued the whole people and brought it under their own authority.

And the governor questioned him, saying: “Are you the King of the Jews?” Pilate asks nothing else about him except whether he is the King of the Jews, because he feared that someone might assume tyranny, as Theudas had done. For this was why he himself governed the province: to prevent such a thing.

Jesus said to him: “You say so.” Whenever he spoke to them, Truth spoke truth, and with moderation, so that no one could reproach him either for excessive speech or for silence.

When he was accused by the chief priests and the elders of the people, he answered nothing. If he had wished to answer everything as he could have done, he would have been released, and redemption would not have been necessary [Col. 1486D].

Then Pilate said to him: “Do you not hear how many testimonies they bring against you?” Pilate urged him to defend himself because he wanted to release him. And he did not answer him a word, so that the governor marveled greatly. He marveled because he did not wish to excuse himself as other men do when they are condemned to death.

For who, unless he were dying for God, would not act with every possible urgency to avoid dying?

On the feast day the governor was accustomed to release to the people one prisoner whom they wished. Life was granted to one condemned man out of reverence for the feast.

He had an eminent prisoner—that is, notorious for his wickedness—called Barabbas. *Bar* means “son”; *rabbi* means “teacher”; understand, “their teacher,” that is, the teacher of the Jews. From that day they have been sheltered and ruled by the devil, who lies in wait like a robber for the Lord’s sheepfold, until they are converted.

When they had assembled, Pilate said to them: “Whom do you want me to release to you: Barabbas, or Jesus who is called Christ?” For he knew that they had handed him over out of envy.

How much envy accomplishes among human beings! Behold, the Lord possessed nothing in this world except food and clothing, and he served everyone by preaching and healing the sick; yet, through the faction of the leading men, they hated and killed him, and chose one who had never done anything except evil.

Such are peoples. Whoever possesses power easily turns those below him toward his own will, however great the number may be. They do not consider who is more righteous, but turn toward whatever they understand their leader to want. Such things happen because of gifts, as it is written: “Riches add many friends, but even those whom a poor man had depart from him.”

While he was sitting on the tribunal. “For the condition,” or “on account of the matters belonging to the tribe.” His wife sent word to him.

Before he came into the palace, Pilate labored greatly to have the Lord released. But when his wife sent word that, after daybreak, she had seen many things about him in a dream, he exerted himself still more.

“Have nothing to do with that righteous man.” That is: “Do him no harm, and do not harm yourself.” “For I have suffered many things today in a dream because of him”—understand, many dreams—sent by angels.

For the devil and his followers were striving to have the Lord crucified, supposing that he was truly a man. It is not surprising that angels came to this woman, since God also spoke to Balaam and an angel appeared to Cornelius [Col. 1487C].

But the chief priests and the elders persuaded the crowds to ask for Barabbas and to destroy Jesus. There is no worse sin than envy. Behold, Pilate’s wife and Pilate declare the Lord righteous, while the traitor and the leaders mislead the people so that they choose Barabbas, who had done them many evils, including murder and robbery, and hand over to death the Lord, who had performed many good works for them.

Even now such is the custom among many: whatever they see or hear their leaders praise, they praise without examination; whatever they see those leaders condemn, they condemn. But whenever someone hears another person praised or blamed, each person ought to guard himself, lest he call good evil or evil good, because woe will come upon the one who does this.

The governor answered and said to them: “Which of the two do you want me to release to you?” Because he could not persuade the leaders to release the Lord, he referred the matter to the whole people, so that, if the leaders wished to destroy him out of envy, the people—who had experienced his many benefits—might ask that he live. For if the common people had asked for him, Pilate would have preserved him alive against the will of the leaders. Or perhaps the priests knew this and had already persuaded the crowds to choose Barabbas.

But they said: “Barabbas.” Such is the custom today: for one word from a leader, they abandon the truth.

Pilate said to them: “What then shall I do with Jesus who is called Christ?” Pilate said all these things in order to release him.

They all said: “Let him be crucified.” Six days earlier they had cried: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord”; now they cry: “Let him be crucified.” During those six days he did nothing other than preach to you until evening. How did he commit the sins for which you cry, “Crucify him”?

The governor said to them: “Why, what evil has he done?” Pilate had held the office for many years; he had neither heard nor seen any evil of his, nor had you. But they cried out more and more: “Let him be crucified.” They did not state a charge, because they did not know one; they cried out, “Crucify him,” like people who had been misled.

When Pilate saw that he was accomplishing nothing toward releasing him, but that rather a riot was developing, the priests, perceiving that Pilate wanted to release him, brought forward the charge: “If you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend” [Col. 1488B].

Fearing both these words and the possibility of a popular revolt—for the nation was very ready to stir up sedition—he showed everyone how unjustly they were acting by washing his hands before the people. As though he were saying in words:

“Behold, these men who possess the law of God and claim to keep his commandments are doing what I, who am foreign to their law, wish to be free from. I am innocent of the blood of this righteous man. I know that he is righteous, and you want to kill an innocent man. You be guilty, not I; you will see to it yourselves.”

And the whole people answered: “His blood be upon us and upon our children.” Because Pilate declared himself innocent, they answered: “Let us be guilty, so that the blood of this man may be required from us and from our children.”

The Jews were heard. The Lord exacted his blood from them through Vespasian and Titus: in Jerusalem, as though in a prison, on the very day of Passover on which they had committed this sacrilege against the Savior; and there those murderers perished by a most evil death [Col. 1488C].

Then he released Barabbas to them; but after scourging Jesus, he handed him over to them to be crucified. Pilate scourged him unwillingly because Roman law prescribed that anyone who was to be crucified should first be scourged.

Thus the Lord was handed over to the soldiers to be beaten, and they cut with scourges that most sacred body and that breast capable of containing God. The column to which he was bound still exists in Jerusalem. O, who then could have believed that the Creator of all things was being treated in that place and at that time? And how wretched were those who were present there!

They have frequently heard the saying: “Blessed are the wombs that did not bear and the breasts that did not nurse”; and they still have cause to say it.

It should be noted that the text says “he handed him over to them,” that is, to their will. Although the soldiers received him, he was handed over to them, and they took possession of him. The soldiers supplied their hands and the wood, but the Jews killed him, because both Pilate and the soldiers acted unwillingly in what they did. Yet Pilate was not innocent, because he could have released him if he had wished. If someone who can help does not help one who is destined to perish, he kills him.

Then the soldiers, taking Jesus into the praetorium. This was the place where Pilate sat, called the Lithostratos. They led him into Pilate’s house. *Lithos* in Greek means “stone” in Latin; *Lithostratos* means “paved with stone.” *Praetorium* is derived from *praetor*, “governor.”

They gathered the whole cohort [Col. 1489A]. The very cohort that had apprehended him was waiting there, in case some disturbance should arise. Thus they gathered the people, because no king can exist without a people.

And they stripped him of his garments and wrapped him in a scarlet cloak. That scarlet cloak was placed around him in place of the purple with which kings were accustomed to be clothed. There is also a kind of red purple very similar to scarlet.

And weaving a crown of thorns, they placed it on his head. In place of the golden diadem they put a crown of thorns; in place of the scepter that kings customarily carry, they placed a reed in his hand. They did all these things in mockery, because he had been accused of saying that he was a king.

The crown of thorns was a branch cut from thorn bushes, bent like a circle and placed upon his head. The reed was given to him because it grows abundantly in that land, and because of its lightness everyone there carries one in his hand.

Allegorically, the thorns signify our sins, which he took upon his body so that he might die on the cross for our sins, although he himself had committed no sin. He held a reed in his hand to show that he would destroy all poisonous things. Or he held the reed in order to write the sacrilege of the Jews, since the Greeks and other nations write with a reed.

And kneeling before him. It was customary in this way to worship a king or his princes. Because Mordecai refused to do this before Haman, Haman wished to destroy him together with his offspring.

“Hail, King of the Jews.” *Ave* is a Latin word, and has no other forms except *ave* and *avete*. It is a word of greeting, as among the Greeks *chaire* and *chairete* (χαῖρε, χαίρετε). In Hebrew it is called *Salam lekh* [Col. 1489C].

And spitting on him, they took the reed and struck his head. By their spitting and striking his head they showed that they had not done what they were doing for any good purpose.

As they went out, they found a man of Cyrene named Simon. John says that Jesus himself first carried the cross and that afterward they encountered a certain Simon. Spiritually, this indicates that the Lord carried his own cross—namely, mortification in his body, because all sins were dead in him—and afterward the Gentile people carried and carry it, following his footsteps.

Cyrene is a city of Libya and is interpreted as “heir”; Simon means “obedient.” Because the Gentile people were obedient to the preachers, they became heirs of that inheritance. Hence the Jewish people gloried in the adoption of sons.

And rightly he was coming from a village. “Village” is *pagos* in Greek, from which *pagani*, “pagans,” is derived. This is fitting for the Gentile people, because, coming from paganism, they began to follow Christ and imitate him.

They compelled him—that is, they imposed on him the task of carrying the cross behind Jesus. And they came to a place called Golgotha. The Evangelist explained what Golgotha is: *Calvariae*, “of the skull,” with “place” understood. It is a Syriac word, not a Hebrew one, although the Hebrews called the place by that name.

Because the skulls of condemned men were removed there, it was a place outside the city. It pleased God to die there where criminals were punished, so that the banner of virtues might be raised, and so that, just as he endured the cross and the other insults for us, he might also endure this.

Sedulius beautifully described how he was upon the cross, saying:

> And lest anyone be unaware that the form of the cross is worthy of worship,
>
> which, by mighty design, bore the Lord in triumph:
>
> from it the four regions of the square world are gathered.
>
> From the head of the radiant author the East shines forth
>
> toward the West; the stars are touched by his sacred feet.
>
> The North is held by his right hand; his left raises the central axis,
>
> and all nature lives from the limbs of its Creator;
>
> and Christ, embraced by the cross, governs the whole world on every side.

And they gave him wine to drink mixed with gall. It was the same bad wine that they gave him afterward; they gave it now either supposing that he was thirsty from carrying the cross, or because the robbers had asked for it. And when they had given it to them, they also gave it to the Lord; or, as Luke says, “The soldiers mocked him, offering vinegar.”

Allegorically, the Lord’s vineyard—the Jewish people—had been turned into bitterness, so that it produced bitter wine. But when it says, “And when he had tasted it, he would not drink,” it shows that he tasted a little and removed it from his mouth.

After they had crucified him, they divided his garments by casting lots. John explains this more fully: the four soldiers divided the other garments among themselves. But because the tunic was seamless, they cast lots to determine whose it should be. This signified that the Gospel would be disseminated through the four corners of the earth, while his Church would be one throughout the whole world. For although the expanses of the earth are separated, the elect are nevertheless one body of Christ, and there is one catholic Church—that is, universal.

“And sitting down, they kept watch over him”: they waited for him to die and to ensure that no one removed him until the governor gave the order.

“And they placed above his head the written charge against him: ‘This is Jesus, the king of the Jews.’” It was the Roman custom that whenever someone was condemned to death, after the entire judgment had been completed, the charge for which he was being killed was written down and read aloud at the place where he was to be punished. In accordance with this custom, Pilate ordered it to be written; and because he was angry with the Jews, since they were crucifying him, he dictated the title in this form. When the Jews asked that it be written differently, he said: “What I have written, I have written.” But it pleased God that it should be written in this way, so that the Jews, even against their will, might acknowledge that he is the king of the whole earth and of themselves. To the spiritual Jews as well—that is, to confessors—he is a gracious king.

It was written in three languages: in Hebrew, on account of the Jews; in Greek, because the nobles of the Romans spoke Greek; and in Latin, on account of the Romans. These three languages are also the most excellent in the whole world, both because of their perfection and because of the peoples who spoke them. Hebrew was the mother of languages. Greek was honored on account of its wisdom, since the Greeks are wiser than all other nations, and because it is more sonorous than the other languages. Latin was honored on account of the Romans, who at that time ruled the world.

[Col. 1490C]

“Then they crucified two robbers with him, one on his right and one on his left.” Whether the Jews wish it or not, everything is being enacted mystically, although they themselves think the punishment shameful. Behold, the Lord, the physician, is crucified, so that it may be shown that he is the judge of the good and the evil among the people. And just as at the judgment the good will be placed on the right and the evil on the left, so now the good man is on the right and the evil man on the left.

“But those passing by blasphemed him, shaking their heads.” Those who, because of envy, had previously been unable to bear seeing him when he performed miracles now walked before him, because at that time they saw him as they had always wished to see him. They shook their heads, as those customarily do who consider themselves superior to people whom they despise.

“Ha! You who destroy the temple of God.” *Vah* is an interjection expressing delight, because they rejoiced when they saw what they had always desired. Among the ancients *vah* was a complete interjection, although it is common to many nations. In order to win the favor of rulers, ordinary people used to say such things; and the rulers, so that the people might repeat them more insistently, later said the same things themselves, showing that they approved what had been said.

Similarly, the chief priests also said: “He saved others; he cannot save himself.” The Pharisees, unwillingly and against their will, bear witness to Christ that he had saved others. This is apparent from the fact that, if he wished, he could free himself from his present danger.

“If he is the king of Israel, let him now come down from the cross, and we will believe in him.” The Jews’ greatest stumbling block was that the Lord had called himself the Son of God and the king of the Jews; they continually repeat and reproach him for this. When they say, “Let him now come down from the cross,” they either speak as though this were impossible, as if he could not do it, or else the demons were prompting them to say it, because they were already perceiving Christ’s power: they saw all the elements thrown into confusion and understood that he was the creator of the world. They regretted that they had crucified him, just as the apostle Paul says: “For if they had understood, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory.”

The robbers who had been crucified with him also reproached him in the same way. By the figure called *sylepsis*, both robbers are introduced as having blasphemed him, although according to Luke one blasphemed while the other confessed him. It is also possible that at first both blasphemed, but afterward one of them, when he saw the elements thrown into confusion, was converted and believed him to be the Lord.

That same robber possessed three virtues on the cross itself, through which he obtained the Lord’s grace: faith, hope, and charity. He had faith because he believed that the man whom he saw dying beside him would reign. He had hope because he requested the rewards for which we hoped, saying: “Remember me, Lord, when you come into your kingdom.” He had charity because, amid the torments, he sought to correct his companion, saying: “Do you not fear God, since you are under the same condemnation?”

Therefore he deserved to hear: “Today you will be with me in paradise.”

[Col. 1490D]

That is, in the place where the rich man saw Lazarus with Abraham. It is rightly called paradise in comparison with the other regions of hell. We also believe that those whom the Lord freed from the punishments of hell were placed there until, ascending into heaven, he led them all with him into the eternal Jerusalem. For just as the Lord was the firstborn from the dead, so he first introduced his own body and soul into heavenly paradise, and afterward the others—which had not happened before he ascended into heaven, forty days later.

“From the sixth hour darkness came over the whole earth until the ninth hour.” Because the Lord ascended the cross at the sixth hour, the sun concealed its rays for the three hours during which the Lord was on the cross. And just as he hung on the gibbet for three hours, so he lay in the tomb for three days. Just as the three hours of his passion were not completed in their entirety, so he did not lie in the tomb through all three days; rather, a part is understood from the whole.

The Jews suspected that there had been an eclipse of the sun or the moon at that time; but there was not, because a solar eclipse can occur only at the rising of the moon, and a lunar eclipse only at the old moon.

The Lord hung on the cross at the hour when Adam sinned in paradise. For it is written that Adam heard the voice of God walking in paradise after midday. At the same hour in which Adam introduced death, the second and true Adam conquered death. And just as the Lord hung on the cross for three hours, so Adam remained in paradise for three hours.

“And around the ninth hour Jesus cried out with a loud voice,”

[Col. 1491A]

saying: “Eli, Eli, lamma sabacthani.” The same verse is given in the Hebrew language out of reverence for the Lord, because it is his prayer; therefore it has not been translated. In Hebrew it does not contain “look upon me,” as it does in our Psalters, nor does it contain “my” except once, nor does the Greek either. In Greek it is said: “Ὁ Θεὸς, ὁ Θεὸς μου, ἵνα τί ἐγκατέλιπές με,” that is, “O God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”

He speaks these words in the person of the man who was suffering, because, as it were, everything had been fulfilled according to the Jews’ will when they saw him dying on the cross. The *l* should not be joined to the *i*, but pronounced separately, nor should it have an aspiration at the beginning. For *El* is the first of the ten names by which God is called among the Jews, and it is found at the end of Hebrew names, such as Michael, Gabriel, and Raphael. In Greek it is said to be ἴσχυρος, that is, “strong.”

But some of those standing there and hearing this said: “This man is calling Elijah.” The soldiers said this because they were ignorant of the Hebrew language. But the Jews also said it in mockery, changing it into an evil sense, as they did with the rest. For *Eli*, too—the name of the prophet—is interpreted as “my God.”
