“And immediately one of them ran, took a sponge, filled it with vinegar, placed it on a reed, and gave him a drink.” As Luke reports, the soldiers did this in mockery; yet it had also been prophesied, and the Lord, because he knew that this had been prophesied about him and that it had not yet been fulfilled, said: “I thirst.” That is: “I know that this has been prophesied concerning me; let what has not yet been fulfilled now be fulfilled. Then everything that was prophesied about my passion will be accomplished.”

This drink was appropriately given to Christ, because just as vinegar comes from good wine, so the Jews had become evil from a good ancestry.

“Jesus, crying out again with a loud voice”—that is, so that those standing around might hear. John, writing what he cried out, says: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit.” The very man who was said to have been abandoned by the Father entrusted his soul to him, and commended it to the one by whom his body and soul had been created—that is, to the divinity.

In Greek this is said, *eis cheiras sou parathesomai to pneuma mou*: “εἰς χεῖράς σου παραθήσομαι τὸ πνεῦμά μου,” that is, “Into your hands I will commend my spirit.” It is good for a Christian to say this when he is about to depart from the body, following the example of the Lord, who spoke in this way.

“He gave up his spirit”—that is, his soul. For where he had earlier said, “I have power to lay down my soul,” they now say, “He gave up his spirit.” What is giving up the spirit, then, except laying down the soul as well? The soul is so called because it gives life; the spirit either because of its spiritual nature or because it breathes in the body. Likewise, the *animus* is a part of the soul, namely, the soul’s will; the mind is also a part of the soul, namely, memory. All these are joined to the soul in such a way that they are one thing, while the soul receives different names according to its different functions.

“And behold, the veil of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom.” Before the Holy of Holies hung a very costly curtain, beyond which no one entered except the high priest, and he only once a year. What was within was called the Holy of Holies, because the Jews had nothing holier. The ark had been there before Jeremiah concealed it, and the mercy seat was there as well. It could be seen from one side, while the rest was hidden on the other; it is called a veil because it veiled—that is, concealed—the interior.

Another veil hung on the outside, between the first altar and the people. The Jews say that this veil was torn. It was not the first veil of the temple that was torn, so that it might show that all sacred things were to pass over to the gentile people. Formerly it was said: “God is known in Judah”; now it is said: “From the rising of the sun to its setting, the name of the Lord is worthy of praise.”

[Col. 1491B]

“And the earth was shaken, and the rocks were split.” Josephus reports that the lintel, which was of immense size, was broken and divided, and that at that very time even the angelic powers cried out: “Let us depart from these dwellings.”

In all these signs of the elements, the creator must be recognized, for whose death the elements are shaken. Mystically, the hearts of the gentiles were to be shaken and opened to the confession of God. They were indeed opened at that time, but the dead among them did not rise until after the Lord had risen, so that he might be the firstborn from the dead. No immortals rose before him; rather, all died again, as Lazarus did. These, however, rose immortal and ascended with the Lord when he ascended.

The dead are called “sleeping” throughout all the divine Scriptures, and the place where they rest is called κοιμητήριον, that is, “dormitory,” in the Greek language, so that it may be truthfully shown that all will rise at the end of the world.

“And coming out of the tombs after his resurrection.” When it says “his resurrection,” this refers both to “they rose” and to “coming out of the tombs.”

“They came into the holy city.” Jerusalem is still called holy because of the Lord’s temple, the vessels that had been sanctified there, and the many holy people who were living there, even though we do not possess an account of all of them. For afterward we find that the apostles prayed there and observed every form of religious worship until its destruction, in the forty-second year after his ascension. That period had been given to them for repentance.

And because they refused to repent, two bears emerged against them—Vespasian and Titus—from the thicket of the gentiles; they killed eleven hundred thousand of them and led away one hundred thousand.

When it says that they “appeared to many,” it shows that this was not a general resurrection but a particular one: those whom God held dear rose, and they appeared to those who had been chosen to know God’s mystery.

[Col. 1491C]

“But the centurion and those with him who were guarding Jesus, when they saw the earthquake and the things that were happening, were greatly afraid.” This centurion, as we find written, was Longinus, who, on Pilate’s order, opened the Lord’s side. Pilate did not want his legs to be broken along with those of the robbers, since that was a very cruel and dishonorable act, and he did not want the Jews to say that he had not been dead but had merely suffered a spasm.

Yet nothing caused the centurion such amazement as the fact that, when he wished and when he said, “Into your hands I commend my spirit,” he then died. Other human beings are neither born when they wish nor die at the hour they choose. In this especially he recognized that he was God, and therefore believed and was baptized. He was later also killed for Christ by the prefect Octavius.

Not he alone, but the soldiers as well glorified God.

“There were also many women there, watching from a distance, who had followed Jesus from Galilee, ministering to him.” It was customary among the Jews for women to minister from their own resources to the prophets and preachers of the law, supplying them with food and clothing, and there was no reproach among them on this account among the gentiles. Because this could give rise to scandal, blessed Paul did not make use of it. Hence he says: “Do we not have the right to take a woman along with us, as Cephas and the others do?”

They ministered to the Lord from their resources so that they might reap his spiritual words—not because the Lord needed their material goods, but so that he might show that preachers rightly deserved such support. The Lord too, although he was God, chose such companions and ministers that no complaint could be raised against them.

[Col. 1491D]

Among them were Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Joseph, and the mother of the sons of Zebedee. Mary Magdalene was the woman from whom he had cast out seven demons. Mary, the mother of James and Joseph, was the Lord’s maternal aunt, because she was the sister of Saint Mary. She is called *matertera*, as if to say “another mother.” The mother of the sons of Zebedee was there serving her sons with the Lord.

“When evening had come.” The law commanded that anyone who had been hung on a gibbet should be taken down by evening. This was in accordance with what Joshua had been commanded to do concerning the five kings; for this reason their legs were broken, so that they might die and be removed.

“A certain rich man came.” The evangelist does not say that this man was rich out of any desire to boast, but to show that he was able to obtain the Lord’s body because he was rich and held the rank of a member of the council, one of its counselors. Poor men did not dare approach such a powerful governor, because he paid no attention to what Solomon said: “Whoever despises the poor sins.” Our own people, who have been commanded to gather in the poor, despise them; how much more did that pagan.

“A certain man from Arimathea.” Arimathea is Ramatha, the city of the prophet Samuel in the region of Samnium, near Diospolis.

“Named Joseph.” This was not the Lord’s foster father, since that man was poor; nowhere else in the Gospel is this Joseph mentioned, except here. From this it is shown that the Lord had many disciples about whom we have no written account, who did not follow him but carried out God’s works in their own homes.

He approached Pilate and asked for Jesus’ body. His status is shown by the fact that he approached Pilate himself and sent no one else in his place; and he himself dared to bury the man who had been condemned.

[Col. 1492A]

They relate concerning him that the Jews, for this reason, put him into custody, and that on the very night of the Lord’s Resurrection the house in which he was confined was lifted into the air, and that the Lord came and brought him out. Later, when the Jews sought the Lord’s body from the soldiers, the soldiers said: “Give us back Joseph, and we will give you back the body.” Then Pilate ordered that the body be returned.

This Joseph was a man of great dignity according to the world and according to God: he was powerful enough to obtain the body and worthy to carry out the ministry of burial.

From this Joseph the first psalm is understood to have been sung: “Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the wicked,” and so forth.

“And Joseph took the body and wrapped it in a clean linen cloth.” *Sindon* means linen cloth, one that had been newly purchased and from which nothing had previously been made. He wrapped the Lord’s body in it together with spices.

It was already close to the observance of the Sabbath, and therefore he could do nothing else except place spices around the body and wrap it in the linen cloth. He placed it in the tomb without a covering, so that after the Sabbath he could return with additional spices and then anoint the Lord carefully. But because Joseph was confined in custody by the Jews, and the poor women could not make preparations on the following day, they intended to complete this on the third day, if they found the body.

From this custom a practice has prevailed in the Church: when the Lord’s body is consecrated on the altar, it is consecrated not on silk or dyed cloth but on linen. We read that this was established by blessed Sylvester in the deeds of the pontiffs.

This simple burial of the Lord also condemns the extravagance of the rich, who do not wish to be without their riches even in the tomb.

“And he placed it in his own new tomb, which he had hewn in the rock.” It was placed in a new tomb so that, if someone else had previously been placed there, there might be doubt about who had risen. Just as no one lay before or after him in the womb of Saint Mary, so no one lay before or after him in this tomb.

He was placed in hewn rock so that, if it had been constructed from small stones, people might have believed that the body had been stolen by undermining the foundations of the burial mound. All these things were done for the sake of our faith.

Formerly people were buried in houses. But when the stench began to kill those living there, the Romans ordered by public edict that people should not be buried either in a house or in a city. Since it then seemed burdensome to bury relatives and friends under the open sky, they returned to the ancient form of burial, excavating tombs in the rocks or crypts beneath the earth and burying people there.

Hence many such places are still found both near Rome and in other lands, such as the cemetery of Callistus, where Saint Cecilia lay, together with Saint Urban and many soldiers.

They report concerning that tomb that it is a mountain above natural rock, where the earth is said to stand; in the rock itself a crypt has been hewn, and in that crypt a sarcophagus has been cut into the northern side. It is seven feet long and three palms high. Elsewhere, the crypt itself is so high that a man standing inside can scarcely touch the ceiling with an outstretched hand, and it is round in shape.

We can gather a similar description from the tombs excavated in our own land. The rock itself is white with a reddish tint. It was open on the south, from which the Lord’s body was brought in, and above the rock there was a garden. Now, however, the place is enclosed, and a basilica has been consecrated in the crypt itself.

“And he rolled a large stone against the entrance of the tomb and departed.” Joseph rolled the stone there so that no beast might enter and touch the Lord’s body, although there was also an enclosure around it for the care of the garden.

“Mary Magdalene and the other Mary were there.” These are the Marys mentioned above: the sister of Lazarus and the mother of James and Joseph.

[Col. 1492B]

Mary, because of her excessive grief at what she had seen on the cross, could not go to the tomb. But this sister of Lazarus recognized her liberation very well, and she surpassed men and women in serving the Lord. While the others returned to their homes, these women watched how the body was placed, so that at the proper time they might offer him the service of their devotion.

“On the next day, which is after the preparation day.” *Parasceve* is a Greek name, translated into Latin as *praeparatio*, “preparation”; we call it the sixth day, Friday, on which the Lord was crucified. It is called “preparation” because on that day the Jews prepared what they usually ate on the Sabbath.

The Lord was pleased to be crucified on the sixth day because Adam sinned on the sixth day and was expelled from paradise on that same day. Those souls are like those who prepare for the Lord, through good works, a place of rest in their hearts.

They say to Pilate on the Sabbath: “Lord, we remember that that deceiver, while still alive, said: ‘After three days I will rise again.’”

Behold, the Jews served our salvation and progress in this matter, because we have not only the evangelists but also the guards as witnesses of the Lord’s resurrection. This is what those who fight against God do: they strive to prevent what they do not want to happen, and in doing so they prepare what God has ordained.

They acted very well when they sealed the stone and appointed guards, for they made us more certain of the Lord’s resurrection. Yet it should also be observed that the thought still prevailed in Judea among those people who, because of envy, could not bring themselves even to name him, but called him “the deceiver.” If you had known what the guards were going to announce, you would never have appointed them to guard the tomb.

Pilate said to them: “You have a guard; go, secure it as you know how.” This does not mean that the Jews had the soldiers under their own authority, but it is as though he had said: “Behold, I give you a guard. Arrange how it is to be guarded, so that you will have nothing to say.”

They went and secured the tomb—that is, by means of the guard and the sealing. Since it was the Sabbath, they desired nothing else and did nothing more than what could be done by command. It is apparent that the tomb was nearby, since they dared to walk there on the Sabbath.

It should also be noted that Joseph, though he was from Ramathaim, wished to be buried near Jerusalem, so that he might rise there with the many saints who lay there.

The persecutors of the Lord are recorded to have met the following ends.

[Col. 1492C]

First, Herod, who wished to kill him, killed innocent children on his account and ordered all the divine Scriptures to be burned, so that people would think that his own offspring came from the royal line of David. He also married Mariamne, the daughter of Aristobulus, so that his descendants might possess the kingdom forever. But because he acted unjustly and against God’s will, he soon fell.

He did not reign more than three years after the slaughter of the innocents. He was consumed externally by a sacred or wasting fire, while his entire body putrefied within. His breath emitted a foul odor; his feet and genitals were swollen; and, in addition to all this, he suffered a severe fever.

He had already killed his wife Mariamne and their three sons by her—Aristobulus, Hyrcanus, and Antipater—as well as three others. Yet amid these sufferings he ordered all the sons of the nobles to be confined in one place. He summoned his father-in-law and said to him: “I know that the Jews will rejoice at my death. But if you were willing, I would have mourners at my funeral: once I was dead, you would kill the sons of the nobles, and then I would have mourners at my funeral.”

His father-in-law promised to do this, but did nothing. When Herod died, he ordered them all to be released. After the illnesses had grown severe in him, he took a knife, ostensibly to peel an apple, and killed himself; thus he died.

Archelaus, his son, died in exile at Vienna. Herod the tetrarch, the son of Herod, who beheaded John and agreed with Pilate during the Passion, was exiled to Lyons. Another Herod, Herod’s grandson and the son of Aristobulus, who beheaded James, the brother of Saint John, died after worms had eaten him from within for five days. Pilate killed himself with his own hand.

“On the evening of the Sabbath, as it began to dawn toward the first day of the week.” *Vespere* is named from the star that commonly rises as the day begins to grow dark. “On the evening of the Sabbath”—that is, on the Sabbath evening that begins to grow light—nevertheless belongs to the first day of the week.

Before the Lord’s coming, the day preceded the evening. Whoever wished to celebrate a complete day celebrated the day first and then the evening and night, to signify that Adam came from paradise into the world as from light into darkness, from innocence into sin. After the resurrection, however, evening and night preceded, to show that through Christ we have come again from sin to innocence.

The fact that different times for the women are described in the Gospels is not a falsehood but results from the frequency of the women’s visits.

“They came on the evening of the Sabbath.” They came after the evening of that day, while it was still dark—that is, they came at first light. Thus “on the evening of the Sabbath” means, as it were, “during the night that follows the Sabbath.”

On the very day when he suffered, they returned and prepared spices and ointments. On the Sabbath they remained silent in accordance with the command of the law, observing the Sabbath from one evening to the next. Therefore, after the Lord had been buried, as long as work was permitted—that is, until sunset—they were occupied in preparing the ointments; and what they could not obtain then, they bought after the Sabbath had passed, so that they might come and anoint Jesus.

*Vespere* is found in both the masculine and feminine gender, among Greeks as well as Latins. Yet the Greeks pronounce it *hespera*, with an aspiration, while we say *vespere*, with *v*. In many words that pass into our language, we use either *s* or *v* in place of their aspiration; thus they say *hex*, while we say *sex*.

The Lord lay in the tomb for forty hours, and for this reason he appeared to them for forty days.

“And behold, there was a great earthquake.” The earthquake occurred on account of the guards, so that they might be terrified, not dare to hinder those who came, and yet, having seen the truth, announce it. Nothing terrifies mortal hearts so much as thunder and an earthquake.

Spiritually, these two women are the two peoples, Jewish and gentile. The earthquake is the shaking caused by God through the preaching of the Holy Spirit. “An angel of the Lord”: the service of the angels, through whom that ministry was completed.

“He rolled away the stone.” He did not do this to open a path for the Lord, but to show the women that the Lord had already departed, and to teach that the barriers of hell had been cast down and overcome.

“He sat upon it.” He sat there to show that Christ had conquered everything—both death and corruption. When he was born, angels appeared standing, to show that he would have to fight with the devil.

“His appearance was like lightning.” This too was for the terror of the guards. The nominative should have *v* here. He appeared in lightning because of the guards’ fear.

“And his clothing was like snow.” This was done to soothe the women, so that he might appear in one aspect. The guards, however, were terrified by him because of their fear. He appeared in this manner on account of the guards, and also to signify that the one whom he announced would be terrifying to the reprobate but gentle to the righteous. In the lightning there was the terror of fear; in the snow, the gentleness of love.

“But the angel answered and said to the women.” Another evangelist says that the women were saying: “Who will roll away the stone for us?” To this the angel is said to have answered. First he drives away their fear, for it is customary and rational that fear should be removed first, since a person cannot understand well while afraid.

Afterward they hear the answer to what the women themselves had been saying: “Do not be afraid.” As if he said openly: “Let those who do not love Jesus be afraid, because these terrible things happened on their account. But you who seek Jesus, do not be afraid, because I came to serve the one whom you too have come to serve; we have one God and one will.”

“For I know that you seek Jesus who was crucified.” Because I know that you have come to serve the Crucified One, I do not want you to fear either me or the earthquake.

“He is not here.” You seek his body; he is not here. For by his divinity he is everywhere.

“For he has risen.” He rose by himself, needing no one’s help, because he lay down for as long as he wished and rose when he wished.

“As he said.” When he foretold his death.

“Come and see the place.” If you do not believe my words, at least believe your eyes when you see the empty tomb. As the Lord is good, so also is his messenger. If some proud person had said something to another, he would not want that person to seek confirmation with his eyes after his words. But the holy angel, even though the women asked nothing, directs them after his words to examine the evidence with their eyes.

“Where they placed him.” Joseph, namely, and Gamaliel and Nicodemus.

“And go quickly and tell his disciples that he has risen.” Because the disciples fled while you always remained, and because you frequently sought him here, be their messengers, so that those who were men and nevertheless feared more than you may learn through you, who are the weaker sex.

“Tell Peter also.” Because a woman caused him to deny, let a woman cause him to confess; and let the one who was separated from the disciples through a woman be restored to them again through a woman.

“And behold, he will go before you into Galilee.” That is, he will precede you into Galilee. Although you will see him elsewhere, you will see him there in the general appearance to the disciples, where there are no murderers who killed him.

Typically, Galilee is interpreted as “migration made” or “revelation.” The Lord is rightly seen in Galilee, so that by the very location of his body he might speak to the disciples of the mystery of his resurrection. He is seen in Galilee because he had already migrated from death to life, from corruption to incorruption, and from punishment to glory. Following the example of the disciples, let us also migrate from sins to virtues. Then we shall see the Lord in this age by the mind, and in the future face to face.

“They went out quickly from the tomb with fear and great joy.” A double state of mind had taken possession of the women: fear and joy. One arose from the magnitude of the miracle, the other from their desire for the risen one. Yet both, in the manner of women, were impelled to hasten and announce it to the disciples. A woman had announced death to a man and incited him to evil; now a woman announces life to men.

“And behold, Jesus met them and said: ‘Greetings.’” Because they had shown great care in coming to the tomb and now hurried again to announce the Lord, they rightly deserved to have the Lord meet them, so that the curse of Eve upon women might be undone through women.

“They approached and took hold of his feet.” These women approached, took hold of his feet, kissed them, and worshiped him, because they believed that he was God. But to the woman who doubted that he was God it was said: “Do not touch me.”

Many say that this was one and the same Mary Magdalene: she doubted at first, but afterward, corrected by the Lord’s voice, deserved to kiss the Lord’s feet and worship him.

Then he said to them: “Do not be afraid.” It is natural for human beings to fear when they see something beyond their nature, especially for women. Since they saw an incorrupt and glorified body beyond human nature, they were frightened. Their fear was first driven away so that they might understand what was being said with a sound mind.

“Go and announce to my brothers.” The apostles are called the Lord’s brothers because in his mercy he had granted them the right to call the Lord Father, saying: “Our Father,” and so forth. He had commanded that we invoke no other father as the author of our authority except his Father; and he himself, as firstborn, also became a brother through the resurrection.

“That they should go into Galilee; there they will see me.” The Lord was seen by some disciples before they went into Galilee, but the general appearance to the disciples occurred there, where there were no murderers who had killed him.

By words and deeds the Lord commends himself and his works to the disciples. Because he had passed from corruption to incorruption and from mortality to immortality, he was, as it were, seen in Galilee. For Galilee is interpreted as “migration made” or “revelation.”

I have read in a certain book that one part of the city of Jerusalem was called Galilee, the part that the Galileans had built.

“There they will see me.” That is, they will see me, the one who was killed, and not merely a spirit.

Sedulius writes that the risen Lord first appeared to Mary his mother. For he says:

> [lacuna] At this dawn of light  
>  
> The virgin mother and the other mothers together came lamenting,  
>  
> With the familiar offering of an aromatic harvest.

To the tomb. When they had gone, behold, some of the guards came into the city [Col. 1500B]. The soldiers were permitted to witness something of the Lord’s resurrection, but under terror, so that they did not dare to prevent it. Nevertheless, they were not commanded to announce it, because they had come with evil intent; therefore they did not deserve to become messengers of the Lord, but rather of their own torments. They reported everything that had happened. Since they were not Jews, they did not conceal the truth or distort it in a malicious sense—until the Jews corrupted them. And when they had assembled with the elders and taken counsel, they gave the soldiers a large sum of money. Money is called silver. Hence in Greek it is called *argyron* (“silver”). Behold the Jews who had said to the Lord, “Come down from the cross, and we will believe you”: he rose from the tomb, which is the greater thing, and they not only did not believe, but also took silver from the Lord’s temple [Col. 1500C] and gave it for a lie, saying, “Say that his disciples came and stole him while we were asleep.” A wise person quickly detects the truth and the lie that appears in both claims. Now the Jews are recommending an obvious lie. If they were asleep, how did they know who stole him? But if they were awake, why did they not prevent it? And this report was spread among the Jews—namely, what the soldiers had said. Pilate also heard about that money; thus we find it in his letter to Tiberius concerning the Passion of Saint Peter.

The eleven disciples went to Galilee. Eleven went because the twelfth had been killed. And concerning the apostles, the Evangelist speaks only on account of their dignity; for the other disciples and the women also went to the mountain where Jesus had appointed them. To the mountain—that is, Tabor—which he had chosen both for speaking of secret matters and for worship. He had appointed it before the resurrection, when he had foretold his Passion, and after the resurrection, through the women. And when they saw him, they worshiped him, but some doubted. Luke shows the reason for their doubt when he says: “Thinking that they were seeing a spirit.” For they thought that they had seen only his spirit, because the body they saw was more subtle than other bodies, being already immortal and incapable of suffering. “They thought they were seeing a spirit.” But some doubted. Their doubt increased our faith, when his side was shown more clearly to Thomas, together with the places of the nails in his hands and feet.

And Jesus approached and spoke to them, saying. By approaching more closely and speaking, he removes their doubt that the one who was seen and spoke was also a body [Col. 1501A]. “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me.” Authority was given to the one who shortly before had been crucified and had died, and who had risen. For according to his divinity he had always possessed it, since for him to have this is the same as to be this. He who shortly before had been made a little lower than the angels was raised above the angels. By “heaven and earth” the whole creation is understood. In a typological sense: as he previously reigned in heaven, so through the faith of believers he reigns on earth.

“Go, therefore, teach all nations.” A most beautiful order: first they are to be taught who God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are, through whom the forgiveness of sins takes place; and that unless someone believes with the heart and confesses with the mouth, he does not have forgiveness of sins. When a person has understood these things, then he ought to be baptized. For if he is [of age?] (sic) and has not believed these things, he is baptized in vain, like an animal or a piece of metal. But for little infants forgiveness is granted on account of the faith of those who answer for them, as is said concerning the paralytic: “When Jesus saw the faith of those who were bringing him, he said to the paralytic, ‘Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven you.’”

“Baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.” As there is equality in the Trinity, so there is equality in the invocation and immersion: the immersion must be celebrated with each name. “Baptizing,” that is, washing; for just as it washes externally, so it washes the mind internally. And therefore the rite is performed with such an element, so that what a person sees being done outwardly, he may believe is likewise being done inwardly, since sins are, as it were, certain impurities of souls.

“Teaching them to observe everything that I have commanded you.” Above, he commanded them to teach belief in God and the forgiveness of sins that takes place in baptism for those who believe and confess, and who also possess faith. Now he commands that those who are baptized be taught what they must observe, so that they may carry the garment they received in baptism undefiled before the tribunal of Christ, and because there is one baptism and it cannot be repeated. “Everything,” he says, “that I have commanded you”—that is, all the commandments which I commanded, or entrusted, to you for safekeeping, so that those who have been baptized in the Trinity may do everything that has been commanded.

“Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age.” What does he mean by saying, “Behold, I am with you,” when elsewhere he says, “These are the words that I spoke to you while I was still mortal, as you are”? When he promises, “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age,” he speaks of the presence of his divinity and of the help by which the Lord is near to all who call upon him in truth. As long as they were alive, he was with them in all their invocations; and now they see his face in contemplation of his glory. Because he was withdrawing bodily, he promised the presence of his divinity, so that they would not lose faith although they did not see his body.

God is everywhere, and his divine presence is also with the reprobate, since he sees and penetrates everything. But he is with the elect in another way: so that he may accomplish their will and direct them according to his good pleasure, as the Psalmist says: “He will do the will of those who fear him, and he will hear their prayer and save them.” Whoever says that he must be with the disciples until the end of the age shows that he knows the day of judgment, and demonstrates that the disciples must exist after death.

Behold, he shows that two natures belong to him: one that was withdrawing bodily, and another whose divinity he was promising. Therefore let Eutyches, the abbot and monk, be silent—he who, after the assumption of humanity, denied that Christ existed in two natures, and asserted that there was in him only one, divine nature.

When he was proclaiming these things, and no one could refute him, the emperor Martianus assembled a synod of six hundred and thirty bishops in the city of Chalcedon against him. For forty days the bishops debated with him and his six monks, but they could not refute them. Then, finding himself in distress, the emperor said to the whole assembly:

“Behold, we have abandoned our idols and the pleasures in which we pagans delighted, and now, having renounced our pleasures, we are prepared to suffer hell for our faith. But know this: unless I learn with complete truth what I ought to believe, I shall return with the whole world to the pleasures of the age, so that, if I lose eternal life, I may at least enjoy the pleasure of the world and not grieve in that life over having lost both. Behold, all you bishops, you cannot refute these seven, who say that the nature of the Word of God and of the flesh is one; and they say that you are heretics, while you, in turn, consider them heretics. Yet you cannot overcome them in debate, and therefore I do not know whom I ought especially to believe. You who ought to be the pillars and rulers of the churches, find a plan by which the world may not perish—the world that has been entrusted to you by the Lord.”

Then the bishops replied [Col. 1502C]: “Let us all pray to the Lord, that he may show his peoples who speaks the truth and who speaks falsely.”

Then someone came forward and said that a certain man named Achatius had been shut up in a rock for thirty years, like Saint Simeon, and worked miracles; and that there was another hermit on the Jordan, a man of equal reputation. At the bishops’ counsel, the emperor ordered them to go there and bring those men.

When two bishops had come to Achatius’s cave, they told him the command of the emperor and of the bishops. He replied: “I shall not leave this cave alive, because I can neither walk nor debate.” A rock had indeed been cut to the measure of his small body, so that he could turn neither this way nor that, but lay enclosed in the rock as though praying. Bread and drink were given to him through a window. Whatever left his body in the process of human cleansing fell through an opening onto the ground.

Therefore, when the bishops saw that he did not wish to come out, they ordered the cave to be destroyed and him to be expelled. Then he began to implore them not to expel him alive; but the bishops, for the sake of the people’s salvation, did not heed him. When he had been brought out, he was as stiff as he had been while in the cave, and could neither rise nor walk. Nevertheless, they carried him on horseback to the emperor, together with the other hermit.

The emperor said to them: “Whatever impediment we have caused you, we have caused for the salvation of the whole world. For behold, there are seven monks who say that there was one nature of the Son in the Son of God after the assumption of the flesh. All the bishops and the others with them deny this, but in debate they cannot refute them. Unless you come to our aid, we shall all return again to paganism, because we do not know what we ought to believe.”

Achatius replied: “I cannot contend with words, because it is a long time since I ceased debating or reading syllogisms. But these men have studied this from childhood until now. The teacher of the nations instructed his disciple, saying: ‘Do not contend with words, for it is useful for nothing except the overthrow of those who hear.’ Therefore it is necessary to turn to God, so that he himself may show who believes more rightly, if he wishes his Church to be saved.”

Then he asked whether there was nearby a place where God demonstrated his power and signs through someone. They told him that the holy virgin Euphemia frequently displayed miracles in those who sought God through her intercession, at a distance of about two miles from the city.

The emperor went there with the entire synod. When they had arrived, Achatius ordered her tomb to be opened. When they had opened it, she appeared to be lying as though asleep on a bed. The king came and kissed her on the breast, followed by the bishops and the whole people.

After this, the aforementioned man ordered the bishops and monks each to write down and seal his faith. When they had done this, he placed the writings upon her breast in the sight of the king, the bishops, and the heretics. Afterward they all left the basilica, and all the entrances around it were closed and sealed with the rings of the king, the bishops, and the heretics.

Achatius said to the whole assembly: “Fast and pray for three days around the basilica, so that the Lord may show us whose faith he approves.”

They did as he had commanded. On the third day Achatius said to the bishops and heretics: “Look carefully at your seals, to see whether they are intact, so that no doubt may arise afterward.”

The bishops and heretics replied: “Our seals are intact, because both our men and theirs have kept watch in turn by day and night. Whatever God shows us, we shall believe without doubt and shall not contradict it.”

Then they opened the doors and came to the virgin’s tomb. They saw that she had raised one document from her breast and placed it upon her mouth, kissing it with folded hands; but another, as though gnawed and reduced to pieces by mice, she was trampling under her feet. Yet they did not know which was which.

Achatius said to the assembly: “Do you see that she kisses one faith, through which she was saved, and tramples another beneath her feet? What do you think?”

They all replied: “We shall submit ourselves to the faith which she kisses.”

When her hands had been lifted from above the document, it appeared that the document of the bishops was intact, while that of the heretics had been gnawed away. When they saw this, everyone glorified God and was strengthened in his faith. The heretics likewise, seeing these things, threw themselves at Achatius’s feet, believed as they found written in the intact document, and repented of their error.

Afterward they brought those good men back to their places. They shut the first man again in his cell, as he had been before, and released the other into his solitude. Thus the Lord saved his Church from the error of the faithless.

We too, the children of the churches, ought to pray that almighty God may preserve it unshaken and undefiled until the end of the age, so that it may meet him on the day of judgment without stain or wrinkle [Col. 1504C]. May our Lord Jesus Christ, who shed his blood for it, grant this—he who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 1503C]

CHRISTIANUS DRUTHMARUS, MONK OF CORVEY: A BRIEF EXPOSITION ON LUKE THE EVANGELIST

(*Bibliotheca veterum Patrum*, same location)

Luke himself rose to write the Gospel so that the pseudo-evangelists would not have the opportunity to preach falsehoods, since Gospels had falsely been written under the name of the twelve apostles. David divided the priests, Levites, and families into twenty-four courses, and the eighth course was Abijah’s, so that he might be shown as the herald of the New Testament.

“Righteous before the Lord.” No one is righteous before the Lord if justice is not formed from simplicity of mind. First comes the commandment, afterward justification. When we judge correctly, we seem to sing the Lord’s justifications. Praise arises from lineage, conduct, equity, duty, commandment, and justification.

“And it fell to him by lot.” Incense was not then to be placed; rather, according to the ancient order, Abijah succeeded the others in that particular year. Incense was offered on the tenth day of the seventh month, the day of expiation or propitiation, which occurs sometimes in September and sometimes in October because of the moon’s varying course.

“He will turn the hearts of the fathers to the children.” It is the prudence of the righteous not to presume justice from the works of the Law.

Silence was both a sign and a punishment for unbelief. When angels are sent to us, they fulfill their ministry outwardly in such a way that they nevertheless never cease inwardly through contemplation, because he is not circumscribed.

“After these days.” Clearly, the days of Zachariah’s service. After the day of expiation, a change of priesthood took place. Alternatively: through Zachariah the Jewish priesthood is signified, and through Elizabeth the barrenness of the Law, because it brought nothing to perfection. Although it flourished in the time of Moses and afterward, at the Lord’s coming it was, as it were, worn out by old age.

The priesthood of God knows secret things. The dull stand outside and remain hidden for five months, because the Lawgiver, through the five books, announces the mysteries of Christ in riddles; or the Law prefigures Christ’s dispensation in five ages.

“His father was Joseph.” He expressed the opinion of the common people. Many are adopted whom they call sons.

“For a sign that will be opposed.” For this is known concerning the sect: it will be opposed everywhere. “A stone of stumbling,” so that what is hidden from many may be revealed. It was uncertain which of the Jews would receive the grace of Christ and which would reject it.

Anna, said to have been of venerable conduct and worthy age, is said to have borne witness to Christ, and signifies the Church. The number of years of her widowhood, during which she wandered in the world, is seven times twelve, making eighty-four: seven pertains to the course of this age, and twelve to the perfection of apostolic teaching. Whoever devoted the whole time of his life to apostolic institutions serves the Lord for eighty-four years. The seven years she had remained with her husband signify the time of the Lord’s incarnation, because perfection is signified by seven.

Anna means “the grace of God”; Phanuel, “the face of God”; Aser, “blessed”; and he was eighth in order of birth.

“They returned to Nazareth.” Luke omitted what Matthew said: that the Lord had been brought back from Egypt.

“Wisdom and the grace of God.” Wisdom according to the flesh, because the fullness of divinity dwells bodily in him. Grace, as John says: “Full of grace and truth.” What John calls grace, Luke calls wisdom.

“And he went up at Passover.” Luke is rightly likened to a calf, since he narrates concerning Zachariah. Mary sends the Lord to the temple with an offering. Likewise John, not with his parents; and afterward he places the disciples praising God in the temple.

“But when Christ was twelve years old.” When the time had come, he began to reveal both his natures, so that little ones would not be ashamed to learn from elders and so that God’s willingness to listen to human beings would be shown. To prevent the weak from daring to teach, he did not teach until he was thirty years old.

“They were astonished at his understanding.” For they saw that he was young in age. As a human being he questioned the elders; as God he answered, so that the elders and the learned might marvel.

“Jesus increased in wisdom, age, and grace.” Age refers to the flesh, wisdom to the soul, and grace to natural understanding, which is granted on account of reason.

Herod and his brothers were sons of another Herod; among them, Archelaus, their brother and Herod’s, reigned for ten years. Annas was before Caiaphas, who held office in the very year in which the Lord was crucified.

“From stones, children of Abraham.” Paul says concerning these: “But if you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s seed.”

“The axe.” Christ, who is held by the handle, cuts by his divinity. The tree is the human race.

It appears that around the time of the Lord’s birth there was peace for twelve years, so that what the prophet said might be fulfilled: “They shall beat their swords into plowshares and their spears into pruning hooks,” so that the apostles might travel throughout the world.

“The first census,” which described the whole world, or certainly began the first time when Quirinius came to Syria. Augustus signifies Christ; the consuls, preachers. A denarius was paid for ten bronze coins, signifying the Decalogue.

“The axe at the roots,” when the whole offspring is removed at once.

“Whoever has two tunics.” Since a tunic is more necessary than a cloak, this commands us to share even necessities with our neighbors.

“In fire.” That is, in the purification of sanctification and the testing of tribulation. The Holy Spirit is also named by the word “fire.” Hence it is said: “You will be baptized with the Holy Spirit.”

The separation of a righteous judgment is signified by the chaff; the threshing floor is the Church. The chaff signifies those who are instructed in divine mysteries; the weeds, those who do not deign to hear the divine commandments [Col. 1506A].

John the Baptist represents the figure of the Law.

“Heaven was opened” on our account; and on our account the Holy Spirit, and so forth.

“In you I have established my pleasure.” That is, through you to accomplish what pleases me, because he regretted not having created this man.

“Thirty years old.” The cord was thirty cubits long, in accordance with faith in the Holy Trinity and the operation of the Decalogue; it enclosed the sea and held six measures. Joseph was brought out of prison in his thirtieth year. David was made king in his thirtieth year. Ezekiel saw the heavens opened in his thirtieth year. The tabernacle was thirty cubits long.

Jacob and Heli were brothers. When Heli died, Jacob fathered Joseph by Heli’s wife. Matthew, through forty-two generations, signifies the labor of the Church in the present age. Luke, ascending through seventy-seven generations from Christ to God, signifies that after baptism and the forgiveness of sins the Church will ascend to heaven.

In Matthew’s generations, Christ’s taking upon himself our sins is signified. In Luke’s generations, Christ’s forgetting of sins is signified. The one descends; the other ascends.

Luke took this genealogy from the Septuagint edition, placing Enoch in the seventieth position, to signify that those who have fulfilled the Decalogue spiritually will be transferred to rest.

“You shall not tempt.” He was being prompted, as though he were a human being, to test by some sign how great he was—that is, how much he could accomplish with God. This is done wrongly when it is done in such a way.

“Until the time.” Later he approached, not in order to tempt, and after the three deceptions had been set forth he says that every temptation had been brought to completion, since these embrace the origins of all vices. As John says: “Everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life.”

And in the Gospels they are excluded from eternal life by only three concerns. The first is a property, the second oxen, the third a wife. Desire for a wife, like gluttony, belongs to the desire of the flesh. The purchase of a property, on account of avarice, looks toward the pride of life; the testing of the oxen belongs to curiosity, which is vainglory.

Against these the Lord commanded us to be armed with a threefold weapon: fasting against the desire of the flesh, almsgiving against avarice, and prayers against boastfulness.

In the second book Josephus repeats what the Lord had previously done, namely in the first year; others assign it to the second.

“By the power of the Spirit.” He speaks of signs of miracles. First the Lord displayed signs of power through wisdom. He had given the Jews the command: “Be still and see.” And the synagogue was called a house.

He was anointed in the Jordan above his companions with spiritual oil and heavenly power.

“The day of retribution,” when the Son of Man will come in glory.

The Lord opened the book—that is, he opened Scripture—and returned it to the attendant, signifying the apostles. He stood when he was incarnate; but when he ascended into heaven, he returned it folded, because not everything is to be said to everyone.

It was fulfilled because, just as he had foretold, he both performed great deeds and preached greater ones. They bore witness that he was the one about whom the prophets had foretold [Col. 1507A].

“The son of the craftsman.” For the Father of Christ works through fire and spirit.

“Cure yourself.” That is, he commands him to perform miracles in his own homeland.

The Lord did not wish to die any other death than on the cross.

A teacher’s word is spoken with authority when he does what he teaches.

“Leave [us alone].” “Cease tormenting me.”

This confession does not proceed from good will, because it is not followed by a reward. Since the devil was the first to sin, his tongue was therefore the first to be closed.

“And it harmed him in nothing.” It did not weaken him in his limbs.

Human beings cast out demons by the word of God; Christ by his own authority.

The man who was freed signifies the human mind; the woman signifies the flesh restrained from desire.

The devil did not think that he would be condemned by the Lord’s death.

The Sea of Galilee, the Sea of Tiberias, and Gennesaret are one and the same. The nets are so called as things that retain. They were not submerged, but were endangered [Col. 1507B].

The sacrifice of his body had not yet begun, because the old should not be taken away until the new had come.

He prays on the mountain; he preaches in the city; and he gives sufficiently clear examples of both the contemplative and active life.

Capernaum was also called the city of Christ, since by illuminating it with his powers he had made it his own.

The four virtues are sobriety, wisdom, justice, and courage.

The paralytic is the sinful person; the crowd is the habit of sinning; the house is sacred Scripture, under its rules, because it is beneath a veil that can be understood. “With the bed”: that is, he must know Christ together with the flesh; and to carry away the bed means to restrain that flesh through continence.

To go home and to paradise means either the inner guardianship.

The healthy are those who do not wish to establish their own righteousness.

Whoever fasts, unless incorporated into the members of Christ, does so in vain.

John fasted in order to increase merit; Christ, without sin, forgave sins [Col. 1507C].

“No one drinking old wine.” He means the Jews.

“On the second-first Sabbath.” That is, on the second Sabbath, at the first incarnation: second because the first commandment came through the Law, first because it had been observed by the righteous before the Law.

The loaves were baked before the Sabbath and placed on the Sabbath in two golden dishes with incense, until that Sabbath.

The Hebrew letter P is not pronounced.

Alphaeus was called Cleopas, and Alphaeus means “learned.”

Judas Thaddaeus Scarioth: “memory of death.”

“Seaside,” from the sea, where Tyre was located.

You will rarely find a sick person cured on a mountain. And although Christ speaks generally, he nevertheless raises his eyes more particularly toward the disciples.

Matthew, on account of the resurrection, sets down five beatitudes [Col. 1507D].

Luke embraces the virtues: in poverty, temperance; in hunger, justice; in mourning, prudence, knowing for whom they ought to weep; in perfection, fortitude, so that they may be able to endure. The Lord possessed all these.

“Prophets,” he means false prophets.

“Sin unto death.” An attack upon charity and brotherhood; for this reason Paul does not pray for Alexander.

“To everyone who asks.” That is, honorably and justly.

Bad fruit is the work of the flesh: fornication, and so forth. The fruit of the Spirit is goodness and charity.

Thorns are the cares of the age. The foundation, singular, is Christ; foundations, plural, are teachers.

Digging is the intention that removes all earthly things from the hearts of the faithful.

Morally, foundations are the good thoughts or intentions of each person.

The flooding of the river signifies the gates of hell, or the restraint of the flesh [Col. 1508A].

The devil’s house is the world.

“Without a foundation,” because every sin lacks substance or the distinction of the final judgment.

“He was about to die.” Why is he said to have been about to die when he did not? Because in reality he would have died if he had not lived through the Lord’s prayers.

The centurion approached God in faith. The Lord displayed humility by going, and power by healing while absent.

He refused to go to the ruler’s son, lest he seem to honor wealth; here he went, lest he seem to despise social condition.

This man represents the people of the nations.

The elders whom he sent are the good men of the Church, accompanied by one hundred men. This signifies the perfection of virtues.

The ark was built over one hundred years. Abraham received a son at one hundred years of age. Isaac found a hundredfold. The hundred passes from the left to the right; the hundredth psalm sings of mercy.

John sends disciples to the Lord so that they may believe in him. Therefore the Lord performed miracles and said: “Blessed is whoever is not scandalized in me.”

“He who is least in the kingdom of God”: either the Lord or an angel.

God is justified through baptism, when all people, by confessing their own sins, justify themselves.

“They rejected it in themselves,” or “against themselves.”

Some think this was said in the person of the Lord, others in the person of the Evangelist; and through these words he explains what concerns the Pharisee.

“Your generation”—concerning them we sang to you, the prophets.

“Who said to them”: religious dancing is agility of the limbs; singing is exultation; lamentation is “turn back to me with fasting.”

The disciples are the children of wisdom.

Mary anointed the Lord with ointment: first in Galilee, and second in Bethany [Col. 1508C]. The Church—or the soul—in the present celebrates the mysteries of his flesh; in the future, the glory of eternity. What she presented to him shamefully, she repeated entirely in the Lord.

The Pharisees signify the Jewish people. The house of the Pharisee is the custody of the Law. “He reclined”: he appeared in the flesh.

The two debtors are the two peoples, or the Pharisee and the woman. The moneylender is the Creator.

Chorazin: “my ministry.”

Joanna: “the grace of the Lord,” or “the merciful Lord.”

Susanna: “lily.”

Mary here: “bitter sea.” Magdala: “tower.”

In the rock there was no persevering love, nor in the lamps the denarius of perfection.

The active and contemplative life are in the Decalogue. In the active life there is love of neighbor; in the contemplative life, love of God.

The lamp is the word of God; the chosen vessel is the flesh, or the vessel of avarice; earthly pleasures are the bed; the body is the lampstand.

Whoever has the same love of the word will be given the understanding to comprehend.

The boat here signifies the cross.

Gerasa, “a settler who casts out,” or “a stranger who casts out,” signifies the Gentile world.

The notable city across the Jordan, joined to Gilead.

Through the staff which, according to Mark, is to be carried, the power of receiving those who are subject is signified.

And by commanding them not to wear two tunics, he commanded them to proceed not doubly but simply.

The different places at table of the diners signify the different churches throughout the world.

“Fifty,” because the fiftieth psalm is the psalm of repentance.

“The day of assumption”: he means the time of the Passion.

“I was seeing Satan.” Not only now, but earlier, when he fell.

“Your names are written,” as though recorded in letters and eternally fixed in God’s memory [Col. 1509A].

“You have revealed them to little ones.” He opened the mysteries of his coming to the apostles.

“By fear”: he condemns sharpness of intellect.

“Everything has been handed over to me.” That is, everything chosen, so that they may come to me.

“No one knows who the Son is except the Father, nor who the Father is except the Son and anyone to whom the Son wishes to reveal him.” Since this applies to both—to the Son and to the Father.

“Which of you?” The Lord is understood as the friend.

“At midnight”: in tribulation.

“In his bread”: the understanding of the Trinity.

The friend who comes from the road is our mind, which returns from earthly things to God.

The door is the understanding of divine speech.

The children of the master of the house are preachers of the truth in rest.

“And understanding is given through faith”: there is a human being.

Bread is charity; stone, hardness; fish, faith, because of baptism; serpent, unbelief; in the egg, hope; scorpion, despair [Col. 1509B].

Evil lovers of the age are earthly goods, which seem to us to have been given as good by God.

This confession is for praise, because Martha and Mary, and the disciples, were diligent in hearing the Lord’s secrets.

The lamp is humanity; the vessel, the light; divinity, the lampstand; the Church, the lamp. “Under the bushel”: under the measure of the Law, or within the boundaries of the Jewish people.

“The lamp of our body” is more intent; the body is our works: “Put to death your members that are upon the earth.”

“You who tithe these things”: your almsgiving is new, and I do not warn you about these things.

“With one finger”: that is, you do not fulfill even the smallest matters.

It is a sin not to build monuments to the prophets, but to love their killer. You consent to their works by inflicting injuries upon the Lord who had been foretold to them by the prophets.

“The wisdom of God”: he himself, plainly.

Through Abel and Zechariah are meant martyrs of both ranks, martyrs and laity—namely, those devoted to the service of the altar.

“The key of knowledge” is the humility of Christ.

“To enter” means not to be content with the surface of the letter, but to penetrate into the secrets of deeper understanding.

A teacher is one who taught by example.

“He neither enters nor permits others to enter.”

The leaven of the Pharisees is hypocrisy.

Take care not to imitate hypocrites, because a time will come when their hypocrisy will be revealed.

In the temple of the Lord, a wooden flooring was built five cubits above the ceiling.

*As* [*assis*], if declined, is masculine.

The *dipondius* is a type of very light weight composed of two *asses*.

“Does God have no care for you, when he has care for sparrows?”—the word “he says” is understood. But knowledge is one thing, care another.

“Are you not worth more than they?” That is, of greater value. It should be read as pertaining to comparison of number. “But you are worth more”: that is, you are of greater merit, dignity, and estimation before God than the countless bodies or kinds of sparrows that are counted.

The person who knowingly understands the works of God but attacks them through envy will not be forgiven. He slanders Christ and calls the works of the Holy Spirit Beelzebub; such a person will not be forgiven.

The soul is more than the body. Here “soul” is used for this life, as in the saying: “Whoever loves his soul.”

“You are worth more than they.” That is, you are more precious.

“Which of you?” That is, to add to his stature.

“Passing over.” He passes from judgment and returns to the kingdom.

“Who” is used because of difficulty, not impossibility—that is, something rare. Elsewhere it is used for impossibility, as in “Who is like you?”—that is, no one [Col. 1510A].

“Above all the joys of the heavenly kingdom.” Not so that only the learned may possess the Lord, but so that they may enjoy eternal possession more abundantly than the other saints.

“Those who are learned will shine, and those who instruct many in righteousness.”

In the one wicked servant the whole people of the wicked is represented.

Not knowing is one thing; refusing to know is another.

The fire-bearing one signifies the grace of the Holy Spirit.

“Blood,” he says, is used for kindling: first he must be drenched by it, and thus the hearts must be inflamed. And the ardor within us was troubled and constricted by afflictions during the time of the Passion, not because of fear of death, but because of the delay of our redemption.

Five in one house: father and mother, son and daughter, daughter-in-law or mother-in-law. The synagogue is Christ; the daughter is the Church [Col. 1510B].

The cloud is the flesh of Christ rising again, from which the rain of preaching proceeds—[the word] “proceeds” is understood. The south wind is the heat of tribulation.

“What about yourselves—why do you not judge what is right?” That is, what a human being is; nor can he be ignorant either of the evils he ought to avoid or of the good things he ought to desire.

The *minutum*, or *quadrans*, appears to be a fourth part of an ounce, and a fifth part in the temple court.

Sacrifices were carried by laypeople inside to Pilate.

The mallet-maker’s mouth—the devil—mixed good works with vices and destroyed many, as also happened to those eighteen upon whom the tower in Siloam fell, namely, first to Cain.

They signify those who imitate the name of the Lord under an unlawful appearance, because the name of the Lord is written with the same letters.

The tower of Siloam, which is interpreted as “sent,” signifies the Lord [Col. 1510C].

“Upon whomever it falls, it will crush him.” Alternatively, we ought to build the tower of virtues.

The vineyard is the house of Israel. The fig tree is the synagogue. The cultivator of the vineyard is the order of teachers.

“Cut it down by its branches”: the preaching of the apostles.

“I will dig”: “I will preach the dung of the wicked.”

“What it has done”: “I will recall it.”

“If it bears fruit”—he did not add “who,” because he saw that the person was more inclined toward evil.

The bent woman is a part of the synagogue, because she believed.

“By fourteen”: that is, six ages and six periods of the Lord’s visitation, directed toward earthly things.

“He saw”: by predestination. “He called”: through teaching. “He laid hands”: spiritual gifts.

The man is Christ; the rising is the Church; the mustard seed is the word of the Gospel, which the man Christ received from divinity.

The branches are the diversities of doctrines; or Christ himself, whom Joseph buried in the garden [Col. 1510D].

The leaven is love of God and neighbor, until we fulfill all the commandments.

They seek to enter out of love of salvation, but they will not be able to do so because of the harshness of the way.

“He will shut the door”: he will remove the place of repentance.

“We ate in the more obscure places of Scripture; we drank the clearer ones.”

Weeping comes from the tree; gnashing of teeth from the cold. A twofold Gehenna is shown.

I cast out demons and complete healings, today and tomorrow, and on the third day I am brought to completion. This refers to his body, which is the Church. Demons are expelled when all the nations believe in him after abandoning their ancestral superstitions, and healings are completed when one lives according to his commands. After the devil and this world have been renounced, all the way to the end of the resurrection, the Church will be brought to completion as though on the third day—that is, to evangelical fullness. The Church will also be completed through the immortality of the body; or, “today and tomorrow” refers to the present and the future, while “the third day” refers to the time when he preached after rising and brought to completion everything written about himself.

He did not forbid brothers or others to imitate him, but distinguished that imitation from almsgiving. Therefore he does not say, “lest it become sin for you,” but “retribution.” There are, however, certain banquets called revelries. Revelries are luxury and banquets. If someone acts simply according to the example of Job’s sons, as in other brotherly duties, God will be the rewarder.

He eats bread in the kingdom of God if he has deserved to enjoy Christ in the sacrament of the Incarnation, though many do so more with the mouth than with the heart. Therefore he tells a parable about them: when an army twice as large comes against one half its size, they examine us, who are scarcely prepared in our outward deeds alone, with regard to both body and thought.

The first robe is the garment of innocence. The servants are preachers. The ring is the seal of faith on the hands, so that faith may shine forth through works. The sandals on the feet are the office of evangelizing. The calf is Christ. The kids among them are Christ. One of the servants is some prophet from the Holy Spirit.

“Everything that the Father has is mine.” He said this of the things that pertain to the Father’s divinity. This parable can also be applied to two persons, the penitent and the just.

“They were laughing at him.” Because the Law and the Prophets did not command that people should thereby abound in all good things—indeed, overflow with them—if they observed the Law. “Woe to the person through whom scandal comes,” that is, the Pharisees mocked the Lord’s teaching and turned others away from believing in him.

It is more useful for an innocent person to end his bodily life by the most dreadful punishment than, by harming a brother, to deserve the perpetual death of the soul. That is, the “little one” is the person scandalized against righteousness; one must not be concerned about a brother’s scandal.

“Seventy times seven”: four hundred and ninety times. “Increase our faith,” because the Lord had said above, “If you were not faithful in what belongs to another.” Therefore he taught these things.

The mustard seed, when gargled, cleanses the head. The pestle signifies persecution; through the tree of virtues, all trees are signified; or the word of the Gospel sent among the nations is intended.

A servant plowing or feeding is understood to be any teacher. He returns from the field when, having interrupted his preaching, he returns to his conscience. To him he did not immediately say, “Pass at once from this life into the eternal one,” but, “Apply yourself to virtues.” To gird oneself is to bind the mind against every evil thought.

If one human being asks many services of another, how much more does our Creator? “Useless servants,” because your Lord does not need your benefit.

“The one who is on the roof”: in the height of virtues. “His vessels”: carnal desires. “In the field”: in the Church.

“Wife”: those who, in tribulation, look back without hope in divinity. “On that night”: in that tribulation. “In bed”: in repose, that is, in idleness—not occupied with secular business or ecclesiastical concerns.

“One will be taken,” namely, those who act for God’s sake. “The other will be left,” namely, those who act otherwise.

“Two women grinding”: those established among the congregations who are governed by female teachers—so called because it is fitting for them to be governed by the learned. The women grinding also signify the circuit and continual movement of temporal affairs.

“One will be taken”: the portion that has entered into marriage solely for the sake of producing offspring, and has distributed its earthly substance for God’s sake.

“Two in the field”: preachers in the Church. “One will be taken”: the one who announces the word of God for the Lord’s sake. There are three orders of preachers: the continent, the married, and the teachers.

“Where the body is, there the eagles will be gathered”: where the Lord is, and the elect with him, who are satisfied with his passion as with flesh. The eagle flies higher, defends itself from serpents by means of a stone, and is baptized in the Jordan.

“To pray always”: always to do what is just.

“There was a certain judge in a city.” Parables are presented either by similarity or by dissimilarity. This judge is introduced not by similarity but by dissimilarity, showing, namely, how much God cares for those who entreat him and for himself.

“Do you think he will find…?” The Lord shows that the charity of the good will exist on the day of judgment. He does not doubt, however, but argues, as Paul does: “I think that I too have the Spirit of God.”

For two reasons the just are said to pray for vengeance against the wicked. There are four forms by which a proud person, when he thinks he has goodness, considers it given to him for his merits: either he boasts that he possesses what he has by virtue of his uniqueness, or he wants to possess what he has.

“Do not become children in understanding, but in malice”; or, as children in learning, not contradicting. He does not offer counterarguments but receives faithfully, like sheep.

This ruler had heard the word about entering the kingdom of heaven through children; therefore he asks by what merits of works he might enter. He does not testify that he himself is not a good teacher, but that no teacher is good without God.

“The eye of a needle”: the narrowness of sufferings through which he deigned to mend our torn nature.

“With God it is possible”: namely, that a rich person may become a poor person belonging to Christ, and may be humble, and so forth.

“In this age”: that is, in the fellowship of all Christians.

Zacchaeus is said to have been justified; he signifies the gentile people. The sycamore signifies the cross, because it is mocked by many. To climb up means to believe in the crucified one; to descend means that, if we knew Christ according to the flesh, now we know him no longer in that way.

The nobleman is Christ. The distant country is the Church: either because the Church cries out to him from the ends of the earth, or because salvation is far from sinners.

[Col. 1512D]

Ten minas. The number ten pertains to the Law. He chose disciples instructed in the Law and gave them ten minas, because he caused them to understand the sayings of the Law spiritually. The mina, which the Greeks call *mna* (μνᾶ), is weighed in drachmas.

The citizens are the Jews; “he will return” means “to judgment”; “that he might know” means “that he might make known.”

The first servant is the order of teachers who were commanded, among the circumcised, to preach one mina—that is, one God and one faith. He acquired ten minas: the Jewish people. “In a little” means in the word of God.

The ten cities are souls coming through the word of the Law to the grace of the Gospel. Another servant is the blind man who preached to the uncircumcised; the five minas signify the gentile world devoted to the five senses.

“Be over five cities”: that is, be great and exalted over those whom you instructed.

The money is the word of the Gospel.

Bethphage means “house of the jaw”; it was a village of priests. Bethany was nearby. The city is the Church over the tomb of Lazarus, because before his passion, by teaching, he filled many people with the gifts of pious confession and spiritual obedience.

“On the mountain”: that is, in the Lord himself, who refreshes the light of spiritual charisms with anointings.

Two are sent, either because of the twofold charity or because of speech and action. Those who opposed them were teachers of errors.

Half a year had passed during which the Lord had not returned to Galilee when he came to his passion.

“If these were silent, they would cry out when he himself was silent, through the splitting of the rocks.”

“The tombs were opened”: spiritually, the gentiles, who are called stones.

The city signifies either this world or the mind of each individual.

[Col. 1513B]

When he was received by the Jews, it was the tenth day of the month: God had commanded that the lamb be taken.

For two reasons the truth is concealed: from the unworthy person who seeks it, and from the person who seeks it wickedly and therefore is incapable of it.

The first servant sent to the vineyard is Moses, whom they provoked. The second is David, of whom he said, “Who is our portion?” The third is the chorus of the prophets. “Perhaps” is said ambiguously, so that free will may be left to human beings.

“The stone”: that is, to take away the faith of Christ. The sinner who believes in God is crushed when he sins. Upon such people it will fall from above in judgment, with the punishment of destruction.

In the moral sense, every person becomes the Lord’s vineyard through baptism. The servants are the Law, the Psalms, the Prophets, or another Scripture of the Lord. He kills it and drives the Holy Spirit away from himself.

The treasury was a chest with an opening above, placed beside the altar on the right. For those entering the house of the Lord there were two. Spiritually, this is said of the love of God and neighbor.

The widow is the Church; the rich are the Jews presuming upon their righteousness.

“Terror”: the things that come from heaven. A star resembling a sword hung above Jerusalem for an entire year.

“Great signs”: chariots and armed horsemen were seen rushing through the air. A heifer led out for sacrifice gave birth to a lamb.

“Then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains.” Ecclesiastical history relates that all the Christians fled across the Jordan to a city called Pella, until the desolation was complete.

“Until the times of the nations are fulfilled”: that is, until their multitude believes.

“The roar of the sea and the waves”: because the sea, destined to be destroyed, will send beforehand signs of its agitation.

Matthew also narrates the actual presence of the judgment; Luke narrates what precedes it.

“Those who seem to flourish in this world will wither.” “Generation” means the human race, or specifically the Jews.

“The heaven that will pass away” is not the ethereal or starry heaven, but the atmospheric heaven in which the birds of heaven fly—the very heaven whose waters perished.

Passover: the first day, when the lamb was killed. Unleavened Bread: the following day, when they went out from Egypt, and then for seven days. These signify the entire period of our life, during which we must flee from Egypt.

[Col. 1514A]

“They began to accuse him.”

Peter ran—something John says that he himself did; but Peter had done it, and because Luke mentioned it, John remained silent.

A *stadium* is an eighth of a mile: that is, sixty stadia make eight miles and a half. This accords with those who were certain about the death and burial but doubtful about the resurrection.

The resurrection took place after the seventh day of the week. The number eight is appropriate to the resurrection. Those disciples were walking, grieving that he had died. They completed the sixth and seventh days because they did not doubt that he had rested in the tomb. Of the eighth they completed only half, because they did not believe fully in the resurrection.

The person who gives false testimony against God sells money, and so does the person who destroys brotherly concord.

“I will not drink from the fruit of the vine.” This can be understood either simply or mystically.

In the bread, water is signified; in the wine, water is also signified, as he showed by the water representing the people upon the table. This table is heavenly glory.

“Behold, Satan has demanded you, to sift you.” Satan’s demanding means his longing to afflict the elect.

“When I sent you without purse, and so forth.” Some virtues must always be maintained; others need not be, such as hunger, thirst, vigils, nakedness, and reading. Similarly, in this passage he commands them, for persecution, to have money necessary for food, and even a sword.

The two swords suffice as a testimony to the Savior’s voluntary suffering. One signifies the apostles’ boldness; the other, which was not drawn, signifies his patience.

“About a stone’s throw.” They intended to throw a stone at him—that is, they directed against him the intention of the Law written on stone.

Agony means eagerness or confidence.

“As drops of falling blood.” This signifies the earth watered by blood and by his prayers, so that he might cleanse the disciples’ faith through his blood and by his death restore the world to life.

“Allow this, up to here”: that is, do not be disturbed by what is about to happen; permit them to seize me.

When he had asked, Peter struck. The servant signifies the Jewish people, “of the high priest,” from whose prompting they chose Barabbas. Peter shows that, by divine judgment, the hearing of the Law had been taken away from them. In the healing of the ear, he signifies those among the Jews who believed.

They did not come bodily through the rulers and priests, but mentally, because Herod was a Jew by nature and religion; therefore Pilate sent Jesus to him.

The white garment is what the Church says in the Song of Songs: “My beloved is white and ruddy.”

The column placed in the Church on Mount Zion displays the traces of the Lord’s blood.

Barabbas signifies the Antichrist.

Cyrene is a city of Libya and means “heir.”

Mary Magdalene was the sister of Lazarus. Joanna was the wife of Chuza, Herod’s steward. Mary of James was the sister of Saint Mary.

[Col. 1515]

CHRISTIANUS DRUTHMAR OF CORVEY, MONK: A SHORT EXPOSITION ON JOHN THE EVANGELIST.

(*Bibliotheca veterum Patrum*, in the same place.)

[Col. 1515A]

Grace for grace: first faith, then the remission of sins and eternal life.

“From his fullness we have received.”

The Law was given through Moses and displayed sins; that is, it displayed the remission of sins. Truth is knowledge of him and the granting of eternal life.

The Trinity, one God, sent John to baptize. John knew certain things about the Lord and was taught certain things in baptism—namely, that the Lord himself would baptize through all his servants, and that it would be called his baptism, not someone else’s.

Deceit is present when one thing is done and another is pretended.

In Nathanael he praised the confession of sin. The leaves of the fig tree signify Nathanael’s sins. The people who believed from among the Jews are signified; Philip signifies the preachers.

The angels are the preachers, ascending above the Son of Man, above his Church.

[Col. 1515B]

Each person ascends, as Paul did: “He heard words in paradise that it is not permitted for a human being to speak.” He descends when he says: “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal.”

John was standing: that is, in the persecution of virtues, from which he deserved to contemplate the height of divinity.

The disciples were standing because they followed his teacher in good works.

“Seeing Jesus walking”: that is, living among human beings on earth and displaying progress in life.
