The Lamb: because he was to be sacrificed for us and, through the wool of his fleece, to offer examples of virtue.

The two disciples are rightly mentioned, because whoever follows the Lord ought to walk adorned with the gift of twofold charity.

He saw them, because the Lord both approves and assists those who have good intention.

By their asking where he was staying, he teaches that all who follow the Lord in their deeds should do so for eternal life.

It was the tenth hour, because whoever wishes to come to the Lord’s dwelling must have completed the Law contained in ten words.

They remained for one day, because “one day in your courts is better than thousands.”

Just as Andrew brought his brother to the Lord, so each person ought to bring his neighbor to the Lord.

Jesus looked at him with the inward eyes of his heart and spoke the name he had received from his parents, as well as the name he fittingly imposed upon the Church and its foundation.

“I say that Christ Jesus was a minister of the circumcision,” that is, its executor.

Nathanael means “house of God” or “my God.”

The third day: the third age of the world. First, before the Law, through the example of the patriarchs; second, under the Law, through the writings of the prophets; third, under the grace of the Gospel.

The Lord’s mother is the synagogue. She was called a woman, just as Eve was called: “As soon as she was made,” he says, “he formed her into a woman.”

The six vessels are the stony hearts of the saints, set forth as an example for believers through the six ages of the world.

“According to the purification of the Jews,” because the Law was given to them alone.

“Two measures each”: the love of God and neighbor. “Three”: because of the mystery of the Trinity. The servants are the apostles.

“By filling”: that is, by understanding.

The first water jar was under Abel; the second, under Noah; the third, under Abraham; the fourth, under David; the fifth, under Jesus—the people brought back from captivity. The seventy years signify the fullness of good works; life is understood through the gifts of the Holy Spirit.

In the sixth age the Lord appeared, and he changed that water into wine.

The dining room signifies the three orders in the Church: the married, the continent, and the teachers.

By the dove the Holy Spirit is understood; by the oxen, the preachers; by the sheep, the people.

Forty-six years, because Christ was from Adam; and Adam is interpreted there as forty-six.

The oxen signify heavenly doctrine; the sheep, works of purity and piety; the doves, the spirit.

They sell oxen who provide God’s teaching for earthly profit. They sell sheep who perform works of piety for human favor. They sell doves who hand over the grace of the Holy Spirit for a price and for the sake of popular opinion. They sell money who openly serve earthly things.

The cords signify the multitude of sins. “He poured out the money”: he removes the figures of the things they loved.

The first building of the Temple, under Solomon, took seven years. Under Zerubbabel, it took forty-six years.

The conception of a human being in the womb resembles milk for six days; for nine days, blood; on the twelfth day it becomes solid; on the eighteenth it is strengthened. Six, nine, twelve, and eighteen total forty-five. Add one, by which it is divided into limbs, and there are forty-six.

Nicodemus: its interpretation is not supplied here [reading incomplete].

“If I told you earthly things”: that is, “Destroy this temple.”

“Heavenly things.”

“The Spirit breathes where he wills.”

“No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended.”

Concerning purification—that is, through baptism—the question was whether John or Christ was greater.

“For God does not give the Spirit by measure,” that is, to the Son. To other human beings he gives through the Spirit in the word of wisdom, and so forth.

“The Father loves the Son and has given everything into his hand,” so that he may be understood to be equal to the Father.

Aenon means “dedication”; and [uncertain reading: *cehe*]: Salim. Sichar means “conclusion”; Sichem means “shoulder.”

“He is wearied from the journey.” The taking on of flesh is his journey. The sixth hour signifies the sixth age of the world. The well signifies the depth of our dwelling. The woman is the Church from the gentiles. The water jar is desire; the water is the pleasure of the world.

The gift of God is the Holy Spirit; the water is the fountain of life; the five husbands are the five bodily senses.

The reapers signify the prophets and patriarchs born from the seed below. The apostles arose. “Let the one who sows and the one who reaps rejoice together.” The apostles and prophets announce Christ to the pagans.

He remained for two days and gave the twofold commandment of charity: that is, to hear what the Son is and to see what he is.

“From death to life”: from the death of unbelief to the life of faith.

“Those who hear will live”: that is, those who obey or heed.

“He gave life to the Son”: that is, he begot the Son. By begetting him, he gave him life in himself.

Heretics said that this resurrection of souls had already taken place.

“The Father judges no one,” because the form of a servant, which was judged, will judge at the end, and divinity will not be seen there.

“I do not do my own will”: that is, not my will alone.

“He shows everything to the Son.” By not doing, he shows it to the Son; but by showing, the Father does it through the Son. Doing and showing are one.

“He will show him greater things”: having taken everything upon himself, that is, the resurrection of bodies.

“As the Father raises the dead, so also the Son gives life to whom he wills.” That is, the resurrection of souls is similar to the resurrection of bodies.

“The Father judges no one.”

The twenty-five stadia signify the Law, because five times five makes twenty-five. But before the Gospel came, this Law lacked perfection. Perfection is comprehended in the number six, because God perfected the world in six days. Let five be multiplied by six, so that the Law may be fulfilled through the Gospel: five times six makes thirty.

Christ came. At first he speaks summarily; afterward he recapitulates how he came and shows that he crossed the sea on foot, not by ship.

“God the Father sealed him”: to place a sign means to seal.

The Jews said: “Moses gave manna; you give barley.”

“Everything that the Father gives me I will not cast out.” This concerns the eternal life of which it was said: “Enter into the joy of the Lord.”

[Col. 1517C]

“Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood”: that is, whoever remains in me, and I in him.

“When you see the Son of Man ascending where he was before.” Then you will understand that he did not speak of the flesh of the body, because human flesh profits nothing for eating.

A person remains in God whose member he is; he himself remains in us when we are his temple.

“Whoever perseveres will be saved.”

He did not wish to walk in Judea. He was providing an example for his followers.

“My time has not yet come”: either the time of rejoicing, which will be on the day of judgment, or the time of the passion.

“Go up to this feast”: where you seek human glory.

The Feast of Booths (*Scenopegia*) is in this world as in a desert, and Christ is hidden.

“Where I am, you cannot come.” He did not say, “where I will be,” but “where I am,” according to his divinity.

“If anyone thirsts, let him come to the streams of living water.” Charisms, gifts, or charity are understood.

The Spirit had not yet been given so abundantly as after his resurrection, because “the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.”

Why after the resurrection? Because the apostles were more perfect in preserving the Spirit, so that it might blaze in our resurrection.

“My sheep hear my voice”: that is, whoever perseveres, and so forth.

“I came so that they may have eternal life”: those entering the Church, so that they may have it more abundantly in eternal life. They enter the Church through faith; “he will go out” means “to eternal life.”

“As the Father knows me, and I know the Father.” This is established in the fact that I know the Father and am known by the Father.

“Because I lay down my life for my sheep”: that is, by the love with which I die for my sheep, I show how much I love the Father.

“The feast of Dedication took place.” The Jews celebrated the day of the Dedication three times. First, when Solomon dedicated the Temple in October, on the tenth day of that month. Second, when it was dedicated by those who had returned from Babylon. Third, when it was dedicated again by Judas Maccabaeus, in December, on the twenty-fifth day of that month.

“Father, glorify your Son.” By this likeness he gave us an example of what we ought to do and say in temptation.

“I have glorified him”: this occurred before the ages; it also occurred when the Magi saw the star that revealed him, when the Spirit appeared over him in the form of a dove, and when he was transfigured on the mountain.

“I will glorify him”: when he rises and ascends into heaven.

“Now is the judgment of the world.” Here “judgment” means discernment, as in the Psalmist.

“Now the prince of this world”: that is, the devil.

“He will be cast out”: namely, from the hearts of many of the elect.

“I will draw everything to myself”: that is, everything from which the devil will have been expelled. He did not say “everyone,” but “everything”—body and soul, and everything else predestined or chosen.

“If I am lifted up”: “if” means “when.”

“Who is this Son of Man?” Above he said: “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified”; and he said: “The light is still with you for a little while.”

Christ seems to have said: “He remains in the house forever.”

“Do not let the darkness seize you”: that is, if you deny his humanity.

“Therefore they could not believe.” Here it must be understood that they did not wish to believe, just as it was said of the Lord: “If we do not believe him, he remains faithful; he cannot deny himself.” This does not mean that human beings cannot change, but that those who pursue vital things cannot believe.

“I judge no one”: that is, not now.

“The word that I have spoken”: that is, myself.

“He gave life to the Son”: that is, by begetting him.

“Now the Son of Man has been glorified,” because, when the unclean spirit had gone out, all remained clean.

“And immediately he will glorify him,” namely, through his passion and resurrection.

“You seek me,” and, as he said to the Jews, “Where I am going, you cannot come”; and I say this to you now. He did not say “now” to the Jews; it is understood.

“If it were otherwise, I would have told you.” That is, if there were not many dwellings prepared in my Father’s house, I would have told you.

He prepared them for us when he died for us.

“If I go away”: that is, through the absence of his flesh.

“Philip, whoever sees me…” He desired to see the Father, supposing that the Father was greater.

“He will do greater things”: he also said this concerning the salvation of the gentiles, which they would accomplish.

“Because I am going to the Father, and whatever you ask, I will do.”

“And another Paraclete”: that is, so that they may have more.

“I will ask the Father”: through his humanity; “I will give” means through his divinity.

“I live”: immediately, through the resurrection, immortal.

“And you will live”: immortal at the end.

“Whoever has my commandments”: that is, in memory.

“And keeps them”: that is, in action.

“I will love him”: that is, so that he may reach the vision of truth.

“And I will reveal myself to him”: implicitly, through the same charity.

“And the word, which is himself…” In the first instance he did not say “my peace,” but in the second he did. The former is worldly; the latter everlasting.

[Col. 1519A]

“Because of the word that I have spoken to you”: that is, because of belief, since without the word there is no baptism.

For us to remain in Christ and Christ in us is beneficial to us, not to him.

“I have kept the Father’s commandments”: that is, so that I might die for human beings.

“Let your joy be complete”: that is, to have fellowship with him.

It is one thing to be a servant through fear and another to be a servant through love.

“I have made everything known to you”: this signifies that he knew what he was going to do.

“Go willingly, and bear fruit by working.”

“If I had not come, they would not have sin.” This means the sin of unbelief by which they despised believing in him, and also the sin of murder by which they killed him.

“He proceeds from the Father, and I will send him.” These are one, because he proceeds from the Father and the Son and comes of his own accord.

“He will testify about me”: that is, so that he may make them believe in me.

“I did not tell you these things from the beginning”: that is, concerning the promise of the Holy Spirit, or the expulsion of the synagogue—namely, concerning the killing, and so forth.

“He will convict the world.” The Spirit of truth will convict the world concerning these matters, but only Judea, as though he were saying: “He will pour charity into your hearts.”

“A human being has been born into the world.” What is to be understood is either that Christ has risen or that the Church will give birth to children for eternal life.

“You will not ask me”: that is, you will not question me.

“You have asked for nothing.” This is because they had not asked in the name of Jesus.

“You will not ask.” He said this of the future, when they would have sufficient understanding.

“Because you loved me.” It is understood that the Father first loved them freely and caused them to believe in the Son and love him.

“I came forth from the Father.” It is understood: because, in the form in which he is equal to the Father, he appeared lesser in the creature he assumed.

“And I came into the world”: that is, in the form of a servant, he presented himself to the lovers of this world.

“I left the world”: that is, he brought his humanity to the majesty of the Father.

“Behold, now you are speaking plainly.” The apostles, still inexperienced, thought that he had spoken plainly because they were unable to grasp the depth of what had been given.

“Now we know.” The Lord, knowing their thoughts, spoke about the things they wished to ask.

“Do you now believe?” Jesus said. “Behold, the hour is coming—indeed, it has come—when you will be scattered, each to his own.” What is understood is: into the fear of unbelief.

“In me you may have peace”: that is, you do not lack faith; or, they may have peace among themselves and love one another.

“The glory that you gave me I have given them”: that is, knowledge of the almighty Father in the Son.

[Col. 1520A]

“Across the brook Cedron.” *Cedron* is a Greek plural genitive, which can mean “of cedars.”

“Or go up to the following days; I am not going up.” Namely, he did go up to this first one.

“I came so that those who do not see may see.” And those who did see—that is, thought they saw—did not wish to believe in him and therefore remained blind.

The evangelists call the tomb of God a rounded place, at whose entrance a stone had been rolled. The sepulchre, however, is the place within the little structure, on the northern side of the tomb, where the Lord’s body rested. The stone that had been rolled away was divided, and two altars were made above it.

The tomb of Saint Mary is in the Valley of Jehoshaphat, in the basilica in which she was once buried. But concerning that same tomb—how or at what time, or by what persons, her holy little body was removed—no one can report with certainty.

The bodies of Simeon and of Joseph, the Lord’s foster-father, are buried in another basilica in that same valley, between Mount Zion and the Mount of Olives, in the Valley of Jehoshaphat.

“Salt of the earth” is said of salt that is found in the earth and is not made from water. Hence the Lord says: “You are the salt of the earth.”

In the region of Trachonitis there is a spring called Phiala, from which underground springs arise for one hundred twenty stadia as far as Caesarea Philippi, which is also called Paneas, after Mount Panium, where the Jordan’s sources divide into the Jor and the Dan. Shortly afterward they join and form a river, flowing for one hundred twenty stadia as far as the city of Julia. Then it forms Lake Gennesar, which is also called Chinnereth.

Concerning locusts and wild honey. Locusts are the smallest kind found in that land; their little bodies are thin and short, about the length of a finger. Because their flight is short, they resemble the leaps of light frogs. They are easily caught in the grasses and, when cooked in oil, provide food for the poor.

As for wild honey: there are small trees with broad, round leaves, of a milky color and honeyed taste. The nature of their leaves is very fragile. Those who wish to eat them first rub them between their hands and then eat them. This is the wild honey found in the forests.

The place where the Lord fed five thousand people is on this side of the Sea of Galilee. Beyond [uncertain reading: *attatum*], it has a spring from which those in Capernaum drink, beside Lake Chinnereth.

Mount Tabor rises thirty stadia high and is twenty-four stadia across its side—this last measurement being understood.

IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 851. AURELIANUS, MONK OF REOMÉ.

[Col. 1521]

HISTORICAL NOTICE ON AURELIANUS.

(*Fabricius, Bibliotheca medii et infimae Latinitatis*)

[Col. 1521A]

Aurelianus, a cleric of the church of Rheims—[Note: [Col. 1521A] Or rather a monk of Reomé, as Martene relates. [Col. 1522A] See the note below on Bernard. EDIT.]—wrote to Bernard, arch cantor and later bishop, according to Sigebert, chapter 110, a regular Tonary, or a work on the rules of the musical modes, which they call tones or tenors, and on the names of these.

In *Adversaria* XLV, 7 and 21, Barthius suspects that this Aurelianus forged letters spuriously attributed to Martial of Limoges. He is led by no other argument than the fact that the *Life and Acts of Martial of Limoges* circulate under Aurelianus’s name, published at Paris in 1522, octavo, and with Abdias at Basel in 1552, folio. Add the *Acta Sanctorum*, 30 June, volume V, page 535.

But that fictitious Aurelianus claims to have been Martial’s hearer and consequently nearer to the time of the apostles. Our Aurelianus, who wrote on music, is noted by Trithemius, chapter 294, as having lived around the year of Christ 900.

[Col. 1521C]

AURELIANUS’S [Note: [Col. 1521C] From an Elno manuscript of approximately eight hundred years.] LETTER TO BERNARD, ARCH CANTOR AND FUTURE ARCHBISHOP

Prefixed to a book on Music composed by him.

(Martene, *Amplissima Collectio*, volume I, page 122.)

HERE BEGINS THE PREFACE TO THE SCIENCE OF MUSIC.

[Col. 1521B]

To Bernard, noblest among Christian nobles, most excellent among men, most nobly raised to the summit of apostolic honor, likewise adorned with imperial dignity, and flourishing in every kind of virtue in Christ—archcantor and, as I hope, the called and future true archbishop of the whole holy Church: Aurelianus, your native servant, formerly of the monastery of Saint John of Reomé, now cast off, yet still yours—and, whether the world wishes it or not, yours—yours, I say, yours, and the least servant of all Christ’s servants.

Because I recognized no one else besides yourself as outstanding in natural talent and renowned for learned training in harmonic philosophy, I was asked by the brothers [Col. 1521C] to set down an extensive account of certain rules of melodies, which they call tones or tenors, and also of the names of the things themselves. For this reason I have directed this series of letters to the judgment of your nobility and dedicated it to your name, so that, if they seem worthy of approval, they may be entrusted to memory; but if otherwise, may be consigned to oblivion.

For I know that very noble singers are to be found. Yet in this art, I confess, I have seen no one skilled except yourself. Some of our own people indeed know many musical regulations [Col. 1522B]. Nevertheless, although they were ancient, nowhere, as I think, is a musician found; and so, from what I was able to find scattered through the sayings of the ancients, as well as from what I heard from you and from others, I myself have striven to compose a new work—with the help of Him who gave the gift, and without whom we can do nothing; to Him also I render devoted thanks.

With these matters briefly prefaced, recognize that I love, welcome, honor, and admire you, remembering your kindly affection toward me—you who loved me sincerely, admonished me, taught me, and nourished me. Observe also that I honor reconciled friendships sincerely, and do not, in accordance with the saying of Plautus, hold a stone in one hand while offering bread with the other.

I shall certainly say something to make a very noble and stern man laugh, so that you may sometimes imitate Crassus, whom Lucilius says to have laughed only once in his life. I shall say what, whenever I often ask it, I cannot keep myself from laughing. We used to lament that you were excessively patient; but, as I see, you raised your hand for a long time and suspended the blow, so that you might strike forcefully, and your silence was deliberate restraint, not consent.

You know very well why I have said this: I learned it by experience in my own case. Therefore I daily sing that prophetic saying: “I will endure the wrath of the Lord until he justifies my cause.” For many ways seem right to men which afterward are found to be crooked. Yet often a treasure is stored in earthen vessels [Col. 1523A].

In the Gospel, an importunate woman at last deserved to be heard; and when the door had been shut with the servants inside, even in the middle of the night a friend received loaves from a friend. God himself, whom no powers can overcome in opposition to him, is overcome by the prayers of the tax collector. Nineveh stood firm through its tears. Christ, I say, joyfully embraces the returning prodigal son. Paul, from a persecutor, becomes the greatest preacher. Tears restore Peter, who denied him three times, to his proper place of love. The one to whom more is forgiven loves more. The whole flock is passed over in silence, while the angels in heaven rejoice over the soul of one sick sheep.

If this seems unworthy to anyone, let him hear the Lord say: “Friend, if I am good, why is your eye evil?” Farewell, my portion—or rather, if you deign it, the unity of my soul; staff of the blind, food of the hungry, hope of the wretched, comfort of the mourners [Col. 1523B], ornament of the Church, light of the world. Do not despise the soul of your fellow servant, for whom Christ died.

*The preface ends.*

# The Chapters of the Work Prefaced Above Begin

I. On the praise of the discipline of music.

II. On its name and inventors, and how the forms of numbers were discovered.

III. That there are three kinds of music.

IV. That human music has distinct parts.

V. On the names of the voices.

VI. That music has the greatest harmony with number.

VII. What distinguishes a musician from a singer.

VIII. On the eight tones.

IX. What is assigned to the tones themselves.

X. On the authentic protus.

XI. On the plagal protus.

XII. On the authentic deuterus.

[Col. 1523C] XIII. On the plagal deuterus.

XIV. On the authentic tritus.

XV. On the plagal tritus.

XVI. On the authentic tetrardus.

XVII. On the plagal tetrardus.

XVIII. The second treatment of the tones.

XIX. A rule by which the density, rarity, density, and depth of the verses of all the tones may be distinguished.

XX. That there exist melodies composed according to this discipline, which, in accordance with the constitution of earlier fathers, are sung as preludes in the church day and night.

## After Chapter 20 the Following Is Read

The book *On the Discipline of the Musical Art* ends. I have compiled it according to my ability, from whatever sources I could gather, with Christ’s help, at the request of the brothers, and have briefly confined it within the compass of a single little book. I have offered it for reading and examination to my most reverend lord and abbot Bernard [Note: [Col. 1523D] In the old catalogue of the abbots of the monastery of Réomé, cited by Peter Roverus in his history of that monastery, there is found a Bernard, bishop of Autun, who is said to have presided over the Réomé community around the year 846. Moreover, in a privilege granted to Hereticus, abbot of Corbie, in 843 at the assembly of Germigny, Bernard, abbot of Saint John of Réomé, subscribed. But the document does not give his episcopal title, nor does he occupy a place in the commonly received list of the bishops of Autun. Roverus considers him to be the same as Berno, to whom Charles the Bald gave the bishopric of Autun, and for whose benefit Wenilo, archbishop of Sens, wrote to Amolo, bishop of Lyons, asking him to invest him with the episcopal character for that see. This letter of his is preserved in Lupus of Ferrières, no. 81. But here he is called not a bishop but a future archbishop; which see he was to hold is entirely unknown. Bernard, archbishop of Lyons, certainly existed, but somewhat later.], who is indeed to become an archbishop. I beg, ask, and entreat you, prudent singer—whoever you are—that if you find anything blameworthy in it, you indicate to me what must be corrected and cease to slander me.

But when you see that something has been done orderly and reasonably, give thanks with me to God, who granted it, and recognize that among the ancients it was considered just as shameful to be ignorant of music as of letters. For both the world itself and the heaven above us are said, according to the teaching of the philosophers, to bear within themselves the resonance of harmony.

Music moves the affections of human beings and summons the senses into different dispositions. In war also it restores the strength of combatants; and the more vehement the blast of the trumpet, the stronger the spirit becomes for battle. It also draws beasts, serpents, birds, and dolphins to listen, as we have said above, insofar as we were able, in praise of the discipline of music.

And why say more? [Col. 1524B] The art of music surpasses all the arts. The reader of the Apocalypse will not doubt that the angels also offer praises to God in the manner of this discipline in the starry heights. Moreover, we are taught by many examples that the voices of angels are heard resounding on earth. I shall present two of them here.

The memory of the ancients records, unless I am mistaken, that a certain monk from the monastery of Saint Victor [Note: [Col. 1524D] That is, of Saint Victurius, bishop of Le Mans, whose name was once borne by a monastery near the river Sarthe at Le Mans; it is mentioned in the *Acts of Saint Domnole*, vol. III of the *Analecta*, and in a charter of Charlemagne, ibid., p. 264.]—which is near the city of the Cenomanni—went, for the sake of prayer, to the basilica of Saint Michael the Archangel on Mount Gargano. Spending the night in vigil before the doors of the church, he heard a choir of angels singing the responsory that is sung on the feast of the apostles, namely:

**R.** “The citizens of the apostles and the household of God have arrived today,” etc.

**V.** “Send forth, O Lord, your spirit.”

When he came to Rome, he recounted what he had heard and committed it to memory for the clergy of the Roman Church. They changed the verse, namely:

**V.** “Their sound has gone out into all the earth.”

This is sung not only by them but also by the whole Church.

In a city called Auxerre, they say, there lived a devout priest who, among his other religious practices, had adopted this custom: whenever the signal for the basilica was sounded, he would immediately rise and promptly prepare the church. While he was flourishing in such practices, one night, as he was leaving his own house—which was attached to the wall of a basilica dedicated in honor of Saint Alban the martyr—he heard a choir of angels singing the *alleluia* with harmonious voices, together with Psalm 148 [Note: [Col. 1524D] This practice of singing *alleluia* with each verse of Psalm 148 in the manner prescribed here, once customary on all Sundays, as this passage shows, later became proper to Septuagesima Sunday.], until the end of the Psalter. Listening attentively at the door of that oratory with astonished ears, he learned the melody.

It was the custom to sing the *alleluia* with the preceding psalm only on Sundays: in the first verse it was repeated once, in the second twice, in the third three times, and in the third it was again repeated from the beginning [Col. 1525A]. As I think, it is fittingly sung in honor of the holy and undivided Trinity.

So that the truth of the matter might become clear to everyone, he summoned the clergy after the completion of Matins and committed it to their memory. In this way it departed from the recesses of his heart, so that nothing remained except the word of praise—and rightly so: the one to whom heavenly things had been revealed had handed them on to others, and, although moved by a love of what was good, he remained for others a means of offering praises to God, while the matter itself withdrew from his own memory.

The following account, which blessed Gregory relates in the books of the *Dialogues* about a certain boy, agrees with this event. When the boy had learned heavenly words and knew the peculiarities of many languages, he came to himself and began to reveal who would depart from that place, how many there would be, and when they would leave. Therefore, tearing his own limbs, he breathed out his final and life-giving spirit [Col. 1525B].

The apostle Paul, fearing this in his own case, says: “I heard secret words which it is not lawful for a human being to speak.” And John is commanded not to write what was uttered by the voices of the seven thunders.

*The end.*

I send you this little book, my most beloved and greatly desired abbot Bernard, which I have edited according to my ability, for reading and examination. I beg you to deign to intercede for me before the merciful Judge on account of the frailties of both my body and my soul, most noble of the noble.

For as long as the spirit covers these limbs, as long as we enjoy the passage of this life, I promise, vow, and pledge that you will always resound upon my tongue. From this day forward there will be no page of ours [Col. 1525C] that does not sound forth the name of Bernard, venerable, noble, holy, [Col. 1526A] devout, and kind. Wherever the monuments of our speech reach, you will travel forth with my writings, most noble of Christians; for you will never die in my books.

Both sexes will always hear me speaking about you—the old, the young, the child, the stranger, and the citizens. Why do I say these things? Because Abraham’s son is tested and found more faithful; Joseph is sold in Egypt so that he may feed his father and brothers; Hezekiah is terrified by approaching death, and, bathed in tears, is granted fifteen additional years of life.

The apostle Peter is shaken by the Lord’s passion, and, weeping bitterly, hears: “Feed my sheep.” Paul—the ravening wolf and younger Benjamin—is blinded in ecstasy and surrounded by the sudden horror of darkness; he calls upon the Lord whom he had long persecuted as a human being [Col. 1526B]. The one to whom more is forgiven, as we stated in the little preface, loves more.

You know, my most reverend father, that many, not content with their own destruction, wish to make more people share in death, as though the multitude of sinners diminished the crime. Nevertheless, now and always I say this, and I want you to hold it firmly on my behalf: whoever proves faithless toward you and disparages or whispers against you, or attempts or says anything hostile to your interests, is to be regarded as so alien to our party that I wish to know neither what he is doing nor where he is. Let him himself finally see where he can obtain absolution.

May the grace of heavenly assistance preserve your holy fatherhood and always strengthen you for the defense of his holy Church.

Amen, amen, amen. May it be, may it be, may it be. Amen.

## FIRST PART OF THE BOOK OF THE PONTIFFS, CONTAINING THE LIVES OF THOSE WHO FLOURISHED FROM THE TIME OF SAINT APOLLINARIS TO ECCLESIUS. 459

Prologue.—The author opens the sources for writing history, asserts their reliability, exaggerates the difficulty of the work, and implores the aid of the Godhead. 459

First chronological-historical dissertation.—On the date of the first twelve bishops [Col. 1530], especially on the period of the sees of Agapitus, Marcellinus, and Severus, and on their succession. 461

Chapter I.—The disagreement of Jerome, Rubeus, and Baronius concerning the question. The arguments of both sides are set out. The opinions of Bollandus and his associates. Summary of the statements. 461

Chapter II.—The disadvantages of each of the views presented. Three bishops alone are insufficient to fill a period of 142 years. The acts of the ancient bishops were almost unknown to ancient writers. Were churches dedicated to the saints and very frequent assemblies of Christians already present in the time of Aurelian? Agapitus II is unknown to everyone who wrote before Rubeus. The Roman council was wrongly postponed to the year 348. Marcellinus occupied the see between Agapitus and Severus. The same difficulty occurs in Bollandus’s view. Agnellus asserts that Marcellinus lived for a sufficiently long time. 467

Chapter III.—Several Roman councils under Julius. Controversies concerning their number, occasion, and date. The acts of the earlier Roman synod are regarded as spurious by Pagius, Labbe, and the critics. The succession of the bishops of Milan. Julius Firmicus Maternus was certainly not bishop of Milan. Passages from the work *On the Mysteries of Profane Religions* elucidated. 469

Chapter IV.—The age of Severus is established from the *Life of Geminianus*. There is no need to multiply the Agapiti or Severi. The succession of the bishops of Ravenna is certain; the rest is obscure. Agnellus’s reliability and sincerity. 474

Brief admonition concerning the verses prefixed to the *Life of Saint Apollinaris*. 475

Dedications of churches to saints later than the age of Apollinaris. The Ravennate patrician Rufus is distinct from his homonymous counterpart, the bishop and martyr of Capua. The Capitolium of Ravenna. The inventions of more recent writers rejected. At what time Saint Apollinaris was crowned with martyrdom. An encomium of him from an ancient martyrology. 477

Observations on the *Life of Saint Exuperantius*.—What was the Silver City, and what was meant by *processus*? Agnellus’s reliability. The other things related about Exuperantius were unknown to Agnellus. 526

## LIFE OF SAINT JOHN ANGELOPTES. 527

Chapter I.—A brief encomium of John. The construction of the basilica of Saint Lawrence and the chapel of Saint Stephen. The acts of Lauricius. 527

Chapter II.—The arrival of Attila. John’s encounter with him. Attila is appeased. 530

Chapter III.—Odoacer is defeated by Theodoric, who takes possession of Ravenna. John appeases the king and makes him favorable to the Ravennates. Other matters concerning Theodoric. 533

Chapter IV.—The spurious privilege of Valentinian in favor of the church of Ravenna. Valentinian adorns and fortifies Ravenna. 535

Chapter V.—The church of the Holy Cross built by Galla Placidia. Singleida constructs another church of Saint Zacharias. Other matters concerning Galla Placidia. 536

Chapter VI.—The death of Galla Placidia. Aquileia captured by the Huns. The basilica of Saint John the Evangelist is built. 537

Chapter VII.—Saint John sees an angel during the celebration of Mass. His death and tomb. 538

Chapter VIII.—The author’s reflections on the *Life of Saint John*. 538

Observations on the *Lives of Saint John Angeloptes and John II*.—Chronological recapitulation. The office of the chamberlains. The place of the *subditae* in basilicas. What does Agnellus mean by the word “monastery”? Were the bodies of the dead buried inside basilicas? Several matters relating to chronology in the age of Attila and Theodoric. Their acts elucidated. Valentinian’s privilege for the church of Ravenna is spurious. The paternal and maternal genealogies of Galla Placidia. Certain liturgical matters. 541

## LIFE OF SAINT PETER CHRYSOLOGUS. 553

Chapter I.—Peter’s birthplace and church. The heresy of Eutyches. The letter of Chrysologus written on that occasion. 553

Chapter II.—The ordination of Peter Chrysologus commanded from heaven. 556

Chapter III.—Buildings constructed under Peter’s care. His synchronism with Projectus of Imola. The funeral of Saint Barbatus. 557

Chapter IV.—Peter foresees and foretells his own death. He proceeds to Imola and dies there. The site of his tomb. 558

Observations on the *Life of Saint Peter Chrysologus*.—Peter’s age investigated. The account of his election as resulting from divine impulse is defended against Dupin. Agnellus acknowledges that the church of Ravenna was subject to the Roman Church. Peter’s letter to Eutyches. Whether he wrote another. Whether he wrote the final sections of that letter. Whether the *Tricolos* building was erected by Chrysologus. The Petrine church. Whether the chapel of Saint Andrew was built by Chrysologus. Gifts presented to the church of Imola. 559

## LIFE OF SAINT AURELIANUS. 567

Single chapter.—A few details about Aurelianus. Complaints concerning pressing work. Interpretation of the verse from the psalm, “You have broken,” and so forth. The death of Aurelianus and his tomb. 567

Observations on the *Life of Saint Aurelianus*.—Are the beginnings of the monastery of Pomposa indicated here? The age of Agnellus when writing this and postponing the remaining matters to another time. Aurelianus was contemporary with Hormisdas. 570

## SECOND PART OF THE BOOK OF THE PONTIFFS, CONTAINING THE LIVES OF THOSE WHO FLOURISHED FROM THE TIME OF ECCLESIUS TO GEORGE. 570

Chronological-historical dissertation.—On the periods of Ecclesius, Ursinus, Victor, Maximianus, and Agnellus.—The chronology transmitted by Rubeus. Matters in Agnellus relating to chronology considered. The chronology arranged. The acts and dates of Silverius and Vigilius examined. The series of years investigated. 571

## LIFE OF SAINT ECCLESIUS. 583

Chapter I.—The church and image of the Blessed Virgin. The period of Ecclesius. The basilica of Saint Vitalis praised. The death and tomb of Ecclesius. 583

Chapter II.—Disputes between the Ravennate clergy and the bishop are settled. The letter of Pope Felix. Further details concerning the death of Ecclesius. 585

Observations on the *Life of Saint Ecclesius*.—Was the basilica of Saint Vitalis built at Justinian’s expense? The emperor did not attend its dedication. The monogram does not belong to Narses. Julianus Argentarius is a profession, not a surname. The inscription of Isaac the Strategos. Analysis of Felix’s Constitution. 589

## LIFE OF SAINT URSICINUS. 597

Chapter I.—Analysis of secular history. The church of Saint Apollinaris completed by Julianus Argentarius. 597

Chapter II.—Agnellus’s reflections on the sacred synaxis. The death and tomb of Ursicinus. 597

Observations on the *Life of Saint Ursicinus*.—Agnellus’s historical statements corrected or explained. 599

## LIFE OF SAINT VICTOR. 599

Chapter I.—A silver ciborium of the Ursian Church. An *endothis* offered. Baths constructed for the clergy. 599

Chapter II.—The decoration of the fountain at the Petrine church. An attack on vices. The death and tomb of Victor. 601

Observations on the *Life of Saint Victor*.—Rubeus errs knowingly and willingly. The use of the ciborium. What is an *endothis*? The building at the Petrine fountain. 602

## LIFE OF SAINT MAXIMIANUS. 603

Chapter I.—The homeland of Maximianus. A treasure is found, part of which is presented to Justinian while the remainder is concealed by a shrewd stratagem. He is ordained bishop. By gentleness of character and conduct he reconciles the Ravennates, who had turned against him. 603

Chapter II.—The church of Saint Stephen is built. Monasteries or chapels beside the basilica. Materials miraculously prepared within the space of one night. 605

Chapter III.—A forest in Istria assigned to the church of Ravenna. Crowns placed on the *Tricolos* building. 607

Chapter IV.—The church of Blessed Mary at Pola. The church of Saint Andrew restored. The body of Saint Andrew at Constantinople. The beard of that apostle. Crowns and dedications of various buildings. 607

Chapter V.—The writings of Maximianus, together with a fragment from his *Analogy*. Certain matters of secular history. 608

Chapter VI.—Small chrism vessels and several *endothes*. A golden cross. Ecclesiastical books corrected by Maximianus. An attack on vices. 610

Chapter VII.—The death and tomb of Saint Maximianus. The translation of relics. 611

Observations on the *Life of Saint Maximianus*.—How could the pallium have been requested from the emperor? Which church of Saint Stephen is meant? Maximianus came to Constantinople only once after obtaining the see. Was the building of Saint Andrew an oratory or a church? Which Vitalis is meant in the poems of Venantius Fortunatus? When were the relics of Saint Andrew at Constantinople? What is a *bandus*? The disturbances in the Alexandrian Church as related by Maximianus. Certain matters of secular history. What are *chrismataria*? Books for ecclesiastical use: missals. 612

## LIFE OF SAINT AGNELLUS. 617

Chapter I.—Agnellus was first married and a soldier, then a deacon. As he was dying, he named his niece as heir. 617

Chapter II.—The churches and possessions of the Goths are donated by Justinian to the church of Ravenna. Several are listed. Special details concerning the church of Saint Martin. A mystical interpretation of the painting existing in it. 619

Chapter III.—The fountain at Blessed Martin’s is reconciled and adorned. A silver cross. The estate of Argenta acquired; the church of Saint George founded. Certain secular matters. The death of Agnellus. His epitaph. 621

Observations on the *Life of Saint Agnellus*.—The date of Bishop Agnellus. His letter to Armenius. The title of the ordained man. Transfer from one title to another. The churches of the Arians. The two Arian baptismal fonts at Ravenna. The inscription in Rubeus differs from Agnellus’s. Secular matters reserved for examination in the following dissertation. 622

Chronological-historical dissertation.—On the dates of Peter the Elder, John, Marinianus, and both Johns. 623

Chapter I.—The dates of the bishops mentioned are transmitted differently by Rubeus and Agnellus. The argument must be divided and treated under definite headings. 623

Chapter II.—The ordination of Peter the Elder must be distinguished from his election. The reason for the longer interregnum. The beginnings of Bishop John. The basilica of Saint Severus restored. An inscription relating to the matter. John’s death assigned to a definite time. 624

Chapter III.—The entry of the Lombards into Italy. The death of Narses. The epoch of the Lombard kingdom differs from the epoch of their entry into Italy. Sigonius defended against the criticism of Camillo Peregrini. 626

[Col. 1534] Chapter IV.—Marinianus sits in the Roman council of the year 595. The year of the death of Gregory the Great. Rubeus corrected. 630

Chapter V.—The bubonic plague. Further discussion of the epoch of Alboin. Battles among the Frankish kings. When the destruction of the monastery of Cassino occurred. The daughter of King Agilulf captured by Callinicus. She was returned around the time of Marinianus’s death. 631

Chapter VI.—Two Johns of that name. The years of both bishops. Agnellus supplemented from Paul. The secular matters related by Agnellus are considered. 633

## LIFE OF PETER THE ELDER. 635

Chapter I.—The basilica of Saint Severus begins to be repaired. Peter is ordained at Rome. After his ordination the Ravennates come to meet him with acclamations. 635

Chapter II.—The entry of the Lombards into Italy. Ticinum besieged. The statue of Theodoric that had stood at Ravenna is described. It is carried by Charlemagne to Aachen. 635

Chapter III.—Italy is ravaged. Ravenna is thrown into alarm. Narses dies after destroying the glory of the Romans. 637

Chapter IV.—Alboin is beheaded through the agency of his wife Rosamund. Rosamund is honorably received at Ravenna by Longinus. There she dies of poison. The death and tomb of Bishop Peter. 637

Observations on the *Life of Peter the Elder*.—The ordination of Peter the Elder without fasting. Statues erected for Theodoric. What is meant by the name “Venetiae.” The history of Alboin’s murder differs in some respects from Paul’s account. 641

## LIFE OF JOHN THE ROMAN. 641

Single chapter.—John’s homeland. The basilica of Saint Severus completed and the body of Saint Severus transferred. John’s death. His tomb and epitaph at the oratory of Saints Mark, Marcellinus, and Felicula. 641

Observations on the *Life of John the Roman*.—Some matters concerning the use of the pallium. What are *mappulae*? Andrew, to whom Saint Gregory’s letter is addressed, was certainly not a bishop. Monks were numerous at Ravenna. The *apocrisiarius* of the Roman see at Ravenna. John the bishop defended against the charge of schism, contrary to Rubeus, Blondus, and Sigonius. The year in which the church of Saints Mark, Marcellus, and Felicula was consecrated. 643

## LIFE OF MARINIANUS. 645

Chapter I.—The family and homeland of Marinianus. Saint Gregory’s *Pastoral Book*. An attack on simoniacal bishops. 645

Chapter II.—Contemporary events connected with Marinianus from history. His death and epitaph. 647

Observations on the *Life of Marinianus*.—Marinianus as monk and priest. Was he abbot of the brethren’s cell? The *Pastoral Book* was written to John, not to Marinianus. The occasion on which it was written. The arguments of all Saint Gregory’s letters written to John and Marinianus. 648

## LIFE OF JOHN. 655

Single chapter.—There is an unceasing attack on the vices of his age. John’s tomb and the time of his episcopate are indicated. 655

## LIFE OF JOHN. 657

Chapter I.—The fleet is redeemed with the Church’s resources on three occasions. A further admonition to the bishops concerning moral conduct. 657

Chapter II.—Wars and truces between the Lombards and the Romans. The actions and fate of John and Eleutherius. Phocas becomes emperor. The Roman Church is the mother of all the Churches. The Pantheon is dedicated. Wars in the East. The beginnings of the Emperor Heraclius. The death and tomb of John. 658

Chronological-historical dissertation.—On the dates of the following bishops of Ravenna: Bon, Maurus, Reparatus, Theodore, Damianus, and Felix. 659

Part I.—Rubeus’s syntax is explained. Many things related in it without authority cannot be maintained. Agnellus is compared with Anastasius. The sees are arranged chronologically. 659

Part II.—The established order is disturbed by Papebroch’s chronology of the Roman pontiffs. It is reconsidered. 663

## LIFE OF BON. 667

Single chapter.—Images are placed for the Ravennate bishops. A further exhortation to the bishops. The death and tomb of Bon. 667

Observations on the *Life of Bon*.—The custom of placing portraits of bishops in the church. The same concerning emperors. The first incursions of the Saracens. 670

## LIFE OF MAURUS THE SCHISMATIC. 669

Chapter I.—Maurus, deacon and abbot of Saint Bartholomew. Having become bishop, he contends with the Roman pontiff. 669

Chapter II.—Benedict, deacon of Sicily, is administrator. The wealth of the Sicilian Patrimony belonging to the church of Ravenna. The *manipularius* is sent to Sicily again and returns rich. 671

[Col. 1535] Chapter III.—Maurus refuses to go to Rome when summoned by the pontiff. Punished with an anathema, he dares to pronounce an anathema against the Roman pontiff. The death of both men. 671

Chapter IV.—The stone of the tomb. The Emperor Lothair carried it off to Gaul. The body of Blessed Apollinaris transferred from the *ardica* to the middle of the basilica. The epitaph of Maurus. 673

Observations on the *Life of Maurus the Schismatic*.—The church’s steward, in Latin *vicedominus*. Abbots among the clergy of Saint Bartholomew; the abbey of Ravenna. The seats of the bishops of Ravenna at synods. The decree obtained by Maurus from Constantine. Chronological matters corrected; the succession of the exarchs supplemented from it. Autocephaly arose and turned into schism. Agnellus refuted. 674

## LIFE OF REPARATUS. 679

Single chapter.—The gifts of Reparatus. He obtains many things from the emperor. It is decreed that an elected bishop of Ravenna may remain in Rome no longer than eight days. Images of Reparatus and the emperors. Complaints against the bishops of his age. 679

Observations on the *Life of Reparatus*.—Reparatus sought to obtain autocephaly under Maurus. He was taken from a monastery. Which monastery was he taken from? He obtains a privilege from Pogonatus, which supports concord rather than autocephaly. 681

## LIFE OF THEODORE. 681

Chapter I.—The fourth part customarily given to the clergy is abolished. Documents favorable to the clergy are collected and consumed by fire. 681

Chapter II.—The monastery, or oratory, of Blessed Theodore, built by Theodore the exarch. The piety of that exarch. Joannicius flourishes. Further details concerning him. 684

Chapter III.—The clergy withdraw from Theodore on Christmas Day. The dispute is settled through the exarch. The clergy are restored to their former position. 685

Chapter IV.—Theodore submits to the Roman pontiff. Leo II confirms the decrees under Agatho, after certain conditions have been accepted. Theodore’s death and the duration of his see. 688

Observations on the *Life of Theodore*.—Theodore defended against Agnellus’s criticisms. Theodore the exarch distinct from Calliopa. Certain matters relating to discipline and to the autocephaly of the bishop of Ravenna indicated. 689

## LIFE OF DAMIANUS. 691

Chapter I.—A boy is restored to life, but after being signed with chrism dies again. Joannicius returns to Ravenna. 691

Chapter II.—The citizens of Ravenna were accustomed to fight among themselves. The factions took their names from the city gates. A great slaughter of people occurred; thereafter several were killed treacherously and secretly. A public prayer is proclaimed; the authors of the crime are discovered and punished. 691

Chapter III.—Several matters are related concerning a certain anonymous man living in the age of Damianus. Damianus himself is praised. 694

Chapter IV.—John, abbot of Saint John beyond Caesarea. He conducts the affairs of his church at Constantinople. Through the aid of demons he comes to Ravenna in a single night. He repents of what he has done. 695

Chapter V.—The conversion of a certain Jew. The homeland and education of Damianus. The burning of the Ravennate archive. The death of the pontiff. His epitaph. 697

Observations on the *Life of Damianus*.—What is related here about the boy restored to life is related elsewhere and differently by Rubeus. The rite of signing is elucidated from certain unpublished materials. The abuse of civil warfare had ceased at Parma a few years earlier. What is attributed to Damianus was wrongly said of another. The story told about John the abbot is fabulous. The rite was borrowed from the monks. The barbarism of that age is evident from the epitaph. 698

## LIFE OF SAINT FELIX. 701

Chapter I.—The appearance, character, and writings of Felix. He is both abbot and steward. Some details about Bishop George. 701

Chapter II.—Justinian, who here is called Constantine, is expelled after his nose and ears are cut off. He returns to imperial power. Revenge against the Ravennates. Felix is captured and blinded. 701

Chapter III.—A new crisis for the Ravennates. George, son of Joannicius, is elected duke with supreme authority. He arranges everything for war outside and inside the city. 704

Chapter IV.—Joannicius is killed by a savage slaughter. Justinian is killed. After seeing the head of Justinian, which she had desired, Joannicius’s sister dies. 705

Chapter V.—Philippicus frees Felix and bestows many gifts on him. As he returns to Ravenna, Felix becomes famous for miracles. Because of these, the emperor heaps honors and privileges upon him and restores him to his own see. He builds a house called “Felix’s.” 707

Chapter VI.—Before the disaster described above, Joannicius had arranged the sacred offices. His genealogy. His piety proved by a miracle. Other matters relating to this. 709

Chapter VII.—The works of Felix. He deposits the relics of the saints. He asks that his own writings be consumed by fire. He collects the sermons of Saint Peter Chrysologus. His death, tomb, and epitaph. 710

[Col. 1536] Observations on the *Life of Saint Felix*.—Agnellus is silent about Felix’s disputes with the Roman pontiff. Later writers report things that are by no means true. The causes of Justinian’s anger against the Ravennates. Other matters omitted by Agnellus. Certain matters related by Agnellus neglected by Rubeus. Agnellus’s genealogy from Joannicius. Felix numbered among the saints. An ecclesiastical writer. 711

Chronological excursus on the period of the remaining Ravennate pontiffs about whom Agnellus writes.—The mutilated and meager lives of the following bishops. What Rubeus and Ughellus report. The periods of Liutprand, Aldeprand, Rachis, and Aistulf. The names of the pontiffs Stephen and Paul transposed in Agnellus. Other matters relating to the dates of the Ravennate pontiffs. 715

## LIFE OF JOHN. 721

Chapter I.—Ravenna is captured by the treachery of its citizens under Liutprand. John goes into exile. He is restored through the care of Epiphanius the *scriniarius*. Epiphanius also takes revenge on John’s enemies. 721

Chapter II.—A battle between the Ravennates and a Greek *ministraticus* [reading uncertain], accompanied by a prodigy. Because of this, the day of Saints John and Paul is made a feast. The death of John. 722

Observations on the *Life of John*.—This John is the sixth of that name. Why was he called the fifth? Particulars concerning Ravenna’s capture by Liutprand’s army. The fleet destroyed. John went into exile, not because of the Iconoclasts. The office of the *scriniarii*. The events related concerning the Ravennate victory belong to an uncertain time. The River Pantheum, or Paterenum: which river was it? 723

## LIFE OF SERGIUS. 725

Chapter I.—Sergius, formerly a layman and married man, becomes bishop. His wife Euphemia becomes a deaconess. The clergy are hostile to the bishop. The bishop creates new priests and deacons. After the matters are settled, the two groups minister in different dress and in different ranks. 725

Chapter II.—The arrival at Ravenna of Pope Zacharias, who had anointed King Pippin. He celebrates Mass and presents an *endothis*. Aistulf offers gifts both at Rome and at Ravenna. He restores the Petrine church. Other details concerning him. 725

Chapter III.—Sergius is brought before a tribunal by the Roman pontiff, as having been ordained contrary to the canons. A new pontiff restores Sergius to his see. Sergius gives thanks to Saint Nicholas. 726

Chapter IV.—The pontiff comes to Ravenna. The clergy plot unspeakable things against him. The deacon Uviliaris offers wiser counsel. The pontiff carries away several things. Sergius threatens the region as exarch. Those responsible for the attack on the pontiff are taken to Rome. Other matters concerning Sergius. Some things are missing. Everything must be read cautiously. 728

Observations on the *Life of Sergius*.—The truth of the narratives in the *Life of Sergius* concerning the Roman pontiffs. The new clergy ordained by Sergius. The deacons’ shoulder garment. The monastery of Saint Hilary at Galiata. The time during which Sergius was detained at Rome. The boundaries of the Ravennate territory. The copyist’s inept additions to this codex. 729

## LIFE OF LEO. 733

Single chapter.—He attracts Charles to Italy and shows the route through Martin. Desiderius is captured. Adelgisus flees. 733

Observations on the *Life of Leo*.—Leo is found to be a man of sufficiently disreputable character. How he first showed the route to the Franks coming into Italy. No bishop intervened between Gratiosus and Valerius. 733

## LIFE OF JOHN. 733

Chapter I.—The life is acephalous. Something concerning disputes with the bishop. The ecstasy of John the abbot. 733

Chapter II.—The disastrous effects of an unjust curse cast upon an innocent man. John’s unhappy death. 735

Observations on the *Life of John*.—The dispute between the bishop and the clergy indicated. What Rubeus relates about John. What is *calicodimia*? 736

## LIFE OF GRATIOSUS. 737

Chapter I.—King Charles at Ravenna. He dines with the bishop. The simplicity of Gratiosus, for which Charles praises him. 737

Chapter II.—The author’s prophecy, attributed to Gratiosus. The death and tomb of Gratiosus. 737

Observations on the *Life of Gratiosus*.—The monastery of Saint Apollinaris in Veclo. The prodigies indicated here do not belong to the age of Gratiosus. The matters that Agnellus appends to the *Life of Gratiosus* are wrongly attributed to Gratiosus. 740

## LIFE OF MARTIN. 741

Chapter I.—The age of Martin when he was ordained by Leo III. His tall stature. He bestows on the author the monastery of Saint Mary at Blachernae. He fortifies the church of Saint Euphemia. Pippin and Charles die. The basilica of Saint Apollinaris in Classe is repaired at the expense of the Roman pontiff. Martin is summoned to Rome by that pontiff, who has been offended. John of Arles is presented with gifts at Ravenna. 741

Chapter II.—Leo III dies. Stephen succeeds him and celebrates Mass at Ravenna, displaying the Savior’s sandals. The Emperor Louis presents a silver table to the church of Ravenna. 743

Observations on the *Life of Martin*.—The date and certain deeds of Martin. The period of John of Arles. The silver table bequeathed by Charles to the church of Ravenna. The Savior’s sandals. 744

## SOME MATERIALS FROM THE LIFE OF PETRONACIUS COLLECTED BY THE COPYIST. 745

Observations on Petronacius.—He could not have sworn allegiance to Charles. Agnellus wrote part of the book while Petronacius was seated in the see. The title “cardinal priest” in the church of Ravenna is later than Agnellus. Certain supplementary matters. 745

## LIFE OF GEORGE. 745

Chapter I.—Gregory IV consecrates George. He plunders the church’s treasures. At Pavia he lifts the daughter of Lothair from the sacred font. Prodigies. The death of Louis the Pious. Wars among his sons. 745

Chapter II.—George obtains permission to be sent with legates by the pontiff to Gaul for the sake of peace. The pomp and extravagance with which he travels. The battle of Fontenay. George is captured and subjected to insults. Charles’s wife intercedes for him. On his return, he is cruel toward his priests. He dies. 747

Observations on the *Life of George*.—Many things said about George by Rubeus are untrue. Lothair’s daughter was called Rotrude, not Geltrude. Irmingard was her mother. The prodigies are considered in relation to chronology. What particular point is established by the matter concerning the bread and offerings? 750

Notice to the reader. 751

Reverend Fathers and archbishop-pontiffs of the church of Ravenna, transmitted in summary and in sequence. The work was that of one man up to 1286, and from then until the present day the work of another. 751

Concerning Aurelianus, the twenty-third archbishop; Ecclesius, the twenty-fourth; Ursicinus, the twenty-fifth; Victor, the twenty-sixth; and Maximianus, the twenty-seventh. 783

Concerning Agnellus, the twenty-eighth archbishop; Peter the Elder, the twenty-ninth; John the Roman, the thirtieth; Mauritius, the thirty-first; and John, the thirty-second. 784

Concerning John, the thirty-third archbishop; Bon, the thirty-fourth; Maurus, the thirty-fifth; Reparatus, the thirty-sixth; Theodore, the thirty-seventh; Damianus, the thirty-eighth; Felix, the thirty-ninth; and John, the fortieth. 785

Concerning Sergius, the forty-first archbishop; Leo, the forty-second; John, the forty-third; Gratiosus, the forty-fourth; John, the forty-fifth; Valerius, the forty-sixth; Martin, the forty-seventh; and Petronacius, the forty-eighth. 786

Concerning George, the forty-ninth archbishop; Deodatus, the fiftieth; and John, the fifty-first. 787

## ACTS OF THE ROMAN COUNCIL. 787

The Chronicle follows. 792

Concerning Romanus, the fifty-second archbishop; Dominicus, the fifty-third; John, the fifty-fourth; and John, the fifty-fifth. 792

Annotation. 792

Concerning Constantius, the fifty-sixth archbishop. 792

Concerning Peter, the fifty-seventh archbishop; Honestus, the fifty-eighth; John of Pavia, the fifty-ninth; and Herbertus, the sixtieth. 793

Admonition concerning the following Constitution. 793

## HERE BEGINS THE SACRED CONSTITUTION OF THE LORD EMPEROR OTTO.

issued on the twelfth day before the Kalends of October, in the twelfth indiction, in the third year of the pontificate of Pope Gregory V; promulgated through the hands of Gerbert, archbishop of the holy church of Ravenna, at that synod in which Arnulf, bishop of Milan, was deprived of the papacy, in the basilica of Blessed Peter called the Golden Cell; and all the bishops who were present signed it. 793

The Chronicle follows. 793

Concerning Neomutus, the sixty-first archbishop; Frederick, the sixty-second; Arnold, the sixty-third; Herbert, the sixty-fourth; and Gebhard, the sixty-fifth. 794

Concerning Himfrid, the sixty-sixth archbishop; Henry, the sixty-seventh; and Gilbert, the sixty-eighth. 795

On Walter, archbishop LXIX; Moses, archbishop LXX. 795

**HISTORY OF THE TRANSFER OF THE BODIES OF THE SAINTS RAGNOBERTUS AND ZENO.** 891
