FRECULPHUS, BISHOP OF LISIEUX.

HISTORICAL NOTICE. 915

THE TWO VOLUMES OF FRECULPHUS’S CHRONICLES. 917

Preface to the first volume. 917

The author’s hexameter poem to his teacher Elisachar. 919

HERE BEGINS THE FIRST VOLUME, CONTAINING A HISTORY OF EVENTS FROM THE BEGINNING OF THE WORLD TO THE NATIVITY OF THE SAVIOR. 919

BOOK ONE. 919

CHAPTER ONE.—On the fact that nearly all historians began to weave their histories from Ninus, king of the Assyrians. 919

CHAPTER II.—Why the human being was created last among creatures. 920

CHAPTER III.—How the human being was created in the image and likeness of God. 920

CHAPTER IV.—On the obedience given to the human being by God. 921

CHAPTER V.—On the tree of the knowledge of good and evil in paradise, and on the tree of life. 921

CHAPTER VI.—On Abel, who was killed by his brother Cain, and on the punishments Cain endured. 921

CHAPTER VII.—On the origin of the two cities. 922

CHAPTER VIII.—How God spoke to the first human beings, and on what is written: “If you offer rightly, but do not divide rightly, have you not sinned?” 922

CHAPTER IX.—On what is written: “Cain knew his wife, and she bore him Enoch, after whose name he called the city that he had built”; and how this can be reconciled with the fact that three human beings, who were then the only ones, built a city. 923

CHAPTER X.—That the Greek and Latin philosophers have a different opinion about the first age of the world from that of the Hebrews. 925

CHAPTER XI.—On Seth, son of Adam, who pleased God, and on his sons and grandsons, who discovered wisdom wondrously down to the seventh generation and eventually wrote it on pillars. [Col. 1540] 926

CHAPTER XII.—On Enoch, who was taken away, and who also left his prophecies in writing. 926

CHAPTER XIII.—On the sons of Seth, who displeased God after the seventh generation. 927

CHAPTER XIV.—On the sons of God who took the daughters of men as wives. 927

CHAPTER XV.—Whether the people of the first age lived without wives through so many spans of years, since we read that they fathered sons only after many years. 927

CHAPTER XVI.—On Methuselah: whether he lived fourteen years after the Flood, as seems to be stated in Genesis. 928

CHAPTER XVII.—On what is said: “Vengeance shall be taken sevenfold on Cain, but on Lamech seventy-sevenfold.” 928

CHAPTER XVIII.—On the wrath of God, and on what is written in Genesis: “It repents me that I made man,” although there is no repentance in God, in whom foreknowledge is certain. 929

CHAPTER XIX.—On what God says: “Their days shall be one hundred and twenty years.” 929

CHAPTER XX.—On Noah, and how, tenth from Adam, he became the leader of his people. 929

CHAPTER XXI.—On the size of the ark and its chambers. 930

CHAPTER XXII.—That we read that two of the unclean animals and seven of the clean animals were in the ark. 931

CHAPTER XXIII.—Whether the tiniest and useless little creatures were in the ark. 931

CHAPTER XXIV.—How the animals that are thought unable to live without meat could have lived in the ark. 931

CHAPTER XXV.—On Noah’s entry into the ark; where the ark came to rest after the Flood; the number of years from Adam to Noah; and what the philosophers of the nations thought about the ark. 932

CHAPTER XXVI.—On what seems impossible to certain people: that human beings lived nine hundred years. 932

CHAPTER XXVII.—How the whole human race was propagated from Noah’s three sons, and what parts of the world they occupied. 933

CHAPTER XXVIII.—On the interpretation of Falech as “division,” because in his days the division of languages took place; also on the building of the tower and its builder, Nimrod, and on what the wise men of the nations thought about it. 935

CHAPTER XXIX.—On the statement that Assur went out from the land of Shinar and built Nineveh. 937

CHAPTER XXX.—Why, when Ham sinned, his son Canaan received the sentence of punishment. 937

CHAPTER XXXI.—How “May God enlarge Japheth, and may he dwell in the tents of Shem” is to be understood. 937

CHAPTER XXXII.—On what is written: “From Shem were born [descendants]; he was the father of all the sons of Eber, the elder brother of Japheth.” 938

CHAPTER XXXIII.—Since Genesis makes no mention of anyone from Noah to Abraham, whether there was any righteous person. 938

CHAPTER XXXIV.—How the statement that the Lord descended is to be understood; that “they will not desist from their thoughts until they complete them in action”; and how seventy-two languages began throughout the lands from Noah’s three sons. 939

CHAPTER XXXV.—On the number of years from the Flood to the birth of Abraham, concerning which Josephus and the Septuagint interpreters, or Eusebius, hold a different view from what is contained in the Hebrew text. 940

CHAPTER XXXVI.—How Terah went out from Chaldea with Abraham, Lot, and Aram, and came into the land of Canaan. 941

CHAPTER XXXVII.—After the death of Abraham’s father Terah, what the Lord is read to have said to Abraham: “Go out from your land and from your kindred,” etc., although he had previously left it with his father; also concerning Nahor, Abraham’s brother, and matters pertaining to this question. 941

CHAPTER XXXVIII.—Since the years of some people’s lives are recorded, why the years of others are passed over in Genesis. 943

CHAPTER XXXIX.—Whether the father of Milcah was himself the father of Iscah, or who Iscah was. 943

CHAPTER XL.—How Sarah, although she was taken by Pharaoh, is not believed to have been violated by him. 943

CHAPTER XLI.—Who the armed men were whom Abraham is read to have counted. 943

CHAPTER XLII.—Who Melchizedek was, the king of Salem who received tithes from Abraham. 943

BOOK TWO. 945

CHAPTER ONE.—On Joseph’s exaltation, and why the children of Israel departed from there; the partly incomplete and partly false account of the pagan historians. 945

CHAPTER II.—The patriarch Jacob’s clear prophecy concerning Christ’s coming. Also when Greece began to use grain. 946

[Col. 1541] CHAPTER III.—On Joseph’s death and the affliction of the children of Israel that immediately followed. 946

CHAPTER IV.—Callithias, the first man to hold the priesthood at Argos. Also the time when Atlas was a distinguished astrologer. 947

CHAPTER V.—From where Syria received its name. 947

CHAPTER VI.—At what time, and together with which contemporaries, Moses learned the philosophy of the Egyptians. 947

CHAPTER VII.—At what time the kingdom of the Athenians began. Also the contest between the gods Neptune and Minerva over the naming of Athens. 948

CHAPTER VIII.—On the history of Moses’ birth, exposure, upbringing, life, and deeds, both in Ethiopia and in Egypt. 949

CHAPTER IX.—On the parricides of the sons of Danaus and of Aegisthus; Egypt’s first name; and Busiris’s tyranny there. 954

CHAPTER X.—On Procne and Philomela, and on Cathmus, king of Thebes. 954

CHAPTER XI.—Games instituted in honor of Apollo; the time when Hercules flourished and Dionysus revealed the vine. Also on the Flood under Deucalion and the conflagration under Phaethon. 955

CHAPTER XII.—Troy and Achaea. Triptolemus distributed grain throughout the cities. Hercules brought Theseus back from the underworld. 956

CHAPTER XIII.—On the abduction of Ganymede; Medea’s slaughter of her little children; and the beheading of the prostitute Gorgo. 957

CHAPTER XIV.—On Deborah the prophetess, and on the transfer of the Argive kingdom to Mycenae. 958

CHAPTER XV.—At what time Ilium and Troy were founded; the Golden Age of Saturn. 958

CHAPTER XVI.—On Liber and his Bacchic rites. Likewise on Daedalus and the Sphinx, and also on the Argonauts; finally on the Scythians, the Amazons, and the island of Scaza. 959

CHAPTER XVII.—Carthage founded by Dido. Hercules instituted the Olympic contest and killed Antaeus, son of Earth. The ten-year Trojan War begins. When it finally ended, Aeneas, seeking other settlements for himself, came to Latium, etc. 964

CHAPTER XVIII.—Samson, judge of the Hebrews; Aeneas, the first king of the Latins; and after him Ascanius, etc. The historians also relate that the story of Ulysses’ escape from Scylla occurred at this time. 967

CHAPTER XIX.—After Eli the priest died, the prophet Samuel succeeded him, and Saul was appointed the first king of the Hebrews. 968

CHAPTER XX.—David was appointed the first Hebrew king from the tribe of Judah. Some believe that Homer also flourished at the same time. Codrus, king of the Athenians, and how he freed his country. 969

CHAPTER XXI.—Two calculations of the years from Adam to Solomon and the building of the Temple: one according to Eusebius and Saint Jerome, and the other according to Josephus’s reckoning. 970

BOOK THREE. 971

CHAPTER ONE.—How David rose from a shepherd’s life to kingship and greatly enlarged his kingdom. 971

CHAPTER II.—On the expenses, arrangements, and order of the priests that David prepared for building the Lord’s Temple. 971

CHAPTER III.—On Solomon: how nobly he was raised to the kingdom and how magnificently he buried his father. This became evident when Hyrcanus, after many years, dug open his tomb and carried away countless sums of money. Herod later did the same. 972

CHAPTER IV.—The thirty-first Assyrian ruler, Lausthenes, in whose time Solomon completed the Lord’s Temple, using the friendship of Hiram, king of Tyre; and what writers among the nations thought about both men. 974

CHAPTER V.—The thirty-second Assyrian ruler, Piritiabes, during whose reign the Hebrew kingdom was divided and King Shishak of Egypt also plundered the Lord’s Temple; and what an educated writer among the nations thought about this. 974

CHAPTER VI.—The thirty-third Assyrian ruler, Ophrataeus, during whose time the wicked King Ahab reigned over part of Israel, under whom Elijah lived. Also what Menander wrote about the drought of that period. 975

CHAPTER VII.—The thirty-fourth Assyrian ruler, Ophratenes, during whose reign Tiberinus was king of the Latins. Homer is also said to have lived then, as did Lycurgus the lawgiver and Joiada the righteous high priest of the Temple, who lived 130 years after Moses, as sacred history relates. 976

CHAPTER VIII.—The thirty-fifth Assyrian ruler, Acrazapes, during whose reign the prophet Zechariah, son of the priest Joiada, was killed between the Temple and the altar. At that time Sylvius Romulus also established a stronghold among the hills where Rome now stands. 976

[Col. 1542] CHAPTER IX.—The thirty-sixth Assyrian ruler, Thonos, called Concoloros and Sardanapalus, who was more corrupted than a woman. For this reason he was despised and overthrown by Arbaces, commander of the Medes, and the Assyrian kingdom collapsed together with him. 977

CHAPTER X.—The first Median ruler, Arbaces: during his reign Hosea, Isaiah, Amos, and Jonah prophesied. Like springs, they burst forth into prophecy, when the first Babylon fell and the second began to arise, namely Rome, under whose rule Christ was born. 978

CHAPTER XI.—The second Median ruler, Sosarmus: during his reign the first Olympiad began; the kingdoms of the Lacedaemonians and Corinthians came to an end, while the kingdom of the Lydians began. At that time the tyrant Phalaris in Sicily justly punished the author of a most wicked deed. The holy prophets also began to preach the salvation of the nations. 978

CHAPTER XII.—The third Median ruler, Madidus: during his reign the ten tribes called Israel were transferred to the mountains of the Medes, and the Cuthaeans, who are called Samaritans, were settled in their region in their place. Romulus, after killing his grandfather and brother, founded Rome. At this time the Erythraean Sibyl also lived; she prophesied openly about Christ. 980

CHAPTER XIII.—The fourth Median ruler, Cardicas: during his reign Numa was king of the Latins, instituting many vain and superstitious practices. 982

CHAPTER XIV.—The fifth Median ruler, Deioces: under him Manasseh was led captive to Babylon and, by doing penance, earned release. Tullus was king of the Romans; he instituted many measures contributing to the dignity of the state, and the cities founded at that time are recorded. 983

CHAPTER XV.—The sixth Median ruler, Phraortes: under him Josiah was king of the Jews, and Ancus Marcius was king of the Romans. 984

CHAPTER XVI.—The seventh Median ruler, Cyaxares: during his reign Josiah, king of the Jews, was killed; the Jews were oppressed by various calamities, and their kings were afflicted by an unhappy fate among the Egyptians and Babylonians. Tarquinius Priscus was king of the Romans; he enlarged the Senate and devised many notable and splendid institutions by which the dignity of the empire was made conspicuous. 984

CHAPTER XVII.—The eighth Median ruler, Astyages: during his reign Jerusalem was captured and the Temple burned. The Jews were led captive into Babylon. The great strength of Nebuchadnezzar and the remarkable deeds he accomplished by courage and action are briefly recorded, as is what writers among the nations said about him. The question is also raised: since the Babylonian kings possessed such extraordinary strength, why is the number of years reckoned according to the Median kings? Also concerning the sufferings of the prophet Jeremiah; why he unwillingly went down to Egypt; and how he foretold the devastation of Egypt. Also concerning Pythagoras and the seven wise men of Greece who lived in those times. 986

CHAPTER XVIII.—How Cyrus the Persian destroyed the empire of the Medes, defeated his maternal uncle Astyages in war, overthrew Babylon, divided the river Gyndes into 460 channels, and, marching against Lydia, captured King Croesus. Finally, after accomplishing many brave deeds, he perished in Scythia with his entire army. Under him the Jews were released from captivity. At that time Tarquinius, surnamed Superbus, ruled the Roman kingdom; and he was expelled because of his tyranny and arrogance, while the Romans simultaneously abolished royal power. 990

CHAPTER XIX.—Cambyses, the second king of the Persians, prohibited the rebuilding of the Temple at Jerusalem and conquered Egypt in war. The Magi succeeded him, but Darius rebuked their audacity, exposed their deceptions, and himself became king. He ordered the building of the Lord’s Temple, which had been begun under Cyrus and was completed by his command. 994

BOOK FOUR. 995

CHAPTER ONE.—Darius, the fourth king of the Persians, made war against the Scythians; he conquered Asia and Macedonia and fought the Athenians on the plain of Marathon, where he lost two hundred thousand of his army and, defeated, fled back to Persia. 995

CHAPTER II.—During his reign Brutus and Collatinus, after the expulsion of the kings, were appointed the first consuls among the Romans. The events that took place among the Romans in those days are also related, as well as how the laws of the state were administered for 243 years under kings, then for 464 years through consuls, tribunes, and dictators, and again through consuls. 996

CHAPTER III.—On Melcho, king of the Carthaginians, who fought unsuccessfully in Sicily and, returning home, killed himself with his own hand. 997

CHAPTER IV.—On Ezra: how, having won the favor of King Xerxes, he returned to Jerusalem with a great crowd of Jews and many gifts. 998

CHAPTER V.—On Nehemiah, who rebuilt the walls of Jerusalem and gathered inhabitants there. 998

[Col. 1543] CHAPTER VI.—How Xerxes is said to have had 700,000 armed men from his kingdom and 300,000 auxiliaries, as well as 1,200 ships with rams and 3,000 cargo ships in his army; how Leonidas, commander of the Spartans, opposed him with 4,000 men and almost defeated him; and how afterward Themistocles, commander of the Athenians, overcame his army in a naval battle. Xerxes, defeated and having lost his forces, disgracefully fled to his homeland. 998

CHAPTER VII.—During the reign of Artaxerxes, the books of Pythagoras were burned by the Athenians. Also a memorial of the philosophers who lived then, namely the Milesians, the physician Hippocrates, and Socrates. 1001

CHAPTER VIII.—On Mamilius, commander of Tusculum, who subdued the Latins; on the first contest held at Rome; on the great plague that almost consumed Roman strength; and on other events that took place among the Romans at that time. 1002

CHAPTER IX.—On the seventy weeks foretold by Daniel, which were completed in the final year of Nero’s empire. 1003

CHAPTER X.—During the reign of Darius, surnamed Nothus, concerning the wise men who flourished at that time. The Romans then requested laws from the Athenians and wrote them on the Twelve Tables. They expelled the consuls and appointed decemvirs, and the great evil that arose from this, together with the events that befell them in those days. 1003

CHAPTER XI.—On the conflict among the Sicilians, namely between the people of Catana and Syracuse, who sought aid from the Lacedaemonians and Athenians; on the occasion of which not only Sicily but all Greece was worn down by the gravest wars. 1004

CHAPTER XII.—How Artaxerxes fought against and defeated his brother Cyrus; on the earthquake in Sicily and the severe eruption of Mount Etna; on the plague that struck the Athenians; and on the troubles of the Romans. 1005

CHAPTER XIII.—On the Gauls who burned, devastated, and finally sold Rome. 1005

CHAPTER XIV.—In what period Socrates and Plato flourished. 1006

CHAPTER XV.—During the reign of Artaxerxes, also called Ochus, John, the high priest of the Jews, killed his brother Jesus in the Temple. Because of this crime the Jews suffered many grievous calamities. 1008

CHAPTER XVI.—How Artaxerxes proclaimed peace to the Greeks and added the defeated Egypt to his empire. 1008

CHAPTER XVII.—In what period a great plague cruelly devastated Rome, and the earth opened in the City and swallowed alive Curtius, a knight. At that time the Gauls also, conspiring against the Romans, were defeated three times. 1009

CHAPTER XVIII.—On the unusually prolonged night, and on true stones falling from heaven and severely striking the earth. This happened when Alexander the Great of Macedon was born. Aristotle was also renowned in those days, and Plato died. 1010

CHAPTER XIX.—That, during the reign of Arxes, Roman matrons were discovered engaged in a criminal poisoning plot. Philip, king of the Macedonians and father of Alexander the Great, meanwhile waged many wars, overthrew cities, and subdued countless nations. 1010

CHAPTER XX.—On the most serious battles fought between the Samnites and Romans in those days. The Romans were defeated by the Samnites and sent under the yoke of servitude; later the Romans, victorious under their commander Papirius, defeated the Samnites and threw off the yoke. 1013

CHAPTER XXI.—During the reign of Darius, whom Alexander killed, Jaddus, leader and priest of the Jews, expelled his brother Manasseh from the priesthood because he had married the daughter of the satrap of Samaria. On this occasion a temple was built on Mount Garizim, modeled on the Jerusalem Temple. 1015

CHAPTER XXII.—In what period Alexander, having gained the kingdom of the Macedonians after his father’s death, performed great and remarkable deeds among his own people, first defeated the Parthians in war, then, subjugating Egypt and Syria, reached Jerusalem, which he left unharmed and honored the Temple with gifts. Later, after destroying the Parthian forces in two battles, he finally killed Darius, being most cruel toward foreigners and impious toward his own kin. 1015

CHAPTER XXIII.—After Alexandria was built in Egypt and the Persian empire destroyed, Alexander held the monarchy of the world for five years. He defeated numerous peoples, marched against India and subjugated it, and overcame and captured the other inaccessible nations situated around the shores of the Ocean. Finally, returning to Babylon, he died after drinking poison. 1019

CHAPTER XXIV.—On the wars fought between the Romans, Samnites, and Gauls at the time when Alexander was devastating the East, and on the many hardships caused by their mutual conflicts. 1020

CHAPTER XXV.—How Alexander obtained the monarchy and among whom he cruelly divided the kingdom he had acquired; and what portion fell to each. [Col. 1544] 1022

CHAPTER XXVI.—After Alexander, king of the Macedonians, died, his commanders destroyed one another in mutual wars. 1023

CHAPTER XXVII.—How Ptolemy, Alexander’s successor, captured Jerusalem by deceit and led many Jews captive with him into Egypt. 1025

CHAPTER XXVIII.—On the battles fought by the people of Tarentum against the Romans together with Pyrrhus, king of Epirus, who was the first to bring elephants with him into Italy; how they were defeated and subdued by the Romans; and on the various portents that occurred at that time. Also that all Italy was then subjected to the Romans. 1026

BOOK FIVE. 1029

CHAPTER ONE.—The text of the narrative: how Ptolemy Philadelphus honored Eleazar, the Jewish high priest, with gifts and honored the Temple; how he also released more than one hundred thousand Jewish captives; and how he summoned seventy of the wisest elders to come to him and ordered them to interpret the divine laws. 1029

CHAPTER II.—On the various battles between the Romans and Carthaginians by land and sea, and on the countless multitude of men killed on both sides; these most wretched wars continued uninterruptedly for twenty-five years. 1033

CHAPTER III.—At what time an unusual fire and inundation of waters nearly destroyed the City. 1036

CHAPTER IV.—During the reign of Ptolemy Euergetes, Jesus composed the Book of Wisdom, while Josephus won such favor with King Judah that he was appointed commander not only of Judaea and Samaria but also of Syria and Phoenicia. 1036

CHAPTER V.—At the same time the Parthians withdrew from the yoke of the Macedonians, and the Romans lived peacefully for one year without war—something that had not happened to them for 450 years, that is, since the time of King Numa. Thereafter followed great and grievous wars fought between the Romans, the Gauls, the Histri, and the Illyrians. 1037

CHAPTER VI.—During the reign of Ptolemy Philopator, 60,000 Jews were killed by Antiochus, and they suffered from him the events contained in the Third Book of the Maccabees. 1038

CHAPTER VII.—In what period Hannibal, the Romans’ most hostile enemy, set out from Spain with a large army and came into Italy. Remaining there continuously for thirteen years, he fought grave and extensive wars against the Romans and wore them down almost to the point of utter despair. Also how, recalled from Italy to Africa, he was defeated there by Scipio, although previously he had very often been victorious. And while the Romans were being oppressed by an internal enemy whom they could not endure in their homeland, with which foreign peoples he undertook wars. 1039

CHAPTER VIII.—King Ptolemy Epiphanes, through his commander named Scopas, brought Lower Syria, Judaea, and Samaria under his rule, although Antiochus had recently taken them from his power. Antiochus again defeated Scopas and subjected the same regions to his own rule. 1044

CHAPTER IX.—An account of how Philip, king of the Macedonians, defeated by the Romans, gave his son Demetrius as a hostage. Likewise Nauides, commander of the Athenians, defeated by the Romans, gave his son Armenes as a hostage. Various nations were subjected to the Romans along with them. Antiochus, king of Syria, was also defeated with all his forces and compelled to pay tribute by land and sea. 1045

CHAPTER X.—How Antiochus occupied Egypt but, terrified when the Romans issued a warning, withdrew from it; then, marching against Jerusalem, plundered the Temple, set up an altar there, polluted it with unclean sacrifices, devastated and destroyed the city, and built a fortress in it to house Macedonian troops. He led part of the population captive and put another part to the sword; he compelled the survivors to live according to the customs of the nations and ordered those who resisted to suffer various punishments. Also where this evil was believed to have begun. 1046

CHAPTER XI.—In what period the Romans slaughtered countless multitudes in Spain and destroyed more than 300 towns. The Macedonian War, rightly counted among the greatest wars, was also fought at that time. The Third Punic War likewise arose. When it was concluded, Carthage was utterly destroyed by fire and sword, in the six hundredth year after its foundation. 1048

BOOK SIX. 1051

CHAPTER ONE.—How Mattathias, resisting the edicts of Antiochus, vindicated the ancestral laws, placed Judas in command of the people, and how Judas himself attained the chief priesthood. 1051

CHAPTER II.—During the reign of Ptolemy Euergetes, Simon attained the chief priesthood after Jonathan’s death. 1053

CHAPTER III.—On the destruction of the extremely wealthy city of Tyre, and how Achaea was subjected to the Romans through the consul Metellus. In those times an androgyne was seen at Rome, after which portent a great plague followed. Viriathus, a Lusitanian of pastoral origin, also defeated and routed the Romans in various battles. Finally, he was killed by his own men. [Col. 1545] 1054

CHAPTER IV.—How the king of the Parthians subjected Babylon and various nations to his empire. At that time Brutus defeated in battle the Gallaeci, who were bringing aid to the Lusitanians in Further Spain. The proconsul Lepidus, while attempting to attack the harmless Vaccaei in Spain, was defeated by them after losing his army. At that time the slaves who were conspiring at Rome were also soon killed. 1055

CHAPTER V.—In what period Numantia was destroyed by Scipio Africanus, and Attalus, king of Asia, by his will caused the Roman people to succeed him; his brother invaded the kingdom, to the ruin of the Roman people and his own destruction. 1056

CHAPTER VI.—At that time a conspiracy of slaves spread far and wide, and soon they were destroyed after being compelled by punishments imposed by their masters or by the Roman consuls. At that time Mount Etna also vomited unusually fierce fires beyond measure, while in Africa an enormous swarm of locusts plunged into the sea and was thrown back upon the shore, polluting the air and bringing an excessive plague upon mortals. 1057

CHAPTER VII.—On John, son of Simon, who was called Hyrcanus: how he captured many cities of the Syrians, Samaritans, and Idumaeans in successfully waged wars, and grew old in complete peace and prosperity. Also how his son Aristobulus, who was the first after the Jewish people’s return from Babylonia to assume the royal title, killed his mother and his brother Antigonus, and himself died detestably after scarcely completing a year of his reign. 1058

CHAPTER VIII.—On the rebuilding of Carthage, and on the revolt of slaves that arose at Rome in hope of liberty; how the Gauls of the Allobroges and the Gauls of the Arverni were likewise defeated and destroyed by the Romans. At that time an eruption of Mount Etna afflicted the people of Catana. 1060

CHAPTER IX.—On Jugurtha, king of the Numidians, and on the consuls who fought against and defeated him. 1061

CHAPTER X.—On the Roman consuls who, fighting unsuccessfully against the Gauls, were defeated and killed. Against those Gauls, in vengeance for the consuls and to defend the frontiers, Marius was appointed consul for the fourth and fifth time and sent out. He killed 440,000 Gauls, apart from the women and children, who killed themselves; meanwhile, in Asia and Syria, the rulers who were then reigning… 1062
